title:
Neoagarotetraose
from Marine Red Algae Attenuates
Hypertensive Vascular Remodeling by Targeting FoxO4 to Inhibit Mitochondrial
Superoxide Generation
abstract:
Oxidative stress
is a key driver of hypertensive vascular remodeling.
Neoagarotetraose (NA4), a marine-derived oligosaccharide, possesses
potent antioxidant activity, but its effects on hypertension remain
unexplored. Here, we investigated the role of NA4 in vascular smooth
muscle cells (VSMCs) from spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) and
in SHR in vivo. NA4 treatment significantly reduced mitochondrial
superoxide, H 2 O 2 levels, and NADPH oxidase activity
in SHR-VSMCs and suppressed their hyperproliferation and migration.
RNA-seq identified FoxO4 as a significantly downregulated target.
FoxO4 overexpression enhanced ROS production and VSMC dysfunction,
and these effects were reversed by NA4. In SHR, oral administration
of NA4 (200 or 250 mg/kg/day) for 4 weeks lowered blood pressure,
attenuated vascular remodeling, and reduced arterial FoxO4 expression
and superoxide generation. Collectively, NA4 ameliorates hypertensive
vascular remodeling, and molecular docking suggests a potential interaction
between NA4 and the FoxO4-ROS axis, highlighting its potential as
a functional food ingredient for hypertension management.
journal: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry

sections.introduction:
Oxidative
stress (OS), characterized by an imbalance between pro-oxidants
and antioxidant defenses, is a critical driver of vascular remodeling
in hypertension. This process is intimately
linked to the dysfunction of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs),
which, upon exposure to excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), undergo
aberrant proliferation and migration, leading to arterial stiffening
and elevated blood pressure. , The primary sources
of this ROS burden in the vasculature are the NADPH oxidases and dysfunctional
mitochondria, both of which are activated under hypertensive conditions. , Excessive ROS production from these sources not only disrupts cellular
redox homeostasis but also directly promotes the phenotypic switching
of VSMCs that underlies pathological vascular remodeling. While endogenous antioxidant systems exist, they
are often overwhelmed in hypertension, underscoring the urgent need
for targeted interventions capable of breaking this self-perpetuating
cycle of oxidative injury and vascular dysfunction. Neoagarooligosaccharides (NAOS) are a class of novel
β-1,3-linked
functional oligosaccharides derived from agarose, which have attracted
considerable attention due to their high safety profile and diverse
biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hypoglycemic,
antiatherosclerotic, and antitumor effects. Among these, neoagarotetraose (NA4) displays a particularly potent
scavenging effect on hydroxyl radicals compared with other oligosaccharides
such as neoagarobiose (NA2), neoagarohexaose (NA6), and neoagarooctaose
(NA8). Recent studies have also demonstrated
its protective effects against age-related neuronal damage. These findings suggest that NA4 holds promise
as a functional food ingredient for health management. However, despite
its robust antioxidant capacity, the role of NA4 in hypertension-associated
oxidative stress and vascular remodeling remains unexplored. Therefore,
this study aims to investigate the regulatory effects of NA4 on redox
signaling pathways in the context of hypertension and vascular remodeling,
as well as the underlying mechanisms. The forkhead box O (FoxO)
transcription factor family, comprising
FoxO1, FoxO3, FoxO4, and FoxO6, features a conserved forkhead-associated
helix domain that facilitates genomic DNA binding, thereby orchestrating
diverse biological processes. Among these,
FoxO4 serves as a critical regulator of gene networks governing OS,
insulin signaling, cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and longevity. Recent studies have highlighted the functional
importance of FoxO4 in oxidative-stress-related pathologies; for instance,
it plays a significant role in protecting lens epithelial cells from
oxidative damage, and it has been shown
to alleviate myocardial ischemia in aged hearts by regulating oxidative
stress. Nevertheless, the role of FoxO4
in hypertensive vascular remodeling remains unexplored, and whether
marine-derived oligosaccharides, such as NA4, can modulate FoxO4-mediated
oxidative stress in the vasculature is unknown. In this study,
we demonstrate that the marine-derived oligosaccharide
NA4 attenuates hypertensive vascular remodeling by targeting FoxO4.
Using SHR and primary VSMCs, we show that NA4 effectively lowers blood
pressure and alleviates oxidative stress, as evidenced by reduced
mitochondrial superoxide generation while suppressing VSMC proliferation
and migration. Notably, we identified FoxO4 as a previously unrecognized
mediator of oxidative stress in the context of hypertensive vascular
remodeling. Collectively, our findings reveal a novel regulatory mechanism
involving FoxO4 and highlight NA4, a marine-derived bioactive oligosaccharide,
as a promising functional food component for the management of hypertension.
sections.na4 preparation:
NA4 was prepared
according to a previous method. , The purity of NA4 was
96.53% (w/w), which was determined by high-performance liquid chromatography.
sections.primary culture of vsmcs:
VSMCs were
procured from the tunica media of the thoracic aorta of WKY and SHR
rats. Briefly, the tunica media was digested
with 0.4% collagenase (Gibco, NY, USA) for 30 min. Cells were cultured
in DMEM supplemented with 20% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and antibiotics
at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . Upon reaching 90% confluence,
cells were passaged, and those from passages 2–6 were used
for experiments. Cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting
Kit-8 (Dojindo, Japan).
sections.experimental animals:
Male WKY and
SHR rats (systolic blood pressure of >150 mmHg) were obtained from
Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. All animal
procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use
Committee of the Third Institute of Oceanography, Ministry of Natural
Resources (TIO-IACUC-07-2024-03-07) and were conducted in accordance
with the international guidelines. Rats were housed under controlled
conditions with a 12 h light–dark cycle and free access to
standard chow and water. NA4 (200 or 250 mg/kg/day), captopril (30
mg/kg/day), or saline was administered daily by gavage for 4 weeks.
At the end of the experiment, rats were euthanized by an intraperitoneal
injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg).
sections.rna sequencing\n(rna-seq) analysis:
VSMCs derived from SHR were treated with
NA4 (300 μM) or PBS
for 24 h. Total RNA was extracted using the Trizol reagent (Invitrogen,
NY, USA), and RNA integrity was assessed using the Agilent Bioanalyzer
2100 (Agilent, CA, USA). RNA-seq was performed by Majorbio Biopharm
Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China), with three biological replicates
per group. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using
DESeq2 with an adjusted p value < 0.05 and a fold-change
threshold of >1.2-fold. The cutoff is indicated by dashed lines
in
the volcano plot. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were performed using
the GO and KEGG databases. The RNA-seq data have been deposited in
the NCBI database under accession number PRJNA1256135.
sections.foxo4 overexpression in vsmcs:
VSMCs
were transfected with either pcDNA3.1 plasmid (negative control) or
FoxO4 overexpression plasmid (50 nmol/L) using Lipofectamine 3000
(Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s
protocol. After 24 h, cells were harvested for subsequent experiments.
sections.vsmc migration assay:
VSMC migration
was assessed utilizing the scratch assay and Boyden chamber assay. For wound healing, a linear scratch was made
in confluent VSMC monolayers using a 1 mL pipet tip. Images were captured
at 0 and 24 h to assess wound closure. For the Boyden chamber assay,
VSMCs were seeded in the upper chamber of 8 μm pore-size Transwell
inserts (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) in serum-free medium, with
10% FBS in the lower chamber as a chemoattractant. After 24 h, nonmigrated
cells were removed, and migrated cells were stained with 1% crystal
violet and quantified from five random fields per well.
sections.vsmc proliferation assay:
VSMC proliferation
was assessed by proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) protein
expression and EdU incorporation assays. EdU incorporation was detected using an EdU staining kit (RiboBio,
Guangzhou, China) following the manufacturer’s protocol, and
PCNA protein levels were determined by Western blot.
sections.dhe fluorescence staining:
Intracellular
and vascular ROS levels were assessed using dihydroethidium (DHE)
staining. VSMCs grown on coverslips were
incubated with 10 μM DHE (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai,
China) at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark. For arterial tissues,
frozen sections (20 μm) were incubated with 10 μM DHE
for 5 min. Fluorescence images were captured using a fluorescence
microscope.
sections.nox activity assay:
NOX activity was
quantified using the lucigenin-derived chemiluminescence method. , Briefly, samples were incubated with 5 μM lucigenin and 100
μM NAD­(P)­H, and luminescence was recorded using a luminometer.
NOX activity was expressed as mean light units (MLU)/min/mg protein.
sections.measurement of mitochondrial superoxide:
Mitochondrial superoxide production was quantified using the MitoSOX
Red method. VSMCs were seeded in 24-well
plates, treated for 24 h, and then incubated with 5 μM MitoSOX
Red at 37 °C for 10 min in the dark. Fluorescence images were
captured using a fluorescence microscope, and intensity was quantified
using the ImageJ software.
sections.measurement of h 2 o 2 levels:
H 2 O 2 levels were
measured
using the Amplex Red Assay Kit (Life Technologies, MD, USA) according
to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, cells were incubated with 50 μM Amplex Red and 0.1
U/mL horseradish peroxidase (HRP), and absorbance was recorded at
560 nm.
sections.immunohistochemistry:
Tissue sections
were stained for FoxO4 and PCNA using specific primary antibodies
(Aifang Bio, Changsha, China) followed by HRP-conjugated secondary
antibodies (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, CA, USA). The staining intensity
was quantified using the ImageJ software.
sections.masson\u2019s\nstaining:
Collagen
deposition in the aorta and mesenteric arteries was evaluated using
Masson’s trichrome staining. The proportion of blue-stained
collagen fibers was quantified using the ImageJ software.
sections.blood pressure measurement:
Systolic
blood pressure was measured weekly in conscious rats using a noninvasive
tail-cuff system (PowerLab). Rats were acclimated at 28 °C for
10–20 min prior to measurement, and the average of 10 consecutive
readings was used for analysis.
sections.rt-qpcr:
Total RNA was extracted
from tissues and cells and reverse-transcribed into cDNA. Quantitative
real-time PCR was performed using specific primers (sequences listed
in Table ) on a real-time
PCR system. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2 –ΔΔCt method.
sections.western\nblot analysis:
Protein expression
was analyzed by Western blotting. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE,
transferred onto PVDF membranes, and incubated with primary antibodies
against FoxO4, PCNA, and GAPDH (Proteintech, IL, USA) followed by
HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Signals were detected by chemiluminescence.
sections.statistical analysis:
Data are expressed
as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Comparisons between two groups
were performed using Student’s t test, and
multiple-group comparisons were analyzed by one-way or two-way ANOVA
followed by Bonferroni’s post hoc test. Statistical significance
was set at P < 0.05. All n values
indicate the number of independent biological replicates (cell samples
or animals) as specified in each figure legend.
sections.impact of na4 on the redox signaling of:
Dose–response experiments showed that 300 μM NA4 optimally
reduced SHR-VSMC hyperproliferation without nonselective cytotoxicity
( Figure S1 ). DHE staining revealed that
superoxide production was significantly elevated in SHR-derived VSMCs
compared with WKY-derived cells, and NA4 treatment markedly reduced
this increase ( Figure A,B). Consistent with these findings, MitoSOX Red staining demonstrated
that mitochondrial superoxide levels were also higher in SHR VSMCs
and were significantly attenuated by NA4 treatment ( Figure C,D). Additionally, H 2 O 2 levels were elevated in SHR VSMCs, and NA4 effectively
reduced these levels ( Figure E). To further evaluate the involvement of NADPH oxidase in
the antioxidant action of NA4, total NOX activity was measured. NA4
significantly inhibited the elevated NOX activity observed in SHR
VSMCs ( Figure F).
In contrast, NA4 did not significantly alter superoxide production,
H 2 O 2 levels, or NOX activity in VSMCs derived
from WKY rats. These observations indicate that the antioxidant properties
of NA4 likely function through modulating NOX-mediated and mitochondrial
superoxide formation, with a selective effect on pathological VSMCs.
sections.impact of na4 on the migration\nand prol:
OS functions as a critical factor in facilitating
VSMC migration and proliferation. To
investigate whether the antioxidant properties of NA4 could reduce
the migration and proliferation of VSMCs in SHR, wound healing and
Boyden chamber assays were conducted to assess migratory capacity.
The findings revealed increased migratory ability of SHR VSMCs, which
was significantly inhibited by NA4 treatment ( Figure A,B). Additionally, the proliferation of
VSMCs, evaluated through PCNA expression and EdU incorporation, was
elevated in SHR, and NA4 effectively reduced this level of proliferation
( Figure C–E).
In contrast, NA4 showed no notable effects on the migration and proliferation
of the WKY VSMCs. These observations suggest that NA4 inhibits VSMC
migration and proliferation in the SHR.
sections.na4 downregulates foxo4 expression in sh:
RNA sequencing was performed in SHR-derived VSMCs treated with
PBS or NA4 (300 μM) for 24 h. Volcano plot analysis revealed
pronounced alterations in gene expression, with significant downregulation
of Foxo4 and modest decreases in Gpx4 and Sod2 ( Figure A,D). Heatmap analysis confirmed distinct
expression patterns of oxidative-stress-related genes between groups
( Figure B), and GSEA
demonstrated significant enrichment of oxidative stress signaling
pathways ( Figure C).
Transcriptomic validation confirmed that Foxo4 mRNA was significantly
reduced in NA4-treated cells, whereas the decreases in Gpx4 and Sod2
were less pronounced ( Figure D). These results indicate that NA4 selectively downregulates
FoxO4 expression at the mRNA level in SHR-VSMCs, with FoxO4 being
the most substantially affected transcript among the antioxidant genes
examined. Consistently, Western blot analysis showed that NA4 treatment
also reduced FoxO4 protein expression, and mRNA quantification further
confirmed the downregulation ( Figure S2 ). Together, these data demonstrate that NA4 suppresses FoxO4 expression
at both the mRNA and protein levels in SHR-VSMCs.
sections.molecular\ndocking predicts a potential:
Molecular docking analysis between
NA4 and FoxO4 showed a binding energy of −6.5 kcal/mol ( Table ). Multiple hydrogen
bonds within 0.35 nm were identified, involving residues Ser96, Arg98,
Arg97, Asn103, Asn157, Tyr106, His161, and His156 ( Figure E–G). These docking
results suggest a potential interaction between NA4 and FoxO4, providing
a theoretical basis for future experimental validation. Notably, the
predicted binding site is located near the DNA-binding domain (DBD)
of FoxO4, raising the possibility that NA4 may interfere with FoxO4’s
transcriptional activity by blocking its access to DNA.
sections.foxo4 overexpression attenuates the anti:
To validate the involvement of FoxO4
in the NA4-mediated inhibition of OS, this study performed a FoxO4
overexpression experiment in VSMCs combined with NA4 treatment. The
results indicated that cotreatment with FoxO4 overexpression and NA4
did not negatively affect cell viability ( Figure S3 ). The successful overexpression of FoxO4 was confirmed by
elevated FoxO4 protein levels, and NA4 treatment effectively mitigated
this upregulation ( Figure A), further validating FoxO4 as a target of NA4. FoxO4 overexpression
led to significantly increased superoxide and H 2 O 2 production in VSMCs derived from both WKY and SHR, effects that
were markedly suppressed by NA4 treatment ( Figure B–D and Figure S4 ). Similarly, elevated FoxO4 levels enhanced the total NOX
activity, which was reversed by NA4 ( Figure E). These findings indicate that NA4 attenuates
FoxO4-mediated oxidative stress in VSMCs, positioning FoxO4 as a critical
mediator of the antioxidant effects of NA4.
sections.foxo4 overexpression reverses\nthe inhib:
To assess
whether FoxO4 regulates the inhibitory effects of NA4 on VSMC migration
and proliferation, an overexpression experiment was conducted in combination
with the NA4 treatment. The results demonstrated that FoxO4 overexpression
enhanced the migratory capacity of VSMCs from both WKY and SHR, while
NA4 treatment effectively mitigated this increase ( Figure A,B). Similarly, FoxO4 overexpression
promoted VSMC proliferation in both WKY and SHR, an effect that was
suppressed by NA4 treatment ( Figure C,D and Figure S5 ). These
findings suggest that FoxO4 serves as a crucial mediator in regulating
the suppressive impact of NA4 on VSMC migration and proliferation
in the SHR.
sections.impact of na4 on blood\npressure and vas:
Absorption of NA4 into the bloodstream
was verified by oral administration of a fluorescent probe NA4-CY7.
In vivo imaging showed systemic fluorescence signals ( Figure S6 ), indicating intestinal absorption
and distribution. A 4 week gavage experiment was then conducted in
WKY and SHR rats to evaluate the therapeutic potential of NA4 in hypertension
and vascular remodeling. NA4 administration resulted in a sustained
reduction in blood pressure and heart rate in SHR ( Figure A), and the higher concentration
of NA4 exhibited the most pronounced effect, outperforming the positive
drug control group. Masson staining of aortic and mesenteric artery
(MA) samples revealed a pronounced increase in collagen fiber deposition
in SHR, a hallmark of vascular remodeling, which was significantly
attenuated by NA4 treatment ( Figure B,C). Immunohistochemical analysis further demonstrated
elevated PCNA levels in the aorta and MA of SHR, an effect that was
prevented by NA4 administration ( Figure D,E). These findings indicate that NA4 effectively
mitigates hypertension-induced vascular remodeling.
sections.impact of na4 on foxo4 and os in the art:
To validate the mechanistic insights from
VSMC experiments, the impact of NA4 on FoxO4 expression was further
investigated in vivo. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed that FoxO4
staining was elevated in the aortas and mesenteric arteries of SHR,
whereas NA4 treatment significantly reduced this upregulation ( Figure A,B). Consistent
with the in vitro findings, MitoSOX Red staining demonstrated that
mitochondrial superoxide levels were also higher in SHR arteries and
were significantly reduced by NA4 treatment ( Figure C,D). Additionally, H 2 O 2 levels in arterial homogenates were elevated in SHR, and NA4 effectively
decreased these levels ( Figure E). The total NOX activity was also increased in SHR arteries
and was significantly inhibited by NA4 ( Figure F). These in vivo results further substantiate
that NA4 alleviates vascular remodeling in SHR by targeting the FoxO4–oxidative-stress
signaling pathway.
sections.discussion:
Vascular remodeling is a
central factor in the development of hypertension
and its complications, with OS playing a pivotal role in promoting
VSMC migration, proliferation, and vascular remodeling. The primary novel finding of this study is that
NA4 effectively inhibits the hyperproliferation and exaggerated migration
of VSMCs derived from SHR by attenuating the excessive OS. Mechanistically,
we identify FoxO4 as a key mediator of this process: FoxO4 is upregulated
in SHR-VSMCs, and NA4 suppresses its expression, thereby alleviating
OS and subsequent VSMC dysfunction. Furthermore, FoxO4 overexpression
enhances VSMC migration and proliferation, effects that are reversed
by the NA4 treatment. These findings reveal that NA4 alleviates vascular
remodeling and hypertensive symptoms in SHR arteries through the inhibition
of the FoxO4-OS signaling pathway, positioning NA4 as a promising
antioxidant with therapeutic potential for hypertension and related
vascular diseases. Numerous natural products have been investigated
for their antihypertensive
effects, with many plant-derived compounds, such as apocynin, resveratrol,
and curcumin, shown to lower blood pressure primarily through the
inhibition of NADPH oxidase activity and attenuation of oxidative
stress. However, these phenolic compounds
often face limitations including poor water solubility, limited bioavailability,
and predominantly terrestrial sourcing. In contrast, NA4 is a marine-derived oligosaccharide with distinct
advantages: its high water solubility ensures superior bioavailability.
And its production from renewable red algal waste aligns with sustainable
development principles, a critical consideration for functional food
ingredients. Notably, emerging evidence
suggests that marine-derived bioactive compounds may exhibit more
potent antioxidant activities than their terrestrial counterparts
due to the unique marine environment. Recent studies have demonstrated that polysaccharides from red seaweeds
effectively modulate hypertension-associated biomarkers by regulating
the renin–angiotensin system and reducing oxidative stress, while extracts from brown algae such as Ecklonia cava have been shown to decrease vascular
calcification through mitochondrial ROS suppression. Building upon these findings, the present study demonstrates
that NA4 effectively alleviates oxidative stress in VSMCs and arteries
of SHR by suppressing NADPH oxidase activity, a mechanism shared with
certain plant-derived compounds but achieved by NA4 with the added
benefits of marine origin and favorable physicochemical properties.
Given that oxidative stress drives VSMC proliferation and migration,
the inhibitory effects of NA4 on these processes in SHR likely stem
from its antioxidant activity. Furthermore, given the well-established
link between oxidative stress and inflammation in vascular disease
pathogenesis, the antioxidant properties of NA4 may also contribute
to anti-inflammatory effects, collectively reducing VSMC dysfunction
and vascular remodeling in hypertension. FoxO4, a member of
the FoxO transcription factor family, is regulated
by multiple post-translational modifications that determine its nuclear
localization and transcriptional activity. In the cardiovascular system, FoxO4 has been implicated in atherosclerosis, vascular injury responses, and myocardial infarction. However, its role in hypertensiona condition intimately
linked to oxidative stress and vascular remodelinghas remained
unexplored. Notably, our RNA-seq data showed that NA4 significantly
downregulated FoxO4, whereas the decreases in Gpx4 and Sod2 were less
pronounced. This pattern suggests that NA4 primarily targets FoxO4.
It is well established that FoxO4 binds to the SOD2 promoter and transcriptionally
upregulates SOD2 under oxidative stress. Although GPx4 is not a direct FoxO4 target, FoxO family members
can indirectly influence GPx4 expression via redox-dependent pathways. In hypertensive vascular remodeling, FoxO4 drives
NADPH oxidase-derived ROS production, while SOD2 and GPx4 serve as
mitochondrial antioxidant defenses. The mild decreases in Gpx4 and
Sod2 after NA4 treatment likely reflect a reduced cellular demand
for ROS scavenging following suppression of FoxO4-driven oxidative
stress rather than direct transcriptional inhibition. Comparison with other reported FoxO4 inhibitors.
Previous studies
have identified several compounds that inhibit the FoxO4 function.
Curcumin, a natural polyphenol, downregulates the AKT/FoxO pathway
and promotes FoxO4 nuclear translocation in hepatoma cells. Punicalagin inhibits the AKT-FoxO4 signaling
axis to reduce excessive autophagy and exert neuroprotective effects. The most specific FoxO4 inhibitor is the interfering
peptide FoxO4-DRI, which blocks the FoxO4-p53 interaction and induces
senolysis. Additionally, marine-derived
compounds such as SZ-685C have been shown to suppress the Akt/FoxO
pathway. Most of these known inhibitors
act indirectly through upstream kinases or by disrupting protein–protein
interactions. In contrast, our molecular docking suggests that NA4
may bind directly near the DBD of FoxO4, potentially acting through
a distinct mechanism. However, it should be noted that molecular docking
alone does not prove a direct physical interaction. Future studies
using surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cellular thermal shift assay
(CETSA), or coimmunoprecipitation are required to validate the direct
binding between NA4 and FoxO4. The present study demonstrates
that FoxO4 is significantly upregulated
in VSMCs and arteries of SHR, establishing it as a key mediator of
hypertensive vascular pathology. Functionally, we found that NA4 treatment
suppressed both mitochondrial superoxide generation and NADPH oxidase
activity in SHR-VSMCs, and these effects were reversed by FoxO4 overexpression,
indicating that NA4 reduces ROS production from both mitochondria
and NOX through the downregulation of FoxO4. This regulatory relationship
between FOXO transcription factors and ROS sources is supported by
evidence from other diseases: in diabetic kidney disease, a NOX-FoxO3a
signaling axis has been identified. In
intervertebral disc degeneration, oxidative stress upregulates NOX2/4
while downregulating FoxO4, hinting at a negative correlation. More directly, FoxO1 suppresses miR-92b to derepress
NOX4 in ischemic stroke. Although direct
evidence for FoxO4 binding to NOX promoters is currently lacking,
the high homology among FOXO family members raises the possibility
that FoxO4 may similarly regulate NOX expression in the vasculature.
Notably, the pro-oxidative, pro-proliferative role of FoxO4 in hypertension
contrasts with its protective functions reported in atherosclerosis and its context-dependent dual roles in cancer, highlighting the tissue- and disease-specific
nature of FoxO4 signaling. Our identification of NA4 as a novel upstream
modulator of FoxO4 that suppresses its elevated expression and attenuates
downstream ROS production thus reveals a previously unrecognized regulatory
axis in hypertension. Consistent with our in vitro findings,
oral NA4 (200–250
mg/kg/day) lowered blood pressure, attenuated vascular remodeling,
and reduced FoxO4 expression and superoxide generation in SHR arteries,
supporting its translational potential. This dose is consistent with
or lower than those used in previous NA4 studies (100–2500
mg/kg/day) , and is well below the no-observed-adverse-effect
level (NOAEL) of 5000 mg/kg/day for NAOs in rats. Other marine-derived oligosaccharides, e.g., potassium
alginate oligosaccharides, show antihypertensive effects in SHR at
300–600 mg/kg/day. Using body
surface area normalization (factor 6.2), our NA4 dose translates to
a human equivalent of 32–40 mg/kg/day (1.9–2.4 g/60
kg adult), which is feasible given NA4’s high safety and solubility. In summary, this study demonstrates that NA4 attenuates oxidative
stress, VSMC dysfunction, and vascular remodeling in hypertension
through the suppression of FoxO4. Notably, the effects of NA4 are
specific to pathological conditions, as no significant changes were
observed in normotensive WKY rats, suggesting that NA4 selectively
targets disease-associated signaling pathways without disrupting physiological
homeostasis. This pathological context-dependent action distinguishes
NA4 from broad-spectrum antioxidants that may interfere with essential
redox signaling. At the molecular level,
NA4 suppresses the FoxO4-ROS axis, a mechanism that differs from classical
antihypertensive agents such as captopril (which primarily inhibits
ACE) and plant-derived compounds like
resveratrol (which activates SIRT1) or apocynin (which directly inhibits
NOX assembly). , Furthermore, the marine origin
of NA4 confers unique advantages including high water solubility,
sustainable production from algal waste, and favorable biosafety profile, , distinguishing it from terrestrial-derived polyphenols that often
face bioavailability limitations. At
the tissue level, NA4 effectively attenuated remodeling in both large
(aorta) and small (mesenteric) arteries, indicating broad therapeutic
potential across different vascular bedsa critical consideration
given that hypertension differentially affects various vessel types. The concordance between in vitro and in vivo
findingsdemonstrating consistent FoxO4 downregulation, reduced
ROS production, and attenuated VSMC proliferationprovides
strong mechanistic evidence for the FoxO4-OS axis as a central driver
of hypertensive vascular pathology. Collectively, these findings position
NA4 as a promising marine-derived functional food ingredient that
targets a previously unrecognized FoxO4-mediated oxidative pathway
in hypertension, offering a mechanistic alternative to existing therapeutic
approaches. Although current antihypertensive therapies have
achieved partial
success in controlling blood pressure, they remain limited by issues
such as poor patient compliance and adverse effects associated with
long-term medication use. Furthermore,
existing treatments predominantly focus on blood pressure regulation
while failing to adequately address critical pathological processes
such as vascular remodeling and OS. NA4,
as a novel functional food component, exhibits unique advantages in
mitigating OS and vascular remodeling through the suppression of the
FoxO4-OS signaling pathway, potentially offering superior vascular
protective effects compared to conventional therapies. However, our
NA4-CY7 imaging experiment only qualitatively shows intestinal absorption;
it does not directly demonstrate the pharmacokinetics of native NA4,
as the fluorescent tag may alter its properties. Therefore, future
studies should establish true bioavailability using LC–MS/MS.
Additionally, to enhance tissue specificity toward diseased arteries
and VSMCs, nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation with vascular
homing peptides (e.g., targeting VCAM-1 or smooth muscle cell markers)
could be explored. Other future studies should validate direct NA4-FoxO4
binding using SPR, CETSA, or co-IP; evaluate NA4 effects on endothelial
cells (NO, barrier, ROS); and test NA4 in other hypertension models,
long-term safety, and combination therapy. Addressing these questions
will advance NA4 as a functional food ingredient for hypertension.

title: The emerging role of prostate-specific membrane antigen–targeted radioligand therapy in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
abstract: Abstract The treatment of metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) has evolved in recent years towards combination therapy, enhancing survival outcomes when compared with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone. However, many patients who are eligible for combination therapy are still receiving ADT monotherapy, and a significant proportion of those treated with doublet combinations still experience suboptimal outcomes. Furthermore, the value of adding docetaxel to an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)/ADT doublet in mHSPC has not been delineated, particularly in patients with low-volume disease, and chemotherapy toxicity and tolerability remain a major concern for patients. This review addresses the significant unmet need for additional or novel treatment strategies for mHSPC, utilizing prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)–targeted radioligand therapy (RLT) in a combination regimen that uses a non-chemotherapeutic approach for the treatment of mHSPC. PSMA-targeted RLT has been shown to improve survival outcomes in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) previously treated with ARPIs +/− taxanes and is now under evaluation for the treatment of mHSPC, given its demonstrated success in the mCRPC space. Thus, continued education on RLT and its use for patients with mHSPC is important to optimize patient care. This review provides a brief outline of the mHSPC treatment landscape, focusing on the challenges and unique considerations faced by healthcare professionals when treating these patients. We also evaluate the potential role of RLT in surmounting these challenges, discussing potential barriers and solutions to its integration as a treatment for mHSPC.

sections.introduction: In recent years, metastatic prostate cancer treatment has moved towards combination therapy, resulting in improved survival compared with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone. 1 However, with nearly 400 000 prostate cancer-associated deaths reported globally in 2022, and over 500 000 projected to occur by 2030, 2 , 3 there remains an urgent need for alternative, effective treatments. 4 Metastatic disease that has not yet developed resistance to ADT is generally referred to as metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC). 5 Despite initial high response rates to ADT, mHSPC remains largely incurable. 5 Typically, most patients with mHSPC will develop metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) within 1 year of treatment with ADT alone. 1 , 5 In the absence of curative treatments, prolonging survival is the main goal of treatment for mHSPC 5 ; it is also important that treatment is well tolerated and that the patients’ quality of life is preserved as much as possible. 6 The standard of care (SoC) for patients with mHSPC has shifted from ADT monotherapy towards combinations of ADT with androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) with or without chemotherapy (eg, docetaxel), which remain underused in clinical practice despite having been shown to improve survival rates. 6–8 Treatment options for patients with mHSPC with low-volume disease have also expanded, and now patients may receive local therapy to the prostate in addition to metastasis-directed stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) to limited sites of metastatic disease when all sites can be safely treated to an ablative dose. 9–14 Advances in the treatment of mCRPC have guided therapeutic approaches for mHSPC, 15 with many therapies first approved for mCRPC showing greater overall survival (OS) benefits when used earlier in the disease course. 16 Radiopharmaceuticals (including radioligand therapy [RLT]) are an important treatment approach for patients with mCRPC. 4 , 17 RLTs are systemic therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals consisting of a ligand that binds to the target proteins on the tumor cell, the chelator and linker that attach the ligand to the radioisotope, and a radioisotope, which enables visualization or treatment of tumor lesions ( Figure 1 ). 18 Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a type II transmembrane protein 19 with high expression (approximately 80%) on prostate cancer cells. 20 Notably, PSMA is not exclusively expressed in prostate tissues; it has been observed in the cell membranes in other tissues, including breast, ovary, skin, liver, intestines, kidneys, salivary glands, and neovasculature. 21–23 Based on the positive results from the phase 3 VISION ( NCT03511664 ) and PSMAfore ( NCT04689828 ) studies, the PSMA-targeted RLT lutetium-177 vipivotide tetraxetan ( 177 Lu-PSMA-617) is approved for use in patients with PSMA-positive mCRPC who have been treated with ARPI therapy and who are considered appropriate to delay taxane-based chemotherapy or have received prior taxane-based chemotherapy. 24–26 177 Lu-PSMA-617 is the most clinically established RLT and is currently being evaluated in the mHSPC setting, with several ongoing clinical trials investigating its use across differing disease characteristics ( Table 1 ). The latest data from the phase 3 PSMAddition trial, presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress 2025, further support the continued assessment of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 as a potential treatment option in PSMA-positive mHSPC. 27 Other RLTs have been evaluated for the treatment of mCRPC and mHSPC; although discussion of these is out of the scope of the manuscript (which mainly focuses on FDA-approved agents), a recently published paper by Almedia et al. provides a comprehensive review of the available evidence on RLT in mHSPC and mCRPC. 28 Investigating PSMA-targeted RLT in the mHSPC setting leverages the presence of PSMA expression earlier in the disease trajectory, potentially providing benefit from RLT before the emergence of castration-resistance mechanisms that can limit later-stage interventions. 29 If proven to provide clinical benefit, the approval of RLTs for the treatment of mHSPC could address unmet clinical needs by providing a new therapeutic option in patients with known PSMA-expressing disease. However, in such a rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape, healthcare professionals (HCPs) managing mHSPC need to remain apprised of the latest advancements and ongoing clinical trials in order to optimize the multidisciplinary implementation of new treatments into everyday clinical practice. Here, we consider the challenges and unique considerations within the mHSPC setting and discuss how future treatment strategies, including PSMA-targeted RLTs, may address these to improve patient outcomes.
sections.treatment guidelines: While initial treatment for mHSPC continues to center around targeting androgen receptor pathways, 5 treatment paradigms have evolved considerably. 30 , 31 Current US treatment guidelines (2023-2025) recommend treatment intensification using doublet therapy comprising ADT with an ARPI (abiraterone, apalutamide, or enzalutamide, with darolutamide now also approved). 1 , 32–35 Triplet therapy consisting of ADT with docetaxel and either abiraterone or darolutamide may also be considered in patients with high-volume disease. 1 , 32 Upfront treatment intensification has been shown to offer significant survival benefits compared with previously employed sequential strategies or ADT monotherapy. 6 , 36–42 However, US real-world evidence suggests that a significant proportion of patients are still treated with ADT monotherapy, with HCPs citing costs and treatment sequencing as barriers to treatment intensification with hormone therapy. 7 , 8 , 43
sections.existing unmet treatment needs: While ADT+ARPIs +/− chemotherapy have been shown to improve clinical outcomes, 7 , 44 most patients with mHSPC experience disease progression, and survival gains can be modest, especially among patients with suboptimal prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response (>0.2 ng/mL). 6 , 45–47 Chemotherapy toxicity and tolerability remain a major concern for patients; the TRIPLE-SWITCH trial ( NCT06592924 ) and ASPIRE trial ( NCT06931340 ), which aim to investigate whether the addition of docetaxel to ADT and apalutamide improves OS in patients with mHSPC and to assess the tolerability of this treatment regimen, are currently open for accrual and are expected to report out in 2031. 48 , 49 This is a key consideration, given that both treatment side effects and disease progression have significant negative impacts on patients’ quality of life (QoL). 50 , 51 Disease progression despite the introduction of ADT plus an ARPI into the treatment landscape highlights the heterogeneous nature of mHSPC and the limitations of solely targeting the androgen receptor pathway for disease control. 6 , 45–47 There is, therefore, a need for targeted treatments in mHSPC with alternative mechanisms of action to delay progression, and improve disease control and OS, while maintaining QoL. 52 Movement towards improved personalization of therapy in mHSPC is the ultimate goal, 53 with integrated biomarker-based strategies being tested, 54 , 55 and RLT, which utilizes PSMA positivity on positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) as a biomarker. 56–67 RLT could offer a new targeted treatment addition that builds upon the efficacy of current SoC regimens. Based on promising results in patients with mCRPC, RLT could allow for taxane-free combination regimen, improve survival outcomes, and delay deterioration in QoL with tolerable safety, as discussed below.
sections.rlt use in the mcrpc setting: There is increasing interest in earlier use of target-directed RLTs for mHSPC, based on promising results in the mCRPC setting ( Table 2 ). 68 The phase 3 VISION randomized controlled trial (RCT) was a pivotal trial that first demonstrated the benefit of RLT in mCRPC. 72 Treatment with 177 Lu-PSMA-617 plus SoC significantly prolonged radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) and OS, and delayed time to worsening in health-related QoL (HRQoL) in patients with PSMA-positive mCRPC. 72 Similarly, in the phase 3 RCT PSMAfore, investigators showed that 177 Lu-PSMA-617 prolonged rPFS and delayed time to worsening pain and HRQoL versus a change in ARPI in patients with PSMA-positive mCRPC who had progressed once on prior ARPI therapy and had not been exposed to a taxane-containing regimen. 24
sections.current data for rlt use in mhspc: Although current data are limited, there is emerging evidence to suggest that patients at an earlier disease stage may benefit from PSMA-targeted RLT. This is supported by findings from the PSMAfore RCT, in which 177 Lu-PSMA-617 prolonged rPFS compared with a change in ARPI in the pre-chemotherapy setting. 24 Investigating PSMA-targeted RLT in the mHSPC setting leverages the presence of PSMA expression earlier in the disease trajectory and has the potential to provide benefit before the emergence of treatment-induced evolutionary pressure, androgen receptor-independent growth pathways, intra-patient inter-metastatic heterogeneity, and neuroendocrine differentiation, which are frequently observed in mCRPC. 48 , 68 , 78–82 Additionally, the impact of ADT on PSMA and potential enhancement of RLT efficacy in the hormone-sensitive phase is, of interest, but is yet to be determined. 83 While some studies have observed a short-term increase in PSMA within 2-4 weeks of ADT initiation, other findings suggest a reduction in PSMA uptake during this period. 84–86 Moreover, studies investigating the long-term use of ADT (median use 230 days) showed significantly reduced PSMA expression and lesion visibility. 87 These findings highlight the heterogeneous effect of ADT on PSMA expression and should be considered in PSMA PET imaging. The application of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 is currently being evaluated within the mHSPC setting in several clinical trials of patients with differing disease characteristics ( Table 1 ). 57–63 , 65 , 67 , 69–71 This includes the multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase 2 RCT UpFrontPSMA ( NCT04343885 ), which compared the effectiveness of 2 cycles of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 followed by docetaxel versus docetaxel alone in patients with mHSPC starting ADT. 65 , 88 Initial findings have shown that patients with high-volume, PSMA-avid disease (diagnosed within 12 weeks of screening commencement) had higher rates of undetectable PSA (≤0.2 ng/mL) at 48 weeks compared with those who received docetaxel alone (41% [25/61] vs 16% [10/61], odds ratio 3.9; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.6-9.4; P = .002; Table 1 ). 65 Moreover, with a median follow-up of 2.5 years, no new safety signals have emerged, but additional data from longer follow-ups are required. 65 Other trials are ongoing. 56–59 , 63–67 , 69 , 70 The prospective, open-label, phase 3 RCT PSMAddition ( NCT04720157 ) compares 177 Lu-PSMA-617 in combination with SoC versus SoC alone in untreated or minimally treated patients with PSMA-positive mHSPC, with results from the second interim rPFS analysis reported early 2025. 27 , 60–62 , 76 A total of 1144 patients were randomized to receive 177 Lu-PSMA-617 every 6 weeks for up to 6 cycles plus modern-day SoC (ARPI and ADT), or SoC alone, with a primary outcome measure of rPFS. 27 , 60–62 Secondary outcomes include HRQoL, pain, and time to castration resistance. At the second interim rPFS analysis (data cutoff January 13, 2025), 177 Lu-PSMA-617 plus ADT+ARPI reduced the risk of radiographic progression or death by 28% versus ADT+ARPI alone (hazard ratio [HR] 0.72; 95% CI: 0.58-0.90; P = .002). At the first interim OS analysis (using the same cutoff), a positive but non-significant trend was observed, favoring 177 Lu-PSMA-617 plus ADT+ARPI (HR 0.84; 95% CI: 0.63-1.13; P = .125). As data were immature, crossover and follow-up continue. Secondary endpoints at this time point, including overall response rate, progression-free survival (PFS), time to mCRPC, and time to PSA progression, also favored the 177 Lu-PSMA-617 plus ADT+ARPI combination, notably the proportion with PSA nadir <0.2 ng/mL at 48 weeks (87% vs 75%). 76 Furthermore, in PSMAddition, the safety of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 in mHSPC was consistent with its established mCRPC profile, supporting a favorable benefit–risk balance and good tolerability when combined with ADT+ARPI in treatment-naïve or minimally treated patients with PSMA-positive mHSPC. 27 These interim results suggest 177 Lu-PSMA-617 may be efficacious in earlier disease settings, with the potential to increase disease control compared with ADT and ARPI alone for rPFS. Notably, 177 Lu-PSMA-617 combined with ADT and ARPI may offer a new taxane-free combination, benefiting patients with comorbidities or concerns about chemotherapy-related toxicity, an unmet need in real-world practice. 89 However, data collection for OS and long-term safety is ongoing. Furthermore, PSMAddition did not include patients with rapidly progressive disease requiring urgent exposure to taxane-based chemotherapy (as defined by the investigators), for whom triplet therapy remains the SoC. 48 , 90 Another key consideration in selecting patients who may benefit from PSMA-targeted RLT is tumor biology. PSMAddition included patients with high-volume metastatic disease (including those with visceral metastases) and supports the finding that PSMA-targeted RLT is a treatment option in this population for patients with sufficient PSMA expression. 72 , 90–92 However, trial data by site of metastasis and PSMA expression intensity are not yet available. Understanding if PSMA-RLT provides clinical benefit over chemotherapy in patients, such as those with visceral disease and lower PSMA expression, will be crucial. Where possible, biopsy of new visceral metastasis should be considered to identify neuroendocrine differentiation. Treatment of mHSPC is moving towards biomarker-directed strategies. For example, the AMPLITUDE trial ( NCT04497844 ) demonstrated the PFS benefit of abiraterone + niraparib, a poly (ADP ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) that may be a treatment option for patients with homologous recombination repair-mutated mHSPC; however, data on OS and long-term safety are pending. It has been suggested that combining RLT- and PARPi-based therapy may have a possible synergistic effect, but this approach remains untested. 93 Furthermore, patients with phosphatase and tensin homolog-deficient mHSPC demonstrated rPFS benefit from dual blockade of the PI3K/AKT and AR pathways with capivasertib + abiraterone versus placebo + abiraterone in the phase 3 CAPItello-281 trial. 55 Until data can confirm efficacy, optimal targeted treatment strategies remain unclear and require individualized decision-making. The potential role of RLT in delaying castration or disease recurrence in patients with PSMA-positive oligometastatic prostate cancer and avoiding ADT-related adverse events is under active investigation. The multicenter, open-label, phase 2 RCT BULLSEYE ( NCT04443062 ) evaluated 177 Lu-PSMA-617 monotherapy versus deferred ADT in patients with oligometastatic HSPC (≤5 metastatic lesions, PSA doubling time <6 months); at a median follow-up of 27 months, 177 Lu-PSMA-617 dramatically reduced disease progression (7% vs 93%; P < .0001) and prolonged median PFS to 25 months versus 5 months (HR 0.07, 95% CI, 0.03-0.17; P < .0001), with predominantly low-grade adverse events and no treatment-related serious adverse events. 57 In the single-institution, open-label, phase 2 LUNAR trial ( NCT05496959 ), neoadjuvant [ 177 Lu]Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT significantly prolonged PFS versus SBRT alone in oligorecurrent mHSPC (median 17.6 vs. 7.4 months; HR 0.37; P < .0001), without increased toxicity. 94 Preliminary data from a pilot study of SBRT combined with 177 Lu-PSMA-617 in mHSPC with 1–3 metastatic lesions ( NCT05079698 ) further suggest that combining RLT with metastasis-directed therapy could achieve undetectable PSA levels without recourse to hormone therapy. 77 Taken together, these results support a potential major shift in treatment options for oligometastatic prostate cancer and have informed the design of the ongoing multicenter, open-label, phase 3 PSMA-DC trial ( NCT05939414 ), which is evaluating 177 Lu-PSMA-617 after SBRT in approximately 450 patients. 67 , 95 In parallel, ongoing studies such as the CCTG PR.21 trial continue to expand the evidence base for PSMA-targeted RLT across the prostate cancer disease continuum. 96
sections.considerations for the implementation of: Earlier treatment with RLT may necessitate additional monitoring for late-onset adverse events, 97 as patients with mHSPC have a longer median survival than patients with mCRPC (7 years vs 4 years, respectively). 6 , 98 For instance, in a retrospective analysis of long-term renal toxicity in patients with mCRPC undergoing ≥4 cycles of 177 Lu-PSMA-I&T (median number of cycles, 6), 45% of patients had moderate (>15%) to severe (≥30%) decreases in estimated glomerular filtration rate from baseline within 12 months of treatment initiation. 99 Renal toxicity of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 is currently being investigated as part of a global, prospective, long-term follow-up safety study of adult participants with prostate cancer who received ≥1 dose of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 from phase 1-4 clinical trials ( NCT05803941 ). 100 Current publications have estimated the absorbed renal dose for 177 Lu-PSMA-617 is lower than that of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T RLT, reported as 0.4 ± 0.2 to 0.8 ± 0.3 Gy/Gbq versus 0.7 ± 0.2 Gy/Gbq, respectively. 101 In patients receiving RLT, renal toxicity can be mitigated by ensuring the patient remains well hydrated and urinates frequently; performing kidney function laboratory tests between treatment cycles; management of tumor-related renal obstruction and withholding, reducing the dose, or discontinuing treatment based on severity of renal toxicity. 26 , 102 Of note, RLT should be avoided in patients with urinary tract obstruction or hydronephrosis due to urinary stasis within the renal collecting system. 101 In addition to concerns about renal toxicity, introducing RLT earlier in the disease course raises the possibility of suppressing bone marrow reserve 103 and potentially limiting future treatment options. 103 In the final safety analysis of the phase 3 PSMAfore trial (median follow-up: 34.27 months) in the pre-chemotherapy mCRPC setting, hematologic adverse events were more common with 177 Lu-PSMA-617 compared with an ARPI change; however, these events were predominantly grade 1-2, with a median time to resolution of 1.77 months. 34 Moreover, the incidence of grade ≥3 hematologic toxicity was higher in VISION than PSMAfore, suggesting that patients who are more heavily pre-treated may have greater risk of hematologic toxicity. 34 , 104 Long-term follow-up of safety data from VISION and PSMAfore will be used to monitor late myelosuppression. 100 Additionally, prospective trials are needed to further characterize long-term toxicities associated with RLTs in order for patients to make fully informed decisions about the risks and benefits of early RLT and to optimize supportive management. Responses to therapies following RLT are also of importance and were recently investigated in a real-world study (PRECISION) of 152 patients with mCRPC who progressed on 177 Lu-PSMA-617 and received subsequent guideline-recommended therapies (ARPIs or taxanes). Among evaluable patients ( n = 30), 46.7% experienced reduced serum PSA levels by 50% and 40.0% had PSA levels by 80% responses, suggesting that treatment with 177 Lu-PSMA-617 does not preclude responses to subsequent therapies. 105 While RLT is being investigated in a number of different studies, in both the mCRPC and mHSPC settings, it is important to remember that considerations differ between mCRPC and mHSPC due to underlying clinical differences, including the overall health of the patient. The patient’s age, presence of comorbidities, and ability to tolerate toxicities must be considered, resulting in complex needs for individual patients. 6 , 106 When considering patient populations, it is important to recognize the differences between those in clinical trials and those in real-world clinical practice. 107 In the mHSPC setting, clinical trial populations often include more de novo patients, while real-world practice will likely involve a broader patient population, including those who have undergone radical treatment prior to developing metachronous metastases. 6 Additionally, patients in clinical practice tend to range more broadly in age, fitness, and competing comorbidities that can complicate application of trial data to real-world settings. 108 More research is needed in dosing optimization to maximize therapeutic benefit while keeping toxicities to a minimum. RLT may augment the current mHSPC treatment paradigm in several ways. Firstly, RLT in the mHSPC setting may allow for taxane-free combination regimens in patients with high-volume PSMA-avid disease, enabling another option for shared decision-making based on patient preferences as head-to-head comparative data are not available. Investigations are ongoing to determine whether oligometastatic disease identified with PSMA PET may be treated with RLT and metastasis-directed treatment and allow for an ADT-sparing approach in this select group of patients. Finally, the potential synergistic effect between ARPI and PSMA-targeted RLT on treatment efficacy in mHSPC is of interest, with results from ongoing trials awaited.
sections.challenges and proposed solutions associ: While there is a potential role for RLT in the mHSPC space, there are a number of challenges that will need to be addressed before it can be fully integrated into patient care. Logistics, access to treatment, patient selection, and regulatory requirements represent key considerations for the broader implementation of RLT in mCRPC. 97 Below, we discuss unique aspects of moving RLT into the mHSPC setting.
sections.education: One of the challenges associated with RLT implementation may include HCPs’ reluctance to shift to treatments that are newly used outside of previous treatment settings. 108 Real-world data show that ADT monotherapy is commonly used for patients with mHSPC despite data suggesting that it is an inferior approach compared with novel hormone agents or chemotherapy with or without ADT. 108 For example, a multicenter international survey of mHSPC treatment demonstrated that up to 47% of patients received ADT monotherapy, while novel hormonal agents ± ADT and chemotherapy ± ADT regimens were used in 31% and 19% of patients, respectively. 108 These findings suggest an opportunity for other combination therapies to be integrated and a need for ongoing HCP education. Enhanced educational resources that clearly communicate new data and guidelines, such as digital and social media campaigns, webinars, and hybrid conferences, serve an important role in supporting urologists and oncologists and can facilitate the integration of emerging evidence into clinical practice. Similarly, patient-focused websites and open-access plain language publications are critical in educating patients on their treatment options, which will in turn support shared decision-making.
sections.practical considerations: Practical considerations and barriers also exist regarding the incorporation of RLT into standard mHSPC management ( Figure 2 ), with three key steps required: the widespread implementation of PSMA PET imaging (to determine patient eligibility), the expansion of RLT services at current medical centers (to cover the additional patients in the mHSPC population), and the establishment of new RLT centers to ensure equitable access. 97 , 109 Financial, operational, and practical planning will be required for new and expanded centers to provide effective, high-quality services. 97 Obtaining licenses for radioactive materials, implementing the necessary infrastructure upgrades, providing dedicated spaces for RLT, training and deploying staff, and disposing of radioactive waste may contribute to substantial upfront costs when starting a new RLT program, which could be an obstacle for many centers. 97 With the potential for increased use of RLT, pending its approval in the mHSPC setting, there will be a need to shift towards more coordinated input from the multidisciplinary team, including medical oncologists, urologists, nuclear medicine specialists, radiation oncologists, pharmacists, nurse practitioners, and administrative staff. 97 RLT centers should invest in systems of care that ensure all administrative aspects of RLT delivery (such as scheduling, reimbursement, and patient monitoring) run smoothly, and planning documents that clearly delineate the full list of required tasks should be employed to fully optimize patient outcomes. 97 Patient selection for RLT has been complicated by lack of standardized reporting for PSMA PET scans. 110 Several reporting frameworks for PSMA PET have been proposed, such as the VISION read criteria, 111 PSMA-RADS, 112 PRIMARY, 113 and PROMISE (molecular imaging tumor/node/metastasis system, version 1.0/version 2.0). 110 , 114 More recently, the Standardised PSMA PET/CT Analysis and Reporting Consensus (SPARC) has provided a unified framework for PSMA PET/CT analysis and reporting, serving as a reference standard for future clinical implementation. Integration of these common PSMA PET reporting criteria under one umbrella is expected to improve the interpretation and communication of imaging findings between nuclear medicine specialists and treating clinicians, thereby supporting consistent patient selection for RLT. 117 These established PET criteria may be augmented with evolving standards on the use of post-treatment [ 177 Lu]Lu-single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT)/CT as a supplementary imaging tool to assess on-treatment response. 118 However, prospective trials assessing the value of quantitative SPECT/CT are currently lacking, though this method is being used in phase 2 studies of RLT ( NCT06216249 and NCT06288113 ). 119–122 Patients receive RLT in designated, restricted areas of therapy centers. 123 These areas need to be staffed with appropriate medical providers, as well as facilities to prepare and administer RLT. 123 Currently available RLT agents can be administered in regulated areas without additional shielding (a larger, more isolated room may not require shielding at all). 115 , 124 Another primary consideration should be the availability of a designated restroom for patients receiving RLT or other diagnostic or therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals. 115 , 124 Sufficient room for radioactive waste storage is also strongly recommended. 97 , 115 Finally, a robust treatment and follow-up strategy should be implemented, so that appropriate counseling and educational materials can be provided to the patient and their caregivers, including general and radiation safety instructions for both during and after RLT. 123
sections.licensing: In the US, new medical centers starting RLT and current centers using new radioactive materials require a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or from an agreement state. 97 , 125 To apply for a license, the center must define 1) an authorized user (AU) of the RLT, who should be a board-certified physician who has completed radiation-therapy–specific training per NRC guidelines; 2) a dedicated space for delivery and management of RLT; and 3) a radiation safety and waste management program. 97 , 124
sections.staff training and deployment: All staff should receive in-house training on radiation safety and familiarize themselves with the RLT workflow to prepare for their new role. 97 This training should include the management of common adverse events associated with RLT. 97
sections.day-to-day operations: PSMA PET imaging prior to PSMA-directed RLT is required for visual assessment of sufficient PSMA uptake and to exclude sites of disease on CT without PSMA uptake. Quantitative parameters such as the maximum standardized uptake value (SUV max ) or total tumor volume may have additional roles in patient selection. 97 , 126–128 PSMA expression may differ between mHSPC and mCRPC. A recent single-center retrospective study found that PSMA-targeted PET/CT scans in patients with mCRPC had a higher SUV max and more frequent distant metastases than those in patients with mHSPC. 129 Furthermore, while PSMA expression can be heterogeneous in mCRPC due to the impact of prior therapies and the emergence of resistance mechanisms, PSMA is usually uniformly expressed in mHSPC. 130 , 131 Further considerations for medical centers choosing to offer PSMA PET imaging include establishing a fully integrated multidisciplinary team 116 and the standardization of PSMA PET reporting. 110 Some smaller, community-based centers may not have PET scanners available, which may make obtaining functional imaging data problematic. 97 Allowing patients to be referred to PSMA PET imaging at a larger center could solve this issue; the creation of a “tumor board” meeting to review potential patients for RLT could also bridge this gap. Communication between multidisciplinary team members for imaging interpretation, patient response, and laboratory results will result in the best treatment decisions. Multidisciplinary team collaboration is necessary for managing RLT treatment schedules, patient scheduling, and aligning with radiopharmaceutical ordering and supply. 97 Key learnings from RLT in clinical trials and real-world practice also emphasize the importance of AUs for establishing an appropriate workflow within the clinical team for laboratory checks, ordering drugs, administration, and other considerations. 97 Ensuring HCP awareness of the patient radiation instructions is also important, so that these instructions can be effectively reinforced throughout the clinic. 97 Appropriate scheduling of laboratory checks prior to treatment is mandatory for patient safety. 97 Furthermore, the timeframe for laboratory and clinical checks should allow sufficient time to review and order any necessary doses, with a buffer of time for RLT delivery (1-2 weeks) to allow for any delays. 97
sections.future directions: With ADT use alone, progression from mHSPC to mCRPC typically occurs within 1 year of treatment, and the median OS for patients with mCRPC is 42 months. 5 , 132 There is a need to delay progression to castration-resistant disease in patients with mHSPC, which should not only prolong survival but also delay time to deterioration of QoL due to cancer-related symptoms. 5 , 6 , 133 Therefore, ongoing HCP education regarding emerging combination treatment strategies for mHSPC is required. Given that up to ∼50% of patients in recent mHSPC clinical trials (TITAN and ENZAMET) did not attain undetectable levels of PSA (defined as ≤0.02 ng/mL and <0.2 ng/mL in TITAN and ENZAMET, respectively) after doublet or triplet therapy, 37 , 38 , 134 , 135 emerging combination approaches could address the unmet need for new treatment options. Several ongoing trials are currently assessing novel applications for 177 Lu-PSMA-617 in different mHSPC patient populations ( Table 1 ), including PSMAddition, which met its primary endpoint of rPFS at interim analysis (data cutoff January 13, 2025) and demonstrated that treatment with 177 Lu-PSMA-617 is associated with prolonged rPFS and a trend towards improved OS in this setting ( Table 2 ). There remains variation in and uncertainty around the use of treatment intensification strategies for mHSPC in clinical practice. 89 , 136 The addition of new therapies to clinical practice will face similar challenges to those seen with the integration of ARPIs in combination with ADT, such as concerns about drug tolerability, the lack of clinical evidence on OS, and questions on treatment sequencing. 89 The implementation of RLT for the treatment of mHSPC could be facilitated by addressing educational gaps and training needs for HCPs and potential issues surrounding reimbursement. In addition, data from other ongoing clinical trials will help to better define patient populations with mHSPC. For example, the PEACE6 program of trials assesses multiple patient groups and treatment combinations for mHSPC for better treatment selection, 137 including the PEACE6-Vulnerable trial of ADT with or without darolutamide in de novo mHSPC patients with metastases and frailty 138 and the PEACE6-Oligo (PRESTO) trial of ablative radiotherapy in patients with oligometastatic mHSPC. 139
sections.conclusion: Over the past decade, treatment options for mHSPC have improved outcomes, though there is still significant scope for further progress, and new therapeutics and strategies are urgently needed. Recent advances in imaging technology and radiopharmaceuticals are changing the treatment landscape of mCRPC and have the potential to change the treatment paradigm of mHSPC as well. Better understanding of key barriers to the application of new treatment strategies, such as PSMA-targeted RLT, will enable judicious implementation of these treatments into clinical practice when approved and therefore improve future treatment outcomes of mHSPC.

title: Transcription-independent induction of rapid-onset senescence is integral to healing
abstract: Cellular senescence plays key roles in tissue repair, tumour suppression and ageing. Here we identify a rapid, transcription‑independent senescence response in skin following injury. Within minutes to hours after wounding, skin cells at the edge of injury display hallmark features of senescence. This response involves the utilization of pre‑existing Cdkn1a mRNA through the removal of nuclear export inhibitors, which enables Cdkn1a transcript translation and rapid p21 protein accumulation. These cells enter stable cell‑cycle arrest and secrete pro‑migratory and pro‑inflammatory factors that promote tissue repair, including re‑epithelialization. Experimental suppression of this rapid senescence, either genetically or pharmacologically, markedly delays wound closure, whereas inhibition during later phases of repair has no effect. Our findings establish rapid‑onset senescence as a mechanistic requirement for efficient tissue regeneration.

sections.main: Cellular senescence is defined as a state of cells initiated with cell cycle arrest and entails changes on the levels of the transcriptome, proteome, secretome and others 1 , 2 . Senescent cells can be distinguished by a combination of markers, including cell cycle inhibitors: p21 CIP1/WAF1 protein (hereafter referred to as p21), which is encoded by Cdkn1a gene (whose transcript/messenger (mRNA) is also denoted as Cdkn1a mRNA) and p16 INK4A ( Cdkn2a gene) 2 , 3 , reduction in Lamin B1 (LMNB1) 4 , senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) 5 , DNA damage 6 , 7 and accumulation of lipids in senescence (ALISE) phenotype 8 , 9 . Senescent cells accumulate during ageing and have been causally implicated in pathologies of many age-related diseases 10 . Despite the synonymous meaning of ‘senescent’ and ‘old’, senescent cells are found not only in ageing organisms but also in wounds 11 – 14 . While eliminating p16 + cells has been shown to delay skin wound healing in healthy mice 12 , it remains unclear how the timing and mechanism of senescence induction affects healing. The decisive stage of the response of skin to wounding is the immediate recruitment of its cells to guide the healing process 15 . Our recent findings indicate that signalling pathways become active within minutes following skin injury and exhibit spatiotemporal control that shapes the healing process 13 . It is thus reasonable to expect that additional processes are induced just as quickly in the skin, as a rapid response to damage. While senescence has been shown to be integral to the wound response 12 , 13 , 16 , the current paradigm for this field holds that cellular senescence requires at least several days from the time of insult to develop 1 , 12 , 17 . However, these results are based primarily on experiments introducing damaging stimuli, such as in cultured human fibroblasts in vitro and in animal models or preneoplastic conditions 18 , as well as treated with doxorubicin or subjected to X-ray 1 , 13 , 17 , and the timing necessary for induction of senescence in physiological processes in vivo is unknown. The question on the temporal dynamics of cellular senescence in a physiological context stands as a challenge and needs to be addressed for the field to understand what senescent cells are and what they do in vivo. Assessing how senescence induction occurs in wounds, we discovered that p21 + senescent cells appear as early as 90 min after injury. Utilizing p21-lineage-tracing mice, we here show that senescence induction is persistent and that senescent cells are removed after injury is healed. Rapid senescence induction is transcription-independent, with high basal levels of Cdkn1a transcripts present in homeostatic skin, allowing these cells to produce p21 protein immediately upon injury. Mechanistically, Cdkn1a transcripts lose proteins that are known to restrict their nuclear export, which in turn permits interaction with translation initiation factors and promotes translation. Notably, interfering with the senescence machinery or eliminating senescent cells impairs wound healing, but only if carried out during the early stage of the healing process. Thus, our data support the concept that the rapid onset and transcription-independent induction of senescence is pivotal for the healing process, and its modulation might provide new therapeutic avenues. Throughout the research project, we adhered to the Guidelines for Minimal Information on Cellular Senescence Experimentation in vivo (MICSE) 2 to ensure a high level of reliability in identifying and analysing senescent cells.
sections.p21 + cells present a robust response to: Healing involves an interplay between different structures, including epidermis and dermis, their predominant types of cells such as keratinocytes and fibroblasts, which are all involved in migration and re-populating the injury site (Fig. 1a and ref. 15 ). To investigate the role of senescence in healing we made full-thickness excision wounds in mice and collected samples at days 3, 7, 12 and 28 post-wounding. We found that a large number of cells stained positive for p21 protein (which we refer to as p21 + cells in the manuscript), are present throughout the process of healing (Fig. 1b, c and overview in Extended Data Fig. 1a,c ) in all compartments of the skin. Various skin cell types become p21 + upon injury, including dermal fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 1c–e ), keratinocytes (Fig. 1b,c and overview in Extended Data Fig. 1a ) and myocytes of the underlying panniculus carnosus (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g ), among others. While the total number of p21 + cells remains constant throughout the process of healing (Extended Data Fig. 1b,d ), the concentration of p21 + keratinocytes and fibroblasts per mm 2 decreases as the volume of skin involved in healing and number of cells within the regrowing skin increase (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1e ). We found that among these time points the highest concentration of p21 + keratinocytes and fibroblasts can be observed at 3 days post-wounding (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1e ). Of note, there are no p21 + cells in homeostatic, unwounded skin nor are there any after wound closure (skin was collected 4 weeks after wounding, which corresponds to about 2 weeks after wound closure) (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–e ). The wounding-associated increase in the number of p21 + cells in mice was confirmed in porcine skin 7 days after wounding, where samples collected from healed wounds had a lower number of p21 + keratinocytes than samples collected from skin excised from wounds where healing was still ongoing (Extended Data Fig. 1h–j ).
