sections.summary: In the study period, with the exception of 2023, MSDs were the main contributor to consultations in Dutch general practice. The proportion of MSCs varied between 11.3% (95% CI = 11.3 to 11.3) and 12.6% (95% CI = 12.6 to 12.6). Lower limb disorders (31–33%) and females (60%) had the highest proportion of MSCs, while consultations for the trunk (8.2–9.2%) occurred least frequent. Present study showed that the majority of MSCs occurred in the 45–54 age category and in subsequent older age categories. Finally, this study showed that the proportion of MSCs compared with total consultations from all other ICPC chapters by age was highest around the ages of 10–15 years (13.5–12.9%) and 42–61 years (13.3–13.9%).
sections.comparison with existing literature: The usefulness of studies on the proportion of MSCs encountered by GPs is influenced by the age composition, size of the study population, as well as the duration of the study periods. In general, consultation rates may be influenced by whether patients with specific complaints (e.g. low back or neck pain) seek care from allied health professionals. Interpretation of our findings requires consideration of the healthcare context, as the Dutch system is characterised by mandatory GP registration and a gatekeeping role for access to secondary care, while patients also have the option of consulting paramedical professionals without referral through direct access [ 19 , 20 ]. This organizational context suggests that the accessibility of allied health services may influence the number of musculoskeletal consultations in general practice. To date, no systematic reviews were found with an overview of prevalence- and incidence figures of MSCs in generale practice. Current international research on musculoskeletal care in general practice primarily relies on short study periods, small sample sizes, and limited use of centralized databases [ 12 – 14 ]. In comparison with the findings of the NIVEL study [ 5 ], the results of the present study indicate that musculoskeletal and dermatological disorders constitute prominent contributors to the overall burden of disease. Multiple international studies conducted in general practice settings, using loco-regional databases, have reported that musculoskeletal conditions comprise a variable share of consultations, with prevalence estimates ranging from 8.7% to 25% [ 24 – 28 ]. It should be noted that consultation prevalence per ICPC chapter may vary considerably due to factors including geographic variation, demographic composition of the patient population, and structural differences in healthcare systems [ 29 ]. The study by Jordan et al. [ 24 ], using data from an English regional database over the course of one year (2006), found that the back was the most common individual region recorded (591 people consulting per 10,000 registered persons), followed by the knee (324/10,000). In children, the foot was the most common region. Consistent with our study, Jordan et al. utilized a centralized database. However, theirs was regional rather than national in scope. Furthermore, their study covered a one-year period, whereas our research spanned seven years. In a Swedish study involving individuals aged 18 to 65 years who sought care at primary health care centers, 2,000 patient records were examined over a three-year period [ 14 ]. Nearly 60% presented MSDs, with upper limb (34%) and lower limb (28%) issues being the most commonly reported. These symptoms were especially prevalent among younger and middle-aged adults, and more frequently observed in women (56%). The substantial discrepancy in the proportion of consultations for MSDs (12% versus 60%) is primarily attributable to differences in the study populations, specifically the inclusion of individuals of all ages in our study, compared to working-age individuals in the study of Wiitavaara et al. [ 14 ]. During a one-week study period, Keavy et al. found that MSDs among patients aged 12 to 92 years accounted for 21% of consultations at a general practice in an urban community in England, United Kingdom [ 15 ]. The mean age of patients presenting with an MSDs was 59 years, with the lumbosacral spine (18%) and the knee (17%) being the most commonly affected anatomical regions. Goff et al. [ 13 ] conducted a prospective, diary-based study documenting MSDs encountered by general practice registrars over a one-month period. MSDs accounted for 17% of all consultations, with back disorders representing the most frequently recorded category (29%), followed by disorders of the lower limb (27%) and upper limb (15%). Consistent with the study by Jordan et al. [ 24 ] and Wiitavaara et al. [ 14 ], the back and lower limb were identified as the most frequently recorded MSDs regions. In comparison to our study, lower limb disorders were documented more frequently than back disorders. The overrepresentation of women in consultations for MSDs is likely attributable to their higher frequency of general practice visits relative to men [ 30 – 32 ]. Our findings indicated that the proportion of MSCs relative to the total number of consultations was the highest, among other age groups, in the 10–15-year age category. A possible explanation is provided by Kamath et al., who described musculoskeletal injuries as a frequent reason for primary care consultations in the paediatric population, attributing their prevalence in part to the high levels of physical activity, including sports and exercise, among children and adolescents [ 33 ]. Our study showed that within the consultations for MSDs, the most consultations were for patients between 55 and 64 years and 75 + years. Since other studies included different age groups in their populations, their results regarding age distribution are not directly comparable to those of our study. Rekola et al. [ 34 ] showed that the rate of people visiting a primary healthcare doctor for musculoskeletal symptoms was highest in men aged 45–54 years and in women aged 55–64 years. Lutz et al. [ 35 ] showed that the median age of the global population would be 37.3 years in 2050 and 45.6 years in 2100. Since the proportion of MSD mainly increases with age, it can be expected that there will be more consultations for MSD, as the life expectancy of the world population increases. With the aging population and increased life expectancy, people become more susceptible to health problems, particularly MSDs [ 1 ]. Jacobse et al. reported a relatively high proportion of diagnostic errors related to MSDs, which may be partially explained by the high prevalence of MSCs in general practice and insights from studies on professional error [ 36 , 37 ]. These demographic changes, diagnostic errors, and the associated increase in MSCs emphasize the need for efficient deployment of healthcare professionals and rethinking care models to ensure accessibility and quality of care. Based on these findings, it can be argued that adequate attention to the teaching of MSDs is essential during medical school, general practice training, and ongoing postgraduate education for GPs. To ensure and optimize the delivery of care for patients with MSDs, effective collaboration is essential among GPs (trainee), GPwSI in musculoskeletal system, allied health professionals, and hospital-based specialists.
sections.strengths and limitations: This study has both strengths and limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first retrospective cohort study measuring proportions of MSCs, that used the data of more than 2.5 million patients who were representative of the general Dutch population. The use of centralized registration data can be seen as a strength of this study, as almost all Dutch citizens are registered with a general practice. The majority of patients with MSDs first report to and are assessed by their GP (gatekeeper), since going directly to an emergency department for MSDs is discouraged. Another strength of this study was the long-term study period. This allowed us to compare the results across the different years and gives us the opportunity to provide more reliable estimations of the burden of MSDs. A limitation of current study is that it only included information registered by the GP in the EHRs. It is plausible that patients consulted their GP without the consultation being recorded by the GPs. We assume that not registered consultations are evenly distributed over MSCs and the total number of consultations. Another limitation of present study is that the results of this study depend on the accuracy of the registration in the information systems by the GP, where the documented data were assigned to a new or existing ICPC code, ‘care service code,’ and/or ‘integrated care code [ 38 , 39 ]. This may have led to certain consultations not being adequately documented by the GP. Given our definition of a consultation, it was assumed that not all actual patient-GP contacts were recorded, potentially leading to an underestimation of the true number of registrations. To address both limitation within time constraints, we reviewed a small sample that included narrative data from the free-text fields but lacked an ICPC code, ‘care service code’, or ‘integrated care code’ and determined whether it was a (musculoskeletal related) consultation. These consultations were included in the total number of consultations, but we were unable to determine to which chapter the complaints belonged. As a result, the percentage of MSCs reported in this study may have been lower than it is in the real world. The clustering by body region remains, to date, an arbitrary process, for which no clear international consensus has yet been reached, which limit comparison with existing literature.
sections.conclusions and implications of this stu: MSDs accounted for a substantial number of consultations in (Dutch) general practice and most frequently involve consultations for the lower limb and spine. Females accounted for more MSCs, and the highest proportion of consultations involved people in the older age categories. With population aging and increased life expectancy, MSCs may constitute a larger proportion of total consultations in (Dutch) general practice.

title: Minimal Systemic Exposure with Maximal Delgocitinib Cream Use in Patients with Severe Chronic Hand Eczema in the DELTA 2 Randomized, Vehicle-Controlled, Double-Blind, Phase 3 Trial
abstract: Introduction Delgocitinib cream is a topical pan-Janus kinase inhibitor approved for adults with moderate to severe Chronic Hand Eczema (CHE) in the USA, Canada, European Union, and multiple other countries. Here, we assessed the systemic exposure of twice-daily topical application of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g in adults with moderate to severe CHE treated under normal or maximal use conditions in the DELTA 2 trial and compared with the systemic exposure in adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (AD) from a delgocitinib cream phase 1 AD trial. Methods Blood sampling was performed 2–6 h after delgocitinib cream application at weeks 1, 4, and 16 in DELTA 2. In the delgocitinib cream phase 1 trial, blood sampling was performed prior to application and at six timepoints (0–12 h) post-application on day 1 and day 8. Geometric mean delgocitinib plasma concentrations were calculated in DELTA 2 and peak delgocitinib plasma concentrations (geometric mean C max ) were calculated in the phase 1 trial. Results In DELTA 2, patients treated with delgocitinib cream under normal ( n = 294; body surface area [BSA], 1.48%; application, 7.3 g/week) or maximal use conditions ( n = 19; BSA, 2.17%; application, 13.7 g/week) showed geometric mean delgocitinib plasma concentrations at week 1 of 0.19 ng/mL ( n = 268) and 0.58ng/mL, respectively. In the phase 1 trial, patients ( n = 14; BSA, 33.6%; application, 72.3 g/week) showed a geometric mean C max of 1.20 ng/mL ( n = 13) on day 8. Conclusion Delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g resulted in minimal systemic exposure among adults with moderate to severe CHE, including those treated under maximal use conditions. Low systemic exposure was also observed in adults with moderate to severe AD, despite substantially greater BSA involvement and higher delgocitinib cream usage, highlighting the properties of delgocitinib cream’s novel formulation. Trial Registration NCT03826901 (phase 1, delgocitinib cream); study start date: 20 February 2019; primary completion date: 29 October 2021; study completion date: 29 October 2021. NCT04872101 (DELTA 2); study start date: 25 May 2021; primary completion date: 27 December 2022; study completion date: 6 January 2023. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s13555-026-01767-1.

sections.key summary points: Why carry out this study? Delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g, a topical pan-Janus kinase inhibitor approved for adults with moderate to severe Chronic Hand Eczema (CHE), was formulated with minimal penetration-enhancing excipients, and without the addition of propylene glycol and polyethylene glycol, to limit systemic exposure. We evaluated the systemic exposure of delgocitinib cream in adults with severe CHE who applied the highest amounts during the DELTA 2 trial and compared the results with the systemic exposure observed in a phase 1 trial of adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (AD) who had substantially greater body surface area involvement and higher delgocitinib cream usage. What was learned from the study? Twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g resulted in minimal systemic exposure among adults with moderate to severe CHE, including those treated under maximal use conditions. Adults with moderate to severe AD, who applied nearly 10 times more delgocitinib cream compared with adults with moderate to severe CHE, showed low systemic exposure, highlighting the properties of delgocitinib cream’s novel formulation. Based on these data, systemic pharmacological effects are unlikely to be observed with topical applications of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g in patients with moderate to severe CHE.
sections.introduction_1: Chronic Hand Eczema (CHE) is an inflammatory skin disease defined as hand eczema that persists for longer than 3 months or recurs at least twice within 1 year [ 1 ]. The key symptoms of CHE are pain and pruritus, with the clinical signs including erythema, scaling, edema, lichenification, hyperkeratosis, vesicles, and/or fissures [ 1 ]. Topical corticosteroids (TCS) are typically utilized as the short-term, first-line treatment in patients with CHE. However, TCS use has shown limited efficacy with prolonged use (even when used intermittently) and has been associated with adverse events (AEs), such as dermal atrophy and tachyphylaxis [ 1 , 2 ]. Delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g is a topical pan-Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor approved in the USA, Canada, European Union, and multiple other countries for the treatment of moderate to severe CHE in adults for whom TCS are inadequate or inappropriate [ 3 – 6 ]. In the DELTA 1 and DELTA 2 phase 3 trials, treatment with twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g was associated with both significant improvement in all efficacy endpoints versus cream vehicle and a favorable safety profile similar to that of cream vehicle in adults with moderate to severe CHE [ 7 ]. In the head-to-head DELTA FORCE phase 3 trial, twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g demonstrated superior efficacy and a more favorable safety profile compared with oral alitretinoin for up to 24 weeks in adults with severe CHE [ 8 ]. Systemic exposure and safety are central considerations when evaluating topical therapies for dermatological diseases. In 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a class-wide Boxed Warning for JAK inhibitors indicated for the treatment of inflammatory disorders based on data in patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with oral tofacitinib and concomitant methotrexate who showed an increased risk for serious AEs [ 9 , 10 ]. This Boxed Warning label is included with the FDA-approved oral (i.e., abrocitinib, upadacitinib) and topical (i.e., ruxolitinib cream) JAK inhibitors for the treatment of atopic dermatitis (AD) [ 11 – 13 ]. Delgocitinib cream, which was approved by the FDA without this Boxed Warning label, was formulated with minimal penetration-enhancing excipients, and without the addition of propylene glycol (PG) and polyethylene glycol (PEG), to limit systemic exposure [ 14 ]. Here, we examined the systemic exposure of delgocitinib cream in adults with severe CHE who applied the highest amounts of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g during the DELTA 2 phase 3 trial. We also conducted a post hoc comparison of systemic exposure data between the DELTA 2 trial and a phase 1 AD trial of delgocitinib cream in adults with moderate to severe AD who had substantially greater body surface area (BSA) involvement and higher delgocitinib cream usage.
sections.methods_1: To assess systemic exposure of delgocitinib cream, these analyses examined data from adults with moderate to severe CHE in the DELTA 2 randomized, vehicle-controlled, double-blind, phase 3 trial, including adults with severe CHE (defined as an Investigator Global Assessment of Chronic Hand Eczema [IGA-CHE] score of 4) at baseline who were treated under maximal use conditions. Maximal use conditions were defined as being in the upper quartile of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g use (≥ 10.9 g/week) among patients with severe CHE. The trial design of DELTA 2 (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04872101 ) has been previously described in detail [ 7 ]. Briefly, DELTA 2 was a randomized, double-blind, and vehicle-controlled phase 3 clinical trial in which adults (aged ≥ 18 years) with moderate to severe CHE were randomized 2:1 to twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g or cream vehicle for 16 weeks followed by either a 2-week safety follow-up or transfer to a 36-week extension trial. Blood sampling was performed 2–6 h after delgocitinib cream application at weeks 1, 4, and 16. Systemic exposure of delgocitinib cream in DELTA 2 was compared with that observed in the phase 1 AD trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03826901 ) conducted in adults with moderate to severe AD (25–50% BSA involvement at screening and baseline) who were treated with twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g for 8 weeks. Blood sampling was performed on day 1 (i.e., baseline) and day 8 (i.e., after 1 week of treatment) prior to application and at six timepoints post-application (i.e., 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 h). Blood samples were analyzed using a liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry-based method where the lower limit of quantitation was 5 pg/mL. In DELTA 2, geometric mean delgocitinib plasma concentrations were calculated, whereas peak delgocitinib plasma concentrations (geometric mean C max ) were calculated for the phase 1 AD trial. Prior work has shown that delgocitinib cream maintains a relatively flat pharmacokinetic (PK) profile at steady state [ 15 ]. As such, although DELTA 2 values do not represent true C max , collection of a single sample between 2 and 6 h post-application was considered to be sufficient to adequately characterize delgocitinib plasma concentration. Trial protocols were approved by all relevant ethics committees and institutional review boards (Electronic Supplementary Material [ESM] Table S2 ; [ 7 ]). The trials were conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Council on Harmonization Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice and conformed with all relevant country-specific laws and regulations. All patients, or their legal representatives, provided written informed consent. In DELTA 2, patients at selected trial sites had the additional option to participate in a photography component to capture disease status over time; participating patients were required to provide additional informed consent, including consent for their photographs to be published for scientific and/or commercial purposes.
sections.results_1: In DELTA 2, 75 of 313 delgocitinib cream-treated patients had severe CHE (i.e., IGA-CHE 4) at baseline, and 19 of these patients were treated under maximal use conditions (Table 1 ). Patients treated under maximal use conditions ( n = 19) had a mean baseline BSA involvement of 2.17% and applied, on average, 13.7 g of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g per week. Patients with moderate to severe CHE treated under normal use conditions ( n = 294) had a mean baseline BSA involvement of 1.48% and applied an average of 7.3 g of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g per week. In the phase 1 AD trial, adults with moderate to severe AD ( n = 14) had substantially greater mean baseline BSA involvement (33.6%, range 29.0–50.0%) and application of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g (mean of 72.3 g during week 1; Table 1 ). sections.discussion: These analyses showed that twice-daily treatment with delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g resulted in minimal systemic exposure among adults with moderate to severe CHE, including those treated under maximal use conditions. Low systemic exposure was observed in adults with moderate to severe AD who had substantially greater BSA involvement and delgocitinib cream application. Delgocitinib systemic exposure in adults with severe CHE treated under maximal use conditions was approximately 12 times lower than that observed for the lowest tested oral delgocitinib dose (1.5 mg) in healthy adults (geometric mean C max = 7.2 ng/mL) and 40 times lower when compared with whole blood IC 50 of delgocitinib from an in vitro interleukin-4 release assay (24 ng/mL) [ 15 ]. Among patients with moderate to severe AD, delgocitinib systemic exposure was approximately 6 to 20 times lower than these respective reference values. Systemic exposure concentration thresholds are not yet defined in the peer-reviewed literature or formal guidance documents; however, subnanomolar systemic exposure levels under maximal use conditions are generally considered to be negligible in regulatory practice. Given the increased risk of systemic absorption in damaged skin, topical treatments for CHE should be optimized to maintain efficacy while minimizing absorption into the bloodstream for safety. However, topical treatments for dermatological diseases are typically formulated with certain ingredients to maximize drug delivery [ 16 ]; for example, PG is a common skin penetration enhancer present in nearly two-thirds of formulations of TCS [ 16 – 18 ] as well as in ruxolitinib cream [ 11 ]. PEG is also commonly found in formulations of topical treatments and may indirectly enhance drug delivery by maintaining drug solubility, prolonging skin contact, and/or altering the solvent evaporation profile [ 19 – 21 ]. Delgocitinib cream was developed with minimal penetration-enhancing excipients, and without the addition of PG and PEG, which likely contributed to its observed minimal systemic exposure [ 15 ]. Long-term evaluation of adults with moderate to severe CHE treated for up to 52 weeks found that twice-daily delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g was well tolerated with no major safety concerns [ 22 ]. Additionally, while CHE typically involves lower BSA than other dermatological diseases (e.g., AD, psoriasis), low delgocitinib systemic exposure was also observed in adults with moderate to severe AD who had approximately 22 times the mean baseline BSA involvement compared with adults with moderate to severe CHE in DELTA 2 and applied nearly tenfold more delgocitinib cream. Taken together, systemic pharmacological effects are unlikely to be observed with topical applications of delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g in patients with moderate to severe CHE. A limitation of these analyses was the relatively low number of patients treated under maximal use conditions in the DELTA 2 trial. Additionally, differences in the blood sampling approach between DELTA 2 (single timepoint 2–6 h post-application at weeks 1, 4, and 16) and the phase 1 AD trial (sampling prior to application and at six timepoints post-application at baseline and week 1) resulted in comparison of geometric mean delgocitinib plasma concentrations in DELTA 2 with peak delgocitinib plasma concentrations (geometric mean C max ) in the phase 1 trial and only at week 1 of the treatment period.
sections.conclusion_1: Overall, twice-daily treatment with delgocitinib cream 20 mg/g was associated with minimal systemic exposure in adults with moderate to severe CHE, including in patients who were treated under maximal use conditions. Low systemic exposure was observed in adults with moderate to severe AD, despite substantially greater BSA involvement and higher delgocitinib cream usage, highlighting the novel formulation of delgocitinib cream.

title: Vericiguat Attenuates Vascular Calcification by Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate ‐Protein Kinase G Pathway Mediated Suppression of Matrix Metalloproteinase 10
abstract: Background Vascular calcification (VC), a pathological process driven by the osteogenic transdifferentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), markedly increases cardiovascular mortality. Vericiguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator, has shown vascular protective properties, but its role in modulating VC remains poorly investigated. Methods VC models were generated using the nephrectomy method or an adenine diet. Calcification in rat VSMCs and aortic rings was induced by high phosphate. VC was evaluated by Alizarin Red staining, calcium quantification, alkaline phosphatase activity, and imaging. Transcriptomic profiling and viral vector approaches were used to investigate the role of MMP‐10 (matrix metalloproteinase 10) in vericiguat‐regulated VC. Results Vericiguat treatment significantly reduced aortic calcification and osteogenic markers of VSMCs both in nephrectomy‐induced rats and adenine‐induced mice. It also inhibited calcium deposition and the phenotypic switch of VSMCs from a contractile to an osteoblastic state in both aortic ring and VSMC cultures. Transcriptomic profiling identified MMP‐10 as a key mediator; MMP‐10 was upregulated in VC models, and vericiguat reduced its expression. Overexpression of MMP‐10 reversed the protective effects of vericiguat, and lentiviral‐mediated MMP‐10 knockdown confirmed its procalcific role. Mechanistically, vericiguat increased cGMP‐PKG (cyclic guanosine monophosphate‐protein kinase G) signaling, including phosphorylated vasodilator‐stimulated phosphoprotein and phosphorylated c‐Jun (transcription factor Jun), ultimately downregulating MMP‐10. Conclusions Vericiguat inhibits VSMC osteogenic differentiation and attenuates VC by modulating the cGMP‐PKG‐MMP‐10 axis. These findings support vericiguat as a potential therapeutic candidate for VC.

sections.what is new?: Vericiguat, a soluble guanylate cyclase activator, attenuates vascular calcification in multiple experimental models and suppresses osteogenic differentiation of vascular smooth muscle cells through modulation of the cGMP‐PKG‐MMP‐10 (cyclic guanosine monophosphate‐protein kinase G‐matrix metalloproteinase 10) signaling axis. MMP‐10 is identified as a previously unrecognized mediator of vascular calcification and a downstream effector of soluble guanylate cyclase activation.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Whether long‐term pharmacological inhibition of MMP‐10 can slow the progression of vascular calcification and in turn reduce cardiovascular events in patients with chronic kidney disease, diabetes, or heart failure warrants further investigation.
sections.methods_1: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.animal studies: All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care Committee at Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University, China (Approval number: LAEC‐2025‐031) and conducted in compliance with the US National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (8th Edition, 2011). To minimize confounding estrogenic influences on VC, 22 only male Sprague–Dawley (SD) rats (160–200 g) and male C57BL/6J mice (8 weeks old) were purchased from Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center, housed under standard laboratory conditions with a 12‐hour light/dark cycle, and provided with free access to food and water. To establish VC models, SD rats ( n =6) were subjected to a 2‐step surgical reduction of renal mass (5/6 nephrectomy), followed by procalcified stimulation. Specifically, rats underwent two thirds left nephrectomy under intraperitoneal sodium pentobarbital anesthesia (50 mg/kg), followed by complete right nephrectomy 1 week later. Two weeks post surgery, serum creatinine was measured to assess renal function. Rats were then fed a high‐calcium and high‐phosphorus diet (1.0% calcium, 3.0% phosphate) and administered calcitriol (1 μg/kg, oral gavage, every other day; Aladdin, China) for 8 weeks. 23 , 24 , 25 For the arterial calcification models in mice, 8‐week‐old male C57BL/6J mice ( n =6) were randomly assigned to receive either a standard chow diet (control group) or a high adenine diet (0.25% adenine and 1.2% phosphorus) for 12 weeks. 26 In the vericiguat group, animals received oral vericiguat (10 mg/kg; MCE, Germany) once daily for 8 weeks. To investigate the mechanistic role of MMP‐10, recombinant adeno‐associated virus serotype 9 vectors encoding MMP‐10 under the control of the SM22α (smooth muscle 22 alpha) promoter (adeno‐associated virus‐MMP‐10; OBiO Technology, China) were administered to mice via lateral tail vein injection. Eight weeks after viral administration, aortic tissues were harvested for Western blot analysis to confirm overexpression efficiency. The MMP‐10 cDNA construct sequence is detailed in Table S1 .
sections.cell culture: Primary VSMCs were isolated from the thoracic aortas of 2‐month‐old male SD rats (160–200 g) using the explant method. Briefly, rats were euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg), and thoracic aortas were excised under sterile conditions. The adventitia and endothelium were carefully removed, and the remaining aortic tissue was cut into approximately 1 mm 2 segments. These tissue segments were placed in culture dishes containing growth medium (GM), comprising DMEM supplemented with 20% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO 2 . VSMCs from passages 4 to 11 were used in all subsequent experiments. To induce calcification, VSMCs were cultured in a calcifying medium (CM) consisting of DMEM containing 2% FBS supplemented with 2.6 mM disodium hydrogen phosphate (Na 2 HPO 4 ; Sigma, Germany) for 3 to 7 days, with the medium refreshed every 2 days. 26 In specific experiments, vericiguat (MCE, Germany) was added to the CM at varying concentrations (0.01, 0.1, 1, and 10 μM), and the cells were incubated for 3 to 7 days. Moreover, recombinant rat MMP‐10 (r‐MMP‐10; [MCE, HY‐P700571]) was added to the calcifying medium at a final concentration of 200 mM, alone or together with vericiguat, and incubated under the same conditions. Each experiment was conducted independently at least 4 times ( n = 4).
sections.lentiviral transduction in vsmcs: VSMCs at 80% confluence were transduced with lentiviral vectors carrying either MMP‐10‐overexpressing constructs or control vectors (OBiO Technology, China) at multiplicity of infection of 50 following the manufacturer's protocol. For loss‐of‐function experiments, lentiviral short hairpin RNA targeting MMP‐10 or a nontargeting control was used under the same conditions. The lentiviral vectors contained the MMP‐10 cDNA sequence under the control of a cytomegalovirus immediate‐early promoter to ensure stable and efficient expression. Transduction was performed in the presence of polybrene (6 μg/mL) to enhance infection efficiency. After 24 hours, the medium was replaced with fresh GM consisting of DMEM containing 10% FBS to minimize cytotoxicity. For selection, cells were treated with 1 μg/mL puromycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Each transduction experiment was independently repeated at least 4 times to ensure reproducibility (n=4). Detailed information regarding the MMP‐10 cDNA construct is provided in Table S2 , and the shRNA sequences are listed in Table S3 .
sections.arterial ring organ culture: Thoracic aortas were harvested from 2‐month‐old male SD rats euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg), as previously described. 23 , 24 , 25 Human arterial rings were obtained from the discarded vascular tissues of 38‐year‐old male donor following a limb amputation surgery. The use of these discarded tissues for research was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Zhujiang Hospital (Approval No. 2022SL0270), and the requirement for individual informed consent was waived in accordance with applicable regulations and ethical guidelines. The tissues were carefully cut into 3 to 5 mm rings under sterile conditions and cultured in GM consisting of DMEM containing 10% FBS at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . To induce calcification, the aortic rings were incubated in CM consisting of DMEM containing 10% FBS supplemented with 3.2 mM Na 2 HPO 4 for 8 to 10 days. In certain experiments, 10 μM vericiguat was added to the CM for the entire incubation period. At predetermined time points, the aortic rings were collected for further analysis. Each experiment was independently performed at least 6 times ( n =6).
sections.alizarin red staining: Alizarin Red staining was conducted to assess calcification in VSMCs and arterial tissues following standard protocols. 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 For VSMCs, cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 10 minutes, washed with double‐distilled water, and stained with 2% Alizarin Red solution (pH 4.2; Solarbio, China) for 5 minutes. Excess dye was removed by rinsing with double‐distilled water, and calcium deposits were visualized and imaged using a Leica inverted microscope. To quantify calcification, the bound dye was eluted with 10% formic acid, and the absorbance at 405 nm was measured using a microplate reader. For arterial tissues, aortic rings were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned into 4 to 6 μm slices. The sections were stained with 2% Alizarin Red for 5 minutes, washed to remove excess dye, and imaged under an inverted microscope. Red staining areas, indicative of calcification, were quantified using ImageJ software. Whole‐mount staining of aortic tissues involved fixing the samples in 95% ethanol for 24 hours, followed by overnight staining with 0.003% Alizarin Red solution in 1% potassium hydroxide. After staining, tissues were rinsed with 2% potassium hydroxide and imaged.
sections.calcium content quantification: Calcium content in VSMCs and aortic tissues was measured using a commercial calcium assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, cells or freshly isolated (or frozen) aortic tissues were incubated with 0.6 N hydrogen chloride at 4 °C for 12 hours. For tissues, samples were homogenized before incubation. After incubation, the mixtures were centrifuged and the supernatants collected for calcium quantification using a methyl thymol blue solution. Absorbance was measured at 610 nm using a microplate reader. The remaining cell or tissue pellets were used for protein quantification. Calcium content was normalized to total protein concentration and expressed as millimoles of calcium per gram of protein.
sections.alp activity assay: ALP activity was measured using a commercial ALP Assay Kit (Nanjing Jiancheng, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. For both VSMCs and aortic tissues, proteins were extracted with RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitor. For aortic tissues, samples were homogenized in RIPA buffer before centrifugation. The extracts were centrifuged at 12 000× g for 15 minutes at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. The extracted protein samples were then mixed with a paranitrophenyl phosphate substrate and 4‐aminoantipyrine and incubated at 37 °C for 15 minutes. The reaction was terminated by adding potassium ferricyanide, and absorbance was measured at 520 nm using a microplate reader. ALP activity was calculated as units per milligram of protein by normalizing the results to total protein concentration.
sections.quantitative real\u2010time polymerase c: Total RNA was extracted from VSMCs using TRIzol Reagent (TaKaRa, Japan) following the manufacturer's protocol. The RNA was reverse‐transcribed into cDNA using the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (TaKaRa, Japan). Quantitative real‐time polymerase chain reaction was performed on a 7500 FAST Real‐Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, USA) with SYBR Green Premix (TaKaRa, Japan). Relative mRNA expression levels were calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method, with GAPDH serving as the internal reference gene for normalization. The sequences of primers used are provided in Table S4 .
sections.micro\u2010computed tomography for measu: The extent of aortic calcification was assessed using micro‐computed tomography following established protocols. 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 Animals were euthanized via intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg/kg for rats, 200 mg/kg for mice), and their aortas were promptly harvested and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. The fixed tissues were scanned using a Siemens Inveon Micro‐CT scanner at a resolution of 0.079 mm. The acquired images were analyzed using Siemens Inveon Research Workplace software to quantify calcification levels.
sections.serum biochemical analysis: Two weeks after 5/6 nephrectomy surgery, blood samples were collected from the ophthalmic veins of rats and mice and centrifuged to obtain serum for biochemical analysis. Serum creatinine levels were determined using a colorimetric assay with the BioAssay Systems Creatinine Assay Kit (BioAssay Systems, USA).
sections.quantification of cgmp: cGMP concentrations in VSMCs and aortic tissues were quantified using commercial cGMP ELISA kits (Fankewei, China). For sample preparation, VSMCs were lysed in ice‐cold PBS containing protease inhibitor, with cell disruption achieved through 3 freeze–thaw cycles (−80 °C to room temperature). Aortic tissues were precisely weighted, minced into approximately 1 mm 2 fragments, and homogenized in ice‐cold PBS 1:9 (w/v) supplemented protease inhibitor using a prechilled homogenizer. Following centrifugation (10 000× g , 10 minutes, 4 °C), supernatants were collected for analysis. The assay was performed according to the manufacturer's protocol. Briefly, samples and standards were incubated in antibody‐coated wells, followed by sequential addition of detection antibody and substrate solution. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader, and cGMP concentrations were calculated based on a standard curve. All measurements were performed in duplicate, with appropriate dilution factors applied for accurate quantification.
sections.western blot analysis: Proteins from VSMCs and arterial tissues were extracted using RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS‐PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). The membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk or 5% bovine serum albumin for 2 hours at room temperature and then incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against BMP2, RUNX2, OPN, α‐SMA (alpha smooth muscle actin), MMP‐10, PKG, VASP (vasodilator‐stimulated phosphoprotein), p‐VASP (phosphorylated VASP), c‐Jun (transcription factor Jun), and p‐c‐Jun (phosphorylated c‐Jun). After washing with TBST, the membranes were incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 hours at room temperature. Protein signals were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence kit (Millipore, USA) and imaged with the Amersham Imager 600. Band intensities were quantified using Image J software, with GAPDH serving as the loading control.
sections.rna sequencing analysis: Total RNA was extracted from VSMCs using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The RNA quality and integrity were assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Polyadenylated mRNA was enriched from total RNA using oligo beads to specifically capture mature mRNA transcripts. The enriched mRNA was then reverse transcribed into cDNA, followed by library preparation and sequencing on the BGISEQ‐500 platform (BGI, Shenzhen, China). Gene expression levels were quantified using the Fragments Per Kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads method. Differentially expressed genes were identified based on the criteria of a false discovery rate‐adjusted Q‐value<0.05 and absolute log2 fold change>1.0. Functional enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed genes was conducted using Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway analysis. The enrichment ratio for each term was calculated as the number of candidate genes identified in our study divided by the total number of genes associated with that term in the respective database.
sections.statistical analysis: All continuous variables were expressed as mean±SD. Normality of the data was determined using the Shapiro–Wilk test. For comparisons between 2 groups, an unpaired 2‐tailed Student's t test was used for normally distributed data with equal variances. In cases where variances were unequal, Welch's correction was applied. For data not following a normal distribution, the Mann–Whitney U test was employed. For comparisons involving >2 groups, 1‐way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test was used for normality distributed data with homogeneous variances; otherwise, the Kruskal–Wallis h test followed by Dunn's post hoc test was performed. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 26.0), with a P value<0.05 considered statistically significant.
sections.vericiguat attenuates vc in\u00a0vitro a: To evaluate the anticalcification effects of vericiguat, rat VSMCs and arterial rings (rat and human) were cultured in CM with or without vericiguat treatment (Figure 1A ). In VSMCs, vericiguat treatment (0.01–10 μM) significantly reduced CM‐induced calcium deposition in a dose‐dependent manner, as demonstrated by Alizarin Red staining (Figure 1B and 1C ) and quantitative calcium assays (Figure 1D ). Vericiguat also decreased CM‐induced ALP activity (Figure 1E ). In addition, vericiguat suppressed the mRNA and protein expression of osteogenic markers RUNX2 and BMP2, while restoring α‐SMA expression, indicative of preservation of the contractile phenotype (Figure 1F and 1G ). In the ex vivo model, both rat and human arterial rings cultured in CM for 8 to 10 days developed prominent mineral deposition, as evidenced by Alizarin Red staining, which was significantly alleviated by vericiguat treatment (Figure S1A , S1B , S1F , and S1G ). Vericiguat also reduced calcium content (Figure S1C and S1H ) and ALP activity in these arterial rings (Figure S1D and S1I ). Furthermore, vericiguat downregulated the protein expression of BMP2 and OPN in rat arterial rings (Figure S1E ) and RUNX2 and BMP2 in human arterial rings (Figure S1J ). These findings indicate that vericiguat effectively suppresses VC and VSMC osteogenic differentiation in vitro and ex vivo.
sections.vericiguat reduces vc in\u00a0vivo: To evaluate the in vivo efficacy of vericiguat against VC, chronic kidney disease‐related VC models were established in rats (nephrectomy‐based) and mice (adenine‐based). Vericiguat or saline was administered by oral gavage for 8 weeks (Figure 2A , Figure S3A ). Elevated serum creatinine levels confirmed reduced renal function in both models, providing a procalcific background (Figure S2A and S2B ). Micro‐computed tomography analysis revealed significantly reduced aortic calcification in vericiguat‐treated rats and mice compared with saline controls (Figure 2B , Figure S3B ). Whole‐mount Alizarin Red staining further demonstrated decreased mineral deposition in the aortas of vericiguat‐treated animals (Figure 2C , Figure S3C ). Notably, the extent of calcification exhibited segmental heterogeneity along the aorta. Vericiguat treatment markedly attenuated calcification in the thoracic aorta, whereas mild mineral deposition persisted in the ascending and infrarenal segments. In addition, Alizarin Red staining of aortic cross‐sections showed markedly less calcification in the vericiguat groups (Figure 2D and 2E ; Figure S3D and S3E ). Consistently, calcium content and ALP activity were significantly lower in aortic tissues from vericiguat‐treated rats and mice (Figure 2F and 2G ; Figure S3F and S3G ). Western blot analysis indicated that vericiguat increased expression of the contractile marker α‐SMA and decreased the osteogenic markers OPN and BMP2 in both rat and mouse aortas (Figure 2H , Figure S3H ). Collectively, these findings indicate that vericiguat effectively attenuates aortic calcification and suppresses osteogenic differentiation in vivo.
sections.mmp \u201010 is downregulated by vericig: To further elucidate the mechanism by which vericiguat regulates VC and identify its downstream effectors, we performed the RNA sequencing to characterize the transcriptional profiling changes in VSMCs following vericiguat treatment. A total of 23 differentially expressed genes were identified among the GM, CM, and vericiguat groups, as depicted in the Venn plot (Figure 3A ). Heapmap of these 23 differentially expressed genes revealed that compared with the GM group, MMP‐10 expression in the CM group was upregulated, which was significantly attenuated by addition of vericiguat group (Figure 3B ). Gene Ontology enrichment analysis revealed that multiple ECM‐ and lipid metabolism‐related cellular component, such as extracellular region, extracellular space, and the PCSK9‐LDLR (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9‐low‐density lipoprotein receptor) complex, were significantly enriched in the vericiguat‐treated calcified VSMCs, suggesting a potential role of vericiguat in ECM remodeling and cholesterol metabolism (Figure 3C ; Tables S5 and S6 ). Given that ECM remodeling, characterized by collagen deposition and elastin degradation, is a key driver of VC, these findings imply that vericiguat may influence VSMC phenotypic switch by modulating ECM composition. Additionally, calcium homeostasis‐ and cytoskeletal‐associated cellular components, including myosin complex, dystroglycan complex, and sarcoglycan complex, were also enriched in the vericiguat‐treated calcified VSMCs, further supporting the hypothesis that vericiguat inhibited VSMC osteogenic differentiation and VC by altering ECM. Moreover, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment analysis identified the cGMP‐PKG signaling pathway as significantly enriched in the vericiguat‐treated group (Figure 3D ), aligning with the known role of vericiguat in activating sGC and enhancing cGMP production. To validate the RNA sequencing results, Western blot analysis confirmed that MMP‐10 protein levels were significantly downregulated in the vericiguat‐treated group compared with the CM group, both in VSMCs and rat aorta (Figure 3E and 3F ). Consistent findings were also observed in mice (Figure S4 ). Taken together, these findings suggest that vericiguat inhibits MMP‐10 expression both in vitro and in vivo, potentially by modulating ECM remodeling and VSMC osteogenic phenotypic transition, thereby contributing to its regulatory role in VC.
sections.mmp \u201010 overexpression promotes vc: To investigate the role of MMP‐10 in VC, we overexpressed MMP‐10 in rat VSMCs via lentiviral transduction, achieving a transduction efficiency >80% (Figure S5A ). Robust overexpression of MMP‐10 protein was confirmed by Western blotting (Figure S5B and S5C ). Functionally, MMP‐10 overexpression significantly increased mineral deposition in VSMCs, as evidenced by Alizarin Red staining (Figure 4A ) and its quantitative analysis (Figure 4B ), as well as by elevated calcium content (Figure 4C ). ALP activity was also significantly higher in MMP‐10‐overexpressing VSMCs compared with controls (Figure 4D ). Furthermore, protein expression levels of osteogenic markers OPN and BMP2 were markedly upregulated (Figure 4E ). To further assess the role of MMP‐10 in VC in vivo, we established a mouse model with adeno‐associated virus‐mediated MMP‐10 overexpression under the control of the SM22α promoter, resulting in high transcriptional activity in the medial layer of aortic tissues (Figure S6A ). Western blot analysis confirmed robust overexpression of MMP‐10 protein (Figure S6B and S6C ). Alizarin Red staining demonstrated significantly increased mineral deposition in both whole‐mount aortas and aortic cross‐sections from MMP‐10‐overexpressing mice (Figure 5A and 5B ), with quantification showing a greater Alizarin Red‐positive area compared with controls (Figure 5C ). Notably, increased calcification was observed across the examined aortic regions, consistent with an overall pro‐calcific effect of MMP‐10 overexpression. Consistently, MMP‐10 overexpression led to higher calcium content and ALP activity in aortic tissues (Figure 5D and 5E ). Moreover, the protein expression levels of key osteogenic markers, OPN and BMP2, were markedly elevated in aortic tissues of MMP‐10‐overexpressing mice (Figure 5F ). Taken together, these findings indicate that MMP‐10 overexpression exacerbates VSMC osteogenic differentiation and VC. Conversely, lentiviral mediated MMP‐10 knockdown further confirmed the procalcific role of MMP‐10 in VSMCs (Figure S7 ).
sections.exogenous mmp \u201010 reverses the anti: To investigate whether MMP‐10 mediates the anticalcification effect of vericiguat in vitro, we treated rat VSMCs with vericiguat in the presence or absence of r‐MMP‐10 under calcifying conditions. Alizarin Red staining revealed that vericiguat significantly reduced calcium deposition in VSMCs, whereas addition of exogenous MMP‐10 partially reversed this effect (Figure 6A ). This trend was confirmed by quantification of Alizarin Red staining intensity and measurement of calcium content (Figure 6B and 6C ). In addition, ALP activity—which was decreased by vericiguat—was significantly restored upon treatment with r‐MMP‐10 (Figure 6D ). Similarly, exogenous MMP‐10 reversed vericiguat‐mediated downregulation of the osteogenic markers OPN and BMP2 at the protein level (Figure 6E ). These findings suggest that vericiguat attenuates VSMC calcification, at least in part, through MMP‐10 downregulation.
sections.vericiguat activates the cgmp \u2010 pkg: To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which vericiguat suppresses VC, we investigated its impact on the cGMP‐PKG signaling pathway and c‐Jun‐mediated MMP‐10 expression. ELISA results showed that vericiguat treatment significantly increased intracellular cGMP levels in VSMCs cultured under calcifying conditions (Figure 7A ). Correspondingly, vericiguat upregulated PKG protein expression and promoted phosphorylation of its downstream target VASP, as confirmed by Western blot and densitometric analyses (Figure 7B ). Given that c‐Jun, a component of the AP‐1 (activator protein‐1) transcription factor complex, regulates MMP‐10 expression, 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 we next explored the effect of vericiguat on c‐Jun activation. Bioinformatic analysis (JASPAR database) identified 3 high‐affinity c‐Jun binding sites in the MMP‐10 promoter region (Figure S8 ), suggesting potential transcriptional regulation. Consistently, vericiguat treatment reduced p‐c‐Jun in VSMCs (Figure 7B ), supporting a PKG‐mediated inhibitory effect on c‐Jun activity. To validate these findings in vivo, we analyzed the cGMP‐PKG‐p‐c‐Jun axis in aortic tissues from rats. Vericiguat administration increased cGMP levels (Figure 7C ) and enhanced PKG and p‐VASP protein expression, while concomitantly reducing p‐c‐Jun protein levels in aortic tissues from both species, as demonstrated by Western blot (Figure 7D ). Consistent results were observed in mice (Figure S9 ). Taken together, these findings indicate that vericiguat activates the cGMP‐PKG signaling cascade and suppresses c‐Jun phosphorylation, thereby downregulating MMP‐10 expression.
sections.discussion: This study reveals several key findings regarding the vascular benefits of vericiguat: (1) vericiguat attenuates VC and inhibits osteogenic differentiation of VSMCs; (2) these effects are mediated through activation of the cGMP‐PKG signaling cascade, which inhibits c‐Jun phosphorylation and downregulates MMP‐10; and (3) MMP‐10 is identified as a novel VC inducer. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate that vericiguat directly mitigates VC and to delineate its underlying molecular mechanism. Notably, these findings extend the therapeutic relevance of vericiguat beyond heart failure, suggesting its broader applicability in VC (Figure 8 ). Recent clinical trial has established vericiguat as an effective stimulator of sGC that reduces cardiovascular mortality and heart failure‐related hospitalizations in high‐risk patients. 11 However, heart failure and its common comorbidities—such as chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and aging—are frequently complicated by VC, which further exacerbates cardiovascular risk. 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 To date, most studies on sGC stimulators, including vericiguat, have primarily focused on their hemodynamic and antifibrotic benefits in the context of heart failure or pulmonary hypertension. 10 , 32 Vericiguat has been shown to confer vascular protection by mitigating oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation—key contributors to pathological vascular remodeling. 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 Notably, activation of the NO‐sGC‐cGMP‐PKG signaling pathway has been implicated in preserving the contractile phenotype of VSMCs. 33 These observations suggest that vericiguat, through enhancement of cGMP‐PKG signaling, may suppress VSMC osteogenic differentiation. Elucidating this mechanism may open new therapeutic avenues for preventing VC, particularly in high‐risk populations such as individuals with chronic kidney disease. Our study for the first time uncovers that the cGMP‐PKG‐c‐Jun‐MMP‐10 axis is involved in vericiguat's anticalcific effects, thereby extending its therapeutic scope and providing novel mechanistic insights into the role of MMP‐10 in this process. VC is a complex and multifactorial process characterized by abnormal calcium and phosphate deposition in the vascular wall, often accompanied by ECM remodeling. 20 Under physiological conditions, VSMCs maintain ECM integrity and vascular tone. 34 However, under procalcific conditions, such as uremia, hyperphosphatemia, oxidative stress, or aging, VSMCs undergo osteogenic differentiation and secrete mineralized ECM components. 9 , 19 Importantly, calcification exhibits pronounced segmental heterogeneity along the arterial tree, reflecting regional differences in hemodynamic forces and vascular wall composition. The ascending and infrarenal aortas are known to experience higher mechanical stress, turbulent flow, and elastic‐muscular transitions, which make them more prone to residual calcification even under therapeutic intervention. Our transcriptomic analysis revealed that vericiguat significantly modulated genes involved in ECM remodeling and calcium handling, notably including MMP‐10. As a key enzyme driving ECM turnover, MMP‐10 degrades structural proteins like elastin and collagen that maintain vascular compliance. 35 , 36 Its upregulation is known to promote calcification via facilitating mineral deposition and structural weakening. In the present study, MMP‐10 expression was predominantly detected within the vascular wall. In contrast, vericiguat consistently downregulated MMP‐10 in vascular tissues and VSMCs across rodent models, suggesting a protective role against pathological ECM disruption and VC. These findings align with prior studies highlighting the importance of MMP‐mediated ECM remodeling in vascular mineralization. 37 , 38 Moreover, both gain‐ and loss‐of‐function experiments confirmed that MMP‐10 played a causal role: overexpression aggravated, whereas knockdown attenuated calcium deposition, ALP activity, and RUNX2 expression, thereby validating MMP‐10 as a key mediator of vericiguat's anticalcific action. Furthermore, vericiguat activated the canonical cGMP‐PKG signaling cascade, a central modulator of vascular homeostasis. The cGMP‐PKG axis is well established in vasodilation, anti‐inflammatory responses, and endothelial function. 39 , 40 , 41 Our data now expand its functional scope to include inhibition of VC. Elevated cGMP levels triggered PKG activation and downstream VASP phosphorylation—events that may stabilize the VSMC contractile phenotype and suppress their osteogenic transdifferentiation. 33 , 42 Concurrently, vericiguat reduced the phosphorylation of c‐Jun, a key AP‐1 subunit implicated in osteogenic gene expression and MMP‐10 transcription. 43 , 44 These results suggest that vericiguat interrupts procalcific signaling at multiple levels: upstream via PKG, midstream via inhibition of MAPK (mitogen‐activated protein kinase)/AP‐1 activation, and downstream via suppression of MMP‐10 and osteogenic markers. Although the cGMP‐PKG‐MMP axis is increasingly appreciated, its direct influence on MMP‐10 remains incompletely defined. Prior studies have demonstrated that cGMP signaling can regulate various MMPs through ERK1/2 and AP‐1 interactions. 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 Given that the MMP‐10 promoter harbors multiple c‐Jun binding sites, our findings support a plausible model wherein vericiguat suppresses MMP‐10 transcription via PKG‐mediated c‐Jun inhibition. However, how extracellular MMP‐10 signaling translates into intracellular osteogenic activation remains to be clarified. We speculate that MMP‐10 mediated ECM degradation may release matrix‐bound growth factors such as TGF‐β (transforming growth factor beta) and BMPs or alter cell–matrix interactions, thereby activating downstream MAPK/AP‐1 signaling and promoting osteogenic gene expression and ALP activation. This hypothesis provides a potential explanation for the link between extracellular matrix remodeling and intracellular calcific signaling, which warrants further investigation. Taken together, our results provide compelling evidence that vericiguat alleviates VC through suppression of VSMC osteogenic reprogramming and pathological ECM remodeling, involving the activated cGMP‐PKG‐c‐Jun‐MMP‐10 axis. Nonetheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although our findings suggest a pivotal role for MMP‐10 and ECM‐related pathways in vericiguat‐mediated attenuation of VC, further mechanistic studies—such as genetic or pharmacological manipulation of these targets—are needed to confirm causality and clarify the interplay with cGMP‐PKG signaling. Second, our conclusions are based primarily on rodent models and in vitro experiments, which, despite their value, may not fully reflect the complexity and heterogeneity of human VC. Third, the present study could not definitively resolve the cell type–specific contribution of MMP‐10 to VC. Given the potential involvement of non‐VSMC populations, including stromal or interstitial cells within the vascular wall, future studies employing cell type‐specific genetic models (eg, conditional knockout mice) will be required to clarify the precise cellular sources and functions of MMP‐10 in VC. Fourth, the relatively small number of animals and the absence of direct pharmacokinetic measurements of vericiguat levels limit the ability to confirm systemic absorption and exposure‐response relationships. Although all treated animals exhibited consistent pharmacodynamic responses, future studies including liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry‐based serum quantification of vericiguat are warranted to validate systemic exposure and strengthen translational relevance. Finally, the dosing and duration of vericiguat treatment in animals may not directly correspond to clinical regimens, and the translational applicability of these results should be validated in future preclinical or clinical studies.
sections.conclusions_1: In summary, we reveal that vericiguat downregulates MMP‐10 by activating cGMP–PKG signaling, in turn attenuates VSMC osteogenic differentiation and VC. These findings uncover a novel role of vericiguat in retarding the development of VC beyond its recognized benefits to heart failure. Although preclinical results are promising, further clinical studies are warranted to validate its efficacy and safety in patients at high risk for VC, to reduce cardiovascular events.

title: General dentists’ approach to dental management of patients taking anticoagulants - A National Survey-Based Assessment: pre- and post-procedure practice
abstract: Aim: To determine the pre-operative and post-operative practices of general dentists (GDs) in the community for patients taking vitamin K antagonists (VKA) and direct oral anti-coagulants (DOACs). Methods: An online questionnaire was administered to GD members of the National Dental Practice-Based Research Network. GDs were queried about the interaction with the medical professional prior to dental treatment, use of laboratory tests to assess bleeding risk, measures to control bleeding, and comfort level with delivering dental care. Results: 47.6% and 41.2% of GDs “always” consult with the patient’s physician prior to an extraction in a patient on VKA or DOACs, respectively. 27.1% and 8.7% of GDs use laboratory tests to assess risk for bleeding prior to a dental extraction in patients on VKA and DOAC, respectively. For VKA patients, GDs prefer INR testing (68.4%), and for DOAC patients, most GDs are “unsure” what blood test to use. The most-used hemostatic agents were cellulose (65.1%), collagen (60.6%) and epinephrine infiltration (60.6%). Conclusions: GDs are uncertain about the best approach for patients taking DOACs. INR is not routinely used by most GDs to assess the bleeding risk in patients taking VKA. The most commonly used hemostatic agents are cellulose-based, collagen-based and vasoconstrictors.
