sections.introduction: Ischemic stroke remains one of the leading causes of long-term disability and mortality worldwide and continues to impose a major global socioeconomic burden [ 1 ]. Rather than being understood solely as a vascular occlusive event—or, conversely, as a primarily inflammatory disorder—ischemic stroke is now increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of the neurovascular unit and a complex neurovascular syndrome involving dynamic interactions among endothelial cells, pericytes, astrocytes, microglia, neurons, and immune compartments [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite major advances in reperfusion therapies, including intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy, many patients experience incomplete recovery because of narrow therapeutic windows, incomplete tissue rescue despite successful recanalization, microvascular dysfunction, and reperfusion-associated secondary injury [ 4 ]. These downstream processes involve not only inflammatory cascades, but also endothelial dysfunction, blood–brain barrier disruption, altered neurovascular coupling, and multicellular injury within the neurovascular unit [ 3 ]. Accumulating evidence indicates that the ischemic cascade initiates a temporally orchestrated series of neurovascular and immune responses that critically influence secondary brain injury and subsequent tissue repair. Importantly, these responses do not emerge exclusively within the ischemic parenchyma, but begin early within the vascular compartment through endothelial activation, leukocyte adhesion, platelet–immune interactions, complement signaling, and thromboinflammatory processes [ 5 ]. Complement activation represents an additional mechanistically important component of this response, contributing to leukocyte recruitment, endothelial injury, synaptic remodeling, and reperfusion-associated tissue damage in a temporally dynamic manner [ 5 ]. Early events include activation of resident microglia and astrocytes, endothelial dysfunction, disruption of the blood–brain barrier, and infiltration of peripheral immune cells such as neutrophils, monocytes, and T lymphocytes [ 6 ]. These processes unfold within the disrupted neurovascular unit and contribute to maladaptive amplification of innate and adaptive immune signaling within the ischemic core and penumbra, while simultaneously altering vascular permeability, tissue perfusion, and cellular homeostasis [ 2 , 3 ]. These immune mediators amplify neuronal injury through the release of proinflammatory cytokines—including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6—together with oxidative stress and matrix metalloproteinase activation, thereby further compromising blood–brain barrier integrity and expanding infarct size [ 6 ]. At the same time, this inflammatory response is not uniformly deleterious, as selected immune and glial pathways may also contribute to debris clearance, tissue remodeling, and neurovascular repair during later phases of stroke [ 2 , 3 ]. This biological duality supports the rationale for targeted, stage-specific immunotherapeutic strategies rather than nonspecific immune suppression. Within this broader neurovascular framework, recent mechanistic studies have substantially refined our understanding of post-stroke immune dysregulation, shifting the field toward more precise and mechanism-driven immunomodulatory strategies. Accordingly, immunotherapy in ischemic stroke may be more appropriately viewed not as treatment of an isolated inflammatory disorder, but as selective modulation of one biologically important dimension of a multifactorial neurovascular disease. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses have shown that microglia exhibit substantial heterogeneity rather than conforming to the classical M1/M2 paradigm, with distinct transcriptional states emerging across the acute and subacute phases of ischemia [ 7 ]. These findings suggest that nonspecific immune suppression is unlikely to be sufficient and that precision immunomodulation may represent a more biologically appropriate therapeutic direction. Additional experimental work indicates that targeting immune-cell phenotypes and inflammatory signaling pathways may influence post-stroke injury responses: modulation of mechanisms such as NLRP3 inflammasome activation and AMPK–mTOR signaling has demonstrated promising preclinical findings regarding tissue protection and reparative signaling [ 8 , 9 ], thereby informing the ongoing development of molecular immunotherapies. Metabolic dysfunction within immune cells has emerged as an important regulator of post-stroke neuroinflammation, with impaired immunometabolic homeostasis exacerbating inflammatory signaling, leukocyte dysfunction, and neuronal injury [ 10 , 11 ]. Advances in neuroimmunology have also underscored the importance of adaptive immune responses: CD4⁺ T cells influence microglial activation and functional outcomes, whereas IL-17A–producing γδ T cells have been associated with amplification of post-ischemic inflammatory injury in experimental models [ 12 , 13 ]. Clinical studies further suggest that dynamic changes in lymphocyte subsets may be associated with neurological severity, systemic immune status, and functional prognosis after stroke, although the causal and therapeutic significance of these observations remains incompletely understood. Beyond local neuroinflammation, ischemic stroke also induces systemic immune dysregulation involving brain–periphery crosstalk through neuroendocrine and autonomic pathways. Stroke-induced systemic immunosuppression—characterized by lymphopenia, altered splenic responses, impaired peripheral immune competence, and increased susceptibility to infection—has emerged as a potentially clinically relevant component of post-stroke immunopathology, although its implications for immunotherapeutic timing and patient stratification remain to be fully established. Importantly, post-stroke neuroinflammation does not occur in a biologically neutral host. Common vascular comorbidities—particularly arterial hypertension—may precondition the immune system before stroke onset by promoting myeloid activation, endothelial dysfunction, and chemokine-driven leukocyte recruitment, thereby potentially amplifying secondary inflammatory injury after cerebral ischemia [ 14 , 15 ]. This has important translational implications, as the baseline inflammatory state may influence both the magnitude of post-stroke neuroinflammation and the responsiveness to immunomodulatory interventions. Despite these mechanistic advances, clinical translation has consistently lagged behind biological discovery. Recent consensus frameworks, including STAIR XIII, emphasize that the success of neuroprotective and immunomodulatory strategies is likely to depend on alignment with the temporal dynamics of ischemic injury [ 16 , 17 ]. Rather than a single therapeutic window, ischemic stroke is now understood as a sequence of overlapping pathophysiological phases—including hyperacute (pre-reperfusion), acute (peri-reperfusion), and subacute (post-reperfusion) stages—each characterized by distinct but interconnected mechanisms of injury, inflammation, and repair [ 16 , 18 ]. Inflammatory responses are particularly relevant in this context because they evolve over extended timeframes and contribute not only to early ischemic damage, but also to reperfusion-associated secondary injury and later repair-associated processes [ 13 , 18 ]. This temporal framework provides a biologically plausible rationale for stage-specific immunotherapeutic approaches tailored to the evolving neuroimmune landscape of ischemic stroke [ 13 , 16 – 18 ]. Given these developments, a neurovascularly contextualized and mechanism-oriented synthesis of immunotherapeutic strategies is needed to clarify translational barriers and distinguish mechanistically distinct therapeutic categories. Such an approach may also help guide future clinical trial design in this rapidly evolving field. Therefore, in this systematic review conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement, we systematically and critically evaluate contemporary preclinical and clinical evidence on therapeutic strategies targeting neuroinflammatory and immune-regulatory pathways within the broader neurovascular pathobiology of adult ischemic stroke, while acknowledging the substantial biological, methodological, and translational heterogeneity across the available evidence base. Our objectives are to (1) identify contemporary mechanism-driven immunomodulatory strategies with translational relevance, (2) delineate barriers to clinical translation, (3) distinguish direct immunotherapy from regenerative cell-based approaches with immunomodulatory relevance, and (4) propose priorities for future research aimed at integrating immune-targeted therapies with established reperfusion interventions. For conceptual and translational clarity, the present review does not define “immunotherapy” in a narrow pharmacological sense only. Instead, it evaluates a broader spectrum of therapeutic strategies that either directly target immune/inflammatory pathways or exert clinically relevant immunomodulatory effects within post-stroke neuroinflammation. However, these categories are analyzed separately and should not be interpreted as mechanistically equivalent.
sections.study design: This systematic review and exploratory quantitative synthesis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement [ 19 ], aiming to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor, and were designed to distinguish systematically synthesized evidence from narrative contextual interpretation. The review aimed to identify, systematically synthesize, and critically evaluate evidence on immunotherapeutic interventions for adult ischemic stroke across clinical and translational preclinical studies, and—where appropriate—to quantitatively synthesize comparative clinical trial data.
sections.eligibility framework: The review protocol was structured using the PICO model [ 20 , 21 ]: Population: Adult patients (≥ 18 years) with acute or subacute ischemic stroke Intervention: Direct immunotherapy (molecular or biological), as well as regenerative cell-based therapies with reported or experimentally supported immunomodulatory or neuroinflammation-relevant mechanisms, analyzed as mechanistically distinct but translationally related therapeutic categories Comparator: Standard care (rt-PA, mechanical thrombectomy), placebo, or no treatment Outcomes: Functional recovery, infarct size, inflammatory biomarkers, mortality, and safety This framework was predefined before initiation of the formal database search.
sections.search strategy: A systematic, reproducible search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase was initially conducted in October 2025 and subsequently updated in January 2026 to maximize the likelihood of capturing all eligible studies published through 31 December 2025. The update search was performed using the same databases, search logic, and eligibility criteria as the primary search to ensure methodological consistency across the full review period. Only peer-reviewed, English-language original research articles were eligible for inclusion in the formal systematic synthesis. Review articles, mechanistic syntheses, and conceptual papers were not included in the formal systematic evidence synthesis but were used exclusively to provide biological and translational context in the Introduction and Discussion . The temporal restriction to studies published between 2020 and 2025 was applied to preferentially focus on contemporary mechanism-driven and translational immunotherapeutic strategies that emerged following earlier first-generation anti-inflammatory approaches already comprehensively synthesized in prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The PubMed search strategy was: (“ischemic stroke” OR “cerebral infarction”) AND (immunotherapy OR “immune modulation” OR “neuroinflammation” OR “anti-inflammatory” OR “natalizumab” OR “stem cells” OR “PKM2” OR “STAT3” OR “immune checkpoint” OR complement OR thromboinflammation OR “neutrophil extracellular traps” OR immunosuppression) AND (adults[MeSH Terms]) AND (“2020”[Date—Publication]–“2025”[Date—Publication]). The restriction of the search window to the period January 2020–December 2025 was based on three considerations. First, the immunotherapy landscape for ischemic stroke underwent a substantive transformation around 2019–2020, with the emergence of mechanism-driven, pathway-specific strategies (e.g., PKM2–NF-κB axis modulation, single-cell transcriptomics-informed microglial targeting, second-generation allogeneic cell therapies) that are qualitatively distinct from earlier first-generation anti-inflammatory approaches comprehensively reviewed elsewhere [ 7 , 13 , 22 – 25 ]. Second, restricting the search to the most recent publication period increased the likelihood of capturing studies conducted and reported under contemporary methodological standards, thereby improving comparability across included studies and prioritizing evidence generated under current standards of trial design, reporting quality, and bias assessment [ 26 ]. Third, this temporal scope is consistent with precedent in the neuroinflammation systematic review literature, where comparable or narrower windows have been employed [ 27 , 28 ]. Foundational and historical studies were referenced in the Introduction to preserve contextual continuity. Although this temporal restriction may have limited the historical breadth of the evidence base, it was considered unlikely to materially distort the contemporary translational interpretation of the field, given that earlier foundational studies have already been synthesized in prior systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
sections.inclusion criteria: Studies were eligible if they met the following: Published between January 2020 and December 2025 English language Conducted in adults with ischemic stroke or, in the case of preclinical studies, designed to investigate immunotherapeutic mechanisms considered potentially translationally relevant to adult ischemic stroke Investigated defined immunotherapeutic interventions (molecular or biological) or cell-based regenerative interventions with reported or experimentally supported immunomodulatory, paracrine, or neuroinflammation relevant mechanisms applicable to adult ischemic stroke Reported at least one efficacy or safety outcome Original research: randomized clinical trials, observational studies, or translational preclinical experiments Review articles, narrative reviews, editorials, and conference abstracts were not eligible for formal inclusion in the systematic evidence synthesis. Where such sources were cited elsewhere in the manuscript, they were used exclusively for contextual biological or translational interpretation and were clearly distinguished from the formally included study set. However, selected review and foundational papers were used strictly outside the formal systematic synthesis to provide mechanistic, translational, and historical context and were not considered part of the evidence base.
sections.exclusion criteria: Studies were excluded if they: Addressed hemorrhagic or pediatric stroke. Preclinical studies were excluded if they focused exclusively on descriptive or exploratory pathophysiology without evaluating a defined therapeutic target, immunomodulatory mechanism, or translationally relevant biomarker relevant to adult ischemic stroke. Lacked sufficient full-text or extractable data for eligibility assessment. Were duplicates, reviews, editorials, or conference abstracts.
sections.study selection: The study selection process was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 framework [ 19 ]. A total of 913 records were identified through database searching (PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase), with no additional records identified through other sources. Before screening, 229 records were removed (187 duplicates and 42 non-English publications, reviews, or editorials), leaving 684 records for title and abstract screening. Of these, 477 were excluded because they did not meet the predefined relevance criteria for immunotherapeutic approaches in ischemic stroke. The remaining 207 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which 152 were excluded for predefined reasons. Ultimately, 55 studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. The complete study selection pathway and reasons for exclusion are presented in Fig. 1 . Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles, with disagreements resolved by discussion and consensus. Fig. 1 PRISMA 2020 flow diagram illustrating the identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and inclusion of studies in the qualitative synthesis ( n = 55) and the subsequent selection of trials for the exploratory quantitative meta-analysis ( k = 3; N = 632). [ 19 ] Adapted from Page et al. Reasons for full-text exclusion included hemorrhagic or pediatric stroke, absence of translational therapeutic or biomarker relevance to adult ischemic stroke immunotherapy, lack of an immunotherapeutic intervention, insufficient outcome data, duplicate cohorts, and publication type ineligibility. The supplementary update search did not identify any additional studies that met all predefined eligibility criteria for inclusion in the final qualitative synthesis. Thus, the final evidence base for the qualitative synthesis remained restricted to studies published within the predefined review period (January 2020–December 2025).
sections.data extraction: Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form capturing: Study characteristics (authors, year, study design) Population details Immunotherapeutic intervention type and dosing Sample size and methodology Efficacy outcomes (functional scales, infarct size, perfusion) Secondary outcomes (inflammatory markers, mortality) Adverse events and safety Timing of intervention and follow-up duration Two reviewers independently extracted data to improve methodological consistency and minimize the risk of extraction bias. For studies considered for quantitative synthesis, additional extraction included event counts, comparator arm structure, endpoint definitions, and reported effect estimates with confidence intervals.
sections.quality assessment: Risk-of-bias was assessed using tools appropriate for study design: Randomized clinical trials: Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 (RoB 2) [ 29 , 30 ] Observational studies: Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) [ 31 ] Preclinical studies: SYRCLE’s risk-of-bias tool [ 32 ] For descriptive purposes, randomized controlled trials were interpreted cautiously according to overall RoB 2 judgment, whereas observational studies scoring ≥ 7 points on the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale were interpreted as having relatively higher methodological robustness on the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). Preclinical studies were interpreted qualitatively using the SYRCLE Risk of Bias framework rather than numerical quality scoring. Any discrepancies in quality assessment were resolved through discussion. For randomized controlled trials included in the quantitative synthesis, domain-level risk-of-bias was additionally evaluated and visualized using a RoB 2 traffic-light matrix. Importantly, risk-of-bias assessments were not treated as descriptive variables only, but were explicitly incorporated into the interpretation of study findings and the overall appraisal of evidentiary strength.
sections.data synthesis: Because of substantial heterogeneity in intervention classes, study designs, outcome definitions, and treatment timing, the primary synthesis was structured narrative, informed by predefined categories and methodological grouping [ 29 , 33 ]. Studies were categorized a priori into three predefined and mechanistically distinct groups: Molecular immunotherapy (e.g., PKM2 modulation, STAT3 inhibition, microRNA regulation) Cell-based regenerative therapy with immunomodulatory properties Biological immunotherapy (e.g., monoclonal antibodies such as natalizumab) This classification was applied to minimize the risk of conceptual conflation of mechanistically distinct therapeutic strategies, particularly between direct immunotherapy and regenerative cell-based approaches. For clarity and reproducibility, studies presented in the summary tables were organized according to predefined thematic and methodological groupings rather than order of retrieval. Interventional studies were structured primarily by immunotherapeutic class and then chronologically within each category, whereas mechanistic and clinical trial tables were organized according to conceptual or translational relevance. Comparisons focused on efficacy (functional recovery, infarct size), mechanisms of action, safety, and translational relevance. Studies were also qualitatively analyzed with respect to the timing of intervention relative to stroke onset and reperfusion, in order to assess the alignment of immunotherapeutic strategies with distinct pathophysiological phases of ischemic injury. In addition, an exploratory quantitative synthesis was performed for a subset of completed randomized controlled trials with extractable comparative efficacy data. Full methodological details are provided in the “ Quantitative Synthesis: Materials and Methods ” section. Methodological limitations identified during study quality assessment were incorporated into the interpretation of findings and the overall appraisal of evidentiary strength, rather than being treated as descriptive variables only. To preserve methodological clarity, the formal systematic synthesis was restricted to studies meeting all predefined eligibility criteria and contributing directly to the evidence base on therapeutic interventions or clinically/translationally relevant immunomodulatory mechanisms in adult ischemic stroke. Mechanistic, foundational, and conceptual studies that did not meet formal eligibility criteria for the systematic evidence synthesis were not treated as included efficacy studies and were not incorporated into comparative evidence appraisal. Instead, these studies were used selectively and narratively to support biological interpretation and translational framing and are presented separately as contextual references.
sections.meta-analysis objectives: This exploratory meta-analysis was designed as a hypothesis-generating quantitative extension of the systematic review to explore pooled effect estimates of immunotherapeutic and cell-based interventions on excellent functional outcome at day 90 in adults with acute ischemic stroke, expressed as the odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). The analysis was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement [ 19 ], the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.4 [ 29 ], and the Meta-analysis Of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) reporting guidelines [ 34 ] where applicable. Given the limited number of eligible trials and the heterogeneity of both intervention classes and composite endpoint definitions, this synthesis is characterized as an exploratory meta-analysis and is intended to complement rather than supplant the narrative synthesis presented elsewhere in this review.
sections.study design, data structure, and eligib: As described in the “ Methods ” section, 55 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, of which three randomized controlled trials ( N = 632) were eligible for quantitative analysis. Title and abstract screening of the remaining 684 records led to the exclusion of 477 entries that did not pertain to immunotherapeutic interventions in ischemic stroke. Full-text assessment of the 207 remaining articles resulted in the exclusion of 152 studies for predefined reasons—most frequently, preclinical studies focused exclusively on descriptive or mechanistic pathophysiology without direct therapeutic or translational immunological applicability ( n = 44), focus on hemorrhagic or pediatric stroke ( n = 31), and absence of an immunotherapeutic intervention ( n = 28)—leaving 55 studies eligible for the qualitative synthesis. The complete study selection pathway, including the subset subsequently assessed for quantitative synthesis, is depicted in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1 ). Importantly, the quantitative synthesis was performed exclusively on trials already eligible within the predefined systematic review framework and timeframe. The reference to March 2026 pertains solely to outcome data extraction and verification and does not indicate an extension of the literature inclusion period. Of the 55 studies included in the overarching systematic review, 16 clinical trials (Table 3 ) were subjected to a dedicated eligibility assessment for the quantitative synthesis. Eligibility for the quantitative synthesis was determined by three prespecified criteria that had to be fulfilled jointly: (a) the trial was completed and had sufficiently detailed efficacy results publicly available by the time of data extraction (March 2026), while still falling within the predefined review period of studies published through December 2025; (b) the trial employed a randomized, controlled design with a placebo or standard-of-care comparator arm permitting the computation of an odds ratio (OR) or risk ratio (RR) for binary endpoints, or a standardized mean difference (SMD) for continuous endpoints; and (c) raw numerical data—event counts per arm, means with standard deviations, or reported effect estimates with confidence intervals—were extractable from the primary publication or its supplementary materials. Application of these criteria yielded three trials eligible for the comparative (OR-based) meta-analysis: ACTION [ 35 ], ACTION II [ 36 ], and TREASURE [ 25 ], encompassing a combined sample of N = 637 participants (362 intervention, 275 control). One additional study, SB623 [ 37 , 38 ], was included in a supplementary pre-post analysis exclusively, owing to its open-label, single-arm design, chronic stroke population (6–60 months post-onset), and stereotactic delivery route, all of which precluded its incorporation into the comparative synthesis. The remaining 12 trials were excluded, most frequently because quantitative efficacy results had not been published ( k = 8) or because the trial lacked a comparator arm ( k = 3). Full eligibility assessments with individual rationales are documented in Table S1 (included studies) and Table S2 (excluded studies). Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized extraction form (Supplementary Appendix). Extracted variables comprised: study identifiers (authors, year, NCT registration number, phase), population characteristics (sample size per arm, age, baseline NIHSS, therapeutic window), intervention details (agent, dose, route, timing), and efficacy outcomes (event counts, proportions, OR with CI, risk differences). Any discrepancies were resolved by consensus; inter-rater agreement was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa coefficient [ 39 ]. For ACTION II, which employed a three-arm design (natalizumab 300 mg, natalizumab 600 mg, and placebo in a 1:1:1 ratio), the two active treatment arms were combined into a single intervention group ( n = 179) versus placebo ( n = 91), in accordance with Cochrane Handbook recommendations for multi-arm trials [ 29 ]. The reported OR was adopted directly from the publication, and its sampling variance was recovered algebraically from the confidence interval bounds. The primary efficacy outcome was defined as the proportion of patients achieving an excellent functional outcome at day 90, operationalized as a composite of modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score ≤ 1 and Barthel Index (BI) ≥ 95 (ACTION, ACTION II) or mRS ≤ 1, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) ≤ 1, and BI ≥ 95 (TREASURE). Importantly, the composite endpoint definition differed across trials, with TREASURE employing a more restrictive criterion (mRS ≤ 1, NIHSS ≤ 1, and BI ≥ 95) compared with the ACTION program (mRS ≤ 1 and BI ≥ 95). This definitional heterogeneity represents a non-trivial source of clinical and statistical inconsistency and was explicitly considered in sensitivity and subgroup analyses. Where the primary endpoint in the original trial differed from the present meta-analytic endpoint—as was the case for ACTION, whose prespecified primary outcome was change in MRI infarct volume at day 5 [ 35 ]—the mRS ≤ 1 proportion at day 90 was extracted as a secondary clinical outcome from the published results. For the ACTION trial, the day 90 mRS ≤ 1 outcome was not the prespecified primary endpoint but was selected as a clinically relevant secondary endpoint to ensure comparability across trials reporting functional outcomes.
sections.1.3.1. effect size estimation: The effect size measure employed throughout the comparative analysis was the odds ratio (OR) on the natural logarithmic scale. For consistency, the odds ratio was coded such that values below 1 indicate lower odds of achieving an excellent functional outcome in the intervention group compared with the control. For interpretative clarity, the direction of the odds ratio was defined a priori; however, this coding differs from some conventional meta-analytic presentations and should therefore be interpreted with caution throughout the Results and Discussion. For ACTION and TREASURE, log-ORs and their sampling variances were computed with the Mantel–Haenszel method. For ACTION II, whose raw cell counts were not available per arm owing to the three-arm pooling, the log-OR and variance were derived from the publication-reported OR and 95% CI as described above. Individual study estimates were back-transformed to the OR scale for presentation in forest plots; all modeling was conducted on the log-OR scale. The significance level was set at α = 0.05 (two-tailed) for all inferential tests unless otherwise stated.
sections.1.3.2. meta-analytic model specification: A random-effects model was selected a priori as the primary analytic framework, on the grounds that the included trials differed in their biological class of intervention (monoclonal antibody vs. multipotent adult progenitor cells), composite endpoint definitions, therapeutic windows, and patient populations—factors that make the assumption of a single common true effect unlikely to be biologically or methodologically plausible [ 40 ]. Between-study variance ( τ 2 ) was estimated using the DerSimonian and Laird (DL) method [ 41 ], the most widely adopted moment-based estimator in the meta-analytic literature and the default in RevMan 5.4 [ 42 ]. Because the number of included studies was small ( k = 3), the Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) adjustment was applied to the confidence interval of the pooled estimate [ 43 – 45 ]. The HKSJ correction replaces the standard normal z -based inference with a t -distribution on k − 1 degrees of freedom and incorporates a quadratic adjustment factor, thereby producing wider and more conservative confidence intervals that are better calibrated at small k [ 46 ]. The pooled OR with its 95% HKSJ-corrected CI was used as the principal summary measure for exploratory comparative interpretation.
sections.1.3.3. assessment of heterogeneity: Statistical heterogeneity among the included trials was quantified using three complementary metrics. First, Cochran’s Q statistic was computed as the weighted sum of squared deviations of individual study estimates from the pooled estimate, evaluated against a χ 2 distribution with k − 1 degrees of freedom at a significance threshold of α = 0.10, following the recommendation of Cochrane Handbook §10.10.2 [ 29 ] that a liberal threshold is warranted because the Q test has low statistical power when k is small. Second, the I 2 statistic [ 47 ] was reported to express the proportion of total variability attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than sampling error, interpreted according to the conventional benchmarks: < 25% (low), 25–75% (moderate), and > 75% (high). Third, the between-study variance τ 2 and its square root τ (the standard deviation of the true effect distribution) were reported to characterize the absolute magnitude of heterogeneity on the log-OR scale. Confidence intervals for τ 2 and I 2 were obtained using the Q -profile method [ 48 ].
sections.1.3.4. subgroup and moderator analysis: Given the biologically grounded heterogeneity between the two intervention classes represented in the analysis—monoclonal antibody-mediated immunotherapy (natalizumab, targeting α4-integrin/VLA-4 to block leukocyte transmigration across the blood–brain barrier) and allogeneic cell therapy (HLCM051/MultiStem, a multipotent adult progenitor cell product with paracrine immunomodulatory properties)—a prespecified subgroup analysis stratified by biological class was conducted. Subgroup-specific random-effects estimates were computed, and the test for subgroup differences was performed using a mixed-effects model with biological class as a categorical moderator variable. It is noted that the cell therapy subgroup contained a single trial (TREASURE; k = 1), for which no pooled subgroup estimate was generated; instead, the individual point estimate with its 95% CI was reported without a summary diamond.
sections.1.3.5. sensitivity analyses: Three preplanned sensitivity analyses were performed to evaluate the robustness of the pooled estimate. First, a leave-one-out (LOO) analysis was conducted by sequentially removing each study from the meta-analysis and recomputing the pooled OR, thereby assessing whether any single trial exerted a disproportionate influence on the summary effect [ 49 ]. Given that k = 3, each LOO iteration reduced the analysis to k = 2, and the resulting estimates were interpreted as exploratory. Second, a fixed-effects (common-effect) model was fitted as a comparator to the primary random-effects model, providing an assessment of the sensitivity of results to the choice of meta-analytic framework. Third, the influence of the heterogeneous composite endpoint definition was evaluated by comparing the overall estimate inclusive of TREASURE (whose composite additionally requires NIHSS ≤ 1) against the mAb-only subgroup in which composite definitions were more closely aligned.
sections.1.3.6. risk of bias assessment: Methodological quality of the included randomized controlled trials was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool [ 30 ], which evaluates five domains: (D1) bias arising from the randomization process, (D2) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (D3) bias due to missing outcome data, (D4) bias in measurement of the outcome, and (D5) bias in selection of the reported result. An overall risk-of-bias judgment was derived for each study. Assessments were performed independently by two reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. RoB 2 results are presented as a traffic-light matrix integrated into the primary forest plot (Fig. 2 ), with green (low risk), yellow (some concerns), and red (high risk) indicators for each domain per study, in accordance with the visualization conventions endorsed by Cochrane [ 50 ]. Fig. 2 Forest plot depicting the exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of excellent functional outcome (composite endpoint) at day 90 across three randomized controlled trials. Effect sizes are expressed as odds ratios (OR) on a logarithmic scale. Square size is proportional to inverse-variance weight; the diamond represents the pooled OR with its 95% Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ)-corrected confidence interval. The traffic-light matrix on the right displays Risk-of-Bias 2 (RoB 2) domain-level assessments
sections.1.3.7. assessment of publication bias: Assessment of publication bias was planned a priori and included visual inspection of a funnel plot [ 51 ] depicting individual study effect estimates against their standard errors, supplemented by Egger’s regression test for funnel plot asymmetry [ 52 ]. However, both the funnel plot and the Egger test are acknowledged to possess insufficient statistical power when the number of studies falls below 10 [ 29 , 53 ] (§13.3.5). Accordingly, the funnel plot and Egger test are presented for methodological transparency only and should not be interpreted as reliable evidence regarding the presence or absence of publication bias. This limitation is disclosed in accordance with GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) guidance on rating down for publication bias [ 54 ].
sections.1.3.8. supplementary pre\u2013post analy: For the SB623 trial [ 37 , 38 ], which lacked a control group, a within-subject pre–post effect size was computed as Hedges’ g (the bias-corrected standardized mean difference) using the formula g = d × J , where d = Δ M /SD and the correction factor J = 1 − 3/[4( n − 1) − 1] adjusts for small-sample upward bias in Cohen’s d [ 55 ]. The variance of g was estimated as Var( g ) = (1/ n + g 2 /2 n ) × J 2 . The resulting effect size estimates are presented in a separate supplementary forest plot (FP-5) and were not pooled with the comparative RCT data, as the absence of a control arm precludes attribution of the observed change to the intervention.
sections.software and reproducibility: All statistical computations and forest plot generation were performed in R version 4.3.3 [ 56 ] using the metafor package version 4.6–0 [ 57 ] for effect size computation, random-effects modeling, heterogeneity estimation, leave-one-out analysis, funnel plot construction, and the meta package version 7.0–0 [ 58 ]. Risk-of-bias visualizations were implemented following the RevMan-style recipe documented by Viechtbauer (2024) [ 59 ].
sections.limitations: Methodological limitations included heterogeneity in study designs, intervention timing, dosing protocols, endpoint definitions, small sample sizes (particularly in early-phase trials), and language restrictions, all of which were explicitly considered in the interpretation of findings. Despite these limitations, PRISMA compliance, systematic screening, and validated quality assessment tools support the methodological transparency and overall internal consistency of the review process, although they do not eliminate the limitations inherent to the available evidence base. These constraints were particularly relevant to the exploratory quantitative synthesis, which was intentionally restricted to a very small number of completed randomized trials with extractable comparative outcome data. Consequently, the pooled estimates should be interpreted cautiously and viewed as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory evidence of clinical efficacy.
sections.results: The study selection process is summarized in Fig. 1 . In total, 913 records were identified through database searching. After removal of duplicates and ineligible publication types, 55 studies met all predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the formal qualitative synthesis. Of these 55 studies, 24 were classified as preclinical or translational, 16 as clinical trials, and 15 as observational or biomarker-oriented studies, reflecting the broad translational scope represented within the included evidence base, although the methodological and clinical heterogeneity across study categories should be taken into account when interpreting the overall findings. A subset of 16 clinical trials was subsequently evaluated using predefined eligibility criteria for quantitative synthesis, of which three randomized controlled trials fulfilled all criteria for inclusion in the comparative meta-analysis. In addition to the 55 studies formally included in the qualitative systematic synthesis, selected mechanistic, foundational, and conceptual references were incorporated narratively to support biological interpretation and translational framing. These contextual sources were not eligible for the formal systematic evidence synthesis, were not used for comparative efficacy interpretation, and were not counted among the included studies. The number of included studies increased progressively from 2020 to 2025, with a marked rise after 2022 and the highest concentration observed in 2023–2025, suggesting increasing publication activity in this area over the review period. The results are organized around three complementary tables that collectively illustrate the translational pathway from mechanistic insight to clinical application. Table 1 summarizes original interventional studies—including molecular, cellular, and biological immunotherapeutic strategies—evaluating efficacy, functional outcomes, and safety in preclinical and clinical settings. Table 2 presents selected contextual mechanistic and foundational studies used to support the biological plausibility and translational interpretation of immunomodulatory strategies in ischemic stroke; these studies were not part of the formal systematic evidence synthesis and were not used for comparative efficacy appraisal. Table 3 consolidates clinical studies of direct immunotherapy and regenerative cell-based therapies with immunomodulatory relevance in adults with ischemic stroke. Together, these tables provide an integrated overview of the formal interventional evidence base and its broader mechanistic context.
