sections.methodological quality and risk of bias: Formal methodological quality and risk-of-bias assessment was conducted for all studies included in the formal systematic synthesis using design-specific validated tools. Randomized clinical trials were evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, observational studies using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS), and preclinical animal studies using SYRCLE’s Risk of Bias tool. Overall, the methodological quality of the included evidence was variable and reflected the developmental stage of the field. Randomized clinical trials were predominantly judged as having low risk-of-bias or some concerns, with the main limitations related to selective reporting, endpoint structure, or incomplete reporting of allocation procedures. Observational studies generally showed moderate methodological quality, although limitations related to sample size, confounding, and comparability of cohorts were common. Preclinical studies frequently demonstrated incomplete reporting of randomization methods, allocation concealment, and blinding, which reduced confidence in internal validity despite often strong mechanistic relevance. Importantly, these methodological assessments informed the interpretation of study findings, the appraisal of translational relevance, and the cautious interpretation of the exploratory quantitative synthesis; however, residual methodological uncertainty remained across several study domains. Studies are grouped by immunotherapeutic class (molecular, cellular, biological) and ordered chronologically within each category. Study quality was assessed using design-specific validated tools: RoB 2 for randomized clinical trials, NOS for observational studies, and the SYRCLE Risk-of-bias tool for preclinical studies. These assessments informed the interpretation of evidentiary strength and translational relevance across studies. Table 1 presents representative interventional studies selected to illustrate the major mechanistic classes identified in the review; the full study-level dataset is provided in Supplementary Table S1 .
sections.molecular immunotherapy: Molecular immunotherapy studies primarily targeted intracellular inflammatory and immunometabolic signaling pathways implicated in post-stroke neuroinflammation. Among the included preclinical studies, PKM2 inhibition represented one of the more extensively investigated mechanistically targeted strategies within the currently available preclinical literature and was associated with reduced infarct volume, attenuated thromboinflammatory responses, decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, and improved neurological outcomes in experimental models. Additional mechanistic work suggests that PKM2 may function upstream of NF-κB– and inflammasome-related inflammatory signaling, supporting its potential relevance as a molecular therapeutic target [ 3 ].
sections.cell-based regenerative therapy with imm: Studies involving mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs), progenitor cell products, and related cell-based interventions generally suggested multimodal regenerative, paracrine, neurotrophic, and immunomodulatory effects across both preclinical and early-phase clinical settings. Importantly, these approaches are more appropriately interpreted as regenerative cell-based therapies with immunomodulatory properties rather than as classical immunotherapies sensu stricto. Reported findings included modulation of inflammatory signaling, promotion of reparative and inflammation-resolving immune states, enhancement of neurovascular repair, and signals toward improved motor or functional recovery. However, clinical efficacy remained inconsistent and was limited by small sample sizes, variable study designs, and heterogeneity in treatment timing, cell source, and delivery route [ 61 , 62 ].
sections.biological immunotherapy: Biological immunotherapy studies were predominantly represented by monoclonal antibody–based approaches aimed at limiting leukocyte trafficking or immune cell infiltration into the ischemic brain. Natalizumab was the most extensively studied agent in this category and demonstrated a generally acceptable short-term safety profile within the available randomized clinical trials, although consistent functional benefit was not demonstrated. Other biologically targeted approaches remained largely preclinical or insufficiently developed for efficacy assessment within the review period [ 35 , 36 ].
sections.mechanistic and foundational studies (ta: Studies are organized by conceptual relevance (foundational/contextual, innate immune–microglial–immunometabolic mechanisms, and adaptive immune mechanisms) and ordered chronologically within thematic groupings where applicable. These studies were used narratively to contextualize the biological plausibility and translational rationale of immunotherapeutic strategies rather than to contribute comparative efficacy data. While Table 1 focuses on interventional studies evaluating immunotherapy in clinical and preclinical models, Table 2 presents mechanistic and foundational research supporting the biological plausibility of these therapeutic approaches and was included to aid biological and translational interpretation rather than comparative efficacy assessment. The included contextual studies highlight key components of the post-stroke immune response, including microglial heterogeneity, T-cell subset dynamics, innate lymphocyte activity, and inflammatory cytokine signaling, thereby identifying potential targets for immunomodulation. Collectively, these findings support the view that post-stroke immunomodulation likely involves coordinated interactions between innate and adaptive immune compartments, rather than by a single dominant cellular population.
sections.clinical studies on direct immunotherapy: Table 3 provides a structured overview of 16 clinical studies included in the formal systematic synthesis evaluating direct immunotherapeutic interventions, alongside regenerative cell-based therapies with immunomodulatory relevance, in adults with ischemic stroke. These studies cover various clinical phases (Phase I–III) and employ diverse interventions, including monoclonal antibodies (e.g., natalizumab), mesenchymal stem cells derived from bone marrow or umbilical cord, and other progenitor cells such as JTR-161 (dental pulp stem cells). Among these 16 clinical studies, only a minority provided completed, extractable comparative efficacy data suitable for quantitative synthesis. The limited number of studies eligible for quantitative synthesis primarily reflects the absence of published efficacy data in otherwise methodologically relevant trials, rather than overly restrictive eligibility criteria. Most ongoing, early-phase, or single-arm studies were retained for qualitative appraisal only because efficacy outcomes had not yet been published, comparator arms were absent, or endpoint definitions were not sufficiently harmonized for pooled analysis. The clinical study populations predominantly comprised adults in the acute phase of ischemic stroke, with eligibility criteria commonly based on neurological impairment (NIHSS) and pre-stroke functional status (mRS). Primary study objectives focus on improvement of neurological function, patient independence, and reduction of infarct volume, while cellular therapy studies additionally examine changes in imaging parameters and inflammatory markers. From a safety perspective, the included trials monitored adverse events related to the administration of cells or drugs, including infusion reactions, neurological deterioration, laboratory abnormalities, and serious adverse events. Across reported studies, these interventions were generally reported as well tolerated within the limitations of the available studies, with serious adverse events occurring infrequently. Studies are grouped by intervention type and translational maturity (biological immunotherapy; cellular immunotherapy with available efficacy data; and ongoing/early-phase or registered trials) and ordered within groups accordingly. The first column provides study identifiers in the format “Author et al. (Year)” for published trials, or study name/NCT identifier with “(results pending)” for ongoing or unpublished studies, ensuring consistency with Tables 1 and 2 .
sections.pooled effect estimate across all eligib: The exploratory random-effects model yielded a pooled odds ratio of 0.87 (95% CI, 0.27–2.77; t =  − 0.52, p = 0.66), indicating no statistically significant difference between immunotherapeutic or cell-based interventions and placebo with respect to the proportion of patients achieving excellent functional outcome at day 90. No statistically significant evidence suggestive of consistent clinical efficacy was identified within the constraints of the currently available and methodologically heterogeneous evidence base. The point estimate fell below unity and, under the coding applied in this analysis, nominally reflected lower odds of achieving an excellent functional outcome in the intervention group than in the control group. However, the confidence interval was wide and encompassed effect estimates compatible with both potential benefit and potential harm, reflecting the substantial imprecision inherent to an analysis of k = 3 trials with heterogeneous interventions. Individual study estimates ranged from OR = 0.60 (ACTION II; 95% CI, 0.39–0.93) to OR = 1.24 (ACTION; 95% CI, 0.58–2.64), with ACTION II being the only trial whose confidence interval excluded the null (see Fig. 2 ).
sections.between-study heterogeneity: Moderate statistical heterogeneity was observed across the three included trials. Cochran's Q statistic was 3.73 (df = 2, p = 0.16), which did not attain conventional significance at the recommended α = 0.10 threshold but should be interpreted cautiously given the low power of the Q test at small k . The I 2 statistic was 46.3%, falling within the moderate range (25–75%) per the Higgins and Thompson (2002) benchmarks, and indicating that approximately half of the observed variance in effect estimates was attributable to genuine between-study differences rather than sampling error. The estimated between-study variance was τ 2 = 0.1029 ( τ = 0.321 on the log-OR scale). These heterogeneity parameters may reflect substantial biological and methodological diversity among the included trials: ACTION and ACTION II evaluated natalizumab (a monoclonal antibody targeting α4-integrin) within a ≤ 24-h therapeutic window, whereas TREASURE assessed an entirely different therapeutic modality—intravenously administered allogeneic multipotent adult progenitor cells (MAPC)—with a broader 18–36-h treatment window and a more restrictive composite endpoint definition.
sections.subgroup analysis by biological class of: Prespecified subgroup analysis stratified by biological class revealed divergent point estimates between the two intervention categories, although neither attained statistical significance (see Fig. 3 ). Within the monoclonal antibody (anti-α4 integrin) subgroup, comprising ACTION and ACTION II (combined n = 426), the pooled OR was 0.80 (95% CI, 0.01–73.33), reflecting extreme imprecision driven by the conflicting direction of the two constituent estimates (ACTION: OR = 1.24; ACTION II: OR = 0.60) and the attendant high residual heterogeneity ( I 2 = 62%). The cell therapy subgroup contained a single trial (TREASURE; OR = 1.20; 95% CI, 0.49–2.92), for which no pooled subgroup estimate was computed. The formal test for subgroup differences did not demonstrate a statistically significant interaction between biological class and treatment effect ( χ 2 = 0.48, df = 1, p = 0.49), though this test was underpowered at k = 3. These subgroup findings should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating only. Fig. 3 Forest plot stratified by biological class of intervention. Blue squares denote the monoclonal antibody subgroup (natalizumab; ACTION, ACTION II); the red square denotes the cell therapy subgroup (HLCM051/MultiStem; TREASURE). Subgroup-level and overall pooled estimates are shown as diamonds. Heterogeneity statistics are reported for the overall model
sections.sensitivity analyses: leave-one-out and: The leave-one-out analysis revealed that the pooled estimate was sensitive to the exclusion of individual trials, a finding expected at k = 3, where each study commands substantial leverage (see Figure FP-4 in Supplementary materials). Excluding ACTION II—the largest trial and the sole study with a confidence interval excluding the null—shifted the pooled OR to 1.22 (95% CI, 0.69–2.17), changing the direction of the pooled point estimate across the null value. Residual heterogeneity dropped to I 2 = 0.0% upon removal of ACTION II, suggesting that the directional inconsistency between ACTION II (OR = 0.60) and the other two trials was the principal source of the observed between-study variance. Conversely, excluding either ACTION (pooled OR = 0.76; 95% CI, 0.40–1.44) or TREASURE (pooled OR = 0.80; 95% CI, 0.40–1.61) preserved the sub-unity direction of the overall estimate, though neither exclusion yielded a statistically significant result. The fixed-effects sensitivity model produced a pooled OR of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.55–1.10; p = 0.16), directionally concordant with the random-effects estimate but with a narrower confidence interval, as expected when the between-study variance component is not modeled. This instability of the pooled estimate further highlights the limited robustness and exploratory nature of the current evidence base and reinforces the exploratory nature of the meta-analysis.
sections.risk of bias in the included trials: Domain-level RoB 2 assessments are displayed within the traffic-light matrix in Fig. 2 . All three trials employed double-blind, placebo-controlled designs with adequate randomization procedures (D1: low-risk for ACTION II and TREASURE; some concerns for ACTION owing to limited reporting of allocation concealment details). Performance bias was assessed as low-risk or some concerns across trials, with no evidence of unblinding. Missing outcome data (D3) posed minimal concern, as all three trials reported modified intention-to-treat analyses with low attrition rates. Outcome measurement (D4) was adjudicated as low-risk in all trials, given the use of validated, assessor-blinded neurological scales (mRS, NIHSS, BI). The most notable domain-level concern pertained to the selection of the reported result (D5): ACTION received a high-risk rating because the mRS ≤ 1 outcome at day 90 was a secondary endpoint and was originally reported with a 90% rather than 95% confidence interval, necessitating post-hoc recalculation; ACTION II received some concerns because of the post-hoc three-arm pooling required for meta-analytic compatibility. TREASURE was rated low-risk across all five domains. Overall risk-of-bias judgments were “some concerns” for ACTION and ACTION II and “low risk” for TREASURE. Given the very small number of eligible comparative trials ( k = 3), no formal quantitative analysis examining the association between risk-of-bias profile and effect size was performed. Instead, the potential influence of study quality on effect estimates was explicitly incorporated qualitatively into the interpretation of pooled and individual study effects.
sections.assessment of publication bias: Visual inspection of the funnel plot (see FP-4a in Supplementary materials) revealed an asymmetric distribution of the three study estimates, with ACTION II (the largest trial) positioned to the left of the pooled estimate and the two smaller trials to the right. However, with only k = 3 studies, no reliable inference regarding publication bias can be drawn from the funnel plot, as its interpretive validity requires a minimum of approximately 10 studies [ 53 ]. Egger’s regression test for funnel plot asymmetry yielded t = 4.19 (df = 1, p = 0.15), with a limit estimate of b =  − 1.28 (95% CI, − 4.53 to 1.98). Although the t -statistic was numerically large, the test did not attain significance, and at k = 3, the Egger test possesses negligible statistical power. Accordingly, the present analysis does not provide a reliable basis for confirming or excluding the presence of publication bias because of the very limited number of eligible studies, and this limitation was taken into account in the overall interpretation of certainty and evidentiary strength [ 53 ]. Accordingly, no conclusions regarding the presence or absence of publication bias can be drawn from this analysis.
sections.summary and conclusions of the quantitat: The present exploratory meta-analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant pooled effect or consistent evidence suggestive of clinical benefit for immunotherapeutic or cell-based interventions with respect to excellent functional outcome at day 90 in adults with acute ischemic stroke (OR = 0.87; 95% CI, 0.27–2.77; p = 0.66). The wide confidence interval, spanning effect estimates compatible with both potentially meaningful benefit and potential harm, likely reflects three major methodological constraints: a small number of eligible trials ( k = 3), moderate between-study heterogeneity ( I 2 = 46%), and the application of the HKSJ correction, which, while methodologically appropriate, further widens the interval at small k . Several findings of the quantitative synthesis merit emphasis. First, ACTION II was the only trial whose confidence interval excluded the null (OR = 0.60; 95% CI, 0.39–0.93), yet under the coding applied in this analysis, an OR below unity corresponded to a lower probability of achieving the composite excellent-outcome endpoint in the natalizumab group relative to placebo. This finding should be interpreted cautiously in the clinical context and aligns with the original trial’s conclusion that natalizumab did not confer functional benefit in acute ischemic stroke [ 36 ]. Second, the leave-one-out analysis confirmed that ACTION II exerted the greatest leverage on the pooled estimate, such that its exclusion reversed the direction of the point estimate (OR from 0.87 to 1.22), underscoring the fragility of the overall synthesis. Third, TREASURE, the sole cell therapy trial, demonstrated no treatment effect at day 90 (OR = 1.20; 95% CI, 0.49–2.92; risk difference = 0.5%), although exploratory post hoc analyses at 365 days reported by Houkin et al. identified a trend favoring HLCM051 on selected long-term functional endpoints [ 25 ]. The supplementary SB623 analysis yielded a large pre–post effect size (Hedges’ g =  − 0.96) in a chronic stroke population, suggesting a potential association that modified mesenchymal stem cell implantation may be associated with neurological improvement; however, the absence of a control arm renders this finding hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The assessment of publication bias was constrained by the small number of studies. Egger’s regression test did not reach significance ( t = 4.19, p = 0.15), but this result carries no inferential weight at k = 3. The risk-of-bias evaluation identified “some concerns” in two of the three trials, primarily in the domain of selective outcome reporting; only TREASURE received an overall “low risk” judgement across all RoB 2 domains. In aggregate, the currently available quantitative evidence remains insufficient to support firm conclusions regarding treatment efficacy for either monoclonal antibody-mediated immunotherapy or intravenous cell therapy in acute ischemic stroke. This overall null finding should be interpreted in light of the exploratory nature of the analysis, the limited and heterogeneous trial base, and the conservative statistical framework applied. The field would benefit from the publication of pending trial results—most notably MASTERS-2 ( NCT03545607 ) and J-REPAIR ( NCT04608838 ), both of which employ endpoint definitions compatible with the present synthesis—and from the conduct of adequately powered, harmonized multicenter trials designed to resolve the clinical equipoise identified by this meta-analysis. Until such data become available, the current evidence base is more appropriately interpreted as being of low to very low certainty, principally because of serious imprecision and indirectness arising from heterogeneous composite endpoint definitions across trials.
sections.synthesis: Taken together, the evidence summarized across Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 and the exploratory quantitative synthesis suggest potential translational relevance of these approaches while also underscoring the substantial methodological and clinical limitations of the currently available evidence base of mechanistically distinct strategies, including direct immunotherapeutic approaches and regenerative cell-based therapies with immunomodulatory relevance in adult ischemic stroke. Substantial variability in study design, intervention timing, dosing, delivery route, and endpoint definitions contributes to heterogeneous findings and limits robust inference regarding clinical efficacy. Accordingly, further well-designed, adequately powered, and methodologically harmonized trials are required to better define the therapeutic potential and optimal positioning of these strategies within the evolving neurovascular treatment framework. To integrate these findings into a biologically coherent translational framework, Fig. 4 summarizes the stage-dependent neuroimmune landscape of ischemic stroke, highlighting the dynamic interplay between tissue-damaging and repair-associated inflammatory processes across the evolving phases of injury and recovery. This framework reflects the current understanding that post-stroke neuroinflammation involves temporally dynamic and biologically heterogeneous processes. Fig. 4 Stage-dependent neuroinflammation and immunometabolic regulation in adult ischemic stroke This schematic illustrates the dynamic balance between detrimental and reparative neuroimmune responses across the temporal phases of ischemic stroke, spanning the hyperacute, acute/peri-reperfusion, subacute/post-reperfusion, and chronic recovery stages. The left side represents the pro-inflammatory axis associated with acute tissue injury, including neutrophil infiltration, Th1-associated immune responses, IFN-γ signaling, cytokine amplification, blood–brain barrier disruption, oxidative stress, and maladaptive microglial activation. The right side depicts the anti-inflammatory and repair-associated axis, characterized by regulatory immune populations (including Treg, Th2, and Breg cells), inflammation resolution, remyelination, angiogenesis, neuroimmune repair signaling, and functional recovery. At the center, the “immunometabolic hub” highlights convergent intracellular pathways of translational relevance—PKM2, NF-κB, STAT3, and NLRP3—which may integrate metabolic stress with inflammatory amplification and immune-cell state transitions after ischemic injury. The figure provides a conceptual overview of the temporally evolving neuroimmune landscape of ischemic stroke [ 16 – 18 , 83 ]. This conceptual framework illustrates the current understanding that post-stroke neuroinflammation may represent a temporally shifting immunobiological continuum rather than a strictly unidirectional pathological process.
sections.interpretation of findings: This systematic review is broadly consistent with the current understanding that neuroinflammatory responses represent an important and sustained component of ischemic stroke pathophysiology, but that these responses unfold within a broader neurovascular context involving endothelial dysfunction, blood–brain barrier disruption, thromboinflammatory signaling, and multicellular injury–repair interactions across the neurovascular unit [ 83 , 84 ]. In the context of contemporary stroke care, the translational relevance of neuroinflammation is particularly evident in relation to reperfusion-based treatment. Although recanalization remains the cornerstone of acute ischemic stroke management, successful vessel reopening does not fully prevent secondary tissue injury. Reperfusion itself may amplify inflammatory cascades involving oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, blood–brain barrier disruption, and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Unlike ultra-early neuroprotective strategies, immunomodulatory interventions may remain biologically relevant during peri- and post-reperfusion phases, supporting their investigation as adjunctive rather than competing therapeutic approaches [ 17 , 18 ]. This translational framing is further supported by growing recognition that reperfusion-associated injury is shaped not only by parenchymal inflammation, but also by thromboinflammatory mechanisms involving endothelial activation, neutrophil extracellular traps, complement-related innate immune signaling, and peripheral immune–vascular crosstalk. This is particularly relevant because neutrophil extracellular traps and related thromboinflammatory mechanisms may contribute not only to blood–brain barrier injury and microvascular dysfunction, but also to incomplete reperfusion and persistent tissue vulnerability despite successful recanalization. As summarized in Fig. 5 , the therapeutic strategies identified in this review can be conceptualized as acting at three distinct but complementary levels: intracellular inflammatory signaling, intercellular immunoregulatory and reparative networks, and systemic immune trafficking. This distinction may provide a useful conceptual framework within the present review and supports the interpretation that direct immunotherapy and regenerative cell-based therapy should not be treated as interchangeable intervention classes, even when both influence post-stroke neuroinflammation. Fig. 5 Translational architecture of neuroinflammation-targeted interventions in adult ischemic stroke This perspective is strongly supported by recent STAIR XIII consensus statements, which highlight that therapeutic efficacy in ischemic stroke is highly dependent on matching intervention strategies to specific temporal phases of injury. In particular, therapies targeting early ischemic cascades must be administered within a narrow hyperacute window, whereas interventions modulating inflammatory responses may retain efficacy in later stages, including during and after reperfusion. This distinction may carry translational implications, as it suggests that immunotherapy may help address one of the major limitations of traditional neuroprotective approaches—namely, the restricted therapeutic time window. Accordingly, immunotherapy is best conceptualized as a temporally adaptive adjunct to reperfusion-based care rather than as a static standalone intervention [ 16 ]. The evidence summarized across Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 suggests that molecular, biological, and cell-based strategies with immunomodulatory relevance appear biologically plausible and have demonstrated generally acceptable safety profiles within the currently available studies in early clinical translation, although the available evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. However, consistent and clinically meaningful efficacy signals have not yet been demonstrated, particularly when these interventions are evaluated as standalone rather than adjunctive therapies. This interpretation is supported by the exploratory pooled analysis, which yielded a null overall estimate with moderate heterogeneity and substantial imprecision [ 25 , 36 , 60 , 85 – 88 ]. Notably, the pooled estimate must also be interpreted in light of the methodological profile of the included trials, as even modest differences in selective reporting, endpoint definition, or analytical structure may disproportionately influence effect size estimates in such a small evidence base. These conclusions must also be interpreted in light of the methodological profile of the included evidence, as internal validity limitations were more frequent among preclinical and early-phase translational studies than among completed randomized clinical trials. A further important limitation of the quantitative synthesis is the heterogeneity in composite endpoint definitions across trials, which may have influenced both the direction and magnitude of estimated treatment effects. An important methodological limitation concerns the statistical power of the available clinical evidence [#18]. Among the 16 trials cataloged in Table 3 , none was a completed confirmatory Phase III efficacy trial designed and powered to detect a clinically meaningful treatment effect on functional outcome endpoints. The three largest completed trials—ACTION ( n = 161), ACTION II ( n = 265), and TREASURE ( n = 206)—were Phase II or Phase II/III studies powered primarily for safety, dose-finding, or proof-of-concept objectives. Post hoc power considerations suggest that these sample sizes would provide only limited power to detect moderate treatment effects. Accordingly, the absence of statistically significant efficacy signals should not be interpreted as evidence of therapeutic futility, but rather as a limitation of underpowered early-phase designs. The field may therefore still be considered to remain in a state of unresolved clinical equipoise and requires adequately powered, preregistered Phase III trials with harmonized endpoints [ 89 – 91 ]. An additional translational consideration is that post-stroke neuroinflammation is strongly modified by the host’s pre-existing vascular and immune status [ 6 , 13 , 14 ]. Experimental evidence from hypertensive stroke models suggests that arterial hypertension may amplify post-ischemic innate immune activation through increased chemokine expression, enhanced myeloid cell recruitment, and greater infiltration of monocytes, macrophages, and granulocytes into the ischemic brain [ 14 , 92 ]. Notably, these inflammatory changes have been associated with larger infarct volumes despite comparable early lesion size, supporting the concept that comorbidity-driven immune priming may aggravate secondary injury after stroke [ 14 ]. This reinforces the view that immunotherapeutic strategies should be interpreted and designed within the broader context of patient-specific inflammatory heterogeneity rather than assuming a uniform post-stroke immune response [ 6 , 13 ]. Among molecular strategies, targeting immunometabolic regulators such as PKM2 has been identified as a potentially relevant translational target within preclinical and early translational research within preclinical and early translational research. Dhanesha et al. identified PKM2 in neutrophils as a key mediator of post-stroke thromboinflammatory responses. Both genetic deletion of PKM2 in myeloid cells and pharmacological inhibition with ML265 reduced infarct volume, attenuated proinflammatory cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and limited neutrophil extracellular trap formation, leading to improved cerebral perfusion and motor recovery [ 85 , 93 , 94 ]. Complementary studies further suggest that PKM2-driven signaling via STAT3 and focal adhesion kinase promotes angiogenesis and neurogenesis, supporting the potential therapeutic relevance of immunometabolic modulation in ischemic stroke [ 95 ]. Emerging evidence further supports PKM2 as a convergent immunometabolic regulator linking inflammatory amplification with innate immune activation in ischemic stroke [ 96 ]. In parallel, inhibition of the JAK2/STAT3 axis has been shown to suppress cGAS-mediated neuronal senescence and neuroinflammation, further reinforcing STAT3-related signaling as a plausible upstream target within post-ischemic inflammatory cascades [ 97 , 98 ]. Regenerative cell-based therapy, particularly mesenchymal stromal/stem cell (MSC)-based approaches, may hold translational potential owing to its pleiotropic paracrine, neurorestorative, and immunomodulatory properties. Preclinical and translational evidence suggests that MSCs exert therapeutic effects primarily through paracrine and regenerative mechanisms, including secretion of trophic factors, cytokines, extracellular vesicles, and other bioactive mediators, while also contributing to secondary immunomodulatory rebalancing, including paracrine signaling, modulation of microglial and lymphocyte phenotypes, and direct mitochondrial transfer to T lymphocytes. This mitochondrial transfer has been reported to influence the Th17/Treg axis, reduce oxidative stress, restore mitochondrial membrane potential, and partially reverse pathological shifts in T-cell differentiation and exhaustion states. Importantly, disruption of mitochondrial function within MSCs abolishes these immunomodulatory and neuroprotective effects, highlighting mitochondrial transfer as one potentially important mechanism contributing to the observed therapeutic effects of regenerative cell-based therapy in ischemic stroke models [ 25 , 60 , 86 , 88 , 94 , 99 ]. Early-phase clinical trials, including those evaluating allogeneic products such as MultiStem, have generally demonstrated favorable safety profiles with signals toward functional improvement, although statistical significance has been limited by cohort size, variable endpoints, and heterogeneous treatment timing [ 87 ]. Notably, the SB623 study, although not eligible for comparative meta-analysis, demonstrated a large within-subject effect size in a chronic stroke population, suggesting that regenerative cell-based strategies may warrant further investigation in later neurorestorative phases in later, neurorestorative phases rather than in the acute setting targeted by most randomized trials. These findings suggest that MSC-based therapies may require optimized dosing, standardized delivery routes, and combination with reperfusion strategies to achieve robust clinical benefit [ 25 , 60 , 99 ]. Accordingly, MSC-based interventions in ischemic stroke are more appropriately framed as regenerative cell therapy with immunomodulatory properties rather than as a subtype of immunotherapy in a strict mechanistic sense [ 61 , 62 , 86 ]. In contrast, biological immunotherapies targeting leukocyte trafficking, exemplified by monoclonal antibodies such as natalizumab, have thus far yielded neutral efficacy results despite acceptable safety profiles. In the ACTION II trial, natalizumab administered within 24 h of stroke onset did not significantly improve functional outcomes at 90 days [ 36 , 100 ]. Earlier experiences with nonselective immune blockade, including enlimomab, further highlight the potential risks of broadly suppressing immune responses in the acute phase of stroke [ 100 ]. Collectively, these findings may indicate that biological agents targeting single immune pathways could have limited efficacy when used as monotherapy within the currently available clinical framework and may be better positioned as components of multimodal treatment strategies. This interpretation is also consistent with the broader view that post-stroke inflammation is distributed across multiple temporally dynamic immune pathways, thereby limiting the likelihood that single-target blockade alone will yield reproducible clinical benefit. In this context, targeting upstream regulators such as PKM2 may represent a potentially broader mechanistic strategy, as it simultaneously influences multiple downstream inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, rather than selectively inhibiting a single cytokine or receptor [ 96 ]. Taken together, the available evidence suggests a translational continuum in which molecular immunomodulatory strategies currently provide comparatively strong mechanistic rationale within the currently available preclinical literature, regenerative cell-based approaches have shown preliminary signals suggestive of possible functional benefit in selected early-phase studies, and biological therapies have thus far contributed more to safety characterization than to reproducible efficacy demonstration. Within this framework, interventions targeting immunometabolic regulators, microglial signaling pathways, or selective adaptive immune rebalancing appear to warrant further investigation in future translational studies, although these directions remain to be validated in adequately powered and biologically stratified clinical trials [ 25 , 83 , 84 , 96 , 97 ]. This schematic summarizes the principal levels of therapeutic intervention identified in the present review and compares their mechanistic depth, translational maturity, therapeutic window, and clinical positioning. Three complementary but mechanistically distinct intervention domains are shown: (1) molecular strategies targeting intracellular inflammatory and immunometabolic signaling pathways (e.g., PKM2, NF-κB, NLRP3), (2) cellular regenerative strategies with immunomodulatory properties (e.g., mesenchymal stromal/stem cells, engineered regulatory immune-cell approaches), and (3) biological immunotherapies targeting systemic immune-cell trafficking and leukocyte–endothelial interactions (e.g., natalizumab, cytokine-directed blockade). The lower panel provides a comparative translational summary, emphasizing that these approaches differ substantially in biological scope, clinical maturity, therapeutic timing, and translational rationale. Collectively, the figure supports a stage-specific and integrated treatment framework in which molecular precision, cellular repair, and systemic immune modulation are viewed as complementary rather than interchangeable strategies. This distinction is particularly important when interpreting cell-based therapies, which often combine immunomodulatory, neurotrophic, and reparative effects within a broader regenerative framework. More broadly, MSC-based approaches should not be interpreted in isolation or conceptualized as classical immunotherapy in the strict mechanistic sense. Rather, they appear to represent one component of a broader post-stroke immunoregulatory and reparative network involving coordinated interactions between innate and adaptive immune populations [ 13 , 61 , 62 , 84 , 101 ]. In this framework, repair-associated macrophages may contribute to phagocytosis, remyelination, angiogenesis, and tissue remodeling, whereas adaptive immune subsets—including Th1, Th17, and Treg populations—help shape whether the inflammatory milieu remains tissue-destructive or transitions toward resolution and repair [ 70 , 102 , 103 ]. An additional emerging dimension of stroke immunology involves immune checkpoint signaling, including PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4, and Tim-3 pathways, which may function as context-dependent regulators of post-stroke immune activation and immune exhaustion. Although these pathways remain only preliminarily explored in intervention-oriented stroke studies, they may represent areas for future investigation as potential future targets for selective immunoregulatory strategies aimed at limiting maladaptive inflammation while preserving reparative immune function. Importantly, contemporary evidence increasingly supports a move away from binary polarization models and nonspecific immunosuppression toward selective, stage-specific immune rebalancing informed by cellular heterogeneity, functional state, and immunometabolic context. Accordingly, therapeutic interpretation should increasingly rely on functionally defined and transcriptomically informed immune states rather than on simplified M1/M2 categorizations [ 7 , 101 – 103 ].
sections.comparison with other studies: The findings of this review are consistent with recent syntheses indicating that most immunomodulatory interventions for ischemic stroke remain at an early translational stage, with relatively few strategies supported by robust clinical efficacy data [ 16 – 18 , 28 ]. In particular, molecular approaches targeting PKM2-, STAT3-, and related RNA-regulated inflammatory pathways have shown anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective effects across multiple preclinical studies in preclinical models, although their relevance to human stroke pathobiology remains to be established [ 24 , 85 , 95 – 98 ]. Likewise, recent syntheses of MSC-based therapies support favorable safety profiles and suggest that their therapeutic activity is driven predominantly by paracrine, neuroregenerative, and neurovascular repair mechanisms, with immunomodulation representing an important but non-exclusive component of their biological action. Functional outcomes, however, remain variable and are influenced by substantial heterogeneity in cell source, dose, timing, and delivery route [ 27 , 86 ]. The lack of functional benefit observed with natalizumab parallels earlier studies targeting leukocyte adhesion, reinforcing the notion that ischemic stroke involves highly dynamic and multifactorial immune responses that may not be adequately addressed by single-target interventions [ 36 ]. Emerging approaches aimed at enhancing regulatory T-cell function or selectively modulating pathogenic immune subsets may offer opportunities for more personalized immunotherapy and could synergize with molecular or cellular strategies [ 84 , 88 , 104 ]. Notably, recent studies published in 2025 further support a shift toward more refined immunomodulatory strategies, emphasizing immune cell heterogeneity, immunometabolic regulation, and adaptive immune responses. At the same time, the broader stroke immunology literature increasingly points to additional underexplored therapeutic dimensions—including stroke-induced systemic immunosuppression, peripheral immune organ responses, complement-related innate cascades, and immune checkpoint signaling—which remain only partially represented in the current intervention-focused evidence base. Greater integration of these pathways may be particularly important for understanding why apparently promising anti-inflammatory strategies fail to translate uniformly across biologically heterogeneous patient populations [ 8 ]. From a therapeutic standpoint, these observations support a shift toward integrated treatment paradigms combining recanalization with targeted immunomodulation. Rather than viewing reperfusion and immunotherapy as separate strategies, emerging evidence suggests that their combination may provide complementary therapeutic effects by simultaneously restoring blood flow and mitigating inflammation-driven secondary injury [ 16 – 18 ]. Crucially, the success of such combined strategies will likely depend not only on target selection but also on precise temporal alignment with evolving ischemic, reperfusion-associated, and reparative phases of injury. Such approaches may include inhibition of key inflammatory mediators (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), modulation of inflammasome activation (e.g., NLRP3), regulation of microglial activation states and neuroimmune signaling, and targeting of immune cell trafficking or immunometabolic pathways [ 84 , 97 , 98 ]. Notably, these strategies align with recent expert recommendations advocating for multi-target and stage-specific therapeutic approaches that address the dynamic and multifactorial nature of post-stroke inflammation [ 16 – 18 , 83 ]. Taken together, the present findings suggest that the limited clinical efficacy observed to date should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence against the broader therapeutic concept of immunomodulation in ischemic stroke, but may instead reflect a mismatch between biological complexity and current trial design frameworks. Future progress will depend on aligning immunomodulatory strategies with the temporal, cellular, and metabolic heterogeneity of post-stroke neuroinflammation, rather than applying uniform interventions across biologically distinct patient populations.
sections.limitations_1: Several limitations of the current evidence base should be acknowledged. First, substantial heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, intervention classes, dosing regimens, endpoint definitions, and treatment timing limits comparability and constrains quantitative synthesis [ 17 – 19 , 49 , 51 , 57 ]. Although an exploratory meta-analysis was technically feasible, and the interpretability and generalizability of the pooled estimates were substantially constrained, its interpretability was limited by the very small number of eligible randomized trials, moderate between-study heterogeneity, and differences in endpoint definition and analytical structure across studies. These limitations were compounded by endpoint harmonization challenges and the fragility of pooled estimates in sensitivity analyses [ 17 – 19 , 49 , 51 , 57 ]. These concerns are reinforced by the variable methodological quality and risk-of-bias profile across the included evidence base, particularly among preclinical and early-phase translational studies, where incomplete reporting of randomization, blinding, and allocation procedures remains common [ 25 , 36 , 60 , 86 , 88 , 99 ]. In addition, although mechanistic and foundational studies were incorporated to support biological interpretation and translational framing, these sources were not used to infer comparative therapeutic efficacy and should be interpreted as contextual rather than confirmatory evidence. Second, translational gaps persist between preclinical and clinical research, as animal models incompletely recapitulate the biological and clinical complexity of human ischemic stroke, comorbidities, or immune aging, contributing to frequent failures in clinical translation [ 85 , 93 , 96 ]. Third, the optimal therapeutic window for immunomodulation remains insufficiently defined and is likely to differ across mechanistically distinct intervention classes. As emphasized in recent STAIR XIII recommendations, therapeutic efficacy is highly dependent on the temporal alignment between intervention and the evolving pathophysiological processes of ischemic stroke. Early interventions may interfere with endogenous repair mechanisms, whereas delayed treatment may fail to adequately suppress established inflammatory cascades. The lack of standardized, phase-specific treatment frameworks across studies represents a major barrier to translation and highlights the need for future trials explicitly incorporating time-stratified therapeutic approaches [ 36 , 83 , 84 ]. Additional limitations include the lack of validated human biomarkers for patient stratification, such as circulating PKM2, STAT3 activation, or neutrophil extracellular trap markers, as well as relatively short follow-up durations in most clinical trials [ 85 , 95 – 97 ]. Finally, restriction to English-language publications published between January 2020 and December 2025 may have introduced language-related selection bias and reduced historical breadth; however, this decision was made a priori to prioritize contemporary, methodologically comparable, and clinically relevant evidence reflecting the current phase of development in stroke immunotherapy [ 86 ]. Another important limitation of the current translational evidence base is the insufficient incorporation of comorbidity-associated immune heterogeneity. Common stroke comorbidities, particularly arterial hypertension, may alter baseline immune activation and thereby influence both the magnitude of post-stroke neuroinflammation and the responsiveness to immunomodulatory treatment. This issue remains underrepresented in both preclinical modeling and clinical trial design [ 14 ]. Accordingly, studies with favorable biological or clinical signals but important methodological constraints were interpreted cautiously and considered hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
sections.future directions: Recent comprehensive reviews of inflammatory biomarkers in ischemic stroke further support a paradigm shift toward biomarker-driven and precision immunotherapy approaches. Over the past decade, increasing emphasis has been placed on cytokine profiling, composite inflammatory indices, and their integration into prognostic and translational models. In particular, markers such as IL-6, CRP, and NLR have consistently emerged as correlates of stroke severity, functional outcome, and post-stroke complications. Importantly, these biomarkers may also serve as actionable tools for patient stratification in immunotherapy trials, helping identify individuals most likely to benefit from targeted interventions such as cytokine blockade, inflammasome inhibition, or cell-based immunomodulation [ 83 ]. Accordingly, future immunotherapy trials should move beyond descriptive biomarker reporting toward prospectively integrated immune profiling for patient selection, treatment timing, and mechanistic response assessment. Such designs may be particularly valuable for distinguishing patients with predominantly thromboinflammatory, innate immune–dominant, or maladaptive adaptive immune signatures, thereby improving biological matching between intervention and disease state. Furthermore, recent data emphasize the importance of temporal and phase-specific interpretation of biomarkers, as the same mediators may exert divergent effects depending on the stage of stroke. This dynamic perspective is particularly relevant for designing immunomodulatory strategies that require precise timing to balance neuroprotection and immune-mediated repair. Future research should prioritize large, multicenter phase III trials with rigorous methodology, standardized protocols, and stratification based on stroke severity, comorbidities, and time from symptom onset [ 25 , 83 , 84 ]. Specifically, forthcoming trials should be powered to detect effect sizes in the range of OR = 1.3–1.5 for composite functional endpoints (e.g., mRS ≤ 1 combined with BI ≥ 95 at day 90), which would likely require enrolment of approximately 500–800 participants per arm under conventional statistical assumptions depending on control-arm event rates and allocation ratio [ 105 ]. Adaptive platform trial designs incorporating interim analyses, dose optimization, and biomarker-driven enrichment strategies may provide a pragmatic approach to achieving adequate statistical power while preserving efficiency and ethical flexibility [ 106 ]. The MASTERS-2 trial ( NCT03545607 ) [ 72 ], if completed and fully reported, may represent the first major Phase III dataset in this field and may provide important additional evidence within this evolving field. Integration of immunotherapy with reperfusion strategies may mitigate reperfusion-associated neuroinflammatory injury, while multimodal approaches combining molecular, cellular, and biological interventions may yield synergistic effects when applied within optimized therapeutic windows [ 25 , 60 , 70 , 85 , 104 ]. Finally, long-term follow-up and mechanistic validation in human studies are essential to establish durable efficacy, assess late adverse effects, and define the true risk–benefit profile of immunotherapeutic strategies in ischemic stroke [ 25 , 36 , 60 , 87 , 88 ]. In particular, future strategies should incorporate selective targeting of adaptive immune components, including CD4⁺ T-cell subsets, to achieve precise modulation of neuroinflammatory responses across different stages of stroke. Such approaches may support the future development of more biologically stratified immunotherapeutic approaches tailored to the temporal and biological heterogeneity of ischemic stroke [ 8 ]. Future therapeutic strategies should prioritize immunometabolic modulation, biomarker-guided patient stratification, and cell-type-specific immune targeting as central components of stroke immunotherapy. Additional priority areas include thromboinflammatory pathways, complement-related innate signaling, systemic immune dysregulation after stroke, and peripheral immune organ responses—particularly splenic and lymphoid compartment remodeling—which may offer clinically relevant but currently underdeveloped therapeutic entry points. In particular, the PKM2–NF-κB–NLRP3 axis and coordinated regulation of reparative versus pathogenic immune populations may provide a potentially more integrative biological framework for future investigation than broadly nonspecific single-target immunosuppression approaches. Future trials should therefore align treatment timing, immune profiling, and combination with reperfusion therapies to better reflect the evolving neuroimmune phases of ischemic stroke, consistent with recent STAIR XIII recommendations [ 16 , 83 , 88 , 96 , 102 , 103 ].
