sections.impacts of pandemic response on pharmacy: Participants in this study described many ways the pandemic changed pharmacy practice, including changes in access to other healthcare services, lab services, and specialists; changes to drug supply; changes in demand for pharmacy services; and greater scope and greater acceptance of community pharmacists by the public.
sections.increased demand of pharmacist services: During the pandemic, access to primary care and acute care services (e.g., physician and nurse practitioner run clinics and emergency rooms) was limited to curb the spread of COVID-19. Participants felt that community pharmacists were more accessible for patients than other primary care providers during the pandemic: ‘Not to criticize physicians… they were taking safety precautions the same as everybody else. But it’s just kind of like everyone went off the grid…. But the pharmacy’s open 9:00[AM] to 9:00[PM]. So that’s where the people would come. ’ (NS8, woman, consultant, rural, 11–15 years in practice) As a result of limited access to primary care due to the pandemic, pharmacists described difficulty reaching other primary care providers: ‘During COVID, because of the rules that came out and the risks that were there, a lot of primary care practitioners, such as physicians, dentists… weren’t working in their usual offices or usual setting, it was a lot tougher to reach them… So, the communication between other health care professionals definitely took a hit during… the initial first wave of COVID’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice) Participants felt they were more accessible than other providers, resulting in increased pressure and responsibility: ‘There’s actually a whole lot of bitterness right now between pharmacy and docs (doctors) because through March and April and May [2020], pharmacists …worked like crazy… that level of responsibility is like no one else took on… Everyone else went into hiding, and then we came out of hiding. Like we were full tilt. … there were times at work when I’m sure my staff went home and thought what in the name of God are we doing this for when nobody else is doing it, really? But for anybody just to be able to walk in the door at any given time, sick or not sick, really…’ (NS1, woman, staff, rural, 16+ years in practice) Although there were challenges in accessing other primary care providers, there were some positive aspects for participants such as increased rapport with patients: ‘Doing the extra services and renewals for these patients who couldn’t get a hold of their physicians helped us really get to know them a bit better because we’d have… lengthier conversations… I really feel like the care the patients are getting is better.’ (NS2, woman, manager, rural, 11–15 years in practice) Participants shared that lab services were less available during the pandemic for non-COVID-19 testing. Participants would typically review lab results before refilling prescriptions but were unable to during the pandemic due to lab restrictions.: ‘We’ve seen… our hypothyroid patients wondering why they can’t just get a refill on their [thyroid medication] that they’re going to need forever… you don’t have a recent lab work, we can only go so far.’ (NS6, man, owner, rural, 16+ years in practice) Patients received less routine monitoring from specialists, who were limiting the patients they saw due to the pandemic. This left some patients seeking reassurance and information from pharmacists.: ‘Our diabetics that are no longer being monitored by the diabetic educator… they’re approaching us. And unfortunately, other than the… self-monitoring glucose values that they’re bringing in, we’re kind of limited in what we can do.’ (NS6, man, owner, rural, 16+ years in practice)
sections.changes to drug supply: Participants described increased workload due to patient fears about drug shortages: ‘ in and amongst all that COVID was the rush of filling double, triple prescriptions because people were panicking ’(NS1, woman, staff, rural, 16+ years in practice). The government of Nova Scotia put a restriction of 30 days on all prescription refills early in the COVID-19 lockdown to protect drug supply during shortages: ‘During the first wave of COVID, we saw a reduction in the supply of medication from our wholesalers… Our college… the Nova Scotia College of Pharmacists, had put a restriction on the supply of medication to 30 days at a time unless it was in our professional judgment that a patient should receive more.’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice) Although some participants were ‘supportive ’ of the 30-day limit (NS11, man, manager, rural, 16+ years in practice), others shared challenges associated with the policy. Participants described being ‘burned out ’ as ‘the workload tripled ’ (NS7, woman, owner, rural, 6–10 years in practice) due to more frequent dispensations. The work to find alternatives to medications was also not remunerated: ‘And it’s really, really, really a lot of work… right now we’re dealing with [thyroid medication] which is like a medication that like everybody’s on, and a bunch of doses are short. And the time it takes to pretty much fix it is just so much. And… We don’t get reimbursed for that’ (NS4, woman, relief, both urban and rural, 0–5 years in practice) A participant also described how drug shortages and policies to protect supply ‘fractured’ their relationship with patients: ‘I think the intention was… to try and protect the drug supply. But what it did was kind of fracture some of our relationships with our patients because they’re based on trust… it was eroding that really important relationship. And the government… they put this in place but then didn’t defend us because it was their decision. Didn’t allow us the autonomy… in making decisions for what was in the best interests of our patients… those who can’t afford to bill [pay the dispensing fee] every month, or those who can’t come in every month. It felt like we were just kind of, ‘Here, you’re going to do 30 days at a time,’ and then ‘Sayonara,’ once the chips all fell.’ (NS7, woman, owner, rural, 6–10 years in practice)
sections.changes in scope and acceptance of commu: During the pandemic, pharmacists were able to renew prescriptions for a longer time (expanding from 180 days limit up to a year): ‘So our prescription renewal service… we could do up to six months for regular maintenance medications… And then suddenly, no, there’s not really a hard stop on that. As long as it’s in the best interest of the patient, just keep going.’ (NS11, man, manager, rural, 16+ years in practice). Participants found that requests for prescribing increased, saying ‘It’s probably triple, quadruple [what] it was… before COVID’ (NS1, woman, staff, rural, 16+ years in practice). This increase in prescribing was sometimes due to patients transferring their prescriptions from pharmacies near their workplace to pharmacies near their home: ‘During the first wave, we had a big influx of transfers from [large chain pharmacies] and whatnot in the city because people who were working in the city… would get their prescriptions there when they were in the city. But now they weren’t.’ (NS9, woman, staff, rural, 6–10 years in practice). Other times, this was due to patients not seeing their primary care provider: ‘we definitely did… a lot more prescribing services during COVID for patients with doctors… That was the main increase or change that I saw.’ (NS9, woman, staff, rural, 6–10 years in practice). During the pandemic, some pharmacists found they were doing fewer injections, particularly travel-related immunizations: ‘We used to do other travel-related immunizations, but that has certainly not been as prominent since COVID.’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice). Other pharmacists found there was increased demand for injections, particularly contraceptive injections and immunizations. Patients wished to update other vaccinations before the COVID-19 vaccine became available: ‘We’ve seen requests for more injections… People are looking to get the full slate of immunizations, knowing that they want to get it done before a COVID immunization is available. (NS6, man, owner, rural, 16+ years in practice). A participant shared that patients who were previously hesitant to get the influenza vaccine were motivated to get it early in the pandemic: it was the beginning of COVID. So, all these people who are really hesitant to get a flu shot were now like, Okay, I should probably get the flu shot. So, we did so many vaccines at that point.’ (NS4, woman, relief, urban and rural, 0–5 years in practice). Participants spoke positively about expansions on the injections they could administer: ‘We’ve kind of almost got a set list of what we’re able to inject and what we’re not able to inject. And then around April or May, [Nova Scotia College of Pharmacists, the pharmacy regulator in the province] just said, no, pretty much if it’s intramuscular, you can inject it…If it fits in the best interest of the patient, go for it.’ (NS11, man, manager, rural, 16+ years in practice) However, a participant shared that some changes were not well-supported by additional training: ‘ pharmacists could always inject people aged five and older. But during COVID they lowered the age to two… I think it was a COVID-related change. Which we got no extra training on.’ (NS9, woman, staff, rural, 6–10 years in practice) Despite challenges during the pandemic, several participants found that a ‘silver lining’ was that the pandemic ‘gave us that extra push’ (NS2, woman, manager, rural, 11–15 years in practice) in terms of role expansion and acceptance that was ‘ way overdue’ (NS8, woman, consultant, rural, 11–15 years in practice): ‘Since the pandemic, I felt much more useful in my role. I feel like I play a pivotal role in primary care now. And I did before, but COVID I think really pushed it ahead for a lot of people in terms of who they were going to turn to for advice or for care or for follow-up.’ (NS8, woman, consultant, rural, 11–15 years in practice) Some of the outcomes of expanded roles also meant community pharmacists were happier about the work they were doing. ‘you get a bit more job satisfaction out of it. Because you’ve got patients you can help where you couldn’t help them before.’ (NS11, man, manager, rural, 16+ years in practice)
sections.impact of pandemic response on patient h: Participants described concerns about changes in their patients’ health: ‘you talk to people and they’re different than before. They’re distant. They’re alone. They’re fighting with their spouses…. And they’re not being healthy. They’re not exercising. They’re not going to the gym. They’re not doing all those things. They’re not playing hockey or whatever it was in the summertime that the majority would normally do.’ (NS1, woman, staff, rural, 16+ years in practice) Participants especially noted impacts on mental health and increased prescribing for antidepressants: ‘ [Class of antidepressant medication] prescriptions have increased. And… dose increases. And it’s not necessarily in just the young population that people always assume. I think it’s everybody.’ (NS4, woman, relief, both urban and rural, 0–5 years in practice) Patients also struggled to pay for their medications due to job loss: ‘We definitely have more patients [at pharmacy that requires social worker referral] because of people who have lost their jobs and stuff like that. So, we’re getting more referrals, for sure. So more maybe low to middle income patients that didn’t have trouble paying for their medications before, but now do.’ (NS2, woman, manager, rural, 11–15 years in practice)
sections.impact of pandemic response on community: Participants described increased burnout during the pandemic, and fear of COVID-19 infection.
sections.burnout: Participants described increased workload and burnout during the pandemic: ‘It was hard on mental health, for sure. Sometimes you would feel so overworked and under-staffed. Just the day-to-day activities really got to you. You’d get home and you’d just be worn out, completely exhausted. And after doing that for several months in a row, that takes a toll on your mental health.’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice)
sections.fear of covid-19 infection: Participants felt at risk of contracting COVID-19 and did not feel well protected despite staying open during the initial stages of the pandemic. This was exacerbated by people who were sick going to pharmacies as patients and community pharmacists did not have access to personal protective equipment (PPE) during the initial stages of the pandemic. Participants shared that they were in a unique situation compared to other primary care providers because they were expected to remain available for in-person care, whereas many other primary care providers switched to virtual care: ‘More sick people every day walk into a pharmacy than any doctor’s office… So, it is a place that needs to be protected. If you’re going to have community spread somewhere like a grocery store, you could just as easily have it in a pharmacy. So, our staff need to be protected. We were being asked to do triple the work… be there to fix all these situations in health care while everyone else is being told to stay at home and being praised.’ (NS7, woman, owner, rural, 6–10 years in practice) Participants conveyed COVID-19 infection concerns. The initial stages of the pandemic were especially problematic for participants as not much was known about COVID-19, how the disease was transmitted, and what portion of the population was more at risk of complications. Furthermore, there was a lack of access to PPE and patients were going into the pharmacy to seek medication and PPE. ‘We couldn’t get masks, We couldn’t get hand sanitizer. You’re just worried about your own safety. And I have a young family. So, I was worried about that – coming home and spreading whatever to them… it’s basically impossible to socially distance in the pharmacy from your co-workers… you’re doing everything you can in your power to keep yourself safe. But someone else that you’re working beside may not be. So that was stressful as well.’ (NS9, woman, staff, rural, 6–10 years in practice)
sections.infection prevention and control: Participants recommended that some aspects of the infection prevention and control guidelines remain post-pandemic, as patients visiting pharmacies for treatment are more likely to be ill, and having PPE and proper sanitation measures in pharmacies could reduce exposure and spread of communicable diseases to pharmacists and other patients. ‘I kind of hope we are more conscientious in terms of illness, and people maybe choose to wear a mask when they’re not feeling well.’ (NS2, woman, manager, rural, 11–15 years in practice).
sections.virtual care: Several participants wished to retain virtual care modalities post-pandemic. The ease of communication with patients and convenience of synchronous virtual care options appealed to community pharmacists: ‘I will do a UTI (assessment to prescribe with or without resulting in a prescription) over the phone. And I would love to continue to do that. Renewals over the phone.’ (NS1, woman, staff, rural, 16+ years in practice)
sections.retaining pandemic scope of practice: Participants described the value in maintaining roles that were expanded during the pandemic, particularly around prescription renewals and renewing or prescribing controlled substances: ‘I do like the fact that physicians and nurse practitioners can phone in prescriptions for narcotics and controlled substances now. I think they would probably tell you they find it easier… I do believe other provinces don’t require duplicate or triplicate prescriptions for narcotics, and it’s worked out fine for them.’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice)
sections.expanding community pharmacist roles and: Policy shifts occurred during the pandemic that allowed community pharmacists to provide more care within their scope of practice. Participants recommended expanding the role of pharmacists in the recovery stage and beyond. As one participant explained, ‘I can contribute so much more but you have to untie my hands’ (NS8, woman, consultant, rural, 11–15 years in practice). Several participants wished to expand their roles further by getting involved in ‘the Bloom program’ [a community pharmacy initiative geared towards increasing and improving mental health and addictions care] (NS2, woman, manager, rural, 11–15 years in practice patients). A participant also recommended the ability for pharmacists to refer patients to specialists: ‘Somebody didn’t have a family doctor, and they have diabetes and kidney disease and heart disease. Well, sure, I can maybe request blood work, but in reality maybe they should be seen by an endocrinologist or a heart specialist. So, the ability to make those kind of referrals would be nice.’ (NS5, man, manager, rural, 6–10 years in practice) Participants also demonstrated a need for funding mechanisms to support the work they do helping patients navigate the health system: ‘Trying to help people navigate… the silos that health care functions in, there’s a lot of time spent on that. There isn’t a monetary value there. I think it’s valuable service to the patients… I think that we should be able to bill MSI (Medical Service Insurance, Nova Scotia’s publicly funded health insurance plan) for every phone call that triages a patient in or out of the emergency room.’ (NS3, woman, staff, urban, 6–10 years in practice) Others echoed this sentiment, and felt that their work should be further supported through remuneration by the government: ‘You have disease states that are well within the means of pharmacists maintaining and supervising. You have a push for collaborative health. Well, you’re leaving one aspect of it kind of in the shadows. And you have, you know, processes that they could do to save the system money. Yes, there will be a financial contribution that will have to be made and will have to be reimbursed for some of these services. But overall, you’re going to have a better outcome at a cheaper price.’ (NS6, man, owner, rural, 16+ years in practice) To support these roles, a participant also recommended greater communication between providers through a communication portal such as One Patient, One Record (a patient record which is accessible to health practitioners that will make it easier and more efficient for healthcare practitioners to deal with patients issues that has been discussed, but not yet implemented in Nova Scotia): ‘It would just all make sense if we were all on…like the whole One Patient, One Record, and everybody had access. So, if you’re a health care provider and you’re within the circle of care, there are some basic things that you should be able to access.’ (NS8, woman, consultant, rural, 11–15 years in practice)
sections.discussion: Participants shared numerous ways the COVID-19 pandemic response impacted routine pharmacy practice, including reduced access to other primary care providers, reduced access to laboratory services, drug shortages, increased demand for certain services, and expansion and acceptance of the scope of practice of pharmacists in community pharmacies. Participants detailed impacts on patient health and wellbeing, reporting an increase in physical and mental health concerns during this time. Participants also described increased burnout and stress among community pharmacists. Looking to the pandemic recovery period, participants recommended retaining some of the changes implemented during the pandemic and expanding their primary care roles post-pandemic to further support patients. Community pharmacists reported a perceived reduction of access to other primary care providers (e.g., family physicians and laboratory services) during the pandemic. Similar findings were reported by Gleeson et al . ( 2022 ), where due to pandemic restrictions, family physicians could only carry out telephone consultations (Gleeson et al ., 2022 ). As pharmacies stayed open for in-person visits and medication pick-ups, pharmacists may have felt that they were more physically accessible. The availability of medications during the pandemic, especially in the initial phases, decreased and this may have been attributed to increased demand of certain medications (e.g., analgesics and vitamin C) (Romano et al ., 2021 ). Community pharmacists often had to ration medication supply to be able to cope with the demands of their patients who may have felt they needed to hoard medication (Lee et al ., 2021 ) due to the uncertainty surrounding the pandemic and its duration. Community pharmacists experienced an expansion of their roles during the pandemic (Lee et al ., 2021 ), and had to adopt additional responsibilities (e.g., education about the prevention of COVID-19) to fulfill the needs of their patients. Funding support for some assessment and prescribing (e.g., renewals) was also made available to assist in role expansion. This was especially important as community pharmacists were frontline primary care providers offering face-to-face services when other primary care providers were perceived to be unavailable (Gleeson et al ., 2022 ). While this may have been necessary to support patients and was perceived by community pharmacists as offering more autonomy in their work, questions remain on whether these responsibilities should be adopted under the normal purview of community pharmacists post-pandemic and how to adequately train and compensate community pharmacists. For example, although pharmacists in our study reported trying to alleviate anxiety concerns in patients with respect to the pandemic, all pharmacists may not have had enough training on providing additional supports for patients’ mental health. Despite this, a recent study conducted in Canada demonstrated that pharmacists were able to provide mental health supports such as medication management, non-pharmacologic approaches and supportive conversations, and identification of resources (e.g., referrals, wellness checks, consulting with physicians) (Ashcroft et al ., 2024 ). Additionally, although pharmacists in our study reported seeing increased prescribing of antidepressants to try and alleviate some of the mental health issues patients may have been facing, previous studies showed that dispensation rates of antidepressants reduced slightly in 2020 and returned to previous levels (Uthayakumar et al ., 2022 ). An expansion of roles and responsibilities of community pharmacists occurred during the pandemic. Understanding the impact the adoption of these additional responsibilities may have on other primary care providers (e.g., family physicians and nurse practitioners) under their normal scope of practice is important. Family physicians, nurse practitioners, and community pharmacists are all autonomous professions, and while they cannot dictate each other’s practices, integrating community pharmacists into primary care teams and having more collaborative frameworks to address patient needs could help address challenges in primary care (Jorgenson et al ., 2013 ; Khaira et al ., 2020 ). Knowing that community pharmacists could use their knowledge and skills during a public health emergency to meet the needs of patients highlights how valuable community pharmacists are to the delivery of primary care. Some community pharmacists in our study noted an increase in job satisfaction with the expansion of roles. This contrasted with the findings of a previous study where increased workloads, which could result from the expansion of scope, resulted in reduced job satisfaction and higher stress (Lea et al ., 2012 ) Approximately 80% and 51% of pharmacists surveyed reported having a history of burnout or secondary traumatic stress, respectively (Lea et al ., 2012 ). During the pandemic, stress and burnout may have increased due to anxiety caused by the uncertainty regarding COVID-19, pharmacists’ personal safety, the safety of patients visiting the pharmacies, and additional workload. Therefore, while pandemic recovery and future pandemic response policies and plans should cater to the expansion in roles of community pharmacists, measures must also be taken to ensure the wellbeing of community pharmacists (Elbeddini et al ., 2020 a, 2020 b) is maintained for them to effectively practice, serve the needs of their patients, and prevent community pharmacy attrition due to burnout (O’Donnell et al., 2024 ). Resources such as additional personnel, appropriate remuneration, appreciation, involvement in decision-making, and leadership training for skilled clinicians can help to address burnout as community pharmacists are taking on increased workload and complexity following the pandemic (Reed, 2023 ; Canadian Pharmacists Association, 2023 ). Moving to the recovery stage of the pandemic, health systems will need to address the backlog in patient care (Mathews et al ., 2023 b). Pharmacists have a key role to play in the pandemic recovery stage in continuing to provide important primary care services, as well as opportunities to expand services that might not have been accessed or available during the pandemic. The COVID-19 pandemic altered primary care, introducing innovations and expanding scope of practice (Hayden and Parkin, 2020 ). We also saw greater acceptance of pharmacists by patients (Canadian Pharmacists Association, 2023 ; Hoti et al., 2020 ). As health services resume normal provision of primary care, community pharmacists could play a larger role in supporting patients, including those who have no other primary care providers following them (Hayden and Parkin, 2020 ). Given community pharmacists are accessible (Tsuyuki et al ., 2018 ; Yang and Son, 2023 ), optimally utilizing community pharmacists’ expertise within primary care may help reduce pressures faced by other primary care providers, if they were able to offer a larger array of publicly funded services. At the time of writing, publicly funded and delivered services in Nova Scotia, such as community pharmacy primary care clinics (CPPCC), provide extended pharmacy primary care services at no charge (i.e. publicly funded) in Nova Scotia. These services include assessment and prescribing for common ailments, chronic disease management (diabetes, asthma, COPD), prescription adaptation and therapeutic substitution and provision of additional public health funded vaccines beyond COVID-19 and influenza vaccines (Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia, 2023). Many of these services, when provided outside of the CPPCC, still require additional fees for some or all patients including medication reviews; minor ailment assessment and prescribing; smoking cessation programs; and several vaccinations and injections such as human papilloma virus, hepatitis A and B, vitamin B12, and injectable hormonal contraception (Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia, 2023).
sections.limitations: For this study, we interviewed community pharmacists in one Canadian province during early waves of the COVID-19 pandemic. Community pharmacists in Nova Scotia have a broader scope of practice than many other provinces. Findings may not resonate with those in other jurisdictions and may not account for policy changes that emerged since the time of data collection. However, findings may still hold relevance in other jurisdictions where regular pharmacy practice was similarly impacted. The results may also be of benefit to jurisdictions considering the expansion of the role of pharmacists in primary care in providing support around the care that can be provided.
sections.conclusion: The COVID-19 pandemic response had a major impact on community pharmacy practice and community pharmacists. As health systems have moved to the pandemic recovery stage, there will be an increase in demand for health services that were delayed during the pandemic, and higher acuity of patient needs. Community pharmacists are vital to primary care provision and should be enabled to provide expanded care to support pandemic recovery efforts and beyond.

title: The State of the Art in Chronic Prurigo Nodularis
abstract: Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN) is a highly burdensome chronic inflammatory dermatosis characterized by intensely pruritic papulonodular lesions that may persist for years. Its pathophysiology reflects a neuro–immune–fibrotic axis in which type-2 cytokines (IL-4/IL-13/IL-31), neuropeptides, and profibrotic signaling interact to sustain the itch–scratch cycle and dermal fibrosis. CPN predominantly affects older adult women and is frequently associated with dermatologic, neuropsychiatric, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. Definition, nomenclature, and management remain areas of debate, with relevant differences between European and US consensus documents. The therapeutic landscape has expanded with dupilumab and nemolizumab, the only agents currently supported by phase III evidence, whereas JAK inhibitors remain promising but investigational options that require careful safety contextualization. This narrative review synthesizes current knowledge on CPN, from definition and epidemiology to etiopathogenesis and evolving therapy, while highlighting persistent unmet needs in diagnosis and management.

sections.key summary points: Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN) is a debilitating inflammatory skin disease defined by intense, chronic itch and nodular lesions that significantly impair a patient’s quality of life and psychological well-being. The disease is driven by a self-perpetuating “itch–scratch cycle” involving a complex neuro–immune–fibrotic axis where type-2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, and IL-31) and neuropeptides promote persistent inflammation and skin fibrosis. CPN is a highly heterogeneous condition frequently associated with a broad range of comorbidities, including atopic dermatitis, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and psychiatric disorders such as anxiety and depression. The therapeutic landscape is currently shifting from empirical, off-label treatments toward targeted biologics, with dupilumab and nemolizumab being the only agents currently supported by high-level phase III clinical evidence. There remains a critical need for standardized clinical guidelines and personalized “treat-to-target” strategies to address existing gaps in managing special populations and the neurogenic components of the disease.
sections.introduction: Chronic prurigo nodularis (CPN), referred to as prurigo nodularis (PN) in much of US literature, is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by intensely pruritic papulonodular lesions that may persist for years or even decades [ 1 – 9 ]. Patients experience not only intractable itch but also pain, stinging, burning, and tingling, which promotes repeated scratching, scarring, and a substantial disease burden. Moderate-to-severe disease can impair quality of life to a degree comparable with other chronic disorders such as hypertension or arthritis [ 10 ]. This burden is further amplified by frequent comorbidities, including atopic dermatitis, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and psychiatric disorders, which contribute to the marked heterogeneity of CPN [ 11 ]. Despite the diversity of associated conditions, all cases of CPN share a common pathophysiologic mechanism known as “the itch–scratch cycle”, in which uncontrollable itch leads to persistent scratching and the subsequent development of the nodular cutaneous lesions [ 12 , 13 ]. Recent molecular and histopathological studies highlight the role of a neuro–immune–fibrotic axis in which type-2 cytokines (IL-4/IL-13/IL-31), neuropeptides, and profibrotic pathways drive the itch–scratch cycle, epidermal acanthosis, and fibrosis [ 14 ]. Currently, there is no universally accepted definition of CPN and no standardized clinical guidelines for its management. Existing expert consensus documents propose largely empirical therapeutic strategies, with limited guidance on treatment sequencing, combinations, optimal duration, or management of special populations [ 1 , 15 ]. One of the major unmet needs in CPN care is the development of clear therapeutic algorithms. Recent advances, particularly the approval of dupilumab and nemolizumab [ 16 , 17 ], the only agents supported by phase III evidence, together with emerging JAK inhibitors, are reshaping the treatment landscape. This narrative review synthesizes current knowledge on CPN, including its definition, epidemiology, etiopathogenesis, and clinical impact. It also integrates evidence from clinical trials and real-world studies to support clinicians in the diagnosis, assessment, and management of this challenging condition.
sections.methods: We performed a targeted literature search in MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, and the Cochrane Library from January 2015 to September 2025. The strategy combined MeSH/Emtree terms and free-text keywords related to CPN/PN, epidemiology, pathophysiology (including IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, neuroimmune pathways, and fibrosis), diagnosis, patient-reported outcomes, and treatments (dupilumab, nemolizumab, JAK inhibitors). Search terms also covered emerging biologics and their targets (e.g., vixarelimab/OSMRβ, barzolvolimab/CDX-0159/KIT, rocatinlimab/OX40, stapokibart/CM310/IL-4Rα, SHR-1819/IL-4Rα), alongside class terms (e.g., oncostatin-M/OSM, IL-4 receptor, OX40 antagonists, KIT inhibitors). We included human studies in English or Spanish that addressed CPN definition or classification, epidemiology, comorbidities, pathophysiology, diagnosis, outcome measures, or treatment. We prioritized clinical practice guidelines, systematic reviews or meta-analyses, randomized and prospective interventional studies, large observational cohorts, and selected seminal mechanistic studies. We excluded reports centered on other chronic pruritic disorders without extractable CPN data, nonprimary literature not relevant to the objectives, and isolated case reports except when they illustrated an emerging therapy with no higher-level evidence. Reference lists of key reviews and guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional records. The final narrative synthesis included 127 references. Because this review was conceived as a narrative review rather than a systematic review, a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-style screening flow, formal risk-of-bias assessment, and a prospectively recorded record-level denominator for all screened citations were not available; this limitation is now stated explicitly to avoid overstating methodological rigor. However, we describe the search process to enhance transparency and adhere to the principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) [ 18 ].
sections.definition: Although dermatologists generally share a clear clinical understanding of what CPN is, its nomenclature has historically been a source of confusion. In the USA, the term prurigo nodularis (PN) is preferred and is used to encompass all chronic prurigo variants, as it is considered sufficiently descriptive (ICD-10: L28.1) [ 15 ]. In contrast, in Europe, chronic prurigo is employed as the umbrella term, with CPN designated as its nodular subtype [ 1 , 2 ]. Chronic prurigo is therefore used as a broad category that includes several clinical morphologies, such as papular, nodular, plaque, or umbilicated types of the same disease. The term chronic prurigo was used in literature prior to the establishment of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology Task Force in 2018 with the purpose of reaching expert consensus on the definition and classification of prurigo associated terms [ 1 ].
sections.epidemiology: Data on the incidence and prevalence of CPN remain scarce and heterogeneous, partly because the disease is underrecognized, and case ascertainment differs across datasets [ 19 ]. Reported prevalence ranges from 9 to 210 per 100,000 in Europe and the USA [ 8 ]. In large European and US cross-sectional studies, older adults predominate, with mean ages of 64 and 56 years, respectively, although cases also occur in other age groups, including children [ 10 , 20 – 22 ]. No consistent sex association has been demonstrated, with rates similar to the general population or only slightly higher in women in some cohorts [ 8 , 10 , 20 , 22 , 23 ]. In England, epidemiological data indicate an increase in CPN prevalence from 2.49 per 10,000 inhabitants in 2007 to 8.8 per 10,000 inhabitants in 2019 [ 24 ]. These findings differ from those of Morgan et al., who reported a prevalence of 3.27 per 10,000 inhabitants in 2018 and an incidence of 2.88 per 100,000 inhabitant-years between 2008 and 2018 [ 25 ]. However, these studies used markedly different methodologies [ 25 , 26 ].
sections.etiopathogenesis: The etiology of CPN remains unclear in most reports. The disease frequently occurs in association with dermatologic, systemic, neurologic, or psychiatric disorders, although it can also appear without an identifiable underlying condition [ 1 , 6 , 22 ]. Ortiz de Frutos et al. classified CPN according to etiological factors and comorbidities into four groups: (1) dermatological disease-related CPN, most commonly linked to atopic dermatitis and less often to psoriasis, lichen planus, or hypertrophic lupus; (2) systemic/metabolic disease-related CPN, including diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, hematologic and hepatobiliary disease, and drug-induced pruritus; (3) psychiatric disease-related CPN, associated with obsessive–compulsive, impulse control, or anxiety–depressive disorders; or (4) idiopathic CPN, defined as CPN without an associated disease, representing a very small proportion of cases [ 27 ]. These diverse comorbid profiles contribute to marked clinical heterogeneity. Etiology and comorbidities are often intertwined, and it is frequently unclear whether one condition precedes or results from the other or how CPN and comorbidities mutually influence each other [ 28 ]. Despite these differences, patients share a common pathophysiologic mechanism: the itch–scratch cycle, maintained by a complex interplay of immunologic, environmental, and disease-related factors (Fig. 1 ) [ 1 , 6 , 22 ]. Advances in molecular and histopathologic research have substantially improved our understanding of CPN, which is now considered a multifactorial disorder driven by immune dysregulation, neuronal sensitization, and—unlike most other chronic pruritic diseases—a prominent profibrotic response [ 14 ]. sections.immune dysregulation: Changes in the skin of patients with CPN perpetuate the itch–scratch cycle, causing chronic nonhistaminergic pruritus and persistent inflammation [ 12 , 29 – 31 ]. When the epithelium is damaged—by scratching or by proinflammatory cytokines and pruritogenic mediators—keratinocytes release itch-inducing mediators (thymic stromal lymphopoietin, IL-33, cathepsin S, kallikreins) that activate sensory neurons [ 12 , 29 ]. Additional pruritogenic and type-2 cytokines from eosinophils, basophils, type-2 innate lymphoid cells, Th2 lymphocytes, and mast cells (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, histamine, tryptase) further stimulate these neurons and contribute to producing itching (Fig. 1 ) [ 12 , 32 – 34 ]. Within this microenvironment, eosinophils and mast cells are particularly relevant. Eosinophils release neuropeptides, eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN), eosinophil protein X (EPX), and major basic protein; ECP and EDN, which are neurotoxic, are markedly elevated in CPN skin [ 35 ]. Mast cells are an important source of oncostatin M and show high IL-31RA expression in CPN, and mast cell–associated mediators and receptors (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, MRGPRX2, PAR2) also contribute to disease pathogenesis [ 36 ]. Type-2 inflammation is central in CPN. IL-4, IL-13, and IL-31 directly activate sensory neurons via their receptors (Fig. 1 ) [ 37 , 38 ]. IL-4 and IL-13 signaling through IL-4Rα sensitizes neurons to subthreshold levels of other pruritogens, including IL-31, a key pruritogen in CPN [ 12 , 38 – 42 ]. Moreover, type-2 cytokines participate in feedback loops, as IL-4 induces IL-31 expression and release by Th2 cells, further amplifying pruritus and inflammation [ 38 ].
sections.neural dysregulation: CPN is also characterized by structural and functional alterations of cutaneous nerves. In the epidermis, intraepidermal nerve fiber density is reduced but returns to normal after lesion resolution; nerve growth factor (NGF) receptor–immunoreactive fibers and protein gene product (PGP)-9.5+ fibers are likewise decreased [ 35 , 43 ]. In the dermis, however, neuronal hyperplasia is observed, with PGP-9.5 and NGF receptor staining showing significantly denser immunoreactive structures than in healthy controls [ 35 , 43 , 44 ]. Chronic activation of sensory neurons—by scratching or pruritogenic mediators—induces neurogenic inflammation and peripheral sensitization [ 29 , 30 ]. Activated neurons release neuropeptides (calcitonin gene-related peptide, substance P, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide) that stimulate immune cells to produce IL-4, IL-13, and other mediators, which in turn further activate neurons, creating a self-reinforcing loop. These signals are transmitted to the central nervous system, eliciting itch and perpetuating the itch–scratch cycle (Fig. 1 ) [ 45 ].
sections.fibrotic response: Cutaneous fibrosis is a defining histopathological feature of CPN [ 9 , 46 ]. It arises from repeated tissue injury and represents a reparative response to stimuli such as scratching [ 47 ]. Pruritus-related mediators, including neuropeptides and histamine, also promote dermal inflammation and fibrosis (Fig. 1 ) [ 46 ]. However, type-2 cytokines are the main fibrotic drivers: IL-4 and IL-13, essential for normal wound healing, become pathogenic when dysregulated, activating profibrotic pathways that induce excessive fibroblast proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition [ 47 , 48 ]. Fibroblasts in CPN display a WNT5A+ phenotype, are apoptosis-resistant, and enhance dermal fibrosis and type-2 inflammation via periostin release [ 49 , 50 ]. IL-31 further activates IL-31RA on fibroblasts, altering genes involved in proliferation and collagen synthesis, thereby contributing to fibrosis [ 51 ]. CPN is also characterized by a hyperkeratotic epidermis with irregular epidermal hyperplasia, focal parakeratosis, papillary dermal fibrosis, and inflammatory infiltration [ 52 ]. IL-22, produced in type-3 (Th17/Th22) responses, is a key proinflammatory cytokine driving these epidermal changes. It promotes keratinocyte proliferation, fuels skin inflammation, and modulates wound healing and epidermal differentiation, with elevated levels detected in both skin and serum of patients with CPN [ 52 , 53 ].
sections.comorbidities: A systematic review identified diseases related to CPN and grouped them into: (1) pruritic diseases that may lead to or coexist with CPN, (2) inflammatory diseases, and (3) age-related diseases, more frequent in older adults, in whom CPN is also more common [ 11 ]. Studies from several countries similarly show that many conditions are more prevalent in CPN, notably, atopic dermatitis, asthma, diabetes, hyperlipoproteinemia, heart failure, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic kidney disease [ 11 , 27 , 28 , 54 – 56 ]. Up to 50% of patients with CPN have a history of atopy, and the term “atopic dermatitis with a prurigo phenotype” is often used, although the temporal relationship between dermatitis and prurigo is unclear [ 11 ]. Single-cell RNA sequencing has shown molecular differences: oligoclonal cytotoxic T cells are present in atopic dermatitis but not in CPN, and type 2 myeloid responses are stronger in atopic dermatitis, whereas CPN is dominated by a stromal response (fibrosis, angiogenesis, collagen remodeling, neurogenesis) [ 57 ]. Among systemic comorbidities, chronic kidney disease is particularly relevant. Although many patients with chronic kidney disease and pruritus do not develop prurigo, chronic kidney disease–associated pruritus and CPN share dermatologic, neuropathic, and immune dysregulation features [ 58 ]. Renin–angiotensin system dysregulation may also contribute to both CPN lesions and kidney disease [ 59 , 60 ]. Other systemic associations include infectious, endocrinologic, cardiovascular, and neoplastic diseases such as lymphoma, likely linked to inflammatory imbalance, neural dysregulation, or a profibrotic tendency. In hepatic disease, Marani et al. found that patients with CPN (versus atopic dermatitis) showed gene signatures associated with liver disease, liver fibrosis, and chronic hepatitis [ 61 ]. The most prevalent metabolic comorbidities are type 2 diabetes (≈ 35%) and chronic liver disease (≈ 16%), both capable of causing peripheral neuropathy and supporting a role for neural dysregulation in CPN pathogenesis [ 20 , 62 ]. Psychiatric comorbidities, especially anxiety (45.6%) and depression (16.4%), are also common [ 7 , 63 ]. Sleep disturbance is frequent and associated with elevated C-reactive protein levels, which in turn increase cardiovascular risk [ 64 ]. In one analysis, patients with CPN were clustered into: class 1, atopy (high atopic burden, no psychiatric or cardiovascular disease, lower mean age 38.7 years); class 2, neuropsychiatric (high neuropsychiatric burden, 68.9% women); class 3, high comorbidity burden (multiple chronic pruritic, neuropsychiatric, cardiopulmonary, and atopic diseases); and class 4, chronic and cardiopulmonary diseases [ 65 ]. This stratification may aid clinical and therapeutic decision-making. In a multicenter study of 513 patients with CPN with various comorbidities, itch intensity (worst itch intensity in the previous 24 h, worst itch numeric rating scale [WI-NRS]) was significantly associated only with hypertension—hypertensive patients reported more intense pruritus—whereas quality of life (Five-Item Life Quality Questionnaire, 5-PLQ) was significantly worse in those with concomitant depression [ 66 ].
sections.impact on patients: Patients with CPN experience a multidimensional burden, affecting both physical and psychological health [ 10 ]. Beyond intense itch and papulonodular lesions with excoriations and scarring [ 1 , 10 , 13 , 22 ], they frequently report pain and somatosensory symptoms such as stinging, burning, tingling, and heat/cold dysesthesia [ 13 , 22 ]. Compared with other chronic conditions with pruritus, the itching experienced by patients with CPN is among the most severe, with an intensity of 7 out of 10 [ 7 , 10 , 22 ]. More than 53% report skin pain (skin pain-numeric rating scale (NRS) ≥ 3), and more than 54% report burning, stinging, or tingling (burning/stinging/tingling-NRS ≥ 3) [ 7 ]. Although nodules may gradually resolve, they often leave scarring and hyper- or depigmentation, especially if undertreated, adding considerable psychoaffective distress [ 67 , 68 ]. This burden leads to marked impairment in quality of life, comparable to other pruritic dermatoses (notably contact dermatitis and lichen planus) and systemic diseases such as hypertension, stroke, coronary artery disease, and arthritis, through sleep disturbance, absenteeism, and disruption of daily activities, particularly in those with higher itch scores [ 1 , 7 , 10 , 69 – 74 ]. Emotional well-being is also affected, with frequent anxiety, depression, anger, disgust, shame, and helplessness and increased use of antidepressants and anxiolytics [ 1 , 7 , 75 ]. Patients with CPN show higher odds than those with atopic dermatitis of behavioral and eating disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, substance abuse, schizophrenia, and self-harm [ 19 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that they are 1.3-, 1.9-, and 2-fold more likely to experience depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation/self-harm, respectively, than healthy controls, although causality remains unclear [ 76 ]. The overall burden is further amplified by comorbidities [ 3 , 10 , 15 , 19 , 22 ]. A higher Charlson Comorbidity Index in CPN (1.53) compared with atopic dermatitis (0.53) and psoriasis (1.16) is associated with greater use of specialist healthcare services [ 77 ].
sections.diagnosis and evaluation of chronic prur: CPN includes several lesion types, with papulonodular lesions being the most common [ 8 ]. Different prurigo lesions may coexist, and no subtype lesion necessarily reflects a more advanced or chronic stage [ 5 , 6 , 23 ]. Papulonodular lesions can range from a few to hundreds, typically distributed bilaterally and symmetrically on the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs [ 5 , 6 , 8 , 78 ]. The “butterfly sign” may be observed, with sparing of areas inaccessible to scratching, classically the mid-back [ 6 , 23 ]. Ulcerations may also occur, irrespective of CPN subtype [ 79 ]. There is no consensus on whether CPN is a distinct disease or a consequence of other conditions; therefore, current guidelines seek to harmonize diagnostic criteria. European and American documents diagnose CPN clinically using three main signs or symptoms, summarized in Table 1 . Both require chronic pruritus lasting at least 6 weeks [ 1 , 2 , 15 , 80 ]. The European guideline additionally emphasizes multiple localized or generalized pruritic lesions and a history or signs of repeated scratching, whereas the American consensus highlights nodular lesions plus repeated scratching, pinching, or rubbing [ 1 , 15 , 80 ]. Terminology also differs: “chronic nodular prurigo” in Europe versus “prurigo nodularis” in the USA (Table 1 ). Differential diagnosis remains essential, and Table 2 highlights the main alternatives and distinguishing features [ 2 , 3 , 15 , 81 – 83 ]. In 2024, Spanish dermatologists proposed a diagnostic algorithm aligned with European criteria [ 27 ]. It accepts all lesion types (not only nodules) and uses history and examination to guide both differential diagnosis and etiologic categorization, integrating signs and symptoms, quality of life, productivity, patient-reported outcomes, and comorbidities. Final diagnoses fall into four categories: CPN associated with dermatologic disease, systemic/metabolic disease, psychiatric disease, or idiopathic CPN. This categorization is mainly intended to guide etiologic work-up and multidisciplinary management rather than to define distinct drug regimens for each subgroup [ 27 ]. sections.disease evaluation and control tools: CPN severity and disease control can be assessed with several tools and scoring systems (Table 4 ), which collectively capture lesion activity, itch intensity, quality of life, sleep, and patient-perceived control [ 2 , 3 , 68 , 73 , 85 – 90 ]. One of the most widely used clinician-reported measures is the Investigator’s Global Assessment for PN (IGA-PN) [ 2 , 85 ]. Others tools, such as the Prurigo Activity Score (PAS), provide greater granularity but are less practical for routine care, although a shorter version is available [ 2 , 86 ]. Table 4 Tools for the evaluation and control of chronic prurigo nodularis [ 2 , 3 , 68 , 73 , 85 – 90 , 93 ] Assessment Tool Clinician evaluation • Investigator’s Global Assessment Nodular Prurigo (IGA PN) • Prurigo activity score (PAS) Patient-reported outcomes • Pruritus (worst itch) numerical rating scale (WI-NRS) • Pruritus visual analog scale (VAS) • Pain numerical rating scale (NRS) • Prurigo Control Test (PCT) • ItchyQoL Quality of life and psychological assessment • Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) • EuroQoL-5 dimensions (EQ-5D) • Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) Sleep assessment • Sleep numerical rating scale (NRS) • Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) • PROMIS Sleep Disturbance Short Form 8a IGA-PN is popular because of its simplicity. It evaluates both disease activity (IGA-PN-A) and stage (IGA-PN-S) using a 5-point scale based on the number of active lesions (0, clear [no nodules] to 4, severe [> 100 dome-shaped palpable nodules]) [ 2 , 85 ]. Quality of life is crucial in CPN. The most commonly used tool is the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), which is almost always impaired [ 88 ]. DLQI is a ten-item questionnaire assessing the impact of skin disease over the previous week; each item scores 0–3 (maximum 30), with higher scores indicating worse quality of life [ 88 ]. The Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) is also useful; it includes 14 items (7 for anxiety, 7 for depression), each subscale scored 0–21 (0–7, normal; 8–10, borderline; 11–21, abnormal) [ 89 , 90 ]. To date, only DLQI has been formally validated in CPN, on the basis of phase III dupilumab trials in adults; therefore, other phenotypes and settings may be underrepresented [ 91 ]. Therefore, when possible, DLQI should be complemented with prurigo-specific tools such as the Prurigo Control Test (PCT) and/or ItchyQoL. One of the most recent instruments is the PCT, developed and validated to assess disease control from the patient’s perspective. It comprises five items covering the previous 2 weeks, each scored 0–4 (total 0–20; 0 = worst control, 20 = complete control) [ 92 ]. PCT is easy to use in routine practice and supports more focused, meaningful communication between patients and clinicians. The ItchyQoL is a pruritus-specific quality-of-life questionnaire that assesses symptoms, functional impairment, and emotional impact of chronic itch. It consists of 22 Likert-scale items scored from 1 (never) to 5 (all the time) and summed to generate domain and total scores, allowing sensitive monitoring of disease burden and treatment response [ 93 ]. Among sleep measures, the sleep NRS is widely used because of its simplicity: patients rate sleep quality over the previous 24 h on a 0–10 scale (10 = worst, 0 = best), although confusion about the direction of the scale can complicate interpretation.
sections.treatment of chronic prurigo nodularis: The main goals of CPN treatment are to rapidly reduce pruritus, interrupt the itch–scratch cycle, heal lesions, and restore skin integrity. Contemporary consensus documents and treat-to-target proposals define meaningful response as clear or almost clear skin (IGA-PN 0/1) together with a clinically relevant reduction in itch intensity, usually at least 4 points on the WI-NRS or peak pruritus numeric rating scale (PP-NRS) [ 15 , 27 , 80 , 94 ]. Because CPN burden is multidimensional, treatment assessment should also include quality of life, sleep, and patient-perceived control (Table 4 ), and management should incorporate evaluation of associated disease, psychiatric burden, and underlying triggers [ 3 , 95 ]. For practical purposes, the therapeutic evidence can be divided into three tiers. High-quality evidence is currently limited to the phase III trials for dupilumab (PRIME/PRIME2) and nemolizumab (OLYMPIA1/OLYMPIA2), in which combined improvement in itch and lesion clearance represents a key response criterion [ 96 , 97 ]. Intermediate-level evidence comes from phase II trials of agents such as JAK inhibitors. By contrast, most traditional off-label treatments summarized in Table 5 are supported only by small prospective cohorts, retrospective series, or case series. Off-label systemic agents may be useful in selected patients, especially when access to biologics is limited, but they are constrained by variable efficacy, monitoring burden, cumulative toxicity, and sparse long-term data. Even for targeted agents, important practical limitations remain, including long-term safety, cost, reimbursement restrictions, and unequal access across health systems. sections.dupilumab: Dupilumab is a recombinant human IgG4 monoclonal antibody that blocks IL-4 signaling via the type I receptor (IL-4Rα/γc) and both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling via the type II receptor (IL-4Rα/IL-13Rα) [ 16 ]. PRIME and PRIME2 were randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trials in patients with CPN inadequately controlled with topical therapy [ 96 ]. They enrolled 151 and 160 patients, respectively, randomized to placebo or dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks (600-mg loading dose) for 24 weeks plus 12 weeks of follow-up; low-to-moderate potency topical corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors were allowed [ 96 ]. Clinically meaningful itch improvement was significantly more frequent with dupilumab than with placebo (≥ 4-point WI-NRS reduction at week 24: 60% versus 18% in PRIME, and 58% versus 20% in PRIME2; both p < 0.0001), as was clear/almost clear skin (IGA-PN 0/1 at week 24: 48% versus 18% in PRIME, and 45% versus 16% in PRIME2; both p < 0.001) (Table 6 ). These benefits were consistent across baseline lesion severity and were similar in patients who were atopic and who were nonatopic. No patients discontinued dupilumab, and no new safety signals emerged; conjunctivitis rates were low and comparable to placebo in PRIME (2.7% in both arms) and only slightly higher with dupilumab in PRIME2 (3.9% versus 0%) [ 96 ]. Together with nemolizumab, dupilumab currently represents one of the two therapies with the strongest evidence base in CPN.
sections.nemolizumab: Nemolizumab is a humanized IgG2 monoclonal antibody that inhibits IL-31 signaling by selectively binding IL-31RA [ 17 ]. Its efficacy and safety were evaluated in the phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled OLYMPIA1 (24 weeks) and OLYMPIA2 (16 weeks) trials [ 97 , 102 ]. OLYMPIA1 enrolled 286 patients and OLYMPIA2 274, who were randomized to nemolizumab (60-mg loading dose followed by 30 or 60 mg according to baseline weight) or placebo every 4 weeks. At week 16, a ≥ 4-point reduction in PP-NRS was achieved by 58.3% of patients receiving nemolizumab versus 16.7% receiving placebo in OLYMPIA1 and by 56.3% versus 20.98% in OLYMPIA2 (both p < 0.0001), with maintenance through week 24 in OLYMPIA1. IGA 0/1 rates were 26.3% versus 9.4% and 37.7% versus 11.0%, respectively ( p < 0.0001) (Table 6 ). Most adverse events were mild or moderate; headache (6.6% versus 4.4%) and atopic dermatitis (5.5% versus 0%) were the most common events reported with nemolizumab [ 97 , 102 ]. These phase III data place nemolizumab alongside dupilumab at the top of the current therapeutic evidence hierarchy in CPN.
sections.jak inhibitors: Oral JAK1 inhibitors include abrocitinib [ 103 ], upadacitinib [ 104 ], and povorcitinib [ 105 ]. Among them, povorcitinib currently has the strongest CPN-specific dataset, based on a randomized phase II study. Patients were assigned to povorcitinib 15 mg ( n = 36), 45 mg ( n = 36), 75 mg ( n = 37), or placebo ( n = 37) for 16 weeks. A ≥ 4-point reduction in WI-NRS was achieved by 54.1% of patients receiving povorcitinib versus 8.1% receiving placebo, and 48.6% achieved IGA-PN 0/1 versus 5.4% with placebo. Benefit was maintained through the extension phase up to week 40 [ 105 ] (Table 6 ). Despite this promising signal, JAK inhibitors should currently be contextualized as investigational or selected-use options in CPN rather than as evidence-equivalent alternatives to dupilumab or nemolizumab. The available CPN-specific datasets remain early phase or derived from small real-world cohorts, and none have been specifically designed to assess long-term safety in this population. Importantly, the safety profile of JAK inhibitors warrants careful consideration in CPN, particularly given that the patient population is predominantly older (mean age 56–64 years) and carries a high comorbidity burden, including diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease [ 106 ]. Accordingly, when JAK inhibitors are considered in CPN, an individualized risk–benefit assessment and close monitoring of safety parameters are essential.
sections.emerging therapies: Several emerging biologics are being investigated for CPN. The anti-OSMRβ monoclonal antibody vixarelimab achieved rapid itch reduction and clear or almost clear skin in about one third of patients in a phase IIa prurigo nodularis study [ 107 ]. IL-4Rα–blocking antibodies such as rademikibart (CBP-201) have shown robust efficacy in phase II atopic dermatitis trials and are being developed for type 2-driven dermatoses [ 108 , 109 ]. The OX40 antibody rocatinlimab and the anti-KIT antibody barzolvolimab are also in phase II development in type-2 inflammatory or mast cell–driven diseases, with promising antipruritic activity that may translate to CPN [ 110 , 111 ]. At present, however, these agents remain investigational in CPN and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than practice-changing.
sections.real-world evidence: Real-world evidence complements clinical trials by reflecting broader case-mix and routine-use safety [ 112 ], but in CPN, it remains dominated by uncontrolled small studies. Using the eligibility criteria summarized in Table 7 , we identified 44 real-world studies: 9 case series, 19 prospective series, and 16 retrospective series. Most cohorts were small, heterogeneous, and at risk of selection and reporting bias, therefore, these data should be used mainly to support feasibility, tolerability, and external validity rather than to infer comparative efficacy. Reported responses were sometimes substantial, but toxicity and discontinuation were non-negligible, particularly with thalidomide and methotrexate [ 101 , 113 , 114 ]. Since 2023, the most informative prospective cohorts have involved dupilumab, with consistent improvement in itch, lesion clearance, and quality of life, together with more limited but encouraging signals for abrocitinib and upadacitinib (Table 8 ) [ 103 , 104 , 115 , 116 ]. Table 8 Key recent prospective real-world series in chronic prurigo nodularis Dupilumab ( n = 73) [ 116 ] Abrocitinib ( n = 25) [ 103 ] Upadacitinib ( n = 10) [ 104 ] Percentage of patients with a reduction in the NRS score for itching ≥ 4 points 84.9% week 12 80% week 12 100% week 4 PP-NRS score (basal score → end score) 7.9 → 5.2 week 2 → 2.1 week 12 → 1.9 week 16 9.2 → 2.0 week 12 8.1 → 1.5 week 4 → 0.8 week 12 → 0.8 week 24 IGA score (basal score → end score) 3.5 → 3.3 week 2 → 1.9 week 12 → 1.6 week 16 3.6 → 2.5 week 12 3.4 → 2.3 week 4 → 1.4 week 12 → 1.0 week 24 DLQI score (basal score → end score) 16.6 → 12.5 week 2 → 7.21 week 12 → 6.5 week 16 19.0 → 8.9 week 12 17.8 → 3.4 week 4 → 1.8 week 12 → 0.6 week 24 Safety • Dry eyes ( n = 1; 1.4%) • No serious adverse events were reported • No treatment discontinuations or withdrawals • Acneiform eruption ( n = 2; 10%) • No serious adverse events were reported • No treatment discontinuations or withdrawals • Dyslipidemia ( n = 1; 10%) • No serious adverse events were reported • No treatment discontinuations or withdrawals DLQI Dermatology Life Quality Index, IGA Investigator’s Global Assessment, PP-NRS pruritus peak numeric rating scale, NRS numerical rating scale Recent retrospective studies largely confirm the rapid antipruritic and lesion-level benefit of dupilumab observed in clinical trials [ 117 – 122 ]. Limited real-world experience with nemolizumab also suggests meaningful improvement, but cutaneous adverse events have been reported and require monitoring [ 123 , 124 ]. Overall, the main value of real-world evidence at present is to confirm the effectiveness of the approved biologics in more diverse patients and to highlight safety and access issues that are less visible in randomized trials.
sections.current guidelines for the treatment of: The International Forum for the Study of Itch (IFSI) guideline (2020) and the European and US expert consensuses propose stepwise approaches to CPN diagnosis and management, but they are consensus-based, nonpersonalized, and largely pre-phase III with respect to dupilumab and nemolizumab; consequently, they provide limited patient-tailored therapeutic guidance [ 15 , 80 , 84 , 101 , 125 ]. These documents consistently begin with trigger control and topical anti-inflammatory therapy and then escalate to phototherapy or systemic agents, but they differ in how explicitly they separate neural-directed from immune-directed options. One consensus proposes an algorithm that starts with high-potency topical corticosteroids for flares, calcineurin inhibitors for maintenance, and capsaicin for localized disease, with phototherapy or systemic agents added when response is inadequate [ 125 ]. The Japanese consensus is broadly similar but recommends reevaluating the diagnosis and considering biopsy if all treatment lines fail [ 84 ]. Notably, most guidelines were developed before the availability of phase III biologic data and therefore rely heavily on off-label treatments supported by lower-quality evidence. This helps explain why frequently used therapies such as antihistamines continue to appear prominently despite the limited mechanistic rationale for histamine blockade in CPN [ 24 , 80 , 126 ]. The recent SWITCH algorithm moves closer to a treat-to-target model by linking therapeutic decisions to pruritus, lesion count, quality of life, and sleep [ 94 ]. Building on that concept, Fig. 2 provides a simplified pragmatic algorithm that prioritizes high-level evidence when available, reserves off-label or investigational agents for selected circumstances, and emphasizes repeated reassessment every 3–6 months.
sections.unmet needs in chronic prurigo nodularis: Despite recent progress, the management of CPN is currently facing urgent unmet needs, which highlight the necessity for clearer therapeutic strategies: First, harmonized terminology, diagnostic criteria, and therapeutic guidance are still needed across regions; current recommendations remain largely consensus-based and leave substantial room for variability in practice [ 127 ]. Second, treatment sequencing and combination strategies remain poorly defined. Clinicians still lack evidence-based guidance on when to escalate, switch, taper, or combine systemic and topical therapies. Third, the neurogenic and fibrotic components of CPN remain undertargeted. Although these pathways are biologically central, therapies specifically directed at neural sensitization or fibrosis are still limited [ 127 ]. Fourth, long-term data and guidance for special populations are scarce, including children, older adults, pregnant patients, and individuals with major cardiometabolic or psychiatric comorbidity. Finally, access remains a major unmet need: even when biologics are available, cost, reimbursement restrictions, and health-system inequities may delay the use of the agents with the strongest evidence. These gaps underscore the complexity of CPN and the need for more practical and personalized guidance. Future research should prioritize biomarker-informed phenotyping, pragmatic comparative trials, long-term safety data, and digital endpoints to better define CPN subtypes and treatment response.

title: Feasibility and safety of coronary catheter rolling technique (Jahanzeb technique) for radial artery catheterization on arterial perforation and radial artery patency
abstract: Background Transradial access is widely used for coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI); however, complications such as radial artery spasm, perforation, and occlusion remain clinically relevant. Jahanzeb’s Coronary Catheter Rolling Technique (JCRT) is a novel method designed to improve catheter navigation and reduce vascular trauma. Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety and clinical outcomes of JCRT compared with the conventional radial catheterization technique. Methods In this prospective, non-randomized comparative study 4,697 patients undergoing elective coronary angiography or PCI via radial access were included. Patients were allocated to JCRT ( n = 1,519) or the standard technique ( n = 3,178). Primary endpoints were arterial perforation and radial artery occlusion. Secondary endpoints included major bleeding, radial artery spasm, thrombosis, and patient and physician satisfaction. Outcomes were analyzed using odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and multivariable logistic regression was performed. Results JCRT was associated with a significantly lower overall complication rate (7.6% vs. 11.0%; OR: 0.66, 95% CI 0.52–0.92; p = 0.037). Significant reductions were observed in major bleeding (4.3% vs. 7.1%; OR: 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.81; p = 0.024), radial artery spasm (2.1% vs. 4.9%; OR: 0.41, 95% CI 0.27–0.63; p = 0.011), arterial perforation (1.6% vs. 3.8%; OR: 0.41, 95% CI 0.24–0.71; p = 0.032), and radial artery occlusion (2.8% vs. 6.3%; OR: 0.43, 95% CI 0.29–0.63; p = 0.006). On multivariable analysis, JCRT remained associated with reduced complications after adjustment (adjusted OR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.51–0.93; p = 0.021). Patient and physician satisfaction scores were significantly higher with JCRT ( p < 0.001). Conclusion JCRT is a feasible and safe technique associated with reduced vascular complications and improved satisfaction. Further multicenter randomized studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

sections.introduction: Coronary artery disease (CAD) continues to pose a significant global health burden and the diagnosis and treatment of these conditions often necessitate coronary angiography (CA) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [ 1 ]. Radial access has gained popularity as a preferred approach for these procedures due to its reduced risk of significant bleeding, lower vascular complications, and overall improved patient comfort compared to the traditional femoral approach [ 2 ]. However, challenges persist particularly in achieving and maintaining radial artery patency and minimizing complications such as arterial perforation [ 3 ]. The Coronary Catheter Rolling Technique or JCRT can be a potential solution to enhance the success and safety of radial artery catheterization. Named after the pioneering interventional cardiologist Dr Jahanzeb, this technique involves a unique rolling motion of the catheter at the radial artery access site, aiming to reduce the risk of complications like arterial perforation and maintain radial artery patency during and after the procedure. This study aims to comprehensively investigate the feasibility and safety of JCRT in the context of radial artery catheterization, specifically focusing on assessing its impacts on arterial perforation and radial artery patency. By closely examining the outcomes and potential benefits of this innovative approach, this study aims to provide valuable insights to the existing body of knowledge in interventional cardiology.
sections.study design and ethical approval: This prospective, non-randomized comparative study was conducted at Basharat Hospital (Study ID: BH/23/012) in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board and written informed consent was secured from all participants prior to enrollment.
sections.study population: Consecutive patients undergoing elective coronary angiography or percutaneous coronary intervention via radial artery access were included. Patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction requiring primary PCI, those with hemodynamic instability, prior documented radial artery occlusion or inability to provide informed consent were excluded. Patients were allocated to either JCRT or the standard technique based on operator discretion and familiarity with the technique.
sections.procedural technique: All procedures were performed by experienced interventional cardiologists. In the standard technique group, catheter advancement was performed using conventional linear manipulation over a guidewire. In the JCRT group, after successful radial artery cannulation, a 0.035-inch soft-tip hydrophilic guidewire was advanced into the ascending aorta. A 5–6 French diagnostic or guiding catheter was then introduced. The JCRT technique involves controlled advancement of the catheter using alternating clockwise and counterclockwise rotational movements while maintaining gentle forward pressure. This rolling motion facilitates smoother catheter navigation through the radial and brachial arteries and minimizes resistance within the vessel lumen. Particular care was taken to avoid forceful catheter manipulation in both groups. Patient and physician satisfaction were assessed using a standardized Likert scale immediately after the procedure. Patient responses were self-reported, while physician assessments were recorded by the operating cardiologist at the end of the procedure. Satisfaction outcomes were not blinded, which may introduce reporting bias.
sections.data collection: Baseline demographic and clinical variables including age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, body mass index and prior cardiovascular history were recorded. Procedural details and complications were prospectively documented. Radial artery patency was assessed clinically and confirmed with Doppler ultrasonography prior to discharge.
sections.endpoints and definitions: The primary endpoints were arterial perforation and radial artery occlusion. Arterial perforation was defined as angiographically confirmed contrast extravasation. Radial artery occlusion was defined as absence of antegrade flow on Doppler ultrasonography or clinical absence of a palpable pulse. Secondary endpoints included major bleeding defined according to Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) criteria; radial artery spasm, defined as patient-reported pain associated with resistance to catheter advancement; hematoma at the access site; thrombosis, defined clinically and confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography; infection at the access site; and patient and physician satisfaction assessed using a Likert scale.
sections.statistical analysis: A sample size of approximately 4,500 patients was estimated to provide 80% power to detect a relative reduction of at least 20% in complication rates assuming a two-sided alpha level of 0.05. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation and were compared using the independent samples t-test. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages and were compared using the chi-square test. Effect sizes are reported as odds ratios (OR) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI). Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to evaluate the association between JCRT and clinical outcomes after adjustment for potential confounders including age, sex, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, radial artery diameter as well as procedural variables such as sheath size, anticoagulation strategy and operator experience. A two-tailed p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Model assumptions were assessed prior to analysis, and goodness-of-fit was evaluated using appropriate statistical tests. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 26 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).
sections.study population and flow of participant: A total of 4,921 patients were screened for eligibility during the study period. Of these, 546 patients were excluded due to predefined criteria, including not meeting inclusion criteria ( n = 372), declining participation ( n = 115), or other reasons ( n = 59). The final study cohort comprised 4,375 patients, of whom 1,519 (34.7%) underwent catheterization using JCRT and 2,856 (65.3%) underwent the standard technique. All enrolled patients completed the study and were included in the final analysis. The study flow is illustrated in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Study Flow Diagram of Patient Enrollment and Allocation. Flow diagram illustrating the selection and allocation of patients included in the study. A total of 4,921 patients were assessed for eligibility, of whom 546 were excluded based on predefined criteria. The remaining 4,375 patients were allocated to either the Jahanzeb’s Coronary Catheter Rolling Technique (JCRT) group ( n = 1,519) or the standard technique group ( n = 2,856). All allocated patients were included in the final analysis
