title: Remodeling the marrow fat niche: BMAT in cancer bone metastases and hematological malignancies
abstract: Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) is a dynamic component of the marrow microenvironment that influences tumor persistence, therapy response, and skeletal integrity. Recent work shows that marrow adipocytes function not only as metabolic partners for malignant cells but also as stress-responsive components of bone marrow niche remodeled by tumor progression and cancer therapy. Reciprocal signaling between tumor cells and adipogenic lineage populations alters lipid mobilization, redox balance, and stromal differentiation, creating microenvironments that support tumor cell survival under metabolic and therapeutic stress. Cancer therapies can reprogram adipocyte and stromal populations, generating inflammatory or senescent niches that persist beyond active disease and influence residual tumor behavior. At the same time, adipogenic cells contribute to marrow repair, highlighting the need to distinguish regenerative from tumor-permissive states. Spatial heterogeneity across skeletal sites, and its evolution during treatment, adds an additional layer of complexity to how BMAT regulates tumor behavior in bone. Here, we review recent advances that are redefining the role of BMAT in cancer progression and therapy response.
journal: Current opinion in endocrine and metabolic research

sections.introduction: Bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) is a metabolically active and spatially heterogeneous component of the marrow microenvironment that influences hematopoiesis, bone remodeling, immune cell metabolism, and tumor behavior [ 1 – 5 ]. Its role as a metabolic fuel source and pro-survival niche for marrow-resident metastatic solid tumors and hematologic malignancies has become increasingly appreciated [ 2 , 4 , 6 – 8 ]. Over the past several years, accumulating evidence has broadened the recognized role of BMAT in cancer progression and therapy response. BMAT is now viewed as a stress-responsive and plastic niche that is dynamically remodeled by both tumor growth and associated treatment. This review highlights recent advances that redefine our understanding of the interplay between BMAT remodeling and tumor behavior within malignant bone microenvironments ( Table 1 ).
sections.new insights into tumor-driven bmat remo: It is now widely accepted that BMAT remodeling by both the hematological malignancies and bone-metastatic tumors is reciprocal: tumor cells actively reprogram marrow adipocytes by inducing lipolysis, while adipocytes enhance lipid uptake and transport in tumor cells, collectively reshaping tumor metabolism [ 7 , 9 ]. Mechanistically, tumor-induced lipolysis is driven by a combination of soluble factors, stress signaling, and bidirectional tumor-adipocyte communication [ 10 ]. BMAT responses vary by skeletal site. Although marrow adipocytes are plastic and can undergo remodeling, delipidation, or functional reprogramming, as observed in leukemia [ 11 , 12 ], multiple myeloma [ 13 ], and bone metastasis [ 14 ], they are generally less susceptible to lipolysis than white adipocytes from peripheral adipose depots, and this resistance is not uniform [ 15 ]. In AML, regulated adipocytes in hematopoietic-rich regions (rBMAds) are depleted in response to leukemic cells, whereas constitutive BMAds (cBMAds) are comparatively resistant to delipidation, highlighting depotspecific BMAd plasticity [ 12 ]. These differences raise important questions about how tumors access lipid stores in more stable marrow niches. A recent important study from the Scheller laboratory suggests that the apparent lipolytic resistance of cBMAT is not permanent but rather reflects a homeostatic state [ 16 ]. Although sympathetic signaling has historically been viewed as the principal regulator of adipocyte lipolysis, this elegant study identifies adaptive, catecholamine-independent pathways capable of mobilizing lipids in response to systemic or local stress. They show that stable adipocyte depots, including cBMAT, can undergo ATGL-dependent lipolysis independent of local sympathetic input when nutrient and endocrine conditions shift, such as during hypoglycemia, reduced insulin signaling, or tumor-induced cachexia. These mechanisms may be particularly relevant in tumor-bearing marrow, where inflammatory cytokines, nutrient competition, and hypoxia could engage non-adrenergic lipolytic programs to sustain lipid mobilization. Notably, a direct transfer of lipolytic cAMP signaling from breast cancer cells to white adipocytes by GJB3 gap junctions has recently been reported [ 17 ], suggesting that contact-dependent mechanisms may further amplify lipid mobilization. Whether similar mechanisms contribute to lipid mobilization by tumors residing within the marrow niche remains to be determined.
sections.emerging mechanisms shaping bmat-tumor c: A current view of the field is that metabolic coupling, adipokine signaling, and microenvironment-mediated resistance are central features of adipocyte—tumor interactions in bone [ 10 ]. Systemic states such as obesity, age, as well as conditions of energy deficit such as anorexia influence marrow adiposity [ 1 ], while adipokine-driven signaling links marrow fat to bone remodeling and tumor-supportive niche function [ 18 – 20 ]. This evolving perspective frames BMAT as a dynamic and state-dependent regulator of tumor behavior shaped by tumor-derived signals and host metabolism. Mechanistically, adipocyte-derived fatty acids remain front and center in supporting tumor survival, operating through multiple metabolic routes, including fatty-acid oxidation, membrane synthesis, lipid storage, and stress-protective remodeling [ 7 ]. Increasingly, however, lipid-handling pathways are being recognized not simply as passive fuel sources but as components of coordinated stress-adaptation programs that enable tumor persistence within adipocyte-rich marrow niches. Under hypoxic conditions, chronic myeloid leukemia cells were reported to increase glutamine-dependent CD36-mediated fatty acid uptake, a response associated with enhanced survival and maintenance of leukemic stem-cell populations in the adipocyte co-culture systems [ 21 ]. In multiple myeloma cells, inhibition of acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain (ACSL) enzymes was recently shown to suppress proliferation and induce mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting the importance of converting fatty acids into metabolically useable acyl-CoA pools to sustain tumor fitness in marrow environments [ 22 ]. Complementing this work, an in vivo CRISPR activation screen identified acyl-CoA-binding protein (ACBP/DBI) as a driver of bone metastatic growth, linking acyl-CoA availability to mitochondrial function and tumor survival in the skeletal niche [ 23 ]. Furthermore, targeting fatty acid binding proteins (FABPs) was shown to disrupt MYC signaling and cell-cycle progression in pre-clinical models of multiple myeloma [ 24 ], reinforcing the role of lipid trafficking in coordinating proliferative and metabolic programs within adipocyte-rich niches [ 25 , 26 ]. Beyond lipid acquisition and trafficking, lipid-modifying enzymes that buffer metabolic stress are emerging as important regulators of tumor adaptation within marrow niches. In bone-metastatic prostate cancer models, inhibition of the ER-resident desaturase stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD) suppresses tumor progression in adipocyte-rich bone through mechanisms involving ER stress, mTOR dysregulation, and DNA-damage signaling [ 27 ]. This is consistent with recent work showing that high SCD expression is associated with adverse outcome and enrichment of unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis in relapsed or chemo-refractory AML, and that pharmacologic SCD inhibition induces lipotoxicity and cell death across genetically diverse AML models [ 28 ]. Notably, even in models with limited single agent sensitivity, SCD inhibition increased chemotherapy-induced DNA damage and synergized with conventional cytotoxic therapy to prolong tumor cell survival in vivo , indicating that metabolic perturbation can prime leukemic cells for a second therapeutic hit. Together with observations in pre-clinical lung cancer bone metastasis models in which combined inhibition of fatty acid synthesis and chemotherapy restored chemosensitivity in adipocyte-rich bone [ 29 ], these findings suggest that targeting tumor lipid handling enhances therapeutic response across marrow malignancies. This may occur through limiting desaturation or de novo synthesis, thereby destabilizing adipocyte-supported metabolic buffering.
sections.therapy-driven bmat remodeling: Therapy-associated increases in marrow adiposity have long been observed, but recent studies now clarify the mechanisms and functional consequences of these changes, positioning BMAT as an active component of therapy-remodeled marrow niches that impact tumor progression and therapeutic response [ 10 ]. Compelling recent work demonstrates that cytotoxic therapy can induce senescence preferentially within murine marrow adipogenic lineage populations, including CXCL12-abundant reticular (CAR) cells and bone marrow adipocytes [ 30 ]. These cells upregulate senescence associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors, including RANKL, to drive osteoclastogenesis while simultaneously reducing osteoblastogenic capacity, thereby uncoupling bone remodeling. Importantly, targeting stress-activated MK2 signaling (a downstream effector of p38 MAPK that regulates inflammatory SASP phenotype) or pharmacologically clearing senescent adipo-lineage cells (e.g., using senolytics) mitigated bone loss without compromising chemotherapy efficacy. These findings indicate that therapy-associated BMAT remodeling is not a transient phenomenon but a persistent stromal response with functional consequences. In this context, therapy-induced senescence may create a stromal environment that supports survival of residual tumor cells during post-therapy adaptation. Radiation and chemotherapy can also bias mesenchymal stromal progenitors toward adipogenesis at the expense of osteoblastogenesis, contributing to sustained marrow adiposity and impaired bone regeneration. Although therapy-induced adipogenesis has been recognized for years [ 9 , 10 , 31 , 32 ], recent lineage-resolved studies in mice demonstrate that these adipogenic shifts arise from defined stromal populations and persist in marrow niches that are also exploited by malignant cells [ 33 , 34 ]. Importantly, adipogenic lineage expansion is not uniformly detrimental. Marrow adipogenic lineage precursors (MALPs) can support marrow recovery following chemotherapy [ 33 ], as these late-stage adipogenic progenitors resist early cytotoxic depletion, transiently expand, and adopt proliferative and myofibroblast-like states that promote vascular and stromal repair. Genetic ablation of MALPs impairs hematopoietic and microenvironmental recovery after treatment, and similar transient expansion and myofibroblast conversion of MALPs has been observed after radiation injury, where their ablation was shown to impair restoration of marrow cellularity and vasculature [ 34 ]. This duality suggests that therapeutic strategies targeting BMAT must consider timing and cellular state, as interventions that broadly suppress adipogenesis could impair marrow recovery while still leaving processes that support tumor cell survival intact. Together, these findings highlight BMAT as a niche that can be simultaneously reparative and permissive under conditions of therapeutic pressure. Other disease-relevant therapies further illustrate how treatment can reshape marrow niches. Bone-targeted agents such as radium-223, used in prostate cancer bone metastases, alter bone remodeling dynamics and have been associated with longer-term microenvironmental changes including increased marrow adiposity [ 35 ]. This suggests that therapies directed at skeletal lesions can also remodel stromal and adipogenic compartments in ways that influence residual tumor cells, immune populations, and subsequent treatment responsiveness. Endocrine therapies represent another major clinical axis of BMAT remodeling: androgen deprivation therapy increases marrow adiposity and suppresses bone formation [ 36 ], and estrogen depletion in breast cancer similarly favors adipogenic allocation and contributes to skeletal fragility [ 37 – 39 ]. Glucocorticoids, widely used in ALL, lymphoma, and myeloma regimens, are potent pharmacologic drivers of adipogenesis that promote adipocyte differentiation while suppressing osteoblast programs [ 40 ]. Because all of these agents are often administered repeatedly or chronically, their effects may accumulate and compound BMAT remodeling due to therapy, with potential consequences for marrow recovery, niche signaling, and tumor persistence. The clinical relevance of therapy-associated BMAT remodeling was recently reinforced by the phenome-wide association and Mendelian randomization analysis of UK Biobank participants [ 41 ], which demonstrated associations between cancer therapy exposure, including chemotherapy and radiation, and increased marrow fat fraction across skeletal sites. Notably, higher bone marrow fat fraction showed site-specific associations with malignancies including breast and prostate cancer bone metastases and multiple myeloma, aligning with preclinical evidence that marrow adipocytes can promote tumor cell survival and therapeutic resistance. These findings suggest that BMAT remodeling is a clinically measurable consequence of treatment exposure and a reflection of altered marrow niche function. Defining when such remodeling supports tissue repair versus tumor persistence will be critical for understanding how treatment shapes long-term disease outcomes and skeletal recovery.
sections.emerging mechanisms responsible for pers: As BMAT is remodeled by both tumor growth and treatment, adipocyte-rich marrow niches may become key determinants of how tumor cells survive therapy and persist. Single-cell analyses in murine myeloma models demonstrate that malignant cells induce inflammatory and oxidative stress programs across non-hematopoietic niche populations and bias mesenchymal differentiation toward adipogenic lineages that support tumor growth [ 42 ]. Therapy-associated BMAT changes may therefore build upon pre-existing stromal polarization induced by the tumor, rather than arising de novo . In this setting, marrow niches rich in adipocytes are likely to influence how tumor cells respond to therapy. Adipocytes can reduce effective drug exposure by metabolizing lipophilic agents such as daunorubicin, while simultaneously supplying fatty acids that sustain mitochondrial metabolism and redox balance during therapy-induced stress [ 43 ]. Tumor-induced adipocyte lipolysis may further promote resistance to agents such as docetaxel by increasing local lipid availability and reinforcing stress-adaptive metabolic programs [ 27 , 44 , 45 ]. These lipid-supported tumor survival pathways should be considered not only as drivers of proliferation but also as mechanisms that allow tumor cells to remain viable under therapeutic pressure without requiring active cell cycling. Consistent with this interpretation, recent work in human T-ALL samples and murine models reported enrichment of quiescent tumor populations within adipocyte-dense marrow regions [ 46 , 47 ], suggesting that such niches may support low-cycling states compatible with minimal residual disease. Bone marrow adipocytes have also been implicated as regulators of disseminated tumor cell (DTC) reactivation by providing free fatty acids that fuel mitochondrial metabolism and support proliferative outgrowth of previously dormant cells [ 48 ]. Marrow adipocyte interaction with other components of bone marrow niche, including osteoclast-mediated remodeling, loss of osteoblast-derived quiescence signals, and inflammatory cues, collectively shape dormancy escape [ 48 ]. This extends the role of BMAT beyond therapy tolerance, suggesting that the same metabolic and signaling interactions that support survival during treatment may also influence the timing and probability of dormancy escape. Therapy-driven BMAT remodeling may therefore shape not only whether tumor cells survive treatment but also how and when they re-enter the cell cycle. A key priority moving forward will be to define how lipid-rich marrow niches influence tumor cell tolerance to metabolic and oxidative stress, and how adaptation to stress induced by lipids supports survival of dormant populations versus their eventual reawakening.
sections.biogeography of bone marrow niche - spat: A major emerging direction in the BMAT-cancer field is the need to understand marrow niches in a spatially resolved and human-relevant context. Bone marrow adipose tissue is not uniformly distributed across the skeleton [ 49 ], and recent work suggests that tumor cell behavior and fate, including persistence, dormancy, and therapy responsiveness may depend on the specific microenvironments in which tumor cells reside [ 8 , 10 ]. Spatial and single-cell approaches are therefore becoming essential for defining the biogeography of marrow niches and for determining whether adipocyte-rich regions possess distinct immune, stromal, or vascular signatures that influence tumor fate. Recent mapping of human marrow niche architecture using single-cell transcriptomics and multiplexed imaging has begun to define location-specific niche states and their association with disease progression and therapy exposure [ 50 ]. These spatial analyses enable investigation of whether BMAT-rich regions harbor unique inflammatory, metabolic, or senescence-associated programs and whether these signatures correlate with quiescence or relapse risk. As spatially resolved datasets become more comprehensive, it should become possible to define how niche location influences tumor persistence and therapeutic response. Despite rapid mechanistic progress, translation of BMAT biology into clinically relevant systems remains a major challenge. While metabolic coupling and adipocyte-driven signaling are now well established, major limitations remain in existing model systems, particularly in recapitulating human marrow architecture, adipocyte heterogeneity, and vascular context [ 8 ]. Recent methodological advances have begun to address this gap. New three-dimensional adipose culture systems and extracellular matrix-mimicking hydrogels are emerging as experimental models for testing of adipocyte-tumor interactions in therapy-relevant settings, including endocrine and metabolic stress conditions [ 51 ]. Emerging human bone marrow organoid systems that incorporate mesenchymal, endothelial, and hematopoietic lineages, provide increasingly physiologic platforms for modeling tumor-niche interactions and therapy response [ 52 ]. However, current organoids largely lack adipocyte compartments, in part because adipogenic differentiation requires specific metabolic and mechanical conditions, mature adipocytes are fragile and difficult to maintain in long-term culture, and BMAT is tightly integrated with bone, hematopoietic, and vascular niche components [ 53 ]. Incorporating adipogenic lineages while preserving physiologic niche architecture therefore remains a key technical barrier for next generation BMAT-based models [ 53 ]. Continued development of physiologically faithful models will be essential for linking BMAT heterogeneity with clinical outcomes [ 4 ]. Advances in quantitative imaging are also beginning to bridge preclinical and clinical studies. Proton density fat fraction (PDFF) MRI and related techniques provide non-invasive methods to quantify marrow adiposity and detect dynamic changes associated with aging, radiation, and therapy exposure, including increases in marrow fat fraction and decreases during marrow regeneration or hematopoietic recovery [ 54 ]. Specifically, in preclinical mouse models, PDFF measurements correlate strongly with histologic adiposity and capture spatial and temporal variability in marrow fat content [ 54 ]. Ongoing clinical studies are now extending these approaches to patients, including longitudinal imaging of marrow fat fraction in individuals undergoing chemotherapy and transplantation (e.g., NCT03422731 ), supporting their translational relevance. In parallel, spatial transcriptomic approaches, applied in both preclinical models and human tissue samples, enable high-resolution mapping of stromal lineage heterogeneity within the marrow, including adipogenic progenitor populations that localize to distinct niches and support leukemic cell survival and chemoresistance in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia [ 55 ]. Population-level and clinical imaging analyses further support the concept that marrow adiposity is a quantifiable and therapy-responsive phenotype [ 56 , 57 ], raising the possibility that BMAT could serve as a biomarker of marrow niche state and long-term treatment effects.
sections.outlook and future directions: Over the past several years, BMAT has shifted from being viewed primarily as a passive lipid reservoir to a dynamic, state-dependent component of the bone marrow niche that shapes tumor behavior, therapy response, and skeletal health ( Figure 1 ). This shift highlights several outstanding questions. First, a clearer understanding of how tumor- and therapy-driven signals converge over time to remodel BMAT, and how long these changes persist, will be important for establishing how residual tumor cells adapt and survive in bone marrow niche. Second, because adipocyte-rich marrow niches appear to support tumor persistence by buffering metabolic and oxidative stress and stabilizing low-proliferative states, identifying the specific lipid and stress adaptation pathways that support tumor survival in these environments will be an important next step. Third, adipogenic lineage populations can also contribute to marrow repair. Distinguishing reparative from tumor-permissive BMAT states will therefore be critical when considering therapeutic intervention. Finally, because marrow adiposity varies across skeletal sites and niche states appear to differ in their capacity to support persistence or repair, defining when BMAT is tumor-permissive versus adaptive will be central to future work. Linking mechanistic insights from pre-clinical studies to patient-relevant systems will be essential for determining whether adipocyte-rich niches represent targetable vulnerabilities or reflect broader remodeling of bone marrow microenvironment that supports tumor progression and therapy evasion. In this context, the widespread clinical use of metabolic therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists underscores the need to understand how systemic metabolic interventions influence bone microenvironment and skeletal health [ 58 ]. Although current data primarily address skeletal and metabolic outcomes, their potential to impact BMAT remodeling or tumor—niche interactions is plausible and represents an important, largely unexplored area for future investigation.

title: METTL7A is a key regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease progression
abstract: Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase and thiol methyltransferase enriched in hepatocytes, has been implicated in cancer biology, yet its role in hepatic lipid metabolism and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) remains unknown. Hepatic steatosis was induced in HepG2 and Huh7 cells using oleic acid (OA). The role of METTL7A was examined through shRNA-mediated knockdown, RNA sequencing, lipid metabolic assays, and rescue experiments. Protein interactions were assessed via mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation. An AAV-shMETTL7A mouse MASLD/NAFLD model was used to validate in vivo relevance. METTL7A expression was significantly upregulated in OA-induced steatotic hepatocytes. METTL7A silencing mitigated lipid accumulation, improved cell viability, reduced LDL-C, TC, and TG levels, and restored HDL-C. Transcriptomic profiling identified PLIN5 as a key downstream target reduced upon METTL7A depletion. Mechanistically, METTL7A knockdown inhibited PI3K/AKT activation and suppressed PLIN5 expression. Mass spectrometry revealed SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein, and SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation, PI3K/AKT activation, and PLIN5 levels in METTL7A-deficient cells. In vivo, AAV-mediated METTL7A knockdown alleviated hepatic steatosis, normalized serum lipid profiles and liver injury markers, and reduced SAPCD2, PLIN5, FAS, and ACC while increasing HSL expression. METTL7A is a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis that promotes steatosis by sustaining SAPCD2 expression and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and PLIN5 expression. Targeting METTL7A may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MASLD/NAFLD. sections.introduction: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly named nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to a wide range of liver conditions marked by abnormal fat deposition in hepatocytes among individuals who drink little or no alcohol 1 . It has become one of the most prevalent chronic liver disorders worldwide, strongly associated with metabolic dysfunction and affecting roughly 30% of the global population 2 . MASLD/NAFLD is generally classified into two forms: metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver/nonalcoholic fatty liver (MAFL/NAFL) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis/nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) 3 . MAFL/NAFL involves simple steatosis without notable inflammation or fibrosis and is often viewed as relatively mild, though progression can occur. In contrast, MASH/NASH features steatosis accompanied by inflammation and hepatocellular damage, which may advance to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or even hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) 3 , 4 . Key contributors to MASLD/NAFLD include obesity, type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia, genetic susceptibility, and unhealthy lifestyle habits 5 , 6 . At present, few medications have been approved in the United States specifically for MASLD/NAFLD or MASH/NASH therapy 5 , 7 . Current management focuses on reducing excess weight through lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy, or bariatric and endoscopic procedures, and correcting metabolic abnormalities 8 , 9 . Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular pathways driving hepatic lipid accumulation is urgently needed for novel therapy development. Hepatic steatosis develops when lipid acquisition exceeds lipid disposal—that is, when fatty acid uptake and de novo lipogenesis outpace fatty acid oxidation and lipid export. In MASLD/NAFLD, both hepatic fatty acid uptake and lipogenesis are elevated, whereas the compensatory increase in fatty acid oxidation is insufficient to normalize lipid levels 10 . Several molecular pathways have been implicated in regulating hepatic lipid deposition 11 . For instance, the PI3K/AKT pathway plays a vital role in regulating hepatic glucose and lipid metabolism 12 . Additionally, key enzymes such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FAS) drive de novo lipogenesis in hepatocytes 11 , while hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) facilitates lipolysis and mobilizes triglycerides in the liver 13 . Despite these insights, the mechanisms governing hepatic lipid metabolism remain incompletely defined. Methyltransferase-like protein 7A (METTL7A), also known as TMT1A, is an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer prognosis and therapeutic resistance 14 – 17 . It is a member of the METTL7 family, which also includes METTL7B 18 . Although METTL7A is abundantly expressed in hepatocytes 19 , its function in hepatic lipid metabolism and its potential contribution to MASLD/NAFLD pathogenesis have not yet been investigated. In this study, we first established an MASLD/NAFLD cellular model by treating HepG2 and Huh7 cells with oleic acid (OA), which led to increased METTL7A expression. We then depleted METTL7A in OA-treated HCC cells and evaluated their viability and lipid metabolism-related parameters. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs), among which PLIN5, a key regulator of MASLD/NAFLD and lipid metabolism 20 , was significantly downregulated. Screening for PLIN5-interacting proteins revealed SAPCD2 as a potential mediator of PLIN5 function in OA-treated hepatocytes. Consistently, knockdown of SAPCD2 led to the downregulation of both PLIN5 and PI3K. Overexpression of SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient cells decreased cell viability and promoted lipid synthesis. Finally, using an MASLD/NAFLD mouse model, we confirmed the role of METTL7A in regulating hepatic lipid metabolism.
sections.cell culture: HEK293T cells were cultured in 90% DMEM (IMC-305) with 10% FBS (Gibco, A5670801) and penicillin–streptomycin (IMMOCELL, 15,070,063). HepG2 cells (IM-H038) were maintained in the specified medium (IM-H038-1). Huh7 cells (IM-H040) were kept in specialized medium (IM-H040-1). All these cell lines and culture media were sourced from IMMOCELL. Cell culture was maintained in a designated culture incubator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 3311E) provided with 5% CO₂ at 37 °C.
sections.cell viability assay: To assay cell viability, 0.2 mL full medium containing 1 × 10 4 HepG2 or Huh7 cells was inoculated into each well of 96-well plates. Following 24 h of culture, 20 µL of MTT solution (5 mg/mL, Beyotime, ST316) was added to each well. Four hours later, the liquid was discarded, and 0.15 mL DMSO was applied to each well. The crystal was then dissolved by continuous shaking for 10 min. OD 490 values of the plate were evaluated using a Thermo Fisher Scientific microplate reader (A51119500C).
sections.plasmid construction: To overexpress METTL7A or SAPCD2, their coding sequence was respectively ligated into the pECMV-3 × FLAG or pLVX-CMV-HA-pGK-puro backbone. The resulting vector was named Flag-METTL7A or SAPCD2 OE. In order to deplete METTL7A, its targeting shRNAs were inserted into the pLKO.1-puro backbone. Three shMETTL7A constructs were produced: shMETTL7A-1, shMETTL7A-2, and shMETTL7A-3. A non-specific shRNA (shNC) was constructed to function as a control. All the resulting plasmids were subjected to Sanger sequencing to ensure sequence accuracy before being used for functional assays. Table 1 shows the details of primers. Plasmid transfection was performed using Lipofectamine® 2000 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11668-019) when cells reached 70–80% confluence. Table 1 Primer details for plasmid generation. sections.quantitative pcr (qpcr): The RaPure Total RNA Kit (Magen, R4011-02) was employed to extract total cellular and tissue RNA, following the manufacturer’s instructions. Genomic DNA was digested, and RNase-free water was applied to elute RNA. The purified RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using All-in-One First-Strand SuperMix containing dsDNase (Nuoyang Biotech, EG15133S). qPCR was performed using ChamQ SYBR Color qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q431-02) on a QuantStudio 3 system (ThermoFisher, A28573 ). Relative targeted gene expression was determined based on the 2 –ΔΔCt method, normalizing to 18S. The primers used for qPCR are listed in Table 2 . Table 2 Primer details for qPCR. sections.western blot: Cells or liver tissues were washed with PBS and then lysed using RIPA buffer with vortexing and sonication on ice. The resulting lysates were then centrifuged, and the supernatant was transferred into fresh tubes. The protein concentration was measured with a BCA kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23,227). A 20 μg aliquot of each denatured sample was separated by 10% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto activated PVDF membranes. Next, the membranes were incubated with 5% nonfat milk for 1 h to minimize background. After incubating with primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight, the membranes were washed and then kept in secondary antibody solution for 1 h. Following another round of washing, the membranes were incubated with enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) and then exposed to X-ray film to visualize the bands. ImageJ was used for band grayscale value quantification. The antibodies used for Western blotting are listed below: METTL7A (ImmunoWay, YN8429, 1:500), PI3K (Proteintech, 20,584–1-AP, 1:500), P-PI3K (Cell Signaling Technology, #17,366, 1:500), AKT (Proteintech, 60,203–2-Ig, 1:500), P-AKT (Proteintech, 80,455–1-RR, 1:500), PLIN5 (Proteintech, 26,951–1-AP, 1:500), SAPCD2 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, PA5-60,632, 1:500), HA-tag (Proteintech, 51,064–2-AP, 1:500), Flag-tag (Proteintech, 20,543–1-AP, 1:1000), β-actin (Proteintech, 20,536–1-AP, 1:500), HRP-Anti-Rabbit IgG (Proteintech, SA00001-2, 1:10,000), HRP-Anti-Mouse IgG (Proteintech, SA00001-1, 1:10,000).
sections.rna-seq and data analysis: Total RNA was extracted and purified from OA-treated HepG2 cells (shNC or shMETTL7A) using the method described above. For library preparation, 1 µg of RNA per sample was processed with the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina® (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA fragment selection and purification were performed using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter), and library quality was evaluated with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100. Clustering of index-coded libraries was carried out on the cBot Cluster Generation System using the TruSeq PE Cluster Kit v3-cBot-HS (Illumina). Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates were performed and analyzed for each experimental condition. For data processing, raw reads containing adapter sequences or low-quality bases were removed to obtain high-quality clean reads. Filtering was conducted using fastp software (v0.23.4) with a Phred quality threshold of ≥ 20. Reads were first aligned to an rRNA database using Bowtie2 (version 2.2.8), and rRNA-aligned reads were excluded. The remaining clean reads were used for transcript assembly and gene expression quantification. A reference genome index was constructed, and paired-end clean reads were aligned to the reference genome (GRCh38) using HISAT2 (version 2.4) with default parameters. Mapped reads were assembled using StringTie (version 1.3.1) in a reference-guided mode, and raw expression counts were enumerated using featureCounts (v2.0.2). Transcript abundance was quantified as TPM using RSEM. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed with the R package gmodels (version 2.19.1). Differential expression analysis was conducted using DESeq2 R package (version 1.42.1), and genes or transcripts with an absolute log 2 fold change > 1 ( |log 2 (FC)|> 1) and an adjusted P -value (padj < 0.05) were considered differentially expressed. Functional enrichment analyses were carried out using clusterProfiler (version 4.10.1).
sections.measurement of high-density lipoprotein: The levels of HDL-C, LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT were measured using commercial assay kits according to the manufacturers’ instructions: HDL-C and LDL-C (Beyotime, S0213S), TC (Yeasen, 60723ES60), TG (Beyotime, S0219M), AST (Solarbio, BC1565), and ALT (Solarbio, BC1555). Absorbance was recorded using a Thermo Fisher Scientific microplate reader (A51119500C).
sections.oil red o staining: Oil Red O staining was used to assess lipid droplet accumulation in liver cells. Cells or tissues were first fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min and washed with PBS. Next, the fixed samples were treated with 0.5% Oil Red O solution prepared in isopropanol (Beyotime, C0157S) for 5 min at 37 °C in the dark. Finally, stained samples were then examined and imaged using a BX51 inverted OLYMPUS microscope equipped with a digital camera.
sections.mass spectrometry (ms): Protein bands from control HepG2 cells and those overexpressing Flag-METTL7A were cut from Coomassie-stained gels, destained, and subjected to in-gel digestion. Proteins were reduced, alkylated, and digested with trypsin (enzyme-to-protein ratio 1:50) at 37 °C for approximately 20 h. The resulting peptides were desalted, dried, and reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid (FA) before storage at − 20 °C. Peptide separation was carried out by nanoHPLC on a nanoElute system (Bruker) at 300 nL/min using a 25 cm × 75 μm, 1.9 μm C18 column (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Mobile phase A contained 0.1% FA in water, and mobile phase B consisted of 0.1% FA in 99.9% acetonitrile. The gradient program was: 0–18 min, 5–35% B (linear); 18–20 min, 35–80% B (linear); 20–30 min, 80% B (isocratic). MS was performed on a timsTOF Pro in positive ion mode (1.5 kV spray voltage) with a scan range of 100–1700 m/z. Data were collected in PASEF mode (eight MS/MS scans per cycle) with a cycle time of 0.95 s, charge states 0–5, and a dynamic exclusion of 24 s. Raw files (.d format) were analyzed using MaxQuant (v1.6.14) for protein identification against the appropriate databases.
sections.co-immunoprecipitation (co-ip): Cells were rinsed with ice-cold PBS and then lysed in pre-chilled RIPA buffer. The resulting lysates were scraped and transferred to centrifuge tubes. After continuous shaking on a platform at 4 °C for 20 min, the lysates were centrifuged. The supernatant was then collected as total cell lysate (TCL). For IP assays, the samples were mixed with Protein G Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10003D) pre-treated with either anti-HA (Proteintech, 66,006–2-Ig) or anti-FLAG (Proteintech, 66,008–4-Ig) antibody at 4 °C for 2 h. After three rounds of washing with lysis buffer, the beads were mixed with elution buffer for a few minutes, and the eluted proteins were collected, denatured, and analyzed via Western blotting.
sections.establishment of the masld/nafld mouse m: C57BL/6 J female mice 21 , 22 (6 weeks old) were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of the Basic Laboratory of the 900th Hospital. After one week of acclimation, the mice were randomly assigned to four groups using a computer-generated random number sequence, including Control, Model, Model + shNC, and Model + shMETTL7A, with six mice per group. Mice in the Control and Model groups received an intravenous injection of 0.1 mL sterile saline, while mice in the Model + shNC and Model + shMETTL7A groups were injected with 0.1 mL rAAV2/8 (5 × 10 11 vg, OBiO) carrying shNC or shMETTL7A under the control of a U6 promoter via the tail vein. The rAAV2/8 vector was selected to ensure high-efficiency transduction specifically targeting liver tissues. One week later, mice in the Control group were fed a standard chow diet, whereas those in the remaining groups were given a high-fat diet (HFD, Research Diets, D12492) for two months. At the end of the experiments, the mice were fasted for 12 h before being anesthetized with 5% isoflurane for induction and 1% isoflurane for maintenance. Orbital blood was collected for serum biochemical analysis. The mice were then euthanized, and liver tissues were harvested for imaging. Subsequently, half of each liver sample was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for histological analysis, while the remaining tissue was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA and protein extraction. To ensure unbiased evaluation, sample processing, histological examinations, and lipid quantification were performed by investigators blinded to the group allocations. All C57BL/6 J female mice were euthanized at approximately 4 months of age via cervical dislocation. At the time of sacrifice, the average body weight of the mice was approximately 25–28 g. The study adheres to the 3Rs (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) principles to minimize animal suffering. All animal experiments were approved by the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of 900th Hospital of PLA Joint Logistic Support Force (Code of Ethics: 2024–32).
sections.statistical analysis: GraphPad Prism (version 9) was utilized for data analysis and plotting. Data are shown as mean ± standard deviation (SD). In the bar-dot plots, each data point indicates values from a biological replicate, and values for MTT and qPCR assays reflect the mean of technical triplicates. The specific statistical tests applied for each quantification are described in the corresponding figure legends. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.mettl7a expression is upregulated in an: To investigate the potential role of METTL7A in MASLD/NAFLD, we first optimized the in vitro steatosis model conditions using a concentration gradient of OA. HepG2 and Huh7 cells were treated with various concentrations of OA for 24 h, and cell viability was evaluated using MTT assays. Based on the cell viability results and the efficiency of intracellular lipid deposition assessed by Oil Red O staining, optimal and non-toxic concentrations of 1 mM for HepG2 cells and 200 μM for Huh7 cells were selected for subsequent experiments, which align with widely used protocols to induce lipid accumulation 23 , 24 . Huh7 cells exhibited cytotoxicity above 200 μM, whereas HepG2 cells maintained high viability up to 1 mM. Both cell lines displayed marked intracellular lipid deposition as detected by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 1 A, B). qPCR and Western blotting revealed significant increases in METTL7A mRNA and protein levels in OA-treated HCC cells compared with controls (Fig. 1 C, D). These results suggest that METTL7A may contribute to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes. Fig. 1 METTL7A expression is elevated in an in vitro MASLD/NAFLD model. ( A ) MTT analysis of cell viability in HepG2 and Huh7 cells treated with a concentration gradient of oleic acid. ( B ) Representative Oil Red O staining images and corresponding quantification of intracellular lipid droplet areas in HepG2 and Huh7 cells treated with indicated concentrations of OA for 24 h. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) qPCR analysis of METTL7A mRNA levels in OA-treated versus control HepG2 and Huh7 cells. ( D ) Western blot analysis showing increased METTL7A protein expression following OA treatment. β-actin served as a loading control. Unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used for statistical significance evaluation. Mock refers to cells treated with an equivalent amount of the solvent used to prepare OA. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.mettl7a knockdown mitigates lipid accumu: To define METTL7A’s function in hepatic lipid metabolism, we generated three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs. qPCR analysis in HEK293T cells showed effective knockdown by all constructs, with shMETTL7A-1 achieving the greatest suppression (Fig. 2 A); thus, it was selected for further experiments. In both HepG2 and Huh7 cells, METTL7A depletion markedly reduced OA-induced lipid accumulation as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 2 B). MTT assays showed that METTL7A silencing partially rescued the OA-induced decrease in cell viability (Fig. 2 C). Consistent with reduced lipid accumulation, METTL7A knockdown significantly lowered LDL-C, TG, and TC levels while increasing HDL-C in OA-treated cells (Fig. 2 D). At the molecular scale, METTL7A depletion was confirmed by qPCR and Western blotting (Fig. 3 A, B). Moreover, METTL7A deficiency downregulated ACC and FAS expression while upregulating HSL in OA-treated hepatocytes (Fig. 3 B). These findings indicate that METTL7A acts as a positive regulator of lipid accumulation. Fig. 2 METTL7A knockdown reduces lipid accumulation and improves cell viability in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR validation of three METTL7A-targeting shRNAs in HEK293T cells, identifying shMETTL7A-1 as the most effective construct. ( B ) Oil Red O staining of HepG2 and Huh7 cells with or without METTL7A knockdown following OA treatment. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( C ) MTT assay showing that METTL7A depletion partially rescues OA-induced reduction in cell viability. ( D ) Biochemical measurements of LDL-C, TG, TC, and HDL-C levels in control and OA-treated cells with or without METTL7A silencing. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was used for P-value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 3 METTL7A knockdown alters lipogenic and lipolytic gene expression in OA-treated hepatocytes. ( A ) Western blotting validation of METTL7A knockdown efficiency in HepG2 and Huh7 cells with the specific treatments. ( B ) qPCR assessment of lipid metabolism–related genes, showing reduced ACC and FAS expression and increased HSL levels upon METTL7A depletion in cells under different treatments. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was utilized to determine P -values. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.depletion of mettl7a causes reduced expr: To delineate the mechanism by which METTL7A promotes lipid deposition in OA-treated HCC cells, we performed RNA-seq using control and METTL7A-deficient HepG2 cells exposed to OA for 24 h. Among the DEGs, PLIN5 attracted our attention due to its known function in hepatic lipid metabolism. qPCR and Western blotting validated the RNA-seq data, showing that PLIN5 expression was greatly decreased in OA-treated METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. Notably, PLIN5 expression was also strongly induced by OA treatment, similar to METTL7A (Fig. 4 A and B). We also investigated the activation of PI3K/AKT pathway, a key player in hepatic lipid metabolism. Western blotting indicated that the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (P-PI3K and P-AKT), which represents activation of the pathway, was enhanced by OA in both cell lines; however, this effect was nullified by METTL7A depletion (Fig. 4 C). These observations demonstrate that METTL7A facilitates lipid accumulation in the hepatocytes by inducing PLIN5 and the PI3K/AKT pathway. Fig. 4 METTL7A regulates PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT pathway activation during lipid loading in HCC cells exposed to OA. ( A ) qPCR analysis of PLIN5 expression in control and METTL7A-deficient cells treated with OA. ( B ) Western blot analysis confirming reduced PLIN5 protein levels upon METTL7A knockdown. ( C ) Western blot analysis showing increased phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT in response to OA treatment, and suppression of this activation by METTL7A depletion. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test was employed for statistical significance assessment. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.mettl7a interacts with sapcd2 in hcc cel: To further explore how METTL7A regulates PLIN5 and PI3K/AKT signaling, a preliminary MS screening was initially performed as an exploratory approach using control and Flag-METTL7A–expressing HepG2 cells, with candidates cross-referenced against PLIN5 interactors in BioGRID 25 . Among the candidates, SAPCD2 emerged as a candidate of interest (Fig. 5 A) because it is also reported to activate PI3K/AKT signaling 26 . Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP revealed a potential band corresponding to SAPCD2 (Fig. 5 B). Exogenous co-IP assays verified the interaction between overexpressed METTL7A and SAPCD2 in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 C). Furthermore, endogenous co-IP assays confirmed that native METTL7A physically interacts with endogenous SAPCD2 under physiological conditions in HepG2 and Huh7 cells (Fig. 5 D). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting revealed that METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells exhibited significantly reduced SAPCD2 expression (Fig. 5 E and F). These findings suggest that METTL7A may regulate PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT activation in hepatocytes through SAPCD2. Fig. 5 METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 and maintains its expression in HCC cells. ( A ) Venn diagram showing the 369 potential METTL7A-interacting proteins based on the MS results. ( B ) Coomassie blue staining of proteins pulled down by IP targeting the Flag-tag. The arrow points to the potential band corresponding to SAPCD2. ( C , D ) Co-IP demonstrating physical interaction between METTL7A and SAPCD2. TCL, total cell lysate. ( E , F ) qPCR and Western blot analyses showing reduced SAPCD2 expression in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. Unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used for statistical significance evaluation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.sapcd2 is required for oa-induced pi3k/a: To define the functional role of SAPCD2, we first validated its knockdown and overexpression efficiencies in hepatocytes (Fig. 6 A, B). Western blotting revealed that OA stimulation significantly upregulated METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 expression, alongside increased PI3K and AKT phosphorylation. SAPCD2 silencing suppressed OA-induced p-PI3K and p-AKT levels and abolished PLIN5 upregulation without altering METTL7A (Fig. 6 C, D). Conversely, SAPCD2 overexpression further enhanced PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and PLIN5 expression (Fig. 6 C, D). Consistent with these molecular changes, Oil Red O staining demonstrated that SAPCD2 knockdown significantly attenuated OA-induced intracellular lipid accumulation, whereas SAPCD2 overexpression further exacerbated lipid droplet deposition in both cell lines (Fig. 6 E). These results indicate that SAPCD2 acts downstream of METTL7A to mediate OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression. Fig. 6 SAPCD2 mediates OA-induced PI3K/AKT activation and PLIN5 expression. ( A , B ) Western blot analysis of SAPCD2 knockdown ( A ) and overexpression ( B ) efficiencies in hepatocytes. ( C , D ) Western blot analysis of SAPCD2, METTL7A, total/phosphorylated PI3K and AKT, and PLIN5 expressions in OA-stimulated HepG2 ( C ) and Huh7 ( D ) cells transfected with shSAPCD2 or SAPCD2 OE. ( E ) Oil Red O staining to evaluate intracellular lipid accumulation in OA-stimulated HepG2 and Huh7 cells transfected with shSAPCD2 or SAPCD2 OE. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.overexpression of sapcd2 rescues lipid a: To evaluate whether SAPCD2 mediates the lipogenic effects of METTL7A, we overexpressed SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HepG2 and Huh7 cells. SAPCD2 overexpression restored lipid accumulation in OA-treated METTL7A-knockdown cells, as shown by Oil Red O staining (Fig. 7 A). MTT assays indicated that cell viability decreased upon SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells (Fig. 7 B). Furthermore, SAPCD2-overexpressing METTL7A-deficient HCC cells expressed higher levels of LDL-C, TG, and TC, along with lower levels of HDL-C (Fig. 7 C). Additionally, qPCR and Western blotting uncovered that overexpression of SAPCD2 significantly increased the expression of PLIN5 in OA-induced METTL7A-deficient HCC cells (Fig. 8 A and B). qPCR also showed that SAPCD2 overexpression led to downregulated levels of HSL and upregulated expression of FAS and ACC (Fig. 8 A). Western blotting indicated that the PI3K/AKT pathway activation was enhanced by excessive SAPCD2 in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells exposed to OA (Fig. 8 B). These data suggest that SAPCD2 is a critical mediator of METTL7A’s role in promoting lipogenesis in OA-treated HCC cells. Fig. 7 SAPCD2 overexpression rescues lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient HCC cells. ( A ) Oil Red O staining showing upregulation of lipid accumulation in METTL7A-knockdown HepG2 and Huh7 cells upon SAPCD2 overexpression. Lipid droplet areas was performed using ImageJ software. ( B ) MTT assay showing reduced cell viability when SAPCD2 is overexpressed in METTL7A-deficient, OA-treated cells. ( C ) Biochemical analysis demonstrating increased LDL-C, TG, and TC and decreased HDL-C after SAPCD2 overexpression. One-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test were utilized for P -value calculation. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3). Fig. 8 SAPCD2 enhances PI3K/AKT activation and lipogenic gene expression in METTL7A-deficient hepatocytes. ( A ) qPCR showing that SAPCD2 overexpression reverses METTL7A knockdown–induced changes in PLIN5, FAS, ACC, and HSL expression. ( B ) Western blot analysis showing upregulation of PLIN5 expression and PI3K/AKT phosphorylation by SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient cells. Statistical analysis was done by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
sections.mettl7a knockdown alleviates hfd-induced: To validate these findings in vivo, we established a mouse model of MASLD/NAFLD and infected the mice with AAV carrying shNC or shMETTL7A. Compared to the control group, livers from the Model and Model + shNC groups appeared pale, consistent with steatosis, whereas the Model + shMETTL7A group exhibited darker liver coloration, suggesting reduced lipid content (Fig. 9 A). Histological analysis using H&E and Oil Red O staining confirmed that METTL7A knockdown substantially attenuated steatosis (Fig. 9 B and C). Biochemical assays revealed elevated LDL-C, TC, TG, AST, and ALT and reduced HDL-C in the Model and Model + shNC groups, all of which were partially normalized by METTL7A knockdown (Fig. 9 D). qPCR and Western blotting verified efficient METTL7A knockdown in the liver (Fig. 9 E and F). Expression of PLIN5, SAPCD2, FAS, and ACC was reduced, while HSL levels increased upon METTL7A silencing (Fig. 9 E and F). PI3K/AKT activation, elevated in the Model and Model + shNC groups, was markedly suppressed in METTL7A-deficient livers (Fig. 9 F). Collectively, these results demonstrate that METTL7A promotes hepatic lipid accumulation. Fig. 9 METTL7A knockdown alleviates HFD-induced hepatic steatosis in MASLD/NAFLD mice. ( A ) Liver morphology showing pale, steatotic livers in Model and Model + shNC mice, and reduced discoloration following AAV-shMETTL7A treatment. ( B , C ) H&E and Oil Red O staining showing reduced hepatic lipid accumulation in METTL7A-deficient mice. ( D ) Biochemical analysis of liver lipid parameters and serum liver enzymes (LDL-C, TC, TG, HDL-C, AST, ALT). ( E , F ) qPCR and Western blot showing decreased METTL7A, PLIN5, SAPCD2, ACC, and FAS, and increased HSL expression, along with reduced PI3K/AKT activation in shMETTL7A-treated mice. Oil Red O staining images were quantified using ImageJ software. P -value calculation employed one-way ANOVA and Tukey’s HSD post-hoc test. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3, N = 6 mice per group).
sections.discussion: In this study, we identify METTL7A as a previously unrecognized regulator of hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD progression. Although METTL7A is known as an m 6 A RNA methyltransferase implicated in cancer biology and also functions as a thiol methyltransferase in the liver, playing an essential role in drug metabolism, its metabolic functions in hepatocytes have remained unclear. Our findings demonstrate that METTL7A expression is markedly elevated during hepatocellular lipid loading and that METTL7A actively drives steatosis both in vitro and in vivo. These results broaden our understanding of METTL7A’s role in liver physiology. The mechanism by which lipid accumulation induces METTL7A overexpression in hepatocytes remains unknown. Previous studies show that METTL7A mRNA expression is regulated by several noncoding RNAs, including miR-6807-5p, LINC01123, miR-654-5p, and miR-27a, across different biological contexts 27 – 29 . Notably, these noncoding RNAs also modulate hepatic lipid metabolism and MASLD/NAFLD 30 , 31 , raising the possibility that they may regulate steatosis by targeting METTL7A. Additionally, METTL7A transcription can be influenced by DNA methylation 32 , but whether this mechanism contributes to its increased expression under steatotic conditions remains to be clarified. Importantly, validation of METTL7A upregulation in liver tissues from MASLD/NAFLD patients will strengthen its clinical relevance. To elucidate the mechanism underlying METTL7A’s lipogenic function in hepatocytes, we performed transcriptomic analyses and identified PLIN5 as a key candidate. PLIN5 is a central regulator of intracellular lipid metabolism, essential for lipid storage and oxidation 33 – 35 . Consistent with METTL7A’s pro-lipogenic role, PLIN5 knockout mice exhibit impaired lipid accumulation in the heart and skeletal muscle and show resistance to MASLD/NAFLD and HCC, whereas PLIN5 overexpression induces cardiac steatosis 20 , 35 . In our study, METTL7A silencing markedly reduced PLIN5 expression and intracellular lipid accumulation, suggesting that PLIN5 may serve as a critical mediator of METTL7A function. Nevertheless, functional rescue experiments are needed to confirm this hypothesis. Given that PLIN5 transcription is sensitive to upstream signaling, we examined the PI3K/AKT pathway, a canonical regulator of hepatic lipogenesis that promotes PLIN5 expression in OA-treated HepG2 cells 36 . OA stimulation activated PI3K/AKT signaling, whereas METTL7A knockdown abolished this activation, indicating that METTL7A acts upstream of PI3K/AKT and PLIN5 to promote lipid deposition. To further investigate how METTL7A influences PI3K/AKT signaling, we conducted MS-based interactome profiling and identified SAPCD2 as a METTL7A-interacting protein. SAPCD2 is known to enhance PI3K/AKT pathway activity and has been implicated in metabolic reprogramming in cancer 37 . In this study, we demonstrate that METTL7A not only preserves SAPCD2 expression but also physically interacts with it in hepatocytes. Crucially, SAPCD2 overexpression in METTL7A-deficient cells restored lipid accumulation, reversed changes in lipogenic and lipolytic gene expression, reactivated PI3K/AKT signaling, and increased PLIN5 levels. These findings highlight SAPCD2 as a central mediator of METTL7A-driven lipogenesis. However, the biological significance of the METTL7A–SAPCD2 interaction remains unclear. Since SAPCD2 is predicted to interact with PLIN5, it will be important to determine whether METTL7A, SAPCD2, and PLIN5 form a functional complex in hepatocytes. Additionally, although METTL7A is recognized as a dual methyltransferase, our current data primarily highlight its physical interaction with SAPCD2 and its necessity for maintaining the SAPCD2/PI3K/AKT/PLIN5 axis. Whether this regulation is strictly dependent on METTL7A’s enzymatic activity or involves a scaffolding function remains an open question. Future work involving the characterization of catalytic-dead METTL7A mutants or m6A-specific assays will be required to fully dissect these biochemical nuances. Furthermore, while our present findings establish METTL7A as a critical regulator of early-stage hepatic steatosis, its precise involvement in advanced MASH progression and immune cell infiltration warrants further systemic metabolic profiling in future studies.
sections.conclusion: Collectively, our findings identify METTL7A as a novel regulator of hepatic lipid homeostasis. Mechanistically, METTL7A interacts with SAPCD2 to sustain its expression, thereby activating the PI3K/AKT pathway and enhancing PLIN5-mediated lipid storage. These results suggest that METTL7A may represent an attractive therapeutic target for MASLD/NAFLD. Future studies are needed to determine whether targeting METTL7A confers therapeutic benefits in more advanced disease stages, including MASH/NASH and fibrosis.
