title: Artificial intelligence-driven real-time assistance in minimally invasive surgery: a technology-oriented narrative review
abstract: Although minimally invasive surgery is a standard surgical approach because of its proven benefits to patient outcomes, it imposes increased cognitive demands on surgeons because of limited visualization, lack of tactile feedback, and constraints in instrument manipulation. These challenges have been partially mitigated by robot-assisted surgery, while recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have established intraoperative AI as a key technology enabling real-time support of surgical perception, decision-making, and instrument control. Here, we review the key AI technologies used during the intraoperative phase of endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery, including anatomical and lesion recognition, instrument detection and tracking, surgical phase and workflow analysis, real-time tissue characterization, image-guided and augmented navigation, AI-assisted instrument control, and multimodal event detection. We also discuss key clinical integration challenges and future research directions focused on foundation and self-supervised learning paradigms, and human–AI collaborative system design.

sections.introduction: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), which is standard practice in many surgical specialties, offers substantial clinical benefits like reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stays, faster recovery, and lower infection rates by minimizing incision size and tissue disruption. It includes various techniques, e.g., laparoscopy, endoscopy, and robot-assisted surgery (RAS), aiming to achieve therapeutic goals with minimal invasiveness [ 1 ]. However, MIS poses significant challenges for surgeons, including the lack of direct operative field visualization, limited tactile feedback, and constrained degrees of freedom for surgical instruments. For instance, endo-laparoscopic surgery relies almost exclusively on two-dimensional (2D) or otherwise restricted visual input, making it difficult to interpret complex anatomical structures and execute precise maneuvers, as well as increasing the surgeon’s cognitive load. RAS, which was developed in response to these limitations of MIS, extends the surgeon’s perceptual and motor capabilities within a minimally invasive environment. RAS can be viewed as a technological evolution that augments human dexterity and precision through enhanced visualization, tremor filtration, motion scaling, and intuitive instrument control, rather than as a mere subcategory of MIS [ 2 ]. Robotic systems contribute to improved clinical outcomes like reduced postoperative complications and shorter recovery times by enabling surgeons to perform complex procedures with greater precision and efficiency while maintaining low invasiveness [ 3 , 4 ]. Consequently, robotic platforms are a central component of modern MIS [ 5 ]. The da Vinci Surgical System, developed by Intuitive Surgical in the late 1990s and first introduced clinically in 1999, is the most prominent example of an RAS platform [ 6 ]. This system is widely adopted worldwide, and it integrates surgeon-controlled robotic arms, an ergonomic console, and high-definition three-dimensional (3D) endoscopic imaging to precisely replicate the surgeon’s hand movements with enhanced dexterity and tremor suppression [ 7 , 8 ]. By supporting meticulous tissue manipulation and suturing through small incisions, while providing a stable and immersive operative view, this configuration enables complex procedures to be performed with greater control and improved outcomes when compared with conventional laparoscopic techniques. Although the da Vinci system has dominated the robotic surgery market for more than two decades, with over 7,500 installations worldwide and more than 11 million procedures performed as of early 2023 [ 9 , 10 ], the expiration of key patents and growing demand for more flexible and cost-effective robotic solutions have accelerated the emergence of alternative platforms, including Hugo RAS, Versius, Senhance, Dexter, and MONARCH [ 11 ]. These next-generation systems increasingly incorporate modular architectures, enhanced data integration, haptic feedback, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled functionalities, reflecting ongoing efforts to improve flexibility, accessibility, and technological capabilities in robotic surgery [ 9 , 11 ]. Representative commercial and emerging robotic surgical platforms are summarized in Table 1 . The integration of AI into the intraoperative phase has built on these advances and is one of the most significant recent developments in MIS and RAS. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, which have emerged as core components of this evolution, enable the analysis of large-scale, multimodal intraoperative data in real time [ 12 – 14 ]. AI-driven systems can support intraoperative decision-making through real-time visual perception, lesion and anatomical structure recognition, surgical instrument tracking, workflow and phase recognition, navigation assistance, safety validation, and semiautonomous instrument control [ 15 – 17 ]. Thus, the convergence of AI and robotic systems extends the surgeon’s capabilities beyond mechanical precision and can potentially enhance intraoperative safety, personalize surgical strategies, and improve overall surgical outcomes. Currently, most clinically deployed robotic systems do not operate in fully autonomous surgery. Instead, they function as assistive technologies that preserve surgeon-led decision-making, while compensating for perception, dexterity, or experience limitations. Nevertheless, the increasing role of intraoperative AI as a foundational component of future surgical systems is underscored by the rapid growth of research on DL-based surgical video analysis and autonomous or semiautonomous robotic functions [ 18 – 21 ]. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the AI technologies used during the intraoperative phase of endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery. We systematically examine major application domains based on diverse data modalities, including surgical video, robotic telemetry and kinematic logs, instrument and force sensors, and operating-room contextual and physiological signals. We also highlight persistent technical, clinical, and regulatory challenges that limit broader integration. This review aims to clarify the evolving role of intraoperative AI as a key driver of next-generation minimally invasive and robotic surgical practice by synthesizing current advances and outlining future research directions.
sections.literature search strategy: This review focuses on AI technologies applied during the intraoperative phase of endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in major scientific databases, including PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Google Scholar, to identify relevant clinical and engineering-oriented studies. The search covered articles published between January 2011 and December 2025, and the final search was performed on December 15, 2025. Only studies published in English were included. The search strategy combined keywords related to intraoperative AI and MIS, including “intraoperative AI,” “laparoscopic vision,” “robotic surgery,” “surgical navigation,” “augmented reality,” “surgical workflow recognition,” and “autonomous or semiautonomous surgical systems.” The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) studies focusing on endo-laparoscopic or robotic surgery; (2) studies in which AI methods were applied during surgery in real-time or near real-time; and (3) studies addressing intraoperative perception, decision support, guidance, control, or safety-related tasks. Studies limited to preoperative planning, simulation-only environments, or postoperative outcome prediction without intraoperative relevance were excluded. A total of 642 studies were initially identified, and 621 remained after removing duplicates. Following title and abstract screening, 271 studies were assessed for full-text eligibility. Finally, 69 representative studies were included in this review based on their methodological relevance, clinical significance, and technical contribution. Given the rapid evolution and heterogeneity of intraoperative AI research, this study adopts a technology-oriented narrative review approach rather than a formal systematic review or meta-analysis. The selected studies were categorized into key technical domains to provide a structured overview of current methodologies, clinical applications, and future research directions.
sections.intraoperative artificial intelligence t: Recent advances in AI have enabled a broad range of intraoperative applications in endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery, including lesion and anatomical structure recognition, surgical tool detection, workflow analysis, tissue characterization, image-guided navigation, and autonomous or semiautonomous instrument control. These technologies aim to enhance surgical perception, decision-making, and procedural safety through the real-time analysis of intraoperative data. Although AI-enabled medical devices have achieved substantial clinical adoption in radiology and computer-aided diagnostic systems, the translation of similar technologies into real-time surgical assistance remains comparatively limited despite increasing research activity and technological progress [ 22 , 23 ]. To provide an overview of the current evidence, Table 2 summarizes representative studies on intraoperative AI according to their primary tasks, methodologies, and data types. Together, these studies illustrate both the rapid technological progress and the remaining technical, clinical, and regulatory challenges that hinder broader clinical adoption. The following sections review the major application domains of intraoperative AI in endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery.
sections.lesion and anatomical structure recognit: The foundation of intraoperative AI technologies lies in real-time visual perception and scene understanding of surgical videos. Endoscopic camera images are the sole source of intraoperative information in MIS. Therefore, AI-based visual recognition plays a critical role in compensating for the inherent limitations in human perception. However, frequent visual obstructions by smoke or bleeding, dynamic illumination changes, occlusion by surgical instruments, and continuous deformation of organs during manipulation make understanding surgical video streams challenging. Consequently, robust DL models capable of reliably recognizing lesions and anatomical structures are the cornerstone of the intraoperative AI pipeline [ 24 ]. Lesion recognition is the process of detecting, classifying, and visualizing clinically relevant abnormalities like tumors, metastatic lesions, inflammatory changes, and fibrosis or adhesions. Failing to identify subtle or atypical lesions can directly affect surgical outcomes and prognosis. Accordingly, to reduce observational errors by surgeons, recent studies have explored AI-based systems that automatically detect peritoneal surface metastases or intra-abdominal metastatic lesions from laparoscopic exploration videos [ 25 ]. While lesion recognition is often performed using conventional RGB images, integrating near-infrared fluorescence imaging can substantially enhance lesion-to-background contrast. In clinical practice, indocyanine green is the most widely used fluorescent agent, and it has been applied to tumor detection, margin delineation, anatomical liver segmentation, and biliary structure visualization during procedures like hepatectomy. AI techniques have been recently introduced to quantitatively analyze fluorescence signals or to automatically segment tumor regions in fluorescence-guided surgical images. As a result, AI convergence with fluorescence-guided surgery is increasingly regarded as a key extension of lesion recognition methodologies in intraoperative settings [ 26 ]. Lesion and organ recognition focuses on determining the presence of specific targets, while segmentation aims to precisely delineate their boundaries at the pixel level. Using DL to automatically segment organs and anatomical structures in laparoscopic images enables a wide range of real-time assistance functions, including overlaying anatomical contours onto the surgical field and highlighting regions that should be avoided to prevent iatrogenic injury. Early studies primarily evaluated the feasibility of convolutional neural network (CNN)-based models in automatically segmenting individual organs using selected laparoscopic video frames. Subsequent research expanded towards semantic segmentation approaches that comprehensively segment multiple organs and tissue types across the entire surgical scene [ 27 , 28 ]. Efforts have also been made to improve the stability and accuracy of organ boundary estimation, e.g., kidney edge detection, for reliable foundational information for image-guided navigation systems [ 29 ].
sections.surgical tool detection and segmentation: Surgical tools, the primary actuators that directly execute surgical interventions, are one of the most critical components in operative procedures. Therefore, accurate surgical instrument recognition and tracking are as essential as the identification of organs and lesions, constituting a core element of intraoperative AI systems [ 30 ]. Real-time estimation of the position, shape, pose, and temporal motion is required for reliable tracking of surgical tools within the surgical field. This information is foundational data for higher-level AI functionalities, including surgical navigation, automation, and safety assessment. Surgical instrument detection aims to determine the presence of instruments within an image or to localize specific tools using bounding boxes or landmark representations. Early studies introduced CNN-based approaches to detect instruments and their location in laparoscopic or robot-assisted surgical videos, primarily focusing on demonstrating feasibility for real-time deployment [ 31 ]. Subsequent research extended these approaches to address precise manipulation requirements in robotic surgery via instrument-specific landmark detection or tool position estimation using stereo vision techniques [ 32 ]. Anchor-free CNN-based architectures have recently been proposed to enable faster and more robust real-time surgical instrument detection in robot-assisted surgical environments [ 33 ]. While instrument detection focuses on identifying tools or their approximate location, instrument segmentation aims to distinguish instrument regions from surrounding tissues and background, and to delineate their precise shapes at the pixel level. Surgical instruments can be segmented at different levels, including binary, semantic, and instance segmentation, where individual instruments are separately identified. Generally, detection corresponds to coarse-level localization centered on instrument position, whereas segmentation enables more precise surgical assistance by clearly defining boundaries between instruments and adjacent tissues. Numerous studies have reported CNN-based approaches for instrument segmentation in laparoscopic and robotic surgery videos, including methods combining real clinical images with synthetic data [ 34 ]. Unsupervised or weakly supervised segmentation techniques employing approaches like cycle-consistent adversarial networks and semantic diffusion have been proposed to mitigate the high cost of manual annotation [ 35 , 36 ]. Multiple instruments appear simultaneously and partially occlude or intersect with one another in real surgical scenes, necessitating multi-instrument instance segmentation to distinguish each tool as an independent object. The “mask-then-classify” strategy, a representative approach with demonstrated robust performance in complex multi-tool environments, provides the basis for higher-level analyses, such as instrument collision detection and tool-specific motion analysis [ 37 ]. Furthermore, modeling tool–tissue interactions to jointly identify the instrument, target tissue, and the surgical action being performed [ 38 ] is regarded as key to enabling technology for improved intraoperative safety and advancement towards semiautonomous and autonomous surgical systems. Overall, CNNs are the most widely adopted DL models for surgical instrument detection and segmentation. Additionally, autoencoder-based architectures have been employed for dimensionality reduction and representation learning, particularly in segmentation tasks and unsupervised learning [ 36 ]. Collectively, these DL approaches improve the accuracy and robustness of surgical instrument perception and are essential building blocks for the next generation of intelligent surgical assistance and automation technologies.
sections.procedure and surgical phase recognition: Procedure and surgical phase recognition refers to techniques that automatically interpret the current stage and temporal context of an ongoing operation based on surgical video and instrument information. Surgical phase recognition enables classification of the current operative state by integrating visual features with the motion of surgical instruments, and it can be extended to real-time, context-aware assistance, including subsequent step anticipation and situation-aware decision support [ 39 ]. Early studies focused on classifying surgical phases using frame-level visual features extracted from surgical videos. Temporal models combining CNN-based spatial features, recurrent neural networks, and long short-term memory (LSTM) architectures have been widely adopted to better capture the continuity and the sequential structure of surgical workflows [ 40 , 41 ]. These approaches have evolved beyond coarse phase recognition towards the automatic segmentation and recognition of finer-grained surgical gestures and procedural steps within each phase [ 42 ]. An increasing number of studies have recently incorporated kinematic data, e.g., instrument position, velocity, and joint angles acquired from robotic surgical systems in conjunction with video data. Trajectory segmentation and motion analysis enable quantitative characterization of instrument movement patterns, contributing to learning from demonstration, skill analysis, and improved accuracy in surgical context recognition [ 43 ]. Such trajectory-based analyses have been extended to tasks like knot tying, path planning, and autonomous or semiautonomous tool manipulation, which are closely related to surgical automation [ 44 ]. In parallel, surgical phase recognition has progressed towards context-aware assistance that accounts for instrument usage sparsity and uncertainty, supporting early anomalous event detection and the prediction of surgical workflow evolution [ 45 ]. Procedure and surgical phase recognition technologies have collectively become fundamental building blocks for understanding surgical workflow, objective skill assessment, intelligent intraoperative assistance, and development of semiautonomous and autonomous surgical systems.
sections.real-time tissue characterization: Real-time tissue characterization, which is essential for optimal surgical outcomes while minimizing unintended tissue damage and complications, is a critical component of intraoperative AI. Because tissue morphology and spatial relationships continuously change during surgery, surgeons must make rapid decisions under constrained visual conditions with limited or no tactile feedback. In this context, DL/ML models play a crucial role by analyzing real-time video streams and intraoperatively acquired imaging data to promptly classify tissues and characterize their properties, thereby supporting intraoperative decision-making. Real-time tissue characterization includes a range of tasks, including vessel segmentation, tissue boundary detection, classification of healthy versus pathological (e.g., cancerous) tissues, uncertainty-aware segmentation, and modeling tissue retraction and deformation. These systems can distinguish different tissue types, such as normal tissue, tumors, and vascular structures, based on their visual appearance, texture, and morphological features by leveraging advanced image processing techniques together with ML and DL models. Real-time identification and segmentation of high-risk structures, e.g., blood vessels, is critical for reducing intraoperative bleeding and defining safe operating regions. Real-time vessel segmentation and reconstruction techniques have been integrated with virtual fixtures to support safe instrument manipulation in microsurgical and robot-assisted surgical environments [ 46 ]. In parallel, DL-based approaches for automatic classification of healthy and pathological tissues have been investigated, further expanding the applicability of real-time tissue characterization in surgical assistance [ 47 ]. Among DL-based approaches, the U-Net architecture is the most widely adopted framework for real-time tissue segmentation and characterization. Spatiotemporal U-Net variants combined with LSTM modules have also been proposed to incorporate the temporal information inherent in surgical videos [ 48 ]. Additionally, generative adversarial networks and various CNN variants have been employed to improve segmentation accuracy and generalization performance. Beyond tissue recognition, these techniques have demonstrated the potential to enable autonomous functions, such as active tissue retraction and manipulation in robot-assisted MIS, highlighting their relevance for the development of semiautonomous and autonomous surgical systems [ 49 ].
sections.image-guided navigation and augmented gu: Image-guided navigation is a representative intraoperative AI application aimed at enhancing the surgeon’s spatial awareness during surgery by registering intraoperative images with preoperative imaging data, such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging, and intuitively presenting internal anatomical structures. Early approaches largely relied on manual processes to register preoperative 3D CT models with 2D laparoscopic images. DL-based methods have recently been introduced to automate key steps, including 3D model construction, structure identification in CT images, and corresponding structure detection in real-time surgical videos. These AI-driven 2D/3D registration techniques, which include image-to-image and image-to-patient registration, enable more robust and accurate alignment, even in realistic surgical environments characterized by organ deformation and motion [ 50 , 51 ]. Fig. 1 shows a representative AI-based 2D/3D registration pipeline for image-guided navigation combining segmentation-based position and scale estimation with learning-based or tracking-based orientation estimation to generate real-time 3D overlays on endoscopic video [ 51 ]. Such frameworks highlight how DL can support initialization and continuous update of anatomical registration during surgery. The registered 3D anatomical information is typically presented as augmented reality (AR) overlays on the live surgical view, allowing surgeons to visualize critical anatomical structures, lesion locations, resection margins, and risk regions in real time. Navigation systems that integrate real-time 3D model registration with AR overlays improve intraoperative visualization, support precise target localization and access path planning, and reduce the operating surgeon’s cognitive load. Recent studies have proposed AR guidance systems that automatically generate patient-specific 3D models from DL-based organ and lesion segmentation and overlay them directly onto live endoscopic video streams [ 52 , 53 ]. Additionally, AI-based augmented guidance frameworks can integrate outputs from multiple intraoperative AI modules, including lesion and organ recognition and segmentation, surgical instrument segmentation and tracking, instrument trajectory analysis, tissue characterization, validation of the critical view of safety [ 54 ], and risk zone identification. This integrated information can be extended through virtual fixtures to target localization, optimal trajectory guidance, and the definition of safe operating regions, thereby simultaneously improving surgical precision and minimizing unintended tissue injury. Collectively, image-guided navigation and AR-based augmented guidance are core technologies that enable intelligent surgical navigation and the development of robot-assisted, semiautonomous, and autonomous surgical systems.
sections.artificial intelligence-assisted and sem: AI-based motion assistance aims to compensate for the surgeon’s physical and cognitive limitations by enhancing the stability and precision of instrument manipulation. Representative techniques include tremor reduction, motion scaling, and virtual fixtures, which are particularly effective in robot-assisted surgical environments. Tremor reduction and motion scaling stabilize fine instrument movements by attenuating involuntary hand motion and scaling the surgeon’s inputs, thereby enabling precise manipulation. These assistive control strategies preserve the surgeon’s intent while suppressing unintended instrument motions, thereby improving safety in micro-suturing and procedures performed near critical neurovascular structures. Furthermore, shared control and virtual fixture paradigms prevent inadvertent entry into risk zones and maintain stable tool paths by allowing AI systems to guide or constrain instrument motion based on predefined safe regions or optimal trajectories. Such approaches are regarded as collaborative assistance strategies, whereby AI supports the surgeon through human–AI collaboration, rather than replacing them. Task automation, the most advanced application of intraoperative AI, focuses on well-defined subtasks, such as suturing, knot tying, cutting, and camera control. Most systems adopt a semiautonomous approach rather than full autonomy, with AI performing repetitive or standardized surgical actions under direct surgeon supervision. Reliable workflow and surgical phase recognition, together with objective skill assessment, are a fundamental prerequisite for such automation. CNN- and LSTM-based models have been widely used to recognize the current surgical phase and activity from operative videos, and to anticipate subsequent actions, thereby determining when automation can be safely applied and to what extent [ 55 , 56 ]. Autonomous workflow recognition plays a critical role in structurally understanding the flow of tasks and resources in the operating room and in enabling context-aware assistance [ 57 – 59 ]. Skill assessment functions as a safety-critical control layer that dynamically modulates the level of automation. AI systems can adapt the degree of automation or disengage automated functions when necessary, by quantifying the surgeon’s stability, consistency, and efficiency based on instrument tracking and trajectory analysis [ 60 – 63 ]. This paradigm enables human-in-the-loop automation, maintaining the surgeon’s decision-making authority while reducing their cognitive workload. Additionally, task automation is closely linked to surgical planning. For example, path-planning algorithms based on preoperative CT imaging can be used to recommend or partially automate instrument trajectories during specific surgical stages [ 64 ]. Collectively, safely governed by workflow recognition and skill assessment, task automation has emerged as a central component of semiautonomous surgical systems.
sections.event detection using multimodal signals: Multimodal signal-based event detection, a key extension of intraoperative AI beyond visual perception, aims to enable early identification of abnormal situations and potential complications during surgery. Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating surgical video and kinematic data from robotic systems, force/torque signals, audio streams, and physiological biosignals into DL frameworks can substantially improve the accuracy and reliability of intraoperative event recognition by capturing complementary aspects of the surgical process [ 65 – 67 ]. A representative experimental setup for multimodal signal acquisition in robotic surgery combines synchronized visual, kinematic, and force measurements during controlled tool–tissue interactions [ 68 ]. A da Vinci Research Kit is used in this setup to acquire camera images, robotic motion data, and contact force signals from an artificial silicone tissue mounted on a force-sensing platform. Multimodal datasets can be collected to model normal and abnormal interaction patterns by systematically varying instrument positions and configurations. Physiological signals like electrocardiography and photoplethysmography, which reflect real-time changes in a patient’s systemic condition, can be leveraged to detect early signs of bleeding, pain responses, or cardiovascular instability. In parallel, kinematic data, including instrument position, velocity, acceleration, and joint angles, provide critical cues for identifying abnormal instrument manipulation, abrupt trajectory changes, or repetitive error patterns. These signals enable the detection of deviations from the expected surgical workflow when combined with surgical phase and workflow recognition. Time series-based anomaly detection models that fuse visual, kinematic, and physiological information can learn subtle temporal patterns associated with emerging adverse events, allowing warning issuance before such events are clinically evident to the surgeon. This facilitates timely intervention, mitigates the severity of complications, and contributes to improved patient outcomes.
sections.challenges and future directions: It is essential to address algorithmic performance, practical constraints, and the requirements of real surgical environments for clinical translation of intraoperative AI. One of the most critical challenges is real-time performance under resource constraints. Functions like AR overlays, surgical phase recognition, skill assessment, and closed-loop robotic assistance must operate with minimal latency to avoid disrupting surgical workflow. Even small delays can interfere with surgical flow and decision-making, particularly in applications involving semiautonomous actions like tissue retraction or instrument guidance. Therefore, achieving an appropriate balance between model complexity and real-time deployability remains an important problem [ 15 , 49 ]. Data availability, quality, and standardization are also fundamental challenges. High-quality, large-scale surgical datasets remain limited, and standardized protocols for data acquisition, annotation, and sharing across institutions are lacking [ 69 ]. However, some studies have constructed task-specific datasets for skill evaluation or adverse event analysis, often combining kinematic and procedural data [ 70 ]. Multimodal datasets integrating video, robotic kinematics, and physiological signals face additional obstacles, including heterogeneous data formats, sensor noise, incomplete metadata, and stringent anonymization requirements. Because of these limitations, models are frequently trained on small, non-representative datasets, which constrains their generalizability and clinical reliability. Generalization and transferability across surgical procedures, platforms, and environments are also major challenges. Many DL models demonstrate performance degradation when applied to different endoscopic systems, unfamiliar tissue types, or new operating room conditions. Translation is further complicated by the gap between simulation-based training and real clinical deployment. Addressing these issues will require robust domain adaptation strategies, semi-supervised and self-supervised learning paradigms, and data augmentation techniques capable of capturing anatomical and procedural variability across patients and institutions [ 15 ]. Regulatory, ethical, and liability considerations play a decisive role in the adoption of intraoperative AI. AI-assisted and semiautonomous surgical systems can have serious consequences in case of errors, necessitating rigorous evaluation frameworks and clear accountability structures. Recent efforts, e.g., the IDEAL (Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, and Long-term study) framework for surgical robotics, emphasize staged development, comparative evaluation, and long-term monitoring to ensure safety and effectiveness throughout the lifecycle of robotic surgical technologies [ 71 ]. Furthermore, data privacy issues become increasingly salient as advanced analyses incorporate physiological signals and detailed behavioral data [ 69 ]. Finally, human–AI trust and interpretability remain critical barriers to widespread clinical acceptance. The black box nature of many DL models limits the surgeon’s confidence and hinders meaningful integration into decision-making processes. Clinicians often require transparent, intuitive explanations to understand why a particular output or recommendation was generated, even when AI systems demonstrate strong predictive performance, e.g., in skill assessment or workflow analysis. Explainable AI and explainable robotics approaches that highlight contributing video frames, instrument trajectories, or decision constraints are therefore essential for fostering trust and enabling effective human–AI collaboration in the operating room [ 72 ]. Future research should prioritize foundation and self-supervised learning for surgical video representation, multimodal fusion of visual, kinematic, and physiological data, and human-centered AI system design that explicitly accounts for clinical safety, regulatory compliance, and the surgeon’s trust. It is crucial to address these challenges for intraoperative AI to evolve from experimental prototypes to reliable, interpretable, and widely adopted tools in routine surgical practice.
sections.conclusion: AI is fundamentally reshaping the paradigm of intraoperative decision-making by combining real-time visual perception, decision support, instrument assistance, and safety validation within the surgical workflow. AI-driven intraoperative assistance enables a more accurate recognition of anatomy and lesions, context-aware understanding of surgical workflow, and safer, more precise instrument manipulation in endo-laparoscopic and robotic surgery through motion assistance and semiautonomous functions. As they mature, these technologies hold the potential to simultaneously improve surgical accuracy, safety, and efficiency, while reducing the surgeon’s cognitive burden. Continued progress in real-time performance, data standardization, generalizability, regulatory readiness, and interpretability will be essential to ensure clinical adoption. This will position intraoperative AI as a core decision-support framework and a defining component of future surgical practice.

title: Impact of different PSMA PET-based eligibility criteria on outcome of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA radioligand therapy using [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7/[ 18 F]rhPSMA-7.3 (Flotufolastat)
abstract: Background [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA radioligand therapy (RLT) is key in treating metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Various PSMA agents and eligibility criteria for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT have been described. We retrospectively assessed applicability and outcomes using Blue Earth Therapeutics’ (BET) phase I study criteria with [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7 and Flotufolastat ([ 18 F]rhPSMA-7.3), comparing them to VISION trial-based PSMA PET/CT criteria. Patients eligible for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT, as assessed by an interdisciplinary board, were retrospectively stratified into four groups based on whether their PSMA PET scans with Flotufolastat met BET (B + /B-) and/or VISION (V + /V-) criteria. Outcome parameters like PSA response, PSA progression-free survival (PSA-PFS), and overall survival (OS) were compared, and reasons for (in-)eligibility by BET or VISION were analyzed. Results In total, 191 mCRPC patients from our institutional database were included, of which 138 underwent [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7.3 and 53 [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7. 161 (84.3%) met both criteria (V + /B +), 13 (6.8%) were ineligible (V-/B-), and 17 (8.9%) met VISION but not BET criteria (V + /B-). No patient was BET-eligible without also fulfilling VISION criteria. Of the 30 patients excluded by BET criteria, 17 (56.7%) lacked the “majority” tumor volume criterion; 10/13 (76.9%) excluded by VISION had visceral metastases with lower PSMA expression than the liver. In the subgroups V + /B + , V + /B-, and V-/B-, a PSA response > 50% was present in 62/157 (39.5%), 2/17 (11.8%), and 0/13 (0%) patients, respectively. V + /B + patients had the significantly longest PSA-PFS compared to V + /B- and V-/B- (PSA-PFS: 4.3 months (95% CI 3.4 – 5.2) vs. 1.5 months (95% CI 1.4 – 1.6) vs. 2.8 months (95% CI 0.0 – 6.5), p = 0.002) and a trend towards longer OS (14.9 vs. 13.1 vs. 7.7 months, p = 0.065). Conclusion Multiple similarities between BET and VISION eligibility criteria (V + /B +) prior to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT were observed, with the majority of patients fulfilling both. Positivity in both criteria was associated with the best outcome. Data from our pilot cohort suggest that the criteria for BET’s phase I trial select patients more strictly for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT than VISION criteria, while OS did not significantly differ between the three different groups. sections.introduction: [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA radioligand therapy (RLT) has become a cornerstone for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) [ 1 – 3 ]. [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT is highly effective with low toxicity [ 2 , 4 , 5 ] and was also recently FDA-approved in mCRPC prior to first-line chemotherapy [ 6 ]. Patients who receive [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT usually undergo prior PET imaging to determine target expression for treatment suitability and agents such as [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11, [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7.3 (POSLUMA®), and [ 18 F]DCFPyL (Pylarify®) are commonly used to screen for sufficient PSMA-ligand uptake [ 7 ]. However, according to the SNMMI/EANM guidelines, all PSMA agents are suitable for selecting patients for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT [ 8 ]. To date, the PET-based criteria used to select patients are frequently inconsistent in clinical routine and often even differ between prospective clinical trials. In 2021, the VISION trial, a multicenter randomized phase III study involving 831 patients with mCRPC, assessed the effectiveness of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 plus standard of care compared to standard of care alone. Before treatment, patients underwent [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT imaging to confirm PSMA-positive status and were only admitted to therapy if they fulfilled a set of PSMA PET-based criteria. The trial findings demonstrated significantly longer overall survival (OS) and radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) for patients receiving [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 than the standard of care alone [ 2 ]. [ 177 Lu]Lu-rhPSMA-10.1 is another therapeutic PSMA-targeting agent that has shown promising results for treating mCRPC [ 9 – 11 ]. It has already been demonstrated in patients treated with up to 6 cycles that [ 177 Lu]Lu-rhPSMA-10.1 displays moderately low toxicity and encouraging declines in PSA levels [ 10 , 11 ]. This agent is currently being explored in a prospective, multicenter, non-randomized trial by Blue Earth Therapeutics ( NCT05413850 , Registration Date: 20/05/2022). Patients in this trial undergo a Flotufolastat PET scan prior to therapy to assess treatment eligibility, and are required to present with at least one PET/CT-visible lesion with a PSMA expression score higher than liver uptake. They are excluded from therapy if they show any of the following: lymph node > 10 mm short axis and uptake ≤ blood pool, bone metastasis with soft tissue component with uptake ≤ blood pool, visceral metastasis > 10 mm long axis and uptake ≤ liver, or majority of all metastases (based on a visual assessment) ≤ liver. Considering the frequently high cost of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT and the sometimes limited benefit, careful patient selection is important to optimize the average benefit per patient. It has been demonstrated that PSMA PET/CT-related findings, such as specific types of metastases (i.e., visceral metastases), low SUVs in PSMA PET, or PSMA-negative tumor lesions, are predictive factors linked to unfavorable treatment outcomes and responses to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT [ 12 – 15 ]. For that reason, the 2021 TheraP trial, based on previous findings [ 16 ], excluded patients with FDG-positive/PSMA-negative (discordant) lesions from RLT to optimize response rates [ 17 ]. However, it is also known that patients with lower PSMA expression, which would not have been eligible for the VISION trial, can respond to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT [ 18 ]. Based on advice from the FDA to broaden access to novel [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA agents for patients, including those with low PSMA-expressing tumors but also excluding patients with negative prognostic PET features, a new set of criteria has been developed for this [ 177 Lu]Lu-rhPSMA-10.1-based phase I trial (BET-PSMA-121). In this study, we retrospectively assessed how the BET-PSMA-121 eligibility criteria align with those of the VISION trial, and whether these differences affect patient outcomes.
sections.patients: We reviewed data from our institutional database and included all patients who received [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T from October 2017 to August 2021 and underwent imaging via ([ 18 F]rhPSMA-7 or Flotufolastat PET/CT with a median interval of 21 days prior to treatment (IQR: 12–34.5; range, 0–219). Patients treated at our institution were deemed eligible for therapy and discussed in an interdisciplinary tumor board. From this group, 191 consecutive patients were selected, all of whom had previously received second-line hormonal therapy and taxane-based chemotherapy. The retrospective analysis was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Technical University of Munich (permit number 2018–115) and is in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The requirement to obtain informed consent for publication of the data was waived.
sections.pet imaging: ([ 18 F]rhPSMA-7 and Flotufolastat were synthesized according to Wurzer et al. [ 19 ]. The substance was administered to patients via an intravenous bolus, followed by an intravenous injection of diuretics (furosemide). The PET acquisition started approximately 60 min after the injection. All patients underwent examination on a Biograph mCT or a Biograph Vision scanner (Siemens Healthineers). A diagnostic CT scan was initially performed during the portal venous phase, 80 s after the intravenous injection of an iodinated contrast agent, followed by the PET scan. Each patient received a diluted oral contrast agent (300 mg of Telebrix; Guerbet). The PET scans were conducted in 3-dimensional mode, with an acquisition time of 3–4 min per bed position, or 1.1–1.5 mm/s using the flow technique. Emission data were adjusted for randoms, dead time, scatter, and attenuation and were iteratively reconstructed using ordered-subsets expectation maximization (4 iterations, 8 subsets), followed by a post-reconstruction smoothing Gaussian filter (5 mm full width at half maximum).
sections.image analysis and definition of pet eli: Metastatic patterns were assessed according to the miTNM classification [ 20 , 21 ] (N1/M1a: presence of lymph node metastases; M1b: presence of bone metastases; and M1c: presence of visceral metastases), derived from ([ 18 F]rhPSMA-7 and Flotufolastat PET imaging, for every patient. All patients were assessed by a board-certified nuclear medicine physician (with > 5 years of experience) to determine if they met (showcased by a “ + ”) the imaging-based eligibility criteria for the BET (B) and the VISION trial (V), and stratified into four groups depending on their eligibility: 1) V + /B + , 2) V + /B-, 3) V-/B + , and 4) V-/B-. The criteria utilized for this analysis from BET and VISION are shown in Table 1 . PSMA expression was described based on the miPSMA Expression Score [ 20 ], with 0 signifying a tracer uptake below blood pool, 1 ≥ blood pool but < liver, 2 ≥ liver but < parotid gland, and 3 ≥ parotid gland. Table 1 Comparison of PET-based eligibility criteria of VISION vs. BET trial PET-based eligibility in BET’s phase I/II trial PET-based eligibility in VISION Inclusion criterion at least one lesion visible on the CT/MRI > liver uptake (1 lesion PSMA score ≥ 2) ≥ 1 PSMA-positive lesion in any organ of any size Exclusion criterion • Lymph node > 10 mm short axis with PSMA score 0 • Visceral metastasis > 10 mm long axis with PSMA score ≤ 1 • Bone metastasis with PSMA-negative soft tissue component with PSMA score 0 • Majority of tumor volume (based on qualitative visual assessment) from lymph node and/or bone lesions with PSMA score ≤1 (“majority criterion”) • Lymph node ≥ 2.5 cm short axis with PSMA score ≤ 1 • Visceral metastasis ≥ 1 cm with PSMA score ≤ 1 • Bone metastasis with PSMA-negative soft tissue component ≥ 1 cm defined by PSMA score ≤ 1 In short, VISION criteria exclude any patient who fulfills at least one of the following abnormalities with uptake ≤ liver (miPSMA score 0 or 1) in the baseline PET scan: lymph nodes ≥ 2,5 cm, solid organ/parenchymal metastases ≥ 1 cm, and/or bone metastases with soft tissue component ≥ 1 cm (Table 1 ). BET criteria similarly exclude any patient with at least one of the following: lymph nodes > 1 cm with miPSMA score 0, bone metastases with negative (miPSMA score 0) soft tissue components, as well as visceral metastases > 1 cm and miPSMA score 0 or 1 (Table 1 ). Additionally, BET criteria exclude a patient when, based on a visual assessment by the assessing physician, the majority of lymph nodes and/or bone lesions exhibit PSMA levels ≤ liver (miPSMA score 0 or 1) (“majority criterion”) (Table 1 ).
sections.[ 177 lu]lu-psma-i&t rlt: [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T was synthesized and radiolabeled as reported by Weineisen et al. [ 22 ]. The preparation of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T complied with good manufacturing practices and the German Medicinal Products Act (Arzneimittelgesetz §13 2b). In total, we administered 750 cycles of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT, with a median of 4 cycles per patient (ranging from 1 to 10 cycles). Treatment was discontinued in cases of radiographic and/or clinical signs of progression and/or severe toxicity. Patients received an intravenous treat ment with an average standard activity of 7.4 GBq of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T every 5 to 16 weeks (median of 6 weeks), which could be slightly adjusted based on laboratory test results and tumor burden.
sections.psa response and psa progression: PSA levels and their relative change between cycles were assessed. According to the Prostate Cancer Clinical Trials Working Group 3 [ 23 ], a PSA response was defined as a PSA decline of at least 50% from baseline. PSA progression was defined as either a PSA increase of at least 25% and at least 2 ng/mL above the nadir following an initial PSA decline or a PSA increase of at least 25% and at least 2 ng/mL from baseline in cases with no PSA decline.
sections.psa progression-free survival: PSA-PFS was defined as the time from the first cycle of RLT to the time of PSA progression or until the time of death if progression had not been observed.
sections.overall survival: OS was defined as the time from initiation of RLT until death from any cause. Patients who were alive or lost to follow-up were censored at the last date they were known to be alive.
sections.statistical analysis: Kaplan–Meier graphs and t-tests were generated using SPSS Statistics, version 29.0.2.0 (IBM Corp.) for Mac. Other statistical calculations and waterfall plots were performed and generated via Microsoft Excel for Mac, version 16.92. All statistical tests were conducted for the entire cohort and after stratification by eligibility criteria. Kaplan–Meier tests were calculated for survival analyses. A p-value < 0.05 was rated as statistically significant. Cohen’s κ calculations were performed with Microsoft Excel for Max, version 16.92, and agreement between sets of eligibility criteria was rated according to the benchmarks established by Landis & Koch, with κ < 0.0 signifying poor strength, 0.0–0.2 slight, 0.21–0.4 fair, 0.41–0.6 moderate, 0.61–0.8 substantial, and 0.81–1.0 almost perfect agreement [ 24 ].
sections.patient characteristics: A total of 191 patients with a median age of 74 years were analyzed. Patient characteristics and pre-treatments are presented in Table 2 . Of the 191 patients, 138 (72.3%) underwent imaging via Flotufolastat, while the remaining 53 (27.7%) underwent [ 18 F]rhPSMA-7 PET/CT. A separate analysis of the Flotufolastat subcohort was performed and is included in the Supplementary Material. At baseline, loco-regional lymph node, distant lymph node, bone, and visceral metastases were present in 109 (57.1%), 123 (64.4%), 175 (91.6%), and 59 (30.9%) patients, respectively. The median durations of treatment and follow-up were 4 months (range, 0–35 months) and 12 months (range, 0–62 months), respectively. Two patients died shortly after the first cycle of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T (three weeks and one month, respectively), and three other patients had missing follow-up data regarding their PSA, meaning that we could only assess PSA-PFS and PSA response for 186/191 patients (97.4%). As of June 2024, 162 patients (84.8%) have deceased. sections.comparison of [ 177 lu]lu-psma rlt eligi: V + /B + : A total of 161/191 patients (84.3%) were classified as eligible for both BET and VISION (V + /B +) (Supp. 1). V + /B-: 17/191 (8.9%) qualified for VISION only, while 15/17 of them were BET-ineligible due to the majority of the metastases having less uptake than the liver (“majority criterion”), the other two patients had PSMA-negative lymph node metastases (> 10 mm short axis and uptake ≤ liver) (Fig. 1 , Supp. 1). V-/B-: 13/191 patients (6.8%) were ineligible using both sets of eligibility criteria (V-/B). 7/13 were excluded from both studies solely due to PSMA-negative visceral metastases (6/13 had low uptake according to BET, 1/13 was negative in BET), 2/13 solely due to PSMA-negative lymph nodes, and 1/13 because of PSMA-negative soft tissue component of bone metastases (Fig. 1 ). Two other patients simultaneously exhibited PSMA-negative visceral metastases (VISION + low uptake in BET) and fulfilled BET’s majority criterion. One patient had both PSMA-negative visceral metastases (VISION + low in BET) as well as bone metastases with PSMA-negative soft tissue component in VISION (Supp. 2). V-/B + : No patient was eligible based on BET criteria while ineligible by VISION’s criteria. Fig. 1 Flotufolastat PET/CT images of a patient excluded from BET due to a PSMA-negative paraaortic lymph node metastasis. ( A ) MIP, ( B ) CT image, ( C ) PET scan, ( D ) CT scan with PET scan overlay. PSMA-negative lymph node metastasis visible in (B), but not in ( C , D ) (SUVmax 1.6), while the remaining metastases presented with a heterogenous PSMA expression ( A ). Due to the size < 2.5 cm of the lymph node ( B ), this patient was suitable according to VISION criteria (SUVmean liver: 5.0. SUVmean blood pool: 1.8)
sections.clinical outcomes: PSA response: PSA response and PSA-PFS could be assessed for 186/191 patients (97.4%). Out of the 186 patients, 107 (57.5%) exhibited an initial PSA decline, with 64 (34.4%) achieving a 50% reduction in PSA levels. In 77 cases (41.4%), PSA values increased under PSMA RLT; 74 patients (39.8%) exhibited 25% PSA progression. In two cases (1.0%), PSA values were stable after PSMA RLT. In the subgroups V + /B + , V + /B-, and V-/B-, a > 50% PSA response was present in 62/157 (39.5%, 95% CI 31.8–47.6%), 2/17 (11.8%, 95% CI 1.5–36.4), and 0/13 (0%, 95% CI 0–24.7%) patients, respectively. The median time from baseline to assessment of PSA response was 73 days (IQR: 42–133; range: 0–1243 days). The median PSA change from baseline to final assessment (best response or progression) was -16% (IQR: -77.1% to 51.0%, range: -100 to + 5660%). A PSA waterfall plot illustrates the best PSA response across the subgroups and for the entire cohort (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Waterfall plot depicting best PSA response in percentage for each patient: In the subgroups V + /B + , V + /B-, and V-/B-, a > 50% PSA response was present in 62 of 157 (39.5%, 95% CI 31.8–47.6%), 2 of 17 (11.8%, 95% CI 1.5–36.4), and 0 of 13 (0%, 95% CI 0–26.5%) patients, respectively PSA-PFS: Median PSA-PFS for the entire cohort was 3.9 months (95 CI, 2.9–4.9 months). PSA-PFS differed significantly between the three groups with 4.3 months (95% CI, 3.4–5.2 months) vs. 1.5 months (95% CI, 1.4–1.6 months) vs. 2.8 months (95% CI 0.0–6.5 months) for the subgroups of V + /B + , V + /B- and V-/B-, respectively (p = 0.002). sections.cohen\u2019s \u03ba: The overall agreement between the two trials’ eligibility criteria was determined. For the complete cohort (161 eligible by both standards, 17 eligible only according to VISION, 13 completely ineligible), κ was moderate at 0.56.
sections.discussion: Certain (bio-)markers, including imaging-based ones such as PSMA-negative metastases, can predict a poorer response to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT [ 25 ]. To provide well-suited mCRPC patients with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA therapy, there have been multiple attempts to develop ideal selection criteria prior to therapy [ 13 , 14 , 26 – 28 ], such as those from the VISION and BET trials. Considering the mixed responses to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA therapy reported in some patients, establishing optimal selection criteria is crucial to identify and offer RLT to those most likely to benefit. The VISION trial excluded patients with metastases (visceral, bone with a soft tissue component, lymph node) expressing low PSMA levels (miPSMA score 0 or 1) from [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT [ 2 ]. The BET trial introduced more detailed criteria, such as the majority criterion, which excludes patients in whom the majority of tumor volume shows less uptake than the liver, and is somewhat more permissive regarding lymph node metastases. In this retrospective analysis, we applied both sets of election criteria to the same group of mCRPC patients to determine whether different eligibility thresholds identified different cohorts and influenced responses to therapy with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Under VISION criteria, 174/191 patients (91.1%) were eligible, compared to 161/191 patients (84.3%) under BET. No patient in our cohort was included in BET but excluded from VISION (V-/B +). Most patients were eligible under both, which correlated with better OS and PFS outcomes, indicating that V + /B + effectively stratifies optimal candidates for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA therapy. The VISION exclusion criterion for bone metastases specifies “bone metastasis with PSMA-negative soft tissue component (uptake ≤ liver) ≥ 1 cm”. BET’s equivalent is similar but without the size limit, thus including VISION’s criterion. For lymph nodes, BET defines them as “ > 10 mm short axis with uptake ≤ blood pool,” whereas VISION excludes lymph nodes only when “ ≥ 2.5 cm short axis with PSMA ligand uptake ≤ liver.” Despite VISION’s stricter uptake criterion, it allows patients with low-expressing lymph nodes < 2.5 cm, as their PSMA-expression is not a selection factor. BET’s “majority criterion” was designed to include patients with low-expressing lesions in principle, but restrict against a predominant pattern of low-expressing disease. We hypothesized a case in which a lymph node metastasis would meet BET but not VISION criteria (V-/B +), concluding that it would need to be > 2.5 cm in size with low but not negative tracer uptake (> blood pool and < liver). While possible, we did not observe this in our cohort. BET’s criterion regarding visceral metastases is identical to VISION’s. Overall, both trials exclude a similar number of patients (13 for VISION, 15 for BET) from therapy (V-/B-). Of the 13 V-/B- patients, 7/13 were excluded solely due to PSMA-negative (PSMAscore ≤ 1) visceral metastases. Considering that V-/B- had the worst survival data of the three sub-groups, the criteria that led to V-/B- might be successful for the prediction of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT-ineligibility. The remaining differences mostly involve the “majority criterion” in BET, which excludes 15/17 V + /B- patients; notably, two such patients responded with over 50% PSA decrease (92% and 95%), respectively. The remaining two V + /B- patients had PSMA-negative lymph nodes. Since VISION does not use the majority criterion, the 15 aforementioned patients were classified as V + , reducing the total eligible population under BET’s stricter rule. The V + /B- group showed the worst PSA-PFS but no significantly decreased OS; however, the small sample size limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Future prospective studies should assess whether the application of both criteria sets enhances prognostic accuracy in mCRPC patients. In summary, BET’s criteria, particularly due to the majority criterion, are more restrictive than VISION’s within this cohort. Including the majority criterion and BET’s lymph node criterion appears to exclude patients who would not profit from RLT. The requirements regarding visceral metastases are identical between the two sets, and the absence of size restrictions within BET’s bone metastasis criterion had a limited impact compared to VISION’s. There are several limitations to our study. It was retrospective, leading to some uncertain data, such as missing follow-up PSA values. Treatment decisions were made clinically, so minor deviations from recommended eligibility criteria were at the discretion of the treating nuclear medicine physician. Since follow-up treatments after [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT are unknown to us, they may also have impacted PSA-PFS. Additionally, the disproportionately small sizes of the V-/B- and V + /B- cohorts relative to V + /B + reduce our study’s statistical power. Differences in tracer uptake with various diagnostic tracers should also be noted. While 72% of our patients, like those in the BET patient cohort, underwent Flotufolastat PET scans, the VISION trial used [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 for eligibility assessments. Although these tracers differ slightly in aspects such as half-life and imaging resolution, they are all considered appropriate for detecting PSMA-expressing prostate cancer as per guidelines. Furthermore, differences in outcomes may be attributable to our use of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-I&T, as opposed to VISION’s use of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617, and BET’s use of [ 177 Lu]Lu-rhPSMA-10.1. Lastly, the assessment of the PET/CT scans was conducted by a single experienced nuclear medicine physician, which represents a methodological limitation as interobserver variability could not be assessed. This absence of an interobserver reliability assessment may have introduced bias in the PET eligibility classification. To reduce subjectivity and improve reproducibility, future studies should ideally employ multiple independent readers for image analysis.
sections.conclusion_1: Most patients fulfilled both BET and VISION eligibility criteria prior to [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (V + /B +) and were associated with the best patient outcomes. Our data suggest that the criteria for BET’s phase I trial select patients more strictly for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT than VISION criteria, with a mismatch in 8.9% of cases between VISION and BET (V + /B-) criteria, while overall survival did not differ significantly between the three groups. The implementation of both criteria in prospective trials will further compare BET and VISION PET-based eligibility criteria.

title: Spatially interpretable artificial intelligence framework to tailored neoadjuvant dual HER2 blockade in HER2-positive breast cancer
abstract: Neoadjuvant dual HER2 blockade with trastuzumab and pertuzumab plus chemotherapy represents the current standard-of-care for HER2-positive breast cancer. However, treatment responses remain heterogeneous, underscoring the lack of clinically practical tools for predicting treatment efficacy and informing personalized therapy. Here, we developed HER2-LADDER (Layered AI-based Dual-targeteD anti-HER2 Recommendation), a spatially interpretable and clinically accessible artificial intelligence framework that integrates clinicopathological and spatial topological features from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) slides. Using these spatially derived features, HER2-LADDER accurately predicted response to neoadjuvant TCbHP/PCbHP, achieving AUCs of 0.944 in the model construction cohort ( N = 276), 0.917 in the temporal validation cohort ( N = 82), and 0.869 in the trial-based validation cohort ( N = 85). On the basis of HER2-LADDER scores, patients were stratified into Low (highly responsive), Medium (responsive), and High (resistant) groups, identifying candidates for treatment de-escalation (THP or TCbH/PCbH), standard-of-care (TCbHP/PCbHP), or alternative regimens (e.g., next-generation anti-HER2 antibody‐drug conjugates), respectively. Importantly, Xenium in situ profiling further revealed biological correlates underlying model predictions, including HER2-enriched tumor cell aggregation and neutrophil-helper T-cell interactions, thereby highlighting the mechanistic interpretability of the model. Collectively, HER2-LADDER unites digital pathology and high-resolution spatial profiling into a clinically accessible AI framework, offering a robust, transparent, and biologically grounded tool to tailor individualized HER2-targeted therapy optimization.

sections.introduction: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive (HER2+) breast cancer accounts for ~15–20% of all breast cancer subtypes and is characterized by aggressive behavior and poor prognosis. 1 , 2 Biologically, HER2 is a member of the ErbB receptor tyrosine kinase family. When overexpressed or amplified, HER2 promotes receptor dimerization and activates downstream pathways such as PI3K/AKT and MAPK, thereby enhancing tumor-cell proliferation, survival, and invasion. 3 , 4 Although such activation drives tumor progression and contributes to worse clinical outcomes, this biological dependency also makes HER2 an actionable therapeutic target. Monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab can inhibit HER2-driven signaling and mediate antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, fundamentally changing the natural history of this disease. 5 The clinical development of anti-HER2 therapy has therefore reshaped the treatment paradigm for HER2-positive breast cancer. Compared with chemotherapy alone, the advent of trastuzumab markedly reduced the recurrence risk and improved overall survival (OS). 6 , 7 In the neoadjuvant setting, the NOAH trial demonstrated that incorporating trastuzumab into chemotherapy improved 3-year event-free survival from 56 to 71% in patients with HER2-positive locally advanced or inflammatory breast cancer. 8 Subsequently, dual HER2 blockade further improved neoadjuvant efficacy. In the NeoSphere trial, the addition of pertuzumab to trastuzumab and docetaxel increased the pathological complete response (pCR) rate from 29.0 to 45.8%. 9 PEONY further confirmed this benefit in an Asian population. 10 , 11 Then, a series of clinical trials optimized the chemotherapy backbone, and laid the groundwork for the standard regimens such as platinum-taxane dual-targeted regimens (TCbHP/PCbHP), which are now widely recommended in clinical guidelines worldwide. 2 , 12 – 14 Despite these therapeutic advances, treatment response remains markedly heterogeneous across patients with HER2-positive breast cancer. 15 Clinically, this heterogeneity creates a two-sided challenge: some patients may maintain excellent outcomes with less intensive strategies, including chemotherapy de-escalation, 16 – 18 whereas others show a suboptimal response despite standard therapy and may eventually require treatment adaptation, including next-generation antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) 4 , 14 or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). 19 , 20 These clinical realities make pretreatment response stratification increasingly important, yet robust and clinically actionable tools remain limited. Existing predictive approaches predominantly rely on biomarkers such as HER2 amplification status 21 and CD8-positive tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (CD8+ TILs). 22 , 23 Although these biomarkers are informative, they lack sufficient granularity and precision to effectively distinguish responders from nonresponders. Additionally, sequencing-based predictive assays, 24 – 28 while promising, may face substantial practical limitations, including high costs and limited clinical accessibility, which modestly restrict their widespread clinical implementation. 29 Taken together, these limitations highlight the need for clinically accessible approaches that can better capture treatment-relevant tumor biology. 30 One practical route toward this goal is to leverage routine pathology slides, which are already generated in standard care and preserve rich information on cell morphology, microenvironmental composition, and tissue architecture. 31 Recent work has shown that artificial intelligence applied to histopathology can recover clinically relevant biological signals that were previously thought to require dedicated molecular assays. For example, a recent multicenter study demonstrated that deep learning on histopathological images, combined with clinicopathological variables, could estimate Oncotype DX recurrence risk and chemotherapy benefit, supporting the broader concept that routine pathology can serve as a surrogate substrate for treatment-relevant biomarker discovery. 32 Our previous study, which investigated biomarkers of response to a next-generation ADC, SHR-A1811, further suggested that integrating baseline hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) morphology with HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) features could predict response to anti-HER2 ADC therapy. 33 HER2 IHC provided information on both target expression intensity and its spatial distribution, whereas H&E captured complementary features of cell morphology, tissue architecture, and the surrounding microenvironment. This multimodal integration may therefore better reflect treatment-relevant tumor biology than either modality alone. 33 While that work had clear boundaries: it was developed and validated in a relatively small cohort, and its clinical scope was limited to ADC response. Nevertheless, it did inspire us that such a scalable and clinically applicable framework could also be applied to standard dual HER2 blockade to achieve more precise therapeutic decision-making. Against this background, we developed HER2-LADDER (Layered AI-based Dual-targeteD anti-HER2 Recommendation), a digital pathology framework that integrates routine clinicopathological variables with spatially resolved morphological and topological features extracted from baseline H&E and HER2 IHC whole-slide images (WSIs). By leveraging routinely available biopsy specimens, this approach enables spatially informed and clinically accessible prediction of treatment response. In this study, we established and validated HER2-LADDER across real-world and clinical trial cohorts and demonstrated robust predictive performance and generalizability. Beyond risk prediction, the framework provides layered treatment recommendations aligned with contemporary de-escalation and consideration of alternative regimens. By linking spatial tumor organization to therapeutic outcomes using standard pathology slides, our work introduces a biologically interpretable and scalable strategy to support precision decision-making in patients with HER2-positive breast cancer.
