title:
A Theranostic
Study of 177 Lu-Labeled Anti-ADAM9
Antibody for the Treatment of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract:
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is highly aggressive
with
limited diagnostic and therapeutic options. ADAM9 is overexpressed
in TNBC and may serve as a theranostic target. Therefore, this study
aims to develop [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810, an ADAM9-targeted
probe, and evaluate its targeting specificity, imaging capability,
efficacy, and safety in TNBC models. ADAM9 expression in TNBC cells
was assessed by flow cytometry, and the probe was constructed by conjugating 177 Lu to the ADAM9-specific antibody 48HZ810 via DOTA, after
which binding specificity, affinity, and internalization were evaluated
using radioligand binding, immunoreactive fraction, and internalization
assays. In vivo targeting and pharmacokinetics were further analyzed
by SPECT/CT imaging and biodistribution studies, while efficacy, safety,
and mechanisms were assessed via tumor growth, body weight, survival,
hematology, histopathology, and immunofluorescence. High ADAM9 expression
was confirmed in BT-549 cells, and [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
showed >99% radiochemical purity and stability, high affinity ( K d : 3.75 ± 0.72 nmol/L), and specificity
(Bmax: 422.5 ± 17.85 nmol). The tumor was clearly visualized
at 72 h, with peak uptake at 96 h (8.56 ± 0.69%ID/g), and the
probe significantly inhibited tumor growth (TGI: 46.04% vs antibody:
18.14%) and improved survival (70% vs antibody: 50% vs control: 0%),
with no significant toxicity observed. The antitumor activity was
mediated by DNA damage, apoptosis induction, and proliferation suppression.
Overall, the first ADAM9-targeted theranostic probe, [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810, was successfully developed, demonstrating excellent
tumor targeting, antitumor efficacy, and safety in TNBC models, and
validating ADAM9 as a viable theranostic target.

sections.introduction:
Breast cancer is the most
common cancer among women worldwide and
remains one of the most challenging malignancies. In 2022, it accounted for 11.6% of new cancer
cases and 6.9% of cancer-related deaths, with survival depending on tumor stage and molecular subtype. Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), defined
by the absence of ER, PR, and HER2 expression, represents 15–20%
of all breast cancers. The lack of these
receptors limits targeted therapies. TNBC is highly aggressive, with
frequent recurrence and poor survival, and is considered the subtype with the worst prognosis. The five-year mortality rate reaches 40%, and due to the absence of effective targeted
treatments, TNBC remains the most challenging
subtype in breast cancer therapy. Developing
novel therapeutic strategies is, therefore, an urgent priority in
TNBC management. Targeted radionuclide therapy (TRT) represents
a cutting-edge modality
in oncology that enables precise tumor
delivery of radionuclides through targeting vectors such as antibodies,
peptides, or small molecules, thereby
achieving effective lesion eradication while markedly reducing radiation
damage to normal tissues and ultimately
improving the efficiency and safety of cancer diagnosis and treatment. Among available radionuclides, 177 Lu has emerged as an ideal choice for theranostic applications owing
to its favorable physical properties, including a 6.7-day half-life,
β-particle emission with a mean energy of 133 keV, and a tissue
penetration range of 670 μm, enabling the induction of DNA strand
breaks and tumor cell death. With the
successive FDA approvals of agents such as [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-TATE
for neuroendocrine tumors and [ 177 Lu]­Lu-PSMA-617 for prostate
cancer, , TRT has transitioned to an established therapeutic
paradigm. In this context, TNBC poses a major challenge within the
TRT framework due to its lack of effective therapeutic targets, high
aggressiveness, and poor prognosis. Therefore, applying this precision
strategy to TNBC through novel radiopharmaceuticals is critical for
overcoming current therapeutic limitations and improving patient outcomes. ADAM9 is a multifunctional membrane-anchored glycoprotein that mediates proteolysis and cell adhesion and is closely associated with tumor invasiveness
and poor prognosis. It is overexpressed
in TNBC cells and patient samples, promoting tumor aggressiveness. ADAM9 is also overexpressed in multiple cancers − and is recognized as an important cancer biomarker and therapeutic
target. , Previous studies have shown that microRNA-1298
inhibits breast cancer progression by targeting ADAM9. Theranostic strategies targeting MT1-MMP and
TROP-2 have made significant progress, with preclinical studies demonstrating
specific imaging and effective targeted therapy in TNBC. , Despite these advances, a systematic preclinical evaluation of an
ADAM9-targeted monoclonal antibody, 48HZ810, as a theranostic probe
in TNBC remains lacking. Therefore, this study successfully developed
a novel ADAM9 theranostic probe, [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810,
and systematically evaluated its diagnostic and therapeutic potential
in TNBC, offering a new strategy for precision treatment.
sections.cell lines and cell culture:
Three
STR-validated human triple-negative breast cancer cell lines (BT-549,
HCC1806, MDA-MB-468) were obtained from Wuhan Procell. BT-549 and
HCC1806 were cultured in RPMI-1640, and MDA-MB-468 in DMEM, all with
10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Cells were incubated
at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . − Passages were limited
to six months, and cells were harvested at 75–90% confluence
for experiments.
sections.establishment of animal models:
Female
BALB/c nude mice (6–8 weeks old) were obtained from Sichuan
Paxiwell and acclimatized in an SPF facility (22 ± 2 °C,
50 ± 5% humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle). The xenograft model
was established by subcutaneous inoculation of logarithmic-phase BT-549
cells (1 × 10 7 ) mixed with Matrigel (1:1, 100 μL)
into the right axilla. Tumor volume and health were monitored daily.
sections.flow cytometric analysis of in vitro cel:
Cells (5 × 10 4 /well) were seeded in
96-well U-bottom plates and centrifuged (1300 rpm, 5 min, 4 °C).
After two washes with prechilled FACS buffer (95% PBS, 5% FBS), cells
were incubated on ice with a monoclonal antibody (15 μg/mL)
for 60 min. After washing, cells were incubated with a fluorescent
secondary antibody for 30 min in the dark. Following a final wash,
cells were resuspended in 200 μL of buffer. A total of 3000
events were acquired using a FACSCalibur flow cytometer and analyzed
with FlowJo v10.8.
sections.modification of 48hz810:
The 48HZ810
antibody was ultrafiltered (50 kDa, 13,000 rpm, 4 °C, 10 min)
to remove impurities, then washed three times with prechilled PBS
(pH 7.4). The purified antibody was mixed with DOTA (10:1 molar ratio,
20 nmol/μL in DMSO) and incubated (37 °C, 70 rpm, 1 h).
An equimolar reducing agent was added, and the reaction was continued
for another 1 h. The final product was collected after three washes
with 0.5 M sodium acetate buffer (pH 5.5) via ultrafiltration and
stored for later use.
sections.synthesis of [ 177 lu]\u00adlu-dota-48hz:
DOTA-48HZ810 and 177 LuCl 3 (1:2 molar ratio)
were reacted at 42 °C for 1 h with brief agitation every 10 min.
Radiolabeling yield was determined by thin-layer chromatography. Aliquots
(2 μL) were spotted on silica gel fiber strips and developed
using 0.5 M sodium citrate buffer (pH 5.5). Radiochemical purity was further analyzed by high-performance liquid
chromatography.
sections.in vitro stability evaluation:
To
assess in vitro stability, 5 μL of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
was mixed with 20 μL of saline, PBS (pH 7.4), or RPMI-1640 (with
10% FBS). Radiolabeling yield was measured by TLC at various time
points (4 to 192 h) at room temperature to evaluate stability under
different media conditions.
sections.radioligand cell binding and blocking as:
Radioligand cell binding assay: 5 × 10 4 cells were
preincubated with 12 concentrations of unlabeled antibody (2-fold
serial dilutions, initial 50×) at 200 rpm for 30 min. Then, 12
concentrations of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 (2-fold serial
dilutions, initial 5 μCi) were added and incubated for 1 h at
room temperature for nonspecific binding. For total binding, cells
were incubated directly with 12 concentrations of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
under the same conditions. Blocking assay: 12 concentrations of unlabeled
antibody (2-fold serial dilutions, initial 50× EC 50 ) were incubated with cells at 200 rpm for 30 min, followed by the
addition of 12 concentrations of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
(2-fold serial dilutions) for another 1 h. All samples were washed
three times (FACS buffer, 4 °C, 2800 rpm, 4 min). Bound and unbound
radioactivity was measured using a gamma counter to evaluate the targeting
binding characteristics.
sections.immunoreactive fraction determination:
For the unblocked group, logarithmic-phase cells (8 × 10 5 per 200 μL) underwent 12 2-fold serial dilutions. For
the 100% blocking control, cells were similarly diluted, then incubated
with 12 2-fold serial dilutions of unlabeled antibody (initial 50×
EC 50 ) for 30 min, centrifuged (3000 rpm, 5 min), and the
supernatant was removed. Then, 200 μL (0.2 μCi) of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 was added to each tube, incubated (100
rpm, 1 h), centrifuged, washed twice with PBS, and cpm was measured.
A scatter plot (cells/tube vs total cpm/(measured cpm – 100%
blocked cpm)) was generated, linear regression (y = ax + b, R 2 ≥ 0.99) was fitted, and the immunoreactive fraction
was calculated as 100% × 1/b.
sections.internalization assay:
Logarithmic-phase
cells were seeded (2 × 10 4 /well) in 12-well plates
and cultured overnight. [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 (0.2 μCi)
was added and incubated for 0, 4, 24, or 48 h. At each time point,
the supernatant and PBS washes were collected as the extracellular
fraction. Surface-bound activity was recovered with 0.1 M glycine–HCl
(pH 2.7, 10 min). The internalized fraction was obtained by lysis
with 1% SDS (10 min). Radioactivity in each fraction was measured
with decay correction. The internalization rate was calculated as
[internalized/(surface-bound + internalized)] × 100%.
sections.single-photon emission computed tomograp:
Tumor-bearing mice ( n = 3) were intravenously injected with 11.1 MBq of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 (100 μL). SPECT/CT scans were performed
at 4, 24, 72, 96, 144, 168, and 192 h postinjection under 2.5% isoflurane
anesthesia. Quantitative analysis used AMIDE software. Standardized
uptake values were calculated based on attenuation-corrected activity
and body weight. %ID/g for organs was determined using spherical ROIs
(2–3 mm in diameter). Time-activity curves were generated to
characterize dynamic tracer biodistribution.
sections.biodistribution:
Tumor-bearing mice
( n = 3) were intravenously injected with 0.74 MBq
of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 (100 μL). At 4, 24, 72,
96, 144, 168, and 192 h postinjection, the mice were euthanized. Tissues
(heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, pancreas, stomach, intestine,
muscle, bone, tumor, and blood) were collected, wet-weighed, and measured
for radioactivity using a gamma counter with decay correction ( 177 Lu half-life: 6.65 d). Biodistribution was quantitatively
analyzed as %ID/g.
sections.dosimetry estimation:
Based on the
biodistribution data, mean absorbed doses were estimated using the
OLINDA/EXM software with the ICRP 89 adult male reference phantom.
Time-integrated activities (MBq·h/MBq) were obtained by integrating
the time–activity curves, from which the mean absorbed doses
to organs (mGy/MBq) were calculated. Effective doses (mSv/MBq) were
calculated based on ICRP 103 tissue weighting factors. Animal data
were extrapolated to humans using organ mass scaling. In addition,
tumor doses were estimated using the OLINDA/EXM spherical model (1
g, 5 g, 10 g), and these results are model-based approximations.
sections.radiopharmaceutical therapy:
BT-549
tumor-bearing mice (tumor volume 50–150 mm 3 ) were
randomly assigned to radionuclide therapy, antibody therapy, and control
groups ( n = 15 per group). Mean initial tumor volumes
were 75.65 ± 20.02 mm 3 , 71.5 ± 19.5 mm 3 , and 73.79 ± 17.16 mm 3 , respectively. Mice received
tail vein injections of 11.1 MBq [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
(100 μL), 150 μg 48HZ810 antibody (100 μL), or an
equal volume of normal saline. Body weight and tumor dimensions (W 2 × L × 0.5) were monitored
every 3 days. After 30 days, five mice per group were euthanized and
blood was collected for a complete blood count using a MEK722 analyzer.
Tumors and major organs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for H&E
and immunofluorescence analysis. The remaining mice were monitored
for survival and euthanized upon reaching humane endpoints (moribund,
>20% weight loss, or tumor volume ≥1500 mm 3 ).
sections.48hz810 antibody dose-escalation study:
Because 48HZ810 antibody monotherapy at 7.5 mg/kg exhibited only
limited therapeutic efficacy in the antitumor experiments of this
study, it remained difficult to determine whether this outcome resulted
from insufficient antibody dosing or reflected an intrinsic limitation
of antibody monotherapy in this model. To further investigate this
issue, a supplementary antibody dose-escalation experiment was conducted.
Specifically, tumor-bearing mice were treated with 48HZ810 antibody
monotherapy at 10 mg/kg and 30 mg/kg, and antitumor efficacy, survival
benefit, and safety were systematically evaluated. BT-549 tumor-bearing
mouse models with tumor volumes of approximately 40–70 mm 3 were randomly assigned to a high-dose group, a low-dose group,
and a control group, with five mice per group, and the mean initial
tumor volumes were 57.22 ± 7.2 mm 3 , 54.54 ± 6.17
mm 3 , and 53.37 ± 9.78 mm 3 , respectively.
Mice in the high-dose group received a tail vein injection of 48HZ810
at 30 mg/kg in a volume of 100 μL, mice in the low-dose group
received a tail vein injection of 48HZ810 at 10 mg/kg in a volume
of 100 μL, and mice in the control group received an equal volume
of normal saline. Body weight was monitored every 3 days using a calibrated
electronic balance, and tumor length and width were measured with
calipers to calculate tumor volume using the formula W 2 × L × 0.5. Survival was simultaneously monitored and survival
curves were generated, and mice were euthanized and the experiment
was terminated upon reaching humane endpoints defined as a moribund
state, body weight loss exceeding 20%, or tumor volume reaching 1500
mm 3 .
sections.statistical analysis:
All experimental
data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 10.4.1 software. Results are
presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). For comparisons
between two groups, a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t -test was used. For comparisons among three or more groups,
one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post
hoc test was performed. For tumor growth and body weight data measured
repeatedly over time, two-way repeated measures ANOVA followed by
Tukey’s post hoc test was used. Survival analysis was performed
using the Kaplan–Meier method with the log-rank test, and hazard
ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using
the Mantel–Haenszel method. A p -value <0.05
was considered statistically significant.
sections.safety statement:
All experiments
involving radionuclides were conducted in strict accordance with the
institutional radiation safety regulations. Appropriate shielding,
contamination monitoring, and radioactive waste disposal procedures
were implemented. No unexpected or unusually high safety hazards occurred
during the study.
sections.adam9 expression in triple-negative brea:
Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated significant
differences in ADAM9 expression among three triple-negative breast
cancer cell lines, with low expression in MDA-MB-468 cells, intermediate
expression in HCC1806 cells, and markedly high expression in BT-549
cells, and flow cytometry further confirmed that the binding capacity
of the antibody to target cells remained unchanged after the conjugation
of the 48HZ810 antibody with DOTA ( Figure A).
sections.synthesis and quality control of [ 177 l:
We successfully prepared the radiolabeled
conjugate of 48HZ810 by coupling 177 Lu via the DOTA chelator
to generate the ADAM9-targeted theranostic probe [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810.
The DOTA-to-48HZ810 ratio was approximately 7.52 ( Figure S1 ). HPLC analysis confirmed that the radiochemical
purity (RCP) of 48HZ810, DOTA-48HZ810, and [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
exceeded 99% ( Figures S2–S4 ), and
TLC analysis demonstrated a labeling yield greater than 99% for [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 ( Figure S5 ). Stability studies showed that after incubation for 8 days at room
temperature in normal saline (NS), phosphate-buffered saline (PBS),
and RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum, [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 maintained a labeling yield above 99% in all three
media ( Figures S6–S17 ).
sections.radioligand cell binding and blocking as:
Radioligand cell binding assays in three triple-negative breast
cancer cell lines demonstrated that the cellular uptake of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 was markedly dose-dependent, with a maximal binding
capacity (Bmax) of 422.5 ± 17.85 nmol and an equilibrium dissociation
constant ( K d ) of 3.75 ± 0.72 nmol/L
for BT-549 cells (radioligand binding: 0.83% vs blocking: 0.12%),
a Bmax of 222.0 ± 9.25 nmol and a K d of 5.99 ± 1.0 nmol/L for HCC1806 cells (radioligand binding:
0.83% vs blocking: 0.24%), and a Bmax of 120.0 ± 4.0 nmol and
a K d of 2.49 ± 0.40 nmol/L for MDA-MB-468
cells (radioligand binding: 0.89% vs blocking: 0.12%) ( Figure B).
sections.cell immunoreactivity and internalizatio:
Cell immunoreactivity fraction analysis showed that
the immunoreactive fraction of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 in
BT-549 cells was 79.24% ( Figure C). Internalization assays in BT-549 cells demonstrated
a progressive, time-dependent intracellular uptake of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810, with rates of 0.20 ± 0.16%, 0.94 ±
0.21%, 4.94 ± 0.68%, and 15.22 ± 1.30% at 0, 4, 24, and
48 h, respectively, showing statistically significant differences
among groups ( p < 0.001, Figure D).
sections.in vivo spect/ct imaging of [ 177 lu]\u0:
Mouse SPECT/CT imaging demonstrated that
at 24 h postinjection, [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 began to
accumulate in tumors. At 72 h postinjection, tumors were clearly visualized.
During 4–192 h postinjection, tumor uptake of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 progressively increased and remained high after
72 h, whereas radioactivity uptake in nontarget organs decreased over
time, indicating significantly longer tumor retention than in nontarget
organs ( Figure A).
Further region-of-interest delineation enabled quantitative analysis
of radioactivity uptake in tumors, heart, liver, lung, muscle, bone,
and intestine. The maximum tumor uptake occurred at 96 h, with a mean
%ID/g of 8.56 ± 0.69, after which tumor uptake gradually declined
while remaining at 6.47 ± 0.59 at 192 h. Radioactivity uptake
in nontarget organs such as the heart, liver, and lung progressively
decreased over time, with mean %ID/g values at 192 h of 2.09 ±
0.79 for the heart, 3.01 ± 0.14 for the liver, and 1.04 ±
0.26 for the lung. During 4–192 h postinjection, radioactivity
uptake in muscle, bone, and intestine remained very low, showing a
slight initial increase followed by a time-dependent decrease. The
mean %ID/g ranges were 0.4567 ± 0.0611 to 1.307 ± 0.82 for
muscle, 0.44 ± 0.18 to 1.023 ± 0.75 for bone, and 0.52 ±
0.21 to 1.44 ± 0.24 for intestine ( Figure B).
sections.in vivo biodistribution of [ 177 lu]\u00:
Biodistribution studies demonstrated
that [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 exhibited pronounced tumor-targeting
properties in vivo. Tumor uptake of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
increased in a time-dependent manner, reaching a peak at 96 h (12.35
± 0.95%ID/g), followed by a gradual decline, while remaining
at 7.71 ± 1.63%ID/g at 192 h. Blood clearance kinetics showed
that peak blood uptake occurred at 4 h with a value of 6.49 ±
0.40%ID/g and progressively decreased over time, declining to 2.19
± 0.36%ID/g at 96 h when tumor uptake peaked, and further clearing
from circulation by 192 h with a blood uptake of 0.42 ± 0.13%ID/g.
The liver and kidney both exhibited peak uptake at 4 h, with values
of 1.84 ± 0.28%ID/g and 1.37 ± 0.14%ID/g, respectively,
which were higher than those of other nontarget tissues but gradually
decreased over time to 0.61 ± 0.15%ID/g and 0.41 ± 0.12%ID/g
at 192 h ( Figure C).
From 4 to 192 h after injection of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810,
the tumor-to-blood uptake ratios ranged from 0.22 ± 0.05 to 19.45
± 6.98, the tumor-to-liver uptake ratios ranged from 0.79 ±
0.20 to 13.53 ± 5.30, and the tumor-to-kidney uptake ratios ranged
from 0.44 ± 1.05 to 19.28 ± 4.99 ( Figure D).
sections.dosimetry estimates:
On the basis
of the biodistribution data, absorbed doses to organs and spherical
tumor masses were estimated. Organ mean absorbed doses and effective
doses are presented in Table . Among the evaluated organs, the osteogenic cells (bone surfaces)
received the highest absorbed dose (1.49 × 10 –01 mGy/MBq), followed by the heart wall (1.24 × 10 –01 mGy/MBq) and the liver (5.97 × 10 –02 mGy/MBq).
The total effective dose was 1.73 × 10 –02 mSv/MBq.
Absorbed doses for spherical tumor masses of different sizes are shown
in Table , demonstrating
a marked decrease with increasing tumor mass: 3.73, 0.754, and 0.378
mGy/MBq for 1, 5, and 10 g lesions, respectively.
sections.therapeutic efficacy of [ 177 lu]\u00adl:
At day 30, the normalized tumor volume in the radionuclide therapy
group was 221.2 ± 112.4 mm 3 , which was significantly
lower than that in the other two groups (control group: 415.7 ±
158.7 mm 3 ; antibody therapy group: 334.6 ± 154.8 mm 3 ). The tumor growth inhibition rate (TGI%) was 46.04% in the
radionuclide therapy group and 18.14% in the antibody therapy group.
Statistical analysis of tumor volume revealed significant tumor growth
inhibition in the radionuclide therapy group ( p <
0.0001), whereas no statistically significant inhibition was observed
in the antibody therapy group ( p > 0.05). The
difference
in tumor volume progression between the radionuclide therapy group
and the antibody therapy group was statistically significant ( p < 0.01) ( Figure A). Survival analysis revealed that the median survival time
was 46 days in the control group and 68 days in the antibody therapy
group, whereas survival was significantly prolonged in the radionuclide
therapy group and the median survival was not reached. At the end
of the 30-day treatment period, the survival rates of the radionuclide
therapy group and the antibody therapy group were both 100%, whereas
that of the control group was 80%. When half of the mice in the control
group had died (day 46), the survival rates were 100% in the radionuclide
therapy group and 90% in the antibody therapy group. At the end of
the 70-day observation period, the survival rate remained 70% in the
radionuclide therapy group, declined to 50% in the antibody therapy
group, and reached 0% in the control group. Further statistical analysis
revealed a significant difference in survival curves between the control
group and the radionuclide therapy group ( p = 0.0008).
Compared with the control group, the hazard ratio (HR) for death in
the radionuclide therapy group was 0.10, with a 95% confidence interval
(CI) of 0.03–0.33. Body weight in all groups of tumor-bearing
mice showed a gradual increase, and weight gain in the radionuclide
therapy group was lower than that in the control group, with a statistically
significant difference between groups ( p < 0.05)
( Figure B).
sections.dose-escalation study of the 48hz810 ant:
The normalized tumor volume at day 30 was 440.5 ± 97.13 mm 3 in the high-dose group, 423.5 ± 165.9 mm 3 in the low-dose group, and 568.2 ± 54.8 mm 3 in the
control group, with no significant difference between the high-dose
and low-dose groups at the end of treatment, whereas tumor volumes
in both treatment groups were lower than those in the control group,
with statistically significant intergroup differences ( p < 0.05). The tumor growth inhibition rate (TGI%) was 33.22% in
the high-dose group and 26.92% in the low-dose group, indicating only
mild tumor suppression in both groups. Survival analysis showed that
the median survival time was 40 days in the control group and 45 days
in the low-dose group, while no deaths occurred in the high-dose group.
At the end of the 30-day treatment period, survival rates were 100%
in both the high-dose and low-dose groups compared with 60% in the
control group. At the end of the 50-day observation period, all mice
in the control group had died, the survival rate in the low-dose group
declined to 40%, whereas the survival rate in the high-dose group
remained 100%. Further statistical analysis revealed that the high-dose
group exhibited significantly prolonged survival compared with the
control group ( p = 0.0039, HR = 0.05, 95% CI: 0.0075–0.33),
whereas the low-dose group showed no significant survival benefit
( p = 0.2489, HR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.084–1.67).
Body weight in tumor-bearing mice from all groups showed a gradual
increase, with significantly greater weight gain in the high-dose
group than in the other two groups, and the intergroup differences
were statistically significant ( p < 0.01) ( Figure D).
sections.toxicity evaluation of [ 177 lu]\u00adlu:
At 30 days after administration, hematological analysis of the
control, antibody treatment, and radionuclide therapy groups showed
that red blood cell, white blood cell, hemoglobin, and platelet counts
remained within the normal range with no statistically significant
differences among the groups ( Figure A). Hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed no significant
differences in cellular morphology or tissue architecture among major
organs in the control, antibody treatment, and radionuclide therapy
groups, and no evident pathological alterations were observed in the
major organs of any group ( Figure B). Immunofluorescence staining of 53BP1, γH2AX,
BRCA1/2, Caspase-3, and Ki67 showed that 53BP1 fluorescence intensity
was significantly higher in the radionuclide therapy group than in
the control group ( p < 0.05; Figure A), and γH2AX fluorescence
intensity was significantly higher in the radionuclide therapy group
than in both the control group and the antibody treatment group ( p < 0.0001; Figure B). BRCA1/2 fluorescence intensity was significantly
higher in the control group than in the antibody treatment group and
the radionuclide therapy group (control group vs antibody treatment
group: p < 0.01; control group vs radionuclide
therapy group: p < 0.001; Figure C). Caspase-3 fluorescence intensity was
significantly increased in both the radionuclide therapy group and
the antibody treatment group compared with the control group (radionuclide
therapy group vs control group: p < 0.0001; antibody
treatment group vs control group: p < 0.001; radionuclide
therapy group vs antibody treatment group: p <
0.01; Figure D). The
fluorescence intensity of Ki67 was significantly higher in the control
group than in the antibody treatment group and the radionuclide therapy
group (control group vs antibody treatment group: p < 0.0001; control group vs radionuclide therapy group: p < 0.0001; antibody treatment group vs radionuclide
therapy group: p < 0.01; Figure E). The differences in 53BP1, γH2AX,
BRCA1/2, Caspase-3, and Ki67 among the groups were all statistically
significant.
sections.discussion:
This study demonstrates
for the first time the diagnostic and therapeutic
value of ADAM9 as a specific molecular target in TNBCs. ADAM9 exhibits
a distinct high-expression pattern in TNBC. The probe [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 enables precise detection of primary or metastatic
lesions, shows significant tumor inhibition, and has a favorable safety
profile. This work represents a major breakthrough in TNBC theranostics
and provides a highly specific, novel strategy for TNBC patients. Flow cytometry confirmed the specific high expression of ADAM9
in BT-549 cells, consistent with previous studies. Radioligand binding
assays demonstrated the high affinity and specific binding of ADAM9
to BT-549 cells. A TNBC mouse model with high ADAM9 expression was
established, and [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 was successfully
synthesized. SPECT/CT enabled clear visualization of primary and metastatic
lesions at 72 h postinjection with time-dependent accumulation, providing
a noninvasive diagnostic tool with clinical translational potential.
At 192 h, slightly higher nonspecific accumulation was observed in
the liver, indicating a need for further pharmacokinetic optimization. In the targeted radionuclide therapy experiment,
a clear difference
in tumor volume progression was observed between the radionuclide
therapy group ([ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810) and the antibody
therapy group (48HZ810). The radionuclide therapy group exhibited
significant tumor growth inhibition due to precise ADAM9 targeting
and sustained radiation damage from 177 Lu β-particles.
In contrast, the 48HZ810 antibody alone did not show statistically
significant tumor suppression. However, published literature indicates
that anti-ADAM9 antibodies can exert antitumor effects by suppressing
downstream signaling pathways. We hypothesize that the lack of significant
efficacy with the 48HZ810 antibody likely resulted from an insufficient
dosage. The supplementary dose-escalation study of the 48HZ810 antibody
demonstrated that 48HZ810 monotherapy at doses of 10 mg/kg and 30
mg/kg exerted only limited inhibitory effects on tumor growth in TNBC
mouse models, primarily manifesting as delayed tumor progression,
without significant tumor regression or a clear survival benefit.
Previous studies have shown that antibodies targeting ADAM9 mainly
modulate tumor progression-related phenotypes such as cell migration
and invasion by suppressing phosphorylation of downstream EGFR and
ERK signaling pathways rather than directly inducing tumor cell death, , a characteristic that may partially explain the limited antitumor
activity observed in this supplementary study even at higher antibody
monotherapy doses. Collectively, these findings further suggest that
the therapeutic efficacy of 48HZ810 monotherapy in this TNBC mouse
model is constrained not only by dose but also by the intrinsic biological
properties of antibody monotherapy, thereby underscoring the necessity
of enhancing local cytotoxic effects through radionuclide conjugation
while preserving target specificity. This study systematically demonstrates
for the first time the effectiveness of ADAM9 as a radionuclide therapy
target in TNBC, supporting the therapeutic potential of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810. We systematically evaluated the in vivo
safety of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810. Pharmacokinetic analysis
showed rapid clearance
from circulation, with a 93.42% clearance rate between 4 and 192 h,
reducing hematological toxicity and bone marrow suppression risk.
Complete blood count and histopathological analysis confirmed no hematological
toxicity, and major organs showed no radiation-induced injury. Circulating
[ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 exerts minimal effects on leukocytes
and low cytotoxicity to blood cells and exhibits favorable in vivo
safety. This study performed the first systematic internal dosimetry
assessment
of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810, providing key data for evaluating
its radiation safety and therapeutic window. It should be noted that
tumor doses were estimated using a spherical model and represent model-based
approximations and not actual patient tumor doses. Furthermore, the
extrapolation of animal data to humans involves inherent variability.
According to the RADAR guidelines, animal-extrapolated data tend to
underestimate human organ self-doses. Therefore, human dosimetry data
require further validation in clinical studies. Further mechanistic
studies showed that [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810
upregulated γH2AX and 53BP1, indicating increased DNA double-strand
breaks and DNA damage response activation. Downregulation of BRCA1/2
suggested suppressed homologous recombination repair, exacerbating
genomic instability. Caspase-3 was robustly activated and Ki 67 was markedly reduced, indicating apoptosis induction
and proliferation suppression. These findings demonstrate that [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 exerts antitumor efficacy against TNBC
by inducing DNA damage, disrupting repair homeostasis, promoting apoptosis,
and suppressing proliferation. The clinical significance of
this study extends beyond that of
TNBC. Given the ADAM9 overexpression in multiple malignancies, the
[ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 theranostic strategy has potential
for expansion to other ADAM9-overexpressing tumors. Although mild
nonspecific liver accumulation was observed, antibody optimization
could improve the pharmacokinetic profile. These findings validate
ADAM9-targeted therapy and provide an innovative option for patients
with advanced metastatic solid tumors including TNBC. The limitations
of this study lie in the fact that the imaging
and therapeutic evaluations were primarily conducted in a single-cell-line-derived
xenograft (CDX) model with high ADAM9 expression, and systematic validation
across models with varying ADAM9 expression levels is lacking. In
addition, differences between CDX models and those of human triple-negative
breast cancer (TNBC) may limit their clinical translatability. Therefore,
future validation in multiple CDX models with heterogeneous ADAM9
expression as well as in patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models is
warranted to enhance the comprehensiveness and generalizability of
the conclusions. On the other hand, mild nonspecific liver accumulation
of [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 may reduce its diagnostic and
therapeutic performance and cause a certain degree of radiation damage
to normal tissues, and future optimization of the antibody structure
may improve the targeting specificity and address this issue.
sections.conclusion:
This study systematically
validates the potential of ADAM9 as a
theranostic target for TNBC, and the successfully developed ADAM9-targeted
theranostic probe [ 177 Lu]­Lu-DOTA-48HZ810 not only enables
noninvasive tumor visualization by SPECT/CT imaging but also exhibits
pronounced tumor growth inhibition through the synergistic effects
of antibody-mediated targeting and radionuclide therapy, while pharmacokinetic
analysis confirms its high blood clearance rate and favorable biosafety
without inducing hematological toxicity or damage to major organs.
Despite limitations such as nonspecific hepatic accumulation, further
optimization through antibody engineering strategies could enhance
its targeting performance, and these findings not only provide a novel
approach for TNBC theranostics but also lay the foundation for the
development of precision diagnostic and therapeutic platforms for
other ADAM9-overexpressing tumors.

title: Closing the Gap: Examining Representation of Women in Ischemic Heart Disease Guideline Studies
abstract: Background This study aimed to evaluate the representation of women in cardiovascular clinical trials referenced in the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines, given the historical underrepresentation of women in such trials, which limits generalizability and perpetuates health care disparities. Methods We conducted a systematic review of studies referenced in American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines for chronic coronary artery disease, chest pain, and coronary artery revascularization. Data extraction focused on study type, publication year, total study population, and proportion of women enrolled. Participation‐to‐prevalence ratios were calculated to assess gender representation relative to disease prevalence among women in the United States. Results Our systematic review encompassed 1690 studies revealing persistent underrepresentation of women across all guideline areas: revascularization (29.5%), chronic coronary artery disease (33.3%), and chest pain (40%). Participation‐to‐prevalence ratios ranged from 68.2% to 83.2%, indicating substantial gaps in representation compared with disease burden. Trends over 4 decades showed variability in women's inclusion, with some improvement but minimal overall progress. Conclusion Despite increased awareness and advocacy, our findings highlight ongoing gender disparities in cardiovascular research. Proactive strategies are needed to enhance women's participation in clinical trials, ensuring equitable and effective health care interventions. Addressing these disparities is critical for developing tailored treatments and improving cardiovascular outcomes globally. Future research should prioritize identifying and overcoming barriers to women's enrollment in cardiovascular trials to promote inclusive clinical practice and mitigate health care disparities.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what are the clinical implications?: Underrepresentation of women in pivotal cardiovascular trials limits the generalizability of evidence used to develop guidelines, potentially leading to less effective treatment strategies for half of the patient population. Proactive efforts to improve enrollment of women in cardiovascular research are critical to ensuring equitable, evidence‐based care and improving outcomes for women with ischemic heart disease.
sections.methods_1: The data and analytic methods used in this study can be made available by the corresponding author upon request to allow for replication or further analysis. Institutional review board approval was not required for this study because it used publicly available, deidentified data extracted from published guideline‐referenced studies and did not involve human subjects or protected health information. This study involved data extraction from the 2021 AHA/ACC/American Society of Echocardiography/CHEST/Society for Academic Emergency Medicine/Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography/Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines , 2023 AHA/ACC/American College of Chest Physicians/American Society for Preventive Cardiology/National Lipid Association/Preventive Cardiovascular Nurses Association Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease: A Report of the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines , and 2021 ACC/AHA/Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Intervention Guideline for Coronary Artery Revascularization: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guideline . Studies referenced within these guidelines included clinical trials, prospective, and retrospective studies, systematic reviews, guideline papers, and studies lacking a specified population were excluded. Data extraction was performed by F.A., J.A., and K.D., with verification conducted by A.A and F.S. Extracted information included study name, publication date, study type, total study population, and the proportion of women included. Clinical trials were segregated for separate analysis. Although most cited studies report participants' sex assigned at birth rather than gender identity, we use the term “gender” throughout this article because the disparities we examine are driven not only by biological differences but also by gender‐based social, structural, and systemic factors that influence study design, enrollment, and interpretation. This study did not involve identifiable human subjects or protected health information and therefore did not require institutional review board approval according to institutional policies.
sections.statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data, including counts and percentages for categorical variables. The proportion of women included in each guideline category was assessed both individually and collectively. A 5‐year average was calculated to depict trends over time. No inferential statistical tests were performed, as the primary aim was to provide a descriptive overview of gender representation trends. To gauge representation, the participation‐to‐prevalence ratio (PPR) was computed for each guideline category, derived by dividing the percentage of women included in the cited studies by the percentage of women within the disease population. The latter percentages were obtained from Global, Regional, and National Burden of Cardiovascular Diseases for 10 Causes, 1990 to 2015 and Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics—2024 Update: A Report From the American Heart Association . 9 , 10 A PPR rate <0.8 indicates underrepresentation of women, whereas a rate >1.2 suggests overrepresentation. Furthermore, to evaluate broader trends in how gender and disparities are discussed in cardiovascular research, we performed a PubMed search to assess the number of studies published each year. The search combined terms such as “coronary artery disease,” “chest pain,” “revascularization,” and “ischemic heart disease” with “women,” “gender,” or “disparities.” We then reviewed the annual publication counts to observe how often these topics have been addressed in the literature over time.
sections.results_1: The ACC/AHA Guideline papers for chronic coronary disease (CCD), chest pain, and revascularization cited 3209 studies in all. Each citation was carefully examined, removing repeated studies, meta‐analyses, subanalyses, systematic reviews, special reports, and studies that did not mention the number of women included (Figure 1 ). The final number of studies included in our analysis was 1690 (Table 1 ). The revascularization guidelines referenced 1085 studies, of which 558 (51.5%) were excluded, resulting in 527 (48.5%) studies included in our analysis. 8 Among these included studies, 280 (25.8%) were RCTs. Participation of women in the included studies stood at 29.5%, with 6 of the studies lacking any representation of women. Similarly, the CCD guidelines cited 1260 studies, with 636 (50.5%) being excluded, leaving 624 (49.5%) studies for analysis. 7 Within these included studies, 364 (28.8%) were RCTs. Participation of women in the CCD studies was slightly higher at 33.3%, with 7 studies lacking representation of women. In the chest pain guideline, 864 studies were cited, of which 325 (37.5%) were excluded, resulting in 539 (62.5%) studies included in our analysis. 6 Among the included studies, 123 (14.2%) were RCTs. Notably, participation of women in chest pain studies was higher at 40%, although 2 studies lacked inclusion of any women.
sections.chest pain guidelines: In the chest pain guideline, the trend of participation among women over the years displayed considerable variation, ranging from 14.1% in 1979 to a peak of 71.2% in 2005 (Table S1 ). The 5‐year average ranged from 36.2% to 45.9% over the past 4 decades, reflecting an overall positive trend in inclusion of women (Figure 2 , Table S2 ). Further analysis focused on the representation of women in RCTs, with the overall percentage of women participating in RCTs being 40.3% (Table S3 ). Additionally, the trends when comparing non‐RCT versus RCT studies in participation of women have been relatively equal. However, in recent years the gap is increasing, specifically, in 2020 non‐RCT studies enrolled an average of 44.1% women and RCT studies averaged 28.3% in women inclusion (Figure 3 ).
sections.chronic coronary disease guideline: In the CCD guideline, the trend of participation of women across the years exhibited variability, ranging from 12.5% in the earliest studies in 1976 to a peak of 47.7% in 2004 (Table S1 ). Overall, there has been an upward trend in inclusion, with the 5‐year average ranging between 20% and 25% in the 1990s and ∼37.1% to 42.5% in the 2000s (Figure 4 ). Further analysis focused on the representation of women in RCTs revealed an overall percentage of inclusion of 31.2%. Early RCTs, starting from 1976 and extending into the 1990s, generally exhibited <25% participation of women. The 5‐year average was lowest in the 1990 to 1994 period at 21.1%, compared with 44.5% in the 2000 to 2004 period (Figure 5 ). Additionally, we compared the trend of women participation for RCT versus non‐RCTs and interestingly we found a large discrepancy between the 2 groupings. Specifically in 2020, non‐RCT studies averaged 51.3% participation of women whereas RCT studies averaged a nominal 26.1% (Figure 5 , Table S4 ).
sections.coronary artery revascularization guidel: Within the revascularization guideline, the trend of participation of women exhibited variability, ranging from 0% in 1982 and 1985 to a notable peak of 48.6% in 1997 (Table S1 ). Over the 4 decades analyzed, the highest 5‐year average of participation that included women was 36.4% observed from 1990 to 1994, and the lowest 5‐year percentage was 29.7% recorded from 2015 to 2019. (Figure 6 ). When focusing specifically on RCTs within the revascularization guideline, the percentage of women included was 30.2%. However, the trend in RCT participation showed fluctuations, with the highest percentage recorded at 72.9% in 1993 and the lowest at 13.3% in 1984. Overall, the trend in RCT participation demonstrated a downward trajectory in the 5‐year average of participation of women cited in the revascularization guideline paper, and the gap between non‐RCT and RCT studies has grown in recent years. Specifically, in 2020, the average percent of women participation in non‐RCT studies was 45.1% compared with just 27.2% in RCT studies (Figure 7 ). These findings were summarized in Figures 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 .
sections.participation to prevalence ratio of wom: Within the total CVD prevalence among women in the United States estimated at 48.8%, the PPR in CCD studies was 68.2%. The PPR of revascularization studies when compared with the burden of coronary artery disease is 68.8%. In terms of chest pain and angina pectoris statistics, with a prevalence of 48.1% among women in the United States, the PPR in chest pain studies was 83.2% (Table 2 ).
sections.trends of gender disparities over the ye: To provide context for our findings, we performed a supplementary literature search using PubMed to explore how often gender and disparities are addressed in studies related to chest pain, chronic coronary disease, and revascularization. We used the same keyword strategy described previously and tracked the number of relevant studies published each year. This helped illustrate a growing interest in these issues across the broader cardiovascular research landscape. Specifically, the number of publications surged from 0 in 1985 to >1600 by 2023 (Table S5 ). This trend highlights growing recognition and acknowledgment of gender disparities in cardiovascular research. However, many of these studies may only mention disparities rather than systematically examining the root causes, suggesting the need for more focused investigations. We plotted the number of studies published using these keywords against the percentage of women's participation in trials (Central Illustration) to explore the relationship between awareness and actual representation.
sections.discussion: To our knowledge, this study is the first to comprehensively assess the inclusion of women in studies used to develop guidelines for the management of ischemic heart disease. Our findings reveal persistent and significant underrepresentation of women in all ACC/AHA guidelines pertaining to chest pain, chronic coronary artery disease, and revascularization with no discernible improvement observed over time. These findings emphasize the urgent need to recruit more women into pivotal RCTs, which are most important in informing clinical guidelines. Although most clinical trials report sex assigned at birth rather than gender identity, we use the term gender throughout this article to emphasize the influence of gender‐based assumptions and biases on study design, enrollment, and implementation. This approach highlights how both recognized and unrecognized societal and systemic factors can contribute to the underrepresentation of women in cardiovascular research. Additionally, it is imperative for physicians to recognize and address the fact that the low rate of inclusion of women may affect the care of 51% of the population. Our analysis of 1690 studies spanning from 1971 to 2022, reveals a consistent pattern of notably lower participation of women across all 3 guideline areas, with rates of 29.5%, 33.3%, and 40% for revascularization, chronic coronary artery disease, and chest pain guidelines, respectively. Our findings align with prior research highlighting gender ratio discrepancies in cardiac trials. 11 For instance, Jin et al.'s study of 740 cardiovascular clinical trials from 2010 to 2017 found that women accounted for only 38.2% of participants. 12 Similarly, Tahhan et al.'s research on heart failure trials demonstrated ongoing gender disparities post‐2001, with a PPR <0.8 for older patients and women. 13 Furthermore, we found complete absence of participation among women in 15 studies cited in the guidelines, 5 of which explicitly focused on men only, predominantly conducted before 1990 by the Veterans Affairs Office of Research. These findings underscore the historical and persistent underrepresentation of women in cardiovascular research, raising concerns regarding the generalizability and effectiveness of treatments primarily tailored to men. The implications of gender disparities in clinical trials extend beyond mere representation; they affect clinical decision‐making and guideline development. Scott et al.'s investigation found disease‐specific variations in representation of women within trials used to support Food and Drug Administration‐approved cardiovascular drugs, highlighting the potential consequences of underrepresentation on evidence‐based practice. 14 These findings emphasize the critical need for increased women's representation in cardiovascular research to ensure more equitable and effective treatment strategies for all patients. Efforts to address these disparities have been ongoing, notably with the passage of the National Institutes of Health Revitalization Act in 1993, which aimed to ensure equitable inclusion of women and underrepresented populations in clinical research. 15 , 16 This spurred a notable surge in advocacy aimed at enhancing participation of women in large clinical trials and a substantial increase in publications addressing these gaps. These efforts are also evident within the guideline papers themselves. Notably, guideline papers on chest pain and CCD have dedicated sections highlighting these crucial differences. Moreover, the significance of disparities in care was underscored as a key takeaway in the top 10 messages of the revascularization and chest pain guidelines. 6 , 8 These efforts acknowledging biases within guidelines represent important steps toward addressing gender disparities in cardiovascular research and clinical practice. A critical question remains: does this heightened awareness effectively translate into increased representation of women as CVD research progresses? The trend of inclusion reflected in our study fails to show a parallel rise (central illustration). Understanding the factors contributing to underrepresentation of women in clinical trials is essential for effective interventions. Melloni et al.'s study highlighted the impact of clinical indication on enrollment of women, showing higher participation rates in trials focused on hypertension and diabetes compared with coronary artery disease and heart failure. 16 Additionally, differences in gender preferences, perceptions, and behaviors toward trial participation underscore the need for gender‐specific recruitment approaches. Previous research indicates that women are more often enrolled in primary prevention studies of CVD rather than in secondary prevention, possibly due to physician bias in participant selection and the later onset of CVD in women compared with men. 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 However, other evidence suggests that women are also underrepresented even in primary prevention trials, such as the early statin trials (eg, WOSCOPS [West of Scotland Coronary Prevention Study] and AFCAPS/TexCAPS [Air Force/Texas Coronary Atherosclerosis Prevention Study]) 23 , 24 Moreover, studies suggest that women's lower willingness to participate in cardiac trials, particularly RCTs, is influenced by concerns about added risk and time inconvenience. 25 , 26 However, we should counter the belief that women are reluctant to participate in clinical studies. Evidence shows that women enrolled without hesitation in significant numbers in studies such as the WHI (Women's Health Initiative), WISE (Women's Ischemia Syndrome Evaluation), and the St. James WTH (Women Take Heart) Project. 27 , 28 , 29 However, much of the existing literature is not directed at women. This lack of focus on women may also stem from a shortage of female investigators, which leads to less consideration of women‐specific concerns and factors that would encourage their participation. These differences in gender highlight the importance of tailoring trial recruitment strategies to address gender‐specific behaviors and perceptions. Acknowledging the limitations of our study, the exclusion of systematic reviews, guideline papers, statements, and studies without a specified population could result in the absence of relevant data that may have provided additional information. Additionally, some individual years have peaks much higher than the average percentage of women; however, this is likely attributable to the limited number of studies published that year, with a few studies focusing predominantly on women, thereby skewing the annual data. This highlights the importance of evaluating 5‐year averages as seen in Figures 2 , 4 , and 6 , which provide a more stable and representative trend over time. Also, we focused on only 3 guidelines papers that we believed most relevant in patients with coronary artery disease. It is also important to note that the guidelines do not include every study considered during their development and we did not review and include the full evidence tables that often contain additional studies. Because of this, our analysis may not reflect the complete body of evidence used by the guideline committees. Lastly, the calculated PPRs were based on US estimates of disease prevalence and may not fully reflect the current burden. We also acknowledge that most included studies report sex assigned at birth; our use of gender throughout the article emphasizes the social and systemic factors influencing participation rather than a direct measurement of gender identity.
sections.conclusions: In conclusion, our findings emphasize the urgent necessity for sustained proactive measures to address gender disparities by including women in practice‐changing cardiovascular research. Achieving gender parity in trial enrollment is imperative for ensuring equitable health care delivery and improving cardiovascular outcomes for all individuals. Future research should prioritize identifying barriers that decrease representation of women in ischemic heart disease trials to promote evidence‐based, gender‐inclusive clinical practice.

title: Infective endocarditis surgery using conventional prosthetic valves versus homograft: the IESCOPO study protocol
abstract: Background According to the prevailing view among experts in the field of surgical research, homografts should be used preferentially over both conventional xenografts and mechanical prostheses in cases of infective endocarditis (IE). The rationale for this recommendation is that homografts possess a greater degree of resistance to infection. Nevertheless, the existence of comparative evidence that validates this assertion is scant. Methods A comprehensive search of the databases of three tertiary academic centres yielded a total of 775 adult patients (aged 18 years or over) who underwent surgical procedures for active IE involving the heart valves during the period from 2005 to 2024. The evaluation of short- and long-term outcomes was conducted using propensity score analysis to reduce baseline confounding between patients receiving homografts and those receiving conventional prosthetic valves. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to create weighted cohorts with balanced baseline characteristics. Discussion This study hypothesizes that the nature of the results in question will serve to minimize biases related to institutional volume and surgical experience in the case of homograft implantation when compared to conventional prosthetic valves. Participating centers must maintain an infective valve surgery program, with provisions to guarantee postoperative follow-up and management of late complications from valve surgeries for infective endocarditis. The data that will be collected will provide valuable insight into the comparative effectiveness of various surgical approaches, both standard and advanced, in valve replacement surgery for IE. This will be achieved using conventional prosthetic valves versus cryopreserved homograft. It is further expected that this comprehensive analysis will contribute significantly to the development of robust international guidelines. Trial registration Clinical Trial Gov. Com. ID: NCT05253469; IRB. ID: 2,022,011,054. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13019-026-04088-8.

sections.introduction: The reappearance of infection following valve replacement for infectious endocarditis (IE) is a matter of major clinical significance. Consequently, there has been considerable discussion about which prosthesis represents the optimal choice in this setting. This process can be traced back several decades [ 1 – 7 ]. According to the prevailing surgical principles, the utilisation of autologous or allogeneic tissue is deemed to be the superior approach when compared with the use of synthetic material in an infected area. In light of the preference to avoid the utilisation of foreign artificial materials, as evidenced in the use of conventional mechanical or stented xenograft valve prostheses, the utilisation of homografts has garnered advocacy from some scholars. Favorable outcomes have been documented, particularly in cases involving prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) and other intricate and invasive lesions, such as root abscess development [ 8 – 14 ]. The majority of the extant research, however, consists of unblinded observational investigations devoid of conventional prostheses suitable for use as comparators [ 8 – 14 ]. Nevertheless, obstacles to the utilisation of homografts persist. It is evident that the process of implantation is technically more complex than that of other procedures. The subject is universally taught. In the contemporary era, homografts are utilised in the vast majority of instances as a means of full aortic root reconstruction. The aggressive nature of this procedure may, however, constitute the primary disadvantage associated with its recommendation to patients who already face a high risk of operative mortality [ 1 – 4 , 15 , 16 ]. Furthermore, the resilience of homografts is understood to be limited, with this aspect potentially acting as a constraining factor, especially amongst younger patients. It is important to note that such grafts are comparatively limited in availability [ 17 ]. The process of cryopreservation is a prerequisite. Consequently, the supposition that homografts are obligatory may, in practice, constitute an impediment to the judicious surgical management of patients afflicted with IE [ 18 – 22 ]. Notwithstanding the existence of a robust corpus of opinion, the extant data set is limited in scope, precluding a comprehensive comparison of operative outcomes for homograft versus the utilisation of conventional prosthetic valves in the context of IE. This is a subject that has been the focus of extensive discussion. After reviewing the evidence, a protocol has been developed to access data from the three institutions exhibiting analogous referral patterns, all from a common patient pool. This protocol will also gather divergent perspectives on the optimal prosthesis. We are pleased to inform you that this unique dataset has been identified for analysis. The objective of this study was to compare short- and long-term outcomes for homograft versus conventional prosthetic replacements in patients with active IE involving the AV requiring surgical therapy.
sections.methods and analysis: The IESCOPHO (Infective Endocarditis Surgery Using Conventional Prosthetic Valves versus Homograft) study is a retrospective, multicentre study. A review of a database that had been carefully managed over time was carried out. This database included patients who had undergone surgery for treating infective endocarditis from 2005 to 2024. We conducted a retrospective analysis of three distinct valve replacement types, employing a 1:1:1 ratio: standard valve replacement (SVR), using either a conventional mechanical valve prostheses (MVP) or a stented xenograft valve prostheses (SXVP); or cryopreserved homograft (C-Ho) (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Study design schematic. BP, bioprosthetics; BVD; bioprosthetic valve dysfunction; IESCOPHO; Infective Endocarditis Surgery Using Conventional Prosthetic Valves versus Homograft; MACCE; major adverse cardiac or cerebrovascular event; MV; mechanical valve; SVR, standard valve replacement During the designated study period, a total of 775 patients who met the study’s criteria were included. The study is being conducted in three research centers in France that performed the surgeries. (Box 1 ) A select group of sites was enrolled in an imaging substudy (see the online supplemental material S1). According to the latest estimates, the imaging substudy is expected to enroll 120 patients from each of the designated groups. (see online supplemental material S1) . The primary objective of this study will be to focus on patients diagnosed with native valve endocarditis or prosthetic valve endocarditis who are scheduled to undergo surgery within 15 days or elective surgery. Patients who are admitted to the hospital with emergency symptoms, such as embolized vegetations and left ventricular dysfunction, will not be included in the protocol. The subanalysis constitutes a component of a project submitted to the European Commission, New Tracers for Imaging in Infective Endocarditis (NTIIE). The project is available at the following URL: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/EU4H-2025-HERA-PJ-1-a . A review of patient data will inform future research. This study combines CT imaging with 18-flurorodeoxyglucose (18FDG-PET) positron emission tomography (PET) to show metabolic activity. Leukocyte single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is used to show regions of metabolic activity. Inflammation is a significant research area with potential for advancement. The following approach is recommended for patients who meet the relevant criteria to receive a surgical procedure, as outlined in the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases Infective guidelines. A wide range of targeting modalities have been evaluated in preclinical studies; however, most have yet to be translated into clinical practice. This protocol aims to provide an analysis of both the most promising tracer candidates for non-invasive molecular imaging of infections and the issues that impede clinical translation. ( https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/EU4H-2025-HERA-PJ-1-a .) The present study was formally endorsed by the institutional review board, and the requirement for individual patient consent was waived. The database is the subject of constant updating and maintenance. The document under consideration was composed by clinical information analysts. The collection of data is subject to regular validation through the implementation of internal and external controls. Preoperative and postoperative variables are entered prospectively during the patient’s in-hospital stay, and follow-up data are entered on subsequent encounters. The collection of follow-up data for survival and reintervention was achieved through a thorough examination of the electronic medical records, followed by contacting the referring physicians and, when necessary, communicating directly with the patients and their families. The data concerning patients with IE who have undergone surgical valve replacement have been systematically organized in a Microsoft Access datasheet. (Redmond, Washington, USA). The current data collection instrument is intended to include predetermined baseline, operative, and outcome variables. Patient enrolment began in 2005, with the aim of completing the study by freezing the prospective dataset for retrospective statistical analysis by 31/12/2024. (Online supplementary NCT05253469) It is important to note that the sequence of events delineated in this chronology is contingent on the findings that may be revealed by any ensuing interim analyses that may be undertaken. Approval for the execution of this investigation is to be sought from the institutional review board or local ethical committee (IRB 202201054), in accordance with local legislation. The present study has been duly registered on the ClinicalTrials.gov database, with the identifier NCT05253469. (see Online supplemental material S2).
sections.characterization of patient populations: The following inclusion criteria have been established for the study: patients must demonstrate a medical history of IE, with the presence of valve regurgitation (VR) as an accompanying symptom. In addition, patients must have undergone one of the following surgical procedures: The standard valve replacement procedure is performed using either a conventional MVP or a SXVP, or alternatively with the use of a partial or complete C-Ho ( Fig. 1 ). The study is open to participants of all genders, races and ethnicities.
sections.infectious diseases criteria for infecti: The Duke Criteria, which were originally published in 1994 [ 23 ] and revised in 2000 [ 24 ], are the most common means of diagnosing IE. The primary function of the aforementioned entity was to serve as a research instrument, with the objective of standardising the definition of a condition that is characterised by clinical variability. Their presence established a foundation for a series of multinational investigations that led to a significant advancement in our comprehension of the illness [ 25 – 29 ]. Nevertheless, the microbiology, diagnostics, epidemiology and therapeutic management of IE have undergone substantial modification since the introduction of these criteria. An illustrative example of this phenomenon is represented by endovascular cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs), comprising permanent pacemakers. The presence of cardioverter-defibrillators has been documented in a minimum of 10% of temporary IE case investigations [ 28 ]. Furthermore, these devices have been recognised as a substantial risk factor for infection [ 30 , 31 ]. The incidence of infection in transcatheter-implanted valves has been demonstrated to be a significant concern. The incidence of PVE has been shown to be comparable to that of surgically implanted valves. It is an increasingly prevalent component of the condition. In light of recent advancements in the field, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) has proposed amendments to the Modified Duke Criteria in 2015 [ 32 ]. However, recent advances in the field necessitate further modifications to the formal diagnostic criteria for infective endocarditis. The ISCVID (International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases) Criteria Working Group has incorporated these novel diagnostic approaches into the 2023 Duke-ISCVID Pathogenic Criteria of Definite IE. The Pathological Criteria for Definite IE in the Modified Duke Criteria were predicated on the identification of either microorganisms or histopathological evidence of active IE in operative or post-mortem samples. The 2023 Duke-ISCID IE criteria have undergone a thorough elucidation and expansion, incorporating recent advancements in genetic and molecular research. The subsequent protocol will provide a comprehensive overview of tissue staining techniques. The utilisation of these methodologies is for the purpose of detecting etiological microorganisms, thereby enabling a definitive diagnosis of IE. A plethora of contemporary laboratory diagnostics, including 16S/18S ribosomal RNA gene polymerase chain reaction (PCR), novel sequencing techniques [ 33 ] and fluorescent in situ hybridisation, [ 34 ] can facilitate our capacity to diagnose infectious endocarditis. For instance, fluorescence in situ hybridization A combination of PCR/sequencing (FISHseq) with the investigation of infected prosthetic heart valves has been proven to result in a 30% increase in the detection and clarification of causative microorganisms when compared with conventional blood and valve culture methods [ 34 ]. As demonstrated, [ 34 ] the employment of fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in combination with PCR/sequencing (FISHseq) for the analysis of infected prosthetic heart valves results in enhanced detection and clarification of causative microorganisms when compared with conventional blood and valve culture methods, exhibiting a 30% increase in efficacy. The conclusion of the ISCVID Working Group is that the original structure for differentiating definite, possible, and rejected IE on the basis of Major and Minor Clinical Criteria should remain unaltered. The addition of a third domain, designated ‘surgical’, was made to the two domains that had been previously identified. As outlined in Table 1 [ 35 , 36 ] and Table 2 [ 35 – 46 ] of the Clinical Criteria, the study-protocol encompasses microbiological and imaging components. sections.assessment of cardiopulmonary status: The following methodologies are employed for the purpose of evaluating the cardiovascular and respiratory systems: The Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) status of angina should be documented, along with a 12-lead ECG (Supplementary Table 1). The New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification should also be included (Supplementary Table 2). A comprehensive TTE is conducted, encompassing an evaluation of aortic valve gradients (mean and peak), areas, indices, and the extent of regurgitation. This extensive assessment should also comprise a measurement of left ventricle systolic function (global and segmental).It is imperative that this initial echocardiogram is conducted within 90 days prior to the enrolment process. Cardiac imaging is an essential part of the pre-enrolment evaluation process. This imaging should include TEE, CT or 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose ([18F]FDG PET/CT imaging) to determine the area of infection in the heart structure. This qualifying cardiac imaging must be performed within one year before enrolment in patients with PVE, unless contraindicated. The assessment of patients suffering from PVE will include the evaluation of the occurrence of stenosis and coronary artery disease using the invasive techniques of left and right heart catheterisation. Cardiac catheterisation is to be conducted within one year of enrolment, unless there exists a contraindication. The SYNTAX score constitutes a mandatory element in the assessment of significant native coronary artery disease (CAD). A full lung check is vital for patients with a history of respiratory diseases.
sections.clinical laboratory tests: The following text comprises a comprehensive compendium of clinical laboratory tests. These include white blood cells (WBC), haemoglobin (Hgb), and platelet count. Further diagnostic procedures may include the measurement of prothrombin time (PT) or the international normalized ratio (INR), as well as the assessment of creatine kinase (CK)/CK-MB and troponin levels. The maximum time period for the conduction of these tests is 72 h prior to the valve implant procedure.

sections.therapeutic intervention: We conducted a retrospective evaluation of patients who underwent PVE surgery, and the following elements were analyzed in the archived documentation. Valve implantation was scheduled as a priority within 30 days of the presentation of the informed consent form. According to protocol, the medical examination and inclusion in the prospective registry for assignment must occur 14 and 21 days prior to the designated date of operation. In patients with native valve endocarditis (NVE), the distribution across cohorts depends on age, reproductive status, and the extent and severity of the infection at admission. The date of valve implantation is designated as day 0. The preliminary encounter (day 0) is for scheduling and calculating visit windows. Patients who undergo stenting, mechanical bioprosthesis, or homograft procedures remain enrolled and complete the study through year 19, according to the study procedure and schedule. Before valve implant, a patient’s cardiovascular system must be evaluated. This includes medications to regulate cardiovascular function and anti-thrombotic/anti-coagulant therapies. Adverse event assessment is also part of the process, supplemented by transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) or TEE, and supra-aortic doppler or TEE if needed. The recommended anticoagulation/antithrombotic regimen is in Table 8 .
