sections.methods: The data and materials used to conduct this research study will not be made publicly available.
sections.study design: The Closure of Muscular VSDs with the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder PAS ( ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT00647387 ) was a single-arm, observational, multicenter, postmarket clinical investigation designed to characterize the safety and effectiveness of the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder in patients ≥5.2 kg. This weight cutoff corresponds to the lower weight limit specified in the Food and Drug Administration approved Instructions for Use which was determined based on the analysis of premarket study data, where a higher rate of major complications was observed in patients weighing <5.2 kg. The study was approved by the institutional review boards of each participating clinical investigational site, and informed written consent was obtained from each patient or legally authorized representative before study participation.
sections.patient population: Enrollment criteria included patients with complex congenital muscular VSDs of significant size to warrant closure and at high risk for a standard transatrial or transarterial surgical VSD closure based on anatomic factors or the overall medical condition. Specific criteria to warrant VSD closure included VSDs with any of the following: (1) a large-volume left-to-right shunt (pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio > 2:1); (2) pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary artery pressure >50% systemic); or (3) clinical symptoms of congestive heart failure. Patients with a history of pulmonary artery banding with a VSD that, in the opinion of the treating investigator, warranted closure were also eligible for enrollment. Anatomic factors that were considered high risk for a standard surgical closure included a muscular VSD with a location requiring an extensive right ventriculotomy or a left ventriculotomy for surgical repair; a muscular VSD that had a failed surgical repair; the presence of multiple apical and anterior muscular VSDs (Swiss cheese septum); and a posterior apical muscular VSD covered by trabeculae. The VSD pattern for each patient was characterized as being a single VSD, multiple VSDs, or a Swiss cheese septum by the study investigator at each clinical site. Patients with either multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum were analyzed as 1 group when comparisons were made with the group of patients with a single VSD. Patients with severe elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance (>7 Wood units), right-to-left shunting (not associated with a tight pulmonary artery band), and irreversible pulmonary vascular disease were excluded from the study. Patients requiring closure of a perimembranous VSD or a postmyocardial infarction VSD, or VSDs with a distance <4 mm from the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) or atrioventricular valves (mitral and tricuspid), were also excluded. Other exclusion criteria were patients with active infection and those who were unable to take anti-platelet therapy.
sections.patient enrollment: Enrollment into the study was initially prospective before VSD closure. However, due to slow enrollment, retrospective enrollment was allowed beginning in 2016. Once retrospective enrollment began, all patients at each clinical site were screened for enrollment if they met the eligibility criteria, which included the potential to provide a minimum of baseline, procedure, 1-year, and 5-year echocardiography imaging. To mitigate bias, retrospectively enrolled patients were excluded from the technical success end point analysis.
sections.study end points: The primary effectiveness end points were technical success (defined as a device successfully implanted in the VSD), acute procedure success (defined as a defect with ≤2 mm residual shunt at the conclusion of the procedure through/around the muscular VSDs that underwent device occlusion, excluding additional VSDs that were not closed), and shunt closure success (defined as residual shunt ≤2 mm at the 1-year follow-up visit, as assessed by an independent centralized Echocardiography Board). The primary safety end point was the proportion of patients with any serious adverse event (SAE) within 12 months of the procedure. For this study, all SAEs were included in the primary safety end point regardless of cause, which included device-related, procedure-related, and unrelated SAEs.
sections.patient follow-up: Patient follow-up occurred before hospital discharge and at 30 days, 6 months, 1 year and annually through 5 years post-implant. At each follow-up, the residual shunt was assessed using a transthoracic echocardiogram. The baseline and 1-year echocardiograms were reviewed by an independent centralized echocardiography board. All SAEs were adjudicated by an independent centralized clinical events committee.
sections.device: The Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder is a self-expanding nitinol wire mesh device consisting of 2 flat symmetrical discs that are linked together by a central cylindrical waist with a diameter intended to correspond to the size of the VSD. 4 The device is available in 8 different waist diameters ranging from 4 to 18 mm in increments of 2 mm. The left and right disc diameters for the 4-mm device are 9 mm, and for the remaining device sizes are 8 mm larger than the waist diameter. All 8 device sizes have a uniform waist length of 7 mm. To improve closure, the discs and waist are filled with polyester patches, which are sewn securely within the device with polyester thread. Radiopaque marker bands located at the center of the right and left discs provide visualization of the device under fluoroscopy. The device size (waist diameter) is selected to be up to 2 mm larger than the largest VSD diameter, as assessed by transesophageal echocardiography or angiography at end-diastole. The device may be implanted using either an antegrade or retrograde approach using a 5F to 9F delivery sheath depending on the device size. 4 , 5
sections.statistical methods: This is a single-arm descriptive study. Categorical data are reported as a count and percentage. Continuous data are reported as mean±SD or as a median with interquartile range. The range may also be provided within square brackets to present the minimum and maximum values. Patient survival was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method. Patients with a death or unknown survival status were censored at the last known date reported alive. Data were analyzed using SAS software, version 9.4 (Chicago, IL).
sections.study cohort: The study enrolled 92 patients at 28 clinical sites in the United States (N=27) and Canada (N=1) between May 2008 and February 2020. Baseline patient demographics and medical history are shown in Table 1 . The median patient age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.8–5.8 years), with 54.3% being female. Approximately one-third of patients were between 3 months and 1 year of age, and ≈50% of patients weighed between 5.2 and 10 kg (Figure 1 ). Approximately 70% of patients were at high risk for surgical VSD repair due to the overall medical condition, with ≈36% of all patients having a prior pulmonary artery banding procedure and 15% having had a prior surgical closure of a muscular VSD. Patients with a prior pulmonary artery banding were generally recommended to undergo VSD closure combined with de-banding due to the onset of cyanosis. The median patient follow-up was 5.0 years (interquartile range, 4.6–5.4 years), with 96.1% of eligible patients completing the 5-year follow-up ( Figure S1 ).
sections.vsd characteristics: The VSD characteristics and procedural details are shown in Table 2 . Almost half (48.9%) of patients had a single VSD, 34.8% had multiple defects, and 16.3% had a multi-fenestrated Swiss cheese septum. A total of 155 VSDs were identified among 92 patients on the baseline echocardiogram, which included ≈41% apical muscular VSDs, 34% mid-muscular VSDs, 15% anterior muscular VSDs, 5% posterior muscular VSDs, 3% perimembranous VSDs, and 2% inlet VSDs. Seventy-five percent (75%) of the patients had a VSD with a pattern and location that would require an extensive right ventriculotomy or a left ventriculotomy during a surgical VSD repair, as determined at each individual site’s Heart Center. The average measured VSD size was 6.3±2.6 mm (2.0–14.0), and 82.6% of VSDs had a left-to-right shunt. Six patients without pulmonary hypertension had VSDs with a right-to-left shunt at the time of VSD closure associated with the presence of a tight pulmonary artery band. Hemodynamic assessment before VSD closure demonstrated an average pulmonary-to-systemic blood flow ratio of 2.1±1.0 for VSDs with left-to-right shunt (N=76); 1.3±0.5 for VSDs with bidirectional shunt (N=10); and 1.0±0.4 for VSDs with right-to-left shunt (N=6).
sections.procedure outcomes: An Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder was successfully implanted in muscular VSDs in 94.6% (87/92) of patients overall, and for prospectively enrolled patients (N=80), technical success was achieved in 93.8% (75/80; Table 3 ). In most cases (N=75; 81.5%) transesophageal echocardiography was used for the implant procedure, while angiography alone was utilized in 10 (10.9%) cases, transthoracic echocardiography alone in 5 (5.4%) cases, and intracardiac echocardiography in 2 (2.2%) cases. Five patients (5.4%) had an unsuccessful implant where a device was not implanted due to interference with the mitral valve (N=1); causing intraprocedural second-degree atrioventricular block requiring device removal (N=2); or due to technical difficulties associated with device recapture necessitating surgical removal or inadvertent device release leading to transcatheter retrieval using a snare (N=2). In another 5 of the 92 patients a second transcatheter procedure was performed to close additional VSDs with the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder such that overall, there were 97 implant procedures performed, with an average procedure time of 226±112 minutes. Within the first 2 years following transcatheter muscular VSD closure with the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder, there were 5 other patients who underwent closure of additional muscular VSDs using a surgical approach in 4 patients and using a perventricular approach in 1 patient (Table 3 ). Transcatheter closure was attempted in 136 muscular VSDs (average of 1.5±1.0 per patient) with an implant success rate of 91.9% (125/136) and an intraprocedural VSD closure rate (defined as a residual shunt ≤2.0 mm) of 78.0% (96/123). The 2 most frequently implanted device sizes were the 6 mm (29.4%) and 8 mm (27.8%) occluders. A single device was implanted in 75% of patients (N=69), and ≥2 devices were implanted in 20% (N=18) of patients. Among the 18 patients implanted with multiple devices, a single procedure was used to implant the devices in 12 patients, and 2 procedures were used to implant the devices in 6 patients.
sections.vsd closure: Acute procedural closure success was achieved in 78.0% of patients (71/91), and at 1 year post-implant the shunt closure success increased to 94.4% (68/72). Between 2 and 5 years post-implant shunt closure success further increased and remained consistently >98% (Figure 2 ). There were no patients in the study who developed hemolysis following VSD closure. Two (2.2%) patients had an additional transcatheter procedure to close a residual shunt through a defect associated with the original implant at 1 and 2.3 years, respectively, following the initial procedure. One patient was treated by adding a second Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder into the residual defect, and the second patient was treated by adding a different Amplatzer occluder into the residual defect (Table 3 ).
sections.adverse events: During the first year post-implant SAEs of any cause occurred in 52.2% (47/90) of patients. Overall, there were 153 all-cause SAEs and 23 non-SAEs reported over the 5 years of follow-up. The majority of the SAEs (N=126) were not procedure- or device-related but were submitted for adjudication in accordance with the study protocol. Throughout the study, SAEs occurred in more patients with either multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum (35/47 patients, 74%) compared with patients with a single VSD (16/45 patients, 36%; P <0.001). Patients with multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum tended to undergo VSD closure at a younger age compared with patients with a single VSD (median age at VSD closure of 19.6 versus 27.4 months); and had a history of undergoing more previous cardiac surgery before undergoing VSD closure (72% versus 42%, P =0.003). Procedure-related SAEs occurred in 20 (21.7%) patients, and device-related SAEs occurred in 7 (7.6%) patients as summarized in Table 3 . Non-SAEs occurred in 17 (18.5%) patients with none being procedure- or device-related. Intraprocedural hemodynamic instability occurred in 4 patients (weight 5.2–13.4 kg), with a jugular venous approach used in 3 patients and a femoral venous approach in 1 patient. All procedure- and device-related SAEs occurred within 9 days post-implant, except for 1 heart failure SAE that was reported 18 months post-implant in association with a device-related tricuspid regurgitation.
sections.surgical device explant: A total of 3 patients underwent surgical explant of the device. One patient had an intraprocedural device embolization due to inadvertent entanglement of the left disc within the mitral valve chordae requiring premature device release which was managed with a surgical device explant. The second patient with preexisting diastolic dysfunction had a Swiss cheese ventricular septum and underwent multiple VSD closures using multiple devices (N=6) during 2 separate transcatheter procedures 5 days apart. These resulted in an injury and entrapment of the tricuspid valve that required surgical explant of 2 devices 9 days later, with tricuspid valve repair and surgical closure of 2 VSDs. This patient had a preexisting diagnosis of restrictive cardiomyopathy and a small left ventricle and ultimately underwent orthotopic heart transplantation 9 months later. The third patient with preexisting diastolic dysfunction had multiple apical VSDs and underwent successful transcatheter VSD closure during 2 separate procedures 1 year apart without procedure- or device-related complications. This patient ultimately underwent orthotopic heart transplantation (the native heart was removed with 3 devices within it) due to preexisting restrictive cardiomyopathy with severe left ventricular diastolic dysfunction 18 months following the initial transcatheter VSD closure procedure. Both patients who underwent heart transplantation were found on histopathology of the native heart to have complete tissue coverage of the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluders with a neoendothelium and no evidence of a residual defect associated with the occluders.
sections.complete heart block: There was 1 patient with a Swiss cheese ventricular septum and prior surgery to close a membranous and muscular VSDs who underwent a successful transcatheter closure of a muscular VSD with a single device. This patient developed intraprocedural device-related third-degree heart block with cardiac arrest that required a permanent pacemaker, which was implanted 1 day following VSD closure and had no further device- or procedure-related complications through 5 years of follow-up.
sections.stroke: Two strokes were reported in the study. One patient developed a thrombus on the aortic valve on the same day following a successful transcatheter closure of an apical VSD with a single device. The patient subsequently underwent thrombus and pulmonary artery band removal 1 day later, which was complicated by a stroke with left hemiparesis postoperatively. This patient had no further device- or procedure-related complications through 5 years of follow-up. The second patient had a history of an aortic arch repair and underwent a successful transcatheter closure of a mid-to-apical VSD with a single device followed by a planned pulmonary artery band removal and an additional surgical aortic arch repair for residual obstruction. Three days postoperatively the patient developed an ischemic stroke with hemiparesis. Subsequently, the patient had no further device- or procedure-related complications through 5 years of follow-up.
sections.heart failure: There was 1 patient with multiple apical VSDs who underwent successful transcatheter closure of 1 VSD with a single device but had a moderate residual shunt causing ongoing heart failure 5 days post-implant that was successfully managed with pulmonary artery banding and resulted in no residual shunt at 5 years of follow-up. Another patient with a Swiss cheese septum underwent a successful transcatheter closure of an apical VSD with a single device but had severe tricuspid regurgitation and a residual shunt through the remaining VSDs requiring pulmonary artery banding 11 months post-implant. This patient had ongoing heart failure and 6 months later underwent surgical closure of the remaining VSDs through a left ventriculotomy with repair of the tricuspid valve and removal of the device, which apparently entrapped tricuspid valve tissue and caused severe valvular regurgitation. Both of these patients had no further procedure- or device-related complications through 5 years post-implant.
sections.survival: The 5-year survival was 97.5%, with 2 patient deaths that occurred ≈2.5 years post-implant, which were unrelated to the procedure or device (Figure 3 ). One death was due to an intracerebral hemorrhage following an unrelated tricuspid valve-in-valve procedure, and the second death was due to septicemia from an infected indwelling catheter used for total parenteral nutrition in a patient with liver failure.
sections.discussion: In this PAS, the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder demonstrated low rates of serious complications and high rates of effective transcatheter VSD closure in patients weighing ≥5.2 kg through 5 years of follow-up. Acute technical implant success was achieved in almost 94% of patients. Residual shunts, though common at the time of implant, resolved over time, with long-term shunt closure documented in >98% of patients at 5 years. Survival at 5 years was 97.5%, with no device- or procedure-related deaths. There was a low rate of device-related SAEs (<8%), with nearly all occurring within 10 days post-implant. The management of newborns with moderate or large VSDs can be complex depending on the presence of associated congenital heart defects, anatomic factors, and overall clinical status. 6 Under most circumstances surgical intervention to close the VSD is delayed to allow for spontaneous closure. 2 , 3 However, depending on symptoms and the need to perform other concomitant surgical procedures earlier intervention may be required. 1 In symptomatic patients with a large left-to-right VSD shunt who may not be suitable candidates to undergo surgical closure, pulmonary artery banding may be used to temporize symptoms and as a bridge to a more definitive closure procedure while the infant grows. 7 In patients without the protection of pulmonary artery banding, careful monitoring of cardiac function and pulmonary vascular resistance is essential to ensure the infant does not progress to having irreversible pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome. 8 In children with complex muscular VSDs who may be at high risk for standard surgical closure consideration may be given to utilizing transcatheter VSD closure to avoid potential complications associated with an invasive surgical procedure. 1 – 3 Children with multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum pattern at high risk for undergoing surgical VSD closure may benefit from transcatheter closure using ≥1 devices. Following a successful transcatheter VSD closure, additional interventions may be performed to remove or adjust a previously placed pulmonary artery band, and in some children, it may be necessary to perform additional transcatheter interventions or surgery to close additional VSDs or manage a residual shunt, as demonstrated in this study. In this PAS, ≈50% of patients (47/92) had either multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum, and many patients had either a previous surgical closure of a muscular VSD (15.2%) or pulmonary artery banding (35.9%). Patients enrolled in the study were at high risk for surgical VSD closure based on anatomic factors or the overall medical condition. Transcatheter VSD closure using the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder was successfully performed in >94% (87/92) of patients, with most patients being implanted with a single device (75%). In some patients with multiple VSDs or a Swiss cheese septum, reintervention to close additional VSDs was performed using a transcatheter (N=5), surgical (N=4), or perventricular approach (N=1). From a clinical standpoint, there are some important considerations that may be derived from this long-term follow-up study, given that existing literature on long-term follow-up of VSD closure devices is limited and clouded by data that include a variety of devices and perimembranous VSD closure. 9 – 11 One noteworthy consideration is that nearly all residual shunts (defined as residual flow through the VSD that received a device) disappeared on follow-up. Given the complex nature of many of these defects, immediate residual shunts are common, as was seen in this study. The fact that the data presented here verify that these residual shunts are mostly insignificant, and when present, resolve over time is valuable information for operators performing these procedures and health care providers following these patients. Consistent with the results of this study long-term follow-up studies 9 – 11 demonstrate a high shunt closure rate (95% to 100%) among patients who underwent transcatheter muscular VSD closure using the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder. The Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder is implanted within the muscular portion of the interventricular septum, where the device becomes incorporated into the muscular septum and residual shunts may become sealed with device healing and the endothelialization process. Histopathologic examination performed in 2 of the patients from this study who underwent heart transplantation at 9 and 18 months post-implant demonstrated complete tissue coverage of the occluders with a neoendothelium. This finding is consistent with prior studies where it was shown that the majority of the device becomes covered with a neoendothelium within 10 weeks post-implant and completely covered within 7 to 10 months post-implant. 12 It is important to note that in both of the patients who underwent heart transplantation, restrictive physiology with diastolic dysfunction was present before muscular VSD device closure and not as a consequence of the implanted muscular VSD occluders. Closure of the muscular VSDs with devices was performed to improve their clinical scenarios, but ultimately heart transplantation was required due to their preexisting restrictive cardiomyopathies. In the long-term follow-up study by Białkowski et al, 11 there was 1 patient who underwent successful transcatheter closure of 2 muscular VSDs using 2 separate Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluders during the second year of life and ultimately underwent orthotopic heart transplantation due to an underlying restrictive cardiomyopathy from endocardial fibrosis 16 years later at the age of 18 years. Consistent with the findings from this study, histopathologic examination 16 years post-implant demonstrated complete neoendothelialization of both devices without any evidence of thrombus formation, inflammatory reaction, or calcification. 13 Another consideration based on the results from this study is the low rate of long-term device-related SAEs. Specifically, in long-term follow-up, we observed no cases of device-related cardiac erosion, late occurrence of new valvular damage, or endocarditis from the devices, unlike cardiac implants in other locations. 1 , 14 – 16 Long-term safety data, as observed in this study and similarly reported in other studies, 9 – 11 are necessary to validate the excellent acute results seen with the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder when comparing to surgical VSD closure techniques. As demonstrated in this study transcatheter muscular VSD closure may be utilized as an alternative to a surgical VSD repair, particularly in patients with multiple prior surgical procedures who may be at high risk for reoperation and those with a favorable VSD location for a transcatheter approach to avoid complications associated with an open cardiac surgical approach. Although several patients in this study who were deemed high risk for a surgical VSD repair ultimately were referred to surgery to undergo closure of additional VSDs or due to complications of heart failure from incomplete VSD closure or device migration, a surgical approach compared with transcatheter closure, is associated with a higher risk for blood loss and transfusion, infection, and a prolonged hospital stay. 17 , 18 In addition, a surgical approach involving a left ventriculotomy may have the potential to result in more arrhythmias, left ventricular dysfunction, and late left aneurysm formation. 2 , 3 In addition to having a lower risk for complications a transcatheter approach for VSD closure may be favored due to offering better access to the VSD within a trabeculated right ventricle, a quicker recovery, and cosmetically to avoid a surgical scar. Thus, a transcatheter approach may have benefits over surgical muscular VSD closure in standard-risk patients as well.
sections.study limitations: Due to the limited number of patients with a complex congenital muscular VSDs at high-risk for surgical closure, enrollment into the study was slow and took almost 12 years to complete. To accelerate study completion retrospective enrollment of patients into the study was allowed beginning in 2016, which resulted in the addition of 12 (13%) patients. Since retrospective enrollment of patients has the potential to bias the interpretation of study results, retrospectively enrolled patients were excluded from the technical success end point analysis; however, all other analyses included all 92 patients.
sections.conclusions: Transcatheter closure of complex muscular VSDs in patients ≥5.2 kg using the Amplatzer Muscular VSD Occluder was found based on this study, to be safe and effective, with >94% shunt closure success at 1 year post-implant and a low rate of device-related complications (<8%). The availability of a safe and effective transcatheter treatment option for children with complex muscular VSDs provides an important alternative to surgical VSD closure that should be considered whenever encountering high-risk patients for a standard surgical approach.

title:
Caffeic Acid
Ameliorates l ‑Methionine-Induced
Hyperhomocysteinemia, Leading to Decreased Adult Neurogenesis and
Oxidative Stress Status in Adult Rats
abstract:
Chronic l -methionine ( l -met) treatment
induces
hyperhomocysteinemia, which impairs neurogenesis and memory by increasing
oxidative stress. Caffeic acid (CA) possesses antioxidant properties
that reduce brain oxidative damage and promote neurogenesis. This
study investigated the neuroprotective effects of caffeic acid against
the impact of l -met on hippocampal neurogenesis. Forty male
Sprague–Dawley rats were randomly assigned to four groups ( n = 10 per group): Control, l -met, CA, and CA+ l -met. Rats received daily oral gavage of l -met (1.7
g/kg) and/or CA (40 mg/kg) for 28 days. The results demonstrated that
CA ameliorated l -met-induced decreases in DCX and Sox-2-positive
cells in the SGZ of the dentate gyrus, as shown by immunofluorescence
staining. CA also reversed the l -met-induced decreases in
hippocampal protein expression of Nrf2, Sox-2, and BDNF, as determined
by Western blotting. Furthermore, CA alleviated l -met-induced
oxidative damage and decreased antioxidant enzyme activity in the
prefrontal cortex (PF) and hippocampus. These findings demonstrate
CA’s ability to counteract neurotoxicity induced by l -methionine.

sections.introduction:
Currently, the prevalence
of dementia is increasing worldwide,
affecting millions of people. Dementia
is becoming more prevalent globally and a significant public concern,
affecting learning, memory, and cognitive function. Several studies have demonstrated that the production of
free radicals leads to oxidative stress, causing damage to lipids,
proteins, and nucleic acids. This damage contributes to the acceleration
of neurodegenerative diseases associated with dementia. , l -methionine ( l -met) is an essential, nonpolar
amino acid commonly found in foods such as meat, fish, eggs, sesame
oil, and cereal grains. l -Met
serves as a substrate for several important biomolecules, including
cysteine and taurine. Through a methylation pathway, it is converted
to homocysteine (Hcy) via a methylation pathway. Excessive levels of Hcy are associated with the production
of oxidative agents that cause neuronal damage through highly reactive
free radical agents. This, in turn, disrupts the redox system in neuronal
cells, inducing and accelerating lipid peroxidation events. Chronic l -met treatment at 1.7 g/kg
of animal weight elevates Hcy levels, inducing hyperhomocysteinemia
(HHcy). This can lead to cerebrovascular disorders such as stroke
and vascular dementia. Furthermore, administering l -met 1.7 g/kg for 28 days can lead to decreased cell proliferation,
cell survival as well as increased cell cycle arrest, resulting in
spatial and recognition memory deficits. Neurogenesis continuously generates newborn neurons in the
hippocampal
dentate gyrus throughout life; however, it declines with age and is
disrupted by negative factors affecting the neurogenesis process. Conversely, hippocampal neurogenesis and neuroprotective
qualities are enhanced through exposure to an enriched environment
and compounds derived from plant-based sources, including hesperidin,
asiatic acid, chrysin, and CA. , − Caffeic acid (CA), a hydroxycinnamic acid, is a natural phenolic
compound present in plants and foods such as tomatoes, berries, tea,
coffee, and red wine. − CA exhibits antioxidant properties and effectively
scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to the neutralization
of lipid peroxidative markers. A previous
study investigated the effects of CA at the doses of 20 and 40 mg/kg
on oxidative stress and antioxidant enzyme activities. CA 40 mg/kg demonstrates its ability to improve memory
deficits associated with cell proliferation and survival, decrease
cell cycle arrest, and effectively enhance antioxidant enzyme activities
and reduce neuronal apoptosis and oxidative stress in both l -met and aging models. , This study aims to explore how
CA 40 mg/kg affects the oxidative state, antioxidant enzyme activity,
and the expression of specific protein markers linked to neurogenesis
and neural stem cells. This research may ultimately uncover a new
way that CA mitigates the detrimental effects of hyperhomocysteinemia.
sections.materials and methods:
In all experiments,
male Sprague–Dawley rats aged 4–5
weeks and weighing 200–220 g were purchased from Nomura Siam
International Co., Ltd., Bangkok, Thailand, and used in all experimental
procedures. They were housed in a stainless-steel cage (28 ×
47 × 18 cm) and maintained under a 12 h light/dark cycle at 28–30
°C. The rats had unlimited access to food and water. The experiment
methods were accepted by the Khon Kaen University Ethics Committee
in Animal Research (reference number AICUC-KKU-87/65). Before any
drugs were administered, the rats were randomly housed for 7 days
to acclimate to their surroundings. The CA and l -met supplier
was Sigma-Aldrich Chemical Co. (Saint Louis, MO, USA). The rats were
randomly assigned to four groups: the vehicle group; the l -met ( l -Met) group ( l -met 1.7 g/kg/day, dissolved
in 0.1% w/v Carboxyl Methyl Cellulose [CMC]); the CA group (CA40 mg/kg/day,
a dose from previous study, dissolved in propylene glycol); and the
CA combined with l -met (CA+ l -met) group. Oral gavage
was used to administer both CA and l -met. The vehicle (propylene
glycol and 0.1% w/v CMC) was given to the animals in the vehicle group
by oral gavage. All treatments, including l -met, CA, and
vehicle, were initiated on the same day and continued for 4 weeks
( Figure ).
sections.tissue preparation:
Rat brains were
fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Sigma-Aldrich, Inc., USA). The
brains were then serially sectioned at a thickness of 40 μm
in the coronal plane using a cryostat (Cryostat Series HM550, Microm
International, A.S. Science Co. Ltd., Walldorf, Germany). The sections
were kept in the cryoprotective buffer at 4 °C. A systematic
random sampling method was used and every eighth section along the
length of the dentate gyrus was selected to obtain nine sections per
brain for DCX and Sox-2 staining. Immunofluorescence staining was
then used to assess hippocampal neurogenesis.
sections.determination of hippocampal neural stem:
The sex-determining region Y-box 2 (Sox-2) immunofluorescence
staining method was used to investigate cell development, self-renewal,
and pluripotency. Forty-micron sections
were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-Sox-2 (1:400, Abcam,
USA). On the second day, the sections were treated with Alexa 568
goat antirabbit IgG (1:500, Invitrogen, USA) at room temperature for
60 min and counterstained with DAPI (1:6000, Molecular Probes, Eugene,
OR, USA). Finally, each section was mounted with glycerol.
sections.determination of immature neurons (dcx):
Cell differentiation
into immature neurons was analyzed using the
doublecortin microtubule-associated protein staining method. Serial
sections of frozen brains were prepared along the length of the dentate
gyrus in the coronal plane. The antimouse monoclonal IgG primary doublecortin
antibody (1:100, Santa Cruz, USA) was applied to the sections and
incubated overnight at 4 °C. The following day, the sections
were incubated with rabbit antimouse IgG Alexa Fluor 488 antibody
(1:300, Invitrogen, USA) for 60 min and then counterstained with propidium
iodide (1:6000, Sigma-Aldrich, Inc., St. Louis, USA) for 30 s. Ultimately,
each section was mounted using glycerol and coverslipped for fluorescence
microscope examination using the free-floating approach. Staining
was applied to each section, and three cell layers in the subgranular
zone of the upper and lower blades of the DG were counted to determine
the presence of DCX-positive cells.
sections.biochemical assessment:
After homogenizing
tissue samples from the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex on ice with
cold deionized water to prepare a 100 mg/mL solution, the mixture
was centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant
was then carefully collected.
sections.measurement of malondialdehyde\n(mda):
MDA level is the end product of lipid peroxidation,
and its levels
are measured using the thiobarbituric acid reactive substance (TBARS)
assay. , A 100 μL aliquot of the supernatant
was mixed with a solution of 20% acetic acid (pH 3.5), 0.8% thiobarbituric
acid (TBA), and 8.1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS). The mixture was
heated to 95 °C for 1 h. Once cooled to room temperature, deionized
water was added. Afterward, the mixture was centrifuged at 4000 rpm
for 10 min at room temperature. A 15:1 pyridine and n-butanol solution
was then added to the mixture. The supernatant was collected to measure
absorbance at 540 nm using a microplate reader. The data were expressed
in nmol/mg protein, and the reaction was performed in triplicate.
sections.measurement of catalase (cat) levels:
The CAT enzyme activity measurement technique is based on the method
described by Weydert. A 96-well plate
containing 10 μL of the supernatant and 30% hydrogen peroxide
(H 2 O 2 ) in a 50 mM potassium phosphate buffer
(pH 7.0) was used to initiate CAT enzyme activity. The reaction was
then rapidly stopped using 2.5 M sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ). After gently mixing the solution with potassium permanganate
(KMnO 4 ), absorbance was measured at 540 nm using a microplate
reader.
sections.measurement of glutathione peroxidase (g:
The procedure described by Eyer, Podhradsky, and Weydert
was adapted to measure GPx enzyme activity. , A cocktail solution was prepared using sodium azide (NaN3), 50 mM
glutathione, β-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (β-NADPH),
and glutathione reductase (GR). To initiate the reaction, 60 μL
of the supernatant was combined with 30% H 2 O 2 and the cocktail containing 5,5′-dithiobis­(2-nitrobenzoic
acid) (DTNB). After incubating the mixture in a dark chamber for 10
min, absorbance was measured at 405 nm using a microplate reader.
sections.measurement of superoxide dismutase (sod:
SOD activity was measured using a method adapted from
Weydert. The cocktail included 216 mM potassium phosphate buffer (pH
7.8), 1.1 mM cytochrome C solution, 0.108 mM xanthine solution, and
10.7 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid solution (EDTA). Each measurement
was performed at room temperature. To initiate the reaction, 700 μL
of the cocktail and 25 μL of the supernatant were mixed in a
96-well plate, followed by the addition of xanthine oxidase solution
to stop the cytochrome C reaction. Absorbance at 540 nm was measured
using a microplate reader from minute 0 to minute 5. The data were
reported in protein units per mg. The biochemical assessment reaction
was performed in triplicate.
sections.western\nblotting analysis:
Hippocampal
tissue samples were homogenized on ice in lysis buffer to a concentration
of 100 mg/mL solution. The homogenate was then centrifuged at 13,000
rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatant was collected.
Protein concentrations were measured using a Nanodrop spectrometer.
For the analysis of BDNF, Nrf2, and Sox-2, proteins were separated
by SDS-PAGE using a 12% separating gel. Following separation, the
samples (30 μg proteins per lane) were transferred onto nitrocellulose
membranes (GE Healthcare Life Sciences, Freiburg, Germany). The membrane
was then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary
antibodies: Sox-2 (1:1000, ab97959, Abcam, Cambridge, UK), Nrf2 (1:1000,
ab31163, Abcam, Cambridge, UK), BDNF (1:1000, ab108319, Santa Cruz
Biotechnology, TX, USA), and anti-GAPDH (1:20,000, Abcam, Cambridge,
UK). The membranes were incubated for 60 min at room temperature with
the following secondary antibodies: antirabbit (1:2000, DAKO, Glostrup,
Denmark), antigoat (1:2000, DAKO, Glostrup, Denmark), or antimouse
(1:2000, DAKO, Glostrup, Denmark), depending on the primary antibody
used. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence
(ECL) Western blot detection system (GE Healthcare, Buckingham, UK).
The relative optical density of the protein bands was quantified using
ImageJ software (version 1.53a, Wayne Rasband, National Institutes
of Health, USA). The data were expressed as the optical density of
each protein band relative to that of the GAPDH housekeeping protein.
All experiments were performed in triplicate, and the protein bands
of interest were compared to this internal control.
sections.homocysteine serum levels:
Blood samples
were collected from the lateral tail veins. The serum homocysteine
level was estimated using a Roche Cobas homocysteine enzymatic analyzer
to determine l -met levels using a method based on the principle
that assesses the cosubstrate conversion product instead of Hcy. First
step: free hydrogen is created by reducing oxidized hydrogen bonds.
Next step: Hcy reacts with SAM, a cosubstrate, in a reaction catalyzed
by Hcy S-methyltransferase to produce l -met and SAH. SAH
is measured via a series of coupled enzyme reactions at the Immunology
and Clinical Chemistry Laboratory, Faculty of Medicine, Khon Kaen
University.
sections.statistical analysis:
Statistical
parameters were calculated using GraphPad Prism software (Version
7.04). Results are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance
was set at p < 0.05. Data normality was assessed
using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk test ( p > 0.05) with IBM SPSS Statistics 29. A One-way ANOVA
was
used to analyze Hcy serum level followed by Dunnett post hoc testing,
Sox-2 and DCX immunofluorescence-positive cells, protein expression
(from Western blotting analysis), antioxidant enzyme activities, and
MDA followed by Bonferroni post hoc testing. Animal weight gain was
analyzed using two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni post hoc testing.
sections.effect of ca and l -met on animal\nbody:
Animals receiving 40 mg/kg
of CA and l -met showed no significant difference in the body
weight compared to the control group ( F (81, 560)
= 0.8001, P > 0.05; Figure ). However, l -met administration
significantly increased homocysteine serum levels in both the l -met and combined groups compared to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 0.3101, P = 0.0045, R 2 = 0.5569) and the combined group ( F (3, 20) = 0.1136, P = 0.0388, R 2 = 0.6089), respectively. However, the combined
group showed significantly lower Hcy serum levels compared to the l -met group ( F (3, 20) = 0.3101, P = 0.0467, R 2 = 0.5569; Figure B).
sections.effect of ca and l -met on hippocampal\n:
With chronic l -met administration,
Sox-2 is widely used as a marker for cell self-renewal and pluripotency
of neural stem cells ( Figure A-D). The results showed a significant decrease in Sox-2-positive
cells in adult rats treated with l -met compared to the vehicle
and combined groups ( F (3, 20) = 0.2338, R 2 = 0.8223, P = 0.0002 and P < 0.0001, respectively). On the other hand, both the CA and combined
groups showed a significant increase in Sox-2-positive cells compared
to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 0.2338, R 2 = 0.8223, P = 0.0031 and P = 0.0428, respectively). These findings suggest that CA
may enhance and prevent the reduction of neural stem cells caused
by l -met ( Figure E).
sections.effect of ca and l -met on immature\nneu:
DCX has become a widely used marker for immature
neurons in the adult neurogenesis process ( Figure A-D). The results for the l -met
group revealed a significant decrease in DCX-positive cells compared
to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 2.294, P < 0.0001, R 2 = 0.8535). In contrast,
the CA group showed a significant increase in DCX-positive cells compared
to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 2.294, P = 0.0019, R 2 = 0.8535). Moreover, the
combined group exhibited significantly higher DCX-positive cells compared
to the l -met group ( F (3, 20) = 2.294, P < 0.001, R 2 = 0.8535).
However, there were no significant differences in DCX-positive cells
between the vehicle group and the combined group ( F (3, 20) = 2.294, P = 3420, R 2 = 0.8535; Figure E).
sections.effect\nof ca and l -met on antioxidant\:
MDA levels: Animals treated with l -met alone exhibited significantly higher MDA levels in both the
hippocampal region and prefrontal cortex compared to the vehicle group
( F (3, 20) = 10.8, P = 0.0328, R 2 = 0.6832, and F (3, 28) =
0.5147, P = 0.0134, R 2 = 0.6353). However, both the caffeic and combined groups showed
significantly decreased MDA levels in the hippocampal tissues compared
to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 10.8, P = 0.0399, P = 0.0280, R 2 = 0.6832; Figure A), as well as in prefrontal cortex tissue ( F (3,
28) = 0.5147, P = 0.0228, P = 0.0222, R 2 = 0.6353, respectively; Figure B). CAT levels: The l -met
group showed a significant decrease
in CAT levels in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compared to
the vehicle group ( F (3, 28) = 1.012, P = 0.0313, R 2 = 0.6103; F (3, 28) = 0.133, P = 0.0424, R 2 = 0.6112). In contrast, both the caffeic and combined groups
exhibited a significant increase in CAT levels in hippocampal ( F (3, 28) = 0.133, P = 0.0077, P = 0.0402, R 2 = 0.6112) and prefrontal
cortex tissue ( F (3, 28) = 1.012, P = 0.0253, P = 0.0194, R 2 = 0.6103) compared to the vehicle group ( Figure C and D). SOD
levels: A significant reduction of the SOD levels was observed
in the l -met group compared to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 0.7466, P = 0.0036, R 2 = 0.7815; F (3, 20) = 0.9164, P = 0.0014, R 2 = 0.7682). In
contrast, the SOD levels in the CA and combined groups were significantly
higher than those in the vehicle group in both the hippocampus ( F (3, 28) = 1.012, P = 0.0253, P = 0.0194, R 2 = 0.6103; Figure E) and prefrontal cortex ( F (3, 20) = 0.9164, P = 0.0256, P = 0.0344, R 2 = 0.7682; Figure F). GPx levels:
The GPx levels in the CA and combined groups in hippocampus
( F (3, 20) = 0.5757, P = 0.0014, P = 0.0181, R 2 = 0.7885) and
prefrontal cortex tissue ( F (3, 28) = 0.3817, P = 0.0425, P = 0.0294, R 2 = 0.6247) were significantly higher compared to the
vehicle group. In contrast, the l -met group showed a significant
decrease in GPx levels compared to the vehicle group in hippocampus
( F (3, 20) = 0.5757, P = 0.0043, R 2 = 0.7885; Figure G) and prefrontal cortex tissue ( F (3, 28) = 0.3817, P = 0.0134, R 2 = 0.6247; Figure H).
sections.effect of ca and l -met on the expressio:
Western blotting
analysis revealed a significant reduction in the expression of Nrf2,
Sox-2, and BDNF in the hippocampus of rats treated with l -met compared to the vehicle group ( F (3, 20) = 0.6496, P = 0.0457, R 2 = 0.7209); ( F (3, 20) = 5.4, P = 0.0263, R 2 = 0.7196); ( F (3, 20) = 1.508, P = 0.0159, R 2 = 0.7855). On
the other hand, a significant increase in hippocampal protein expression
of Nrf2, Sox-2, and BDNF was observed in both the CA group ( F (3, 20) = 0.6496, P = 0.0045, R 2 = 0.7209; F (3, 20) = 5.4, P = 0.0064, R 2 = 0.7196; F (3, 20) = 1.508, P = 0.0003, R 2 = 0.7855) and the combined treatment groups ( F (3, 20) = 0.6496, P = 0.0181, R 2 = 0.7209; F (3, 20) = 5.4, P = 0.352, R 2 = 0.7196; F (3, 20) = 1.508, P = 0.0163, R 2 = 0.7855) when compared to the vehicle group. Furthermore,
the group receiving both CA and l -met exhibited significantly
higher levels of Nrf2, Sox-2, and BDNF expression compared to the l -met group ( F (3, 20) = 0.6496, P < 0.0001, R 2 = 0.7209); ( F (3, 20) = 5.4, P < 0.0001, R 2 = 0.7196); ( F (3, 20) = 1.508, P < 0.0001, R 2 = 0.7855)
as shown in Figure .
sections.discussion:
The major finding of this
current
study is that l -met-treated
rats exhibited a decrease in hippocampal neurogenesis, as evidenced
by a reduction in the expression of the Sox-2 and DCX-positive cells
in the hippocampal dentate gyrus. In this study, chronic administration
of l -met caused a significant increase in Hcy serum levels
compared to the vehicle group. These findings confirm previous studies
reporting that excessive l -met results in hyperhomocysteinemia,
which in turn induces neuroinflammation and impairs neurogenesis. The main mechanism of l -met-induced
neurogenesis impairment is likely related to increased oxidative stress
in the hippocampus. This stress develops
during HHcy as the thiol groups generate ROS, including H 2 O 2 , superoxide, and hydroxyl radicals. These impair redox
and homeostasis, resulting in increased lipid peroxidation and neuronal
damage. CA possesses potent antioxidant
properties that may neutralize MDA levels, thereby increasing antioxidant
enzyme activity and reducing serum Hcy levels by eliminating free
radicals caused by elevated Hcy accumulation. Furthermore, l -met increased MDA levels and decreased the
expression of Nrf2, Sox-2, and BDNF in the hippocampal region, while
also lowering the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as CAT, GPx,
and SOD. On the other hand, CA improved
antioxidant activity by lowering MDA levels and increasing the expression
of DCX and Sox-2-positive cells, as demonstrated by immunofluorescence
staining. Additionally, CA administration ameliorated the l -met-induced decrease in Nrf2, Sox-2, and BDNF expression. Throughout life, adult neurogenesis occurs in the subventricular
zone of the lateral ventricles and in the SGZ of the dentate gyrus. According to our current research, rats treated
with l -met exhibited a significant reduction in the expression
of Ki-67 and BrdU-specific cells. The
Sox-2 transcription factor can increase cell survival and proliferation
by activating the PI3K/AKT pathway through its connections with tyrosine
kinase pathways. In this interaction, AKT phosphorylates Sox-2, affecting
its stability, nuclear localization, and activity, while Sox-2, in
turn, acts as a downstream target that encourages stemness and therapeutic
resistance. Sox-2 moderates Notch1 signaling
to maintain the precursor pool in the adult SGZ, and there is a positive
correlation between Sox-2 and nestin expression. , Previous
studies have reported that deletion of Sox-2 in adult rats results
in a loss of hippocampal neurogenesis, because Sox-2 is required for
maintaining the proliferation of NSCs and intermediate progenitor
cells (IPCs), and Sox-2 in adult rats disappears as these cells differentiate
into neuroblasts. In the present
study, the l -met group showed a significant
decrease in the neuronal stem cell marker Sox-2 and the immature neuron
marker DCX compared to the vehicle group. These results demonstrate
that l -met administration contributes to a reduction in hippocampal
neurogenesis. This finding is consistent with a previous study on
brain aging induced by D-galactose, which reported that reduced Sox-2
expression negatively affects cell proliferation associated with the
neurogenic niche. However, CA treatment
led to a significant increase in Sox-2-positive cells compared to
the vehicle group. Interestingly, the combined administration of CA
and l -met can improve Sox-2-positive cell levels compared
to both the vehicle and the l -met groups, as well as enhance
cell differentiation compared to the l -met group in the SGZ
of the hippocampal dentate gyrus. These findings suggest that CA can
mitigate the negative effect of l -met by preventing the reduction
of neuronal stem cell expression and promoting cell differentiation.
The current study supports previous findings that hyperhomocysteinemia
causes apoptosis, neuronal damage, and inflammation. However, CA can
also lessen the adverse effects of l -met through strong antioxidant
properties, which protect against free radical-induced oxidative stress. , , , Oxygen-centered free radicals are known as ROS. Oxidative stress refers to the biological damage
caused
by an excess of ROS. An imbalance between ROS production and the cell’s
antioxidant capacity leads to oxidative stress. According to a previous study, chronic l -met administration
showed a significant increase in Hcy serum levels associated with
oxidative agent production via homocysteine thiolactone, which is
a highly reactive radical unstable electron atom. In this study, rats that received l -met exhibited
increased ROS production, leading to oxidative stress and a significant
rise in MDA levels due to lipid peroxidation in the hippocampal and
prefrontal cortex regions compared to the vehicle group. Moreover,
increased oxidative stress in the hippocampus is likely the primary
cause of neuronal damage and memory impairment, resulting from the
sulfur-containing property of Hcy. Oxidative
stress, brain defects, and cognitive and memory dysfunction are all
significantly influenced by HHcy. Recent
findings indicate that chronic l -met consumption is associated
with a significant decline in the enzymatic activities of GPx, CAT,
and SOD. However, these declines were prevented with the administration
of CA. Furthermore, treatment with CA
mitigated these effects, suggesting that oxidative stress plays a
role in the interaction between CA and l -met. Interestingly,
the current study found that the increase in Nrf2
expression in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampal regions was
associated with a rise in antioxidant enzyme levels. In order to preserve cellular redox equilibrium, Nrf2 plays
a crucial role in maintaining cellular redox balance by regulating
the production of antioxidants. During
oxidative stress, the disruption of Keap1 and Nrf2 interaction triggers
Nrf2 translocation into the nucleus, where it binds to the antioxidant
response element (ARE). Following this,
Nrf2 stimulates the transcription of numerous genes related to detoxification
and antioxidants, including those encoding enzymes like heme oxygenase-1
(HO-1), CAT, SOD, and GPx. These enzymes
lessen free radicals and oxidative stress in cells. Consequently,
the Nrf2/ARE signaling pathway serves as a defense mechanism for antioxidants. This study found that the l -met group
exhibited a significant decrease in Nrf2 expression compared to the
vehicle and combined groups. In contrast, both the CA group and the
CA with l -met group showed a significant increase in Nrf2
expression in the hippocampus. Similarly, a prior study demonstrated
that the CA micronutrient protects the brains of mice from Aβ-induced
neurodegeneration and memory impairment through the Nrf2-HO-1 signaling
pathway in an AD rat model. Additionally,
a CA polyphenol ester derivative prevents oxidative stress-induced
neuronal cell apoptosis and scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment
by activating Nrf2/HO-1 signaling. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin essential
for processes such as neurogenesis and neuronal survival. BDNF also
has significant affects both presynaptic and postsynaptic levels,
making it a crucial modulator of synaptic plasticity. The BDNF signaling pathway enhances the activity of the
cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) transcription factor,
which regulates nerve cell survival and promotes synaptic plasticity
and neurogenesis. , This study found that l -met administration was associated with a significant decrease in
hippocampal BDNF expression compared to the vehicle and combined groups.
However, treatment with CA prevented the decreases in BDNF expression
in both the CA and combined groups compared to the vehicle group.
Supporting this, previous studies have shown that increasing BDNF
expression and reducing neuroinflammatory reactions can help mitigate
cognitive impairment. Dietary methionine restriction may reduce cognitive
impairment in sleep-deprived mice and CA significantly increased the
expression of these markers in the brains of mice given Aβ injections. Moreover, the binding of BDNF to its TrkB (Tropomyosin
receptor Kinase B) receptor facilitates the dimerization and autophosphorylation
of cytoplasmic tyrosine residues, initiating the activation of a diverse
array of signaling pathways, including ERK, PI3K, and the generation
of second messengers such as cAMP, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3)
and Ca 2+ crucial for neural development, survival, and
plasticity that promote neuronal growth. A study in hippocampal neurons revealed that BDNF activates Nrf2,
evidenced by BDNF-induced increases in Nrf2 gene targets. Conversely,
Nrf2 activation with fluoxetine raises BDNF expression levels in a
mouse model of anxiety and depression. Furthermore, a recent study found that while antioxidant therapy
restores redox equilibrium, lower hippocampal levels of BDNF in a
model of depressed rats result in decreased nuclear translocation
of Nrf2, causing persistent oxidative stress. These findings demonstrate that CA effectively increased BDNF expression
via bidirectional crosstalk, thereby improving Nrf2 translocation
to the nucleus and enhancing oxidative enzyme activities after binding
with TrkB receptor. This process is essential for memory, neurogenesis,
and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus. Numerous investigations
have demonstrated that individuals with AD and other neurodegenerative
diseases exhibit ectopic expression of stem cells, such as Sox-2 and
immature neurons like DCX in the hippocampal dentate gyrus. BDNF can enhance the migration of NSCs expressing
Sox-2. Conversely, Sox-2 regulates BDNF gene expression, as well as
NSC survival, proliferation, and differentiation into neurons. These
interactions frequently cooperate to create a synergistic loop for
neurogenesis. This study showed that
Sox-2 expression in the CA and combined groups was significantly higher
than in the vehicle group in the hippocampus. The interaction between
the Nrf2 and Sox-2 pathways is crucial for maintaining cell pluripotency,
stemness, and survival, particularly in cancer and development. Nrf2
shields cells from oxidative stress, while Sox-2 controls stem cell
identity. Nrf2 can affect Sox-2 expression, and both pathways work
together to regulate genes essential for self-renewal and stress resistance.
sections.conclusions:
The neuroprotective effects
of CA against
hyperhomocysteinemia
in adult rats are demonstrated by the increase in neural stem cells,
an immature neuron marker, as well as a decrease in MDA overproduction.
Additionally, a rise in GPx, CAT, and SOD activity was observed in
the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. These discoveries may lead
to future therapies for cognitive impairment.

title: Clinically integrated multi-modal transformer framework with cross-modal gated fusion and clinical nomogram for automated Kellgren-Lawrence grading of knee osteoarthritis on x-ray images
abstract: Background We developed a multi-modal Transformer framework integrating knee radiographs with clinical covariates to enable automated, objective, and generalizable ordinal Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading. Methods A total of 2,703 anteroposterior knee radiographs were retrospectively collected from three independent medical centers (January 2018 - December 2024). Data from two centers ( n = 1,953) were used for model development and internal five-fold stratified cross-validation, while the third center ( n = 750) served as an independent external test set. The proposed framework combines a Swin Transformer-Base image encoder with a clinical feature Transformer through a novel Robust Cross-Modal Gated Fusion (RCGF) module employing bidirectional cross-attention and uncertainty-aware dynamic gating via Monte-Carlo dropout. Ordinal prediction was performed using Consistent Rank Logits (CORAL). Eight classifier architectures were systematically compared, encompassing multi-modal models, unimodal image-only baselines, and a clinical-only model. Results The proposed RCGF framework achieved a Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) of 0.900 (95% CI: 0.877–0.921), macro-averaged AUC of 0.930 (95% CI: 0.910–0.950), and balanced accuracy of 87.6% on the independent external test set, significantly outperforming all baseline models including BioViL-T (QWK = 0.850) and MedViT (QWK = 0.830; all FDR-corrected p < 0.001). Sensitivity for severe Osteoarthritis (OA) (Grade 4) reached 83.5% (95% CI: 79.1–87.4%), with specificity 95.3%. The clinical nomogram demonstrated excellent calibration (calibration slope = 0.98, Brier score = 0.072, C-statistic = 0.940) and superior net benefit over treat-all and treat-none strategies across all clinically relevant decision thresholds. Conclusion This multi-modal Transformer framework with uncertainty-aware gated fusion provides robust external generalizability for ordinal knee OA severity grading and delivers a clinically actionable nomogram. The approach has strong potential to reduce radiologist workload and facilitate objective assessment on routine clinical radiographs, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12891-026-10043-4.

sections.introduction: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) represents the most prevalent joint disease worldwide and a major cause of chronic pain, disability, and reduced quality of life. It affects over 500 million individuals globally, with radiographic evidence present in approximately 37% of women and 27% of men aged over 60 years [ 1 ]. The socioeconomic burden is enormous, with direct and indirect costs exceeding $200 billion annually in high-income countries, projected to rise sharply with population aging [ 2 ]. Accurate severity assessment is critical for risk stratification, treatment planning, and monitoring disease progression. The current gold standard, the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading system, is semi-quantitative, suffers from substantial inter-observer variability (Cohen’s κ = 0.45–0.65 in community radiological settings), and depends heavily on the expertise of musculoskeletal radiologists [ 3 , 4 ]. This variability imposes a direct clinical cost: patients in settings without specialist coverage may receive suboptimal or delayed care. Although deep learning approaches have shown promise in automating knee radiograph interpretation [ 5 – 7 ]. several important limitations persist. Most models perform binary classification (OA versus non-OA) rather than full ordinal grading across the five KL levels, losing clinically relevant severity information [ 5 , 8 ]. The majority of published studies rely on single-center data with only internal validation, limiting generalizability across heterogeneous imaging protocols, scanner vendors, and patient populations [ 9 , 10 ].Critically, most existing frameworks are unimodal (image-only) and fail to incorporate readily available clinical risk factors [ 11 , 12 ]. Even when multi-modal approaches are attempted, they typically rely on simple concatenation or late-fusion strategies that lack robustness to domain shift and fail to model uncertainty in feature integration [ 6 , 13 ]. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel multi-modal Transformer-based framework that integrates high-resolution knee radiographs with key clinical covariates through a Robust Cross-Modal Gated Fusion (RCGF) module. Unlike conventional fusion methods, RCGF employs bidirectional cross-attention combined with an uncertainty-aware dynamic gating mechanism based on Monte-Carlo dropout, enabling adaptive weighting of each modality while explicitly addressing inter-center domain shift. Ordinal prediction is achieved using the Consistent Rank Logits (CORAL) framework to preserve the natural ordering of KL grades [ 8 ]. The model was developed and internally validated using five-fold cross-validation on data from two medical centers ( n = 1,953) and externally tested on an independent third center ( n = 750). While Swin Transformer, CORAL, MC-Dropout, and clinical feature fusion are individually established methods, their principled integration into a unified uncertainty-aware cross-modal gated fusion framework for ordinal knee OA grading, combined with multi-center external validation and a validated clinical nomogram, has not been previously reported. The novelty of this work lies in this specific combination and its rigorous clinical validation, rather than in any single component.

sections.study population and dataset: This retrospective multi-center study was approved by the institutional review boards of all three participating centers, with a waiver of informed consent due to the de-identified nature of the data. The study was conducted and reported in accordance with the TRIPOD + AI guidelines for transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Zhejiang Wanli University (approval no. 62576319), with a waiver of informed consent due to the fully de-identified nature of the data. A total of 2,703 anteroposterior knee radiographs were collected from three independent medical centers between January 2018 and December 2024. Center 1 contributed 980 radiographs (790 patients) and Center 2 contributed 973 radiographs (782 patients); these two centers (combined n = 1,953 from 1,572 patients) constituted the development cohort used for five-fold stratified cross-validation. Center 3 ( n = 750 from 612 patients) served as an independent external test set with no overlap with the development cohort. Detailed imaging acquisition parameters for each center are provided in Supplementary Table S2. Inclusion criteria were: age ≥ 40 years, standard weight-bearing AP knee radiograph of diagnostic quality, and complete availability of all six predefined clinical variables. Exclusion criteria included: previous total or unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, acute fracture, primary or metastatic bone tumor, septic arthritis, severe motion artifact, or incomplete clinical records. In total, 247 radiographs were excluded (Center 1: 83, Center 2: 91, Center 3: 73), primarily due to motion artifact ( n = 104) and incomplete clinical data ( n = 87). Knee OA severity was graded independently by two board-certified musculoskeletal radiologists (Radiologist A: 14 years of experience; Radiologist B: 11 years of experience) using the standardized Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) system, blinded to clinical information and each other’s assessments. Inter-observer agreement was substantial (Quadratic Weighted Kappa = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.84–0.90; intraclass correlation coefficient = 0.91). Discrepancies (occurring in 8.3% of cases) were resolved by consensus at a joint review session. KL grade definitions followed published criteria: Grade 0, no radiographic features of OA; Grade 1 (doubtful), doubtful joint space narrowing with possible osteophytic lipping; Grade 2 (minimal), definite osteophytes with possible joint space narrowing; Grade 3 (moderate), multiple osteophytes, definite joint space narrowing, with mild sclerosis; Grade 4 (severe), large osteophytes, marked joint space narrowing, and severe sclerosis with possible bony deformity. The demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1 . The two cohorts were well-matched across all baseline characteristics (all p > 0.05). sections.image preprocessing and data augmentatio: All DICOM images were exported and converted to 8-bit PNG format. Knee joints were automatically localized and cropped using a YOLOv8 detector pre-trained on the MS-COCO dataset and fine-tuned on 2,400 knee radiographs from the publicly available Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset (mean intersection-over-union [IoU] = 0.941; mAP@0.5 = 0.962). Images were subsequently resized to 384 × 384 pixels and enhanced with Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE; clipLimit = 2.0, tileGridSize = 8 × 8). Normalization followed ImageNet channel statistics (mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]; SD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]). Training-time augmentation was performed using the Albumentations library (v1.3.1) and included random horizontal flip ( p = 0.50), rotation within ± 15°, brightness/contrast adjustment (± 0.15), additive Gaussian noise (σ = 5–15), RandomResizedCrop (scale = 0.85–1.00), MixUp (α = 0.20), and CutMix (α = 1.0). No augmentation was applied to validation or external test sets.
sections.clinical feature encoding: Six clinically relevant variables were selected according to ACR and OARSI guidelines for knee OA risk assessment: age, body mass index (BMI), history of significant knee injury or trauma, previous knee surgery (meniscectomy or ACL reconstruction), occupational physical loading level (high vs. low/sedentary), and smoking status (current/former vs. never). These variables were selected based on their established association with knee OA severity in the epidemiological literature [ 14 ] and their routine availability in clinical practice. All continuous variables were z-score normalized; categorical variables were binary-encoded prior to input into the clinical encoder.
sections.training details and hyperparameters: The framework was implemented in PyTorch (v2.1) and trained on 4 × NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs. The optimizer was AdamW with weight decay λ = 0.01. Learning rates were set to 5 × 10⁻⁵ for the backbone and 1 × 10⁻⁴ for the fusion module and classification head, with cosine annealing schedule and a 5-epoch linear warm-up. Effective batch size was 32 (per-GPU batch = 16 with 2-step gradient accumulation). To address class imbalance (Grade 4: 7.8% of development data), class-weighted sampling was applied with inverse-frequency weights [1.00, 1.16, 1.05, 1.35, 3.25] for Grades 0–4, respectively. The total training loss combined three terms: L_total = L_CORAL + 0.30 × L_CE (weighted) + 0.20 × L_focal (γ = 2.0). The weighting coefficients (0.30 and 0.20) were determined via grid search over the candidate values {0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50} for each term, optimizing validation QWK across five folds; the selected combination yielded the highest and most stable cross-validated performance. Training ran for a maximum of 60 epochs with early stopping (patience = 8 epochs) based on validation QWK; the proposed RCGF converged at epoch 52 ± 3 (mean ± SD across five folds). The best model checkpoint (highest mean QWK across folds) was selected for external evaluation.
sections.clinical nomogram construction and valid: The AI-derived continuous severity score (CORAL output probability of KL ≥ 2) was combined with the six selected clinical variables through multivariable ordinal logistic regression with proportional-odds assumption. The nomogram was internally validated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples (Harrell’s optimism-corrected C-statistic). Calibration was assessed using the calibration slope, Brier score, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) was performed across threshold probabilities of 0.05–0.95 to assess net clinical benefit against treat-all and treat-none reference strategies.
sections.model interpretability: Swin-adapted Grad-CAM++ [ 18 ] generated class-specific activation heatmaps highlighting anatomically relevant features such as osteophytes, joint space narrowing, and subchondral sclerosis. Cross-modal attention rollout [ 19 ] was applied to quantify the relative attention weight directed by each modality toward the other. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values (TreeSHAP for XGBoost; GradientSHAP for the neural architectures) were computed to quantify the contribution of each clinical variable to model predictions. t-SNE dimensionality reduction was applied to image embeddings before and after RCGF fusion to visualize class separability and inter-center domain alignment.
sections.statistical analysis: Model performance was evaluated using confusion matrices, one-versus-rest ROC curves, QWK (primary endpoint), macro-averaged AUC, balanced accuracy, and per-class sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score. Eight classifiers were compared: the proposed RCGF, a simple late-fusion baseline, MedViT [ 13 ], BioViL-T [ 20 ] ( adapted for knee radiographs as a unimodal image-only baseline by removing its text encoder and fine-tuning solely the vision backbone on our dataset, consistent with prior domain-transfer benchmarks), ResNet-50 [ 21 ], EfficientNet-B7 [ 22 ], ViT-B/16 [ 23 ], and a clinical-only XGBoost model. All 95% confidence intervals were computed with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. FDR correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method) was applied for all pairwise comparisons. Inter-rater agreement was assessed with Quadratic Weighted Kappa and intraclass correlation. Calibration was assessed with Brier score and ECE. Statistical comparisons used DeLong’s test (AUC) and McNemar’s test (accuracy). All analyses were conducted in Python (scikit-learn v1.4, SciPy v1.11) and R (v4.3.2), with statistical significance set at two-sided p < 0.05 after FDR correction.
sections.comprehensive model comparison: Eight classifier architectures were systematically evaluated across training, internal five-fold cross-validation, and independent external test sets. Performance is reported as mean ± SD for training and internal validation, and as point estimates with 95% bootstrap CIs for the external test set. Results are summarized in Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table S1. As shown in Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table S1, the proposed RCGF framework achieved the highest performance across all datasets and all metrics. The minimal gap between internal validation and external test QWK (ΔQWK = 0.016: validation 0.884 → external 0.900) confirms excellent generalizability. The proposed RCGF significantly outperformed all seven baselines (all p < 0.001, FDR-corrected), with absolute QWK improvements of + 0.050 over BioViL-T, + 0.070 over MedViT, + 0.081 over ViT-B/16, + 0.088 over EfficientNet-B7, and + 0.111 over ResNet-50. Fig. 3 Heatmap of key performance metrics (Accuracy, QWK, AUC, and Brier Score) for all eight evaluated classifiers across training, internal validation, and independent external test sets (mean ± SD for training/validation; point estimates with 95% CI for external test set). Darker colors indicate superior performance. The proposed RCGF (top row) achieves the highest scores across all metrics and datasets, with a minimal gap between internal validation and external test results, confirming robust generalizability across centers

sections.ablation study: Systematic ablation results are presented in Table 3 . Removing uncertainty-aware gating reduced QWK by 0.040 ( p < 0.001), representing the single largest individual component contribution. Replacing CORAL with standard softmax cross-entropy reduced QWK by 0.068 ( p < 0.001), underscoring the importance of preserving ordinal structure. Removing the clinical encoder reduced QWK by 0.060 ( p < 0.001), and the corresponding balanced accuracy reduction (87.6% → 82.5%) confirms that clinical covariates provide information complementary to and non-redundant with the radiographic signal. Removing class-weighted sampling combined with focal loss reduced balanced accuracy most markedly (87.6% → 79.3%), confirming the critical importance of these strategies for Grade 4 detection. To verify the robustness of these findings, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by repeating the ablation across the five cross-validation folds on the development set. The relative ranking and magnitude of each component’s contribution were consistent across all folds, supporting the reliability of the reported performance drops on the external test set. sections.clinical nomogram performance: The integrated clinical nomogram, which combines the AI-derived continuous severity score with the six clinical covariates, exhibited outstanding calibration and clinical utility in the independent external test set (Fig. 6 ). As illustrated in Fig. 6 a, the calibration curve closely followed the ideal diagonal line across the entire range of predicted probabilities, achieving a calibration slope of 0.97, an intercept of 0.00, and a Brier score of 0.072 (Table 4 ). The minimal deviation confirmed by the Platt recalibration line indicates excellent reliability of the probability estimates without systematic over- or under-prediction. DCA (Fig. 6 b) further demonstrated that the nomogram provided substantially higher standardized net benefit than the treat-all or treat-none reference strategies across all clinically relevant high-risk thresholds (0.05–0.95), with positive net benefit maintained even at more conservative cost: benefit ratios. These results, together with the discrimination performance (C-statistic = 0.940; 95% CI: 0.920–0.958), confirm that the nomogram delivers accurate, well-calibrated, and clinically actionable individualized predictions of KL grade ≥ 2, supporting its potential for objective risk stratification in routine radiographic assessment of knee osteoarthritis. By visually weighting the complementary contributions of radiographic AI output and established epidemiological risk factors, the nomogram provides clinicians with transparent, actionable probability estimates that consistently outperform treat-all or treat-none strategies across clinically relevant decision thresholds, thereby supporting objective triage, treatment planning, and patient counseling in both specialist and resource-limited settings. sections.training and validation loss curves: Figure 12 presents training and validation loss curves for all eight architectures across 60 epochs. The proposed RCGF achieved the lowest final combined loss (L_total = 0.412 ± 0.018 at convergence) with the smallest train–validation gap (ΔL = 0.031 ± 0.009), consistent with its strong external generalizability. Early stopping was triggered at epoch 52 ± 3 (mean ± SD across folds). All baseline models showed progressively larger generalization gaps, with XGBoost exhibiting the steepest divergence after epoch 15. Late-fusion was the closest baseline with a final validation loss of 0.487 ± 0.022.
