A smaller gap between training and validation loss indicates better generalization. The proposed RCGF (dark blue) achieves the lowest final combined loss and the smallest train–validation gap among all models, consistent with its superior external test performance. Larger gaps observed in baseline models suggest overfitting to the training data
sections.principal findings: This study demonstrates that a multi-modal Transformer framework integrating knee radiographs with structured clinical covariates through an uncertainty-aware gated fusion mechanism achieves state-of-the-art performance for ordinal knee OA severity grading, with robust generalizability across three independent imaging centers. The proposed RCGF framework achieved a QWK of 0.900 on the external test set, substantially exceeding the typical human inter-observer agreement (QWK = 0.60–0.80) reported in community radiological settings [ 3 , 4 ], and significantly outperforming all eight evaluated baseline architectures. The ΔQWK = 0.016 between internal validation and external test set confirms that the model generalizes effectively across different scanner vendors and imaging protocols within the studied region; however, prospective validation across geographically and ethnically diverse populations remains necessary before clinical translation. The uncertainty-aware gating mechanism, validated through systematic ablation (ΔQWK = 0.040 upon removal; p < 0.001), demonstrated the most critical individual contribution to performance among all model components. This finding underscores the importance of explicitly modeling epistemic uncertainty in multi-modal fusion, rather than treating each modality as equally reliable regardless of input quality or domain. The CORAL ordinal head further contributed meaningfully (ΔQWK = 0.068 vs. softmax CE), confirming that exploiting the natural rank ordering of KL grades is not merely a modeling preference but a clinically significant design choice that reduces severity-skipping misclassifications. Beyond performance gains, the combination of CORAL ordinal prediction with uncertainty-aware gated fusion represents a paradigm shift in multi-modal OA grading. CORAL ensures that predictions respect the inherent clinical ordering of disease severity, preventing clinically implausible grade-skipping errors. The uncertainty-aware gating explicitly models the reliability of each modality at inference time, enabling the framework to down-weight unreliable inputs rather than propagating fusion errors. Together, these components provide a foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support that is absent from conventional late-fusion or concatenation-based approaches.
sections.comparison with prior work: Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved automated Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) grading of knee osteoarthritis from plain radiographs, yet most studies remain constrained by unimodal (image-only) designs, reliance on internal validation, simple fusion strategies, or the need for domain-specific fine-tuning. Pi et al. [ 24 ], developed an ensemble deep-learning network on 8,260 images from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset, achieving 76.93% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.7665; Grad-CAM visualizations confirmed anatomically relevant focus on the joint space. However, their evaluation was limited to internal validation, precluding assessment of cross-center generalizability. Nasef et al. [ 5 ]. appropriately highlighted a pervasive limitation in the field: many models that perform adequately on internal test sets fail to generalize to external datasets due to domain shift and suboptimal training convergence. Their work underscores the critical need for rigorous external validation, an essential standard that the present study satisfies with a large independent test cohort. Vaattovaara et al. [ 4 ]. evaluated a deep-learning model trained on the Multicenter Osteoarthritis Study (MOST) and tested on an external dataset of 208 radiographs, reporting a multiclass quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.820 and balanced accuracy of 0.693. Their model demonstrated performance comparable to four human readers (radiologists and an orthopedic surgeon), yet remained strictly unimodal and utilized a relatively small external cohort. More recently, Alkhatatbeh et al. [ 25 ] introduced KL-FuseNet, a multitask architecture fusing global (ConvNeXt-Base) and local (ResNet-50) features. On internal OAI data, the model attained a QWK of 0.881 (accuracy 70.3%); however, zero-shot transfer to an independent Chinese cohort ( n = 2,295) dropped accuracy to 66.1%. Selective fine-tuning recovered performance to 80.0% accuracy and QWK 0.950, illustrating persistent domain-shift challenges even with sophisticated feature fusion. On the multimodal side, Ma’aitah et al. [ 26 ] proposed a Vision Transformer + BERT framework for joint image–text embedding on the OAI dataset, achieving 82.85% accuracy, 84.54% precision, and 82.89% recall. Although this represents a valuable step toward multimodal learning, the study relied exclusively on internal validation and employed standard embedding concatenation without advanced cross-modal attention or uncertainty quantification. In contrast, the present study advances the field on multiple fronts. We introduce a true multi-modal Transformer framework that integrates high-resolution knee radiographs with six routinely available clinical covariates (age, BMI, history of knee injury, previous surgery, occupational loading, and smoking status) through a novel Robust Cross-Modal Gated Fusion (RCGF) module employing bidirectional cross-attention and Monte-Carlo dropout–based uncertainty-aware dynamic gating. This design achieved a superior externally validated QWK of 0.900 (95% CI: 0.877–0.921) and balanced accuracy of 87.6% on a sizable independent test set ( n = 750) without any fine-tuning or domain adaptation, outperforming all seven evaluated baselines (including BioViL-T and MedViT) with statistically significant margins (all FDR-corrected p < 0.001). Furthermore, the incorporation of Consistent Rank Logits (CORAL) for ordinal prediction, systematic ablation studies quantifying each component’s contribution, and a validated point-based clinical nomogram with excellent calibration and decision-curve net benefit provide both higher ordinal consistency and direct clinical translatability that are absent from prior unimodal or late-fusion approaches. Large general-purpose multimodal models such as Med-Flamingo exceed 7 billion parameters and lack ordinal specialization, making them impractical for resource-constrained clinical deployment. Attention-based feature refinement strategies have shown consistent improvements across diverse medical image analysis tasks [ 27 ]. Collectively, these comparisons demonstrate that the proposed RCGF framework not only surpasses recent state-of-the-art results in externally validated multiclass performance but also addresses key translational gaps. domain robustness without retraining, clinical covariate integration, explicit uncertainty modeling, and actionable decision support. thereby representing a meaningful step toward objective, scalable, and generalizable radiographic osteoarthritis assessment.
sections.clinical relevance of modality contribut: The ablation results confirmed that the clinical encoder contributes a QWK gain of + 0.060 and a balanced accuracy gain of + 5.1% points over the image-only baseline, a clinically meaningful increment representing approximately 38 additional correctly classified radiographs in the external test set. The SHAP analysis identified age and BMI as the dominant predictors, consistent with established epidemiological evidence [ 14 ]. Notably, occupational loading and knee injury history contributed substantially to moderate-grade predictions, consistent with the mechano-biological understanding that repetitive joint loading and prior structural trauma accelerate cartilage degradation [ 14 ]. These findings are consistent with clinically coherent predictive pathways and provide supportive evidence against spurious correlations; however, interpretability tools such as Grad-CAM++, SHAP, and attention rollout suggest rather than prove causal or anatomical correctness, and should be regarded as complementary analyses supporting model transparency. A center-stratified analysis further confirmed that the QWK improvement attributable to the clinical encoder was consistent across sites (development centers: ΔQWK = + 0.061; external center: ΔQWK = + 0.058), supporting the reliability and cross-center consistency of the structured clinical data.
sections.deployment considerations: The proposed framework achieves an inference time of 28 ms per image on an NVIDIA A100 GPU and an estimated 180–220 ms on a standard clinical workstation CPU, both within acceptable range for asynchronous PACS worklist integration. The model does not require specialized hardware beyond a standard radiology workstation and can be implemented as a background analysis tool that generates KL grade suggestions alongside routine radiograph interpretation. Integration with PACS systems via DICOM SR, regulatory approval (CE marking, FDA 510(k)), and prospective clinical validation of workflow impact remain necessary steps before broad clinical adoption. Cross-attention fusion mechanisms have further demonstrated practical applicability in clinical imaging workflows [ 28 ].
sections.limitations: Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the number of Grade 4 cases in the external test set ( n = 60, 8.0%) is relatively small. Although sensitivity for Grade 4 reached 83.5%, the wider confidence interval compared with other grades reflects this sample size constraint; external validation in a dataset enriched for severe disease is warranted. Second, the clinical variables were limited to six routinely available factors; inclusion of lower-limb alignment measurements, inflammatory biomarkers, or genetic risk factors may further improve performance but was precluded by inconsistent availability across the three centers. Third, this study used retrospective data from three centers in a single geographic and ethnic region; prospective validation across geographically and ethnically diverse populations is required before broad clinical translation. Furthermore, systematic data on comorbidities and ethnic diversity were not available across all three centers, which limits assessment of model generalizability to broader patient populations. Future work should include validation on publicly available datasets such as the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) and the Multicenter Osteoarthritis Study (MOST) to further confirm reproducibility across independent cohorts. Fourth, while the nomogram was internally validated with bootstrap resampling, prospective external validation of its clinical decision-making utility has not yet been performed. Fifth, although the development and external test cohorts were well-matched across baseline characteristics, this also means the model has not yet been evaluated under stronger domain shift conditions, such as imaging from different countries, different ethnic populations, portable radiograph systems, or low-resource clinical settings. Such validation represents a critical priority for future work prior to broad clinical deployment.
sections.conclusion_1: This multi-modal Transformer framework with Robust Cross-Modal Gated Fusion provides robust, externally validated performance for automated ordinal knee OA severity grading from plain radiographs, achieving a QWK of 0.900 on an independent external test set, substantially exceeding both human inter-observer agreement and all seven evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The uncertainty-aware gating mechanism effectively addresses inter-center domain shift, the CORAL prediction head preserves ordinal grade structure, and the validated clinical nomogram translates model outputs into individualized probability estimates suitable for clinical decision support. With inference times compatible with routine clinical workflow and interpretability tools confirming anatomically coherent model behavior, this framework represents a promising step toward objective radiographic OA assessment; however, prospective validation in geographically and ethnically diverse populations is required before clinical deployment. Prospective multi-center validation of the clinical workflow impact is warranted prior to widespread implementation.

title:
Short- and
Long-Acting Psychedelics: Structure–Activity
Relationships, Pharmacology, and Implications for Neuropsychiatric
Therapeutics
abstract:
Psychedelics have re-emerged as promising therapeutics
for neuropsychiatric
disorders, including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder,
and substance use disorders. While their beneficial effects are largely
attributed to serotonin 2A (5-HT2A) receptor activation, psychedelics
exhibit substantial diversity in chemical structure, receptor binding
kinetics, metabolism, and duration of action. These differences underpin
the distinction between short-acting psychedelics like N,N -dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and 5-methoxy-DMT, and long-acting compounds
like lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and mescaline. Short-acting
psychedelics may offer advantages in clinical settings where brief
therapeutic sessions are preferred, while long-acting agents may be
relatively more effective for clinical outcomes. This review highlights
the chemistry, structure–activity relationships, and pharmacology
of both short- and long-acting psychedelics. We examine key functional
group modifications that influence receptor binding affinity, efficacy,
and duration. By integrating insights from synthetic chemistry, pharmacology,
and clinical effects, this review provides a framework for rational
psychedelic drug development aimed at producing next-generation antidepressants,
anxiolytics, and substance use disorder treatments with controlled
and predictable clinical effects.

sections.introduction:
Psychedelics have re-emerged
as promising tools in neuroscience
and psychiatry as potential treatments for conditions such as depression,
anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and substance use
disorders (SUDs). − Psychedelics refer to compounds that alter consciousness
through activation of brain 5-HT2A receptors. Psychedelics may be
the earliest known class of psychopharmacological agents. Examples
include Soma, a substance revered in ancient India and celebrated
in the Rigveda through numerous hymns, and psilocybin mushrooms, known
as teonanacatl or “god’s flesh” used by Aztec
shamans in healing and rituals. These substances played central roles
in spiritual and ceremonial practices across cultures. − The resurgence of interest in psychedelics is driven by renewed
scientific focus and growing clinical evidence demonstrating the therapeutic
potential of both classic compounds, such as lysergic acid diethylamide
(LSD), psilocybin, and N,N -dimethyltryptamine (DMT),
and novel synthetic analogs. − The 5-HT2A receptor subtype,
a primary target for psychedelics,
is located in the central and peripheral nervous system and is present
at both pre- and postsynaptic regions. The 5-HT2A receptors are G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) that
couple to the G q/11 subtype. Activation of G q/11 stimulates phospholipase C (PLC) function, which hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol
4,5-bisphosphate to diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol triphosphate
(IP3). DAG can activate protein kinase C (PKC) and mediates a wide
variety of cellular processes, whereas IP3 triggers the release of
calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, which activates multiple intracellular
signaling pathways. In addition to G-protein
signaling, β-arrestin is another downstream effector of 5-HT2A
receptors, mediating receptor desensitization, internalization, and
downregulation of GPCR signaling. Although
the hallucinogenic effects of psychedelics are thought to be mediated
primarily through 5-HT2A receptor activation, some studies suggest
that 5-HT2A activation may only partially explain the therapeutic
actions of these compounds. , This has raised interest
in developing nonhallucinogenic 5-HT2A-targeting therapeutics with
retained clinical potential. Some studies have proposed that psychedelics
favor Gq-mediated signaling relative to β-arrestin pathways
compared with nonpsychedelic compounds; however, the literature remains
mixed. A recent study by Ippolito et
al. demonstrated that 5-HT2A agonists activated both Gq and β-arrestin
pathways, and that ligand bias did not distinguish psychedelics from
nonpsychedelics. Instead, nonpsychedelic compounds exhibited lower
overall efficacy, leading the authors to conclude that reduced efficacy,
rather than biased agonism, may better differentiate psychedelic from
nonpsychedelic 5-HT2A agonists. At least 14 distinct serotonin (5-HT) receptors have been identified
to date. In addition to affinity at 5-HT2A
receptors, psychedelics such as psilocybin, LSD, and DMT bind to other
5-HT receptor subtypes. Interactions
with other receptors including subtypes of 5-HT receptors appear to
be responsible for the adverse effects of psychedelics. For instance,
activation of the 5-HT2B receptor by fenfluramine, pergolide, and
other potent 5-HT2B agonists is responsible for producing valvular
heart disease. Thus, developing selective
5-HT2A agonists may result in novel psychedelic therapeutics with
reduced side effects. Psychedelics can be broadly classified
into short-acting and long-acting
compounds based on their duration of action. , Short acting psychedelics have a rapid onset and brief duration
of subjective effects, typically lasting less than 1–2 h. In
contrast, effects of long-acting psychedelics can last up to 30 h. − Long-acting psychedelics like psilocybin have shown promise in producing
both rapid and enduring relief of depressive symptoms. Long-acting psychedelics have a disadvantage,
in that their clinical use is resource intensive as they require patients
to be monitored by clinicians for a relatively long duration. Short-acting agents may offer advantages in
clinical settings where reduced time burden and control over psychoactive
effects are desirable. Advances in medicinal
chemistry have enabled the synthesis of novel compounds that fine-tune
pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties with varying durations
of action. Common in vivo behavioral models used to study
the effects of psychedelics include drug discrimination and the head-twitch
response (HTR). Drug discrimination is a well-established behavioral
pharmacology technique used to assess discriminative stimulus effects
of pharmacological compounds; compounds that share discriminative
stimulus effects generally share central nervous system (CNS) receptor
mechanism(s) of action. Drug discrimination
is particularly useful for evaluating whether test compounds share
pharmacological mechanisms of action with a training drug that has
an established mechanism of action. The HTR is characterized by rapid,
side-to-side head shakes that occur following 5-HT2A receptor activation
by psychedelics. The HTR is a convenient screening strategy to distinguish
hallucinogenic from nonhallucinogenic compounds because unlike drug
discrimination, HTR does not require acquisition of learned behavior
and days to months of extensive training. Potency to produce the HTR
has been shown to correlate with ED 50 values of 5-HT2A
agonists obtained from drug discrimination studies. Dose–response curves generated in HTR experiments
typically exhibit an inverted U-shaped pattern, which may reflect
activation of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2C receptors at higher doses of psychedelics
and other behavioral effects that interfere with the HTR. Although HTR is faster and more convenient compared
to drug discrimination, HTR is susceptible to false positives or negatives
due to polypharmacology of certain drugs (multiple sites of action
or lack of selectivity for the 5-HT2A receptor) and antagonism studies.
Antagonists can also have ″off-target″ effects that
interfere with the animal being able to show the HTR. This review provides a comprehensive examination
of the structural,
pharmacological, and functional properties of short- and long-acting
psychedelics. We highlight structure–activity relationships
(SAR), receptor binding dynamics, and metabolic pathways. Emphasis
is placed on both clinically relevant compounds and investigational
analogs, bridging insights from synthetic chemistry, pharmacology,
and clinical outcomes. A deeper understanding of the interplay between
chemical structure, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics is essential
for the rational development of psychedelics as safe and effective
therapeutics.
sections.tryptamines:
The tryptamine class
of psychedelics have close structural similarity to serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine),
an endogenous neurotransmitter. Serotonin and tryptamines both share
an indole ring and an ethylamine side chain; however, psychedelic
tryptamines typically possess N,N -dialkyl substitutions
on the terminal amine, a modification that is critical for their hallucinogenic
activity. SAR studies demonstrate that
tryptamine psychedelics rely on a constrained framework in which the
indole–ethylamine core is preserved. SAR investigations have examined the impact of substitutions on
the indole ring, modifications to the pyrrole moiety, alterations
to the side chain, and changes to the terminal amine. − DMT is considered the prototypical tryptamine psychedelic,
exhibiting a 5-HT2A receptor affinity ( K i ) of 127 nM in rat cortical homogenates. , However, DMT has poor oral bioavailability due to rapid first-pass
metabolism by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A). Structural modifications to the indole ring have produced analogs
with substantially enhanced affinity for the 5-HT2A receptor. For
example, 5-methoxy-DMT and 4-hydroxy-DMT (psilocin) have higher affinity
than DMT, with K i values of 14 nM and
6 nM, respectively. Fluorination of the
indole ring at the 6- and 7-positions of psilocin results in a 2-fold
decrease in 5-HT2A receptor affinity. , , The bioisosteric replacement of the phenyl ring with
thiophene, as well as the substitution of the pyrrole ring with thiophene
or furan, resulted in compounds with reduced 5-HT2A receptor affinity
compared to DMT, highlighting the critical role of the indole scaffold
in maintaining high 5-HT2A binding affinity. , Side-chain modifications further influence receptor interactions.
α-Methylation yields a chiral center, where the S -isomer displays higher 5-HT2A affinity ( K i = 46 nM) than the R -isomer ( K i = 130 nM). Additionally, α-methyltryptamine
shows improved metabolic stability because it is resistant to MAO-mediated
oxidation. Ethyltryptamines, which are
α-ethyl tryptamines have been found to be neurotoxic. Substitution on the amine with ethyl or isopropyl
moieties resulted in compounds with 2-fold lower affinity than psilocin,
and substitution with isobutyl groups markedly decreased affinity
at the 5-HT2A receptor ( K i = 260 nM) compared
to psilocin ( K i = 6 nM). N,N -dialkyl substitution with ethyl or
isopropyl moieties results in orally stable molecules. Figure summarizes the structural
modifications of the tryptamine class and their corresponding 5-HT2A
receptor binding affinities.
sections.pharmacodynamics:
DMT is a potent
hallucinogen that is widely found in nature, both as an endogenous
compound in animals and as an alkaloid in various psychedelic plants.
For centuries, it has been used in traditional brews such as ayahuasca , which combines DMT-containing plants with monoamine
oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)-containing plants to enable oral activity. Beyond its recreational and ceremonial use,
DMT has shown significant therapeutic potential, particularly as an
anxiolytic, antidepressant, and antipsychotic agent. , − In addition to its primary mechanisms of action at
the 5-HT2A receptor, which mediates psychedelic effects, DMT binds
to sigma-1 receptors, trace amine-associated receptors, adrenergic
receptors (α, β1, and β2), and other serotonin receptors
( Table ). , − DMT binds to ligand-gated receptors, and binds with relatively low
affinity at neurotransmitter transporters such as serotonin transporters
(SERT) ( K i = 6 μM), norepinephrine
transporters (NET) ( K i = 6 μM),
dopamine transporters (DAT) ( K i = 22 μM),
and vesicular monoamine transporters 2 (VMAT2) ( K i = 93 μM). , Glennon et al. evaluated the 5-HT receptor binding
affinity of
several tryptamine analogs, including DMT, using the rat stomach fundus
preparation method. Employing a drug
discrimination assay, Glennon et al. showed that classical hallucinogens,
such as DMT, act as agonists at 5-HT2A receptors. In 1989, Sadzot et al. determined the binding affinity
of DMT using radioligand binding assays and reported that the affinity
of DMT in rat cortex was greater than in human cortex. Additional in vivo studies
suggested that the discriminative stimulus effects of DMT are primarily
mediated through 5-HT2A receptors, whereas 5-HT2C receptors do not
appear to play a significant role. Carbonaro
et al. reported that M100907, a selective 5-HT2A receptor antagonist,
dose-dependently attenuated the HTR induced by DMT, further supporting
the involvement of 5-HT2A receptors in mediating DMT’s hallucinogenic
effects. Moreover, studies using 5-HT2A
knockout 129S6/SvEv mice confirmed the critical role of 5-HT2A receptors
in DMT-induced HTR. In preclinical
behavioral studies assessing mood-related outcomes,
Cameron et al. found that DMT produced anxiety-like behavior without
modifying locomotor activity per se. DMT significantly reduced immobility
and increased swimming behavior in the forced swim test, indicative
of antidepressant-like effects. Similarly,
Lima da Cruz et al. demonstrated that a single dose of DMT decreased
depression-like behavior in rodents by improving anhedonia and enhancing
motivation and reward-related processes ( Table ).
sections.pharmacokinetics:
DMT is rapidly
metabolized in the body, primarily by MAO-A and hepatic cytochrome
P450 enzymes, resulting in a short plasma half-life of approximately
5–15 min ( Table ). CYP2D6 plays a major role in its
biotransformation, catalyzing oxidative deamination and N-demethylation,
while CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2E1 contribute to a lesser extent. Co-administration with MAOIs, such as the β-carboline
alkaloids harmine, harmaline, and tetrahydroharmine found in Banisteriopsis caapi (a key component of ayahuasca) prevents
the oxidative deamination of the orally labile DMT. In humans, intravenous doses produce peak plasma concentrations
at approximately 2 min and an initial plasma elimination half-life
of about 5–6 min, followed by a slower terminal phase of 15
min; subjective effects typically peak around 5 min and resolve by
30 min. In rabbits, intravenously administered
radio-labeled DMT crosses into the brain within 10 s, becomes undetectable
in plasma and urine within 24 h, yet trace amounts (0.1% of the dose)
remain in brain tissue up to 7 days postinjection. The principal metabolite of DMT is indole-3-acetic acid
(IAA), formed through oxidative deamination by MAO-A followed by oxidation
via aldehyde dehydrogenase ( Figure ). Other intermediates
include DMT N-oxide and N -methyltryptamine (NMT),
which contribute to the formation of IAA, along with other metabolites
such as tryptamine derivatives, 6-hydroxy-DMT analogs and tetrahydro-β-carbolines.
Although substantial research has been conducted on DMT metabolism,
challenges remain in the simultaneous quantification of its metabolites,
especially due to potential interference from dietary sources of indole
acetic acid produced in the gut.
sections.clinical studies:
DMT is under
investigation for multiple neurologic and psychiatric conditions.
Due to extensive first-pass metabolism, oral administration is impractical.
Clinical trials have used intravenous and inhaled formulations (e.g., NCT05901012 , NCT05695495 ) and these trials have focused on evaluating
DMT’s pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, tolerability and
preliminary efficacy. In a double-blind, Phase 1 trial ( NCT05559931 ),
a 1.5 mg intravenous bolus followed by a 6-h infusion (0.105 mg/min)
was administered either once or over six sessions across a two-week
period. Results are pending. A related
Phase 1 study ( NCT05384678 ) assessed dose-dependent subjective and
autonomic responses across a range of bolus and infusion dosing. At
a 1.8 mg/min infusion rate, participants reported a “good drug
effect”, while higher doses were associated with increased
anxiety and ego dissolution. Self-selected doses in the titration
arm of the study mirrored those in the acute dosing arm (1.8 mg/min). , In a separate open-labeled study conducted in 2022 ( NCT04711915 ),
intravenous DMT (0.1–0.3 mg/kg) was administered to participants
with major depressive disorder (MDD) and healthy controls. In this
study, transient elevations in heart rate and blood pressure were
observed, along with reductions in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale
(HAMD-17) scores 24 h postinfusion. A Phase 2a trial ( NCT06094907 ) for treatment-resistant depression
(TRD) evaluated vaporized DMT (15 mg acclimatization followed by a
60 mg) with ∼40–60 min of psychotherapeutic integration.
Participants experienced rapid and sustained reduction in Montgomery−Asberg
Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) scores over 3 months, with concurrent
decreases in suicidal ideation. Psychedelic effects were brief and
intense, and adverse events (e.g., pharyngeal discomfort, cough, headache,
and nausea) were mild and transient. DMT is also being investigated for alcohol use disorders. In an
ongoing randomized, placebo-controlled Unity trial in the UK, the
neurophysiological effects of DMT, lisuride, and d-cycloserine are
being compared using EEG and MRI scans of participants. A Yale-sponsored
clinical trial ( NCT06070649 ) evaluates two infusion strategies, (1)
0.3 mg/kg over 5 min followed by 60 min of saline, and (2) 0.2 mg/kg
over 5 min followed by 60 min of maintenance infusion at 0.01 mg/kg/min.
This trial is assessing the safety, tolerability and efficacy of DMT
in alcohol use disorders. New
clinical trials have recently opened to expand the evaluation
of DMT into additional therapeutic domains. One trial is assessing
acute analgesic effects of DMT ( NCT06180759 , recruiting), while another
compares the subjective profile of multiple psychoactive compounds
in volunteers ( NCT06772753 ). , Further mechanistic
studies are using EEG, MRI ( NCT06624137 , recruiting) and FDG-PET techniques
( NCT06252506 , pending results) to map the effects of DMT on learning,
perception, and brain energy metabolism. , Collectively, these studies shape the translational framework for
DMT as a fast-acting, scalable psychedelic intervention, with potential
implication across multiple neurologic disorders.
sections.pharmacodynamics_1:
The 5-methoxy
analog of DMT is found in certain plants and animals, and is also
endogenously produced in humans. Unlike
its parent compound, 5-methoxy-DMT has selectivity for 5-HT1A receptors
(1.9–3 nM), which is approximately 300–1000 times higher
than its affinity for 5-HT2A receptors. 5-MeO–DMT, like DMT, also binds to the monoamine transporters
SERT ( K i = 2,032 nM) and NET ( K i = 2,859 nM). A drug discrimination study
by Winter et al. in male Fischer-344 rats demonstrated that 5-MeO–DMT
exerts discriminative stimulus effects primarily through 5-HT1A receptors,
as these effects were antagonized by the selective 5-HT1A antagonist
WAY-100635, but not by the selective 5-HT2A antagonist M100907. In a separate study, 5-MeO–DMT reduced
locomotor activity in animals, an effect attributed to 5-HT1A receptor
activation. In contrast, in
vivo experiments in mice showed that 5-MeO–DMT induces
the HTR through activation of 5-HT2A receptors ( Table ). Halberstadt
et al. demonstrated a dose-dependent induction of HTR by 5-MeO–DMT,
and confirmed the role of 5-HT2A receptors using 5-HT2A receptor knockout
mice, in which the HTR was abolished. Collectively, these findings suggest that the behavioral effects
of 5-MeO–DMT result from activation of both 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A
receptors. Winne et al. investigated the effects of 5-MeO–DMT
in an
anxiety-like behavioral model and found that a single dose produced
short-term anxiolytic effects. Nogueira
et al. assessed 5-MeO–DMT in the elevated plus maze (EPM) and
open field (OF) tests, revealing mixed anxiolytic and anxiogenic effects.
However, this study also showed that 5-MeO–DMT had anxiolytic
effects in stressed animals, suggesting its potential as a therapeutic
agent for anxiety-related psychiatric disorders ( Table ).
sections.pharmacokinetics_1:
The metabolism
of 5-MeO–DMT and DMT is similar, with the primary pathway involving
MAO-A–mediated oxidative deamination, leading to the formation
of the indoleacetic acid (IAA) analog ( Figure ). Another major pathway involves Phase II
metabolism, forming 5-hydroxy glucuronide and sulfate conjugates.
Additional metabolites include 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
and 5-hydroxy-DMT (bufotenine), formed via N-demethylation and O-demethylation,
respectively. A minor metabolic route involves N-oxidation of the
indole ring. , In vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that CYP2D6 plays a central
role in the O-demethylation of 5-MeO–DMT to form bufotenine,
its active metabolite. Additional cytochrome P450 enzymes, including
CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2E1, contribute to a lesser extent, consistent
with the metabolic profile observed for DMT. In animal models, 5-MeO–DMT exhibits rapid absorption and
elimination, with peak plasma concentrations reached within 5–7
min following intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration in mice, and a
terminal half-life ranging from 12 to 19 min. Nonlinear pharmacokinetics have been demonstrated in mice,
where higher doses (10–20 mg/kg) lead to disproportionately
larger increases in AUC and decreased systemic clearance, consistent
with a saturable (Michaelis–Menten) elimination process, likely
due to MAO-A saturation. In humans,
early phase clinical data from a single-ascending-dose study indicate
that plasma elimination half-lives ranged between 15 and 27 min, confirming
a rapid elimination profile.
sections.clinical studies_1:
5-MeO–DMT
is under investigation for psychiatric indications, where rapid onset
and short duration may offer therapeutic benefit. A Phase 1 study
( NCT05347849 ) of BPL-003, an intranasal formulation of 5-MeO–DMT,
evaluated doses ranging from 1 to 12 mg in healthy participants. BPL-003 demonstrated rapid absorption (Tmax:
4–15 min), dose-dependent increase in psychedelic effects that
began quickly and subsided quickly, and no serious adverse events.
These data support the compound’s potential for short-duration
psychedelic interventions. GH Research is developing GH001, a vaporized
5-MeO–DMT formulation, initially evaluated in healthy volunteers
( NCT04640831 ) and subsequently in individuals with treatment-resistant
depression as part of a Phase 1/2 study ( NCT04698603 ). Participants
received either a single 12 mg or 18 mg dose or underwent individualized
dosing guided by tolerability and intensity thresholds. The individualized
dosing arm demonstrated higher remission rates (based on standard
depression scales) than a fixed-dose group. Adverse effects were generally
mild to moderate (transient anxiety, headache, and sensory changes),
and no serious adverse events reported. −
sections.pharmacodynamics_2:
Bufotenine,
or 5-hydroxy- N,N -dimethyltryptamine (5-HO–DMT,
also known as N,N -dimethylserotonin), is a naturally
occurring tryptamine alkaloid primarily found in plants and is an
active metabolite of 5-MeO–DMT. Bufotenine binds to several serotonin receptor subtypes, with reported
affinities of 182 ± 35 nM at 5-HT2A and 234 ± 27 nM at 5-HT2C
receptors. , Bufotenine also binds to the
5-HT1A and 5-HT1B receptors, albeit with higher affinity at 5-HT1A
than 5-HT1B. Bufotenine has low potency
for producing hallucinogenic effects, primarily due to its poor ability
to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB). In contrast, structurally related analogs such as 5-MeO–DMT
and 4-hydroxy-DMT (psilocin) demonstrate significantly greater BBB
permeability, likely due to their higher lipophilicity and enhanced
partition coefficients compared to bufotenine. The high polarity and ionization potential of bufotenine
are key factors limiting its BBB penetration and, consequently, its
central psychoactive effects.
sections.pharmacokinetics_2:
Bufotenine was
initially believed to be primarily metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic
acid (5-HIAA) via oxidative deamination catalyzed by monoamine oxidase
A (MAO-A). However, studies have shown that pretreatment with MAO-A
inhibitors, while reducing 5-HIAA levels, did not lead to an increase
in bufotenine concentrations. This suggests that MAO-A–mediated
deamination may not be the primary metabolic pathway for bufotenine,
or that inhibition of this pathway may activate alternative metabolic
routes ( Figure ). , Phase II conjugation pathwaysspecifically glucuronidation
and sulfationconvert bufotenine into more hydrophilic forms.
Glucuronidation and sulfation of bufotenine occur through liver enzymes,
notably UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (e.g., UGT1A6) and sulfotransferases
(e.g., SULT1A3). When MAO-A is inhibited, Phase II pathways become
more prominent, as bufotenine avoids primary deamination and instead
is excreted as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. 173 Bufotenine
formed from 5-MeO–DMT is eliminated quickly in mice, where
it peaks at 13 min with an apparent half-life of 22 min. , In rats given bufotenine directly, concentrations drop quickly and
are almost undetectable after 8 h. In
humans, bufotenine’s effects are brief: in controlled self-administration
experiments, intranasal free-base had onset within 5 min, peaked at
35–40 min, and ended by 90 min, and vaporized bufotenine (2–8
mg) produced similar short-lived effects.
sections.clinical studies_2:
Bufotenine is
rarely considered for clinical development because of its low BBB
accumulation and rapid metabolic inactivation following oral administration.
A hypothesis was proposed that coadministration with ephedrine, found
in toad secretion, can transiently enhance BBB permeability and potentiate
the hallucinogenic properties of bufotenine. In one of the first dose-escalation
studies, intravenous bufotenine (116 mg over 3 min) induced
dose-dependent peripheral and central effects. Symptoms like chest
tightness and facial paresthesia were observed at lower doses, while
pupillary dilation, nystagmus, hyperpnea, and transient visual hallucinations,
emerged at doses ≥ 4 mg. No significant changes in blood pressure
were observed, and repeated exposure was well tolerated. Potential peripheral effects of bufotenine
identified in preclinical in vitro studies include
actions on human cardiac 5-HT4 receptors to increase heart rate and
contractility. However, these effects have not been confirmed in vivo . Taken together, the
combination of low BBB permeability, metabolic instability and high
peripheral burden, makes bufotenine an unlikely candidate for clinical
psychedelic development unless substantial advances in delivery strategies
or chemical modifications occur.
sections.pharmacodynamics_3:
RE-104 and RE-109
are ester prodrugs of 4-hydroxy- N,N -diisopropyltryptamine
(4-OH-DiPT) and 4-hydroxy- N,N- dimethyltryptamine
(psilocin), respectively. In a study by Bryson et al., RE-104, despite
primarily being identified as a prodrug, was found to bind with low
affinity to 5-HT2A ( K i = 4300 nM) and
5-HT2B ( K i = 1,800 nM) receptors ( Table ). In vivo , RE-104 induced HTR in rats and
significantly reduced immobility time in the forced swim test, findings
consistent with antidepressant-like activity ( Table ). Similar to
RE-104, 1 mg/kg RE-109 significantly decreased immobility time in
animals in the forced swim test. The
diisopropyl substitution improved 5-HT2A receptor affinity relative
to the dimethyl analog but resulted in poor aqueous solubility, reducing
its bioavailability. This limitation was addressed by incorporating
a glutaroyl group, yielding a zwitterionic structure with enhanced
solubility. ,
sections.pharmacokinetics_3:
The rapid hydrolysis
of the prodrugs RE-104 and RE-109 results in the formation of their
active hydroxytryptamine counterparts, leading to a relatively short
half-life and duration of action (t 1/2 = 35 min; duration
= 2–3 h), in contrast to the slower conversion of psilocybin
to psilocin (t 1/2 = 1.5–2 h; duration = 6–8
h). , The primary metabolites of these prodrugs
are their active 4-hydroxy derivatives, followed by oxidative metabolism
and N-dealkylation to produce indoleacetic acid (IAA), which is subsequently
cleared via glucuronidation by UGT1A10 and UGT1A9 ( Figure ). , CYP2D6/CYP3A4 mediate minor oxidative routes and MAO-A produces
only small amounts of deaminated metabolites; human CYP isoforms for
RE-104 remain insufficiently defined. ,
sections.clinical studies_3:
Both compounds,
RE-109 and RE-104 were developed by Reunion Neuroscience, Inc., but
RE-104 was prioritized for clinical studies. Currently, RE-104, a
4-OH-DiPT prodrug, is in development as a subcutaneous, short-acting
psychedelic for the treatment of mood disorders. In a 2025 randomized,
double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-ascending-dose study in healthy
volunteers with prior psychedelic experience, RE-104 demonstrated
a favorable safety profile at doses of ≤ 30 mg. Doses above
this threshold were associated with moderate to severe side effects,
most commonly nausea, sinus tachycardia, restlessness, and headache.
The duration of psychedelic effects was 3–4 h, notably shorter
than those of psilocybin, but with a compatible safety profile (ACTRN12622000713796). In the Phase 2 study ( NCT06342310 ) for
postpartum depression by RECONNECT, a single 30 mg subcutaneous dose
of RE-104 produced a mean reduction of 23 points in MADRS score at
Day 7, compared with 17.2 points in the 1.5 mg active control arm.
Seventy one percent of patients on RE-104 achieved remission (MADRS
< 10) by day 7 vs 41% in the control arm. Clinical responses and
remission rates in patients were sustained by day 28 on follow-up,
confirming the desired outcome of treatments. The findings showed
that RE-104 was well-tolerated, with mild to average complaints of
nausea and headache in patients, consistent with the effects produced
by other medications in this class. In parallel, a pharmacokinetics study ( NCT06659263 ) enrolled 14
postpartum participants who received a single 30 mg subcutaneous dose
of RE-104. Levels of RE-104 in the breast milk were evaluated over
7 days for peak concentration ( C max ),
time to peak ( T max ), and half-life ( t 1/2 ). Preliminary data indicate a favorable
safety profile of RE-104 in this subpopulation of patients. Following these findings, a REKINDLE
study ( NCT07002034 ) is planned
to evaluate RE-104 in patients with adjustment disorder and depression.
This Phase 2 study will assess changes in MADRS score in participants
at day 14 following a 30 mg subcutaneous injection. Secondary objectives
include the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) and safety through
14 days and at 42-day follow-up.
sections.pharmacodynamics_4:
Extensive research
has focused on the synthesis of psilocin analogs to develop prodrugs
based on 4-acetoxy and 4-hydroxy alkyltryptamine scaffolds. The incorporation
of a 4-acetoxy group has been shown to enhance brain uptake, potentially
increasing potency. Both 4-acetoxy and
4-hydroxy alkyltryptamines have demonstrated comparable potency and
subjective effects in humans. 193 Psilocin binds to 5-HT2A
receptors ( K i = 6 ± 5 nM or 107.2 nM 77 ), whereas psilocybin
has negligible affinity at 5-HT2A receptors ( K i > 10,000 nM) ( Table ). Psilocin also binds
to SERT,
albeit with a lower affinity ( K i = 3,801
nM). Psilocybin and psilocin exhibit
discriminative stimulus effects in rodents; these effects are primarily
mediated by 5-HT2A receptor activation, as evidenced by antagonism
with highly selective 5-HT2A receptor ligands. Gatch et al. reported
that psilocin fully substituted for the discriminative stimulus effect
of 0.5 mg/kg 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-methylamphetamine (DOM) with an ED 50 of 0.33 ± 0.18 mg/kg ( Table ). Similarly,
Callahan et al. showed that psilocybin substituted for LSD and mescaline
in drug discrimination assays. Psilocybin
substitution in LSD- and DOM-trained animals was blocked by the 5-HT2A
antagonist M100907 but not by the 5-HT1A antagonist WAY-100635, indicating
the necessity of 5-HT2A receptor activation. Psilocybin also induces the HTR with a U-shaped dose–response
curve, peaking approximately 5 min postadministration. , , , The results of studies reported in Erkizia-Santamaría et
al. suggested that 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT1A receptors mediate psilocybin-induced
HTR. Evidence continues to grow
for the therapeutic potential of psilocybin in psychiatric conditions.
In chronically stressed mice, a single psilocybin dose reversed anhedonia
independent of 5-HT2A receptor activation. Psilocybin (2.5 mg/kg) also produced rapid and sustained antidepressant-like
effects in naïve and corticosterone-exposed mice. García-Cabrerizo et al. reported longer-lasting
effects in males following repeated administration, which could indicate
sex-dependent pharmacokinetic differences in the metabolism of psilocybin. In a marble-burying test of obsessive-compulsive
disorder (OCD), Singh et al. reported that psilocybin significantly
reduced burying behavior independent of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors. In contrast, Wojtas et al. found no evidence
of antidepressant or anxiolytic effects in Wistar Han rats across
multiple behavioral assays. Harari et
al. reported that psilocybin induced acute anxiety-like behaviors,
reduced center time in the open field, and increased avoidance of
the light component in the light-dark test; psilocybin-induced anxiety
was not reversed by ketanserin, suggesting non-5-HT2 A /2B/2C mechanisms. Regarding substance
use disorders, Floris et al. found that psilocybin (3 mg/kg) did not
reduce heroin intake but attenuated relapse in a rat model of heroin
self-administration. However, Pohořalá
et al. reported no effect of psilocybin (1 and 2.5 mg/kg) on cocaine-seeking
behavior in mice and rats ( Table ).
sections.pharmacokinetics_4:
After rapid
dephosphorylation of psilocybin to psilocin, the primary metabolic
pathway involves glucuronidation, followed by oxidative metabolism
via MAO, similar to other tryptamines. A key structural feature influencing BBB permeability and
metabolic stability lies in the position of the hydroxy groupspecifically,
4- versus 5-hydroxy substitution. The inability of 5-hydroxy-DMT (bufotenine)
to efficiently cross the BBB is attributed to its higher basicity
compared to 4-hydroxy-DMT (psilocin), with respective p K a values of 9.67 and 8.47. The difference in BBB permeability is primarily due to psilocin’s
ability to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, which reduces N-protonation
and O-deprotonation, effectively masking polar functional groups and
increasing the compound’s partition coefficient, thereby enhancing
BBB permeability. The intramolecular
hydrogen bonding facilitates a pseudoring conformation that reduces
susceptibility to MAO-mediated degradation, further contributing to
the metabolic stability of psilocin ( Figure ). , Psilocybin acts
as a prodrug and its plasma exposure is driven
by psilocin; intact psilocybin is usually undetectable in plasma. , Psilocin’s typical human half-life is 2–3 h (e.g.,
2 h in pooled analyses; 3 h in a clinical PK study), while subjective
effects last 5–7 h after oral dosing. , , After dephosphorylation, psilocin
is primarily cleared by O-glucuronidation. UGT1A10 is the principal
isoform responsible for psilocin O-glucuronidation, with UGT1A9 playing
a secondary role. Oxidative metabolism by CYP2D6 (forming norpsilocin/oxidized
psilocin) and CYP3A4, together with limited MAO-A deamination, occurs
only to a minor extent, whereas in vivo clearance
is dominated by UGT-mediated O-glucuronidation.
sections.clinical studies_4:
Clinical development
of psilocybin has significantly accelerated across psychiatric and
neurologic indications, with over 200 clinical trials being reported
in the clinical trials database. In a landmark 2016 trial ( NCT00465595 )
in cancer patients, a high dose of psilocybin (22–30 mg/70
kg) produced sustained antidepressant and anxiolytic effects for six
months. It reliably initiated mystical-type experiences, rated among
participants as “the most meaningful and spiritually significant
events.” Dose-related increase
in blood pressure, heart rate, and nausea were observed, with tolerability
declining at higher doses. In major depressive disorder, a Phase
2 trial ( NCT03181529 ) comparing 25 mg psilocybin with niacin (100
mg) demonstrated rapid symptom reduction at Day 8 and met the primary
end point at Day 43. Treatment was generally well-tolerated, with
headache and nausea as the most common adverse effects ( NCT03866174 ). In treatment-resistant depression, a single
25 mg oral dose of psilocybin significantly reduced MADRS scores,
and conferred additional benefits after repeated dosing over 6 months.
Adverse events were mostly transient and mild to moderate, though
one participant experienced persistent genital arousal ( NCT05029466 ). A comparative Phase 1 trial ( NCT02033707 ) found
that while dextromethorphan (DXM) (400 mg/70 kg) and psilocybin (10–30
mg/70 kg) produced meaningful subjective effects in healthy volunteers,
psilocybin yielded stronger positive psychological responses and better
tolerability. Early phase trials
have also demonstrated efficacy of psilocybin
in alcohol and tobacco use disorders, leading to a wave of ongoing clinical trials to assess psilocybin
in various substance use disorders (cocaine: NCT02037126 , methamphetamine: NCT06899594 , opioid: NCT06067737 , NCT06160284 , and cannabis: NCT06660381 ).
Trials have expanded to include assessments on stress ( NCT06768944 ),
burnout ( NCT06814522 ), eating disorders ( NCT05035927 ), obsessive compulsive
disorder ( NCT06992999 ), anxiety ( NCT00979693 ), pain management ( NCT06001749 , NCT05068791 ), and many others. Additionally, adjunctive strategies,
such as transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS),
are being evaluated to enhance memory consolidation and retain behavioral
integration gained during the psychedelic experience ( NCT05866471 ). Subpsychedelic doses of psilocin are of interest for the development
of potential therapeutics to treat mood, cognitive, and sleep disorders
without inducing hallucinogenic experiences. A Phase 1 study ( NCT05317689 )
sponsored by University of California, San Diego, is currently comparing
the pharmacokinetic and subjective effects of oral psilocin or psilocybin
with sublingual psilocin in healthy volunteers aged 20–55 years
with prior psychedelic exposure. Outcomes of this study include tolerability,
subjective responses (via standardized self-report instruments), and
vital monitoring, with results pending. Psilocin’s clinical use has been limited by its chemical
instability in the presence of oxygen, reducing its shelf life and
complicating formulations. On the other hand, chemically stable psilocin
exhibits interindividual variability in metabolic conversion and oral
bioavailability. To address these limitations, a separate Phase 1
study ( NCT06035900 ) evaluated psilocin mucate (L-130), a novel stable
salt form. A single 4 mg oral dose (equivalent to 2 mg psilocin base)
was well tolerated by healthy volunteers, with no reports of psychedelic-like
effects or cognitive changes during the monitoring period, as assessed
using the Mini-Mental State Evaluation (MMSE) test. The formulation
demonstrated rapid absorption ( T max ∼
0.7 h) and consistent pharmacokinetics, with preliminary data suggesting
near 100% oral bioavailability. End points also included self-reported
mood and anxiety measures, with immediate anxiolytic response reported
in most participants and mild mood-enhancing effects persisting in
a subset. While more clinical trials
are required, the existing data fully support the therapeutic development
of L-130.
sections.phenylethylamines:
Phenylethylamines
share a structural scaffold with neurotransmitters like dopamine,
amphetamine, and norepinephrine, which are not psychedelically active.
This class of compounds exhibits markedly different subjective effects
in humans with subtle chemical modifications, resulting in a dramatic
SAR profile underpinned by complex pharmacology. − Mescaline represents the prototypical structure of this class,
and its α-methyl derivative, particularly the R-isomer, shows
relatively high binding affinity at 5-HT2A receptors. β-position
modifications, including hydroxy and methoxy substitutions, preserve
hallucinogenic activity in humans. Substitutions
on the phenyl ring are commonly found in the 2,4,5-trisubstituted
pattern, with oxygen-containing groups at the second and fifth positions
critical for psychedelic activity. Hydrophobic
groups at the fourth position (e.g., alkyl, halogen, or trifluoromethylthio)
have been shown to increase potency, likely by improving pharmacokinetic
properties such as BBB permeability. In contrast, polar substituents
(hydroxy, amine, and carboxylic acid) at the fourth position tend
to reduce 5-HT2 affinity ( K i > 25,000
nM) compared to the 4 unsubstituted, 2,5-substituted analog ( K i = 5,200 nM). An additional strategy involves constraining methoxy groups in cyclic
structures to improve permeability by stabilizing hydrogen bond acceptors.
For instance, tethering the 2,5-dimethoxy moiety into a dihydrofuran
ring yielded an analog with high 5-HT2A affinity ( K i = 0.04 nM) and potent psychedelic activity. Modifications at the α- and N-positions
were also explored; α-alkylation generally retained receptor
affinity, while N-alkylation was not well tolerated. Structure activity relationships for the phenylethylamine
class are shown in Figure .
sections.pharmacodynamics_5:
Mescaline is
a naturally occurring alkaloid found in the peyote cactus that binds
to multiple receptors. , Mescaline exerts discriminative
stimulus effects that are mediated by central serotonergic receptor
function. In a study conducted in rats,
mescaline produced biphasic effects on locomotor activity: low doses
reduced locomotion, whereas a high dose (100 mg/kg) induced hyperlocomotion. These changes in activity were blocked by the
selective 5-HT2A receptor antagonist M100907, suggesting that mescaline’s
effects are mediated via 5-HT2A receptor activation. In zebrafish, mescaline dose-dependently increased
locomotor activity and reduced immobility in the novel tank test,
indicative of anxiolytic-like effects. At the highest dose tested (20 mg/L), mescaline also enhanced shoaling
behavior, suggesting a potential role in modulating social behavior. In another study, Halberstadt et al. showed
that mescaline induced HTR in mice, with an ED 50 of 6.51
mg/kg. Assessment of prepulse inhibition
(PPI) of the acoustic startle response found that mescaline-induced
PPI deficits were attenuated by pretreatment with a 5-HT2A receptor
antagonist. These results further support the conclusion that the
behavioral effects of mescaline are mediated predominantly through
5-HT2A receptor activation.
sections.pharmacokinetics_5:
In placebo-controlled
trials with healthy participants, oral mescaline reaches peak plasma
levels at about 2 h, has a plasma elimination half-life of 3.5 h,
and produces subjective effects that typically last 8–12 h. In pooled human data, urinary recovery after
oral mescaline is primarily dominated by unchanged mescaline (approximately
53% overall), with 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylacetic acid (TMPAA) contributing
approximately 31% over the 24–30 h period. Biotransformation proceeds mainly via oxidative deamination
by MAO to 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylacetaldehyde, followed by aldehyde
dehydrogenase oxidation to TMPAA or alcohol dehydrogenase reduction
to the corresponding alcohol; N-acetylation and O-demethylation occur
as minor routes.
sections.clinical studies_5:
In 2024, a double-blind,
placebo-controlled, crossover study (NCT04849103) evaluated the subjective,
autonomic, and pharmacokinetic effects of oral mescaline (100–800
mg) in healthy participants. A subset of volunteers received 800 mg
of mescaline with 40 mg of ketanserin, a 5-HT2A receptor antagonist.
Subjective effects emerged above 100 mg of mescaline and were dose-dependent
in intensity and duration. While blood pressure elevation plateaued
at 200 mg, heart rate increases were dose-dependent. The most frequent
adverse effects, nausea and emesis, were reported at the 800 mg dose.
Co-administration of ketanserin markedly attenuated the subjective
effects of 800 mg mescaline, confirming 5-HT2A receptor mediation
of mescaline’s psychedelic profile ( NCT04849013 ). A second randomized, placebo-controlled
crossover study ( NCT04227756 ) compared LSD (100 μg), psilocybin
(20 mg), and mescaline (300 mg, 500 mg) in healthy participants. Despite
differences in duration, with the longest effect produced by mescaline,
followed by LSD, and then psilocybin, all three compounds produced
comparable alterations in consciousness, as assessed by standardized
psychometric scales.
sections.pharmacodynamics_6:
3.2.2.1.1 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI) The binding
affinity ( K i ) and potency (EC 50 ) of DOI at the 5-HT2A receptor has been reported as 3.2 ± 0.8
nM and 1.8 ± 0.7 nM, respectively ( Table and Figure ). The discriminative stimulus effects of DOI (2.5 mg/kg)
were attenuated by the 5-HT2A antagonist M100907 and by the 5-HT2C
antagonists SB 206,553 and SB 242,084. However, other studies showed that the discriminative stimulus effects
of DOI (0.75 mg/kg) in rats were only attenuated by the 5-HT2A antagonist
M100907 and not by 5-HT2C receptor-selective antagonists. , DOI produced an inverted U-shaped dose–response in changing
locomotor activity, with higher doses decreasing locomotion. This hypolocomotion, unlike DOI-induced hyperactivity,
was not present in 5-HT2A knockout mice, but was reversed by 5-HT2C
antagonism, suggesting opposite roles for 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors
in mediating the locomotor effects of DOI. Glennon et al. were the first to report DOI-induced HTR in Sprague–Dawley
rats, and Canal et al. found that DOI-induced HTR was suppressed in
5-HT2C knockout mice and by 5-HT2C antagonists in wild-type animals. , DOI also produced anxiolytic-like effects in the Four-Plate Test
(FPT), which were blocked by α 2 -adrenergic agonists,
highlighting adrenergic interactions. Ripoll et al. confirmed that these effects were mediated by 5-HT2A
receptors, as only the 5-HT2A antagonist SR 46349B but not the 5-HT2B/C
antagonists SB 206553 and RS 10–2221 suppressed DOI’s
anxiolytic-like behavior. Recent studies
evaluating reinforcing effects showed that DOI reduced fentanyl intake
and relapse in rats, with sex-specific differences in reinforcement
modulation where males were more sensitive to DOI than females, indicating
that DOI may be more effective in males than females. In cocaine and ethanol self-administration
assays in mice and rats, DOI suppressed intake in a 5-HT2A-dependent
manner, without affecting inactive lever presses or total fluid intake. − In a heroin–alcohol co-use model measured with progressive
ratio self-administration methods, DOI decreased heroin intake (blocked
by M100907) but had no effect on alcohol intake. 3.2.2.1.5 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-methylamphetamine
(DOM) DOM is a relatively selective 5-HT2 receptor
agonist, with higher
affinity for 5-HT2 A /2C than 5-HT1A receptors ( Table and Figure ). Drug discrimination studies in Fischer 344 rats confirmed that animals
could distinguish DOM from saline. DOM
substituted for LSD with an ED 50 of 0.186 mg/kg, which
was attenuated by ketanserin, indicating 5-HT2 A /2B/2C
receptor mediation ( Table ). , The same group showed that DOM
exhibited a U-shaped dose–effect function for both HTR and
locomotion in mice, which was reversed by ketanserin and M100907. In 5-HT2A knockout mice, DOM failed to induce
HTR, confirming 5-HT2A involvement. In
rhesus monkeys trained to self-administer fentanyl, DOM did not enhance
fentanyl self-administration, suggesting a lack of coabuse liability
with opioid agonists. 3.2.2.1.2 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-bromoamphetamine (DOB) The reported K i of DOB at 5-HT2A receptors
is 25 nM with an EC 50 of 0.2 nM ( Table and Figure ). DOB substituted fully
for LSD in mice with an ED 50 of 0.16 mg/kg and exhibited
longer-lasting effects than LSD which was antagonized by M100907,
indicating 5-HT2A receptor mediation. , DOB also
fully substituted for DOM in rats with an ED 50 value of
0.09 mg/kg. DOB produced wet dog shakes
in rats, which was attenuated by ketanserin, and HTR in mice with
an ED 50 of 0.23 mg/kg ( Table ). , These findings support
a prominent role of 5-HT2A receptors in mediating DOB’s behavioral
effects. 3.2.2.1.3 2,5-dimethoxy-4-ethylamphetamine
(DOET) DOET binds to 5-HT2 receptors with a K i of 100 nM and shares discriminative stimulus
effects (ED 50 of 0.23 mg/kg) with DOM in DOM-trained animals
( Table , ,
and Figure ). , As with DOM, DOET increased locomotion in mice at 25 mg/kg in a
dose-dependent manner. On the other
hand, Halberstadt et al. observed that DOET exerted an inverted U-shaped
effect on locomotor activity, with high doses (10 mg/kg) reducing
movement and low doses (0.3 and 1 mg/kg) increasing it. Additionally, DOET dose-dependently decreased
investigatory behavior, such as nose-poking and rearing. Recent studies show that DOET induces HTR in
mice with an inverted U-shaped dose–response, with an ED 50 of 0.2 mg/kg, and peak effects at 1 mg/kg ( Table ). 3.2.2.1.4 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-chloroamphetamine (DOC) The binding affinity ( K i ) of DOC
at
the 5-HT2A receptor is 4 ± 0.45 nM with an EC 50 of
2.91 ± 0.66 nM ( Table and Figure ). Eshleman et al. showed that DOC (0.3–10
mg/kg) decreased locomotor activity in mice, with effects lasting
up to 80 min. A low dose (0.3 mg/kg)
caused hyperactivity, whereas a high dose (10 mg/kg) produced hypoactivity. DOC also substituted for DOM (ED 50 = 0.3 mg/kg) and LSD (ED 50 = 0.39 mg/kg). Halberstadt et al. reported an ED 50 of 0.32 mg/kg for DOC-induced HTR ( Table ). Mice treated
with DOC showed increased place preference for the drug-paired compartment,
and rats had higher self-administration compared to controls, suggesting
reinforcing and abuse-related potential. However, these results with DOC in mice suggesting abuse-related
potential do not generalize to most other 5-HT2A receptor agonists,
implicating some other mechanism of action.
sections.pharmacokinetics of dox compounds:
DOX compounds, or 4-substituted-2,5-dimethoxyamphetamines, such as
DOC, DOI, DOB, DOM (STP), and DOET, are long-acting phenethylamine
psychedelics, with durations of actions in humans of 12–24
h (DOC), 16–30 h (DOI), 18–30 h (DOB), 8–20 h
(DOM), and 5–20 h (DOET). − Across the DOX series
(DOC, DOI, DOB, DOM, DOET), in vitro and urine-metabolite
studies indicate that the primary biotransformation is O-demethylation
(with DOM additionally undergoing benzylic side-chain methyl hydroxylation),
mediated predominantly by CYP2D6.
sections.clinical studies_6:
Clinical trials
involving the DOX compounds for therapeutic use are extremely limited
in modern research. Despite early clinical evaluation in the mid-to-late
1960s, the DOX compounds have not advanced for several reasons. , , These compounds have exceptionally
long duration of actions complicating clinical supervision and increasing
the risk of prolonged adverse psychological effects relative to shorter-acting
psychedelics. − The emergence of shorter-acting serotonergic psychedelics
with more manageable pharmacokinetic profiles further shifted research
priorities away from DOX compounds. In addition, the amphetamine backbone
of the DOX series confers sympathomimetic effects, which were evident
in early clinical reports and raised safety concerns distinct from
nonamphetamine serotonergic psychedelics. Finally, the regulatory climate following the late-1960s scheduling
of hallucinogens, combined with public health concerns surrounding
DOM misuse, effectively halted further clinical investigation. ,
sections.ergolines:
Ergolines are tetracyclic
molecules derived from alkaloid sources and represent a chemical class
that includes LSD. Due to their structural complexity giving rise
to synthetic challenges, SAR studies have been limited and are primarily
centered around LSD ( Figure ). The two chiral centers of LSD reveal the
importance of chirality influencing hallucinogenic activity, as 5R,8R-isomer
is the sole ergoline possessing biological activity. Substitution with a halogen at the 2-position of the indole
ring in LSD, abolishes psychedelic activity and acts as an antagonist
at the 5-HT2A receptor. Reduction of the
double bond between the C9 and C10 positions diminishes activity,
and similarly, hydrogenation of the C2–C3 double bond reduces
potency to approximately one-eighth that of LSD. , In contrast, substitution of the N(6)-methyl group with longer alkyl
chains has been shown to enhance potency.
sections.pharmacodynamics_7:
LSD binds to
multiple receptor systems, including serotonergic (e.g., 5-HT2A, 5-HT1A,
5-HT2C), dopaminergic (D2, D4), adrenergic receptors, and serotonin
transporters ( Table ). , Drug discrimination studies show that LSD
produces discriminative stimulus effects with 5-HT2A receptors playing
a dominant role. The discriminative
stimulus effects of LSD are time-dependent: early effects (15–30
min) are mediated by 5-HT2A receptors, while later effects (60–90
min) involve D2 receptors. M100907 only
partially blocks the discriminative effects of LSD, and 8-OH-DPAT
partially substitutes, implicating 5-HT1A involvement. LSD-induced HTR (ED 50 = 0.039 mg/kg)
is attenuated by M100907. , The behavioral effects
of LSD are absent in β-arrestin 2 knockout mice and present
in wild-type and β-arrestin 1 knockouts, highlighting a β-arrestin
2–dependent mechanism. Glutamate
systems also modulate LSD effects; mGlu2/3 antagonists enhance the
potency of LSD, while mGlu2/3 agonists attenuate the discriminative
stimulus effects of LSD. LSD enhances
sociability in mice at does that do not alter locomotion. A single dose reduced depressive-like behavior
for up to 5 weeks in the forced swim test. Acute LSD had sedative effects in zebrafish, while repeated low
doses reduced anxiety in rodents. , , LSD decreased ethanol intake without affecting total
fluid intake, though it did not alter relapse in alcohol-deprived
rats. , Chronic LSD administration caused long-lasting
hyperlocomotion, social deficits, and anhedonia. Overall, LSD produces complex, time- and receptor-dependent
behavioral effects, making it a valuable tool for studying serotonergic
signaling and psychiatric disorders ( Figure ). Several LSD analogs have emerged with varying pharmacological
profiles.
1-Propanoyl-lysergic acid diethylamide (1P-LSD) induces HTR in mice
with an ED 50 of 0.159 mg/kg and is less potent than LSD;
its effects are blocked by the 5-HT2A antagonist M100907, and it acts
as a prodrug for LSD. , 6-Norlysergic Acid Diethylamide
(nor-LSD), a metabolite of LSD, exhibits greater affinity and efficacy
at 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B receptors than LSD itself. 6-Allyl-6-nor-LSD (AL-LAD) fully substitutes for LSD in
drug discrimination assays and is more potent (ED 50 = 13
nmol/kg vs 46 nmol/kg for LSD), and has relatively high 5-HT2A receptor
binding affinity ( K i = 8.1 nM), though
it is less potent than LSD in HTR assays (ED 50 = 0.0742
mg/kg). , , Lysergic
Acid Amide (LSA), also known as ergine, binds to D2 and 5-HT2 receptors
and shows in silico affinity for multiple 5-HT subtypes,
particularly 5-HT1D; however, in vitro studies reveal
lower affinity than LSD at 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 receptors. , , 6-Ethyl-6-nor-LSD (ETH-LAD)
binds strongly to both dopamine and serotonin receptors ( Table ) and is more potent
than LSD in discrimination studies ( Table ). , Its isomer N-ethyl-Nisopropyllysergamide
(EIPLA) induces HTR in mice with an ED 50 of 0.102 mg/kg,
indicating reduced potency compared to LSD. 6-Propyl-6-nor LSD (PRO-LAD) also shows high 5-HT receptor affinity,
induces oxytocic effects in the rat uterus, and substitutes for LSD
with comparable potency in trained animals. , Collectively, these analogs highlight structural modifications that
differentially influence serotonergic and dopaminergic receptor interactions,
potency, and behavioral effects. The binding and efficacy profiles
of the LSD analogs are listed in Table .
sections.pharmacokinetics_6:
LSD is rapidly
absorbed when administered orally, reaching peak plasma concentrations
typically within 1.5–2 h ( Table ). It follows linear, first-order elimination kinetics
up to 12 h post-ingestion, with a plasma half-life of 3.6 ± 0.9
h; however, a slower terminal phase extends the elimination to 8.9
± 5.9 h. Despite plasma clearance,
the subjective psychedelic effects of LSD persist for approximately
8–12 h. Extensive hepatic metabolism
is mediated largely by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, producing several inactive
metabolites including the major urinary product 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-LSD
(O–H-LSD) and nor-LSD.
sections.clinical studies_7:
Clinical interest
in LSD has led to a wave of early- and late-phase trials, assessing
anxiolytic, mood-enhancing and psychotropic properties of this compound.
In a Phase 1 crossover study, healthy
volunteers received 75 μg intravenous LSD and placebo in separate
sessions. LSD produced robust psychological effects, but also increased
the likelihood of psychosis-like symptoms in participants. Further,
a double-blind comparison study ( NCT03604744 ) found that oral LSD
(100 and 200 μg) and psilocybin (30 mg) produced comparable
subjective effects, though the 200 μg LSD dose was linked to
stronger ego dissolution. Psilocybin increased blood pressure more
than LSD, whereas LSD increased heart rate more than psilocybin. However,
both LSD and psilocybin showed comparable cardiostimulant properties. Building on this work, in a Phase 2 trial ( NCT03153579 ),
participants with generalized anxiety, including those with terminal
illness, received two 200 μg LSD (oral solution) and 2 placebo
sessions across a 48-week period. LSD
treatment resulted in significant reduction in anxiety and depression
which lasted up to 16 weeks following the last injection. Only one
severe adverse effect (transient anxiety and delusional reaction during
session) was reported. A parallel placebo-controlled trial ( NCT03790358 )
of low-dose LSD (26 μg) in participants with depression found
mood improvements, particularly in participants with higher baseline
depressive symptoms. The treatment was
well-tolerated, with no severe adverse effects. One of the most
advanced programs involves MM120, an orally disintegrating
tablet of LSD. A Phase 2b clinical trial ( NCT05407064 ) identified
100 μg as the optimal dose, with 48% remission at week 12 in
generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), with only mild-to-moderate transient
adverse effects. As of 2025, MindMed
entered MM120 into three Phase 3 trails: Voyage ( NCT06741228 ) and
Panorama ( NCT06809595 ) for treatment of GAD, and Emerge ( NCT06941844 )
for treatment of MDD. −
sections.perspective:
Recent research and clinical
data support the therapeutic potential
of psychedelics in treating CNS disorders, including depression, anxiety,
and substance use disorders. However, the critical unresolved question
remains: What is the optimal pharmacokinetic (short-acting or long-acting)
and pharmacodynamic (5-HT2A affinity, selectivity, and efficacy) profile
for translating this class of agents into mainstream clinical practice?
Addressing these questions will help refine implementation of psychedelic-assisted
therapies. Short-acting psilocybin analogs, such as RE-104 and
vaporized 5-MeO–DMT,
demonstrate rapid onset of action, a duration of action ranging from
15 min to 2 h, aligning their use with the constraints of clinical
sessions. The clinical potential of short-acting compounds was well
demonstrated in recent Phase I/II trials, signifying their ability to induce rapid antidepressant responses,
often within 7 days, which is better than the delayed onset of action
typical of conventional antidepressants. Their favorable safety profiles
and potential for multiphasic dosing regimens provide additional benefits
for potential individualized therapy and outpatient care. On
the other hand, long-acting psilocybin derivatives provide the
advantage of sustained receptor engagement and deeper psychological
immersion. They induce prolonged 5-HT2A receptor activation and neuroplasticity-related
downstream signaling, resulting in antidepressant effects that can
last for several months. Their metabolic stability and ability to
permeate the BBB contribute to robust efficacy in trials with cancer-related
depression, treatment-resistant depression, and alcohol use disorders.
However, the downside of their use is extended hallucinogenic experiences
and the need for intensive clinical infrastructure, which may limit
accessibility. The field now faces a critical inflection point.
While short-acting
agents may offer benefits of broader clinical utilization, especially
in outpatient settings, long-acting psychedelics may remain necessary
for deep psychotherapeutic work to treat resistant cases of depression
in patients with complex or chronic conditions. Intermediate-acting
agents with durations of action approximately 2–4 h may retain
the robust therapeutic efficacy of psychedelics while reducing clinical
burden associated with prolonged monitoring. For example, bretisilocin
(GM-2505), a rapid-acting psychedelic with a 2 h duration of action,
was recently acquired by AbbVie and is currently in Phase II clinical
trials. Future directions should focus
on head-to-head comparative trials, real-world effectiveness studies,
and biomarker-guided personalization strategies to determine which
patients benefit most from each modality. Overall, the optimal
psychedelic therapy is not only defined by
the optimal duration of action alone but requires precision matching
between compound properties, clinical goals, and individual neurobiology.
Bridging this gap will require integrated efforts across molecular
pharmacology, clinical neuroscience, and health systems implementation.
sections.conclusion:
Short- and long-acting psychedelics
offer distinct pharmacological
and therapeutic profiles that collectively expand the landscape of
psychedelic-assisted interventions. Short-acting agents, such as DMT
and 5-MeO–DMT, provide rapid onset and brief duration, making
them attractive for controlled, time-limited clinical settings. In
contrast, long-acting compounds like psilocybin and LSD allow for
extended therapeutic engagement, which may be advantageous in certain
psychiatric contexts. Advances in medicinal chemistry and receptor
pharmacology have illuminated how structural modifications influence
receptor affinity, signaling pathways, and metabolic stability; factors
that ultimately shape both duration of action and clinical utility.
These insights guide the development of next-generation psychedelics
with optimized efficacy, safety, and dosing parameters. Moving forward,
a structure-informed approach that integrates both pharmacokinetic
and pharmacodynamic considerations will be essential for harnessing
the full therapeutic potential of psychedelic compounds across a range
of neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: Abnormal adnexal uptake in 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT: from physiological variants to malignant characterization
abstract: Background The adnexal region in females presents complex imaging due to the menstrual cycle. Accurate diagnosis is crucial for effective tumor treatment. This study aims to assess the clinical utility of abnormal adnexal uptake on 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT for early and precise lesion characterization. Methods This study retrospectively analyzed all female patients with abnormal adnexal uptake on 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT at our institution from November 2021 to June 2024. Semiquantitative analysis of PET/CT imaging parameters was performed, combined with serum tumor markers and immunohistochemical markers. Pathological findings or imaging follow-up ≥ 6 months served as the gold standard for evaluating the diagnostic performance of 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT. Results The study included 121 female patients with a mean age of 53.8 ± 12.2 years (18–80 years). A total of 184 adnexal lesions with abnormal uptake were identified. Pathology/follow-up confirmed 82.6% as malignancies, comprising 84 primary and 16 metastatic cases. Additionally, 2 borderline tumors and 19 benign lesions were detected. The positive predictive value was 83.5%. SUVmax differed significantly among primary malignant, metastatic, and benign lesions (12.52 ± 5.41 vs. 9.78 ± 3.39 vs. 5.52 ± 4.17). In the subset of patients with available pathological specimens, SUVmax showed weak to moderate positive correlations with Ki-67 ( r = 0.361, p < 0.001) and p53 ( r = 0.419, p < 0.001). Notably, the mean SUVmax in the Ki67 > 20% group was significantly higher than in the Ki67 ≤ 20% group ( p < 0.001). ROC analysis showed an AUC of 0.85 of SUVmax alone for diagnosing malignant adnexal lesions, increasing to 0.89 when combined with tumor markers. Discussion 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT demonstrates high diagnostic performance for ovarian lesions. Among pathologically confirmed cases, SUVmax correlates with proliferative activity and malignant potential, supporting its role in diagnostic optimization.
