sections.introduction: Statistics show that up to 35% of premenopausal women and 17% of postmenopausal women carry adnexal lesions, with a trend toward onset at a younger age [ 1 ]. These lesions encompass a spectrum of changes from benign to malignant. When evaluating adnexal lesions, the primary considerations are whether emergency surgical intervention is necessary and the potential impact on fertility. Secondary considerations include differentiation between benign and malignant lesions, as well as staging. Ovarian malignancies, given their subtle onset, are often diagnosed at advanced stages. They have the highest mortality rate among gynecological cancers, posing a severe threat to women’s health and survival [ 2 , 3 ]. Tumor markers play a crucial role in disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. Serum CA125 is the most widely used indicator for assessing ovarian lesions, with abnormal elevation in approximately 80% of patients with epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) or fallopian tube cancer, particularly in postmenopausal women [ 4 – 6 ]. A meta-analysis revealed that CA125 has a sensitivity of 69–87% and a specificity of 81–93% for detecting cancer in postmenopausal women. However, up to 20% of patients still exhibit normal CA125 levels, and the marker is not expressed in pure mucinous carcinoma [ 7 ]. Other markers, such as CEA, CA153, and CA199, also provide some indication of adnexal lesions, but their specificity is relatively low. Therefore, accurate diagnosis requires comprehensive evaluation combining these markers with other clinical information [ 8 ]. Compared with conventional imaging, molecular imaging techniques—particularly positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)—can provide deeper insights into disease heterogeneity and biological characteristics. PET/CT has been incorporated into routine protocols for preoperative evaluation and postoperative follow-up of ovarian cancer. 18 F-FDG remains currently the most widely used PET tracer. However, its specificity is relatively low, especially in the female reproductive system [ 9 – 12 ]. Certain physiological changes, such as follicular cysts and hemorrhagic corpus luteum, can result in false-positive 18 F-FDG uptake. This not only leads to potential misdiagnosis but may also obscure underlying pathological changes [ 9 , 13 , 14 ]. Bacanovic et al. reported a case where a hemorrhagic follicle mimicked a malignant tumor on 18 F-FDG imaging [ 15 ]. In a study by Minamimoto et al., 80 women underwent 18 F-FDG PET/CT screening for suspected ovarian cancer, with 19 cases were subsequently confirmed as benign [ 16 ]. These findings underscore the limitations of 18 F-FDG PET/CT in accurately detecting lesions within the female reproductive system. In recent years, 68 Ga-FAPI has been widely used in PET imaging and has demonstrated exceptional performance in early tumor detection, treatment planning, and postoperative assessment [ 17 ]. Fibroblast activation protein (FAP), a type II transmembrane serine protease, is absent or minimally expressed in normal adult tissues but is highly expressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts in over 90% of epithelial tumors. Its presence correlates with tumor invasiveness and poor prognosis. Previous research has shown that 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT exhibits a favorable target-to-background ratio in the female reproductive system, characterized by high tumor uptake and low background activity. The maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) for ovarian cancer has been reported to range from 6 to 10, although with significant interindividual variability [ 17 ]. However, studies directly evaluating adnexal tumors and non-neoplastic conditions using 68 Ga-FAPI remain limited. Distinguishing the nature of abnormal uptake in the adnexal region, whether physiological, inflammatory, or tumor-related, remains an urgent challenge for clinicians and nuclear medicine specialists. Previous studies have established correlations between p53 and Ki-67 expression and radiotracer uptake on 18 F-FDG PET/CT [ 18 , 19 ]. However, the relationship between 68 Ga-FAPI uptake and immunohistochemical findings remains inconclusive. This study retrospectively analyzes 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT images to determine the clinical significance of increased abnormal uptake in the adnexal region. It further explores the diagnostic efficacy of 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT in conjunction with common tumor markers and immunohistochemical indicators, aiming to provide valuable reference information for the future diagnosis and treatment of adnexal diseases.
sections.patients: This retrospective study analyzed all female patients who underwent 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT at the Department of Nuclear Medicine of our hospital from November 2021 to June 2024 for oncological evaluation (e.g., staging, restaging, or detection of unknown primary tumors based on clinical suspicion). From this cohort, clinical data were systematically reviewed using a standardized case report form. The recorded data included patient demographics, clinical symptoms, levels of serum tumor markers (CA125, CA19-9, CA15-3, CEA) measured within one week prior to the PET/CT scan, and detailed histopathological reports when available. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) female patients aged 18–80 years; (2) presence of newly discovered abnormal uptake in the adnexal region on PET/CT, with the nature of the lesion undetermined at the time of imaging. Exclusion criteria were: (1) history of reproductive system tumors; (2) history of prior surgery or specific treatment (e.g., chemotherapy, radiotherapy) targeting the adnexal region in question; (3) lack of definitive pathological confirmation or sufficient follow-up data (≥ 6 months) to determine the final nature of the adnexal lesion. Histopathological analysis (from biopsy or surgical specimens) served as the gold standard for diagnosis whenever possible. For lesions with pathological confirmation, immunohistochemical markers relevant to tumor grading and prognosis, specifically p53 expression status and the Ki-67 proliferation index, were documented from pathology reports. For patients without pathological verification, a composite clinical-imaging reference standard was used. Follow-up assessments consisted primarily of ultrasound, contrast-enhanced CT or pelvic MRI, combined with clinical evaluation and serum tumor marker tests. The first follow-up was typically conducted within 3 months after the PET/CT scan, with subsequent evaluations every 3 to 6 months thereafter. A minimum follow-up of 6 months was required for inclusion in the final analysis to ensure reliable determination of the lesion’s biological behavior. Adnexal lesions were considered malignant based on the following criteria: (a) typical malignant characteristics confirmed by imaging and laboratory tests; (b) clear evidence of significant disease progression on serial imaging studies during follow-up; or (c) substantial remission of the lesion following institution of anti-cancer therapies (e.g., chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy). Benign lesions were defined as those showing stability or regression without specific anti-tumor treatment over the follow-up period. This study was approved by the hospital ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all patients.
sections.pet/ct image acquisition and analysis: Two experienced nuclear medicine physicians conducted a consensus evaluation of the 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT images. Any adnexal uptake exceeding background blood pool activity was included in the study. For patients with bilateral lesions, the lesion with the highest SUVmax was selected as the representative lesion for that patient. The maximum diameter of each lesion was measured, and a fixed circular region of interest (ROI, 1.5 cm in diameter) was delineated in the area of highest uptake. Tracer uptake was quantified using the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax). To obtain background activity, the mean standardized uptake value (SUVmean) was measured by placing a 3-cm spherical volume of interest (VOI) within the right lobe of the liver, carefully avoiding major blood vessels and biliary structures. The tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) was calculated as SUVmax (tumor) / SUVmean (liver). The diagnostic efficacy of 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT for adnexal malignancy was assessed by comparison with final pathology results and/or follow-up findings.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 7.0 and IBM SPSS Statistics 23.0. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and for homogeneity of variances using Levene’s test. Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± SD, and non-normally distributed data as median (interquartile range). Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages. ROC curve analysis with area under the curve (AUC) was used to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of PET parameters. For two-group comparisons, the independent-samples t-test (normal distribution) or Mann-Whitney U test (non-normal) was used. For multiple group comparisons: one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test when normality and homogeneity of variances were satisfied; Welch’s ANOVA with Games-Howell post hoc test when variances were unequal; and Kruskal-Wallis H test with Dunn’s post hoc test for non-normally distributed data. Correlations between PET parameters and tumor markers or immunohistochemical indices were assessed using Pearson (normal distribution) or Spearman (non-normal) correlation coefficients.
sections.patient characteristics: Figure 1 presents the study flowchart. A total of 121 female patients (mean age: 53.8 ± 12.2 years; range: 18–80 years) were included. We identified 184 adnexal lesions with abnormal 68 Ga-FAPI uptake. Bilateral uptake was observed in 63 patients, and unilateral uptake in 58 patients (31 left, 27 right). Based on the reference standard, 100 patients (82.6%) were confirmed as having malignant, including 84 with primary malignancies and 16 with metastases. Additionally, we identified 2 borderline tumors, 7 benign lesions, and 12 cases attributed to physiological uptake. Detailed patient demographics are summarized in Table 1 . Fig. 1 Study flowchart. sections.imaging features: The characteristics of the adnexal lesions are detailed in Table 2 . Among the malignancies, high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma was the most prevalent subtype, accounting for 57.0% of cases. Malignancies (primary and metastatic) exhibited predominantly solid or cystic-solid morphology (Fig. 2 ), with mean SUVmax values of 12.52 ± 5.41 and 9.78 ± 3.39, and mean diameters of 7.59 ± 3.96 cm and 5.43 ± 3.42 cm, respectively. In contrast, uptake of non-malignancy uptake (including physiological variations, cysts, abscesses, borderline tumors, mature teratomas, and serous cystadenofibroma) was predominantly cystic (Fig. 3 ), with a significantly lower mean SUVmax of 5.52 ± 4.17 and a mean diameter of 5.31 ± 5.94 cm. A statistically significant difference in SUVmax was observed among the three groups (Welch’s F (2, 38.01) = 20.69, p < 0.001). Specifically, SUVmax was significantly higher for primary malignancies than for both non-malignancy ( p < 0.001) and metastases ( p = 0.032). Furthermore, metastatic lesions demonstrated significantly higher SUVmax than non-malignancy ( p = 0.004). No significant difference in mean lesion diameter was observed among the three groups ( p > 0.05) (Fig. 4 ). sections.correlation of pet parameters with serum: Tumor marker levels measured within one week prior to PET/CT were analyzed. Elevated levels were observed in a subset of patients (CEA: 28, CA125: 106, CA15-3: 79, CA19-9: 53), with the majority occurring in the malignant group (CEA: 23, CA125: 91, CA15-3: 66, CA19-9: 44). No significant correlation was found between the degree of elevation (stratified into < 2-fold, 2–5 fold, 5–10 fold, and > 10-fold) of any tumor marker and the PET parameters SUVmax or TBR ( p > 0.05 for all).
sections.correlation of pet parameters with histo: Immunohistochemistry data were available for 86 lesions (from biopsy or surgical specimens). Among 75 lesions with available data, the mean p53 expression rate was 64% ± 25%. Excluding tumor types with fewer than 3 cases, the mean Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 57% for high-grade serous carcinoma, 42% for clear cell carcinoma, and 38% for endometrioid carcinoma. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis revealed a statistically significant positive correlation between SUVmax and both Ki-67 ( r = 0.361, p < 0.001) and p53 expression rate ( r = 0.419, p < 0.001). TBR showed a marginally stronger correlation with these markers than SUVmax alone (Table 3 ). Lesions with a Ki-67 index > 20% (a commonly used clinical threshold) demonstrated a significantly higher mean SUVmax than those with Ki-67 ≤ 20% ( p < 0.001). sections.discussion_1: This study systematically evaluated the diagnostic value of 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT for focal abnormal uptake in the female adnexal region with a relatively large sample size, and further explored the association between its quantitative parameters and tumor biomarkers. The results indicate that 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT has high diagnostic efficacy for malignant adnexal tumors. Its semi-quantitative parameters, SUVmax and TBR, not only effectively differentiate benign from malignant lesions but also show a modest but statistically significant positive correlation with key immunohistochemical markers reflecting tumor proliferative activity (Ki-67) and malignant transformation (p53). The modest strength of these correlations suggests that while 68 Ga-FAPI uptake is associated with proliferative activity and p53 status, it is not a direct surrogate for these markers. Although 18 F-FDG PET/CT has been widely used for malignant tumors, its specificity in the female adnexal region is limited [ 20 ]. Physiological uptake (such as menstrual cycle-related ovarian changes) and benign inflammatory lesions often lead to false positives. 68 Ga-FAPI targets activated cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in the tumor microenvironment, which are expressed at extremely low levels in normal ovarian tissue [ 21 , 22 ]. CAFs play a significant role in tumor proliferation, invasion, and metastasis by secreting various growth factors and cytokines and degrading extracellular matrix proteins [ 23 ]. Lactate and ketone bodies produced by CAFs are transported to adjacent tumor cells to fuel glycolysis, further promoting tumor proliferation and metastasis [ 17 , 24 ]. For patients with adnexal masses but atypical features on conventional imaging, 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT can provide crucial molecular-level information to assist in characterization. Semi-quantitative parameter thresholds can serve as decision-support tools, helping to avoid unnecessary invasive procedures. This study confirmed that the SUVmax of malignancies was significantly higher than that of benign lesions, providing a reliable quantitative basis for differential diagnosis. Cihan et al. evaluated FAPI uptake in healthy tissues of cancer patients, reporting that normal ovaries had an average FAPI uptake of 1.7 (SUVmax 0.3–5.87), while glandular cells in the fallopian tubes showed moderate FAP expression with no significant differences between premenopausal and postmenopausal women [ 21 ]. Notably, while the literature suggests that baseline expression of FAP in normal ovarian tissue is not affected by the menstrual cycle [ 25 ], the physiological uptake observed in this study (e.g., in the corpus luteum) indicates that cycle-related physiological structures or benign lesions themselves may become sources of FAPI uptake due to local repair, angiogenesis, and other processes accompanied by fibroblast activation [ 26 , 27 ]. Therefore, the key to interpreting abnormal adnexal FAPI uptake lies in differentiating “pathological” from “non-malignancy”activation, rather than simply identifying malignancy. The SUVmax differences and TBR values established in this study provide an objective reference for this purpose. Another important finding of this study is the positive correlation between SUVmax and both the Ki-67 index and p53 expression. This finding is not coincidental but is rooted in the biological function of FAP. CAFs are core regulators of the tumor microenvironment, directly promoting tumor proliferation, invasion, and metastasis by secreting growth factors, cytokines, and remodeling the extracellular matrix. A high Ki-67 index indicates active tumor cell proliferation [ 28 , 29 ], and this state is often accompanied by a more activated stromal environment. Similarly, p53 mutation or loss leads to genomic instability and malignant progression [ 30 ], and such highly malignant tumor clones typically recruit more CAFs to support their growth. Therefore, the high uptake of 68 Ga-FAPI, which reflects CAFs activity, is associated with Ki-67 and p53. This association reveals the synergistic co-evolution between activated stroma and tumor invasiveness during disease progression. This result suggests that imaging information from 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT may non-invasively reflect the intrinsic invasiveness potential of the tumor. In this study, there was no significant correlation between serum tumor marker levels and SUVmax. Although CA125 was elevated in 90% of malignant cases, its well-documented rise in various benign conditions (such as endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease) limits its diagnostic specificity [ 31 , 32 ]. This lack of correlation underscores that these biomarkers and FAPI uptake reflect fundamentally distinct biological processes. For example, serum CA125 is a glycoprotein secreted into the systemic circulation, indicative of tumor burden and secretory activity, whereas SUVmax on 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT quantifies the localized density of activated cancer-associated fibroblasts within the tumor microenvironment. Consequently, they provide complementary rather than overlapping information. Their combination offers complementary diagnostic value, as supported by our data showing that combining SUVmax with markers such as CA125 increased the diagnostic AUC from 0.85 (SUVmax alone) to 0.89.
sections.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective design may introduce selection bias; all patients underwent PET/CT due to suspected malignancy, which may overestimate the performance of FAPI in truly incidental lesions. Second, the lack of a direct head-to-head comparison with ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT prevents a quantitative assertion within this dataset that 68 Ga-FAPI is superior to 18 F-FDG, although theoretical advantages exist. Third, the number of cases with benign and borderline tumors is relatively small. Larger samples are needed in the future to further refine the uptake characteristics of various lesions. Finally, whether FAPI uptake can independently predict treatment response and prognosis requires verification through prospective follow-up studies.
sections.conclusion: In conclusion, 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT is a molecular imaging technique with high diagnostic efficacy for adnexal lesions. Its quantitative parameters, SUVmax and TBR, can not only effectively differentiate benign from malignant lesions, but also serve as non-invasive biomarkers reflecting stromal activation associated with tumor proliferative activity and p53 status, providing a new dimension for preoperative risk assessment. Combining these parameters with serum tumor markers can further optimize diagnostic accuracy. The results of this study provide strong evidence supporting the application of 68 Ga-FAPI PET/CT in the precise diagnosis and individualized management of adnexal lesions, particularly in challenging cases.

title: Osteoporosis in children and adolescents with transfusion-dependent thalassemia and the diagnostic value of different indicators
abstract: Background The study aimed to investigate the prevalence of osteoporosis in children and adolescents with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) and evaluate the diagnostic value of different osteoporosis indicators. Methods Clinical data were collected from children and adolescents with TDT treated with blood transfusion between March 2022 and January 2024 at Huizhou Central People’s Hospital and Huizhou First Hospital. The patients were grouped according to the presence of osteoporosis (International Society for Clinical Densitometry [ISCD] criteria). Results Of 138 patients included in the study, 48 (34.8%) had osteoporosis. The patients with osteoporosis mainly had asymptomatic grade I fractures of the spine. Using the dual-X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) standards from the World Health Organization, height-corrected TBLH Z-score ≤-2 was associated with osteoporosis (30.4% vs. 14.9%, P = 0.035), displaying 30.4% sensitivity and 85.1% specificity. According to the Chinese DXA standards, height-corrected and age-specific Z-scores ≤-2 were not associated with osteoporosis. Conclusion The prevalence of osteoporosis among children and adolescents with TDT was 34.8%, indicating the need for screening for osteoporosis in that population. In TDT, the diagnosis of osteoporosis requires early detection of spinal fractures because bone density assessed by DXA is of limited value. sections.introduction: Thalassemia is a group of hereditary blood disorders caused by mutations in the globin genes, resulting in impaired hemoglobin production [ 1 – 5 ]. About 5% of the world population carries a thalassemia mutation [ 3 , 4 , 6 ]. In China, over 200 million individuals carry at least one mutated allele for a globin gene, with two provinces (Guangdong and Guangxi) accounting for 40% of the cases [ 7 ]. Patients with transfusion-dependent thalassemia (TDT) require lifelong regular red blood cell transfusions [ 1 , 3 , 8 ]. One of the most common complications of thalassemia is osteoporosis, observed in 22.9% of the patients in the OPTIMAL CARE study (291 male and 293 female patients of 25.4 ± 13.9 years old from Lebanon, Italy, Iran, Egypt, United Arab Emirates, and Oman) [ 9 ] and 22.3% in the study by Karimi et al. [ 10 ] (726 patients aged 2.5–80 years from Iran, Italy, Turkey, Greece, Oman, Qatar, Jordan, Cyprus, and the United Kingdom). Patients with thalassemia major and intermedia may present skeletal complications such as reduced bone mineral density (BMD), spontaneous fractures, and spinal deformities. Patients with β-thalassemia often have lower BMD compared with individuals without thalassemia and have a higher fracture prevalence that increases with age [ 3 , 6 ]. In recent years, expert groups have emphasized that osteoporosis in TDT constitutes a major cause of morbidity and requires structured, disease-specific guidance for screening, diagnosis, and management across the lifespan [ 11 , 12 ]. Osteoporosis in children and adolescents with TDT will inevitably lead to an escalating fracture risk in adulthood. The development of osteoporosis and osteopenia in patients with TDT is primarily attributed to ineffective erythropoiesis and subsequent bone marrow expansion. In addition, severe iron overload, often found in patients with TDT due to repeated blood transfusions, may directly interfere with osteoid maturation and mineralization [ 3 , 6 ]. Iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine or deferasirox also contributes to the risk of osteoporosis [ 3 , 6 , 8 ]. Few studies have comprehensively investigated osteoporosis in children and adolescents with TDT. Gaudio et al. [ 13 ] suggested that the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children with TDT should not rely solely on BMD measurements because of the interference from the growing skeleton. In addition, BMD deficit may be exaggerated in patients with iron overload [ 14 ]. Several knowledge gaps persist regarding the diagnosis and risk factors for osteoporosis in children and adolescents with TDT. Furthermore, there is a lack of comparisons of different criteria of BMD for the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents with TDT. Current osteoporosis guidelines increasingly recognize the role of vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) as an integral component of fracture risk evaluation, because even asymptomatic vertebral fractures substantially increase the risk of subsequent fractures and may be missed when relying solely on areal BMD [ 11 , 12 , 15 ]. In this context, integrating VFA with densitometric measurements is particularly relevant in TDT, where spinal deformities, growth impairment, and altered bone geometry can complicate the interpretation of BMD and lead to underdiagnosis of clinically important vertebral fractures [ 11 , 12 , 15 ]. Available data regarding TDT patients suggest early and periodic assessment of bone health, including lumbar spine and hip BMD, evaluation for vertebral fractures, and timely initiation of pharmacological and supportive interventions to prevent fractures and preserve quality of life [ 16 ]. However, these data are largely derived from adults, and robust evidence on optimal diagnostic thresholds and imaging strategies in pediatric and adolescent TDT populations remains limited. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the prevalence of osteoporosis in children and adolescents with TDT and evaluate the diagnostic value of different BMD criteria for osteoporosis.
sections.study design and patients: The present study included children and adolescents with TDT treated with blood transfusion between March 2022 and January 2024 at Huizhou Central People’s Hospital and Huizhou First People’s Hospital. The study was approved by the ethics committees of Huizhou Central People’s Hospital and Huizhou First Hospital (approvals #ky112022097 and #HZFH2023002). The patients or their legal guardians signed the informed consent forms. The inclusion criteria were (1) met the diagnostic criteria for TDT [ 3 , 11 , 12 , 17 ], including β thalassemia major, transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia intermedia, and transfusion-dependent α-thalassemia intermedia, (2) 5–18 years old, (3) without bone marrow transplantation or gene therapy, (4) without anti-osteoporosis treatment (e.g., bisphosphonates), and (5) agreed to participate in the study. The exclusion criteria were (1) suffering from other chronic diseases (e.g., severe liver or renal function impairment, mental retardation, chromosomal abnormality, long-term use of glucocorticoids, hereditary osteopathy, etc.), (2) non-removable objects in the body that can affect BMD assessments (e.g., prosthesis, steel plates, etc.), (3) height or weight exceeding the instrument’s detection range, i.e., height > 197.5 cm or weight > 204 kg, (4) pregnancy, (5) participated in research involving ionizing radiation in the past year, or (6) incomplete data. All participants in this study were transfusion-dependent. The initiation of transfusion was based on hemoglobin levels persistently being < 70 g/L or hemoglobin being > 70 g/L but accompanied by severe anemia symptoms, growth and developmental delays, facial deformities, pathological fractures, or significant extramedullary hematopoiesis. The participants were receiving transfusions of allogenic red blood cells every 2–5 weeks [ 17 , 18 ]. At the study centers, patients on regular transfusion were managed according to disease‑specific thalassemia guidelines, under which pre‑transfusion hemoglobin levels are intentionally maintained at 90–105 g/L as part of a hypertransfusion regimen, rather than at the lower thresholds commonly used in the general population [ 3 , 17 , 19 ].
sections.data collection: Age, sex, diagnosis, time of starting blood transfusion, average hemoglobin before blood transfusion, and average ferritin in the last year were extracted from the patient’s medical records data. Questionnaires (presented in the Supplementary Materials) were administered to the patient’s family members to collect information on the use of iron chelation drugs, whether splenectomy was performed, and whether there were previous fractures. Trained pediatric endocrinologists performed standard height and weight measurements of the patients to calculate body mass index (BMI). They also determined Tanner’s staging for each patient. Asymptomatic osteoporosis was diagnosed based on the presence of painless spine fractures [ 20 ]. The fractures were graded as grades I (height of the vertebrae decreased by 20% to 25%), II (height of the vertebrae decreased by 25%-40%), and III (height of the vertebrae decreased by > 40%) (Fig. 1 ). The 2019 International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD) criteria for osteoporosis diagnosis in children and adolescents are (1) spine fracture resulting from low trauma without localized disorders, or (2) if no spinal fracture is present, a BMD Z-score ≤-2.0 accompanied by a significant history of fracture, i.e., ≥ 2 long bone fractures before the age of 10 years or ≥ 3 long bone fractures occurring before the age of 19 years [ 21 ]. The diagnostic criteria for spinal fractures were based on the Genant semiquantitative determination method [ 22 ]. Fig. 1 Examples of the grades and types of asymptomatic spine fractures. A Normal. B Grade I compressive deformation. C Grade I wedge-shaped deformation. D Grade I double-convex deformation. E Grade II compressive deformation. F Grade III compressive deformation The imaging examinations included lateral spine film to assess spinal fractures and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) to measure BMD. The DXA assessments for children and adolescents were based on the lumbar spine (L1-L4) and total body less head (TBLH) [ 23 , 24 ]. Age-specific and height-corrected BMD Z-scores were obtained using the World Health Organization (WHO) [ 25 , 26 ] and Chinese [ 27 ] reference values. Fasting blood samples were taken before blood transfusion for routine blood counts, electrolytes, liver and kidney function, blood lipids, serum ferritin, endocrine function, and bone turnover markers.
sections.statistical analysis: SPSS 26.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) was used for statistical analysis. Continuous data that conformed to the normal distribution were described as means ± standard deviations and analyzed using Student’s t-test. Continuous data that did not conform to the normal distribution were described as medians (interquartile range [IQR]) and analyzed using the rank sum test. Categorical data were described as n (%) or [n/n total (%)] and analyzed using the chi-squared test. Considering the characteristics that change with increasing age, height [ 28 ], BMI [ 29 ], IGF-1 [ 30 ], AMH [ 31 , 32 ], PINP, and β-CTX [ 33 ] were analyzed using standard deviation scores (SDS). The different parameters for the diagnosis of osteoporosis were calculated using contingency tables. Sensitivity (true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives), specificity (true negatives divided by true negatives plus false positives), positive predictive value (true positives divided by true positives plus false positives), and negative predictive value (true negatives divided by true negatives plus false negatives) were calculated. The Youden index was calculated as sensitivity + specificity − 1. Two-sided P -values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.
sections.characteristics of the patients: During the study period, 184 patients with TDT (5–18 years old) received blood transfusions at Huizhou Central People’s Hospital or Huizhou First People’s Hospital. Among them, 139 underwent a DXA examination and lateral spine examination, but one patient with comorbid Turner syndrome (TS) was excluded. Therefore, 138 patients were included in the present study. Based on the presence of spine fractures, the prevalence of osteoporosis was 34.8% (48/138), without significant differences between β-thalassemia (34.6%, 37/108) and α-thalassemia (36.7%, 11/30). When stratified into 2-year age intervals, the prevalence of osteoporosis was 33.3% in those aged 5–6 years, 35.3% in 7–8 years, 39.1% in 9–10 years, 37.5% in 11–12 years, 33.3% in 13–14, 33.3% in 15–16 years, and 26.7% in 17–18 years. Among the 48 patients with osteoporosis, 45 had asymptomatic grade I mild thoracic or lumbar fractures (45/48, 93.8%), presenting as compression deformities, wedge deformities, or biconcave deformities. Two patients (4.1%) had moderate grade II fractures characterized by compression and deformation of T12 or L5. One patient (2.1%) had grade III severe fractures characterized by compression and deformation of T5, T7, T8, and T9. Among the 48 patients with vertebral fractures, 83 fractured vertebral levels were identified. Fifteen patients had multiple vertebral fractures, ranging from two to nine affected levels. The most frequently involved vertebra was L5 (31/48, 64.6%), followed by T12 (9/48, 18.8%), L1 (7/48, 14.5%), T11 (6/48, 12.5%), and L4 (5/48, 10.4%). The types of deformation included grade I compressive deformations ( n = 38 fractures), grade I wedge-shaped deformations ( n = 31 fractures), grade I double-convex deformations ( n = 8 fractures), grade II compressive deformations ( n = 2 fractures), and grade III compressive deformations ( n = 4 fractures). Among the patients who could not be diagnosed with osteoporosis according to the ISCD standard, seven patients (7/90, 7.8%) had a history of limb fractures. There were no significant differences between the osteoporosis and non-osteoporosis groups regarding demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics (all P > 0.05) ( Table 1 and Supplementary Table S1 ) . sections.discussion: In the present study, the prevalence of osteoporosis among children and adolescents with TDT was 34.8%, indicating the need for screening for osteoporosis in that population. The results suggested that in patients with TDT, the diagnosis of osteoporosis requires the early detection of spinal fractures because BMD assessed by DXA is of limited value. These findings can potentially enhance the management of children and adolescents with TDT and improve their long-term outcomes. Recent recommendations on vertebral fracture assessment emphasize that identifying morphometric vertebral deformities is a critical component of osteoporosis evaluation, because many vertebral fractures are clinically silent yet strongly predict future fracture risk and adverse outcomes. These data support integrating systematic spine imaging (e.g., VFA or lateral spine radiographs) into routine bone health assessment rather than relying on DXA-derived BMD alone [ 15 , 34 ], which is consistent with the present findings in pediatric TDT. In the present study, the prevalence of osteoporosis among patients with TDT (34.8%) was higher than that of 23% of patients with β-thalassemia aged 2.5–80 years and from several countries [ 9 , 10 ]. On the other hand, the prevalence of osteoporosis in TDT has been reported to vary widely from 18% to 75% [ 35 – 38 ], depending upon the diagnostic criteria, transfusion status, iron chelation therapy status, and patient age. Of note, those previous studies [ 35 – 38 ] were performed in adults or the general population of patients regardless of age. Studies revealed a higher prevalence of fractures in patients with TDT than in non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia [ 39 , 40 ]. Previous studies in children are limited by small numbers of patients but suggest a prevalence of osteoporosis of 10.5%-10.8% [ 41 , 42 ]. A recently developed guideline dedicated to osteoporosis in transfusion-dependent thalassemia underscores that skeletal complications, particularly vertebral and long-bone fractures, remain a major cause of morbidity despite advances in transfusion and chelation therapy and recommends proactive case-finding using both BMD and vertebral imaging in this high-risk group. These recommendations align with our observation that a substantial proportion of pediatric patients with TDT already fulfill diagnostic criteria for osteoporosis, highlighting the need to implement structured, guideline-based screening pathways from childhood to mitigate cumulative fracture burden over the life course [ 11 , 12 ]. The early screening and diagnosis of osteoporosis in patients with TDT is important to reduce the fracture risk and related complications [ 43 ]. It is particularly important in children and adolescents since such patients are at a very high risk of fracture in adulthood [ 44 ]. Unfortunately, the present study did not identify any demographic, clinical, or biochemical factors that could help identify patients needing more aggressive screening and prevention strategies. The discrepancies among studies can be due to several factors, including the sample size, the variables included in the study, the characteristics of the study population, and the diagnostic criteria and reference values. Patients with TDT are more at risk of having traditional factors associated with low BMD and fractures, such as physical inactivity, small body weight, and nutritional deficiencies [ 3 , 45 , 46 ]. Other non-traditional factors have been reported to be associated with low BMD in patients with TDT, including genetic factors [ 47 ], bone marrow expansion [ 48 ], iron toxicity [ 49 ], and hormonal imbalances [ 50 ]. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels are associated with low BMD in TDT [ 43 ], but it was not observed here. Therefore, those results emphasize the importance of monitoring for spine fractures. In the present study, osteoporosis was diagnosed using the ISCD criteria [ 21 ]. Among the patients who could not be diagnosed, seven patients (7/90, 7.8%) had a history of limb fractures, and their height-corrected TBLH-BMD (WHO criteria) Z-score showed no statistically significant difference compared with those with osteoporosis, highlighting the complexity of the diagnosis. It also emphasizes the importance of preventing fractures among patients without a formal diagnosis of osteoporosis. No osteoporosis diagnosis does not imply a low fracture risk, and these patients need to be closely monitored. Indeed, fracture risk remains high in all patients with TDT [ 13 , 51 , 52 ]. TBLH-BMD height-corrected Z-score ≤-2 based on the WHO reference values was associated with osteoporosis, while BMD height-corrected Z-score ≤-2 based on the Chinese reference values was not associated with osteoporosis. Indeed, the WHO and the Chinese reference values were derived from different populations. Surprisingly, the present study included Chinese patients who might be expected to fit the Chinese reference values more than international values, mainly derived from Caucasian populations. Since TDT significantly affects somatic development [ 9 , 10 ], it could explain the discrepancy of Chinese patients with TDT not matching the Chinese reference values. Indeed, all patients with TDT suffer from some growth retardation [ 53 ], and about 33% of patients with TDT have a short stature [ 54 ]. Iron overload, a consequence of repeated blood transfusions [ 1 ], is also an issue since it may cause growth retardation and organ damage in children with TDT [ 55 ]. The differences between the two reference values can explain the discrepancy observed here in the diagnosis of osteoporosis. TBLH-BMD height-corrected Z-score ≤-2 (WHO reference values) was reported to be associated with osteoporosis in patients with types 2 and 3 spinal muscular atrophy [ 56 ]. In the present study, TBLH-BMD height-corrected Z-score ≤-2 had a low sensitivity for osteoporosis, indicating that it cannot be used for detecting osteoporosis, but it had a high specificity, suggesting that it could be used to rule out other diagnoses. It has been suggested that all patients with TDT should start to undergo BMD screening at age 8 to detect osteoporosis as soon as possible [ 57 ]. A study from Hong Kong indicated that DXA was insufficient to predict the fracture risk [ 52 ], supporting the present study. Additional studies are necessary to determine the optimal screening strategy and its impact on patient prognosis. Nevertheless, the present study suggests that because the diagnostic value of BMD changes with different criteria, screening for spinal fractures is more important than screening for BMD for the diagnosis of osteoporosis in TDT. Nevertheless, the present study was cross-sectional, and not all patients had reached the 19-year threshold for determining the history of pediatric TDT-related osteoporosis. In addition, the fracture risk can evolve over time. Therefore, follow-up studies are important to determine the actual risk of pediatric TDT-related osteoporosis. The present study had several limitations. First, the patients were recruited from only two centers in Huizhou, and all patients were from a single geographical area, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to broader populations. Secondly, children < 5 years old were excluded because there are no WHO reference standards for children < 5 years old. Third, the biochemical analyses were limited to routine tests conducted at the authors’ hospital for patients with TDT. Fourth, complaints like pain, limitation of movement, or neurological symptoms or signs were not collected. Finally, only patients without osteoporosis treatment (e.g., bisphosphonates) were included, and no data were available about those on treatment; such patients should be the focus of future studies.
sections.conclusion_1: In conclusion, the prevalence of osteoporosis among children and adolescents with TDT was 34.8%, indicating the need for attention and screening. In TDT, the diagnosis of osteoporosis requires the early detection of spinal fractures because NMD assessed using DXA is of limited value.

title: Lipidomic Markers of Tobacco Use and Cessation Associated With Cardiovascular Risk Factors: A Longitudinal Study in American Indian Individuals
abstract: Background Research is warranted to identify lipidomic markers longitudinally associated with tobacco smoking and cessation and examine their associations with cardiovascular risk metrics. Methods Using untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry, we measured 1542 lipids among 1845 American Indian individuals at 2 visits (~5.5 years apart). Information on smoking and cessation was collected using questionnaires at both visits. Using mixed‐effects linear regression, we first identified lipids associated with current smoking between current and never smokers and past smoking between former and never smokers. Random effects were used to account for family relatedness and within‐individual correlations across visits. We then investigated whether longitudinal changes in smoking‐related lipids were associated with smoking cessation that occurred between baseline and follow‐up. We examined the longitudinal associations of a lipidomic score and each lipid with various cardiovascular risk metrics. Results Concentrations of 126 named lipids differed between current and never smokers (false discovery rate<0.05), whereas none differed between former and never smokers. Smoking cessation during the study period was associated with a decrease in phosphatidylcholine(p‐16:0/2:0)/phosphatidylcholine(o‐16:1/2:0) at false discovery rate <0.05, an upregulated lipid in current smokers. At P <0.05, cessation was linked to decreases in 8 of 50 upregulated lipids (eg, lysoglycerophospholipids) and increases in 11 of 76 downregulated lipids (eg, sphingomyelins). The lipidomic score and multiple individual lipids were associated with blood pressure, waist circumference, C‐reactive protein, fasting glucose, insulin resistance, and insulin sensitivity. Conclusions Current smoking, but not past smoking, is associated with a broad range of lipidomic markers in American Indian individuals. Longitudinal profiling reveals suggestive evidence of lipidomic markers recovering after cessation. Once validated, these findings may elucidate key lipid pathways underlying the effects of smoking and cessation.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: Current smoking, but not past smoking, was associated with a wide range of novel lipidomic markers in a large cohort of American Indian participants, and longitudinal lipidomics tracked potential recovery in key lipidomic markers following smoking cessation, such as lysoglycerophospholipids and sphingomyelins. Smoking‐related lipidomic markers were longitudinally associated with various cardiovascular risk metrics, suggesting potential lipid pathways through which smoking may contribute to cardiometabolic risk in this high‐risk population.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Future studies are needed to confirm these findings across different population settings.
sections.ethics approval and consent to participa: The SHFS protocols were approved by the institutional review boards of the participating institutions and the American Indian Tribes. All participants provided informed consent at baseline.
sections.data availability: The phenotype data used in this study can be requested through the Strong Heart Study ( https://strongheart‐study.org/ ). The lipidomic data are available upon request to the corresponding author.
sections.study sample: The SHFS is an ongoing longitudinal study designed to investigate genetic, metabolic, and behavioral risk factors for CVD in American Indian people. Initially, 2780 tribal members (aged ≥14 years) were recruited from 13 participating tribal communities across Arizona, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Oklahoma. Participants' eligibility based on race was verified using tribal rolls provided by the local Bureau of Indian Affairs and tribal offices. 18 The current analysis included 2 examinations conducted ∼5.5 years apart: the baseline visit in 2001 to 2003 and the follow‐up visit in 2006 to 2009. Both examinations included a standardized personal interview and physical examination, and fasting blood sample collection for laboratory tests. Lipidomic profiling was performed on 1957 and 1948 participants at baseline and follow‐up respectively. More detailed laboratory methods and overall SHFS design and methods were described previously. 19 , 20
sections.assessments of tobacco smoking: Data on smoking status were collected via structured questionnaires at both baseline and follow‐up visits. Smoking status was categorized into current, former, or never smokers. Participants who had smoked ≥100 cigarettes in their lifetime and were smoking at the time of the interview were classified as current smokers. Those who had smoked ≥100 cigarettes but were not current smokers at the time of the interview were classified as former smokers. In longitudinal analyses of smoking cessation, we defined cessation as reporting current smoking at baseline but quitting smoking (former smoker) at follow‐up.
sections.assessment of cardiovascular risk metric: Cardiovascular risk metrics included systolic and diastolic blood pressure, waist circumference, CRP (C‐reactive protein), fasting glucose, insulin resistance, and insulin sensitivity. Blood pressure and anthropometric measures including waist circumference were measured using standard methods during physical examinations. 19 Fasting blood samples were collected after overnight fasting. CRP was assessed using an immunoturbidometric method (Vitros Chemistry Products, number 6801739, Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Rochester, NY) on a Vitros 5,1 platform (Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Rochester, NY). Fasting glucose was measured by standard laboratory methods. 19 Insulin resistance was assessed by homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance, which was calculated as: homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance =fasting glucose (mg/dL)×insulin (μU/mL)/405. Insulin sensitivity was estimated by calculating the Quantitative Insulin Sensitivity Check Index: Quantitative Insulin Sensitivity Check Index =1/(log insulin [mU/L]+log baseline glucose [mg/dL]).
sections.assessments of covariates: During personal interviews, we collected sociodemographic information (age, sex, and education), alcohol use status, medical history, and use of prescription medications. 19 , 20 Alcohol use status included current/former/never drinkers. Habitual physical activity levels were assessed using pedometers at baseline and follow‐up. Specifically, steps/day over a 7‐day period were calculated by averaging the total number of steps recorded each day, except when bathing or swimming. Height and weight were measured through standard physical examinations. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as body weight (kg) divided by the square of height (m 2 ). Participants' use of prescription medications, including antihypertensive and lipid‐lowering agents, was recorded using structured questionnaires. Participants were classified as having hypertension if they had a systolic blood pressure ≥140 mm Hg, a diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg, or reported use of antihypertensive medications.
sections.lipidomic data acquisition, processing,: Lipidomic data acquisition, processing, and normalization methods are described in Data S1 and previous publication. 21 , 22 Briefly, we used untargeted liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry to quantify the relative abundance of molecular lipid species in fasting plasma samples at baseline and follow‐up. After preprocessing (eg, batch effect correction using Systematic Error Removal using Random Forest software 23 ) and quality control, we obtained data of 1542 lipid species (518 named, 1024 unknown) across 14 named lipid classes from 1957 participants at baseline, and 1948 participants at follow‐up.
sections.inclusion and exclusion criteria: The current analyses included participants who (1) attended clinical examinations at both baseline and follow‐up; (2) were free of overt CVD at baseline, and (3) had complete data on tobacco smoking, lipidomic profile, and covariates at both visits. Figure 1 presents the detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria. After excluding those with missing data on lipidomics, tobacco smoking, or covariates, we included 1845 participants with complete data at both baseline and follow‐up.
sections.statistical analysis: Figure 1 shows the flowchart for participants selection and the analytical approach. Statistical analyses were carried out using R version 4.5.1. Before the analysis, lipidomics data and continuous variables were standardized to zero mean and unit variance.
sections.lipidomic markers associated with tobacc: We examined current and past smoking separately. First, we used mixed‐effects linear regression to identify lipidomic markers associated with current smoking among current and never smokers. We considered baseline and follow‐up data as repeated measurements for an individual to capture the longitudinal association between lipidomic profile and smoking status across 2 time points. In these models, relative abundance of each lipid was the dependent variable, and current smoking (yes/no) was the independent variable. We selected covariates based on prior literature and domain knowledge. Covariates included age, sex, center, education (years), BMI (kg/m 2 ), alcohol use (never/former/current), physical activity (steps/day), fasting glucose (mg/dL), lipid‐lowering drug use (yes/no), and hypertension status (yes/no). The family relatedness among the participants and correlation within the same individual between 2 time points were accounted for by including random intercept terms. We adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure and defined statistical significance as a false discovery rate (FDR) of <0.05. Second, we identified lipidomic markers associated with past smoking, by repeating the models in former and never smokers. We further compared the results for current and past smoking.
sections.lipidomic marker changes associated with: Among current smokers at baseline, we examined whether quitting smoking during the study period (ie, between baseline and follow‐up) was associated with longitudinal changes in the identified lipidomic marker, compared with continued smoking. In these models, the 5.5‐year change in lipid levels (ie, follow‐up minus baseline) served as the dependent variable, and smoking cessation status (yes/no) served as the independent variable. We adjusted for the same set of covariates described above (at baseline level), plus the baseline lipid level, and accounted for the 5.5‐year change in BMI instead of baseline BMI.
sections.smoking\u2010related lipidomic markers a: We then assessed the clinical relevance of the identified lipidomic markers in relation to cardiovascular risk metrics across 2 time points. Mixed‐effects linear regression models were used, with baseline and follow‐up measurements modeled as repeated observations within each individual. Specifically, each smoking‐related lipid was the independent variable, and each risk metric was the dependent variable. We included random intercept terms to account for the family structure and within‐individual correlation. The models were adjusted for age, sex, study center, education, BMI, alcohol consumption, ambulatory physical activity levels, lipid‐lowering medication use, and hypertension at the study examination.
sections.lipidomic score of current smoking: We constructed a lipidomic score using the identified named lipids associated with current smoking at FDR<0.05. The score was computed by summing standardized lipid concentrations, each weighted by its regression coefficient. To assess a linear trend in lipidomic scores (outcome) across current, former, and never smokers, smoking status was treated as an ordinal variable (predictor) in a mixed‐effects linear model with a random intercept for family structure, and the P value for the ordinal term was the P ‐trend. We assessed the clinical relevance of the lipidomic score by examining its associations with cardiovascular risk metrics across baseline and follow‐up. We used mixed‐effects linear regression, adjusting for the same covariates used in single‐lipid models, both with and without additional adjustment for smoking status.
sections.pathway enrichment analyses: Significant lipids (FDR<0.05) were used as the target list in enrichment analyses. We used the Lipid Pathway Enrichment Analysis 24 to identify metabolic pathways that are associated with tobacco smoking. The background list was the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes Database list of lipids. Additionally, we conducted enrichment analysis using the Lipid Ontology 25 database to identify associated ontology terms. For Lipid Ontology enrichment, the background list included all annotated lipids in our study. Fisher's exact test was used to determine the statistical significance of each pathway/Lipid Ontology term.
sections.sensitivity analyses: To reduce the risk of overadjustment in our main analyses (ie, identifying lipidomic markers associated with smoking and cessation), we additionally performed minimally adjusted models. Specifically, we repeated the main analyses in current versus never smokers, adjusting only for age, sex, center, education (years), alcohol consumption (never/former/current), physical activity (steps/day) and lipid‐lowering medication use (yes/no). For the lipids identified, we further examined whether their longitudinal changes were associated with smoking cessation among the subset of current smokers, adjusting for the same covariates as before and baseline level of the lipid. To evaluate the robustness of our findings on the lipidomic score, we performed a sensitivity analysis to construct the score and test associations in separate data sets. We first obtained beta coefficients using data from the “Oklahoma” and “Arizona” centers (n=978), and then calculated the lipidomic score for participants in “South Dakota” center (n=789) and tested the associations between the score and cardiovascular risk metrics.
sections.characteristics of study participants: The Table 1 summarized the characteristics of the participants at each study visit by smoking status. Among the 1845 participants included, about 62% were female. Their baseline mean age was 40 years and mean BMI was 32 kg/m 2 ; at baseline, about 29% and 18% of the participants had hypertension and diabetes, respectively. The prevalence of smoking was 40% at baseline and 37% at follow‐up. At both baseline and follow‐up, current smokers were more likely to report current alcohol use and had fewer years of education, lower BMI, and a lower prevalence of hypertension and diabetes.
sections.lipidomic markers associated with curren: In total, 397 lipid species (126 named) were associated with current smoking compared with never smoking at FDR<0.05, independent of sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical covariates (Figure 2 ; Table S1 ). These lipids include 11 out of 14 lipid classes. Specifically, they consist of mostly glycerophospholipids (eg, phosphatidylcholines and PC plasmalogens), followed by sphingomyelins and triacylglycerols. Among them, 50 lipids were positively associated with current smoking (ie, upregulated markers) and 76 were inversely associated (ie, downregulated markers). Effect sizes of current smoking on lipid levels ranged from −0.27 to 0.26 SD compared with noncurrent smoking status (Beta ranged from −0.27 [95% CI, −0.35 to −0.19] to 0.26 [95% CI, 0.18 to 0.34]). Notably, all the identified triacylglycerols were upregulated, whereas most phosphatidylcholine plasmalogens and sphingomyelins were downregulated.
sections.lipidomic markers associated with past s: Among the 1542 lipids measured, none significantly differed between former versus never smokers (all FDR>0.05), suggesting minimal difference in lipidomic profile between former and never smokers in general. At P <0.05, 60 lipids were associated with past smoking, including 35 that were also associated with current smoking with same direction of associations (Table S2 ).
sections.lipidomic marker changes associated with: Among the 735 current smokers at baseline, 202 (27%) reported quitting smoking at follow‐up. Phosphatidylcholine(p‐16:0/2:0)/phosphatidylcholine(o‐16:1/2:0), an upregulated lipid in smokers, showed significant longitudinal decrease associated with smoking cessation (FDR<0.05). At a nominal P <0.05 level, 8 (of 50) upregulated lipids in smokers showed a decrease over 5.5 years associated with smoking cessation, including mainly lysoglycerophospholipids; meanwhile, 11 (of 76) downregulated lipids in smokers showed increases associated with smoking cessation, including mostly sphingomyelins (Figure 3 ; Table S1 ).
sections.smoking\u2010related lipidomic markers a: Most of the current smoking‐related lipidomic markers (124 of 126) were associated with alterations in at least 1 of the cardiovascular risk metrics at FDR<0.05. (Figure 4 ; Table S3 ). Most upregulated lipids in smokers were positively associated with blood pressure, waist circumference, CRP, fasting glucose, and insulin resistance, and negatively associated with insulin sensitivity. Meanwhile, the downregulated lipids mostly showed the opposite direction of associations. Notably, the smoking‐related triacylglycerols, which were upregulated lipids, exhibited strong associations with nearly all risk factors. Among the downregulated markers, long‐ and very long‐chain unsaturated sphingomyelins (≥36 carbons) were predominantly linked to metabolic risk measures, for example, indices of glucose/insulin homeostasis.
sections.lipidomic score of current smoking_1: We calculated the lipidomic score based on the 126 named lipid species associated with current smoking at FDR<0.05. The highest scores were observed for the current smokers, followed by former and never smokers ( P ‐trend <0.05). After adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical risk factors, the lipidomic score was longitudinally associated with higher blood pressure, waist circumference, circulating CRP, fasting glucose, and insulin resistance and with lower insulin sensitivity (FDR<0.05). The associations remained significant after further adjusting for smoking status (Figure 5 ).
sections.pathway enrichment analyses_1: Among the 126 named lipids associated with current smoking (FDR<0.05), 71 were matched to the Human Metabolome Database. Using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway database, the top pathways reaching significance included glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism and sphingolipid signaling pathway. For lipid ontology enrichment, 106 out of 126 (84%) lipids were matched to Lipid Ontology. The top enriched terms for the smoking‐related lipids were ceramide phosphocholines (sphingomyelins), plasma membrane, and sphingolipids (Figure S1 ).
sections.sensitivity analyses_1: After removing BMI, fasting glucose and hypertension status in the models, the results remain largely unchanged. In total, 84% of the current smoking‐related lipids (106 of the original 126 named lipids) remain significant in sensitivity analyses, and 95% of the cessation‐associated lipids (18 of the original 19 lipids) remained significant at P <0.05. Phosphatidylcholine(p‐16:0/2:0)/phosphatidylcholine(o‐16:1/2:0) remained the one lipid with longitudinal change associated with smoking cessation at FDR<0.05 (Table S4 ). Using the beta coefficients derived from “Oklahoma” and “Arizona” centers data, we constructed the lipidomic score comprising the 126 smoking‐related lipids in the “South Dakota” center data. Consistent with the main results, the score was the highest among current smokers, followed by former and never smokers. The lipidomic score was associated positively with blood pressure, waist circumference, circulating CRP, fasting glucose, and insulin resistance and inversely with insulin sensitivity (FDR<0.05), with or without adjusting for smoking status (Figure S2 ).
sections.discussion: Based on the unique longitudinal lipidomics data from a large cohort of American Indian adults, we have several important findings. First, we identified 126 lipidomic markers of current smoking across a wide range of the lipidome, suggesting extensive lipidomic alterations associated with current smoking. Many of these lipids have not been reported previously. Second, past smoking showed limited associations with lipids, suggesting largely similar lipidomic profiles between former and never smokers. Third, at a nominal level, smoking cessation during the study period was associated with longitudinal decreases in many upregulated lipids in smokers (eg, lysoglycerophospholipids) and increases in downregulated lipids (eg, sphingomyelins). This suggestive evidence shows that longitudinal lipidomics may capture partial recovery of the lipid profile following smoking cessation, corroborating the observed lack of difference between former and never smokers. Lastly, we demonstrated the clinically relevance of the lipidomic markers, individually or combined as a composite score, through their associations with cardiovascular risk factors over time. These observational findings, although causality cannot be inferred, suggest key lipid pathways potentially involved in the biological effects of smoking and cessation. We identified glycerophospholipids (eg, phosphatidylcholines and plasmalogens) as the predominant lipid class associated with smoking. Additionally, disrupted glycerophospholipid metabolism is the primary pathway enriched among smoking‐related lipids. Interestingly, lysoglycerophospholipids (eg, lyso‐phosphatidylcholines and lyso‐phosphatidylethanolamine) were mostly upregulated among current smokers compared with nonsmokers, whereas the majority of the smoking‐related phosphatidylcholinesand plasmalogens were downregulated among current smokers, while. This aligns with previous metabolomics‐based studies. In an experimental study where the metabolomic profile of 105 current smokers was measured after smoking cigarettes, 26 smoking induced acute changes of multiple glycerophospholipids. In addition, they observed an elevated lysophosphatidylcholine (16:1) level in smokers compared with nonsmokers, which was confirmed in our study. In studies of European population, 11 , 15 , 27 altered phosphatidylcholines, plasmalogens, and phosphatidylethanolamines were the major altered lipids among smokers compared with nonsmokers. The association of altered glycerophospholipids with smoking was also observed in the Chinese population. 12 We further reported that a large number of glycerophospholipids had consistent direction of associations with smoking and cardiovascular risk metrics, that is, lipids were positively associated with both current smoking and cardiovascular risk or inversely associated with both. Glycerophospholipids are major structural components of cell membranes and are mainly responsible for maintaining membrane fluidity and enabling cell signaling. 28 Previous studies have shown that the disrupted glycerophospholipids is involved in the development of coronary artery disease, 29 , 30 heart failure, 31 subclinical peripheral artery disease, 32 and hypertension 33 in American Indian and other population groups. Our study suggests that altered glycerophospholipid metabolism could be a potential pathway linking tobacco smoking to the pathogenesis of CVD. We observed that former and never smokers had limited differences in lipidomic profiles, which is in line with a previous study measuring 140 metabolites in a European population. 11 In their study, 19 out of 21 smoking‐related metabolites were found not significantly different between former and never smokers. Similarly, a study conducted in a Japanese population found that the metabolomics profile of former smokers was more similar to that of never smokers than to current smokers. 9 In support of our findings, 1 animal study also showed that accumulation of lipids on the mouse aortic walls was attenuated following smoking cessation, suggesting a potential for lipid profile recovery after quitting smoking. 34 Combined with our longitudinal findings, the evidence points to a possible reversal of smoking‐related lipidomic alterations after cessation, although our findings should be interpreted with caution, as most cessation‐related lipids did not survive multiple testing correction. The associations of triacylglycerols and tobacco smoking were widely reported by many studies, including meta‐analyses. 16 , 17 , 35 However, previous studies were limited by lipid panel measurements. Using untargeted lipidomics approach, we observed that multiple long‐ and very long‐chain unsaturated triacylglycerols species were upregulated among current smokers, such as triacylglycerol(50:2), triacylglycerol(52:1), and triacylglycerol(54:2). These smoking‐related triacylglycerols were consistently associated with multiple cardiovascular risk metrics, including strong associations with blood pressure, waist circumference, glucose, and insulin homeostasis metrics. Triacylglycerol is an important lipid class that plays a crucial role in energy metabolism and storage. Nicotine, the major psychoactive substance in tobacco products, is known to regulate energy expenditure, 36 which could be an explanation of the observed association between triacylglycerols and tobacco smoking. Prior research has linked many triacylglycerol species to higher risks of CVD, 30 , 37 , 38 including triacylglycerol(54:2), which was an upregulated marker for tobacco smoking in our analyses. It is possible that tobacco smoking influences triacylglycerol levels, including key lipid species that promote CVD risk. We reported a wide range of lipid classes associated with current smoking. Many lipids associated with smoking revealed by our analyses, such as sphingomyelins, have not yet been extensively investigated in relation to smoking. Of note, 1 animal study 34 showed that smoking exposure induced changes in various lipid classes in the aortic tissue of mouse, including cholesterol esters, phospholipids (eg, phosphatidylcholinesand plasmalogens), sphingomyelins, and ceramides. Our study added valuable population‐based evidence linking smoking to altered lipid metabolism across the human lipidome. The first strength of our study is the unique longitudinal lipidomics approach with high coverage of lipidome. We measured >1500 individual lipid species across 14 named lipid classes at 2 time points, enabling a comprehensive investigation of the lipidome and its longitudinal changes. Second, we measured multiple cardiovascular risk metrics to assess the clinical significance of the smoking‐related lipids. Third, we had a comprehensive collection of sociodemographic information, lifestyle factors and history of diseases, which allows for the thorough adjustment for confounders in our analyses. Meanwhile, several limitations should also be noted. First, our study is observational in nature, thus cannot establish any causal relationship among lipid concentrations, smoking and cardiovascular risks, although the longitudinal design can help reduce concerns of reverse causality. Second, among the >1500 detected lipids, many remain unannotated and require further characterization. This limits the opportunity for discovery, pathway analysis and the interpretation of smoking‐ and cessation‐related lipid alterations. Third, the focus on American Indian participants may limit the generalizability of the findings to other populations. Lastly, smoking status was self‐reported, which may introduce misclassification; in addition, cotinine measurements and more detailed smoking exposure information (eg, passive smoking exposure, duration of smoking, time since cessation, and pack‐years) were unavailable for this analysis, limiting our ability to assess dose–response relationships.
sections.conclusions_1: In summary, our study identified novel lipidomic markers of current smoking among American Indian adults, some of which showed trends suggestive of partial recovery after smoking cessation at a nominal level; however, these observations should be interpreted with caution. In contrast, past smoking had limited associations with lipidomic profiles. Smoking‐related lipids were associated with cardiovascular risk metrics over time. Future studies are warranted to confirm our findings in different population settings.

title: Non-tobacco nicotine dependence is associated with increased complications following clavicle open reduction internal fixation
abstract: Background Tobacco dependence is well established to impair bone healing and increase postoperative complications. However, the independent effects of nicotine, separate from combustion-related factors, remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of non-tobacco nicotine dependence (NTND) following open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of clavicle fractures, including midshaft and lateral fracture subtypes. Methods A retrospective cohort study was performed using a large national database. Patients undergoing ORIF of clavicle fractures were identified using procedural and diagnostic codes. Patients with non-tobacco nicotine dependence (e.g., vaping, patches, or gum) were identified and propensity score matched to (1) patients without nicotine exposure and (2) patients with tobacco nicotine dependence. In a secondary analysis, patients were stratified by fracture type (midshaft and lateral), and outcomes were compared between nicotine exposure and no nicotine exposure within each subgroup. Outcomes were assessed at 90 days and 1 year and included medical complications, number of opioid prescriptions, and implant-related outcomes. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Results After matching, 936 non-tobacco nicotine users were identified. Non-tobacco nicotine dependence was associated with increased implant removal at 90 days (RR 2.50) and higher opioid prescriptions ( p < 0.05). At 1-year, non-tobacco nicotine use was associated with increased implant removal (RR 1.74), infection (RR 1.73), and nonunion (RR 1.78) ( p < 0.05). In direct comparisons between non-tobacco nicotine and tobacco nicotine users ( n = 897), there were no significant differences in postoperative complications or implant-related outcomes (all p > 0.05). In fracture-specific analyses, nicotine use was associated with increased infection (RR 2.17), nonunion (RR 1.42), and implant removal (RR 1.24) in midshaft fractures ( p < 0.05), with no significant differences observed in lateral fractures. Conclusion Non-tobacco nicotine dependence was associated with increased risks of infection, opioid utilization, implant removal, and nonunion following clavicle fracture fixation. These associations were observed predominantly in midshaft fractures, with no significant differences in lateral fractures. These findings suggest that non-tobacco nicotine dependence may carry a risk profile similar to that of tobacco use. Level of evidence III. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00402-026-06377-2.

sections.introduction: Clavicle fractures are a relatively common orthopedic injury, accounting for 2.6-5% of all adult fractures [ 1 ]. Clavicle fractures most commonly occur in adolescent and young adult males, with peak incidence between ages 13 and 20 [ 2 ]. The rate of surgical fixation has been increasing in recent years, with an estimated 445% increase from 2000 to 2022 [ 3 ]. Surgical fixation offers the advantage of faster healing, higher union rates, higher short-term patient satisfaction, and a cosmetic appearance more closely resembling typical anatomy [ 4 ]. Due to the increase of operative management in clavicle fractures, it is essential we understand the factors that might predispose patients to complications to help guide clinical decision making. Tobacco use has been well established to increase fracture nonunion rates, heighten infection risk, and impede wound healing [ 5 ]. While, cigarette smoking has been declining in the United States for decades, non-tobacco nicotine dependence has been on the rise, partially due to the public perception that alternative nicotine forms, like vapes, are safer [ 6 ]. Additionally, nicotine pouch use among US teenagers and young adults nearly doubled between 2023 and 2024, with approximately 13% reporting active use in 2024 [ 7 ]. Despite popular belief that non-tobacco nicotine products are safer than smoking, these products may carry similar risks for orthopedic surgery recovery. Given the increasing use of non-tobacco nicotine especially among adolescents and young adults, who represent a large portion of clavicle fracture patients, its impact on fixation outcomes remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the effect of non-tobacco nicotine dependence on complication rates following open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of clavicle fractures, including midshaft and lateral fracture subtypes. We hypothesized that non-tobacco nicotine dependence would significantly impede wound healing and fracture union and predispose patients to infection.
sections.study design: This retrospective cohort study aimed to assess the risk of postoperative complications at 90 days and 1 year in patients with non-tobacco nicotine dependence undergoing open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of clavicle fractures, using data from the TriNetX database. TriNetX aggregates deidentified records from 170 healthcare organizations, covering more than 180 million patients, and provides real-time access to a wide range of electronic health information, including diagnoses, procedures, medications, and laboratory values. Institutional review board approval was not required because only deidentified aggregated data were accessed. We used International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes to identify patients with clavicle fractures and corresponding procedural codes for ORIF.
sections.cohort selection: Patients who underwent ORIF of clavicle fractures were identified using Current Procedural Terminology codes (CPT-23515). These patients were further categorized into three cohorts based on preoperative exposure: non-tobacco nicotine dependence (NTND), tobacco dependence, and controls without nicotine exposure. The NTND cohort was defined as patients with a diagnosis of nicotine dependence excluding cigarette, chewing tobacco, or other combustible tobacco product use (ICD-10: F17.x excluding F17.21, F17.22, F17.29, and Z72.0), consistent with non-combustible nicotine exposure such as e-cigarettes, patches, or gum. The tobacco dependence cohort was defined as patients with a diagnosis of nicotine dependence related to combustible tobacco products (ICD-10: F17.2x and Z72.0). Control patients were those undergoing ORIF of clavicle fractures with no documented history of nicotine dependence or use (ICD-10: Z87.891, F17). The three cohorts were mutually exclusive. Patients with any combustible tobacco code (ICD-10 F17.2x or Z72.0) were excluded from the NTND cohort, so that no patient could contribute to more than one exposure group; this prevented overlap between the tobacco and non-tobacco cohorts and excluded dual users from the NTND group. In a secondary analysis, patients with any nicotine exposure (tobacco or non-tobacco) were compared to those without nicotine exposure and stratified by fracture location (midshaft vs. lateral). Midshaft (ICD-10 S42.02-) and lateral/distal (ICD-10 S42.03-) clavicle fractures were defined using mutually exclusive ICD-10 codes, and propensity score matching was performed separately within each fracture-location subgroup. A complete list of all ICD-10 and CPT codes used to define exposures, fracture locations, and outcomes is provided in Supplementary Table 1. Patients were required to have a documented encounter within 1 year prior to surgery to establish exposure status.
sections.statistics: For all outcomes of interest, risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed using the TriNetX system, with p values less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. Categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-squared test, whereas continuous variables were evaluated using Student t-tests. Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 fashion using nearest-neighbor matching without replacement (caliper of 0.1 pooled standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score). The propensity model included age, sex, race, body mass index, hemoglobin A1c, and the comorbidities reported in Table 1 (hypertension; hyperlipidemia; type 2 diabetes mellitus; chronic lower respiratory disease; chronic ischemic heart disease; acute kidney failure and chronic kidney disease; diseases of the liver; disorders of bone density and structure; and concomitant fracture of the ribs, sternum, or thoracic spine). Covariate balance was assessed using standardized mean differences (SMDs) rather than p values alone, with an SMD < 0.1 considered well balanced; all covariates achieved an SMD < 0.1 after matching.
