Analysis of distribution of 8-hydroxyguanine (8-OHG: a marker of oxidative DNA damage) by immunohistochemical staining of E13 neural tube revealed that 8-OHG high NPCs exhibited a TOMM20 low profile in the subventricular zone of mouse developing neural tube (Fig. 3 B). Findings in vitro disclosed a similar co-localization of 8-OHG and TOMM20 in NPCs at t=30 min post-induction of differentiation (Fig. 3 B). To complement DNA-level evidence of oxidative damage, the abundance of malondialdehyde (MDA, a by-product of lipid oxidation) was assessed in differentiating NPCs in vitro. Fluorometric quantification of the level of MDA showed increasing concentration of the compound in differentiating NPCs from t=30 min to t = 2 h (Fig. 3 C). Evidence of enhanced oxidative stress compelled us to ask whether mitochondrial degeneration was in part or entirely a consequence of the oxidative damage. To answer this question, we were required to manipulate mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), a task which was not possible without deeper mechanistic insight into mitochondrial ROS production upon induction of differentiation. Generation of ROS by a forward electron flow or a reverse electron transport (RET) [ 40 ] in the mitochondrial electron transport chain was investigated. NPCs were harvested and incubated with a complex I inhibitor, rotenone (100nM), and a complex III inhibitor, antimycin A (1µM), for 10 min in DPBS. Rotenone, upon association with complex I, decreases ROS production via RET in mitochondria oxidising the complex II substrate succinate but amplifies ROS production in mitochondria respiring on complex I substrates [ 41 ]. Antimycin A amplifies generation of ROS in mitochondria respiring on complex I or II substrates [ 42 ]. After incubation with the inhibitors for 10 min, neural induction medium was added to trigger production of ROS and oxidation of DCFH (2′,7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein) was used to detect production of ROS [ 43 ] (Fig. 3 D). While inhibition of complex III by antimycin-A resulted in slight reduction of the level of ROS, exposure to rotenone triggered a marked decrease in production of ROS (Fig. 3 D, left). This pattern of responsiveness to inhibitors was consistent with RET (reverse electron transport) as the main mechanism for amplification of ROS immediately after induction of differentiation. Notably, application of dynarrestin to prevent IOC, reduced the level ROS with an effectiveness comparable to that of rotenone (Fig. 3 D, right) suggesting that fusion of mitochondrial and nuclear membranes somehow triggers RET and amplifies ROS. Two proposed mechanisms for induction of RET include an over-reduction of the available pool of coenzyme Q and a high proton motive force (Δp), both of which render the forward electron flow thermodynamically unfavourable. Given that IOC amplifies ΔpH component of Δp due to influx of protons associated with nuclear-encoded RNAs [ 5 ], we investigated whether an amplified ΔpH exceeds the thermodynamic threshold for induction of forward electron flow. Mitochondria were isolated from NPCs at baseline and T = 0.5 h post-induction of differentiation and resuspended in 500 µl of RNase-free water. RNase-A was then employed to degrade RNAs in the mitochondrial intermembrane space and release the RNA-associated protons [ 5 , 44 ]. The difference in proton release after RNase-A treatment at baseline and T = 0.5 h, denoted ΔΔpH T0:T0.5 (ΔpH T0.5 -ΔpH T0 ), was ≈ 0.17 units (Fig. 3 E). Based on a conservative calculation that the apparent ΔΔpH T0:T0.5 reflects a ≈ 5314-fold dilution of protons upon release from the mitochondrial intermembrane space to the water-electrode interface (see methods and supplementary Fig. S6 for details), the corrected ΔΔpH T0:T0.5 within the intermembrane space was estimated as ≈ 3.4. Using the Nernst equation at 37 °C, a ΔΔpH of 3.4 corresponds to an electrical potential difference of 210mV (see methods). That is, the locally generated Δp via activity of the electron transport chain is amplified by 210mV owing to imported protons via IOC. A favourable thermodynamic condition for forward electron transport requires that the reduction potential difference of the NAD + /NADH and CoQ/CoQH 2 redox couples (ΔE h ) for 2 electrons to transport across complex I must be large enough to allow pumping of 4 protons against the proton motive force (Δp) across the mitochondrial inner membrane or 2ΔE h > 4Δp [ 45 ]. Findings suggest that a conservative 4Δp of 840mV contributed entirely by imported protons exceeds 2ΔE h (760mV), a condition that is conducive to RET (Fig. 3 E). It was concluded that the early shift to an oxidizing milieu is a consequence of RET-induced ROS in response to IOC-mediated import of RNA-associated protons. Surprisingly, when NPCs were harvested at T = 0.5 h post-induction of differentiation and the impact of rotenone and antimycin-A on ROS activity was probed, oxidation of DCFH was not impacted by either inhibition of complex I, or by suppression of complex III (Fig. 3 F, left). However, application of 1mM oxaloacetate diacetate, a competitive inhibitor of complex II, attenuated the production of ROS (Fig. 3 F, right). The latter finding is in agreement with the suggested role of complex II in contributing to ROS production [ 41 ]. Further, pre-exposure to oxaloacetate prevented mitochondrial degeneration as evidenced by an increased copy number of mitochondrial DNA upon induction of differentiation (Fig. 3 G). Together, findings suggested that while an early wave of ROS production by complex I is triggered by IOC-mediated RET, a second wave of ROS production ensues owing to the activity of complex II respiring on succinate. Given that accumulation of succinate is partially dependent on β-oxidation of odd chain free fatty acids, we tested whether suppression of β-oxidation reduces oxidative stress in mitochondria and abolishes mitochondrial decline following the induction of differentiation. NPCs were incubated with 1µM etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyl transferase-I (CPT-I), which prevents shuttling of long chain free fatty acids to mitochondria [ 46 ] (supplementary Fig. S7). In parallel, (R)-Bromoenol lactone ((R)-BEL) was used at a concentration of 10µM to inhibit mitochondrial calcium-independent phospholipase A2-γ (iPLA2γ). Enzymatic activity of iPLA2γ protects mitochondria from oxidation-induced lipid peroxidation and dysfunction [ 47 ] and inhibition of the enzyme is expected to amplify the impact of ß-oxidation on mitochondria. To determine the efficiency of inhibitors in altering mitochondrial redox state by modulating ß-oxidation, we deployed MitoTracker red CMXRos (50nM) which is retained in mitochondria by forming covalent bonds with the redox-sensitive thiol groups of proteins. Hence, a shift to an oxidizing milieu can be detected by diminished retention of the dye within mitochondria [ 48 ]. NPCs were pre-treated by adding the inhibitors to spent growth medium one hour before induction of differentiation. NPCs were then detached, washed, and incubated with neural induction medium containing MitoTracker Red CMXRos. Cells were immediately transferred to an optical reader to record the intensity of MitoTracker Red CMXRos (recording frequency: 1/sec) at a baseline temperature of 37 °C. Upon induction of neural differentiation, etomoxir-treated NPCs showed 1.5-fold increased retention of the dye which contrasted sharply with pronounced reduction of the retained dye in mitochondria of (R)-BEL-treated NPCs (supplementary Fig. S7). The observed impact of etomoxir confirmed previous findings that ß-oxidation of fatty acids is a major contributor to oxidative stress within mitochondria. MitoTracker Green was employed to provide an indication of mitochondrial protein mass in differentiating NPCs. Etomoxir increased the apparent mitochondrial protein mass by 1.6-fold as opposed to a reduction by 1.6-fold of the mitochondrial protein mass in the presence of (R)-BEL (supplementary Fig. S7). Notably, combined application of the inhibitors effectively offset the impacts observed upon application of individual compounds (supplementary Fig. S7). NPCs were pre-treated with etomoxir (1 h) prior to induction of differentiation and the impact of this treatment on mitochondrial degeneration during differentiation was explored by quantification of mitochondrial DNA (mDNA). This treatment partially abolished the metabolic flux of mitochondrial populations (Fig. 3 H) observed during differentiation of control NPCs (Fig. 1 F). To confirm the role of ROS in triggering mitochondrial degeneration, cultured NPCs were exposed to 50µM H 2 O 2 in spent growth medium (supplementary Fig. S7). Ultrastructural analysis of H 2 O 2 -treated cells disclosed features of mitochondrial degeneration within 15 min of exposure (supplementary Fig. S7) that were indistinguishable from degenerative changes triggered by neural induction in vivo and in vitro (Fig. 1 D, E). It was concluded that while RET-induced ROS were essential for initiation of the metabolic reprogramming that eventually leads to mitochondrial degeneration, the activity of complex II is essential for continued accumulation of ROS and for eventual degeneration of mitochondria. Considering the evidence for the involvement of complex II in triggering mitochondrial degeneration we investigated the molecular basis for this phenomenon. One possibility was that RET-generated ROS damage mitochondrial complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) [ 49 ], prompting a search for evidence of depletion of components of this complex by analysing the LC/MS data. This analysis revealed decreased abundance of the nuclear-encoded components of complex I by t = 0.5 h post-induction of differentiation, an observation that contrasted sharply with the increased abundance of subunits of complex II (Fig. 3 I, left). Mitochondria-encoded subunits of the electron transport chain were also depleted at t = 0.5 h post-induction of differentiation to a considerably greater extent than nuclear-encoded proteins (Fig. 3 I, right). Corroborating the LCMS profile, the analysis of mitochondrial-encoded mRNAs (meRNAs) isolated at defined time points after the induction of neural differentiation revealed significant depletion of three selected meRNAs encoded by the heavy strand (or H-strand) of the mouse mitochondrial genome, namely Rnr1, Nd5 and Cox1 (Fig. 3 J). Succinate dehydrogenase is the only component of the electron transport chain whose subunits are not encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Therefore, the emerging picture suggested that RET-induced ROS production by complex I not only initiates a redox-dependent metabolic reprogramming that leads to accumulation of succinate, but it also causes a depletion of the mitochondrial electron transport chain components except for nuclear-encoded complex II which respires on succinate and amplifies ROS production. Central to this phenomenon was a decline of mRNAs encoded by the mitochondrial genome concurrent with ROS-mediated metabolic reprogramming so that electrons transferred to complex II were used to generate ROS rather than being transported to upstream or downstream components of the electron transport chain. The basis for elimination of mRNAs encoded by the mitochondrial genome was investigated.
sections.a single-stranded mitochondrial dna remo: A preliminary clue regarding transcriptional decline of mitochondria was provided by ultrastructural analysis of the replicating mitochondrial DNA (Fig. 4 A, left). While ultrastructural features typical of the strand displacement model of mitochondrial DNA replication were present, a second low molecular weight product that appeared to be a single stranded DNA (ssDNA) was also observed (Fig. 4 A, right). Partial degradation of this band following incubation with exonuclease I (2 units/20µl reaction buffer) confirmed that the band mainly consisted of a single stranded DNA (Fig. 4 B). However, the low molecular weight fragments generated as by-products of exonuclease I activity suggested the presence of duplex regions that hindered the enzymatic activity of exonuclease I. Such duplex regions have been reported to be mitochondrial DNA replication intermediates composed of RNA hybridised to the H-strand of mtDNA [ 50 ]. To explore whether the duplex region contains hybridised RNA, isolated mitochondrial DNA was incubated with 2U of RNase H for 30 min (Fig. 4 B). This led to reduced intensity of the ssDNA suggesting the presence of RNA/DNA duplex regions. Fig. 4 Emergence of a mitochondrial single-stranded DNA upon induction of neuronal differentiation. Subsequent dissipation of the protons gradient is expected to amplify mitochondrial thermogenesis We then used a gel electrophoresis mobility shift assay (EMSA) by employing S9.6 antibody that recognises RNA/DNA duplex. To exclude any non-specific binding of S9.6, we utilised a double-stranded DNA corresponding to a PCR-amplified fragment of Rnr1 locus of mDNA. Further, a higher molecular weight band corresponding to the double-stranded mDNA served as the internal control for the specificity of binding of S9.6 to RNA-DNA duplex. After 20 min of incubation with S9.6, delayed migration of the ssDNA both at t = 30 and 60 min after induction of differentiation was noted, while migration of the double stranded high molecular weight band corresponding to mtDNA remained unaffected (Fig. 4 C). These results supported the interpretation of RNase H treatment indicating that the ssDNA contains RNA/DNA duplex regions. To determine the identity of ssDNA, two biotinylated oligonucleotide baits complementary to the L- and H-strands of mtDNA were utilised. After isolation of the ssDNA using Dynabeads MyOne Streptavidin T1, only the H-strand of mDNA was detected (Fig. 4 D). This finding accorded with previous reports that the parental H-strand of mtDNA can be identified as mitochondrial replication intermediates in association with L-strand transcripts [ 51 ]. By employing 11 specific primer sets spanning mouse mtDNA, it was confirmed that ssDNA encompasses the full length of the H-strand of mitochondrial DNA (Fig. 4 D). Having confirmed the identity of ssDNA as mitochondrial H-strand, we then explored the occupancy pattern of this ssDNA by meRNAs. Isolated ssDNA-bound meRNAs were reverse transcribed using superscript III. The resultant cDNA library was analysed using qPCR in the background of ssDNA. Unequal representation of hybridised meRNA characterised by a reduction of the level of bound transcripts from the 5′ towards the 3′ end of the H-strand was noted (Fig. 4 E). A potential explanation for this observation was that preferential degradation of these meRNAs by processive exonuclease activity of mitochondrial RNase-H1 in 3′ to 5′ direction [ 52 ] would lead to under-representation of 3′-meRNAs. To test the validity of this hypothesis mitochondrial RNase-H1 and Mgme1 (Mitochondrial genome maintenance exonuclease 1) were inhibited by employing RNAi. The underlying logic was that just as inhibition of RNase-H1 is expected to increase the level of meRNAs encoded on H strand of mtDNA in RNAi RNase−H1 -treated cells (e.g. Nd-5), inhibiting degradation of ssDNA by targeting the nuclease Mgme1 should increase the level of ssDNA and thus expand the scope of activity of RNAse-H1 leading to amplified degradation of the meRNAs. In this experiment Nd-6 was selected as a control gene encoded on the L strand of mtDNA. After application of RNAi, the level of Nd-5 meRNA encoded by the H-strand of mDNA increased significantly, whereas the level of Nd-6 which is encoded by the L-strand of mDNA remained unaffected by RNAi treatment of NPCs (Fig. 4 F). Findings were consistent with a model of DNA replication in which the parental H-strand of mDNA is generated in an uncoupled manner from the L-strand (Fig. 4 G). This strand could function as a natural antisense DNA which hybridises to the meRNAs triggering RNase-H-mediated degradation of the transcripts (Fig. 4 G). Three specific questions needed to be addressed to gain functional insight into the proposed model of post-transcriptional regulation of meDNAs. Why is the single-stranded H-strand not protected by mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein-1 (Ssbp1)? Why are the meRNAs hybridised to the H-strand despite a capacity to form a secondary structure? Finally, why is the replication of H and L-strands uncoupled leading to generation of the single-stranded H-strand during neural differentiation? Of the three questions, the most accessible concerned the hybridization of meRNAs which indicated a loss of RNA secondary structure following the induction of differentiation. It was reasoned that mitochondrial generation of heat during neuronal differentiation [ 14 ] could potentially explain a loss of meRNA secondary structure and hence the next set of experiments were designed to address the mitochondrial thermal flux. To record the temperature at nanoscale with high accuracy, an L-DNA molecular beacon (l-MB) [ 53 ] probe was introduced into NPCs via electroporation [ 14 ]. This approach, however, provides restricted information due to variation of the intracellular copy number of the probe across the population coupled with limitations of assessing the probe by live imaging microscopy including phototoxicity at a high frame rate. In this study, NPCs were detached, mixed with l-MB (at a ratio of ≈ 10 10 probes/NPC) and suspended in 20 µl of spent growth medium (18 h post-incubation) or neural induction medium. The mixture was immediately transferred to a qPCR thermal cycler and the florescence signal of l-MB was recorded at a baseline temperature of 37 °C and at 1 s intervals (Fig. 4 H). While the temperature of NPCs in spent growth medium remained stable at 37 °C, we recorded a mean cross-population temperature of 44.6 °C within t=5 min of inducing differentiation followed by a gradual decline of the temperature to 42 °C by t=10min (Fig. 4 H). This thermal output approximates to thermogenesis at an average rate of 10nW/NPC which is higher that the reported average energetic output of 2.2 nW for a typical eukaryotic cell [ 54 ], but lower that the thermal output of zebrafish embryos at the 2-cell stage (30nW/cell) [ 55 ]. A mitochondrial lysate was then prepared using a sucrose gradient, mixed with l-MB and transferred to a qPCR thermal cycler and the florescence signal was recorded at a baseline temperature of 37 °C and at 1 s intervals. In state 3 mitochondria (with access to 1mM pyruvate, 1mMADP and 2mMPi) temperature approached 55°C within seconds and then gradually elevated to 58 °C (Fig. 4 I). This recorded peri-mitochondrial temperature using l-MB was in close agreement with the reported mitochondrial temperature of 54 °C by Terzioglu et al. who used protein reporters of temperature to record the thermogenic output [ 56 ]. Findings together with those of others [ 56 , 57 ] suggest that mitochondrial temperature could rise significantly (≈ 15 °C) upon full activation of oxidative phosphorylation which is expected to establish an ultimate Δp of 210mV. While metabolomic reprogramming upon induction of neuronal differentiation renders the electron transport chain inactive, it was noted above that imported protons via IOC amplify ΔpH component of Δp by 210mV (Fig. 3 E). Replicating the measurement of thermal flux in dynarrestin-treated NPCs following incubation in NIM revealed an attenuated thermogenic capacity thereby strengthening the role of IOC in amplifying thermal flux (Fig. 4 J). Further supporting evidence for the notion of IOC-mediated thermogenesis was afforded by RNase-A treatment of the isolated mitochondria in the presence of l-MB to record the temperature (Fig. 4 K). While RNase-A treatment triggered a spike in temperature to 48 °C within seconds of application, the RNase-A-treated mitochondria lost capacity to maintain this temperature afterwards. The latter observation is compatible with the proposed role of RNA as a carrier for protons in the intermembrane space [ 44 ], whose loss diminishes the capacity of the organelle to generate an effective ΔpH. Therefore, it is proposed that IOC-mediated import of protons from the nucleus not only triggers RET, but it also leads to a concurrent elevation of temperature upon dissipation of the proton gradient (Fig. 4 L), a notion that was consistent with an increased level of mRNAs encoding mitochondrial uncoupling proteins upon induction of differentiation (supplementary Fig. S8).
sections.mitochondrial oril functions as a nanoth: Given the evidence for asymmetric replication of mitochondrial DNA by uncoupling the polymerisation of the light and heavy strands, we focused on investigating the putative uncoupler. It is known that both the secondary structure (i.e. a conserved stem loop) and the primary sequence of OriL are required for initiating replication of the light strand of mDNA [ 23 ]. To investigate if melting of the secondary structure of OriL uncouples the replication of the L-strand and H-strand of mDNA, a synthetic 37-mer oligonucleotide corresponding to A 5159 -T 5195 of mouse mtDNA with a 5′ fluorophore, 6-FAM, and a 3′ quencher, ZEN-Iowa Black FQ, was utilised to study the melting kinetics of OriL. The probe was dissolved in 50ul of 0.1 mM TE buffer (final concentration: 1mM) and transferred to a qPCR thermal cycler. The intensity of fluorescent signal was recorded at 1 s intervals as a function of increasing temperature (25 °C to 75 °C). The synthetic OriL analogue exhibited a melting temperature (T m ) of 51 °C with > 90% of melting events occurring between 41 °C and 55 °C under the specified ionic conditions (Fig. 6 A). This initial analysis of T m was done in the absence of any counter-ion. As expected, increasing the concentration of Na + increased the T m of the synthetic OriL analogue by presumptive shielding of the phosphate groups (Fig. 6 A). However, under physiological conditions ions are unlikely to interact entirely with the stem loop, as proteins function as a competing pool for sequestering ions. To address this scenario, we repeated the previous experiment with the highest concentration of NaCl in the presence of acetylated bovine serum albumin (5%) (Fig. 6 B). Inclusion of 5% BSA alone did not alter the melting kinetics of the synthetic OriL (Fig. 6B). Upon addition of 40mM NaCl, however, BSA completely neutralised the stabilising impact of counter-ions (Fig. 6 B) while inclusion of the osmolyte PEG200 in TE buffer reduced the T m of the OriL in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 6 C). The apparent destabilisation of OriL by osmolytes is consistent with the reported impact of these molecules in reducing the stability of a DNA helix [ 61 ]. Ca 2+ , a critical regulator mitochondrial function, had little impact on destabilisation of the synthetic OriL at low nM concentrations (Fig. 6 D, left). However, incubation of isolated mitochondria with Ca 2+ triggered significant enrichment of the mitochondrial ssDNA consistent with the open state of the OriL and uncoupled replication of the heavy and light strands of mitochondria (Fig. 6 D, right). This was expected as Ca 2+ functions as an allosteric activator of key enzymes in the Krebs cycle, particularly isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase [ 62 ], thereby enhancing mitochondrial thermogenic capacity. We concluded that while the synthetic minimal OriL has an inherent T m of 51 °C, the apparent T m could be fine-tuned to adapt to the functional state of mitochondria. We then sought an alternative method of determining the T m of OriL as a molecular beacon reports the separation of the fluorophore and the quencher due to melting of the 5′ and 3′ termini of the synthetic OriL raising the possibility of reporting a partial melting as full melting. A single-stranded mini-chromosome corresponding to the H-strand of mDNA was synthesized by CircLigaseII-mediated circularisation of the region of mDNA containing the OriL and extending to the proximal upstream region (-40 bp: C5119-G5158) and the downstream region (+ 45 bp: A5196-T5242) of the OriL. The melting dynamic of the mini-chromosome was compared to that of an isolated OriL using the intercalating dye Sybrgreen I (Fig. 6 F). Inclusion of OriL in a mini-chromosome altered the melting dynamics of OriL from a sigmoidal to a hyperbolic mode leading to a reduction of the apparent Tm by 7 °C (Fig. 6 F). An explanation for reduction of the apparent T m of the OriL in a mini-chromosome was that forces applied to the 5′ and 3′ termini of the hairpin amplify the breathing kinetics [ 63 ] of the DNA helix leading to a reduction of the T m of OriL. To probe the impact of stem and loop breathing kinetics on melting dynamics of OriL, two mutations were introduced into OriL and the impact on T m was studied. To attenuate breathing of the DNA helix, C 5183 was mutated to T 5183 , a substitution that increases the length of the stem by 1 bp while simultaneously reducing the size of the loop by 2 bp (ΔT m high O L ). To amplify the breathing dynamics of the DNA helix, an intra-stem mismatch was introduced by mutating C 5163 to T 5163 (ΔT m low O L ). A 5′ fluorophore, 6-FAM, and a 3′ quencher, ZEN-Iowa Black FQ, was utilised to study the melting kinetics of the mutated OriLs. While the T m of ΔT m high O L increased by 4 °C, that of ΔT m low O L decreased by 11 °C confirming the notion that amplifying the breathing dynamics of the DNA helix alters the melting dynamics of OriL (Fig. 6 G). Together, findings indicated that OriL functions as a thermal switch with melting kinetics that are within the range of the thermogenic capacity of mitochondria. Considering the importance of DNA secondary structure in recruiting mitochondrial RNA polymerase to OriL [ 23 ], we explored whether thermal flux suppresses the polymerisation of the parental H-strand of mitochondrial DNA by denaturing the OriL stem loop. We initially probed binding affinity of mouse recombinant Polmrt to a single-stranded circular DNA corresponding to mouse mitochondrial H-strand containing the OriL along with the proximal upstream region (-40 bp: C5119-G5158) and the downstream region (+ 45 bp: A5196-T5242) of the OriL (OriL Wt ). Variations of this circular single-stranded mini-chromosome were also synthesized in which a C 5163 to T 5163 (ΔT m low O L ) and a C 5183 to T 5183 (ΔT m high O L ) were introduced (Fig. 6 H) to alter the T m of the OriL as discussed above (Fig. 6 G). The mini-chromosome and Polmrt were incubated in TE buffer for 15 min, at a temperature of 25 °C and 37 °C in a thermal cycler. To stabilise the association of Polmrt and OriL via molecular crowding [ 64 ] and to precipitate the complex [ 65 ], polyethylene glycol (mw:8000, PEG8000) was added to a final concentration of 10% just before collecting the polymerase/OriL complex by centrifugation at 20000 g for 2 min. The ssDNA was then purified using phenol-chloroform extraction and quantified using qPCR. No significant difference was observed in the quantity of pulled-down ΔT m high O L between samples incubated at 25 °C and 37 °C (Fig. 6 H). However, a significantly smaller amount of OriL Wt and even lower quantity of ΔT m low O L were recovered from the sample incubated at 37 °C compared to that incubated at 25 °C (Fig. 6 H). This is consistent with as estimated Tm of 47 °C for ΔT m high O L (7 °C lower than the isolated ΔT m high O L ) which retains its secondary structure both at 25 °C and 37 °C, whereas OriL Wt (Tm = 42 °C) and ΔT m low O L (Tm = 31 °C) reside in a partially denatured state at 37 °C decreasing the affinity of Polmrt to OriL. Findings were validated using an in vitro model of mitochondrial H-strand replication adapted from Korhonen et al. [ 66 ]. Mitochondrial mini-chromosomes were incubated with mouse recombinant Polmrt, recombinant DNA polymerase gamma (Pol-γ), and Ssbp1 in a reaction mix containing rNTPs and dNTPs for 40 min at 25 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C (Fig. 6 I). DNA was purified using phenol-chloroform extraction and quantified using qPCR. When OriL Wt was used as a template, the quantity of replicated DNA at 37 °C was > 50% less than for incubation at 25 °C. Increasing the reaction temperature to 50 °C decreased the rate of replication of DNA by > 80% compared to incubation at 25 °C (Fig. 6 I). Further, the rate of replication of DNA in reactions with ΔT m high O L was higher than that of OriL Wt at 37 °C and 50 °C, whereas no such difference was observed between the rate of replication of ΔT m low O L and that of OriL Wt (Fig. 6 I). It is noteworthy that these results are conservative estimates of the impact of stem loop on polymerisation rate as DNA polymerases follow Arrhenius kinetics [ 67 ] and increasing the temperature from 25 °C to 37 °C (or from 37 °C to 50 °C) is expected to increase the extension rate of the polymerase by an average of ≈ 31% for a reported activation energy of 17 kcal/mol [ 68 ]. We therefore concluded that OriL operates as a nanothermometer that melts in response to an increased thermal flux, thereby reducing the affinity of Porlmrt to OriL and uncoupling the replication of the heavy and light strands of mDNA ( Fig. 6 J ).That is, thermal flux not only triggers partial denaturation of meRNAs and a concurrent destabilization of Ssbp1, but also suppresses the replication of the H strand of mDNA leading to release of the parental H strand as a single-stranded DNA which hybridises to denatured meRNAs, followed by RNaseH-mediated degradation of these transcripts. An outstanding question was whether IOC not only uncouples the replication of mitochondrial H- and L-strand, but also triggers replication of the mitochondrial genome.
sections.mitochondrial dna replication is trigger: To probe the relevance of IOC to replication of the mitochondrial genome, we asked if accumulation of the ssDNA by asymmetric replication of mtDNA would occur in the absence of inter-organellar communication. IOC was prevented by application of dynarrestin (25µM, 1 h prior to induction of differentiation) or by RNAi-mediated inhibition of Lis-1 using a cocktail of two DsiRNAs (18 h prior to induction of differentiation). Following the induction of differentiation, we did not observe significant accumulation of ssDNA in either treatment group (Fig. 7 A). To complement these results, mitochondria were isolated at t=30 min after induction of differentiation (mito 0.5 h ). The isolated mitochondria, which contained ssDNA/meRNA duplex, were incubated in EB buffer (2mM Pi) supplemented with pyruvate and ADP (Fig. 7 B, left). In isolated mito 0.5 h , the ssDNA/RNA duplex was rapidly degraded. Supplying ADP/Pi (state 3 mitochondria) accelerated the degradation rate of the duplex compared to state 0 mitochondria (Fig. 7 B, right). We concluded that isolated mitochondria appeared to be deprived of DNA replication cues. It also appeared that amplified thermal flux (triggered by supplying ADP/Pi) was not sufficient to trigger the replication process. To confirm this, we replicated the experiment with state 3 isolated mito 0.5 h at different temperatures to test whether the thermal flux could trigger generation of ssDNA (Fig. 7 C, left). The rate of degradation of ssDNA/meRNA duplex increased in a temperature-dependent manner (Fig. 7 C, right). Further, a reduction of double-stranded mtDNA in a temperature-dependent manner suggestive of mitochondrial degeneration was noted (Fig. 7 C, right). Therefore, it appeared that thermal flux increases the enzymatic activity of RNase-H1 in a temperature-dependent manner but does not trigger replication of mtDNA. A conclusion derived from these experiments was that isolated mitochondria lack a factor required for DNA replication. An essential clue was provided by the observation that in mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, mutation targeting the Rrm2B subunit of ribonucleotide reductase reduces the mitochondrial pool of dNTPs leading to mDNA replication arrest [ 69 ]. Likewise, other reports highlighted a competition between nucleus and mitochondria for acquisition of dNTPs [ 17 ]. Fig. 7 IOC stimulates replication of mDNA by supplying nucleotides. After isolation of mitochondria from NPCs, dNTPs were added in an equimolar ratio of 2mM, along with 10mM pyruvate, 2mM ADP, and 2mM Pi and the isolated organelles were incubated at 25 °C and 42 °C for 40 min (Fig. 7 D). Increased copy number of mtDNA suggested that supplying dNTPs triggers the replication of mitochondrial genome (Fig. 7 D, right). Simultaneously, access to dNTPs resulted in significant accumulation of ssDNA in isolated mitochondria after 40 min of incubation (Fig. 7 D). While increased temperature appeared not to affect the level of ssDNA (Fig. 7 D, middle), a comparison with Fig. 7 C revealed that equal levels of ssDNA 25 °C and 42 °C occurred despite significant amplification of RNAseH1-mediated degradation of ssDNA at 42 °C, suggesting a significant boost of ssDNA generation at 42 °C. On the other hand, RNAi-mediated targeting of the subunits of ribonucleotide reductase, Rrm1 and Rrm2, to restrict the supply of dNTPs to mitochondria 16 h prior to induction of differentiation resulted in a significant reduction of ssDNA/meRNA duplex following induction of neuronal differentiation (Fig. 7 E). Further, mitochondrial degeneration in RNAi Rrm1 and RNAi Rrm2 NPCs was markedly less than the control NPCs undergoing neuronal differentiation (Fig. 7 F). Considering that ribonucleotide reductase catalyses the conversion of nucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) or triphosphates (NTPs) to deoxynucleotides [ 70 ], it seems plausible that IOC supports replication of mtDNA by supplying NDPs to ribonucleotide reductase after importing and degradation of nuclear-encoded RNAs via PNPase [ 5 ]. However, the trigger for initiation of replication at O H (Origin of replication of H-strand) remains unclear. One possibility is that while some 95% of mitochondrial replication events are terminated after about 650 nt [ 71 ], supplying dNTPs could potentially reduce the frequency of aborted replication events [ 72 ] rather than directly inducing replication of mtDNA. Nonetheless, validation of this hypothesis requires extensive experimentation beyond the scope of the present paper.
sections.ioc-mediated mitochondrial degeneration: Finally, we asked if IOC-mediated mitochondrial degeneration operates as a negative autoregulation mechanism that is invoked upon mitochondria-nucleus fusion to diminish the number of mitochondria poised for successive waves of interaction with the nucleus. Integration of such negative feedback is expected to reduce the rate of neuronal differentiation driven by IOC [ 5 ]. To test this proposition, we employed two strategies to reduce the level of mitochondrial ssDNA. Cells were treated with 1mM hydroxy urea (HU), a specific inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase, for 1 h prior to induction of neuronal differentiation. HU-treated NPCs exhibited an increased level of pro-neural transcription factor Ngn1 at t = 2 h post-induction of differentiation compared to the control cells (Fig. 8 A). Mouse NPCs were then transfected to express Ssbp P92> L92 or E. coli Ssb followed by induction of neuronal differentiation. Quantifying the level of mRNA encoding pro-neural transcription factor, Ngn1, revealed significant upregulation of the level of this transcript in NPCs expressing Ssbp P92> L92 (≈ 3 fold) or E. coli Ssb (≈ 4 fold) by day 3 of differentiation (Fig. 8 B). An interpretation of this finding was that enhanced stability of Ssbp P92> L92 (or introduction of the thermally stable E. coli Ssb into NPCs) boosts the impact of IOC on driving neuronal differentiation by preventing mitochondrial degeneration (Fig. 8 C). We studied neuronal markers in differentiating NPCs to confirm these findings. Interestingly, immunohistochemical detection of neuronal differentiation markers, Tubulin-β3 and NeuN, revealed a different picture; the level of these proteins in NPCs expressing Ssbp P92> L92 or E. coli Ssb at day 1 and 3 of differentiation was lower than that of the control cells (Fig. 8 D). In contrast, the level of phalloidin/F-actin was higher in the control cells compared to the transfected cells (Fig. 8 D). Considering that induction of autophagy is required to facilitate emergence of a new proteomic profile during the early stage of neuronal differentiation [ 73 ], we wondered if inhibition of mitochondrial degeneration in Ssbp P92> L92 or E. coli Ssb is responsible for uncoupling of the transcriptional and proteomic profiles in differentiating NPCs. We initially asked if the autophagic flux corresponds to the timeline of mitochondrial degeneration upon induction of differentiation. Probing the timeline of macro-autophagy revealed increased levels of Sqstm1 (p62), LC3, and ubiquitinated proteins by t=60 min followed by a reduction of the level of these proteins between t=60 min and t=90 min (Fig. 8 E). We then asked if mitochondrial decline contributes to the observed amplification of autophagy during neuronal differentiation. To probe this notion, we studied the autophagy in NPCs expressing Ssb E. coli using a fluorescent reporter of autophagic flux. Cells expressing Ssb E. coli were co-transfected with a reporter vector of autophagy, ptfLC3, and neuronal differentiation was induced after 16 h. Monitoring for GFP and RFP, to visualize autophagosomes (appearing yellow) and autolysosomes (appearing red), revealed a significant reduction of the autophagic flux in Ssb E. coli NPCs after 24 h of incubation in the differentiation medium (Fig. 8 F). This finding was consistent with a reduction of autophagic flux in Ssb E. coli NPCs. Therefore, we asked whether the reduced autophagic flux was linked to events that trigger mitochondrial degeneration or whether it is a direct energetic consequence of mitochondrial degeneration. NDPs support replication of mDNA, while an amplified ΔpH triggers RET and enhances thermal flux. The increased thermal flux stimulates formation of ssDNA/meRNA duplex and the subsequence degradation of meRNAs reprograms activity of the electron transport chain leading to amplified production of ROS by complex II respiring on succinate To arrest mitochondrial transcription and induce mitochondrial degeneration we employed the established method of using the intercalating dye, ethidium bromide (EtBr: 2 µg/mL), for 2h [ 74 ]. Analysis of two meRNAs, Nd5 and Nd6, encoded on H and L-strands respectively of the mitochondrial genome, disclosed near-linear reduction of the level of both mRNAs within a period of 2 h from the application of the intercalating dye (Fig. 8 G), a reduction rate equivalent to that observed in differentiating NPCs. Mitochondria from EtBr-treated NPCs showed ultrastructural features similar to those of NPCs 1 h after induction of differentiation, namely a reduction of the number of internal cristae and disappearance of the matrix (Fig. 8 ). However, we did not observe noticeable evidence of enhanced autophagic flux upon mitochondrial decline in EtBr-treated cells (Fig. 8 G). We therefore focused on an alternative hypothesis that amplified production of ROS is responsible for induction of autophagy [ 75 ]. TEM analysis of H 2 O 2 -treated cells (supplementary Fig. S7) provided evidence of amplified autophagosome formation (Fig. 8 H) corroborating reports that oxidative stress is a major inducer of autophagy [ 76 ]. We concluded that ssDNA-dependent production of ROS not only propels a decline of mitochondria but also induces a concurrent wave of macro-autophagy (Fig. 8 I). In the proposed model, mitochondrial decline operates as a negative autoregulatory mechanism to regulate the rate of IOC and hence the scope of transcriptional remodelling of NPCs by IOC [ 5 ]. The concurrent induction of autophagy facilitates remodelling of the proteome by eliminating the existing proteins and emergence of a new protein profile after translation of the remodelled transcriptome (Fig. 8 I).
sections.discussion: Here, we provide evidence for a novel mitochondrial degeneration mechanism that is triggered by inter-organellar communication (Fig. 8 J). Central to this negative autoregulation mechanism is IOC-mediated thermal flux that uncouples replication of the heavy and light strands of mitochondrial DNA by denaturing the Origin of replication of the light strand. Accordingly, completion of the replication of the L-strand leads to release of the non-replicated parental H-strand as a single stranded DNA which hybridises to mRNAs encoded by the heavy strand. Degradation of ssDNA-bound mRNAs by mitochondrial RNase H completes this cycle by shutting down electron transport chain components encoded by the mitochondrial genome. Continued activity of complex II respiring on succinate leads to significant amplification of ROS and degeneration of mitochondria. The resultant decline of mitochondrial populations operates as a negative autoregulation mechanism that reduces the rate of neuronal differentiation driven by IOC. A key facet of IOC that triggers the cascade of events culminating in mitochondrial degeneration is significant amplification of mitochondrial proton motive force (Δp) owing to the release of RNA-associated protons imported from the nucleus. Under homeostatic conditions, mitochondrial Δp is established by the activity of the electron transport chain pumping protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space of mitochondria. Hence establishment of Δp by this mechanism is subject to regulation by two respiratory control mechanisms discussed earlier. While the first control mechanism is triggered by inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase in an amplified state of proton motive force (Δp) [ 6 , 7 ], the second mechanism of respiratory control requires allosteric inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase at a high ATP/ADP ratio [ 8 , 9 ]. ATP exerts this inhibitory effect by binding to the matrix domain of the subunit IV of cytochrome c oxidase [ 10 ]. IOC-mediated acquisition of RNA-associated protons from the nucleus provides an alternative route for establishment of an amplified Δp [ 5 , 44 ] that is independent of the activity of the electron transport chain and hence is not subject to regulation by known respiratory control mechanisms. A corollary of such an amplified Δp is enhanced mitochondrial thermogenic capacity which uncouples replication of the L- and H-strand of mitochondrial genome. Mitochondrial DNA appears to replicate via two different mechanisms [ 77 ]. According to the strand displacement model of DNA replication [ 78 ], synthesis of L- and H-strand DNA proceeds continuously (i.e. without synthesis of Okazaki fragments) but in an unsynchronised manner [ 79 ]. Synthesis of L-strand beings only after 11 kb of H-strand has been synthesized. During replication of the L-strand, the parental single-stranded H-strand is covered and protected by mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein (mtSsbp) [ 80 ]. General dynamics of the alternative RITOLS model ( r ibonucleotide i ncorporation t hrough o ut the l agging s trand) of mitochondrial DNA replication are similar to those of strand displacement replication with a key difference [ 51 , 81 ]. In the RITOLS model, processed RNA molecules rather than mtSsbp cover the displaced single-stranded parental H-strand [ 82 ]. While the physiological significance of RITOLS and underlying circumstances that promote this mode of DNA replication remain largely unknown, findings presented herein partially address these questions. Our findings complement the RITOLS model of DNA replication by demonstrating an inherent thermal instability of mtSsbp which enables binding of the competing meRNAs to the single-stranded mtDNA. This instability of mtSsbp is underpinned by Pro92-mediated destabilisation of the protein which triggers its dissociation from ssDNA at an elevated temperature. Supporting our findings, Cha et al. identified a point mutation in mtSsbp which leads to Arg91 > Gln91 [ 83 ] leading to further destabilisation of the protein due to a diminished capacity for salt bridge formation in this region. This mutation impeded multimer formation, reduced DNA-binding affinity of mtSsbp, and led to significant reduction of mtDNA copy number and mitochondrial ATP synthesis [ 83 ]. Similarity of our disclosed mechanism of mitochondrial replication to RITOLS suggest that both describe a single phenomenon, a quasi-replication that attenuates the transcriptional profile of mitochondria by RNase-H-mediated degradation of ssDNA-bound meRNAs. This quasi-replication phenomenon is similar to asymmetric replication of plasmid DNA that generates a single-stranded DNA with potential to be converted to double-stranded DNA [ 84 ]. In bacteria, the asymmetric replication and generation of ssDNA has an important pro-survival function. During conjugation of Gram-negative bacteria, rolling circle replication occurs in an asymmetric manner and while the leading strand is replicated in the donor organism, the single-stranded lagging strand is transferred and replicated in the recipient cell [ 85 ]. It appears that the quasi-replication of the mitochondrial genome is yet another variation of the asymmetric rolling-circle mechanism adapted to alter mitochondrial activity by regulating mitochondrial transcriptional profile. Subsequent to the generation of mitochondrial ssDNA, meRNAs hybridize to it leading to emergence of RNA-DNA hybrids that are targeted by mitochondrial RNase-H1. RNase-H is present in all major kingdoms of life with the conserved functionality of eliminating R-loops (RNA/DNA hybrids) that arise during replication of DNA [ 86 ]. In mitochondria, RNase-H1 performs a more specialised function of processing RNA primers to allow site-specific initiation of mtDNA replication [ 87 ]. Here we report that RNase-H performs an additional task of modulating the transcriptional landscape of mitochondria. This function is similar to the activity of synthetic DNA antisense oligonucleotides in reducing the level of both cytoplasmic mRNAs and nuclear-retained RNAs in an RNase H1-dependent manner [ 88 ]. A major consequence of mitochondria-intrinsic RNA degradation by an RNase H1-dependent mechanism is that all the components of the electron transport chain have subunits encoded by the mitochondrial genome except complex II whose components are nuclear encoded. Therefore, selective degradation of meRNAs provides an opportunity for complex II to function in isolation leading to an amplified generation of ROS. In recent years, mitochondrial complex II has emerged an important producer of ROS [ 41 , 89 – 91 ]. Aside from ROS production via forward and reverse electron flow at high concentration of succinate (> 5mM), complex II can produce significant quantities of ROS directly when the concentration of succinate is 0.5mM or less. While respiration on succinate is a prerequisite for generation of ROS by succinate dehydrogenase, higher concentrations of the metabolite appear to prevent access of oxygen to FAD of the complex [ 41 ]. A source of succinate is β-oxidation of odd chain fatty acids. This provides a partial explanation for our finding that β-oxidation of fatty acids contributes to neuronal differentiation. Corroborating this notion, Yanes et al. reported that a metabolic shift to oxidize fatty acids promotes differentiation dynamics of NPCs [ 92 ]. Maximal ROS generation by mitochondrial complex II at the FAD site also requires inhibition of electron transfer both toward complex I via reverse electron flow and toward complex III via forward electron flow. As noted above, ssDNA-mediated degradation of meRNAs encoding components of the electron transport chain enables complex II to function in isolation leading to amplified ROS production by this complex. Attenuation of meRNAs is complemented by RET-induced oxidative damage to mitochondrial proteins. Triggering of RET by IOC is central for initiation of β-oxidation of free fatty acids by shunting of the metabolic flux from the upper glycolysis pathway to lipogenesis. Sufficient amplification of proton motive force (Δp) by IOC to fulfill the thermodynamic requirement for RET means that the Δp for pumping 4 protons against the proton motive force (4Δp) must exceed the reduction potential difference of the NAD + /NADH and CoQ/CoQH 2 redox couples in transporting 2 electrons across the complex I (ΔE h= 760mV) [ 45 ]. Due to biophysical constraints, such as increased permeability of mitochondrial membrane s at a high voltage [ 93 ], surpassing the thermodynamic threshold for induction of RET by importing protons from the mitochondrial matrix would be challenging. IOC, on the other hand, bypasses these biophysical constraints by importing RNA-associated protons from the nuclear matrix [ 5 , 44 ]. The imported RNA is degraded via exonuclease activity of mitochondrial polynucleotide phosphorylase (PNPase) which releases H + along with nucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) [ 5 , 44 ]. The released protons not only trigger RET but also, upon dissipation, amplify the thermal flux. While the role of an amplified thermal flux in neuronal differentiation has been reviewed elsewhere [ 4 ], our findings add a novel dimension to the existing knowledge by demonstrating that mitochondria accommodate evolutionary adaptations that enable sensing the thermal flux aside from the thermogenic capacity. These adaptations include a replication mode that responds to thermal flux and a single-stranded DNA binding protein with a structural adaptation that brings about thermal instability. Considering that thermal flux plays a major role in mitochondrial degeneration, we propose the term “Calamortis” (Cala: from calor , meaning heat, Mortis : death) to describe this mode of mitochondrial degeneration.
sections.scope and limitations of the study: An important limitation of our findings in vitro is that we have not validated the results in different cell lines or primary cells. This concern is partially addressed by findings in vivo that corroborate the in vitro results. However, it remains to be investigated whether the reported mitochondrial degeneration occurs upon differentiation of other cell lineages. From a mechanistic perspective, the exact role of ROS in induction of mitochondrial degeneration remains unclear at this stage. One explanation is that ROS-mediated DNA damage triggers the depletion of mtDNA. However, the outcome of RNAseH1 inhibition and introduction of the stable mtSsbp along with experiments in which the biphasic nature of ROS generation was investigated argue against this likelihood to some extent. We noted that inhibition of RNaseH1-mediated degradation of meRNAs and transfection of mitochondria with the stable mtSsbp (P21 > L92 or E coli SSB) was sufficient to prevent the reduction of the level of mtDNA. Arguably, these interventions affect the second phase of ROS production (i.e. the rise of complex II as the generator of ROS). However, significant production of ROS via IOC-mediated RET (phase I) remains unaffected in these experiments. Therefore, while oxidative damage is the root cause of organellar degeneration, it does not appear to be caused by direct oxidative damage to mtDNA. Other possibilities, that remain to be investigated, include mitochondrial lipid peroxidation or oxidative damage to key susceptible mitochondrial proteins such as Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel 1 (Vdac1). From a methodological perspective, while the reduction of the abundance of mRNAs of interest is indicative of the efficiency of RNAi, the absence of protein-level validation of RNAi remains a current limitation of this study. Issues such as the absence of antibodies that recognise the alternatively spliced mitochondrial isoform of RNaseH1 rendered this task challenging.
sections.conclusion and future directions: The functional significance of IOC-mediated mitochondrial degeneration is to provide a negative autoregulatory mechanism to decelerate neuronal differentiation. Accordingly, the described phenomenon can be viewed as an anti-differentiation mechanism. Several interesting questions arise from this observation. In our experiments, we noted that a subpopulation of mitochondria undergoing IOC enter the degenerative pathway. A potential explanation for this apparent heterogeneity of response is an inherent resistance to the redox-mediated degeneration. Potentially, this could be the result of heterogeneity of mitochondrial antioxidant response giving rise to a resistant subpopulation. A second plausible explanation is concerned with the mechanism of heat build-up as mitochondria become metabolically active. It can be argued that mitochondria not only generate heat endogenously but also receive heat from other surrounding metabolically active mitochondria; a bystander effect. Hence, it is expected that once mitochondrial degeneration exceeds a threshold, the thermal flux (due to mitochondrial decline) will decrease, sparing the remaining mitochondria. It is also conceivable that a combination of these mechanisms may be involved in setting up an upper limit for mitochondrial decline. At a cellular level, it is of interest whether IOC-mediated mitochondrial degeneration can be calibrated to orchestrate the rate of neuronal differentiation. Also, it remains to be established whether this form of mitochondrial degeneration is specific to neuronal differentiation or represents a general mechanism underlying cellular differentiation. Beyond developmental relevance, it is intriguing to consider whether the observed mechanism represents a vulnerability that is exposed in pathological conditions affecting the nervous system.

sections.mice: C57BL/6J mice (6–12 weeks of age) were obtained from Animal Resources Centre (WA, Australia). Diet and water were provided ad libitum, and standard light cycles were used. Standard protocols were followed to minimize animal suffering.

sections.immunohistochemistry: Tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde in Sorensen’s phosphate buffer pH: 7.4, for 4 h at 4 °C. Cultured cells were fixed in the same fixative for 25 min at room temperature. For IHC staining, sections/cells were incubated with 0.1 M PBS, 1% BSA, 0.1% Tween-20, and 5% normal goat serum for 40 min. Sections/cells were incubated with the primary antibodies overnight at 4 ˚C and secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Specificity controls were carried out by incubating sections with rabbit or mouse IgG negative control antibodies.
sections.antibody characterisation: Rabbit monoclonal anti-TOMM20 (Abcam, catalogue no. ab186735) recognises mouse, and human Tomm20. The antibody recognises a single band (≈ 16 kDa) in Western blots corresponding to the molecular weight of Tomm20. Mouse monoclonal anti-8-Hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine antibody (Abcam, catalogue no. ab48508) detects 8-Hydroxy-2’-deoxyguanosine in IHC. The antibody has been validated and used by many laboratories (Citations: 167 as per manufacturer’s website). The antibody has been validated and used by many laboratories (Citations: 628 as per manufacturer’s website). The antibody recognises a single band (≈ 55 kDa) in Western blots corresponding to the molecular weight of the protein. Anti-NeuN antibody (Abcam, catalogue no. ab177487) is a rabbit monoclonal antibody that detects NeuN in IHC. The antibody has been validated and used by many laboratories (Citations: 868 as per manufacturer’s website). The antibody recognises two bands at 46,48 kDa in Western blots generated from a single NeuN gene by alternate splicing (i.e. as a result of inclusion or absence of 47 amino acids from exon 12).
sections.image analysis: To measure the linear intensity of fluorescence signals along a designated path, the intensity of a signal of interest was recorded along a traced line using the plot profile plugin of ImageJ software.
sections.live-cell tau-sted nanoscopy: NPCs were plated in glass-bottom petri dishes (World Precision Instruments) and incubated overnight in growth medium. PKmito ORANGE (Spirochrome, cat no. CY-SC053) was added to cell culture media (1:1000 dilution as per manufacturer’s instructions) and NPCs were incubated 1 h prior to live‐cell imaging. Live-cell nanoscopy was performed with a laser scanning confocal microscope, Leica DMi8, Stellaris 8 (Leica Microsystems) with fluorescence lifetime imaging (FaLCon) and STED (Stimulated emission depletion) capabilities (775 nm depletion laser) with a 100x/1.4 HC PL APO Oil STED white objective. PK Mito Orange was imaged with the super-continuum laser tuned to 591 nm excitation with and without depletion at 775 nm and emission between 600 and 680 nm analysed with a HyD S detector.
sections.transmission electron microscopy: For TEM analysis, tissues were fixed in Karnovsky’s fixative overnight at room temperature followed by post-fixation in OsO4 for 1 h. Preparations were dehydrated in graded alcohols and embedded in low viscosity resin (TAAB Laboratory and Microscopy, United Kingdom). Ultrathin sections were mounted on Pioloform/formvar coated slot grids, stained in uranyl acetate and lead citrate and examined in a JEM-2200FS field emission electron microscope. For ultrastructural analysis of replication intermediates, DNA was extracted from mitochondria isolated from NPCs at t = 0.5 h after induction of differentiation using phenol-chloroform isolation method. TEM copper grids 600 mesh (EMS) were covered with a very thin carbon film (2–4 nm) to facilitate deposition and spreading of replicating mitochondrial DNA. Seven microliters of the isolated DNA (conc. 280ng/µl) were deposited on the carbon-coated grid for 5 min and a 2% (w/vol) solution of aqueous UrAc was used for rinsing and staining of DNA molecules. Blotting was done using a filter paper and the grids were visualised in a JEM-2200FS field emission electron microscope.
sections.laser capture microdissection: Laser microdissection and pressure catapulting (LMPC)–LMPC was conducted on a PALM Micro Beam instrument (Carl Zeiss) equipped with 495- and 595-nm excitation FITC and TRITC filters. Tomm20 immuno-stained samples were visualized by using a 20× objective and FITC filters, and LMPC was performed by using the same objective under freeze mode (UV energy: 68–72, UV focus: 76–78, cutting speed: 25).
sections.gene expression analysis: RNA was isolated using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen). After DNase treatment, reverse transcription of the extracted RNA was carried out using a mixture of 1 µL of oligo-dT/random hexamer, 4 µL of total RNA, 1 µL of dNTP Mix (10 mM each), 4 µL of 5x First-Strand synthesis Buffer, 1 µL of 0.1 M DTT, 1 µL of RNaseOUT (40 units/µL), 1 µL of SuperScript-IV reverse transcriptase (200 units). Reverse transcription was performed at 50˚C for 50 min followed by 55˚C for 15 min. RNA was subsequently digested with RNAase H. To design primers, gene sequence data and exon/intron boundaries were obtained from GenBank database. In each of the primer sets (except the mitochondrial primers), the common 3΄ or 5΄ primer spanned the adjacent exons to prevent amplification of genomic DNA.

sections.rna interference: For small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated knockdown of Pnpt1, cells were electroporated with a cocktail containing 200 nM of two siRNAs. The sequences of DsiRNAs targeting mRNAs of interest are as follows: Lis-1 siRNA-1: sense: 5′-rArArArArGrArArGrArArUrUrUrArCrGrUrCrArGrGrUrGGA-3′. antisense: 5′-rUrCrCrArCrCrUrGrArCrGrUrArArArUrUrCrUrUrCrUrUrUrUrGrC-3′. Lis-1 siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rUrGrGrArUrGrUrArGrArUrUrGrArGrCrUrUrArUrUrArAAT-3′. antisense: 5′- rArUrUrUrArArUrArArGrCrUrCrArArUrCrUrArCrArUrCrCrArGrA-3′. Rnase-H1 siRNA-1: sense: 5′- rCrCrUrUrUrArArArArArUrCrArArUrArUrArUrUrArCrUAA − 3′. antisense: 5′- rUrUrArGrUrArArUrArUrArUrUrGrArUrUrUrUrUrArArArGrGrUrC − 3′. Rnase-H1 siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rGrUrArCrArGrGrGrArArArGrArUrGrUrGrArUrCrArArCAA − 3′. antisense: 5′- rUrUrGrUrUrGrArUrCrArCrArUrCrUrUrUrCrCrCrUrGrUrArCrUrU − 3′. ExoG siRNA-1: sense: 5′- rArCrCrArUrUrGrGrUrArUrUrCrArArCrArGrArArGrUrCAT − 3′. antisense: 5′- rArUrGrArCrUrUrCrUrGrUrUrGrArArUrArCrCrArArUrGrGrUrArA-3′. ExoG siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rArUrGrUrUrUrGrGrArUrArGrUrArUrCrArGrGrArCrCrUTT − 3′. antisense: 5′- rArArArGrGrUrCrCrUrGrArUrArCrUrArUrCrCrArArArCrArUrCrU − 3′. Mgme1 siRNA-1: sense: 5′- rArGrArArArArArCrUrCrUrUrArCrGrArArGrCrArGrUrAGA − 3′. antisense: 5′- rUrCrUrArCrUrGrCrUrUrCrGrUrArArGrArGrUrUrUrUrUrCrUrUrC-3′. Mgme1 siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rCrCrUrArArCrArUrGrUrUrArUrArUrCrArArGrUrUrGrCAA − 3′. antisense: 5′- rUrUrGrCrArArCrUrUrGrArUrArUrArArCrArUrGrUrUrArGrGrUrU − 3′. Rrm1 siRNA-1: sense: 5′- rGrCrArArUrUrArCrUrCrArUrCrArGrCrUrArArArGrArCCT-3′. antisense: 5′- rArGrGrUrCrUrUrUrArGrCrUrGrArUrGrArGrUrArArUrUrGrCrUrU − 3′. Rrm1 siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rCrUrArArArGrUrCrArUrUrGrUrCrCrGrArArArUrCrUrGAA − 3′. antisense: 5′- rUrUrCrArGrArUrUrUrCrGrGrArCrArArUrGrArCrUrUrUrArGrUrG − 3′. Rrm2 siRNA-1: sense: 5′- rGrCrUrArUrGrArUrGrGrUrArCrArGrUrArArArUrUrCrUGA-3′. antisense: 5′- rUrCrArGrArArUrUrUrArCrUrGrUrArCrCrArUrCrArUrArGrCrArU − 3′. Rrm2 siRNA-2: sense: 5′- rGrCrArUrCrGrArUrArUrUrCrUrGrGrCrUrCrArArGrArAAC − 3′. antisense: 5′- rGrUrUrUrCrUrUrGrArGrCrCrArGrArArUrArUrCrGrArUrGrCrArA − 3′. For electroporation in RNAi, cells were harvested, mixed with Dsi-RNA (i.e. siRNA) and resuspended in 400 µl of electroporation buffer (106 cells/400µl). Electroporation buffer comprised 20mM HEPES, 135mM KCl, 2mM MgCl2, 0.5% Ficoll 400 and 2mM ATP/5 mM glutathione (pH 7.6). Electroporation was carried out at 1700 V/cm, 700µs, four pulses at 1-s intervals. The efficiencies of RNAi for Lis-1, RnaseH1, ExoG, Mgme1, Rrm1, and Rrm2 were determined using real-time qPCR as 72%, 80%, 68%, 74%, 78%, 72%, respectively. While the reduction of the abundance of mRNAs of interest is indicative of the efficiency of RNAi, the absence of protein-level validation of RNAi remains a current limitation of this study. To this end, absence of antibodies that interact with the alternatively spliced mitochondrial isoform of RNaseH1 with a mitochondrial targeting sequence rendered this task challenging. A Negative Control DsiRNA (Integrated DNA Technologies) were used for transfection of control samples.
sections.isolation and functional analysis of mit: Mitochondria were isolated based on the method developed by Frezza et al. [ 95 ]. Briefly, NPCs (10 7 cells) were harvested, washed and resuspended in 3 ml of ice-cold IB buffer (10mM Tris–MOPS, 1mM EGTA/Tris, 0.2 M sucrose, pH to 7.4). The cells were then homogenized using a Teflon pestle. Homogenized cells were centrifuged twice at 600 g for 5 min at 4 °C to isolate nuclei. Mitochondria were isolated by additional centrifugation of the supernatant from the previous step at 7,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. Mitochondria were then resuspended in EB buffer (10mM KCl, 10mM Tris/MOPS, 1mM EGTA/Tris, and 1mM KH 2 PO 4 , pH to 7.4) and checked using Mitotracker Red under a fluorescence microscope to ensure that mitochondria were viable before further experimentation.
sections.quantification of ros: The cell permeable probe, 2′-7′-Dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA), was used to monitor generalised oxidative stress (i.e. ROS production). To measure ROS production, NPCs were harvested at defined time points, resuspended in PBS and incubated for 10 min with 2µM DCFH-DA at 37 °C. The cells were then washed and resuspended in GM or NIM at a final density of 10 6 cells/well and a total volume of 100 µl in a 96-well plate. The plates were transferred into a real-time PCR machine and accumulation of DCF was recorded at 10-second intervals by recording fluorescence at 530 nm after excitation of the sample at 485 nm.
sections.induction of mitochondrial depletion: In order to deplete mitochondria, Ethidium bromide was added to NPCs in spent growth medium at a final concentration of 2 µg/mL [ 96 ]. The cells were then returned to CO 2 incubator and harvested at defined time points as per the main text.
sections.measurement of thermal flux: The L-DNA molecular beacon (MB) was designed as described elsewhere. Molecular beacons were labelled with a 6-FAM reporter dye at the 5′ end, and an Iowa Black FQ quencher at the 3′ end (Integrated DNA Technologies). The sequence of MB is as follows: FAM-GCGAGTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTCTCGC-IBFQ To measure the temperature, MB was mixed with thermogenic units (cells/mitochondria) to a final concentration 1µM in a total volume of 50 µl. The mixture was then transferred to a real-time PCR machine (Stratagene® Mx3000P) to record the intensity of FAM signal that is detected upon melting of the molecular beacon and separation of the fluorochrome from the quencher. During an initial equilibration step at 25 °C for 30 s, the signal was recorded at a rate of 1/sec. In a second incubation step at 37 °C, thermal flux of mitochondria/cells was recoded for 30 min at a rate of 1/sec. The fluorescence signal intensity was then converted to temperature (°C) using a calibration curve generated from inactive thermogenic units (i.e. cells in PBS without access to glucose or mitochondria in EB buffer without access to pyruvate). This method ensures accurate conversion of fluorescence signal intensity to temperature (°C) as the presence of inactive thermogenic units alters the emission characteristics of the FAM signal. To generate a calibration curve, FAM signals were collected after an initial equilibration step at 25 °C for 30 s by increasing the temperature in steps of 5 °C (each step 20 s). Mean values of 20 recordings for every thermal step were used generate a calibration curve used for conversion of fluorescence signal intensity to temperature (°C).
sections.small molecule inhibitors: Dynarrestin was applied at a final concentration of 25µM one hour prior to induction of differentiation. To induce differentiation, the growth medium was replaced with NIM containing 25µM Dynarrestin (Sigma, cat no. SML2332). To modulate forward and reverse electron flow, NPCs were harvested and incubated with a complex I inhibitor, rotenone (100nM, cat no. R8875), and a complex III inhibitor, antimycin A (1µM, cat no. A8674), for 10 min in DPBS. After incubation with the inhibitors for 10 min, neural induction medium was added to trigger production of ROS. To inhibit lipid ß-oxidation, NPCs were incubated with 1µM etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyl transferase-I. (R)-Bromoenol lactone ((R)-BEL, cat no. 10006800) was used at a concentration of 10µM to inhibit mitochondrial calcium-independent phospholipase A2-γ (iPLA2γ).
sections.measurement of atp level: ATP levels were measured using ATP-Glo™ Bioluminometric assay as per manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence measurements were performed using SpectraMax i3 Multi-Mode Microplate Reader with a delay time of 5 s, an integration time of 100 milliseconds, and a read height of 5.86 mm. Measurements were done in standard 96-well standard opaque plates.
sections.metabolomic analysis: For cell metabolite extraction (refer to Rabinowitz’s method), a buffer consisting of acetonitrile: methanol: water in the ratio between 4:4:2 (20% water) and 0.1mM formic acid was used. The extraction buffer was then pre-chilled in a -30 °C freezer. To extract the metabolites, 5 ml of the pre-chilled extraction buffer was added to the T7 flasks containing NPCs (~ 2 × 10 7 cells/time point), pre-washed gently with 10 ml ice-cold PBS. Flask surface was scraped and then incubated on ice for 3 min. 435uL of neutralizing buffer (15%w/v NH4HCO3) was added and the cell slurry transferred into 15 ml falcon tubes and stored at -80 C. Just before LCMS metabolite analysis, the cell slurry was thawed and vortexed before taking e 200uL into a fresh microfuge tube and centrifuged at 15,000 g 4 °C for 10 min. The supernatant was transferred into HPLC vials and assayed promptly. LCMS was carried out using a Poroshell 120 HILIC-Z column (2.7 μm, 2.1 × 150 mm, Agilent) at 30 °C on a Vanquish-TSQAltis LC-MS/MS system. The pair of mobile phase buffers used were 95:5 (v/v) water: acetonitrile containing 20 mM ammonium hydroxide and ammonium acetate (Buffer A) and 100% acetonitrile (Buffer B) flowed at 200 µL/min. MS acquisition was performed in positive and negative SRM mode to measure energy cofactors, amino acids, glycolytic and TCA cycle metabolites. Authentic standards were used to calibrate metabolite MRMs and determine analytes’ retention times. The injection volume was 5 µL. HESI source settings were 3500 V (positive) and 2500 V (negative) and vaporizer temperature 275 °C. Scheduled acquisition was carried out across the 30-minute LC program. Instrument data was extracted using ProteoWizard MSConvert (3.0.21128-7376ae988) and in-house MATLAB (2024a) scripts.
sections.lipidomic analysis: A 1-butanol/methanol (BUME, 1-butanol: methanol = 1:1 v/v containing 5 mM ammonium formate) single phase lipid extraction method was used for lipid extraction. Briefly, washed cell pellets contained in 15 mL tubes were resuspended in 500 µL 0.1 mM Tris-HCl with 100 µM BHT (pH 7.9) before being transferred to 1.5 mL Eppendorf tubes. Cells were then sonicated to generate cell lysates (Branson, Amp 30% for 30 s). All the above steps were done on crushed ice. 10 µL of cell lysate was transferred into a fresh tube and first spiked with 10 µL of diluted Avanti Splash Lipidomix (10% dilution), serving as lipid class specific internal standards (ISTD). Then, 100 µL BUME solvent was added and mixed thoroughly in a water bath sonicator for 60 min and finally centrifuged 16,000 g for 10 min (room temperature). Supernatants were then carefully transferred to inserted LC glass vials for subsequent LC/MS analysis. A targeted LC/MS lipidomics method was applied, capable of detecting > 600 lipid species encompassing 36 lipid classes/subclasses, using a TSQ Altis triple quadrupole mass spectrometer equipped with a H-ESI source and coupled with a Vanquish Horizon liquid chromatography (LC) system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). Briefly, autosampler injection volume was 5 µL and temperature was set 10 °C. Liquid chromatographic separation was achieved with a 100*2.1 mm Supelco Ascentis ® Express C18, 2 μm UHPLC Column (Sigma Aldrich, NSW, AU) attached to a SecurityGuard™ ULTRA C18 guard column (Phenomenex, CA, USA), with 35 °C column oven temperature. A binary gradient buffer system was used as the mobile phase throughout the 23 min run time at flowrate of 0.3 mL/min. Solvent A comprised acetonitrile/H 2 O = 6:4, 10 mM ammonium formate, 5 µM phosphoric acid and 0.1% (v/v) formic acid; solvent B comprised isopropanol/acetonitrile/H 2 O = 90:9:1, 10 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% (v/v) formic acid. Positive and negative scheduled single reaction monitoring (SRM) modes were applied to acquire targeted lipidomic data. Raw LC/MS-MS data examination, deconvolution and manually peak integration (when necessary) were performed using Skyline. The exported spreadsheets containing peak areas were subsequently tidied and converted to concentrations using in-house Python scripts utilizing Numpy and Pandas packages.
