sections.proteomic analysis: The samples were solubilized using 150 µl of 1% SDC in 100 mM TEAB, heated to 95 °C for 5 min, cooled then incubated with 1U of Benzonase for 15 min at 37 °C. An aliquot (25 µl) of the suspension was transferred to two PBI Barocycler tubes and lysed, reduced and alkylated in the PBI Barocycler for 60 min at 56 °C. The mixture was diluted with 120 µl of Rapid digestion buffer and 1.5 µg of trypsin added. Enzymatic digestion was in the PBI Barocycler for 30 min at 56 °C. The reaction was terminated and SDC precipitated by adding 5 µl of 100% formic acid, vortexed and centrifuged for 30 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred to a clean tube, diluted with 760 µl of 0.5% formic acid and loaded onto a Phenomenex C18 SPE cartridge. Peptides were eluted and dried to completeness in the RVC. The peptides were resuspended in 30 µl of 0.5% formic acid, centrifuged for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was transferred to clean low-bind tubes. Peptide quantitation was performed using the nanodrop N60 using setting OD = 1.0. The samples were acquired using the TripleTOF5600 + mass spectrometer. A total of 2 µg of total peptide/protein was used for LC-MS/MS analysis on the TripleTOF 5600 + mass spectrometer. The tryptic peptides were first loaded onto the TRAP column and then separated using a Waters Acuity UPLC M-class CSH C18 1.7 μm particle size analytical column using a 95 min LC-MS/MS method. Data was acquired using Information Dependent Acquisition (IDA) LC-MS/MS method. The raw LC-MS/MS data was processed using SCIEX Protein Pilot 5.0 and MS-GF+ software. The processed data was searched against the SWISS-PROT database.
sections.analysis of merna melting profile: After isolating mitochondria from NPCs, meRNAs were extracted using Qiagen RNeasy kit. An on-column DNase digestion was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol to exclude DNA contamination. The extracted meRNAs were then dissolved in RNase-free 18mΩ water (concentration: 2 µg/ 50 µl). To investigate the impact of temperature on the global melting profile of meRNAs, the intercalating dye Sybrgreen I was added to meRNAs (concentration: 1 µg/mL). As a complementary method, the metachromatic dye, acridine orange, was utilised at a concentration of 1 µg/mL. After adding the intercalating dyes, an optical reader was used to record the fluorescence signal.
sections.thermal stability shift assay: Assays were performed in a 96-well plate for real-time PCR using a protein thermal shift™ dye kit (Applied Biosystems). The reaction mix contained 5 µL of protein thermal shift™ buffer, 2.5 µL of diluted protein thermal shift™ dye (8×), 5 µL of recombinant protein of interest (400pmol), in 7.5 µL of RNase-free water. In experiments with Polmrt, RNA was added in an equimolar ratio with the protein. Likewise, Ssbp1 and ssDNA were used in an equimolar ratio. A real-time thermocycler Stratagene ® Mx3000P was used for collecting data from 25 to 80 °C, sampling every 1 °C.
sections.molecular dynamics: The open-source GROMACS tool was used to simulate the temperature-dependent dynamics of mouse mitochondrial Ssbp1 (AlphaFold ID: AF- Q9CYR0 -F1-v6). Simulations were performed using the water model of SPC/E and OPLS/AA force-field. Equilibrating simulations under an NVT (isothermal-isochoric) ensemble, followed by an NPT (isothermal-isobaric) ensemble were performed at 298 K until the root mean-square deviation (RMSD) was stable. The root mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) values were calculated with Gromacs 4.5 through the Galaxy platform. Mutation of Pro-92 to leu-92 in silico was performed using PyMOL. Both RMSD and RMSF were calculated with Gromacs package.
sections.phylogenetic analysis: To perform phylogenetic analysis, 344 orthologues of mouse mitochondrial Ssbp1 were retrieved from Uniprot database and aligned using Jalview software. Likewise, 244 orthologues of E. coli Ssb were retrieved from Uniprot database and aligned using Jalview software. Sequence logos were generated using WebLogo application.
sections.thermal hybridization chain reaction: Thermal hybridisation chain reaction (t-HCR) is based on iterative hybridization of two hairpin DNAs, a synthetic analogue of OriL (A 5159 -T 5195 ) and another half-complementary hairpin with a similar T m to OriL. OriL: 5′- TGAAGATGGCCCCTTTTTTTTTTTACCGCCATCTTCA − 3′. Complementary OriL: 5′-AAAAGGGGCCATCATCATGAAGATGGCGGTAAAAAAA-3′. As the temperature approaches the T m of OriL, denatured hairpins could hybridise in a chain reaction whereby 3′-complementary OriL (highlighted orange) hybridises to 3′-OriL (highlighted red). This generates a 3′overhang in double-stranded DNA corresponding to 5′-complementary OriL (highlighted green) to which another 5′-OriL (highlighted blue) can hybridise exposing 3′-OriL as a single-stranded DNA. This event completes one hybridization cycle, only to start a new hybridization cycle for as long as the condition of T hybridisation =T m is met. Therefore, the length of the double-stranded product corresponds to the duration of time in which T hybridisation =T m . When the temperature exceeds the annealing temperature of OriL and complementary OriL (T hybridisation > T m ), the hybridization reaction will cease despite existence of the two stem loops in a denatured stage.
sections.synthesis of mitochondrial single-strand: To synthesize a single-stranded mitochondrial H-strand, a methodology was required to enable circularization of a single-stranded DNA oligomer in a splint-independent manner. A single-stranded DNA oligomere corresponding to the H-strand of mDNA was synthesized corresponding to a region of mDNA containing the OriL and extending to the proximal upstream region (-40 bp: C5119-G5158) and the downstream region (+ 45 bp: A5196-T5242) of the OriL: TTTTTC GGCGGTAGAAGT AGATTGAAGCCAGTAATAGGGTATTTACCTGTCGTAGCAAATTAATTCTTGTAGAGAAATCTCTACTAAG ACTTCTACCGCC ATTTTTT Annealing of the complementary stem region of the oligomer facilitates approximation of the 5′ and 3′ terminals prior to ligation. To circularise the synthetic H-strand, 2µL of the oligomer (0.5 pmol/µL), 2µL CircLigase II 10X Reaction Buffer, 1µL 50 mM MnCl 2 , 1µL CircLigase II ssDNA Ligase (100 U), and 14µL nuclease-free water were mixed and incubated at 60 °C for 1 h. The enzyme was then inactivated by incubation at 80 °C for 10 min. The efficiency of circularization was checked by running a DNA gel in which near-complete conversion to a circular DNA was detected. The circularised D-strand was then purified using a phenol-chloroform isolation method.
sections.expression and purification of recombina: Synthesis of recombinant proteins was achieved using a methodology described by Korhonen et al. [ 66 ]. Synthetic DNA fragments encoding mouse mitochondrial Ssbp1, Polγ (DNA polymerase subunit γ-1), and Polmrt containing a His 6 tag at the N terminus were cloned into the pBacPAK9 vector (Clontech). The plasmid constructs were used to prepare Autographa californica nuclear polyhedrosis virus recombinant for the proteins of interest. Expression of the recombinant proteins was achieved in Spodoptera frugiperda (Sf9) cells maintained in suspension in SFM 900 medium (Gibco-BRL) and containing 5% fetal calf serum at 27 °C. To purify the proteins, cells were transferred to a lysis buffer containing 25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 20 mM 2-mercaptoethanol, and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma) and lysed using a Dounce homogeniser type B. The recombinant proteins were purified using a Ni 2+ -NTA matrix using the methodology described by Falkenberg et al. [ 97 ]. The purity of isolated proteins was checked by SDS-PAGE under reducing condition (purity > 90%) and the identity of recombinant proteins was confirmed by LC/MS.
sections.in vitro mitochondrial mini-replisome: The circularised single-stranded mitochondrial H-strand (OriL Wt , or the mutated versions (ΔT m low O L , or ΔT m high O L ); final concentration 5 nM) was added to a reaction mixture containing 25 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.6), 5 mM magnesium chloride, 1 mM DTT, 100 µg/ml BSA, 4 mM ATP, 10% glycerol, 250 µM dATP, 250 µM dTTP, 250 µM dGTP, 250 µM dCTP, 100 µM UTP, 100 µM GTP, 100 µM CTP, and 2U of SUPERase·In RNase Inhibitor. The reaction mixture also contained 200 pmol of mtSSB, 50 pmol of POLγ, and 50 pmol of Polmrt. The reactions were run for 40 min at 25 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C. The DNA was then purified using phenol-chloroform extraction and quantified using real-time qPCR.
sections.statistical analysis: Prism software was used for the statistical analysis of data. The relative expression level of genes of interest and that of mDNA were analysed using non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test. Error bars represent ±1SD.

title: Association of the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio with cardiovascular disease: a cross-sectional study based on NHANES
abstract: Purpose To examine the association between the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio (SVR) and prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD) in a nationally representative U.S. population. Methods We analyzed data from the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), 2011–2018. Associations of SVR with composite CVD and its subtypes (heart failure [HF], coronary heart disease [CHD], angina pectoris [AP], myocardial infarction [MI], or stroke) were estimated using multivariable logistic models; linear trend across SVR tertiles was tested, and nonlinearity was assessed using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models. Subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity. Results The sample comprised 9,997 participants. In multivariable-adjusted logistic models, higher SVR was associated with lower odds of CVD (Model 4: OR = 0.44; 95% CI 0.29–0.67; P < 0.001), with a dose–response (P for trend = 0.001). In subtype analyses, the highest SVR category was associated with lower odds of HF (OR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.18–0.96; P = 0.047), CHD (OR = 0.28, 95% CI 0.11–0.71; P = 0.011), and MI (OR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.11–0.94; P = 0.045), with significant trends for all three outcomes (P for trend < 0.05). RCS models showed nonlinear associations of SVR with composite CVD, CHD, and MI, but not with HF, stroke or AP. Subgroup analyses detected interactions for poverty-income ratio (PIR) and BMI strata (both P for interaction = 0.005). Conclusion Higher SVR may be a potential CVD risk marker, whereas associations with AP and stroke were weak or non-significant. Prospective validation is warranted. Level of evidence : Level V—cross-sectional observational study. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40519-026-01865-1.

sections.purpose: To examine the association between the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio (SVR) and prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD) in a nationally representative U.S. population.
sections.methods: We analyzed data from the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), 2011–2018. Associations of SVR with composite CVD and its subtypes (heart failure [HF], coronary heart disease [CHD], angina pectoris [AP], myocardial infarction [MI], or stroke) were estimated using multivariable logistic models; linear trend across SVR tertiles was tested, and nonlinearity was assessed using restricted cubic spline (RCS) models. Subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity.

sections.introduction: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide and a major source of loss of healthy life years. Although established behavioral and metabolic risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, tobacco use, and unhealthy diet, are well characterized, growing evidence highlights additional determinants, particularly body fat distribution and skeletal muscle mass [ 1 – 3 ]. Visceral adiposity has been closely linked to impaired glucose tolerance, insulin resistance, and other metabolic disturbances, which have been associated with CVD incidence, progression, and prognosis [ 4 , 5 ]. By contrast, higher skeletal muscle mass has been associated with more favorable cardiometabolic profiles, characterized by better glycemic control and attenuated inflammation [ 6 – 9 ]. Clinical studies have reported that individuals with CVD have lower skeletal muscle mass than healthy controls [ 7 , 8 ]. Among patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation, lower psoas muscle mass has been associated with higher 12-month risks of CVD events and mortality [ 10 – 12 ]. Because skeletal muscle and visceral fat may exert opposing effects on metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis, an index integrating both components may better reflect cardiometabolic imbalance than either component alone. In this context, the skeletal muscle mass-to-visceral fat area ratio (SVR) has emerged as a potentially informative body composition-based indicator [ 13 – 15 ]. However, the available literature directly evaluating SVR remains limited. Existing studies have more often focused on metabolic abnormalities, whereas evidence regarding the association between SVR and clinically defined cardiovascular disease remains scarce [ 16 , 17 ]. In this study, we analyzed data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), in which dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) was used to quantify appendicular lean mass (arms and legs) and VFA. We then examined associations between SVR and prevalent CVD and its major subtypes—heart failure (HF), coronary heart disease (CHD), angina pectoris (AP), myocardial infarction (MI), and stroke.
sections.data source: This study utilized data from NHANES ( https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/ ) collected during 2011–2018. NHANES is a nationally representative, continuous surveillance program administered by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) under the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Employing a complex, multistage, stratified probability sampling design, it yields estimates representative of the U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population. Specifically, it integrates standardized questionnaires, physical examinations, laboratory measurements, and dietary surveys to collect comprehensive health and nutrition information. This multifaceted approach enables the assessment of dietary intake, chronic disease prevalence, behavioral risk factors, and environmental exposures. NHANES serves as a foundational resource for public health monitoring, policy-making, and epidemiological research.
sections.study population: This cross-sectional study examined the association between SVR and CVD. Participants were excluded based on the following criteria: (1) age < 20 years (n = 16,539); (2) missing DXA measures required to calculate SVR (n = 11,874) or missing CVD status (n = 25); and (3) missing data in key covariates (n = 712 in total). The final analytic sample comprised 9,997 adults. Participant flow is shown in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Participant selection flowchart for NHANES 2011–2018
sections.dxa measurements and svr calculation: Whole-body DXA scans were performed in participants aged 8–59 years, excluding pregnant individuals, those who had used radiographic contrast agents (e.g., barium) within the past 7 days, and those exceeding the DXA table limitations (weight > 450 lbs or height > 6 ft 5 in). All DXA examinations were conducted by trained and certified radiology technologists, with rigorous quality control maintained throughout the entire process to ensure accuracy. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) were evaluated using Hologic APEX software, with measures of fat area, mass, and volume at the intervertebral level between L4 and L5. Appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM) was calculated as the sum of lean mass in the arms and legs, and SVR was defined as ASM divided by VFA (kg/cm 2 ) [ 18 ].
sections.cardiovascular disease ascertainment: CVD was ascertained from self-reported physician diagnoses collected via a standardized medical condition questionnaire. Participants were queried about prior diagnoses of HF, CHD, AP, MI, or stroke; those reporting any of these conditions were classified as having CVD [ 19 ].
sections.definition of covariates: The covariates collected in this study encompassed demographic characteristics (age, sex, race, education level, poverty-income ratio [PIR], and marital status), lifestyle factors (smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical activity level, total energy intake, and body mass index [BMI]), and medical comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, cancer, kidney impairment, and hyperuricemia). Smoking status was classified into three categories: never smokers (smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lifetime), former smokers (smoked at least 100 cigarettes but were not currently smoking), and current smokers (smoked at least 100 cigarettes and continued smoking at the time of the survey). Alcohol consumption was defined as having consumed at least 12 alcoholic beverages in the past 12 months. Hypertension was determined on the basis of any of the following: systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90 mmHg, self-reported physician diagnosis, or current use of antihypertensive medication. Diabetes was identified if participants met one or more of the following criteria: fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2 h plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5%, self-reported physician diagnosis, or current antidiabetic therapy. Dyslipidemia was considered present if any of the following applied: total cholesterol ≥ 200 mg/dL; triglycerides ≥ 150 mg/dL; low-density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥ 130 mg/dL; high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ≤ 40 mg/dL (men) or ≤ 50 mg/dL (women); or current use of lipid-lowering medication. Kidney impairment was defined as a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥ 30 mg/g. Physical activity was categorized into high and low levels, according to a previously validated method [ 20 ].
sections.statistical analysis: All statistical analyses were conducted using sample weights to account for the complex survey design of NHANES and to ensure nationally representative estimates. Specifically, the 2-year MEC examination weight (WTMEC2YR) was applied as the sampling weight, SDMVSTRA was used as the stratification variable, and SDMVPSU as the primary sampling unit [ 21 ]. Detailed information on the weighting strategy is available on the official CDC website ( https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/analyticguidelines.aspx#sample-design ). Incorporating these design elements ensured that the estimates, standard errors (SEs), and 95% confidence intervals appropriately reflected the U.S. non-institutionalized civilian population [ 22 ]. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population. Missing data were handled as follows: (1) participants with missing values in the primary exposure or outcome variables were excluded; (2) for covariates, if the proportion of missingness was < 5%, those observations were deleted; if > 5%, multiple imputation was employed—predictive mean matching (PMM) was used for continuous variables, and logistic regression imputation for categorical variables. For normally distributed continuous variables, results were presented as mean ± SE, and group comparisons were conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). For non-normally distributed continuous variables, data were reported as median (Q1, Q3), and comparisons were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis rank-sum test. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies (percentages), and differences between groups were assessed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. To evaluate the association between SVR and CVD, we fitted four multivariable logistic regression models with increasingly comprehensive covariate adjustment: Model 1, unadjusted; Model 2, adjusted for sex, age, race, PIR, marital status, and education level; Model 3, additionally adjusted for BMI, smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and total energy intake; and Model 4, further adjusted for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, serum uric acid, renal impairment, and cancer. The same modeling framework was applied to individual outcomes, including HF, CHD, AP, MI, and stroke. Tests for linear trends across SVR tertiles were conducted using median values of each category as a continuous variable. Potential nonlinearity in the SVR–CVD association was examined using restricted cubic splines (RCS) based on the covariate set in Model 4. Subgroup analyses were conducted across strata defined by age, sex, education level, PIR, BMI, smoking status, alcohol consumption, and histories of hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia, with interaction tests performed to evaluate effect modification and support the robustness of the findings.
sections.association between svr and cardiovascul: Table 2 presents multivariable logistic regression estimates for the associations of SVR tertiles with composite CVD and its subtypes (HF, CHD, MI, AP, and stroke); P for trend across tertiles was evaluated in a series of progressively adjusted models. The results demonstrated a significant inverse association between SVR and the prevalence of composite CVD. Compared with the lowest tertile (T1, SVR ≤ 0.20), individuals in both the intermediate tertile (T2, SVR = 0.20–0.34) and the highest tertile (T3, SVR > 0.34) had lower odds of CVD, although the associations were attenuated after progressive adjustment. In the fully adjusted model (Model 4), the odds ratios for T2 and T3 were 0.57 (95% CI 0.38–0.86; P = 0.012) and 0.44 (95% CI 0.29–0.67; P < 0.001), respectively, with a significant dose–response trend across SVR tertiles (P for trend = 0.001). sections.subgroup analyses of svr in relation to: As shown in Fig. 3 , the association between SVR and CVD remained statistically significant across most subgroups, with no evidence of interaction in the majority of strata (P for interaction > 0.05), indicating broadly consistent associations across population groups. All analyses were survey-weighted to account for the complex, multistage sampling design and were conducted using multivariable logistic regression. Notably, significant interactions were observed for PIR and BMI (P for interaction = 0.005 for both), suggesting that these factors may modify the SVR–CVD association. Fig. 3 Forest plot of subgroup analyses for the association between SVR and CVD. Age, sex, race, PIR, education level, marital status, smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical activity level, BMI, energy intake, cancer, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, renal impairment, uric acid were adjusted in the subgroup analysis. SVR skeletal muscle mass to visceral fat area ratio, PIR poverty income ratio, BMI body mass index, CVD cardiovascular disease, OR odds ratio, CI confidence interval In the subgroup with moderate income (PIR = 1.3–3.5), the association between SVR and CVD was statistically significant (OR < 0.01; 95% CI < 0.01–0.12; P = 0.004). By contrast, no significant associations were observed for PIR < 1.3 (OR = 0.86; 95% CI 0.34–2.15; P = 0.748) or PIR > 3.5 (OR = 0.08; 95% CI < 0.01–4.31; P = 0.214), suggesting a stronger association of SVR with CVD in the middle PIR group. Similarly, in BMI-stratified analyses, the association was not significant for BMI < 25 (OR = 0.81; 95% CI 0.29–2.25; P = 0.693) but was significant for BMI 25–29.9 (OR = 0.03; 95% CI 0.01–0.77; P = 0.034) and BMI ≥ 30 (OR < 0.01; 95% CI < 0.01–0.11; P = 0.002), indicating a stronger association of SVR with CVD among overweight and obese participants.
sections.discussion: To our knowledge, few prior studies have directly examined SVR in relation to the prevalence of CVD. In the present cross-sectional analysis, higher SVR was significantly associated with lower odds of composite CVD. Similar inverse associations were also observed for several major subtypes, particularly HF, CHD, and MI, suggesting a potential cardioprotective role of a more favorable muscle-fat distribution. However, these associations were not uniform across all subtype analyses. These results reinforce the beneficial contribution of skeletal muscle mass to cardiovascular health and underscore the detrimental role of visceral adiposity in CVD pathogenesis. Taken together, our findings suggest that SVR may serve as a useful integrated body-composition marker associated with cardiovascular health and highlight the potential importance of overall body composition, especially the balance between skeletal muscle and visceral fat, in understanding CVD burden. These results may be explained by multiple biological mechanisms. The adverse effects of VAT on cardiovascular events have been extensively studied [ 23 , 24 ]. Compared with subcutaneous adipose tissue, VAT harbors larger adipocytes,adipocyte hypertrophy promotes adipose-tissue dysfunction, and hypertrophic adipocytes exhibit insulin resistance. Insulin resistance can contribute to CVD via endothelial dysfunction, sodium retention, heightened sympathetic activity, and vascular hypertrophy. As a metabolically active tissue, VAT secretes multiple proinflammatory and metabolic mediators, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and leptin [ 13 – 15 ]. Elevated circulating leptin concentrations have been shown to predict incident CVD [ 25 , 26 ], and increases in several proinflammatory cytokines are mechanistically implicated in the development and progression of CVD [ 27 , 28 ]. Building on this, the role of skeletal muscle in cardiovascular health and overall well-being is equally critical. In a study including 469,830 UK Biobank participants, a slow walking pace and lower muscle mass were associated with a higher incidence of CVD. The pathophysiological mechanisms linking muscle mass with CVD risk and mortality are complex and warrant further investigation. As a principal site of glucose and lipid metabolism, an increase in muscle mass may help stabilize metabolic homeostasis and is associated with multiple health benefits, including enhanced insulin sensitivity, reduced inflammatory levels, and an increased metabolic rate. Chronic systemic inflammation is a key driver of skeletal muscle wasting and declines in muscle quality and is associated with increased risks of CVD and mortality [ 29 ]. Moreover, inflammatory and oxidative-stress pathways that impair muscle health overlap with those implicated in CVD, promoting the release of actin from skeletal myocytes and cardiomyocytes and perpetuating a vicious cycle [ 30 ]. Consistent with these mechanistic considerations, our results show that a higher SVR, an indicator of greater muscle mass relative to visceral adiposity, is significantly associated with a lower odds of composite CVD,this association remains robust after adjustment for age, BMI, and other potential confounders. These findings highlight the potential importance of considering both visceral adiposity and skeletal muscle mass in relation to cardiovascular health. Prior studies have examined the joint influence of skeletal muscle and visceral adiposity on CVD from an integrated perspective, but the operational definitions and measurement indicators have differed. In a UK-based prospective study (n = 452,931; ages 40–69; mean follow-up, 5.1 years), individuals with sarcopenic obesity (SO), defined by low grip strength together with elevated BMI, had a higher risk of CVD than those with low grip strength alone or obesity alone. In a prospective study of the general Japanese population (n = 2,490), dynapenic obesity (low grip strength plus obesity) was likewise significantly associated with incident CVD [ 31 ]. By contrast, a prospective study of British men aged 60–79 years (n = 4,111, mean follow-up, 11.3 years) found that SO defined by mid-upper arm circumference and waist circumference was not significantly associated with CVD risk [ 32 ]. Similarly, a community-based U.S. study of older adults (n = 3,366,ages ≥ 65 years) showed that SO was unrelated to CVD risk when defined by skeletal muscle mass and waist circumference; when defined by grip strength and waist circumference, only a borderline statistically significant association was observed [ 33 ]. In addition, a cross-sectional study following the definition by Lopes et al. [ 34 ] and using the muscle quality index as the measure of muscular status found limited predictive performance for CVD and mortality [ 2 ]. Overall, evidence points to an association between composite muscle-fat phenotypes and CVD risk, but findings remain inconsistent owing to divergent SO definitions, metric selection, adiposity assessment methods, and differences in populations and follow-up. To strengthen comparability across studies, it will be important to standardize terminology and adopt harmonized thresholds. In analyses across cardiovascular disease subtypes, we observed that, in fully adjusted models, participants with CHD, HF, or MI had lower SVR than participants without these conditions. Adiposity contributes substantially to the major risk factors for CHD—hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes—and may itself be an independent risk factor for atherosclerosis and incident CHD events [ 35 ]. Similarly, an analysis based on NHANES suggested a nonlinear dose–response association between the VAI and CHD [ 36 ]. Excess adiposity and ectopic fat deposition upregulate pro-atherogenic inflammatory mediators, increase vascular wall stress, and cause myocardial injury, thereby promoting left ventricular hypertrophy and remodeling; these processes ultimately culminate in diastolic and systolic dysfunction and progression to HF [ 37 ]. In addition, obesity increases circulating blood volume and cardiac output requirements, further augmenting volume and pressure overload and thereby exacerbating HF. Sarcopenia may contribute to ventilatory inefficiency and exercise intolerance in patients with congestive heart failure and has been associated with reduced survival in this population. Prior studies have shown that the prevalence of sarcopenia among patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction is approximately 20% higher than in healthy individuals [ 38 ], suggesting a bidirectional, mutually reinforcing pathophysiological link between sarcopenia and HF. Excess adiposity may increase the risk of MI through sustained systemic inflammation and its long-term effects on coronary atherosclerosis. Madala et al. reported that overweight was closely associated with a younger age at the first occurrence of non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction [ 39 ]. Sato et al. further observed that, among patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, lower skeletal muscle mass was independently associated with a lower left ventricular ejection fraction and an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including all-cause mortality, nonfatal MI, nonfatal ischemic stroke, hospitalization for HF, and unplanned revascularization [ 40 ]. By contrast, the attenuated associations for AP and stroke after full adjustment may reflect heterogeneity across CVD subtypes. In contrast to HF, CHD, and MI, which are more directly linked to adiposity-related atherosclerotic burden, myocardial remodeling, and metabolic dysfunction, AP is a symptom-based and potentially more heterogeneous clinical entity, whereas stroke comprises pathophysiologically distinct subtypes with different risk profiles [ 41 , 42 ]. In addition, because these outcomes were self-reported, misclassification may have varied across subtypes, which could have further weakened the observed associations. Subgroup analyses revealed significant interactions of BMI and PIR with the association between SVR and CVD. Among individuals who were overweight or obese, the protective association of a higher SVR with CVD appeared more pronounced, underscoring the importance—particularly in higher-BMI groups—of increasing skeletal muscle mass while reducing the burden of visceral adiposity. In addition, the inverse association between SVR and CVD was stronger among participants with intermediate income levels, indicating effect modification by PIR. This pattern may reflect the influence of broader socioeconomic context: in lower-income groups, limited access to healthcare, poorer diet quality, heightened psychosocial stress, and adverse environmental exposures may obscure the benefits associated with higher SVR; whereas in higher-income groups, greater access to health resources, more favorable lifestyle behaviors, and earlier clinical interventions may already lower baseline CVD risk, thereby attenuating the incremental contribution of SVR. Compared with prior research, this study employed SVR as an integrated indicator of body composition and analyzed a large, nationally representative U.S. sample, enabling a comprehensive assessment of the SVR–CVD relationship with extensive covariate adjustment to reduce bias and evaluate robustness.
sections.strengths and limitations: This study has several strengths. First, it was based on NHANES, a nationally representative survey with standardized protocols, which enhances the generalizability and reliability of the findings in the U.S. adult population. Second, to our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between SVR and CVD. Third, beyond overall CVD, we further evaluated the associations between SVR and specific CVD subtypes, providing a more nuanced understanding of the cardiometabolic relevance of SVR. Fourth, we conducted subgroup analyses and explored potential nonlinear associations, which strengthened the robustness and interpretability of the findings. Nevertheless, several limitations warrant consideration. First, cardiovascular disease was identified based on validated self-reported questionnaires rather than clinical adjudication or medical record review, which may introduce recall bias and disease misclassification. Second, although survey weights were applied to improve the representativeness of the estimates, a substantial number of participants were excluded because SVR could not be calculated, mainly due to missing DXA-derived appendicular lean mass or visceral fat area data. As these exclusions may not have occurred at random, residual selection bias cannot be ruled out. Third, because this study is cross-sectional, causal inference is not possible and reverse causation cannot be excluded; whether higher SVR directly lowers cardiovascular risk remains uncertain. Fourth, although DXA is among the reference standards for body-composition assessment, its precision may be affected by body habitus and participant positioning. Fifth, despite broad adjustment for potential confounders, residual and unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out. Future studies should employ prospective designs to validate these findings and to delineate heterogeneity in the association between SVR and cardiovascular risk across populations, thereby elucidating potential biological mechanisms. In parallel, intervention research should examine whether dietary and lifestyle modifications can improve SVR and, in turn, reduce cardiovascular risk. In sum, our study supports consideration of integrated body-composition metrics in clinical assessment and offers new insights and directions for subsequent research.
sections.conclusion_1: In summary, higher SVR was associated with lower odds of composite CVD. This inverse association was mainly observed for HF, CHD, and MI, whereas the findings for AP and stroke were attenuated after full adjustment, suggesting heterogeneity across CVD subtypes. These findings support a potential association between integrated body composition and cardiovascular health, but the clinical utility of SVR requires confirmation in prospective studies.
sections.what is already known on this subject?: Previous studies have shown that lower muscle mass and greater visceral adiposity are each associated with higher cardiovascular risk, and that composite muscle–fat phenotypes such as SO may also be related to CVD. However, findings have been inconsistent because prior studies used heterogeneous definitions and indicators.
sections.what this study adds?: To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between SVR and overall CVD, as well as major CVD subtypes, in a nationally representative U.S. population. Higher SVR was associated with lower odds of composite CVD and several major subtypes, particularly HF, CHD, and MI. Nonlinear and subgroup analyses further suggested that the association between SVR and CVD differed across outcomes and appeared more pronounced among participants with overweight/obesity and those with moderate income.

title: Association between self-purchased medication use and gastric disease among Chinese adults: a cross-sectional analysis based on CHARLS 2018 data
abstract: Background Gastric diseases are a major health burden, especially in East Asia, with high incidence and mortality rates. While Helicobacter pylori infection and poor lifestyle behaviors are established risk factors, the impact of drug-related gastric injury in aging populations remains underexplored. In China, polypharmacy is common among older adults, with nearly 40% using self-purchased medications without professional guidance. Similar trends are observed in other aging societies, highlighting the global challenge of unregulated drug use. Existing studies lack adjustments for comorbidities, prediction tools, and methodological innovation. This study analyzes CHARLS 2018 data to: (1) examine the relationship between self-purchased medication use and gastric disease, and (2) identified strongly associated groups, such as patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetes. Methods We included 19,752 participants from the CHARLS database. Participants were divided into gastric disease and control groups based on DA007_10 questionnaires. We compared baseline characteristics, including self-purchased medication use, between groups. Multivariate logistic regression models were used to assess the correlation between self-purchased medication use and gastric disease. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve evaluated Model 3’s predictive performance. Stratified analysis was conducted to assess the stability of the results. Results Significant differences were observed between the gastric disease ( n = 659) and control ( n = 5,428) groups in factors such as ethnicity, self-reported health status, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, chronic lung diseases, liver disease, kidney disease, smoking history, and medication use. In all models, self-purchasing medication was associated with an increased prevalence of gastric disease (adjusted OR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.46–2.09, p < 0.001), including Model 3 (adjusted OR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.46–2.09, p < 0.001). The model demonstrated moderate discriminatory ability in distinguishing individuals with and without gastric disease (AUC = 0.71). Stratified analyses revealed that the association between self-purchased medication use and gastric disease risk was consistent across covariates, with stronger effects observed in participants with CKD (adjusted OR = 1.89) and diabetes (OR = 1.82). Conclusions This study found that self-purchasing medication was positively correlated with the risk of gastric disease in Chinese older adults (adjusted OR = 1.75), and the association was stronger among those with chronic kidney disease (adjusted OR = 1.89) or diabetes (OR = 1.82). This finding provides a reference for the risk stratification and prevention strategies of gastric disease. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12889-026-27616-6.

sections.introduction: Gastric diseases constitute a major global health burden, with particularly high incidence and mortality in East Asia. In this region, the age-standardized incidence of gastric cancer reaches 28.3 per 100,000, and the mortality rate is 17.6 per 100,000, both markedly higher than the global average [ 1 ]. Helicobacter pylori infection (global prevalence > 50%) [ 1 ] and adverse lifestyle factors are recognized as core risk factors for Gastric diseases. While preliminary evidence has linked certain medications to gastric injury [ 2 – 4 ], important gaps remain in understanding the epidemiology and underlying mechanisms of drug-induced gastric injury in aging populations—a group characterized by high polypharmacy rates (e.g., Chinese elderly take a mean of 4.2 medications per person, with 38.7% reporting self-purchased medication use [ 3 , 4 ]). For instance, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) irreversibly inhibit cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), thereby reducing prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂) levels by more than 80% and increasing the risk of ulcers by 2-4-fold [ 5 – 7 ]. Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt gut microbiota homeostasis, thereby increasing the risk of H. pylori colonization by 3.2-fold [ 8 ]. Although eradication of H. pylori can reduce gastric cancer incidence by 47% [ 9 ], drug-induced gastric injury, particularly among older adults exposed to polypharmacy, remains an underexplored pathway requiring tailored prevention strategies. Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPIs) use induces sustained hypochlorhydria (median gastric pH elevated from 1.4 to 5.8; duration at pH > 4 prolonged 5-fold [ 10 , 11 ], thereby significantly promoting small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and Clostridium difficile infection (RR = 1.74) [ 12 ]. Furthermore, emerging evidence indicates synergistic effects between medications and environmental carcinogens. For example, the combination of NSAIDs and a high-salt diet increases gastric cancer risk 5.2-fold [ 13 ], highlighting the importance of multifactorial risk assessment for gastric diseases. Against the backdrop of China’s rapidly aging population, polypharmacy is becoming increasingly severe. CHARLS data reveal a high polypharmacy burden, with participants taking an average of 4.2 medications per person. The prevalence of self-purchased medication use was 38.7% overall, and significantly higher in rural areas (52.1%, p < 0.001) [ 3 , 14 ]. This trend mirrors global challenges in aging societies. For instance, Watanabe reported that in Japan, where cultural acceptance of self-medication is high, over 45% of the elderly individuals routinely purchase OTC drugs without professional consultation, primarily for chronic pain and digestive symptoms [ 15 ]. Such cross-border parallels highlight the urgent need for international collaboration in regulating non-prescription medication access, particularly in rural and underserved regions. Critically, over 40% of the elderly individuals obtain medications without prescriptions due to highly accessible over-the-counter (OTC) markets and insufficient medication supervision systems [ 1 , 16 ]. Despite growing concern, current research faces four critical limitations. First, most observational studies inadequately adjust for confounding effects and fail to account for comorbidities such as chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 60 mL/min) and diabetes mellitus [ 17 , 18 ]. Second, there is a lack of dedicated risk prediction tools. Existing gastric cancer prediction models (e.g., the Hong Kong model developed by Wong et al.) [ 19 ] do not incorporate drug exposure variables and demonstrate only modest discrimination (AUC = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.64–0.72), failing to meet the requirements of precision screening [ 20 ]. Third, a deficiency in methodological innovation is evident, with only 12.3% of relevant studies utilizing advanced metrics like Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI) and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) to quantify model optimization [ 21 ]. Fourth, most studies use a binary definition of self-purchased medication (yes/no) without distinguishing drug subclasses (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics, PPIs) or quantifying the number of concurrent medications, precluding dose–response analysis based on polypharmacy burden and detailed assessment of high-risk drug combinations. This study develops a comprehensive analytical framework to address these gaps identified earlier by leveraging the nationally representative CHARLS 2018 cohort (baseline n = 19,752). We present three key methodological innovations. First, we constructed sampling-weighted multivariate logistic regression models that progressively incorporated 12 sociodemographic and clinical covariates (Additional file 1) to mitigate confounding [ 22 ]. Second, we applied advanced evaluation metrics, including Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI) and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI), to quantify model optimization. Third, we conducted stratified analyses to identify vulnerable subgroups—such as individuals with chronic kidney disease or diabetes—among whom the risk of self-purchased medication-associated gastric injury was found to be amplified [ 18 ]. The public health significance of our work is twofold. On the methodological front, our study provides a validated risk assessment tool (AUC = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.68–0.74) for drug-induced gastric injury in aging populations in China, for which dedicated tools were previously lacking [ 21 ]. On the translational front, our findings provide evidence-based policy levers, including potential revisions to the National Essential Medicines List (e.g., imposing restrictions on high-dose NSAIDs) [ 23 ] and optimization of community-based gastric disease screening programs (e.g., prioritized risk-stratified allocation of endoscopy) [ 24 ]. Beyond pharmacological mechanisms, our study underscores the intersection between self-purchased medication safety, socioeconomic disparities, and rural–urban differences, highlighting the urgency of policy-level interventions. Collectively, these innovations establish a new evidence base for self-purchased drug safety research in aging societies and offer actionable strategies for precision prevention and regulatory reform.
sections.study population: The CHARLS database ( https://charls.pku.edu.cn/ ) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey of middle-aged and older adults (aged ≥ 45 years) in mainland China, designed to serve as a high-quality public micro-database [ 22 ]. All participants provided written informed consent, and all data are publicly available through the official platform. In this study, we included all individuals who participated in the 2018 CHARLS survey ( n = 20,866). Three core datasets were utilized: the Health Status and Functioning module, the Demographics module, and the Household Information module. After merging, an initial cohort of 19,752 participants was obtained. We then applied the exclusion criteria step by step. First, we excluded participants without information on stomach or digestive diseases ( n = 4,406). Next, participants with missing covariate data were excluded ( n = 9,250). Finally, we excluded individuals without information on medication use ( n = 9). After these exclusions, the final analytical sample consisted of 6,087 participants (Fig. 1 ) [ 22 ]. Fig. 1 Flowchart of participant selection from the CHARLS 2018 cohort (Gastric disease group: n = 659; Control group: n = 5,428)
sections.gastric disease and self-purchased medic: In this study, the diagnosis of ‘gastric disease’ and ‘self-purchased medication use’ depended on the questionnaires. Specifically, participants who answered “yes” to DA007_10 (“Diagnosed with Gastric disease by a Doctor”) were classified as having a gastric disease, while those who answered “yes” to EF001_W4 (“Self-purchased medication use”) were classified as having used self-purchased medications. A “no” response was regarded as an absence of gastric disease or non-use of self-purchased medications, respectively.
sections.covariates: Here, gender, ethnicity, type of residential address, education, marital status, self-reported health status, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, chronic lung diseases, liver disease, kidney disease, ever smoked, frequency of drinking alcoholic beverages. Detailed grouping information is shown in S1.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical analyses were performed using R (v. 4.3.1) software. Here, 6,087 subjects were divided into the gastric disease and control groups based on the questionnaire of DA007_10. Weighted counts and percentages were calculated using the tableone package (v. 0.13.0) [ 25 ] to describe baseline characteristics, and weighted chi-square tests were used to compare differences between the two groups across various characteristics ( p < 0.05). We then applied weighted multivariate logistic regression to examine the association between self-purchased medication use and gastric disease, expressed as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Three models were constructed: Model 1 (unadjusted), Model 2 (adjusted for age and ethnicity), and Model 3 (fully adjusted for all covariates). The first quartile of self-purchased medication use served as the reference group. Then, the prediction ability of Model 3 was assessed by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve using the pROC package (v 1.18.0) [ 21 ]. To further compare model accuracy and discrimination, we calculated Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI) and Integrated Discrimination Improvement (IDI) using the nricens (v.1.6) and PredictABEL (v.1.2.4) packages. Finally, stratified analyses were performed with the survey package (v.4.4-1) [ 26 ] to assess the robustness of associations across all covariates. To further describe the model’s capacity to differentiate between participants with and without gastric disease, we calculated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for Model 3. It is important to note that this analysis serves as a descriptive measure of discrimination rather than a validation of a predictive model, given the cross-sectional design.
sections.baseline characteristics: In CHARLS, 6,087 subjects from 2018 were grouped into gastric disease ( n = 659) and control ( n = 5,428) groups. The weighted chi-square test suggested that the ethnicity, self-reported health status, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, chronic lung diseases, liver disease, kidney disease, ever smoked, and taking any purchased medicine were significant between the gastric disease and control groups ( p < 0.05) (Table 1 ). Of 659 participants with gastric disease, 434, or 65.9%, had taken any purchased medicine. sections.the relationship between taking any purc: To further assess the association between self-purchasing medication and gastric disease, this study constructed three regression models. In Model 1, which did not adjust for confounders, self-purchasing medication was positively correlated with gastric disease (OR = 2.23, 95% CI = 1.88–2.64, p < 0.001). In Model 2 adjusted for age and ethnicity, the above relationship remained unchanged (OR = 2.20, 95% CI = 1.86–2.61, p < 0.001). In addition, in Model 3, which adjusted for all covariates, self-purchasing medication still showed a significant positive correlation with gastric disease (OR = 1.75, 95% CI = 1.46–2.09, p < 0.001) (Table 2 ). Furthermore, the AUC value was 0.71 in Model 3, which indicated that the model had a certain degree of discriminatory power (Fig. 2 ). sections.nri and idi: NRI and IDI analyses were performed, which showed that the predictive performance of the models improved sequentially with the gradual adjustment for covariates. Compared to the unadjusted Model 1, the overall predictive performance of Model 2 improved slightly (NRI = 1.69%, IDI = 0.37%, p < 0.05) (Table 3 ). After further adjusting for all covariates, the predictive performance of Model 3 was significantly improved compared to both Model 1 (NRI = 19.32%, IDI = 5.77%, p < 0.001) and Model 2 (NRI = 18.5%, IDI = 5.39%, p < 0.001) (Table 4 ). Regarding the correct reclassification of cases, compared to Model 2, Model 3 correctly reclassified 25.95% more cases upward (NRI + = 0.2595) while incorrectly reclassified 7.48% of non-cases upward (NRI − = -0.0748), indicating that the model’s sensitivity increased while its specificity decreased slightly (Table 5 ). In conclusion, the results of the NRI and IDI consistently demonstrated that Model 3, which was fully adjusted for confounders, possessed superior predictive performance and discriminatory ability. sections.stratified analysis: effect modification: Our stratified analyses confirmed significant effect modification by specific comorbidities (interaction p -values: CKD < 0.01; diabetes = 0.03). Among participants with chronic kidney disease, the risk of gastric disease in those who self-purchased medications was approximately 1.89 times that of those who did not (adjusted OR = 1.89, 95% CI 1.52–2.35). Similarly, among participants with diabetes, this risk was approximately 1.82 times that of those who did not self-purchase medications (adjusted OR = 1.82, 95% CI 1.47–2.25), a value higher than the average strength of the association observed in the overall population (OR = 1.75). In all stratified analyses, consistent with the pre-specified hypothesis, lower odds of gastric disease were observed in those who did not self-purchase medications compared to those who did (pooled OR = 0.57, 95% CI 0.48–0.68; p < 0.001). Effect estimates for other covariates are detailed in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3 Forest plot of stratified analyses for the association between self-purchased medication and gastric disease
sections.discussion: This multivariable logistic regression analysis based on the nationwide CHARLS cohort (Model 3) revealed a significant positive correlation between self-medication behavior and gastric diseases in the Chinese elderly population. Notably, the observed magnitude of this risk was higher than two categories of known risks: one is the genetic predictive association of smoking and alcohol consumption with overall gastrointestinal diseases in Asian populations derived from Mendelian randomization analyses [ 16 ]; the other is the traditional lifestyle-related risk factors reported in previous observational studies, such as the association between smoking and peptic ulcers, and the link between heavy alcohol consumption and gastritis [ 5 , 27 – 29 ]. This comparison suggests that the risk posed by unsupervised self-medication may be comparable to, or even exceed, that of some traditional lifestyle-related risks. It should be pointed out that the exposure indicator in this study was a binary variable, only reflecting the presence or absence of self-medication behavior, and did not further distinguish between drug subclasses (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors), dosage, duration of use, or polypharmacy. Therefore, the following discussion on pathophysiological mechanisms is primarily based on inferences from existing pharmacological literature rather than direct data support from this study. Nevertheless, the observed association in this study is biologically plausible and may be related to the use of high-risk medications commonly involved in self-medication. From a pharmacological perspective, the potential mechanisms of several common classes of drugs may provide explanations for this association. First, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) irreversibly inhibit cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing the production of gastric mucosal protective prostaglandin E2, thereby impairing key protective functions such as mucus secretion, bicarbonate transport, and mucosal blood flow [ 5 – 7 , 12 ]. Experimental studies have shown that the gastric ulcer area in experimental animals treated with indomethacin was significantly larger than in the control group [ 7 ]. Additionally, NSAIDs may interfere with the repair process of gastric stem cells, further exacerbating gastric mucosal injury [ 30 ]. Second, long-term use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) may also pose potential risks. Existing studies have indicated that PPI use is associated with an increased risk of gastric mucosal metaplasia, which aligns with the overall direction observed in this study [ 11 , 31 ]. The mechanism may involve PPIs causing a sustained increase in intragastric pH by inhibiting gastric acid secretion, thereby creating conditions for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth [ 10 , 11 ]. Studies have shown that the incidence of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth is higher in PPI users compared to non-users, and the risk increases with prolonged use [ 11 ]. Third, the widespread use of broad-spectrum antibiotics may have indirect effects by disrupting the intestinal microbial ecosystem. Antibiotics can lead to a decrease in microbial diversity [ 8 , 12 ], and this microecological change may create favorable conditions for Helicobacter pylori colonization. Some studies suggest that the risk of H. pylori adhesion increases after antibiotic use [ 8 ]. Although the effectiveness of probiotic interventions is still under investigation, some evidence indicates they may help reduce related risks [ 32 ]. The above mechanisms suggest that these medications, commonly used in self-medication, may each affect gastric mucosal health through their respective pathways, highlighting the potential risks associated with medication behavior lacking professional guidance. It is further important to note that although PPIs are often used to prevent NSAID-induced gastric mucosal injury, this protective effect may not completely offset the potential risk in high-risk patients or situations involving concurrent use of multiple ulcerogenic drugs [ 11 , 12 , 27 ]. This phenomenon suggests that unsupervised polypharmacy may lead to more complex cumulative effects. In addition to the cumulative effects of the drugs themselves, patients’ underlying health conditions may also influence their risk of gastric disease. Subgroup analyses in this study found that the association between self-medication and gastric disease was more pronounced in certain patient groups with complications. For example, among participants with chronic kidney disease (CKD), those who self-medicated had approximately 1.89 times the risk of gastric disease compared to those who did not; among diabetic patients, this risk was approximately 1.82 times. This result suggests that individuals with these underlying conditions may be more susceptible to drug-related gastric injury. Mechanistically, in CKD patients, certain accumulated toxins in the body may interfere with mucosal repair processes by activating inflammatory pathways, thereby compromising the integrity of the gastric mucosal barrier [ 18 , 33 – 36 ]. In diabetic patients, chronic hyperglycemia may affect gastric motility, leading to delayed gastric emptying, which prolongs the contact time between the gastric mucosa and potentially harmful substances, increasing the risk of gastric disease [ 17 , 28 , 33 ]. Therefore, medication management for these high-risk populations should be more cautious in clinical practice. For patients with renal insufficiency, the use of NSAIDs with clear nephrotoxicity should be avoided where possible; alternative medications such as selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors could be considered, along with enhanced clinical monitoring [ 12 , 27 ]. For diabetic patients, vigilance is needed regarding the potential risks of certain drug combinations. For instance, the concurrent use of some sulfonylureas and macrolide antibiotics may increase the risk of hypoglycemia, necessitating risk-stratified management in clinical practice to ensure patient medication safety. As a supplement to the regression analysis, this study further evaluated the model’s discriminatory ability at the individual level. The results showed that Model 3 demonstrated a certain level of discriminatory ability in distinguishing between gastric disease cases and non-cases, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.71. Model performance evaluation indicated that, compared to the simplified model, the fully adjusted model showed improvement in risk reclassification. Both the integrated discrimination improvement and the net reclassification improvement indices indicated that the adjusted model had higher accuracy in identifying individual risk. Based on this finding, future exploration could involve integrating such models into existing public health service frameworks to optimize the allocation of screening resources. For example, individuals assessed as high-risk could be prioritized for endoscopic examination, while those at intermediate risk could be considered for annual monitoring using serological tests [ 20 , 24 ]. Of course, the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of such strategies still require further validation in real-world studies [ 20 ]. Regarding the prevalence of self-medication behavior, in addition to drug accessibility and regulatory factors, the public’s level of medication knowledge is also noteworthy. Surveys have shown that some elderly individuals primarily obtain information for using over-the-counter medications from sources other than professional medical personnel [ 15 ]. Therefore, alongside improving drug regulatory laws and strengthening prescription drug sales management in accordance with the latest national drug classification standards [ 37 ], enhancing the public’s rational medication literacy is also particularly important. For example, regulations concerning the dispensing of high-risk NSAIDs should be strictly enforced to curb their illegal sales [ 1 , 16 , 23 , 38 ]; for patients requiring long-term use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), it is recommended to establish monitoring plans to periodically assess the necessity and potential risks of continued use [ 39 ]. Furthermore, integrating gastric disease risk assessment into routine health management services for the elderly may help identify high-risk individuals more effectively, facilitating an extension from individual diagnosis and treatment to population-level prevention [ 14 , 19 , 20 , 24 , 40 – 42 ]. The methodological improvements in this paper also hold potential translational significance. First, compared to traditional models, the weighted covariate adjustment employed in this study helps reduce selection bias, enhancing the representativeness of the study results for the rural elderly population, thus partially addressing the limitations present in previous hospital-based studies [ 22 ]. Second, the analysis of the net reclassification improvement index showed that, compared to the baseline model, the fully adjusted model improved predictive accuracy, providing a methodological reference for predictive research in the field of medication safety. Furthermore, based on the reallocation of existing public health service funds [ 14 , 42 ], this risk stratification strategy has preliminarily demonstrated high operational feasibility in pilot areas, suggesting that it may offer a reference implementation pathway for potential nationwide promotion without significantly increasing the financial burden. These explorations collectively represent an attempt to advance the research from theoretical risk assessment towards preventive strategies. This study has several limitations. First, some participants in the original data were excluded from the final analysis due to missing information. Although statistical weighting was applied, selection bias may still exist, affecting the generalizability of the results [ 22 ]. Future research should focus on improving data completeness. Second, the definition of the self-medication variable was relatively simplistic, measured only as a binary indicator without distinguishing specific drug categories, dosages, or usage patterns. Given that different drugs have markedly different effects on the gastric mucosa, this limits the clinical interpretability of the results. Subsequent studies should link electronic health records or drug monitoring systems to obtain granular medication data for stratified analyses [ 4 ]. Third, the outcome variable “gastric disease” relied entirely on participant self-report. Although this questionnaire item has been used in previous studies [ 22 , 43 ], it remains subject to recall bias and does not distinguish between specific disease subtypes. Future studies should validate outcomes using objective sources such as clinical diagnostic records, gastroscopy results, or medical insurance claims data. Fourth, limited by the data, this study was unable to assess the impact of high-dose medication or the combined use of multiple drugs, nor did it consider the potential gastric mucosal irritancy of non-active ingredients; these factors may lead to an underestimation of the risk [ 4 , 5 , 11 , 12 ]. Fifth, although the model adjusted for several covariates, there may still be unmeasured important confounders, such as Helicobacter pylori infection status and high-salt diet. Their absence could result in residual confounding, so caution is warranted when interpreting the association, and future prospective studies should systematically collect such information. Finally, as a cross-sectional study, this research cannot determine the temporal sequence between self-medication and gastric disease, nor can it rule out the possibility of reverse causation—that is, gastric discomfort might lead to self-medication behavior. Future studies should adopt longitudinal designs to establish a clear temporal relationship and explore changes in medication behavior before and after the onset of gastric disease to more accurately assess the direction of causality.
sections.conclusion: Based on data from the CHARLS study, this research found a significant positive correlation between self-purchased medication behavior and the risk of gastric diseases among middle-aged and older adults in China, an association that was notably amplified among those with comorbid chronic kidney disease or diabetes. These findings suggest that self-purchasing medication, as well as its interaction with chronic conditions, is a potential risk factor worthy of attention in gastric disease screening for middle-aged and elderly populations. This offers valuable insights for clinical risk identification and the optimization of community-based chronic disease management strategies. Future efforts should strengthen the monitoring and regulation of non-prescription medication use.
