sections.safety: During the double-blind period, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 18.8% (3/16) of patients receiving HDM3010 QD, 12.5% (1/8) receiving vehicle QD, 25.0% (4/16) receiving HDM3010 BID, and 55.6% (5/9) receiving vehicle BID, yielding an overall TEAE incidence of 26.5% (13/49). No TEAE occurred in ≥ 2 patients. Most TEAEs were grade 1 or 2. A single resolved grade 3 hypertensive aggravation occurred in one patient in the HDM3010 BID group and was considered possibly unrelated to study treatment. No TEAEs or serious adverse events resulted in treatment discontinuation or study withdrawal, and no AESIs. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were infrequent, occurring in 4.1% (2/49) of participants, all in the HDM3010 groups (one each in the QD and BID cohorts). One patient in the HDM3010 QD group experienced grade 1 elevated free triiodothyronine and transient grade 1 application-site pruritus and pain, all of which resolved without intervention. Another patient in the HDM3010 BID group developed grade 1 elevated alanine aminotransferase which resolved without treatment interruption and concurrent grade 2 elevated gamma-glutamyl transferase; this patient had a pre-existing history of fatty liver disease and positive serology for hepatitis B core and e antibodies. HDM3010 demonstrated favorable local tolerability without an apparent dose-related pattern (Online Resource Table S1 ).
sections.pk: PK analyses were conducted in 32 patients with PN. The median initial administered doses on D1 were 9.53 mg in the QD group and 12.7 mg in the BID group. Following the initial dose on D1, systemic exposure was low in both cohorts. The geometric mean C max was higher in the BID group than in the QD group (1.14 vs. 0.513 ng/mL), whereas geometric mean area under the concentration–time curve (AUC 0– t ) values were similar (7.73 vs. 7.44 h·ng/mL, respectively) (Online Resource Table S2 ). After multiple doses, the drug concentration reached a steady state, with reduced peak-to-trough fluctuations compared to the first dose. The observed accumulation ratio is approximately 3–4 (Online Resource Figs. S2 – 3 ). Plasma concentration–time profiles on D29 demonstrated stable and sustained exposure at extremely low levels throughout the dosing interval (Online Resource Fig. S3 ).
sections.efficacy: During the double-blind period, HDM3010 showed a consistent trend toward greater improvement in pruritus compared with vehicle. Higher proportions of participants achieved a ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline in weekly average WI-NRS scores in the HDM3010 groups than in the vehicle groups at weeks 1, 2, and 4, with response rates increasing over time. Greater mean reductions from baseline in the WI-NRS, IGA PN-S, and IGA PN-A scores were also observed with HDM3010 relative to vehicle (Figs. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ). Although these differences did not reach statistical significance, likely because of the limited sample size, the directionally consistent findings across endpoints provide preliminary evidence supporting the potential efficacy of HDM3010 in PN. Fig. 1 Proportion of patients achieving a ≥ 4-point improvement from baseline in weekly average Worst Itch Numerical Rating Scale (WI-NRS) score Fig. 2 Change from baseline in weekly average Worst Itch Numerical Rating Scale (WI-NRS) score Fig. 3 Change from baseline in Investigator’s Global Assessment for Prurigo Nodularis–Stage (IGA PN-S) score Fig. 4 Change from baseline in Investigator’s Global Assessment for Prurigo Nodularis–Activity (IGA PN-A) score To further illustrate lesion-level improvement, three representative patient cases are presented. As shown in Online Resource Fig. S4 – 7 , from baseline to week 4, treatment with HDM3010 was associated with a reduction in the number and size of nodular lesions, decreased erythema and infiltration, and improvement in pruritus-related excoriations.
sections.discussion: This study demonstrated that topical 1.5% ruxolitinib gel (HDM3010) was generally safe and well tolerated in adults with PN. The incidence of TEAEs was comparable between HDM3010- and vehicle-treated groups. PK analyses confirmed rapid absorption following initial administration; however, key systemic exposure parameters remained at relatively low levels in both cohorts. Across multiple efficacy endpoints, including improvement in WI-NRS scores and reductions in IGA PN-S and IGA PN-A scores, HDM3010 consistently demonstrated positive trends relative to vehicle, supporting its favorable safety, tolerability, and low systemic exposure, and providing preliminary evidence of clinical benefit. Management of PN remains challenging. Conventional topical therapies (corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors) are limited by local adverse effects or systemic risks, and further constrained by a lack of high-level evidence supporting their efficacy in PN, restricting their utility. Although approved biologics (dupilumab, nemolizumab) represent advances, and systemic JAK inhibitors show potential efficacy, both carry risk linked to systemic exposure. In contrast, topical delivery of ruxolitinib gel enables localized drug exposure at lesional sites while mitigating systemic risks associated with oral JAK inhibition. This localized therapeutic approach is particularly relevant for PN, a chronic condition often requiring sustained treatment, in which cumulative systemic risk is a major clinical concern. The safety profile observed with HDM3010 is consistent with that reported for other topical JAK inhibitors. TEAEs were comparable to vehicles and TRAEs were infrequent, typically mild to moderate in severity. These findings align with phase III TRuE-PN1 and TRuE-PN2 data for ruxolitinib cream in PN, which similarly demonstrated low rates of application-site reactions and no grade ≥ 3 TRAEs [ 21 ]. Comparable safety outcomes were reported in phase III trials in atopic dermatitis, in which ruxolitinib cream showed similar or lower adverse event rates compared with vehicle [ 22 ]. Collectively, these data support the favorable safety profile of topical JAK inhibition in inflammatory skin diseases [ 23 ]. Mechanistically, topical JAK1/2 inhibitors may disrupt the interferon-gamma (IFNγ)–CXCL10–CD8 + T cell trafficking axis within the lesional area, thereby achieving therapeutic effects while minimizing systemic immunosuppression, which may underlie the observed tolerability of ruxolitinib gel [ 16 , 18 , 24 – 27 ]. While the whole-blood JAK2 inhibition IC 50 of orally administered ruxolitinib is 281 nM, HDM3010 exhibits rapid cutaneous absorption and minimal systemic exposure (steady-state mean peak concentration < 7 ng/mL, < 10% of the oral IC 50 )—a pharmacokinetic profile providing a mechanistic basis for minimizing risks typical of systemic JAK inhibition [ 28 ]. These findings are consistent with earlier studies in healthy volunteers demonstrating substantially lower systemic exposure with HDM3010 compared with the reference ruxolitinib cream (the geometric mean ratios (T/R) for C max , AUC 0– t , and AUC 0–∞ were 29.29%, 33.38%, and 34.33%, respectively). Although limited by sample size and treatment duration, HDM3010 demonstrated efficacy trends across multiple clinically relevant endpoints that were consistent with phase III data for ruxolitinib cream. Pooled analyses from the TRuE-PN1 and TRuE-PN2 trials showed that topical 1.5% ruxolitinib cream rapidly and significantly improved pruritus and skin lesions, with sustained superiority over vehicle early in treatment. Improvements in itch and clinical signs were evident as early as week 2 and were maintained through week 24 [ 21 ]. In the present study, although statistical significance was not achieved, directional improvements in WI-NRS, IGA PN-S, and IGA PN-A scores paralleled these phase III findings. The numerically higher response rates observed in the QD group may reflect a greater proportion of patients with milder baseline disease; nevertheless, the BID group, which included a higher proportion of moderate-to-severe cases, demonstrated comparable improvement trends, suggesting potential efficacy across disease severities. Mechanistically, HDM3010 is postulated to attenuate JAK-dependent pruritus signaling in sensory neurons while suppressing cytokine-driven inflammation within lesional skin [ 18 ]. This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. As a phase I/II study, the sample size in each cohort was relatively small and the treatment duration was limited to 8 weeks, which precludes definitive conclusions regarding the long-term safety and efficacy of HDM3010. In addition, the study population was predominantly composed of patients with moderate-to-severe disease (79.6%), which, although representative of a clinically refractory population, may limit generalizability to patients with milder PN. Future phase III randomized controlled trials with larger cohorts, longer treatment durations, and broader disease severity representation are warranted to confirm the long-term safety and efficacy of HDM3010.
sections.conclusions_1: In this phase I/II randomized clinical trial, HDM3010 demonstrated a favorable safety and tolerability profile, minimal systemic exposure, and consistent trends toward greater improvement in pruritus and skin lesion severity compared with vehicle in adults with PN. Collectively, these findings support the continued clinical development of HDM3010 as a novel topical therapeutic option for PN and provide a rationale for subsequent, larger-scale clinical trials to further establish its efficacy and long-term safety.

title: Severe peripheral neuropathy secondary to acute intermittent porphyria caused by a rare HMBS gene mutation: a case report
abstract: Background Peripheral neuropathy is caused by numerous etiologies, such as immune, infectious, neoplastic, metabolic, toxic, traumatic, vasculitic, hereditary factors, etc. Each etiological type has no special manifestation, and the misdiagnosis rate is relatively high. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare disease, often complicated by peripheral nerve injury, and can develop sequelae after delayed diagnosis or treatment. Case presentation A 26-year-old female patient presented with recurrent abdominal pain, limb numbness and weakness, and autonomic neuropathy. Symptoms aggravated and respiratory and circulatory failure develop gradually, following the recurrence of the disease. She was initially diagnosed with neurosis, intestinal obstruction, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. She underwent treatment for inflammatory peripheral neuropathy, including intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and plasmapheresis; however, no improvement in symptoms was observed. Clinical assessment revealed brown urine that turned reddish-brown after sunlight exposure. Whole exome sequencing (WES) identified a mutation in the HMBS gene (exon 10, c.651G > C, p.Gln217His), which was confirmed through Sanger sequencing and diagnosed as rare AIP with severe peripheral nerve damage. Numbness and weakness gradually improved after the initiation of hemin therapy and high-carbohydrate therapy. Conclusion The AIP is an easily missed or misdiagnosed disease. In the absence of timely and effective intervention, patients are at risk of developing irreversible and permanent neurological damage. It is essential for clinicians to enhance their awareness of the disease to ensure prompt diagnosis, appropriate treatment, and avoidance of triggering factors. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12883-026-04893-7.

sections.background_1: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS) gene, resulting in decreased activity of porphobilinogen deaminase in the heme biosynthesis pathway [ 1 ]. The estimated prevalence of AIP is 5–10 cases per 100,000 persons, with acute attacks manifesting in less than 1% of mutation carriers, indicating remarkably low clinical penetrance [ 2 , 3 ]. Peripheral neuropathy represents a severe but well-recognized neurological manifestation of AIP, typically presenting as a motor-predominant axonal neuropathy that may progress to tetraparesis and respiratory insufficiency [ 4 ]. The clinical spectrum ranges from mild distal weakness to a Guillain-Barré-like syndrome, often accompanied by autonomic dysfunction [ 2 , 5 ]. Here, we describe a patient with AIP who presented with severe and irreversible peripheral neuropathy as the predominant clinical feature, highlighting the diagnostic challenges associated with this rare neurological presentation.
sections.clinical history and physical examinatio: A 26-year-old ethnic Han woman from China with a history of abdominal pain, limb weakness, and respiratory failure was admitted to the Department of Neurology on October 6, 2023. She was healthy in the past with no known family history of neurological disorders. Ten months ago, she had abdominal pain and bloating, limb numbness, and weakness after an uncertain infection complicated by fever. On severe days, she requires assistance from family members for ambulation. Antipyretic treatment was administered at the local clinic. These symptoms last more than ten days and gradually return to normal. Eight months ago, similar symptoms relapsed, lasted for 20 days before recovery, and she had a clinical suspicion of neurosis. One month ago, the symptoms described above recurred. She presented with low-grade fever (around 37.5 °C), abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, poor appetite, and loose stools with normal flatulence. Plain film examination, barium meal studies, and abdominal computerized tomography (CT) scans were carried out and excluded intestinal obstruction. Her condition progressively deteriorated with tetraplegia, with only slight finger movement remaining. Disease gradually developed aphasia, dysphagia, and seizures, which suggested the probable involvement of the central nervous system. Then respiratory and circulatory failure aggravated two days before admission to our department. On admission to our department, the patient was confused, and her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 169/119 mmHg, pulse 152/min and regular, body temperature 38.5 °C, and a respiratory rate of 20/min with machine assistance. The neurological examination was limited due to poor patient cooperation. Tetraplegia (0/5, Medical Research Council scale), global muscle hypotonia, and absent tendon reflexes were observed. No pathological reflexes were elicited.
sections.clinical misdiagnosis, treatment, and th: The results of clinical examination and laboratory tests are shown in Table 1 . Guillain-Barré syndrome was suspected as the potential diagnosis. Immunoglobulin therapy was initially given at a dose of 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days, followed by plasma exchange therapy one month after the immunoglobulin treatment. Regrettably, no significant improvement was observed regarding the patient’s limb numbness, or weakness symptoms, other than allowing for intermittent disconnection from the ventilator. Complications, such as deep venous thrombosis, ventilator-associated pneumonia, malnutrition, and sweeny, should be given corresponding treatment. Electromyography of the four limbs revealed multifocal peripheral nerve damage, with no abnormalities in repetitive electrical stimulation (Table 2 ). Head, cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and intracranial magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) demonstrated no evident abnormalities (Fig. 1 ). sections.genetic diagnosis, therapeutic adjustmen: The patient showed little improvement after sufficient immunotherapy. There was no evidence of a tumor or poisoning. So inherited metabolic diseases should be considered. So we exposed her urine to sunlight and found the color changed to reddish-brown (Fig. 1 ). Then carried Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) analysis and detected a mutation in the HMBS gene (exon 10, c.651G > C, p.Gln217His). Sanger sequencing confirmed this mutation in both the proband’s father and brother, who were asymptomatic (Fig. 2 ). This mutation has not been identified in normal population databases (1000Genome, MutIn Database, ESP6500, ExAC). The mutation site has not yet been cataloged in the ClinVar database. The REVEL software assigned a score of 0.979 (> 0.75 indicates predicted pathogenicity), while the ClinPred software yielded a score of 0.9998 (> 0.5 indicates predicted pathogenicity). MutationTaster assessed a pathogenicity score of 1, and conservative prediction is shown in Fig. 2 . Both SIFT and PolyPhen-2 software predicted deleteriousness in protein function. Employing the tertiary protein structural prediction model known as 3EQ1 successfully revealed alterations within protein structure (Fig. 2 ). It is noteworthy that this mutation has been described in the literature previously. The patient, a 31-year-old female, upon presentation exhibited recurrent abdominal pain and significant gastrointestinal hypomotility, which manifested as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and abdominal distension [ 6 ]. This variation is considered likely pathogenic according to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics [ 7 ]. Supplemented by symptomatic supportive care, and active limb rehabilitation therapy. Significant improvements were observed in the muscle strength of both upper limbs (4/5; MRC scale) and both lower limbs (3/5; MRC scale) after six months, but the tendon reflexes remained abolished. The patient continued rehabilitation therapy after removal of the tracheostomy tube.
sections.discussion: AIP is a main form of acute hepatic porphyria (AHP) that can cause severe neurological symptoms involving the central, autonomic, and peripheral nervous system after severe (abdominal) pain [ 8 – 10 ]. AIP exhibits significant geographic and ethnic variability in HMBS mutation prevalence. In the Chinese population, the estimated prevalence of pathogenic HMBS variants is approximately 1 in 1,765 individuals [ 11 ], which differs from that in European populations [ 3 ]. This epidemiological context highlights the rarity of severe AIP-related peripheral neuropathy in our patient population. Acute attacks are more frequent in women, especially in the post-pubertal age group [ 12 ]. The neurologic damage occurs due to the accumulation of the porphyrin precursors, porphobilinogen, and aminolevulinic acid. Depending on the clinical presentation, the main differential diagnoses are Guillain-Barré syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis, or acute myelitis [ 10 , 13 , 14 ]. Severe AIP-related peripheral neuropathy is rarely reported in the literature [ 6 ]. The patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, limb numbness and weakness, and autonomic neuropathy. Peripheral neuropathy and seizure-like episodes emerged, then aggravated to respiratory and circulatory failure following the recurrence of the disease. Neurophysiological examination shows the involvement of both axons and myelin, predominantly affecting the lower limbs. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed during the late stage of seizures exhibited no discernible lesions, suggesting a presentation similar to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome [ 15 ]. Autonomic symptoms mainly manifested as intractable nausea, vomiting, tenderness upon palpation of the lower abdomen, and tachycardia. CSF results are normal, as previously reported [ 8 ]. Electrophysiological studies revealed reduced amplitudes and conduction velocities, while F-wave persistence rates remained normal—a finding that distinguishes this condition from Guillain-Barré syndrome. The conventional treatment modalities for Guillain-Barré syndrome, including intravenous immunoglobulin G (IVIG) and plasma exchange, showed limited efficacy in this patient. WES identified a mutation in the HMBS gene, which was confirmed through Sanger sequencing and diagnosed as AIP. Following the confirmation, treatment comprised administration of hemin and high-carbohydrate therapy while incorporating rehabilitation exercises targeting limb function. Medications metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes (such as barbitone, valproic acid, and metoclopramide) were avoided throughout the treatment process. Gradual recovery of muscle strength was observed in the patient’s condition over time. The patient intermittently presented with chest tightness, tachycardia, and tea-colored urine, suggesting the presence of acute AIP episodes during the recovery phase. Following administration of hemin and high-carbohydrate therapy, a notable amelioration of symptoms was observed with no further exacerbations. AIP always gets delayed diagnosis or misdiagnosis due to relative rarity, nonspecific symptoms, and similarities with other diseases. Prompt initiation of treatment and avoidance of triggers are pivotal in effective management. Failure to promptly intervene or inadequate intervention may result in enduring neurological damage. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, as a single case report, the generalizability of our findings is inherently limited, and the observed phenotype may not represent the full spectrum of HMBS-related neuropathies. Second, while nerve conduction studies confirmed severe axonal loss, a nerve biopsy was not performed given the patient’s condition, which could have provided additional insights into the underlying pathology. Although this report provides valuable insights into AIP-related neuropathy, the findings should be validated in prospective studies with larger sample sizes. Further research, including functional studies of the HMBS mutation, is needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the severe axonal damage observed in this patient.

title: Associations of Brain Morphology and Cognitive Function With Ambulatory Estimated Pulse Wave Velocity
abstract: Background Inconsistent links between arterial stiffness and cognition may reflect limited cognitive tests and unaccounted diurnal pulse wave velocity variation. To bridge this knowledge gap, we investigated 24‐hour ambulatory estimated pulse wave velocity (ePWV) and its association with dementia‐related neuroimaging and cognitive function in hypertension. Methods We assessed 893 patients with hypertension aged ≥50 years (mean age, 67.2 years; 52.3% women), including brain magnetic resonance imaging (n=545), global cognitive testing (n=623), and ambulatory ePWV measurements. White matter hyperintensity and hippocampus were quantified via Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12 and Statistical Parametric Maps 12. Cognition was assessed via the Mini‐Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Results Among 623 tested participants, the prevalence of mild cognitive impairment was 10% (Mini‐Mental State Examination, n=62) and 18.5% (Montreal Cognitive Assessment, n=115). Cognitive scores decline with higher white matter hyperintensity burden and lower hippocampal volume ( P ≤0.024). Higher 24‐hour ePWV quartiles showed graded associations with higher white matter hyperintensity volume and lower hippocampal volume (both P <0.001) and lower cognitive scores ( P ≤0.037). Multivariable models showed each 1‐SD (+1.2 m/s) increment in 24‐hour ePWV were associated with 2.00±1.74 mL greater white matter hyperintensity volume ( P =0.004), and 0.54±0.14 mL smaller hippocampal volume ( P <0.001), independent of age, systolic blood pressure, and other confounders. These associations persisted after further adjustment for carotid–femoral PWV, which itself showed no independent association ( P ≥0.18). Results were consistent for daytime and nighttime ePWV and across key subgroups. Conclusions Ambulatory ePWV is an independent risk factor for dementia‐related brain pathology. Targeting arterial stiffness represents a promising strategy for dementia prevention.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: To bridge the knowledge gap on inconsistent links between arterial stiffness and cognitive decline due to limited cognitive tests and unaccounted diurnal pulse wave velocity variation, we investigated 24‐hour ambulatory estimated pulse wave velocity in relation to neuroimaging and cognitive function in patients with hypertension.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Over and beyond traditional risk factors, increased arterial stiffness, as measured by ambulatory estimated pulse wave velocity, is independently associated with greater white matter hyperintensity burden and smaller hippocampal volume. Novel strategies targeting arterial stiffness represent a promising avenue for the prevention and mitigation of dementia.
sections.data availability: All available data are shown within the article and the online Supplemental Material . The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.study cohort: Our study participants were consecutive patients hospitalized at the translational research ward of the Department of Hypertension, Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China. We adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. 16 The Ethics Committee of Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine approved the study. All study participants gave informed written consent. From February 2021 to April 2025, 1967 patients aged ≥50 years who had undergone 24‐hour central hemodynamic recordings were recruited. After exclusion of patients who lacked both brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and cognitive function assessment (n=1056), whose ambulatory BP and ePWV recording included <8 daytime and 4 nighttime qualified readings (n=18), the number of participants statistically analyzed totaled 893, of whom 270 had isolated brain MRI data, 348 had isolated cognitive function assessment, and 275 had both brain MRI data and cognitive function assessment (Figure S1 ).
sections.bp and arterial properties: We programmed validated 17 Mobil‐O‐Graph PWA monitors (IEM, Stolberg, Germany) to obtain BP and ePWV readings at 20‐minute intervals from 06:00 am to 10:00 pm and at 30‐minute intervals from 10:00 pm to 06:00 am . ePWV was calculated from noninvasively measured BP and peripheral waveforms processed with the validated 18 ARCSolver method (AIT Austrian Institute of Technology, Vienna, Austria). This algorithm estimates ePWV using a model that incorporates the patient's age, central systolic BP, and characteristic impedance obtained via wave separation analysis. The ARCSolver software also grades the quality of the signal from 1 to 4. Results of excellent or good quality are labeled 1 and 2 and include >80% and 50% of the cardiac cycles during signal acquisition, respectively. Grade 3 results are estimated from <50% of the recorded cycles. Grade 4 indicates missing results. The analysis was limited to hemodynamic measurements of grade 1 or 2 quality and to the first 24 hours of ambulatory recordings that contained a minimum of 8 daytime and 4 nighttime readings. Daytime and nighttime intervals were defined using sleeping time reported by diary cards. The daytime, nighttime, and 24‐hour BP and ePWV means were weighted for the time interval between consecutive readings. The readings taken during siesta were excluded when calculating daytime hemodynamic indices. The daytime‐to‐nighttime change in ePWV was defined as daytime ePWV minus nighttime ePWV. A subgroup of 625 participants allowed us to compare the association between carotid–femoral and ambulatory ePWV in relation to brain morphology (n=360) and cognitive function (n=504). The carotid and femoral arterial waveforms at the patient's right side were measured by applanation tonometry. Trained technicians used a high‐fidelity SPC‐301 micromanometer (Milar Instruments, Houston, TX) interfaced with a laptop computer, running the SphygmoCor software version 9.0 (AtCor Medial, West Ryde, New South Wales, Australia). 19 Pulse wave travel distance was the distance from the suprasternal notch to the femoral sampling site minus the distance from the suprasternal notch to the carotid sampling site. Pulse transit time was the average of 10 consecutive heartbeats. PWV is the ratio of the travel distance in meters to transit time in seconds.
sections.brain mri and cognitive function assessm: Brain MRI was performed using the 3.0 Tesla MR scanner (GE Architect). The scanning protocol included 3‐dimensional T1‐weighted images (repetition time, 8.1 ms; echo time, 2.7 ms; field of view, 240×240 mm 2 ; slice thickness, 0.5 mm; flip angle, 8.0°; number of excitations, 1), T2‐weighted images (repetition time, 6.5 ms; echo time, 140 ms; field of view, 12.0×12.0 mm 2 ; slice thickness, 2.40 mm; flip angle, 160°; number of excitations, 1), and fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery sequences (repetition time. 6.5 ms; echo time, 140 ms; field of view, 12.0×12.0 mm 2 ; slice thickness, 2.40 mm; flip angle, 160°; number of excitations = 1). Data processing workflow consisted of a voxel‐based processing using the Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12 (Structural Brain Imaging Group, University of Jena, Jena, Germany) and the Statistical Parametric Maps 12 software, 20 running in Matlab (R2017a; The Mathworks Inc., Natick, MA). Images were visually checked for artifacts as well as undergoing the standard quality assurance protocol for image homogeneity implemented in Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12 software. Regions‐of‐interest volumes were estimated and quantified on the basis of the Cobra atlas in Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12 toolbox. For further details of the brain imaging data acquisition and preprocessing, see Expanded Methods (Data S1 , Figure S2 ). Among all the regions of interest estimated in the current study, we focused on volumes of white matter hyperintensity (WMH), hippocampus, middle temporal gyrus, and superior parietal gyrus, which were significantly associated with Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE)/Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. The global cognitive function was assessed using the Chinese version of the MMSE and MoCA, via the face‐to‐face interview with the well‐trained technician. Both tests have a total score of 30 points. Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) was defined using education‐adjusted cutoff points. For MMSE, the cutoff scores were 25, 27, and 29 for subjects with no education, primary (elementary), and secondary (junior) and above, respectively. 21 For MoCA, the cutoff scores were 13, 19, and 24 for subjects with no education, primary (elementary), and secondary (junior) and above, respectively. 22
sections.other measurements: Participants wore light indoor clothing without shoes for body weight measurement. Body height was measured to the nearest 0.5 cm. Body mass index was the weight in kilograms divided by the height in meters squared. After the participants had fasted overnight, venous blood samples were drawn for the measurement of serum creatinine, serum total and high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and plasma glucose. Diabetes was defined as a fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L or a 2‐hour postfood plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L on an oral glucose tolerance test or the use of antidiabetic agents. 23 Smoking and drinking were defined as self‐reported current smoking and drinking alcohol at least weekly during the past year, respectively. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was estimated from serum creatinine, according to the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equation. 24
sections.statistical analysis: For database management and statistical analysis, we used the SAS software version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC). Means were compared using the large‐sample Z test or ANOVA. Proportions were compared by Fisher's exact test. A Cochran–Armitage trend test was performed for the linear trend. Statistical significance was a 2‐sided probability of ≤0.05. We performed univariable and multivariable ANOVA to study the distribution of brain morphology volumes across quartiles of 24‐hour ePWV. We performed multivariable linear regression analysis to study the association of 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV with brain morphology volumes and MMSE/MoCA scores. The adjusted analysis of brain morphology was for total intracranial volume. Fully adjusted models further accounted for sex, age, body mass index, heart rate and systolic BP, current smoking and drinking, serum high‐density lipoprotein and low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, eGFR, and diabetes. For ambulatory ePWV included in multivariable models, the assumption of linearity was assessed using restricted cubic spline with 3 internal knots located at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of their distributions. Departure from linearity was evaluated using a Wald test for the nonlinear spline components. In patients who had both ambulatory ePWV and carotid–femoral PWV measured (n=625), concordance between the 2 PWV assessments was studied by correlation analysis, intraclass correlation coefficient analysis, and the Bland–Altman method after normalization. For normalization, each PWV measurement was centered by subtracting its mean and scaled by dividing by the corresponding SD. Multivariable linear regressions were performed to explore the association between ambulatory and carotid–femoral PWV and brain morphology, after being mutually adjusted one for another. Finally, sensitivity analyses were performed to replicate the results for the multivariable‐adjusted correlations according to age (≥65 years) and eGFR (≥60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ) and in the presence of a history of cardiovascular disease and primary hypertension.
sections.characteristics of participants: The 893 study participants had a mean±SD age of 67.2±6.6 years, and included 467 (52.3%) women, 350 (39.2%) patients with diabetes, and 819 (91.7%) patients on antihypertensive treatment (Table 1 ). The proportions of cigarette smoking and alcohol intake were 0.2% and 0.2%, respectively, among women and 37.3% and 20.7%, respectively, among men. Overall, mean values were 25.6±3.3 kg/m 2 for body mass index, 78.7±17.0 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 for eGFR, and 1.20±0.29 and 2.62±0.85 mmol/L for serum high‐density lipoprotein and low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, respectively. The median number (5th–95th percentile) of 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime BP measurements were 59 (43–65), 40 (26–49), and 16 (10–22), respectively. The corresponding values for ePWV were 55 (36–63), 37 (21–47), and 15 (9–21), respectively. Twenty‐four‐hour BP and ePWV averaged 129.7±14.6/78.6±10.5 mm Hg and 9.5±1.2 m/s, respectively. Systolic/diastolic BP, heart rate, and ePWV significantly decreased from the daytime to nighttime by 6.3/6.6 mm Hg, 9.3 beats/min and 0.2 m/s, respectively ( P <0.001; Figure S3 ). Across increasing quartiles of 24‐hour ePWV, participants were significantly ( P <0.001) older and had higher systolic BP and higher prevalence of diabetes. Concurrently, we observed significant trends of increasing WMH volume ( P <0.001) and decreasing hippocampal volume and MMSE/MoCA scores ( P ≤0.037; Table 1 ). Among 623 tested participants, the prevalence of MCI was 10% (MMSE, n=62) and 18.5% (MoCA, n=115).
sections.correlations between brain morphology an: Men had a larger total intracranial volume compared with women (1506.3 versus 1335.1 mL, P <0.001) and hippocampal volume (6.75 versus 6.29 mL, P <0.001) and tended to have higher WMH volume (7.31 versus 6.63 mL, P =0.17). In both sexes, WMH volume was significantly higher with older age ( P for trend<0.001), whereas the opposite was true for hippocampal volume ( P for trend<0.001; Figure 1 ). The correlations between cognitive function, assessed by MMSE/MoCA scores, and brain morphology were statistically significant ( P ≤0.024) for specific regions: positively with the volumes of the hippocampus, middle temporal gyrus, and superior parietal gyrus (correlation coefficients, 0.140–0.206), and inversely with WMH volume (correlation coefficients, −0.147 to −0.139; Table S1 ). MMSE and MoCA scores increased from 25.6 to 26.4, and from 22.8 to 24.7, respectively, across increasing quartiles of hippocampal volume (Figure 2 ). Similar trends were observed for middle temporal gyrus and superior parietal gyrus (Figure S4 ). A nonsignificant decreasing trend was observed for WMH volume (Figure 2 ).
sections.associations of ambulatory epwv with bra: A significant gradient was observed across 24‐hour ePWV quartiles, with increasing WMH volume from 4.39 to 9.24 mL and decreasing hippocampal volume from 6.81 to 6.21 mL, after accounting for total intracranial volume ( P <0.001). The inverse association with hippocampal volume remained statistically significant in a model fully adjusted for sex, age, body mass index, 24‐hour heart rate, 24‐hour systolic BP, current smoking and drinking, serum high‐density lipoprotein and low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, eGFR, and diabetes ( P =0.042; Figure 3 ). The volumes of the middle temporal gyrus and superior parietal gyrus also exhibited inverse associations across 24‐hour ePWV quartiles in analysis adjusted for total intracranial volume but not in fully adjusted analysis (Figure S5 ). Restricted cubic spline analyses showed no significant deviation from linearity for 24‐hour ePWV included in the multivariable models ( P ≥0.07); therefore, linear terms were retained. In fully adjusted multivariable regression analyses, each 1‐SD increment (+1.2 m/s) in 24‐hour ePWV was significantly associated with 2.00±1.74‐mL greater WMH volume, and 0.54±0.14‐mL smaller hippocampal volume (Table 2 ). The results were consistent when 24‐hour ePWV was replaced with daytime and nighttime ePWV (Table S2 ). In addition, the daytime‐to‐nighttime change in ePWV was significantly and inversely associated with WMH volume, each 1‐SD increment (+0.37 m/s) in ePWV change was associated with 0.75±0.23‐mL smaller WMH volume. No other association between the daytime‐to‐nighttime ePWV change and measures of brain morphology or cognitive function reached statistical significance in fully adjusted models (Table S2 ). Compared with subjects without MCI, those with MCI (MMSE defined, n=62) exhibited significantly higher nighttime ePWV (9.73 versus 9.40 m/s, P =0.040), with higher 24‐hour and daytime ePWV that did not reach statistical significance (n=561, 9.52 versus 9.30 m/s, P =0.067; 9.86 versus 9.60 m/s, P =0.085, respectively). MCI, defined by MoCA score (n=115), showed significantly higher 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV compared with subjects without MCI (n=508, 9.77 versus 9.50 m/s, P =0.024; 9.82 versus 9.58 m/s, P =0.039; and 9.68 versus 9.38 m/s, P =0.013, respectively).
sections.sensitivity and subgroup analyses: Further analysis showed consistent results on the regression coefficients for 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV in relation to the WMH and hippocampal volume across subgroups according to age (≥65 years), eGFR (≥60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ), and in the presence of a history of cardiovascular disease and primary hypertension (Table S3 ). A subgroup analysis was performed to compare carotid–femoral PWV with ambulatory ePWV in 625 subjects. The correlation coefficients between carotid–femoral PWV and 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV were 0.43, 0.42, and 0.44, respectively ( P <0.001). The intraclass correlation coefficients between carotid–femoral PWV and 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV were 0.39, 0.38, and 0.40, respectively ( P <0.001). After normalization of both PWV indices, Bland–Altman analysis was conducted to assess the agreement between the carotid–femoral and ambulatory ePWV (Figure S6 ). The mean differences (±1.96 SD) were 0.004±2.086 normalized unit for 24‐hour ePWV, 0.002±2.107 for daytime ePWV, and 0.004±2.071 for nighttime ePWV. In a further subgroup of 360 subjects with both carotid–femoral and 24‐hour PWV measurements and brain morphology, significant associations with WMH and hippocampal volumes were observed for ambulatory ePWV measurements, either 24‐hour, daytime, or nighttime, even after adjustment for carotid–femoral PWV but not for carotid–femoral PWV in multivariable models (Table 3 ). No significant evidence of nonlinearity was observed for PWV measures in the multivariable models ( P ≥0.29).
sections.discussion: The key findings of the current study can be summarized as follows. First, the expected age‐related patterns of cognitive decline, as assessed by MMSE and MoCA scores, were accompanied by decreased hippocampal volume and increased WMH burden. Second, higher ambulatory ePWV was independently associated with lower hippocampal volume and greater WMH volume, even after adjustment for BP and other covariates. Third, these significant associations for ambulatory ePWV persisted after adjustment for carotid–femoral PWV. In contrast, carotid–femoral PWV itself showed no independent associations with these brain structural measurements. Our observation on hippocampal atrophy and WMH accumulation as markers of cognitive impairment is consistent with the results of several previous studies. 25 An inverse relationship between arterial stiffness and cerebral small‐vessel disease has been well established. 3 , 4 , 26 However, the role of PWV in the deterioration of brain structure 12 , 13 , 27 , 28 , 29 and function 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 in relation to cognition remains controversial. In a systematic review of 28 large‐scale studies published from 2007 to 2022, Aimagambetova and coworkers highlighted the overwhelming reliance on a single office visit for PWV assessment, with carotid–femoral PWV being the predominant method (n=24). 30 Our study advances this field by using 24‐hour ePWV and adjusting for ambulatory BP, in contrast with 4 previous studies that only adjusted for hypertension status. 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 Furthermore, among 12 studies that included MRI data, 3 , 4 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 31 , 32 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 6 quantified WMH volumes, 27 , 28 , 29 , 32 , 35 , 36 and 6 others focused on other markers of cerebral small‐vessel disease 3 , 4 , 26 , 31 , 37 or white matter free water. 38 Nevertheless, in a recent population‐based study in 1488 adults, 12 whose ages ranged from 22.8 to 83.9 years, each 1‐SD (+3.2 m/s) higher brachial–ankle PWV was associated with 0.08 mL (95% CI, 0.04–0.13) smaller hippocampal volume, and hippocampal volume partially mediated the association between PWV and MoCA scores. 12 The significant associations we observed were confined to ambulatory ePWV and brain morphology, a pattern consistent with findings from the Framingham Offspring Study. 35 In that study, higher carotid–femoral PWV was associated with lower total cerebral brain volume, greater WMH volume, and a higher prevalence of silent cerebral infarcts; however, the associations with neurocognitive outcomes, specifically logical memory‐delayed recall and Trails B‐A score, did not reach statistical significance. 35 Despite the close correlations between cognitive function and brain morphology (Table S1 ), structural brain changes, such as those assessed by WMH and hippocampal volumes, may precede detectable cognitive decline and serve as earlier markers of neurodegeneration, particularly given the limited sensitivity of global cognitive tests. Although the brain constitutes only 2% of the total body weight, it is densely vascularized with high‐flow, low‐resistance perfusion, receiving up to 20% of cardiac output. This results in a close coupling between cerebral blood flow and systemic hemodynamics. This reliance makes the constant cerebral blood flow dependent on stable systemic hemodynamics, with arterial stiffness being a primary factor that can disrupt this equilibrium. Increased arterial stiffness transmits excessive pulsatile energy into the cerebral microvasculature, which can impair cerebral flow regulation and contribute to cognitive decline. 2 While not directly assessed in the present study, impaired cerebral perfusion resulting from heightened transmission of pulsatile energy may mediate the observed associations between arterial stiffness and neurodegeneration. Supporting this hypothesis, a retrospective cohort study of 112 participants reported significantly lower cerebral blood flow in posterior cingulate, parietal, medial temporal, frontal, and occipital cortices in individuals with faster rates of aortic stiffening. 39 Future studies examining the mediating mechanisms linking PWV to cognitive dysfunction are warranted. Although no interventional studies have specifically targeted arterial stiffness to improve cerebrovascular function and resilience against cognitive decline, drugs that reduce arterial stiffening may be particularly beneficial for mitigating cognitive impairment in aging. A post hoc analysis of SPRINT‐MIND (Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial–Memory and Cognition in Decreased Hypertension) investigated the association between formula‐based PWV, calculated with age and mean BP, and cognitive outcomes in 4278 patients undergoing intensive BP lowering to a systolic BP of <120 mm Hg and 4285 patients on a standard target of <140 mm Hg. Compared with the bottom tertile, the top tertile of PWV was associated with higher risk of probable dementia (hazard ratio [HR], 1.70 [95% CI, 1.08–2.68]) and MCI (HR, 2.35 [95% CI, 1.71–3.23]). The study further introduced the concept of PWV response after antihypertensive treatment, whose PWV increased by ≤0.15 m/s from baseline to the 12‐month follow‐up. Within the intensive treatment group, PWV nonresponders exhibited a significantly higher incidence of probable dementia or MCI compared with treatment responders (log‐rank test, P =0.002). 40
sections.clinical implications: Given the established physiological importance of arterial stiffness in cerebrovascular disease, vasoactive drugs that target arterial stiffness and pulsatile hemodynamics 41 represent a promising therapeutic avenue of mitigating cognitive decline. This potential is supported by the LACI‐2 (Lacunar Intervention Trial‐2) study, 42 in 363 participants assigned in a 2×2 factorial design to receive isosorbide mononitrate, cilostazol, both, or no study drug for 12 months. Compared with those participants not receiving the particular drug, treatment with isosorbide mononitrate alone was associated with a significantly reduced odds of cognitive impairment (adjusted odds ratio, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.36–0.86]). This benefit was also observed for the combination therapy of isosorbide mononitrate with cilostazol (adjusted odds ratio, 0.44 [95% CI, 0.23–0.85]). Notably, this protective effect was achieved independent of BP changes. The means BP in the isosorbide mononitrate group was 143.0/84.0 mm Hg at baseline and 143.0/82.4 mm Hg at 12 months, which was 1.83/0.45 mm Hg higher than in the group not receiving the drug. 42 By acting as a nitric oxide donor and a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, respectively, isosorbide mononitrate and cilostazol improve endothelial function, leading to reduced arterial stiffness. 2
sections.strengths and limitations: Our study moved beyond current knowledge in several ways. First, we comprehensively assessed 24‐hour, daytime, and nighttime ePWV, moving beyond a single office measurement. A direct comparison revealed that ambulatory ePWV, unlike carotid–femoral PWV, was consistently associated with brain health, offering a potential explanation for previous negative findings based solely on office readings. Second, our study extended the measurements beyond cognitive scores to include more regional specificity in neuroimaging, such as hippocampal atrophy and WMH accumulation, which are known to precede the onset of MCI. Third, our analytical approach rigorously accounted for ambulatory BP levels and hence allowed for exploring independent associations. Notwithstanding these strengths, the present study must also be interpreted within the context of its limitations. First, the cross‐sectional design of our study does not allow making inferences about causality or temporality. Previous meta‐analyses of 9 longitudinal studies have reported pooled effect sizes for the association between PWV and global cognition, executive function, and memory of −0.21, −0.12, and −0.05, respectively. 8 However, these assessments were based on clinic rather than ambulatory PWV measurements, underscoring the need for longitudinal studies using ambulatory PWV. Second, fewer patients with carotid–femoral PWV measurements may limit the statistical power to detect any association between a single visit of PWV and markers of cognitive impairment. Third, the generalizability of our findings may be limited, as the study was a hospital‐based study conducted in an Asian population, which has a higher propensity for stroke compared with community‐based or other ethnic cohorts. Although a similar inverse association between 24‐hour ePWV and brain atrophy was observed in a small community‐based Austrian cohort (n=84), 15 further validation in more diverse populations is warranted. Fourth, although we adjusted for major confounders including age and ambulatory BP, residual confounders cannot be fully excluded. Specifically, data on lifestyle behaviors and psychosocial factors were not available, which may have influenced the observed associations.
sections.perspectives: Over and beyond traditional risk factors, increased arterial stiffness, as measured by ambulatory ePWV, is independently associated with cognitive decline. With established treatments for neurocognitive disorders offering limited efficacy, novel strategies that address modifiable vascular mechanisms, particularly those influencing large‐artery and cerebrovascular function, represent a promising avenue for the prevention and mitigation of dementia.

title: Histology-validated comparison of angioscopy, IVUS, and OFDI for assessing stent strut coverage in femoropopliteal arteries with thin neointima
abstract: In-stent thrombotic occlusion remains a major clinical challenge after femoropopliteal stenting, and delayed healing is believed to contribute to this problem. However, conventional intravascular imaging may struggle to evaluate vascular healing due to limited resolution, particularly in thin neointima. This study aimed to validate the diagnostic performance of angioscopy for assessing endothelial strut coverage in thin neointima using histology as the reference standard. In a healthy swine model, 22 femoropopliteal arteries were evaluated one month after stenting. Ex vivo angioscopy, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), and optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) were performed. Endothelial strut coverage was assessed in segments with neointimal thickness < 1000 μm (thin neointima) using histology as the gold standard. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) for detecting endothelial-covered struts were calculated. A total of 112 co-registered image sets were obtained, of which 62 were classified as thin neointima. Histology identified endothelial-covered struts in 8 of 62 segments (12.9%). Angioscopy color assessment showed a sensitivity of 100%, specificity of 92%, PPV of 60%, and NPV of 100%. In contrast, IVUS and OFDI demonstrated a high sensitivity for detecting endothelial-covered struts; however, overestimated coverage and failed to distinguish endothelial-covered struts from fibrin-covered struts (sensitivity 100%, specificity 0%, PPV 15%). While IVUS and OFDI overestimate endothelial stent coverage in thin neointima, angioscopy offers superior diagnostic accuracy for identifying fibrin-covered struts and may serve as a valuable modality for assessing vascular healing in femoropopliteal arteries, potentially facilitating the optimization of antithrombotic therapy. sections.introduction: The global prevalence of lower extremity artery disease (LEAD) in adults is estimated at 9.7%, and LEAD is a growing global health concern, leading to a significant increase in both endovascular therapy (EVT) and surgical bypass procedures [ 1 – 3 ]. In recent years, EVT has become the primary treatment strategy for femoropopliteal lesions, and drug-eluting stents (DES) have improved outcomes [ 4 ]. However, the long-term clinical outcomes of femoropopliteal stenting, including bare metal stents and DES, remain suboptimal compared to those in coronary artery interventions [ 5 ], and in-stent thrombotic occlusion remains a major clinical issue [ 6 ]. A previous study has reported that the 1-year restenosis rate after femoropopliteal DES implantation was 12.9%, of which 71% were attributable to in-stent occlusion [ 7 ]. A central goal of post-stent vascular healing is complete endothelialization of stent struts. In coronary arteries, incomplete endothelial strut coverage is a well-established substrate for thrombotic complications [ 8 – 10 ], and confirming coverage in vivo could inform antithrombotic strategy. This concern is heightened in the femoropopliteal segment, where delayed vascular healing is believed to contribute to poorer clinical outcomes [ 11 ]. Previous case reports have demonstrated that delayed vascular healing after DES implantation has been associated with adverse events such as restenosis and stent thrombosis [ 12 , 13 ]. Furthermore, prior angioscopic studies have demonstrated that fibrin deposition around the struts is prone to thrombus attachment and may contribute to stent thrombosis [ 14 ]. Accordingly, accurate in vivo assessment of endothelialization and fibrin coverage is clinically crucial. Although intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) are widely used, their limited resolution often hinders the precise evaluation of neointimal strut coverage [ 15 ]. In contrast, angioscopy offers direct en-face visualization, potentially overcoming these resolution constraints. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility and clinical utility of in vivo angioscopy for assessing stent coverage and thrombus formation [ 16 ]. However, its diagnostic utility in peripheral arteries remains unestablished. Therefore, the present study aimed to validate the accuracy of angioscopy for assessing strut coverage in thin neointima using histology as the reference standard.
sections.study framework: This study represents a sub-study of our broader preclinical swine femoropopliteal stent model project, which originally included a total of 18 swine (36 femoropopliteal arteries) [ 17 ]. The primary objective of the overarching study was to evaluate the differences in stent behavior among various stent types—including bare nitinol and drug-eluting stents—in a healthy, poor below-the-knee runoff model. From this primary cohort, we conducted two focused imaging-based sub-studies. The first sub-study evaluated the characterization of in-stent restenosis tissue using OFDI, IVUS, and angioscopy in segments with thick neointima (≥ 1000 μm), which included 22 arteries from 11 swine. The second imaging sub-study, which constitutes the current investigation, specifically focused on imaging–histology validation in segments with thin neointima (< 1000 μm), utilizing 22 arteries from 11 swine.
sections.animal model and stent implantation proc: The study protocol received approval from the Japanese Association for Laboratory Animal Science (Approval No. IVT22-90, S23-058). All animals were maintained in accordance with the Animal Welfare Act and Public Health Service guidelines. This preclinical ex vivo validation study employed a healthy swine model to investigate vascular healing following femoropopliteal artery stenting, as previously reported [ 17 ]. Briefly, dual antiplatelet therapy was initiated two days prior to the procedure. Under general anesthesia, a 6-French guiding catheter was introduced into the common femoral artery. To reproduce a clinically relevant poor below-the-knee runoff condition—known to be associated with adverse outcomes after femoropopliteal intervention [ 18 ]—coils (VortX-18 Diamond coil, Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) were deployed in the tibial artery. Thereafter, one of three stent types—bare nitinol stents (Innova; strut thickness about 220 μm; Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA), fluoropolymer-based paclitaxel-eluting stents (Eluvia; drug dose 0.167 µg/mm², strut thickness about 220 μm; Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA), or polymer-free paclitaxel-eluting stents (Zilver PTX; drug dose 3.0 µg/mm², strut thickness about 220 μm; Cook Corporation, Bloomington, IN, USA)—was implanted in each femoral artery. All implanted stents were 6.0 × 40 mm in size. All experimental procedures adhered to institutional animal care standards.
sections.vessel harvesting and preparation: At one month, follow-up angiography was performed to evaluate the vascular state. The swine were then euthanized with intravenous pentobarbital and/or potassium. Stented vessels were excised, pressure-perfused with 0.9% saline to remove residual blood, and subsequently fixed by perfusion with 10% formalin. Post-fixation radiography confirmed complete stent expansion without evidence of fracture.
sections.ex vivo intravascular imaging acquisitio: After formalin fixation, the stented arteries were imaged ex vivo while immersed in a 0.9% saline bath. Imaging was performed from the distal to the proximal segments using angioscopy (VISIBLE; FiberTech, Chiba, Japan), IVUS (AltaView, Terumo, Tokyo, Japan), and OFDI (LUNAWAVE, Terumo, Tokyo, Japan). IVUS images were acquired at a pullback rate of 0.5 mm/s, and OFDI images at 20 mm/s [ 19 ]. All imaging data were analyzed at our institution. The stented segments were evaluated at 1-mm intervals. Angioscopic assessment evaluated both neointimal color and coverage grade. Neointimal color was classified as either white or red [ 20 ]; struts covered by white neointima in angioscopy were defined as endothelial-covered struts, whereas those surrounded by red neointima were defined as fibrin-covered struts. Additionally, neointimal coverage was graded using a 4-point scale [ 14 ]: grade 0 (struts fully visible); grade 1 (struts bulging but translucently visible); grade 2 (struts embedded but translucently visible); and grade 3 (struts fully embedded and invisible). In this study, only grade 3 was defined as endothelial-covered struts. For IVUS and OFDI, struts were defined as covered if any identifiable tissue signal (> 0 μm) was visible overlying the struts. This 0 μm threshold was chosen to reflect previous clinical studies, where any detectable tissue layer is often interpreted as an indicator of the coverage, regardless of its thickness [ 15 , 21 ].
sections.histological processing and definition o: Following imaging, stented arteries were embedded in methyl methacrylate resin. The stented segments were cut at 3 mm intervals, and 4–6 μm thick sections were prepared and stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Movat Pentachrome for light microscopic evaluation [ 17 , 22 , 23 ]. Although stents were 40 mm in length and sectioned at 3 mm intervals, not all sections were suitable for final analysis. Sections with significant processing artifacts or inadequate tissue preservation were excluded prior to image co-registration. Neointimal coverage of each strut was classified as either endothelial-covered or fibrin-covered struts according to the following definition. Endothelial coverage was defined as the presence of luminal endothelial cells overlying struts and an underlying smooth muscle cell layer (Fig. 1 ) [ 15 , 24 ]. Struts covered only by fibrin thrombus were considered fibrin-covered. Each segment was defined as endothelial coverage if more than 90% of the struts were endothelial-covered. Fig. 1 Definition of strut coverage. Representative photomicrographs of endothelial-covered struts ( A ) and fibrin-covered struts ( B ) stained with Movat Pentachrome. Endothelial-covered struts were defined as the presence of luminal endothelial cells overlying struts and an underlying smooth muscle cell layer. High-power Movat Pentachrome and hematoxylin and eosin staining images show endothelial-covered (A’ and A’’) and fibrin-covered struts (B’ and B’’). Arrows indicate endothelial cells
sections.image and histology co-registration: Imaging frames from angioscopy, IVUS, and OFDI were co-registered to histological sections using anatomic landmarks and measured distances from stent edges. The analysis focused exclusively on segments where the neointimal thickness was less than 1000 μm based on histological evaluation, which were defined as the “thin neointima group” (Fig. 2 ). Neointimal thickness was defined as the maximum neointimal thickness measured within each histological section, rather than an average thickness across the segment. The predefined cutoff of 1000 μm was therefore applied to the maximum measured thickness per segment. Only segments that fulfilled all the following predefined criteria were included in the final analysis: [ 1 ] adequate histological quality without sectioning artifacts [ 2 ], successful co-registration across angioscopy, IVUS, OFDI, and histology, and [ 3 ] histologically confirmed neointimal thickness < 1000 μm. The primary diagnostic accuracy assessment was subsequently performed on the thin neointima group. Two experienced investigators (N.N. and S.T.), who were blinded to the histological findings, independently evaluated all images to determine coverage status for each modality. Fig. 2 Lesion flowchart for the current study. From 22 swine femoropopliteal arteries, 112 matched images were evaluated. Segments were classified by neointimal thickness: thin (< 1000 μm) vs. thick (≥ 1000 μm). Thin neointima segments were evaluated by angioscopy, IVUS, and OFDI. IVUS: intravascular ultrasound; OFDI: optical frequency domain imaging
sections.statistical analysis: Using histological findings as the gold standard, the diagnostic accuracy of each imaging modality for distinguishing endothelial-covered struts was assessed by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) at the segment level. To address the potential within-animal correlation among multiple histological sections, all diagnostic metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV) were first summarized on a per-animal basis. Each animal was treated as an independent observational unit, and the mean values of each metric were calculated across animals. To estimate the variability and 95% confidence intervals (CI) of these metrics while considering within-animal clustering, we performed cluster bootstrap resampling (2,000 iterations) at the animal level. This method appropriately accounts for the non-independence of observations from the same animals and provides a valid CI for diagnostic performance. Inter-observer agreement between two independent investigators was evaluated for each imaging modality. Cohen’s kappa coefficient was calculated when applicable, and percent agreement was reported when kappa could not be reliably estimated due to limited variability in classification. All statistical analyses were performed using JMP software version Student Edition 18.0 (SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina, USA) and Python software version 1.10.1 (SciPy library; Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, Delaware, USA).
sections.baseline animal and angiographic outcome: All swine completed the scheduled one-month observation period without significant adverse events. Follow-up angiography demonstrated no evidence of vessel dissection, ectasia, or aneurysm. Post-fixation radiographs of the stented arteries confirmed complete stent expansion without fractures. Furthermore, all tibial arteries subjected to coil embolization were fully occluded, accompanied by the development of bridging collateral vessels supplying the affected regions.
sections.histological findings and cohort descrip: A total of 36 femoropopliteal arteries from 18 swine were included in the experimental model. Of these, 112 co-registered sections from 22 arteries in 11 swine fulfilled the predefined criteria—adequate histological quality and successful multimodality co-registration—and were eligible for analysis. Based on maximum neointimal thickness per histological section, 62 sections were classified as thin neointima (< 1000 μm) and included in the primary analysis, whereas 50 Sect.  (44.6%) were categorized as thick neointima (≥ 1000 μm). Within the thin neointima group, the median neointimal thickness was 57 μm (IQR 27–247 μm; range 15–824 μm). Histological evaluation identified 8 of the 62 segments (12.9%) with endothelial-covered struts (Table 1 ). sections.diagnostic accuracy in thin neointima (<: Using histology as the gold standard, the diagnostic performance of each imaging modality for detecting endothelial-covered stent struts was assessed in the thin neointima (Tables 1 and 2 ; Figs. 3 and 4 ). Inter-observer agreement was assessed prior to diagnostic accuracy analysis. For IVUS and OFDI, kappa could not be reliably estimated because one observer classified nearly all segments into a single category; percent agreement was 100% and 98.4%, respectively. Angioscopy demonstrated substantial agreement (κ = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.66–0.99). Angioscopic assessment based on neointimal color accurately detected endothelial-covered segments, with a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 100–100), a specificity of 92% (95% CI: 79.9–100), a PPV of 60% (95% CI: 0.0–100), and an NPV of 100% (95% CI: 100–100). Assessment based on coverage grades identified 13 segments (21.0%) as grade 3, showing acceptable diagnostic performance: sensitivity 67% (95% CI: 20.0–100), specificity 84% (95% CI: 66.7–97.2), PPV 49% (95% CI: 16.7–85.7), and NPV 95% (95% CI: 87.1–100). However, the PPV for both color and coverage grade assessments was approximately 50–60%, suggesting that angioscopy tended to overestimate endothelial coverage—particularly in segments with thick, fibrin-rich neointima—resulting in false positives (Fig. 5 ). In contrast, the diagnostic utility of IVUS and OFDI was limited in this cohort. Both modalities showed a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 0%, with a PPV of 15% and an undefined NPV (Table 3 ). These modalities consistently overestimated endothelial coverage in thin neointima, misclassifying fibrin coverage as endothelial coverage.
