title: STAT3 Signaling in Spinal Cord Injury: Neurochemical Mechanisms Linking Neuroinflammation, Mitochondrial Stress, and Glial Remodeling
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating neurological disorder marked by profound disturbances in cytokine signaling, redox balance, mitochondrial homeostasis, and glial-neuronal communication. Although many therapeutic strategies have been explored to attenuate secondary injury, effective molecularly targeted interventions remain limited. Increasing evidence identifies signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) as a central signaling node in the neurochemical response to SCI. Recent studies indicate that STAT3 exhibits pronounced spatiotemporal and cell-type-specific activation after SCI. Depending on the upstream trigger and cellular compartment involved, STAT3 can amplify or restrain neuroinflammation, shape astrocyte and microglial reactivity, influence mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress, modulate ferroptosis and apoptosis, and alter the regenerative state of the injured spinal cord. In this review, we frame STAT3 not simply as a downstream effector of the JAK/STAT cascade, but as an integrative regulator of SCI neurochemistry that links cytokine-driven signaling to metabolic stress, glial remodeling, and axonal repair. We emphasize how injury phase, cell type, and subcellular localization influence STAT3-dependent outcomes, discuss emerging therapeutic strategies that converge on STAT3-centered pathways, and outline the key challenges that must be addressed for precise translational targeting.

sections.introduction: Preclinical SCI research has addressed both experimental therapeutic delivery systems and early molecular repair responses, including resveratrol-based biodegradable nanoparticles and mTORC1-dependent activation of neural stem/progenitor cells [ 1 , 2 ]. Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a severe neurological disorder caused by traumatic or non-traumatic insults to the spinal cord [ 3 ]. It frequently results in permanent motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction and imposes a substantial burden on patients, families, and healthcare systems worldwide [ 3 ]. Recent advances in surgical management, pharmacological intervention, stem cell-based therapy, neuromodulation, and brain-computer interface-assisted rehabilitation have created new opportunities for functional restoration after SCI [ 4 – 7 ]. Nevertheless, effective strategies for limiting secondary injury and achieving durable neurological recovery remain insufficient. Secondary injury after SCI is not a single event but a dynamic and evolving neurochemical cascade involving cytokine release, redox imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction, excitotoxicity, glial reactivity, and multiple forms of regulated cell death. These interconnected processes drive tissue degeneration but also shape the conditions for repair. Among the signaling pathways implicated in this secondary phase, the JAK/STAT axis—and particularly STAT3—has emerged as a central hub linking inflammatory signals to metabolic adaptation and cell fate decisions [ 8 ]. Experimental evidence further indicates that STAT3 can promote corticospinal remodeling and functional recovery after SCI [ 9 ]. Beyond SCI, context-dependent STAT3 signaling has also been implicated in fibrotic remodeling, oncogenic signaling, and denervation-associated muscle fibrosis, underscoring its broader biological relevance [ 10 – 12 ]. Importantly, STAT3 is neither uniformly detrimental nor uniformly beneficial. Its biological consequences depend on injury stage, cell type, upstream ligand environment, and subcellular localization. In neurons, glia, and vascular-associated cells, STAT3 can support survival and remodeling under some conditions while promoting chronic inflammation, maladaptive gliosis, or oxidative injury under others. This context dependence is essential for understanding how STAT3-dependent molecular signaling is translated into neurochemical imbalance, cellular dysfunction, and reparative remodeling after SCI. In this review, we argue that STAT3 should be viewed as a context-dependent integrator of post-injury neurochemical remodeling rather than a simple linear pathway component. By focusing on how STAT3 connects cytokine signaling, mitochondrial stress, ferroptotic vulnerability, astrocyte reactivity, and regenerative responses, we aim to provide a broadly applicable mechanistic framework and to highlight where future studies should move from descriptive association toward causal, phase-specific, and cell-specific intervention.
sections.structure, function, and neurochemical r: The biological functions of STAT3 are closely tied to its structural organization and post-translational regulation. For SCI, the most relevant question is not only how STAT3 is activated, but how its activation is coupled to cytokine receptor signaling, mitochondrial adaptation, and redox-sensitive pathways in the injured nervous system.
sections.structure and function of stat3: STAT3 is one of the most extensively studied members of the STAT family and consists of 770 amino acids. From the N-terminus to the C-terminus, STAT3 contains six highly conserved domains: the N-terminal domain (NTD), coiled-coil domain (CCD), DNA-binding domain (DBD), linker domain (LD), Src homology 2 (SH2) domain, and transcriptional activation domain (TAD) [ 13 – 16 ]. The NTD contributes to dimer stability, cooperative DNA binding, and nuclear translocation. The CCD mediates interactions with transcriptional cofactors and regulatory proteins. The DBD recognizes and binds specific DNA elements in target genes, whereas the LD stabilizes DNA-binding activity and connects adjacent domains structurally. The SH2 domain is critical for phosphotyrosine recognition and STAT3 dimerization, while the TAD contains regulatory phosphorylation sites that modulate transcriptional efficiency [ 13 – 16 ]. Through the coordinated actions of these domains, STAT3 regulates diverse biological processes, including cell proliferation, differentiation, survival, immune responses, and tissue repair. This multifunctional architecture helps explain why STAT3 can serve as both a homeostatic regulator in the CNS and a context-dependent driver of pathology or repair after SCI. The domain organization of STAT3 and the major phosphorylation sites relevant to SCI are summarized in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Domain organization of STAT3 and major regulatory sites relevant to cytokine, redox, and injury-associated signaling in SCI
sections.regulation of stat3 activity: STAT3 activity is regulated by multiple post-translational modifications that collectively determine its activation status, intracellular localization, stability, and transcriptional output. Tyrosine phosphorylation at Tyr705 represents the classical and most extensively characterized mode of activation [ 16 , 17 ]. In response to cytokines and growth factors, upstream kinases such as JAK family members phosphorylate STAT3 at Tyr705, thereby promoting dimerization, nuclear translocation, DNA binding, and transcriptional activation [ 16 – 18 ]. In addition to Tyr705 phosphorylation, serine phosphorylation at Ser727 is another important regulatory event. Ser727 can modulate transcriptional activity, mitochondrial signaling, and neuroprotective responses [ 19 ]. In the CNS, Tyr705- and Ser727-related programs may cooperate or diverge in a context-dependent manner to influence neuronal survival, axonal regeneration, and inflammatory signaling. STAT3 activity is also shaped by acetylation, methylation, and ubiquitination. Acetyltransferases such as p300/CBP can acetylate STAT3 and alter its DNA-binding capacity or transcriptional selectivity [ 20 , 21 ]. Histone-modifying enzymes and methylation-related mechanisms may further refine STAT3-dependent transcription by influencing chromatin accessibility and target-gene preference [ 22 ]. In addition, ubiquitination mediated by specific E3 ligases affects STAT3 stability and turnover, thereby contributing to fine control of signal duration and intensity [ 23 , 24 ]. Taken together, these regulatory layers allow STAT3 to respond dynamically to extracellular and intracellular stimuli. This multilayered control is particularly relevant in SCI, where inflammatory mediators, oxidative stress, and altered energy metabolism converge to produce a highly dynamic neurochemical environment.
sections.expression of stat3 in the central nervo: STAT3 is widely expressed in the CNS and participates in both developmental and injury-related processes. Its spatial distribution, temporal activation profile, and cell-type specificity are therefore highly relevant to understanding its functions after SCI.
sections.stat3 in spinal cord physiology and inju: STAT3 should be considered in relation to the cellular architecture and functional demands of the spinal cord rather than only as a broadly expressed CNS transcription factor. In the spinal cord, STAT3-responsive pathways are relevant to motor neurons, interneurons, ascending and descending axons, oligodendroglial lineage cells, astrocytes, microglia/macrophages, endothelial cells, pericytes, and ependymal or progenitor-like populations. These cell types participate in segmental motor control, sensory transmission, myelination, barrier maintenance, inflammatory surveillance, and repair responses; therefore, changes in STAT3 signaling can influence both neural circuit integrity and the lesion microenvironment after SCI. Under physiological conditions, STAT3 contributes to CNS development and homeostasis. It participates in the differentiation and functional regulation of neural progenitor cells during embryonic nervous system development [ 25 ]. STAT3 is broadly expressed in the CNS and is engaged by multiple cytokine- and growth factor-dependent pathways [ 26 ]. It has been implicated in neuronal survival, synaptic maintenance, axonal regeneration, and astrocytic differentiation. For example, increased STAT3 activity has been associated with attenuation of tau-induced synaptic deficits and promotion of neuronal survival [ 27 ], whereas exercise-induced changes in STAT3 phosphorylation have been linked to retinal ganglion cell axon regeneration and neuroprotection [ 28 ]. In neural stem cells, STAT3 also regulates astrocytic differentiation through control of GFAP expression and interactions with pathways such as NF-kB [ 29 ]. These general CNS functions are directly relevant to the spinal cord because the same STAT3-linked processes—neuronal survival, axonal growth capacity, glial differentiation, and cytokine responsiveness—are redirected after SCI. In the injured spinal cord, survival-associated STAT3 signaling may influence motor-neuron and interneuron vulnerability, axonal regenerative competence, and glial support functions. At the same time, STAT3-dependent regulation of astrocytic differentiation and GFAP-related programs provides a mechanistic bridge from physiological glial homeostasis to reactive astrogliosis and scar-related remodeling. Under pathological conditions, STAT3 exhibits even more complex and context-dependent roles. It has been implicated in neuroinflammation, metabolic stress, ischemic injury, neurodegeneration, tumor biology, and immune regulation [ 30 – 43 ]. In some settings, STAT3 contributes to neuroprotection, repair, or anti-inflammatory responses; in others, it promotes cytokine production, oxidative damage, or maladaptive glial activation. These observations suggest that STAT3 is better understood as a context-dependent regulator whose effects vary according to cell type, subcellular localization, and disease stage, rather than as a uniformly pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory signal. In the spinal cord, this duality becomes especially important because STAT3-dependent signaling can contribute to both protective and maladaptive outcomes within the same lesion environment. Acute or spatially restricted STAT3 activity may support lesion containment, barrier stabilization, and cell survival, whereas prolonged or cell-type-inappropriate activation may amplify inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress, gliosis, neuropathic pain, or scar-associated inhibition of axonal growth. Thus, rather than presenting STAT3 as a general CNS factor, we use these physiological and pathological observations as a basis for interpreting how STAT3 coordinates spinal cord-specific responses to injury. This framing provides a more targeted transition to the following discussion of spatiotemporal STAT3 activation after SCI.
sections.spatiotemporal characteristics of stat3: Previous studies have shown that STAT3 expression is detectable in the developing CNS and may increase progressively over time in selected brain regions [ 44 – 47 ]. After injury, STAT3 activation is often rapid and spatially restricted to specific cell populations. Following SCI, prominent astrocytic nuclear localization of activated STAT3 can be observed within hours after injury, and pSTAT3 remains elevated during the subacute phase [ 48 , 49 ]. In addition to the injured spinal cord, SCI can also engage JAK/STAT-related signaling in peripheral tissues; for example, inhibition of JAK1/2 tyrosine kinases has been shown to reduce neurogenic heterotopic ossification after SCI [ 50 ]. Together, these observations suggest that SCI-associated JAK/STAT signaling can extend beyond the lesion core and that STAT3-related responses are dynamic, cell-type-specific, and injury-stage-dependent. In the acute phase, astrocytic nuclear pSTAT3 near the lesion border is closely associated with early astroglial responses, lesion-border organization, and scar-related tissue remodeling after SCI [ 48 , 49 ]. In immune and glial populations, STAT3-related signaling may lead to different outcomes depending on the upstream cue: IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling has been linked to glial activation and neuropathic pain, whereas BMP7-, extracellular vesicle-, and regulatory T cell-related mechanisms have been associated with attenuation of neuroinflammation or promotion of anti-inflammatory microglial/macrophage responses [ 51 – 55 ]. During the subacute-to-chronic phase, persistent astrocytic STAT3-related signaling may shape GFAP-associated astrogliosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and glial scar formation, while excessive glial STAT3-associated inflammatory signaling may contribute to pain-related maladaptation [ 48 , 54 , 56 – 65 ]. In parallel, neuron- or axon-associated STAT3-related pathways may support regeneration-associated gene expression, axonal sprouting, corticospinal or sensory axon regeneration, and repair-permissive microenvironmental remodeling [ 66 – 71 ]. These examples reinforce the need to report the timing, cellular source, phosphorylation readout, and subcellular localization of STAT3 activation in future SCI studies.
sections.neurochemical and cellular mechanisms of: STAT3 has emerged as a central signaling node in SCI because it links extracellular cues to diverse pathological and reparative programs. In neurochemical terms, STAT3 sits at the intersection of cytokine signaling, oxidative metabolism, mitochondrial function, glial communication, and transcriptional reprogramming. The sections below summarize how these linked mechanisms shape injury progression and recovery.
sections.exosome-mediated regulation of stat3 aft: Exosomes are small extracellular vesicles secreted by various cell types and widely distributed in biological fluids. They carry proteins, lipids, mRNAs, and microRNAs and thereby mediate intercellular communication. In SCI, growing evidence suggests that exosomes regulate STAT3-related signaling pathways and contribute to inflammation control, barrier repair, and neural regeneration [ 72 – 75 ]. Pericyte-derived exosomal miR-210 has been reported to modulate JAK1/STAT3 signaling after SCI, thereby protecting mitochondrial function, preserving tight junction proteins, repairing the blood-spinal cord barrier, reducing inflammatory cytokine release, and improving motor recovery [ 72 ]. Exosomes from endothelial progenitor cells carrying miR-222-3p regulate the SOCS3/JAK2/STAT3 axis and promote macrophage polarization toward the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, which in turn attenuates glial scar formation and supports myelin and axonal repair [ 73 ]. Similarly, hypoxia-preconditioned mesenchymal stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles enriched in miR-21 influence astrocyte phenotype switching through the JAK2/STAT3 pathway and help create a more reparative microenvironment [ 74 ]. Schwann cell-derived exosomes containing MFG-E8 have also been shown to regulate the SOCS3/STAT3 pathway, suppress STAT3 phosphorylation, and promote anti-inflammatory macrophage/microglial polarization [ 75 ]. Overall, these observations indicate that exosome-mediated regulation of STAT3 represents an important mechanism in the injured spinal cord and may provide new opportunities for precision modulation of the post-injury microenvironment. These findings also highlight that exosome-mediated STAT3 regulation after SCI is highly context dependent rather than uniformly activating or inhibitory. Moreover, the STAT3 signaling pathway after spinal cord injury is determined by factors such as exosome sources, loading components, receptor cell types, and the injury background, rather than by a unified activation or inhibition model. These exosome-mediated, cell-type-dependent effects on STAT3 signaling are summarized in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Exosome-mediated regulation of STAT3 after SCI. Pericyte-derived exosomal miR-210 regulates JAK1/STAT3 signaling to support blood-spinal cord barrier repair and mitochondrial protection. Endothelial progenitor cell-derived exosomal miR-222-3p modulates the SOCS3/JAK2/STAT3 axis to promote M2 macrophage polarization, reduce glial scarring, and support myelin/axon repair. Hypoxic mesenchymal stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles enriched in miR-21 influence astrocyte phenotype switching through JAK2/STAT3 signaling and attenuate inflammation. Schwann cell-derived exosomal MFG-E8 regulates the SOCS3/STAT3 pathway, suppresses STAT3 phosphorylation, and promotes anti-inflammatory macrophage/microglial polarization
sections.stat3 in neuroinflammation, cytokine sig: Neuroinflammation is one of the core pathological events after SCI, and STAT3 is deeply involved in coordinating this response. Injury-induced activation of resident glial cells, recruitment of peripheral immune cells, and disruption of tissue homeostasis lead to sustained production of cytokines, chemokines, proteases, and oxidative mediators that can expand tissue damage. However, inflammatory signaling after SCI is not purely destructive; it also participates in debris clearance, lesion containment, and tissue remodeling. STAT3 therefore operates at a critical intersection between damaging inflammation and adaptive immune reprogramming. A growing body of work indicates that STAT3 signaling, particularly through the JAK2/STAT3 axis, regulates inflammatory factor production, glial responses, and macrophage/microglial polarization after SCI. CD44 and the long non-coding RNA SNHG1 enhance inflammatory signaling and tissue-damaging responses through JAK2/STAT3 activation [ 76 , 77 ]. Conversely, transneuronal delivery of hyper-interleukin-6 can enable functional recovery after severe SCI, highlighting the context-dependent reparative potential of cytokine/STAT3-related signaling [ 78 ], whereas interventions such as Ruxolitinib, miR-34c, and Fisetin attenuate inflammatory amplification and improve microenvironmental homeostasis through modulation of STAT3-related pathways [ 79 – 81 ]. MicroRNAs also exert bidirectional effects: miR-21a-5p promotes neurotoxic A1 astrocyte polarization and inflammation [ 82 ], and additional miR-21-focused experimental work further supports the relevance of miRNA-mediated regulation in SCI [ 83 ], whereas miR-22-3p, miR-29a, and miR-17-5p have been linked to enhanced regenerative capacity or improved neural recovery through STAT3-associated cascades [ 84 – 86 ]. Importantly, not all of these studies establish STAT3 as the sole causal mediator; in many cases, STAT3 appears to function as part of a broader signaling network shaped by cell type, injury stage, and upstream context. Other regulators, including BMP7, 4D-sEVs, lncRNA Kcnq1ot1, and ACY1215, also shape post-injury inflammatory responses through direct or indirect control of STAT3 signaling [ 51 – 53 , 87 – 89 ]. In parallel, the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 axis and related pathways such as p38 MAPK/NF-kB/STAT3 have been implicated in neuropathic pain by regulating astrocyte and microglial activation after SCI [ 54 – 56 , 90 – 94 ]. Additional intervention studies involving neural scaffolds, IL-4/OEC-mediated immune regulation, hydrogel-based JAK2/STAT3 inhibition, Alpinetin, DANCR/ACTN4/STAT3 signaling, and biomaterial-based modulation further support the relevance of STAT3-associated inflammatory networks in SCI repair [ 95 – 100 ]. Taken together, current evidence suggests that STAT3 is best understood not simply as a pro-inflammatory switch, but as a context-dependent regulator of immune-cell programming and glial signaling. A key task for future studies will be to define when STAT3 suppression is beneficial and when excessive inhibition might interfere with lesion containment or reparative remodeling (Table 1 ). sections.stat3 and neuronal apoptosis after sci: Neuronal apoptosis is a major component of secondary injury after SCI and contributes substantially to tissue loss and neurological dysfunction. Following primary mechanical damage, neurons are exposed to oxidative stress, inflammatory mediators, excitotoxicity, and mitochondrial impairment, all of which can activate apoptotic pathways. STAT3 is intricately involved in this process. In H2O2-stimulated spinal cord neuron models, increased STAT3 expression has been associated with activation of the p38 MAPK pathway, upregulation of Bax and cleaved caspase-3, downregulation of Bcl-2, and aggravation of neuronal apoptosis [ 101 ]. By contrast, interventions that modulate STAT3 signaling can reduce inflammasome activation, enhance autophagy, or attenuate apoptosis [ 102 ]. Stem cell-based interventions have also been linked to STAT3-dependent anti-apoptotic effects [ 103 ]. Wogonin suppresses inflammation and apoptosis through the STAT3 signaling pathway after SCI [ 104 ], while KLF7 has been reported to attenuate neuronal injury through anti-apoptotic signaling in a traumatic brain injury model, indicating that STAT3-associated survival pathways may extend beyond SCI-specific models [ 105 ]. Notably, Wogonin, KLF7-related anti-apoptotic signaling, Falcarindiol, EGFR activation, and neural stem cell-based combination therapies each influence Bax/Bcl-2/caspase-related pathways via STAT3 or JAK2/STAT3 signaling, thereby altering apoptotic vulnerability and promoting neuroprotection [ 104 – 108 ]. Overall, the literature supports a role for STAT3 in neuronal survival signaling after SCI, while also indicating that the direction of this effect depends on model context and upstream regulatory cues. Key studies connecting STAT3-associated pathways with neuronal apoptosis are summarized in Table 2 . sections.stat3, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are major drivers of secondary damage after SCI. Injury-induced disruption of mitochondrial homeostasis leads to impaired ATP production, excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, altered mitophagy, and activation of downstream cell-death pathways. Emerging evidence indicates that STAT3 is involved in these events through both canonical transcriptional programs and non-canonical mitochondrial actions [ 49 , 109 – 115 ]. On the one hand, phosphorylated STAT3 has been linked to inhibition of FOXO3a nuclear translocation, suppression of mitophagy-related pathways such as PINK1/Parkin, and decreased antioxidant defense, including reduced SOD2 activity, thereby promoting ROS accumulation and oxidative injury [ 109 ]. Consistent with a broader glial mitochondrial role of STAT3, disruption of astrocyte STAT3 signaling has been reported to decrease mitochondrial function and increase oxidative stress in vitro [ 111 ]. On the other hand, mitochondrial or contextually activated STAT3 has also been associated with preservation of bioenergetic homeostasis, modulation of stress-responsive genes, and support of injury-adaptive metabolic programs [ 49 , 110 ]. These apparently divergent findings may reflect differences in cell population, subcellular localization, timing, phosphorylation status, and whether STAT3 activity is measured as a driver of injury progression or as a compensatory response to metabolic stress. Mechanistically, STAT3 should be considered not only as a cytokine-responsive nuclear transcription factor but also as a compartment-sensitive regulator linking receptor-dependent signaling to mitochondrial respiration, redox balance, and cellular stress adaptation. Mitochondrial STAT3 has been shown to support optimal electron transport chain complex I/II activity, whereas mitochondrial-targeted STAT3 can preserve complex I-dependent respiration, reduce cytochrome c release, and attenuate ischemia-induced ROS generation through partial modulation of electron flow [ 112 , 115 ]. Although these findings were largely derived from non-SCI models, they provide an important mechanistic framework for interpreting STAT3-dependent mitochondrial adaptation in the injured spinal cord. This compartmental distinction is also relevant to the different biological implications of Tyr705 and Ser727 phosphorylation. Tyr705 phosphorylation primarily couples STAT3 to the canonical dimerization–nuclear translocation–DNA-binding axis, whereas Ser727 is required for maximal transcriptional activation and appears to be particularly important for mitochondrial STAT3 function [ 113 ]. In mitochondrial models, STAT3-dependent regulation of respiration can be dissociated from canonical Tyr705-dependent transcriptional activity: DNA-binding-defective or Y705F STAT3 can retain mitochondrial effects, whereas S727A disrupts restoration of electron transport chain activity and S727D can rescue complex I/II function [ 112 ]. Similarly, mitochondrially restricted STAT3 supports Ras-dependent metabolic remodeling in a Ser727-dependent manner, further indicating that Ser727 may couple STAT3 to bioenergetic regulation independently of classical nuclear signaling [ 114 ]. Accordingly, the relationship between STAT3 and oxidative injury in SCI should not be reduced to a simple pro-oxidant or antioxidant model. The strongest current interpretation is that STAT3 tunes the balance between mitochondrial resilience and mitochondrial failure in a highly context-dependent manner. Within this framework, Tyr705-related signaling may mainly reflect cytokine-driven nuclear transcriptional responses, whereas Ser727-related signaling may integrate transcriptional amplification with mitochondrial electron transport, metabolic adaptation, and ROS control. Future studies should therefore distinguish nuclear versus mitochondrial STAT3, Tyr705- versus Ser727-related signaling, and neuron- versus glia-dominant responses when evaluating STAT3 as a metabolic therapeutic target. The dual roles of STAT3 in oxidative injury and mitochondrial adaptation are illustrated in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3 Context-dependent roles of STAT3 in mitochondrial homeostasis and oxidative stress after SCI
sections.stat3 in astrocyte reactivity and scar-r: Astrocytes are central regulators of the post-injury microenvironment, and reactive astrogliosis is a defining feature of SCI. STAT3 signaling has long been recognized as a major determinant of astrocyte activation, phenotype transition, and scar formation [ 57 – 65 , 116 , 117 ]. Yet the biological significance of astrocytic STAT3 is more nuanced than a simple equation of ‘more STAT3 = worse outcome’. Reactive astrocytes can limit lesion spread, help restore barrier functions, and isolate inflammatory damage [ 48 ], whereas persistent maladaptive astrocyte responses can contribute to chronic inflammation, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan (CSPG)-rich scar formation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired axonal extension [ 118 ]. Several studies have shown that excessive or dysregulated STAT3 activation promotes neurotoxic A1-like astrocyte features, inflammatory mediator production, and glial scar-associated changes [ 57 – 63 ]. Calycosin reduces A1 astrocyte reactivity and glial scar markers by inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation [ 57 ], whereas Hv1 knockout decreases A1 astrocyte accumulation through the ROS/STAT3 pathway [ 58 ]. Similarly, suppression of abnormal JAK2/STAT3 activation through HDAC3 depletion or restoration of miR-19b-1-5p reduces astrocyte migration, GFAP expression, and scar-related remodeling [ 59 ]. However, classic work on astrocytic STAT3 also indicates that complete disruption of STAT3-dependent astrogliosis can impair lesion containment and worsen tissue organization, underscoring the need for calibrated rather than indiscriminate inhibition [ 48 ]. In the context of scar-related remodeling, STAT3-dependent astrocyte reactivity contributes not only to astrocyte activation but also to the structural reorganization of the lesion border. Activated astrocytes proliferate, migrate toward the lesion margin, upregulate glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and interact with extracellular matrix components to form a scar-associated boundary that initially restricts inflammatory spread and protects spared tissue [ 48 ]. When persistent or excessive, STAT3-associated astrocytic programs may promote extracellular matrix remodeling, CSPG accumulation, maintenance of a pro-inflammatory glial phenotype, and formation of a non-permissive substrate for axonal extension [ 57 – 65 , 116 – 118 ]. Therefore, STAT3-mediated scar remodeling should be interpreted as a dynamic process involving both protective lesion containment and chronic inhibitory remodeling, rather than simply as astrocyte activation alone. STAT3 also interacts with inflammatory and reparative signaling programs to shape astrocyte behavior across injury stages. Through crosstalk with NF-kB and cytokine signaling, STAT3 can amplify acute inflammatory responses [ 60 ]; conversely, interventions such as Zeb2os knockdown, quercetin-loaded mesenchymal stem cell-derived vesicles, N-acetylcysteine, and miR-124-overexpressing Schwann cells can attenuate maladaptive astrogliosis or scar-forming capacity by suppressing STAT3-related signaling [ 61 – 65 ]. Ginsenoside Rg1 further highlights the contextual nature of astrocytic STAT3, as distinct downstream programs may favor astrocyte-to-neuron conversion or pro-angiogenic support [ 116 , 117 ]. Thus, an important translational question is not whether astrocytic STAT3 should be turned on or off, but how its timing, magnitude, and cell-state specificity can be modulated to preserve protective astrogliosis while limiting chronic scar-related inhibition. Overall, astrocytic STAT3 lies at the boundary between protective lesion containment and maladaptive chronic remodeling. This dual positioning makes it one of the most compelling, but also one of the most challenging, STAT3-related targets in SCI. sections.stat3 and axonal regeneration following: Axonal regeneration is a major determinant of functional recovery after SCI, yet the intrinsic regenerative capacity of CNS neurons is limited. STAT3 has been identified as a key signaling molecule involved in promoting axonal regeneration through multiple mechanisms [ 66 – 71 ]. STAT3 can cooperate with transcription factors such as KLF7 and MEF2 to induce regeneration-associated genes, thereby promoting axonal sprouting and sensory axon growth after dorsal column injury [ 66 ]. It also participates in intrinsic neuronal redox signaling linked to NOX2- and PKC-dependent regeneration [ 67 ]. In addition, mTOR-STAT3 signaling has been implicated in enhanced corticospinal and sensory axon regeneration following Lipin1 depletion [ 68 ]. At the same time, modulation of STAT3 influences the extracellular environment that determines regenerative success. Mesenchymal stem cell-based therapies combined with electroacupuncture reduce astrocyte activation and glial scar formation by suppressing STAT3 phosphorylation [ 70 ], whereas graphene-collagen composite hydrogels modulate inflammatory polarization and support axonal regeneration partly through STAT3-related mechanisms [ 71 ]. Together, these findings indicate that STAT3 shapes axonal regeneration through both neuron-intrinsic and microenvironmental mechanisms. sections.proposed stat3-related mechanisms: ferro: In addition to the better-established roles of STAT3 in neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, mitochondrial stress, astrocyte reactivity, and axonal regeneration, several emerging mechanisms may further explain how STAT3 participates in SCI progression and repair. Among these, ferroptosis and photobiomodulation (PBM)-associated signaling deserve separate consideration, but they are best presented as proposed or developing mechanisms because the current evidence remains partly indirect and context dependent. Ferroptosis has attracted increasing attention as a mechanism of SCI pathogenesis because it directly links several core features of secondary injury, including iron dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, lipid peroxidation, antioxidant failure, and progressive neuronal loss [ 119 – 122 ]. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis is driven primarily by iron-dependent oxidative damage to membrane lipids and insufficient detoxification of lipid peroxides. This mechanism is highly relevant to SCI, where hemorrhage, mitochondrial injury, inflammatory activation, and redox imbalance can create a lesion microenvironment that favors lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic vulnerability. Bioinformatic analyses of SCI samples have identified ferroptosis-related gene signatures and suggested that these pathways are associated with acute injury progression [ 119 ]. Additional SCI-related gene analyses further implicate ferroptosis-related pathways in injury pathogenesis and redox-related signaling networks [ 121 , 122 ]. Experimentally, modulation of ferroptosis-related pathways has been linked to neuronal survival after SCI, supporting the view that ferroptosis is not merely a secondary biochemical marker but a potentially targetable contributor to tissue degeneration and functional outcome [ 120 ]. Therefore, ferroptosis deserves attention in SCI research because it provides a mechanistic bridge between oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, neuronal death, and therapeutic neuroprotection. STAT3-related mechanisms are particularly relevant in this context because STAT3 is positioned at the intersection of cytokine signaling, redox homeostasis, mitochondrial adaptation, and cell-death regulation. In SCI, STAT3 activation is highly context dependent, and its effects may differ according to injury phase, cell type, subcellular localization, and upstream inflammatory or metabolic cues. Ferroptosis-related studies further support this duality. One key experimentally supported mechanism is the Syvn1/STAT3/GPX4 axis. Syvn1-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination stabilizes STAT3, promotes its nuclear translocation, and enhances transcription of GPX4, a major ferroptosis-suppressive enzyme that limits lipid peroxide accumulation and helps preserve ROS balance [ 120 ]. Through this pathway, STAT3 may protect neurons by strengthening GPX4-dependent lipid peroxide detoxification and reducing ferroptotic cell death. Conversely, sustained or dysregulated STAT3 activation may indirectly promote ferroptotic susceptibility by intensifying oxidative stress, weakening antioxidant defenses, or interacting with HIF-1alpha- and Nrf2-related signaling networks [ 121 , 122 ]. Thus, the STAT3-ferroptosis relationship should not be interpreted as uniformly protective or detrimental. Instead, STAT3 should be viewed as a context-sensitive regulator that may either restrain ferroptosis through GPX4-dependent antioxidant protection or contribute to ferroptotic vulnerability when oxidative and inflammatory signaling becomes excessive. PBM represents another proposed STAT3-related mechanism in SCI. Experimental studies indicate that PBM can attenuate neurotoxic astrocyte and microglial activation, reduce inflammatory mediator production, limit glial scar-associated responses, and improve motor recovery, at least partly through modulation of STAT3-associated signaling [ 123 – 125 ]. Mechanistically, PBM has been linked to suppression of Lcn2/JAK2-STAT3 crosstalk, miR-330-5p-mediated regulation of macrophage polarization, and inhibition of the JAK2/STAT3/AQP4 axis involved in spinal cord edema [ 123 – 125 ]. These findings suggest that STAT3 may serve as one molecular convergence point through which PBM reshapes the inflammatory, glial, and edema-related microenvironment after SCI. However, because PBM can also affect mitochondrial function, vascular responses, oxidative metabolism, and immune signaling, further causal validation is needed before PBM can be defined as a specifically STAT3-guided intervention. Taken together, ferroptosis and PBM illustrate two emerging areas in which STAT3-related signaling may influence SCI progression and repair. The ferroptosis-related evidence justifies growing attention because it connects iron-dependent lipid peroxidation with neuronal death, oxidative stress, and functional prognosis after SCI. The STAT3-centered evidence is important because STAT3 links cytokine-driven injury responses with GPX4-mediated antioxidant protection, ROS balance, mitochondrial adaptation, and inflammatory remodeling. Future studies should determine whether STAT3 acts as a causal mediator or a downstream marker in these mechanisms, define the relevant cell types and injury phases, and test whether selective modulation of STAT3-related pathways can preserve neuronal survival and improve functional recovery after SCI.
sections.therapeutic modulation of stat3 signalin: A growing number of studies highlight the therapeutic relevance of STAT3 in SCI and suggest that rehabilitation-based, pharmacological, biomaterial-based, and extracellular vesicle-centered interventions converge on STAT3-related signaling. The translational appeal of STAT3 lies in its position at the interface of inflammation, metabolism, mitochondrial regulation, and glial-neuronal communication. Treadmill training has been shown to enhance neural function recovery in SCI models, partly through activation of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway and attenuation of apoptosis [ 126 ]. Network pharmacology studies likewise identify STAT3 as a hub target across candidate therapeutic strategies [ 127 ]. Age-specific bioinformatics and anoikis-related analyses further implicate STAT3-associated pathways in post-injury cellular responses and functional recovery [ 128 , 129 ]. Metabolomic work also shows that Danshen extract (Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge) attenuates SCI in a rat model, although whether this effect is directly mediated through STAT3-centered signaling requires further validation [ 130 ]. Protein-interaction and bibliometric analyses additionally highlight STAT3-related inflammatory networks and neuromodulation research as important areas for future SCI therapeutics [ 131 ]. At the same time, the field still relies heavily on indirect modulation of STAT3, and the neurochemical specificity of many reported interventions remains insufficiently defined. Future therapeutic work will therefore need to distinguish direct STAT3 targeting from broader pathway perturbation and to establish when modulation of STAT3 improves metabolic resilience, when it restrains inflammatory signaling, and when it may interfere with necessary reparative responses. Overall, current evidence supports the view that STAT3 is not only a mechanistic regulator in SCI but also a practical intervention node. However, because its effects are stage-dependent and cell-specific, successful translation will likely require precise neurochemical stratification rather than blanket inhibition or activation.
sections.conclusions and future directions: STAT3 is a multifunctional signaling molecule that exerts pivotal yet highly context-dependent effects in spinal cord injury. Across the current literature, its importance lies not simply in belonging to the JAK/STAT pathway, but in integrating multiple neurochemical dimensions of secondary injury, including cytokine signaling, redox imbalance, mitochondrial dysfunction, ferroptotic pressure, glial remodeling, and regenerative plasticity. The major challenge is that the biological consequences of STAT3 activation vary according to injury phase, cell type, subcellular localization, and model system. This variability explains why STAT3 can appear protective in some experimental settings and deleterious in others. For the field to move forward, studies must more clearly distinguish nuclear versus mitochondrial STAT3 actions, acute versus chronic signaling effects, and descriptive pathway associations versus genuine causal dependence. Several priorities emerge from the current literature. First, the therapeutic window for modulating STAT3 across acute, subacute, and chronic SCI remains poorly defined. Second, greater emphasis is needed on cell-specific manipulations in astrocytes, microglia/macrophages, neurons, and vascular-associated cells. Third, future work should better integrate neurochemical readouts—including oxidative balance, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory mediator profiles—with behavioral and histological outcomes. Finally, more selective intervention strategies and clinically relevant delivery systems are required if STAT3-centered therapies are to progress beyond preclinical promise. In summary, STAT3 should be regarded as a context-dependent integrator of neuroinflammation, glial remodeling, metabolic stress, and regenerative signaling after SCI. This framework may help future studies define more precise therapeutic windows, identify cell-specific mechanisms, and develop translational strategies for STAT3-centered pathway modulation.

title: Serotonin 5-HT7 receptor signaling modulates inflammatory responses and survival after myocardial infarction
abstract: Background Myocardial infarction (MI) is among the leading causes of death worldwide, and a precisely regulated inflammatory response is essential for effective cardiac repair and long-term outcome. The serotonergic system regulates immune cell functions, yet its contribution to post-MI remodeling is incompletely understood. Methods Here, we investigated the role of serotonin receptor 7 (5-HT7R) in post-infarction inflammation and outcome after permanent left anterior coronary artery ligation in mice, and complementary analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) obtained from patients with acute MI. Results Three days after MI, 5-HT7R mRNA expression was significantly upregulated in the infarct region compared to remote myocardium and sham operated mice. RNA-sequencing of isolated murine CD11b + cells demonstrated high 5-HT7R expression in cardiac macrophages during the acute phase, which was confirmed by immunohistochemistry. Systemic 5-HT7R-knockout did not affect basal cardiac function but resulted in impaired left ventricular function and enhanced inflammatory signatures 14 days after MI without changes in infarct size. Pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R signaling with the selective agonist LP-211 increased survival after MI, although global systolic function among survivors was not improved. Transcriptomic profiling of cardiac macrophages 3 days after MI revealed bidirectional regulation of inflammatory and metabolic programs depending on 5-HT7R activity, including altered expression of Got1 and S100A9 . Complementary, in PBMCs from MI patients Got1 expression was reduced, while S100A9 was increased, and both correlated with 5-HT7R expression. Conclusions These data suggest 5-HT7R as a regulator of post-MI immune responses and a potential target to improve repair and survival. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-026-08423-4.

sections.background_1: Myocardial infarction (MI) followed by heart failure (HF) remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Despite advances in therapeutic interventions, including percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and pharmacological treatments targeting the neurohumoral system, such as β-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, mortality associated with HF is still high after MI [ 1 , 2 ]. Following cardiac injury, ischemic cell death initiates a complex cascade of cellular and molecular processes that drive cardiac inflammation, remodeling, and tissue repair [ 3 , 4 ]. Modulators of the inflammatory response are therefore considered to be effective therapeutic targets to minimize cardiac damage and preserve cardiac function. Among immune cells, macrophages play a pivotal role in post-infarction remodeling through their dynamic polarization and functional plasticity. However, current therapies are unable to efficiently modulate the inflammation and remodeling processes, thus limiting their impact on long-term cardiac function and survival after MI. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms governing inflammation and remodeling is essential for the development of effective interventions. One potentially promising target is the serotonergic system (5-HT system). Beyond its well-established role in the central nervous system, the 5-HT system regulates the function of various immune cells, and is also affected in various cardiovascular diseases [ 5 , 6 ]. Notably, patients after acute MI exhibit an elevated risk of developing major depressive disorders (MDD), while patients with MDD or other severe psychiatric disorders are frequently affected by cardiovascular disease associated with increased morbidity and mortality, suggesting a bidirectional link between serotonergic signaling, cardiovascular pathology, and inflammatory responses [ 7 – 9 ]. Our recent data demonstrate that serotonin receptor 7 (5-HT7R) is expressed in human macrophages and modulates their functions [ 10 ]. In M1-like macrophages, pharmacological 5-HT7R activation with the highly selective agonist LP-211 reduced phagocytic and migratory ability. In addition, LP-211 treatment altered the secretory profile across all macrophage subtypes indicating that modulation of 5-HT7R activity may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for inflammatory diseases [ 10 ]. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that 5-HT7R contributes to the regulation of the inflammatory response after MI and that modulation of the 5-HT7R expression or activity influences cardiac inflammation, remodeling, and survival. In the present study, we therefore investigate the regulation of 5-HT7R signaling in context of MI, aiming to identify if the 5-HT7R is a regulator of post-MI immune responses and a potential target to improve cardiac repair and survival.
sections.myocardial infarction: Sibling male mice (age 12 to 16 weeks) WT and 5-HT7R-KO (B6;129 SvEv -Htr7 tm1Sut , JAX-ID. 019453 [ 11 ]), were used in all studies except for time course data (C57BL6/N, purchased from Charles River Germany). Myocardial infarction (MI) was induced by permanent occlusion of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) or sham operation in age-matched mice as described previously [ 12 , 13 ]. Briefly, one day before surgery, 500 mg/ml metamizol (Ratiopharm) was supplied via the drinking water and maintained until 7 days after surgery. On the day of operation mice received a combination of butorphanol (2 mg/kg body weight (BW), CP Pharma) and carprofen (2 mg/kg BW, CP Pharma) in 0.9% sodium chloride solution (Carl Roth) via subcutaneous injection. Animals were anesthetized with 4% isoflurane (Baxter Deutschland GmbH), intubated and artificially ventilated. Anesthesia was maintained using 1–2% isoflurane. After local disinfection, local anesthesia (0.5% xylocaine, Aspen) was administered prior to the left thoracotomy in the 5 th intercostal space. After opening the pericardium, the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery was ligated with a 6.0 Prolene suture (Ethicon). To induce large infarcts, the suture was positioned just below the auricular level. Successful coronary occlusion was indicated by significant color changes in the ischemic region. Mice were randomly assigned to experimental groups. In sham-operated mice, the suture passing around the LAD artery was not tied. Data were collected at baseline and after 3 days, 7 days or 14 days post-MI, as indicated. Mice suffering intraoperative death and mice with an MI size < 20% were excluded from the study.
sections.lp-211 treatment after mi: Starting on day one after surgery, 0.025 mg/10 g body weight of LP-211 (Sigma Aldrich) in 0.9% sodium chloride solution was injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) once daily until the end of the experiment. Control animals were administered an i.p. injection of 0.9% sodium chloride solution accordingly until the end of the experiment.
sections.infarct size measurements: Infarct size measurements were performed on longitudinal myocardial sections stained with Picro-Sirius red F3BA as the ratio of scar length to LV circumference [ 13 ]. In brief, hearts were retrogradely perfused (2 min; 80 mmHg) with PBS (pH 7.4) containing 50 mM KCl (Sigma Aldrich/Merck) and 200 U/ml heparin (Ratiopharm), followed by in situ paraformaldehyde-fixation. Hearts were cut longitudinally through the center of the scar, and 6 µm sections were prepared and stained with Picro-Sirius red F3BA (Sigma Aldrich/Merck) [ 14 ]. MI sizes were determined in the first three midventricular sections from the midline of the scar, representing the full scar dimensions. Epicardial and endocardial infarct lengths and circumferences were measured, and the epicardial and endocardial infarct ratio was determined by dividing each infarct length by circumference. MI size was calculated as [(epicardial infarct ratio+endocardial infarct ratio)/2] x 100 [ 15 ] and is presented as the mean of the three midventricular sections.
sections.echocardiography: Transthoracic 2D echocardiography was performed to assess contractile function in 5-HT7R-KO and in corresponding WT mice on anesthetized mice as described previously [ 16 , 17 ]. In brief, contractile function and heart rate were assessed by serial echocardiography using the Vevo 3100 system (VisualSonics) at baseline and after 3 days or 14 days post-MI (as indicated). Anesthesia was induced with 2% (in 100% oxygen) isoflurane, followed by maintenance at 0.5–1% isoflurane via a special vaporizer for rodents delivered by a small nose cone (VisualSonics). For echocardiographic image acquisition, the animal was placed in a supine position on a prewarmed platform and the body temperature was maintained as close to 37 °C as possible during the entire procedure. Echocardiographic measurements were obtained 5 min following the induction of anesthesia when the heart rate had stably recovered to exclude the variation in cardiac function created by anesthesia induction. Parasternal short- or long-axis views were recorded in B-mode at the level of the papillary muscle, and still images were used to measure left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD) and LV end-systolic diameter (LVESD) and calculate fractional shortening (FS; [LVEDD – LVESD]/LVEDD x 100) in short-axis view and fractional area change (FAC; [end-diastolic area (LVEDA) – end-systolic area (LVESA)/end-diastolic area ×100) in long-axis view.
sections.human peripheral blood mononuclear cell: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from MI patients ( N = 18) were isolated from blood taken 3 ± 1d after insult in EDTA containing S-Monovette® tubes (Sarstedt) as described before [ 18 ]. Blood from healthy volunteers ( N = 11) served as control. Blood samples were 1:2 diluted in PBS (Sigma-Aldrich) and loaded on top of 12.5 ml Bicoll Separating Solution (1.077 g/ml, Biochrom). For separation, the tubes were centrifuged for 30 minutes at 800 ×g at room temperature without the brake. The PBMC layer was removed as completely as possible with a pipette, then diluted 1:3 with PBS and centrifuged at 300 ×g for 10 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and the cells were washed again with PBS. Centrifugation was continued at 200 ×g for another 10 minutes. After isolation, the PBMC cell pellets were directly lysed in TRIzol® reagent (Invitrogen) for RNA isolation and gene expression analysis.
sections.rna isolation, cdna synthesis, qrt-pcr a: Total RNA from murine hearts was isolated with TRIzol® reagent (Invitrogen) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. cDNA synthesis using Superscript III (Invitrogen), 2 µg of total RNA and random hexamer primers (Sigma-Aldrich) was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocols as previously described [ 19 ]. Semi-quantitative real-time PCR using the SYBR green dye method (SYBR Green qPCR 2x Mastermix-Kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was performed with the AriaMX Real-Time PCR System (Agilent Technologies). Sequences of qRT-PCR primers used in this study are provided below. mRNA expression levels were normalised using the 2 -ΔΔCT method relative to 18S or HPRT. Expression of mature miR-29a-3p (Applied BioSystems) was determined by miR-qRT-PCR on an ABI7500 cycler (Applied BioSystems) and was normalized using the 2 -ΔΔCT method relative to U6 as previously described [ 20 ].

sections.macrophage isolation from infarcted mous: Isolation of neutrophils, macrophages and fibroblasts from basal and infarcted WT hearts after 1d and 7d post-MI or from infarcted 5-HT7R-KO, WT and WT with LP-211 hearts 3 days post-MI was performed after collagenase digestion followed by antibody binding and magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) as described previously [ 19 , 21 ]. In brief, 3 days after MI, LVs were excised and washed with Hanks balanced salt solution (HBSS; Merck). Aortic and pulmonary vessels and atria were removed. Tissues were minced into small pieces and digested for 3 × 15 min at 37 °C with 0.1% collagenase type II (Worthington) and DNase I in HBSS. The digested suspension was filtered through a 30 μm filter. After red blood cell lysis, enrichment of Ly6G + cells (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–092-332) and CD11b + macrophages (Miltenyi Biotec, 130–049-601) was achieved by sorting the cells using microbeads and the MACS system (Miltenyi Biotec). Flow through was collected as CD11b - fibroblasts. Isolated cell fractions were directly lysed in TRIzol® reagent (Invitrogen) for RNA isolation.
sections.library generation, quality control, and: 100 ng of total RNA per sample were utilized as input for rRNA depletion procedure with ‘NEBNext® rRNA Depletion Kit (Human/Mouse/Rat), 96 rxns’ (New England Biolabs, E6310X) followed by stranded cDNA library generation using ‘NEBNext® Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina’ (New England Biolabs, E7760L). All steps were performed as recommended in user manualE7760 (Version 1.0_02-2017; NEB) except that all reactions were downscaled to 2/3 of initial volumes. cDNA libraries were barcoded by dual indexing approach, using ‘NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina − 96 Unique Dual Index Primer Pairs’ (New England Biolabs, 6440S). All generated cDNA libraries were amplified with 10 cycles of final PCR. One additional purification step was introduced at the end of the standard procedure, using 1.2x ‘Agencourt® AMPure® XP Beads’ (Beckman Coulter Inc., A63881). Fragment length distribution of individual libraries was monitored using ‘Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity DNA Assay’ (Agilent Technologies, 5067–4626). Quantification of libraries was performed by use of the ‘Qubit® dsDNA HS Assay Kit’ (ThermoFisher Scientific, Q32854 ).
sections.library denaturation and sequencing run: Equal molar amounts of individually barcoded libraries were pooled for a common sequencing run in which each analyzed library constituted around 8.3% of overall flowcell / run capacity. The library pool was denatured with NaOH and was finally diluted to 1.8 pM according to the Denature and Dilute Libraries Guide (Document # 15048776 v02; Illumina). 1.3 ml of the denatured pool was loaded on an Illumina NextSeq 550 sequencer using a High Output Flowcell (400 M cluster) for single reads (Illumina, 20024906). Sequencing was performed with the following settings: Sequence reads 1 and 2 with 38 bases each; Index reads 1 and 2 with 8 bases each.
sections.bcl to fastq conversion: BCL files were converted to FASTQ files using bcl2fastq Conversion Software version v2.20.0.422 (Illumina).
sections.raw data processing and quality control: Before downstream analysis, all FastQ files were quality-checked and filtered using fastp v0.23.4 [ 22 ]. The parameter -q 30 was used to filter out bases with a Phred score lower than 30. All other settings were run with default parameters. After quality control and quantification, the read depth for all samples ranged between 14 and 22 million reads, with an average of 17 million reads. Salmon v1.10.2 was used to quantify transcript expression [ 23 ]. GRCm39 was used as the reference genome to build a decoy-aware index. This genome was obtained from Ensembl release 112 [ 24 ]. Once the index was built, the quant command was run with the -l A and –validateMappings arguments. To generate a matrix of raw counts, the output from salmon was imported to R and summarized to gene level using the package Tximeta 1.24.0 [ 25 ]. A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was run on log2 transformed counts to visualize the primary sources of variation and potential outliers. PCA plots were generated with ggfortify [ 26 ].
sections.normalization and differential expressio: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using edgeR v4.4.2 [ 27 ] and annotated with AnnotationDbi v1.68.0 and org.Mm.eg.db v3.20.0 [ 28 , 29 ]. Prior to differential expression analysis, normalization by library size was performed using the edgeR functions calcNormFactors and normLibSizes, and low-expressed genes were removed using filterByExpr. Pairwise comparisons were then performed among all three groups. Volcano plots and Venn diagrams were generated using ggplot2, ggrepel, and ggvenn [ 30 – 32 ]. Heatmaps showing normalized gene expression were generated using the ComplexHeatmap package [ 33 ].
sections.biological process and pathway overrepre: Over-representation analysis (ORA) of biological processes and pathways was conducted using ClusterProfiler v4.14.6 with the Gene Ontology (GO), Reactome, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) databases [ 34 – 37 ]. Genes with a nominal p -value < 0.05 were used as queries, and all detected genes were used as the background set. Upregulated and downregulated genes were analyzed separately. To identify connections between overrepresented terms, gene networks were constructed using the cnetplot function from the Enrichplot package [ 38 ]. Dot plots showing overrepresented terms were also generated using Enrichplot.
sections.multiplex assays of cardiac murine tissu: For multiplex analysis, samples from the infarct region of 5-HT7R-KO and WT hearts 3 days post-MI were isolated with the Bio-Plex® cell lysis kit (Bio-Rad, 171304011) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The protein concentration of the lysates was measured with Bradford reagent (Bio-Rad) and LV lysates were diluted with Bio-Plex sample diluent to a protein contration of 1 mg/ml. The Bio-Plex Pro™ Mouse Cytokine 23-plex Assay (Bio-Rad, M60009RDPD) was used as recommended by the manufacturer and measured with the Bio-Plex 200 system (Bio-Rad).
sections.histology and immunostaining: Histological, immunohistological and morphological analyses were performed 3 days and 14 days after sham operation or MI. For cardiac morphological analyses, hearts were embedded in Tissue-Tek O.C.T Compound (Sakura Finetek) and frozen at −80 °C until sectioning. Subsequently, 6 µm cryosections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), wheat germ agglutinin (WGA, Vector Laboratories Inc., RL-1022) or IB4 (isolectin B4)-fluorescein (Vector Laboratories Inc., B-1205) as described previously [ 12 ]. The cross-sectional area was determined on longitudinal cryosections after wheat germ agglutinin/Hoechst staining. Analysis was done on maximum-intensity projcetions of five centred planes using “HeartJ” plugin in ImagJ with minor modifications [ 39 ]. To analyze cardiac 5-HT7R levels, immune cells status and angiogenesis, 6 µm LV cardiac slices were stained with respective antibodies. In brief, cardiac slices were washed with PBS, blocked and permeabilized using 10% donkey serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch) and 0.3% Triton X-100 (Sigma Aldrich) for 45 min. The slices were stained overnight using primary antibodies recognizing CD68 (Novusbio, NBP2-33337), CD80 (Abcam, ab106162), CD206 (R&D Systems, AF2535), CD31 (eBioscience™, Invitrogen, 14–0311-82), Nestin (ThermoFisher, PA5-143578), and 5-HT7R (BioRad, AHP1343) at 4 °C. Following secondary antibodies were used: Alexa Fluor® 488 AffiniPure™ Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H+L) (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111–545-003), Alexa Fluor® 546 Goat anti-Rat IgG (H+L) (Dianova, A-11081), Alexa Fluor® 594 AffiniPure™ Donkey Anti-Goat IgG (H+L) (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 705–585-147), Alexa Fluor® 647 AffiniPure™ Goat Anti-Armenian Hamster IgG (H+L) (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 127–605-160), Alexa Fluor® 647 AffiniPure Donkey Anti-Chicken(Jackson ImmunoResearch, 703–605-155), DyLight® 649 Donkey Anti-Rat IgG (H+L) (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 712–495-153), Alexa Fluor® 488 Anti-Mouse (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 715–545-150), Cy3 Anti-Rabbit (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 711–165-152) and counterstained with Hoechst 33342 trihydrochloride, trihydrate (Invitrogen) or 4′,6-Diamidino-2-phenylindol (DAPI; Sigma Aldrich). The tissue was imaged on a Zeiss LSM780 with a LD C-Apochromat with a 40x/1.2 W objective and Zen 2012 imaging software. Each fluorophore/dye was imaged in online-fingerprinting mode with pre-defined spectra of single-stained slices. The evaluation was conducted blinded on maximum-intensity projections applying custom-written Matlab scripts. In each cardiac slices two regions of the scar, border, and remote area were captured with a pixel size of 0.208 µm (1024 × 1024 pixels; 212.55 × 212.55 µm), pixel dwell time 1.57 µs. Manders correlation coefficient was determined using a custom-written Matlab script and averaged on four regions per animal.
sections.statistical analyses: Database management and statistical analyses were performed with the PRISM version 7.0 and version 11.0 statistical programme (GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla). Data are presented as mean ± SD. Differences between groups were analysed by Student’s t -test with or without Welch’s correction or ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests. A non-parametric Mann-Whitney test was performed on data not fitting a Gaussian distribution (as analysed by D’Agostino and Pearson omnibus normality test or Shapiro-Wilk normality test for small sample sizes). A P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Data are depicted as * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001.
sections.5-ht7r is predominantly expressed in inf: To investigate whether the 5-HT7R expression is regulated in the heart after MI, we quantified 5-HT7R mRNA levels in the infarcted (scar) area and in the remote myocardium 3, 7 and 14 days post-MI and compared them with LVs from sham-operated WT mice (Fig. 1 A, B). Upregulation of cardiac stress and hypertrophy marker atrial natriuretic peptide ( ANP ) together with increased expression of inflammatory markers, including the macrophage-associated genes Adgre1 , CD80 and CD206 , confirmed effective cardiac injury and initiation of inflammatory and remodeling processes (Fig. 1 B; Supplementary Fig. S1 A-C). Notably, 5-HT7R mRNA expression was significantly increased exclusively in the infarcted (scar) region during the acute phase 3 days post-MI (Fig. 1 B). This time point coincides with the peak of inflammatory activity after MI before the beginning transition from M1 to M2 macrophage polarisation [ 4 ]. To explore potential post-transcriptional mechanisms underlying this transient upregulation, we performed miRNA target prediction analysis using TargetScanMouse 7.2, which identified miR-29a-3p as a putative regulator of 5-HT7R expression. Consistent with increased 5-HT7R mRNA levels, miR-29a-3p expression was markedly reduced in the infarct region compared to the remote myocardium 3 days after MI, and compared to the LV of sham-operated controls (Fig. 1 C), suggesting miRNA-mediated regulation of 5-HT7R expression in response to cardiac injury. ( D ) Relative mRNA expression of 5-HT7R in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of MI patients ( N = 18) 3 ± 1d after insult compared to healthy controls ( N = 11) normalized to 18S rRNA. ( E ) Experimental scheme of isolation of neutrophils, fibroblasts, and macrophages by MACS separation technique. ( F ) 5-HT7R expression in macrophages, neutrophils and fibroblasts basal, 1 and 7 days post-MI ( N = 3). Macrophage 5-HT7R expression is normalized to fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM), whereas neutrophil and fibroblast expression is shown relative to GAPDH expression. Statistical analysis was performed using ( B ) ordinary One-Way ANOVA with Šídák multiple comparison post hoc test, ( C ) One-Way ANOVA followed by post hoc tests with Bonferroni’s correction ( D ) unpaired, two-tailed t -test and ( F ) ordinary One-Way ANOVA with tukey multiple comparison post hoc test To assess clinical relevance, we analyzed peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from patients 3 ± 1 days after acute MI. PBMCs from MI patients exhibited significantly higher 5-HT7R mRNA expression compared with healthy controls (Fig. 1 D), supporting translational relevance of the observed regulation. To further characterize cell-specific expression patterns, Ly-6 G + neutrophils, CD11b - fibroblast and CD11b + macrophages were isolated from mouse hearts under basal conditions and at 1 and 7 days post-MI using magnetic-activated cell sorting (MACS) separation (Fig. 1 E). RNA-sequencing (RNA-Seq) analysis from CD11b + macrophages revealed a pronounced increase in 5-HT7R expression at 1 day post-MI, whereas Ly-6 G + neutrophils showed reduced 5-HT7R expression at this timepoint. In contrast, the 5-HT7R expression in CD11b - fibroblasts remained unchanged (Fig. 1 F). Moreover, expression of 5-HT7R-related signaling partner Cd44 was significantly upregulated in macrophages 1 day after MI, whereas expression of others downstream signaling molecules including Cdc42 , Mmp9 , RhoA , G α S and G α 12 was not significantly altered (Supplementary Fig. S1 D). Immunofluorescence staining for 5-HT7R in combination with the macrophage markers CD68, CD80 and CD206 on infarcted WT hearts confirmed robust expression of 5-HT7R in macrophages within the scar and border zone, which was supported by positive Mander’s correlation coefficient. In contrast, the remote myocardium showed only low signal intensity for all four markers, indicating minimal expression outside the infarcted area (Fig. 2 A, B). Baseline echocardiographic analysis revealed that 5-HT7R-KO mice at the age of 3–4 months show normal cardiac function compared to WT mice (Supplementary Table S1 ). Moreover, heart weight (HW), body weight (BW), lung weight (LW) and the HW/BW or LW/BW ratio did not differ between genotypes under basal conditions (Table 1 ). However, assessment of the cardiac inflammatory milieu by Bioplex analysis revealed elevated baseline chemokine and cytokine levels in sham-operated 5-HT7R-KO mice compared with WT controls, including IL-1a, IL-1b, IL-3, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, IL-13, IL-17, GM-CSF, CXCL1, MCP-1, MIP-1b, TNF-a. 3 days following MI, 5-HT7R-KO hearts experienced a more pronounced increase in IL-1a, IL-5, and CXCL1 levels compared to WT mice (Supplementary Fig. S2 ), indicating an enhanced inflammatory response in the absence of 5-HT7R signaling. Interestingly, 14 days post-MI, 5-HT7R-KO mice displayed a significantly greater decline in LV function and increased markers of tissue inflammation compared with WT mice, while the survival rates and infarct size did not differ between genotypes (Fig. 3 A–F, Table 1 ). Sham-operated 5-HT7R-KO and WT mice showed comparable cardiac function at this time point, confirming that the observed functional impairment was MI-dependent. These findings provide first evidence that endogenous 5-HT7R signaling is important for cardiac integrity and cardiac function during post-infarction remodeling. sections.modulation of 5-ht7r activity after mi i: To investigate whether modulation of 5-HT7R signaling affects post-infarction tissue remodeling, cardiac angiogenesis and fibrosis development were analysed 14 days after MI in hearts from WT, 5-HT7R-KO and WT mice treated with the selective 5-HT7R agonist LP-211 (WT+LP-211) (Supplementary Fig. S4 , Supplementary Fig. S5 ). Quantitative immunofluorescence analysis of endothelial markers revealed that 5-HT7R-KO mice displayed an angiogenic response in the infarct border zone comparable to WT mice. In contrast, LP-211-treated animals revealed a significantly increased capillarization in the border zone, as indicated by increased mean fluorescence intensity of the endothelial marker CD31 and active angiogenesis marker nestin (Supplementary Fig. S4 A-B), suggesting that pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R promotes post-infarction neovascularization. To assess whether altered 5-HT7R signaling influences cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or vascular density in non-injured myocardium, cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area and capillary density were analyzed in the remote myocardium. No significant differences were observed among WT, 5-HT7R-KO, and WT+LP-211 groups, indicating that neither genetic ablation nor pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R affects cardiomyocyte size or baseline vascular architecture outside the infarcted area (Supplementary Fig. S5 A-B). In addition, cardiac remodeling was evaluated by Sirius red polarization microscopy to quantify collagen deposition and maturation within the scar and border zone. Total collagen content within the scar was comparable across all experimental groups. Detailed analysis of collagen fiber composition revealed no differences in the ratio of thick (orange-red) to thin (yellow-green) birefringent collagen fibers between WT, 5-HT7R-KO, and WT+LP-211 mice (Supplementary Fig. S5 C-F), indicating that 5-HT7R signaling does not significantly influence collagen organization or scar maturation at this stage after MI. Collectively, these data demonstrate that pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R enhances neoangiogenesis in the infarct border zone after myocardial infarction, as evidenced by increased endothelial marker expression, without affecting cardiomyocyte size, capillary density in remote myocardium, or scar composition.
sections.5-ht7r activation influences the molecul: To investigate underlying molecular pathways, Ly6G - CD11b + macrophages were isolated from infarcted mouse hearts 3 days post-MI followed by RNA-Seq and comprehensive pathway analysis (Fig. 4 A–E; Supplementary Fig. S6 ). Comparative transcriptomic profiling revealed substantial changes in gene expression upon genetic ablation or pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R. Specifically, 1003 genes were differentially expressed in macrophages from 5-HT7R-KO mice compared with WT controls, whereas 1041 transcripts were significantly regulated in macrophages from WT mice treated with the selective 5-HT7R agonist LP-211 relative to WT macrophages (Fig. 4 B, C). Notably, 338 genes (19.8% of all regulated transcripts) were shared between both comparisons, which likely represent key downstream targets of 5-HT7R signaling thus highlighting the regulatory role of the receptor in shaping macrophage responses during the early post-infarction phase (Fig. 4 B). Starting one day after surgery, WT animals received a daily injection of LP-211. On day 3 after surgery macrophages were isolated and subjected to RNA sequencing. ( C ) Heatmap indicates differently expressed genes between macrophages of WT and LP-211-treated WT mice. Each column dataset corresponds to one animal. Upregulated genes are shown in red and downregulated genes in blue Gene ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis revealed that modulation of 5-HT7R activity predominantly affected transcriptional programs associated with inflammatory signaling, immune regulation and wound healing processes (Fig. 4 D, E, Supplementary Fig. S6 D). Gene enrichment analysis further revealed the complex and coordinated regulaton of inflammatory pathway networks in macrophages both upon LP-211-mediated receptor activation and in absence of 5-HT7R siganling, underscoring the role of this receptor in post-MI macrophage biology (Fig. 4 E, Supplementary Fig. S6 E). Among the differentially regulated genes, two particularly interesting gene candidates were identified, namely S100 Calcium Binding Protein A9 ( S100A9 ) and Glutamic-Oxaloacetic Transaminase 1 ( Got1 ), both of which are known to be involved in post-MI inflammatory and metabolic responses, but have not previously been linked to serotonergic signaling. We found that expression of Got1 was significantly reduced in macrophages from 5-HT7R-KO mice compared with WT macrophages, whereas macrophages from LP-211-treated WT mice exhibited increased Got1 expression relative to WT controls (Fig. 5 A). In contrast, S100A9 expression was higher in macrophages from 5-HT7R-KO mice compared to WT macrophages, while the observed elevation through LP-211 treatment did not reach statistical significance. Such bidirectional regulation of inflammatory and metabolic genes, including Got1 and S100A9 , suggests that 5-HT7R signaling can be involved in controlling macrophage-driven inflammatory responses and early remodeling processes in the infarcted myocardium.
