( A ) mRNA expression of Glutamic-Oxaloacetic Transaminase 1 (Got1) and S100 Calcium Binding protein A9 (S100A9) in macrophages isolated from the mouse heart 3 days post-MI, determined by RNA-sequencing. ( B ) Relative mRNA expression of Got1 and S100A9 in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of MI patients ( N = 18) 3 ± 1d after insult compared to healthy controls ( N = 11) normalized to 18S rRNA. ( C ) Correlation analysis of Got1 and S100A9 expression against 5-HT7R expression in human PBMCs. Axis values show ΔCT values normalized to 18S, so lower numbers indicate greater expression levels. Simple linear regression and correlation analysis revealed positive correlation for 5-HT7R expression and Got1 in PBMCs of patients 3 days after MI (R 2 = 0.3345; p = 0.0104) and for 5-HT7R expression and S100A9 in Ctrl subjects (R 2 = 0.4338; p = 0.0275) and MI patients (R 2 = 0.2235; p = 0.0476)
sections.regulation of got1 and s100a9 expression: To assess the translational relevance of the identified target genes in the human system, we analyzed expression levels of Got1 and S100A9 in PBMCs isolated from patients 3 ± 1 days after acute MI. These PBMCs have previously been shown to exhibit significantly increased 5-HT7R expression after MI (Fig. 1 D). In line with the murine data, PBMCs from MI patients displayed significantly reduced Got1 mRNA expression and concomitantly increased S100A9 expression compared with healthy control individuals (Fig. 5 B). Importantly, expression levels of both Got1 and S100A9 showed a positive correlation with 5-HT7R mRNA expression, with this association being particularly pronounced in PBMCs from MI patients (Fig. 5 C). These findings support the clinical relevance of Got1 and S100A9 as downstream targets of 5-HT7R signaling.
sections.discussion: Current research focuses on identifying novel molecular targets to improve patient outcomes after MI. In this context, the serotonergic (5-HT) system has emerged as an attractive candidate [ 5 ]. In the present study, we identify 5-HT7R as a relevant modulator of the inflammatory response after MI. We demonstrated that 5-HT7R expression is transiently upregulated during the acute phase after MI both in human PBMCs and in mouse hearts. The modulation of 5-HT7R appears to be regulated post-transcriptionally via the expression of miRNAs. Importantly, this upregulation is mainly confined to inflammatory cells, in particular macrophages located in the infarct and border regions of the heart, suggesting that 5-HT7R signaling may be specifically involved in immune cell-mediated processes during early post-infarction remodeling. To assess the functional relevance of 5-HT7R signaling in vivo, we combined genetic and pharmacological approaches. Systemic deletion of 5-HT7R did not affect cardiac function under basal conditions but resulted in significantly impaired left ventricular function and increased inflammatory signatures 14 days after MI, despite unchanged infarct size. These findings indicate that 5-HT7R signaling is dispensable for normal cardiac homeostasis but becomes critical during post-infarction repair. Conversely, pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R using the selective agonist LP-211 [ 40 , 41 ] significantly improved survival after MI. Of note, no significant differences in cardiac function were detected between WT mice treated with LP-211 and untreated WT controls. This lack of functional differences might be explained by survivor bias, as animals with severely impaired cardiac function predominantly died during the subacute phase after MI (2–7 days), mainly due to cardiac rupture. Consequently, differences between groups were reflected primarily in mortality rather than in cardiac function among surviving animals. Previous work from our group and others has shown that 5-HT7R signaling regulates macrophage morphology, motility and cytokine secretion in vitro and in vivo [ 10 ]. Extending these observations, our data suggest that 5-HT7R activation modulates the inflammatory phenotype of cardiac macrophages during the acute phase after MI. Consistently, LP-211 treatment altered macrophage composition within the infarcted myocardium and was associated with reduced inflammatory marker expression, supporting the concept that 5-HT7R signaling contributes to fine-tuning of post-infarction inflammation. To gain mechanistic insight, we performed transcriptomic profiling of cardiac macrophages isolated 3 days after MI. RNA-sequencing revealed extensive transcriptional reprogramming upon both genetic deletion and pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R, with a substantial overlap of differentially expressed genes in the two conditions. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted inflammatory signaling, chemotaxis, angiogenesis and wound healing processes as key targets of 5-HT7R modulation. Notably, LP-211 treatment reduced expression of IL-6, a cytokine strongly implicated in adverse post-MI remodeling and poor outcome [ 42 – 44 ], suggesting a potential mechanism underlying the observed survival benefit. Among the differentially regulated genes, we identified S100A9 and Got1 as particularly interesting candidates. Both genes have been previously linked to MI pathology but had not been connected to serotonergic signaling. [ 45 , 46 ]. Got1 plays a central role in cellular amino acid metabolism and has been associated with improved survival in MI patients [ 46 ]. In line with our observation of reduced Got1 expression in PBMCs from MI patients early after infarction, Mouton et al. reported decreased Got1 levels in the remote myocardium of C57BL/6J mice at 3 and 7 days after MI, whereas Got1 expression was increased in macrophages within the infarct scar at later stages [ 47 ]. Moreover, high Got1 levels in the blood plasma of patients with acute MI have been associated with improved survival, supporting the concept of Got1 as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target [ 46 ]. In our study, pharmacological activation of 5-HT7R was associated with increased Got1 expression in cardiac macrophages during the acute phase after MI, suggesting that serotonergic signaling may support the maintenance of Got1 expression under inflammatory conditions. We therefore propose that 5-HT7R signaling may limit inflammation-induced metabolic reprogramming of immune cells, thereby contributing to the preservation of Got1 levels and facilitating resolution of inflammation. Consistent with this notion, activation of 5-HT7R signaling in the acute phase after MI could attenuate inflammatory metabolic rewiring of macrophages and PBMCs [ 48 – 50 ], which has been shown to suppress Got1 expression, and thereby potentially influence post-infarction outcome. At the mechanistic level, these effects may involve activation of Gαs-cAMP-PKA-CREB axis and ERK/mTOR pathways, which possibly attenuate NF-κB/HIF-1α–driven glycolytic polarization and maintain malate-aspartate shuttle activity [ 51 – 56 ]. As a result, Got1 expression remains preserved, supporting cell metabolism and effective resolution of inflammation. Interestingly, we observed a correlation of 5-HT7R expression with S100A9 levels in PBMCs. We also show that S100A9 expression is significantly upregulated in human PBMCs during the acute phase after MI. Consistent with these findings, we detected increased S100A9 levels in macrophages isolated from the hearts of 5-HT7R-KO mice 3 days post-MI compared to WT mice. S100A9 -expressing macrophages play a critical role in the early inflammatory response after MI by amplifying tissue damage, while also contributing to the transition toward a reparative phase through promotion of fibrosis [ 32 ]. Experimental administration of S100A9 induces neutrophil and macrophage infiltration, modulates macrophage polarization, enhances infarct wall thinning and reduces ejection fraction in mice [ 5 , 24 ]. In line with these reports, we observed a significantly reduced ejection fraction in 5-HT7R-KO mice 14 days after MI compared to WT mice, which may be linked to elevated S100A9 expression in cardiac macrophages during the acute phase 3 days post-MI. Importantly, previous studies demonstrated that short-term inhibition of S100A9, either by pharmacological blockade or macrophage-targeted S100A9 siRNA, restores key biological processes that are otherwise impaired after MI [ 4 , 22 ]. In contrast, prolonged inhibition of S100A9 negatively affects cardiac repair and counteracts the beneficial effects of short-term intervention, underscoring the importance of precise temporal control of S100A9 activity during the dynamic inflammatory phases following MI [ 24 ]. Importantly, we were able to highlight a potential clinical relevance of targeting 5-HT7R signaling by demonstrating that isolated PBMCs from human patients’ blood in the acute phase (3±1 days) after MI showed regulated mRNA expression levels of Got1 and S100A9 , which positively correlated with 5-HT7R expression levels.
sections.limitation of the study: Certain limitations should be acknowledged. 5-HT7R signaling is known to impact various physiological functions, including thermoregulation, circadian rhythm, learning, sleep, and more. Therefore, 5-HT7R agonists, such as LP-211, can possibly exert effects on recovery after MI through a plethora of processes, and might not be limited to the regulation of macrophages. Further, we did not uncover how LP-211 treatment positively regulates survival without improving cardiac function, and if effects would be consistent in female mice.
sections.conclusions_1: In summary, we demonstrate that 5-HT7R signaling is transiently upregulated in inflammatory cells after MI and plays a critical role in shaping the post-infarction inflammatory response. Loss of 5-HT7R signaling aggravates cardiac dysfunction, whereas pharmacological activation improves survival after MI. These effects are associated with modulation of macrophage gene expression programs, including pathways linked to inflammation and metabolism. Our findings identify 5-HT7R as a novel and potentially druggable target to fine-tune immune responses and improve outcomes after MI.

title: Hypercalcitoninemia in chronic kidney disease: an old issue, a new perspective?
abstract: Objective Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has been reported in association with hypercalcitoninemia, but the calcitonin (Ct) values to expect in CKD patients are unknown. This study aimed to evaluate Ct levels in CKD patients using an accurate chemiluminescent immunoassay. Methods Two population datasets were analyzed: Group 1 consisted of 9,450 anonymous subjects with Ct and creatinine measurements; this group was subdivided according to eGFR into a control series (eGFR ≥ 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , n = 4,294) and a CKD series (eGFR < 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , n = 4,022). Group 2 consisted of 135 patients with CKD (78.5% in stage 5). Renal function and Ct levels were retrospectively evaluated. Results The Group 1 CKD series had a median Ct of 1.0 ng/L (IQR: 1.0–2.8 ng/L), 181 patients (4.5%) had Ct > 10 ng/L and ≤30 ng/L, and 35 patients (0.9%) had Ct ≥ 30 ng/L. Median Ct differed significantly according to CKD stage: 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–2.40 ng/L) in stage 2; 1.20 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–4.30 ng/L) in stage 3; 2.80 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–6.75 ng/L) in stage 4; and 4.55 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–11.30 ng/L) in stage 5 ( P < 0.001). Median Ct in the control series was 1.0 ng/L (IQR: 1.0–2.9 ng/L). Ct levels >10 ng/L were significantly associated with CKD stage and were observed in 16.7% of stage 4 patients and 31.1% of stage 5 patients vs 4.3% of controls ( P < 0.001). In Group 1, Ct levels were significantly correlated with creatinine ( P < 0.001). In Group 2, median Ct was 3.7 ng/L (IQR: 1.0–7.0 ng/L), 25 patients (18.5%) had Ct levels >10 ng/L, and Ct levels were not associated with renal function. Conclusions Ct levels may be mildly elevated in advanced CKD; until stage 3, the increase is negligible.

sections.introduction: Calcitonin (Ct) is a peptide hormone secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid and is known to be the most sensitive marker of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) ( 1 ). Ct levels may be mildly elevated in conditions other than C cell disease, being differential diagnosis between non-neoplastic hypercalcitoninemia and MTC pivotal in performing an adequate diagnostic workup. Significantly elevated Ct levels (>100 pg/mL) have a high positive predictive value in the diagnosis of MTC, whereas mildly elevated Ct levels require careful evaluation of the potential causes of non-neoplastic hypercalcitoninemia and further investigation ( 2 ). Chronic autoimmune gastritis, autoimmune thyroiditis, smoking, use of proton pump inhibitors (PPI), and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are among the conditions that have been reported to lead to non-neoplastic hypercalcitoninemia ( 3 , 4 , 5 ). The impact of many of these conditions on Ct levels has recently been questioned now that more accurate assay kits for measuring Ct, such as chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA), are available in clinical practice ( 6 , 7 , 8 ). Previously used methods, such as radioimmunometric assays (RIAs), were less specific for Ct and prone to interference from Ct precursors, which could overestimate the measured level. Nonetheless, as with other biomarkers, Ct measurement is still prone to laboratory interference ( 3 , 9 , 10 ). The vast majority of studies investigating the influence of CKD on Ct levels have been carried out using RIA methods ( 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ), and Ct has rarely been measured with more accurate assays in this context ( 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ). Moreover, it is still not clear at which CKD stage Ct levels significantly rise, as it is difficult to evaluate the significance of mild Ct elevation in patients with CKD and thyroid nodular disease in clinical practice ( 16 , 17 , 18 ). The aim of our study was to evaluate Ct levels in patients with CKD using an accurate measuring method in order to investigate the association between Ct and glomerular filtration rate.
sections.materials and methods: Two separate datasets were compiled: a retrospective dataset of anonymous subjects (Group 1) and a retrospective clinical cohort of CKD patients being followed up at the Nephrology Unit of our hospital (Group 2).
sections.group 1 \u2013 anonymous subjects: The Laboratory Medicine Unit of the University Hospital of Padua provided us with anonymous data obtained from subjects whose Ct levels had been measured at the laboratory between 2013 and 2023. We included these measurements in our analyses only if a simultaneous creatinine measurement was also available. The subjects’ sex and age were also recorded. The data, which came from 9,450 blood samples, were collected retrospectively, anonymously, and consecutively. Of the 9,450 blood samples, 413 samples with Ct levels >100 ng/L were excluded from the analysis as being highly suspicious for MTC. A further 721 were excluded because there were no corresponding glomerular filtration rates estimated by CKD-EPI. We analyzed the remaining 8,316 samples, of which 4,294 subjects with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥ 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were assigned to the ‘control series’ and 4,022 with eGFR < 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 were assigned to the ‘CKD series’ ( Fig. 1 ).
sections.group 2 \u2013 clinical cohort of ckd pa: From April 2023 to June 2024, we consecutively enrolled patients with CKD in follow-up at the Nephrology Unit of the University Hospital of Padua and whose Ct, creatinine, and eGFR had been previously evaluated in a single blood test at the local laboratory. We also considered procalcitonin (proCt) levels and biochemical data on calcium–phosphate metabolism, where available. The inclusion criteria were as follows: CKD, stable for at least 3 months, with eGFR < 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; written consent to participation in the study; previous evaluation of plasma Ct levels by CLIA at the local Laboratory Unit. The exclusion criteria were as follows: diagnosis of autoimmune chronic gastritis; previous or current diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumors; age < 18 years. We ultimately enrolled 135 patients and obtained their anthropometric, clinical, and biochemical data from clinical records. If patients’ Ct levels were above the laboratory upper limit of normality (10 ng/L), a second Ct measurement, where available, was also considered. In dialysis patients, pre-dialysis Ct measurement was considered. This study was performed in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Local Ethical Committee (Padua General Hospital, Comitato Etico per la Sperimentazione Clinica (CESC), ethics code number: 405n/AO/23). All patients in Group 2 gave written informed consent to participate in the study. No informed consent was necessary for Group 1 as the data were collected anonymously and contained nothing of a sensitive nature.
sections.laboratory: Ct levels were measured with a LIAISON® Calcitonin II-Gen CLIA kit (DiaSorin Inc., USA). The method has an analytical sensitivity of ≤1.0 ng/L, a functional sensitivity of ≤3.0 ng/L, and an upper reference limit of 10.0 ng/mL. Procalcitonin levels were measured with a LIAISON BRAHMS PCT II-Gen CLIA kit (DiaSorin, Italy). Analytical sensitivity was 0.04 ng/mL, and the upper reference limit was 0.5 ng/mL. Calcium and phosphate were measured using the colorimetric method (reference ranges: calcium 2.10–2.55 mmol/L; phosphate 0.87–1.45 mmol/L). PTH and 25-OH vitamin D were analyzed using the chemiluminescent method (reference ranges: PTH 6.5–36.8 ng/L; 25-OH vitamin D: 47.8–190.3 nmol/L). Plasma creatinine levels were measured using the enzymatic method, and eGFRs measured with the CKD-EPI method were provided by the laboratory. CKD stages were defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) classification based on eGFR, as follows ( 20 ): stage 1: eGFR ≥ 90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; stage 2: eGFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; stage 3: eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; stage 4: eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; stage 5: eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . All laboratory data were measured at the Laboratory Unit of the University Hospital of Padua.
sections.statistical analysis: The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to assess the normal distribution of the variables. Normally distributed parameters were expressed as the arithmetic mean ± the standard deviation; non-normally distributed parameters were expressed as median, interquartile range (IQR), and range of minimum and maximum value. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ct was considered both a quantitative variable and a categorized variable, in the latter case as either ≤10 ng/L or >10 ng/L. ProCt was considered a quantitative variable and a categorized variable, in the latter case as either ≤0.04 ng/mL or >0.04 ng/mL. Creatinine and eGFR were considered continuous variables, and CKD stages were defined according to the KDIGO classification. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were analyzed with the Mann–Whitney or Kruskal test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were analyzed with the chi-squared test. All statistical analyses were run in the MedCalc® statistical software, version 22.023 (MedCalc Software Ltd, Belgium; https://www.medcalc.org ; 2024).
sections.group 1: The CKD series of Group 1 consisted of 4,022 anonymous subjects, of which 1,421 (35.3%) were females and 2,601 (64.7%) were males; the median age was 61 years (IQR: 53–68 years; range: 20–74 years). Of these, 3,422 (85.1%) were in CKD stage 2, 478 (11.9%) in stage 3, 48 (1.2%) in stage 4, and 74 (1.8%) in stage 5. Median creatinine was 81.0 μmol/L (IQR: 72.0–93.0 μmol/L; range: 55.0–1,523.00 μmol/L), and median eGFR was 77.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (IQR: 67.0–84.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; range: 3.0–89.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ). The control series of Group 1 consisted of 4,294 anonymous subjects. The distributions by sex, age, creatinine, and eGFR of the CKD series and the control series are reported in Table 1 . The median Ct of all Group 1 subjects was 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–2.90 ng/L; range: 1.00–99.6 ng/L). Median Ct levels were significantly higher in females (2.70 ng/L, IQR: 1.00–5.00 ng/L) than in males (1.00 ng/L, IQR: 1.00–1.30 ng/L) ( P < 0.0001). There was no statistically significant difference in median Ct levels between controls and the entire CKD series, the former being 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–2.90 ng/L; range: 1.00–99.40 ng/L) and the latter 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–2.80 ng/L; range: 1.00–99.60 ng/L) ( P = 0.248). In the CKD series, we found a significant association between Ct level and CKD stage. The median Ct levels by CKD stage were as follows: stage 2, 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–2.40 ng/L; range: 1.00–99.6 ng/L); stage 3, 1.20 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–4.30 ng/L; range: 1.00–91.90 ng/L); stage 4, 2.80 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–6.75 ng/L; range: 1.00–26.6 ng/L); and stage 5, 4.55 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–11.30 ng/L; range: 1.00–29.70 ng/L) ( P < 0.001). Ct levels differed significantly between all stages, except for stages 4 and 5, which were not significantly different from each other. Median Ct was significantly lower in stage 2 than in the control series, while from stage 3 onward, it was significantly higher than in the controls ( P < 0.001) ( Fig. 2 ). We also found a significant difference in the distribution of Ct levels categorized as ≤10 ng/L or as >10 ng/L according to renal function, the most advanced CKD stages being significantly associated with Ct > 10 ng/L ( P < 0.001) ( Table 2 ). In the CKD series, Ct was ≤10 ng/L in 3,806 (94.6%) cases, >10 ng/L and ≤30 ng/L in 181 (4.5%) cases, and >30 ng/L and <100 ng/L in 35 (0.9%) cases, which means that 5.4% of these subjects had Ct values higher than 10 ng/L. We found a positive correlation between Ct and creatinine levels ( R 2 = 0.014, y = 2.2095 + 0.008428x, P < 0.001) and a negative correlation between Ct and eGFR ( R 2 = 0.010, y = 5.9947–0.04071x, P < 0.0001) in CKD stages 2, 3, and 4, but no correlation in stage 5 ( Fig. 3 ).
sections.group 2: We enrolled 135 patients with CKD, 92 (68.1%) of which were males and 43 (31.9%) were females. The median age at enrollment was 74 years (IQR: 59.0–82.8 years; range: 25.0–93.0 years). Of these patients, 104 (77%) were undergoing dialysis treatment, while 31 (23%) had CKD that did not require this treatment. Other information, such as the patients’ smoking status, use of PPI, and anthropometric data, is reported in Table 3 . Seven (5.2%) patients had stage 2 CKD, 17 (12.6%) stage 3, five (3.7%) stage 4, and 106 (78.5%) stage 5. All but two of the 106 patients in stage 5 were undergoing dialysis treatment. Median creatinine was 646.5 μmol/L (IQR: 160.0–868.5 μmol/L; range: 76.0–1,407.0 μmol/L), and median eGFR was 6.5 mL/min/1.73 m 2 (IQR: 5.0–35.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; range: 3.0–88.0 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ). The etiologies of renal disease in Group 2 patients are reported in Table 4 . There were no significant differences between the sexes in either creatinine levels or eGFR. The median levels and IQRs of calcium, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D, and PTH were, respectively, 2.23 mmol/L (2.12–2.35 mmol/L), 1.36 mmol/L (1.08–1.65 mmol/L), 40.5 nmol/L (21.0–65.0 nmol/L), and 161.0 ng/L (74.0–281.5 ng/L). The median Ct level was 3.7 ng/L (IQR: 1.0–7.0 ng/L; range: 1.0–24.2 ng/L). There was a statistically significant difference between the sexes in median Ct levels, which were 1.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–3.98 ng/L; range: 1.0–19.8 ng/L) in females and 4.65 ng/L (IQR: 1.35–9.30 ng/L; range: 1.0–24.2 ng/L) in males ( P < 0.001). Ct levels were <1 ng/L in 35 (25.9%) patients, ≥1 ng/L and ≤10 ng/L in 75 (55.6%) patients, and >10 ng/L in 25 (18.5%). None of the patients had a Ct level >30 ng/L. There was no statistically significant difference between the dialysis and non-dialysis patients in median Ct levels, which were 3.50 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–7.75 ng/L; range: 1.0–24.2 ng/L) in the former and 4.00 ng/L (IQR: 1.53–6.48 ng/L; range: 1.0–14.8 ng/L) in the latter. Patients with Ct levels >10 ng/L for whom post-dialysis measurements were available exhibited higher median Ct values after dialysis than before, although the difference did not reach statistical significance (median pre-dialysis Ct: 12.2 ng/L (IQR: 11.3–21.6 ng/L; range: 10.4–21.8 ng/L); median post-dialysis Ct: 19.55 ng/L (IQR: 13.50–28.40 ng/L; range: 8.50–96.90 ng/L); P = 0.06). There was no significant correlation between Ct and creatinine levels, nor between Ct and eGFR. We found no statistically significant differences in Ct levels according to CKD stage: median Ct was 2.30 ng/L (IQR: 1.55–5.75 ng/L; range: 1.0–14.8 ng/L) in stage 2, 4.40 ng/L (IQR: 2.65–7.05 ng/L; range: 1.0–12.6 ng/L) in stage 3, 3.80 ng/L (IQR: 1.28–8.18 ng/L; range: 1.2–12.3 ng/L) in stage 4, and 3.50 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–7.70 ng/L; range: 1.0–24.2 ng/L) in stage 5 ( P = 0.79). Among patients with elevated Ct levels (>10 ng/L), we found no significant association between Ct level and CKD stage: Ct levels were >10 ng/L in 14.3% of patients in stage 2, 11.8% in stage 3, 20% in stage 4, and 19.8% in stage 5 ( P = 0.87). Repeat Ct measurements were taken for all 25 patients with Ct levels >10 ng/L, and elevated levels were confirmed in nine of them. These nine patients underwent thyroid ultrasound to rule out the presence of suspicious nodules: four had no nodules, while five had small nodules without features suggestive of malignancy. No signs of autoimmune thyroiditis were observed. Their Ct levels, dialysis treatment, and ultrasound findings are reported in Table 5 . We found no statistically significant associations between Ct and age, weight, BMI, smoking status, use of PPI, calcium, phosphate, PTH, or 25-OH vitamin D. The median proCt level was 0.13 ng/mL (IQR: 0.04–0.42 ng/mL; range: 0.04–0.88 ng/mL); proCt was undetectable (<0.04 ng/mL) in 22 (34.9%) patients. Ct and proCt levels were not correlated ( P = 0.087). Median proCt was higher in dialysis patients than in non-dialysis patients: 0.41 ng/mL (IQR: 0.26–0.55 ng/mL; range: 0.12–0.55 ng/mL) in the former; 0.04 ng/mL (IQR: 0.04–0.05 ng/mL; range: 0.04–0.14 ng/mL) in the latter ( P < 0.001) ( Fig. 4A ). We found no significant differences in proCt levels between CKD stages 2, 3, and 4, but median proCt levels were significantly higher in stage 5 patients than in stage 2–4 patients, respectively, 0.39 ng/mL (IQR: 0.23–0.54 ng/mL; range: 0.05–0.88 ng/mL) and 0.04 ng/mL (IQR: 0.04–0.04 ng/mL; range: 0.04–0.04 ng/mL) ( P < 0.001) ( Fig. 4B ). ProCt was detectable (≥0.04 ng/mL) in 24.1% of patients with CKD stages 2–4 and in 100% of stage 5 CKD patients, a statistically significant difference ( P < 0.001). Finally, we found proCt values to be significantly related to creatinine levels ( R 2 = 0.44, y = 0.01875 + 0.0004280x, P < 0.001) and eGFR ( R 2 = 0.37, y = 0.4533–0.01110x, P < 0.001) ( Fig. 4C ).
sections.discussion: Calcitonin is a highly sensitive marker for MTC, but its low specificity is problematic, especially when it is only mildly elevated. The American Thyroid Association Guidelines for the management of MTC advise clinicians that misleadingly high Ct levels can occur with a variety of clinical diseases other than MTC, including chronic renal failure. With respect to the evaluation of Ct, CLIAs are confirmed as highly sensitive and specific for monomeric Ct ( 3 ). CKD is one of the leading causes of death in this century. Approximately 850 million people worldwide are estimated to have kidney disease, which is reported to be the third fastest-growing cause of death globally ( 20 , 21 , 22 ). Given the high prevalence of CKD, accurate Ct measurement in this broad population of patients is crucial to avoid either unnecessary treatment or underestimating its clinical significance. Since the initial observations on small series, subsequent studies have shown that Ct levels are elevated in patients with CKD ( 11 , 12 , 23 , 24 ). In these studies, Ct was measured using RIA methods, mostly in patients being treated with chronic hemodialysis, and was reported to be higher than the normal range. In a 1995 study on a small series of patients, Messa et al. found that subjects with normal renal function and CKD patients with eGFR > 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 had similar Ct levels, with a mean of approximately 10 ng/L in both groups. However, the mean Ct value was 34 ng/L in patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , measured by RIA ( 13 ). Our study corroborates previous findings that CKD patients with eGFR > 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 have, on the whole, similar Ct values to controls. Nevertheless, the median Ct values in our study were lower than those previously reported for both groups, possibly reflecting the better accuracy of the assessment method. Approximately 30% of dialysis patients have been reported as having increased Ct values ( 15 , 19 , 25 ). More recently, Borchhardt et al. reported a median Ct value of 31 ng/L in a cohort of 17 patients with stage 4 and stage 5 CKD before kidney transplant, although measurement was made by CLIA in only a subset of cases. In a second study by the same group, the median Ct of 15 patients with CKD with C cell hyperplasia (CCH) was found to be as high as 35 ng/L ( 16 , 17 ). It is only in recent years that studies have measured Ct levels in CKD patients using CLIA for the whole series ( 18 , 19 ). Notably, Sabia et al. reported a median Ct of 8 ng/L in a cohort of 31 patients with dialysis-dependent CKD ( 18 ). Akan et al. reported a median Ct level of 8 ng/L in 283 dialysis patients, with no difference between pre- and post-dialysis measurements ( 19 ). In our study, Ct levels measured with accurate CLIA methods were higher than 10 ng/L in 5.4% of CKD patients as a whole. Looking at only those patients with end-stage renal disease (stage 5), median Ct was 4.55 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–11.30 ng/L) in the anonymous subjects dataset and 3.50 ng/L (IQR: 1.00–7.70 ng/L) in the clinical cohort. Ct was >10 ng/L in approximately 30% of the former group and 20% of the latter. Our study substantially confirms previous observations that Ct can be expected to be higher than the normal range in 20–30% of patients in end-stage CKD, although the Ct levels in our study were substantially lower than those previously reported ( 15 , 18 , 19 , 25 ). The difference between older findings and our own is likely to be mainly related to the assay used for measuring Ct, as two-site and two-step immunoassays are more accurate in recognizing mature Ct as distinct from Ct precursors, which are particularly abundant in the case of CKD ( 3 , 9 ). Furthermore, the above-mentioned studies focused exclusively on end-stage renal disease and paid little attention to patients with moderately reduced GFR. An apparent inconsistency in our results is that Ct levels were significantly associated with creatinine and eGFR among the anonymous subjects (Group 1), whereas the association was not significant in our smaller cluster of clinical CKD patients (Group 2). In our opinion, there are several reasons for this discrepancy. First, there were probably too few subjects in the Group 2 clinical cohort for the positive correlation between creatinine and Ct, and the negative correlation between eGFR and Ct, to reach statistical significance. The discrepancy could also be attributed to the different distributions of CKD stages in the two populations, as only 1.8% of the anonymous Group 1 subjects were in stage 5, against 78% of Group 2 CKD patients. We also found that in Group 1, the median Ct level increased from one CKD stage to the next up to stage 4, but stages 4 and 5 did not significantly differ from each other. The inconsistency is therefore only apparent, and the results are, after all, consistent if the different CKD stages in the two groups are taken into account. Moreover, since NET and chronic autoimmune gastritis were exclusion criteria for enrollment in Group 2, and PPI use and smoking were not significantly associated with Ct levels in this group, advanced-stage CKD may be considered an independent risk factor for increased Ct levels. However, as the anonymized data from Group 1 did not include information on comorbidities, the potential contribution of these conditions could not be evaluated on a larger scale. One of the greatest strengths of our study is the very high number of patients – the largest so far reported in the literature in a clinical setting – which included not only subjects with very compromised renal function, but also a large number of patients at the less advanced CKD stages. Moreover, using a modern measurement method, the CLIA, across the entire cohort allowed us to accurately assess Ct levels. Our study has some limitations. First, we were unable to correlate Ct levels with potential confounders in Group 1, such as comorbidities known to be associated with elevated Ct levels. Second, no definitive diagnostic conclusion, other than CKD, could be drawn for Group 2: patients with Ct levels above the reference range did not undergo fine-needle aspiration biopsy as no suspicious thyroid nodules were identified. In addition, the inclusion of two distinct populations with different distributions of CKD stages precluded direct comparison of the results of the two groups. Moreover, the exclusion of records with Ct levels >100 pg/mL may have resulted in an underestimation of the median Ct levels among the CKD patients in Group 1. Finally, because the laboratory records were anonymized, it was not possible to determine whether patients with MTC had also been included in the analysis. However, the large number of records examined, the exclusion of patients with Ct levels >100 ng/L, and the rarity of MTC should mitigate this potential bias. A previous study by Fugazzola et al. used a baseline Ct cutoff of >30 pg/mL for females and >34 pg/mL for males to differentiate MTC from non-MTC patients ( 26 ). In our series, only 0.9% of the laboratory samples and none of the clinical cohort had Ct levels higher than 30 ng/L, so there is a very low probability that MTC patients were included in our dataset. Finally, in a single study in which Ct was measured by both CLIA and RIA, Borchhardt et al. proposed a Ct cutoff of 50–150 ng/L to discriminate between MTC and CCH in patients with CKD and observed that 250 ng/L was the lowest Ct value among MTC patients on dialysis ( 17 ). In Group 2, Ct values for patients with CKD under dialysis treatment were below the reported cutoff for MTC diagnosis, further supporting the very low probability that MTC patients were included in our dataset. In the clinical setting of Group 2 patients, we also evaluated proCt levels according to renal function and found them to be significantly related to creatinine and eGFR, with a significant difference between dialysis and non-dialysis patients. These findings, the opposite of those for Ct in the same population, were also confirmed by the absence of a correlation between Ct and proCt in our population. A study by Wu et al. found that serum concentrations of proCt were higher in patients with CKD than in healthy controls. Increased proCt has been related to a reduction in renal clearance and partly to a condition of low-grade chronic inflammation ( 27 ). Elevated Ct levels, on the other hand, have been reported as being secondary to CCH associated with CKD: the two different mechanisms potentially explain the different behaviors of the two markers according to dialysis and their reciprocal independence ( 13 , 18 ). Interestingly, in our series, we did not find statistically significant differences in Ct levels according to chronic dialysis treatment, which may be explained by the high number of dialysis patients (77%) in our clinical population of CKD patients. The correlation between Ct and creatinine that was observed in the anonymous records was not confirmed in CKD stage 5, which may be related to the fact that elevated Ct in end-stage renal disease is not related to reduced filtration, but rather is secondary to increased C cell hormone secretion ( 13 , 18 ). Consequently, the observed increase in Ct after dialysis, although not statistically significant, may be secondary to a reduction in circulating blood volume induced by dialysis. Our results suggest that proCt is not a suitable complementary marker for the diagnosis of MTC in patients with CKD, particularly in those requiring dialysis. We recently asserted that the combined use of Ct and proCt may improve diagnostic accuracy in patients with mildly elevated Ct levels, using a proCt cutoff of 0.04 ng/mL ( 28 ). However, this finding does not apply to the CKD population examined in the present study, where proCt levels of all patients with stage 5 CKD and 24% of those in earlier stages were ≥0.04 ng/mL. This means that the use of proCt as a complementary diagnostic marker for MTC in this setting may lead to significant overtreatment. Although we have no definitive confirmation of the presence or absence of MTC in our series, we believe that proCt may be more of a confounding factor than a reliable diagnostic tool in CKD patients, particularly in advanced renal disease, where chronic inflammation may contribute to persistently elevated proCt levels. Secondary hypercalcitoninemia is an important issue, and current guidelines state that serum Ct levels may be elevated in different thyroid- and non-thyroid-related conditions, such as CKD ( 3 ). Our group recently found no increase in Ct levels, measured by CLIA, in patients with chronic autoimmune gastritis, regardless of the presence of autoimmune thyroiditis ( 7 ). In the present study, we confirmed that Ct levels may be elevated in CKD patients, although the median Ct lies within the normal range in all stages of CKD.
sections.conclusion: The present study confirms that Ct levels increase in patients with CKD, continuing to rise with advancing CKD stage, and in significant relation to creatinine and eGFR. However, overall, we found that median Ct lies within the normal range in all stages of CKD and is only slightly higher in CKD patients than in controls. Ct is significantly elevated for clinical practice only from stage 4 and is higher than the normal range in approximately 30% of stage 5 CKD cases, although absolute Ct levels measured by CLIA are often only slightly above the normal range. The use of proCt in patients with CKD warrants careful consideration, as it may potentially lead to overtreatment in cases of mildly elevated Ct levels.

title: Possible Diagnostic Error in Cervical Artery Dissection: Analysis of STOP ‐ CAD Study
abstract: Background Cervical artery dissection (CeAD) is a common cause of stroke in young adults but is frequently misdiagnosed due to its nonspecific symptoms. This study examines factors associated with possible diagnostic error in CeAD and evaluates its impact on patient outcomes. Methods We conducted a secondary analysis of the STOP‐CAD (Antithrombotic Therapy for Stroke Prevention in Cervical Artery Dissection) study, which is a multicenter international study of adult patients admitted with CeAD. Possible diagnostic error was defined as the presence of CeAD symptoms within 30 days before the index CeAD diagnosis. The comparison group included patients diagnosed on their first medical encounter. Multivariable regression was used to identify factors associated with possible diagnostic error. Primary and secondary outcomes included ischemic stroke, death, and modified Rankin Scale score <2. Results Of 4012 patients (mean age 47.5 years, 44.6% female), 663 (16.5%) experienced possible diagnostic error. Among these, 224 (33.8%) reported to have ischemic stroke before CeAD diagnosis. Patients with possible diagnostic error were younger (odds ratio [OR], 0.89, P <0.001), more likely to have a history of migraines (OR, 1.35, P =0.007), and more likely to present with headaches (OR, 1.43, P <0.001), but less likely to show focal neurologic signs (OR, 0.68, P <0.001). There was no significant difference between groups in ischemic stroke after diagnosis (adjusted OR, 0.96, P =0.86), 90‐day modified Rankin Scale score <2 (adjusted OR, 1.04, P =0.80), or death (adjusted OR, 0.58, P =0.34). Conclusions One in 6 patients with CeAD experienced a possible diagnostic error, particularly those who were younger, had migraines, or presented with headaches and nonfocal symptoms.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: In a large international STOP‐CAD (Antithrombotic Therapy for Stroke Prevention in Cervical Artery Dissection) cohort, ~1 in 6 patients with cervical artery dissection had a prior health care encounter within 30 days before diagnosis for symptoms attributable to dissection. Despite diagnostic delay, possible diagnostic error was not associated with a higher risk of ischemic stroke after diagnosis, worse functional outcomes or increased mortality.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Cervical artery dissection should remain a key diagnostic consideration in younger patients presenting with new or atypical headache or neck pain, even in the absence of focal neurologic deficits.
sections.methods_1: Aggregate data are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. Institutional review board approval was obtained from each participating center to perform the study. Patient consent was waived due to the retrospective design of the study. This article was written in adherence to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist for observational studies.
sections.study design: This was a planned secondary analysis of the multicenter, cross‐sectional, international, retrospective STOP‐CAD (Antithrombotic Therapy for Stroke Prevention in Cervical Artery Dissection) study, which included patients presenting to an acute care hospital with a diagnosis of CeAD without major trauma. 5 Adult patients aged 18 and older diagnosed with CeAD were identified using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision ( ICD‐9 ; 443.21, 443.24) and Tenth Revision ( ICD‐10 ) codes (I77.71, I77.74 and I77.75). Details of the study including inclusion and exclusion criteria were previously described. 5
sections.possible diagnostic error: For the purposes of this analysis, possible diagnostic error of CeAD was defined as presence of possible CeAD symptoms (such as headache, cervical or neck pain, Horner's syndrome, focal neurologic deficit, transient neurologic symptoms, peripheral cranial nerve palsy, dysphagia, tinnitus, retinal infarct, amaurosis) in a medical encounter within 30 days before the index CeAD diagnosis. The comparison group without possible diagnostic error consisted of patients with CeAD diagnosis made on first medical encounter. We chose the 30‐day window based on prior literature, as this period is reported to be high risk for recurrent stroke after cerebrovascular events and large studies investigating possible diagnostic error have used a similar time definition. 6 , 7 , 8 The STOP‐CAD data abstraction forms included questions to ascertain whether a patient may have presented with CeAD symptoms to a medical setting before their index CeAD diagnosis (possible diagnostic error). These questions were presented in the following sequential order in the data abstraction form using branching logic, whereby subsequent questions would appear only if the answer to Question 1 was “yes”: Question 1: Was the patient seen by a health care professional within the past 30 days for similar symptoms? Question 2: In which setting was the [CeAD] diagnosis not made [possible diagnostic error]? Question 3: Did the patient have an ischemic stroke after the initial encounter, but before [CeAD] diagnosis? 4 Question 4: In what setting was the diagnosis made? Possible diagnostic error was defined as a “yes” answer to Question 1. For Question 2, the misdiagnosis setting was divided into ED, outpatient neurology clinic, outpatient primary or urgent care, or other. We defined the possible diagnostic error of CeAD as having any medical encounter in the ED or office settings within 30 days before CeAD hospitalization for any neurological symptom reported above attributable to CeAD.
sections.covariates: The following covariates were included: Demographic variables: age, biological sex, Race (White, Black, Asian, American Indian or Alaska, or Unknown), Hispanic ethnicity. Comorbidities/medications: hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, migraine, active smoking, recent COVID infection, recent upper respiratory infection, known connective tissue disease, cervical manipulation, pregnancy, postpartum, use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Clinical presentation: ischemic versus nonischemic symptoms (headache, neck pain, tinnitus, Horner's syndrome) on presentation during both possible diagnostic error encounter and during encounter for index hospitalization, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score during encounter for index hospitalization. Imaging findings: normal baseline computed tomography scan, dissection location (single vertebral dissection, single carotid dissection, single intracranial dissection, multivessel dissection), acute infarct on imaging, occlusive dissection, presence of partially occlusive thrombus, intracranial extension, or pseudoaneurysm. All imaging variables were evaluated during the index diagnosis encounter, as no imaging data are available for encounter with possible diagnostic error.
sections.study outcomes: Our primary outcome was ischemic stroke after index CeAD diagnosis within 180 days. Strokes occurring between the initial possible diagnostic error encounter and the index diagnosis date were reported by sites but not included as outcome as strokes occurring in this time interval were not confirmed. Secondary outcomes included death and excellent functional outcome defined as 90‐day modified Rankin Scale score <2 from the time of CeAD diagnosis.
sections.statistical analysis: We compared the aforementioned covariates among patients with and without possible diagnostic error using rank sum test for continuous variables and χ 2 test for categorical variables. We used multivariable regression to identify factors associated with possible diagnostic error. The following covariates included in multivariable regression models were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and prior literature on CeAD and diagnostic delay: age, female sex, race, hyperlipidemia, migraine, postpartum state, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use, presenting with headache, presenting with neck pain, presenting with focal deficit, dissection vessel location, acute infarct on imaging, occlusive dissection, and pseudoaneurysm. Univariable analyses were performed for descriptive purposes only and were not used to determine covariate inclusion. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to assess the association between possible diagnostic error and the primary and secondary outcomes of interest. Specifically, models evaluating ischemic stroke and mortality were adjusted for demographic factors and imaging markers of dissection severity (age, female sex, occlusive dissection, partially occlusive thrombus, multivessel dissection, intracranial extension; mortality also adjusted for National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score). Models evaluating functional outcome were adjusted for age, female sex, and baseline stroke severity (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score). These covariates were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and factors known to influence stroke outcomes or dissection severity. Analyses were performed using STATA SE 18.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Analyses were conducted using a 2‐sided significance level of 0.05. Missing data were not imputed.
sections.baseline characteristics: Of 4023 STOP‐CAD study patients, 4012 were included in this substudy after excluding 11 patients with unavailable variables about possible diagnostic error. The mean±SD age of included subjects was 47.5 (13.3) years and 1788 (44.6%) were women. A total of 663 (16.5%) had a medical encounter for symptoms attributable to CeAD within 30 days preceding the index CeAD diagnosis (the possible diagnostic error group). Of these, 314 were seen in the ED, 272 in primary care/urgent care clinics, 65 in the inpatient setting, 33 in outpatient neurology clinics, and 32 in other settings. Fifty patients had >1 encounter with possible diagnostic error. Out of 663 patients in the possible diagnostic error group, 584 had an encounter 0 to 15 days before the date of index diagnosis and 78 had an encounter 16 to 30 days before index diagnosis (encounter date missing on 1 patient). Among patients with a preceding encounter with possible diagnostic error, 224 (33.8%) had an ischemic stroke reported between the initial encounter with possible diagnostic error and the CeAD index diagnosis encounter and 11 (1.7%) had an additional ischemic stroke within 180 days after index diagnosis. The median time from any symptom onset to diagnosis was 1 day for the entire cohort (interquartile range, 0–6) and 75% of patients were diagnosed within 6 days from symptom onset (Figure S1 ). The median time from symptom onset to diagnosis was significantly higher in patients with possible diagnostic error (7 days [interquartile range, 3–14]) compared with patients without possible diagnostic error (1 day [interquartile range, 0–4], P <0.001).
sections.factors associated with possible diagnos: Table 1 depicts the univariate comparisons of patients with versus without possible diagnostic error. After adjustment, younger age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.89 with a 10‐year increase [95% CI, 0.83–0.95], P <0.001), history of migraine headache (aOR, 1.35 [95% CI, 1.09–1.67], P =0.007), presentation with headache (aOR, 1.43 [95% CI, 1.19–1.71], P <0.001), and absence of focal neurologic signs or symptoms (absence of focal deficit, Horner's or cranial nerve palsy) (aOR, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.56–0.83], P < 0.001) were independently associated with possible diagnostic error (Table 2 ).
sections.association between possible diagnostic: In adjusted analyses, there was no significant difference in the 180‐day ischemic stroke incidence (aOR, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.63–1.48], P =0.86), excellent 90‐day functional outcome (aOR, 1.04 [95% CI, 0.76–1.44], P =0.80), and death at 90 days (aOR, 0.58 [95% CI, 0.19–1.8], P =0.34) among patients with CeAD with and without possible diagnostic error (Table 3 ).
sections.discussion: In this large, multicenter, international STOP‐CAD substudy, 1 in 6 patients with CeAD experienced possible diagnostic error, defined as a prior health care encounter attributable to CeAD within 30 days before their index diagnosis. Younger age, history of migraine headaches, presence of headache, and clinical presentations without focal neurologic deficits were associated with a higher likelihood of possible diagnostic error. Importantly, we did not find a significant difference in 180‐day ischemic stroke risk, excellent functional outcome, or death among patients with CeAD with and without preceding possible diagnostic error. Our rate of possible diagnostic error of CeAD was greater than in a prior study using administrative claims data from a large heterogeneous cohort of patients from 2 states, which reported a CeAD misdiagnosis (type of possible diagnostic error) in 1 in 30 patients in ED settings. 3 Our higher rate of possible diagnostic error may be due to a longer time interval (30 days in our study versus 14 days in the prior study) and the inclusion of encounters in a variety of non‐ED outpatient settings. Additionally, our use of detailed clinical data through chart reviews may have allowed for the inclusion of more comprehensive neurological symptoms, including nonfocal presentations that are known to be diagnostically challenging, potentially leading to the identification of more encounters with possible diagnostic error. Our study identified several risk factors associated with possible diagnostic error of CeAD. We found that younger patients had a higher likelihood of having possible diagnostic error, which is consistent with prior studies examining possible diagnostic error of stroke. 3 , 6 , 9 In fact, one study showed that younger patients under the age of 44 years were 7 times more likely to have a probable stroke misdiagnosis compared with patients older than 75 years of age. 6 A recent study on misdiagnosis of CeAD using administrative claims data showed that the mean age among patients with probable misdiagnosis in the ED setting was 43.3 years compared with 53 years in patients without probable misdiagnosis. 3 Patients with a history of migraine headaches or presenting with headache were more likely to have possible diagnostic error, which is similar to what is reported in the stroke diagnostic error literature. Migraine is a known stroke chameleon, often incorrectly diagnosed in cases of missed stroke. 6 , 10 , 11 Diagnosing cerebrovascular conditions in patients who present with a history of migraines, headache, and otherwise minimal neurological deficits is challenging. 12 , 13 Headache is a common presenting symptom in patients with CeAD, it often precedes focal neurologic deficit, and at times it is the only clinical presentation along with neck pain. 14 , 15 There are no specific features that help distinguish dissection‐associated headache from other causes of headaches. Although inclusion of headache predominant presentations may overestimate true diagnostic error, excluding such presentations would risk underestimating delayed in recognition, particularly among nonischemic presentation. Thus, our findings should be interpreted as reflecting challenges in early recognition rather than inappropriate care at the initial encounter. Clinicians need to use caution when evaluating patients with headache and keep CeAD in the differential to initiate timely and appropriate workup. The goal of highlighting headache‐predominant presentations is not to suggest that all patients with headache or neck pain should undergo vascular imaging. Given the high prevalence of benign headache disorders, indiscriminate imaging could lead to substantial overtesting and false‐positive evaluations. Rather, our findings emphasize maintaining clinical awareness of CeAD in patients with new, atypical, or severe head or neck pain, particularly in younger individuals. Careful clinical judgment is required to balance timely recognition of CeAD with appropriate and judicious use of diagnostic resources. Additionally, patients with nonischemic clinical presentation were more likely to experience possible diagnostic error, which is also consistent with prior stroke literature. Stroke protocols generally capture focal neurological symptoms, but not isolated headache or neck pain, which are often the initial symptoms in CeAD and tend to precede focal ischemic symptoms. 16 CeAD diagnosis should be considered in patients who present with new or worsening headache or neck pain. 7 Moreover, a quarter of patients with carotid dissection have an associated partial Horner syndrome, which if present with new or worsening headache could suggest carotid dissection and help with timely diagnosis. 1 , 17 In addition, we found that patients without possible diagnostic error were more likely to receive intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy during index hospitalization compared with patients who experienced possible diagnostic error. Although the exact reason for this is unclear, it is possible that patients without possible diagnostic error had more typical acute stroke presentations, facilitating rapid recognition and access to acute stroke care, which contributed to be absence of possible diagnostic error. Importantly, one third of patients with possible diagnostic error were found to have a stroke between the possible diagnostic error encounter and before the index diagnosis. These events occurred before confirmed CeAD diagnosis, were not adjudicated, and may not have been preventable. Therefore, they should be interpreted as descriptive in nature rather than as evidence of harm from diagnostic delay. Nevertheless, this finding underscores the close time proximity between symptoms onset and ischemic events and highlights the importance of timely recognition and treatment of CeAD, to reduce the risk of future ischemic stroke. 16 Lastly, we did not find any difference in outcomes among CeAD patients with and without possible diagnostic error, which is keeping in line with the previous literature. 3 We may be overestimating the number of possible diagnostic errors, as some encounters were likely not related to subsequent hospitalization for CeAD. Alternatively, we could be underestimating the rate of diagnostic errors, as some patients likely did not return for evaluation, sought care at different medical centers, or died before an accurate diagnosis could be made. It is also possible that patients who experience diagnostic errors are low‐risk individuals, whose outcomes remain unchanged despite the diagnostic error. Our findings that patients with possible diagnostic error were less likely to present with focal deficits or have acute infarcts or occlusive dissection on imaging, compared with patients without possible diagnostic error, might support this hypothesis. However, it remains unclear whether timely and accurate diagnosis of patients who initially experience a diagnostic error leads to improved outcomes or reduces harm. Our study has several important limitations. An important limitation of this study is the inability to determine whether prior health care encounters truly represented diagnostic error, as many presentations included nonspecific symptoms, for which immediate vascular imaging may not have been indicated. Thus, our definition of possible diagnostic error may overestimate true misdiagnosis while at the same time, undercapture external encounters. Thus, the findings should be interpreted as identifying presentations associated with delayed recognition rather than definitive diagnostic error. Not all encounters within 30 days before CeAD diagnosis may be related to subsequent CeAD detection. Although some may represent instances of severely delayed or missed diagnosis of CeAD, others could have had symptoms similar but unrelated to CeAD. Differentiating recurrent migraine symptoms from musculoskeletal neck pain or symptoms that would prompt further CeAD workup is important in the allocation of imaging resources in the emergency department or outpatient settings. Also, strokes reported to have occurred between the time interval of possible diagnostic error and final diagnosis were not adjudicated or confirmed, compared with stroke outcomes that occurred after the index correct diagnosis, which were all confirmed by site investigators. These events should be considered descriptive in nature and not interpreted as evidence of harm attributable to diagnostic delay. In addition, our study is retrospective and prone to ascertainment bias. Lastly, diagnosis of CeAD was identified using ICD 10 codes and not prospectively, and detailed data with regard to a possible diagnostic error encounter such as hospital type (teaching versus nonteaching) and clinician level or experience (years in practice) were not collected. However, studying diagnostic error would not be feasible prospectively, and retrospective data sets are the only way to study root causes of diagnostic error. On the other hand, retrospective data sets may be limited by documentation, and prior medical encounters might not be systematically documented.
sections.conclusions_1: One in 6 patients eventually diagnosed with CeAD experienced a prior health care encounter for symptoms attributable to CeAD, with one ‐third having an ischemic stroke after the possible diagnostic error encounter. This was especially common in younger patients with a history of migraines and a headache or nonfocal clinical symptoms.

title: Primary health care experiences of Indian immigrants living with chronic illnesses in Australia: a qualitative study
abstract: Aim: To explore the primary health care experiences of Indian immigrants living with chronic illnesses in Australia. Background: Primary health care is integral for managing health issues for people living with chronic illnesses. Despite Indian migrants being the largest overseas-born population in Australia to use primary health care services for their chronic illnesses, at this time, limited literature reports on their experiences in Australia. Methods: A qualitative exploratory approach was adopted for this study. Through purposive sampling, 11 participants were recruited, and data was collected using semi-structured interviews. The interviews were transcribed verbatim and thematically analysed. Findings: Three themes and six sub-themes emerged from the thematic analysis. The first theme ‘being a mix of experiences’ presented participants’ positive and negative experiences related to communication, compassion, quality of care and length of consultations. The second theme ‘facilitators to accessing primary health care services in Australia’ described the benefits of telehealth and having a common cultural background as that of the general practitioner. Meanwhile, the third theme ‘barriers to accessing primary health care services in Australia’ identified unavailability of preferred GPs and waiting times and delays for in-person appointments as barriers that hindered access to PHC services in Australia. Conclusion: Primary health care experiences of Indian immigrants with chronic illnesses in Australia were a mix of positive and negative experiences, similar to that of other immigrants. Faster accessibility and compassionate services among migrants were highlighted to be needing extra attention by way of further research and acknowledging the unique diversity of individuals.

sections.introduction: Chronic illnesses are prolonged conditions lasting for at least six months, which have persistent effects on quality of life and require ongoing care and management from a multidisciplinary health care team (Australian Health Minister’s Advisory Council, 2017 ; Gordon et al ., 2018 ). Around 41 million people die each year as a result of chronic illnesses, equating to 74% of deaths globally (World Health Organization, 2023 ). In 2022, 171,500 deaths (90% of all deaths) in Australia were due to chronic illnesses and around 12.6 million people (49.9%) residing in Australia for at least 12 months were living with at least one chronic condition (Australian Bureau of Statistics [ABS], 2023 ). Primary health care (PHC) delivers essential early interventions that facilitate prevention, early detection, and treatment by a multidisciplinary team of health care professionals for people living with chronic illnesses in the community (Bierman et al ., 2021 ; World Health Organization, 2023 ). The Australian health care system comprises of a public and private sector (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare [AIHW], 2025 ). Medicare, Australia’s universal health insurance scheme is a federal funded programme. It provides free or subsidized treatment for Australian citizens, permanent residents, and visitors from countries with reciprocal health agreements who use public hospitals, community services, and general practitioners (GPs) (AIHW, 2022 ). Private health insurance provides Australian citizens with the option to access private hospitals, specialists, dental care, and allied health services that are not fully covered by Medicare (AIHW, 2025 ). Nursing services are provided in both public and private sectors and, therefore, are funded by either Medicare or private health insurances (Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 2025 ). Over the years, PHC in Australia has evolved to adapt to the changing health care needs of the diverse population, of which, over 30% was born overseas (ABS, Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2026 ). However, culturally and linguistically diverse immigrants with complex health care needs face challenges of accessing suitable health care and navigating Australia’s complex health system (Department of Health, 2022 ; Mengistu et al ., 2023 ). These include language barriers (Kay et al ., 2016 ), lack of recognition of cultural diversity, and limited levels of cultural competence (Harrison et al ., 2019 ). Chinese immigrants, particularly the elderly and those with poor English proficiency, faced language and communication problems and had difficulties navigating the health care system and resources (Jin et al ., 2020 ; Zhang et al ., 2020 ). Vietnamese immigrants reported to have similar access barriers by way of language difficulties and a lack of health information available in their language (Jin et al ., 2020 ). Furthermore, travel time, cultural and religious differences and affordability affected accessibility among African immigrants (Anaman-Torgbor et al ., 2017 ). These issues influence poor heath service utilization and, consequently, increase the risks of unmanaged chronic health conditions. Indian immigrants in Australia are the largest group born overseas, with a population of 916,000, and thus, the largest group to avail Australia’s PHC services (ABS, Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2026 ). One in three Indian immigrants in Australia has a chronic condition which is managed and treated through PHC (AIHW, 2022 ; Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, 2022 ). People of Indian cultural background in Australia are at a higher risk of insulin resistance and have the third-highest prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus (Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, 2022 ). Back pain, depression, hypertension and heart disease were the most reported diseases in an Australian study (Nisar et al ., 2025 ). South Asian immigrants in the UK, US, Norway and Canada are at a higher risk of abdominal obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia and impaired glucose intolerance, which directly contribute to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus (Mahadevan et al ., 2023 ). In America, one in four deaths among Indian immigrants is caused by cardiovascular disease (Gidwani et al ., 2021 ). Deficiency in Vitamin D is also common among Indian immigrants living in countries such as the UK, US, Canada, South Africa, and Australasia (Darling, 2020 ; Partha, 2024 ). Apart from Indian immigrants being the largest immigrant group in Australia, and the largest to use PHC services to manage their chronic health conditions, they consider medical expertise, responsiveness, and inclusion in decision making processes when assessing the quality of the health care they receive (Chatterjee and Srinivasan, 2013 ). Communication due to socio cultural differences is reported to be a barrier in accessing health care among south Asian migrants (Adhikari et al ., 2021 ; Nisar et al ., 2022 ). However, the specifics for Indian immigrants in PHC is lacking in empirical research. While the above evidence explores the access and decision-making issues experienced by migrants, the current study focuses solely on the experiences of Indian immigrants with PHC services in Australia. Considering the large proportion of Indian immigrants with chronic illnesses that are managed through PHC, their cultural variations and ethno-specific healthcare needs warrant concerted information on their experiences with PHC services.
sections.aim: To explore the PHC experiences of Indian immigrants living with chronic illnesses in Australia.
sections.study design and setting: A qualitative exploratory approach was adopted using virtual semi-structured interviews that facilitated in-depth exploration of personal experiences of Indian immigrants regarding PHC services across Australia, a topic that remains under-explored (Denzin and Lincoln, 2018 ). This approach facilitated deeper insights that form the foundation of more specific research in future. Rigour was maintained throughout the study by meeting four criteria as recommended by Hammarberg et al ., ( 2016 ). These criteria were trustworthiness, credibility, applicability, and consistency. Trustworthiness was achieved by presenting a detailed description of the study purpose and process, including how decisions were made and how data was generated. Credibility was achieved by using robust quotes and contextual details to support the findings, along with details on reflexivity. Detailed descriptions of the sampling, recruitment, data collection and data analysis methods, and participant information are presented to achieve applicability. Additionally, presenting detailed findings that were verified by all members of the research team helped achieve consistency. The guidelines for Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies (Tong et al ., 2007 ) and the Consensus Reporting Items for Studies in Primary Care (CRISP) checklist (Phillips et al ., 2023 ) were followed. A social constructionism perspective guided this study. This perspective supports the notion that there are multiple realities and that one’s understanding of the world and, therefore, their perception of reality depends upon dynamic social and cultural contexts of the time (Burr and Dick, 2017 ; Doyle et al ., 2019 ). Social constructionism has a number of assumptions including social reality being socially constructed, and reality not being an objective truth. Guided by these assumptions, we utilized semi-structured interviews that enabled participants to provide their subjective experiences of accessing PHC for the management of their chronic illnesses. Social constructionism assumes that multiple realities are possible. This informed the adequate attention that we paid to each of the participants’ interview transcripts in the course of data analysis. Even when participants provided competing and contrasting responses to the interview questions, our understanding of the social constructionism assumption that there is no single correct and factual reality guided the wide presentation of participants’ subjective quotes.
sections.study participants, sampling, and recrui: Participants were eligible for inclusion in this study if they (1) identified as Indian immigrants in Australia, (2) were aged 18 years and over, (3) had an existing chronic condition that had been diagnosed for at least 6 months, for which they were utilizing PHC services, and (4) were willing to participate. The exclusion criteria for this study were people who could not converse in the English language and people who self-reported with any cognitive impairment that would prevent them from providing informed consent and, thus, participating in the interview. Purposive sampling was used to intentionally recruit participants who met the inclusion criteria. Self-identified adult Indian immigrants with chronic illnesses were considered central to obtaining an in-depth understanding of their lived experiences. Participants were informed of the study using a flyer that was posted on unpaid social media platforms, including personal Facebook and WhatsApp community groups between April and May 2024. These platforms have been successfully used in previous studies to recruit research participants from diverse communities and geographical areas efficiently (Darko et al ., 2022 ; Pathak et al ., 2025 ). Examples of Facebook groups used in this study included ‘Indian Mums of Australia’, ‘Indian Families Connect (Sydney)’, ‘Blacktown Indian Community – Sydney’, and ‘Penrith LGA Indian Community Group’. These groups provide members with opportunities to reach out for help, support, and advice, and allow for social and community connections and networking. The first author (RS) is an Indian migrant in Australia and a member of these groups (not an administrator). There are a few similar WhatsApp groups of which the researcher is a part. These provide more localized connections and ease of access to a diverse range of potential participants. Such groups include ‘Glenmore Park Mums’ Group’ and ‘Penrith LGA Unity Group’. However, despite using social media recruitment, this did not result in a favourable outcome, perhaps due to the sensitive nature of the topic. It was anticipated that interviewing 10 to 15 participants would provide adequate data to identify common patterns and recurring themes to gain deeper insights into Indian immigrants’ experiences with PHC services. However, data collection was stopped after engaging 11 participants, as no new concepts were identified for this exploratory study (Vasileiou et al ., 2018 ; Braun and Clarke, 2022 ;). A participant information sheet detailing the aims of the study, data collection method, confidentiality, and voluntary participation and withdrawal was provided to interested participants. They were also provided with an informed consent form which they were asked to read, understand, and sign prior to participation. They were able to seek any clarification and ask further questions before providing their written consent and taking part in an individual interview. Before the commencement of the interview, another opportunity was provided to participants for any questions or clarifications. Their consent and willingness to participate and have their unidentifiable data used in this and further related research and publication was confirmed. They were reinformed that they could withdraw at any stage and/or refuse to answer any questions, without repercussion. No incentives were provided to participants.
sections.data collection: Data for this study was collected through semi-structured interviews conducted and recorded virtually via Zoom. This was due to the convenience that remote interviews provided to participants and to ensure the comfort of a familiar environment, potentially allowing them to express their thoughts more easily (Pocock et al ., 2021 ; Taherdoost, 2023 ). Participants were given the option to turn their video off prior to the interview and all the interviews were audio recorded. These interviews were conducted by the first author (RS), a registered nurse and researcher working in PHC. The researcher received training in qualitative interviewing techniques. To ensure methodological rigour and interviewer confidence, the first interview was conducted jointly with an experienced qualitative researcher from the team. Participants were required to provide pseudonyms to which they were referred to in this study. An interview guide with open-ended questions was utilized (Appendix A). This guide was informed by the expertise and experience of the research team and after examining existing literature while ensuring that the questions addressed the research topic. The semi-structured interviews ranged from 30 minutes to one hour, allowing for a relatively set agenda and predetermined questions while permitting probing and clarification and hence, facilitating the collection of rich data (Taherdoost, 2023 ). Participants were asked to share their experiences regarding the PHC services they used for the management of their illnesses. The interviewer took brief notes during the interviews, followed by detailed contextual descriptions and reflections from the interviews. The recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim, and data was stored securely in password-protected documents and folders on a secure file-sharing platform on the university’s network ( Privacy and Personal Information Protection Act 1998 (NSW), pt 2, div 1 ; Western Sydney University, 2022 ; National Health and Medical Research Council, 2023 ).
sections.data analysis: Data analysis was commenced simultaneously with data collection to ensure adequacy of data until no new concepts were introduced (Braun and Clarke, 2022 ; Klem et al ., 2022 a). Analysis of the data from the transcribed interviews was guided by Braun and Clarke’s ( 2023 ) six phases of thematic analysis of qualitative data, namely, phase one: familiarization with the data; phase two: generating initial codes; phase three: generating themes; phase four: reviewing potential themes; phase five: defining and naming themes; and phase six: producing the report. The first phase involved the first author (RS) becoming familiar with the data to identify similarities and differences across the dataset. Then, initial codes were generated before descriptive themes and subthemes were identified, reviewed, defined, and named by the research team (RS, OO, SP, AL). The themes and subthemes reflected the participants’ experiences as understood and collectively interpreted by the research team. This non-linear and iterative process was documented in NVivo 14 (Lumivero, 2023 ) to track the evolution of the codes and their prospective themes by the research team, thereby facilitating a transparent process of data analysis (Byrne, 2022 ; Braun and Clarke, 2023 ). Additionally, debriefing during weekly meetings, and maintaining an audit trail with a detailed log of the research processes and decisions was maintained (Cope, 2014 ; Klem et al ., 2022 b). This included records of the research process such as interview transcripts, stages of data analysis, and draft reports. Furthermore, rich, vivid, and verbatim participant quotations were used to confirm that the analysis presented was collated directly from the collected data. Member checking was not used in this study as the research team felt that revisiting the sensitive areas of chronic illnesses and PHC experiences and the potential reporting of negative experiences may be triggering.
sections.researcher reflexivity: It is important to acknowledge that the first author (RS) who conducted interviews of participants, is an Indian immigrant and a registered nurse working in PHC, positioning her as an insider with shared experiences to those of the participants. Of the other researchers, SP is also an Indian immigrant, and all (SP, OO, and AL) are registered nurses who have had experiences caring for Indian immigrants. As such, it was imperative to address the role, biases, assumptions, prejudices, beliefs, attitudes, and learning of the research topic to eliminate potential bias in the design of the study, recruitment of participants, collection and interpretation of data, and writing of the findings (Berger, 2015 ; Teh and Lek, 2018 ). This was achieved via a reflective journal and weekly debriefing meetings held by the research team where perspectives, interpretations and assumptions from the interviews were critically reflected upon to ensure credibility throughout the duration of this study.
sections.ethical considerations: This study was approved by the institutional Human Research Ethics Committee (Approval Number: H15813 ).
