sections.theme 1: a mix of experiences: Participants revealed positive and negative experiences with using Australian PHC services for the management of their chronic illnesses. Mixed experiences with communication, its effect on the quality of care, and negative consequences of inadequate lengths of consultations were described.
sections.\u2018everything is at one place\u2019: The participants described the PHC setting as a one-stop shop where ‘everything is at one place’ (Sandy). They valued having other services available in the same clinic, including pathology, radiology, physiotherapy, and dental services. This, according to them, proved to be much more convenient, ‘… and you know the place and the people, so things become easier’ (Sandy), than having to visit different places for different tests for which they had to often wait for at least a week before getting an appointment. They described these experiences as being ‘just easier’ (Shaf) because ‘you don’t need to go to different places’ (Raul).
sections.experiences with treatment and managemen: The participants presented a mix of experiences with the treatment and management of their chronic illnesses in the PHC setting. All participants were satisfied with their current GPs’ informative communication about the causes of their chronic illnesses, treatment and management regimes, potential side effects of treatments, and reasons for medication changes. Bree was visibly impressed by the ‘very clear’ communication from her GP, especially about ‘what the side effects could be’ of her new medication, as was Pur, who felt his GP was ‘happy to answer questions and was very understanding and very kind about it’, making him feel that his concerns were adequately addressed without any judgement. Dal was impressed with the amount of information and education she was provided with to manage her diabetes with ‘diet, exercise and medication’. When Roi first saw her GP for her knee pain, she really appreciated the level of understanding he showed towards ‘the pain and my concern about what the diagnosis would be’. Sandy also found his GP to be ‘very thorough’ and was glad that he ‘listens and addresses any concerns’. While participants described positive communication experiences with their current GPs, some had concerns about previous GPs’ poor language skills and limited efforts in building rapport, which affected the quality of care that was provided. Bindu described being ‘sent back with some Panadol’ when she was in a lot of pain and felt some GPs need to show more care and ‘understand when somebody is really in pain’. Bree compared her experiences with doctors in India and Australia and felt that doctors in India were ‘more competent’ than some of those she had seen in Australia. Nee shared similar beliefs about the competency of doctors in India, who she believed were ‘some of the brightest doctors across the globe’ along with the technological advancements within the Indian health care system. She thought that the Australian doctors did not have the same level of expertise and believed that this was due to the ‘vast experience’ Indian doctors gained from the large population in India. Almost half of the participants felt that some GPs did not provide an adequate amount of time for their face-to-face consultations. They felt ‘rushed’ (Nee) and were often ‘out from the GP’s room within a couple of minutes with a prescription’ (Vik). They stated that they felt like the GP did not want to listen to them. This experience was contrary to the participants’ expectations. They emphasized that the time they spent with their GP during face-to-face consultations provided them with limited opportunities to communicate and discuss their health concerns. Bindu, who was living with multiple chronic illnesses appeared disappointed and described that she expected GPs to listen, understand her issues, and ask questions to try and help treat her, but ‘felt neglected’ instead: You come in; they don’t even listen to you properly. And then they just give you medication or just send you out. I feel like they don’t have that much time to listen to you. I’m getting the same answer lots of times. I feel like it’s not right, you know, until they don’t examine you. They didn’t check anything. They didn’t ask the questions regarding the situation, and they send you with some medication. I feel like that’s not right. (Bindu) While participants acknowledged that GPs had many patients to see, they felt it was important that they received adequate consultation time. The participants reported that thorough assessments and examinations were not being conducted during the short consultations and, consequently, their GPs could not understand their symptoms, were dismissive of their concerns and were unable to provide a holistic approach to their care. Sandy described one interaction where he felt his previous GP ‘did not understand’ his concerns about his migraines, ‘started joking’ and wanted to ‘finish the consultation like he has done his part and now you are on your own’. He mentioned that he felt reassured after reading ‘some online resources’. Nee described an experience where she felt her GP was being ‘hasty’ and she was not able to explain her concerns: I was like, at least give me two minutes, or maybe 3 minutes. Just don’t rush me. And yeah, they just write the prescription, and they’ll be like off you go, scoot now. So yeah, that was not very nice. (Nee) Study participants confessed that they changed from one GP clinic to another due to these issues: Sometimes my previous GP was like oh you’re just overthinking or you’re just working really hard. Maybe that’s why this is happening. You have to reduce this or that, you don’t need to worry. But after I think three to four months later you change the GP, go to different one and then you find out no, you’re going through something really serious and you need a treatment for that. (Bindu) Sandy also preferred ‘not to go’ to his previous GP if his symptoms ‘were not very bad’ and eventually changed to a different GP.
sections.experiences with reception staff: Though not directly involved in the provision of care and management of their chronic illnesses, participants acknowledged the important role of the reception staff in the PHC setting. Bindu described this succinctly, ‘sometimes I feel like receptionists make a big difference. Some of them are really welcoming of you and some of them are just there.’ According to most participants, the reception staff facilitated a homely atmosphere and managed patients with different levels of needs. Bree describes the reception staff at her small GP practice: ‘they knew, you know, every patient by name. They knew good history, so it was quite homely atmosphere’. However, Nee and Raul described the communication from some reception staff as ‘frustrating’ (Nee) and needing improvement for a compassionate health care experience. According to these participants, the lack of communication about waiting times, especially when this is exceeded beyond acceptable times, added to feelings of stress and disappointment. For example, Nee, who was living with multiple chronic illnesses, expressed her frustration about the reception staff who became ‘annoyed’ when she asked them why there was a delay with her scheduled appointment. Nee explained that the reception staff did not provide a reason for the delay and did not understand that patients also had work commitments and limited time: The reception is not very vocal in terms of why we have the delay, and they also seem annoyed if you go ahead, and you know if you ask them why is there a delay at all. They do not give you a reason. They’re like, ok, there are seven patients before you, just eight patients before you. But a lot of them like, really seem annoyed. (Nee) Some reception staff were described as ‘rude’ (Roi), ‘cranky’ (Victor) and lacking empathy and compassion. Nee described her experiences of being treated differently due to perceived ethnic differences: They’re different in the way they treat, you know, people of the white race and they’re different to the people who are of, let’s say, the Indian race or, you know, some other ethnicity. I think people of the white race get more privilege. This behaviour is more, you know, it’s more predominant in again, receptionists who are white in race. Some of them not all. Some of them are really pleasant. But it does not happen so much with receptionists who are of the Indian cultural background or maybe some other ethnicity. (Nee)
sections.theme 2: facilitators to accessing phc s: This theme presents the facilitators in accessing PHC services in Australia as described by the participants. These include the ongoing convenience of telehealth and the benefits of a shared cultural background with that of their GP.
sections.telehealth: While talking about telehealth as an important facilitator of their access to PHC, almost all of the participants made specific reference to the recent global COVID-19 pandemic as the catalyst. During that time, most of the participants explained that they did not need to see their GP in person as much and, therefore, opted for the much-appreciated telehealth services that became increasingly available. Roi stated that after her initial knee examination, she did not need to ‘see him too often’. The option of telehealth consultations proved to be invaluable for the participants during, and post, COVID-19. Nee described telehealth as being ‘really accessible’ and ‘one of the best things to happen’. Participants described the convenience of having an appointment with their GP over the phone, without having to go in person, for urgent prescriptions, non-urgent blood test results, and consultations that did not require a physical examination. According to them, they did not only save travel and waiting time, but they also received timely care. Nee was happy to not ‘spend time in transporting’ and sitting in the waiting room’ while receiving more prompt’ care through telehealth. For more than half of the participants, telehealth had become the preferred method of consultation when they did not need to see their GP in person. Shaf elaborated on this point. Unless there’s something I need to show him, I prefer doing it on the phone. I think because he knows my history and, you know, he knows me well, I think it’s more convenient. Unless obviously there’s something I need to physically show him. (Shaf) Given that almost all of the participants were full-time workers, they appreciated the flexibility of telehealth consultations in seeking health care despite their busy schedules. Telehealth facilitated timely access to PHC services, talk to their GP over the phone, and were able to finish their telehealth consultations within ‘ten to 15 minutes (Nee). According to Roi, with telehealth, there was ‘pretty much no wait time’.
sections.cultural background of gp: The participants established that having a GP from the same cultural background facilitated better communication and a greater level of understanding between them and their GP. Despite living in Australia for over thirty years, Roi and Victor still preferred having a GP of a similar cultural background. These participants felt that the GP was able to provide a greater level of understanding and was perceived to have more of a ‘sympathetic approach’. Similarly, Nee appreciated her GP’s ability to identify potential illnesses that they had experienced within the Indian community: My current GP is of the Indian background, and he had dealt with so many Indians before so he was able to sort of identify that these are the ailments that I could have. So, from that perspective, I think it was helpful that he was from the Indian background. (Nee) Having the same cultural background as their GP facilitated better communication by way of similar languages and a greater understanding of dietary requirements. Being able to communicate in their own language was beneficial for participants as they felt that they could explain themselves better and understand the PHC provider more effectively. For instance, Dal appreciated that their GP had some understanding of their food preferences and options, providing a better understanding of the required dietary changes to help control her type 2 diabetes mellitus: If GP is from the same country or same culture, it’s better he can explain you better. Like I love my food, so it’s very hard to explain to the other GP. I feel so comfortable to explain my current situation more easily. (Dal)
sections.theme 3: barriers to accessing phc servi: The participants in this study identified unavailability of their preferred GP and waiting times and delays for in-person appointments as barriers that hindered their access to PHC services in Australia.
sections.unavailability of preferred gp: Participants in this study preferred to see a regular GP who supported their health care needs; someone they were able to see when needed and someone who was able to provide them with the care needed to manage their chronic conditions. As Vik described it: ‘a dedicated family GP. However, this proved to be a barrier to accessing timely and relevant PHC services. Bindu found it difficult to get an appointment with her regular GP on several occasions and had to wait for at least one week to be seen: sometimes they’re really busy and you have to wait for a week time, sometimes two weeks’. The inability to access her preferred GP when needed also posed challenges in receiving timely and continued care for Bree. She summarizsed her experience: It was only one doctor on a day so if she was unwell or not coming in, I didn’t have any other option but to go to a completely different person or completely different practice’. Furthermore, some of the participants felt helpless when they reported not getting a GP with specialized expertise in areas such as mental health, Not all the clinics in the locations I’ve been at have had mental health professionals, or then they haven’t had mental health professionals who are free within the next few weeks (Pur). GPs providing bulk-billed services were preferred by participants and having to pay a co-payment because bulk billing was not available was a significant deterrent. Pur was ‘not bothered’ to contact GPs for an appointment when their website specified that they did not offer bulk-billed services. He also cancelled an appointment after he reached the GP clinic and found out that bulk billing was not an option: There was one time when I went to a clinic where there wasn’t any specification about bulk billing. Before I went in for my appointment, I found out that there’s no bulk billing. And so, I asked him, if I can, you know, this isn’t what I was expecting. I would like to not go to the appointment, and they cancelled it. (Pur) He was also disappointed about having to pay the same amount of co-payment for telehealth consultations as others did for face-to-face consultations. He questioned, ‘why am I paying the same amount of co-pay for something that’s done over the phone?. The increasing number of clinics charging a co-payment was a growing concern among participants as they believed that this would limit the number of bulk-billed PHC services, increase PHC costs, and, consequently, reduce access to PHC services: We know that people will avoid going to the GP because if they have to pay, so that’s something that has to be looked into and it should not be taken lightly by the government. It should be kept as a free service for primary care. (Bree)
sections.long waiting times: Long waiting times to see their GP in-person were identified as a major barrier to seeking PHC. When an appointment was not available, participants had to attend the GPs’ clinics without an appointment and wait between half an hour to three hours. Bindu described having to wait ‘for more than one hour’, even when she was in ‘so much pain’: And you don’t get the appointment, so you have to walk in. But even with an appointment these days, I find it is difficult. You still have to wait longer than your scheduled time’. Long waiting times deterred participants from returning to the clinic and contributed to their preference for telehealth consultations. Roi stated that she avoided going to the clinic, even when she felt that she needed to see her GP face-to-face, and preferred telehealth ‘“as much as possible now’. Consistently long waiting times caused a lot of frustration among participants. Waiting for their GP for around an hour every time, even when they had an appointment, affected other aspects of their lives. Raul was frustrated when he summarized this issue: Everybody here is taking time off from something that they’re doing. Either kids’ pick-up or work or something, and if you’ve got to wait for like an hour every time then you kind of lose one hour just waiting there. For participants who did not have the option of working from home, ‘almost half a day’ (Nee) was often spent waiting for an appointment to see their GP. Nee stated that she ‘expected a delay of maybe half an hour or 45 minutes’ but became frustrated when she had to wait ‘two hours’ one day and decided to leave ‘the clinic altogether and was like I’ll maybe come another day or go to a different GP’.
sections.discussion: Mixed experiences of treatment and management of chronic illnesses within PHC were shared by the participants in this study. This is similar to previous studies that reported on migrants’ experiences with treatment and management of chronic illnesses in PHC settings. Trusting relationships with GPs were found to be significant in chronic disease management among Indian immigrants in the UK (Sidhu et al ., 2016 ). Contrasting evidence reported that a lack of concern, rudeness, and poor communication were the experiences of young adult migrants in Greater Western Sydney, Australia (Raymundo et al ., 2021 ) and South Asian migrants in Tasmania, Australia (Terry et al ., 2011 ). An unapproachable nature of GPs, along with their inattentiveness, contributed to participants losing confidence and feeling discontent with PHC services, leading them to seek PHC service elsewhere (Vakil et al ., 2023 ). In the current study, most participants shared positive experiences of receiving compassionate and emotionally supportive care from their GPs, and this facilitated trusting GP-patient relationships. Meanwhile, some participants felt that their concerns were dismissed with poor communication and compassion, resulting in their experiences of sub-optimal care, changes in their GPs and delays in accessing care. Having a mixed health care experience presents the PHC system to the risk of losing the trust of its users. Having a GP of the same cultural and linguistic background was not a necessity for most participants in this study. It is important, though, to note that in the current study, the participants acknowledged having a GP of the same cultural and linguistic background as a facilitator to better PHC access. They explained that a common culture and language facilitated better communication and understanding between participants and their GP and, in turn, enabled better comprehension of health information. This is similar to previous studies among Asian, African, and Middle Eastern immigrants in Australia that reported the importance of speaking in English to communicate their needs, as well as comprehend their health care providers and educational resources (Khatri and Assefa, 2022 ; Lakin and Kane, 2023 ). In both the UK and Canada, language and cultural barriers led to limited knowledge about their chronic illnesses and prevented optimal use of PHC services (Sidhu et al ., 2016 ; Rishworth et al ., 2022 ), highlighting the preference of GPs with common cultural and linguistic backgrounds. In this study, issues with untimely access to PHC services and insufficient consultation time were highlighted. Similarly, recent research identified long waiting times as impediments to access for South Asian and other migrants with family and work commitments in Australia, Canada, America and Europe, often leading to limited advice regarding the management and treatment of their chronic illnesses (Rishworth et al ., 2022 ; Vakil et al ., 2023 ). Statistical evidence from the ABS ( 2025 ) also reported longer than acceptable waiting times to get an appointment with a GP for 26% of people aged 15 years and above. Participants in the current study highlighted having to wait unacceptably long times to be seen by their GP for booked appointments, followed by insufficient times given by their GP during the consultations. This is contrary to the situation reported in a study conducted in India, where the maximum amount of time most participants had to sit and wait in the clinic before being seen for their prebooked GP appointment was ten minutes, and they were satisfied with the amount of consultation time provided (Ardey and Ardey, 2015 ). The long waiting in the current study is a serious issue given that timely health care is one of the measures suggested by the World Health Organization ( 2023 ) for achieving the PHC pillar that focuses on meeting the lifelong health needs of people. An important explanation for the increasing waiting time may be attributed to a shortage of GPs (Australian Medical Association [AMA], 2022 ). There is growing community demand for GPs, however, GPs are not only opting for fewer working hours, but GP training places are not being filled (AMA, 2022 ; Behera et al ., 2022 ). Extended freezing of Medicare rebates and lack of government support for general practice may be responsible for these shortages, along with a lack of streamlined processes aimed at integrating and registering internationally qualified GPs (AMA, 2022 ). Freezing of Medicare rebates also means that some GPs are opting for private billing instead of offering bulk-billed consultations. Bulk billing is payment option in Australia, whereby a range of health care services, including GP consultations, are billed to the government, instead of the patient, at the discretion of the service provider (Services Australia, 2024 ). With private billing, the consultations are billed directly to the patient, sometimes, with the option for the patient to receive a rebate from Medicare (The Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, 2025 ). Access to Medicare rebates in Australia depends on one’s immigration status, through which the eligibility for Medicare services is determined (Services Australia, 2024 ) and, therefore, not all immigrants are able to receive rebates after private billing in PHC. The out-of-pocket expenses for these patients reduce accessibility to timely and affordable PHC services.
sections.strengths and limitations: From an extensive search of the current literature, it appears that this study may be the first to specifically explore the PHC experiences of Indian immigrants in Australia. However, self-selection of participants in this study presented limitations by way of potential bias and lack of diversity. Most of the participants were middle-aged residents who were highly educated, engaged in full time employment, and spoke fluent English. This presents a lack of diversity and potential bias in the findings as the experiences of younger and older Indian immigrants, students, those with lower levels of education, working in other types of employment or unemployed, and limited English proficiency were not gleaned. Additionally, all participants were from New South Wales, a state with the second largest population of Indian immigrants, and the perspectives of those living in other states were not obtained.
sections.recommendations for future research: The participants in this study were highly educated, middle-aged Indian immigrants who spoke fluent English and lived in metropolitan Sydney. However, the Indian diaspora in Australia is a diverse mix of younger, middle-aged, and elderly immigrants with varying levels of education and English fluency and engaged in a range of professions. They also reside in urban and regional areas across Australia. Therefore, further research is needed to gain a better understanding of the PHC experiences of the diverse Indian immigrant population in Australia, including those with financial hardship. Furthermore, it would be beneficial to learn the perspectives of PHC providers for a better understanding of immigrant PHC experiences in Australia, and to provide an insight into the PHC system for immigrants.
sections.policy implications: Health policies in Australia aim at improving migrants’ experiences with PHC, however, it is necessary to understand the way they identify themselves as culturally diverse individuals who are shaped by their unique backgrounds and experiences within and beyond their ethnicity. Directing funding to research and PHC services that aim to address these gaps would promote a more holistic approach in providing timely, compassionate, and culturally appropriate care to address the needs and expectations of Indian and other immigrants in Australia.
sections.practice implications: Ongoing training on culturally responsive health care for health care providers in PHC setting, including GPs and reception staff, along with more culturally responsive health promotion strategies would enable better access to and quality of PHC.
sections.conclusion: This study highlights the importance of timely and compassionate PHC for Indian and other immigrants living with chronic illness in Australia. A commitment to meeting the lifelong health needs of culturally diverse groups requires that the Australian health care system attend to the ongoing untimely access to PHC services. While the findings of this study presented common experiences among Australian immigrants, it is the first study to specifically present those described by Indian immigrants alone.

title:
From
Leuco to Blue: Photochemical Redox Amplification
for Small-Molecule Immunodetection
abstract:
Sensitive enough
detection of small-molecule toxins and many other
target analytes remains challenging for immunoassays that rely on
stoichiometric reporters or enzymatic cascades. Here we introduce
an enzyme-free, light-gated amplification strategy that teams up stabilized
leucomethylene blue (LMB) derivatives with antibody recognition and
photoredox cycling. As a proof-of-concept, we designed a stable LMB
precursor (δ-BLMB) and a BLMB–zearalenone (ZON) conjugate
that undergo rapid, selective photo-oxidation to methylene blue (MB)
only under the assay illumination. Electrochemical analysis has established
δ-BLMB as a redox precursor to MB, while time-resolved luminescence
of [Ru­(phen) 3 ] 2+ (RP3) photocatalyst revealed
diffusion-limited quenching ( k q = 2.68
× 10 9 M –1 s –1 )
consistent with dynamic electron transfer to the precursor. Mechanistic
studies show that blue light activates RP3 to generate acyl-radical
and MB – intermediates via O 2 -independent
pathways; red light is then used to excite nascent MB to drive a secondary
photocatalytic reductive cycle that regenerates MB through radical/anionic
intermediates, yielding exponential signal growth. We have validated
immunoassay integration using ZON-specific monoclonal antibodies in
bead-based and plate formats, demonstrating specific, light-triggered
fluorescence that reports competitive binding. Its implementation
with sequential two-color illumination demonstrates selective system
activation and precise control of the signal amplification (300-fold).
This photochemical approach provides stable, long-term reagents that
can be tailored to the target species and offers a potentially general
strategy for developing enzyme-free, high sensitivity immunoassays
for small analytes.

title: Real-World Ritlecitinib Treatment of Severe Alopecia Areata in the United States: Patient Characteristics and Physician Satisfaction According to a Secondary Database Analysis
abstract: Introduction Ritlecitinib, an oral, selective dual inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK) 3 and tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) family kinases, is approved for treating severe alopecia areata (AA) in patients aged ≥ 12 years in the USA. This study describes characteristics, treatment satisfaction, and success among adults initiating ritlecitinib. Methods A sample of US dermatologists treating adults who received ritlecitinib for severe AA were surveyed between November 2023 and June 2024. Demographics, clinical characteristics, treatment history, satisfaction, and health-related quality of life were analyzed overall, among recent initiators, and stratified by treatment duration. Results A total of 123 adults were included (mean age 37.1 years; 57% male; 79% white; 88% commercial insurance). Mean disease duration was 2.1 years. At ritlecitinib initiation ( n = 93), mean scalp hair loss was 71% and 73% had worsening AA. The proportion of patients with hair regrowth increased with longer treatment duration, 49% among those with < 3 months of treatment ( n = 18/37) to 82% with > 6 months ( n = 28/34). Physicians reported many recent initiators ( n = 26) felt moderate/severe embarrassment (84%), frustration (73%), and anxiety (65%) due to their AA. Among patients with available data ( n = 102), ritlecitinib was the first AA treatment for 46%. Treatment goals ( n = 123) included reducing hair loss (94%), improving quality-of-life (41%), and achieving long-term control (32%). Reasons for selecting ritlecitinib ( n = 113) included its ability to reduce scalp hair loss (38%), cost–benefit ratio (28%), and safety profile (25%). Satisfaction with AA control was 54%, 68%, and 85% after < 3 ( n = 20/37), 3–6 ( n = 27/40), and > 6 months ( n = 29/34), respectively, of ritlecitinib treatment. Conclusions Many patients experienced psychological burden due to their AA around the start of treatment. Ritlecitinib was chosen for its efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness. Hair regrowth, disease stability, and treatment satisfaction increased with longer ritlecitinib treatment duration suggesting sustained treatment is important for achieving treatment goals. sections.key summary points: Why carry out this study? Ritlecitinib, a dual JAK3/TEC kinase inhibitor, is approved for the treatment of severe alopecia areata (AA) in patients ≥ 12 years of age, but data on its use in real-world clinical practice and its impact on patients’ health-related quality of life (HRQOL) remain limited. Understanding patient characteristics; treatment patterns, goals, and satisfaction; and the impact on HRQOL can help guide dermatologists in optimizing AA management and aligning treatment expectations for their patients. What was learned from the study? Ritlecitinib was used as first line AA treatment in nearly half of patients and was associated with improvements in hair regrowth, disease stability, and satisfaction the longer the patient was on treatment, emphasizing the value of sustained treatment in achieving treatment goals. Physicians selected ritlecitinib primarily for its efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness. Many patients experience psychosocial burdens around the time of initiating treatment, highlighting the unmet need for effective treatments for patients with severe AA.
sections.introduction_1: Alopecia areata (AA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by patchy or complete nonscarring hair loss on the scalp, with or without additional loss of facial and/or body hair [ 1 ]. The clinical presentation of AA is unpredictable and can vary by the extent and location of hair loss including scalp, eyebrows, eyelashes, facial hair, and body hair; in severe cases it can progress to alopecia totalis (complete loss of scalp hair) or alopecia universalis (complete loss of scalp, face, and body hair) [ 2 ]. The global prevalence of AA is estimated to range from 0.58% to 2% [ 3 – 6 ]. In the USA, a large, cross-sectional survey found the self-reported point prevalence and lifetime prevalence to be 1.1% and 2.5%, respectively [ 4 ]. AA has an unpredictable disease course; some patients will spontaneously recover while many will experience periods of relapse and remission and some will progress to more severe forms of AA, which can be more difficult to treat [ 2 , 7 , 8 ]. In addition to hair loss, AA negatively impacts patients’ health-related quality of life (HRQOL), which is an important consideration when determining the severity of a patient’s AA [ 9 ]. Psychosocial and emotional impacts of AA are consistently observed, with patients reporting mental health issues including feeling sad/depressed and embarrassed/ashamed along with avoidance of social situations and impacts on work productivity and major life decisions [ 10 – 14 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 37 studies found that the prevalence of depressive disorders and anxiety disorders were higher among patients with AA compared with the general population and that 7–17% of patients had depressive or anxiety disorders that required care or medication [ 15 ]. This study found that, among patients with AA, the prevalence and odds ratio (OR) of depressive symptoms (37%; OR, 2.70) and anxiety symptoms (34%; OR, 3.07) were higher than that of depressive disorders (9%; OR, 1.38) and anxiety disorders (7–17%; OR, 1.51–1.69). Traditional treatments for AA have included topical, intralesional, and systemic corticosteroids; immunosuppressants; phototherapy; and topical calcineurin inhibitors [ 8 , 16 ]. Newer, US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapies are also available, including ritlecitinib, an oral, selective dual inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK) 3 and tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) family kinases [ 8 , 17 ]. Although there are, at the time of writing, no US treatment guidelines for AA, guidelines and consensus statements from other regions include JAK inhibitors as efficacious treatment options for adult patients with AA [ 18 – 21 ]. Ritlecitinib demonstrated efficacy and safety in the pivotal ALLEGRO phase 2b/3 study (NCT3732807) in adults and adolescents, and in June 2023, ritlecitinib 50 mg once-daily (QD) was FDA-approved for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents 12 years and older [ 17 ]. As approved kinase inhibitor treatments for AA are relatively new, limited data exist describing how dermatologists are integrating them into real-world clinical practice, or the impact of such treatments on patients. The objective of this study was to describe patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and HRQOL along with treatment history, satisfaction, and success among adult patients with severe AA who were treated with ritlecitinib in the USA. Analyses were stratified by ritlecitinib treatment duration and by recent ritlecitinib initiation (within 2 months of the survey).
sections.study design and patient population: A secondary database analysis was performed using data from the Adelphi Real World AA II US Disease Specific Programme ™ (DSP)—a cross-sectional survey of US dermatologists and their consulting patients with AA in routine clinical practice. Patients aged ≥ 18 years who were diagnosed with physician-assessed severe or very severe AA (referred to hereafter as “severe”) in the USA and receiving ritlecitinib at the time of the survey were included in the analysis (Fig. S1 ). The overall severity of AA was assessed by survey respondents’ answers to the question “What is/was your overall assessment of the severity of AA symptoms in this patient based on your own definition of the terms mild, moderate, severe, and very severe?” The DSP was conducted between November 2023 and June 2024 and collected de-identified information from patient medical records and the most recent consultation (Fig. S1 ). A convenience sample of dermatologists in the USA who were actively involved in managing the cases of at least seven adult patients (age ≥ 18 years) with AA monthly were recruited to participate. Eligible dermatologists were asked to complete a physician survey and patient record forms (PRFs) for the next seven consecutively consulting adult patients with AA (one patient with mild, three patients with moderate, and three patients with severe disease, as evaluated subjectively by each physician). US dermatologists were consulted in the development of the survey to ensure that questions were phrased to align with terminology that would resonate with most dermatologists. PRFs were completed at a single point in time but had an element of retrospective data collection as physicians were able to use patients’ medical records when completing the PRFs. Data collection was performed in compliance with the European Pharmaceutical Marketing Research Association code of conduct and Adelphi Real World standard operating procedures and are submitted for review to the Pearl Institutional Review Board.
sections.outcomes: Outcomes included baseline patient demographics, clinical characteristics, treatment characteristics, treatment history, physician-reported HRQOL and psychological burden, physician-reported treatment goals, physician-reported satisfaction with treatment, and physician perception of treatment success. HRQOL and psychological burden included the impact of AA on patients’ daily lives and feelings about their disease and its management as reported to their physician (e.g., avoidance of social interactions, impairment in ability to conduct normal daily activities, impairment in ability to work/study, frustration, stress, annoyance, anxiety/worry, and depression/low mood). To assess patients’ quality of life close to the time of treatment decision-making, but before the effect of treatment could have reasonably occurred, psychosocial burden was analyzed among the subgroup of patients who initiated ritlecitinib within 2 months of the survey (ie., “recent initiators”). A 2-month window for the survey was selected to proxy baseline burden to align with routine clinical practice, in which follow-up visits to assess AA treatment effectiveness typically occur 3–4 months following treatment initiation.
sections.statistical analysis: Descriptive statistics were reported for each objective, for the overall cohort sample (patients receiving ritlecitinib) and each subgroup. Subgroups included ritlecitinib treatment duration (< 3 months, 3–6 months, > 6 months), and recent initiators.
sections.ethical approval: A complete description of the methods of the survey has been previously published and validated [ 22 – 24 ]. Permission was obtained from the owner of the Adelphi Real World AA II US DSP to use the database for this study. Using a check box, patients provided informed consent for use of their anonymized and aggregated data for research and publication in scientific journals. Data were collected in such a way that patients and physicians could not be identified directly; all data were aggregated and de-identified before receipt. Data collection was undertaken in line with European Pharmaceutical Marketing Research Association guidelines and as such it does not require ethics committee approval. Each survey was performed in full accordance with relevant legislation at the time of data collection, including the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act legislation [ 25 ].

Overall, 88% had commercial insurance, and 78% were working full- or part-time. Of these 123 patients, 26 were recent initiators with a mean (SD) age of 34 (11.9) years with 35% being male, 85% being White, 96% having commercial insurance, and 73% working full- or part-time (Table 1 ). sections.psychosocial burden among recent ritleci: Among the subset of patients who recently initiated ritlecitinib ( n = 26), dermatologists assessed patient HRQOL and psychological burden prior to initiating ritlecitinib. Dermatologists reported that prior to starting ritlecitinib, 69% of patients learned to manage their AA; however, HRQOL impacts were still experienced including that AA is a major problem in everyday life and causes considerable problems with day-to-day activities (69%), as well as causing considerable emotional upset (65%), and the patient has become disheartened about achieving better control due to poor performance of available treatments and lack of new treatment options (38%; Fig. 2 A). Dermatologists also reported that, prior to initiating ritlecitinib, 85%, 73%, and 65% of patients had moderate/severe embarrassment, frustration, and anxiety, respectively, due to their AA, and the majority had moderate/severe fear of persistence of the condition, stress, avoidance of social interactions, and annoyance (81%, 73%, 69%, and 65%, respectively; Fig. 2 B). sections.treatment history and treatment selectio: Among patients with known ritlecitinib treatment duration ( n = 111/123 [90%]), measured from the start of ritlecitinib to the date of the survey, mean (SD) ritlecitinib treatment duration was 4.8 (3.2) months and the proportion of patients with a ritlecitinib treatment duration of < 3 months, 3–6 months, and > 6 months was 33% ( n = 37/111), 41% ( n = 46/111), and 25% ( n = 28/111), respectively (Table 4 ). Among patients in the overall cohort ( N = 123), 84% were receiving ritlecitinib monotherapy, and 16% were receiving concomitant therapies, which included intralesional corticosteroids, topical corticosteroids, oral corticosteroids, or other treatment (Table 4 ). Among those with data on the number of previous lines of AA treatment received ( n = 102/123 [83%]), patients had a mean (SD) of 1.8 (0.9) lines of treatments, and ritlecitinib was the first treatment for 46% ( n = 47/102) of these patients (Table 4 ). Among patients ( n = 60/123 [49%]) with data for AA therapies received before initiating ritlecitinib, 33% ( n = 20/60) received topical corticosteroid, 30% ( n = 18/60) intralesional corticosteroid (e.g., triamcinolone), 18% ( n = 11/60) oral corticosteroid, 18% ( n = 11/60) another JAK inhibitor (oral or topical), 15% ( n = 9/60) systemic immunomodulator, 7% ( n = 4/60) intravenous injected corticosteroid, 5% ( n = 3/60) topical immunomodulator, and 12% ( n = 7/60) other treatment (Table 4 ). sections.discussion: This real-world, cross-sectional survey of dermatologists treating patients with severe AA in the USA demonstrates the impact of ritlecitinib treatment on patients’ AA, including improvements in scalp hair regrowth, how ritlecitinib is being integrated into real-world clinical practice, and physician satisfaction. Overall, patients who received ritlecitinib had improvements in scalp hair regrowth from the time of ritlecitinib initiation to the time of survey with a reduction in mean percentage of SHL and an increase in the proportion of patients reported as having improving hair-regrowth status. The proportion of patients with hair regrowth, the mean percentage of scalp hair regrowth, and quality of hair regrowth all increased with longer treatment duration. It should be noted that it is plausible that those patients who improve are more likely to continue treatment, while those who do not are more likely to discontinue early. Disease status and disease severity also improved with increased ritlecitinib treatment duration, as did physician-reported satisfaction with the current control of their patient’s AA and the proportion of physicians who considered the ritlecitinib treatment regimen to be a success. Improvements in hair regrowth with ritlecitinib treatment were also observed in the ritlecitinib clinical trials. In the ALLEGRO-2b/3 study, there was a higher proportion of female patients, a slightly lower proportion of White patients, and slightly higher extent of scalp hair loss at baseline compared with the present survey. In ALLEGRO-2b/3, the proportion of patients with response based on Severity of Alopecia Tool (SALT) score ≤ 10 and ≤ 20 was significantly higher among patients receiving ritlecitinib versus placebo at Week 24 and continued to increase through Week 48 [ 17 ]. Similar results were demonstrated for the adolescent population in ALLEGRO-2b/3 [ 26 ]. In addition, in the ongoing long-term extension study, ALLEGRO-LT ( NCT04006457 ), which included patients rolled over from ALLEGRO-2b/3 as well as de novo patients, the proportion of patients with SALT score ≤ 10 and ≤ 20 increased from Month 12 to Month 24 among patients who rolled over from ALLEGRO-2b/3 [ 27 ] and was maintained from Month 12 to 24 among de novo patients [ 28 ]. Our survey demonstrated that patients receiving ritlecitinib in real-world practice also experience improvements in scalp hair regrowth over time. In addition to assessing scalp hair regrowth, the ALLEGRO-2b/3 study also demonstrated increasing rates of eyebrow and eyelash response through Week 48 among patients with abnormal eyebrows or eyelashes at baseline but did not examine hair regrowth in other body regions [ 17 ]. The survey data collected in the present study now provide insight into hair regrowth over a range of body regions and demonstrated that the proportion of patients with facial hair (beard or mustache) regrowth over time increases with duration of ritlecitinib treatment. Overall, the present study expands our understanding of the efficacy of ritlecitinib from the clinical trials and demonstrates the real-world impact ritlecitinib can have for patients with AA, highlighting the importance of sustained treatment, although longer-term follow-up data will be needed to further understand the impact of ritlecitinib treatment in real-world clinical practice. The present survey also demonstrated how AA impacted HRQOL among patients who recently initiated ritlecitinib. Physicians reported that a majority of patients had learned to manage their AA prior to initiating ritlecitinib, but for many it was still a major problem in everyday life and caused considerable psychosocial burden. Physicians reported that the majority of their patients felt embarrassed, frustrated, stressed, annoyed, and anxious/worried; feared persistence of the condition; and avoided social interactions prior to initiating ritlecitinib. These findings support previous studies on the psychosocial burden among patients with AA. In an online survey of 216 patients in the USA, 85% of respondents said that coping with AA was a daily challenge, and 85% reported making different life decisions regarding relationships, career, or education due to their AA [ 11 ]. In a survey of 26 patients with AA in Finland, 23% reported a psychiatric diagnosis of anxiety, which was often received after the diagnosis of AA [ 29 ]. In the study in Finland, the impact of AA on HRQOL was correlated with the extent of hair loss; however, a US survey of 259 patients found that impacts of AA on quality of life were not correlated with the degree of SHL, but rather with patient’s perception of disease severity [ 12 ]. Overall, AA has been consistently demonstrated to negatively impact patient quality of life, which is an important component of assessing the severity of disease [ 9 ]. In the present study, the majority of patients were receiving ritlecitinib monotherapy, which aligns with current treatment guidelines [ 18 , 19 ]. Our survey did not explicitly capture whether AA treatments were prescribed or received outside of the survey dermatologist’s clinic. However, dermatologists completed the patient forms using information available in patients’ medical records. Therefore, prior treatments prescribed by other healthcare professionals or at other clinics may have been included if they were documented in the medical record. Just under half of patients received ritlecitinib as their first line of treatment, and the most common treatments prior to ritlecitinib were topical and intralesional corticosteroids [ 18 ]. This could suggest that patients may not have had a satisfactory response to these treatments and their AA may have progressed prior to initiating ritlecitinib. Physician-reported treatment goals and reasons for choosing ritlecitinib reflected the psychosocial burden of AA with the most common goals, including improving quality of life and reducing psychological impact, in addition to goals that address the clinical characteristics of AA (reducing scalp hair loss, achieving long-term control, and reducing eyebrow hair loss). Similar treatment goals were reported in a survey of dermatologists and patients with AA in Europe [ 30 ]. Reducing scalp hair loss was the most common treatment goal in the European survey (92% of patients) followed by improving quality of life (49%), reducing psychological impact (38%), and achieving long-term/chronic control of the condition (29%) [ 30 ]. The most common physician-reported reason for choosing the current therapy in the European survey was reducing scalp hair loss. In the present study, reducing scalp hair loss was the most common physician-reported reason for choosing ritlecitinib, and this decision is supported by clinical trials and other studies in adults and adolescents that demonstrated the efficacy of ritlecitinib in reducing scalp hair loss [ 17 , 26 – 28 ]. Other common physician-reported reasons for choosing ritlecitinib in the present study included the good overall safety profile and safe for long-term use. The safety profile of ritlecitinib has been demonstrated in the ALLEGRO clinical trial program [ 17 , 26 – 28 , 31 ], of which an integrated safety analysis demonstrated that ritlecitinib is well-tolerated with an acceptable safety profile up to ~5 years [ 32 ]. Physicians provided data on consecutively consulting patients meeting the eligibility criteria, thus reducing the chance of selection bias; however, generalizability of the study results to the wider patient population may be impacted in a few ways beyond the limited sample size. First, participants from the AA DSP did not constitute a true random sample, and participation was influenced by the willingness to complete the record forms. Second, the patient sample may have been more severely affected by their disease and/or treatment due to their consulting nature and patients who consulted more frequently were more likely to be included in the patient sample. Third, study data are self-reported by participants, as no independent verification was possible due to the nature of the DSP methodology. Fourth, as the study used data from real-world clinical practice, not all outcomes relevant to these patients were able to be captured, and some data may be missing for the selected outcomes. Fifth, a minority of patients were not receiving ritlecitinib monotherapy, which may be a confounding factor. Sixth, as patients’ SHL and disease severity were reported only for the time periods at treatment initiation and at the time of survey, data were not available on whether patients had responded and subsequently relapsed between treatment initiation and the survey. And finally, as patients currently on treatment may be more likely to feel satisfied with their therapy (i.e., did not discontinue due to lack of efficacy, safety issues, or other unsatisfactory events), satisfaction results cannot be generalized.
sections.conclusions_1: Despite many patients managing the impacts of their severe AA, in this study dermatologists reported substantial negative emotional and daily-life effects among patients due to their AA before initiating ritlecitinib. Ritlecitinib was chosen by dermatologists for its efficacy, safety profile, and cost–benefit ratio and used in nearly half of patients as first-line treatment for severe AA. As ritlecitinib treatment duration increased, disease stability, hair regrowth, physician satisfaction, and perceived treatment success also increased. While selection bias should be considered, results emphasize the importance of sustained treatment for the management of patient expectations and achieving AA treatment goals.

title: Association of Polygenic Risk Scores With Aortic Valve Calcium: The Multi‐Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis
abstract: Background Aortic valve calcification (AVC) is the primary process leading to aortic stenosis. We examined whether polygenic risk scores (PRS) are associated with AVC beyond traditional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Methods We included 6812 participants in MESA (Multi‐Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) with computed tomography‐measured AVC at Visit 1. Using previously published PRS we calculated weighted PRS, standardized within each ancestry group. The cross‐sectional association per 1 SD higher PRS with AVC >0 was examined using multivariable logistic regression modeling with Bonferroni correction. The mean age was 62 years old, 53% were female, and 913 (13.4%) had AVC >0 at baseline. Results The PRS for coronary artery disease (hazard ratio [HR], 1.16 [95% CI, 1.07–1.26]), systolic blood pressure (HR, 1.1 [95% CI, 1.020–1.2]), low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.06–1.25]), and lipoprotein(a) (HR, 1.11 [95% CI, 1.02–1.20]) were significantly associated with AVC, whereas the other PRS including coronary artery calcium (HR, 1.02 [95% CI, 0.94–1.10]) and C‐reactive protein (HR, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.89–1.05]) were not. In sex‐stratified analyses, the PRS for coronary artery disease, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) were significantly associated with AVC >0 for both sexes ( P <0.05), whereas the systolic blood pressure PRS was borderline significant for women (HR, 1.10 [95% CI, 0.97–1.25]) and significant for men (HR, 1.11 [95% CI 1.00–1.24]). Conclusions Our results confirm the role of atherogenic lipids in the pathogenesis of AVC and suggest that systolic blood pressure and the genetic risk factors for CAD are also important risk factors. The lack of association for the coronary artery calcium PRS with AVC >0 strongly suggests significant differences exist in the calcification pathways for AVC and coronary artery calcium.

sections.what are the clinical implications?: These results confirm the importance of atherogenic lipids as risk factors for AVC and we show that the polygenic risk scores for systolic blood pressure is significantly associated with AVC, highlighting systolic blood pressure as an important underrecognized risk factor for AVC and as a potential treatment target. These results help to better understand the pathogenesis and risk factors for AVC, which is vital in the ongoing process to identify treatment strategies to slow or prevent the development of AVC and aortic stenosis.
sections.methods_1: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. MESA (Multi‐Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) is a prospective cohort study comprising 6814 participants without known CVD at baseline from 6 field centers across the United States, with the baseline visit conducted between the years 2000 and 2002. A detailed description of the cohort design, and participant sampling has previously been reported. 17 Institutional review boards at each study site reviewed and approved the study. All participants provided written informed consent. There were 2 participants without baseline visit AVC data who were excluded from this analysis. Genotype data were available on the remaining 6812 participants and collected concurrently at the baseline MESA visit (2000–2002). An Affymetrix 6.0 SNV array was used to perform SNV genotyping. 18 The 1000 Genomes cosmopolitan phase 3 version 5 reference haplotypes were used to impute SNVs. Individuals who were closely related, as determined by pi‐hat relatedness >0.2, were excluded by random removal for 1 of each pair. The EIGENSOFT package was used to examine population stratification using SNV genotypes and to confirm the self‐reported race or ethnicity. 19 , 20 , 21 All ancestry outliers were removed from the analyses. Previously published PRS scores for CAD, CAC, and the CVD risk factors of blood pressure, low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), triglycerides, Lp(a), CRP (C‐reactive protein), and diabetes were used for these analyses (Table 1 ). The MESA cohort comprised a small percentage of the derivation cohorts for the following PRS: systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), CRP, CAC, LDL‐C, triglycerides, and diabetes but not for the PRS for CAD or Lp(a). The PRS derivation cohorts were multiethnic cohorts, except for the cohorts used for the BP PRS. The weighted PRS for each participant was calculated as PRS i = ∑ i k β ^ j × dosage ij where PRS i is the polygenic score for subject i ; dosage ij is the posterior probability of being a heterozygous (probability ≈1.0) or homozygous (probability ≈2.0) effect allele carrier after imputations for subject i and variant j ; κ is the number of independent variants in the polygenic score for subject i ; and β ^ j is the weight for variant j obtained from genome‐wide association study summary statistics. The PRS was then standardized within each ancestry group, starting with self‐reported ancestry followed by exclusion of outliers based on principle components. 19 AVC was quantified at MESA Visit 1 via electronic beam computed tomography scanner at 3 field centers and multidetector computed tomography at the other 3 field centers. These 2 imaging modalities have equivalent reproducibility for the measurement of cardiac calcification. 22 The scan images were processed and interpreted at a centralized reading center (Harbor‐UCLA). AVC was defined as calcification of the aortic valve leaflets and calcification that extended from the aortic valve leaflets into the aortic root. 23 The scans were performed without intravenous contrast and the Agatston method was used to quantify AVC values. 24 Accordingly, calcified lesions were included only if they had a peak density of at least 130 Hounsfield units and an area of at least 1 mm 2 , in order to avoid false positive values. There was low intrareader (4.4%) and interscan (9.7%) variability for AVC scores. 23 For these analyses AVC was quantified as absent (AVC=0) or prevalent (AVC >0) as our primary aim was to examine whether or not the individual PRS are causally associated with AVC rather than the association with the burden or amount of AVC. 25 We also performed sensitivity analyses examining the association of AVC as a continuous variable. AVC was examined as a log transformed variable using ln(AVC +1), because it is zero inflated and right skewed. 26 Baseline demographic information and medical history including sex, race, ethnicity, and smoking status was self‐reported at Visit 1. SBP and DBP were measured in triplicate and recorded as the mean of the second and third values. Hypertension was defined as ≥140/90 mm Hg or use of an antihypertensive medication. Triglycerides were measured using overnight fasting samples sent to the Collaborative Studies Clinical Research Laboratory (Minneapolis, MN). LDL‐C was calculated using the Friedewald method, except for participants with triglycerides ≥400 mg/dL in whom LDL‐C was not calculated. 27 Lp(a) was measured using a latex‐enhanced turbidimetric immunoassay (Denka Siken) by Health Diagnostic Laboratory (Richmond, VA). 28 hs‐CRP (high‐sensitivity CRP) was measured using the BNII nephelometer via a particle‐enhanced immunonephelometric assay (N High Sensitivity CRP, Dade Behring Inc, Deerfield, IL). 29 Diabetes was defined as a fasting glucose of ≥126 mg/dL or the use of blood glucose lowering medication. Hypertension was defined as a BP of ≥140/90 mm Hg to be consistent with prior MESA publications, a definition used by some but not all BP guidelines. 30 , 31
sections.statistical analysis: Demographic data including CVD risk factor information were stratified by the presence or absence of AVC. Differences between groups were evaluated using the Student’s t test for quantitative traits, and chi‐square test for binary traits. We tested the association of each of the individual 9 PRS with the matching clinical phenotype to ensure that the PRS were significantly associated with the expected traits. Pairwise correlation was performed for the 9 PRS to evaluate the potential overlapping effect. To examine the association between each individual PRS and the risk of AVC>0, we carried out logistic regression analysis for each PRS using progressively adjusted models as follows: Model 1: age, race, ethnicity, sex, field center Model 2: model 1 + hypertension, diabetes, LDL‐C, triglycerides, hs‐CRP, and smoking status Model 3: model 2 + Lp(a). Stratified multivariable logistic regression modeling was also performed to examine for potential differences by sex and race or ethnicity and reported graphically using Model 1 adjustment variables. A Bonferroni corrected P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant for the primary analyses. For secondary analyses of sex and race or ethnicity stratified differences, a non‐Bonferroni corrected P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant due to the lower power of these stratified analyses. Logistic regression modeling was also performed with stepwise backwards elimination of the PRS to examine which PRS were independently associated with AVC. We examined the continuous variables 1 SD higher value PRS score in order to maintain comparability due to the different measurement values. For categorical variables, the reference group was absence of disease or risk factor. For sensitivity analyses of AVC as a continuous variable, linear regression modeling was used adjusted for the variables in model 1. In order to further examine the causal association between SBP and LDL‐C with AVC, Mendelian randomization was performed using 1780 SNVs PRS for SBP traits and 442 SNVs for LDL‐C traits. We did not perform Mendelian randomization to examine the association between CAD and AVC, as CAD is not thought to be a direct causal risk factor for AVC and our primary goal is to examine risk pathways for AVC. Instead, we performed sensitivity analyses for the CAD PRS stratified by concordance and discordance of AVC and incident CAD.
sections.results_1: Overall, participants with AVC >0 were older, more likely to be male, and had a greater burden of CVD risk factors (Table 2 ). White participants had the highest prevalence of AVC >0 (45.3%) and Chinese participants had the lowest prevalence of AVC >0 (7.4%). As regards relationships between the PRS, there was a moderate correlation between SBP and DBP, but otherwise the correlation between the individual PRS was low (Figure 1 ). Each of the 9 individual PRS were very strongly associated with the matching clinical phenotype (Table 3 ). Using model 3 adjustment variables, there was a significant association with the odds for AVC >0 for the PRS of CAD (odds ratio [OR],1.16 [95% CI, 1.07–1.26], P =0.002), SBP (OR, 1.112 [95% CI, 1.0–1.201], P =0.036), and LDL‐C (OR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.06–1.25], P =0.003). The PRS for Lp(a) was not significantly associated with AVC >0 using model 3 variables (OR, 1.11 [95% CI, 1.02–1.20], P =0.135) but was significant using model 2 variables that do not include the clinical measurement of Lp(a) (OR, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.12–1.30], P <0.001). There were no significant associations for the risk of AVC >0 for the PRS for CAC, DBP, CRP, or diabetes (Table 4 ). The PRS for triglycerides had a nominally significant association that was not significant after Bonferroni correction. In the stepwise selection analysis that included the clinical variables as well as the PRS, the PRS for CAD and SBP were significant (Table S1 ). The PRS for Lp(a) and LDL‐C were not significant in the stepwise model, because the quantitative variables for clinically measured Lp(a) and LDL‐C were already significant in the stepwise multivariable model. The overall association of individual PRS with AVC >0 was similar for men and women (Figure 2 ). Both women and men had a significant association for the PRS of CAD, LDL‐C, and Lp(a) with AVC >0, whereas the PRS for SBP was significant for women (OR, 1.13 [95% CI, 1.00–1.27]) and men (OR, 1.14 [95% CI, 1.00–1.27]) when analyzed separately (Table S2 ). The association of individual PRS with AVC >0 were generally similar across the different races and ethnicities (Figure 3 and Table S3 ). In Mendelian randomization analyses, for every 5 mm Hg higher in SBP there was a 16% higher odds for AVC >0 (OR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.05–1.28], P =0.002) and for every 10 mg/dL higher LDL‐C there was a 21% higher odds for AVC >0 (OR, 1.207 [95% CI, 1.11–1.32], P <0.001). The CAD PRS was significantly associated with AVC alone, CAD alone, AVC without incident CAD, and incident CAD without AVC (Table S4 ). Sensitivity analyses examining the 4 PRS significantly associated with AVC >0 also showed a significant association with AVC when AVC was examined as a continuous variable (Table S5 ).
sections.discussion: To best of our knowledge this is the first article to investigate the association of individual PRS with AVC. We show that PRS for CAD, SBP, LDL‐C, and Lp(a) are significantly associated with an increased risk for AVC >0. Our PRS results are consistent with prior genome‐wide association study analyses demonstrating that LDL‐C and Lp(a) are associated with AVC. Furthermore, these results provide insights into other risk factors for AVC and the pathobiology of AVC. Of particular interest, these results suggest that SBP is an important and underrecognized risk factor for AVC. Of further importance, the significant results for the CAD PRS suggest that the genetic pathways leading to CAD and AVC are shared. In contrast, our results highlight that the genetic pathways for calcification of the aortic valve and coronary arteries are different. Additionally, the nonsignificant results for the CRP PRS support prior findings that inflammation measured by CRP is not an independent or causal risk factor for AVC, similar to other findings that CRP is not a causal risk factor for CAD. 4 , 32 , 33 It is well established that AVC and CAD have shared risk factors. 3 However, our study also demonstrates that beyond shared risk factors such as hyperlipidemia and hypertension, the underlying genetic pathways that promote CAD itself are shared with AVC. Accordingly, when we examined the correlation between the different PRS, there was little overlap between the CAD PRS and the PRS for individual risk factors such as LDL‐C, Lp(a), etc, which strongly suggests pathways beyond traditional atherosclerotic CVD risk factors are shared by CAD and AVC. Understanding these differences and commonalities may provide insights into novel treatment targets and for therapies that may have the potential for preventing both CAD and AVC. In contrast to the shared genetic pathways for AVC and CAD, we found that the PRS for CAC was not associated with AVC. This finding supports our understanding of CAC as part of the atherosclerosis process within the intima of the coronary vasculature, while AVC is a distinct process on the nonvascular aortic valve leaflets. 34 , 35 Coronary atherosclerotic plaques begin as noncalcified lipid rich plaques. Over time the death of smooth muscle, oxidative stress, and inflammation promote intimal calcification. Healing of ruptured coronary plaques also contributes of the development of CAC. 36 , 37 , 38 On the other hand, aortic valve leaflets become damaged over time leading to fibrosis and calcification. Lipid deposition within the aortic valves, particularly oxidized lipids promote calcification via fibroblasts. 39 In the later stages of AVC and AS, the AVC process is driven primarily by osteogenic pathways. 40 , 41 We also found that PRS for CRP was not significantly associated with AVC. Although inflammation is commonly considered a risk factor for AVC, our work and that of others have demonstrated that higher hs‐CRP levels were not independently associated with AVC or AVC progression. 4 , 32 However, higher hs‐CRP appears to modify the risk for AVC, as higher hsCRP levels in conjunction with higher Lp(a) levels were associated with a much higher risk for AVC than higher Lp(a) levels alone in the MESA study. 4 Accordingly, these results highlight the important of further work to better understand the concordant and discordant pathways for CAD and AVC. Currently, there are no approved medications to treat AS and the only intervention is aortic valve replacement. To date, efforts toward slowing the progression of AVC and preventing severe AS have focused on LDL‐C lowering with the largest trials showing no benefit. 42 , 43 , 44 However, our results showing a significant association of the LDL‐C and Lp(a) PRS with AVC further support the importance of these causal atherogenic lipid pathways and the need for further investigation into lipid‐lowering therapies to prevent the formation of AVC or progression to severe AS. Indeed, exploratory analyses have suggested benefit among appropriately selected participants and for individuals treatment with PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitors. 45 , 46 Lp(a), which is ≈90% genetically determined is a strong risk factor for AVC and has been implicated as stronger atherogenic risk factor than LDL‐C. 4 , 47 , 48 In this regard, the Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS (Randomized Double‐Blind, Placebo‐Controlled, Multicenter Trial Assessing the Impact of Lipoprotein(a) Lowering With Pelacarsen [TQJ230] on the Progression of Calcific Aortic Valve Stenosis) trial will begin enrollment soon to test the Lp(a) lowering agent Pelacarsen. Beyond lipid‐lowering therapies, our findings show that SBP is an important underappreciated risk factor for AVC. A small number of studies have shown expression of angiotensin‐converting enzymes and angiotensin II Type I on aortic valve macrophages. 49 , 50 A recent Mendelian randomization of plasma protein levels has also recently linked angiotensin‐converting enzymes as a causal pathway for the development of AS and suggested that the risk for AS associated with angiotensin converting enzyme exposure may be extend beyond SBP level. 51 An association between hypertension with calcific aortic valve disease has also been observed, although these studies were primarily conducted among older adults and examined AVC or AS measured by echocardiography, which does not detect calcific aortic valve disease until a later stage of the disease compared with computed tomography measured AVC. 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 Additionally, our results show an OR of relatively comparable magnitude for the PRS of SBP, LDL‐C, and Lp(a), suggesting that the relative magnitude of contribution to AVC for elevated SBP may be in keeping with that of atherogenic lipids. In our study the primary aim was to explore underlying pathways for AVC. However, there is a growing interest in the use of PRS to identify individuals at increased risk for CVD. 7 To date studies have shown mixed results for whether or not the PRS improve CVD risk prediction beyond traditional risk factors or CAC scoring. 8 , 9 , 19 , 56 , 57 However, an important distinction is that currently there is no recommended screening algorithm for AVC or AS. Therefore, our results showing that individuals with an elevated PRS for either LDL‐C, Lp(a), SBP, or CAD are more likely to have AVC is an incremental step toward developing a method for the identification of individuals who have an increased risk for AVC. Future studies are planned to develop a specific PRS for AVC. An important limitation of this study is that the analyses are cross‐sectional. Aside from the PRS for SBP and DBP, the other PRS were derived from multiethnic cohorts, although European ancestry was the predominant race or ethnicity for all PRS derivation cohorts. The MESA cohort is part of the CHARGE (Cohorts for Heart and Aging Research in Genomic Epidemiology) and GLGC (Global Lipids Genetic Consortium), which were used to derive the PRS for some (eg.,LDL‐C, triglycerides, and CRP, etc) but not all of the PRS. However, the MESA cohort comprised <5% of participants for the CHARGE Consortium and<1% of participants for the GLGC. 15 , 16 Strengths of this analysis include the 9 different individual PRS, which had a low correlation with each other, except for SBP and DBP. The use of PRS also allows for examination of causal associations to determine underlying pathways for AVC.
sections.conclusions_1: These results confirm the importance of atherogenic lipids as risk factors for AVC and provide important insights to help better understand nonlipid pathways underlying AVC. Importantly, we show that the PRS for SBP is significantly associated with AVC, highlighting SBP as an important underrecognized risk factor for AVC and as a potential treatment target. These results also demonstrate shared genetic pathways for CAD and AVC but different pathways for calcification of the aortic valves and coronary arteries. Overall, these results help to better understand the pathogenesis and risk factors for AVC, which is vital in the ongoing process to identify treatment strategies to slow or prevent the development of AVC and AS.
