title: Ki-67 as a treatment decision modifier in breast cancer
abstract: Abstract Ki-67 is widely used in breast cancer; however, the fraction of patients in whom it meaningfully alters treatment decisions is not well established. Using a guideline-based approach anchored in National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) recommendations (v2.2026), we identified clinical scenarios in which Ki-67 directly modifies adjuvant therapy decisions and estimated their prevalence using population-level data and complementary datasets, recognizing that fully annotated datasets capturing all relevant clinicopathological variables remain limited. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that only a small fraction of patients meet the combined criteria of HR+/HER2− subtype, T2 stage, grade 2 histology, and Ki-67 ≥ 20%. This estimate, compared to population-scale ( n = 117 990 patients) and curated datasets ( n = 1356 patients), indicates that the clinically relevant subset remains in the low single digits (3-5%). Ki-67 impacts care only in specific decision settings, particularly near clinically relevant thresholds where small analytic variation may translate into treatment changes; outside these contexts, its routine use has limited evidence for clinical utility. Its application should therefore be selective, context-dependent, and focused on scenarios in which threshold-adjacent precision is clinically consequential.

sections.practical considerations: First, knowing the clinical setting is the basis to understand meaningful use of Ki-67 ( Figure 1A ). From a biological perspective, Ki-67 is an intuitively appealing marker of tumor proliferation and perceived aggressiveness, which in clinical practice often leads to its use as an additional decision-support tool beyond strictly guideline-defined contexts. The low prevalence of guideline-defined evidence-based indications where Ki-67 meaningfully alters management argues against routine Ki-67 testing in all breast cancer cases. This practice supports diagnostic stewardship, tissue preservation, and cost containment. For example, in some laboratories, Ki-67 is proposed as part of multi-marker panels. 9 , 10 While technically possible, our analysis illustrates the implied extra effort of >90% without guideline-compliant actionability ( Figure 1B ). Second, for these specific clinical settings and indications, it is of crucial importance to know the decision threshold ( Figure 1C ). When Ki-67 is used to modify treatment decisions, a one percentage point shift in the score can have substantial consequences. For example, a Ki-67 score of ≤13.25% has been evaluated as a criterion to de-escalate local therapy in the LUMINA cohort study. 11 In this context, a difference of less than one percentage point can meaningfully inform clinical decisions. By contrast, the same degree of variability may be clinically inconsequential when Ki-67 is reported as 14% and the relevant decision threshold is 20%. In these settings, analytic and interpretive variance become clinical variance. Therefore, knowing the clinical setting and decision threshold is important to avoid unintentional imprecision. Accordingly, the funnel presented here reflects scenarios in which Ki-67 itself functions as a decision-modifying variable, rather than the overall prevalence of adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitor use. Third, knowing the relevant decision threshold has another important practical implication: it allows precision efforts to be focused where they matter most, namely, in cases with Ki-67 scores near the decision threshold ( Figure 1C ). Precision in this context refers to prioritizing time, expertise, and quality controls for cases in which small differences in Ki-67 scoring could alter management. While standardized, visual, and careful assessment is one option, visual scoring alone may lack sufficient reproducibility around clinical thresholds. Accordingly, resource optimization may also include digital image analysis and AI-enabled quantification tools. These can aid in objective Ki-67 assessment and help mitigate reproducibility concerns, 12 especially in cases with Ki-67 scores near the relevant decision threshold. Fourth, complete and well-annotated clinicopathological data are a prerequisite for the clinically meaningful use of Ki-67. In our analysis, even seemingly straightforward classifications (ie, tumor stage, nodal status, grade, and receptor status) were not consistently available, leaving insufficient context for clinical use of Ki-67. More liberal Ki-67 ordering practices cannot substitute for complete staging, grading, and receptor assessment. This aligns with ongoing efforts by professional organizations such as the College of American Pathologists , the American Society for Clinical Pathology , and the International Ki-67 in Breast Cancer Working Group , which emphasize standardized assessment and context-specific use of Ki-67. Greater attention to data integrity will be essential to translate biomarker insights into reliable clinical practice. Importantly, this analysis does not argue against Ki-67 as a biomarker, but for its meaningful and context-specific use. Ki-67 remains clinically relevant for luminal subtype refinement, prognostic enrichment, trial eligibility, and assessment of treatment response in the neoadjuvant setting, where changes in Ki-67 correlate with outcome. 13 However, its use as a decision tool is limited by analytic and interpretive variability, including pre-analytic factors, scoring methods, inter-observer reproducibility, and inconsistent decision thresholds; limitations repeatedly highlighted by expert reviews and professional societies 13 , 14 contributing to ongoing controversy and, in some settings, removal from regulatory labels. Differences in how Ki-67 is applied across adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitor programs further emphasize the need for standardized assessment and interpretation. 15 Ki-67 plays distinct roles across trials, regulatory authorization, and guideline implementation. Historically, Ki-67 has been widely used as a prognostic biomarker reflecting tumor proliferation. With the emergence of prospective trials evaluating adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitors, including the monarchE 7 and NATALEE 1 trials, Ki-67 ≥ 20% was incorporated to define high-risk subgroups. In 2021, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved adjuvant abemaciclib for HR+/HER2− early breast cancer with high-risk features, requiring Ki-67 ≥ 20% as a companion diagnostic for treatment selection. 16 This designation facilitated initial regulatory approval and clinical adoption by providing a measurable threshold for patient selection (=market entry). However, in 2023, 17 the FDA removed the Ki-67 companion diagnostic requirement following longer-term analyses of monarchE demonstrating benefit independent of Ki-67 status, 18 alongside ongoing concerns regarding assay variability and reproducibility. 19–21 As a result, Ki-67 has transitioned to a context-specific decision modifier reflecting that biomarker roles evolve with clinical, evidentiary, and regulatory context. 22 Thereby, Ki-67 in breast cancer exemplifies how a (prognostic) biomarker can be elevated to a companion diagnostic for treatment selection and market entry, then later repositioned as evidence and practice evolve. Similarly, regulatory approvals evolve with emerging scientific evidence in accordance with principles of regulatory science. 17 Notably, in assembling these estimates, we were struck by the limited availability of datasets with complete patient-level annotation. In population-scale datasets, substantial missingness or the need for sequential restriction markedly reduces the analyzable cohort. 23 As a result, we were unable to identify a single, readily available dataset that captures these variables jointly at the patient level to directly assess their dependence structure. This limitation has broader implications, including for AI/ML applications, where robust methods to address sparse and/or systematically missing data remain an unmet need. In an era of increasingly resource-constrained oncology care, even familiar biomarkers benefit from periodic re-examination, not to diminish their value, but to align their use with demonstrable, guideline-anchored clinical impact.

title: Changes in Medication Use After Medicare Part D Annual Out-of-Pocket Spending Caps
abstract: This cohort study reports on changes in prescription drug use after the Inflation Reduction Act implemented out-of-pocket spending caps.

sections.question: How did prescription drug use change after the Inflation Reduction Act implemented annual out-of-pocket spending caps in Medicare starting in 2024?
sections.findings: In this cohort study using a difference-in-differences framework of 3053 medications covering 92.9% of gross Medicare Part D spending in 2023, prescriptions for medications paid by Medicare increased after the out-of-pocket cap was implemented in 2024 compared with those paid by commercial insurance; this change was most pronounced among the highest-cost medications, with a 22.7% increase in 2024-2025.
sections.meaning: Results of this study suggest that implementing annual out-of-pocket caps in Medicare was associated with higher use of medications and that the policy improved Medicare-insured patients’ access to costly medications.
sections.importance: The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) implemented annual out-of-pocket spending caps to the Medicare Part D prescription medication benefit in 2024; the caps were lowered to $2000 in 2025. It remains unclear how this policy affected medication access.
sections.objective: To evaluate changes in prescription medication fills in the Medicare population after the implementation of the IRA.
sections.design, setting, and participants: This study used data from an all-payer pharmacy database (Symphony Health Metys) to evaluate changes in quarterly prescription fills for medications reimbursed by Medicare and commercial insurance from 2022 to 2025. Using an event study, difference-in-differences framework, changes in per-capita prescriptions for medications before and after the Medicare annual out-of-pocket spending caps were implemented in 2024 were compared. Because out-of-pocket caps are most relevant for patients using expensive medications, medications were stratified based on monthly cost: low (<$100), medium ($100-$829), high ($830-$6999), and very high (≥$7000).
sections.results: Among 3053 medications covering 92.9% of gross Medicare Part D spending in 2023, 1534 (50.2%) were low cost, 882 (28.9%) were medium cost, 455 (14.9%) were high cost, and 182 (6.0%) were very high cost. After the spending caps were implemented, average medication use increased in Medicare compared with medication use in commercial insurance, with larger increases for higher-cost medications. In pre-post difference-in-differences analyses, there was no change in Medicare vs commercial use of low-cost, medium-cost, or high-cost medications. Very-high-cost medication use increased by 22.7% (95% CI, 6.0% to 42.0%; P = .01). Use of medications in Medicare increased over time in event-study analyses, although CIs were wide; by the fourth quarter of 2025, the use of medications in Medicare compared with commercial insurance increased from baseline by 4.1% (95% CI, −3.4% to 12.3%) for low-cost medications, 20.7% (95% CI, −10.7% to 63.0%) for medium-cost medications, 23.1% (95% CI, 2.7% to 47.4%) for high-cost medications, and 35.9% (95% CI, −4.1% to 92.3%) for very-high-cost medications.
sections.conclusions and relevance: This study found that medication use increased after implementation of Medicare annual out-of-pocket cost caps, particularly among the highest-cost medications. These results suggest that the policy substantially improved patient access to high-cost medications for Medicare-insured patients.
sections.introduction: Medicare Part D provides prescription medication coverage for more than 57 million US individuals, including most adults older than 65 years. 1 Since its enactment in 2006, Part D has required substantial cost-sharing by patients, including a deductible, 25% cost-sharing up to a catastrophic level of spending ($7400 in 2023), and unlimited 5% cost-sharing after this threshold. 2 As the cost of prescription medications increased over the last 2 decades, this approach became increasingly untenable, with patient costs exceeding $10 000 for some expensive medications, such as oral chemotherapy medications and biologics. 3 , 4 Higher cost-sharing is associated with medication nonadherence and worse clinical outcomes, including higher mortality. 5 , 6 , 7 In a 2022 survey, 1 in 5 adults older than 65 years reported cost-related medication nonadherence. 8 To help Medicare patients, US Congress implemented several changes to the Part D program in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022. 9 Starting in January 2024, the IRA eliminated cost-sharing after patients reached the catastrophic spending limit, effectively capping patients’ annual out-of-pocket costs to approximately $3300. 10 In January 2025, the annual out-of-pocket spending cap was lowered to $2000. By one estimate, the $2000 spending cap was expected to lower costs for approximately one-fifth of Medicare beneficiaries. 11 The IRA also includes several other changes to Part D, including shifting more financial liability from the government to private Part D plan sponsors for patients with high-cost medications, changing how the maximum out-of-pocket cost threshold was calculated, and expanding which patients were eligible for low-income subsidies; these subsidies substantially lower out-of-pocket costs for those who qualify. 4 These changes in the Part D program—particularly the annual out-of-pocket spending cap—could improve medication access and affordability for the millions of US residents with Medicare, particularly for high-cost medications previously associated with out-of-pocket costs of thousands of dollars. The goal of this study was to measure changes in medication use by Medicare-insured patients after the implementation of the annual out-of-pocket spending caps compared with changes in use of the same medications by commercially insured patients.
sections.data sources and medication cohort: In this cohort study, we identified medications covered by Medicare Part D using the public Medicare Part D spending dashboard data from 2023, which was the year prior to the out-of-pocket spending caps and the most recent data available (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 ). 12 We excluded vaccines and insulins, 2 classes of medications subject to separate out-of-pocket limits for Medicare beneficiaries during this time. 13 , 14 We also excluded medications with no use in the reference quarter (2023 quarter [Q] 4), the most recent quarter prior to the start of the IRA Part D reforms (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 ). Medications were defined by active ingredient and brand vs generic status since brand name medications typically cost more than generic medications (eMethods in Supplement 1 ). The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline for observational research. This project was exempt from review and informed patient consent because it was deemed not to represent human participants research by the Massachusetts General Brigham Institutional Review Board. To measure changes in medication use over time, we linked this cohort at the medication level to Symphony Health Metys, an all-payer retail pharmacy database that estimates nationally representative counts of prescriptions based on a large sample of retail, mail-order, and long-term care pharmacies (eMethods in Supplement 1 ). Generic and brand name formulations were treated as separate entities during this linkage given that they typically have different prices. We benchmarked Metys against the Medicare Part D dashboard to measure what percentage of prescriptions Metys captured in its dataset (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 ). We used these data to measure the estimated number of filled prescriptions reimbursed by Medicare or commercial insurers from the first quarter of 2022 through the fourth quarter of 2025, the most recent full quarter of data available at the time of analysis. We excluded a small number of medications that could not be linked to data from Symphony Health Metys (unlinked medications represented 0.4% of 2023 gross Medicare Part D spending). To account for changes in the size of the Medicare Part D and commercially insured populations over time, we used quarterly national Medicare Part D and commercial insurance enrollment estimates from public Medicare Part D enrollee files and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey (eMethods in Supplement 1 ). Medicare enrollment did not change substantially from pre-IRA historical trends over the study period.
sections.exposure and covariates: The primary exposure was enactment of annual out-of-pocket spending caps in Medicare in January 2024. We chose 2024 as the start of our intervention period because this was the first year the IRA implemented a spending cap in Medicare Part D (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ); although the spending cap was higher in 2024 (approximately $3300) than in 2025 ($2000), we presumed that the impact of adding a cap may be larger than the impact caused by lowering the cap in 2025. Additionally, low-income subsidy expansions under the IRA took effect in January 2024. We hypothesized that this policy would disproportionately affect access to the most expensive medications, because patients using these medications would reach the spending cap early in the year and have no cost-sharing for remaining prescription fills. We thus stratified medications based on monthly cost into 4 categories: low (<$100), medium ($100-$829), high ($830-$6999), and very high (≥$7000). Monthly costs were determined based on mean annual spending per Medicare beneficiary using the 2023 Part D dashboard data (most recent year available) and reflect gross spending prior to any confidential rebates. The $830 threshold was chosen because medications above this threshold can be designated in specialty tiers subject to higher cost-sharing requirements by Part D plans that might be more sensitive to out-of-pocket costs. 15 The $7000 threshold was selected because medications above this cost would likely lead patients to reach the $2000 out-of-pocket cap after filling a single month’s supply. 15 In sensitivity analyses, we further stratified high-cost medications at $830 to $2999, $3000 to $4999, $5000 to $6999, and $7000 or more.
sections.outcome measures: The primary outcome was the quarterly number of prescriptions per capita for each medication, calculated by dividing the number of filled prescriptions in Medicare or commercial insurance by the number of Medicare or commercial enrollees in the calendar year.
sections.statistical analysis: We used a difference-in-differences analysis to compare changes in the use of medications in Medicare before and after the Medicare annual out-of-pocket caps were implemented in January 2024 compared with changes in the use of the same medications in the commercially insured population. Data were analyzed at the medication-quarter insurance-type level with longitudinal panel estimates at the medication-insurance–type level. We clustered errors at the medication-insurance–type level to account for repeated measures over time. We used ordinary least-squares models to estimate the quarterly number of prescriptions per capita, and the outcome was log-transformed so that model results could be interpreted as relative changes over time. We calculated the overall average treatment effect comparing quarters before (2022-2023) and after (2024-2025) the policy change. We also calculated quarter-specific effects using an event study framework to measure changes over time. 16 Models included fixed effects for each medication (to account for time-invariant differences between drugs and to focus the analysis on within-drug changes in use) and calendar quarter (to account for within-year seasonal variation). To better reflect national trends, the primary results were weighted based on the number of Medicare prescriptions for each drug in the baseline study quarter (fourth quarter of 2023). This was done so that common medications contributed more to results than rarely prescribed medications. Unweighted results were also reported. We evaluated whether models satisfied the parallel-trends assumption using models of the untransformed and log-transformed outcomes using an interaction term between quarter and treatment group (Medicare vs commercial) in the 8 preintervention quarters. Separate models were created for medications in each cost group. To ensure that differences between Medicare and commercial plans were related to the implementation of the Medicare Part D out-of-pocket spending caps implemented in January 2024, we performed a falsification test in which we treated the first quarter of 2023 as the exposure. To illustrate how changes in medication use varied across therapeutic categories, we performed a subgroup analysis by therapeutic category among the high- and very-high-cost categories; these groups were combined to adequately power the subgroup analyses (eMethods in Supplement 1 ). Analyses were considered significant based on 2-sided tests with statistical significance defined as P < .05. Analyses were performed in Stata version 18.1 (StataCorp).
sections.results_1: The analysis included 3053 medications, covering 92.9% of gross Medicare Part D spending in 2023. Overall, 1534 (50.2%) medications were low cost, 882 (28.9%) were medium cost, 455 (14.9%) were high cost, and 182 (6.0%) were very high cost. The median monthly costs were $15 for low-cost (IQR, $7-$39), $253 for medium-cost (IQR, $159-$395), $2392 for high-cost (IQR, $1358-$4616), and $11 196 for very-high-cost (IQR, $8609-$18 091) medications. The most common therapeutic category for low-cost medications was gastroenterological (286 of 1534 [18.6%]), while the most common category for very-high-cost medications was oncology (65 of 182 [35.7%]) ( Table 1 ). In analyses benchmarking our dataset, Symphony Health Metys, to the Medicare Part D dashboard, the percentage of prescriptions captured by Metys decreased over time (eg, from 92% to 88.2% for low-cost medications), which could bias our results toward the null (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 ). The most prescribed medications for Medicare beneficiaries by cost category in the fourth quarter of 2023 were atorvastatin for low cost (15 061 045 prescriptions), apixaban for medium cost (4 865 374 prescriptions), bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir for high cost (136 822 prescriptions), and nintedanib for very high cost (117 979 prescriptions) ( Table 2 ). Trends in the mean per-capita use of medications in each of the 4 cost categories are presented in Figure 1 . The use of low-cost medications decreased over time in both cohorts (Medicare: 67 976 prescriptions per million in the first quarter of 2022 to 66 979 in the fourth quarter of 2025; commercial: 32 902 to 30 691), medium-cost medications increased in both cohorts (Medicare: 21 742 to 28 512; commercial: 6740 to 8769), high-cost medications remained stable in commercial insurance (733 to 738) and increased in Medicare (705 to 973), and very-high-cost medication use decreased in the commercial insurance population (352 to 302) and increased in Medicare (830 to 1229). Trends in the log-transformed data were similar (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 ). Prior to the Medicare spending caps, average changes in medication use were similar in Medicare and commercial insurance, and each group satisfied the parallel-trends assumption (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 ). In the primary (pre-IRA vs post-IRA) difference-in-differences analyses, there was no significant change in Medicare vs commercial use of low-cost medications (difference-in-differences estimate, 3.9%; 95% CI, −1.2% to 9.4%; P = .14), medium-cost medications (20.4%; 95% CI, −7.4% to 56.4%; P = .17), or high-cost medications (14.1%; 95% CI, −1.3% to 32.0%; P = .08). There was a 22.7% (95% CI, 6.0% to 42.0%; P = .01) increase in the use of very-high-cost medications after the spending cap in Medicare compared with commercial insurance. In event study analyses, differences between the Medicare and commercial groups increased over time ( Figure 2 ). By the fourth quarter of 2025, mean changes in medication use were 4.1% higher (95% CI, −3.4% to 12.3%; P = .29) for low-cost medications, 20.7% higher (95% CI, −10.7% to 63.0%; P = .22) for medium-cost medications, 23.1% higher (95% CI, 2.7% to 47.4%; P = .02) for high-cost medications, and 35.9% higher (95% CI, −4.1% to 92.3%; P = .08) for very-high-cost medications. Confidence intervals were wide due to heterogeneous trends among individual medications. In a falsification test evaluating changes in the 2023 calendar year, the overall difference-in-differences estimators were not significant for any of the 4 cost categories (eFigure 3, eTable 4 in Supplement 1 ). Among the high- and very-high-cost medications, CIs were wide and results not statistically significant, although point estimates were directionally consistent with pooled results ( Figure 3 ). Using alternate cost thresholds, medication use in Medicare vs commercial insurance increased by 8.9% (95% CI, −9.0% to 30.3%; P = .35) for medications costing $830 to $2999 monthly, 10.3% (95% CI, −9.6% to 34.5%; P = .33) for medications costing $3000 to $4999, and 54.1% (95% CI, −13.8% to 175.3%; P = .14) for medications costing $5000 to $6999 (eFigure 4, eTable 5 in Supplement 1 ). In unweighted models, results were more homogeneous across medication pricing levels. In 2 period difference-in-differences estimates the use of low-cost medications in Medicare increased by 9.2% (95% CI, 6.6% to 11.8%; P < .001), medium-cost medications by 11.8% (95% CI, 8.2% to 15.5%; P < .001), high-cost medications by 7.9% (95% CI, 3.5% to 12.4%; P < .001), and very-high-cost medications by 13.6% (95% CI, 6.3% to 21.5%; P < .001) (eFigure 5, eTable 6 in Supplement 1 ). In sensitivity analyses excluding 2025, the use of very-high-cost medications increased by 13.0% (95% CI, 0.3% to 27.4%; P = .045); other groups did not change significantly (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 ).
sections.discussion: In this cohort study using difference-in-differences analysis, the use of medications in Medicare increased relative to commercial insurance after annual out-of-pocket costs were enacted for Medicare Part D in 2024. The differences increased over time after the policy took effect, and the differences were generally larger among higher-cost medications. For example, the use of very-high-cost medications increased by 35.9% by the last quarter of 2025 compared with use of the same medications by commercially insured individuals. These findings suggest that the Part D annual out-of-pocket spending caps enacted under the IRA in 2024 were associated with substantially increased patient access to high-cost medications, with major implications for clinical treatment decisions and government health care spending. Our results provide important additional evidence of the salutary impact of out-of-pocket spending caps on patients’ access to medications. 11 , 17 , 18 Most prior studies have focused on caps for specific medications or classes of medications, such as insulin and vaccines, finding smaller effects on use. 13 , 14 State-level caps on out-of-pocket costs for insulin 19 , 20 and specialty medications 21 were not associated with increased use, perhaps because many of the commercially insured patients affected by these caps already had lower out-of-pocket costs. By contrast, the Part D annual spending caps in the IRA applied to all medications and represented a large reduction in cost for many patients who previously could pay $10 000 or more for some expensive medications. As a result, the magnitude of increased use was higher than seen in most prior studies. Our results are generally aligned with a prior study that found a substantial increase in the use of oral oncology medications in Medicare after the Part D spending caps in 2024; our study included a much broader range of drugs and more time after the policy took effect. 22 Another study 23 found that patient-reported cost-related medication nonadherence decreased among those with Medicare in 2024 compared with those with commercial insurance, which aligns with the increases in use observed in the current study. These results suggest that the caps may have achieved the intended policy goal of improving access and adherence to medications. For example, before the cap, many patients abandoned new prescriptions for many high-cost categories of medications, 4 and such rates of abandonment have decreased after the caps. Although some of the higher use after the spending caps is likely related to patients accessing needed medications, there could also be some substitution of lower-cost medications with higher-cost alternatives, now that patients may pay similar out-of-pocket costs and thus have limited incentives to select the lower-cost options. Similarly, the caps might incentivize some shifting from injection and infusion medications reimbursed by Medicare Part B to retail medications reimbursed under Medicare Part D. For example, patients with cancer may pay less out of pocket for oral cancer treatments covered under Part D rather than infused medications covered under Medicare Part B, which continues to have unconstrained 20% cost-sharing. Whether the changes we observed will translate to better patient outcomes is likely to be disease-specific, because increased medication use could reflect both high-value and low-value care. Further study of whether the increasing use of high-cost medications by Medicare-insured patients translates to improved clinical outcomes for Medicare Part D–insured patients will be needed. In the short term, the increased use of high-cost medications will raise the government’s spending on the Medicare Part D program. 15 The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the Medicare Part D redesign would increase Medicare spending by $60 billion from 2022 to 2031. 24 However, spending increases exceeded expectations from 2024 to 2025; the substantial growth in the use of high-cost medications observed in our study may partially explain this rapid increase in spending. 25 Much of this added cost will be borne by taxpayers who fund Medicare; some of the cost may be passed on to Medicare beneficiaries in the form of higher premiums, although premium increases have been restricted by the IRA and premium stabilization demonstrations through 2026 that have allocated billions of additional federal dollars to the program to prevent premium increases. But if these programs are not continued and if premiums do eventually increase, this could result in some Medicare-insured patients leaving the voluntary Part D program altogether. The higher costs might also lead to changes in how private plan sponsors offer coverage; in 2024-2025, plans became less generous in subsidizing out-of-pocket costs (before patients reached the annual cap) and some plans left the Part D marketplace altogether. 15 , 26 Under the IRA, the additional costs of funding a more generous Part D benefit were expected to be offset by lower costs from other policies, such as Medicare price negotiation, which was expected to save $100 billion from 2022 to 2031. 27 , 28 However, in 2025, US Congress eliminated an estimated $9 billion of these savings by excluding many rare disease medications from qualifying for negotiation. 29 , 30 Additionally, the IRA introduced a new Medicare Discount Program that requires manufacturers to reimburse Medicare for 20% of medication costs after patients reach the annual out-of-pocket spending cap. For very-high-cost medications, this will translate into discounts of approximately 20% that will offset higher spending related to their increased use. 31
sections.limitations: Our study has several limitations. We used aggregated medication-level data, so we were unable to make direct inferences about patient-level adherence or clinical outcomes and could not account for different effects among patients taking multiple medications. Furthermore, small-volume, high-cost prescriptions may contribute to large CIs. We were unable to exclude Medicare-insured patients unaffected by the caps, including those with low-income subsidies, which meant that the results may reflect an underestimate of the increase in use among Medicare-insured patients without these subsidies. There was substantial variation in the trends in use of individual medications; thus, we may not have been adequately powered to detect differences between Medicare and commercial insurance in all price groups or violations of the parallel-trends assumption. We estimated medication costs using 2023 Medicare spending data, but prices can change over time, which could lead to some misclassification of medications in the cost groups. Our measure of monthly cost was imprecise because it was calculated based on annual Medicare spending per beneficiary, which could lead to misclassification for drugs typically not used for a full year. Similarly, our per-capita estimates for Medicare enrollees may be imprecise as not all Medicare beneficiaries are continuously enrolled during the calendar year; this could bias results toward the null. Our dataset may undercount Medicare prescriptions, biasing our results to the null. We measured changes in use based on the quarterly prescriptions filled, which could change if patients fill a different amount of the medication, such as switching from 30-day to 90-day supplies. 32 However, because we compared usage patterns for the same medications in Medicare and commercial insurance, this would only affect the results if trends differed between these insurance types. We used commercial insurance as a comparison for Medicare, and there may be different trends in the use of medications in these 2 different populations, including if medications are used for different indications; however, the results met parallel-trends assumptions, suggesting that these differences did not bias the results. We could not disentangle the effects of the out-of-pocket caps from other policies implemented by the IRA, including expanded eligibility for low-income subsidies in 2024 and introduction of a program in 2025 that allowed patients to pay out-of-pocket costs across the calendar year. However, these programs affected a very small number of beneficiaries compared with the annual out-of-pocket caps. Our results only reflect trends in the first 2 years after the Medicare spending caps; although we found that the use of medications increased over time, these trends may change in subsequent quarters and it will be important to update these analyses as newer data become available. Use of medications in Medicare in subsequent years may be affected by other policies, including lower prices for some medications negotiated by Medicare that began to take effect in 2026. 33
sections.conclusions: In this study, the implementation of annual spending caps in Medicare Part D under the IRA was associated with increased use of prescription medications, particularly for very-high-cost medications. These results suggest that the policy may have substantially improved patients’ access to high-cost medications, and the magnitude of these changes has important implications for future policies to address Medicare Part D spending by patients and the government.

title: Description of the Tranquillo Phase 3 Clinical Trial Designs/Study Protocols to Assess Ritlecitinib in Adults and Adolescents with Nonsegmental Vitiligo
abstract: Introduction Ritlecitinib is an oral, selective inhibitor of JAK3 and TEC family kinases under investigation for the treatment of nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV). In a phase 2b study, ritlecitinib was efficacious and well tolerated over 48 weeks. The Tranquillo phase 3 program comprises three studies aiming to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of once-daily 50-mg and 100-mg ritlecitinib in adult and adolescent patients with NSV. Methods Tranquillo ( NCT05583526 ), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 52-week trial, compares the efficacy and safety of once-daily 50-mg ritlecitinib vs placebo ( N ≈ 600). Tranquillo LTE ( NCT06163326 ), a randomized, double-blind, withdrawal and dose-up titration 52-week extension study, investigates the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of once-daily 50-mg and 100-mg ritlecitinib and durability of response with once-daily 50-mg ritlecitinib following participation in Tranquillo ( N ≈ 400). Tranquillo 2 ( NCT06072183 ) comprises two parts: Part I, a 52-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study with 52-week extension with randomized dose-up/dose-down titration comparing once-daily 50-mg and 100-mg ritlecitinib with placebo ( N ≈ 1000), and Part II, a de novo 52-week nonrandomized, open-label once-daily 100-mg ritlecitinib arm ( N ≈ 450). Participants are aged ≥ 12 years (Tranquillo 2: ≥ 18 years) with clinical diagnosis of active or stable NSV for ≥ 3 months, body surface area involvement 4%–60%, facial body surface area ≥ 0.5%, Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI) ≥ 0.5, and Total (T)-VASI ≥ 3. Planned Outcomes Tranquillo’s primary efficacy endpoint is the proportion of participants achieving ≥ 75% improvement in F-VASI from baseline (F-VASI75) at Week 52; T-VASI50 at Week 52 is a coprimary efficacy endpoint in the US and a key secondary endpoint globally (other than US). Tranquillo LTE’s primary endpoint is safety. Tranquillo 2’s primary efficacy endpoint is F-VASI75 at Week 52; T-VASI50 at Week 52 is a coprimary efficacy endpoint in the US and a key secondary endpoint globally (other than US). In all three studies, the safety and tolerability of ritlecitinib are assessed throughout. Graphical abstract available for this article. Clinicaltrials.gov Registrations NCT05583526 , NCT06163326 , NCT06072183 . Graphical abstract

sections.digital features: This article is published with digital features, including an infographic, to facilitate understanding of the article. To view digital features for this article, go to 10.6084/m9.figshare.31573417
sections.background: Vitiligo is an autoimmune skin disease characterized by pigment loss due to the destruction of melanocytes. Vitiligo has an estimated global prevalence of 0.36% to 2% and can affect people of all sexes, races, ethnicities, and ages [ 1 – 4 ]. The most common type is nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV), occurring in 84% to 95% of cases, which manifests as symmetrical patches of depigmentation and confers an unpredictable disease course [ 1 – 3 ]. Vitiligo can often affect a patient’s psychosocial health, and patients with vitiligo experience higher rates of anxiety and depression [ 2 , 4 – 8 ]. The pathogenesis of vitiligo is complex and can involve multiple factors, from genetic predisposition to oxidative stress, resulting in recruitment of cytotoxic CD8 + T-cells to the location of melanocytes and the production of cytokines and chemokines and leading to further immune system activation and recruitment [ 9 – 12 ]. Cumulatively, this leads to melanocyte destruction [ 9 – 12 ]. The Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription proteins (JAK/STAT) pathway, in particular JAK3, and the tyrosine kinase expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (TEC) family kinase members play a vital role in vitiligo pathogenesis. Their roles include increasing the activity and expression of cytokines such as IFN-γ and IL-2, which leads to the activation and recruitment of CD4 + and cytotoxic CD8 + T-cells and tissue-resident memory T-cells [ 13 – 17 ]. Inhibition of both JAK3 and the TEC family kinases in patients with NSV was shown to decrease biomarkers associated with vitiligo pathogenesis [ 18 ]. Treatments for vitiligo include phototherapy, topical or oral corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and immunotherapies, as well as ruxolitinib, a topical JAK1/2 inhibitor (limited in clinical trials to topical application on ≤ 10% of a patient’s body surface area) [ 19 – 22 ]. However, these treatments often have limited efficacy, especially in patients with large areas of depigmentation, long-term safety concerns, or both [ 23 ]. No targeted oral systemic treatment is currently approved for NSV, highlighting an unmet need. Ritlecitinib is an oral, selective irreversible inhibitor of JAK3 and the TEC family kinases that is under investigation for the treatment of NSV [ 24 ]. In a phase 2b study ( NCT03715829 ), ritlecitinib 50 mg once daily (QD) (with or without an initial 4-week 100- or 200-mg QD loading dose) was efficacious and well tolerated in adults with active NSV over 48 weeks, demonstrating significant improvement vs placebo on centrally read Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI) scores at Week 24, with further efficacy observed up to Week 48 [ 24 ]. Exposure-response findings indicate that doses of ritlecitinib > 50 mg QD may provide additional efficacy [ 25 ]. In trials, 100-mg QD doses of ritlecitinib in patients with rheumatoid arthritis for up to 24 weeks and 200-mg doses QD in patients with ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, or rheumatoid arthritis for up to 8 weeks were generally safe and well tolerated [ 26 – 29 ]. In completed and ongoing studies on alopecia areata and vitiligo, over 1600 participants have received ritlecitinib in doses ranging from 50 to 200 mg QD, which were generally safe and well tolerated [ 24 , 30 – 33 ].
sections.objectives: Here, we present an overview of the Tranquillo phase 3 program, which comprises three phase 3 studies aiming to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and 100 mg QD in adult and adolescent participants with NSV: Tranquillo ( NCT05583526 ), Tranquillo Long Term Extension (LTE) ( NCT06163326 ), and Tranquillo 2 ( NCT06072183 ). The comprehensive program will assess efficacy by measuring repigmentation on both the face and entire body and seek to determine the safety and tolerability of both short- and long-term treatment with ritlecitinib. Tranquillo LTE and Tranquillo 2 will additionally study the impact of dose titration and randomized withdrawals to investigate optimal dosing strategies.
sections.tranquillo: Tranquillo is a phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter clinical trial designed to compare the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD with those of placebo in adult and adolescent participants with NSV. The primary objective of Tranquillo is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD vs placebo in participants with NSV. The study includes a 30-day screening period, a 52-week treatment period, and either a 4-week follow-up period or, for those eligible, entry into the extension study Tranquillo LTE (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Study design for the Tranquillo clinical trial. LTE long-term extension, QD once daily At baseline, participants are randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive either ritlecitinib 50 mg QD or placebo for 52 weeks. Participants are stratified based on Fitzpatrick skin type (FST) and age. FST stratification includes three strata: FST I and II, FST III and IV, and FST V and VI. Age stratification includes two strata: adolescent participants < 18 years and adult participants ≥ 18 years, with a target enrollment of approximately 5% of the total population being adolescents. Participants with active or stable NSV are enrolled without formal stratification or capping. Efficacy evaluations include outcomes at Weeks 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 52. Outcomes at all time points in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD group are being compared with those in the placebo group.
sections.tranquillo lte: Tranquillo LTE is a phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, parallel-group, randomized withdrawal and dose-up titration extension study designed to investigate the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and ritlecitinib 100 mg QD, and durability of response with ritlecitinib 50 mg QD in adults and adolescents with NSV following their participation in the Tranquillo study for 52 weeks. The primary objective is to evaluate the long-term safety and tolerability of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and 100 mg QD based on the incidence of adverse events, treatment-related adverse events, and serious adverse events leading to discontinuation and the incidence of clinically significant laboratory abnormalities. The study includes a 30-day screening period, a 52-week treatment period, and a 4-week follow-up period (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Study design of the Tranquillo LTE clinical trial. DUT dose-up titration, LTE long-term extension, NR non-randomized, QD once daily, RDRN randomized dose-ranging non-responders, RDRS randomized dose-ranging sub-threshold responders, RW randomized withdrawal Arm allocation is informed by response status at Week 52 of the Tranquillo study, the treatment received in the Tranquillo study, and age (Table 1 ). For those who received ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks during the Tranquillo study, adult and adolescent responders (defined as those who had ≥ F-VASI75 and/or ≥ T-VASI50 at Week 52 of the Tranquillo study) are randomized 1:1 to either continue ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks or switched to placebo for 52 weeks (randomized withdrawal). Adult sub-threshold responders (defined as those who had at least ≥ F-VASI50 but < F-VASI75 and/or at least ≥ T-VASI33 but < T-VASI50 at Week 52 of the Tranquillo study) are randomized 1:1 to either continue ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks or dose up to ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks (dose-up titration). Adolescent subthreshold responders and adult and adolescent non-responders (defined as < F-VASI50 and < T-VASI33 at Week 52 of the Tranquillo study) receive placebo for 52 weeks (non-randomized). Table 1 Definitions of responses used in Tranquillo clinical program Response at week 52 Threshold Responder ≥ F-VASI75 and ≥ T-VASI50 ≥ F-VASI75 ≥ T-VASI50 Sub-threshold responder F-VASI50 to < F-VASI75 and T-VASI33 to < T-VASI50 F-VASI50 to < F-VASI75 T-VASI33 to < T-VASI50 Non-responder < F-VASI50 and < T-VASI33 F-VASI Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index, T-VASI Total Vitiligo Area Scoring Index For those who received placebo for 52 weeks during the Tranquillo study, adult and adolescent responders continue to receive placebo for 52 weeks (non-randomized). Adult sub-threshold responders are randomized 2:1 to receive either ritlecitinib 100 mg QD or ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (randomized dose-ranging sub-threshold responders). Adult non-responders are randomized 2:1 to receive either ritlecitinib 100 mg QD or ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (randomized dose-ranging non-responders). Adolescent sub-threshold responders and non-responders receive ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (non-randomized). Efficacy evaluations include outcomes at Weeks 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 52. Outcomes at all time points in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD and 100-mg QD groups are being compared with those in the placebo group unless otherwise specified. Safety evaluations include outcomes at all time points for the entire patient population.
sections.tranquillo 2: Tranquillo 2 comprises two parts. Part I is a phase 3, 52-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter study (Part Ia) plus 52-week randomized dose-up/dose-down titration extension (Part Ib) designed to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and ritlecitinib 100 mg QD compared with placebo in adult participants with NSV. Part II is a de novo 52-week non-randomized, open-label ritlecitinib 100-mg QD arm to support the safety database. The primary objectives of Tranquillo 2 are to compare the efficacy of ritlecitinib 100 mg QD vs placebo and to evaluate the safety and tolerability of ritlecitinib over time in participants with NSV. Part I includes a 30-day screening period, a 52-week placebo-controlled treatment period, a 52-week dose-up/down titration extension period, and a 4-week follow-up period. Part II includes a 30-day screening period, a 52-week treatment period, and a 4-week follow-up period (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Study design for the Tranquillo 2 clinical trial. DDT dose-down titration, DUT dose-up titration, NR non-randomized, QD once daily, RDRN randomized dose-ranging non-responders, RDRS randomized dose-ranging sub-threshold responders In Part Ia, participants are randomized in a 3:1:1 ratio to receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD, ritlecitinib 50 mg QD, or placebo QD for 52 weeks. Participants are stratified based on FST into three strata: FST I and II, FST III and IV, and FST V and VI. At Week 52, participants in Part Ia enter Part Ib, with treatment response in Part Ia at Week 52 informing Part Ib treatment arm allocation (Table 1 ). For those who received 100 mg QD for 52 weeks during Part Ia, responders (defined as those who had ≥ F-VASI75 and/or ≥ T-VASI50 at Week 52) are randomized 1:1 to either continue ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks or receive ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (dose-down titration), sub-threshold responders (defined as those who had at least ≥ F-VASI50 but < F-VASI75 and/or at least ≥ T-VASI33 but < T-VASI50 at Week 52) continue ritlecitinib 100 mg for 52 weeks, and non-responders (defined as < F-VASI50 and < T-VASI33 at Week 52) receive placebo for 52 weeks. For those who received ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks during Part Ia, responders continue ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks, sub-threshold responders are randomized 1:1 to either continue ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks or receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks (dose-up titration), and non-responders receive placebo for 52 weeks. For those who received placebo QD for 52 weeks during Part Ia, responders continue receiving placebo for 52 weeks, sub-threshold responders are randomized 2:1 to either receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks or receive ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (randomized dose-ranging sub-threshold responders), and non-responders are randomized 2:1 to either receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks or receive ritlecitinib 50 mg QD for 52 weeks (randomized dose-ranging non-responders). In Part II, all participants receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD for 52 weeks in an open-label manner. Those enrolled in Part II do not proceed to the extension period. Efficacy evaluations include outcomes at Weeks 24, 36, and 52. Outcomes at all time points in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD and 100-mg QD groups are being compared with those in the placebo group.
sections.sample selection: In brief, eligible participants for all 3 studies include individuals aged ≥ 12 years (for Tranquillo and Tranquillo LTE) or ≥ 18 years (for Tranquillo 2) with a clinical diagnosis of NSV (as previously defined) [ 24 ] for at least 3 months, with active or stable disease status evaluated at baseline. Participants must have a body surface area involvement of 4% to 60%, excluding palms, soles, or dorsal aspect of the feet, and body surface area ≥ 0.5% involvement on the face. Additionally, participants must have F-VASI ≥ 0.5 and T-VASI ≥ 3. Exclusion criteria include any psychiatric condition including recent or active suicidal ideation or behavior, other forms of vitiligo, or other diseases or conditions affecting the skin. Prohibited medications include moderate to potent CYP3A inducers and moderate sensitive or sensitive CYP3A substrates. See Table 2 for a list of prohibited concomitant medications. sections.tranquillo_1: In the Tranquillo study, selection and testing of the primary and key secondary endpoints are region specific as a result of negotiations and agreements with global regulators. In the US, F-VASI75 and T-VASI50 at Week 52 are co-primary endpoints, while F-VASI75 at Week 52 is the primary endpoint and T-VASI50 at Week 52 is a key secondary endpoint for Global (other than US) study sites. Both F-VASI75 and T-VASI50 are clinically meaningful endpoints, with T-VASI50 representing clinically meaningful improvement for patients across the whole body (including face). F-VASI75 represents the most clinically meaningful and socially impactful improvement for patients who have lesions on their face. Both endpoints will be controlled for family-wise Type I error rate, and there are no implications to the interpretation of the study results. In the US, the coprimary efficacy endpoints are the comparison of the proportions of participants achieving F-VASI75 at Week 52 and the proportion of participants achieving T-VASI50 at Week 52 among those receiving ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and those receiving placebo (Table 3 ). Globally (other than the US), the primary efficacy endpoint is the comparison of the proportion of participants achieving F-VASI75 at Week 52 among those receiving ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and those receiving placebo. Table 3 Endpoints for the Tranquillo clinical trial US coprimary efficacy endpoints Global (other than US) primary efficacy endpoint F-VASI75 a Week 52 F-VASI75 a Week 52 T-VASI50 a Week 52 All countries primary endpoint Safety Throughout study US key secondary endpoints Global (other than US) key secondary endpoints F-VASI75 a Weeks 24 and 36 F-VASI75 a Weeks 24 and 36 T-VASI50 a Weeks 24 and 36 T-VASI50 a Weeks 24, 36, and 52 %CFB in F-VASI/T-VASI Weeks 24, 36, and 52 %CFB in F-VASI/T-VASI Weeks 24, 36, and 52 T-VASI75 a Week 52 PGIS-F/PGIS-V b Weeks 24, 36, and 52 PGIS-F/PGIS-V b Week 52 CFB change from baseline, F-VASI Facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index, PGIS-F Patient Global Impression of Severity–Face, PGIS-V Patient Global Impression of Severity–Overall Vitiligo, T-VASI Total Vitiligo Area Scoring Index a Proportion of participants achieving this measurement b Participants achieving PGIS-F/PGIS-V response, which is defined as a 1-point improvement in facial/total body vitiligo in participants with mild, moderate, or severe facial/total body vitiligo at baseline or a 2-point improvement in participants with very severe facial/total body vitiligo at baseline Key secondary endpoints for the US include the comparison of the proportion of participants achieving F-VASI75 at Weeks 24 and 36, the proportion of participants achieving T-VASI50 at Weeks 24 and 36, and the mean percent change from baseline (CFB) in F-VASI and T-VASI at Weeks 24, 36, and 52 in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD group vs placebo group, and the proportion of participants achieving T-VASI75 at Week 52 in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD group vs placebo group. Patients also report on their perception of disease severity at certain visits using the Patient Global Impression of Severity–Face (PGIS-F) and Patient Global Impression of Severity–Vitiligo (PGIS-V, used to assess total body extent of vitiligo). For PGIS-F and PGIS-V, a response is defined as a 1-point improvement in facial or total body vitiligo, respectively, in participants with mild, moderate, or severe facial or total body vitiligo at baseline or a 2-point improvement in participants with very severe facial or total body vitiligo at baseline, respectively. The comparisons of the proportions of participants achieving PGIS-F response at Week 52 and the proportions of participants achieving PGIS-V response at Week 52 between those in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD and placebo groups are also key secondary endpoints. Global (other than the US) key secondary endpoints include the comparison of the proportion of participants achieving F-VASI75 at Weeks 24 and 36; the proportion of participants achieving T-VASI50 at Weeks 24, 36, and 52, and the mean percent CFB in F-VASI and T-VASI at Weeks 24, 36, and 52 in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD group vs placebo group. The comparisons of the proportions of participants achieving PGIS-F response at Weeks 24, 36, and 52 and the proportions of participants achieving PGIS-V response at Weeks 24, 36, and 52 between those in the ritlecitinib 50-mg QD and placebo groups are also key secondary endpoints. sections.sample size: Tranquillo is enrolling approximately 600 participants, with approximately 400 participants randomized to receive ritlecitinib 50 mg QD and approximately 200 participants randomized to receive placebo. Tranquillo LTE is enrolling approximately 400 participants who completed the Tranquillo study to receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD, ritlecitinib 50 mg QD, or placebo QD, based on their responder status, age, and dose at Week 52 in Tranquillo. Tranquillo 2 is enrolling approximately 1000 participants in Part I, with 600 randomized to receive ritlecitinib 100 mg QD, 200 participants to receive 50 mg QD, and 200 participants to receive placebo. An additional approximately 450 patients are enrolled in Part II. The sample sizes in Tranquillo and Tranquillo 2 yield higher power (≥ 89%) of conclusion of efficacy under alternative hypotheses. The sample size in Tranquillo LTE assumes approximately 85% of those that complete Tranquillo will enter Tranquillo LTE.
sections.statistical analyses: In general, numbers and percentages will be presented for binary variables. Number, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum will be presented for all continuous variables. Analysis of binary endpoints will be conducted using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel approach adjusting for stratification factor of FST. Large sample approximation will be used to test the superiority of ritlecitinib 50 mg QD or ritlecitinib 100 mg QD vs placebo (where applicable) at the stated time points and to form 95% CIs and calculate P values. For treatment comparison using continuous endpoints, the data will be analyzed using an analysis of covariance model, which will include treatment group, baseline value of the endpoint, FST, and age (where applicable) as covariates. The mean treatment difference, its 95% CI, and its P value will be obtained. Missing data will be considered as non-response for binary endpoints and imputed with worst observation carried forward for continuous endpoints. Safety data will be summarized descriptively and presented in tabular and/or graphical format. No comparative analyses will be performed on the non-randomized cohorts within Tranquillo LTE, Tranquillo 2 Part Ib, or Tranquillo 2 Part II.
sections.strengths: Overall, the Tranquillo program comprehensively explores ritlecitinib, a targeted systemic treatment, in a large and varied cohort of approximately 2050 patients with active and stable NSV spanning all FSTs and a broad range of affected percent body surface area over the course of up to 104 weeks. Collectively, these three studies provide insights into the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of ritlecitinib, both on the face and body, and after both short- and long-term treatment, in patients with NSV. Additionally, the inclusion of dose-up titration, dose-down titration, and randomized withdrawal arms in the study designs will provide valuable information on the effects of ritlecitinib dosage changes and the impact of treatment interruptions on patient responses to ritlecitinib.
sections.limitations: The Tranquillo program may be limited by the complexity of the comprehensive study design. To aid in understanding, where possible, published results will include graphics and plain language summaries so that physicians, caregivers, and patients can access and understand the information.
sections.ethics and dissemination: These studies are being conducted in accordance with the protocols and with the consensus ethical principles derived from international guidelines, including the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 and its later amendments and CIOMS International Ethical Guidelines; applicable International Council for Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines; and applicable regional laws and regulations, including privacy laws. The protocols, protocol amendments, and other relevant documents are reviewed and approved by the sponsor and submitted by the investigator for review and approval by the institutional review board/ethics committee before each study can be initiated. All participants or their legally authorized representative must provide written informed consent for their participation in the trial. The results of the trials described here will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal for publication.

title: The effect of concept mapping–based self-care education on quality of life in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a non-randomized quasi-experimental study
abstract: Objective In addition to pharmacological treatments, self-care education is crucial for managing chronic conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Concept mapping, a visual and learner-centered educational strategy, has shown potential in improving self-care engagement. However, evidence for its effectiveness in rheumatoid arthritis populations remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of concept map–based self-care education on quality of life in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Results Following the intervention, participants in the experimental group showed significantly better outcomes compared to the control group in overall quality of life (P < 0.001) and most domain-specific measures, including Activities, Movement, and Energy (P = 0.007); Mood/Emotions (P < 0.001); and Physical Contact (P = 0.015), with moderate to large effect sizes. However, no significant difference was observed in the Self-Care domain (P = 0.300). Within-group analyses revealed significant improvements in quality of life across all domains in the intervention group (all P < 0.05), whereas no changes were observed in the control group (all P > 0.05). Therefore, concept mapping, as a structured and visual educational strategy, may enhance patients’ understanding of complex self-care information and improve quality of life among individuals with rheumatoid arthritis. Trial registration : The protocol of this clinical trial has been registered in the Iranian Clinical Trial Registration Center (registration code: IRCT20230405057828N1). Registered 23 June 2023- registered while recruiting, https://www.irct.ir/ .

sections.introduction: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic inflammatory autoimmune disorder that primarily affects synovial joints and is clinically characterized by symmetrical polyarticular pain, swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, and fatigue [ 1 , 2 ]. Persistent synovitis, as the pathological hallmark of RA, leads to progressive cartilage destruction, bone erosion, and irreversible structural joint damage when inadequately managed [ 3 , 4 ]. Beyond joint involvement, RA is a multisystem disease with extra-articular manifestations such as rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, peripheral neuropathy, vasculitis, and hematologic abnormalities, all of which can substantially compromise overall health status and survival [ 5 , 6 ]. Globally, the prevalence of RA has been estimated at approximately 460 cases per 100,000 individuals between 1980 and 2019 [ 7 , 8 ]. In Iran, the incidence of RA is reported to affect 0.37% of the total population [ 9 ]. The chronic and progressive nature of RA, alongside its clinical burden and long-term functional consequences, including severe impairments in physical function, psychological well-being, and social participation, leads to substantial reductions in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) [ 10 – 13 ]. Therefore, the adoption of comprehensive management strategies, extending beyond pharmacological interventions, is critical to reduce disability and the long-term burden of the disease [ 14 ]. Among non-pharmacological approaches, self-care plays a pivotal role in the management of chronic diseases. Self-care encompasses individuals’ abilities to maintain health, prevent disease progression, and manage symptoms independently or in collaboration with healthcare professionals. Unlike conventional patient education, which primarily focuses on information delivery, self-care emphasizes active patient engagement. This involvement helps patients develop the confidence, autonomy, and position them as valuable contributors to their own care and decision-making processes [ 15 , 16 ]. Evidence from other chronic neurological and inflammatory conditions, such as multiple sclerosis, indicates that educational interventions focused on self-care can improve quality of life and psychological resilience [ 17 ]. To optimize the effectiveness of such interventions, they should be grounded in robust and innovative pedagogical frameworks, such as Ausubel’s theory of meaningful learning. According to this theory, meaningful learning occurs when new information is actively integrated with pre-existing cognitive structures, with prior knowledge serving as an anchor for the assimilation of new concepts. In this context, concept mapping represents an instructional strategy that operationalizes meaningful learning [ 18 , 19 ]. Concept mapping, originally developed by Novak in the 1980s, consists of graphical representations composed of nodes and connecting lines. Each node represents a concept, while the linking lines illustrate the relationships and propositions between concepts. A concept map may include multiple interconnected nodes and links organized in a hierarchical structure, in which more general and inclusive concepts are positioned at the top or center, and more specific concepts are arranged at lower levels. This structured organization facilitates the integration of prior knowledge with new information, thereby promoting meaningful learning, enhancing critical thinking and problem-solving skills, and supporting deeper knowledge assimilation [ 20 – 22 ]. Despite the profound multidimensional impact of RA on HRQoL, there is limited evidence on the integration of concept map–based self-care education into clinical practice for this population. The scarcity of rigorous interventional studies examining this instructional strategy represents a critical gap in nursing science, particularly regarding its potential to enhance the effectiveness of self-care education and improve quality of life outcomes. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of concept map–based self-care education on quality of life in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
sections.study design and setting: This study adopted a quasi-experimental design with intervention and control groups. The study was conducted at the rheumatology clinic of Imam Khomeini Hospital, affiliated with Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran, from September 2023 to December 2023 .
sections.study population and eligibility criteri: The study population consisted of all patients with a confirmed diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis who attended the rheumatology clinic of Imam Khomeini Hospital during the study period. Participants were eligible for inclusion if they were aged 18–60 years, possessed sufficient literacy to engage with the educational materials, had a confirmed diagnosis of RA by a licensed rheumatologist, were able to use CD-based educational resources, and provided voluntary informed consent to participate in the study. Participants were excluded if they had a diagnosis of other chronic medical conditions (e.g., cardiovascular disease, asthma, or cancer), had a documented psychiatric disorder, were unwilling to continue participation, or failed to attend the scheduled educational sessions.
sections.data collection instruments: Data were collected using two instruments: a demographic characteristics questionnaire and the Rheumatoid Arthritis Quality of Life (RAQoL) questionnaire.
sections.demographic characteristics questionnair: Participants’ demographic and clinical characteristics were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire, including age, sex, level of education, marital status, employment status, perceived economic status, duration of disease, frequency of hospitalization due to RA, and medications used.
sections.rheumatoid arthritis quality of life (ra: Quality of life was assessed using the RAQoL questionnaire, a validated disease-specific instrument comprising 30 dichotomous (yes/no) items. The RAQoL, originally developed by Jasani et al. [ 24 ], is designed to evaluate the impact of RA on multiple aspects of daily functioning. In this instrument, a response of “yes” indicates that a need or problem is present and is scored as 1, whereas a response of “no” indicates that the need is met and is scored as 0. Total scores range from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating poorer quality of life. The questionnaire encompasses four domains: activities, movement, and energy (10 items); self-care (8 items); mood and emotions (8 items); and physical contact (4 items). The validity and reliability of the RAQoL have been well documented. Zlatkovic-Svenda et al. [ 25 ] reported a correlation coefficient of 0.94, supporting its validity in patients with RA. The Persian version of the RAQoL Questionnaire has previously been translated and culturally adapted for the Iranian population with RA. Furthermore, its psychometric properties, including reliability and construct validity, have been rigorously confirmed [ 26 ]. In the present study, content validity was evaluated by a panel of 10 faculty members from the Tehran School of Nursing and Midwifery, and their feedback was incorporated into the final version of the instrument. Reliability was assessed using a test–retest approach in 15 patients with RA, with a 10-day interval between administrations. Internal consistency, assessed using Cronbach’s alpha, was 0.704, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.889, indicating acceptable internal consistency and strong temporal stability.
sections.intervention: All required institutional permissions and ethical approvals were obtained before the initiation of data collection. Participants were provided with a detailed explanation of the study objectives and procedures, and written informed consent was obtained in accordance with ethical guidelines. For the control group, baseline data (pretest) were collected before the intervention period. Participants then received routine education as part of standard clinical care during regular outpatient visits, delivered by physician assistants. This education primarily addressed immediate clinical concerns, such as symptom management and medication instructions, and was not delivered within a structured or comprehensive educational framework. In addition, patients received routine printed educational materials, including pamphlets and brochures related to RA. No scheduled or interactive educational sessions were conducted for the control group. One month after the pretest, post-intervention data were collected. Following completion of recruitment and data collection for the control group, enrollment of the intervention group commenced. After baseline assessment (pretest), participants in the intervention group received a self-care education programme based on concept mapping. The intervention was delivered in two individual, face-to-face sessions, each lasting 45–60 min, with a two-week interval between sessions. Individual delivery was chosen to facilitate active engagement, tailored explanations, and responsiveness to participants’ questions. Educational content was presented using a laptop and delivered in a step-by-step manner at an appropriate pace to support comprehension. All sessions were conducted in a quiet, pre-arranged setting to minimise distractions. Throughout the intervention, participants’ questions and concerns regarding their condition were addressed to promote effective learning. The first session (45 min) focused on disease awareness, clinical manifestations, diagnostic processes, and general corrective and therapeutic approaches. The second session (60 min) addressed a broader range of self-care topics, including nutrition, sleep and rest, physical activity and rehabilitation, the influence of weather on symptoms, use of hot and cold compresses, marriage and family life, pregnancy and breastfeeding, vaccination, travel considerations, anxiety and depression, and strategies for ongoing disease management and continuity of care (Table 1 ). Table 1 content of self-care training sessions for RA patients Session Duration Topic 1 45 min Understanding the disease, clinical manifestations, diagnosis of the disease, and various corrective and therapeutic methods 2 60 min Principles of nutrition, sleep and rest, exercise, rehabilitation, the effect of weather on the disease, the use of hot and cold compresses, marriage, pregnancy, breastfeeding, vaccination, travel, anxiety and depression and how to control and continuously care for the disease The educational programme consisted of 20 concept maps developed by the researcher using Mindomo software and organised in a hierarchical structure. Seven concept maps addressed disease recognition, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and therapeutic approaches, while 13 concept maps focused on self-care and lifestyle-related topics, including nutrition, rest, exercise, rehabilitation, environmental factors, psychosocial issues, and long-term disease management. The content and structure of the concept maps were reviewed by three faculty members from the School of Nursing and Midwifery with expertise in patient education and rheumatology nursing, and their feedback was incorporated to enhance clarity and content validity. At the conclusion of the two educational sessions, participants in the intervention group received the concept map-based educational materials in CD format. Post-intervention data for the intervention group were collected one month after completion of the final educational session. The extended interval in the intervention group was necessary to allow sufficient time for participants to engage with the educational materials and potentially translate acquired knowledge into practice before outcome assessment. During the follow-up period, participants were contacted weekly via scheduled telephone calls to encourage review of the educational materials, respond to questions, and support continued engagement. Brief questions were used to confirm participation and understanding. Participants were also encouraged to contact the researcher by telephone if additional questions or concerns arose. At the end of the study, the educational CD was provided to participants in the control group to ensure equitable access to the educational content, in accordance with ethical principles. Due to the nature of the educational intervention, blinding of participants and the researcher was not feasible. However, efforts were made to minimise potential bias through standardised data collection procedures and consistent follow-up across study groups.
sections.ethics consideration: All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations (Declaration of Helsinki). This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Tehran University of Medical Sciences (Ethics code: IR.TUMS.FNM.REC.1401.187). Participants were informed about the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, and the confidentiality of their personal information. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection.
sections.trial registration: The protocol of this clinical trial has been registered in the Iranian Clinical Trial Registration Center (registration code: IRCT20230405057828N1). Registered 23 June 2023- registered while recruiting, https://www.irct.ir/ .
sections.statistical analysis: Data were analysed using SPSS software (version 16.0). Both descriptive and inferential statistical methods were employed. Descriptive statistics included frequency distributions for categorical variables and mean and standard deviation for continuous variables. For inferential analyses, the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate, was used to assess baseline homogeneity of categorical variables between the control and intervention groups. Before conducting parametric analyses, the normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. The results indicated that quality-of-life total scores and domain-specific scores were approximately normally distributed in both groups at baseline and post-intervention (p > 0.05), supporting the use of parametric tests. Independent-samples t-tests were conducted to compare quality of life scores and their domain-specific dimensions between groups at baseline and post-intervention. Within-group changes over time were examined using paired-samples t-tests. In addition to inferential statistics, effect size (Cohen’s d) and their 95% confidence intervals were reported. For between- group comparisons, Cohen’s d was calculated using pooled standard deviations. For within-group comparisons, Cohen’s d for dependent samples (dz) was computed based on the paired t statistic. A significance level of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.
sections.results_1: In the intervention group, 45 participants were initially recruited. Of these, 35 participants (77.8%) completed both educational sessions and the post-intervention assessment, while 10 participants (22.2%) discontinued participation before completion of the educational sessions. In the control group, 37 participants were enrolled, of whom 35 (94.6%) completed the post-test; two participants (5.4%) withdrew during the study period. The reported reasons for withdrawal were personal and non–study-related, including time constraints, family obligations, transportation difficulties, and lack of availability to attend scheduled sessions. Notably, no withdrawals were attributed to dissatisfaction with the intervention, adverse effects, or disease-related complications. All participants who remained in the intervention group adhered fully to the intervention protocol, attended both scheduled educational sessions, participated in the planned weekly telephone follow-ups, and completed the post-intervention assessment (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Participant flow diagram The mean age of participants was comparable between groups, with 44.55 years in the intervention group and 44.74 years in the control group. Women constituted the majority of the sample in both groups (74.3% and 62.9%, respectively). In terms of marital status, 62.9% of participants in the intervention group and 54.3% in the control group were single. Regarding clinical characteristics, 28.6% of participants in each group reported a disease duration of 6 months to 2 years. Additionally, over half of the participants had no prior history of hospitalization (54.3% in the intervention group and 51.4% in the control group). Comparative analyses revealed no statistically significant differences between the intervention and control groups across demographic and clinical variables, indicating baseline homogeneity (Table 2 ).
