sections.introduction: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is among the most common types of cancer worldwide and is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths. Due to the absence of specific symptoms early stages, 85% of patients with HCC present were diagnosed at an advanced stage and distant metastases [ 1 , 2 ]. Despite the progress has been made in the molecular mechanism of pathogenesis and drug therapy, there is still challenging to deliver effective therapy due to tumor heterogeneity, metabolic reprogramming, tumor recurrence and drug resistance [ 3 , 4 ]. Therefore, it is necessary to explore the tumor microenvironment and identify more precise prognostic biomarkers for HCC patients. The recent discovery of lactylation, an epigenetic modification involving the addition of a lactyl group to lysine residues in chromatin, has expanded the understanding of the complex mechanisms regulating gene transcription [ 5 ]. This novel modification has been shown to directly stimulate gene expression. Research has confirmed two pathways for lysine lactylation. The first involves P300-catalyzed conversion of L-lactate into lactoyl-CoA, which then mediates lactylation. The second pathway involves methylglyoxal-derived lactoylglutathione (LGSH), which can mediate protein lactylation non-enzymatically, and LGSH can be further hydrolyzed by glyoxalase 2 (GLO2) into glutathione and D-lactate [ 6 ]. Recently, lactylation has emerged as an important event that modulates tumorigenesis [ 7 ], tumor metabolism [ 8 ], and tumor immune response. For example, research found that histone lactylation could drive the tumor progression., which could be reversed by activating the Hippo pathway [ 9 ]. Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α lactylation promoted angiogenesis and vasculogenic mimicry in prostate cancer [ 10 ]. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications represent the most prevalent type of RNA modifications, exerting significant influence on various aspects of RNA biology, including nuclear processing, translation efficiency, and mRNA stability [ 11 ]. These modifications play a crucial role in the regulation of gene expression and signal transduction [ 11 ]. Abnormalities in the m6A RNA modification machinery have been implicated in various diseases, particularly cancer, where they contribute to tumor progression by affecting cell proliferation, differentiation, migration, and apoptosis [ 12 ]. Recent findings suggest that lactylation and m6A modifications may interact and jointly regulate pathological processes. In the development of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), crosstalk between AECs and myofibroblasts via lactylation and m6A is thought to accelerated the progression of IPF [ 13 ]. Furthermore, METTL16, a recently discovered RNA m6A methyltransferase, lactylation at site K229 is induced by cuproptosis in development of gastric cancer [ 14 ]. In tumor immune microenvironment, lactate accumulated potently induced METTL3 upregulation via H3K18 lactylation, and the upregulated METTL3 mediated m6A modification, which is responsible for immunosuppressive capacity of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells [ 15 ]. Furthermore, M6A methylation modification has been reported to promote histone lactatation-driven tumor progression in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma [ 16 ]. Therefore, the crosstalk between lactylation and m6A modifications represents an emerging area of research with potential implications for our understanding of complex disease processes like tumor. Revealing the molecular mechanisms underlying two epigenetic modifications may uncover novel therapeutic targets. However, the crosstalk histone lactylation and m6A modification in the development of HCC is still unclear. With the rapid development of bioinformatics and the establishment of the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), genome, proteome, transcriptome, and metabolome are explored to the tumorigenesis mechanism and biomarkers for the prognosis and therapy of cancer [ 17 , 18 ]. To help understand the role of histone lactylation and m6A in HCC development, we analyzed the expression of lactylation-m6A related genes and constructed a prognostic signature for HCC patients in TCGA cohort. We further analyzed prognostic signature in tumor immune microenvironment and drug prediction. Our study may provide more data for the prognostic biomarkers and molecular mechanisms in HCC.
sections.data collection: The RNA-sequence data, somatic mutation data, copy number variation (CNV) data, and clinicopathological data pertaining to HCC patients were extracted from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA; https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/repository ). The clinicopathological information of HCC patients within the TCGA dataset was detailed in Supplementary Table (1) The lactylation-related genes were collected from previous studies [ 5 , 19 , 20 ], and a total of 332 lactylation-related genes were included and were presented in supplementary Table (2) An external validation dataset consisting of gene expression data for 231 HCC patients was acquired from The International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) ( https://docs.icgc-argo.org/docs/data-access/icgc-25k-data ). The normalization of gene expression data was executed using the Perl programming language ( http://www.perl.org/ ). Data analysis was performed with R software (version 4.3.1) and R Bioconductor packages.
sections.identification of correlation, different: Pearson correlation analysis was utilized to discern crosstalk genes between lactylation-relevant genes and a set of 23 m6A-linked genes, adopting rigorous selection criteria of correlation magnitude > 0.5 and statistical significance at P < 0.01. Lactylation modification-related DEGs were identified on basis of the following criteria: false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05 and a log2 fold change > 1. Subsequently, the univariate Cox analysis was performed to confirm the prognostic intersection genes (IGs) ( P < 0.05). A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was then assembled using the STRING online resource ( http://string-db.org/cgi/ ), with edges exhibiting an interaction score surpassing 0.2 deemed statistically significant and incorporated into the network representation.
sections.identification of hcc subtypes: HCC patients in TCGA dataset were divided into different subtypes through an unsupervised methodology by the ConsenSuClusterPlus R package. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify the ability of the clusters to discriminate between subtypes. The differences over survival rate were compared between subtypes by K-M analysis.
sections.enrichment analysis: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was used to analyze the remarkable enrichment pathways between high- and low- risk groups via the R package “clusterProfiler”, “org.Hs.eg.db”, and “enrichplot”. P < 0.05 was regarded as statistically enriched. For each group, we calculated the correlation between the expression values of all genes in each sample and the average expression profile of that group. The genes used here were based on the entire transcriptome sequencing data, encompassing all annotated genes across the whole genome.
sections.immune cell infiltration, tumor mutation: Calculation of the tumor mutation burden (TMB) was performed according to the equation: TMB = (total mutation/total covered bases) ×10 6 . A comparison of TMB levels between the high- and low-risk groups was undertaken using TCGA cohort data, with the “maftools” package facilitating the examination of mutation data in each risk category. To evaluate the association between risk score and tumor-infiltrating immune cells, seven algorithms – XCELL, TIMER, QUANTISEQ, MCPCOUNTER, EPIC, CIBERSORT-ABS, and CIBERSORT—were applied to calculate Spearman correlations. The ESTIMATE algorithm was utilized to determine the stromal score, immune score, and estimate score. Use the “ggplot2” R package to create an immune correlation Lollipop chart, which is used to display the correlations between multiple immune characteristics and core genes.
sections.the prediction of drug sensitivity: The R package “oncoPredict” was used to predict the drug sensitivity. Simply, the gene expression data from this dataset was used as the input. The drug screening data and fitting models provided by the GDSC (Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer) database were taken as the training benchmark. Through the algorithm, the predicted values of the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) for each sample to specific drugs were calculated in batches. The final results were used to evaluate the potential differences in drug sensitivity between patients classified as high- and low-risk.
sections.cell culture and transfection: The human HCC Huh-7 cell line was obtained from the China Center for Type Culture Collection (Wuhan, China). The cell line was cultured in medium DMEM (Hyclone, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Siji Green, China) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, USA) at 37℃ in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . The TCOF1 and HDAC1 siRNAs (The siRNA sequences: TCOF1: GACGCTTCATATAGATGTGTA; HDAC1: CGTTCTTAACTTTGAACCATA) were synthesized by Ruibo Biotechnology (Guangzhou, China). Those siRNA were transfected into Huh-7 cell using Lipofectamine™ 3000.
sections.wound healing and transwell assays: The wound healing assay was conducted to assess cell migratory capacity. Briefly, cells in 6-well plates, approaching approximately 90% fusion, were scratched with a sterile 10 µL pipette tip to create a central wound in each well. Following a 24-hour incubation, photographs were taken using an inverted microscope to determine gap in at least three randomly selected fields. The migration distance was determined by Image J software. Cell invasion ability was measured by Transwell assays using 24-well Transwell chambers with 8 μm polycarbonate membranes (Millipore, MA, USA) and was performed as previously described [ 21 ].
sections.statistical analysis: All data were explored and visualized with the use of the R 4.3.1 software. For each analysis, P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant, * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001.
sections.analysis of lactylation-m6a related gene: The flowchart of the study is shown in Fig. 1 . By correlation analysis, we identified 207 crosstalk genes between and lactylation and m6A, and the co-expression network was shown in Fig. 2 A. We identified the lactylation-related DEGs between normal and HCC tissues which included 125 upregulated genes and 1 downregulated gene (Fig. 2 B). Then, 87 intersection genes (IGs) were identified from 207 lactylation-m6A related genes and 126 DEGs (Fig. 2 C). To further explore the function of m6A-lactylation related genes in HCC, GO functional enrichment analysis based on IGs was implemented. The biological processes (BP) were involved in RNA export from nucleus, RNA localization, nucleic acid transport, RNA transport, and establishment of RNA localization (Fig. 2 D). The cellular components (CC) included chromosomal region, nuclear speck, chromosome, centromeric region, and condensed chromosome. The molecular functions (MF) included tubulin binding, chromatin DNA binding, and single-stranded RNA binding. The KEGG results indicated that the IGs were involved in the cell cycle, p53 signaling pathway, and drug metabolism (Fig. 2 E). According to Fig. 2 F, these intersection genes were mutated in 12.64% of samples, and PRKDC exhibited the highest mutation frequency (6%). Fig. 1 Flow chart of this study Fig. 2 Analysis of lactylation-m6A related genes and DEGs in HCC patients. A Co-expression network indicating the correlation between m6A and lactylation. B Heat map exhibiting lactylation-related DEGs between normal and HCC tissues. C Venn diagram showing the DEGs and lactylation-m6A genes. D Histogram of Gene Ontology enrichment. E KEGG analysis. F Mutational landscape of m6A-lactylation related DEGs
sections.identification of hcc subtypes based on: Univariate Cox regression analysis was employed to identify 67 prognostic IGs (Fig. 3 A). Then HCC patients in TCGA cohort were separated into two clusters according to the expression of prognostic IGs (Fig. 3 B, and Fig. S1 ), resulting in 293 cases assigned to cluster-1, and 50 cases of cluster-2. The PCA performed in all HCC samples revealed that there was little overlap between the two clusters (Fig. 3 C). Survival analysis demonstrated that patients in cluster-2 had a significantly decreased survival rate compared to those in cluster-1 (Fig. 3 D). A Sankey diagram was employed to illustrate the association between clusters and corresponding clinical traits (Fig. 3 E). The results show that in the cluster 2 subgroup, the proportion of males is high and the number of deaths is also large. Wihle the majority of the females are concentrated in cluster 1 and had a relatively favorable prognosis. In addition, infiltration indicated that there were differences in naive B cell, memory B cell, CD4 T cells M0/M1 macrophages and neutrophils between two clusters (Fig. 3 F). Fig. 3 Identification of HCC subtypes. A Forest plot of prognostic lactylation-m6A related DEGs. B Consensus clustering of 2 subtypes. C Principal component analysis based 2 clusters.Red: cluster1; Blue: cluster2. D K-M analysis between cluster1 and cluster2. E Sankey diagrams showing the interchangeable relationships among clusters, grade, gender and status. F Box plot for comparing the infiltration of immune cells between cluster1 and cluster2. * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01; *** P < 0.001; ns not significant
sections.constructing a lactylation and m6a relat: Then, the 67 prognosis-related IGs were subjected to Lasso regression analysis in TCGA cohort. According to the minimum criteria, a risk signature based on 7 prognosis-related IGs (G6PD, PRKDC, HDAC1, CCT5, KIF2C, TCOF1 and PPM1G) was to establish (Fig. 4 A, B). Risk score per patient = TCOF1*(0.013) + HDAC1*(0.003) + PPM1G*(0.013) + CCT5*(0.003) + KIF2C*(0.024) + PRKDC*(0.003) + G6PD*(0.005). Based on their risk scores relative to the median value, patients were classified into low- or high-risk groups. K-M survival curves demonstrated that patients in the high-risk group exhibited significantly lower survival rates compared to their low-risk counterparts (Fig. 4 C). The predictive ability of the model had been verified through the ROC value, which showed its success in predicting HCC patient survival in the TCGA cohort (1-year AUC = 0.791, 3-year AUC = 0.699, and 5-year AUC = 0.649) (Fig. 4 D). PCA and t-SNE analyses further verified this prognostic model separated the high-risk patients from low-risk group in TCGA cohort (Fig. 4 E, F). Risk survival status plots revealed a negative association between risk scores and patient survival, as higher scores correlated with shorter overall survival in TCGA cohort (Fig. 4 G, H). Furthermore, a heatmap highlighted the elevated expression of the risk genes in the high-risk group, implicating their role in the poorer prognosis observed in these patients (Fig. 4 I). Further analysis revealed that, regardless of age (Fig. S2A, B), tumor grade (Fig. S2C, D), gender (Fig. S2E-F), or stage (Fig. S2G, H), patients in the high-risk group consistently experienced more reductions in survival. These results collectively indicated that the risk model was a robust prognostic predictor and independent of key clinical and pathological factors. Fig. 4 Constructing a lactylation and m6A related prognostic model. A Identification of optimal parameters by Lasso Cox regression analysis based on the minimum criteria. B Distribution of coefficients. C K-M analysis between the high- and low-risk groups. P < 0.001. D Time-dependent ROC analysis for the 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS of the prognosis. E PCA and t-SNE ( F ) analysis of the TCGA cohort based on the risk score. Distribution of the risk scores ( G ), survival status ( H ), and expression ( I ) of the seven risk genes in the TCGA cohort Data from ICGC was utilized to verify the accuracy and generalizability of the risk signature. Firstly, patients in ICGC cohort were stratified into high- and low-risk groups using the same equation applied in TCGA analysis. Consistent with the TCGA findings, patients with high-risk score in ICGC cohort displayed significantly shorter survival time (Fig. S3A). According to PCA and t-SNE analysis, these 7 risk genes could be assigned to different risk groups of HCC patients in ICGC cohort (Fig. S3B, C). The distribution of the risk score, survival status of each patient and expression of these 7 risk genes were exhibited in Fig. S3D-F. To investigate the independence of the risk score as a predictor of HCC patient prognosis, univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were conducted for the TCGA and ICGC cohorts. As shown in Fig. S4A-B, the risk score was a statistically significant independent predictor of patient survival in TCGA cohort (for univariate Cox analysis, risk score, HR = 1.448, 95% CI   1.315–1.595, P < 0.001; for multivariate Cox analysis, HR = 1.405, 95% CI   1.258–1.568, P < 0.001). As similar with the results in TCGA cohort, the risk score was also proved to be an independent factor in ICGC cohort (Fig. S4C, D). In summary, these results demonstrated our risk signature might be an independent factor to predict the prognosis of HCC patients.
sections.the correlation of tmb and prognostic si: We investigated the copy number variation (CNV) in the seven risk genes across all HCC samples. As shown in Fig. 5 A, while KIF2C and HDAC1 showed a decrease in copy number, the remaining five risk genes all displayed increased copy numbers. It had been reported that TMB was a biomarker that indicated response to immunotherapy. Hence, we procured mutation data for HCC patients from the TCGA database and computed TMB values for each subject to explore the association between TMB and our prognostic signature. The findings revealed that the top 20 driver gene with frequency of alterations significantly differed between high- and low-risk groups (Fig. 5 B, C). Moreover, patients with high TMB values had a poorer prognosis compared to those with low TMB (Fig. 5 D). Importantly, HCC patients who had the high-TMB combined with a high-risk score patients had a worst prognosis (Fig. 5 E). These results indicated that the prognostic signature could reflect the genomic stability for HCC patients. Fig. 5 The correlation of TMB and prognostic signature. A Diagram of the copy number frequencies of prognostic model related genes. Waterfall diagram of the top 20 driver genes with the highest alteration in high ( B ) and low-risks groups ( C ). D K-M analysis of the high and low-TBM groups. P < 0.001. E Survival analysis of high/low TMB combined with high/low risks
sections.correlation analysis between the risk sc: To investigate the biological differences between the high- and low-risk groups, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was conducted on the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways for each group. The top ten enriched pathways in high-risk group were predominantly correlated with cell cycle, DNA replication, ECM receptor interaction, and intestinal immune network (Fig. 6 A). While, the low-risk group was highly enrichment in drug metabolism, fatty acid metabolism and other metabolic processes (Fig. 6 B). Furthermore, we observed a positive correlation between the risk score and immune cell type (specifically B cell, T cell CD4+, Th1, Th2 e.g.), highlighting the potential impact of the immune microenvironment on the risk stratification (Fig. 6 C). Indeed, the high-risk group displayed a higher immune score and a lower stromal score compared to the low-risk group (Fig. 6 D). Given the critical role of immune checkpoints in dictating responses to immunotherapy, we analyzed the expression of immune checkpoints related genes in high- and low-risk groups. Multiple costimulatory molecules, such as CD70, TNFRSF4/9/14, IFNG, IL-1B, IL-2RA, and HMGB1, were upregulated in high-risk group (Fig. 6 E). Some coinhibitory molecules, such as VEGFA, SLAMF7, CTLA4, IL-10, LAG3 and EDNRB were showed a higher in high-risk group (Fig. 6 F). These results proved that our risk score possibly predict the immunotherapy for HCC patients. Fig. 6 Correlation analysis between the risk score and tumor microenvironment. Enrichment analysis of GSEA pathways in high ( A ) and low-risk ( B ) groups. C The correlation between risk score and immune cell infiltration by various immunocytes analysis methods. D Analysis of the differences in tumor microenvironment score between high- and low-risk groups. E The expression of inhibitory immune checkpoints between high- and low-risk groups. F The expression of stimulatory immune checkpoints between high- and low-risk groups. * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01;*** P < 0.001
sections.prediction drug sensitivity: In consideration of the GSEA analysis showed that the low-risk genes were enriched in drug metabolism, we proceeded to compare drug sensitivity between the high- and low-risk groups by IC50. As showed in Fig. 7 , some drugs such as 5-fluorouracil, afatinib, crizotinib, cediranib, taselisib and stauroporine were more sensitive for patients in high-risk group. While entinostat, irinotecan, KRAS inhibitor, cisplatin, axitinib and topotecan were more sensitive to the treatment for patients in low-risk group. Those data suggested that the risk score may predict the response of patients to treatment with certain drugs. Fig. 7 Prediction drug sensitivity. The prediction of IC50 values in high- and low-risk groups for A 5-fluorouracil, B afatinib, C crizotinib, D cediranib, E taselisib, F stauroporine, G entinostat, H irinotecan, I KRAS inhibitor, J axitinib, K topotecan and L cisplatin
sections.the protein expression of risk genes: The protein levels of these 7 risk genes were explored in the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) database. As shown in Fig. S5A, the expression of TCOF1, HDAC1 and PRKDC was upregulated in HCC tissue than normal tissue. While, the expression of G6PD, CCT5, KIF2 and PPM1G were very low or no detected in HPA database. In addition, we found that the expression of PRKDC was no correlation with the prognosis of patients. Further analysis showed that TCOF1 (Fig. S5B) and HDAC1 (Fig. S5C) was positive with M0 macrophages, Tregs, and memory B cells, while negative with M1/M2 macrophages, neutrophils and monocytes.
sections.tcof1- and hdac1-silencing inhibited the: In order to further explore the role of TCOF1 and HDAC1 in HCC development, we used the siRNA to silence TCOF1 and HDAC1 in Huh-7 cell, respectively (Fig. 8 A). As shown in Fig. 8 B, cell invasion ability decreased significantly by silencing TCOF1 and HDAC1. Similarly, wound healing analysis also verified that silencing TCOF1 and HDAC1 inhibited the migration of Huh-7 cell (Fig. 8 C). Our results demonstrate that TCOF1 and HDAC1 influence migration and invasion of Huh-7 cell. Fig. 8 TCOF1- and HDAC1-silencing inhibited the cell migration and invasion. A The mRNA level of TCOF1 and HDAC1 were detected by RT-PCR after transfected with siRNA. B The invasion ability was measured by Transwell assay. C Wound healing analysis was used to explore the migration of Huh-7 cell. * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01;*** P < 0.001
sections.discussion: Lactate, an end-product of intracellular glycolysis, has evolved from being a metabolic waste product to a molecule with recognized significance in both physiological and pathological processes, particularly in the context of cancer. This paradigm shift was sparked by the discovery of the Warburg effect, which highlights the aberrant reliance of tumor cells on aerobic glycolysis for energy production, leading to excessive lactate accumulation [ 22 ]. Lactate has since been implicated in two core characteristics of cancer: immune evasion and metabolic reprogramming [ 23 ]. Recent studies have exhibited that lactate mediate protein modification, regulate genes expression in macrophages, somatic cells, and cancer cells by lysine lactylation [ 24 ]. As one of the most ubiquitous types of posttranscriptional modification, m6A is reported to involve in the development and progression of numerous diseases, including cancer. As two important modification methods, m6A and lactylation play crucial roles in the regulation of cellular functions, and recent research had discovered that there was a close interaction between them. For example, histone lactylation-regulated METTL3 promotes ferroptosis via m6A-modification in sepsis-associated lung injury [ 25 ]. It was reported that tumor-associated fibroblasts regulated m6a modifications and stability through lactate production, and influenced tumor progression [ 26 ]. Lactylation mediates serine metabolism and m6A methylation modification, participating in a new mechanism for HCC resistance to lenvatinib [ 27 ]. Therefore, further investigation into the roles of m6A and lactylation modification in the immune microenvironment, prognosis, and immunotherapy of HCC is of great significance. In our study, a prognostic model was formulated based on the lactylation-m6A related genes and HCC patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups. The K-M survival analysis revealed significantly a poor survival among high-risk patients relative to their low-risk group. Similar findings were replicated in the ICGC dataset. Notably, accumulating evidence underscores the predictive relevance of TMB, not only in the context of immunotherapy, but also when combined with chemotherapy [ 28 , 29 ]. We found that patients who had the high-TMB combined with a high-risk score had a poorer prognosis. The high-risk score in our study takes into account not only TMB but also other clinical and molecular characteristics. This means that even among patients with high TMB, those classified as high-risk may carry additional unfavorable prognostic factors that could mask the potential benefits associated with TMB. Furthermore, not all patients with high TMB received immunotherapy. Therefore, for those high-TMB patients who did not receive appropriate immunotherapy, their natural disease course may not have been influenced by TMB-related immune responses, potentially leading to poorer prognoses. At the same time, we also recognize that the limited sample size in this study may have led to insufficient statistical power in specific subgroup analyses, which could potentially affect the statistical significance and generalizability of the results. The characteristics of elevated immune score and decreased stromal score in the high-risk group present a dual nature in treatment. Although the absence of the extracellular barrier may enhance the accessibility of drugs, the nature of immune infiltration—dominated by inhibitory subpopulations driven by the lactate-m6A axis – indicates the presence of a “cold” functional state in a “hot” cellular environment. This implies that while these tumors are not excluded by fibrosis, they may exhibit intrinsic resistance to checkpoint blockade alone, necessitating combination strategies that target the underlying metabolic-epigenetic drivers of immunosuppression. We further investigated the protein expression of risk genes (G6PD, PRKDC, HDAC1, CCT5, KIF2C, TCOF1 and PPM1G) in HAP database. Consistent with the expression of RNA level, the protein expression of TCOF1, HDAC1 and PRKDC was upregulated in HCC tissue than normal tissue. While, the protein of G6PD, CCT5, KIF2 and PPM1G were very low or no detected in in HPA database which probably be due to post-translation modification or degradation of protein. K-M survival analysis showed the high expression of TCOF1 and HDAC1 was correlated with a shorter survival time, but PRKDC had no influence for patients’ survival. As a gene related to m6A, TCOF1 had been reported to be associated with the immune microenvironment of HCC [ 30 ]. Recent studies found that TCOF1 probably appears to be antitumorigenic or protumorigenic depending on the tumor type and conditions. One research reported that TCOF1 downregulation was observed in human T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) cells and TCOF1 haploinsufficiency promoted an increased incidence of T-ALL in mice [ 31 ]. Conversely, upregulation of TCOF1 is observed in triple-negative breast cancer [ 32 ], HCC [ 33 , 34 ] and correlates with a poor prognosis. Mechanically, TCOF1 regulates KRAS-activated genes, epithelial‐mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes, and promotes the expression ribosomal RNA production which is a hallmark of cancer [ 34 ]. Histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) is one of the classes I HDACs, and impacts physiology by not only directly regulating transcription via deacetylation of histones but also enzyme through activity direct deacetylation [ 35 ]. In T cell-mediated immune diseases, HDAC1 acted as the key regulator to acute and chronic adaptation to environment stimuli such as allergen, stress [ 36 , 37 ]. However, the regulatory function of HDAC1 on inflammatory signaling is paradoxical, as it can either stimulate or inhibit such responses, contingent upon the specific contextual cues or extracellular stimuli encountered [ 35 ]. Similarity, HDAC1 also have complex role in regulating cell proliferation, such as an acceleration for cancer cells [ 38 ] and an anti-proliferative effect for endothelial cells. HDAC1 was identified as the critical direct m6A target in bipotent progenitor [ 39 ]. Overexpression of HDAC1 was supposed to be associated with tumor progression and metastasis [ 40 , 41 ]. HDAC1 was also involved in drug resistance by regulating the genes expression [ 42 ]. Several HDAC inhibitors have exhibited promising results in the treatment for multiple carcinoma [ 43 ]. In our study, we identified that TCOF1 and HDAC1 were the key prognostic genes for HCC patients and more research is needed to further reveal the role of these two genes in HCC progression. However, there is still some limitations in our study. The first limitation is that protein lactylation is a novel field, more and more lactylation-related genes will be discovered in the future. Secondly, this study uses the oncoPredict computational prediction, which is based on a gene expression association model from public databases. The results are algorithmic inferences and have not yet been verified by experimental or clinical data. Thirdly, our in vitro functional experiments were primarily conducted using the Huh-7 cell and future studies employing a broader panel of HCC cell lines (e.g., HepG2, MHCC97H) and patient-derived organoids will be necessary to fully confirm the generalizability of these mechanisms. Finally, the complex interaction between HCC cells and the immune microenvironment in the context of lactation-m6A modification remains an area for further study.
sections.conclusion: In summary, our research might provide a novel perspective for forecasting the prognosis of HCC patients and uncovered the relationship between lactylation-related genes and HCC. Our results provided great potential for advancing research of lactylation and m6A in HCC.

title: Association between timing of surgery and postoperative outcomes in older adults with distal femur fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Introduction The association between surgical timing and clinical outcomes in older adults with distal femur fractures remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate whether earlier surgery is associated with improved outcomes in this population. Materials and methods In accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, two independent reviewers searched MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from inception to October 8, 2024. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality, and secondary outcomes included longer-term mortality and postoperative complications. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Results Of 6,101 records screened, 16 retrospective cohort studies comprising 31,213 patients met the inclusion criteria. Early surgery was not associated with reduced 30-day mortality (adjusted odds ratio [OR]: 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.56–1.05; low-certainty evidence) or with longer-term mortality at 90 days (crude OR: 0.91, 95% CI: 0.51–1.60), 180 days (crude OR: 0.46, 95% CI: 0.12–1.77), or 1 year (crude OR: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.34–1.09). Similar findings were observed for postoperative complications: cardiac complications (OR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.48–1.07), pulmonary complications (OR: 1.07, 95% CI: 0.77–1.47), and pulmonary embolism (OR: 1.14, 95% CI: 0.62–2.16). Heterogeneity across outcomes was low to moderate, and definitions of early surgery varied among studies. Overall, this meta-analysis did not demonstrate a clinically meaningful association between surgical timing and short-term clinical outcomes in older adults with distal femur fractures. Sensitivity analyses consistently suggested lower mortality with earlier surgery, likely reflecting stricter definitions of early surgery and improved control of time-related bias. Conclusions This meta-analysis did not demonstrate a clinically meaningful association between surgical timing and short-term clinical outcomes in older adults with distal femur fractures. Given the heterogeneity in definitions and study designs, high-quality prospective studies with standardized timing are warranted. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00402-026-06296-2.

sections.introduction_1: Distal femoral fractures represent a significant clinical challenge in aging societies, where optimizing management and improving outcomes are pressing priorities. Although they account for 3–7% of all femoral fractures and are relatively uncommon overall [ 1 ], in older adults they represent the second most frequent fragility fracture after hip fractures [ 2 ]. These injuries are challenging to manage due to their high mortality and complication rates, which are comparable to or even exceed those associated with hip fractures [ 1 , 3 – 5 ]. Early surgical intervention is recommended for hip fractures. A systematic review and meta-analysis (SRMA) demonstrated that timely surgery reduces both mortality and postoperative complications in this population [ 6 , 7 ]. In contrast, evidence regarding the impact of surgical timing on outcomes after distal femoral fractures is limited and inconclusive [ 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 – 13 ]. Some studies suggest that early surgery may increase morbidity and mortality, whereas others report no significant association [ 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 – 13 ]. Consequently, the optimal timing of surgery for distal femoral fractures has not been clearly established [ 1 ]. Notably, no SRMA has yet clarified the relationship between surgical timing and postoperative outcomes in this patient population. We aimed to examine the association between the timing of surgery and postoperative outcomes, including mortality and complications, in older adults with distal femoral fractures.
sections.study design: This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 14 ]. The study protocol was prospectively registered in a public repository (registration ID: mu5q8). The PRISMA flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1 , and the completed checklist is provided as Supplementary Table 1.
sections.search strategy: We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and EMBASE (Dialog) from database inception to October 8, 2024, and updated the search on December 14, 2025, without restrictions on publication language or year. We also searched for ongoing or unpublished studies using the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Platform (ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov. (Supplementary Tables 2–6). Additionally, we reviewed references of included articles and articles citing the included studies using CitationChaser ( https://estech.shinyapps.io/citationchaser/ ).
sections.eligibility criteria: Study design: We included studies that reported stratified outcomes for patients who underwent surgery for distal femur fractures, including cohort studies and case series. All types of publications were eligible, including published and unpublished articles, conference abstracts, and letters. We applied no restrictions on language, country, observation period, or publication year. Case reports and biomechanical studies were excluded. Participants/population: We included studies that recruited participants aged 60 years or older from any setting, such as the general population, research cohorts, or clinical populations, as most distal femur fractures in this age group result from osteoporotic fractures [ 3 , 11 – 13 ]. We included interventions such as open reduction and internal fixation, total knee arthroplasty (TKA), AO screws and K-wires, cannulated screws, and external fixation for distal femur fractures. Exposure: The main exposure was the timing of surgery after hospital admission. Eligible patients were classified into early or delayed surgery groups. Early surgery was defined as occurring within 2 days of admission, consistent with previous studies of distal femur and hip fractures [ 3 , 7 , 15 ]. We also included studies that defined early surgery as within 2 days of injury or did not specify whether timing was measured from admission or injury. Comparison: The control group consisted of patients who underwent surgery three or more days after admission for distal femur fractures.
sections.outcome of interest: The primary and secondary outcomes were selected and prioritized based on their clinical importance and in accordance with the consensus core outcome set for patients with hip fractures [ 16 , 17 ]. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality, defined as death occurring during the hospital stay or within 30 days after surgery, consistent with previous studies [ 6 , 18 – 20 ]. The secondary outcomes were: (1) 90-day, 180-day, and 1-year mortality; (2) pulmonary complications, as defined by the original authors [ 17 ]; (3) cardiac complications; (4) deep vein thrombosis (DVT); (5) pulmonary embolism (PE); and (6) additional surgery, defined as surgery or readmission related to the initial treatment [ 17 ].
sections.data screening and extraction: Two reviewers (SH and one of TT, TS, YI, or SN) screened titles and abstracts. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then reviewed. Other relevant studies were identified by manually searching the reference lists of included studies. Data were extracted by independent reviewers using a prepiloted data extraction form. We attempted to contact study authors to clarify information or request additional data as necessary. Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and if necessary, a third reviewer (NY, NS) acted as an arbiter. For effect measures, we extracted both univariable and multivariable estimates. For univariable analyses, we extracted the number of events and participants in each group. For multivariable analyses, odds ratios (ORs) were prioritized. When both hazard ratios (HRs) and ORs were reported, the measure most frequently used across studies was selected for the primary meta-analysis, and the alternative measure was used for sensitivity analyses.
sections.quality assessment: Two reviewers (SH and one of TT, TS, YI, or SN) assessed the quality of each included article using the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool [ 10 ]. When necessary, study authors were contacted. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved by discussion, and if consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer (NY or NS) arbitrated. For the QUIPS assessment, we defined the following confounders: age, sex, comorbidity, fracture type, and the type of surgery [ 3 , 11 , 12 , 21 ]. Studies adjusting for all these confounders were rated as having a low risk of bias in the confounding domain. Overall risk of bias was rated low if all QUIPS domains were low, moderate if one domain was moderate or high, and high if two or more domains were high.
sections.data synthesis: Binary outcomes, including mortality and postoperative complications, were summarized as ORs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Pooled ORs were calculated using the Mantel–Haenszel method with a random-effects model, and pooled HRs were calculated using the inverse variance method with a random-effects model. When both crude and adjusted ORs were reported, adjusted ORs were used for the primary synthesis. Meta-analyses were conducted separately for crude and adjusted estimates. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, with values ≥ 75% considered high. Forest plots were constructed to illustrate study outcomes, and sensitivity analyses were conducted for primary outcomes to assess robustness. Publication bias was not evaluated using funnel plots or Egger’s test because fewer than ten studies were available for each outcome. Statistical analyses were performed using RevMan version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark). A two-sided P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.subgroup analysis: To explore potential effect modifiers on the primary outcomes, subgroup analyses were prespecified according to: (1) sex (men versus women), (2) age (< 75 years versus ≥ 75 years), (3) history of comorbidities (present versus absent), (4) type of surgery (fracture fixation versus arthroplasty), and (5) presence of other implants such as TKA or total hip arthroplasty (present versus absent).
sections.sensitivity analysis: Sensitivity analyses were performed for the primary outcomes to evaluate the robustness against methodological decisions. For 30-day mortality, early surgery was redefined as within 24 h rather than 48 h. For 180-day mortality, time from admission was used instead of time from injury, and cases with uncertain timing were included. For 1-year mortality, both adjusted HRs based on time from injury and admission and crude ORs based on time from injury, admission, and uncertain cases were analyzed. Furthermore, to explore the impact of clinical heterogeneity related to surgical procedures, we conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding studies involving arthroplasty for the crude ORs of 90-day and 1-year mortality. We also planned sensitivity analyses for operative time and blood loss, if sufficient data were available. Across all analyses, we examined whether the direction and consistency of the associations were maintained compared with the main analysis.
sections.summary of findings table: We created a Summary of Findings table for 30-day mortality, pulmonary complications, cardiac complications, and pulmonary embolism. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach [ 22 ]. This approach considered eight domains influencing certainty, including factors that may reduce certainty (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias) and factors that may increase certainty (large effect, dose–response, and plausible confounding). Certainty was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low. One reviewer (SH) performed the assessment, which was verified by another (NY). Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, if needed, adjudication by a third reviewer (NS). Reasons for downgrading were reported in the Summary of Findings table. The median event rate in the comparison group across included studies was used as the baseline risk.
sections.difference between protocol and review: Exposure was initially defined only as time from admission; however, in the review, it was broadened to include time from injury and cases with unclear timing. Although only 1-year mortality was prespecified as a secondary outcome, 90-day and 180-day mortality were additionally analyzed. The meta-analysis was initially planned to combine crude and adjusted estimates; however, these were analyzed separately in the final review.
sections.study selection and characteristics: After screening 6,280 records, we included 16 studies (31,213 patients) in the final analysis (Fig. 1 ). Of 30 reports sought for retrieval, 14 were excluded after full-text review because of wrong design ( n = 5), wrong population ( n = 7), or wrong intervention ( n = 2); details of these studies and reasons for exclusion are provided in Supplementary Table 7. Fig. 1 Preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis (PRISMA) 2020 flow diagram illustrating the study selection process. By contacting study authors, we obtained unpublished data from four studies. The included studies were conducted in multiple regions, with the majority originating from the United States and the majority being multicenter cohorts (Table 1 ; Supplementary Table 8). sections.secondary outcomes: For 90-day, 180-day, and 1-year mortality, early surgery was not significantly associated with lower mortality (90-day: 3 studies, 536 patients, crude OR: 0.91, 95% CI: 0.51–1.60, I² = 9%; 180-day: 2 studies, 354 participants, crude OR: 0.46, 95% CI: 0.12–1.77, I² = 55%; 1-year: 3 studies, 351 patients, crude OR: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.34–1.09, I² = 0%, Fig. 2 B–D). Low-certainty evidence suggested that early surgery may result in little to no difference in cardiac complications (2 studies, 7,408 patients: OR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.48–1.07; I² = 5%, Fig. 3 A). Very low-certainty evidence indicated that the effect of early surgery on pulmonary complications (4 studies, 7,641 patients: OR: 1.07, 95% CI: 0.77–1.47; I² = 0%, Fig. 3 B) and pulmonary embolisms (2 studies, 7,335 patients: OR: 1.14, 95% CI: 0.62–2.16; I² = 0%, Fig. 3 C) remained highly uncertain. No significant differences were observed for cardiac complications (low-certainty evidence), pulmonary complications (very low-certainty evidence), or pulmonary embolism (low-certainty evidence). Early surgery was not significantly associated with reduced rates of DVT (3 studies, 7,283 patients, crude OR: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.54–1.04, I² = 0%, Fig. 3 D) and additional surgery (3 studies, 4,635 patients, crude OR: 0.98, 95% CI: 0.57–1.67, I² = 0%, Fig. 3 E). sections.discussion: Our meta-analysis of 16 studies found that the pooled evidence was insufficient to determine whether early surgery reduces mortality in older adults with distal femur fractures. The certainty of the evidence regarding surgical timing in this population was low. No clear benefit was observed for complications, with certainty ratings ranging from low to very low. Therefore, the effect of surgical timing on clinical outcomes remains uncertain. Early surgery in older adults with distal femur fractures was associated with little or no difference in 30-day mortality. Evidence from comparable hip-fracture cohorts and current guidelines supports surgery within 24–48 h [ 6 , 7 ]. In our analysis of 29,309 patients, earlier surgery was not significantly associated with reduced mortality (adjusted OR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.56–1.05), likely reflecting limited statistical power, residual confounding, or clinical heterogeneity rather than a definitive absence of effect. Sensitivity analyses also favored early surgery, likely reflecting the use of stricter timing definitions and analytic strategies intended to reduce time-related bias. Overall, because the evidence was of low certainty and the primary analysis was nonsignificant, we cannot make a strong recommendation. However, given consistent findings from sensitivity analyses, a cautious, conditional suggestion to operate within 48 h of admission appears reasonable when feasible. Our SRMA found no significant association between early surgery and an overall reduction in complications among older adults with distal femur fractures. This result aligns with several previous studies that also failed to demonstrate a clear benefit of earlier intervention in reducing postoperative complications [ 2 , 3 , 10 ]. Several factors may explain these findings as follows: (1) heterogeneity in fracture type and surgical technique [ 2 , 15 ]; (2) variability in definitions and assessments of complications [ 4 , 10 ]; (3) differences in patient comorbidities and perioperative optimization [ 2 , 9 , 12 , 13 ]; and (4) attenuation of any potential mortality benefit by temporary external stabilization, which allows pain control and upright positioning [ 23 ]. In contrast, some evidence suggests that early surgery may reduce specific complications, such as urinary tract infections or acute coronary syndromes [ 2 , 4 ]. Taken together, these considerations indicate that postoperative complications are influenced by multiple interacting factors, and surgical timing alone is unlikely to account for their occurrence. The primary strength of this study is that it is the first SRMA to quantify the effect of early surgery on mortality and complications in older adults with distal femur fractures. Another strength is our adherence to transparent reporting and rigorous methodology by following PRISMA guidelines, the Cochrane Handbook, and GRADE recommendations. We also contacted original authors and obtained unpublished data, including separate results where available. As a clinical implication, we conditionally recommend targeting surgery within 48 h of admission once the patient is medically optimized. Previous studies have reported that earlier surgery is associated with shorter hospital stays and lower healthcare costs, and in some analyses with reduced mortality [ 3 , 4 , 24 ]. However, evidence also indicates that surgery should proceed only after comprehensive preoperative assessment to ensure patient safety [ 2 , 25 ]. Although our analysis found the low-certainty evidence and no clear mortality benefit, these findings support medically optimized early surgery—ideally within 48 h—as a clinically and economically meaningful strategy. Our study has several limitations. First, the number of patients included was small, resulting in wide CIs and reduced statistical precision. Given the rarity of distal femur fractures [ 3 ], larger, multicenter prospective studies are needed to strengthen the evidence base. Second, all included studies were retrospective cohort studies, making them prone to selection bias and information bias. Third, although some studies reported adjusted estimates [ 4 , 8 ], many relied on crude ORs. Several studies did not adequately control for key confounders, such as comorbidities, fracture type, and surgical techniques, highlighting the need for future investigations with rigorous adjustment for confounding. Additionally, the inclusion of different surgical procedures may have contributed to clinical heterogeneity. Because procedure-specific outcomes were rarely reported, we were only able to assess this issue by excluding studies involving arthroplasty in sensitivity analyses for crude 90-day and 1-year mortality. Excluding arthroplasty increased heterogeneity and widened the CIs, resulting in imprecise estimates. Fourth, our findings were not validated in other settings or populations. Reports were concentrated in a small number of countries—primarily the United States, with limited data from Japan, parts of Europe, and China—which may limit generalizability. Fifth, definitions of early surgery varied across studies, some measured timing from admission, whereas others used time from injury, and the time zero for follow-up was not aligned. These issues likely introduced exposure misclassification and immortal time bias, potentially distorting effect estimates. Sixth, heterogeneous outcome definitions and incomplete or inconsistently timed reporting of early postoperative and preoperative complications limited cross-study comparability and may have biased between-study comparisons. Finally, we did not assess outcomes such as healthcare costs, functional recovery, or quality of life. Although our review focused on mortality and major complications, future research should incorporate these broader clinical and economic outcomes. Addressing these limitations will be crucial to generating high-quality evidence that informs clinical practice and guideline development. In conclusion, our findings suggest that the effect of early surgery for distal femur fractures in older adults remains uncertain due to low-certainty evidence. Notably, when more stringent timing definitions and strategies to reduce time-related bias were used, sensitivity analyses indicated a potential benefit of earlier surgery; however, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the observational character of the data. High-quality prospective studies are needed to clarify whether surgical timing improves clinical outcomes. These findings support ongoing efforts to clarify the role of early surgery in older adults with distal femur fractures, better understand processes of care that may influence postoperative outcomes, and confirm these findings through further high-quality research.

title: Ramucirumab induces apoptosis in Caco-2 cells via mitochondrial impairment and caspase activation
abstract: Ramucirumab, a monoclonal antibody that targets vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 (VEGFR-2), is primarily known for its ability to inhibit angiogenesis in a variety of cancer types. Its direct cytotoxic mechanisms in colorectal cancer cells, especially those related to mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-mediated apoptosis, are inadequately elucidated. This work aims to examine the involvement of mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and caspase activation in mediating ramucirumab induced cytotoxicity in Caco-2 cells. MTT (3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazolyl-2)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) tests were used to measure cell viability and cytotoxicity, respectively by exposing Caco-2 cells to ramucirumab for 24 h. Flow cytometry was used to analyze apoptosis and cell cycle distribution. Hoechst 33342, rhodamine 123 and carboxy-H 2 DCFDA staining was used to examine nuclear condensation, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and intracellular ROS, respectively. Additionally, the expression of the apoptotic markers caspase-3 and caspase-7, and levels of VEGF was quantified. Ramucirumab enhanced the release of LDH, and significantly ( p < 0.05) decreased cell viability with increasing concentration and IC 50 value was estimated as 780 µg/ ml. A significant ( p < 0.05) increase in the apoptotic cell population and cell cycle arrest primarily at the S-phase was observed. Nuclear condensation and fragmentation were observed and mitochondrial membrane potential was found to be decreased, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction. Additionally, oxidative stress (ROS) and VEGF was elevated and cleaved caspase-3 and caspase-7 were significantly upregulated, indicating caspase-mediated apoptosis. In conclusion, by causing cell cycle arrest and inducing apoptosis via mitochondrial malfunction and caspase pathway activation, ramucirumab demonstrates anti-cancer action against Caco-2 cells. These findings provide new perspectives on ramucirumab's wider anti-tumor potential beyond angiogenesis inhibition.

sections.introduction: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is still a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide and it is the third most common type of cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death in 2020. Due to resistance to conventional treatments, the development of novel treatment strategies are urgently desired (Ferlay et al. 2020 ; Sung et al. 2021 ). A significant contemporary strategy for treating colorectal cancer involves the development of drugs that target the angiogenesis pathway to inhibit the proliferation and spread of cancer cells, such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (Muro et al. 2020 ; Hansen, et al. 2021 ). Compensatory resistance mechanisms can restrict the efficacy of anti-angiogenic treatments that target VEGF signaling, such as bevacizumab, despite improved results (Cremolini et al. 2020 ). Ramucirumab, a monoclonal antibody against VEGF receptor-2 (VEGFR-2), is approved for advanced gastric and non-small cell lung cancers and many other types of cancer (Goel et al. 2016 ; Debeuckelaere, et al. 2019 ; Refolo et al. 2020 ). Despite lacking approval for colorectal cancer, numerous preclinical and experimental research have investigated its potential anti-tumor properties in colorectal cancer models, especially on angiogenesis inhibition and tumor development (Tabernero et al. 2015 ). However, its direct effects on colorectal cancer cells remain unclear. In contrast to bevacizumab's neutralization of VEGF ligands, ramucirumab's suppression of VEGFR-2 may disrupt both angiogenic and tumor-intrinsic survival pathways, offering a double therapeutic advantage (Spratlin et al. 2010 ). Normal cells have a balance between proangiogenic and anti-angiogenic factors; if this balance is disrupted for any reason, cancer develops (Colombo and Porretto 2023 ; Jain 2005 ). A recent study found that VEGFR-2 is expressed on both endothelial and epithelial cancer cells, where it initiates pro-survival signaling cascades such as PI3K/AKT and ERK (Wei et al. 2019 ). Inhibition of these pathways may result in apoptosis by generating mitochondrial dysfunction, which is characterized by cytochrome c release, caspase activation, and loss of membrane potential (ΔΨm) (Green and Kroemer 2004 ). Furthermore, the accumulation of ROS, a known consequence of disrupted growth factor signaling that can lead to DNA damage and apoptotic cell death, may exacerbate oxidative stress (Trachootham et al. 2009 ). Although ramucirumab's anti-angiogenic properties are well established, its capacity to directly cause mitochondrial-mediated apoptosis and ROS-dependent cytotoxicity in colorectal cancer cells has not been fully investigated. Recent data indicates that mitochondrial integrity and oxidative stress are pivotal in modulating cancer cell survival and apoptosis in colorectal cancer (Wu et al. 2024 ). Therefore, the present work was aimed to examine whether ramucirumab promotes apoptosis in Caco-2 cells via mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and caspase-dependent mechanisms, revealing new anti-tumor mechanisms beyond angiogenesis inhibition. The direct anticancer effects of ramucirumab were evaluated in this study using Caco-2 cells, a reliable model for colorectal cancer. By combining viability (MTT), cytotoxicity (LDH), and apoptosis assays (flow cytometry, caspase-3/7 activation), we demonstrated that ramucirumab suppresses proliferation and induces apoptotic cell death. As shown by Hoechst 33324 staining, we mechanistically link these effects to nuclear fragmentation, ROS overproduction, and mitochondrial depolarization. Our findings indicate that ramucirumab may have supplementary cellular effects beyond angiogenesis suppression in an in vitro colorectal cancer cell model; nevertheless, these results are confined to a single cell line and necessitate further validation in clinical samples and in vivo systems.
sections.cell culture: The colon carcinoma cells Caco-2, obtained from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC; Manassas, VA, USA). The cells were cultured in a cell culture minimum essential medium (MEM)/DMEM supplemented with 1% penicillin/streptomycin and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37 o C with a supply of 5% CO 2 . Cells grown as adherent monolayers and exponentially growing cells harvested by trypsinization. The cell viability was assessed using trypan blue staining and quantified using a Bio Rad TC20 automated cell counter. Cells were cultured in 96-well plates, 6-well plates, or flasks based on experimental protocols. The proliferating cells were rinsed with PBS and subjected to trypsinization. The harvested cells were centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C, thereafter diluted with medium to a density of 1 × 10 5 cells/ml and utilized in the tests.
sections.cell viability assessment using mtt assa: The MTT assay was utilized to investigate the cytotoxicity of ramucirumab against Caco-2 cells as described by Mosmann, ( 1983 ) using a commercial assay kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). Caco-2 cells were cultured in 96-well plates (70–80% confluence) and subjected to two-fold successive dilutions (62–2000 µg/mL) of ramucirumab (obtained from Illy-Lilly Co. Indianapolis, USA), for 24 h, alongside an untreated control. Then, the MTT solution (5 mg/mL) was added to each well and further incubated for 3- 4 h. The resultant formazan crystals were solubilized in DMSO, and absorbance was quantified at 550 nm utilizing a microplate reader (BioTek®, Winooski, VA, USA). The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) was ascertained using concentration–response analysis of cell viability data derived from the MTT experiment. Absorbance measurements were recorded for each concentration of ramucirumab, and the mean values from independent experiments were computed and shown as percentage cell viability in relation to untreated control cells. A concentration–response curve was created by graphing percentage cell viability versus the drug concentration. The IC 50 value was determined as the concentration that results in a 50% decrease in cell viability relative to the control group.
sections.lactate dehydrogenase (ldh) activity: The LDH leakage out of Caco-2 cells was assessed as described previously (Decker and Lohmann-Matthes 1988 ), using a commercial kit (Abcam®, Cambridge, UK). Cells were grown at a density of 1 × 10 4 cells per well in 96-well plates and exposed to specified concentrations (62–2000 µg/mL) of ramucirumab for 24 h. After centrifuging the 96-well plate, 100 µl of supernatant was transferred into fresh 96- well plate, and then the LDH reaction mixture was added to each well in accordance with the manufacturer's guidelines. Absorbance was quantified at 450 nm, and LDH release (%) was determined in relation to the control.
sections.detection of cytomorphological changes: The Caco-2 cells were seeded at a confluence of 70% in a 6- well plate and incubated for overnight. Then the cells were treated with the selected concentrations (125, 250 and 500 µg/ml) of ramucirumab for 24 h at 37 °C. The cells were examined under an inverted microscope (Olympus IX51, Tokyo, Japan) fitted with digital camera, the cytomorphological alterations were compared with those cells in control group.
sections.measurement of vegf in cell culture medi: Highly sensitive Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay kit (Molequle-On, New Zealand) utilized for in vitro quantitative assessment of human VEGF in the culture media of ramucirumab treated Caco-2 and control cells (Rodriguez et al. 1998 ). All reagents and working standards are prepared in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. We calculated the quantity of microwell strips necessary for testing based on the desired sample count and the number of wells needed for blanks and standards. 100 μl of the standard is introduced into the specified well, followed by the addition of samples to each well corresponding to their respective numbers, and then incubated for 90 min at 37 °C with agitation. Each well is aspirated and washed, and the process is repeated three times for a total of four washes. By filling each well with wash solution (350 μl) using a multichannel pipette and then completely removing the liquid at each step. After the last wash, any remaining wash solution is removed by aspiration or filtration and the plate is inverted and wiped with a clean paper towel. Finally, 100 μl of biotin-conjugated anti-VEGF antibody working solution added to each well, and incubated for 60 min at 37 °C with shaking. This step was repeated for washing and 100 μl of Streptavidin-HRP working solution was added to each well, and incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. Finally, after washing step, 100 μl of substrate solution was added to each well and incubate for 15 min at 37 °C in the dark. 50 μl of Stop solution was added to each well. The plate was gently tapped to ensure complete mixing. The absorbance was read at wavelength of 450 nm using a Synergy microplate reader (BioTek®, Winooski, VA, USA) and then, the VEGF percentages were calculated.
sections.assessment of intracellular reactive oxy: The intracellular ROS generated in Caco-2 cells were assayed as previously reported (Wang and Joseph 1999 ), utilizing the cell-permeable fluorescent probe 2′,7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (H₂DCFDA), by using a commercial ROS Detection Kit (Molecular Probes, USA). Cells were cultured in 96-well black-bottom plates and subjected to specified concentrations (125, 250, and 500 µg/mL) of ramucirumab for 24 h. Cells were subsequently incubated with 25 µM carboxy-H₂DCFDA for 20 min at 37 °C in the absence of light. Following PBS washing, fluorescence intensity was measured utilizing a microplate reader (excitation: 485 nm; emission: 528 nm). Intracellular ROS levels were quantified via endpoint fluorescence analysis subsequent to carboxy-H2DCFDA labeling. Fluorescence intensity levels were standardized against untreated control cells designated as 100%, and utilized for comparative evaluation of oxidative stress among experimental groups.
sections.activity assay of caspase 3 and caspase: Caspase-3/7 activities in the Caco-2 cells were measured following the earlier reported method by Adamova et al. ( 2014 ), with Caspase-Glo 3/7 Assay Kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Cells were cultured in 96-well plates (1 × 10 4 cells/well) and exposed to the specified concentrations of ramucirumab for 24 h. Subsequent to treatment, caspase reagent was introduced and incubated at ambient temperature for one hour. Luminescence was quantified with a microplate reader and reported relative to the control group.
sections.detection of apoptosis using annexin v-f: To investigate early apoptosis, late apoptosis and necrosis induced by ramucirumab by flow cytometry, a commercial kit (FITC Annexin V Apoptosis Detection Kit, BD Pharmingen™, USA) was used following the protocol provided (Rieger et al. 2011 ). The Caco-2 cells were seeded and then treated with the various concentrations of ramucirumab including untreated control, as mentioned above for 24 h. The cells were incubated with annexin V- FITC/PI for 20 min and incubated in the dark. After that, the cells were analyzed on a flow cytometer (Cytomics FC500, Beckman Coulter, USA), with a total of 10,000 events were recorded for each sample, and the data were analyzed using CXP software (version 2.3). Flow cytometric analysis was conducted via a sequential gating technique. Cellular debris was initially eliminated using forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) criteria. Doublets were eliminated by FSC-A versus FSC-H gating to ensure the analysis of single-cell populations. The gated population was subsequently examined for Annexin V–FITC and PI fluorescence. The dot plot analysis was categorized into four quadrants according to fluorescence signals: Annexin V −/PI − denotes viable cells, Annexin V +/PI − indicates early apoptotic cells, Annexin V +/PI + signifies late apoptotic cells, and Annexin V −/PI + represents primary necrotic cells.
sections.cell cycle distribution analysis by flow: The cell cycle analysis was performed as described previously (Darzynkiewicz et al. 2017 ), using a commercial assay kit (BioVision, USA) and executed according to the instructions provided by the manufacturing company. Caco-2 cells were cultured on 6-well plates and exposed to ramucirumab at concentrations of 125, 250, and 500 µg/mL for 24 h. Then, the cells were trypsinized and fixed with chilled ethanol (70%) drop by drop with vortexing and kept for 1 h at 4 °C. After that the cells were stained with a working mixture of propidium iodide (PI) for 30 min in the dark condition. Finally, the cells were analyzed by flow cytometer (Cytomics FC500, Beckman Coulter, USA) with a total of 10.000 events observed for each sample.
sections.analysis of nuclear morphology by hoechs: The nuclear morphological alterations in Caco-2 cells that underwent apoptosis were probed by Hoechst 33342 staining method (Crowley et al. 2016 ). The cells were plated on coverslip-loaded on a six-well plate overnight. Then, the cells were treated with the different concentrations of ramucirumab (125, 250 and 500 µg/ml) for 24 h. After fixing with formaldehyde, the cells were labeled with Hoechst 33342 stain for 10 min. Subsequently, the cells were washed with PBS, and then the nuclear morphology alterations were examined under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX41, Tokyo, Japan), equipped with a digital camera and suitable filter, at an excitation wavelength of 346 nm and emission wavelength of 497 nm. Nuclei were specifically assessed for chromatin condensation, nuclear fragmentation, and the development of apoptotic bodies. Nuclei that display homogeneous and diffused light blue color represent viable cells, while nuclei that display bright blue color nucleus with condensed and fragmented nuclei represent apoptosis. For the quantitative analysis of nuclear staining, the Caco-2 cells were grown in black-bottomed 96 well plate and then assayed as mentioned above. The fluorescence intensity signal was measured using the microplate reader (BioTek®, Winooski, VA, USA) at 346 nm for excitation and 497 nm for emission and compared with untreated cells which was set as 100%.
sections.measurement of mitochondrial membrane po: The mitochondrial membrane potential in Caco-2 cells was measured (Scaduto and Grotyohann 1999 ), using Rhodamine 123 probe (Molecular Probes, OR, USA). The cells were seeded on cover slip- loaded 6 well plate and then exposed the selected concentrations of ramucirumab (125, 250 and 500 µg/ml) and incubated for 24 h. The harvested cells were stained with a working solution of Rhodamine 123 for 10 min in the dark. After that, the cells were washed with 1X PBS and then observed under fluorescence microscope (Olympus BX41, Tokyo, Japan) fitted with suitable filter and digital camera. Correspondingly, in the quantitative estimation the cells were grown into black bottomed 96 well plate and then processed as aforementioned. The quantification of the fluorescence intensity was measured in a plate reader (BioTek®, Winooski, VA, USA) at excitation wavelength of 507 nm and emission wavelength of 529 nm, and compared to the control which was assumed to be 100%.
sections.statistical analysis: All experiments were conducted independently in triplicate. Each experiment consisted of three to six replicates. IC 50 values were derived from dose–response curves via nonlinear regression analysis of normalized cell viability data acquired from the MTT experiment. Nonlinear regression fitting was conducted using GraphPad Prism software (version 10.4.2) utilizing the dose–response inhibition model with varied slope values. Quantitative data were evaluated utilizing one-way ANOVA, followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparison post hoc test (GraphPad Prism software, 10.4.2). Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation, with significance determined at p < 0.05.
sections.cell viability by mtt assay: Caco-2 cells were exposed to six different concentrations of ramucirumab ranging from 62 – 2000 µg/ml (two - fold dilutions) for 24 h. The results of cell viability evaluation using MTT assay were shown in Fig. 1 . A general trend of decreasing cell viability with increasing concentrations of ramucirumab was observed (14 – 68%), but slight variability at intermediate concentrations was noted. The proliferation of Caco-2 cells was reduced to 14% in the lowest concentration of 62 µg/ml while in the highest concentration of 2000 µg/ml, the viability was decreased to 68%. The IC 50 value was estimated as 780 µg/ml under the present experimental conditions. Fig. 1 Cytotoxicity of ramucirumab evaluated by MTT assay on Caco-2 cells treated in different concentrations as indicated for 24 h. Data were presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments. Significant at * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.0001, compared with controls ( n = 6)
sections.lactate dehydrogenase (ldh) leakage assa: The induction of membrane damage in Caco-2 cells leading to release of LDH in the culture medium was evaluated by LDH leakage assay. Caco2 cells were treated with twofold dilutions of six different concentrations of ramucirumab (62 – 2000 µg/ml) for 24 h. The results of LDH assay were presented in the Fig. 2 , in which highest concentrations (1000 and 2000 µg/ml) showed a significant (p < 0.05) release of LDH in a concentration dependent manner, while the lower concentrations were insignificant. The highest percentage of LDH release of 64% were recorded in the highest concentration used (2000 µg/ml) when compared to untreated controls. However, in the lowest concentrations (62 µg/ml) the increase in LDH release was only 5% which was found to be not significant. Fig. 2 Cytotoxicity in Caco-2 cells measured by LDH release assay after 24 h post treatments with different concentrations of ramucirumab. Data were presented as mean ± SD from three independent experiments. Significant at * p < 0.05 and ** p < 0.001, compared with untreated control ( n = 6)
sections.analysis of cytomorphological changes: The cytomorphological alterations Caco-2 cells were observed under inverted microscope and representative images were presented in Fig. 3 . The cells were exposed to three sub-lethal concentrations of ramucirumab (125, 250 and 500 µg/ml) for 24 h. The untreated control cells (Fig. 3 A) appeared to have a normal cell morphology firmly attached to the surface. In contrast, treatment with ramucirumab revealed explicit cytomorphological changes (Fig. 3 B, C, and D). These alterations mainly included cell shrinkage, changes in the cell architecture, cell detachment appeared as rounded cells, and a decline in cell density. Many cells found to be loosely attached to the surface. Fig. 3 Cytomorphological changes observed in the Caco-2 cells post 24 h treatment of ramucirumab and observed under Phase contrast inverted microscope. A - Control, B - 125 µg/ml, C - 250 µg/ml, and D - 500 µg/ml. Magnification 100X. ( n = 3)
sections.detection of vegf in cell culture medium: The levels of VEGF in the cell culture medium after exposing Caco-2 cells to ramucirumab for 24 h was measured by sandwich ELISA assay. As depicted in the Fig. 4 , quantification of VEGF in caco2 cells revealed a significant ( p < 0.05) increase when compared to the control untreated cells which was calculated as 245 pg/ml. In the lowest concentrations of 125 µg/ml, it was increased to 254 pg/ml which was not significant. In contrast, in 250 and 500 µg/ml concentrations of ramucirumab, VEGF was increased to 310 and 365 pg/ml, respectively. These findings suggest that Caco-2 cells may secrete more VEGF when VEGFR-2 is blocked by ramucirumab. Fig. 4 VEGF levels in caco2 cells were quantified in cell culture medium using a sandwich ELISA assay via a commercial kit. Caco-2 cells were treated as indicated with Ramucirumab (125, 250, and 500 µg/mL) for 24 h. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Significant at * p < 0.05 and ** p < 0.001, compared to the untreated control ( n = 6)
sections.detection of intracellular reactive oxyg: The generation of intracellular ROS was evaluated by staining the cells by carboxy-H 2 DCFDA fluorescence marker. The fluorescence intensity was measured post-exposure to Caco-2 cells with ramucirumab. As illustrated in Fig. 5 , a significant elevation in ROS production levels were recorded. The quantitative analysis revealed a significant ( p < 0.05) increase in the percentage of ROS, 37%, 34% and 45% in 125, 250 and 500 µg/ml concentrations respectively, relative to control (100%). Fig. 5 The quantification of intracellular Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels in Caco-2 cells exposed to ramucirumab in different concentrations for 24 h. The fluorescence intensity was measured after staining the cells with carboxy-H 2 DCFDA fluorescence marker. The data were presented as mean ± SD for experiments performed in triplicate. (Significant at *** p < 0.001 and *** p < 0.0001, compared to untreated control, n = 6)
sections.caspase 3/7 activity assay: To determine whether ramucirumab inhibits the growth of Caco-2 cells via apoptosis pathway, the changes in the activity of Caspase 3/7 was measured because these are the main enzymes that mediate apoptosis. As demonstrated in Fig. 6 , the treatment of Caco-2 cells with ramucirumab at the concentrations of 125, 250 and 500 µg/ml resulted in a significant ( p < 0.05) activation of caspase 3/7 which were observed to 27%, 34% and 64% respectively, when compared to control which was considered to be 100%. Fig. 6 Effect of Ramucirumab on activation of caspase 3/7 post 24 h exposure measured in Caco-2 cells. Data were expressed as mean ± SD for experiments performed in triplicate (Significant at ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, and *** p < 0.0001, compared to untreated control, n = 3)
sections.apoptosis analysis using annexin-v/pi as: The results of apoptosis analysis in Caco-2 cells using flow cytometry method is presented as dot plots in Fig. 7 (A-D). The treatment with ramucirumab showed a remarkable induction of apoptosis in all the concentrations. The highest fraction of early apoptosis (16.1%) was recorded at the lower concentration (125 µg/ml) (Fig. 7 B). Simultaneously, the highest percentage of late apoptotic cells (3.1%) and necrotic cells (16.7%) was detected at the higher convention (500 µg/ml) after 24 h of treatment (Fig. 7 D). The proportion of viable cells were reduced as the concentration of ramucirumab increased. In contrast, control cells showed about 98.5% viable cells (Fig. 7 A). ( A ) Control ( B ) 125 µg/ml ( C ) 250 µg/ml ( D ) 500 µg/ml ( n = 3). As shown in the figure, the dot plot analysis was categorized into four quadrants (A1, A2, A3 and A4) according to fluorescence signals: A1 (Annexin V −/PI +): Necrotic cells, A2 (Annexin V +/PI +): Late apoptotic, A3 (Annexin V −/PI −): Viable cells, A4 (Annexin V +/PI −): Early apoptotic cells
sections.cell cycle distribution analysis: Flow cytometry-based cell cycle analysis primarily demonstrates cell cycle arrest if the cells in the G0/G1 phase is accumulated. The results of cell cycle analysis using flow cytometry and PI-staining as presented in histograms (Fig. 8 A-D). The exposure to Caco-2 cells with ramucirumab did not show cells accumulation in G1 phase however, the percentage of cells in S-phase were increased in all treatments 2% to 5% which suggests S-phase cells accumulated without moving to G2/M phase due to DNA damage or impaired DNA synthesis completion. Remarkably, the proportion and sub-G1 cells increased in treatment group implicating induction of apoptosis.
