sections.detection of nuclear morphological chang: Hoechst 33324 stain is a fluorescent nuclear dye mainly used to detect the different characteristic features of apoptosis process. Hoechst 33324 binds to structurally damaged DNA fragments and emits stronger blue fluorescence. After staining the control and ramucirumab treated Caco-2 cells, nuclear morphological changes were observed under a fluorescent microscope and the representative images were shown in Fig. 9 (A-D). The control Caco-2 cells were regular in morphology and showed an intact nuclear architecture (Fig. 9 A), while the treated cell nuclei were densely stained by the dye, and even appeared to be fragmented and showed enhanced fluorescence intensity, which suggested the apoptosis of cells (Fig. 9 B – D). The Quantitative estimation of Hoechst staining using spectrofluorometry showed a significant ( p < 0.05) increase in fluorescence intensity from 9%, 55% and 75% in low to high concentration of ramucirumab relative to untreated cells (100%), which indicated nuclear DNA damage and apoptosis. The fluorescence images as depicted in Fig. 10 (A – D) showed diminution of the mitochondrial membrane potential in a concentration- dependent manner, indicated to disruption of mitochondrial function and apoptosis triggering particularly at the highest concentration (500 µg/ml) compared with control which emitted highly green fluorescence. sections.discussion: VEGFR-2 is the target of the monoclonal antibody ramucirumab, which is mainly used in cancer treatment to prevent angiogenesis. Ramucirumab interacts with high affinity and specificity to the extracellular ligand-binding epitope of VEGFR-2. This obstructs the binding of VEGF-A to VEGFR-2, resulting in the suppression of VEGF-A signaling, which consequently decreases tumor angiogenesis and proliferation. Ramucirumab possesses the potential to block several activities triggered by VEGF activation of VEGFR-2 (Tabernero et al. 2015 ; Verdaguer et al. 2016 ; Goel et al. 2016 ). However, its direct impacts on colorectal cancer cells, such as Caco-2, are still being studied. More recently, combination treatment options utilizing ramucirumab have been examined using diverse cancer models. Ramucirumab coupled with gold nanoparticles exhibited higher cellular recognition, uptake, and accumulation, leading to increased cytotoxicity in gastric cancer cells (Fan et al. 2021 ). The combination of sorafenib and ramucirumab exhibited synergistic anticancer effects in hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2 cells), characterized by enhanced apoptosis, reduced proliferation, and suppression of angiogenesis (Taha et al. 2022 ). Furthermore, the concomitant administration of ramucirumab and 5-azacytidine (5-Aza) has been documented to augment therapeutic efficacy in hepatocellular carcinoma cells (HuH-7) (Almasoud et al. 2024 ). Using a variety of assays, such as MTT, LDH, cell cycle and apoptosis analysis, caspase activation, ROS detection, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and Hoechst nuclear staining, this study assesses the effect of ramucirumab on Caco-2 cells. Cell viability and proliferation are reflected in the MTT assay, which quantifies cellular metabolic activity. In Caco-2 cells treated with ramucirumab, a significant fall in absorbance ( p < 0.05) indicates a loss in cell viability and an anti-proliferative effect. Similar findings from earlier research on VEGFR-2 inhibitors showed that inhibiting VEGFR-2 signaling decreased the development of cancer cells (Spratlin et al. 2010 ). The concentration-dependent response observed aligns with findings that higher ramucirumab concentrations enhance growth inhibition in tumor models (Zhu et al. 2013 ). By monitoring the release of lactate dehydrogenase following membrane injury, the LDH assay assesses cytotoxicity. Ramucirumab-induced cytotoxicity is indicated by elevated LDH levels in treated cells. Cell death may be the outcome of disturbed survival signaling pathways downstream of VEGFR-2 (Fuchs et al. 2014 ). The idea that ramucirumab not only prevents proliferation but also encourages cell death is supported by the association between decreased cell viability observed in MTT assay and increased LDH release. Ramucirumab treated Caco-2 cells showed enhanced apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, according to flow cytometry analysis. A significant (p < 0.05) accumulation in the G0/G1 or G2/M phase indicates cell cycle blocking, potentially as a result of VEGFR-2-mediated pro-survival signal suppression (Wilke et al. 2014 ). Additionally, cell cycle analysis showed an increased sub-G1 population and Annexin V/PI staining confirm apoptosis induction. These findings are consistent with studies showing that VEGFR-2 inhibition triggers apoptotic pathways in cancer cells (Youssoufian et al. 2007 ). The elevation of VEGF levels noted after ramucirumab treatment may indicate a compensatory feedback mechanism triggered by the suppression of VEGFR-2 signaling. Inhibiting receptor-mediated signaling can interfere with downstream angiogenic pathways and cellular equilibrium, resulting in the increase of VEGF expression as a biological effort to re-establish angiogenic signaling. Nonetheless, despite increased VEGF levels, angiogenic signaling is suppressed due to receptor inhibition at VEGFR-2, obstructing downstream activation of endothelial proliferation and vessel formation. Comparable elevations in VEGF have been seen in anti-angiogenic therapy contexts and do not signify augmented angiogenesis; instead, they indicate receptor-level pathway blockage (Jayson et al. 2016 ). Caspase-3 and −7 are executioner caspases required for apoptosis. The induction of apoptosis by either intrinsic or extrinsic routes is confirmed by increased activity of these caspases in treated cells. By interfering with death receptor signaling or mitochondrial integrity, ramucirumab may trigger caspase cascades (Elmore 2007 ). This is consistent with findings in other treatments that target VEGFR-2, where caspase-dependent apoptosis is a major mode of action. In cancer, reactive oxygen species contribute to both survival and death. Increased ROS levels in ramucirumab-treated cells show oxidative stress as a contributing factor to apoptosis. Excessive ROS can damage biological components, including DNA and mitochondria, leading to cell death (Trachootham et al. 2009 ). The elevation of intracellular ROS during Ramucirumab treatment is likely attributable to mitochondrial malfunction and redox imbalance caused by the suppression of VEGFR-2 signaling. Under normal condition, the activation of VEGFR-2 stimulates pro-survival pathways including PI3K/Akt, which aid in preserving cellular redox equilibrium. Inhibiting this route can compromise antioxidant defenses and increase ROS generation (Karar & Maity 2011 ; Trachootham et al. 2009 ). Mitochondria are a principal intracellular generator of ROS, primarily due to electron leakage from the electron transport chain during oxidative phosphorylation. Impairment of mitochondrial function can exacerbate ROS production, establishing a positive feedback loop between oxidative stress and mitochondrial injury. Increased levels of ROS can lead to a decline in mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), promoting the release of pro-apoptotic proteins such cytochrome c and the subsequent activation of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway (Tait & Green 2010 ). The findings in this study indicate that the elevated levels of ROS, alongside mitochondrial depolarization and caspase-3/7 activation, corroborate the theory that ramucirumab triggers death in Caco-2 cells via a ROS-mediated mitochondrial route. The current study does not explicitly differentiate between mitochondrial and non-mitochondrial sources of reactive oxygen species (e.g., NADPH oxidases); however, the significant correlation between ROS production and mitochondrial dysfunction implies that mitochondria are a primary contributor. Subsequent research employing ROS scavengers or mitochondrial-specific probes will be necessary to ascertain the exact origin of ROS. Moreover, the precise sequence and hierarchy of these signaling events cannot be conclusively determined from the existing data. The lack of pathway-specific inhibitors hinders the differentiation between upstream and downstream processes. Future research utilizing targeted inhibitors or genetic methodologies will be essential to clarify the specific signaling cascade responsible for these effects. It is important to acknowledge that DCFDA-based endpoint ROS tests have many methodological constraints, such as vulnerability to photo-oxidation, auto-oxidation, dye leakage, and possible fluorescence interference during washing processes. Consequently, the current findings ought to be regarded as a relative signal of intracellular oxidative stress rather than an absolute quantitative assessment of ROS generation. ROS produced after ramucirumab exposure to Caco-2 cells may originate from various intracellular sources. Mitochondria are acknowledged as primary sources of cellular ROS, yet other enzymatic systems such as NADPH oxidases, xanthine oxidase, cytochrome P450 enzymes, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), cyclooxygenases, and endoplasmic reticulum stress pathways can also play substantial roles in oxidative stress during pathological conditions (Liou and Storz 2010 ; Forrester et al. 2018 ). The current investigation indicated mitochondrial participation by observed mitochondrial membrane depolarization, elevated ROS production, and the activation of caspase-dependent apoptosis. The precise origin of ROS was not explicitly examined, so the role of non-mitochondrial oxidative processes remains unexcluded. Future evaluation utilizing ROS scavengers, pathway-specific inhibitors, and organelle-targeted probes will be necessary to clarify the exact source of ROS generated by ramucirumab in colorectal cancer cells. Intrinsic apoptosis is characterized by mitochondrial malfunction, which is indicated by a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Ramucirumab treated cells displayed reduced ΔΨm, suggesting mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and cytochrome c release, activating caspase-9 and downstream effectors (Green and Kroemer 2004 ). This method is consistent with the observed caspase-3/7 activation and emphasizes the significance of mitochondrial apoptosis in ramucirumab’s cytotoxicity. Hoechst staining demonstrated nuclear condensation and fragmentation in treated cells, hallmark markers of apoptosis. This morphological alteration is consistent with mitochondrial malfunction and caspase activation, indicating that ramucirumab causes apoptotic cell death as opposed to necrosis (Krysko et al. 2008 ). The existence of apoptotic bodies further validates the flow cytometry and caspase activity data. The current data indicate that Ramucirumab induces apoptosis in Caco-2 cells by reducing mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), oxidative stress, and activating executioner caspases. These events activate the intrinsic apoptotic pathway (Elmore 2007 ; Tait and Green 2010 ). However, complete mechanistic validation requires the identification of upstream regulatory proteins including Bax and Bcl-2, cytochrome c release, and caspase-9 activation, which were not assessed in this work. Our findings indicate a molecular sequence wherein ramucirumab mediated VEGFR-2 suppression generates oxidative stress, induce mitochondrial malfunction, and activates the caspase dependent intrinsic apoptotic pathway in Caco-2 cells. This study examined downstream apoptotic mechanisms in Caco-2 cells with ramucirumab, a targeted VEGFR-2 inhibitor. However, the study lacks mechanistic controls such non-specific IgG treatment, VEGFR-2 expression validation, and comparison with other VEGFR-2-targeting drugs. The current work provides robust association evidence for this pathway, however, additional research with pathway-specific inhibitors is necessary to verify direct effects.
sections.conclusions: In this study, the anti-tumor efficacy of ramucirumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting VEGFR-2, was investigated in Caco-2 colorectal cancer cells utilizing various functional assays. Our results consistently show that ramucirumab treatment decreases cell viability, causes cytotoxicity, stops the advancement of the cell cycle, and initiates apoptosis, all of which suggest that it may be a useful therapeutic agent against colorectal cancer. The possible mechanisms involve are inhibition of cell proliferation via VEGFR-2 inhibition, induction of oxidative stress and mitochondrial malfunction and activation of caspase-dependent apoptosis. Although these data indicate potential direct effects beyond the inhibition of angiogenesis, they are presently confined to a singular in vitro model. Additional research employing various colorectal cancer cell lines and in vivo models is necessary to confirm the wider applicability and translational significance of these findings.

title: Topical Timolol Beyond Infancy: A Retrospective Study of Its Use in Persistent Infantile Hemangiomas
abstract: Introduction Infantile hemangiomas (IH) usually undergo spontaneous involution; however, some lesions remain visible after infancy and may cause psychosocial distress in children and their families. Evidence regarding the effectiveness of topical beta-blockers when treatment is initiated after infancy remains limited. Methods This real-world study evaluated the efficacy of topical timolol therapy in children aged 1–5 years with persistent IH. Children with IH were evaluated at a specialized vascular anomalies center in Ukraine between 2019 and 2024. Parents of children older than 1 year with persistent visible IH associated with psychosocial distress were offered vascular laser therapy or topical timolol treatment. Because topical therapy could be administered safely at home under remote medical supervision during ongoing military action, all families chose this option. A short initial treatment period of 2–4 weeks was used to assess the therapeutic response, and treatment was continued if improvement was observed. Results A total of 2419 children with IH were evaluated during the study period. Among them, 1287 patients used topical timolol as monotherapy. Treatment was initiated after the age of 1 year in 113 patients with persistent lesions. Positive outcomes were observed in 1151 (98.04%) patients who started therapy before the age of 1 year and in 78 (69.03%) patients who initiated treatment between 1 and 5 years of age ( p < 0.001). Topical timolol 0.5% demonstrated limited effectiveness in older children, whereas switching to topical timolol 1% resulted in clinical improvement. In six patients previously treated with systemic beta-blockers, topical timolol remained effective even after systemic therapy had lost effectiveness. Natural involution of IHs may be partially responsible for the positive effect observed in some of our patients. Conclusions These findings suggest that topical timolol 1% may provide clinically meaningful improvement in persistent IH beyond infancy and support telemedicine-based treatment when access to in-person care is limited.

sections.key summary points:
Why carry out this study? Topical timolol is a well-established treatment for infantile hemangiomas during the first year of life. Some children older than 1 year continue to have visible hemangiomas that cause psychosocial 
distress. Evidence regarding the efficacy of topical timolol in this older age group remains limited. This study aimed to determine whether topical timolol remains effective in children aged 1–5 years with persistent infantile 
hemangiomas. What was learned from the study? Topical timolol 1% demonstrated clinically meaningful efficacy and a favorable safety profile in the 
majority of children aged 1–5 years.
sections.introduction_1: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy [ 1 ]. The incidence of IH in the general newborn population ranges from 1.1% to 2.6% but increases to up to 12% by 1 year of age. Approximately 30% of IHs are present at birth, whereas 70–90% appear during the first 4 weeks of life. Most IHs occur sporadically. Although IH occurs in all racial groups, it is more common in white infants and less frequent in infants of African or Asian descent [ 2 ]. Observation is often recommended by physicians because many IHs undergo spontaneous involution. However, children with visible IH may become targets of bullying. Skin disease-related bullying may begin as early as 3 years of age and may persist into adulthood [ 3 ]. The presence of IH in a child, along with repeated questions from others about the child’s appearance, may also have a negative psychosocial impact on parents [ 4 ]. Consequently, parents who initially follow physicians’ recommendations to observe IH until the age of 1 year but do not observe regression may insist on initiating treatment in older children. When necessary, referral to a hemangioma specialist and/or initiation of therapy should be considered as early as 1 month of age, as earlier treatment is associated with better cosmetic outcomes. The goal of therapy is to inhibit growth and accelerate involution while minimizing permanent sequelae [ 5 , 6 ]. Timolol maleate 0.5%, a nonselective beta-blocker, is considered a well-tolerated, safe, and effective treatment for small, thin, superficial IHs. It has been reported to be comparable to oral propranolol for superficial lesions, with a lower rate of systemic adverse effects, and superior to topical corticosteroids [ 5 , 7 ]. Typically, the 0.5% solution or gel is applied twice daily, and most studies have demonstrated significant reductions in IH color and size compared with laser therapy, placebo, or observation. Adverse effects are usually limited to local reactions such as irritation, whereas systemic events similar to those seen with propranolol therapy are rare [ 6 ]. Although topical beta-blockers are most effective when initiated during the proliferative phase of IH, some patients present later with persistent lesions that cause psychological or social distress. There is limited evidence regarding the rationale for, and outcomes of, initiating treatment in children older than 1 year when parents or patients decline further observation because of visible disfigurement and the associated psychosocial burden [ 8 ]. An effective treatment option for IH in older children is the 595-nm pulsed dye laser (PDL) [ 9 , 10 ]. However, because of military conflicts, pandemics, and natural disasters, a substantial number of patients may have limited access to laser treatment. In such circumstances, topical timolol may be considered an alternative therapy. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of initiating topical timolol maleate treatment in children older than 1 year with IHs.
sections.methods_1: Children with IHs who were evaluated and treated at our vascular anomalies center between 2019 and 2024 were included in the study. Children older than 1 year who had not previously received treatment, because physicians had recommended an observation strategy, were treated because of persistent lesions and the associated psychosocial impact (e.g., bullying, avoidance, or social withdrawal). All patients demonstrated minimal or no signs of spontaneous regression at presentation. Patients included both low-risk cases (small lesions located on the trunk or limbs) and moderate-risk cases (facial or scalp lesions, lesions in skin folds, or lesions larger than 5 cm). For children aged 1–5 years, two treatment options were offered: vascular laser therapy or topical timolol. Parents were informed that the effectiveness of topical timolol in older children could not be guaranteed. Because of safety concerns related to ongoing military action, many parents were unable to visit the clinic for laser therapy and therefore agreed to start treatment with topical timolol for a 1-month test period. Topical timolol 0.5% was initially prescribed to the first ten children older than 1 year whose parents requested active treatment. At follow-up examination after 2–4 weeks, nine of these ten children showed no clinical improvement. After discussion with the parents, treatment was continued with topical timolol 1% gel, after which clinical improvement was observed in all cases. Consequently, all subsequent patients older than 1 year were treated with topical timolol 1% gel. Topical timolol gel (0.5% or 1%) was applied to the IH 2–3 times daily under occlusion for 2–3 h. If lightening of the IH color was observed within 2–4 weeks, treatment was continued with photographic monitoring every 2 months. If no signs of lightening or regression were observed during the first month of treatment, it was discontinued. Treatment continued as long as progressive lightening of the IH was noted. The treatment duration varied between 3 and 10 months (minimal and maximal). Especially for our online teledermatology consultation service, we have developed standards and algorithms for photo documentation, video instructions for patients, and even patented two algorithms for online consultations—one for patients and the other for doctors. We teach patients photography standards according to our algorithms, which has greatly facilitated this process. All photos obtained according to these algorithms are taken under the same lighting, from the same angle, and under the same patient conditions. Only if the quality of the photo meets the established standards and requirements does the operator of the online service accept the photo for consultation; if the photo does not meet the standard, the operator explains what needs to be changed and how the photo should be retaken. All photos are collected in the patient’s digital medical record over the course of treatment and follow-up. In all cases, the parents were trained to measure the child’s heart rate at home using a pulse oximeter and to record the results in diaries, which they then sent to us. The parents also independently monitored the child’s blood glucose level. In addition, all patients underwent a mandatory monthly examination by a pediatrician or family doctor, including blood pressure measurement and electrocardiography (ECG). Categorical variables were described as number and percentage ( n , %). Differences between groups were analyzed using the chi-square test. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) and its subsequent amendments. Ethical approval was granted by the local ethics commission of the Dr. Bogomolets Institute of Dermatology and Cosmetology (Protocol No. 2311025/1). Written informed consent for participation in the study and for publication of clinical images and data was obtained from the parents of all patients.
sections.results_1: A total of 2419 infants with IHs were evaluated at the hemangioma and vascular malformation treatment center between 2019 and 2024. Of these, 1287 patients used topical timolol as monotherapy. The remaining patients were either managed by observation because treatment was not required, treated with systemic beta-blockers, treated with a combination of systemic and topical beta-blockers, or referred for vascular laser therapy if they were older than 5 years of age. Among the 1287 patients treated with topical timolol, 891 (69.23%) were girls and 396 (30.77%) were boys. The age at initiation of treatment with topical beta-blockers is presented in Table 1 . No systemic adverse effects were observed. These patients subsequently underwent treatment with a 595-nm PDL, with a positive effect. Six children older than 1 year had previously been treated with systemic beta-blockers in other clinics. In all of these patients, systemic therapy had been discontinued after the age of 1 year because no further clinical effectiveness was observed. Treatment with topical timolol was initiated no earlier than 3 months after discontinuation of systemic beta-blocker therapy. As a result of persistent lesions and the psychosocial impact of IH, parents requested further treatment with topical beta-blockers. All six patients demonstrated a positive clinical response to topical timolol 1% therapy (Figs. 2 , 4 , 6 , and 8 ). In all 113 cases, follow-up was conducted via telemedicine consultations, and treatment efficacy was assessed on the basis of clinical photographs.
sections.discussion: Our study demonstrated that topical timolol 1% therapy may be effective in children aged 1–5 years with persistent IHs. Clinical improvement was observed in 69% of patients in this age group. Although the effectiveness of topical beta-blockers was significantly higher in children treated before the age of 1 year, these findings suggest that a substantial proportion of older children may still benefit from topical therapy. Previous studies have consistently shown that early initiation of treatment is associated with better outcomes in IHs. Rapid growth of IH typically occurs between 5.5 and 7.5 weeks of life, and most lesions stop proliferating after 6 months. Ng et al. evaluated the efficacy of topical timolol as primary monotherapy for facial IHs before 12 months of age and reported clinically significant improvement in 47–88% of patients, depending on the age at treatment initiation [ 11 ]. Similarly, a large multicenter retrospective cohort study of 731 patients treated with topical timolol reported that risk of disfigurement was the most common indication for therapy (74%), and lesion thickness, duration of therapy, and subtype of IH were significant predictors of treatment response [ 12 ]. Other studies have also demonstrated that younger age at treatment initiation and smaller lesion size are associated with better therapeutic outcomes [ 13 – 15 ]. Consistent with these observations, our results showed significantly higher treatment efficacy in children younger than 1 year compared with those aged 1–5 years. However, no statistically significant differences were observed among the 1–1.5 year, 1.5–2 year, and 2–5 year age subgroups. These findings suggest that although earlier treatment remains preferable, the therapeutic window for topical beta-blocker therapy may extend beyond infancy. Persistent IHs may therefore retain sensitivity to beta-blocker treatment even several years after the proliferative phase. An important clinical observation of our study was the limited effectiveness of topical timolol 0.5% in children older than 1 year. In the initial group of patients treated with this concentration, the majority did not demonstrate clinical improvement during the first weeks of therapy. After switching to topical timolol 1% gel, clinical improvement was observed. These findings suggest that higher concentrations of topical timolol may be required to achieve a therapeutic response in persistent IHs in older children. Another notable observation was the response to topical timolol in patients who had previously received systemic beta-blocker therapy. In all such cases, systemic treatment had been discontinued after the age of 1 year because no further clinical effectiveness was observed. Topical timolol therapy was initiated at least 3 months after discontinuation of systemic beta-blockers, and all patients demonstrated clinical improvement. These observations suggest that IHs may retain sensitivity to locally administered beta-blockers even after the effectiveness of systemic therapy has declined. This finding warrants further investigation. Topical timolol treatment in our cohort was administered under occlusion using plastic film and monitored remotely via telemedicine consultations because of safety risks associated with ongoing military action. These observations suggest that topical timolol therapy may be particularly suitable for the remote management of selected patients with IHs when access to in-person care is limited. The fact that topical timolol treatment was selected by families who had no access to laser treatment may not compromise the generalizability of our findings. The safety profile of topical timolol reported in the literature is generally favorable. A systematic review of complications associated with topical timolol therapy reported that local irritation was the most frequently observed adverse event, typically presenting as mild scaling, pruritus, or superficial skin changes [ 16 ]. Systemic adverse events were rare and occurred in approximately 1.2% of cases. Studies evaluating the systemic absorption of topical timolol have detected measurable serum or urinary levels in some patients, but these concentrations were generally low and were not associated with clinically significant cardiovascular effects [ 17 ]. Nevertheless, monitoring of heart rate and blood pressure has been recommended in infants receiving topical beta-blocker therapy, particularly when it is applied over large surface areas or in younger patients [ 18 ]. Gallegos et al. suggested that 0.5% topical timolol may be safely applied in patients who have no contraindications [ 19 ]. Safety depends on careful screening of patients for contraindications to timolol use in dermatologic conditions. Screening should include assessment of risk factors and the presence of cardiopulmonary disease [ 20 ]. We followed these recommendations in our study. A recent study by Yang et al. also reported mild adverse events associated with topical timolol 0.5% eye drops used for IH treatment, including local irritation and transient systemic symptoms [ 15 ]. Importantly, most reported systemic adverse events were observed in adults or older patients with significant comorbidities [ 21 ], whereas pediatric patients with IHs generally tolerate topical therapy well. In our cohort, no adverse effects were reported in patients treated with topical timolol 1% gel. Our previous clinical experience also demonstrated the potential role of telemedicine in the management of complicated IHs. In a previously published case report, successful treatment of an ulcerated IH using systemic antibiotics and topical beta-blockers was achieved via telemedicine consultations during periods when in-person medical care was limited [ 22 ]. Although such circumstances were initially related to military action, this experience highlights the broader potential of remote management of selected vascular anomalies during pandemics, natural disasters, or other situations limiting access to healthcare. The relatively small number of patients older than 1 year included in subgroup analyses represents a limitation of the present study. Nevertheless, the available data were sufficient for statistical analysis and did not demonstrate any trend toward a further decline in treatment efficacy among older age subgroups within the 1–5 year age range. We compared children younger than 1 year and those older than 1 year who were treated with different concentrations of topical timolol. However, even the lower concentration of topical timolol showed superior efficacy in younger children compared with the higher concentration used in older children. The late proliferative phase of IH, characterized by slower growth, is usually completed by 9–12 months of age, but growth can extend beyond 36 months, with the latter defining late growth. Usually, a period of relative stabilization is present, followed by spontaneous regression over several months or even years. The involution phase starts around 12 months of age and usually lasts for 3 to 9 years. While some studies predicted final involution at approximately 10% per year, other studies indicated that involution ends at a median age of 3 or 4 years and that most hemangiomas cease to improve after 3–5 years of age [ 23 – 25 ]. Couto et al. estimated that involution ceased at a median age of 36 months, and 92% of IHs completed involution by 48 months [ 26 ]. A change in IH color and texture marks the involution phase, during which the lesion becomes more violaceous-gray, soft, and compressible [ 6 ]. The incidence of residual lesions varies widely depending on the study and has been reported in 25–69% of untreated hemangiomas [ 25 ]. Superficial nodular hemangiomas showed significantly more residual lesions (74%) than deep hemangiomas (25%) [ 27 ]. It is therefore not possible to exclude the possibility that natural involution of IHs may be partially responsible for the positive effect observed in some of our patients. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that spontaneous involution in the majority of children of different ages occurred by chance exactly after the initiation of topical timolol treatment. We observed significant lightening of IHs during the first 2–4 weeks of treatment in responders. No signs of regression in those patients were seen during the previous year. Lightening and regression of IHs persisted during the consequent 3–10 months treatment period. Therefore, we consider that the positive effect achieved is directly related to topical timolol use. All photographs were taken according to our algorithms under the same lighting, from the same angle, and under the same patient conditions, which reduces potential limitations. A higher concentration of topical timolol may lead to an increase in systemic adverse effects. However, no systemic adverse effects were observed. Taken together, our findings highlight three clinically relevant observations: topical timolol therapy may remain effective beyond infancy, higher concentrations of timolol may be required to achieve a therapeutic response in older lesions, and treatment can be successfully administered under remote medical supervision.
sections.conclusions_1: Treatment with topical beta-blockers in patients younger than 12 months demonstrated a positive response in 98% of cases, with minimal adverse effects. However, topical timolol therapy may also be effective in children aged 1–5 years, with clinical improvement observed in 69% of patients with persistent IHs. A short initial test period of topical therapy (2–4 weeks) may help determine whether the IH retains sensitivity to beta-blocker treatment. Topical timolol 0.5% demonstrated limited effectiveness in older children, whereas switching to topical timolol 1% resulted in clinical improvement in previously non-responsive lesions. Our observations also suggest that IHs may retain sensitivity to topical beta-blocker therapy even after systemic beta-blocker treatment has been discontinued because of loss of clinical effectiveness. Topical timolol therapy may also be suitable for the remote management of selected patients under medical supervision when access to in-person care is limited. Topical timolol 1% may therefore represent a practical therapeutic option for persistent IHs in children aged 1–5 years.

title: Mechanisms ofra Tetmethylpyrazine in spinal cord injury: a narrative review
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is characterized by irreversible loss of motor and sensory function, imposing a substantial burden on patients and their families. Tetramethylpyrazine (TMP), a bioactive compound derived from traditional Chinese medicine, possesses a wide range of pharmacological activities and has demonstrated potential therapeutic effects in the treatment of SCI. Therefore, this article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanisms by which TMP promotes spinal cord repair. This review compiles a large body of in vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies, including a total of 86 publications documenting the effects of TMP on SCI. The results indicate that the mechanisms by which TMP exerts its effects in SCI treatment include promoting nerve regeneration, improving vascular dysfunction, exerting anti-inflammatory effects, inhibiting neuronal apoptosis, reducing oxidative stress, regulating iron metabolism, maintaining ion homeostasis, alleviating pyroptosis, and modulating autophagy. Through these mechanisms, TMP contributes to the restoration of spinal cord morphology, motor function, and electrophysiological parameters in experimental animal models. Clinical reports on the use of TMP injection for SCI are relatively limited, and its clinical efficacy requires further investigation. The combined application of nanotechnology or hydrogels provides an efficient targeted delivery and sustained-release system for TMP in the spinal cord, thereby significantly enhancing its bioavailability. Overall, TMP shows promising potential in SCI treatment and may serve as a valuable adjunctive therapeutic strategy.

sections.introduction: Patients with spinal cord injury (SCI) frequently experience a range of neurological deficits, including partial or complete loss of sensory and motor functions below the level of injury. For instance, cervical spine injuries often result in quadriplegia, while thoracic spine injuries result in paraplegia, with severe cases potentially being life-threatening. Annually, approximately 930,000 new SCI cases are reported, and an estimated 27.04 million individuals are affected globally. SCI not only significantly impacts an individual’s quality of life but also imposes a considerable socioeconomic burden, with the estimated lifetime cost per person reaching approximately 2.35 million USD [ 1 , 2 ]. Currently, clinical treatment options for SCI remain limited. Patient recovery primarily depends on surgical decompression and pharmacological interventions, and the ongoing search of more effective alternative therapies remains one of the key research focuses for this condition. Modern pharmacological studies have shown that the active components of traditional Chinese medicine exert their effects through multi-target and multi-pathway mechanisms, demonstrating significant therapeutic benefits in conditions like SCI. Among them, tetramethylpyrazine (TMP), an alkaloid derived from ligustrazine, has been shown to promote cell proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, induce vasodilation, regulate immune responses, exert anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, and enhance tissue microcirculation. TMP has been used in the treatment of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, including myocardial infarction, cerebral ischemia, brain injury, and Alzheimer’s disease. TMP also demonstrates neuroprotective effects in SCI and is increasingly regarded as a promising therapeutic candidate for this condition [ 3 ]. Meta-analyses have shown that TMP, the main active component of Ligusticum chuanxiong, is significantly more effective in reducing SCI-induced inflammation than other traditional Chinese medicines, such as Salvia miltiorrhiza (Danshen) [ 4 ]. This article provides a comprehensive review of the clinical applications, as well as in vivo and in vitro experimental studies, of TMP and its mechanisms of action in SCI repair. The aim is to present new therapeutic options for the clinical treatment of SCI. The main content of the article is summarized in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Graphical abstract. (The image was created using Photoshop)
sections.materials and methods: This was a narrative review.
sections.sources of data: The search strategy in this section was designed to be broad. Relevant data were obtained from both Chinese and English literature published before August 2025. These studies were sourced from PubMed, Springer, Web of Science, Cochrane, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI). Boolean operators were used to combine search terms, specifically linking ‘SCI’ OR ‘spinal cord injury’ with ‘tetramethylpyrazine’ OR ‘TMP’ using the ‘AND’ operator to ensure a comprehensive collection of literature in both languages.
sections.inclusion criteria: Literature from the five databases was screened, with duplicates removed. Studies closely related to the research objectives and content of this paper were selected. The included studies had to focus on in vitro, in vivo, or clinical research on the use of TMP in the treatment of SCI.
sections.exclusion criteria: Non-Chinese and non-English literature; reviews, abstracts, conference papers, short reports, and newspaper articles; studies involving combination therapies or comprehensive treatment regimens where TMP’s independent contribution could not be demonstrated; articles lacking detailed research methods or with incomplete data or figures; and literature not aligned with the research objectives. The screening process is outlined in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Flow diagram for identifying eligible studies. (The image was created using Photoshop)
sections.data extraction: Two authors independently screened all included studies and performed data extraction. Discrepancies were resolved through consultation with a third author. Information such as authors, publication date, study design, animal species, disease modeling method, drug dosage, intervention duration, and outcome measures was extracted.
sections.results of the review: This section summarizes the findings from previously published in vivo and clinical studies evaluating TMP in SCI. The results are detailed below.
sections.molecular structure of tmp: Tetramethylpyrazine (TMP, C₈H₁₂N₂) is a bioactive monomer extracted from the traditional Chinese medicinal herb Chuanxiong. The chemical structure of TMP is shown in Fig. 3 . TMP is an amide-type alkaloid with a pyrazine core substituted by four methyl groups. The unique molecular structure of TMP underlies its diverse pharmacological activities [ 5 ]. The pyrazine ring is a relatively planar, electron-deficient system that serves as the core pharmacophore, contributing to TMP’s broad therapeutic effects. ITMP exhibits antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory properties, and also regulates autophagy, angiogenesis, vasodilation, and endothelial function [ 6 ]. Additionally, the four highly symmetric methyl groups increase the molecule’s lipophilicity, allowing TMP to effectively penetrate the blood–brain barrier, making it a promising candidate for treating central nervous system diseases. Fig. 3 Chemical structure of TMP. (The image was created using in Draw software)
sections.clinical application of tmp in sci: Currently, two salt forms of TMP have been approved for clinical use: TMP hydrochloride and TMP phosphate. TMP is a lipophilic alkaloid with poor water solubility. By combining TMP with hydrochloric acid or phosphoric acid, its water solubility and drug stability are significantly improved, enhancing its absorption and utilization in the human body, making it better suited for clinical application. In the treatment of SCI, TMP injection is typically diluted in 5% glucose injection or sodium chloride injection and administered via intravenous drip. Currently, there are limited reports on the use of TMP injection alone for SCI treatment, with only three studies available. Wu Xi administered TMP injection continuously for 14 days to 36 patients after SCI surgery. The motor and sensory function scores at 3, 6, and 12 months post-operation were all higher than those in the conventional treatment group, demonstrating that TMP can promote the recovery of motor and sensory function after SCI surgery, without any adverse effects on surgical recovery [ 7 ]. Du FT found that in patients with SCI, the high-dose group (240 mg) showed better postoperative motor scores and higher levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, Nrf2, GCLc, and GCLm in the cerebrospinal fluid compared to the low-dose group (120 mg) [ 8 , 9 ]. herefore, it was concluded that TMP may promote SCI recovery by improving oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, with higher doses providing better therapeutic effects. The clinical study information is presented in Table 1 . Although the above reports provide some evidence of the efficacy of TMP in promoting SCI recovery, and no adverse reactions have been reported so far, preliminary evidence suggests that TMP may be a beneficial adjunctive treatment option. sections.rodents: A total of 65 in vivo studies have investigated the effects of TMP using rodent models, including SD rats, C57BL/6 mice, and Wistar rats. The acute SCI model is primarily established through a modified Allen’s weight-drop method. One study employed balloon occlusion of the thoracic aorta to induce a spinal cord ischemia model. TMP is typically administered via intraperitoneal injection at a dose of 200 mg/kg [ 10 ]. The mechanisms through which TMP promotes SCI repair are multifaceted. These include enhancing neural repair, improving vascular dysfunction, exerting anti-inflammatory effects, inhibiting cell apoptosis, providing antioxidant benefits, improving iron metabolism, and regulating ion homeostasis. These mechanisms are interconnected and work synergistically at the molecular and cellular levels. Through multi-target and multi-pathway regulation, TMP ultimately facilitates both structural and functional repair of SCI at the tissue and functional levels. Promote nerve regeneration .
sections.upregulation of neurotrophic factors: Nerve growth factor (NGF) is a neuroprotective substance produced by neurons, glial cells, and others in the damaged spinal cord through autocrine and paracrine mechanisms. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is an essential neurotrophic factor for maintaining neuronal survival, promoting neuronal differentiation, and supporting myelination. Zhou Y found that TMP can upregulate the expression of NGF and BDNF in the injured segment of the spinal cord [ 11 ]. Wang GQ found that TMP promotes the upregulation of CAP-43 expression after SCI, which is also an important growth protein related to neural development and repair [ 12 ]. Yang F found that TMP can also promote the expression of neurotrophic factor NT-4 and TrkA after acute SCI [ 13 ]. TrkA is a high-affinity receptor for neurotrophic factors, and neurotrophic factors must bind to this receptor to initiate cellular signaling pathways and exert their biological effects.
sections.reduction of glial scars: The formation of glial scars is considered a major obstacle to axonal regeneration. The proliferation and hypertrophy of astrocytes (AS) is one of the factors that contribute to the formation of glial scars [ 14 ].In the inflammatory response, the key enzyme cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) can hydrolyze membrane phospholipids to release arachidonic acid, thereby promoting the occurrence of the inflammatory cascade, activating astrocytes, and facilitating glial scar formation. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), as a cytoskeletal protein of astrocytes, is a marker of astrocyte activation. Chen X found that after TMP intervention, the positive area expression of GFAP and cPLA2 started to be lower than the model group on the third day. Furthermore, 21 days after SCI, HE staining showed that the model group had already developed glial scars, while the TMP group only exhibited ischemic changes. TMP effectively inhibited the excessive hypertrophy of activated astrocytes and delayed glial scar formation. However, not all scar characteristics form inhibitory barriers. During the acute to subacute stages, the proliferation of astrocytes is responsible for isolating the injury site to reduce the diffusion of cytotoxic molecules and inflammatory cells to adjacent, undamaged tissue. In addition, astrocytes around the injury may provide local nutritional support and promote angiogenesis [ 15 ]. Qi W found that early SCI, after TMP intervention, the number of GFAP-positive cells increased compared to the model group, reaching a peak on day 7 and then gradually decreasing [ 16 ]. However, the decrease was smaller than the increase observed before day 7, indicating that TMP promotes the activation of astrocytes during the acute phase to enhance endogenous repair mechanisms. This finding does not contradict the previous study, one of which focused on the increase in GFAP-positive cells during the acute phase, while the other observed a reduction in GFAP-positive cell area during the chronic phase. This suggests that TMP does not simply upregulate or downregulate GFAP expression but exerts “biphasic” regulation on astrocytes, thereby maximizing the potential for neural repair.
sections.promotion of neural stem cell proliferat: Endogenous neural stem cells (ENSCs), as pluripotent neural stem cells, are located in the central canal region of the spinal cord of adult mammals. They are activated after SCI and then differentiate into various neural cells, promoting endogenous repair and regeneration [ 17 ]. Qi W found that after TMP intervention, the number of proliferating cell markers (BrdU+) and the expression of neural stem/progenitor cell markers (Nestin+) were significantly increased, promoting the proliferation and differentiation of endogenous stem cells [ 18 ]. (2) Improvement of vascular dysfunction .
sections.vasodilation to improve blood supply: Endothelin is present in various organs and tissues, such as the spinal cord and heart. It is the most potent and long-lasting endogenous vasoconstrictor substance discovered to date, causing vasospasm and exacerbating ischemia after SCI. Thromboxane A2 (TXA2) is a potent bioactive substance synthesized and released by platelet microvesicles, which strongly promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) is primarily found in endothelial cells, and the nitric oxide (NO) it produces can dilate blood vessels and inhibit platelet aggregation and adhesion. Several studies have found that after SCI, TMP intervention significantly reduces the levels of endothelin [ 19 ] and thromboxane A2 in the damaged spinal cord tissue of rats, while increasing eNOS expression in the early stages of injury [ 20 ].
sections.inhibition of endothelial cell apoptosis: Endothelial cells are an important component of the blood-spinal cord barrier. SCI can lead to endothelial cell apoptosis, further increasing the permeability of the blood-spinal cord barrier and exacerbating secondary damage to the microvasculature [ 21 ]. The integrity of the vascular structure is a prerequisite for the normal function of the blood-spinal cord barrier. Li DZ found through experiments that after injecting TMP into rats with SCI, the number of endothelial cell apoptoses at different postoperative time points in the TMP group was lower than in the control group [ 22 ]. They suggested that TMP can inhibit endothelial cell apoptosis after acute SCI and simultaneously increase the density of micro vessels. HU found that after injecting TMP into rats with SCI, endothelial cell apoptosis was significantly reduced [ 23 ]. Subsequently, using Micro CT scanning, they discovered that the TMP group had better indicators of vascular quantity, vascular volume fraction, and vascular continuity in the spinal cord tissue compared to the control group, thus proving that TMP can promote angiogenesis by inhibiting endothelial cell apoptosis. Additionally, the main components of micro vessels, such as endothelial cells, type IV collagen, laminin, as well as type I collagen and type XVIII collagen, which regulate vascular regeneration, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) like MMP-2 and MMP-9 [ 24 ], which have a degrading effect on type IV collagen, all play a leading role in maintaining the integrity of the blood-spinal cord barrier. TMP can reduce the expression of matrix metalloproteinases MMP-2 and MMP-9, promote the expression of type IV collagen, laminin, and type I collagen in the early stages after SCI, as well as enhance the expression of type XVIII collagen [ 22 ]. It also inhibits endothelial cell apoptosis, promotes angiogenesis, increases microvascular density, improves vascular morphology, thereby alleviating neural damage.
sections.improvement of hemorheology: Hemorheology is the study of the flow properties and changes in blood and its components. It reflects changes in the internal environment of the circulatory system. After SCI, microcirculatory disorders are closely related to changes in hemorheology. Liu G found that on the 7th day after SCI, TMP significantly reduced whole blood viscosity (at low, high, and medium shear rates) and plasma viscosity [ 25 ]. On the 14th day, TMP increased the red blood cell deformability index. TMP can improve the hypercoagulable state of blood after SCI, promote the repair of microcirculation, and to some extent, prevent complications such as deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs after SCI.
sections.promotion of angiogenesis: PGC-1 factors are involved in intracellular oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis. They can activate estrogen receptor ERR, thereby upregulating vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) gene expression and promoting angiogenesis. He ZY found that TMP can upregulate PGC-1α/ERR-α, improving blood circulation after SCI [ 26 ]. Zhou Y, through vascular immunofluorescence double labeling and synchrotron micro-CT, observed that TMP can multidimensionally promote vascular repair and improve microcirculation after SCI [ 27 ]. In terms of two-dimensional structure, it significantly increases the microvascular density and the number of new blood vessels in the damaged area. In the more detailed three-dimensional structure, it mainly acts on functional micro vessels (diameter < 40 μm), accelerating the remodeling of a more intact microvascular three-dimensional network by increasing total vascular capacity, reducing vascular tortuosity, and enhancing the connectivity of the vascular network. Wu TD also observed that TMP can significantly increase blood flow perfusion in the damaged spinal cord (vascular volume fraction, VVF) [ 28 ], dilate micro vessel diameters, promote the recovery of micro vessel numbers, upregulate the expression of VEGF, and promote angiogenesis, thereby enhancing the recovery of microcirculation. (3) Anti-inflammatory . The expression of C-reactive protein in the serum of rats after SCI was significantly increased. After the addition of TMP, the expression of C-reactive protein was significantly reduced compared to the model group, indicating that TMP can improve the inflammatory microenvironment in rats with SCI [ 29 ].
sections.regulation of interleukins: Interleukins play a significant role in transmitting information, activating and regulating immune cells, mediating T and B lymphocyte activation, and contributing to inflammation. Li XM found that after SCI in rats, the injection of TMP led to an increase in interleukin 10 (IL-10) and a decrease in interleukin 18 (IL-18) expression [ 30 ]. TMP can restore neurological function after SCI by inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting the expression of anti-inflammatory factors. Wang C found that TMP can reduce the expression of various pro-inflammatory cytokines (including IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-18), and these effects can be reversed by the HO-1 inhibitor (ZnPP) and the Akt inhibitor (LY294002) [ 31 ]. TMP inhibited the reduction of Akt phosphorylation and increased the expression of Nrf2 in rats after SCI. This inhibitory effect was suppressed by LY294002 but not by ZnPP. Therefore, TMP can improve the inflammatory response after SCI through the Akt/Nrf2/HO-1 pathway. TMP first activates the Akt signaling, which further activates the transcription factor Nrf2. Activated Nrf2 enters the nucleus, binds to the promoter region of the HO-1 gene, and upregulates the expression of HO-1. Abnormal activation of signaling pathways such as STAT3 can promote the secretion of IL-17. Zhang N found that TMP can effectively inhibit the phosphorylation of STAT3 and the expression of IL-17 after SCI [ 32 ]. TMP can suppress STAT3 activity, reduce IL-17 levels, and promote spinal cord recovery. High expression of COX-2 catalyzes the production of large amounts of prostaglandins, particularly PGE2. PGE2 is a potent pro-inflammatory factor that further amplifies the inflammatory response. Microglia are the primary immune cells in the central nervous system. After SCI, microglia are rapidly activated. Moderate activation in the early stages after injury helps clear debris, but excessive activation releases large amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Shin JW found that TMP treatment can also reduce COX-2 expression after SCI and attenuate microglial activation at 48 h post-SCI [ 33 ]. Additionally, TMP promotes the polarization of microglia from the M1 type to the M2 type, thereby protecting neurons [ 34 ]. In addition, the NF-κB pathway is involved in regulating the inflammatory response after SCI. Abnormal activation of NF-κB in neurons and glial cells can upregulate NF-κB-dependent pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, leading to the infiltration of inflammatory cells and exacerbating secondary damage [ 35 ]. Liu G found that TMP reduced the protein expression of TNFR1, IκB-α, and NF-κB p65 in spinal cord tissue. The inhibition of the inflammatory response by TMP may be related to the modulation of the TNFR1/IκB-α/NF-κB p65 signaling pathway [ 36 ]. Hu JZ and Xiao ZM found that TMP not only regulates the expression of IL-10 and IL-18 after SCI but also promotes the expression of IκB-α, inhibiting the expression of MIF and NF-κB [ 37 ]. They suggested that the mechanism by which TMP reduces NF-κB may involve the inhibition of MIF expression, leading to increased expression of IκB-α. Additionally, P2 × 7R is an important member of the purinergic receptor family, triggered by ATP, leading to the release of inflammatory and immune mediators. Fan X found that after TMP treatment, the number of activated microglia (IBA-1+) expressing P2 × 7R (P2 × 7R+/IBA-1 + cells) in spinal cord tissue was significantly reduced [ 38 ]. TMP also significantly decreased the expression levels of key proteins in the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, including NLRP3 and activated Caspase-1, as well as downregulated the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 induced by SCI. Therefore, TMP effectively improves the inflammatory response after SCI by targeting the P2 × 7R/NLRP3 axis.
sections.inhibition of neutrophil infiltration: Neutrophils can rapidly infiltrate the injury site within 24 h after SCI, thereby mediating the inflammatory response. Myeloperoxidase is a heme protein, and external stimuli can lead to the accumulation of neutrophils, which in turn release myeloperoxidase. Fan LH found that myeloperoxidase activity in spinal cord tissue significantly increased in response to ischemia-reperfusion injury, while TMP treatment notably reduced myeloperoxidase activity in the injury area and decreased neutrophil infiltration [ 10 ]. P-selectin is expressed on the surface of activated endothelial cells and platelets, and it mediates initial cell adhesion, initiating the adhesion and migration cascade of leukocytes, especially neutrophils. Once neutrophils are activated by adhesion, they release neutrophil elastase (NE), which promotes the expression of IL-2 and IL-6, thereby exacerbating the inflammatory response. Li JH found that TMP can inhibit the expression of P-selectin in spinal cord tissue after acute SCI in rats, reduce the levels of neutrophil elastase, and alleviate secondary damage caused by the inflammatory response [ 39 ]. (4) Inhibition of neuronal apoptosis .
sections.regulation of the caspase family: Caspases are Ca²⁺-dependent proteases. After acute SCI, Caspases can induce neuronal apoptosis [ 40 ]. Shen ZX found that in SCI rats treated with TMP, the expression of Caspase-3 decreased at all postoperative time points, reaching the lowest value on the 7th day [ 41 ]. TMP can inhibit neuronal apoptosis by regulating the expression of Caspase-3. The expression of Fas-associated death domain protein (FADD) activates the caspase cascade to execute apoptosis. Wang SX found that in the TMP injection group, the expression of Caspase-8 and FADD decreased at different postoperative time points [ 42 ].
sections.regulation of the bcl-2 family: The Bcl-2 family is closely associated with cell apoptosis. Bcl-2 protein inhibits apoptosis, while Bax protein antagonizes its effect, forming a positive and negative regulation system for cell apoptosis [ 43 ]. Sun HY found that TMP can promote the expression of Bcl-2 and inhibit the expression of Bax after SCI [ 44 ]. A significant change in numerous miRNAs was observed in rats after SCI, with miR-214-3p being significantly upregulated. miRNA is a short non-coding RNA, and miR-214-3p is a pro-apoptotic factor in SCI. It directly targets Bcl-2 mRNA, leading to the degradation of Bcl-2 protein, thereby accelerating neuronal apoptosis in the spinal cord. Fan YZ confirmed that TMP inhibits cell apoptosis in vivo by reducing miR-214-3p levels and increasing Bcl2l2 expression [ 45 ]. Wang G found that TMP can upregulate the expression of miRNA-24 in spinal cord tissue after SCI in rats, while simultaneously downregulating the expression of the pro-apoptotic Bim protein in the Bcl-2 family [ 46 ]. Huang JH found that TMP can inhibit neuronal apoptosis by increasing the expression of miRNA-21 and decreasing the expression of pro-apoptotic genes such as FasL, PTEN, and PDCD4 [ 47 ]. In addition, Sun HY also found that TMP reduces neuronal apoptosis and inhibits the occurrence of secondary damage by suppressing the expression of the pro-apoptotic gene c-fos after SCI [ 48 ]. (5) Antioxidant stress Malondialdehyde (MDA) is the end product of lipid peroxidation and is cytotoxic. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an endogenous antioxidant that acts to protect cells. Pu QL found that TMP can increase the SOD activity in spinal cord tissue and inhibit the generation of MDA, showing significant antioxidant damage protection [ 49 ]. The Nrf2 pathway is involved in regulating oxidative stress injury, and its downstream molecule HO-1 can degrade heme and exert antioxidant effects by regulating free iron metabolism. Under physiological conditions, Nrf2 binds with Keap1 to form the Nrf2-Keap1 dimer. In the case of redox imbalance, the Keap1 dimer is competitively bound by P62, which disrupts the binding with Nrf2 and releases its transcriptional function. Tao JW found that in the TMP group, the expression levels of Nrf2, HO-1, and P62 in spinal cord tissue were higher than those in the model group, while the expression of Keap1 was significantly lower than that in the model group [ 50 ]. Additionally, ROS expression was lower in the TMP group compared to the model group. These findings preliminarily demonstrate that TMP can exert neuroprotective effects by regulating antioxidant activity through the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway. In addition, Liu G found that TMP inhibits oxidative stress after SCI, which may also be related to the regulation of the TNFR1/IκB-α/NF-κB p65 signaling pathway [ 36 ]. Huo LY found that the decrease in PKD1 gene expression after SCI is associated with significant oxidative stress, and TMP effectively reversed this response [ 3 ]. (6) Improvement of iron metabolism After SCI, ruptured red blood cells release a large amount of free iron ions (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺), which accumulate at the injury site, causing local iron metabolism disorders, known as iron overload. Through the Fenton reaction, a large amount of reactive oxygen species is generated, inducing ferroptosis in neuronal cells. Regulating iron metabolism disorders is of great significance for SCI repair [ 51 ]. Fan X found that after TMP intervention, the expression of FTH1 and FTL proteins was promoted following SCI [ 52 ]. It is known that FTH1 and FTL can bind free iron ions to form ferritin, thereby reducing the content of free iron ions and regulating iron metabolism [ 53 ], therefore, the average absorbance value of Prussian blue staining in spinal cord tissue was significantly reduced compared to the model group, indicating that TMP can reduce iron deposition. After SCI, local iron overload and stress can activate a series of lipid peroxidation reactions, both of which can induce ferroptosis following SCI [ 54 ]. GPX4 is a cysteine-containing, glutathione-dependent enzyme and a key regulator of ferroptosis. It converts glutathione into oxidized glutathione, thereby reducing lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress damage [ 55 ]. Tao JW found that in the TMP group, compared to the model group, the protein expression levels of GPX4, ferritin heavy chain, and iron export proteins in spinal cord tissue were increased [ 56 ]. At the same time, glutathione and SOD levels were elevated, and MDA levels were reduced. Additionally, the expression of neuron-specific nuclear protein in spinal cord tissue was increased. Based on this, it is inferred that TMP can exert neuroprotective effects by regulating lipid peroxidation and iron metabolism to inhibit neuronal ferroptosis. ACSL4 is a key isomerase that can convert polyunsaturated fatty acids into unsaturated fatty acid phospholipids, thereby increasing the cell’s sensitivity to ferroptosis [ 57 ]. Liu G found that TMP improved the microstructure of mitochondria, reduced the levels of ROS, GSH, MDA, and SOD, increased GPX4 levels, and simultaneously reduced ACSL4 levels and inhibited glial scar formation. Additionally, the effects of TMP could be reversed by using RSL3, a GPX4 inhibitor [ 58 ]. These findings suggest that TMP may alleviate ferroptosis and lipid peroxidation through the GPX4/ACSL4 axis. The transcription factor NRF2, which is the nuclear factor of NFE2L2, regulates the transcription of most ferroptosis-related genes by binding to antioxidant response elements [ 59 ]. Tao JW found that compared to the model group, the TMP group showed increased expression of NRF2, and the levels of iron metabolism-related molecules FTH1, FTL, and FPN1 were higher in the TMP group. This preliminary evidence suggests that TMP regulates iron metabolism and the NRF2/ARE pathway [ 60 ]. (7) Regulation of ion homeostasis
sections.antagonism of calcium ion influx: After SCI, the imbalance of ion homeostasis involves various ion abnormalities and cellular dysfunctions, such as calcium overload, potassium efflux, and sodium influx. Particularly, calcium ions are critical, as the significant increase in cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ exacerbates vasospasm and ischemia, damages mitochondrial function, and acts as an essential cofactor promoting cell necrosis and apoptosis [ 61 ]. Li GH found that after TMP treatment, the activity of spinal cord mitochondrial PLA2 and the concentration of MDA were reduced, while the activity of SOD and Ca²⁺-Mg²⁺-ATPase was increased [ 62 ]. TMP antagonized calcium ion influx and alleviated oxidative stress-mediated damage to mitochondrial membrane structure and function. Sun HY found that after injecting TMP into rats with SCI, the levels of Ca²⁺ and water content in the spinal cord tissue were reduced, alleviating electrolyte imbalance in the injured spinal cord area and preventing a series of pathological responses caused by intracellular calcium overload [ 63 ].
sections.inhibition of potassium ion efflux: Li H found that TMP can inhibit the outward delayed rectifier potassium current in the anterior horn motor neurons of rats with complete spinal cord transection, stabilize the membrane potential, and protect spinal cord neurons [ 64 ]. (8) Anti-pyroptosis Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death, primarily characterized by inflammasome formation, caspase and GSDMD activation, and the extensive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. This process disrupts cellular integrity and exacerbates the inflammatory response [ 65 ]. Tao B found that TMP intervention could downregulate the protein expression of NLRP3, ASC, Caspase-1, and GSDMD in the pyroptosis pathway following spinal cord injury (SCI). Additionally, TMP was shown to suppress NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway [ 34 ]. (9) Regulation of autophagy Autophagy is a crucial defense mechanism that maintains cellular metabolism and homeostasis by eliminating protein aggregates and damaged organelles. By activating autophagy, cell death can be inhibited, offering neuroprotective effects in SCI [ 66 ]. Macrophages, key components of the immune system, can phagocytose damaged tissue debris and pathogens, regulate inflammation, and assist in tissue repair. Song XM observed that TMP intervention increased both the number of autophagosomes and the expression level of LC3Ⅱ protein in spinal cord macrophages following damage [ 67 ]. Therefore, TMP may effectively repair SCI in rats, with its molecular mechanism likely linked to the activation of autophagy in spinal cord macrophages. TMP demonstrates powerful potential in treating SCI, highlighting its multifaceted and multi-target characteristics. It exerts its effects through various pathways at the cellular and molecular levels, including antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anti-inflammatory pathways. TMP also exhibits network-based regulation, enabling precise intervention at key molecular or pathway hubs within the pathological network of SCI. This allows for the effective modulation of multiple interconnected pathological and physiological processes, resulting in synergistic therapy and comprehensive repair. For instance, TMP inhibits apoptosis, promotes angiogenesis, and supports neural regeneration and repair by decreasing miR-497-5p expression while increasing EGFL7 expression [ 68 ];Furthermore, TMP reduces inflammation, oxidative stress, and other responses following SCI by downregulating the NF-κB pathway.
