sections.heterogeneity analysis: Education level groups conducted the heterogeneity analysis for several theoretical and methodological reasons. First, education level serves as a proxy for socioeconomic status and health literacy, both of which significantly influence the adoption of health behaviours and sleep hygiene practices. Second, educational attainment affects individuals’ access to health information and their ability to implement lifestyle modifications effectively. Third, previous literature suggests that the relationship between physical activity and sleep outcomes varies across different socioeconomic strata. Education level was selected over other demographic factors (such as income or occupation) because it remains relatively stable throughout adulthood and is less susceptible to reverse causation bias in longitudinal studies. In this study, heterogeneity analyses were conducted to examine differences in factors influencing sleep duration among middle-aged and older adults from different educational background groups. Please refer to Fig. 4 for further details. Fig. 4 Forest Plot of Heterogeneity Analysis by Education In the primary school and below education level group, the effect of marital status on sleep duration was significantly positive ( β = 0.389, p < 0.001). In contrast, in the junior high school education level group, the effect was not significant ( β = 0.136, p > 0.1). In the high school and above education level group, marital status had a significantly positive impact ( β = 0.272, p < 0.05). The squared term of age was significantly positive in both the primary school and below group (β = 0.000, p < 0.10) and the junior high school group ( β = 0.001, p < 0.05). However, the squared age term coefficient was insignificant in the high school and above group ( β = 0.000, p > 0.10). The interaction term between males and age was significantly negative in the lower secondary education level group ( β = -0.114, p < 0.05), but not significant in the primary school and below ( β = -0.051, p > 0.1) and high school and above groups ( β = -0.022, p > 0.1). The interaction term between females and age was not significant across the three education groups. Regarding chronic disease, the coefficient was significantly negative only in the high school and above education level group ( β = -0.097, p < 0.10), with no significant effect in the junior high school or primary school and below groups. Drinking behaviour had a significantly negative effect ( β = -0.095, p < 0.05) in the primary school and below group, whereas alcohol consumption had a non-significant effect in the junior high school and high school and above groups. For physical activity, the direct effect was negative in the primary school and below group ( β = -0.113, p > 0.1) and significantly negative in the middle school group ( β = -0.266, p < 0.10). The interaction between physical activity and time was significantly positive in the middle school group ( β = 0.094, p < 0.05). In contrast, neither the direct effect nor the interaction term for physical activity was significant in the high school and above group. Heterogeneity analyses underscore the significant moderating role of education level in the factors affecting sleep duration in middle-aged and older adults. The findings from the heterogeneity analysis reveal that the long-term cumulative benefits of physical activity on sleep duration are most pronounced in the middle school education group. The effect of social activities and sleep duration is significant only in the primary school and below group. These results underscore the significant moderating role of education level in how these behaviours affect sleep over time.
sections.temporal effects of exercise: physical a: Interestingly, the data revealed a crucial temporal dynamic for physical activity, showing that while a short-term, immediate association with sleep duration might be negative, the long-term, cumulative engagement has a robust positive effect. This pattern strongly suggests that the full realisation of sleep benefits from physical activity is not instantaneous but necessitates long-term adherence. Consistent and sustained physical activity gradually enhances sleep duration by regulating physiological rhythms, effectively alleviating psychological stress, and improving overall physical function [ 22 ]. This finding provides a nuanced perspective beyond cross-sectional studies by demonstrating the ‘maturation’ of the protective effect of exercise over time, a mechanism previously linked to better health and overall well-being in older adults [ 23 ].
sections.impact of social activity on sleep durat: Notably, a positive, though comparatively more modest, long-term effect of social activity on sleep duration was also confirmed in our longitudinal analysis. Active participation in social activities is theorised to provide crucial emotional support, effectively mitigating feelings of loneliness and, indirectly, improving sleep outcomes by enhancing mental health [ 24 ]. Specifically, social engagement can improve both the subjective experience and objective quality of sleep by decreasing loneliness and depressive symptoms, particularly among older adult individuals living alone or widowed [ 25 ]. Furthermore, social activity may indirectly enhance sleep duration by promoting cognitive function and fostering psychological resilience [ 26 ]. This cumulative benefit, although smaller than that observed for physical activity, reinforces the idea that over time, the psychosocial benefits of social integration progressively strengthen their positive influence on sleep health.
sections.differential mechanisms of exercise: phy: Surprisingly, our findings suggest distinct temporal patterns that align with theoretical physiological and psychosocial pathways, although specific biological mechanisms were not directly tested in this model.ageingactivity appears to exert a more direct and substantial long-term effect, primarily through physiological mechanisms, such as optimising circadian rhythms, enhancing cardiovascular function, and regulating neuroendocrine markers. In contrast, social activity contributes to sleep improvement indirectly, predominantly via psychosocial mechanisms, in which sustained engagement reduces feelings of loneliness and alleviates depressive symptoms, thereby fostering emotional support and overall mental well-being [ 27 , 28 ]. This novel separation of long-term mechanisms reinforces the theoretical framework proposed in Fig. 5 , providing empirical evidence for the ‘Cumulative Bridge’ concept, where sustained behavioural inputs lead to greater long-term sleep benefits. Notably, our heterogeneity analysis revealed a significant moderating effect of educational attainment on the long-term impact of health behaviours on sleep duration. Specifically, the most pronounced long-term cumulative benefits of physical activity were observed among the middle school education group, whereas the positive temporal effect of social activities was evident only in the primary school and below group. This differential impact suggests that educational level serves as a critical proxy for health literacy and socioeconomic status, influencing both the adoption of and the physiological response to lifestyle modifications [ 29 – 30 ]. Individuals with lower educational attainment may have less access to comprehensive health information or structured exercise facilities, making the adoption of regular physical activity a greater health gain [ 31 – 32 ], which subsequently translates into a stronger temporal effect on sleep. These findings resonate with the ‘Fundamental Cause Theory’ of health disparities, which posits that individuals with higher socioeconomic status (proxied here by education) are better positioned to deploy flexible resources—such as health literacy and agency—to maximise the health returns of behavioural interventions. The pronounced effect in the educated groups suggests that education may enhance the ‘efficiency’ of translating physical activity into sleep benefits through better adherence and sleep hygiene practices. Prior research also highlights that health literacy—closely linked to educational level—is a determinant of adopting and maintaining healthy behaviours, including sleep-related practices [ 33 – 34 ]. Moreover, meta-analytic evidence suggests that socioeconomic status moderates the conversion of behavioural intentions into actual physical activity [ 35 ]. From a theoretical perspective, the fundamental cause theory underscores that education, as a key component of socioeconomic status, persistently shapes health disparities by providing or limiting access to flexible resources such as knowledge, social support, and power [ 36 ]. This is a crucial novel finding that directly informs policy interventions, underscoring the necessity of designing targeted, educationally sensitive public health programs to maximise the sleep benefits for the most vulnerable segments of the ageing population. Furthermore, the visualisation in Fig. 5 dynamically illustrates the ‘Cumulative Bridge’ concept, with the temporal trends providing a clear interpretation of the short-term adverse and long-term positive effects of physical activity on predicted sleep duration. Specifically, in the initial waves, the predicted sleep duration for the exercise group (blue line) declines more steeply than for the non-exercise group (red line), which is consistent with the estimated immediate adverse direct effect of exercise. However, over subsequent follow-up periods, this trajectory reverses: the exercise curve’s decline substantially slows, while the non-exercise curve continues its descent, leading to a gradually widening gap in favour of the sustained exercise group in later waves. This dynamic shift clearly demonstrates how the long-term engagement effect effectively mitigates age-related declines in sleep duration, supporting the idea that the protective effect of physical activity on sleep duration increases cumulatively over time by improving cardiovascular function, regulating melatonin secretion, and reducing cortisol levels [ 37 ]. In contrast, the impact of social activity on sleep duration suggests a positive effect that emerges earlier, as it helps alleviate loneliness and depressive symptoms, provides emotional support, and enables middle-aged and older adults to experience better sleep early on [ 38 ]. Unlike activity, improving sleep through social activity primarily occurs through psychological pathways, with limited direct effects on physiological mechanisms [ 39 ]. Nevertheless, the findings highlight that activity and social activity act as complementary components in health interventions [ 40 ]. exercise offers long-term physiological benefits, while social activity can effectively alleviate stress and loneliness in the short term [ 41 ]. Fig. 5 Interaction Effect Diagram, Note: wave1: first wave survey; wave2: second wave survey; wave3: third wave survey; wave4: fourth wave survey
sections.effects of marital status, drinking beha: The fixed-effects model robustly confirmed that marital status provides a substantial protective effect on sleep duration in middle-aged and older adults. Marital relationships are believed to indirectly enhance sleep duration by reducing stress perceptions, providing consistent emotional support, and promoting adherence to healthy behaviours [ 42 ]. Moreover, the quality of the marriage relationship critically affects sleep outcomes: high-quality relationships are associated with reduced sleep disorders, while marital conflict can negatively affect sleep [ 43 ]. Conversely, the present study found a consistent and significant negative association between drinking behaviour and sleep duration, suggesting that chronic alcohol consumption is a critical, yet modifiable, factor contributing to the reduction of sleep quality and duration in this demographic. Although alcohol may initially aid sleep onset, the consensus is that it disrupts sleep architecture, leading to fragmented sleep and early awakening problems [ 44 – 45 ]. This negative influence is further compounded as chronic consumption may increase the risk of insomnia and sleep disorders by affecting the balance of neurotransmitters [ 46 ]. Finally, the interaction effect of sex and age showed a greater age-related decline in sleep duration in women. This gender-specific acceleration may be attributed to hormonal fluctuations, particularly during the menopausal stage in women, which can substantially increase the prevalence of sleep disorders [ 47 ].
sections.limitations: This study has several important limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, sleep duration was measured via self-reported questionnaires, which may introduce recall and social desirability biases. Objective sleep measurement devices could provide more accurate assessments in future studies. Second, the study experienced attrition across the nine-year follow-up period, which may introduce selection bias if dropout was related to sleep patterns or health behaviours. Third, the generalizability of findings may be limited to the Chinese cultural context, and cross-cultural validation would strengthen the evidence base. Fourth, although we controlled for several important confounders, unmeasured variables, such as specific mental health conditions, detailed medication use, sleep disorders, and environmental factors, may influence the observed relationships. Fifth, the discrete-time specification, while interpretable, may not capture more nuanced temporal dynamics that could be revealed by continuous-time modelling. Finally, the study measures sleep duration rather than comprehensive sleep quality, which includes factors such as sleep efficiency, sleep latency, and subjective sleep satisfaction. Furthermore, our reliance on a binary exposure measure precludes the examination of intensity-specific dose-response relationships. Additionally, while we propose physiological and psychosocial mechanisms to explain the observed associations, we lacked the specific biomarkers or intermediate psychological variables to conduct formal mediation analyses, making these mechanistic interpretations theoretical rather than empirical. We also acknowledge the potential for bidirectional relationships, or reverse causality, where individuals with superior sleep health may possess the energy reserves necessary to initiate and sustain physical activity. While our fixed-effects strategy controls for time-invariant individual heterogeneity, dynamic selection bias remains a possibility. However, the observed gradual widening of the sleep duration gap over time supports the hypothesis of a cumulative protective effect of activity rather than a selection effect in which good sleepers simply start exercising.
sections.conclusions: This study finds that long-term participation in and social activities positively affects sleep duration, with physical exercise showing a more pronounced long-term impact. Marital status significantly protects sleep duration, while alcohol consumption has a notable negative effect on sleep time. The non-linear relationship between age and sleep duration, along with gender differences, further underscores the complexity of sleep issues in middle-aged and older adults. Building on existing research, this study further validates the multi-dimensional impact of health behaviours on sleep duration, emphasising the complementary role of physical exercise, physical activity, and social activities. The findings suggest specific policy directions: (1) Public health programs should emphasize sustained, long-term physical activity engagement rather than short-term intensive interventions, given the temporal dynamics observed; (2) Community-based social activity programs should be integrated with physical activity initiatives to maximize complementary benefits; (3) Health education should address alcohol consumption patterns as part of comprehensive sleep hygiene promotion; (4) Interventions should consider the differential effects across educational levels, with particular attention to lower-educated populations who showed stronger responses to behavioral interventions.

title: Nuclear export of R-loop by the DDX1 and XPO1 complex promotes senescence-associated secretory phenotype and inflammaging
abstract: Cellular senescence contributes to inflammaging in part through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). R-loops, three-stranded nucleic acid structures, contribute to innate immune response in cancers; however, the role of R-loops in senescence and inflammaging remains largely unknown. Here we show that nuclear-derived cytoplasmic R-loops promote the SASP and inflammaging. We detect an accumulation of nuclear-derived R-loops in the cytoplasm of senescent cells with an enrichment in alpha-satellite repeats. These cytoplasmic R-loops localize into cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCFs) and activate the cGAS–STING innate immune pathway to drive the SASP. We identify the exportin-1 (XPO1)–DEAD-Box helicase 1 (DDX1) complex as essential for the nuclear export of R-loops and their subsequent localization into CCFs. Inhibition of XPO1 with KPT-330 suppresses nuclear R-loop export and its localization into CCFs, attenuates the SASP, mitigates age-associated inflammation and extends healthspan. These findings reveal nuclear export of R-loops as a potential target for suppressing age-associated inflammation.

sections.main: Cellular senescence is characterized by a stable cell cycle arrest and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) that contributes to chronic inflammation during tissue aging, known as inflammaging 1 – 3 . Notably, the SASP is linked to innate immune response through formation of cytoplasmic chromatin fragments (CCFs) and the associated persistent DNA damage response 4 – 7 . R-loops are DNA–RNA hybrid-containing three-stranded nucleic acid structures that are distributed across the genome. R-loops are important intermediates in transcription, DNA replication and repair 8 , 9 . Persistent R-loops stalling causes double-stranded breaks and compromise genome stability 9 , 10 . Thus, formation and timely removal of R-loops in the genome are tightly regulated. Cells employ various mechanisms such as helicases to resolve R-loop structures by unwinding the duplex hybrids 8 , 11 . Beyond their nuclear roles, DNA damage triggers the release of cytoplasmic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and DNA–RNA hybrids to activate innate immune responses in pathological contexts such as chronic inflammation and cancer 12 – 14 . Despite both the SASP and R-loops being linked to persistent DNA damage response, innate immune response and chronic inflammation, the role of R-loops in SASP and its potential implication in inflammaging remains largely unexplored.
sections.cytoplasmic accumulation of nuclear-deri: To investigate R-loop dynamics during senescence, we performed MapR, an antibody-independent and catalytically inactive RNase H-dependent CUT&RUN-based method for genome-wide R-loop profiling 15 , in proliferating and oncogenic HRAS G12V -induced senescent (OIS) IMR90 embryonic human lung fibroblasts (Supplementary Fig. 1a–c ). R-loops are typically associated with the loci of actively transcribed genes 9 , 15 , 16 . Previous studies showed that there is a global reduction in gene transcription in senescent cells and aged tissues 17 , 18 . Consistently, we observed a global decrease in R-loop signals in senescent compared to proliferating cells (Fig. 1a ). Fig. 1 Nuclear-derived accumulation of cytoplasmic R-loops promotes the SASP. a , Heatmaps of genome-wide MapR signal intensity in control and OIS IMR90 cells. b , Slot-blot analysis of R-loop levels in whole cell lysates, cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions from equal numbers of control and OIS IMR90 cells. Relative intensity was qualified with NIH ImageJ and normalized to control levels in whole cell or indicated fractions. SE, short exposure; LE, long exposure. c , The cytoDRIP-seq workflow. d , The genomic distributions of peaks from cytoDRIP-seq and nuclear DRIP-seq (NuDRIP) in OIS IMR90 cells. Promoter regions are defined as ±2 kb from the TSS; gene bodies are defined as entirety of gene, including introns and excluding promoter regions; terminator regions are defined as 300 bp downstream of TTS; and intergenic regions refer to the rest in the genome. Rep, replicate. e , Genomic tracks showing senescence-specific cytoDRIP signals at sites with nuclear R-loop formation. The red bar shows the peak. ALR, alpha-satellite repeat. f , Slot-blot analysis of R-loop levels in whole cell lysates and cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions from equal numbers of control and OIS IMR90 cells with or without treatment of pharmacological XPO1 inhibitor KPT-330 (100 nM) or XPO1 knockdown. Relative intensity was qualified with NIH ImageJ and normalized to control levels in whole cells or indicated fractions. g , Slot-blot analysis of R-loop levels in whole-cell lysates and cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions from equal numbers of OIS IMR90 cells with or without cytoplasmic expression of RNase H (RH-NES). Relative intensity was qualified with NIH ImageJ and normalized to control levels in whole cell or indicated fractions. h , i , Immunoblot analysis of the indicated proteins in control and OIS IMR90 cells with or without RH-NES expression ( h ). In addition, expression of representative SASP genes in the indicated cells was measured by RT–qPCR ( i ). j , Expression of representative SASP genes in the control and OIS IMR90 cells with or without KPT-330 treatment was measured by RT–qPCR. Data represent mean ± s.e.m. n = 3 biologically independent experiments unless otherwise stated. P values were calculated using a two-tailed t -test. Source data We next examined whether the subcellular distribution of R-loops is altered during senescence. Consistent with the MapR results, we observed an overall decrease in R-loop levels in senescent compared to proliferating cells (Fig. 1b ); however, while the levels of nuclear R-loops were reduced, we observed an increase in its cytoplasmic levels in senescent cells (Fig. 1b ). To determine the origin of cytoplasmic R-loops accumulated in senescent cells, we conducted cytoplasmic DNA–RNA hybrid immunoprecipitation (DRIP) sequencing (CytoDRIP-seq) analysis 13 using S9.6 antibody in proliferating and senescent cells (Fig. 1c ). To limit the issue that S9.6 antibody can also bind to double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) 19 , we used ssDNA moiety of the hybrids for sequencing and obtained highly reproducible signals (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). The sequencing reads were predominantly mapped to nucleus with the rest mapped to mitochondria genome (Extended Data Fig. 1b ). Notably, the peaks identified in senescent cells were less than those in control proliferating cells (Extended Data Fig. 1c ). Of note, nearly half of these peaks were mapped to intergenic regions (Fig. 1d ). As nuclear R-loops are enriched for certain repetitive elements 8 , we determined whether cytoplasmic R-loops overlapped with those repeats in senescent cells. We discovered that cytoDRIP regions were specifically enriched for alpha-satellite repeats (Extended Data Fig. 1d ), which overlapped with sites that form nuclear R-loops in senescent cells (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 1e ). Moreover, despite cytoDRIP regions mapped to smaller areas in the genome compared to nuclear DRIP regions, their peak strength was highly correlated with nuclear DRIP-seq levels (Extended Data Fig. 1f ). These data suggest that cytoplasmic R-loops accumulated during senescence are primarily derived from a small subset of nuclear R-loops with an enrichment in alpha-satellite repeats. Nuclear R-loops and their derived RNA–DNA hybrids can be targeted by nucleotide excision repair endonucleases and exported to the cytoplasm in a nuclear export protein exportin-1(XPO1)-dependent manner where they engage innate immune sensors including cGAS 12 , 13 , 20 , 21 . For example, endonucleases XPF and XPG are involved in R-loops excision from nuclear chromatin 10 , 13 , 21 . Thus, we next asked whether they play a role in the cytoplasmic accumulation of R-loops. Notably, both XPF and XPG were upregulated in senescent cells (Extended Data Fig. 2a ). Knockdown of either XPF or XPG in senescent cells led to a decrease in the cytoplasmic R-loop level (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b ), further supporting the nuclear origin of cytoplasmic R-loops. Finally, to determine whether cytoplasmic R-loops are exported from nucleus, we treated senescent cells with KPT-330, an inhibitor that blocks nuclear export 22 . Indeed, treatment with KPT-330 reduced the accumulation of cytoplasmic R-loops, while increased R-loop levels in the nucleus (Fig. 1f ). A similar observation was made by short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated knockdown of XPO1 in senescent cells (Fig. 1f ). Together, these data support that cytoplasmic R-loops originate from the nucleus and are actively exported in senescent cells.
sections.cytoplasmic r-loops localize to ccfs and: Cytoplasmic nucleic acids are known to activate innate immune signaling, which drives SASP during senescence 4 . To determine whether cytoplasmic R-loops accumulated in senescent cells contribute to the SASP, we expressed cytoplasm-localized RNase H1 with nuclear export signal (RH-NES) 13 in senescent cells to selectively digest cytoplasmic R-loops (Supplementary Fig. 2a ). Indeed, RH-NES significantly reduced cytoplasmic R-loop levels without affecting nuclear R-loop levels (Fig. 1g ), which correlated with the suppression of IRF3 signaling and SASP genes expression (Fig. 1h,i ). This suggests that cytoplasmic R-loops contribute to the innate immune response in senescent cells. Notably, senescence markers such as senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity (SA-β-gal) and p21 expression remained unchanged (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Fig. 2b,c ). This indicates that the SASP suppression by RH-NES expression was not a consequence of overcoming senescence. Similar observations were made in therapy-induced senescent ovarian cancer OVCAR3 cells (Supplementary Fig. 3 ). Moreover, reducing cytoplasmic R-loop levels in senescent cells through XPF or XPG knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 2c ) or by inhibiting nuclear export via KPT-330 or XPO1 knockdown also impaired the SASP (Fig. 1f,j and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e ). These findings support that cytoplasmic R-loops promote the SASP. Senescent cells undergo a global chromatin reorganization and fragmentation 12 . Following the nuclear envelope breakage, the chromatin fragments appear in the cytoplasm as CCFs 23 . CCFs play a critical role in driving the SASP 5 , 24 . Given that cytoplasmic R-loops were accumulated during senescence, we next examined the spatial localization of cytoplasmic R-loops. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed strong colocalization of R-loops and CCFs, marked by γH2AX, in senescent cells (Fig. 2a,b ). Notably, these signals were sensitive to RNase H treatment, confirming that the antibody-detected signal was derived from R-loop structure (Supplementary Fig. 4a,b ). Further, as the S9.6 antibody also recognizes dsRNA, though the affinity is much lower compared to that for R-loop structures, we stained dsRNA in senescent cells. Notably, the dsRNA signal was not detected in CCFs (Supplementary Fig. 4c,d ). Together, these data suggest that R-loops localize to CCFs in senescent cells. Fig. 2 R-loops localize to CCFs in the cytoplasm. a , b , Immunostaining for γH2AX and S9.6 in control and OIS IMR90 cells ( a ). Arrows indicate an example of γH2AX and S9.6 colocalized CCF. γH2AX-positive CCFs that were positive for S9.6 in OIS IMR90 cells were quantified ( b ). Scale bars, 10 μm. c , Immunoblot analysis of the indicated proteins in control and OIS IMR90 cells with or without lamin B1 knockdown. d , e , Cells with γH2AX-positive CCF ( d ) and with CCF positive for both S9.6 and γH2AX ( e ) were quantified in OIS IMR90 cells with or without lamin B1 knockdown. f , Slot-blot analysis of R-loop levels in the cytoplasmic fraction from equal numbers of OIS IMR90 cells with or without lamin B1 knockdown. Relative intensity was qualified with NIH ImageJ and normalized to control levels. g , h , γH2AX-positive CCFs that were positive for S9.6 ( g ) and cells with γH2AX-positive CCF ( h ) in OIS IMR90 cells with or without KPT-330 treatment (100 nM) were quantified. i , j , Fluorescently labeled DNA–RNA hybrids were transfected into OIS IMR90 cells and analyzed for their localization into CCFs ( i ). The arrow indicates an example of a DNA–RNA hybrid localized to a CCF. The percentage of CCFs positive for the DNA–RNA hybrids was quantified ( j ). Scale bar, 10 μm. k – m , Schematic of CCF fractionation ( k ). Solubility of CCF-localized R-loops was measured by slot-blot analysis in each fraction; cytoplasmic and chromatin protein markers were analyzed by immunoblot for validation ( l ). Relative intensity was qualified with NIH ImageJ and normalized to control levels in indicated fractions ( m ). Data represent mean ± s.e.m. n = 3 biologically independent experiments unless otherwise stated. P values were calculated using a two-tailed t -test. Source data To determine whether CCFs are required for cytoplasmic R-loop-induced SASP, we treated the senescent cells with trichostatin A (TSA), a histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi), to suppress CCF formation 24 . Indeed, a low dose of TSA reduced both CCF formation and SASP gene expression in senescent cells without affecting senescence-associated growth arrest (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d ). Notably, RH-NES expression in TSA-treated senescent cells failed to further suppress the SASP (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f ), suggesting that CCFs are required for cytoplasmic R-loop-induced SASP in senescent cells. Together, these findings are consistent with the notion that cytoplasmic R-loops localize to CCFs and contribute to the SASP induction. We next explored the relationship between CCF formation and cytoplasmic R-loops accumulation. As downregulation of lamin B1 compromises integrity of the nuclear envelope and elevates CCF 23 , 25 , we knocked down lamin B1 in senescent cells (Fig. 2c ). Indeed, CCF formation was significantly increased by lamin B1 knockdown (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3g ), which was accompanied by an increase in R-loop positive CCFs (Fig. 2e ); however, the level of cytoplasmic R-loops was not increased by lamin B1 knockdown as determined cytoDRIP (Fig. 2f ). These findings suggest that cytoplasmic R-loops are not a consequence of nuclear envelope breakdown and CCF formation. Indeed, senescent cells with KPT-330 treatment that suppressed the R-loop nuclear export (Fig. 1f ) decreased R-loop localization into CCF without affecting CCF formation (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 3h ). Consistently, shXPF or shXPG that decreased cytoplasmic R-loop levels (Extended Data Fig. 2b ) also decreased R-loop localization into CCF without decreasing CCF formation (Extended Data Fig. 3i–k ). We next directly determined whether cytoplasmic R-loops can localize into CCF. Toward this goal, we transfected fluorescently labeled RNA–DNA hybrids into senescent cells. Indeed, the transfected hybrids localized into CCFs in senescent cells (Fig. 2i,j ). In contrast, transfected fluorescently labeled dsRNA failed to localize into CCFs in senescent cells (Supplementary Fig. 4c,e ). These results show that the cytoplasmic RNA–DNA hybrids can be recruited to CCFs. Consistently, analysis of eluted fractions of purified CCFs from increasing salt concentrations showed that the hybrids were most abundant in the soluble fractions of CCFs (Fig. 2k–m ). Together, these results are consistent with a model whereby R-loop nuclear export and CCF formation are two independent processes and localization of R-loops into CCFs occurs in the cytoplasm after their nuclear export.
sections.the xpo1\u2013ddx1 complex mediates r-lo: We next investigated the mechanism underlying R-loop nuclear export and localization to CCFs. Notably, XPO1 does not directly bind R-loops (Fig. 3a ), implying the involvement of adaptor proteins. To identify candidate R-loop-binding proteins (RBPs), we performed cytoplasmic R-loop pulldown followed by liquid chromatography (LC)–tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis in control proliferating and senescent cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a ). Among 1,745 RBPs identified, 1,087 were enriched in senescent cells (more than 1.5-fold enrichment in two biologically independent experiments) (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 1 ). To enable R-loop export, candidate proteins are expected to be nuclear-localized. By combining Gene Ontology Cellular Component annotation and UniProtKB database, we identified 367 nuclear-localized RBPs. Cross-referencing with a known CCF protein component 26 yielded 194 candidates that showed enrichment for 11 functional subsets, including helicases (Fig. 3b,c ). Notably, helicases are known to bind to R-loops 11 , 27 . We focused on DDX1, a DEAD-box RNA helicase with a known role in the DNA damage response 28 , 29 , due to its strong enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 4b ). Indeed, we validated that DDX1 interacted with R-loops (Fig. 3d ). We next examined the localization of DDX1 in senescent cells. Consistent with its interaction with R-loops in senescent cells, we observed a colocalization of DDX1 and R-loops in CCFs (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d ). Moreover, analysis of CCF fractionations revealed the presence of DDX1 in soluble fractions in which R-loops are enriched (Fig. 2o,p and Extended Data Fig. 4e ). To determine whether DDX1 directly binds to the R-loop structure, we assembled R-loops for biochemical assays 30 (Supplementary Fig. 5 ). The electrophoresis mobility shift assay (EMSA) showed that DDX1 bound to R-loop structures in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 3g ). Of note, although DDX1 was previously reported to resolve the RNA–DNA duplex 29 , we did not detect its unwinding ability in resolving a three-stranded R-loop structure (Fig. 3g ). Fig. 3 Cytoplasmic R-loops localize into CCF through nuclear export mediated by the XPO1/DDX1 complex. a , Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of XPO1 and R-loops using the S9.6 antibody in the cytoplasmic fraction from control and OIS IMR90 cells. b , c , LC–MS/MS analysis of cytoplasmic RBPs from control and OIS IMR90 cells. FC, fold change. d , Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of DDX1 and R-loops using S9.6 antibody in the cytoplasmic fraction from control and OIS IMR90 cells. e , f , Immunostaining for DDX1 and S9.6 in OIS IMR90 cells ( e ). Despite a decrease in total XPO1 protein expression in senescent cells, we observed an enhanced interaction between DDX1 and XPO1 in senescent compared to proliferating cells (Extended Data Fig. 4f ). XPO1 recognizes the leucine-rich NES, which is typically composed of four hydrophobic residues separated by 1–3 linker residues (Φ-X 1–3 - Φ -X 2-3 - Φ -X 1–3 - Φ motif) 31 . Notably, DDX1 contains an NES in its C-terminal domain (Fig. 3h ). This was accompanied by impaired R-loop localization into CCFs without affecting CCF formation itself (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 5c,d ). Consistently, the SASP was impaired by DDX1 knockdown in senescent cells (Fig. 3l and Extended Data Fig. 5e ), and this suppression is not due to an overcome of senescence per se (Extended Data Fig. 5f,g ). Replacement of endogenous DDX1 with ectopically expressed wild-type DDX1, but not an NES-mutant DDX1, in senescent cells restored R-loop’s localization into CCFs (Fig. 3m,n ). These data suggest that the nuclear export function of DDX1 is required for R-loop export and associated SASP induction. Notably, both wild-type and NES-mutant DDX1 interacted with R-loops, suggesting the observed changes in NES-mutant DDX1 expressing cells are not due to its inability to interact with R-loops (Extended Data Fig. 5j ). Indeed, XPO1 inhibitors significantly decreased the colocalization of DDX1 and R-loops in CCFs without impairing their interaction (Extended Data Fig. 5k–m ). These findings suggest that DDX1 is required for R-loop nuclear export and its subsequent localization into CCF. As DDX1 is an RNA helicase, we next determined whether its enzymatic activity is important for its role in R-loop nuclear export. Toward this goal, we ectopically expressed an enzymatic activity defective K52A-mutant DDX1 (ref. 32 ) in senescent cells with endogenous DDX1 knockdown and observed no significant changes in R-loop localization into CCFs or the SASP gene expression (Fig. 3m,n and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i ). Finally, to demonstrate directly the role of DDX1 in R-loop nuclear export, we performed cytoDRIP-seq in senescent cells with or without DDX1 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 6a–e ). We noticed a trend toward decrease in nuclear-derived cytoplasmic R-loops in DDX1 knockdown cells compared to controls (Extended Data Fig. 6b ). Notably, DDX1 knockdown led to loss of alpha-satellite repeats from cytoplasm of senescent cells (Figs. 1e and 3o and Extended Data Fig. 6d,e ). We further validated this finding by performing fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) assay with probes designed from these alpha-satellite regions (Fig. 3p–r ). Consistently, RNA-immunoprecipitation (RIP)-seq using an anti-DDX1 antibody also showed a significant enrichment for alpha-satellite repeats in senescent compared to control cells (Extended Data Fig. 6f ). Together, these findings support that the XPO1–DDX1 complex function as a key mediator of R-loop nuclear export and its localization to CCFs to promote the SASP in senescent cells.

sections.targeting r-loop nuclear export suppress: Sterile inflammation, also known as ‘inflammaging’, is a hallmark of tissue aging 2 , 3 . Cellular senescence contributes to tissue aging partially through the SASP. Given the critical role of cytoplasmic R-loops in promoting the SASP, we next explored the implications of this mechanism in inflammaging. Due to lack of commercially available inhibitors for DDX1, we treated chronologically aged mice (22 months old) with the XPO1 inhibitor KPT-330 to suppress the R-loop’s nuclear export. We focused on our analysis in liver because cellular senescence is widely implicated in age-dependent liver dysfunction and senescent hepatocytes in aged liver is associated with the SASP and senescence-associated distension of centromeric satellites 40 , 41 . We first stained mouse livers for expression of p21, a marker of senescence 41 . Consistent with our in vitro data, treatment with KPT-330 did not significantly affect p21-positive senescent hepatocytes or CCF formation in aged mouse livers (Fig. 7a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a ). Notably, CCF formation was highly correlated with senescent hepatocytes in aged mouse livers (Extended Data Fig. 9b ). We next stained for R-loops in mouse livers. In contrast to young mouse liver, a diffuse pattern of R-loops across the whole cell with a significant accumulation in the cytoplasm was observed in aged hepatocytes, which was markedly reversed by KPT-330 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d ). Notably, R-loop localization to CCFs in hepatocytes of aged mouse livers was significantly decreased by KPT-330 treatment (Fig. 7c,d ). This reduction in cytoplasmic R-loops was accompanied by decreased expression of proinflammatory SASP factors and reduced immune cell infiltration as determined by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and immunohistochemistry for CD3 and CD68 (Fig. 7e–h and Extended Data Fig. 9e,f ). Furthermore, KPT-330 treatment attenuated liver fibrosis as measured by collagen accumulation and lowered plasma cholesterol levels in aged mice (Fig. 7i,k ), both of which are linked to chronic inflammation 41 , 42 . Likewise, the increase in plasma alanine transaminase (ALT) level, a marker of hepatocyte damage, in aged mice was significantly decreased by KPT-330 treatment (Fig. 7l ). sections.discussion: R-loops are critical regulators of genomic stability, while their dysregulation has been implicated in cancers and inflammation 13 , 14 . Here, we identify a mechanism by which a subset of nuclear R-loops is exported to the cytoplasm during senescence, where it localizes to CCFs and activates the cGAS–STING pathway, thereby driving the SASP and contributing to inflammaging. Notably, these R-loops are released from chromatin in the nuclear in an XPF/XPG-dependent manner, and are exported into cytoplasm in a XPO1/DDX1-dependent and CCF formation-independent manner. Thus, our findings provide a mechanistic basis by which cytoplasmic R-loops promote innate immunity through their nuclear export and localization into the CCFs during senescence. Our data support a sequential mechanism at cell biology level for R-loop localization to CCFs (Extended Data Fig. 7l ). We demonstrated that DDX1 is required for R-loop export from nuclei to cytoplasm and their subsequent localization to CCFs (Fig. 4e ). Due to the compartmental distribution (nuclei versus cytoplasm), the interaction between DDX1 and cGAS can only occur in the presence of hybrid in the cytoplasm because they can each interact with R-loops (Fig. 4b ), but not themselves directly (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e ). Once in cytoplasm, the localization of DDX1 and R-loops to CCFs are cGAS dependent because of the binding between cGAS and R-loops and localized concentration of cGAS at CCFs. Hence, both cGAS and DDX1 are required for R-loop localization to CCFs (Fig. 5e,h ). Biochemically, cGAS can bind an R-loop without DDX1 (Fig. 4k ). Indeed, DDX1 does not affect cGAS activity toward R-loops as determined by 2′3′-cGAMP production (Fig. 4l ). Thus, DDX1 is required for the cGAS–R-loop association in the cytoplasm (Fig. 4b ) due to DDX1-dependent R-loop nuclear export. Although DDX1 was the focus of this study, our data suggest that additional RBPs may contribute to R-loop export and/or its localization into CCFs, as not all R-loop-positive CCFs are DDX1-positive (Extended Data Fig. 5a ). Based on the RBPs that we discovered (Extended Data Fig. 4b ), future studies are warranted to systematically define the R-loop export machinery. Notably, while cGAS has been reported to interact with XPO1 in several cancer cell lines 44 , we did not detect this interaction in senescent primary human IMR90 cells (Fig. 5a ), highlighting cell- and/or context-specific differences in this interaction. Our work also links centromeric R-loops (previously associated with replication stress 8 ) to innate immune response during senescence. Consistently, centromeres undergo distension of centromeric satellites during senescence 45 , which facilitates their transcription during senescence and aging 46 , 47 . The large size and repetitive nature of these nuclear-derived transcripts as determined by cytoDRIP-seq may protect them from degradation and promote robust immunogenicity to activate the cGAS–STING pathway 34 . In addition to the presence of nuclear-exported R-loops, we observed mitochondria-derived R-loops in the cytoplasm of senescent cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b ); however, inhibition of R-loop nuclear export was sufficient to attenuate activation of the cGAS–STING pathway and the associated SASP. These findings suggest that, although we cannot exclude a potential contribution from mitochondria-derived R-loops, nuclear-derived R-loops play a dominant role in this process. Consistent with our findings, selective inhibitors of nuclear export extend lifespan in worms and flies by nuclear enrichment of longevity-associated transcription factors such as HLH-30/TFEB 48 . Our study revealed that in addition to regulating transcription in the nuclei, inhibition of nuclear export suppresses inflammaging by preventing activation of innate immunity by exported R-loop in the cytoplasm. Complementing results obtained using nuclear export inhibitor KPT-330, we identified XPO1 adaptor-DDX1 and performed DDX1 knockdown and rescuing with ectopic wild-type or mutant DDX1 experiments together with biochemical, molecular and cellular assays to show that the DDX1/XPO1-mediated nuclear export of R-loops is critical for cytoplasmic function in senescent cells; however, a limitation of our study is that we cannot formally rule out the possibility that other XPO1 substrates may also contribute to the observed phenotypes. In addition, although targeting this process was associated with a beneficial effect on lifespan (Extended Data Fig. 9h ), this finding remains preliminary, given the small sample size and the exclusive use of female mice. Future studies employing larger and sex-balanced cohorts are warranted to definitively establish the potential of targeting this pathway for lifespan extension. In summary, we uncover a role for R-loop nuclear export in driving innate immune response through the CCF–cGAS–STING signaling axis during senescence. Our findings suggest that targeting R-loop nuclear export offers a promising strategy for mitigating inflammaging.

sections.retrovirus and lentivirus production and: Retrovirus was produced using Phoenix cells 50 . Lentivirus was produced in 293FT cells with packaging plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher, cat. no. 11668019) based on the manufacturer’s instructions. IMR90 fibroblasts infected with viruses encoding the puromycin resistance gene were selected using puromycin (1 μg ml −1 ).
sections.colony-formation assay: Cells were seeded in six-well plates at a density of 3,000 cells per well and cultured for 10 days before staining with 0.05% crystal violet for visualization. Analysis was performed based on integrated density using the NIH ImageJ (1.48v).
sections.qpcr with reverse transcription: Extracted RNA was used for qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) using a high-capacity complementary DNA reverse transcription kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat. no. 4368814). Quantitative PCR was performed using a QuantStudio 3 real-time PCR system. The following primers were used for reverse-transcriptase qPCR: Human GAPDH Forward: 5′-GTCTCCTCTGACTTCAACAGCG-3′, Reverse: 5′-ACCACCCTGTTGCTGTAGCCAA-3′; Human IL1B Forward: 5′-AGCTCGCCAGTGAAATGATGG-3′, Reverse: 5′-GTCCTGGAAGGAGCACTTCAT-3′; Human IL6 Forward: 5′-ACATCCTCGACGGCATCTCA-3′, Reverse: 5′-TCACCAGGCAAGTCTCCTCA-3′; Human IL8 Forward: 5′-GCTCTGTGTGAAGGTGCAGT-3′, Reverse: 5′-TGCACCCAGTTTTCCTTGGG-3′; Human DDX1 Forward: 5′-CCTGGATGAAGCTGATGGGC-3′, Reverse: 5′-GCAAAGTGGCAGAGCAAACA-3′; Human XPO1 Forward: 5′-CTACATCTGCCTCTCCGTTGCT-3′, Reverse: 5′-CCAATACTTCCTCTGGTTTAGCC-3′; Human IFNB Forward: 5′-CTTGGATTCCTACAAAGAAGCAGC-3′, Reverse: 5′-TCCTCCTTCTGGAACTGCTGCA-3′; Human CXCL10 Forward: 5′-CCATTCTGATTTGCTGCCTTATC-3′, Reverse: 5′-TACTAATGCTGATGCAGGTACAG-3′; Human TLR3 Forward: 5′-GCGCTAAAAAGTGAAGAACTGGAT-3′, Reverse: 5′-GCTGGACATTGTTCAGAAAGAGG-3′; Human DDX58 Forward: 5′-CACCTCAGTTGCTGATGAAGGC-3′, Reverse: 5′-GTCAGAAGGAAGCACTTGCTACC-3′; Human IFIH1 Forward: 5′-GCTGAAGTAGGAGTCAAAGCCC-3′, Reverse: 5′-CCACTGTGGTAGCGATAAGCAG-3′; Human LMNB1 Forward: 5′-GAGAGCAACATGATGCCCAAGTG-3′, Reverse: 5′-GTTCTTCCCTGGCACTGTTGAC-3′; Human XPF Forward: 5′-CGCAGAGCTAACCTTTGTTCGG-3′, Reverse: 5′- TCCGCAAAGCAGTGAGATAGCG-3′; Human XPG Forward: 5′- GATGCGGAAGATTCGCTCCATG-3′, Reverse: 5′- GCTTTCCAGGAACATCTGTCCG-3′; Mouse Gapdh Forward: 5′-CATCACTGCCACCCAGAAGACTG-3′, Reverse: 5′-ATGCCAGTGAGCTTCCCGTTCAG-3′; Mouse Il1b Forward: 5′-TGTGCAAGTGTCTGAAGCAGC-3′, Reverse: 5′-TGGAAGCAGCCCTTCATCTT-3′; Mouse Ccl2 Forward: 5′-GAAGGAATGGGTCCAGACAT-3′, Reverse: 5′-ACGGGTCAACTTCACATTCA-3′; Mouse Ccl5 Forward: 5′-GCTGCTTTGCCTACCTCTCC-3′, Reverse: 5′-TCGAGTGACAAACACGACTGC-3′.
sections.senescence induction and sa-\u03b2-gal s: For ER:RAS senescence induction, IMR90 cells were infected with retrovirus encoding a 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (4-OHT) inducible ER:RAS construct (pLNC-ER:Ras, Addgene #67844), after 4 weeks of selection with G418 (400 μg ml −1 , Gibco). Cells were maintained with lower dose of G418 (200 μg ml −1 ) and for induction, cells were treated with 4-OHT at a final concentration of 100 nM. Cells were collected to examine the expression of ER-RAS and other markers at indicated time points. For senescence induced by oncogenic HRAS G12V (ref. 50 ), IMR90 cells were infected with retrovirus encoding HRAS G12V construct followed by puromycin selection. Cells were collected to examine the expression of RAS and other markers at indicated time points. In addition, senescence was induced by treatment of cisplatin in OVCAR3 (750 nM for 3 days followed by drug-free culture for 3 days). Specifically, for SA-β-gal staining, cells were fixed using 2% formaldehyde and 0.2% glutaraldehyde in PBS and washed twice with PBS. The cells were then incubated overnight in X-gal solution (150 mM NaCl, 40 mM Na 2 HPO 4 , pH 5.7, 2 mM MgCl 2 , 5 mM K 3 Fe(CN) 6 , 5 mM K 4 Fe(CN) 6 and 1 mg ml −1 X-gal) at 37 °C in a non-CO 2 incubator. For mouse liver tissue, frozen sections were fixed and stained at pH 5.5 for 5–8 h.
sections.conditioned medium: For conditioned medium collection, the senescent cells were cultured in DMEM with 0.5% FBS for 7 days, filtered and mixed with DMEM containing 40% FBS at a ratio of 6:1 to generate conditioned medium with 5% FBS. For the stimulation of tumor cell growth, conditioned medium was collected from control or RAS-induced senescent cells incubated in serum-free DMEM for 12 h. The conditioned medium was filtered and mixed with DMEM + 2% FBS to generate culture medium containing 0.5% FBS. TOV21G cells were cultured in the conditioned medium and refreshed every day. The cancer cell growth was determined by counting the number of cells on day 7.
sections.antibody array analysis: The antibody array for secreted factors was performed using a Quantibody Human Inflammation Array 3 (RayBiotech, cat. no. QAH-INF-3) based on the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, conditioned medium was generated from cells following a PBS wash and incubation in serum-free DMEM for 48 h. Conditioned medium was filtered (0.2 μm) and incubated on the array overnight at 4 °C. Following incubation, the array was washed five times with Wash Buffer I and then twice with Wash Buffer II at room temperature. The array was then incubated with the biotinylated antibody cocktail for 2 h at room temperature before being washed three times with Wash Buffer I and then twice with Wash Buffer II at room temperature. The array was then incubated with Cy3 equivalent dye-conjugated streptavidin for 1 h at room temperature. Following incubation, the array was washed three times with Wash Buffer I and then washed twice with Wash Buffer II. The signals were then measured using Amersham Typhoon laser scanner and quantified with NIH ImageJ software (1.48v) followed by normalization to the cell number from which the conditioned medium was generated.
sections.2\u20323\u2032-cgamp measurement: A 2′3′-cGAMP enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit (Cayman Chemical, cat. no. 501700) was used to analyze the cellular endogenous level of 2′3′-cGAMP following the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, 2 × 10 6 cells were incubated in 200 μl lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat. no. 78501) on ice for 30 min. After 30 min centrifugation at 11,200 g , the supernatant was collected for 2′3′-cGAMP measurement following the manufacturer’s instructions. For determination of 2′3′-cGAMP level in mouse plasma, the plasma was diluted at 1:6 for the ELISA.
sections.cgas activity assay: Recombinant cGAS was incubated with the indicated nucleic acids in 20 μl of cGAMP synthesis buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 5 mM MgCl 2 , 2 mM ATP and 2 mM GTP) at 37 °C for 90 min. The 2′3′-cGAMP was extracted with 80% methanol and analyzed using the ELISA kit (Cayman Chemical, cat. no. 501700).
sections.r-loop annealing: The oligonucleotides used in all the biochemical assays were DNA-1: Cy5-GCCGTCGCATGACGCTGCCGAATTCTACCACGCGATTCATACCTGTCGTGCCAGCTGCTTTGCCCACCTGCAGGTTCACCTCGTCCCTGG; DNA-2: Cy3-CCAGGGACGAGGTGAACCTGCAGGTGGGCAAAGCAGCTGGCACGACAGGTATGAATCGCGTGGTAGAATTCGGCAGCGTCATGCGACGGC; RNA: AF488-GCAGCUGGCACGACAGGUAUGAAUC. DNA oligonucleotide stock was made at 10 μM and RNA oligonucleotide stock at 100 μM and stored at −80 °C. Duplex DNA or duplex hybrids were formed by mixing 0.5 μl of each oligonucleotide in annealing buffer 1 (10 mM Tris, pH 7.6, 100 mM NaCl and 1 mM EDTA) and incubated at 95 °C for 5 min followed by slowly cooling to 21 °C in a Thermo Cycler (Bio-Rad). R-loops were assembled by mixing 8 μl DNA duplex and 1 μl RNA in annealing buffer 2 (90 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 90 mM borate and 10 mM MgCl 2 ) in a total volume of 20 μl for 2 h at room temperature. Excess RNA was removed using NucAway spin columns (Ambion). The purified assembled R-loops were used for unwinding assays, EMSA and cGAS activity assay.
sections.ddx1 helicase unwinding assay: Recombinant DDX1 was incubated with assembled R-loops in 20 μl reaction buffer (12.5 mM MOPS, pH 7.0, 25 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, 30 mM KCl, 50 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgCl 2 , 0.1% Tween-20, 1.5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and 5 mM ATP) at 30 °C for 60 min. Then we took 4 μl and mixed this with 3 μl of 50% glycerol and 3 μl H 2 O, loaded the mixture onto an 8% acrylamide gel and carried out electrophoresis at 60 V for 2 h. The gels were then subjected to analysis using an Amersham Typhoon laser scanner.
sections.electrophoretic mobility shift assays: Recombinant cGAS was incubated with the indicated nucleic acids in the reaction buffer (25 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl and 5% glycerol) at room temperature for 20 min. The mixtures were loaded on 1% agarose gel using an electrophoresis buffer (45 mM Tris and 45 mM boric acid, pH 10.0). The gels were then subjected to analysis using an Amersham Typhoon laser scanner.
sections.fluorescence in situ hybridization: A Cy3-labeled DNA probe was synthesized at Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT): Cy3-GAATCTGCAAGTGGATAT. The probe was resuspended in formamide to make a 50 μM stock and mixed in hybridization buffer (10% dextran sulfate, 50% formamide, 2× SSC, 1 mM EDTA and 50 mM sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.0). Cells were fixed in 4% PFA for 10 min at room temperature and permeabilized in 70% ethanol at 4 °C overnight before incubating with 10 μl 500 nM pre-denatured (85 °C, 10 min) probes at 37 °C overnight. Then the cells were washed three times with wash buffer (50% formamide and 2× SSC) and were subjected to 1 μg ml −1 DAPI staining for 5 min at room temperature, followed by washing with 2× SSC, 1× SSC and finally water for 2 min each at room temperature. We mounted the coverslip on a slide with antifade mounting medium and observed the fluorescence under a Confocal Leica SP8 laser scanning microscope.
sections.immunoblotting and immunofluorescence: For immunoblotting, protein was isolated by lysing cells or tissues in 1× sample buffer (10% glycerol, 2% SDS, 0.01% bromophenol blue, 0.1 M DTT and 62.5 mM Tris-HCl, pH 6.8). Equal amounts of proteins were loaded and separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred to a PVDF membrane. The membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk in TBS/0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) for 1 h at room temperature and then incubated with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight in 4% BSA/TBS + 0.025% sodium azide. The next day, the membrane was washed with TBST for 10 min at room temperature and then incubated in HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies. Following incubation with the secondary antibodies, the membrane was washed in TBST for 10 min at room temperature for four times and then incubated with SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for visualization on film. For immunofluorescence staining, cells on coverslips or tissues from frozen section were fixed with 4% PFA for 15 min at room temperature. Cells/tissues were washed twice with PBS followed by permeabilization with 0.2% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min. For immunostaining for R-loops using S9.6 antibody, cells/tissues were fixed and permeabilized in ice-cold methanol for 15 min. After washing twice, cells/tissues were blocked with 1% BSA in PBS for 20 min at room temperature. Cells/tissues were incubated with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight. The next day, cells/tissues were washed three times in PBS and probed with Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondary antibody (Life Technologies) for 1 h at room temperature. Cells/tissues were washed and subjected to 1 μg ml −1 DAPI staining for 5 min at room temperature, after washing four times with PBS, the slides were sealed and imaged using a Confocal Leica SP8 laser scanning microscope.
sections.co-immunoprecipitation: For endogenous DDX1 and XPO1 interaction, the cells were lysed in ice-cold lysis buffer containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 10% glycerol, 10 mM NaF, 1%Triton X-100 and 10 mM DTT, supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, cat. no. 4693116001) and maintained gentle rotation at 4 °C for 30 min. The supernatant was incubated with anti-XPO1 antibody or rabbit IgG at 4 °C overnight, and then 20 μl Dynabeads protein A/protein G magnetic beads were added. The lysate beads mixture was incubated at 4 °C under gentle rotation for 2 h. The mixture was then put on a magnetic stand and washed three times before boiling with 2× SDS loading buffer for immunoblot analysis.
sections.purification of cytoplasmic dna\u2013rna: A total of 5 × 10 6 noncrosslinked cells were lysed in 1 ml Cyto-lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40 and 2 mM EDTA, supplemented with protease inhibitor cocktail) on ice for 30 min. After 10 min of centrifugation at 11,200 g , the supernatant was collected with the addition of 10 μg ml −1 RNase A followed by incubation with S9.6 antibody or mouse IgG at 4 °C overnight. Dynabeads protein A/protein G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were preblocked with 0.5% BSA/PBS at 4 °C for 2 h and were then added to the immunoprecipitated samples under gentle rotation at 4 °C for 2 h. The mixture was then put on a magnetic stand and washed three times, the DNA–RNA hybrids-binding proteins were eluted with 50 mM glycine (pH 2.5): 1 M Tris (pH 8.5) (20:1) buffer. The eluted samples were collected for subsequent analysis.
sections.lc\u2013ms/ms analysis and data processi: Samples were briefly electrophoresed on a 10% TGX precast gel (Bio-Rad, cat no. 4561033), after which, the entire gel lanes were excised and subjected to trypsin digestion. LC–MS/MS was conducted using a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) interfaced with an UltiMate 3000 nano UPLC system (Thermo Scientific). Peptides were first loaded onto a PepMap100 trap column (0.3 × 5 mm, 5 μm C18 resin; Thermo Scientific) and then separated via reverse-phase LC using a BEH C18 nanocapillary analytical column (75 μm i.d. × 25 cm, 1.7-μm particle size; Waters). Separation was achieved over a 90-min gradient formed by solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). Eluted peptides were analyzed by the mass spectrometer set to repetitively scan m / z from 350 to 1,950 in positive ion mode. Full MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 60,000, followed by data-dependent MS/MS scans at 15,000 resolution for the 20 most abundant ions surpassing a 20,000 intensity threshold. Peptide match was set as preferred, the exclude isotopes option was enabled and charge-state screening was applied to discard unassigned ions as well as singly charged and >4 charged species. Peptide sequences were identified using MaxQuant (v.2.3.1.0) 51 . MS/MS spectra were searched against the UniProt human protein database (downloaded on 21 July 2022) and a common contaminants database. The search parameters included full tryptic specificity allowing up to two missed cleavages, static carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues and variable modifications for Met oxidation, protein N-terminal acetylation and Asn deamidation. Consensus identification lists were generated with false discovery rates set at 1% for both protein and peptide identification.
sections.slot-blot analysis for dna\u2013rna hybr: A total of 5 × 10 6 cells were collected and resuspended in 1.6 ml of TE buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8 and 0.1 mM EDTA) and incubated with 41.5 μl of 20% SDS and 5 μl of proteinase K at 55 °C overnight. DNA was extracted gently with phenol–chloroform. Precipitated DNA was washed with 70% ethanol, resuspended gently in TE buffer and digested with digestion buffer (50 U HindIII, EcoRI, BsrGI, XbaI and SspI, 10 mM DTT, 2 mM spermidine and BSA) at 37 °C overnight. Half the DNA was treated with digestion buffer containing 3 μl of RNase H as negative control. The digested DNA was purified using phenol–chloroform extraction, DNA from equal cell counts were loaded onto a nylon membrane (Cytiva, cat. no. RPN203B), UV-crosslinked and incubated with S9.6 antibody for R-loop detection. For R-loop detection in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, 5 × 10 6 cells were lysed in 1.6 ml Cyto-lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40 and 2 mM EDTA) on ice for 30 min. After centrifuging at 11,200 g for 30 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was collected as the cytoplasmic fraction. Pelleted nuclei were resuspended in 1.6 ml TE buffer and labeled as the nuclear fraction. Both fractions were incubated with 41.5 μl of 20% SDS and 5 μl of proteinase K at 55 °C overnight followed by phenol–chloroform extraction as described above.
sections.ccf fractionation to assess r-loop solub: A total of 5 × 10 8 cells were incubated in DMEM containing 10 μg ml −1 cytochalasin B for 30 min at 37 °C. The cell pellet was dounced and homogenized in prechilled lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 2 mM magnesium acetate, 3 mM CaCl2, 0.32 M sucrose, 0.1 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT, 0.1% NP-40, 0.15 mM spermine, 0.75 mM spermidine and 10 μg ml −1 cytochalasin B, pH 8.5 at 4 °C). After fixation with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min, an equal volume of 1.6 M sucrose buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.1 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT, 0.3% BSA, 0.15 mM spermine and 0.75 mM spermidine, pH 8.0 at 4 °C) was added. In a 50-ml tissue culture tube, 10 ml of the homogenate was added on top of the sucrose buffer gradient (20 and 15 ml containing 1.8 and 1.6 M sucrose, respectively). The gradient was centrifuged (12,000 g ) for 20 min at 4 °C. After removing the top 3 ml of the gradient, the next 15-ml CCF-containing fraction was diluted with an equal volume of ice-cold PBS. The solution was filtered through a 5-μm low-protein-binding Durapore polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane (Millipore, cat. no. SLSV025LS). Ice-cold 5× PBS was added into the CCFs, which were centrifuged (12,000 g ) for 30 min at 4 °C. The pellet was collected as CCF fraction. To assess the solubility of CCF-localized R-loops, CCF pellet was resuspended in 300 μl buffer A (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 50 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl 2 and 0.05% Triton X-100), samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as fraction A. Next, the pellet was resuspended in 300 μl buffer B (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl 2 and 0.05% Triton X-100), samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as fraction B. Next, the pellet was resuspended in 300 μl buffer C (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 250 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl 2 and 0.05% Triton X-100), samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as fraction C. Next, the pellet was resuspended in 300 μl buffer D (50 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgCl 2 and 0.1% Triton X-100), samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 g for 15 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as fraction D. The remaining pellet was resuspended in buffer B supplemented with 5 mM CaCl 2 and 3 U micrococcal nuclease (Thermo Fisher), incubated at 37 °C for 10 min, and the supernatant was collected as chromatin fractionation after centrifugation at 15,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. Whole-cell lysates and isolated chromatin using Pierce Chromatin Prep Module (Thermo Fisher, cat. no. 26158) were prepared as controls.
sections.dna\u2013rna hybrid immunoprecipitation: DRIP-seq was performed as previously described with minor modifications 13 . A total of 1.2 × 10 7 cells were collected and fractionated using the Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Extraction kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The cytoplasmic or nucleoplasmic fractions were incubated with 0.4% SDS and 40 μg ml −1 of proteinase K for 90 min at 37 °C. The samples were resuspended in ultrapure water and normalized to equal cell counts, adjusted to 550 mM NaCl and treated with RNase A (1 μg ml −1 ) for 30 min. For RNase H treatment, the samples were digested overnight with RNase H (0.4 U μl −1 ). For immunoprecipitation, the samples were resuspended in TE buffer and precleared with Dynabeads protein A/protein G for 1 h in binding buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 150 mM NaCl and 0.5% sodium deoxycholate). Precleared samples were then incubated with S9.6 antibody or control mouse IgG overnight at 4 °C with rotation. Then, Dynabeads protein A/protein G magnetic beads were added, and the mixture was incubated for 2 h at 4 °C with rotation. Bound beads were washed with TSE buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 2 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS and 150 mM NaCl) and then with TE buffer. Elution was performed in 200 μl elution buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 8.0, 10 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS and 8 μl of 20 mg ml −1 proteinase K) for 50 min at 50 °C. The eluted samples were resuspended in TE buffer and sonicated to a peak fragment size of 300 bp using a Covaris ME220 machine (10% duty factor, 200 cycles per burst, 75 peak incident power and 60 s per tube). DNA libraries were synthesized from ssDNA using xGen ssDNA & Low-Input DNA Library Prep kit (IDT) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The libraries were sequenced in a 150-base pair paired-end run on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 system by the Wistar Genomics Facility.
sections.mapr-seq: A total of 2 × 10 6 cells were washed twice with 1 ml wash buffer (20 mM HEPES. pH 7.5, 0.15 M NaCl, 0.5 mM Spermidine and 1 mM protease inhibitors) and immobilized on concanavalin A-coated beads at room temperature. For each group, immobilized cells were divided equally into two tubes and resuspended in 50 ml wash buffer containing 0.02% digitonin (Dig-wash). GST-MNase and GST-RHΔ-MNase proteins were added to a final concentration of 1 mM and incubated at 4 °C with rotation. The beads were washed three times, resuspended in 100 μl Dig-wash buffer and placed on ice. Then, 2 μl 0.1 M CaCl 2 was added to activate MNase and digestion was carried out for 30 min on ice. Reaction was stopped by adding equal volume of 2× STOP buffer (340 mM NaCl, 20 mM EDTA, 4 mM EGTA, 0.02% digitonin, 5 μg RNase A, 5 μg linear acrylamide and 2 pg ml −1 heterologous spike-in DNA). The samples were incubated at 37 °C for 10 min to release the chromatin fragments and centrifuge at 16,000 g for 5 min at 4 °C. Supernatants were transferred to new tubes with 2 μl 10% SDS and 5 μg proteinase K added and incubated at 70 °C for 10 min. Quickly spun down and add 300 μl phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol mix, centrifuge at 16,000 g for 5 min at room temperature, the upper aqueous phase was transferred to a new tube containing 0.5× volume of 7.5 M NH 4 OAc and 4 μl of linear acrylamide, followed by addition of 2.5× volume of ice-cold 100% ethanol and stored at 80 °C for at least 1 h. After centrifuging at 16,000 g for 30 min at 4 °C, the pellets were washed with 1 ml 75% ethanol and spun down at 16,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. Then, we removed the supernatant and air dried the pellets for 2 min. We dissolved the pellets in 20 μl TE buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8 and 0.1 mM EDTA). We took 7 μl DNA for library construction using a NEBNext Ultra DNA Library Prep kit for Illumina (NEB, cat. no. 7370) and the libraries were sequenced in a 75-bp single-end run on Illumina NextSeq 500 system by the Wistar Genomics Facility.
sections.rna-ip and rt\u2013qpcr analysis: Anti-DDX1 RIP was carried out using a Magna RIPRNA-binding protein immunoprecipitation kit (Millipore, cat. no. 17-700). In brief, for each immunoprecipitation, 2 × 10 7 cells were collected and lysed in 100 μl RIP Lysis Buffer with RNase inhibitor and protease inhibitor. The lysate was subjected to immunoprecipitation using 20 μg anti-DDX1 antibody (Invitrogen, cat. no. 703141). The immunoprecipitated RNA was extracted using phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (125:24:1) (Thermo Fisher, cat. no. AM9720), followed by RNA library construction using Illumina Stranded Total RNA Prep with Ribo-Zero Plus kit (Illumina) and sequenced in a 75-bp paired-end run on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 system by the Wistar Genomics Facility.
sections.in vivo mouse models: For xenograft mouse model, cells (TOV21G: senescent fibroblasts at a ratio of 1:1, 2 × 10 6 cells) were suspended in 100 μl PBS: Matrigel (1:1) and unilaterally injected subcutaneously into the right dorsal flank of 6–8-week-old female immunocompromised nonobese diabetic/severe combined immunodeficiency (NOD/SCID) gamma (NSG) mice. Tumor size was measured on the indicated days. Tumor size was determined using the following equation: tumor size (mm 3 = ( d 2 × D )/2, where d and D are the shortest and the longest diameter, respectively. For hydrodynamic tail-veil injection, 8-week-old female C56BL/6 mice (Charles Rivers Laboratory) were used. For each injection, endotoxin-free transposon-based construct expressing NRas G12V (25 μg) together with endotoxin-free transposase plasmid (5 μg) were mixed at a volume of 10% of the mouse body weight were delivered into the mice within 5–8 s as previously described 39 . Mice were killed 6 or 14 days after injection, livers were collected and embedded in OCT (Fisher, cat. no. 23-730-571) followed by flash freezing. For the XPO1 inhibitor treatment, the aged C57BL/6J mice (22 months) were obtained from the National Institute on Aging aged rodent colonies and were randomly grouped into three groups. Oral gavage administration was given once every 3 days with 20 mg kg −1 KPT-330 in solvent (2% dimethylsulfoxide + 40%PEG300 + 5% ddH 2 O) or solvent alone for 5 weeks. The mice were killed and the tissues and blood samples were collected for correlative studies. For body composition analysis, treatments were given in aged C57BL/6J female mice (23 months) weekly with 20 mg kg −1 KPT-330 for 2 months. Mouse body composition (visceral fat mass and posterior skeletal muscle mass) was performed by MRI analysis. Posterior skeletal muscles include hindlimb and paraspinal muscles starting from the top level of the right kidney. Lifespan in aged C57BL/6J female mice (23 months) treated with vehicle or KPT-330 (20 mg kg −1 , weekly, for 2 months) was followed using reported criteria 52 . Mice were medicated for non-life-threatening conditions by experienced veterinarians. The experimental end point was recorded when the mice were found dead or at the time of killing if they were unlikely to survive longer than 48 h (for example severely moribund).
sections.mouse plasma levels of il-6, tnf, choles: Mouse plasma levels of IL-6 and TNF were determined using ELISA kits (Proteintech, cat. no. KE10007 and KE10002). In brief, mouse plasma was diluted at 1:8 for IL-6 measurement and 1:16 for TNF measurement. Then, 100 μl of diluted serum was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. After a total of four washes, 100 μl of detection antibody solution was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. After a total of four washes, 100 μl of streptavidin–HRP solution was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 40 min. After a total of four washes, 100 μl of TMB substrate solution was added to each well and incubated at room temperature for 15–20 min with protection from light. Then, 100 μl of Stop solution was added to each well and absorbance at a wavelength of 450 nm was recorded on a microplate reader. Mouse plasma levels of cholesterol were determined using RayBio Total Cholesterol Colorimetric Assay kit (RayBiotech, cat. no. MA-TC). The plasma samples were diluted at 1:5 for the measurement following the manufacturer’s instruction. Mouse plasma levels of ALT activity were determined using ALT activity assay kit (RayBiotech, cat. no. MA-ALT). No dilution of plasma samples was required for the assay following the manufacturer’s instruction.
sections.picrosirius red staining: Liver collagen fibers were stained using a Picrosirius Red Staining kit (Polysciences, cat. no. 24901). The paraffin-embedded mouse liver sections were used following the manufacture’s instruction. After staining, the fibrotic area was quantified.
sections.immunohistochemistry: Fresh mouse liver tissues were fixed overnight in 4% PFA in PBS at 4 °C or embedded in OCT compound for cryosection. For immunohistochemistry staining, the slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated, quenched in 0.6% hydrogen peroxide in methanol for 15 min and boiled for 40 min in either 10 mM citrate (pH 6.0) buffer or Tris–EDTA (pH 9.0) buffer for antigen retrieval. The slides were incubated with BlockAid Blocking Solution (Invitrogen, cat. no. B10710 ) for 1 h at room temperature and then incubated overnight with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer at 4 °C. The slides were further incubated with biotinylated secondary antibodies, followed by ABC solution and developed with 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (Vector Laboratories). The slides were finally counterstained with hematoxylin, dehydrated and mounted with Permount (Thermo Fisher). For quantification, 20–30 ×10 fields per mouse were counted.
sections.mapr-seq_1: FastQC (v.0.11.9) was used to check qualities of the raw FASTQ reads. Raw MapR reads were aligned to human genome reference GRCh38 using Bowtie2 (v.2.4.5) algorithm 53 . Peaks were called for each sample using corresponding background sample as control by MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1) 54 with parameters -broad broad-cutoff of 0.1. Peaks were annotated using R library ChIPseeker (v.1.39.0) 55 . Promoter regions were defined as ±2 kb of transcription start site (TSS) and transcription termination site (TTS) regions were defined as 300 bp downstream of the TTS. Gene bodies include exons and introns but exclude the promoter regions. The difference in count per million mapped reads normalized MapR signals between testing samples and their corresponding background samples were calculated using deepTools (v.3.5.4) 56 bamCompare. The relative signals around TSS were calculated and plotted using deepTools (v.3.5.4) computeMatrix and plotHeatmap. All statistical analyses were carried out in R (v.4.2.3).
sections.cytodrip-seq: Quality assessment of CytoDRIP and nuclear DRIP reads were carried out using fastQC (v.0.11.9). Adaptor sequence and low-quality ends were trimmed using trim-galore (v.0.6.10) and cutadapt (v.4.5). Trimmed cytoDRIP and nuclear DRIP reads were aligned to human genome reference GRCh38 using Bowtie2 (v.2.4.5) algorithm 53 . Picard v.2.27.4 ( http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard ) MarkDuplicates was used to remove PCR duplicates. Peaks were called against corresponding IgG/RH samples using MACS2 (v.2.2.7.1) 54 with narrow peak settings and visualized using signal per million reads normalization in IGV 57 . Peak annotation was carried out similarly to MapR. Read coverages for the entire genome were calculated using deepTools (v.3.5.4) command multiBamSummary bins. Pearson correlation to show reproducibility between replicates were calculated using deepTools (v.3.5.4) command plotCorrelation with options -skipZeros-removeOutliers. SAMtools (v.1.16.1) 58 idxstats was used to calculate reads mapped to nuclear or mitochondrial standard chromosomes. bedtools (v.2.30.0) 59 was used to obtain coverage in each experiment over the peaks. University of California, Santa Cruz RepeatMasker annotations were used for DNA repeat elements. The cytoDRIP peaks were subsampled 10,000 times using bedtools shuffle from within all nuclear DRIP peaks. A Jaccard coefficient by bedtools Jaccard was calculated for each randomized peak set and the z -score was calculated from the resulting distribution, as previously described 13 . Overlapping cyto-peaks and repeat elements were identified by bedtools intersect. Nuclear DRIP-seq signals at cytoDRIP regions and cytoDRIP-seq signals were calculated using bedtools multicov.
sections.rip-seq: Quality assessment of RIP-seq reads were carried out using fastQC (v.0.11.9). Adaptor sequence and low-quality ends were trimmed using trim-galore (v.0.6.5) and cutadapt (v.1.18). Trimmed RIP-seq reads were aligned to human genome reference GRCh38 using STAR (v.2.7.10b) 60 with parameters –winAnchorMultimapNmax 100 –outFilterMultimapNmax 100 for TE elements. Aligned reads were summarized at the gene and TE level by TEtranscripts (v.2.2.3) 61 . Annotation of transposable elements (TEs) was performed using ‘GRCh38_GENCODE_rmsk_TE.gtf’ annotation ( https://hammelllab.labsites.cshl.edu/software/#TEtranscripts ) based on the University of California, Santa Cruz RepeatMasker database. Differential expression analysis of TEs was carried out by TEtranscripts and R package DESeq2 (ref. 62 ).
sections.statistics and reproducibility: No statistical test was used to predetermine sample size but our sample sizes are similar to those reported in previous publications 5 , 26 . The sample size for each experiment is stated in the figure legends. For measuring 2′3′-cGAMP level in mouse plasma, one sample from aged vehicle group was beyond the detection range according to the ELISA kit instructions and was thus excluded (Extended Data Fig. 9g ). Data distribution was assumed to be normal, but this was not formally tested. Experimental groups were indiscriminately allocated. The investigators were blinded to group allocation during data collection and analysis. Experiments were repeated at least three times independently unless otherwise stated in figure legends with similar results. All statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad). All bar graphs show mean values with error bars (s.e.m. as defined in figure legends). An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t -test was used for comparison between two groups.
