We did not assess whether predictors of PPC consultation changed over time following implementation of the embedded model. Future studies are needed to examine whether integrated PPC models can reduce disparities in referral patterns between cancer and non-cancer populations.
sections.discussion: This ten–year evaluation demonstrates that embedding PPC specialists within existing pediatric services can produce sustained improvements in advance care planning and interdisciplinary collaboration. The marked increases in DNR documentation, structured family meetings, and PPC consultations indicate that shared–care integration effectively lowers referral barriers and normalizes palliative involvement within routine practice. These findings are consistent with prior studies showing that early PPC engagement enhances communication quality and promotes goal–concordant decision–making [ 12 – 15 ]. The substantial growth in structured family meetings observed in our cohort is particularly noteworthy. Repeated, proactive conversations allow families to clarify prognosis, explore values, and prepare for difficult decisions. Previous work has demonstrated that such communication reduces decisional conflict and improves caregiver satisfaction [ 16 – 18 ]. Our results suggest that institutionalizing these discussions through a shared PPC model may meaningfully strengthen advance care planning processes. However, the relatively low proportion of documented family meetings may reflect underdocumentation or variability in clinical practice, as discussions regarding prognosis and goals of care may have occurred outside of formally recorded meetings. This finding also highlights an opportunity to improve the standardization and documentation of structured family meetings in pediatric end-of-life care. Despite these gains, ICU deaths and high–intensity treatments remained common. Similar patterns have been reported internationally across pediatric oncology and critical care populations, where aggressive interventions frequently persist near the end of life even after PPC involvement [ 19 – 21 ]. These findings suggest that consultation alone may be insufficient to substantially alter location-of-death outcomes. As increasing numbers of children live longer with complex chronic conditions, the demand for coordinated palliative support across prolonged illness trajectories continues to grow. Logistic regression analysis showed that cancer diagnosis and increasing age were associated with a higher likelihood of PPC consultation, whereas absence of a family meeting was associated with lower PPC involvement. These findings suggest that referral patterns may still be influenced by underlying disease characteristics and care processes. The interpretation of regression results may depend on the reference groups used, and careful attention is required when interpreting the direction of associations. We did not assess whether predictors of PPC consultation changed over time following implementation of the embedded model. Future studies are needed to examine whether integrated PPC models can reduce disparities in referral patterns between cancer and non-cancer populations. Several mechanisms may explain this persistence. Children with complex chronic conditions often experience unpredictable deterioration, limiting opportunities for planned discharge. In addition, limited pediatric hospice availability and caregiver concerns regarding home care may restrict transitions outside the hospital. Studies examining place of death suggest that community–based services and home palliative support are critical for enabling non–ICU deaths [ 22 – 25 ]. From a systems perspective, shared PPC models appear particularly feasible and scalable. Embedding specialists within primary teams preserves continuity of care, reduces stigma associated with referral, and facilitates earlier collaboration. Similar integration frameworks have been proposed as sustainable strategies for expanding pediatric palliative capacity without major structural reorganization [ 26 – 28 ]. Policy initiatives may further enhance these effects. International experts increasingly advocate that PPC be considered a standard component of pediatric oncology and critical care rather than an optional service [ 29 – 32 ]. Our findings provide real–world evidence from an Asian healthcare system where PPC has historically been underutilized, demonstrating that integration can produce meaningful improvements over time. Cultural expectations favoring life-prolonging treatment and limited availability of pediatric hospice services in Taiwan may contribute to the persistence of ICU deaths. These contextual factors highlight the importance of culturally responsive and community-based palliative care models in Asian healthcare systems. This study has limitations, including its retrospective design and data derived from two centers. In addition, information regarding prior PPC involvement and reasons for hospital admission was not consistently available and therefore was not included in the analysis. The use of all pediatric decedents as the denominator may overestimate or underestimate the proportion of patients who required PPC services, as palliative care needs were not defined using standardized criteria across the study period. In addition, the study did not assess whether documented DNR orders or advance care plans were consistently honored in clinical practice. The implementation of the embedded PPC model may not have been uniform across all clinical teams, and variations in practice patterns could not be fully captured. Although family meetings were conducted with participation from palliative care team members, detailed documentation of all multidisciplinary participants was not consistently available. This is partly because structured family meeting records were maintained as separate paper-based forms and were not fully accessible through the electronic medical record system used in this retrospective study. As a result, the full composition of the care team involved in each meeting could not be determined. Furthermore, although high rates of ICU utilization at the end of life were observed, we were not able to directly assess whether this reflected misalignment between care delivery and family preferences, as patient and family perspectives were not systematically documented. In our setting, critically ill pediatric patients are commonly managed in intensive care units to provide advanced life-sustaining treatment. Transition to general wards typically occurs only when a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order is established and further life-sustaining interventions are no longer pursued. This practice pattern may partly explain the high proportion of ICU utilization observed and suggests that ICU-based end-of-life care does not necessarily indicate misalignment with family preferences. Nevertheless, the large cohort and decade–long observation period provide valuable insight into evolving practice patterns. Continued efforts to promote earlier referral, strengthen interdisciplinary education, and expand community resources are needed to further improve alignment between care delivery and family preferences. Overall, early, integrated PPC should be regarded as an essential element of high–quality pediatric healthcare [ 33 ].
sections.conclusions_1: Implementation of a shared pediatric palliative care model was associated with sustained improvements in advance care planning, interdisciplinary communication, and utilization of palliative services over time. Embedding palliative specialists within primary pediatric teams may contribute to reducing referral barriers and facilitating the integration of palliative care into routine clinical practice. Despite these gains, the persistence of ICU deaths and high-intensity treatments underscores the influence of structural, cultural, and resource-related factors on end-of-life care patterns. Expanding community-based services, strengthening caregiver support, and promoting earlier referral strategies may be necessary to further align care delivery with family preferences. In healthcare systems where pediatric palliative care has historically been underutilized, shared-care integration represents a feasible and scalable approach to improving care quality. Early and integrated PPC should be recognized as a fundamental component of high-quality pediatric healthcare. These findings support the integration of pediatric palliative care as a core component of child health systems and may inform policy development in regions where services remain underutilized.

title: DNAJB4/HLJ1 protects against acetaminophen-induced liver injury by attenuating ER stress via HSP70
abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) remains a leading cause of acute liver failure; however, current clinical strategies lack reliable biomarkers, predictors of susceptibility, and effective therapeutic interventions. Among these etiologies, acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is the most common cause of DILI worldwide. Heat shock proteins (HSPs), particularly members of the HSP40 family, are central regulators of cellular stress responses, yet the specific role of DNAJB4/HLJ1 in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity remains poorly defined. To address this gap, we employed DNAJB4/HLJ1-deficient mice ( Dnajb4 −/− ) to investigate the function of DNAJB4/HLJ1 in APAP-induced liver injury. Following APAP administration (> 400 mg/kg), Dnajb4 −/− exhibited exacerbated hepatic necrosis, elevated liver enzymes, and enhanced c-jun/JNK activation compared with Dnajb4 +/+ controls. Metabolic profiling revealed altered APAP metabolism, with reduced detoxification products and excessive oxidative metabolites, and pronounced glutathione (GSH) depletion. Transcriptomic analysis implicated DNAJB4/HLJ1 in metabolism, protein folding, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress via interaction with HSP70. Consistently, ATF6, XBP1, and CHOP expression confirmed aggravated ER stress in Dnajb4 −/− livers. AlphaFold-Multimer modeling and co-immunoprecipitation validated physical interaction between DNAJB4/HLJ1 and HSP70. Restoration of DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression attenuated ER stress, c-jun/JNK activation, and liver injury, while pharmacological inhibition of ER stress confirmed its mechanistic involvement. Collectively, these findings identify DNAJB4/HLJ1 as a previously unrecognized regulator of stress signaling in APAP-induced hepatotoxicity. By modulating ER stress within the integrated cellular stress network, DNAJB4/HLJ1 limits injury progression and promotes hepatocellular resilience, highlighting its potential as a novel therapeutic target for preventing or mitigating DILI. Graphical Abstract 1. DNAJB4/HLJ1 acts as a critical safeguard against acetaminophen-induced liver njury. 2. Its loss rewires APAP metabolism, driving toxic NAPQI accumulation and GSH collapse. 3. DNAJB4/HLJ1 partners with HSP70 to restrain ER stress and halt JNK-driven damage. 4. Reinstating DNAJB4/HLJ1 restores cellular resilience, revealing a targetable defense in drug-induced liver injury (DILI). sections.introduction: Since the late twentieth century, the clinical significance of DILI has markedly increased. DILI accounts for a major proportion of acute liver failure (ALF) cases in developed countries, with annual incidence rates of 14–19 per 100,000 individuals (Sgro et al. 2002 ). Mortality can be substantial, reaching up to 50% in severe cases (Hosack et al. 2023 ). Common causes include prescription drugs, herbal remedies, and dietary supplements, particularly in individuals with underlying liver disease or metabolic dysfunctions (Hosack et al. 2023 ; Ravindra et al. 2023 ). DILI manifestations fall into two broad categories, including intrinsic and idiosyncratic. The intrinsic form is predictable and dose-independent, exemplified by acetaminophen (APAP) toxicity, whereas the idiosyncratic form occurs unpredictably, even at therapeutic doses of agents such as NSAIDs, antibiotics, and cardiovascular drugs (Hoofnagle and Björnsson 2019 ). APAP is among the most widely used over-the-counter medications for pain and fever relief. Although safe at therapeutic doses, it remains the leading cause of drug-induced ALF (Jaeschke and Ramachandran 2024 ). Its hepatotoxicity primarily arises from the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by hepatic glutathione (GSH). In overdose or GSH depletion, NAPQI accumulation triggers oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hepatocellular necrosis. Despite decades of study, the mechanisms governing the transition from reversible stress to irreversible liver failure remain unclear, and there is an urgent need for novel hepatoprotective strategies beyond N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), particularly for late-presenting patients. Current research efforts are directed toward modulating oxidative stress and minimizing the associated liver injury (Hibino et al. 2023 ; Umbaugh and Jaeschke 2021 ). Recent evidence implicates broader cellular stress pathways, particularly endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, as additional contributors to APAP hepatotoxicity. Persistent ER stress activates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which, when unresolved, leads to hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis (Chen et al. 2023 ). Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are essential chaperones maintaining ER function and cell survival under stress. Although HSPA5 has been linked to APAP-induced liver injury, whether other HSP family members modulate hepatotoxic responses remains unclear (Xiang et al. 2024 ). Given the functional diversity of HSP subfamilies, including HSP70s, HSP90s, and HSP40s (DNAJ) co-chaperones, certain HSPs beyond HSPA5 may either protect against or exacerbate liver injury. However, the involvement of these alternative HSPs in the pathogenesis of DILI has not been systematically explored. Moreover, whether modulation of specific HSPs could serve as a therapeutic strategy to mitigate APAP-induced hepatotoxicity remains largely uninvestigated. DNAJB4/HLJ1, a ~ 40 kDa co-chaperone of HSP40/DNAJ family, regulates ordered protein folding (Frydman et al. 1994 ). The DNAJ family comprises three subtypes (A, B, and C), based on sequence homology, with DNAJB being the largest subgroup (Ohtsuka and Hata 2000 ). Despite its high expression in the liver, the potential role of DNAJB4/HLJ1 in hepatic drug metabolism and its involvement in modulating DILI have not been previously explored. In this study, we demonstrate that DNAJB4/HLJ1-deficient mice ( Dnajb4 −/− ) exhibit significantly exacerbated liver injury following APAP administration compared to wild-type mice ( Dnajb4 +/+ ). Metabolite analysis using customized mass spectrometry revealed impaired detoxification capacity in Dnajb4 −/− , leading to elevated levels of the toxic APAP metabolite NAPQI and subsequent GSH depletion. Mechanistically, the absence of DNAJB4/HLJ1 impairs hepatocellular capacity to adapt to APAP-induced cellular stress triggered by oxidative drug metabolites and is associated with enhanced ER stress signaling in the injured liver. Conversely, hepatic re-expression of DNAJB4/HLJ1 mitigates APAP-induced injury by promoting hepatocellular resilience, recapitulating the protective effects observed with pharmacological inhibition of maladaptive ER stress. Collectively, we identify DNAJB4/HLJ1 as a previously unrecognized regulator of the hepatic response to xenobiotic-induced stress. By placing DNAJB4/HLJ1 within the interconnected cellular stress network triggered by toxic drug metabolites, this study expands current understanding of DILI pathogenesis and provides a conceptual foundation for exploring DNAJB4/HLJ1 as a potential therapeutic or preventive target in clinical settings.
sections.dnajb4/hlj1 is highly expressed in the l: We first examined DNAJB4/HLJ1 protein levels across organs of Dnajb4 +/+ (Fig. 1 A). Semi-quantitative densitometric analysis normalized to β-actin indicated that DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression was higher in the liver than in several other tissues examined. However, expression was also detectable in multiple organs, including muscle, heart, and testis (Fig. 1 B). To explore its physiological function, we generated Dnajb4 −/− by gene targeting (Supplemental Fig. 1 ). Focusing on hepatic tissue, we performed Gene Set Enrichment Analysis using transcriptomic data comparing livers from Dnajb4 −/− and Dnajb4 +/+ (Fig. 1 C), which revealed enrichment of protein refolding, lipid oxidation, carbohydrate kinase activity, acute phase response, drug metabolism process, and high-density lipoprotein particle regulation, suggesting that DNAJB4/HLJ1 may act as a stress-responsive protein in response to chemical and physiological insults such as DILI. Heatmaps below each enrichment plot illustrate the relative expression of leading-edge genes within each pathway
sections.loss of dnajb4/hlj1 increases susceptibi: APAP overdose is a major cause of DILI and is well characterized in experimental models. To assess the role of DNAJB4/HLJ1, we performed a dose-escalation APAP study. Both Dnajb4 +/+ and Dnajb4 −/− exhibited dose-dependent liver injury; however, Dnajb4 −/− showed greater susceptibility (Supplemental Fig. 2 ). At lower doses (≤ 200 mg/kg), liver injury was minimal, and genotype differences were not apparent. In contrast, at higher doses (≥ 600 mg/kg), the injury approached near-maximal in both groups, thereby obscuring genotype-dependent differences. Therefore, we selected 400 mg/kg APAP for subsequent experiments because it produced a clear and reproducible difference between genotypes without excessive injury. Mice were treated with 400 mg/kg APAP via intraperitoneal injection, and liver tissues and blood samples were collected at 3, 6, and 24 h post-treatment (Fig. 2 A). Gross examination at 24 h revealed more severe liver damage in Dnajb4 −/− compared with controls (Fig. 2 B). Histological analysis showed that liver injury in Dnajb4 −/− was evident as early as 3 h and progressively worsened by 24 h (Fig. 2 C). Quantification of necrotic areas confirmed significantly greater liver damage in Dnajb4 −/− at both 6 and 24 h following APAP administration (Fig. 2 D). To biochemically evaluate these findings, serum levels of liver enzymes were measured (Fig. 2 E-F). Both AST and ALT were significantly elevated in Dnajb4 −/− , indicating more extensive hepatocellular injury. Given the established role of c-Jun and JNK in APAP-mediated liver toxicity, we next examined hepatic c-Jun and JNK activation in Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 2 G), which was consistent with the aggravated liver injury phenotype. Interestingly, we also observed differential expression of HSP70, a key molecular chaperone implicated in protection against APAP-induced liver injury (Tsuji and Akagi 2025 ). In Dnajb4 +/+ , APAP treatment induced robust hepatic upregulation of HSP70; however, this response was absent in Dnajb4 −/− . Together, these findings indicate that DNAJB4/HLJ1 protects against APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, potentially by modulating stress responses and maintaining chaperone function. sections.metabolites shift toward napqi derivativ: APAP is primarily metabolized into non-toxic glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, while a small fraction is converted into the reactive intermediate NAPQI by CYP enzymes. NAPQI is normally detoxified by conjugation with GSH to form APAP-GSH, which is subsequently converted into APAP-cysteine (APAP-cys) and APAP-NAC. During overdose, excessive NAPQI depletes GSH, leading to NAPQI accumulation, ER stress, and liver injury (Fig. 3 A). To characterize APAP metabolic profiles, we quantified APAP-derived metabolites in mouse livers by coupling an Agilent 1290 Infinity UHPLC system with a Jet Stream electrospray ionization source to an Agilent 6460 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer for targeted molecular analysis in multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode. Mass spectrometric conditions were established and optimized for each metabolite, including analyte-specific and internal standard-specific MRM transitions, fragmentor voltages, collision energies, and ESI mode (Supplemental Table 1). Under these conditions, chromatographic patterns and retention times for each metabolite were determined (Supplemental Fig. 3 ), as well as their measurable concentration ranges and corresponding regression equations (Supplemental Table 2). Representative analyses of liver samples collected 6 h after APAP administration demonstrated that APAP metabolites could be clearly identified and quantitatively measured, each displaying distinct chromatographic profiles in Dnajb4 +/+ and Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 3 B). Quantitative and proportional analyses across time points revealed that compared with Dnajb4 +/+ , Dnajb4 −/− exhibited reduced levels of detoxification and de-oxidation metabolites, but significantly elevated levels of NAPQI-derived metabolites (Fig. 3 C). Specifically, at 3 h post-APAP administration, Dnajb4 +/+ displayed significantly higher levels of APAP-glucuronide, APAP-sulfate, and APAP-GSH than Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 3 D). In contrast, at 6 h post-treatment, APAP-cys and APAP-NAC levels were markedly higher in Dnaj4b −/− (Fig. 3 E). Furthermore, 24 h after APAP exposure, GSH levels were significantly lower in Dnajb4 −/− , consistent with sustained GSH depletion (Supplemental Fig. 4 ). Together, these findings indicate that the absence of DNAJB4/HLJ1 shifts hepatic APAP metabolism toward toxic NAPQI intermediates, thereby exacerbating liver injury. sections.minimal differences in metabolizing enzy: To test whether altered enzyme expression contributed to the observed metabolic shift, we analyzed key phase I and phase II enzymes involved in APAP metabolism, including CYP2E1, CYP1A2, CYP3A4, UGT1A1, UGT1A6, UGT1A9, and SULT1A1 (UGT, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase; SULT, sulfotransferase), in livers from Dnajb4 +/+ and Dnajb4 −/− before and after APAP treatment (Fig. 4 ). At the mRNA level, only Ugt1a6 was significantly higher in Dnajb4 +/+ compared with Dnajb4 −/− under basal conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed for other enzymes (Fig. 4 A). At the protein level, we focused on the major phase I enzymes CYP2E1 and CYP3A4. CYP2E1 was significantly higher in Dnajb4 +/+ before treatment, but no significant differences were observed under other conditions (Fig. 4 B). Overall, these results suggest that the metabolic changes in Dnajb4 −/− are not primarily driven by differences in expression of major metabolic enzymes.
sections.enhanced er stress underlies apap-induce: To investigate the mechanisms underlying APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, we examined markers of ER stress, as oxidative stress and protein misfolding caused by toxic APAP metabolites are known to activate the UPR (Hionides-Gutierrez et al. 2025 ). Following APAP treatment, the global ER stress sensor BiP, along with the three major UPR branches—ATF6, IRE1, and PERK—were generally upregulated in Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 5 A). Specifically, in the ATF6 pathway, cleaved ATF6 levels were significantly increased after APAP exposure. In the IRE1 pathway, although phosphorylated IRE1 levels were not markedly altered, its key downstream effector XBP1s was robustly upregulated in Dnajb4 −/− . In the PERK pathway, the downstream pro-apoptotic marker CHOP was also significantly increased in Dnajb4 −/− after APAP treatment (Fig. 5 B). In contrast, hepatic HSP70 expression in Dnajb4 −/− exhibited a decreasing trend compared with Dnajb4 +/+ after APAP challenge, although this difference did not reach statistical significance. Together, these findings indicate that APAP-derived NAPQI is associated with enhanced ER stress-related signaling in the injured liver, and the absence of DNAJB4/HLJ1 resulted in the impaired capacity to modulate this stress response, thus leading to more severe and sustained hepatocellular injury. Fig. 5 Loss of DNAJB4/HLJ1 alters hepatic ER stress response upon APAP treatment. A Western blot analysis of ER stress-related protein in livers from wild-type ( Dnajb4 +/+ ) and knockout ( Dnajb4 −/− ) mice at basal conditions and 6 h after acetaminophen (400 mg/kg) treatment. Analyzed proteins include HLJ1, HSP70, and three major downstream signaling pathways: the ATF6 pathway, the IRE1 pathway, and the PERK pathway, related to ER stress. α-tubulin was used as a loading control. B Quantification of protein levels normalized to α-tubulin. Data represent mean ± SD. (n = 3 per group). *p < 0.05
sections.potential co-modulation of er stress res: To further probe the molecular mechanisms underlying DNAJB4/HLJ1-mediated hepatoprotection, we performed transcriptomic analyses integrating both experimental and public datasets (Fig. 6 ). Specifically, we analyzed two transcriptomic datasets, GSE148204 and GSE205201 , which represent liver samples from Dnajb4 +/+ and Dnajb4 −/− , and liver samples collected at different time points following APAP administration in mice, respectively. Genes exhibiting a fold change of ≥ 1.5 and statistical significance (p < 0.05) were subjected to process network and Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analyses (Fig. 6 A). Process network analysis revealed significant enrichment of pathways related to ER stress, protein folding, and DNA damage responses. Consistently, GO process analysis highlighted enrichment in metabolic processes, stress responses, and responses to oxygen-containing compounds. These findings suggest that DNAJB4/HLJ1 deficiency and APAP-induced liver injury share common stress-response signatures. To further delineate shared molecular features, we performed an intersection analysis using a Venn diagram (Fig. 6 B) and identified 29 genes significantly altered across datasets (Supplemental Table 3). Among these genes, Hspa1b , a member of the HSP70 family, emerged as a prominent stress-responsive candidate. In the independent APAP time-course dataset ( GSE205201 ), both Hspa1a and Hspa1b exhibited strong and time-dependent induction following APAP exposure (Fig. 6 C), consistent with the established role of HSP70 chaperones in proteostasis and adaptive ER stress responses. We next examined the expression dynamics of DNAJ family members under APAP treatment using the same dataset (Fig. 6 D). Notably, Dnajb4 expression increased significantly in a time-dependent manner following APAP exposure. Collectively, these results support a co-induction or a co-modulation role for DNAJB4/HLJ1 and HSP70 in coordinating hepatic ER stress responses triggered by oxidative and metabolic stressors. Fig. 6 Transcriptomic analysis reveals altered stress and metabolic gene responses in DNAJB4/HLJ1-deficient mouse liver following APAP treatment. A Process network and gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between wild-type ( Dnajb4 +/+ ) and knockout ( Dnajb4 −/− ) mice livers ( GSE148204 ) (left), and APAP- vs. vehicle-treated livers at 3 and 6 h post-injection ( GSE205201 ) (middle and right). Top enriched biological processes or networks are ranked by -log(p) value. B Venn diagram illustration for the overlap of metabolic process-related DEGs among three comparisons, including Dnajb4 +/+ vs. Dnajb4 −/− , APAP vs. vehicle at 3 h, and APAP vs. vehicle at 6 h. C Heatmap of hepatic Hsp gene expression in mouse livers after APAP treatment (top), highlighting the significant upregulation of APAP-induced Hsp70 ( Hspa1a / Hspa1b ) (red arrow) (bottom). (n = 5 per group) D Heatmap of differential expression of Dnajb family members in mouse livers after APAP treatment (top). Dnajb4 is highlighted (red arrow) and quantification at different time points after APAP treatment showed significantly upregulated (bottom). (n = 5 per group) Data represent mean ± SD. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001 * p < 0.05
sections.dnajb4/hlj1-hsp70 interaction strengthen: Based on transcriptomic results, we first employed AlphaFold-Multimer to predict potential interaction partners of DNAJB4/HLJ1 that may coordinate the cellular response to APAP-induced ER stress (Supplemental Table 3). Among the 29 proteins that were significantly altered across multiple datasets, HSPA1B, a member of HSP70, exhibited the highest predicted template modeling (pTM) and inter-chain predicted template modeling (ipTM) scores in structural interaction modeling with DNAJB4/HLJ1 (ipTM = 0.65, pTM = 0.6), prompting further validation. These results suggest that HSPA1B has the strongest potential to interact with DNAJB4/HLJ1, based on protein structure compatibility and inter-chain interface reliability. To further assess the spatial confidence of residue-level interactions between DNAJB4/HLJ1 and HSPA1B, we analyzed the predicted aligned error (PAE) plot generated by AlphaFold-Multimer modeling (Fig. 7 A). The analysis revealed high confidence in the spatial positioning of DNAJB4/HLJ1 residues 1–80 and 168–337 with HSPA1B residues 1–600 and 600–641, respectively, indicating probable binding interfaces. Structural visualization using ChimeraX showed that the DNAJB4/HLJ1 J-domain (JD) interacted with the interdomain region between the substrate-binding and nucleotide-binding domains (SBD and NBD) of HSPA1B, consistent with the canonical binding mode of J-domain proteins. Furthermore, T637, E640, and D642 of HSPA1B were predicted to form hydrogen bonds with K205, K209, T212, and K302 of the C-terminal domain (CTD-I) of DNAJB4/HLJ1. In addition, hydrophobic interactions between P636 and I638 of HSPA1B and W208, I214, and F216 of DNAJB4/HLJ1 further stabilized the interface between the EEVD tail of HSPA1B and CTD-I of DNAJB4/HLJ1 (Fig. 7 B). Because commonly available antibodies recognize the HSP70 family rather than specifically distinguishing the isoform HSPA1B, subsequent experiments were performed using a general HSP70 antibody, and the term HSP70 is used in the following experimental analyses. Co-immunoprecipitation assays confirmed a physical interaction between DNAJB4/HLJ1 and HSP70 in mouse liver tissues (Fig. 7 C), with a notable enhancement in binding observed 6 h after APAP treatment. These data demonstrate a dynamic HLJ1–HSP70 interaction in response to stress. Fig. 7 DNAJB4/HLJ1 interacts with HSPA1B (HSP70) as demonstrated by in silico modeling and co-immunoprecipitation assays. A Predicted aligned error (PAE) plot from AlphaFold-Multimer modeling of DNAJB4/HLJ1 and HSPA1B interaction (ipTM = 0.65, pTM = 0.6). Lower PAE values (dark green) indicate higher confidence in spatial positioning between residues, suggesting potential binding interfaces. B Structural model of DNAJB4/HLJ1 (cyan) and HSPA1B (purple) generated from AlphaFold-Multimer. Binding interfaces are highlighted, including J-domain (JD) interaction, C-terminal domain-I (CTD-I) hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic contacts (cyan: DNAJB4/HLJ1; purple: HSPA1B). C Co-immunoprecipitation analysis confirming DNAJB4/HLJ1-HSP70 interaction in mouse liver lysates following acetaminophen administration (0 and 6 h). DNAJB4/HLJ1 was immunoprecipitated and probed for HSP70 (left panel), and reciprocally, HSP70 was immunoprecipitated and probed for DNAJB4/HLJ1 (right panel). Input and IgG controls are included to validate specificity. ipTM, inter-chain predicted template modeling; pTM, predicted template modeling
sections.dnajb4/hlj1 reconstitution in knockout m: Given that DNAJB4/HLJ1 modulates ER stress and alleviates APAP-induced liver injury, we next examined whether hepatic re-expression of DNAJB4/HLJ1 could mitigate liver damage caused by reactive drug metabolites (Fig. 8 ). To this end, we employed hydrodynamic tail vein injection in mice to re-express DNAJB4/HLJ1 specifically in the liver (Fig. 8 A). DNAJB4/HLJ1 was re-expressed 36 h prior to APAP administration, after which liver tissues were harvested for histopathological evaluation and analysis of ER stress markers and associated signaling pathways. Protein and DNA analysis confirmed successful reconstitution of DNAJB4/HLJ1 in the livers of Dnajb4 −/− following hydrodynamic injection (Fig. 8 B). As a control for evaluating re-expression efficiency, a plasmid encoding GFP was administered using the same approach, and fluorescence microscopy revealed robust GFP expression throughout the hepatic lobules (Fig. 8 C). Histopathological analysis demonstrated that hepatic re-expression of DNAJB4/HLJ1 markedly attenuated APAP-induced hepatic injury in Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 8 D). Consistent with this protective effect, expression of ER stress markers, including CHOP and IRE1, was significantly reduced in the livers of DNAJB4/HLJ1-reexpressing Dnajb4 −/− (Fig. 8 E). Moreover, phosphorylation of c-Jun and JNK, which are key mediators of APAP-induced hepatotoxicity, was also decreased following DNAJB4/HLJ1 re-expression (Fig. 8 F). Finally, to further clarify the role of ER stress in the process by which DNAJB4/HLJ1 counteracts APAP toxicity, we employed tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), a pharmacological inhibitor of ER stress (Supplemental Fig. 6 ). TUDCA was administered to Dnajb4 −/− 2 h prior to APAP injection, and liver and blood samples were collected 12 h after APAP treatment for subsequent analysis (Supplemental Fig. 6 A). The results demonstrated that TUDCA treatment effectively reduced ER stress (Supplemental Fig. 6 B). Consistently, TUDCA attenuated APAP-induced elevations in serum AST and ALT levels and alleviated liver injury, as evidenced by histopathological assessment (Supplemental Fig. 6 C and D). Overall, these findings provide proof-of-concept that restoring DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression in the liver restrains maladaptive stress signaling, including ER stress–associated pathways, and mitigates APAP-induced hepatic injury. Fig. 8 Exogenous DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression mitigates APAP-induced liver injury in DNAJB4/HLJ1-deficient mice. A Schematic of the experimental timeline. Mice received hydrodynamic tail vein injections of plasmids encoding either GFP as a control or DNAJB4/HLJ1 (50 µg DNA/2 mL per 20 g mouse). After 36 h, mice were injected intraperitoneally (i.p.) with APAP 400 mg/kg, and liver samples were collected 24 h later. B Western blot analysis for validating DNAJB4/HLJ1 protein expression and PCR for Dnajb4 knockout genotype in liver tissue of wild-type (WT, Dnajb4 +/+ ) and knockout (KO, Dnajb4 −/− ) alleles. C Fluorescence imaging of GFP by the dissecting fluorescence microscope in whole liver samples. GFP expression was confirmed for the efficiency of the transgene. Scale bar = 0.5 mm. D Representative H&E-stained liver sections showing APAP-induced necrosis in different experimental groups. Quantification of necrotic area indicates that exogenous DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression is significantly reduced in KO mice compared to GFP controls. Scale bar = 200 µm. Data are presented as mean ± SD. *, p < 0.05 E Western blot analysis of DNAJB4/HLJ1 and ER stress related proteins, CHOP and IRE1, expression in liver lysates from mice treated with APAP. CHOP and IRE1 levels were reduced in DNAJB4/HLJ1-expressing Dnajb4 −/− . F Western blot analysis of phosphorylated and total c-jun and JNK. DNAJB4/HLJ1 expression reduced APAP-induced c-jun/JNK pathway activation in Dnajb4 −/− . β-actin served as a loading control in all blots
sections.discussion: DILI remains a leading cause of acute liver failure worldwide, with limited therapeutic options, particularly in cases of APAP overdose (Hoofnagle and Björnsson 2019 ; Li et al. 2021 ). While ER stress is increasingly implicated in APAP hepatotoxicity, the regulatory role of HSPs in this context remains incompletely defined, limiting the development of targeted interventions. Given the abundant hepatic expression of DNAJB4/HLJ1, we investigated its physiological function in APAP-induced liver injury using a DNAJB4/HLJ1-deficient mouse model. Dnajb4 −/− exhibited enhanced accumulation of NAPQI-derived conjugates, impaired GSH recovery, aggravated necrosis, and heightened ER stress activation, indicating increased vulnerability to APAP challenge. As excessive NAPQI formation and delayed GSH regeneration are key drivers of ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction (Yan et al. 2018 ), these findings implicate DNAJB4/HLJ1 as a protective regulator of hepatocellular injury. Although no broad genotype-dependent alterations in major APAP-metabolizing enzymes were observed, modest basal differences in CYP2E1 protein and Ugt1a6 mRNA were noted. Given the central role of CYP2E1 in APAP bioactivation (McGill and Jaeschke 2014 ; Nelson 1990 ), even subtle variation may influence early NAPQI generation and cannot be entirely excluded. However, the absence of consistent, large-scale enzymatic changes suggests that altered phase I or II metabolism is unlikely to be the primary driver of the aggravated phenotype. Due to the extreme reactivity and short half-life of NAPQI, we quantified downstream conjugates, which are widely accepted surrogate markers of NAPQI burden (Jaeschke et al. 2012 ; James et al. 2003 ). Notably, these metabolites are also influenced by GSH availability and cellular redox status. The sustained GSH depletion observed in Dnajb4 −/− therefore suggests that increased conjugate levels likely reflect compromised detoxification capacity and reduced stress resilience, rather than solely enhanced bioactivation. Collectively, these findings support a multifactorial model in which DNAJB4/HLJ1 deficiency lowers the threshold for metabolic and proteostatic stress, thereby amplifying ER stress signaling and hepatocellular injury during APAP challenge. We compared liver transcriptomic profiles from Dnajb4 −/− and APAP-treated wild-type mice and identified shared stress-response signatures. Among the candidates, HSPA1B emerged prominently in our selected transcriptomic analysis, although both HSPA1A and HSPA1B were significantly induced following APAP challenge. In silico modelling further suggested a potential structural distinction, revealing that murine HSPA1B contains an additional proline insertion (P628) adjacent to the C-terminal EEVD motif, resulting in a marked bend in the EEVD tail (79.6° vs. 34.8° in HSPA1A; Supplemental Fig. 5 ). Prior studies have established that HSP70 activity is modulated by its EEVD motif through interactions with co-chaperones (Johnson et al. 2022 ), and that the EEVD-CTD-I binding is crucial for relieving DNAJB autoinhibition and initiating HSP40-70 cycling (Faust et al. 2020 ). Consistent with these mechanisms, our structural model suggested that the altered EEVD orientation in HSPA1B may enhance its compatibility with the HLJ1 CTD-I domain (ipTM = 0.65 vs. 0.31 in HSPA1A-HLJ1), potentially contributing to the preferential implication observed in the murine transcriptomic networks. Notably, proteomic studies have demonstrated that DNAJ/HSP40-HSP70 partnerships are inherently selective and tissue-specific (Piette et al. 2021 ; Shemesh et al. 2021 ), supporting the concept that even subtle conformational differences may bias chaperone pairing. We acknowledge that our biochemical validation used a general HSP70 antibody, which cannot distinguish HSPA1A from HSPA1B. Due to the lack of reliable isoform-specific antibodies and the high sequence similarity between HSPA1A and HSPA1B in mice, our data support DNAJB4/HLJ1 interaction with inducible HSP70 under APAP stress rather than definitive HSPA1B-specific binding. We note that direct functional validation of their interaction in vivo was not performed, as such approaches remain technically challenging. Notably, murine HSPA1A and HSPA1B differ by only a single proline near the EEVD motif, while the human isoforms are identical, suggesting that DNAJB4/HLJ1 may act broadly through HSP70 in humans, making isoform distinction less biologically relevant. A growing body of evidence implicates ER stress as a contributing mediator in DILI pathogenesis. The liver’s extensive ER network, required for protein synthesis and xenobiotic metabolism, makes hepatocytes particularly vulnerable to misfolded protein accumulation. During APAP overdose, excess NAPQI formation burdens the ER’s folding machinery and triggers the UPR, contributing to hepatocellular damage (Hionides-Gutierrez et al. 2025 ). Members of the DNAJ/HSP40 family support proteostasis by cooperating with HSP70s, and several DNAJB proteins have established roles in ER protein quality control and stress adaptation (Kampinga et al. 2019 ). For example, DNAJB12 inactivation sensitizes cells to ER stress-induced apoptosis by impairing the degradation of pro-apoptotic protein BOK through ER-associated degradation (ERAD) (Sopha et al. 2017 ). Consistent with these functions, our transcriptomic data suggest that DNAJB4/HLJ1 is associated with UPR and protein folding pathways, and Dnajb4 −/− mice show heightened ER-stress markers after APAP challenge. Moreover, the KO mice exhibited a slower decline in APAP-cys and APAP-NAC levels, suggesting impaired resolution of APAP-induced cellular stress. Although direct ER localization of DNAJB4/HLJ1 has not been demonstrated, previous work showed that DNAJB4/HLJ1 participates in ERAD-dependent clearance of misfolded E-cadherin (Simões-Correia et al. 2014 ). Future experiments, such as validating subcellular localization and potential interactions with ERAD components, will confirm whether this effect is direct or indirect. Beyond ER stress, APAP-induced injury is strongly driven by oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, marked by robust JNK activation (Jaeschke and Ramachandran 2024 ). Given the close interdependence of ER and mitochondria, and the essential roles of DNAJ/HSP40 proteins in maintaining mitochondrial protein homeostasis (Kampinga et al. 2019 ), disruptions in ER proteostasis may further amplify mitochondrial damage. The IRE1 branch of the UPR can activate JNK, which translocates to mitochondria and binds Sab, inhibiting the respiratory chain and amplifying superoxide production in a feed-forward loop (Urano et al. 2000 ; Win et al. 2014 ). In addition, prolonged ER stress can perturb Ca 2 ⁺ homeostasis, further compromising mitochondrial function (Makio et al. 2024 ). Consistent with the enrichment of mitochondrial maintenance pathways observed in our transcriptomic data, these mechanisms may indicate that DNAJB4/HLJ1 contributes to broader hepatoprotective responses during APAP challenge. Interestingly, our transcriptomic analyses also identified choline kinase α gene ( Chka ) as significantly upregulated in both APAP-treated wild-type and Dnajb4 −/− livers. Chka catalyzes the first step of phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, and its increased expression is often associated with membrane biogenesis and metabolic rewiring in stressed conditions (Ren et al. 2025 ). Although Chka inhibition is known to trigger ER stress-induced apoptosis via CHOP activation (Sanchez-Lopez et al. 2013 ), its elevation here more likely reflects a compensatory response to heightened proteostatic stress, as prolonged UPR signaling is known to induce lipogenic pathways (Moncan et al. 2021 ). In metabolic contexts such as MASLD, where basal ER stress, impaired UGT expression, and altered phospholipid remodeling are present (Ernst et al. 2024 ), DNAJB4/HLJ1 deficiency may further exacerbate injury, potentially engaging alternative cell-death mechanisms such as ferroptosis. These findings may indicate that HLJ1 participates in an HSP70-independent regulatory axis involving metabolic enzymes such as Chka, warranting further mechanistic investigation in predisposed metabolic dysfunction-related DILI. In several forms of DILI, pharmacologic agents such as diclofenac, carbamazepine, and nefazodone activate ER stress pathways through Nrf2 and MAPK signaling, involving downstream effectors including JNK, ERK1/2, and p38 (Fredriksson et al. 2014 ; Ren et al. 2016 ). Hepatoxicity driven by ER stress thus remains a significant clinical challenge. To attenuate ER stress, small molecules such as salubrinal and 4-PBA have shown protective effects in models of MASLD, autoimmune hepatitis, and chemotherapy-induced liver injury (Fan et al. 2024 ; Li et al. 2020 , 2024 ). Despite these advances, strategies that directly target the endogenous chaperone network, particularly the HSP40/HSP70 axis, remain largely unexplored in the context of DILI. Our study demonstrated that restoring DNAJB4/HLJ1 restrains maladaptive stress signaling, including ER stress–associated pathways, and mitigates APAP-induced liver injury, providing preliminary evidence that modulation of HSP40 activity may represent a previously untouched protective mechanism. Consistent with this, pharmacologic attenuation of ER stress in Dnajb4 −/− partially rescues APAP-induced liver injury, supporting a functional contribution of ER stress to the aggravated phenotype. While APAP hepatotoxicity is classically attributed to mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by ROS generation, our findings suggest that ER stress is required for the development of APAP-induced liver injury under these conditions. Although therapeutic efficacy remains to be established, these results highlight HSPs as biologically grounded and potentially novel targets across DILI etiologies. A limitation of our study is that we primarily focused on early, acute mechanisms of APAP-induced liver injury. Prior work has shown that sterile inflammation and immune cells, including Kupffer cells, monocyte-derived macrophages, and neutrophils, play important roles in the regenerative phase following moderate APAP overdose (Jaeschke and Ramachandran 2024 ). Since a whole-body knockout was performed in our model, we cannot exclude the possibility that its loss in immune or stromal cells contributed to the observed phenotype. Future investigations in these mechanisms will be necessary to dissect these contributions. We also did not analyze the influence of genetic polymorphisms or expression variability. DILI susceptibility is strongly affected by individual polymorphisms in drug-metabolizing enzymes (Ingelman-Sundberg et al. 2007 ). Similarly, isoforms and expression variability in HSPs may also modulate DILI outcomes, which remains to be explored. Our work provides a conceptual foundation to understand how co-chaperones may influence DILI progression, highlighting a novel path for mechanistic studies and therapeutic interventions. In summary, we demonstrate that DNAJB4/HLJ1 contributes to hepatocellular resilience against APAP-induced injury by modulating stress signaling, including ER stress-associated pathways, within the broader cellular stress network. While NAC remains the only approved antidote for APAP toxicity, its limited efficacy once hepatocellular injury is established underscores the need for alternative strategies. The identification of DNAJB4/HLJ1 as an endogenous modulator of liver resilience highlights a promising avenue for therapeutic exploration.
sections.animal experiments: Dnajb4 -targeted mice were generated using a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC; bMQ341C24) encompassing the Dnajb4 genomic region, which was subcloned into the pL253 vector to construct the targeting plasmid. In 129 Sv embryonic stem (ES) cells, the endogenous allele was disrupted via homologous recombination by introducing a modified allele harboring a neomycin resistance cassette flanked by loxP sites in intron 1, along with an additional loxP site inserted into intron 2. Correctly targeted ES clones were identified by Southern blot analysis and subsequently subjected to transient transfection with pCAGGS-NLS-Cre to mediate deletion of exon 2 (~ 1.9 kb). Following selection, genomic DNA from targeted ES cells was extracted and further validated by Southern blotting using α−32P-dCTP-labeled probes, as previously reported (Luo et al. 2022 ). Recombinant ES cells were microinjected into C57BL/6 blastocysts to produce chimeric mice, and germline transmission was confirmed through mating with C57BL/6 animals. The resulting mutant line was backcrossed for ten generations to establish a congenic background.
sections.genotyping: Genomic DNA was isolated from mouse tail biopsies using a DNA Purification Kit (Promega, USA). Genotyping was performed by PCR with primer pair I1F/I1R to detect the wild-type allele and I1F/I2R to identify the knockout allele. The primer sequences were as follows: I1F, 5′-AGGCTTGCTGTCTAAGGTGATG-3′; I1R, 5′-GTGCAGGTACCTGTGAAGGTC-3′; and I2R, 5′-ACGTTCAAAGCTATCATAGTC-3′.
sections.transcriptomic analysis: Transcriptomic profiling was conducted following the Affymetrix GeneChip Expression Analysis Technical Manual, consistent with previously published procedures (Leu et al. 2017 ). Briefly, total RNA (8 μg) extracted from independent liver samples of Dnajb4 + / + and Dnajb4 −/− mice was reverse-transcribed using a T7 primer with the One-cycle cDNA Synthesis Kit (Affymetrix, Santa Clara, CA). The resulting cDNA was purified and subsequently subjected to in vitro transcription in the presence of biotin-labeled ribonucleotides (IVT Labeling Kit; Affymetrix). The labeled RNA was then fragmented, and an aliquot was hybridized overnight to the Mouse Genome 430 2.0 GeneChip (Affymetrix). After hybridization, arrays were processed using the manufacturer’s amplification staining protocol, followed by scanning with an Affymetrix GeneChip Scanner 3000 7G. Image acquisition and initial data processing were carried out using GeneChip Operating Software (GCOS) version 1.4. All experiments were performed with three independent biological replicates per group. Differentially expressed genes were identified using a twofold change threshold with false discovery rate (FDR) control ( p < 0.05) implemented in GeneSpring GX 14.8 (Silicon Genetics, Redwood City, CA). Functional enrichment analysis was conducted using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) to interpret biological significance. FDR values were estimated based on 1,000 Monte Carlo permutations, and normalized enrichment scores (NES) were calculated to account for gene set size and enable comparison across datasets. All transcriptomic datasets, including raw and processed files, have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession number GSE148204 .
sections.pharmacological treatment in animal mode: Pharmacological interventions in mice included the establishment of an APAP-induced acute liver injury model and the use of TUDCA to inhibit ER stress. For the APAP-induced acute liver injury model, APAP (MCE, Cat#. HY-660005) was dissolved in 0.9% normal saline at 37 °C and administered via intraperitoneal injection. The final dosage was determined according to experimental design. Serum and liver samples were collected at 3, 6, and 24 h post-injection for subsequent biochemical, histological, and molecular analyses. For ER stress inhibition, mice were treated with TUDCA based on the previous study with minor modifications (Luo et al. 2024 ). Briefly, TUDCA (100 mg/kg body weight; MCE, Cat#. HY-19696A) was dissolved in PBS and administered via intraperitoneal injection 2 h prior to APAP administration. Mice were sacrificed 12 h after APAP treatment, and liver tissue and blood samples were collected for histopathological evaluation, liver function, and molecular analysis.
sections.histopathological and serum biochemistry: Livers were fixed in 10% formalin, paraffin-embedded, sectioned, and stained with Hematoxylin–Eosin. ImageJ Software is used to circle and quantify the necrosis area. For biochemical analysis, blood samples were collected from the submandibular region at different time points (0, 3, 6, and 24 h), clotted at room temperature for 20 min, and centrifuged at 2000 g for 10 min. The serum is collected and stored at −80℃ for biochemical analysis. Serum ALT and AST are analyzed by using Cobas c111 (Roche).
sections.metabolites analysis by mass spectrometr: Liver samples were mechanically disrupted prior to metabolite extraction, which was performed using 20% methanol in MS-grade solvent to recover APAP-related metabolites. Analytical measurements were conducted on an Agilent 1290 Infinity UHPLC platform coupled to an Agilent 6460 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer equipped with a Jet Stream electrospray ionization source. For chromatographic resolution, analytes were separated on a ZORBAX® Eclipse Plus C18 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm; Agilent) maintained at 40 °C. The binary mobile phase system consisted of water with 0.02% formic acid (phase A; ultrapure, 18.2 MΩ) and methanol containing 0.02% formic acid (phase B; LC–MS grade). The gradient was programmed to increase the proportion of phase B from 5 to 30% over the initial 6 min, followed by a ramp to 90% B during the subsequent 4 min. A post-run equilibration of 2 min was included before the next injection. The flow rate was fixed at 0.3 mL/min, and 5 μL of each sample was introduced into the system. Detection was performed under both positive and negative ionization settings. Source parameters included a drying gas temperature of 350 °C (11 L/min), nebulizer pressure at 45 psi, and sheath gas delivered at 350 °C with a flow rate of 10 L/min. The capillary voltage was set to 3.5 kV, and the nozzle voltage to 500 V, with identical settings applied in both ion modes.
sections.real-time quantitative pcr: Total RNA was isolated using NucleoZOL reagent (Takara Bio, #740,404.200). For cDNA synthesis, 2 μg of RNA was reverse-transcribed with the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, Cat# 4368814). Quantitative PCR was conducted using SYBR Green Master Mix on a QuantStudio 3 system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The reverse transcription reaction conditions were set at 25 °C for 10 min, 37 °C for 120 min, followed by 85 °C for 5 min. Relative mRNA expression levels were normalized to β-actin and calculated using the 2^ − ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are provided in Supplemental Table 4.
sections.immunoblotting and immunoprecipitation: Tissue protein extraction and Western blot analysis were performed as described previously, with modifications to accommodate the experimental design of this study. Briefly, tissues were homogenized in lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and equal amounts of total protein (30 μg per lane) were loaded for SDS-PAGE to ensure consistent protein input across samples. For normalization, β-actin or α-tubulin was used as an internal loading control depending on the experimental context. Within each experimental set, the same internal reference was applied consistently for all groups. Although β-actin may exhibit tissue-specific expression variability due to differences in cellular composition and cytoskeletal abundance among organs (Eaton et al. 2013 ), equal protein loading was primarily ensured by BCA quantification prior to electrophoresis, and internal controls were used for normalization within each experiment. All antibodies used in this study are shown in Supplemental Table 5. The immunoprecipitation and immunoblot were performed according to the protocol as previously described with minor adjustments (Chen et al. 2014 ). Liver tissues were lysed using T-PER Tissue Protein Extraction Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich). For co-immunoprecipitation assays, lysates were prepared in IP lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors and mechanically sheared by repeated passage through a 21-gauge needle. Protein A/G agarose beads were incubated with 1 μg of anti-HSP70 antibody (Cat#10,995–1-AP, Proteintech) in 400 μL of 1 × TBS on a vertical rotator for 4 h at 4 °C. Subsequently, 200 μL of lysate containing 1 mg total protein was added, and the mixture was further incubated overnight at 4 °C with gentle rotation. Beads were then washed, and bound proteins were eluted by resuspension in 4 × sample buffer containing 2-mercaptoethanol (Cat# M3148, Sigma-Aldrich), followed by heating at 95 °C for 10 min. The resulting supernatants were subjected to SDS-PAGE analysis.
sections.glutathione measurement: Liver glutathione was measured by Glutathione Assay Kit (Cayman, Cat#703,002) following the manufacturer’s protocol.
sections.structural modeling: Protein interaction predictions were performed using AlphaFold-Multimer ( https://alphafoldserver.com ) with default parameters (Abramson et al. 2024 ; Evans et al. 2022 ), and visualized by ChimeraX (Meng et al. 2023 ). Protein sequences were retrieved from UniProt, and the canonical sequence was used for analysis when multiple isoforms exist. Predictions with an inter-chain predicted template modeling (ipTM) score above 0.6 were considered potential interactors and selected for subsequent validation.
sections.re-expressing dnajb4/hlj1 by hydrodynami: Hydrodynamic gene delivery was performed as described previously with slight modifications (Liu et al. 1999 ). For in vivo re-expression, either pcDNA3.1-DNAJB4/HLJ1 or control pcDNA3.1-eGFP plasmid was prepared. A total of 50 μg plasmid DNA diluted in 2 mL normal saline was rapidly injected into the tail vein of Dnajb4 + / + and Dnajb4 −/− mice within 6–8 s. Following injection, mice were allowed a 36-h recovery period to permit protein expression. Subsequently, APAP was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 400 mg/kg. Animals were euthanized 24 h after APAP treatment, and liver tissues were collected for gross imaging using a fluorescence stereomicroscope, followed by histological examination.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical analyses were performed using Student’s t-test implemented in Microsoft Excel or GraphPad Prism 8. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), where n indicates the number of biological replicates or animals. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Longitudinal Adherence Trajectories to Statins and Antithrombotic Therapy After Ischemic Stroke and Their Impact on Low‐Density Lipoprotein Control and Cardiovascular Outcomes
abstract: Background Adherence to secondary prevention therapies after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack is often suboptimal, and the clinical implications of adherence patterns remain unclear. This study identified adherence trajectories to statins and antithrombotic agents and evaluated their associations with lipid control and cardiovascular outcomes. Methods Using the Chang Gung Research Database linked to Taiwan's population claims data, we identified patients with first‐ever acute ischemic stroke/transient ischemic attack between 2012 and 2018 who survived ≥1 year and initiated secondary prevention. Monthly adherence was measured by proportion of days covered and classified using group‐based multitrajectory modeling. The primary outcome was a composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, and myocardial infarction; secondary outcomes included individual components and all‐cause death. Results Among 13 299 eligible patients (mean age, 65.6 years; 60.3% men), 4 adherence trajectories were identified: dual high adherence (46.7%), antithrombotic‐only adherence (35.1%), early dual discontinuation (12.2%), and gradual dual decline (6.0%). Dual high adherence achieved the greatest low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol reduction (−24.3%) and lowest mortality rate. Early dual discontinuation was associated with higher risks of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.57 [95% CI, 1.31–1.88], recurrent ischemic stroke/systemic embolism (aHR, 1.60 [95% CI, 1.31–1.95]), myocardial infarction (aHR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.02–2.14]), and all‐cause death (aHR, 1.56 [95% CI, 1.36–1.79]). Poor adherence had greater adverse impact among patients with baseline low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥100 mg/dL, younger adults, and men. Conclusions Adherence trajectories were strongly associated with low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol and major cardiovascular outcomes. Sustained dual adherence conferred substantial protection, whereas early discontinuation markedly increased recurrent ischemic and mortality risks.

sections.background: Adherence to secondary prevention therapies after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack is often suboptimal, and the clinical implications of adherence patterns remain unclear. This study identified adherence trajectories to statins and antithrombotic agents and evaluated their associations with lipid control and cardiovascular outcomes.
sections.methods: Using the Chang Gung Research Database linked to Taiwan's population claims data, we identified patients with first‐ever acute ischemic stroke/transient ischemic attack between 2012 and 2018 who survived ≥1 year and initiated secondary prevention. Monthly adherence was measured by proportion of days covered and classified using group‐based multitrajectory modeling. The primary outcome was a composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, and myocardial infarction; secondary outcomes included individual components and all‐cause death.
sections.results: Among 13 299 eligible patients (mean age, 65.6 years; 60.3% men), 4 adherence trajectories were identified: dual high adherence (46.7%), antithrombotic‐only adherence (35.1%), early dual discontinuation (12.2%), and gradual dual decline (6.0%). Early dual discontinuation was associated with higher risks of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.57 [95% CI, 1.31–1.88], recurrent ischemic stroke/systemic embolism (aHR, 1.60 [95% CI, 1.31–1.95]), myocardial infarction (aHR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.02–2.14]), and all‐cause death (aHR, 1.56 [95% CI, 1.36–1.79]).
