sections.what is new?: In a large real‐world cohort of patients with first‐ever acute ischemic stroke/transient ischemic attack, group‐based multitrajectory modeling identified 4 distinct 12‐month adherence patterns to statins and antithrombotic therapy (dual high adherence, antithrombotic‐only adherence, early dual discontinuation, and gradual dual decline). These adherence phenotypes were strongly associated with low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol control and cardiovascular outcomes, with dual high adherence showing the greatest low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol reduction while early dual discontinuation was linked to higher risks of the composite outcome and all‐cause death.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Future studies should test whether targeted, scalable adherence‐support strategies (eg, structured postdischarge follow‐up, pharmacist‐led programs, or digital interventions) can shift patients away from early discontinuation/decline trajectories and reduce recurrent ischemic events and death.
sections.methods_1: Data and materials are not available for sharing due to institutional restrictions.
sections.data source: The Chang Gung Research Database is derived from the Chang Gung Memorial Hospital system, a large multicenter health care network in Taiwan. The Chang Gung Research Database is a multi‐institutional electronic health record database that captures routine clinical encounters, including emergency, inpatient, and outpatient care, without disease‐specific enrollment or research‐based selection. It covers ≈20% of outpatient visits and 12% of inpatient encounters in Taiwan. 22 In this study, the Chang Gung Research Database was linked to nationwide claims data from the Health and Welfare Data Science Center, covering >99% of the Taiwanese population. The linked data set provides longitudinal information on diagnoses, prescriptions, laboratory tests, and clinical events across care settings. The study period spanned January 1, 2011, to December 31, 2022. Institutional review board approval was obtained (Permit No. 202300443B0C602), which waived the requirement for informed consent due to the use of deidentified data.
sections.study cohort: We identified patients hospitalized for a first‐ever acute IS or transient ischemic attack (TIA) between 2012 and 2018 using validated International Classification of Diseases , Ninth / Tenth Revision , Clinical Modification ( ICD‐9 / 10‐CM ) codes (Table S1 ) and required confirmatory brain imaging, such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, during the index hospitalization. Patients without baseline LDL‐C measurements from the index hospitalization were excluded to accurately assess the association between statin adherence and changes in lipid profiles. Patients were excluded if they lacked baseline LDL‐C values, had prior cerebrovascular or cardiovascular events, died within 1 year of the index date, lacked sufficient follow‐up for adherence assessment, or experienced recurrent ischemic events during the 12‐month adherence assessment window to avoid reverse causation. The index date was defined as the hospital discharge date to align the start of follow‐up with initiation of outpatient secondary prevention therapy. Because adherence was assessed on the basis of outpatient prescription claims, defining the index date as the discharge date avoids exposure misclassification and minimizes immortal time bias.
sections.study outcomes: The primary outcome was a composite of recurrent IS, systemic embolism, and myocardial infarction. Secondary outcomes included individual components and all‐cause death. Outcomes were identified using ICD‐9 / 10‐CM codes based on hospital discharge diagnoses (Table S1 ). ICD‐9 / 10‐CM codes for IS, systemic embolism, and myocardial infarction have been validated in Taiwan's national health databases with high positive predictive value, supporting the accuracy of outcome ascertainment. 23 , 24 , 25 To ensure temporal ordering and avoid immortal time bias, adherence trajectories were defined during the 12‐month postindex window, and follow‐up began thereafter. Patients were followed prospectively until the occurrence of the outcome of interest, death, loss to follow‐up, or the end of data availability (December 31, 2022), whichever came first.
sections.covariates: Baseline characteristics included age, sex, smoking and drinking status, laboratory data (renal and liver function, lipid profile, and glycated hemoglobin), comorbidities (Charlson Comorbidity Index, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and dyslipidemia), and medication use (antihypertensive, antithrombotic, and lipid‐lowering therapies) within 365 days before the index date. Information on acute stroke management, including intravenous thrombolysis (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator) and endovascular thrombectomy, was also collected. Stroke severity was assessed using the validated claims‐based Stroke Severity Index (SSI), a proxy for the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, and categorized as mild (SSI ≤5), moderate (SSI 5 to ≤12), or severe (SSI >12). 26 , 27 In addition to baseline lipid‐lowering and antithrombotic therapy, concomitant medications during follow‐up (antihypertensive agents, antidiabetic agents, histamine‐2 receptor antagonists, proton pump inhibitors, and NSAIDs) were captured. Statin intensity (high, moderate, or low) was defined as the category with the greatest cumulative days supplied during the first year after discharge. When equal durations occurred, the higher‐intensity category was assigned. Medication use was defined as receiving >28 days of prescriptions for a given medication category within 365 days before the index date (for baseline covariate) and during the follow‐up period. To characterize health care use, the frequency of neurology follow‐up visits and LDL‐C monitoring was additionally recorded.
sections.proportion of days covered and group\u20: Statins included atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin, pitavastatin, lovastatin, and fluvastatin. Antithrombotic therapy was defined as use of antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, dipyridamole, cilostazol, and ticlopidine) or oral anticoagulants, including warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban). Monthly adherence to secondary prevention, statins, and antithrombotic agents was measured using the proportion of days covered (PDC). PDC values were calculated on the basis of prescribing dates, days of supply, and the actual refill occurrences in the full population database provided by the Health and Welfare Data Science Center. The total number of days covered in each 30‐day period after the index date was divided by 30, yielding PDC values ranging from 0 to 1. Group‐based multitrajectory modeling was used to classify patients according to similar adherence patterns over the 12 months following the index date. This method was selected because it captures heterogeneous, real‐world adherence behavior over time and provides greater clinical interpretability than static thresholds such as PDC ≥80%. A multitrajectory framework was applied to jointly model adherence to both antithrombotic agents (antiplatelet or anticoagulant) and statins across multiple indicators. 28 , 29 Model selection was based on the Bayesian information criterion, average posterior probability (>0.7), ≥5% group size, and acceptable odds of correct classification. 29 , 30 Detailed model specifications are provided in Tables S2 and S3 .
sections.statistical analysis: Baseline characteristics were compared using the χ 2 test and the Kruskal–Wallis test. The crude cumulative incidence of study outcomes was presented as percentages and incidence rates per 1000 person‐years across PDC trajectory groups. Associations between adherence trajectories and outcomes were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusting for baseline and time‐varying covariates. LDL‐C analyses were restricted to complete cases (available in 71% of patients). Stratified analyses were performed by age, sex, baseline LDL‐C, and stroke severity. Analyses were conducted using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC), with trajectories modeled using Proc Traj. A 2‐sided P <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.study population: A total of 24 931 patients hospitalized for acute IS or TIA met the initial inclusion criteria. Of these, 17 382 had a first‐ever acute IS/TIA between 2012 and 2018. After excluding patients without ≥1 year of follow‐up or without any secondary prevention therapy, 13 299 patients were included in the final cohort (Figure 1 ). The mean age of the overall cohort was 65.64±13.33 years, and 60.3% of patients were men. Most patients were nonsmokers (60.5%) and did not report alcohol consumption (71.1%) before. Stroke severity was predominantly mild (SSI ≤5, 75%), and few patients received acute reperfusion therapies (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator, 3.2%; endovascular thrombectomy, 0.3%; Table 1 ).
sections.adherence trajectories: Among 13 299 patients receiving secondary prevention therapy, 4 distinct adherence trajectories were identified using group‐based multitrajectory modeling (Figure 2 ; Tables S2 and S3 ). The trajectory groups were (1) dual high adherence (46.7%): consistently high adherence to both statins and antithrombotic agents with minimal decline over 12 months; (2) antithrombotic‐only adherence (35.1%): persistently high adherence to antithrombotic therapy but low or absent statin use; (3) gradual dual decline (6.0%): moderate to high baseline adherence followed by a steady reduction in both therapies through month 12; and (4) early dual discontinuation (12.2%): lowest initial adherence with rapid decline, reaching approximately half of baseline level within 3 months. Trajectory definitions and model justification are summarized in Table S4 .
sections.antithrombotic and statin use across adh: Baseline characteristics and medication use varied substantially across adherence groups (Table 1 ). Patients in the dual high adherence and antithrombotic‐only adherence groups maintained high adherence to antithrombotic therapy at 12 months (PDC ≥0.8). The dual high adherence group had the highest baseline LDL‐C (123.2±37.4 mg/dL), with 76.2% having LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL. Most patients in this group received moderate‐intensity statins (75.9%). In contrast, the antithrombotic‐only adherence group demonstrated lower baseline LDL‐C (98.8±27.7 mg/dL) and limited statin use (14.1%), although 44.8% had LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL. Patients in the gradual dual decline and early dual discontinuation groups had baseline LDL‐C levels of 118.9±40.0 mg/dL and 109.9±33.4 mg/dL, respectively, with >60% exceeding 100 mg/dL. Statin use was uncommon in the early dual discontinuation group (35.2%). In contrast, all patients in the gradual dual decline group received statins, but only 52.6% received antithrombotic therapy during follow‐up. The nonuser group exhibited higher stroke severity (mean SSI, 6.6±4.8), and 49% had LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL despite receiving neither statins nor antithrombotic therapy.
sections.ldl \u2010c changes across adherence tra: LDL‐C levels and their 1‐year changes varied substantially across adherence groups (Table 2 ). The dual high adherence group achieved the lowest follow‐up LDL‐C (86.6±31.0 mg/dL) and the greatest percentage reduction (−24.3%). The gradual dual decline group showed a smaller reduction (−12.2%; follow‐up LDL‐C 95.9±36.4 mg/dL). In contrast, LDL‐C increased in the antithrombotic‐only, early dual discontinuation, and nonuser groups (+11.6%, +7.9%, and +13.1%, respectively). Among patients with available follow‐up lipid measurements, LDL‐C goal attainment (<100 mg/dL) were highest in the dual high adherence group and lowest in the nonuser and antithrombotic‐only groups.
sections.association between adherence trajectori: The median overall follow‐up time in our cohort was 6.31 years (interquartile range, 4.62–8.28 years). During follow‐up, the composite cardiovascular outcome occurred in 14.1% of patients (23.6 per 1000 person‐years). Incidence was highest in the early dual discontinuation group and lowest in the dual high adherence group. Recurrent IS or systemic embolism occurred most frequently in the early dual discontinuation group (22.6 per 1000 person‐years), followed by the gradual dual decline group (19.7 per 1000 person‐years). All‐cause death was lowest in the dual high adherence group (34.9 per 1000 person‐years) and highest in the early dual discontinuation and gradual dual decline groups (54.5 and 44.9 per 1000 person‐years, respectively) (Table S5 ). With respect to cause of death, intracerebral hemorrhage accounted for ≈2.3% of deaths in the cohort, and no deaths were attributed to other critical bleeding events based on ICD‐10 classifications. In adjusted analyses (Table 3 ), early dual discontinuation was associated with significantly higher risks of the composite cardiovascular outcome (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.57 [95% CI, 1.31–1.88]), recurrent IS or systemic embolism (aHR, 1.60 [95% CI, 1.31–1.95]), and myocardial infarction (aHR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.02–2.14]), compared with dual high adherence. All‐cause death was similarly elevated in the early dual discontinuation (aHR, 1.56 [95% CI, 1.36–1.79]) and gradual dual decline groups (aHR, 1.23 [95% CI, 1.06–1.42]).
sections.stratified analysis: Stratified analyses demonstrated that the adverse impact of poor adherence was consistent across key clinical subgroups (Figure 3A through 3C ). The association between poor adherence and the composite cardiovascular outcome was strongest in patients aged <65 years (aHR, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.41–2.34]), with attenuated but still elevated risks observed in those aged 65 to 74 years. Similar age‐related gradients were noted for recurrent ischemic events and all‐cause death. Sex‐specific analyses showed higher relative risks in men, with significant increases in composite cardiovascular outcome (aHR, 1.81 [95% CI, 1.45–2.25]) and recurrent IS (aHR, 1.92 [95% CI, 1.50–2.46]). In women, associations were smaller and not statistically significant for some outcomes. Among patients with baseline LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL, poor adherence was associated with a 61% to 68% higher risk across outcomes, whereas those with LDL‐C <100 mg/dL showed weaker and generally nonsignificant associations. Elevated risks were also observed among patients with mild to moderate stroke severity (SSI ≤12).
sections.main findings: This study identified 4 distinct longitudinal adherence trajectories to statins and antithrombotic therapy in patients with acute IS/TIA. Sustained dual adherence was consistently associated with greater LDL‐C reduction and the lowest risks of major cardiovascular events and all‐cause death. In contrast, early discontinuation of both therapies was associated with substantially higher risks of recurrent ischemic events and death. The adverse impact of poor adherence was most pronounced in younger patients, men, those with baseline LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL, and individuals with mild to moderate stroke severity.
sections.gaps in secondary prevention and ldl \u2: Adherence to secondary prevention therapies during the first year after acute IS/TIA remains suboptimal, aligning with prior reports showing adherence rates of 52% to 61% for statins and 66% to 78% for antithrombotic agents. 17 , 18 , 31 , 32 , 33 In our cohort, nearly one fifth of patients followed trajectories characterized by early discontinuation or progressive decline. At baseline, 61.8% of patients had LDL‐C levels above guideline targets, and a substantial proportion remained uncontrolled at 1 year despite treatment initiation, consistent with findings from the T‐SPARCLE (Taiwanese Secondary Prevention for Patients With Atherosclerotic Disease) registry. 21 These treatment gaps likely reflect the evolving LDL‐C targets over the study period, transitioning from <100 mg/dL in earlier recommendations to <70 mg/dL and, more recently, <55 mg/dL for very‐high‐risk patients. 12 , 14 , 34 , 35 Undertreatment was particularly evident among patients with LDL‐C levels between 70 and 100 mg/dL. Poor adherence, particularly early statin discontinuation, was associated with rising LDL‐C levels over 1 year, suggesting that both inadequate treatment initiation and declining adherence contribute to suboptimal lipid control. These findings underscore the need for routine lipid monitoring, adherence reinforcement, and timely treatment intensification to meet contemporary LDL‐C goals. 36
sections.adherence trajectories and cardiovascula: Distinct longitudinal adherence patterns were strongly and independently associated with cardiovascular outcomes. Patients in the early dual discontinuation group experienced a 60% higher risk of the composite outcome compared with those with dual high adherence (aHR, 1.60 [95% CI, 1.31–1.95]), and elevated all‐cause death was observed in both the early dual discontinuation and gradual dual decline groups. These findings align with prior population‐based studies showing that low adherence or low medication possession ratios are associated with 60% to 70% higher risks of recurrent stroke and death. 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 Several mechanisms may underlie these associations. Discontinuation of statins has been linked to rebound increases in LDL‐C, heightened inflammatory activity, and endothelial dysfunction, all of which may promote plaque instability and recurrent ischemic events. 41 , 42 Likewise, interruption of antithrombotic therapy reduces platelet inhibition or anticoagulant effects, thereby rapidly restoring a prothrombotic state. Poor adherence may also coincide with reduced engagement in routine follow‐up and lipid surveillance, limiting opportunities for treatment optimization. Together, these factors likely contribute to the increased vascular and mortality risks associated with early discontinuation or progressive adherence decline. Beyond statistical categorization, these adherence phenotypes likely reflect heterogeneous real‐world clinical scenarios. Patients classified as having antithrombotic‐only adherence may represent individuals with lower baseline lipid burden, physician noninitiation of statin therapy, perceived intolerance, or other clinical considerations. Because detailed prescribing rationale was unavailable, these interpretations should be considered exploratory. Early dual discontinuation may reflect poststroke disability, frailty, adverse effects, competing comorbidities, or reduced health care engagement after discharge. The detrimental impact of poor adherence was most pronounced among younger patients, men, and those with elevated baseline LDL‐C. Among adults aged <65 years, poor adherence increased the risk of recurrent IS by 82%, consistent with prior evidence of higher long‐term vascular vulnerability in younger stroke survivors. 43 , 44 Male patients also exhibited stronger associations, including nearly 2‐fold higher recurrence risk with early discontinuation, consistent with literature suggesting a greater dependence on statin therapy in men. 45 Poor adherence further amplified risk among patients with baseline LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL, underscoring the interaction between inadequate treatment exposure and elevated atherosclerotic burden. These findings identify younger, male, and hyperlipidemic patients as key groups who may benefit from targeted adherence‐support interventions.
sections.strengths and limitations: This study has several strengths. First, it is among the few to apply group‐based multitrajectory modeling to jointly characterize adherence to both statins and antithrombotic therapy, enabling identification of clinically relevant adherence phenotypes and their associations with lipid control and cardiovascular outcomes. Second, the use of the multi‐institutional Chang Gung Research Database linked with Taiwan's nationwide claims data allowed comprehensive capture of prescriptions, laboratory results, and outcome events across care settings, supporting robust longitudinal follow‐up and enhancing generalizability. Third, this design highlighted persistent real‐world gaps in statin initiation and lipid monitoring, particularly among patients with baseline LDL‐C levels of 70 to 100 mg/dL, an increasingly important group under evolving lipid‐lowering recommendations. Several limitations should also be acknowledged. First, adherence was inferred from prescription refill data rather than directly observed medication‐taking behavior. Although linkage across databases enabled near‐complete capture of dispensed medications, this approach remains subject to inherent limitations of refill‐based measures. Second, follow‐up LDL‐C testing was not uniformly performed, with measurements available in 71.7% of patients. LDL‐C change analyses therefore relied on complete cases, which may introduce selection bias if patients with more frequent testing differed systematically from those without follow‐up measurements. Third, detailed pathogenetic classification of IS was not uniformly available in the database. Although atrial fibrillation status and antithrombotic treatment patterns were captured, residual heterogeneity in stroke mechanisms may exist. Prior population‐based studies in Taiwan have reported that small‐vessel occlusion accounts for the largest proportion of IS cases (37.7%), followed by large‐artery atherosclerosis (27.7%) and cardioembolism (10.9%). 46 Intracranial atherosclerosis is more prevalent in Asian than in Western populations, 47 , 48 and differences in stroke pathogenesis and health care systems, including access to care and medication affordability, may influence event rates and treatment patterns. Although sustained adherence was associated with improved outcomes, caution is warranted when extrapolating these findings to Western populations or to health care care systems with substantially different structures. Residual confounding from unmeasured factors, such as infarct size and poststroke lifestyle behaviors, cannot be excluded. In addition, patients without any secondary preventive medication were not included in the trajectory modeling, as the objective was to characterize adherence patterns among treated individuals. Nonusers may represent a distinct clinical phenotype, and their exclusion limits direct comparison with treated populations.
sections.conclusions_1: Sustained dual adherence to statins and antithrombotic therapy was associated with the most favorable cardiovascular profile, yielding greater LDL‐C reduction and substantially lower risks of recurrent ischemic events and all‐cause death. Early discontinuation of both therapies was associated with the highest vascular events and mortality rates, accompanied by worsening lipid control. Persistent undertreatment, particularly among patients with baseline LDL‐C levels of 70 to 100 mg/dL, highlights a critical gap in contemporary secondary prevention. These findings identify adherence as a modifiable, high‐impact cardiovascular risk factor and underscore the need for systematic adherence monitoring, timely treatment intensification, and targeted support for vulnerable subgroups, particularly younger patients and those with elevated baseline LDL‐C, to optimize long‐term vascular outcomes after IS.

title: Overcoming fratricide of CD86 targeting CAR-T cells by defined logic-gate CAR strategy
abstract: Despite its remarkable success in the treatment of several hematological malignancies, cellular immunotherapy using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells faces significant challenges when treating refractory/relapsed or myeloid malignancies such as AML, CML or multiple myeloma. To overcome the pronounced heterogeneity of such diseases, the search for suitable tumor-associated antigens recently led to surface antigens of the B7 protein family as potential CAR-T cell targets. Using the example of CD86-targeting, we highlight a considerable pitfall of CAR-T therapy which utilizes B7-family proteins as a prominent group of T cell (activation) associated antigens. In a consistent set of in vitro and in vivo experiments we could demonstrate that fratricide among pre-activated CD86-specific CAR-T cells strongly reduces their overall survival and efficacy in tumor killing as recently shown for B7-H3/CD276-targeting CARs. Therefore, we propose a defined combinatorial antigen recognition concept via dual-chain CAR-T cells that incorporate an “AND-gate” mechanism through CD19 primary CAR activation and CD86 conditional co-stimulation to circumvent a severely limited outcome. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s40164-026-00791-3.

sections.supplementary information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s40164-026-00791-3.
sections.to the editor: A safe target-antigen is crucial for CAR-T cell therapy, as disease-associated antigens are frequently expressed on healthy cells. Here, we focus on the B7-family protein CD86 as a recently identified, attractive target-antigen example in hematologic malignancies [ 1 – 3 ]. Our recently published “AND-gate” CAR with superior safety and efficacy compared to a second-generation CAR [ 1 ] uses CD86 as a conditional co-stimulator. In this context, we highlight characteristics of T cells expressing both CD86 and CD86-specific CARs. While transcriptomics confirmed elevated CD86 in NHL lymph nodes [ 4 ] (Fig. 1 A), we verified this at protein-level on primary DLBCL cells and human leukemia/lymphoma lines (SuppFig.1 A, B). Furthermore, we observed a continuous increase of CD86 expression on healthy human T cells (Fig. 1 B), which reached densities after initial activation similar to those of primary lymphoma cells (Fig. 1 C). Fig. 1 CD86 is expressed on tumor cells but also on activated T cells. a Comparison of transcriptional abundance in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and healthy lymph node samples show up-regulation of CD86 in a public dataset analyzed by Brune et al. 4 . b Mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of CD86 (red) along with the activation marker CD25 (blue) was assessed by flow cytometry prior to stimulation (baseline), and on day 2 and day 4 after activation with anti-CD3 (OKT3, 200 ng mL − 1 ) and anti-CD28 (15E8, 100 ng mL − 1 ) antibodies ( n = 2 donors). ( c ) CD86 expression density on primary healthy and malignant hematological samples in comparison to activated T cells arranged in following groups: [1] CD3 + healthy donor T cells, activated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 and IL-2, according to methods; [2] CD19 + healthy donors B cells; [3] primary CD19+/CD5 + CLL cells; [4] CD19 + primary DLBCL cells. CD86-expression was analyzed via FACS by binding of CD86 antibody in the respective populations. d CAR-T cells were incubated on a pre-coated 96well plate. Coating was either PBS (no stim), anti-CD152/CTLA4 antibody Ipilimumab (1 µg mL − 1 ) or anti-CD3 antibody OKT3 (1 µg mL − 1 ) plus anti-CD28 antibody 15E8 (5 µg mL − 1 ). After 72 h, IFN-γ secretion into supernatants of cultivated cells were analyzed via sandwich ELISA. Bars represent means of triplicates of 3 donors; error bars are SEM. e , f Characterization of CD86 targeting CAR-T cells in comparison to T cells without CAR on day 6 after start of retroviral transduction: cell death / apoptosis was detected by FACS via APC-conjugated Annexin-V and 7-AAD binding in bulk cell population. CD86-expression on T cells was analyzed via FACS by binding of CD86 antibody in the CD3 positive population. All statistical analyses were done by unpaired students’ t-test We designed a second-generation CAR with CTLA4-binding-domain (SuppFig.1 C) to investigate how CD86-expression on T cells affects CD86-CAR-mediated activation. IFN-γ release was induced not only by specific CAR-activation, but also in the absence of activating agents (Fig. 1 D). After transduction, the proportion of apoptotic CAR-T cells increased (Fig. 1 E) and CD86 + T cells were eliminated accordingly (Fig. 1 F), suggesting CTLA4-BBz CAR-induced fratricide. As a potential solution, we tested dual-chain CAR-variants (SuppFig.2 A): “19-BB/CTLA4-z”: CD86-binding activates via CD3z, CD19-binding conditionally co-stimulates via 4-1BB. “19-z/CTLA4-BB”: vice versa composition [ 1 ]. T cells with 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR killed fewer co-cultured CD19 + /CD86 + tumor cells and produced less IFN-γ than 19-z/CTLA4-BB CAR-T cells (SuppFig.2B). Unstimulated 19-BB/CTLA4-z and CTLA4-BBz CAR-T cells secreted more IFN-γ via auto-activation compared to 19-z/CTLA4-BB and 19-BBz CAR-T cells (SuppFig. 2 C). Blocking of CTLA-4 during the transduction of T cells (SuppFig.2D) revealed the impact of CD86-binding on potential fratricide: apoptosis rates decreased in 19-BB/CTLA4-z and CTLA4-BBz CAR-T cells while CD86-expression was increased in presence of Ipilimumab (Fig. 2 A, B). To further investigate fratricide, we co-cultivated CAR-T cells with re-activated autologous PBMCs as CD86 + “victim cells”. 19-BB/CTLA4-z and CTLA4-BBz CAR-T cells eliminated these PBMCs, whereas 19-z/CTLA4-BB and 19-BBz CAR-T cells did not (Fig. 2 C; SuppFig.2E). CAR-activation in CAR-transduced Jurkat reporter-cells [ 5 ] led to distinct expression-levels of NFAT-eGFP and NF-kB-CFP. In contrast to second-generation CARs, both dual-chain CARs only fully activate when both CAR-antigens are present. Interestingly, the 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR induced lower levels of co-stimulatory transcription factor NF-kB (SuppFig. 2F). Deeper mechanistic insights were gained from bulk RNA-sequencing of CAR-T cells after transduction. T cells with the 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR exhibited potent activation, proliferative signaling and inflammatory response in comparison with 19-z/CTLA4-BB CAR (Fig. 2 D). Fig. 2 Defined CD19/CD86 dual-chain CAR concept can circumvent CD86-directed fratricide. a PBMC were retrovirally transduced in presence or absence of anti-CTLA-4 antibody Ipilimumab (20 µg mL − 1 ). Cell death / apoptosis on day 6 after start of retroviral transduction was detected by FACS via Annexin-V and 7-AAD binding in bulk cell population and compared between blockade and no blockade ( n = 4 donors). b CD86 cell surface expression was analyzed by FACS in parallel ( n = 4 donors). c Fratricide detection was performed by co-culturing freshly transduced CAR-T cells with re-activated fluorescent dye-labeled autologous T cells (“victim cells”). After 24 h hours, quantification of “victim cells” was done via FACS (triplicates of n = 3 donors). All bar plots (a-c) represent mean ± SEM. Significance levels (a-c) derived from paired ( a , b ) or unpaired (c) t-tests. CAR rates [%]: 19-BBz (78/53.5/58.5), 19-z/CTLA4-BB (65/42.2/42.7), 19-BB/CTLA4-z (51/24.1/38.5), CTLA4-BBz (48/19/33). d Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of hallmark pathways [ 6 ] in monocultured 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR T cells compared to 19-z/CTLA4-BB controls shortly after transduction, derived from bulk RNA-sequencing. (Left) Dot plot illustrating the top differentially enriched hallmark pathways [ 6 ] in the 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR. The x-axis represents the GeneRatio. Dot size corresponds to the number of core enriched genes (Count) within the pathway, and the color gradient indicates the statistical significance (adjusted p-value). (Right) Ridge plot displaying the expression density distribution of the core enriched genes for each corresponding hallmark pathway ( n = 3 donors). e Comparison of long-term in vivo efficacy of 19-z/CTLA4-BB and 19-BB/CTLA4-z dual-chain CAR-T cells in a xenograft mouse model: immunodeficient animals were grafted with 2e5 CD19 + fLuc expressing Raji lymphoma cells via tail vein. After confirmation of engraftment, two groups (each n = 7) were intravenously injected with 2e6 dual-chain CAR-T cells. Kaplan-Meier plot of overall survival percentage is shown with the corresponding numbers at risk for each time-point. Statistical significance of the study outcome was confirmed by Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test and Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test. f , g Tumor luminescence (LagoX, Spectral Instruments Imaging) and hCD19 + cell count in peripheral blood were analyzed at different time points in consistent xenograft model, intravenously engrafted with 5e5 fLuc Raji cells. Following groups were injected with 5e6 (CAR) T cells: w/o CAR ( n = 3), 19-BBz ( n = 3), 19-z/CTLA4-BB and 19-BB/CTLA4-z (each n = 4). Persistence of hCD3 + cells and percentage of hCD86 in hCD3 + in peripheral blood of these mice were analyzed via FACS in parallel. All analyses were performed on Beckman Coulter CytoFLEX S. Significance levels derived from multiple t-test comparison between dual-chain CAR T groups To demonstrate in-vivo relevance in a xenograft mouse model, we first verified efficacy of 19-z/CTLA4-BB CAR-T cells (SuppFig.3 A) and then conducted a long-term comparison of both dual-chain CAR-T variants in Raji-engrafted mice (SuppFig.3B). Treatment with 19-z/CTLA4-BB CAR-T cells prolonged survival, confirming limited efficacy of 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR-T cells (Fig. 2 E; Supp. Figure 3 C, D). To determine whether these findings are consistent with fratricide, we investigated persistence and CD86-expression of dual-chain CAR T cell variants in another xenograft model. Despite some effects regarding tumor burden and hCD19 + cells in peripheral blood (Fig. 2 F), only a few human T cells were detected in the 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR group (Fig. 2 G). Most remarkably, T cells in the 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR group vanished and the few remaining cells were CD86-negative (Fig. 2 G; SuppFig. 4A). Spleen, bone marrow and liver tumors (w/o CAR group) showed no traces of CD86 + 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR T cells (SuppFig.4B). While CD86 has been suggested as a promising CAR-T target [ 2 , 3 ], our findings add an important caveat to these conclusions by demonstrating potential off-tumor reactivity. We observed insufficient selectivity towards lymphoma cells using CTLA4-BBz or 19-BB/CTLA4-z CAR-T cells, resulting in elimination of activated T cells and other CD86 + immune cells like CD14 + monocytes (SuppFig.5 A-C). Although using a CTLA-4-derived binding-domain, we suggest that antibody-derived CD86-specific second-generation CARs may insufficiently distinguish between tumor cells and CD86-expressing immune cells. Different CAR-designs (CD28 vs. 4-1BB) [ 3 ] might explain variations in fratricide susceptibility and need further comparative investigation. Limitations of CAR-T cell efficacy due to fratricide are well-known when targeting T cell-associated antigens [ 7 – 11 ], and a gene knock-out might be a successful bypass strategy [ 12 ]; however, for B7-family proteins impact on T cells needs to be carefully investigated. Therefore, our data suggest that targeting CD86 via CD3zeta-activating CARs requires caution due to its expression on immune cells, but it can serve as a safe target for conditional co-stimulation. The success of the “AND-gate” CAR architecture depends on strict separation of activation and co-stimulation. This distinction is biologically important and highly relevant for future CAR-T design in order to develop safe and efficient CAR-T cells and circumvent limited efficacy due to fratricide.

title: Beyond Psoriasis Area and Severity Index and Body Surface Area: An Italian Delphi Consensus on the Definition of Moderate Psoriasis
abstract: Introduction Moderate psoriasis, despite its clinical relevance, remains inconsistently defined in current guidelines, leading to heterogeneous treatment decisions and variable access to systemic therapy. A unified, clinically meaningful definition is currently lacking. To establish a consensus-based, operational definition of moderate psoriasis, we conducted a two-round modified Delphi process involving expert dermatologists. Methods Fifteen Italian dermatologists with recognized expertise in psoriasis participated in a Delphi survey composed of 18 statements addressing clinical severity, quality of life, symptoms, involvement of special areas, and treatment response. Consensus was defined as a median score ≥ 7 with interquartile range (IQR) ≤ 2, or ≥ 75% of ratings ≥ 7, on a scale going from 1 (completely disagree) to 10 (completely agree). Statements not reaching consensus in Round 1 were revised according to participants’ comments and re-evaluated in Round 2. Results In Round 1, 12 of 18 statements reached consensus. Six statements required revision owing to ambiguity or insufficient operational clarity. After refinement, including clearer definitions of early and frequent relapses, specification of Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) thresholds, and explicit mention of difficult-to-treat or highly visible areas, all six statements achieved consensus in Round 2. Ultimately, consensus was obtained for all 18 statements. Conclusions This Delphi process produced a comprehensive and clinically actionable definition of moderate psoriasis, emphasizing a multidimensional view of severity that extends beyond Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) or Body Surface Area (BSA). These consensus-based criteria may support earlier access to systemic therapies, including biologics and small molecules, and improve harmonization in both clinical practice and research.

sections.key summary points: Why carry out this study? Moderate psoriasis lacks a clear and consistent definition in current guidelines, leading to variability in treatment decisions and access to systemic therapies. Traditional clinical scores, such as PASI and BSA, often underestimate disease burden, particularly in patients with involvement of special areas or significant quality-of-life impairment. What was learned from the study? This two-round modified Delphi consensus defined moderate psoriasis as a multidimensional construct integrating objective severity, symptoms, quality of life, special areas, and treatment response. Moderate psoriasis cannot be identified solely by intermediate PASI or BSA values, but by the overall clinical and psychosocial impact of the disease. The proposed framework supports earlier use of targeted systemic therapies, including biologics and small molecules, and may improve consistency in clinical practice.
sections.introduction_1: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory disease that primarily affects the skin, with a global prevalence estimated at approximately 2–3% of the general population [ 1 ]. Lesions most commonly occur on the elbows, knees, scalp, and lumbosacral region, but the disease can involve any cutaneous site [ 1 ]. Certain locations, such as the scalp, face and neck, hands, nails, and genital area, are often referred to as special or sensitive areas, as their involvement can cause a disproportionate impact on patients’ quality of life, even when the overall affected body surface area (BSA) is limited [ 2 ]. Treatment strategies for psoriasis depend largely on disease severity [ 2 ]. According to current guidelines, mild psoriasis is usually managed with topical therapies, such as topical corticosteroids (TCS) and vitamin D analogues, often in fixed combinations. Although TCS are typically the first-line treatment, they often prove inadequate for patients with involvement of sensitive or difficult-to-treat areas. Conversely, moderate-to-severe psoriasis generally requires systemic treatments, including conventional agents and innovative therapies, including biological drugs and small molecules [ 3 – 5 ]. The Italian Guidelines, in line with European recommendations, define eligibility for systemic therapy on the basis of the presence of a Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) > 10, or a Body Surface Area (BSA) > 10%, or a Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) > 10 [ 3 ]. Additional criteria have been introduced to “upgrade” otherwise mild cases to a moderate-to-severe category, including the involvement of visible areas, extensive scalp psoriasis, genital disease, nail dystrophy affecting at least two fingernails, and recalcitrant plaques [ 3 ]. However, this approach has been increasingly criticized for its limited sensitivity to the real burden of disease and its binary view of severity [ 6 ]. In response to these limitations, the International Psoriasis Council (IPC) has recently challenged the traditional dichotomous classification of mild psoriasis versus moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Through a modified Delphi consensus, the IPC proposed a simplified system distinguishing only between candidates for topical therapy and candidates for systemic therapy. According to this definition, patients should be considered candidates for systemic therapy if they meet at least one of the following criteria: (1) BSA > 10%, (2) involvement of special areas, or (3) failure of topical therapy [ 6 ]. Despite these efforts, no internationally accepted definition of moderate psoriasis exists [ 7 ]. This gap leads to inconsistent clinical decision-making and inequitable access to systemic therapy, underscoring the need for a pragmatic and clinically grounded definition. To address this unmet need, we conducted a modified Delphi consensus aimed at identifying and validating clinical, functional, and patient-reported criteria for the characterization of moderate psoriasis in real-world clinical practice.
sections.study design: The Delphi method is a structured, iterative process that gathers the opinions of experts through a series of anonymized voting rounds, aiming to achieve convergence of views on a specific topic. This approach is particularly suitable for areas in which evidence is limited or heterogeneous, and expert clinical judgment is needed to support standardization [ 7 , 8 ]. This Delphi panel consisted of 15 Italian dermatologists with recognized experience in psoriasis management and clinical research, representing both academic and hospital-based settings across different regions of Italy. All panelists had authored peer-reviewed publications or participated in multicenter studies in the field of inflammatory skin diseases, and plaque psoriasis in particular. To minimize potential bias, each participant was blinded to the responses of the others during the voting phase.
sections.development of statements and the voting: An initial list of 18 statements was developed by the scientific committee on the basis of a literature review of current psoriasis classification systems, treatment guidelines, and real-world evidence on disease burden and treatment outcomes. Statements covered clinical severity (PASI, BSA, PGA), difficult-to-treat areas, symptom burden, quality-of-life impairment, psychosocial impact, and comorbid conditions. Each statement was formatted as an affirmative sentence to be rated on a 1–10 numeric agreement scale, where 1 indicated “strongly disagree” and 10 “strongly agree.” Panelists independently rated each statement through an anonymized online form. For each statement, both central tendency and dispersion were analyzed to evaluate the degree of consensus among participants. The Delphi technique was conducted according to established methodological standards [ 8 , 9 ] and in line with previous consensus studies in dermatology [ 7 , 10 ]. Two complementary definitions of consensus were applied: Percentage-based criterion: consensus was reached when ≥ 75% of panelists assigned a score ≥ 7 on the 1–10 scale. Robust criterion: consensus was defined as a median score ≥ 7 combined with an interquartile range (IQR) ≤ 2, ensuring that agreement was both high and consistent among respondents. Statements meeting both criteria were considered to have reached a strong consensus. Statements failing to meet either threshold were classified as “no consensus” and identified as potential candidates for revision in a subsequent Delphi round. Qualitative feedback from Round 1 was thematically analyzed and used to revise statements that did not reach consensus. The survey was administered via a secure online platform (Google Forms).
sections.ethical approval: Institutional review board approval was exempted for this study as its procedures did not include human subjects and did not deviate from good clinical practice. All the involved dermatologists gave their approval for the study to be published. All the dermatologists who were part of the consensus were involved in the writing and/or revision of the manuscript. All the dermatologists who participated in the consensus were aware of the objective of the study, and they all knew that the manuscript would be published. The participants gave written informed consent.
sections.statistical analysis: Given the ordinal nature of Delphi data, nonparametric statistics (median and IQR) were used. Descriptive statistics were calculated for each statement, including the number of respondents, median, IQR, and percentage of ratings ≥ 7. All analyses were performed using standard statistical software (Microsoft Excel and Python 3.11). Results are presented in tabular form, summarizing for each statement the median, IQR, percentage of high agreement, and whether the predefined consensus thresholds were achieved.
sections.results_1: A total of 15 dermatologists completed both rounds of the Delphi process. During the first round, all 18 statements proposed for defining moderate psoriasis were evaluated according to the two prespecified consensus criteria (median ≥ 7 with IQR ≤ 2, or ≥ 75% of ratings ≥ 7). In total, 12 statements reached agreement, while 6 (numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, and 16) fell below at least one of the thresholds (Table 1 ). Panelists’ comments highlighted several recurring issues: the need to distinguish inadequate response to topical therapy from poor adherence; the potential overlap between systemic treatment failure and intrinsic disease severity; uncertainty about the use of subjective burden in the absence of validated tools; and the need to refine numerical thresholds for QoL impairment and the involvement of special areas. These six statements were therefore revised to include clearer operational definitions, such as the timing of early relapse, the frequency of flares, the use of DLQI ≥ 10 or repeated scores > 5, and the explicit mention of difficult-to-treat or sensitive areas. The revised statements were then resubmitted in Round 2 and received a remarkably high level of agreement. sections.synthesis of expert perspectives: Across both rounds, the panel consistently emphasized that moderate psoriasis cannot be identified solely by intermediate PASI or BSA values (Table 3 ). Instead, it emerges as a multidimensional construct integrating: limited but clinically meaningful objective involvement (e.g., PASI/BSA 3–10%); the presence of difficult-to-treat or highly visible areas; persistent symptoms such as itch or pain; a significant quality-of-life impact, particularly when DLQI ≥ 10 or repeatedly > 5; inadequate or unstable control with appropriate topical therapy; and the contextual severity added by systemic comorbidities. Table 3 Summary of consensus-based criteria defining moderate psoriasis Domain Key criteria Objective severity PASI 3–10, BSA 3–10 Special areas involvement Scalp, face/neck, genital, nails, palmoplantar Symptoms Itch, pain Impairment of quality of life DLQI ≥ 10 or persistent DLQI > 5 Treatment response Inadequate control with topical therapy, early or frequent relapse PASI Psoriasis Area and Severy Index, BSA body surface area, DLQI Dermatology Life Quality Index The panel’s feedback supports a model in which the functional and psychosocial burden of disease carries equal, if not greater, weight than traditional severity metrics. This echoes the evolving framework proposed by the International Psoriasis Council and is strongly aligned with recent literature showing that patients with BSA 3–10% derive quality-of-life improvements comparable to those with more extensive involvement when treated with systemic therapy [ 6 ].
sections.discussion: Moderate psoriasis remains a conceptually heterogeneous entity, and current severity classifications fail to capture its clinical and psychosocial complexity. This modified Delphi consensus sought to establish a clinically meaningful and patient-centered definition of moderate psoriasis, a category for which no standardized or internationally accepted criteria currently exist. The two-round structure of the process allowed not only the identification of areas of agreement but also the refinement of contentious concepts through iterative feedback. Figure 1 provides a visual synthesis of the multidimensional criteria we used to define moderate psoriasis. Fig. 1 Conceptual multidimensional framework defining moderate psoriasis according to the Delphi consensus. Moderate psoriasis is defined through the integration of multiple domains including objective disease extent (PASI and BSA), involvement of special areas, symptom burden, quality-of-life impairment, and response to topical therapy. The coexistence of these elements identifies patients who may be candidates for systemic treatment despite not fulfilling traditional severity thresholds. PASI Psoriasis Area and Severy Index, BSA body surface area, DLQI Dermatology Life Quality Index
sections.expert perspectives and interpretation o: Agreement was strongest for statements emphasizing functional and psychosocial burden rather than purely quantitative severity scores. All participants recognized that involvement of special or visible areas, such as the scalp, face, genital region, or nails, can substantially impair daily life and justify systemic therapy even in patients with low PASI or BSA. This mirrors prior work from the International Psoriasis Council (IPC), which proposed a shift from numeric thresholds toward a treatment eligibility-based classification [ 6 ]. Conversely, disagreement was observed in statements linking disease severity to treatment adherence or prior failures. Some experts considered nonadherence a behavioral rather than disease-related factor (Statement 1), while others noted that difficulty maintaining control with topical therapy reflects the intrinsic chronicity and treatment fatigue typical of moderate disease. Similarly, statements attributing “moderate” status solely to previous systemic therapy failure (Statement 3) were seen as potentially conflating refractoriness with severity, highlighting the need for distinct conceptual categories. These diverging opinions underscore the multifactorial nature of psoriasis severity, where biological activity, treatment responsiveness, and psychosocial adaptation interact dynamically. Several participants emphasized that the patient’s perception of disease plays a decisive role in therapy selection (Statements 4–7). Comments often stressed the importance of shared decision-making, especially when psychosocial distress, occupational limitations, or social withdrawal are present despite limited BSA. Such perspectives align with recent evidence showing that subjective disease burden can outweigh objective measures when assessing overall severity [ 6 , 11 ]. The high level of consensus on these items supports a paradigm in which moderate psoriasis is characterized not merely by intermediate severity scores, but by a clinically meaningful impact on life quality and functionality. Interestingly, comments on statements addressing comorbid immune-mediated diseases (Statement 17) revealed unanimous agreement that coexisting psoriatic arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease necessitates systemic therapy, even with minimal skin involvement. This view reinforces the growing perception of psoriasis as a systemic condition rather than a localized skin disease.
sections.refinement through the second delphi rou: In the first round, most statements addressing quality of life, symptom burden, psychosocial impact, and difficult-to-treat areas achieved strong agreement. By contrast, six statements failed to meet consensus, largely owing to conceptual ambiguity. These primarily involved the interpretation of inadequate response to topical therapy (Statements 1 and 2), the distinction between treatment refractoriness and intrinsic severity (Statement 3), the exclusively subjective assessment of disease burden (Statement 5), the DLQI threshold proposed to reclassify mild disease (Statement 9), and the definition of “moderate” involvement of special areas (Statement 16). The qualitative comments from Round 1 were instrumental in reshaping these statements. Panelists emphasized the need to distinguish behavioral factors (e.g., poor adherence) from true disease severity, to integrate patient-reported outcomes with objective parameters rather than use them in isolation, and to adopt operational definitions (e.g., timing of relapse, number of flares, DLQI thresholds) that reflect everyday clinical practice. Following revision, all six statements reached a clear consensus in Round 2, confirming that the refined formulations aligned more closely with real-world clinical reasoning. This second-round convergence reinforces the robustness of the final set of criteria and demonstrates that disagreement in Round 1 stemmed more from wording, not from true conceptual discord among experts.
sections.context within the current literature: Our findings strongly converge with the evolving framework proposed by the International Psoriasis Council (IPC) and are supported by recent real-world evidence [ 6 ]. In a large CorEvitas registry analysis, Strober et al. compared outcomes of patients with moderate (BSA 3–10%) and severe (BSA > 10%) psoriasis treated with risankizumab [ 12 ]. Remarkably, both groups achieved comparable improvements in skin clearance and in quality of life, as measured by the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) [ 12 ]. This observation reinforces the idea that patients traditionally labeled as “moderate” experience a disease burden disproportionate to their objective skin involvement, and that effective systemic treatment can produce substantial QoL gains similar to those seen in more extensive disease [ 12 , 13 ]. From a clinical standpoint, these findings underscore that the impact of psoriasis on daily functioning and psychological well-being should weigh as heavily as lesion extent in defining disease severity and guiding treatment choice. Failing to recognize this could lead to undertreatment of a population that can achieve significant benefit from timely systemic intervention [ 13 ]. Importantly, this evolving perspective also supports the use of targeted systemic therapies, including biologics and small molecules, in selected patients with moderate psoriasis whose disease burden remains inadequately controlled with topical therapy. As a matter of fact in the past years, Horner et al. [ 14 ] and Armstrong et al. [ 15 ] confirmed that patients with limited but high-impact disease derive notable psychosocial and symptomatic improvement when treated systemically, supporting a multidimensional definition of severity that includes patient-reported outcomes and life impact alongside PASI and BSA. From a health policy perspective, the absence of a clear operational definition of moderate psoriasis contributes to inequalities in access to systemic therapy across countries. Recent EADV and IPC working groups have called for harmonized criteria that incorporate patient-reported outcomes, involvement of special areas, and treatment refractoriness [ 16 , 17 ], all elements that were also validated by our Delphi panel. We strongly believe that our recommendations emphasize both the importance of subjective symptoms and involvement of sensitive areas, intending to further promote access to innovative treatments, also for patients with more limited PASI and BSA. In addition, compared with the IPC definition, which focuses mostly on treatment eligibility, we believe that our model provides a more practical definition of moderate psoriasis by integrating specific clinical and patient-reported outcomes that could be easily incorporated into real-world clinical practice (Table 3 ).
sections.limitations and future directions: A key strength of this study lies in the high level of expertise and engagement of the participating dermatologists, who collectively contributed decades of clinical experience and a detailed understanding of psoriasis across different care settings. The two-round structure enabled the identification and correction of conceptual ambiguities, allowing the panel to converge toward a set of operational criteria with strong clinical relevance. Another strength is the explicit integration of both objective and patient-reported domains, reflecting the multidimensional nature of moderate psoriasis. Moreover, the criteria proposed here are simple enough to be implemented in routine practice and may support more timely identification of patients who would benefit from systemic therapy. However, some limitations must be acknowledged. Delphi studies inherently rely on expert opinion, and the perspectives captured here, while valuable, may not fully represent the diversity of clinical practices beyond the Italian context. The absence of patient input may also limit the breadth of viewpoints, particularly regarding lived experience and perceived burden. Finally, while operational definitions were refined to enhance clarity, further validation through prospective real-world studies will be necessary to determine the applicability and impact of these criteria in different healthcare environments.
sections.conclusions_1: This Delphi consensus provides a coherent and clinically meaningful framework for defining moderate psoriasis, a category that has long lacked operational clarity. By integrating objective severity, symptom burden, quality of life, involvement of special areas, and responsiveness to topical therapy, the final criteria reflect the true complexity of the condition. The full agreement reached across two rounds underscores the robustness of the proposed definitions. These criteria may help standardize clinical decision-making, facilitate earlier access to targeted systemic therapies, including biologics and small molecules, and guide future research. Further validation in real-world populations will be important to confirm their generalizability.

title: Individualized blood pressure management and postoperative organ dysfunction in older hip fracture patients: a study protocol for a single-center, randomized, controlled trial
abstract: Background Postoperative organ dysfunction is a leading cause of death and disability following hip fracture surgery in older patients. Intraoperative hypotension is a major modifiable risk factor for this complication, yet the optimal management strategy to prevent it remains controversial. We hypothesize that an individualized blood pressure management strategy is superior to standard management in reducing postoperative organ dysfunction. Methods This single-center, randomized, controlled trial will enroll 180 patients aged 65–85 years with hip fractures under general anesthesia. Eligible patients will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to the individualized management group (targeting systolic blood pressure within ± 10% of baseline) or the standard management group (reactive management, where intervention is initiated only if systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or decrease of > 30% from baseline). A universal mean arterial pressure target of ≥ 65 mmHg will be maintained for all patients. The allocated hemodynamic management strategy will be maintained throughout surgery and during the post-anesthesia care unit stay. The primary outcome is a composite of dysfunction in at least one organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and neurological) within 7 days after surgery. Secondary outcomes include the components of the primary outcome, intraoperative variables (including hemodynamic management data, fluid balance, blood loss, and serum lactate levels), intensive care unit and hospital stay, and all-cause mortality within 30 days after surgery. Discussion This randomized controlled trial aims to determine whether individualized blood pressure management reduces postoperative organ dysfunction more effectively than standard management in older hip fracture surgery patients. If proven effective, this proactive approach may represent a significant advance in clinical practice, moving from reactive hypotension correction to preventive stabilization, potentially reducing major complications, shortening hospital stays, and improving functional recovery. The results will provide important evidence to guide hemodynamic management during general anesthesia in this vulnerable population, contributing to standardized, evidence-based protocols for enhancing perioperative outcomes. Trial registration Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400093838. Registered on 12 December 2024. This manuscript presents the study protocol; participant recruitment is ongoing and results will be reported upon trial completion. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12877-026-07594-5.

The allocated hemodynamic management strategy will be maintained throughout surgery and during the post-anesthesia care unit stay. The primary outcome is a composite of dysfunction in at least one organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and neurological) within 7 days after surgery. Secondary outcomes include the components of the primary outcome, intraoperative variables (including hemodynamic management data, fluid balance, blood loss, and serum lactate levels), intensive care unit and hospital stay, and all-cause mortality within 30 days after surgery.
sections.discussion: This randomized controlled trial aims to determine whether individualized blood pressure management reduces postoperative organ dysfunction more effectively than standard management in older hip fracture surgery patients. If proven effective, this proactive approach may represent a significant advance in clinical practice, moving from reactive hypotension correction to preventive stabilization, potentially reducing major complications, shortening hospital stays, and improving functional recovery. The results will provide important evidence to guide hemodynamic management during general anesthesia in this vulnerable population, contributing to standardized, evidence-based protocols for enhancing perioperative outcomes.
sections.trial registration: Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400093838. Registered on 12 December 2024. This manuscript presents the study protocol; participant recruitment is ongoing and results will be reported upon trial completion.

sections.background_1: Hip fracture is a common and serious injury among older patients, associated with a one-year mortality rate as high as 30% [ 1 ]. Survivors often face long-term challenges, including multiple systemic complications, disability, increased risk of refracture, and substantial healthcare costs [ 2 ]. The anesthetic management of hip fracture surgery commonly involves either neuraxial or general anesthesia. While both are acceptable, general anesthesia is frequently preferred or necessitated in cases of patient agitation, anticoagulation, difficult positioning, or anticipated prolonged and complex surgery [ 3 – 5 ]. However, general anesthetic agents can induce significant arterial and venous vasodilation, reduce systemic vascular resistance, and cause hemodynamic instability [ 6 ]. These effects are compounded by the age-related impairment of cardiovascular autoregulation and a high prevalence of comorbidities, which collectively render older hip fracture patients particularly susceptible to intraoperative hypotension (IOH) [ 7 ]. IOH is a well-established risk factor for hypoperfusion of vital organs, leading to adverse outcomes such as postoperative delirium [ 8 ], acute kidney injury (AKI) [ 9 , 10 ] and myocardial injury [ 11 ], ultimately worsening the prognosis. The prevalence of IOH in this population is high. A large UK study reported that 61.0% of older hip fracture patients experienced a mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 65 mmHg, and 91.3% had a reduction in systolic blood pressure (SBP) > 20% from baseline [ 12 ]. Despite its high prevalence and strong association with poor outcomes, there is no consensus on the optimal definition or management strategy for IOH. Current guidelines primarily recommend avoiding excessive hypotension (e.g., a > 30% decrease from baseline or an absolute SBP < 90 mmHg) and maintaining MAP ≥ 65 mmHg [ 13 , 14 ]. This approach is inherently reactive, as treatment is initiated only after hypotension occurs. Furthermore, the fixed threshold of MAP ≥ 65 mmHg may not be optimal for all patients, as it fails to account for individual variations in baseline blood pressure and autoregulatory thresholds. In contrast to this reactive approach, an emerging paradigm is individualized or preemptive blood pressure management, which aims to maintain SBP within a narrow range (e.g., ± 10%) of baseline. This strategy has shown promise in reducing postoperative organ dysfunction in patients undergoing major abdominal surgery [ 15 , 16 ], suggesting that proactive stabilization may be superior to reactive correction. However, high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials is lacking specifically in older hip fracture patients. Therefore, we hypothesize that an individualized blood pressure management strategy (targeting SBP within ± 10% of baseline) will reduce the incidence of postoperative organ dysfunction compared to a standard management strategy (preventing SBP < 90 mmHg or a decrease of > 30% from baseline) in older patients undergoing hip fracture repair under general anesthesia.
sections.study design: This randomized controlled trial was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Qilu Hospital of Shandong University (No. KYLL-202406–008-2; October 9, 2024) and registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400093838, December 12, 2024). This study has been conducted since December 2024 and will be completed by June 2026 in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Standard Protocol Items for Randomized Trials (SPIRIT) guidelines. A total of 180 participants will be randomly assigned to either an individualized or a standard treatment group. The research pattern is shown in Fig. 1 . The participant timeline is demonstrated in Table 1 .
