sections.trial objectives: The primary objective of this study is to determine whether individualized blood pressure management reduces the incidence of a composite of organ dysfunction within 7 days after surgery compared with standard management in older hip fracture patients.
sections.research objects: Older patients (aged 65–85 years) who are scheduled to undergo hip fracture surgery under general anesthesia.
sections.inclusion criteria: Age between 65 and 85 years; American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grades I-III; Patients who are planning to undergo surgery for a unilateral hip fracture under general anesthesia; Provision of signed written informed consent from the patient or their legally authorized representative.
sections.exclusion criteria: Severe uncontrolled hypertension (SBP ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure [DBP] ≥ 110 mmHg) at rest before surgery; History of acute cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events (e.g., acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, acute cerebral infarction) within 30 days prior to surgery; Previous history of major neurological or psychiatric disorders that would preclude accurate assessment of postoperative delirium or cognitive function, including but not limited to: moderate to severe Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson's disease, prior stroke with significant residual cognitive or functional deficit, or psychosis; Severe pre-existing organ dysfunction, defined as any of the following: Cardiac: New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV heart failure or left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 30%. Respiratory: Home oxygen therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) < 50% of predicted. Hepatic: Child–Pugh class C liver cirrhosis. Renal: Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 30 mL/min/1.73m 2 or on chronic renal replacement therapy (dialysis). Multiple fractures or other trauma; Requirement for any vasopressor or inotrope infusion at the time of screening or hospital admission for the hip fracture, regardless of duration or indication; Current participation in another interventional clinical trial; Inability to communicate effectively, or severe hearing/visual impairment preventing reliable outcome assessment.
sections.withdrawal criteria: Participant Initiated: Participants may withdraw at any time without penalty. Reasons will be documented if provided. Investigator Initiated: The principal investigator may discontinue a participant for: Major protocol deviation (e.g., unplanned change in anesthesia or surgery). Loss to follow-up (inability to complete the 7-day primary outcome assessment). A serious perioperative complication where continuation is not in the participant's best interest. A Serious Adverse Event (SAE) probably or definitely related to the intervention. Data Handling: The primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle. Data collected until withdrawal will be included unless consent for data use is explicitly revoked.
sections.randomization and blinding: Eligible participants will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either the individualized or standard management group. The randomization sequence will be computer-generated by an independent statistician using block randomization with varying block sizes (of 4 and 6), stratified only by age group (65–74 years vs. 75–85 years) to ensure balance across this key prognostic factor. To guarantee allocation concealment and balance between groups throughout the trial, sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes will be used. The envelopes will be stored by an independent coordinator and opened by the attending anesthesiologist immediately prior to anesthesia induction. Due to the nature of the intervention, the anesthesiologist performing the intervention cannot be blinded. However, participants, postoperative outcome assessors, and data analysts will remain blinded to group assignment throughout the trial.
sections.preoperative interview: Within 24 h prior to surgery, eligible patients will undergo a comprehensive preoperative assessment. This includes evaluation of general status, medical history, physical examination, and laboratory results to determine ASA physical status and Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score. The study's purpose, procedures, risks, and benefits will be explained in detail to the patient and their legally authorized representative. Written informed consent for both routine anesthesia and trial participation will be obtained. The reference blood pressure will be obtained under standardized, pain-stabilized conditions. On the day before surgery, after achieving effective analgesia (Numerical Rating Scale [NRS] score ≤ 3) with Flurbiprofen Cataplasms (initiated upon admission and supplemented with rescue opioids as needed), the patient will rest supine for 5 min. Three consecutive SBP measurements will then be taken at 2-min intervals. If the variation between any two readings exceeds 10%, the series will be repeated after an additional 5-min rest. The mean of three stable measurements will be recorded as the reference SBP.
sections.intraoperative monitoring: Standard monitoring will be established upon operating room arrival. Prior to induction, advanced monitoring will be initiated with a radial arterial catheter under local anesthesia for continuous blood pressure monitoring and arterial blood gas sampling. The arterial line will be connected to a LiDCOrapid system (LiDCO Ltd., United Kingdom) for stroke volume (SV), stroke volume variation (SVV), cardiac index (CI) measurement to guide goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) and vasopressor titration. Depth of anesthesia will be monitored using the Bispectral Index (BIS). All arterial pressure (SBP, DBP, MAP) and heart rate (HR) will be recorded electronically, with values extracted every 5 min for subsequent analysis.
sections.anesthesia induction and intervention: After preoxygenation, general anesthesia will be induced with intravenous sufentanil (0.2–0.3 μg/kg), etomidate (0.1–0.2 mg/kg), and rocuronium (0.6 mg/kg). An i-gel supraglottic airway will be inserted, and mechanical ventilation will be commenced. Hemodynamic management will begin immediately post-induction. In the individualized management group, a continuous peripheral intravenous infusion of norepinephrine (10 μg/mL) will be started at 0.02 μg/kg/min and titrated to maintain SBP within ± 10% of the baseline, with a maximum dose of 0.2 μg/kg/min. In the standard management group, intermittent intravenous boluses of norepinephrine (10 μg) will be administered as rescue therapy only if hypotension occurs (defined as SBP < 90 mmHg or a > 30% decrease from baseline). For all patients, the MAP will be maintained at ≥ 65 mmHg as a universal minimum target [ 17 ]. If target blood pressure cannot be maintained at the maximum dose, rescue therapy (e.g., dopamine 2–5 μg/kg/min or epinephrine 0.01–0.05 μg/kg/min) will be initiated based on real-time hemodynamic monitoring. Finally, an ultrasound-guided supra-inguinal fascia iliaca compartment block (S-FICB) with 35 mL of 0.25% ropivacaine will be performed on the surgical side for postoperative analgesia.
sections.anesthesia maintenance: Anesthesia will be maintained with sevoflurane titrated to a BIS value of 40–60. Mechanical ventilation will be set to a tidal volume of 8 ml/kg with respiratory rate adjusted to maintain end-tidal CO₂ between 35–45 mmHg. Supplemental bolus doses of rocuronium, sufentanil, and remifentanil may be administered as needed. GDFT will be guided by the LiDCOrapid system. A fluid challenge of 250 mL lactated Ringer’s solution will be administered over 10 min; an increase in SV of ≤ 10% will be considered indicative of fluid non-responsiveness, establishing the optimal SV. SVV will be maintained at ≤ 13% throughout surgery (S2 Appendix).
sections.recovery of anesthesia: At the end of surgery, anesthetic administration is terminated and the patient is transferred to the postanesthesia care unit (PACU), where the same intraoperative hemodynamic management strategy is maintained. The laryngeal mask airway is removed once the patient responds to commands and demonstrates adequate spontaneous ventilation. Pharmacologic reversal agents are administered if indicated for persistent respiratory depression. Patients will be observed for at least 30 min after extubation and must achieve a modified Aldrete score of ≥ 9 before discharge to the ward.
sections.postoperative analgesia: Upon ward or ICU admission, a standardized intravenous patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) protocol is initiated. The PCA solution contains sufentanil 1 µg/mL (100 µg diluted in 100 mL normal saline) and is programmed with a basal infusion of 2 mL/h, a bolus dose of 2 mL, and a 15-min lockout interval. Nurses instruct patients to self-administer boluses for breakthrough pain (NRS > 3). Respiratory rate, sedation level, and pain intensity are monitored and documented at 4-h intervals to ensure safety.
sections.primary outcome: The primary outcome is a composite of at least one organ system dysfunction (including respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and nervous system) in patients within 7 days after surgery. The occurrence and severity of organ dysfunction should be assessed daily and evaluated during follow-up assessments (For specific definitions of organ system dysfunction, please refer to the S1 Appendix).
sections.secondary outcomes: The secondary outcomes encompass the components of the primary outcome, other postoperative clinical events (including systemic inflammatory response, infection, and thromboembolic events), intraoperative variables (hemodynamic data, fluid balance, and serum lactate levels), postoperative recovery measures (pain score, durations of ICU and hospital stay), and all-cause mortality within 30 days after surgery. More details are provided in the S2 Appendix. Hemodynamic variables, collected from anesthesia induction until PACU discharge, will consist of the total dosage of norepinephrine administered; the incidence of intraoperative hypotension (defined as SBP < 90 mmHg or a decrease > 30% from baseline, or MAP < 65 mmHg); the total dosage of urapidil administered; the incidence of intraoperative hypertension (defined as SBP > 160 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure > 90 mmHg) [ 15 ]; and the occurrence and management of severe bradycardia (defined as heart rate < 40 beats per minute).
sections.follow-up procedures: To ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the primary outcome within 7 days after surgery, a structured follow-up and data collection procedure will be implemented (Table 1 ). Blood samples are planned to be collected from all patients on postoperative days 1, 2, and 7. For patients discharged earlier, detailed guidance and assistance will be provided to facilitate their return for clinical assessment and blood sampling on day 7. If an in-person return is not possible, a blinded assessor will conduct a structured telephone interview to collect information on clinical symptoms. Concurrently, laboratory test results that are routinely available from other healthcare institutions during this period will be collected. The primary composite outcome will be adjudicated based on all clinical and laboratory data obtained up to postoperative day 7.
sections.adverse events: Adverse events (AEs) primarily include respiratory depression, bradycardia, nausea and vomiting, chills, anaphylactic shock, and cardiac arrest. Any unexpected AEs occurring during the trial will be promptly managed. In the event of a serious adverse event (SAE), regardless of its relationship to the intervention, the investigator will document it in detail in the source records, complete the case report form (CRF), and sign and date the entries contemporaneously.
sections.data collection and management: All participants will be evaluated at baseline. All data will be collected using paper-based CRFs. Hard copies of the CRFs will be stored in locked cabinets with restricted access. Data from the CRFs will be entered into a secure electronic database. Access to the database will be limited to authorized study personnel who have signed a confidentiality agreement. All participant personal information will be de-identified and kept strictly confidential throughout the study. Anonymized datasets may be made available for secondary research purposes upon reasonable request to the corresponding author and with approval from the institutional review board.
sections.sample size estimation: The sample size calculation was based on the primary composite outcome of postoperative organ dysfunction. A previous cohort study reported incidences of 51.7% vs . 38.1% for standard and individualized management, respectively [ 15 ]. However, the particularly high vulnerability of older hip fracture patients is demonstrated by elevated rates of intraoperative hypotension (approximately 60%) [ 18 ], postoperative AKI (7.6% to 11.3%) [ 18 – 20 ], and myocardial injury (14%) [ 18 ], we anticipate a higher baseline risk in our standard care group and a potentially larger treatment effect. Therefore, to ensure the study is adequately powered to detect a conservative and clinically significant effect, we assumed a 55% incidence of the primary outcome in the standard management group and a 30% incidence in the individualized management group. Using a chi-square test in PASS 15 software with a two-sided α of 5% and 90% power, a minimum sample size of 82 patients per group was calculated. To account for an anticipated 10% dropout rate, a total of 180 patients (90 per group) will be enrolled. This calculation employs a conservative effect size estimate, anticipating a higher baseline risk of organ dysfunction in our frail older hip fracture population compared to the referenced study in major abdominal surgery [ 15 ], thereby ensuring adequate power to detect a clinically meaningful difference.
sections.statistical analysis: All analyses will be performed using SPSS (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). A two-sided P -value < 0.05 will be considered statistically significant. The primary outcome will be compared between groups using the chi-square test. To account for potential baseline imbalances, the primary analysis will be supplemented with a multivariable logistic regression model adjusting for age (as a continuous variable) and ASA physical status classification. The normality of continuous data will be assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Continuous variables will be summarized as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges and compared using the independent samples t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables will be presented as numbers (percentages) and compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. For secondary analyses, the relationships between the intervention and the primary outcome will be further explored using multivariable logistic regression, adjusting for key baseline covariates. Repeated-measures data (e.g., SBP over time) will be analyzed using generalized estimating equations. Time-to-event data will be analyzed with the Kaplan–Meier method and the log-rank test. The ITT principle will be applied for all analyses. Any missing data will be handled using complete-case analysis.
sections.discussion_1: This randomized controlled trial is designed to evaluate whether an individualized blood pressure management strategy (targeting SBP within ± 10% of baseline) can reduce postoperative organ dysfunction more effectively than a standard reactive management strategy in older patients undergoing hip fracture surgery under general anesthesia. The underlying mechanism is hypothesized to be through preemptive stabilization of hemodynamics, thereby minimizing exposure to IOH and maintaining personalized organ perfusion pressures tailored to individual autoregulatory thresholds. The primary goals of anesthetic management in hip fracture patients are to mitigate postoperative complications and facilitate early recovery and functional rehabilitation [ 21 ]. IOH is a well-established, independent risk factor for a spectrum of adverse outcomes, including AKI, myocardial injury, and postoperative delirium [ 22 , 23 ]. Notably, cardiovascular events and AKI are leading contributors to the high 30-day mortality observed after non-cardiac surgery, with up to one-third of deaths potentially attributable to perioperative myocardial injury [ 23 ]. Consequently, optimizing intraoperative hemodynamics is paramount for improving outcomes in this vulnerable geriatric population [ 24 ]. General anesthetic agents induce vasodilation and reduce systemic vascular resistance, compromising cardiovascular compensatory mechanisms [ 25 ]. This is particularly detrimental in older patients with diminished physiological reserve and impaired autoregulation. Evidence consistently demonstrates that blood pressure deviations exceeding 30% from baseline are associated with prolonged recovery and increased mortality [ 26 , 27 ]. This underscores the limitations of a one-size-fits-all approach using fixed thresholds (e.g., MAP < 65 mmHg or SBP < 90 mmHg) and supports the rationale for individualized targets based on preoperative baseline values. In the previous study, Futier et al. [ 15 ] demonstrated that individualized SBP management during major abdominal surgery reduced postoperative organ dysfunction. We hypothesize that an individualized perfusion pressure management strategy, guided by baseline blood pressure and initiated preemptively before hypotensive events, may improve tissue oxygenation and microcirculation in older hip fracture surgery patients, thus mitigating multi-system ischemic injury. The choice of norepinephrine as the primary vasopressor is based on its favorable pharmacological profile for this population. Unlike phenylephrine, which is a pure α-agonist and can reduce heart rate and cardiac output, norepinephrine possesses both α- and β-adrenergic activity. Its β1-effects provide mild positive inotropy, supporting cardiac output, while its vasoconstrictive effects improve venous return. This profile facilitates a more stable elevation in blood pressure with less impact on heart rate compared to pure vasoconstrictors. Furthermore, compared to ephedrine, which exhibits tachyphylaxis and variable effects [ 28 ], a continuous low-dose infusion of norepinephrine offers more predictable and titratable control, making it ideally suited for preemptive stabilization [ 29 ]. While concerns exist regarding vasopressor use and renal perfusion [ 29 ], the protocol employs low doses aimed at preventing profound hypotension, which is a greater threat to renal autoregulation. Evidence from animal models suggests norepinephrine can effectively restore microcirculatory flow during hypotension without compromising gut oxygenation [ 30 ]. This study has several limitations. First, as a single-center trial, the generalizability of our findings may be limited. However, the single-center design enhances internal validity by standardizing the intervention and perioperative care. Second, in compliance with our institutional ethics committee guidelines, we excluded patients over 85 years of age. While this enhances safety for our initial investigation, it means our results may not be directly extrapolated to the very older population, who represent a significant proportion of hip fracture patients and may derive substantial benefit from such management strategies. Future research should specifically address this age group. Lastly, the composite primary outcome, while designed to capture the overall burden of organ dysfunction, may mask specific effects on individual organ systems. However, it provides a holistic measure of patient-centered morbidity. Despite these limitations, this trial is poised to provide high-level evidence regarding the efficacy of individualized blood pressure management in reducing postoperative multi-organ dysfunction among geriatric hip fracture patients. Our findings are expected to contribute to the development of standardized, evidence-based clinical protocols aimed at optimizing perioperative outcomes and improving survival and functional recovery in this vulnerable population.

title: Longitudinal Degeneration of Microstructural and Structural Connectivity Patterns Following Stroke
abstract: BACKGROUND: Stroke causes neurological impairment through local plasticity mechanisms, such as synaptic sprouting, and large-scale network reorganization. Although poststroke Wallerian degeneration is well established, whether white matter (WM) tracts’ remodel over time to support behavioral recovery remains controversial. We investigated whether longitudinal changes in WM microstructure and structural connectivity are coupled to poststroke behavior, and how structural connectivity reorganization relates to local disconnection microstructure. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study (Washington University, St. Louis; 2016–2018), patients with first-time stroke underwent diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and behavioral assessments at 2 weeks and 3 months poststroke; healthy controls were assessed twice. Latent factorial analysis was applied to behavioral and microstructural data from diffusion tensor imaging and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging. Primary measures were whole-brain structural connectivity gradient divergences computed from tractography, microstructural diffusion parameters extracted from both WM and cortical regions disconnected by the lesion, and behavioral factors. Linear mixed models (adjusted for sociodemographic values) assessed longitudinal changes, linear regression assessed brain-behavior associations, and machine learning algorithms assessed differences between healthy controls and stroke. RESULTS: Seventy-nine patients (age, 60±12 years; 43% female; diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging: 48 at 2 weeks and 26 at 3 months) and 33 age-matched healthy controls were included. At 2 weeks, patients with stroke exhibited diffuse whole-brain alterations in WM organization. These widespread changes were closely linked to microstructural abnormalities in WM pathways disconnected by the lesion. Notably, WM degeneration progressed between 2 weeks and 3 months poststroke. Whole-brain structural connectivity alterations were associated with cognitive deficits acutely but not at 3 months, whereas microstructural parameters in disconnected tracts were primarily related to motor impairment. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with predominantly mild-severity stroke, we observed widespread and progressive alterations in WM microstructure that persists beyond the lesion and continues to evolve over time. Although acute structural disconnection relates to behavioral deficits, chronic WM degeneration appears largely uncoupled from functional recovery.

sections.data availability: Data used for this study are publicly available at www.humanconnectome.org/study/hcp-young-adult/data-releases . The clinical data are available upon request by the corresponding author. For this prospective longitudinal cohort study with a parallel healthy control (HC) group, patients with first-ever ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke were enrolled at Washington University in St. Louis (2016–2018) and followed at 2 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year (not reported). Inclusion required age ≥18 years, clinical stability, and objective neurological deficits; exclusions were multifocal lesions, reduced vigilance, major neurological/psychiatric, systemic comorbidities, or life expectancy <1 year (full criteria in Supplemental Section S1.1 ). Age-, sex-, and education-matched HCs were recruited among patients’ relatives during the same period and assessed twice (1 month apart). Matching was performed at the group level. Patients and HC underwent identical behavioral and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessments (baseline and follow-up). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants per institutional review board procedures at Washington University. This article follows the STROBE reporting guidelines (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies). 25 Figure S1 shows the enrollment diagram. Participants underwent an extensive behavioral battery, administered typically on the same day as the imaging session (lasting ≈2.5 hours), representing an update of a validated battery previously used, 26 and assessing memory, language, visuospatial attention, executive, and motor functions ( Supplemental Sections S1.2.1 through S1.2.5 ). A dimensional reduction approach was applied through a hierarchical factor analysis with orthogonal (varimax) rotation ( Supplemental Section S1.2.6 ). The resulting behavioral factors were compared between stroke and HC using a 2-sample t test, and between the subacute and chronic stroke phases with a paired t test. Stroke severity was quantified using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score both at hospital admission and at the time of the subacute assessment. A 3T Siemens Prisma scanner collected neuroimaging data. Acquisition imaging parameters and preprocessing details are reported ( Supplemental Section S1.3 ).
sections.sc gradients: Whole-brain SC patterns were assessed through gradient analysis, a technique allowing to identify continuous axes of variation in brain connectivity and capture the hierarchical organization of brain networks. 27 Details are given in Supplemental Section S1.4.1 . In line with the literature, 28 we selected the first 3 principal gradients to provide a balanced representation of the connectivity pattern. To quantify variability in the gradients, we applied a gradient divergence (GD) measure for each brain parcel, normalized between 0 and 1, with higher values indicative of connectivity patterns that deviate more strongly from controls (the GD formula is reported in Supplemental Section S1.4.2 ). Briefly, GD captures how far each brain parcel’s connectivity profile departs from the control-derived gradient space, with higher values indicating greater divergence from typical SC patterns. For the networkwise analysis, GDs were averaged based on the correspondence between the Schaefer parcellation and the Yeo 7-network template. 29 To visualize key connectivity features, we examined the relationship between the first 2 gradients by identifying extreme parcels (from HC) along the Cartesian axes within each network. Structural pathways from these points, for both intrahemispheric and interhemispheric connectivity, were traced using a normative streamline map. 30
sections.microstructural diffusivity: Diffusion processed data were used to estimate both diffusion tensor imaging and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging measurements, fed into a latent factorial analysis ( Supplemental Section S1.5 ). To confirm the latent factorial analysis microstructural patterns, the same method was applied in an independent sample of n=1065 individuals from the Human Connectome Project ( Supplemental Section S1.6 ). Microstructural analyses focused on (1) contralesional GM and (2) WM tracts structurally disconnected from the lesion. For the contralesional GM, the binarized and Montreal Neurological Institute-registered lesion mask was flipped along the y axis. These regions of interest were segmented into GM and WM according to the Harvard-Oxford atlas. WM tracts were based on SDC patterns embedding the lesion into a normative template to assess the probability of disconnections within the normative connectome. 20 To visualize SDC patterns, we applied a principal component analysis, and components >10% variance were visualized. We tested disconnection probability thresholds of 40%, 60%, and 80%. To minimize partial volume effects, a shell region, created by inflating lesion borders by 4 voxels, was excluded from tracts.
sections.sc gradients_1: To ensure the robustness of results, we performed different complementary analyses. First, we assessed whether the distributions of the relationship between the main gradients were different between cohorts by means of structural equation modeling ( Supplemental Section S1.7.1 ). Specifically, we assessed whether group (HC; stroke) influenced the association between gradients at the network level. Intraconnectivity and interconnectivity SC gradients were analyzed independently and considered significant with a P FDR <0.05. Second, we summarized gradient values across brain parcels, projecting data into a 2-dimensional space using the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection algorithm. 31 For each participant, parcelwise gradient values were reduced to 2 components. A multivariate ANCOVA was performed to test group differences in this 2-dimensional space (controlling for sociodemographic variables). A support vector machine was used to classify stroke and controls based on Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection embeddings ( Supplemental Section S1.7.2 ). Furthermore, we assessed GD parcel-level differences through a 1-sample t test in stroke (as the GD metric was derived from controls, thus preventing the possibility of an unbiased direct comparison between groups). Zero represents a perfect alignment with the control’s gradient templates, so positive t-scores indicate areas where the stroke group’s GD values differ from this baseline. For visualization, only parcels with t-scores exceeding T=5 were plotted, to highlight brain regions with the highest deviations from controls. Finally, we performed a network-level analysis comparing stroke and controls using directly gradient values (in place of GD). For stroke, hemispheres ipsilesional to the lesion were flipped to the left, with the right hemisphere treated as contralesional. Each parcel was assigned to one of the Yeo network. 29 Absolute gradient values were computed per parcel to avoid cancelation of opposing values within the same network and then averaged at the network level. An ordinary least squares regression was used to compare stroke and controls, controlling for sociodemographic outcomes. We tested the main effects of diagnosis and network, as well as their interaction (diagnosis×network).
sections.microstructural differences between stro: Microstructural diffusion factors obtained from latent factorial analysis (hereafter termed latent microstructure) within SDC maps were compared between stroke and HC. We created a mean template from controls for the latent factor maps. For each patient, the corresponding SDC maps were used as a mask in the control’s template. Values within the individual and template maps were compared by means of a nonparametric independent test (Mann-Whitney U test; P <0.05). Moreover, we applied a voxelwise analysis comparing latent-microstructure factors between controls and subacute stroke ( Supplemental Section S1.8 ).
sections.microstructural-disconnection correlates: We tested whether the disconnected GM also showed microstructural abnormalities. Pathological mechanisms in the disconnected GM tissue have been demonstrated in an animal model 32 but never in humans. To achieve this aim, we assessed whether contralesional latent microstructure could predict the likelihood of the contralesional area being disconnected from the lesion. A linear regression analysis was applied, including as independent variables all the latent-microstructural values within the GM contralesional tissues and the structural degree of disconnection as the dependent variable. In addition, we investigated whether GM regions disconnected from the lesions exhibited worse microstructural values compared with unconnected regions ( Supplemental Section S1.9 ).
sections.longitudinal analysis: We used the linear mixed model to compare network-GD values longitudinally in stroke (subacute versus 3 months), with networks and individuals as random factors. Separate models were run for intrahemispheric and interhemispheric gradients in both ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres (4 models). Similarly, we compared latent-microstructural factors over time within SDC masks. All LLM analyses included sociodemographic covariates. To assess the robustness of results, both sets of analyses were performed on the full data set (all-available-data analysis) and on patients with diffusion-weighted MRI data at both timepoints (complete-case analysis). The complete-case analysis was specifically conducted to verify whether the longitudinal effects were comparable when restricting the sample to patients who completed both baseline and 3-month scans, thereby reducing the possibility that the observed results were driven by systematic characteristics of participants who did not return for follow-up (eg, differences in disease severity).
sections.behavioral correlates: We assessed the parcelwise relationships (Pearson) between behavioral latent factors with intrahemispheric and interhemispheric GD for subacute and chronic stages, separately. This analysis was performed independently for intraconnectivity and interconnectivity ( P FDR <0.05). The relationship between latent-microstructural properties and behavioral performance was assessed by means of a linear regression (R 2 robustness was evaluated via 1000 bootstrap resamples [95% CI]). Latent-microstructural values within SDC and lesion masks were included as predictors for behavior. The analysis was repeated independently for subacute and chronic stages ( P FDR <0.05). Outliers exceeding 2× the interquartile ranges were removed to avoid inclusion of biased values. For SDC, we considered the more lenient threshold (40%).
sections.connectivity organization and microstruc: We examined the relationship (linear regression model) between gradient organization and microstructure, assessing whether deviations in GD from controls were linked to biological mechanisms in disconnected tracts. Microstructural factors within SDC tracts were related to GD separately for intrahemispheric and interhemispheric connectivity and for ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres. A global GD value was calculated by averaging parcelwise GD. Latent-microstructural parameters in SDC-ROIs were used as predictors of global GD ( P <0.05). We also conducted this analysis at the network level ( P FDR <0.05). All analyses were performed in patients with subacute stroke, using SDC maps 40% probability.
sections.sensitivity analyses: Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the analyses, including analyses examining the potential differential impact of subcortical versus nonsubcortical (cortical or cerebellar) lesions on diffusion-derived metrics ( Supplemental Section S1.10 ).
sections.results: Seventy-nine patients (age=60.1±11.5 years; education=13.3±2.5) and n=33 age-matched HC were included. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale scores at evaluation indicated that most patients presented with mild impairment (mean, 4.5±4.5) although a minority of patients showed higher initial severity (Table). Patients and HC were matched for age (T=0.927; P =0.356), education (T=−0.897; P =0.372), and sex (X 2 =1.433; P =0.231). N=29 HC performed MRI exam (age=57±11 years; education=13.7±2.6), of whom n=22 repeated the MRI visit 1 month apart (session 2). A total of n=48 patients had available MRI data at the baseline visit (age=59±11 years; education=13.5±2.2), while n=26 repeated the exam at the 3-month follow-up (age=59±11 years; education=13.8±2.2). No differences were observed between the stroke baseline imaging cohort and the cohort of controls performing MRI at the first session (age: T=−0.55; P =0.58; education: T=0.38; P =0.71; and sex: X 2 =3.06; P =0.08). No significant differences were observed between patients who completed the 3-month MRI follow-up and those who did not in terms of age, sex, education, lesion volume, or baseline clinical severity (all comparisons P >0.39; Figure S2 ). Figure 2 shows the lesion frequency maps.
sections.latent behavioral factors: Latent factorial analysis was used to assess the latent behavioral space. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin score (computed to evaluate the sampling adequacy for latent factorial analysis) showed a value suggestive of adequacy (0.813). We identified 5 main factors explaining ≈50% of the variance. The first factor loaded on verbal memory, language, and executive functions (13.3% variance; hereafter referred to as the language-verbal-memory). The second (12.2%) and third (8.1%) factors reflected right and left motor functions, respectively (right motor and left motor factor). The fourth (6.4%) captured visual memory, working memory, and general attention (visuospatial-memory-attention component); the fifth (6.38%) related to lateralized visuospatial performance on the Posner task (lateralized attention factor; Figure S3 ). Due to the left-right structure of this last factor, absolute values were used. The analysis repeated on the stroke-only (subacute) sample yielded similar results ( Figure S4 ). These factors differed significantly between HC and patients with subacute stroke ( P <0.05; Figure 3 ). At 3-month follow-up (n=33), patients improved in motor (left: P =0.046; right: P =0.002) and lateralized visual attention ( P =0.030), while language-verbal memory and visuospatial-attention factors showed nonsignificant improvements ( Figure S4 ).
sections.structural connectivity: Figure 2 shows the surface representation of the SC gradients obtained in HC intrahemispherically (variance=52%) and interhemispherically (variance=71%). Gradients are data-driven axes of SC covariance that mathematically captures the principal organization of WM and describe variability along posteroanterior, ventral-dorsal, and callosal directions. In HC, the first intrahemispheric connectivity gradient ( intra G1) explained 22% variance, the second ( intra G2) 17%, and the third ( intra G3) 13%. For the interhemispheric connectivity, inter G1, inter G2, and inter G3 explained 32%, 24%, and 15% variance, respectively. Supplemental Section S2.1 provides an anatomic description of the gradients. Figure S5A shows the parcelwise top 10% gradient values. The spatial patterns of these gradients were replicated in HC at both sessions ( Figure S5B ; parcelwise spatial correlation >0.992 across the gradients). Similar average-group patterns were found between patients with stroke (subacute) and controls, highlighting that gradient values captured similar connectivity axes in the 2 groups ( Figure S6 ). An intuitive understanding of the anatomic organization of the gradients emerges from their bivariate relationships. The relationship between intra G1 and intra G2 highlighted an SC pattern transitioning from a posterior-anterior axis (highest intra G1-G2 values) to a superior-inferior pattern (lowest intra G1-G2 values) and then returning to an anterior-posterior axis (intermediate intra G1-G2 values), forming a virtual U-shaped trajectory in the embedded gradient space (Figure 4 A) that reflects a continuous reorganization of dominant connectivity patterns rather than a discrete anatomic pathway. Tracts connected with the parcels with the highest intra G1-G2 values include the geniculocalcarine tract or the inferior frontal-occipital fasciculus. In contrast, tracts connected with the lowest intra G1-G2 values include the corticospinal tract. Notably, the relationship between inter G1 versus inter G2 captures the organization of callosal fibers from the anterior (highest inter G1 values) to the posterior (lowest inter G1 values) portion (Figure 4 B). This interpretation was validated by comparing the inter G1 versus inter G2 values with the average corpus callosum fibers from the Human Connectome Project (Figure 4 C). In summary, the gradient structure allows for mapping in a compact way the whole-brain organization of the SC.
sections.microstructure: Diffusion tensor imaging and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging maps from the 2 sessions of the HC showed high reproducibility ( Figure S7A ). From these maps, we reported 3 main latent diffusion factors ( dwi Fs; Figure 2 ). The first factor ( dwi F1; 52% variance) loaded on axial diffusivity, radial diffusivity, mean diffusivity, and isotropic volume fraction. Higher values were predominantly observed in the cerebrospinal fluid, aligning with the loadings on diffusion metrics. The second factor ( dwi F2; 28% variance) loaded on fractional anisotropy and orientation dispersion index, with opposite directions, indicating a latent space capturing diffusivity orientation. Anatomically, divergent values were expressed in the GM and WM tissues, the latter showing lower values (higher anisotropy in the WM). The third factor ( dwi F3; 15% variance) loaded positively on both fractional anisotropy and intracellular volume fraction (Figure 4 D and 4 E). This factor showed a spatial distribution similar to the myelin map distribution from Glasser et al, 33 suggesting a microstructural pattern preferentially expressed along major WM pathways, which are enriched in highly myelinated fibers (Figure 4 F). An additional analysis computing the latent space independently of the stroke cohort echoed these findings ( Figure S7B ). The latent-microstructural space reported in the second session of HC was used to project microstructural data of patients with stroke. Due to the novelty of the reported patterns, we assess the robustness of this latent diffusion tensor imaging-neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging microstructural space in a large independent cohort (Human Connectome Project). The results were in line with the findings on the stroke data set and highly reproducible across the 2 independent data sets (Washington University and Human Connectome Project; Supplemental Section S2.2 ; Figure S8 ).
sections.cross-sectional analysis: First, we assessed whether the distribution of the relationship between gradients was similar between patients and HC. While, qualitatively, the pattern was similar between cohorts (Figure 4 A and 4 B), patients with stroke showed a more widespread distribution, with significant differences for both intra G1- intra G2 and inter G1- inter G2 mapping to different networks ( Supplemental Section S2.3 ). Differences between cohorts were confirmed by the multivariate ANCOVA analysis applied to the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection space for both intraconnectivity (ipsilesional hemisphere: F=6.70; P =0.0022; contralesional: F=3.43; P =0.0376) and interconnectivity (ipsilesional: F=8.51; P =0.0005; contralesional: F=4.01; P =0.0225). Furthermore, we assess the classification accuracy of the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection space, segregating controls and stroke. Support vector machine reached a classification accuracy of 89% and 96% for the interhemispheric and intrahemispheric SC gradients, respectively (Figure 5 A). Details for the support vector machine hyperparameters’ validation are given in Supplemental Section S2.4 . Finally, we performed a parcelwise finer analysis by means of a 1-sample t test applied to the GD. Although the lesions were heterogeneous in location, most of them concentrated in the middle cerebral artery distribution (Figure 2 A); yet, the cortical parcels showing the greatest divergence from HC also involved regions away from the middle cerebral artery distribution (Figure 5 B). Group differences were further confirmed at the network level when analyses were applied directly to gradient values rather than GD scores ( Supplemental Section S2.5 ; Figure S9 ). These findings indicate that subacute stroke lesions induce widespread alterations of the structural connectome, affecting both the ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres.
sections.longitudinal analysis_1: For the all-available-data sample, the linear mixed model analysis for the ipsilesional hemisphere showed a significant time effect for both intra GD (T=3.406; P =0.001) and inter GD (T=3.035; P =0.003). A significant effect was also observed when considering the contralesional hemisphere ( intra GD: T=3.431; P =0.001; inter GD: T=2.667; P =0.008; Figure 5 C). Results were confirmed in the complete-case sample ( Tables S1 and S2 ). These findings indicate a chronic degeneration of the structural connectome from 2 weeks to 3 months.
sections.cross-sectional analysis_1: First, a qualitative description of the SDC in patients with stroke was performed through a descriptive principal component analysis. Two main factors (>66% variance) were reported, loading within the left and the right hemisphere, consistent with the lesion frequency map (Figure 2 ). SDC maps were used as masks for microstructural analysis. We found a significant group difference for dwi F2 (loading on fractional anisotropy and orientation dispersion index). The results were consistent across multiple SDC thresholds (60%: U=1277; P =0.033; 80%: U=1135; P =0.024), while the 40% threshold showed a trend toward significance ( P =0.06). No significant differences emerged for the other factors ( P >0.6; Figure 6 A). The specific involvement of dwi F2 was confirmed by the exploratory voxelwise analysis, reporting higher dwi F2 values in stroke, subacutely, compared with HC (p FWE <0.05). No significant voxels were reported for dwi F1 and dwi F3 ( Supplemental Section S2.6 ; Figure S10 ). The linear regression analysis showed significant results at the subacute stage ( adj r2=0.625; P <0.0001). Specifically, higher disconnection probability was accompanied by lower dwi F2 (coef: −0.244; P <0.001) and higher dwi F3 (coef: 0.132; P =0.012), with a reversed (and expected) effect of these factors on GM compared with WM. Results were echoed by the bootstrapping procedure (F=21.65; P <0.0001; Figure 6 B). To generalize these findings, we ran a separate analysis in which we compared brain regions with the highest and the lowest probability of disconnections based on the SDC values. A significant effect was found for dwi F2 (Figure 6 C). The result was highly stable across the random selection of parcels with the lowest probability. Moreover, dwi F2 showed the highest differences between parcels compared with dwi F1 and dwi F3 assessed with a 1-way ANOVA (F=347; P <0.00001; np 2 =0.32). Results were replicated when excluding the subcortical parcels from the analysis (F=26.3; P <0.00001; np 2 =0.15; Figure S11 ). These results indicate a significant linear relationship between the degree of WM disconnection and the alteration of the diffusion properties of the disconnected GM.
sections.longitudinal analysis_2: Longitudinal changes in SDC latent-microstructural parameters were significant for dwi F3, consistently for the different probability thresholds in the all-available-data (40%: T=2.124 [95% CI, 2.5–97.5]=0.113–0.752; P =0.043; 60%: T=2.747 [95% CI, 2.5–97.5]=0.022–0.133; P =0.011; and 80%: T=2.128 [95% CI, 2.5–97.5]=0.006–0.150; P =0.043). SDC regions (independently of the threshold) showed, on average, lower values at the chronic stage compared with the subacute stage. Because dwi F3 loads on the main myelinated tracts, its reduction chronically strongly supports longitudinal degeneration (Figure 6 D; Table S1 ), potentially reflecting a combination of processes including demyelination, axonal degeneration, and secondary inflammatory or neurodegenerative mechanisms. Results were confirmed by the complete case ( Table S2 ). A post hoc sensitivity analysis, evaluating whether microstructural latent factors computed at the individual level produced consistent results, confirmed the longitudinal degeneration findings ( Supplemental Section S2.7 ). Similar to the gradient analysis, the microstructural properties of the disconnected tracts further degenerate from the subacute to the chronic stage.
sections.correlations between wm alterations and: At the subacute stage, stroke-related changes in intrahemispheric GD were significantly associated with deficits in language-verbal memory, visuospatial-memory, and attention-neglect. Motor deficits were not significantly associated with GD (Figure 7 A). At the chronic stage, we found no significant behavioral association with the intrahemispheric GD. A weak association was found for the interhemispheric GD with visuospatial-memory-attention and lateralized-neglect components (extended data are reported in Figure S12 ). Contrary to SC gradients, subacute motor left deficits were associated with latent-microstructural parameters of disconnected WM (r 2 =0.37; P FDR =0.015 [95% CI, 0.146–0.690]). The remaining behavioral factors did not show significant associations (Figure 7 B). The relationship between SDC latent-microstructural parameters and left motor deficits remained significant at the chronic stage (r 2 =0.42; P FDR <0.005 [95% CI, 0.237–0.639]; Figure 7 B). Chronically, there was also a significant association between the SDC latent microstructure with the visuospatial-memory-attention ( P FDR =0.020) and language-verbal-memory factors ( P FDR =0.020) although these associations were of lower magnitude (r 2 =0.20 with 95% CI, 0.091–0.394, and r 2 =0.19 with 95% CI, 0.095–0.391, respectively).
sections.relationship between whole-brain gradien: Previous studies have documented widespread changes in the WM poststroke but have not related these changes to the site of lesion. Hence, it is important to establish if the degree of local disconnection relates to the degree of global SC abnormalities. For this analysis, only dwi F2 and dwi F3 were considered, given the marginal contribution of dwi F1 to the results. Microstructural outcomes within the SDC ROI were significantly predictive of the global GD value (intrahemispheric contralesional: R 2 =0.186; P =0.020; intrahemispheric ipsilesional: R 2 =0.224; P =0.008; interhemispheric contralesional: R 2 =0.228; P =0.011; and interhemispheric ipsilesional: R 2 =0.167; P =0.041). As GD increased (higher dissimilarity from HC), in the disconnected WM tracts, dwi F2 increased, and dwi F3 decreased, indicating microstructural alterations compatible with axonal disorganization, while potentially also reflecting contributions from other biological processes such as edema or inflammatory responses ( Figure S13 ; Table S3 ). At the network level, these results were largely confirmed ( Figure S13 ). This analysis links for the first time the degree of WM disconnection caused by stroke lesions to widespread changes in the structural connectome organization.
sections.sensitivity analysis: These findings were confirmed by multiple sensitivity analyses ( Supplemental Section S2.8 ; Figure S14 ).
sections.discussion: One of the most influential results in the past decade has been realizing the importance of brain networks’ disconnection caused by focal lesions. 12 , 34 Here, we demonstrated for the first time 3 related findings: progressive SC degeneration, relations between microstructural degeneration in disconnected tracts and connectome reorganization, and stage-specific dissociations in brain-behavior relationships between the subacute and follow-up stages. Through gradient mapping, 27 we identified 3 SC gradient maps. In patients, these gradients showed, subacutely, widespread differences, in line with previous studies that found poststroke SC alterations 17 , 35 and FC changes. 5 , 12 , 34 The structural changes were large enough that a patient with stroke could be clearly distinguished from HC (accuracy around 90%). When the SC gradients were remeasured after 3 months, we showed a growing deviation from the HC’s template. This is interesting as local synaptic sprouting and remodeling of the WM have been proposed as a mechanism of recovery in animal models, 24 , 36 and most recovery has already occurred at 3 months. 37 However, our results are in line with other human studies, showing progressive poststroke structural degeneration. 18 , 19 , 38 The progressive structural WM degeneration observed here contrasts with prior studies showing FC normalization correlating with recovery of function. 13 , 39 Since, at the subacute stage, changes in FC are closely aligned with alterations of SC, 16 it follows that structural and FC trajectories progressively diverge during recovery, with structure degenerating, while function normalizes. These findings are consistent with the idea that adaptive FC reorganization could contribute to behavioral recovery, especially in more redundant cognitive networks where the link between structure and function is weaker. 40 However, because FC was not directly assessed, this comparison should be interpreted as a contextualization within the existing literature. Similarly, it is important to highlight that gradients represent descriptive SC-covariance axes. Thus, rather than being interpreted as specific anatomic pathways, gradients provide a principled low-dimensional framework to summarize large-scale structural reorganization, enabling the tracking of widespread and progressive deviations in poststroke connectome organization. Beyond SC, we described a latent-microstructural space showing high reliability in condensing complex diffusion metrics into stable components. Three dwi Fs were identified robustly in independent cohorts. When these latent diffusion microparameters were mapped to GM and WM regions identified as disconnected, 20 we found, subacutely, disorganization in disconnected regions. This pattern is consistent with decreased fractional anisotropy in WM, hence fiber disorganization, and decreased orientation dispersion index in the GM, hence loss of neurite dispersion suggestive of cortical deafferentation. Disconnected regions showed further degeneration from 2 weeks to 3 months, as indicated by a decrease in a measure suggestive of myelination. Interestingly, changes of latent microparameters in disconnected tissue partially but significantly explained the SC distance between stroke and HC. Microstructural latent factors predicted GD values in stroke, suggesting a complex relationship between SC and microstructural alterations. These findings suggest a cascade, whereby focal lesions drive microstructural degeneration in disconnected tracts and subsequent connectome reorganization. Despite ongoing structural decline, behavioral recovery occurred, indicating reliance on functional adaptation (likely via synaptic reweighting of surviving connections) rather than structural restoration. We measured behavior using a large battery, finding 5 factors that explained about 50% of the behavioral variance, consistent with previous studies in focal and neurodegenerative diseases. 41 – 43 While, in stroke, they likely reflect both the correlated topography of vascular lesions 44 and the low dimensionality of FC abnormalities, 5 , 8 more generally, they are thought to reflect loss of neural entropy 45 caused by any neurological disorder. Interestingly, different behavioral deficits showed a dissociated pattern of behavioral correlation with SC. Cognitive functions robustly correlated at the subacute stage with SC gradients. The topography was highly specific with left hemisphere alterations related to verbal-language-memory, bilateral alterations for visuospatial-memory-attention, and lateralized attention. Interestingly, motor deficits did not correlate with changes in whole-brain structural organization but rather with the microstructural latent factors of disconnected tracts that included, commonly, the corticospinal tracts. Importantly, our sample predominantly comprised patients with low-severity, mainly subcortical strokes, although consistent with previous literature. 46 , 47 This lesion profile likely emphasizes the role of focal WM disconnection in motor impairment. The correlation between WM changes and behavior weakened at 3 months, a time when behavioral recovery is nearly complete. 37 SC gradient 3-month changes were weakly or not related to cognitive tasks, which indicates a decoupling between SC and cognitive performance. Given that normalization of FC correlates with the behavioral recovery, 39 our results show that behavioral recovery may depend on synaptic reweighting of residual structural connections in the context of longitudinal structural degeneration, at least in mild-to-moderate stroke. This view is also consistent with recent work in nonhuman primates highlighting the role of transmodal association cortex in poststroke recovery. 13 In contrast to the cognitive domains, motor deficits (subacute and chronic stages) correlated with latent-microstructural parameters of disconnected regions. Because the lesion distribution was mainly located in the central WM underlying brain motor regions, and the main patterns of disconnection were correspondingly centered around the central sulcus, including the corticospinal tracts, the association between motor deficits and the microstructure of disconnected regions indicates the importance of local damage/disconnection in accounting for motor and sensory deficits. 8 , 26 , 39 , 42 These results should be interpreted considering several limitations. Gradients depend on methodological choices (eg, tractography algorithm, seeding, and filtering) and parcellation scheme, which shape the connectivity matrices. Although these decisions were guided by established literature and validated in HC, replication across alternative pipelines would further support the generalizability of the results. Interpretation of gradients is also more complex than established methods, with no consensus on their meaning. Consequently, gradients should be viewed primarily as descriptive tools for summarizing connectivity organization rather than as direct biological markers. Despite the absence of differences between patients who completed the MRI follow-up and those who did not, sample attrition remains a limitation. Future investigations with larger longitudinal cohorts will be necessary to confirm these findings. In addition, lesion heterogeneity represents a limitation; although sensitivity analyses addressed cortical versus subcortical lesions, the sample size did not allow for more detailed stratified analyses. Furthermore, the dissociation between chronic SC degeneration and behavior may, at least partly, reflect ceiling effects in behavioral measures or limited sensitivity of the structural indices used in this study. Nonetheless, several strengths stand out. Multishell diffusion data enhanced tractography reliability. The longitudinal design offered insights into stroke evolution, and integrating microstructural, connectivity, and behavioral data revealed novel latent patterns.

title: Gut fungal signatures in colorectal cancer and their potential for supporting diagnosis: a multi-cohort metagenomic analysis
abstract: Background Colorectal cancer (CRC) is influenced by host factors and environmental exposures that shape gut microbial ecosystems. Although bacterial and viral alterations in CRC have been widely investigated, the role of gut fungi remains underexplored, partly because of their low biomass and the limited availability of well-curated fungal reference genomes. Methods We conducted a large-scale metagenomic analysis across 9 publicly available cohorts comprising 1,433 fecal samples to characterize CRC-associated fungal alterations and fungal-bacterial co-abundance patterns. The predictive value of microbial signatures was assessed using LASSO and random forest models, with external validation performed in 6 independent cohorts comprising 272 samples. Results Multi-cohort analysis revealed CRC-associated alterations in gut fungal community structure and selected diversity measures. Differential abundance analysis identified 15 fungal species with recurrent changes across cohorts. Among them, Saccharomyces cerevisiae c86 and Trichophyton rubrum c61 showed predominant enrichment in healthy controls, whereas Barnettozyma c122 and Pseudopithomyces c302 showed predominant enrichment in CRC. Fungal-only models exhibited limited standalone predictive capacity. However, integrating fungal features with bacterial biomarkers modestly improved CRC prediction performance compared with bacterial-only models. In external validation, the random forest-based fungal-bacterial model increased the mean AUC from 0.722 to 0.762, with improved AUCs in 5 of the 6 validation cohorts. Conclusions This study suggests that CRC is associated with gut fungal dysbiosis and supports the exploratory value of gut fungal signatures as adjunctive features in microbiome-based CRC prediction models. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating fungal communities into CRC microbiome research while emphasizing the need for prospective and mechanistic validation. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-026-08403-8.

sections.background_1: Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a major global health burden, causing more than 500,000 deaths annually and ranking as the third most common cancer worldwide [ 1 ]. Epidemiological projections suggest that CRC incidence will continue to rise and may become one of the most prevalent cancers in the coming decades [ 2 ]. Although multiple risk factors have been associated with CRC, including environmental exposures [ 3 ], genetic predisposition [ 4 ], chronic inflammatory conditions [ 5 ], metabolic disorders (diabetes and obesity) [ 6 ], and lifestyle factors (excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, and dietary patterns characterized by high red/processed meat intake and low fruit/vegetable consumption) [ 6 , 7 ], the precise etiological mechanisms remain incompletely understood due to the disease’s remarkable heterogeneity and complex pathogenesis. The gut microbiota, comprising bacteria, fungi, and viruses, serves as a critical interface between environmental exposures and host physiology, playing a key role in maintaining human physiological homeostasis and has been implicated in various disease states [ 8 ]. Accumulating evidence suggests that gut microbial dysbiosis is associated with a range of pathological conditions, including obesity [ 9 ], Parkinson’s disease [ 10 ], hypertension [ 11 ], renal diseases [ 12 , 13 ], inflammation, and atherosclerosis [ 14 ]. Furthermore, there is growing evidence indicating a mechanistic association between specific bacterial taxa and the pathogenesis of CRC [ 15 ]. For instance, an enrichment of Fusobacterium spp. [ 16 ], pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli , and enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis has been consistently observed in CRC patients [ 17 ]. Moreover, distinct bacterial signatures including Fusobacterium nucleatum , Porphyromonas asaccharolytica , Gemella morbillorum , and Clostridium difficile have been identified as potential diagnostic biomarkers for CRC [ 18 ], highlighting the clinical relevance of microbial profiling in oncology. Equally important are the contributions of viruses to CRC development. The gut virome exhibits CRC-associated alterations [ 19 ], with oncolytic viruses not only inducing the body’s anti-tumor immune response through the presentation of tumor antigens but also promoting CRC cell death via selective replication in malignant cells. Furthermore, Brunovirus and Hpunavirus show positive correlations with CRC proliferation, whereas Lubbockvirus displays an inverse association [ 20 ]. These findings, corroborated by our previous research as well as studies conducted by Yang et al. [ 21 , 22 ], position the gut virome as a promising diagnostic tool for CRC detection. In contrast to the well-established research on gut bacteriome and virome, studies focusing on fungi in CRC are remain underexplored. This disparity is primarily due to the relatively low abundance of fungi in the human gut, which accounts for approximately 1% of the total microbial biomass, as well as the limited availability of well-annotated fungal reference genomes that are essential for accurate sequence alignment. These technical limitations have frequently led to the neglect of fungal communities in conventional metagenomic studies [ 23 ]. However, emerging evidence emphasizes the significant impact of the imbalance in fungal community composition on different disease status. For example, Aspergillus sydowii has been shown to play a pivotal role in shaping the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in lung adenocarcinomas, despite its low biomass. This fungal species promotes tumor progression and is associated with markedly poorer clinical outcomes [ 24 ]. Similar oncogenic roles have been identified for Malassezia species in the development of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and for Blastomyces species in breast cancer pathogenesis [ 25 , 26 ]. Collectively, these observations suggest that alterations in the gut mycobiome may influence the initiation and progression of CRC. Another major challenge in CRC microbiome research is the inconsistency across studies caused by technical and biological heterogeneity, including differences in sample processing, sequencing platforms, analytical pipelines, geography, diet, and host background [ 27 , 28 ]. Large-scale integrative analyses across multiple cohorts are therefore needed to identify more reproducible microbial features and evaluate their diagnostic relevance. In this study, we systematically analyzed nine publicly available shotgun metagenomic datasets comprising 1,433 fecal samples from CRC patients and healthy controls. Using a standardized analytical pipeline and a curated human-associated fungal genome catalog, we characterized CRC-associated fungal alterations, evaluated fungal-bacterial co-abundance patterns, and assessed the diagnostic value of fungal signatures alone and in combination with bacterial biomarkers. Our findings provide a multi-cohort view of CRC-associated gut mycobiome alterations and highlight exploratory fungal signatures that may complement existing microbiome-based CRC detection models.
sections.publicly available metagenomic datasets: We systematically identified CRC studies published between 2014 and 2024 that utilized shotgun metagenomic sequencing of human fecal samples from large cohorts through the NCBI database. Our primary analysis included 9 eligible cohorts comprising metagenomic datasets from 1,433 samples, including 641 CRC patients (the CRC group) and 792 healthy controls (the CTR group). The following accession IDs: PRJNA706060 (Gao_2022 et al.) [ 29 ], PRJNA961076 (Grion_2023 et al.) [ 30 ], PRJNA731589 (Liu_2022 et al.) [ 31 ], PRJNA758208 (Xu_2022 et al.) [ 32 ], PRJDB4176 (Yachida_2019 et al.) [ 33 ], PRJNA763023 (Yang_2024 et al.) [ 34 ], PRJEB10878 (Yu_2015 et al.) [ 35 ], PRJEB6070 (Zeller_2014 et al.) [ 36 ] and PRJEB7774 (Feng_2015 et al.) [ 37 ] were used to download datasets from NCBI Sequence Read rchive (SRA) database. In addition, the 6 validation cohorts included 272 samples, comprising 146 CRC patients and 126 healthy controls. The following accession numbers PRJEB12449 (Vogtmann_2016 et al.) [ 38 ], PRJNA389927 (Hannigan_2018 et al.) [ 39 ], PRJNA447983 (Thomas_a_2019 et al.) [ 40 ], PRJNA447983 (Thomas_b_2019 et al.) [ 40 ], PRJEB70916 (Sadeghi_2024 et al.) [ 41 ] and CNP0002641 (Chen_2023 et al.) [ 21 ] were also downloaded. Sample size and details of sample collection of retrieved cohorts is reported in (Table S1 ). Detailed information on gender, age, BMI, country, DNA extraction method, and sequencing platform for all samples is summarized in (Table S2 ).
sections.construction of gut fungal genome catalo: We established a high-quality human-associated fungal genome catalog through rigorous multi-step curation of NCBI resources. Initially, we downloaded 16,634 fungal genomes in February 2025, removing 1,384 low-quality (N50 length < 2,000 bp or number of scaffolds > 10,000) or a mixture of multiple genomes, remaining 15,250 genomes retained as a reference for further analyses. Meanwhile, to ensure accurate fungal identification and the purity of the reference genomes, we adapted methods from published articles [ 42 ]. Specifically, all fungal candidate sequences were aligned against the NCBI bacterial nucleotide (NT) database using BLASTN, and any sequences exhibiting significant homology to prokaryotic genomes (identity > 95%) were removed. We identified a total of 1,490 fungi species associated with humans. These strains were then clustered into 317 non-redundant human-associated fungal species based on an average nucleotide identity (ANI) threshold of 95%.
sections.processing of metagenomic sequencing dat: We performed rigorous quality control on each sample using fastp v0.20.164 [ 43 ], implementing the following filtering criteria: (1) removal of reads < 90 bp; (2) exclusion of reads with mean Phred score < 20; (3) removal of reads with an average complexity < 30%; (4) removal of reads where > 30% of their bases have a Phred quality score < 20; and (5) removal of unpaired-end reads. The detailed statistics for raw reads, filtered reads, and final fungal counts for each sample are provided in (Table S2 ). For comprehensive characterization of the gut bacteriome, we aligned metagenomic reads from both CRC patients and healthy controls against the Unified Human Gastrointestinal Genome (UHGG) reference database [ 44 ]. Following alignment, we systematically excluded reads mapping to the bacterial rRNA/tRNA gene sequences, resulting in the identification of 2,354 prokaryotic species. Relative abundance of these species was calculated by normalizing each sample, with phylum and genus level relative abundances obtained by summing the abundances of species within the same taxonomic group. To ensure specific detection of fungal communities, we implemented a rigorous filtering method specifically to minimize the impact of potential contaminants. Specifically, quality-controlled reads were sequentially aligned against three reference databases: (1) the MetaPhlAn4 bacterial genome database [ 45 ], (2) the complete chm13 v2.0 human genome, and (3) the SILVA rRNA gene database [ 46 ]. Through this multi-step alignment strategy that effectively eliminated reads of human or prokaryotic origin. Subsequently, we mapped the remaining reads to our curated gut fungal genome catalog using Bowtie2 with optimized parameters, employing the settings ‘--end-to-end’ [ 47 ]. To ensure high-confidence taxonomic assignment, only alignments with a sequence identity of at least 90% were retained, ultimately identifying 273 fungal species. To eliminate potential batch effects arising from different sequencing platforms, we performed batch effect correction using the MMUPHin pipeline. Subsequently, to estimate fungal relative abundance, mapped reads assigned to each fungal genome were first normalized by genome length to reduce bias caused by differences in genome size. The resulting length-normalized counts were then rescaled within each sample to a TPM-like scale by dividing each value by the total length-normalized counts and multiplying by one million. Taxon-level fungal abundances were calculated by summing the relative abundances of all species assigned to the corresponding taxon.
sections.statistical analyses and visualization: All statistical analyses were performed in R software version 4.1.2, and visualizations were generated using the ggplot2 package. Microbial diversity was assessed at the species level. Species richness was defined as the number of detected microbial species with relative abundance > 0 in each sample. Alpha diversity was evaluated using Shannon’s index calculated with the diversity function in the vegan package. Beta diversity was assessed using principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis dissimilarity matrices, and group differences were tested by permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) using the adonis2 function in the vegan package. Differential microbial signatures between CRC patients and healthy controls were identified separately within each of the 9 discovery cohorts using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. For fungal species, features with p < 0.05 and fold change (FC) > 1.2 were considered significant. For bacterial species, features with FDR-adjusted q < 0.05 and FC > 1.2 were retained. P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. To improve reproducibility across cohorts, only microbial species showing significant differential abundance in at least 3 cohorts were retained for downstream analyses. For meta-analysis, fungal relative abundances were first transformed using the arcsine square-root transformation. Differences between CRC patients and healthy controls were then summarized using Hedges’ g effect sizes calculated with the escalc function. Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q test and I² statistics with the rma function. Bacterial-fungal co-abundance relationships were evaluated using both Spearman correlation and SparCC analysis. For Spearman analysis, correlations with coefficient > 0.3 and q < 0.05 were considered significant. SparCC analysis [ 48 ] was performed on bacterial and fungal read count profiles using fastspar v0.0.10 with --iterations 20 [ 49 ]. Statistical significance was assessed using 1,000 bootstrap iterations, and correlations with coefficient > 0.3 and p < 0.05 were considered significant. CRC prediction models were constructed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and random forest (RF). Three validation strategies were applied: intra-cohort validation, cross-cohort validation, and leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation. For intra-cohort validation, 10 repeats of stratified 10-fold cross-validation were performed within each cohort, and feature selection was conducted strictly within the training folds. LASSO models were fitted using the cv.glmnet function with alpha = 1 and family = “binomial”, and the optimal λ was selected using lambda.min. RF models were trained with ntree = 999 and seed = 123. For cross-cohort validation, models were trained on one cohort and tested on another. For LOCO validation, models were trained on 8 cohorts and tested on the held-out cohort, with feature selection repeated within each training set. External validation was performed by training models on all 9 discovery cohorts and testing them on 6 independent validation cohorts. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) calculated with the pROC package. Feature importance was determined using permutation-based importance in RF models and coefficient magnitude in LASSO models.CRC prediction models were constructed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and random forest (RF).
