Though, baseline Faith was positively associated with 3-month Peace ( β = .32, p = .004), 3-month Peace was not significantly associated with 15-month PCS ( β = .11, p = .32). These effects remained nonsignificant when controlling for baseline Peace.
sections.discussion: This study examined how patient-reported spiritual well-being in newly diagnosed women with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy was associated with health-related QoL over 1 year. As 90% of the sample was within the first 6 weeks of initial cancer diagnosis, these results contribute to the literature by clarifying the longitudinal impact of spirituality during the challenging early treatment period including during chemotherapy. Consistent with hypotheses and extending the findings of prior cross-sectional research, this study found that greater faith at baseline was associated with higher levels of meaning and peace 3 months later, which in turn was associated with greater mental health-related QoL assessed 15 months after study entry. Additionally, meaning, but not peace, mediated the association between baseline faith and physical health-related QoL, consistent with previous research suggesting a stronger association between meaning and physical QoL (Peterman et al. 2014 ) and other studies suggesting that meaning is a particularly robust mediator (Canada et al. 2023 ). Thus, faith appears to be indirectly associated with subsequent health-related QoL via greater meaning and peace. Further, by controlling for baseline meaning in the model, we were able to demonstrate that the indirect association of faith on mental health-related QoL was also mediated by the change in meaning over time. In other words, greater faith was associated with an increase in meaning during active treatment, which led to greater mental health-related QoL 1 year later. These findings replicate and extend prior work by several researchers who have found faith to be indirectly associated with health-related QoL via meaning and peace in cross-sectional samples (Edmondson et al. 2008 ; Park et al. 2008 ; Canada et al. 2016 ; Merluzzi et al. 2023 ). For example, Canada et al. ( 2016 ) highlighted the indirect role of faith in promoting well-being through existential factors such as meaning and peace in a large cross-sectional sample of cancer survivors. Using the same sample, Canada et al. ( 2023 ) reported that the positive associations of religious service attendance and certainty regarding one’s belief in God with mental and physical health QoL were mediated by meaning, further suggesting that religious faith informs one’s meaning-making in difficult circumstance, which in turn influence QoL. Like the current study, peace was not found to be a mediator in Canada et al.’s study (Canada et al. 2023 ). Current results also align with Merluzzi et al. ( 2023 ), who found that surrendering control to a higher power – one specific aspect of faith – was indirectly associated with well-being through a combined meaning/peace variable in a cross-sectional sample of over 500 cancer survivors. The longitudinal nature of our study provides further evidence that one’s faith, or system of meaning, informs subsequent perceptions of meaning and peace, which in turn shape QoL. Examining the direct association between baseline faith and 15-month QoL was not the primary goal of this study, given existing evidence that faith has a weaker direct association with QoL relative to meaning or peace (Canada et al. 2016 ) and the theoretical and empirical rational for examining faith in conjunction with meaning and peace when considering QoL outcomes (Park 2013 ). Thus, it is not surprising that 3 of the 4 mediation models did not support a direct association between Faith and QoL. However, one model did suggest a surprising direct negative association between Faith and subsequent physical health-related QoL: greater baseline faith was associated with poorer physical health-related QoL in the model including Meaning as the mediator. This suggests that, when variance in physical health-related QoL explained by Meaning is accounted for, the association between Faith and physical health-related QoL may be negative. In other words, faith in the absence of meaning may be unhelpful in terms of physical QoL. It is possible that individuals with high faith but low meaning might experience more spiritual distress that would impede health-promoting behaviors. However, this finding needs to be interpreted with caution due to the exploratory nature of these analyses.
sections.limitations: Limitations of the current study are primarily related to selection of participants for the original Tibetan yoga study. The current sample was relatively financially wealthy, and greater income was associated with better mental and physical QoL. Older women and those with higher levels of education may be over-represented as they were more likely to provide complete self-report data in the parent study. This study also excluded women engaged in psychological treatment or support or who believed they needed psychological or psychiatric services. The current sample reported normative levels of QoL, particularly mental health-related QoL, which may also reflect selection bias for women who chose to join this study of a yoga intervention. It may have been more challenging to detect significant associations between aspects of spirituality and mental health-related QoL due to ceiling effects in this sample.
sections.implications and conclusions: This study suggests that faith, understood as strength and comfort in one’s beliefs in the face of adversity, may be an important precursor to spiritual peace and especially meaning, which demonstrates robust associations with better long-term mental and physical QoL. Importantly, participants in this study were newly diagnosed and undergoing active treatment, suggesting that spiritual resources at the outset of the cancer experience can impact later functioning. One recent study suggests that meaning changed the most over time among cancer survivors (compared to faith and peace) and was positively associated with social support and adaptive coping, suggesting that this is a malleable factor (Park et al. 2024 ). Clinicians working with this population may benefit from attending to patients’ spiritual needs early in care, particularly to foster meaning and peace. Psychological interventions such as Meaning-Centered Psychotherapy (MCP) may be particularly useful in helping patients reconnect with a sense of meaning during cancer treatment. MCP is a brief, structured, cancer-specific psychological intervention designed to address loss of meaning, identity, and purpose after cancer diagnosis. In fact, in writing about how MCP might be useful for breast cancer survivors, Lichtenthal et al. ( 2017 ) echoed the current findings: “meaning is hypothesized to be both an intermediary outcome (a construct to be enhanced in its own right) and a mediator, driving improvement in multiple psychological distress outcomes (e.g., by redirecting attention toward meaningful activities)” (p. 57). MCP is flexible, allowing individuals to integrate their own religious or spiritual beliefs into the therapeutic process. Other interventions that may help to bolster meaning in cancer include Dignity Therapy and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (Sauer et al. 2024 ; Seiler et al. 2024 ). Each of these interventions elicit the patient’s most important values and beliefs to encourage behaviors that are ultimately health-promoting. The current study builds on a substantial body of research suggesting that religion and strength or comfort in one’s faith work through intermediary constructs of meaning and peace to improve cancer patients’ QoL. Longitudinal studies are especially needed to examine how religiosity, spirituality, and meaning evolve over time, how best to intervene upon these constructs, and what impact such changes have on individuals with cancer, their families, and the healthcare teams who support them.

title: Balloon‐Expandable Versus Self‐Expanding Prostheses for Transcatheter Treatment of Patients With Low‐Flow, Low‐Gradient Aortic Stenosis
abstract: Background The use of balloon‐expandable valves (BEVs) or self‐expanding valves (SEVs) for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in patients with low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG‐AS) has been poorly investigated. Aim of this study is to evaluate the procedural and clinical outcomes of patients with severe low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR with current‐generation prostheses. Methods This registry‐based, multicenter, cohort study included consecutive patients with low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high‐volume Italian centers. The study population was divided into 2 groups according to the use of BEVs or SEVs. The primary outcome was all‐cause mortality up to 1 year. Results The study involved 1380 patients; 592 (42.9%) underwent TAVR with BEVs, and 788 (57.1%) with SEVs. At discharge, BEVs were linked to higher mean transvalvular gradients ( P <0.001) and a higher percentage of moderate predicted patient‐prosthesis mismatch ( P <0.001) compared with SEVs. After propensity score weighting, the Cox analysis showed no difference for the risk of the primary outcome (adjusted hazard ratio [HR]:1.23; 95% CI: 0.88–1.72), cardiovascular mortality (adjusted HR:1.37; 95% CI: 0.94–1.97), stroke (adjusted HR:1.83; 95% CI: 0.85–3.95), and myocardial infarction (adjusted HR:1.03; 95% CI: 0.40–2.69) between groups; however, the use of BEVs was associated with a significantly higher risk for HF hospitalization up to 1 year (adjusted HR: 1.54; 95% CI:1.05–2.25). Conclusions In this real‐world study on TAVR treatment for patients with low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis, there was no difference in mortality rates between BEVs and SEVs up to 1 year. However, the use of BEVs was linked to less favorable hemodynamic performance and a higher risk of HF hospitalization. Registration URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ ; Unique identifier: NCT06589063 .
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: Balloon‐expandable valves and self‐expanding valves have advantages and limitations that may influence the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement. However, comparative data between these 2 valve technologies in the high‐risk scenario of low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis are still limited. LOW‐transcatheter aortic valve replacement is the largest registry on patients with low‐flow, low‐gradient aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Absence of significant differences for the risk of all‐cause mortality was observed between the balloon‐expandable valves and self‐expanding valves up to 1 year. However, the use of balloon‐expandable valves was associated with less favorable hemodynamic performance and with a higher risk of heart failure hospitalization compared with self‐expanding valves.
sections.methods_1: Because of the sensitive nature of the data collected for this study, requests to access the data set from qualified researchers trained in human subject confidentiality protocols may be sent to University Study of Salerno at ggalasso@unisa.it .
sections.study population: This registry‐based, multicenter cohort study included patients with LFLG‐AS undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high‐volume Italian centers and enrolled in the LOW‐TAVR (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Severe Low Flow, Low Gradient Aortic Stenosis) registry. Patients were accepted as candidates for TAVR after the Heart Team's decision‐making process, based on comprehensive surgical risk, clinical, echocardiographic, and computed tomography assessments. For this study, the registry population was divided into 2 groups based on the use of SEV or BEV. Patients undergoing valve‐in‐valve procedures and those undergoing implantation of uncommon prostheses (fewer than 5 implants in the registry) were excluded.
sections.low \u2010 tavr registry: LOW‐TAVR is a real‐world, retrospective, and prospective multicenter Italian registry designed to evaluate the characteristics and clinical outcomes of patients with severe LFLG‐AS undergoing TAVR ( NCT06589063 ). The registry included all‐comers patients with a confirmed diagnosis of LFLG‐AS undergoing TAVR with implantation of current‐generation prostheses from January 2019. The list of devices implanted is reported in Table S1 . LFLG‐AS was defined by aortic valve area <1 cm 2 or an indexed aortic valve area ≤0.6 cm 2 /m 2 , mean transaortic gradient <40 mm Hg, and stroke volume index <36 mL/m 2 according to current guidelines. 1 LFLG‐AS was classified according to left ventricular ejection fraction values in classical (<50%) and paradoxical (≥50%) forms. Dobutamine stress echocardiography was systematically performed in patients with left ventricular ejection fraction <50% to exclude pseudo‐severe AS. Calcium volume assessment by computed tomography was also performed in patients with paradoxical LFLG‐AS to confirm the severity of AS. All patients underwent transthoracic echocardiography at hospital admission and before discharge. Patients were followed by clinical visits or phone contact at 1 and 12 months, and yearly thereafter. In‐hospital and follow‐up outcome measures were defined according to the Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC) 3 statement. 12 Study data were collected and managed using REDCap electronic data capture tools hosted at the Department of Medicine, Surgery, and Dentistry of the University of Salerno. Remote electronic data monitoring was systematically performed to search and actively correct missing and/or inconsistent information. The registry adheres to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The institutional review boards approved the protocol. All patients were informed about their participation in the registry and provided written informed consent.
sections.tavr planning, procedure, and pre\u2010d: A systematic preoperative work‐up was performed in patients with severe LFLG‐AS who were eligible for TAVR, including contrast‐enhanced computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and ilio‐femoral axes, using 64‐row or higher scans with cardiac cycle synchronization. The procedural planning, including arterial access approach, device type and size, pre‐dilation, and post‐dilation, was at the operator's discretion. Non‐femoral access was restricted to patients with complex ilio‐femoral anatomy and peripheral arterial disease, who were not amenable to conventional arterial access. Technical success was defined as freedom from mortality, successful arterial access, delivery of the device and retrieval of the delivery system, correct positioning of a single prosthetic heart valve into the proper anatomical location, and freedom from surgery or intervention related to the device or major vascular, access‐related, or cardiac structural complications. 12 Mean aortic valve gradient and the presence and severity of paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) by transthoracic echocardiography were systematically assessed before discharge. PVR was classified using a 5‐class grading scheme (from none/trace to severe) according to the VARC‐3 definition. 12 The predicted prosthesis‐patient mismatch (PPM) was evaluated using the effective orifice area (EOA) derived from the normal reference value for each model and size of prosthesis. 13 , 14 , 15 PPM was categorized as severe (<0.65 cm 2 /m 2 ) or moderate (>0.65–0.85 cm 2 /m 2 ) in the non‐obese population, and as severe (<0.55 cm 2 /m 2 ) or moderate (>0.55–0.70 cm 2 /m 2 ) in the obese population (body mass index >30 kg/m 2 ). 12
sections.study outcome measures: The primary outcome of this study was all‐cause death up to 1 year. The secondary outcomes were cardiovascular death, hospitalization for heart failure (HF), stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI). Other outcomes of interest included in‐hospital and 30‐day outcomes according to the VARC‐3 definitions.
sections.statistical analysis: Normally distributed variables were expressed as mean ± SD and variables with a skewed distribution were reported as median with interquartile range. Differences between groups were assessed using independent‐samples t tests with Welch correction. Categorical variables were compared with the Chi‐squared test, or Fisher exact test, as appropriate. Ordinal variables were compared with the Kendall's Tau‐c test. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) were also calculated to evaluate differences between groups independent of the sample size. SMD value >0.1 reflects the presence of potential imbalance between groups. Survival free from all‐cause death was displayed using Kaplan–Meier curves stratified for BEV or SEV. The unadjusted and adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for the outcomes of interest were calculated using the Cox proportional hazards regression model and reported as hazard ratios (HR) with their 95% CI. The proportional hazards assumption was verified by visually inspecting the log–log plots and with the Schoenfeld residuals test. Continuous covariates were modeled linearly, consistent with prior literature and clinical plausibility. Formal assessment of nonlinearity and interaction effects was not performed. We used the propensity score weighting (PSW) technique to account for potential selection bias in treatment assignment between the BEV and SEV groups. Inverse probability of treatment weights based on propensity scores were applied to estimate the average treatment effect, with extreme weights (at the 5th/95th percentile) trimmed to mitigate the influence of outliers. The PSW model was developed using a parsimonious approach, incorporating all baseline covariates significantly associated with the exposure and/or the primary outcome at univariable regression analysis, as well as variables considered clinically relevant in the context of TAVR. 16 Differences between the SEV and BEV groups before and after weighting were assessed using standardized mean differences (SMDs), a statistical measure that evaluates the magnitude of differences between 2 groups independently of the sample size. An SMD below 0.10, which reflects an optimal balance across all covariates included in the propensity score models, was achieved (Figure S1 ). A sensitivity analysis was conducted to further adjust for the pre‐discharge mean transvalvular aortic gradient and the presence of moderate or severe PPM. The consistency of the study results was assessed within patient subgroups with classical or paradoxical LFLG‐AS forms, according to prosthesis size (≤23 mm or >23 mm) and aortic valve area (≤430 mm 2 or >430 mm 2 ); the estimated interaction effect was expressed as P interaction . The rate of missing baseline values, if any, is shown in Table S2 . Missing data were handled using multiple imputations with the method of chained equations according to Rubin's rules. 17 For all tests, a P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.3.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and IBM SPSS Statistics (version 25).
sections.results_1: The study included 1380 patients (median age 83; 50.4% female); of these, 592 (42.9%) underwent TAVR using BEV, and 788 (57.1%) underwent TAVR using SEV (Table 1 ). The SEV group showed a higher percentage of women ( P =0.001) and a higher prevalence of history of pacemaker implantation ( P =0.033) than the BEV group. Conversely, the use of SEV was significantly lower in patients with diabetes ( P =0.024), atrial fibrillation ( P =0.001), and smokers ( P <0.001). European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II was significantly higher in the BEV than in the SEV group ( P <0.001). The mean aortic valve gradient was higher in patients treated with SEV ( P =0.014). No difference was reported regarding the other echocardiographic characteristics between groups. The use of pre‐dilation ( P <0.001) and post‐dilation ( P <0.001) was significantly higher in patients undergoing SEV implantation compared with BEV group. The percentage of VARC‐3 technical success was high (97.1%) and comparable between groups. The percentage of PVR was significantly higher in the SEV group ( P <0.001), but this result was related to the higher percentage of mild PVR. There was no significant difference in the percentage of mild–moderate or more severe PVR between groups (Figure 1 ). Patients who underwent TAVR with BEV showed a higher mean transvalvular gradient at discharge (10.6±4.7 versus 7.3±3.9, P <0.001). These results were confirmed in patients with prosthesis >23 mm (9.6±3.9 versus 6.9±3.4, P <0.001) and in those with prosthesis ≤23 mm (12.5±5.4 versus 10.6±6.4, P =0.034). In the BEV group, the measured EOA indexed at discharge was smaller than the predicted EOA indexed (1.47±0.49 versus 1.66±0.19, P <0.001); in the SEV group, the measured EOA indexed at discharge was lower than the predicted EOA indexed (1.84±0.63 versus 2.09±0.31, P <0.001). A higher percentage of moderate, but not of severe, predicted PPM was reported in the BEV group compared with the SEV group ( P <0.001; Figure 1 ). As expected, a higher percentage of moderate (29.4% versus 16.2%, P <0.001) and severe (25.7% versus 13.1%, P <0.001) measured PPM was reported in the BEV group compared with the SEV group. The rate of in‐hospital adverse events is reported in Table 2 . All‐cause death occurred in 19 (1.4%) patients, MI in 6 (0.4%), and transient ischemic attack/stroke in 20 (1.5%), with no significant differences between groups. Up to 30 days, VARC‐3 device success was reported in 90.8% of cases, with no significant differences between the BEV and SEV groups. Also, there was no significant difference in the percentages of all‐cause death, stroke, and MI between groups (Table 2 ). Up to 1 year (median 328 [106–365] days; complete 1‐year FU was available in 810 patients), the primary outcome was reported in 167 patients (Table 2 ). The unadjusted Cox regression analysis showed a significantly higher risk for the primary outcome (HR: 1.46; 95% CI: 1.08–1.98; Figure S2 ), cardiovascular death (HR: 1.58; 95% CI: 1.13–2.19), and HF hospitalization (HR: 1.77; 95% CI: 1.26–2.51) in the BEV group. No difference in the risk of stroke and MI between groups was observed. There were no violations of the proportional hazards assumption in the analyses for all the outcomes of interest. The PSW‐adjusted Cox regression analysis showed no significant difference in risk of the primary outcome (adjusted HR: 1.23; 95% CI: 0.88–1.72), cardiovascular death (adjusted HR: 1.37; 95% CI: 0.94–1.97), stroke (adjusted HR: 1.83; 95% CI: 0.85–3.95), and MI (adjusted HR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.40–2.69) up to 1 year between the BEV and SEV groups (Figure 2 ). Conversely, the risk for HF hospitalization was significantly higher in patients treated with BEVs compared with those treated with SEVs (adjusted HR: 1.54; 95% CI: 1.05–2.25). This result was confirmed after adjustment for the pre‐discharge mean transvalvular aortic gradient and the presence of moderate or severe PPM (adjusted HR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.02–2.29). Risk of adverse events based on PVR degree post‐TAVR is shown in Supplemental Table 3 , while the annual distribution of BEV and SEV implantations is presented in Supplemental Table 4 . The estimates for the risk of the primary and secondary outcomes were consistent in patients with classical and paradoxical LFLG‐AS forms, with no significant interaction between groups (Figure 3 ). In subgroup analyses stratified by prosthesis size and aortic valve area, the primary outcome was consistent between BEVs and SEVs, with no statistical interaction between subgroups. Among the secondary outcomes, a significantly higher risk of HF hospitalization up to 1 year was observed in the BEV group compared with the SEV group in patients undergoing implantation with a prosthesis >23 mm and in those with an aortic valve area >430 mm 2 (Figures S3 and S4 ).
sections.discussion: This is the first registry‐based, multicenter cohort study investigating the safety and effectiveness of current‐generation BEV and SEV prostheses in the high‐risk clinical scenario of patients with LFLG‐AS undergoing TAVR. The main findings of this study can be summarized as follows: BEVs and SEVs were both safe and effective, since they were associated with a high procedural success rate and with a low percentage of in‐hospital complications; At discharge, SEVs showed a lower mean transvalvular gradient and a lower percentage of moderate predicted PPM than BEVs. The use of SEVs was associated with a higher percentage of PVR than BEVs, but this difference was related to the higher percentage of mild PVR in the SEV group; After adjusting for potential confounders, the risk for the primary outcome up to 1 year was comparable between BEVs and SEVs groups; however, patients treated with BEV showed a higher risk of HF hospitalization up to 1 year; The primary and secondary outcome results were consistent in patients with classical and paradoxical LFLG‐AS forms, and in patients receiving prostheses ≤23 mm and >23 mm. Most of the evidence on procedural and long‐term outcomes of current‐generation TAVR prostheses comes from populations of patients with high‐gradient AS. 18 , 19 Many studies have confirmed the safety and efficacy profiles of both technologies, highlighting specific technical and hemodynamic features that guide the choice between them in everyday clinical practice. 7 , 8 However, translating existing knowledge from high‐gradient AS into the setting of LFLG‐AS may be challenging because of the high clinical risk profile and the “low‐flow state” of these patients. Our registry‐based study reported comparable percentages of VARC‐3 device success for both valve technologies and confirmed the rates of periprocedural and in‐hospital complications observed in the high‐gradient AS setting for BEVs and SEVs. 7 , 19 The use of SEVs resulted in a lower mean transvalvular gradient at discharge and a lower percentage of moderate predicted PPM compared with BEVs. The lower residual gradient after valve implantation in SEVs compared with BEVs is well established in previous studies on high‐gradient AS. 7 , 20 , 21 However, this is the first study confirming that the use of SEVs is associated with a lower mean transvalvular gradient compared with BEVs, even in the LFLG‐AS setting. This result may be related to multiple factors, including the supra‐annular design of most SEV technologies, SEV geometry, which increases the EOA and promotes a more laminar flow, and the more frequent use of BEVs in small annuli. 19 , 22 , 23 In this study, the PPM was estimated using the predicted EOA according to the prosthesis model and size, and then classified according to the patient's body surface area. 13 , 14 , 15 The use of predicted EOA over the EOA measured by Doppler echocardiography was preferred in this LFLG‐AS population, since the low‐flow state can determine incomplete opening of the prosthetic leaflets. Thus, the measured EOA may be lower than in patients with normal‐flow conditions, potentially leading to the overestimation of PPM (pseudo‐PPM). 14 In a previous study including 1088 patients, the use of predicted EOA reclassified the majority of patients with PPM to no PPM following TAVR, particularly in those with a low‐flow state. Also, the predicted PPM had a stronger association with clinical outcomes and was less affected by the variability of the PPM measured by TTE. 14 We also reported a higher percentage of PVR after TAVR in the SEV than in the BEV groups. This difference, however, was related to the higher percentage of mild PVR in SEVs; mild‐to‐moderate or more severe PVR, which have been associated with a negative prognostic impact, were comparable between groups. 24 This result is consistent with recent studies evaluating PVR in patients with high‐gradient AS undergoing TAVR with current‐generation prostheses. 8 , 25 , 26 The primary finding of this study is the absence of a statistically significant difference in the risk of all‐cause mortality between patients treated with BEVs and those receiving SEVs. This result is consistent with prior evidence on patients with high‐gradient AS undergoing TAVR, reporting comparable survival outcomes between these prosthesis technologies. 18 , 19 , 27 , 28 We also report a significantly higher risk of HF hospitalization in the BEV compared with the SEV group, which was not previously described in the high‐gradient AS setting. 18 , 19 , 27 The higher residual transvalvular gradients and the higher prevalence of moderate PPM could partially explain the higher risk of HF hospitalization observed in the BEV group. LFLG‐AS is characterized by a more advanced cardiac damage than high‐gradient AS and by a “low‐flow state”, which is the low forward output from the left ventricle secondary to afterload mismatch, impaired myocardial contractility, and restrictive physiology. In addition, patients with LFLG‐AS have more comorbidities, a worse clinical status, and increased fragility than patients with high‐gradient AS. 5 , 6 , 11 , 29 In this high‐risk population undergoing TAVR, we hypothesize that the residual pressure overload associated with the use of BEVs may lead to persistently elevated left ventricular wall stress, resulting in increased myocardial work and impaired perfusion of the subendocardial layers. These mechanisms may determine myocardial fibrosis and unfavorable left ventricular remodeling, resulting in a higher incidence of HF hospitalizations. Notably, the outcome results were consistent across patients' subgroups with classical and paradoxical LFLG‐AS forms, as well as across subgroups stratified by prosthesis size and aortic valve area, confirming the absence of a modification effect of these conditions on the study results.
sections.study limitations: Our results should be interpreted considering certain limitations. Although we performed a PSW Cox analysis to account for baseline patient‐related characteristics, we cannot exclude a residual selection bias secondary to other concealed confounders. The LOW‐TAVR protocol does not include systematic verification of echocardiographic measurements in a core laboratory. However, this study evaluated parameters commonly used in clinical practice, particularly in high‐volume TAVR centers, and our echocardiographic findings are consistent with previous studies on LFLG‐AS. 5 , 11 This study does not provide echocardiographic information during follow‐up, including stroke volume and measured PPM, as this information is not mandatory in the LOW‐TAVR registry and was not systematically collected. However, this study was not designed to assess echocardiographic changes after TAVR, but to investigate clinical outcomes in patients undergoing TAVR with different prosthesis technologies. There is concern about discordance between echocardiographic and invasive mean gradients after TAVR. 30 However, invasive hemodynamic parameters were not systematically collected and could not be used for the aim of the present analysis. Although this study represents the largest investigation of this topic to date, it may not have sufficient statistical power to evaluate differences in outcomes across subgroups with paradoxical or classical LFLG‐AS forms. The follow‐up period of 1 year may have limited the study's ability to assess the association between the exposure and clinical outcomes. Also, our registry did not allow outcome analysis for patients stratified by prosthetic type (models and manufacturers) because of the sample's over‐fragmentation.
sections.conclusions_1: This study, which included the largest real‐world population with LFLG‐AS undergoing TAVR, confirmed that both current‐generation SEVs and BEVs are safe and effective, as they were associated with a low percentage of procedural and in‐hospital complications and a high percentage of device success. Although the risk for all‐cause mortality was not significantly different between BEVs and SEVs groups, the use of BEVs was associated with a higher incidence of HF hospitalization up to 1 year. The more favorable hemodynamic performance of SEVs compared with BEVs, in terms of mean transvalvular gradient and predicted PPM, might partially explain this result in this high‐risk TAVR population. This observational evidence requires confirmation through large, randomized studies.
