title: The Importance of Achieving High Treatment Targets in Atopic Dermatitis: A Narrative Review
abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is associated with a significant physical, psychological, social and economic burden and a decreased quality of life. There is a relationship between disease burden and the level of disease severity and control. The burden of AD largely depends on skin lesions, itch and sleep disturbances, although other aspects also play a role. Even though treat-to-target approaches have been proposed for AD in recent years, studies showed that many patients with AD continue to perceive disease burden despite the achievement of the established treatment targets. This prompted the conception of the Aiming High in Eczema/Atopic Dermatitis (AHEAD) recommendations, which included novel optimal targets for both clinician- and patient-reported outcomes, the achievement of which is defined as minimal disease activity or MDA. This narrative review appraises studies that show that the achievement of elevated treatment targets results in multiple benefits. Aiming high helps to achieve more in patients with AD.

sections.key summary points: Atopic dermatitis (AD) causes considerable physical, psychological, social and economic burdens, affecting the quality of life of patients with AD. A relationship exists between disease burden and its severity and control. Setting ambitious goals has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with AD.
sections.introduction: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is the most common inflammatory skin disorder, affecting up to one-fifth of the global population [ 1 ], with over 200 million people currently suffering from it [ 2 ]. Amongst skin conditions, AD tops the statistics of non-fatal years lived with disability [ 3 ] with an increasing prevalence, especially in high-income countries [ 4 , 5 ]. In a cross-sectional study, the point prevalence of AD in the adult population in the EU was 4.4% [ 6 ]. A systematic review of incidence and prevalence data in Europe suggested that, compared to the twentieth century, there has been an increase in both parameters in the twenty-first century; however, this was confirmed by several but not all studies [ 7 ]. AD is a heterogeneous condition that can manifest itself with varying degrees of severity, ranging from mild to severe. More than 60 scoring systems have been developed to assess the severity of the disease. The assessment is based on the intensity and extent of lesions and symptoms (e.g. itch). Scoring atopic dermatitis (SCORAD), Investigator Global Assessment (IGA) and Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) are the most commonly used scoring systems in AD [ 8 ]. The same scores are used to assess the response to treatment, and in clinical trials, EASI improvement is the preferred clinician-reported outcome (CRO) measure. The subjective burden of AD is better reflected by patient-reported outcomes (PRO) including Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure (POEM), Patient-Oriented Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (PO-SCORAD), numerical rating scale (NRS)-itch, numerical rating scale (NRS)-sleep and quality of life scores such as Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI). Mental health is frequently assessed through the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) [ 8 , 9 ]. The care plan for adults affected by AD is stepwise and depends on the severity of the disease [ 10 ]. The emergence of new innovative treatments in the past 10 years has resulted in improved treatment outcomes. This article reviews the burden of disease in AD and explores the concept that the achievement of high treatment targets can result in important benefits for the patient.
sections.materials and methods: We performed a non-systematic literature search using the advanced search builder in PubMed for either “atopic dermatitis” or “atopic eczema”, combined with the following terms: “burden”, “treat-to-target”, “minimal disease activity”, and “EASI90” in the Title/Abstract field, as well as “itch” in the Title field only. The searches were limited to the 2015–2025 decade and only records in English were considered. Both original articles and reviews were considered. Further relevant references were identified through both bibliographic mining and forward citation searching.
sections.ethical approval: Ethical approval was not applicable as this article is based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors.
sections.disease burden: AD is associated with a significant physical, psychological, social and economic burden and a decreased quality of life [ 11 – 16 ]. From the physical point of view, the burdensomeness of AD largely depends on skin manifestations of the disease, such as skin redness, eczematous lesions, flaking/scaling and related symptoms (itch and pain) [ 16 – 18 ]. In a recent study of 88 patients with AD, over 75% of them experienced itch, skin redness, and dry and flaky skin every 1–3 days [ 17 ]. Disease flares worsen the burden of AD, and severe disease is associated with a higher number of flares than mild AD [ 14 ]. Patients experiencing both itch and skin pain had more body areas affected and were more bothered by their symptoms than those without; they also reported worse daily work impairment, sleep disruption and diminished quality of life [ 18 ]. Sleep disturbances, due to itching, are an important part of disease burden in AD and the most common sleep problems in adults with AD are difficulty in falling asleep, frequent nighttime awakenings and consequently daytime sleepiness [ 19 , 20 ]. The relationship between AD and sleep is bidirectional as a vicious circle exists [ 19 ]: patients with more severe disease take longer to fall asleep and report a higher number nights out of previous 7 nights with sleep disturbances than individuals with mild disease [ 14 ]. Using appropriate moisturisers, cleansing routines and fabric selection can impact the burden of skin symptoms [ 21 , 22 ]. Physical burden of AD is also linked to the fact that the disease is associated with multiple, atopic and non-atopic, comorbidities. Amongst others, the atopic comorbidities include asthma, rhinitis, conjunctivitis and food allergy, whereas non-atopic comorbidities such as autoimmune, cardiovascular, endocrine, infectious, ocular, psychiatric diseases and certain cancers have been reported [ 23 ]. The comorbidities and their pathophysiological relationship with AD are reviewed elsewhere [ 23 , 24 ]. Psychology-wise, patients with AD, especially those with inadequately controlled disease, have higher levels of anxiety and depression than matched controls from the general population as shown by a study conducted on 1860 patients with AD in Europe [ 25 ]. Almost 80% of patients with AD suffered from mood changes and this is percentage was higher (94%) at worst point of AD, whereas mood changes were associated with time spent managing AD and the severity of AD [ 13 ]. More severe disease was associated with lower mental health scores in the short form (SF)-12 health survey (which consists of 12 questions covering physical functioning and social functioning, emotional and mental health [ 26 ]) and lower HADS scores [ 14 , 16 ]. Several mechanisms affect the link between AD and mental health, such as poorly controlled AD, sleep disturbances, itch, inflammation and coping patterns [ 27 ]. Relevant associations between depressive symptoms, fatigue and work productivity highlight the disease burden caused by the psychological components of AD. In fact, productivity loss was strongly associated with depressive symptoms ( r = 0.68) and fatigue ( r = 0.60) [ 28 ]. In addition, about 25% of patients with moderate-to-severe AD are affected by alcohol use disorder [ 29 ]. This again can create a vicious circle, as smoking and excessive alcohol consumption negatively impact AD [ 30 ]. Regarding the social aspects of the disease, inclusive of relationships and sex life, there are no conclusive data. Some studies suggested that the relationships were not affected, one stated that sexual dysfunction remained little explored, and another study found that AD disrupted sexual function, and lowered libido and reproductive desire of women [ 31 – 34 ]. The disease affects other family members and patients and family members deal with time-consuming treatment regimens, dietary requirements and household changes [ 35 , 36 ]. There is a dearth of data on the families of adults with AD as most studies were conducted in paediatric patients and their families [ 35 ]. In a population-based cross-sectional study, AD was shown to limit lifestyle (51.3%), lead to avoidance of social interaction (39.1%) and impact activities (43.3%) [ 16 ]. Even patients with mild AD reported lifestyle limitations and avoidance of social interactions, although more severe disease results in a higher level of activity impairment [ 14 , 16 ]. As a result, a significantly higher proportion of patients with AD are very dissatisfied with life (crude OR 2.22 (1.45–3.40); p = 0.0006) [ 16 ]. Regarding the economic burden, a systematic review of 22 unique studies showed that total costs of AD reach over €20,000 per person per year in patients with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe disease [ 37 ]. Both direct (expenditures on prescription medicines, hospitalisations, and visits to healthcare providers) and indirect (absenteeism and presenteeism, career modification, and reduced quality of life) costs contribute to these spendings [ 37 , 38 ]. In Europe, moderate-to-severe AD resulted in significant indirect (up to €14,000 per patient per year) and direct (up to €7000 per patient per year) costs as documented by a study in France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK [ 39 ]. Regarding the healthcare utilisation, one study showed that 21.6% of patients with AD and 37.9% of patients with inadequately controlled AD reported at least one emergency department visit in the previous 6 months versus 16.5% of controls without AD, and 93.1% of patients with AD versus 84.2% of those without AD had at least one clinician visit (both p < 0.001) [ 40 ]. Similarly, another study showed that patients with severe disease (determined by the EASI score) required more healthcare or acute care visits than patients with clear skin in the previous 6 months (6.6 vs. 3.7) [ 14 ]. Together, these data show that disease control is a way of reducing healthcare utilisation. Also in a study that analysed Medicare insured adults, patients with AD showed greater utilisation of outpatient services, outpatient pharmacy services and short-term disability benefits than individuals in the control group without AD [ 41 ]. AD has a negative impact on work productivity and can be linked to bulling and discrimination [ 14 , 28 , 42 , 43 ]. On average, estimated absenteeism and presenteeism in workers with AD were 10.9 days/year and 13.1 days/year respectively [ 43 ]. Stratifying the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) scores according to the EASI score severity strata, Eyerich et al. showed that compared to mild disease, severe AD was associated with higher percentages of absenteeism (4.3% vs. 15.6%), presenteeism (19.8% vs. 40.6%), overall productivity impairment (22.5% vs. 44.9%) and hours missed from work (1.5 h vs. 6.1 h) (all p < 0.0001) with values for moderate AD falling between those seen in mild and severe disease [ 14 ]. Absenteeism and presenteeism were more pronounced in individuals who experienced discrimination, with 33.9% of workers with AD feeling discriminated against due to their disease [ 43 ]. Patients with AD and high levels of embarrassment and those on systemic therapy miss approximately 1.5 more days at work than those who perceive no embarrassment [ 44 ]. Some people may need to change type of work because of their AD and jobs in healthcare, catering, cleaning, hairdressing and car repair should be avoided [ 35 ]. Thus, as mentioned for the individual domains, there is a relationship between disease burden and the level of disease severity and control. Indeed, adults with AD report a substantial burden in multiple domains that are significantly higher in individuals with severe disease and poorly controlled [ 14 , 40 , 45 ]. Also, the severity of AD and the use of topical treatments, the frequency and the amount of time spent managing symptoms showed strong associations with the burden of the disease and decreased quality of life [ 13 , 46 ]. Interestingly, the highest disease burden was reported in geographic clusters including those with the lowest use of systemic therapies [ 14 ]. Many patients feel that physicians, mainly the non-dermatologists, underestimate the burden of their disease and erroneously treat AD as a skin condition only [ 17 ]. Individual disease burden should be gauged to deliver the most appropriate treatments that fulfil the patient’s needs and expectations [ 47 ]. Taken together, we can state that AD poses a considerable burden that extends beyond physical symptoms, significantly impacting patients’ emotional wellbeing, social interactions and economic stability. Addressing this burden requires comprehensive strategies that encompass clinical management, psychological support and economic considerations [ 37 ].
sections.benefits of elevated treatment targets: The identification of AD’s “treatable traits” in 2020 by the European Task Force on Atopic Dermatitis was important for the future implementation of the treat-to-target approach in AD. Treatable traits must be clinically relevant, identifiable and measurable. The Task Force survey established that itch, skin lesions and sleep problems were the top-ranking treatable traits in AD [ 48 ]. Subsequently, the International Steering Committee produced, through an eDelphi process, a treat-to-target framework for shared decision-making on systemic treatment continuation, modification or discontinuation in AD. Three-month and 6-month treatment target goals were proposed for five disease scores: EASI (EASI50 at 3 months and EASI75 or EASI ≤ 7 at 6 months), SCORAD (SCORAD50 at 3 months and SCORAD75 or SCORAD ≤ 24 at 6 months), Worst-Pruritus-NRS (WP-NRS) (WP-NRS reduction of at least 3 points at 3 months and absolute score ≤ 4 at 6 months), DLQI (a reduction of at least 4 points at 3 months with an absolute DLQI ≤ 5) and POEM (absolute POEM ≤ 7 at 6 months). Moreover, 3- and 6-month targets for the Patient self-reported Global Assessment of disease severity (PtGA) were introduced to assess the patient’s broad perception of AD activity. According to this algorithm, if the PtGA target plus at least one disease domain target are achieved, treatment can be continued. Otherwise, treatment modification should be taken into consideration [ 45 ]. This framework was later adapted for local settings, e.g. Italy or Canada [ 49 , 50 ]. Despite the advancements in defining treatment targets, a post hoc analysis of the MEASURE-AD study showed that approximately 45% of 1434 adults with AD who were candidates/received systemic therapy and met more than one 6-month treatment target (as defined by [ 45 ]) continued to have a moderate or severe disease activity, in terms of EASI, SCORAD, WP-NRS, POEM and DLQI [ 51 ]. This analysis suggested that the treatment targets mentioned above may not be high enough to provide a real benefit for the patients and prompted the conception of the Aiming High in Eczema/Atopic Dermatitis (AHEAD) recommendations that established a novel approach to AD management combining shared decision-making with the concept of minimal disease activity (MDA) [ 52 ]. The AHEAD recommendations introduced moderate and optimal targets for CROs (EASI, SCORAD, IGA and BGA) and PROs (NRS, POEM, HADS, DLQI). MDA was defined as the simultaneous achievement of at least one CRO and one PRO optimal target (see Fig. 1 for optimal targets) [ 52 ]. Fig. 1 Summary of the optimal treatment targets according to AHEAD recommendations [ 52 ]. AHEAD Aiming High in Eczema/Atopic Dermatitis, BSA body surface area, DLQI Dermatology Life Quality Index, CRO clinician-reported outcomes, EASI Eczema Area and Severity Index, EASI75/90 75%/90% improvement in EASI, HADS-A Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety, HADS-D Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Depression, IGA Investigator’s Global Assessment, NRS Numeric Rating Scale, POEM Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure, PRO patient-reported outcomes, SCORAD SCORing Atopic Dermatitis, SCORAD75 75% improvement in SCORAD, WP worst pruritus Interestingly, a post hoc analysis of three clinical trials (i.e. Measure Up 1, Measure Up 2, and AD Up) showed that greater degrees of clinical responses were linked to more robust improvements in multiple dimensions impacted by AD, such as skin pain, sleep, anxiety, depression and DLQI, in a stepwise pattern. Indeed, improvements and response rates for both CROs and PROs were higher in the subgroup of patients who simultaneously achieved EASI90 and WP-NRS 0/1, i.e. the MDA, compared to patients achieving EASI90 alone or WP-NRS 0/1 alone. For example, the percentage of patients achieving DLQI 0–1, which means no impact on quality of life, was 18% for those who reached EASI90 but not WP-NRS 0/1, 40% for those who reached WP-NRS 0/1 but not EASI90, and 73% for those who reached both EASI90 and WP-NRS 0/1 [ 53 ]. It should be underlined that this combined endpoint was first used in the Level Up study, which confirmed superiority of upadacitinib over dupilumab in the treatment of moderate-to-severe AD measured as simultaneous achievement of EASI90 and WP-NRS 0/1 at week 16 [ 54 ]. Moreover, patients who achieved optimal treatment targets, compared to individuals who achieved moderate or no treatment targets, had greater improvements in health-related quality of life. Also, patients who achieved MDA more frequently reported improvements in health-related quality of life than patient who achieved only optimal CRO targets or optimal PRO targets [ 55 ]. The analysis of the TARGET-DERM AD registry data demonstrating that achieving optimal treatment targets for both itch resolution and skin clearance markedly enhances patient-reported AD outcomes further substantiates the importance of achieving higher outcomes. In that study of 1920 patients with AD, the odds ratios of achieving ideal PROs (POEM 0–2, Sleep-NRS 0/1, and Pain-NRS 0/1, DLQI 0/1) were the highest in patients who simultaneously achieved optimal targets for skin clearance (IGA 0/1) and itch resolution (WP-NRS 0/1) [ 56 ]. Thus, the study confirmed the validity of the AHEAD recommendations and the importance of aiming for higher treatment targets.
sections.conclusions: Considerable progress has been made in understanding the pathophysiology of AD, and these insights have led to the development of innovative therapies. Despite these advances, patients still do not experience complete benefit from treatment. Increasing evidence suggests that achieving higher treatment goals yields greater advantages for patients. Achieving near or total clearance of skin lesions and relief from itching, i.e. the MDA, is linked to significant improvement across all aspects of the disease, including sleep disturbances, skin pain and overall quality of life. This comprehensive burden reduction is an outcome all dermatologists should aim for. Nevertheless, achieving MDA in routine clinical practice remains challenging, as access to both prescription and over-the-counter therapies varies across countries of residence. Such disparities frequently persist irrespective of medication cost or reimbursement eligibility.

title: Seed priming with melatonin enhances salt stress tolerance in triticale through coordinated regulation of antioxidant defense, osmotic homeostasis, and phytohormone signaling
abstract: Background Seed germination and early seedling establishment in triticale ( ×Triticosecale Wittmack ) are highly vulnerable to salinity stress. Seed priming has emerged as a potent and cost-effective strategy to enhance salt tolerance during these critical developmental stages. However, the physiological mechanisms through which melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine, MT) priming alleviates salt stress in triticale remain poorly understood. Methods In this study, four treatments were applied: CK (control), MT (melatonin priming without salt stress), S (non-primed seeds under salt stress), and MS (melatonin-primed seeds under salt stress). We comprehensively assessed the effects of MT priming on seed germination, seedling growth, photosynthetic performance, and key physiological indicators under saline conditions. Result The results revealed that MT priming significantly increased the germination rate by 26.87% compared to non-primed seeds under salt stress. Moreover, seedling height and fresh weight in the MS treatment were significantly higher by 3.86% and 36.00%, respectively, than those in the S group. These enhancements were attributed to the upregulation of antioxidant enzyme activities, including superoxide dismutase and peroxidase, which effectively reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation and mitigated oxidative damage. Additionally, MT priming improved Na⁺/K⁺ homeostasis and stimulated the biosynthesis of osmoregulatory compounds such as soluble sugars and proteins. Notably, MT application also increased endogenous gibberellin levels while reducing abscisic acid content in both seeds and seedlings under salt stress. Conclusion Melatonin alleviates the detrimental effects of salt stress on seed germination and seedling growth in triticale by modulating antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and hormonal homeostasis.

sections.introduction: As the starting point of plant growth and development, seed germination quality and seedling establishment directly determine the subsequent growth and development of crops and the final yield [ 1 , 2 ], which is the basis of agricultural production ‘complete, complete and strong seedlings’. At present, the problem of soil salinization is prominent [ 3 ], 50% of cultivated land is affected by soil salinity [ 4 ], and the stage of seed germination and seedling establishment is the most sensitive period to salt in the whole growth cycle of crops [ 5 ]. Salt stress inhibits crop germination and growth through a variety of ways. First of all, salt stress interferes with the absorption process of water by plants, resulting in a series of physiological and structural changes in seeds, which is the fundamental reason for the decrease of seed germination rate [ 6 ]. High concentration of salt can significantly delay the seed germination time, prolong the germination cycle, reduce the germination rate, and seriously hinder the seedling establishment. Salt stress will not only cause osmotic stress and ion toxicity, but also induce excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), causing oxidative damage. Excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species will destroy the structure of cell membrane, resulting in increased permeability of cell membrane, and interfere with normal physiological and metabolic processes such as plant photosynthesis and hormone balance, and ultimately inhibit plant growth and development [ 7 , 8 ]. Therefore, how to maintain the healthy growth of plants and slow down the inhibition of salt stress on crop growth and development is of great significance to ensure the high and stable yield of crops. Triticale ( × Triticosecale Wittmack ) is an artificially synthesized crop by hybridization of wheat ( Triticum ) and rye ( Secale ) and chromosome doubling [ 9 ]. It contains the advantages of both parents, and has the characteristics of strong resistance, high yield and wide adaptability [ 10 – 13 ], and has good feeding quality, which plays an important role in agriculture, food and feed. Triticale itself has a certain salt-tolerant ability and has become an important crop for saline-alkali land improvement. However, salt stress still significantly inhibits seed germination [ 14 ], destroys the chloroplast structure at the seedling stage, reduces photosynthetic performance, and then reduces dry matter accumulation [ 15 , 16 ], forming growth inhibition, which in turn leads to a decrease in forage yield. Therefore, it is of great significance to explore efficient and feasible salt stress mitigation measures to promote the popularization and planting of triticale in saline-alkali areas. Seed priming technology is an effective strategy to alleviate crop stress and improve seed resistance [ 17 – 19 ]. By precisely controlling water and temperature conditions, this technology enables seeds to absorb water in advance before germination, initiates the process of physiological and biochemical metabolism in the early stage of germination, and then ensures the orderly germination of seeds, improves the quality of seed germination [ 20 , 21 ], and enhances the antioxidant capacity of seeds during germination and seedling growth [ 22 , 23 ]. Seed priming technology can improve the germination rate of seeds under suitable environment and adversity conditions, and the promotion effect under adversity conditions is more significant [ 24 ]. At present, a variety of substances have been used for seed priming research. For example, gibberellin (GA 3 ) priming can improve seed germination performance and seedling establishment process under salt stress by regulating ABA catabolism [ 25 , 26 ]. Priming with β-aminobutyric acid (BABA) can promote the accumulation of proline, total carbohydrates, total protein and nitrate reductase, and enhance the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD) and guaiacol peroxidase, thereby increasing the photosynthetic rate of mung bean seedlings under salt stress and reducing malondialdehyde content [ 27 ]. Compared with the above trigger substances, melatonin (MT), as a new type of plant signal molecule, has shown unique advantages in enhancing salt tolerance of cereal crops in recent years, providing a new idea for salt stress relief. Melatonin can help plants resist various environmental stresses by scavenging excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), regulating plant hormone balance, and activating stress-related gene expression. Studies have shown that melatonin plays a key role in hormone-regulated species: under salt stress, melatonin effectively enhances the salt tolerance of cotton by promoting the accumulation of auxin and gibberellin, reducing the content of ABA, and activating the defense signals of salicylic acid and jasmonic acid [ 28 ]. In addition, MT priming can up-regulate the expression of OPR, a key enzyme in jasmonic acid synthesis, and promote the synthesis of jasmonic acid (JA), thereby reducing oxidative damage, which is manifested as increased seed germination rate, robust seedling growth, and enhanced antioxidant capacity [ 29 ]. In terms of salt tolerance of grains, the positive effect of MT priming has been confirmed: after MT priming, the germination potential and germination rate of wheat seeds under salt stress were significantly increased, and the amylase activity was enhanced, thereby reducing the inhibition of salt stress on seed germination. At the same time, melatonin priming can also improve the salt tolerance of maize [ 30 ]and wheat [ 31 ]seedlings by strong antioxidant enzyme activity and scavenging reactive oxygen species. In addition, under drought stress, MT priming can enhance the ability of triticale to scavenge reactive oxygen species, increase energy supply and antioxidant enzyme activity, and effectively alleviate the adverse effects of drought stress [ 32 ]. The above studies have shown that MT initiation has broad application potential in enhancing crop stress resistance through multi-channel synergy. At present, the mechanism of MT as a plant growth regulator in regulating plant abiotic stress has been widely confirmed, but the research on the regulation mechanism of MT seed priming technology on triticale seed germination and seedling establishment under salt stress is still obviously insufficient. Based on this, this study used triticale as the research object to explore the mechanism of melatonin seed priming alleviating salt stress on triticale seed germination and seedling growth. This study mainly solves the following key scientific problems: (1) Screening the optimal concentration of MT priming to alleviate the germination of triticale seeds under salt stress; (2) The regulation mechanism of MT priming on antioxidant system and osmotic adjustment substances in triticale seedlings under salt stress was revealed. (3) Regulation of MT priming on endogenous hormone content in triticale seeds and seedlings under salt stress. In this study, the synergistic pathway of ‘antioxidant defense-osmotic regulation-hormone regulation’ mediated by MT was systematically analyzed, and the physiological mechanism of MT-induced regulation of salt tolerance of triticale was elucidated, which provided theoretical basis and practical reference for saline soil cultivation.
sections.experimental design: The experiment was carried out between October and December 2023 under controlled laboratory conditions at Hebei Agricultural University. Triticale seeds (cultivar ‘Jisi No. 2’) were kindly provided by the Dryland Farming Institute of the Hebei Academy of Agriculture and Forestry Sciences. Melatonin (MT, purity ≥ 98%) was sourced from Sigma-Aldrich (USA).
sections.screening of the optimal mt concentratio: Uniform and plump triticale seeds were surface-sterilized with 75% (v/v) ethanol for 10 min, followed by thorough rinsing with distilled water to remove all residual ethanol. The seeds were then immersed in different concentrations of MT solutions—10, 20, 50, 100, and 200 µM (designated as MT10, MT20, MT50, MT100, and MT200, respectively)—at a seed-to-solution ratio of 1:5 (w/v). Priming was conducted at 15 °C for 12 h in darkness, with a non-primed group serving as the control. After treatment, the seeds were rinsed three times with distilled water, air-dried at 25 °C until their original weight was restored, and stored at 4 °C for further use. The selection of melatonin concentrations was based on the effective concentration ranges reported in relevant studies on melatonin treatment for stress resistance in monocotyledonous plants. The concentration gradients set in this experiment covered low, optimal, and high concentrations [ 24 , 32 ]. The primed seeds were evenly distributed on moist qualitative filter paper in 15-cm Petri dishes, with 30 seeds per dish. Each dish was treated with 10 mL of either 100 mM NaCl solution (salt stress group) or distilled water (control group), following the method described by Fu, et al. [ 31 ]. The seeds were then incubated in darkness at 25 ℃ for 7 days under a constant humidity of 80%. The optimal MT concentration for priming was determined based on measurements of germination potential and germination rate. Five biological replicates were set for the seed germination experiment, and three biological replicates with one technical replicate for the seedling growth experiment. All experiments were performed independently and repeated, and conducted in a greenhouse with strictly consistent experimental conditions to ensure the reliability of the results.
sections.seed germination experiment: Four experimental treatments were established as follows: non-primed seeds irrigated with water (CK), seeds primed with 50 µM MT (the optimized concentration determined previously) and irrigated with water (MT), non-primed seeds irrigated with 100 mM NaCl solution (S), and seeds primed with 50 µM MT and irrigated with 100 mM NaCl solution (MS). All cultivation conditions were maintained as described in Section  " Screening of the Optimal MT Concentration for Seed Priming ". Radicle length, germ length, and fresh weight of the seeds were measured on the 3 rd and 7 th days after treatment initiation, with five biological replicates per treatment.
sections.seedling growth experiment: Salt treatment was initiated when the plants reached the two-leaf one-heart stage. Four treatments were applied: non-primed seeds irrigated with water (CK), seeds primed with 50 µM MT (the previously determined optimal concentration) and irrigated with water (MT), non-primed seeds irrigated with 100 mM NaCl solution (S), and MT-primed seeds irrigated with 100 mM NaCl solution (MS). The seed priming protocol followed the same method as described for the germination experiment. Seeds exhibiting uniform radicle emergence were selected and sown in cultivation pots (36 cm × 24 cm) filled with 4 L of water, with 60 seeds per pot and three biological replicates per treatment. Light conditions during seedling growth: photoperiod 14 h/10 h (day/night), light intensity 600 µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹, ambient temperature 27 ℃/23 ℃, relative humidity 75%, with 1 h of aeration per day. Photosynthetic and physiological traits were measured on days 0, 5, and 10 of salt stress, with three replicates per treatment.
sections.morphology and biomass measurement: In the seedling growth experiment, three representative plants were selected for analysis on days 0, 5, and 10 following salt stress treatment. Plant height was measured using a standard ruler. Subsequently, the plants were oven-dried at 105 °C for 30 min and then at 80 °C until a constant weight was achieved to determine dry biomass. The root systems were carefully spread on a scanning tray and scanned using an EPSON Perfection V700 scanner (Epson, Suwa, Japan) at a resolution of 600 dpi. The resulting images were analyzed with WinRHIZO root analysis software (Regent Instruments Inc., Quebec City, Canada) to quantify total root length (cm), root surface area (cm²), root volume (cm 3 ), and average root diameter (mm).
sections.determination of photosynthetic paramete: In the seedling growth experiment, the total photosynthetic pigment content and net photosynthetic rate of the leaves were determined. Approximately 0.1 g of functional leaf samples was immersed in 10 mL of 95% ethanol and extracted in darkness for 24–48 h. Absorbance at wavelengths of 665, 649, and 470 nm was measured using a UV-2450 spectrophotometer (Shimadzu Corporation, Kyoto, Japan). The total photosynthetic pigment content was calculated based on the formula described by Liao, et al. [ 34 ]. The net photosynthetic rate was measured on the penultimate fully expanded leaf of triticale using a LI-6400XT portable photosynthesis system (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). Measurements were conducted under a photosynthetic photon flux density of 500 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and a CO₂ concentration of 400 µmol mol⁻¹.
sections.determination of physiological index: In the seed germination experiment, the activities of α-amylase and β-amylase were assayed using commercial kits from the Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (catalog numbers: C016-1-2 and C016-2-1, respectively). The contents of auxin (IAA), GA₃, and ABA were quantified using ELISA kits provided by Enzyme-Linked Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (catalog numbers: ml147100, ml072782, and ml077235, respectively). During the seedling growth experiment, a series of physiological parameters were measured. MDA content, hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) content, SOD activity, peroxidase (POD) activity, Pro content, SS content, soluble protein (SP) content, Na + content, and K + content were determined using assay kits from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (catalog numbers: A003-3-1, A064-1-1, A001-3, A084-3-1, A107-1-1, A145-1-1, A045-2-1, C002-1-1, and C001-2-1, respectively). The superoxide anion (O 2 − ) content was measured with a kit from Beijing Soleibao Technology Co., Ltd. (catalog number: BC1290). The contents of IAA, cytokinin (CTK), GA₃, ABA and MT were determined using plant hormone ELISA kits provided by Enzyme-linked Biotechnology Co., Ltd., with the corresponding catalog numbers ml147100, ml820295, ml072782, ml077235, and ml104018, respectively. This method quantitatively determines the levels of the aforementioned hormones in plant tissues through antigen-antibody specific reactions, combined with enzyme-catalyzed color development.
sections.statistical analysis of data: Data analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel 2024. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted with SPSS Statistics 27, and significant differences among treatment means were tested by the LSD method at the p < 0.05 level. Correlation analysis was carried out using Origin 2024, and bar charts and other figures were plotted with GraphPad Prism 10.1.2.
sections.screening of optimal mt seed priming con: Salt stress significantly inhibited the seed germination process, whereas melatonin (MT) priming effectively alleviated this inhibitory effect. The alleviating effect of MT priming was concentration‑dependent: 10, 20 and 50 µM MT improved germination indices including GP, GR, GI and VI of seeds under salt stress, while the alleviating effect gradually weakened as the concentration increased to 100 and 200 µM. Among them, the 50 µM treatment showed the optimal alleviating effect. Salt stress significantly reduced seed fresh weight by 27.81% ( p < 0.05). After priming with 50, 100 and 200 µM MT, seed fresh weight was significantly increased by 51.31%, 29.67% and 20.25%, respectively ( p < 0.05), with the most pronounced effect observed in the 50 µM treatment group. In contrast, MT priming effectively mitigated these effects, resulting in increases of 31.28% in radicle length, 21.91% in germ length, and 20.88% in fresh weight compared to the S treatment ( p < 0.05). sections.effects of mt priming on photosynthetic: Salt stress significantly influenced the photosynthetic characteristics of triticale. Compared with CK, MT treatment markedly enhanced the leaf photosynthetic pigment content (Fig. 4 A). sections.effects of mt priming on malondialdehyde: MDA, a primary end-product of membrane lipid peroxidation, serves as a reliable indicator of the extent of cell membrane damage. In the present study, salt stress significantly increased MDA content in triticale leaves (Fig. 6 A), indicating substantial membrane injury. Although MS treatment reduced MDA accumulation to some extent, the difference was not statistically significant. Regarding ROS metabolism, the S treatment resulted in significantly elevated levels of H₂O₂ and O 2 − on both day 5 and day 10 of salt stress compared to CK (Fig. 6 B, C). The MS treatment effectively mitigated this oxidative burst, reducing H₂O₂ content by 31.38% and 24.36%, and O₂ − content by 23.08% and 16.67%, respectively, relative to the S group ( p < 0.05). These findings suggest that MT priming alleviates salt-induced oxidative damage by enhancing ROS scavenging, thereby helping to maintain membrane integrity and cellular viability. Our results demonstrated that salt stress significantly suppressed the activities of SOD and POD in triticale leaves on both day 5 and day 10 (Fig. 7 A, B), indicating a compromised antioxidant capacity. In contrast, MT priming markedly restored the activities of these enzymes. By day 10 of salt stress, SOD and POD activities in the MS group were increased by 12.05% and 25.59%, respectively, compared to the S treatment ( p < 0.05). Collectively, these results demonstrate that MT enhances oxidative stress tolerance primarily by reinforcing the antioxidant enzyme system, thereby reducing oxidative damage under salt stress conditions. sections.effect of mt priming on osmotic adjustme: Under salt stress, plants activate osmotic adjustment mechanisms to maintain cellular homeostasis—an essential physiological strategy for coping with adverse conditions. The results of this study revealed that salt stress significantly induced Pro accumulation in triticale leaves (Fig. 8 A). Notably, MS treatment further increased Pro content, demonstrating a synergistic effect with salt stress. In contrast, both SP and SS contents significantly decreased by the 5 th day of salt stress compared to CK (Fig. 8 B, C). However, MS treatment resulted in significantly higher levels of SP and SS relative to the salt-stressed group. These findings indicate that MT helps maintain cellular homeostasis under salt stress through the regulation of key osmotic adjustment substances.
