sections.introduction: Uncontrolled hypertension remains a global challenge, and only 14% of hypertensive patients are controlled [ 1 ]. In sub-Saharan Africa, hypertension control is poor [ 2 ], with a high prevalence, estimated at 46% of the adult population [ 3 ]. This inflicts a substantial burden on the healthcare system [ 4 ]. In Ghana, more than one in four adults has hypertension, and this high prevalence has persisted for decades and is similar in both urban and rural populations [ 5 ]. Managing hypertension helps to reduce the risk factors associated with cardiovascular diseases [ 6 , 7 ] albeit, hypertension management faces several challenges at multiple levels. Health system-level barriers include a lack of affordable services and resources. Healthcare provider-level barriers include communication gaps, inadequate counselling, long waiting hours for appointments, a lack of national guidelines for hypertension treatment, and a lack of support. Patient-level barriers include not adhering to medication, irregular follow-up visits, a lack of awareness of blood pressure (BP) targets, poor help-seeking behaviours, reluctance to change behaviours, perceived side effects of antihypertensive medication, self-medication, a lack of family support, financial hardship, a lack of awareness of BP complications, and comorbidities [ 8 ]. In Nepal, the reported barriers to hypertension management include the absence of symptoms, reluctance to take medicine, low perceived seriousness of the disease, challenges in behaviour change (diet and exercise), lack of family support, and a lack of communication with and trust in providers [ 9 ]. Similarly, barriers and challenges have been noted among people living with hypertension in Ghana. These challenges include limited physical activities, psychological challenges, socioeconomic factors, and poor coping strategies [ 10 , 11 ]. Non-adherence to antihypertensive medication remains a problem in Ghana. This is reportedly driven by perceived ineffectiveness of the medication, barriers to smoking and alcohol cessation, palpitations, poor sleep, and decreased sexual drive [ 12 ]. In Ghana, health system-level barriers to hypertension control include a lack of appropriate knowledge of hypertension, skills, and resources, inadequate antihypertensive medications, and long distances to the hospital [ 13 ]. Psychoeducation is an evidence-based approach that integrates health information, behavioural guidance, and emotional support. Psychoeducational programme is a non-medical intervention that empowers individuals and family members to manage their health conditions [ 14 ]. It may help motivate patients by focusing on the psychological aspects of self-management, enhancing adherence to good practice. Baccolini et al. reported that a psychoeducational approach is feasible and effective in supporting patients with diabetes at high risk of first- or recurrent foot lesions, increasing their adherence to self-care practices [ 15 ]. Additionally, psychoeducational programmes improve medication adherence in the management of bipolar disorders [ 16 ]. Mahyuvi and Nursalam [ 17 ] reported that social cognitive theory-based psychoeducation directly changed the mindset of patients with ischemic stroke to improve their depression and help them control their BP. In Ghana, there are three hypertension management programmes. These include the Community-based Hypertension Improvement Project (ComHIP), Community-based Blood Pressure Monitoring, and the Healthy Heart Africa programme. However, the (ComHIP) was implemented between 2014 and 2019 in selected districts in Ghana as a task-sharing model aimed at improving hypertension detection, linkage to care, and long-term management. Although ComHIP demonstrated promising outcomes, it has not been adopted nationwide. Rather, it remains a project-specific initiative whose strategies continue to inform hypertension service delivery in some districts. Integrating psychoeducational components into these programmes may strengthen patients’ and families’ capacity to manage hypertension more effectively [ 15 – 17 ], leading to optimal control and decreasing complications related to hypertension. The study aimed to explore and describe the support needs expressed by patients with hypertension in an urban primary care setting in Ghana to inform the development of a psychoeducational programme to support the management of hypertension.
sections.materials and methods: The study adhered to the COREQ (Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research) guidelines. COREQ domains informed the design of the interview guide, the documentation of researcher reflexivity, the data collection procedures, and the analytic transparency. The checklist is provided as supplementary material.
sections.study design: The study used a qualitative descriptive design to examine and describe the needs of patients with hypertension without applying a pre-existing theoretical framework. This approach is appropriate for obtaining straightforward descriptions of participants’ experiences and perspectives, particularly in areas with limited prior research.
sections.study setting and recruitment: The study was conducted in two public health facilities: one regional hospital and one district hospital, all in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana. The Greater Accra region is the most urbanised in the country, with 87.4% of its population living in urban centres. Accra is the capital city of the Greater Accra region and Ghana. The Greater Accra region is bordered in the north by the Eastern Region, east by the Volta Region, south by the Gulf of Guinea, and west by the Central Region. These public health facilities operate hypertension clinics that provide routine blood pressure (BP) monitoring, medication review, and referral services. They serve predominantly low- to middle-income urban and peri-urban populations, making them suitable contexts for exploring the support needs of patients with hypertension. The study was conducted at the Family Medicine Department and Internal Medicine Department, as well as the Diabetic/Hypertension Support Centre and the General Outpatient Department. Maximum variation sampling of purposive sampling was used to recruit participants with similar characteristics but different experiences, which are unique to one another, resulting in shared rich experiences of the phenomenon under study [ 18 ]. The purpose of the study was discussed with staff working at the two recruitment facilities. Two nurses working in the clinics assisted the researcher in identifying eligible participants based on predefined inclusion criteria provided by the research team. While this facilitated access to participants with lived experience of hypertension, it may have introduced selection bias toward individuals who were more engaged with care and able to communicate their experiences. Further, the nurses reviewed the patient files, selected potential participants, and introduced them to the researcher. The researcher had no relationship with potential participants prior to the study. The participants were informed of the study’s purpose, and patients who volunteered to participate in face-to-face interviews signed an informed consent form before the interviews. Only a few (four) participants did not consent to the study; two of them indicated time constraints, while the remaining two participants did not provide any tangible reasons. The people who did not participate in this study were not denied healthcare services. Data collection proceeded concurrently with analysis, and interviews were conducted until data saturation, which is the point where additional interviews yielded no new concepts or insights [ 19 ]. This point was reached by the thirty-fifth interview.
sections.inclusion and exclusion criteria: Thirty-five people living with hypertension were recruited for the study (Table 1 ). Participants aged 18 years and above who were diagnosed with hypertension for one year or more and were visiting hypertension clinics were included in the study. Participants aged 18 years and above were included because they are legally capable of providing informed consent and independently managing their hypertension. The requirement of at least one year post-diagnosis ensured that participants had sufficient experience living with hypertension and interacting with the healthcare system to meaningfully reflect on their support needs. Clinic attendance was necessary because the study focused on individuals engaged in ongoing hypertension care. Hypertension clinic attendance in the study setting is predominantly female, which shaped our sample characteristics. Participants who had been diagnosed with hypertension for less than one year and who had any other disease or mental condition were excluded from the study.
sections.data collection: The data were collected over three months (April 2024 to July 2024). Data were collected during semi-structured face-to-face interviews on appointment days. Permission was also sought from the participants to audio-record the interviews and take notes during the interviews. Each interview began with an introduction from the interviewer, the first author, a female Assistant Lecturer (PhD candidate and Registered General/Public Health Nurse), who is experienced in qualitative research and does not work in a hospital setting. The interviewer also engaged participants in a general conversation to establish a good rapport before explaining the purpose of the study. The participants were assured that their participation and their information would remain confidential. This facilitated participants’ relaxation before the start of the interview and encouraged their willingness to share their experiences during the interview. All the interviews were conducted on the hospital premises, specifically, a private area next to the nurse’s station. Twelve (12) interviews were conducted in English, whereas the remaining 23 were conducted in the local dialect (Akan and Ga). Field notes were also taken to observe the nonverbal cues expressed by the participants. These included sighing, changes in facial expression, fidgeting of fingers, and silence by some participants while their experiences were recorded. Each interview session was audio-recorded and lasted between 30 and 60 min. The interviews took place between the researcher and participants, and none of the participants’ interviews were repeated.
sections.research instrument and pilot study: The semi-structured interview guide used in this study was specifically developed by the research team to explore the healthcare needs of people living with hypertension. The guide was informed by a review of relevant literature and expert consultation in hypertension management and qualitative research. The interview guide comprised two sections: section A, participants’ demographic characteristics, and section B, open-ended questions. The interview guide was piloted by recruiting three people living with hypertension from a third health facility. The pilot study strengthened the interview guide to elicit appropriate information. The data was not included in the main study. An English language version of the interview guide is provided as a supplementary file (see Supplementary File 1).
sections.data analysis: Although qualitative data analysis software such as NVivo can facilitate data management, manual coding was used to allow close engagement with the data and identification of patterns consistent with descriptive qualitative research. The data generated were manually analysed using inductive content analysis (ICA). The five steps outlined by Vears and Gillam (2022) for conducting ICA were followed [ 20 ]. The first author familiarised herself with the data by listening to the audio and transcribing the data. Interviews conducted in Akan and Ga were manually transcribed verbatim by a bilingual researcher fluent in both languages. Transcription was done in the original languages to retain participants’ expressions before translation into English. This two-step approach was used to minimise loss of meaning and ensure cultural accuracy during translation. The first author read all transcripts several times to achieve immersion and identified meaningful units, which were labeled with initial codes that connected to participants’ own words. Because the analysis was inductive, a pre-existing codebook was not used. Instead, a provisional code list was created directly from the data and refined throughout the coding process. Codes with similar content were grouped to form preliminary categories, which were further refined into sub-themes and overarching themes. To enhance analytic rigor, a second researcher independently coded a subset of the transcripts. The two researchers compared coding outputs, discussed interpretive differences, and reached consensus through iterative dialogue. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion until agreement was achieved, ensuring the dependability of the coding process. As an example of the coding hierarchy: a meaning unit, such as “worrying is also part because the problems are a lot , you think too much , which increases the blood pressure (BP)” was coded as “worrying about life problems.” This code was grouped under the category “ stress management ” which contributed to the broader theme “Lifestyle modification.” Throughout the analytic process, the research team engaged in reflexive notetaking, maintained an audit trail of coding decisions, and conducted regular peer debriefing sessions to strengthen credibility and confirmability.”
sections.ethical considerations: Ethical approval was obtained from the Faculty of Health Sciences Research Ethics Committee, Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research Institutional Review Board, and Ghana Health Service Ethics Review Committee. Additionally, permission was granted by the management of the two health facilities. Informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection. Participants were provided with a written information leaflet and consent form with detailed information about the purpose of the study, their rights, and any potential risks or benefits, and were assured of the confidentiality and voluntary nature of their participation. Only participants who consented to the study were asked to complete the consent form and included in the study. Consented participants had the free will to decline without consequences for healthcare. All participants’ records were anonymised. Also, all audio recordings were anonymised using unique identification codes and stored on a password-protected computer accessible only to the research team. Transcripts were saved in encrypted folders, and all identifiable information was removed during transcription.
sections.trustworthiness and reflexivity: The three researchers were from different healthcare professions. Two researchers had similar demographic backgrounds, while the third author was from a different ethnic and cultural background. The three authors independently analysed the data and reflected actively on the findings. This was done to deepen data interpretation and understanding of the diversity of experiences of people living with hypertension with differing demographic profiles. The first author’s previous clinical experience in managing people living with hypertension facilitated the in-depth exploration of experiences and the iterative data collection process. Qualitative studies are considered trustworthy if they implement the criteria of credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability [ 21 ]. Credibility is used to evaluate the confidence level generated from the findings and interpretation of a study [ 21 ]. This was ensured by triangulation, member checking, prolonged engagement at the recruitment site [ 21 , 22 ], persistent observation, peer debriefing, collection of reference materials, and a thick description of the data [ 22 ]. Transferability refers to the extent to which an inquiry can be applied in different contexts [ 21 ]. This was ensured by providing a detailed description of the research design, study setting, and methods and durations used for data collection. Dependability is the extent to which the study results are stable [ 22 ], trusted [ 21 ], and reliable [ 23 ]. To ensure this, an audit trail and peer debriefing were established. Finally, confirmability describes the precision and accuracy of the findings as representing the experiences of the participants and not those of the researcher [ 23 ]. To achieve this, reflexive practice, a comprehensive audit trail, and rich quotes were used.
sections.participants characteristics: Thirty-five patients completed the interviews. Participants’ characteristics are summarised in Table 1 . The majority of the participants, 14 (40.0%), were aged between 50 and 59 years. Primarily, participants were females, 31 representing 88.6% of the sample, and the remaining 4 were males, constituting 11.4% of the sample. The predominance of female participants may reflect gendered patterns of health-seeking behaviour in Ghana, where women are more likely to attend routine clinic appointments and participate in health research compared to men. Most of the participants, 13 (37.1%), had no formal education. Many of the females, 12 (38.7%), had no formal education. In terms of employment, most (19), constituting 54.3% were self-employed. The number of years of living with hypertension ranged from 1 to 20 years and above, with the majority, 13 (37.1%), ranging from 1 to 4 years. Participants aged 50–69 years (23/35) formed the majority and primarily expressed concerns related to long-term medication use and lifestyle modification. In contrast, older participants (>/= 70 years, 7/35) emphasised challenges related to medication side effects and physical limitations that affected adherence to exercise recommendations. Younger participants (40–49 years, 5/35) were more likely to focus on maintaining productivity and integrating lifestyle changes into work routines. In terms of gender differences, the sample was predominantly female (31/35), and women frequently discussed dietary practices and family-related influences on hypertension management. Male participants (4/35), although few, raised concerns related to sexual dysfunction and medication side effects, highlighting gender-specific needs. Additionally, participants with no formal education (13/35) expressed a greater need for simple, clear, and repeated explanations, often relying heavily on healthcare providers for guidance. In contrast, participants with higher levels of education (20/35) demonstrated a preference for more detailed information regarding disease mechanisms, treatment options, and complications. Self-employed participants (19/35) reported challenges in adhering to medication schedules and lifestyle modifications due to work demands and irregular routines. Retired participants (9/35) expressed fewer time-related barriers but highlighted financial constraints and dependence on family support. Participants who had lived with hypertension for a shorter duration (1–4 years, 13/35) expressed a stronger need for basic information about the condition. In contrast, those with longer duration (>/= 10 years, 10/35) were more concerned with complications, medication side effects, and long-term disease management.
sections.presentation of findings: We identified four themes and 10 sub-themes from the data generated (Table 2 ). Table 2 Theme and Sub-themes Theme Sub-themes Health information needs from healthcare provider • Blood pressure monitoring and interpretation • Working mechanism of medications • Side effects of medication • Complications of hypertension Lifestyle modification • Dietary modification • Stress management • Importance of exercise Patient self-care • Medication adherence • Attending regular checkups Psychosocial support • Emotional and psychological support
sections.theme 1: health information needs from h: In Ghana, people living with hypertension needed health information. Most participants emphasized the need for healthcare providers to provide appropriate information regarding the disease and management. They indicated their need for health information such as BP monitoring and interpretation, the working mechanism of medications, side effects of medications, and complications of hypertension.
sections.blood pressure monitoring and interpreta: Almost all participants (31/35; 88.6%) emphasised the importance of receiving appropriate information on BP monitoring and interpretation. They want to know how to measure their own BP, how often to check it, and what BP readings mean. Additionally, some participants wanted to acquire their own BP machines to aid with BP profiling at home. ‘I also need teachings on how to use the BP machine to check my BP at home so that I don’t have to always visit a pharmacy or chemical shop to do that.’ (P 04) . ‘I need a BP machine to check whether it is [BP] high or low.’ (P 06) .
sections.mechanisms of medications: Participants wanted to know how the prescribed medications work. They wished to know how antihypertensive medications affect their hearts and bodies. Some participants (12/35; 34.3%) suggested in-depth education on the mechanism of antihypertensive medicines. Compared with generic brands, they prefer to receive prescriptions for good-quality brands of antihypertensive medications. ‘The information I need is how I will take my medications promptly and what the BP medicine does to your heart and body.’ (P 03) . ‘I have been taking BP drugs , yet I don’t know what it actually does to my heart.’ (P 16) . ‘The BP medicines served within the hospitals are not of good quality , and you may end up getting other diseases [shakes a tablet container]. It just doesn’t work for me as expected , so I have stopped taking them [BP medicines].’ (P 09) .
sections.side effects of medication: Nearly all the participants, 30 out of 35 (85.7%), wanted to be educated on the side effects of antihypertensive medications. Ideally, healthcare providers should explain the side effects and how to manage each antihypertensive. A small number of male participants, 4 out of 35 (11.4), predominantly older individuals, complained of sexual dysfunction associated with taking antihypertensive medications. A few participants (4/35, 11.4%) complained about drowsiness following the use of antihypertensive medicines. ‘What I know is the BP drug , that is what it did to me. My sexual ability was reduced , and eventually , I could not perform sexually.’ (P 07) . ‘There are serious side effects when you take BP medicines; personally , I experienced sexual impotence. So that is why I don’t want to take BP medicines.’ (P 31) .
sections.complications of hypertension: Participants expressed concerns about the complications of hypertension, often drawing on the experiences of others. Some participants (4/35) referred to colleagues or acquaintances who had developed complications such as stroke, heart disease e.t.c, which heightened their fear and desire for more information about the condition. In addition, some participants believed that certain treatments, particularly herbal medications, could lead to adverse outcomes or complications. These views reflected participants’ perceptions and sources of information rather than their personal clinical experiences. Some participants narrate their stories as follows. ‘When he (participant colleague) was rushed to the hospital , his BP level and everything were high , so after some time , we saw the right side of his body not working. Therefore , for me , I want to know more about how these dangerous experiences can be prevented.’ (P 20) . ‘Herbal drugs are the cause of stroke and kidney failure currently. Doctors and nurses must educate us on the effect of not complying with treatment.’ (P 35) .
sections.theme 2: lifestyle modifications: The participants acknowledged that lifestyle changes, such as dietary adjustments, stress management and exercise, are critical for hypertension management. Therefore, they indicated that it would be helpful for their doctors and nurses to provide more information on lifestyle changes.
sections.dietary modification: Some participants (16/35, 45.7%) shared their views on modifying their diets, emphasising the need for a low-sodium diet and consuming fruits and vegetables. However, they indicated the need for a dietary programme and voiced the high cost of fruit and vegetables, making it difficult for them to consume the required amounts. The participants indicated the need for information from doctors and nurses regarding dietary modifications. ‘You must reduce salt intake if you have high BP. We need much more detailed information on salt intake.’ (P12) . ‘There’s no specification of the diet. We need information from doctors and nurses to help us know what to eat and what not… .’ (P 27) .
sections.stress management: The participants (11/35, 31.4%) described how persistent worrying, overthinking, and anxiety, especially at night, contribute to elevated BP and insomnia. The financial strain of medication further exacerbates their stress levels, creating a cycle of worry that intensifies their condition. The participants voiced a need for education related to stress management. ‘My BP has made me have many thoughts , so I can’t sleep , especially at dawn. I need some information on how to manage my stress’ (P 11). ‘Because the problems are a lot , I get worried and think too much , which increases my BP. If the doctors and nurses can teach us about stress management , it will help us very much.’ (P 10) .
sections.importance of exercise: The participants indicated a need for information on exercise. This category describes the importance of regular physical activity in managing hypertension. Thirteen (13) out of thirty-five (35) participants (13/35) representing 37.1% acknowledged the positive impact of exercise, such as morning exercise, on BP control. Other participants (7/35, 20%) also highlighted the need for healthcare providers to provide appropriate information and guidance on exercise, while some indicated their difficulty in wanting to exercise. ‘Therefore , I’m told to exercise by my doctor , but I have not started because I don’t know the kind of exercise to do.’ (P 05) . ’…and you have to do exercise too. However , they [healthcare providers] have not educated me on the type and how often I need to do it.’ (P 27 .
sections.theme 3: patient self-care: This theme captures how participants themselves articulated the duties, expectations, and personal obligations they associate with managing their hypertension. Although similar to the concept of self-management, we retained the term “Patient self-care” because it reflects the participants’ own language and the way they framed their roles in adhering to treatment and attending regular clinic visits. The theme refers to the active roles played by patients in managing their hypertension, particularly in adhering to antihypertensive treatments and attending regular checkups. These responsibilities are vital for achieving optimal BP control and preventing complications. The theme is described under medication adherence and attending regular checkups, which provide insight into participants’ experiences.
sections.medication adherence: This reflects the extent to which participants adhered to prescribed antihypertensive regimens to manage their hypertension. Fifteen (15/35) participants’ narratives provide insights into the complex and multifaceted nature of medication adherence, shaped by participants’ attitudes, experiences, beliefs, and external factors. ‘If I take in my drugs and follow the regimen [clears throat] , then it could be managed , but if I default , then I don’t think I’ll ever be healed.’ (P 01) . ‘I stopped the medication twice. I stopped twice…… In addition , then last October (2023) , I was admitted to the hospital because my BP was extremely high.’ (P 017) .
sections.attending regular checkups: Attending regular check-ups is a key responsibility for people living with hypertension. This category highlights participants’ awareness of the importance of checkups and the barriers that may hinder regular attendance. Nearly half 17/35, (48.6%), of the participants shared their view on this. ‘Although I hear the doctors saying hypertension can lead to stroke if it is not well managed , I am unable to go for my appointments unless I am seriously unwell because I spend so much during the visits.’ (P 20) . ‘Oh , so for me , I’m not so rich , and the money I use to go up and down for this BP checkup is a lot , so sometimes I miss my appointment schedule.’ (P 21) .
sections.theme 4: psychosocial support: Psychosocial support reflects the need for emotional encouragement and social assistance to help individuals cope with living with hypertension. The participants’ experiences reveal how significant life stressors are and how supportive systems influence their well-being.
This highlights the critical need for emotional and psychological support in managing the emotional toll of life events and hypertension. Twelve out of thirty-five (12/35) representing 34.3% participants’ narratives revealed the profound psychological impact of traumatic experiences and the desire for support to navigate these challenges. ‘I suffered a shock as a result and was rushed to the hospital where the doctors diagnosed me with hypertension…I was in shock and needed support’. ( P 23 ) ‘I can say that this condition has truly affected my life badly. There’s no joy in my life. Someone to encourage and calm you down is very good when you are in fear.’ (P 13) .
sections.discussion: This study identified a range of informational and psychosocial needs among patients with hypertension. Beyond the descriptive findings, these needs reflect important gaps in patient-centred care and health education within the Ghanaian healthcare context, where limited consultation time and high patient load may constrain effective communication between healthcare providers and patients. The strong demand for information across multiple domains, including medication use, lifestyle modification, and hypertension complications, suggests substantial unmet informational needs among patients. These findings indicate that patients require not only basic knowledge but also a deeper understanding of their condition to support effective self-care. In the Ghanaian context, where healthcare resources may be constrained, and patient education is often limited, these findings highlight the need for structured, context-specific patient education and support systems [ 24 , 25 ]. This suggests the need for improved patient-provider communication and tailored educational interventions to support hypertension management [ 10 , 26 , 27 ]. Variations in needs were observed across participant characteristics. Participants with lower educational levels required simpler and more practical explanations, whereas those with higher education sought more detailed information about disease mechanisms and treatment. Older participants were more concerned about medication-related challenges and physical limitations, while younger participants focused on maintaining daily functioning. In addition, male participants raised gender-specific concerns, particularly regarding medication side effects. These differences highlight the importance of tailoring interventions to individual patient characteristics. In the present study, participants demonstrated limited understanding of key aspects of hypertension, including blood pressure monitoring, medication mechanisms, side effects, and potential complications, underscoring the need for more comprehensive patient education. Participants do not always understand their BP readings or recognise the importance of regular monitoring. Similarly, home BP monitoring is limited by not knowing the benefits of lowering BP, not understanding BP goals, or knowing how to interpret BP values [ 28 ]. Patients who can monitor their own BP are better able to manage their hypertension; however, this may be daunting. Healthcare providers should educate patients on measuring and accurately interpreting BP readings. Regular monitoring can lead to better management of hypertension, ultimately reducing the risk of complications. Fear of potential side effects is a common barrier to medication adherence among participants. Almost all the male participants (3/35; 8.6%) in this study were concerned about the side effects of antihypertensive medications, specifically, the impact on their sexual performance, which was a barrier to treatment adherence. Earlier studies from Ghana reported that antihypertensive agent use was associated with reduced libido and sexual dysfunction [ 10 , 11 ]. Healthcare providers should proactively discuss potential side effects and provide clear information and strategies to manage them. This approach can alleviate patient anxiety and promote adherence to prescribed therapies. Patients need to know the potential complications of uncontrolled hypertension. This information will motivate patients to adhere to treatment and lifestyle modifications. Findings suggest that patients may not fully appreciate the seriousness of hypertension and the potential consequences of its complications. For example, research in rural Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka highlighted that patients have limited knowledge of preventing or treating hypertension, leading to poor management [ 29 ]. Healthcare providers must educate patients about the risks of complications such as stroke, heart disease, and kidney failure to encourage proactive health behaviours. Hypertension can also be managed through lifestyle modification, including dietary modification, stress management, and exercise. Dietary modification is important for controlling high BP. In this study, although participants were willing to eat fruits and vegetables, they complained that these foods were expensive, making compliance difficult [ 10 ]. Stress management is an important aspect of effective hypertension care, as chronic stress is a well-known contributor to hypertension. However, people living with hypertension often do not know how to reduce their stress through techniques such as mindfulness, relaxation exercises, and social support systems, which are known to help regulate BP and improve mental well-being. The participants in this study attributed their stress to persistent worrying, overthinking, and anxiety, especially at night, which contributed to elevated BP and insomnia. They also mentioned that medication was expensive. Similarly, Atibila et al. reported that hypertensive patients experience fear and anxiety and complain about expensive BP medications [ 10 ]. Exercise is essential for managing hypertension. Regular physical activity improves cardiovascular fitness, promotes weight control, and lowers BP. However, about 20/35 (57.1%) participants in the present study remained unaware of the necessary types and amounts of exercise, such as engaging in at least 150 min of moderate aerobic activity weekly. These findings are consistent with those of Chen and colleagues [ 25 ]. Hypertension and physical inactivity are the primary causes of premature death [ 30 ]. Providing appropriate education and resources will motivate people living with hypertension to engage in exercise. The findings highlight the importance of patient self-care in hypertension management, particularly with regard to medication adherence and regular attendance of check-ups. Medication adherence refers to patients taking their medications as prescribed and following the correct dosage, timing, and frequency. Participants in this study demonstrated suboptimal adherence to antihypertensive medications, with some (7/35; 20%) considering discontinuation and others (4/35; 11.4%) resorting to herbal remedies, highlighting the need for improved patient education and adherence support. Earlier studies from Ghana reported that hypertensive patients believed that traditional medicines could cure hypertension and were more likely to use them [ 4 , 31 ]. Medication adherence is closely associated with the level of trust and communication between patients and healthcare providers, as well as patient education and self-efficacy. Kvarnstrom et al. (2021) further reported that well-informed patients and trusting relationships with healthcare providers are central to improving medication adherence [ 32 ]. Self-efficacy empowers patients to manage their disease and adjust to medications if needed. Regular medical appointments allow for continuous monitoring, early detection of potential issues, and timely adjustments to treatment plans. These checkups foster collaborative engagement between patients and healthcare providers, enhancing communication and shared decision-making. The participants in the present study emphasised the need to attend regular medical checkups. They recognised that checkups could help them to manage their hypertension and allow doctors to review their medications. Similarly, Kvarnstrom, Airaksinen, and Liira (2018) reported that regular interactions between providers and patients during check-ups provide opportunities to address barriers to adherence and reinforce the importance of following treatment regimens [ 33 ]. In our study, the participants revealed profound emotional and psychological distress, which exacerbated their stress. The participants reported feeling anxious, afraid, and helpless, and very few (5.7%) experienced worsening symptoms at night. Participants struggled to articulate their struggles or seek adequate support, which further compounded their emotional burden. Patients mentioned that they were stressed about the cost of medication, leading to feelings of hopelessness and despair. The participants in our study highlighted the need for emotional and psychological support systems to help them cope with the challenges of managing hypertension. Previous studies have shown that a substantial proportion of patients with hypertension experience psychological distress, including depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms [ 34 – 36 ]. Hence, reduced psychological distress may result in improved self-care, increasing the probability of improved hypertension control; thus, psychological interventions may be necessary for managing hypertension [ 37 ]. Psychosocial needs extended beyond emotional support to include the influence of participants’ immediate social environment. Family practices, particularly dietary habits and salt consumption, played a significant role in shaping participants’ ability to adhere to recommended lifestyle modifications. In some cases, lack of family support or conflicting social norms created barriers to behaviour change, particularly in relation to diet and smoking. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating family social networks and community contexts into hypertension management strategies [ 14 , 31 , 38 – 41 ]. Although the study setting provides components of hypertension care, including patient education, routine BP monitoring, medication review, and referral services, the findings suggest that these may not be sufficiently structured, consistent, or tailored to meet patients’ specific informational and psychosocial needs. Based on the primary findings outlined earlier, strengthening and formalizing these existing approaches through structured psychoeducation could help address these gaps by equipping patients with clear, actionable knowledge about their condition. Psychoeducation has been shown to improve disease insight, medication adherence, and self-management behaviours among individuals with chronic illnesses [ 42 ]. In the context of hypertension, psychoeducational strategies such as guided information sessions, demonstration of blood pressure monitoring, and clearer explanation of medication regimens have been associated with improved self-efficacy and better blood pressure control [ 42 ]. Strengthening the content and delivery of health information by healthcare providers may therefore enhance patients’ understanding and engagement with their hypertension management. The themes on lifestyle modification and patient responsibility also align with established behaviour-change theories. The Health Belief Model (HBM) posits that individuals adopt preventive behaviours when they perceive susceptibility, severity, benefits, and low barriers [ 43 ]. Participants in this study expressed challenges related to diet, exercise, and regular monitoring, which may reflect perceived barriers such as cost, knowledge gaps, or low confidence. Psychoeducation grounded in HBM constructs, particularly perceived benefits and self-efficacy, may enable patients to adopt and sustain lifestyle changes. The theme on psychosocial support further highlights the emotional demands of living with hypertension. Participants reported stress, worry, and the need for emotional assistance, emphasizing the importance of addressing the psychological burden associated with chronic disease. Previous studies have shown that psychosocial distress is associated with poor blood pressure control, reduced adherence, and greater cardiovascular risk [ 44 ]. Behaviour-change models such as Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) emphasize the role of social support, self-regulation, and observational learning in sustaining long-term health behaviours [ 45 ]. Incorporating SCT-informed strategies such as peer support groups, family involvement, and collaborative care could help mitigate psychosocial barriers and enhance coping. These findings are consistent with recommendations from established hypertension guidelines, which emphasize patient education, lifestyle modification, and psychosocial support as key components of effective hypertension management [ 46 , 47 ]. In the Ghanaian context, similar priorities are reflected in national treatment guidelines, which highlight the importance of patient-centered care and adherence support [ 48 ]. However, despite the availability of such guidelines, gaps remain in their implementation at the patient level, particularly in relation to effective communication and ongoing patient support. In Ghana, several hypertension programmes have been implemented to improve awareness, screening, and management, including the Community-based Hypertension Improvement Project (ComHIP), Community-based Blood Pressure Monitoring initiatives, and the Healthy Heart Africa programme. These interventions emphasise early detection, patient education, and improved access to care [ 49 ]. Evidence from Ghana demonstrates that while programmes such as ComHIP have improved hypertension awareness and access to care, challenges remain in sustaining long-term patient engagement and adherence [ 4 , 7 , 50 , 51 ]. However, despite the presence of these programmes, participants in this study continued to express unmet needs, particularly regarding a detailed understanding of hypertension, medication use, and psychosocial support. This suggests potential gaps in the implementation, reach, or patient-centeredness of these interventions, particularly at the level of sustained patient engagement and individualized education. The findings of this study, therefore, do not necessarily indicate the absence of interventions, but rather highlight the need to strengthen existing programmes by enhancing patient-provider communication, tailoring education to individual needs, and incorporating psychosocial and family-level support. This is particularly relevant in the Ghanaian context, where health system constraints and variations in service delivery may affect the consistency and effectiveness of programme implementation [ 4 ]. Overall, linking the study’s themes with psychoeducation and behaviour-change models suggests that hypertension management should extend beyond biomedical treatment to include educational, behavioural, and psychosocial interventions. Embedding theory-informed psychoeducation into hypertension clinics may strengthen patients’ knowledge, readiness for lifestyle change, and emotional resilience, ultimately contributing to improved blood pressure control and quality of life. The gender imbalance observed in this study, with far more women than men participating, may be partly attributed to differences in health-seeking behavior. In Ghana, research shows that women are more likely than men to attend routine health services and preventive care, while men often underutilise outpatient services due to social norms around masculinity and prioritisation of work responsibilities [ 52 ]. Moreover, qualitative studies suggest that traditional gender roles discourage men from seeking care: men may view health-seeking as a sign of weakness or believe they should tolerate illness without medical help [ 53 ]. The findings of this study may be transferable to other chronic non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, obesity, and hyperlipidaemia, where patient education, lifestyle modification, and psychosocial support are similarly important.
sections.strengths and limitations: This study aimed to explore and describe the support needs of people living with hypertension. The strengths of this study are associated with the semi-structured in-depth interviews conducted. This allowed us to explore patients’ support needs in managing hypertension, yielding rich information that may increase awareness and understanding among healthcare providers, enhancing hypertension management. Another strength is that the thick description of the study may be transferable to some settings with similar characteristics, despite the sample size, which may compromise generalizability. However, the study experienced some limitations. Firstly, the study was conducted in two health facilities in an urban setting, but only in one region (Greater Accra) out of the 16 regions in Ghana. This decision was due to the limited financial and time resources required in conducting the study. Therefore, the findings may not necessarily reflect the actual situation in Ghana, including rural settings, considering diversity in geographical location, socioeconomic background and status, and allocation of health resources. Future studies should consider other geographical locations. Additionally, the data were self-reported by participants, which could lead to social desirability bias, which may result in some information being overstated or underestimated. Again, the recruitment through clinic nurses may have introduced selection bias, as nurses may have approached patients perceived as more articulate or cooperative. A key limitation of this study is the limited gender variability, with men being underrepresented. This may restrict the transferability of findings to male patients with hypertension. Additionally, the predominantly female sample (approximately 88%) limits the study, which may reflect local clinic attendance patterns and may influence the types of needs expressed, hence affecting the transferability of findings. Another limitation is that the urban Ghanaian context, characterised by high clinic attendance and structured chronic care, may limit transferability to rural or resource-limited settings. Therefore, adaptation should consider health system structure, literacy levels, and access to educational support. Lastly, although an area was created for conducting interviews to ensure privacy as compared to having a room, there were a few circumstances in which the interviewer encountered background noise, which might have affected the free flow of interviews.
sections.recommendations for future research: The researchers recommend the development, implementation, and evaluation of the effectiveness of psychoeducational programmes in improving long-term adherence and self-care behaviours among people living with hypertension.
sections.implications for the profession and pati: These findings may assist healthcare providers in providing comprehensive care with emphasis on integrating psychosocial support in the management of people living with hypertension.
sections.implications for policy and practice: Identifying the support needs of individuals living with hypertension can inform the development of context-appropriate management programmes that consider dietary practices, health beliefs, and social dynamics within diverse populations.
sections.relevance to clinical practice: Addressing the support needs of people living with hypertension warrants exploring their healthcare needs and heeding to the voiced-out support needs, fostering comprehensive management of their condition.
sections.conclusion_1: This study identified several patient-expressed needs among people living with hypertension in Ghana, particularly in relation to understanding blood pressure monitoring, medication use, lifestyle adjustments, and sources of psychosocial support. Participants also described experiences of emotional strain, including feelings of anxiety and concern about their condition. These findings suggest that incorporating basic psychosocial guidance into routine hypertension care may better align with patients’ expressed concerns. Future psychoeducational interventions may benefit from including simple counselling messages and stress-management strategies tailored to patients’ individual needs. Given that the study sample was predominantly female, these findings may particularly reflect the experiences and support needs of women living with hypertension.

title: Untargeted metabolomics and proteomics reveals cocoa-mediated mitigation of valproic acid-induced dysregulation in a zebrafish model of autism: pilot study
abstract: Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by behavioral impairments and limited therapeutic options. Emerging evidence suggests that plant-derived polyphenols may offer neuroprotective benefits. Objectives This pilot study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of polyphenol-rich cocoa extract in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced zebrafish model of ASD. Methods Zebrafish were exposed to 3 μM VPA, cocoa powder providing 2.5 μM (–)-epicatechin, a combination of both, or left untreated. Behavioral phenotyping was conducted using DanioVision and gut morphology was assessed. Untargeted metabolomic and proteomic profiling was performed followed by univariate and multivariate analyses. Results VPA exposure induced ASD-like behavioral hyperactivity, and severe gastrointestinal abnormalities. Cocoa co-treatment ameliorated both behavioral performance and gut architecture. Metabolomic profiling revealed VPA-associated disruptions in neurotransmission, methylation, mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis. Proteomic profiling showed elevated levels of trafficking protein particle complex subunit 11, proteasomal ubiquitin receptor, betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase 1 (BHMT-1), and desmoplakin-A, consistent with genotoxic stress and impaired protein trafficking. Cocoa co-treatment normalized BHMT-1 and desmoplakin-A expression and mitigated broader metabolic dysregulation. Conclusion Collectively, these results suggest that polyphenol-rich cocoa may represent a promising multi-targeted nutraceutical approach for mitigating ASD-related neurodevelopmental and metabolic disturbances. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s11306-026-02482-w.
