sections.discussion: This study utilizes a smart insole system to monitor gait parameters, providing new insights into the association between BMI and specific kinematic and dynamic gait characteristics.
sections.adjustment of walking patterns from effi: This study revealed that RSS of underweight individuals was significantly higher than that of other BMI groups, and RSS presented a very strong negative linear correlation with BMI ( p < 0.001). This may be attributed to their lower body mass, which reduces exercise inertia and energy expenditure, facilitating easier limb initiation and swing. Furthermore, lower joint loads and swing resistance contribute to greater flexibility, which is also reflected in the weak negative linear correlations of SL and SLA with BMI ( p < 0.05). However, underweight individuals often exhibit muscle fiber atrophy and reduced metabolic capacity, leading to diminished muscle strength and endurance, particularly in the dorsiflexor muscles [ 19 ]. To counteract body sway caused by muscular insufficiency during the support phase, they may unconsciously adopt a faster lower-limb swing to improve walking efficiency. This adaptation also results in a significantly higher percentage of single support time (%SST) and percentage of swing phase time (%SPT) (both p < 0.001), a lower percentage of double support phase time (%DSPT) ( p < 0.05), which were moderately negatively and positively correlated with BMI, respectively. In overweight individuals, excess body mass significantly increases lower-limb joint pressure and muscular energy consumption. Their gait demonstrates distinct adaptive adjustments consistent with the above BMI-dependent trends: to reduce the instantaneous impact force and muscular work per step, they actively shorten their SL, and the reduction in distance per step is not compensated by step speed (SS) or cadence (Cad), as no significant linear or nonlinear correlations were found between BMI and SS, Cad ( p > 0.05). The single-leg support time is unconsciously shortened, while the double-support phase time is extended to facilitate a faster transfer of the center of gravity [ 20 ]. Similar adaptive gait characteristics have been observed in studies of the elderly [ 21 ]. Notably, multiple studies have not consistently identified clear gait parameter differences between young overweight and normal-weight groups [ 22 , 23 ]. This may be because young people’s muscle strength, joint elasticity, and cardiopulmonary function are at their peak, which can compensate for the extra weight, and such subtle differences in RSS, %SST, %SPT and %DSPT can be accurately captured by smart insoles. When body mass progresses to obesity, excessive load exacerbates joint pressure and cardiopulmonary burden, leading to altered skeletal muscle recruitment patterns (e.g., overactivation of the soleus and tibialis anterior during single support [ 24 ]), impaired contraction function (e.g., poor quadriceps function [ 6 ]), and structural changes (e.g., muscle fibrosis and structural disorganization [ 25 ]). To conserve energy and maintain stability, obese individuals further shorten their step length and reduce walking speed, thereby decreasing muscular work per unit time [ 26 ], while extending the %DSPT to gain a wider support base [ 27 , 28 ]. Concurrently, chronic load compresses and thickens anterior ankle structures (e.g., tendons and ligaments), but no significant correlation was found between BMI and MPFA, MDFA or FRA [ 29 ] ( p > 0.05), meaning the impact of BMI on ankle joint angle parameters lacks statistical evidence in this study.Although long-term load stimulation can induce lower-limb muscle hypertrophy and an increase in absolute strength, relative muscle strength (normalized to body weight) actually decreases [ 30 ]. While the aforementioned gait adjustments in obese individuals may reduce short-term joint load and improve stability, prolonged excessive muscle co-activation increases the risk of strain, and a shift in muscle fiber type compromises endurance [ 31 ]. This not only predisposes individuals to gait disorders and falls but also accelerates joint degeneration, increasing the incidence of conditions like osteoarthritis and tendinitis [ 32 ].
sections.the compensatory mechanism for phasic di: Our study identified statistically significant differences in PPP of all five foot regions among underweight, normal-weight, overweight, and obese groups ( p < 0.05), and all PPP indicators presented positive linear correlations with BMI ( p < 0.002). In particular, the PPP-M, PPP-A, and PPP-H were significantly higher in the overweight and obese groups compared to the normal-weight and underweight groups, and these three indicators showed a progressive increase with the rise of BMI ( p < 0.001), which aligns with findings from Liu et al. [ 33 ]in elderly women and is likely related to weight-induced gait adaptations. Body weight is the primary source of plantar pressure, and an elevated BMI significantly increases the body’s vertical load. During walking, different regions of the foot distribute this load. The heel, as the initial contact point, bears the brunt of the impact, and its PPP-H naturally rises with BMI [ 34 ], consistent with the conclusions of Choi et al. [ 31 ]. Sustained high heel pressure can lead to local pathologies like plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendinitis [ 10 ].The foot arch is a key structure for cushioning and distributing pressure. Prolonged compression from excess weight can lead to the relaxation of soft tissues like the plantar fascia, potentially resulting in arch collapse and valgus [ 35 ]. Following arch collapse, pressure in the metatarsal region increases accordingly [ 36 ], with the medial metatarsals being more affected [ 34 ]. This abnormal load distribution further impairs lower-limb alignment, causing excessive internal rotation of the knees and hips [ 37 ], which accelerates articular cartilage wear and increases the risk of osteoarthritis, leading to chronic tension and strain in lower-limb muscles [ 22 , 38 ]. Notably, no significant linear correlations were found between BMI and all COP indicators (COP-L, Max COP-ML and Max COP- AP ). Although parabolic regression found an inverted U-shaped nonlinear relationship between Max COP-ML and BMI (cut-off: 24.14), this nonlinear trend lacks sufficient statistical power to confirm a definite association, and thus cannot be regarded as a BMI-dependent adaptive characteristic of the COP. The lateral metatarsal region is less affected by medial arch collapse, and the phalangeal region only bears short-term push-off loads [ 39 ]. Obese individuals compensate by shortening their step length and reducing push-off force, which mitigates inter-group pressure differences in this area. Nevertheless, increased body load can still cause injuries to the phalanges and soft tissues, including stress fractures [ 40 ]. In contrast to the high plantar pressure in individuals with high BMI (BMI > 24), our study shows that underweight individuals have generally lower peak plantar pressure than the normal-weight group, consistent with Shen et al. [ 41 ]. Biomechanically, excessively low plantar pressure indicates insufficient transmission of ground reaction forces to the lower limbs. Normal mechanical loading is a crucial stimulus for chondrocyte activity [ 6 ]. Chronic underloading may deprive cartilage of adequate stimulation, leading to reduced nutrient supply and slowed matrix synthesis, potentially triggering degenerative changes such as thinning and loss of elasticity [ 42 ]. Furthermore, underweight individuals often have insufficient nutrient intake, exacerbating deficiencies in bones, cartilage, and muscles. However, the hypothesis that this results in structural abnormalities and reduced tissue stability reflected in COP indicators is not supported by statistical results in this study, as no significant association was found between BMI and COP parameters. Although the characteristics of some gait parameters and their mechanisms align with relevant studies, the inter-group differences in this study were not always statistically significant. This may be because the participants were young, with strong muscles, good joint elasticity, and flexible neural regulation, allowing them to compensate for weight differences through fine gait adjustments, thereby attenuating inter-group disparities.
sections.limitations: This study utilized a smart insole system to monitor gait parameters, which provides novel insights into the association between BMI and specific kinematic as well as kinetic gait characteristics. Cross-sectional design and causality: The cross-sectional nature of the study only allows for the identification of correlations between BMI and gait parameters, not causal relationships. We cannot determine whether BMI changes induce gait adaptations or if inherent gait patterns influence weight regulation over time. Longitudinal studies tracking BMI and gait parameters over years are needed to clarify causal directions. Uncontrolled confounding factors: Key variables such as physical activity levels, exercise habits, shoe-wearing preferences, and foot morphology (e.g., arch height) were not systematically collected or controlled. These factors may independently influence gait parameters and plantar pressure distribution, potentially confounding the association between BMI and gait adaptations. For example, regularly active individuals with high BMI may have stronger lower limb muscles, leading to different gait compensatory mechanisms compared to sedentary individuals with the same BMI. Limited generalizability: The study population consists of healthy college students (18–28 years old) with no underlying musculoskeletal diseases. This homogeneous group has strong neuromuscular plasticity and compensatory capacity, which may differ from older adults, individuals with chronic conditions, or non-student populations. Thus, the findings cannot be directly generalized to these groups. Simplified testing scenario: Gait data were collected during a standardized 10-meter linear walk, which does not reflect complex real-life scenarios (e.g., climbing stairs, turning, uneven terrain). Gait adaptations to BMI may differ in more dynamic environments, limiting the ecological validity of the results.
sections.conclusion_1: Human gait is a complex motor behavior resulting from the dynamic balance achieved through integrated neural regulation, muscular force, and skeletal support. Using smart insole technology to analyze the gait parameters of college students across different BMI levels, this study found that several parameters showed significant differences and a consistent trend of change among underweight, normal-weight, overweight, and obese groups. These findings reveal the specific gait adaptation mechanisms the body employs to manage load and maintain balance across a mass gradient. This work provides a feasible technical method and quantitative indicators for the early screening of BMI-related gait abnormalities and for monitoring adolescent sports health.
sections.use of generative ai: During the preparation of this work, the authors used generative AI technology for language polishing and readability improvement. Following the use of this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as necessary and take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

title:
Programmable Functionalizations
of Tetramethylpiperidine
N‑Oxyl (TEMPO)–Acrolein Linchpins Derived from Alkoxyallenes
abstract:
Allenes are versatile precursors for constructing complex
molecular
frameworks, yet oxidative transformations to install C–C or
C–heteroatom bonds across the C1–C3 framework rely on
inconvenient reagents and yield overoxidized byproducts and unstable
intermediates that limit downstream diversification. Herein, we report
a general strategy to access multifunctional C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acrolein
linchpins from simple alkoxyallenes. These TEMPO-acrolein intermediates
enable orthogonal transformations of all three carbons of the initial
allene framework into heterocyclic scaffolds that include pharmaceutically
relevant quinoxalines, imidazoles, oxazoles, and thiazoles. Finally,
the utility of this new strategic paradigm is demonstrated through
a concise, metal-free synthesis of the natural product clathrodin.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

sections.introduction:
Allenes are the simplest cumulenes, comprised
of three contiguous
unsaturated carbon atoms in the form of two orthogonal alkenes. Their distinctive electronic and geometric features
enable the installation of functionality across the entire C1–C3
framework of the allene, positioning these precursors as unique three-carbon
synthons in synthesis. Allenes can be
prepared from inexpensive, commercially available precursors and have
emerged as valuable building blocks for complex molecules, as exemplified
in the total syntheses of epoxomicin and rocaglamide ( Scheme A ). Despite these advances, general strategies able
to fully exploit the synthetic potential of allenes, particularly
through programmed, multisite functionalizations, remain an ongoing
challenge. In this context, oxidative allene trifunctionalizations
that furnish chemically distinct sites of reactivity ( Scheme B ) are attractive,
but are often limited by harsh or inconvenient reagents, overoxidation,
poor functional group tolerance, and the generation of unstable intermediates. , Once the oxidation step is initiated, intermediates are not isolable,
hampering the ability to program subsequent reactivity in a divergent
and tunable manner. Our group has a long-standing interest
in methods for allene trifunctionalization
( Scheme B ). Early work leveraged intramolecular nitrene transfer as a key
step to ultimately form amine-containing stereotriads, but an intermolecular
version of this chemistry was unsuccessful. , More
recently, we described an intermolecular electrooxidation of aryl-disubstituted
allenes capable of functionalizing all three allene carbons. Unfortunately, the scope was restricted to 1,1′-Ar/Me
substituted allenes, furnished poor yields and offered limited opportunities
for diversification. We envisioned leveraging electron-rich
and readily synthesized
alkoxyallenes as precursors to multifunctional,
isolable intermediates that act as versatile platforms for downstream
diversifications. We were especially interested in underexplored C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO adducts that combine
the stability of a TEMPO-protected enol with the reactivity of a conjugated
carbonyl system ( Scheme C ). Herein, we report selective alkoxyallene oxidation
to C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acroleins that function as versatile synthetic
linchpins. In contrast to our previous work with aryl allenes, this
chemistry gives rise to downstream orthogonal reactivity at the vinyl-TEMPO
and carbonyl sites for elaboration into heterocycles and bioactive
molecules. The mild reaction conditions, facile access to the alkoxyallene
precursors, broad functional group compatibility, and versatility
of this method provide a practical, programmable platform to transform
alkoxyallenes into complex molecular architectures, as demonstrated
by the synthesis of the pyrrole-imidazole alkaloid clathrodin.
sections.results and discussion:
The TEMPO group is widely employed
in organic synthesis, most commonly
as a persistent radical trap in mechanistic studies. Beyond this role, well-established methods to install C­(sp 3 )-TEMPO groups, particularly those adjacent to carbonyl groups,
are known. These include electrochemical and photoredox strategies,
as well as enantioselective α-oxyamination reactions mediated
by organocatalysis. Furthermore, alkene
difunctionalizations, as exemplified by azidooxygenations reported
from the Lin and Studer groups, provide access to C­(sp 3 )-TEMPO adducts that can be transformed into alcohols and ketones. , In contrast to C­(sp 3 )-TEMPO compounds, C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO adducts are comparatively rare and have not been well-explored. , We envisioned regioselective reaction of an alkoxyallene with TEMPO + , followed by hydrolysis ( Scheme C ) would furnish a product with
a unique combination of a stable enol ether and a conjugated carbonyl
group. These C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acroleins have the potential
to function as programmable linchpins, where the carbonyl and enol
handles can be diversified in an orthogonal manner to deliver new
heterocycles without the need for transition metal catalysis. Allene 1 was selected as a nonvolatile model substrate;
while other alkoxyallenes (e.g., methoxyallene) can be used, their
low boiling points and relative instability made determining overall
mass balance in our initial studies challenging. Optimized conditions
combine 1 with TEMPO + in 1:1 THF:H 2 O at 0 °C for 15 min ( Figure A, for full screening results, see Tables S2–S5 in the Supporting Information ). Increasing
the temperature to 25 °C or the time to 30 min resulted in decreased
yields of 2 , suggesting it may be prone to decomposition
( Figure A). In addition
to benzyl alkoxyallenes, tetrahydropyran (THP)-protection was tolerated.
Reaction in either acetonitrile or acetone gave lower yields, while
a 10:1 THF:H 2 O solvent mixture did not substantially affect
the outcome. A 1:10 THF:H 2 O mixture or H 2 O only
gave low conversion of 1 to 2 due to poor
substrate solubility. The scalability of the reaction was demonstrated
on a 1-gram scale
of 1 (6.84 mmol), affording TEMPO-acrolein 2 in 92% isolated yield as a crystalline white solid ( Figure B). Electrochemical oxidation
could also be employed using TEMPO instead of TEMPO+, delivering 2 in a comparable 77% yield ( Figure C, Supporting Information for details). The reaction exhibits good chemoselectivity
to form 2 even in the presence of other oxidizable functional
groups. Additives,
including alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, and heterocycles, gave good
conversion of 1 to 2 (72–93% yields)
and could be recovered in most cases ( Figure D). As 1 has a lower oxidation
potential than the alkene, alkyne, alcohol, and thiophene additives,
it engages TEMPO + BF 4 – in a
productive manner, while the anilines
oxidize in preference to 1 . Both radical and polar mechanisms
were considered in a brief computational study ( Figures S6 , S7 in the Supporting Information ) and appear plausible. The alkoxyallene may directly attack TEMPO+
to form an oxocarbenium ion, followed by hydrolysis; alternatively, oxidation of the allene to a radical cation,
followed by trapping with TEMPO, could form the TEMPO-acrolein adduct.
sections.reaction scope:
With a reliable method in hand to access 2 , the generality of the transformation was examined. We prioritized
substrates that introduce both structural complexity and useful handles
for further elaboration to highlight the utility of C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acroleins as programmable synthetic linchpins. Three key
features were of interest in the exploration of scope: (i) the ability
of the method to tolerate complex and strained precursors; (ii) the
potential for diastereoselective reactions to furnish stereochemically
rich scaffolds, and (iii) versatility in the installation of functionality
at C1 and C3 of the original allene. C1-monosubstituted alkoxyallenes
contain an acidic proton; treatment of 1 with n BuLi and various electrophiles furnishes disubstituted
allenes of the general structure 3 ( Figure ). Ketones ( 3a – n ), aldehydes ( 3p – u ), and an alkyl halide ( 3o ) readily furnished more elaborate alkoxyallenes, while a 1,3-disubstituted
allene 7 was accessed via prefunctionalization at C3
of the alkyne precursor 6 , followed by base-mediated
isomerization ( Figure , bottom left). Optimized conditions from Figure A were employed to evaluate the scope of
the oxidation
( Figure ). While most
alkoxyallenes could be prefunctionalized and isolated prior to oxidation,
the instability of certain substrates necessitated a one-pot protocol,
where crude intermediates were directly subjected to oxidation without
isolation. In these cases, complete conversion of the allene required
increased TEMPO + loading to quench residual base from the
preceding step. Under these conditions, 1 was converted
to cyclic TEMPO-acroleins 4a and 4b in good
yields. Acyclic alkoxyallenes 3c – d and
heterocycle-derived ketones 3e–g were transformed
to the corresponding TEMPO-acroleins 4c – d and 4e – g , respectively,
in moderate yields and modest dr for 4f . Precursors derived from natural products bearing ketones, including
(−)-carvone ( 3h ), (−)-menthone ( 3i ), cholestenone ( 3j ), and estrone ( 3k ),
were competent substrates, affording 4h – k in moderate yields ( Figure A). Steric interactions between the TEMPO and the ketone
framework are likely responsible for reduced yields, but the ability
to incorporate both functional group and stereochemical complexity
into the products underscores the versatility of this method. Finally,
alkoxyallenes derived from strained cyclic ketones, such as cyclobutanone
( 3l ), N -Boc azetidinone ( 3m ), and oxetanone ( 3n ), underwent oxidation to 4l–n , followed by a Wagner-Meerwein shift to deliver
ring-expanded products 5a – c . Note
these rearranged products reverse the position of the carbonyl and
alcohol groups as compared to 4a – k ( Figure B). Treatment of the anion of 1 with MeI gave the 1,1-disubstituted
allene 3o , which was converted to the corresponding TEMPO-acrolein 4o in good yield ( Figure C). A series of alkoxyallenes derived from aldehydes 3p – u , including citronellal, senescialdehyde
and (−)-myrtenal, were smoothly converted to the TEMPO-acroleins 4p – u ( Figure D). Notably, TEMPO-acrolein 2 itself could be employed as an electrophile to furnish 4u , introducing additional sites for diversification. Finally, 1,3-disubstituted
alkoxyallenes 7a and 7b , derived from alkynes 6v and 6w , successfully underwent oxidation to
yield the TEMPO-acroleins 4v and 4w respectively
( Figure E). Collectively,
these results demonstrate that a broad array of alkoxyallenes can
be converted into structurally diverse TEMPO-acroleins under mild
conditions, enabling convergent access to a unified class of multifunctional
TEMPO-acroleins as useful entry points for downstream synthetic elaborations.
sections.synthetic applications:
With mild conditions in hand
to generate diverse TEMPO-acroleins, we next evaluated the potential
of 2 as a diversifiable building block for the synthesis
of pharmaceutically relevant scaffolds. A defining feature of these
intermediates is the presence of two orthogonal reactive sites: a
conjugated aldehyde and a vinyl-TEMPO moiety. The vinyl-TEMPO moiety
acts as a protected enolate that may react with various electrophiles
( E ) to reveal an α-functionalized ketone ( Scheme A , right).
Meanwhile, the aldehyde group in 2 offers a versatile
entry point to classical aldehyde transformations to access a wide
range of other useful functional groups and heterocycles ( Scheme A , left). Representative examples that showcase the synthetic
utility of 2 are highlighted in Schemes B-D . Iodination of 2 furnished
trielectrophile 8 in 90% yield ( Scheme B ), which underwent a one-pot
condensation with 1,2-phenyldiamine to deliver the quinoxaline 9 in good yield. Quinoxaline
derivatives are of particular interest in medicinal chemistry due
to their broad range of physiochemical and biological properties;
the modularity of 2 provides a straightforward entry
into this valuable scaffold. In
a similar fashion, azidation of 2 , followed by
condensation with 1,2-phenyldiamine, afforded the azido-quinoxaline 10 in 69% yield. Subsequent Cu-catalyzed 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition
delivered triazole 9 in 55% yield. , These complementary pathways illustrate the potential for either
divergent polar (iodination) or radical (azidation) reactivities of
the TEMPO-acrolein motif. , Engaging the
carbonyl reactivity of 2 ( Scheme B ) via condensation
with 1,2-phenyldiamine, followed by oxidation, delivered the benzimidazole 12 , which was converted to α-iodo ketone 13 in quantitative yield. Isocyanate condensation
with phenyl toluenesulfonylmethyl isocyanide (Ph-TosMIC) and 2 afforded oxazole 14 in moderate yield, which
underwent iodination and S N 2 displacement with 2-mercaptopyridine
to afford imidazole 15 . A
similar isocyanate condensation was conducted on a precondensed variant
of 2 with 4-bromobenzylamine to afford imidazole 16 ; sequential treatment with I 2 and thiourea afforded
the heterobisaryl 17 . Oxazoles,
imidazoles, and thiazoles are naturally occurring secondary metabolites
derived from amino acids and show significant bioactivities. Julia-Kocienski olefination of 2 with tetrazole 18 and lithium bis­(trimethylsilyl)­amide
(LiHMDS) gave 19 ; iodination and condensation with 2-aminopyrimidine
gave
imidazo­[1,2-α]­pyrimidine 20 , a key precursor to
pyrrole-imidazole alkaloid (PIA) natural products. Finally, TEMPO-acrolein 4 proved amenable
to an iodination–condensation sequence to access more elaborate
heterocycles ( Scheme C ). For example, iodination of the α-ketol rearrangement
product 5a , followed by condensation with thiourea, yielded
thiazole 21 . Similarly, ketone adducts 4e and 4b were transformed into quinoxalines 22 and 24 via iodination and condensation with 1,2-phenylenediamine
and 4-bromo-1,2-diaminobenzene, respectively. Subsequent NaH-mediated
cyclization furnished heterospirocycles 23 and 25 , providing rapid entry to structurally complex scaffolds
in only three steps from benzoxyallene 1 and avoiding
the use of precious metal catalysis. Collectively, these transformations
demonstrate that TEMPO-acroleins function as three-carbon synthons
with programmable, site-selective reactivity at each position. To further highlight the potential of 2 as a useful
building block, it was applied to the total synthesis of clathrodin
( Scheme D ). Clathrodin is a pyrrole-imidazole
alkaloid isolated from the Caribbean sponge Agelas clathrodes and is structurally related to the brominated congeners oroidin
and hymenidin. The compound exhibits diverse biological activities
that include antimicrobial, antihistaminic, and cytotoxic properties. We envisioned a route in which the imidazole
fragment would arise from an imidazo­[1,2-α]­pyrimidine, itself
accessible from condensation of an α-halo ketones. Leveraging the vinyl-TEMPO motif as a protected
α-iodo ketone, the remaining fragment was installed through
Julia-Kocienski olefination of 2 , followed by iodination
and condensation to yield 20 ( Scheme B, right). From the imidazo­[1,2-α]­pyrimidine 20 , acid-mediated phthalimide deprotection afforded amine 26 in 96% yield. Subsequent amide coupling with the pyrrole
fragment gave 27 , and the last hydrazine-mediated deprotection
delivered clathrodin 28 in five steps from TEMPO-acrolein 2 with an overall yield of 22% with no precious metal catalysis.
sections.conclusion:
In summary, we have developed a new strategy
for versatile and
programmable allene reactivity through the use of C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acroleins as a unifying intermediate. This mild and operationally
simple strategy converts readily accessible alkoxyallenes into stable,
isolable C­(sp 2 )-TEMPO-acroleins as multifunctional intermediates.
The unique combination of a conjugated carbonyl moiety and a vinyl-TEMPO
motif enables orthogonal and sequential reactivity, supporting both
polar and radical transformations. This dual reactivity allows modular
access to structurally diverse heterocycles, including quinoxalines,
imidazoles, oxazoles, and thiazoles. Finally, the power of this multifunctional
platform is illustrated by a concise synthesis of clathrodin.

title: Latest in Resuscitation Research: Highlights from the 2025 American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.goal directed cardiopulmonary resuscitat: Xavier Jouven, MD, PhD (Université Paris Cité, Paris, France) showed that although changes in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) guidelines increased the estimated chest compression fraction from roughly 59% in 1998 to 68% to 69% under the 2010 to 2020 guidelines, an unintended result was more prolonged untreated ventricular fibrillation (VF) per cycle, increasing from about 11 seconds to 72 seconds. Because most VF recurrences occur within a minute post shock, this fixed 2‐minute cycle can delay needed defibrillation. Continuous rhythm analysis during CPR, using detectors that distinguish ECG rhythms despite compressions, could allow earlier shocks and shorten VF duration to 7 to 17 seconds while also increasing chest compression fraction to ∼75%. Daniel M. Rolston, MD, MSHPM (Northwell, New York, NY) presented on Doppler ultrasound guided CPR and highlighted its potential as a physiologic monitor in the future. He reviewed his team's prior work revealing Doppler ultrasound was more accurate than manual palpation and EtCO 2 for pulse detection, 1 , 2 especially when using peak systolic velocity measurements; and others' work showing it did not prolong interruptions. 3 Additionally, Dr Rolston presented their recently published study identifying intracompression Doppler ultrasound waveforms, which also demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy (88.9%) for subsequent pulse detection. 4 He closed with limitations and technologic advancements needed to expand use of Doppler ultrasound in diverse cardiac arrest settings. Sam Parnia, MD, PhD (NYU Langone Health, New York, NY) detailed the use of electroencephalography and cerebral oximetry to investigate cortical activation and recall of cognitive experiences that occur during resuscitation of in‐hospital cardiac arrest. His multicenter work in AWARE II (Awareness During Resuscitation II) showing intra‐arrest bursts of organized brain activity on electroencephalography and patient‐reported memories of consciousness/awareness challenged the assumption that the brain is entirely inactive in low‐flow cardiac arrest states. 5 These findings aligned with the clinical phenomenon of CPR‐induced consciousness, in which patients display outward signs of awareness, such as eye opening or purposeful movement, despite the absence of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Together, AWARE II and CPR‐induced consciousness provide preliminary evidence that the brain may not be entirely quiescent during CPR, underscoring the need for further research into the role of cerebral perfusion optimization during resuscitation. Hal Harry Shaffner Jr, MD (Johns Hopkins Medicine, Baltimore, MD) highlighted how patient‐specific physiology determines where an individual lies along the cardiac–thoracic pump continuum and how this should inform a personalized approach to chest compressions. He reviewed experimental and translational work comparing different physiologic targets for CPR optimization, including end‐tidal CO 2 –guided versus diastolic blood pressure–guided strategies, 6 and presented data from a neonatal and juvenile piglet model demonstrating that individualized, EtCO 2 ‐optimized compressions outperformed fixed‐depth standard CPR. 7 He also described emerging methods for dynamically adjusting hand position based on real‐time EtCO 2 responses to improve forward blood flow, underscoring the broader concept that chest compressions should be physiologically titrated rather than delivered as a one‐size‐fits‐all intervention.
sections.late\u2010breaking resuscitation science: This session was moderated by Anne Grossestreuer, PhD (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center) and Ari Moskowitz, MD, MPH (Montefiore Einstein). Robert Sutton, MD, MSCE (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) presented the first pediatric description of airway opening index, a metric to infer airway patency during CPR. Airway opening index was calculated from the oscillations in the end‐tidal waveform associated with each ventilation during chest compressions in a prospective multicenter observational study of 99 pediatric patients with in‐hospital cardiac arrest. A target airway opening index of 3 0.35 (range 0 [closed] to 1 [open]) was identified, which was associated with improved survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome and improved immediate postarrest physiology (lower lactates) despite similar CPR durations. 8 Paul Chan, MD, MS (Saint Luke's Mid America Heart Institute and the University of Missouri‐Kansas City) presented his work on the association between the Resuscitation Quality Improvement program for CPR training and cardiac arrest survival in hospitals. Using the Get With the Guidelines—Resuscitation registry they matched hospitals that implemented Resuscitation Quality Improvement, which uses high frequency (every 3 month) rather than every 2‐year CPR training, with those that did not. They then conducted a difference‐in‐difference analysis to compare the 2‐year postintervention versus 2‐year preintervention in‐hospital risk adjusted cardiac arrest survival and ROSC rates at Resuscitation Quality Improvement versus control hospitals. There was no difference in survival or ROSC in the hospitals implementing Resuscitation Quality Improvement. 9 Sam Parnia, MD, PhD (New York University Langone Hospital, New York, NY) presented his work on goal‐directed CPR using cerebral oximetry as a novel physiological target. Patients were randomized to usual care or cerebral oximetry where those with saturations <60% received physiologic brain directed resuscitation including changing chest compression characteristics (rate, depth, mechanical) or administering higher/additional vasopressors, steroids, or red blood cells. They included 93 patients and found no difference in sustained ROSC between the physiologic CPR group (58.7%) and the control group (68.1%). 10 Lars Wik, MD, PhD (Oslo University Hospital) presented a block‐randomized out‐of‐hospital clinical study evaluating the hemodynamic effects of adding active decompression with a piston device to standard mechanical CPR. Use of the device, which lifts the chest 3 cm above neutral position during decompression, compared with standard mechanical CPR, was associated with higher end tidal and systolic and mean arterial blood pressure at 5, 10, and 30 minutes of CPR and higher cerebral oximetry at 5 and 10 minutes of CPR. 11
sections.american heart association/japanese circ: The American Heart Association and Japanese Circulation Society Joint Session highlighted complementary perspectives from the United States and Japan on cardiac arrest prevention, population outcomes, and pharmacologic strategies, with a particular focus on young patients and registry‐based analyses. Dianne L. Atkins, MD (University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA) opened the session by emphasizing the importance of primary prevention of sudden cardiac arrest in children and young adults. She highlighted that many arrests in this population are attributable to inherited arrhythmia syndromes or structural heart disease with recognizable ECG abnormalities. Dr Atkins contrasted Japan's long‐standing school‐based ECG screening programs, implemented nationally since the 1990s, with screening practices in the United States, which remain largely limited to preparticipation athletic evaluations. She noted that broader screening efforts would require standardized ECG interpretation, stakeholder engagement, and scalable data infrastructure, with emerging machine learning tools offering potential future solutions. Tsukasa Yagi, MD, PhD (Nihon University Hospital) presented updated national data from the All‐Japan Utstein Registry, describing long‐term trends in out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrest outcomes. He demonstrated steady increases in bystander CPR and public access defibrillation rates over time, accompanied by improvements in survival, particularly among adults. Outcome gains among pediatric and adolescent patients were more modest, especially for nonshockable rhythms. Dr Yagi also highlighted sex‐based differences in bystander response among adolescents and young adults, with lower rates of bystander CPR and defibrillator use for female patients, underscoring the need for targeted public education. Mitsuaki Nishikimi, MD (Hiroshima University Hospital, Japan) focused on the role of epinephrine in nonshockable out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrest, emphasizing heterogeneity within this group, particularly between pulseless electrical activity and asystole. Using a registry‐based analysis with time‐dependent propensity score matching, he demonstrated that earlier epinephrine administration was more strongly associated with return of spontaneous circulation and survival in patients with asystole compared with those with pulseless electrical activity. Neurologic outcome differences were less consistent. These findings supported the concept that rhythm‐specific and time‐sensitive pharmacologic strategies may be important, while highlighting the need for prospective validation. Catherine Ross, MD (Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, MA) concluded the session by presenting the EpiDose trial, a randomized dose‐effect study evaluating periarrest epinephrine bolus dosing for hypotension in the pediatric intensive care unit. The trial compared 1.0 microgram per kilogram versus 0.5 microgram per kilogram dosing, with the primary outcome defined as short‐term systolic blood pressure response. Enrollment was limited by feasibility and funding constraints, resulting in a small sample size. Although higher‐dose epinephrine showed nonsignificant trends toward greater blood pressure increases and fewer repeat doses, substantial interpatient variability was observed. Dr Ross emphasized the operational challenges of conducting exception‐from‐informed‐consent trials in inpatient pediatric settings and highlighted important lessons for future physiologically targeted resuscitation studies.
sections.artificial intelligence \u2010powered li: This session was moderated by Dana Edelson, MD, MS (University of Chicago, Chicago, IL) and Michael Sayre, MD (University of Washington, Seattle, WA) and discussed new artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that could revolutionize resuscitation science and improve cardiac arrest outcomes. Natalia Trayanova, PhD (Johns Hopkins University) opened the session with an overview of advanced AI approaches for predicting cardiac arrest in high‐risk populations, focusing on deep learning models that integrate raw cardiac magnetic resonance imaging data with clinical variables. Dr Trayanova emphasized that multimodal deep learning substantially outperformed current guideline‐based approaches for stratifying the risk of lethal arrhythmias. Importantly, deep learning applied to raw magnetic resonance imaging scans could extract latent features not captured in routine clinical image interpretation, offering a path toward more precise and individualized risk assessment. Jacob Hutton, PhD (University of British Columbia, Vancouver, BC) presented the use of AI on wearable device data to improve outcomes through the early detection of unwitnessed out‐of‐hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs). His group trained their algorithms on physiological data from several patient cohorts including those in hospice, undergoing medically assisted death or withdrawal of life support in the intensive care unit, and healthy volunteers. Dr Hutton's work illustrated both the promise and the challenges of wearable‐based cardiac arrest detection: although machine learning approaches show clear potential, achieving high‐trust, clinically deployable systems will require richer data sets, improved modeling strategies, and careful attention to performance in real‐world conditions. Cindy Hsu, MD, PhD, MS (University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI) presented an update from her AI in CPR Optimization Grant funded by the American Heart Association. She described one of the primary barriers to the personalization of OHCA care as an inability to measure coronary perfusion pressure during CPR. Dr Hsu then provided a road map for INSIGHT‐CPR, a noninvasive sensor that uses an AI algorithm to provide real‐time blood pressure feedback during CPR. Lars Wik, MD, PhD (Oslo University Hospital, Norway) described one of the main challenges of OHCA care as identifying when ROSC occurs and introduced the idea that ballistocardiography signals could be used to develop an algorithm for automating this process. Sixty data segments from six patients who experienced OHCA were collected from both monitor/defibrillator files as well as ballistocardiography signals, which measure mechanical cardiac activity through body surface vibrations, on the carotid artery and chest. They successfully extracted fluctuations from the ballistocardiography signal representative of effective heartbeats and subsequently developed an AI algorithm that could detect ROSC.
sections.\u201cshock\u201d\u2010ing debates in ca: This session comprised 2 debates surrounding the “2025 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care”. 12 The first was titled “Resuscitation Guidelines: take ‘em’ or leave ‘em?’” with Michael Donnino, MD (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA) arguing the “con” position of the guidelines and Ashish Panchal, MD (The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH) arguing the “pro” position. Dr Donnino discussed how certain therapies dictated by advanced cardiovascular life support algorithms were not supported by high‐quality evidence, for example the 2‐minute interval of chest compressions between pulse checks. He also included clinical scenarios in which there were differences in practice and nuances not captured by the guidelines. He argued for the inclusion of differing viewpoints and historical changes in the guidelines and for a more open discussion of controversies, practice variation, and knowledge gaps. Dr Panchal followed with a discussion on the merits of the guidelines, including standardizing care, improving patient outcomes, and helping identify knowledge gaps. He emphasized that hospitals and emergency medical services agencies with the best outcomes had systems of quality assurance and standardized guidelines in place. 13 , 14 He agreed that although some variation of practice exists and there is room for furthering knowledge, having an established guideline‐driven standard of care protects patients and provides a frame of reference for medical decision making. In the second debate, “An Electrical Brawl: Double Sequential External Defibrillation vs Standard Defibrillation,” Sheldon Cheskes, MD (University of Toronto, Toronto, ON) argued for the use of double sequential external defibrillation and Charles Deakin, MD (University of Southampton, UK) argued in favor of standard defibrillation. Dr Cheskes, first author of the DOSE‐VF (Double Sequential External Defibrillation for Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation) trial, discussed the study's findings that patients randomized to double sequential external defibrillation had improved neurologic outcomes and higher percentage of patients surviving to hospital discharge compared with the standard group. 15 He also mentioned the promising results of the Double‐D pilot data using early double sequential external defibrillation (before 3 standard defibrillation attempts) showing improved survival (pilot data presented by Akil Awad, PhD, Karolinska Institutet, Solna, Sweden) at the European Resuscitation Council Congress in Rotterdam, October 2025. Dr Deakin rebutted with the argument that pad placement and the resultant vector may have explained the results of the DOSE‐VF trial. He also raised concerns regarding treatment compliance, misclassification of refractory versus recurrent ventricular fibrillation, and early closure of the trial, which may have biased results.
sections.best of the best abstract oral session: Roos Edgar, MSc (Radboud University Medical Center, Netherlands) presented “Towards Smartwatch‐Based Cardiac Arrest Detection: Validation in Shockable Cardiac Arrest,” the validation work of a wearable smartwatch to detect cardiac arrest using a photoplethysmography algorithm. 16 Fifty‐six patients from 4 university hospitals, who underwent induced cardiac arrest during implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator implantation (14 patients) or ventricular tachycardia ablation (42 patients), had the wristband applied during the procedure. Sensitivity of the device was 100% for VF and 90% for pulseless ventricular tachycardia detection, with 9 false positive alerts in the latter group. Patty Gessner, DNP (Ascension Illinois Alexian Brothers Medical Center, Elk Grove Village, IL) presented “The Benefits of Proactive versus Reactive Rapid Response Activations” in which she described rapid response activations using an AI early warning tool Electronic Cardiac Arrest Risk Triage. These ‘proactive’ rapid response activations were compared with standard ‘reactive’ protocols. Of a total of 16 589 rapid response activations, 39% were “proactive” based on Electronic Cardiac Arrest Risk Triage, representing about 6 activations per day. 17 One out of 6 patients received an intervention and 1 out of 36 was transferred to higher level of care. Jacob Hutton, PhD (University of British Columbia) in his talk “If It Can Help Someone, Then They Want to Do It: End of Life Studies for Wearable Cardiac Arrest Detection,” discussed feasibility and implementation of the use of wearable technology for cardiac arrest detection and data collection in patients at end‐of‐life for device validation. Patients undergoing Medical Assistance in Dying procedures and patients in hospice were prospectively enrolled. Data from 64 patients were collected, representing about 28% of patients who were approached for consent. The study found that wearable‐based research in end‐of‐life settings was feasible, yielded useful data, and participant feedback was positive. 18 So‐Young Jeon, MD (Chungnam National University Hospital, Republic of Korea) presented “Beyond Blood‐Brain Barrier Disruption and Molecular Weight: Compartmental Kinetics of S100B and NSE [Neuron‐Specific Enolase] for Neurological Prognostication After Cardiac Arrest.” In this retrospective observational study of registry data from 111 survivors of OHCA treated with targeted temperature management who had a lumbar catheter in place, the levels of S100B and neuron‐specific enolase were investigated for use in neuroprognostication using serum and cerebrospinal fluid levels. 19 The investigators found that serum S100B peaked early after ROSC and then declined despite persistently elevated levels in the cerebrospinal fluid, compared with neuron‐specific enolase, which peaked at 72 hours and remained elevated in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. The findings suggested that S100B may have utility in the early phase rather than the late phase for neuroprognostication, whereas elevated neuron‐specific enolase remained a more consistent predictor of poor neurological outcome over time.
sections.beating the unexpected: predicting and p: This session was moderated by Sana Al‐Khatib, MD, MHS (Duke University) and Sara Stephens, PhD, MPH (Baylor University). Enrico Baldi, MD, PhD (Fondazione IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo di Pavia, Italy) presented “A Tale of Mandatory Screening in Pediatric Non‐Professional Athletes,” his team's research on screening nonprofessional athletes for cardiac causes of potential sudden cardiac death in Italy. He compared the cost of screening with the potential monetary benefit of implementing such screening for hospital systems. He reinforced the value of presports screening with impressive data demonstrating improved cardiovascular outcomes for children whose pathologies were identified at presports screenings. Gregory Webster, MD, MPH (Northwestern University, Chicago, IL) presented his team's work on evaluating families referred after a child had a cardiac arrest to determine potentially heritable causes of the sudden cardiac death. He described the importance of autopsy reports on screening guidance and future care for patients affected by identifiable causes of sudden cardiac death. Importantly, follow up screening in children alone yielded an identifiable diagnosis in only 10% of cases. Dr Webster highlighted that thorough evaluation of both parents markedly improved the likelihood of finding a potentially heritable cause. Bjorn Knollman, MD, PhD (Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN) shared his team's work on targeted therapies for arrhythmogenic sudden cardiac arrest. He explored the genetic mechanisms involved in sudden cardiac death outlining the key role of calcium channelopathies in many of these arrests and highlighted the importance of screening patients for specific variants of long QT syndrome. He noted that children with structural heart defects are at especially high risk of sudden cardiac death and that dantrolene is an exciting, effective treatment to decrease ventricular arrhythmias in children whose ventricular arrhythmias are associated with structural heart defects.
sections.targeting inflammation to improve cardia: This session was moderated by Teresa May, DO (Maine Medical Center, Portland, ME), Jing Li, MD (University of Illinois Chicago), and Tiffany Ko, PhD (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, PA). Edy Kim, MD, PhD (Brigham and Women's Hospital, Boston, MA) opened the session by presenting mechanistic insights into early innate immune activation after cardiac arrest. His team showed that by 6 hours after ROSC, immune cell transcriptomes differed markedly between patients who later achieved good versus poor neurologic outcomes, but these differences disappeared by 48 hours, highlighting initial hours after cardiac arrest may represent a window for therapeutic intervention in the resolution of inflammation. 20 He noted that targeting single inflammatory pathways such as IL‐6 (interleukin‐6) was unlikely to be effective given the complexity of postarrest immune responses. 21 Instead, he described approaches aimed at enhancing endogenous protective mechanisms, including activation of the Nectin‐2/TIGIT (T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains) immune checkpoint pathway, stimulation of sulfatide‐responsive natural killer T cells, and delivery of IL‐10 messenger RNA via myeloid‐targeted nanoparticles, all of which have improved inflammatory profiles and neurologic outcomes in preclinical models. David Seder, MD (Maine Medical Center) discussed adaptive immunity and its protective role after cardiac arrest. He presented compelling evidence that CD73‐expressing lymphocytes, which generate immunoregulatory adenosine (a key anti‐inflammatory mediator), are associated with survival and reduced inflammatory injury. 22 Conversely, he showed that immature CD10‐negative neutrophils were disproportionately elevated in nonsurvivors and migrated into the brain, contributing to delayed neuroinflammation. 23 He concluded that CD73‐positive lymphocytes promote adenosine generation, enhance microcirculatory perfusion, and suppress inflammatory myeloid activity, whereas immature CD10‐negative neutrophils drive delayed tissue injury. Based on these findings, he proposed future therapeutic strategies aimed at augmenting CD73 lymphocytes, strengthening adenosinergic pathways, modulating immature neutrophil activity, and ultimately exploring immunomodulatory approaches in human trials. Wei Yang, PhD (Duke University, Durham, NC) then shifted attention to the subacute phase after cardiac arrest which is marked by profound immunosuppression, characterized by severe lymphopenia and significant thymic and splenic atrophy. He demonstrated that this immune collapse is driven by activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis and heightened glucocorticoid signaling, triggered in part by increased hypothalamic cytokines such as IL‐1β and TNF‐α (tumor necrosis factor alpha). 24 Using T‐ and B‐cell specific glucocorticoid receptor knockouts, as well as pharmacologic blockade with the glucocorticoid receptor antagonist, his team showed that preserving lymphocyte development reduces lymphoid organ atrophy, lowers bacterial infection burden, and improves neurologic recovery. He concluded that postcardiac arrest immunity progresses through 2 distinct phases, an early inflammatory surge followed by a delayed glucocorticoid mediated immunosuppressive state, which may contribute to postarrest infections and represents a promising therapeutic target. Laust Obling, MD, PhD (Copenhagen University Hospital, Denmark) presented results from the STEROHCA (Steroid Treatment After Resuscitated Out‐of‐Hospital Cardiac Arrest) randomized controlled trial, which evaluated a single prehospital dose of high‐dose methylprednisolone administered immediately after ROSC. 25 The intervention produced a marked early anti‐inflammatory response, with significantly lower IL‐6 and several other proinflammatory cytokines at 24 hours, alongside higher early IL‐10 levels. Patients receiving steroids exhibited more stable hemodynamics, requiring less norepinephrine and overall vasoactive support during the first 48 hours. Although biomarkers of brain injury did not differ between groups, adjusted analyses indicated a possible survival advantage. He emphasized that the trial established the feasibility and safety of early glucocorticoid therapy in the prehospital setting and noted that these findings set the stage for larger outcome‐powered trials currently underway.
sections.basic/translational abstract oral sessio: Jun Hagiwara, MD, PhD (Nippon Medical School, Tokyo, Japan/Becker Laboratory, Feinstein Institute, Manhasset, NY) presented delayed mitochondrial transplantation in a 10‐minute rat cardiac arrest model. 26 Animals received intravenous mitochondria at 30 and 60 minutes post ROSC; mitochondrial transplantation was associated with improved neurological function at later time points (48–72 hours) and reduced histologic evidence of neuronal degeneration and microgliosis (IBA‐1 [ionized calcium‐binding adaptor molecule 1]), supporting a delayed therapeutic window and implicating postresuscitation neuroinflammation as a potential modifiable pathway. Clark G. Owyang, MD (Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY) described the establishment of a swine extracorporeal CPR (ECPR) platform integrating biventricular pressure–volume loop assessment during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) flow ramping. 27 Following 10 minutes of no‐flow VF and a 10‐minute low‐flow CPR period, animals were cannulated for fem‐fem ECMO, then ramped across stepwise flows (15 → 30 → 45 → 60 mL/kg/min). With increasing ECMO flow, both ventricles showed reductions in stroke volume and progressive ventriculoarterial uncoupling, with more pronounced uncoupling in the right ventricle, highlighting the importance of chamber‐specific physiology during eCPR and providing a translational platform for studying personalized resuscitation and ECMOmanagement. Louis Silva, MD (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) presented a pediatric swine asphyxial arrest study linking noninvasive cerebral optical monitoring to an invasive marker of cerebral metabolic injury. 28 Using hybrid diffuse optical spectroscopy to measure cerebral oxygenation metrics during CPR and cortical microdialysis to quantify lactate–pyruvate ratio after ROSC, the group trained machine‐learning models showing that mean cerebral tissue oxygen saturation and oxyhemoglobin features during early CPR segments explained a meaningful portion of subsequent peak lactate–pyruvate ratio variance. These data supported the feasibility of using optical signals obtained during CPR as real‐time correlates of cerebral metabolic stress. Laura Faiver, MD (University of Pittsburgh, PA) presented a clinical translational study evaluating cerebral physiology in comatose patients after cardiac arrest monitored with jugular bulb catheters. 29 She focused on the jugular venous–arterial CO 2 gap as a pragmatic adjunct to jugular venous oxygen saturation interpretation, hypothesizing that CO 2 gap could distinguish diffusion‐limited hypoxia (eg, perivascular edema/microvascular dysfunction) from impaired oxygen use in patients with elevated jugular venous oxygen saturation. In a single‐center retrospective cohort, jugular venous oxygen saturation decreased after hyperosmolar therapy primarily among patients with an elevated cerebral CO 2 gap, suggesting the CO 2 gap may help identify a treatment‐responsive subgroup and motivating prospective protocolized validation. The final abstract, presented by Darci Anderson (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) used hybrid diffuse optical methods (frequency‐domain diffuse optical spectroscopy plus diffuse correlation spectroscopy) to compare cerebral hemodynamics across CPR strategies in a pediatric swine asphyxia arrest model. 30 Piglets were randomized to hemodynamic‐directed CPR targeting higher versus lower systolic/diastolic pressure goals, or to depth‐directed CPR. In intention‐to‐treat analyses, targeting higher blood pressure did not yield clear improvements in cerebral oxygenation or blood flow, largely because many animals could not sustain the higher systolic target over the CPR epoch; in a per‐protocol analysis restricted to animals meeting targets, higher pressure targeting increased cerebral oxygenation without a corresponding increase in cerebral blood flow, underscoring both the physiologic appeal and the practical challenges of consistently achieving aggressive hemodynamic targets during resuscitation.
sections.clinical abstract oral session: This session was moderated by Audrey Blewer, PhD, MPH (Duke University) and Ryan Coute, DO (University of Alabama at Birmingham). Alexander Presciutti, PhD, MSCS (Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA) began the session by presenting his work on a resilience intervention titled Recovering Together after Cardiac Arrest, designed for survivors of cardiac arrest and their caregivers. Using a mixed‐methods design, his team confirmed the feasibility of the Recovering Together after Cardiac Arrest intervention and observed clinically meaningful reductions in emotional distress among participants. 31 Kunihiko Maekawa, MD (Hokkaido University Hospital, Japan) then presented his research examining the association between bystander CPR type and outcomes following drowning‐related cardiac arrest. 32 Using national data from the All‐Japan Utstein OHCA registry, his team found that both compression‐only CPR and conventional CPR with rescue breathing were associated with improved survival, with conventional CPR resulting in the highest likelihood of a neurologically favorable outcome. David Seder, MD (Maine Health, Portland, ME) presented his work titled “Brain Oxygen and ICP [Intracranial Pressure] Optimization in Severe Post‐Cardiac Arrest (BOOSCA).” He outlined a novel clinical protocol for invasive intracranial pressure and brain tissue oxygenation monitoring and management in selected patients after cardiac arrest. 33 In a cohort of 10 patients, his team found that intracranial hypertension and brain hypoxia were treatable, and that targeted management may reduce secondary neurological injury during the postcardiac arrest period. Guro Kruger, MD (Trondheim University Hospital, Norway) introduced the audience to her team's efforts to identify ROSC after defibrillation using a hands‐free carotid Doppler ultrasound system (RescueDoppler). 34 The team analyzed 36 shocks across 13 patients with various causes. Twelve patients had some form of spontaneous circulation present on the Doppler demonstrating that this technology could identify a successful defibrillation in real time. Tom Aufderheide, MD, MS (Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, WI) shared results from a real‐world implementation of the Zoll Real BVM technology to improve ventilations during OHCA within the target rate (8–12 breaths/min) and volume (500–600 mL/breath). 35 Two hundred seventy‐eight patients were enrolled over a 15‐month period. The Real BVM technology was activated after 3 months. There was a statistically significant change in the compliance of ventilation parameters after the activation without any change in the chest compression performance measures.
sections.max harry weil early career award compet: Three finalists, Mohammad Abdel Jawad, MD, MS (St. Luke's Hospital Kansas City, MO), Lindsay Shepard, MD, MSCE (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia), and Sara Stephens, PhD, MPH (Baylor University, Waco, TX) competed in the Max Harry Weil Award Competition for Resuscitation Science. Dr Jawad presented a study from CARES (Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival) that found a graded inverse relationship between time to bystander CPR and survival outcomes in pediatric OHCA. 36 Dr Shepard presented her work identifying novel ventilation rate thresholds associated with improved survival outcomes in children with in‐hospital cardiac arrest. 37 Dr Stephens' presentation also focused on pediatric OHCA, outlining differences in characteristics between children of different races and ethnicities. 38 Following the presentations, an international panel of expert judges awarded the 2025 Max Harry Weil Early Career Investigator Award to Dr Shepard. The 3CPR Mid‐Career Award recognizes a midcareer investigator whose endeavors and achievements have made a significant impact on cardiopulmonary care and resuscitation science. This year's awardee was Jonathan Elmer, MD, MS (University of Pittsburgh). Dr Elmer presented his vision for the future of resuscitation science, with an emphasis on safeguarding scientific integrity against censorship and other external threats.
sections.funding opportunities: Glenn Dillon, PhD (American Heart Association) and Norman Paradis, MD (Zoll Foundation, Chelmsford, MA) provided an overview of current and forthcoming funding opportunities for investigators at all career stages. The session opened with Dr Dillon announcing that the American Heart Association, the largest nongovernmental funder of cardiovascular research in the United States, 39 had allocated a record level of research funds for FY2025 to 2026. These funds will be used to expand existing mechanisms across career stages, increase support for early‐career investigators, provide 1‐year extensions for projects originally scheduled to conclude in 2025, and launch several new funding initiatives. Dr Paradis then highlighted funding opportunities available through the Zoll Foundation for early‐stage investigators. He emphasized that “early‐stage” is defined not by the investigator's age but by their level of research experience. Eligible applicants should be nonindependent investigators (ie, those without R‐level awards as principal investigator) working under the mentorship of an established investigator with relevant scientific expertise. The Zoll Foundation supports a broad range of applicants, including paramedics, nurses, PhD scientists, and physician–scientists.
sections.pumped up: unveiling the opportunities o: This session was moderated by Remle Crowe, PhD (ESO Solutions, Inc., Austin, TX), Adam Gottula, MD (The University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN), Katrina Augustin, MD (Mayo Clinic, Rochester. MN), and Anna Condella, MD (University of Washington). The discussion centered on emerging strategies, implementation challenges, and system‐level considerations surrounding ECPR for refractory OHCA. Georg Trummer, MD (University of Freiburg, Breisgau, Germany) opened the session with a presentation on controlled automated reperfusion of the whole body, a next‐generation approach to ECPR designed not only to provide circulatory support but also to actively counteract whole‐body ischemia–reperfusion injury. 40 He described controlled automated reperfusion of the whole body as a therapeutic platform rather than a support device, engineered to restore perfusion with precise pressure, flow, and metabolic control. He highlighted historical limitations of conventional ECMO, the physiological challenges of prolonged CPR, and preclinical evidence showing that controlled reperfusion can markedly reduce myocardial edema and improve organ recovery after prolonged cardiac arrest. Next, Andrea Elliott, MD (University of Minnesota) addressed real‐world implementation challenges in ECPR. She emphasized that the success of an ECPR program depends on 3 key components: patient selection, timing, and cannulation strategy. She noted that refractory VF/ventricular tachycardia with witnessed arrest and immediate bystander CPR remains the most promising target population, although survival declines substantially with each minute of delay. She discussed barriers to effective ECPR implementation, including transport logistics, early identification of eligible patients, rapid emergency department activation, trained teams, and readiness, which implies continuous availability. Her presentation underscored that ECPR outcomes depend as much on system design as on the procedure itself. The session then shifted to a dynamic debate examining whether field‐initiated ECPR should be adopted. Melissa Vogelsong, MD (Stanford University, Stanford, CA) argued in favor of prehospital initiation, presenting a scenario of refractory VF where intra‐arrest transport and early cannulation could offer the only pathway to survival. She highlighted the substantial proportion of patients who remain in shockable rhythms long enough to benefit from ECPR and summarized emerging data suggesting that reducing low‐flow time, even by minutes, could be lifesaving. Her argument framed field ECPR as a logical extension of high‐performance emergency medical services care in select systems capable of rapid response and coordinated workflow. In contrast, Jose Cabanas, MD, MPH (The University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC) articulated the challenges, risks, and system‐level implications of attempting ECPR in the field. He mentioned that geography, transport times, staffing, and overall emergency medical services resource constraints fundamentally limit scalability. He argued that ECPR is not primarily a scientific challenge but an infrastructure challenge that demands multidisciplinary coordination among emergency medical services, cardiology, surgery, critical care, and hospital leadership. He raised safety concerns related to intra‐arrest transport, lack of universal clinical consensus, and the risk of diverting resources from interventions with broader population impact, such as improving on‐scene CPR and defibrillation. He underscored that only systems that consistently achieve survival with good neurologic function through conventional care should consider expanding into ECPR.
sections.conclusions: The 2025 American Heart Association Resuscitation Science Symposium brought together investigators from across disciplines to present advances spanning basic, translational, clinical, and implementation science in resuscitation. Across sessions, recurring themes included increasing emphasis on physiologically guided CPR, refinement of monitoring strategies during and after cardiac arrest, and growing attention to survivorship, equity, and system‐level performance. Novel technologies, including Doppler‐based hemodynamic assessment, cerebral monitoring, andAI–enabled tools, highlighted the field's continued shift toward more individualized and data‐informed resuscitation care. At the same time, debates surrounding guideline implementation, defibrillation strategies, and ECPR underscored persistent knowledge gaps and the importance of rigorous evaluation before widespread adoption. Collectively, the work presented at Resuscitation Science Symposium 2025 reflected a maturing resuscitation science ecosystem that increasingly integrates mechanistic insight, clinical trial data, and health systems research to improve outcomes after cardiac arrest. Continued collaboration, thoughtful translation of emerging evidence, and attention to implementation and equity will be essential to realizing the full impact of these advances.
