Traditional small molecules, such as betulin, fatostatin, and PF-429242, interfere with the canonical SREBP pathway by inhibiting nuclear transcriptional activity, blocking SCAP translocation, or suppressing S1P processing, respectively. However, their tissue selectivity and off-target effects remain major obstacles to clinical translation. By contrast, the novel Insig1/2 loop 1 short peptide represents a more sophisticated strategy: By competitively binding to phosphorylated PCK1, a tumor-specific activation node, it precisely blocks oncogenic signal-driven non-canonical SREBP activation. Although its peptide nature relies on advanced delivery systems, the concept of ‘precisely intervening with aberrant signals while preserving normal feedback’ paves a new direction for the development of safer and more effective metabolic-antitumor therapies.
sections.upstream pathway inhibitors: The upstream pathways of SREBPs include key regulatory nodes such as the PI3K-AKT pathway and mTORC1 pathway. Aberrant activation of these pathways drives SREBP activation, thereby promoting lipid synthesis and tumor progression. Corresponding targeted inhibitors can indirectly inhibit SREBP activity by blocking upstream signal transduction. The PI3K-AKT pathway regulates the translocation and activation of SREBPs. As a classic PI3K-specific inhibitor, LY294002 targets PI3K, an upstream activator of AKT. LY294002 blocks PI3K-mediated AKT activation, thereby disrupting the translocation of SREBP's cochaperone SCAP from the ER to the Golgi apparatus. Ultimately, it inhibits the processing and maturation of SREBP-1c and SREBP-2, downregulates the expression of their downstream genes related to cholesterol and FA synthesis, and reduces lipid synthesis in tumor cells ( 164 ). In HCC, LY294002 blocked the AKT/mTOR pathway, thereby inhibiting SREBP1 activity and lipogenesis ( 165 ). In in vitro experiments on human ccRCC 786-O cells, treatment with LY294002 for 48 h suppressed the mRNA expression of PI3K, Akt and mTOR in a concentration-dependent manner. This indicated that LY294002 can reduce the activation level of SREBP [that is, decreased nuclear SREBP (n-SREBP)] by inhibiting this core pathway in ccRCC cells, demonstrating its inhibitory effect on the upstream pathways of SREBP ( 166 ). Du et al ( 164 ) further demonstrated that LY294002 significantly inhibited statin-induced SREBP-2 processing and activation in 13A/PS cell experiments. Additionally, it suppressed IGF-1-triggered SREBP activation, thereby reducing intracellular synthesis of cholesterol and FA. Collectively, these findings highlight LY294002 effective blocking effect on the upstream pathways of SREBP. AKT Inhibitors, AKT can phosphorylate PCK1 to endow it with protein kinase function, which in turn phosphorylates Insig1/2. This phosphorylation impairs the cholesterol-binding capacity of Insig1/2, releasing the SCAP-SREBP complex to promote SREBP activation. AKT inhibitors can suppress the kinase activity of AKT, preventing the phosphorylation of PCK1 and subsequent phosphorylation of Insig1/2. This blocks the aberrant activation of SREBP at the source, reducing tumor lipid synthesis. Additionally, in triple-negative BC (TNBC) ( 167 ), AKT inhibitors suppressed its regulation of SREBP-2, preventing tumor cells from surviving through cholesterol synthesis compensation. It has been revealed that when AKT inhibitors are combined with statins, they can inhibit the SREBP-related cholesterol homeostasis pathway, leading to GGPP depletion and impaired protein geranylgeranylation in tumor cells, ultimately inducing cell death ( 167 ). The two agents exhibited a synergistic lethal effect, providing a basis for combination therapy targeting the upstream pathways of SREBP. The mTORC1 serves as a critical upstream regulatory node for SREBP. Its sustained activation maintains SREBP-1 activity, promoting lipid synthesis in tumor cells to resist ferroptosis. As a mTORC1-specific inhibitor, CCI-779 directly reduces mature SREBP-1 levels, suppresses expression of its downstream target gene SCD1, and decreases mono-unsaturated FA synthesis. This approach disrupts tumor cell resistance to ferroptosis while simultaneously severing the mTORC1-SREBP1-mediated lipogenesis pathway ( 168 ). In cancer cells harboring mutations in the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, CCI-779 treatment can effectively restore the sensitivity of cancer cells to the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 and reduce the level of mature SREBP1. In animal models, the combination of mTORC1 inhibitors and ferroptosis inducers achieved nearly complete tumor regression, an effect dependent on the inhibition of the SREBP1 pathway ( 134 ). These pathways regulate numerous cellular processes, with SREBP inhibition being one of their effects. They serve as key nodes connecting cell growth signals and metabolic reprogramming and have been extensively studied in various models of cancers and metabolic diseases.
sections.downstream key enzyme inhibitors: In addition to upstream pathway inhibitors, inhibitors targeting key downstream enzymes in SREBP-driven malignant tumor progression have also demonstrated significant therapeutic potential. Key enzymes in the FA synthesis pathway, such as ACC and FASN, are important downstream targets of SREBPs. As a rate-limiting enzyme in FA synthesis, ACC catalyzes the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, providing substrates for FA synthesis. ACC inhibitors (for example, ND-646) suppress ACC activity to reduce malonyl-CoA production, thereby blocking FA synthesis ( 169 ). In various cancer cell experiments, ACC inhibitors significantly reduced the level of FA synthesis in tumor cells, inhibited tumor cell proliferation, and induced cell apoptosis. For instance, in non-small cell LC cells, treatment with ACC inhibitors downregulated the expression of genes related to intracellular FA synthesis, resulting in significant inhibition of cell proliferation. Moreover, when combined with chemotherapeutic drugs, the antitumor effect was enhanced ( 170 ). In HCC, ACC inhibitors suppressed FA synthesis in HepG2 cells, reduced propionyl-CoA and FA synthesis in rat livers, inhibited tumor proliferation, and enhanced survival rates in tumor-bearing rats when used alone or in combination with the multi-kinase inhibitor sorafenib ( 169 ). In summary, ACC inhibitors represented by ND-646 can effectively disrupt the essential lipid supply for rapid tumor cell proliferation by specifically targeting the rate-limiting enzyme in the first step of FA synthesis. They demonstrated promising antitumor potential in preclinical studies. This strategy provides a significant direction for developing novel therapies targeting metabolic vulnerabilities in tumors. FASN inhibitors, FASN is a key multifunctional enzyme in the FA synthesis pathway that catalyzes the synthesis of long-chain FAs from malonyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. FASN is highly expressed in various tumor tissues and is closely associated with malignant tumor progression and poor prognosis. FASN inhibitors (for example, C75) affect tumor cell function at three levels by reducing FA synthesis: i) Membrane structure disruption: Decreasing the phospholipid content of cell membranes and inhibiting tumor cell migration and invasion ( 171 ); ii) Energy deprivation: Blocking the supply of FAs as energy substrates and suppressing mitochondrial OXPHOS ( 172 ); iii) signaling pathway interference: Reducing the production of lipid-derived signaling molecules (for example, prostaglandins and phosphatidylinositol) and inhibiting oncogenic pathways such as NF-κB and Wnt ( 173 , 174 ). Chen et al ( 175 ) demonstrated that in addition to inhibiting cytoplasmic FASN, C75 can also bind to HsmtKAS, a key enzyme in the mitochondrial FA synthesis pathway. This action reduces lipoic acid production, impairs mitochondrial function, and leads to accumulation of ROS and decreased cell viability. Impaired mitochondrial function directly cuts off an important energy supply pathway for tumor cells, while also affecting lipid synthesis and indirectly disrupting the integrity of the tumor cell membrane. In TNBC experiments, C75 inhibited FASN activity to downregulate the expression of downstream target genes in the SREBP1 pathway, thereby reducing lipid synthesis. Concurrently, it suppressed tumor cell glycolysis and glutaminolysis, achieving ‘multi-metabolic pathway blockage’ ( 176 ). In addition, key enzymes in the cholesterol synthesis pathway, such as HMGCR, are also important downstream targets of SREBPs. As a rate-limiting enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway, HMGCR catalyzes the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonic acid, a crucial step in cholesterol synthesis. Statins, including simvastatin and atorvastatin are common HMGCR inhibitors ( 177 ). In tumor therapy, statins can reduce intracellular cholesterol levels in tumor cells and affect cell membrane fluidity and function ( 178 ), and also regulate tumor cell metabolism and proliferation by modulating the SREBP signaling pathway ( 143 ). Studies have shown that statins exhibited antitumor effects in various tumors, such as PC, BC and colorectal cancer (CRC). They can inhibit tumor cell proliferation, induce cell apoptosis, suppress tumor metastasis, and enhance therapeutic efficacy when combined with other antitumor drugs ( 179 – 181 ). Roy et al ( 182 ) further confirmed that when statins are combined with apalutamide for the treatment of advanced PC, they prolonged patients' overall survival. The statins inhibit tumor cell proliferation by regulating the androgen receptor signaling pathway. In addition, they interfere with the structure of membrane lipid rafts in tumor cells, affecting cancer cell signal transduction and forming a synergistic anticancer effect with apalutamide. It has been shown that long-term treatment with BRAF inhibitors led to epigenetic silencing of PGC-1α in melanoma cells, thereby forming a highly invasive drug-resistant subpopulation ( 183 ). As HMGCR inhibitors, statins can specifically target this subpopulation: The suppression of PGC-1α reduces the expression of RAB6B and RAB27A. Statins decrease the prenylation levels of these two RAB proteins, reducing their membrane association, leading to disruption of integrin localization and downstream signals required for growth, and ultimately inhibit the proliferation of drug-resistant melanoma cells. In addition, statins can precisely block the MVA pathway, disrupt cholesterol homeostasis in p140Cap BC cells, impair cell membrane fluidity, and interfere with lipid raft-related signal transduction, ultimately significantly reducing the survival rate of this type of BC cell. Whether used alone or in combination with chemotherapeutic drugs, statins decreased the survival rate of p140Cap BC cells ( 184 ) These downstream key enzyme inhibitors directly act on critical enzymes in the metabolic pathways regulated by SREBPs, precisely interfering with the metabolic processes of tumor cells, and providing new strategies and directions for tumor therapy.
sections.combination therapy strategy: Targeting the SREBP pathway reshapes tumor lipid metabolism, improves the TME, and alleviates immunosuppression. It forms multi-dimensional synergy with chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), significantly enhancing antitumor efficacy and overcoming drug resistance. The main core mechanisms are: i) Metabolic reprogramming sensitization: Inhibiting SREBP reduces de novo synthesis of FAs/cholesterol, decreases membrane fluidity and drug efflux, and increases the accumulation of chemotherapeutic/targeted drugs. Collectively it impairs tumor energy reserves and offsets drug resistance-related metabolic compensation (for example, PI3K/AKT/mTOR-driven lipid synthesis bypass) ( 185 ); ii) TME immune remodeling: Downregulating tumor PD-L1 and CD47, enhances CD8+T cell infiltration and cytotoxicity; inhibits SREBP-dependent functions and PD-1 expression of intratumoral Tregs, reducing immunosuppression; promotes macrophage M1 polarization and decreases M2-type pro-tumor markers, enhancing antigen presentation ( 186 ). Combination with chemotherapy [for example, SREBP inhibitors (Fatostatin/FGH10019) + docetaxel] can increase the proportion of membrane unsaturated lipids, enhance membrane permeability and drug accumulation; inhibit SREBP downstream targets HMGCS1/IDI1, and promote PARP cleavage and apoptosis. In PC3 ×enograft tumors, the tumor inhibition rate of the combination group reached 78%, which was 40% higher than that of the monotherapy group; the accumulation of docetaxel in tumor tissues increased by 2.1-fold, the proportion of membrane unsaturated FAs increased by 65%, the level of cPARP cleavage increased by 3.5 times, and the proportion of apoptotic cells reached 45% ( 185 ). SREBP inhibitor (Pen-H) + 5-fluorouracil (5-Fu) inhibits SREBP1-mediated lipogenesis, blocks tumor metabolic compensation, and enhances DNA damage and cell cycle arrest. In a gastric cancer model, compared with monotherapy, the combined treatment of Pen-H and 5-Fu exhibited a stronger inhibitory effect on cell proliferation and tumor growth ( 185 ). SREBP1 Inhibitor + Paclitaxel/Carboplatin: Obesity upregulates SREBP1, which alters the TME and induces chemoresistance; inhibiting SREBP1 can reverse this process and restore chemosensitivity. After treatment with standard-of-care chemotherapy combined with an SREBP1 processing inhibitor, tumor recurrence is significantly reduced, and the peritoneal immune landscape is also altered ( 187 ). The combination of gemcitabine (GEM) and nab-paclitaxel (nab-PTX) can inhibit the proliferation and de novo lipogenesis of pancreatic cancer cells. The specific mechanism is that the combination of GEM and nab-PTX induces ATP depletion in pancreatic cancer cells and activates AMPK, which in turn inhibits the expression and nuclear translocation of SREBP1, ultimately suppressing de novo lipogenesis in pancreatic cancer cells ( 188 ). In combination with targeted therapy, SREBP peptide inhibitor + lenvatinib blocks the PCK1-Insig1/2 interaction to inhibit SREBP activation, cuts off the alternative lipid energy source of tumors, and overcomes anti-angiogenic resistance. In a HCC model, the tumor volume of the combination group was reduced by 35% compared with the monotherapy group, and the survival period was prolonged by 30% ( 163 ). SREBP inhibitor + PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitor induce dual inhibition of the upstream activation pathway and downstream metabolism of SREBP, blocking the positive feedback loop of ‘PI3K activation → SREBP nuclear translocation → lipid synthesis’. In various solid tumor models, the combination overcomes monotherapy resistance and synergistically inhibits proliferation and metastasis. In a melanoma model, the tumor growth inhibition rate reached 70% (monotherapy <35%), and the Akt-SREBP positive feedback loop was blocked ( 31 ). In combination with ICIs, regorafenib + ICI: Regorafenib reverses immunosuppression and enhances ICI efficacy by regulating the IFN-γ/NSDHL/SREBP1/TGF-β1 axis. Regorafenib inhibits SREBP1 through restoring NSDHL, thereby reducing the production of the immunosuppressive factor TGF-β1, decreasing Treg infiltration, and improving the tumor immune microenvironment ( 189 ). Targeting the SREBP pathway achieves significant synergistic enhancement of the efficacy of chemotherapy, targeted therapy and ICIs through triple coordination of metabolism, immunity and signaling pathways, with particularly prominent potential in tumors with active lipid metabolism and immunosuppressive phenotypes. Future clinical trials are needed to further verify the safety and efficacy of combination regimens and optimize biomarker-guided personalized treatment strategies.
sections.challenges and future outlook: Despite the great potential of SREBPs as anticancer targets, translating SREBP-targeted strategies into clinical practice faces substantial challenges, numerous of which are rooted in the complex, context-dependent biology of SREBPs and limitations of the current tools. The major hurdles, controversies and contradictory findings in the field are discussed below, and specific recommendations for future research are provided.
sections.context-dependent and paradoxical functi: A critical and nuanced aspect of lipid reprogramming is that while SREBP activity overwhelmingly drives tumor progression, its continuous hyperactivation can create context-dependent vulnerabilities under specific metabolic stresses. In most malignancies, including HCC, BC, ccRCC, PC, CRC and hematological malignancies, SREBP1 and SREBP2 are consistently recognized as oncogenic drivers that promote lipogenesis, proliferation, invasion and drug resistance. However, emerging evidence suggests that under certain extreme metabolic contexts, aberrant SREBP signaling may become detrimental for cancer cell survival ( 190 , 191 ). Mechanistically, this context-dependency may arise from: i) The dominant SREBP isoform and downstream lipid outputs (SREBP1-associated fatty-acid programs vs. SREBP2-linked cholesterol/MVA pathways); ii) tissue-specific metabolic crosstalk with other pathways such as p53 or Wnt signaling; iii) harsh metabolic microenvironments including nutrient deprivation, severe hypoxia, or lipid-induced ER stress (lipotoxicity) ( 121 ); and iv) differences in cellular stress responses, such as altered sensitivity to ferroptosis driven by polyunsaturated FA accumulation ( 192 ). This complexity means that while SREBPs are potent oncogenic drivers, targeting them requires an intricate understanding of the tumor's metabolic state, as their hyperactivation might render certain cancer cells exquisitely vulnerable to specific metabolic or oxidative stressors. Future studies must clarify these context-specific metabolic trade-offs before broad clinical application.
sections.major limitations of current srebp-targe: Existing therapeutic approaches targeting SREBPs suffer from multiple critical limitations that impede clinical translation: i) Lack of tumor specificity and off-target toxicities. SREBPs are essential for physiological lipid homeostasis in liver, adipose tissue and intestinal cells; therefore systemic inhibition causes hepatotoxicity, hyperlipidemia, metabolic disorders, or intestinal dysfunction, which severely limits safe dosing; ii) poor druggability of SREBP TFs, SREBPs are conventionally considered ‘undruggable’. Thus, most current agents instead target SCAP, S1P, or downstream enzymes, which only indirectly block SREBP activity and often have off-target effects; iii) compensatory metabolic resistance. Tumors frequently activate bypass pathways such as enhanced lipid uptake, FA oxidation, or autophagy to resist SREBP inhibition, leading to therapeutic failure; iv) variable efficacy across preclinical models. Numerous SREBP inhibitors showed robust effects in cell culture but weak antitumor activity in vivo , partly due to poor pharmacokinetics, low tumor penetration and rapid metabolism ( 193 ); v) Lack of predictive biomarkers. There are still no validated clinical biomarkers to identify ‘SREBP-addicted’ tumors, which leads to potential treatment failure in unselected patients.
sections.specific recommendations for future rese: The following focused research directions are proposed to overcome the aforementioned limitations and resolve contradictory evidence:
sections.i) precise biomarkers and functional str: Future studies should identify biomarkers that can predict functional dependence on the SREBP pathway. Such biomarkers may include specific genomic features, metabolomic signatures and lipidomic profiles. For example, lipidomic alterations associated with therapeutic resistance may enable selection of SREBP-dependent subgroups. Liquid biopsy approaches based on the tumor metabolic characteristics (for example, circulating cell-free DNA methylation profiling and lipidomics) may further support non-invasive patient stratification and response monitoring ( 194 , 195 ).
sections.ii) improved tumor-selective delivery: As selectivity is central to safety, delivery systems should be optimized to enhance intratumoral exposure while reducing normal-tissue effects. Nanocarriers (for example, pH-sensitive liposomes) and targeted delivery modalities such as antibody-drug conjugates may improve drug accumulation at the tumor sites and potentially improve therapeutic index ( 196 , 197 ). Beyond tumor accumulation, future research should quantify tumor penetration depth, intracellular delivery efficiency and exposure-response relationships.
sections.iii) rational combination strategies to: Single-agent SREBP inhibition may trigger adaptive metabolic rewiring. Hence, combination strategies that target complementary metabolic checkpoints or transcriptional adaptation mechanisms may enhance efficacy. For instance, combining SREBP pathway inhibition with epigenetic regulators (for example, HDAC inhibitors) or metabolic checkpoint inhibitors (for example, glutaminase inhibitors) may help overcome resistance arising from network-level compensation.
sections.iv) synthetic lethality and vulnerabilit: Synthetic lethality provides a route to tumor specificity. Systematic identification of gene mutations or metabolic vulnerabilities that interact with SREBP pathway inhibition may yield tumor-selective therapeutic opportunities. Such approaches should be functionally validated using patient-derived models.
sections.v) temporal and spatial intervention bas: SREBP activity can change during tumor progression, metastasis, and in response to prior therapies. Therefore, future studies should optimize treatment timing (for example, relative to chemotherapy or immunotherapy) and evaluate how SREBP-targeting affects therapy-resistant populations or metastasis-initiating cells.
sections.conclusion: SREBPs represent a fundamental metabolic nexus that links oncogenic signaling with the aberrant lipid phenotypes essential for tumor progression. The present review has synthesized evidence demonstrating that SREBPs are not merely passive downstream effectors, but active drivers of a self-reinforcing feedback loop that sustains membrane synthesis, redox balance and immune evasion. However, the prevailing ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach for targeting SREBPs is increasingly challenged by emerging evidence of cancer-type-specific functions and adaptive metabolic rewiring. The transition from broad-spectrum lipid inhibition to individualized precision medicine remains the most critical frontier. Future research must prioritize the identification of robust biomarkers to define ‘SREBP-addicted’ tumor subtypes and explore synthetic lethal vulnerabilities that can overcome the compensatory resistance. By shifting focus toward the spatial and temporal dynamics of SREBP signaling within the TME, next-generation interventions can move beyond the preclinical stage to achieve clinical breakthroughs. Ultimately, deciphering the contextual duality of SREBP biology is crucial for unlocking its full therapeutic potential in lipid-dependent malignancies. In summary, SREBPs are not merely lipogenic enzymes but master integrators of oncogenic signals and metabolic outputs. Their targeting, when guided by precision medicine principles, offers a viable path to improve the outcomes in patients with lipid-addicted cancers.

title: Comparison of perioperative chemotherapy and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in locally advanced resectable distal esophageal/esophagogastric junction (EGJ) adenocarcinomas
abstract: Objective To compare the real-world outcomes of perioperative chemotherapy (ChT) and neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in patients with locally advanced resectable distal esophageal and esophagogastric junction (EGJ) adenocarcinomas, with respect to pathological response, overall survival (OS), and recurrence-free survival (RFS). Materials and methods This retrospective cohort study included 119 patients treated between 2016 and 2025 at a tertiary oncology center. Patients received either perioperative ChT ( n = 68) or neoadjuvant CRT ( n = 51) followed by curative-intent surgery. Baseline clinicopathological characteristics were comparable between groups. Survival outcomes were analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared with the log-rank test. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were constructed to identify independent prognostic factors for OS. Results A total of 119 patients were included, with comparable baseline characteristics between groups. Neoadjuvant CRT achieved higher pathological complete response and downstaging rates ( p = 0.034 and p = 0.005), but no significant difference in overall survival (OS) ( p = 0.944) or recurrence-free survival (RFS) ( p = 0.449) was observed. In subgroup analyses, neoadjuvant CRT showed a trend toward improved OS in EGJ stage II ( p = 0.078) and a significant RFS benefit in distal stage II ( p = 0.014), whereas perioperative ChT demonstrated a significant OS advantage in EGJ stage III ( p = 0.020). Treatment modality was not an independent predictor of OS, while nodal involvement was the strongest adverse prognostic factor. Conclusion Neoadjuvant CRT improved pathological response but did not provide a survival advantage over perioperative chemotherapy in the overall population. Subgroup analyses suggested stage- and location-dependent differences, although these findings are hypothesis-generating. Both strategies showed comparable survival outcomes, supporting individualized treatment selection. Larger prospective studies are needed for validation.

sections.introduction: Locally advanced resectable (cT2–T4 or cN1–3, M0) esophageal and esophagogastric junction (EGJ) adenocarcinomas represent a major global health challenge due to their rising incidence and persistently high mortality. In this patient population, long-term survival can only be achieved through multimodal treatment approaches. Currently, perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT constitute the principal therapeutic strategies. The survival benefit of perioperative ChT was first demonstrated in the MAGIC trial, in which perioperative administration of epirubicin–cisplatin–5-FU (ECF) significantly improved both OS and disease-free survival (DFS) [ 1 ]. Subsequently, the phase III FLOT4 trial established the FLOT regimen as the contemporary standard for perioperative treatment, demonstrating higher pathological complete response (pCR) rates, superior survival outcomes, and improved tolerability compared with ECF [ 2 ]. Neoadjuvant CRT was introduced by the CROSS trial, which reported a substantial survival advantage, particularly in squamous cell carcinoma, and a more modest yet clinically meaningful benefit in adenocarcinoma [ 3 ]. Although the CROSS regimen increased pCR rates, the optimal treatment strategy for adenocarcinoma remains controversial. The Neo-AEGIS phase III trial directly compared these approaches and reported improved tumor regression and pCR rates with CRT; however, no superiority in OS or DFS was demonstrated compared with perioperative ChT [ 4 ]. Importantly, because most patients in the chemotherapy arm received the ECF regimen, these findings may not fully reflect outcomes achievable with modern FLOT-based regimens. This limitation was addressed by the ESOPEC trial, which demonstrated superior OS and RFS with perioperative FLOT compared with Neoadjuvant CRT (CROSS) [ 5 ]. Similarly, the TOPGEAR trial showed that the addition of CRT to perioperative ChT improved pathological response without translating into a statistically significant survival benefit [ 6 ]. Based on accumulating evidence, current guidelines (NCCN v4.2025) recommend perioperative FLOT chemotherapy as a preferred treatment strategy for locally advanced resectable esophageal and EGJ adenocarcinomas [ 7 ]. Despite these contemporary randomized phase III trials, several important knowledge gaps persist. Trial populations often differ from real-world cohorts in terms of comorbidity burden, performance status, treatment adherence, and evolving chemotherapy practices. Moreover, subgroup-specific real-world data focusing on anatomically distinct entities such as distal esophageal and esophagogastric junction adenocarcinomas remain limited. In addition, the interaction between nodal burden, tumor localization, and treatment modality outside strictly controlled trial settings has not been fully characterized. Therefore, real-world evidence is needed to complement randomized data and to inform individualized treatment decisions in routine clinical oncology practice. In this study, we aimed to compare treatment responses as well as OS and RFS between patients treated with perioperative ChT and those receiving neoadjuvant CRT in a real-world institutional cohort, and to evaluate the concordance of our findings with contemporary international evidence.
sections.data collection: This retrospective cohort study included patients diagnosed with locally advanced resectable esophageal and esophagogastric junction (EGJ) adenocarcinoma who underwent multimodal treatment at our hospital between 2016 and 2025. A total of 119 patients were enrolled in the study following a review of the institutional oncology database and medical records. Inclusion criteria were histopathologically confirmed diagnosis of esophageal or EGJ adenocarcinoma, locally advanced resectable disease according to TNM classification (cT2–T4 and/or cN1–3, M0), receipt of curative-intent perioperative ChT or neoadjuvant CRT, planned and performed surgical treatment, availability of complete pre-operative clinical and radiological data, and a minimum follow-up period of 6 months. Exclusion criteria were metastatic disease at baseline (M1), histological subtypes other than adenocarcinoma (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma), receipt of palliative treatment only, incomplete treatment, inability to undergo surgery, missing data, and age < 18 years. Patients were stratified into two groups based on the treatment regimen administered: perioperative ChT ( n = 68) and neoadjuvant CRT ( n = 51). Patient characteristics, including age, gender, tumor localization, clinical stage, treatment protocol, progression and mortality status, and follow-up duration, were recorded. Clinical staging was performed according to the TNM classification, based on CT, PET/CT, and endoscopic evaluation results. Treatment response was classified postoperatively as complete response, partial response, stable disease, or progressive disease. Ethical committee approval for the study was obtained, and all data were anonymized to ensure patient confidentiality. Clinical nodal stage was categorized according to the AJCC/UICC TNM classification as N0, N1, N2, and N3. For consistency, identical nodal definitions were applied across baseline descriptive tables and multivariable regression models. Flow diagram illustrating patient selection and cohort derivation is provided (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow Diagram of Patient Selection and Cohort Derivation
sections.statistical analysis: In this study, the sociodemographic, clinical, surgical–pathological, and survival outcomes of patients receiving perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT were compared. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA); all tests were two-sided, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± standard deviation or median according to distribution characteristics, whereas categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. For comparisons of baseline characteristics between treatment groups, Pearson’s chi-square test was used for categorical variables when expected cell counts were adequate, and Fisher’s exact test was applied when they were not. Independent samples t-test was used for continuous variables. This approach was applied to assess whether baseline clinical parameters—such as age, sex, tumor localization (distal/EGJ), clinical T stage, clinical N stage, and overall clinical stage—were balanced between the two treatment groups. Within the scope of surgical and pathological outcomes, resection status (R0/R1), pathological T stage, pathological N stage, and overall pathological stage were compared according to treatment groups. Pearson’s chi-square test was used for multilevel categorical variables such as pathological T stage and pathological staging, while Fisher’s exact test was preferred in tables with low event counts or small expected cell frequencies. This allowed evaluation of the relationship between neoadjuvant CRT and pathological response/downstaging, as well as potential differences compared with perioperative ChT, based on objective postoperative pathological data. For survival analyses, OS was defined as the time from diagnosis to death from any cause; patients who were alive were censored at the last follow-up date. RFS was defined as the time from surgery to the first RFS; cases without events were censored at the last follow-up date. OS and RFS probabilities were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and differences between treatment groups were evaluated using the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. For clearer clinical interpretation, 2-year and 5-year survival rates and median survival times (with 95% confidence intervals when applicable) were reported. In subgroups where the median could not be calculated, the “median not reached” approach was adopted and displayed as “–” in the tables, reflecting that survival probability did not fall below 50% during follow-up. To assess the independent effects of treatment strategy and selected prognostic variables on OS, multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were constructed. This retrospective study adopted a multivariable regression approach to evaluate the independent effect of treatment modality on survival. Treatment type (perioperative ChT or neoadjuvant CRT) was included as the primary explanatory variable in all multivariable models. Covariates to be included in the models were selected based on clinical relevance, previously established prognostic factors in the literature, and the characteristics of the dataset. In this context, age, sex, tumor location, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, and pathological variables were considered as potential confounding factors. Given the relatively limited study population and the low number of events in some subgroups, the number of variables included in each model was deliberately restricted to preserve model stability and reduce the risk of overfitting. Accordingly, a stepwise modeling strategy was adopted. Model 1 included clinical variables, Model 2 included pathological variables, and Model 3 represented a parsimonious model including only the key prognostic indicators. In addition, treatment type was retained as the main independent variable in all multivariable models. In accordance with reviewer recommendations, the modeling strategy was planned stepwise and three separate models were reported: (i) Clinical Model (Model 1): Included age (continuous), sex, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, tumor localization, and treatment type, in order to evaluate the simultaneous effects of preoperative clinical factors. (ii) Pathological Model (Model 2): Included age and sex together with pathological stage (T categories) and resection margin status (R1), aiming to investigate the prognostic value of postoperative pathological features. (iii) Parsimonious Model (Model 3): To increase model stability and reduce the risk of overfitting, this model focused only on key pathological markers and was limited to pathological nodal status (N stage) and resection margin status (R1). Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals were reported for these models, and results were presented in forest plot format to facilitate visual comparison. Subgroup analyses were prospectively planned to evaluate the consistency of survival differences within clinically relevant subgroups (e.g., distal vs. EGJ localization and combinations of clinical Stage II–III) and were interpreted as exploratory/hypothesis-generating. However, in certain subgroups with very low event counts or marked imbalance between treatment arms, Cox models failed to converge or produced excessively wide confidence intervals. To avoid misleading interpretations, hazard ratios were not reported in subgroups where reliable estimates could not be generated; instead, findings were presented by jointly evaluating the overall pattern of Kaplan–Meier curves and log-rank test results in a transparent and cautious manner. Hazard ratios were presented with 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.2 statistical software. Among the constructed models, Model 1 (clinical model) was defined as the primary multivariable model addressing the main research question. Models 2 and 3 were considered sensitivity analyses and are presented in the supplementary materials. Detailed chemotherapy regimen information was not included in the analysis due to incomplete and heterogeneous documentation across patients. Inclusion of such variables could introduce misclassification bias and reduce the internal validity of comparisons; therefore, treatment was analyzed at the strategy level (perioperative ChT vs. neoadjuvant CRT).
sections.sociodemographic, baseline clinical, and: In Table 1 , the sociodemographic and clinical characteristics of patients who received perioperative ChT ( n = 68) and neoadjuvant CRT ( n = 51) were compared. No statistically significant difference was observed between the groups in terms of mean age (65.77 ± 10.37 vs. 62.27 ± 13.96; p = 0.122). Similarly, the categorical age distribution (< 60 and ≥ 60 years) was comparable between the groups ( p = 0.182). The distribution of clinical T stage (T1–T3) and clinical N stage (N1–N3) was also similar between treatment groups ( p = 0.965 and p = 0.458, respectively). When recurrence status was compared, no significant difference was identified between the groups ( p = 1.000), indicating a similar distribution of recurrence rates across treatment groups. Although no statistically significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics and follow-up outcomes, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Given the retrospective and non-randomized nature of the study, residual confounding cannot be excluded, even in the absence of statistically significant differences between groups. Therefore, subsequent survival analyses were interpreted within the context of potential baseline imbalances inherent to observational study designs. Overall, no statistically significant differences were observed between the groups regarding sociodemographic characteristics, baseline clinical stage, administered treatment regimens, mortality, or recurrence rates (all p > 0.05). Although no statistically significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of full comparability between groups. Given the retrospective and non-randomized design, residual confounding may still influence the observed associations, and therefore subsequent analyses should be interpreted within this context.
sections.surgical and pathological outcomes: In Table 2 , surgical and pathological characteristics were compared between the treatment groups. No statistically significant difference was observed between the neoadjuvant CRT and perioperative ChT groups in terms of resection status (R0/R1) ( p = 0.221, Fisher’s Exact test). This finding indicates that both treatment approaches yielded similar outcomes with respect to achieving negative surgical margins. The distribution of pathological T stage differed significantly between the groups ( p = 0.034, Pearson’s Chi-square test). The neoadjuvant CRT group demonstrated a higher proportion of T0 cases, representing pathological complete response, whereas advanced T stages (particularly T3–T4) were more frequently observed in the perioperative ChT group. This suggests that neoadjuvant CRT may have a more pronounced effect on tumor regression and pathological downstaging. No statistically significant difference was found between the groups in terms of pathological N stage ( p = 0.663). The similar distribution of lymph node involvement indicates that the two treatment groups were comparable regarding nodal response. Although no statistically significant differences were observed, residual confounding cannot be excluded. In contrast, a significant difference was observed in overall pathological staging ( p = 0.005). The neoadjuvant CRT group had a higher proportion of Stage 0 patients, whereas Stage III patients were more prevalent in the perioperative ChT group. These findings support the notion that the pathological downstaging effect was more pronounced in the neoadjuvant CRT group. sections.overall survival (os) analysis: Upon examination of Table 3 , the median OS for the entire cohort was calculated as 53.0 months (95% CI: 42.3–63.7), with survival probabilities of 65.4% at 2 years and 37.9% at 5 years. These findings indicate a considerable accumulation of events during long-term follow-up, with the survival curve showing a marked downward trend around the 5-year time point. Median OS was 36.0 months (21.9–50.1) in the perioperative ChT group and 54.0 months (40.5–67.5) in the neoadjuvant CRT group. However, the log-rank p-value of 0.944 indicates no statistically significant difference between the OS curves of the two groups. Thus, in this dataset, no OS superiority of either treatment modality was demonstrated in the overall population. In subgroup analyses stratified by distal tumor location and clinical stage, the Distal–Clinical Stage II subgroup showed 2- and 5-year OS rates of 46.2% and 15.4% for perioperative ChT and 66.7% and 26.6% for neoadjuvant CRT. Median OS was 18.0 months (3.3–32.8) for perioperative ChT, whereas for neoadjuvant CRT it was reported as “–”, indicating that the median could not be calculated during follow-up (primarily due to low event count and survival not dropping below 50%). Although the log-rank p-value was 0.164 and therefore not statistically significant, a numerical trend favoring neoadjuvant CRT was observed. In the Distal–Clinical Stage III subgroup, 2- and 5-year OS rates were 54.4% and 29.8% for perioperative ChT, and 51.8% and 26.6% for neoadjuvant CRT. Median OS was 33.0 months (17.3–48.7) in the perioperative ChT group and 30.5 months (2.8–58.1) in the neoadjuvant CRT group. There was no major divergence between the treatment approaches in terms of survival rates or medians, consistent with the log-rank p-value of 0.443, indicating no significant OS difference in Distal Stage III patients. In contrast, more pronounced differences were observed in the EGJ localization subgroups. In the EGJ–Clinical Stage II subgroup, the 2- and 5-year OS rates were 69.4% and 0.0% for perioperative ChT, and 91.7% and 78.6% for neoadjuvant CRT. The log-rank p-value was 0.078, suggesting a borderline significant difference ( p < 0.10). The higher 2- and 5-year OS rates in the neoadjuvant CRT group indicate that the survival curve generally remained higher. However, the 5-year OS rate of 0.0% in the perioperative ChT group may reflect a very small risk set at that time point, where a few events dramatically reduced the survival estimate (this issue is further addressed in the “problematic points” section below). The most notable finding of the study was observed in the EGJ–Clinical Stage III subgroup: the 2- and 5-year OS rates were 85.7% and 51.4% for perioperative ChT, compared with 57.1% and 42.9% for neoadjuvant CRT. Median OS was 70.0 months (46.9–93.1) in the perioperative ChT group and 53.0 months (0.0–150.9) in the neoadjuvant CRT group. With a log-rank p-value of 0.020, a statistically significant OS advantage favoring perioperative ChT was demonstrated in this subgroup. This finding suggests that treatment selection may have a more pronounced impact on OS in patients with EGJ tumors and advanced stage disease; however, given the subgroup nature of this analysis, this interpretation should be made with caution. In subgroup analyses, it should be considered that limited sample size and low event counts in certain categories may lead to greater uncertainty in Kaplan–Meier estimates, particularly at later time points. Specifically, 5-year survival rates may become more variable due to the decreasing number of patients remaining at risk during that time interval. This may result in lower-than-expected survival rates or abrupt changes in 5-year survival estimates in some subgroups. Additionally, in certain subgroups, the median OS time was not reached and is indicated as “–” in the table. This notation signifies that the survival probability did not fall below 50% during the follow-up period and therefore the median value could not be calculated (median not reached). Accordingly, the findings were interpreted not solely based on survival rates at individual time points, but by jointly evaluating the overall pattern of the Kaplan–Meier curves and the results of the log-rank test. Furthermore, the subgroup analyses are exploratory in nature and intended to generate hypotheses. Therefore, the reported p-values should be interpreted cautiously, taking into account the clinical context and the sample size.
sections.recurrence-free survival (rfs) analysis: Upon examination of Table 4 , the 2-year RFS rate was calculated as 91.7%, and the 5-year RFS rate as 65.7%. However, the median RFS time was not reached in the overall analysis. This finding is consistent with the relatively low number of events (recurrences) during the follow-up period and the fact that the survival curve did not fall below 50%. When comparing treatment modalities, no statistically significant difference in RFS was observed between the perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT groups (log-rank p = 0.449). In both groups, the 2-year RFS rates were high, and although differences were observed in long-term (5-year) rates, these differences did not reach statistical significance. In the Distal – Clinical Stage II subgroup, a statistically significant difference was identified between the groups ( p = 0.014). The absence of events in the neoadjuvant CRT group (100% RFS) is noteworthy. In contrast, the perioperative ChT group demonstrated lower 2- and 5-year RFS rates. This finding suggests a potential treatment-related difference within this specific subgroup. In the Distal – Clinical Stage III subgroup, a borderline statistically significant difference was observed ( p = 0.072). The 2- and 5-year RFS rates appeared higher in the perioperative ChT group. However, as the p-value exceeded 0.05, this finding should be interpreted as a trend rather than a statistically significant difference. In the EGJ – Clinical Stage II subgroup, no significant difference was detected between the groups ( p = 0.172). The 2-year RFS rates were similar, while variability was observed in the 5-year rates. Likewise, in the EGJ – Clinical Stage III subgroup, no statistically significant difference was found ( p = 0.402). Although 2-year RFS rates were high in both groups, heterogeneity was present in long-term outcomes. Overall, the RFS analyses demonstrate heterogeneous results across subgroups. While a notable difference was observed in the Distal Stage II subgroup, no statistically significant differences were demonstrated in the other subgroups. In particular, the presence of zero or very few events in certain subgroups prevented the calculation of median survival times and resulted in artificially inflated survival rates. Therefore, the subgroup findings should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive, and should be interpreted with caution rather than used for firm conclusions. Although subgroup analyses were performed as part of the prespecified analysis plan, it should be emphasized that, due to the limited sample size and number of events, these findings need to be interpreted alongside multivariable models and validated in future studies with larger cohorts. Examination of the OS curves in Fig. 2 demonstrates that survival distributions are largely similar between the perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT groups. In both groups, a noticeable decline in survival rates is observed in the early period, followed by a more horizontal plateau phase. Fig. 2 OS According to treatment modality Throughout the follow-up period, the survival curves occasionally intersect and do not exhibit a clear or sustained pattern of separation. This finding supports the absence of a significant long-term OS advantage between the groups. Indeed, the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test revealed no statistically significant difference between the two treatment modalities ( p = 0.944). Censored observations are distributed at regular intervals in both groups, indicating comparable follow-up durations. At later time points, wider step formations are observed in the curves due to the decreasing number of patients at risk. Examination of the Kaplan–Meier RFS curves presented in Fig. 3 shows that high survival rates were maintained in the early period in both treatment groups. Throughout the follow-up period, the curves for the perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT groups largely follow a parallel course, without a distinct or sustained pattern of separation. Fig. 3 RFS According to treatment modality During the early and mid-term follow-up, RFS rates remained above 90% in both groups. At later time points, stepwise declines were observed due to an increase in the number of events and a decrease in the number of patients at risk. However, the difference between the curves appears clinically limited, and the log-rank test did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference between the groups. The regular distribution of censored cases in both groups indicates comparable follow-up durations. Nevertheless, due to the low total number of events and the high censoring rate, uncertainty increases in long-term survival estimates. This finding underscores the need for caution when interpreting long-term RFS rates. In conclusion, when the Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank analysis are considered together, no statistically significant difference in RFS was observed between the treatment modalities.
sections.multivariable cox regressions and subgro: In the primary multivariable Cox regression model (Model 1), the adjusted effect of treatment modality on OS did not reach statistical significance (HR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.48–1.54; p = 0.600). In this study, three separate multivariable Cox regression models were constructed to evaluate the independent prognostic factors affecting OS. In the multivariable Cox regression analysis performed within Model 1, treatment modality, age, sex, clinical T stage, clinical N stage, and tumor location were simultaneously included in the model to evaluate their independent effects on OS. Regarding the treatment variable, no statistically significant difference in survival was observed between patients receiving perioperative ChT and those receiving neoadjuvant CRT (HR = 0.85; 95% CI: 0.48–1.54; p = 0.600). The inclusion of 1 within the confidence interval and a p-value greater than 0.05 indicate that there is no significant difference in survival between the treatment groups. Age was included in the model as a continuous variable, and a one-year increase was not found to have a significant effect on survival (HR = 1.00; 95% CI: 0.97–1.03; p = 0.882). Similarly, for the sex variable, when female patients were evaluated relative to the reference category, no statistically significant difference was observed (HR = 1.26; 95% CI: 0.65–2.46; p = 0.494). For clinical T stage, the hazard ratios for the T2 and T3 subgroups were HR = 1.51 (95% CI: 0.43–5.29; p = 0.515) and HR = 1.96 (95% CI: 0.51–7.50; p = 0.325), respectively. However, the wide confidence intervals and non-significant p-values indicate that this variable is not a statistically significant predictor in the model. When clinical N stage was examined, no significant difference was found for the N1 level (HR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.48–1.96; p = 0.928), whereas a statistically significant increase in risk was observed for the N3 stage (HR = 2.39; 95% CI: 1.11–5.15; p = 0.026). This finding indicates that, after adjustment for other variables, patients with N3 disease have a significantly higher risk of mortality. In terms of tumor location, tumors located at the esophagogastric junction (EGJ) did not show a statistically significant effect on survival compared to distal localization (HR = 0.67; 95% CI: 0.36–1.23; p = 0.196). Overall, the multivariable model demonstrates that only clinical N3 stage is a statistically significant independent prognostic factor, while the other variables do not reach statistical significance. The forest plot findings support these results, showing that only the confidence interval for the clinical N3 subgroup does not cross the reference line of 1, whereas all other variables have confidence intervals that include 1. This visually confirms that most variables in the model do not have a statistically significant effect on survival. Hazard ratios were estimated relative to predefined reference categories. Under these circumstances, reporting hazard ratios could be statistically misleading; therefore, hazard ratios for these specific subgroups were deliberately not presented in the tables and forest plot displays. This approach was adopted to prevent overinterpretation of statistically invalid results and to ensure transparency in the analysis. In line with the reviewers’ comments, the scope of the analyses in this study was expanded, and three separate multivariable Cox regression models were constructed to more comprehensively identify independent prognostic factors for OS. Model 1 included clinical parameters, Model 2 incorporated postoperative pathological variables, and Model 3 was a parsimonious model focusing on the key prognostic indicators. When evaluated together, these models consistently demonstrated the determinant role of nodal involvement on survival. In the clinical model, N3 stage was found to be statistically significant. İn the parsimonious model, pathological N1 and N3 stages independently increased the risk of mortality. Thus, the impact of nodal burden on survival was confirmed across different modeling approaches. Conversely, the lack of statistical significance for variables such as age, sex, tumor location, and resection margin in the multivariable analyses does not imply absence of effect. Rather, it may reflect the relatively limited number of events and small sample sizes in certain subgroups, which may have resulted in widened confidence intervals. Indeed, the presence of broad confidence intervals and borderline significance levels in some categories suggests limited statistical power. Therefore, results were interpreted by considering both the clinical context and the structure of the sample. In response to reviewers’ concerns regarding model stability and the risk of excessive variable loading, the models were deliberately structured in a stepwise and controlled manner. Particularly in the third model, a more simplified approach was adopted, focusing only on the most clinically meaningful variables in order to preserve an appropriate event-to-variable ratio. This strategy reduced the risk of overfitting while allowing the principal prognostic factors to be more clearly identified. Although wide confidence intervals were observed in certain categories due to low event counts in subgroup analyses, this does not undermine the consistency of the findings; rather, it demonstrates that the results were reported with appropriate caution. Overall, the additional analyses strengthened the methodological robustness of the study and contributed to a more detailed and transparent presentation of independent effects on survival.
sections.discussion: In this real-world retrospective cohort of patients with locally advanced resectable distal esophageal and EGJ adenocarcinoma, neoadjuvant CRT was associated with significantly higher pathological complete response and tumor downstaging rates compared with perioperative ChT. However, multivariate analysis results indicate that, despite regression in pathological T stage, no significant improvement in overall survival was observed; this finding suggests a potential dissociation between tumor downstaging and long-term survival benefit. This situation is consistent with several contemporary randomized trials directly comparing multimodal strategies [ 8 – 11 ]. The Neo-AEGIS and TOPGEAR trials demonstrated improved pathological response rates with CRT but did not show clear survival superiority over chemotherapy-based approaches [ 8 , 10 ]. Similarly, the POET trial reported higher pathological complete response rates with CRT compared to chemotherapy; however, this did not result in sustained survival benefit [ 12 ]. Taken together, these studies suggest that improved tumor regression does not uniformly translate into improved long-term survival, particularly in adenocarcinoma subsets. It should also be noted that, although no statistically significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics between treatment groups, this does not imply full comparability. In retrospective observational studies, the lack of statistical significance does not eliminate the possibility of residual confounding. Unmeasured factors such as comorbidity burden, treatment selection bias, and performance status may have influenced treatment allocation and outcomes. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as associative rather than causal. In the overall cohort, survival outcomes were comparable between treatment modalities. This observation is in line with more recent comparative data suggesting survival equivalence between modern perioperative ChT and CRT in adenocarcinoma populations [ 13 – 15 ]. These findings suggest that, in contemporary real-world practice, both strategies may provide similar long-term survival effectiveness when applied to appropriately selected patients. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested potential heterogeneity according to tumor localization and clinical stage. In EGJ-located clinical stage III tumors, perioperative ChT was associated with improved overall survival, whereas in clinical stage II patients, neoadjuvant CRT appeared to be more advantageous. This stage-dependent pattern may be explained by differences in tumor burden and disease biology. In clinical stage III disease, where tumor burden and the risk of micrometastatic spread are higher, systemic disease control becomes more critical, thereby favoring perioperative ChT. In contrast, in stage II disease, where tumors are more localized, enhanced local control achieved with neoadjuvant CRT may translate into improved outcomes. In the ESOPEC trial, the study population predominantly consisted of stage III patients with a higher tumor burden, and the survival benefit was observed in favor of perioperative ChT, which is conceptually consistent with our findings [ 11 , 16 ]. Together, these observations suggest that tumor burden and systemic disease risk may play a key role in determining the relative efficacy of treatment modalities. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution, as they are primarily derived from univariate analyses. In this study, three conceptually structured multivariable Cox regression models were constructed to more robustly evaluate independent prognostic factors for overall survival (OS). In Model 1, which included clinical variables, clinical N3 stage was found to significantly increase the risk of mortality. This finding aligns with prior prognostic analyses highlighting nodal burden as a dominant determinant of survival in esophageal and EGJ adenocarcinoma [ 6 , 17 ]. This finding was further confirmed in the parsimonious model, in which pathological N1 and N3 stages demonstrated independent and significant adverse effects on overall survival. The association between pathological N1 stage and increased mortality risk may reflect a non-linear relationship between nodal burden and survival, as well as the limited sample size within subgroups. Despite the use of different modeling strategies, the persistence of the adverse impact of nodal involvement on survival supports the strong prognostic role of lymph node burden. In contrast, age, sex, tumor localization, pathological T stage, and resection margin status did not retain independent statistical significance in multivariable analyses. Similar findings have been reported in retrospective cohort analyses where event numbers were limited [ 18 – 20 ]. Limited event numbers and subgroup size imbalances likely contributed to wide confidence intervals and reduced statistical power. Indeed, directional trends toward increased mortality risk were observed for some variables; however, statistical significance was not achieved because the confidence intervals included the value of 1. This suggests that sample size and event counts may have been limiting factors for multivariable modeling in this cohort. To address concerns regarding overfitting and model instability, a stepwise modeling strategy was deliberately implemented, including a parsimonious model focusing only on biologically meaningful variables. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) analyses showed no statistically significant differences between treatment modalities in the overall population. However, in univariate analysis, RFS was found to be significantly better in the neoadjuvant CRT group among patients with distally located clinical stage II tumors. Nevertheless, the limited number of recurrence events reduced statistical power and precluded reliable multivariable modeling for RFS. This finding contrasts with results from pooled analyses and comparative phase II studies reporting survival equivalence despite differences in pathological response, and suggests that subgroup-level effects may be unstable due to the small sample size and low event count [ 21 , 22 ]. Therefore, these results should be considered hypothesis-generating. From a clinical standpoint, these results suggest that both perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT represent valid multimodal strategies in routine practice. While CRT may offer superior pathological tumor regression and local tumor control, this advantage does not necessarily translate into improved survival at the population level. Contemporary guideline updates and comparative analyses have likewise emphasized individualized treatment selection rather than uniform superiority claims [ 14 , 23 , 24 ]. The use of three separate models represents a deliberate methodological choice aimed at reducing the potential risk of overfitting and maintaining an appropriate balance between the number of events and the number of variables included in the models. The clinical model incorporated preoperative factors, the pathological model focused on postoperative characteristics, and the parsimonious model included the most biologically and clinically meaningful variables. This stepwise modeling strategy not only strengthens the robustness of the findings but also addresses potential methodological concerns regarding model stability and parameter inflation. In summary, clinical and pathological N3 nodal involvement emerged as the most prominent and independent prognostic factor in this study. The lack of independent statistical significance for other variables does not necessarily indicate a lack of clinical importance; rather, these factors may require further evaluation in larger patient cohorts and prospective studies. The inclusion of additional multivariable analyses has expanded the prognostic assessment of the study and enabled treatment comparisons to be interpreted within a more controlled analytical framework.
sections.limitations: There are several limitations that should be considered in this study. First, the retrospective design and the relatively limited sample size constrained the complexity of the multivariable modeling. Although multivariable Cox regression analyses were performed, the number of covariates included in the models was intentionally restricted in order to preserve model stability. Second, the subgroup analyses were exploratory in nature, and the results should be interpreted with caution, particularly in subgroups with a low number of events. Finally, causal inference methods such as propensity score matching were not applied, as they could have further reduced the effective sample size in subgroup analyses and consequently decreased statistical power. Additionally, the absence of propensity score–based methods may limit the ability to fully adjust for treatment selection bias.
sections.conclusion_1: In this real-world retrospective cohort of patients with locally advanced resectable distal esophageal and EGJ adenocarcinoma, neoadjuvant CRT was associated with higher pathological complete response and tumor downstaging rates; however, this advantage did not translate into a statistically significant overall survival benefit in the overall population compared with perioperative chemotherapy. Exploratory subgroup analyses demonstrated heterogeneity according to tumor location and clinical stage, with a trend toward improved OS with neoadjuvant CRT in EGJ clinical stage II disease and a significant RFS benefit in distal clinical stage II patients, whereas a statistically significant OS advantage was observed with perioperative ChT in EGJ clinical stage III tumors. These subgroup findings were derived from univariate analyses and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating. In multivariable models, treatment modality was not an independent predictor of survival, while nodal involvement, particularly advanced nodal stage, consistently emerged as the strongest adverse prognostic factor. Overall, these findings suggest that perioperative ChT and neoadjuvant CRT provide comparable survival outcomes at the population level, while treatment response may vary according to disease characteristics, supporting a personalized approach to treatment selection. Given the retrospective design, limited sample size, and low event numbers in subgroup analyses, these results require validation in larger prospective studies.

title: Barriers and enablers for publishing results of randomized trials: a cross-sectional survey of principal investigators in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Objectives To investigate the views and experiences of principal investigators (PIs) based in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) regarding publication bias of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and strategies to mitigate it. Design Cross-sectional online survey, informed by previous reviews and prior surveys on publication bias. The survey consisted of closed-ended items with Likert scales and optional free text. Setting We emailed invitations to African-based PIs that we identified through the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Participants 6056 invitations were sent, 610 opened the survey, 433 were eligible to partake, and 409 consented and proceeded with the survey. Main outcome measured Awareness and perceived magnitude of publication bias in SSA, experiences of timely publication, non-publication, delayed publication and their perceived effectiveness of mitigating strategies. Results Awareness that all RCTs are to be published was 62.7% (227/362). More than 90% agreed that PIs are responsible for ensuring that their RCTs are published (295/323), and 84% (272/323) within 24 months of completion. Publication bias in SSA scored a median of 71/100 (IQR: 50 – 84) for geographical region and 66 (IQR = 40 –79) for the respondent’s specific field of research. Of the respondents, 63.1% (219/347) published the findings of at least one RCT within 24 months, and 23.6% (82/347) were unable to publish at least one complete RCT. Notably, 74% (246/332) indicated not having had prior training in writing RCT-specific manuscripts. Of the 82 that were unable to publish, their reported reasons for non-publication included 30.5% (25/82) journal rejection, 29.3% (24/82) time constraints, 14.6% (12/82) non-significant or 13.4% (11/82) non-positive results, 13.4% (11/82) methodological concerns and 12.2% (10/82) lack of confidence in writing. 41.2% (143/347) of respondents reported delays greater than 24 months, 47.9% (69/347) attributed time constraint, 38.9% (56/347) time-consuming analysis, and 36.8% (53/347) journal rejection. Of the 332 participants that answered questions on mitigating strategies, the following were suggested to be very effective: 56.6%(188/332) dedicated writing time, 37.1% (123/332) guidance on writing a manuscript and 35.8% (119/332) peer-review prior to submission. Furthermore, 52.7% (175/332) rated the CONSORT checklist as effective/very effective, and 37.4% (124/332) noted artificial intelligence tools somewhat effective. Conclusions SSA PIs note that publication bias is a problem, which is a result of barriers such as time constraints, analysis difficulties, journal rejection, and limited writing support. Enablers include mentorship, dedicated writing time, and structured reporting tools.
