sections.what is new?: Using an imaging‐based classification of hemorrhage‐dominant patterns, rather than relying solely on aggregate lesion counts, we demonstrated that higher vascular amyloid burden is associated with greater hemorrhagic predominance within the cerebral amyloid angiopathy spectrum. The association between amyloid burden and hemorrhagic predominance, together with co‐occurring amyloid‐linked imaging features such as high‐degree centrum semiovale‐enlarged perivascular spaces, supports a graded relationship between vascular amyloid severity and disease expression.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Do individuals with higher vascular amyloid burden exhibit accelerated progression toward hemorrhage‐dominant phenotypes over time, and can this trajectory be modified?
sections.study design and participants: This study used data from an ongoing single‐center observational cohort of patients with CAA at Massachusetts General Hospital, with enrollment procedures described previously. 9 Briefly, participants met the modified Boston criteria for probable or definite CAA. 3 The inclusion criteria included age ≥55 years old and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrating (1) ≥2 hemorrhages (ICH or CMB) restricted to lobar, cortical, and cortico‐subcortical regions (cerebellar hemorrhages allowed) or (2) single lobar, cortical, or cortico‐subcortical hemorrhage accompanied by any degree of cSS; (3) absence of any hemorrhagic lesions in deep brain regions; and (4) absence of any alternative causes for hemorrhagic lesions (excessive warfarin [international normalized ratio >3.0]; blood dyscrasia, antecedent head trauma or ischemic stroke, intracranial tumor, vascular malformation, or vasculitis). Individuals with mild cognitive impairment, dementia, and any other neurodegenerative conditions were excluded based on comprehensive clinical and neuroimaging assessments. 10 , 11 Detailed information, including demographics and risk factors, was prospectively recorded at the time of cohort entry. All participants underwent structural MRI at 3T and 11 C Pittsburgh compound B (PiB) PET imaging, as described below. The study was approved by the local institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent. No photographs, videos, or other identifiable personal information were used. The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.mri acquisition and analysis: All participants underwent a research MRI scan at 3T field strength. The imaging protocol included a 3‐dimensional T1‐weighted multiecho magnetization‐prepared rapid gradient‐echo sequence, fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery, T2‐weighted, and 3‐dimensional susceptibility‐weighted imaging sequences. Imaging markers of CAA, including lobar ICH, lobar CMBs, cSS, and CSO‐EPVS, were identified using established criteria. 12 , 13 ICH was defined as a parenchymal hemorrhage >5 to 10 mm in the largest diameter that does not meet criteria for a CMB. 14 , 15 cSS was scored using a validated multifocality scale. 16 In this scale, each hemisphere was rated as 0 (no cSS), 1 (cSS in 1 sulcus or up to 3 adjacent sulci), or 2 (cSS in ≥2 nonadjacent sulci or >3 adjacent sulci). Right and left scores were summed (range, 0–4), with 0 indicating no cSS, 1 mild/unifocal cSS, and ≥2 severe/multifocal cSS. CSO‐EPVS was rated on axial T2‐weighted images using a validated 4‐point visual scale: 0=no CSO‐EPVS; 1=1 to 10 CSO‐EPVS; 2=11 to 20 CSO‐EPVS; 3=21 to 40 CSO‐EPVS; and 4=>40 CSO‐EPVS. A score of 4 was categorized as high‐degree CSO‐EPVS. 17 ICH, CMBs, and cSS were rated on susceptibility‐weighted imaging and CSO‐EPVS on T2‐weighted images, with each marker assessed independently in separate sessions. The FreeSurfer software suite ( surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu ) was used to calculate WMH volume and estimated total intracranial volume, using an automated fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery‐based method independent of MRI ratings. WMH volume was expressed as a percentage of estimated total intracranial volume to account for individual differences in head size. For participants with large hemispheric ICH, measurements from the contralateral hemisphere were used and doubled to estimate total volume.
sections.hemorrhagic pattern classification: To capture variation in hemorrhagic lesions, participants were categorized based on the relative severity of cSS and CMBs. cSS severity was assessed using the previously defined multifocality score (range, 0–4), and total lobar CMBs were counted on susceptibility‐weighted imaging. Patients were then classified into 4 patterns: cSS‐D: cSS score ≥2 and ≤10 CMBs; CMB‐D: >10 CMBs and cSS score <2; both dominant: cSS score ≥2 and >10 CMB; and nondominant: cSS score <2 and ≤10 CMBs. The classification schema is illustrated in Figure 1 . Among 67 patients with a diagnosis of probable or definite CAA, 5 individuals who met the criteria for the both‐dominant pattern were excluded from further analysis due to low sample size, resulting in a final cohort of 62 participants. Although ICH represents a hemorrhagic manifestation of CAA, it was not incorporated into the dominance classification, given the limited subgroup sizes that would have substantially reduced statistical stability. 18
sections.pet acquisition and analysis: All PET scans were acquired on a Siemens/computed tomography ECAT HR+ scanner (Knoxville, TN) in 3‐dimensional mode and processed as previously described. 19 Briefly, each scan was coregistered to each subject's magnetization‐prepared rapid gradient‐echo MRI using Statistical Parametric Mapping 8 software. MRI‐defined cortical and subcortical regions of interest were transformed into native PET space, and tracer uptake was sampled from each hemisphere. Carbon‐11‐PiB ( 11 C‐PiB) (8.5–15 mCi) was injected as a bolus, with dynamic imaging from 40 to 60 minutes postinjection. The Logan graphical method was used to compute regional distribution volume ratios (DVRs) for each region of interest, using the cerebellar cortex as the reference region. Global cortical PiB DVR was calculated as the mean DVR across cortical regions of interest. In patients with a large ICH, results from the non‐ICH hemisphere were used for the analyses. All PET analyses were performed blinded to MRI ratings and WMH volume measurements.
sections.statistical analysis: Analyses were conducted on the final cohort (n=62), excluding the both‐dominant group due to low sample size. All analyses were exploratory and biologically informed, consistent with the observational study design and sample size, and were intended to characterize associations rather than support causal or predictive inference. Continuous variables are presented as mean±SD or median (interquartile range) depending on distributional characteristics, and categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. Normality was assessed using visual inspection of histograms and Q–Q plots in combination with the Shapiro‐Wilk test. Homogeneity of variance was assessed using visual inspection. Group comparisons among the 3 subgroups (CMB‐D, cSS‐D, and nondominant) were performed using 1‐way ANOVA when parametric assumptions were met or the Kruskal‐Wallis test when they were not, for continuous variables. Categorical variables were analyzed using χ 2 or Fisher exact tests, as appropriate. When a significant overall group effect was identified, post hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted as follows: for ANOVA, Bonferroni‐adjusted pairwise comparisons were used; for Kruskal‐Wallis tests, pairwise comparisons were performed using Mann‐Whitney U tests; and for categorical variables, pairwise comparisons were conducted using χ2 or Fisher exact tests. Bonferroni correction was applied for 3 pairwise comparisons, and adjusted P values are reported. To examine associations between imaging markers and hemorrhage pattern, separate multivariable logistic regression models were constructed for each imaging marker (global cortical PiB DVR, high‐degree CSO‐EPVS, or WMH volume) rather than including multiple imaging predictors in a single model. Dominant hemorrhage pattern was modeled as the outcome (CMB‐D or cSS‐D versus nondominant and CMB‐D versus cSS‐D). This approach was chosen to limit model complexity and reduce the risk of overfitting, given the modest sample size. All regression models were adjusted for age and sex, based on their clinical relevance and established role as demographic confounders in CAA. Effect estimates with 95% CIs are emphasized along with the P values. Given univariate differences in ICH prevalence between the cSS‐D and CMB‐D groups, we further evaluated this association using age‐ and sex‐adjusted logistic regression. Separate regression models were also used to examine the associations between global PiB DVR and CSO‐EPVS (logistic regression) and between global PiB DVR and WMH volume (linear regression, with WMH volume as the dependent variable), each adjusted for age and sex. Because ICH was not incorporated into the dominance classification and represents a clinically distinct hemorrhagic manifestation within the CAA spectrum, sensitivity analyses were performed with additional adjustment for ICH in regression models to assess robustness. 14 , 18 To improve the interpretability of regression coefficients, global cortical PiB DVR and WMH volume were scaled by multiplying by 10 to reflect the effect per 0.1‐unit increase. WMH volume was additionally log‐transformed before modeling to reduce skewness, mitigate the influence of extreme values, and improve the linearity of its association with outcomes. In analyses where WMH was modeled as a dependent variable (linear regression), this transformation also improved residual distributional properties. Model assumptions, including linearity, were assessed using visual inspection of residual plots and were considered reasonable after transformation. All statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 28.0). A 2‐tailed P <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results_1: The final study cohort included 62 patients with a diagnosis of CAA, categorized into 3 groups: CMB‐D (n=31), cSS‐D (n=17), and nondominant (n=14). Baseline demographics and imaging characteristics for each group are summarized in Table 1 . As expected, the groups significantly differed in terms of lobar CMB counts and presence of cSS, whereas demographics did not differ significantly among groups. The overall frequency of ICH did not differ significantly among groups ( P =0.053). However, patients with the cSS‐D pattern showed a numerically higher rate of ICH compared with those with the CMB‐D pattern, and this association was significant in a logistic regression model adjusted for age and sex (odds ratio [OR], 1.65 [95% CI, 1.1–23.0]; P =0.031).
sections.hemorrhage patterns and global cortical: Global cortical PiB DVR significantly differed among groups ( P =0.011, Figure 2 ). In post hoc comparisons, both the CMB‐D and cSS‐D groups had significantly higher PiB DVR relative to the nondominant group ( P =0.033 and P =0.014, Bonferroni‐corrected; Figure 2 ). These associations remained significant in logistic regression models adjusted for age and sex (CMB‐D versus nondominant: OR, 1.8 [95% CI, 1.1–2.8]; P =0.009; cSS‐D versus nondominant: OR, 1.6 [95% CI, 1.1–2.5]; P =0.020; Table 2 ). No difference was observed between the CMB‐D and cSS‐D groups ( P =1.000).
sections.hemorrhage patterns and high\u2010degree: High‐degree CSO‐EPVS significantly differed among groups ( P =0.009, Table 1 ). In post hoc comparisons, both the CMB‐D and cSS‐D groups had significantly higher frequencies of high‐degree CSO‐EPVS compared with the nondominant group (CMB‐D versus nondominant, P =0.018; cSS‐D versus nondominant, P =0.015, each Bonferroni‐corrected), whereas the 2 hemorrhagic groups did not differ from each other ( P =1.000). In logistic regression analyses adjusted for age and sex, high‐degree CSO‐EPVS remained independently associated with both the CMB‐D (OR, 9.3 [95% CI, 1.6–52]; P =0.011) and cSS‐D (OR, 10 [95% CI, 1.6–62]; P =0.013) groups relative to nondominant (Table 2 ).
sections.hemorrhage patterns and wmh volume: Although the overall group difference in WMH volume did not reach statistical significance ( P =0.055), WMH burden was numerically higher in both hemorrhagic‐dominant groups compared with the nondominant group (Table 1 ). These results remained nonsignificant after adjustment for age and sex (CMB‐D versus nondominant, P =0.089; cSS‐D versus nondominant, P =0.058).
sections.association of pib uptake with cso \u201: Patients with high‐degree CSO‐EPVS had significantly higher global PiB DVR than those without (1.46±0.22 versus 1.29±0.25, P =0.007), and this relationship remained independent in a logistic regression model adjusted for age and sex (OR, 1.35 [95% CI, 1.0–1.7]; P =0.016). In a separate linear regression model, global PiB DVR was also independently associated with WMH volume (β=0.25 [95% CI, 0.02–0.94]; P =0.049), again adjusted for age and sex.
sections.sensitivity analyses: All associations remained unchanged in sensitivity analyses that included ICH as an additional covariate (data not shown).
sections.discussion: In this study, we investigated whether amyloid burden varies among patients with CAA with distinct hemorrhagic patterns and whether these patterns are linked to downstream structural consequences. We demonstrated that patients with CAA with either CMB‐D or cSS‐D patterns had greater brain amyloid burden, more frequent high‐degree CSO‐EPVS, and numerically higher WMH volumes compared with those without dominant hemorrhagic lesions. Supporting our main hypothesis, our findings showed that hemorrhage‐dominant patterns (either CMB‐D or cSS‐D) were associated with significantly higher global cortical amyloid load compared with the nondominant group. Previous studies in non‐CAA populations have reported associations between either lobar CMBs or cSS and increased amyloid PET uptake, suggesting that vascular amyloid may contribute to microbleed and siderosis formation. 20 , 21 Within CAA cohorts, 1 study demonstrated increased regional PiB retention in areas affected by lobar CMBs, although similar data for cSS remain limited. 22 Our results extend these observations by demonstrating that both hemorrhagic markers, CMBs and cSS, are associated with elevated global amyloid burden. These findings support models that even within patients with CAA, greater amyloid load promotes brain hemorrhages, which can manifest through diverse lesion types such as microbleeds and siderosis. We also observed that both hemorrhagic‐dominant groups exhibited a higher frequency of high‐degree CSO‐EPVS, a marker of impaired perivascular clearance, and consistently numerically greater WMH volume, reflecting global ischemic injury in CAA. 23 , 24 In multivariable models, high‐degree CSO‐EPVS remained independently associated with both hemorrhagic patterns, whereas WMH volume was consistently numerically higher in hemorrhagic‐dominant groups, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Similar to previous observations, when examined as a continuous measure across the entire cohort, higher PiB uptake was independently associated with both CSO‐EPVS burden and WMH volume, further supporting the hypothesis that these structural markers reflect downstream consequences of vascular amyloid accumulation. 9 , 19 , 25 , 26 Taken together, patients with more hemorrhagic lesions also have broader, likely parallel processes of amyloid‐related brain injury, including impaired perivascular clearance and global ischemic injury. Notably, the only major difference between the cSS‐D and CMB‐D subgroups was that cSS‐D had a substantially higher frequency of ICH, whereas the 2 groups did not differ in PiB uptake or other CAA markers. This singular distinction suggests that the mechanistic pathways leading to ICH may diverge between these patterns, with cSS‐D potentially representing a more ICH‐prone phenotype. This interpretation aligns with prior studies reporting a strong association between cSS and increased ICH risk in CAA. 27 , 28 We also found that the CMB‐D group had a lower frequency of ICH (51.6%) than the nondominant group (78.6%) despite demonstrating a higher amyloid burden, suggesting that factors beyond global amyloid load influence the likelihood of ICH in CAA. This variability in ICH prevalence across subgroups further supports the rationale for using distinct hemorrhagic markers, rather than ICH itself, to define biologically meaningful CAA phenotypes. Although our pattern classification also allowed for a fourth group characterized by both severe cSS and high CMB burden (both dominant), only 5 participants (7.4% of the initial cohort) met criteria for this pattern. This group was excluded from primary analyses due to the small sample size. The rarity of this combination in our study aligns with prior reports showing that cSS typically occurs in individuals with relatively lower CMB counts, supporting the idea that extensive cSS and high CMB burden may reflect distinct pathological mechanisms within the broader CAA spectrum. 8 One proposed mechanism underlying the distinction between cSS and CMBs involves differences in the vascular compartments affected by amyloid pathology. A prior neuropathological study reported that moderate‐to‐severe cSS was associated with more advanced CAA in leptomeningeal vessels, but lower amyloid severity in cortical vessels. 4 In addition, there was no association between the presence of cSS and microbleeds, suggesting that cSS arises primarily from vascular amyloid deposition in leptomeningeal vessels, whereas lobar CMBs may reflect amyloid burden in cortical vessels. This divergence may be further explained by underlying genetic differences. Several studies have linked apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε2 to cSS and APOE ε4 to lobar CMBs, raising the possibility that these genotypes may contribute to distinct vascular injury mechanisms. 5 , 6 , 7 However, these studies are often limited by small sample sizes or meta‐analyses with heterogeneous cohorts, and typically assess cSS and CMBs in isolation. Notably, none included amyloid PET imaging, limiting insights into the interaction between genetic risk, amyloid burden, and hemorrhagic expression. This study has several limitations. The sample size was modest; classification into 3 patterns further reduced the number of participants per group. Given the modest sample size, the regression models were intentionally kept simple. Some effect estimates, especially for dichotomized variables, may appear large with wide CIs and require careful interpretation. Overall, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis‐generating rather than confirmatory. Because the cohort was drawn from a single tertiary center, generalizability to broader clinical populations might be limited. Still, the study leveraged a well‐characterized CAA cohort with comprehensive multimodal imaging. APOE genotype data were not available, preventing analysis of potential genetic contributions to the observed hemorrhagic phenotypes. Future work integrating genetic data will be important for refining mechanistic insight. Our hemorrhage pattern classification intentionally did not account for the presence/absence of ICH, which may have introduced some heterogeneity in the study cohort. To address this, we repeated the regression models by including ICH as an additional covariate in sensitivity analyses. The results were unchanged, supporting the robustness of our findings. The cross‐sectional design limits causal inference, and longitudinal studies are needed to determine the temporal relationship between amyloid, hemorrhagic markers, and structural injury, an effort currently underway. PiB‐PET might not differentiate between vascular and parenchymal amyloid deposition. A previous neuropathological study in 44 participants, 24 of whom had a pathologic diagnosis of Alzheimer disease, reported that parenchymal plaques, but not regional CAA, were associated with PiB uptake. 29 Importantly, that cohort differed substantially from ours; the participants were not clinically symptomatic patients with CAA but predominantly individuals with underlying Alzheimer disease pathology and minimal hemorrhagic markers, making their findings less applicable to a symptomatic CAA population. Still, we aimed to minimize the risk of Alzheimer disease copathology by excluding individuals with mild cognitive impairment or dementia at study enrollment. Finally, despite classifying patients into biologically meaningful subgroups, residual heterogeneity likely exists within each category; however, the simplicity of this classification supports its potential usefulness in both research and clinical settings. Despite these limitations, the consistency of associations across multiple models and sensitivity analyses supports the robustness of our findings and their relevance to understanding CAA mechanisms. In conclusion, our findings support a close association between vascular amyloid burden and hemorrhagic manifestations of CAA, including a high burden of CMBs and severe cSS. The strength of the PiB–dominance association, combined with the observation that patients with hemorrhage‐dominant patterns also exhibit other amyloid‐linked imaging features such as high‐degree CSO‐EPVS, suggests that these phenotypes may reflect overlapping vascular pathways related to amyloid accumulation. These pathways may include impaired perivascular clearance, vascular dysfunction, and vessel wall weakening. A better understanding of these mechanisms may help identify biologically distinct subgroups with implications for prognosis and therapeutic targeting. Overall, our results support the candidate treatment approach of targeting amyloid production, with the goal of lowering vascular amyloid burden and thereby reducing the risk for hemorrhagic lesions. This approach is currently being tested in a clinical trial. 30

title: Minimally Invasive, Echocardiography‐Guided Mouse Model of Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation Recapitulates Cardiac Remodeling and Arrhythmogenesis
abstract: Background Degenerative mitral regurgitation (MR) is a progressive valvular disorder that causes atrial enlargement, cardiac remodeling, heart failure, and arrhythmias. Current rodent models are limited by thoracotomy or intubation, which increase procedural risk and reduce reproducibility. Methods and Results We established a minimally invasive, transthoracic echocardiography–guided mouse model of MR by puncturing the anterior mitral leaflet with a 27G needle introduced through the left ventricular apex. Ten‐week‐old C57BL/6J mice underwent baseline imaging before MR induction, and sham controls received apical puncture without leaflet disruption. Color Doppler confirmed regurgitant jets and increased vena contracta width, with procedural survival exceeding 90%. At 2 weeks, MR mice exhibited significant left heart enlargement, reduced fractional shortening, and myocardial fibrosis compared with sham. Pressure–volume loop analysis demonstrated increased end‐diastolic volume and reduced compliance. RNA sequencing of left atrial tissues revealed enrichment of calcium signaling, apoptosis, and shear stress pathways. Histology confirmed increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis, accompanied by Connexin‐43 downregulation and elevated ryanodine receptor 2 phosphorylation. Programmed atrial pacing induced atrial fibrillation in MR mice, consistent with enhanced arrhythmogenicity and calcium‐handling abnormalities. Conclusions This closed‐chest, echo‐guided murine model reliably induces MR, avoids thoracotomy, and recapitulates key features of human disease, including chamber dilation, fibrosis, and arrhythmia susceptibility. It provides a scalable platform for mechanistic studies, genetic interventions, and drug testing in valvular heart disease.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: A minimally invasive, transthoracic echocardiography–guided mouse model of degenerative mitral regurgitation was developed that reproducibly induces chronic regurgitation, chamber remodeling, and arrhythmogenic changes without thoracotomy.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: This closed‐chest mitral regurgitation model closely mirrors human pathophysiology and provides a practical platform for mechanistic studies and preclinical testing of novel therapies targeting valvular heart disease and atrial remodeling.
sections.animals and mitral valve puncture proced: All procedures have been approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines in Chi‐Mei Medical Center, Taiwan (113–07). All data underlying this article are available upon request. Ten‐week‐old male C57BL/6J mice (30–35 g) were used. Mice were anesthetized with isoflurane (5% induction, 2% maintenance) and monitored with ECG and body temperature support. Baseline echocardiography confirmed normal mitral valve (MV) function. Mice were randomly assigned to the sham or MR groups. For MR induction, a 27G needle was advanced via a transthoracic apical approach under echocardiographic guidance and directed toward the anterior MV leaflet, which was perforated under real‐time imaging (Figure 1A ; Video S1 and S2 ). Sham controls underwent identical preparation without leaflet perforation. MR was confirmed by color Doppler (regurgitant jet, vena contracta width) (Figure 1B ). Animals were excluded if pericardial effusion or acute hemodynamic instability occurred. Postoperative monitoring included serial echocardiography, body weights, survival assessment, and noninvasive blood pressure. A study protocol, including the research question, key design features, and analysis plan, was defined before study initiation.
sections.echocardiographic follow\u2010up: Serial transthoracic echocardiography was performed using a high‐frequency (30–40 MHz) linear array transducer (S‐Sharp Prospect T1 system, Taiwan) with a frame rate >150 Hz. Mice were lightly anesthetized with 1% to 2% isoflurane and placed in the supine position on a temperature‐controlled platform to maintain normothermia. Heart rate was continuously monitored and maintained between 400 and 500 beats per minute to minimize anesthesia‐related cardiac depression. Standard parasternal long‐axis (PLAX) was acquired to assess LA diameter, interventricular septum in diastole, LV internal dimension at end‐diastole, fractional shortening, and MV morphology 16 . LV fractional shortening was measured from M‐mode recordings obtained at the level of the papillary muscles in the parasternal long‐axis view. MR severity was evaluated using color and continuous‐wave Doppler imaging. Color Doppler imaging was performed in the AP4C view with a zoomed‐in region of interest centered on the MV, using optimized Nyquist limits (40–60 cm/s), minimal wall filter, and adjusted color gain just below the noise threshold. Vena contracta width was measured at the narrowest portion of the regurgitant jet immediately downstream from the mitral orifice during systole, with electronic calipers positioned perpendicular to the jet direction. Continuous‐wave Doppler interrogation of the mitral regurgitant jet was performed with careful alignment parallel to the direction of flow to maximize signal intensity. Doppler gain was optimized to avoid signal saturation, and sweep speed was increased (200–300 mm/s) to improve temporal resolution. Regurgitant peak velocity was recorded for MR characterization. For each parameter, measurements were averaged from 3 to 5 consecutive cardiac cycles. To ensure reproducibility, 2 independent observers performed blinded measurements of vena contracta width, with 1 observer repeating assessments twice. Intra‐ and interobserver reliability were evaluated using linear regression and intraclass correlation analysis (Figure S1 ).
sections.mouse blood pressure measurement: Blood pressures were measured using a noninvasive tail‐cuff plethysmography system (CODA High Throughput System, Kent Scientific, Torrington, CT, USA). Mice were acclimated to the restrainer and warming platform (32 °C–34 °C) for 10 to 15 minutes before measurement to minimize stress‐induced variability. Occlusion and volume‐pressure recording cuffs were placed at the base of the tail. For each mouse, ≥10 consecutive valid measurements were obtained, and the average systolic blood pressure was used for analysis. Measurements were performed at the same time of day by a blinded operator.
sections.pressure\u2013volume loop analysis: At study end point, invasive hemodynamic assessment was performed. 17 Mice were anesthetized with urethane (500 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) and the right carotid artery was exposed. A 2.0F conductance catheter (SPR‐838, Millar Instruments, USA) was advanced retrogradely into the left ventricle under pressure guidance. After stabilization, steady‐state pressure–volume loops were recorded using PowerLab (ADInstruments). Closed‐ and open‐chest measurements were performed sequentially. Inferior vena cava occlusion was applied by gentle external compression to derive load‐independent indices. Systolic function was quantified by end‐systolic pressure, volume, +dP/dt, arterial elastance, and the end‐systolic pressure–volume relationship. Diastolic indices included end‐diastolic pressure, volume, –dP/dt, relaxation constant (Tau), and the end‐diastolic pressure–volume relationship.
sections.histology and immunostaining: Post 28 days of MV puncture, mice were euthanized under deep anesthesia by cervical dislocation. Hearts were excised, weighed, and normalized to tibia length. Tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 μm thickness. Hematoxylin–eosin staining was performed for morphology, and Masson's trichrome staining quantified myocardial fibrosis as blue‐stained collagen relative to red‐stained myocardium. Immunofluorescence staining was performed on fixed cells or heart tissue sections using phalloidin–Alexa Fluor 488 to visualize F‐actin and primary antibodies against Connexin‐43 (1:200; Cell Signaling Technology, MA, USA) or wheat germ agglutinin (Biotium, CA, USA), followed by Alexa Fluor–conjugated secondary antibodies. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. Apoptotic cells in cardiac sections were identified using a TUNEL (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase–mediated dUTP nick‐end labeling) assay (BioVision, Milpitas, CA), and cardiomyocytes positive for both F‐actin and TUNEL were quantified as apoptotic cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocyte cross‐sectional area was assessed on LV sections stained with wheat germ agglutinin to delineate cell membranes, and measurements were performed on transversely cut cardiomyocytes with a centrally located nucleus using ImageJ software, with ≥30 cells analyzed per heart by an investigator blinded to group allocation. Fluorescence images were acquired using an Olympus BX51 microscope (Olympus Optical Co. Ltd., Tokyo, Japan), and 10 randomly selected fields per section were quantified using ImageJ.
sections.atrial fibrillation inducibility: Atrial fibrillation (AF) susceptibility was tested by programmed pacing. Under light anesthesia (1%–1.5% isoflurane), a 1.1F octapolar catheter was advanced transesophageally to the posterior left atrium. 18 Burst pacing at 20 Hz (2 milliseconds pulse width, twice diastolic threshold) was delivered for 2 to 3 seconds using a Grass S88 stimulator. Surface ECG monitored rhythm in real time. AF was defined as an irregular atrial rhythm persisting >1 second after pacing. Each mouse underwent 3 to 5 pacing attempts. Inducibility was expressed as the proportion of pacing trials that triggered AF, and duration was measured for each episode.
sections.rna sequencing: Left atrial tissues were harvested from adult C57BL/6 mice (n=3 per group) subjected either to sham operation or surgically induced MR. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, and RNA integrity was verified by Bioanalyzer. Libraries were prepared with poly‐A selection and sequenced on an Illumina platform to generate 150 bp paired‐end reads. After quality control with FastQC, clean reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (GRCm39) using HISAT2. Transcript assembly and quantification were performed with StringTie, and differential expression analysis was carried out with DESeq2. Genes with |log 2 fold‐change|>1 and adjusted P <0.05 were considered significant. Functional annotation and enrichment analyses were conducted using clusterProfiler for Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways. Heatmaps and clustering were generated with pheatmap, and Circos plots were drawn to visualize gene–pathway interactions, highlighting the remodeling signatures in MR atria compared with sham. All original sequencing data have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number GSE325528.
sections.western blot for apoptotic proteins and: Left atrial tissues were homogenized in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Total protein concentration was quantified using the BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein (20–40 μg) were separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. After blocking in 5% nonfat milk, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against cleaved caspase‐3 (1:500; Cell Signaling, MA, USA), Bax (1:500; Cell Signaling, MA, USA), RyR2 (ryanodine receptor 2; 1:500; Cell Signaling, MA, USA), and phosphorylated RyR2 (Ser2814) (1:500; Cell Signaling, MA, USA), followed by horseradish peroxidase‐conjugated secondary antibodies. Proteins were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry in ImageJ. GAPDH (1:5000, Sigma‐Aldrich Co., St. Louis MO, USA) served as the internal loading control.
sections.flow cytometry for cardiomyocyte apoptos: Cardiomyocytes were freshly isolated from left atrial tissues using collagenase digestion and mechanical dissociation, followed by filtration through a 40‐μm mesh to obtain single‐cell suspensions. Cells were incubated with anticardiac troponin T antibody conjugated to FITC to identify cardiomyocytes, and propidium iodide was added immediately before analysis to detect apoptotic/necrotic cells. Flow cytometry was performed on a BD FACSAria III (BD Biosciences). Data were analyzed using FlowJo software, with gating based on forward/side scatter and fluorescence intensity. Propidium iodide + /troponin + cells were quantified as the percentage of apoptotic cardiomyocytes per sample. At least 10 000 troponin‐positive events were acquired per mouse.
sections.statistical analysis: All data are presented as mean ± SEM. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons between 2 groups were performed using unpaired Student's t ‐test for normally distributed variables and the Mann–Whitney U test for nonnormal distributions. For comparisons among multiple groups, 1‐way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test or Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn's correction was applied as appropriate. Categorical variables were analyzed using Fisher's exact test. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan–Meier curves, and group differences were assessed by the log‐rank test. Intraobserver reliability for echocardiographic measurements was assessed in a randomly selected subset of animals using the intraclass correlation coefficient with a 2‐way mixed‐effects model for absolute agreement. Gene expression differences from RNA sequencing were analyzed using DESeq2 with Benjamini–Hochberg correction to control the false discovery rate (<0.05). A 2‐sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (v8.0). All echocardiographic, histological, and Western blot analyses were conducted by investigators blinded to group allocation.
sections.procedural feasibility and survival of m: A minimally invasive, echo‐guided, closed‐chest puncture of the anterior mitral leaflet was performed under transthoracic echocardiographic guidance in C57BL/6J mice. MR was confirmed by color Doppler visualization of new regurgitant jets, with significant increases in vena contracta width, consistent with moderate‐to‐severe MR (Figure 1B ; Videos S3 and S4 ). Animals with pericardial effusion or acute hemodynamic instability were excluded. Following MR induction, body weight and heart rate remained unchanged, but systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressures were lower compared with sham (Figure 1C–G ). Serial echocardiography demonstrated progressive LA enlargement and LV dilation (LV internal dimension at end‐diastole) at 2 and 4 weeks, accompanied by reduced fractional shortening, indicating systolic dysfunction despite no significant changes of interventricular wall thickness (interventricular septum in diastole) (Figure 1H through 1M ). Procedural survival exceeded 90%, with most mortality occurring within the first 10 days, after which survival stabilized (Figure 1N ). Intraobserver reliability of vena contracta measurements showed a good correlation (R 2 =0.972), and interobserver agreement between independent observers remained high (R 2 =0.979), confirming the robustness and consistency of the measurement approach (Figure S1 ). Further, pressure–volume loop analysis demonstrated increased LV end‐diastolic volume and reduced compliance, consistent with volume overload and maladaptive remodeling (Figure 2 ). These findings closely recapitulate hemodynamic alterations observed in patients with chronic MR. The detailed echocardiography and hemodynamic parameters were displayed in Table S1 .
sections.histopathological remodeling: As shown in Figure 3A , after 28 days of MV puncture the autopsy showed a significant hole at the anterior leaflet of MV. Increase of heart weight–to–body weight and heart weight–to–tibia length ratios were observed in MR compared with sham mice (Figure 3B ). Notably, enlarged left heart dimensions were detected in all MR mice (Figure 3C ). Masson's trichrome staining revealed significantly increased interstitial fibrosis in both atrial and ventricular tissues of MR mice compared with sham (Figure 3D and 3E ). By quantifying the cross‐sectional area of wheat germ agglutinin‐outlined, F‐actin–positive cardiomyocytes, we observed that the cell width of cardiomyocyte was similar in MR mice compared with sham controls (Figure 3F through 3G ).
sections.molecular remodeling and apoptosis in mr: To further investigate the impact of MR induced flow stress on transcriptional alternatives, RNA sequencing analysis of LA tissues from 3 sham and 3 MR mice was performed. Gene Ontology enrichment highlighted pathways related to calcium ion transport, oxidative stress, and cytoskeletal organization (Figure 4A ). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway and heatmap clustering analysis showed strong enrichment in fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, calcium signaling, and apoptosis (Figure 4B and 4C ). Circos visualization further illustrated gene–pathway associations, underscoring the molecular reprogramming from apoptosis, calcium signaling to flow shear stress, in atrial tissue during MR‐induced hemodynamic stress (Figure 4D ). Using TUNEL staining, we confirmed elevated cardiomyocyte apoptosis in atria of MR mice compared with sham mice (Figure 5A through 5C ). Flow cytometry also showed increased propidium iodide + /troponin + cardiomyocytes in MR atria (Figure 5D ). Western blot and quantification of Bax, caspase‐3, and cleaved caspase‐3 demonstrated upregulations of apoptotic signaling in MR atria (Figure 5E through 5G ).
sections.af susceptibility and activated calcium: To evaluate whether MR mice also reproduce the phenotype of AF, we performed transesophageal burst pacing and observed in a significantly greater proportion of MR mice compared with sham (Figure 6A and 6B ). Notably, connexin‐43 immunostaining revealed disrupted gap junction expression patterns in MR atria, suggesting impaired electrical coupling (Figure 6C and 6D ). Likewise, protein expressions of connexin‐43 were also downregulated in MR atria (Figure 6E and 6F ). In contrast, increased phosphorylation of RYR2 (Ser2814), a key controller of intracellular Ca 2+ release channel, was also observed in the atria of MR mice, consistent with calcium‐handling abnormalities (Figure 6E and 6G ). Together, these structural alterations indicate maladaptive remodeling, which activates apoptotic pathways and disrupts calcium homeostasis, secondary to MR‐induced flow stress. The presence of atrial fibrosis, gap junction remodeling, and calcium dysregulation likely contributed to enhanced arrhythmogenicity. These results demonstrate that the model reproduces a key clinical complication of degenerative MR and the subsequent AF (Figure 7 ).
sections.discussion: In this study, we developed and validated a novel minimally invasive, transthoracic echocardiography‐guided murine model of MR. This model represents a significant methodological advancement over previous approaches, which relied on open‐chest surgery or large‐animal models. By eliminating thoracotomy, we achieved shorter procedural times, improved postoperative survival, and enhanced reproducibility. Importantly, this model recapitulates the hallmark features of human degenerative MR, including chamber dilation, systolic dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, apoptosis, and arrhythmia susceptibility. Our results highlight the utility of high‐frequency echocardiography for both procedural guidance and postprocedural validation. Color Doppler reliably confirmed leaflet perforation and regurgitant flow, and serial imaging demonstrated progressive remodeling. To note, we have previously applied this minimally invasive MR model in rats to investigate pharmacologic interventions and demonstrated that dapagliflozin significantly improved cardiac function, reduced fibrosis, and mitigated endoplasmic reticulum stress‐related injury. 19 These findings further validate the translational value of this model for testing therapeutic strategies targeting MR‐induced cardiac remodeling and heart failure. The ability to perform repeated noninvasive assessments allows longitudinal follow‐up and reduces animal numbers, aligning with the principles of refinement and reduction in animal research. Our findings suggest that flow stress from regurgitant flow disrupts calcium handling, activates apoptotic pathways, and downregulates connexin‐43, collectively contributing to fibrosis and electrical instability. These results align with previous studies implicating endoplasmic reticulumstress and reactive oxygen species signaling in MR‐induced remodeling. 13 , 20 Also, RNA sequencing analysis of LA tissues from MR mice revealed a distinct transcriptional reprogramming that integrates apoptosis, calcium dysregulation, inflammation, and fibrosis. The upregulation of Bax and cleaved caspase‐3 indicates activation of apoptotic cascades, consistent with atrial cardiomyocyte loss under chronic volume overload. Altered expression of Ryr2 and calcium‐dependent signaling molecules highlights disrupted calcium homeostasis, a key driver of contractile dysfunction and arrhythmogenic substrate formation. 21 , 22 The induction of Mmp2 , Mmp9 , Vcam1 , and Icam1 suggests enhanced extracellular matrix turnover and inflammatory cell adhesion, aligning with histological observations of fibrosis and atrial remodeling in MR. 23 , 24 Enrichment of fluid shear stress–related pathways further support the role of abnormal hemodynamic forces in activating mechanosensitive and oxidative stress responses. 13 , 14 Together, these findings underscore that atrial maladaptation in MR is not a singular process but the convergence of mechanical stress, oxidative damage, and molecular signaling networks, offering potential therapeutic targets to attenuate fibrosis and dysfunction. Compared with previously reported murine models of MR, our transthoracic, echocardiography‐guided mitral leaflet puncture platform offers several important methodological and pathophysiological advantages. Earlier models relied on thoracotomy combined with radiofrequency cauterization to rupture the mitral leaflet, which introduced substantial perioperative risk and variability in lesion size, whereas a more recent closed‐chest approach primarily emphasized ventricular dilation and hemodynamic changes with limited characterization of atrial pathology. In contrast, our model was specifically designed to interrogate MR‐induced atrial cardiomyopathy and reproducibly recapitulates key features of atrial remodeling, including left atrial enlargement, interstitial fibrosis, cardiomyocyte apoptosis, connexin‐43 downregulation, RyR2 hyperphosphorylation, and increased susceptibility to atrial fibrillation. Owing to the high murine heart rate (~500 bpm), repetitive oscillation of the mitral leaflet against the 27‐gauge puncture site generates sustained, physiologically relevant mechanical stress without the need for electrosurgical injury, and autopsy consistently confirmed localized leaflet disruption without collateral thermal damage. Importantly, our analysis of LV remodeling demonstrated comparable cardiomyocyte cross‐sectional areas between sham and MR mice on wheat germ agglutinin‐stained sections, indicating the absence of cell widening; this finding aligns with prior work by Wu et al., which showed that MR predominantly induces longitudinal cardiomyocyte growth consistent with volume overload–driven eccentric remodeling rather than pressure overload–associated hypertrophy. 25 Collectively, these data establish our model as a robust and translationally relevant platform that captures calcium‐handling dysregulation and atrial arrhythmogenesis, thereby enabling mechanistic dissection of MR‐induced atrial disease. Several limitations should be acknowledged when interpreting our findings. First, the surgical puncture model, although reproducible and minimally invasive, does not fully replicate the spectrum of human MR causes, particularly chordae tendineae rupture and the involvement of posterior leaflets. The acute mechanical disruption of the leaflet may differ from chronic remodeling processes, potentially influencing the downstream molecular responses. Second, although MR mice can survive for several months, our study focused on a 4‐week duration, which sufficiently captured atrial cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia but may not fully reflect the long‐term progression of atrial fibrosis, ventricular remodeling, or compensatory adaptations. Third, although we identified key pathways, mechanistic causality was not addressed, and functional studies are required to link specific molecular alterations with arrhythmogenesis. Fourth, in this study MR induction was performed in male mice; however, sex differences may influence MR‐induced remodeling, including the modulatory effects of estrogen signaling on hypertrophy and fibrosis. Future work will extend validation of this MR model to female mice to address these potential sex‐dependent responses. Finally, the use of only young, male C57BL/6J mice limits generalizability across sex, strain, and age, which may influence susceptibility to MR‐induced remodeling.
sections.conclusions_1: We present a reproducible, minimally invasive mouse model of MR that accurately reflects human pathophysiology. This platform enables high‐throughput mechanistic studies, genetic manipulation, and preclinical drug testing, representing an important step forward in translational research for valvular heart disease.

title: Primary Results of the SALAMANDER Registry: A Multicenter Observational Cohort Study
abstract: Background The balance between thromboembolic complications and bleeding risk in anticoagulated patients with atrial fibrillation remains challenging, with left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) representing a potential alternative. Our prospective multicenter study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, safety, technical, and procedural outcomes of the contemporary practice of stand‐alone LAAO. Methods The SALAMANDER (Stand‐Alone Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion for Thromboembolism Prevention in Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation Disease) registry is a real‐world, multicenter, observational cohort study conducted at 16 cardiac centers in Europe between 2010 and 2024, evaluating the safety and efficacy of LAAO using contemporary devices. Results A total of 1660 patients were enrolled, with a median age of 76 (interquartile range, 70–81) years and 38% being women. The median CHA 2 DS 2 ‐VASc score was 4 (interquartile range, 3–5). The most common indication for LAAO was significant bleeding (83.7% of patients), most frequently during treatment with direct oral anticoagulants (68.8%) more than vitamin K antagonists (24.9%). The predominant bleeding sites were the lower (27.9%) and upper (21.7%) gastrointestinal tracts, with 17.4% having a history of hemorrhagic stroke. The most common antithrombotic regimen before the procedure was direct oral anticoagulants (48.9%), while postprocedural therapy most often included dual antiplatelet therapy (50%). The technical success rate was 95.5%, with residual leak (2.2%) and tamponade (1.4%) as the main causes of failure. Procedural success was 90.5%, most often limited by vascular complications (3.7%), periprocedural death (1.1%), and major bleeding (0.7%). Technical and procedural success rates did not differ significantly between the devices used. Conclusions In this large prospective cohort, technical and procedural success rates were similar across all LAAO devices, suggesting comparable safety and efficacy. Postprocedural therapy typically involves dual antiplatelet therapy, with all patients requiring some pharmacological treatment. Registration URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05144958 .

sections.what is new?: In the large multicenter SALAMANDER (Stand‐Alone Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion for Thromboembolism Prevention in Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation Disease) registry, stand‐alone left atrial appendage occlusion using 7 contemporary devices was associated with high technical (95.5%) and procedural (90.5%) success rates, with no meaningful differences between devices. Postprocedural antithrombotic therapy in SALAMANDER was heterogeneous, with antiplatelet‐based regimens most commonly used at discharge.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Prospective studies are needed to define optimal post‐left atrial appendage occlusion antithrombotic strategies that minimize bleeding while maintaining protection from device‐related thrombosis and thromboembolic events.
sections.methods_1: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.study design: The SALAMANDER registry is a real‐life, multicenter, observational study conducted across 16 high‐volume cardiac centers in Europe, with the primary objective of evaluating the safety and efficacy of LAAO using a variety of currently available technologies. 14 Overall, 7 distinct devices have been assessed within the registry framework, representing the technological diversity of current clinical practice. These include (1) AtriClip (AtriCure, Mason, OH), a fully thoracoscopic, epicardial clip system applied externally to occlude the LAA via minimally invasive surgical access; (2) Watchman (Boston Scientific), a percutaneous, endocardial occluder delivered transseptally to seal the LAA from within the atrium; (3) Watchman FLX (Boston Scientific), the next‐generation version of the Watchman device, with enhanced conformability and anchoring features; (4) Amulet (Abbott, Plymouth, MN), a dual‐seal endocardial device comprising a lobe and a disc, suitable for complex LAA morphologies; (5) LARIAT (SentreHeart, Redwood City, CA), a hybrid endo‐epicardial system involving transseptal endocardial guidance and epicardial suture‐based ligation; (6) Lambre (Lifetech Scientific, Shenzhen, China), a self‐expanding, endocardial occluder with a distinctive anchoring mechanism and adaptability to varying appendage anatomies; and (7) Omega (Shape Memory Medical Inc., Santa Clara, CA), an endocardial device using shape memory. The patients' data were collected using an electronic case report form developed by the Polish Cardiac Society and were protected in accordance with the applicable Polish regulations, the General Data Protection Regulation, and institutional standard operating procedures (Data S1 ). The study was conducted in line with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was registered at www.ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05144958 ). The study adhered to Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines for observational studies (Table S1 ). Ethical approval was obtained from the local Bioethics Committee of the Upper‐Silesian Medical Centre of the Silesian Medical University in Katowice, Poland (PCN/CBN/0052/52/139/I/22). Due to the noninterventional, observational nature of this prospective registry, the requirement for informed consent was waived. To minimize potential bias, all participating centers followed standardized data collection procedures with predefined event definitions and protocol‐based measures to ensure cross‐center consistency in reporting. In addition, regular data quality checks, source data verification, and central data validation were performed to ensure the completeness, accuracy, and uniform ascertainment of outcomes across sites.
sections.study population: Patients in the study have been continuously recruited at each participating center to ensure unbiased inclusion of the eligible population. The enrollment period for this analysis spanned from October 29, 2010, to December 19, 2024. Inclusion criteria for the SALAMANDER registry comprise the following: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) diagnosis of paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent nonvalvular AF; (3) increased thromboembolic risk, defined as a CHA 2 DS 2 ‐VASc score ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women; (4) elevated bleeding risk, particularly in patients with a HAS‐BLED score ≥3; (5) history of significant bleeding events; (6) documented bleeding complications while on OAC, including VKAs; (7) presence of comorbid conditions predisposing to bleeding, such as coagulopathies, thrombocytopenia, or end‐stage renal disease requiring dialysis; and (8) failure of oral anticoagulation due to stroke recurrence or associated cerebrovascular abnormalities such as cerebral aneurysm. Participants in this registry met all the inclusion criteria and did not meet any exclusion criteria. Study sites are listed in Table S2 . The flowchart of the study design is presented in Figure 1 .
sections.end point definitions: Clinical and procedural data are collected in accordance with the study protocol and predefined criteria for success and complications, thereby enabling a robust assessment of the safety and efficacy of LAA closure in real‐world clinical practice. The primary outcomes analysis focused exclusively on clinical events occurring during the index hospitalization (from the LAAO procedure until hospital discharge). Imaging outcomes were additionally assessed at a 1‐time control visit within 3 months after the procedure. This study uses structured, prespecified end points based on the definitions outlined in the Munich Consensus. 15 As the SALAMANDER registry is ongoing, postdischarge clinical outcomes are not analyzed in this article, which focuses on baseline characteristics, procedural data, and in‐hospital outcomes. Longitudinal follow‐up outcomes (24 months) will be reported separately once the full data set becomes available to avoid bias related to unequal follow‐up duration and potential temporal changes in device selection and procedural strategies. The primary end point was technical success, defined as complete LAA exclusion without device‐related complications and with no residual peridevice leak >5 mm. Procedural success was defined as achievement of technical success without major periprocedural complications, including vascular injury, thromboembolic events (eg, stroke or air embolism), periprocedural death, or major bleeding. Major bleeding was defined as type 3 or higher according to the Bleeding Academic Research Consortium criteria. Ischemic stroke was defined as an acute focal neurological deficit presumed to be due to ischemia, persisting ≥24 hours, or <24 hours with imaging confirmation of infarction. Transient ischemic attack was defined as a rapid‐onset focal neurologic deficit due to cerebral ischemia, resolving within 24 hours. Systemic embolism was defined as an occlusive thrombotic event in a systemic artery with clinical manifestations. Effective device occlusion is defined as a residual jet ≤5 mm, evaluated intraoperatively or during control visit (transoesophageal echocardiography or computed tomography), depending on the specific device used. Given the heterogeneous nature of available LAAO technologies, including 7 distinct occluder systems—Watchman, Watchman FLX, Amulet, LARIAT, AtriClip, Lambre, and Omega—the study adopted uniform, device‐agnostic definitions of success. Despite differences in design, deployment strategy (endocardial, epicardial, or hybrid), and imaging control protocols, the endpoint definitions were standardized across all devices to enable valid interdevice comparisons. Procedural metrics, including implantation depth, compression ratio, residual leak, need for partial or full recapture, and imaging features (eg, spontaneous echo contrast, coverage of trabeculations), were systematically collected. Device‐specific parameters were reported using a harmonized data structure, and all echocardiographic data were evaluated by a central core laboratory to ensure consistency across the diverse technologies.
sections.statistical approach: Data were summarized using mean±SD and median (interquartile range) for continuous data, and count (percentage) for categorical data. Continuous variables were tested for distribution by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. For comparisons between 2 groups, the unpaired Student's t test or Mann–Whitney U test was applied, depending on data distribution. For comparisons across >2 groups, ANOVA or the Kruskal–Wallis test was used as appropriate. Categorical variables were compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher's exact test. To identify independent predictors of procedural success and clinical outcomes, multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed. Variables with a P value <0.05 in univariable analysis were included in the multivariable model. Results are expressed as odds ratios with 95% CIs. Figures were created in BioRender ( https://biorender.com/ ). Given the minimal extent of missingness and the fact that these variables were not used for building adjusted multivariable models at this stage of the analysis, no imputation procedures were performed.
sections.characteristics of participants: The study enrolled 1660 patients (median age, 76 [interquartile range, 70–81] years; 38% women). A total of 98.7% of patients had AF, and the remaining 1.3% were diagnosed with atrial flutter. The median LVEF was 55%. The most common comorbidities were hypertension (90%), chronic kidney disease (49.9%), and coronary artery disease (37.7%). A prior history of ischemic stroke was reported in 26.3% of patients and systemic embolic events in 12.1%. The median CHA 2 DS 2 ‐VASc was 4 (interquartile range, 3–5). The median HAS‐BLED score was 4 (interquartile range, 3–4). Detailed characteristics of enrolled participants are presented in Table 1 . Patient characteristics according to the implanted device are presented in Table S3 . The most common types of LAA shapes were chicken wing (63.5%), windsock (13.5%), and cauliflower (12.5%). Additional data on the characteristics of LAA are presented in Table S4 .
sections.indications for laao: The most common indication for LAAO was significant bleeding, in 83.7% of enrolled patients. Among these bleeding events, 68.8% occurred during treatment with DOACs and 24.9% during therapy with VKAs. The most frequent bleeding sites were the lower (27.9%) and upper (21.7%) gastrointestinal tracts, and 17.4% had a history of hemorrhagic stroke. The second‐ and third‐most‐common indications were other reasons (8.4%) and failure of OAC (5.6%), respectively. A detailed description of the indications for LAAO is presented in Table 1 .
sections.procedural characteristic: The most frequently used devices were Watchman FLX (39%), Amplatzer Amulet (30.1%), and Watchman (17.5%). General anesthesia was administered to 55.9% of enrolled participants, of which 32.6% received intubated anesthesia. The remaining procedural characteristics are presented in Table 1 .
sections.antithrombotic regimen: Before the procedure, 91.7% of patients received OAC in the form of DOACs (48.9%), VKAs (17.1%), DOACs with single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT; 12%), triple antithrombotic therapy (5.7%) or low‐molecular‐weight heparin (4.1%). The most common antithrombotic regimens after the procedure were DAPT (50%), SAPT (27.3%), and DOACs (9.8%). The percentage distribution of various antithrombotic regimens is presented in Figure 2 . The most common antithrombotic regimen before the procedure, DOACs (48.9%), was most often switched to DAPT (45.4% of all DOAC‐treated patients) or SAPT (24.4% of all DOAC‐treated patients) postprocedurally, while in 18.8% of cases it was continued. Among patients receiving VKAs (17.1% of all patients before the procedure), 58.8% were switched to DAPT, 22.2% to SAPT, and 12% continued their previous regimen. The majority of patients receiving low‐molecular‐weight heparin before the procedure (4.1% of all patients) were switched to DAPT after the LAAO (70.6% of all low‐molecular‐weight heparin–treated participants). Among patients receiving triple antithrombotic therapy before the procedure, 65.3% were treated with DAPT and 31.6% with SAPT following LAAO. An illustrative distribution of changes in antithrombotic therapy is presented in Figure 3 .
sections.primary outcomes: The technical success rate was 95.5%, with the most common causes of failure being residual leak (2.2%) and tamponade (1.4%). The procedural success rate was 90.5%. The most frequent factors of procedural failure were vascular complications (3.7%), periprocedural death (1.1%), and major bleeding (0.7%). Among the 19 periprocedural deaths, the leading causes were cardiac tamponade (5 cases [26.3%]) and major bleeding (4 cases [21.1%]). Urgent cardiac surgery was required in 9 patients, including the need for device removal in 5 cases (55.6%). A detailed description of the primary outcomes is presented in Table 2 . No statistically significant differences were observed among the occluders in technical and procedural success rates, as shown in Table 2 . Detailed results of the univariate analysis are available in Tables S5 and S6 . No statistically significant differences were observed in the frequency of primary outcomes after dividing the analyzed period into 2 time intervals. Year‐by‐year analyses demonstrated stable technical and procedural success rates, whereas the incidence of major bleeding and periprocedural death varied significantly over time ( P <0.001 and P =0.003, respectively). Notably, these adverse events showed lower rates in more recent years compared with earlier peaks, albeit with marked interannual variability. Temporal trends in the frequency of primary outcomes and in the use of individual devices are presented in Tables S7 through S9 .
sections.discussion: This study represents one of the largest European cohorts evaluating the outcomes of stand‐alone LAAO for thromboembolism prevention in patients with nonvalvular AF. Our findings demonstrate that the stand‐alone LAAO procedure is associated with a high technical (95.5%) and procedural (90.5%) success rate, regardless of the device type, reflecting the advances in device technology and operator expertise. Second, we observed a reduction in the use of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in patients undergoing LAAO, highlighting the procedure's potential to minimize long‐term pharmacological burden and associated bleeding risks. These results reinforce the growing evidence supporting LAAO as a viable and effective alternative to long‐term OAC, especially in patients with contraindications or intolerance to anticoagulant therapy. Two general problems are observed in many patients with AF receiving OAC. The first is an inadequate level of anticoagulation due to poor compliance, leading to increased stroke risk, especially for DOAC. The second is an induction of bleeding, which leads to discontinuing the therapy. One real‐world study revealed that ≈30% of patients with nonvalvular AF discontinue OAC in the first 2 years after therapy admission. 16 The most frequently documented reasons for discontinuing anticoagulation were bleeding (13%) and infrequent AF paroxysms (14%). 17 In the United States, analysis of MarketScan data (12 129 patients) revealed that up to 47% of patients with nonvalvular AF discontinued anticoagulation therapy in an average of 120 days, most commonly due to bleeding. 16 Hence, a reliable management option is needed for these patients. Previous real‐world studies, although based on smaller patient cohorts and using a narrower spectrum of devices, demonstrate technical and procedural success rates comparable with the outcomes achieved in our study. One Belgian study involving 457 patients undergoing transcatheter LAAO with the use of either the Watchman or Amplatzer cardiac plug/Amulet device reported a technical success rate of 97.1% and a procedural success rate of 95.9%. 18 The EWOLUTION (Registry on WATCHMAN Outcomes in Real‐Life Utilization) registry, which included 1025 patients undergoing transcatheter LAAO with the Watchman device, demonstrated technical and procedural success rates of 98.5% and 97.3%, respectively. 19 In the ITALIAN‐FLX registry, which included 772 patients, there was a technical success rate of 100% and a procedural success rate of 97.3%. 20 Large randomized clinical trials have shown technical success rates that, while comparable, remain lower: 88% in PROTECT‐AF and 90% in PRAGUE‐17. 12 , 21 The high rates of technical and procedural success reported in both real‐world studies, such as ours, and in randomized clinical trials underscore the safety and feasibility of transcatheter LAAO. In addition, a number of studies showed good performance of external epicardial occlusion devices both in animal studies and clinically implanted concomitantly to open heart surgery and thoracoscopic ablation, revealing no safety issues and nearly 100% of LAA closure with no pouch and stable long‐term results. 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 Different epicardial (AtriClip) and endocardial devices (Watchman, Amulet), are in various stages of development or clinical use with good results in experienced centers. Some doubts about LAAO effectiveness have been formulated in terms of transcatheter techniques. 29 , 30 , 31 There is a debate whether it is related to acute complications, need for bridging anticoagulation, mid‐ and long‐term device leakage, or thromboembolism originating from other parts of the left atrium. 32 , 33 Epicardial clips are able to avoid those weaknesses, while limitations associated with the thoracoscopic intervention, such as the need for short induction and intubation, severely depressed lung function, and previous surgery with left pleural cavity opening, are self‐evident. The optimal antithrombotic regimen following LAAO remains debatable. Despite growing experience with the procedure and, therefore, increasing implantation success rates, there is still no universally accepted postimplantation protocol. Various strategies have been proposed, ranging from DAPT to short‐term OAC, depending on patient bleeding risk profiles. The current evidence on the optimal antithrombotic strategy following LAAO remains conflicting, especially since studies include patients with widely varying bleeding risks and use inconsistent regimens. There is no general consensus on the most effective/safe approach, and clinical practice can vary significantly between centers. 34 While some studies support the use of low‐dose DOACs for reducing thromboembolic and bleeding events, others report no significant advantage over simplified regimens such as SAPT or even no therapy. 35 A network meta‐analysis of 41 studies 36 found that DOAC monotherapy was associated with the lowest rates of thromboembolic events and the highest risk of major bleeding, while DOAC treatment was superior to VKA in reducing all‐cause death by 61%, and DAPT was associated with 50% lower risk of thromboembolic events compared with SAPT. Clinical trial evidence comparing antithrombotic regimes is limited. The ADALA (Low‐Dose Direct Oral Anticoagulation Versus Dual Antiplatelet Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion) trial identified that low‐dose DOAC, in the form of apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, was a superior therapeutic option, reducing the risk of the primary end point (major bleeding, thromboembolic events, and device‐related thrombosis) by 81% at 3‐month follow‐up. 37 Conversely, there are some observational data. For example, findings from the LOGIC (Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion in Patients With Gastrointestinal or Intracranial Bleeding) registry demonstrated no significant differences in overall death, cardiovascular death, thromboembolic events, or bleeding risk between patients receiving SAPT or no antithrombotic therapy and those treated with standard antithrombotic regimens. 38 In the EWOLUTION study, the use of DAPT was comparable (60.8% versus 50% in our cohort), while SAPT was less common (6.9% versus 27.3% in our study). 19 In contrast, John et al reported DAPT use in 72% of their patients, with limited use of DOACs (3.7% versus 9.8% in our cohort). 18 In the SALAMANDER registry, discharge antithrombotic therapy varied not only between centers but also at the operator level (as the choice of postprocedural regimen was left to the operator's discretion). This likely reflects real‐world decision making that is strongly shaped by the individual patient's clinical profile, procedure‐related anatomic considerations, and implant quality (optimal anatomic sealing with stable device positioning). In many cases, the predominant driver is a bleeding‐prone phenotype (frequent prior major bleeding, particularly gastrointestinal or intracranial), in whom even short‐term OAC may be considered unacceptable, favoring DAPT or SAPT. Conversely, a distinct subgroup undergoes LAAO due to perceived OAC failure, that is, thromboembolic events (including stroke) occurring despite anticoagulation, which may prompt some operators to prefer a period of OAC or DOAC‐based therapy after the procedure, even for long‐term use. These patient‐level contrasts, combined with center/operator‐specific decisions, plausibly explain the observed heterogeneity in post‐LAAO regimens. This heterogeneity also mirrors differences between landmark trials. In PROTECT AF and PREVAIL, the postimplant protocol was anchored in short‐term warfarin plus aspirin followed by a transition to antiplatelet therapy, reflecting a strategy that assumes temporary anticoagulation is feasible in many patients. In contrast, PRAGUE‐17 enrolled a high‐risk population and used a more antiplatelet‐forward post‐LAAO approach, which is closer to the DAPT‐dominant practice seen in contemporary bleeding‐driven cohorts such as SALAMANDER. 10 , 11 , 12 Device selection (endocardial versus epicardial) for LAAO is usually determined by LAA anatomy, bleeding risk profile, feasibility of antithrombotic therapy, and institutional expertise. 8 Endocardial systems require transseptal access and implantation within the LAA lumen, necessitating at least a temporary course of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. In contrast, epicardial techniques achieve LAA exclusion without leaving permanent material within the LAA. This fundamental distinction often allows simplification or avoidance of long‐term anticoagulation. 39 Moreover, epicardial systems require pericardial access or surgical exposure, which introduces procedure‐specific risks such as pericardial bleeding, effusion, tamponade, and injury to adjacent structures. 8 Endocardial devices, by contrast, are implanted via a fully percutaneous transseptal approach and are therefore associated with a lower immediate procedural risk profile. Their periprocedural complications are more commonly related to transseptal puncture, device embolization, or access‐site bleeding. 40 In clinical practice, these differences directly influence patient selection and the individualization of periprocedural and postprocedural management strategies.
sections.limitations: The SALAMANDER registry is an observational, real‐world multicenter cohort study. The AF population has been recruited across 2 countries (Poland and Italy), but as with any observational cohort study, there are limitations, including common limitations to observational cohort studies, inadequacy of data recording/capture, and selection bias. Despite selecting high‐volume reference centers to ensure uniform procedural quality, certain data elements were not collected systematically across sites. In this context, a notable example is the lack of detailed information on imaging modalities used during percutaneous LAAO procedures, which reflects the inherent challenges of comprehensive data acquisition in large observational registries. The large overall study cohort is a strength of this study; however, the marked imbalance in sample sizes between device groups limits the ability to reliably compare outcomes, particularly rare events such as tamponade, and therefore warrants cautious interpretation. Finally, as the present cohort is derived exclusively from European populations, the generalizability of these findings to other regions may be limited, given the known ethnic differences in AF‐related complication (ie, stroke and bleeding), 41 , 42 LAA morphology, 43 and the so‐called “East Asian” paradox in relation to antithrombotic therapy effectiveness and safety 44 ; therefore, similarly large prospective cohorts from different populations globally are warranted.
sections.conclusions_1: In one of the largest European cohorts, we show that the stand‐alone LAAO procedure is associated with a high technical and procedural success rate, with potentially comparable outcomes across device types. The reduction in the use of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy in patients undergoing LAAO reduces long‐term OAC use and associated bleeding risks.
