sections.study design and participants: The BAT2 study (Bleeding With Antithrombotic Therapy 2) was an investigator-initiated, prospective, multicenter, observational study involving 52 hospitals across Japan within the Network for Clinical Stroke Trials. 7 , 22 , 23 The BAT2 study was designed to determine the incidence and characteristics of bleeding complications in patients treated with oral antithrombotic therapy and to develop bleeding risk prediction models, including baseline brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data obtained under standardized imaging conditions, using a prospective registry involving institutes across Japan. Patients with cerebrovascular or cardiovascular diseases, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, who newly started or continued taking oral antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants were enrolled from stroke clinics and hospitals from 2016 through 2019. This subanalysis of the BAT2 study aimed to investigate the impact of SVD burden on functional outcomes, using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) to assess functional outcomes. In the BAT2 study, mRS was measured 5× over 2 years, at registration and every 6 months until the end of follow-up. For this subanalysis, patients from the BAT2 study with available mRS data at registration and the final follow-up were selected for analysis. The BAT2 study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02889653 ) and the University Hospital Medical Information Network clinical trial registry in Japan (URL: https://www.umin.ac.jp/ctr ; Unique identifier: 000023669). The overall protocol has been published elsewhere. 22 All study procedures were reviewed and approved by the ethics committees of the participating sites. Written informed consent was obtained from patients or their family members before enrollment. This study follows the STROBE reporting guidelines (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology; Supplemental Material ) for cohort studies.
sections.data acquisition, management, and follow: Baseline clinical information and blood test results were collected. MRI examinations of the brain were acquired at 3T or 1.5T between 90 days before and 14 days after registration. MRI sequences included T1-weighted, T2-weighted, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery, and T2*-weighted imaging. All MRI examinations were interpreted by a central diagnostic committee for white matter hyperintensity (WMH), lacunes, cerebral microbleeds (CMB), and basal ganglia perivascular spaces according to the criteria from the Standards for Reporting Vascular Changes in Neuroimaging. 24 One point for each SVD feature of CMB (≥1 for any CMB), confluent WMH, enlarged basal ganglia perivascular spaces (≥11), and lacunes (≥1) on MRI was summed as the total SVD score, ranging from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 4. 15 For patients in whom one SVD feature was missing, 0 points were awarded for that SVD feature. Details of the acquisition and interpretation of MRI are described elsewhere. 23 Interrater reliability of MRI interpretation by the central diagnostic radiology committee, expressed as median kappa coefficients, was as follows: 0.87 (0.72–0.97) for deep CMB; 0.86 (0.74–0.96) for lobar CMB; 0.68 (0.57–0.86) for periventricular hyperintensity; 0.75 (0.63–0.81) for deep subcortical white matter hyperintensity; 0.61 (0.52–0.81) for basal ganglia perivascular spaces; and 0.75 (0.65–0.98) for lacune. Interrater reliability for these findings showed median kappa coefficients ranging from 0.66 to 0.94. 23 The primary outcome of the BAT2 study was major bleeding, defined by the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis, 25 while secondary outcomes included clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, 26 ischemic events, and death, with ischemic events encompassing ischemic stroke, acute coronary syndrome, systemic embolism, and unplanned revascularization due to ischemia. Enrolled patients were followed up at 6 (±2) months, 12 (±3) months, 18 (±3) months, and 24 (±4) months after registration, with a total of 4 assessments conducted by the principal investigator or a trained study coordinator at each site, either through in-person clinic visits or telephone interviews with the patient or caregiver, to investigate event occurrence and measure mRS. If death occurred during the follow-up period, mRS for all subsequent measurement points was recorded as 6, and death was treated as part of the outcome trajectory.
sections.outcomes: The following outcomes were assessed in the present study: functional decline, defined as an increase in mRS from baseline to the end of follow-up (ΔmRS score ≥1); unfavorable functional outcomes at the end of follow-up, defined as an mRS score of 3 to 6; and all-cause death during the follow-up period. Events occurring during the follow-up period (major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, and ischemic events) were treated as time-dependent covariates, as the timing of each event could influence mRS at the final follow-up. To clarify the impact of event timing on mRS at the final follow-up, events were categorized into 4 time periods: event 1 (registration–6 months), event 2 (6–12 months), event 3 (12–18 months), and event 4 (18–24 months; Figure S1 ). Each event, categorized into 4 time periods, was examined for associations with ΔmRS score ≥1 and unfavorable functional outcomes at the end of follow-up. For major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, and ischemic events, patients with multiple episodes were counted once in each distinct time period; if several episodes occurred within the same period, they were counted only once. If death occurred during the follow-up period, no further events were considered to have occurred.
sections.statistical analysis: Continuous variables are expressed as the mean±SD or median (interquartile range), and categorical variables are presented as the number (%). Differences in categorical variables among the 5 SVD score groups (range, 0–4) were tested with the Pearson χ 2 test, and differences in continuous variables with the Kruskal-Wallis test. For multivariable analysis, logistic regression was used to compare outcomes among the SVD score groups after adjustment for age, sex, premorbid mRS, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, previous stroke, previous acute coronary syndrome, antiplatelet use, anticoagulant use, MRI field strength, and events (major bleeding, clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding, and ischemic events), each categorized into 4 time periods. Events during follow-up were categorized into 4 predefined time periods, and the presence or absence of events in each period was entered as separate covariates. Information on event severity was not available and was not included in the analyses. Detailed definitions of covariates are provided in the Supplemental Methods . Causal mediation analysis used a 4-way decomposition. 27 SVD score was decomposed into its 4 MRI markers (CMB, confluent WMH, extensive basal ganglia perivascular spaces, and lacunes), and the same analyses were performed to test each marker’s association with ΔmRS score ≥1. A 4-way decomposition provides detailed insight into how much of the effect is mediated, how much is due to interaction, how much stems from both mediation and interaction, and how much is attributable to neither. 27 , 28 Severe SVD burden, defined as an SVD score of 3 or higher as reported in previous studies, 7 , 20 was the exposure; major bleeding or ischemic event was the mediator; and ΔmRS score ≥1 was the outcome. The model was further adjusted for age, sex, premorbid mRS, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, previous stroke, acute coronary syndrome, antiplatelet use, anticoagulant use, and MRI field strength. Sex-stratified analyses were additionally performed. Several sensitivity analyses were performed. The first analysis was restricted to patients without major bleeding or ischemic events. Second, a complete-case analysis restricted to patients with available SVD imaging data was conducted. Third, multivariable analyses excluding baseline mRS from the covariates were conducted. Fourth, analyses were performed excluding patients who died during follow-up. Fifth, a proportional odds model for 24-month mRS was conducted with the same covariates as the primary model. Finally, mRS was categorized into 3 levels (0–1, 2–4, and 5–6), and the association between SVD score and a shift toward worse mRS categories was evaluated. Missing data were <1% overall and none for the study outcome, so no imputation was performed. Chronic kidney disease was defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Because these analyses were prespecified, no formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was applied. Statistical significance was set at P <0.05. All analyses were performed with STATA software (version 17.0; SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC).
sections.patient selection: Among the 5378 patients enrolled, 11 had contraindications to MRI, 17 did not undergo MRI for reasons other than contraindication, 24 had incomplete baseline clinical data, 2 had duplicated registrations, 73 had no follow-up data, 1 lacked information on baseline antithrombotic therapy, and 485 had missing data for either baseline or final follow-up mRS, making them ineligible (Figure 1 ). There were differences in patient characteristics according to the availability of data for baseline and final follow-up mRS for the variables of dyslipidemia, history of stroke, history of ischemic stroke, deep vein thrombosis, and current smoking ( Table S1 ). A total of 4765 patients (1573 women; median age, 73 years ([interquartile range, 66–79]); baseline mRS, 0 [0–1]) were included in the present analysis. Of these, 4268 (89.6%) patients had a history of ischemic stroke, with a median interval of 87 days [16–1524] from onset to registration, and were taking antithrombotic agents as secondary stroke prevention. The remaining 497 (10.4%) were receiving antithrombotic therapy for primary prevention of stroke or secondary prevention of cardiovascular diseases, and their characteristics are summarized in Table S2 . Between baseline and the end of follow-up, mRS increased in 967 patients (20.3%), showed no change in 2965 (62.2%), and decreased in 833 (17.5%; Figure S2 ).
sections.patient characteristics by svd score: Calculated total SVD scores were 0 in 857 patients (18.0%), 1 in 1302 (27.3%), 2 in 1182 (24.8%), 3 in 934 (19.6%), and 4 in 490 (10.3%; median total SVD score 2 [1–3]). Table 1 summarizes the patient demographics and clinical characteristics. As the total SVD score increased, older age, higher premorbid mRS, and higher frequencies of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and history of stroke, ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and acute coronary syndrome were observed (all P <0.001).
sections.incidence of events and mrs changes duri: Table 2 summarizes the unadjusted incidence of events and mRS changes during follow-up according to the SVD score. The incidence of major bleeding ( P <0.001), clinically relevant nonmajor events ( P =0.02), and ischemic events ( P =0.001) during the follow-up period increased as the SVD score increased. As the SVD score increased, the proportions of patients with mRS scores of 3 to 6 and of all-cause death likewise increased. Furthermore, as the SVD score increased, the proportion of patients with ΔmRS score ≥1 increased ( P <0.001), with proportions of 13.2% with score 0, 16.1% with score 1, 20.7% with score 2, 28.1% at score 3, and 28.2% with score 4 (Table 2 ; Figure 2 ; Figure S3 ).
sections.association between svd score, functiona: In the multivariable analysis adjusted for covariates, including events during follow-up categorized into 4 time periods, the SVD scores of 3 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.65 [95% CI, 1.27–2.15]) and 4 (aOR 1.62 [1.19–2.19]), compared with the SVD score of 0, were significantly associated with ΔmRS score ≥1, along with major bleeding and ischemic events during the follow-up period (Figure 3 ; Table S3 ). The addition of the SVD score to clinical covariates in the primary analysis resulted in modest but statistically significant improvement in discriminative performance, with the C-statistic increasing from 0.699 to 0.705 (ΔC=0.006; P =0.035). Major bleeding and ischemic events were significantly associated with mRS scores of 3 to 6 at 24 months and all-cause death during the follow-up period. The SVD score was not significantly associated with the mRS score of 3 to 6 at 24 months and all-cause death during the follow-up period ( Table S4 ). When events were coded as occurring during follow-up or not, instead of being divided into 4 time periods, SVD scores of 3 (aOR, 1.64 [1.26–2.14]) and 4 (aOR, 1.62 [1.20–2.19]) were significantly associated with ΔmRS score ≥1, along with major bleeding (aOR, 4.86 [3.05–7.75]) and ischemic event (aOR, 3.20 [2.43–4.22]; Table S5 ) during the follow-up period. For individual SVD markers, the presence of CMB was associated with ΔmRS score ≥1 (aOR, 1.23 [1.05–1.45]). Confluent WMH was associated with ΔmRS score ≥1 (aOR, 1.36 [1.15–1.61]) and mRS score of 3 to 6 at 24 months (aOR, 1.43 [1.15–1.78]; Table S6 ). There was no significant interaction between sex and SVD score for the outcomes ( Table S7 ).
sections.causal mediation analysis of svd burden: Both the controlled direct effect of SVD burden on ΔmRS score ≥1 and the pure natural indirect effect mediated through major bleeding and ischemic events were significant (controlled direct effect, coefficient, 0.498 [95% CI, 0.26–0.73]; pure natural indirect effect, coefficient 0.051 [0.01–0.09]). The controlled direct effect accounted for 73.05% of the total effect (Figure 4 ).
sections.sensitivity analysis: Among patients without major bleeding or ischemic events during follow-up, unadjusted patient clinical characteristics and mRS changes during follow-up by SVD score are summarized in Table S8 . The SVD score increased, the proportion of patients with ΔmRS score ≥1 increased ( P <0.001), with proportions of 12.2% with score 0, 14.8% with score 1, 19.2% with score 2, 24.8% at score 3, and 25.3% with score 4. In the multivariable analysis, SVD scores of 3 and 4, compared with an SVD score of 0, were significantly associated with ΔmRS score ≥1 (SVD score 3, aOR 1.57 [1.19–2.08]; SVD score 4, aOR 1.61 [1.17–2.22]). SVD score of 4 was significantly associated with mRS score of 3 to 6 at 24 months (aOR, 1.63 [1.07–2.49]; Table S9 ). SVD imaging markers were not assessable in 422 patients (8.9%). In the complete-case analysis of SVD data, SVD scores of 2, 3, and 4, compared with an SVD score of 0, were significantly associated with ΔmRS score ≥1 (SVD score 2: aOR, 1.34 [1.01–1.77]; SVD score 3: aOR, 1.82 [1.38–2.41]; SVD score 4: aOR, 1.86 [1.36–2.54]). In addition, an SVD score of 4 was significantly associated with an mRS score of 3 to 6 at 24 months (aOR, 1.64 [1.09–2.47]; Tables S10 and S11 ). The analyses excluding baseline mRS from the covariates ( Table S12 ), the analyses additionally excluding patients who died during follow-up ( Table S13 ), the proportional odds model ( Table S14 ), and the categorical mRS analysis ( Table S15 ) all showed results consistent in direction with the primary analyses.
sections.discussion: Notably, this study investigated the influence of SVD burden on functional outcomes while accounting for ischemic and bleeding events as time-dependent variables. One of the major findings of the present study was that 20.3% of patients receiving oral antithrombotic agents experienced functional decline within 2 years. SVD scores of 3 and 4 were associated with a higher risk of increased mRS score at the end of follow-up, compared with an SVD score of 0. In addition, causal mediation analysis separated the association between SVD burden and the ΔmRS score ≥1 into direct effects and indirect effects mediated by major bleeding or ischemic events. Even without major bleeding or ischemic events, an SVD score of ≥3 was significantly associated with an increase in mRS in the sensitivity analysis. This study suggested that patients with a higher SVD burden may experience functional decline even in the absence of overt bleeding or ischemic events. This study expands on previous studies that have assessed the prognostic value of SVD burden for functional outcomes. Prior studies have reported inconsistent findings regarding the association of each of the SVD imaging features and the SVD score with functional decline. 12 – 14 , 16 – 21 , 29 – 32 Although some studies showed an independent relationship with prognosis, 17 – 19 the SVD score added little incremental predictive value beyond established predictors such as age and baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score. 16 Compared with these earlier studies, the present study included the largest number of participants and evaluated long-term outcomes, thereby providing clearer evidence of the impact of SVD score on functional outcomes. It is also important to assess the influence of ischemic and bleeding events during follow-up on functional decline, as they are likely to have a significant impact. The present study recorded not only strokes but also systemic ischemic and hemorrhagic events that occurred during follow-up. SVD burden may contribute to the risk of functional decline in the absence of significant bleeding or ischemic events. Apart from the effects of ischemic and bleeding events, MRI-defined SVD may contribute to functional decline by disrupting the basal ganglia–thalamo–frontal cortical and frontoparietal circuits, which are critical for motor and cognitive function. 33 , 34 Previous studies have shown associations of SVD with dysphagia, gait disturbance, and parkinsonism, 35 – 38 conditions that are thought to arise from disrupted connections in the basal ganglia–thalamo–frontal cortical and frontoparietal circuits. The present study did not identify the specific symptoms underlying functional decline; however, dysphagia, gait disturbance, Parkinsonism, and dementia are possible contributors. In the analysis of individual SVD markers, confluent WMH emerged as the main contributor to worsening mRS score and disability at the final follow-up. Prior studies using functional MRI have shown that WMH is associated with functional dysconnectivity of basal ganglia–thalamo–frontal cortical circuits, 39 , 40 supporting our finding. MRI-based assessment of SVD, therefore, has prognostic value for predicting disability. The findings of this study indicate that SVD burden not only raises the risk of bleeding and ischemic events 7 but also has an association with functional decline and frailty, which may ultimately restrict patients’ activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living. Therefore, these findings indicate the need to develop therapies targeting SVD directly. Therapeutic options for SVD remain limited. Recent data suggest that isosorbide mononitrate and cilostazol may favorably affect a composite outcome of cognition and activities of daily living. 41 In this study, 15.1% of participants were taking cilostazol, but the sample size was insufficient to confirm efficacy. Intensive blood pressure management has also been reported to slow the progression of MRI-SVD features and reduce the risks of stroke and mortality. 42 – 44 Future studies should evaluate whether cilostazol or intensive blood pressure management improves long-term functional outcomes, with stratification by SVD features in each patient. The strength of this study lies in the large sample size and multicenter recruitment in a real-world setting, reflecting actual clinical experiences. Second, we used standardized multimodal MRI sequences, with validated scales from a central diagnostic radiology committee, ensuring high reliability in neuroimaging interpretation. Third, this analysis treated ischemic and bleeding events during follow-up as time-dependent variables. For example, if the events occur early in the follow-up period, mRS may initially increase and later decrease by the final follow-up due to rehabilitation or the passage of time. By treating these events as time-dependent variables, this study accounted for the temporal fluctuations in their impact on mRS. This study has some limitations. First, almost all participants were Asian, which might limit the generalizability of the results to other ethnicities. Racial differences in the pathophysiology of SVD have been suggested. 45 , 46 Second, this study lacked detailed information on the specific causes of functional decline. Functional outcomes were assessed using the mRS, the most commonly used poststroke outcome measure with established validity, 47 , 48 which is weighted toward mobility. Because SVD affects independence through variable domains, such as cognitive impairment and mood disorders, mRS may not be the optimal measure of functional status. Third, in this study, most participants had prior ischemic stroke and were receiving antithrombotic therapy. Stroke severity data were unavailable. The findings may have limited generalizability. Fourth, functional outcome was assessed only at the end of follow-up. This approach may not fully capture the dynamic relationship between interim events and longitudinal functional trajectories. Finally, causal mediation relies on assumptions, including the absence of uncontrolled risk factors, which may not be fully met in this observational study.
sections.conclusions: Imaging-based assessment of SVD has prognostic value for predicting disability in patients receiving oral antithrombotic agents, mainly for cerebrovascular disease. SVD burden is associated with the risk of functional decline in the absence of significant bleeding or ischemic events. The detection of SVD burden may identify a group of individuals to target for enhanced rehabilitation and preventive strategies.
