sections.introduction: Fragility fractures, defined as fractures resulting from low-energy trauma such as a fall from standing height or less, are a hallmark of underlying osteoporosis and represent a substantial public health challenge globally. They predominantly affect older adults and are associated with increased morbidity, long-term disability, mortality, and significant healthcare costs [ 1 ]. Despite their clinical significance, fragility fractures are often under-recognized and inadequately managed in the emergency department (ED), the most common setting in which fracture diagnosis is made [ 2 ]. This gap in recognition contributes directly to suboptimal secondary prevention, leaving patients vulnerable to subsequent fractures that further compromise quality of life and increase healthcare burden [ 3 , 4 ]. Beyond their clinical consequences, fragility fractures impose a substantial economic and societal burden. In Europe, the direct costs of osteoporotic fractures were estimated to exceed €37 billion annually, with projections indicating a sharp rise due to population aging [ 5 ]. In Italy, a cost-of-illness analysis estimated the annual economic burden of osteoporosis at €2.2 billion in 2017, with approximately 80% of costs attributable to hospitalizations, 16% to drug treatments, and 3% to outpatient care [ 6 ]. Importantly, this estimate likely under-represents the true societal impact, since it does not fully capture indirect costs, productivity losses, and the economic burden borne by informal caregivers. Evidence suggests that these components can be substantial, amplifying the long-term financial implications of fragility fractures for both patients’ families and healthcare systems [ 5 , 7 – 9 ]. Emergency departments serve as crucial points of contact for patients with fragility fractures, offering a unique but under-utilized opportunity for early identification, risk stratification, and prompt initiation of multidisciplinary management strategies [ 2 ]. However, the fast-paced and acute-driven environment of emergency care can impede comprehensive evaluation and timely referral to specialist services such as fracture liaison services (FLS) and osteoporosis clinics [ 4 ]. Recent literature underscores the vital role of multidisciplinary collaboration, encompassing emergency medicine, orthopedics, geriatrics, endocrinology, rehabilitation, nursing, and primary care in improving patient outcomes through integrated fracture management pathways [ 1 , 5 , 6 ]. Evidence supports the implementation of practical, validated scoring systems and screening tools that can be feasibly applied in the emergency setting to facilitate early identification of high-risk individuals [ 4 ]. These tools aim to bridge the current care gap by enabling targeted referrals and personalized interventions aimed at reducing the risk of refracture [ 3 , 10 ]. This paper synthesizes current evidence on the multidisciplinary evaluation of fragility fracture management in the emergency setting and examines barriers to effective care coordination and risk recognition in ED practice. By highlighting these challenges, the study aims to contribute to improved identification of fragility fractures, more consistent referral pathways, and ultimately more effective secondary prevention and long-term patient outcomes.
sections.methods_1: A cross-sectional survey ( Supplementary materials 1 ) was conducted to investigate current practices, awareness, and perceived barriers in the identification and management of fragility fractures in emergency departments. A total of 34 healthcare professionals participated in the survey, including 10 emergency physicians, 11 radiologists, and 13 emergency nurses. The participants were drawn from 10 emergency departments distributed across northern, central, and southern Italy, including first- and second-level departments. The participating centers were based in Naples, Carpi, Milan, Venezia, Foggia, Rome, Ragusa, Reggio Emilia, and Turin, ensuring a broad geographic representation of emergency care settings across Italy. Collectively, these facilities handled approximately 450,000 emergency department visits in 2024. The survey consisted of 16 structured questions designed to explore how different professional figures assess and manage a case of fracture in the emergency setting: They are multiple-choice and open-ended questions covering areas such as patient triage, fracture risk factor assessment (e.g., history of falls, prior fractures, and use of risk-associated medications), interprofessional communication, and discharge practices. The instrument also explored whether existing workflows supported the identification of patients with potential bone fragility. Responses were collected through structured interviews conducted by trained facilitators. Following the survey, a focused expert board, composed of bone health specialists and emergency medicine physicians, reviewed and discussed the results. The purpose of the meeting was to critically review the survey findings, compare them with clinical experience, and explore practical solutions to address identified gaps. Key themes discussed included the discrepancy between reported and actual practices, the under-utilized role of nurses in history taking, and the limited involvement of radiologists in fragility risk assessment. Participants expressed strong support for the need to improve awareness, consistency, and standardization in the assessment of fragility fracture risk within emergency settings. The outcome of this process is the identification of key domains and risk factors relevant to fragility fracture recognition, in line with evidence and variables included in validated algorithms such as FRAX and DeFRA [ 11 – 14 ].
sections.results_1: Developed by a multidisciplinary panel composed of an emergency physician, an endocrinologist, specialists in internal medicine, a radiologist, an orthopedic surgeon, a rheumatologist, an emergency nurse, a health economist, and a gender medicine expert, the questionnaire covered a range of critical topics: recognition of clinical risk factors (such as previous fractures, family history, fear of falling, and balance impairment), evaluation of pharmacological risks (e.g., corticosteroids or hormonal therapies), documentation practices, availability of internal care pathways, and role-specific behaviors and perceptions. It also investigated potential barriers to standardized assessment and explored the perceived utility of a brief screening tool to support early identification and referral. Responses were analyzed by professional role to identify variability in attitudes, workflows, and clinical priorities and served as the foundation for a multidisciplinary expert discussion that followed. Figure 1 a shows how professionals investigate a history of recent or frequent falls and their dynamics. Emergency physicians reported the highest rate, with 60% stating they always assess this, compared to 37% of radiologists and 8% of nurses. Nurses showed greater variability, with a significant share responding “sometimes” or “in all individuals over 50 years of age.” These results highlight a stronger focus among physicians, while in other roles the assessment appears less systematic, potentially limiting early identification of fragility risk. Fig. 1 a Answers to question 1.2: Is a history of recent or frequent falls, and the mechanism of the fall, investigated? b Answers to question 1.3: Is there an investigation into a history of frequent or recent fractures and how they occurred? In line with the question on falls, responses to the investigation of frequent or recent fractures (Fig. 1 b) showed a similarly uneven approach. Among emergency physicians , 80% reported “always” investigating prior fractures , reflecting a strong awareness of fracture history as a risk factor. In contrast, only 12% of radiologists and 9% of nurses reported the same level of attention. The majority in these two groups selected “sometimes” or “in all individuals over 50,” suggesting that the investigation is often limited to specific populations and not part of standard practice across the board. The investigation of medication history as a risk factor for fractures, particularly regarding corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, or adjuvant hormone therapy, revealed clear differences across professional roles (Fig. 2 ). Among emergency physicians, a strong majority reported that they “always” assess this risk factor, with only 10% indicating “rarely” or only in women over 50 years. In contrast, radiologists showed a markedly different pattern: 22% reported doing so “always,” while 60% indicated they rarely or never investigate this information. Nurses showed intermediate behavior, with 40% responding “always” and 40% selecting “rarely or never.” These results highlight the critical role emergency physicians and nurses may play in identifying pharmacological contributors to bone fragility, while radiologists remain largely uninvolved in this aspect of clinical evaluation. Fig. 2 Answers to question 1.13: Is the patient’s medication history investigated as a risk factor for fractures (with particular attention to steroids, anticonvulsants, or adjuvant anti-hormonal therapies for cancer)? Assessment of family history of fracture is another important element in identifying patients at risk of osteoporosis. The investigation of family history of fractures, such as hip or other fracture sites in first-degree relatives, was reported inconsistently across all professional roles (Fig. 3 ). Among emergency physicians, the most frequent responses were “sometimes” (40%) and “rarely/never” (40%), indicating that this aspect is not routinely assessed even by frontline clinicians. Radiologists and nurses showed a similar trend, with the majority also reporting low or occasional investigation of familial risk. These findings show a general low attention to family history in the three professional categories even if at different levels. Fig. 3 Answer to question 1.5: Do you investigate whether there are cases of hip or other fractures in the family, such as in first-degree relatives? Fear of falling and self-reported balance issues are well-known predictors of future fractures and functional decline, particularly in older adults. However, these indicators are not routinely explored in the emergency setting. The assessment of fear of falling or difficulty maintaining balance is inconsistently performed across professional roles (Fig. 4 ). Among emergency physicians, only 50% reported “always” investigating this factor, while the remaining answers were split between “sometimes” and responses limited to specific subgroups. Radiologists showed minimal engagement, with most responses indicating “rarely/never” or “only in individuals over 50.” In contrast, emergency nurses showed a polarized pattern of responses, with only 30% reporting they “always” assess this aspect, while another 30% indicated they “rarely or never” investigate it. These results suggest that, although balance and fall-related fears are clinically relevant for fracture risk, they are variably integrated into emergency assessment routines. Fig. 4 Answer to question 1.16: Do you investigate whether the patient has ever been afraid of falling or has noticed difficulty maintaining balance? The explicit use of the term “fragility fracture” in clinical documentation is critical for the start of the most appropriate pathway. In fact, when asked only to the emergency physicians how frequently they indicate a “fragility fracture” diagnosis at discharge (question n 1.21 Supplementary Materials ), 80% responded “sometimes,” while only a small minority selected “never” (10%) or “other” (10%). Notably, none of the respondents reported indicating it “always.” Across most items, the survey revealed inconsistencies between professional roles and between declared practices and what typically occurs in real-world settings. These findings were critically discussed during the expert panel meeting, where organizational barriers, role-specific limitations, and lack of standardized tools were identified as major contributors to the therapeutic gap. In response, the panel discussed the practical implications of the identified gaps and emphasized the importance of early recognition of fragility fractures in postmenopausal women and men over 50 presenting with specific major fracture types (vertebra, pelvis, femur, humerus, and radius/ulna). The discussion highlighted the need for timely identification of patients at high risk of bone fragility and for structured referral to dedicated care pathways, ensuring appropriate follow-up, specialist evaluation, and secondary prevention. Overall, the expert discussion underscored the clinical relevance of well-established fragility fracture risk factors already recognized in the literature [ 15 – 20 ] and commonly included in validated risk assessment frameworks, highlighting their inconsistent evaluation in routine emergency practice.
sections.discussion: This study offers a qualitative overview of how fragility fractures are identified and managed in emergency settings, based on the perspectives of emergency physicians, radiologists, and nurses from 10 Italian hospitals. While general awareness of osteoporosis appears high across roles, the survey highlights a critical gap between knowledge and clinical practice, particularly in the systematic investigation of risk factors such as prior falls, previous fractures, medication use, and family history. One of the most relevant findings is the lack of uniformity in assessing fall and fracture history. Even though emergency physicians tend to investigate these aspects more consistently than nurses and radiologists, responses across all roles reveal that these assessments are neither standardized nor embedded into clinical workflows. Nurses, often the first point of contact in the ED, frequently limit their history taking to specific populations, and radiologists rarely explore fragility-related risk factors, despite their potential role in identifying low-trauma fractures. Similarly, the investigation of pharmacological risk and family history remains limited, especially outside emergency medicine. This inconsistency undermines early recognition and delays entry into appropriate care pathways. Another key insight is the near-absence of the term “fragility fracture” in discharge documentation. This omission limits both the patient’s awareness of their underlying condition and the ability of downstream providers, such as primary care physicians and fracture liaison services (FLS), to recognize the fracture as a sentinel event requiring secondary prevention. In the absence of structured follow-up systems or automatic alerts, this gap in communication compromises timely initiation of osteoporosis management and contributes to the widening of the therapeutic gap in fragility fracture care. These findings are consistent with previous literature showing that many fragility fractures remain unrecognized in acute care, with the first fracture often failing to prompt appropriate follow-up [ 21 ]. Unlike other acute conditions such as stroke or myocardial infarction, where triage pathways and structured referral protocols are well established, fragility fractures continue to follow the same undifferentiated route as traumatic fractures. This leads to delays in appropriate treatment and prevents timely prevention strategies, despite the known consequences of recurrent fragility fractures on patient outcomes and healthcare systems. The expert panel’s discussion emphasized the need to address the identified gaps through a more structured and shared approach to fragility fracture recognition in the emergency setting. Strengthening early clinical suspicion and improving integration of fragility-related considerations into routine fracture assessment may support more appropriate referral pathways and enhance continuity of care. This perspective aligns with the successful use of structured clinical approaches in other acute domains and supports the long-term goal of improving consistency in fragility fracture identification within emergency departments. Beyond the clinical and organizational implications, our findings also highlight an important economic dimension. Fragility fractures represent a substantial burden for healthcare systems, largely driven by hospitalizations and subsequent rehabilitation [ 5 , 7 ]. In Italy, the annual economic impact of osteoporosis has been estimated at approximately €2.2 billion, of which nearly 80% is attributable to hospital care, while only a small fraction relates to outpatient visits or pharmacological treatment [ 6 ]. Failure to identify and label fragility fractures in the emergency setting, as observed in our survey, is therefore not only a missed clinical opportunity but also a source of inefficient resource use. Recurrent fractures increase the likelihood of repeated admissions and long-term dependency, thereby amplifying both direct healthcare costs and indirect costs associated with loss of independence and caregiver burden. This study presents several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the methodology was qualitative in nature, based on self-reported survey responses rather than objective measurement of clinical practice or outcomes. As such, the results provide insight into declared attitudes and behaviors but do not allow for verification of their consistency with actual clinical performance. Second, a notable discrepancy emerged between reported practices and what is known from the literature about real-world behavior in emergency settings, particularly regarding the roles of radiologists and nurses in assessing fragility risk factors, highlighting the risk of overreporting desirable actions. Third, the survey was not anonymous, which may have further contributed to response bias, especially among professionals less directly involved in patient history taking. Fourth, we did not collect diagnostic data or case-level fracture information, as the purpose of the project was to explore attitudes and organizational practices rather than to evaluate clinical prevalence or appropriateness of diagnosis. Lastly, the emergency department itself represents a highly specific and pressured environment, where time constraints, role fragmentation, and acute care priorities may limit the feasibility of conducting comprehensive risk assessments, regardless of clinicians’ awareness or intentions.
sections.conclusion_1: This study highlights a persistent gap in the recognition and documentation of fragility fractures in emergency departments, despite increasing awareness of their clinical and organizational relevance. The findings underscore the lack of standardized approaches to distinguish fragility-related fractures from traumatic ones at the point of first contact, resulting in missed opportunities for timely referral and secondary prevention. The multidisciplinary discussion highlighted the need for a more structured and shared approach to the assessment of fragility fractures in the emergency setting. Improving consistency in fracture evaluation and early clinical suspicion may facilitate more appropriate care pathways and contribute to reducing the burden of secondary fractures and associated healthcare costs [ 6 ].

title: Yolov7 neural network for pelvic X-rays after total hip arthroplasty: automatically measuring component position parameters- a retrospective feasibility study
abstract: Background After total hip arthroplasty (THA), regular follow-up X-rays are required to evaluate the position of the prosthesis. However, measuring the parameters of prosthesis position consumes a significant amount of time, and there may be variations in the results obtained by different doctors. Purpose To validate the feasibility of an artificial intelligence model for the automated measurement of component position parameters on anteroposterior X-rays after THA. Materials and methods Post-THA anteroposterior X-rays were collected from five hospitals in Inner Mongolia, China. They were divided into training, validation and test sets. The model was divided into left, right, and bilateral THA modules for training. Statistical analysis was performed using Python 3.8 and SPSS 25.0. The accuracy of the model in keypoint detection and measurement were assessed. In addition, we compared the time difference between the model and manual measurements. Results A total of 1050 X-rays were included in the training and validation sets (350 X-rays for each module), and 105 in the test set (35 X-rays for each module). Overall, 80.00–100.00% of the model-predicted keypoints fell within 3 mm of the standard keypoints. The model-predicted values were highly consistent with the standard reference values (intra-class correlation coefficient = 0.89–0.99, r = 0.83–0.99, root mean square error = 0.96–3.43, mean absolute error = 0.78–2.87, mean difference = -1.29–1.17). The model-predicted values were highly consistent with the measurements of senior attending radiologists. The model took an average of 3.2 s to measure an X-ray image, which is significantly shorter than the 751.76 s in manual measurement. Conclusions This study validates the feasibility of the model for rapid and accurate keypoint identification and component position parameter measurement on anteroposterior X-rays. The model holds promise as a diagnostic aid to alleviate clinicians’ workload and facilitate the monitoring of prosthetic positioning changes following THA. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

sections.introduction: Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is an effective treatment that reduces symptoms and significantly improves quality of life in patients with end-stage hip diseases, such as femoral head necrosis, femoral neck fracture, and hip degeneration [ 1 ]. There were approximately 370,000 patients undergoing THA in the United States in 2014 [ 2 ], 37,000 in Canada [ 3 ] and 97,000 in the UK in 2017 [ 4 ], and more than 400,000 in China every year [ 5 ]. As the incidence of diseases, such as osteoarthritis, continues to increase due to the aging population, the number of patients undergoing THA will continue to increase. Owing to evolving medical technology, approximately 95% of hip prostheses can stand for more than 10 years, with some even lasting as long as 30 years [ 6 , 7 ]. Although the life of the prosthesis has been significantly prolonged, dislocation occurs in 0.2% to 10% of patients after THA [ 8 ], and loosening in 1.8% [ 9 ]. Regular follow-up after THA helps detect abnormal position of prosthesis early and facilitates revision surgery. At present, X-ray is preferred for evaluating component position after THA. Many parameters, such as acetabular component abduction and anteversion angles, vertical and horizontal center of rotation (VCR and HCR), femoral offset (FO), and leg length discrepancy (LLD), are used in X-ray evaluation. Moreover, to help early detection of prosthetic abnormalities, regular follow-up should be carried out based on immediate postoperative X-rays every 3 months within one year after THA, and every six months to one year thereafter [ 10 – 12 ]. However, it takes a long time to accurately measure these parameters. Moreover, different geographical location, education levels, and experiences of clinicians may introduce subjective differences in measurement. Clinicians are eager to reduce their workload using current computer technology. As artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithms have continued to develop in recent years, AI has been increasingly used in the medical field, including management of joints, especially the hip. For example, deep learning was used to measure the acetabular index on plain X-ray to screen children for developmental dysplasia of the hip [ 13 ], and to assess the risk of prosthetic dislocation based on post-THA plain X-ray [ 14 ]. The success of these studies demonstrates to some extent the feasibility of applying AI in hip management. Despite the increasing application of AI in THA, few studies have been performed on AI models for automatic measurement and monitoring of component position. Tseng et al. [ 15 ] included post-THA anteroposterior X-rays to train an AI model for measuring component position parameters on plain X-ray (BKNet). In contrast to the model by Tseng et al., which remains relatively simplistic without distinct categorization, our proposed model provides a more granular framework by incorporating three specialized modules. Pouria et al. [ 14 ] established a convolutional neural network model (U-Net) to measure the acetabular component abduction and anteversion angles. However, the model of Pouria et al. has a limited number of measurable parameters and cannot comprehensively assess post-THA component position. In contrast, our model incorporates six distinct parameters, offering a more robust and comprehensive evaluation. The model is divided into three modules (i.e., left, right, and bilateral THA modules), incorporating six key parameters to provide a more comprehensive diagnostic evaluation. This model has been validated as a promising tool to facilitate rapid and precise clinical assessment of component placement.
sections.data sources: A retrospective, multi-center study was conducted using post-THA anteroposterior pelvic X-ray images from five hospitals (Site1, Site2, Site3, Site4, and Site5) in Inner Mongolia. Specifically, 1050 post-THA pelvic anteroposterior X-rays (including 350 each for left, right and bilateral THA) were collected from Site1, Site2, Site3, and Site4 between January 1, 2021 and February 28, 2023 for model training. Additionally, 105 post-THA anteroposterior X-ray images (including 35 images each for left, right and bilateral THA) were collected from Site5 from May 1 to June 30, 2023 for independent external verification (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Multi-center data composition diagram
sections.inclusion and exclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria: patients undergoing unilateral or bilateral THA with bioprostheses. Exclusion criteria: (1) anatomical keypoints (including bilateral teardrops, ischial tuberosities, and lesser trochanters) not clearly visible on X-ray images; (2) asymmetrical pelvic structure; and (3) patients with developmental hip dysplasia, and those with conditions affecting hip radiographic measurements, including local bone defects, bone tumors, and severe degenerative changes of the unaffected joint.
sections.x-ray acquisition parameters: The digital X-ray systems of SIEMENS (Multix Fusion, Germany) and PHILIPS (Digital Diagnost, Netherlands) were used. The patient was placed in a relaxed supine position, with eyes looking straight ahead, upper limbs along the trunk, and lower limbs straight at 15° internal rotation. Images were taken with one-time exposure at distance of 100 cm in the anteroposterior position. The X-ray beam was centered on the upper edge of the pubic symphysis and perpendicular to the patient [ 16 ].
sections.definition of measurement parameters: Acetabular component abduction angle [ 10 ] is defined as the angle between the line connecting the outermost and innermost points of the acetabular component and the line connecting the inferior points of ischial tuberosities. Acetabular component anteversion angle [ 12 ] is calculated according to the formula by Lewinnek, acetabular component anteversion = arcsin(r/R), where r is twice the vertical distance from the inferior point of the short axis of the cup-shaped opening of the acetabular component to the line connecting the outermost and innermost points of the acetabular component, and R is the distance between the outermost and innermost points of the acetabular component. VCR [ 17 ] is defined as the vertical distance from the center of the femoral head (or the center of the femoral head component) to the line connecting the inferior points of the teardrops. HCR [ 17 ] is defined as the distance from the projection of the center of the femoral head (or the center of the femoral head component) on the line connecting the inferior points of the teardrops to the inferior point of the ipsilateral teardrop. FO is defined as the vertical distance from the center of the femoral head to the axis of the proximal femur. (The axis of the proximal femoral is defined as the line connecting two reference points: the midpoint of medullary canal at the level of the inferior point of the lesser trochanter, and the midpoint of the medullary canal at the level 5 cm below the inferior point of the lesser trochanter.) LLD [ 18 ] is the distance between the lines parallel to the line connecting the inferior points of the teardrops through the most prominent points in the middle of the lesser trochanters.
sections.definition of keypoints: The keypoints are defined according to the measurement method of each parameter (Table 1 ). sections.data labeling: The training and validation sets were used to train the model. They were labeled by a senior attending radiologist with at least 20 years of experience in bone and joint X-ray diagnosis (Radiologist 1 from Site3) using the software LabelMe. First, a target frame, which must include the relevant keypoints, was drawn on the upper femurs and acetabula. Keypoints were then labeled within the set target frame. The trained model should be able to automatically predict unlabeled keypoints. The test set was used to evaluate the prediction performance of the model. It was labeled by the model, as well as three senior attending radiologists, Radiologists 1, 2, and 3, independently of each other to ensure objectivity. As there was no reference standard for the coordinate data of keypoints, the average of the keypoint coordinate values obtained by the three radiologists by labeling the test set was used as the reference standard to compare with those predicted by the model [ 19 , 20 ] (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 A - C represent the manually annotated diagrams for left replacement, right replacement, and bilateral replacement, respectively
sections.data processing: Dataset was processed using Python 3.8. First, to improve generalization and alleviate overfitting, we employed several data augmentation techniques—including horizontal flipping, and color space perturbations (Hue, Saturation, and Value). Implemented via the standard YOLOv7 pipeline, these methods enhance data distribution diversity and ensure model robustness against the variability of complex clinical images. Subsequently, the resolution of all images was scaled to 640 × 640 pixels for machine learning. After prediction by the model, the test set images were resampled as original pixels and used for comparison with the labeling results obtained by the radiologists on the original images. The parameters of the post-THA anteroposterior pelvic X-ray were a resolution of 2801 × 2753 and an original pixel size of 0.143 mm.
sections.model construction: The model was divided into three modules for left, right, and bilateral THA for training. The model used in this study was constructed based on the convolutional neural network Yolov7 (version yolov7-w6-pose, released on July 7, 2022). In this study, the network architecture was divided into two parts, i.e., Backbone and Head [ 21 ]. The model architecture utilizes a Backbone for multi-scale feature extraction, capturing deep semantic information through successive downsampling and channel expansion. The Head integrates SPPCSP and E-ELAN-based PAN modules to optimize gradient paths and enhance feature fusion, thereby improving the network’s overall learning efficiency. The workflow consists of three stages: target localization, which automatically defines the Region of Interest (ROI) covering the proximal femur and acetabulum; landmark detection, performed precisely within the localized ROI; and post-processing, where identified keypoints are used to automatically calculate clinical parameters, including acetabular abduction and anteversion angles (Figs. 3 and 4 ). Fig. 3 A - C represent the model prediction diagrams of key points for left displacement, right displacement and bilateral displacement, respectively Fig. 4 The model construction process diagram The experiments were run on CentOS 7.9.2009 with NVIDIA Tesla GPU. The experimental environment is configured with NVIDIA-Tesla-A100-80GB GPU, 8-core 64GB CPU, PyTorch-1.4.0 dependency library, and Jupyter Lab Notebook. Model hyperparameters were as follows: batch-size 16, 500 epochs, img-size 640*640, and 8 workers. The model was optimized using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with an initial learning rate of 0.01, a momentum of 0.937, and a weight decay of 5*10 − 4 . To enhance training stability and facilitate model convergence, a cosine annealing strategy was employed for dynamic adjustment of the learning rate. Loss Function Design: The model was trained using a multi-task joint optimization strategy. The total loss function comprises four components: bounding box regression loss, objectness loss, classification loss, and keypoint regression loss. Specifically, the keypoint regression component employs an L1 loss to penalize the spatial deviations between the predicted keypoints and the ground-truth annotations. To prevent the model from overfitting on small-sample data, this study employs several regularization and control strategies. First, weight decay is applied as a formal regularization technique to constrain model complexity. Second, diverse data augmentation is introduced to broaden the training distribution. Third, the best model selection is conducted based on performance metrics from the validation set. Furthermore, the trend of validation loss is monitored throughout the training process; early stopping is implemented when performance gains plateau, ensuring that the optimal weights are preserved for subsequent evaluation. The model was obtained after 5 h and 36 min of training. In all experiments, the same backbone, Yolov7, was used. To construct the keypoint detection network, pre-training was performed using the ImageNet dataset [ 22 ] to improve the performance of small datasets to meet the requirements of deep learning for large data volumes. The Yolov7 keypoint detection network used optimizes ImageNet by initializing weights to achieve transfer learning. It prevents overfitting of the neural network with a limited number of training images. Yolov7 maintains high-resolution representations throughout the entire process and is suitable for landmark detection on pelvic X-ray images.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical analysis was performed using Python 3.8 and SPSS 25.0. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The distribution of patient age and gender in the training, validation, and test sets was investigated by descriptive statistics.
sections.consistency of image labeling: The Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK) of keypoint labeling was assessed by calculating the distance from labeled point to labeled point between two observers and the percentages of distance differences of 1, 2, 3, and 4 mm [ 20 , 23 ].
sections.accuracy of keypoint detection by the mo: The accuracy of the model in predicting keypoints was measured by PCK [ 20 , 23 ]. The pixel coordinates for calculating PCK are original coordinates of the keypoints. Due to the lack of an objective standard, the average coordinate value of the three radiologists was used as the reference standard.
sections.accuracy of model measurements: Due to the lack of an objective standard, the average measurement of the three radiologists was used as the reference standard for comparison with model predictions. The performance of the deep learning model was evaluated by the Bland-Altman plot, intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), pearson correlation analysis, root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE) and paired t test.
sections.comparison of model and manual measureme: Model and manual measurement time was compared by independent samples t test.

sections.comparison with previous studies: Post-THA X-rays help clinicians understand the position of the implanted prosthesis and monitor the wear and stability of the prosthesis and osteolysis. As the number of patients undergoing THA continues to increase due to the aging population, the workload in postoperative follow-up will inevitably increase significantly. It will definitely consume a lot of time of clinicians. Moreover, there may be subjective differences in the interpretation of imaging data between clinicians with different experiences. In order to address this issue, many researchers have tried to use AI to assess post-THA X-rays [ 24 ]. Pouria et al. [ 14 ] developed a convolutional neural network model based on ResNet18 and included the 5-year follow-up X-ray data of patients undergoing THA, including 1,490 patients with dislocation and 91,094 without dislocation. This model was demonstrated to provide high sensitivity and negative predictive ability, enable quickly assessing the risk of dislocation after THA based on clinical risk factors. In addition, some researchers have developed an AI model for automatic measurement of component position parameters on X-rays after THA. For example, Tseng et al. [ 15 ] included 3,072 post-THA anteroposterior X-rays to train an AI model for measuring component position parameters on plain X-ray (BKNet), which was proven to be able to quickly and accurately measure component position parameters. Pouria et al. [ 14 ] developed a convolutional neural network model (U-Net) to measure the abduction and anteversion of the acetabular component, which included 600 anteroposterior and 600 cross-table post-THA X-rays. This model was found to be no different from clinicians in measurement accuracy, and is expected to be applied in clinical practice and scientific research. The AI model developed in this study identifies keypoints on post-THA X-ray and automatically measures angles and distances through the identified keypoints. It is similar to the keypoint detection model developed by Tseng et al. [ 15 ]. However, our model includes three modules, i.e., left, right, and bilateral THA modules, which were trained separately. Moreover, a target frame was detected first to increase the accuracy of subsequent keypoint detection. The two features make the present model different from the model developed by Tseng et al. [ 15 ]. Regarding the keypoint identification capability at a 5 mm threshold, the BKNET model developed by Tseng et al. achieved a PCK of at least 75%, whereas our model demonstrated superior performance with a PCK of at least 91% under the same threshold, which demonstrate that our model outperformed the model developed by Tseng et al. The model of Pouria et al. [ 14 ] was established by segmentation, whereas the present model is a keypoint detection model. Due to the fundamental differences in the methodologies of these two models, their performance cannot be compared directly. In addition, the present model measures six post-THA component position parameters, whereas that of Pouria et al. [ 14 ] only measures the abduction and anteversion of the acetabular component. The present AI model was demonstrated to accurately identify keypoints on post-THA anteroposterior pelvic X-rays, with a PCK of 80–100% within a 3-mm distance and 91.42–100.00% within a 4-mm distance. It accurately measured acetabular component abduction and anteversion, bilateral FO, VCR, and HCR differences, and LLD, representing an ICC of 0.89–0.98 with the reference standard. The error of this model was comparable to that of senior attending radiologists.
sections.performance of yolov7 relative to other: Yolo, short for “you only look once”, was first proposed by Redmon et al. It is an object detection algorithm based on regression, which can detect objects in real time, but is difficult to detect small objects [ 25 ]. Yolo has undergone multiple updates. Yolov7 is the new version released on July 7, 2022. It was developed by Wang et al. [ 21 ]. Compared to U-Net, which is prone to interference from metallic artifacts during pixel-wise segmentation, and BKNet, which lacks the capacity to capture complex orthopedic features, YOLOv7-W6-Pose offers superior robustness. Its w6 architecture allows for high-resolution processing of X-ray images, ensuring precise localization of key anatomical landmarks and prosthesis centers, which is critical for accurate postoperative geometric measurements. Yolov7 has been rarely used in medicine. The present model was developed based on Yolov7. The results show that Yolov7 is very useful in keypoint detection on plain pelvic X-rays.
sections.analysis of measurement accuracy and mod: The ability to accurately identify keypoints is the fundamental prerequisite for reliable parameter measurement. Any excessive discrepancy between the model-identified landmarks and the ground truth would inevitably lead to variations in measurements, potentially altering clinical outcomes. However, inherent variability in landmark detection is unavoidable due to anatomical complexity. Regarding the acceptable degree of discrepancy, several established benchmarks provide guidance. Chen et al. [ 26 ] suggested that an average distance difference of keypoints between groups within 2.98 mm was considered satisfactory in clinical analysis. In this study, 92–96% of the keypoints labeled by different radiologists fell within a distance of 3 mm, which indicates that independent labeling between radiologists was reliable. The AI model developed in this study yielded a PCK of 80–100% within 3 mm. This performance demonstrates that our model’s precision aligns with established clinical tolerances. Despite its good performance, there were deviations in the predictions of a few keypoints. In particular, the PCK within 4–5 mm was low for the midpoint of medullary canal at the level 5 cm below the inferior point of the lesser trochanter (L_P15 and L_P17 in left THA, R_P15 and R_P17 in right THA, and D_110 and D_210 in bilateral THA). This may be because the reference anatomical landmarks necessary for localization are often located at a significant distance from the target points, complicating the spatial localization process. The midpoint of medullary canal at the level of the inferior point of the lesser trochanter (L_P14 and L_P16 in left THA, R_P14 and R_P16 in right THA, and D_109 and D_209 in bilateral THA) also has an unclear anatomical landmark. However, the model prediction of this point is based on the prediction of the inferior point of the lesser trochanter, which has a clear anatomical landmark. Therefore, the model provided relatively accurate prediction for the midpoint of medullary canal at the level of the inferior point of the lesser trochanter. In the left, right, and bilateral THA modules, the model-predicted values were all highly consistent with the standard reference values, with ICC of 0.89–0.99 and r of 0.83–0.99. Furthermore, the model-predicted values were highly correlated with the measurements of senior attending radiologists, with r ranging from 0.77 to 0.98. In all the three modules, the model-predicted values only had a slightly higher MAE for a few parameters than measurements of a single radiologist. The MAE of the model-predicted values of most parameters was not significantly different from or was smaller than that of the measurements of senior attending radiologists. Comparison shows that the error of the model is comparable to that of senior attending radiologists.
sections.clinical application: Correct prosthesis positioning (including acetabular component anteversion and abduction angles) and restoration of hip biomechanics (including reconstruction of hip rotation center and leg length and offset) are the keys to successful THA. They are also the basis for the long-term stability of the implanted prosthesis. The positioning of the prosthesis can be quantitatively evaluated by measuring the component position parameters on the first plain pelvic X-ray after THA. The position changes of the prosthesis can also be quantitatively monitored by subsequent regular follow-up X-rays. The THA component position parameters selected in this study are internationally recognized indicators. Repeating measurements of these parameters waste the valuable time of clinicians. Moreover, the same patient may not necessarily have all X-rays performed at the same hospital over time. In this case, it is unknown whether the same accurate measurement can be made by radiologists in different regions, with different education levels and experiences. The model developed this study provided comparable predictions of THA component position parameters to the measurements of senior attending radiologists. It can eliminate the differences between radiologists that may be caused by subjective factors to some extent. Moreover, model measurement takes significantly less time than manual measurement. Therefore, this model is expected to be used for measurement in postoperative reexaminations and early detection of changes in component position. When a large change in the component position is found, the patient should be advised to undergo a comprehensive and in-depth examination to prevent further displacement of the prosthesis. The clinical utility of this work lies in providing a validated foundation for future integration into hospital infrastructures, such as Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). By offering transparent visual overlays of keypoints, the model facilitates a transition where clinicians shift from performing manual measurements to verifying AI-generated results. While currently in the validation phase, this approach has the potential to significantly reduce the manual workload of orthopedic surgeons and radiologists, ultimately enhancing the efficiency and standardization of post-operative follow-up. As a clinical decision support tool, our model provides intuitive visual overlays of keypoints. The core of its reliability lies in the precise localization of anatomical and prosthetic landmarks. Since the measurement calculations are mathematically derived from these points, training focuses on enabling clinicians to visually verify the accuracy of keypoint identification against the radiographic anatomy. In cases where landmarks may be misaligned due to severe bone loss or image noise, clinicians can immediately identify the discrepancy and perform manual corrections.
sections.study limitations: Limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, as a feasibility validation, this study focused on standard anatomical conditions; thus, the model’s reliability in complex or extreme cases (e.g., severe deformities or pelvic obliquity) requires further validation. Second, this pilot study did not extensively analyze the impact of patient demographics; BMI, potential variations in bone density and soft-tissue interference across different populations may influence identification precision. Third, predictive deviations persisted at specific landmarks, notably the medullary canal midpoints located 5 cm below the lesser trochanter (L_P15/17, R_P15/17, D_110/210). Admittedly, these limitations also provide clear directions for our future research.
sections.future research: Addressing these limitations will be the primary focus of our future research. Building upon our current findings, we intend to integrate large-scale, multi-center datasets—encompassing diverse demographics and complex pathologies like early loosening—to enhance model robustness and generalization. Crucially, we will refine our algorithmic frameworks to specifically improve the identification efficacy for landmarks with indistinct anatomical features. Furthermore, we plan to explore multimodal data fusion to improve the estimation precision of parameters such as the anteversion angle. Ultimately, we aim to refine this model into a reliable clinical decision-support system for standardized longitudinal tracking and early intervention after THA.
sections.conclusions_1: This study validated the feasibility of an automated model for measuring component position parameters on post-THA pelvic radiographs. With performance in keypoint identification and parameter prediction comparable to that of senior radiologists, the model demonstrates significant potential as a clinical decision-support tool. Upon further refinement, it is expected to alleviate the diagnostic workload of clinicians and provide robust support for the precise monitoring of post-operative component position changes during follow-up.

title: Mortality associated biological age improves independently of weight loss after bariatric surgery
abstract: Obesity increases the risk of common diseases and mortality, placing a significant burden on our aging society. Bariatric surgery results in significant weight loss; however, the amount of associated health gain is currently less studied, particularly in the first two years. We modelled mortality-associated biological age according to established blood markers in a prospective cohort of 505 patients that underwent bariatric surgery. The difference between biological age and chronological age (age acceleration) as a molecular marker of health gain was evaluated at different time points with mixed effects models. At baseline, biological age acceleration was positively correlated to higher smoking exposure as well as increased body mass, particularly in males. Twelve months after surgery, patients were on average 5.55 years younger (slope and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI): -5.55 [-6.12; -4.97]) which remained stable until 24 months. When adjusted for changes in body mass index over time, the effect seizes decreased to 3.32 years younger age at 12 months post-surgery (slope and 95% CI: -3.32 [-4.26; -2.37]), indicating an age-rejuvenating effect – more pronounced in men - beyond weight loss. Individual markers such as glucose and C-reactive protein levels as well as blood cell counts contributing to biological age computation showed a generally more favorable change after surgery. In conclusion, biological age was markedly reduced in patients undergoing bariatric surgery resulting in a 40-50% reduction in expected mortality after two years, particularly in men. Our findings support the use of biological age as a clinically meaningful, patient-centered marker of treatment success after bariatric surgery.

sections.introduction: According to the WHO, obesity is a chronic disease arising from complex interactions among genetics, neurobiological factors, eating behaviors, access to a healthy diet, market forces, and the environment 1 . In recent decades, obesity prevalence has increased globally as countries have experienced increased food security, socioeconomic development, and shifts in diet, physical activity, and societal and individual behavior due to globalization and industrialized food systems. On a global scale, the prevalence of obesity has reached epidemic proportions, with more than 1 billion individuals affected. This surge has manifested in nearly every country resulting in a consistent upward trend in obesity rates 2 with approximately 50% of the German population having a body mass index (BMI) above 27 kg/m 2 3 . Obesity has been identified as a risk factor for a variety of associated diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, musculoskeletal disorders and several types of cancer 4 . The severity of obesity has been demonstrated to be positively correlated with an increased risk of these associated diseases. Weight loss in obesity has been an important aspect for preventing long-term illnesses. The efficacy of a nutritionally balanced diet and increased physical activity, in reducing weight among overweight individuals is often hindered by factors that initially contributed to weight gain such as psycho-social aspects, or lack of adherence to prescribed lifestyle modifications. Bariatric surgery (BS) has been the only approved weight-loss procedure for decades 5 . It typically results in an average reduction of 20% body weight in the first year and 40% in the second year 6 – 8 . This weight loss translates to a reduction of all-cause mortality of about 30–50% 8 and is thus an established treatment of weight reduction. Traditional metrics of weight loss (e.g., changes in BMI or waist circumference or percent body weight) do not distinguish sufficiently between healthy (restorative, loss of fat mass, reduced disease risk) or unhealthy (catabolic, loss of physiological reserves, increased disease risk) weight loss. In particular, the goal of healthy weight loss is to reduce fat mass and therefore reduce future (chronic) disease risks and mortality. In comparison, unhealthy weight loss could be the results of underlying illness, frailty or excessive caloric restriction without exercise, leading to loss of physiological reserves and potentially increased disease risk. Furthermore, unhealthy weight loss could lead to false reassurance scenarios where weight loss occurs without health improvement or even worsening of disease risk 9 . One way to define health in relation to age is to compute biological age which represents the accumulation of organ and molecular damage over time, reflecting how quickly an individual is aging compared to others. Several aging clocks used to compute biological age exist from a variety of data such as DNA methylation 10 , high-throughput omics data 11 or routine blood-based markers 12 . Of particular interest are aging clocks that use markers associated with survival as they are more likely to capture mortality relevant processes and not just general senescence 13 . From those markers, the next step is to derive an aggregate score capturing the underlying liability. Mapping the score against age allows computing the biological age, effectively capturing the expected mortality risk at the individual’s chronological age. In general, it is often more informative to investigate the difference between biological and chronological age, known as age acceleration 14 , since this metric does not depend on an individual’s chronological age and thus reflects faster or slower biological aging compared to the expected trajectory 15 . In this study, evaluated the potential of mortality-related age acceleration as an alternative marker for treatment success following BS. For this purpose, we derived phenotypic aging from blood markers at multiple perioperative time points before and assessed longitudinal changes with and without accounting for body mass index.
sections.study cohort: The prospective investigator-initiated cohort study (BBC – Berlin Bariatric cohort Study) registered at German Clinical Trial Register (DRKS00021263) has been described previously in more detail 16 . Between December 2019 and November 2022, 1068 patients with an indication for bariatric surgery were recruited, of whom 505 underwent surgery. Participants completed detailed clinical questionnaires, and blood and urine samples were collected for laboratory analysis. Participants were followed up to 2 years post-surgery (Table 1 ). Follow-up data were available for 419 patients at 3 months, 386 at 6 months, 347 at 12 months, and 155 at 24 months. The median body mass index (BMI) at baseline was 44.5 kg/m² (range 30.0–78.0). The mean chronological age of the participants was 41.13 years (SD ± 11.24, range 17–69). Approximately 65% of participants reported obesity onset during adulthood.
