sections.surgical procedures: The two main bariatric surgical techniques were laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (SG) and gastric bypass (GB), performed either as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) or omega-loop gastric bypass (OAGB). SG involves longitudinal gastric resection, resulting in the creation of a narrow gastric tube to induce a state of reduced appetite, leading to a decrease in food intake. GB procedures combine restrictive and mild malabsorptive mechanisms by constructing a small gastric pouch and rerouting the small intestine to alter nutrient flow 5 , 17 . Both surgical techniques demonstrated high efficacy, with over 90% of patients achieving ≥20% weight loss relative to baseline 6 .
sections.blood biomarker assessment: Venous blood samples were collected from participants at the time of enrollment and at scheduled follow-up visits at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-surgery. These blood samples were processed on the same day to measure standard hematological and biochemical parameters. From the standard panel, we extracted plasma album, creatinine, C-reactive protein, glucose, alkaline phosphatase levels as well as white blood cell and lymphocyte count, mean corpuscular volume and red cell distribution width, as shown before 12 (Supplementary Table 1 ). The selected biomarkers were subsequently transformed to the appropriate scale (i.e., with appropriate units for use in subsequent analyses) and utilized to compute the phenotypic age acceleration metric (see below).
sections.estimation of mortality risk and phenoty: The estimation of phenotypic age was conducted in accordance with the methodological framework presented elsewhere 12 . Briefly, a Gompertz proportional hazards model was used to select nine biochemical and hematological blood biomarkers (Supplementary Table 1 ) predictive of 10-year mortality risk. The estimated mortality risk was then mapped to chronological age thus allowing the mortality associated prediction of biological age. This approach effectively transforms biomarker-derived mortality risk into a continuous measure of biological aging expressed in years 18 representing the expected mortality at a given chronological age. From the biological age, we derived a measure called age acceleration as a marker of faster or slower biological aging compared to actual age by computing the residual (difference) between biological and phenotypic age. Patients with a positive residual would have faster biological aging and patients with a negative residual would have slower aging than expected. Importantly, the residuals are independent (not correlated) to actual age and thus should not be influenced by differences in age at baseline and increased age during follow-up of the patients.
sections.dimensionality reduction via umap: Dimensionality reduction was performed using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). A non-linear embedding algorithm was designed to preserve both local and global data structures. UMAP allows to visualize relationship between individuals based on the markers supplied to identify clusters and/or identify outliers. We plotted the first two components computed from UMAP for baseline parameters with ggplot 19 and color-coded with a scheme retrieved from the RColorBrewer package.
sections.statistical analysis and presentation of: The correlation between biological (phenotypic) and chronological age using baseline measurements was assessed with linear regression models and the R 2 value was extracted from the model fit. To assess the influence of sex, baseline BMI, type of surgery, smoking status, education and the age of obesity onset on biological age at baseline, we employed multivariate linear regression models. Age acceleration was modelled as the outcome and the above-mentioned variables were jointly examined as exposures. In addition to the regression in all participants, we also fitted models with the same covariates in subgroups of patients stratified by sex, age and baseline BMI. The results of the correlation analyses are presented as correlation plots implemented in the corrplot package in R 20 . To model the longitudinal change in biological age and to account for individual variability, random-intercept linear mixed-effects (LME) models were employed as implemented in the lme4 21 package in R. LME models are an extension of the general linear model, incorporating both fixed effects, which represent the average relationship across all participants, and random effects, which capture deviations unique to each individual. We allowed for random intercepts for each individual by including the study ID as random effect and adjusted all models for sex. In a sensitivity analysis, we also included BMI measured at each time point to account for changes in BMI during follow-up. The changes in biological age at different time points are shown using a beeswarm plot, as implemented in the beeswarm library in R 22 . To illustrate the longitudinal trajectory in biological age while accounting for changes in the BMI of individuals, we extracted the residuals from a linear regression model with age acceleration as the outcome and BMI as the sole predictor. The residuals represent the BMI-adjusted age acceleration (changes in biological age) and were subsequently also visualized using beeswarm plots. In all analyses, p -values below 0.05 were deemed as statistically significant and highlighted with an asterisk in the respective correlation and beeswarm plots.
sections.multidimensional analysis of mortality-a: Mapping nine mortality-associated biomarkers to two parameters with UMAP revealed a continuous, age-ordered distribution of individuals across the two-dimensional manifold (Fig. 1 ). Participants were arranged along a gradual trajectory from younger to older age, without the presence of distinct, separable clusters. This finding indicates a progressive shift in biomarker composition across the aging continuum as expected from age- and mortality-associated markers. Fig. 1 Cluster analysis of 505 obese patients according to mortality-associated biomarkers at baseline. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) was used to map the 9 mortality associated biomarkers to two dimensions for individual patients. Each point represents a single participant, colored according to chronological age (blue: younger, red: older). Distinct clustering patterns by age are observed, with a continuous gradient from younger to older individuals across the UMAP space.
sections.association between chronological age an: Phenotypic age, a composite biomarker-based estimate of biological aging, exhibited a strong linear relationship with chronological age at baseline (R² = 0.725; RMSE = 7.13 years) (Fig. 2 ). Similar correlations were observed in male and female patients (men R² = 0.739, women R² = 0.720). The distribution of data points indicates a considerable inter-individual variability in the difference between phenotypic and chronological age. This deviation, termed “age acceleration” (AgeAccel), is defined as the residual of phenotypic age when chronological age is regressed out. This approach is equivalent to computing the difference between predicted (biological) age and actual (chronological) age. Individuals with higher-than-expected phenotypic age (faster biological aging) demonstrated positive AgeAccel values, while those with lower-than-expected phenotypic age demonstrated negative AgeAccel values (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Relationship between chronological and biological (phenotypic) age in a high BMI cohort. Scatter plot depicting the correlation between chronological age and phenotypic age at baseline. Red points indicate individuals with a higher phenotypic age than chronological age (accelerated biological aging), blue points indicate individuals with a lower phenotypic age (slower biological aging). R 2 = coefficient of determination; RMSE = root mean square error. Generally, AgeAccel was not correlated to chronological age at baseline ( p > 0.05), neither in individuals younger nor older than the median. Thus, heteroscedasticity is unlikely to influence our results, and we opted not to adjust our models for age at baseline or follow-up. To put our results into perspective, we correlated age acceleration against the mortality risk score at baseline and estimated that a one-year reduction in age acceleration results in a relative reduction of the mortality risk by about 8%.
sections.correlation between ageaccel and demogra: Correlation analyses conducted across the entire cohort demonstrated a significant positive correlation between AgeAccel and BMI (slope and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) per standard deviation of BMI: 1.71 years [1.13; 2.3], p = 1.59*10 -8 , Fig. 3 ). This correlation was also significant in all strata analysis except in the lower BMI group (BMI < 44.5: slope per S.D. and 95% CI: 0.05 years [-0.70; 0.81], p = 0.88). Fig. 3 Associations between demographic/clinical variables and Age Acceleration. Shown are the correlations between clinical and demographic factors and age acceleration before surgery across participant subgroups. The color scale denotes the direction of correlations (blue: negative, i.e., younger biological age, red: positive, i.e., older biological age), and bubble size reflects the strength of the association in years. Higher body mass index and smoking were both correlated to faster aging. S.D. = Standard deviation. We found that over all age groups, women were not biologically older or younger than men. However, in individuals over the median age of 42, we found that women are indeed biologically younger than men (slope and 95% CI: -2.78 years [-4.75; -0.81], p = 0.006) (Fig. 3 ). In this age group as well as in the lower BMI group, education level (Highschool diploma; yes vs. no) showed a significant correlation to AgeAccel with higher education resulting in reduced age (slope and 95% CI: -3.6 years [-5.71; -1.48], p = 0.001 and -1.83 years [-3.56; -0.1], p = 0.04, in the younger age group and lower BMI group, respectively). In addition, we observed that smokers had advanced age compared to non-smokers (slope and 95% CI: 1.35 years [0.04; 2.65], p = 0.04). This correlation was more pronounced in male smokers compared to male non-smokers (slope and 95% CI: 3.12 years [0.38; 5.86], p = 0.028).
sections.longitudinal changes in biological age a: Employing mixed-effects models revealed significant postoperative changes in AgeAccel across four follow-up visits at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery (Fig. 4 ). We found that biological age decreases significantly (Fig. 4A ) at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months after surgery by 1.34 years (slope and 95% CI: -1.34 [-1.87; -0.80], p = 1.17*10 -6 ), 4.00 years (slope and 95% CI: -4.00 [-4.56; -3.44], p = 8.33 *10 -42 ), 5.55 years (slope and 95% CI: -5.55 [-6.12; -4.97], p = 1.32*10 -70 ) and 5.27 years (slope and 95% CI: -5.27 [-6.06; -4.49], p = 2.70*10 -37 ), respectively. Those estimates would thus result in a reduction of around 40–50% in all-cause mortality risk 12 and 24 months post-surgery. Fig. 4 Longitudinal changes in biological age following bariatric surgery. Beeswarm plots showing biological age acceleration at baseline and at follow-up after bariatric surgery (BS). Each point represents one individual. Below each plot, the median and 95% confidence intervals are given. A A significant reduction in biological age acceleration is observed at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months post-surgery (mixed effects models adjusted for sex). B After adjustment for BMI, the reduction in biological age at 6, 12 and 24 months post-surgery (mixed effects models adjusted for sex and BMI) remains significant. At 3 months post-surgery, biological age acceleration is slightly elevated, suggesting a transient rise in mortality risk in the early postoperative period, *** p < 0.0001. Since patients lost weight during follow-up, this effect can potentially be explained by reduced BMI instead (since we showed that BMI is correlated to AgeAccel in Baseline). To test this, we adjusted the mixed effects models by BMI measured at each time point (Fig. 4B ). Similar to the results obtained without accounting for BMI, we found that biological age significantly decreased at 6, 12 and 24 months post-surgery by 2.18 years (slope and 95% CI: -2.18 [-3.01; -1.36], p = 2.33 *10 -7 ), 3.32 years (slope and 95% CI: -3.32 [-4.26; -2.37], p = 7.94 *10 -12 ) and 2.93 years (slope and 95% CI: -2.93 [-4.04; -1.82], p = 2.63 *10 -7 ), respectively (Fig. 4B ). However, the decrease was not as pronounced as observed in the unadjusted analysis, indicating that weight loss accounted for around 40–50% of the reduction in biological age. In the early postoperative period (i.e., 3 months post-surgery), biological age was slightly increased by 0.19 years (slope and 95% CI: 0.19 [-0.85; 0.47], p = 0.57), however did not reach a statistical significance compared to baseline on average when accounting for BMI. To see whether those observed effects are influenced by biometric or demographic baseline variables, we fit the same models stratified by sex, age and pre-surgery BMI (Fig. 5 ). Generally, the correlation pattern was similar to the overall analysis including all patients. Nevertheless, we observed a difference in the reduction of AgeAccel during follow-up when accounting for BMI at 12 and 24 months depending on patient sex. We found that biological age decreased more in men at 12 months post-surgery (slope and 95% CI: -4.68 years [-6.59; -2.76], p = 2.39*10 -6 ) compared to women (slope and 95% CI: -2.50 years [-3.65; -1.36] p = 1.86*10 -5 ). This difference remained stable also at 24 months post-surgery. Since the 95% confidence intervals overlap between the estimates and men and women, we did not find a statistically significant difference between the effect sizes, which can be attributed to the limited sample size of male patients in our cohort. Fig. 5 Longitudinal changes in biological age across time points and subgroups. Correlation plots depict correlations between follow-up time points (3, 6, 12, and 24 months post-surgery) compared to baseline and age acceleration across participant subgroups, with and without adjustment for BMI. Color represents the direction and magnitude of correlations (blue: negative, i.e., younger biological age, red: positive/older biological age), while circle size indicates effect strength in years. Asterisks denote statistical significance at p < 0.05. Across all participants, age acceleration showed a progressive negative association with time, reaching the strongest effect at 24 months post-surgery. Adjustment for changes in BMI attenuated the observed correlations by about 50%.
sections.longitudinal changes in biological marke: Generally, most individual markers used to compute biological age (Supplementary Table 1 ) were significantly changed 3 months after surgery and thereafter (Supplementary Figure 1 ). Indeed, we observed reduced levels of glucose, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, C-reactive protein, and white blood cell count, indicating improved metabolic, renal and liver health as well as reduced systemic inflammation. Most markers stayed relatively stable over the rest of the follow-up period. Notably, C-reactive protein and alkaline phosphatase levels continued to decline until 12 months post-surgery, indicating further improvements after the early postoperative period (3 months). When accounting for the rapid weight loss (and thus BMI), we found that the trajectory of most markers is attenuated and showed weaker correlations with the exception of glucose and creatine, which showed a correlation pattern similar to the unadjusted approach and red cell distribution width (RDW), which exhibited slightly higher correlations at three months post-surgery. While weaker, we still found that C-reactive proteins levels decreased, and lymphocyte levels increased after 6 months post-surgery compared to baseline (Supplementary Fig. 1 ).
sections.discussion: In this study, we examined the change in biological age related to overall mortality after bariatric surgery (BS). We could demonstrate for the first time an average reduction of biological age by about 6 years at 12 and 24 months after BS resulting in a strongly decreased mortality. The reduction in age acceleration was attenuated by adjusting for changes in body mass index (BMI) across the follow-up, indicating that most of the rejuvenating effect can be attributed to weight loss. Sex-stratified analyses indicated stronger decreases in males compared to females. Importantly, we saw no biological age rejuvenation at 3 months post-surgery when accounting for BMI reduction at this time point. Our analysis yielded a R² of 0.725 when investigating the correlation between chronological and predicted (phenotypic) age, which is lower than the correlations reported in prior studies (R² ≈ 0.85) 23 . This can be due to cohort-specific characteristics, such as the higher baseline BMI. We note that a notable gap in the research exists concerning the influence of extreme adiposity on biological aging metrics. To date, the number of studies that have examined BMI as a modifying factor in biological age assessment is limited and often relied on self-reported retrospective BMI ascertainment or was only conducted in a cross-sectional setting 18 . In addition, in our cohort, BMI varied greatly among participants. Thus, predicting age from blood markers could yield a lower R 2 value due to this added (and generally understudied) variation. The observed reduction in biological age after surgery was accompanied by a decline in estimated mortality risk of about 40–50% between 6 and 24 months post-surgery compared to baseline. This observation aligns with the findings from studies demonstrating that BS reduces all-cause mortality and improves long-term cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes 5 , 7 at comparable magnitudes. The most significant decreases in biological age were revealed at 12 and 24 months post-surgery. This time frame also corresponds to the period of optimal metabolic normalization following BS 24 , which might be the driving factor behind our findings in addition to the reduction of fat mass during the same period. Across the entire cohort, biological age showed a decline over time following BS. Crucially, we observed that after accounting for BMI, we detected differences in the change of age acceleration after surgery according to sex. Indeed, male subjects showed a more substantial decrease in biological age at 6,12, and 24 months post-surgery compared to women. These findings suggest that biological age reduction following BS may be more responsive in men than in women. This might potentially be explained by our observation that male subjects entered into the intervention with a higher baseline biological age and thus potentially more disease burden. The results of other epidemiological studies support our observations: male patients exhibited a higher prevalence of comorbidities prior to surgery and consequently initiated treatment from a disadvantageous position 25 and could thus have a greater potential for post-surgical improvement. In addition, some studies found a more substantial reduction in fat mass in males compared to females. However, our study did not ascertain fat mass at baseline or beyond, thus we cannot investigate such a link nor control for it in the statistical analyses. In longitudinal studies, there were no observed differences between sexes regarding overall survival 26 – 28 . Importantly, those studies compared average survival between treated and untreated patients in the gender strata, thus could miss individual effects that only appear when investigating markers at multiple time points in the same individual, thus reducing the inter-individual variation. As indicated by the findings of other studies, BMI of men continues to exceed that of women one year post-surgery despite larger weight loss, which could explain why we found differences between sexes when investigating absolute changes in biological age and thus mortality compared to relative changes as prior studies did 27 . In addition to those explanations, stronger alterations in behavioral factors in men compared to women, such as differential adoption of lifestyle modifications, physical activity, or dietary changes, were not captured in this study and may also contribute to the observed gender differences. Alternatively, biological age may be more sensitive to weight reduction in men than in women. However, given the smaller number of male participants, these interpretations should be considered hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. At current, we can only speculate which pathways are responsible for the slightly increased biological age observed at three months when accounting for body mass index, particularly in female participants. This finding can be due to acute postoperative stress responses, including inflammation, immune activation, and wound-healing processes. These processes are known to influence leukocyte-derived biomarkers that are incorporated into biological age calculations. Concurrent elevations in inflammatory and stress-related pathways have been documented in early postoperative bariatric cohorts 29 . Due to the immune modulatory nature of estrogen, a higher response of those markers in women is possible and could explain some of the observed sex differences. In addition, early postoperative food restriction defined as a state of negative energy balance and mobilization of endogenous energy stores may further contribute to this effect by initiating responses similar to those associated with starvation. The latter finding could be explained by the increased red cell distribution width (RDW) observed at 3 months post-surgery, even when accounting for BMI reduction at this time point. Indeed, prior reports found that malnourishing can result in increased RDW 30 , pointing towards an imbalance of nutrition at this stage. Beyond its descriptive value, biological age modeling has important translational implications. The method outlined in this paper could be applied to calculate the health effects of various obesity interventions, including drug treatment (such as GLP-1-receptor agonists) and lifestyle modifications to monitor treatment success and to inform the necessity of additional interventions in case an adequate reduction in biological age is not achieved. In addition, future studies should focus on the impact of weight regain after bariatric surgery and other interventions on biological age. Previous epidemiological studies indicated that moderate weight regain does not translate to an, on average, increased mortality risk and only minor increase in cardiovascular risk 31 . Nevertheless, biological age might offer a more granular evaluation of disease risk after weight regain, since some patients might show resilience against weight gain (i.e., no increased biological age despite weight increase) while other might suffer from a more pronounced negative impact on their biological age and thus mortality risk. Those patients might profit from additional interventions to counter the increased risk. Thus, knowledge on health gain resilience might be crucial to improve health in individuals after weight loss. The application of blood-based biomarkers facilitates scalable, minimally invasive estimation of biological age and mortality risk at the individual level across multiple visits. This approach goes beyond abstract percentage-based descriptions of weight loss and provides patients with tangible, personalized indicators of health improvement. Given the heterogeneity of treatment success in BS and the limitations of weight-based metrics in fully capturing this heterogeneity, biological age may serve as a complementary endpoint to assess individualized therapeutic benefit. A significant strength of this study is the ongoing, prospective data collection within the BBC, which allows the longitudinal evaluation of biological age. The notable number of female participants in this study addresses a significant gap in obesity research, which has historically been male-biased. Furthermore, the cohort spans a wide BMI spectrum (30–78 kg/m²), thereby enabling the assessment of biological aging across levels of adiposity that remain underrepresented in current research. By also evaluating anamnestic markers in this obese cohort allowed us to further shed light on the contribution of those factors to biological age, which seem to be of limited impact in those individuals. However, we also note that BMI is a suboptimal metric for evaluating adiposity and metabolic health. Since current guidelines often define a successful BS as achieving at least 20% weight loss from baseline, we nevertheless opted to use BMI as an important factor in our analyses to monitor weight changes after baseline. Furthermore, the study had a higher attrition rate due to the lack of required follow-ups after surgery leading to fewer observations after 12 and 24 months, which could limit our power to draw further conclusions from the data.
sections.conclusion: The present study demonstrates a substantial reduction in biological age and thus mortality risk after bariatric surgery, with particularly notable effects in the male population. Importantly, we found that a part of the reduction in biological age was independent of BMI changes, suggesting that bariatric surgery exerts systemic benefits beyond weight loss itself. These findings support the use of biological age as a clinically meaningful, patient-centered marker of treatment success that is less abstract and potentially more informative than weight-based metrics alone or metrics that focus solely on beneficial changes in future disease risk.

title: A multi-marker NMR metabolomics signature for the superior detection of chronic and acute systemic inflammation in dogs: a comparative study with C-reactive protein
abstract: Background Identifying inflammatory states is vital in veterinary diagnostics, yet reliable markers for chronic, low-grade inflammation are lacking. This study aims to characterize metabolic alterations in diverse inflammatory conditions and evaluate a novel multi-marker model. Methods Plasma from 175 healthy and 207 diseased dogs (representing infectious, neoplastic, and degenerative pathologies) was analyzed via canine-validated 1H NMR spectroscopy. Logistic regression was employed to identify both general and disease-specific metabolic alterations. A multivariable model was developed using forward stepwise selection, and its diagnostic performance was compared against that of C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin, glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA), and a combination of GlycA and albumin. Results Metabolic changes were observed across all the conditions studied, with some alterations specific to individual diseases and others common across conditions. The final six-metabolite model (albumin, GlycA, pyruvate, alanine, glucose, and phenylalanine/tyrosine ratio) showed excellent performance (AUC=0.82). It significantly outperformed CRP in detecting all chronic diseases (0.68–0.89 vs. 0.46–0.60) and acute gastroenteritis ( 0.86 vs. 0.71). Conclusions Metabolic profiling provides a superior diagnostic approach to CRP, particularly for chronic inflammatory conditions, by capturing systemic signatures that traditional markers miss. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12917-026-05426-7.

sections.background_1: Inflammation is a common biological response observed in numerous diseases that aims to restore homeostasis during and after tissue insult. In addition to conditions typically recognized as inflammatory—such as infectious or autoimmune diseases—many acute and chronic illnesses feature a component of systemic low-grade inflammation [ 1 ]. Chronic diseases often induce systemic inflammation; however, the connection between low-grade systemic inflammation and disease extends beyond this causal relationship. In humans, low-grade systemic inflammation can precede clinical disease onset by as much as a decade [ 1 ], and it contributes to various conditions ranging from diabetes mellitus to Alzheimer’s disease [ 2 ]. Identifying an inflammatory state is crucial in veterinary clinical diagnostics. Inflammatory markers can be used in veterinary medicine to not only confirm the presence of inflammation but also help determine its severity, prognostic implications, and associated morbidity and mortality risks [ 3 ]. While practical biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) effectively identify acute inflammation in dogs [ 4 ], there is a lack of validated biomarkers for chronic low-grade inflammation. Establishing reliable markers for chronic inflammation in dogs could contribute to earlier detection and management of chronic diseases, with potential benefits for canine health and longevity. Inflammation is known to affect metabolism. Unraveling the specific metabolic changes occurring in dogs during inflammation might reveal novel, clinically useful inflammatory markers enhancing the identification of inflammatory conditions. It could also enable the creation of multi-metabolite models with the potential to identify inflammation more accurately than single-marker based diagnostics. Recently, a validated proton nuclear magnetic resonance ( 1 H NMR) spectroscopy-based metabolomics platform for canine plasma and serum samples was established [ 5 ]. This method enables the robust and comprehensive evaluation of over 120 metabolic measures [ 5 ]. The method has proven its usefulness in identifying metabolic changes associated with several canine conditions [ 5 – 9 ] and is a promising tool for studying the metabolic effects of inflammation in dogs. The objectives of this study were to: (i) characterize both common and disease-specific metabolic alterations in dogs; (ii) develop and evaluate the performance of a metabolite-based multivariable model for detecting systemic inflammation in dogs regardless of the specific disease trigger.
sections.study population: We conducted an observational, cross-sectional study on pet dogs. Patients were enrolled by experienced research nurses at four Finnish small animal veterinary hospitals: Eläinsairaala Evidensia Tammisto (Vantaa), Eläinsairaala Mevet (Helsinki), Lahden Eläinlääkäriasema (Lahti), and Espoon Eläinsairaala (Espoo). All dogs fulfilling the inclusion criteria and visiting within the research nurses’ working hours were enrolled provided the owner gave consent. The recruitment period spanned from May 2022 to April 2023. A total of 203 healthy control dogs and 223 dogs diagnosed with predefined common canine diseases participated in the study. The investigated conditions included acute gastroenteritis, pyometra, cutaneous and noncutaneous neoplasia, atopic dermatitis, periodontal disease, urinary tract infection, canine infectious respiratory disease complex, and osteoarthritis. The study population included a diverse cohort of diseases to capture the metabolic intersection of different inflammatory triggers, categorized into acute systemic responses (e.g., cutaneous and noncutaneous neoplasia, pyometra, acute gastroenteritis, urinary tract infection, canine infectious respiratory disease complex) and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation (e.g., osteoarthritis, periodontal disease, atopic dermatitis). This broad clinical cohort was deliberately selected to ensure the resulting multivariable model was not biased toward a single organ system but instead reflected a “pan-inflammatory” metabolic response common to systemic inflammation. The disease had to be in the active phase during enrollment, defined as the period during which a patient exhibited overt clinical signs of the primary condition and/or had diagnostic findings (laboratory, imaging, or histopathological) confirming the disease was not in remission or a subclinical state. Diagnoses were determined based on patient history, clinical signs, findings, and appropriate diagnostic tests tailored to each patient’s condition (Table 1 ). For neoplastic conditions, dogs could be enrolled based on clinical suspicion with their diagnoses later confirmed through subsequent histopathological or cytological examination. The dogs represented a typical clinical population as dogs could present with multiple concurrent conditions, and both treatment-naïve and previously medicated patients were included. Control group inclusion required a physical examination performed within the past three months and a medical history free of indications suggestive of illness. To confirm the health status of control group in-house clinical chemistry analysis was performed via a Catalyst Dx Chemistry analyser using a Chem15 CLIP, and hematology was assessed via ProCyte (both from IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Maine, USA) on study inclusion. For all participating dogs, detailed information on signalment, health status, medication usage, and fasting duration prior to blood sampling was collected. CRP was measured via an in-house clinical chemistry analysis Catalyst CRP Test (IDEXX Laboratories, Inc., Maine, USA), with a reference interval of 0–10.0 mg/L. However, the analyzer detection limits varied among clinics, ranging from lower detection limits of either 1.0 mg/L or 10.0 mg/L, to upper limits of 170 mg/L or 240 mg/L. For metabolomic analysis, 2 ml of blood was drawn via cephalic venipuncture into Vacuette LH Lithium Heparin PREMIUM tubes (2 ml). Plasma volumes ranging from 110 to 500 µl were separated according to the manufacturer’s recommendations and subsequently transferred into cryo tubes (Sarstedt 72.730.005). The samples were refrigerated at the veterinary clinics for up to one week and then transported within three hours under cool-pack conditions. After transportation, the samples were stored at -80 °C for a maximum of five months prior to metabolomic analysis performed by PetMeta Labs Ltd. (Helsinki, Finland) via 1 H NMR spectroscopy. All studied metabolites have been shown to remain stable in the used storage and shipping conditions [ 5 ].
sections.1 h nmr spectroscopy: A targeted 1 H NMR spectroscopy method optimized and validated for dogs was utilized [ 5 ]. The method has been thoroughly described elsewhere [ 5 , 10 , 11 ]. The method is highly automated, from sample processing to the processing of the NMR spectra. The equipment used includes a sample changer SampleJet (Bruker Corp., Billerica, Massachusetts, USA), a PerkinElmer JANUS Automated Workstation with an 8-tip dispense arm with Varispan (PerkinElmer Inc., Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) and a Bruker AVANCE III HD 500 NMR spectrometer with a 5 mm triple-channel (1H, 13 C, 15 N) z-gradient Prodigy probe head [ 10 ]. Sample preparation included light mixing of the sample and removing the possible precipitate by centrifugation, transferring 100 µl of sample to individual NMR tubes, and mixing with sodium phosphate buffer [ 10 , 12 ]. Metabolite quantification in absolute units is achieved by processing the NMR spectra via scripts optimized for canine samples [ 5 ] based on regression modelling [ 11 ]. The proprietary software utilized has integrated quality control [ 11 ]. Quality control also includes detection of samples with suboptimal quality and reporting its cause. The method quantitates 123 measurands, including a detailed lipoprotein analysis, amino acids, fatty acids, triglycerides, cholesterols, glycolysis-related metabolites, albumin, creatinine, and GlycA [ 5 ].
sections.data preprocessing: All manual data review and processing steps were conducted in Microsoft Office Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). The laboratory and health data of all participating dogs were thoroughly reviewed and evaluated by a veterinarian. Seventeen dogs initially assigned to the control group were excluded since their CRP levels, clinical chemistry, hematology results, or general health information indicated either subclinical or clinical disease. Hematology, clinical chemistry and CRP values considered to indicate either clinical or subclinical disease were changes moderate to severe in magnitude, such as alkaline phosphatase over 500 µmol/L, or mild to moderate changes spanning multiple parameters. Control group dogs displaying laboratory parameters slightly outside reference ranges without clear disease indications were flagged for potential exclusion from subsequent analyses if the metabolomics data identified them as outliers. Similarly, the disease status of case-group dogs was meticulously reassessed, resulting in the exclusion of 11 individuals with uncertain or incorrect diagnoses, or, specifically within neoplasia cases, those lacking histopathological confirmation. Metabolomic data were subjected to rigorous quality control. Dogs with extensive missing metabolite data were excluded, resulting in the exclusion of 5 cases and 3 controls. Individual metabolites were assessed for completeness, with those exhibiting more than 20% missing observations removed. Specifically, metabolites such as very large very low-density lipoprotein phospholipids (XL-VLDL PL), esterified cholesterol (XL-VLDL CE), and free cholesterol (XL-VLDL FC)—known for their characteristically low canine levels—were excluded. Next, the metabolomics data were screened for outliers. When control group outliers were identified, their health and laboratory data were reevaluated. Eight dogs exhibiting deviations, including previously noted laboratory abnormalities unrelated to clear disease or moderate alterations in muscle mass or body condition, were excluded. Following these steps, the final dataset comprised 175 control dogs and 207 case dogs. The remaining missing metabolite values were imputed via Random Forest imputation, employing the R [ 13 ] packages missForest version 1.5 [ 14 ], dplyr version 1.1.2 [ 15 ] and tidyverse [ 16 ]. The imputation out-of-bag (OOB) error was 0.136, indicating adequate performance. A separate approach was applied for CRP value imputation: values below the detection limit were imputed as half the detection limit, whereas values exceeding the detection limit were imputed as the detection limit plus 10 mg/L. One pyometra group dog lacking CRP measurements was excluded from analyses involving CRP. Outlier identification, missing value imputation and all statistical analyses were conducted using the R programming environment [ 13 ] (R Core Team, 2023). Metabolite concentrations were quantified in absolute units. To maintain biological integrity and prevent the introduction of unnecessary bias, no normalization, transformation, or scaling procedures were applied to the raw data. Consequently, the statistical framework was specifically restricted to methods validated for absolute quantitative measurements rather than relative abundance data.
sections.statistical analyses: Descriptive statistics were computed to characterize the study groups. The normality of metabolite variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test (stats package, R Core Team, 2023) [ 13 ], which revealed that most metabolites were not normally distributed. P -value adjustments for metabolite analyses were conducted using Bonferroni correction based on the number of principal components (PCs) explaining > 95% of the data variance. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using FactoMineR and factoextra packages, with five PCs explaining 95% of the variance, resulting in a p -value threshold of 0.01 (0.05/5). Initially, general metabolic changes associated with disease were evaluated by comparing the combined case group (dogs diagnosed with one or more diseases) with the healthy control group. To be able to statistically take into account the possible differences in physiological factors and the possible metabolic effects of medications, differences in physiological characteristics (sex, neutering status, fasting duration, and age) between the case and control group were compared between the groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (stats package) [ 13 ]. Significant differences were identified only for age. Given the known influence of age on metabolite concentrations [ 17 ], age was included as a covariate in subsequent analyses. The potential effects of medications administered within 24 h prior to sampling on metabolite levels in the diseased group were also assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (stats package) [ 13 ], revealing no significant differences. Metabolite concentrations between the case and control groups were compared using logistic regression (stats package) [ 13 ] adjusted for age. The case-control status served as the dependent variable, and the results were visualized via bubble plots created with the bubbleHeatmap (version 0.1.1) [ 18 ] and grid [ 13 ] packages. The bubble plots reflected logistic regression p -values and median absolute deviation (MAD) differences from the dataset median. To confirm the robustness of the results, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (stats package) [ 13 ] was also performed. A multivariable logistic regression model to identify inflammatory markers was developed using metabolites that were significant ( p < 0.05) in the univariable logistic regressions. The model, adjusted for age, was constructed through forward stepwise selection on the basis of p -values via the stats package [ 13 ]. Variables were sequentially added until no further metabolites reached statistical significance ( p < 0.05). Akaike information criterion (AIC)-based selection yielded identical metabolites at each step. The multivariable model underwent diagnostic assessment to ensure that the logistic regression assumptions were met. Multicollinearity was evaluated using variance inflation factors (VIF; car package [ 19 ]), revealing no multicollinearity (VIF range: 1.07–1.58). Influential observations were examined through standardized residual plots (broom package [ 20 ]), showing no influential outliers (standardized residuals < 2.6). The linearity of the logit assumption was tested by adding interaction terms between each variable and its natural logarithm; no significant interaction terms were found ( p > 0.05). Variable importance was assessed using the caret package. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation (cvAUC package version 1.1.4) [ 21 ], with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the performance metric. AUC values > 0.7 were considered acceptable, > 0.8 were considered excellent, and > 0.9 were considered outstanding. Next, metabolic changes specific to each disease were investigated individually. Dogs with concurrent conditions were included in the analyses for each relevant disease. To be able to statistically take into account the possible differences in physiological factors and the possible metabolic effects of medications or concurrent diseases, differences in the physiological characteristics of each disease group and the control group were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (stats package) [ 13 ]. While some groups exhibited differences in sex or neutering status compared to controls, group sizes limited statistical adjustments. Considering that the effects of sex and neutering status are very small in magnitude [ 17 ], only age was included as a covariate in logistic regression models. The effects of concurrent diseases and recent medications on metabolite concentrations were evaluated in each studied condition using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (stats package) [ 13 ], which revealed no significant effects, except for higher docosapentaenoic acid percentage in acute gastroenteritis dogs with concurrent illnesses. Due to their negligible effects, concurrent diseases or recent medications were not adjusted for in the subsequent logistic regression analyses. Disease-specific metabolite comparisons between the control group and each disease group were conducted using logistic regression (stats package) [ 13 ], adjusting for age. Bubble plots visualizing logistic regression p -values and MAD differences from control medians were created using bubbleHeatmap (version 0.1.1) [ 18 ] and grid [ 13 ] packages. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (stats package) [ 13 ] validated logistic regression findings, with only minor interpretation differences. Finally, the diagnostic performance of CRP, GlycA, albumin, the GlycA-albumin combination, and the multivariable metabolite model was compared using logistic regression (stats package) [ 13 ]. Performance was assessed and visualized with ROC curves (pROC package) [ 22 ]. AUC values were calculated, and differences in the AUC between CRP and metabolic measures were statistically compared using the DeLong method. The dependent variable for each logistic regression model was disease presence versus control. Differences in CRP and metabolite concentrations across groups were illustrated through box plots generated via the forcats (version 1.0.0) [ 23 ] and ggpubr (version 0.6.0) [ 24 ] packages, incorporating reference intervals for clarity. Final graphical adjustments were completed using Inkscape [ 25 ].
sections.group demography: The demographic characteristics of the study groups are presented in Table 2 . Compared to control dogs, dogs with pyometra, neoplastic diseases, periodontitis, and arthritis were significantly older, whereas those with canine infectious respiratory disease complex were notably younger. All study groups included diverse breeds and mixed-breed dogs. Among noncutaneous neoplasias, the most frequently observed were mammary tumors ( n = 9), lymphoma ( n = 8), leukemia ( n = 3), and mast cell tumors ( n = 3). The most common cutaneous neoplasias were cutaneous mast cell tumors ( n = 9) and lipomas ( n = 7). The prevalence of concurrent diseases varied among disease groups, ranging from 19% in dogs with atopic dermatitis to 52% in those with osteoarthritis. The administration of medication within 24 h prior to sample collection was common, occurring in 51% of the dogs in the case group. These medications included treatments specific to the diagnosed conditions as well as sedatives administered when blood sampling coincided with procedures requiring anaesthesia, such as tumor removal or dental treatments. sections.metabolite associations with overall dis: Several metabolites were robustly associated with overall disease occurrence when the healthy control group was compared with the combined case group, which included all dogs diagnosed with one or more of the studied conditions (Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table, Sheet O1 and O8). Logistic regression and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test yielded highly similar results. Among the strongest associations were the inflammatory markers GlycA and albumin. GlycA levels were elevated in the case group, whereas the level of albumin, a negative acute-phase protein, was decreased. Notable alterations in amino acids included a significant decrease in tyrosine and glycine and an increase in the phenylalanine-to-tyrosine ratio. Among the metabolites related to sugar metabolism, pyruvate showed the most pronounced increase in the case group. Total cholesterol, triglycerides, and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) levels did not differ significantly between the groups, and changes in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels were minor. However, large and small HDL particle numbers (L-HDL and S-HDL), total lipids, cholesterol, and esterified cholesterol concentrations were significantly reduced in the case group, whereas large LDL (L-LDL) variables were notably increased, except for triglyceride levels. sections.metabolite associations with specific di: While some changes in metabolite concentrations were universal across different diseases, multiple diseases also showed disease-specific changes (Fig. 2 , Supplementary Table, Sheet D1). Universal changes across different conditions included decreases in the levels of albumin and tyrosine and increases in the levels of GlycA and pyruvate. An increase in phenylalanine and the phenylalanine/tyrosine ratio was mainly observed in acute diseases. The changes in the other amino acids were relatively disease specific, and all were decreases in concentration. Multiple very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) lipid variables and total triglycerides were increased in dogs with osteoarthritis, periodontitis, neoplastic diseases, and pyometra but decreased in dogs with atopic dermatitis, acute gastroenteritis, and canine infectious respiratory disease complex. The HDL and LDL variables had different signatures. LDL variables, especially L-LDL variables, were increased in dogs with osteoarthritis, pyometra, and noncutaneous neoplasia, with no or few changes in other diseases. Total HDL and total cholesterol remained unaltered in all diseases. Nevertheless, small and large HDL variables were relatively uniformly decreased across multiple conditions. In fatty acid concentrations, a decrease in oleic acid, docosapentaenoic acid, and omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) and an increase in saturated fatty acids were observed in pyometra. Decreased omega-3 PUFA concentrations were observed in periodontitis, pyometra, cutaneous neoplasia, and urinary tract infections. Citrate was reduced in atopic dermatitis, acute gastroenteritis, and canine infectious respiratory disease complex, and acetate followed a similar pattern. Glucose was elevated in periodontitis and pyometra and slightly elevated in the other studied acute conditions. In general, the dogs with atopic dermatitis presented the fewest and slightest metabolic changes. sections.discussion: This study, involving a large clinical cohort of over 380 dogs across multiple clinically relevant inflammatory conditions, was designed to address the critical diagnostic gap in identifying systemic inflammation, particularly in chronic states. The inclusion of a heterogeneous cohort was a deliberate strategy to isolate a universal systemic inflammatory signature. While the studied conditions (ranging from acute infections like pyometra to chronic degenerative states like osteoarthritis) possess distinct primary etiologies, they share a common biological denominator: the activation of systemic inflammatory pathways that alter host metabolism. By including diverse tissue insults, the multivariable model focuses on metabolic intersections rather than organ-specific noise, allowing for the detection of inflammation across a wide clinical spectrum. This approach yielded several significant findings: (i) both acute and chronic inflammatory diseases exhibit measurable systemic metabolic changes; (ii) systemic inflammation is confirmed in conditions previously considered predominantly local, such as osteoarthritis; (iii) despite a shared inflammatory signal, each condition maintains a distinct metabolic profile, and (iv) the newly developed multimetabolite model provides superior diagnostic performance compared with C-reactive protein (CRP), especially for identifying chronic inflammatory conditions. Universal metabolic alterations linked to inflammation are highly valuable for detecting and evaluating inflammatory states in a veterinary clinical context. In routine practice, clinicians often face ‘gray zone’ cases where a patient is symptomatic, but traditional markers like CRP and standard clinical chemistry remain within reference intervals. Our findings highlight that while CRP is a sensitive indicator for high-grade acute conditions like pyometra (AUC = 0.93), its diagnostic utility drops significantly in chronic states such as neoplastic diseases or osteoarthritis (AUC < 0.60). The multivariable metabolite model effectively bridges this gap, maintaining acceptable to excellent performance even when individual markers appear unremarkable, thus providing a higher-definition lens for detecting the subtle, low-grade systemic involvement that is frequently ‘invisible’ on routine blood work. The two strongest contributors to the multimetabolite model were the inflammatory markers albumin and GlycA. Both markers were generally superior to CRP in detecting chronic inflammatory states. Of these two markers, albumin is a well-known negative inflammatory marker, decreasing in concentration during inflammatory episodes [ 3 ] GlycA is a relatively novel composite inflammatory marker combining the 1 H NMR signals of several acute-phase proteins [ 26 ]. Its composite nature makes it a stable and consistent marker of inflammatory stimuli [ 26 ]. Extensively studied in humans, GlycA has been shown to correlate with chronic inflammation, chronic diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality risk [ 1 , 27 – 29 ]. While it has been only recently studied in dogs, elevated GlycA levels have already been observed in dogs across multiple conditions analogous to human diseases, including liver shunts and hepatopathies [ 6 ], Addison’s disease and Cushing’s disease [ 7 ], diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism [ 8 ], lipemia [ 5 ], and during phenobarbital treatment [ 30 ]. Two amino acid measures - the phenylalanine-to-tyrosine (Phe/Tyr) ratio and the individual amino acid alanine - were identified as key predictors in the multivariable model. In this study, amino acid concentrations generally decreased, with the notable exception of phenylalanine. This specific pattern has been historically linked to muscle catabolism during systemic illness, where the body’s protein reserves are mobilized to meet the metabolic demands of the inflammatory response [ 31 – 34 ]. Similar metabolic abnormalities have been documented in dogs suffering from various inflammatory and neoplastic diseases. Crucially, the magnitude of these amino acid shifts, particularly the elevation of the Phe/Tyr ratio, has been shown in veterinary literature to directly correlate with disease severity and prognosis in critically ill canine patients. The inclusion of alanine and Phe/Tyr in the final model underscores its ability to capture the systemic catabolic toll of disease, even in chronic states where traditional markers like CRP are insensitive. Given the identified therapeutic potential of amino acids in mitigating these catabolic effects, our findings suggest that metabolic profiling could eventually guide targeted nutritional interventions or supplementation strategies to improve outcomes in dogs with chronic inflammatory or neoplastic burdens [ 33 , 34 ]. Glucose and pyruvate also contributed to the multimetabolite model, highlighting the altered cellular energy metabolism during inflammation [ 35 ]. Pyruvate levels were almost consistently elevated across the studied conditions, suggesting consistent changes in its metabolism. Elevated glucose levels in acute conditions, particularly pyometra, reflect stress-induced hyperglycemia. Beyond universal shifts, the disease-specific metabolic profiles identified in this study offer significant clinical insight into the systemic impact of localized conditions. A notable finding is the evidence of systemic involvement in conditions traditionally managed as local processes, such as osteoarthritis (OA) [ 36 ] and periodontitis. In OA, metabolic shifts in lipid profiles and amino acids suggest that the disease impact extends far beyond the joint capsule, exhibiting alterations indicative of low-grade systemic inflammation that are undetectable by routine diagnostic methods. Similarly, periodontitis was associated with systemic metabolic alterations, including reduced omega-3 PUFA concentrations and altered glucose metabolism, suggesting that chronic “local” dental disease may have a broader impact on overall metabolic health than previously recognized. The metabolic signature of acute gastroenteritis also demonstrated translational relevance [ 9 ], showing distinct similarities to chronic enteropathy. Both conditions exhibit elevated phenylalanine alongside reduced glycine and fatty acid concentrations; however, acute gastroenteritis is uniquely characterized by specific differences in citrate and acetate levels. Conversely, atopic dermatitis displayed the fewest and slightest metabolic changes, and CRP failed to effectively detect the disease [ 37 ]. This aligns with observations in human medicine, where a systemic inflammatory response is typically only observed in patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, whereas mild disease primarily triggers local responses. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the multimetabolite model is capable of capturing a spectrum of inflammatory responses—from the subtle systemic signals of chronic local disease to the more pronounced signatures of acute systemic insult. The observed changes in omega-3 PUFA are interesting. Supplementation with omega-3 PUFA is popular in dogs and is considered to have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties [ 38 ]. However, the associations between serum fatty acid concentrations and diseases have rarely been studied in dogs. We observed reduced omega-3 PUFA levels in periodontal disease, pyometra, cutaneous neoplasia, and urinary tract infections, with pyometra also showing increased saturated fatty acids and decreased monounsaturated oleic acid. In humans, decreased PUFAs and increased monounsaturated and saturated fatty acids are among the most potent predictors of present disease and disease risk [ 1 ]. Given the potential anti-inflammatory benefits of omega-3 PUFA supplementation, further exploration of fatty acid metabolism and disease susceptibility in dogs is needed. Lipid metabolism in inflammation is also an interesting topic that warrants further study in dogs. Inflammation has been shown to increase VLDL and LDL levels and to decrease HDL levels in humans [ 39 ], and HDL has also been suggested as a negative inflammatory marker in vector-borne diseases in dogs [ 40 , 41 ]. These changes probably reflect an effect of stress on lipid metabolism: increased fat accumulation with less cholesterol carried away from tissues by HDL and increased lipid deposit into tissues by LDL and VLDL. In this study, we used the most comprehensive lipoprotein profiling method available for dogs. The detailed lipoprotein subclass analysis showed that small and large HDL variables were the lipoprotein variables most uniformly associated with inflammatory diseases, whereas the concentrations and compositions of very large HDL particles remained unaltered. Therefore, the overall changes in HDL concentration during inflammation seem to arise from the decreased concentration of the smaller HDL particles. The finding regarding small vs. large HDL particles is a novel sub-clinical insight that traditional veterinary lipid panels (which only measure total HDL/cholesterol) cannot see. This information adds to our understanding of HDL metabolism during inflammation and its properties as a possible inflammatory marker. Like all research, this study has certain limitations. Since metabolism is affected by numerous physiological and environmental factors, it is impossible to fully match the case and control groups for all factors simultaneously. However, the effects of physiological and environmental factors on the studied metabolites have been recently evaluated [ 17 ], and this study was carefully planned to take the most important factors into consideration. Age is known to be one of the main factors affecting metabolite concentrations in healthy dogs [ 17 ]. Therefore, age was considered in the statistical analyses and all models were adjusted for age by including age in the metabolite models as a covariate. All the groups consisted of dogs of a large variety of breeds, and no single breed or breed type dominated any of the groups. The effects of medications and concurrent diseases were also statistically considered and were shown not to affect the results of this study. All dogs participating in this study were recruited in Finland and the generalizability of the findings should be evaluated in other countries. A limitation of the CRP analysis was that the lower detection limit varied between clinics. The discriminatory capacity of CRP might have been better if the detection limit had been 1.0 mg/l in all clinics. However, since CRP was used as an exclusion criterion for the healthy control group, the discriminatory capacity of CRP might also be worse in real life.
sections.conclusions_1: This study confirms that systemic inflammation in dogs, regardless of the underlying primary pathology, produces a measurable and consistent metabolic signature. By integrating six key biomarkers- albumin, GlycA, pyruvate, alanine, glucose, and the phenylalanine/tyrosine ratio - we developed a multivariable model that significantly bridges the diagnostic gap left by traditional CRP testing. The model’s superior performance in chronic conditions suggests a transformative potential for veterinary diagnostics, allowing clinicians to detect low-grade systemic involvement that is typically “invisible” on routine blood work. However, the variation in performance across diseases underscores that while the model is a powerful indicator of systemic insult, it should be used as a complement to organ-specific diagnostics. Future research should focus on validating this model in longitudinal studies to determine its efficacy in monitoring treatment response across diverse canine populations.

title: Aging disrupts spatiotemporal coordination in the cycling murine ovary
abstract: Throughout the female reproductive lifespan, the ovary undergoes hundreds of cycles of follicle development, ovulation and tissue regeneration. How aging disrupts the coordination of such precise, multicellular interactions across time and space is not well understood. Using Slide-seq, a near-cellular spatial transcriptomics method, here we profile 22 mouse ovaries across the reproductive cycle and chronological ages, capturing 610,620 spots across 69 spatial profiles. We develop a novel segmentation pipeline to examine the multicellular dynamics of 358 oocytes, 668 follicles and 236 corpora lutea to find that aging impairs the spatial and temporal coordination required for folliculogenesis even before reproductive cycles cease. These disruptions are characterized by altered immune cell dynamics, inflammatory signaling and global tissue disorganization, which impair the cyclic remodeling required for ovarian function. Our findings reveal how multicellular niches orchestrate ovarian function and demonstrate that age-related breakdown in tissue organization precedes the end of fertility.

sections.main: The ovary is a highly dynamic organ that undergoes repeated cycles of phenotypic switching to orchestrate oocyte maturation, ovulation and endocrine signaling throughout the reproductive cycle 1 , 2 . This ‘homeostatic cycling’ occurs approximately 150–650 times in mice and 300–400 times in humans throughout the female reproductive lifespan 3 , 4 . Chronological aging leads to a progressive decline in reproductive function, ultimately culminating in the cessation of these cycles. Here we investigate the molecular interactions underlying this transition, focusing on the depletion of the ovarian reserve, the loss of precision in cellular interactions and the accumulation of tissue-wide inflammation and fibrosis 5 – 10 . Central to ovarian function are follicles, which are multicellular structures that develop growing oocytes and transform into corpora lutea (CL) after ovulation. Folliculogenesis begins with primordial follicles, consisting of a dormant oocyte encased by flattened granulosa cells (GCs). Follicle activation triggers GC proliferation, first forming preantral follicles that undergo morphological and functional changes to support oocyte growth and then transitioning to the gonadotropin-dependent and steroidogenic antral stage 11 , 12 . Notably, less than 1% of recruited follicles reach ovulation while the rest undergo atresia (that is, controlled follicle death) 13 . After ovulation, follicular remnants transform into the CL, a transient progesterone-producing endocrine structure essential for pregnancy and cycle regulation 12 , 14 . Follicle maturation spans multiple reproductive cycles, approximately 18 days in mice and 375 days in humans, creating an extraordinarily complex tissue environment where dozens (mice) or thousands (humans) of follicles at varying developmental stages share the same physical space with multiple CLs 15 , 16 . The molecular mechanisms coordinating such asynchronous spatiotemporal organization remain poorly defined, underscoring the need for spatially resolved profiling to decode the dynamics of these cellular ecosystems. Prior studies of ovarian aging have focused primarily on follicle depletion and oocyte-intrinsic changes, such as aneuploidy 17 , 18 . However, mounting evidence suggests that dysfunction across the entire ovarian tissue environment also contributes substantially to reproductive decline 7 , 9 , 18 – 20 . Known disruptions include GC signaling 21 – 23 , extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling 24 – 27 and aberrant immune infiltration 9 , 28 – 30 , yet how these events collectively drive ovarian aging remains unknown. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a powerful tool for uncovering cellular heterogeneity and its regulatory mechanisms, it is limited in uncovering insights for ovarian research. Droplet-based scRNA-seq methods often fail to capture mature oocytes due to their large size, which can exceed 70 µm in diameter, leading to a bias toward early-stage oocytes 31 – 34 . Furthermore, scRNA-seq dissociates interacting cell types, thereby losing the spatial context of the follicular niche, whereas coarse spatial transcriptomics lacks the resolution needed to characterize follicular architectures 20 , 35 . Here we present a spatiotemporal atlas of the naturally cycling C57BL/6 J mouse ovary throughout chronological aging. Using Slide-seq 36 , 37 , we generated 69 spatial transcriptomic profiles from 22 biological samples, capturing 610,620 spots at 10 µm resolution during the estrus and metestrus stages. To analyze the cooperative nature of multicellular ovarian structures, we developed a segmentation pipeline that identified 358 primordial and growing oocytes, 668 follicles of which 301 enclosed oocytes and 236 CLs, enabling a high-resolution analysis of their in situ molecular signatures. Our results reveal that aging disrupts the temporal dynamics of both folliculogenesis and CL function. This dysregulation aligns with heightened inflammatory signaling and a global decline in tissue organization, which may compound ovarian dysfunction. Our work demonstrates how the breakdown of coordinated multicellular niches contributes to the age-related decline of reproductive and endocrine function.
sections.spatial transcriptomics reveals multicel: To characterize the multicellular architecture of the ovary, we generated spatial transcriptomics profiles from mice across three reproductive age groups: young (10–12 weeks), middle-aged (36–40 weeks) and old (52–54 weeks) mice 38 . Mice were harvested during the ovulatory (estrus) and post-ovulatory (metestrus) phases, with active cycling confirmed via longitudinal estrous staging (Fig. 1a , Extended Data Fig. 1a , Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 and Methods ). Unsupervised clustering and post hoc annotation resolved all major ovarian cell populations, including oocytes ( Gdf9 ), multiple GC subtypes, theca cells ( Col1a2 ) and two distinct luteal populations ( Parm1 or Akr1c18 ). We also identified epithelial ( Epcam ), fibroblast ( Pdgfra ), smooth muscle ( Tagln ), immune ( Lyz2 ), endothelial ( Flt1 ) and stromal ( Aldh1a1 ) cells (Fig. 1b–d , Extended Data Fig. 1b , Supplementary Tables 3 – 5 and Supplementary Note). To validate these Slide-seq annotations, we also performed whole-ovary single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq). Although snRNA-seq recovered a consistent set of cell types, it showed a notable loss of oocytes and cumulus cells, underscoring the advantage of our spatial profiling for capturing a more comprehensive ovarian cellular atlas (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d ). Fig. 1 A spatiotemporal map of the cycling and aging ovary identifies spatial niches driving folliculogenesis. a , Experimental overview. Mice were staged by vaginal cytology and collected at estrus and metestrus ( n = 22; young 10–12 weeks, middle-aged 36–40 weeks, old 52–54 weeks). Multiple nonadjacent sections per ovary were profiled using Slide-seq, with a minimum gap of 200 µm to avoid resampling the same follicle or CL. Adjacent sections were used for histology. After clustering and cell-type annotation, multicellular segments were defined using an automated segmentation pipeline. b , UMAP of Slide-seq RNA profiles ( n = 610,620 dots at 10 µm resolution) across 69 pucks, colored by post hoc annotation (legend); GC, granulosa cell. c , Mean expression (log-normalized counts, dot color) and proportion of expressing cells (dot size) of marker genes (columns) used to annotate cell types (rows). Spot counts in Supplementary Table 4 . d , Mean cell-type composition across young ( n = 32), middle ( n = 16) and old ( n = 21) pucks. e , Schematic of folliculogenesis and CL formation. GCs proliferate from a single layer around a dormant oocyte in primordial follicles to form preantral follicles, which transition to gonadotropin-dependent antral follicles with fluid-filled antral cavity formation and theca recruitment. GCs differentiate into multiple subtypes. Atresia can occur at any stage of folliculogenesis. After ovulation, GCs luteinize to form the CL, which is subsequently cleared. f , Mean expression (log-normalized counts and variance-scaled) of key hormone receptors and synthesis genes (columns) across segment types (rows), grouped by gonadotropin-independent, gonadotropin-dependent and luteinization stages. Segment counts: preantral ( n = 238), antral mitotic ( n = 191), antral luteinizing ( n = 43), atretic ( n = 181), CL— Parm1 ( n = 87), CL— Akr1c18 ( n = 147); n = 22 mice across all ages. g , Representative H&E sections with corresponding spatial segment maps showing annotated preantral follicles (purple), antral follicles (green-blue) and CLs (yellow). Asterisks denote structures present in either H&E or Slide-seq due to sectioning differences of sampling, rather than an error in the segmentation. h , Segmentation accuracy assessed across n = 347 segments with an available adjacent H&E section for validation; the majority ( n = 311) were correct. Errors included merged segments with other segments, misannotations with incorrect segment types and missed detections by the pipeline. Cohen’s kappa = 0.85. i , Follicle counts from paired H&E sections and Slide-seq segments across pucks (dots) and their means (bars) for young ( n = 32), middle ( n = 16) and old ( n = 21) pucks. Error bars represent standard error of the mean (s.e.m.). Significance was determined by two-tailed t -test; all other bar groups are not significant. We next developed a segmentation pipeline to group anatomically and functionally related spatial spots, namely oocytes, follicles and CLs. Our method identified follicular segments across distinct stages of folliculogenesis, including preantral ( n = 238), antral mitotic ( n = 191), antral luteinizing ( n = 43) and atretic ( n = 181) follicles, supported by the stage-specific expression of known hormone receptors and synthesis genes (Fig. 1e,f , Extended Data Fig. 1e–g , Supplementary Table 6 and Methods ) 39 , 40 . We also identified two spatially segregated CL types, classified as Parm 1 ( n = 87) and Akr1c18 ( n = 147) (Fig. 1h ). Although current resolution limits precluded the identification of squamous GCs in primordial follicles, we identified primordial oocytes through a separate pipeline that expressed additional marker genes such as Sohlh1 and Nobox 41 (Extended Data Fig. 1h and Methods ). All segmentation results for follicles and CLs were validated by manual annotation of adjacent H&E-stained sections (Fig. 1g–i , Extended Data Fig. 1i , Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 , Supplementary Table 5 and Methods ). Furthermore, to provide orthogonal validation of atretic follicles beyond transcriptional signatures 32 , we examined the spatial distribution of immune cells within follicles. As expected 9 , atretic follicles exhibited significant immune infiltration toward the follicle center consistent with clearance, whereas healthy follicles had minimal immune presence (Extended Data Fig. 1j and Supplementary Table 7 ; P < 0.05 antral versus atretic follicles, Tukey’s test). Altogether, these findings demonstrate that our segmentation pipeline accurately captures the multicellular organization and functional heterogeneity of the ovary from spatial transcriptomics data.
sections.oocytes follow coordinated transcription: Although oocytes are traditionally viewed as transcriptionally silent storage units for maternal RNA 42 , recent evidence reveals active transcriptional regulation throughout their maturation 43 – 45 . Indeed, our in situ profiling of oocyte transcriptomes showed that canonical oocyte marker genes were differentially expressed across their follicle stages (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ) 31 , 46 – 48 . Further analysis via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) revealed five distinct oocyte gene programs across their maturation (Fig. 2d , Methods , Extended Data Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Table 8 ). Oocyte program 2, characterized by zona pellucida glycoproteins genes Zp2 and Zp3 , was upregulated in primordial and preantral oocytes, suggesting the synthesis of components essential for follicular assembly following primordial activation 49 , 50 . In contrast, oocyte program 4, enriched in Bmp15 and F-box proteins genes ( Fbxw19 , Fbxw21 , Fbxw24 ) encoding components of the SCF ubiquitin E3 ligase complex controlling cell cycle progression 51 , 52 , emerged in mature antral oocytes, reflecting shifts required for meiotic progression. In mature oocytes, we observed a significant increase in oocyte program 0 ( Bcl2l10 , Btg4 , Tcl1 ), signaling readiness for growth following the gonadotropin surge (Fig. 2e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0001 preantral versus antral; two-tailed t -test) 53 – 55 . Conversely, atretic oocytes failed to maintain the expression of these programs, showing a loss of Padi6 expression and a premature induction of oocyte program 0 (Fig. 2a,e , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 8 ; P = 0.0203 antral versus atretic; two-tailed t -test). Altogether, our findings reveal that oocyte transcription may be dynamically regulated throughout folliculogenesis to govern the switch from oocyte dormancy to maturation. Fig. 2 Oocyte transcriptional dynamics across folliculogenesis and age. a , Mean expression (log-normalized counts and variance-scaled) of oocyte marker genes (columns) across follicle stages (rows). n = 358 oocytes across 22 mice, all age groups; oocyte counts per follicle type in Supplementary Table 8 . b , Principal component (PC) embedding of n = 358 oocyte RNA profiles (dot) colored by its enclosing follicle stage. c , Representative spatial plots of two pucks showing oocytes (colored dots) within their tissue context, colored by enclosing follicle stage; surrounding GC spots shown in gray. d , Expression (color) of oocyte gene programs. sections.aging alters regulators of oocyte matura: Aging leads to both the depletion and functional decline of maturing oocytes 56 , 57 . Consistent with this, we observed a sharp age-associated decrease in oocyte counts across all follicle stages (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table 5 ). Differential expression analysis between maturing oocytes of young and old animals revealed transcriptional alterations, notably the upregulation of the genes encoding the nuclear androgen receptor ( Ar ) and the progesterone-metabolizing enzyme ( Akr1c18 ) (Fig. 2g , Extended Data Fig. 2d , Supplementary Tables 9 and 10 and Methods ). Given their roles in oocyte maturation and meiosis 58 – 60 , their increase may reflect an adaptive shift in response to the altered endocrine landscape of the aging ovary 61 , 62 . Conversely, we observed reduced expression of the insulin-degrading enzyme gene Ide . Because Ide modulates insulin signaling to maintain oocyte quality, attenuating insulin signaling during healthy folliculogenesis 63 , 64 , its downregulation suggests a disruption in metabolic homeostasis 64 , 65 . We also detected the downregulation of the Nlrp9b family genes ( Nlrp9a / b/c ), components of the subcortical maternal complex thought to facilitate the oocyte-to-embryo transition 66 – 68 (Extended Data Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 11 ). Importantly, these trends were consistent in oocytes across follicle types, suggesting that these changes reflect oocyte-intrinsic changes rather than shifts in follicular composition with age (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table 11 ). Together, our results suggest that aging impairs the integration of external cues that guide oocyte maturation, providing a potential mechanistic basis for the age-related decline in oocyte quality.
sections.molecular programs define spatially orga: Next, we investigated how GC states change throughout folliculogenesis. To compare GC organization across hundreds of follicles of varying sizes, we devised a normalized, scaled radial distance from the follicle center. Quantifying GC composition along this radial axis revealed extensive intra-follicle heterogeneity, indicating that transitions between follicle stages are not driven by a synchronized follicle-wide switch, but instead may emerge through the local propagation of changes in cell–cell interactions (Fig. 3a,b , Extended Data Fig. 3a , Supplementary Table 6 and Methods ).
