sections.discussion: In this study, we tested the subgroup hypothesis that small-to-modest effect sizes of SNPs on adverse late reactions may result from some risk factors being conditional on certain other risk factors 15 . By combining the functional RILA assay with two genomic and two clinical features, the PA DT identified six partly nested subgroups. The two SNPs and BMI had significantly larger effects in the low-RILA than in the high-RILA subgroup, whereas hypertension was significant in the high-RILA but not the low-RILA subgroup. In particular, the NBS1 CG&GG genotype was conditional on low-RILA and BMI(high). By contrast, the CTGF TT genotype was protective in both RILA subgroups and dominated over the increased risk associated with low CD4 + RILA. Interaction analysis confirmed that the NBS1 SNP and both clinical features interacted with CD4 + RILA and showed that the association between low-RILA and fibrosis was confined to patients with the combination of non-TT CTGF genotype, CG&GG NBS1 genotype, high BMI, and no hypertension. The six subgroups were aggregated to produce three PA risk groups with five-fold variation in risk, which were verified by robust ML modelling. In particular, 23/24 patients (96%) in the unaggregated PA high-risk group were also identified as high-risk by the combined ML model, demonstrating that this PA subgroup was not a result of overfitting. This provided proof-of-concept that the increased risk associated with the NBS1 G-allele is conditional on other risk factors and that its significance is obscured when analysing the whole cohort. To the best of our knowledge, the present study is the first to show an association of this SNP with fibrosis. The combined ML model incorporated the complex feature interactions by weighing certain risk factors against the combination of other risk factors. The different CAP characteristics of the RF and SVM models can be attributed to differences in the way they handle sample classification. The RF model classifies samples that align with the core characteristics of their respective opposite class, whereas SVM maximises the decision boundary and excels in correctly identifying samples such as inner outliers sharing characteristics with the opposite class. Importantly, both RF and SVM individually outperformed the classical approach to predictive modelling represented by LR. The assignment of seven PA medium-risk patients to the ML high-risk group indicates that, in some cases, other risk-factor combinations or a higher grade of BMI may compensate for the absence of low-RILA or NBS1 (CG&GG). Furthermore, the recessive protection by the CTGF T-allele did not rely on other risk factors. Thus, subgroups may be formed in different ways, probably depending on the role of risk factors in mechanistic pathways. The combined ML model was able to correctly predict 25/30 (83%) fibrosis-positive patients with fibrosis in the high-risk group (13.7% of the cohort) and 121/146 (83%) fibrosis-negative patients in the low-risk group (67% of the cohort), representing a five-fold difference in risk levels (83% and 17.1%, respectively). In a clinical setting, this would potentially enable precise risk stratification by assigning 80% of the patients to the high- and low-risk groups with 17% errors. The identification of a minor group of patients (∼1 in 7) with a 2.8-fold increased risk would allow clinicians to offer high-risk patients an alternative, normal-tissue sparing treatment such as partial-breast radiotherapy with the potential to reduce the overall rate of fibrosis by more than a third. However, the model needs to be validated in an independent cohort before it can be applied routinely outside clinical studies. Although the patients were accrued prospectively, this was an observational study with a moderate sample size, and blood samples for the RILA assay were obtained at the late follow-up examination. However, CD4 + lymphocytes are not part of standard RILA protocols and, as far as is known, no cohort with comparable long-term follow-up is available, so a new study will be needed for external validation before clinical application. The AUC was similar for the PA and ML approaches, but the more robust, combined ML model performed marginally better than PA with respect to assigning more fibrosis-positive patients to the high-risk group and more fibrosis-negative patients to the low-risk group, with minimal losses of accuracy while decreasing the size of the medium-risk group. This resulted in a smaller medium-risk group and additional patients assigned to the high- and low-risk groups, suggesting that the more robust, combined ML model may weigh high values of some risk factors against the absence of others. However, these explorative observations on small numbers of patients need to be confirmed in a large study. To the best of our knowledge, no other predictive model has identified a subgroup of high-risk patients with a 2.8-fold increased risk (83.3%) compared with the whole cohort (30.1%). It is important to note that the PA cutpoints for CD4 + RILA and BMI were not used in ML modelling, which used continuous values. However, stochastic fluctuations in distributions of features between different cohorts could potentially affect the sensitivity of the ML models. To address this issue, stratified 10-fold cross-validation was performed, indicating overall solid reproducibility, but marginally higher stability of the RF compared to the SVM model. Nevertheless, the generalisability of the model and the quantitative risk of fibrosis in the risk groups need to be confirmed in an independent data set. PRSs comprising a few dozen SNPs showed highly significant associations with late reaction in breast cancer patients at two-year follow-up, but data on the predictive performance were not presented 8 . LR was used in an early breast cancer cohort incorporating several clinical and genomic features, which reported a misclassification error of 34% 26 . Only a few studies have used ML modelling for predicting late normal tissue reactions after radiotherapy. In a previous study, six different ML models were used to predict radiotherapy outcome and three toxicities in patients treated for different cancers ((non-)small-cell lung cancer, head-and-neck cancer, meningioma) 27 . The models were developed and evaluated on 12 separate datasets, but no best model was found for all datasets. For the RF model, a broad range of AUC values was found with a median of 0.725, i.e., comparable to the simpler and biologically more specific model in the present study. A pre-conditioned random forest regression (PRFR) with SNPs from a GWAS on prostate cancer patients yielded AUC values of 0.55–0.70 in ROC analysis for four genitourinary toxicities, and optimal performance required at least 75% of several hundreds of SNPs 10 . More recently, the REQUITE cohort has been used to validate candidate SNPs identified from the literature with modest results 25 . A similar approach, selecting sets of 13 interacting SNPs, yielded AUC values of 0.78 for late urinary frequency ≥gr.2 and 0.71 for late haematuria ≥gr.1, but just 0.63–0.68 for three other endpoints 24 . Using only five features, the present model performed on par with much more complex models and has scope for further improvement. The general question whether a predictive test will indeed widen the therapeutic window may be addressed by a cost-benefit analysis as estimated for effects on normal lung tissue relative to adjusting radiotherapy prescription dose according to genomic markers of non-small cell lung cancer radiosensitivity 28 . In the case of breast radiotherapy, intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) with 50 kV X-rays results in hardly any fibrosis if given alone without EBRT 29 but a cost-benefit assessment will need to be included as part of a carefully planned, prospective clinical trial. Regarding mechanistic aspects, the association of low RILA values with increased risk of fibrosis emphasises that lymphocyte apoptosis is not a surrogate for the radiosensitivity of patients’ normal tissue cells and instead supports an involvement of the immune system in radiation-induced fibrosis 15 . A low rate of apoptosis in irradiated CD4 + lymphocytes might enhance the production of cytokines, attract inflammatory immune cells to the irradiated tissue, and drive polarisation towards a pro-fibrotic response 17 , 19 , 30 . The CD4 + subtypes Th2 and Th17 are pro-fibrogenic via secreted cytokines and their effects on fibroblasts and ECM deposition (reviewed in ref. 31 ). T reg cells control Th17, and the Th17/T reg ratio has been associated with fibrosis, but T reg cells also secrete TGF-β1 and IL-10, which stimulate and inhibit ECM deposition, respectively, and have been reported to have pro- or anti-fibrogenic effects 31 . The CTGF minor allele (T) was protective in a recessive fashion against fibrosis and was associated with low CD4 + RILA, although low-RILA was associated with an increased rate of fibrosis. This implies that the direct, protective effect of the TT genotype dominates over the association of low RILA values with increased fibrosis. CTGF plays an important role in the regulation of ECM homoeostasis. Along with TGF-β1 and downstream signaling proteins, CTGF controls the production of collagen and other ECM components 32 – 34 . Preclinical studies have reported that blocking CTGF may stop or, in some cases, even reverse the process of fibrosis development 35 – 37 . A previous study showing an association of the rs9399005 SNP with systemic sclerosis reported a higher affinity of regulatory proteins for the minor allele (T) compared to the major (C) allele and detected an alternative isoform of CTGF mRNA 38 . Our in vitro study on fibroblast strains with different CTGF genotypes showed that the T-allele influences expression levels of CTGF itself and a large number of DEGs, especially after irradiation, thus supporting the notion that the CTGF rs9399005 SNP has a regulatory function with biological consequences. Further, preliminary in-silico analysis indicated significantly higher binding affinity of transcription factors to the region containing the T allele, and binding was much more frequent on the minus strand from which CTGF is transcribed (Sami et al., in preparation). However, considering the relatively small number of fibroblast strains and potential confounding effect between the genotypes and the cell proliferation due to stochastic interactions, further studies are needed to reveal and confirm the indicated biological function of the CTGF rs9399005 SNP. The NBS1 gene product, nibrin, is a key component of the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) complex, which plays a critical role in detecting and stabilizing DNA double-strand breaks during repair. The SNP (rs1805794) is located in the exon region responsible for interaction with Sp100 nuclear antigen (SP100), near the BRCA1 C-terminal (BRCT) domain, and a nearby mutation (176:Tyr→Ala) was reported to block radiation-induced phosphorylation 39 . Previously, no association was found with acute normal-tissue reactions 40 nor with telangiectasia at 4.3 years mean follow-up after radiotherapy 41 . Although the risk of hypertension is known to increase with overweight, multivariate analysis showed that the effects of BMI and hypertension were independent. The data-driven BMI cutoff defined by the PA algorithm (BMI = 24.4 kg/m 2 ) is close to the WHO threshold for overweight in females (BMI = 25 kg/m 2 ), indicating that the PA cutpoint was biologically meaningful. A high BMI has been associated with increased risk of liver fibrosis, which may be related to an enhanced inflammatory state associated with visceral fat 42 , 43 . Large breast size and hypertension were associated with fibrosis after hypofractionated radiotherapy 44 . Furthermore, hypertension is a risk factor for myocardial fibrosis 45 – 47 and has been implicated in the development of liver and kidney fibrosis 48 . In conclusion, the present study provides proof-of-concept for the subgroup hypothesis that certain risk factors for breast fibrosis after radiotherapy are conditional on the presence of other risk factors. Thus, a significant association within a subgroup may be obscured in the classical approach by statistical ‘noise’ from complementary subgroups. Robust ML modelling confirmed the subgroup hypothesis with five-fold variation in risk and identified a smaller subgroup of high-risk patients, thus enabling biologically-aware risk stratification. Using just five features, risk stratification by this approach improved prediction over classical regression models and performed on par with more complicated models using dozens or hundreds of SNPs or other risk factors. If externally validated in an independent cohort, these advances could potentially enable more precise risk assessment of late toxicity for patients receiving breast cancer radiotherapy. The approach may even have broader applicability in personalised medicine, especially if additional interacting risk factors are identified in the future.
sections.patients, treatments, and endpoints: All patients belonged to the German ISE cohort on radiation sensitivity, recruited prospectively during 1998-2001 from the Rhine-Neckar region in Germany 49 . The median age of the patients was 59 years at the time of breast cancer diagnosis, and the patients had been treated with breast-conserving surgery followed by RT, without chemotherapy. Adjuvant RT was given to the whole breast (50.0 Gy in 2.0 Gy/fraction or 50.4 Gy in 1.8 Gy/fraction) followed by a tumour-bed boost of 6 to 16 Gy (median: 10 Gy, 2.0 Gy/fx; n = 83), or with 56.0 Gy given in 2.0 Gy fractions without a boost. Ethics approval for the original follow-up was obtained from the ethics committee of the Medical Faculty, Heidelberg University (approval number: 062/2002), with an amendment for the late follow-up, including RILA (approved on 17.12.2010). Fibrosis and telangiectasia were scored according to the LENT-SOMA scoring system, and blood samples were taken with written informed consent according to the Declaration of Helsinki principle 19 . Patient scores were dichotomised with grades 0–1 considered fibrosis/ telangiectasia-negative, and grades 2-3 considered fibrosis/telangiectasia-positive. At median follow-up of 11.6 years (10.3–12.8 years), positive rates were 30.6% for fibrosis and 9.5% for telangiectasia in 252 patients with RILA data, and DNA was available from 238 patients. RILA was performed at the time of the late follow-up, as previously described 19 .
sections.candidate snp selection, genotyping, and: Based on a pilot screening, three candidate SNPs, rs9399005 in the CTGF gene, rs1805794 in NBS1 , and rs373759 in ATM , were selected for genotyping by allele discrimination with real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction. DNA was extracted from whole blood or buffy coat using FlexiGene DNA kits (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), as previously described 50 . Genotyping was performed by allelic discrimination using TaqPath™ qPCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Massachusetts, US) with appropriate primer solutions and analyzed on a StepOnePlus™ machine (Applied Biosystems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Primer ordering IDs were: C_30290305_20 (rs9399005), C_26470398_30 (rs1805794), C_1039777_20 (rs373759). Validation of ambiguous genotypes, and genotyping of the rs9399005 SNP for selecting fibroblasts from the GENEPI cohort was performed by Sanger sequencing (primers included in Supplementary Table S3 ). A power analysis for additive genetic models was performed in R, using the Power Genetics library 51 for 238 samples for a power of 0.8 at α = 0.05. Minor allele frequencies (MAF) for Utah residents with Northern and Western European (CEU) ancestry in the 1000 Genomes Project dataset were used 52 .
sections.cell culture and irradiation: Tests of phenotypic effects of the rs9399005 ( CTGF ) genotypes were performed with early-passage skin fibroblasts from a local biobank established with written informed consent as part of the European GENEPI project by ESTRO and EURATOM 53 , 54 (Medical Ethics Commission II, Universitätsmedizin Mannheim, approval number 184/04). Early-passage fibroblast cultures were grown in AmnioMAX TM C-100 medium (Thermo Fisher, Darmstadt, Germany), supplemented with 7.5% AmnioMAX TM C-100 supplement, 7.5% foetal bovine serum (HyClone, Fisher Scientific GmbH, Schwerte, Germany), 2 mM glutamin, and penicillin/streptomycin. For clonogenic cell survival, the colony formation assay (CFA) was performed as described previously 55 , 56 . Cell irradiation was performed with 6 MV X-rays from a clinical therapy machine, and dosimetry was part of routine quality checks.
sections.gene expression analysis: Total cellular RNA was extracted on day 0 from non-irradiated fibroblasts and on day 2 from irradiated and non-irradiated fibroblasts using Qiagen RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA sequencing was performed by a commercial company, and raw data were obtained as FASTQ files. Raw gene read counts from the RNA-seq data were calculated with the Kallisto (pseudoalignment) program. Gene normalisation (voom function) and differential gene expression (DGE) analysis were performed with the limma package in R. Nominal p-values were calculated using the moderated t-test and were adjusted for multiple testing by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method.
sections.feature independence and subgroup analys: Test of collinearity between the features was performed by the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) method in Python using the “variance_inflation_factor” function from the “statsmodels” library.
sections.machine learning (ml) models: The development of RF and SVM classifiers is presented schematically in Supplementary Fig. S9 . The RF algorithm is based on creating a large number of decision trees (DTs) on different training subsets of the whole data set and making the final prediction by majority vote of the DTs. The SVM model was developed with a Radial Basis Function kernel, and classification based on the differences of inner outliers, or samples that are most similar to the opposite class (i.e., fibrosis negative samples that are similar to fibrosis positive samples vs fibrosis positive samples that are similar to fibrosis negative samples). The whole process was performed by using the Python programming language and the Scikit-Learn framework for Python 57 . The hyperparameter values used in the models were defined by applying the GridSearchCV function from the Scikit-Learn library (Python) and 10-fold stratified CV with applied standard scaler in a pipeline, using AUC as referent selection metric. The parameter values were as follows: RF model: Max depth (of the trees) = 5, Max leaf nodes = 30, Max samples used per tree = 0.9 (of the whole cohort), Min samples per leaf = 3, Min samples per split =10, Number of estimators (trees) = 500. SVM model: Regularization parameter (C) = 20, Gamma = 0.05, Class weights = balanced (automatically balanced according to the ratio between the classes), Kernel = Radial Basis Function (RBF). Non-indicated parameters kept default values (according to Scikit-Learn). Because of the intermediate sample size of the cohort, Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) was used and implemented in all downstream analysis and evaluation methods. This means that the prediction for each sample was made based on the model trained on the rest of the cohort, as presented in Fig. S9 . The stability of the final models was verified by additional stratified 10-fold cross-validation repeated ten times. To compute the error rates with stratified 10-fold cross-validation, the whole dataset was randomly split into 10 subgroups (folds), preserving the ratio of fibrosis-positive and fibrosis-negative samples (~30% of fibrosis-positive samples) in each subgroup. Each subgroup was then used as a test set, while training the models on the other nine subgroups, calculating error rates of predicted fibrosis status in the test and training sets. Thus, ten pairs of error rates were obtained from ten train-test pairs. The whole process was repeated 10 times, making ten new subgroups each time, which created 100 train-test pairs in total. Error rates and standard deviations for training and test datasets were calculated from all 100 pairs of error rates. The RF and SVM models were compared with Logistic Regression (LR: a linear model) and other commonly used ML models: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB: an ensemble model), K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN), and Naïve Bayes Classifier (NBC). Model performance was evaluated by precision (positive and negative predictive values), accuracy, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC), and Cohen’s kappa coefficient. All models were created using the Scikit-Learn library, except XGB, which was developed from the XGBoost library 58 . The LOOCV method was applied to all models.
sections.tests for feature and model evaluation: The characteristics of the models were evaluated by the cumulative accuracy profile (CAP), with predicted probabilities of positive outcomes (based on the predictions from LOOCV) as a function of the proportion of the dataset. The accuracy ratios (AR) were determined as the ratio of the areas under the curve of the test model vs. the perfect model. The influence of each feature on the models was evaluated by the Permutation Feature Importance test, which scores the average decrease of model accuracy when values of each feature are shuffled multiple times (LOOCV performed for each permutation). This implies shuffling values in each feature a number of times, every time repeating the whole model construction process and measuring the accuracy of the model. Finally, the importance of each feature is presented as an average decrease in model accuracy after shuffling the values for that feature. The statistical significance of the final models was evaluated by a permutation test 59 . The dataset was shuffled a number of times (i.e., 1000 times), each time making predictions based on the developed models (LOOCV applied) and calculating accuracies. This way, the distribution of accuracies for randomized datasets was created. The p-value is calculated as the fraction of randomized datasets where the accuracy is higher than in the original dataset. Data manipulation and mathematical calculations were performed with NumPy 60 and Pandas 61 Python libraries. The related figures were created in the Matplotlib library for Python 62 .
sections.statistical analysis: Basic statistical analyses were performed with JMP statistical software (SAS, Böblingen, Germany). Associations between categorical variables were assessed using contingency table tests. For 2 × 2 tables, Fisher’s exact test (two-tailed) was used; for tables larger than 2 × 2, Pearson’s χ² test was applied (as implemented in JMP). For non-parametric testing of continuous parameters between two groups, the Mann-Whitney U test, and for comparing more than two groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test were used. Potential subgroups were identified by partition analysis (PA), which creates a decision tree (DT) by a number of consecutive dichotomous splits. The risks of fibrosis in complementary subgroups were compared by contingency analysis using Fisher’s exact test. The effect of BMI on the RILA-fibrosis relationship according to HTN status was determined using the ‘Fit model’ linear model function.

title: Nanoparticles that target nonamyloid and nontau pathways in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder whose progression involves multiple pathways beyond the canonical amyloid and tau cascades. Neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and lysosomal impairment represent key nonamyloid and nontau pathways; preclinical evidence suggests that targeting these pathways may aid in the development of more effective treatments, although clinical validation remains pending. Owing to their ability to cross the blood‒brain barrier and their potential for precise targeting, nanostructured materials represent promising tools for modulating these pathways in preclinical models. Lipid, chitosan, and gold nanoparticles, when employed as carriers of anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds such as curcumin and resveratrol, have been shown in animal studies to reduce neuroinflammation and improve mitochondrial function. NPs functionalized with ligands such as triphenylphosphonium specifically target mitochondria, reducing oxidative stress and increasing ATP production by increasing drug bioavailability. Polymeric and carbon nanostructures improve lysosomal function and restore cellular homeostasis. These technologies slow disease progression by reducing neuroinflammation, improving mitochondrial dynamics, and enhancing autophagy processes. This article provides a strictly narrative review of recent advances in the use of nanostructured materials for targeting nonamyloid and nontau pathways in AD and to examine the therapeutic potential of this technology in the development of effective strategies to combat this disease.

sections.introduction: AD is the most common form of dementia; it primarily affects elderly individuals and is characterized by progressive neuronal loss. As a result of rising global life expectancy, AD has emerged as one of the most significant health challenges of the twenty-first century [ 1 ]. If the age-specific incidence rate of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementia continues to grow at the pace observed over the past decade, it is projected that 115.8 million disability-adjusted life years could be lost annually by 2050. For decades, AD research has been largely shaped by the "amyloid cascade" and "tau hyperphosphorylation" hypotheses, which have guided therapeutic development. However, the repeated failure of clinical trials targeting amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau proteins underscores the multifactorial nature of the disease and highlights the urgent need to explore alternative pathological mechanisms. The evidence indicates that the NANT pathway plays important roles in the development of AD, including neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, lysosomal defects, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, synaptic damage, and neurovascular impairments. These processes often occur before the formation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, indicating their involvement in the early stages of the disease. Chronic neuroinflammation caused by microglial activation and the astrocyte response leads to neuronal damage through the secretion of inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species (ROS) [ 2 ]. Similarly, mitochondrial dysfunction leads to energy deficiency and oxidative stress, exacerbating neuronal vulnerability. Defects in lysosomal function and autophagy result in the accumulation of toxic proteins, whereas ER stress disrupts protein balance and calcium homeostasis and activates apoptotic pathways. The loss and dysfunction of synapses, which strongly correlate with cognitive decline, are influenced by glial phagocytosis and metabolic disturbances [ 3 ]. Furthermore, recent studies have identified disruptions in the gut‒brain axis (GBA) and epigenetic changes as fundamental factors in Alzheimer’s disease pathology, opening new avenues for therapeutic targets [ 4 ]. A critical conceptual advancement in the therapeutic approach to AD lies in distinguishing between pathologies that are fundamentally driven by Aβ aggregation and those capable of autonomous initiation and propagation, even if they subsequently converge with or amplify amyloid-related toxicity. For example, neuroinflammatory processes can be activated systemically through peripheral immune challenges or by genetic risk factors such as TREM2 variants, resulting in microglial dysregulation and synaptic loss before substantial amyloid plaque deposition [ 5 ]. Similarly, deficits in mitochondrial bioenergetics represent a core feature of aging and are particularly severe in carriers of the APOE4 allele, regardless of amyloid load, indicating a parallel and contributory pathway to neuronal susceptibility [ 6 ]. The nanostrategies discussed in this review are engineered to target these upstream or concomitant dysfunctions. Their therapeutic promise stems from their potential to alter disease progression by correcting failures in essential cellular homeostasis. This provides a complementary or alternative strategy to amyloid reduction, particularly in contexts where therapies centered on amyloid have demonstrated limited clinical efficacy. AD is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial disorder in which amyloid and tau pathology represents only part of the pathogenic landscape. This narrative review synthesizes nanostructured materials engineered to modulate NANT pathways implicated in AD. We map seven convergent axes of pathology—neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and bioenergetic failure; lysosomal impairment and autophagy disruption; ER stress and proteostasis imbalance; neurovascular compromise; gut–brain axis signaling; and epigenetic regulation—and assess how engineered nanoparticles influence these processes at the cellular and subcellular scales. Rather than focusing on a single axis or on carrier properties alone, the work integrates mechanistic insights from diverse nanoplatforms and contrasts targeted delivery with nontargeted approaches. We discuss translational considerations for multipathway strategies and outline design principles for multifunctional nanoplatforms, including multiligand surface functionalization and combinatorial payloads, which collectively realize a systems-level nanomedicine framework for AD. The translational potential is underscored by the capacity of nanostructured platforms to cross the BBB and deliver payloads to subcellular targets [ 7 ], enabling simultaneous modulation of multiple pathogenic cascades in AD.
sections.literature search and selection methodol: This work constitutes a strictly narrative review that synthesizes recent advances in nanotechnology targeting nonamyloid, non‑tau pathways in AD. Although a structured literature search strategy was applied to ensure comprehensive source identification, the subsequent thematic synthesis, critical appraisal, and discussion adhere to a narrative framework rather than a formal systematic review or meta-analysis protocol.. The search strategy targeted three primary electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. A defined set of search terms, including “AD,” “nanoparticle,” “nanomedicine,” “neuroinflammation,” “oxidative stress,” “mitochondrial dysfunction,” “synaptic plasticity,” “neurogenesis,” “blood–brain barrier,” and “non‑amyloid,” was applied to titles, abstracts, and keywords. The selection process adhered to explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. The included studies consisted of articles published from 1997–2026 that investigated nanotherapeutics or nanodiagnostics in experimental models of AD, with a primary focus on mechanisms independent of amyloid-β or tau pathology. Articles whose principal objective involved amyloid‑targeting or tau‑targeting strategies were excluded, alongside editorials, conference abstracts, and non‑English publications. Selected high‑impact reviews and seminal earlier publications were consulted solely for contextual purposes. All retrieved records underwent an initial screening on the basis of title and abstract. The full texts of potentially relevant articles were then obtained and evaluated for final inclusion. This evaluation prioritized studies with clearly described methodologies and results obtained from established AD models. The objective of this structured process was the identification of original research that demonstrated innovative nanomaterial designs and contributed to conceptual frameworks beyond the classical amyloid and tau pathways. Relevant data on nanomaterial properties, experimental conditions, model parameters, and outcomes were extracted and integrated into the subsequent narrative synthesis.
sections.modulation of neuroinflammation via nano: Neuroinflammation is a pathological process in neurodegenerative diseases such as AD. This condition is characterized by the activation of microglia and astrocytes, which release inflammatory cytokines and ROS, exacerbating damage to neurons [ 8 ]. Microglias, which are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), play dual roles in neuroinflammation. Under pathological conditions, they polarize into two distinct phenotypes, M1 and M2. The M1 phenotype is inflammatory and involves the secretion of cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), and interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β), leading to neuronal death [ 8 , 9 ]. In contrast, the M2 phenotype is anti-inflammatory and produces factors such as interleukin 10 (IL-10) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which have neuroprotective effects and aid in tissue repair. This polarization mechanism is a therapeutic target for modulating neuroinflammation and reducing the progression of inflammatory diseases [ 8 ]. Nanostructured materials are suitable tools for targeting neuroinflammation because they have the ability to cross the BBB and can deliver drugs to the desired site in the brain [ 10 ]. Among these materials are lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), chitosan nanoparticles, and gold nanoparticles, which have shown high potential [ 8 , 9 ]. LNPs, which include solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), are particularly effective at increasing bioavailability and precise drug targeting. In murine models of AD, SLNs containing resveratrol significantly reduce brain inflammation by lowering TNF-α and IL-1β levels in Alzheimer’s disease models [ 8 , 11 ]. Additionally, CUR, a natural compound with powerful anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, plays a role in inhibiting pathological processes associated with neurodegenerative diseases [ 12 ]. Using SLNs to carry CUR, in addition to increasing its bioavailability, helps improve the penetration of this compound across the BBB and enhances its effectiveness in target areas of the brain [ 13 ]. SLNs containing methylthioadenosine (MTA) have also increased the bioavailability of the drug in the brain fourfold and and demonstrated neuroprotective effects in murine models of demyelination, underscoring the broader potential of lipid nanocarriers for CNS delivery [ 8 ]. Claims of direct symptomatic improvement in human MS patients are not supported by the cited preclinical data. The mechanisms of action of nanostructured materials in modulating neuroinflammation are complex. Controlled drug release is an important feature that provides long-term therapeutic effects and reduces systemic toxicity (8, 9). Furthermore, some nanoparticles reduce oxidative stress through mechanisms such as inhibiting ROS or delivering antioxidants to damaged neurons [ 14 ]. Silver nanoparticles coated with CUR (CUR-Ag NPs), for example, have shown favorable performance in combating oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators [ 15 ]. Additionally, mitochondrion-targeted nanoparticles, especially those functionalized with TPP + , have also demonstrated efficacy in improving mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis, which is considered a key factor in neurodegenerative diseases [ 16 ]. Overcoming these limitations requires interdisciplinary collaboration to optimize nanoparticle formulations, understand structure‒activity relationships, and establish regulatory frameworks for CNS-targeted therapies. Future research should focus on expanding multidrug nanoformulations by combining phytochemicals with other therapeutic agents, such as anti-inflammatory drugs or gene therapies, to increase their efficacy and reduce risks. Moreover, the integration of nanotechnology with advanced treatments, such as CUR-containing nanoliposomes targeting beta-amyloid deposits, paves the way for advanced therapeutic interventions (Fig. 1 )[ 17 ]. sections.the role of nanoparticles in combating m: Oxidative stress is a biochemical process resulting from an imbalance between the production and elimination of ROS [ 26 ]. ROS are natural byproducts of cellular processes that have important signaling functions under controlled conditions, but when their levels increase, they can damage DNA, proteins, and lipids. The brain is highly susceptible to oxidative damage due to its high energy demand, elevated oxygen consumption, abundance of peroxidizable unsaturated fatty acids, and high levels of catalytic iron for ROS production [ 27 , 28 ].
sections.mitochondrial dysfunction in alzheimer\u: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the main pathways of ROS production in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases such as AD and is independent of amyloid or tau. This dysfunction is characterized by impaired energy metabolism, increased oxidative stress, and an imbalance in calcium homeostasis, all of which play a role in neuronal damage and disease progression [ 29 ]. Furthermore, comparisons of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) with nuclear DNA (nDNA) have shown that oxidative damage to mtDNA in Alzheimer’s disease patients is 10 to 20 times greater than that to nDNA, indicating the greater sensitivity of mtDNA to ROS-induced damage and the important role of mitochondria in the progression of oxidative stress in AD [ 30 ]. Other studies on cell lines whose mtDNA was isolated from Alzheimer’s disease patients have shown that these cells produce higher levels of ROS and free radicals than control cells do. This finding confirms a direct link between mtDNA mutations, excessive ROS production, and the initiation or exacerbation of neurotoxic processes in Alzheimer’s disease (Fig. 2 ) [ 31 ]. Fig. 2 Mitochondrion-targeted nanoparticles rescue neuronal bioenergetics by scavenging ROS, repairing mtDNA damage, and restoring ATP production in neurodegenerative conditions. GSH-AuNPs: glutathione-conjugated gold nanoparticles; CeO 2 NPs: cerium oxide nanoparticles; ROS: reactive oxygen species; mtDNA: mitochondrial DNA Recent advances in nanotechnology have provided new opportunities to combat mitochondrial dysfunction. These advances have focused mainly on the development of nanoparticles capable of directly improving mitochondrial function, including cerium oxide nanoparticles (CeO 2 NPs) and nanoparticles functionalized with various groups that specifically target mitochondria. GSH-AuNPs also improve mitochondrial function and increase ATP production by maintaining the mitochondrial membrane potential, cytochrome c distribution, and respiratory chain activity. The protective effects of these nanoparticles are also stabilized by regulating the expression of genes related to mitochondrial biogenesis (such as PGC-1α, NRF-1, and Tfam) [ 32 ].
sections.mitochondria-targeting ligands: The mitochondrial membrane’s high negative electrical potential limits entry of anionic molecules [ 33 ]. To overcome this barrier, nanoparticles employ mitochondrion-targeting ligands including TPP⁺, tetramethylrhodamine-5-isothiocyanate, mitochondrial peptides, dequalinium, and natural compounds such as hypericin and glycyrrhetinic acid [ 34 ]. Among these ligands, TPP⁺ has been extensively investigated as an effective mitochondriotropic moiety because of its favorable safety profile and capacity to traverse mitochondrial membranes. The conjugation of TPP⁺ to nanoparticles enhances their lipophilicity and exploits the negative mitochondrial membrane potential (approximately − 180 mV), facilitating preferential partitioning into the mitochondrial matrix under experimental conditions. Multiple independent preclinical studies report that TPP⁺-functionalized nanocarriers achieve enhanced subcellular accumulation compared with untargeted formulations. However, these observations remain confined to rodent and cell culture models, and clinical translation requires rigorous validation of in vivo pharmacokinetics, off-target tissue distribution, and dose-dependent toxicity profiles. Seven distinct nanocarrier systems functionalized with TPP⁺ have demonstrated successful mitochondrial delivery in preclinical models of brain disorders, including (i) ceria NPs [ 35 ], (ii) PAMAM dendrimers conjugated to N-acetylcysteine [ 36 ], (iii) red blood cell membrane-camouflaged human serum albumin NPs loaded with CUR [ 37 ], (iv) RBC membrane-coated nanostructured lipid carriers for resveratrol [ 38 ], (v) PLGA-b-PEG-TPP + copolymers for antiretrovirals [ 39 ], (vi) tetrahedral DNA framework NPs [ 40 ], and (vii) Cu 2 ₋ₓSe-based NPs for CUR delivery [ 41 ]. The lipophilic cationic character of TPP⁺ enables these nanoparticles to bypass the impermeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane to anionic therapeutics, resulting in increased intramitochondrial drug concentrations. Consequently, compared with nontargeted formulations (5–50 mg/kg), TPP⁺-functionalized nanoparticles achieve therapeutic efficacy at substantially lower doses (2–5 mg/kg for CUR), thereby minimizing systemic exposure while preserving mitochondrial bioenergetics, the membrane potential, and dynamics [ 16 ]. CeO 2 NPs possess unique redox properties derived from their ability to switch between Ce 2 ⁺ and Ce 3 ⁺ oxidation states. This feature allows them to scavenge ROS effectively. Studies using transgenic mouse models of AD have shown that CeO 2 NPs significantly reduce oxidative stress and thereby slow the progression of dementia [ 42 – 44 ]. The synthesis methods and biological effects of these nanostructured materials play important roles in their efficiency. CeO 2 NPs are usually synthesized via precipitation or hydrothermal methods to achieve precise control over the size, shape, and surface chemistry of the particles. Surface modifications with biocompatible polymers or functional groups further enhance the stability and targeting capability of these particles. Preclinical data have shown that CeO 2 NPs, when administered intravenously at doses of 0.1 to 10 mg/kg, significantly reduce ROS levels and improve mitochondrial dynamics [ 42 ]. These targeted approaches not only increase mitochondrial ATP production but also restore the membrane potential and reduce mitochondrial degradation [ 45 ]. Additionally, CUR, an antioxidant, prevents neuron death by reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress, but its targeted delivery to the mitochondria of brain neurons remains challenging. In this context, biomimetic nanoparticles coated with red blood cell membranes (RBC-NPs) have been engineered to efficiently deliver CUR to neuronal mitochondria. These nanoparticles are functionalized with the T807 ligand to facilitate BBB penetration and triphenylphosphine (TPP + ) for mitochondrial targeting and are collectively designated T807/TPP + -RBC-NPs. These nanoparticles ensure high stability, controlled drug release, biocompatibility, and prolonged circulation in the blood. CUR loaded in these nanoparticles (CUR-loaded T807/TPP + -RBC-NPs) inhibits neuron death by reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress and improves Alzheimer’s disease symptoms both in vitro and in vivo (Fig. 3 ) [ 37 ]. sections.comparison of targeted and nontargeted n: A comparative analysis of mitochondrion-targeted and nontargeted nanoparticles demonstrated context-dependent advantages in experimental models (Tables 2 , 5 ). However, direct performance comparisons are complicated by substantial heterogeneity in study design, including divergent transgenic backgrounds, dosing paradigms, and administration routes across the reviewed literature. Notably, while TPP⁺-functionalized formulations have demonstrated therapeutic efficacy at reduced dosages (2–5 mg/kg CUR equivalent) in head-to-head preclinical evaluations [ 16 , 37 ], untargeted carriers in parallel neurodegenerative models often require higher systemic exposures (5–50 mg/kg) to achieve comparable biochemical outcomes [ 50 , 51 ]. Furthermore, the dynamic protein corona that forms in vivo can differentially mask targeting ligands depending on administration route, adding another layer of complexity to cross-study interpretation [ 52 – 56 ]. Within these constraints, mitochondrion-targeted nanoparticles have consistently demonstrated enhanced modulation of bioenergetic regulators (e.g., PGC-1α, SIRT1) in comparative preclinical studies (Table 2 ), supporting their potential for superior subcellular delivery. Standardized head-to-head evaluations across identical animal models, dosing schedules, and routes remain scarce, underscoring the need for harmonized preclinical benchmarks before clinical extrapolation. To rigorously evaluate these bioenergetic improvements, contemporary studies increasingly rely on direct functional assays rather than indirect behavioral proxies. Quantitative assessments of mitochondrial competence now routinely incorporate oxygen consumption rate (OCR) profiling, ATP-linked respiration measurements, and maximal respiratory capacity assays, which provide objective, pathway-specific readouts of nanoparticle efficacy [ 16 , 57 ]. The reliability of these core metabolic endpoints is consistently reinforced through orthogonal validation, including high-resolution respirometry, cytochrome c oxidase activity assays, and ultrastructural analysis of cristae morphology. This methodological rigor ensures that observed therapeutic benefits reflect genuine restoration of mitochondrial bioenergetics rather than compensatory or off-target physiological adaptations. While the dose-sparing effect achieved through mitochondrial targeting markedly lowers the risk of off-target toxicity, these findings must be contextualized within established safety thresholds. Although both targeted and untargeted CUR dosing regimens currently exceed the 0–3 mg/kg allowable daily intake for human dietary consumption, the substantial exposure reduction afforded by precise subcellular delivery represents a clinically meaningful step toward mitigating systemic burden and potential hepatorenal strain [ 37 , 58 ]. These comparative outcomes collectively demonstrate that therapeutic efficacy in mitochondrial dysfunction pathways is governed primarily by targeting precision rather than mere nanoscale dimensions. The convergence of evidence across multiple independent preclinical studies validates core nanostructural design principles for NANT interventions and highlights the critical need for standardized, mechanism-driven evaluation frameworks to accelerate clinical translation.
sections.protein corona formation and its implica: Upon intravenous administration, nanoparticles undergo rapid adsorption of plasma proteins within seconds to minutes, forming a dynamic biomolecular corona that confers a new biological identity distinct from their engineered physicochemical properties [ 54 ]. This corona layer frequently masks surface-conjugated targeting ligands through steric hindrance, substantially diminishing active targeting efficiency in vivo compared with in vitro observations [ 52 , 53 ]. For example, transferrin-functionalized nanoparticles exhibited diminished cellular targeting following corona formation in human plasma [ 55 ]. Recent in vivo corona characterization studies revealed that nanoparticles accumulating in the murine brain parenchyma frequently possess coronas enriched with apolipoprotein E and clusterin, which may facilitate receptor-mediated transcytosis across the experimental BBB [ 55 , 56 ]. This dynamic shift from engineered ligand targeting to corona-mediated biological identity represents a critical pharmacological consideration. Corona composition is highly sensitive to plasma protein variability, disease stage, and administration route, necessitating standardized in vitro-to-in vivo correlation studies before clinical translation.
sections.nanostructures targeting lysosomal dysfu: Lysosomal dysfunction in AD involves defective acidification, impaired enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D), vATPase proton pump defects, altered TFEB-mediated biogenesis, and disrupted endosome-lysosome trafficking. These impairments lead to accumulation of toxic substrates and neuronal death [ 60 , 61 ]. The application of nanostructures in targeting and regulating lysosomal activity is helpful in the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease [ 62 ]. Several nanostructures selectively accumulate in lysosomes, help repair lysosomal damage and restore the optimal pH of lysosomes [ 63 ]. Nanostructures such as polymeric nanoparticles, including PLGA, have also been effective in improving lysosomal function. These particles lower the lysosomal pH and increase protein degradation activity [ 64 ]. Furthermore, carbon nanostructures such as single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) also play a role in modulating lysosomal function. These nanoparticles reduce oxidative stress and improve mitochondrial function [ 65 ]. Surface-characterized nanoparticles (nanoparticles whose surface properties—including surface chemistry, surface charge, hydrophilic/hydrophobic properties, presence of ligands, polymer coating, and functional groups—are identified via analytical methods) are also intelligently directed toward lysosomes and enhance autophagy processes [ 66 ].
sections.structural carbon nanoparticles: graphen: Carbon-based nanoparticles encompass a diverse family of structures, including graphene oxide (GO), carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and fullerenes, which have garnered significant attention for AD therapy because of their unique physicochemical properties. Owing to their high surface area, exceptional mechanical strength, and versatile functionalization capabilities, these materials are robust platforms for drug delivery, neuroprotection, and bioimaging. For example, graphene oxide sheets have been shown to mitigate oxidative stress and improve cognitive function in transgenic AD models [ 67 , 68 ]. Similarly, carbon nanotubes can be engineered to ferry neurotrophic factors across the BBB and promote neuronal survival [ 69 ]. The inherent optical and electrical properties of these materials further enable their use as contrast agents for near-infrared imaging, facilitating noninvasive monitoring of disease progression [ 67 ]. However, their long-term biocompatibility and potential neurotoxicity require careful surface engineering and rigorous toxicological evaluation [ 70 ].
sections.carbon dots (cds): A distinct and rapidly advancing subclass within carbon nanoparticles is CDs. These quasispherical nanoparticles (2–10 nm) exhibit exceptional biocompatibility, low toxicity, tunable fluorescence, and ease of surface functionalization. Unlike their structural counterparts, CDs offer unique advantages for simultaneous diagnosis and therapy [ 71 ]. In addition to their established role in Aβ theranostics [ 72 ], the intrinsic physicochemical properties of CDs, such as their potent antioxidant capacity and facile surface engineering, position them as systems with adaptable potential for engaging NANT pathways [ 71 , 73 ]. The proven efficacy of these compounds in scavenging ROS and their ability to conjugate with various therapeutic ligands theoretically enable them to target key NANT processes such as neuroinflammation and oxidative stress [ 73 ]. Furthermore, their small size facilitates efficient BBB penetration and promotes renal clearance, minimizing the risk of long-term accumulation [ 74 ]. This combination of properties suggests that strategically engineered CDs may have the potential to evolve into a convergent nanoplatform for multitarget interventions addressing both amyloid and NANT pathologies in AD.
sections.synaptic disorders and synaptic plastici: Loss of synapses is a common and early sign of AD, and the extent of this loss correlates with the severity of cognitive decline [ 75 ]. Studies have shown that microglia and astrocytes play important roles in synapse elimination. In the disease state, these cells phagocytose both healthy and damaged synapses and contribute to the spread of damage. The complement system, especially the molecules C1q and C3, is involved in this process and tags synapses for removal by microglia. Studies indicate that activation of the metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1) in rodent models of AD leads to phagocytosis of glutamatergic synapses by microglia. This process occurs through the upregulation of the complement protein C1q, which is regulated by mGluR1. Activation of mGluR1 causes dephosphorylation of the FMRP protein and increases local translation of C1q mRNA at synapses. The increase in C1q, in turn, stimulates the phagocytosis of synapses by microglia, resulting in synapse loss and cognitive impairments. Inhibition of mGluR1 signaling or a reduction in C1q expression reverses this process and improves synaptic and cognitive function [ 76 ]. Additionally, changes in the expression of inflammation-related genes, such as TREM2 and APOE, lead to increased synapse elimination [ 77 , 78 ]. In recent years, clinical studies have focused on the development of synaptic biomarkers, such as SV2A proteins, neurogranin, and SNAP25, in cerebrospinal fluid to enable early diagnosis of this disease. PET imaging with SV2A ligands has also made it possible to observe synapse loss in the living brain. New treatments targeting interactions between synapses and glial cells, such as CSF1R inhibitors and anti-C1q antibodies, are being tested. These approaches aim to slow disease progression by preserving synaptic integrity [ 79 , 80 ]. Mitochondria play an important role in synaptic processes, and dysfunction of synaptic mitochondria contributes to synapse degradation in AD, as mitochondria are crucial for maintaining synaptic health. Reduced energy production and oxidative stress caused by mitochondrial dysfunction lead to impaired synaptic function and ultimately neuronal death [ 81 ]. Nanostructures such as magnetic or carbon nanoparticles can be used as drug carriers or antioxidant agents to target mitochondria. These materials can facilitate improved mitochondrial function and reduce cellular damage [ 82 ]. Additionally, nanostructures can assist in imaging synaptic changes in the early stages of disease [ 83 ]. Imaging via magnetic nanoparticles has shown that the gradual loss of synapses often begins decades before the onset of clinical symptoms and is initially evident in areas such as the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus. A reduction in synaptic density and dysfunction, especially in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, is associated with episodic memory impairment. NPs, as MRI theranostic agents, can target damaged regions for both early diagnosis through precise imaging and targeted delivery of synapse-repairing drugs. Given that the severity of cognitive impairments is more closely linked to synapse loss than to amyloid or neurofibrillary deposits, the use of surface-functionalized nanoparticles aids in improving targeting and therapeutic performance at the synaptic level. These nanoparticles adapt their biological surface properties to the biological environment and more effectively bind to damaged synapses [ 84 ]. Synaptic plasticity, i.e., the ability of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time in response to increased or decreased activity, is a fundamental mechanism in learning, memory, and cognitive functions. This dynamic process is regulated by complex molecular pathways such as calcium signaling, the regulation of neurotrophic factors, and receptor trafficking. However, synaptic plasticity is highly susceptible to damage caused by oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disruption of calcium homeostasis, which are characteristic features of many neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and Huntington’s disease [ 85 ]. These pathological conditions disrupt the delicate balance necessary for maintaining neuronal communication and lead to decreased cognitive function and gradual degeneration of the nervous system. Consequently, strategies aimed at enhancing synaptic plasticity have emerged as important therapeutic targets for combating neurological disorders.
sections.nanostructures modulating er stress in a: ER stress plays a significant role in the progression of AD, primarily through the accumulation of misfolded proteins, disruption of homeostasis, increased oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, which result in neuronal dysfunction and cell death [ 86 , 87 ]. According to several studies, the Presenilin1 (PS1) protein and amyloid precursor protein (APP) exhibit heightened responses to ER stress. PS1 is involved in regulating the calcium balance within the ER. The enzyme SERCA (Sarco/ER Ca2⁺-ATPase), which is responsible for transferring calcium from the cytosol into the ER, along with ER-associated calcium channels such as the inositol trisphosphate receptor and ryanodine receptor, are influenced by the function of the PS1 protein. Mutations in PS1 linked to familial Alzheimer’s disease (FAD) cause alterations in the activity of these calcium transport channels. These changes in the calcium concentration within the ER are considered stable and effective factors that induce stress in this network [ 88 ]. In this context, the use of nanostructures as a novel tool to modulate ER stress in neurodegenerative diseases has been proposed. For example, quercetin-modified nanoparticles (Qc@SNPs) have been designed, which, after crossing the BBB with the help of microbubbles and ultrasound, effectively accumulate in the brain parenchyma. In preclinical models, these nanoparticles have been reported to protect nerve cells by targeting ER stress through reducing neuronal apoptosis, modulating inflammatory responses, regulating calcium homeostasis, and decreasing oxidative stress. The results of behavioral tests, such as the Morris water maze test, revealed that treatment with the Qc@SNPs significantly improved learning and memory in an Alzheimer’s disease mouse model. This smart drug delivery system (Qc@SNP-MBs) is not only considered a safe and effective method for crossing the BBB but also offers a new strategy for treating neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease by regulating ER stress. The Qc@SNP-MB nanodrug system, composed of quercetin-modified sulfur nanoparticles (Qc@SNPs) and microbubbles, facilitates focused ultrasound-mediated BBB permeabilization in preclinical models. Following intracranial delivery, experimental data indicate reduced ER stress markers, attenuated oxidative damage, and improved behavioral performance in murine models through modulation of calcium homeostasis and suppression of apoptotic pathways (Fig. 4 ) [ 87 ]. These outcomes are confined to acute/short-term animal paradigms and do not yet reflect chronic human disease progression. Fig. 4 Nanostructures alleviate ER stress in Alzheimer’s disease by restoring proteostasis, calcium homeostasis, and redox balance thereby preventing neuronal apoptosis and cognitive decline. ER: endoplasmic reticulum; ROS: reactive oxygen species; ONOO – : peroxynitrite; BBB: blood‒brain barrier; SA: syringic acid; GSH-AuNPs: glutathione-conjugated gold nanoparticles; Qc@SNPs: quercetin-modified sulfur nanoparticles; CHOP: C/EBP homologous protein Recent studies have also shown that nanoparticles containing plant metabolites such as syringic acid (SA), which regulate ER stress, have protective effects on nerve cells. These compounds prevent neuronal cell death by inhibiting ER stress signaling pathways, including reducing the expression of the genes encoding ATF-6, caspase-8, and caspase-3. SA-containing designed nanoparticles not only cross the BBB but also show high potential for improving neuronal cell function by targeting ER disorders. In vivo studies have shown that these nanoparticles increase the survival of neuroblastoma cells (SH-SY5Y) by reducing oxidative stress and inflammation [ 83 ]. Furthermore, glutathione-conjugated gold nanoparticles (GSH-AuNPs) have demonstrated neuroprotective potential by reducing ER stress, which is evident through the regulation of ER stress markers such as Bip, C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP), and ASK1 and the restoration of calcium homeostasis in neural stem cells. These nanoparticles combat oxidative damage by enhancing the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and increasing the expression of enzymes such as SOD, catalase, and HO-1. By simultaneously targeting ER stress, oxidative damage, and mitochondrial dysfunction, GSH-AuNPs provide a comprehensive environment for protecting nerve cells against neurodegeneration [ 32 ]. Research by Huang et al. [ 89 ] also revealed that ER stress and the related process called ER-phagy are involved in the pathology of AD. Peroxynitrite (ONOO – ), an important biomarker, participates in the initiation and exacerbation of these processes. In one study, a smart fluorescence nanosensor based on AIEgen named DHQM, which has the ability to specifically target the ER network and detect ONOO – , was designed. This sensor, with high sensitivity, was able to track ONOO – fluctuations in an aluminum-induced Alzheimer’s disease cell model through fluorescence imaging. Ferroptosis (a recently discovered type of programmed cell death) is distinct from classical types of cell death, such as apoptosis. This process is iron-dependent and is associated with iron accumulation and severe lipid peroxidation in the cell membrane, leading to cell damage and death) induced by aluminum, leading to excessive production of ONOO – , which in turn activates and exacerbates ER stress. This nanosensor not only provides a valuable tool for understanding the pathological mechanisms of Alzheimer’s disease at the ER network level but also suggests new therapeutic methods for identifying important pathways [ 89 ]. Recent advances in nanocarrier engineering have enabled simultaneous modulation of lysosomal function through single multifunctional platforms (Table 3 ). These systems incorporate stimuli-responsive elements and dual-targeting ligands to address the interconnected nature of subcellular pathologies in AD. sections.nanostructures modulating neurovascular: Cerebrovascular disorders and the role of the BBB in AD have recently attracted significant attention. The investigation of targeted nanoparticles to improve cerebral vascular function and repair the BBB is an important part of NANT treatment [ 95 ]. The neurovascular unit (NVU) includes endothelial cells, pericytes, astrocytes, microglia, and neurons, which together maintain homeostasis in the brain. In AD, disruption of the NVU leads to a reduced cerebral blood supply, increased BBB permeability, and neuroinflammation, all of which independently contribute to neuronal damage and cognitive decline, separate from beta-amyloid plaques or tau protein [ 96 , 97 ]. Owing to their unique physicochemical properties and ability to cross the BBB, nanostructures have provided new therapeutic approaches for restoring NVU function and alleviating vascular deficiencies. One important component of the NVU is endothelial cells, which are damaged in AD, resulting in reduced vasodilation and cerebral blood flow. NPs designed to deliver vascular protective agents or antioxidants can target endothelial cells and reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. Polymeric nanoparticles containing nitric oxide donors or antioxidant enzymes have been shown to significantly improve endothelial function and microcirculation in preclinical models. These nanoparticles overcome the limitations of conventional therapies by increasing drug availability and providing controlled release at the site of vascular injury [ 18 , 98 , 99 ]. Other characteristics of neurovascular disorders in AD include the loss of pericytes, which leads to BBB disruption and the infiltration of toxic substances into brain tissue. Nanostructures designed to preserve pericyte survival or stimulate pericyte regeneration effectively maintain BBB stability. NPs that deliver growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) to the target site have the potential to increase pericyte proliferation and strengthen vessel walls. Additionally, nanoparticles modified with targeted ligands can selectively bind to pericytes and facilitate therapeutic effects at the desired location [ 96 , 100 , 101 ]. Astrocytes and microglia, which constitute the glial components of the NVU, become activated under neurovascular disorder conditions and release inflammatory cytokines that contribute to vascular and neuronal damage. Nanoparticles capable of modulating glial activity by delivering anti-inflammatory agents or inhibitory RNA molecules have been developed to reduce neuroinflammation [ 98 ]. For example, LNPs containing siRNAs targeting inflammatory pathways inhibited microglial activity in animal models and improved vascular function. Similarly, Ralvenius et al. [ 23 ] used LNPs to deliver siRNAs specific to a gene called PU.1 to the brain. When these nanoparticles were injected intrathecally into mice, the uptake of mRNA into the brain increased, and within 12 h, they were able to silence approximately 92% of the PU.1 gene. This resulted in reduced production of inflammatory substances in the mouse brain and helped decrease neuroinflammation. Another application of nanostructures is regulating ionic balance and oxidative stress within the NVU. Metal oxide nanoparticles such as CeO 2 have inherent antioxidant properties and can protect vascular cells against oxidative damage. These nanoparticles are designed to cross the BBB, accumulate in damaged brain regions, and continuously provide neurovascular protection [ 102 ]. Another area where nanostructures have high potential is enhancing the function of the glymphatic system (the brain’s waste and toxin clearance system, which is impaired in AD due to NVU dysfunction) [ 103 ]. When magnetic nanoparticles are combined with external magnetic fields, they guide drugs to perivascular spaces, thereby facilitating the removal of metabolic toxins and improving interstitial fluid flow [ 104 ]. Furthermore, recent advances in nanotechnology have enabled the creation of biomimetic nanoparticles that mimic cellular vesicles such as exosomes. These nanoparticles can safely and effectively cross the BBB and target specific types of vascular cells. These nanoparticles are capable of delivering miRNAs or other regulatory molecules that stimulate angiogenesis, stabilize the endothelial wall, and support neurovascular communication [ 105 ].
sections.nanotechnology-based modulation of the g: Modulation of the GBA via nanotechnology is a method employed to combat AD (Table 4 ). This axis directly addresses the complex bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal system and the CNS. The GBA includes a network of neural, immune, and metabolic pathways that regulate brain function and behavior. Recent evidence has shown that disruption of this axis plays a role in the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease. Changes in the composition of the gut microbiota (known as dysbiosis) lead to increased intestinal permeability, systemic inflammation, damage to the BBB, neuroinflammation, neuronal damage, and associated complications, including Alzheimer’s disease [ 106 ] . Considering the limitations of conventional treatments in targeting these systemic factors affecting AD, nanotechnology offers novel strategies for modulating the GBA through microbiome engineering, targeted drug delivery, and immunomodulation. Nanostructures can restore gut microbial balance by selectively delivering prebiotics, probiotics, or antimicrobial agents[ 107 ]. Chiral gold nanoparticles alter the gut microbiota composition in Alzheimer’s disease animal models, improve cognitive function outcomes, and reduce neuroinflammation. These nanoparticles have increased levels of beneficial metabolites, such as indole-3-acetic acid, which can cross the BBB and exhibit neuroprotective effects [ 108 ]. Chitosan-based nanoparticles have been used to encapsulate beneficial bacteria or bioactive compounds, enhancing their stability and targeted release in the intestinal lumen. These nanoparticles protect probiotics from gastric degradation and improve their colonization efficiency, thereby facilitating a better microbiome composition associated with reduced systemic inflammation and improved neurodegenerative outcomes such as Alzheimer’s disease [ 109 , 110 ]. Sodium oligomannate (GV-971), a seaweed-derived compound, has been shown to modulate the gut microbiota composition and reduce neuroinflammation in models of AD. Currently, phase four clinical trials are underway to confirm the efficacy of this drug, highlighting the importance of nanoformulations in enhancing bioavailability and drug properties [ 111 ]. In addition to microbiome modulation, preclinical studies suggest that nanotechnology enables targeted delivery of anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective agents to mitigate downstream effects of experimental microbiome dysbiosis. Gut-derived inflammatory mediators may enter systemic circulation and modulate central inflammatory tone via vagal afferents and peripheral immune trafficking [ 112 ]. Human translational evidence for this cascade remains limited and requires longitudinal clinical cohorts. Lipid nanoparticles functionalized with bacterial extracellular vesicles have been engineered to deliver miRNAs that specifically target the commensal Lactobacillus rhamnosus, thereby increasing bacterial proliferation and the production of indole-3-carboxaldehyde. This approach has been shown to restore intestinal barrier integrity and mitigate inflammation in colitis models, potentially preventing the translocation of bacterial endotoxins such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS), which can activate glial cells and exacerbate neuronal damage [ 113 ].Additionally, nanogels containing resveratrol and selenium based on chitosan (Res@SeNPs@Res-CS-NPs) with a high loading capacity (64%) have been designed to reduce inflammation and oxidative stress in Alzheimer’s disease models accompanied by metabolic disorders by the modulation of the gut microbiota. These nanogels improve insulin resistance and lipid accumulation by adjusting the Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes ratio and modulating glucose-related metabolic disorders through the JNK/AKT/GSK3β pathway. Moreover, by reducing LPS production and resulting neuroinflammation, these nanoparticles restore gut microbiota homeostasis. Furthermore, Res@SeNPs@Res-CS-NPs exerts protective effects by regulating bacteria associated with oxidative stress and inflammation, such as Enterococcus and Ruminococcus. This nanosystem has high potential for treating AD accompanied by metabolic disorders by improving cognitive function in animal models [ 114 ]. Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs), which enhance the effects of probiotics, especially Lactobacillus casei ATCC 393 (L. casei ATCC 393-SeNPs), can improve the balance of the gut microbiota. This combination not only strengthens intestinal barrier function by increasing antioxidant capacity and regulating the immune response but also increases the levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and neurotransmitters. These changes lead to reduced microglial activation and protect neurons against oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Additionally, intervention with L. casei ATCC 393-SeNPs modulates the Akt/CREB/BDNF signaling pathway, which is effective in improving cognitive impairment. Therefore, SeNPs enriched with probiotics have significant therapeutic potential in Alzheimer’s disease models through the modulation of the microbiota-GBA [ 115 ]. Studies have shown that CS@Se nanoparticles have significant therapeutic effects on Alzheimer’s disease models by modulating the microbiota-GBA. These nanoparticles restore the gut microbiome balance by increasing the diversity and richness of the gut microbiota, increasing the abundance of beneficial bacteria such as Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and reducing the abundance of harmful bacteria such as Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria. The resulting changes lead to reduced systemic inflammation and improved intestinal barrier function, which in turn prevents the entry of bacterial toxins such as LPS into the bloodstream. Moreover, CS@Se helps reduce oxidative stress and neuroinflammation by increasing the production of neuroprotective metabolites such as SCFAs. CS@Se nanoparticles play an important role in maintaining neuronal health by enhancing mitochondrial function and improving the synaptic structure in the hippocampus. Moreover, CS@Se prevents overactivation of microglia and the creation of an inflammatory environment in the brain by reducing the abundance of inflammatory bacteria such as Helicobacteraceae. These multiple mechanisms indicate that CS@Se has high potential for improving cognitive and neurological disorders in AD through the regulation of the GBA (Fig. 5 ) [ 116 ].
