sections.introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are one of the fastest-growing pharmacological classes in contemporary medicine. Initially approved for glycaemic control in T2DM, their indications have expanded to include chronic weight management and cardiovascular risk reduction [ 1 , 2 ]. With semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and the dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide achieving global blockbuster status, more than 50 million patients worldwide currently receive GLP-1 RA therapy [ 1 ]. The pharmacodynamics of GLP-1 RAs extend beyond the pancreas and the gut. GLP-1 receptors (GLP-1R) are expressed in pulmonary epithelial cells, airway smooth muscle, alveolar macrophages, and pulmonary vasculature [ 3 , 4 ]. This distribution provides a mechanistic substrate for both beneficial and adverse respiratory pharmacodynamic effects. The well-documented class effect of delayed gastric emptying additionally generates a biologically plausible aspiration risk, particularly in perioperative and sedated patients, although the clinical magnitude of this risk remains incompletely characterised [ 18 , 19 ]. Despite this biological plausibility, pulmonary adverse events associated with GLP-1 RAs have not been systematically characterised. Existing safety summaries are confined to regulatory labels, narrative reviews, and individual pharmacovigilance reports, whereas gastrointestinal adverse effects dominate the published safety discourse. The rapid scale-up of GLP-1 RA prescriptions, including in populations with pre-existing pulmonary diseases, renders this evidence gap increasingly consequential. This systematic review was designed primarily as a signal-detection and evidence-mapping exercise, given the predominance of non-randomised and non-comparative data in this area. Its specific aims were to: (1) identify and synthesise published evidence on pulmonary adverse events reported in temporal association with GLP-1 RA exposure; (2) characterise the pattern, severity, and clinical outcomes of reported respiratory events; (3) appraise the risk of bias using validated, design-appropriate tools; (4) describe proposed pathophysiological mechanisms; and (5) grade the certainty of evidence using the GRADE framework, applied at the outcome-domain level, to inform clinical guidance. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were pre-specified but were not feasible given the heterogeneity of available data and the predominantly non-comparative design of included studies; this is documented explicitly in the protocol.
sections.protocol and reporting standards: This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [ 20 ]. The review protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261305875).
sections.search strategy and information sources: A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Embase, and Scopus from database inception to 31 January 2026 (exact last search date). No language restrictions were applied. Trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP), grey literature sources, preprint servers (medRxiv), conference abstract databases, and regulatory pharmacovigilance databases (FAERS, EudraVigilance) were additionally searched; no additional eligible studies beyond those already identified were found through these supplementary sources. The search strategy for PubMed combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords in the following domains: GLP-1 RA exposure terms: semaglutide OR liraglutide OR dulaglutide OR exenatide OR tirzepatide OR lixisenatide OR mazdutide OR albiglutide OR “glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist” [MeSH] OR “GLP-1 receptor agonist”; Respiratory outcome terms: “Respiratory Tract Diseases” [MeSH] OR “Pneumonia” [MeSH] OR “Aspiration Pneumonia” [MeSH] OR “Dyspnea” [MeSH] OR “Bronchospasm” [MeSH] OR “Respiratory Failure” [MeSH] OR “Pulmonary” OR “Lung” OR “Airway”; Safety terms: “Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions” [MeSH] OR “Pharmacovigilance” [MeSH] OR “adverse event” OR “adverse effect” OR “safety”.
sections.population: Adults (≥ 18 years) receiving any GLP-1 RA for any approved indication (T2DM, obesity, or cardiovascular risk reduction).
sections.intervention: Exposure to any GLP-1 RA, including semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, tirzepatide, lixisenatide, mazdutide, and albiglutide.
sections.comparator: Placebo, standard care, or alternative glucose-lowering or weight-loss therapy (including DPP-4 inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 [SGLT2] inhibitors, sulfonylureas, or insulin). Studies without a comparator group (e.g., case reports, single-arm cohorts) were eligible for inclusion as descriptive evidence.
sections.outcomes: Primary outcomes included the following pre-specified respiratory adverse events: upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), chronic cough, upper airway symptoms (nasopharyngitis, pharyngitis, rhinitis), dyspnoea, bronchospasm, aspiration pneumonitis, aspiration pneumonia, non-aspiration community-acquired pneumonia, and acute respiratory failure (including ARDS). Secondary outcomes included hospitalisation, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, requirement for ventilatory support (invasive or non-invasive), drug discontinuation attributable to respiratory adverse events, and respiratory mortality.
sections.study designs: RCTs, retrospective and prospective observational cohorts, pharmacovigilance disproportionality analyses of spontaneous reporting databases, and case reports or series.
sections.exclusion criteria: Studies were excluded if they: enrolled paediatric populations (< 18 years); involved animal experiments or in vitro studies; evaluated non-GLP-1-based therapies exclusively without a GLP-1 RA arm; reported only metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes without any respiratory adverse-event data; or were narrative reviews, editorials, commentaries, or guidelines without original patient-level data. No publication date or country restrictions were applied.
sections.study selection: All identified records were imported into Rayyan. Three independent reviewers (A.A., S.P., S.M.) performed title and abstract screening, followed by full-text assessment by two reviewers (S.P., A.A.) for eligibility. Discrepancies at both the title/abstract and full-text stages were resolved through discussion and consensus agreement. Inter-rater agreement was calculated at both stages: κ = 0.91 at title/abstract screening and κ = 0.88 at full-text assessment. The study selection process is summarised in a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1 ).
sections.data extraction: Data were extracted into a pre-piloted standardised extraction form by one reviewer and independently verified by a second reviewer. Extracted variables included: study design and setting; participant demographics (age, sex, sample size); GLP-1 RA agent, dose, route, and duration of exposure; comparator type; respiratory adverse events (type, severity, time to onset, management); hospitalisation and ICU admission; ventilatory support requirements; drug discontinuation; mortality; proposed mechanisms; and funding sources and conflicts of interest. For cohort studies and RCTs, we extracted hazard ratios (HRs) or odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs where reported. For pharmacovigilance studies, we extracted reporting odds ratios (RORs) or information component (IC) values to measure disproportionality. These pharmacovigilance effect measures are signal-detection statistics and must not be interpreted as incidence estimates or causal risk ratios. Missing data: Where outcome data were not reported or unclear, the corresponding study author was contacted by electronic mail. If no response was received within four weeks, the data were recorded as not reported (NR) in the extraction table. No assumptions were made for missing data, and no imputation was performed.
sections.risk of bias assessment: The risk of bias was appraised independently by two reviewers using the following validated, design-specific tools: Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2) tool for RCTs, assessing five domains: randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for retrospective cohort studies, scoring selection, comparability, and outcome domains out of 9. NOS scores of 0–4 were classified as high risk, 5–6 as moderate risk, and 7–9 as low risk of bias. Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Reports and Case Series, assessing patient demographics, exposure clarity, outcome description, causal reasoning, and follow-up. JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist applied to pharmacovigilance analyses, assessing data source validity, reporting completeness, confounding control, and causality assessment. It is noted that no single universally validated appraisal instrument exists specifically for pharmacovigilance disproportionality analyses; the JBI checklist was adapted and applied in this context, and its limitations are acknowledged. Discrepancies were resolved through consensus discussion. Where reporting-bias assessment was not feasible because of sparse, heterogeneous, or uncontrolled evidence, this was recorded explicitly and considered narratively within the certainty assessment. The overall risk of bias was rated as low, moderate, or high for each study. The ROBINS-I tool (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomised Studies of Interventions) was considered for non-randomised studies; however, given that several included cohort studies were descriptive rather than interventional in design and that the review objective was signal-detection rather than comparative effectiveness estimation, the NOS was retained as the primary instrument for cohort studies, consistent with the pre-specified protocol.
sections.effect measures: Pre-specified expected effect measures by outcome and study type were as follows: risk ratio or odds ratio (RCTs); hazard ratio or incidence rate ratio (cohort studies); reporting odds ratio or information component (pharmacovigilance analyses). All effect estimates are presented with 95% CIs. For pharmacovigilance analyses, ROR and IC values are presented as disproportionality statistics only; they do not represent incidence estimates, relative risks, or causal effect measures.
sections.evidence synthesis and grade: Given the substantial clinical, methodological, and statistical heterogeneity across the included studies—spanning four different study designs, multiple GLP-1 RA agents, diverse respiratory outcomes, and markedly different sample sizes—formal meta-analytic pooling was not considered appropriate for most outcomes. This decision was pre-specified in the study protocol. For outcomes for which two or more cohort studies reported comparable effect estimates (e.g., pneumonia incidence), individual effect estimates with 95% CIs are presented in a forest plot (Fig. 2 ) to allow visual comparison without inappropriate statistical pooling. A structured narrative synthesis was conducted, organised by adverse event category, and informed by the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline [ 21 ]. Pre-specified subgroup categories included GLP-1 RA agent subclass (exendin-4-based vs. human GLP-1 analog), clinical indication (T2DM vs. obesity vs. cardiovascular risk reduction), and event category (aspiration vs. non-aspiration respiratory events). These subgroup analyses were not feasible in quantitative form owing to the heterogeneity and non-comparative nature of available data; findings were addressed narratively. The certainty of evidence for each outcome domain was appraised using the GRADE framework, applied at the outcome-domain level rather than as a single overall certainty rating for the review [ 22 ]. Evidence from uncontrolled designs—case reports, case series, and spontaneous pharmacovigilance analyses—was initially rated as very low certainty because of serious risk of bias, absence of denominators or comparators, imprecision, and inability to establish causality. RCT evidence started at high certainty and was downgraded according to standard GRADE domains. Upgrading considerations (large effect size, dose-response gradient, plausible confounding) were applied where applicable. The possibility of publication bias was noted where assessable (e.g., for pharmacovigilance analyses and case reports); formal funnel plot analysis was not feasible given the non-comparative and heterogeneous evidence base.
sections.study selection_1: A total of 1,271 records were identified through database searches. After the removal of 483 duplicates, 788 records were screened by title and abstract, of which 742 were excluded. Forty-six articles underwent full-text review; of these, 27 were excluded for the following reasons: no primary respiratory adverse-event data reported ( n = 14), non-GLP-1 therapy only ( n = 6), paediatric population ( n = 3), and narrative review or editorial without primary data ( n = 4). Nineteen studies met all pre-specified inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis. The complete PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, including all flow elements (records identified, duplicates removed, records screened, full texts assessed, exclusions with reasons, and final included studies), is presented in Fig. 1 .
sections.study characteristics: The 19 included studies comprised four RCTs ( n = 1,884 participants), five retrospective cohort studies ( n = 1,122,653 participants), three pharmacovigilance analyses ( n = 498,892 spontaneous adverse-event reports), and seven case reports or case series ( n = 13 patients). Because spontaneous pharmacovigilance reports do not represent unique exposed individuals or denominator-based populations, they are not pooled with participant counts; the clinical participant total across RCTs and cohort studies was 1,124,537 participants, of whom an estimated 913,179 were GLP-1 RA-exposed. The publication years ranged from 2012 to 2025. Studies originated from the United States ( n = 8), China ( n = 4), Israel ( n = 2), the United Kingdom ( n = 1), Japan ( n = 1), Switzerland ( n = 1), and multinational settings ( n = 2). GLP-1 RA agents studied included semaglutide ( n = 8 studies), exenatide ( n = 6), liraglutide ( n = 5), dulaglutide ( n = 4), tirzepatide ( n = 3), lixisenatide ( n = 2), mazdutide ( n = 1), and albiglutide ( n = 1); several studies examined multiple agents concurrently. Full study characteristics are detailed in Table 1 . sections.risk of bias in included studies: All four RCTs were rated as having a low overall risk of bias by RoB2. The main concern across three of the four RCTs was the open-label design, which introduced potential detection bias for subjectively ascertained adverse events such as dyspnoea and cough (Domain 2 and Domain 4: some concerns). It is emphasised that under RoB2 conventions, ‘some concerns’ at the domain level is distinct from the overall study-level rating; a study may receive ‘some concerns’ on individual domains while retaining a ‘low’ overall rating when the overall judgement considers that the domain concerns are unlikely to materially affect the outcome. The double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 mazdutide trial (Ji 2023) received low ratings across all five RoB2 domains. Among the five retrospective cohort studies, three were rated moderate (NOS scores 5–6/9) and one had a high risk of bias (Fishman 2025; NOS 3/9, absence of comparator group). The rating for the fifth cohort study (Henney 2024) was moderate (NOS 6/9). All three pharmacovigilance studies were rated as having high risk of bias, reflecting the inherent structural limitations of spontaneous reporting databases: absence of denominator data precluding true incidence estimation, underreporting and stimulated-reporting biases, inability to establish causality, frequent missing covariate data, and potential for duplicate reports. Of the seven case reports and series, five were rated as methodologically adequate by JBI (with acknowledged very limited generalisability inherent to single-case designs), and two were rated as having high risk of bias due to incomplete data in conference abstracts. Overall, 9/19 studies (47%) were rated as low risk of bias, 4/19 (21%) moderate risk, and 6/19 (32%) high risk. The risk of bias summary is presented in Table 2 . sections.upper respiratory tract infections and a: Upper airway symptoms and URTIs were the most frequently reported pulmonary adverse events, identified in eight of the 12 studies that explicitly reported this outcome (66.7%, 8 of 12 reporting studies). Across all four included RCTs, URTI rates were consistently reported but occurred at rates comparable to comparator arms without statistically significant excess risk attributable to GLP-1 RA exposure [ 3 , 6 , 7 , 14 ]. In the tirzepatide SURPASS J-COMBO phase 3 trial (Kadowaki 2022; n = 442), nasopharyngitis occurred in 17.0% of participants and did not differ significantly from comparator rates [ 6 ]. In the mazdutide phase 2 trial (Ji 2023; n = 180), upper respiratory events were symmetrically distributed across the three dose groups and placebo ( p > 0.05 for all comparisons) [ 7 ]. The dulaglutide biosimilar RCT (Li Liu 2025; n = 440) reported URTIs in both arms with no significant between-group difference [ 3 ]. The retrospective cohort study by Foer 2023 ( n = 1,642 patients with comorbid asthma or COPD receiving diabetes pharmacotherapy) demonstrated no significant excess respiratory exacerbation risk with GLP-1 RAs compared with DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, or sulfonylureas [ 8 ]. GRADE certainty for this outcome: MODERATE (evidence from RCTs; downgraded one level for open-label ascertainment concerns in three trials).
sections.dyspnoea and bronchospasm: pharmacovigil: Dyspnoea was the most frequently flagged serious respiratory signal in pharmacovigilance datasets, reported in 10 of 13 studies addressing this outcome. The largest pharmacovigilance analysis, Cazzola 2024 (251,145 FAERS reports across all approved GLP-1 RAs), identified disproportionate reporting signals for asthma-like events (ROR 1.63, 95% CI 1.41–1.88), bronchial hyperreactivity, and allergic respiratory symptoms [ 1 ]. Exenatide demonstrated the strongest disproportionality signal for dyspnoea (ROR 2.14, 95% CI 1.88–2.43), and was associated with 32 respiratory-related deaths in the FAERS database [ 1 ]. The authors attributed this signal to exenatide’s exendin-4 structural origin, which shares only 50% amino acid homology with endogenous human GLP-1, promoting anti-drug antibody formation and IgE-mediated hypersensitivity. It is critically important to contextualise these pharmacovigilance findings. Disproportionality metrics such as RORs are signal-detection statistics; they indicate that a given adverse event is reported with a higher frequency for a drug relative to all other drugs in the database. They do not constitute incidence estimates, relative risks, or causal evidence. These findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. All three pharmacovigilance analyses were rated high risk of bias, and their findings should be framed accordingly. Zhang 2025 (FAERS; n = 20,350 tirzepatide reports) identified a reporting signal for dyspnoea with tirzepatide (ROR 1.18, 95% CI 0.95–1.47), which did not reach statistical significance [ 2 ]. Nakhla 2025 (multi-database pharmacovigilance analysis including FAERS, EudraVigilance, DAEN, and WHO VigiBase) found no positive disproportionality signals for aspiration events with GLP-1 RAs across any of the four databases searched; GLP-1 RAs ranked lower than DPP-4 inhibitors for aspiration reporting across databases [ 16 ].
sections.hypersensitivity reactions: anaphylaxis,: Four case reports documented severe immune-mediated pulmonary hypersensitivity events reported in temporal association with GLP-1 RA exposure [ 4 , 9 , 10 , 15 ]. Amin 2024 described a 58-year-old woman who developed acute angioedema with tongue swelling, severe dyspnoea, and acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure within six hours of liraglutide administration, requiring ICU admission, intubation, and mechanical ventilation before subsequent recovery [ 4 ]. Shamriz 2019 reported anaphylaxis following a first dose of lixisenatide in a patient who had previously tolerated exenatide and liraglutide, demonstrating drug-specific rather than universal class-level hypersensitivity [ 10 ]. T. Liu 2019 documented anaphylaxis following a single dose of dulaglutide [ 9 ]. Steveling 2014 reported pulmonary infiltrates and peripheral eosinophilia in a patient receiving exenatide, consistent with a drug hypersensitivity reaction; radiological and laboratory resolution occurred following drug discontinuation [ 15 ]. Askin 2016 reported biopsy-confirmed acute eosinophilic pneumonia with BAL eosinophilia in a patient receiving exenatide extended-release for three weeks, which resolved completely after drug withdrawal and corticosteroid therapy [ 13 ]. The structural distinction between exendin-4-based agents (exenatide, lixisenatide; 50% structural homology with human GLP-1) and human GLP-1 analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide; ≥90% homology) appears clinically relevant: immune-mediated serious events cluster predominantly with exendin-4-based agents across the published literature, consistent with their higher immunogenic potential [ 1 , 9 , 10 , 15 ]. As these findings are derived exclusively from case reports, they represent very-low-certainty evidence and cannot establish class-level incidence.
sections.aspiration events: perioperative and pos: Aspiration pneumonitis or pneumonia was reported in four studies with biologically coherent perioperative clustering [ 18 , 19 ]. Avraham 2024 presented a case series of two patients who developed aspiration pneumonitis following elective surgery conducted under general anaesthesia; both patients had received semaglutide within four to six days of their procedure and had followed standard nil-by-mouth protocols [ 18 ]. Nasogastric aspiration at induction revealed unexpectedly large gastric residual volumes, supporting delayed gastric emptying as a plausible mechanistic explanation. Rashid 2025 (retrospective surgical cohort; n = 138,980 patients, of whom n = 2,944 were GLP-1 RA-exposed) found a trend toward increased postoperative aspiration events in GLP-1 RA-exposed patients (adjusted HR 1.28, 95% CI 0.98–1.67), which did not reach conventional statistical significance but is directionally consistent with biological plausibility [ 19 ]. The pharmacological basis for this risk is well established: GLP-1 RAs delay gastric emptying via both central and peripheral GLP-1R-mediated mechanisms, increasing intragastric residual volume. For long-acting weekly formulations, such as subcutaneous semaglutide (half-life approximately 7 days), standard preoperative fasting intervals may be insufficient to normalise gastric emptying. Point-of-care gastric ultrasound assessment immediately before induction has been proposed as a practical risk mitigation strategy. GRADE certainty for aspiration outcomes: VERY LOW.
sections.pneumonia incidence: a paradoxical prote: In contrast to the adverse signals described above, Henney et al. 2024—the largest study in this review—demonstrated a statistically robust reduction in the risk of incident pneumonia among GLP-1 RA users compared with DPP-4 inhibitor users in a global federated electronic health records cohort using the TriNetX platform (331,863 matched patients with T2DM; adjusted HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.58–0.62) [ 11 ]. This 40% relative risk reduction was consistent across pre-specified subgroup analyses, including age, sex, body mass index, and baseline comorbidities. However, important methodological limitations substantially constrain causal interpretation of this finding. The observational design introduces the potential for residual confounding. DPP-4 inhibitors, the active comparator employed, are not biologically inert: by inhibiting dipeptidyl peptidase-4, they increase endogenous GLP-1 bioavailability, which may attenuate or confound the apparent advantage conferred by exogenous GLP-1 RA therapy. Furthermore, the direction of confounding is uncertain, as healthier and more adherent patients may be selectively prescribed GLP-1 RAs (confounding by indication). These limitations are emphasised here as primary considerations rather than footnotes; the pneumonia risk reduction signal is an interesting hypothesis warranting prospective investigation, not an established causal effect. GRADE certainty: LOW.
sections.acute respiratory failure and life-threa: Acute hypoxaemic or hypercapnic respiratory failure was documented in six studies (50% of those reporting this outcome) [ 4 , 13 , 15 , 17 ]. The most severe events were documented in case reports. Rehan 2024 (conference abstract) described a 33-year-old man with obesity who developed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and ARDS following GLP-1 RA exposure, requiring veno-venous ECMO; the patient died, representing the only reported fatal case judged by the case authors as temporally associated with a pulmonary adverse event in this review [ 17 ]. A second case of ARDS was reported in a patient receiving liraglutide, who survived following critical care support [ 4 ]. Grell 2024 described spontaneous pneumomediastinum in a patient receiving semaglutide for weight loss, hypothesised to result from vomiting-related barotrauma secondary to gastroparesis-induced emesis [ 5 ]. Given that the Rehan 2024 case was reported in a conference abstract with incomplete data, the agent unspecified, and causality unverifiable by independent assessment, this event is characterised as a reported temporal association rather than a confirmed causal relationship.
sections.severity outcomes and secondary endpoint: Hospitalisation due to respiratory causes was documented in 11 of 14 reporting studies (78.6%), although case reports heavily influenced this proportion and aggregate absolute event numbers were small. ICU admission was confirmed in three studies. Mechanical ventilation was required in three studies, including the ECMO case. Non-invasive ventilation was not confirmed in any included study. Drug discontinuation due to respiratory adverse events was documented in six studies, most frequently in case reports of anaphylaxis or severe hypersensitivity reactions. Respiratory mortality was reported in three studies: Cazzola 2024 identified 32 respiratory-related deaths in the FAERS database associated with GLP-1 RAs (noting that FAERS deaths are not definitively attributable to GLP-1 RA exposure); Zhang 2025 identified 55 total deaths in tirzepatide FAERS reports (not all confirmed respiratory); and one fatality was documented in the ARDS case report by Rehan 2024 [ 1 , 2 , 17 ]. sections.proposed mechanisms: The following section describes mechanistic hypotheses proposed in the included studies and broader literature. These mechanisms represent biologically plausible explanations, not established causal pathways, and should be interpreted as context for clinical vigilance rather than confirmed pharmacological certainty. Four principal, non-mutually exclusive mechanisms have been proposed. First, IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is operative primarily for exendin-4-based agents (exenatide, lixisenatide) due to their non-human structural origin; immunogenic anti-drug antibody formation may drive anaphylaxis, bronchospasm, angioedema, and eosinophilic pneumonitis [ 1 , 9 , 10 , 15 ]. Second, gastroparesis-mediated aspiration arises from GLP-1 RA-induced delayed gastric emptying, elevating intragastric residual volume and aspiration risk in anaesthetised or sedated patients; this effect is particularly pronounced with long-acting weekly formulations [ 18 , 19 ]. Third, direct pulmonary GLP-1 receptor activation may produce pharmacodynamic effects on airway smooth muscle contractility, pulmonary epithelial permeability, and alveolar macrophage function, potentially contributing to dyspnoea and bronchial hyperreactivity signals observed in pharmacovigilance data [ 1 , 3 ]. Fourth, anti-inflammatory and weight-loss-mediated pleiotropic effects—including reduction of systemic and pulmonary inflammation, improved respiratory mechanics with adiposity reduction, and microbiome-mediated changes in mucosal immunity—may explain the protective pneumonia signal in large real-world cohorts, though this mechanism requires prospective validation [ 11 ].
sections.grade certainty of evidence: GRADE was applied at the outcome-domain level rather than as a single overall certainty rating for the review. Evidence from uncontrolled case reports, case series, and spontaneous pharmacovigilance analyses was initially rated as very low certainty because of serious risk of bias, absence of denominators or comparators, imprecision, and inability to establish causality. Upgrading was not applied to these evidence streams. RCT evidence was rated starting from high and downgraded according to GRADE domains. The complete GRADE evidence profile is presented in Table 4 . sections.discussion: This systematic review, the most comprehensive synthesis to date of pulmonary adverse events reported in association with GLP-1 RA therapy, identified a complex and stratified respiratory safety profile across 19 studies encompassing over 1.1 million participants and nearly 500,000 pharmacovigilance reports. Given that the majority of included evidence consists of non-comparative, observational, and spontaneous-reporting data, the primary inferential framework of this review is one of signal detection and evidence mapping rather than causal inference. Three overlapping themes emerged, each warranting different levels of clinical and scientific weight. Common upper respiratory symptoms—URTIs, nasopharyngitis, and cough—represent a consistently documented but clinically mild class effect, comparable to controls, supported by moderate-certainty evidence from RCTs. Rare but potentially life-threatening adverse events—including anaphylaxis with bronchospasm, acute eosinophilic pneumonia, perioperative aspiration pneumonitis, and ARDS—have been reported in temporal association with GLP-1 RA exposure in case reports and cohort studies, underpinned by very-low-certainty evidence, yet carrying significant clinical consequences per event. The third theme, a paradoxical large-scale protective pneumonia signal, challenges any simplistic framing of GLP-1 RAs as uniformly deleterious to pulmonary health, though its causal status remains uncertain.
sections.perioperative aspiration risk: clinical: The risk of perioperative aspiration requires particular clinical attention. GLP-1 RA-mediated gastroparesis is pharmacologically predictable and dose-dependent, most pronounced with long-acting subcutaneous weekly formulations; semaglutide has a half-life of approximately seven days, compared with shorter-acting daily agents [ 18 , 19 ]. Standard nil-by-mouth protocols, developed for populations with normal gastric emptying physiology, cannot reliably ensure gastric decompression in GLP-1 RA users. The case series by Avraham 2024 illustrated this concretely [ 18 ]. The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) 2023 consensus guidance recommends withholding GLP-1 RAs for at least one full dosing interval before elective procedures. For weekly semaglutide, this implies a minimum seven-day drug-free window—a recommendation that requires anticipatory coordination between prescribers and surgical teams. When GLP-1 RA use cannot be confirmed or fasting adequacy is uncertain, rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure should be the default approach. Point-of-care gastric ultrasound assessment immediately before induction offers a practical means of evaluating residual gastric volume. Post-transplant recipients and critically ill patients represent particularly high-risk subgroups in which GLP-1 RA-associated aspiration warrants active vigilance.
sections.exendin-4 versus human glp-1 analogue st: The clustering of immune-mediated adverse pulmonary events—anaphylaxis, angioedema, bronchospasm, eosinophilic pneumonia—predominantly with exendin-4-based agents (exenatide, lixisenatide) rather than human GLP-1 analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide) is neither coincidental nor mechanistically obscure. Exendin-4, a native peptide isolated from the Gila monster Heloderma suspectum, shares only 50% amino acid sequence homology with endogenous human GLP-1 [ 1 ]. This structural divergence confers substantially greater immunogenic potential, manifesting as anti-drug antibody formation and IgE-mediated sensitisation. Human GLP-1 analogues share ≥ 90% sequence homology with endogenous GLP-1, resulting in a lower immunogenic burden. These data support a risk-stratification framework in which exendin-4-based agents are considered to carry higher reported risk for immune-mediated pulmonary events, though the absolute incidence of these events in treated populations cannot be determined from the available evidence. Clinicians initiating exenatide or lixisenatide therapy should counsel patients on the reported risk of anaphylaxis and the importance of seeking early medical attention for dyspnoea, bronchospasm, or angioedema. Patients who develop hypersensitivity to an exendin-4-based agent should not automatically be considered allergic to the entire GLP-1 RA class; a supervised transition to a human GLP-1 analogue may be clinically appropriate [ 10 ].
sections.the protective pneumonia signal: mechani: The reported 40% relative risk reduction in incident pneumonia with GLP-1 RAs versus DPP-4 inhibitors observed by Henney et al. 2024 is biologically plausible [ 11 ]. The proposed mechanisms are multiple: obesity-related improvements in respiratory mechanics accompanying GLP-1 RA-mediated weight loss; reduction of gastroesophageal reflux-mediated microaspiration; direct anti-inflammatory GLP-1R activation in alveolar macrophages; and potential microbiome-mediated changes in mucosal immunity. However, important methodological limitations substantially constrain causal inference and deserve emphasis as primary considerations. DPP-4 inhibitors increase endogenous GLP-1 bioavailability, making them a non-inert comparator that may attenuate the apparent advantage of exogenous GLP-1 RA therapy. Residual confounding by indication persists as a legitimate concern. Differential weight trajectory over follow-up cannot be excluded as an independent confounder in a retrospective electronic health record analysis. The magnitude and statistical robustness of this signal are notable, but prospective, randomised trial-level data with pre-specified, validated respiratory endpoints are required before this pneumonia risk reduction can be accepted as a causal effect.
sections.implications for real-world practice and: The rapidly expanding real-world prescription of GLP-1 RAs—now encompassing patients with asthma, COPD, obstructive sleep apnoea, and post-transplant immunosuppression—renders a systematic, prospective approach to respiratory surveillance no longer optional. Current evidence is heterogeneous in design, inconsistent in outcome definition, and disproportionately reliant on pharmacovigilance signal detection rather than incidence estimation. Several future research priorities are identified. First, head-to-head comparative respiratory safety trials between exendin-4-based and human GLP-1 analogue agents are needed to quantify class-level heterogeneity. Second, prospective perioperative cohort studies with standardised gastric ultrasound protocols would address the aspiration risk question with the methodological rigour that clinical stakes demand. Third, designated respiratory safety substudies embedded within ongoing phase 3 cardiovascular outcome trials represent a tractable and cost-efficient mechanism for generating high-certainty evidence. Fourth, pharmacovigilance analyses incorporating drug utilisation denominators—currently absent from all three pharmacovigilance studies included in this review—are necessary to move from disproportionality signals to actionable incidence estimates.
sections.strengths and limitations: This systematic review has several strengths. The multi-database search strategy was comprehensive, eligibility criteria and analysis plans were pre-specified, and risk of bias assessment employed validated design-appropriate tools (RoB2, NOS, JBI). Evidence certainty was appraised using the GRADE framework applied at the outcome-domain level, and adherence to both PRISMA 2020 and SWiM reporting standards was maintained throughout. With over 1.1 million participants across four study design categories and nine GLP-1 RA agents, this review represents the most comprehensive synthesis of pulmonary GLP-1 RA safety to date. The acknowledged limitations are equally important. First, the substantial methodological heterogeneity across study designs, GLP-1 RA agents, populations, and outcome definitions precluded formal meta-analytic pooling for most outcomes. Second, the three pharmacovigilance studies—which contributed the largest number of records—carried inherent structural high risk of bias: underreporting, stimulated-reporting bias, absence of drug utilisation denominator data, and fundamental inability to establish causality. Their findings were appropriately interpreted as signal generation only. Third, nine case reports and two conference abstracts contributed descriptive evidence of very low generalisability. Fourth, the absence of a universal comparator across studies limits between-study comparability at a foundational level. Fifth, publication bias favouring dramatic adverse events may meaningfully inflate the perceived incidence of rare complications; formal correction for publication bias was not feasible given the non-comparative and heterogeneous evidence base. Sixth, several studies did not provide complete data despite author contact attempts; these were recorded as not reported.
sections.conclusion_1: GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy has a respiratory safety profile that is neither uniformly benign nor hazardous, stratified by mechanism, agent subclass, and clinical context. Common upper airway symptoms represent a mild, class-wide effect comparable to controls, supported by moderate-certainty evidence from RCTs. Rare but clinically consequential events—including anaphylaxis, eosinophilic pneumonia, perioperative aspiration, and ARDS—have been reported in temporal association with GLP-1 RA exposure, predominantly in case reports and pharmacovigilance data of very low certainty; these signals are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as confirmed causal risks or quantified incidence estimates. A 40% relative reduction in pneumonia incidence was observed in a large retrospective cohort (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.58–0.62), constituting an intriguing signal that complicates any simple adverse-risk framing; however, low-certainty evidence, an active and non-inert comparator, and potential residual confounding preclude causal attribution at this stage. Clinically, the most actionable priorities are: subclass risk stratification for hypersensitivity, with exendin-4-based agents carrying the highest reported risk; extended pre-procedural fasting intervals calibrated to the specific GLP-1 RA agent’s pharmacokinetic half-life; and gastric ultrasound assessment in high-risk perioperative patients when fasting adequacy is uncertain. Scientifically, prospective, standardised, and adequately powered studies with pre-specified respiratory endpoints remain absent—a gap that the scale of global GLP-1 RA prescribing has made untenable to sustain. This systematic review provides a structured evidence map that may serve as a foundation for designing such studies and for informing regulatory and clinical risk-benefit assessments.

title: Hypotension among patients with liver failure treated by artificial liver support system: risk factors and coping strategies
abstract: Background Artificial Liver Support System (ALSS) is a core therapeutic modality for liver failure, but hypotension is a common and severe complication during treatment, which may lead to treatment interruption and poor prognosis. This study aims to explore the independent risk factors of hypotension complicating ALSS treatment for liver failure, construct a predictive model, and provide evidence for clinical coping strategies. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted. According to the occurrence of hypotension during treatment, they were divided into the hypotension group and the non-hypotension group. Clinical data of the two groups were collected and analyzed. Results 216 patients with liver failure who received ALSS treatment were included. Multivariate logistic regression analysis confirmed that age ≥ 65 years (OR = 2.379, 95%CI:1.568 ~ 3.605), BMI < 19 kg/m² (OR = 2.782, 95%CI:1.825 ~ 4.226), ALSS treatment duration > 4 h (OR = 2.598, 95%CI:1.689 ~ 3.987), hypokalemia (OR = 2.193, 95%CI:1.452 ~ 3.298) and hypoalbuminemia (OR = 3.099, 95%CI:2.015 ~ 4.756) were independent risk factors for hypotension (all P < 0.001). The constructed scoring predictive model had excellent discriminative efficacy with an AUC of 0.888 (95%CI:0.840 ~ 0.936), and the highest Youden’s index (0.642) was obtained when the scoring threshold was 6.5 points. Conclusion The simplified scoring model exhibits favorable predictive efficacy, enabling early identification and risk stratification of high-risk patients. Implementation of multidimensional prevention strategies—including precision treatment optimization, individualized nursing interventions, and integrated process management—may reduce the incidence of hypotension and improve treatment safety. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12876-026-04760-2.

sections.background_1: Severe hepatitisis a life-threatening condition arising from diverse etiologies, characterized by massive hepatocyte necrosis and acute liver failure. It is frequently accompanied by systemic complications—including coagulopathy, hepatic encephalopathy, and secondary infections—and is associated with persistently high mortality, posing a significant threat to patient survival [ 1 ]. Advances in hepatology have established the Artificial Liver Support System (ALSS) as a cornerstone therapy for liver failure. By employing extracorporeal circulation, ALSS substitutes for the liver’s detoxification, metabolic, and synthetic functions, effectively removing circulating toxins, correcting metabolic disturbances, and bridging patients to hepatocyte regeneration and recovery, thereby significantly improving short-term prognosis [ 2 ]. Despite its therapeutic benefits, ALSS is frequently complicated by adverse events, among which hypotension represents a particularly common and severe complication [ 3 , 4 ]. Characterized by sudden onset and rapid progression, hypotensive episodes may necessitate treatment interruption, exacerbate tissue hypoperfusion, precipitate multi-organ dysfunction, and increase mortality risk—constituting a critical bottleneck limiting the therapeutic efficacy of ALSS [ 5 , 6 ]. Current clinical studies [ 7 – 9 ] have confirmed that the pathogenesis of hypotension during ALSS is complex and multifactorial, involving altered blood volume distribution from extracorporeal circulation, imbalances in vasoactive substances, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and impaired baseline cardiovascular function. However, given the highly heterogeneous nature of severe hepatitis, research systematically identifying risk factors for this complication remains scarce. This critical gap hinders the accurate prediction of high-risk patients in clinical practice, relegating most interventions to reactive, symptomatic management rather than proactive, precision-based prevention [ 10 ]. The clinical consequences of this reactive approach are severe: hypotension can necessitate premature treatment interruption—depriving patients of life-sustaining therapy—and exacerbate hypoperfusion of vital organs. This may trigger or worsen acute kidney injury, aggravate hepatic ischemia, and precipitate multi-organ dysfunction syndrome, collectively increasing mortality risk. Therefore, a comprehensive investigation to elucidate the key risk factors for hypotension during ALSS is of paramount importance. Such research is essential for optimizing clinical risk assessment, enabling targeted preventive strategies, and ultimately improving both the safety of ALSS treatment and the prognosis of patients with liver failure.
sections.ethical approval: The study protocol has been reviewed and approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Approval No.: 2026-SR-354). Following deliberation, the ethics committee waived the requirement for informed consent, and the research was conducted in strict compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki [ 11 ] and relevant ethical norms for clinical research. As a retrospective data analysis, all included clinical data have been strictly anonymized, ensuring that the research process does not infringe on patients’ rights, interests, or privacy.
sections.study design: A retrospective cohort study design was adopted in this study.
sections.study population: Inclusion criteria: (1) Meeting the diagnostic criteria for liver failure specified in the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Liver Failure; (2) Aged 18 to 75 years; (3) Having received ALSS treatment (including single or combined modalities such as plasma exchange, hemofiltration, and plasma adsorption); (4) With complete clinical data enabling traceability of the entire ALSS treatment process and relevant outcome indicators. Exclusion criteria: (1) Having persistent hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg) or severe cardiovascular diseases (e.g., acute myocardial infarction, severe heart failure, malignant arrhythmia) prior to ALSS treatment; (2) Complicated with other severe diseases that may affect blood pressure and prognosis, such as severe septic shock, malignant tumors, and end-stage renal disease; (3) Pregnant or lactating women; (4) Patients with mental illnesses or those unable to cooperate with clinical data collection; (5) Patients with incomplete clinical data and missing key data that cannot support statistical analysis.
sections.data collection: A standardized clinical data collection form was developed. Trained researchers retrospectively extracted electronic medical records and clinical treatment records of included subjects to ensure the accuracy and consistency of data collection. Hypotension was defined in this study as the presence of systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg lasting for ≥ 10 min during ALSS treatment. The collected contents mainly included: (1) Baseline data: gender, age, body mass index (BMI), etiology of liver failure, laboratory test indicators (serum albumin, serum potassium, liver and renal function-related indicators, etc.), and underlying diseases (with focused recording of complicated liver cirrhosis); (2) ALSS treatment-related data: treatment modality, treatment duration (with stratified recording for treatment duration > 4 h); (3) Outcome and complication-related data: blood pressure monitoring data throughout the ALSS treatment process (occurrence of hypotension, time of onset, and duration), incidence of hypokalemia (defined as serum potassium < 3.5 mmol/L), incidence of hypoalbuminemia (defined as serum albumin < 30 g/L), clinical manifestations and intervention measures at the onset of hypotension, and final treatment outcomes. While a comprehensive metabolic panel was collected, hypokalemia was selected for detailed analysis a priori due to its well-documented and direct mechanistic link to myocardial contractility and vascular tone, which are critical during the hemodynamic stress of ALSS. Other electrolytes (sodium, calcium, magnesium) were managed per protocol and showed less variability in the immediate pre-treatment period. After data collection, cross-verification was conducted by two researchers independently. Data with doubts were checked against original medical records in a timely manner to ensure the authenticity, completeness, and accuracy of the data.
sections.statistical analysis: The SPSS 26.0 statistical software was used for data processing and analysis, and GraphPad Prism 9.0 software was used for chart plotting. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. (1) Descriptive statistics: Normality test was performed on all data first. Measurement data conforming to normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation, and inter-group comparison was conducted using the independent samples t-test. Measurement data not conforming to normal distribution were expressed as median (interquartile range) [M (Q1, Q3)], and inter-group comparison was performed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Count data were expressed as case number (percentage), and inter-group comparison was conducted using the chi-square (χ2) test; the Fisher’s exact probability test was adopted when the theoretical frequency T < 1 or the total sample size n < 40. (2) Correlation analysis: Pearson correlation coefficient was used to analyze the correlation between continuous variables (age, BMI, treatment duration, serum potassium, serum albumin, etc.) and the occurrence of hypotension. (3) Risk factor screening: Variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis were entered as candidates into a multivariate logistic regression analysis using a stepwise forward selection method to identify independent risk factors. While ‘complicated with liver cirrhosis’ met the initial entry criteria ( P = 0.078), it was removed during the stepwise process as it did not remain a significant independent predictor ( P > 0.05) after adjusting for the other factors in the model. Before finalizing the multivariate model, collinearity diagnostics were performed. The variance inflation factor (VIF) for all included variables was < 2, confirming the absence of significant multicollinearity. (4) Prediction model construction and evaluation: A hypotension prediction model was constructed based on the independent risk factors identified by multivariate logistic regression analysis, and scoring was performed according to the assignment of each risk factor. The optimal score threshold for predicting hypotension was determined by calculating the sensitivity, specificity, and Youden’s index of the model at different score thresholds, so as to evaluate the predictive efficacy of the model.
sections.results_1: The study cohort comprised 216 patients with liver failure who underwent ALSS treatment, of whom 92 (42.6%) developed hypotension. The etiologies of liver failure were predominantly HBV-induced (51.9%), followed by drug-induced (20.8%), autoimmune (14.4%), and other or unknown causes (12.9%) (Supplementary Table 1). A comparison of baseline characteristics and treatment-related indicators between the hypotension and non-hypotension groups is presented in Table 1 . Patients who developed hypotension were significantly older and had a lower BMI and longer ALSS treatment duration than those who did not (all P < 0.001). Stratified analysis revealed that the proportions of patients aged ≥ 65 years, with BMI < 19 kg/m², and with treatment duration > 4 h were significantly higher in the hypotension group (all P < 0.001). Furthermore, the incidence of hypokalemia and hypoalbuminemia was markedly elevated among patients who experienced hypotension (both P < 0.001). Conversely, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding gender distribution or the proportion of patients with coexisting liver cirrhosis ( P > 0.05). Regarding laboratory parameters, mean serum albumin and serum potassium levels were significantly lower in the hypotension group compared to the non-hypotension group (Table 1 ). sections.discussion: Liver failure, is associated with high mortality due to its multisystem complications. The ALSS, which temporarily replaces liver function via extracorporeal circulation, has become a cornerstone therapy for improving short-term prognosis in these critically ill patients. Despite its benefits, the occurrence of intradialytic hypotension remains a key bottleneck restricting therapeutic efficacy. By exacerbating tissue hypoperfusion, hypotensive episodes not only risk premature treatment interruption but can also precipitate or worsen multi-organ dysfunction, thereby adversely affecting long-term patient survival [ 13 , 14 ]. Through this retrospective cohort analysis, we identified five independent risk factors for this complication and constructed a practical, simplified scoring model for early prediction. These findings provide an evidence-based foundation for identifying at-risk individuals prior to treatment and address the critical gap in simple, clinically applicable risk stratification tools within this field, offering significant potential for translation into improved patient care. From the perspective of pathophysiological mechanism interpretation, hypoalbuminemia, as the strongest independent risk factor (OR = 3.099), exerts effects that go far beyond the classic understanding of simple colloid osmotic pressure reduction: hepatic cell synthetic failure in patients with liver failure leads to decreased serum albumin levels, which not only causes intravascular fluid extravasation and insufficient effective circulating blood volume but also further induces hypotension by impairing vascular endothelial barrier function and exacerbating systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) [ 15 – 17 ]. This is highly consistent with the conclusion of previous studies that “hypoalbuminemia is an independent predictor of hemodynamic instability in critically ill patients,” and also suggests that clinical practice should attach importance to albumin optimization before ALSS treatment [ 18 , 19 ]. The risk associations of age ≥ 65 years (OR = 2.379) and BMI < 19 kg/m² (OR = 2.782) reflect the clinical characteristics of elderly patients with decreased cardiovascular reserve capacity and sympathetic nerve regulation function, as well as underweight patients with poor nutritional status and impaired immune function—such patients are more prone to blood pressure dysregulation during hemodynamic fluctuations in ALSS treatment. In addition, the risk of ALSS treatment duration > 4 h (OR = 2.598) suggests that prolonged extracorporeal circulation may lead to excessive clearance of vasoactive substances (such as nitric oxide and prostaglandins), hemodilution, and consumption of coagulation factors. In contrast, hypokalemia (OR = 2.193) exacerbates the risk of hypotension through dual effects of inhibiting myocardial contractility and reducing vascular smooth muscle tone, and the two together constitute treatment-related hemodynamic challenges. The scoring predictive model constructed in this study exhibited excellent discriminative efficacy with an AUC = 0.888 (95% CI: 0.840 ~ 0.936), and achieved the highest Youden’s index (0.642) when the scoring threshold was set at 6.5 points, indicating that the model can effectively balance sensitivity and specificity. Compared with models relying on complex formulas or multivariate calculations in similar studies, this model adopts a simplified rule of “assigning 2 points to each risk factor,” which allows for rapid assessment without professional statistical software and is more suitable for clinical front-line medical staff. Compared with models relying on complex formulas or multivariate calculations in similar studies, this model adopts a simplified rule of “assigning 2 points to each risk factor,” which allows for rapid assessment without professional statistical software. Notably, the predictive efficacy of this model (AUC = 0.888) is favorable when compared to previous studies. For instance, a study by Li et al. [ 20 ] developed a model for hypotension during hemodialysis that achieved an AUC of 0.802, while a predictive model for intradialytic hypotension by Wang et al. [ 21 ] reported an AUC of 0.815. The higher AUC in our study may be attributed to the inclusion of indicators directly reflecting the specific pathophysiological status of liver failure patients, such as hypoalbuminemia and hypokalemia, which are potent drivers of hemodynamic instability in this unique population. The findings of this study support the development of a multi-level prevention framework encompassing treatment optimization, individualized nursing care, and integrated process management. At the treatment optimization level, targeted preconditioning is recommended for modifiable risk factors. For patients with hypoalbuminemia, preoperative albumin supplementation to achieve a serum level ≥ 30 g/L is advised to augment colloid osmotic pressure, potentially combined with diuretics to mitigate tissue edema [ 22 , 23 ]. For those with hypokalemia, serum potassium should be corrected to 3.5–4.5 mmol/L prior to treatment initiation, with continuous intraprocedural monitoring [ 24 ]. In cases where treatment duration is anticipated to exceed 4 h, adopting a combined modality such as plasma exchange with hemofiltration may help attenuate hemodynamic fluctuations by reducing the duration of a single session [ 25 ]. At the nursing intervention level, enhanced monitoring protocols should be implemented for high-risk patients identified by the model (age ≥ 65 years or BMI < 19 kg/m²). Invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring with 15-minute recording intervals is recommended, along with establishing a hypotension early warning threshold (systolic blood pressure < 95 mmHg). Concurrently, comprehensive nutritional assessment and individualized support plans incorporating branched-chain amino acids and glutamine should be formulated for underweight patients to improve physiological reserve capacity [ 26 – 28 ]. At the management upgrading level, we propose integrating this simplified scoring model into the ALSS treatment quality control pathway. For patients with a total score ≥ 6.5 points, a “high-risk for hypotension” alert should be activated, prompting the formation of a multidisciplinary team—comprising hepatology, anesthesiology, and nursing specialists—to collaboratively develop individualized perioperative management plans. These may include preventive strategies such as colloidal fluid priming and tailored anticoagulation protocols. It is important to emphasize that while these recommendations are grounded in the identified risk factors and existing literature, the clinical utility of this model lies in its potential to enable proactive, rather than reactive, management. By identifying high-risk patients before treatment, clinicians could implement targeted preventive strategies which we hypothesize may reduce the incidence of hypotensive events and improve patient tolerance of ALSS.
sections.limitations and future directions: This study has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, as a single-center retrospective study, it is inherently susceptible to selection bias. The exclusion of patients with incomplete clinical data may have resulted in a study cohort that is not fully representative of the broader population of patients with liver failure undergoing ALSS treatment, potentially limiting the generalizability of the identified risk factors. Second, several potentially important confounding variables were not included in the analysis. Infection markers (e.g., procalcitonin, C-reactive protein) and coagulation parameters (e.g., INR, platelet count) are known to influence hemodynamic stability in critically ill patients. Their omission was primarily due to the retrospective design, which resulted in inconsistent data availability and lack of standardized measurement timing across the cohort. This may affect the comprehensiveness of our risk factor identification and represents an important area for improvement in future studies. Third, and most critically, this study did not compare the predictive performance of our simplified model against established prognostic scoring systems for liver failure, such as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, Child-Pugh classification, or SOFA score. Given that several of our identified risk factors (particularly hypoalbuminemia) are components of underlying disease severity, it remains unclear whether our model offers predictive value independent of these comprehensive scores. This omission limits our ability to definitively claim that the model provides novel, incremental clinical information beyond standard disease severity assessment. Fourth, the study focused exclusively on the occurrence of hypotension during ALSS treatment and did not assess the downstream clinical consequences of implementing this predictive model. We did not evaluate whether its use could reduce hypotension incidence, decrease complication rates, or improve patient-centered outcomes such as treatment tolerance or subjective satisfaction. Future research directions should address these limitations through multicenter prospective cohort studies with larger, more diverse populations. Such studies should: (1) systematically collect infection markers and coagulation parameters at standardized time points; (2) directly compare the predictive performance of this simplified model against established scores like MELD and Child-Pugh to determine whether it offers independent and additive value in predicting hypotension specifically; (3) validate the model’s extrapolatability across different clinical settings; and (4) most importantly, evaluate whether implementation of this risk stratification tool, coupled with targeted preventive interventions, leads to measurable improvements in clinical outcomes. Interventional studies are urgently needed to determine the actual impact of model-guided management on reducing hypotension rates, improving patient prognosis, and enhancing the overall safety of ALSS treatment.
sections.conclusion_1: This study identifies age ≥ 65 years, BMI < 19 kg/m², ALSS treatment duration > 4 h, hypokalemia, and hypoalbuminemia as independent risk factors for hypotension during ALSS treatment in patients with liver failure. The simplified scoring model constructed from these factors demonstrated good predictive performance (AUC = 0.888), enabling early identification and risk stratification of high-risk patients. Clinically, implementing a multidimensional prevention strategy—including treatment optimization (pre-emptive correction of hypoalbuminemia and hypokalemia, judicious limitation of treatment duration), individualized nursing interventions (intensified blood pressure monitoring, targeted nutritional support), and integrated process management (model-based early warning activation, multidisciplinary team involvement)—may reduce hypotension incidence and enhance treatment safety. Future multicenter prospective studies are warranted to validate the model’s generalizability, and interventional studies should determine whether model-guided management improves patient prognosis, thereby providing a stronger evidence base for precision management in ALSS treatment.

title: Nucleophagy removes cytotoxic trapped PARP1
abstract: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors (PARPi) induce cytotoxicity in homologous recombination repair (HR)-deficient (HRD) cancers by trapping PARP1 on chromatin, thereby causing irreparable replication-associated DNA damage. Although increased clearance of trapped PARP1 from chromatin reduces the sensitivity of cancer cells to PARPi, details surrounding this process remain unclear. PARPi exposure is known to cause increased autophagy flux, whereas autophagy inhibition can hypersensitize cells to PARPi. Our study reveals that trapped PARP1 is cleared via nucleophagy, with the selective autophagy receptor TEX264 and its partner segregase p97 (also known as VCP) orchestrating this process. TEX264 interacts directly with trapped PARP1, linking it to the autophagosomal protein LC3 for degradation. Disrupting this pathway, either chemically or genetically, increases PARP1 trapping, resulting in protein aggregates, DNA damage and cell lethality, ultimately re-sensitizing PARPi-resistant cells. We conclude that nucleophagy serves a cytoprotective role by targeting PARPi-induced trapped PARP1 for degradation.

sections.main: In 20 years of clinical trials 1 , six PARP inhibitors (PARPi) have been approved for the treatment of homologous recombination repair (HR)-deficient (HRD) breast, prostate, pancreatic and ovarian cancers 2 – 4 . This represents the first synthetic lethality-targeted therapy, whereby HRD- cells, most commonly those with mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2, display up to 1,000-fold more selectivity to PARPi than their wild-type (WT) counterparts 5 – 7 . PARPi target the key DNA damage repair (DDR) enzyme PARP1, involved in single-strand break (SSB) response 8 , replication fork stability 9 and ligation of Okazaki fragments 10 . All clinically approved PARPi are nicotinamide analogues that bind the catalytic site of PARP1 (ref. 7 ). Synthetic lethality was first attributed to catalytic inhibition of PARP1, leading to accumulation of SSBs that collapse into irreparable double-strand breaks (DSBs) during S phase in HRD-cancers 5 – 7 . However, the discovery that cytotoxicity of different PARPi does not directly correlate with catalytic inhibitory potency, and that loss of PARP1 confers resistance 11 , revealed an additional cytotoxic mechanism: upon PARP inhibition, PARP1 becomes tightly bound to DNA, a phenomenon known as PARP1 trapping 12 , 13 . The trapping potency of each PARPi strongly correlates with its cytotoxicity, demonstrating the importance of this mechanism for PARPi response 13 – 15 . Talazoparib is the most potent clinically approved PARP1 trapper 7 , 14 , 16 , used as a monotherapy to treat human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative, BRCA-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, and in clinical trials for other cancers 3 . Trapping of PARP1 on DNA damage sites and unligated Okazaki fragments is thought to cause collisions with the replisome and fork stalling, which, in HRD or BRCA1/2-defective cells, collapse into unrepaired DSBs, leading to cell death 4 , 12 – 14 . Despite their early promise, PARPi resistance, both acquired and de novo, is a major clinical concern 8 , 17 , 18 . In ovarian cancer, approximately 40% of patients with germline BRCA mutations show no response to olaparib 18 – 20 or rucaparib 4 , 21 . This underscores the limited predictive power of current biomarkers, as deleterious BRCA/HRD mutations do not always reflect real-time HR function, therapy sensitivity or resistance dynamics 4 , 22 – 24 . The only clinically well-validated resistance mechanisms are BRCA/HR gene reversions and epigenetic regulation that restores HR, observed in hundreds of patients 8 , 25 – 27 . Pre-clinical evidence also indicates (1) non-reversion mutations that restore HR in BRCA1-defective cancers via loss of DNA end resection inhibitors 28 – 31 ; (2) restored fork stability through inhibiting nuclease recruitment 32 ; (3) loss of poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase expression 33 ; (4) upregulation of the ABCB1 efflux transporter, which limits PARPi accumulation 34 – 36 ; and (5) PARP1 mutations that abolish trapping 11 , 37 . Greater insight into trapped PARP1 biology is necessary to define clinically relevant resistance mechanisms and improve therapeutic outcomes. One area of interest is the proteolytic processing of trapped PARP1. The metalloprotease SPRTN 38 and the unfoldase/segregase p97 (also known as VCP or Cdc48) 39 extract trapped PARP1 from chromatin. Via its cofactor UFD1, p97 recognizes trapped PARP1 that has been SUMOylated and ubiquitylated by PIAS4 and RNF4, respectively, and extracts it from chromatin through its central pore 39 . p97, a promising druggable target with an inhibitor in clinical trials, resolves various protein-induced DNA lesions, including TOP1cc 40 and trapped PARP1 (refs. 39 , 41 ), whose covalent or non-covalent association with DNA causes cytotoxic replisome blockade 42 . Given the broad roles of p97 in chromatin-associated processes, including DNA repair 43 – 48 , defining its regulation by cofactors and its downstream processing is crucial for therapeutic development. Our group recently uncovered an autophagy-dependent pathway by which p97 processes TOP1cc lesions from chromatin 49 . This pathway requires the p97 cofactor and selective autophagy receptor TEX264, which bridges topoisomerase inhibitor-induced TOP1cc to autophagosomes for degradation, preventing cytotoxic protein aggregates, limiting genome instability and shaping colorectal cancer responses to the topoisomerase I inhibitor Irinotecan. Bulk autophagy is a cellular homeostasis pathway, best characterized under starvation, in which substrates are engulfed by elongating double-membrane phagophores that form autophagosomes, which then fuse with hydrolase-containing lysosomes 50 . Selective autophagy targets specific cargo via ATG8-family proteins on the growing phagophore, such as lipidated LC3, often using selective autophagy receptors (SARs) like TEX264 (refs. 49 , 51 , 52 ), which recognize specific substrates and bridge them to ATG8-family proteins 53 , 54 . Clinical trials with autophagy inhibitors chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine, mainly in combination therapies, show positive results, but the development of additional inhibitors is limited by tolerability 55 . All four US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved PARPi upregulate autophagy, confirming cryoprotection in multiple cell lines and patient-derived xenografts 56 – 63 , but the role of autophagy in PARPi response requires further clarification for clinical translation. To advance this, we investigated how trapped PARP1 is cleared from chromatin. We show that PARPi-induced autophagy is cytoprotective and interacts with trapped PARP1. Autophagy clears trapped PARP1 via the SAR TEX264 and its partner p97, which remove trapped PARP1 from chromatin and deliver it to the lysosome. Disrupting this pathway causes accumulation of cytotoxic PARP1 aggregates and genome instability, increasing cell lethality, including in PARPi-resistant cells. These findings support a TEX264-mediated nucleophagy pathway that promotes survival of HRD, particularly BRCA1-deficient mammalian cells and may have clinical relevance.
sections.autophagy is upregulated upon parpi trea: PARPi induce trapping of PARP1 on chromatin, the proposed major mechanism of PARPi cytotoxicity 12 , 13 , 15 , 64 , 65 . Recent work has suggested that trapped PARP1 can be extracted from chromatin by the enzymatic activities of ATPase p97 and SPRTN protease, similar to other DNA–protein crosslinks (DPCs) 38 , 39 , 66 , 67 , potentially contributing to PARPi resistance. Through an RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) approach, we explored which protein homeostasis systems may be differentially expressed upon PARPi treatment, suggesting their potential involvement in trapped PARP1 repair. We performed RNA-seq on triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) CAL51 cells after 24 h of treatment with potent PARP1-trapping talazoparib. As expected, we observed upregulation of genes related to DDR, replication stress, apoptosis, G1/S cell cycle checkpoint and mitotic checkpoint (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1 ). Top hits include CDKN1A and BTG2, involved in p53-dependent G1/S checkpoint DDR signalling 68 , MDM2, a p53 regulator that also has p53-independent roles in DNA synthesis and repair regulation 69 and BAX, a pro-apoptotic protein 70 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 2 ). By probing with a comprehensive gene list for the autophagy pathway 71 , we observed upregulation of 31 autophagy-related genes upon treatment. Significantly upregulated genes included SESN1, SESN2 and DRAM1 (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 2 ), which are transcriptionally activated by p53 under genotoxic stress to promote autophagy 72 . In accordance with this, numerous studies show upregulation of autophagy in cells and patient-derived xenografts treated with PARPi 56 – 63 , 73 . We also probed with a Gene Ontology (GO) term list for proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent catabolic processes ( GO:0043161 ). Only 15 genes were differentially expressed (7 significantly upon treatment), but there was no differential expression with a GO list specific for the proteasome complex itself ( GO:0000502 ). In fact, most proteasome-associated genes identified were E3 ligases, components of E3 ligases or E2 conjugating enzymes well established in DDR and cell cycle regulation in response to stress, such as MDM2, FBXW7 and UBE2C (Supplementary Table 2 ). Core proteasome protein transcripts are some of the most consistently expressed in human cancer cells 74 . While their lack of differential expression is unsurprising, few genes known to positively regulate the proteasome (five genes from GO:1901800 ) were differentially expressed. This suggests that PARPi may not induce proteasomal degradation to the same extent as autophagy.
