sections.introduction: Valve-sparing aortic root replacement (VSARR) preserves the patient’s native aortic valve (AV), eliminating the need for lifelong anticoagulation and maintaining natural haemodynamics. Despite its proven clinical benefits in appropriately selected patients, VSARR is a technically demanding procedure that is performed relatively infrequently and carries a long-term risk of reintervention. 1–3 Currently, VSARR is performed in centres of varying annual volumes, and recommendations on annual caseloads required to perform VSARR are lacking. Centralization of specialized healthcare services has become a pivotal aspect to improving the quality of medical procedures. Conceptually, by concentrating cases in higher-volume centres, surgeons and medical teams become more experienced, which has been associated with improved patient outcomes across various medical disciplines. 4 This association between volume-outcome (V-O) has been well-documented, leading to the establishment of specific annual case volume thresholds that define centres of excellence for several procedures. 5–9 However, determining these thresholds for complex procedures like VSARR poses significant challenges due to limited procedural frequency, low event rates, and data variability. We evaluated V-O associations for VSARR using prospective registry data from the Heart Valve Society Aortic Valve (HVS AV) Database and aimed to identify a data-driven annual case volume threshold to define high-volume centres.
sections.ethical statement: Access to the HVS AV Database was granted by the HVS Scientific Committee. Participating centres obtained approval from their local ethics committee/IRB or a formal waiver. Written consent was obtained when required and waived where permitted. Erasmus MC approved participation (MEC-2020-0890). Data handling followed each site’s regulations and HVS AV Database governance. The HVS AV Database, and consequently this study, follows the WMA Declarations of Helsinki (2013) and Taipei (2016).
sections.protocol and registration: This study is an analysis of prospectively collected registry data from the HVS AV Database. This registry, including governance, has been described in detail elsewhere. 10 The protocol was reviewed by the HVS AV Database Scientific Committee prior to data release. De-identified data were extracted on October 14, 2024 for all participating centres contributing VSARR cases within the inclusion window.
sections.data collection: All elective primary VSARR cases with complete data on timing of death, reintervention, and early postoperative outcomes were included in the study. Patients in the HVS AV database were operated on between 1996 and 2023. A CONSORT-style flow diagram illustrating the selection of patients from the HVS AV database is provided in Supplementary Material S1 .
sections.outcome measures: The primary outcomes were the association between annual institutional volume and (i) early postoperative outcomes (in-hospital or within 30 days after surgery), including mortality, thromboembolic events (transient ischaemic attack [TIA], stroke, or peripheral arterial embolism), intraoperative conversion to valve-replacement surgery, early reinterventions, and early recurrent aortic regurgitation (AR) grade 2 or higher, and (ii) AV reintervention-free (AVRF) survival, defined as survival without having undergone reintervention at follow-up. Reintervention was defined as any repeat surgical or transcatheter procedure on the AV or root, including valve replacement, redo VSARR, or full root replacement. Conversion was defined as valve replacement performed after completion of VSARR, excluding cases where VSARR was abandoned after primary intraoperative valve assessment. A composite end-point of early adverse events was created and included all-cause mortality, reintervention, thromboembolic events, intraoperative conversions to valve replacement, and recurrent AR grade 2 or higher, as these outcomes collectively reflect early procedural safety and surgical expertise. Secondary outcomes comprised the separate end-points of the early composite end-point, long-term survival, long-term freedom from reintervention, and long-term AVRF.
sections.statistical analysis: Baseline characteristics were presented as means and standard deviations (SDs) or medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs). Distribution was tested using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Annual institutional case volume was calculated as the mean number of VSARR procedures per year of registry participation per centre. For descriptive purposes, the baseline and procedural characteristics, as well as early and late outcomes, were presented for the overall sample and retrospectively stratified by the AVRF-derived threshold (see Results section). Comparisons between categorical data were made using the χ 2 -test, while continuous data were compared using Mann-Whitney U or Student’s T-test for continuous data, depending on their distribution. Follow-up completeness was calculated using the Modified Clark’s Completeness Index C* . 11 , 12 Long-term outcomes were analysed using time-to-event methods. Overall survival rates were assessed using Kaplan-Meier estimates and compared using Cox proportional hazards models with the frailty parameter (centre) as a random-effects term. 13 The proportional hazards assumption for EuroSCORE II was evaluated using Schoenfeld residuals. Cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) were plotted to present absolute risks of reintervention and death. The method to derive the threshold that could define a high-volume centre was previously described in detail and validated by multiple studies. 6 In short, for early outcomes, the rate of the primary end-point was plotted on the y-axis and the annual institutional case load was plotted on the x-axis, after which a restricted cubic spline (RCS) model was applied, consisting of 3 knots (for model optimization). Then, for long-term outcomes, a hazard ratio (HR) was calculated per centre, using the adjusted survival of the overall sample as reference, excluding the centre of interest, per calculation (for one specific centre). The HR per centre is then plotted on the y-axis, with the centre’s corresponding annual case volume on the x-axis. Uncertainty margins (95% CIs) were recalculated to “variance” (squared SD). In the figures, smaller spheres indicate larger variance (and more uncertainty) and therefore less weight in the analyses. The potential non-linear association between annual case volume and the HR per centre was subsequently investigated using an RCS model. For model optimization, these analyses were performed for centres that contributed more than 30 cases per centre in total. Additionally, as a sensitivity analysis, the data of centres contributing 0-10, 10-20, and 20-30 cases to the registry were merged as if being one centre and subsequently entered into the model. In line with previous studies aimed at the determination of a case volume that can define a high-volume centre, 5–9 the threshold was determined by the “elbow of the curve.” 14 , 15 At this point on the curve, an increase in case volume no longer yields a significant improvement in the survival rate. 16 For the current analyses, we used R Statistics Version 3.6.0 (R foundation, Vienna, Austria), using the “survival,” “ggplot2,” “pathviewr” (for the elbow analysis), and “discfrail” (frailty Cox model) packages.
sections.missing data: Variables with missing data are indicated in the tables. Across all baseline characteristics used in the outcome analyses, missing data resulted in the exclusion of fewer than 5% of patients; therefore, complete-case analysis was performed. For survival analyses, patients with missing follow-up data for the end-point of interest were censored at their last known follow-up date.
sections.avrf survival: The primary long-term outcome of the study was the AVRF-survival. Cox proportional hazards analyses demonstrated a significant non-linear association between annual case-volume and AVRF-survival in centres that performed >30 cases in the registry ( P = .0023; Figure 1 ), with an elbow at 11 cases/year (95% CI, 10-12). Based on this analysis, the threshold defining a high-volume centre was determined and the cohort was stratified into patients undergoing VSARR in centres performing <12 or ≥12 cases/year. Their baseline characteristics can be appreciated in Tables 1 and 2 in retrospect.
sections.patient and procedural characteristics: Baseline patient characteristics are presented in Table 1 . Mean age was 51.0 (SD: 14.2) years; 85.6% were male. The LVEF prior to surgery was good (>50%) in 86.7% of patients. Table 2 shows the procedural characteristics. Valve morphology was predominantly tricuspid (62.3%), followed by bicuspid (36.2%). Only aortic cross-clamping time and concomitant aortic (hemi-)arch surgery showed a statistically significant difference.
sections.early outcomes and v-o association: Due to low early adverse event rates, only observational analyses were made. Early mortality occurred in 0.86% (23/2668) of patients, and early AV-related reintervention in 0.49% (13/2665). Thromboembolic events were reported in 1.64% of all patients (43/2663; stroke n = 25; TIA n = 12; peripheral embolism n = 6). Thirteen intraoperative conversions to valve replacement were performed; 9 in the <12 cases/year group and 4 in the ≥12 cases/year group ( Table 2 ; P = .174). Early recurrent AR grade ≥2 occurred in 2.3% (59/2541) of patients (grade 2: n = 57; grade 3: n = 2) and was significantly more frequent in centres performing <12 cases/year (48/1239 vs 11/1302; P < .001). Post-hoc analyses similarly showed higher early AV-related reintervention risks in lower-volume centres, 0.82% (11/1337; <12 cases/year) versus 0.15% (2/1318; ≥12 cases/year) ( P = .014). Early mortality (1.0%; 14/1344 versus 0.69%; 9/1311; P = .319) and thromboembolic events (1.49%; 20/1344 versus 1.59%; 21/1319; P = .875) did not differ significantly between lower- and higher-volume centres. No significant non-linear association between annual case volume and the early composite outcome was observed in the analysis of centres contributing >30 cases ( P = .8003; Figure 2 ).
sections.long-term survival and freedom from rein: Overall median follow-up was 3.7 years (IQR 0.9-6.7 years) with a follow-up duration of 11 960.68 patient years. Median follow-up was 2.47 years (IQR: 0.21-5.37) in <12 cases/year centres and 5.03 (IQR 1.82-8.23) in ≥12 cases/year centres. Follow-up completeness was 55.61% for the entire cohort. Kaplan-Meier analyses show the long-term survival across the cohort in Supplementary Material S2 ; the estimated overall survival of the entire cohort was 98.4% (95% CI, 97.8-99.0%), 95.8% (95% CI, 94.8-96.8%), and 87.1% (95% CI, 84.6-89.6%) at 1, 5, and 10 years, respectively. Figure 3 shows the CIFs of death and AV-reintervention. Linearized incidence rates of mortality and AV-related reoperation are reported in Table 3 .
sections.sensitivity analyses: Sensitivity analyses, including centres contributing fewer than 30 cases in total to the registry, demonstrated consistent results ( Supplementary Materials S3 and S4 ), and the identified volume thresholds were robust across various modelling strategies. The predictive performance of EuroSCORE II was evaluated for survival using Cox regression. EuroSCORE II was significantly associated with mortality (HR 1.19, 95% CI, 1.15-1.24, P < .001) and AVRF (HR 1.14, 95% CI, 1.09-1.18, P < .001), not with reintervention (HR 1.03, 95% CI, 0.95-1.11, P = .520). Additionally, the proportional hazards assumption for EuroSCORE II was not violated for both mortality ( P = .138) and reintervention ( P = .150). This supports the validity of the time-constant HRs applied in the primary Cox regression models.
sections.discussion: Valve-sparing aortic root replacement is a safe and effective procedure in contemporary practice, with low early complication rates and durable long-term outcomes. 17–21 This is particularly relevant given the relatively young age of our patient population and the long life expectancy after a successful procedure. The 2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for Valvular Heart Disease recognize the growing role of VSARR in appropriately selected patients. 22 This procedure is increasingly performed in dedicated centres, reflecting a possible shift from replacement to repair in aortic root surgery 17–21 Our analysis showed a significant non-linear V-O association for long-term AVRF-survival within the HVS AV Database, in which institutional annual volumes ranged from 3 to 25 procedures per year. While early outcomes were uniformly low, centres performing ≥12 VSARR procedures annually were associated with superior long-term outcomes. This suggests experience and institutional exposure contribute to success but should be interpreted in context. Our findings on exposure are consistent with earlier analyses in other surgical procedures where similar volume thresholds have been identified. 5–9 The registry reflects a historical cohort spanning over 25 years, during which annual VSARR volumes increased, particularly in the last decade. As a result, the association observed here is shaped by evolving surgical practice, patient selection, and perioperative management across time. Moreover, the registry includes exclusively David and Yacoub procedures; other valve-sparing strategies, such as isolated AV repair (AVP) or more complex AVP techniques involving extensive leaflet repair or double annuloplasty, were not included. Proficiency in David or Yacoub techniques does not automatically translate to expertise in AVP, and vice versa, and outcomes observed in our study cannot be generalized across all forms of valve-sparing surgery. Our findings must be viewed considering several important nuances. First, referral and acceptance practices may differ between centres. Highly experienced, high-volume institutions may treat patients with more complex pathology or borderline indications and may still achieve durable outcomes despite higher inherent procedural difficulty. Conversely, some centres may concentrate on less complex cases. These centre-specific patterns cannot currently be quantified in the registry, therefore the association should not be interpreted as a sole causal effect of volume. Current guidelines recommend that complex procedures such as VSARR be performed in Heart Valve Centres with high procedural volumes and excellent clinical outcomes. 22 Although no specific threshold is provided, they advocate for a network model in which complex interventions are performed in the upper quartile of centres by volume and performance. Our results suggest, within the limits of this dataset, that an annual case volume of ≥12 may be beneficial to valve-durability and patient longevity. This number should not be interpreted as a rigid cutoff, but rather as an opportunity for lower-volume centres to reflect on their current practice and consider strategies for structured growth. Centres aiming to build expertise in VSARR should first gain experience in AV and root surgery. They can then consider starting with less complex, elective VSARR cases, such as isolated aneurysms without significant valve pathology, and gradually increasing procedural exposure and complexity. Ensuring consistent exposure to the procedure is key to retaining improved patient outcomes. The trend towards valve preservation is reinforced by our findings. Valve-sparing aortic root replacement avoids prosthetic valve-related complications, maintains native valve haemodynamics, and offers excellent short- and long-term outcomes, especially in high-volume centres. VSARR offers a compelling alternative to valve replacement, particularly in younger patients where prosthetic valve durability and anticoagulation may be of concern.
sections.limitations: Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, as a retrospective registry analysis, selection bias and residual confounding remain possible, despite the adjustment for EuroSCORE II. Second, the registry spans over 25 years during which changes in techniques, patient selection, and perioperative care may influence comparability across centres. In addition, annual institutional volume was calculated as a mean across each centre’s period of participation in the registry. This static measure does not capture temporal changes in expertise or innovations in surgical and peri-/postoperative care, potentially biasing results towards centres with long-standing programs. Third, procedural complexity (eg, severity and morphology of aortic insufficiency or the number of leaflets treated) was not accounted for in our analysis. Although these factors may influence surgical difficulty and long-term outcomes, no standardized or validated method exists to reliably quantify procedural complexity. This limits our ability to determine whether the V-O association reflects true effects of procedural exposure or differences in patient populations. Fourth, surgeon-specific volumes were unavailable due to privacy restrictions, preventing assessment of the relative contributions of operator- versus institutional-level experience. Finally, modelling required the aggregation of low-contributing centres into surrogate categories. Although sensitivity analysis supported the findings, this may obscure heterogeneity between individual centres.
sections.conclusion: In this multicentre registry-based analysis, a significant association between institutional case volume and long-term AVRF survival following elective VSARR was observed. Based on our analyses, an institutional volume of 12 or more elective VSARRs annually is associated with long-term valve durability and survival. This high-volume threshold represents a benchmark for centres and surgeons already experienced in AV and/or root surgery, not a minimum for initiating VSARR, and should be interpreted within the registry’s limits. Further research incorporating procedural complexity, surgeon-level data, and contemporary populations is required to refine these benchmarks.
sections.supplementary material: Supplementary material is available at EJCTS online.
sections.conflicts of interest: None declared.
sections.funding: None declared.

title: Epigenetic programming by H3K23ac defines lineage fate of Meg3 + haematopoietic stem cells and drives immune ageing
abstract: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) produce all blood and immune cells throughout life, but ageing progressively impairs their function, generating excessive myeloid and megakaryocyte cells at the expense of lymphocytes. This lineage imbalance contributes to immune decline, chronic inflammation and increased disease susceptibility in the elderly, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we show that a specific Meg3 + HSC subset (CD150 hi Sca1 hi CD24 hi CD201 + CD9 + CD63 + long-term HSCs) expands dramatically during ageing and drives this lineage skewing. Using multi-omics profiling, we found that inflammatory signals increase H3K23ac levels in aged Meg3 + HSCs, enhancing PU.1 activity through recruitment of the reader protein TRIM24. This epigenetic mechanism promotes excessive megakaryocyte and myeloid production. Of note, disrupting H3K23ac–TRIM24 interaction in aged HSCs restored balanced lineage output and reduced inflammatory signals. Our findings reveal a key mechanism linking inflammation to HSC ageing and identify potential therapeutic targets for reversing ageing-related immune decline.

sections.main: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) sustain lifelong blood and immune cell production, but ageing leads to the accumulation of functionally impaired HSCs with skewed lineage output, characterized by increased myeloid and megakaryocyte (MK)/platelet production and reduced lymphoid potential 1 – 4 . Accordingly, these ageing-related changes in HSCs drive declining immune function, contributing to increased pathogen susceptibility, poor vaccine responses, chronic inflammation and elevated risk of cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration and cancer in the elderly 5 – 8 . Nevertheless, despite recognized drivers of ageing such as DNA damage 9 , epigenetic modifications 10 , shifts in cell polarity 11 and disruptions in metabolic/proteostasis processes 12 , 13 , which collectively impact HSC lineage fate decisions, the precise mechanisms governing HSC fate during ageing remain inadequately understood. HSCs are functionally heterogeneous under steady-state and reconstitution conditions, with distinct lineage-biased subsets such as MK/platelet-biased HSCs 14 . An alternative model posits that such lineage bias reflects uni- or oligopotent self-renewing progenitors within the phenotypic HSC compartment 15 . Recent single-cell sequencing of human and murine haematopoietic progenitors has uncovered cellular and molecular diversity underlying haematological diseases 4 , 16 – 19 , yet unravelling the global mechanisms of HSC lineage decisions remains challenging and requires integrating single-cell transcriptomic, epigenomic and functional approaches across steady-state and ageing contexts. In this study, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile two defined subsets within CD150 hi myeloid-biased HSCs (SH-HSCs and SL-HSCs) alongside CD150 lo lymphoid-biased HSCs 1 , 20 , 21 , capturing a spectrum of lineage specification and commitment states. We mapped haematopoietic differentiation trajectories and identified Meg3 + HSCs as the developmental apex. These cells expanded markedly starting in middle age, accompanied by dynamic transcriptional changes linked to histone modification and MK/myeloid differentiation. Transplantation assays revealed an altered ability to replenish myeloid, lymphocytes and MKs, and declined self-renewal capacity in middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs. Multi-omics profiling of Meg3 + HSCs unveiled increased H3K23ac level in middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs, mediated by a pioneer transcription factor p65/RELA-KAT6A activation in response to inflammatory signals. H3K23ac-associated genes were enriched in MK/platelets and myeloid cell differentiation pathways, highlighting the critical role of H3K23ac in modulating HSC fate decision during ageing. Mechanistically, H3K23ac recruited TRIM24 to enhance the transcriptional activity of PU.1. Interfering the binding of TRIM24 and H3K23ac in aged HSCs rescued MK/platelets and myeloid lineage skewing and reduced senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Collectively, our study delineates the dynamic changes associated with ageing in HSCs, and the underlining mechanisms driving lineage skewing and immune ageing.
sections.cd150 hi and cd150 lo lt-hscs encompass: A previous study delineated a shift of proportion between CD150 hi myeloid-biased and CD150 lo lymphoid-biased HSCs during ageing 22 . We refined the characterization of lineage-biased HSC subsets by further subdividing CD150 hi myeloid-biased long-term (LT)-HSCs based on Sca1 and CD24 expression into CD150 hi Sca1 hi CD24 hi (SH-HSCs) and CD150 hi Sca1 lo CD24 lo (SL-HSCs), alongside CD150 lo lymphoid-biased HSCs (CL-HSCs) (Extended Data Fig. 1a ). In young mice, SH-HSCs and SL-HSCs were present at similar numbers. With ageing both subsets increased in proportion and absolute number in bone marrow, whereas CL-HSCs decreased proportionally but remained stable in absolute number (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c ). Transplantation into lethally irradiated recipients revealed distinct reconstitution capacities. SH-HSCs contributed ~40% donor chimerism at 8 weeks that remained stable over 20 weeks, whereas CL-HSCs and SL-HSCs achieved only ~20% and ~10%, respectively. SH-HSCs generated a myeloid-biased output, whereas SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs produced 60–70% lymphocytes, indicating balanced or lymphoid-biased fates (Extended Data Fig. 1d–f ). Fig. 1 Single-cell transcriptome map of CD150 hi Sca1 hi CD24 hi LT-HSCs (SH - HSCs), CD150 hi Sca1 lo CD24 lo LT-HSCs (SL-HSCs) and CD150 lo LT-HSCs (CL-HSCs). a , b , Flow cytometry analyses of the CD150 hi Sca1 hi CD24 hi LT-HSCs (SH-HSCs), CD150 hi Sca1 lo CD24 lo LT-HSCs (SL-HSCs) and CD150 lo LT-HSCs (CL-HSCs) in LT-HSCs, of young, middle-aged and aged mice, respectively. Representative t -distributed stochastic neighbour embedding ( t -SNE) plots show the concatenated flow cytometry data ( a ). Frequencies and absolute numbers of SH-HSCs, SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs in LT-HSCs ( b ). Statistical significance was calculated across different HSC subsets of the same age and the same HSC subset across different age groups. Black P values indicate comparisons within the same HSC subset across ages; turquoise, yellow, and tangerine P values denote comparisons among different HSC subsets in young, middle-aged and aged mice, respectively. Young, n = 16 mice; middle-aged, n = 16 mice; aged, n = 7 mice. Data are from five biological independent experiments. c , t -SNE visualization of the HSC subsets. Top: coloured by manual annotation of cell identity. Bottom: coloured by sample ID (SH-HSCs, SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs). n = 2,790 cells. d , Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualizations show the integration result of SH-HSCs, SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs, iHSCs (from GSE116530 ) and Vwf + HSCs (from GSE188118 ). Source data To delineate the transcriptional landscape of these subsets, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of SH-HSCs, SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs from young mice. Integration of SH-HSCs, SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs revealed six distinct clusters (Fig. 1c ), highlighting the transcriptional heterogeneity within immunophenotypically defined HSC subsets 23 . To compare these HSC subsets with previously defined HSCs, we integrated our scRNA-seq data with immunophenotyped HSCs (iHSCs) and Vwf + HSC data generated using SMARTseq2 (refs. 24 , 25 ) (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1g ). The combined HSCs still segregated into six clusters as defined above, with full integration of three datasets (Fig. 1e ). SH-HSCs mainly consisted of C0 and C4. C1 mainly arose from SL-HSCs. C2 was primarily derived from SL-HSCs and CL-HSCs, whereas C3 was almost exclusively from the CL-HSC fraction (Fig. 1c,e ). In comparison, HSC-LT (CD34 − CD135 − LSK) 26 comprised only about 30% C0, whereas ESLAMSK (CD201 + CD150 + CD48 − CD45 + Sca1 + cKit + ) 27 and fraction I (CD150 + CD41 − CD34 − LSK) 15 had over 75% C0. And either balanced or biased Vwf + HSCs were a mixture of HSC subsets defined above (Fig. 1e ). In summary, various immunophenotypically defined HSCs exhibited heterogeneity and could be further classified into the sub-clusters defined in this study. We next annotated the clusters based on the most highly expressed marker genes. For instance, C0 shows high expression of genes such as Meg3 , Procr , Hes1 and Hlf . Among these, Meg3, a tumour-suppressive long non-coding RNA, is dispensable for HSC maintenance, but highly and specifically expressed in HSCs 28 . Notably, Meg3 was expressed in 50% of C0 and at a significantly higher level (81-fold) compared with other clusters. In contrast, Hlf and Hes1 were coexpressed in C1(Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1 ). Accordingly, Meg3 was selected as the representative marker for C0, and the remaining clusters were annotated using the same approach (Fig. 1f ). Meg3 + HSCs, Pf4 + HSCs and Clec4d + HSCs predominantly remained in G0/G1 phase, whereas the rest were in a relatively activated phase (Fig. 1g ). Consistently, most SL-HSCs were in quiescent phase, whereas CL-HSCs exhibited the highest proportion of proliferative HSCs and SH-HSCs were in between (Extended Data Fig. 1h ). Meg3 + HSCs and Pf4 + HSCs exhibited high expression of genes essential for maintaining HSC stemness, such as Hlf 29 , 30 , Meis1 (ref. 31 ) and Hes1 (ref. 32 ). Surface marker genes Procr (encoding CD201) and Cd74 were highly expressed in Meg3 + HSCs, while Ifitm1 and Cd63 were enriched in both Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs (Fig. 1f ). Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) of transcriptome and regulons of key transcriptional factors both revealed enrichment of Gene Ontology (GO) terms related to ‘cell fate determination’, ‘T cell differentiation’ and ‘B cell differentiation’ in Meg3 + HSCs (Fig. 1h , Extended Data Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 1 ), indicating features of stemness and multipotential differentiation. Notably, Pf4 + HSCs showed marked upregulation genes driving MK and platelet development, including Pbx1 (ref. 33 ), Pf4 (refs. 34 , 35 ), Plek 36 , Fli1 (ref. 37 ), Stat4 (ref. 38 ) and Gata2 (ref. 39 ) (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2a ). Correspondingly, GO terms such as ‘megakaryocyte differentiation’ were enriched in Pf4 + HSCs (Fig. 1h , Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 1 ). Clec4d + HSCs exhibited pathways related to ‘T cell differentiation’, and displayed high activity of transcriptional factors predicted to promote early T cell differentiation, including Egr1 (ref. 40 ), Sox4 (ref. 41 ), Fos 42 , Zmiz1 (ref. 43 ) and Myb 44 , 45 (Fig. 1f,h , Extended Data Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 1 ). Integrative analysis of three HSC subsets with downstream lymphoid progenitors that recently been reported to give rise to T lineages 46 – 48 revealed a direct developmental trajectory from Clec4d + HSCs to thymus-seeding progenitors (TSPs) 46 , 48 . Consistently, genes involved in thymus seeding ( Ccr7 and Ccr9 ) 49 and early T cell development ( Sox4 (ref. 50 ), Fos 51 and Lyl1 (ref. 52 )) were upregulated along the putative path (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e ), supporting a potential differentiation trajectory from Clec4d + HSCs to T lineages. Rhd + Mt2 lo and Rhd + Mt2 h HSCs shared common transcriptional factor and surface marker features, including Gata1 , a critical erythroid development transcriptional factor 53 and Rhd , a gene encoding Rh blood type D antigen 54 (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2a ). Pebp1 hi HSCs shared common features with Clec4d + HSCs, such as ‘regulatory T cell differentiation’ and ‘CD8 + αβT cell differentiation’ (Fig. 1h and Supplementary Table 1 ). Despite enrichment in GO terms regarding erythrocyte differentiation, genes regulated erythroid development, such as Gata1 (ref. 53 ), Rhd 55 and E2f4 (ref. 56 ), were reduced in Pebp1 hi HSCs, reflecting decreased potential for erythroid differentiation (Fig. 1f ).
sections.meg3 + hsc sits at the apex of the hsc d: To assess lineage bias among these HSC subsets, we employed the STEMNET algorithm 57 (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g ). STEMNET positioned the Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs subsets along the B lineage, T lineage and MK/platelet branches, indicating their propensity to give rise to lymphocytes and MK/platelets. Pf4 + HSCs exhibited higher MK/platelet lineage potential (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g ), consistent with the upregulation of Plek , Pf4 and Pbx1 (Fig. 1f ). Conversely, Clec4d + HSCs showed the highest potential towards CD8 + T lymphocytes, whereas their potential to generate MK/platelets lineage decreased compared with Pf4 + HSCs (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g ). Rhd + Mt2 lo , Rhd + Mt2 hi and Pebp1 hi HSCs were predicted to primarily contribute to the erythroid lineage. Notably, HSC sub-clusters exhibited a lower myeloid potential than other cell types (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g ), aligning with previous findings that myeloid-biased MPPs serve as a potent source of myeloid amplification 58 . Overall, quiescent LT-HSC subsets, including Meg3 + , Pf4 + and Clec4d + HSC, maintained a higher differentiation potential of lymphocytes and MK/platelets, whereas the potential to develop the erythroid lineage increased in Rhd -expressing HSCs. To infer developmental trajectories of HSC subsets, we employed various computational approaches, including Monocle3 (Fig. 1i ), force-directed graph (FDG), diffusion map and partition-based approximate graph abstraction (PAGA) (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b ). All three models collectively indicated Meg3 + HSC as the trajectory origin (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b ). Meg3 + HSCs connected directly to Pf4 + HSCs, followed by Clec4d + and Rhd + Mt2 lo HSCs (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b ), with concurrent downregulation of genes related to stemness, including Hes1 (ref. 32 ), Hlf 29 , 30 , Meis1 (ref. 59 ), Erg 60 and Gata2 (ref. 61 ) (Extended Data Fig. 3c ). Monocle3 and FDG visualization also identified two branches from Rhd + Mt2 lo HSCs, leading to erythroid-bias differentiation ( Rhd + Mt2 hi HSC, fate 1) or increased T-lineage potential ( Pebp1 hi HSCs, fate 2; Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 3a ). Genes regulating erythrocyte differentiation, erythroid components and mitochondria function, such as Gata1 (ref. 53 ), E2f4 (ref. 56 ), Hmbs 62 , Rhd 63 and Mcp1 (ref. 64 ), upregulated along the fate 1, whereas genes promoting T cell development 65 – 68 , inhibiting erythrocyte differentiation 69 or regulating mitochondria function 70 , 71 , such as Timm13 , Tcf12 , Mrpl12, Tcf3 and Pebp1 , increased along the fate 2 (Extended Data Fig. 3c ). Collectively, these data provide a comprehensive view of putative haematopoietic differentiation trajectories. To investigate HSC subset microenvironments, we classified bone-marrow niche cells and analysed interactions between niche clusters and HSC subsets (Extended Data Fig. 3d–g ) 72 , 73 . This revealed distinct interactions between each HSC subset with niches, including endosteal (osteoprogenitors, osteolineage cells and chondrocytes), arteriolar (arterial/arteriolar epithelial cells (ECs) and pericytes) and sinusoidal (sinusoidal ECs and pericytes) 74 niches. Arteriolar/endosteal niches support lymphoid differentiation, whereas the sinusoidal niche favours myeloid output 75 – 78 . Meg3 + HSCs and Pf4 + HSCs interact with arterial/arteriolar ECs via Esam - Esam and Jam2 - Jam3 signalling to support self-renewal 79 , 80 , whereas signals from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), sinusoidal ECs and pericytes to Meg3 + HSCs through Angpt1 - Tek and Jag1 - Notch1 may regulate quiescence and repopulation 81 , 82 . In comparison, Clec4d + HSCs interact with sinusoidal ECs, pericytes and periosteal cells via Icam1-Itgal signalling (Extended Data Fig. 3e–g and Supplementary Table 1 ), suggesting a distinct niche preference.

sections.characterization of the self-renewal cap: To evaluate lineage differentiation potential, we transplanted sorted Meg3 + , Pf4 + and Clec4d + HSCs (from dTomato + CD45.2 + mice) into lethally irradiated recipients (dTomato⁻CD45.2 + ), with equal numbers of LT-HSCs as controls (Extended Data Fig. 5a ). Due to partial loss of dTomato fluorescence in donor-derived T and myeloid cells (Supplementary Fig. 2 ), we used CD45.2 to identify T cells, B cells and myeloid cells. Over 40 weeks, Meg3 + HSCs showed higher reconstitution than LT-HSCs, indicating superior self-renewal and stemness, whereas Pf4 + HSCs showed lower reconstitution and Clec4d + HSCs the lowest (Extended Data Fig. 5b ). At 20 weeks, all subsets generated platelets, erythrocytes, myeloid cells, B/T lymphocytes and dendritic cells (Extended Data Fig. 5c ). Pf4 + and Meg3 + HSCs exhibited high platelet reconstitution (12.7% versus 10.8%), while Clec4d + HSCs showed minimal MK/platelet but increased erythroid output. Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs produced balanced lineages (~30% T, ~50% B and 10–20% myeloid), whereas Clec4d + HSCs predominantly gave rise to T cells with reduced B cells. By 40 weeks, Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs were skewed towards myeloid cells with fewer lymphocytes and dendritic cells, whereas Clec4d + HSCs increased platelet output (Extended Data Fig. 5c ). End-point analysis confirmed that Meg3 + HSCs reconstituted most robustly across bone marrow, spleen and lymph nodes. Clec4d + HSCs preferentially reconstituted T cells in spleen and nodes. In primary recipients, Meg3 + HSCs regenerated all HSC subsets including themselves, Pf4 + HSCs reconstituted all except Meg3 + HSCs, and Clec4d + HSCs mainly gave rise to Rhd + Mt2 hi , Rhd + Mt2 lo and Pebp1 hi HSCs, supporting the predicted trajectories (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g ). To further assess self-renewal capacity, we performed secondary transplantation 20 weeks after primary transplantation (Extended Data Fig. 5h–m ). Meg3 + HSCs maintained the highest reconstitution and multilineage potential, albeit with less pronounced myeloid/MK skewing, and self-renewed while generating the other five subsets. In contrast, Pf4 + and Clec4d + HSCs had drastically reduced reconstitution, indicating limited self-renewal. Notably, Meg3 + HSCs achieved higher chimerism and LT-HSC proportions in secondary recipients, possibly due to the young recipient niche (2-month-old) 94 (Extended Data Fig. 5d,g,j,m and Supplementary Fig. 3 ).
sections.middle-aged meg3 + hscs exhibit altered: As Meg3 + HSCs expanded during ageing and exhibited marked transcriptional changes, we transplanted either young or middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs (CD45.1 + CD45.2 + dTomato + ) into age-matched recipients (CD45.2 + ) to assess their stemness and lineage potential (Fig. 3e–n ). Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated reduced reconstitution capacity of middle-aged cells in both peripheral blood and lymphoid organs, suggesting compromised self-renewal capacity. Furthermore, compared with young Meg3 + HSCs, middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs exhibited increased differentiation into CD11b + myeloid cells along with decreased proportions of CD3 + and CD19 + lymphoid cells in peripheral blood and lymphoid organs. Notably, in the thymus, T cells derived from middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs were more frequently arrested at the CD4 − CD8 − stage (Fig. 3f–j ). Additionally, a higher proportion of CD41 + MKs were found in bone marrow reconstituted with middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs. MKs of different ploidy levels perform distinct functions: low-ploidy (2N) immune-modulating MKs, intermediate-ploidy (4N-8N) niche-supporting MKs, and high-ploidy (16N-32N) platelet-producing MKs 95 . Middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs preferentially gave rise to 2N immune-modulating and 16N-32N platelet-producing MKs, whereas young Meg3 + HSCs predominantly generated 4N-8N niche-supporting MKs (Fig. 3k ). Reconciled with that, middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs showed significantly enhanced potential to generate MK-biased Pf4 + HSCs during differentiation, which aligns well with the MK analysis results (Fig. 3l–n ). These findings collectively demonstrate that Meg3 + HSCs exhibit increased myeloid/megakaryocytic differentiation potential during ageing, consistent with our previous bioinformatics analysis (Fig. 2f,h ).

Ageing-related hyperacetylated proteins were mainly enriched in myeloid cell differentiation, cellular responses to lipid and DNA repair, in both middle-aged and aged Meg3 + HSCs, whereas platelet activation-associated proteins showed increased acetylation in middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs (Extended Data Fig. 6g–l and Supplementary Table 4 ), suggesting that altered acetylation contributes to lineage skewing.
sections.enrichment of h3k23ac on genes associate: ssGSEA indicated altered histone acetylation in middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs (Fig. 2f and Supplementary Table 2 ). Acetylome profiling further revealed increase H3K18/K23ac in both middle-aged and aged Meg3 + HSCs (Fig. 4c ), in contrast to our previous finding that H3K23ac, but not H3K18ac, increased in aged HSCs 96 . Corroborating this, intracellular flow cytometry confirmed elevated H3K23ac without a concurrent increase in H3K18ac in aged Meg3 + HSCs (Extended Data Fig. 7a ). We next employed confocal microscopy, confirming a significant increase in H3K23ac during HSC ageing (Fig. 4d,e and Extended Data Fig. 7b,c ). In contrast, H4K16ac, a histone mark linked to HSC quiescence and activation 99 , exhibited an opposite trend (Fig. 4d,f ). Notably, H3K23ac increased more prominently in aged Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs than in Clec4d + HSCs, possibly owing to varying expression of Kat6a and Hdac6 across these subsets (Extended Data Fig. 7d–f ). Elevated H3K23ac was also detected in middle-aged MPP3 cells and various progenitor populations, including common myeloid progenitors (CMPs), granulocyte–monocyte progenitors (GMPs), MK progenitors (MKPs) and common lymphoid progenitors(CLPs) (Extended Data Fig. 7g,h ). To illustrate genes directly regulated by H3K23ac, we performed CUT&Tag in young, middle-aged and aged Meg3 + HSCs (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Table 5 ). H3K23ac peak enrichment significantly increased in middle-aged and aged Meg3 + HSCs (Fig. 4h ). Overlapping genes with H3K23ac-enriched transcription start site (TSS) regions (±3 kb) with transcriptome data from Meg3 + HSCs showed that H3K23ac-associated genes in middle-aged and aged Meg3 + HSCs were mainly involved in MK/platelet and myeloid differentiation. Examples of such genes include Gp5 (ref. 100 ), Hoxa7 (ref. 101 ), Trib1 (ref. 102 ), Hif1a 103 , Myc 104 and Fes 105 . In contrast, H3K23ac-enriched genes in young HSCs were mainly linked to the chromatin three-dimensional (3D) structure and interferon (IFN) signalling (Fig. 4i,j , Extended Data Fig. 7i and Supplementary Table 5 ). H3K23ac in middle-aged Meg3 + and Pf4 + HSCs also enriched in TFs including Msi2 (ref. 106 ), Gata2 (ref. 107 ), Runx1 (ref. 108 ), Runx2 (ref. 109 ), Hoxa7 (ref. 110 ) and Tcf3 (ref. 111 ), which formed a transcriptional regulatory hub to activate pathways related to cell cycle progression and proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 7j,k and Supplementary Table 5 ). To further investigate the overlap between H3K23ac peaks and open chromatin regions (OCRs), we conducted a joint analysis of published ATAC-seq data of young and middle-aged HSCs 84 , 112 with H3K23ac CUT&Tag data. Colocalization of H3K23ac and OCRs revealed notable differences in chromatin accessibility between the two age groups (Fig. 4k ), and genes with H3K23ac-enriched OCRs in middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs were strongly associated with platelet activation and myeloid cell differentiation pathways (Fig. 4l and Supplementary Table 5 ). To confirm the role of H3K23ac in HSC lineage decision, we overexpressed the gain-of-function mutant H3K23Q (mimicking constitutive acetylation), the loss-of-function mutant H3K23R or wild-type (WT) H3K23 in young HSCs (Extended Data Fig. 8a ). Compared with H3K23R, H3K23Q significantly promoted CD41 + MK/platelet and myeloid differentiation at the expense of B220 + lymphocytes, a finding further supported by co-transfer experiments, which also revealed reduced stemness in H3K23Q-overexpressing HSCs (Extended Data Fig. 8b–g ). CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq analysis in WT or H3K23Q-overexpressing cells revealed increased overlap between H3K23Q peaks and OCRs at MK- and myeloid-related genes and pathways, including CEBPA 113 , STAT3 (refs. 114 , 115 ), CLEC5A 116 , VAV 1 (ref. 117 ) and TSPAN32 (ref. 118 ), with corresponding enrichment of PU.1, ELF4 and SPIB motifs in these overlapping promoter regions (Extended Data Fig. 8h–l and Supplementary Table 6 ). Collectively, our results indicate an essential role for H3K23ac in the lineage decision of aged Meg3 + HSCs.

sections.disrupting trim24-h3k23ac binding decrea: Next, we tested whether modulating PU.1 could reverse MK and myeloid lineage skewing. Knocking down PU.1 in middle-aged HSCs significantly reduced MK/platelet frequency and absolute numbers. It also decreased the absolute numbers of B and myeloid cells without altering their relative proportions, due to markedly decreased total differentiated cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a–h ), indicating a broader role for PU.1 in haematopoietic differentiation. Consistent with this, PU.1 knockdown profoundly altered histone acetylation profiles (Extended Data Fig. 10i ). Thus, directly targeting PU.1 failed to correct lineage skewing. TRIM24 binds H3K23ac via its bromodomain, and IACS-9571 specifically disrupts this interaction 135 , 136 . We therefore tested whether blocking the TRIM24–H3K23ac interface could modulate lineage output in aged HSCs. IACS-9571 treatment dose-dependently reduced MK/platelet and myeloid output, while promoting B cell differentiation in aged HSCs (Fig. 7a–c ). sections.disrupting the h3k23ac\u2013trim24 inter: We next sought to test whether disrupting H3K23ac–TRIM24 interaction in vivo produced similar effects. Due to the short half-life of IACS-9571, we turned to a genetic approach. sections.discussion: In this study, we delineated the transcriptional landscape of age-associated lineage specification and commitment within the HSC compartment, uncovering a spectrum of cell states among LT-HSCs. We identified Meg3 + HSCs as the apex of the HSC hierarchy, capable of replenishing all haematopoietic lineages with the highest reconstitution capacity. During ageing, Meg3 + HSCs expanded markedly and exhibited altered transcription factors, metabolism and histone modifications, giving rise to MK- and myeloid-biased HSCs. H3K23ac increased significantly during early ageing, and its upregulation was closely associated with MK/platelet and myeloid skewing in Meg3 + HSCs, driven by inflammatory signals via the p65/RELA–KAT6A axis. Mechanistically, H3K23ac recruits TRIM24 to enhance PU.1 transcriptional activity, and disrupting this interaction suppressed PU.1 function and rescued MK/myeloid skewing while reducing SASP in aged HSCs. Together, our findings provide insights into the mechanisms underlying HSC development, ageing and lineage fate decisions. Single-cell studies have revealed extensive heterogeneity across haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, including a continuum of core progenitor states where pre-myeloid and pre-lymphoid fates coexist, whereas erythroid and megakaryocytic programmes remain more distinct 145 , 146 . However, whether early fate decision within LT-HSCs follows similar rule has remained unclear. Here, we identified incipient MK/platelet potential in the Pf4 + subset, consistent with recent reports of multipotent but MK/platelet-biased HSCs in humans and mice 4 , 14 , 147 . Accordingly, Pf4 + and Meg3 + HSCs exhibited MK/platelet bias while maintaining multipotency, and Meg3 + HSCs remained heterogeneous in single-cell assays, yielding restricted, dual and multipotent outputs 147 (Extended Data Fig. 10u ). Both subsets generated MK/platelets, potentially with different kinetics or functional outputs 25 , 148 , or provide a shortcut path to generate platelets upon ageing. Consistent with this, middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs generated significantly more Pf4 + HSCs and mature MKs. Notably, although CD48 − MKPs, which directly generate MK/platelets from HSCs 85 , 148 , 149 , increased with age in steady-state mice, middle-aged Meg3 + HSCs generated fewer CD48 − MKPs after transplantation than young counterparts (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 10v,w ), possibly reflecting accelerated downstream differentiation into MKs. Previous studies have attributed age-related myeloid and MK/platelet skewing primarily to the expansion of lineage-biased HSC subsets 1 , 21 , 150 , 151 . Here, we show that altered lineage fate decisions originate at the haematopoietic apex, with significant expansion and epigenetic remodelling in Meg3 + HSCs. Although epigenetic changes, such as H3K56ac and H4K16ac, critically influence HSC ageing 10 , 152 – 154 , the histone acetylation landscape in aged HSCs has remained incompletely understood. We characterized this landscape in Meg3 + HSCs and identified increased H3K23ac, a mark elevated in aged human haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) 155 and associated with several cancers 122 , 156 , but whose function in HSCs was unknown. Notably, we established a direct link between proinflammatory signals (IL-1α, LPS, poly(I:C)) and H3K23ac induction via NF-κB signalling, providing evidence that inflammatory cues during ageing imprint the HSC epigenome and reshape lineage output. p65/RELA functions as a pioneer transcription factor (TF) in determining H3K23ac specificity by recruiting KAT6A. In contrast, PU.1 expression does not determine H3K23ac. Although PU.1 has been reported to drive myeloid skewing in aged HSPCs 157 – 159 , the mechanism of its target selection remains unclear. Our findings support a model in which PU.1 is recruited to the open chromatin sites marked with elevated H3K23ac, contributing to lineage fate decisions in HSCs. These findings reconciled with previous evidence that chromatin context constrains PU.1 binding 160 . In addition, unlike the transit activation of p65/RELA, PU.1 exhibited consistent upregulation and nucleus entre in middle-aged HSCs. Therefore, we collectively unveiled a critical mechanism by which proinflammatory sustained H3K23ac to regulate HSC fate decision by navigating PU.1. Notably, KAT6A also mediates H3K23 propionylation (H3K23pr) via the BRPF1–KAT6 complex 161 . Given that distinct histone acylations may cooperate in transcriptional regulation 162 , it is possible that H3K23 acetylation and propionylation act together during HSC ageing to regulate lineage-associated genes, warrants further investigation. Aged HSCs directly contribute to senescent immune remodelling and inflammaging through skewed lineage differentiation 163 – 168 . Recent studies suggest that depleting myeloid-biased HSCs may rejuvenate aged immunity and alleviate inflammaging 22 . Our findings extend this concept by showing that interfering with H3K23ac/TRIM24/PU.1 activity in aged HSCs can rebalance lineage differentiation and reduce SASP. We deliberately avoided directly targeting KAT6A, given its additional activity on H3K9, H3K14 and H3K27 (ref. 169 ), and instead used IACS-9571 or a TRIM24 bromodomain mutant to specifically disrupt the H3K23ac–TRIM24 interaction. This approach more precisely interrogates the H3K23ac-associated pathway and may hold therapeutic potential for alleviating senescent immune remodelling and inflammaging.
