title: Management of endotracheal tube dislodgement during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery: a multicenter cross-sectional survey study
abstract: Objective To investigate the awareness, clinical management practices, and training needs of otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists regarding endotracheal tube dislodgement (ETTD) during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery. Methods A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists from multiple hospitals in China through the WeChat “Questionnaire Star” platform. Results A total of 321 valid questionnaires were collected (220 from the Otolaryngology Department and 101 from the Anesthesiology Department). A total of 61.1% of clinicians reported prior exposure to ETTD. More years of clinical practice were associated with higher self-reported awareness and greater reported numbers of ETTD cases. Educational background significantly influenced otolaryngologists’ reported awareness and anesthesiologists’ self-reported number of ETTD cases. Significant interdisciplinary differences were observed in the definition of high-risk populations, perceived main causes, and methods for detecting ETTD. Emergency reintubation was predominantly performed by anesthesiologists. In a small proportion of cases, ETTD led to complications, ICU admission, or death and triggered medical disputes. A total of 95.6% of the participants thought training on ETTD-related knowledge was necessary. Conclusions A high proportion of clinicians in both specialties reported prior exposure to ETTD during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery. Significant differences in the understanding and management of ETTD between otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists were observed. Although such discrepancies correlated with differences in the years of clinical practice and educational background, a causal relationship could not be established. Interdisciplinary collaboration and standardized training regarding ETTD must be strengthened to improve perioperative safety. sections.introduction: Endotracheal tube dislodgement (ETTD) is a life-threatening emergency complication during the perioperative period [ 1 ]. It is the third most common adverse event for patient safety in Taiwan, China [ 2 ]. Studies have reported that 20% of children who experience unplanned extubation, including accidental removal of anesthesia intubation or ETTD, develop significant cardiovascular events requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation or vasoactive medication administration [ 3 , 4 ]. These events also lead to prolonged ICU stays and total hospital stays, along with a corresponding increase in medical costs [ 5 – 7 ]. Transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgeries carry a high ETTD risk because of limited surgical access, the frequent intraoperative manipulation of instruments such as suspension laryngoscopes, and the need for repeated adjustment of the patient’s head position [ 8 ]. Once ETTD occurs, it can rapidly result in hypoxemia, hypercapnia, airway injury, and even cardiac arrest and death [ 9 ]. ETTD poses serious risks; however, systematic research on its management in transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery remains scarce [ 10 ], and clinical practice relies heavily on individual experience, with no standardized protocols. Moreover, due to differences in professional perspectives, otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists hold divergent perceptions regarding the risk factors and management strategies for ETTD, which may compromise the efficiency of multidisciplinary teamwork [ 11 ]. Therefore, this study aims to reveal the awareness, identification, management, and training needs regarding ETTD among otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists through a multicenter cross-sectional survey; explore the roots of interdisciplinary differences in the perception of ETTD; and provide a basis for optimizing the management of perioperative safety.
sections.study design and participants: This multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted from August 1 to September 30, 2025. The questionnaires were distributed to otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists performing or administering anesthesia for transoral oropharyngeal surgeries across China via national academic conferences, validated professional WeChat groups, and hospital research departments. This study was conducted and reported in strict accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement for cross-sectional studies.
sections.survey instrument: Electronic questionnaires were distributed via the “Wenjuanxing” platform on WeChat, which consists of two versions for the Departments of Otolarology and Anesthesiology. The questionnaire was accompanied by a brief introduction to the purpose of this study, voluntary nature, and confidentiality. The questionnaire mainly consisted of the following three parts (Supplementary material): Basic information (8 items), including age, sex, education, years of clinical practice, professional title, institution type, teaching hospital affiliation, and hospital administrative grade; ETTD management (17 items), including awareness, case exposure, risk assessment, detection methods, emergency response, and complications; Training needs (3 items), including willingness to participate in ETTD training and reasons for nonattendance.
sections.analysis of the content validity of the: The preliminary questionnaire was compiled based on the relevant international literature and expert consensus [ 12 ]. Prior to its official distribution, the questionnaire was reviewed, revised and polished by 5–8 senior experts in the Departments of Anesthesiology and Otolaryngology to ensure satisfactory content validity.
sections.statistical methods: The data were analysed using SPSS 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables are reported as the means ± SDs or medians (IQRs) based on the normality of the distribution. Group comparisons were performed using t tests, one-way ANOVA, or nonparametric equivalent tests (Mann–Whitney U test and Kruskal–Wallis H test), as appropriate. Enumeration data are presented as n (%), with the chi-square (χ²) test used for between-group comparisons. Multivariate ordinal logistic regression analyses were performed to adjust for the potential confounding factors of years of clinical practice and educational background and to examine their independent effects on the level of ETTD awareness and the number of self-reported ETTD cases. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
sections.basic information of the participants: A total of 321 valid questionnaires were included after responses with logical inconsistencies (e.g., age < years of clinical practice), implausible title–experience mismatches, or a completion time < 3 min were excluded. The final sample included 220 otolaryngologists (68.5%) and 101 anesthesiologists (31.5%). No significant intergroup differences were observed in age, sex, professional title, institution type, teaching hospital status, or hospital grade. However, otolaryngologists had higher educational attainment (more master’s/doctoral degrees; χ² = 13.52, p < 0.001), while anesthesiologists had more clinical experience (Z = − 2.308, p = 0.021) (Table 1 ). sections.differences in the understanding and ris: Anesthesiologists reported significantly greater ETTD awareness than otolaryngologists ( χ² = 28.93, p < 0.001). Both groups agreed that suspension laryngoscope-based oropharyngolaryngeal surgery was associated with the highest ETTD risk ( χ² = 12.36, p = 0.006) and that ETTD most commonly occurred during the removal of the laryngoscope or mouth gag ( χ² = 6.28, p = 0.046); however, 8.9% of anesthesiologists could not specify the highest-risk surgical type. A significant discrepancy in defining the age group most susceptible to ETTD was observed. Otolaryngologists regarded preschool children aged 4–6 years as the most vulnerable to ETTD, whereas anesthesiologists identified infants and toddlers aged 0–3 years as the high-risk group ( χ² = 58.72, p < 0.001). Otolaryngologists attributed intraoperative ETTD primarily to inadequate tube fixation, whereas anesthesiologists attributed it to an improper surgical technique ( χ² = 32.15, p < 0.001). Additionally, 61.4% of anesthesiologists named the Otolaryngology Department as the clinical setting with the greatest ETTD risk—reinforcing transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery as a key risk factor (Table 2 ). sections.self-reported cases, identification, man: A total of 61.1% of participants reported at least one prior exposure to an ETTD event; anesthesiologists had significantly greater exposure than otolaryngologists ( χ² = 11.85, p = 0.008). In terms of the case distribution, for both otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists, the number of reported ETTD cases was predominantly concentrated in the range of 1–5 cases, accounting for 49.6% and 66.3%, respectively. All anesthesiologists detected ETTD within 5 min, and none missed it ( χ² = 8.32, p = 0.040). Otolaryngologists relied mainly on a clinical self-assessment; anesthesiologists relied on monitor alerts ( χ² = 98.45, p < 0.001). Reintubation, which was typically performed by anesthesiologists, with or without preoxygenation, was the most common response. Although most ETTD events did not cause severe complications or disputes, both groups reported cases in which patients developed complications, required ICU admission, died, or litigation occurred (Table 3 ). sections.effects of the years of clinical practic: The univariate analysis using the χ² test (Tables 4 and 5 ; Fig. 1 ) showed that the years of clinical practice positively affected both the self-reported awareness level and the number of ETTD cases among physicians in both departments. Specifically, with increasing years of clinical practice, the awareness level of ETTD was significantly increased for both otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists (otolaryngology: χ² = 15.103, p < 0.001; anesthesiology: χ² = 62.372, p < 0.001), indicating an obvious effect of cumulative experience (Table 4 ; Fig. 1 ). Moreover, the number of self-reported ETTD cases increased markedly with more years of clinical practice by physicians in both departments (otolaryngology: χ² = 18.765, p < 0.001; anesthesiology: χ² = 22.342, p < 0.001), indicating a time accumulation effect. Notably, senior physicians with more years of clinical experience in the anesthesiology department reported greater exposure to ETTD cases (Table 5 ; Fig. 1 ). A multivariate ordered logistic regression model was further applied to evaluate interdepartmental differences and the independent effects of the interaction between the confounders of the number of years of clinical practice and educational background on the outcomes. As observed for the effects of the number of years of clinical practice and educational background on reported ETTD knowledge level (Table 6 ), the number of years of clinical practice (adjusted for educational background) was an independent factor influencing the reported ETTD knowledge level of physicians in both departments. Compared with physicians with 1–5 years of working experience, those with 6–10 years and more than 10 years of working experience had significantly greater knowledge levels. A stratified analysis based on educational background (adjusted for working years) revealed that a master’s degree or higher was an independent factor for a higher reported ETTD knowledge level of physicians in the otolaryngology department ( β = 0.482, p = 0.017, OR = 1.62), whereas the educational background had no independent effect on the ETTD knowledge of physicians in the anesthesiology department ( p = 0.289), suggesting that this discrepancy was confounded mainly by working years. sections.analysis of training needs: The vast majority of physicians in both departments (95.6%) deemed that receiving standardized training on ETTD was quite necessary or highly necessary. Specifically, 75.0% of the otolaryngologists and 74.3% of the anesthesiologists considered this training extremely necessary. Approximately two-thirds of all the physicians were willing to participate in relevant training. The primary reasons for unwillingness to attend training were busy work schedules with limited spare time, as well as the perception that the clinical incidence of intraoperative ETTD was low in daily practice (Table 8 ). sections.discussion: This cross-sectional survey revealed a high prevalence of self-reported ETTD events (61.1%) during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery. Moreover, significant differences were identified between otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists regarding ETTD-related knowledge, risk assessment, self-reported cases, event recognition, and clinical management. Except for significant differences in the number of years of clinical practice and educational attainment between the two groups of physicians, no statistically significant differences in age, sex composition, professional title distribution, type of medical institution, teaching hospital affiliation, or hospital grade were observed.
sections.self-reported high prevalence of ettd ex: This study revealed that 61.1% of the participating physicians reported prior exposure to ETTD. Senior physicians reported more cases, reflecting both its high frequency and time accumulation effect. Greater clinical experience was also significantly associated with deeper understanding of ETTD by physicians in both specialties, indicating an effect of accumulated experience. In contrast, junior physicians showed limited ETTD knowledge, highlighting the need to strengthen risk awareness training early in professional development [ 13 ]. Physicians in both specialties agreed that suspension laryngoscope-based oropharyngolaryngeal surgery carried the highest ETTD risk and that ETTD most commonly occurred during the removal of the laryngoscope or mouth gag (60.6% of cases). This finding likely reflects both mechanical tube traction during the procedure and reduced vigilance for tube protection near the surgical end.
sections.root causes of interdisciplinary cogniti: Anesthesiologists identified infants (0–3 years) as the highest-risk group for ETTD, likely because of the shorter tracheal length [ 14 ], increasing the risk of dislodgement during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery. In contrast, otolaryngologists regarded preschool children aged 4–6 years as the highest-risk group for ETTD. This difference likely reflects practice patterns: otolaryngologists perform fewer surgeries on infants [ 15 ], whereas common procedures such as tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy predominantly involve children over 3 years of age. Anesthesiologists attributed ETTD primarily to “improper surgical technique”, while otolaryngologists regarded “inadequate endotracheal tube fixation” as the main cause, revealing a cross-specialty attribution bias. This finding reflects a lack of shared mental models in interdisciplinary collaboration, potentially undermining communication and teamwork efficiency [ 16 ].
sections.identification of and emergency response: Notably, most clinicians in both specialties could detect ETTD events immediately, with 96.0% of participants identifying ETTD events within 3 min, which reflected the effectiveness of the current intraoperative monitoring system. However, the primary approaches for ETTD detection differed notably between the two disciplines. Anesthesiologists most commonly recognize ETTD by monitoring alarms (84.1%), whereas otolaryngologists rely more on self-inspection or notification from anesthesiology colleagues [ 12 ]. While these findings illustrate the current preferences for ETTD identification strategies, our questionnaire did not evaluate whether clinicians fully depend on a single detection method. Future studies should adopt multiple-choice questions or direct on-site observations to clarify whether the overreliance on a single detection approach is prevalent and whether it poses potential clinical risks. Although the vast majority of ETTD episodes are managed successfully during surgery without subsequent complications, both otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists have encountered severe adverse outcomes associated with ETTD, including ICU admission, mortality, and subsequent medical disputes [ 17 ].
sections.in-depth analysis of the influence of th: Univariate and multivariate ordered logistic regression analyses confirmed that the number of years of clinical practice had a stable positive effect on physicians’ reported knowledge level and number of ETTD cases in both departments, further verifying the core roles of the “experience accumulation effect” and “time accumulation effect” [ 18 ]. Specifically, more years of clinical practice are associated with greater clinical participation and richer professional experience, which in turn increase physicians’ ETTD knowledge and likelihood of exposure to ETTD events. Notably, ETTD events are jointly encountered and identifiable by physicians from both departments. The greater number of reported cases among senior anesthesiologists cannot be simply attributed to greater perceptual sensitivity [ 19 ] or a higher true incidence; instead, it may be explained by their broader surgical involvement (not limited to otolaryngology procedures), greater willingness to report these events, and potential systematic underreporting among otolaryngologists [ 20 , 21 ]. Thus, the positive association between more years of clinical practice and more self-reported ETTD cases among anesthesiologists reflects the combined effects of cross-departmental exposure opportunities, reporting behaviours, and underreporting magnitude rather than a simple accumulation of true incidence. Educational background exerted distinct effects depending on the department of the clinician: a master’s degree or higher was independently associated with higher reported ETTD knowledge levels among otolaryngologists but with more reported ETTD cases among anesthesiologists. The higher ETTD knowledge level observed in otolaryngologists with higher educational backgrounds may stem from their greater professional demand for expertise in airway anatomy and ETTD, as well as their stronger theoretical foundations and literature acquisition capabilities [ 22 , 23 ], which facilitate an in-depth understanding of ETTD. Additionally, more highly educated otolaryngologists are more likely to participate in academic training and learning guidelines, which further improves their understanding of ETTD. In contrast, no significant difference in reported ETTD knowledge by educational background was observed among anesthesiologists. This result may be because their knowledge system relies more on clinical protocols and simulation training than on academic qualifications [ 24 ]. Inconsistent self-evaluation criteria for ETTD knowledge between physicians in the two departments may also contribute to these findings, as higher-educated anesthesiologists may adopt stricter self-assessment standards. The greater number of reported ETTD cases among anesthesiologists with higher education levels may be related to their broader coverage of multiple operating rooms. Specifically, higher-educated anesthesiologists tend to systematically record adverse events, adhere to reporting norms, and have a lower recognition threshold for ETTD [ 25 ], leading to more reported cases. Thus, educational background affects anesthesiologists mainly in terms of reporting behaviour rather than the theoretical understanding of ETTD. Importantly, the number of reported cases is not equivalent to the true incidence rate of ETTD. Since ETTD events are jointly encountered by surgical and anesthesiology teams, the present findings should be interpreted as the moderating effects of clinical working years or educational background on ETTD reporting behaviour rather than direct causes of the risk of ETTD occurrence.
sections.urgency of training needs and interdisci: A total of 95.6% of the physicians expressed a strong demand for professional training, indicating deficiencies in the current training system. Traditional single-department models are inadequate for complex airway safety management; interdisciplinary, multidisciplinary crisis resource management training is therefore essential [ 26 , 27 ]. Future ETTD training should include (1) the simulation of high-risk scenarios, e.g., tube dislodgement during suspension laryngoscopy or paediatric airway emergencies; (2) technical integration, e.g., the use of visual endotracheal tube fixation devices; and (3) team-based communication and collaboration drills. By replicating real-world situations, this training aligns team understanding, standardizes management protocols, and strengthens the collective response to ETTD. Given the interdepartmental differences in how experience and education affect ETTD understanding and exposure, training and management strategies must reflect each specialty’s distinct professional profile. In the anesthesiology department, highly educated clinicians should play a leading role in ETTD prevention, and targeted training should be provided for junior physicians to accelerate their experience accumulation. In the otolaryngology department, interdisciplinary collaboration with the anesthesia team should be strengthened to increase vigilance against ETTD risks. Regardless of the education level, otolaryngologists must maintain vigilant intraoperative monitoring of the tube status to reduce the number of blind spots in ETTD risk management caused by differences in disciplinary perspectives.
sections.limitations of this study and future pro: This study still has several limitations. (1) Recruiting participants through academic conferences, professional WeChat groups, and academic networks might result in an overrepresentation of academically oriented clinicians, leading to selection bias and preventing the full generalization of the conclusions of this study to all otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists who perform or administer anesthesia for transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgeries across the country. (2) Participants reported past events from memory, which may be subject to recall bias. (3) This study was a cross-sectional survey, and the results reflected only the prevalence of self-reported events by clinicians, rather than the true incidence of events per surgical procedure or per unit time. (4) Test-retest reliability was not assessed in this study. Therefore, the temporal stability of the responses to the questionnaire is unknown. (5) Information on specific types or design parameters of endotracheal tubes (e.g., the presence or absence of cuffs, tube length, or brand) was not collected in this study. Previous studies have shown that the structural characteristics of endotracheal tubes, especially their cuff-related properties, may affect the risk of ETTD [ 9 , 28 ]. Due to the lack of relevant data on endotracheal tube types, we were unable to evaluate whether the type of endotracheal tube had a confounding effect on the study outcomes. (6) Limitations in the questionnaire design (e.g., the question on ETTD identification adopted a single-choice format) were noted. (7) Due to the inherent limitation of the cross-sectional study design, the observed intergroup differences in this study could not be clearly distinguished as being caused by differences in actual exposure levels or reporting bias, and accurate causal inferences could not be made. Based on the limitations of this study, several directions for future research should be pursued. First, multicenter prospective studies with representative sampling, including nonacademic and community hospitals, are needed to improve generalizability. Second, longitudinal cohort designs should be employed to calculate the true incidence of ETTD per surgical procedure or per unit time and to eliminate recall bias. Third, the questionnaire should undergo a test–retest reliability assessment with an appropriate time interval (e.g., 2–4 weeks) to confirm its temporal stability. Fourth, detailed endotracheal tube specifications (e.g., cuff design, tube length, and brand) must be collected to evaluate whether the tube type confounds the ETTD risk. Fifth, questionnaire-based studies should adopt multiple-answer formats or intraoperative observations for questions on the detection method to better capture real-world clinical practice. Finally, objective clinical documentation (e.g., incident reports and electronic medical records) should be used alongside self-reported surveys to distinguish true differences in exposure from reporting bias across specialties.
sections.conclusions_1: Episodes of ETTD are not uncommon during transoral oropharyngolaryngeal surgery and represent a critical threat to perioperative safety. Significant interdisciplinary differences were observed between otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists in their understanding and management of ETTD. The years of clinical practice and educational level were associated with self-reported ETTD awareness levels and case numbers. Critically, because ETTD was experienced simultaneously by both specialists, the higher reported prevalence among anesthesiologists could not be interpreted as a superior detection ability but rather as reflecting broader surgical exposure or potential underreporting by otolaryngologists. Most clinicians strongly desire ETTD training. Interdisciplinary collaboration, standardized training and team protocols, and specialty-specific strategies are recommended to improve perioperative safety.

title: Using Robotics to Improve Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair of the Mitral Valve
abstract: Transcatheter valve repair presents significant challenges due to the mechanical limitations and steep learning curve associated with manual catheter systems. This paper investigates the use of robotics to facilitate transcatheter procedures in the context of mitral valve edge-to-edge repair. Specifically, the study builds upon the MitraClip ™ (Abbott, USA), a widely used commercial system for mitral valve repair, adapting it for robotic actuation to evaluate potential performance improvements. The complex handle-based control of a clinical repair device is replaced by intuitive robotic joint-based control via a game controller. Manual versus robotic performance is analyzed by decomposing the overall device delivery task into motion-specific steps and comparing capabilities on a step-by-step basis in a phantom model of the heart and vasculature. Metrics include procedure duration and clip placement accuracy. Results demonstrate that the robotic system can reduce procedural time and motion errors while also improving accuracy of clip placement. For the most commonly treated middle leaflet segment, mean delivery time is reduced from 146.6sec to 76.2sec while mean clip positioning error is reduced from 3.1mm to 0.6mm. These findings suggest that robotic assistance can address key limitations of manual systems, offering a more reliable and user-friendly platform for complex transcatheter procedures.

title: Clinical Management of Helicobacter Infection in Captive Baboons ( Papio anubis and Papio hamadryas ), and Isolation and Molecular Characterization of Three Novel Helicobacter Species
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Helicobacter spp. are gastric or enterohepatic bacteria that can be commensal, opportunistic, or pathogenic. Few studies have evaluated Helicobacter spp. in baboons. Methods Twenty‐seven captive baboons were surveyed for Helicobacter spp. by fecal PCR, and a subset evaluated by culture. Nine baboons were treated with oral “triple therapy” with clarithromycin (10 mg/kg), amoxicillin (10 mg/kg), and omeprazole (20 mg) once daily for 10 days. Results All baboons were positive for Helicobacter spp., including H. macacae (78%), H. suis (19%), and H. pylori (15%). Three novel Helicobacter species were identified by whole genomic sequencing, for which we propose the names Helicobacter papionis , H. simiae , and H. papionifaecis. Treatment was safe and effective for H. pylori , H. suis , and H. macacae , but did not eliminate the novel Helicobacter spp. Conclusions Species‐specific assays should guide treatment of Helicobacter spp. infections in baboons. Further epidemiologic studies are needed to inform clinical management.

sections.introduction: The genus Helicobacter comprises Gram‐negative, spiral‐shaped, microaerophilic, fastidious bacteria grouped by tissue tropism: gastric species colonize the stomach while enterohepatic Helicobacter species (EHS) colonize the small intestine, large intestine, and hepatobiliary tree. Gastric species include H. pylori and H. heilmannii ‐like organisms (HHLOs) [ 1 , 2 ]. H. pylori is a human pathogen linked to gastritis, gastric ulceration, gastric adenocarcinoma, gastric lymphoma, and rarely inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) [ 3 , 4 ]. EHS are associated with IBD, enteritis, colitis, and proctitis, bacteremia, and neoplasia in humans, often in immunocompromised patients [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]. In humans, non‐human primates (NHPs), dogs, and cats, Helicobacter spp. infection may be subclinical, but during illness may also be opportunistic pathogens [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Among NHPs, Helicobacter spp. have been most extensively studied in macaques, with gastric species including H. pylori , HHLOs, and H. suis , and EHS including H. cinaedi and H. macacae [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ]. Infection in macaques may be asymptomatic or associated with gastritis, chronic diarrhea, and intestinal adenocarcinoma [ 12 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. There is limited literature regarding Helicobacter in baboons (Table S1 ), with gastric species more often described. H. pylori and HHLOs have been observed in the gastric mucosa and parietal cells of wild‐born olive baboons ( Papio anubis ) [ 20 , 21 ] but are not always present, even in baboons with lymphoplasmacytic gastritis [ 16 , 22 ]. While one group posited HHLOs were commensal, others found HHLOs to be associated with gastritis [ 23 , 24 ]. Two studies have isolated EHS from baboons, with homology to H. macacae and H. cinaedi but unknown clinical relevance [ 25 , 26 ]. It is unclear if Helicobacter are commensals, pathobionts, or pathogens in baboons. Here, a case of gastritis in an olive baboon led to detection of an unidentified Helicobacter spp. and its genetic sequence, prompting colony‐wide surveillance to assess the prevalence of Helicobacter spp. in our baboons and ultimately leading to the isolation and characterization of three novel Helicobacter species.
sections.study population and humane care guideli: Twenty‐seven baboons from two colonies, including 11 male and 1 female olive baboons ( Papio anubis ) from colony A, and 14 male olive baboons and 1 male hamadryas baboon ( Papio hamadryas ) from colony B, were included (Table S2 ). All baboons in this study were housed at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) at an AAALAC International‐accredited facility, in accordance with the Animal Welfare Act (7 U.S.C. 2131), Animal Welfare Regulations (Title 9 C.F.R.) and the 8th Edition of the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals [ 27 ]. Baboons were maintained under protocols approved by the JHU Animal Care and Use Committee and were singly‐housed for protocol‐related purposes or behavioral management. The authors confirm that the ethical policies of the Journal of Medical Primatology , as noted on the journal's author guidelines page, have been followed. Animals in this study were not on protocols investigating hepatobiliary or gastrointestinal (GI) disease, or infectious disease. Colonies were 4 miles apart, in buildings that also housed rodents; the facility with Colony A also housed macaques, marmosets, pigs, sheep, dogs, cats, and ferrets.
sections.data collection: Medical records were reviewed for age, origin (captive‐bred vs. wild‐born, facility of birth, intermediate facility, facility immediately prior to arrival at our institution) and tenure at our facility (Table S2 ). Four baboons were originally caught from the wild (all Papio anubis ), and the remaining animals were captive‐bred. Baboons arrived from six facilities. Ages ranged from 3.5 to 27.3 years (mean 18.3 years) with a tenure of 2–21.9 years (mean 13.7 years). The date of birth for wild‐born animals was estimated as 1 year prior to capture or the earliest medical record. Medical records were examined for GI signs such as inappetence, vomiting, regurgitation, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia. Eight baboons had a history of acute GI signs, all either self‐limiting or resolved with treatment before the start of study (Table S2 ). No major medical history was present in any animals. Major medical history was defined as clinical concerns (apart from superficial wounds, dermal masses, dental pathology, osteoarthritis, or alopecia) or sedation/anesthetic events (apart from routine preventive or protocol‐related procedures). No animals had prior fecal PCR testing for Helicobacter spp. or were previously treated for Helicobacter spp.
sections.sample collection: For PCR, feces were collected and stored at 4°C for up to 24 h or frozen at −80°C until shipment to a diagnostic laboratory (IDEXX BioAnalytics, Columbia, MO 65201). In Colony A, additional fecal samples were collected 2 weeks and 14–16 months after completing antibiotic treatment. For culture, fecal samples from 16 baboons (seven from Colony A collected at least 18 months after completion of antibiotics, and 9 from Colony B) were stored in 20% glycerol in Brucella broth at −80°C until shipment on dry ice to MIT. In a subset of animals euthanized for unrelated reasons, post‐mortem fecal, gastric, gall bladder, liver, small intestine, and colon samples were collected and stored at −20°C for up to 24 h, then frozen at −80°C until shipment to the diagnostic laboratory.
sections.histopathology: Tissue samples were fixed in 10% neutral‐buffered formalin and paraffin‐embedded. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin or Warthin–Starry and examined by a board‐certified veterinary anatomic pathologist. Images were collected on a Nikon Eclipse 80i microscope with a Y‐TV55 adaptor and Morrell camera and processed in Adobe Photoshop 25.9.0, following anatomic pathology guidelines [ 28 ].
sections.fecal sample real\u2010time pcr , conven: Fecal samples underwent genus‐wide Helicobacter spp. real‐time PCR assay and species‐specific real‐time PCR assays to detect H. cinaedi /canicola , H. macacae , H. pylori , and H. suis . Real‐time PCR assays were based on the IDEXX BioAnalytics proprietary service platform (IDEXX Laboratories, Westbrook, ME). Samples were homogenized and total nucleic acids were extracted and tested by fluorogenic hydrolysis probe‐based real‐time PCR assays using a commercially available instrument (LightCycler 480, Roche Applied Science, Indianapolis, IN) and master mix (LightCycler 480 Probes Master, Roche Applied Science). Assay‐specific positive and negative controls were included for each run and positive samples were retested for confirmation. A multiplexed hydrolysis‐probe‐based real‐time PCR assay targeting a eukaryotic gene ( 18SrRNA ) and bacterial gene ( 16SrRNA ) was performed for each sample to demonstrate nucleic acid recovery and absence of PCR inhibition. To limit uninterpretable sequencing results due to coinfection, only samples from animals negative for the four species‐specific real‐time PCR assays but positive on genus‐wide Helicobacter spp. assay were assessed for atypical Helicobacter sequences. The literature suggests that 16SrRNA sequences should not be used to solely identify unknown Helicobacter isolates, as they are often highly conserved among Helicobacter spp. [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] Moreover, there is some evidence for horizontal 16 S rRNA gene fragment transfers; thus, 16SrRNA similarity does not always correctly reflect Helicobacter phylogenetic relationships [ 29 , 32 , 33 ]. We therefore also utilized additional genes throughout this study. The 16SrRNA , 23SrRNA , and/or gyrB genes were amplified using conventional PCR (primers shown in Table S3 ) then submitted for Sanger sequencing (GENEWIZ, South Plainfield, NJ) [ 34 ]. BioEdit [ 35 ] v.7.2.5 and Sequencher software (Gene Codes Corporation, Ann Arbor, MI) were used to assemble reads into contigs. Regions of poor‐quality sequence and primer binding sequences were removed. Sequencing results with multiple traces were excluded. Contigs were compared to GenBank sequences and to whole genome sequences of novel species subsequently identified in this study using BLAST software [ 36 ].
sections.antibiotic treatment: Oral “triple therapy” of amoxicillin (10 mg/kg), clarithromycin (10 mg/kg), and omeprazole (20 mg/baboon) once per day for 10 days was given to nine baboons in colony A. Baboons did not receive other antibiotics between diagnosis and follow‐up fecal PCRs.
sections.bacterial isolation: Feces in freeze media (~200 mg) were directly placed on CVA (cefoperazone, vancomycin, and amphotericin) or TVP (trimethoprim, vancomycin, and polymyxin B) plates (Remel Laboratories, Lenexa, KS), or filtered through 0.65 or 0.45 μm filters onto blood agar plates. Plates were incubated under microaerobic conditions (80% N 2 , 10% CO 2 , and 10% H 2 ) at 37°C. Suspected Helicobacter spp. were identified by morphology and Gram stain.
sections.pure isolate and paraffin\u2010embedded: Microbial DNA was extracted from pure isolates using the Roche High Pure PCR Template Preparation Kit (Roche Life Science, Basel, Switzerland) according to manufacturer protocols. Isolates were confirmed as Helicobacter species by 16S rRNA sequencing using conserved primers (Table S3 ). Isolates were speciated by heat shock protein 60 ( hsp60 ) and RNA polymerase subunit B ( rpoB ) sequencing, which has been previously used to identify phylogenetic relationships among Helicobacter species [ 30 , 33 ]; primers are shown in Table S3 . PCR‐amplified products were subjected to Sanger sequencing. Sequence alignments and phylogenetic analysis were performed via Geneious bioinformatics software (Geneious v.7.1.7, Biomatters Ltd., Auckland, New Zealand). For Helicobacter PCR of paraffin‐embedded tumor, the Qiagen FFPE tissue kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) was used to extract DNA. PCR was performed with C97/H676 and C97/C98N primers (Table S3 ) using the High‐Fidelity PCR System (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN).
sections.whole genome sequencing: Genomic DNA was prepared for Illumina MiSeq sequencing (2 × 300 bp) by the BioMicroCenter at MIT using the Nextera Flex library prep kit. Default parameters were used for all bioinformatics tools. Raw sequenced reads were decontaminated of adapter sequences and quality trimmed using BBDuk (v.37.17; parameters: ktrimr, k23, mink11, hdist1, tpe, tbo, qtrimrl, trimq10, and qin33) [ 37 ] followed by de novo contig assembly and genome annotation using the Comprehensive Genome Analysis pipeline (The Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV‐BRC), https://www.bv‐brc.org/ ). Genomes were deposited in NCBI under GenBank Accession numbers in Table S6 . Using OrthoFinder [ 38 ], concatenated core protein sequences were determined, followed by MAFFT for multi‐sequence alignment and FastTree to infer approximate maximum‐likelihood phylogenetic trees. Taxonomic classification of genomes was supported by average nucleotide identity (pyANI, v.0.2.10) [ 39 ] and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (Genome‐to‐Genome Distance Calculator, v.3.0) [ 40 ]. Protein annotations were searched for the virulence factors flagellin, gamma‐glutamyltranspeptidase, High‐Temperature Requirement A, Cytotoxin‐associated gene A, Vacuolating cytotoxin A, Neutrophil‐activating protein A, catalase, Cytolethal distending toxin, Campylobacter invasion antigen B, and Fibronectin‐like protein A.
sections.biochemical characterization: The RapID NH System (Remel Laboratories, Lenexa, KS) was performed, including tests for oxidase, catalase, nitrate reduction, indoxyl acetate hydrolysis, urease, phosphatase activity, γ‐glutamyl transferase, growth at 42°C, growth with 1% glycine, and resistance to nalidixic acid and cephalothin (30 mg disks) [ 41 ].
sections.transmission electron microscopy: Two isolates per novel species were imaged by transmission electron microscopy. 24–48‐h blood agar cultures were collected into 1× PBS. Bacterial concentration was adjusted to 0.05 OD/mL with PBS to decrease background effects. Samples were placed on formvar/carbon mesh grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Montgomery County, PA), negatively stained with Uranyless Solution (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Montgomery County, PA), and examined under a Jeol 2100F transmission electron microscope.
sections.statistical analysis: Each animal was coded as 1 (positive) or 0 (negative) for H. macacae , H. suis , or H. pylori . A binomial general linear mixed model was used to compare infection rates by housing colony (A vs. B), housing room (A1 vs. A2 vs. B1 vs. B2), origin (wild‐born or captive‐born), birth location for captive‐born (one of three facilities), and housing facility prior to arrival at our institution (one of six facilities). A logistic regression was performed to assess the effect of age and tenure at our facility on the likelihood of being positive with H. macacae , H. suis , or H. pylori . Analyses were run in R v.4.1.1 [ 42 ].
sections.case study 1: During a routine experimental procedure, a 16‐year‐old intact male olive baboon (baboon #1, colony A) demonstrated marked regurgitation of partially digested blood. Gastric endoscopy revealed erythematous and inflamed mucosa without obvious ulceration. Three gastric mucosal biopsies were collected from separate sites. Radiographs revealed right cranial lung lobe consolidation, concerning for aspiration pneumonia. The patient was managed with gastroprotectants, antinausea medication, and antibiotics (enrofloxacin 5 mg/kg IM for 5 days). Gastric biopsy demonstrated frequent argyrophilic spiral organisms within gastric glands, consistent with Helicobacter spp., and mild neutrophilic inflammation (Figure 1 ). Fecal PCR was positive for Helicobacter spp., but negative for H. macacae , H. pylori , H. suis , and H. cinaedi . A portion of the Helicobacter 16SrRNA gene was sequenced from fecal nucleic acids, revealing an unidentified Helicobacter sequence.
sections.colony survey: Twenty‐seven baboons were surveyed for Helicobacter using fecal real‐time PCR. All baboons were positive for Helicobacter spp. with 78% positive for H. macacae , 19% positive for H. suis , 15% positive for H. pylori , and 0% positive for H. cinaedi /canicola (Table 1 , Figure 2 ). Co‐infections were present in 30% of cases; all 4 animals positive for H. pylori were co‐infected with H. macacae , and 4 of the 5 animals positive for H. suis were co‐infected with H. macacae . The prevalence of H. macacae was similar between colony A (75%) and colony B (80%). There was no effect of colony or housing room on positivity with H. macacae , H. suis , or H. pylori (Table S4 ). There was an effect of captive‐born status on positivity with H. macacae ( Z = −2.29, SE = 1.31, p = 0.022) with 87% (23/27) of captive‐born baboons positive for H. macacae compared to only 25% (1/4) of wild‐born baboons. Animals born at Facility 1 ( Z = 2.46, SE = 1.55, p = 0.014) also had a significantly higher likelihood of positivity for H. macacae compared to wild‐born animals. The only hamadryas baboon in the study, baboon #20, tested positive for H. macacae ; to our knowledge, this is the first report of H. macacae in P. hamadryas . There were no statistical effects of captive‐born status or birth facility on H. suis or H. pylori prevalence, nor of age or time at the facility on H. macacae , H. suis , or H. pylori prevalence.
sections.initial identification of novel helicoba: On initial colony survey, five animals (two from colony A, three from colony B) were positive for Helicobacter at the genus‐level but negative on species‐specific assays. Eight additional baboons in colony A met criteria after antibiotic treatment. Feces from these 13 animals were subjected to 16SrRNA ± 23SrRNA and gyrB gene sequencing. Sequences from baboons #2 and #14 had 100% 16SrRNA homology to H. macacae strains (MIT 99‐5501 and MIT 99‐5504) but only 93.3%–97.7% homology with 23SrRNA sequences and 85.5%–86.7% homology with gyrB sequences from H. macacae . Feces from the other 11 baboons (#1, 3–10, 13, and 19) yielded 16SrRNA sequences with > 99% identity with H. fennelliae (NCTC 11613), H. cinaedi Mainz strain (CCUG 33804/R‐927), baboon isolate MIT 03‐7674 colon, and macaque isolate MIT 99‐10781, but lower homology for 23SrRNA and gyrB sequences. These results suggested the presence of undescribed species.
sections.treatment and fecal pcr follow\u2010up: Due to potential adverse impacts of Helicobacter infection on experimental outcomes, one investigator elected to pursue treatment. Nine baboons from colony A were treated with oral triple therapy (amoxicillin (10 mg/kg), clarithromycin (10 mg/kg), and omeprazole (20 mg)) once daily for 10 days. Treatment was well tolerated. Fecal real‐time PCR performed 2 weeks post‐treatment demonstrated 100% clearance of H. macacae , H. suis , and H. pylori , yet eight of nine animals remained positive for Helicobacter at the genus level (Table 2 ). At 14–16 months post‐treatment, all baboons were positive for Helicobacter spp., but only two were identifiable at the species level (Table 2 ).
sections.case study 2: Eight months following the initial Helicobacter diagnosis, baboon #14 from colony B presented for acute obtundation with marked gastric dilatation and was euthanized due to poor prognosis. Necropsy revealed chronic‐active gastritis and a tumor expanding and compressing the cystic bile duct and neck of the gall bladder, histologically consistent with a cholangiocarcinoma (Figure 3 ). Moderate periportal to bridging chronic hepatitis was also present, as well as mild to moderate chronic‐active enterocolitis. No organisms consistent with Helicobacter were appreciated on Warthin–Starry stained sections from the tumor, liver, gall bladder, stomach, small intestine, or colon. Additionally, scrolls of paraffin‐embedded tumor were negative for Helicobacter by 16S rRNA PCR. However, H. suis was identified by PCR in feces and fresh tissue from necropsy (stomach, liver, gall bladder, small intestine and colon). The colon was also positive for H. macacae . Fecal PCR also yielded undescribed Helicobacter sequences identical to this animal's original sample.
sections.isolation and characterization of three: Approximately 22 months (Colony A) and 8 months (Colony B) after the initial survey, fecal samples were cultured from 16 baboons (seven in Colony A and nine in Colony B). Samples that tested positive for Helicobacter spp. but negative for H. macacae were preferentially chosen for culture. A total of 11 Helicobacter isolates were obtained (two in Colony A and nine in Colony B). Sequencing of the 16S rRNA , hsp60 and rpoB genes and phylogenetic analysis revealed three novel taxa that clustered separately from other Helicobacter species (Figure S1 ). The presence of three novel taxa was subsequently confirmed by whole genome sequencing of two isolates per novel taxon, for which we propose the names H. papionis , H. simiae , and H. papionifaecis (Figure 4 ). H. simiae and H. papionifaecis were phylogenetically closer to each other than to H. papionis. H. papionifaecis was closely related to H. macacae . Average nucleotide identity (ANI) calculated between novel and existing Helicobacter genomes revealed that the novel species were below the 95% similarity threshold to differentiate species, and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (DDH) showed that the novel species were below the 70% similarity threshold to differentiate species (Table S5 ). Thus, we confirmed that the three novel species are distinct from each other and from other known Helicobacter species. Genome summary statistics are presented in Table S6 . H. papionifaecis had a substantially larger genome than the other two novel species, at 2.78 and 2.89 Mb for isolates 23‐1056 and 23‐1059, respectively. All sequenced isolates contained the gene encoding the virulence factor flagellin, and all but 23‐1046 T2 ( H. simiae ) contained the gene encoding catalase. The novel species were negative for other major virulence factors, including CagA. The 16S rRNA , 23S rRNA , and gyrB sequences from initial characterization were also evaluated using BLAST against whole genome sequences from pure isolates to confirm identity. A comparison of the biochemical and phenotypic characterizations of the three novel species and other Helicobacter species is provided in Table S7 . All isolates were oxidase‐positive, urease‐negative, negative for γ‐glutamyl transferase activity, positive for alkaline phosphatase hydrolysis, negative for nitrate reduction to nitrite, and unable to grow in 1% glycine but able to grow at 42°C. H. papionis and H. papionifaecis were catalase‐positive, while H. simiae was catalase‐negative. Indoxyl acetate hydrolysis was present in all isolates of H. papionis , one of five isolates of H. simiae , and two of four isolates of H. papionifaecis . All three novel species were resistant to the antibiotic nalidixic acid, while H. simiae and H. papionifaecis were also resistant to cephalothin. Transmission electron microscopy was performed for two isolates from each novel species, with representative images from one isolate each shown in Figure 5 . Cells from H. papionis were 1.2–1.5 μm long and 0.3–0.4 μm wide. The organism was comma‐shaped with a single, unipolar, sheathed flagellum. Cells from H. simiae were 2.6–4.3 μm long and 0.2–0.3 μm wide. The organism had curved to spiral shape with bipolar, sheathed flagella. Cells from H. papionifaecis were 3.1–4.4 μm long and 0.2–0.4 μm wide. The organism was curved with bipolar, sheathed flagella. No organisms had periplasmic fibers.
sections.discussion: This is the first colony‐wide survey of Helicobacter infection in baboons using molecular diagnostics and the first study to isolate novel Helicobacter spp. from baboons. Using a combination of genus‐level Helicobacter real‐time PCR and species‐specific real‐time PCR assays, we found that H. macacae is highly prevalent in our baboon colonies, with H. suis and H. pylori at lower prevalences. Thirteen baboons tested positive for Helicobacter spp. but negative on four species‐specific real‐time PCR assays, suggesting that they might be infected with species or strains of Helicobacter spp. that had not been previously identified in NHPs. Further investigation using culture and molecular diagnostics led to the isolation and characterization of three novel Helicobacter species: H. papionis , H. simiae , and H. papionifaecis . These species were genetically, morphologically, and biochemically distinct. All three species were resistant to the synthetic quinolone nalidixic acid, and H. simiae and H. papionifaecis were resistant to cephalothin, a first‐generation cephalosporin. The heterogeneity in antibiotic susceptibility observed among these novel Helicobacter species suggests that genus‐level identification of Helicobacter should be followed by species‐specific characterization to guide antibiotic therapy. H. macacae , H. suis , and H. pylori were not cultured from any fecal samples, including baboons that were PCR‐positive for these species. This is in part due to intentional selection of samples for culture that were suspected to be mono‐infected by novel species. Additionally, because the samples for PCR and culture were collected at different times, intermittent shedding of the pathogen could impact test congruency. Furthermore, the ability to detect gastric species of Helicobacter by fecal PCR may be limited by their tissue niche deep in the gastric glands; thus, gastric biopsy with culture would be more sensitive; due to invasiveness, we did not employ this method here. The greater sensitivity of PCR compared to culture and the commercial availability of PCR assays led us to use PCR to assess treatment efficacy against Helicobacter in this study. There are no studies on treatment for Helicobacter spp. in baboons, nor for EHS in any NHPs. Oral combinations of a proton‐pump inhibitor, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin, with or without bismuth subsalicylate, have been utilized successfully to treat gastric Helicobacter ( H. pylori in humans, rhesus macaques, and Japanese macaques, and H. suis in a rhesus macaque) [ 8 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 ]. In rhesus macaques, H. pylori has also been managed with metronidazole, amoxicillin, and bismuth subsalicylate, but with only partial success due to metronidazole resistance [ 43 ]. There is sparse guidance on the treatment of EHS in human patients. Intravenous antibiotic therapy for several weeks appears to be effective in human clinical reports, but such regimens would often be impractical to implement for NHPs, and difficult to justify in animals without clinical signs [ 6 ]. In our study, oral triple therapy with once daily amoxicillin, clarithromycin, and omeprazole was safe and effective to treat H. macacae , H. pylori , and H. suis in baboons. Animals remained negative for H. macacae and H. pylori by fecal PCR for over 1 year, suggestive of clearance or long‐term suppression. Despite initial 2‐week post‐treatment negative results, two baboons later became positive for H. suis , which may be new infections or recrudescence. The successful treatment of H. macacae is particularly informative for primate veterinarians. Further research is indicated to investigate how baboons acquire these apparently prevalent Helicobacter spp. infections. H. papionis was only found in Colony A, while H. simiae was restricted to Colony B and H. papionifaecis was predominantly found in Colony B, with one individual positive in Colony A. We found no correlation between species‐specific Helicobacter positivity and colony or housing room, suggesting that transmission among adult baboons may not be common. Despite a small sample size, we also found that three of the four wild‐born animals were negative for H. macacae , H. suis , and H. pylori , despite having been at our institution for over 14 years and with other baboons housed in proximity. In captive rhesus macaques, newborns are infected with H. pylori via oral‐oral exposure within 24 h of life [ 47 ]. Host adaptation to H. pylori also appears to play a role in macaques [ 48 ]. While EHS have been less studied in NHPs, chronic subclinical infections with H. macacae and H. cinaedi may be common in macaques [ 13 , 49 ]. Zoonotic or zooanthroponotic transmission of Helicobacter between humans and NHPs may also occur [ 50 , 51 , 52 ]. Further characterization of natural Helicobacter infections in baboons is thus also essential for biosafety and risk assessment with regard to personnel exposure. On necropsy, we identified subclinical pathology of the hepatobiliary and/or gastrointestinal systems in 4/6 animals, including a cholangiocarcinoma in baboon #14, representing the first such case documented in an olive baboon. Gall bladder adenocarcinomas have been rarely reported in baboons, with three cases in hamadryas baboons, three in Guinea baboons ( Papio papio ), and no reports in several large retrospective studies [ 53 , 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 59 ]. Although Helicobacter was not identified within the tumor microscopically or by PCR, this baboon was PCR‐positive for H. suis and H. macacae in feces and tissues, and positive for H. simiae by fecal culture. Since EHS are associated with hepatobiliary tumors in humans, chronic Helicobacter spp. infection in this baboon could have participated in tumorigenesis [ 60 , 61 , 62 , 63 , 64 , 65 ]. Further investigation of the potential sequelae of chronic Helicobacter infection in baboons is therefore needed to inform clinical management. Given the apparently high prevalence and chronicity of Helicobacter infection in predominantly healthy baboons, we hypothesize that these organisms may be commensals or pathobionts. We also suspect that conspecific transmission may occur in baboons with isolated colonies having distinct Helicobacter species or strains, but that transmission among adult baboons may not be very common and may be influenced by other factors which merit further study—for example, age of first exposure, coinfection with other Helicobacter strains, or health status. Triple therapy treatment achieved prolonged clearance of H. macacae and H. pylori . This is the first published treatment protocol for Helicobacter in baboons and represents an evidence‐based refinement to the management of this species. However, triple therapy treatment was ineffective at clearing the novel Helicobacter species, and isolates showed antibiotic resistance in vitro, suggesting the response to treatment is likely bacterial species‐specific and highlighting the value of species‐specific assays to guide management and therapy.

title: Targeting the mevalonate pathway with statins overcomes acquired resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: The emergence of covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors has revolutionized the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet acquired resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we systematically identified statins as potent agents capable of overcoming acquired resistance to KRAS G12C inhibitors through high-throughput screening of 1,971 FDA-approved compounds. Statin treatment preferentially induced cell death in resistant cells, markedly impairing tumor growth both in vitro and in vivo. Proteomic profiling and pathway analysis revealed upregulation of the mevalonate (MVA) pathway in resistant cells. Genetic silencing of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR) and pharmacologic inhibition of the MVA-geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) branch recapitulated the effects of statins. Mechanistically, MVA-GGPP signaling promoted Yes-associated protein (YAP) activation, whereas disruption of this axis by statins or geranylgeranyl transferase I (GGTase-I) inhibitors impaired YAP-driven transcription and cell survival. Combination therapy with simvastatin and KRAS G12C inhibitors delayed resistance onset and enhanced antitumor efficacy across multiple in vivo models, with acceptable tolerability. These findings identify the MVA-GGPP-YAP pathway as a therapeutic vulnerability in acquired KRAS G12C inhibitor resistance and support repurposing statins to improve KRAS G12C -targeted therapy. title: “Highly committed but overwhelmed by constraints”: a qualitative study of officials’ and health staff’s perspectives on the prison mental health system in Cambodia
abstract: Background Prisoners have been identified in various international studies as one of the populations most vulnerable to mental health problems, yet the system’s response has been notably limited. Enhancing the prison healthcare system to effectively address the challenges involved a complex undertaking compounded by the prevailing constraints and stressors faced by both inmates and prison staff, particularly in low- and middle-income countries such as Cambodia, where research is lacking. This study aimed to examine the perceptions of prison officials and healthcare staff regarding the health system’s challenges in addressing prisoners’ mental health and well-being and to explore strategies to improve the Cambodian prison healthcare system. Methods Three focus group discussions were conducted in three prisons located in various regions of Cambodia with a total of 15 participants (11 prison health staff and four prison officials). A qualitative content analysis was applied to the collected data. Results Despite limited resources, the current prison healthcare system managed to provide basic healthcare, refer severe cases, and implement certain preventive measures. However, our study revealed a lack of mental health focus within the system, although certain emotional support was provided by healthcare staff to prisoners with mental health issues. Staff displayed commitment but expressed a sense of resignation due to skills and resource constraints. Participants recommended various strategies, such as increasing awareness and offering vocational training to prisoners and room leaders, intense training for healthcare staff, and enhancing governance and external support to strengthen the prison healthcare system to foster the mental health and well-being of prisoners. Conclusions Addressing the mental health needs within the prison setting in Cambodia demands an urgent reform of the current prison healthcare system. This entails a comprehensive collaborative effort among governmental institutions, placing emphasis on enhancing the skills and capabilities of inmates, room leaders and prison staff. Moreover, it is also essential to establish stronger partnerships with external organizations to improve health system governance.
