sections.kaplan\u2013meier analysis: Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated that higher postoperative nadir serum potassium levels were significantly associated with lower 28-day and 90-day mortality ( p = 0.006). Among the three groups of patients stratified by the postoperative nadir serum potassium level, the patients with the serum potassium level > 4 mmol/L had the lowest mortality rate, and the advantage in survival rate became more pronounced with the prolongation of follow-up time (Fig. 2 A). During the initial two weeks, the difference of survival rates among the three group was not significant, with the group of postoperative nadir serum potassium level between 3.5 and 4 mmol/L demonstrating the highest survival rate. However, subsequent analysis revealed that the group with serum potassium levels exceeding 4 mmol/L experienced a significantly reduced rate of survival decline and ultimately maintained the highest survival rate. The mortality rate of the group with postoperative serum potassium level below 3.5 mmol/L was markedly higher compared to the other two groups till 90 days (Fig. 2 B). Fig. 2 K-M curve of 28-day and 90-day survival in SAVR patients. ( A ) Kaplan-Meier survival curve for 28-day all-cause mortality ( P = 0.006). ( B ) Kaplan-Meier survival curve for 90-day all-cause mortality ( P < 0.001)
sections.rcs and roc analysis: RCS showed a non-linear relationship between postoperative nadir serum potassium and mortality (Fig. 3 ). The optimal threshold was identified as 3.55 mmol/L. However, given the difficulty of achieving precise decimal-level control in clinical practice, a practical interpretation is that postoperative nadir serum potassium should not fall below 3.5 mmol/L. Each 1 mmol/L increase of postoperative nadir serum potassium was associated with a 60% reduction in 28-day mortality (OR = 0.40; 95% CI: 0.24–0.69). Before covariate adjustment, the area under the curve (AUC) of the predicted values of the 28-day and 90-day mortality rates of SAVR patients by the postoperative lowest serum potassium level was 0.636 and 0.697 respectively, and the optimal thresholds were both 3.55 mmol/L. After adjustment for age, gender, BMI, heart failure, COPD, beta-blockers, antidiabetic drugs, diuretics, peripheral vascular diseases, BUN, and Creatinine, the AUC of the predicted values of the 28-day and 90-day mortality rates of SAVR patients by the postoperative lowest serum potassium level was 0.770 and 0.789 respectively, and the optimal thresholds were 2.70 and 3.03 mmol/L, respectively (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 Nonlinear association between nadir potassium and 28-day mortality Fig. 4 ROC curves of nadir postoperative potassium for predicting 28-day and 90-day mortality in SAVR patients: Comparison of unadjusted and adjusted models
sections.secondary outcomes: In the unadjusted model and the models adjusted by sequentially adding demographic characteristics (sex, age, BMI), preoperative medications (beta-blockers, antidiabetic drugs, diuretics), comorbidities (heart failure, COPD, peripheral vascular diseases), and indexes of kidney (BUN, Creatinine), the odds ratios (OR) of AKI were 0.59 (0.49, 0.71), 0.61 (0.50, 0.73), 0.64 (0.53, 0.77), 0.66 (0.55, 0.80), and 0.54 (0.44, 0.66) respectively. We also observed a significant negative association between postoperative serum potassium level and the risk of AKI. However, with the gradual inclusion of demographic characteristics, preoperative medications and comorbidities, the OR value slowly increased from 0.59 to 0.66. The standardized regression coefficients (β) of the length of hospital stay were − 7.04 (− 7.73, − 6.35), − 7.27 (− 7.96, − 6.57), − 6.28 (− 6.91, − 5.65), − 6.06 (− 6.69, − 5.44), and − 6.20 (-6.83, -5.57) respectively; the β values of the length of ICU stay were − 4.76 (− 5.16, − 4.37), − 4.85 (− 5.25, − 4.45), − 4.73 (− 5.13, − 4.33), − 4.62 (− 5.02, − 4.22), and − 4.70 (-5.10, -4.30) respectively. In Model 2 adjusted for demographics, the absolute values of β for the length of hospital stay and ICU stay increased, while in Models 3 and 4, the absolute values of β gradually decreased. We also examined the association between postoperative nadir serum potassium and arrhythmia using the same sequential adjustment strategy. In the unadjusted model (OR = 0.995, 95% CI: 0.357–2.770, P = 0.992) and the fully adjusted model (OR = 1.229, 95% CI: 0.293–5.154, P = 0.778), no statistically significant association was observed. Detailed results are presented in Supplementary Table S1.
sections.subgroup analysis: Figure 5 presents the forest plot of subgroup analyses. The association between postoperative nadir serum potassium and 28-day mortality was consistent across most subgroups, including sex (female: 0.23[0.19–0.28]; male: 0.48[0.39–0.58]), age (< 65 years: 0.73[0.60–0.89]; ≥65 years: 0.29[0.24–0.35]), BMI (< 30: 0.23[0.19–0.28]; ≥30: 0.97[0.80–1.18]), heart failure (no: 0.27[0.22–0.33]; yes: 0.69[0.57–0.84]), COPD (no: 0.40[0.33–0.49]; yes: 0.35[0.29–0.43]), beta- blocker (no: 0.44[0.36–0.54]; yes: 0.37[0.30–0.45]), antidiabetic drug (no: 0.35[0.29–0.43]; yes: 1.34[1.10–1.63]), diuretic (no: 0.39[0.32–0.47]; yes: 0.59[0.48–0.72]), and peripheral vascular disease (no: 0.42[0.35–0.51]; yes: 0.36[0.30–0.44]). While sub-group analysis also suggested potentially stronger effects in female patients (OR = 0.23), older adults aged ≥ 65 years (OR = 0.29), non-obesity individuals (BMI < 30, OR = 0.23), and those without heart failure (OR = 0.27). However, interaction tests did not reach statistical significance in these subgroups (all p > 0.05). A borderline interaction was observed for heart failure status ( p = 0.080). Notably, among patients receiving antidiabetic drugs, higher nadir potassium was unexpectedly associated with increased 28-day mortality (OR = 1.34), which contrasts with the protective effect observed in other subgroups. This paradoxical finding may be explained by residual confounding, such as the severity of diabetes, insulin use versus oral agents, or concurrent renal impairment. It is also possible that antidiabetic drugs affecting potassium homeostasis (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors) were differentially distributed. Given the small sample size in this subgroup ( n = 167, 5.8%), chance findings cannot be excluded, and this result should be interpreted with caution. Fig. 5 Forest plot of odds ratios for the association between nadir potassium and 28-day mortality across subgroups, with interaction P-values
sections.discussion: This study found a U-shaped association between postoperative nadir serum potassium and 28-day mortality in patients undergoing SAVR. Patients with postoperative nadir serum potassium level > 4.0mmol/L had the lowest 28-day and 90-day mortality rates, shorter hospital and ICU length of stay, and a lower risk of postoperative AKI. Additionally, as the postoperative nadir serum potassium level increased, the OR value of 28-day mortality showed a significant downward trend. The association of higher postoperative nadir serum potassium with short term mortality was consistent across different patient subgroups. In the present study, the reference level for serum potassium in logistic regression models was set at 3.5 mmol/L. This cutoff was chosen based on the conventional clinical definition of hypokalemia (serum potassium < 3.5 mmol/L), which is widely accepted in clinical practice and has been used as a reference in numerous prior studies investigating potassium-related outcomes [ 11 , 12 , 21 ]. Using this clinically meaningful reference level facilitates the interpretation of odds ratios and enhances the comparability of our findings with existing literature. These findings are consistent with previous studies that demonstrated the risks of both hypokalemia and hyperkalemia. Moreover, this is the first study to identify a specific threshold of postoperative nadir serum potassium in patients undergoing SAVR. To date, the “optimal” range of potassium remains unclear. Although 3.5-5.5mmol/L is currently considered safe, it is still difficult to define a critical value associated with the lowest risk of death and other clinical outcomes in patients undergoing SAVR [ 12 – 14 ]. Hypokalemia leads to an increased concentration gradient of potassium ions across the myocardial cell membrane, reduced potassium efflux, and a decrease in the resting potential negativity of myocardial cells, thereby affecting cell excitability [ 15 , 16 ]. Since cardiac repolarization depends on potassium influx, hypokalemia prolongs the action potential and increases QT dispersion (reflecting electrical heterogeneity). Hypokalemia is also a strong independent predictor of mortality in heart failure (HF), and patients taking non-potassium-sparing diuretics have higher all-cause and cardiac mortality rates in patients with HF [ 17 , 18 ]. In a study of 6,073 patients with HF, the risk of death was relatively increased by 2.3 times in patients with a serum potassium level < 3.5mmol/L [ 19 ]. In a cohort of 142,087 patients from the US Veterans Affairs database, the risk of death was 1.3 times and 1.6 times higher in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) patients with intermittent and persistent hypokalemia, respectively [ 20 ]. A study on coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) showed that the 90-day mortality risk was increased in patients with postoperative hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, and normal-range hypokalemia (3.5-3.9mmol/L), while the relative risk was smaller in patients with normal range of potassium (4.7-5.0mmol/L), and the all-cause mortality rate increased in patients with potassium levels outside the range of 4.2-5.2mmol/L [ 21 ]. Another study showed that patients with a serum potassium level below 3.5 mmol/L (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.12–1.66) and those with a serum potassium level above 4.6 mmol/L (HR 2.46, 95% CI 1.66–2.74) had an increased mortality rate within 60 days in patients with hypertension, compared with those with a serum potassium level of 3.5–4.6 mmol/L. Moreover, serum potassium level below 3.0 mmol/L was significantly associated with mortality (HR 2.46, 95% CI 1.05–5.74), and patients with serum potassium level between 3.0 and 3.4 mmol/L also had an increased risk of death [ 22 ]. A study of 2,660,609 patients from the US National Inpatient Sample database demonstrated a 1.9-fold higher in-hospital mortality risk in hypokalemic patients [ 23 ], and multiple prior studies have linked hypokalemia to increased mortality in cardiovascular disease patients [ 24 – 28 ]. Consistent with the U-shaped association between postoperative nadir serum potassium and 28-day mortality observed in our study, unadjusted mortality in unselected cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) patients was also U-shaped related to admission serum potassium, including subgroups with ACS, HF, AKI and CKD [ 29 ]. This U-shaped relationship has been further confirmed in other studies: a UK cohort of 21,334 newly diagnosed HF patients showed a 2-fold higher mortality risk in any hypokalemia (< 3.5 mmol/L) after mortality correction [ 30 ]; a Danish National Registry study of 19,549 chronic HF patients found that serum potassium < 3.8 mmol/L was associated with a 3-fold higher 90-day mortality risk compared with 4.2–4.4 mmol/L and a 2.4-fold higher risk compared with 3.5-5.0 mmol/L [ 31 ]; similar correlations were also observed between post-randomization potassium levels and cardiovascular mortality in HFpEF patients [ 32 ], and between serum potassium and all-cause mortality as summarized in a JACC review [ 33 ]. Although the U-shaped potassium-mortality association exists in both SAVR and HF patients, potassium exerts a distinct perioperative-specific effect on death risk in SAVR patients. Postoperatively, SAVR patients have stunned myocardium due to surgical trauma and ischemia-reperfusion injury, with extremely fragile electrophysiological and systolic functions, resulting in far greater sensitivity to hypokalemia than HF patients. In the specific context of SAVR, the U-shaped association between postoperative nadir potassium and mortality carries distinct clinical implications. First, surgical aortic valve replacement involves cardiopulmonary bypass, aortic cross-clamping, and cardioplegic arrest, all of which predispose the myocardium to reperfusion injury and electrical instability. In this setting, even transient hypokalemia may act as a proximate trigger for malignant arrhythmias, whereas hyperkalemia is often iatrogenic and less common. Second, the nadir potassium typically occurs early postoperatively due to hemodilution, diuresis, and stress-related catecholamine surge, making it a modifiable and time-sensitive target. Third, the U-shaped relationship underscores that both ends of the potassium spectrum are harmful, but the mechanisms differ: hypokalemia primarily increases arrhythmic risk, while hyperkalemia may reflect renal dysfunction or excessive supplementation. Therefore, potassium management after SAVR should aim to avoid extreme deviations rather than achieving a single “optimal” value. Mild hypokalemia can directly induce malignant arrhythmias, exacerbate myocardial injury, and synergize with abrupt postoperative volume load changes to increase acute cardiogenic adverse event risk, acting as a key trigger for perioperative acute death—whereas hypokalemia-related risks in HF patients are mostly cumulative effects of chronic pathological processes, and mild hypokalemia generally does not directly cause acute death. In addition, potassium disorders in SAVR patients are mostly short-term stress-induced postoperative abnormalities due to cardiopulmonary bypass and volume fluctuations, rather than the chronic compensatory abnormalities from long-term RAAS activation and chronic medication use in HF patients. Rigorous perioperative monitoring and rapid intervention also significantly attenuate the lethal effect of hyperkalemia in SAVR patients, unlike in HF patients where hyperkalemia is also a major mortality risk factor. Furthermore, prompt perioperative correction of hypokalemia in SAVR patients can directly block the acute pathological cascade with marked immediate benefits and a narrow intervention window, thus requiring a more stringent and aggressive potassium management strategy than that for HF patients to effectively avoid hypokalemia-related short-term mortality. However, an ICU study showed that patients with an average serum potassium of 3.5-4.0 mmol/L and low potassium variability had the lowest mortality rate (3.7%), and even those with mild hypokalemia (3.0-3.5 mmol/L) had significantly lower in-hospital mortality than patients with 4.0-4.5 mmol/L [ 34 ]. For SAVR patients, cardiac function and electrolyte balance are critical for postoperative recovery, and hypokalemia exerts a more pronounced impact on cardiac function, potentially triggering complications such as arrhythmias and increasing mortality. While overactivated RAAS and diuretic use can cause hypokalemia, and ACEI/ARB and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) use can lead to hyperkalemia in both populations, the underlying physiological mechanisms differ. HF patients often develop hyperkalemia due to reduced potassium excretion from insufficient renal perfusion, whereas aortic regurgitation patients undergoing SAVR have left ventricular dilation and dysfunction caused by diastolic blood regurgitation, which alters myocardial cell physiological characteristics and renders this population more sensitive to potassium fluctuations. Additionally, previous studies analyzing the correlation between postoperative serum potassium and 90-day mortality in CABG patients focused on the first serum potassium level within 7 days postoperatively, enabling simultaneous evaluation of hyperkalemia and hypokalemia on mortality [ 21 ]. In contrast, the present study analyzes postoperative nadir serum potassium in SAVR patients, which provides greater guiding significance for maintaining the minimum postoperative serum potassium level and preventing postoperative hypokalemia. There are several limitations in this study. First, this is a retrospective, single-center study, which precludes causal inference. Second, the predominantly U.S.-based cohort may limit external generalizability. Third, unmeasured confounders, such as intraoperative factors or dietary intake, could also influence the outcomes. It is also important to note that the nadir serum potassium represents a single extreme value rather than the average or cumulative potassium status during the postoperative period. Therefore, our findings should not be interpreted as advocating for maintaining potassium at or above 3.55 mmol/L at all times, but rather as identifying a threshold below which the risk of mortality increases significantly. Fourth, patients with lower nadir potassium levels had higher APACHE III scores and were older, indicating greater baseline illness severity. Therefore, nadir potassium may serve as a prognostic marker rather than a direct causal factor, and residual confounding cannot be fully excluded. Fifth, among the samples excluded due to the lack of blood potassium measurement levels in the ICU, the majority also had missing data on the length of ICU stay. This part of the samples might have had data missing because of a relatively short ICU stay, which could lead to the exclusion of samples of early postoperative deaths, causing a certain degree of bias. Additionally, the unexpected interaction between antidiabetic drug use and nadir potassium warrants further investigation in larger, prospective cohorts with detailed medication classification and diabetes severity adjustment.
sections.conclusion_1: In patients undergoing SAVR, the postoperative nadir serum potassium level is independently associated with 28-day mortality. A threshold of 3.55 mmol/L was identified, which can be practically interpreted as maintaining postoperative nadir serum potassium no lower than 3.5 mmol/L to reduce short-term mortality. However, this threshold should not be interpreted as a target level to be maintained constantly, nor does it imply that higher potassium levels are beneficial for prognosis. The nadir value represents only the lowest single measurement during ICU stay and does not reflect overall potassium homeostasis throughout the hospitalization period.

title: Geometric coronary constraints and anatomical feasibility of redo TAVR in Asian patients with Evolut valves: A CT-based simulation study
abstract: Redo transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) when implanting a second transcatheter valve within a tall-frame self-expanding valve can be challenging because of unfavorable coronary-related anatomy. However, computed tomography (CT)-based data in Asian patients with smaller aortic root dimensions remain limited.This study aimed to evaluate the CT-based geometric coronary constraints by simulating implantation of a balloon-expandable SAPIEN 3 (S3) within a previously implanted self-expanding Evolut valve in Asian patients. Consecutive patients who underwent TAVR using Evolut at a single center between May 2021 and May 2023 and had post-procedural CT were analyzed. Virtual S3-in-Evolut implantation was simulated at three depths (node 4: low; node 5: intermediate; node 6: high). Geometric coronary constraint was assessed based on the relationship between the neo-skirt plane and coronary ostia and the valve-to-aorta distance. Among 113 patients, the distribution of geometric coronary constraint differed by simulated S3 implantation depth. With high S3 implantation (node 6), severe, intermediate, and low constraint were observed in 63.7%, 23.9%, and 12.4% of patients, respectively; with intermediate implantation (node 5), in 31.0%, 29.2%, and 39.8%; and with low implantation (node 4), in 3.5%, 16.8%, and 79.6%. In multivariable analysis, smaller sino-tubular junction diameter was independently associated with severe geometric coronary constraint.Geometric coronary constraints that may affect coronary access after redo TAVR with S3-in-Evolut configurations depend on the implantation depth of both the index Evolut and the simulated S3. However, the hemodynamic significance and clinical impact of these geometric findings require validation through flow studies. sections.introduction: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is increasingly used to treat younger patients with lower surgical risk and longer life expectancy. There is a significant body of data demonstrating the durability of transcatheter aortic valves (TAVs) up to 7 years [ 1 – 3 ]. However, like surgical aortic bioprostheses, structural valve degeneration of TAVs can occur over time and may eventually lead to repeat intervention [ 4 , 5 ]. In these cases, implantation of a second TAV inside a failed TAV (TAV-in-TAV) is a therapeutic option and the number of TAV-in-TAV procedures is expected to grow [ 6 ]. A major concern of a TAV-in-TAV procedure is that the leaflets of the first TAV would form a neo-skirt-covered stent when tilted up by a second TAV, which directly or indirectly obstructs the coronary ostium. This risk is increased with tall-frame supra-annular self-expanding valves (SEV), due to the higher leaflet position creating a taller leaflet neo-skirt [ 7 , 8 ]. Previous studies conducted primarily in the United States have reported that the potential geometric coronary constraint during redo TAVR, simulated by implanting a balloon-expandable SAPIEN 3 (S3) valve (Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, California) within an Evolut (Medtronic, Minneapolis, Minnesota) SEV, ranged from 46% to 75% in the context of high S3 implantation [ 7 , 9 ]. However, comprehensive post-TAVR computed tomography (CT) assessments stratifying the severity of geometric coronary constraint by initial Evolut implantation depth and subsequent S3 implant position remain limited. Furthermore, although prior studies have shown that smaller aortic valve complexes are associated with severe geometric coronary constraint in TAV-in-TAV procedures, no data are currently available regarding this risk among Asian patients, who typically exhibit smaller aortic root anatomy [ 7 , 9 ]. Therefore, we sought to utilize post-TAVR CT analysis to evaluate geometric coronary constraints and anatomical feasibility in TAV-in-TAV by simulating implantation of a S3 within Evolut SEV in various initial Evolut implant depths and subsequent S3 implant positions.
sections.study population: We screened consecutive patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR using the Evolut TAV at Shonan Kamakura General Hospital between May 2021 and May 2023. The decision to proceed with TAVR was made with the consensus of a dedicated heart team including experienced clinical and interventional cardiologists and cardiothoracic surgeons. The selection of the type and size of TAV were at the discretion of the treating physician. For the purpose of this study, patients without electrocardiography (ECG)-gated contrast-enhanced post-TAVR CT data, those with poor CT image quality, those who underwent valve-in-valve TAVR, or those with TAV embolization were excluded from the analysis. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Tokushukai Group Ethical Committee (approval number: TGE02332-024).
sections.pre-tavr ct analysis: Details of the CT imaging acquisition protocol and processing have been previously reported [ 10 ]. For annulus, Sinus of Valsalva (SOV), sinotubular junction (STJ), and atrioventricular dimensions, analysis was performed according to the current guideline [ 11 ]. The STJ height and coronary height were measured from the annular plane to the lowest point of STJ, and inferior border of each coronary ostium in a stretched multiplanar image, respectively.
sections.second tav sizing and positioning: The post-TAVR CT scans were used to implant virtual S3 inside the Evolut valves. For the S3-in-Evolut implantation, the S3 size was determined based on the CT measurements of the expansion of index TAV and native aortic annular dimension. Three different S3 implantation positions (low, intermediate, and high) were evaluated. In the low implantation position, the S3 outflow was aligned with Evolut node 4, in the intermediate position with node 5, and in the high implantation position with node 6 (Fig. 1 ). We assumed that the index TAV leaflet would be pushed completely open by the second TAV, thereby establishing a neo-skirt and sealing the stent frame circumferentially up to the S3 outflow level after TAV-in-TAV. The neo-skirt plane (NSP) is defined as the plane at the top of the neo-skirt. sections.post-tavr ct display settings: To delineate the TAV-frame boundary and minimize blooming artifacts, measurements were performed using a standardized default display setting of WW/WL = 1,800/800 HU [ 12 ]. We confirmed the robustness of valve-to-aorta (VTA)-related measurements by repeating the analysis under two alternative window settings (WW/WL = 1600/800 and 2000/800 HU).
sections.post-tavr ct analysis and definition: To assess CT-identified geometric coronary constraints, two reference planes were identified: the NSP and the coronary risk plane (CRP). The CRP was defined as the plane parallel to the aortic annulus at the base of each coronary ostium and was established for both the left coronary artery (LCA) and the right coronary artery (RCA). In the short-axis view, the distance between the simulated redo-TAV complex and the adjacent aortic wall was measured and defined as the VTA distance. To account for stent frame thickness and blooming artifacts inherent to CT imaging, the VTA distances were measured from the midline of the stent frame. Depending on the anatomical level, the VTA distance was assessed at three locations: (i) valve-to-coronary (VTC), (ii) valve-to-aortic sinus (VTAoS), and (iii) valve-to-STJ (VTSTJ). Each measurement was obtained for both the LCA and the RCA. Geometric coronary constraint assessment was performed using the NSP, CRP, and corresponding VTA measurements for both coronary ostia, as previously described [ 13 ]. When the NSP was positioned below the CRP, the case was classified as low geometric coronary constraint. When the NSP was located above the CRP, the narrowest of the three VTA measurements was used to further stratify the geometric constraint severity. Geometric coronary constraint severity was stratified by VTA using a three-tier framework: severe (VTA < 2.0 mm), intermediate (2.0 mm ≤ VTA < 4.0 mm), and low (VTA ≥ 4.0 mm) (Fig. 1 ). The overall geometric coronary constraint for each patient was determined based on the higher constraint severity classification of the two coronary arteries. To assess the robustness of classification to the choice of cutoff, we performed a multi-threshold sensitivity analysis by varying the lower VTA threshold from 1.0 to 4.0 mm in 0.5-mm increments. For each threshold, we recalculated the proportion classified as severe geometric coronary constraint and plotted the results by simulated S3 outflow level. The implantation depth of the index Evolut valve was defined as the mean distance from the inflow edge of the TAV to the floor of the sinus of Valsalva, measured at each coronary cusp. For patients identified as having severe geometric coronary constraint, leaflet modification techniques, such as the bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction (BASILICA) procedure may be an option to mitigate leaflet-induced coronary obstruction [ 14 ]. However, if commissural posts of the index TAV overlap with the coronary ostia, leaflet modification may be technically unfeasible or suboptimal, as the posts may remain in front of the coronary ostia even after successful leaflet laceration, thereby compromising coronary flow. To assess this, the overlap between the first TAV commissural posts and each coronary ostium was analyzed using end-diastolic phase data. Coronary overlap involving the LCA and RCA was considered severe when the neocommissure and coronary orifice were separated by an angle of 0° to 20°, as previously described [ 15 , 16 ].
sections.measurement reproducibility: Two observers independently remeasured left and right VTA in a randomly selected subset of 30 cases spanning the observed VTA range. Inter-observer agreement was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) with a two-way random-effects model, absolute agreement, single measures, and Bland-Altman analyses reporting the mean difference and 95% limits of agreement. The primary observer repeated the measurements after an interval of at least 14 days to assess intra-observer repeatability using the same metrics. ICC values were interpreted according to established guidelines (< 0.50 = poor, 0.50–0.75 = moderate, 0.75–0.90 = good, and > 0.90 = excellent agreement) [ 17 ].
sections.statistical analysis: Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation for normally distributed continuous variables or as median and interquartile range (IQR: 25–75%) for non-normally distributed continuous variables. Categorical variables are expressed as numeric values and percentages. Comparison of continuous variables was performed using the Student’s t -test or Mann–Whitney U test, depending on the variable distribution. The chi-square or Fisher’s exact test was used to compare categorical variables. Left and right VTA was summarized as continuous variables by simulated S3 outflow level (node 4–6) using median and interquartile range and visualized using box plots. Univariate logistic regression modelling identified initial preprocedural clinical characteristics, CT anatomical parameters, and procedural variables associated with severe coronary constraint following S3 outflow at Evolut node 6 implantations for the overall cohort. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with severe geometric coronary constraints in case of high S3 implants. Covariates were selected based on clinical relevance and univariate associations ( p < 0.10). The complete results of univariate logistic regression analyses for all baseline clinical characteristics, CT anatomical parameters, and procedural variables are provided in Supplemental Table S1 . To avoid multicollinearity, annulus perimeter (instead of annulus area) and mean SOV diameter (instead of SOV diameters toward the left and right coronary cusps) were selected as representative CT metrics for the final multivariable model. No other relevant multicollinearity was detected. Additionally, the optimal cut-off points for the predictors for severe geometric coronary constraint were determined on a univariate level by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and Youden’s J statistic. The odds ratios (OR) with associated 95% confidence intervals (CI) and Wald p-values for the continuous variables are reported. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 24.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA) and R software version 3.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results: For this redo TAVR CT-based analysis, we screened 142 consecutive patients for eligibility during the study period. After excluding 29 patients according to the criteria (valve-in-valve:12, no post-TAVR contrast-enhanced CT: 10, poor CT image quality: 5, TAV embolization:2), 113 patients were included in this study and post-TAVR CT scans were analyzed for implantation of a virtual second TAV in 3 different positions. Baseline characteristics of the study population are shown in Table 1 . The median age of the study cohort was 85 years, 63.7% were female, and the median Society of Thoracic Surgeon risk score was 5.3% (3.6%−7.1%). A size 23, 26, 29, 34 mm Evolut TAV was implanted in 7.1%, 48.7%, 40.7%, and 3.5% of patients, respectively. Pre- and post-dilatation was performed in 26.5% and 1.8% of TAVR procedures, respectively. sections.vta measurements: VTA decreased with higher simulated S3 implantation. Median (IQR) left VTA was 4.9 (3.8–6.5) mm at node 4, 4.1 (2.6–6.3) mm at node 5, and 2.4 (0.7–3.6) mm at node 6. Median (IQR) right VTA was 5.3 (4.2–6.3) mm at node 4, 4.3 (1.6–6.0) mm at node 5, and 2.1 (0.8–4.3) mm at node 6 ( Supplemental Figure S1 ). Inter-observer agreement was excellent for both left and right VTA (ICCs: 0.96; 95% CI, 0.92 to 0.98, and 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96 to 0.99, respectively), with small mean differences and narrow 95% limits of agreement on Bland-Altman analyses. Intra-observer repeatability was similarly high for both left and right VTA (ICCs: 0.98; 95% CI, 0.95 to 0.99, and 0.98; 95% CI, 0.95 to 0.99, respectively), with small mean differences and narrow 95% limits of agreement on Bland-Altman analyses ( Supplemental Figure S2 ).
sections.ct-identified geometric coronary constra: Geometric coronary constraint differed markedly by simulated S3 implantation depth. With high S3 implantation (node 6), severe, intermediate, and low constraint were observed in 63.7%, 23.9%, and 12.4% of patients, respectively. With intermediate implantation (node 5), the corresponding proportions were 31.0%, 29.2%, and 39.8%. With low implantation (node 4), severe constraint was uncommon (3.5%), whereas intermediate and low constraint accounted for 16.8% and 79.6%, respectively ( Graphical abstract ). Across VTA thresholds from 1.0 to 4.0 mm, the proportion classified as severe geometric coronary constraint increased monotonically for all simulated S3 implantation depths. Notably, the relative gradient by implantation depth remained consistent across thresholds, with node 6 showing the highest proportion of severe constraint, followed by node 5 and node 4 (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Multi-threshold sensitivity analysis for severe geometric coronary constraint according to simulated SAPIEN 3 implant depth.The x-axis shows the valve-to-aorta (VTA) threshold (1.0–4.0 mm, 0.5-mm increments) and the y-axis shows the proportion of patients classified as having severe geometric coronary constraint. Curves are stratified by simulated SAPIEN 3 (S3) implantation depth within the index Evolut valve (node 4, node 5, and node 6)

A high implant depth (< 3 mm) of the Evolut was observed in 38.9% of patients. Severe geometric coronary constraint became more frequent as the index Evolut was implanted more shallowly and as the simulated S3 was implanted higher. In the worst-case scenario of a shallow index Evolut implant combined with a high S3 implant, severe constraint was observed in 70.5% of patients. In the best-case scenario of a deep index Evolut implant combined with a low S3 implant, no patient met criteria for severe constraint (Fig. 3 ). With a low S3 implant position, severe constraint was uncommon (3.5%) irrespective of the index Evolut implant depth. The predicted constraints according to the size of the index Evolut are shown in Supplemental Figure S3 . sections.overlap between the first tav commissura: In a coronary-level analysis, overlaps between the first TAV commissural posts and coronary ostium were observed in 22.0% (11 of 50) in LCA and 15.4% (8 of 52) in RCA among coronary arteries classified as having severe geometric coronary constraint with high S3 implantation (node 6) in Evolut.
sections.predictors of severe geometric coronary: Predictors of severe coronary constraint with a high S3 implant position (node 6) are listed in Table 2 . In univariate analysis, female sex and smaller aortic root dimensions, lower STJ height, and lower coronary height were associated with a greater likelihood of severe coronary constraint. Among procedural characteristics, a shallower implantation depth of the index Evolut was associated with severe geometric coronary constraint ( Table 2 ) . In multivariable analysis, smaller STJ diameter was independently associated with severe geometric coronary constraint (Table 3 ). The final multivariable logistic regression model demonstrated good discriminative performance for identifying severe geometric coronary constraint, with a C-statistic (area under the ROC curve) of 0.86. ROC analyses showed the following cut-offs for severe constraint: annulus perimeter < 72.1 mm, mean SOV diameter < 29.8 mm, mean STJ diameter < 26.7 mm, left/right STJ height < 19.1/18.6 mm, left/right coronary height < 14.9/15.1 mm, and index Evolut implantation depth < 4.0 mm. sections.discussion: In this study, we assessed CT-identified geometric coronary constraints and anatomical feasibility for redo TAVR in Asian patients with prior self-expanding Evolut valves by simulating S3-in-Evolut configurations at different index Evolut and redo S3 implantation depths. The major findings of this study are as follows: (1) CT-identified geometric coronary constraint varied markedly by simulated S3 implantation depth within the index Evolut valve: with a high S3 position (node 6), 63.7% ( n = 72) of patients met criteria for severe geometric coronary constraint, compared with 31.0% ( n = 35) at the intermediate position (node 5) and 3.5% ( n = 4) at the low position (node 4). (2) The severity of geometric coronary constraint was influenced by the implantation depths of both the index Evolut and the simulated S3. (3) Among coronary arteries classified as having severe geometric coronary constraint, coronary overlap suggesting limited anatomical feasibility for leaflet modification was observed in approximately one in five cases due to coronary–commissural misalignment. This study assessed geometric coronary constraints using static CT measurements but did not evaluate actual coronary blood flow. While narrow VTA distances may pose anatomical challenges, the hemodynamic significance remains unvalidated. Fluid dynamics analysis would be necessary to determine the relationship between VTA distance and flow velocity/pressure gradients, validate the 2 mm cutoff, and identify optimal S3 positioning. Until such validation is performed, our findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating data rather than definitive risk stratification.
sections.optimal implantation depth of s3 in a fa: Our findings demonstrated that implantation of the S3 at a lower position within the index TAV reduced the neo-skirt height, thereby lowering the likelihood of geometric coronary constraint, consistent with previous CT-based simulation studies. By using a balloon-expandable TAV inside a failed SEV, the operator can adjust the position of the S3, thereby influencing the NSP and subsequent likelihood of geometric coronary constraint. A lower implantation position, with the S3 outflow aligned at node 4, can reduce the neo-skirt height by up to 7.6 mm compared with node 6 [ 18 ]. However, a potential drawback of lower S3 implantation is the residual index TAV leaflet tissue which may overhang the S3. Although in-vitro studies of S3-in-Evolut configurations showed favorable hemodynamic outcomes across both low and high S3 positions regardless of the extent of leaflet overhung, the long-term clinical impact remain unknown [ 18 ]. This should be confirmed by further clinical studies of real TAV-in-TAV cases with longer-term follow-up. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of precise preprocedural CT assessment and individualized procedural planning, including positioning of the second TAV, to reduce the likelihood of geometric coronary constraint.
sections.implantation depth of index evolut tav t: Our study showed that deeper implantation of the index TAV was associated with a lower likelihood of geometric coronary constraint in future TAV-in-TAV. However, deeper implantation depth may increase the risk of postprocedural conduction disturbances, which are associated with higher mortality [ 10 ]. As TAVR expands to younger and lower-risk populations, determining patient-specific implantation depth becomes increasingly important to balance the competing risks of geometric coronary constraint in future TAV-in-TAV and conduction disturbances after the index procedure. This decision should be based on the anticipated need for future redo TAVR, the anatomical characteristics of the aortic valve complex, and the risk of conduction disturbances. Furthermore, anatomical characteristics and the choice or implantation depth of the index TAV may preclude future redo TAVR in some patients. The heart team should carefully determine the most appropriate initial treatment strategy (TAVR versus surgery) at the time of the first procedure. A tailored decision-making approach based on clinical and anatomical factors is essential for optimal lifetime management of patients with aortic stenosis.
sections.predictors of severe geometric coronary: In this study, CT-derived measurements reflecting a smaller aortic valve complex were associated with a higher likelihood of severe geometric coronary constraint in cases of high S3 implantation. Among these variables, a smaller STJ diameter emerged as the independent predictor in multivariable analysis, underscoring the critical role of the STJ in determining geometric coronary constraint after redo TAVR. It may be argued that Asian patients, who typically have smaller aortic valve complexes, are at a higher likelihood of geometric coronary constraint compared with Western populations. However, CT analysis from the Evolut low risk trial conducted primarily in the United States showed that 75% of patients were classified as severe geometric coronary constraint at a high S3 implantation position (node 6), whereas 47% and 20% were identified as severe geometric coronary constraint at intermediate (node 5) and low (node 4) implantation positions, respectively. These findings are similar to our results in Asian patients using identical methodology and a high-risk cut-off of VTA < 4 mm. Although a smaller aortic valve complex is generally associated with an increased CT-identified geometric coronary constraint in TAV-in-TAV for a given index Evolut valve size, the Evolut TAVs used in Asian patients with smaller anatomy were also correspondingly smaller than those used in prior studies involving American cohort [ 9 ]. In the majority of S3-in-Evolut configurations, a smaller Evolut TAV results in a reduced neo-skirt height, potentially mitigating the severe geometric coronary constraint [ 18 ]. Taken together, native aortic root anatomy, particularly the size of the STJ, in combination with TAV size appears to be a key determinant of geometric coronary constraint, rather than small aortic dimensions alone. Therefore, in patients with borderline annular dimensions at index TAVR, potential future coronary access difficulty and geometric coronary constraint should be carefully considered when selecting a larger TAV, particularly in the presence of a proportionally smaller STJ relative to the aortic annulus.
sections.feasibility of leaflet modification proc: Our analysis showed that overlap between coronary arteries and TAV neo-commissures occurred in approximately 20% of coronary arteries among classified as having severe geometric coronary constraint with high S3 implantation (node 6) in Evolut. For the Evolut TAV system, inserting the delivery system with the flush port oriented at the 3 o’clock position has been shown to enhance the success rate of achieving commissural alignment in prior studies [ 10 , 15 ]. However, in this study, overlap of one or both coronary ostia with the TAV commissural posts was still observed in approximately one in five patients, even when this technique was employed. One potential explanation is that variations in aortic anatomy, including the eccentricity of coronary ostia relative to the SOV, orientation of the native aortic valve, and tortuosity of the aorta, differ substantially among patients. Future refinements in TAV and delivery system design are warranted to improve the feasibility of achieving precise commissural alignment. This finding suggests that leaflet modification strategies such as BASILICA may be technically limited in a subset of anatomies, because catheter traversal and controlled laceration may be challenging when the target leaflet region is adjacent to a neo-commissural post. In such cases, alternative management strategies should be considered, including coronary protection with a pre-positioned guidewire and standby stent, careful depth trade-offs to lower the neo-skirt relative to the coronary ostia, and heart-team discussion regarding redo-TAVR versus surgical options in anatomically unfavorable scenarios. Given the expanding indications for TAVR in younger patients, the number of redo TAVR is expected to increase. Our findings underscore the importance of comprehensive preprocedural CT assessment to evaluate the likelihood of geometric coronary constraint by analyzing the 3-dimensional geometric interactions between the portion of the redo-TAV combination covered with the neo-skirt and aortic root. These findings suggest that even among Asian patients with smaller aortic valve complexes, careful selection of the initial Evolut implantation depth and the secondary S3 implantation position can significantly reduce severe geometric coronary constraint in TAV-in-TAV. When planning TAVR in younger low-risk patients, implantation depth and commissural alignment of the index TAV as well as the second TAV positioning during TAV-in-TAV should be carefully optimized to increase the feasibility of redo TAVR.
sections.limitations: First, this study evaluated only static geometric relationships and did not assess actual coronary blood flow. The association between VTA distance and hemodynamically significant flow compromise remains unvalidated. Fluid dynamics analysis and clinical outcome studies are needed to determine whether these geometric constraints result in clinically meaningful coronary flow impairment. Second, the VTA cut-off values used for stratification, particularly the 2.0-mm threshold, are empirical and were not validated against hemodynamic assessments or clinical events. Because the relationship between VTA and functional coronary impairment is likely continuous, future studies correlating CT-based metrics with flow/hemodynamic measurements and clinical outcomes are needed to determine the optimal thresholds. Third, the neo-skirt plane definition assumes full leaflet displacement and does not incorporate patient-specific leaflet overhang or native leaflet height. Fourth, leaflet overhang or incomplete displacement could alter both hemodynamics and geometric relationship between the TAV-in-TAV complex and aortic root, particularly at lower redo TAV positions. Future work should incorporate patient-specific leaflet modeling that includes both native and index TAV leaflets and validation against flow and clinical data. Fifth, only four patients (3.5%) were classified as severe geometric coronary constraints with low S3 implantation at node 4, which limited our ability to identify predictors of geometric coronary constraints in this subgroup. Sixth, our results cannot be applied to TAV-in-TAV configurations except S3-in-Evolut. Finally, CT cannot assess the leaflets of the native aortic valve or the neointimal (pseudo endothelial) coverage of the implanted TAV device. These unresected native leaflets and neointimal tissue may persist after the index TAVR and contribute to geometric coronary constraints.
sections.conclusions: In redo TAVR involving implantation of a balloon-expandable S3 valve within a prior supra-annular Evolut SEV in Asian patients, CT-identified geometric coronary constraints that may affect coronary access depend on native aortic root anatomy and the implantation depths of both the index and redo valves. Our findings suggest that preprocedural CT assessment of geometric coronary constraints may help identify patients requiring additional procedural planning for redo TAVR. However, the clinical impact of these geometric findings and optimal S3 positioning strategy require validation in actual redo-TAVR cases with clinical outcome assessment.

title: Association of Dietary Patterns and Genetic Risk With Cardiovascular Disease in UK Biobank Cancer Survivors
abstract: Background The extent to which diet influences cardiovascular risk in survivors of cancer is not well established. We therefore assessed how adherence to various dietary patterns relates to the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD) in this population. Method This study included 10 414 survivors of cancer from the UK Biobank who were free of CVD and had completed at least two 24‐hour dietary recalls. Adherence at baseline to the Alternative Healthy Eating Index 2010 (AHEI‐2010), alternate Mediterranean diet, dietary approaches to stop hypertension, and EAT‐Lancet diet was examined in relation to incident CVD, and Cox models were used to derive hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs for CVD incidence. Results The mean age of participants was 59.49±7.00 years, and 37% were men in our study. Over a median follow‐up of 13.12 years, 1331 incident CVD events were documented. In the fully adjusted model, the HRs for the highest versus lowest tertiles of adherence were 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72–0.97) for alternate Mediterranean diet, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.66–0.87) for AHEI‐2010, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.72–0.94) for dietary approaches to stop hypertension, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.74–0.97) for EAT‐Lancet. Specifically, higher adherence to the alternate Mediterranean diet, AHEI‐2010, dietary approaches to stop hypertension, and EAT‐Lancet diets was associated with lower risks of ischemic heart disease (HR, 0.77–0.85), while the AHEI‐2010, dietary approaches to stop hypertension, and EAT‐Lancet diets were also linked to reduced risk of heart failure (HR, 0.74–0.88) and the AHEI‐2010 and EAT‐Lancet diets with lower stroke risk (HR, 0.81–0.83). No significant interaction between the genetic risk of CVD and diet pattern was observed. Conclusions These results indicate that following a healthy diet is linked to a reduced risk of CVD among survivors of cancer, regardless of their genetic risk.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what are the clinical implications?: Our findings provide actionable dietary strategies for cardiovascular risk management in survivors of cancer, supporting the promotion of healthy dietary patterns.
sections.methods: All data generated or analyzed in this study can be obtained from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.study participants: The UK Biobank is a prospective, large‐scale cohort study that enrolled >500 000 participants aged 40 to 69 years from 22 centers throughout the United Kingdom between 2006 and 2010. Study methods and data collection procedures have been extensively documented in previous publications. 23 , 24 Approval for the study was granted by the North West Multi‐Centre Research Ethics Committee, and all participants gave written informed consent. It was conducted in accordance with UK Biobank data access protocols under approval number 300908. In this study, information on cancer diagnoses (excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer) was obtained via linkage with national cancer registries in England, Wales, and Scotland (details available at https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/showcase/docs/CancerLinkage.pdf ). Cancer cases were classified according to International Classification of Diseases , Tenth Revision ( ICD‐10 ) codes C00 to C96 (excluding C44), and Ninth Revision ( ICD‐9 ) codes 140 to 208 (excluding 173). 25 The participant selection process for this study is illustrated in Figure S1 . A total of 502 131 individuals were initially recruited; however, 365 380 were excluded due to missing dietary data. Individuals with no prior cancer diagnosis at baseline (n=125 595) and those with preexisting CVDs at baseline, including ischemic heart disease (IHD), heart failure (HF), and stroke (n=752), were also excluded. Ultimately, 10 404 survivors of cancer were included in the final analysis.
sections.outcomes: The primary outcomes included incident CVD events, encompassing total CVD and its major subtypes: IHD, HF, and stroke. Events were identified using ICD‐10 codes: I20 to I25 for IHD, I50 for HF, and I60 to I64 for stroke. 11 Health outcomes were determined through linkage with Hospital Episode Statistics and national death registries, with follow‐up extending from baseline to December 8, 2022, for participants in England and Wales, and to December 19, 2022, for those in Scotland.
sections.diet quality assessment: A 24‐hour web‐administered dietary questionnaire was used to measure intake in the UK Biobank. 26 Approximately 300 000 individuals were invited by email to complete 4 questionnaires between February 2011 and April 2012. Since the number of participants who completed 3 or 4 surveys was too small, we included only those who had completed at least 2 questionnaires in the calculation of the diet score on the basis of previous studies. 16 , 27 The alternate Mediterranean diet (aMED) score is derived from the Mediterranean dietary pattern originally proposed by Trichopoulou and later modified to reflect US dietary practices. 28 In this scoring system, participants receive 1 point for consuming amounts above the study median for whole grains, vegetables, nuts, legumes, fruits, and the ratio of monounsaturated to saturated fats, and fish, and 0 points for consumption below the median. In contrast, higher‐than‐median consumption of red and processed meats is scored 0, whereas lower consumption receives 1 point. A daily alcohol intake of 5 to 25 g earned 1 point, whereas all other consumption levels were scored 0. Across participants, aMED scores ranged from 0 for lowest adherence to 9 for highest adherence (Table S1 ). As a revised version of the Healthy Eating Index, the Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI) focuses on foods and nutrients linked to chronic disease prevention. 27 In the present study, we used the 2010 updated version, modified for application in the UK Biobank. 29 The score allocates 0 to 10 points across 11 dietary components. Transfat intake was excluded due to unavailable data, and seafood intake was used as a proxy for omega‐3 consumption. For each component—vegetables, whole grains, fruits and fruit juices, sugar‐sweetened beverages, nuts and legumes, sodium, red and processed meats, seafood, and alcohol—intermediate intakes were scored proportionally, while values outside the defined range received 0 or 10 points. Across participants, scores ranged between 0 and 100, with 0 denoting lowest and 100 denoting highest adherence (Table S2 ). The DASH diet was created with the goal of reducing blood pressure. 30 The DASH score used in this study was developed following the methodology of Fung et al. 31 Food groups were categorized into sex‐specific quintiles. Higher quintiles of fruits, whole grains, legumes, vegetables, nuts, low‐fat dairy, and lower sodium intake received higher scores, whereas higher intakes of sugar‐sweetened beverages, and red and processed meats received lower scores. Across participants, summed scores varied from 8 for lowest adherence to 40 for highest adherence (Table S3 ). We constructed an EAT‐Lancet diet index following a previous study based on key food groups, including whole grains, protein sources, tubers and starchy vegetables, fruits, vegetables, legumes, dairy, added fats, and sugars. 16 In this index, each component was scored from 0 to 10 proportionally up to the recommended intake, and from 10 to 0 for intakes above the recommendation. The overall score spanned 0 to 130, with higher scores indicating stronger adherence to the EAT‐Lancet diet (Table S4 ). For participants who completed at least two 24‐hour dietary questionnaires, dietary intake was calculated separately for each questionnaire and subsequently averaged. Dietary scores were generated on the basis of these mean values. A total of 136 751 participants with complete dietary data were then categorized into tertiles (tertiles 1, 2, and 3) according to the distribution of scores within the study population.
sections.assessment of covariates: In the UK Biobank cohort, information on covariates was collected using standardized questionnaires and laboratory procedures, including age (continuous), sex (female or male), race (White or other), educational attainment (college degree or not), smoking status (never or current/former), alcohol consumption (low‐ or high‐risk), body mass index, and physical activity levels. Race was self‐reported by participants in the UK Biobank and categorized according to the UK Biobank classification system (eg, White, Black, Asian, and others). Data on comorbidities, such as diabetes and hypertension, were obtained from ICD codes, self‐reports, or medication records. We also included biomarkers such as estimated glomerular filtration rate, hemoglobin A 1c , low‐density lipoprotein, high‐density lipoprotein, total cholesterol, and C‐reactive protein. Socioeconomic deprivation was assessed using the Townsend Deprivation Index, which is calculated from national census data and postal codes and considers factors including unemployment, household overcrowding, and car and home ownership; lower Townsend Deprivation Index scores indicate higher socioeconomic status. Data on preexisting conditions were collected from both self‐reports and hospital inpatient records. Participants were considered regularly physically active if they completed at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise weekly, 75 minutes of vigorous exercise weekly, or an equivalent mix of both. 23 Low‐risk drinking was characterized by moderate alcohol intake, meaning up to 1 daily drink for women and 2 for men (1 drink=8 g ethanol in the United Kingdom), with relatively consistent consumption. 23 The CVD polygenic risk score (PRS) was sourced from the UK Biobank release (“Standard PRS,” Category 301) and has been thoroughly validated. 16 Participants with PRS above the median were classified as “high genetic risk,” and those at or below the median as “low genetic risk,” consistent with previous studies. 16
sections.statistical analysis: Continuous variables were summarized as means±SDs, and categorical variables as percentages, with χ 2 tests applied to categorical data and 1‐way ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests used for continuous data. For missing covariate data, we applied multiple imputation using chained equations, creating 10 imputed data sets and combining the results according to Rubin's Rules. Details of variables and imputed missing data are shown in Table S5 . Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs were calculated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression to assess associations. Independent variables in the analysis were the dietary scores, which were categorized into tertiles to create comparable adherence groups, with the lowest tertile serving as the reference. Trends were assessed by modeling tertiles as continuous variables. The classification of dietary data into tertiles was based on the distribution of dietary variables in the entire UK Biobank cohort. We fitted a series of progressively adjusted models, with model 1 controlling for age, sex, and race; model 2 further controlled for Townsend Deprivation Index, education level, estimated glomerular filtration rate, hemoglobin A 1c , C‐reactive protein, total cholesterol, high‐density lipoprotein, low‐density lipoprotein, smoking, alcohol intake, body mass index, physical activity, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease on the basis of model 1. The continuous diet scores were modeled using restricted cubic splines with 3 knots to assess potential nonlinearity in their associations with the outcome. Kaplan–Meier analysis was applied to determine cumulative CVD incidence across dietary score categories, with log‐rank tests used to evaluate differences. We evaluated additive interactions between genetic risk and dietary patterns by calculating the relative excess risk due to interaction and the attributable proportion, each accompanied by a 95% CI. Subgroup analyses in the UK Biobank were conducted by stratifying participants according to age, sex, alcohol consumption, smoking status, genetic risk, physical activity, and presence of hypertension. To assess the robustness of our findings, we conducted several sensitivity analyses: (1) excluding participants who died within the first 12 months of follow‐up; (2) excluding those who developed CVD within the first 12 months; (3) restricting the analysis to complete cases; (4) excluding participants with baseline diabetes or hypertension; and (5) further adjusting for history of chemotherapy and genetic risk as a continuous variable. All analyses were performed using R version 4.2.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria), and a 2‐sided P value of <0.05 was regarded as statistically significant.
sections.results_1: Baseline characteristics of the UK Biobank participants are summarized in Table 1 . The average age of participants was 59.49±7.00 years, with 37% being men. Survivors of cancer who developed CVD tended to be older, have higher rates of smoking, greater body mass index, lower levels of physical activity, lower educational attainment, and a higher prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease at baseline. In contrast, participants in the highest tertiles of the aMED, DASH, AHEI‐2010, and EAT‐Lancet diet scores were more likely to be women, engage in more physical activity, have higher education, lower body mass index, smoke less, consume less alcohol, and have fewer comorbidities. Additional details are provided in Tables S6 through S9 . Figures S2 and S3 show the distribution of different dietary patterns among the participants included in our analysis and in the entire UK Biobank cohort. Across 13.12 years of median follow‐up, 1331 participants developed CVD, including 898 cases of IHD, 289 cases of stroke, and 363 cases of HF. Restricted cubic spline analyses showed no evidence of nonlinear associations between dietary scores and CVD risk, with P values for nonlinearity of 0.097 for aMED (Figure 1A ), 0.158 for AHEI‐2010 (Figure 1B ), 0.301 for DASH (Figure 1C ), and 0.250 for EAT‐Lancet (Figure 1D ). The Kaplan–Meier curves demonstrated a significantly reduced cumulative incidence of CVD in the highest tertile compared with the lowest (Figure 2 ). Each of the 4 dietary patterns—aMED, AHEI‐2010, DASH, and EAT‐Lancet—showed an inverse association with CVD risk (Table 2 ). The highest versus lowest tertiles yielded HRs of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72–0.97) for aMED, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.66–0.87) for AHEI‐2010, 0.82 (95% CI, 0.72–0.94) for DASH, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.74–0.97) for EAT‐Lancet, with all trends statistically significant ( P ‐trend<0.001) in the fully adjusted model. Each score was analyzed per 1‐SD increase to allow direct comparison; AHEI‐2010 showed the numerically strongest inverse association, with a 13% lower CVD risk (Table S10 ). In cumulative analyses based on the number of scores above the median, a graded inverse association was observed, indicating progressively lower CVD risk with increasing adherence (Table S11 ). A consistent association pattern was observed across different cardiovascular outcomes. Specifically, greater adherence to the aMED pattern at baseline was linked to a reduced risk of IHD, with an HR of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.64–0.92; P for trend=0.003; Table 3 ). Similarly, greater adherence to the AHEI‐2010 was linked to a reduced risk of IHD (HR, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.66–0.92]; P for trend=0.003), stroke (HR, 0.83 [95% CI, 0.67–0.99]; P for trend=0.043), and HF (HR, 0.80 [95% CI, 0.70–0.93]; P for trend=0.007). Participants with higher DASH scores also showed a lower likelihood of developing IHD (HR, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.70–0.96]; P for trend=0.015), and HF (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.75–0.98]; P for trend=0.042). Furthermore, greater adherence to the EAT‐Lancet diet was associated with reduced risks of IHD (HR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.73–0.99]; P for trend=0.045), stroke (HR, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.64–0.95]; P for trend=0.043), and HF (HR, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.63–0.89]; P for trend=0.014). Figure 3 presents the joint associations of diet quality and PRS with CVD incidence. Relative to individuals with both elevated genetic risk (PRS median or greater) and poor adherence to the aMED pattern (aMED less than median), those who maintained high aMED adherence despite high genetic risk had a 21% reduction in CVD risk, while participants with low genetic risk but low aMED adherence experienced a 25% lower risk. Moreover, individuals with both low genetic risk and high aMED adherence had a 31% lower CVD risk. Similar patterns were observed for the AHEI‐2010, DASH, and EAT‐Lancet dietary scores, as presented in Figure 3 . Furthermore, we conducted an additive interaction analysis and found no interaction between dietary patterns and genetic risk (Table S12 ). In sensitivity analyses, the associations remained stable across multiple models (Tables S13–S18 ). Stratified analyses yielded consistent results (Figures S3–S7 ), and no significant interactions were detected. In addition, analyses stratified by cancer type (Table S19 ) showed that, although some associations were not statistically significant, interaction tests indicated no significant heterogeneity (all P >0.05).
sections.discussion: Among survivors of cancer enrolled in the UK Biobank, those who maintained higher adherence to the aMED, AHEI‐2010, DASH, and EAT‐Lancet dietary patterns showed significantly lower CVD risk over a median 13.12‐year follow‐up. Specifically, participants in the highest tertile of adherence showed a 17% lower risk for the aMED, 23% lower for the AHEI‐2010, 18% lower for the DASH, and 15% lower for the EAT‐Lancet. The association between adherence to healthy dietary patterns and cardiovascular risk among survivors of cancer has been explored in several previous studies. For example, Ergas et al studied 3415 women recently diagnosed with breast cancer and found that those most closely following the DASH diet had lower risks of multiple cardiovascular outcomes, including HF, arrhythmias, valvular disease, cardiac arrest, and CVD‐related death, compared with women in the lowest adherence group. 21 They also reported that higher scores on a healthy plant‐based diet index were linked to a lower risk of HF, while stronger adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with reduced odds of developing arrhythmias. 21 However, Ergas et al did not observe significant associations between adherence to these dietary patterns and the risks of IHD or stroke. Differences in study populations may partly explain the inconsistent findings. Ergas et al focused exclusively on women with breast cancer from a US population, whereas our study included survivors of multiple cancer types, both sexes, and a European population. Such heterogeneity in cancer type, sex distribution, and geographic background may differentially influence cardiovascular risk profiles and diet–disease associations. Lan et al conducted a cross‐sectional study involving roughly 3400 individuals who had survived childhood cancer, and they observed that higher adherence to the AHEI‐2015 (odds ratio, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.75–1.03]), DASH (odds ratio, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.71–1.01]), and aMED (odds ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.84–1.00]) dietary patterns was associated with a trend toward reduced CVD risk among women, while in men, only higher AHEI‐2015 scores were also linked to a lower, though not statistically significant, risk. 22 Bellissimo et al conducted a cross‐sectional study involving 113 survivors of cancer with various cancer types and found that better dietary fat and carbohydrate quality—specifically, higher intake of unsaturated fatty acids and fiber—was associated with improved cardiac function, whereas greater sucrose consumption was linked to poorer cardiac function. 20 Furthermore, Bonaccio et al examined around 800 long‐term survivors of cancer and reported that individuals who more closely followed a Mediterranean dietary pattern had reduced risks of cardiovascular death. 32 However, the above studies primarily focused on specific cancer populations, such as patients with breast cancer or adult survivors of childhood cancer, and were often limited by small sample sizes or cross‐sectional designs within US populations. Consequently, the evidence on the association between dietary patterns and CVD risk among survivors of cancer remains insufficient. In contrast with these prior studies, our investigation was based on a large prospective cohort of 10 404 European survivors of cancer and comprehensively evaluated 4 different dietary patterns in relation to both overall and specific cardiovascular outcomes. We observed that greater adherence to healthy dietary patterns was associated with lower risks of overall CVD, including IHD, stroke, and HF. These findings provide robust population‐based evidence from a British cohort, suggesting that healthy dietary patterns may confer cardiovascular benefits not only in the general population but also among individuals with a history of cancer. Previous studies in the general population have demonstrated that PRSs for CVD capture cumulative genetic susceptibility and can substantially improve cardiovascular risk stratification beyond traditional risk factors. 33 , 34 , 35 Importantly, several previous studies have explored the interplay between genetic predisposition and dietary intake in relation to CVD risk, 36 , 37 evidence on whether PRSs modify the association between diet and CVD among survivors of cancer is still scarce. In our analysis, we observed that the inverse relationship between adherence to a healthy diet and CVD risk was largely independent of CVD PRS. While no significant statistical interaction was detected, the combined analysis indicated that greater adherence to a healthy diet might partially counterbalance an elevated genetic susceptibility to CVD. Overall, these results indicate that adherence to a healthy diet could play a significant role in preventing CVD among survivors of cancer, regardless of their inherited genetic risk. Our results extend the existing literature by demonstrating that, among survivors of cancer, a population at elevated cardiovascular risk, higher adherence to healthy dietary patterns was associated with lower CVD risk across both high and low genetic risk groups, supporting the notion that genetic predisposition does not negate the cardiovascular benefits of a healthy diet. The cardiovascular benefits of Mediterranean, DASH, AHEI‐2010, and EAT‐Lancet–style diets in survivors of cancer likely operate through multiple, converging mechanisms. Adopting healthy dietary patterns, as assessed in this study, supports higher consumption of plant‐based foods, whole grains, nuts, and fish, which may confer protective effects against chronic diseases and early death through diverse biological processes. 38 Evidence suggests that higher intake of dietary fiber, vegetables, and fruits can lower cholesterol and blood pressure, decrease inflammation and platelet aggregation, and enhance vascular as well as immune function. 39 , 40 Recent meta‐analyses have shown that higher dietary fiber intake is linked to a lower risk of CVD. 41 , 42 Nuts, seeds, vegetables, fruits, and whole grains are rich in antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, carotenoids, and phenolic compounds, which neutralize free radicals and limit oxidative damage. 43 These nutrients may also reduce low‐density lipoprotein oxidation, platelet aggregation, and inflammation, thereby helping to prevent arterial plaque formation. 43 , 44 Together, these effects may help mitigate treatment‐induced endothelial damage and reduce persistent prothrombotic and proatherogenic activity after cancer therapy.
sections.strengths and limitations: Key strengths of this study are its prospective design, long‐term follow‐up, use of rigorously validated dietary scores, and reliance on clinically verified cardiovascular outcomes with high diagnostic reliability. Nonetheless, some limitations must be noted. First, the lack of detailed information on cancer characteristics, including tumor stage, histological type, and specific treatments, as well as data on cancer recurrence, limited our ability to assess cardiovascular risks associated with specific therapies. Second, although the data set encompassed a wide range of cancer types, the sample size for each subtype was relatively small, limiting our ability to reliably determine if the relationship between diet and cardiovascular risk differed across cancer subtypes. Third, as in all observational studies, the possibility of residual confounding remains despite controlling for a wide range of covariates, including lifestyle factors linked to healthy eating. Moreover, selection bias may be present because participants in the UK Biobank are volunteers, with repeat assessors tending to be older and more educated than the overall population. Finally, only baseline dietary data were collected, and we were unable to account for potential changes in dietary habits or other covariates over time. Future research should therefore explore how longitudinal changes in dietary patterns contribute to the risk of CVD.
sections.conclusions_1: In this extensive UK population–based cohort of survivors of cancer, higher adherence to the aMED, AHEI‐2010, DASH, and EAT‐Lancet diets was linked to a reduced risk of CVD, including IHD, HF, and stroke. These results emphasize the importance of integrating regular evaluations of dietary quality into survivorship care strategies and underscore the need for additional research aimed at establishing dietary guidelines specifically designed for individuals who have survived cancer.

title: Effectiveness of an Intervention to Improve Guideline‐Directed Medications for Patients With Acute Heart Failure: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: Background Guideline‐directed medical therapy during the transitional period is crucial for improving outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. We investigated whether a simplified transitional care intervention could increase guideline‐directed medical therapy adherence in patients with acute heart failure (HF). Methods This multicenter, open‐label randomized trial enrolled 982 patients with acute HF. The transitional care intervention included a discharge checklist, HF education, and telephone monitoring. The primary outcome was achievement of high guideline adherence indicator, defined as the prescription of all 3 guideline‐directed medical therapy drugs (renin‐angiotensin system blockades, beta blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) at 6 months. Both modified intention‐to‐treat and per‐intervention analyses were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of intervention components. Results Among 982 participants (mean age, 62.4±15.5 years; 64.5% male), there was no statistical difference in the proportion achieving a high guideline adherence indicator between the intervention and control groups (49.6% versus 44.6%; OR, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.86–1.45; P =0.37). No significant differences were observed in the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score or clinical outcomes. In the per‐intervention analysis, patients who received all components showed significantly higher guideline adherence indicator achievement compared with those who received no components (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 1.56 [95% CI, 1.07–2.27], P =0.02). Conclusions In this randomized trial of patients with acute HF, although the simplified transitional care intervention did not increase high guideline adherence indicator achievement, implementation of all intervention components was associated with improved guideline adherence. Our findings emphasize that implementation fidelity is the key challenge in optimizing transitional care for HF management. Registration URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT04900584 .
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease
