sections.aca regulates sirt1-mediated deacetylati: Next, we sought to explore the potential molecular mechanisms by which ACA regulates Pkm2 to exert its therapeutic effects. NAD serves as an important co-substrate for the Sirtuins family, which participates in maintaining mitochondrial metabolic homeostasis, neurodegeneration, and regulating immune inflammation by sensing changes in NAD levels [ 35 , 36 ]. ACA selectively upregulated Sirt1 mRNA in LPS-stimulated microglia, whereas other Sirtuin family members (Sirt2-7) showed no obvious changes under our conditions (Fig. 5 A). Consistent with this, STRING protein-protein interaction analysis of key NAD-catabolic genes (Gapdh, Pkm, Aldoa, Eno1, Eno1b) together with Sirt1-7 identified Pkm and Sirt1 as central hubs with a strong predicted interaction, supporting a plausible connection between Sirt1 and Pkm-related NAD metabolism (Fig. 5 B). Cellular IF further confirmed that ACA attenuated the LPS-induced upregulation of Pkm2 in BV2 cells while enhancing the expression of Sirt1 (Fig. 5 C-E). Sirt1 relies on NAD to maintain its deacetylase activity [ 37 ]. Recent studies have found that Sirt1 can inhibit the activity of Pkm2 through deacetylation [ 38 ]. Overexpression of Sirt1 in BV2 cells was successfully achieved and confirmed by plasmid transfection (Fig. 5 F). Consistent with previous studies [ 34 ], co-immunoprecipitation (CO-IP) confirmed a physiological interaction between Sirt1 and Pkm2 when overexpress Sirt1 and Pkm2 (Fig. 5 G-H), and inflammatory stimulation was accompanied by increased Pkm2 acetylation (Fig. 5 I-J). To determine whether Pkm2 deacetylation is mediated by Sirt1 rather than class I/II histone deacetylases (HDACs), we treated LPS-activated BV2 cells with the SIRT1 inhibitor sirtinol and the pan-class I/II HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA) at literature-informed [ 38 ], non-cytotoxic working concentrations that was verified by Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assays before use (Fig. S7A). We showed that only sirtinol increased Pkm2 acetylation, suggesting that the deacetylation of Pkm2 in activated microglia under inflammatory stimulation may predominantly depend on Sirt1 activity (Fig. 5 K-L). ACA reduced LPS-induced Pkm2 acetylation, and this effect was reversed by sirtinol (Fig. 5 M-N). Consistently, plasmid experiments showed that Pkm2 overexpression increased its acetylation, whereas Sirt1 overexpression suppressed Pkm2 acetylation, and sirtinol partially abrogated this suppression (Fig. 5 O-P). To pinpoint the critical acetylation sites of Pkm2 in this inflammatory state, we performed acetylation modification proteomics on BV2 cells stimulated with LPS. The Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis revealed that Pkm2 underwent acetylation at five specific lysine residues: K311, K505, K166, K433, and K270 in response to inflammatory stress (Fig. 6 A). To further examine the relationship between these sites and Sirt1, we co-transfected K166A, K270A, or K433A mutants with or without Plas-Sirt1 and performed Co-IP assays. Among these mutants, K270A was associated with a marked reduction in detectable Pkm2-Sirt1 interaction (Fig. 6 D-E). This finding supports the view that K270 may represent an important deacetylation site associated with Pkm2-Sirt1 interaction. To validate this hypothesis, we mutated K166, K270, and K433 to glutamine (Q) to simulate acetylation, followed by co-transfection with or without Plas-Sirt1. Consistent with previous results, we found that overexpression of Sirt1 diminished the acetylation level at the K270 site (Fig. 6 F-G). Groups annotated with different letters (A to D) differ significantly, whereas groups sharing a letter are not significantly different Next, we interrogated the three-dimensional structure of Pkm2 (AlphaFold model AF- P52480 -F1, residues 1-531) with emphasis on the K270 acetylation site and performed a structure-guided virtual screen from a commercial compound database (MCE Compound Library) containing 80,000 inhibitors. Based on the docking scores of small molecules within the amino acid pocket containing the K270 site of Pkm2, we concentrated our efforts on identifying the top five small molecule inhibitors, including HY-112431 A, HY113082 , HY-P0046, HY-F0004, and HY-106443B, which have previously been reported to be associated with inflammation, metabolic disorders, and neurological diseases [ 39 – 45 ]. Guided by previous work, we screened candidate inhibitors in BV2 cells using CCK-8 viability assays and reverse transcription and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qRT‑PCR) for iNOS, and identified five compounds (HY-112431A, HY-113082, HY-106443B, HY-F0004 and HY-P0046) at concentrations that preserved cell viability while exhibiting reproducible anti-inflammatory activity (Fig. S7A-J). CO-IP assays showed that several candidate compounds reduced Pkm2 acetylation under LPS stimulation, with HY-113082 producing the most pronounced effect (Fig. 6 J-K). Molecular docking analysis further revealed that HY-113082 was accommodated within the binding pocket of Pkm2 and established a direct hydrogen bond with the K270 residue, with a bond length of 2.2 Å, which indicates a particularly tight and stable interaction (Fig. 6 L). Functionally, HY-113082 markedly attenuated LPS-induced transcriptional upregulation of proinflammatory mediators, confirming its potent anti-inflammatory activity in BV2 cells (Fig. 6 M). To determine the optimal intraocular concentration of HY-113082, we first evaluated its effects on retinal morphology following IR injury. HE staining revealed that IR markedly reduced the thickness of the IPL, whereas intravitreal administration of HY-113082 mitigated this structural loss in a dose-dependent manner, with 5 nM exhibiting the most pronounced protective effect (Fig. S8K-L). Based on these findings, we proceeded to in vivo experiments using the selected concentration. IF staining of RGCs showed that HY-113082 significantly improved RGCs survival after IR injury, and co-administration with ACA was accompanied by further improvement (Fig. 6 N-O). Consistent with these histological observations, Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) demonstrated that HY-113082 alone reduced the IR-induced upregulation of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, whereas the combination of HY-113082 with ACA elicited an even stronger suppression of these pro-inflammatory cytokines (Fig. 6 P). Moreover, WB analysis indicated that HY-113082 decreased the ratio of p-P65/P65, while co-treatment with ACA further reinforced this inhibitory effect on NF-κB activation (Fig. 6 Q-R). Besides, Targeting the Pkm2-K270 site with HY-113082 favorably modulated immunometabolism, as intracellular NAD levels increased and rose further with ACA co-treatment (Fig. S8M). HY-113082 also curtailed LPS-evoked mtROS and restored mitochondrial membrane potential, while ACA potentiated these improvements in mitochondrial metabolic function (Fig. S8N-Q). Taken together, these results support that Pkm2-K270 is a functionally relevant acetylation site in activated microglia and that HY-113082, a K270-pocket-prioritized compound, can phenocopy part of the anti-inflammatory and mitochondrial benefits observed with ACA. In combination with the Sirt1-dependent deacetylation evidence above, these data are consistent with a model in which ACA-associated microglial protection involves, at least in part, Sirt1-linked regulation of Pkm2 acetylation at K270.
sections.knockout of microglial pkm2 abolishes th: To investigate the role of microglial Pkm2 in retinal IR injury, we inserted LoxP sites into exon 10 of the Pkm2 gene and generated conditional knockout mice using the LoxP/Cre system, with homozygosity confirmed by PCR genotyping (Fig. 7 A-C). Baseline retinal architecture was indistinguishable between Pkm2 fl/− Cx3cr1 Cre and Pkm2 fl/fl Cx3cr1 Cre mice, as shown by HE sections and quantification of IPL thickness (Fig. 7 D-E). After retinal IR, Pkm2 fl/fl Cx3cr1 Cre mice displayed higher RGCs survival than Pkm2 fl/− Cx3cr1 Cre controls, and intravitreal ACA further improved RGCs preservation (Fig. 7 F-G). However, combining ACA with the K270-targeting inhibitor HY-113082 in the knockout background did not yield additional neuroprotection (Fig. 7 F-G), indicating that the inhibitor’s efficacy depends on microglial Pkm2. Consistently, microglial activation was attenuated in Pkm2 fl/fl Cx3cr1 Cre retinas, as evidenced by reduced Iba-1 + cell density engaging RGCs axons within the ganglion cells layer and a shift away from hypertrophic, amoeboid, and phagocytic morphology, and ACA produced further reductions, whereas HY-113082 conferred no extra effect in the knockout (Fig. 7 H-I). ELISA of retinal homogenates showed that Pkm2 deletion lowered IR-induced IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, and that ACA further suppressed these cytokines, whereas the anti-inflammatory effect of HY-113082 was not apparent in the absence of microglial Pkm2 (Fig. 7 J). In line with these in vivo data, LPS-challenged BV2 cells transfected with siPkm2 did not gain additional suppression of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α when HY-113082 was added to ACA (Fig. 7 K). Fig. 7 Knocking out Pkm2 in microglia reduces retinal IR injury and abrogates HY-113028-mediated enhancement of ACA’s protection. ( A ) Schematic diagram of Pkm2 fl. mouse construction. ( B and C ) Agarose gel electrophoresis was used to identify mouse genotypes. ( D ) Representative HE-stained images of retinal sections between Pkm2 fl/− Cx3cr1-Cre and Pkm2 fl/fl -Cx3cr1-Cre groups. Red scale bar, 200 μm; Black scale bar, 50 μm. ( E ) Measurements of retinal IPL thickness. n = 4/group. ( F ) Representative retinal whole mounts labeled with RBPMS (red) and TUJ-1 (green) showing RGCs among groups at 7 days after retinal IR injury. Scale bar, 100 μm. ( G ) Quantification of RGCs survival rate. n = 4/group. ( H ) Representative retinal whole mounts labeled with Iba-1 (red) and TUJ-1 (green) showing microglia in the GCL layer among groups at 3 days after retinal IR injury. Scale bar, 100 μm. ( I ) Statistical analysis of Iba-1 + microglia density. n = 4/group. ( J ) Bar plots showing the protein levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α among groups at 3 days after retinal IR injury measured by ELISA. n = 4/group. ( K ) Bar plots showing the mRNA levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in BV2 cells among groups. n = 4/group. The data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA [(G), (I), (J), and (K)] or Student’s t-test (E), and all data are expressed as the mean ± SD. ns, nonsignificant, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, and**** p < 0.0001 Collectively, these data indicate that microglial Pkm2 deletion is associated with enhanced ACA-mediated neuroprotection, as reflected by reduced RGCs loss and dampened retinal inflammation after IR. Moreover, in the microglial Pkm2-deficient background, the added benefit of the K270-targeting inhibitor HY-113082 was no longer evident, supporting target dependence. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that ACA protects RGCs via anti-inflammatory mechanisms and may concurrently improve mitochondrial metabolism in association with reduced microglial Pkm2 K270 acetylation.
sections.aca counters rgcs apoptosis via microgli: To further validate our in vivo findings and explore the interaction between microglia and RGCs, we isolated primary RGCs (pRGCs) and established a co-culture system of pRGCs and BV2 cells to determine whether ACA exerts its effects on RGCs through modulation of microglia (Fig. S9A-B). We initially extracted pRGCs and confirmed their identity through IF staining for POU domain class 4 transcription factor 1 (BRN3A) and TUJ-1 (Fig. S9A). The WB analysis showed that following oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R), pro-apoptotic markers (Bax, cleaved-casp3) significantly increased while the anti-apoptotic marker (Bcl-2) significantly decreased (Fig. S9C-F). Upon ACA treatment, Bax levels significantly decreased, while cleaved-casp3 showed no significant change, and Bcl-2 levels were significantly elevated (Fig. S9C-F). Notably, when BV2 cells and RGCs were subjected to OGD/R separately before co-culture, pro-apoptotic markers (Bax and cleaved-casp3) in RGCs significantly increased compared to RGCs undergoing OGD/R alone, while anti-apoptotic markers (Bcl-2) further declined (Fig. S9C-F). This indicates that microglia exacerbate RGCs damage in the context of hypoxic-ischemic injury. When BV2 cells and pRGCs were separately treated with ACA after OGD/R and then co-cultured, Bax and cleaved-casp3 in pRGCs were significantly reduced and Bcl-2 was increased compared with pRGCs treated directly with ACA after OGD/R (Fig. S9C-F). These findings support the possibility that ACA may enhance the protective role of microglia on RGCs. Given the damaging role of Pkm2 during hypoxic-ischemic conditions, we overexpressed Pkm2 in BV2 cells prior to co-culture with RGCs (Fig. S9G). We found that BV2 cells overexpressing Pkm2 increased RGCs apoptosis (Bax and cleaved-casp3) relative to the pcDNA3.1 control group by decreasing their anti-apoptotic capacity (Bcl-2) (Fig. S9H-K). Additionally, we previously confirmed that the Sirt1 inhibitor, sirtinol, weakens the protective effects of ACA. Upon treatment with sirtinol and ACA after OGD/R, we observed a significant increase in the pro-apoptotic marker Bax and cleaved-caspase-3, along with a decrease in Bcl-2 levels, compared to the ACA-only group (Fig. S9L-O). To assess whether inhibiting the K270 site aligns with our in vivo findings, we treated BV2 cells with ACA and HY-113082 after separate OGD/R modeling and subsequently co-cultured them with RGCs. We found HY-113082 significantly enhanced the therapeutic effects of ACA, resulting in a marked decrease of Bax and cleaved-casp3, while an increase in anti-apoptotic levels (Bcl-2) in RGCs (Fig. S9P-S). In summary, these results suggest that the protective effect of ACA on RGCs in this in vitro system is largely associated with its modulation of microglial state rather than a direct action on RGCs alone. Furthermore, manipulating Pkm2 expression and its K270-associated regulation in microglia appears to influence the efficacy of ACA in protecting RGCs.
sections.discussion: This study provides evidence supporting intravitreal ACA as a potential neuroprotective strategy for preserving RGCs after retinal IR, possibly through reprogramming microglial immunometabolism. Our data indicate that retinal IR induces pronounced inflammatory activation and mitochondrial dysfunction, accompanied by increased NAD catabolic pathway activity in microglia. ACA treatment was associated with attenuation of these changes, relative preservation of retinal NAD levels, and improvement of mitochondrial structural and functional readouts, together with reduced neuroinflammatory responses and RGCs loss. Mechanistically, the present data suggest that ACA regulates Pkm2 acetylation in a Sirt1-dependent context, with K270 appearing to be a functionally relevant regulatory site. Consistent with this, genetic reduction of Pkm2 enhanced the protective effect of ACA, and the K270-directed inhibitor HY-113,082 decreased Pkm2 acetylation and further increased ACA-associated protection in vivo. This additional effect was no longer observed in microglia-specific Pkm2 conditional knockout mice, supporting the dependence of HY-113,082 on microglial Pkm2 in this context. Retinal IR is characterized by microglial activation and aggregation around neurons, altering the immune microenvironment through increased cytokine and chemokine secretion and vascular permeability, leads to rapid loss of RGCs with thinning of IPL and pronounced metabolic perturbations, with microglial activation driving and exacerbating this degeneration [ 46 ]. Prior studies indicated that modulating microglial neuroinflammation could protect RGCs, although the directness or indirectness of this relationship remains incompletely resolved. In our study, scRNA-seq mapped retina-wide transcriptional changes and highlighted an immune-metabolic response centered in microglia, while complementary in vivo and in vitro experiments showed that IR-associated inflammation coincides with bioenergetic stress characterized by diminished NAD, and disrupted mitochondrial structure and function. Although these observations place retinal IR within an immunometabolic framework in which metabolic disequilibrium co-evolves with inflammatory activation, our interpretation is still based primarily on dissociation-based scRNA-seq and endpoint molecular assays rather than direct metabolic flux measurements. Accordingly, future studies incorporating real-time and cell type-resolved metabolic flux analyses will be important for refining this framework. Early studies have shown that ACA can mitigate cardiac IR injury by reducing ROS. However, the specific mechanisms underlying this effect remain unclear [ 47 ]. As research increasingly elucidates actions of ACA beyond glucose lowering, encompassing anti-inflammatory, mitochondrial, and organ-protective effects, ACA, alongside rapamycin, metformin, and NAD enhancers, is considered one of the most promising interventions for robustly delaying aging [ 48 ]. Our data in the retinas showed that ACA conferred measurable neuroprotection and immune quieting in acute IR injury. We demonstrated that intravitreal administration of ACA protects the retina against IR injury, as reflected by partial preservation of IPL thickness and improved RGCs survival. Consistently, GO analysis revealed significant upregulation of pathways related to phototransduction and visual perception, which collectively substantiated the neuroprotective potential of ACA to rescue retinal neuronal injury. From a translational perspective, it is also worth noting that retinal IR is frequently used as an experimental proxy for injurious components that appear across several vision-threatening disorders, including diabetic retinopathy (DR) and glaucoma, where ischemia or hypoxia, metabolic stress, and neuroinflammation can converge to promote progressive neurodegeneration [ 2 ]. In DR, where chronic hyperglycemia and retinal metabolic stress are accompanied by inflammatory amplification and microglial activation [ 49 , 50 ], ACA is conceptually attractive not only because it is an established metabolic drug, but also because its anti-inflammatory and mitochondrial-modulating properties reported in other organs raise the possibility that it could influence the retinal inflammatory microenvironment in a manner complementary to vascular-targeted therapies. In glaucoma and related optic neuropathies, in which RGC vulnerability is increasingly understood to reflect an interaction between mechanical stress, metabolic fragility, and immune activation, our findings provide a mechanistic rationale to consider whether ACA might be leveraged to stabilize NAD-centered metabolic resilience and thereby restrain maladaptive inflammatory signaling [ 51 , 52 ]. Importantly, these implications should be interpreted cautiously, because the present study does not directly model the chronic pathophysiology of DR or glaucoma, and it remains to be established whether ACA delivers durable benefit when injury evolves over longer time scales. Accordingly, future work will need to evaluate ACA in retinal IR-related disease contexts, including DR and glaucoma, with careful consideration of dosing, treatment window, route of administration, and long-term safety, to clarify how broadly the immunometabolic framework proposed here may extend beyond the acute IR setting. Microglia, the principal resident immune cells of the central nervous system, can perpetuate tissue damage when dysregulated and thereby endanger neuronal survival through excessive inflammation [ 53 ]. Owing to the neuroanatomical continuity of the retina with the brain, a feed-forward loop ensues in which microglial activation amplifies RGC dysfunction and, as injured RGCs release damage-associated signals, oxidative stress intensifies and damages mitochondrial membranes and mitochondrial DNA, diminishing bioenergetic capacity and neural transmission [ 54 ]. Prior evidence that ACA suppresses hypothalamic gliosis and cytokine production substantiates its anti-neuroinflammatory profile [ 55 , 56 ]. Taken together, these observations are consistent with the possibility that ACA can restrain neuroinflammatory responses. Concordant with these observations, our in vivo and in vitro experiments demonstrate that ACA attenuates microglial activation, lowers M1-associated markers, increases M2-associated markers, and dampens NF-κB signaling. While these data support microglia as a major contributor to the protective effects observed in our models, a limitation is that we did not mechanistically validate ACA’s effects on other resident immune cells of the retina. Future work should delineate modulatory effects of ACA on these populations to refine our understanding of the retinal immune microenvironment. Mounting work indicates that mitochondrial metabolism shapes myeloid effector states, and ACA has been reported to reprogram macrophages toward a salutary M2-like phenotype [ 21 ]. Consistent with these observations and with evidence that ACA reverses pre-degenerative metabolic imbalance in Leigh syndrome mice [ 20 ], we showed that ACA was associated with reduced microglial metabolic stress, including attenuation of NAD catabolic signatures, improvement of mitochondrial ultrastructure, and partial correction of bioenergetic dysfunction. These findings suggest that ACA engages additional metabolic regulatory nodes that influence neuroinflammatory progression and support a model in which ACA modulates microglial immunity through mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming. In line with this framework, our co-culture experiments indicate that, although direct ACA treatment of OGD/R-injured RGCs conferred only limited benefit, a more pronounced anti-apoptotic effect occurred when RGCs were co-cultured with ACA-pretreated microglia. This pattern is consistent with the possibility that ACA alters the microglial state in a manner that is more supportive of neuronal survival. One possible explanation is that ACA shifts microglia toward a less pro-inflammatory and more reparative phenotype, while also preserving NAD homeostasis and thereby improving the metabolic milieu available to stressed neurons. Although our data indicate that ACA is associated with mitigation of retinal IR injury in parallel with reduced NAD catabolism, our scRNA-seq analysis also revealed concurrent down-modulation of glycolysis, pyruvate metabolism, and ATP metabolic programs. The extent to which these pathways are directly regulated by ACA, as opposed to changing secondarily with inflammatory resolution, remains unclear and will require further mechanistic dissection in future studies. Due to the significant influence of alternative splicing on the activity of Pkm, two mutually exclusive exons 9 form Pkm1, and exon 10 gives rise to Pkm2, thereby presenting different active conformations [ 57 ]. Under physiological conditions, Pkm2 predominantly exists as a tetramer in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, but hypoxia or altered metabolic states promote the dimeric form, which supports transcriptional programs and inflammatory signaling [ 58 , 59 ]. In contrast, Pkm1 remains a constitutively active tetramer that drives oxidative ATP production, highlighting the isoform-specific metabolic roles of Pkm [ 60 ]. In our study, we observed that Pkm1 protein levels did not change significantly in the acute phase of retinal IR injury, while Pkm2 was robustly upregulated, suggesting selective involvement of Pkm2 in IR-induced pathology. Pkm2 has gained attention for its dual function in metabolism and inflammation and is increasingly being explored as a potential therapeutic target in neuroinflammatory disorders [ 61 ]. It can act as a coactivator for transcription factors implicated in the activation of the hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α), signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3), which regulate proinflammatory genes [ 62 ]. Elevated Pkm2 expression correlates with enhanced metabolic demand and M1-biased polarization of microglia [ 63 ]. Beyond polarization, Pkm2 facilitates microglial migration to sites of injury, as demonstrated by α-synuclein-mediated engagement of Pkm2 that drives metabolic reprogramming and enhances migration following spinal cord injury [ 64 ]. Importantly, accumulating evidence also indicates that Pkm2 regulates mitochondrial metabolism in addition to inflammation. Pkm2 translocation into the nucleus has been shown to influence mitochondrial biogenesis and redox balance, which links its conformational state to bioenergetic stress responses [ 65 , 66 ]. These studies support a model in which Pkm2 acts at the intersection of inflammatory signaling and metabolic rewiring. While we do not exclude that Pkm2 may also engage other metabolic programs that shape microglial immunity, our current readouts and sampling windows indicate a predominant involvement of NAD catabolic processes in retinal IR, although this inference will require validation with expanded cohorts and orthogonal metabolic assays in future work. In this context, our work demonstrated that ACA suppresses IR-induced Pkm2 upregulation and potentiates the protective effects of Pkm2 deletion, thereby supporting the possibility that ACA may act as a pharmacological enhancer of Pkm2-targeted interventions. Complementary work in macrophages has shown that Pkm2 knockdown prevents LPS-induced M1 polarization [ 67 ] and that myeloid Pkm2 deletion reduces atherosclerosis by suppressing inflammatory signaling and inhibiting inflammation [ 68 ]. Our results extend these findings. We found that overexpression of Pkm2 in microglia promoted a shift toward the M1 proinflammatory phenotype and activated the NF-κB pathway, reinforcing the idea that high Pkm2 levels drive inflammatory polarization. Conversely, knockdown of Pkm2 in BV2 cells suppressed LPS-induced inflammation, downregulated proinflammatory markers, and promoted an M2-like anti-inflammatory phenotype. Importantly, Pkm2 silencing not only reduced inflammatory signaling but also restored mitochondrial morphology and bioenergetic function, revealing a dual role in controlling both inflammation and metabolism. In vivo, targeted knockout of Pkm2 in microglia partially reduced RGC apoptosis-like changes and attenuated neuroinflammation after retinal IR, consistent with prior reports that Pkm2 inhibition exerts neuroprotective effects in other contexts [ 33 , 69 ]. These findings should nevertheless be interpreted with caution. While our data support Pkm2 as an important regulatory node linking inflammatory activation to metabolic stress, other ACA-responsive pathways may also contribute to the overall protective phenotype. Further studies using broader metabolic profiling and cell type-resolved approaches will be required to clarify the relative contribution of Pkm2 within the wider immunometabolic network engaged by ACA. Previous studies have shown that the function of Pkm2 is highly dependent on post-translational modifications including acetylation, phosphorylation, and SUMOylation [ 70 , 71 ]. Protein acetylation is now recognized as a central post-translational modification in metabolic regulation, as nearly all NAD metabolic and TCA cycle enzymes are subject to acetylation [ 72 , 73 ]. Sirtuins, a family of NAD-dependent deacetylases [ 74 ], couple acetylation status to NAD availability. In tumor models, T cell-derived IFN-γ suppresses Pkm2 activity and reduces NAD levels, thereby impairing Sirt1-mediated deacetylation and reprogramming tumor stemness [ 75 ]. NAD homeostasis is a critical factor that influences neurodegeneration and neuroprotection. Increasing levels of NAD provide neuroprotection in multiple cell and animal models of disease and in human clinical trials [ 76 ]. Recent animal and human studies have uncovered metabolic dysfunction occurring early in RGCs in glaucoma, in particular the critical dependency of RGCs on sufficient levels of NAD [ 77 – 79 ]. Sirt1 can directly interact with and deacetylate the RelA/p65 subunit of the NF-κB complex, thus playing an important role in the termination of NF-κB driven inflammatory responses and enhancing the resolution of inflammation [ 80 ]. However, regulation of the Sirt1-Pkm2-NAD axis in neuroinflammation has remained unexplored. Our study reveals that Pkm2 is closely associated with NAD catabolism in microglia, accompanied by reduced NAD levels. Although silencing Pkm2 partly increased NAD, the effect was more pronounced with concurrent ACA treatment, suggesting that ACA may impose additional constraints on NAD catabolism, consistent with GO analysis of scRNA-seq. We further found that the regulation of Pkm2 by ACA appears to involve Sirt1-mediated post-translational acetylation. When Sirt1 deacetylase activity was pharmacologically inhibited with sirtinol, Pkm2 acetylation increased and the anti-inflammatory effect of ACA was correspondingly attenuated. However, this interpretation should be made with caution, as sirtinol-based inhibition does not fully exclude the involvement of other deacetylation-dependent mechanisms. Further studies combining site-specific acetylation analysis with direct metabolic flux measurements will be needed to define the extent to which this axis accounts for the NAD-preserving and anti-inflammatory effects of ACA. Sirtuin family members are increasingly recognized as regulators of Pkm2, acting through acetylation at discrete sites that differ according to disease context. Sirt2 loss promotes Pkm2 acetylation at K135, altering hepatic glucose metabolism under stress [ 81 ], while Sirt3 deacetylates Pkm2 at K433 to suppress apoptosis in lung IR injury [ 82 ]. In Parkinson’s disease models, Sirt1 deacetylates Pkm2 at K135 and K206, thereby lowering enzymatic activity and lactate production and reducing glial activation [ 38 ]. Nevertheless, under inflammatory conditions the Sirt1 deacetylation sites on Pkm2 remained undefined. Here, we close this gap. Using LC/LC-MS and CO-IP, we identified K270 as a site on Pkm2 associated with inflammatory acetylation changes, and our results further suggested that this residue is responsive to Sirt1 activity and is modulated after ACA treatment. Furthermore, we validated in vitro and in vivo that the K270-targeting inhibitor HY-113082 can enhance ACA-associated protection, with reduced RGC apoptosis-related changes and attenuated neuroinflammation. In this study, leveraging the molecular docking score at the K270 site of Pkm2, we employed virtual drug screening to identify the top five small-molecule inhibitors associated with metabolism or inflammation from a library of 80,000 candidates. These inhibitors showed the ability to reduce Pkm2 acetylation. Subsequent in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that inhibition of Pkm2 K270 residue acetylation in microglia conferred partial anti-inflammatory effects and protection of RGCs, with enhanced therapeutic efficacy observed upon combination with ACA. Among these candidates, HY-113082 emerged as the most effective compound in our screening pipeline, providing a theoretical foundation for future investigations into Pkm2 acetylation-related mechanisms. Nevertheless, constrained by economic and ethical considerations, our screening approach exhibited limitations, as it did not encompass broader libraries of small-molecule inhibitors. Future studies should explore whether additional compounds possess deacetylating activity at K270 to expand therapeutic options. In summary, our study provides evidence that ACA exerts a protective effect in retinal IR injury and is associated with preservation of RGCs. Combining scRNA-seq with in vivo and in vitro experiments, we delineated a microglial immunometabolic mechanism involving a Pkm2-NAD checkpoint. ACA was associated with reduced NAD catabolism and with enhanced Sirt1-mediated deacetylation of Pkm2 at K270, accompanied by microglia-driven neuroinflammation and restores mitochondrial homeostasis. HY-113082 further strengthened these ACA-associated effects in a Pkm2-dependent context. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for considering ACA-related metabolic modulation as a potential therapeutic direction in retinal IR and possibly other neuroinflammatory conditions.
sections.experimental design: For molecular biology experiments, three technical replicate experiments were performed for each sample and the data were averaged. In vitro experiments, assays were performed on cells in three wells for each experiment to obtain an average count. In general, 3 to 30 biological replicates in each group were used in this study. The exact numbers of biological replicates in different experiments were stated in the figure legends. Sample sizes for all experiments were determined on the basis of prior studies with α = 0.05, power = 0.8, and an estimated effect size ≥ 2.
sections.ethics statement: All animal breeding and experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the guidelines of Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology (ARVO). The animal protocols used were pre-approved by the animal ethics committee at Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, Sun Yat-sen University (Guangzhou, China; approval no. ID: 2025021).
sections.animal and retinal ir model: C57BL/6J male mice (6–8 weeks of age) were purchased from the Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center and housed in a Specific Pathogen Free animal facility at the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center. Mice were randomly assigned to the following groups: blank group, sham group, and retinal IR group with or without drug treatment. In the blank group, mice received no ocular manipulation. In the sham group, mice underwent anterior chamber cannulation using the same procedure as the IR group, but without elevation of intraocular pressure. The retinal IR models were established as described previously [ 83 ]. Prior to the operation, mice were anesthetized with 1% pentobarbital sodium injected intraperitoneally and topical anesthesia of the cornea was administered with tetracaine hydrochloride. We carefully inserted a 30G needle connected to a normal saline (NS) bottle into the anterior chamber of the mice’s eyes. IOP was increased to 110 mmHg by elevating the NS bottle to a height of 150 cm and maintained for 1 h.
sections.intravitreal injection: Intravitreal injections of the drug were performed immediately after the IR model or sham operation were established. A 3 µl volume was slowly injected into the intravitreal cavity using a Hamilton syringe fitted with a 32-gauge microneedle. ACA (800 µg/ml, MCE, USA) and HY-113082 (5nM, MCE, USA) were dissolved freshly in control vehicle (phosphate-buffered saline, PBS) and were used within 2 h. In addition, to evaluate the potential effect of ACA itself in the absence of IR injury, mice in the Blank + ACA group received the same intravitreal volume and concentration of ACA at the beginning of the experiment. The siPkm2 (2 nmol/eye) and the negative control (NC), provided by KeyGEN BioTECH (China), were dissolved in sterile distilled water and administered three times: 7 days and 3 days prior to the induction of retinal IR, respectively.
sections.cell culture and treatment: The mouse BV2 cells line (RRID: CVCL_0182) was kindly provided by Wuhan Pricella BiotechnologyCo.,Ltd. Vendor authentication by short tandem repeat (STR) profiling showed > 80% concordance with the reference BV-2 profile, indicating no cross-species or human-cell contamination. The cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% (vol/vol) fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA), and 1% penicillin/strep tomycin (PS, Gibco, USA) in a sterile humidified environment at 37 °C and 5% CO 2 . Cultures were inspected daily by light microscopy to confirm the absence of bacterial or fungal contamination, and screened monthly for Mycoplasma Stain Assay Kit (Beyotime, China), with all tests remaining negative throughout the study. pRGCs were obtained from C57BL/6J mouse pups at postnatal day 2–4. Following euthanasia, the eyes were carefully enucleated, and all surrounding tissues were removed before isolating the retinas. Retinal tissue was finely chopped with ophthalmic scissors and incubated for 30 min in a digestion solution containing papain (8 mg/mL, Worthington, USA) and DNase I (15 U/mL, Sigma-Aldrich, USA). The resulting suspension was filtered and then resuspended in Neurobasal medium supplemented with B-27, penicillin–streptomycin, and 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were seeded onto dishes precoated with poly-D-lysine and laminin (Sigma-Aldrich, USA). To establish an inflammatory model, BV2 cells were exposed to 1 µg/ml of LPS (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 24 h. The treatment group (50µM ACA, MCE, USA; 10µM HY-113082, MCE, USA) was pre-treated for 6 h before adding LPS, and then they were combined with LPS to treat BV2 cells for 24 h.
sections.he staining: The eyeballs were enucleated and fixed in FAS Fixator (Servicebio, China) for 24 h. Subsequently, the samples were embedded in paraffin and sectioned into 10-µm-thick sections stained with HE solution. Images of the stained sections were obtained with Leica DMi8 microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar Deutschland, Germany). The thickness of IPL of four cross-sectional areas (500 and 1000 μm from the optic nerve head of both nasal and temporary retina) was measured by CaseViewer v2.4 (3DHISTECH Ltd., Budapest, Hungary).
sections.if staining: For retinal whole mount, the mice were first transcardially perfused with NS solution, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Then, the eyeballs were enucleated and fixed in 4% PFA for 2 h. The retinas were carefully harvested and permeabilized in 0.5% Triton X-100. After blocking, the collected retinas were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the samples were incubated with species-compatible secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature (RT). The retinas were then tiled on glass slides and cut into a four-leaf clover shape. Following previously published approaches for retinal flat-mount regional sampling [ 84 – 86 ], images were acquired using a Leica DMi8 (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar Deutschland, Germany). In each quadrant, regions located approximately 1 mm and 2 mm from the margin of the optic disc were defined as the central and peripheral fields, respectively. The average number of RBPMS or Iba-1-positive cells of both central and peripheral areas was counted as the mean density of all retinas per group. For retinal frozen section, the eyes were enucleated and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. The eyecups were cryoprotected in 30% sucrose at 4 °C until they sank, embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound, and frozen at -80 °C overnight. Tissues were cryosectioned at 10 μm thickness and collected onto glass slides. Prior to staining, sections were brought to room temperature, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 10 min, and blocked with 5% donkey serum supplemented with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were then incubated with the primary antibody overnight at 4 °C. After primary incubation, sections were washed three times with PBS and incubated with the appropriate fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were washed three times with PBS, counterstained with DAPI for 5 min, and washed three additional times with PBS. Finally, sections were mounted with antifade mounting medium, coverslipped, and imaged using a Leica DMi8 microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar Deutschland, Germany). For cell labeling, cells grown on cell slides were fixed in 4% PFA for 15 min at RT. The cells were incubated in appropriate concentrations of serum and 0.3%Triton X-100 for 1 h. After incubation with primary antibodies overnight, the samples were washed and incubated with the appropriate secondary anti-body for 1 h. Cell nuclei were stained by 4,6-diamidino 2-phenylindole (DAPI, Bioss, China) for 10 min. Images were captured using a Leica DMi8 microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar Deutschland, Germany). The sources and dilutions of all antibodies for IF are listed in Table S2.
sections.qrt\u2011pcr: The total RNA of retinas and cells were extracted using the RNA-Quick Purification Kit (Goonies, China). RNA purity and concentration were determined using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (ND-1000, NanoDrop Technologies, USA). Subsequently, the extracted RNA was transcribed into cDNA using Evo M-MLV RT reagent kit (Accurate Biology, China). qRT-PCR was performed using the SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Accurate Biology, China) in the Light Cycler 480 RealTime PCR System (Roche Molecular Systems, Inc., SUR). Relative mRNA expression levels were normalized to the expression of β-actin gene in the same samples and calculated using the comparative cycle threshold method (2-ΔΔCt method). The primers targeting corresponding mouse genes are listed in Table S3.
sections.wb analysis: Total protein was extracted from the retinas and cells using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis solution (Beyotime, China) and separated on 8%-12% (wt/vol) gradient polyacrylamide gels according to a standard procedure. The levels of target proteins were normalized to β-actin from the same sample (set as 1.0). The primary antibodies and their respective dilutions are detailed in Table S2.
sections.scrna-seq analysis: The data analysis pipeline in our study was described on the 10x Genomics ( www.10xgenomics.com/ ) and the Seurat official website ( https://github.com/satijalab/seurat ). ScRNA-seq libraries were prepared using the 10×Genomics kit. The CellRanger (version 7.1.0) count commands were utilized to demultiplex and barcode the sequencing data. Downstream analyses were conducted using the R Seurat package (version 4.4.0), unless indicated otherwise. Following rigorous quality control (with a mitochondrial gene ratio of less than 10%, and detected genes ranging from more than 200 to fewer than 7,500), a total of 60,223 cells were retained for further analysis (12,602 cells from Blank, 28,759 cells from IR and 18,862 cells from ACA). The “FindMarkers” function within the Seurat package was employed to carry out differential expression analysis, identifying genes with | Log2 (Fold Change) | > 0.1 and P value < 0.05 as DEGs.
sections.gene functional analysis: DEGs were mapped to functional Gene Ontology (GO) terms using the web-based tool Metascape. A selection of representative GO terms and pathways was visualized with the R package ggplot2 (version 3.4.3).
sections.gsea: Gene sets related to selective pathways were downloaded from MSigDb ( https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp ). GSEA of IR-DEGs and ACA-DEGs mapped to corresponding gene sets was performed using R package GSEABase (version 1.56.0).
sections.scoring of biological processes: The R package AUCell (version 1.8.1) [ 87 ] was used to score the pathway activity of individual cells. We used an expression matrix to calculate the gene expression ranking in each cell by the “AUCell_buildRankings” function with default parameters. After downloading the canonical path databases from the KEGG, and GO databases, pathways were used to score each cell. The “AUCell_calcAUC” function was used to calculate the area under the curve (AUC) value based on gene expression rankings.
sections.metabolic phenotyping: Metabolic phenotyping for NAD+/NADH quantification in retinas and BV2 cells were dissociated to cell lysate samples and compounds of cell lysate samples were measured following the manufacturer’s instructions (NAD+/NADH assay kit, Beyotime, China). Results were calculated according to the standard curve generated by using standards from the kits and were determined by chemiluminescence.
sections.mmp measurement and mtros staining: MMP was assessed using a tetramethylrhodamine, methyl ester (TMRM) probe (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and Mito-SOX Red (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was used to detect mtROS. The Hoechst (Biosharp, China) was used to stain the nuclei of living cells. Briefly, target cells were seeded in 24-well plates (NEST, USA), treated accordingly, and stained with TMRM or Mito-SOX Red staining solution at 37 °C for 30 min. Cells were imaged under a Leica DMi8 (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar Deutschland, Germany).
sections.tem: Cells were collected and fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde-2.5% glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), pH 7.3, at 4 °C overnight. After washing three times with phosphate buffer, the cells were post-fixed in 1% osmium tetroxide (Structure Probe) for 30 min. The samples were dehydrated and stained with 1% aqueous uranyl acetate (Structure Probe). The structures of mitochondria were observed under an H-7500 transmission electron microscope (Hitachi, Tokyo, Japan) at 80 kV.
sections.cck-8 assay: Cell viability was assessed using a CCK8 kit (Goonie, China). Briefly, cells were seeded into 96-well plates and treated with the indicated concentration of specific medicine for 24 h. Next, 10 µl of CCK-8 buffer was added to each well and incubated at 37 ℃ for 1 h. Absorbance at 450 nm in each well was then measured via a multimode reader.
sections.protein\u2013protein interaction (ppi) n: Based on the retinal specific upregulated DEGs, we utilized STRING [ 88 ] to conduct the PPI network, which was visualized with Cytascape software (v3.9.1). Then, the hub genes were selected by CytoHubba plugin with six different algorithms [ 89 ].
sections.sirna and plasmids: BV2 cells were plated and grown to 70%-80% confluency at the time of transfection. The transfection complexes were prepared with KeygenMAX 3000 (KeyGEN BioTECH, China) and siRNA (50 nM) in Opti-MEM (ThermoFisher Scientific, USA). Following transfection for 4–6 h, the transfection complexes were removed, and BV2 cell culture medium was added to continue incubation for 24–48 h before proceeding with subsequent experiments. The sequences of siRNAs are listed in Table S3. The coding sequence of Pkm2 and Sirt1 were synthesized and incorporated into pcDNA3.1 using endonuclease site of NheI and XhoI (Keygen BioTECH, China). BV2 cells were transfected with plasmid overexpressing Pkm2 or/and Sirt1(0.2 µg/µL) by KeygenMAX 3000 (KeyGEN BioTECH, China) and DNA enhancer (KeyGEN BioTECH, China). Following transfection for 4–6 h, the transfection complexes were removed, and BV2 cell culture medium was added to continue incubation for 24–48 h before proceeding with subsequent experiments. The oligos sequences are listed in Table S3.
sections.co-ip: After collecting BV2 cells subjected to different treatments, pre-chilled RIPA lysis buffer was added. The cells were subjected to sonication and then left on ice for 30 min. To remove cellular debris, the mixture was centrifuged at 10,000×g for 20 min at 4 °C. One milliliter of the supernatant was then mixed with 0.2 µg of the primary antibody in a 1.5 mL EP tube and incubated at 4 °C for 1 h. Following this, the solution was incubated overnight at 4 °C with 20 µL of Protein A/G Plus-Agarose (Santa Cruz, China) on a rotating mixer. The beads were collected by centrifugation at 2,500 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C and washed three times with PBS. After washing, 40 µL of sample loading buffer was added to the beads, and the mixture was boiled in a water bath at 100 °C for 10 min. Following centrifugation at 2,500 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was collected and used for WB analysis. The primary antibodies and their respective dilutions are detailed in Table S2.
sections.lc-ms/ms spectrometry analyses: Cells were lysed in pre-cold lysis buffer containing 8 M urea, 1% protease inhibitor, 3 µM TSA (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 50 mM nicotinamide (NAM, Sigma-Aldrich, USA). The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4℃. Cell debris was discarded and supernatant was kept on ice. Protein concentration in super natant was measured by BCA kit according the manufacturer’s instructions (Beyotime, China). The obtained protein samples were subjected to subsequent trypsin enzymatic hydrolysis, peptide modification enrichment and then was analyzed by liquid chromatography followed by liquid chromatog raphy-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions (PTM Bio, China).
sections.computational screening: The data file for the structure of the mouse Pkm2 protein was downloaded from the AlphaFold database. All heterogeneous atoms were removed, followed by molecular docking. High-throughput virtual screening was performed by MCE Co., Ltd. under HTVS, SP, and XP modes. The compounds were selected based on scoring values, conformation and structural diversity. Protein–ligand interactions were obtained by PyMOL version 1.7.4.5.
sections.elisa: Mice were anesthetized after different treatment and the retinas was used for ELISA. ELISA was performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. The following ELISA kits were used for detection: Mouse IL-1β ELISA Kit (RayBiotech, China), Mouse IL-6 ELISA Kit (RayBiotech, China) and Mouse TNF-α ELISA Kit (RayBiotech, China).
sections.construction and identification of trans: The Pkm2 fl/fl mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (USA) and the Cx3cr1-Cre mice were purchased from Cyagen Biotechnology Co., Ltd (China). One Step Mouse Genotyping Kit (Vazyme, China) was used for PCR experiments to identify the genotypes of the mice, with the procedures carried out according to the instructions provided by the reagent manufacturer. Pkm2 primers: F: 5’-CCT TCA GGA AGA CAG CCA AG-3’, R: 5’-AGT GCT GCC TGG AAT CCT CT-3’ (Homozygotes: one band with 680 bp, Heterozygotes: two bands with 680 bp and 578 bp, Wildtype allele: one band with 578 bp). Cx3cr1-Cre primers: F1: 5’-GAC ATT TGC CTT GCT GGA C-3’, R: 5’-GCA GGG AAA TCT GAT GCA AG-3’ (Wildtype: N.A. Targeted: 380 bp).
sections.ogd/r model: The OGD/R model was established as described previously [ 23 ]. In brief, OGD/R was induced by washing cells twice with PBS, replacing medium with serum- and glucose-free media and placed under conditions of 5% CO 2 and 95% N 2 in a 37 °C incubator for 3 h, then returned to the normal environment (37 °C, 5% CO2 and normoxic conditions) and complete medium (DMEM with 10% FBS and glucose [4.9 g/L]) for 24 h.
sections.cell treatment for co-culture: To maximally simulate interactions between microglia and RGCs, BV2 cells were co-cultured with pRGCs in transwell chambers. In brief, BV2 cells (4 × 10⁴ cells per well) treated with siRNA, plasmid or mutant, or treated with different conditions (ACA, sirtinol or HY-113082) were inoculated into 0.4-micron transwell chambers and placed in a 12-well plate above pRGCs (1 × 10⁵ cells per well), and co-cultured for 24 h.
sections.quantification: ImageJ software ( https://imagej.net/ij/ ) was used for the quantification of retinal whole mount, retinal section, WB, CO-IP, IF, MMP, and mtROS.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical analysis was conducted using GraphPad Prism 10 software. Power analysis by PASS software was used to ensure proper sample size. All values for each group were presented as Mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Parametric and nonparametric tests were used according to the homogeneity of variance. According to different comparison situations, statistical differences were analyzed using Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA, as appropriate, with Sidak’s or Turkey’s multiple comparisons test. P < 0.05 indicated that the difference was statistically significant. Significance levels are indicated as ns for not significant, * for P < 0.05, ** for P < 0.01, *** for P < 0.001, and **** for P < 0.0001.

title: Comparing clinical decision-making between colposcopists and large language models in cervical dysplasia management: a pilot prospective multicenter study
abstract: Purpose This prospective multicenter study aimed to compare the decision-making abilities of board-certified colposcopists and two commercially available large language models (LLM), ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5, in cervical dysplasia management. Methods Twenty-three anonymized real-life patient cases with multiple-choice (MC) questions regarding treatment decisions were used to assess answer quality. Ten board-certified colposcopists and the two LLMs addressed the MC questions. The gold standard was defined by two guideline authors. LLMs were prompted to justify their responses. Concordance rates were calculated and compared across all questions and histopathological subgroups, including cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), unspecific histopathological results, and cervical cancer cases. Results Clinicians and LLMs achieved similar overall concordance rates compared to the gold standard (69.6% for clinicians, 69.6% for ChatGPT-4o, and 65.2% for ChatGPT-5). ChatGPT-5 outperformed clinicians in precancerous lesions (81.8% vs. 66.4%), while clinicians excelled in complex cases with unspecific histopathology (86% vs. 60%). Clinicians showed a tendency to overtreat low-grade lesions (CIN I), opting for more intensive surveillance. ChatGPT-4o performed better than ChatGPT-5 in cervical cancer cases, though both models struggled with these scenarios. Conclusion This study highlights the potential of LLMs as decision support tools in cervical dysplasia management, particularly for straightforward cases like precancerous lesions. However, clinicians remain superior in handling complex or ambiguous cases. The tendency of clinicians to overtreat low-grade lesions may offer the potential to test the implementation of a decision support tool for those cases. While LLMs show promise, exploring open-ended clinical scenarios and integrating retrieval-augmented generation could enhance their practical application. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00404-026-08498-w.

sections.introduction: Managing cervical dysplasia is a fundamental part of cervical cancer prevention and gynecological routine work. Yearly, around 39.000 patients are seen and treated in certified dysplasia units in Germany [ 1 ]. High-quality diagnostics and early treatment might then prevent the occurrence of cervical cancer, ensure patients’ health, and reduce healthcare costs. Hence, treatment decisions are standardized and based on regularly updated guidelines [ 2 , 3 ]. Nevertheless, in contrast to cancer therapy, all decisions are made without a certified board being involved. To ensure quality standards, colposcopists are certified after finishing specific training courses and an exam to manage these cases. Still, clinical decision-making might vary between practitioners due to several influencing factors [ 4 – 6 ]. To support clinicians, artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems, for instance, in colposcopic image recognition, are the focus of recent developments [ 7 ]. In breast cancer screening, double evaluation (AI/clinician) is already improving workflows, diagnostic specificity, and therefore patient safety [ 8 – 10 ]. Further support could be implemented in AI-based clinical decision support for therapeutic recommendations. This has not yet been evaluated in the context of dysplasia management. Previous work proved the outstanding performance of large language models (LLM) in multiple-choice (MC) questions from medical exams, including case-related therapy decisions [ 11 , 12 ]. Even though real-life patient casuistics might prove to be more complex than medical exam MC questions, the existing potential of broad, commercially available LLM tools is undeniable. These systems can process and analyze natural language input such as medical guidelines, studies, and patient casuistics, and provide the user with a structured treatment recommendation based on the provided input. The capability of LLMs in guideline-based decision-making has been shown previously in early breast cancer [ 13 – 16 ]. Still, limits such as incorrect reasoning or hallucinations require further studies. For this purpose, Roy et al . developed a classification scheme to further characterize wrong output justifications and allow a better understanding of false reasoning in complex question situations [ 17 ]. With the release of the OpenAI Inc. (San Francisco, CA, USA) ChatGPT-5, hope arises for more sufficient and comprehensible recommendations. In cervical dysplasia treatment, the comparability and potential benefits of LLM-supported decision-making have not yet been evaluated. Therefore, we conducted a first-of-its-kind prospective multicenter study comparing treatment recommendations for cervical dysplasia patients by 10 certified colposcopists as well as ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 on an MC questionnaire. Additionally, the LLM was prompted to justify its output, which was then further classified.
sections.casuistics, gold standard, and colposcop: Adapted and anonymized real-life patient cases with cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), uncertain histopathology, or cervical cancer treated in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology of Hannover Medical School were used to prepare 30 casuistics. Each case included a question concerning the treatment recommendation in an MC manner with four answer possibilities. The casuistics included different complexities to cover the spectrum of cervical dysplasia. The patient cases were structured and shortened to therapeutically relevant details (e.g., age, family planning, medical preconditions, and previously performed surgery) and histological classification if available. Information extent varied in width and depth, but was sufficient to answer the MC questions. The gold standard was defined by two authors of the German AWMF (“ Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wissenschaftlichen Medizinischen Fachgesellschaften e.V. ”, engl. Working Group of Scientific Medical Societies) cervical cancer prevention guideline to ensure guideline concordance. After this process, seven cases were excluded due to answer variations between the experts (2 cases) or ambiguous cases (5 cases). The final 23 cases, MC questions and correct answers are displayed in Supplemental File 1. For our prospective multicenter approach, a total of 10 specialized colposcopists certified by the “ Arbeitsgemeinschaft Zervixpathologie und Kolposkopie e.V. ” (AG-CPC, engl.: Board of the German Society of Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology) were involved. Participants are practicing at different-sized facilities (private practice, hospital, university clinics) with several years of clinical experience.
sections.llm and prompt engineering: ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 were accessed via the OpenAI online login and used in default mode. Settings such as temperature or the amount of tokens cannot be modified via the online login and are set based on an internal algorithm triggered by the prompt. A paid license was deployed to guarantee the most recent versions. Casuistics were prompted in groups of 5 on the 20th of July 2025 (ChatGPT-4o) and on the 19th of October 2025 (ChatGPT-5). A new conversation was opened for every input. The prompt was designed to be simple and requested a justification for both the selected answer and the rejected answers, partially following the prompt Roy et al . [ 17 ] used, leading to the following input: Please answer the multiple-choice questions in the attached Word document and use both attached PDF documents as a basis for your answers. Only one answer per question is permitted. Please justify your answer and explain why the other options are incorrect. Casuistics and prompts were provided in German to match the guideline language.
sections.medical guidelines: The LLMs were provided with the latest versions of the AWMF guidelines on cervical cancer prevention (Version 1.1, March 2020; [ 2 ]) and on diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up care for patients with cervical cancer (Version 2.2, March 2022; [ 3 ]). Both are written in German language, consisting of text, tables, and diagrams, and are available in PDF format. The documents were uploaded without preprocessing.
sections.classification of incorrect llm output: To gain deeper insights into incorrect LLM answers, these were classified according to the error taxonomy proposed by Roy et al. [ 17 ]. This scheme was developed based on wrong LLM answers to USMLE ( United States Medical Licensing Examination ) MC questions, and the results yielded the existence of 4 error categories: reasoning-based error , knowledge-based error, reading comprehension error, and non-error, with multiple errors occurring simultaneously.
sections.data analysis: Since this was designed as a pilot study, a power analysis was not conducted beforehand. All answers were summarized in an analysis table and compared to the gold standard. The number of correct answers across clinicians was calculated for each question in percentage. The resulting values were averaged for each diagnosis (CIN I with n = 3, CIN II with n = 4, CIN III with n = 4, cervical cancer with n = 7, or unspecific pathology with n = 5), and across all questions. Due to the limited number of cases and the structure of the data, a statistical analysis could not be performed, so the results were analyzed descriptively. Given the small number of cases in certain subgroups (e.g., CIN I), the analyses are exploratory in nature and should be interpreted with caution. Cohen’s Kappa [ 18 ] was calculated to quantify inter-rater agreement between the two guideline authors. To quantify answer variability, Shannon entropy [ 19 ] was calculated for the clinicians’ answers for each question and visualized in a heatmap plot generated using Matplotlib version 3.10.3 and Seaborn version 0.13.2 in Python [ 20 , 21 ]. To ease interpretability, the resulting values were normalized to values between 0 and 1 using the maximum entropy, as proposed, e.g., by Wilcox [ 22 ]. High answer variability results in high entropy, whereas entropy is zero if all clinicians choose the same answer option. Further information about the methods can be found in Supplemental File 2. For each of the casuistics answered incorrectly by ChatGPT, the reasoning for choosing the final (incorrect) answer was further analyzed qualitatively and classified according to the error taxonomy proposed by Roy et al. [ 17 ].
sections.analysis of clinical answers: From 30 cases, 5 cases were excluded from analysis due to question ambiguity stated by the guideline authors. For the remaining total of 25 cases, the guideline authors agreed in 23 cases. Cohen’s Kappa was calculated to 0.8845, indicating high agreement. All participating clinicians were board-certified by the AG-CPC and received the casuistics with the MC questions. Answers were collected anonymously and compared to the gold standard. Across all cases, clinicians achieved a mean concordance rate of 69.57% with the gold standard (Fig. 1 a). The answer heterogeneity between all clinicians is shown in Fig. 1 b, indicating different opinions across 19 of 23 cases (82.6%). After dividing the casuistics into subgroups of histopathological diagnoses, clinicians reached a score of 66.36% for precancerous lesions (Fig. 2 a). If separated into the CIN subgroups, the following concordance rates were achieved: 46.67% for CIN I, 67.5% for CIN II, and 80% for CIN III (Fig. 2 b), indicating discrepancies in the management of low-grade lesions. In case of unspecific histopathology or cervical cancer casuistics, participating colposcopists reached a concordance rate of 86% and 62.86%, respectively (Fig. 2 a). Fig. 1 Answer concordance of colposcopists, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 with the gold standard and answer entropy among colposcopists. a Overall answer concordance (in percent) of certified colposcopists ( n = 10), ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 on 23 dysplasia cases with multiple-choice questions and four answer possibilities in comparison to the gold standard. b Heatmap of normalized Shannon entropy illustrating the answer variability. Each heatmap value was calculated from the answers of n = 10 colposcopists choosing one answer out of four possible answer options. The value “0” (dark green) shows complete homogeneity, whereas “1” (yellow) indicates the maximal heterogeneity Fig. 2 Answer concordance of colposcopists, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 by case subgroups compared to the gold standard. a Answer concordance (in percent) of certified colposcopists ( n = 10), ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 with the gold standard divided in histopathological subgroups CIN ( n = 11), unspecific histopathology ( n = 5) and cervical cancer ( n = 7). b Answer concordance (in percent) of certified colposcopists ( n = 10), ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 with the gold standard divided in CIN subgroups CIN I ( n = 3), CIN II ( n = 4) and CIN III ( n = 4) Analyzing the wrong answers revealed a clinical tendency for the safest treatment option rather than the gold standard option for CIN I. For example, in the case of a 26-year-old patient with transformation zone type I and a histopathological CIN I (case 4), 70% of clinicians favored a second invitation to the dysplasia unit with re-biopsy after 6 months, whereas the gold standard recommended cytological control at the treating gynecologist’s practice. A comparative qualitative analysis of the colposcopists’ responses to histopathological CIN II cases revealed both overtreatment and undertreatment, without a distinct trend. In contrast, for CIN III cases, the incorrect answers primarily involved undertreatment.
sections.llm output and clinical comparison: Overall, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 reached similar concordance rates with 69.57% and 65.22%, respectively (Fig. 1 a). Interestingly, the older version was capable of slightly outperforming the newer model. When analyzing the subgroups, ChatGPT-4o achieved a concordance rate to the gold standard of 72.73% for CIN, 60% for unspecific histopathology, and 71.43% for cervical cancer casuistics (Fig. 2 a). Within the precancerous lesions, ChatGPT-4o reached concordance rates of 66.67% for CIN I, 50% for CIN II and 100% for CIN III cases (Fig. 2 b). In comparison, ChatGPT-5 achieved concordance rates of 81.82% for CIN, 60% for unspecific histopathology, and 42.86% for cervical cancer cases (Fig. 2 a). When analyzing the CIN subgroups, ChatGPT-5 reached concordance rates of 66.67% for CIN I, 75% for CIN II, and 100% for CIN III casuistics (Fig. 2 b). Consequently, the newer model exhibited superior performance in addressing the treatment of precancerous lesions, overall and for the CIN II subgroup. However, the older model demonstrated superiority in the management of cervical cancer cases. In contrast to clinical answers, both ChatGPT versions showed greater concordance with the gold standard for precancerous lesions, with ChatGPT-5 achieving the highest results, while clinicians proved superiority for challenging cases with unspecific histopathology. Interestingly, for cervical cancer cases, ChatGPT-4o as well as the clinicians reached higher concordance rates than the ChatGPT-5 model. Regarding case 21 with cervical cancer, both models referenced the recently published SHAPE study [ 23 ], not yet implemented in the German guideline, but already into clinical routine. Interestingly, ChatGPT-4o used the study results and chose the correct answer, demonstrating the use of sources outside the guideline and a failure to adhere to the specified prompt. ChatGPT-5 also referred to the SHAPE study but did not utilize the results, stating that the study “… has not yet been fully implemented; currently not standard …”. In summary, this proved the greater capabilities of ChatGPT-5 to follow a given prompt and the model’s superior reasoning in this case, despite choosing the clinically incorrect answer.
sections.analysis of incorrect llm output: In contrast to Roy et al. [ 17 ], the prompt in our study explicitly instructed the models to use the relevant guidelines that were uploaded simultaneously. Interestingly, in some cases, the answer parts could not be clearly assigned to one of the seven error types. Therefore, the upper taxonomy level proposed by Roy et al . , consisting of four top-level error categories: non-error type, reasoning-based error, knowledge-based error, and reading comprehension error , was applied [ 17 ]. For ChatGPT-4o, within a total of seven incorrect answers, seven errors were identified, of which one was classified as a non-error type , four as reasoning-based errors , and two as knowledge-based errors (Fig. 3 a). For ChatGPT-5, within the total of eight incorrect answers, ten errors were classified, of which three belonged to a non-error type , four to reasoning-based errors , two to knowledge-based errors , and one to reading comprehension error (Fig. 3 b). Fig. 3 Distribution of top-level error types in incorrect answers of ChatGPT. Error types refer to the error taxonomy proposed by Roy et al. [ 17 ]. Multiple errors per incorrect answer were possible. a Results of ChatGPT-4o. b Results of ChatGPT-5 All non-error type errors belonged to the subtype non-error type 1 (reasonable response), where the models gave a reasonable answer despite choosing the incorrect answer option . Reasons for this error type were, e.g., recent study updates (case 21; ChatGPT-5) or interpretable guideline scope (case 8; both models). Detailed classification results can be found in Supplemental File 3.
sections.discussion: In this study, we conducted a first-of-its-kind prospective multicenter analysis comparing clinical decision-making of ten board-certified colposcopists with two commercially available LLMs (ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5) in cervical dysplasia management. Overall, our results showed similar concordance rates to the gold standard with higher answer concordance by ChatGPT-5 for precancerous lesions, whereas clinicians outperformed the LLMs in complex cases. Even though clinical decision-making regularly follows national and international guidelines, differences can arise between clinicians due to varying contextual factors or therapeutic preferences [ 5 ]. In cervical dysplasia management, treatment decisions are based on the patient’s history, a Papanicolaou (PAP) smear, human papillomavirus (HPV) testing, colposcopy, and, most importantly, a histopathological sample diagnosing a precancerous lesion and altogether estimating the risk of developing cervical cancer. As spontaneous regression rates are high, up to 90%, for low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, active surveillance is frequently the chosen treatment option [ 24 ]. Nevertheless, the answer concordance rate within the CIN I subgroup by the participating clinicians was the lowest for all precancerous lesions. The given answers mainly included overtreatments such as short-term re-colposcopy or re-biopsy. Even though a re-visit might not harm the patient, relevant additional healthcare costs arise consequently within a country, estimated for the United States of America at several billion dollars per year [ 25 ]. A survey interviewing clinicians about overtreatment by Lyu et al . revealed that practitioners estimate around 20.6% of the overall medical care as unnecessary, with the leading reasons being fear of malpractice and patient pressure/request [ 26 ]. Therefore, solutions are needed to support clinicians with their choice of treatment and reduce the risk of potentially unnecessary visits or diagnostics. Since board decisions regarding oncological patient care are impractical to implement into daily dysplasia management, an LLM-based decision support tool might offer additional guidance in those cases. Nevertheless, indicating a treatment decision can be a highly patient-specific task with several influencing factors. Still, recent publications indicate the capabilities of LLM decision support tools, for instance, in emergency internal medicine cases [ 27 ]. Challenges with commercially available LLMs arise if treatment decisions are verified for guideline compliance or if the input prompt demands a literature reference, as those models are vulnerable to hallucinations [ 28 , 29 ]. Our overall results showed that the deployed LLMs are equivalently capable of recommending an MC question-based guideline-compliant treatment in cervical dysplasia management compared to board-certified colposcopists, but with relevant differences. Since ChatGPT-5 outperformed the clinicians for precancerous lesions, those cases could serve as a future use-case for clinical implementation of an LLM-based decision support tool. Even though no statistical tests were applied, we considered the higher concordance rate as clinically relevant. Still, given the small sample size, these results must be considered exploratory. For other gynecological pathologies, e.g., breast cancer, similar conclusions were drawn for LLM decision support tools, and focusing on early breast cancer cases for initial proof-of-concept studies was suggested [ 13 ]. In comparison, the data confirmed the high relevance of board-certified colposcopists for complex cases with unspecific histopathological results due to the superior concordance rate. Regarding the cervical cancer cases, the concordance rates should be viewed as exploratory because colposcopists are not necessarily trained oncologists and may not serve as the optimal test cohort. Additionally, due to the outdated German cervical cancer guideline and existing new clinical trials (e.g., SHAPE), it is expected that clinical practice will differ from the guideline to provide up-to-date treatment [ 23 ]. This circumstance is reflected in the conflicting reasoning of the LLM versions. ChatGPT-4o recommended the treatment because of the existing SHAPE publication, but ignored the prompt. ChatGPT-5, on the other hand, advised against it since it is not yet part of the provided guideline. To overcome this conflict, an updated, machine-readable guideline is needed for follow-up projects. While the AWMF cervical cancer prevention guideline (2020–2022) predates the formalized 2023 risk-based management framework of the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP) [ 30 ], several of its core elements—such as HPV-centered management, persistence-based triage, and extended follow-up after high-grade lesions—already reflect a risk-adapted clinical rationale. However, in contrast to the ASCCP approach, these strategies are not anchored in quantitatively defined risk thresholds but rely on algorithm-based decision pathways. This temporal and methodological difference should be acknowledged when interpreting our findings. For clinical practice, this implies that management according to AWMF guidelines remains broadly aligned with risk-adapted care but may offer less granularity in risk stratification. In comparison, the ASCCP framework enables more individualized decision-making based on explicit risk estimates, which may be particularly relevant in borderline constellations or complex follow-up scenarios. Nevertheless, the advantages of bounding an LLM to a certain knowledge base also come with limitations: Edge cases may not be incorporated in the guideline, e.g., therapy for patients of high age with comorbidities. These complex cases require the knowledge of an experienced clinician who can weigh up the patient-specific risks and benefits, as these case details go beyond the guideline’s scope. Nevertheless, to allow meaningful utilization of such tools, future projects are needed to evaluate the performance in an open question manner to better reflect clinical practice. Furthermore, cloud-hosted LLMs are easy to access for initial studies but certainly lack the required data safety to enable daily usage with real-life patient data. Moreover, models are usually trained on vast amounts of data, which is not necessarily specific to use cases in daily clinical routine. Specific documents like guidelines must be accessed for answering, and citation of relevant text parts is crucial for reliable results. For this purpose, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [ 31 ] enhanced LLMs are recently attracting attention as this technique can reduce hallucinations, can be deployed locally in compliance with data safety requirements, and with a tailored database (e.g., medical guidelines). Using this method, Tung et al . developed a RAG-enhanced LLM system for prostate cancer screening that provided a guideline-compliant answer in 95.5% of the 220 cases, outperforming junior clinicians by a large margin [ 32 ]. Reasoning-based error was the major error type in both models’ answers. This finding is in line with the results of Roy et al . and Liévin et al . [ 17 , 33 ]. Challenges in assigning proper classes mainly arose from the fact that the LLMs were instructed to use two specific guidelines. Thus, a statement not supported by the guideline could be classified either as an unsupported medical claim ( knowledge-based error ) or a hallucination of information ( reading comprehension error) . Nevertheless, we kept our classification tight to the taxonomy description and categorized these errors as knowledge-based errors and used the hallucination of information error for reading comprehension failures concerning the presented casuistic. This highlights the need for a taxonomy suitable for open-book settings like in our study or in RAG-based systems. To provide more insights into the failure origins in the processing pipeline, RAG could be used. In conclusion, this pilot study demonstrates that both board-certified colposcopists and LLMs like ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 achieve similar overall concordance rates with the gold standard in cervical dysplasia management. While LLMs excelled over the clinicians in precancerous lesions, clinicians outperformed LLMs in complex cases with unspecific histopathology. The tendency of clinicians to overtreat low-grade lesions underscores the potential for decision support tools to reduce unnecessary healthcare costs. Still, considering the small sample size, a sufficiently powered follow-up study is needed for verification. Due to the chosen test cohort, the results for cervical cancer cases should be viewed as preliminary. LLMs, while effective, require updated guidelines and enhanced data safety for practical applications. Future research should explore their use in open clinical scenarios and integrate retrieval-augmented generation to minimize errors. These findings suggest a promising role for LLMs in supporting clinicians, particularly in straightforward cases, while emphasizing the need for further refinement.
