sections.data processing using iramuteq software: Through the Descending Hierarchical Classification (DHC) method, it was possible to identify that the overall corpus consisted of 26 texts/interviews, comprising 4,328 text segments (TS), of which 3,988 TS were retained (92.14%). The corpus presented 151,743 word occurrences, including 6,988 distinct forms, of which 2,984 corresponded to hapax, that is, words that appear only once. Thus, the analyzed corpus was organized by the software into five emerging classes: class 1, composed of 561 TS (13.05%); class 2, with 1,045 TS (24.31%); class 3, with 1,089 TS (25.34%); class 4, with 1,155 TS (26.87%); and class 5, with 448 TS (10.42%), as presented in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Dendrogram of the Descending Hierarchical Classification. Graphical representation of the division of the corpus into five lexical classes, resulting from textual processing using IRaMuTeQ software In view of this, based on the reading of the text segments (TS) processed by IRaMuTeQ and derived from the textual corpus, it was possible to identify units of meaning (corpus excerpts with relevant meaning) and to name the classes, which are considered intermediate categories in the DTA process [ 15 ]. In addition, the software generated a dendrogram (Fig. 2 ), which also contributed to naming the intermediate categories, as it highlights the words with the highest frequency within each class. Fig. 2 Dendrogram with lexical classes and associated words. Representation of the Descending Hierarchical Classification, highlighting the thematic classes and the terms with the highest frequency and statistical association in each class, based on corpus processing using IRaMuTeQ software Therefore, although the DHC generated five classes, only three were considered in the analysis. After reading the text segments of class 1, it was found that its content did not address the objective of the study, as it primarily referred to aspects of clinical practice, without mentioning pedagogical approaches or strategies. Likewise, class 5 was not further explored, as its TS indicated elements already encompassed within the other analyzed classes. Thus, classes (intermediate categories) 2, 3, and 4 were analyzed.
sections.category 2: faculty understanding of sof: According to the dendrogram presented in Fig. 2 , the most frequent word was “soft skills,” followed by the words “faculty,” “training,” “skill,” among others. Therefore, this category illustrates faculty members’ perceptions of soft skills, considerations regarding training related to these competencies, the skills investigated in the data collection instrument, as well as soft skills indicated beyond these as essential to nursing education, presented in Subcategories 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively.
sections.subcategory 1: faculty perceptions of so: Participating faculty members describe soft skills as fundamental in nursing education, emphasizing that such competencies underpin professional practice and should receive greater attention from institutions. According to some participants, they are considered even more determinant than technical skills, as illustrated in the excerpts below. I think soft skills are extremely important , and they should be discussed more within institutions so that they can be more effectively implemented. (IND25-D) I think they are the main skills we need to have […] technical aspects we can develop without difficulty […] the structured course sequence is there for that […] But without these skills , the soft skills , you cannot fully develop the proposal , the profile of what it means to be a nurse. (IND20-C) I believe that soft skills are more important than hard skills for professional success. (IND11-C)
sections.subcategory 2: training on soft skills: Participating nursing faculty members reported the importance of training initiatives on this topic, as they understand that these skills, in addition to being essential, tend to be the most difficult to develop in nursing education. Although none of the participants reported having attended specific training using the terminology “soft skills,” some mentioned having participated in more focused training activities, such as those related to communication. The more I reflect on it , the more I realize that we need to work on this type of competency and skill within nursing , because it is the most difficult part. (IND16-C) I have never received any type of training regarding this [soft skills] , but I consider them extremely important , because it is impossible to talk about nursing without talking about these skills. (IND07-A) I have taken training courses focused on communication […] one was offered by the university […] and others I pursued on my own , seeking them out independently; they were not institutionalized. (IND05-B)
sections.subcategory 3: soft skills investigated: With regard to the soft skills addressed in the data collection instrument, participating faculty members commented on interpersonal skills, highlighting communication and teamwork as fundamental in the teaching–learning process in nursing education. They emphasized that communication influences decision-making, interpersonal relationships, and work organization. Furthermore, teamwork was also described by participants as fundamental, since nurses do not work in isolation and depend on their relationship with the team to ensure the best possible care for patients. Communication is the foundation of the entire process […] the way it is conveyed , the content , shapes your decision-making , shapes your interpersonal relationships , shapes the organization of your work […] I would say it is fundamental for education and for students’ development. (IND05-B) Communication is extremely important — what to say , how to say it , to whom to say it , the right moment to speak , and even when not to speak — it is an essential skill in the teaching–learning process. (IND07-A) Teamwork may be the second most important soft skill in nursing practice , because , after all , nurses do not work alone. If we do not maintain good relationships with the team , which is our support base , we will not be able to provide adequate care. (IND26-D) Still related to interpersonal skills, the soft skills of leadership and empathy were also highlighted. In participants’ accounts, leadership is emphasized as a competency established in the National Curricular Guidelines and as fundamental to nurses’ performance as team leaders. Empathy, in turn, was described as being associated with the ability to understand others and as a foundation for the development of various soft skills. Leadership is of utmost importance; it is a competency established in the curricular guidelines , so nurses do need to develop leadership , they are the leaders of the team. (IND11-C) The need for empathy […] is necessarily centered on the possibility of understanding others. And in order to develop all those soft skills , or most of them , you really need to recognize the other person. (IND05-B) With regard to intrapersonal skills, participating faculty members emphasized critical thinking, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence. They highlighted that critical thinking distinguishes nurses in professional practice, that problem-solving is part of the daily routine of the profession, and that emotional intelligence supports the development of other soft skills. Critical thinking is essential […] nurses are trained to have a distinguishing feature , and that distinguishing feature is not the technical skills they are able to perform because they are nurses , but rather the ability to think critically about situations […] it is necessary for them to develop this critical perspective regarding everything they experience. (IND16-C) Problem-solving , I believe , is a very important skill , not only for professional practice but for life. In nursing , we are constantly dealing with and trying to resolve problems and conflicts , whatever they may be; this skill is extremely important. (IND08-A) I think emotional intelligence is the foundation for all other soft skills […] At some point , a soft skill will be hindered depending on your emotional intelligence; your leadership will be hindered if you do not have emotional intelligence. (IND01-C) In participants’ accounts, communication and relational skills were frequently prioritized and directly associated with decision-making and the organization of nursing work.
sections.subcategory 4: soft skills considered es: In addition to the soft skills directly addressed in the data collection instrument, participating faculty members identified other skills they described as essential for students’ development in undergraduate nursing education. Various skills were mentioned, including socioemotional, relational, organizational, and professional aspects. Among the socioemotional aspects, self-awareness, resilience, flexibility, tolerance, availability, compassion, situational awareness, and sincerity were highlighted by participants. Selected excerpts are presented below, in which faculty members emphasize that self-awareness is the foundation for the development of other soft skills and that emotional resilience is necessary in light of the emotionally demanding situations experienced in the profession. I think self-awareness may be what stands out the most , because without self-awareness we are not truly able to develop all the other competencies. (IND26-D) I think working on emotional resilience is also very important , considering that we are in unhealthy environments , with people who are , most of the time , ill , sick , or in the process of dying in many situations. (IND08-A) Regarding relational aspects, active listening, bonding, negotiation, respect, solidarity, and conflict resolution were highlighted by participants. As an example of these skills, faculty members emphasized the importance of developing the soft skill of conflict resolution during training, describing the presence of reactive behaviors in practice settings. Another participant further described conflict resolution as being associated with the management of dilemmas present in everyday professional practice, as evidenced in the excerpts below. I think conflict resolution […] people tend to be quite reactive , and I believe this has greatly affected the settings we are part of , such as hospitals. I think learning how to resolve conflicts , how to mediate conflicts , is a very important skill that needs to be developed. (IND11-C) I think [another essential soft skill for development in undergraduate nursing education] is the issue of conflicts and dilemmas; we will always have to resolve something in a way that may be less harmful , and conflict is similar and operates within that same context. I believe conflict resolution , and the management of dilemmas , are essential. (IND02-B) In addition, organizational and professional aspects were mentioned that some participating faculty members consider essential for development in undergraduate nursing education, such as responsibility, organization, commitment, time management, autonomy, decision-making, and ethical issues. As exemplified below, participants mention time management as necessary for the performance of future nursing professionals, considering the responsibilities they will assume in different settings. Furthermore, one participant highlights the importance of ethical and moral issues in the development of soft skills within the health context. I think time management […] because soon the students will be graduating , they will be taking responsibility for primary care units , inpatient units , and they need to learn how to manage their time. (IND08-A) I do not know if I could call it a soft skill , but I think so; what permeates all of them are ethical and moral issues […] I think that when we work in the health field , reflecting on ethical and moral issues is a major contribution to integrating all the other soft skills. (IND01-C) Overall, participants identified soft skills that extend beyond those traditionally outlined in curricula, encompassing socioemotional, relational, organizational, and ethical–moral dimensions.
sections.category 3: pedagogical approaches and s: The most frequent word in this category was “practical,” followed by the words “assessment,” “instrument,” and “course,” as well as other slightly less frequent terms such as “approach,” “strategy,” “simulation,” and “case study.” Thus, throughout this category, the pedagogical approaches and strategies reported by participants to promote the development of soft skills are presented. Active methodologies were mentioned several times by faculty members as an approach to facilitate the development of soft skills, and were described as promoting closer engagement with students and their active role in the teaching–learning process. I use active methodologies […] I try , in every class I design , to start from lived experiences so that I can discuss with the students based on reality. And we can also go beyond the technical aspect and discuss the broader context. (IND16-C) I think that when we work with active methodologies , we have the possibility of being a bit closer to the students. Listening more , allowing them to bring their own experiences and backgrounds. I think that through more active methodologies […] we are able to work on these skills , the soft skills. (IND19-D) I think that any approach based on active methodologies will support the development of soft skills , because it ultimately reinforces the role of the student as the protagonist of their own learning process. (IND11-C) Participants report that they encourage students’ reflection and autonomy through examples from practice, as well as by returning questions in the form of new questions, which was described as an approach related to the soft skills of communication and problem-solving. We encourage communication all the time […] in theoretical classes , I usually use examples from my own practice , of course. And I try to take a reflective approach so that they think about how communication should be , how it actually is , and what its importance is for health promotion. (IND21-C) As for an approach to communication , I do not have a specific framework to tell you about […] in the past , when students asked me a question , I would immediately answer it. Now , when they ask me a question , I return the question to them , so that they can research it , seek out the knowledge , and then bring it back for us to discuss. (IND23-C) I think the approach to problem-solving is daily; again , it involves exposing students to reality and , whenever possible , not giving them immediate answers. I return questions and challenge the students […] (IND06-A) . Participating faculty members emphasize that emotional intelligence and empathy are also addressed mainly through examples and conversations with students. Likewise, they described the soft skill of teamwork is developed based on examples from their professional practice. For emotional intelligence and empathy , I bring examples from my professional experience , situations I have already gone through , and I say , look , in this situation , if you take this path , it will not turn out well […] But if you choose a different approach , to minimize a conflict or some difficulty , you could handle it this way , perhaps. It is about approaching it through conversation , holding a meeting , trying to clarify a misunderstanding with a patient or a team member. (IND18-D) I think that when it comes to emotional intelligence and empathy , we rely a lot on examples […] what we have been doing is talking one-on-one about situations that we see require attention , because many times people do not come forward on their own. (IND20-C) As for a pedagogical approach to teamwork , both in theory and in practice , we always try to bring examples from our own work when engaging with students. Through examples […] we show them the need for teamwork. We also share the difficulties we experienced when we were unable to develop this work with teams , whether due to the group or the faculty member. (IND20-C) Consequently, case studies were frequently mentioned by participants as strategies used for the development of various soft skills, including all the skills investigated in the data collection instrument. Case studies were described as mediating strategies between theory and practice, and as supporting the problematization of complex situations and the development of critical thinking. In addition, paper-based cases were also highlighted by participants as a strategy for developing certain soft skills, such as communication, teamwork, critical thinking, problem-solving, and ethical aspects. In this context, selected excerpts are presented below for illustration. I think that to develop communication , for example , these case studies , in practice , require them to train communication skills both with the patient and with the team. Because they will have to talk to the patient , gather some information or clarify doubts with the team as well , and they will have to talk among themselves in order to present the case study and develop the care plan. (IND04-B) We always end up working on problem-solving through case studies , but it is always simulated. How would you resolve the situation? […] Show how you would do it , which model you would apply , how you would reach the solution […] (IND11-C) . For critical thinking , we make extensive use of paper-based cases; if they are not in practice settings , we bring paper-based cases into the classroom for discussion. Based on a case we have already experienced , we present it in order to bring them the context of care , and then we engage in dialogue. (IND12-B) Another pedagogical strategy highlighted by participants was clinical simulation, mentioned at various points by several faculty members as applicable to the development of all the soft skills investigated in the instrument. Clinical simulation was described as an intentional strategy, in which faculty members report greater opportunities to observe, prompt, and assess the development of multiple soft skills in an integrated manner. Participants also described that simulation enables the definition of which soft skills will be addressed, observe students’ behaviors, and develop skills such as communication, leadership, and teamwork, as illustrated below. But I rely heavily on simulation; I think we are able to structure it , plan very specific objectives , and even define which soft skills we want to work on in a given scenario. (IND18-D) While the student is there , often carrying out that simulation for a specific condition , it may also involve communicating difficult news to a family member. It may also involve teamwork , the way the student is working with the rest of the team to resolve that situation. (IND11-C) Clinical simulation , for example , we are going to provide care , the patient is in cardiac arrest , even if it is basic life support , right there you can already identify who will assume leadership. Or no one assumes leadership , no one leads the process , which creates a rather chaotic situation. (IND14-D) The portfolio was mentioned by seven participants as a pedagogical strategy, as faculty members described it as enabling students to express themselves and elaborate on their lived experiences and feelings. In this regard, participants also described portfolios as useful for developing and assessing skills such as emotional intelligence, empathy, and responsibility. I believe that a pedagogical strategy to assess empathy and emotional intelligence is the portfolio […] often in the portfolio students bring up their feelings regarding a particular field placement or practice setting […] that is where they tend to express themselves , how they felt , many mention empathy , how much they were able to put themselves in the patient’s or colleague’s place. (IND08-A) […] I ask them to develop a portfolio […] one of the topics is breaking bad news; we address issues such as abortion , organ donation , among others. For each topic , they are expected to bring something more creative to present in the portfolio at the end of the course. I believe this encourages them to also take responsibility in constructing their own knowledge. (IND04-B) The flipped classroom and problem-based learning (PBL) were cited by five and six participants, respectively. These strategies were described as promoting reflective and self-regulatory processes, and as expanding students’ active role in the development of their competencies. Participants also reported that these strategies foster the development of skills such as critical thinking, for example, by encouraging questions formulated based on students’ readings. Last semester we carried out a flipped classroom activity […] we tried to build on the students’ readings and on what they identified there , bringing forward some questions to try to develop this critical thinking. (IND23-C) I think that […] the flipped classroom , problem-based learning , among others , will facilitate this process , this development of skills for the student. (IND11-C)
sections.category 4: perceived difficulties in pr: In Category 4, the most frequent words were “person,” “time,” “world,” and “difficulty,” among others with lower frequency, such as “cell phone” and “maturity.” Therefore, this category presents aspects reported by participants as challenges in promoting soft skills in teaching, such as the subjectivity involved in teaching these competencies, students’ emotional immaturity and preference for hard skills, as well as the impacts of technology and difficulties with concentration, illustrated in Subcategories 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
sections.subcategory 1: subjectivity in teaching: Participants associated the difficulty of teaching soft skills both with the absence of objective instruments and with students’ emotional immaturity. They also reflect that many of these skills are addressed implicitly in teaching, which makes them difficult to recognize. According to the faculty members, many students have difficulty understanding the importance of these skills and are not always open to the process. Regarding the teaching of soft skills , I see that perhaps the greatest difficulty we face is that we sometimes receive students who are very immature from an emotional standpoint […] not that this cannot be trained […] but sometimes we realize that students do not have the necessary emotional maturity , even those at the end of the program. (IND26-D) To teach soft skills , I think there is also the difficulty of their own subjectivity , and perhaps of the student’s difficulty in understanding whether that is important or not. Students are not always open to it either. (IND19-D) […] it is also an issue that , since we do not yet have a protocol or a checklist , it ends up being more subjective. (IND11-C) I think the greatest difficulty is that these are much more qualitative than quantitative issues , and they are also very transversal […] both we and the students do not always realize that we are teaching them something about leadership […] something about critical thinking […] Another point is that we do not speak about it explicitly , saying , look , we are going to work on leadership […] I think that is another difficulty. (IND08-A)
sections.subcategory 2: students\u2019 preference: Participants also reported that, when attempting to introduce activities related to soft skills, they encounter limited receptivity from students, who prioritize the teaching of hard skills, contributing to other skills being less valued. In participants’ accounts, the predominant appreciation of technical skills among students reinforces the perception of soft skills as secondary, making their legitimation within the educational process more difficult. I see difficulty in teaching soft skills because I do not see students interested in these concepts; they are more interested in technique. They want to learn how to perform procedures , how to insert an IV , the hard skills; that is what they are interested in. (IND13-D) […] I notice students’ lack of interest in this area; sometimes we bring something into the classroom […] to try to work on these skills , and students find it boring , they think they are wasting time […] I think one of the first difficulties is this barrier with students , because they have this perception that hard skills , techniques , procedures are more important , and they prioritize that. (IND11-C)
sections.subcategory 3: use of technologies and d: In participants’ accounts, the constant use of technologies and students’ difficulty concentrating are challenges for the development of soft skills. Students were described as having difficulty maintaining attention, engaging in in-depth reading, and reflecting on the proposed situations. The intensive use of digital technologies was described as a factor that may compromise the attention and reflective depth necessary for the development of soft skills. I notice difficulties […] I think technology helps us a lot […] but it also undermines students’ ability to think […] I see students struggling to think , to reflect , to engage in more in-depth reading […] in a classroom with 60 students , 40 of them have their cell phones on. (IND06-A) There are moments that are a bit more challenging […] today , young people come from a more immediate kind of education […] they have difficulty with reading , with going deeper , with stopping to listen […] in general , we struggle to ensure that everyone has the same level of perception and even to avoid distraction , in the sense of truly focusing on what we are proposing at that moment. (IND22-C) Transversally across the three analytical categories, the results indicate that, although faculty members widely recognize the relevance of soft skills in nursing education, their promotion occurs predominantly in an implicit, non-systematized, and pedagogically unintentional manner. Soft skills emerge primarily as indirect outcomes of teaching practices, especially associated with the use of active methodologies, reflective strategies, and practical experiences, rather than as explicitly planned, assessed, or institutionally guided objectives. Overall, the findings suggest that, although soft skills are widely recognized as important, their incorporation into pedagogical practices is not consistently structured.
sections.discussion: The results indicate that faculty members in this study recognize the importance of soft skills in nursing education, attributing to these competencies a central role in enhancing professional practice. Based on participants’ self-reports, these competencies were described as essential to teaching and to the development of professional practice. This perception converges with international findings that identify the teaching of soft skills as a fundamental element for strengthening interpersonal interactions and improving health care delivery, as observed among nurse educators in South Africa [ 16 ]. Thus, the results suggest that recognition of the formative value of these competencies is shared among the participants and aligns with findings from other educational contexts. However, this interpretation should be considered with caution, as it is based on self-reported data and may reflect perspectives aligned with socially or professionally desirable expectations. However, although participants acknowledge the relevance of soft skills, the findings suggest a significant gap regarding formal training for their teaching. None of the participants reported having received institutionally structured training aimed at the pedagogical development of these competencies, which may reflect the specific institutional context of the participating universities. This result suggests that the teaching of these competencies tends to rely on individual faculty initiative, rather than structured institutional strategies. This pattern observed among participants is consistent with what has been described in the international literature, which shows that nursing faculty, despite recognizing the importance of soft skills, often assume individual responsibility for teaching them, highlighting the fragility of institutional strategies for faculty development [ 17 ]. This mismatch between recognition and formative support, as reported by participants, indicates that the teaching of soft skills remains largely dependent on individual initiative and insufficiently structured within the curriculum, often being understood as something that develops through practice rather than through intentional pedagogical planning. With regard to the soft skills investigated in the data collection instrument, participants highlighted, based on their reports, both interpersonal and intrapersonal skills as essential to the teaching–learning process in nursing education. Communication emerged as a structuring competency in training, being associated with decision-making, interpersonal relationships, and work organization. This centrality attributed to communication in participants’ accounts is supported by the educational literature, which recognizes communication skills as fundamental tools in the relationship between nursing professionals and patients, with a direct impact on care outcomes [ 18 ]. Thus, the findings suggest that communication is a central competency within the context of this study, reinforcing its relevance in the investigated setting. Similarly, teamwork was mentioned by participants as one of the main competencies for nursing practice, considering that nurses work in integration with other health professionals. Collaboration among team members was associated with the promotion of more person-centered care and improved care outcomes, both for patients and for health services, as highlighted by McLaney et al. [ 19 ]. Therefore, the findings indicate that teamwork is understood by the faculty members in this study as a soft skill inseparable from professional nursing practice. Other interpersonal skills, such as leadership and empathy, were also emphasized by participants. Leadership was recognized as a fundamental competency for nurses’ performance as team leaders, as reported by participants, reinforcing the need for its development beginning in undergraduate education in order to prepare future professionals to work in different care settings [ 20 ]. Empathy, in turn, was understood as a transversal skill capable of supporting the development of various soft skills. This understanding, as expressed in participants’ accounts, is supported by the literature, which identifies empathy as a factor contributing to increased leadership effectiveness and the strengthening of professional relationships [ 21 , 22 ]. Within the domain of intrapersonal skills, participating faculty members highlighted critical thinking, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence as relevant competencies for nursing education. Critical thinking was understood as a distinguishing feature of nurses in professional practice, as reported, particularly in light of the complexity of care contexts. This finding converges with the literature pointing to the need for transformations in health education in order to prepare professionals capable of critically analyzing situations and responding reflectively to contemporary challenges [ 23 ]. Complementarily, studies indicate that the development of problem-solving skills is closely related to critical thinking, since pedagogical strategies based on problematization foster the analytical reasoning of nursing students [ 24 ]. Emotional intelligence was also identified by participating faculty members as a foundation supporting the development of other soft skills, a perception supported by studies that highlight this competency as essential to professional nursing practice, with implications for ethical aspects, crisis management, and quality of care [ 25 ]. Furthermore, evidence from a systematic review indicates that training in emotional intelligence contributes to stress reduction and the enhancement of communication skills, reinforcing its relevance within the educational context [ 26 ]. Beyond the skills initially investigated, participating faculty members expanded the set of soft skills considered essential to nursing education, incorporating socioemotional, relational, organizational, and professional competencies. Among the socioemotional aspects, self-awareness was identified as a foundation for the development of other soft skills, as it fosters critical reflection and the construction of professional identity throughout the educational process. This understanding is aligned with the literature that recognizes self-awareness as a component of emotional intelligence and as a factor associated with nurses’ professional performance [ 27 , 28 ]. Participating nursing faculty members also emphasized the importance of emotional resilience, considering the emotionally demanding situations experienced in professional practice. Studies indicate that resilience contributes to reducing emotional strain and burnout, as professionals with higher levels of this competency demonstrate greater adaptability to stressors and lower levels of emotional exhaustion [ 29 , 30 ]. These findings suggest the importance of educational strategies to support the development of resilience in nursing education, although this interpretation is grounded in participants’ accounts within a specific educational, institutional and regional context. With regard to relational aspects, conflict resolution was highlighted by participating faculty members as a skill that needs to be developed during training. Evidence from studies involving nurses working in intensive care units indicates moderate levels of conflict, even in atypical contexts such as the COVID-19 pandemic, emphasizing collaboration as the primary strategy for resolution [ 31 ]. These findings suggest that conflict management is a relevant competency for nursing practice and point to the importance of its intentional inclusion in the educational process. The soft skills considered essential by participating faculty members also encompassed organizational and professional aspects, such as time management and ethical–moral issues. Time management was associated, in participants’ accounts, with the ability to handle simultaneous demands, balance personal and professional life, and reduce stress related to work overload, as evidenced in the literature [ 32 ]. Likewise, the development of ethical–moral competencies was recognized as fundamental for analyzing complex situations and making well-grounded ethical decisions, contributing to improvements in the quality of health care [ 33 ]. The results also indicate that participants use different pedagogical approaches and strategies to promote the development of soft skills in nursing education, with emphasis on the use of active methodologies. These approaches were described by participants as facilitating closer interaction between faculty and students, as well as strengthening students’ active role in the teaching–learning process. This finding converges with the literature pointing to a progressive transition from traditional pedagogical models to student-centered approaches, which favor the development of transversal competencies such as communication, teamwork, and autonomy [ 34 , 35 ]. However, as these findings are based on participants’ reports, the absence of direct observation limits the ability to assess how these strategies are implemented in actual teaching practice. In the present study, active methodologies do not emerge merely as didactic techniques, but as pedagogical devices that enable greater student engagement with real or simulated professional practice situations. Based on participants’ reports of using strategies that stimulate reflection, problematization, and active participation, faculty members indicate a broadened understanding of soft skills teaching, aligned with pedagogical proposals that foster the development of critical thinking and student autonomy. These findings are consistent with evidence that the use of active methodologies contributes to more positive student attitudes toward communication, teamwork, and stress management [ 34 ]. It is important to consider that the adoption of active methodologies, although relevant, may not be sufficient in itself to ensure the development of soft skills, which may indicate the need for greater attention to pedagogical intentionality in their implementation. It is pertinent to acknowledge that the effects of these strategies may vary according to how they are planned and conducted, particularly with regard to the explicit articulation of objectives related to soft skills. Among the pedagogical strategies mentioned, case studies were widely used by participating faculty members as a means of articulating theory and practice. This strategy was associated with the development of various soft skills, such as communication, teamwork, critical thinking, and problem-solving. The literature indicates that case-based learning promotes the problematization of complex situations and stimulates students’ critical reflection, in addition to contributing to greater self-confidence and satisfaction in the learning process when compared to traditional lecture-based methods [ 36 , 37 ]. Thus, the findings suggest the potential of case studies as a pedagogical strategy for the integrated development of technical and non-technical competencies. Complementarily, participating faculty members reported the use of paper-based cases as a pedagogical resource to deepen classroom discussions, particularly when students were not engaged in practice settings. This strategy was associated with the stimulation of critical thinking and problem-solving, as it requires analysis, information seeking, and decision-making. Evidence indicates that the use of paper-based cases fosters reflection on real professional practice situations, contributing to the development of these soft skills within the context of nursing education [ 37 , 38 ]. Clinical simulation stood out as one of the most relevant pedagogical strategies for the development of the investigated soft skills. Participating faculty members reported that simulation enables the prior definition of pedagogical objectives, the observation of students’ behaviors, and the integration of multiple competencies within a safe and controlled environment. This finding is consistent with studies identifying simulation as an effective strategy for strengthening communication, leadership, teamwork, and critical thinking, in addition to contributing to increased student self-confidence and satisfaction [ 39 , 40 ]. In this way, clinical simulation can be understood as an intentional and structured approach to the development of soft skills in nursing education. The use of portfolios was also mentioned as a pedagogical strategy that fosters reflection on experiences lived in different learning settings. Participating faculty members associated this strategy with the development of soft skills such as emotional intelligence, empathy, and responsibility, since the portfolio allows students to express feelings, perceptions, and learning derived from their experiences. The literature highlights the portfolio as a resource capable of integrating teaching, learning, and assessment, stimulating critical-reflective reasoning, autonomy, and decision-making in nursing education [ 41 , 42 ]. In addition, the flipped classroom and problem-based learning were identified as pedagogical strategies used by some participating faculty members to promote the development of soft skills. From a conceptual perspective, the flipped classroom presupposes students’ prior study of the content, so that in-person time can be dedicated to discussion, problematization, and deeper exploration, rather than being limited to group presentations, with which it is sometimes mistakenly associated. In the reports, the flipped classroom was linked to the expansion of space for reflective discussions in class, while problem-based learning was associated with the stimulation of critical thinking and problem-solving. Evidence indicates that these strategies foster student engagement and the development of competencies such as communication, cooperation, autonomy, and time management, particularly when combined within the educational process [ 43 , 44 ]. Overall, the results indicate that participating faculty members draw on different pedagogical strategies to promote the development of soft skills, with emphasis on approaches that stimulate reflection, active participation, and engagement with professional practice situations. However, the findings suggest that these strategies are often adopted sporadically and depend largely on individual faculty initiative, which may indicate the need for greater pedagogical systematization and institutional support to consolidate the teaching of soft skills in nursing education. In this regard, mechanisms such as faculty performance evaluation and career progression criteria may contribute to encouraging and valuing pedagogical practices aimed at the development of these competencies. The results also indicate that, although participants recognize the importance of soft skills in nursing education, their promotion in teaching is permeated by various pedagogical, institutional, and relational difficulties. Among the main challenges identified in participants’ reports are the subjectivity of these competencies, students’ emotional immaturity, the prioritization of technical skills, and the impact of the intensive use of technologies on the teaching and learning process. Although some of the challenges reported by faculty members are related to the specific nature of soft skills, the findings suggest that certain difficulties may also reflect broader aspects of the contemporary educational context. Elements such as the intensive use of digital technologies, classroom distraction, and issues related to students’ emotional maturity are not exclusive to the teaching of soft skills but permeate the educational process as a whole. Such factors may intensify the perceived difficulties, indicating the need for pedagogical strategies that take into account transformations in contemporary educational dynamics. The subjectivity associated with soft skills was mentioned as a factor that hinders both their teaching and evaluation. Participating faculty members reported the absence of clear protocols, instruments, or frameworks to guide the approach to these competencies, which contributes to their being addressed in an implicit and transversal manner, without explicit pedagogical intentionality. This perception is supported by the literature, which identifies the lack of conceptual consensus and standardization as one of the main barriers to the systematic incorporation of soft skills into education, particularly when compared to hard skills, which are traditionally associated with more objective assessment criteria [ 45 ]. Associated with this subjectivity, students’ emotional immaturity was identified as an additional difficulty in the development of soft skills. Participating faculty members reported that many students demonstrate resistance or limited openness to reflecting on socioemotional and relational aspects, which restricts engagement in activities aimed at these competencies. This finding is consistent with studies indicating that students’ recognition of the importance of soft skills tends to occur later, particularly when they begin to experience clinical practice settings more intensively [ 46 ]. Thus, the appreciation of these competencies appears to be conditioned by practical experience, which makes their continuous promotion throughout the educational process more challenging. Another relevant challenge identified by participants refers to students’ preference for the teaching of hard skills to the detriment of socioemotional and relational competencies. The reports indicate that activities aimed at developing soft skills are sometimes perceived by students as secondary or less relevant when compared to technical and procedural skills. This perception is corroborated by the literature, which points out that nursing students frequently associate professional competence with the mastery of psychomotor skills, contributing to the devaluation of soft skills in the educational process [ 46 ]. This preference may also be interpreted as reflecting the reproduction of a traditional educational model centered on memorization and content transmission, experienced throughout students’ prior educational trajectories. In this context, more problematizing pedagogical proposals oriented toward autonomy may generate resistance, which may, in turn, affect the recognition and appreciation of soft skills within the educational process. In addition, participating faculty members highlighted the intensive use of digital technologies as a factor that negatively interferes with the development of soft skills. The constant presence of electronic devices in the classroom was associated with difficulties in concentration, reduced depth of reading, and diminished reflective capacity among students. Evidence suggests that frequent use of technologies, especially for purposes unrelated to the educational process, may compromise students’ attention and active participation, interfering with activities that require listening, reflection, and interaction, which are fundamental aspects for the development of soft skills [ 47 , 48 ]. Taken together, the identified challenges suggest that the difficulties in promoting soft skills in teaching are not limited to individual factors related to students or faculty members but reflect broader structural and pedagogical limitations. The absence of clear guidelines, insufficient faculty training, a training culture centered on technical skills, and the impacts of digital technologies may create a scenario that hinders the intentional and systematic incorporation of these competencies into nursing education. Thus, the findings point to the need for institutional strategies that recognize soft skills as essential components of professional education, promoting their explicit integration into curricula, faculty pedagogical development, and the creation of learning environments that foster reflection, interaction, and student engagement. Nevertheless, these considerations should be interpreted with caution, considering the context-specific nature of the study and the use of self-reported data, which may influence how soft skills are perceived and described, and therefore limit the transferability of the findings to other educational contexts.
sections.limitations: This study presents some limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. First, the data were obtained exclusively through interviews with faculty members and are therefore based on self-reported accounts. This characteristic may influence the perceptions presented, as the responses reflect how participants interpret and describe their own pedagogical practices. Furthermore, although the interviews were conducted with cameras on, the virtual format may have influenced the dynamics of the dialogue and limited aspects of interaction that might have been more broadly perceived in face-to-face encounters. In addition, the possibility of social desirability bias cannot be ruled out, considering that faculty members may have emphasized aspects perceived as socially or professionally desirable, particularly regarding the value attributed to soft skills and the use of pedagogical strategies aligned with contemporary approaches. Another limitation concerns the absence of direct observation of pedagogical practices in teaching settings. The inclusion of observational methods could have expanded the understanding of how soft skills are effectively promoted in everyday teaching activities, allowing for triangulation between discourse and practice. Moreover, participants were affiliated with federal public universities in a single region of Brazil, which delimits the findings to this institutional and regional context. Although the inclusion of multiple institutional settings contributes to the diversity of perspectives, the results should not be generalized to other educational contexts without due caution. Despite these limitations, the study offers relevant contributions by deepening the understanding of the incorporation of soft skills into nursing education and providing support for future reflections and investigations that may expand and complement the findings presented here.
sections.conclusion: The findings of this study suggest that, among the participating faculty members, there is recognition of the relevance of soft skills in the context of nursing education, as well as reports of the use of different pedagogical approaches and strategies to promote their development, particularly through active methodologies and learning environments that stimulate critical reflection, autonomy, and students’ active role. However, the absence of specific training for teaching these competencies, reported by a significant proportion of faculty members, reveals a formative gap that calls for investment in continuing education processes. The findings also indicate that faculty members expand the set of soft skills initially addressed in the data collection instrument, incorporating competencies of a socioemotional, relational, organizational, and ethical nature. Despite this broadened recognition, relevant challenges persist in promoting these competencies in teaching, such as the subjectivity associated with soft skills, students’ emotional immaturity, the predominant appreciation of technical skills, and the impacts of the intensive use of technologies on concentration and reflective capacity. In this sense, the results suggest that, although technical mastery is indispensable in nursing education, the intentional and systematic development of soft skills is equally essential for building a more comprehensive professional education. It is evident, however, that the absence of structured theoretical-pedagogical frameworks to guide the teaching of these competencies contributes to their unsystematic and predominantly implicit approach. Thus, the adoption of structured institutional strategies aimed at integrating these competencies into curricula and promoting faculty pedagogical development is fundamental to strengthening the educational process. Therefore, investing in faculty training for the teaching of soft skills may strengthen professional nursing education and contribute to improving the quality of health care. This study points to the need for intentional and institutionally supported strategies to integrate soft skills into nursing curricula, promoting a more comprehensive education aligned with the contemporary demands of professional practice.

title: CFD-driven optimization and experimental validation of venturi-based thrombectomy devices in a circle of willis
abstract: The geometry of the Circle of Willis poses major challenges for mechanical thrombectomy, where device navigability and effective thrombus removal determine treatment success. This study investigated the performance of venturi-inspired aspiration thrombectomy devices in a simplified cerebral artery segment representative of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), a frequent site of occlusion. Five designs (30°, 45°, 60° venturi, 7/11° taper, and cylindrical control) were assessed using a combined computational–experimental framework. On the computational side, unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) simulations were performed in ANSYS Fluent 19.2 with k–ε turbulence closure. Blood–clot interactions were modeled using a Volume of Fluid (VOF) multiphase formulation with Carreau–Yasuda non-Newtonian rheology. In vitro, stereolithography-fabricated prototypes were tested with porcine thrombi in silicone arterial phantoms. CFD predicted extraction times of 2.12 s for the control and 1.64 s for the 45° venturi, with efficiency plateauing beyond 45°. Experimental results confirmed this trend, showing the 45° design as optimal and all venturi devices outperforming the control. Fragmentation analysis revealed a trade-off, with the 60° venturi producing more than twice the fragments of the 30°. These findings demonstrate that venturi taper geometry critically influences aspiration efficiency and fragmentation and establish CFD–experiment integration as a foundation for optimizing next-generation thrombectomy devices.

sections.introduction: Stroke remains the second leading cause of death worldwide and a primary contributor to long-term disability 1 . According to the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study, ischemic stroke accounts for approximately 85% of all stroke cases and continues to increase in prevalence despite advances in preventive and acute care strategies 2 . Over the past decade, endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) has revolutionized the treatment of large-vessel occlusion (LVO), with multiple landmark trials and subsequent meta-analyses demonstrating significantly improved outcomes compared to medical therapy alone 3 , 4 . Nonetheless, substantial challenges persist. Recanalization failure, thrombus fragmentation, and distal embolization remain common even when using current-generation stent retrievers and aspiration systems 5 – 7 . These limitations underscore the ongoing need for device innovation, informed by hemodynamic principles and validated through rigorous experimental and computational evaluation.
sections.the circle of willis: collateral hub and: The Circle of Willis (CoW) is the brain’s principal arterial collateral system, playing a critical role in redistributing flow during arterial occlusion. However, anatomical studies indicate that a complete CoW, featuring intact anterior and posterior communicating arteries, is present in fewer than 50% of individuals 8 , 9 . Variations such as hypoplasia or absence of communicating arteries significantly affect compensatory flow pathways and influence ischemic burden and stroke prognosis 10 , 11 . Functional studies show that the CoW operates as a pressure-dissipating system under physiological conditions but becomes a crucial collateral route during stenosis or occlusion 9 , 10 . Experimental and computational models have demonstrated that CoW anatomy and vessel caliber strongly modulate embolic trajectories, perfusion heterogeneity, and thrombectomy outcomes 5 , 8 . Beyond static anatomical classification, recent CFD studies have demonstrated that even subtle variations in CoW geometry can profoundly alter collateral flow patterns and shear stress distributions under pathological states 12 – 14 . Patient-specific modeling across hundreds of subjects has enabled functional phenotyping of CoW integrity and its relationship to embolic risk 13 – 15 . MR angiography and hemodynamic modeling have further shown how variations in communicating artery caliber affect posterior collateral sufficiency and anterior circulation compensation 11 , 16 . Several large-scale studies, such as those by Vrselja et al. 9 and Alastruey et al. 8 , highlighted how anatomical variants of the CoW alter cerebral perfusion and collateralization. More recent studies, including Sriwastwa et al. 5 , have linked CoW variants with stroke outcomes following revascularization therapy. Advanced imaging and simulation methods (Hendrikse et al. 10 ; Behland et al. 13 ) continue to refine our understanding of CoW physiology and pathophysiology, reinforcing the importance of incorporating CoW variation in both clinical and computational thrombectomy studies .
sections.aspiration thrombectomy and device desig: Direct aspiration thrombectomy has emerged as a practical and efficient alternative to stent retrievers, offering procedural simplicity, lower device cost, and favorable clinical outcomes in select patients. However, aspiration success depends on a complex interplay of factors, including catheter inner diameter, tip geometry, applied vacuum pressure, thrombus composition, and alignment with the thrombus 17 , 18 . While bench-top and clinical studies have shown that larger-bore aspiration catheters improve first-pass effect and recanalization rates, increased stiffness may compromise deliverability in tortuous vessels 12 . Physics of thrombus ingestion remains a subject of ongoing investigation. Turk et al. 19 demonstrated that suction-based thrombus retrieval, particularly with the direct aspiration first-pass technique (ADAPT), can achieve high rates of successful recanalization with reduced procedure times. Jakobek et al. 20 further showed in vitro that catheter position relative to collateral pathways significantly alters aspiration performance and embolic clearance. Together, these findings reinforce the importance of catheter geometry, positioning, and suction force in optimizing aspiration thrombectomy design and outcomes.
sections.computational modeling in thrombectomy r: Computational modeling is a crucial tool in thrombectomy research, enabling in silico analysis of mechanical procedures. This approach allows researchers to simulate the interaction between devices and blood thrombuss, considering factors like thrombus composition and material properties. For example, Fregona et al. 21 showed that red blood cell-rich thrombuss are more prone to fragmentation. Bridio et al. 22 developed a low-dimensional surrogate model for rapid strain estimation, while Luraghi et al. 23 evaluated the performance of combined stent-retriever and aspiration techniques. Other work has focused on creating patient-specific models of the cerebral vasculature 24 , proposing new models for thrombus deformation during aspiration 25 , and modeling the effects of microthrombi on tissue oxygenation 26 . This research, which also includes a consensus-based review on using these methods for regulatory purposes 27 , demonstrates that computational modeling is essential for improving our understanding of thrombectomy mechanics and developing better devices and strategies.
sections.beyond laminar flow: turbulence and bloo: While blood flow in cerebral arteries is often modeled as laminar, recent studies challenge this assumption in the context of complex geometries and device-induced disturbances. Saqr and Zidane 28 identified non-Kolmogorov turbulence regimes in arterial flow, characterized by inverse energy cascades with potential implications for endothelial mechanobiology. Such turbulence may emerge in aneurysmal sacs, near bifurcations, or during active aspiration. Additionally, the non-Newtonian nature of blood must be accounted for in CFD simulations. The Carreau–Yasuda model has been validated as a physiologically realistic representation of shear-dependent blood viscosity, outperforming Newtonian approximations 29 , 30 . The importance of considering both turbulence and non-Newtonian effects in blood flow simulations, initially highlighted by Saqr and Zidane 28 , has been further underscored by recent research. Studies such as those by Cheng et al. 31 and Calzetta et al. 32 have advanced our understanding of turbulence and its energy spectrum in physiological and non-Newtonian fluids. Furthermore, Garven et al. 33 and Chauhan et al. 34 have demonstrated these principles in specific biomedical applications, including multiscale modeling for pediatric cardiovascular systems and the hemodynamics of bileaflet mechanical heart valves, respectively. These collective findings validate the ongoing efforts to develop more physiologically realistic models.
sections.novelty and study objectives: A critical gap in current thrombectomy research lies in the lack of integrated approaches that combine CFD optimization with experimental validation in physiologically realistic environments. The present study aims to address this gap by evaluating venturi-inspired aspiration thrombectomy device geometries using both CFD and in-vitro testing in a Circle of Willis model. In addition to clot extraction efficiency, the present study also evaluates visible clot fragmentation in the in-vitro experiments as a secondary outcome, since fragmentation may influence the practical safety and effectiveness of aspiration thrombectomy. The CFD framework employed Unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) simulations in ANSYS Fluent 19.2 to solve the governing equations of incompressible, unsteady flow in a simplified cerebral artery segment representative of the CoW, focusing on the middle cerebral artery (MCA), a frequent site of occlusion. A Volume of Fluid (VOF) multiphase model was implemented to capture blood–thrombus interactions, with blood modeled as a non-Newtonian fluid via the Carreau–Yasuda law and thrombi represented as highly viscous deformable occluding phases positioned downstream of the catheter tip within the VOF framework. Turbulence was modeled using the standard k–ε closure within a URANS framework. While this approach does not resolve turbulence spectra, flow instabilities observed in the simulations are later interpreted in light of recent reports of transitional turbulent kinetic energy cascades in cerebral arteries 28 , providing a physiologically relevant context for understanding aspiration-induced unsteadiness. The objectives were: To evaluate multiple venturi geometries (30°, 45°, 60° curved; 7/11° straight; plus a control design) and quantify their influence on flow dynamics and thrombus extraction efficiency in the CFD model, while assessing fragmentation experimentally in the in-vitro tests. To validate Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) predictions, which utilize an Eulerian-Eulerian approach, against experimental results using porcine thrombus models; and To assess the performance of various designs of aspiration-based thrombectomy devices within a Circle of Willis phantom. The study emphasizes their extraction efficiency in the middle cerebral artery (MCA), which is a key component of the CoW that branches off the internal carotid artery and is a frequent location for thrombus occlusion.
sections.methods: Five designs of aspiration based thrombectomy device (30°, 45°, 60° curved, 7/11° straight, and a cylindrical control) were investigated through computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and bench-top experiments. Simulations were performed in ANSYS Fluent 19.2 using the URANS framework with the standard k–ε turbulence closure. The choice of a URANS turbulence closure was motivated by the pulsatile, aspiration-driven, and geometry-disturbed nature of the present flow, together with previous reports indicating that cerebral hemodynamics may depart from purely laminar behavior and may exhibit transitional, non-classical turbulent features under complex unsteady conditions. Within this framework, the standard k–ε model was selected as a robust and computationally efficient two-equation closure for the present comparative parametric study, in which all device geometries were evaluated under identical operating conditions. The primary objective of the CFD analysis was to establish the comparative ranking of device performance, rather than to resolve detailed near-wall turbulence structure or turbulence spectra. In this context, the standard k–ε model was considered appropriate because of its established robustness, stable convergence behavior, and wide use in mean-flow engineering simulations. While the k–ω SST model is an important alternative for flows with stronger adverse pressure gradients, separation, and enhanced near-wall sensitivity, a single turbulence-model framework was retained across all simulated geometries to ensure direct comparison of device-performance trends 35 , 36 . This model captures mean unsteady separation and shear but does not resolve turbulence spectra; spectral interpretations are deferred to the Discussion. A Volume of Fluid (VOF) multiphase model was implemented to capture blood–thrombus interactions: blood was treated as a Carreau–Yasuda non-Newtonian fluid, while thrombi were represented as highly viscous deformable occluding phases positioned downstream of the catheter tip. The Courant number was maintained below unity, and a time step of 0.001 s was used to resolve the pulsatile inlet waveform and turbulence-like fluctuations. In parallel, experimental validation was performed using porcine blood thrombus in silicone tube. This model represented a simplified segment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) within the CoW to replicate its anatomical complexity. This combined numerical–experimental methodology ensured reproducibility, physiological fidelity, and rigorous testing of device designs.
sections.boundary conditions: At the inlet, a prescribed time-dependent axial velocity boundary condition was applied directly at the inlet plane of the computational domain. The temporal waveform was represented using a Fourier series with a fundamental frequency of 2 Hz (120 bpm). To preserve physiological waveform asymmetry, harmonics were retained up to the fifth order (≤ 10 Hz). The spatial velocity distribution at the inlet was assumed to be uniform across the inlet section of the simplified axisymmetric artery model; that is, the pulsatility was imposed through the time variation of the inlet velocity magnitude, rather than through an upstream inlet extension used to generate a developed profile. This choice was made to provide a controlled and identical inflow condition for all simulated device geometries in the present comparative study. The imposed waveform consisted of systolic and diastolic phases, with velocity varying between 0.1 m s −1 and 0.5 m s −1 , as shown in Fig. 1 . This choice is supported by reports that more than 90% of the pulsatile energy in the internal carotid and cerebral arteries is contained in harmonics below 6 Hz, with the dominant contributions occurring between 1 and 4 Hz 28 , 39 , 40 . This cyclic flow, with a period of 0.5 s, consists of systolic and diastolic phases. During systole, the velocity varies sinusoidally, peaking at 0.5 m/s and reaching a minimum of 0.1 m/s. This pulsatile profile is shown in Fig. 1 . The mean Reynolds number, calculated using the generalized Metzner–Reed correlation, was approximately 345 for a vessel diameter of 4 mm, a value within the transitional regime and therefore supporting the adoption of a turbulence model 28 . A diameter of 4 mm was selected based on morphometric data of the Circle of Willis, where the proximal cerebral arteries typically exhibit diameters around this value 41 . Fig. 1 Inlet velocity profile. The outlet boundary was set to a constant suction pressure of –30 kPa, corresponding to the experimental vacuum system. Vessel walls were treated as no-slip boundaries, and near-wall resolution was handled using a boundary-layer inflation strategy adjacent to the solid walls. The thrombus was modeled as a 20 mm occlusion placed 3 mm downstream of the catheter tip. A 20 mm long thrombus with 4 mm diameter was positioned 3 mm downstream of the catheter tip, representing full occlusion of the vessel. The thrombus was represented as a highly viscous deformable occluding phase with density 1080 kg m −3 and dynamic viscosity 0.35 Pa s, according to Talayero et al. 42 . Within the present VOF framework, this treatment corresponds to a fluid-like clot surrogate rather than a solid-mechanics viscoelastic constitutive model.
sections.computational domain and numerical detai: The computational domain was constructed as a 2D axisymmetric geometry to reduce computational cost while preserving symmetry, since the aspiration device and vessel were coaxially aligned. Figure 2 illustrates the general computational arrangement of the artery–device–thrombus system used in the CFD simulations, whereas the detailed CAD geometries of the individual device configurations investigated in this study are provided in Table 1 . The simulated artery was modeled as a 30 mm long straight segment with an internal diameter of 4 mm, corresponding to the silicone tubing used in the experiments. The aspiration device lumen was modeled with a diameter of 3 mm, attached coaxially to the artery. A 20 mm long thrombus with the same diameter as the artery (4 mm) was placed 3 mm downstream of the catheter tip, representing a 100% occlusion. An adapted interaction region was defined around the thrombus to capture the multiphase interface. The thrombus was modeled as the secondary phase and represented as a highly viscous deformable occluding phase with density 1080 kg m −3 and dynamic viscosity 0.35 Pa s. Thus, within the present VOF framework, the clot was treated as a fluid-like surrogate phase rather than as a solid body with a separately defined viscoelastic constitutive law. For the VOF model, explicit time integration was employed to track multiphase interactions. Each simulation was run for eight cardiac cycles; the first three cycles were discarded to remove start-up transients, and the final five were used for analysis. Convergence was defined as residuals below 10 −5 for velocity and continuity and below 10 −6 for turbulent viscosity.
sections.mesh independence: Grid independence was evaluated to ensure numerical accuracy while minimizing computational cost. The near-wall meshing strategy was kept consistent throughout the mesh-independence study. Specifically, the same wall-boundary treatment and inflation approach were retained for all mesh levels, and refinement was introduced through changes in the overall grid density rather than by altering the near-wall treatment itself. Due to the similarity of the venturi-style devices, the 45° geometry was selected as a representative case for the mesh refinement study. Simulations were performed with progressively refined grids, and the maximum velocity at the catheter tip was monitored at a representative timestep (0.07 s). Results showed negligible variation in velocity and shear stress beyond 4000 finite volumes, confirming mesh convergence. Accordingly, the final simulations were performed with 4000–5000 finite volumes, which provided a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The mesh convergence study yielded a maximum velocity of approximately 2.3 m/s, consistent with the expected suction-driven flow regime. Residuals were converged at 10 −5 for velocity and continuity and 10⁻⁶ for turbulent viscosity, with a time step of 0.001 s ensuring numerical stability. Figure 3 shows computational mesh of the artery–device–thrombus configuration used in the CFD simulations. However, Fig. 4 represents the mesh independence analysis for the 45° venturi geometry. sections.device design and fabrication: Five designs of aspiration based thrombectomy device were investigated: three curved venturi designs with taper angles of 30°, 45°, and 60°, one straight taper geometry (7/11°), and a cylindrical control. Geometries were created in ANSYS DesignModeler 19.2. Prototypes were manufactured using stereolithography (SLA) 3D printing with standard resin material to achieve high dimensional accuracy. The fabrication route was selected because the device geometry required a minimum wall thickness of 0.5 mm, which was compatible with the available SLA process. All prototypes were fabricated using the same manufacturing route and post-processing procedure, including washing, curing, and polishing of the tip region, to maintain consistency across the tested geometries. Each printed device was attached to rigid silicone catheter tubing, which provided sufficient support and prevented detachment during recanalization attempts, as shown in Fig. 5 . Silicone was chosen over other common polymers such as nylon or polyurethane due to its inert properties and resistance to interaction with blood. Fig. 5 Printed device attached to rigid silicone catheter tubing. Table 1 shows the aspiration based thrombectomy device designs.
sections.experimental setup: The experimental system was constructed to validate the aspiration performance of the venturi-inspired devices under physiologically relevant conditions. A soft silicone tube with a length of 150 mm and an inner diameter of 4 mm was used to represent a simplified cerebral artery. The material had a measured Young’s modulus of 1.68 MPa, consistent with vessel compliance reported in literature 43 . N-saline solution was used as a substitute for blood. The solution was prepared by dissolving 9 g of sodium chloride in 1 L of water and mixing thoroughly. Prior to each trial, the interior wall of the silicone tube was lubricated with N-saline to facilitate clot insertion and reduce wall friction. In addition to wall compliance, clot motion in the silicone phantom may also be influenced by surface friction and wettability at the clot–wall interface. In the present experiments, these effects were not independently characterized, but the same silicone material and the same N-saline pre-lubrication protocol were used throughout in order to maintain consistent interface conditions across all runs. The aspiration system consisted of a vacuum pump connected via a PVC tube to a vacuum flask. A pressure gauge was integrated into the system and adjusted to maintain a constant negative pressure of − 30 kPa. The catheter was connected to the arm of the vacuum flask, with the probe inserted halfway into the silicone tubing to secure the assembly. Figure 6 illustrates both (a) the schematic diagram of the experimental setup for in-vitro validation of venturi-inspired aspiration devices and (b) a photograph of the real physical apparatus. Fig. 6 The experimental setup for in-vitro validation of venturi-inspired aspiration devices. Cylindrical porcine clots, 20 mm lengths with 4 mm diameter, were prepared, induced with thrombin, incubated at 37 °C, and stored at 4 °C for 24 h before use. During each trial, a clot segment was inserted into the silicone phantom, with N-saline added to both ends of the tubing to ensure hydration and smooth insertion. The probe tip was then positioned 3 mm proximal to the clot before aspiration was initiated. All in-vitro trials were conducted using the same experimental protocol, including identical nominal clot dimensions, the same silicone phantom geometry, a fixed probe-tip offset of 3 mm from the clot, N-saline lubrication of the tubing prior to insertion, and a constant applied suction pressure of − 30 kPa, in order to maintain consistency across replicates. Figure 7 shows the prepared porcine clot (a) and its insertion into the soft silicone tube (b, c), which was used to represent the simplified cerebral artery in the in-vitro setup. Fig. 7 Porcine clot preparation and insertion into the experimental phantom. ( a ) Prepared cylindrical porcine clot. ( b , c ) Clot inserted into the soft silicone tube, representing the cerebral artery model. Each device geometry was tested in ten replicates. The primary endpoint was the clot extraction time, defined as the duration required for ≥ 95% clot removal. Secondary endpoints included recanalization success rate, clot fragmentation, and residual clot length. In the present experiments, fragmentation was assessed qualitatively by visual inspection after each run. A fragment was defined as a visibly discrete residual clot piece remaining in the silicone phantom or at the device entrance region after aspiration, separate from the main clot body. Fragmentation was recorded as the number of such visible residual pieces per run; fragment mass was not measured. The experimental work did not involve any live vertebrates or animal sacrifice. Porcine blood clots were prepared from commercially obtained porcine blood purchased from a licensed food supplier. All experiments were conducted in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations of Aston University (Birmingham, UK) and in line with the ARRIVE guidelines 44 for studies involving animal-derived materials.
sections.results: The performance of venturi-inspired thrombectomy devices was evaluated through in-vitro experiments and CFD simulations. In-vitro testing was conducted first to quantify clot extraction times, recanalization rates, and fragmentation across the five device geometries. These results were then complemented by CFD simulations, which provided detailed insight into suction velocities and pressure fields, and allowed direct comparison with experimental findings. Together, experimental and computational outcomes were used to assess device performance and to identify the optimal design.
sections.in-vitro evaluation of device performanc: Prototype devices were fabricated by stereolithography and tested in vitro using porcine thrombi within silicone arterial phantoms, with ten independent replicates performed for each geometry (30°, 45°, 60° venturi, 7/11° taper, and cylindrical control). In terms of extraction times, all venturi-inspired devices achieved faster clot removal than the cylindrical control, which required 1.57 s on average. The 30° venturi recorded the longest extraction time among the venturi designs at 1.51 s, while the 45° and 60° venturi achieved shorter times of 1.20 and 1.25 s, respectively. The 7/11° venturi (1.27 s) performed comparably to the 60° device, indicating that performance gains plateaued beyond 45°. These outcomes are shown in Fig. 8 , which presents the mean extraction times for all devices. Fig. 8 Mean extraction time for all venturi-inspired designs tested in-vitro. Error bars represent standard deviation across n = 10 replicates for each geometry. To quantify experimental repeatability, the extraction-time data were further analyzed across the ten replicates for each geometry. The results were 1.51 ± 0.09 s for the 30° venturi, 1.20 ± 0.11 s for the 45° venturi, 1.25 ± 0.12 s for the 60° venturi, 1.27 ± 0.12 s for the 7/11° venturi, and 1.57 ± 0.19 s for the cylindrical control. The corresponding coefficients of variation (CVs) were 5.8%, 9.4%, 9.9%, 9.3%, and 11.9%, respectively. These values indicate moderate variability while preserving the same overall ranking across repeated trials, with the 45° venturi remaining the fastest design and the cylindrical control remaining the slowest.
