sections.what is new?: In a large, real‐world cohort of adults with type 2 diabetes at moderate cardiovascular risk, individual SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitor medications demonstrated comparable cardiovascular benefits, supporting the overall class effect observed in prior studies. Empagliflozin showed a modestly decreased risk of major adverse cardiovascular outcomes compared with canagliflozin and dapagliflozin, driven primarily by a reduction in all‐cause mortality, with more pronounced relative differences over time.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Factors underlying the observed differences in all‐cause mortality, including the specific causes of death most impacted, and widening differences between medications over time, will need to be further explored.
sections.data availability: This study was conducted using deidentified data from Optum Labs Data Warehouse and linked 100% sample of Medicare fee‐for‐service claims. These data are third‐party data owned by Optum Labs and contain sensitive patient information; therefore, the data are available only upon request. Interested researchers engaged in Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) compliant research may contact connected@optum.com for data access requests. The data use agreement requires researchers to pay for rights to use and access the data. These data are subject to restrictions on sharing as a condition of access.
sections.study design and data sources: This is a retrospective study emulating a target trial examining head‐to‐head the comparative cardiovascular effectiveness and glycemic safety of different SGLT2i among adults with T2D at moderate risk of cardiovascular disease. 21 Specifications of the target trial and its emulation are detailed in Table S1 and the analytic approach is visualized in Figure S1 . This trial emulation was a prespecified secondary analysis within a larger trial emulation that sought to compare SGLT2i, GLP‐1 receptor agonists, DPP‐4 inhibitors, and sulfonylureas among adults with T2D at moderate cardiovascular risk with respect to cardiovascular (primary) and other secondary end points; the protocol was preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05214573 ) and results of the main analysis were published elsewhere. 10 The study was deemed exempt by the Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board and is reported according to the Reporting of Studies Conducted Using Observational Routinely Collected Health Data and Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology reporting guidelines. 22 , 23 We used deidentified medical and pharmacy claims from the Optum Labs Data Warehouse, which includes enrollees in commercial and Medicare Advantage health plans across the United States, linked to the 100% sample of Medicare fee‐for‐service claims, thereby including a diverse cohort with a wide range of ages, racial and ethnic groups, income levels, geographic regions, health systems, and health plans across the United States. 24 , 25 Optum Labs Data Warehouse and Medicare fee‐for‐service claims were linked on personal identifiers and then deidentified by Optum Labs before being made available to researchers, allowing us to analyze the data as a single cohort and follow patients as they switched between included plans.
sections.study population: We identified adults ≥21 years who filled a new prescription for an SGLT2i (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or ertugliflozin) between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2021 (Figure S2 ). Bexagliflozin was not included as it was approved by the Food and Drug Administration in January 2023. The date of the first fill was used as the index date for each patient. Patients were required to have a second consecutive fill of the same SGLT2i (with no more than 30‐day gap in days covered) and no fill for an alternative SGLT2i within 30 days of the index date to confirm use and tolerance (emulating a wash‐in period of a target RCT); in a sensitivity analysis, we set the second SGLT2i fill date as the index date, excluding 2571 patients who experienced any study outcome between the first and the second SGLT2i fill dates. Patients were required to have 12 months of enrollment before the index date to ascertain baseline covariates, including cardiovascular risk, and to ensure new use of study drugs. We subsequently excluded patients with missing or conflicting sex, year of birth, or US region; a fill for any SGLT2i or insulin (Table S2 ) during the baseline 12 months; a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, pregnancy, or metastatic cancer during the baseline 12 months (Table S3 ); and with low (<1%) or high (>5%) annualized risk of MACE, calculated using the Annualized Claims‐Based MACE Estimator 17 as in prior work, resulting in a cohort of individual with moderate cardiovascular risk (estimated 1%–5% annualized risk of MACE). Due to small sample size (N=335) in the ertugliflozin arm, it was excluded from analyses. We also excluded index years 2014 and 2021 due to violation of the positivity assumption, with too few patients starting empagliflozin in 2014 and canagliflozin in 2021.
sections.independent variables: Baseline covariates included demographic characteristics ascertained from enrollment files on the index date (age, sex, race, ethnicity, and US region) and medications (Table S2 ) and comorbidities (Table S4 ) ascertained from pharmacy and medical claims, respectively, during the baseline 12‐months period. Unknown race, ethnicity, region, and prescriber data were analyzed as distinct subcategories; there were no other missing data. Included variables were identified by the study team and a Patient Stakeholder Advisory Group, which was formed to provide feedback on study design, implementation, and dissemination. 26
sections.outcomes: The primary outcome was MACE, defined as the composite of myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, or all‐cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included expanded MACE (composite of MACE, HF hospitalization, and arterial revascularization), individual components of expanded MACE, hospitalization or emergency department visit for hyperglycemic crisis (eg, diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state; examined concurrently due to their frequent co‐occurrence and potential misclassification), hospitalization or emergency department visit for hypoglycemia, and severe genitourinary tract infection. 27 Outcome definitions are detailed in Table S5 .
sections.statistical analysis: Our primary analyses were time‐to‐event models within an intention‐to‐treat (ITT) framework, where included patients were followed from the time of the first‐observed use of an SGLT2i to either the end of the study (December 31, 2022), disenrollment from an insurance plan in our database, or death, whichever came first. We first estimated propensity score models for initiating each SGLT2i drug (versus the other 2, as ertugliflozin was excluded from analysis) using a diverse set of individual binomial prediction algorithms in the super learner ensemble ( Supplemental Methods ), 28 including baseline covariates detailed in Tables S2 and S4 . The super learner framework allows for flexible estimation of an ensemble predictor with the theoretical properties of cross‐validation for model selection to control for overfitting. 29 Stabilized weights were used to be robust to extreme values. 30 Stabilized inverse propensity scores were used to establish the weighted study cohorts. Inverse probability of treatment weighted median (95% CI) follow‐up times were calculated for each study arm using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. 31 We evaluated the balance across study drugs after weighting using standardized mean differences (of the baseline covariates, 32 calculated for each pairwise comparison). We planned to include any baseline covariates with maximum standardized mean difference >0.10 (across all pairwise comparisons) as adjustment variables in the outcome models. The stabilized inverse propensity score weights were incorporated into Cox proportional hazards models (1 for each outcome) with all treatment groups. For the outcomes that did not include mortality, all‐cause mortality was considered as a competing risk and cause‐specific models were used. 33 Results are reported as hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CI for all pairwise comparisons, using simulation to estimate the 95% CIs for the different contrasts. A single overall omnibus test was conducted at the 0.05 significance level. For each model, we tested the proportional hazards assumption for treatment group using the Grambsch and Therneau test, 34 , 35 planning to estimate piecewise models for ≤1, 1 to 2, and >2 years after index in the event that there was evidence the HRs vary across time, based on a P value <0.05. We used these models to estimate the adjusted (absolute) event rates within 1, 2, and 3 years after treatment initiation. Cumulative incidence curves were also estimated by first taking the pseudo values of the Kaplan–Meier estimate at each unique event time and then applying propensity scores weighted averages of the pseudo values. 36 , 37 Isotonic regression was then applied to enforce monotonicity of the cumulative incidence curve. 38
sections.sensitivity analyses: To evaluate the sensitivity of treatment effects to potential unmeasured confounders, we examined the falsification end point of hospitalization for appendicitis (Table S5 ) using the same approach as our primary analysis. 39 , 40 Two additional sensitivity analyses were conducted using an as‐treated approach, whereby patients were censored upon (1) discontinuation of the assigned treatment (no fills after 30 days beyond the dispensed pill count), death, disenrollment from the health plan, or end of the study period, whichever came first; and (2) discontinuation of the assigned treatment, addition of another glucose‐lowering drug (including a different SGLT2i) or insulin, death, disenrollment from the health plan, or end of the study period, whichever came first. Data management activities were conducted using SAS 9.04 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC), and analyses were conducted using R version 4.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
sections.results_1: We identified 142 362 adults who initiated canagliflozin (N=45 273), dapagliflozin (N=19 229), or empagliflozin (N=77 860) between 2015 and 2020 (Figure S2 ). Doses of the initiated drugs are detailed in Table S6 . Before inverse probability of treatment weighting, patients differed on many baseline covariates (Table S7 ), but after inverse probability of treatment weighting, standardized mean difference was >0.10 only for the health plan/data source variable (standardized mean difference=0.103) (Table 1 ), which we subsequently included in the outcome models as the sole adjustment variable in addition to the medications dependent variable. The final (weighted) study population had 42 877 individuals in the canagliflozin group [median weighted follow‐up time: 1076 days (95% CI, 1066–1087)], 17 871 in the dapagliflozin group [median weighted follow‐up time: 1035 days (95% CI, 1023–1046)], and 76 485 in the empagliflozin group [median weighted follow‐up time: 1032 days (95% CI, 1026–1039)]. Across the groups, patients were ∼66 years old, 43% were women, 75% were non‐Hispanic White, 82% were treated with metformin, and 11% were treated with GLP‐1 receptor agonists. Tables 2 and 3 and Figure1 present results of the ITT analyses comparing the SGLT2i drugs. Comparison of predicted probabilities of all study outcomes (ie the proportions of patients experiencing each outcome) at 1, 2, and 3 years after treatment initiation demonstrates that patients treated with empagliflozin experienced the lowest rate of MACE: 1.7% of patients at year 1, 3.8% of patients at year 2, and 6.2% of patients at year 3 (Table 2 ). In contrast, dapagliflozin was associated with the highest probability: 1.9% of patients at year 1, 4.4% of patients at year 2, and 7.2% of patients at year 3. Rates of hospitalizations for HF were low overall and similar across study arms: 0.2% at year 1, 0.5% to 0.6% at year 2, 0.9% to 1.0% at year 3. Rates of genitourinary infection were 4.5% to 4.6%, 7.1% to 7.3%, and 9.0% to 9.2% at 1, 2, and 3 years after treatment initiation, respectively, with a lower rate among those treated with canagliflozin than with dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. Rates of hyperglycemic and hypoglycemic crises were low in all study arms. Pairwise comparisons of the relative hazards (Table 3 ) showed that empagliflozin was superior to canagliflozin with respect to MACE (HR, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.87–0.97]), driven almost entirely by reduced risk of all‐cause mortality (HR, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.80–0.94]). Notably, empagliflozin was also associated with a slightly higher risk of arterial revascularization procedure than canagliflozin (HR, 1.06 [95% CI, 1.01–1.12]). There was no difference between dapagliflozin and canagliflozin, or between empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, with respect to any of the examined outcomes. There was also no difference between empagliflozin and canagliflozin with respect to expanded MACE, stroke, MI, hospitalization for HF, genitourinary tract infection, or hyperglycemic or hypoglycemic crises. Because the proportional hazards assumption was violated for all outcomes, we calculated the piecewise HRs for follow‐up of ≤1, 1 to 2, and >2 years from treatment initiation (Table 4 ). Early during treatment (≤1 year), empagliflozin was associated with modestly higher risks of MACE, expanded MACE, stroke, and revascularization compared with canagliflozin; and modestly higher risks of expanded MACE and revascularization dapagliflozin. With longer follow‐up, however, this association reversed, with empagliflozin showing lower risks of adverse cardiovascular events when compared with canagliflozin and dapagliflozin. We repeated the analyses using the second SGLT2i fill date as the index date for outcome ascertainment. All results, shown in Table S8 , were consistent with the main analyses, except there was no longer a statistically significant difference in risk of arterial revascularization between canagliflozin and empagliflozin, with HR 1.05 (95% CI, 0.99–1.10). Sensitivity analyses conducted per the as‐treated approach, censored when patients discontinue the assigned treatment (Table S9 ), revealed no significant differences in outcomes among the arms, except modestly increased risk of revascularization with empagliflozin versus canagliflozin (HR, 1.08 [95% CI, 1.01–1.16]). Similarly, when censoring patients upon discontinuation of assigned treatment or initiation of another medication (Table S10 ), empagliflozin was associated with higher risk of expanded MACE compared with canagliflozin (HR, 1.09 [95% CI, 1.02–1.17]) driven primarily by revascularization risk (HR, 1.09; [95% CI, 1.02–1.18]). Table S11 shows the median follow up times for each sensitivity analysis. In the falsification analysis, conducted under the ITT approach, there was no difference in the risk of hospitalization for acute appendicitis (Table S12 ).
sections.discussion: In this large nationwide study of adults with T2D at moderate cardiovascular risk initiating SGLT2i therapy, comparing empagliflozin, canagliflozin, and dapagliflozin head to head under the target trial emulation framework, 21 empagliflozin use was associated with modestly lower risk of MACE (8% risk reduction), mostly driven by all‐cause mortality (14% risk reduction), compared with canagliflozin, with no significant differences between empagliflozin and dapagliflozin or dapagliflozin and canagliflozin. Thus, our findings suggest that although empagliflozin may be modestly better than canagliflozin in this population, these drugs are largely comparable overall, and any SGLT2i may be appropriate for cardiovascular risk reduction among those at moderate risk for cardiovascular disease. These analyses, made possible by the size and heterogeneity of our national, multipayor cohort, complement existing clinical trials and observational studies that have not directly compared across the different drugs within the SGLT2i class nor examined these medications among adults at moderate cardiovascular risk. 12 , 15 , 41 As such, these data provide important information to inform formulary design decisions and clinical decision‐making for the two thirds of adults with T2D who have moderate cardiovascular risk. 17 Our findings build upon prior indirect evidence from network meta‐analyses, including the 2023 study by Chen et al. that compared different SGLT2i in people with and without T2D, using data from 14 placebo‐controlled RCTs of the individual SGLT2i drugs. 12 They found that among people with T2D, empagliflozin was associated with a lower risk of all‐cause mortality than dapagliflozin (HR 0.81 [95% CI 0.69–0.96]) but found no difference between canagliflozin, ertugliflozin, or sotagliflozin (a dual SGLT1 and SGLT2 inhibitor that was not included in our analyses as it is a different pharmacologic class) and dapagliflozin (which was the reference group for all pairwise comparisons in this network meta‐analysis). In a more recent network meta‐analysis by Kani et al. that examined the same drugs but included 21 placebo‐controlled RCTs including participants with and without T2D, there was no difference between the different SGLT2i drugs on any cardiovascular outcome or all‐cause mortality. 11 However, this is indirect evidence, pooling outcomes from heterogeneous trials, and not focused on those with moderate CVD risk. Our findings are also largely consistent with earlier observational studies, though similar to the RCTs, none of the observational studies directly compared across the available SGLT2i drugs nor focused on patients at moderate cardiovascular risk. In a Japanese study comparing CVD outcomes in 25 315 adults with T2D and without preexisting cardiovascular disease initiating SGLT2i therapy, there was no difference in HF, MI, stroke, or all‐cause mortality between the drugs. 42 However, this study did not fully account for baseline differences between the treatment arms that likely impacted treatment assignment and did not compare across all SGLT2i treatment groups. In a separate analysis comparing dapagliflozin with empagliflozin in adults with T2D in Korea, dapagliflozin showed a lower risk of HF‐related hospitalizations or deaths (HR, 0.84[ 95% CI, 0.71–0.99], P =0.04) and cardiovascular death (HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.62–0.92], P =0.006), but not in MI or stroke. 43 Similarly, Balata et al.'s study comparing echocardiographic outcomes of dapagliflozin and empagliflozin therapy found empagliflozin to be have greater effects on left ventricular remodeling, but this study focused on people with HF and had unequal rates of T2D in each group. 16 It will be important to compare our findings to the ongoing pragmatic RCT examining empagliflozin versus dapagliflozin ( ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06642272 ) being conducted in Denmark, though that trial is not limited to people with T2D nor is it stratified or subset to particular levels of cardiovascular risk. A recent large US‐based study by Shin et al. found no difference between canagliflozin and empagliflozin, or between dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, with respect to the primary outcomes of MI or stroke; however, it also did not compare the SGLT2i drugs head to head. 15 In this study, there was also no difference between the examined pairs with respect to all‐cause mortality (where their findings diverge from ours), but this secondary analysis was limited by the lack of death data in their largest included database. A direct comparison between canagliflozin and dapagliflozin also cannot be extrapolated from the other 2 comparisons; although the treatment arms within each 2‐drug comparison were balanced on key baseline covariates and confounders, the 2 comparisons themselves had very different cohorts, varying with respect to the prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidities, cardiology specialty care, health care use, and concurrent use of GLP‐1 receptor agonist and metformin drugs. Moreover, this study used a per‐protocol analysis without accounting for potentially informative censoring; yet, with 60% to 70% of censoring occurring due to treatment discontinuation, this may have an important effect on study results. Indeed, in our study, results of the secondary per‐protocol analysis differed from those of the primary ITT analysis for some comparisons, underscoring the potential impact of informative censoring. Thus, our results provide robust and—for the first time—direct evidence on the comparative effectiveness of the 3 most used SGLT2i agents, supporting clinical decision‐making for the dominant population of adults with T2D living with moderate cardiovascular risk. Additionally, our study focused specifically on patients at moderate cardiovascular risk, whereas Shin et al. and others either included all patients with T2D or focused on those with higher risk levels, which may obscure heterogenous treatment effects that exist as a function of baseline cardiovascular risk. 18 In our primary ITT analysis, empagliflozin was modestly superior to canagliflozin in our primary outcome of MACE—a composite of MI, stroke, or all‐cause mortality—with no difference in HF hospitalizations and slightly more instances of arterial revascularization. Most benefit for empagliflozin was seen with all‐cause mortality, with a 14% relative risk reduction. There are several mechanisms that might explain the observed benefits of empagliflozin relative to canagliflozin, though none have been definitively explored. Empagliflozin is a more selective SGLT2i, whereas canagliflozin exhibits dual SGLT2 and SGLT1 inhibition. This selectivity may lead to empagliflozin's greater hemodynamic effects through osmotic diuresis and natriuresis. Empagliflozin was also shown to have different effects on gut microbiota, enhancing favorable short‐chain fatty acid‐producing bacteria and reducing potentially harmful species. 44 Notably, although the empagliflozin EMPA‐REG (Empagliflozin Cardiovascular Outcome Event Trial in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Patients) trial and the canagliflozin CANVAS (Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study) trial showed overall similar reductions in 3‐point MACE (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, and cardiovascular death) compared with placebo, benefits in cardiovascular and all‐cause mortality were seen in EMPA‐REG but not in CANVAS. 45 , 46 , 47 Additionally, we observed a modestly higher risk of arterial revascularization procedure with empagliflozin than canagliflozin, which may reflect differences in procedure use, competing risks, or residual confounding. This finding requires further study. However, our results may also reflect different treatment trajectories among patients initiating the empagliflozin, since its benefit emerged with longer follow‐up in the ITT analysis after many patients already discontinued treatment and the as‐treated sensitivity analyses showed no difference in MACE between the different SGLT2i drugs. Nevertheless, overall differences between the SGLT2i drugs were small and likely clinically insignificant. We also detected evidence of nonproportional hazards in all comparisons, indicating changes in the relative effects over time. Most notably, in the ITT analysis, empagliflozin was initially (within the first year of treatment) associated with higher relative risk of MACE compared with both dapagliflozin and canagliflozin, driven primarily by higher risk of stroke, but this association reversed with longer follow‐up, such that by 2 years of follow‐up (as in the overall analysis), the relative risk of MACE (and stroke) was lower among those treated with empagliflozin. Importantly, the absolute differences in event rates between the study drugs were small, particularly during the first 2 years after treatment initiation, with much greater magnitude of both relative and absolute differences seen beyond 2 years of treatment. Although the reason for this will need to be explored, this finding is consistent with earlier observations in the EMPA‐KIDNEY (Study of Heart and Kidney Protection With Empagliflozin) and EMPEROR‐Reduced (Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction) trials that demonstrated benefits of empagliflozin (relative to placebo) persisting even after treatment discontinuation, though effects waned over time. 48 , 49 By exploring serious cardiovascular outcome variability within the SGLT2i class, our study expands the knowledge base on risk and benefits of individual SGLT2i drugs, facilitating patient‐centered, evidence‐based care. However, it also has limitations. Even with rigorous analytic methods, there is potential for residual unmeasured confounding. To mitigate this risk, we used the super learner ensemble method to estimate propensity scores, including a wide range of relevant confounders, and included a falsification end point of appendicitis hospitalizations, finding no difference between the study drugs. We were also unable to specifically examine cardiovascular mortality nor delineate what, specifically, is driving the difference in all‐cause mortality seen between the empagliflozin and canagliflozin arms. Identifying cause of death in large population‐based studies is generally infeasible due to the inability to link to death certificate data to administrative claims and consortia electronic health record databases. 50 , 51 Clinical variables such as hemoglobin A1c, blood pressure, and lipid profiles were also not available in claims, and we were not able to assess their impact on study outcomes, though SGLT2i are generally comparable with respect to these end points. Nevertheless, our findings are strengthened by the inclusion of a large nationwide cohort of patients under routine care conditions, including diverse age groups, races and ethnicities, income levels, geographic regions, and health systems and practices. By including enrollees in private, Medicare Advantage, and different traditional Medicare Part D plans, we were able to unbiasedly examine different SGLT2i drugs to the extent not possible in single payor or single health system cohorts. We conducted rigorous head‐to‐head comparisons across the 3 commonly used SGLT2i drugs allowing for direct comparisons across the agents. As other studies have suggested, prior cardiovascular risk may affect SGLT2i outcomes. 18 , 42 , 52 Indeed, clinical trial of the individual SGLT2i drugs focused primarily on individuals at high cardiovascular risk, and our results extend the evidence on cardiovascular risk reduction with SGLT2i to those at moderate cardiovascular risk, who make up two thirds of adults with T2D. 17 Our findings therefore help address a major knowledge gap in T2D management and complement other analyses in T2D populations at various levels of cardiovascular risk.
sections.conclusions_1: In this large nationwide observational study emulating a target trial that directly compares canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin in adults with T2D at moderate cardiovascular risk, we found that these agents exert similar effects on outcomes of importance to patients and that differences between these agents are likely small in magnitude.

title: ‘We feel abandoned out here’: teamwork dilemmas among rural health professionals in distributed emergency settings
abstract: Background In rural northern Sweden, community hospitals serve as essential first-response centres. During emergencies, general practitioners remotely collaborate on-call with on-site nurses via videoconferencing. This setup of geographically distributed teams enables healthcare delivery across long distances. However, little is known about how healthcare professionals make sense of and negotiate roles and responsibilities in such distributed emergency settings. Hence, the aim of this study was to analyse how healthcare professionals position themselves and others in interprofessional teams when collaborating in distributed emergency settings in rural areas. Methods Interprofessional focus group interviews ( n = 17) were conducted with staff (one nursing assistant, one registered nurse and one physician per focus group) at community hospitals in rural northern Sweden, following full-scale, simulated, in-situ team training. The analysis was inspired by Billig’s concept of ideological dilemmas and Wetherell’s concept of interpretative repertoires. Results Participants drew on three interpretative repertoires—Involvement, Responsibility and competence, and Control and dependency—to account for teamwork in distributed emergency settings. Across these repertoires, participants accounted for involvement as both enabled and difficult to sustain, responsibility as not readily transferred, and control as limited and dependent on others’ accounts. These ways of accounting reflected ongoing dilemmas, as professionals positioned themselves in relation to competing demands when acting under conditions of distance, uncertainty and mediated access to the clinical situation. Conclusions Distributed teamwork reshapes the conditions for collaboration in emergency care, as roles and responsibilities become continuously negotiated in relation to tensions concerning involvement, responsibility and control. As a result, collaboration is unevenly achieved and cannot be taken for granted. Clinical trial number Not applicable.
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine

sections.background_1: Effective teamwork is crucial in delivering high-quality healthcare, as communication errors and poor teamwork often lead to adverse outcomes [ 1 ]. In an emergency, strong leadership that promotes shared mental models, clear communication and defined roles is essential to ensure precise coordination around the patient [ 2 , 3 ]. While effective teamwork is vital for patient safety [ 2 , 4 , 5 ], team dynamics are often described under the assumption that all team members, including the team leader, are physically present in the same location as the patient [ 2 ]. This perspective may not fully capture the dynamics of distributed teams, in which team members are geographically distributed and use technology to communicate [ 6 ]. In a distributed team, team communication must adapt to the physical absence of team members and the use of technology [ 7 ], while leadership, roles and responsibilities may need to be redefined and negotiated across distance. Research on teamwork in distributed teams has focused on ad-hoc student teams dealing with hypothetical tasks [ 8 ] and settings outside healthcare [ 9 ], often with inconsistent findings [ 10 – 13 ]. Although distributed teams face challenges similar to those of co-located teams, their limited face-to-face interaction [ 7 ] can complicate teamwork [ 14 ] and increase workload [ 15 ]. Furthermore, communication and coordination can be more challenging without established trust or familiarity, which are difficult to build in distributed teams [ 16 ]. Advanced research on distributed teams has been conducted in fields such as aviation [ 17 ] and business [ 18 ], but healthcare’s unique demands, which include urgent tasks and patient safety, require empirical studies specific to this context. Moreover, previous research in non-healthcare settings has primarily focused on the structural and functional aspects of teamwork, such as communication, coordination and workload [ 19 , 20 ], while paying less attention to how team members make sense of and negotiate their roles in distributed settings. In rural northern Sweden, the absence of conventional hospitals, combined with challenges that include long distances, limited accessibility and severe weather conditions, has driven the need for innovative healthcare solutions [ 21 ]. As one such solution, community hospitals (CHs) serve as first-response centres in sparsely populated areas [ 22 ]. Despite their limited capacity, CHs operate 24/7, offering various services that include primary care, emergency treatment and diagnostic capabilities [ 22 ]. During on-call periods, CHs are supported by distributed teams [ 6 ], with general practitioners (GPs) participating remotely while nursing assistants (NAs) and registered nurses (RNs) provide on-site care. Thus, the team members in these distributed teams collaborate through technology [ 21 ], which enables GPs to manage multiple CHs simultaneously and remotely, addressing emergencies across long distances. This creates a context in which roles and responsibilities are not always clear and must be worked out in practice by professionals collaborating at a distance, through technology and across different professions. Although distributed teams may face unique challenges [ 15 ], there is limited understanding of how healthcare professionals make sense of their roles in practice in rural emergency settings. Such processes are central in distributed emergency care, where roles are not always clearly defined but must be actively worked out in interaction [ 19 ]. To address this limitation, a discourse psychology (DP) approach was used to explore how teamwork is constructed in distributed emergency settings in rural areas. Rather than focusing on what teamwork is, DP makes it possible to examine how teamwork is made meaningful by participants [ 23 ]. In this study, we analyse how healthcare professionals talk about teamwork in distributed emergency settings, focusing on how they account for, justify and negotiate roles and responsibilities. The analysis focuses on interpretative repertoires [ 24 ], which are understood here as recurring ways of talking about teamwork; on subject positions [ 24 ], which reflect how roles and responsibilities are constructed; and on ideological dilemmas [ 25 ], which capture tensions between competing expectations in teamwork within this context. The aim of this study was therefore to analyse how healthcare professionals position themselves and others in interprofessional teams when collaborating in distributed emergency settings in rural areas.
sections.design: This study is part of a broader research programme titled Teamwork in Geographically Dispersed Emergency Teams in Rural Settings (TIGER), which aims to improve rural emergency care by redefining teamwork in geographically dispersed teams [ 26 – 32 ]. The aim of this study was to analyse how team members position themselves and others within interprofessional teams while collaborating in a distributed setting during simulated emergencies. We employed a qualitative design inspired by DP [ 32 ]. To support completeness in reporting, we used the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Results (COREQ) guidelines [ 33 ].
sections.setting: This study was conducted in the rural inland areas of northern Sweden and involved seven CHs in southern Lapland. These CHs are essential for providing first-response care, being situated in one of Europe’s least densely populated regions, with less than one person per square kilometre in some areas [ 21 ]. Moreover, the rural and often elderly population presents unique healthcare demands. Staff members at CHs manage a range of chronic and acute conditions [ 34 ] – a challenge compounded by a shortage of healthcare workers [ 35 ]. Some CHs are up to 350 km away from the nearest urban hospital with specialised care [ 22 ]. Ambulance services are based near CHs, yet residents often face long waiting times due to the long distances, which are made worse by challenging weather conditions such as snowy roads. With no private healthcare alternatives, the CHs serve nearly all local residents (500–6000 per rural community). These CHs are primary healthcare centres, providing family medicine, maternal care, minor surgery, palliative care and 24/7 emergency care. Staff at CHs include NAs, RNs, resident physicians, GPs, midwives, physiotherapists and occupational therapists [ 22 ]. These professions differ in educational background and scope of practice. In Sweden, NAs complete vocational training at the secondary school level [ 36 ], while RNs hold at least a bachelor’s degree after 3 years of university studies. Many RNs pursue additional specialist training, such as in district nursing or midwifery, which requires an additional 1.5–2 years to achieve a master’s degree [ 37 ]. GPs complete a 5.5-year master’s degree, followed by a 2-year internship and 5 years of specialist training [ 38 ]. RNs and NAs provide immediate care on-site during on-call hours, while GPs are on call for a larger area and connect via videoconferencing to join the distributed team. If videoconferencing cannot be utilised, telephone consultation may be the only option, as travelling between CHs for medical assessments is often too time-consuming in acute situations, risking delays that could prevent timely intervention [ 21 ].
sections.participants: All NAs, RNs and GPs employed at all seven rural CHs in northern Sweden were eligible for inclusion in this study. Recruitment was facilitated through the manager of each CH, who distributed information about the study to all staff. Participation was voluntary and based on staff availability. A total of 51 medical staff members participated: 13 NAs, 21 RNs and 17 GPs. Consequently, 17 three-person focus groups were organised. Of these, 13 focus groups included one NA, one RN and one GP, while the remaining four comprised two RNs and one GP. No participants declined or dropped out. Participants’ ages ranged from 35 to 51 years (median 42), with most being female ( n = 42/51). Participants’ work experience spanned 6–26 years (median 16), and 26% had prior experience working in a distributed setting. Detailed participant characteristics are presented in Table 1 .
