sections.introduction: With the acceleration of global population aging, the worldwide elderly population is projected to surge from 1 billion to 2.1 billion between 2019 and 2050 [ 1 ]. With the growth of the elderly population and the extension of life expectancy, the prevalence of dementia is also rising rapidly posing enormous challenges for patients, families, healthcare systems, and governments [ 2 ].Analysis from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 indicates that the number of people living with dementia worldwide is expected to increase from 57 million in 2019 to 153 million by 2050 [ 3 ]. China, which has both the largest elderly population and the highest number of dementia cases globally [ 4 ], is projected to have more than 15 million individuals affected by dementia by 2050 [ 3 ]. Consequently, the accurate screening and prevention of dementia are crucial for reducing the associated disease burden. Motor cognitive risk syndrome (MCR) is defined as a condition in older adults without dementia or mobility disability, characterized by subjective cognitive complaints and slow gait speed [ 5 ]. Previous studies indicate its prevalence varies across countries and populations, ranging from 2% to 27% [ 6 – 8 ]. There is growing evidence that MCR is an early risk factor for dementia [ 5 , 9 , 10 ]. Individuals with MCR exhibit a 2.2-fold higher risk of developing cognitive impairment or dementia compared to cognitively normal older adults [ 9 ]. Compared with formal diagnostic evaluation for mild cognitive impairment or dementia, which may involve neuropsychological testing, neurological examination, informant history, and sometimes imaging or laboratory assessment, MCR can be identified using a simpler clinical approach [ 7 , 11 , 12 ]. Because it relies on subjective cognitive complaints and gait speed, MCR may be particularly useful as an early screening construct in primary care and in resource-limited settings [ 13 , 14 ]. Importantly, early identification of MCR may contribute to dementia prevention by flagging individuals at elevated risk for closer follow-up, more comprehensive cognitive evaluation, and earlier management of modifiable risk factors. In addition, MCR is associated with increased risks of falls, disability, and mortality [ 8 , 15 ]. Given its substantial prevalence and association with adverse outcomes, identifying individuals at higher risk of MCR and understanding factors related to MCR may inform risk stratification and support earlier identification and monitoring of older adults vulnerable to cognitive–motor decline. Depression is a prevalent mental disorder globally, particularly prominent among older adults [ 16 ]. Accumulating evidence indicates that depressive symptoms may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease [ 17 ], cancer [ 18 ], dementia, and mortality [ 19 ], representing a major global disease burden. In recent years, growing research has focused on the associations between depressive symptoms and MCR, cognitive function, and gait. For example, a Chinese cohort study demonstrated that depression is an independent risk factor for MCR in community-dwelling older adults [ 20 ]. Evidence from meta-analyses further indicates that depression increases the risk of developing MCR in the elderly population [ 21 ]. Hao et al. identified a bidirectional association between depression and cognitive function [ 22 ]. Based on a community cohort study involving older adults without dementia or depression, Brandler et al. found that higher levels of depressive symptoms were associated with poorer objective gait performance [ 23 ].Collectively, these findings suggest that depressive symptoms are a significant factor associated with MCR in older adults. While previous studies have explored the relationship between depression and MCR, most have assessed depressive symptoms at only a single time point, thereby overlooking the dynamic nature and trajectory patterns of these symptoms. Identifying distinct trajectory patterns of depressive symptoms through repeated measurements would facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of their dynamic progression and complex relationship with MCR. Currently, the relationship between longitudinal trajectories of depressive symptoms and MCR among older adults in China remains unclear. Therefore, the present study utilized longitudinal data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), a nationally representative prospective cohort study, to identify long-term trajectories of depressive symptoms in older adults and examine their associations with MCR.
sections.data sources: The data used in this study were derived Eligible participants from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) ( https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/ ). This project is a nationwide follow-up survey designed to gather data on the health status and quality of life of Chinese people aged 45 and above. Participants were chosen through a multistage sampling approach based on probability proportional to size (PPS), covering 150 counties across 28 provinces in China. The baseline wave of CHARLS began in 2011, and subsequent surveys were conducted in 2013, 2015, 2018, and 2020. The Biomedical Ethics Committee of Peking University approved the study (IRB00001052–11015), and all participants signed a written informed consent. Detailed information about CHARLS has been reported in a previous study [ 24 ]. The analysis used data from the 2011 baseline survey and data from the 2013 and 2015 follow-up surveys. Given that gait speed measurements, essential for constructing the definition of Motoric Cognitive Risk Syndrome (MCR), were only systematically collected during the 2011, 2013, and 2015 waves of the CHARLS survey, we utilized baseline data from 2011 along with follow-up data from 2013 to 2015. This approach ensured consistent measurement of MCR and enabled the examination of its association with trajectories of depressive symptoms. Eligible participants were aged 60 years or older, had complete data on depressive symptoms, and were free of MCR at baseline. The participant selection process is illustrated in Fig. 1 . To maximize the sample size and better characterize the trajectory of depressive symptoms, no participants were excluded based on cognitive risk syndrome. Among the 17,708 participants at baseline, we first excluded 4,136 individuals who did not participate in the subsequent two waves of surveys. Next, 7,810 individuals under 60 years of age at baseline were excluded as walking speed was not measured in participants below 60. Additionally, 2,008 participants were excluded due to incomplete data on depressive symptoms across the three survey waves. Ultimately, data from 3,754 participants were used to explore depressive symptom trajectories. To investigate the relationship between depressive symptom trajectories and MCR, additional exclusion criteria were applied. Individuals who self-reported physician-diagnosed memory-related diseases (Alzheimer’s disease, cerebral atrophy, and Parkinson’s disease) or disability history at baseline were excluded from the analysis. Furthermore, individuals with MCR at baseline and those lacking MCR-related information in the follow-up waves were also excluded from the analysis. Finally, 2,298 participants were included in the MCR outcome analysis. Fig. 1 Flowchart of participant selection from the CHARLS database
sections.assessment of depressive symptoms: The short version of the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10) was used to assess depressive symptoms in older adults. The CES-D-10 has been validated and widely used in China to measure depressive symptoms in adults [ 25 ]. The scale contains a total of 10 items, each with four response options based on the frequency of symptoms in the past week: (1) 0 points for rarely or hardly ever (< 1 day); (2) 1 point for sometimes or a small portion of the time (1–2 days); (3) 2 points for often or moderately often (3–4 days); and (4) 3 points for most or all of the time (5–7 days). Notably, items 5 (I feel hopeful about the future) and 8 (I felt happy) are reverse-coded. The total score ranges from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating greater severity of depressive symptoms. The scale has been demonstrated to exhibit satisfactory reliability and validity in the Chinese older adult populations and is a reliable instrument for screening depressive symptoms [ 26 ]. In the present study, the internal consistency of the CES-D-10 was assessed at each survey wave. Cronbach’s alpha coefficients were 0.803 in 2011, 0.753 in 2013, and 0.793 in 2015. The diagnosis of depressive symptoms specific items saw Supplementary Table 1.
sections.assessment of motoric cognitive risk syn: Based on the original criteria of Verghese et al. [ 5 ], MCR is defined as the co-occurrence of subjective cognitive complaints and slow gait speed, in the absence of dementia or mobility disability. In the CHARLS study, cognitive complaints were assessed by asking participants, “How do you rate your current memory?” Respondents were required to choose one of five response options: excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor. Participants reporting “fair” or “poor” were classified as having cognitive complaints. Gait speed was calculated as the average time taken to complete two walks along a 2.5-meter straight path. A 2.5-meter straight walkway was prepared and delineated with tape. Participants were instructed to walk along the pathway at their self-selected usual pace. The use of walking aids, such as canes or walkers, was permitted when needed. The duration required to complete the walkway was recorded with a stopwatch. The test was conducted twice, and the average time from the two trials was used to calculate walking speed in meters per second. Slow gait was defined as walking speed at least 1.0 standard deviation (SD) below the age- (< 75 or ≥ 75 years) and sex-specific mean values for the cohort [ 20 ].
sections.covariates: Covariates were selected a priori based on previous literature [ 14 , 27 ]. These covariates were chosen to account for demographic characteristics, lifestyle, and health-related factors that may confound the association between depressive symptom trajectories and MCR. In CHARLS, all data were collected through a standardized questionnaire administered by trained interviewers. Demographic characteristics included: age (continuous), gender (male or female), education level (illiterate, primary school or below, junior high school or above), residence (urban or rural), and marital status (married or other). Lifestyle factors included smoking status (never, current, former), drinking status (never, < 1/month, ≥ 1/month), body mass index (BMI), social participation (yes or no). Health status was obtained from self-reported physician-diagnosed chronic diseases, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, pulmonary disease, cancer, liver disease, stroke, heart disease, kidney disease, gastric disease, and arthritis. Participants were categorized into three groups based on the number of chronic conditions: none, 1, or ≥ 2. A detailed description of the relevant covariates can be found in Supplementary Table S1.
sections.statistical analysis: Data processing and analysis were performed using Stata 17.0 and SPSS 25.0. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Normality of continuous variables was assessed using visual inspection of histograms and normal probability plots. In descriptive statistics, continuous variables (age) with skewed distributions were presented as medians (Q₁, Q₃) and examined by the Kruskal-Wallis test and Mann-Whitney test. Categorical variables (gender, education level, residence, marital status, smoking status, drinking status, BMI, social activity participation, number of chronic diseases) were expressed as frequencies and percentages, and analyzed using chi-square tests. This study utilized the “traj” command in Stata 17.0 to implement group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) for identifying depressive symptom trajectories between 2011 and 2015. GBTM classifies individuals with similar developmental patterns through maximum likelihood estimation to identify multiple potential developmental trajectories in the population [ 28 ]. Based on previous research into depressive symptoms, we hypothesized two to seven distinct trajectories [ 29 ]. We started with models incorporating the highest polynomial order (cubic), then sequentially tested quadratic slopes, linear terms, or intercepts to capture potential trajectory shapes. Model fit was assessed using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), log-likelihood (LL), and entropy values, with smaller AIC, BIC, and LL values alongside higher entropy values suggesting better fit. Additionally, the goodness-of-fit between the model and the data was assessed by employing the Average Posterior Probability (AvePP) for each trajectory group. All groups had AvePP values above 0.70, indicating good model fit [ 30 ]. Additionally, each trajectory group was required to account for more than 5% of the total participants to ensure clinical representativeness. Associations between different depressive trajectories and MCR were explored using binary logistic regression analyses. We constructed 3 separate models. Model 1 was an unadjusted model that included only depressive symptom trajectories. Model 2 adjusted for demographic characteristics (age, gender, education level, residence, and marital status). Model 3 further adjusted for lifestyle factors and health status (smoking status, drinking status, BMI, social activity participation, number of chronic diseases).
sections.sensitivity analysis: To address potential bias arising from baseline imbalance across depressive symptom trajectory groups and from attrition-related selection, we conducted weighted sensitivity analyses. First, we applied multinomial propensity-score weighting (inverse probability of treatment weighting, IPTW) to improve baseline comparability across the four trajectory groups. A multinomial logistic regression model including baseline demographic characteristics, lifestyle, and health-related covariates was used to estimate group membership probabilities; stabilized weights were constructed and trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Weighted logistic regression with robust standard errors was then used to estimate the associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident MCR. Second, to assess potential selection bias due to loss to follow-up and missingness, we constructed stabilized inverse-probability-of-censoring weights (IPCW) using the same baseline covariates to model the probability of being included in the analytical sample. Weighted logistic regression models with robust standard errors were then fitted to estimate the associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident MCR.
sections.identification and characteristic of dep: After screening, 3,754 participants were included in the depressive symptom trajectory analysis with a median age of 65.00 (62.00, 70.00) years. Using Group-Based Trajectory Modeling (GBTM), we observed decreasing absolute values of both AIC and BIC with increasing numbers of trajectory groups. The 5-trajectory model demonstrated lower AIC and BIC values compared to the 4-trajectory model, with all fit indices meeting recommended thresholds (AvePP > 0.7, each trajectory group proportion ≥ 5%; see Supplementary Table S1).However, the five-trajectory solution did not meaningfully distinct groups compared to the four-trajectory model. Furthermore, the entropy value for the four-trajectory model exceeded that of the five-trajectory model. Combining model parsimony and clinical interpretability, we ultimately selected the four-trajectory model, which comprised two linear trajectories and two quadratic trajectories. As shown in Fig. 2 , the four depressive symptom trajectories were named based on their characteristics as follows: low-stable ( n = 2491, 66.4%), high-decreasing ( n = 561, 14.9%), medium-increasing ( n = 499, 13.3%), and high-stable ( n = 203, 5.4%). Low-stable: individuals in this trajectory maintained low depressive symptom scores throughout the follow-up period. High-decreasing: individuals in this trajectory reported higher depressive symptom scores at baseline and a gradual decrease in depressive symptom scores during follow-up. Medium-increasing: participants had CESD-10 scores close to 10 at baseline and the first follow-up, followed by a marked increase at the second follow-up. High-stable: participants maintained high depressive symptom scores throughout follow-up. Participant characteristics by depressive symptom trajectory are shown in Table 1 . Individuals in the other three trajectories, compared to the low-stable trajectory, were more likely to be female, not have a partner, have lower education levels, live in rural areas, not participate in social activities, not smoke, not drink, and have a higher number of chronic conditions. sections.characteristics of motoric cognitive ris: Table 2 shows the characteristics of the 2,298 participants who were included in the analysis of the association between depressive symptom trajectories and the motoric cognitive risk (MCR) syndrome. Compared with excluded participants, those included in the final analysis were younger and had higher educational attainment. Standardized mean differences indicated moderate differences for age and education, and small to moderate differences for several sociodemographic characteristics and baseline depressive symptoms scores (Supplementary Table S2). The included participants had a median age of 65.0 (62.0, 69.0) years. During the 4 years follow-up period (2011–2015), 207 individuals were diagnosed with MCR in 2015. sections.association of depressive symptoms traje: Table 3 shows the results of the logistic regression modelling of the relationship between depressive symptom trajectories and MCR in older adults. Compared with the low-stable depressive symptoms group in Model 1 (unadjusted), the high-decreasing group (OR = 1.92, 95%CI [1.31, 2.82], P < 0.001), the medium-increasing group (OR = 1.93, 95% CI [1.29, 2.88], P = 0.001), and the high-stable group (OR = 4.17, 95% CI [2.54, 6.86], P < 0.001) had higher odds of MCR. This association remained significant after adjusting for baseline demographic factors (Model 2) and lifestyle and health status factors (Model 3). sections.discussion: This study utilized a nationally representative sample to describe the heterogeneous trajectories of depressive symptoms in older Chinese adults and to analyze the relationship between depressive symptom trajectories and MCR. We identified four distinct depressive symptom trajectories: low-stable, high-decreasing, medium-increasing, and high-stable. After delineating these distinct trajectories, we examined their associations with MCR and found that, compared to those with the low-stable trajectory, the other three trajectories were all significantly associated with MCR. This study, based on the GBTM method, identified four significantly distinct depressive symptom trajectories: low-stable trajectory (66.4%), high-decreasing trajectory (14.9%), medium-increasing trajectory (13.3%), and high-stable depressive trajectory (5.4%). The depressive symptom trajectories identified in this study are similar to findings from previous studies based on CHARLS data [ 29 , 31 ], which further enhances our confidence in the stability of the study results. Approximately 19% of older adults exhibited moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms throughout the follow-up period with no improvement. Although 14.9% of older adults showed remission of depressive symptoms, they still exhibited moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms at baseline and the first follow-up. Similar to previous research findings [ 32 – 34 ], individuals with more depressive symptoms were more likely to be female, have lower socioeconomic status, and bear a greater comorbidity burden. China has the world’s largest population and is facing an increasingly severe aging crisis; substantial depressive symptoms among older adults will impose a significant medical and care burden. Therefore, it is necessary to strengthen the prevention and long-term management of depressive symptoms among older adults in China, especially targeting groups who are female, have low socioeconomic status, and bear a heavy comorbidity burden. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to report the association between depressive symptom trajectories and MCR risk. Specifically, compared to the low-stable trajectory, individuals in the medium-increasing trajectory and the high-stable trajectory had a significantly higher likelihood of developing MCR. Among them, individuals in the high-stable trajectory had the highest risk of MCR (OR = 3.65). This indicates that individuals with persistently high depressive symptoms face greater health challenges, emphasizing that individuals with persistently high depressive symptoms should be prioritized for depression interventions aimed at preventing MCR. Notably, individuals in the high-decreasing trajectory also had a high risk of developing MCR, although their CESD-10 scores decreased from 13.7 to 8.1. This result is similar to that of Xiang et al., who found that even a trajectory of reduced depressive symptoms was associated with poorer cognitive performance [ 35 ]. Our findings suggest that even short-term episodes of depressive symptoms can have long-term negative effects on an individual’s cognition and gait speed, highlighting the importance of early of early identification of depressive symptoms. Although both our study and previous research [ 20 ] have indicated an association between depressive symptoms and MCR, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. Here are several possible illustrations to explain the association between them. First, the behavioral pathway suggests that individuals with worsening depressive symptoms are more likely to experience unhealthy lifestyle behaviors, such as sedentary behavior, reduced physical activity, smoking, and poor sleep, all of which are established risk factors for MCR [ 27 , 36 ]. Second, the psychological pathway points out that increased sensitivity to social threats in individuals with worsening depressive symptoms may elevate perceived stress levels. The Rugao Longevity and Aging Study showed that high levels of perceived stress increase the risk of MCR in older adults [ 37 ]. Third, the physiological pathway indicates that depressive symptoms may be associated with inflammatory responses. A recent study showed that inflammatory responses are an independent risk factor for MCR [ 38 ]. Finally, previous studies have shown that maintaining adequate muscle strength is key to preventing the decline of physical functions such as gait. When older adults have depressive symptoms, it can easily lead to sarcopenia [ 39 ]. Sarcopenia, in turn, affects their physical function, subsequently leading to slow gait and cognitive decline in older adults, thereby increasing MCR risk [ 40 ]. It is noteworthy that it has long been recognized that depressive symptoms often co-occur with early cognitive impairment, though the causal direction between the two remains unclear [ 41 ].Overall, our findings indicate that patterns of persistent or worsening depressive symptoms are associated with higher risks of new-onset MCR, with the highest risk observed among those maintaining consistently elevated symptom levels. These discoveries expand upon prior evidence linking depressive symptoms to cognitive-motor vulnerability by underscoring the potential significance of symptom dynamics over time. From a public health perspective, MCR has been associated with a range of adverse outcomes, including cognitive decline, dementia, falls, disability, and mortality, and may therefore help identify older adults who warrant closer monitoring. Although MCR diagnosis does not itself constitute dementia prevention, it may contribute to prevention efforts indirectly by identifying older adults at elevated risk who may benefit from closer follow-up and multidomain interventions targeting potentially modifiable risk factors. Understanding how depressive symptom courses relate to this cognitive–motor risk phenotype may help identify subgroups who could benefit from closer monitoring and more comprehensive cognitive and motor assessment. This study has several limitations. First, because this was an observational study, causality cannot be inferred. Although we adjusted for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and health-related covariates, residual confounding remains possible. Second, several variables, including depressive symptoms, subjective cognitive complaints, and some covariates, were assessed by self-report. In particular, the subjective memory item used to define cognitive complaints may be influenced by mood, personality, reporting tendencies, and level of insight, and may not fully correspond to objective cognitive impairment [ 42 ]. This may have introduced some misclassification in MCR ascertainment and may have affected the estimated associations. Recent literature suggests that self-reported and informant-reported cognitive complaints may offer different but complementary information [ 42 , 43 ]. Therefore, the subjective cognitive complaint component of MCR in this study should be interpreted cautiously, and future research using informant reports or objective cognitive markers would be valuable. Third, the analytical sample was restricted to participants with complete repeated depressive symptom data and available MCR-related data. Because participants with incomplete data could not be classified into depressive symptom trajectories, selection bias is possible if excluded individuals differed systematically from those included. Although the IPCW analyses yielded results similar to the primary analyses, bias related to missingness and attrition cannot be fully excluded. Fourth, although CHARLS is a nationally sampled cohort, our final analytical sample should not be assumed to be fully nationally representative because of the age restriction and complete-case requirements. Therefore, the generalizability of these findings should be interpreted with caution. Fifth, the follow-up period was relatively short and MCR was identified using available survey items rather than a full clinical diagnostic workup. Longer follow-up and studies incorporating more detailed neuropsychological and clinical assessments are needed to confirm the present findings. Finally, the study population consisted of older Chinese adults, which may limit extrapolation to other ethnic, cultural, or healthcare settings.
sections.conclusion: In summary, this study classified depressive symptom trajectories among the older Chinese population into four distinct patterns: low-stable, high-decreasing, medium-increasing, and high-stable. The findings revealed that individuals with increasing, persistently high, or even decreasing depressive symptoms faced a higher risk of developing MCR. These findings suggest that the longitudinal course of depressive symptoms may be informative for risk stratification and earlier identification of older adults vulnerable to cognitive–motor decline in community settings.

title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Estrogen receptor β activation impairs mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and affects malignant mesothelioma cell growth in vitro and in vivo
Comparison of spread patterns and survival outcomes in uterine carcinosarcoma versus grade 3 endometrioid endometrial cancer
abstract: Purpose To compare the clinicopathologic characteristics, dissemination patterns, and survival outcomes of uterine carcinosarcoma (CS) and grade 3 endometrioid adenocarcinoma (G3EAC), focusing on nodal distribution and the impact of complete surgical staging. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 105 patients (43 CS, 62 G3EAC) who underwent primary surgical treatment at a single tertiary center between 2000 and 2016. A focused analysis was performed on a high-quality subgroup of 80 patients (76.2%) who underwent systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods, and independent prognostic factors were evaluated via Cox proportional hazards regression models. Results CS patients were significantly older than G3EAC patients ( p = 0.005). While CS showed lower rates of deep myometrial invasion (44.2% vs. 67.7%; p = 0.016), it was associated with significantly higher positive peritoneal cytology (30.8% vs. 7.0%; p = 0.002). Overall lymph node metastasis rates were comparable between the groups (35.9% vs. 24.6%; p = 0.230). CS was associated with a significantly lower 5-year PFS (35.6% vs. 63.4%; p = 0.042), particularly in Stage IA disease (median PFS 7.7 months), and a trend toward lower 5-year OS (41.1% vs. 64.0%; p = 0.088). Multivariable analysis identified advanced age as the sole independent predictor of poor prognosis (OS HR 1.043, p = 0.021; PFS HR 1.039, p = 0.032). Notably, combined chemoradiotherapy (CRT) effectively eliminated the survival gap between histologies (5-year OS: 72.7% for CS vs. 70.0% for G3EAC; p = 0.590). Conclusion Uterine carcinosarcoma exhibits minimal local invasion but high systemic aggressiveness. Traditional markers of local spread, such as myometrial invasion, are less predictive for CS. Systematic surgical staging remains essential, and multimodal adjuvant CRT is crucial to mitigating the inherent survival disadvantage of CS. sections.introduction: Uterine carcinosarcoma (CS), malignant mixed Müllerian tumor, was traditionally classified as a subtype of uterine sarcoma. It is a biphasic neoplasm composed of malignant-appearing epithelial and mesenchymal elements (D’Angelo and Prat 2010 ). However, accumulating evidence suggests that CS is more closely related to carcinoma than to true sarcoma. According to current data, CS represents a metaplastic carcinoma arising from a single malignant clone (McCluggage 2002a ). Histologic and molecular studies have consistently demonstrated that carcinosarcomas are monoclonal; the sarcomatous component develops from the carcinomatous element, which is the determining factor in tumor behavior. Metastases of carcinosarcomas mostly contain the carcinomatous component, a finding proven by rigorous histopathological examination (Sreenan and Hart 1995 ). Consequently, adjuvant treatment strategies for CS should be similar to those used for high-grade endometrial carcinomas, rather than being sarcoma-based. High-grade (grade 3) endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinomas (G3EAC) and CS were compared in the present study with respect to patterns of spread and prognosis. Further biological insights highlight the dominance of the epithelial component. Investigations using vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) immunostaining and CD34-based assessment of microvessel density (MVD) demonstrated significantly higher VEGF expression and MVD in epithelial compared with mesenchymal elements (Emoto et al. 1999 ). Tumors with lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) exhibited higher VEGF expression, suggesting that angiogenesis is primarily driven by the carcinomatous component. Proliferation studies using MIB-1 (Ki-67) also demonstrated higher mitotic and proliferation indices in the carcinomatous component (Nicòtina et al. 1997 ). Additionally, matrix metalloprotease-7 expression was significantly stronger in epithelial elements, supporting a key role of the carcinomatous component in invasion and tumor progression (Tanimoto et al. 2000 ). Molecular analyses of X-chromosome inactivation patterns and loss of heterozygosity have further confirmed the monoclonal histogenesis of CS (Kounelis et al. 1998 ). Identical p53 and KRAS mutations identified in both tumor components prove their monoclonal nature (Abeln et al. 1997 ). These biological findings have shifted adjuvant treatment strategies toward regimens used for high-grade endometrial carcinomas, incorporating systemic chemotherapy (CTx) and, where indicated, radiation therapy (RT) to improve local control (Rijswijk et al. 1994 ; Omura et al. 1983 ). More recently, integrated molecular analyses from large-scale genomic studies have demonstrated that CS clusters molecularly with high-grade endometrial carcinomas rather than uterine sarcomas (Cherniack et al. 2017 ; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al. 2013 ). CS is surgically staged according to the FIGO system, similar to endometrial carcinoma, with disease stage being the most important prognostic factor. Complete surgical staging includes total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO), and systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection. Lymphadenectomy is recommended as it provides accurate staging and may be associated with improved survival (Nemani et al. 2008 ; Park et al. 2010 ). Given the historical evolution of treatment paradigms, the objective of the study was to compare CS and G3EAC in a cohort where comprehensive surgical staging was prioritized, evaluating clinical behavior and prognosis within the framework of these biological insights. Beyond comparing clinical characteristics, our study specifically aims to evaluate whether modern adjuvant strategies, particularly combined chemoradiotherapy (CRT), can bridge the survival gap between these two aggressive histologies—a phenomenon we describe as the ‘equalizing effect’.
sections.study design and patients: This retrospective cohort study included 105 patients (43 CS and 62 G3EAC) who underwent primary surgical treatment at a single tertiary university hospital between December 2000 and November 2016. All procedures were performed by gynecologic oncologists. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee (No: GO 17/792 − 37). Patients were staged according to the 2009 FIGO classification system. Follow-up data were collected through electronic medical records and telephone interviews until July 2018 or death. The initial diagnosis was based on the final pathology reports from our institution’s specialized gynecological pathologists. While a pathology re-review was not performed at the time of this analysis, all cases underwent institutional pathology board review during the initial diagnostic process. Progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the interval from the date of primary surgery to the date of first recurrence or death from any cause. Any of these were considered an event. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the interval from the date of primary surgery to the date of death from any cause. Recurrence was confirmed via radiological imaging (computed tomography [CT], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], or PET-CT) or pathological validation through biopsy or surgical specimens.
sections.surgical procedures: All surgical procedures were performed via open laparotomy. Complete surgical staging—defined as TAH-BSO and systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection—was performed in 34 (79%) CS and 46 (74%) G3EAC patients. The remaining patients underwent TAH-BSO with pelvic lymphadenectomy or TAH-BSO alone based on clinical judgement and patient comorbidities. Cytoreductive surgery was required in only two patients ( n = 2) due to extensive intraoperative disease.
sections.statistical analysis: Continuous variables were analyzed using Student’s t -test or Mann–Whitney U test, based on the assessment of normality. Categorical data were compared using chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests. Survival outcomes, including five-year OS and PFS, were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared via the log-rank test. Median follow-up time was calculated using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were utilized to identify independent prognostic factors, including age, FIGO stage, histology, and peritoneal cytology. From an initial cohort of 105 patients, a complete case analysis was performed for the multivariable models, resulting in a final analyzed cohort of n = 94. Eleven cases were excluded due to missing data in peritoneal cytology ( n = 9) or other clinical covariates ( n = 2). Variables were selected for the multivariable models based on a twofold approach: univariable significance ( p < 0.05 for age and peritoneal cytology) and established clinical relevance in the literature (histology, FIGO stage) regardless of its univariable p-value. To ensure the stability of the regression models and prevent overfitting, the ratio of events per variable (EPV) was maintained above the recommended threshold of 10. The multivariable model for PFS included 43 events, providing an EPV ratio of 10.75 (Omnibus test, p = 0.012). OS model included 41 events, yielding an EPV ratio of 10.25 (Omnibus test, p = 0.018). The proportional hazards assumption was verified by both visual inspection of log-log plots and the use of time-dependent covariates, which confirmed that the assumption was met ( p = 0.462 for PFS and p = 0.266 for OS). Given its clinical relevance, the impact of adjuvant RT was evaluated in a separate sensitivity analysis. An interaction term (histology × RT) was tested to assess whether the effect of adjuvant treatment differed between subtypes. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. All tests were two-sided, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.
sections.baseline clinicopathologic characteristi: A total of 105 patients were included, 43 (41%) had CS and 62 (59%) had G3EAC. CS patients were significantly older (mean age: 67.4 ± 8.8 vs. 62.1 ± 9.8 years; p = 0.005), with a mean age difference of 5.38 years (95% CI 1.67–9.08). While G3EAC was associated with more frequent deep myometrial (≥ 50%) invasion (67.7% vs. 44.2%, p = 0.016), positive peritoneal cytology was substantially more common in the CS group (30.8% vs. 7.0%, p = 0.002). Median tumor size (6.0 cm vs. 5.0 cm; p = 0.051) and LVSI prevalence (60.9% vs. 68.5%; p = 0.516) were comparable (Table 1 ). The distribution of clinical and pathological features for the entire cohort is presented in Table 1 . Discrepancies in the total number of patients for certain variables, such as peritoneal cytology ( n = 9 missing) and LVSI ( n = 28 missing), are due to incomplete data in the retrospective records; for peritoneal cytology, occasional procedural omissions or logistical challenges over the 16-year retrospective period. sections.nodal and surgical characteristics: A comprehensive nodal assessment was performed in 96 patients (39 CS, 57 G3EAC). Median retrieved lymph nodes were 27 (IQR, 17–40), and 33 (IQR, 17–44), respectively ( p = 0.573). Overall lymph node metastasis (LNM) rates were 35.9% for CS and 24.6% for G3EAC ( p = 0.230). Pelvic (30.8% vs. 19.3%; p = 0.196) and para-aortic lymph node involvement (23.5% vs. 17.4%; p = 0.497) were similar between groups (Table 2 ). Although the mean number of metastatic nodes was numerically higher in the CS group (2.49 ± 5.15) than in the G3EAC group (1.19 ± 4.55), this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.083). sections.survival outcomes and recurrence pattern: Median follow-up for the entire cohort was 61.4 months (95% CI 55.0–67.8). Recurrence was radiologically confirmed in all patients (100%, n = 22), with additional pathological validation performed in 40.9% ( n = 9) of these cases. Recurrence occurred in 30.2% ( n = 13) of CS and 14.5% ( n = 9) of G3EAC patients ( p = 0.052, Table 2 ). Recurrence patterns differed by histology: CS failures were more disseminated, frequently involving distant sites (distant metastasis:7, abdominal:4, pelvic:1, vaginal cuff:1), while G3EAC recurrences were more localized to the vaginal cuff or peritoneum (distant:3, abdominal: 4, pelvic:1, vaginal cuff:1). Five-year PFS was significantly lower in the CS group compared with G3EAC (35.6% vs. 63.4%; p = 0.042; Fig. 1A). Median PFS was 19.4 months (95% CI 7.7–31.1) for CS versus not reached for G3EAC. Similarly, CS showed a clinical survival disadvantage in 5-year OS (41.1% vs. 64.0%; p = 0.088), with a median OS of 32.9 months versus 106.1 months for G3EAC. Although the CS group showed a more aggressive decline in the early follow-up period (Fig. 1B), the difference in 5-year OS did not reach statistical significance. Although the carcinosarcoma group showed a more aggressive decline in the early follow-up period, the difference in 5-year OS did not reach statistical significance. Vertical ticks indicate censored observations. Number at risk is provided below each graph. Abbr: EAC, endometrioid adenocarcinoma.
sections.early-stage disease (stage ia and ib): In Stage IA disease ( n = 21), CS exhibited a markedly aggressive course despite being uterine-confined. Five-year OS and PFS rates for CS were both 28.6%, compared with 60.0% and 63.0% for G3EAC (OS p = 0.095; PFS p = 0.077). Median PFS for Stage IA CS was only 7.7 months (95% CI 5.6–9.8) and median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI 3.9–30.0), whereas medians were not reached for G3EAC. For Stage IB disease ( n = 31), 5-year OS was 50.0% for CS versus 72.1% for G3EAC ( p = 0.174), and 5-year PFS was 40.0% and 73.2%, respectively ( p = 0.122). Median PFS and OS for CS were 17.4 and 32.8 months, while neither was reached for G3EAC.
sections.advanced-stage disease (stage iii and iv: In Stage III disease ( n = 26), the survival gap was less pronounced; 5-year OS was 54.3% for CS and 77.1% for G3EAC ( p = 0.607), while 5-year PFS rates were 50.6% and 68.6%, respectively ( p = 0.668). Both groups demonstrated poor outcomes in Stage IV ( n = 17). Median OS was 11.1 months (95% CI 7.7–14.4) for CS and 17.9 months (95% CI 8.9–26.9) for G3EAC ( p = 0.844). Median PFS was 7.0 months (95% CI 0.0–19.6) for CS and 8.7 months (95% CI 7.5–9.8) for G3EAC ( p = 0.614).
sections.impact of adjuvant treatment modalities: Survival outcomes across the cohort were analyzed by adjuvant strategy: CRT, CTx only, RT only, and no adjuvant treatment.
sections.chemoradiotherapy (crt) group: In patients receiving CRT, survival outcomes were comparable between the two histological subtypes, suggesting that intensified multimodal treatment may mitigate the aggressive biological nature of CS. The 5-year OS rate was 72.7% for CS versus 70.0% for G3EAC ( p = 0.590), with median OS of 87.6 and 106.1 months (95% CI 13.2–199.0), respectively. The 5-year PFS rates were also similar (63.6% vs. 60.0%; p = 0.502). Notably, median PFS was 70.8 months (95% CI 0.0–169.6) for G3EAC and was not reached for CS, suggesting sustained remission in CS patients treated with CRT.
sections.chemotherapy (ctx) only group: Among patients treated with CTx alone, CS showed a trend toward inferior outcomes, though this did not reach statistical significance. The 5-year OS was 22.2% for CS versus 60.0% for G3EAC ( p = 0.493). The median OS for CS was 32.9 months (95% CI 0.0–68.4), while the median OS for the G3EAC group was not reached. Similarly, 5-year PFS was 19.0% for CS versus 62.5% for G3EAC ( p = 0.370), with a median PFS of 19.9 months (95% CI 11.8–28.0) for CS, not reached for G3EAC.
sections.radiotherapy (rt) only group: RT as a single modality was associated with a survival disadvantage in this sub-group analysis for CS compared with G3EAC, highlighting the systemic nature of CS spread. The 5-year OS was significantly lower for CS at 33.3% versus 75.8% for G3EAC ( p = 0.009; median OS: 14.3 months [95% CI 4.8–23.7] vs. not reached). Similarly, 5-year PFS was 25.0% for CS and 77.9% for G3EAC ( p = 0.003; median PFS: 7.3 months [95% CI 0.0–19.7] vs. not reached).
sections.no adjuvant treatment group: Both groups demonstrated poor survival in the absence of adjuvant treatment. The 5-year OS was 30.0% for CS and 31.1% for G3EAC ( p = 0.743), with median OS of 9.8 months (95% CI 4.8–14.9) and 32.5 months (95% CI 0.0–88.1), respectively. Five-year PFS rates were 30.0% for CS and 31.1% for G3EAC ( p = 0.677).
sections.multivariable and sensitivity survival a: Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify independent prognostic factors for OS and PFS (Table 3 ). In univariable analyses, increasing age and positive peritoneal cytology were significantly associated with both poorer OS and PFS. Histological subtype was significantly associated with PFS in the univariable model ( p = 0.045), with CS demonstrating worse outcomes than G3EAC, although its association with OS did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.091). Notably, advanced FIGO stage (III–IV vs. I–II) was not significantly associated with OS or PFS in the univariable models ( p > 0.05). To further investigate this finding, a subgroup analysis of treatment modalities was conducted (Supplementary Table S1 ). This revealed a distinct treatment distribution: 32.2% (20/62) of Stage I–II patients received no adjuvant therapy, whereas 88.4% (38/43) of Stage III–IV patients underwent intensive multimodal treatment. sections.sensitivity analysis of adjuvant radioth: Given the therapeutic impact observed in univariable analysis, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by including adjuvant RT in the multivariable model. In this model, adjuvant RT remained significantly associated with improved OS (HR 0.476; 95% CI 0.242–0.935; p = 0.031), while its association with PFS approached statistical significance (HR 0.527; 95% CI 0.275–1.010; p = 0.054). Importantly, no significant interaction was observed between histologic subtype and RT for either OS or PFS ( p > 0.05), indicating that the beneficial effect of RT was consistent across both histologies (Table 3 ).

sections.clinicopathologic features and peritonea: In this high-quality cohort, CS patients were significantly older (mean age 67.6 ± 9.1 vs. 61.2 ± 8.6 years, p = 0.002). Regarding uterine-confined features, deep myometrial invasion (≥ 50%) was identified in 55.9% (19/34) of CS and 71.7% (33/46) of G3EAC patients ( p = 0.218). Positive peritoneal cytology was significantly more frequent in the CS group (28.1% vs. 8.8%; p = 0.034).
sections.nodal distribution and metastatic burden: As detailed in Table 4 , median retrieved lymph nodes were 31.5 for CS and 37.5 for G3EAC ( p = 0.174). Despite lower rates of deep invasion, LNM was numerically more frequent in CS (41.2%) than G3EAC (28.3%; p = 0.469). Pelvic LNM occurred in 32.4% of CS and 21.7% of G3EAC ( p = 0.286), while para-aortic involvement was detected in 23.5% and 17.4%, respectively ( p = 0.497).
sections.survival analysis of the staged cohort: Survival outcomes within the completely staged subgroup demonstrated a persistent clinical disadvantage for CS (Table 4 ). Median PFS for CS was 32.9 months (95% CI 14.3–51.4), while it was not reached for G3EAC ( p = 0.062; 5-year PFS rates: 41.7% vs. 72.5%). Median OS for CS was 43.2 months (95% CI 0–111.2), vs. not reached for G3EAC ( p = 0.092; 5-year OS rates: 46.4% vs. 73.6%). Although these differences did not reach statistical significance, they reflect the inherent biological aggressiveness of CS even with accurate nodal mapping. Recurrence patterns showed that upper abdominal/peritoneal relapses occurred in 17.6% of CS and 13.0% of G3EAC patients.
sections.discussion: The present study provides a comparative analysis of CS and G3EAC, focusing on their distinct pathophysiological behaviors and prognostic trajectories. Our results demonstrate that while these two high-grade malignancies are managed under similar protocols, they exhibit fundamentally different dissemination modes. CS displays a more systemic and aggressive phenotype from the clinical outset, supporting its understanding as a metaplastic carcinoma (McCluggage 2002a , 2002b ; Cherniack et al. 2017 ). Our observations regarding the distinct clinical behavior of CS and G3EAC are further supported by recent 2025 literature. Dagher et al. ( 2025 ) similarly emphasized the heterogeneity among high-grade endometrial carcinomas, demonstrating that CS exhibits both higher peritoneal cytology positivity and the poorest survival outcomes when compared to G3EAC. Furthermore, in advanced-stage disease, our results align with Conforti et al. ( 2025 ), who demonstrated that histological subtype is a major determinant of survival outcomes even beyond disease stage.
sections.age and the biological paradox of dissem: A primary distinction in our cohort was the significantly higher age of patients in the CS group, consistent with the established literature characterizing CS as a disease of the elderly, typically presenting in the sixth and seventh decades of life (Cherniack et al. 2017 ). Beyond demographics, the most striking finding was the “surgical paradox”: while G3EAC exhibited a higher incidence of deep myometrial invasion (67.7% vs. 44.2%; p = 0.016), CS demonstrated a more aggressive systemic profile. Despite less frequent deep local penetration, the CS group showed significantly higher positive peritoneal cytology (30.8% vs. 7.0%; p = 0.002) and distant organ metastasis. This suggests that CS possesses an inherent systemic aggressiveness, likely driven by EMT (Chaffer et al. 2016 ). This cell plasticity allows for early peritoneal seeding and distant failure independent of traditional markers of uterine invasion, such as myometrial depth (Tanimoto et al. 2000 ).
sections.lymphophilic nature independent of myome: In endometrial cancer, deep myometrial invasion is traditionally established as the primary predictor of LNM. Across our entire cohort, however, the incidence of overall LNM was not significantly different between the two subtypes (35.9% for CS vs. 24.6% for G3EAC, p = 0.230), despite the significantly higher deep myometrial invasion in G3EAC. This indicates that while deep myometrial invasion remains a reliable predictor for G3EAC, it is less predictive for CS. In the CS group, nodal risk remained high even with superficial myometrial invasion. This underscores that CS histology itself drives lymphatic dissemination independent of anatomical depth (Park et al. 2010 ).
sections.survival disadvantage and the frailty of: When evaluating the entire cohort, the clinical impact of this biological aggressiveness is most evident in survival outcomes. Our findings suggest a trend towards a survival disadvantage for CS compared to G3EAC, most notably in PFS (5-year PFS: 34.9% vs. 61.3%; p = 0.016). This gap was particularly notable in Stage IA disease ( n = 21), where CS exhibited a markedly aggressive course despite being uterine-confined. For Stage IA CS, the 5-year OS and PFS rates were both 28.6%, compared with 60.0% and 63.0% for G3EAC (OS p = 0.095; PFS p = 0.077). The median PFS for Stage IA CS was only 7.7 months (95% CI 5.6–9.8) and the median OS was 17.0 months (95% CI 3.9–30.0), whereas medians were not reached for G3EAC. These clinical observations in Stage IA CS should be interpreted with caution given the small subgroup size; however, they may be partially explained by the adjuvant treatment distribution in our cohort. Specifically, 66.7% (6/9) of Stage IA CS and 41.7% (5/12) G3EAC patients received no adjuvant therapy during the study period. This lack of adjuvant treatment, combined with the inherent systemic aggressiveness of CS, likely contributed to the rapid disease progression observed even in early-stage disease. These findings suggest that even at the earliest FIGO stage, CS carries a substantially worse prognosis than G3EAC (D’Angelo and Prat 2010 ; Cherniack et al. 2017 ), necessitating its management as a systemic disease from diagnosis. However, as our observations regarding Stage IA CS are based on a very small subgroup, these findings should be interpreted with caution and regarded as exploratory only.
sections.the equalizing effect of multimodal adju: A major finding is that while CS patients receiving only RT had poorer outcomes than their G3EAC counterparts ( p = 0.009), this survival gap was effectively eliminated in the combined CRT group (5-year OS: 72.7% for CS vs. 70.0% for G3EAC; p = 0.590). Our exploratory observations on the ‘equalizing effect’ of CRT suggest a potential systemic nature for CS. While single-modality RT provides local control, it fails to address the high risk of distant and peritoneal failure inherent to CS (Galaal et al. 2013 ; Powell et al. 2010 ). Therefore, a multimodal approach incorporating both the local benefits of RT and the systemic coverage of CTx is essential to achieve comparable outcomes.
sections.independent prognostic factors: multivar: Our multivariable analysis, identified advanced age as the sole independent predictor of poor prognosis for both OS (HR: 1.043; p = 0.021) and PFS (HR: 1.039; p = 0.032). Interestingly, FIGO stage did not emerge as a significant predictor of survival in our cohort. This finding likely reflects a combination of the intensive multimodal management of advanced-stage patients and the significant proportion of early-stage patients (32.2%) who did not receive adjuvant therapy during the study period. The high recurrence potential of CS and G3EAC even in early stages, when left untreated, appears to have narrowed the prognostic difference between early and advanced-stage disease in our series. Furthermore, in sensitivity analysis adjuvant RT was significantly associated with improved OS (HR: 0.476; p = 0.031), providing a 52.4% reduction in the risk of mortality. This emphasizes that beyond the histology, patient-specific factors—primarily age—and the optimal treatment combinations are the primary determinants of outcome.
sections.insights from the completely staged subg: To eliminate the confounding effect of stage migration, we performed a focused analysis on the completely staged subgroup ( n = 80). In this high-quality surgical cohort, the survival difference between histologies did not reach statistical significance (PFS p = 0.062; OS p = 0.092). However, the 23.5% para-aortic involvement in CS underscores the necessity of systematic staging (Park et al. 2010 ). Omitting this step could lead to significant understaging, as superficial uterine findings in CS do not preclude a substantial upper lymphatic burden (Nemani et al. 2008 ).
sections.strengths and limitations: We acknowledge that our study is primarily limited by its retrospective design and small subgroup sample sizes, rendering secondary analyses exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. However, despite these limitations, a major strength is the high quality and uniformity of the surgical management. Specifically, 76.2% of our patients underwent systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy and all patients operated via laparatomy, providing a “clean” cohort for the accurate analysis of nodal distribution and significantly reducing the risk of stage migration. Furthermore, the single-center nature of our study at a tertiary university hospital provided a significant advantage in terms of consistency across surgical techniques, standardized pathological interpretations, and uniform adjuvant treatment strategies, thus minimizing the inter-institutional variability often encountered in multi-center datasets. Additionally, the long median follow-up of 61.4 months (95% CI 55.0–67.8) ensures a robust and reliable assessment of 5-year survival outcomes and long-term recurrence patterns in these aggressive malignancies.
sections.conclusion_1: In conclusion, our study suggests that CS and G3EAC exhibit markedly different local invasion patterns despite a similar risk for lymphatic dissemination. CS follows a more aggressive systemic phenotype characterized by early peritoneal seeding and a high lymphatic burden, even in cases with superficial uterine involvement. While our results are limited by the cohort size and should be considered hypothesis-generating, this “surgical paradox“ highlights that traditional markers of local invasion, such as deep myometrial invasion, are significantly less predictive of spread in CS compared with G3EAC. Importantly, our multivariable analysis identified advanced age as the sole independent predictor of poor prognosis for both OS and PFS in these high-grade malignancies. Furthermore, while CS carries an inherent survival disadvantage, our findings suggest that this gap can be effectively mitigated through a multimodal adjuvant approach. The ‘equalizing effect’ observed in our cohort provides a clinical signal that the survival gap might be mitigated through a multimodal approach. However, these findings require validation in larger, prospective trials. While CS exhibits a general survival disadvantage across the entire cohort (PFS p = 0.016), this disparity narrows in completely staged patients and is effectively eliminated by combined CRT. Therefore, comprehensive surgical staging remains essential, and treatment strategies should be optimized with a focus on multimodal therapies to improve clinical outcomes in this high-risk patient population.

title: Determinants of the quality of life of patients with NF2 -related schwannomatosis and validation of the Dutch NFTI-QOL questionnaire
abstract: NF2 -Related Schwannomatosis ( NF2 -SWN) is a rare tumor predisposition syndrome characterized by heterogeneous clinical manifestations that substantially impact quality of life (QOL). In this diverse patient population, a disease-specific QOL instrument is essential for both research and clinical decision-making. Insight into factors associated with QOL may further facilitate the tailoring of management strategies to individual patient needs. This study aimed to validate the Dutch version of the NF2 Impact on Quality of Life questionnaire (NFTI-QOL) and to identify factors associated with QOL in Dutch patients with NF2 . Following forward‑ and backward‑translation, the NFTI-QOL was administered to NF2 -SWN patients alongside the SF‑36, EQ‑5D and PANQOL. The NFTI-QOL was repeated after one week. Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To provide clinical context, questionnaires were also administered to patients with sporadic vestibular schwannoma (sVS). 64 NF2 -SWN and 51 sVS patients completed the questionnaires. The NFTI-QOL demonstrated good validity and reliability. In multivariate linear regression, dizziness (β = 2.533, p = 0.027) and facial weakness (β = 4.064, p = 0.008) were significantly associated with QOL, whereas hearing complaints were not. Surprisingly, overall QOL did not differ between NF2 -SWN and sVS patients, whereas patients with sVS even reported poorer hearing-related QOL. The Dutch NFTI-QOL is a reliable instrument for assessing QOL in NF2-SWN patients. Dizziness and facial weakness were associated with lower QOL, while hearing problems were not. sections.introduction: NF2 -Related Schwannomatosis ( NF2 -SWN, formerly Neurofibromatosis type 2 or NF2 ) is a rare, autosomal dominant tumor predisposition syndrome with an estimated incidence of 1:50.000 [ 1 ]. The hallmark lesions are bilateral vestibular schwannomas (VS) [ 2 ]. Additionally, intracranial and spinal meningiomas, ependymomas and schwannomas as well as peripheral schwannomas throughout the body may develop [ 3 ]. These different types and locations of tumors result in a variable phenotype. The clinical manifestations of NF2 -SWN typically include progressive bilateral hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, and tinnitus, and patients also experience various other neurological deficits affecting vision, mobility, and sensation. This diverse symptomatology leads to substantial variation in disease burden and functional impairment, yet often compromises quality of life (QOL) [ 4 – 6 ]. As curative treatment options are lacking, the aim of NF2 -SWN management is to prevent or rehabilitate function loss as much as possible, with the ultimate goal of preserving quality of life. Current management options comprise active surveillance, surgery, radiotherapy and pharmacotherapy. Although treatment strategies are mostly guided by the standard objective measures such as tumor progression or the extent of objective neurological function loss, these measures have been shown to have limited correlation with the patients’ QOL [ 7 ]. Moreover, the therapy itself may negatively impact QOL. This highlights the need for a comprehensive understanding of the factors that influence QOL in NF2 -SWN patients and for tools that reliably capture this. QOL is a multidimensional construct encompassing physical, psychological, social, environmental, functional and personal aspects of well-being [ 8 ]. While generic QOL-instruments are aimed at measuring these broader domains, they do not sufficiently reflect the specific multisystem nature of NF2 -SWN or the problems that have been found most relevant to NF2 -SWN patients [ 9 ]. Disease-specific instruments may therefore provide complementary insight. To address this gap, a NF2 -SWN-specific questionnaire ‘Neurofibromatosis 2 Impact on Quality of Life’ (NFTI-QOL) was developed in 2012 [ 10 ]. This short and concise disease-specific questionnaire has been validated in English and translated into German [ 11 ]. As of yet, no validated Dutch version is available. A Dutch version of the NFTI-QOL would support clinical care and research not only in the Netherlands but also in other Dutch speaking NF2 -SWN populations (for instance in Belgium). Furthermore, QOL in Dutch NF2 -SWN patients has not yet been systematically investigated. Identifying the factors associated with QOL may guide interventions and supportive care beyond tumor-directed treatment [ 12 ]. The aims of this study are to validate the Dutch version of the NFTI-QOL, to deploy it in a Dutch patient cohort and identify factors that determine the quality of life of NF2 -SWN patients.
sections.translation of nfti-qol into dutch: The NFTI-QOL was translated into Dutch following the internationally accepted guidelines for translation of patient-reported outcome measures [ 13 , 14 ]. Two native Dutch speakers with near-native proficiency in English independently performed forward translation. Subsequently, the Dutch version was translated back into English by two native English speakers with near-native proficiency in Dutch. After both translation steps, differences between the two translations were discussed by both translators until consensus was reached. Discrepancies between the backward translation and the original English version were discussed by all translators until resolved. Finally, the resulting Dutch translation was assessed for clarity and readability by an additional native Dutch speaker. The final Dutch version of the NFTI-QOL is provided in the Supplementary Materials (Appendix 1).
sections.study design and participants: This prospective study included patients with NF2 -SWN and a comparison group of patients with a (unilateral) sporadic vestibular schwannoma (sVS). Recruitment took place between July 2025 and February 2026 at the Leiden University Medical Center, a national tertiary referral and expertise center for NF2 -SWN and VS, and through the Dutch NF2 -SWN patient association (NFVN). Inclusion criteria for NF2 -SWN patients were (1) age ≥ 18 years, (2) a diagnosis of NF2 -SWN based on the criteria by Plotkin et al. (2022) and (3) a good proficiency in Dutch [ 2 ]. All patients known to the NF2 -SWN expertise center were invited by email, and an open invitation was distributed through the patient association. After providing informed consent, patients received questionnaires either through an online link using Castor EDC [ 15 ] or on paper, depending on patient preference. To provide contextual comparison of QOL domains, a reference group of patients with sVS was recruited. This population was selected because patients experience vestibulocochlear symptoms similar to those in NF2 -SWN, albeit unilaterally rather than bilaterally, but do not have the additional intracranial and spinal tumors characteristic of NF2 -SWN. Inclusion criteria for sVS patients were (1) age ≥ 18 years, (2) a diagnosis of unilateral vestibular schwannoma and (3) good proficiency in Dutch. Exclusion criteria were (1) suspected NF2 -SWN and (2) suffering from visual impairment, neurological disease or neuropathies not related to the vestibular schwannoma. Patients were recruited through the vestibular schwannoma care pathway at the LUMC and approached by email or during a visit at the outpatient clinic. Frequency matching was used to obtain comparable age and sex distributions between both groups.
sections.questionnaires: NF2 -SWN patients received patient-reported outcome measures in addition to a set of questions on demographic and clinical status, including age, age at onset, education level, and hearing rehabilitation. All instruments were sent at once. To assess test–retest reliability, the NFTI-QOL was sent a second time one week after completion of the baseline questionnaires. sVS patients received the same set of questionnaires once. The online and paper versions were identical in content, and the order of questionnaires was fixed for all participants. The NFTI-QOL is a disease-specific questionnaire consisting of eight items covering different domains of QOL: dizziness/imbalance, hearing problems, facial weakness, sight problems, mobility, outlook on life, pain, and anxiety/depression. Each item is scored on a four-point scale, yielding a total score between 0 and 24, with higher scores reflecting worse QOL [ 10 ]. Concurrent validity was assessed using three additional validated patient-reported outcome measures. The 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and the EQ-5D-5L were included as generic health-related QOL-instruments, and the Penn Acoustic Neuroma Quality-of-Life scale (PANQOL) was used as a disease-specific measure relevant to sVS patients [ 16 – 18 ]. All three instruments have validated Dutch versions [ 19 – 21 ]. In these questionnaires, higher scores indicate better functioning.
sections.data collection: Clinical information was collected from the patients’ electronic health records when available, and included audiological, neurological, and genetic data. Audiometric evaluation consisted of both pure tone audiometry and word recognition scores (WRS). Pure tone averages (PTA) were calculated by averaging thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz. If no measurement was available at 3 kHz, the average of 2 and 4 kHz was used [ 22 , 23 ]. Facial nerve function was assessed using the House-Brackmann scale [ 24 ]. Genetic data were extracted from the clinical genetics report when available and classified according to the validated NF2 -SWN genetic severity classification by Halliday [ 25 ]. In cases of uncertainty regarding interpretation or classification, a Clinical Geneticist with expertise in NF2 -SWN was consulted. Information on prior treatments, including surgery, radiotherapy and bevacizumab therapy, was collected from the medical record. The relationship between NFTI-QOL scores and disease burden was assessed using three different measures of disease severity. Clinician-reported severity was derived from a validated symptom-based scoring system and classified into mild, moderate, and severe disease [ 26 ]. Genetic severity was classified into five levels according to the validated genetic severity score by Halliday [ 25 ]. Patient-reported disease severity was assessed using a single self-reported item included in the questionnaire, in which participants rated the overall impact of NF2 -SWN on their quality of life as none or mild, moderate, or severe.
sections.power calculation: According to the COSMIN (COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement Instruments) guidelines, a sample size between 50 and 99 participants is considered adequate for assessing reliability and validity of a patient-reported outcome measurement instrument [ 27 ]. We therefore aimed to recruit at least 50 NF2 -SWN and 50 sVS patients for the validation of the Dutch version of the NFTI-QOL questionnaire.
sections.statistical analyses: Descriptive statistics were calculated for demographical and clinical factors. Group differences were calculated using independent samples t-tests and Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables. For correlations, Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients were used. All analyses were performed on a complete‑case basis. For each questionnaire, standard scoring algorithms were applied to calculate domain, component, and total scores according to the respective scoring manuals [ 10 , 18 , 28 , 29 ]. Internal consistency of the NFTI-QOL was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha (α) for the total score. Test–retest reliability was evaluated by calculating the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Concurrent validity was examined by computing Spearman correlation coefficients between total scores of NFTI-QOL and the physical and mental health component summery scores of the SF-36 and the total scores of the EQ-5D and PANQOL. Correlations were interpreted according to the criteria described by Evans [ 30 ]. Associations between disease severity and NFTI-QOL scores were evaluated using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. To identify symptoms independently associated with quality of life, a multivariate linear regression model was computed. Because of the limited sample size and to prevent overfitting, a set of predictors was selected a priori based on clinical relevance and existing literature. Assumptions for linear regression were assessed. Additional univariate associations were explored to identify demographic or clinical parameters potentially associated with QOL. As an exploratory contextual comparison, NFTI-QOL domain and total scores were compared between NF2 -SWN patients and sVS patients. All statistical analyses were performed with IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 29.0 (released 2022, IBM Corp, Armonk, NY).
sections.ethics: The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board and conducted in full compliance with the ethical standard of the 2024 Declaration of Helsinki.
sections.results: 70 NF2 -SWN patients and 61 sVS patients provided informed consent. 64 NF2 -SWN patients (91%) completed the first four questionnaires. 51 patients with sVS completed the questionnaires (84%). There were no missing responses to questions in the surveys. Baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1 . The NF2 -SWN and sVS groups were comparable in age and sex due to frequency matching. Nine patients (14%) were included from other centers. For these patients, detailed clinical information could not be retrieved as electronic records were not accessible to the researchers. For an additional four patients, records were available but incomplete or outdated. Therefore, descriptive analyses of clinical parameters are based on the remaining 51 patients, unless otherwise specified. NFTI-QOL domain scores for NF2 -SWN patients are reported in Supplementary Table S1 . Internal consistency was good for the total NFTI-QOL score (α = 0.804). Test–retest reliability was assessed in 61 patients who completed both assessments. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for the total score was 0.915, indicating excellent reliability. Regarding concurrent validity, total NFTI-QOL scores correlated strongly with total scores of the PANQOL ( ρ = − 0.755, p < 0.001), the physical component summery score (PCS) of the SF-36 ( ρ = − 0.786, p < 0.001) and EQ-5D ( ρ = − 0.783, p < 0.001). Genetic disease severity was not associated with NFTI-QOL scores (Spearman’s ρ = 0.272, p = 0.053). Patient-reported severity correlated moderately with NFTI-QOL scores (Spearman’s ρ = 0.577, p < 0.001).
