Given the difference in tumor laterality, WRS were evaluated separately for the best- and worst-hearing ear. In the NF2- SWN cohort, 83% of patients had good hearing in the best ear, 6% had serviceable hearing, and 11% had non-serviceable hearing in their best hearing ear. In contrast, in the sVS cohort, all patients (100%) demonstrated good hearing in the best ear. Analysis of the worst-hearing ear showed non-serviceable hearing in 41% of NF2 -SWN patients and in 27% of sVS patients, serviceable hearing in 13% of NF2 -SWN patients and 16% of sVS patients, and good hearing in 33% and 57%, respectively. In other words, only 33% of NF2- SWN patients had good bilateral hearing versus 57% of sVS patients.
sections.discussion: This study represents the validation and deployment of a disease-specific QOL instrument for NF2 -SWN in a NF2 -SWN patient cohort in the Netherlands. The Dutch translation of the NFTI-QOL demonstrated to be a reliable questionnaire for use in Dutch patients with NF2 -SWN. The NFTI-QOL was intentionally designed as a concise and clinically practical disease-specific instrument. As a result, not all individual contributing domains of quality of life are captured in detail. Nonetheless, the NFTI-QOL showed strong correlations with both generic and vestibular schwannoma-specific QOL questionnaires, as well as with clinician-reported and patient-reported disease severity, consistent with previous literature [ 31 , 32 ]. These findings support its ability to capture disease burden on quality of life. Compared with previously published NF2 -SWN cohorts from the United Kingdom and Germany, the Dutch cohort showed lower NFTI-QOL scores, indicating a better overall QOL (mean NFTI-QOL: 7.0 vs. 9.4 and 9.2, respectively) [ 10 , 32 ]. Several factors may contribute to this difference. The Dutch cohort had a higher mean age at diagnosis (36 years) compared to the average age at diagnosis reported in the literature (20–29 years) [ 33 , 34 ], and a lower rate of inherited NF2 -SWN (7% vs. 23–56% in the literature) [ 35 , 36 ]. These factors in themselves may indicate that the disease phenotype may be milder in this Dutch study population. Unfortunately, direct comparisons of the current cohort with the studies from Germany and the United Kingdom with respect to these factors are hampered by limited data on the clinical and genetic characteristics of these cohorts. Even so, the current Dutch cohort indeed comprised more patients with disease classified as mild (59% vs. 18% and 44%). As NFTI-QOL outcomes correlate well with clinician-reported and patient-reported disease severity, differences in the average QOL between these cohorts may be explained by differences in the case-mix. Additionally, general population-based quality of life indices (i.e. the general quality of life index and the specific health care index) are known to be higher in the Netherlands than in the UK or Germany, which may also affect disease specific quality of life [ 37 ]. A striking finding is that the overall QOL did not differ between patients with NF2 -SWN and sVS, as assessed with NFTI-QOL, EQ-5D and SF-36. This is surprising as NF2 -SWN patients face a more complex multisystem tumor syndrome causing multiple neurological deficits and a more uncertain prognosis, whereas sVS patients suffer from a sporadic tumor typically affecting audiovestibular function only. The absence of this difference in perceived QOL suggests that it does not solely depend on objective disease severity or the multitude of objective functional impairments, but is probably also substantially influenced by the context of the disease, personality traits and coping abilities. Another possible explanation is the difference in time since diagnosis. Because patients with sVS were age-matched, their average age at diagnosis was higher than that of NF2-SWN patients, resulting in a shorter time since diagnosis. This may have provided less opportunity for the sVS patients to develop coping strategies and allow psychological adaptation over time. Our analyses demonstrate that facial and vestibular symptoms are important determinants of disease-specific quality of life in patients with NF2 -SWN, whereas hearing impairment was not independently associated with overall quality of life. Vestibular dysfunction is highly prevalent in NF2 -SWN patients, but has not been studied extensively. Better understanding and management of this important factor in NF2 -SWN patients could potentially improve their QOL. The strong association between facial symptoms and poorer QOL is consistent with the literature [ 6 , 38 ]. Surprisingly, hearing loss was not identified as an independent determinant of overall QOL in NF2 -SWN patients. What is more, NF2 -SWN patients had better scores on the hearing domain of the NFTI-QOL than sVS patients, despite having worse audiometric outcomes. We hypothesize that in sVS patients, unilateral hearing loss may be experienced as a major functional decline because audiovestibular problems are the predominant clinical feature of the disease, while in NF2 -SWN patients, hearing loss may represent only one of a plethora of neurological deficits that contribute to the overall disease burden, potentially diminishing its relative impact on perceived quality of life. Evaluation of other potential factors in NF2 -SWN-related QOL revealed that the number of treatment modalities and radiotherapy as prior treatment were negatively associated with QOL. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the exploratory nature of these analyses, and it remains uncertain whether the observed associations in NF2 -SWN reflect the impact of treatment on QOL. An alternative explanation could be that the number and type of treatments are indirect indicators of disease severity. The association between NF2 -SWN-related QOL and radiotherapy has been observed before [ 6 ]. To date, data on treatment-related QOL in NF2 -SWN remain scarce precluding definite conclusions on the effects of different treatment modalities on patient-reported outcomes in NF2 -SWN. Nonetheless, these findings stress the necessity to carefully weigh the potential risks of active treatment against the expected benefits. The main limitation of this study is the relatively limited size of the patient cohort, which is inherent to the rarity of NF2 -SWN. Even so, the number of patients exceeds the required number as stipulated in the COSMIN guidelines for the validation of patient-reported outcome measurement instruments. Moreover, with an estimated prevalence in the Netherlands of 300–400 patients, the study cohort constitutes approximately 20% of the total Dutch NF2 -SWN population. An additional limitation is the cross-sectional design that does not allow for evaluation of longitudinal changes. Causality can therefore not be determined when examining contributing factors of QOL. The NFTI-QOL has now been implemented in routine NF2 -SWN care in our center, enabling longitudinal assessment of QOL and the evaluation of treatment strategies in the future. Finally, although all known patients were invited to participate, participation bias cannot be ruled out. However, this potential bias may plausibly act in both directions: on the one hand, patients with more severe disease manifestations may be more motivated to participate in a study such as this, while on the other hand the burden associated with study participation may conversely lead these same patients to decline involvement.
sections.conclusion: The Dutch NFTI-QOL is a reliable instrument for assessing disease-specific quality of life in Dutch speaking NF2 -SWN patients. Facial and vestibular symptoms showed strong correlations, while hearing loss was not significantly associated with quality of life. Notably, overall QOL did not differ between NF2 -SWN and sporadic vestibular schwannoma patients and patients with a sporadic (unilateral) vestibular schwannoma even reported poorer hearing-related QOL despite better objective hearing levels. This suggests that the relationship between QOL and objective physical impairment is complex and other factors play a major role.

title: Medically tailored meals receipt and healthcare utilization and costs in Massachusetts’ Medicaid demonstration
abstract: Smaller quasi-experimental studies and short-term controlled trials of medically tailored meals (MTMs) have shown health benefits for several conditions, but MTMs have not been evaluated in large-scale policy initiatives. Multiple US states are now implementing MTMs in Medicaid, the health insurance program for low-income individuals, yet their impact has not been evaluated. We investigated changes in hospitalizations, emergency department (ED) visits and healthcare costs among 1,866 MTM recipients and 1,372 comparators from 2020 to 2023 across 11 health systems in Massachusetts. Both groups met eligibility criteria for diet-related conditions and food insecurity. We used propensity overlap-weighted generalized estimating equations to compare a 6-month baseline period to the program period. MTM receipt (mean, 6.7 months) was associated with 31% fewer hospitalizations (adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) = 0.69 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.58−0.82)), 20% fewer ED visits (aIRR = 0.80 (95% CI: 0.72−0.89)) and US$3,433 lower total healthcare costs (95% CI: $−1,215 to −$5,651). Healthcare cost reductions offset 98% of the MTM program costs during the enrollment period. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses, a negative control test and a secondary comparison group. In stratified analyses, MTM receipt was net cost-saving among participants with cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, depression, diabetes or high comorbidity. This large MTM policy evaluation informs consideration of ‘food is medicine’ therapies in clinical care.

sections.main: Poor diet is a leading cause of death, disability and acute healthcare utilization globally, causing half a million deaths annually in the United States alone 1 . Healthy food access is worsened by food insecurity, a marker of financial strain or poverty reflecting inadequate access to food for a healthy and active life 2 , which is associated with poor health 3 – 5 and higher healthcare utilization 6 – 8 . ‘Food is medicine’ (FIM) interventions, which include provision of free, healthy food through clinical care, have emerged as a therapy to improve nutrition and health among patients with diet-sensitive conditions and food insecurity 9 , 10 . Many FIM programs were initially supported by philanthropy, making services challenging to scale in clinical settings. However, insurance coverage for FIM is expanding through US policy initiatives. Medicaid, the joint federal−state health insurance program for 71 million Americans with low income or disability, offers states flexibility to test whether therapeutic innovations improve health and are budget neutral through Section 1115 demonstrations 11 . In Massachusetts’ Medicaid (MassHealth) 1115 demonstration from 2017 to 2022, US$149 million was authorized for the novel Flexible Service Program (FSP), enabling newly created accountable care organizations (ACOs) to partner with social service organizations to address patient nutrition needs 12 . Although federally required evaluations of Section 1115 demonstrations in Massachusetts and North Carolina have evaluated the overall nutrition and/or housing programs 13 , 14 , the impact of MTMs, the most intensive and expensive nutrition intervention, has not been reported. MTMs are fully prepared, home-delivered meals tailored by a registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) for individuals with diet-sensitive conditions (for example, diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease) who often also have food insecurity and/or activity limitations 15 . Smaller quasi-experimental MTM evaluations and short-term trials suggest that patients with various diet-sensitive conditions who receive meals for 6 months or longer may experience better disease management, have fewer hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) admissions and have lower healthcare expenditures 16 – 19 . However, not all MTM studies have found significant reductions in healthcare utilization, in particular short-term trials testing very brief MTM programs (2−10 weeks) after hospital discharge 20 – 22 . Among 16 states with ongoing or pending Section 1115 waivers that include nutrition services 11 , 23 , Massachusetts was the first with large-scale MTM implementation, providing an important opportunity to evaluate the impact of such a program on healthcare utilization and cost. We investigated changes in hospitalizations, ED visits and healthcare costs associated with MTM receipt among all Medicaid members receiving the intervention across 11 participating ACOs. We compared recipient outcomes to those of eligible Medicaid members not receiving MTMs, accounting for sociodemographic characteristics, comorbidities and healthcare utilization prior to the program period, using multiple model specifications to test the robustness of our findings. We also conducted a negative control test, fitting similar models on time periods prior to the program period to assess whether differences between groups were observed when there was no intervention. This large quasi-experimental evaluation of MTM policy informs consideration of FIM therapies in clinical care.
sections.mtm intervention: All MTMs were provided by Community Servings 24 , a nonprofit Boston-based organization with statewide reach and the largest MTM provider in the demonstration with 11 ACO contracts. Ten meals (five lunches and five dinners) plus snacks were home delivered once per week, typically for 6 months with the possibility for renewal after clinical reassessment. Some participants were enrolled in a one-time, 3-month program created in response to the COVID-19 pandemic (2020 only), and one ACO initiated a 3-month program, typically reenrolling members (often for more than 1 year), based on provider recommendations. Meals were tailored by RDNs to address each patient’s diagnosis, comorbid conditions and dietary preferences (for example, vegetarian or soft meal options) from 15 different meal plans ( Supplementary Information ). Prior to starting services, all MTM recipients had an initial nutrition assessment and counseling session with an RDN to confirm health conditions and discuss preferences and restrictions to establish the appropriate meal plan. Participants could attend three additional counseling sessions that included nutrition education and printed materials focused on the participant’s medical conditions and goals. In practice, uptake of nutrition counseling was low: 5% of participants attended three sessions, 10% attended two, 23% attended one and 62% did not attend any additional nutritional counseling sessions. Bilingual RDNs and telephonic translation services allowed staff to communicate in the participant’s primary language. MTMs were provided for the FSP recipient only, as MassHealth was not authorized to fund meals to household members. MTM costs for all ACOs were US$125 per person per week. This is the amount paid by ACOs to comprehensively cover all of Community Servings’ program costs, including food, nutritional counseling, delivery and administrative and facility costs.
sections.baseline characteristics: Among the 1,866 adult Medicaid ACO members in the primary study sample who were enrolled in MTMs for more than 90 days, the mean (s.d.) age was 47.8 (11.6) years, 60.2% were female and 37.7% were non-Hispanic White (Table 1 ). Characteristics for the secondary population of all MTM recipients regardless of their program duration, including those receiving an emergency 90-day COVID-19 MTM program, are provided in Supplementary Table 1 . The comparison group of FSP-eligible but not enrolled food-insecure Medicaid ACO members included 1,372 adults who were slightly younger, modestly more likely to identify as non-Hispanic White and had lower prevalence of cardiometabolic conditions but similar education, employment, language, social stressors and behavioral health conditions as comparators. MTM recipients had similar baseline rates of hospitalizations and ED visits as comparators but higher mean total healthcare costs. After propensity score weighting, all baseline sociodemographics, social stressors, comorbidities and utilization values were equivalent in the two groups (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1 ). sections.association of mtms with healthcare util: After overlap propensity score weighting, MTM recipients experienced 31% fewer hospitalizations (adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) = 0.69 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.58−0.82)), 20% fewer ED visits (aIRR = 0.80 (95% CI: 0.72−0.89)) and $3,433 lower total healthcare costs (95% CI: −$1,215 to −$5,651) while receiving meals (Table 2 ). By contrast, there was no change in primary care visits between MTM recipients and comparators (aIRR = 0.99 (95% CI: 0.97−1.01)), which was consistent across secondary and stratified analyses (Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 ). Absolute risk reductions in hospitalizations for the primary population were −443 (−671 to −216) per 1,000 individuals treated and −403 (−621 to −184) per 1,000 individuals treated for ED visits (Supplementary Table 4 ). The absolute risk reductions are a function of the relative effect size associated with MTM receipt and high rates of healthcare utilization in this population. Weighted GEE models assess the change (that is, difference-in-difference) between treatment and comparison group outcome measurements during the 6 months prior to starting the FSP MTM program and during MTM enrollment. For healthcare utilization, models report IRRs. An IRR <1 indicates a reduction in healthcare utilization for MTM enrollees relative to the comparison. Statistical significance: * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001. All P values are two-sided. Findings were consistent across four sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Table 5 ), underscoring that results were robust across multiple model specifications. Findings were also consistent among an alternate comparison group of managed care organization (MCO) members with cardiometabolic conditions who were never referred to the program (FSP was available only to ACO members) (Supplementary Tables 5 and 6 ). We also conducted a negative control test that assessed changes in healthcare utilization and costs between the treatment and comparison groups during a time period in which the treatment group did not receive meals. In the negative control analyses, no significant differences were observed between the treatment and comparison groups for any outcomes (Supplementary Table 7 ), supporting our hypothesis that we would not see reductions in utilization or costs at these arbitrary timepoints outside of the MTM treatment period. Stratified analyses demonstrated similar relative reductions in hospitalizations and ED visits among MTM participants, versus comparators, who had baseline cardiovascular disease (CVD), diabetes, chronic kidney disease or depression and anxiety disorders (Table 3 ). However, given the high costs of these conditions, total healthcare cost reductions were greater among MTM recipients with these conditions, most notably CVD (−$10,450 (−$18,597 to −$2,303)) and chronic kidney disease (−$12,312 (−$23,526 to −$1,098)). Stratified by overall medical comorbidity, among those in the lowest tertile (Diagnostic Cost Group (DxCG) < 3.1), no significant reductions in healthcare utilization were evident, whereas significant reductions were observed among those in the highest tertile (DxCG > 8.4), with total healthcare cost reductions of $9,733 (−$15,505 to −$3,961) (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 2 ). In analyses stratified by COVID-19 period (2020−2021 versus 2022−2023), a larger point estimate for hospitalizations was observed in years 2022−2023 (aIRR = 0.56 (95% CI: 0.41−0.77)) than in years 2020−2021 (aIRR = 0.77 (05% CI: 0.63−0.93)), although healthcare cost reductions were similar in both time periods (Supplementary Table 3 ). No change in ED visits was observed in years 2020−2021 during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, in secondary analyses among all participants regardless of MTM program length, MTM receipt was associated with reductions in hospitalizations (aIRR = 0.74 (95% CI: 0.62−0.89)) and ED visits (aIRR = 0.82 (95% CI: 0.71−0.94)), but differences in total healthcare costs while receiving meals were not statistically significant (−$1,086 (−$3,000 to $826)) (Supplementary Table 8 ). Colored bars represent the mean per-person healthcare cost reductions stratified by level of medical morbidity. Error bars represent 95% CIs for the difference in the change in healthcare costs between the MTM treatment group and the comparison group. n = 629 (treatment) and n = 457 (comparison) for the first tertile; n = 629 (treatment) and n = 457 (comparison) for the second tertile; n = 628 (treatment) and n = 456 (comparison) for the third tertile. DxCG scores are routinely used by MassHealth in managed care risk adjustment and report total medical morbidity scores, with higher scores signifying higher medical morbidity. In this study population, the first tertile is defined as DxCG < 3.1; the second tertile as 3.1 ≤ DxCG ≤ 8.4; and the third tertile as DxCG > 8.4. Estimates for healthcare cost reductions associated with MTM receipt are generated from GEEs with overlap weights created from propensity scores. The propensity score model included member demographics, social risk indicators, prior health care utilization, diagnostic history and random effect for referral ACO. Two-sided P value for change in healthcare costs in the third tertile of medical morbidity was <0.001. Two-sided P value for changes in healthcare costs for the first and second tertiles was >0.05.
sections.discussion: In this analysis of Massachusetts’ Medicaid Section 1115 demonstration, 1,866 adults receiving MTMs for at least 3 months had 31% fewer hospitalizations and 20% fewer ED visits than 1,372 eligible but not enrolled adults. Total per-person healthcare costs among MTM recipients declined by $3,433 during enrollment over an approximately 7-month period. Reductions in healthcare costs offset 98% of MTM costs ($3,512 per person), resulting in total net costs of only $14.90 per person per month during the active program period. Higher cost reductions and substantial net cost savings were observed among participants with CVD, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, depression or greater overall comorbidities. No difference was observed in primary care visits, indicating continued engagement with routine clinical care and lower likelihood of confounding in primary outcomes by overall reduced healthcare engagement among MTM recipients. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses, comparison groups and negative control time periods. These findings have clinical and policy implications for innovations in health insurance coverage of MTMs to address diet-related diseases and healthcare costs. Thirteen US states have approved Medicaid Section 1115 demonstrations to implement FIM programs, including MTMs, and three US states have waivers pending federal approval 11 , 25 . Our results support the potential for substantial health gains with MTMs targeted to similar populations at essentially no overall net cost and large net savings for particular Medicaid populations with high-risk conditions. Reductions in healthcare utilization and costs occurred over an approximately 7-month period while individuals were receiving MTMs, underscoring rapid improvements in health. In secondary analyses of all individuals receiving MTMs, including those receiving MTMs for ≤90 days, reductions in hospitalizations and ED visits were still identified, but changes in total healthcare costs were smaller and not statistically significant. In other contexts, healthcare utilization has not been reduced in short-term trials testing brief (2−10-week) MTM programs after hospital discharge 20 – 22 . Overall, this suggests that longer enrollment periods may be more likely to be associated with healthcare cost reductions. We cannot confirm meal adherence because we lacked dietary data. However, a randomized controlled trial of a similar meal service by the same organization, Community Servings, found significant improvements in dietary quality and food security among MTM recipients with diabetes and food insecurity 26 . Likely, participants in our study experienced similar dietary improvements as they received a nearly identical meal program (additionally, half of our study population also had diabetes). MTM program start and end dates were anchored on actual delivery dates, and all meals were home delivered once weekly, ensuring that participants received food. Finally, because comparators did not receive nutritional counseling, effects should be interpreted as a joint effect of healthy food delivery and nutrition counseling, although there is evidence that supplemental nutritional counseling within FIM programs may have little added benefit on health outcomes 20 , 27 , and uptake of nutritional counseling was low in our study. Recent Medicaid Section 1115 demonstrations have generally included multiple interventions to address social needs and improve health, including nutrition, housing and transportation supports. Healthy food access is unique among these in being both a social determinant of health and a direct, biological determinant of health that modulates disease pathways through improved nutrition. Observed improvements in healthcare utilization and costs among MTM recipients are likely attributable to multiple causal pathways: better nutrition by medical tailoring of meals by dietitians 26 , improved food security and fewer financial tradeoffs between food and other urgent needs such as rent or utilities 28 , 29 , more stable mental health 16 , 28 , 29 and greater medication adherence 17 . Our study was not designed to tease out these causal pathways, and results likely reflect a combination of interconnected factors. Our findings align with results from North Carolina’s Medicaid Section 1115 demonstration, which found that provision of nutrition services (including some MTMs but primarily food boxes with raw ingredients) and housing navigation assistance to over 14,000 Medicaid members were associated with net cost savings by 8 months after enrollment 14 . The food-insecure Medicaid population in North Carolina had some differences from our sample, with more participants living in rural areas, identifying as non-Hispanic Black and having lower healthcare costs. Together, these studies, implemented in different contexts and populations, strengthen the evidence that innovations targeting food insecurity and nutrition can reduce acute healthcare utilization and thus improve member well-being in meaningful ways. It also suggests that our findings could be generalizable to other state Medicaid programs outside of Massachusetts. Our findings support the need to test MTM and other FIM interventions in additional contexts. FIM trials are being conducted in Australia and China, and hospital-based MTMs are being provided in Rwanda, where therapeutic nutrition may help address the double burden of malnutrition 30 . In Switzerland, a trial testing an intensive hospital-based nutrition program for patients with heart failure with malnutrition found reductions in mortality and major cardiovascular events 31 . Further clinical and implementation research is needed to determine effects of FIM in different national contexts, particularly given global trends toward increasing non-communicable chronic diseases, greater medical spending, rural disinvestment and health disparities. Limitations in our approach should be considered. First, because receipt of MTMs was not randomly allocated, selection bias is possible. Comparisons of MTM recipients with eligible members who did not enroll may overstate effects if unmeasured differences in health-seeking behaviors drove enrollment decisions among MTM recipients. Additional unmeasured differences could bias findings in either direction. Similar results from the secondary comparison group of MCO members who were never screened or referred to FSP support our primary findings because this sensitivity analysis protects against selection bias related to FSP uptake. The analysis with MCO comparators focused on the prominent diet-related conditions in the treatment group (a strength), yet these comparators may have less social risk because we could not confirm food insecurity among MCO Medicaid members (a limitation). Second, most participant characteristics were similar between MTM participants and comparators, although unweighted differences show that comparators were slightly younger and had lower rates of cardiometabolic illness. However, all weighted characteristics were equivalent. To account for potential confounding, we employed overlap propensity score weights that balanced sociodemographics, social risk factors, medical comorbidities, ACO sites, concurrent enrollment in other Section 1115 demonstration programs and preceding (baseline) healthcare utilization and costs. Results were robust across several sensitivity analyses and a negative control test with different analytical approaches, each with complementary strengths, limitations and assumptions, underscoring that our findings are not dependent on our primary modeling choice. Third, although exact start and end dates were available for most participants, a minority (<5%) had their start dates estimated with quarters of enrollment provided by MassHealth. Fourth, we evaluated MTMs provided by an established nonprofit organization with a commitment to community and high-quality nutrition standards serving a high-risk population 32 ; results may be less favorable with a lower-quality program or among healthier patients with less social and economic adversity. Finally, due to the substantial time required for claims and encounters adjudications, at this time we could not assess if there were any lasting effects after the program ended as these data are not yet available. If healthcare cost reductions among MTM recipients were to continue after the program ends, then the meal services could be even more cost-effective. In conclusion, a large MTM program embedded in a major US health insurance program was associated with significant reductions in hospitalizations, ED visits and total healthcare costs among adults with diet-sensitive medical conditions and food insecurity, informing consideration of FIM therapies in clinical care.
sections.study design and setting: We used a propensity score weighted, difference-in-difference analysis of adult MassHealth members with one or more complex medical conditions and food insecurity comparing participants who received MTMs versus those who did not receive MTMs. Our study period spans the MTM program launch in January 2020 (coinciding with the COVID-19 outbreak) through March 2023, the end of MassHealth’s first FSP contract period with ACOs within the 1115 demonstration. Medicaid administrative data from 2019−2023, including eligibility, claims and encounters, were linked with member characteristics collected by 11 ACOs in FSP administrative data and enrollment data from Community Servings 24 , the major provider of MTMs in the demonstration. This study was determined to be ‘not human subjects research’ by the UMass Chan Medical School institutional review board (IRB) and the Tufts Health Sciences IRB because it was part of the independent evaluation of MassHealth’s Section 1115 demonstration, required by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. As such, the need for ethical approval for this study was waived.
sections.study population: Eligibility for demonstration nutrition programs, including MTMs, required ACO enrollment, age under 65 years, experiencing food insecurity and meeting at least one of five health needs-based criteria: (1) behavioral health diagnosis; (2) complex physical diagnosis such as diabetes or CVD; (3) high ED utilization; (4) high-risk pregnancy; or (5) limited activities of daily living or instrumental activities of daily living 33 . Additional eligibility details are provided in the Supplementary Information . The treatment group comprised individuals who received at least one MTM delivery, with program start at the first meal delivery (start date) and end at the last meal delivery (end date). MTM program dates were obtained from Community Servings data for eight of 11 ACOs that signed data-sharing agreements for this analysis. For the remaining three ACOs, MassHealth provided calendar year quarters of MTM program period, from which start and end dates were defined as the mid-points of the first and last quarter of enrollment (impacting 82 individuals (4.4%) of the treatment group). Comparators were adult ACO members screened eligible for nutrition FSP who received no such services. MassHealth administrative records document reasons for not receiving services as (1) lost contact during referral process ( n = 736, 53.6%); (2) declined services ( n = 447, 32.6%); (3) left ACO or moved ( n = 33, 2.4%); and (4) other ( n = 174, 12.7%). ACO members in the comparison group were assigned the paired start and end dates of a randomly selected MTM recipient, stratified by the year in which study MTM recipients and comparators were screened as food-insecure to align with their period of FSP eligibility. Randomization created equivalent observation times between the treatment and comparison groups, in addition to balance across calendar years to account for secular trends during the study period. We required all participants to have at least 6 months of MassHealth coverage before their start date and at least 3 months of MassHealth coverage after their start date to be included in the analyses. Pandemic-related policy changes made maintaining Medicaid coverage easier for members during our study period, and overall MassHealth coverage churn was low at less than 3% annually 34 . Our primary analysis focused on members receiving at least 3 months (>90 days) of MTMs, due to evidence that briefer durations may be insufficient to impact healthcare utilization 20 , 21 , because 3 months was the shortest program hypothesized by ACOs to improve utilization and to exclude participants receiving a temporary, shorter COVID-19 relief program. Secondary analyses retained all participants regardless of MTM program lengths. Randomization of comparators’ program dates was conducted once for the primary population enrolled >90 days (treatment n = 1,866; comparison n = 1,372) and again for the secondary population (treatment n = 2,882; comparison n = 1,400). The slight difference in comparison group sample size is due to requiring sufficient MassHealth coverage before and after the randomly assigned start date.
sections.outcomes: Medicaid claims and encounters data provided access to utilization and cost outcomes for study participants across Massachusetts, regardless of where they sought care. Co-primary outcomes included changes in unplanned hospitalizations (excluding planned and elective surgeries), ED admissions and total healthcare costs. These were operationalized using measure definitions and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) code sets consistent with quality measures used by MassHealth performance accountability for ACOs 35 . Healthcare costs reflect paid amounts from all adjudicated claims. An ED visit that led to a hospital admission was counted as a hospitalization only to avoid double-counting outcomes. We examined primary care visits as a secondary outcome, hypothesizing that MTMs would reduce acute healthcare use but not primary care use. A reduction in primary care visits could also suggest reduced engagement with primary care (generally not considered beneficial for health).
sections.covariates: We modeled a comprehensive set of sociodemographics, social risk factors, clinical conditions and prior utilization data that could represent potential sources of confounding. Covariates were measured using MassHealth claims data and FSP administrative data. Sociodemographics included age at enrollment, sex, race/ethnicity, employment, education, primary language and referring ACO. Social stressors included Neighborhood Stress Score-7 (ref. 36 ) (an area-level measure of socioeconomic stress based on address), tobacco use, alcohol abuse, substance use disorder, homelessness, housing insecurity and disability status (eligibility for Medicaid due to disability or being a client of the Department of Mental Health or the Department of Developmental Services). Clinical conditions were derived from ICD-10-CM codes going back 1 year prior to participants’ start dates and included 24 diagnoses selected to reflect FSP eligibility (Table 1 ). We also used ICD-10-CM codes to calculate total medical morbidity risk scores, including based on diagnoses (DxCG) 37 and prescription dispensing (RxCG) 38 , anchored on the year prior to each participant’s start date. These risk scores were developed for, and are routinely used by, MassHealth in risk adjustment for managed care payment. Finally, baseline healthcare utilization in the 6 months prior to MTM enrollment included hospitalizations, ED visits, total healthcare costs and primary care visits. All study participants could receive FSP housing services, including housing search and navigation assistance, one-time provision for rental deposits or moving costs or home modifications such as filters or air conditioning units for members with asthma. They could also enroll in the Community Partners Program 39 , which collaborates with community-based organizations to provide care management and coordination to Medicaid members with substantial behavioral health needs, addiction and/or long-term care needs. Analyses accounted for concurrent enrollment in FSP housing services and Community Partners programs.
sections.statistical methods: To address potential confounding due to selection bias, we first created propensity score overlap weights. Propensity score models incorporated all aforementioned covariates as predictors of MTM treatment using a generalized linear mixed model with a binomial link and random intercept for members’ ACO to account for clustering 40 . Using these propensity scores, overlap weights were calculated in which MTM recipients were assigned a weight equal to 1 minus their propensity score, and comparators were assigned a weight equal to their propensity score. This achieves balance between treatment and comparison groups on all covariates included in the propensity score (Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 1 and 6 ) and emphasizes study participants equally likely to be in either the treatment group or the comparison group, mimicking a key attribute of clinical trials 41 . Overlap weights overcome shortcomings of other propensity score approaches such as matching, which can reduce sample sizes, or inverse probability of treatment weights, which can emphasize outliers and bias results 41 . MTM program effects were estimated using difference-in-difference models comparing changes between MTM recipients and comparators from a 6-month baseline period to the MTM program period (see Supplementary Figs. 1 – 3 for parallel trends assessment). All outcomes were top-coded at the 99.5th percentile. We used overlap-weighted, generalized estimating equation (GEE) models with a negative binomial link for counts of inpatient hospitalizations, ED visits and primary care visits and an identity link for healthcare costs. In each analysis, the variable of interest was the interaction term quantifying the difference in change (from the baseline to the MTM program period) for MTM participants in contrast to the change for the comparison group. Weighted GEE models did not adjust for covariates already included in the propensity scores but did adjust for MTM program length. GEE models employed an independent correlation structure accounting for multiple measurements (one baseline measurement and one program measurement per participant). All analyses were conducted in Stata version 19 software. We evaluated stratified analyses by clinically relevant subgroups by having (1) CVD, diabetes and chronic kidney disease because these conditions have causal nutritional pathways and their clinical management is highly sensitive to diet; (2) depression and anxiety disorders, because these were common FSP eligibility criteria and food insecurity is associated with worse mental health; and (3) overall morbidity score (DxCG) by tertiles of risk. We also performed analyses stratified by calendar year of enrollment (2020−2021 and 2022−2023), given the coincidence of the FSP launch with the COVID-19 emergency in early 2020. Propensity scores were recalculated and overlap weighting was repeated for each subgroup analysis. We conducted several sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our findings to different model assumptions. First, an unadjusted, unweighted GEE model produced crude effect estimates. Second, an unweighted GEE model that adjusted for covariates tested differences between propensity score weights and covariate adjustment. Third, alternate propensity score weights were created, excluding baseline outcome measures, testing whether regression to the mean could have been introduced by including baseline values of outcome variables, which may occur if baseline values differ meaningfully between treatment and comparison groups 42 . Fourth, we evaluated a secondary comparison group drawn from Medicaid MCO enrollees who were ineligible for FSP and were never screened or referred to the program. This group included Medicaid members aged 18−64 years with hypertension, diabetes, CVD or chronic kidney disease, reflecting the most common diet-related conditions in the MTM group (77% of the treatment group had at least one of these conditions). This analysis included clinically similar study participants as only treatment and secondary comparison group members with major cardiometabolic conditions were included. However, food insecurity screening data were not available in the MCO population (100% of the treatment group had food insecurity); therefore, the secondary comparators may have experienced less social risk than the primary comparison group. However, these secondary comparators were not prone to potential selection bias correlated to program uptake. Finally, we conducted a negative control test by fitting similar models on time periods prior to the actual baseline and intervention periods for the primary analysis. Specifically, we compared changes in outcomes between the treatment and comparison groups in months 12−7 prior to the true baseline period (that is, negative control baseline period) and in months 6−1 prior to the true baseline period (that is, negative control program period). These arbitrary periods did not overlap with MTM receipt or the baseline period of our study; thus, we hypothesized that this analysis would not show significant differences in outcomes during this time.

title: Pediatric pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of guanabenz for the treatment of vanishing white matter
abstract: Vanishing White Matter (VWM) is a leukodystrophy with cystic cerebral white matter degeneration, resulting in neurological decline and premature death. There is currently no treatment. Guanabenz, a central α 2 -adrenergic receptor agonist, ameliorates the disease in VWM mouse models. We aimed to evaluate the validity of a translational guanabenz pediatric pharmacokinetic model, to explore the concentration-toxicity association, and to estimate brain guanabenz concentrations using a biomarker of biological effect and toxicity. Translational modelling was performed to determine the potentially effective guanabenz dose. During a phase 1/2 clinical trial for pediatric VWM patients, this model was evaluated and the correlation between guanabenz concentrations and side-effects was explored. Translating rodent PK/PD models and adult PK models, the estimated pediatric target dose of guanabenz was 2 mg/kg/d, with a minimum effective dose of 1 mg/kg/d and a maximum of 10 mg/kg/d. PK modelling was performed with 32 trial participants, aged 2.4–12.9 years. Evaluation of the translational model showed an underprediction with a median prediction error of -50% with oral doses between 1.04 and 1.68 mg/kg/d. Hallucinations were an unexpected side-effect. A trend was seen in the correlation between the decrease in mean arterial blood pressure and hallucinations. The developed translational model was able to predict plasma concentrations within acceptable range of 2-fold prediction error. The plasma concentrations reached were above the predicted minimal effective dose. Hallucinations were a dose limiting adverse event and the predicted optimal dose may have been underestimated. Blood pressure may be useful as a non-invasive biomarker in future studies. This clinical trial was registered under number: 2017-001438-25 on 28/11/2018. sections.introduction: Vanishing White Matter (VWM) is a leukodystrophy that most often presents in children between two and six years of age 1 – 4 . It causes cystic degeneration of the cerebral white matter, leading to motor and cognitive decline and premature death 4 . The disease course and age at death are extremely variable, with age of onset as best predictive variable of disease course, especially in very early onset 4 . Currently, there is no approved therapy for this severe disease. VWM is caused by pathogenic variants in the genes EIF2B1-5, encoding the 5 subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B) 5 , 6 . eIF2B is conditional for mRNA translation per se and central in regulating the rate of mRNA translation and protein synthesis. It is pivotal to downregulate protein synthesis upon activation of the integrated stress response (ISR). Various types of physiological stress activate enzymes that phosphorylate initiation factor eIF2, which then inactivates eIF2B, activating its downstream targets and inhibiting protein synthesis 7 – 11 . A feedback loop in the ISR via stress-induced growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible protein (GADD34) restores eIF2B activity and reduces ISR activation. In VWM, pathogenic variants in eIF2B reduce its activity, leading to constitutive activation of the downstream ISR. In mouse models for VWM, the degree of ISR activation correlates with severity of clinical disease and white matter pathology. Inhibition of ISR with the eIF2B activator ISRIB resulted in improvements in neuropathology and motor skills in these VWM mice 12 . We therefore postulated that the abnormal activation of the ISR plays a central role in VWM pathophysiology and that the ISR is potential target for treatment of VWM 12 . Guanabenz is a central acting α 2 -adrenergic receptor agonist, which has been trialed and registered in 1973–1983 as a treatment for hypertension in adults. Additionally, it has a known effect on GADD34 in the ISR. We showed in VWM mice that guanabenz reduces ISR activation and ameliorates the clinical disease and brain pathology 1 , 13 . A clinical trial was, therefore, initiated in pediatric patients with VWM. Guanabenz is lipophilic drug that is well absorbed (75%) after oral administration. The Cmax is observed around 2–5 h after a single oral dose. Guanabenz is 90% bound to plasma proteins is metabolized via CYP1A2 and passes the blood brain barrier via passive transport. No data on guanabenz were available for the pediatric population. Translational pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) modelling was performed to determine the safe and potentially effective doses of guanabenz for children. This PKPD model was then used to design the dosing schedule and PK-sampling in the phase 1/2 clinical trial, which investigates the safety, tolerability and efficacy of guanabenz in children with VWM. The PKPD aims of this currently ongoing trial were to evaluate the validity of the translational guanabenz pediatric PK-model, to explore the concentration-toxicity association and, to assess the possibility of estimating the guanabenz concentration in the brain using an early non-invasive biomarker of biological effect and toxicity. For the latter, blood pressure measurements were chosen, as guanabenz’ antihypertensive effect is due to binding to α 2 -adrenergic receptors in the brain 14 . Thus, the relationship between guanabenz and the decrease in blood pressure was investigated.
sections.trial and patricipants: The trial is an ongoing open-label single-center study at the University Medical Center Amsterdam in children with DNA-confirmed VWM with onset ≤6 years and disease duration ≤8 years, with approval of the Dutch Central Ethics Committee (CCMO) ( https://www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ctr-search/trial/2017-001438-25/NL ) and written informed consent from the participant’s parents or legal guardians. Each participant’s age, body weight, body temperature, heart rate and blood pressure were recorded during the trial. Side-effects and adverse events were recorded and severity graded, applying NCI CTCAE version 5.0.
sections.dosing and sampling: On the first day of the trial, VWM patients were administered approximately 0.5 mg/kg guanabenz in oral capsules: approximately 5-fold higher than the adult 4 mg BID antihypertensive starting dose 21 . Subsequently, doses were given once daily in the evening to minimize possible guanabenz’s sedative effects during the day. Under daily clinical supervision, the dose was titrated upwards in 1 mg/kg increments every three days or smaller increments over a longer period if mild or moderate side effects occurred. Alternatively, doses were administered twice daily if better tolerated. The dose titration ended if the maximum individual tolerated dose or the maximum dose, determined by translational analysis was reached (Fig. 1 a) For the pharmacokinetic analysis, once a year venous samples were taken at time points of just before and 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, and 12 h after administration of Guanabenz. Additionally, dried blood spot (DBS) samples of 30µL each were taken annually on the same day as the venous sampling before intake and 2 and 3 h after, as well as every three months just before and occasionally 2 h after administration (Fig. 1 b). Per protocol, full PK-sampling, was performed in 15 patients with a body weight below 15 kg and in 15 with a body weight of 15 kg and higher. After completion of these cohorts, PK-sampling was minimized. The pharmacodynamic properties of guanabenz were assessed through adverse events, diastolic and systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and body temperature, which were measured frequently during periods of pharmacokinetic assessment and the drug titration. Fig. 1 Design of the translation modeling and phase 1/2 study.
sections.bioanalytical method: The DBS and venous samples were analyzed using a validated LC-MS/MS method in an ISO-certified pharmaceutical laboratory at the Amsterdam University Medical Centre. The lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) of this method was 0.1 µg/L and the upper limit was 500 µg/L. The between-day coefficient of variation percentage (CV%) was less than 11.4%. Agreement between DBS and plasma concentrations was evaluated using linear modelling. Additional covariates of age, body weight, height, sex, time after dose, and lag time between the sampling times of both sampling types were evaluated in a stepwise fashion. A resulting model and its predicting variables were considered significant if the p-value of ANOVA’s F-test, compared to the null or parent model, was lower than the α-level of 0.05. The final model’s structure was thereafter incorporated into the pharmacokinetic analysis to assess both sampling types’ data simultaneously.
sections.pharmacokinetic modelling: A population pharmacokinetic analysis was conducted using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling with NONMEM ® (version 7.4.2, ICON PLC, Dublin, Ireland) with first-order conditional estimation (FOCE-I), supported by Pirana (version 3.0.0, Certara, Princeton, NJ, USA). SCM and bootstrap analysis were conducted using Perl-speaks-NONMEM (version 5.3.0, Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden). Data processing and graphical imaging of data were performed in R (version 4.2.1, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with Rstudio (version 2022.02.3, Rstudio, Boston, MA, USA) and the ggplot2 and cowplot packages. Linear modeling of PK data was done in R using the stats package and visualized with the ggfortify package. Prediction-corrected visual predictive checks were generated in R with the vpc package. The Kaplan-Meier analysis and visualization were performed in R using the survival and survminer packages. For the translational modelling animal the effective and toxic doses from literature 13 , 22 were translated to brain AUC values using previously described data in rodents studies 15 , 17 . This was then comibned with human adult data combined to predict the PK profile and accumulation of Guanabenz in the brain in children with VWM at clinical doses (Figs. 1 and 2 ) 19 .The animal PK-data were extracted from 2 preclinical models using a plot extractor tool 15 , 17 . Parameter estimation was performed using NONMEM ® (version 7.4.2, ICON PLC, Dublin, Ireland) with first-order conditional estimation (FOCE-I), supported by Pirana (version 3.0.0, Certara, Princeton, NJ, USA). To evaluate the accuracy of the model, goodness-of-fit plots PRED vs. observed and CWRES vs. time were made. R (4.3.2) was used with Rstudio (2023.12.1.402) for data processing and visualization. For the model building, one- and two-compartment models were compared to determine which structural model best described the guanabenz PK. Afterwards, inter-individual variability (IIV) on each of the model’s parameters was assessed in a stepwise matter and residual variability was assessed in both additive, proportional and combined error models. The detailed description of model development and evaluation can be found in the supplementary methods. Fig. 2 Translational model used to predict brain AUC values in children. With effective and toxic doses derived from studies by Tribouillard-Tanvier ( d ) et al. and Witkamp et al. ( e ) translated using mouse PK and KPT and RPT values values derived from the rodent studies by Vieira et al. ( a ) and Meacham et al. ( b ) and the adults PK parameters derived from Lasseter et al. ( c ) 13 , 15 , 17 , 19 , 22 .
sections.pharmacodynamic analysis: Sequential PKPD analyses were used to investigate the concentration-response relationships. The PK profile of each individual for the entire study’s duration was simulated by using the dose adjustment logs and the final individual’s PK parameter estimates. Subsequently, the concentration-toxicity relationship was analyzed and compared to adult data to estimate the PD translation.
sections.translational model development: To approximate the observed mouse and rat pharmacokinetic data in plasma 6 , 11 , linear compartmental models were applied to the median of the observed plasma PK data Both rat and mice plasma PK-data showed a bilinear shape, indicating the presence of a distribution and a terminal phase, characteristic of a two-compartment model. Initially, the PK parameters for mice were allometrically scaled from the estimated rat PK parameter values. However, this shows an underprediction of the observed concentrations in mice. Therefore, parameter estimation was done in NONMEM. For the initial estimations preclinical PK parameters from rodents (mouse and rat) as well as from adult patients were scaled to paedicatric PK as described in Table 1 . Simulations were performed for a number of doses (0.25 mg/kg/day–10 mg/kg/week) and the predicted guanabenz concentrations and AUC ss in both plasma and brain compartments are summarized in supplemental Table 1 .
sections.translational pkpd analysis: The developed two-compartment model showed adequate predictions of the plasma and brain concentration time profile (AUC and Cmax) in both mice and rats, when compared with data after a single dose of 32 and 100 µg/kg in rats, and 10 mg/kg in mice (Supplemental Fig. 2 ) 15 , 17 . These models were therefore used for further simulation purposes. 2 mg/kg and 4.5 mg/kg daily doses were effective in previous tissue and mouse models 13 ), and produced predicted brain AUC ss of 7.71 mg*h/L and 17.36 mg*h/L respectively. Simulations were performed with the current pediatric model for children 3 years of age (supplemental Figs. 3 and 4 ), which showed steady state concentrations much higher in brain than in plasma. A predicted brain AUC ss of 8.5 mg*h/L is reached with a daily dose of 1 mg/kg, and a brain AUC of 17.1 is reached with a dose of 2 mg/kg (Supplemental Table 1 ). The latter dose was therefore estimated as target dose and 1 mg/kg daily as minimum effective dose. Additional simulations were done for children of ages 2, 5, and 10 years, which showed a decrease of Cmax in the brain with increasing age. (Supplemental Figs. 3 and 4 ). Rodent studies showed acute toxicity at dosages of 40 mg/kg 22 . At similar plasma AUC, a daily dose of 10 mg/kg was estimated to be the maximum dose in children. In conclusion, these analyses suggested 2 mg/kg as target dose, with a minimal dose of 1 mg/kg and maximum of 10 mg/kg (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Predicted plasma pharmacokinetics in mice associated with beneficial results and corresponding predicted dose-exposure in children, suggesting a minimum effective dose of 1 mg/kg and an optimal dose of 2 mg/kg. This figure shows the predicted Guanabenz range at steady state in terms of AUC in brain (left) or plasma (right) (Y-axis) at once daily dosing in mg/kg (X-axis). The predicted pediatric plasma and brain AUC in children, with allometrically scaled parameters from adults 19 is shown with the solid dark grey line; The predicted pediatric AUC with allometrically scaled parameters from rodents is depicted in dashed grey lines; The predicted AUC in mice and rats are depicted with dotdashed, and dotted lines, respectively. sections.pharmacokinetic sample analysis results: The Guanabenz PK dataset comprised 521 measurements, of which 56 were below the LLOQ of 0.1 µg/L, all but one taken before the patients received the first guanabenz dose and therefore omitted from the analysis. The remaining 466 consisted of 190 and 138 venous samples from the titration phase and year 1 sampling, respectively. For the DBS samples, 90 were taken at baseline, 24 at 1 year, and a total of 79 in the 3-monthly sampling times. For the validation of DBS measurements, a total of 84 venous measurements were matched to DBS measurements at similar sampling times, where the median difference in time (range) was 0.12 (−0.45–0.67) hours (supplemental Figure S5 A). DBS concentrations correlated linearly with venous concentrations, with a correction factor of 0.78 ( p <.001 compared to 1, adjusted R 2 = 0.9832). No other covariate resulted in a significant improvement. This analysis shows that DBS measurements could serve as a valuable addition to the PK dataset and its analysis as they reflected the venous measurements well, albeit with the following considerations. The diagnostic plots’ residuals (supplemental Figure S5 B) indicated increased variability in DBS samples. DBS samples were taken at home by parents or legal guardians, and the absence of hematocrit measurements to normalize the DBS measurements may explain the additional variability. Therefore, all population PK model predictions including DBS samples were optimized by adding a parameter for the ratio between the two sampling types, and two separate error models.
sections.pharmacokinetic modeling: The model developed using only rodent PK data showed a prediction error of 100% when extrapolating to children. By extrapolating adult PK parameters an overall under-prediction of the measured concentrations (Fig. 4 C) was observed, with a median PE% of −50.0, within the defined limits (Table 1 ) 28 . For the population PK model, the structural model that best described the data was a one-compartment model with a first-order absorption rate (K a ) and CL. A two-compartment model was not able to be adequately fitted to the data, giving relative standard error percentages (RSE%) for the peripheral volume and inter-compartmental clearance parameter estimates in excess of 100%. The model that best described the RUV was a proportional error model for both venous and DBS measurement types. The following IIVs were incorporated, in the following order, on CL (∆OFV = −117.7), V (∆OFV = −68.1), and K a (∆OFV=−7.81). The subsequent SCM showed body weight to be a significant covariate of CL (∆OFV=−18.12, p <.001) and V (∆OFV=−36.2, p <.001). The parameter estimates of the final PK model can be seen in Table 1 . PcVPCs and goodness-of-fit plots (Fig. 4 A,B) showed that the parameter estimates and corresponding IIVs were able to describe the PK data well and could explain its variability. The final model’s predictions showed a median PE% of −4.5. The original adult extrapolated PK parameters of CL, V, and K a were within the 95% CI of the final PK-parameters. Likewise, the allometric scaling exponents showed to be adequately within the 95% CI, with the exponent for body weight on V being near the lower range. Fig. 4 Plots for evaluation of the final population PK model’s fit. Consisting of pcVPCs ( n = 250) with the venous measurements of the baseline and year one sampling period (A) and diagnostic plots of all measurements (B). pcVPCs of the simulation ( n = 250) with the extrapolated adult guanabenz parameters (C).
sections.mean arterial pressure modelling: We hypothesized that mean arterial pressure could be an early non-invasive biomarker of biological effect and toxicity, if the MAP associated with the central adverse events incidence observed in children. If this hypothesis is correct, MAP may be suitable as a biomarker for guanabenz brain concentrations. First, MAP was modeled using a dataset consisting of 2106 systolic and diastolic blood pressures during the titration phase. For the structural model, the concentration-response relationship was best described by the E max function. Thereafter, the addition of an effect compartment (∆OFV=−26,806 and an exposure-driven tolerance through EC 50 (∆OFV = −104.3) significantly improved the model (combined ∆OFV=−422.008) compared to the base model. Following this, IIVs were assigned on the following parameters: EC 50,BL (∆OFV=−61.5) and the effect compartment’s rate constant, k e (∆OFV=−58.4). The final PD model’s parameter estimates are shown in Table 3 . The pcVPCs (Fig. 5 ), showed a good fit to the data, although the variability was under-explained. They also showed a decrease in effect after several days of guanabenz intake, albeit partly due to sparse sampling during the time point of maximum effect. The goodness-of-fit plots (Fig. 5 B) overall supported the model’s fit, although they did show predictions with high CWRES. sections.discussion: In this study, we showed that by using rodent and adult PK/PD data, we were able to adequately derive an possible effective dose for a phase 1 clinical trial of guanabenz in children with VMW. Observed concentrations were less than two-fold higher than those predicted on basis of the adult model. During the clinical trial the potentially minimal effective dose was reached in all patients through dose titration, but the potentially optimal dose of 2 mg/kg was not reached, due to off target toxicity. The occurrence of tolerance prevents the use of MAP as biomarker for long-term response, but a trend was observed of early onset hypotensive drug effects and risk of hallucinations future dose. Further concentration-efficacy and -toxicity analyses are needed to evaluate the balance between efficacy and toxicity and may guide further treatment optimization. The fact that toxicity was seen at a dose below the predicted optimal dose may indicate that brain concentrations in children were underpredicted, even though we corrected for the difference in brain mass between rodents, humans and children specific. Guanabenz is passively transported into the brain and we know from literature that PS values for these drugs are conserved between species 18 . This means that the permeability-surface area product (PS) for passive diffusion is conserved when adjusted for differences in brain microvascular endothelial surface area across species. As this PS value is expressed as ml/min/g tissue we performed additional analysis correcting for the brain weight of children with different ages. However, this does not take into account structural differences in lipophilicity of the brain between species. In fact in humans, white matter account for around half of the total brain mass while this is only around 10% in mice 29 ” Guanabenz is a lipophilic drug and human brains have much more white matter than rodents, which could result in accumulation of guanabenz in the human compared to the rodent brain. As a result, it is possible that we underpredicted brain concentrations in humans, particularly in this pediatric population, leading to a lower-than-anticipated effective dose. This may also have contributed to the unexpected occurrence of hallucinations, which limited the use of higher doses in children. Direct measurements of brain concentrations in children are not feasible, therefore we evaluated if MAP could be used as a non-invasive biomarker for guanabenz brain concentrations. To this end we developed a population PD model and explored its correlation with the occurrence of hallucinations. This PD model consisted of an E MAX concentration-response relationship, an effect compartment, and a tolerance component. The effect compartment was warranted as the time point of the maximum decrease in MAP followed after the time point of the maximum guanabenz concentration. Tolerance was best described by increasing EC 50 , not by decreasing E MAX . This was primarily due to the fact that while the dosages were titrated upwards, the effect size remained stable and the effect duration did not increase. The effect duration remained below 24 h, so a persistent effect was not observed as C trough increased. The tolerance might be attributed to the homeostatic regulation in response to the altered hemodynamics 30 , 31 or by downregulation of α2-adrenergic receptors with spare receptors, as with spare receptors the decrease in the amount of available receptors decreases the EC 50 , while the E MAX can remain largely unaffected 32 – 34 . The occurrence of tolerance prevents the use of MAP as biomarker for long-term response. However, the PD model used to associate the individual hypotensive drug effects with the occurrence of hallucinations. In this small dataset, a rapid decrease in MAP appeared to trend toward an increased risk of hallucinations. Further investigation is needed to determine whether early MAP changes could serve as a biomarker for toxicity. Our modeling approach has some limitations. First of all although the prediction error was within the defined limits for pediatric studies it was still relatively large considering that enzyme ontogeny should not play a major role especially as guanabenz is metabolized via CYP1A2 which matures before the age of 2. This may be explained by the fact that that the literature on pharmacokinetics of guanabenz is very limited. The study that was used for the extrapolation was the study of Lasseter et al. from 1984 which analyzed the pharmacokinetics of guanabenz in 20 patients, of which 10 had liver insufficiency. Therefore the adult PK was based only on 10 adult patients who received a lower dose. However by re-estimating the model we have been able to accurately describe the PK of guanabenz in children. However it should be noted that the youngest patient in our study was 2 years of age. At this age the blood brain barrier permeability as well as the metabolic route of guanbenz (via CYP1A2) has matured, as a result our findings cannot be readily extrapolated to younger children 35 , 36 . In addition in the PK translation only age with respect to brain mass was implemented, but no other adjustments were performed for species or disease state. This may have affected the results since the amount of white matter may influence the brain concentrations of guanabenz due to its high lipophilicity. Future research should try to take this into account by incorporating this effect possibly by the use of MRI data. Another limitation of our study is that only total concentrations were measured while guanabenz is highly protein bound, with about 90%. However there is no information available about interspecies variability in protein binding of guanabenz, and all available literature is on total concentrations. Furtheremore, it is important to note that because VWM is a rare disease the population size was very small. As a result analysis to determine covariates are likely to be underpowered and only trends could be observed. Finally, the hematocrit values of DBS samples were not measured and the measured guanabenz concentrations could therefore not be normalized with a standard hematocrit value 37 , 38 . This, alongside the fact that DBS samples could be sampled at home, resulted in a higher proportional error compared to venous samples. However, the linear modelling between the two sampling types showed a good correlation between the two methods, albeit with a correction factor. DBS guanabenz PK-samples can therefore be considered suitable alternative to venous samples in an outpatient setting. Second, the final PK model showed under-predictions of the steady state C MAX values. Given that the model showed a high CV% and shrinkage for the IIV on K a , this is likely due to limited sampling in the absorption phase (< 2 h after dosing). Future PK-sampling schemes in children should allow assessing maturation of the absorption processes. The PD-modeling was hypothesis driven only. For MAP predictions, the circadian rhythm was specifically sampled protocol, nor implemented into the model, which might have affected the determination of the concentration-response relationship as doses, except those taken during PKPD assessments, were taken in the evening. The occurrence of hallucinations as dose limiting effect allowed us to use a TTE modeling, but further modeling of other AEs would require repeated event modeling and allow further dose optimization. With the data on MAP we made optimal use of all the information to predict brain concentrations. For future perspective it would be of interest to combine this information in a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling, like the one by Verscheijden et al. and be able to possibly link CSF concentrations to actual brain concentrations. In conclusion, we were able to translate preclinical and adult data to adequately predict plasma concentrations in children. This data was used to predict an minimal and optimal effective dose, of which the minimal effective dose was reached during the clinical study. The fact that the optimal effective dose was not reached may indicate an underprediction of brain concentrations in our translational model. Therefore, the optimal effective dose may be lower than initially predicted. Indeed, brain AUC predictions using the final re-estimated model showed a generally higher AUC for all doses (Fig. 3 ). Therefore in future research this needs to be evaluated further possibly using a biomarker, like early onset hypotension, to evaluate the concentration - toxicity/efficacy relationships of guanabenz.
