title: AI and network biology for rational polypharmacology in signaling drug design: a review
abstract: The complexity of disease-causing signaling networks is indicative of the failure of single-target therapeutics to work, particularly because of feedback, redundancy and activation of compensatory responses. The review describes the recent movement to network pharmacology and purposeful polypharmacology facilitated by the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and massive biological knowledge graphs. This review explains how machine learning and graph neural networks can be used to characterize molecular interactions systematically, predict targets that are of disease relevance, as well as priorities on multi-target intervention strategies. Generative models and reinforcement-based learning strategies are addressed to create compounds and combinations of drugs designed to modulate networks, and not individual protein inhibition. It describes the experimental validation processes, such as CETSA, NanoBRET, and Perturb-seq, and patient-derived models and MIDD systems to aid the translational evidence. Data quality, bias, interpretability, and reproducibility are taken into consideration. In sum, this review presents a feasible and combined model of AI-assisted network-mediated drug discovery.

sections.introduction: The contemporary diseases are like network problems: the pathways cross-talk, compensate and reroute upon perturbation. Single-target drugs may not treat such system responses and may cause abrupt loss of activity or even toxicity 1 , 2 . Polypharmacology is the intentional adjustment of various targets to alter a disease network towards an improved health state, rather than inhibiting one of the nodes 3 . Polypharmacology, characterized by the systematic design of small compounds targeting many therapeutic sites, presents a revolutionary approach to address biological redundant behavior, network adjustment, or the development of resistant drugs in intricate disease processes 4 . Network biology has transformed the concept into work tools. It encodes genes, proteins, and metabolites as graphs and proceeds to identify hubs, bottlenecks and modules explaining the ability of perturbing one node to rewire entire systems 5 – 7 . The selection of targets, biomarker discovery, drug repurposing and in silico screening are now guided by those network maps in network medicine and network pharmacology 8 , 9 . Experimental reviews and multi-omics articles demonstrate the application of such approaches in the areas of oncology, cardiovascular disease, and complicated disorders.
sections.limitations of traditional drug discover: Target-based screening simplifies complicated biology to single-assay tests. The leads that had appeared promising in one biochemical or cellular assay usually fail in the animal or human system due to the absence of tissue exposure, network compensation, and off-target effects in those assays 10 , 11 . All such failures indicate the issue of translation disjunction between simplified screens and organismal biology. Due to that gap, reviewers and researchers insist on complementary strategies that predict earlier emergent behavior 12 , 13 . Multi-target design, phenotypic screens, multi-omics, organoids and organ-on-chip models, and enhanced in silico translational tools are currently suggested as means of identifying safety and efficacy liabilities before expensive clinical studies 14 – 16 .
sections.rise of ai and network biology integrati: AI is applied to high-dimensional heterogeneous biology. It acquires structural, sequential, omics, and clinical representations. Deep models applied to graphs transmit information along the edges to encode the context 17 . This allows predicting drug-target associations, network modules, adverse events and treatment response. Even a multi-modal network of proteins, drugs, and clinical phenotypes has been predicted by graph convolutional networks to predict specific side-effects of drug pairs 18 . With these tools, rational polypharmacology can be done: the multi-target profiles are selected to reiterate signaling flow, as opposed to blocking a single enzyme 19 . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the AI-based network pharmacology workflow connects network construction, predictive modeling, and therapeutic design. Fig. 1 AI-based network pharmacology integrated workflow: network construction to predictive modeling and therapeutic design 223 . A The metagraph, a schema of the network types. B The hetnet visualized. Nodes are drawn as dots and laid out orbitally, thus forming circles. Edges are colored by type. C Metapath counts by path length. The number of different types of paths of a given length that connect two node types is shown. For example, the top-left tile in the Length 1 panel denotes that Anatomy nodes are not connected to themselves (i.e. no edges connect nodes of this type between themselves). However, the bottom-left tile of the Length 4 panel denotes that 88 types of length-four paths connect Symptom to Anatomy nodes. CC BY 4.0 © 2017 eLife, Cambridge, United Kingdom.
sections.scope of the review: This is a review concerning network lens signaling design. It searches graph-based and learning-based methods that have the capability of multi-target reasoning. It emphasizes models, that is, pathway topology associated with quantifiable outcomes. It also deals with the data resources, validation and translational feedback involving prediction and experimentation. It is an operational vision: show how AI and network biology can improve the reduction of attrition through the development of network-sensitive interventions based on the cross-talk, redundancy, and feedback of networks. In contrast with other reviews of network-pharmacology that mainly concentrate on target identification or drug-disease interactions, this review is unique in its integration of network biology with the artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks, exposure response, and translational limits, and how AI-controlled network modulation can be implemented to realize rational polypharmacology during signaling-driven drug design. Schematic diagram of AI model → network inference → experimental validation → PK/PD → clinic translation in a closed loop is shown in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 AI/ML modeling, network inference, experimental validation, PK/PD modeling and clinical translation for signaling-based drug design and polypharmacology shown in a closed-loop framework.
sections.systems and network biology foundations: It is important to know the backgrounds of systems and network biology to be able to explain how cellular organization and molecular interactions affect drug responses 20 . Biological processes are manifested in networks and not linear pathways, and these structures determine the response of cells to perturbations, such as drug exposure or a genetic perturbation 5 . These frameworks form the conceptual framework of network pharmacology, polypharmacology and signaling pathway mapping as discussed in the next subsections.
sections.overview of biological networks: The biological systems do not have a linear pathway but dynamic webs of molecular interactions. Biological networks consist of highly connected graphs made up of genes, proteins, and metabolites, which regulate processes of signaling, metabolism, and cell homeostasis 21 , 22 . These networks are arranged in such a way that they spell out how cells adapt to any disturbances, like drug binding or gene mutations 6 . The highly connected nodes, known as hubs, are essential to stability, and the edges are the biochemical or regulatory relationships 23 . One of the initial network models, like protein–protein interaction maps, the clusters of disease genes can be seen to be partitioned into modules, as opposed to being randomly distributed across the interactome 24 . Network biology offers a conceptual and computational realization of disease as network failures and to draw up interventions in the form of protocols re-establishing normal connectivity 25 .
sections.principles of network pharmacology: Network pharmacology provides this systems perspective to drug discovery. It is a method of combining both molecular interaction networks and pharmacological information to explain the action of drugs on many targets at once 26 . The method focuses on the emergent attributes of synergy, redundancy, and feedback, which are inaccessible to the traditional methods of single targets. The pleiotropic effects and off-target actions can be predicted by the position of a drug in the network, which is also known as its topological fingerprint 27 . The most important ones are node degree, betweenness and modularity. Such parameters are used to locate key nodes whose modulation can give the desired network state with the least side effects 28 , 29 . In the current algorithm, the drug-target and disease networks are overlaid to identify the intersections or disease modules, which can be acted upon to achieve the greatest possible therapeutic effect 30 . Figure 3 summarizes the typical drug–disease association and repurposing workflow driven by heterogeneous biomedical graphs. Fig. 3 Provides an overview of the typical process of drug-disease association prediction and repurposing based on heterogeneous graphs of biomedical knowledge, embedding algorithms, and machine-learning classifiers 191 . a The node sequence generation process through teleport-guided random walk. When arriving at a drug/disease node, the random walker selects an action between network traversing and teleport operation based on the teleport factor τ. b The embedding space generation process with heterogeneous Skip-gram model. The heterogeneous Skip-gram performs negative sampling process from the same node types. c The embedding vector space enables computational analysis including clustering of entities and distance-based analysis. d Drug-disease association prediction using XGBoost classifier with subtracted vectors of drug and disease embedding vectors as input. e Repurposing candidate drugs are prioritized using the trained XGBoost classifiers. Given a query disease of interest, all unlabeled drug-disease pair vectors are pass through the trained classifiers to obtain treatment probabilities. These probabilities are then averaged to yield a ranked list of candidate drugs based on their average treatment possibility. CC BY 4.0 © 2020 Nature Communications, London, United Kingdom.
sections.mapping signaling pathways: The cascades like MAPK, PI3K–AKT that respond to this include NF-kB, and mTOR, all of which possess feedback, time control, and cross-talk 31 . Network mapping transforms assembled databases of pathways (e.g., Reactome, KEGG, STRING) 32 – 34 into computational graphs over which signaling flux may be simulated. With these coupled with omics information, it is possible to determine dysregulated subnetworks in disease conditions 35 . The network inference problem has now been solved by AI to directly reconstruct signaling topologies using transcriptomic or phosphoproteomic data by directly comparing the two substances, which has been shown to better resolve and cover 36 . This type of integration prepares the basis of forecasting the manner in which concomitant perturbations, such as multi-target drugs or combinations, restructure signaling equilibrium.
sections.emergence of polypharmacology in a netwo: Polypharmacology was previously considered to be a bad thing due to off-target promiscuity. Network pharmacology replaces it with an exploitable property and is able to overcome pathway redundancy and resistance mechanisms 37 . Multi-target compounds such as imatinib, sorafenib, and vorinostat have long-lasting effects as they inhibit a combination of several different kinases or epigenetic controllers. These computational predictions of such useful poly-target profiles are now made using AI models that have been trained on chemogenomic data and network data 38 , 39 . Polypharmacology scholars have dominated the industry as an element in the industry design philosophy, and a phenomenon, as opposed to an incidentality of disease treatment 40 . Table 1 compares the foundational concepts, analytical goals, and tools that distinguish systems biology from network pharmacology. sections.historical and computational evolution: The development of drug discovery has advanced to early systems pharmacology that was based on mechanistic pathway models by building on data-driven network pharmacology and, most recently, AI-assisted analysis 41 . Early ODE-based simulations provided a mechanism understanding but were not scalable, thus giving way to the development of graph-based modeling that represented multi-pathway interactions 42 . As biological networks grow and multi-omics datasets have become available, machine-learning and graph embeddings have become increasingly important. These methods enable the extraction of features automatically, reposition drugs and predict the impact of network perturbation 20 . As shown in Fig. 4 , the field of network pharmacology has evolved from early conceptual models toward modern AI-driven analytical frameworks. Fig. 4 Trends in evolution and research in network pharmacology. History of key conceptual advances in network pharmacology between the early drug–target network models (2007) and synergistic and mechanism-oriented models (2015–2022). CC BY 4.0 © 2022 Frontiers in Pharmacology, Lausanne, Switzerland.
sections.early systems pharmacology approaches: The field of systems pharmacology was introduced in the early 2000s to describe the effects of drugs in whole-cell systems. It used kinetic modeling, simulations at the level of differential equations and omics data to analyze the propagation of perturbations in pathways 43 , 44 . These models uncovered the fact that biologically plausible tends to cover the target inhibition, which explains the loss of power of single-target therapies in vivo 45 . But these frameworks had a high level of parameterization and could not be easily scaled to more than a small number of pathways 46 . In 2005, interest shifted to network pharmacology, where the cell was considered an interconnected graph, and not a system of equations. The change in concept transformed the deterministic kinetics with topological reasoning and paved the way to the discovery of data 47 .
sections.network-based drug repositioning: Known drugs and disease genes were mapped to interactomes using network algorithms to determine overlapping or adjacent modules. It was projected that drugs with targets adjacent to disease nodes were to have therapeutic potential 48 . Adding further protein–protein interaction and gene-expression signatures, disease ontologies to the mix enhanced the accuracy 49 . Thousands of biomedical entities were incorporated heterogeneously in Hetionet as they related to new drug-disease relationships. The methods based on graphs formed the basis of contemporary network analysis with AI enhancements 50 .
sections.transition to ai-augmented network analy: Machine learning changed the nature of network pharmacology as it automated the process of feature extraction and relationship discovery. Similarity measure techniques have been substituted with graph embeddings that represent a representation of nodes as continuous vectors that represent topology, along with biological context 51 , 52 . These algorithms are predictive of drug-target interactions, toxicity and synergy using raw networks directly. Omics, structural, and phenotypic data are also combined into one learning framework by AI 53 . Multi-target multi-objective design of chemical entities can be done by knowledge-graph reasoning and deep generative models 54 . As summarized in Table 2 , computational strategies in network pharmacology have progressed through multiple generations of methodological innovation. These conceptual backgrounds are elaborated in later parts to cover algorithmic examinations (Section 4) and the issues around information quality, benchmarking, and assessment (Section 6). sections.ai and machine-learning frameworks in ne: AI has taken center stage in deriving actionable information on the intricate biological networks. Knowledge-graph models and explainable AI can improve interpretability, enabling the ability of the models to connect molecular features to biological processes 55 , 56 . The following section provides an overview of the key AI paradigms used in network pharmacology and how they can be used to rationalize multi-target drug design.
sections.supervised and unsupervised learning app: Machine learning has been a focal point in the new network pharmacology, which can analyze high-dimensional and high dimensionalbiological data. Figure 5 provides an overview of the key supervised and unsupervised AI models used across pharmaceutical and network-based drug discovery. Random forests, support vector machines, and gradient-boosted trees are supervised learning algorithms trained on labeled datasets. These datasets typically contain known drug-target interactions, side-effect associations, and pathway memberships 57 , 58 . Recent advancements combine both multi-omics and chemical-structure data in order to boost the predictive quality and also increase the generalization across diseases 59 . Fig. 5 Different supervised and unsupervised AI learning models and tools applied in pharmaceutical and network pharmacology for drug discovery, optimization, and prediction 224 . CC BY 4.0 © 2023 MDPI, Basel, Switzerland. Unsupervised learning, on the other hand, determines inherent patterns in biological networks without labeling biological networks beforehand 60 . Clustering, principal-component analysis and autoencoder approaches have been used to cluster drugs and genes into mechanistic modules that are associated with disease-relevant pathways successfully 61 . These models reveal emergent polypharmacological signatures, clusters of compounds that act on shared latent spaces and not the individual targets, because they embed medications, targets and signaling pathways into shared latent spaces 62 .
sections.deep learning for polypharmacology: Network pharmacology has been converted to deep learning by learning molecular and biological data directly. Graph Convolutional and Attention Networks (GCNs, GATs) represent the drug-target and disease relationship as a graph, both in terms of chemical and topological properties 18 , 63 . The networks, such as Hetionet and STRING are accurate predictors of drug interactions and polypharmacy effects using these models. Compounds are now designed by generative models, including VAEs, GANs, and diffusion networks, to target multiple targets to facilitate rational polypharmacology 64 . By combining omics, structural, and phenotypic data, AI has transformed network pharmacology to be now predictive and design-led drug discovery rather than descriptively mapping it 65 .
sections.knowledge graphs and multi-omics integra: Based on the knowledge graph and incorporating concepts in Section 3, heterogeneous multi-omics analyses are combined to do causal reasoning, link prediction, and drug-disease inferences with AI models. These graphs, combined with multi-omics integration, can be used to determine the causal flow of genetic variation. Such flow associates molecular signaling to phenotypic outcomes. DrugKG and DeepDrug models combine the features of proteomic, transcriptomic and chemical-structure to provide new drug-disease relationships 66 – 68 .
sections.explainable ai (xai) in network drug des: Although deep models are predictive, they lack biological interpretability due to their lack of transparency. Explainable AI methods solve this problem by measuring the importance of which network nodes, molecular substructures or pathways generate predictions 69 . SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, integrated gradients, and attention weights are methods that are used in identifying important determinants of activity. Methodologies like (XAI) (Explainable AI), notably SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), have gained prominence in elucidating DL-based models of multi-target prediction. The SHAP system identifies and ranks molecular characteristics that significantly help in the classification of compounds and activity estimation, thus enhancing mechanistic interpretation. Contrasting research on descriptor-based and GNNs (graph-based neural network) models has shown that SHAP examination effectively clarifies essential molecular descriptors as well as structural motifs identified by GNNs, offering knowledge about the factors influencing the prediction of molecular characteristics and various target behavior profiles. These applications emphasize the significance of XAI systems in enhancing accessibility, resilience, or biological credibility of AI-powered network pharmacology models 70 . Cooperationally, XAI-controlled Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have identified signal motifs with the engines of most predicted synergy among PI3K inhibitors of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), consistent with computational prediction, and have discovered known feedback loops 71 , 72 . This openness would introduce biological trust and promote AI-based relations regarding regulatory adoption.
sections.reinforcement and generative learning fo: Reinforcement learning (RL) maximizes actions, chemical modifications, docking poses, or target choices, should they be based on reward functions based on network effects or based on their predicted efficacy 73 , 74 . Models of Deep RL, which have been trained on docking and network feedback, have produced multi-target kinase inhibitors with balanced selectivity and low toxicity 75 . Current developments in AI, specifically DL (deep learning), RL (reinforcement learning) or generative modeling had been expedited the identification and multi-target agent’s optimization. By combining modeling that is ligand-based modeling, structure-based docking, network pharmacology, or assessment at the systems level, these emerging AI-driven frameworks allow the dual or multi-target drug’s de novo design. In particular, current generative models have been developed for de novo compounds attacking pairs of proteins that are physiologically co-dependent, along with docking simulations showing that these compounds have beneficial binding free energies or preserved binding directions in comparison with existing single-target inhibitors. In a single case, inhibitors like dual MEK1/mTOR were designed using a generative RL system. This resulted in the production of 32 potential compounds, most of which showed substantial decreases in cell viability at very small concentrations or above-50% inhibition of these two targets. These outcomes highlight the promise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods to convert hypotheses produced from networks into polypharmacological entities that have been verified through experimentation 76 . This progress bridges the gap between prediction and design to enable the autonomous AI systems to propose compounds that are in agreement with network-pharmacological reasoning 4 . sections.applications in signaling drug design: The signaling pathways form one of the most complex and therapeutically important networks in the biology of diseases and are the best targets of AI-based network pharmacology 77 . The modeling of cross-talk, feedback loops, and pathway coupling among systems, including PI3K–AKT–MAPK and JAK/STAT, can help AI to discover critical points of intervention, opportunities for repurposing drugs, and synergistic combinations of drugs 78 .
sections.targeting pathway cross-talk and feedbac: The greatest contribution of network pharmacology to signaling-based therapeutics is that it allows cross-talk and feedback between dominant pathways to be captured 79 . Conventional mono-target inhibitors tend to induce a compensatory response which reinstates downstream activity, leading to drug resistance 80 . Recent AI-based models of networks determine the key central hubs to mediate such resilience. As an example, deep-learning systems incorporating PI3KAKTMTOR and MAPK cascade information can be used to predict which dual/sequential inhibition sites would produce long-term inhibition of oncogenic signaling 81 , 82 . The graph-based causal inference outcome reveals feedback regulators such as PTEN and SOS1, which show how (secondary) targets stabilize signaling flux 83 . These predictions can be used to rationally design multi-target inhibitors/combination regimens that will pre-empt resistance. As depicted in Fig. 6 , major cancer-relevant signaling pathways such as AR and PI3K/AKT/mTOR are highly interconnected and exhibit therapeutic cross-talk. sections.case studies: cancer and neurodegenerati: Multi-pathway inhibition has become a common practice in the field of oncology. The next step is improved by AI-driven models, which combine both phosphoproteomic and interactome data to identify synergistic drug pairs 84 , 85 . Network modeling of neurodegeneration shows that there are common inflammatory and mitochondrial modules in Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Huntington’s diseases 86 . It has been found that machine-learning studies on transcriptomic and metabolomic networks identified hub nodes, including NFKB1, MAPK1 and SIRT1, which facilitate neuroinflammation and energy metabolism together 87 , 88 . These findings assist in making polypharmacological compounds to serve oxidative stress and signaling dysregulation.
sections.drug repurposing via network inference: The use of network-based inference is advantageous to drug repurposing. Embeddings of knowledge graphs and link prediction methods infer the indirect reactions between known drugs and the new diseases based on their mutual entangledness with gene or pathway links 89 . Hetionet and DrugRep platforms have been effective in predicting already existing drugs that have potential anti-fibrotic, anti-viral or neuroprotective capability 90 . The models particularly work well to indicate diseases whose molecular pathways are overlapping with repositioned drugs being able to hit convergent network motifs 91 .
sections.synergy prediction and combination thera: One of the most difficult objectives in pharmacology is to be able to predict synergistic effects. The network models designed using AI consider both topological proximity and dynamic coupling among targets to predict the synergy scores 92 . Combination-space deep-reinforcement-learning methods are currently being studied to analyze the combinatorial drug space based on pathway-level simulations 93 . Incidentally, one study has used graph attention networks to filter pairs of kinase inhibitors to find pairs that both disrupt MAPK and JAK/STAT loops together. This predictive synergy modeling can forecast useful low-dose multi-drug regimens with minimal adverse interactions 64 , 94 . Interaction networks, perturbation signatures, and disease associations are now available on large-scale platforms (e.g., OpenTargets, STRING and LINCS), but these present heterogeneity and ontology alignment challenges as well as batch effects 96 . It is also critical to have relevant benchmark data and metrics that would allow a fair evaluation of the model performance in the link prediction, re-purposing, and synergy problems. sections.primary databases: The modern network pharmacology is using the open-access resource to integrate targets, pathways and perturbation data. Genetics, expression, and literature-based targeted disease associations are made available through OpenTargets under CC0, making them easier to reuse and benchmark 97 . STRING supplies organism-wide protein–protein interaction networks annotated with evidence-based confidence scores, enabling structured network analysis and the selection of reliable interaction subsets for downstream modeling 98 . LINCS L1000 also gives signatures of chemical and genetic perturbations at LINCS L1 (CC BY 4.0), which are commonly used in repurposing and synergy screening 99 . Graph-based learning and network-based therapeutic discovery are made possible by a combination of these resources.
sections.data curation and integration challenges: Heterogeneity is an essential issue in network pharmacology: entity names, identifiers, ontologies, and evidence provenance are often different among datasets, and the quality as well as granularity of evidence provenance are highly heterogeneous 100 . Comparability across laboratories as well as cell types is further complicated by batch effects, including in transcriptomic signatures of the LINCS L1000 platform 101 . Using persistent identifiers, FAIR metadata practices, and well-documented analytic pipelines helps reduce data drift and improve consistency across heterogeneous data sources 102 .
sections.benchmark datasets for model validation: The benchmarks must indicate the prediction task. To predict links and re-use them, time-split edges of Open Targets graphs or Hetionet-type graphs should be used to prevent leakages of future knowledge 103 . PPI sense Tasks Hold-out STRING edges by publication date or evidence channel. Exact reruns can be done in case of public releases and versioned snapshots 104 .
sections.evaluation metrics: Select measures that are congruent with outcome distributions. AUROC is widespread but optimistic when there is an imbalance in the classes. AUPRC and precision NDCG are better indicators of the early-retrieval requirement of candidate lists 105 , 106 . In the case of affinity or response regression, report the concordance index and report RMSE/MAE. In combination studies, synergy metrics should be used in the same direction as the design: Bliss, Loewe, HSA, and ZIP 107 . Calibration of reports (e.g. Brier score) in cases where the information in the probabilities is used to make downstream decisions. Molecular generalization: use scaffold or time-based splits 108 .
sections.reproducibility and fair data practices: The guidelines of FAIR make use of DOIs, persistent identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and frequently open licensing. In order to have reproducibility, share code, copy exact datasets, and specifications of the environment used and random seeds 109 . Add Results/Model cards to the chart training statistics, data split, performance metrics, as well as literature limitations 110 . It is a process that bridges the target-engagement assays, functional genomics and translational models in a closed-loop workflow that revamps and refines the drug design via recurring feedback. sections.bridging ai predictions to wet-lab targe: Predication on the network should translate to the target cell engagement. Label-free CETSA identifies thermal stabilization of endogenous proteins on ligand binding, and is now capable of endorsing high-throughput adaptations toward screening 112 . It authenticates on-target action within intact cells and tissues and has the capacity to profile several proteins via the MS readout. Live-cell NanoBRET is used to complement CETSA through the binding and residence time of inhibitors against individual kinases in live cells 113 . It is isoform-selective, sensitive, and quite suitable for ranking chemical series before animal studies.
sections.functional genomics to confirm causal no: Single-cell CRISPR screens can be used to test whether predicted nodes actually regulate pathway outputs, e.g., Perturb-seq. These multiplex gene perturbations and concomitantly measure transcriptomes to give causal edges, feedbacks, and compensatory modules underlying polypharmacology 114 . Time-split designs guarantee minimal leakage due to the effects of batching 115 .
sections.translational models: organoids, pdx, an: Network predictions are related to disease biology with patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) 116 . PDOs maintain the epithelial structure and, alongside the air-liquid or co-culture, stromal/immune components can be formulated to test immunotherapy. PDXs offer in vivo pharmacology with human-mouse microenvironment discontinuities 117 . They all give preference to combinations that cross-talk and can be handled with tolerable toxicity.
sections.pk/pd, model-informed development, and c: In a variety of signaling biology and polypharmacology applications, AI-based models have shown strong quantitative behavior. The reported values of the AUROC to prioritize targets, infer the activity of pathways, and predict drug-target interaction ranges typically between 0.75 and 0.92, with the AUPRC values in the range between 0.30 and 0.70, which depict a better performance in highly disproportionate biological samples 118 , 119 . Notably, network-based and multi-task learning models are generally more accurate than single-target or isolated prediction models, and gains of synergy prediction of 10–30% or 0.05–0.15 synergy prediction 8AUROC have been reported in many studies 120 , 121 . In addition to predictive accuracy, AI-directed decision-making has been approximated to lower rates of drug discovery failure in early-stage drug discovery by ~2040% of early-stage drug discovery failures because of enhanced target selection, compound prioritization, and use of mechanisms in candidate screening 122 , 123 . Such quantitative metrics collectively underscore the concrete translational benefits of incorporating AI or network biology into rationale polypharmacology or signaling-based design of drugs. In reaching the clinic, predicted multi-target effects should match with exposure responses. Model-Informed Drug Development (MIDD) possesses connections with the preclinical information to human dosing in terms of population PK/PD, founded on exposure response and simulation-innovation trial design 124 . These frameworks are now guided by regulators, which allows quantitative decision-making of combinations and adaptive designs.
sections.clinical translation of ai-guided polyph: In one case of triple breast cancer, Tang et al. 125 identified effective target pairings by combining kinase target’s network analysis along profiles of drug-target or expression data. Kinases such as Aurora-B and ZAK were identified by their pipeline as a potentially effective co-targeting approach. siRNA/CRISPR are the combinatorial knockdown and drug combination experiments demonstrated that suppression of both kinases Aurora-B or ZAK induced much more cytotoxicity versus either individually. The interaction across the pathways of p53 or p38 MAPK was implicated for this synergy by dynamic signaling modeling, demonstrating how artificial intelligence-based network pharmacology can uncover context-specific multiple-target processes. Munson et al. 76 developed “POLYGON” by utilizing deep-reinforcement learning, which is a de novo compound estimated to block two kinases simultaneously. They taught the computer to reward compounds that target both proteins (and therefore were similar to drugs) by concentrating on cancer-related pairings. They produced 32 excellent candidates for dual inhibition of MEK1/mTOR and generated new scaffolds for the purpose of pairing ten kinase, of which one is experimentally confirmed. At micromolar concentrations, the majority of hits demonstrated more than 50% inhibition of the two MEK1 or mTOR activity, thus decreased cancer cell viability. The study shows an artificial intelligence-based polypharmacology technique combining target selection of multi-omics-informed and in vitro testing.
sections.closed-loop workflows: The CETSA/NanoBRET determines the interaction, plus the Perturb-seq/phospho-proteomics observes the change of the networks 126 . The PDO/PDX evaluates the effectiveness, and the PK/PD models project clinical doses. The models are updated by feeding the results back to them 127 . sections.challenges, limitations, and risk mitiga: AI models based on networks can provide very powerful solutions, yet their effectiveness is determined by the quality of the data, biological plausibility, and accountable execution 128 . Current resources are subject to biases, gaps and batch effects, which may bias predictions. There are still problems of translation of multi-scale evidence in cell models to human systems because of inconsistencies in exposure, signaling dynamics and assay context 78 .
sections.data quality and completeness: Section 6 elaborates on the heterogeneity of data, coverage bias, batch impacts, and problems related to FAIR. This section emphasizes their subsequent consequences on system complexity or reducing risk. Effective mitigations within the ontology consist of splits of the time-based data based on leaking future knowledge, harmonization of ontologies, and systematic uncertainty tagging. Triangulating through (combining) multiple resources (e.g., Open Targets + STRING + Reactome + ChEMBL) minimizes bias in a single source and smooths out company benchmarks 129 .
sections.model-level risks: overfitting and limit: All deep models on massive graphs may fit good hub patterns, literature popularity, or assay artifacts as opposed to causal biology. Absence of mechanistic constraints gives rise to link predictions that are biologically implausible and false synergy 130 . Trains are pronounced to pathway priors, long separate the forest paths, and balance five degrees along with XAI to highlight the stipulating nodes and edges 131 . sections.multi-scale integration barriers: The scaling of cell-line or organoid activity at the human dosage needs uniformity through all PK/PD, tissue exposures, and target occupancy. Multi-omics fusion has the potential to overweight transcriptomics and underspend phospho-signaling or proteoforms 132 . Synthesize development Model-informed development (MIDD) between preclinical exposure response and clinical endpoints, feedback inference based on longitudinal phospho-proteomics, and assay to trial design uncertainty propagation 133 .
sections.ethical, regulatory, and dataset governa: Networks associated with patients create privacy and governance concerns. Privacy-preserving or federated learning assists; however, traceable provenance and recorded informed consent are fundamental 134 , 135 . To be regulatory-ready, analysis plans must be finalized before training to avert post hoc modeling adjustments and p-hacking 136 . sections.emerging and future directions: The future of network pharmacology is broader than the present predictive and design capabilities due to the rapid development of computational biology and AI 137 . Emerging technologies integrate richer biological signals, distributed clinical datasets, and network optimization to enable personalized therapeutic decision-making 138 . These advances, including multi-modal and federated learning, quantum optimization, digital-twin modeling and autonomous AI platforms, provide new approaches to current weaknesses in scalability, interpretability and translation.
sections.multi-modal and federated learning: Future approaches to network-pharmacology will combine chemistry, structure, transcriptomics, phospho-proteomics, proteoforms, imaging and clinical features in a latent space. Multi-modal encoders have the capability of aligning small-molecule graphs to pathway graphs and patient-level signals, allowing the model to reason based on ligand substructures up to pathway flux and phenotypes 139 , 140 . Federated learning extends this to non-central institutions of patients. Training is done locally on site-restrained EHRs or omics, or images and only gradients or parameters are exchanged. This maintains privacy and enhances the diversity of cohorts and minimizes the domain shift 141 . The major engineering complications are client-drift, non-IID data, label imbalance and secure aggregation. It will be necessary to combine federated averaging with domain adaptation and calibration before these models can apply to prospective decision support 142 . sections.quantum computing for network optimizati: Hard network problems underlying polypharmacology design, such as the choice of target set on large graphs within potency, exposure and toxicity limits, are under investigation using quantum methods 143 . Forms can be transformed to quantum annealers/variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) hybrids in the form of QUBO or Ising objectives. Hybrid quantum–classical workflows provide near-term utility but require careful encoding, noise management, and classical validation to avoid overstated benefits 144 , 145 . They need to focus on strong problem encoding, noise-sensitive expectation estimation, and classical bases so that they do not over-claim benefit.
sections.digital twins and personalized network m: A digital-twin system keeps a patient-specific state vector genotype, longitudinal laboratory, therapies, tumor or tissue signaling and exposure history associated with an executable model network 146 . The twin receives new observations and makes updates to parameters, predicts response and proposes an intervention that can guide the signaling modules to remission with acceptable toxicity 147 . In the case of combination therapy, the twin can model dose schedules and order sequencing, and project uncertainty to clinical endpoints. In practice, twins will begin with organ- or pathway-level abstractions which are associated with quantifiable biomarkers, and as data become available, should proceed to multi-organ PK/PD and immune context 148 .
sections.autonomous ai\u2013network platforms: The self-governing platforms form the connection between: hypothesis → design → test → learn. Genference Agents suggest multi-target chemistries on a network constraint; the lab automation validates the interaction with the target and the changes of the pathway; it promotes the feedback of results on retraining the policy 149 , 150 . Safe deployment entails guardrails, mechanistic filters intentionally exposing goals, thresholds of uncertainty, or curious human oversight of prospectively registered Insights plans 151 . It is not aimed at a hands-off discovery engine, but a human-in-the-loop paradigm that makes use of cycles through. sections.pharmaceutical adoption of network-based: There is a growing establishment of AI and network pharmacology in drug discovery and combining design by pharmaceutical companies. Companies such as AstraZeneca and Novartis, Sanofi, GSK, and Bayer have deployed giant knowledge graphs between chemical, omics, and clinical data to discover polypharmacology patterns and new indications, including AstraZeneca Knowledge Graph, GSK BioGraph and Bayer PharmaGraph 153 , 154 . These systems are linked with phenotypic screens and CRISPR libraries, which provide AI feedback on the experiment reactions and detect early off-target activities at the start of validation of predictions 155 .
sections.cost\u2013benefit and r&d efficiency: The integration of network-AI is mostly relevant during the early phase of attrition of drug R&D, where an estimated 60% of failures are due to incorrect target choice or unforeseen toxicity 156 . Companies design predictive off-network effects and alternative ways to mitigate wasted chemistry cycles and in vivo research 157 . The 2024 life-sciences report by Deloitte reported a decline in preclinical cost per candidate of flexibility by an average of 30%, and the cost per candidate in lead optimization lagged by 25 years in the event of project adoption of network-AI triage 158 . Major costs can be substantially leveraged through computational reuse. After training, network models could be reused across programs without the need for wet-lab work setup 157 .
sections.regulatory frameworks: The regulators are instituting structures concerning MIDD and submissions using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) 159 . GMLP guidance provided by the FDA (2023) has discussed the principles of data provenance, model traceability and explainability that are directly applied to network-AI pipelines 160 . On the same note, the Big Data Steering Group suggests transparent documentation of algorithms, pre-registration of learning objectives and reference datasets in auditing algorithms to EMA 161 . Models of network-pharmacology are well placed to meet these regulatory expectations, since they are directly generating mechanistic evidence, not correlative evidence 162 .
sections.collaborative and open innovation models: Research in network-AI is moving to an open-science (precompetitive) model in which collaboration is the force behind innovation 163 , 164 . Programs such as MELLODDY, Pistoia Alliance, IMI eTRANSAFE, and NCATS Translator allow federated learning and integration of underlying knowledge graphs between the public and private ones without revealing proprietary data 165 . These frameworks are reinventing drug discovery with common infrastructure, standardized assessment and regulatory-ready AI systems with the help of open benchmarks such as Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) 166 . Table 9 highlights real-world industrial implementations of network-AI platforms and their documented benefits across pharmaceutical R&D. Table 9 Industrial adoption and translational value of network-AI systems Sector/organization Implementation focus Example platform or consortium Documented benefit Reference AstraZeneca Knowledge-graph for target–disease–compound integration AstraZeneca Knowledge Graph (AZ-KG) Improved portfolio triage; multi-target prediction 218 GSK Predictive safety & target prioritization BioGraph embedding platform 20% faster target-safety review 219 Bayer Clinical evidence graph for trial selection PharmaGraph Earlier identification of combinatorial opportunities 220 MELLODDY Consortium Federated ML across pharma FedBio joint pipeline Privacy-preserving multi-site training; improved AUC + 0.05 164 eTRANSAFE/Pistoia Alliance Translational safety and preclinical reuse Open ToxNet/ToxHub Enhanced regulatory traceability, FAIR compliance 221 NCATS Biomedical Translator Public-private network knowledge graph Translator KG Accelerated repurposing insights for rare diseases 222
sections.future roadmap (2025\u20132035): It is predicted that AI-based network pharmacology will be developed into standardized, clinical-aligned systems within the next decade, developed out of experimental frameworks 30 . Mid-term innovations will grow into patient-specific modeling, federated learning and hybrid optimization. Over the long term, the more autonomous and ethically regulated AI platforms will facilitate ongoing and network-sensitive drug discovery and individual therapeutic design 167 . Figure 12 summarizes the projected roadmap for AI-enabled network pharmacology from 2025 to 2035. Fig. 12 Future roadmap (2025–2035) of short, middle, and long-term directions of network pharmacology and AI integration. Author-generated schematic.
sections.short-term goals (2025\u20132027): The next three years will be focused on standardization and reproducibility. Current network-AI models vary in data representation, metrics of evaluation, and interpretability, and it is not easily cross-studied 168 . Standards Graph schema and ontologies Graph schema and benchmark datasets are being standardized in global initiatives like FAIR-Pharma, TDC, and OpenTargets. These are done to facilitate reproducible workflows that can be used in regulatory applications 169 . Research on explainable AI (XAI) and mechanistic integration done on a parallel basis will assist in forming trust: testable biological theories will be generated by attention-guided graph neural networks (GNNs) and by causal models of inference as opposed to being black-box predictions 170 . The emphasis will be placed on experimental validation: The AI suggests imported signatures will be experimentally validated by CETSA, NanoBRET, or Perturb-seq assays, which will be verified as relevant in the real world 171 .
sections.mid-term objectives (2028\u20132030): Network pharmacology will proceed to multi-scale personalization by 2028. Individualized predictions of drug synergy and toxicity using patient-derived organoids, digital-twin models, and jointlyomics and imaging data 172 , 173 . Quantum-hybrid optimization, in order to reach a balance between efficacy and toxicity, deployment of a digital twin in early trials to simulate dose and combinations, and equilibration of real-world evidence are all part of mid-term goals to constantly retrain network-AI systems 174 . Certification technologies that ensure AI models in drug development and route are hyper-regulated will be formalized by regulatory agencies, in the same way the ISO/ICH is structured 175 .
sections.long-term vision (2031\u20132035): The long-term vision consists of a completely autonomous but open-ended discovery-development ecosystem 176 , 177 . AI systems will independently generate hypotheses, generate compounds, simulate network effects, and arrange robot validation in AI-driven pharmacology laboratories 178 . Future systems composed of quantum computing, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and the digital-twin ecosystem will enable future design of therapies: drugs will be co-optimized depending on dynamic patient states, controlling dosage, timing and combinations based on individual-patient-specific signaling feedback 179 , 180 .
sections.conclusion: This concluding part is a summary of the key findings of the review and points out how network biology and AI modeling are transforming approaches to signaling-based drug discovery. Combining multi-omics information, biological networks and predictive machine-learning systems, network pharmacology can provide better methods to identify both targets, drug combinations, and repurposing opportunities. This review indicates that signaling diseases are network-based and react more to polypharmacology than single-target regulation. All proteins, pathways, phenotypes, and drugs are mapped using network biology, whereas AI models can suggest the possibility of targets, combinations, and the possibility of repurposing. A knowledge graph is a form of generalizing omics, structural, and clinical data. This framework, together with the exposure response model, enhances the dosing process and minimizes failures due to compensatory signaling and off-target effects. The coverage and quality of edges in organisms, tissue and disease stages are not uniform. There are numerous interactions which are situation-specific or temporal, and even they remain underrepresented in curated graphs. There are still model risks, learning to choose a shortcut based on the graph degree or modeling publication bias, learning poorly when applied to novel cohorts, and being poorly aligned with PK/PD feasibility. Digital twins must have sustained information incorporation, supreme uncertainty, and medically acknowledged update principles. Such areas of governance gaps are transparent provenance, consent tracking of multi-institution learning, and reproducible and regulator-ready benchmarks. Highlight time-separated and degree-informed benchmarking to avoid information leakage and shortcut learning. Integrate graph learning with mechanistic restrictions to maintain pathway logic and/or biophysical relevance. Extend multi-mode data assimilation with phospho-proteomics, spatial omics and longitudinal. Federate and privacy-preserving systems using drift control and calibration on the per-site level. Develop and future validate medical individual digital twins associated with biomarkers and exposure statistics. Network-conscious AI does not discover single targets, but rather coordinates network parts. It allows the combination therapy to be rationally combined, multi-target to be balanced, and the indication to be expanded across related diseases. There is improved benefit-risk in a clinical setting that is informed by models and adaptive schedules occurring due to cross-talk and feedback. Knowledge-graph and digital-twin systems personalize therapy by matching mechanism, exposure and patient state to form a learning health discovery system which advances with each experiment and patient interaction. Unlike previous reviews, which mostly focus on descriptive network analyses, the current work acknowledges a mature and prospective framework that relates network biology, explainable and generative AI, PK/PD feasibility, as well as translational validation, which promotes the field of practical applicability of network-based polypharmacology in a more advanced manner.

title: Neuroprotective Agents for Photoreceptor Rescue Following Experimental Retinal Detachment in Rodents: A Systematic Review
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate neuroprotective interventions for photoreceptor preservation in rodent models of retinal detachment (RD). Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar identified studies evaluating neuroprotective agents in rodent RD models. The primary outcome was a reduction in terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL)-positive cells quantified on retinal tissue sections (histology-based); secondary outcomes included preservation of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) and electroretinography (ERG). Risk of bias was assessed using the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) tool. Results Thirty-six studies (2007–2025) met inclusion criteria: 19 rat, 12 mouse, and 5 combined-species. Interventions included small molecules and recombinant proteins ( n = 30), monoclonal antibodies ( n = 3), peptides ( n = 2), and extracellular vesicle therapy ( n = 1). Eight (22.2%) evaluated US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved agents for non-retinal indications. Anti-inflammatory interventions achieved the highest median TUNEL reduction (84.5%, interquartile range [IQR] = 62.3%–88.1%), followed by anti-inflammatory/antioxidant approaches (70.8%, IQR = 54.3%–76.0%), metabolic modulators (59.6%, IQR = 42.9%–64.8%), and anti-apoptotic agents (59.0%, IQR = 56.6%–69.3%). Between-group differences were not statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.32). Quantitative ERG data were available in only six studies (16.7%). The risk of bias was largely unclear across selection and performance domains, with assessor blinding most reported (63.9% low risk). Ten studies additionally evaluated genetically modified backgrounds as complementary mechanistic strata ( n = 11 experiments). Conclusions Inflammation-targeted therapies showed the most consistent numerical photoreceptor rescue across rodent RD studies. With eight studies evaluating FDA-approved agents, the field has clear repurposing opportunities; closing the translational gap will require rigorously designed, functionally oriented preclinical trials that reflect clinically realistic treatment delays.

sections.protocol registration and eligibility: This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251177792) on December 17, 2025, prior to data extraction and analysis. Literature searches and screening were conducted prior to registration. Studies were included if they: (1) used rodent models (rat or mouse) of experimental RD; (2) administered any pharmacological or biological agent intended to be neuroprotective; (3) included a concurrent control group (vehicle, placebo, or no treatment) subjected to the same RD model; (4) reported quantitative outcome measures for photoreceptor survival or death, including terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) assay quantified on retinal tissue sections (histology-based), outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness, or electroretinography (ERG); and (5) were peer-reviewed articles published in English. Studies were excluded if they: (1) were in vitro, ex vivo, or computational studies without in vivo validation; (2) used non-rodent animal models; (3) were reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, or conference abstracts without full data; (4) lacked quantitative outcome measures for photoreceptor survival; (5) investigated only surgical techniques without pharmacological intervention; or (6) compared only active interventions without a vehicle or no-treatment control; or (7) reported photoreceptor apoptosis or cell-death outcomes only by flow cytometry of dissociated retinal cells (including flow-cytometric TUNEL or apoptosis-marker quantification such as cleaved caspase) without histology-based section quantification on retinal tissue, to ensure methodological consistency across the synthesis; or (8) used genetic deletion or knockout as the sole intervention without administration of a pharmacological or biological neuroprotective agent, to maintain the agent-intervention focus of this synthesis (transgenic comparisons were retained only when reported within otherwise eligible agent-intervention studies and were treated as complementary mechanistic strata rather than primary interventions).
sections.literature search and selection: A systematic literature search was conducted across 4 electronic databases from inception through April 25, 2025: MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar (first 200 results). The search strategy used a three-domain approach combining Medical Subject Headings, Emtree terms, and free-text keywords (see the full Boolean syntax in the Supplementary Methods ): • Domain 1 (Animal Model): rodent, rat, mouse, mice, and murine. • Domain 2 (Condition): “retinal detachment,” “detached retina,” “retinal separation.” • Domain 3 (Intervention/Outcome): neuroprotect*, “neuroprotection,” “neuroprotective,” “neuroprotectant,” “neuronal protection,” “photoreceptor survival,” “retinal neuroprotection,” “neuroprotective agents,” “neuroprotective therapy.” Database-specific search strings were constructed using Boolean operators (AND, OR) and truncation symbols adapted for each database's syntax. No date restrictions were applied. Records were managed and screened in Covidence systematic review software by two independent reviewers (authors K.G.B. and D.B.). Screening proceeded through title/abstract and full-text phases. Inter-rater agreement was substantial for abstract screening (κ = 0.803) and perfect for full-text screening (κ = 1.0). All conflicts were resolved through discussion between the two reviewers without requiring third-party adjudication. Of 46 full-text articles assessed, 36 met the inclusion criteria.
sections.data extraction and risk of bias: Two reviewers (authors K.G.B. and D.B.) independently extracted data using a pre-piloted, standardized extraction form. Discrepancies were resolved by discussion and consensus. Data were extracted directly from text, tables, and figures; when outcome data were presented only in graphical format, WebPlotDigitizer was used to extract numerical values. 22 Extracted variables included: bibliographic details (first author, year, and journal); study design (randomization, blinding, and sample size per group); animal model characteristics (species, strain, sex, age, method of RD induction, and duration of detachment); intervention details (agent name, dose, route, timing, and frequency); and outcome measures (TUNEL-positive cell counts, ONL thickness, and ERG amplitudes). Pharmacological details, including US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval status and mechanism of action, were also recorded. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool for animal studies, comprising 10 domains: selection bias (sequence generation, baseline characteristics, and allocation concealment), performance bias (random housing, investigator blinding, and random outcome assessment), detection bias (assessor blinding), attrition bias, reporting bias, and other biases. 23 Each domain was scored as 0 (low risk), 1 (unclear risk), or 2 (high risk). Results were summarized descriptively by domain rather than by aggregate numerical scoring, consistent with SYRCLE methodology recommendations.
sections.data analysis: The primary outcome was the percentage reduction in TUNEL, calculated as [(TUNEL_Control − TUNEL_Treated)/TUNEL_Control] × 100; complete calculations for all interventions are provided in Supplementary Tables S1 a to S1 c. TUNEL outcomes were harmonized by computing percent reduction relative to control; day 3 post-detachment was preferentially selected a priori for temporal consistency, corresponding to the peak of photoreceptor apoptosis reported across experimental RD models. When day 3 data were unavailable ( n = 4 pharmacological and n = 4 transgenic), outcomes were extracted at the nearest reported timepoint and annotated accordingly in the figures and supplementary tables. Secondary outcomes included ONL thickness (mean difference in micrometers or percentage preservation) and ERG amplitudes (a-wave and b-wave, mean difference in microvolts). Interventions were classified by primary mechanism of action: anti-apoptotic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory/ antioxidant (dual mechanism), metabolic modulation, or other. Interventions were categorized by primary mechanism as stated in the original study; overlap with secondary pathways is acknowledged. Metabolic Modulator interventions target cellular metabolism, including energy metabolism (glycolysis and pyruvate kinase activation), iron homeostasis/ferroptosis inhibition, and hypoxia-related pathways (hypoxia-inducible factor [HIF] stabilization). Statistical analyses were performed using Python 3.12 (scipy, pandas, and matplotlib). Non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis) were used for between-group comparisons given the non-normal distribution of effect sizes. Correlations were assessed using Spearman's rank coefficient. Planned subgroup analyses examined: species (rat versus mouse), transgenic status (wild type versus genetically modified), route of administration (subretinal, intravitreal, intraperitoneal, and oral), treatment timing relative to detachment, and risk of bias level.
sections.study selection: The systematic search yielded 449 records across 4 databases. After removing 141 duplicates, 308 unique records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 262 were excluded based on predetermined criteria. A full-text assessment of 46 articles identified 36 studies that met all eligibility criteria ( Fig. 1 ). Ten full-text articles were excluded, with the most common reason being lack of full-text availability ( n = 9), followed by use of non-rodent models ( n = 1). Inter-rater agreement was substantial for abstract screening (κ = 0.803) and perfect for full-text screening (κ = 1.0).
sections.study and intervention characteristics: The 36 included studies 17 , 18 , 24 – 57 (2007–2025) were authored by 32 unique first authors and 23 unique senior authors (see the Table ). Species distribution comprised rat ( n = 19, 52.8%), mouse ( n = 12, 33.3%), and both ( n = 5, 13.9%); 10 studies (27.8%) used genetically modified models, evaluated as complementary mechanistic strata within otherwise eligible agent-intervention studies (see Supplementary Table S1 c). RD was induced predominantly via subretinal sodium hyaluronate injection (one study used carboxymethylcellulose), with day 3 post-detachment as the predominant assessment timepoint (88.9%). Interventions included small molecules and recombinant proteins ( n = 30), monoclonal antibodies ( n = 3), peptides ( n = 2), and extracellular vesicle therapy ( n = 1), administered via intraperitoneal (36.1%), subretinal (30.6%), intravitreal (13.9%), or oral (13.9%) routes ( Fig. 2 ). Eight studies (22.2%) evaluated agents with FDA approval for non-retinal indications, representing potential repurposing candidates.
sections.therapeutic efficacy by mechanism of act: Twenty-seven intervention arms from 36 studies provided quantifiable TUNEL data for the primary synthesis ( Fig. 3 , see Supplementary Table S1 a); 10 additional intervention arms were excluded due to use of alternative endpoints ( n = 5), non-quantifiable TUNEL data ( n = 3), or function as mechanistic probes demonstrating worsened outcomes ( n = 2; see Supplementary Table S1 b). Of note, some studies contributed both included and excluded intervention arms. Anti-inflammatory interventions ( n = 6) achieved the highest median TUNEL reduction at 84.5% (interquartile range [IQR] = 62.3%–88.1%), followed by combined anti-inflammatory/antioxidant approaches ( n = 7, 70.8%, IQR = 54.3%–76.0%), metabolic modulators ( n = 4, 59.6%, IQR = 42.9%–64.8%), and anti-apoptotic agents ( n = 8, 59.0%, IQR = 56.6%–69.3%). Two interventions using other mechanisms achieved a median of 50.2% (values 32.7% and 67.6%). Despite the 25.5 percentage-point difference between anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic categories, the between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance (Kruskal-Wallis H = 4.65, P = 0.32). Given heterogeneity and small category sizes, these numerical medians should be interpreted as exploratory signals rather than definitive rankings. Notably, necrostatin-1 was evaluated in two studies targeting the necroptosis pathway via RIPK1 inhibition, 29 , 35 however, Dong et al. used propidium iodide (PI)-based membrane integrity endpoints rather than TUNEL (see Supplementary Table S1 b). An additional study reported suppression of necroptosis markers with rapamycin-based therapy via autophagy activation (see Supplementary Table S1 b). 46
sections.secondary outcome measures: ONL thickness or cell count data were reported in 35 studies (97.2%); interventions achieving >70% TUNEL reduction generally preserved ONL thickness, with anti-inflammatory approaches showing sustained protection in long-term studies (>1 month). Quantitative ERG data were available in only 6 studies (16.7%), precluding robust assessment of functional outcomes; among these, interventions achieving >60% TUNEL reduction generally preserved a-wave and b-wave amplitudes.
sections.subgroup analyses: Planned subgroup analyses examined species, transgenic status, route of administration, and treatment timing as potential sources of heterogeneity; only the species comparison revealed a statistically significant difference. Among the 27 intervention arms, arms from mouse studies ( n = 11) showed significantly higher median TUNEL reduction than arms from rat studies ( n = 12, 77.1% vs. 61.5%, P = 0.039); 4 arms from studies using both species were excluded. Analysis of 11 individual genetically modified model experiments (10 studies) revealed heterogeneous responses: monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) −/− (+82.6%) and LPR (+75.0%) models demonstrated the highest TUNEL reductions, whereas interleukin-6 (IL-6) −/− (−113.4%) and heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) −/− (−205.6%) exhibited increased photoreceptor death, confirming complex pathway interactions where eliminating individual mediators of inflammation or stress response may disrupt compensatory protective mechanisms ( Fig. 4 ). Among administration routes, subretinal delivery achieved the highest numerical efficacy (68.5%) versus oral the lowest (51.1%), but differences were not significant ( P = 0.861). Most studies ( n = 32, 88.9%) initiated treatment concurrent with detachment induction; 3 studies examining therapeutic windows reported reduced efficacy when treatment was delayed beyond 24 hours.
sections.risk of bias assessment: Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool across 10 domains for all 36 studies, and results were summarized descriptively by domain ( Supplementary Table S2 ). Assessor blinding (Q7) was the most frequently reported safeguard (63.9% low risk). However, randomization was documented in only 5.6% of studies, and neither allocation concealment nor investigator blinding was reported in any. This pattern of poor reporting across the selection and performance bias domains limits confidence in internal validity, consistent with the broader preclinical literature. 58 , 59
sections.publication trends: Publication frequency increased over time, with 39% of studies published since 2019. Early studies (2007–2012) focused on single-target anti-apoptotic interventions, whereas recent investigations increasingly explored novel mechanisms, including ferroptosis inhibition, metabolic reprogramming, and extracellular vesicle therapeutics.
sections.discussion: This systematic review of 36 preclinical studies (2007–2025) yielded 3 main results: (1) anti-inflammatory treatments showed the highest numerical median TUNEL reduction (84.5%), although the between-group comparison was not statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis P = 0.32) and should be interpreted as an exploratory signal; (2) 8 studies (22.2%) evaluated agents with FDA approval for non-retinal indications, indicating opportunities for drug repurposing; and (3) despite 36 preclinical studies over 18 years, none has been approved for clinical use, indicating a persistent translational gap. The high degree of efficacy of the various treatments, such as neutralization of tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α; 92.1%), inhibition of MCP-1 (88.9%), inhibition of macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) (85.7%), and depletion of microglia with PLX3397 (83.3% reduction in acute TUNEL, but no improvement in long-term photoreceptor survival) 56 suggests that the upstream immune modulation may interfere with several death-effector pathways simultaneously. This interpretation is strengthened by the finding that not only microglia, but also peripheral monocytes and neutrophils, actively promote photoreceptor death, 60 and that the RPE itself mounts an innate immune defense and recruits immune cells to the subretinal space. 61 The numerically higher efficacy of anti-inflammatory agents (median TUNEL reduction 84.5% vs. 59.0% for anti-apoptotics) is in line with the accumulating evidence that the innate immune response, microglial activation, and monocyte infiltration, is a central driver of photoreceptor death in retinal degenerative conditions, including RD. 3 , 62 The TREM-2-deficient mice showed accelerated photoreceptor death due to impaired microglial phagocytic clearance and compensatory infiltration of macrophages and neutrophils. 63 Moreover, inhibition of CSF-1R with PLX5622 worsened the acute outcome in the Okunuki et al. study, indicating that microglia are neuroprotective in the immediate post-RD period. 64 However, the immune modulation must be precisely calibrated rather than broadly suppressive. TNF-α activates caspase-8-dependent apoptosis 32 and regulates photoreceptor autophagy, 65 blurring the distinction between the two mechanistic categories. Pan-caspase inhibition paradoxically increases RIP kinase-mediated necroptosis, a compensatory switch demonstrated by Trichonas et al. and Dong et al. 29 , 35 The relative ineffectiveness of anti-apoptotics reinforces the need for upstream intervention. Moreover, photoreceptor death after RD involves at least four overlapping pathways: apoptosis, necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis, 29 , 55 , 66 – 68 with the FSP1-CoQ10-NADH and GSH-GPx4 axes identified as protective mechanisms against ferroptosis in the RPE. 69 , 70 This apoptosis-necroptosis crosstalk extends beyond RD: RIP3-mediated microglial necroptosis drives neuroinflammation in diabetic retinopathy, 71 and the RIPK1-RIPK3-MLKL axis contributes to ganglion cell death in glaucoma. 72 Qin et al. provided direct experimental evidence that simultaneous inhibition of apoptosis, necroptosis, and ferroptosis improved ganglion cell survival beyond the effects of single-pathway inhibition. 73 Deferiprone, which we have included in this review as an example of iron-mediated ferroptosis, exemplifies this expanding mechanistic landscape. 57 These observations help to explain the greater efficacy of anti-inflammatory therapies that modulate the inflammatory milieu rather than inhibiting individual death effectors. The paradoxical photoreceptor death in IL-6 −/− and HSP70 −/− knockout mice further illustrates this complexity: the elimination of individual mediators disrupts compensatory protective networks whose net effect is beneficial. Eight studies (22.2%) evaluated 10 drugs (9 distinct interventions, including one combination of nelfinavir and ritonavir) already approved by the FDA for nonretinal indications (2 studies each tested 2 approved drugs), including minocycline, 27 , 74 , 75 edaravone, erythropoietin, selumetinib, pexidartinib, deferiprone, nelfinavir, and ritonavir (used in combination), doxazosin, and guanabenz. However, the translation of these preclinical data into clinical practice is hampered by the specificity of these drugs. These examples illustrate that FDA approval alone is insufficient to predict ophthalmic translational feasibility; each agent must be evaluated for its pharmacological profile, ocular safety, and suitability for the surgical workflow that RD requires. ONL1204 (xelafaslatide), a first-in-class small peptide Fas-receptor antagonist with orphan drug designation for macula-off RD, is the only drug from our review to have reached a clinical trial (NCT05730218); the contrast-sensitivity primary endpoint was not met at week 24, 76 although a subgroup analysis of pseudophakic patients showed a 1 to 2 line improvement in visual acuity; a phase Ib study demonstrated favorable safety in geographic atrophy. 77 Doxazosin is associated with intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, complicating the cataract surgery often required after RD surgery 78 ; and deferiprone carries a 1% to 2% risk of agranulocytosis, requiring weekly monitoring. 57 , 79 The fact that only a single agent has reached a clinical trial after nearly 2 decades of preclinical research is itself a measure of the translational gap. Schmidt-Pogoda et al. found that 69% of preclinical stroke studies reported positive results, whereas only 6% of phase III clinical trials did. 80 This discrepancy is not unique to RD, but reflects a systemic failure in neuroprotection research that requires structural explanation. 81 In ophthalmology, two phase III trials of memantine for neuroprotection in glaucoma (2298 patients, 48-month follow-up) failed to show efficacy, 82 resulting in the pharmaceutical industry's reluctance to engage with neuroprotection. 83 Tsilidis et al. confirmed this pattern in 4445 animal studies of 6 different neurodegenerative diseases, finding a nearly twofold excess of statistically significant results. 84 Nevertheless, several of the compounds in our review are advancing through the clinical trial process in adjacent retinal conditions, providing translational context. Oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), the parent compound of tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA; 50.5% TUNEL reduction in our review), has been shown to cross the blood-retina barrier in patients with retinitis pigmentosa (phase 1; NCT02841306), and a recent systematic review has confirmed TUDCA's neuroprotective effects in a wide range of retinal disease models. 85 Kamuvudine-8, related to kamuvudine-9 evaluated in our review, 54 has been found to be well tolerated in a phase 1 trial for the treatment of geographic atrophy (NCT06164587). 86 These developments, together with systematic evidence of neuroprotective efficacy in other retinal degenerative conditions, 87 , 88 suggest that the mechanistic pathways identified in RD neuroprotection research may have broader translational relevance across retinal degenerative conditions. 83 The emerging paradigm of multi-drug combinations, as demonstrated by Leinonen et al. with tamsulosin, metoprolol, and bromocriptine for mutation-agnostic photoreceptor protection, 89 may prove to be more effective than single-agent approaches, given the convergent death pathways identified here.
sections.strengths and limitations: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic review of neuroprotection in RD models, using the SYRCLE risk of bias tool. The limitations of this review are: (i) the exclusive use of rodent models, which limits anatomic translation because of the absence of the macula, but rodent models are the standard platform for mechanistic neuroprotection research; (ii) the reliance on TUNEL, which primarily detects apoptosis, but necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis can also produce TUNEL-positive signal, which may under-represent the protection afforded by non-apoptotic agents; (iii) limited ERG data, which prevents robust assessment of function; (iv) the mechanistic classification is inherently reductive; for example, Fas signaling participates in inflammatory cell recruitment beyond apoptosis initiation, and TNF-α engages caspase-8-dependent apoptosis beyond its inflammatory role; (v) the Domain 3 search terms were neuroprotection-specific, which may miss mechanistic RD studies not framed as neuroprotection; the four candidate publications named by the reviewer were nevertheless excluded by independent eligibility criteria (intervention type or outcome modality).
sections.conclusions_1: This systematic review of 36 preclinical studies (2007–2025) demonstrates that anti-inflammatory interventions achieve the highest numerical photoreceptor rescue in rodent RD models. Bridging the persistent translational gap will require preclinical trials that incorporate functional outcome measures, clinically realistic treatment delays, and standardized reporting practices to advance neuroprotective strategies toward clinical application.

title: Clinical Effectiveness of Sodium‐Glucose Cotransporter‐2 Inhibitors Among Older Patients Hospitalized for Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction
abstract: Background SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2) inhibitors (SGLT2i) reduce cardiovascular events in randomized controlled trials of patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but these trials enrolled outpatient, relatively younger patients (median age 66–67). The effectiveness of SGLT2i in older patients hospitalized for HFrEF in routine US clinical practice is not well studied. Methods This study included Medicare beneficiaries aged ≥65 years hospitalized for HFrEF and eligible for SGLT2i in Get with the Guidelines–Heart Failure between July 1, 2021 and June 30, 2023. Primary outcomes were 30‐day and 1‐year all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission. Association between SGLT2i and outcomes was assessed with Cox regression and overlap weighting using propensity score estimates. Results A total of 8847 patients were eligible for but not prescribed SGLT2i at hospital admission (Median age 77; 40% women; median left ventricular EF 28%); 1464 (16.5%) patients were initiated on SGLT2i by discharge. Findings were consistent across subgroups based on age, sex, race, ethnicity, diabetes status, chronic kidney disease status, and left ventricular EF. Conclusions Among older patients hospitalized for HFrEF, SGLT2i initiation by time of discharge was independently associated with reduced all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission. These findings support SGLT2i use to improve postdischarge outcomes among older patients hospitalized for HFrEF in routine US practice.
