sections.background: SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2) inhibitors (SGLT2i) reduce cardiovascular events in randomized controlled trials of patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but these trials enrolled outpatient, relatively younger patients (median age 66–67). The effectiveness of SGLT2i in older patients hospitalized for HFrEF in routine US clinical practice is not well studied.
sections.methods: This study included Medicare beneficiaries aged ≥65 years hospitalized for HFrEF and eligible for SGLT2i in Get with the Guidelines–Heart Failure between July 1, 2021 and June 30, 2023. Primary outcomes were 30‐day and 1‐year all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission. Association between SGLT2i and outcomes was assessed with Cox regression and overlap weighting using propensity score estimates.

sections.what is new?: Among older patients hospitalized for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a new prescription of sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 inhibitors at time of hospital discharge is independently associated with improved postdischarge outcomes, including survival and readmission.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: These real‐world findings support the clinical benefits noted in randomized controlled trials of sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 inhibitors for older patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. These data support the routine use of such medications for eligible patients at the time of discharge.
sections.data source and data availability: The GWTG‐HF (Get With The Guidelines–Heart Failure) registry is a national, observational, ongoing HF quality improvement program supported by the American Heart Association. The registry includes patients hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of new or worsening HF. Patient‐level information is collected on consecutive patients with HF admitted to the hospital by trained personnel at each participating medical center. Data include demographics, medical history, laboratory and imaging results, discharge medications, contraindications to medications, and discharge status. All participating centers receive either human research approval to enroll cases without individual patient consent under the common rule, or a waiver of authorization and exemption from subsequent review by their institutional review board. An internet‐based patient management tool (IQVIA, Parsippany, NJ) serves as the data collection and coordinating center for the GWTG programs; the Duke Clinical Research Institute is the data storage and analytic center and has an agreement to analyze the aggregate limited data for research purposes. Data‐sharing agreements require an application process for researchers to access GWTG data; researchers can submit proposals to use GWTG for research purposes via the American Heart Association website. Additional information regarding the analytic methods and study material may be available upon request from the Duke Clinical Research Institute. The Institutional Review Board at Duke University Health approved this study. Registry participants aged ≥65 years with fee‐for‐service Medicare coverage were linked to Medicare inpatient claims using a validated approach. 8
sections.study population: The study included patients with HF aged ≥65 years who were hospitalized for HFrEF between July 1, 2021 and June 30, 2023, linked to Medicare fee‐for‐service, and discharged alive with a primary diagnosis of HF (Figure S1 ). Other inclusion criteria included a left ventricular EF (LVEF) ≤40% and complete information on discharge prescription status and contraindications for SGLT2i. Exclusion criteria included patients with a documented contraindication to SGLT2i, discharge to hospice care or palliative care, leaving against medical advice, history of heart transplantation or ventricular assist device, history of type 1 diabetes, and history of dialysis or an estimated glomerular filtration rate <20 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 .
sections.exposure: The exposure variable for all analyses was prescription of SGLT2i at index hospitalization. For patients with multiple eligible hospitalizations during the study, the first hospitalization was chosen as the index hospitalization. In the primary analysis, we compared patients who were newly prescribed SGLT2i at discharge to those patients not prescribed SGLT2i at discharge. For sensitivity analysis, we compared patients prescribed SGLT2i at discharge regardless of prior use (ie, in‐hospital SGLT2i continuation or initiation) to those patients not prescribed SGLT2i at discharge (prevalent user analysis).
sections.study outcomes: The prespecified primary end points were all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission at 30 days and 1 year. Secondary end points included the composite of HF readmission or all‐cause death at 30 days and 1 year, as well as incident renal events, defined by inpatient claims for acute kidney injury (AKI) hospitalization and hospitalization for end‐stage kidney disease (ESKD)/dialysis.
sections.statistical analysis: Baseline characteristics were compared between patients prescribed SGLT2i at discharge versus those not prescribed SGLT2i at discharge. Categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages and continuous variables were presented as medians with 25th and 75th percentiles. To test for differences between groups, chi‐square tests or Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical variables and Wilcoxon rank sum tests were used for continuous variables. Absolute standardized mean differences as a percentage were used to represent a measure of effect size; a percent absolute standardized difference greater than 10% indicated an imbalance between groups. To address treatment selection bias, overlap weighting was used, which has previously shown advantages over inverse probability weights. 9 , 10 A propensity score for prescription of SGLT2i was estimated with a multivariable logistic regression model including demographics, comorbidities, laboratory values, discharge medications, and hospital factors as used in prior GWTG‐HF studies. 11 Adjustment variables were prespecified and selected based on clinical relevance after consideration of confounders specific to this study. The distributions of the propensity scores were plotted to assess overlap in propensity to receive treatment (Figure S2 ). For the overlap‐weighted analysis, patients were weighted by the probability of being in the opposite exposure group, that is, the overlap weights for “treated” patients were the probability of not being prescribed SGLT2i and for those “untreated” were the probability of being prescribed SGLT2i at discharge. To assess balance after weighting the standardized differences were recalculated for the baseline characteristics; these were also depicted graphically (Figure S3 ). To describe patient outcomes, unadjusted and adjusted (weighted) cumulative incidence of each outcome at 30 days and 12 months after discharge were compared. Follow‐up was censored early if the patient lost Medicare fee‐for‐service coverage. The log‐rank test of the Kaplan–Meier hazards for mortality‐based end points and Gray's test of the cumulative incidence functions for the hospitalization end points were computed to compare exposure groups. Cox proportional hazards models were fit to estimate the association between SGLT2i prescription and each time‐to‐event outcome. Readmission outcomes were assessed using the cause‐specific hazards model, which estimates hazard ratios among those still alive and at risk for an incident event. Unadjusted and adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated; adjusted HRs were obtained from Cox models using the overlap propensity weights. Models accounted for hospital variation using the robust sandwich variance. Model assumptions, including the proportional hazard assumption, were checked. Negative control “falsification” analysis was performed to assess for potential residual confounding of the association between prescription for SGLT2i and clinical outcomes. Falsification end points selected were gastrointestinal bleed hospitalization at 1 year and hospitalization for influenza or COVID‐19 at 1 year. These end points were analyzed similar to the end points described previously. SGLT2i prescription was anticipated to be unrelated to the falsification outcomes (HRs of 1). HRs that deviate from the null would indicate possible residual confounding, which might also suggest contamination of our estimates of associations between SGLT2i and the primary outcomes. Interaction analyses were performed to determine whether adjusted associations between SGLT2i prescription and clinical outcomes varied by subgroups of interest (age, sex, race, ethnicity, diabetes status, chronic kidney disease status, and LVEF). The reference group was the unexposed subgroup in each stratum. Assessment was done by fitting Cox models as described, with additional terms in the model for subgroup and the interaction between subgroup and SGLT2i prescription. Statistical analyses were performed using SAS software (version 9.4, SAS Institute, Cary, NC). Missing values were excluded from descriptive summaries. For propensity score covariates, low levels of missingness (<5%) were singly imputed; multiple imputation under the fully conditional specification method was otherwise used, with 20 imputed data sets. Model‐based results were aggregated across imputed data sets using Rubin's rules. Model diagnostics for logistic regression were assessed a priori. Potential nonlinearity in continuous covariates was evaluated and appropriate transformations applied; restricted cubic splines were used for the nonlinear covariates. Correlations of adjustment factors were examined and overall model fit was further assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness‐of‐fit test, which did not indicate lack of fit. Two‐tailed P value <0.05 was considered significant for all statistical tests.
sections.baseline characteristics: Between July 1, 2021 and June 30, 2023, 8847 patients met study eligibility criteria (Figure S1 ), with an index hospitalization for HFrEF and eligible for but not prescribed SGLT2i at the time of hospital admission. Overall, 1464 (16.5%) patients were newly initiated on SGLT2i at discharge. Baseline characteristics are available (Table 1 ). Before overlap weighting, patients newly initiated on SGLT2i tended to be younger with fewer medical comorbidities, with the exception of diabetes. After application of overlap weights, there were no concerning imbalances in baseline characteristics between the 2 groups, with few exceptions (angiotensin receptor‐neprilysin inhibitor at admission; length of stay; admission at a heart transplant hospital) (Table 2 ). Median age was 77; 40% were women; 83% were Non‐Hispanic White, 11% were Non‐Hispanic Black, and 4% were Hispanic; median LVEF was 28%; and comorbid conditions were frequent.
sections.new initiation versus no initiation of s: Patients newly initiated on SGLT2i at hospital discharge had lower unadjusted cumulative incidence of all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission at 30 days and 12 months, compared with patients not prescribed SGLT2i (Table 3 ). There was no difference in hospitalization for AKI or for ESKD/dialysis. After application of overlap weighting for confounding adjustment, initiation of SGLT2i at discharge was independently associated with lower all‐cause mortality (adjusted HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.67–0.86]; P <0.001), all‐cause readmission (adjusted HR, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.81–0.97]; P =0.009), and HF readmission (adjusted HR, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.75–0.95]; P =0.004), compared with those not prescribed SGLT2i over 12‐month follow‐up (Table 4 ; Figure 1 ). Initiation of SGLT2i at discharge was not associated with hospitalization for AKI or for ESKD/dialysis and was not associated with either falsification end point in adjusted analyses (Table 4 ; Tables S1 and S2 ).
sections.subgroup and sensitivity analyses: Primary outcome findings were consistent across subgroups based on age, sex, race, ethnicity, diabetes status, chronic kidney disease status, and LVEF (all P for interaction ≥0.05) (Figure 2 ). Sensitivity analysis included 16 863 patients discharged with SGLT2i regardless of use before admission (prevalent user analysis). Overall, 3812 (22.6%) patients were discharged with SGLT2i. Patients prescribed SGLT2i were younger, more often male, and had higher rates of diabetes (Table S3 ). After application of overlap weighting, baseline characteristics were similar between the 2 groups (Table S4 ). In unadjusted and adjusted models, SGLT2i prescription at discharge was independently associated with lower all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission, compared with those not prescribed SGLT2i over 12‐month follow‐up (Tables S5 and S6 ; Figure S4 ). SGLT2i prescription at discharge was not associated with hospitalization for AKI or for ESKD/dialysis in adjusted models. Missingness data are available (Tables S7 and S8 ).
sections.discussion: In this real‐world clinical practice population of older US patients hospitalized for HFrEF, SGLT2i initiation by time of discharge was independently associated with reduced all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission, compared with those not discharged on SGLT2i. Importantly, in terms of safety there was no difference in hospitalization for AKI or for ESKD/dialysis. Findings were robust in subgroup analyses. Sensitivity analyses including SGLT2i prescription regardless of use at admission were also consistent. These findings further support the effectiveness and safety of SGLT2i in patients hospitalized with HFrEF, including those who are older with frequent comorbid conditions. In a meta‐analysis of DAPA‐HF 2 (Study to Evaluate the Effect of Dapagliflozin on the Incidence of Worsening Heart Failure or Cardiovascular Death in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure) and EMPEROR‐REDUCED (Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction), 3 SGLT2i was associated with a 13% reduction in all‐cause death (pooled HR, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.77–0.98]). 4 Similarly in our current study, SGLT2i initiation was independently associated with lower all‐cause mortality (adjusted HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.67–0.86]). Clinical benefit was noted within days to weeks of SGLT2i initiation in these randomized controlled trials 12 , 13 ; an early clinical benefit was also observed in the present study. However, the recent DAPA‐ACT‐HF‐TIMI 68 (Dapagliflozin and Effect on Cardiovascular Events in Acute Heart Failure–Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68) trial showed a nonsignificant reduction in cardiovascular death or worsening HF event in the first 2 months after an HF hospitalization with in‐hospital initiation of SGLT2i therapy (HR, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.68–1.08]). 14 Despite this finding, a subsequent meta‐analysis published in the same article analyzed DAPA‐ACT‐HF‐TIMI 68 alongside SOLOIST‐WHF 15 (Effect of Sotagliflozin on Cardiovascular Events in Participants With Type 2 Diabetes Post Worsening Heart Failure; primary outcome: total cardiovascular death, hospitalization, or urgent visit for HF) and EMPULSE 16 (A Study to Test the Effect of Empagliflozin in Patients Who Are in Hospital for Acute Heart Failure; primary outcome: stratified win ratio); the authors reported a class effect of inpatient initiation of SGLT2i, reducing the risk of cardiovascular death or worsening HF event (HR, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.41–0.80]). Notably, our current study assesses a patient population older than patients in pivotal trials (79 versus 67 years old), with a higher proportion of female participants, a higher baseline NT‐proBNP (N‐terminal pro‐B‐type natriuretic peptide), and a lower estimated glomerular filtration rate. Data from the ambulatory‐based NCDR (National Cardiovascular Data Registry) PINNACLE (Practice Innovation and Clinical Excellence) registry suggest that as of 2023, outpatient use of SGLT2i for eligible patients with HFrEF is about 29%. 6 For inpatient use, a study from GWTG‐HF between 2021 and 2022 suggests that 20% of eligible patients receive SGLT2i after a hospitalization for HFrEF. 7 Real‐world assessment of SGLT2i effectiveness for HFrEF is limited but largely supports our findings. A recent study by Gautier et al. looked at >50 000 HF hospitalizations in France between 2021 and 2023 and assessed the clinical impact of SGLT2i prescription at discharge, including >16 000 patients with HFrEF; SGLT2i prescription was associated with a lower risk of the composite end point of all‐cause death or HF hospitalization (adjusted HR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.67–0.75]), a lower risk of all‐cause death (adjusted HR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.65–0.74]) and a lower risk of HF hospitalization (adjusted HR, 0.71 [95% CI, 0.64–0.78]). 17 The study did not assess for renal outcomes. However, like our cohort, patients were older and had more medical comorbidities than in randomized controlled trials. To our knowledge, there is no comparable study performed in the United States, where current usage rates are much lower than in the Gautier study, where use of SGLT2i for patients with HFrEF reached 70% by 2023. 6 , 7 , 17 Similarly, there is no comparable study of patients with LVEF >40%. Randomized trial evidence demonstrates clinical benefit in these patients as well, yet data from the PINNACLE registry suggest outpatient use for these patients is about 13% 1 , 6 , 18 , 19 ; subsequent GWTG‐HF analyses will thus evaluate the clinical effectiveness of new SGLT2i prescription after HF hospitalization among patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction. It is clear that implementation of SGLT2i for HF can improve at a population level, but barriers in the United States may differ from those noted elsewhere in the world. SGLT2i for HFrEF are cost effective and could potentially prevent 34 000 deaths in the United States annually 20 , 21 ; however, cost, clinical inertia, bias, and uncertainty of treatment effect likely contribute to the slow adoption in the United States. Although the SGLT2i class has been available in the United States for treatment of diabetes since 2013, it was approved by the Food and Drug Administration for HFrEF only in 2020 before being formally recommended for all patients with HF in the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology HF guidelines. 1 Estimated out‐of‐pocket costs remain high, where a 30‐day supply can range from $500 to $800. 22 Furthermore, there is a tendency to defer initiation of GDMT until after the acute hospitalization, despite evidence that patients discharged without GDMT are >75% likely to remain off GDMT at 1 year. 23 , 24 , 25 Because barriers are present at the patient, clinician, and system level, multipronged initiatives to improve GDMT have shown promise; interdisciplinary HF teams, audit and feedback mechanisms, formalized discharge protocols, and electronic health record interventions may increase the use of GDMT—including SGLT2i—in routine practice. 26 , 27 Given the mortality and readmission benefits noted in both randomized controlled trials and real‐world populations, action is needed to address the barriers limiting eligible patients from receiving such an important medical therapy.
sections.limitations: Despite adjustment for several demographic and clinical variables and the use of a rigorous statistical method, selection biases and residual measured/unmeasured confounding may still be present and thus influence the primary outcomes. The data set does not allow for assessment of prescription decisions and thus cannot account for factors related to socioeconomic status, compliance, and insurance coverage. This includes the fact that Medicare Advantage enrollees were not included in the study. In addition, the inclusion of only new users of SGLT2i means the patient population is selective; external validity may be limited. The use of treatment groups defined by discharge SGLT2i prescription meant the study did not account for potential crossover—either by subsequent SGLT2i initiation or discontinuation—after the index hospitalization. Although an analysis from CONNECT‐HF (Care Optimization Through Patient and Hospital Engagement Clinical Trial for Heart Failure) has shown that discharge prescription of GDMT is associated with high subsequent fills and adherence, 28 this study did not directly assess postdischarge adherence or persistence of discharge therapy, and these factors could contribute to associations with clinical outcomes. Subsequent changes in the remaining GDMT regimen were also not accounted for in the study. The falsification end points were prespecified and informed by prior literature, 29 but choosing such end points is challenging for SGLT2i given the broad range of medication effects; these end points may not have been entirely neutral to SGLT2i use. Finally, the low use of diuretics at discharge (60%) may not truly reflect underuse, as the data are captured only as a prescription at discharge and not reliably captured as missing or not prescribed.
sections.conclusions_1: In this real‐world population of older US patients hospitalized for HFrEF, new SGLT2i prescription by time of discharge was significantly associated with reduced all‐cause mortality, all‐cause readmission, and HF readmission. These results complement the existing data available from randomized controlled trials and registry data and suggest that the clinical benefit of SGLT2i extends to routine US practice.

title: Incremental Prognostic Power of Coronary Flow Reserve and Artificial Intelligence–Enabled ECG – Derived Filling Pressure in Angina With Nonobstructive Coronary Arteries
abstract: Background Coronary flow reserve reflects microvascular function, whereas filling pressure indicates myocardial hemodynamic burden. In angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries, abnormalities in either could contribute to a supply–demand mismatch; however, their combined prognostic significance remains unclear. Methods Patients with angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries who underwent invasive coronary reactivity tests were studied retrospectively. Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) was coronary flow reserve <2.5. An artificial intelligence–enabled ECG marker of elevated filling pressure (AIEFP) was applied as a scalable prognostic marker of myocardial hemodynamic stress. Associations with major adverse cardiovascular events were evaluated using Cox regression and propensity score overlap weighting. Results Among 1957 patients with angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries (median age, 51.8 years; 67.2% women), CMD+ was identified in 26.4% and AIEFP+ in 6.6%. Over 8 years, 204 patients (10.4%) experienced major adverse cardiovascular events. In nested models, both CMD (hazard ratio [HR]=1.42 [95% CI=1.13–1.78]; P =0.002) and AIEFP (HR=2.28 [95% CI=1.67–3.11]; P <0.001) remained associated with major adverse cardiovascular events after adjustment. Adding AIEFP to the base model improved model fitness (Δχ 2 =23.65, P <0.001; ΔAkaike Information Criterion=−21.7) and modestly improved discrimination (ΔHarrell concordance index=0.02, P =0.02). In a 4‐group model, adjusted risks increased in a graded manner. Overlap‐weighted analysis after covariate balance demonstrated distinct temporal risk trajectories: CMD+/AIEFP+ had the highest 1‐year risk (12.7%), and AIEFP+ had the highest cumulative 8‐year risk (57% in CMD− and 51.8% in CMD+). Conclusions CMD and AIEFP provide complementary prognostic information, with AIEFP remaining significantly associated with outcomes after multivariable adjustment. A dual‐axis framework integrating myocardial hemodynamic stress (AIEFP) and microvascular function (coronary flow reserve) may enhance risk stratification and enable identification of clinically distinct angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries phenotypes with divergent trajectories.

Integrating myocardial hemodynamic stress (artificial intelligence–enabled ECG marker of elevated filling pressure) with microvascular vasodilatory capacity (coronary flow reserve) revealed divergent short‐ and long‐term risk trajectories, with myocardial stress conferring substantial cumulative risk even in the absence of overt microvascular dysfunction.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: In a heterogeneous population with angina with nonobstructive coronary arteries, a dual‐axis framework integrating ECG‐derived myocardial hemodynamic burden and invasive coronary physiology may refine prognostic stratification by distinguishing myocardial‐ and microvascular‐dominant risk phenotypes, thereby supporting more tailored assessment and longitudinal follow‐up.
sections.transparency and openness statement: This study adheres to the AHA Journals' implementation of the Transparency and Openness Promotion Guidelines. The data supporting this study's findings are not publicly available because of institutional policies and restrictions related to patient privacy. The data may be made available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and with appropriate institutional approvals. The analytic methods used in this study are described in sufficient detail within the article and Supplemental Materials to allow replication of the results.
sections.study design and population: This retrospective, single‐center, cohort study included all patients aged ≥18 years with symptoms of stable angina who were found to have nonobstructive coronary artery disease (<50% stenosis in all epicardial vessels) on clinically indicated elective coronary angiography and invasive coronary reactivity test (CRT) at the Mayo Clinic between 1993 and 2023. Exclusion criteria were as follows: LV ejection fraction <50%, the absence of a research‐quality 12‐lead ECG within 2 weeks of the CRT procedure, an incomplete physiological assessment, or insufficient follow‐up data. The Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board (No. 05‐004191) approved the study protocol. The present study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki for the investigation of human subjects, and all participants provided written informed consent before enrollment in the registry.
sections.coronary angiography and crt: Patients presented to the cardiac catheterization laboratory in a fasting state, with cardiovascular medications withheld for at least 48 hours. All participants underwent diagnostic coronary angiography following standard protocols. Subsequently, CRT was performed to evaluate coronary microvascular function. From 1993 through 2021, CFR was measured using a Doppler flow wire system (FloWire, Philips/Volcano) positioned within a 2.2‐F coronary infusion catheter (Transit Microcatheter, DePuy Synthes Companies) advanced into the mid left anterior descending artery. Incremental intracoronary bolus injections of adenosine (18–72 μg) were administered through the guiding catheter to achieve maximal hyperemia. CFR was calculated as the ratio of the average peak coronary flow velocity during hyperemia to baseline average peak velocity. 27 , 28 Beginning in 2022, CFR assessment was performed using a thermodilution‐based technique with a dual‐sensor PressureWire (PressureWire X; Abbott Vascular Inc) connected to a CoroFlow console. The wire, positioned in the mid left anterior descending artery, incorporates a pressure transducer and 2 thermistors that measure the mean transit time of a rapidly injected cold saline bolus at rest and during adenosine‐induced hyperemia. Because mean transit time decreases as coronary flow increases, CFR was derived as the ratio of mean transit time at baseline/that at hyperemia. 29 , 30 CMD was defined as CFR <2.5. 31 , 32
sections.ai \u2010 ecg for elevated filling press: To noninvasively index myocardial hemodynamic burden, we applied a validated, officially released AI‐ECG model (ResNet‐18 convolutional neural network) to standard 10‐second 12‐lead ECGs acquired within 2 weeks before CRT. The model outputs probabilities for 4 grades of diastolic function (0–3). 25 Consistent with the model specification, AIEFP was defined as the sum of the predicted probabilities for diastolic dysfunction grades 2 and 3. A specified probability threshold of ≥0.264, corresponding to the optimal operating point identified in the development and validation study, was used to classify increased filling pressure. This binary construct demonstrated robust discrimination for elevated filling pressure (area under the curve, 0.911), with a high negative predictive value (94.5%) and prognostic performance comparable to echocardiographic assessment. Accordingly, AIEFP was applied as a predefined binary marker (+/−) in all analyses and used for patient stratification alongside CFR. Additionally, we performed an internal assessment of model performance within our cohort with ANOCA.
sections.clinical assessment and follow\u2010up: Baseline demographic data, cardiovascular risk factors, medical history, and laboratory results were extracted from the electronic health record by trained investigators blinded to the study's primary hypotheses. The primary end point was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), a composite of all‐cause mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or hospitalization for HF. Mortality was ascertained through a systematic review of hospital records and linkage to the Minnesota Death Index. Nonfatal myocardial infarction was defined according to the Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction, requiring a rise and/or fall in cardiac troponin with at least 1 value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, accompanied by evidence of myocardial ischemia (eg, symptoms, new ischemic ECG changes, or imaging evidence). 33 HF was diagnosed with any cardinal symptoms and abnormal findings of echocardiography, NT‐proBNP (N‐terminal pro‐B‐type natriuretic peptide) level, and HF hospitalization was defined as an unplanned admission for worsening symptoms of HF requiring intravenous diuretic therapy. 34 All events were independently adjudicated by at least 2 physician investigators blinded to biomarker data, using a combination of institutional databases, death certificates, and detailed medical record review to ensure rigor and consistency. Time to event was calculated as the period between the date of procedure and the first occurrence of an MACE that documented a clinical event in the medical record or registry. Patients without an MACE were censored at their last follow‐up.
sections.statistical analysis: All statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 4.5.1) and SPSS (version 29, IBM Corp). A 2‐sided P <0.050 was considered statistically significant. Continuous variables were presented as medians with interquartile ranges and compared using the Kruskal‐Wallis test for 4‐group analyses or the Mann–Whitney U test for 2‐group analyses. Categorical variables were presented as counts and valid percentages and compared using the χ 2 test or Fisher exact test, as appropriate. To account for imbalanced group sizes and provide scale‐independent estimates of group differences, effect sizes (η 2 for continuous data and Cohen h or Cramer V for categorical data) were calculated in addition to P values and are reported in the Supplemental Materials . All survival analyses were performed using complete‐case data, as all patients in the analytic cohort had complete information on the primary exposures (CFR and AIEFP), outcome (MACE), and the prespecified covariates used in the multivariable models. Missing data were limited to descriptive characteristics not used in modeling and represented <20% of observations.
sections.univariate and multivariable prognostic: Unadjusted MACE‐free survival distributions were evaluated with Kaplan–Meier curves and global/pairwise log‐rank tests with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment. Multivariable Cox proportional‐hazards models were constructed hierarchically using prespecified clinically relevant covariates. Nested models were used to evaluate the incremental association of CMD, AIEFP, and their interaction with outcomes. Akaike Information Criterion was used as a secondary index of relative model parsimony, whereas likelihood‐based testing and discrimination metrics were used to assess incremental prognostic information. To ensure model stability, the variance inflation factor was calculated for all predictors; models containing any variable with a variance inflation factor ≥10 were excluded to prevent multicollinearity. Base model with clinically relevant covariates and CMD Model 1+AIEFP CMD×AIEFP interaction Incremental model performance was assessed using complementary metrics reflecting distinct aspects of prognostic modeling. Improvement in model fit was evaluated with likelihood‐ratio testing of nested Cox models and change in Akaike Information Criterion, with Akaike Information Criterion interpreted as a measure of relative fit and parsimony rather than discrimination. Prognostic discrimination was assessed using Harrell concordance index, and change in discrimination with addition of AIEFP was quantified using both ΔC and the integrated discrimination improvement. A final model incorporating the 4 predefined CMD/AIEFP phenotypes generated adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for MACE. Proportional‐hazards assumptions were tested using Schoenfeld residuals, and precision was validated by 1000 bootstrap resampling. Prespecified sensitivity analyses were performed stratified by CFR measurement technique and additionally adjusted for enrollment year to assess the robustness of the prognostic association of AIEFP.
sections.confirmatory analysis with propensity sc: To verify robustness of the phenotype‐based findings and minimize residual confounding, propensity‐score overlap weighting was applied to achieve covariate balance across 4 groups. Propensity scores for phenotype membership were estimated using generalized boosted models. Covariate balance was assessed with standardized mean differences (<0.10 indicating adequate balance). Weighted Cox regression estimated aHRs for MACE, and weighted Kaplan–Meier estimators provided 1‐ and 8‐year absolute risks, yielding clinically interpretable short‐ and long‐term risk trajectories in a balanced pseudopopulation.
sections.study population and grouping distributi: From an initial cohort of 2307 patients with ANOCA, 1957 met the eligibility criteria and were ultimately included (Figure 1 ). The individuals were predominantly women (67.2%, N=1316) with a median age of 51.8 (43.3–60.6) years. Overall, CMD was present in 26.4% (N=516) of patients, and AIEFP in 6.6% (N=129) of patients with ANOCA. Based on CMD and AIEFP status, patients with ANOCA were stratified into 4 distinct groups: CMD−/AIEFP−: N=1379 (70.4%) CMD+/AIEFP−: N=449 (22.9%) CMD−/AIEFP+: N=62 (3.2%) CMD+/AIEFP+: N=67 (3.4%) Among AIEFP+ patients, 51.9% had concurrent CMD+, whereas only 12.7% of CMD+ patients had AIEFP+, underscoring the partial but clinically relevant overlap between microvascular dysfunction and elevated filling pressure. Within this cohort, the AI‐ECG model was reassessed against echocardiographic markers of elevated filling pressure, demonstrating robust discrimination (area under the curve=0.79).
sections.baseline characteristics: Baseline characteristics of the total cohort, along with stratification by AIEFP status, are presented in Table 1 . Patients with AIEFP+ were older (65.3 versus 51.1 years) and more frequently women (79.8% versus 66.4%). The cardiometabolic comorbidity burden was higher in the AIEFP+ group, with a greater prevalence of hypertension (67.4% versus 42.2%) and diabetes (21.7% versus 10.9%). In contrast, body mass index, obesity, smoking history, family history of coronary artery disease, and hyperlipidemia were similar between the groups. Laboratory profiles were consistent with increased myocardial and systemic stress among AIEFP+ patients, characterized by markedly higher NT‐proBNP levels (252 [150–488] versus 66.5 [37–123] pg/mL), modestly higher renal indexes, higher glycemic markers, and lower hemoglobin concentrations. Inflammatory burden assessed by hs‐CRP (high‐sensitivity C‐reactive protein) was comparable between groups. Medication use reflected a greater cardiovascular disease burden in AIEFP+ patients, including higher use of angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (25.6% versus 14.2%) and β‐blockers (51.2% versus 32.1%), whereas the use of aspirin and calcium‐channel blockers was similar. Cardiac structure, coronary physiology, and invasive hemodynamics differed substantially by AIEFP status. AIEFP+ patients had higher left atrial volume index (34 [28–42] versus 27 [23–34] mL/m 2 ), lower CFR (2.4 [2.1–2.9] versus 2.9 [2.5–3.4]), higher prevalence of CMD (51.9% versus 24.6%), modestly lower left ventricular ejection fraction (60% [54%–65%] versus 62% [59%–65%]), and higher left ventricular end‐diastolic pressure (20 [15–24] versus 16 [12–20] mm Hg). AI‐ECG derived atrial fibrillation probability was markedly higher in the AIEFP+ group (18.1% [3.9%–35.5%] versus 0.9% [0.3%–3.1%]), supporting internal biological coherence of the AIEFP phenotype (Tables S1 and S2 ).
sections.prognostic analyses: In up to 8 years’ follow‐up (median, 6.7 years), MACEs occurred in 204 patients (10.4%), comprising 93 all‐cause deaths (4.8%), 50 nonfatal myocardial infarctions (2.6%), and 61 HF hospitalizations (3.1%). The absolute numbers and proportions of MACE events across CMD/AIEFP phenotypes were as follows: CMD−/AIEFP− (111 events among 1379 patients; 8.0%), CMD+/AIEFP− (57/449; 12.7%), CMD−/AIEFP+ (16/62; 25.8%), and CMD+/AIEFP+ (20/67; 29.9%). In unadjusted Kaplan–Meier analyses, both CMD+ and AIEFP+ were individually associated with significantly lower MACE‐free survival (log‐rank P <0.001 for both; Figure 2 ). When stratified into the 4 groups, a graded, stepwise decline in MACE‐free survival was observed (global log‐rank P <0.001; Figure 3 ). All pairwise phenotype comparisons remained significant after Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment ( P <0.001), except for CMD−/AIEFP+ versus CMD+/AIEFP+ ( P =0.545), where wide 95% CIs were driven by few patients and higher event rates. Nested model analysis demonstrated that addition of AIEFP to the base model containing clinical covariates and CMD significantly improved model fit (likelihood‐ratio test Δχ 2 =23.65, P <0.001; ΔAkaike Information Criterion=−21.7; Tables S3–S7 ). This was accompanied by a modest but statistically significant improvement in discrimination, with Harrell concordance index increasing from 0.66 (95% CI, 0.63–0.69) to 0.68 (95% CI, 0.64–0.70) (ΔC=0.02, P =0.02). The integrated discrimination improvement further supported incremental discrimination when AIEFP was included. The CMD×AIEFP interaction was not statistically significant ( P =0.697), suggesting no evidence of multiplicative interaction between CMD and AIEFP. These findings indicate that AIEFP provides prognostic information not captured by clinical covariates and invasive microvascular measures. In a 4‐group multivariable Cox model, risk increased progressively and in a stepwise manner across the phenotypes. Compared with the CMD−/AIEFP− as a reference group, the aHR for MACE was 1.45 (95% CI, 1.13–1.86) for CMD+/AIEFP−, 2.42 (95% CI, 1.59–3.69) for CMD−/AIEFP+, and 3.12 (95% CI, 2.05–4.74) for CMD+/AIEFP+ (Table 2 ). These results, consistently reproduced across 1000 bootstrap resampling validations, underscore the robustness of the proposed 4‐tier risk stratification scheme (Table S8 ). Sensitivity analyses accounting for enrollment timing, modeled continuously and by study era (pre‐2010 versus post‐2010), demonstrated no association between enrollment period and outcomes, with no impact on covariate effect estimates. Formal interaction testing in the full cohort revealed no evidence of effect modification by CFR measurement technique (interaction P =0.990), supporting the robustness of the findings across CFR method.
sections.confirmatory analysis using propensity s: A confirmatory analysis using propensity score overlap weighting was performed, achieving excellent covariate balance across the 4 groups (all standardized mean differences <0.10; Figure S1 ). This procedure resulted in a small effective sample size in the 2 highest‐risk strata (effective sample size≈60 in each; Table S9 ). The weighted Cox models confirmed the primary results, highlighting each group's strong, independent prognostic significance (Table 3 ). In the doubly robust model, both CMD−/AIEFP+ (aHR=3.37 [95% CI=1.82–6.23]) and CMD+/AIEFP+ (aHR=3.37 [95% CI=1.71–6.61]) groups were associated with the highest risk of MACE relative to the reference group. The CMD+/AIEFP− group conferred a more modest, although still significant, increase in risk (aHR=1.58 [95% CI=1.21–2.07]). Interestingly, analysis of absolute risk in the balanced cohort revealed distinct risk trajectories across phenotypes (Figure 4 ). The CMD+/AIEFP+ group carried the highest short‐term risk (1‐year MACE absolute risk: 12.7%). Additionally, both groups with AIEFP+ demonstrated markedly elevated cumulative long‐term risk (8‐year MACE absolute risk: 57.0% CMD− and 51.8% CMD+).
sections.main findings: The current study demonstrated that integrating a noninvasive AI‐derived ECG marker of elevated filling pressure (AIEFP) with invasive CFR could refine risk stratification in ANOCA. This dual framework assessment of myocardial hemodynamic stress and microvascular function identified distinct phenotypes with divergent clinical trajectories, demonstrating that myocardial load and microvascular capacity contribute in complementary ways to adverse outcomes. These findings highlight this signal as a potential practical tool to improve prognostic evaluation.
sections.myocardial vulnerability and microvascul: In ANOCA, symptoms and outcomes often reflect a bidirectional coupling between the coronary microvasculature and the myocardium rather than microvascular dysfunction alone. 35 , 36 Prior studies suggest that myocardial hemodynamic stress and microvascular dysfunction frequently coexist in ANOCA‐related syndromes. 37 , 38 The present study extends these observations by integrating invasive coronary physiology with an ECG‐derived myocardial stress signal applied for prognostic stratification. In our cohort, just over half of patients with AIEFP positivity also exhibited CMD, consistent with prior evidence that microvascular dysfunction is common in clinical states characterized by elevated filling pressures, including HF with preserved ejection fraction. 14 , 39 Meta‐analytic data indicate CMD in up to 71% of HF with preserved ejection fraction cases, with impaired CFR present in ≈62%. 40 , 41 The observed overlap is consistent with prior reports linking CMD and diastolic dysfunction across related clinical syndromes. Conversely, only a minority of patients with CMD were AIEFP positive in the present study, a proportion lower than the reported prevalence of echocardiographic diastolic dysfunction in comparable CMD populations. 37 , 42 This distinction, compared with the broader prevalence of any grade of diastolic dysfunction among patients with CMD, suggests that AIEFP identifies the subset in whom myocardial stress has progressed to clinically meaningful hemodynamic burden and worse outcome, thereby refining prognostic prediction within CMD. The resulting partial overlap is therefore expected and biologically plausible. Impaired coronary flow reserve does not uniformly translate into elevated myocardial filling pressures, and the ECG‐derived signal should not be interpreted as a surrogate for comprehensive diastolic assessment. Instead, AIEFP identifies a smaller, higher‐risk subset characterized by sustained myocardial hemodynamic burden, thereby refining prognostic stratification within CMD using a widely available tool.
sections.complementary prognostic contributions o: A central finding of this study is the additive prognostic value of the ECG‐derived myocardial hemodynamic stress marker (AIEFP) when considered alongside invasive coronary flow reserve. In adjusted models, the CMD−/AIEFP+ phenotype conferred a significantly higher risk of MACEs than the CMD+/AIEFP− phenotype. This suggests that in the population with ANOCA, a noninvasive signal of myocardial hemodynamic burden may identify clinical risk not necessarily captured by microvascular vasodilatory capacity alone. 18 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 The observed complementary behavior of these markers is consistent with established physiological principles describing a bidirectional coupling between the myocardium and the microcirculation. Mechanistically, chronically increased wall stress and elevated filling pressures have been shown to decrease microvascular perfusion by shortening the diastolic perfusion window and increasing extravascular compressive forces, particularly in the subendocardium. Our results are consistent with prior translational pressure‐overload models, which demonstrate that chronically increased wall stress impairs subendocardial perfusion, potentially leading to a secondary microvascular dysfunction superimposed on, or independent of, primary endothelial disease. 48 , 49 Conversely, primary microvascular dysfunction may trigger subendocardial ischemia, which promotes myocardial stiffening and further elevates filling pressures. 18 , 50 However, we cannot exclude shared underlying mechanisms that contribute to each independently.
sections.unmasking distinct clinical trajectories: Although recent registry data suggest that the average patient with ANOCA may have a prognosis similar to the general population, 51 our findings highlight that invasive and AI‐enhanced phenotyping can identify high‐risk biological subsets, specifically those with CMD and elevated filling pressures, who experience higher rates of HF hospitalization and mortality. These observations indicate that clinical risk in ANOCA is not uniformly distributed but is concentrated within physiologically defined phenotypes with divergent trajectories. After overlap weighting, integration of CMD and AIEFP status revealed distinct risk trajectories. The CMD+/AIEFP+ group had the highest early event rate (12.7% at 1 year), consistent with a brittle hemodynamic state combining impaired microvascular reserve and elevated diastolic load. In contrast, CMD−/AIEFP+ exhibited the steepest long‐term risk accumulation (57% at 8 years), reflecting progressive myocardial remodeling despite preserved perfusion. CMD+/AIEFP− showed intermediate risk (37%), suggesting that isolated microvascular dysfunction primarily drives ischemic vulnerability. Collectively, these patterns suggest that myocardial hemodynamic stress is associated with earlier and more sustained risk accumulation than impaired CFR alone. This aligns with prior studies linking low CFR to subclinical diastolic dysfunction and with evidence that combined CMD and diastolic dysfunction markedly increase HF with preserved ejection fraction hospitalization risk. 3 , 41 , 52 , 53 Together, AIEFP and CFR delineate complementary axes of vulnerability: AIEFP captures resting diastolic load, whereas CFR reflects cumulative ischemic burden. Their integration defines temporally distinct yet additive pathways of risk, supporting a unified framework for precision phenotyping and mechanism‐guided investigation in ANOCA.
sections.clinical implications: a scalable progno: From a clinical perspective, the primary value of the AI‐ECG–derived filling pressure signal lies in its role as a scalable prognostic layer rather than a diagnostic alternative to echocardiography. Although echocardiography remains the reference standard for structural and functional assessment, it is resource intensive, is subject to interobserver variability, and often yields indeterminate diastolic classifications. In contrast, the ECG‐derived signal evaluated here provides a widely available, low‐cost marker of myocardial hemodynamic vulnerability that can be applied longitudinally and across care settings. When integrated with invasive coronary physiology, this signal may offer a scalable adjunct for prognostic enrichment by identifying patients in whom myocardial stress contributes meaningfully to adverse outcomes, even in the absence of overt systolic dysfunction or microvascular impairment.
sections.competency in medical knowledge: Integration of invasive CFR and an AI‐ECG marker for elevated filling pressure (AIEFP) provides a complementary framework for prognostic assessment in ANOCA, capturing both vascular and myocardial stress domains. The presence of this ECG‐derived signal may indicate a higher‐risk myocardial phenotype and help prioritize patients for closer evaluation of myocardial hemodynamic burden and individualized longitudinal management, rather than serving as a diagnostic or therapeutic determinant. 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 , 58
sections.translational outlook: AI‐ECG–derived myocardial stress signals may provide a scalable adjunct for prognostic risk stratification in ANOCA. Prospective studies will be required to assess whether such risk stratification meaningfully informs clinical evaluation pathways or improves long‐term outcomes.
sections.strengths and limitations: The strengths of this study include the large, well‐phenotyped cohort with invasive coronary physiology measurements, long‐term follow‐up with adjudicated end points, and a confirmatory propensity score–based analysis. Nevertheless, several limitations merit consideration. This was a single‐center, retrospective study; a prospective, multicenter study with standardized echocardiographic acquisition is required to generalize prognostic performance for clinical deployment. Two CFR assessment techniques (Doppler and thermodilution) were used; however, sensitivity analyses demonstrated consistent results. The AI‐ECG–derived filling pressure marker, although previously validated against echocardiographic measures of diastolic function, represents an indirect, resting surrogate and does not capture instantaneous invasive or exercise‐induced change in hemodynamics. However, its role in identifying a high‐risk phenotype remains clinically significant. Longitudinal medication data were incomplete, limiting assessment of time‐varying treatment effects. Finally, the confirmatory analysis yielded a reduced effective sample size in the highest‐risk strata, underscoring the need for larger studies to support clinical generalizability.
sections.conclusions_1: Integrating invasive coronary flow reserve and an AI‐derived ECG marker of elevated filling pressure distinguishes clinically meaningful ANOCA subgroups with divergent short‐ and long‐term prognoses. Leveraging AI‐ECG, a routinely available test, offers a practical means of identifying a higher‐risk myocardial phenotype. Together, this dual‐axis approach provides a scalable framework for refined prognostic stratification and exploratory phenotypic classification in ANOCA.

title: Robotic single-port plus one-port radical cholecystectomy: description of surgical techniques with video
abstract: Radical cholecystectomy is the standard procedure for gallbladder (GB) cancer, offering the possibility of cure. Many surgeons have increasingly expanded surgical indications following the growing trend of robotic surgery in hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery. This study presents our experience with several robotic single-port (SP) plus one-port radical cholecystectomies using the da Vinci system (Intuitive Surgical). Data from five patients who underwent robotic SP radical cholecystectomy for GB cancer between April 2024 and December 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. All patients presented with imaging findings suggestive of localized GB cancer (T2 or lower). The median operative time was 145 minutes (range, 121–153 minutes), and the median number of harvested lymph nodes was five (range, five to eight). The median hospital stay after surgery was 6 days (range, 6–7 days), with no major complications reported. Robotic SP radical cholecystectomy is a safe and feasible option for GB cancer.

sections.introduction: Gallbladder (GB) cancer is the most predominant malignancy of the biliary tract and is associated with high mortality. Surgical resection is currently the only curative option, with radical cholecystectomy being the standard procedure for resectable GB cancer [ 1 ]. Radical and simple cholecystectomies involve several surgical procedures. However, unlike laparoscopic cholecystectomy, which gained widespread acceptance in the early 1990s, laparoscopic radical cholecystectomy was initially considered a contraindication during the same period. One primary reason for this was the technical difficulties associated with the procedure, such as lymph node (LN) dissection around the hepatoduodenal ligament and liver resection [ 2 ]. Advances in surgical techniques and devices have helped overcome these challenges. Recent studies have shown that the surgical outcomes of laparoscopic radical cholecystectomy are similar to those of open radical cholecystectomy [ 3 ]. As a result, laparoscopic radical cholecystectomy is now an acceptable treatment for GB cancer. However, technical difficulties continue to pose challenges for young surgeons performing the procedure. The robotic approach could offer a solution to technical challenges, as it has advantages such as tremor filtration and enhanced wrist articulation. Several studies have confirmed the feasibility and safety of robotic radical cholecystectomy, supporting the growing trend of robotic surgery in hepatobiliary and pancreatic (HBP) surgery [ 4 ]. The da Vinci single-port (SP) system (Intuitive Surgical) was recently introduced to expand surgical indications from simple cholecystectomies to more complex procedures such as distal pancreatectomies and left lateral sectionectomies [ 5 ]. However, no studies have reported on the clinical outcomes of robotic SP radical cholecystectomy. This case series reports our initial experience with five patients undergoing robotic SP radical cholecystectomy for GB cancer using the da Vinci SP system, focusing on the surgical technique and early outcomes.
sections.enrolled patients: Data from five patients who underwent robotic SP radical cholecystectomy for GB cancer between April 2024 and December 2024 at Severance Hospital in Seoul, Korea were retrospectively reviewed. Presumed patients without hepatic invasion (T2 or lower) on preoperative imaging studies were enrolled [ 6 ]. Their clinicopathological data during the peri- and postoperative periods were reviewed and analyzed. The first SP radical cholecystectomies were performed on April 5, 2024.
sections.detailed procedures: The robotic SP was introduced through a transumbilical site, with an additional 5-mm port placed on the right side. During the procedure, conventional robotic instruments, including bipolar forceps, scissors, and clips, were used. The lesser sac of the stomach was incised and dissected to expose the common hepatic arteries. The LN dissection along the common hepatic artery (No. 8) was dissected, and tissue dissection was performed toward the left side of the hepatoduodenal ligament (No. 12p), which extended the hilar area. Skeletonization of the dissection around the hepatoduodenal ligament (No. 12a) provided a clear view of the cystic duct’s origin from the common bile duct. After cystic artery ligation and division, the cystic duct was ligated and divided at its junction with the common bile duct. The resection margin of the cystic duct was sent to a pathologist for frozen section analysis. The LN dissection around Calot’s triangle (No. 12b) and the posterior common bile duct was performed, with dissection directed toward the posterior surface of the pancreatic head (No. 13). Cholecystectomy, including full-thickness dissection with the use of a cystic plate, is typically performed during GB detachment from the liver. If the tumor was located on the hepatic side, an extended cholecystectomy (i.e., en bloc resection including liver parenchyma over 1 cm deep) was performed to achieve clear margins. After detachment, the specimen was extracted through the umbilicus, and a drain was placed through the 5-mm-port site ( Supplementary Video ).
sections.clinical characteristics of the patients: Table 1 presents the clinicopathological characteristics of the five patients. The median age of the patients was 76 years (range, 74–77 years), and their median preoperative carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were 48.3 U/mL (range, 44.0–54.2 U/mL). The median operation time was 145 minutes (range, 121–153 minutes), and the median number of harvested LNs was five (range, five to eight). The median hospital stay after surgery was 6 days (range, 6–7 days), and no major complications were observed.
sections.discussion: This case series reports the immediate surgical outcomes of robotic SP radical cholecystectomy for GB cancer. Although only five patients were analyzed owing to their initial experience, safe and feasible clinical outcomes without major complications were observed. Radical cholecystectomy involves the removal of the GB (colecystectomy) and lymphadenectomy. Owing to its anatomical location, the extent of resection for GB cancer varies depending on the clinical status. The GB is attached to the liver in the subhepatic area, connected to the common bile duct for biliary drainage, and lies adjacent to the duodenum. Therefore, radical resection of GB cancer varies from a simple cholecystectomy to a more extensive hepatopancreatoduodenectomy [ 3 ]. In most cases, surgeons can predict and determine the extent of resection based on preoperative imaging studies. However, the optimal extent of lymphadenectomy remains controversial. Several guidelines, including those of the AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer), UICC (Union for International Cancer Control), and the Japanese Society of Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery, provide recommendations on the extent of lymphadenectomy during radical cholecystectomy [ 7 , 8 ]. For example, all these guidelines agree on the need for LN dissection around the hepatoduodenal ligament (No. 12), but they differ on including LN dissection at the posterior surface of the pancreatic head (No. 13). Although there is no consensus on the dissection of No. 13 LNs, several studies have highlighted the oncological impact of dissection in this area. If surgeons consider performing No. 13 LN dissection, the laparoscopic approach becomes challenging owing to its inherent limitations. Unlike pancreatoduodenectomy, where the head and duodenum of the pancreas are often resected, these structures must be reserved during radical cholecystectomy. Occasionally, their anatomical structure obstructs a clear surgical view, requiring wide Kocher maneuvers. Furthermore, most laparoscopic instruments are rigid, limiting options for addressing these challenges in a laparoscopic setting. On the robotic platform, a robotic arm with multiple degrees of freedom and wrist articulation can easily access the posterior surface of the pancreatic head with minimal Kocherization. This is a key advantage of using the robotic platform [ 9 ]. Furthermore, unlike the multiport system, the camera of the da Vinci SP system can be angulated to provide a bird’s-eye view of the surgical field, similar to that in an open approach. This unique feature distinguishes the SP system from other robotic platforms. So far, there is no study comparing SP and a multiport system for robotic radical cholecystectomy. Comparing the SP system indirectly with the multiport system, which was compared with the laparoscopic platform, revealed similar perioperative and immediate postoperative outcomes [ 10 ]. However, the SP system showed a relatively lower number of harvested LNs compared to the multiport system. It seemed that a selection bias related to enrolled relatively early-stage patients in the initial period for the SP system may have occurred. For statistical analysis, further experience, including a sufficient number of cases, is mandatory. This case series has some limitations. First, as the first study to report robotic SP radical cholecystectomy, we selectively enrolled patients and all patients had confirmed T2 stage cancer. While no significant issues occurred during wedge resection of the liver using the SP robotic platform, further experience with T3 or T4 stages is essential for more extensive hepatectomies, such as segment 4b + 5 resection. Second, this study is a case series, and no statistical comparisons were made between laparoscopic and multiport robotic radical cholecystectomy. Larger studies are needed for statistical analyses and to provide conclusive evidence. Nonetheless, this case series is valuable as it introduces a novel treatment modality for GB cancer. To our knowledge, this is the first case series of robotic SP radical cholecystectomy for GB cancer and meaningfully demonstrates that robotic reduced-port radical cholecystectomy using the SP system is technically feasible and safe in selected early-stage GB cancer. Further studies are needed to evaluate long-term oncologic outcomes. Overall, robotic SP plus one-port radical cholecystectomy appears to be a safe and feasible option for treating GB cancer. Further studies are needed to validate and generalize these findings.

title: Peripheral Circulating Exosomes Induce Sepsis-associated Liver Injury by Up-regulating STAT1 to Promote Autophagy and Regulating the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 Axis to Promote Ferroptosis
abstract: Peripheral exosomes have been implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple organ dysfunction during sepsis. However, their role in sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of circulating exosomes on hepatic injury and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms of SALI. A murine sepsis model was established via intraperitoneal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Peripheral exosomes were isolated and co-cultured with murine hepatocytes (AML12 cells). RNA sequencing identified Signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) as a key regulator in exosome-induced liver injury. Since STAT1 functions upstream of the ferroptosis-related solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11)–glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis, further in viv o and in vitro experiments were conducted to clarify its mechanistic role. In vitro , exosomes derived from septic mice enhanced inflammatory responses in AML12 cells via STAT1-mediated autophagy and modulation of the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis, leading to ferroptosis. Inhibition of STAT1 abrogated these effects, whereas STAT1 overexpression potentiated them. In vivo , septic exosomes (sep-Exo) induced liver injury in mice, while suppression of STAT1 abolished the regulatory effects of sep-Exo on ferroptosis, autophagy, and hepatic inflammation. Our findings reveal a novel mechanism underlying SALI, whereby peripheral exosomes upregulate STAT1 to induce autophagy and modulate the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis, thereby promoting ferroptosis and hepatic inflammation during sepsis. Graphical Abstract Peripheral circulating exosomes induce SALI by upregulating STAT1 to promote autophagy and modulating the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 axis to induce ferroptosis Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10753-026-02495-6.

sections.graphical abstract: Peripheral circulating exosomes induce SALI by upregulating STAT1 to promote autophagy and modulating the SLC7A11-GSH-GPX4 axis to induce ferroptosis
sections.supplementary information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10753-026-02495-6.
sections.introduction: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by dysregulated host responses to infection, leading to acute and progressive organ dysfunction [ 1 ]. It remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide [ 2 ]. Despite advances in early antibiotic administration, fluid resuscitation, and multi-organ support strategies, the overall prognosis for patients with sepsis remains unsatisfactory [ 3 ]. Therefore, elucidating the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying sepsis-induced organ injury is essential for improving clinical outcomes. The liver plays a pivotal role in metabolism and immune regulation, contributing to energy storage, detoxification, coagulation, and hormonal homeostasis [ 4 ]. Increasing evidence suggests that hepatic dysfunction is a common and severe complication of sepsis, significantly influencing disease progression and patient prognosis [ 5 ]. As a frontline immune organ, the liver is often among the first organs affected during sepsis and frequently exhibits severe injury [ 6 ]. Excessive microbial burden and the ensuing cytokine storm can trigger hyperactivation of inflammatory pathways, leading to disruption of homeostasis and hepatocellular death [ 7 , 8 ]. Clinically, the mortality rate in septic patients with hepatic dysfunction has been reported to range from 54% to 68% [ 4 ], underscoring the urgent need to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI). Ferroptosis, a regulated form of cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has emerged as a critical contributor to multiple organ failure during sepsis. The solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11)–glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) axis represents a core antioxidant defense system that protects cells from oxidative stress-induced ferroptosis. Dysregulation of this pathway may accelerate the progression of septic organ injury. Given the liver’s essential role in iron storage and metabolism, hepatocytes are particularly susceptible to ferroptotic death under conditions of iron overload. Excessive accumulation of free iron can exacerbate oxidative damage and impair hepatic function, particularly under lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory stress. Although several studies have linked ferroptosis to sepsis pathophysiology [ 9 , 10 ], the upstream molecular mechanisms initiating this process remain poorly understood. Exosomes, nanosized extracellular vesicles secreted by a wide range of cell types, including platelets, endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cells [ 11 ], are key mediators of intercellular communication. They transport bioactive molecules such as lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids, thereby regulating the biological behavior of recipient cells [ 12 ]. Growing evidence indicates that exosomes play crucial roles in both local and systemic inflammatory responses. In septic mouse models, serum-derived exosomes promote macrophage proliferation and inflammatory activation [ 13 ], while neutrophil-derived exosomes deliver miR-30-5p to induce macrophage polarization and pyroptosis [ 14 ]. These findings suggest that exosomes actively participate in the pathogenesis of sepsis; however, their specific contribution to SALI remains incompletely understood. Signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1), a member of the STAT transcription factor family, is a key downstream effector of the interferon-mediated Janus kinase–signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK–STAT) signaling pathway [ 15 ]. Upon activation, STAT1 translocates to the nucleus and binds specific DNA elements to regulate gene expression. During inflammatory responses, STAT1 directly interacts with the HMGB1 promoter (− 1700 to − 700 bp), thereby enhancing transcription of this late inflammatory mediator [ 16 ]. Elevated STAT1 activity has been observed in septic patients, where it acts as a central signaling hub integrating multiple inflammatory pathways to amplify cytokine production [ 17 ]. However, whether STAT1 functions as a critical molecular link between circulating exosomes and ferroptosis-mediated hepatic injury in sepsis remains unclear. Based on these observations, we hypothesized that peripheral circulating exosomes contribute to SALI by modulating the STAT1 signaling pathway. To test this hypothesis, we established an LPS-induced murine sepsis model and isolated circulating exosomes from septic mice. Through a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments, we demonstrated that these exosomes induce hepatocyte injury, promote autophagy, and trigger ferroptosis. RNA sequencing further identified STAT1 upregulation as a pivotal event in this process. Mechanistic analyses revealed that peripheral circulating exosomes induce autophagy and ferroptosis via STAT1-dependent regulation of the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis. Collectively, this study uncovers a novel pathological pathway through which circulating exosomes mediate SALI, providing new insights into potential therapeutic strategies for sepsis.
sections.patients and control subjects: The study protocol, procedures, and recruitment of patients and control subjects were approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University, China (IACUC No. IRB-AF/SC-04/02.0). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University and was performed in accordance with the ethical standards as laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Clinical trial number: IRB number: LC2024-058. A total of 80 patients admitted to the Department of Critical Care Medicine at the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University were enrolled between March 2022 and May 2023, including 40 patients diagnosed with SALI and 40 septic patients without liver injury. Blood samples and clinical data were collected upon admission. The diagnosis of sepsis was established according to the Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3). Inclusion criteria were as follows: Adult patients meeting the Sepsis-3 diagnostic criteria; Liver injury defined by at least one of the following parameters: Total bilirubin (TBIL) > 34.2 µmol/L; Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) > 120 U/L; Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) > 120 U/L. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy, a history of malignancy, drug-induced liver injury, chronic liver disease, autoimmune or metabolic liver disorders, acute liver failure, immunosuppressive or immunodeficiency conditions, and incomplete clinical data that could interfere with statistical analysis. In addition, 20 healthy adult volunteers were recruited from the local community in Harbin as healthy controls. The expression levels of exosome-specific markers, including CD63, CD9, and TSG101, were quantitatively measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels were obtained from routine laboratory test results, and their correlations with serum AST and ALT levels in patients with SALI were further analyzed.
sections.animal model: Male wild-type C57BL/6 mice (6–8 weeks old, weighing 18–25 g) were obtained from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). All mice were maintained under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions in the Hulan Laboratory Animal Center of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University, with controlled temperature (22 ± 2 °C), humidity (55 ± 10%), and a 12-hour light/dark cycle, and were provided ad libitum access to food and water. All animal procedures, including the establishment of the sepsis model and euthanasia, were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Harbin Medical University (IACUC No. 2021100) and conducted in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals issued by the National Institutes of Health.
sections.cell culture: The murine hepatocyte cell line AML12 cells was obtained from Procell Life Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). Cells were cultured in complete AML12 growth medium consisting of a 1:1 mixture of Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium and Ham’s F12 (DMEM/F12; ATCC 30-2006) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; ATCC 30-2020), 10 µg/mL insulin, 5.5 µg/mL transferrin, 5 ng/mL selenium, and 40 ng/mL dexamethasone. Cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂.
sections.lps-induced mouse model of sali: Male SPF C57BL/6 mice were fasted for 12 h with free access to water, followed by water deprivation for 6 h prior to the experiment. All animals were weighed before the start of the experiment. Mice in the control group received intraperitoneal injections of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Mice in the experimental group were intraperitoneally injected with LPS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) dissolved in PBS to induce SALI. The final concentration of the solution was 1.5 mg/mL, corresponding to an LPS dose of 15 mg/kg body weight per mouse. GW4869 (2.5 mg/kg; CM01341, Proteintech, China) was administered intraperitoneally 1 h prior to LPS or PBS injection as pretreatment. Twenty-four hours later, all mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection of an overdose of pentobarbital sodium (100 mg/kg). Blood samples were collected into EDTA-containing tubes, and liver tissues were harvested for subsequent histological analysis.
sections.histological analysis of liver tissues: Liver samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (P0099-3 L, Beyotime, China) for 24 h, embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Histopathological changes were examined using a light microscope.
sections.measurement of serum and cellular ast an: AST and ALT were determined using commercial assay kits (AKAM006M and AKAM019M, Boxbio, China) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. For cellular assays, AML12 cells were harvested by centrifugation at 800×g for 5 min at room temperature. Approximately 5 × 10⁶ cells were lysed in 1 mL extraction buffer and sonicated on ice (20% power, 3 s on/10 s off, for 30 cycles). The lysates were then centrifuged at 8,000×g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatants were collected for analysis. For liver tissue assays, 0.1 g of liver tissue was homogenized in 1 mL extraction buffer and centrifugation at 8,000×g for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant was used for enzymatic assays. The reactions were performed in 96-well plates by sequentially adding reagents according to the manufacturer’s instructions, followed by incubation at 37 °C. Absorbance was measured at 505 nm using a microplate reader, and AST and ALT levels were calculated based on the manufacturer’s formulas.
sections.elisa: Serum levels of exosome markers, including CD63 (ml105153, Mlbio, China), CD9 (CSB-EL004969HU, Cusabio, China), and TSG101 (ml105672, Mlbio, China) were quantified in clinical samples. Levels of inflammatory cytokines interleukin-1β (IL-1β; ml058059, Mlbio, China) and interleukin-18 (IL-18; ml058055, Mlbio, China) were measured in mouse serum and AML12 cell culture supernatants using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
sections.rna extraction and quantitative real-tim: Total RNA was isolated from tissues or cultured cells using TRIzol reagent (YEASEN, 19202ES60). Reverse transcription was performed using the Hifair ® II 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix for qRT-PCR (YEASEN, 11123ES60). Quantitative PCR was conducted using the Hieff ® qRT-PCR SYBR Green Master Mix (YEASEN, 11200ES50) on an ABI 7500 Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The amplification protocol consisted of 95 °C for 5 min, followed by 40 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, 60 °C for 20 s, and 72 °C for 31 s. GAPDH was used as the internal reference gene. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2⁻ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Table 1 . Table 1 Primer Sequences Used for qRT-PCR.
