sections.western blot analysis: Tissues and cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (G2002, Servicebio, China) supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (ST506, Beyotime, China). Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000×g for 5 min, and protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (P0012, Beyotime, China). Equal amounts of protein were mixed with 5× loading buffer (P0015L, Beyotime, China) and boiled for 10 min. Proteins were separated by SDS–PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. After blocking, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using a chemiluminescent substrate (MA0186, Meilunbio, China). Primary antibodies included IL-1β (1:10000, 16806-1-AP, Proteintech, China), IL-18 (1:50000, 10663-1-AP, Proteintech, China), CD63 (1:2000, AB-3713000, Abmart, China), CD9 (1:2000, M050808S, Abmart, China), TSG101 (1:2000, T55985XS, Abmart, China), SLC7A11 (1:4000, 26864-1-AP, Proteintech, China), GPX4 (1:4000, 67763-1-Ig, Proteintech, China), ACSL4 (1:50000, 22401-1-AP, Proteintech, China), Nrf2 (1:2000, 16396-1-AP, Proteintech, China), LC3 (1:8000, 14600-1-AP, Proteintech, China), and p62 (1:50000, 18420-1-AP, Proteintech, China) .
sections.exosome isolation and characterization: Serum samples were collected from LPS-treated mice in EDTA-containing tubes and processed within 2 h. Samples were centrifuged at 3,000×g for 10 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was diluted with seven volumes of PBS. The diluted samples were filtered through 0.22 μm membranes and ultracentrifuged at 200,000×g for 2 h at 4 °C. The resulting pellets were resuspended in PBS and ultracentrifuged again at 200,000×g for 1 h. Purified exosomes were finally resuspended in PBS and stored at 4 °C. Exosome morphology and size distribution were characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA). Expression of exosome marker proteins (CD63, CD9, and TSG101) was confirmed by Western blot analysis.
sections.stat1 inhibition and overexpression: To inhibit STAT1 expression, AML12 cells were pretreated with fludarabine (50 µM; CM00136, Proteintech, China) for 1 h before exposure to exosomes. For STAT1 overexpression, AML12 cells were infected with a lentiviral vector (GL180, pcSLenti-EF1-EGFP-P2A-Puro-CMV-Stat1-3×FLAG-WPRE; H36963 , GeneChem, China). Seventy-two hours after infection, overexpression efficiency was confirmed by Western blot analysis.
sections.autophagy inhibition and activation: In the in vitro experiments, autophagy was inhibited by pre-treating AML12 cells with chloroquine (CQ; 10 µmol/L; C6628, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 1 h prior to exosome exposure. To activate autophagy, AML12 cells were pretreated with rapamycin (20 nmol/L; 553210, Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 1 h before exosome treatment. In the in vivo experiments, autophagy inhibition was achieved by intraperitoneal injection of CQ (60 mg/kg) administered 1 h before exosome injection. For autophagy activation, rapamycin (1 mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally 1 h prior to exosome injection.
sections.in vivo and in vitro exosome treatments: For in vivo experiments, serum-derived exosomes from the corresponding groups were administered via tail vein injection at a dose of 300 µg per mouse. Twenty-four hours after injection, mice were euthanized, and liver tissues were harvested for subsequent analyses. For in vitro experiments, AML12 cells were pretreated with GW4869 (20 µmol/L) for 1 h to minimize the interference of endogenous exosome secretion. GW4869 is a neutral sphingomyelinase inhibitor that suppresses exosome biogenesis and release. After pretreatment, AML12 cells were co-cultured with serum-derived exosomes at a concentration of 100 µg/mL at 37 °C for 24 h. After incubation, cells and culture supernatants were collected for subsequent analyses.
sections.immunofluorescence staining: Cells and liver tissues were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (P0099-3 L, Beyotime, China), permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 10% bovine serum albumin (BSA; A8010, Solarbio, China). Samples were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against GPX4 (1:200, 67763-1-IG, Proteintech, China) or LC3 (1:200, 81004-1-RR, Proteintech, China), followed by incubation with Alexa Fluor-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:500, F2761, Thermo Fisher Scientific, China) for 1 h at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (C0065, Solarbio, China) for 10 min, and fluorescence images were captured using a fluorescence microscope.
sections.detection of reactive oxygen species (ro: Frozen liver sections were incubated with ROS detection reagent (G1045, Servicebio, China) in a humidified chamber at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark. After washing with PBS three times, the sections were stained with DAPI (G1012, Servicebio, China), and mounted using antifade mounting medium (G1401, Servicebio, China). Fluorescence images were obtained using a Nikon ECLIPSE C1 fluorescence microscope (Nikon, Japan).
sections.measurement of fe\u00b2\u207a, tissue ir: Intracellular Fe²⁺ levels were determined using an iron assay kit (E-BC-K881-M, Elabscience, China). Total tissue iron content was quantified using a tissue iron detection kit (AKIC001C, Boxbio, China). Lipid peroxidation, a hallmark of ferroptosis, was assessed by measuring MDA levels (AKFA013M, Boxbio, China).The antioxidant capacity was evaluated by measuring GSH levels (AKPR008M, Boxbio, China), following the manufacturer’s instructions.
sections.rna sequencing and analysis: After 24 h co-culture of AML12 cells with serum-derived exosomes from LPS-treated or untreated mice, total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (YEASEN, 19202ES60). RNA purity and concentration were determined using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA), and RNA integrity was assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). cDNA libraries were prepared using the VAHTS Universal V10 total RNA was extracted for transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) Library Prep Kit (Premixed Version), and sequencing was performed by OE Biotech Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China).
sections.rna interference of stat1: Adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) vectors carrying STAT1 shRNA or scrambled control shRNA were synthesized by GeneChem (Shanghai, China). The targeting sequences were: STAT1-shRNA#1, 5′-GGAGGTCTTTGTTCCCTTTCA-3′; STAT1-shRNA#2, 5′-GGTCTTTGTTCCCTTTCAGAC-3′; Scrambled control, 5′-GGTGTATGGGCTACTATAGAA-3′. AAV8 vectors were injected via the tail vein four weeks before serum exosome administration.
sections.statistical analysis: All data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Comparisons between two groups were performed using Student’s t-test, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was used for multiple-group comparisons. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software (version 9.0).
sections.elevated levels of circulating exosomes: To verify the clinical relevance of our subsequent experiments, a preliminary analysis was conducted using plasma samples collected from patients. The expression levels of the exosome-specific markers CD63, CD9, and TSG101 in human plasma were measured by ELISA. Previous studies have demonstrated that CD63 and CD9, members of the tetraspanin protein family that are highly enriched on exosomal membranes, serve as reliable markers for exosomes, with CD63 exhibiting stable accumulation along the endocytic pathway [ 18 , 19 ]. Notably, Yunjoo Im et al. reported that elevated CD63 levels are associated with the severity of organ failure in patients with sepsis and may serve as a predictor of mortality [ 20 ]. In addition, other proteins such as Alix and TSG101 are involved in exosome biogenesis and membrane trafficking [ 21 ]. Based on these findings, we evaluated serum exosome abundance by quantifying the expression of CD63, CD9, and TSG101. The results revealed that plasma levels of these exosomal markers were significantly higher in patients with sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI, n = 40) than in septic patients without liver injury ( n = 40) and healthy controls ( n = 20) (Figs. 1 A–C). Fig. 1 Increased circulating exosome levels in patients with SALI are positively correlated with serum AST and ALT levels. ( G – I ) Correlation analyses of exosomal markers CD63 ( G ), CD9 ( H ), and TSG101 ( I ) with serum levels of ALT in patients with SALI. ( J – L ) Correlation analyses of exosomal markers CD63 ( J ), CD9 ( K ), and TSG101 ( L ) with serum levels of LDH in patients with SALI. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001 Further correlation analyses demonstrated that the plasma concentrations of the exosomal markers CD63, CD9, and TSG101 were positively correlated with the serum levels of AST and ALT in patients with liver injury (Figs. 1 D–I). To further exclude the possibility that the elevated levels of exosomal markers were attributable to cell necrosis or nonspecific cell lysis, LDH levels were obtained from routine laboratory test results and their correlations with plasma concentrations of CD63, CD9, and TSG101 were analyzed in patients with liver injury. The results showed no significant correlations between LDH levels and these exosomal markers (Figs. 1 J–L), suggesting that the observed increase in exosomal markers was unlikely to result from cell necrosis or nonspecific cellular disruption. Taken together, these findings indicate that circulating exosomes are markedly increased in patients with SALI and may reflect the extent of hepatic injury during sepsis. These findings indicate that the expression levels of exosomal marker proteins were markedly increased in patients with SALI and positively correlated with the severity of hepatic dysfunction. This observation suggests that exosomes may play an important role in the pathogenesis of SALI. Accordingly, we next aimed to elucidate the relationship between exosomes and SALI.
sections.establishment of a mouse model of sali: To investigate the role of serum exosomes in SALI, serum-derived exosomes were isolated from mice with LPS-induced SALI and subsequently administered to healthy mice and normal hepatocytes to assess their pathogenic potential. Initially, a murine model of SALI was established by intraperitoneal injection of LPS ( n = 6). To validate the effectiveness of the model, the serum levels of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β (Fig. 2 A) and IL-18 (Fig. 2 B) were measured using ELISA. Both cytokines were significantly elevated in the LPS-treated group compared with the control group. In addition, the serum levels of hepatic injury markers AST (Fig. 2 C) and ALT (Fig. 2 D) were markedly increased in the LPS group. Consistent with these findings, qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses demonstrated upregulated expression of IL-1β (Fig. 2 E and G), IL-6 (Fig. 2 F), and IL-18 (Fig. 2G) at both the mRNA and protein levels in liver tissues. Histopathological examination further revealed severe hepatic injury in LPS-treated mice, characterized by marked inflammatory cell infiltration, tissue edema, and hemorrhagic lesions (Fig. 2 H). sections.isolation and characterization of periph: To investigate the role of peripheral circulating exosomes in SALI, serum-derived exosomes were isolated from LPS-induced septic mice and control mice. TEM revealed that the isolated vesicles displayed the typical cup-shaped morphology characteristic of exosomes, with diameters ranging from approximately 40–150 nm (Fig. 3 A). NTA demonstrated that the particle size distribution peaked within the 40–150 nm range, which is consistent with previously reported exosome profiles (Fig. 3 B) [ 22 ]. Notably, NTA quantification showed a significantly higher concentration of circulating exosomes in the LPS-treated group than in the control group (Fig. 3 C), suggesting that systemic inflammation promotes exosome release. Western blot analysis further confirmed the expression of the exosomal marker proteins CD9, CD63, and TSG101 in both groups (Fig. 3 D), thereby validating the successful isolation and identity of exosomes. Moreover, the expression levels of these markers were markedly increased in the LPS-treated group compared with the control group (Fig. 3 D), indicating that the development of SALI may be associated with increased exosome activity. sections.peripheral circulating exosomes induce a: Exosomes were successfully isolated from mice and co‑incubated with AML12 cells for 24 h (Fig. 4 A). After 24 h of incubation, the levels of hepatocellular injury markers AST and ALT were markedly elevated in AML12 cells treated with sep-Exo, whereas both parameters were significantly reduced in the con-Exo and GW4869-pretreated groups (Fig. 4 B). To further evaluate the contribution of exosomes to SALI, the expression of proinflammatory cytokines was assessed by ELISA, qRT-PCR, and Western blot. The results showed that IL-1β (Figs. 4 C, H, E), IL-18 (Figs. 4 D, H), IL-6 (Fig. 4 F), and TNF-α (Fig. 4 G) were significantly upregulated in the sep-Exo–treated group, whereas GW4869 pretreatment markedly attenuated these increases. These findings suggest that peripheral circulating exosomes contribute to the progression of SALI. Fig. 4 Peripheral circulating exosomes induce AML12 cell injury through ferroptosis and autophagy. ( P ) Immunofluorescence staining of LC3 in AML12 cells under different treatments (Blue: DAPI; Red: LC3). ( Q ) Western blot analysis of LC3 and p62 protein expression in AML12 cells. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. * P < 0.05, ** P < 0.01, *** P < 0.001 Previous studies have demonstrated that excessive levels of labile iron are hepatotoxic, triggering ferroptosis and exacerbating liver injury under LPS challenge. Increasing evidence indicates a close association between ferroptosis and sepsis [ 9 ]. Moreover, accumulating studies suggest a functional interplay between autophagy and ferroptosis, in which autophagy regulates iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and ROS accumulation [ 23 , 24 ]. To further elucidate the mechanisms underlying exosome-mediated hepatocellular injury, we systematically assessed markers associated with ferroptosis and autophagy. Compared with the con-Exo group, sep-Exo treatment significantly increased intracellular Fe²⁺ (Fig. 4 I) and MDA (Fig. 4 J) levels, while reducing GSH levels (Fig. 4 K). These alterations were partially reversed by GW4869 pretreatment, as Fe²⁺ and MDA levels decreased while GSH levels were restored. At the transcriptional level, qRT-PCR revealed that the mRNA expression of SLC7A11 (Fig. 4 L) and GPX4 (Fig. 4 M) was markedly downregulated in sep-Exo-treated cells, whereas GW4869 pretreatment restored their expression. Consistently, Western blot analysis demonstrated reduced protein levels of SLC7A11, GPX4, and nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2), accompanied by increased expression of acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4) in the sep-Exo group; GW4869 treatment partially restored these protein levels (Fig. 4 O). The SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis is a classical ferroptosis-suppressing pathway [ 25 , 26 ]. Within this pathway, SLC7A11 mediates cystine uptake, promoting cysteine and GSH synthesis, whereas GPX4 utilizes GSH as a cofactor to reduce lipid peroxides, thereby inhibiting ferroptosis [ 25 , 27 ]. The concurrent downregulation of SLC7A11, GSH, and GPX4 observed in our study suggests that sep-Exo may promote ferroptosis by disrupting this protective axis. Furthermore, immunofluorescence analysis revealed that sep-Exo markedly increased intracellular ROS accumulation, which was significantly attenuated by GW4869 pretreatment (Fig. 4 N). Regarding autophagy-related markers, sep-Exo treatment increased LC3 expression while reducing p62 levels, whereas GW4869 pretreatment reversed these alterations (Fig. 4 P and Q). Collectively, these findings indicate that septic serum-derived exosomes (sep-Exo) induce AML12 hepatocellular injury by promoting both ferroptosis and autophagy, likely through modulation of the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 signaling axis.
sections.stat1 is identified as a key differentia: To further elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which septic serum-derived exosomes promote autophagy-and ferroptosis-associated hepatocellular injury, equal amounts of serum exosomes derived from PBS-treated control mice (con-Exo) and LPS-treated septic mice (sep-Exo) were applied to AML12 cells. After 24 h of treatment, total RNA was extracted for transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq). RNA-seq analysis revealed substantial transcriptional differences between the two groups (Fig. 5 A). Principal component analysis (PCA) and sample correlation heatmaps analysis demonstrated high intragroup reproducibility and clear intergroup separation (Figs. 5 B–C), confirming that exposure to different exosomal sources induced distinct global gene expression profiles in AML12 cells. Differential expression analysis identified a total of 1,556 upregulated genes and 1,238 downregulated genes (|log₂FC| > 1, p < 0.05) in the sep-Exo group compared with the con-Exo group. Among the upregulated genes, STAT1 exhibited one of the most pronounced increases in expression (Figs. 5 D–E), suggesting that it may serve as a key transcriptional mediator of the cellular response to septic exosomes. ( G ) Venn diagram showing the overlap between upregulated genes in the sep-Exo group and predicted transcription factors binding to the SLC7A11 promoter region, highlighting STAT1 as the only overlapping candidate gene To explore the potential role of STAT1 in regulating ferroptosis, we retrieved the promoter sequence of the mouse SLC7A11 gene (− 2000 nt upstream to + 100 nt downstream of the transcription start site) from the UCSC Genome Browser and predicted transcription factor binding site (TFBS) using the PROMO database (species: Mus musculus, dissimilarity threshold: 5%). A total of 29 potential transcription factors were predicted to bind within this promoter region. By integrating these TFBS predictions with our RNA-seq differential expression data, STAT1 was identified as a putative upstream regulator of SLC7A11 (Fig. 5 F). Furthermore, cross-comparison analysis revealed that STAT1 was the only overlapping gene between the 1,556 upregulated genes in the sep-Exo group and the 29 predicted SLC7A11-binding transcription factors (Fig. 5 G). These findings strongly suggest that STAT1 may function as a direct upstream regulatory factor of SLC7A11, mediating the pro-ferroptotic effects of septic exosomes during SALI.
sections.peripheral circulating exosomes regulate: To elucidate the regulatory role of STAT1 in exosome-mediated ferroptosis and autophagy during SALI, AML12 cell models with altered STAT1 expression were established. A stable STAT1-overexpressing (OE-STAT1) cell line was generated via lentiviral transduction, whereas STAT1 inhibition was achieved by treating cells with Fludarabine (FLUD, 50 µM). Western blot analysis confirmed a significant downregulation of STAT1 in the FLUD-treated group and marked upregulation in the OE-STAT1 group, indicating successful establishment of the STAT1-modulated models (Fig. 6 B). Given that ferroptosis and autophagy are key mechanisms of septic exosome–induced hepatocellular injury and that transcriptomic analysis suggested STAT1 as an upstream regulator of SLC7A11, we next investigated whether STAT1 modulates ferroptosis via the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis, a canonical ferroptosis-suppressing pathway [ 25 , 26 ]. STAT1 suppression significantly decreased intracellular Fe²⁺ and MDA levels while increasing GSH content, whereas STAT1 overexpression produced opposite effects (Figs. 6 K–M). Consistently, qRT-PCR revealed that STAT1 inhibition upregulated SLC7A11 and GPX4 mRNA, whereas STAT1 overexpression repressed their transcription (Figs. 6 N–O), indicating that STAT1 negatively regulates the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 pathway. sections.peripheral circulating exosomes mediate: To validate the reliability of the above in vitro findings, we further conducted in vivo experiments in C57BL/6 mice. A liver-specific STAT1 knockdown mouse model (sh-STAT1) was established via shRNA lentiviral transfection. qRT-PCR analysis confirmed that among three shRNA constructs, shRNA#1 exhibited the highest silencing efficiency and was therefore selected for subsequent in vivo experiments (Fig. 8 B). To further clarify the role of STAT1 in hepatic inflammation, we quantified the levels of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-18, IL-6, and TNF-α in liver tissues using ELISA, qRT-PCR, and Western blot analyses. The results revealed that sep-Exo treatment markedly upregulated these cytokines, whereas both GW4869 treatment and STAT1 knockdown significantly reversed this effect (Figs. 8 H–M). Collectively, these findings suggest that peripheral circulating exosomes are critical mediators of SALI, with STAT1 acting as a pivotal pathogenic regulator. To elucidate the mechanistic basis of ferroptosis and autophagy regulation in this process, we next assessed the impact of circulating exosomes and STAT1 modulation on key ferroptosis-related parameters. Compared with the con-Exo group, hepatic Fe²⁺ and MDA levels were significantly elevated, whereas GSH content was reduced in the sep-Exo group. Both GW4869 treatment and STAT1 knockdown effectively reversed these changes (Figs. 8 N–P). qRT-PCR analysis revealed that sep-Exo markedly downregulated SLC7A11 and GPX4 mRNA expression, whereas both GW4869 treatment and STAT1 knockdown restored their expression (Figs. 8 Q–R), indicating that STAT1 participates in regulating the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis. Consistently, Western blot results confirmed that sep-Exo decreased SLC7A11, GPX4, and Nrf2 expression while increasing ACSL4 levels; these alterations were reversed by either GW4869 treatment or STAT1 knockdown (Fig. 8 T). Immunofluorescence staining of GPX4 showed a similar pattern (Fig. 8 U). In addition, ROS accumulation was markedly enhanced in sep-Exo–treated mice but was significantly reduced following GW4869 treatment or STAT1 knockdown (Fig. 8 S). Conversely, both GW4869 treatment and STAT1 knockdown attenuated autophagy, as evidenced by decreased LC3/GAPDH and increased p62 expression (Figs. 8 V–W). Notably, the shRNA viral vector alone did not alleviate liver injury induced by peripheral circulating exosomes, as no improvement was observed in the sep + Vehicle or sep + sh-Scr groups (Fig. 8 D-W). In contrast, STAT1 knockdown markedly attenuated exosome-mediated hepatic injury, indicating that the protective effect was specifically attributable to STAT1 modulation rather than nonspecific effects of viral transduction.

sections.discussion: Sepsis remains one of the most formidable challenges in clinical medicine, with its global incidence and mortality continuing to rise and frequently leading to multiple organ dysfunction. Previous studies have shown that sepsis can cause extensive damage to multiple organs, including the kidneys and lungs. For instance, in a septic mouse model, γδ T17 cells were reported to migrate from the intestine to the lungs, where they regulate IL-17A–mediated pulmonary inflammation through the CCL1–Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway in alveolar macrophages [ 28 ]. Another study demonstrated that the histone methyltransferase EZH2 modulates apoptosis and inflammation in sepsis-induced acute kidney injury [ 29 ]. In addition to these organs, the liver is also highly susceptible to septic injury. Chuanhuning has been shown to alleviate sepsis-associated acute liver injury by inhibiting ferroptosis through modulation of the gut microbiota [ 30 ], while CD39 restricts P2 × 7 receptor–mediated inflammatory signaling and mitigates sepsis-induced hepatic damage [ 31 ]. Despite these advances, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying SALI remain incompletely understood [ 32 – 34 ]. LPS, a major endotoxin derived from Gram-negative bacteria, is widely used to establish experimental models of sepsis. In the present study, we successfully established an LPS-induced mouse model of SALI and isolated serum-derived exosomes, which were subsequently characterized and validated for downstream experiments. Exosomes serve as critical mediators of intercellular communication, transferring bioactive molecules such as growth factors, signaling lipids, and genetic material encapsulated within a lipid bilayer [ 35 ]. These vesicles are secreted by multiple cell types and are present in nearly all body fluids [ 36 – 38 ]. Circulating exosomes, in particular, are easily accessible, circulate systemically, and maintain remarkable structural stability, thereby exerting important regulatory functions in both physiological and pathological processes [ 39 ]. For example, serum exosomes derived from diabetic mice can be internalized by aortic endothelial cells, leading to endothelial dysfunction in healthy mice [ 40 ]. Another study demonstrated that blood-borne exosomes can be internalized by dendritic cells to induce donor-specific transplant tolerance [ 41 ]. Notably, recent evidence indicates that circulating exosomal mRNA may serve as an early predictive biomarker for persistent organ failure in acute pancreatitis [ 42 ], while exosomal miR-155 promotes macrophage proliferation and inflammatory activation [ 13 ]. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical roles of circulating exosomes in inflammation-related pathologies. However, their specific contribution to SALI remains poorly understood. In this study, we provide the first evidence that circulating exosomes from septic mice (sep-Exo) can directly induce SALI. Treatment of AML12 hepatocytes with sep-Exo significantly induced inflammatory responses, as evidenced by elevated expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and increased AST and ALT levels, indicating hepatocellular injury. Consistent with these in vitro findings, intravenous administration of sep-Exo into healthy mice reproduced similar liver inflammation and injury. Although previous studies have not directly addressed the mechanism by which serum exosomes contribute to septic liver injury, Gao et al. reported that plasma-derived exosomes carrying miR-1-3p can target SERP1 to induce endothelial dysfunction and thereby promote septic lung injury [ 43 ]. Together with our results, these observations suggest that circulating exosomes from septic mice constitute a pro-inflammatory subpopulation capable of eliciting liver inflammation. Ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, is increasingly recognized as a pivotal mechanism in sepsis pathogenesis [ 44 ]. Extensive evidence indicates that ferroptosis exacerbates inflammation, and targeting ferroptosis can mitigate sepsis-induced multi-organ injury, implying that hepatocellular ferroptosis may play a central role in SALI [ 44 , 45 ]. Supporting this notion, deletion of LCN2 has been shown to aggravate ferroptosis in septic liver injury by modulating PTGS2 [ 46 ], whereas Wenqingyin alleviates SALI by suppressing ferroptosis via activation of the Nrf2 signaling pathway [ 47 ]. Mechanistically, GPX4 detoxifies lipid peroxides using GSH as a reducing cofactor to counteract oxidative injury caused by iron overload. SLC7A11, a cystine/glutamate antiporter, facilitates cystine uptake for GSH synthesis, and its downregulation depletes intracellular GSH and reduces GPX4 activity. Thus, the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis constitutes the core antioxidant defense mechanism against ferroptosis [ 48 , 49 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated the critical regulatory role of this pathway in ferroptosis; for instance, systemic glucose deprivation can trigger disulfide stress and ferroptosis by inhibiting this axis [ 50 ], and suppression of this pathway in vascular smooth muscle cells drives ferroptosis and vascular calcification [ 51 ]. Consistent with these findings, serum exosomes from septic mice induced hepatocyte injury, suppressed SLC7A11, GSH, and GPX4 expression, activated autophagy, and thereby promoted ferroptosis. These results suggest that septic serum exosomes may drive ferroptosis and liver injury by inducing autophagy and disrupting the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis. Autophagy is closely associated with ferroptosis. During ferroptosis, the accumulation of iron and ROS can activate autophagy, while excessive autophagic activity further increases intracellular iron and ROS, establishing a positive feedback loop that accelerates ferroptotic cell death [ 52 ]. Autophagy plays a context-dependent dual role in ferroptosis [ 53 – 55 ]. However, the precise function of autophagy in SALI remains largely undefined. Elucidating the crosstalk between these two processes may provide novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets for sepsis. Although autophagy is physiologically protective, excessive or dysregulated autophagy during sepsis is associated with aggravated inflammation and poorer outcomes. In experimental models, autophagy inhibition alleviates cytokine storm and vascular leakage, indicating a pathological role under specific conditions [ 56 ]. Importantly, extracellular vesicles have been shown to induce both autophagy and ferroptosis in sepsis-induced acute lung injury, further exacerbating inflammatory damage [ 57 ]. Collectively, these findings suggest that excessive autophagy in sepsis may contribute to organ injury, highlighting the need for precise therapeutic modulation. STAT1, a key member of the STAT family, regulates diverse biological processes, including cell proliferation, cell death, and immune responses. Recent studies have highlighted its pathogenic involvement in hepatic ischemia-reperfusion and drug-induced liver injury [ 58 ], yet its role in SALI remains unexplored. Our RNA sequencing data revealed that STAT1 was among the most significantly upregulated genes in AML12 cells treated with sep-Exo, suggesting its potential involvement in exosome-mediated hepatic injury. Functional experiments demonstrated that inhibition of STAT1 attenuated sep-Exo–induced hepatocellular injury and inflammatory cytokine production, whereas STAT1 overexpression further exacerbated these effects. These results were consistent in both in vitro and in vivo models. Previous studies have shown that esculin alleviates early sepsis by suppressing NF-κB and STAT1/3 signaling [ 59 ], and that the IFIH1/IRF1/STAT1 axis promotes sepsis-related inflammatory lung injury via driving M1 macrophage polarization [ 60 ], supporting our observation that STAT1 activation exacerbates septic inflammation. Importantly, we identified STAT1 as an upstream regulator of SLC7A11. Mechanistically, STAT1 activation suppresses SLC7A11 expression, reduces cellular antioxidant capacity, and promotes ferroptosis. Similar mechanisms have been reported in other systems, such as STAT1-mediated inhibition of SLC7A11 inducing ferroptosis in retinal pigment epithelial cells, which can be reversed by STAT1 inhibition [ 61 ]. Consistent with these findings, our data demonstrate that STAT1 inhibition restores SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 signaling and prevents ferroptosis, whereas STAT1 overexpression intensifies ferroptotic damage [ 62 , 63 ]. This study has several limitations. Although our data indicate that circulating exosomes contribute to septic liver injury, exosomes contain diverse bioactive cargos, and the specific pathogenic components responsible for this effect remain to be identified. Further studies are therefore warranted to characterize these molecules and elucidate their precise roles in the pathogenesis of SALI. From a translational perspective, our findings may offer potential therapeutic insights. Previous studies have proposed blood purification strategies aimed at selectively removing pathogenic exosomes and viral particles from the circulation, such as those developed by Aethlon Medical for cancer and hepatitis C treatment [ 32 ]. In this context, our results suggest that targeting circulating exosomes could represent a complementary therapeutic strategy for mitigating liver injury during sepsis. Notably, our study demonstrates that serum-derived exosomes are enriched in the peripheral circulation of septic mice and contribute to SALI through STAT1 upregulation. Activation of STAT1 promotes autophagy while concomitantly suppressing the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis, thereby facilitating ferroptosis. Both in vitro and in vivo , septic serum–derived exosomes were shown to exacerbate hepatocellular injury, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Collectively, these findings provide novel mechanistic insights into the role of circulating exosomes in SALI and identify STAT1-mediated autophagy–ferroptosis signaling as a potential therapeutic target.
sections.conclusion: Our study provides compelling evidence that serum-derived exosomes from LPS-induced septic mice contribute to the pathogenesis of SALI by upregulating STAT1. This activation of STAT1, in turn, induces autophagy and suppresses the SLC7A11–GSH–GPX4 axis, thereby promoting ferroptosis. Collectively, these findings advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying SALI and identify STAT1-mediated exosomal signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sepsis.

title: Reduced Posterior Occlusal Contacts Are Associated With an Increased Risk of Stroke: A Retrospective Study Based on a Japanese Claims Database
abstract: Background Stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, requiring modifiable risk factors for prevention. Oral health, particularly posterior occlusal contact that supports mastication, may influence systemic vascular outcomes; however, its role in stroke remains unclear. This study investigated whether reduced posterior occlusal contact independently predicts stroke in Japanese adults. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data collected from April 2016 to March 2022 from a nationwide health insurance database in Japan. Adults aged 40 to 74 years without a history of stroke were included. Posterior occlusal status was categorized as Eichner A (full posterior occlusal contact), B (partial contact), or C (no contact). The primary outcome was stroke incidence, identified using validated insurance claims. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs), adjusting for demographics, health behaviors, comorbidities, and tooth counts. Results Among 981 543 participants (mean age 49.6±7.0 years; 57.5% male) followed for 2 712 815 person‐years, 7086 strokes occurred. In adjusted Cox models, Eichner B was significantly associated with higher stroke risk than Eichner A (HR, 1.26 [95% CI, 1.10–1.44], P <0.001). Eichner C showed elevated risk, although not statistically significant (HR, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.91–1.50], P =0.229). Associations were observed in both sexes and across age groups. Conclusions Reduced posterior occlusal support was associated with higher stroke risk independent of tooth count and conventional vascular risk. These findings highlight that posterior occlusal support may represent a potential marker of cerebrovascular risk and warrant further investigation into its clinical relevance.

The association was most evident in individuals with partial posterior tooth loss, indicating that moderate occlusal decline may have systemic cerebrovascular effects.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Posterior occlusal status may represent a modifiable marker for stroke prevention, underscoring the importance of maintaining or restoring occlusal contacts through timely dental care.
sections.data availability statement: All data in the Japan Medical Data Center (JMDC) Claims Database are fully anonymized before release; therefore, informed consent from individual participants was not required. The database is available to institutions or researchers who obtain a license from JMDC Inc. (Tokyo, Japan; https://www.jmdc.co.jp/en/ ), a private company that aggregates nationwide health insurance claims and health checkup data. Data supporting the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. These data are not publicly available due to privacy and ethical restrictions.
sections.data source and study design: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the JMDC Claims Database, which includes the medical and dental records of >60 health insurers in Japan. The database covers ∼7.6% of the population, mainly working‐age adults and their dependents under the age of 75 years. It contains encrypted personal IDs, demographics (age and sex), diagnoses, procedures, prescriptions, and annual health checkup results. We analyzed data from April 2016 to March 2022 to study the association between posterior occlusal contact and stroke (Figure 1 ). From the 6 549 778 individuals who underwent health checkups, we excluded those aged <40 years (n=2 140 312), those without dental codes for all 28 teeth in the previous year (n=3 418 231), and those with stroke within 12 months before baseline (n=9692). Missing health data were imputed using the mice package in R with 10 data sets. The final cohort included 981 543 individuals with complete dental and health data and no history of stroke. The study design is illustrated in Figure 2 .
sections.outcome: Stroke included cerebral infarction ( International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision [ ICD‐10 ]: I63), intracerebral hemorrhage (I61), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (I60). 17 The primary outcome was the first stroke during the follow‐up period (April 2016 to March 2022). We identified cases with confirmed diagnoses from claims and excluded suspected cases. The follow‐up ended at the stroke, death, or study end, whichever occurred first.
sections.exposure: We used the Eichner classification to assess the posterior occlusal contact. The JMDC Claims Database lacks tooth counts but records dental procedures, such as periodontal examinations and cleanings. Each tooth had a code, and when multiple codes existed, the latest code was used. Following the previous methods, 18 , 19 we estimated the number of teeth present in the codes. We identified occlusal support zones, opposing premolars, or molars in contact on each side and grouped them into 0 to 4 zones. Eichner A included all 4 intact zones, Eichner B had 1 to 3 intact zones, and Eichner C had none.
sections.covariates: We adjusted for demographics, health behaviors, and comorbidities associated with stroke as available in the claims data. The demographics included insurance status (employee or dependent), age, and sex. Age was calculated from the birth date and grouped into 40 to 59 and 60 to 74 years. Health behaviors included obesity, smoking, alcohol use, and physical activity. Obesity was defined as BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 . Smoking and alcohol use were self‐reported; current smokers had smoked >100 cigarettes within the past 28 days, and current drinkers consumed alcohol daily or occasionally. Physical activity was assessed by questionnaire; ideal activity was defined as ≥30 minutes of exercise twice a week or ≥1 hour of walking daily. Tooth count, excluding third molars, was classified as <20 or ≥20 based on evidence that ≥20 teeth are sufficient for functional mastication. 20 Comorbidities included hypertension, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia. Hypertension was defined as systolic blood pressure (BP) ≥140 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure (BP) ≥90 mm Hg, or use of antihypertensive medications. Hyperglycemia was defined as fasting blood glucose level ≥126 mg/dL or use of glucose‐lowering drugs. Dyslipidemia was defined as low‐density lipoprotein ≥140 mg/dL, high‐density lipoprotein <40 mg/dL, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, or use of lipid‐lowering drugs. Definitions are listed in Table S1 .
sections.statistical analysis: All analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.0.4). The statistical significance level was set at α=0.05. The demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were expressed as means ± SD and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Categorical variables across the 3 Eichner classifications were compared using the chi‐square test. The Anderson–Darling test confirmed that all continuous variables (age, number of teeth, BMI, systolic BP, diastolic BP, fasting blood glucose, low‐density lipoprotein, high‐density lipoprotein, and triglycerides levels) were nonnormally distributed ( P <0.001); therefore, we used the Mann–Whitney U test for group comparisons. Kaplan–Meier curves were plotted to compare stroke incidence among the Eichner groups, and the log‐rank test was used to assess the differences. The proportional hazards assumption was initially evaluated using log–log plots and formally tested using Schoenfeld residuals for each covariate and for the overall model. We used a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model to assess the association between Eichner classification and stroke risk. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs were calculated for both unadjusted and adjusted models. Covariates entered simultaneously into the model included age, tooth group, sex, insurance status, smoking, alcohol use, obesity, hypertension, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and physical activity. Martingale residuals were examined to assess the functional form of covariates and to screen for influential observations. Deviance residuals were evaluated to identify outliers and poorly fitted observations. Variance inflation factors were used to assess multicollinearity. For categorical variables, we calculated the adjusted generalized variance inflation factors to align with the standard thresholds. All values were <2.0, indicating no significant multicollinearity. Four sensitivity analyses were conducted. First, we analyzed only complete cases (n=766 400) and excluded participants with missing health checkup data. Second, we used continuous values (number of teeth, BMI, systolic BP, fasting blood glucose, and low‐density lipoprotein levels) instead of their respective categorical variables. Third, we applied 6‐ and 12‐month induction periods, excluding individuals who developed stroke within these intervals, resulting in sample sizes of 977 688 and 974 792, respectively. Fourth, we defined stroke onset using the ICD‐10 codes I60 to I64 and G459 (n=980 413). Subgroup analyses were stratified by sex (male: n=564 503; female: n=417 040) and age (40–59 years, n=880 299; 60–74 years, n=101 244) to examine the association between Eichner classification and stroke risk.
sections.ethics: This study used anonymized data from the JMDC Claims Database, in accordance with Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information. Informed consent was not required because the data were anonymized under the Next‐Generation Medical Infrastructure Act. According to Japan's ethical guidelines, studies using anonymized data do not require ethics committee approval. The study complied with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
sections.results_1: We analyzed 981 543 participants (mean age: 49.6±7.0 years; 564 503 male and 417 040 female) over a total of 2 712 815 person‐years. During a mean follow‐up of 19.5 months, 7086 individuals (mean age: 53.3±7.7 years; 4620 male and 2466 female) developed stroke. Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics according to Eichner classification: A (n=942 444), B (n=28 510), and C (n=10 589). Stroke incidence was significantly higher in Eichner B and C than in Eichner A ( P <0.001). Diagnostic analyses revealed no meaningful violations of the assumptions of the Cox proportional hazards model. The global Schoenfeld test was not significant ( P =0.55), and no consistent time‐dependent patterns were observed (Table S2 ). Although smoking showed a borderline covariate‐specific result, additional assessment of its Schoenfeld residuals indicated no meaningful time dependence (Figure S1 ). Martingale residuals showed the expected distribution without evidence of nonlinearity (Figure S2 ), and deviance residuals identified few extreme observations (0.3%) with no indication of undue influence (Figure S3 ). Figure 3 presents the Kaplan–Meier curves of stroke incidence according to the Eichner classification. Stroke risk showed significant difference among the 3 groups (log‐rank P <0.001). In the Cox models adjusted for demographics, health behaviors, comorbidities, and tooth count, the Eichner B score was significantly associated with stroke risk (Table 2 and Table S3 ). Eichner B had a 1.26‐fold higher risk than Eichner A (HR, 1.26 [95% CI, 1.10–1.44], P <0.001), whereas Eichner C showed a 1.17‐fold increase (HR, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.91–1.50], P =0.229). Several sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the primary findings. First, an analysis limited to complete cases without multiple imputations produced results consistent with the main analysis (Table S4 ). Second, replacing the categorical variables with continuous values for tooth count, BMI, hypertension, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia yielded similar results (Table S5 ). Third, we applied 6‐ and 12‐month induction periods to exclude participants with potential latent stroke at baseline, and the associations remained stable (Table S6 ). Finally, the redefinition of stroke using alternative ICD‐10 codes did not alter our findings (Table S7 ). Together, these analyses confirmed the robustness of the association between posterior occlusal status and stroke across different model specifications and populations. We also examined the association between the Eichner classification and stroke risk according to sex and age. In men, the Eichner B had a significantly higher risk of stroke than the Eichner A (HR, 1.24 [95% CI, 1.05–1.45], P =0.010), and a similar association was observed in women (HR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.03–1.67], P =0.027). Age‐stratified analyses showed that in the 40 to 59 age group, the Eichner B group had a significantly increased risk (HR, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.04–1.55], P =0.021). In the 60–74 age group, both Eichner B (HR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.09–1.57], P =0.003) and C (HR, 1.39 [95% CI, 1.02–1.90], P =0.038) were significantly associated with higher stroke risk than Eichner A (Tables S8 and S9 ).
sections.discussion: In this longitudinal study, we used a nationwide Japanese claims database to examine the association between posterior occlusal contact, measured using the Eichner classification, and stroke risk. After adjusting for conventional vascular risk factors and tooth count, reduced posterior occlusal contact was associated with a higher risk of incident stroke compared with full occlusion. This association was most consistent with the partial loss of posterior support (Eichner B). Complete loss of posterior contact (Eichner C) showed a directionally similar but nonsignificant overall increase. Importantly, age‐stratified analyses further indicated that these associations were more prominent among older adults, particularly those aged 60 to 74 years, where baseline stroke incidence was higher and event rates allowed more stable effect estimation. The sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of these findings. To our knowledge, this is the first longitudinal study to show that reduced posterior occlusal contact, a key determinant of mastication, independently increases the risk of stroke. Prior research has not identified impaired chewing as a risk factor for stroke, but has instead shown that stroke often impairs chewing, oral sensitivity, and mastication due to neurophysiological damage in the orofacial region. 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 For example, one cohort study found no improvement in chewing efficiency after poststroke dental restoration, and no correlation between occlusal units and mastication in stroke survivors. 24 These findings suggest that poststroke masticatory decline stems mainly from neurological causes rather than dental issues. 26 , 27 In contrast, many studies have associated tooth loss with a higher risk of stroke. 7 , 28 , 29 Because mastication depends on both the number and distribution of occluding teeth, particularly in the posterior region, posterior tooth loss can impair functional occlusion and chewing efficiency. 30 Notably, stroke risk remained significantly elevated in individuals classified as Eichner B, even after adjusting for the number of remaining teeth. This suggests that the partial loss of posterior occlusal support, rather than tooth loss alone, plays a distinct role in increasing stroke risk. A significant interaction was observed between Eichner B and the number of remaining teeth, indicating that the impact of tooth loss is modified by the degree of occlusal support (Table S10 ). The association in Eichner C, which reflects a complete loss of posterior occlusion, weakened and lost significance after adjusting for tooth count. One possible explanation for this is the varying effects of denture use. Many patients in the Eichner C group were likely to use dentures; however, their health effects remain uncertain. Removable partial dentures can restore mastication and improve quality of life, 31 however, denture use increases the risk of cardiovascular diseases, including stroke. 32 As the present data set lacked information on denture status, we could not resolve these conflicting findings. This limitation underscores the need for future studies including data on prosthetic treatments. The association between reduced posterior occlusal support and stroke risk is biologically and clinically plausible, particularly considering the established role of mastication in neurovascular regulation. Chewing activates trigeminal afferents and stimulates cortical regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, thereby enhancing cerebral perfusion and oxygenation. 33 , 34 , 35 Neuroimaging and experimental studies have shown that diminished mastication, which often results from tooth loss or posterior occlusal decline, is associated with cognitive impairment and impaired neurovascular coupling. 36 , 37 Consistent with these findings, our previous study showed that individuals with fewer posterior occlusal contacts as defined by the Eichner classification were at a higher risk of dementia. 16 Together, these results support the notion that the loss of sensory input from mastication may compromise cerebral regulation. As cognitive decline and stroke share common pathophysiological mechanisms, including endothelial dysfunction, blood–brain barrier disruption, and impaired cerebral autoregulation, 38 reduced masticatory stimulation could possibly increase stroke risk through the neurovascular and endothelial pathways. In addition to the neurovascular mechanisms, dietary alterations secondary to impaired mastication represent another plausible pathway linking posterior occlusal loss to stroke. Individuals with reduced occlusion often avoid hard‐to‐chew foods, such as fibrous vegetables, fruits, and lean proteins, leading to diets that are less diverse and nutritionally unbalanced. 39 , 40 , 41 Such dietary changes decrease the intake of cardioprotective nutrients, including antioxidants, fiber, and omega‐3 fatty acids, which play critical roles in the prevention of atherosclerosis and hypertension. 40 , 42 Consequently, compromised masticatory ability may indirectly contribute to the risk of stroke by promoting adverse dietary patterns that deteriorate vascular health. Reduced posterior occlusal contacts were significantly associated with cerebral infarction but not with intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage (Table S11 ). This pattern is consistent with previous studies showing that tooth loss and dental caries increase the risk of cerebral infarction but not hemorrhagic stroke. 6 These differences suggest that oral health has a weaker influence on the mechanisms underlying hemorrhagic stroke. Cerebral infarction is closely linked to atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation, and is modulated by poor oral hygiene and periodontal disease. 43 , 44 In contrast, intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages most commonly result from the sudden rupture of blood vessels, typically due to chronic hypertension or congenital vascular anomalies, such as aneurysms and arteriovenous malformations. 45 , 46 Therefore, the inflammatory and atherogenic pathways that plausibly connect impaired occlusion to infarction are unlikely to contribute substantially to hemorrhagic stroke, which explains the lack of an association in our findings. This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the diagnostic data were based on insurance claims that were not routinely validated against clinical records. Misclassification of stroke diagnoses may have occurred, which could have affected the accuracy of the outcome assessment. Second, this retrospective cohort study identified associations but could not establish causality. Although we found a significant link between posterior occlusal status and stroke, the observational design requires cautious interpretation. Prospective studies with standardized assessments are required to confirm these findings. Third, the study population was limited to working‐age adults from large Japanese companies and their dependents. Older adults (>75 years) were underrepresented, further limiting the generalizability of the study. This age structure also affects the interpretation of the overall estimates, because stroke incidence was low among younger participants and the relatively younger, lower‐risk composition of the reference group may have influenced the magnitude of the effect estimates despite statistical adjustment. The data set may also lack sufficient geographic and socioeconomic diversity, which could introduce a selection bias. Fourth, although we adjusted for common stroke risk factors, unmeasured confounders, such as income, education, occupation, diet, and health care access, may have affected the results. Finally, we lacked data on periodontal status despite its known relation to inflammation and stroke risk. 47
sections.conclusions_1: In conclusion, this observational study demonstrated that a reduced posterior occlusal contact, as defined by the Eichner classification, was associated with an increased risk of stroke, with the association more evident in older adults. Because of the observational design and relatively short median follow‐up, these findings should be considered hypothesis generating rather than causal. Nevertheless, the findings underscore the potential significance of posterior occlusal support as a plausible factor relevant to cerebrovascular risk in aging populations, warranting further examination in prospective and interventional studies to clarify underlying mechanisms and determine whether improving oral rehabilitation influences long‐term cerebrovascular outcomes.

title: Valve‐in‐Valve Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement Versus Redo Surgical Mitral Valve Replacement: Meta‐Analysis of Early and Late Outcomes
abstract: Background Bioprosthetic mitral valve degeneration is traditionally treated with redo surgical mitral valve replacement (redo‐SMVR), but valve‐in‐valve transcatheter mitral valve replacement (ViV‐TMVR) offers a less invasive alternative. Methods Systematic review and meta‐analysis of studies comparing ViV‐TMVR and redo‐SMVR. PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane databases (inception to September 2025) were searched. Meta‐analyses were conducted with random‐effects models to assess patient‐relevant outcomes; Kaplan–Meier‐derived time‐to‐event data were pooled to assess late outcomes. Results Thirteen observational studies met our eligibility criteria, including 15 941 patients (ViV‐TMVR: 5465; redo‐SMVR: 10476). In comparison with redo‐SMVR, ViV‐TMVR was associated with lower risk of in‐hospital mortality (risk ratio [RR], 0.72 [95% CI, 0.57–0.90]; P =0.004), stroke (RR, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29–0.83]; P =0.008), bleeding (RR, 0.43 [95% CI, 0.20–0.94]; P =0.035), acute kidney injury (RR, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.42–0.77]; P <0.001), permanent pacemaker implantation (RR, 0.30 [95% CI, 0.19–0.49]; P <0.001), and shorter hospital length of stay (mean difference,−5.09 days [95% CI, −6.56 to −3.63]; P <0.001). There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in terms of 5‐year survival (hazard ratio [HR], 0.92 [95% CI, 0.81–1.05]; P =0.256); however, the landmark analysis revealed that ViV‐TMVR was associated with lower risk of death in the initial 6 months (HR, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.58–0.83]; P <0.001) but a higher risk beyond 6 months (HR, 1.47 [95% CI, 1.20–1.79]; P <0.001). Conclusions In patients amenable to ViV‐TMVR, this procedure shows a lower initial risk of death and complications, but higher mortality after 6 months in comparison with redo‐SMVR. These findings highlight the importance of striking a balance between upfront surgical risk and estimated life expectancy when selecting interventions.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease
