title: Celiac trunk thrombosis and splenic infarction in a patient with ankylosing spondylitis under adalimumab: a case report
abstract: Background Celiac trunk thrombosis is a rare vascular emergency that can lead to life-threatening complications including bowel ischemia and multi-organ dysfunction. The association between inflammatory autoimmune arthropathies and thrombotic events is well-established, but celiac trunk involvement remains exceptionally uncommon. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges and management considerations in patients with underlying inflammatory autoimmune conditions. Case presentation A 45-year-old male with ankylosing spondylitis under adalimumab presented with acute epigastric pain and bilious vomiting. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography with angiography revealed a 1.5 cm thrombus at the celiac trunk trifurcation with subtotal occlusion of the splenic and common hepatic arteries, high-grade stenosis of the left gastric artery, and subsequent splenic infarction. The patient was managed conservatively with anticoagulation and supportive care, with gradual clinical improvement. Conclusions This case demonstrates that celiac trunk thrombosis should be considered in patients with autoimmune arthropathies presenting with acute abdominal pain, even when initial clinical suspicion points toward more common diagnoses. Early recognition through appropriate imaging is crucial for optimal management and prevention of fatal complications.

sections.background: Celiac trunk thrombosis is a rare vascular emergency that can lead to life-threatening complications including bowel ischemia and multi-organ dysfunction. The association between inflammatory autoimmune arthropathies and thrombotic events is well-established, but celiac trunk involvement remains exceptionally uncommon. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges and management considerations in patients with underlying inflammatory autoimmune conditions.
sections.case presentation: A 45-year-old male with ankylosing spondylitis under adalimumab presented with acute epigastric pain and bilious vomiting. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography with angiography revealed a 1.5 cm thrombus at the celiac trunk trifurcation with subtotal occlusion of the splenic and common hepatic arteries, high-grade stenosis of the left gastric artery, and subsequent splenic infarction. The patient was managed conservatively with anticoagulation and supportive care, with gradual clinical improvement.
sections.conclusions: This case demonstrates that celiac trunk thrombosis should be considered in patients with autoimmune arthropathies presenting with acute abdominal pain, even when initial clinical suspicion points toward more common diagnoses. Early recognition through appropriate imaging is crucial for optimal management and prevention of fatal complications.
sections.background_1: Celiac trunk thrombosis is an extremely rare but serious vascular emergency, accounting for less than 1% of all mesenteric vascular occlusions [ 1 , 2 ]. Because the celiac trunk supplies the liver, spleen, stomach, and proximal duodenum, its occlusion can lead to multi-organ ischemia if left unrecognized [ 2 ]. This type of rare vascular event is particularly noteworthy in patients with conditions like ankylosing spondylitis (AS), a chronic autoimmune arthropathy affecting the axial skeleton [ 3 ]. Ankylosing spondylitis is associated with increased cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk due to systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and procoagulant changes [ 3 ]. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors like adalimumab are well-established treatments for ankylosing spondylitis, and while they improve joint control and can prevent cardiovascular events, rare thrombotic events have been reported with their use [ 4 ]. The co-occurrence of celiac trunk thrombosis and ankylosing spondylitis under adalimumab has not been described in the literature. This highlights the importance of considering rare vascular complications in patients with autoimmune diseases receiving TNF inhibitors.
sections.case presentation_1: A 45‑year‑old male presented to the emergency department with acute epigastric pain starting during the night. The pain was constant, dull, and supraumbilical. He had multiple episodes of bilious vomiting but denied fever or urinary symptoms. Initial labs showed leukocytosis 15 × 10 3 /μL and elevated C‑reactive protein (CRP) 20 mg/L, leading the referring physician to suspect appendicitis. His rheumatologic history included a misdiagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, later reclassified in 2018 as human leukocyte antigen (HLA)‑B27–positive ankylosing spondylitis after bilateral sacroiliac ankylosis was confirmed on imaging. He underwent a biological aortic valve replacement in 2018 for severe insufficiency secondary to nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, with normal coronaries documented. Anticoagulation management following valve replacement consisted of 6 months of warfarin therapy followed by lifelong aspirin therapy. No further anticoagulation work-up was done. Follow‑up echocardiography in 2020 showed left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction (67%) and normal prosthetic valve function. Current medications included aspirin and adalimumab (every four weeks subcutaneous injection; last dose one week prior). His AS was in clinical remission. He had no allergies, previous abdominal surgery, or thromboembolic history. He smoked about 10 cigarettes per day and consumed alcohol socially. On exam, vitals were stable. A systolic murmur was audible over the aortic valve area. Abdominal exam revealed diffuse tenderness, most prominent in the epigastrium, with mild guarding but no rebound or rigidity. Bowel sounds were preserved. Labs at presentation showed white blood cell count 16.2 × 10 3 /µL and CRP 30 mg/L. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with left axis deviation, 1st‑degree AV block, and nonspecific repolarization changes. Contrast‑enhanced computed tomography (CT) with angiography. (Fig. 1 a and b) revealed a 1.5 cm eccentric thrombus at the celiac trunk trifurcation, with subtotal occlusion of the splenic and common hepatic artery origins and severe stenosis of the left gastric artery. Multiple peripheral splenic infarcts were identified. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) showed increased metabolic activity in the artery wall of the truncus coeliacus (Fig. 1 c and d) suggestive of active inflammatory changes. Fig. 1 a ) Axial contrast-enhanced CT image showing an eccentric thrombus (arrow) at the celiac trunk trifurcation. b ) Coronal reconstruction demonstrating subtotal occlusion of the splenic artery origin and consequent splenic infarctions (arrowheads). c ) Fused PET-CT image revealing FDG uptake (arrow) in the wall of the celiac trunk, suggestive of active inflammatory change. d ) Maximum intensity projection (MIP) PET image confirming localized inflammatory activity (arrow) at the site of thrombosis The patient was managed conservatively with therapeutic anticoagulation (low‑molecular weight heparin transitioned to oral anticoagulation), supportive fluids, and analgesia. He subsequently developed hypertensive urgency requiring medical therapy with intravenous urapidil. This was interpreted as multifactorial, likely triggered by a pain-induced catecholamine surge combined with systemic inflammation and sympathetic activation. Renal artery involvement as reason for the hypertensive crisis could be excluded via CT. He recovered gradually and was discharged on long‑term anticoagulation with subcutaneous enoxaparin 80 mg twice per day.
sections.discussion: This case presents a rare manifestation of celiac trunk thrombosis in a patient with ankylosing spondylitis, highlighting several important clinical and pathophysiological considerations. The family physician’s initial misinterpretation of symptoms led to an incorrect suspicion of appendicitis, illustrating the diagnostic challenges inherent in this rare condition. The association between inflammatory arthropathies and increased thrombotic risk is well-established in the literature [ 5 , 6 ]. Chronic inflammation characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis leads to endothelial dysfunction, altered coagulation cascades, and increased platelet reactivity [ 3 , 6 ]. In our case, PET-CT imaging demonstrated active inflammation of the celiac trunk, suggesting that vascular wall inflammation may have contributed to local thrombus formation. The role of TNF-α inhibitors in cardiovascular and thrombotic events remains an area of ongoing debate. Recent studies have shown conflicting evidence regarding the cardiovascular effects of these agents. While some analyses suggest a potential association with elevated risk of specific cardiovascular events, particularly with early initiation [ 4 ], others demonstrate potential cardioprotective benefits through reduced systemic inflammation [ 7 ]. A recent pharmacovigilance analysis of the FAERS database (2004–2024) revealed that adalimumab was associated with the highest number of thrombotic adverse events among TNF-α blockers analyzed, with postpartum thrombosis displaying the strongest signal and deep vein thrombosis being most frequently reported [ 4 ]. Notably, celiac trunk thrombosis was not specifically reported in this dataset, underscoring the rarity of our case. The mechanisms underlying TNF-α blocker-associated thrombosis may include the formation of anti-adalimumab antibodies, which are thought to promote a hypercoagulable state [ 4 ]. In our patient, the disease was in clinical remission at presentation, and therefore anti-adalimumab antibody testing was not performed as it was not clinically indicated. Given the patient’s stable disease state, it remains unclear whether adalimumab, the underlying inflammatory disease, or other factors contributed to the thrombotic event. From a clinical perspective, celiac trunk thrombosis typically presents with acute onset of severe epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and systemic signs of inflammation—all features observed in our patient [ 1 , 2 ]. The nonspecific nature of this presentation can lead to diagnostic delays and potentially catastrophic outcomes, including bowel necrosis, multiorgan failure, and death [ 1 , 2 ]. Splenic infarction, as occurred in this case, is a relatively uncommon diagnosis, with only 10% of cases diagnosed ante-mortem [ 1 ]. The main causes include thromboembolism, acute infection, and hematological diseases [ 8 ]. Early recognition through appropriate imaging, particularly contrast-enhanced CT angiography, is crucial for optimal patient outcomes. Management of celiac trunk thrombosis depends on the extent of occlusion, presence of collateral circulation, and clinical stability [ 8 ]. Treatment options range from conservative management with anticoagulation and supportive care to interventional procedures, including thrombolysis, angioplasty, and surgical revascularization. In this case, the patient’s relatively stable clinical condition and presence of adequate collateral circulation supported the feasibility of conservative management [ 8 ]. The development of hypertensive urgency secondary to splenic infarction in this patient represents an uncommon complication of mesenteric vascular occlusion, and while the exact mechanism remains speculative, several factors may have contributed. The severe visceral pain could have activated segmental spinal reflexes through physiological neuronal connections, causing sympathetic nervous system activation with increased peripheral resistances, heart rate, and stroke volume [ 9 ], potentially triggering a catecholamine surge and leading to vasoconstriction. Additionally, systemic inflammatory mediators released during tissue ischemia might have contributed to endothelial dysfunction and blood pressure elevation [ 10 ]. No evidence of renal artery compromise was seen on imaging. However, it is important to acknowledge that the precise causality cannot be definitively established, and multiple interacting mechanisms likely played a role in precipitating this hypertensive emergency. This case underscores the importance of maintaining high clinical suspicion for atypical presentations of vascular emergencies in patients with inflammatory conditions [ 2 ]. The combination of chronic inflammation, immunosuppressive therapy, and potentially prothrombotic states creates a unique risk profile that requires vigilant clinical assessment.
sections.conclusions_1: Celiac trunk thrombosis, though rare, should be considered in patients with inflammatory arthropathies presenting with acute abdominal pain. CT angiography is the diagnostic modality of choice. Conservative anticoagulation may be suitable in hemodynamically stable patients with adequate collateralization. Clinicians should remain aware of thrombotic complications in ankylosing spondylitis, particularly in patients receiving immunomodulatory therapy.

title: The Texas Abortion Ban and Maternal Mental Health
abstract: This cross-sectional study examines the association of the implementation of Texas Senate Bill 8, which banned abortions after embryonic cardiac activity, with maternal mental health outcomes.

sections.question: Was the implementation of Texas Senate Bill 8 (SB8), which banned abortions after embryonic cardiac activity with no exemptions for congenital anomalies, associated with differences in the prevalence of fair or poor maternal mental health outcomes?
sections.findings: In this cross-sectional study of 4323 mothers in Texas and 152 537 mothers in states without abortion bans, mothers residing in Texas had a statistically significant higher likelihood of reporting fair or poor mental health after SB8 went into effect compared with mothers in states without abortion restrictions. The association was more pronounced among Texas mothers with public health insurance.
sections.meaning: These findings suggest that abortion bans may be correlated with worsening maternal mental health outcomes.
sections.importance: Maternal mental health disorders are among the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality. In the US, the 2022 Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization and ensuing state-level abortion restrictions have raised concerns that such policies may worsen maternal health and mental health outcomes.
sections.objective: To examine the association of the implementation of Texas Senate Bill 8 (SB8) abortion law, which banned abortions after embryonic cardiac activity in September 2021, with maternal mental health outcomes.
sections.design, setting, and participants: This repeated cross-sectional study used a difference-in-differences (DiD) design with pooled data from the 2016 to 2023 National Survey of Children’s Health. The nationally representative sample included US mothers aged 18 to 49 years who lived with at least 1 child aged 0 to 17 years. Data were analyzed from April to October 2025.
sections.exposure: Mothers residing in Texas represented the treatment group, and mothers in states without abortion bans (Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wyoming) served as the control group.
sections.main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was mothers’ self-reported fair or poor mental and emotional health. Logistic regression models, adjusted for child-, mother-, and household-level characteristics, were used to estimate changes in the probability of mental health outcomes for mothers coinciding with SB8 implementation. Similar models were estimated with maternal physical health and fathers’ mental health as outcomes for sensitivity analyses.
sections.results: The sample included 4323 mothers in Texas (47.2% [95% CI, 45.1%-49.4%] aged 30-39 years) and 152 573 mothers in nonban states (47.1% [95% CI, 46.4%-47.7%] aged 30-39 years). Compared with mothers in nonban states, those in Texas experienced a statistically significant increase in the likelihood of reporting fair or poor mental health following SB8’s implementation (DiD estimate, 2.52 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.02-5.01 percentage points). The largest increases were observed among mothers of children with public insurance (DiD estimate, 7.06 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.83-13.29 percentage points). No significant outcomes were observed for mothers’ physical health outcomes or fathers’ mental health in the sensitivity analyses.
sections.conclusions and relevance: In this repeated cross-sectional study, the implementation of an abortion ban in Texas was associated with a worsening of maternal mental health among reproductive-age mothers relative to mothers in states without such bans. These results underscore the association of abortion restrictions with maternal mental health and highlight the need to strengthen support in the post- Dobbs policy environment.
sections.introduction: Mental health disorders affect approximately 1 in 5 US women during the perinatal period, making it one of the leading causes of maternal mortality. 1 , 2 , 3 Most often these conditions remain untreated due to lack of adequate access to mental health care and inequities in the mental health care delivery system. 4 Changes in maternal health care access are often associated with changes in maternal mental health outcomes. In June 2022, the US Supreme Court decision on Dobbs vs Jackson Women’s Health Organization abolished the federal right to abortion, which has been associated with possible reductions in access to maternal care, 5 , 6 and in turn maternal mental health care. 7 , 8 Multiple mechanisms may explain the association of abortion bans with maternal mental health. The presence of abortion bans may create an overarching sense of insecurity and a loss of personal autonomy. 9 For many, the lack of autonomy may contribute to increased anxiety and distress, even for individuals who are not currently pregnant or seeking an abortion. 10 Further, restrictions on future reproductive choices may also be associated with increased anticipatory stress and anxiety, particularly among individuals who wish to retain control over family planning. 10 Restrictive abortion laws, such as mandatory waiting periods, parental consent laws, and travel requirements, create substantial logistical and financial barriers to maternal care. 11 These system-level changes may be associated with access to preventive, reproductive, and mental health care for all mothers, potentially contributing to increased stress and other mental health problems. 12 While some of these mechanisms are more directly relevant to individuals who are pregnant or considering pregnancy, taken together these broader structural and psychosocial pathways may affect the mental health of all reproductive-aged mothers, including those with older children. Research into the effects of abortion restrictions on maternal mental health is limited, 13 despite a growing interest in this topic following the Dobbs decision. 14 Literature in this area has focused mostly on overall population-level mental health rather than examining maternal mental health specifically. 7 , 15 , 16 , 17 In addition, previous research on abortion restrictions has examined different outcomes, such as infant mortality, pregnancy-related mortality, and female mental health, rather than maternal mental health. 14 , 16 , 18 We aim to address these gaps in the literature by examining the association of Texas Senate Bill 8 (SB8) with maternal mental health. SB8 was enacted in September 2021, 19 and at that time was the nation’s most restrictive abortion law, banning abortions after embryonic cardiac activity (as early as 5-6 weeks’ gestation) and offering no exemptions for congenital anomalies. 14 Similar to previous research, 16 we compare mental health outcomes among reproductive-age mothers in Texas with the mental health outcomes of reproductive-age mothers in states that did not restrict abortion in order to estimate the association of abortion bans with maternal mental health. We extend on the existing literature by focusing on reproductive-age mothers. Studying this population is critical because their mental health is closely associated with the well-being and developmental outcomes of their children and the stability of the entire family unit. 20 , 21 Specifically, in this study we use a difference-in-differences (DiD) research design with recent national survey data to test the hypothesis that reproductive age mothers in Texas reported worse mental health status after SB8 compared with reproductive age mothers in states without an abortion ban.
sections.study sample: This cross-sectional study used data from the National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) from 2016 to 2023. The NSCH is an annual, cross-sectional survey that collects parent-reported data on parents’ and children’s physical and mental health, child access to and quality of health care, and child and family sociodemographic characteristics on children ages 0 to 17 years. The NSCH has been used to study maternal mental and physical health. 3 Our study sample included reproductive-age mothers (18-49 years). All female parents were included regardless of biological or adoptive status. 3 In households with 2 female parents, both were included. Parents with missing values for the outcome or covariates were not included. The study was determined exempt from review and the requirement of informed consent by the Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute institutional review board in accordance with the Common Rule because the NCHS was deidentified, public-use data. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline.
sections.outcome measure: Female parent respondents were asked, “If this child’s mother is a primary caregiver and lives in the household, in general, what is the status of mother’s mental and emotional health?” Our primary outcome was whether the mother was reported to have fair or poor mental and emotional health status.
sections.child-level characteristics: Self-reported by the parent, child race and ethnicity were categorized as non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, non-Hispanic White, and non-Hispanic other (including multiracial and any race or ethnicity not otherwise specified) based on categorical levels of the child race variable in the publicly available data. Race and ethnicity were included to examine differential policy impacts and to help isolate the policy effect from preexisting group-level differences. Parent-reported child insurance type was defined as private (including employer and Marketplace coverage), public (including Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program), other (including Tricare, Indian Health Services, and other types of insurance), and uninsured. We also included an indicator for whether the child had special health care needs.
sections.mother-level and household-level charact: Mother-level variables included mother age group (18-29, 30-39, and 40-49 years), education level (high school graduate or less and greater than high school), whether the mother was born in the US, mother marital status (married; not married, living with spouse or partner; never married; divorced; separated; or widowed), and whether the mother was in a same-sex relationship. Household-level variables included household language (English, Spanish, and other), household structure (single parent, 1 child; single parent, 2 children; single parent, ≥3 children; 2 parents, 1 child; 2 parents, 2 children; and 2 parents, ≥3 children), income as percentage of the federal poverty level (<100%, 100%-199%, 200%-399%, and ≥400%), and census region (Northeast, Midwest, South, and West).
sections.statistical analysis: We used a DiD design to estimate the potential association of Texas SB8 with the mental and emotional health of reproductive-age mothers. Mothers residing in Texas were considered the treatment group, and mothers who resided in any non–abortion ban state (Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wyoming) were considered the control group. 14 We considered 2016 to 2020 as the prepolicy period and 2021 to 2023 as the postpolicy period. We first calculated unweighted and weighted descriptive characteristics of the study sample overall and by treatment and control group. We conducted both unadjusted and adjusted event study analyses to confirm the parallel trends assumption held between Texas residents and residents in control states (eTable 1, eFigure 1, and eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 ). All analyses were conducted using the Stata svy command to account for the complex survey design of the NSCH and weighting structure. Finally, we estimated unadjusted and adjusted DiD models (logistic regression) to assess the change in the likelihood of mothers’ fair or poor mental and emotional health outcomes following the abortion ban in Texas compared with mothers in control states. Margins were reported using the Stata margins command for interpretable DiD estimates. Because income as a percentage of the federal poverty level is sparsely populated, the NSCH provides 6 multiply imputed poverty variables and recommends using multiple imputation procedures in the analyses. 22 Stata could not report margins in multiple imputation settings and therefore we did not include income level as a covariate in our adjusted models. After estimating the models on the entire sample, we stratified the analysis by mother’s age, mother’s education, and child’s insurance (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ). We performed 4 sensitivity analyses of the likelihood of (1) fair or poor maternal mental health using linear regression (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 ), (2) fair or poor maternal mental health using 2021 as a washout year (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 ), (3) fair or poor maternal physical health (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 ), and (4) father’s fair or poor mental health to assess the specificity of the observed associations (eTable 6 in Supplement 1 ). Statistical significance was set at a 2-sided P < .05. All analyses were completed using Stata version 19 (StataCorp) from April to October 2025.
sections.results_1: Table 1 presents demographic characteristics of our study sample after stratification by the control group in non–abortion ban states (152 573 individuals; 47.1% [95% CI, 46.4%-47.7%] aged 30-39 years) and treatment group in Texas (4323 individuals; 47.2% [95% CI, 45.1%-49.4%] aged 30-39 years). Children’s racial and ethnic makeup varied by location. In nonban states, the largest group was non-Hispanic White at 50.8% (95% CI, 50.2%-51.4%), followed by Hispanic at 27.0% (95% CI, 26.4%-27.7%), non-Hispanic other race or ethnicity at 13.6% (95% CI, 13.2%-13.9%), and non-Hispanic Black at 8.6% (95% CI, 8.2%-8.9%). Among children in Texas, the largest group was Hispanic at 50.3% (95% CI, 48.1-52.4%), followed by Non-Hispanic White at 32.4% (95% CI, 30.6%-34.3%), non-Hispanic Black at 9.7% (95% CI, 8.4%-11.1%), and non-Hispanic other race or ethnicity at 7.6% (95% CI, 6.8%-8.5%). The prevalence of children with special health care needs was similar between the groups: 17.8% (95% CI, 17.4%-18.2%) in nonban states and 15.8% (95% CI, 15.3%-18.3%) in Texas. Private insurance was the dominant type in both, covering 63.0% (95% CI, 62.4%-63.6%) in nonban states and 54.0% (95% CI, 51.8%-56.2%) in Texas. Notably, the rate of uninsured children and children covered under other insurance in Texas was more than double compared with nonban states, at 11.9% (95% CI, 10.4%-13.7%) vs 4.3% (95% CI, 4.0%-4.5%), respectively. For mother age, the majority in both groups fell into the 30- to 39-year age group (47.1% [95% CI, 46.4%-47.7%] in nonban states and 47.2% [95% CI, 45.1%-49.4%] in Texas). A majority of mothers in both the nonban states and Texas were in the greater than high school group (75.7% [95% CI, 75.1%-74.4%] in nonban states and 67.2% [95% CI, 64.8%-69.4%] in Texas). Similarly, a majority of mothers in both groups were born in the US (73.8% [95% CI, 73.1%-77.4%] in nonban states and 68.5% [95% CI, 66.3%-70.6%] in Texas) and spoke English as the primary language in the household (84.0% [95% CI, 83.5%-84.6%] in nonban states and 77.1% [95% CI, 74.9%-79.1%] in Texas). The DiD analysis results are reported in Table 2 and show a statistically significant increase in the proportion of mothers reporting fair or poor mental health in Texas after the abortion ban, relative to mothers in states without a ban. Specifically, the proportion of Texas mothers reporting fair or poor mental health rose from 4.6% (3.2-6.0) in the preban period to 9.3% (7.3%-11.2%) in the postban period. In contrast, mothers in control states experienced a more modest increase from 5.4% (5.0%-5.8%) to 7.5% (7.1%-7.9%). Our adjusted DiD model, which accounted for the complex survey design of the NSCH and weights and controlled for household covariates, estimated an increase of 2.5 percentage points (95% CI, <0.0-5.0 percentage points) in the likelihood of fair or poor mental health among Texas mothers relative to the control group. We estimated our DiD model for subgroups of mothers stratified by their age group, child’s type of insurance coverage, and education ( Figure ), which revealed the largest statistically significant increase in the reported likelihood was observed among mothers whose children were covered by public insurance, with the estimate showing an increase of 7.06 percentage points (95% CI, 0.83-13.29 percentage points) in mothers reporting fair or poor mental health after the abortion ban in Texas compared with mothers with public insurance in the nonban states. The other age, education, or insurance groups did not show statistically significant differential changes. The sensitivity analysis using linear regression and the Stata margin command found a slight difference in the magnitude of the association compared with our main results, but the overall conclusion remained the same (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 ). Our sensitivity analysis of the association of the Texas abortion ban with mothers reporting fair or poor physical health compared with nonban states did not show any statistically significant association (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 ). The association of an abortion ban with the likelihood of fathers’ reporting fair or poor mental health was also not statistically significant (eTable 6 in the Supplement 1 ).
sections.discussion: This cross-sectional study found that mothers in Texas experienced a significant decline in mental health following the SB8 abortion ban compared with mothers in comparison states without an abortion ban. We found the estimated association to be more pronounced among mothers who were covered by public health insurance. The results of this analysis are consistent with previous literature, which documents significant adverse outcomes associated with abortion restrictions and/or ban on maternal health, 15 , 16 but contribute to the field by providing evidence of a decline in mental health of mothers regardless of whether they were seeking abortion or not. This increase in fair or poor mental health suggests that Texas’s unique legal environment—which includes civil enforcement and no exemptions for congenital anomalies—may have broader implications for health care access more generally. The shortage of medical residents and the exodus of clinicians from the state suggests that the observed decline in mental health may be a negative externality of a strained maternal health infrastructure that affects all mothers, including those past their early reproductive years. 5 , 6 This finding could be associated with several factors that are related to broader negative consequences of an abortion ban for the health care system. For example, compared with states where abortion is accessible, states with restrictive policies may have fewer maternal clinicians, 23 more maternity care deserts, 23 , 24 and higher rates of care delays, 25 which are associated with worse mental health outcomes for mothers. In addition, the literature has found that in states with abortion bans, there has been a documented exodus of clinicians and a decrease in the number of medical residents choosing to train there. 26 , 27 , 28 This shortage of skilled health care professionals can lead to a decline in the overall quality of maternal and reproductive health care, 29 thus potentially having an adverse impact on maternal mental health. Our findings also suggest that the mental health implications of SB8 extend beyond individuals who are pregnant or actively seeking abortion care. While mechanisms such as delayed or foregone pregnancy-related care are likely most salient for mothers of younger children or those considering additional births, broader system-level and psychosocial mechanisms may affect all reproductive-age mothers. These include reduced availability of maternal and reproductive health clinicians, increased care fragmentation, and heightened stress associated with constrained reproductive autonomy. 10 , 11 , 12 Such mechanisms may plausibly relate to mothers of older children through reduced access to preventive care, increased caregiving strain in a constrained health system, and broader stressors linked to policy environments. 23 , 25 The findings of our analysis have several implications for the post- Dobbs health policy landscape. A decline in maternal mental health observed alongside abortion bans may restrict the ability to parent in a safe and healthy environment, thus having a population health influence that goes beyond the direct ramifications of an abortion ban. The findings also highlight the importance of expanding mental health services, especially for mothers, and integrating mental health screenings and support into routine prenatal and postpartum care. We further note that Texas represents a particularly important policy context. SB8 was among the earliest and most restrictive abortion laws, with a unique enforcement mechanism and limited exemptions. As such, Texas may serve as an early indicator of how similar policies might be associated with maternal mental health and health systems functioning in other states.
sections.limitations: Despite using a large national dataset and a DiD research design, the study has several limitations. First, our data are self-reported, which introduces the potential for social desirability bias and recall bias, and thus may result in an underestimation or overestimation of the parent’s mental health status. In addition, the public discourse surrounding SB8 may have increased emotional salience, leading to a heightened awareness (and thus increased reporting) of distress. Because these measures are subjective rather than clinical diagnoses, our results may reflect changes in perceived psychological well-being rather than clinical pathology. Furthermore, the survey relied on parent 1 as the respondent for parent 2 and children in the household. While 69% of our sample was considered parent 1, the proxy-reported measures for parent 2 may also have resulted in underestimation or overestimation of the primary outcome. Second, the DiD approach relies on key causal assumptions, including parallel trends between treatment and control groups, absence of differential concurrent shocks, and stable composition over time. Although our event study analyses support the parallel trends assumption, violations of these assumptions due to unobserved time-varying confounders cannot be ruled out. Third, our data are cross-sectional, which limits our ability to make causal inferences. Fourth, we are unable to directly observe pregnancy status, recency of childbirth, or fertility intentions, which limited our ability to distinguish mechanisms that may differentially affect mothers of younger vs older children. Fifth, SB8 was passed during the COVID-19 pandemic and effects of the COVID-19 pandemic alongside newly legal abortion restrictions may be compounded. Sixth, our study period ended in 2023, 2 years after the SB8 implementation, and our results indicated its short-term impact. Future studies need to assess the long-term impacts.
sections.conclusions: In this cross-sectional study of reproductive-age mothers between 2017 and 2023, we found that residence in a state with an abortion ban was associated with worse mental health outcomes compared with residence in states without such a ban. This finding is particularly relevant after the Supreme Court Dobbs decision and suggests that a negative externality of abortion bans might be adverse maternal mental health outcomes. 21 , 24

title: Associations Between Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat and Venous Thromboembolism Among 118 619 Participants With Metabolic Syndrome: Insights From Epidemiology to Genetic Susceptibility
abstract: Background Metabolic syndrome substantially elevates venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, increasing health care burdens. The Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat (METS‐VF) offers a novel, simplified approach to assess visceral fat. This study evaluates METS‐VF's association with VTE risk and its utility for risk stratification in patients with metabolic syndrome. Methods Using UK Biobank data, we included 118 619 participants with metabolic syndrome free of VTE at baseline. Time‐dependent area under the curve analysis with bootstrap validation identified the strongest VTE predictor. Multivariable Cox models assessed associations of METS‐VF, a VTE‐specific polygenic risk score, and their combination with incident VTE. Mediation analysis evaluated potential mediators. Robustness was assessed through subgroup and sensitivity analyses, including competing risk of death. Results Over a median 12‐year follow‐up, 5162 participants developed VTE. METS‐VF demonstrated stronger association with VTE than traditional metabolic indicators. Highest quartile participants showed significantly increased risks of VTE (hazard ratio [HR], 1.46 [95% CI, 1.33–1.61]), pulmonary embolism (HR, 1.50 [95% CI, 1.33–1.70]), deep vein thrombosis (HR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.34–1.73]), and lower‐extremity deep vein thrombosis (HR, 1.59 [95% CI, 1.38–1.82]). Stratified analysis revealed synergistic interaction between METS‐VF and genetic susceptibility. CRP (C‐reactive protein) and estimated glomerular filtration rate significantly mediated the METS‐VF–VTE association. Conclusions METS‐VF is a significant, independent risk indicator for VTE in patients with metabolic syndrome, demonstrating synergistic effects with genetic risk. The CRP‐ and estimated glomerular filtration rate–mediated association supports METS‐VF's clinical utility in VTE risk stratification.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: The Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat is established as a novel and independent risk indicator for venous thromboembolism and its subtypes in individuals with metabolic syndrome. An additive interaction between the Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat and genetic risk for venous thromboembolism was observed in this population, underscoring their combined effect.
sections.what question should be addressed next?: Future studies should explore the utility of the Metabolic Score for Visceral Fat in capturing “residual” metabolic risk in low‐genetic‐risk populations, while simultaneously refining risk stratification for those already at high genetic predisposition to achieve peak precision in prevention.
sections.methods_1: All methods used in this study were conducted in accordance with the relevant guidelines and declarations. The project was approved under UK Biobank approval number 106027 and adhered to the protocols established by the North West Multi‐Centre Research Ethics Committee as part of the UK Biobank's Research Tissue Bank approval. Given the nature of the UK Biobank's approval framework, no separate ethical approval was required for this specific study. Further details on the UK Biobank's ethical framework can be found at Ethics Advisory Committee ( https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ethics ). All participants in the UK Biobank provided written, informed consent at the time of recruitment. In accordance with the Transparency and Openness Promotion Guidelines implemented by the American Heart Association journals, the data that support the findings of this study will be made available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and subject to a data use agreement.
sections.definition of mets , vte, and study part: MetS was diagnosed on the basis of a modified set of criteria that included 5 components: obesity, defined as a waist circumference (WC) of ≥102 cm for men and ≥88 cm for women; elevated triglycerides with levels of ≥150 mg/dL (≥1.7 mmol/L); elevated blood pressure characterized by a systolic blood pressure of ≥130 mm Hg or a diastolic blood pressure of ≥85 mm Hg, or a baseline diagnosis of hypertension; elevated blood glucose with fasting glucose levels of ≥100 mg/dL (≥5.6 mmol/L), or a baseline diagnosis of diabetes; and reduced HDL‐C with levels of <40 mg/dL (<1.0 mmol/L) for men and <50 mg/dL (<1.3 mmol/L) for women, or the use of lipid‐modifying medications. Participants were diagnosed with MetS if they met ≥3 of these criteria. 15 The study population was derived from the UK Biobank, with an initial cohort of 502 248 participants. Participants with missing data on WC (n=2160) were excluded, followed by those with missing triglyceride levels (n=34 264), HDL‐C levels (n=39 601), and height measurements (n=440). After these exclusions, a total of 425 783 participants remained. Of these, only those diagnosed with MetS (n=123 845) were included in the analysis. Further exclusion was applied to participants with a history of VTE or its subtypes (n=5226), resulting in a final study population of 118 619 participants (Figure 1 ). VTE was identified using the following International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision ( ICD‐10 ), codes: I80 (I80.1, I80.2, I80.3, I80.8, and I80.9), I81, I82 (I82.1, I82.2, I82.3, I82.8, and I82.9), and I26 (I26.0 and I26.9). And the specific subtypes were defined as follows: pulmonary embolism (PE) was identified with codes I26.0 and I26.9. Lower‐extremity DVT (LEDVT) was defined using codes I80.1 (femoral vein), I80.2 (other deep vessels of lower extremities), and I80.3 (lower extremities, unspecified). The broader category of DVT included all LEDVT codes plus thromboses at other sites, using codes I80.1, I80.2, I80.3, I81, I82.1, I82.2, I82.3, I82.8, and I82.9. VTE cases were identified using hospital inpatient admissions and death registry records. Inpatient admissions records were available from the Hospital Episode Statistics for England, the Scottish Morbidity Record for Scotland, and the Patient Episode Database for Wales. Death registry records were available from the National Health Service England for England and Wales, and the Information and Statistics Division for Scotland. Primary and secondary hospital diagnoses and causes of death were recorded using the ICD‐10 coding system. The ICD‐10 codes used to ascertain VTE were selected and validated by the UK Biobank outcome adjudication group. In the UK Biobank data set, follow‐up is primarily conducted through linkage with national routine data sets. In this study, the latest date of VTE confirmation was in January 2024.
sections.measurement of metabolic indexes: The METS‐VF was calculated to estimate visceral adiposity through a hierarchical structure: Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance: The Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance was first calculated 16 : METS − IR = ln 2 × FPG + TG × BMI ln HDL − C where FPG is fasting plasma glucose (mg/dL), TG is triglycerides (mg/dL), BMI is body mass index (kg/m 2 ), and HDL‐C is high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (mg/dL). 2 METS‐VF: The Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance value was integrated with age, sex, and waist/height ratio (WHtR; calculated as waist circumference divided by height) 9 : The formula for calculating METS‐VF is (sex: male = 1, female = 0; age: years): METS − VF = 4.466 + 0.011 ln METS − IR 3 + 3.239 ln WHtR 3 + 0.319 Sex + 0.594 ln Age Detailed formulas for secondary indicators (visceral adiposity index, triglyceride‐glucose index, triglyceride‐glucose index–body mass index, triglyceride‐glucose index–waist circumference, and triglyceride‐glucose index–waist/height ratio) are provided in the Table S1 .
sections.other covariates: Baseline data included information on sex, race, educational level, smoking status, alcohol consumption, income, and physical activity. Smoking status was categorized as never, former, or current smoker. Alcohol consumption was classified on the basis of frequency, with categories including never, former, and current drinkers. Income levels were divided into 5 brackets: <£18 000, £18 000 to £30 999, £31 000 to £51 999, £52 000 to £100 000, and >£100 000. Physical activity was assessed on the basis of the frequency of weekly exercise sessions. Hypertension was defined on the basis of self‐reported history of hypertension, hospital records, systolic blood pressure ≥140 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg, or the use of antihypertensive medications. Diabetes was diagnosed through self‐reported history, hospital records, glycated hemoglobin >6.5%, or fasting blood glucose >7.0 mmol/L. The diagnosis of cancer was based on self‐reported history or hospital records. Given the baseline enrollment period (2006–2010), the anticoagulant medications primarily consisted of warfarin and various heparins.
sections.exclusion and stratification based on vt: The VTE polygenic risk score (PRS) was derived from published data sets of the UK Biobank and calculated using a Bayesian approach. After excluding participants with missing data on the VTE PRS, the final study population comprised 116 977 individuals. Consistent with previous studies, 17 , 18 participants were categorized into different risk groups according to quintiles of the PRS distribution: the lowest quintile (quintile 1) as the low‐risk group, the second to fourth quintiles (quintile 2–quintile 4) as the intermediate‐risk group, and the highest quintile (quintile 5) as the high‐risk group. This stratification allowed for the assessment of VTE risk across different genetic predisposition levels while accounting for the polygenic nature of VTE.
sections.statistical analysis: All analyses were conducted using R software. The predictive performance of METS‐VF and other metabolic indicators for VTE risk was evaluated using the concordance index and time‐dependent area under the curve analysis. To address the inherent overfitting and inflation of accuracy that occurs when a model is evaluated on the same data used for its development, we used bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). This approach allows for the calculation of bias‐corrected estimates, ensuring a more realistic and generalizable assessment of each indicator's discriminatory power. Baseline characteristics of the study participants are presented according to quartiles of the METS‐VF. Continuous variables were assessed for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Normally distributed data are presented as mean±SD, whereas nonnormally distributed data are summarized as median with interquartile range. Categorical variables are expressed as frequency and percentage. Between‐group comparisons were conducted using χ 2 tests for categorical variables, 1‐way ANOVA for normally distributed continuous variables, and the Kruskal–Wallis test for nonnormally distributed continuous variables. The cumulative incidence of outcome events was visualized by Kaplan–Meier curves, and differences between METS‐VF groups were compared using the log‐rank test. To further evaluate the association between METS‐VF and the risk of VTE outcomes, we used Cox proportional hazards regression models with a progressive adjustment strategy: Model 1 was unadjusted; model 2 included adjustments for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors (age, gender, race, educational level, household income, sleep duration, changes in eating habits, smoking status, alcohol consumption, and physical activity); and model 3 further incorporated clinical covariates, including hypertension, diabetes, glycated hemoglobin, total cholesterol, CRP, eGFR, uric acid, as well as the use of aspirin, insulin, lipid‐lowering drugs, anticoagulants, and antihypertensive medications. The proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals, and no material violations were observed. Finally, we also assessed the joint association of METS‐VF and the number of MetS components with VTE risk, applying the same covariate adjustments as in model 3. To investigate potential sources of effect heterogeneity, we examined the associations between METS‐VF and VTE (including subtypes) across various subgroups. These subgroups were based on age (≤60 or >60 years), sex (male or female), and the presence or absence of individual MetS components (elevated WC, elevated triglycerides, elevated blood pressure, elevated fasting glucose, and reduced HDL‐C). Restricted cubic splines were applied to explore nonlinear relationships. If a nonlinear association was identified, a 2‐piecewise Cox regression model (adjusted for model 3 covariates) was fitted on both sides of the inflection point to quantify threshold effects. We used the PRS to determine genetic predisposition to VTE and its subtypes, followed by an evaluation of the joint and interaction association between this genetic susceptibility and METS‐VF. Mediation analysis was performed using a 3‐step approach to assess the potential mediating roles of eGFR and CRP: (1) linear regression models were used to examine the association between METS‐VF and each mediator (eGFR and CRP); (2) parametric survival models were applied to evaluate the relationships of METS‐VF, eGFR, and CRP with VTE‐free survival; and (3) formal mediation analysis was conducted using the R package “mediation” with 1000 simulations, adjusting for model 3 covariates, to estimate the proportion mediated and its 95% CI. To ensure robustness of the findings, we performed several sensitivity analyses: (1) an additional Cox regression model based on model 3 but further adjusted for cancer history; (2) a competing risk analysis using the Fine‐Gray model, treating all‐cause mortality as a competing event, to evaluate the association of METS‐VF with VTE and its subtypes; and (3) analyses to evaluate potential collider bias: (a) 1:1 propensity score matching with a non‐MetS cohort followed by Cox regression (model 3) in the matched set, and (b) testing for interaction between METS‐VF and the number of MetS components within the MetS cohort using Cox regression (model 3) (see Supplementary Material for details). We used multiple imputation with 5 repetitions and chained equations to handle covariates with missing data (<20% missing) before multivariable modeling, with details on missingness summarized in Table S2 . All statistical tests were 2 sided, with P <0.05 defining significance.
sections.selection of optimal vte prediction fact: The concordance index and time‐dependent areas under the curve were used to evaluate the predictive performance of METS‐VF, Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance, visceral adiposity index, triglyceride‐glucose index, triglyceride‐glucose index–body mass index, triglyceride‐glucose index–waist circumference, and triglyceride‐glucose index–waist/height ratio for the risk of VTE. The results demonstrated that METS‐VF exhibited the highest concordance index compared with other metabolic markers (Table S3 ). Moreover, METS‐VF showed superior area under the curve values for predicting incident VTE, PE, DVT, and LEDVT in both short‐, medium‐, and long‐term follow‐ups. The comprehensive comparison indicated that METS‐VF had the best discriminative ability among these metabolic indicators (Figure 2 ). To investigate the association between METS‐VF and the risk of VTE and its subtypes in participants with MetS, we first summarized their baseline characteristics (Table 1 ). Of this population, 5162 incident VTE events were documented over a median follow‐up of 13.2 years (Table S4 ). Initial assessment using Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed that the highest METS‐VF quartile (quartile 4) was consistently associated with the greatest cumulative incidence for overall VTE, PE, DVT, and LEDVT (Figure S1 ). Consistent with these findings, the results from Cox proportional hazards models further demonstrated a graded increase in risk, as detailed by the unadjusted and multivariable‐adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs across METS‐VF quartiles for all end points in Table 2 . In the fully adjusted model (model 3), participants in the highest quartile (quartile 4) had a 46% increased risk of incident VTE (HR, 1.46 [95% CI, 1.33–1.61]), a 50% increased risk of PE (HR, 1.50 [95% CI, 1.33–1.70]), a 52% increased risk of DVT (HR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.34–1.73]), and a 59% increased risk of LEDVT (HR, 1.59 [95% CI, 1.38–1.82]) compared with those in quartile 1. When analyzing METS‐VF as a continuous variable in model 3, each unit increase in METS‐VF was associated with a 53% increase in the risk of incident VTE (HR, 1.53 [95% CI, 1.40–1.67]), a 64% increase in PE risk (HR, 1.64 [95% CI, 1.46–1.84]), a 52% increase in DVT risk (HR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.35–1.70]), and a 60% increase in LEDVT risk (HR, 1.60 [95% CI, 1.41–1.82]).
sections.subgroup analysis of the association bet: Subgroup analyses were conducted using age (with 60 years as the cutoff), sex, and individual components of MetS as binary subgroup variables. The subgroup analysis (Figure 3 ) reveals that the association between Mets‐VF and the risk of incident VTE and PE varies significantly by sex ( P interaction =0.001). Specifically, Mets‐VF demonstrates superior risk stratification ability among female participants with MetS.
sections.cox regression analysis of the associati: Further stratified analyses were conducted on the basis of the number of MetS components among participants. Participants in the quartile 3 and quartile 4 categories of METS‐VF exhibited relatively higher risks of incident VTE across different groups of MetS component counts. Compared with participants who had only 3 MetS components and were in the quartile 1 category of Mets‐VF, those with 5 MetS components and in the quartile 4 category of METS‐VF had the highest risks of incident VTE (HR, 1.48 [95% CI, 1.32–1.67]), PE (HR, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.30–1.77]), DVT (HR, 1.53 [95% CI, 1.30–1.79]), and LEDVT (HR, 1.61 [95% CI, 1.35–1.91]) (Figure 4 ).
sections.rcs curves between mets \u2010 vf and vt: Figure 5 illustrates the relationship between METS‐VF and various types of thromboembolic events. For VTE (panel A; P ‐overall <0.001, P ‐nonlinear=0.003), the inflection point was 7.225. Below this point, each 1‐unit METS‐VF was associated with an increased VTE risk (HR, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.16–1.50]); above it, risk further increased (HR, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.60–2.19]). A similar pattern was observed for PE (panel B; P ‐overall <0.001, P ‐nonlinear <0.001), with an inflection point at 7.285. METS‐VF increases below and above this threshold were associated with significantly higher PE risks, with HRs of 1.31 (95% CI, 1.12–1.54) and 2.39 (95% CI, 1.91–3.00), respectively. Panels C and D show a predominantly linear relationship between METS‐VF and 2 thrombotic outcomes, with hints of nonlinear trends ( P ‐overall <0.001 for both; P ‐nonlinear=0.265 for DVT and P ‐nonlinear=0.537 for LEDVT).
sections.association between mets \u2010 vf and v: The association between VTE‐PRS and the risk of incident VTE was evaluated (Table S5 ). In the fully adjusted model, compared with participants with MetS with low genetic risk, those with high genetic risk had an increased risk of incident VTE (HR, 2.51 [95% CI, 2.29–2.75]), PE (HR, 2.82 [95% CI, 2.49–3.20]), DVT (HR, 2.46 [95% CI, 2.17–2.79]), and LEDVT (HR, 2.72 [95% CI, 2.38–3.31]) among participants with MetS. Further stratified analysis by PRS risk categories revealed that, in the low‐, medium‐, and high‐risk groups, individuals with METS‐VF in the quartile 4 category had a 106%, 63%, and 43% higher risk of incident VTE, a 77%, 78%, and 48% higher risk of incident PE, a 128%, 60%, and 54% higher risk of incident DVT, and an 118%, 68%, and 57% higher risk of incident LEDVT compared with those in the quartile 1 category, respectively (Figure 6A – 6D ). Joint analysis of METS‐VF and PRS showed that, compared with participants with low genetic risk and METS‐VF in the quartile 1 category, those with high genetic risk and METS‐VF in the quartile 4 category had a significantly higher risk of incident VTE (HR, 3.24 [95% CI, 2.65–3.97]), PE (HR, 3.44 [95% CI, 2.64–4.46]), DVT (HR, 3.43 [95% CI, 2.61–4.52]), and LEDVT (HR, 3.94 [95% CI, 2.91–5.33]) (Figure 6E – 6H ). And we assessed the interaction between METS‐VF and VTE PRS on the risk of various thromboembolic events. A statistically significant positive additive interaction was observed for the risks of VTE, PE, and LEDVT, as indicated by the relative excess risk attributable to interaction, attributable proportion due to interaction, and synergy indexes (Table S6 ). Notably, the synergistic effect was most pronounced for PE. In contrast, no significant interaction was found for DVT or on the multiplicative scale for any outcome. Additionally, the integrative model combining the PRS and METS‐VF achieved the highest predictive efficacy for VTE and its subtypes (area under the curve >0.66), significantly outperforming each standalone model (Figure S2 ), underscoring the complementary effect of genetic and metabolic determinants in VTE development.
sections.mediation analysis investigating the rel: To further elucidate the underlying mechanisms linking METS‐VF to the risk of VTE, we conducted a mediation analysis using eGFR and CRP as potential mediators (Figure 7 ). Notably, METS‐VF exhibited a significant negative correlation with eGFR (β±SE=−1.966±0.101; P <0.001) and a positive correlation with CRP (β±SE=2.06±0.038; P <0.001). These results indicate that elevated levels of METS‐VF are associated with decreased renal function (as measured by eGFR) and increased inflammation (as indicated by CRP levels). Mediation models revealed a partial mediating role for both eGFR and CRP. The proportions of the total METS‐VF–VTE association mediated by eGFR were 5.6% for VTE, 5.5% for PE, 5.3% for DVT, and 5.5% for LEDVT. Corresponding proportions mediated by CRP were 5.3%, 4.8%, 5.0%, and 4.8%, respectively.
sections.sensitivity analyses: To evaluate the robustness of our primary findings, we conducted multiple sensitivity analyses. The association between METS‐VF and VTE and its subtypes remained consistent in an additional Cox model that adjusted for history of cancer. Moreover, results were corroborated by a multivariable competing risk analysis with all‐cause mortality as a competing event. These findings collectively support the stability of the observed associations (Tables S7 and S8 ). To address potential collider bias arising from restricting the analysis to individuals with MetS, 2 supplementary analyses were conducted. First, using a propensity score–matched cohort, we matched MetS and non‐MetS participants based on key demographic and clinical variables. Following matching, the 2 groups achieved balance in critical covariates, including age, sex, and race (see Table S9 for postmatching baseline characteristics and Figure S3 for balance diagnostics). In this matched cohort, the association between higher METS‐VF levels and increased VTE risk remained significant and directionally consistent among individuals without MetS (Table S10 ). Second, interaction analysis within the MetS cohort showed no statistically significant effect modification by the number of MetS components for any VTE outcome (Table S11 ). Collectively, these findings suggest that collider bias is unlikely to substantially influence the observed association between METS‐VF and VTE.
sections.discussion: The findings of this study underscore the significant association of METS‐VF with incident VTE risk among individuals with MetS. Our results demonstrate that METS‐VF exhibited a stronger association with VTE risk than other metabolic indicators, as evidenced by a robust, graded increase in the risks of PE, DVT, and LEDVT with increasing METS‐VF levels. This suggests that METS‐VF effectively captures the aspect of metabolic dysfunction most critically linked to thrombotic risk. The stability of this association, confirmed through extensive subgroup, sensitivity, and competing risk analyses, alongside its complementary role to genetic susceptibility, underscores the potential utility of METS‐VF as a robust tool for VTE risk stratification in the population with MetS. Additionally, mediation analysis implicates CRP and eGFR as important mediators in the relationship between METS‐VF and VTE, highlighting potential biological pathways linking metabolic dysfunction to thrombotic risk. METS‐VF is a comprehensive score based on metabolic indicators, used to assess visceral fat levels and associated health risks. 19 Compared with imaging examinations, METS‐VF is low cost and easy to operate, making it suitable for large‐scale screening. Studies have shown that METS‐VF is highly correlated with visceral fat area and shows a stronger association with outcomes than common indicators, such as BMI, WC, and waist/hip ratio. 20 Although it is comparable to WC in some cases, METS‐VF still has high practicality and value for promotion in large populations. The components of MetS are closely associated with the formation of DVT through multiple mechanisms, including alterations in hemorheology, 21 endothelial dysfunction, 22 inflammatory responses, 23 insulin resistance, 24 and so on. Visceral adipose tissue, a core factor of MetS, promotes thrombus formation through these pathways. 25 Excessive visceral adipose tissue is frequently accompanied by dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL‐C. This aberrant lipid profile contributes to a prothrombotic milieu by promoting hemodynamic alterations, such as increased blood viscosity and sluggish blood flow in the venous system, which can predispose to venous stasis, a key component of Virchow triad in VTE pathogenesis. 26 , 27 Abnormal visceral adipose and metabolic factors can damage endothelial cells, reducing the production of nitric oxide and leading to endothelial dysfunction, which, in turn, promotes platelet aggregation and the activation of coagulation factors. 28 Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) secretes various inflammatory factors (such as HMGB1 [high‐mobility group box 1 protein]), which activate immune and inflammatory responses, creating a positive feedback loop that further exacerbates inflammation. 29 These inflammatory factors can activate the coagulation system, increase the hypercoagulable state of the blood, and thereby promote the occurrence of VTE. 30 Additionally, VAT has a lower sensitivity to insulin, making it more prone to insulin resistance, which is closely related to a hypercoagulable state and increases the levels of free fatty acids in the blood. 31 These fatty acids further accumulate on the vascular wall, leading to lipid deposition and endothelial dysfunction. The accumulation of VAT is also closely associated with dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated triglyceride levels and reduced HDL levels. HDL has anticoagulant properties, and its reduced levels weaken this anticoagulant effect, increasing the risk of thrombus formation. 32 In patients with MetS, elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor‐1 levels impair fibrinolysis by inhibiting plasminogen activators, reducing plasmin generation, and thus suppressing fibrin dissolution. Consequently, thrombi are less likely to be dissolved and cleared. 12 MetS is closely associated with tumorigenesis, progression, and thrombosis in a hypercoagulable state. These factors not only increase the risk of cancer through inflammatory responses and proliferation‐promoting mechanisms (eg, breast cancer, 33 colorectal cancer, 34 and renal cancer 35 ) but also significantly elevate the risk of VTE through a hypercoagulable state. Our study further confirmed the significant association of METS‐VF with thrombotic risk through sensitivity analysis of cancer. Anticoagulant drugs play an important role in the prevention and treatment of thrombosis in patients with MetS. 36 In our analysis, we adjusted for the use of anticoagulant drugs to exclude their impact on thrombus formation. The results showed that METS‐VF still exhibited good predictive ability for thrombotic risk in patients with MetS, highlighting its simplicity and effectiveness. Notably, our subgroup analysis revealed that the association between METS‐VF and VTE risk was more pronounced in female participants. This sex‐specific disparity may be attributable to fundamental differences in body composition and fat distribution. Women typically have a higher overall percentage of body fat. 37 Thus, the METS‐VF score, by virtue of its specific reflection of visceral adiposity, may more accurately represent the key pathogenic driver of thrombotic risk in women. Furthermore, hormonal influences, particularly the decline in estrogen during menopause, which is known to shift fat distribution toward a central pattern, 38 could amplify the relative contribution of visceral fat to endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation in women, thereby making METS‐VF a more salient risk indicator in this demographic. In the joint analysis with the VTE‐PRS, we found that METS‐VF is an independent risk factor for VTE in the population with MetS. METS‐VF demonstrated a consistent association with VTE risk across all VTE‐PRS subgroups. Importantly, stratified analysis revealed that this association was strongest in participants with low genetic risk. This finding underscores the complementary roles of genetic and metabolic pathways: in individuals with low genetic susceptibility, VTE development is likely driven more substantially by acquired metabolic factors, making a high METS‐VF score a particularly potent indicator of risk. This effectively supplements the risk not captured by the genetic risk score, highlighting the clinical utility of METS‐VF for risk stratification even in those deemed to have a favorable genetic background. Consequently, integrating METS‐VF into clinical practice could help identify patients with MetS who are at a substantially elevated risk for VTE. These individuals may benefit from more vigilant monitoring and individualized risk assessment, which could guide decisions about the initiation of preventive strategies in accordance with clinical guidelines. Mediation analysis revealed that CRP and impaired eGFR play a significant mediating role in the association between METS‐VF and the incidence of VTE. This finding is consistent with previous studies, which have demonstrated that elevated CRP levels and impaired renal function are associated with an increased risk of thrombosis. 11 , 14 Specifically, CRP, as an inflammatory marker, is closely related to chronic inflammation. Inflammatory responses can activate the coagulation system, leading to a hypercoagulable state and thereby increasing the risk of thrombosis. Moreover, a reduced eGFR, indicative of impaired renal function, is often associated with a prothrombotic state. Patients with renal insufficiency typically exhibit impaired fibrinolytic system function, which further inhibits fibrinolysis and makes thrombi more resistant to dissolution and clearance. The synergistic effect of inflammation and renal impairment significantly increases the risk of VTE, highlighting the important impact of inflammation and renal function on thrombosis in the context of METS‐VF. In patients with MetS, particularly those with high METS‐VF, regular follow‐up and assessment are essential. Moreover, lifestyle changes and management of modifiable risk factors are equally important. 39 Studies have shown that weight loss, the use of glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists or sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, and regular exercise can significantly reduce all‐cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and VTE incidence in patients with MetS. 40 , 41 , 42 Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists and sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors both play important roles in the treatment of MetS. Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists, through mechanisms that promote insulin secretion, suppress appetite, and slow gastrointestinal motility, not only significantly reduce body weight but also improve metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis, reduce plasma glucose and hepatic inflammation, and improve cardiac and renal function. 43 Sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce blood glucose levels by inhibiting renal glucose reabsorption and increasing urinary glucose excretion, and they also provide multiple benefits, including weight reduction, blood pressure lowering, improved insulin resistance, and reduced serum uric acid levels. Additionally, they can reduce cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalization risks, thereby improving cardiovascular outcomes. 44 Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the generalizability of our results is limited by the predominantly European ancestry of the UK Biobank cohort, highlighting the need for validation in more ethnically and geographically diverse populations. Second, because all exposure and covariate data were assessed only at baseline, we could not account for potential changes in metabolic parameters, medication use, or incident comorbidities during follow‐up, which might influence VTE risk. Third, although we adjusted for a PRS of VTE, we did not specifically account for monogenic forms of inherited thrombophilia, which may represent a source of residual genetic confounding. Finally, despite the use of mediation analysis to explore potential pathways, the observational nature of our study design precludes definitive causal inferences about the relationships between METS‐VF, mediating factors, and VTE. In summary, our study suggested that METS‐VF could be a valuable tool for risk stratification in clinical practice and highlights the importance of further exploring the underlying mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets. For patients with MetS, especially those with high METS‐VF, a comprehensive management strategy, including regular follow‐up, anticoagulant therapy when necessary, and lifestyle changes and management of modifiable risk factors, is key to reducing VTE risk and improving cardiovascular prognosis. Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists and sodium‐glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors play a central role in weight reduction and improvement of metabolic syndrome–related complications, providing new directions for the treatment of MetS. Future research should further explore the long‐term effects and mechanisms of these interventions in different populations with MetS.
sections.conclusions_1: In conclusion, this study establishes METS‐VF as a significant and independent risk indicator for VTE events among individuals with MetS. The findings indicate that higher METS‐VF values are significantly associated with increased risks of VTE, PE, DVT, and LEDVT. Subgroup, stratified, and joint analyses confirm its stability and generalizability. Mediation analysis highlights CRP and eGFR as key factors mediating the METS‐VF–VTE relationship, suggesting biological pathways linking metabolic dysfunction to thrombotic risk. These results support the potential use of METS‐VF for VTE risk stratification in clinical practice and emphasize the need for further research into underlying mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
