title:
Serotonin Transporter
Blockade Reduces the Psychedelic-Like
Effects of 4‑Methoxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine and Related Analogs
abstract:
Tryptamine psychedelics induce psychoactive effects via
agonist
actions at serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT 2A ), but the compounds
are generally nonselective. 4-Methoxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-MeO-MiPT) is a 5-HT 2A agonist which also blocks the 5-HT transporter (SERT) and has blunted
visual and other psychedelic effects in humans. Here, we compared
the pharmacology of 4-MeO-MiPT, its 4-hydroxy derivative (4-HO-MiPT),
and related analogs with N- alkyl or 4-alkoxy variations.
We hypothesized that compounds with more potent SERT uptake inhibition
would display reduced 5-HT 2A -mediated psychedelic-like
effects in the mouse head twitch response (HTR) model. In
vitro target profiling revealed potent and efficacious 5-HT
receptor activities for most of the compounds, including 5-HT 2A receptor agonism (EC 50 = 10–118 nM, E max = 72–97% 5-HT). Importantly, 4-MeO-MiPT
and its N , N -diisopropyl (4-MeO-DiPT)
and N -methyl- N -cyclopropyl (4-MeO-McPT)
analogs displayed more potent uptake inhibition at SERT (IC 50 = 17–107 nM) than their 4-OH counterparts (IC 50 = 280–423 nM). Studies administering the drugs subcutaneously
to C57BL/6J mice revealed that 4-HO- and 4-MeO-MiPT (0.03–30
mg/kg) had similar potencies for inducing HTRs (ED 50 =
0.75 vs 0.97 mg/kg), but 4-MeO-MiPT had reduced efficacy ( E max = 77 vs 34 HTRs/30 min). A similar trend
for decreased HTRs was observed for 4-MeO-DiPT and 4-MeO-McPT. Pretreatment
with the SERT inhibitor fluoxetine (10 mg/kg) prior to 4-HO-MiPT,
4-HO-DiPT, or 4-HO-McPT reduced the maximal number of HTRs to levels
observed for their respective 4-MeO analogs. Overall, our data indicate
that 4-MeO-MiPT interacts with 5-HT 2A and other 5-HT receptors,
but the drug also inhibits SERT to reduce the efficacy of psychedelic-like
effects in mice. Therefore, 4-MeO-MiPT and other dual 5-HT 2A /SERT ligands may be therapeutically relevant compounds with reduced
potential for traditional acute psychedelic effects.

sections.introduction:
4-Phosphoryloxy- N , N -dimethyltryptamine
(psilocybin) is a serotonergic psychedelic that is being investigated
as a treatment adjunct for psychiatric conditions such as depression,
anxiety, and substance use disorders, while other psychoactive tryptamines
are increasingly popular as recreational drugs. − Psilocybin and serotonergic psychedelics,
like lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), produce psychoactive effects
in humans and effects in rodents by acting as agonists at serotonin
(5-HT) 2A receptors (5-HT 2A ) in the central nervous system. − Despite strong evidence for the role of 5-HT 2A in mediating
the actions of serotonergic psychedelics, many of the drugs also target
other 5-HT receptor subtypes (e.g., 5-HT 1A receptors or 5-HT 1A ), non-5-HT receptors (e.g., alpha-adrenergic receptors and
melatonin receptors), and nonreceptor proteins (e.g., monoamine transporters). 4-Hydroxy- N,N- dimethyltryptamine
(psilocin) is
the active metabolite of psilocybin. Homologs of psilocin varying
in N -alkyl or 4-position length or bulk have been
synthesized and pharmacologically characterized, with varying degrees
of purported psychedelic subjective effects in humans. , − As an example, 4-hydroxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (miprocin or 4-HO-MiPT) is the isopropyl homolog
of psilocin, which was originally synthesized by Repke and colleagues
( Figure ). Psilocin and miprocin are reported to exert
similar psychedelic subjective effects. , In contrast
to miprocin, its 4-methoxy analog, 4-methoxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-MeO-MiPT), is reported to have
reduced psychedelic effects based on anecdotal accounts. The subjective experiences induced by 4-MeO-MiPT
are described
as less visual, with weaker overall psychedelic subjective effects
that share some similarities with the entactogen 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine
(MDMA) and the 5-methoxy miprocin analog, 5-MeO-MiPT. , 5-Methoxy analogs of psilocin, miprocin, and related 4-hydroxy tryptamines
are also considered psychedelics, , − but its unclear if other 4-MeO tryptamine analogs may have reduced
psychedelic effects akin to 4-MeO-MiPT. The pharmacological target
profiles of 4-MeO-MiPT and miprocin have not been reported or compared,
but it has been shown that 4-MeO-MiPT and the related N , N -diisopropyl analog (4-MeO-DiPT) are 7–50
times more potent at blocking 5-HT uptake via the serotonin transporter
(SERT) (IC 50 = 11–53 nM) compared to their respective
4-hydroxy and 5-methoxy counterparts. Moreover, SERT activity has been implicated in modulating psychedelic-like
effects of psilocybin and other 5-HT 2A agonists in preclinical
studies, − and anecdotal reports suggest that human subjects taking 5-HT selective
reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have reduced psychoactive effects, or
less negative experiences, when exposed to psychedelic drugs in some
cases. − Here, the in vitro pharmacological target
profiles
of miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT were determined to elucidate potential
mechanisms responsible for differences in their reported psychoactive
effects. Based on preliminary screening results and our previous work
characterizing the quaternary tryptammonium and 5-MeO analogs of miprocin
and related tryptamines, , we surmised that bulky N -alkyl groups would confer the highest potency for SERT
uptake inhibition. Therefore, in the present study, the structure
of 4-MeO-MiPT was modified to increase steric bulk at the amine group
or lengthen the 4-position alkoxy chain to examine the structure–activity
relationships (SAR) governing activities at 5-HT receptors (e.g.,
5-HT 2A ) and monoamine transporters (e.g., SERT). Furthermore,
we tested the compounds in the head twitch response (HTR) assay, which
is a translational mouse model used to assess central 5-HT 2A activation and predict relative potencies for inducing subjective
psychedelic effects of drugs in humans. In particular, the acute dose-related
effects of 4-MeO-MiPT and its analogs were tested to determine whether
SERT activity modulates the HTR. Overall, the data show that certain
4-MeO analogs display potent SERT inhibition that dampens their psychedelic-like
effects in mice, consistent with available anecdotal reports in humans.
Hybrid 5-HT 2A /SERT compounds may thus be ideal candidate
therapeutics for clinical indications where reduced psychedelic or
psychoactive effects are desirable.
sections.target profiling of miprocin and 4-meo-m:
Anecdotal
reports suggest that miprocin produces robust psychedelic subjective
effects in humans, whereas 4-MeO-MiPT has blunted effects in this
regard. , , Furthermore,
recent in vitro pharmacological data suggest that
4-MeO-MiPT and its N , N -dialkyl analog,
4-MeO-DiPT, are 5-HT 2A agonists that display more potent
uptake inhibition at SERT relative to their 4-hydroxy counterparts. Therefore, initial studies were conducted to
characterize the comprehensive in vitro pharmacological
target profiles of miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT to identify relevant targets
that may explain their differential subjective effects. The
compounds were screened across 48 potential targets (listed in Materials and Methods ) using fixed 10 μM concentrations
in competition binding studies. Hits were defined as compounds with
>50% inhibition of radioligand binding, and compounds achieving
this
criterion were subjected to full concentration–response testing
to determine affinities ( Figure S1 ). The affinities of the drugs were also assessed
at mouse 5-HT 1A (m5-HT 1A ) and 5-HT 2A receptors (m5-HT 2A ) in postmortem brain tissue preparations
( Figure S1A , Figure S2 ). The affinities at human and mouse receptor subtypes were
similar across compounds. Miprocin had nM affinities at 5-HT 1E , 5-HT 2A , m5-HT 2A , 5-HT 2B , and 5-HT 6 (K i values = 66–695 nM; Figure S1A ), whereas 4-MeO-MiPT had nM affinities at 5-HT 1A , m5-HT 1A , 5-HT 1D , 5-HT 2A , m5-HT 2A , 5-HT 2B , and 5-HT 2C (K i values = 48–810 nM; Figure S1A ). The only common non-5-HT receptor target for miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT
was SERT, but 4-MeO-MiPT had ∼6 times higher affinity (K i value = 41 nM; Figure S1B ). At
non-5-HT receptors, 4-MeO-MiPT had nM affinities for alpha adrenergic
(alpha 2A , alpha 2C ) and sigma-2 receptors ( K i values = 240–843 nM; Figure S1B ). Miprocin had no other targets with nM affinities
outside of 5-HT receptor subtypes and SERT. Overall, the compounds
had similar and overlapping target profiles, but 4-MeO-MiPT displayed
higher affinities for 5-HT 1A and SERT relative to miprocin. Fixed 10 μM screening assays were employed to identify functional
relevance of targets identified in binding assays. Miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT both exhibited agonist activity
at 5-HT 2 receptor subtypes in a Gαq-calcium mobilization
assay, relative to the reference agonist 5-HT ( Figure S1C ). Both compounds had higher activity at 5-HT 2A (87–95% 5-HT) vs 5-HT 2B and 5-HT 2C receptors (43–76% 5-HT). In the Tango screening assay for
arrestin signaling, both miprocin and
4-MeO-MiPT displayed agonist activity at various 5-HT 1 ,
5-HT 2 , and 5-HT 7 subtypes, albeit with low efficacies
(31–59% 5-HT; Figure S1D ). Miprocin
had substantial efficacy at 5-HT 1E (72% 5-HT), whereas
4-MeO-MiPT had substantial efficacy at 5-HT 1D (76% 5-HT)
and 5-HT 7D (91% of 5-HT). In addition to agonist activity
at 5-HT receptors, the compounds displayed inhibition of SERT activity
(81–100% fluoxetine), but had no effect at the dopamine transporter
(DAT) or norepinephrine transporter (NET), or agonist-like effects
at other receptors ( Figure S1E ). The potencies
and efficacies of the drugs at 5-HT 2 receptors were determined
in calcium mobilization assays, revealing that the compounds had similar
potencies at 5-HT 2A and 5-HT 2B receptors (EC 50 = 6–18 nM), but were less potent for activity at
5-HT 2C (EC 50 = 119–325 nM; Figure S3A–D ). Miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT
were full agonists at 5-HT 2A but partial agonists at the
other 5-HT 2 receptors ( E max = 90–102 vs 65–77% 5-HT; Figure S3E ).
sections.functional activities of 4-meo-mipt anal:
Based on screening results and existing structure–activity
studies, , , , we surmised that increasing the 4-position alkoxy
chain length or altering the steric bulk of the N -alkyl chain of 4-MeO-MiPT would provide a series of hybrid 5-HT 2A /SERT ligands. To that end, 15 analogs were synthesized or
procured. Specifically, one series of compounds included 4-alkoxy
chain variants: 4-ethoxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-EtO-MiPT), 4- n -propyloxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-PrO-MiPT),
4-isopropoxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine
(4-iPrO-MiPT), 4-benzyloxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-BnO-MiPT), and 4-neopentyloxy- N -methyl- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-NpO-MiPT) ( Figure S4 ). A second series included N -alkyl chain variants: 4-methoxy- N -methyltryptamine
(4-MeO-NMT), 4-methoxy- N , N -dimethyltryptamine
(4-MeO-DMT), 4-methoxy- N -isopropyltryptamine (4-MeO-NiPT),
4-methoxy- N , N -diisopropyltryptamine

sections.monoamine transporter activities in rat:
The compounds were assessed for their potencies to inhibit neurotransmitter
uptake or stimulate release at DAT, NET, and SERT in rat brain synaptosome
preparations ( Figure ). Kozell et al. previously showed that 4-MeO-MiPT and 4-MeO-DiPT
are 7–50 times more potent (IC 50 = 11–53
nM) at blocking uptake at SERT compared to their respective 4-hydroxy
and 5-methoxy analogs, while maintaining agonist activity at 5-HT 2A . Here, we expand on this this
finding by examining the SERT activities for a series of 4-MeO-MiPT
analogs that act as 5-HT 2A agonists. Across the series, none of the compounds displayed
nM potencies
for uptake inhibition at DAT or NET ( Figure A, Figure S7 ).
By contrast, many of compounds had nM potency for uptake inhibition
at SERT (IC 50 = 17–903 nM). All of the alkoxy chain
variants, and several of the N- alkyl variants (4-MeO-NMT,
4-MeO-NPT, and 4-MeO-NpT), had very weak potency for SERT inhibition
(i.e., >1,000 nM). None of the compounds were SERT-releasing agents
akin to MDMA (EC 50 = 87 nM, Figure S8 ), likely due to the small size constraints for substrate
activity at SERT. Consistent with previous
work, we found that 4-MeO-MiPT and 4-MeO-DiPT were 4–7 times
more potent than their 4-hydroxy analogs for SERT uptake blockade
( Figure A–B).
Importantly, the SERT potency values determined here for 4-MeO-MiPT
and 4-MeO-DiPT in rat brain synaptosomes were nearly identical to
those determined in cells transfected with human SERT. 4-MeO-McPT was 3 times more potent for SERT
uptake inhibition when compared to its 4-hydroxy analog ( Figure A and C). The lack
of SERT uptake inhibition for 4-MeO-NpT vs 4-MeO-3PT and 4-MeO-sBuT
also shows that the highly branched N -neo-pentyl
substitution may be too rigid or bulky to interact with 5-HT receptors
or SERT relative to other compounds assessed. Taken together, our
SERT findings demonstrate that introducing a 4-MeO ring substitution
induces more potent SERT uptake inhibition relative to 4-hydroxy analogs.
Within the 4-position series, lengthening or bulkier substitution
of the alkoxy chain beyond a methoxy group (4-EtO-MiPT, 4-PrO-MiPT,
4-iPrO-MiPT, 4-BnO-MiPT, 4-NpO-MiPT) markedly reduces SERT potency,
such that these analogs show only weak or no measurable SERT inhibition
in our assays ( Figure , Table S2 ). By contrast, within the N -alkyl series, increasing steric bulk on the terminal amine
from small substituents to isopropyl/diisopropyl or cyclopropyl groups
(e.g., 4-MeO-MiPT, 4-MeO-DiPT, 4-MeO-McPT, 4-MeO-DcPT) enhances SERT
uptake inhibition into the low- to midnanomolar range, whereas further
expansion to the highly branched N -neopentyl substitution
abolishes high-affinity SERT inhibition. Lastly, none of the compounds
acted as substrate-type releasers at SERT.
sections.preference of 4-meo-mipt analogs for 5-h:
Using the drug potency values determined from the
SERT uptake inhibition assays and the G protein BRET assays, we determined
the preference of the compounds for SERT ( Figure A) or 5-HT 2A ( Figure B) relative to other targets.
SERT preference for a given drug was calculated by dividing the IC 50 for SERT uptake inhibition by the EC 50 for a
particular receptor subtype. In a similar manner, 5-HT 2A preference was calculated by dividing the EC 50 for 5-HT 2A activation by the EC 50 for a particular 5-HT
receptor subtype. Because drug potency is an inverse function (i.e.,
smaller numerical values indicate higher potencies), lower numerical
values indicate higher preference for either SERT or 5-HT 2A . Preference ratios are categorized as follows: balanced = 0.5–3.5,
SERT preference = values <0.5, and 5-HT receptor preference = >3.5. 4-MeO-MiPT and its desmethyl analog (4-MeO-NiPT)
were both slightly
SERT-preferring but balanced (ratio = 0.61–3.39) across targets
except for showing preference for SERT over 5-HT 1A potency
(ratio = 0.04–0.09). In contrast, 4-MeO–DiPT had high
preference for SERT over all targets assessed (ratio = 0.005–0.16),
except for showing more balanced potencies relative to 5-HT 2B (ratio = 0.81). 4-MeO-DiPT was the most SERT-preferring compound
over 5-HT 2A activity across the series. 4-MeO-DcPT also
exhibited preference for SERT across targets similar to 4-MeO-DiPT,
but its potencies were slightly shifted toward a more balanced potency
profile (ratio = 0.11–0.74). Overall at SERT relative to 5-HTRs,
4-MeO-MiPT analogs with increased steric bulk at the N -alkyl were generally SERT-balanced or preferring vs other targets,
but compounds with smaller N -alkyl substituents or
increased 4-alkoxy chain lengths displayed preferences for 5-HT receptors
over SERT. With respect to 5-HT 2A potencies vs potencies
at SERT
and other 5-HTRs tested, most compounds generally showed 5-HT 2A -preference or were balanced. All compounds preferred 5-HT 2A vs 5-HT 1A activity (ratios = 0.02–0.25),
showing that activity at 5-HT 1A may only be relevant for
these compounds at high doses in vivo . Nearly all
the compounds displayed preference or balance for 5-HT 2A over SERT uptake inhibition, but 4-MeO-DiPT was an exception (ratio
= 6.31) in this regard. Some compounds exhibited slight preference
for 5-HT 2A vs m5-HT 2A or 5-HT 2A β-arrestin2
activities, corroborating slight potency shifts observed in earlier
experiments ( Figure A), but overall the compounds were mostly balanced across species
(i.e., human vs mouse 5-HT 2A ) and second messenger events
monitored (i.e., G αq vs β arrestin signaling).
At 5-HT 2B , the series was generally 5-HT 2A -preferring
or balanced; however, 4-MeO-DiPT, 4-MeO-DMT, and 4-MeO-McPT exhibited
slight preferences for 5-HT 2B (ratios = 2.24–5.09),
a property which has been linked to cardiac valvulopathy after chronic
administration of other serotonergic drugs. − Potency ratios
at 5-HT 2C relative to 5-HT 2A revealed that most
compounds were 5-HT 2A -preferring or balanced, but 4-MeO-NMT
and 4-MeO-DMT showed higher preference for 5-HT 2C potency.
sections.acute effects of 4-meo-mipt analogs in m:
Eleven
of the compounds, plus 4 related analogs, were tested in the mouse
HTR paradigm, a predictive model of 5-HT 2A -mediated psychedelic-like
effects. , , Serotonergic
psychedelics reliably induce the HTR in mice via activity at 5-HT 2A , and drug potencies for C57BL/6J mice in the HTR assay are
correlated with potencies to induce psychedelic effects in humans
across drug chemotypes. Here, the HTR
paradigm was used to compare the psychedelic-like effects of 4-MeO-MiPT
analogs with varying activities at 5-HT 2A vs SERT, as determined
from the in vitro assays. The compounds were administered
subcutaneously (sc.) to C57BL/6J mice at various doses (0.03–30
mg/kg) to construct dose–response curves and examine their
potencies (ED 50 values) and efficacies (maximal number
of HTRs) over a 30 min testing session. In addition to HTR activity,
body temperature changes were also monitored to capture acute effects
known to be mediated by other 5-HT receptors. Across the compounds
tested, the potency range to induce HTRs was 0.09–10.53 mg/kg
( Figure A), while
the range of efficacies for maximal number of HTRs was 20–98
HTRs/30 min ( Figure B). Compounds were considered HTR active if they produced dose-related
increases in HTRs that statistically exceed those produced by vehicle
injections ( Table S3 ). In most cases, HTR
active compounds displayed biphasic, bell-shaped dose–response
curves ( Figure C–F).
The most potent compound to induce HTRs was 4-HO-McPT (ED 50 = 0.09 mg/kg), which displayed potency similar to that of psilocin
reported in prior studies (ED 50 = 0.11–0.17 mg/kg). , Our HTR findings with 4-HO-McPT represent the first report of HTR
potency for this compound. Compared to miprocin, 4-MeO-MiPT induced
less HTRs with slightly weaker potency (ED 50 = 0.76 vs
0.97 mg/kg, E max = 70 vs 39 HTR/30 min),
in agreement with the reduced psychoactive effects of 4-MeO-MiPT reported
in humans. The most efficacious compound was 4-HO-DiPT ( E max = 98 HTRs), and the 4-OH compounds (miprocin,
4-HO-DiPT,
4-HO-McPT) had higher potencies and efficacies when compared to their
respective 4-MeO counterparts (4-MeO-MiPT, 4-MeO-DiPT, 4-MeO-McPT)­( Figure C–F). Relative
to the template structure of 4-MeO-MiPT, 4-MeO compounds with short N -alkyl chains (4-MeO-DMT, 4-MeO-NiPT), and ones with the
excessively bulky N -alkyl chains, failed to induce
the HTR ( Figure , Figures S10–S11 ). Prior research with
4-OH and 5-MeO monoalkyltryptamine analogs shows that compounds with N -alkyl chains smaller than ethyl or isopropyl are HTR inactive,
which may be due to poor brain permeance or other factors. , The finding with 4-MeO-NiPT is noteworthy since this compound is
an identified metabolite of 4-MeO-MiPT ( Table S4, Figure S9 ), but it lacks HTR
activity and is only a minor metabolite. The time-courses of
HTR events induced by the compounds can be
found in Figure G–J
and Figures S9–S10 . Miprocin and
other 4-OH tryptamines displayed higher rates of HTRs across the session
vs 4-MeO-MiPT and other 4-MeO analogs. For nearly all compounds, the
elevations in HTRs generally resolved or returned to near baseline
by the end of the 30 min session. Notably, 4-HO-McPT produced peak
HTR counts in the first 5 min postinjection which resolved within
15–20 min, a time-course that was quicker than other 4-OH compounds.
In a similar manner, 4-MeO-McPT also displayed a quicker time-course
for induction of HTR relative to other 4-MeO compounds that were active. 4-MeO-DMT did not induce HTR in our experiments, even though the
drug was previously shown to substitute for the known psychedelic
compound, 5-MeO-DMT, in rat drug discrimination studies. Given the positive relationship between drug
potencies to induce HTR in mice and potencies to engender psychedelic-like
drug discrimination in rats, we expected
that 4-MeO-DMT would display HTR activity. The ability of 4-MeO-DMT
to substitute for 5-MeO-DMT as a discriminative stimulus could be
related to the predominant 5-HT 1A activity of the training
drug as observed by Winter et al., and
corroborated by mouse HTR studies. , Thus, it is
tempting to speculate that 4-MeO-DMT fails to induce HTR due to its
5-HT 1A activity. Previous results show that hypothermia
produced by psychedelic tryptamines is primarily mediated by activation
of 5-HT 1A . , , , , In the present
study, 4-MeO-DMT produced the most potent and efficacious hypothermia
(ED 50 = 9.89 mg/kg, E max =
−9.0 °C), while the potencies for other compounds were
all >10 mg/kg and no clear peak effects were reached for this end
point. 4-MeO-DMT had sub-μM potency and high efficacy at 5-HT 1A in vitro , in line with its more potent
hypothermic effects in vivo . On the other hand, 4-MeO-McPT
and 4-MeO-DcPT also had sub-μM potencies and high efficacies
at 5-HT 1A in vitro , but still evoked robust
HTR. The 5-HT 2C activity of 4-MeO-DMT was also potent and
efficacious, but this activity was equivalent to the HTR active compound,
4-MeO-McPT. Collectively, the results suggest that agonist activity
of 4-MeO-DMT at 5-HT 1A and 5-HT 2C cannot fully
explain its lack of HTR, so other potential targets of action or pharmacokinetic
mechanisms must be involved. One possibility is that 4-MeO-DMT interacts
with monoamine oxidase (MAO) enzymes, since other tryptamines are
substrates for these proteins (e.g., DMT and 5-MeO-DMT). Follow-up
studies are needed to further explore the reason(s) why 4-MeO-DMT
fails to induce HTR.
sections.sert-selective uptake blocker pretreatme:
Given that the 4-OH compounds were less potent as SERT uptake blockers
yet produced more HTRs relative to their 4-MeO analogs ( Figures and ), we sought to test whether pretreating mice with an SSRI could
decrease the HTRs produced by the 4-OH compounds. Mice were pretreated
with fluoxetine (FLX, 10 mg/kg sc.) 10 min prior to administration
of miprocin, 4-HO-DiPT, or 4-HO-McPT (0.03–30 mg/kg). These
4-OH compounds had 3- to 16-fold lower potencies for SERT uptake inhibition
when compared to their 4-MeO counterparts. Based on the reduced subjective
effects of 4-MeO-MiPT in humans, and preclinical evidence that SSRIs
dampen effects of psychedelic drugs, , , , − , , , we hypothesized that FLX pretreatment would
reduce HTRs induced by the 4-OH analogs. Drug potency values
for inducing HTRs, with and without FLX pretreatment, are shown in Figure A–B for miprocin, Figure E–F for 4-HO-DiPT,
and Figure I–J
for 4-HO-McPT. Corresponding dose–response curves and time-course
data are shown in Figure C–D, G–H, and K–L. The total number of
HTRs induced by miprocin after FLX pretreatment was reduced compared
to miprocin alone, but drug potencies in both treatment conditions
were similar ( Figure A–D, Table S5 ). Notably, the miprocin
plus FLX pretreatment group displayed peak effects matching those
of the 10 mg/kg dose of 4-MeO-MiPT. Similarly, FLX pretreatment prior
to 4-HO-DiPT and 4-HO-McPT reduced the maximal number of HTRs, showing
that the psychedelic-like effects of the 4-OH compounds can be reduced
by increased SERT uptake inhibition ( Figure E–H, Figure I–L, Table S5 ). Overall, the HTR findings suggest that SERT uptake inhibition
can be leveraged to reduce the psychedelic-like effects of certain
5-HT 2A agonists. This notion is consistent with the hypothesis
that the enhanced SERT uptake inhibition by 4-MeO analogs likely mediates
their reduced psychedelic-like effects relative to 4-OH analogs in
mice. These data further suggest that subjective effects of psychedelics
in humans are reduced with compounds that also have potent SERT-mediated
pharmacological effects or with cotreatment of SSRIs. Importantly,
FLX activity did not seem to impact the body temperature decreases
induced by 4-OH analogs at high doses ( Figure S14 , Table S5 ). The effects of 5-HT 1A blockade on psychedelic-like
effects
of 4-MeO-MiPT were also tested, given that 5-HT 1A agonism
was detected with this compound ( Figure S1 , Figure S2 , Figure ). Prior studies show that 5-HT 1A agonist activity can buffer or attenuate the expression of HTRs
and psychedelic subjective effects in humans , , , , − so psychedelic-like effects of
4-MeO-MiPT could be impacted by its 5-HT 1A activity at
high drug doses. Pretreatment with WAY100635 prior to 4-MeO-MiPT revealed
that 5-HT 1A agonist-like activity attenuated psychedelic-like
effects, but only at high doses ( Figure A–C, Figure S13 ). Mice pretreated with WAY100635 prior to 30 mg/kg 4-MeO-MiPT displayed
more HTRs and blunted hypothermic effects ( Figure S14A , Table S5 ). The WAY100635 data
are consistent with a growing body of literature demonstrating the
buffering effects of 5-HT 1A agonism on 5-HT 2A -mediated psychedelic-like effects across species. , , , , Given that several compounds had higher potencies
than 4-MeO-MiPT for functional activity at 5-HT 1A (e.g.,
4-MeO-DMT), this receptor activity and others (e.g., 5-HT 2C ) may play a larger role in attenuating or modulating psychedelic-like
effects of these analogs. , 5-HT 2A agonists that interact with SERT have been identified
here and in prior studies. , , Previous animal experiments have explored the effects of 5-HT 2A agonists after pharmacological inhibition of SERT or genetic
manipulation of SERT expression. For example, repeated or acute SSRI
treatments generally decrease 5-HT 2 receptor binding and
drug-induced HTR counts. , , SERT knockout mice, which have elevated basal concentrations of
extracellular 5-HT in the brain, exhibit decreased HTRs in response
to 5-HT 2A agonists. , By contrast, mice overexpressing
SERT have reduced basal concentrations of extracellular 5-HT and show
increased 5-HT 2A receptor function and DOI-induced HTR. Pharmacological depletion of 5-HT can amplify
psilocybin-induced HTR in mice, while increased extracellular 5-HT
via SSRI treatment attenuates it. Taken
together, the available evidence suggests an inverse relationship
between 5-HT availability and intensity of psychedelic-like effects.
sections.limitations and caveats:
An obvious limitation of the
current study is that we did not measure extracellular levels of 5-HT
in the brain after various drug treatments, and future studies should
address the neurochemical effects of ring-substituted tryptamines.
Nevertheless, the 10 mg/kg dose of FLX used here is known to evoke
modest and sustained increases in microdialysate concentrations of
5-HT in the brain, and engender antidepressant-like effects in rodents. − It is worth noting that FLX has affinity for a variety of receptors,
including 5-HT 2 receptor subtypes, , − which may be relevant to findings of attenuated 5-HT 2A -mediated HTRs. In particular, FLX has reported agonist effects
at 5-HT 2B and 5-HT 2C receptors, − with limited information about efficacy at 5-HT 2A . The potential agonist effects of FLX at 5-HT 2C are most important in the present context, since this receptor
is known to dampen 5-HT 2A -mediated HTR. , However, FLX has much higher affinity at SERT relative to its affinities
at 5-HT 2 receptors (<2 nM vs 20 to >1000 nM), indicating that effects of the drug at these
receptors would only be relevant after high-dose or chronic administration.
Supporting the activity of FLX at SERT vs 5-HT 2 receptors,
it has been shown that the SSRI, citalopram, which does not have relevant
pharmacological effects at 5-HT 2 receptors, can also reduce
psilocybin-induced HTR. Prior investigations
demonstrate that uptake inhibitors targeting DAT and NET can also
modulate the activity of drug-induced HTRs in some cases. For example,
the nonselective uptake inhibitor cocaine can block HTRs induced by
the SERT releasing agent d-fenfluramine. Even though HTRs induced by d-fenfluramine are mediated by indirect
stimulation of 5-HT 2A receptors by increased 5-HT levels,
a variety of catecholamine uptake inhibitors and releasers can blunt
this response, suggesting a complex interplay among monoamine systems
in modulating HTR. − Catecholamine releasing agents like amphetamine can reduce basal
HTR in mice, but this effect is complicated by locomotor stimulation
induced by the drug that could mask the expression of other behaviors. We have recently identified nonselective monoamine
releasers with 5-HT 2 receptor agonist activity that induce
robust HTRs without acute accompanying psychostimulant effects (e.g.,
6-(2-aminopropyl)-1-benzothiophene or 6-APBT). In a similar manner, MDMA and its metabolite MDA are nonselective
monoamine releasers that evoke HTRs, either indirectly via 5-HT release
or by direct actions at 5-HT 2A . , Additionally, MDMA and MDA substitute to varying degrees for the
interoceptive stimulus cues of 5-HT 2A agonists in drug
discrimination studies. − The summed findings suggest there is substantial overlap between
subjective effects of psychedelic 5-HT 2A agonists and MDMA-like
releasing agents, but with some notable differences. , Regarding the psychoactivity of 4-MeO-MiPT and related hybrid
5-HT 2A agonist/SERT inhibitors described here (e.g., 4-MeO-DiPT,
4-MeO-McPT), anecdotal reports from human users indicate that subjective
effects of 4-MeO-MiPT involve “erotic or aphrodisiac”
and “MDMA-like entactogen” effects. , Thus, the effects of 4-MeO-MiPT are similar to those induced by
5-HT releasing agents like MDMA, even though 4-MeO-MiPT displays a
different mechanisms of action at SERT (i.e., uptake blockade vs release).
The available anecdotal evidence shows that 4-MeO-MiPT analogs are
psychoactive to some degree, with reported effects more closely resembling
those of MDMA-like drugs or atypical tryptamines with reported entactogenic
effects at certain doses and reduced visual effects (e.g., 5-MeO-MiPT) , rather than classical psychedelic 5-HT 2A agonist effects. Several of the compounds tested here failed to induce elevated
HTR counts vs vehicle controls (e.g., 4-MeO-DMT, 4-MeO-sBuT, 4-MeO-3PT).
One commonality with these HTR inactive compounds is partial agonist
efficacy at 5-HT 2A ( E max =
51–76% 5-HT). It has previously been proposed that there may
be a G αq “efficacy threshold” at 5-HT 2A that distinguishes HTR active ( E max > 70%) vs HTR inactive compounds ( E max < 70%). However, we show that 4-MeO-NiPT
has a higher 5-HT 2A G αq efficacy than
the proposed threshold ( E max = 81–82%
5-HT) but does not induce psychedelic-like effects on HTR, whereas
4-MeO-McPT has a lower efficacy but still induces the HTR. Thus, the
present findings are not completely consistent with the threshold
hypothesis, at least for this series of compounds, and potentially
may be explained by factors other than 5-HT 2A efficacy
(e.g., brain permeability, polypharmacology, etc.). For example, norpsilocin
(4-hydroxy- N -methyltryptamine or 4-HO-NMT) and its N -ethyl analog (4-hydroxy- N -ethyltryptamine
or 4-HO-NET) both activate 5-HT 2A with full agonist efficacy,
but only 4-HO-NET is HTR active likely due to improved brain permeability
vs norpsilocin. Furthermore, regarding
polypharmacology, the 5-methoxy analog of 4-HO-NET (5-MeO-NET) is
HTR inactive until its 5-HT 1A activity is blocked, showing that non-5-HT 2A efficacy-related
phenomena can also play a role in psychedelic-like effects of 5-HT 2A agonists. The present data are also relevant to ongoing
discussions about
which aspects of 5-HT 2A pharmacology are most critical
for psychedelic-like activity. Kozell et al. concluded that neither absolute G protein efficacy nor potency at
5-HT 2A alone is sufficient to explain psychedelic activity,
and suggested that either (i) network-level amplification mechanisms
or (ii) preferential engagement of 5-HT 2A over other targets
are key determinants. The present results are consistent with the
latter possibility. Compounds such as 4-MeO-MiPT, 4-MeO-DiPT, and
4-MeO-McPT retain high-potency 5-HT 2A agonism but engage
SERT with comparable or greater potency, and this polypharmacology
attenuates their 5-HT 2A -mediated HTR. In other words, strong
engagement of SERT and other targets (such as 5-HT 1A ) appears
to “dilute” the functional impact of 5-HT 2A activation on behavior, in line with the idea that relative selectivity
for 5-HT 2A is a more reliable predictor of psychedelic-like
activity than 5-HT 2A efficacy in isolation. An additional
dimension recently highlighted by Vargas et al. is that classic psychedelics may preferentially access
intracellular pools of 5-HT 2A receptors, which can signal
from endosomal or other compartments and may contribute to their distinctive
plasticity-related and behavioral effects. It will be important in
future work to determine whether 4-MeO-MiPT and its analogs differ
from their 4-hydroxy counterparts in their ability to engage intracellular
5-HT 2A receptors or to access specific neuronal subpopulations,
as such differences could help explain why some high-efficacy 5-HT 2A agonists are non- or weakly psychedelic in vivo .
sections.conclusions:
Overall, our findings indicate that the
reduced psychedelic-like
effects of 4-MeO-MiPT, relative to miprocin, are related to potent
SERT uptake inhibition produced by the 4-MeO analog. 4-MeO-MiPT and
miprocin exhibit similar potency and efficacy at 5-HT 2A , but 4-MeO-MiPT has 7-fold higher potency at SERT and induces less
HTRs in mice. The present findings might explain, at least in part,
why humans anecdotally report reduced subjective effects of 4-MeO-MiPT
when compared to miprocin. The SAR for determining drug potencies
at 5-HT 2A and SERT were studied for a series of 4-MeO-MiPT
analogs, and a number of novel 5-HT 2A /SERT hybrid compounds
were identified. Our findings reveal that adding steric bulk to the
terminal amine substituent of 4-MeO-MiPT analogs increases SERT activity,
whereas lengthening the 4-position alkoxy chain abolishes it. The
present series of compounds represents a set of pharmacological tools
for studying the relative contribution of 5-HT receptors and SERT
in modulating psychedelic-like drug effects in animal models. Finally,
our preclinical findings suggest that 5-HT 2A /SERT hybrid
compounds could have therapeutic utility in clinical contexts where
reduced visual psychedelic effects, or enhanced entactogenic effects,
are warranted.
sections.drugs:
The compounds were one commercial sample (4-MeO-DMT,
Cayman Chemical), one purified from a commercial sample (4-MeO-MiPT,
ChemLogix), and the remaining synthesized using standard organic synthetic
techniques. Full synthetic details and analytical data (including 1 H NMR spectra of novel compounds) are provided in the Supporting Information .
sections.target screening:
Miprocin and 4-MeO-MiPT were screened
at the following potential targets: 5-HT 1A , 5-HT 1B , 5-HT 1D , 5-HT 1E , 5-HT 2A , 5-HT 2B , 5-HT 2C , 5-HT 3 , 5-HT 5A ,
5-HT 6 , 5-HT 7A , Alpha 1A , Alpha 1B , Alpha 1D , Alpha 2A , Alpha 2B , Alpha 2C , Beta 1 , Beta 2 , Beta 3 , BZP rat brain site, D 1 , D 2 , D 3 , D 4 , D 5 , DAT, DOR, GABA A , H 1 , H 2 , H 3 , H 4 , KOR,
M 1 , M 2 , M 3 , M 4 , M 5 , MOR, NET, PBR, SERT, Sigma 1, Sigma 2, AMPA, Kainate rat
brain site, NMDA, NR2B. Assays were generously carried out by the
National Institute on Mental Health Psychoactive Drug Screening Program.
Details of the assay conditions are available online https://pdsp.unc.edu/pdspweb/ . , Details of the methods used to conduct radioligand
binding experiments in mouse brain can be found in previous studies. ,
sections.bioluminescence resonance energy transfe:
For human 5-HT 2A , 5-HT 2B , 5-HT 2C , and mouse 5-HT 2A Gq dissociation assays as measured
by BRET, HEK 293T cells (ATCC) were transfected in a 1:1:1:1 ratio
of receptor: Gαq-Rluc8:β3:GFP2-γ9, as previously
reported. , For 5-HT 1A GoB dissociation assays
as measured by BRET, HEK 293T cells were transfected in a 1:1:1:1
ratio of receptor: GαoB-Rluc8:β1:GFP2-γ2. For 5-HT 2A β-arrestin2 recruitment as measured by BRET, HEK 293T
cells were transfected in a 1:15 ratio of human 5-HT 2A -Rluc8:
GFP2-human βarr2. Cells at approximately 60–80% confluency
were transfected in 10% dialyzed fetal bovine serum (dFBS; Omega Scientific),
and all transfection mixes were prepared in minimal essential medium
(Opti-MEM; Invitrogen) using a 3:1 ratio of TransIT-2020 (Mirus Bio)
μL:μg total DNA. Next day, cells were detached, centrifuged,
resuspended, and plated in 1% dFBS at an approximate density of 30–50,000
cells per well into poly- l -lysine-coated 96-well white assay
plates (Greiner Bio-One). After approximately 24 h, media was decanted
and replaced with 60 μL per well of drug buffer (1× Hank’s
balanced salt solution (HBSS), 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.4), and incubated
for at least 15 min at 37 °C in a humidified incubator before
receiving drug stimulation. Compounds were diluted at 3× in drug
buffer containing 0.3% bovine serum albumin (BSA) fatty acid free
and 0.03% ascorbic acid. Diluted compounds were dispensed as 30 μL
into each well using multichannels and plates were incubated at 37
°C in a humidified incubator until reading. Next, plates were
briefly taken out and coelenterazine 400a (5 μM final concentration;
Nanolight Technology) was added 15 min before reading. After 60 min
of total time for compound incubation in the assay plates, plates
were read in a PheraStarFSX or ClarioStar Plus (BMG Labtech; Cary,
NC) at 1 s per well for at least 15 min for 3–5 cycles. BRET
ratios of 510/400 luminescence were calculated per well and were plotted
as a function of compound concentration. Data were normalized to %
positive control (5-HT) stimulation and analyzed using nonlinear regression
“log­(agonist) vs. response” to yield E max and EC 50 parameter estimates. All assays
were performed in duplicate with at least three independent cell culture
preparations.
sections.uptake and release monoamine transporter:
Monoamine
transporter assays were conducted according to previously described
methods. , − Sprague–Dawley
rats were euthanized via CO 2 narcosis to collect fresh
brain tissue. Tissue from the caudate was used for DAT assays, while
whole brain without the caudate or cerebellum was used for NET and
SERT assays. Synaptosomes from the tissue samples were prepared for
both uptake inhibition and release assays. Tritiated 5-HT, dopamine,
and norepinephrine were utilized for uptake inhibition assays for
each transporter. [ 3 H]­5-HT was used as the radiolabeled
substrate for SERT release assays. To determine best fit values of
interest (IC 50 , EC 50 , E max ), three-parameter nonlinear regression fits were used in
monoamine transporter assays. All assays represent n = 3 experiments performed in triplicate.
sections.animals:
Groups of 24 mice (12 male and 12 female) were
purchased from The Jackson Laboratory (#000664) at 8 weeks of age,
initially housed 4/cage. Animals were housed at the NIDA IRP animal
facilities in Baltimore, MD under a 12/12 h light/dark cycle (lights
on at 6 or 7 AM local time depending on the time of year testing was
conducted). After 1–2 weeks of acclimation to the facility,
all mice were briefly anesthetized with isoflurane and received subcutaneous
transponders (TP500, Avidity Science) that allowed noninvasive temperature
recording using a hand-held reader (DAS-8027 IUS, Avidity Science),
as previously described. , The implanted transponders
were placed in the upper back area, and mice were single housed after
implantation to avoid damage to the transponder.
sections.dose\u2013response and pretreatment stud:
Mouse
HTR methods were carried out as described in previous studies. Briefly,
baseline temperature for each mouse was recorded after brief acclimation
to testing chambers. After baseline temperature readings, mice received
subcutaneous injection of either drug (0.03–30 mg/kg) or vehicle
(saline or 90:5:5 saline:DMSO:Tween 80), and behavior was video recorded
with Hero 7 GoPro cameras (1280 × 960 pixels, 120 frames/sec)
for 30 min postinjection. After the session, body temperature was
recorded to calculate change from baseline to the end of the session.
In antagonist/pretreatment experiments, mice received a sc. injection
of either fluoxetine hydrochloride (FLX, 10 mg/kg, Spectrum Chemical
Manufacturing Corporation), WAY100635 maleate (3 mg/kg, Cayman Chemical
#14599), or saline vehicle 10 min prior to test drug, then mice were
returned to the testing chamber for 30 min. Drug treatments occurred
every 1–2 weeks to avoid tolerance. During the behavioral sessions,
locomotor activity was also monitored to examine the potential effects
of treatments on general behavior or movement (data not shown). For
mouse studies, the drug doses represent the weight of the salt form
used (listed here or in Supporting Information ).
sections.analyses of experimental videos:
Based on training and
validation of the DLC+SimBA HTR detection approach described in detail
in Maitland et al., a new model was
trained on machine learning (ML 30 videos at 640 × 480 resolution,
120 fps downscaled using FFmpeg, a free, open-source software tool
for handling video files ( https://www.ffmpeg.org/ ). Extracted frames taken from 30 videos and 16 animals (then 95%
was used for training) were labeled. The number of total extracted
frames was 600 frames. Thirteen body points were consistently labeled,
including nose, left eye, right eye, left ear, right ear, top of the
skull, three points along the spine, the tail base, and three points
along the tail (see Figure A from Maitland et al.). A ResNet-50-based
neural network was used with default parameters (batch size of 8)
for 500,000 training iterations, when loss typically plateaus. Each
model was validated with 3 shuffles. The train and test errors were
2.22 and 2.87, respectively, representing 2.54% of the mouse’s
total body length from nose to tail base. Next, a behavioral
classifier with 13 user-defined body parts in SimBA from previous
HTR experiments was trained using downscaled 640 × 480 resolution,
120 fps videos from previous HTR experiments which were not included
during DLC pose-estimation model training. The approximate width of
the TruScan chamber was used to define pixels per mm during the Video
Settings step. The outlier correction step was skipped. Features derived
from mouse pose estimation data (32 features) were extracted using
default settings. Classifier training videos were carefully annotated
for the HTR using the default SimBA behavioral annotator GUI. A total
of 20 random historical experimental HTR videos (5.6 h of video recording)
were reviewed and annotated for HTR events. These 20 videos contained
408 HTR events. Each HTR was annotated from the initial movement of
the mouse’s ears until the head returned to its initial resting
state. Random forest models were generated in SimBA with the default
hyperparameters (random forest estimators = 2000, max features = sqrt,
criterion = gini, test size = 0.2, train–test split type =
frames, minimum sample leaf = 1) and included optional model evaluation
settings to generate a classification report, precision-recall curves,
feature importance bar graph, and SHAP score calculations for 100
frames present and 100 frames absent. This model combination was validated
using 38 nonoverlapping historical experimental videos containing
879 HTR events (precision= 95.93, recall = 93.74, F 1 =
94.82). Lastly, HTR scores from new experimental videos included in
this report were compared to HTR scores from a previously described
commercial software-based detection approach (Clever Sys Inc.), showing that scores from both detection methods
were highly correlated ( r > 0.96, data not shown). Hardware and software used : Dell Precision Workstation
T5820 with Intel Xeon Processor W-2223 (3.6 GHz), 32 GB RAM, Windows
11 Pro operating system, and a NVIDIA RTX A100 GPU (video card). Videos
were downscaled using FFmpeg. Pose estimation models were trained
using DLC version 2.3.10. Behavioral classifiers were generated using
SimBA version 2.2.4. HTR detection was also done using the commercial
software package, TopScanLite (Clever Sys Inc.), with the HTR detection
feature (“ear in air” model) included.
sections.statistical analyses:
Dose–response data for
the acute effects of the test compounds on HTR were fit with biphasic
nonlinear regression fits for visualization. Dose–response
data for acute effects of test drugs on body temperature change were
fit with four-parameter nonlinear regression fits (IC 50 > 0). HTR potency values determined for each drug were calculated
using four-parameter nonlinear regression fits of ascending limb doses
(EC 50 > 0). Comparisons of dose–response data
for
acute drug effects (HTR, body temperature change) were conducted via
Welch’s ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s T3 post hoc analyses
comparing all groups to vehicle controls. In antagonist/pretreatment
studies, predetermined dose-by-dose comparisons were made between
no pretreatment and pretreatment groups using a two-way ANOVA (dose
× treatment) with Sidak’s post hoc test. Alpha was set
at 0.05 for all analyses.

title: Enhanced Prediction of Peripheral Artery Disease Using Plasma Proteomics Among Individuals Without Diabetes
abstract: Background Although peripheral artery disease (PAD) is an important diabetes complication, a substantial proportion of cases occur among individuals without diabetes. This study aimed to assess the predictive value of plasma proteomics in the long‐term risk of PAD among individuals initially free of diabetes. Methods Included were 46 508 participants (6046 with prediabetes) without diabetes or major cardiovascular disease at recruitment of the UK Biobank. Using multivariable Cox regression models, a total of 2923 unique plasma proteins were assessed for the associations with incident PAD. Significant proteins were subsequently processed by a trained light gradient boosting machine classifier to determine important proteins. Using receiver operating characteristic analyses, the performance of these important proteins in predicting incident PAD were evaluated, in the whole sample and by glycemic status (normoglycemia and prediabetes). Results During a median follow‐up of 12.7 years, 461 participants developed PAD. There were 107 proteins associated with incident PAD, with 103 positive associations. The LGBM approach identified 9 proteins (eg, WFDC2 [WAP 4‐disulfide core domain protein 2], MMP12 [macrophage metalloelastase], and GDF15 [growth differentiation factor 15]) as the top‐ranked proteins based on their importance ordering. Whereas glycated hemoglobin showed very modest predictive accuracy, a panel incorporating these top proteins showed good performance in the prediction of PAD risk (area under the curve 0.820), and it significantly enhanced the prediction beyond traditional risk factors (raising area under the curve from 0.803 to 0.837, DeLong test P =5.21×10 −3 ). These observations were consistent for participants with normoglycemia or prediabetes. Conclusions Plasma protein biomarkers enhance the prediction of long‐term risk for PAD among individuals without diabetes, regardless of glycemic status.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: In this large‐scale plasma proteomics study of individuals without diabetes, 107 plasma proteins were independently associated with incident peripheral artery disease, implicating important inflammatory and immune‐related pathways. A light gradient boosting machine approach identified 9 top‐ranked proteins, and these plasma protein biomarkers enhance the prediction of long‐term risk for peripheral artery disease among individuals without diabetes, regardless of glycemic status.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: The identified protein panel may facilitate the early identification of at‐risk individuals and better prediction of peripheral artery disease risk, especially for those without diabetes who are not regularly screened for peripheral artery disease.
sections.methods_1: The data that support the findings of this study are available upon application to the UKB ( www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/ ).
sections.study population: The UKB is a prospective population‐based cohort that recruited >500 000 participants aged 37 to 73 years from 22 assessment centers across England, Scotland, and Wales. From 2006 to 2010, participants completed various questionnaires, underwent a range of physical measures, and provided biological samples. The study was approved by the Northwest Multi‐Centre Research Ethics Committee (REC reference for UK Biobank 11/NW/0382) and all study participants provided written informed consent. The UKB‐PPP is a precompetitive consortium of 13 biopharmaceutical companies funding the generation of blood‐based proteomic data in a subset of UKB participants. 13 In our study, among 502 411 participants from UKB, a subset of randomly selected 53 026 participants had information on 2941 protein analytes (reflecting 2923 unique proteins) measured across Olink panels in plasma samples collected at baseline. We excluded participants with prevalent diabetes, PAD, or other major cardiovascular diseases at baseline (n=6518), leaving 46 508 participants in the present analysis. Among these, there were 6046 individuals with prediabetes (39 mmol/mol ≤ glycated hemoglobin [HbA1c] <48 mmol/mol) and 40 462 with normoglycemia (HbA1c <39 mmol/mol).
sections.measurements of plasma proteomics: The baseline blood samples donated by UKB‐PPP study participants underwent proteomic profiling using the Olink Explore 3072 platform (Olink Proteomics), which quantified 2941 protein analytes representing 2923 unique proteins across 8 panels (Cardiometabolic, Cardiometabolic II, Inflammation, Inflammation II, Neurology, Neurology II, Oncology, and Oncology II). The details on the sample collection, plasma sample preparation, plasma profiling using the Olink technology, and quality control were described elsewhere. 13 , 14 There were 830 proteins with ≥25% of their data below the lowest level of detection or with >50% of data failing quality control, which were excluded from the analysis. For the remaining 2093 proteins included, missing values were imputed by half of the lowest values detected. Data were then standardized using rank‐based inverse normal transformation followed by Z score normalization to ensure comparability and standardization across the proteins.
sections.ascertainment of incident pad: Incident cases of PAD during the follow‐up were ascertained from linked hospital and death databases. Date and cause of hospital admissions were identified via record linkage to Health Episode Statistics (England and Wales) and the Scottish Morbidity Records (Scotland). Date and cause of death were obtained from death certificates held by the National Health Service Information Centre (England and Wales) and the National Health Service Central Register Scotland (Scotland). PAD was defined using the International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision ( ICD‐9 ) codes, Tenth Revision ( ICD‐10 ) codes, and the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys Classification of Interventions and Procedures, version 4 codes. A complete list of these codes is provided in Table S1 .
sections.covariates: Information on sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, medical history, and medication use was assessed using touchscreen‐based questionnaires. The Townsend deprivation index was derived to capture area deprivation, with a higher score indicating a higher level of social deprivation. Physical activity was assessed using a self‐reported short‐form international physical activity questionnaire. A healthy diet score was calculated based on the following 6 food groups: vegetables and fruit, red meat, processed meat, whole grains, refined grains, and fish. 15 Blood pressure was measured using the Omron HEM‐7015IT digital blood pressure monitor and calculated as the mean of 2 sitting measures. Total cholesterol was measured using the Beckman Coulter AU580. HbA1c assay was performed using a high‐performance liquid chromatography method (Bio‐Rad Variant II Turbo analyzer, Bio‐Rad Laboratories). Diabetes was defined as self‐reported physician's diagnosis, medication use, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol.
sections.baseline characteristics of the study po: Baseline participant characteristics were presented according to the status of incident PAD, as mean±SD or frequencies (%) where appropriate.
sections.proteomic association analyses: Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for the associations between individual plasma proteins and incident PAD. Follow‐up period was calculated from the date of baseline recruitment to the date of PAD diagnosis, death, or the most recent follow‐up for the approved data set (December 2021), whichever occurred first. The multivariable model was adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, Townsend deprivation index, body mass index, waist circumference, tobacco consumption, alcohol consumption, total physical activity, healthy diet score, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and use of antihypertensive or lipid‐lowering medications. Missing data for continuous covariates were addressed using sex‐specific median values, and categorical covariates were addressed with a missing indicator category. 16 Missingness in continuous covariates was generally low, with most variables showing missingness proportions below 5%, except for HbA1c (5.42%), systolic blood pressure (6.18%), and physical activity (19.41%). To characterize the missing‐data pattern, missingness indicators were modeled against observed baseline participants characteristics as well as outcome information using logistic regression. The results suggested that the missing‐data pattern was unlikely to be strictly missing completely at random and may be more consistent with a missing‐at‐random mechanism (Table S2 ). To evaluate the potential impact of simple missing‐data handling on the main analyses, an additional sensitivity analysis was conducted by restricting the sample to participants with complete data on all continuous covariates and repeating the primary analyses. Bonferroni corrections were applied to assess significant associations ( P <0.05), accounting for the number of proteins tested ( k =2093).
sections.pathway enrichment analyses: To gain insights into the potential biological pathways for the significant proteins, we performed systematic enrichment analyses encompassing Gene Ontology, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, and Reactome pathway analyses using the R package clusterProfiler . Statistical significance was presented as the P value of Fisher's exact test, followed by false discovery rate corrections via the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.
sections.proteins importance ranking: The relative importance of the PAD‐related proteins in the risk prediction of PAD were determined mainly by 2 steps: candidate proteins ranking and sequential forward selection. In the first step, the significant proteins identified from the association analyses were fed into a preliminary trained light gradient boosting machine classifier, and each protein was ranked according to its contribution to model performance based on the information gain, which can be regarded as the predictor's ability to identify future incident PAD. Afterwards, a sequential forward selection strategy was applied, where predictors were added one by one to the newly developed light gradient boosting machine classifier according to the predictor importance ranking. This iterative process continued until the optimal performance in terms of the area under the curve (AUC) was reached, determined when the inclusion of an additional predictor failed to yield a statistically significant improvement in model performance, as assessed by 2 consecutive DeLong tests.
sections.evaluation of model performance in predi: Subsequently, we used the top‐ranked proteins to construct following prediction models with or without plasma proteins, including (1) a single important protein, (2) traditional risk factors, (3) HbA1c, (4) a protein panel including all important proteins, and (5) the protein panel + traditional risk factors. Traditional risk factors consisted of all the covariates included in the aforementioned multivariable models. HbA1c is a well‐established clinical indicator for assessing glucose metabolism, widely used to guide diabetes management and evaluate vascular risk indirectly. Treating HbA1c as a standalone model could allow us to directly compare the predictive performance of protein panel against a marker routinely measured in clinical practice. Receiver operating characteristic analyses were performed to evaluate the performance of the models in predicting PAD. DeLong tests and bootstrap tests with 2000 iterations were adopted to compare whether AUC values differed significantly between models. The data were split into 10 folds based on the geographical locations (East Midlands, London, North East, North West, Scotland, South East, South West, Wales, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and Humber) of participants' recruitment centers. Models were developed and validated using a 10‐fold cross‐validation strategy that the validation set (1‐fold of data) was kept untouched and merely used for evaluation purposes, and the hyperparameters tuning and postcalibration were performed within an inner‐looped cross‐validation within the training sets (9‐fold of data). This process was repeated 10 times, with the folds being shifted for each iteration to serve as training and testing sets. In addition, differences in the expression levels of top‐ranked proteins between individuals with normoglycemia and prediabetes were assessed using 2‐sample t tests. To evaluate the generalizability of the constructed protein‐based prediction models and the robustness of their predictive accuracy, we repeated the receiver operating characteristic analysis across subgroups defined by glycemic status (normoglycemia and prediabetes). All statistical tests were performed using Python (version 3.9) and R software (version 4.4.2, R Development Core Team). Statistical significance was set at 0.05 (2 tailed) unless otherwise stated.
sections.baseline characteristics of the study po: Mean age for the 46 508 participants was 56.28 years at baseline and 20 341 (43.7%) were male. As shown in Table S3 , compared with participants without PAD, those with PAD tended to be older, were more likely to be male, and had a higher Townsend deprivation index. Body mass index, waist circumference, systolic blood pressure, and glycated hemoglobin levels were higher in the group with PAD, whereas they had slightly lower total cholesterol levels. Those with PAD also were more likely to have an unhealthy lifestyle and to use medications for metabolic dysfunction.
sections.associations of plasma proteins with inc: During a median of 12.7 years of follow up, 461 participants experienced incident PAD, among whom 132 participants had prediabetes at baseline. Of the 2093 unique proteins assessed, after the multivariate adjustment, 107 (103 positively and 4 inversely) were significantly associated with incident PAD (Figure 1 ; Table S4 ). By HR, GDF15 (growth differentiation factor 15) showed the strongest positive association and OMG (oligodendrocyte‐myelin glycoprotein) had the strongest inverse association with incident PAD, with HRs of 1.67 (95% CI, 1.46–1.90; P Bonferroni‐corrected =5.21×10 −11 ) and 0.77 (95% CI, 0.70–0.85; P Bonferroni‐corrected =1.78×10 −4 ), respectively. Enrichment analyses implicated multiple biological pathways related to these significant proteins, such as immune response and cell signaling (eg, cytokine‐cytokine receptor interaction, chemokine signaling pathway, signaling by interleukins), cell migration and differentiation (eg, leukocyte migration, osteoclast differentiation), cell structure and extracellular matrix (eg, collagen‐containing extracellular matrix, extracellular matrix organization), metabolism and transport (eg, carbohydrate binding), and signal transduction and gene expression (eg, positive regulation of MAPK [mitogen‐activated protein kinase] cascade) (Figure S1 ).
sections.protein importance ranking: On the basis of the 107 PAD‐related proteins, we further sorted their relative importance in the prediction task (Table S5 ). The predictive importance ranking for these proteins is illustrated in Figure S2 , and the top 30 proteins are detailed in Figure 2A . The predictive capacity for PAD (quantified by AUC) demonstrated rapid enhancement with the initial incorporation of a few top‐ranked proteins, eventually reaching a performance plateau as additional biomarkers were included. Based on sequential forward selection with statistical significance validation, 9 proteins, including WFDC2 (WAP 4‐disulfide core domain protein 2), MMP12 (macrophage metalloelastase), GDF15, CXCL17 (C‐X‐C motif chemokine 17), LAMP3 (lysosome‐associated membrane glycoprotein 3), LRRN1 (leucine‐rich repeat neuronal protein 1), BCAN (brevican core protein), EDA2R (tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 27), and NEFL (neurofilament light polypeptide), were ultimately determined as important proteins for risk prediction of PAD. The associations between these 9 key proteins and incident PAD are presented in Figure 2B .
sections.predictive performance of plasma protein: We then examined the predictive accuracy of the selected important proteins for long‐term risk of PAD, using a 10‐fold cross‐validation approach. As shown in Table S6 , the top 3 important proteins, WFDC2, MMP12, and GDF15, achieved predictive accuracies of 0.743, 0.751, and 0.767, respectively, which largely surpassed the AUC of HbA1c (0.631). Combining these 9 proteins as a protein panel yielded an AUC of 0.820. Adding the protein panel to traditional risk factors attained the best‐performing model for incident PAD, increasing the AUC from 0.803 to 0.837 (DeLong test P =5.21×10 −3 ) (Figure 2C ; Table S7 ). Seven of the 9 top‐ranked proteins exhibited higher expression levels in the group with prediabetes than in the group with normoglycemia, whereas BCAN and LRRN1 levels were higher in the group with normoglycemia (Figure S3 ). Despite these glycemic‐related expression heterogeneities, the protein panel maintained robust predictive performance and demonstrated strong predictive ability for incident PAD across the subgroups defined by glycemic status (Figure 3 ; Table S8 ), with AUC of 0.807 in normoglycemia and 0.792 in prediabetes, both considerably outperforming the AUC of HbA1c (0.555 in normoglycemia and 0.550 in prediabetes). For both subgroups, adding the protein panel substantially improved the prediction accuracy beyond HbA1c and other traditional risk factors (all P values from DeLong test <0.05) (Table S9 ), with AUC increasing from 0.790 to 0.830 in normoglycemia and from 0.721 to 0.795 in prediabetes (Figure 3 ). Among 2733 participants who had diabetes and were free of PAD at baseline, we conducted a supplementary analysis to assess the performance of the 9‐protein panel in predicting PAD risk (115 incident cases). In this group, the protein panel achieved an AUC of 0.718, substantially lower than that for individuals without diabetes (AUC=0.820), suggesting that the identified proteins may capture biological processes beyond the progression of diabetes.
sections.sensitivity analysis: After excluding participants with missingness in continuous covariates, the overall association estimates were highly concordant with those in the primary analysis (Figure S4 ). Although the number of significant proteins decreased to 26, all these proteins were among the 107 significant proteins identified in the primary analysis. Of the 9 top‐ranked proteins, all but 2 proteins (LRRN1 and BCAN) remained significantly associated with incident PAD after Bonferroni correlation (Table S10 ). A 7‐protein panel still showed good predictive performance for incident PAD and significantly improved discrimination beyond the basic model, regardless of glycemic status (Figure S5 ).
sections.discussion: Although PAD is an important macrovascular complication of diabetes, it also occurs among individuals without diabetes. Yet, there has been limited epidemiological evidence regarding the risk prediction of PAD for individuals without diabetes who are less likely to be screened for PAD. In this large‐scale plasma proteomics study of individuals without diabetes, we identified 107 significant protein‐PAD associations potentially involving important inflammatory and immune‐related processes. Among these, 9 proteins (eg, WFDC2, MMP12, and GDF15) were identified as the most important proteins for predicting the long‐term risk of PAD. Although HbA1c showed very modest predictive accuracy, a panel of these key proteins showed good performance in predicting the risk of PAD, and it substantially improved the risk prediction beyond HbA1c and other traditional risk factors, regardless of glycemic status. Recent proteome studies have highlighted the potential of proteomic biomarkers to improve the prediction of vascular conditions. 17 For instance, in the Second Manifestations of Arterial Disease cohort, incorporating 50 proteins into a cardiovascular risk model enhanced the ability of predicting recurrent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. 18 In the Heart and Soul study, a risk score based on 9 proteins performed better than the refit Framingham secondary event risk score in predicting cardiovascular events among patients with stable coronary heart disease. 19 PAD shares many risk factors with other vascular diseases, 20 indicating potential value of proteomic biomarkers in the prediction of PAD risk. Although previous studies have linked proteomic biomarkers to the development or prediction of PAD among individuals with diabetes, 10 relevant evidence remains limited for those without diabetes. In the present study of participants without diabetes, we identified a set of proteins associated with incident PAD. Several of these individual proteins, such as GDF15, PLAUR (urokinase plasminogen activator surface receptor), and MMP12, which are among the top 10 significant proteins in the present study, have previously been proposed as biomarkers for PAD in the general population. 21 , 22 In addition, we found that the identified PAD‐related proteins shared important pathways that have been implicated in the pathogenesis of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases, 23 , 24 , 25 such as immune response and cell signaling, cell structure and extracellular matrix, metabolism and transport, and signal transduction and gene expression. Our findings showed the greatest importance of 9 plasma proteins in predicting incident PAD, with WFDC2, MMP12, and GDF15 ranking as the top 3 proteins substantially contributing to the predictive ability (combined AUC for the 3 proteins: 0.791). WFDC2, also known as human epididymal protein 4, functions as an inhibitor of multiple proteinases, playing a crucial role in modulating the balance between extracellular matrix synthesis and degradation, as well as regulating inflammatory responses. 26 These processes are essential in the development of atherosclerotic vascular disease and the maintenance of plaque stability. 27 WFDC2 has been reported to be associated with cardiovascular events, 26 but its relationship with PAD has not been studied. The positive relationship of plasma WFDC2 with incident PAD, along with its potential as the strongest predictor for PAD, are our novel findings that need further confirmation in future studies. MMP12, a matrix metalloproteinase zinc‐dependent proteolytic enzyme secreted from immunocompetent cells, has been associated with several atherosclerotic cardiovascular conditions, such as intima‐media thickness in the common carotid artery, 28 , 29 coronary events, 30 and large‐artery atherosclerotic stroke. 31 Results from a Swedish cohort study showed that higher MMP12 levels were associated with an increased risk of PAD in the general population. 21 GDF15 is a member of the transforming growth factor family involved in apoptosis and inflammation, and it has been found to be differentially expressed in patients with and without PAD. 32 Higher levels of GDF15 have been associated with an increased risk of PAD in the general population as well as in individuals with diabetes. 21 , 33 HbA1c is commonly used as a clinical marker to guide the management of diabetes and its prognosis. Nevertheless, given the multifactorial nature of PAD pathogenesis and the heterogeneity of clinical manifestations, 34 a single biomarker is unlikely to attain the highest predictive accuracy. In the present study of individuals without diabetes, HbA1c showed only modest ability in predicting the risk of PAD, highlighting the need to discover other biomarkers, alongside phenotypic and clinical features, to improve early risk screening and disease prevention. 32 In our study, a panel of the 9 top‐ranked proteins demonstrated good predictive performance for incident PAD and significantly enhanced the risk discrimination beyond HbA1c and other traditional risk factors. We further found that the predictive performance of the protein panel was similar for individuals with normoglycemia and those with prediabetes. In a previous proteomic analysis of 354 patients undergoing peripheral or coronary angiography, a protein panel showed similar performance in the prediction of obstructive PAD across HbA1c levels. 35 Our study used a larger sample size with a greater number of protein biomarkers, extending the prior knowledge to individuals with normoglycemia or prediabetes. Findings from this large‐scale, machine learning‐driven proteome study of individuals without diabetes may have important significance both for public health and clinical practices. The selected top‐ranked protein biomarkers may shed novel mechanistic insight into the pathological process of PAD that is independent of glucose metabolism. The identified protein panel may facilitate the early identification of at‐risk individuals and better prediction of PAD risk, especially for those without diabetes who are not regularly screened for PAD. Our study benefits from the large sample size, the long‐term follow up, and the high‐throughput proteome analysis, although several potential limitations should be acknowledged. Although a comprehensive assessment of plasma proteins is provided by the UKB‐PPP, there are some proteins that are not captured by the platform. In addition, independent external cohorts with large‐scale proteomics data are unavailable to validate our findings. In the present study, we have implemented a rigorous 10‐fold cross‐validation strategy and confirmed the model performance in predefined subgroups by glycemic status (normoglycemia and prediabetes). This rigorous internal validation is widely used for ensuring model robustness and generalizability, 17 , 36 , 37 which align with recent proteomic studies for biomarker discovery. Moreover, participants in the UKB were predominantly White Europeans, and our findings are yet to be confirmed for other regional or ethnic populations.
sections.conclusions_1: In summary, our large‐scale proteomic analysis identified a group of plasma proteins associated with incident PAD among individuals without diabetes, emphasizing the importance of 9 key proteins (especially WFDC2, MMP12, and GDF15) in predicting the long‐term risk for PAD beyond traditional risk factors including glycemic levels. These findings may provide new insights into the disease mechanisms that are beyond glucose metabolism. Our findings may also have implications for early screening and targeted prevention of PAD among the general population who are unlikely to be regularly screened for the risk of PAD.

title: Hospitalizations and long-term care for older adults with Alzheimer's disease and related dementia: Differences across geographic regions of the United States
abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease and related dementia (ADRD) leads to adverse health outcomes, such as higher risk of hospitalizations and long-term institutionalization. However, little is known about differences in ADRD health outcomes for older adults in the Deep South (DS) compared to those in the rest of the U.S. (non-DS). Objectives: This study aims to examine the prevalence of hospitalization and long-term use of skilled nursing facilities (SNF) among older adults with ADRD, and factors influencing these healthcare utilization outcomes in the DS vs. non-DS regions. Methods: We conducted secondary analyses of claims data for 115,879 Medicare beneficiaries with ADRD in 2013–2015. Modified Poisson regression was used to examine the association of outcomes with individual and context-level factors for Deep South and non- Deep South separately. Results: Hospitalization rates were slightly higher in the Deep South. Utilization of long-term SNF was similar across regions. In adjusted analyses, within each region, differences between non-Hispanic Black and White beneficiaries were not significant. Comorbidities, specialist visits, ADRD drug use, and Medicare/Medicaid dual eligibility were associated with more hospitalizations and SNF use for all beneficiaries in the DS. For beneficiaries in the non-DS region, context-level factors (limited availability of medical resources and poor population health) were significantly associated with healthcare utilization. Conclusions: We identified differences across regions in the factors associated with hospitalizations and long-term SNF stays, with patient-level factors being relevant in the DS region and context-level factors in the non-DS region.

title: Beyond the patient: how providers perceive and experience non-medical barriers in gastrointestinal cancer care
abstract: Purpose Gastrointestinal (GI) cancer care requires coordination across specialties and is sensitive to non-medical barriers like insurance, transportation, and health literacy. Prior survey work at our institution identified these barriers as most prominent during initial treatment planning and as consuming substantial provider time. This qualitative study represents the second phase of a larger effort to inform the development of a transdisciplinary care model designed to address non-medical determinants of care. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled multidisciplinary providers involved in GI cancer care at a large academic health system in the USA. Interviews explored patient- and system-level barriers and opportunities to improve care coordination. Transcripts underwent inductive thematic analysis with double coding. Pearson correlation coefficients assessed covariation among themes and informed the construction of a directed acyclic graph illustrating hypothesized causal relationships among barrier domains. Results We interviewed 30 providers, including physicians ( n = 7), advanced practice providers ( n = 2), nurses ( n = 5), dietitians ( n = 7), social workers ( n = 6), and a care coordinator ( n = 1). Seven interconnected themes emerged: health system, financial, access and logistics, provider capacity, patient knowledge and engagement, social and emotional, and communication and coordination. Structural and financial barriers operated as upstream drivers influencing workflow and access, while logistical and social barriers translated these pressures into downstream inefficiencies and provider strain. Providers consistently supported a transdisciplinary care model to centralize navigation and support. Conclusion Non-medical barriers in GI cancer care undermine patient care, provider capacity, and health system efficiency. These findings provide an actionable framework for developing equitable, efficient, and sustainable cancer care models. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00520-026-10897-3.
