sections.study design, participants, and protocol: This case-control study compared gut microbiome composition among individuals with Alzheimer disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and cognitively healthy controls (CO). A total of 78 participants were recruited by the Brain Research Unit at the University of Eastern Finland between 2018 and 2019. Participants were assigned to 3 groups based on neuropsychological assessment and clinical diagnosis. The CO group included 37 individuals (mean MMSE 28.4±1.5). The MCI group comprised 20 individuals with mild cognitive impairment without dementia (mean MMSE 27.0±1.5). The AD group included 21 individuals diagnosed with prodromal or mild AD before enrollment (mean MMSE 23.9±3.0). Exclusion criteria included diabetes, depression, other neurological disorders such as PD, moderate or severe AD (CDR 2 to 3), and non-AD dementias. Each participant attended 2 study visits. The protocol included a demographic interview, clinical and neurological examination, and ApoE-ε4 genotyping from venous blood. Cognitive performance was assessed using the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer disease neuropsychological battery (CERAD-NB), and disease severity with the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) global score. 11 , 12 Controls were required to show normal cognitive performance and no functional impairment based on CDR and clinical evaluation. Individuals in the MCI group had preserved daily functioning and were classified according to CERAD-NB performance in the absence of biomarker data. AD diagnoses were established before enrollment by a neurologist or geriatrician according to the National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer’s Association (NIA-AA) criteria. 13 AD stage was determined using the CDR global score (0.5 to 1.0). Participants in the AD group underwent neuroimaging (MRI or CT) and laboratory testing for differential diagnosis, and standard clinical treatment was initiated. Biomarker data were not available at the time of recruitment.
sections.cerad-nb: Cognitive performance was evaluated using the Finnish version of the CERAD neuropsychological battery (CERAD-NB), which includes the same subtests as the original English version. 12 The battery consists of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE; range: 0 to 30), the 15-item Boston Naming Test (range: 0 to 15), category fluency for animals, word list learning (range: 0 to 30), word list recall (range: 0 to 10), word list recognition (range: 0 to 20), and constructional praxis (range: 0 to 11). The Finnish version additionally includes delayed recall of constructional praxis (range: 0 to 11) and the clock-drawing test (range: 0 to 6). A CERAD-NB Global Memory Score was calculated by summing word list learning, delayed recall, and recognition (maximum 50 points).
sections.apoe genotyping: ApoE-ε4 is a well-established genetic risk factor for sporadic AD. 14 Genomic DNA was extracted from venous blood using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (QIAGEN). ApoE genotype was determined with TaqMan genotyping assays (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA) targeting 2 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (rs429358 and rs7412). Allelic discrimination was performed on the ABI 7000 platform following standard procedures. 15
sections.fecal sample collection and dna analysis: Participants reported their dietary habits for the week preceding the study visit, including consumption of meat, legumes, vegetables, grains, dairy products, coffee, beer, and alcohol. Information on comorbidities and medications, particularly cardiovascular and metabolic conditions, was also collected. Fecal samples (FS) were collected at home at least 3 days before the first study visit using containers prefilled with DNA stabilizer (PSP Spin Stool DNA Plus Kit; STRATEC Molecular). Samples were stored in home freezers, transported to the Brain Research Unit on ice, and subsequently stored at –80 °C. Sample collection was recommended to occur as close as possible to the study visit. For transport to Helsinki for sequencing, samples were kept on dry ice. DNA from fecal samples was extracted using the PSP Spin Stool DNA Plus Kit (STRATEC Molecular). Detailed extraction and sequencing procedures have been described previously. 7 In brief, the 16S rRNA V3-V4 regions were amplified by PCR and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform (v3 600-cycle kit), producing 326-bp forward and 278-bp reverse reads. Barcodes were selected using BARCOSEL. 16 Primer trimming was performed with Cutadapt v3.7, 17 and quality filtering, ASV inference, and taxonomic classification were conducted using DADA2 v1.18.0 in R v4.0.5. 18 , 19
sections.statistical analyses: IBM SPSS Statistics was used to analyze CERAD-NB subtests and demographic variables. Group differences in categorical variables, such as ApoE-ε4 carrier status and gender, were assessed with χ 2 tests. For continuous variables, including age, education, and CERAD-NB scores, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons was applied. Alpha diversity was assessed at the ASV level using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with a significance threshold of P ≤0.05. Beta diversity was analyzed in R using distance-based multivariate methods (PERMANOVA, vegan package) to evaluate the effects of clinical and technical variables on sequencing data. 7 , 19 , 20 On the basis of PERMANOVA results, differential abundance models were adjusted for arrhythmia and statin use. Differential abundance analyses were performed in R using the DESeq. 2 package. 21
sections.demographics, bowel-related factors, and: In the AD group, 78.9% of participants were APOE-ε4 carriers, compared with 37.8% in the CO group and 35% in the MCI group. The difference was significant between CO and AD ( P ≤0.05). No significant group differences were observed in comorbidities, bowel-related factors, or dietary habits (Table 1 ).
sections.cerad-nb_1: Three CERAD-NB subtests (verbal fluency, word list learning, and word list recognition) and the global memory score differed significantly between CO and MCI ( P ≤0.02). CO and AD differed significantly in all nine subtests ( P ≤0.02). MCI and AD differed in 5 subtests: MMSE, word list learning, word list savings, constructional praxis, and the global memory score (Table 2 ).
sections.differences in the gut microbiome: Comparative analyses of gut microbiome genera were conducted across the CO, MCI, and AD groups (Table 3 , Fig. 1 ). We observed group-level differences in alpha diversity across 5 diversity indices, but no significant differences in beta diversity (Fig. 2 ). When comparing the changing genera between the CO and the AD groups, the amounts of Anaerovorax and an unidentified genus of the Comamonadaceae family increased, while Enterobacter, Absicoccus, Buttiauxella, Raoultella , and Lacticaseibacillus decreased significantly in the AD group. In addition, when comparing the changing genera between the CO and MCI groups, we detected an increase in Falciporphyromonas, Absicoccus , and Ligilactobacillus in the MCI group. The significantly decreased genera in the MCI group were Clostridium_XlVb, Megasphaera, Limosilactobacillus, Lacticaseibacillus, Raoultella , and Buttiauxella. Comparing the AD group to the MCI group, we detected that the relative amounts of Anaerovorax, Paramuribaculum , and 2 unidentified genera of the Comamonadaceae and Flavobacteriaceae families increased significantly, whereas Cetobacterium , Raoultella , and an unidentified genus of the Sutterellaceae family decreased significantly in the AD group.
sections.discussion: Differences in the gut microbiome (GM) have been reported between healthy individuals and patients with neurological disorders such as PD and iNPH. 6 , 7 , 22 In AD, growing evidence suggests that GM contributes to disease pathogenesis, with some studies indicating that alterations may already appear in the preclinical stage. 9 , 23 Associations between AD and the oral microbiome have also been described. 24 Our findings show differences in bacterial genera across the CO, MCI, and AD groups. Notably, several alterations appeared at multiple stages of cognitive decline. The most prominent patterns were decreases in Lacticaseibacillus, Raoultella , and Buttiauxella , already detectable in the MCI group, and increases in Anaerovorax and an unknown genus from the Comamonadaceae family in the AD group. These results suggest a gradual shift in gut microbiome composition along the neurodegenerative continuum. To evaluate their potential as early biomarkers of AD, further research is needed to characterize these relatively unknown genera and clarify their roles within the gut-brain axis. Alpha diversity, reflecting within-sample bacterial diversity, was assessed using 5 indices: Observed, Chao1, ACE, Shannon, and Inverse Simpson. Observed, ACE, and Chao1 indices showed significant differences between CO and MCI as well as between MCI and AD, but not between CO and AD. In contrast, Shannon and Inverse Simpson indices revealed significant alpha-diversity differences across all three groups. Beta diversity, reflecting differences in community composition between groups, did not differ significantly between CO and AD or between MCI and AD. No significant difference was observed between CO and MCI either, although the model indicated that arrhythmia and statin use may influence beta-diversity patterns in this comparison. At the genus level, we identified significant differences between the groups and observed recurring alterations in 5 genera (Fig. 1 ). Lacticaseibacillus, Raoultella , and Buttiauxella decreased in the MCI group compared with controls and declined further in the AD group. In contrast, the AD group showed increases in the Anaerovorax genus and an unidentified genus from the Comamonadaceae family relative to both CO and MCI. These patterns did not align with findings from a recent study on preclinical AD, 9 which may reflect differences in diet, lifestyle, or cultural background. We also observed several genus-level changes that appeared only in specific pairwise comparisons. In the MCI group relative to controls, the genera Falciporphyromonas, Absicoccus , and Ligilactobacillus increased, whereas Clostridium_XlVb, Megasphaera , and Limosilactobactobacillus decreased. In the AD group compared with the MCI group Paramuribaculum and unidentified genera of Flavobacteriaceae increased, while Cetobacterium and an unidentified genus of the Sutterellaceae family decreased. Independently, the AD group showed a reduction in the Enterobacter genus compared with controls. We also observed inconsistent changes in the genus Absicoccus : its abundance increased in the MCI group compared with controls but decreased in the AD group. Although statistically significant, these opposing patterns complicate interpretation. This raises the broader question of whether a genus showing a significant difference between 2 groups (eg, CO vs. AD) should exhibit similar changes in other comparisons. It is also possible that some alterations are reversible, with certain taxa increasing at one stage and declining at another. Given the small sample size, some findings may be spurious. At present, the overall trajectory of microbiome changes across the disease continuum remains unclear, including whether specific alterations occur only at certain stages or lack biological relevance. Further studies are therefore needed. Among the 5 most significantly altered genera, the most clinically interesting genus was Lacticaseibacillus . Taxonomically, it has been an independent genus since 2020, as it was formerly part of the larger genus Lactobacillus . 25 The genus consists of lactic acid-producing species, the most well-known being L. casei, L. paracasei , and L. rhamnosus . Because our bioinformatics pipeline does not resolve taxa to the species level, the specific species present in our samples remain unknown. Nevertheless, lactic acid-producing bacteria are widely used as probiotics, including in functional food products. 26 In murine and rodent studies, L. rhamnosus has been found to suppress the expression of proinflammatory interleukins and interferons. 27 L. rhamnosus GG was also found to improve cognition and reduce neuroinflammation in mice. 28 It has additionally been reported to decrease depression in rats by regulating cortisone pathways, increasing neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine, epinephrine, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor, and modulating GM composition. 29 In a randomized and double-blinded study of MCI patients, L. rhamnosus GG strain supplementation did not change microbiome diversity, although it did improve cognitive performance and induced minor changes in the GM composition. 30 In a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized study, people with MCI received L. rhamnosus GG- supplement for 3 months, and their neuropsychological test results improved. 31 Despite these findings, another human study reported that L. rhamnosus was not more effective than a placebo regarding stress, HPA-function, inflammation, or cognitive performance. 32 In a murine model, L. casei improved gut-barrier integrity and reduced colonic and systemic inflammation, along with decreasing oxidative stress in the brain; however, its effects were stronger when combined with a specific dietary-fiber complex rather than used alone. 33 Another study showed that supplementation with both live and heat-killed L. paracasei increased hippocampal serotonin levels and upregulated genes related to neuroplasticity, anti-inflammatory pathways, and antioxidant functions in mice. 34 In a randomized, double-blind trial in PD patients, a strain of L. paracasei alleviated nonmotor symptoms, although it did not alter the gut microbiome composition. 35 The remaining genera are less well characterized. Raoultella , for example, is a relatively unknown histamine-secreting genus composed of low-virulence, biofilm-forming, lipopolysaccharide-containing bacteria. 36 Although it can cause opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals, its overall clinical relevance remains unclear. 37 Other genera of uncertain significance in our dataset include Buttiauxella , Anaerovorax , and an unidentified genus within the Comamonadaceae family. A recent meta-analysis reported that these genera were not detected in the microbiomes of PD patients, 38 raising the possibility that the observed changes may be more specific to AD. Our independently changing genera Clostridium_XlVb, Megasphaera, Falciporphyromonas, Ligilactobacillus. An unidentified genus of the Sutterellaceae family, Cetobacterium. Paramuribaculum and Flavobacterium are of unknown clinical relevance. The Enterobacter genus consists of opportunistic pathogens, some of which exhibit antibiotic resistance. 39 However, the genus Limosilactobacillus , which decreased in the MCI group compared with the CO group, consists of lactic acid bacteria, the most well-known being L. reuteri . L. reuteri is reported to have protective properties in the gastrointestinal epithelium and has also been associated with immunomodulation. 40 , 41 Finding differences between the groups is in line with the literature, which states that gut microbiome-related factors correlate with progressive neurodegeneration. We detected alpha-diversity differences, but no beta diversity. According to a meta-analysis, microbial diversity is less rich in AD patients compared with healthy controls. 23 However, other preclinical AD studies report that in early AD, diversity may not significantly change. 9 Our participants reported remarkably similar diets: they consumed comparable amounts of meat, vegetables, dairy, and grain products, and preferred darker rye bread over white bread. Intake of beans, noodles, rice, beer, and alcohol was uniformly low. Given that all participants lived in the same geographical and cultural region in Finland, the lack of dietary differences is unsurprising. The typical Finnish diet is characterized by agricultural products, dairy, and meat, 42 suggesting that diet, the major potential confounder, was largely eliminated. Previous studies also indicate that adequate nutrition may help mitigate cognitive decline. 43 , 44 In our cohort, the ApoE ε4 allele was most common in the AD group, where 78.9% carried at least one ε4 allele. In comparison, 35% of the MCI group and 37.8% of controls were ε4 carriers. ApoE ε4 is a well-established genetic risk factor for sporadic AD, whereas ε2 is considered protective and ε3 is largely neutral. 45 The higher ε4 frequency in the AD group is therefore consistent with previous literature and supports the validity of our diagnostic grouping.
sections.strengths and limitations: A key strength of this study is the well‑characterized cohort, which included cognitively healthy controls, individuals with MCI, and patients with early‑stage AD, enabling comparisons across different stages of cognitive decline. The groups were similar in age, sex, and dietary habits, reducing major confounders, and the use of detailed food diaries is a notable advantage over many previous studies. To further minimize confounding, individuals with diabetes, known to exhibit gut microbiome alterations, were excluded. 46 This study also has limitations. Its cross‑sectional design prevents assessment of within‑individual changes over time, and longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the observed patterns. The relatively small sample size, particularly in the MCI and AD groups, limits statistical power and generalizability, underscoring the need for validation in larger cohorts. Another limitation is the absence of biomarker confirmation for MCI and AD diagnoses. At the time of recruitment (2018 to 2019), fluid biomarkers such as plasma p‑tau217 were not yet available, so classification relied on established clinical and neuropsychological criteria. Although this may introduce some diagnostic heterogeneity, it reflects real‑world clinical practice. Importantly, early‑stage alterations have been detected in this same cohort using independent methods, including eye‑movement analysis and tear‑fluid proteomics, 47 – 49 supporting the presence of early disease‑related changes. Focusing on early‑stage AD and including individuals with MCI allowed us to detect microbiome alterations at the earliest stages of cognitive decline. However, variability in diet, gut health, and sample handling may introduce additional noise, and some genus‑level findings may reflect stochastic variation due to the limited sample size. These results should therefore be interpreted with caution.
sections.implications and future studies: One of the most consistent findings in this study was the reduced abundance of the Lacticaseibacillus genus across multiple group comparisons, suggesting a potential link between lower levels of this genus and cognitive decline. Although these results should be interpreted with caution, they identify Lacticaseibacillus as a promising target for further investigation in early-stage AD. More broadly, our findings support the idea that gut microbiome alterations may emerge early in the disease continuum. Future work should examine whether combinations of microbial taxa, rather than individual genera, could enhance the sensitivity and specificity of microbiome-based biomarkers. Longitudinal studies are particularly important to determine whether these microbial changes precede cognitive decline and could contribute to risk prediction. The potential clinical utility of microbiome profiling remains an area of interest. If validated in larger cohorts, gut microbiome signatures could complement existing diagnostic tools. Interventional studies, such as dietary modifications or probiotic supplementation, may also help clarify whether modulating the gut microbiome can influence disease-related processes. However, the associations observed here do not imply causality, and the biological and clinical relevance of the identified genera requires further investigation.
sections.conclusions: Our findings indicate that gut microbiome composition is altered in the early stages of cognitive decline, including in individuals with MCI, and that these changes resemble those observed in AD. Several genera, such as Lacticaseibacillus , Raoultella , and Buttiauxella —showed consistent decreases from cognitively healthy individuals to MCI and AD. These results suggest that gut microbiome alterations may emerge early in the disease process and highlight specific genera as potential candidates for biomarker development. However, validation in larger and longitudinal cohorts is needed to determine their reliability and clinical relevance.

title: The Gut–Oral–Skin–Heart Microbiota Axis and Oxidative Stress: Where Have We Been and Where Are We Going
abstract: Scientific interest in the relationship between cardiovascular disease and the human microbiome has grown substantially in recent years, with particular emphasis placed on the gut microbiota. Emerging evidence suggests, however, that distinct microbial niches—including the skin, oral cavity, and gut—may interact to influence cardiovascular homeostasis through shared pathogenic pathways, most notably oxidative stress and systemic inflammation. Intestinal dysbiosis has been strongly linked to the increased production of microbial metabolites such as trimethylamine N-oxide, which promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative imbalance, and atherogenesis. The oral microbiome has similarly been implicated in cardiovascular pathology through mechanisms encompassing chronic low-grade inflammation, transient bacteremia, and direct vascular colonization by pathogenic species. The contribution of the skin microbiome to cardiovascular risk remains less well defined; nevertheless, chronic inflammatory dermatoses—psoriasis in particular—have been consistently associated with elevated cardiovascular risk, a relationship potentially mediated by systemic immune dysregulation and oxidative stress. This review synthesizes current evidence on the gut–oral–skin–cardiac microbiome axis, underscoring the central role of oxidative stress as a convergent pathogenic mechanism and examining potential therapeutic implications. A more comprehensive understanding of these interconnected systems may inform the development of novel, microbiome-targeted strategies for the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.

sections.key summary points: Alterations in the human microbiome are increasingly recognized as significant contributors to cardiovascular disease, operating through interconnected inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways. This review examines the interdependent roles of the gut, oral, and skin microbiota within a unified microbiome axis, and their collective influence on cardiovascular homeostasis. Key microbial metabolites, including trimethylamine N-oxide, are strongly implicated in endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and the progression of atherosclerotic disease. Chronic inflammatory dermatoses, psoriasis in particular, further substantiate the concept of systemic immune dysregulation as a mediator of elevated cardiovascular risk. A deeper understanding of these microbiome–cardiovascular interactions may inform the development of novel diagnostic biomarkers and microbiome-targeted therapeutic strategies.
sections.introduction: The gut–oral–skin–cardiac microbiome axis represents a complex network of interrelations between distinct microbial ecosystems and their collective impact on host physiology, including skin integrity and cardiovascular function. Among these, the gut microbiota has been extensively studied for its beneficial influence on cardiovascular health [ 1 ]. Scientific evidence indicates that intestinal dysbiosis—an imbalance in the gut microbial community—is associated with several cardiovascular pathologies, such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and heart failure (HF) [ 2 ]. In the context of HF, reduced perfusion can lead to intestinal ischemia and mucosal edema, compromising the gut barrier and facilitating translocation of bacteria and their metabolites into systemic circulation [ 2 ]. This process triggers both local and systemic inflammatory responses, which may subsequently disturb the homeostasis of the skin and oral microbiota [ 3 ]. Further supporting this interconnectedness, disruptions in the oral microbiome have also been implicated in cardiovascular dysfunction. Specific oral bacterial species, such as Streptococcus mutans and Porphyromonas gingivalis , have been directly associated with an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease [ 4 ]. The cutaneous microbiome plays a fundamental role in immunological defense and pathogen resistance. Dysregulation of the skin microbiota contributes to the etiopathogenesis of inflammatory dermatoses, which may indirectly influence cardiovascular health through immune-mediated mechanisms [ 5 ]. The purpose of this review is to present a thorough and integrative summary of existing findings relating the gut, oral, and skin microbiota to cardiovascular disorders, with specific emphasis on oxidative stress as a unifying pathogenic mechanism. By investigating the dynamic interplay between these diverse microbial habitats, this work attempts to outline potential system-level interactions within the gut–oral–skin–cardiac axis and to discover developing translational prospects for risk stratification and targeted therapeutic intervention.
sections.oxidative stress in cardiovascular disea: Recent studies have demonstrated a significant association between intestinal dysbiosis and heightened oxidative stress, alongside systemic inflammation, particularly concerning the cardiovascular system [ 6 – 8 ]. The interplay between the human host and the gut microbiota, as well as the contribution of oxidative stress to cardiovascular pathogenesis, is essential for elucidating mechanisms that affect human health [ 9 ]. The gut microbiota produces a range of metabolites—such as reactive sulfur species (RSS), short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO)—that modulate oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, both of which play pivotal roles in the development of cardiovascular diseases. Notably, TMAO, a key metabolic byproduct of intestinal microbial activity, has been strongly linked to increased oxidative stress in cardiovascular conditions. Evidence suggests that TMAO exacerbates oxidative imbalance by disrupting the equilibrium between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant capacity [ 10 – 12 ]. Moreover, TMAO affects endothelial inflammatory pathways by modulating the availability of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and nitric oxide (NO). It also contributes to platelet hyperreactivity by intensifying oxidative stress within endothelial cells. These pathophysiological mechanisms emphasize TMAO’s critical role in endothelial dysfunction and underscore its potential as a target for further mechanistic and therapeutic investigation in cardiovascular diseases [ 13 , 14 ]. The diverse oral microbiome similarly exerts significant effects on both local and systemic health. Oral microbial communities produce several bioactive compounds, including SCFAs (e.g., butyrate, acetate, and propionate), lactate, hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S), NO, and TMAO. SCFAs have demonstrated anti-inflammatory properties that support oral and cardiovascular homeostasis. H 2 S contributes to vascular tone regulation and inflammatory processes, while NO exerts multifaceted roles in vasodilation and blood pressure regulation. As previously mentioned, TMAO has been implicated in atherosclerosis progression and overall cardiovascular risk [ 15 , 16 ]. The skin microbiota also produces various metabolites, including SCFAs (e.g., acetate, propionate, and butyrate), hydrogen peroxide, lactate, xenobiotics, and organic acids [ 17 ]. However, the specific impact of these skin-derived metabolites on oxidative stress and cardiovascular function remains poorly understood and warrants further exploration (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 The role of the microbiome in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases. Schematic representation of the gut–oral–skin–cardiac microbiome axis and its involvement in cardiovascular pathophysiology. Microbial metabolites—including trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and reactive sulfur species (RSS)—contribute to systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction. Interactions between microbial ecosystems may influence immune activation and vascular remodeling
sections.the gut microbiome in cardiovascular dis: Intestinal bacteria are taxonomically divided into several key phyla, including Actinobacteria, Pseudomonadota, Fusobacteria, and Verrucomicrobiota, with Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes being the predominant families. In HF, reduced perfusion to abdominal organs leads to alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota. This includes decreased oxygen supply to intestinal epithelial cells, resulting in hypoxia and a metabolic shift toward anaerobic pathways [ 2 ]. Current research has elucidated the influence of microbial secondary metabolites—such as bile acids, SCFAs, and TMAO—on cardiovascular diseases and their underlying pathogenic processes. SCFAs positively affect gut mucosal integrity by reinforcing epithelial barrier function and mitigating apoptosis via the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway. Conversely, TMAO may exert direct deleterious effects on the heart by promoting cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, endothelial and arterial inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiomyocytes, ultimately contributing to the progression of HF [ 12 ]. Savi et al. demonstrated that TMAO impairs cardiomyocyte contractility by disrupting intracellular calcium metabolism, leading to diminished calcium clearance and increased glycogen accumulation—findings that provide preliminary evidence for TMAO’s mechanistic involvement in cardiac dysfunction [ 18 ]. Pasini et al. were among the first to report increased levels of pathogenic gut flora—such as Campylobacter , Shigella , Salmonella , Yersinia enterocolitica , and various Candida species—in stool samples from patients with chronic HF compared to healthy controls. Venous congestion within the intestinal wall, a hallmark of chronic HF, exacerbates clinical symptoms and enhances systemic absorption of toxic microbial metabolites [ 19 ]. Comparative studies of healthy individuals and those with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) showed a higher abundance of pro-inflammatory microorganisms in patients with HFpEF [ 20 , 21 ]. At the same time, there was a reduced abundance of anti-inflammatory bacteria (e.g., Lachnospiraceae, Bifidobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae) capable of inducing regulatory T (Treg) cells, including sCD25-positive populations, and peripheral macrophages through butyrate production [ 22 , 23 ]. Consequently, microbial diversity was lower in patients with HFpEF. Eubacterium hallii has been identified as a critical regulator of metabolic balance and intestinal microbial homeostasis through its SCFA production. It can convert glycerol into 3-hydroxypropionic acid (3-HPA), an intermediate in the biosynthesis of cobalamin (vitamin B 12 ) and 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PD), a precursor to propionate [ 24 ]. Cobalamin plays a pivotal role in lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, neurological function, erythropoiesis, and DNA/RNA synthesis in erythroblasts. Vitamin B 12 deficiency leads to elevated homocysteine levels, a recognized cardiovascular risk factor [ 24 ]. Recent evidence has revealed that gut microbiota metabolize phosphatidylcholine into trimethylamine (TMA), which is transported to the liver and subsequently oxidized to TMAO by flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 (FMO3). TMAO actively participates in modulating the biochemical reactivity of several physiologically critical molecules [ 25 ]. Elevated plasma TMAO levels are associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney disease, HF, atherosclerosis, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes—all conditions that significantly heighten the likelihood of major adverse cardiovascular events. Moreover, circulating TMAO levels may serve as a biomarker for HF severity and prognosis [ 26 ].
sections.the skin microbiome in cardiovascular di: Multiple studies have suggested a potential correlation between the presence of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and atopic dermatitis (AD) [ 27 ]. Some research highlights an association between sleep disturbances in individuals with AD and cardiovascular-related insomnia [ 28 ]. Additional hypotheses indicate links among AD, obesity, and metabolic syndrome—recognized as major contributors to cardiovascular dysfunction. Furthermore, these comorbidities are often associated with a sedentary lifestyle frequently observed in patients with AD [ 29 ]. The inflammatory cascade in AD that contributes to cardiovascular pathology is similar to the one observed in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis. The role of T helper type 2 (Th2) cytokines has been established in the pathogenesis of AD; however, their involvement in atherosclerosis remains inconclusive. In contrast, T helper type 1 (Th1) cytokines play a critical role in both rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis, as well as in atherogenesis [ 30 ]. In this context, psoriasis represents one of the most extensively studied models linking chronic cutaneous inflammation to cardiovascular disease [ 31 ]. Psoriasis is a systemic immune-mediated disorder characterized by activation of the Th1 and Th17 pathways, leading to sustained production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), interleukin (IL)-17, and IL-23. These mediators contribute not only to keratinocyte hyperproliferation but also to systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction [ 32 ]. A growing body of epidemiological evidence indicates that patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis exhibit an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction, stroke, and cardiovascular mortality, often independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors [ 33 – 35 ]. Despite these observations, the extent to which the cutaneous microbiome directly modulates cardiovascular risk remains incompletely understood [ 36 ]. Further studies are warranted to elucidate whether skin-derived microbial signals contribute to systemic effects within the gut–oral–skin–cardiac axis. Atopic dermatitis offers additional insights into barrier breakdown and allergen-driven immune activation, whereas psoriasis offers a model of systemic inflammatory load. Disruption of epidermal barrier integrity facilitates allergen penetration through the epithelium, triggering a Th2-mediated immune response. This enhanced Th2 activity leads to B cell stimulation and increased IgE production, which in turn activates basophils and mast cells. Allergens also tend to bind to dendritic cells, promoting their activation and the subsequent release of pro-inflammatory cytokines that exacerbate the existing inflammatory state [ 37 , 38 ]. In a large-scale cohort study conducted in the UK between 1998 and 2015, Silverwood et al. demonstrated an association between AD and various cardiovascular conditions, including myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, HF, atrial fibrillation, and cardiovascular mortality. However, it remains unclear whether this predisposition arises from the underlying disease or from pharmacological interventions used in its management [ 39 ]. Data from three major US surveys—NHANES, the National Health Interview Surveys (NHIS) from 2012, and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2005–2006)—confirmed that AD is associated with an increased risk of peripheral arterial disease, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, stroke, angina, and congestive HF. These findings emphasize the elevated risk of both cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events in individuals with AD [ 40 ]. Moreover, a recent 35-year longitudinal study conducted in Denmark reported approximately a 20% increased risk of developing atrial fibrillation among individuals with AD [ 41 ]. Numerous other studies have confirmed a higher predisposition to cardiovascular events, including coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, HF, ischemic stroke, and peripheral vascular disease, in patients suffering from AD [ 41 – 43 ]. Conversely, an analysis by Thyssen and Egeberg suggested a low likelihood that AD acts as an independent risk factor for CVD. Given these conflicting findings, further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the cellular and molecular underpinnings of this association. Furthermore, as previously noted, the functional role of the cutaneous microbiome and its metabolite interactions with the cardiovascular system remain poorly characterized. Further investigations are essential to explore the potential etiopathogenic link between the skin microbiome and cardiovascular diseases [ 44 ].
sections.the oral microbiome in cardiovascular di: Periodontal diseases have been directly linked to cardiovascular disorders. Numerous studies have confirmed a high prevalence of infections and inflammatory conditions in the periodontal region among individuals with atherosclerosis. Additionally, chronic periodontitis has been associated with increased susceptibility to myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease, stroke, and atherosclerosis [ 45 , 46 ]. Microbial analysis of dental plaque has revealed the involvement of key bacterial species—such as Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans , Tannerella forsythia , Treponema denticola , and P. gingivalis —in the thickening of the intimal and medial layers of the carotid arteries [ 47 ]. Furthermore, experimental animal models have demonstrated that inoculation with P. gingivalis promotes advanced atherosclerotic lesions. For instance, ApoE-knockout mice (apoE −/− ) developed atherosclerotic plaques following bacterial exposure, in contrast to control animals [ 48 ]. Periodontal infections can lead to transient bacteremia, facilitating the invasion of vascular endothelial cells. Oral bacteria employ various mechanisms to evade host immune responses. Notably, oral microbial components have been identified in atherosclerotic plaques, aortic aneurysms, cardiac valves, and within the arterial tree—an area commonly affected by atherosclerotic changes. Specific pathogens, including T. forsythia , A. actinomycetemcomitans , Prevotella intermedia , and P. gingivalis , have been detected in coronary arteries [ 4 , 49 , 50 ]. Substantial evidence supports the notion that systemic inflammation is a major driver of atherogenesis. This has been correlated with elevated circulating levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, TNFα, and monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1), as well as acute-phase proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and fibrinogen. Among these, serum CRP is recognized as a highly reliable biomarker for predicting cardiovascular events and underscores the inflammatory component of atherosclerotic progression [ 51 – 53 ]. CRP contributes to foam cell formation by enhancing macrophage uptake of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and promoting monocyte recruitment to the arterial wall. Additionally, CRP upregulates the expression of endothelial cell adhesion molecules, including ICAM-1, sVCAM-1, and selectins, whose elevated levels have been linked to heightened cardiovascular risk and are regarded as indicators of endothelial activation [ 54 – 56 ]. Emerging studies further indicate that oral microbiota may colonize the gastrointestinal tract and contribute to the development of systemic inflammation, which in turn may play a significant role in the pathogenesis of HF [ 57 ].
sections.limitations: Despite the growing body of evidence linking the microbiome to cardiovascular diseases, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, much of the current literature remains observational in nature, limiting the ability to establish causal relationships between microbial alterations and cardiovascular outcomes. Second, significant heterogeneity exists across studies in terms of population characteristics, methodological approaches, and microbiome profiling techniques, which may affect the comparability and generalizability of findings. Third, while the role of the gut and oral microbiota has been relatively well explored, the contribution of the skin microbiome remains insufficiently characterized, with limited mechanistic and longitudinal data available. Furthermore, the complex interplay between microbial metabolites, host immune responses, and oxidative stress pathways is not yet fully elucidated. Finally, potential confounding factors—including diet, lifestyle, pharmacological treatments, and comorbidities—are not consistently controlled across studies, further complicating interpretation. These limitations underscore the need for well-designed, prospective, and mechanistic studies to better define the role of the microbiome within the gut–oral–skin–cardiac axis.
sections.conclusions: The emerging concept of a gut–oral–skin–cardiac microbiome axis underscores the complexity of host–microbe interactions in cardiovascular disease. While the contribution of the gut and oral microbiota is increasingly well characterized, the role of the skin microbiome remains comparatively underexplored, despite compelling evidence linking chronic inflammatory skin disorders—particularly psoriasis—to heightened cardiovascular risk. A unifying element across these microbial ecosystems appears to be the induction and modulation of systemic oxidative stress and chronic low-grade inflammation, both of which are central to cardiovascular pathophysiology. However, current evidence remains largely associative, and the precise mechanistic pathways linking these microbiome niches to cardiovascular outcomes require further elucidation. Future research should prioritize integrative, multi-omics approaches and longitudinal studies to clarify causal relationships and identify actionable therapeutic targets. In this context, modulation of the microbiome through dietary, pharmacological, and lifestyle interventions may represent a promising avenue for personalized cardiovascular prevention strategies. Ultimately, advancing from compartmentalized models toward a systems-level understanding of microbiome–host interactions may redefine current paradigms in cardiovascular medicine.

title: IL-33 associates with type 2 burden and lung function in paediatric asthma, alongside exploratory IL-33–linked lipid changes
abstract: Background Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is an epithelial alarmin positioned upstream of type 2 (T2) inflammation, yet its clinical correlates and systemic molecular context in paediatric asthma remain incompletely defined. We investigated whether circulating IL-33 is associated with objective disease-burden measures and whether IL-33 elevation co-occurs with exploratory plasma lipid differences. Methods In a paediatric case–control cohort (August 2023–June 2025; asthma n = 60, controls n = 60), plasma IL-33 was quantified by ELISA and related to spirometry (FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEF) and T2 markers (blood eosinophils, total IgE, FeNO). Associations were assessed using correlation analyses and multivariable linear regression treating IL-33 as a continuous exposure (mean-centred ln[IL-33]) with adjustment for age, sex, BMI, and group, plus an Age × IL-33 interaction. ROC analyses were used to describe case–control discrimination within the cohort. Untargeted plasma lipidomics was performed in an exploratory discovery subset (asthma n = 8, controls n = 8) to define differential lipids, IL-33-anchored lipid patterns, and an exploratory six-lipid IL-33-linked score; score–trait associations were evaluated as exploratory analyses with group residualization. Results Compared with controls, children with asthma showed worse lung function and higher T2 burden (all P < 0.001), alongside higher IL-33 (107.1 ± 38.5 vs. 52.4 ± 21.6 pg/mL; P < 0.001). Across the cohort, IL-33 correlated inversely with lung function (FEV1 r = − 0.652; FEV1/FVC r = − 0.585; PEF r = − 0.683; all P < 0.001) and positively with T2 markers (eosinophils r = 0.534; IgE r = 0.583; FeNO r = 0.622; all P < 0.001). In multivariable models, ln(IL-33) remained significantly associated with each outcome after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, and group status, whereas the Age × IL-33 interaction was not significant (all P > 0.05). IL-33 showed case–control discrimination within the cohort (AUC 0.92; cut-off 75.4 pg/mL). In the exploratory lipidomics subset, PCA suggested group separation, although this should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size. Differential lipids were dominated by glycerophospholipids (66.67%), followed by sphingolipids (18.1%). Exploratory IL-33-anchored analyses identified provisional glycerophospholipid/cardiolipin-positive and sphingomyelin-negative lipid patterns. The exploratory IL-33-linked lipid score showed high apparent discrimination within the discovery subset (AUC 0.96; LOOCV AUC 0.97) and, after group residualization, remained directionally associated with lung function and T2 markers. Conclusion In this paediatric case–control cohort, circulating IL-33 was elevated in children with asthma and was significantly associated with objective airflow limitation and systemic type 2 inflammatory burden. Higher IL-33 levels also co-occurred with exploratory plasma lipid differences. These findings should be interpreted as adjusted associations observed within a cross-sectional case–control design and require longitudinal and external validation before any broader biomarker or clinical application can be considered. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12887-026-06947-8.

sections.introduction: Paediatric asthma remains one of the most common chronic respiratory diseases in childhood and is increasingly recognised as a syndrome comprising heterogeneous inflammatory and functional trajectories rather than a single entity. Contemporary frameworks emphasise phenotypes and endotypes to better capture variability in symptoms, exacerbation propensity, airway physiology, and treatment response across development [ 1 – 4 ]. Although guideline-based management has improved outcomes, a substantial proportion of children continue to experience poor symptom control and persistent airflow limitation, highlighting the need for better-characterised biological correlates of clinically meaningful disease burden in paediatric asthma [ 5 , 6 ]. Current clinical biomarkers that support type 2 (T2) endotyping—blood eosinophil counts, fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), and serum total IgE—provide actionable information for risk stratification and, in selected settings, for biologic selection and monitoring [ 6 , 7 ]. However, these markers are downstream readouts and can be discordant with spirometric impairment or symptom control in individual patients, and they do not directly capture epithelial stress signals that initiate and amplify T2 inflammation [ 4 – 6 , 8 ]. Therefore, there is a strong clinical rationale to evaluate upstream epithelial “alarmins” as candidate circulating correlates that may better contextualise T2 burden and airflow limitation. Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is a prototypical epithelial-derived alarmin released upon barrier injury or cellular stress and signals through the ST2 receptor (IL1RL1) expressed on group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s), T helper 2 cells, mast cells, and other immune and structural cell types [ 8 – 11 ]. Genetic and translational evidence implicates the IL-33/ST2 axis in asthma susceptibility and airway inflammatory phenotypes, supporting its upstream role in disease biology [ 10 , 11 ]. At the tissue level, spatial and single-cell analyses of human asthma airway samples identify discrete niches with heightened alarmin expression, including IL-33, reinforcing the concept that epithelial alarm signalling is embedded within the airway wall ecosystem [ 12 ]. Importantly, therapeutic targeting of this pathway has shown clinical benefit in asthma: IL-33 blockade with itepekimab reduced loss-of-control events and improved lung function in moderate-to-severe asthma, and ST2 blockade with astegolimab reduced exacerbations across a broad severe-asthma population [ 13 , 14 ]. Together, these findings motivate renewed efforts to clarify how circulating IL-33 relates to clinically relevant disease-burden measures in children. Despite strong biological plausibility, the clinical relevance of circulating IL-33 in paediatric asthma remains incompletely defined. Recent paediatric studies suggest that serum IL-33 is elevated in childhood asthma and may correlate with spirometric impairment, yet findings can differ by cohort characteristics (e.g., severity spectrum, atopy context) and may be influenced by developmental factors [ 15 – 17 ]. In parallel, asthma is increasingly viewed through an immunometabolic lens, in which membrane lipid remodelling and bioactive lipid classes influence epithelial integrity, receptor organisation, and inflammatory signalling [ 18 , 19 ]. Lipidomic studies in asthma have reported perturbations in glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids—detectable in plasma and airway samples—and have demonstrated that lipid profiles can stratify airway disease and relate to clinical features [ 19 – 21 ]. Mechanistically, phospholipid metabolism is actively reprogrammed during innate immune responses, while sphingolipids and mitochondrial cardiolipin participate in inflammatory programmes and cellular stress signalling, providing plausible links between epithelial stress signals and systemic lipid changes [ 18 , 22 ]. Moreover, epithelial alarmin networks can be cooperative (e.g., TL1A signalling synergising with IL-33), underscoring that upstream alarm pathways are embedded in broader epithelial–immune circuits that may imprint systemic molecular readouts [ 23 ]. However, whether IL-33 elevation in children co-occurs with a coherent plasma lipid remodelling signature, and whether such a signature adds biological interpretability to IL-33 measurement, remain unclear. Our group previously undertook a preliminary IL-33–stratified, asthma-only multi-omics investigation to explore mechanistic links between circulating IL-33 and systemic molecular remodelling. Building on this preliminary framework, the novelty of the present study is that we extend from within-asthma stratification to a paediatric case–control design and evaluate circulating IL-33 as a continuous exposure against objective airflow limitation and T2 inflammatory burden, while deriving an exploratory IL-33–anchored lipid composite to summarise the coordinated lipid remodelling pattern. To address these gaps, we conducted an integrated clinical–lipidomic investigation anchored on circulating IL-33 in a paediatric case–control cohort. We quantified plasma IL-33 and evaluated its associations with objective lung function indices (FEV1, FEV1/FVC, and PEF) and T2 inflammatory burden (blood eosinophil counts, total IgE, and FeNO) using multivariable modelling that treated IL-33 as a continuous exposure and tested an Age×IL-33 interaction. In a matched discovery subset, we performed untargeted plasma lipidomics to characterise case–control lipid alterations and to define IL-33–linked lipid features. Finally, we derived an exploratory IL-33–linked lipid score as a parsimonious composite readout and examined its relationship with IL-33 and clinical traits within the discovery setting. Together, this work aims to clarify how circulating IL-33 aligns with clinically meaningful disease burden in children and to provide lipidomic context that may inform future biomarker refinement and longitudinal validation.
sections.study design and participants: This case–control study was conducted at the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China) between August 2023 and June 2025. Children aged 6–12 years with physician-diagnosed asthma were recruited from the paediatric respiratory clinic, and healthy controls were recruited from routine health examinations. Asthma was diagnosed by paediatric respiratory specialists according to Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) recommendations and standard clinical evaluation. To reduce treatment-related confounding, asthma participants were enrolled at first diagnosis, were not receiving inhaled corticosteroids at enrolment, and were sampled in a stable state rather than during an acute exacerbation. Eligibility criteria were as follows. Inclusion criteria: (1) age 6–12 years; (2) confirmed asthma for the case group, or absence of asthma and other chronic allergic diseases for the control group; and (3) availability of clinical assessments and blood samples. Exclusion criteria: (1) acute respiratory infection or fever within 4 weeks before sampling; (2) systemic corticosteroid use within 4 weeks before sampling; (3) other chronic pulmonary disease (e.g., cystic fibrosis), congenital heart disease, or major systemic illness; and (4) known immunodeficiency or autoimmune disease. The clinical cohort included 60 children with asthma and 60 controls (Table 1 ). Table 1 Baseline characteristics, lung function, type 2 inflammatory markers, and circulating IL-33 levels in the paediatric case–control cohort Variable Control ( n = 60) Asthma ( n = 60) P value Age (years) 9.4 ± 1.4 9.6 ± 1.5 0.590 Sex (male, %) 48.3% 53.3% 0.715 BMI (kg/m^2) 17.4 ± 1.2 17.6 ± 1.3 0.38 FEV1 (L) 2.09 ± 0.31 1.62 ± 0.29 < 0.001 FEV1/FVC (%) 85.21 ± 4.57 77.62 ± 4.88 < 0.001 PEF (L/min) 82.43 ± 3.81 69.11 ± 5.72 < 0.001 Eosinophil count (per/µL) 217.45 ± 76.11 344.74 ± 97.99 < 0.001 Total IgE (IU/mL) 68.7 ± 33.8 147.3 ± 52.1 < 0.001 FeNO (ppb) 24.28 ± 5.97 38.12 ± 5.49 < 0.001 IL-33 (pg/mL) 52.4 ± 21.6 107.1 ± 38.5 < 0.001 Data are presented as mean ± SD for continuous variables and percentage for categorical variables. Between-group comparisons (asthma vs. control; n = 60 per group) were performed using an unpaired t test (or Mann–Whitney U test where appropriate) for continuous variables and the χ² test for categorical variables. Age, sex distribution, and BMI did not differ significantly between groups. In contrast, children with asthma showed significantly lower spirometric indices (FEV1, FEV1/FVC, and PEF) and higher type 2 inflammatory burden (blood eosinophil count, total IgE, and FeNO), alongside markedly elevated circulating IL-33 (all P < 0.001) Ethics approval was granted by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (approval no. LS2022112). Written informed consent was obtained from parents/guardians, and assent was obtained from children when appropriate.
sections.clinical assessments: Demographic information (age, sex) and anthropometrics were recorded at enrolment. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight (kg)/height (m)^2. Lung function was assessed by spirometry following American Thoracic Society standards. Forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), the FEV1/FVC ratio, and peak expiratory flow (PEF) were recorded; the best acceptable manoeuvre was used for analysis. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) was measured as a marker of airway T2 inflammation according to established guidelines using a standardised online technique before spirometry. Peripheral blood eosinophil counts were obtained from routine complete blood counts. Total serum IgE was measured by the hospital clinical laboratory using a standard immunoassay platform (reported in IU/mL).
sections.blood processing and il-33 measurement: Peripheral venous blood was collected and centrifuged within 2 h of collection; plasma was aliquoted and stored at − 80 °C until analysis. Plasma IL-33 concentrations were quantified using a commercially available solid-phase sandwich ELISA (Quantikine Human IL-33 Immunoassay; R&D Systems; Cat. No. D3300B) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The assay sensitivity (limit of detection, LOD) is 1.51 pg/mL, with a stated assay range of 3.13–200 pg/mL for serum/plasma matrices. Plasma samples were assayed in duplicate (50 µL per well), and absorbance was measured at 450 nm (TMB colorimetric readout). A standard curve was generated on each plate using kit standards across the working range, and concentrations were interpolated from the standard curve using four-parameter logistic (4-PL) fitting where supported by the analysis software. Samples with concentrations above the upper limit of quantification were re-measured after dilution using the kit diluent, and final concentrations were back-calculated by applying the dilution factor. Based on the manufacturer’s validation, intra-assay precision shows coefficients of variation (CV%) of 3.7–5.9%, and inter-assay precision shows CV% of 4.4–6.0% across three concentration levels. In our workflow, duplicate measurements were required for each sample; if duplicate variability exceeded predefined acceptance criteria, the sample was re-assayed. No IL-33 measurements in this study were below the LOD; therefore, no < LOD imputation/substitution was applied. For completeness, if < LOD values were encountered in future analyses requiring continuous modelling, a prespecified approach (e.g., substitution with LOD/2) would be used.
sections.discovery plasma lipidomics: Untargeted plasma lipidomics was performed in a discovery subset selected from the full cohort (asthma n = 8; control n = 8). Subset selection used stratified sampling by age and sex to minimise baseline imbalance, and only samples with adequate plasma volume and acceptable pre-analytical quality (e.g., no gross haemolysis) were eligible (Supplementary Table S1). Lipidomics acquisition was performed on a Thermo Vanquish Horizon UHPLC system coupled to a Q Exactive HF-X Orbitrap mass spectrometer. Separation used an Accucore C30 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm, 2.6 μm) at 40 °C with a flow rate of 0.40 mL/min and 2 µL injection volume. Mobile phase A was 10 mM ammonium acetate in acetonitrile: water (1:1, v/v) with 0.1% formic acid; mobile phase B was 2 mM ammonium acetate in acetonitrile: isopropanol: water (10:88:2, v/v/v) with 0.02% formic acid. Data were acquired in positive/negative electrospray ionisation with data-dependent MS/MS, scan range m/z 200–2000, spray voltage + 3000/−3000 V, sheath gas 60 arb, auxiliary gas 20 arb, and source temperature 370 °C; stepped normalised collision energy was 20/40/60. A pooled quality-control (QC) sample was injected periodically across the run to monitor analytical stability.
sections.lipid identification and data processing: Raw LC–MS data were processed in LipidSearch (Thermo Scientific) for baseline filtering, peak detection, alignment, and lipid identification by matching accurate precursor mass and MS/MS spectra against the database (mass error < 10 ppm). When multiple candidates were present, the annotation with the highest MS/MS match score was retained. Isotope-labelled internal standards were added to each sample before extraction and monitored across the analytical batch in both positive and negative ionisation modes to assess extraction/injection consistency and instrument stability. The workflow included three distinct isotope-labelled internal standard substances; because the dataset records signals separately by ionisation polarity, some standards appeared as separate polarity-dependent entries. In this untargeted discovery setting, these internal standards were used for process and instrument monitoring rather than for absolute quantitative calibration. Lipid class assignment followed the internationally adopted LIPID MAPS comprehensive classification system, and identified lipids were grouped into standard lipid categories/classes for downstream summaries (e.g., glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, glycerolipids, sterol lipids, and fatty acyls). Quality-control (QC) injections were used to monitor analytical stability across the run and to check for signal drift. Peak intensities were log-transformed prior to multivariate analyses. Principal component analysis (PCA) and heatmap visualisation were used to assess group separation and QC clustering.
sections.pathway enrichment analysis: For pathway analysis, differential lipid sets (upregulated and downregulated analysed separately) were mapped to KEGG entries where available and tested for over-representation using a hypergeometric (equivalent Fisher’s exact) framework against the background of all annotated lipids detected in the discovery dataset. We report enrichment ratio and nominal P values, consistent with the “ P _value” displayed in the enrichment bubble plots (no adjusted P threshold was used for pathway filtering in the current presentation). Because lipid-to-KEGG mapping coverage is incomplete and only a subset of confidently annotated lipids can be mapped, enrichment results are presented strictly as exploratory functional context and should not be interpreted as evidence of pathway activation or pathway-level specificity.
sections.differential lipid and il-33\u2013anchor: Differential lipids between asthma and controls in the discovery subset were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. P values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR). Lipids with FDR < 0.05 were considered significant; effect sizes were summarised as log2 fold change. Differential lipids were summarised by lipid class (e.g., glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids, glycerolipids, sterol lipids, fatty acyls). To connect lipid alterations to circulating IL-33, correlations between IL-33 and differential lipids were evaluated using Spearman rank correlation. IL-33–positively and –negatively associated lipid patterns were defined based on the direction of association. KEGG over-representation analyses for relevant lipid sets were conducted as described in the ‘Pathway enrichment analysis’ section.
sections.statistical analysis: Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD and categorical variables as counts/percentages. Between-group comparisons used Student’s t test for approximately normally distributed variables and the Mann–Whitney U test otherwise; categorical variables were compared using the χ^2 test or Fisher’s exact test as appropriate. IL-33 and skewed inflammatory markers (FeNO, total IgE, eosinophil count) were log-transformed for regression analyses when indicated by distributional assessment. In the full cohort ( n = 120), associations between circulating IL-33 and clinical outcomes were evaluated treating IL-33 as a continuous exposure. Multivariable linear regression models were fitted separately for each outcome: Outcome ~ lnIL33_c + Age_c + (lnIL33_c×Age_c) + Sex + BMI + Group, where lnIL33_c and Age_c denote mean-centered ln(IL-33) and age, respectively, and Group was coded 0 = control and 1 = asthma. The interaction term tested age-dependent heterogeneity of the IL-33 association. Model fit was summarised using adjusted R^2 and overall model P values (Table 2 ). sections.participant characteristics: A total of 120 children were enrolled (healthy controls, n = 60; asthma, n = 60). Baseline age, sex distribution, and BMI were comparable between groups (all P > 0.05; Table 1 ). In contrast, children with asthma demonstrated marked functional impairment and higher type 2 inflammatory burden, with lower spirometric indices (FEV1, FEV1/FVC, and PEF; all P < 0.001) and higher blood eosinophil counts, total IgE, and FeNO (all P < 0.001; Table 1 ). Circulating IL-33 levels were significantly elevated in the asthma group (107.1 ± 38.5 vs. 52.4 ± 21.6 pg/mL; P < 0.001; Table 1 ). In the lipidomics discovery subset (asthma n = 8; control n = 8), age, sex, and BMI remained balanced (all P > 0.05), while lung function indices, type 2 markers, and IL-33 differed in the same direction as the full cohort (all P < 0.001; Supplementary Table S1).
sections.circulating il-33 is elevated in paediat: Circulating IL-33 was significantly higher in children with asthma than in healthy controls (Fig. 1 A; Table 1 ). Treating IL-33 as a continuous measure across the cohort, IL-33 showed consistent inverse associations with objective lung function indices, including FEV1 ( r = − 0.6522), FEV1/FVC ( r = − 0.5849), and PEF ( r = − 0.6825) (all P < 0.001; Fig. 2 ). Conversely, IL-33 correlated positively with type 2 inflammatory markers, including eosinophil counts ( r = 0.5340), total IgE ( r = 0.5827), and FeNO ( r = 0.6224) (all P < 0.001; Fig. 3 ). Correlation coefficients (r) and corresponding P values are shown in each panel, demonstrating significant positive associations (all P < 0.001) To evaluate whether these relationships persisted after accounting for potential confounding, we fitted multivariable linear regression models for each outcome in the full cohort, including mean-centred ln(IL-33), age, sex, BMI and group status, and an Age×ln(IL-33) interaction. In these models, ln(IL-33) showed significant adjusted associations with each lung function and inflammatory outcome after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, and group status (all P < 0.05; Table 2 ), whereas the Age×ln(IL-33) interaction term was not significant ( P = 0.13–0.71 across outcomes; Table 2 ), suggesting no strong evidence of age-dependent heterogeneity within the studied age range. Although these adjusted associations were statistically significant, the regression coefficients were numerically modest and should not be interpreted as indicating large per-unit clinical effects.
sections.roc analysis shows case\u2013control dis: We next evaluated the extent to which circulating IL-33 separated asthma and control groups within this study cohort. IL-33 achieved an AUC of 0.92 with an optimal cut-off of 75.4 pg/mL (sensitivity 90.0% and specificity 85.8%; Fig. 1 B), indicating substantial case–control discrimination within this paediatric case–control dataset. However, these ROC results should not be interpreted as evidence of validated clinical diagnostic performance.
sections.global lipidomic profiles and differenti: To characterise plasma lipid differences accompanying paediatric asthma, we profiled plasma lipids in the exploratory discovery subset ( n = 16). Unsupervised PCA suggested group separation between asthma and control samples along PC1 (19.50%) and PC2 (15.90%), while pooled QC samples clustered centrally, supporting analytical stability (Fig. 4 A). However, given the very small sample size, sampling effects cannot be excluded and the observed separation should be interpreted cautiously. Differential lipid analysis identified a multi-class case–control difference pattern (Fig. 4 B–C). Class composition analysis indicated that glycerophospholipids dominated the differential feature set (66.67%), followed by sphingolipids (18.1%) and glycerolipids (10.95%), with smaller contributions from sterol lipids (2.38%) and fatty acyls (1.9%) (Fig. 4 D). These findings suggest that glycerophospholipid-enriched differences may be present in the asthma-associated plasma lipidome in this exploratory discovery subset. sections.il-33\u2013anchored lipid patterns and p: To connect the discovery lipid signature to circulating IL-33, we treated plasma IL-33 as a continuous variable and performed Spearman correlation analysis between IL-33 concentrations and the differential lipid species identified in the matched discovery subset. This exploratory analysis identified two provisional IL-33–anchored lipid patterns in the small discovery subset (Fig. 5 . A). The IL-33–positive pattern was mainly represented by glycerophospholipid- and cardiolipin-related species, with representative PE, PC, PS, and CL lipids showing moderate-to-strong positive correlations with IL-33. In contrast, the IL-33–negative pattern included several sphingolipid species, particularly sphingomyelins, among the more prominent inversely correlated features. Correlation magnitudes spanned approximately ρ ≈ 0.56–0.88 for positive associations and ρ ≈ −0.54 to − 0.87 for negative associations, with statistical strength reflected by the −log10( P ) scale (Fig. 5 . A). Sample-level Z-score heatmapping showed direction-consistent abundance differences across samples (Fig. 5 . B), although the very small sample size means that these patterns should be interpreted cautiously and regarded as exploratory rather than stable pattern structure. Fig. 5 IL-33–anchored lipid patterns and exploratory pathway context in the discovery lipidomics subset. A Spearman correlation heatmap between plasma IL-33 and differential lipid species in the discovery subset, ordered by correlation direction and magnitude; colour indicates the correlation coefficient and significance is represented by −log10(P). B Z-score heatmap of IL-33-anchored differential lipids across individual samples, demonstrating direction-consistent abundance differences, with higher abundance of IL-33-positive pattern lipids in asthma and relative enrichment of IL-33-negative pattern lipids in controls. C KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of IL-33-related upregulated and downregulated differential lipid sets (derived from differential lipids that were also directionally associated with IL-33). D KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the global case–control upregulated and downregulated differential lipid sets (asthma vs control), providing broader exploratory metabolic context. In ( C ) and ( D ), dot size reflects the number of mapped lipids and colour denotes pathway P value; the x-axis indicates enrichment ratio. Abbreviations: IL-33, interleukin-33; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes We next contextualised these findings using a two-layer pathway enrichment strategy that separates the global asthma-associated lipid perturbation from the IL-33–anchored component. First, we performed KEGG enrichment on the entire set of case–control differential lipids (asthma vs. control), analysing upregulated and downregulated lipids separately to provide a broad map of metabolic alterations in the discovery subset (Fig. 5 . D). In this global view, the upregulated lipids were primarily linked to systemic lipid handling and energy-related programmes (e.g., cholesterol metabolism, fat digestion and absorption, regulation of lipolysis in adipocytes, lipid and atherosclerosis, with additional signals involving thermogenesis/insulin resistance and glycerolipid metabolism), consistent with widespread remodeling of lipid transport and utilisation in asthma. The downregulated global lipid set showed stronger connections to membrane lipid organisation and inflammatory mediator biology, with enrichment for glycerophospholipid metabolism and sphingolipid-related pathways, alongside fatty-acid–linked annotations (e.g., arachidonic acid metabolism, linoleic/α-linolenic acid metabolism) and cell-death/clearance-related terms (e.g., necroptosis, efferocytosis) (Fig. 5 . D). Collectively, these results outline the overall landscape of lipid dysregulation distinguishing asthma from health in the discovery subset. Second, to isolate the pathway signal most plausibly aligned with IL-33 biology, we repeated KEGG enrichment focusing only on IL-33–related differential lipids (i.e., those differential lipids that were also directionally associated with IL-33), again stratified into IL-33–related upregulated and downregulated subsets (Fig. 5 . C). Compared with the global enrichment, the IL-33–anchored enrichment profile appeared more focused, highlighting annotations broadly related to membrane-lipid remodeling and lipid-mediator signalling. Notably, IL-33–related downregulated lipids remained prominently enriched for glycerophospholipid metabolism and sphingolipid metabolism/sphingolipid signalling, together with fatty-acid mediator pathways (e.g., arachidonic acid metabolism) and immune/stress-associated processes (e.g., efferocytosis and necroptosis) (Fig. 5 . C). This pattern provides exploratory functional context consistent with membrane-lipid remodeling and lipid-signalling alterations, but does not establish pathway specificity, activity, or directionality. Importantly, decreases in intact glycerophospholipid species should not be over-interpreted as reduced pathway “activity,” as they may also reflect increased turnover and remodeling flux under inflammatory or cellular stress conditions. Taken together, the correlation-defined lipid patterns (Fig. 5 . A–B) and the two-layer enrichment framework (Fig. 5 . C–D) provide exploratory, hypothesis-generating context suggesting that asthma in this discovery subset may involve broad lipidomic differences, while the IL-33–anchored component may be related to membrane-lipid-associated features. Within the constraints of limited lipid-to-KEGG mapping and the small exploratory sample size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously as provisional functional context rather than stable mechanistic structure, but they provide a rationale for exploratory derivation of the IL-33–linked composite readout (IL-33–lipid score) evaluated in subsequent analyses.
sections.an exploratory il-33\u2013linked lipid s: To translate the IL-33–anchored lipid pattern into an interpretable quantitative readout, we constructed an exploratory IL-33–linked lipid score in the discovery subset. The score was significantly higher in asthma than in controls (Fig. 6 A) and tracked residualised IL-33 at the individual level after removing group effects ( r = 0.53, P = 0.04; Fig. 6 B). Analyses were performed in the lipidomics discovery subset (asthma n =8; controls n =8). A Box-and-whisker plots show the IL-33–linked lipid score is higher in asthma than in controls ( P <0.01). Shaded band indicates the 95% confidence interval of the fitted trend. D Internal validation by leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) yielded similarly high internally resampled performance estimates (cut-off=0.152; AUC=0.97; sensitivity=90.3%; specificity=89.8%), although these do not substitute for external validation We next evaluated the extent to which the IL-33-linked lipid score separated asthma and control groups within the discovery subset. The score showed high apparent discriminatory performance within this small discovery subset (AUC = 0.96; sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 87.8%; Fig. 6 C); however, because the score was derived and evaluated in the same dataset, these estimates are likely optimistic and should not be interpreted as evidence of validated performance. When assessed using an internal validation approach, the internally resampled performance estimates remained high (AUC = 0.97; sensitivity 90.3%, specificity 89.8%; Fig. 6 D), although this does not substitute for external validation and should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size. Finally, to test whether the lipid score related to clinically meaningful disease burden beyond case–control status, we correlated residualised score values with residualised clinical outcomes (within-group mean-centering). Residualised score was inversely associated with residualised lung function measures, including FEV1 ( r = − 0.76, P = 9.3 × 10^−4), FEV1/FVC ( r = − 0.90, P < 0.05), and PEF ( r = − 0.89, P < 0.05) (Fig. 7 ). Conversely, residualised score correlated positively with residualised type 2 markers, including eosinophil counts ( r = 0.89, P = 6.7 × 10^−5), total IgE ( r = 0.59, P = 0.02), and FeNO ( r = 0.71, P = 2.9 × 10^−3) (Fig. 8 ). Collectively, these exploratory analyses suggest that the IL-33-linked lipid score may reflect plasma lipid differences associated with airflow limitation and type 2 inflammatory burden in this discovery setting.
