sections.discussion: In this paediatric case–control study ( n = 120), circulating IL-33 was elevated in children with asthma compared with healthy controls and was associated with objective measures of disease burden. Across the cohort, higher IL-33 levels were associated with worse airflow limitation (lower FEV1, FEV1/FVC, and PEF) and greater type 2 inflammatory burden (higher blood eosinophils, total IgE, and FeNO). IL-33 also showed substantial case–control discrimination within this dataset (AUC 0.92; cut-off 75.4 pg/mL), although this should not be interpreted as validated clinical diagnostic performance. In the exploratory lipidomics discovery subset ( n = 16; 8 asthma/8 controls), untargeted profiling suggested group separation and identified glycerophospholipid-enriched differential lipid differences. Exploratory IL-33-anchored analyses identified provisional lipid patterns, and an exploratory IL-33-linked score showed high apparent discrimination within the discovery setting and direction-consistent associations with lung function and type 2 markers after residualization for group status. Collectively, these findings support adjusted cross-sectional associations and exploratory lipidomic context rather than independent biological effects or validated biomarker performance. These findings also extend our group’s earlier preliminary work that used IL-33 stratification within paediatric asthma to interrogate IL-33–linked molecular programmes. The present manuscript extends our preliminary within-asthma work by showing, within a larger paediatric case–control cohort, that circulating IL-33 is associated with objective spirometric impairment and T2 inflammatory burden, and by providing an exploratory IL-33-anchored lipid pattern/score framework for future validation. Clinical management of paediatric asthma increasingly integrates biomarkers of type 2 inflammation (blood eosinophils, FeNO, and IgE) because they inform phenotyping and risk stratification [ 5 – 7 , 24 ]. Yet these biomarkers are downstream readouts and may be discordant with lung-function impairment and symptom control in individual patients. Consistent with a mechanistic framework in which epithelial alarmins initiate and amplify type 2 pathways, IL-33 sits upstream of canonical type 2 cascades and has been proposed as a candidate indicator of disease activity [ 8 , 9 ]. In our cohort—enrolled at first diagnosis, ICS-naïve at sampling, and assessed outside acute exacerbations—IL-33 tracked both physiological impairment and systemic type 2 burden, suggesting that circulating IL-33 is associated with clinically relevant measures of disease burden in this case–control cohort, alongside traditional downstream biomarkers. These findings should therefore be interpreted primarily as evidence of directionally consistent adjusted associations, rather than as demonstrating large effect sizes or immediate clinical usefulness at the individual-patient level. Human therapeutic data strengthen the biological plausibility of this axis. In adults with moderate-to-severe asthma, interleukin-33 blockade with itepekimab reduced loss-of-control events and improved lung function, and ST2 (IL1RL1) blockade with astegolimab reduced exacerbations across a broad severe-asthma population [ 13 , 14 ]. Although these trials were conducted in adults, they provide causal evidence that targeting the IL-33/ST2 pathway can modify asthma outcomes, supporting the interpretation that the associations observed here reflect a clinically meaningful pathway rather than an epiphenomenon. The ROC findings for IL-33 in our case–control cohort should therefore be interpreted cautiously as reflecting group separation under controlled conditions within this dataset, rather than as evidence of validated clinical diagnostic performance or as a stand-alone diagnostic test. Our results align with paediatric studies reporting elevated serum IL-33, correlations with spirometric obstruction, and moderate diagnostic accuracy that improves when combined with lung-function parameters and FeNO [ 15 ]. A common concern in paediatric biomarker studies is whether associations are modified by developmental stage. We explicitly tested Age×IL-33 interaction terms in multivariable models and did not observe strong evidence of age-dependent heterogeneity within the 6–12-year range. This suggests that, in this clinically important window, the relationship between IL-33 and disease-burden metrics is directionally stable. However, cross-sectional data cannot establish intra-individual stability or responsiveness to changes in disease activity. Longitudinal sampling across growth trajectories—and across stable and exacerbation states—will be essential to determine whether IL-33 behaves primarily as a state marker, a trait marker, or both. A major contribution of this work is the integration of IL-33 with systemic lipidomic context. Lipidomics studies in asthma have implicated glycerophospholipid and sphingolipid perturbations in plasma and airway-derived samples, and airway lipidomic profiling can stratify asthma phenotypes across severity spectra [ 19 , 20 , 25 ]. In our discovery subset, differential lipids were dominated by glycerophospholipids, consistent with the concept that membrane remodelling is a prominent systemic feature of asthma. Phospholipids influence membrane curvature, vesicular trafficking and receptor microdomain organization, thereby shaping epithelial barrier integrity and immune-cell activation thresholds. Moreover, phospholipid metabolism and membrane homeostasis are actively reprogrammed during innate immune activation. The IL-33-positive pattern included glycerophospholipid- and cardiolipin-related features. Cardiolipin is a mitochondria-enriched phospholipid involved in oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial stress responses, and prior studies have implicated cardiolipin in innate immune regulation and immunometabolism [ 22 , 26 , 27 ]. In the present exploratory dataset, the presence of cardiolipin-related features among IL-33-associated lipids raises a tentative hypothesis that IL-33-high states may coincide with mitochondrial- or membrane-related remodeling; however, these data do not permit firm mechanistic inference. Accordingly, any link between IL-33 and mitochondrial adaptation should be regarded as provisional and hypothesis-generating rather than established by the current study. This tentative interpretation is broadly consistent with prior literature suggesting that IL-33 can influence immune-cell metabolic programmes [ 28 , 29 ], although the present study was not designed to test such mechanisms directly. Given the small size of the discovery subset, the observed lipid patterns should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than as definitive evidence of stable mechanistic patterns. Conversely, the IL-33–negative pattern was enriched for sphingomyelins. Sphingolipids regulate membrane raft structure, receptor clustering and inflammatory signalling; dysregulated sphingolipid pathways have been implicated in asthma pathobiology, and paediatric metabolomic epidemiology links sphingolipid subclasses to childhood asthma traits and lung function [ 30 , 31 ]. The inverse association between IL-33 and multiple sphingomyelins in our discovery subset raises the hypothesis that IL-33–high states may coincide with altered lipid-raft composition or compensatory changes in sphingolipid handling. While our enrichment analyses are hypothesis-generating, the convergence on glycerophospholipid-, sphingolipid-, and arachidonic-acid-related annotations provides exploratory functional context that is broadly consistent with membrane-lipid remodeling, but should not be over-interpreted as pathway-level specificity. Accordingly, the present lipidomic findings are better viewed as provisional functional context than as definitive evidence of pathway-selective remodeling or signaling architecture. To translate the IL-33–anchored lipid signal into an interpretable readout, we constructed a six-lipid IL-33–linked score spanning triglyceride, cardiolipin and glycerophospholipid species. Composite biomarker strategies can improve robustness when single markers are biologically meaningful but noisy, by summarizing coordinated molecular programs into a compact measure and reducing multiple-testing burden. In our discovery subset, the score separated asthma from controls and correlated with residualized IL-33. Importantly, because score components were derived from case–control differential lipids and the subset size was limited, we treated score–clinical associations as exploratory and used residualization for group status to mitigate group-driven confounding. The direction-consistent associations between residualized score and residualized lung function and type 2 markers suggest that the score may reflect disease-burden-related molecular variation in this exploratory discovery setting, rather than functioning solely as a classifier. Overall, our findings indicate that circulating IL-33 is elevated in paediatric asthma and is associated with objective measures of airflow limitation and systemic type 2 inflammatory burden in this case–control cohort. The accompanying lipidomic analyses further suggest that higher IL-33 levels co-occur with exploratory plasma lipid differences, summarised in the discovery setting by an exploratory IL-33-linked lipid score. However, these findings should be interpreted as adjusted associations observed within a cross-sectional case–control design, rather than as evidence of clinical, longitudinal, or monitoring biomarker performance. Longitudinal studies and external validation cohorts will be required to determine the reproducibility, temporal stability, and potential translational relevance of these observations. Strengths of this study include a well-characterized clinical cohort spanning spirometric and type 2 inflammatory domains, and a design that minimized major therapy confounding by enrolling children at first diagnosis without ICS at sampling and outside acute exacerbations. The lipidomics workflow included pooled QC monitoring and an IL-33–anchored analytic strategy that moved beyond case–control differences to identify direction-consistent patterns and pathway context. Our modelling treated IL-33 as a continuous exposure, adjusted for key covariates, and explicitly tested age interaction, addressing frequent reviewer concerns.
sections.study limitations: This study is cross-sectional and single-centre, which precludes causal inference and does not allow assessment of within-child repeatability, temporal stability, treatment responsiveness, or prognostic performance of circulating IL-33. Residual confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded despite adjustment for key covariates, including age, sex, BMI, and group status. The lipidomics component was exploratory and conducted in a small discovery subset ( n = 16; 8 asthma, 8 controls), limiting statistical power and increasing the risk of effect-size inflation, sampling effects, instability of correlation-defined IL-33–linked lipid patterns, and optimistic performance estimates for the composite score even under internal validation. Lipid-to-KEGG mapping coverage is incomplete; enrichment results should therefore be interpreted as exploratory functional context rather than evidence of pathway activation or pathway-level specificity.
sections.recommendations for future research: Replication in larger, multi-centre paediatric cohorts is needed, with phenotype-stratified analyses to test generalisability across asthma subtypes. Targeted quantification should be used to verify the candidate lipids and the parsimonious score with pre-specified modelling and calibration assessment. Longitudinal sampling should evaluate within-child tracking, treatment responsiveness, exacerbation risk, and lung function trajectories, and quantify incremental value beyond established markers (eosinophils, IgE, spirometry). Mechanistic studies should test whether IL-33 signalling can induce membrane-lipid remodelling consistent with the observed pattern.
sections.conclusion_1: In this paediatric case–control cohort, circulating IL-33 was elevated in children with asthma and was significantly associated with objective airflow limitation and systemic type 2 inflammatory burden. Higher IL-33 levels also co-occurred with exploratory plasma lipid differences, including glycerophospholipid/cardiolipin-enriched positive associations and sphingomyelin-enriched negative associations. An exploratory IL-33-linked lipid score summarised this pattern into a compact readout that was associated with clinical burden in the discovery setting. These findings should be interpreted as adjusted associations observed within a cross-sectional case–control design. They do not establish causality, temporal stability, treatment responsiveness, or additive value beyond established biomarkers, and they require longitudinal and external validation before any broader biomarker or clinical application can be considered.

title: Economic Impact of Timely Systemic Treatment of Psoriatic Disease in Comorbidity Risk Reduction: Literature Review and (Early) Economic Assessment
abstract: Introduction Psoriatic disease, including psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, is associated with increased risk of comorbidities (cardiovascular disease, mental health disorders, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity), placing substantial burden on patients and health systems. We aimed to quantify the lifetime economic burden of these four comorbidities in populations with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. We subsequently estimated the potential comorbidity-related gross cost offsets from timely systemic therapy across three diverse country settings (Denmark, the USA and Vietnam). Methods We conducted a literature review to identify data on prevalence, comorbidity risk, treatment-associated risk reduction and cost inputs, followed by development of a static cohort-based economic model from a societal perspective. The model compared untreated/undertreated moderate-to-severe psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis; and systemic treatment scenarios (conventional systemic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs [csDMARDs]; biologic DMARDs [bDMARDs]; and targeted synthetic DMARDs [tsDMARDs]) over a lifetime horizon in Denmark, the USA and Vietnam, reporting total comorbidity cost offsets across direct (healthcare) and indirect (societal) costs. Results Systemic treatment reduced lifetime comorbidity-related direct and societal costs across settings. In the USA, patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis incurred annual direct costs of approximately 4.6 billion USD (indirect 0.6 billion USD), and untreated lifetime burden of about 153.0 billion USD. Treating all patients with bDMARDs yielded an estimated cost offset of 62.9 billion USD in the direct costs and an offset of 8.1 billion USD in the societal costs compared with a fully undertreated population. Equivalent analyses in Denmark and Vietnam reflected similar effects on comorbidity-related costs. The model shows that early systemic therapy yields substantial effect on the direct and societal costs via reduced comorbidity incidence. Conclusions Timely and efficacious systemic treatment of psoriatic disease can significantly reduce lifetime economic burden of comorbidities across diverse healthcare settings. These findings underscore the value of early, proactive management of psoriatic disease and highlight the need for further cost-effectiveness research, including treatment uptake and real-world comorbidity prevention. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s13555-026-01814-x.

sections.key summary points: Why carry out this study? Psoriatic disease increases the risk of several comorbidities, leading to substantial long-term economic burden. The potential cost impact of systemic treatments on reducing comorbidity risk remains unclear. What did the study ask?/What was the hypothesis of the study? Could timely systemic treatment (conventional systemic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs [csDMARDs]; biologic DMARDs [bDMARDs]; and targeted synthetic DMARDs [tsDMARDs]) reduce the lifetime comorbidity-related economic burden in moderate-to-severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis compared with topical/no treatment? What was learned from the study? Systemic therapies, particularly bDMARDs, were estimated to offset comorbidity-related costs by approximately 34–48% across countries. However, the findings need to be interpreted considering the limitations of the model. What has been learned from the study? Systemic treatment may reduce considerable comorbidity-related economic burden, benefiting both patients and healthcare systems. Delays due to treatment ladder requirements may increase comorbidity risk and associated costs, underscoring the importance of timely and improved access to systemic therapies.
sections.introduction_1: Psoriatic disease is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory condition encompassing psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, which share systemic pathogenic pathways [ 1 ]. Approximately 30% of patients with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, underscoring the close clinical relationship between cutaneous and musculoskeletal involvement [ 2 ]. As diagnosis and surveillance improve, global psoriatic disease incidence continues to rise, having increased by an estimated 26.5% between 1990 and 2019 [ 3 – 5 ], revealing a growing burden for patients and health systems. Psoriatic disease is associated with elevated risks of several comorbidities, including cardiovascular disease (CVD) [ 6 , 7 ]; mental health disorders (MHDs) encompassing depression, anxiety and suicidality [ 8 – 10 ]; type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [ 11 ]; and obesity [ 12 ], each compounding morbidity, mortality and costs [ 13 – 21 ]. In the USA, patients with psoriasis and a comorbidity experience roughly double the hospital use and costs of non-comorbid patients [ 22 ]; those with both psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis incur about 9900 USD in additional annual costs, while those with CVD add 8275 USD annually [ 23 ]. Moreover, patients with psoriatic disease face higher comorbidity-related costs than non-psoriatic disease populations [ 24 ]. Beyond financial burden, psoriatic disease and its comorbidities reduce quality of life, work ability and mental well-being. Psoriatic disease and some of its comorbidities share inflammatory pathways, including tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin (IL)-17, IL-23 and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK–STAT) signalling, that drive cutaneous and systemic manifestations [ 25 , 26 ]. Modern biologics and JAK inhibitors target components of these pathways [ 26 – 28 ], while conventional systemics such as methotrexate exert broader immunomodulatory effects that reduce overall inflammatory activity [ 29 , 30 ]. Effective systemic treatment may lower systemic inflammatory load, providing a biologically plausible basis for reduced risks of cardiovascular, metabolic and mental health comorbidities observed in emerging evidence. Recent studies suggest that timely systemic therapy for moderate-to-severe psoriasis can lower risks of developing psoriatic arthritis [ 31 ], CVD [ 32 , 33 ], MHDs [ 34 , 35 ], T2DM [ 34 ] and obesity [ 36 ]. Here, ‘timely’ refers to initiating appropriate systemic therapy early in the disease course, before prolonged inflammation increases likelihood of irreversible joint damage and comorbidities. Consistent with this, international guidelines recommend early detection and management of comorbidities [ 13 , 14 , 37 ]. Previous studies have examined the overall economic burden of psoriatic disease [ 24 , 38 – 42 ], but few have directly assessed the economic impact of systemic treatment on psoriatic disease-related comorbidities. This study quantifies the potential effect of timely systemic treatment on the cost of specific comorbidities in psoriatic disease. We conducted [ 1 ] a literature review to collect data on epidemiology and costs of four comorbidities (CVD, MHDs, T2DM and obesity) and [ 2 ] an economic model estimating lifetime comorbidity costs among patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis in Denmark, the USA and Vietnam. The model evaluates the potential offset in comorbidity-related gross costs that timely treatment with one of three systemic therapy classes could achieve, through a reduction in comorbidity risks. Improving access to effective systemic therapies remains a key priority, as delays in appropriate treatment contribute to preventable burden. Quantifying downstream comorbidity impacts can inform resource allocation, strengthen arguments for early intervention and support efforts to reduce global disparities in psoriatic disease care.
sections.methods_1: This study combined a literature review with a static economic burden model. A protocol was defined a priori, and the review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, including a flow diagram, two-stage study selection and comprehensive referencing. The review and model were developed iteratively to allow available data to inform model structure and ensure methodological transparency and reproducibility.
sections.literature review: A structured, protocol-driven targeted literature review (TLR) was conducted to identify published and grey literature relevant to comorbidity burden and model input parameters in psoriatic disease. The search strategy was predefined and implemented primarily in Embase, with supplementary searches conducted via Google to capture grey literature and additional relevant sources. Eligibility criteria were prospectively defined within the study protocol and refined as appropriate for each model variable. All retrieved records underwent systematic screening by one reviewer, with independent random quality checks performed by a second reviewer to ensure consistency and minimize selection bias. Any discrepancies were resolved through consensus discussion. Data were extracted in a standardized extraction grid to ensure consistency in capturing study characteristics and parameter estimates. Identified evidence was assessed for methodological quality, relevance and applicability to the predefined modelling objectives. While all eligible sources were reviewed, final parameter selection followed predefined prioritization criteria, emphasizing recency, methodological robustness, demographic comparability to the target population, and country-specific relevance where applicable. In instances where direct evidence was unavailable, the most clinically and methodologically comparable relative risk or cost estimates were applied using a structured hierarchy of evidence to preserve internal consistency across comorbidity risks, treatment effects and economic parameters. The target population was defined as adults with moderate-to-severe psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis, representing individuals at elevated risk of comorbidities and the primary candidates for systemic therapy [ 13 , 37 , 43 ]. Four key variable domains guided the structured evidence search: Prevalence of moderate-to-severe psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis. Risk estimates for comorbidities of interest (CVD, T2DM, MHDs and obesity). Impact of treatment classes of different disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) (conventional synthetic DMARDs [csDMARDs], biologic DMARDs [bDMARDs] and targeted synthetic DMARDs [tsDMARDs]) on comorbidity risk reduction. Direct and indirect costs associated with the specified comorbidities in the defined population. Additional model inputs and expanded methodological details, including parameter definitions and evidence selection procedures, are described in the study protocol provided in the electronic Supplementary Materials.
sections.ethical considerations and authorship: No human subjects or animals were involved; ethical approval was not required. The study was conceptually informed by patient advocacy stakeholders. All sources are cited, Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) standards (flowchart and checklist) were followed and funding, conflicts of interest and author contributions (per ICMJE criteria) are disclosed.
sections.literature review findings: The searches identified 600 records, with 151 meeting inclusion criteria. Table 1 summarizes the number of records identified and included by variable. Additional records were identified through ad hoc searches to collect model input data representing life expectancies and demographics for the populations. Denmark, the USA and Vietnam were selected for the economic assessment on the basis of the availability of direct and indirect cost data for moderate-to-severe psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis and regional comorbidity risk data. Literature review results, the PRISMA diagram and the data extraction grid are available in the electronic Supplementary Materials. sections.economic model results: Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis prevalence for each country was estimated by applying prevalence rates to 2025 populations, followed by proportions with moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Comorbidity prevalence was calculated using comorbidity-specific rates (local or proxy). A one-time sustained relative risk reduction reflected systemic treatment effects. Direct (healthcare) and indirect (societal, captured as productivity loss) costs were estimated separately for systemic and non-systemic/no treatment groups. The annual cost reduction represents the difference between the estimates for these groups. Lifetime comorbidity-related cost reduction was calculated by multiplying the annual cost reduction by the remaining life expectancy. Survival gains from reduced comorbidity prevalence were not modelled to avoid added uncertainty.
sections.key model assumptions: Treatment effects were assumed to produce immediate and sustained reductions in comorbidity prevalence over the lifetime horizon, with full adherence to therapy and no contraindications or adverse events. Effects for csDMARDs, bDMARDs and tsDMARDs were estimated from available data on specific treatments within each class and treated as representative averages. Treatment effects on the risks were assumed equal across psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis and consistent across countries. No discontinuation or switching between systemic treatments was modelled; instead, each treatment type was assumed to apply uniformly to all patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis. Consequently, the model does not incorporate treatment mix within countries. With that, comorbidity-related gross cost offsets calculations were performed assuming the entire patient population would be given the specific DMARD being considered. This is not a realistic real-world scenario but provides an estimate of the magnitude of the impact of treatment on comorbidity-related costs.
sections.model findings: denmark: Our calculations estimated that annual direct and indirect costs for the four comorbidities among Danish patients with psoriasis were 24.0 million euros and 30.9 million euros, corresponding to a 29-year burden of 1.4 billion euros. For psoriatic arthritis, annual costs were 58.5 million euros (direct) and 80.4 million euros (indirect), totalling 3.5 billion euros. Systemic treatment substantially reduced this comorbidity-related burden. Treating all patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis with bDMARDs yielded lifetime gross cost offsets of 283.5 million euros (direct) and 330.6 million euros (indirect), a 43.9% offset of the comorbidity-related cost. For psoriatic arthritis, 1.2 billion euros represented a 34.4% offset. The average direct and indirect lifetime cost offsets per comorbid patient were 35,753 € and 43,199 €, respectively. The effect of DMARDs on comorbidity costs in Denmark was lower for csDMARDs compared with bDMARDs (Table 6 ). sections.discussion: This study provides an assessment of how timely and efficacious systemic treatment for psoriatic disease could reduce the economic burden of the four comorbidities studied. Our model synthesized evidence on psoriatic disease comorbidity burden and showed that a proportion of lifetime costs may be preventable through timely systemic therapy, thus potentially offsetting comorbidity-related direct and societal gross cost, depending on the setting. The analysis focused on moderate-to-severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, which are both well-studied and primary candidates for systemic therapy. The effects on the comorbidity-related costs were estimated by comparing an undertreated population with one receiving full systemic treatment; real-world treatment mixes would yield intermediate results. The three modelled countries (Denmark, the USA and Vietnam) reflected diverse health economic contexts. Across all examples, systemic therapy reduced comorbidity-related costs, with bDMARDs showing the greatest effect on comorbidity costs, followed by tsDMARDs and csDMARDs. Some country-specific observations emerged: Denmark’s high societal burden reflects comprehensive national registers and a publicly financed healthcare that reduces the burden on patients; in the USA, direct costs dominate, suggesting that data sources under-report productivity loss, underestimating indirect burden. High out-of-pocket costs highlight affordability challenges in the USA among the 25 million uninsured and 21% underinsured adults [ 47 , 48 ]. Vietnam’s relatively low societal costs likely reflect data gaps; for example, evidence on caregiver burden for T2DM suggests under-reported indirect impacts [ 49 , 50 ].
sections.stakeholder perspectives: For patients, reducing comorbidity risks improves both quality and length of life. Early systemic therapy may reduce additional illnesses, lower medication needs and enhance well-being [ 39 – 41 , 51 ]. Multidisciplinary care further improves outcomes and mental health [ 52 – 54 ], while delayed or insufficient treatment can worsen morbidity and mortality [ 55 ]. For policy-makers, the findings support early, comprehensive psoriatic disease management. Although systemic therapies have upfront costs, the downstream cost reductions due to the effects of systemic treatment may offset these [ 56 ] and should be reflected in Heatlh Technology Assessment (HTA) processes. Expanding access to biosimilars [ 57 – 60 ] may further reduce treatment costs, and strengthening screening for cardiovascular, metabolic and mental health risks remains important for holistic psoriatic disease care and disease prevention.
sections.study strengths: To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the effect of systemic psoriatic disease treatment on comorbidity-related costs, due to reduced comorbidity risks. Integrating a literature review with an economic model enabled synthesis of existing evidence and projection of population-level impacts. By including multiple comorbidities, treatment types, and both direct and indirect costs, this study offers a broad view of the health and economic implications of psoriatic disease. Similar findings in other diseases, such as cardiovascular risks in sleep apnea [ 61 ], late-life depression [ 62 ] and diabetes [ 63 ], reinforce the value of early intervention.
sections.study limitations: The review, while structured, was not fully systematic, and included studies varied in quality and outcome definitions. Limited evidence on long-term treatment effects required assumptions of similar relative risk reductions across treatments and geographies, with durability over a lifetime, which may not accurately reflect real-life experiences. Most included studies were observational and cannot reliably provide causal estimates. Approximately 30% of patients with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis, so overlap between populations could affect risk estimates. The model is a simplified representation of economic benefit from systemic treatment, assuming linear, sustained treatment effects, and disease progression. The side effects of systemic treatment were not modelled. We also assume immediate onset of treatment effect, perfect adherence and sustained reductions in comorbidity risk over the entire time horizon. Real-world treatment patterns, such as delayed response, partial adherence, treatment switching or waning effect, could result in smaller or more variable reductions than those estimated here. The model therefore does not estimate real-world incremental value but rather the comorbidity-related cost offsets attributable to systemic treatment under a full-uptake scenario. Formal deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were also not conducted, as several parameters were based on pragmatic assumptions without sufficient underlying evidence to define reliable parameter distributions or plausible ranges. The model also did not account for concomitant standard preventive care commonly used in patients with psoriatic disease and cardiometabolic risk factors, including statins, antihypertensive therapy, glucose-lowering medications, weight-management interventions or structured mental health treatment. These background interventions can independently manage or prevent the comorbidities modelled and may interact with systemic psoriasis therapies in real-world care pathways. By isolating psoriasis-directed therapy effects, the analysis was intended to estimate the potential contribution of systemic treatment alone; however, excluding broader preventive management may inflate the incremental benefits attributed to systemic therapy. Taken together, these structural assumptions mean that the model should be interpreted as an exploratory scenario analysis designed to illustrate the possible scale of avoidable comorbidity burden rather than a definitive prediction of real-world cost offsets. While uncertainty intervals were not calculated, the model highlights potential underestimation of indirect costs due to data limitations. Importantly, the model and calculations are dependent on data available, such as psoriatic disease prevalence data. Differences in prevalence have been shown across multiple sources. These differences arise primarily from the use of different methodologies to assess how many people live with psoriatic disease. In the USA, for example, the second edition of the Global Psoriasis Atlas estimates 1.12% prevalence of psoriasis [ 64 ], while sources such as the National Psoriasis Foundation and Armstrong et al. (2021) estimate it at 3% [ 65 , 66 ]. It is likely that the real prevalence falls in between these sources, suggesting that the total comorbidity-related burden and gross cost offsets may be higher than we conservatively estimated using the Global Psoriasis Atlas estimate. Most of the identified evidence on treatment-associated risk offsets come from observational studies in which patients receiving systemic therapy often have more severe disease and higher baseline comorbidity risk than untreated groups. Moreover, different treatments within the same group of DMARDs show a different risk reduction estimate, and for some treatments, there is no information on whether and how they may impact comorbidities. As a result, treatment effects derived from these populations may not perfectly reflect risk profiles across the full spectrum of moderate-to-severe psoriatic disease. While this could mean that absolute risk reductions vary across subgroups, the directionality of effect is unlikely to differ, and our population-level model appropriately reflects average expected impacts under a full-uptake scenario. Generalisability of the results is limited; data inputs were derived from a small number of countries, and healthcare structures, access or population characteristics may differ elsewhere. Because lifetime cost projections accumulate effects over extended time horizons, even modest variation in baseline comorbidity prevalence can materially influence the magnitude of estimated cost offsets. In the absence of country-specific epidemiologic data, baseline comorbidity prevalence for Vietnam and Denmark was informed by proxy estimates from China and Germany, respectively, without country-specific recalibration. As a result, even small differences between the proxy and true national prevalence patterns may compound over time and affect projected economic outcomes. The findings should therefore be interpreted as model-based projections generated under stated epidemiological assumptions rather than precise forecasts of country-specific comorbidity-related cost offsets. Only four comorbidities were modelled, leaving others (e.g. hypertension, cancer and inflammatory bowel disease [IBD]) outside of scope. This analysis also did not include the costs of systemic treatments themselves, as these vary substantially across settings, may involve confidential pricing agreements and require jurisdiction-specific inputs to assess total net value. Incorporating treatment costs alongside the avoided comorbidity burden would therefore be an important next step for estimating the full economic value of systemic therapy. Finally, the model assumes 100% systemic treatment uptake with a single therapy type. It is an unrealistic but necessary simplification for early decision modelling. Future analyses incorporating actual treatment mixes, treatment costs or untreated proportions would refine these estimates for more real-world application.
sections.future research: We believe that this work provides an important first perspective on the wider impact of early systemic treatment in reducing the burden of psoriatic disease beyond the skin and joint manifestations. This is particularly relevant when there is still a lack of understanding from many physicians about the increased risk for comorbidities for people living with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Future research using state-transition or microsimulation approaches with longitudinal real-world data would help better capture disease progression, adherence patterns, competing risks, preventive care pathways and temporal changes in treatment effectiveness. Future work should use real-world longitudinal data to better quantify treatment effects on comorbidity risks and improve model accuracy. Cost-effectiveness analyses incorporating Quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and regional data are needed to evaluate long-term value. Expanding evidence in diverse populations will support localized decision-making [ 67 ].
sections.conclusions_1: Our model offers a pragmatic approach to explore the potential economic implications of comorbidity risk reduction associated with timely systemic treatment in psoriatic disease, in settings where longitudinal data remain limited. The findings suggest that timely systemic therapy may offer more than symptom control; it may be associated with reductions in psoriatic disease-related comorbidities and their related healthcare and societal costs. While the analysis relies on necessary epidemiological and structural assumptions, it indicates that systemic treatment may reduce the risk of comorbidities and translate into reduced comorbidity incidence in psoriatic disease, leading to meaningful comorbidity-related cost offsets for the health systems and society. The model development process also highlighted gaps in the available evidence. Future research is needed to strengthen the evidence on the magnitude, durability and causal nature of systemic treatment effects on comorbidity risks, and to support more refined economic evaluations incorporating real-world management patterns. While psoriatic disease remains lifelong condition, its complications may be modifiable, highlighting the importance of further investigation into the long-term burden of psoriatic disease and its comorbidities.

title: Revisiting Glycemic Control Targets: Survival Outcomes by Glycated Hemoglobin Levels Among Patients With Diabetes Under Contemporary Antidiabetic Therapy
abstract: Background Optimal glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) targets for type 2 diabetes remain controversial. Given the evolution of modern antidiabetic therapies, this study aims to reevaluate optimal glycemic targets among patients receiving contemporary glucose‐lowering treatments. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Taiwan University Hospital Integrated Medical Database, including 16 604 patients with type 2 diabetes who initiated dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 inhibitors between 2009 and 2019, with follow‐up through December 2021. Patients were categorized by long‐term mean HbA1c quintiles. Outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (including ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, cardiovascular death), renal outcomes (progression to dialysis, ≥50% estimated glomerular filtration rate decline, or doubling serum creatinine), hospitalization for heart failure, and safety outcomes. Associations were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic spline analyses. Results Compared with the third quintile as reference, the fourth (hazard ratio [HR], 1.22 [95% CI, 1.01–1.47]) and fifth quintiles (HR, 1.36 [95% CI, 1.12–1.64]) were associated with a significantly higher risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. Restricted cubic spline modeling identified significant J‐shaped relationships for both major adverse cardiovascular events and renal outcomes, with the lowest risk observed around an HbA1c of 7%. In contrast, hospitalization for heart failure risk increased linearly with rising HbA1c levels. Notably, sex differences were identified: men showed a linear decrease in cardiovascular risk with lower HbA1c, whereas women exhibited a J‐shaped relationship, indicating increased risks at both glycemic extremes. Conclusion Optimal glycemic targets among patients receiving contemporary therapies differ by outcome and sex. Individualized HbA1c management strategies are essential to balance cardiovascular and renal benefits against potential risks.

sections.what is new?: In patients with type 2 diabetes on contemporary therapies, the relationship between glycated hemoglobin and major adverse cardiovascular or renal events is J shaped, with the lowest risk around a glycated hemoglobin of 7%, whereas the risk for heart failure hospitalization increases linearly with higher glycated hemoglobin levels. Significant sex differences exist, as men demonstrate a linear decrease in cardiovascular risk with lower glycated hemoglobin, whereas women exhibit a J‐shaped relationship with increased risk at both glycemic extremes.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: These findings challenge a one‐size‐fits‐all approach to glycemic control, suggesting that optimal Hb glycated hemoglobin A1c targets should be individualized based on the specific clinical outcome being prioritized—whether it be cardiovascular events, renal protection, or heart failure prevention—and tailored according to patient sex.
sections.methods_1: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. This study was conducted and presented following the recommendations of the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines.
sections.data source: This retrospective cohort study used data derived from the National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) Integrated Medical Database. The NTUH database systematically compiles clinical information from electronic health records of all patient encounters, including outpatient consultations, emergency department visits, and hospitalizations across 10 affiliated medical institutions. These records encompass structured, semistructured, and unstructured data, such as diagnoses, prescriptions, laboratory tests, medical notes, imaging reports, and clinical examinations, stored consistently in standardized formats. Our study population was drawn specifically from patients treated at the NTUH in Taipei, Taiwan, and its Hsin‐Chu branch located in Hsinchu, Taiwan. Ethical approval for this research was obtained from the NTUH Institutional Review Board (NTUH‐REC No. 202211097RINC). Upon approval, this study was granted access to the database covering the period from 2009 to 2021. Given the anonymized nature of the extracted data, the requirement for informed consent was waived. Patients or the public did not participate in the design, implementation, reporting, or dissemination planning of this study.
sections.study cohort: We identified all patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes who received their first prescription of a DPP4 (dipeptidyl peptidase‐4) inhibitor at the NTUH and NTUH Hsin‐chu branch between October 1, 2009 and September 30, 2019 (n=30 787). DPP4 inhibitor users were selected as the primary study population because they constituted the most widely prescribed second‐line therapy in Taiwan during the study period, ensuring a robust sample size. Crucially, the established cardiovascular and renal neutrality of these agents minimizes the confounding influence of drug‐specific harm or pleiotropic effects, 6 , 7 thereby allowing for a clearer assessment of the direct impact of glycemic control itself on long‐term survival and organ protection. From this group, patients who underwent HbA1c testing at least once every 6 months over a 2‐year period were further selected for analysis (n=17 553) (Figure S1 ). The index date was defined as the 731st day following the initial prescription of a DPP4 inhibitor. Accordingly, the exposure of interest—mean HbA1c—was assessed over the 730‐day period immediately preceding the index date. Patients were excluded based on the following criteria 1 : missing demographic information (n=0), 2 age <20 years (n=5), 3 prior history of dialysis before the index date (n=484), 4 occurrence of MACE within 90 days after the index date (n=163), and 5 follow‐up period of <90 days (n=297). After applying these exclusions, a total of 16 604 patients remained eligible for analysis. For the analysis of each outcome, patients were monitored until the occurrence of the respective study outcome, death, or the date of the last medical visit recorded at NTUH or NTUH Hsin‐chu branch, or until the end of database coverage on December 31, 2021, whichever occurred first.
sections.covariate measurements: We analyzed multiple clinical and demographic variables, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, diabetes duration, baseline comorbidities, cardiovascular history, laboratory results, and concurrent medications. Comorbidities assessed included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, peripheral artery disease, carotid artery stenosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, liver diseases, and malignancy. Diabetic complications such as retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, and diabetic foot, alongside the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, were recorded to indicate diabetes severity. Historical cardiovascular events, tracked from 2009 onward, comprised acute myocardial infarction (AMI), ischemic stroke, hospitalization for heart failure (HHF), percutaneous coronary intervention, and coronary artery bypass surgery. Laboratory measurements included serum creatinine (SCr), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum urea nitrogen, potassium, uric acid, alanine aminotransferase, albumin, fasting glucose, HbA1c, cholesterol levels, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and urinary albumin‐to‐creatinine ratio. Concurrent medications were grouped into antidiabetic agents, antihypertensive drugs, antithrombotic therapies, and lipid‐lowering agents.
sections.outcome definitions: This study evaluated both efficacy and safety end points. Efficacy outcomes were classified into cardiovascular, renal, and heart failure (HF) outcomes. The cardiovascular outcomes comprised AMI, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular death, and the composite of MACE, defined as the combination of AMI, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death. AMI and ischemic stroke were identified using inpatient International Classification of Diseases ( ICD ) diagnostic codes; the accuracy of these definitions has been validated in prior studies. 8 , 9 HF outcomes specifically included HHF, cardiovascular death, and their composite end point (HHF plus cardiovascular death). Renal outcomes assessed were the progression to dialysis, a decline in eGFR by ≥50%, doubling of SCr, and a composite renal end point [collectively termed as major adverse kidney events (MAKE)]. Safety outcomes encompassed hypoglycemia, acute hyperglycemic crises (ie, diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state), fracture events, falls, all‐cause hospital admissions, and all‐cause mortality. Events such as HHF, AMI, and ischemic stroke were identified based on the inpatient diagnosis at hospital discharge. Data regarding the timing and causes of death were obtained by linking patient records to the Taiwan National Death Registry, updated up to December 2021. Cardiovascular death was determined using the Standardized Definitions for Cardiovascular and Stroke Endpoint Events in Clinical Trials established by the US Food and Drug Administration. The status of renal function progression was determined by comparing baseline renal function with follow‐up measurements during the study period. New‐onset chronic dialysis was ascertained based on the issuance of a Catastrophic Illness Certificate, through which patients' relevant medical expenses were exempted. Safety outcomes such as diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state were captured from all listed diagnoses during either hospitalization or emergency department visits.
sections.statistical analysis: The linear trend of baseline characteristics across HbA1c quintiles was evaluated using the Cochran–Armitage trend test for categorical variables, linear contrasts from 1‐way ANOVA for continuous variables with approximately normal distributions, and the Jonckheere–Terpstra test for markedly skewed variables (eg, urine albumin‐to‐creatinine ratio). The association between HbA1c quintiles and the risk of outcomes was assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression models, adjusting for all covariates listed in Table 1 (including SGLT2i and GLP‐1RA), with the exception of follow‐up duration. Fasting glucose levels were excluded from the multivariable models due to collinearity with HbA1c. We assessed potential multicollinearity among the remaining covariates using variance inflation factors; all values were <3, indicating no significant concerns (data not shown). In the aforementioned models, HbA1c quintiles were modeled either as a categorical variable (with the third quintile as the reference) to compare intergroup differences, or as an ordinal variable to examine potential linear associations. Because there is no definitive theoretical basis for dividing the cohort into 5 groups, we also performed a sensitivity analysis using quartile groupings to evaluate the robustness of our primary quintile‐based findings. Because categorizing HbA1c into groups—whether using the current quintile approach or any other grouping scheme—is inherently arbitrary and subjective, such discretization inevitably leads to a loss of information embedded in the original continuous variable. To address this limitation, we additionally modeled HbA1c as a continuous variable using restricted cubic splines (RCS). The knots were located in the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of the HbA1c distribution. Adjusted hazard ratios from the RCS models were graphically represented to identify optimal HbA1c thresholds associated with increased or decreased risks. The RCS models were adjusted for the same covariates as in the primary analysis. Nonlinearity in the RCS analysis was assessed by testing the spline terms using a likelihood ratio test. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on key predefined patient characteristics, including age (≥65 versus <65 years), sex, presence or absence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease status (eGFR <60 versus ≥60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ), obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 versus lower BMI), and diabetic microvascular complications. Given the extended study duration (2009–2019), diabetes management evolved substantially, particularly following the introduction of SGLT2i in Taiwan in January 2016. Consequently, we stratified the study period into 2 eras (2009–2015 and 2016–September 2019) and conducted a corresponding subgroup analysis. Interaction effects between subgroup categories and HbA1c quintiles (treated as an ordinal variable) were formally assessed by including interaction terms in the Cox models. The covariates adjusted in the subgroup analyses were identical to those used in the primary analysis. The proportional hazards assumption for the primary exposure—mean HbA1c quintiles—was evaluated across all outcomes by calculating the Pearson correlation between Schoenfeld residuals and ranked survival time. In both the unadjusted and covariate‐adjusted models, these correlations remained small (absolute values <0.15), indicating no significant violation of the proportional hazards assumption (Table S1 ). Statistical significance was determined with 2‐tailed tests, and a P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. The RCS modeling was conducted using R software version 4.4.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the “rms” package. Other statistical analyses were performed using SAS software version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).
sections.baseline characteristics: Table 1 summarizes the baseline characteristics of patients stratified by mean HbA1c quintiles. Patients in the highest quintile (Q5) were younger than those in the lowest quintile (Q1) (63.4 versus 67.2 years) and had a higher mean BMI (26.7 versus 25.7 kg/m 2 ). The proportion of male patients was significantly higher in the lowest quintile compared with the highest. Notably, higher HbA1c quintiles exhibited a significantly elevated prevalence of diabetic complications—including retinopathy (rising from 5.1% in Q1 to 9.0% in Q5), neuropathy (3.6%–6.1%), and nephropathy (10.9%–15.1%)—reflecting increased disease severity despite a shorter duration of diabetes in Q5 compared with Q1 (4.0 versus 4.4 years). Interestingly, eGFR was higher in higher HbA1c quintiles (80.1±36.6 versus 74.5±33.4 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ), likely due to younger age and higher BMI observed in these groups. In contrast, the prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidities—including atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, hypertension, prior stroke, HHF, and previous percutaneous coronary intervention—was significantly higher in the lowest quintile. Consequently, patients in the lowest quintile were more frequently prescribed antihypertensive medications and antithrombotic agents. Regarding antidiabetic therapy, the highest quintile showed substantially greater use of insulin (36.1% versus 2.8%), sulfonylureas (66.2% versus 23.6%), SGLT2i (15.0% versus 4.3%), thiazolidinediones (18.7% versus 3.6%), and alpha‐glucosidase inhibitors (18.3% versus 6.3%). The mean follow‐up duration increased gradually from the lowest to the highest quintile (3.4±2.0 versus 3.9±2.0 years).
sections.risk of major cardiovascular events acro: In univariate analysis, the risks of MACE, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death exhibited J‐shaped relationships across HbA1c quintiles, being significantly higher in both the lowest (Q1) and highest (Q5) quintiles compared with the reference group (Q3) (Table 2 ). The risk of AMI was significantly increased only in the highest quintile (Q5), whereas no significant difference was observed for the lowest quintile (Q1). After multivariable adjustment, the risk of MACE showed a significant, graded increase from the lowest to highest quintiles. This association was driven predominantly by a linear increase in cardiovascular death across quintiles (both P for linear trend <0.05). Although a consistent linear trend was not observed for AMI or ischemic stroke, patients in the highest quintile (Q5) maintained significantly elevated risks for both outcomes compared with the reference group. Similar results were observed across quartiles (Table S2 ). RCS modeling further clarified these associations. The curve for MACE indicated a significant nonlinear J‐shaped relationship ( P for nonlinearity=0.010), characterized by a steep increase in risk at HbA1c levels >7%, whereas risk at levels <7% did not differ significantly from the reference (Figure 1A ). In contrast, no significant association was found between HbA1c and AMI ( P for nonlinearity=0.471; P for linear trend=0.786) (Figure 1B ). The curve for ischemic stroke demonstrated a distinct J‐shaped association ( P for nonlinearity <0.001; P for linear trend=0.014), with significantly elevated risks at both glycemic extremes (Figure 1C ). Conversely, cardiovascular death exhibited a predominantly linear increase in risk >7% HbA1c ( P for nonlinearity=0.101; P for linear trend <0.001), whereas risk remained stable and nonsignificant below this threshold (Figure 1D ).
sections.risk of renal events across levels of hb: In univariate analyses, the risks for all renal outcomes—including MAKE, progression to dialysis, eGFR decline ≥50%, and doubling of SCr—demonstrated J‐shaped trends across HbA1c quintiles (Table S3 ). These J‐shaped associations persisted after multivariable adjustment, indicating elevated risks at both glycemic extremes. Specifically, compared with the reference quintile (Q3), patients in the lowest quintile (Q1) exhibited significantly increased risks for MAKE [hazard ratio (HR), 1.43 [95% CI, 1.23–1.66], progression to dialysis (HR, 1.66 [95% CI, 1.25–2.21]), eGFR decline ≥50% (HR, 1.40 [95% CI, 1.14–1.72]), and doubling of SCr (HR, 1.38 [95% CI, 1.17–1.63]). Similarly, patients in the highest quintile (Q5) showed elevated risks for MAKE (HR, 1.56 [95% CI, 1.34–1.81]), progression to dialysis (HR, 1.77 [95% CI, 1.32–2.38]), eGFR decline ≥50% (HR, 1.47 [95% CI, 1.20–1.81), and doubling of SCr (HR, 1.56 [95% CI, 1.33–1.84]). Consistent results were observed across quartiles (Table S2 ). RCS modeling reinforced these findings, revealing significant nonlinear, J‐shaped associations for all renal outcomes (all P for nonlinearity <0.001) (Figure 2A through 2D ). The risk nadir for all outcomes occurred slightly above 7% HbA1c (MAKE: 7.28%, progression to dialysis: 7.41%, eGFR decline ≥50%: 7.28%, doubling of SCr: 7.2%). Specifically, the HR and 95% CI crossed unity (HR=1) at HbA1c levels of ∼7.0% to 7.6% for MAKE, 7.0% to7.8% for progression to dialysis, 7.0% to 7.6% for eGFR decline ≥50%, and 7.0% to 7.4% for doubling of SCr.
sections.risks of other outcomes across levels of: After multivariable adjustment, no significant differences were observed across HbA1c quintiles for HF outcomes or all‐cause hospitalization (Table S4 ). For all‐cause death, although the highest quintile (Q5) exhibited a significantly higher risk compared with the reference (Q3) (HR, 1.27 [95% CI, 1.10–1.48]), no clear linear trend was evident across quintiles. Hypoglycemia incidence was lowest in Q1 and increased progressively with higher HbA1c quintiles, demonstrating a significant linear trend ( P for trend=0.006). Similarly, the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state increased significantly from lower to higher quintiles, peaking in Q5 ( P for trend <0.001). Risks of falls or fractures did not differ significantly across quintiles. RCS analyses provided further insights. HHF risk showed a linear positive association with HbA1c levels ( P for nonlinearity=0.642; P for linear trend=0.001), increasing alongside HbA1c (Figure 3A ). To address potential reverse causation (eg, worsening HF leading to hyperglycemia), we conducted sensitivity analyses incorporating 6‐ and 12‐month lag periods by excluding events within these intervals. These analyses consistently confirmed the significant linear relationship (Figure S2A and S2B ). All‐cause admission risk demonstrated a significant J‐shaped relationship ( P for nonlinearity <0.001; P for linear trend=0.017), with elevated risks at both glycemic extremes (Figure S3A ). All‐cause mortality exhibited a similar significant J‐shaped association ( P for nonlinearity <0.001; P for linear trend <0.001) (Figure 3B ). Hypoglycemia risk displayed a linear association ( P for nonlinearity=0.234; P for linear trend <0.001), with lower HbA1c corresponding to lower risk (Figure 3C ). For diabetic ketoacidosis/hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, RCS analysis revealed significantly increased risk at HbA1c levels >7% ( P for nonlinearity=0.036; P for linear trend <0.001), whereas risk remained flat below this threshold (Figure 3D ). No significant association was observed between HbA1c and fall risk (Figure S3B ). Finally, fracture risk displayed a J‐shaped curve ( P for nonlinearity=0.027; P for linear trend=0.415); however, CIs were wide and the magnitude of risk elevation was small, with hazard ratios exceeding 2.0 only at HbA1c levels >13% (Figure S3C ).
sections.subgroup analyses of mace: Subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the consistency of the association between HbA1c and MACE across various patient characteristics (Table S5 ). A significant interaction was observed between sex and HbA1c levels ( P for interaction=0.005). Specifically, the results showed a linear increase in risk with rising HbA1c in men, whereas women exhibited a distinct J‐shaped association. A borderline interaction was noted for obesity status (BMI ≥25 versus <25 kg/m 2 ; P for interaction=0.053), though this did not reach statistical significance. No significant interactions were observed for other subgroups, including age (≥65 versus <65 years), history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, renal function (eGFR <60 versus ≥60 mL/min per 1.73 m 2 ), or diabetic microvascular complications. RCS modeling confirmed this significant interaction by sex ( P for interaction=0.001), reinforcing the linear relationship observed in men and the J‐shaped relationship in women (Figure S4 ). Finally, no statistically significant interaction was observed between the study era and the primary outcome ( P for interaction=0.841; Table S6 ).
sections.discussion: In this retrospective cohort study, we observed distinct associations between HbA1c and clinical outcomes in patients with diabetes treated with contemporary therapies. Specifically, MACE and renal outcomes demonstrated significant J‐shaped relationships, characterized by increased risks at both low and high HbA1c levels. In contrast, the risk of HHF showed a linear increase with rising HbA1c. Additionally, clear sex differences emerged: men exhibited a linear increase in MACE risk with rising HbA1c, whereas women showed a distinct J‐shaped association. These findings suggest that optimal HbA1c targets in contemporary diabetes management may need to be individualized based on sex and the specific outcome prioritized. Previous clinical trials investigating the impact of glycemic control on cardiovascular outcomes have yielded inconsistent results. The ACCORD trial reported increased mortality with intensive glycemic control targeting an HbA1c <6%, 2 and the ADVANCE and VADT trials failed to demonstrate significant reductions in cardiovascular events despite not finding higher mortality. 3 , 4 These earlier trials largely used older glucose‐lowering medications, such as sulfonylureas and insulin, which may have contributed to adverse outcomes via hypoglycemia and weight gain. Conversely, observational studies have often diverged from these trial results; for instance, the Swedish National Diabetes Register reported a U‐shaped association for mortality but a curvilinear relationship for cardiovascular outcomes, 10 whereas the UKPDS (United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study) indicated a linear relationship. 11 Consequently, the lack of macrovascular benefit in earlier trials might reflect treatment‐related adverse effects rather than the impact of lower glucose levels per se. In our contemporary cohort, the association between lower HbA1c levels and a reduced risk of hypoglycemia is consistent with this rationale, as patients in the highest HbA1c quintile were significantly more likely to be treated with insulin and sulfonylureas. Furthermore, although contemporary agents like SGLT2i and GLP‐1RA offer independent cardiovascular benefits, our study persisted in finding a J‐shaped relationship between HbA1c and MACE, with the lowest risk observed around 7%. This suggests that the relationship between glycemic control and cardiovascular risk is complex and that targets should be nuanced by patient‐specific factors rather than relying on a universal HbA1c threshold. The lack of a significant association between HbA1c levels and AMI incidence may reflect the high prevalence of baseline secondary prevention in our cohort. Patients in the lowest HbA1c quintile (Q1) were older, had a higher burden of known coronary artery disease, and were more frequently prescribed with antithrombotic agents. This pharmacological protection likely blunted the incremental impact of glycemic control on non‐fatal coronary events. Furthermore, although the atherogenic effects of hyperglycemia often require a multiyear horizon to manifest as clinical AMI—exceeding our mean follow‐up of <4 years—the associations with HF and renal outcomes appeared more immediate. This suggests that glucose lowering may exert more direct hemodynamic or metabolic benefits on HF and kidney function, whereas its role in preventing AMI is potentially overshadowed by contemporary standard‐of‐care in the short term. Therefore, HbA1c remains a critical marker for cardiorenal protection, despite its less sensitive relationship with AMI in this setting. The benefits of glycemic control in reducing diabetic microvascular complications, particularly nephropathy, are well established. Although the ADVANCE trial demonstrated sustained reductions in end‐stage renal disease with intensive control, 12 evidence remains stronger for intermediate markers like albuminuria than for hard clinical end points. 13 In our study, we identified a pronounced J‐shaped relationship between HbA1c and renal outcomes, indicating elevated risks at both glycemic extremes. The increased renal risk at lower HbA1c levels likely involves multiple interacting mechanisms. First, lower HbA1c may reflect malnutrition, chronic illness, or frailty—conditions often associated with advanced chronic kidney disease. Kalantar‐Zadeh et al. described a paradoxical association between lower HbA1c and higher mortality in patients on hemodialysis, suggesting that low HbA1c may indicate poor underlying health rather than effective glucose management. 14 Second, HbA1c variability is an independent predictor of renal deterioration 15 ; notably, intensive therapy in the ACCORD trial reduced microvascular complications only in patients with low glycemic variability. 16 Lastly, chronic kidney disease‐related anemia and reduced erythrocyte lifespan can artificially lower HbA1c, potentially confounding the relationship. Therefore, our findings should be considered hypothesis generating, without supporting definitive conclusions that stringent glycemic control improves or harms renal outcomes. In contrast to the J‐shaped associations observed for MACE and renal outcomes, our study identified a consistent linear relationship between lower HbA1c levels and reduced risk of HHF. This aligns with prior research linking chronic hyperglycemia to HF via mechanisms such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and myocardial fibrosis. 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 Critically, our results extend these findings by demonstrating that this protective linear association persists even at HbA1c levels as low as 5%. Unlike AMI or stroke, where hypoglycemia may negate the benefits of strict control, hypoglycemia does not appear to elevate HF risk. Although it could be hypothesized that the lower risk at lower HbA1c arises from increased prescription of SGLT2i and GLP‐1RA, our cohort actually showed higher usage of these agents in groups with higher HbA1c, and multivariable adjustment confirmed the independent linearity of the association. Thus, optimized glycemic management appears to be a critical strategy specifically for HF prevention. A novel and significant finding of our study is the sex‐specific divergence in the HbA1c–MACE relationship: a linear association in men versus a J‐shaped relationship in women. This suggests that the physiological impact of tight glycemic control differs fundamentally by sex. Several mechanisms may explain why women appear more vulnerable to risks at lower HbA1c levels. First, HbA1c tends to underestimate fasting glucose in men relative to women, possibly due to sex‐specific variations in iron metabolism and erythrocyte lifespan. 22 Consequently, a woman with a “safe” appearing HbA1c may have lower circulating glucose than a man with the same value, placing her closer to hypoglycemic thresholds. Indeed, Færch et al. showed that, independent of anthropometric factors, men consistently had higher fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c levels than women under similar glycemic conditions, indicating inherent physiological differences. 23 Intensive glucose‐lowering therapy may trigger counter‐regulatory stress responses or subclinical hypoglycemia more frequently in women than in men, thereby increasing cardiovascular risk and driving the observed J‐shaped curve. Recognizing these sex disparities is crucial for tailoring individualized glycemic targets in diabetes care. Universal guidelines targeting HbA1c <7.0% may require refinement. Although a strategy of intensive control appears beneficial for men, a target range of 7.0% to 7.5% may be safer for women. These findings underscore the need for future research to be adequately powered to detect sex‐specific interaction effects. Furthermore, because HbA1c lacks sensitivity for glycemic variability, future studies should incorporate continuous glucose monitoring to investigate whether “time‐below‐range” drives the J‐shaped risk curve observed in women. Such precision medicine approaches are essential to transition from generalized targets toward sex‐specific protective strategies. This study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design precludes the establishment of causal relationships, and residual confounding may exist despite robust multivariable adjustments. Second, variability in the timing of HbA1c measurements could affect categorization, though we mitigated this by requiring consistent monitoring. Third, our cohort was drawn from a single health care system; whereas mortality data were linked to a national registry, nonfatal outcomes occurring at outside institutions might be missed. However, we believe this potential bias is non‐differential across HbA1c quintiles, as any under‐ascertainment of outcomes likely occurred with similar frequency across all glycemic groups. Fourth, the requirement for regular HbA1c testing may introduce selection bias, limiting generalizability to patients who are consistently engaged in outpatient care. Finally, our study cohort was defined by the initiation of DPP4 inhibitor rather than SGLT2i or GLP‐1RA, as the latter agents had insufficient usage volume during the earlier study years to constitute a robust standalone cohort. Lastly, although the accuracy of ICD ‐based definitions for major cardiovascular outcomes has been validated in prior studies, some degree of outcome misclassification remains possible. Our findings reflect outcomes in a broad population under standard care with relatively neutral cardiovascular effects, and results may differ among patients treated with newer cardioprotective agents.
sections.conclusions: Among patients with diabetes receiving contemporary therapies, HbA1c levels exhibit J‐shaped relationships with major cardiovascular and renal events, whereas the relationship with HF is linear. Furthermore, men consistently benefited from lower HbA1c targets, whereas women experienced increased cardiovascular risks at both low and high HbA1c extremes, emphasizing the importance of tailoring glycemic goals to individual patient characteristics.

title: Does gestational vitamin D attenuate the negative effects of prenatal depression on offspring emotional and behavioral problems? Findings in the ECHO cohort
abstract: Background Prenatal depression is associated with offspring behavioral problems, but heterogeneity in the strength of this association is not well understood. Maternal vitamin D concentration during pregnancy is important for fetal brain development and may help explain this variability, with potential differences by timing of exposure and maternal race. Methods Using data from 1,451 mother–child pairs in the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes cohort, linear mixed-effects models examined associations between prenatal depressive symptom severity, gestational 25-hydroxy-vitamin D (25[OH]D) concentrations, and internalizing and externalizing behaviors in preschool-aged children. Analyses were stratified by common 25(OH)D deficiency thresholds, prenatal timing, and race. Results Prenatal depressive symptom severity was associated with greater child internalizing ( β = 0.18, 95% CI = 0.11, 0.25) and externalizing ( β = 0.21, 95% CI = 0.14, 0.28) behaviors. Gestational 25(OH)D concentration did not moderate depression effect estimates in adjusted models. In stratified analyses, the association between prenatal depressive symptoms and child externalizing behaviors persisted regardless of 25(OH)D threshold levels, but the association with internalizing behaviors attenuated at 25(OH)D < 20 ng/mL. Timing of 25(OH)D measurement (early/late pregnancy) did not modify relationships. Higher gestational 25(OH)D was associated with fewer externalizing problems among offspring of Black mothers only. Conclusions Prenatal depressive symptoms showed robust associations with child behavioral problems, largely independent of gestational 25(OH)D. However, attenuated risk for internalizing behaviors with low vitamin D levels warrants investigation of social–environmental factors.
