sections.what is new?: VICTORION‐INCEPTION, designed to mimic clinical practice, was the first inclisiran trial in participants with recent acute coronary syndrome and low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C) ≥70 mg/dL, receiving statin therapy or with statin intolerance. Compared with usual lipid‐lowering care, the addition of inclisiran resulted in significantly increased LDL‐C goal attainment and significantly greater LDL‐C lowering at Days 90 through 330.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Inclisiran, in addition to usual care, provides rapid and sustained LDL‐C goal attainment in participants with recent acute coronary syndrome and elevated LDL‐C receiving statin therapy or with statin intolerance, providing a novel LDL‐C–lowering strategy for this high‐risk population.
sections.methods_1: VICTORION‐INCEPTION was a phase 3b randomized, parallel‐group, 330‐day, open‐label trial that enrolled participants at 87 US sites (June 2021–August 2023; Figure 1A ; Table S1 ). Potential participants were identified by principal investigators and invited to contact the study site for screening and inclusion. The study received Institutional Review Board or independent ethics committee approval at each site before initiation and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and International Council on Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Data sets generated as part of the VICTORION‐INCEPTION study are considered commercially sensitive and, as such, are not publicly available. Requests for data supporting the findings in this article should be made to the corresponding author (K.U.K.). Data may be shared in the form of aggregate data summaries and via a data transfer agreement 3 years after publication. Individual patient‐level data are subject to patient privacy and cannot be shared.
sections.eligibility criteria: Adults (≥18 years of age) must have been discharged from an inpatient or outpatient hospitalization for ACS (ST–elevation myocardial infarction [STEMI], non‐ST–elevation myocardial infarction [NSTEMI], or unstable angina) within 5 weeks before screening. Eligible participants had LDL‐C ≥70 mg/dL or non–high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol ≥100 mg/dL at screening and were discharged on statin therapy or had documented statin intolerance (defined as intolerable symptoms with ≥2 different statins tried before screening; Table S2 ). All participants provided written informed consent.
sections.study visits, assessments, and treatment: The study included 5 visits (Figure 1A ). Visit 1 (screening; Days −30 to −1) occurred between hospital discharge and randomization. At Visit 2 (≤30 days after screening; Day 0), eligible participants were randomized 1:1 via interactive response technology to inclisiran + usual care or usual care (further details are in the Supplemental Methods). In the inclisiran + usual care arm, inclisiran sodium 300 mg (284 mg inclisiran equivalent, 1.5‐mL prefilled syringe) was administered subcutaneously by a health care professional on Days 0, 90, and 270. The principal investigator and/or qualified site staff performed study visits in both treatment arms. Usual care was managed by primary treating clinicians other than the principal investigator and included statins and nonstatin LLT as considered appropriate. Initiation or adjustments of concomitant nonstatin LLT, including ezetimibe, anti‐PCSK9 mAbs, bempedoic acid, and inclisiran (if acquired through commercial means in the usual care arm) were permitted. Participants receiving inclisiran were not permitted to receive anti‐PCSK9 mAbs. Participants fasted for ≥8 hours before all visits. Samples for LDL‐C and other lipid biomarkers were collected at each study visit and analyzed by a central laboratory, which used the Friedewald equation to calculate LDL‐C measurements. Treating clinicians could not access study‐obtained LDL‐C values but could perform these assessments at their discretion.
sections.end points: The primary objective of VICTORION‐INCEPTION was to compare LDL‐C lowering with inclisiran + usual care versus usual care at Day 330, assessed with 2 coprimary end points: (1) achievement of LDL‐C <70 mg/dL and (2) percentage change from baseline in LDL‐C. Secondary end points included attainment of prespecified LDL‐C goals (<100 mg/dL [among participants with baseline LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL], <55 mg/dL, ≥50% reduction), absolute change in LDL‐C from baseline, average percentage and absolute change in LDL‐C from baseline across postbaseline visits, changes in other lipids and lipoproteins, changes in concomitant LLT and statin intensity, and statin discontinuation (no use ≥30 days before the end‐of‐study visit). Safety and tolerability were assessed as a secondary end point. The occurrence of MACE was an exploratory end point. Attainment of LDL‐C <40 mg/dL was assessed post hoc.
sections.statistical analysis: Statistical Analyses Software (SAS, version 9.4, SAS Institute, Cary, NC) was used. The study start date in the inclisiran + usual care arm was defined as the first date when inclisiran was administered. For participants in the usual care arm, and those randomized to inclisiran + usual care who did not receive inclisiran, the study start date was considered the day of randomization. Statistical analyses involving LDL‐C were based on calculated LDL‐C measurements. Continuous end points used data as observed per analysis visit; no specific rule for noncompleters was implemented other than using available data up to study discontinuation. For binary end points, a composite strategy was used to address missing data, including data that were missing due to early discontinuation (Supplemental Methods).
sections.sample size: The sample size was calculated for the coprimary end points with adjustment for multiple testing using the Bonferroni procedure. For both coprimary end points, a z test, an allocation ratio of 1:1, a 2‐sided significance level of 0.025, and a targeted power level of 0.85 were used to calculate sample size. For the achievement of LDL‐C <70 mg/dL, with assumed goal attainment of 75% and 55% in the inclisiran + usual care and usual care arms, respectively, a sample size of 242 participants was required. For the percentage change in LDL‐C from baseline, with assumed SD of 40% and mean treatment difference of 15%, a sample size of 306 participants was required. Based on these sample size calculations, a total sample size of 306 with a loss to follow‐up rate of 20% at Day 330 resulted in a final sample size of 384 participants.
sections.primary efficacy end points: The primary analysis time point was Day 330. Both coprimary efficacy end points were analyzed in the full analysis set, which was defined as all randomized participants, according to the treatment arm assigned. Achievement of LDL‐C <70 mg/dL at Day 330 was analyzed using a logistic regression model with treatment and baseline LDL‐C value as explanatory variables. The odds ratio (OR), 2‐sided 97.5% CI for the OR, and P value based on the fitted model are reported. Statistical significance in favor of inclisiran + usual care was shown if the P value at Day 330 was <0.025 and the corresponding OR was >1. In these analyses, participants with missing data were considered nonresponders. Percentage change from baseline in LDL‐C at Day 330 was analyzed using a mixed‐effects model for repeated measurements with treatment, visit (Day 90, Day 270, Day 330), baseline LDL‐C value, treatment‐by‐visit interaction, and baseline‐by‐visit interaction as explanatory variables. Least squares (LS) mean change in each treatment arm, LS mean treatment difference, corresponding 2‐sided 97.5% CIs, and P values are reported. Statistical significance in favor of inclisiran + usual care was shown if the P value at Day 330 was <0.025 and the corresponding LS mean treatment difference was <0. Data collected after participants discontinued treatment were used in the analysis. No additional imputation of missing LDL‐C values was used for this analysis.
sections.secondary end points: All secondary efficacy analyses were conducted in the full analysis set. Summary statistics (mean±SD, median, lower quartile [Q1], upper quartile [Q3], minimum, and maximum) were used to report continuous end points, and frequency counts and percentages were used to report discrete variables. Statistical tests for secondary efficacy end points were conducted against a 2‐sided alternative hypothesis, employing a significance level of 0.05 and corresponding 2‐sided 95% CI. All P values pertaining to the secondary end points are nominal, and no multiplicity adjustment was applied. Safety analyses were performed in the safety set, comprising all participants who received study treatment, according to the treatment received, and were summarized descriptively. Sites assessed adverse events (AEs), clinical laboratory values, and vital signs at each follow‐up visit through to the end‐of‐study visit (Day 330). AEs were also recorded when volunteered by the participant between visits or through physical examination findings, laboratory test findings, or other assessments. Safety analyses summarized the number of participants with AEs by treatment arm and by severity using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (version 27.0) nomenclature for system organ class and preferred term. Study treatment‐related AEs, death, serious AEs, and AEs leading to discontinuation were also summarized.
sections.exploratory end points: The proportion of participants experiencing MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, resuscitated cardiac arrest, and nonfatal ischemic stroke), were summarized. A time‐to‐event analysis was conducted with time to first occurrence of any event in the composite MACE (Table S3 ), as well as time to first occurrence of each of its components, was derived as study day of onset of the corresponding AE, imputing for partially missing dates as needed. To estimate the corresponding hazard ratios of inclisiran + usual care over usual care, Cox proportional hazards models were used, with associated 95% CI and treatment and baseline LDL‐C as explanatory variables; assumptions were not tested. Observation time for participants without the respective event was censored at their end‐of‐study date (date of last participation) or date of death, as applicable. Further details for statistical methods are provided in the Supplemental Methods.
sections.participants: Of 788 individuals screened for eligibility, 388 were not randomized due to not meeting eligibility criteria (n=367), clinician decision (n=14), participant decision (n=6), or death (n=1); 400 individuals were randomized (inclisiran + usual care, n=201; usual care, n=199). Most participants completed the study (overall: 89.0%; inclisiran + usual care: 91.0%; usual care: 86.9%; Figure 1B ); the most frequent reason for study discontinuation was loss to follow‐up (overall: 5.5%; inclisiran + usual care: 6.5%; usual care: 4.5%). Demographics and baseline clinical characteristics were generally balanced between treatment arms (Table 1 ). Index ACS was myocardial infarction [MI] for most (93.0%) participants (STEMI: 39.5%; NSTEMI: 53.5%), and the median time from discharge to initiating study treatment was 34.0 days (Q1–Q3: 26.0–43.0). At the time of index ACS event, 64.5% of participants were receiving LLT, most of whom (96.1%) were receiving statins. Overall, 12.3% of participants had a history of statin intolerance. Most participants with a history of ASCVD were receiving any LLT at the time of index ACS (Table S4 ). At the time of study treatment initiation, 93.8% of participants were receiving statins, with 82.0% receiving high‐intensity statins. Baseline median calculated LDL‐C was 84.0 mg/dL (Q1–Q3: 71.0–103.0) and was similar between treatment arms. Overall, 203 participants received inclisiran (safety set), including 3 randomized to usual care who received inclisiran as permitted in the study design (Table S5 ). Of participants randomized to inclisiran + usual care (N=201, full analysis set), 200 received ≥1 dose of inclisiran, with 100.0%, 95.0%, and 89.5% receiving inclisiran on Days 0, 90, and 270, respectively (Table S5 ).
sections.coprimary end points: Both coprimary end points were met with statistical significance. More participants achieved LDL‐C <70 mg/dL at Day 330 with inclisiran + usual care versus usual care (66.7% versus 28.1%; OR, 5.42 [97.5% CI, 3.29–8.91]; P <0.001; Figure 2A ), with consistent results when missing data were excluded (Table S6 ). A sensitivity analysis showed that the difference in the proportion of participants achieving LDL‐C <70 mg/dL at Day 330 was significant (38.5% [97.5% CI, 28.2–48.9]; P <0.001; Table S7 ). At Day 330, there was a greater percentage change from baseline in LDL‐C with inclisiran + usual care (LS mean: −45.6% [97.5% CI, −51.5 to −39.6]) versus usual care (1.4% [97.5% CI, −4.7 to 7.5]), resulting in a difference of −46.9% (97.5% CI, −55.4 to −38.5; P <0.001; Figure 2B ). Both coprimary end points were also met with statistical significance when analyzed in additional analysis sets, including the per‐protocol set (Tables S8 and S9 ).
sections.changes in ldl \u2010c and other lipids: Among participants with baseline LDL‐C ≥100 mg/dL (inclisiran + usual care, n=62; usual care, n=52), 75.8% versus 40.4% achieved LDL‐C <100 mg/dL at Day 330, respectively (OR, 4.38 [95% CI, 1.92–9.99]; P <0.001; Figure 3A ). Significantly more participants receiving inclisiran + usual care, versus usual care, achieved LDL‐C levels of <55 mg/dL at Day 330 (54.2% versus 13.6%; OR, 8.24 [95% CI, 4.97–13.65]; P <0.001; Figure 3B ). In a post hoc analysis, compared with the usual care arm, significantly more participants in the inclisiran + usual care arm achieved LDL‐C levels of <40 mg/dL at Day 330 (38.3% versus 6.0%; OR, 11.16 [95% CI, 5.72–21.74]; P <0.001; Figure 3C ). Reductions in LDL‐C of ≥50% from baseline at Day 330 were also significantly more frequent with inclisiran + usual care versus usual care (45.3% versus 6.5%; OR, 11.87 [95% CI, 6.33–22.25]; P <0.001; Figure 3D ). Differences in goal attainment between arms were observed from the first postbaseline visit at Day 90 (Figures 2B and 3 ). In the inclisiran + usual care arm, versus usual care, significantly greater percentage reductions in LDL‐C were seen by Day 90 (LS mean difference −51.1% [97.5% CI, −58.1 to −44.1]; P <0.001; Table S10 ). Absolute changes in LDL‐C were consistent with percentage changes across study visits (Table S10 ). The difference between treatment arms in average (ie, across postbaseline study visits) percentage and absolute change in LDL‐C were also statistically significant (−46.7% [95% CI, −52.7 to −40.8] and −37.3 mg/dL [95% CI, −42.4 to −32.2]; both P <0.001; Table S10 ). Individuals' percentage change in LDL‐C showed that most participants in the inclisiran + usual care arm had a decrease in LDL‐C from baseline at Day 330 (91.8%, 157/171), whereas half of participants in the usual care arm experienced a decrease (49.7%, 81/163; Figure S1 ). LS mean differences between inclisiran + usual care and usual care alone in percentage and absolute changes from baseline to Day 330 in other measured lipids and lipoproteins are shown in Figure S2 . Statistically significant LS mean percentage differences were seen in non–high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (−37.7% [95% CI, −44.0 to −31.4]), total cholesterol (−25.5% [95% CI, −30.2 to −20.7]), and apoB (−37.5% [95% CI, −44.8 to −30.3]; all P <0.001). Statistically significant LS mean absolute differences were seen in non–high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (−40.1 mg/dL [95% CI, −47.5 to −32.8]), total cholesterol (−37.7 mg/dL [95% CI, −45.3 to −30.2]), apoB (−28.4 mg/dL [95% CI, −33.0 to −23.9]; all P <0.001), and lipoprotein(a) (−14.0 nmol/L [95% CI, −23.8 to −4.2]; P =0.005).
sections.concomitant llt: At baseline, 82.3% of participants in the inclisiran + usual care arm and 81.7% in the usual care arm were receiving high‐intensity statin therapy. Use of high‐intensity statin therapy decreased at Day 330 to 73.3% and 78.4% in the inclisiran + usual care and usual care arms, respectively (Figure 4 ; Table S11 ). In both treatment arms, few participants had increases in statin intensity at postbaseline visits, and odds of nondecreasing (ie, no change or increasing) statin intensity at Day 330 were lower with inclisiran + usual care than with usual care (OR, 0.43 [95% CI, 0.20–0.93]; P =0.031; Table S12 ). Statin combination therapy use was low at baseline in both arms (9.9% and 8.1%). At Day 330, use of statin combination therapy remained relatively unchanged in the inclisiran + usual care arm (9.6%) and increased to 22.2% in the usual care arm (Figure 4 ). Among participants without a history of statin intolerance (inclisiran + usual care, n=173; usual care, n=178), statin discontinuation rates were similar between arms (14.5% and 18.0%, respectively; Figure S3 ).
sections.exploratory end point: mace: MACE occurred in 3.5% of participants with inclisiran + usual care (n=7) and 7.5% of participants with usual care (n=15; hazard ratio, 0.45 [95% CI, 0.18–1.11]; Table S3 ; Table S13 ).
sections.safety: The proportion of participants with ≥1 AE was comparable between treatment arms (inclisiran + usual care, 58.6%; usual care, 53.3%; Table 2 ). Most frequently reported AEs were COVID‐19 and noncardiac chest pain. Serious AEs occurred in 15.8% and 17.3% of participants in the inclisiran + usual care and usual care arms, respectively, none of which were considered treatment related. Treatment‐related AEs occurred in 10.3% of participants in the inclisiran + usual care arm (Table 2 ; Table S14 ). Treatment‐related AEs at the injection site were reported in 7.9% (n=16) of participants receiving inclisiran + usual care. The maximum severity of treatment‐related AEs at the injection site was mild in most participants (6.9%; n=14), and moderate in 1.0% (n=2). One participant receiving inclisiran + usual care discontinued treatment due to urticaria, which was considered treatment related.
sections.discussion: VICTORION‐INCEPTION demonstrated that early initiation of inclisiran + usual care, within 5 weeks of discharge from ACS hospitalization, resulted in more participants achieving LDL‐C <70 mg/dL (66.7% versus 28.1%) and provided significantly greater LDL‐C lowering versus usual care alone (45.6% reduction from baseline at Day 330 versus 1.4% increase). These findings are more likely to be reflective of inclisiran use as part of routine care, as the study was designed to closely mimic clinical practice, with usual care as the comparator. VICTORION‐INCEPTION provides valuable insights on LDL‐C goal attainment, including <70 mg/dL (coprimary end point), <55 mg/dL (secondary end point), and <40 mg/dL (post hoc end point), in this high‐risk population with ACS and elevated LDL‐C while receiving statin therapy or with statin intolerance. These results are particularly relevant in light of the recently published US guideline that supports the intensification of LLT to achieve LDL‐C <55 mg/dL 11 and the European guideline recommendation for an LDL‐C goal of <40 mg/dL in patients at extreme risk. 36 In the usual care arm of VICTORION‐INCEPTION, only 13.6% of participants achieved LDL‐C <55 mg/dL at Day 330. This is consistent with observational data showing as few as 25% of patients with recent ACS (<1 year) achieve LDL‐C <55 mg/dL and highlights the need for substantial improvements in lipid management to achieve this goal in practice. 2 In the inclisiran + usual care arm, however, 54.2% of participants met this stringent goal. VICTORION‐INCEPTION, as the first study of inclisiran to enroll participants with recent ACS, supports the LDL‐C–lowering effectiveness of inclisiran in this population, with comparable results to prior studies in ASCVD. 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 In ORION‐10 (Inclisiran for Participants With Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease and Elevated Low‐density Lipoprotein Cholesterol) and ORION‐11 (Inclisiran for Subjects With ASCVD or ASCVD‐Risk Equivalents and Elevated Low‐density Lipoprotein Cholesterol), inclisiran reduced LDL‐C by 52.3% and 49.9% at Day 510, respectively. 29 The slightly smaller decrease in VICTORION‐INCEPTION may reflect that ORION‐10 and ORION‐11 were placebo‐controlled studies, whereas VICTORION‐INCEPTION was designed to reflect clinical practice with few restrictions on concomitant therapies. Consistent with prior trials, LDL‐C slightly increased at Day 270, as expected with the measurement being taken when the third dose of inclisiran was due. 29 , 32 Additionally, in the inclisiran + usual care arm, 12 participants experienced an increase in LDL‐C from baseline to Day 330. The extent to which this was driven by behavioral/clinical factors (eg, adherence or changes in background LLT) versus interindividual variability (eg, genetic variation) could not be determined. Early LDL‐C lowering after ACS is associated with reduced risk of MACE. 6 , 14 , 37 The latest guideline for lipid management in patients with ACS recommends reassessing the lipid profile 4 to 8 weeks following hospital discharge to inform treatment intensification. 11 In VICTORION‐INCEPTION, inclisiran initiation fell within this window, with a median time from discharge to starting study treatment of 34.0 days (Q1–Q3: 26.0–43.0). Following inclisiran initiation, LDL‐C lowering was rapid, with significant LDL‐C reduction and goal attainment observed from the first postbaseline visit at Day 90. The LDL‐C–lowering effect of combination statin and nonstatin LLT post ACS has also been demonstrated with the anti‐PCSK9 mAbs evolocumab and alirocumab. 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 In‐hospital initiation of evolocumab post ACS, followed by a second dose at 4 weeks, resulted in a 40.7% greater reduction in LDL‐C from baseline to 8 weeks versus placebo. 21 Similarly, once every 2 week dosing with alirocumab, initiated ≤12 months from ACS hospitalization (median 2.6 months), resulted in LDL‐C levels 61.0% lower than placebo at 12 months. 22 Suboptimal LDL‐C management after an ACS, due to barriers such as insufficient LLT escalation and poor adherence, leads to many patients not achieving LDL‐C goals. 2 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 38 , 39 Indeed, observational studies of US patients with recent ACS (<1 year) show as few as 52.4% receive high‐intensity statin therapy, most of whom receive monotherapy. 2 , 24 , 39 In VICTORION‐INCEPTION, statin discontinuation with inclisiran + usual care was low (14.5%), and comparable to usual care (18.0%), indicating that inclisiran does not negatively affect statin continuation. The study highlights considerable gaps in usual care for this high‐risk patient population, with nearly 3 out of 4 participants in the usual care arm not attaining LDL‐C <70 mg/dL at Day 330. Although participants had elevated LDL‐C before randomization, few in the usual care arm were receiving statin combination therapy at Day 330 (22.2%), suggesting insufficient LLT escalation. Data collected in VICTORION‐INCEPTION, however, may overestimate the degree of LLT intensification in clinical practice due to the Hawthorne effect. 40 Strategies that may increase LLT intensification post ACS include electronic health record alerts and pharmacist‐led interventions; however, the long‐term impact of these types of interventions requires further investigation. 41 , 42 The safety profile of inclisiran in ASCVD is similar to placebo or usual care, with the exception of mild‐to‐moderate injection‐site reactions in 2.6% to 14% of participants. 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 Our study confirms these findings in participants with recent ACS. The numerical trend for reduced composite MACE occurrence with inclisiran + usual care versus usual care alone was similar to that reported in a pooled analysis of ORION‐9, ORION‐10, and ORION‐11; the pooled analysis demonstrated a 25% lower risk of MACE with inclisiran treatment versus placebo. 43
sections.strengths and limitations: The study population was largely reflective of US populations with ACS. 44 , 45 The open‐label design, with usual care as the comparator, was chosen to mimic decision‐making in clinical practice. This allowed for assessment of the impact of inclisiran on background LLT use and statin discontinuation. Additionally, participants' treating clinicians provided LDL‐C management as part of usual care. They could perform LDL‐C measurements at their discretion but were blinded to the study‐obtained LDL‐C measurements. Limitations included that LDL‐C management provided by treating clinicians as part of usual care did not necessarily reflect guideline‐recommended standard of care or best practice. It should also be noted that although the frequently employed Friedewald equation was used to calculate LDL‐C measurements in this study, calculated LDL‐C levels can be erroneously low in patients with hypertriglyceridemia, especially at lower LDL‐C levels. 46 Not all participants in the inclisiran + usual care arm received 3 doses of inclisiran, which may affect observed LDL‐C lowering. Participants randomized to usual care who received inclisiran (as permitted in the study design) were included in the usual care arm for efficacy analyses, which may also have affected analyses. However, this effect was small due to infrequent inclisiran use in the usual care arm (n=3). Although the occurrence of MACE was included as an exploratory end point, the small sample size did not provide adequate power for short‐term evaluation, and study duration did not allow for long‐term evaluation. MACE occurrence will be evaluated by ongoing inclisiran outcomes studies (ORION‐4 [ NCT03705234 ]; VICTORION‐1 PREVENT [ NCT05739383 ]; VICTORION‐2 PREVENT [ NCT05030428 ]). Limitations inherently associated with open‐label trials include the potential for bias and higher participant dropouts compared with blinded trials. 47 Here, the overall noncompletion rate was 10.8% (inclisiran + usual care: 8.5%; usual care: 13.1%), with most noncompletion due to loss to follow‐up (5.5%), which was similar to the overall noncompletion rate of the open‐label VICTORION‐INITIATE trial (9.6%). 32 Importantly, the noncompletion rate was lower than accounted for in the sample size calculations and therefore should not affect the ability to assess coprimary end points. Results here may also have been affected by differences in patient behavior between clinical trials and clinical practice: adherence to background LLT and PCSK9‐targeting therapies, including inclisiran, is typically higher in a controlled study environment versus observational trials. 48
sections.conclusions_1: VICTORION‐INCEPTION was the first prospective, randomized clinical trial to assess the effect of LDL‐C management with inclisiran in participants with recent ACS. Adding inclisiran to usual lipid‐lowering care resulted in significantly increased LDL‐C goal attainment and significantly greater LDL‐C lowering at Days 90 through 330 compared with usual care. Combination LLT was underused in the usual care arm, resulting in low levels of LDL‐C goal attainment. VICTORION‐INCEPTION demonstrates that inclisiran, in addition to usual care, provides an effective strategy to rapidly achieve and maintain guideline‐directed LDL‐C goals ∼1 year post event in participants with recent ACS and elevated LDL‐C (≥70 mg/dL).

title: ARNT2 repression disrupts neuronal identity and promotes glioblastoma growth
abstract: Tumor initiation and progression frequently involve oncogenic programs that favor proliferation at the expense of lineage commitment and differentiation. Here, we identify a MYC-driven mechanism that suppresses neuronal identity in glioblastoma (GBM) through repression of the transcription factor aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator 2 (ARNT2). ARNT2 is highly expressed in the brain, cerebellum, and iPSC-derived neurons but is markedly reduced in GBM tumors and cell lines, where its loss correlates with higher tumor grade and poor survival. Mechanistically, MYC represses ARNT2 expression, and ARNT2 loss results in reduced expression of neuronal and glial identity genes. Although ARNT2 depletion does not alter GBM cell proliferation in vitro, it significantly enhances tumor growth and lipid metabolic remodeling in vivo. Conversely, ectopic ARNT2 expression suppresses tumor burden in both subcutaneous and orthotopic GBM xenograft models and promotes features of neuronal differentiation. Together, these findings identify ARNT2 as a tumor suppressor in GBM and establish MYC-mediated repression of ARNT2 as a critical mechanism by which GBM maintains a proliferative, undifferentiated, stem-like state. sections.introduction: The universal oncogene and transcription factor MYC is activated in most human cancers, where it correlates with disease aggressiveness [ 1 ]. In glioblastoma (GBM), the most aggressive form of brain cancer, MYC is elevated in 60–80% of cases, and its expression increases with glioma grade [ 2 , 3 ]. Transgenic expression of MYC in mouse astrocytic lineages is sufficient to cause gliomas that resemble the human disease [ 4 ]. Activation of MYC downstream of p53 and Pten mutations is associated with impaired neuronal differentiation and enhanced self-renewal capacity of GBM cells [ 5 ]. Importantly, MYC has been shown to play a critical role in GBM progression through regulating genes involved in the cell cycle, metabolism, and differentiation [ 2 ]. As a broad-acting transcription factor, MYC regulates the expression of numerous genes, some directly via binding as a heterodimeric complex with MAX to E-Box motifs in their promoters [ 6 ], and others by cooperating with other pathways to enhance active genes [ 7 , 8 ]. Although the roles of MYC in inducing genes that promote cell growth and metabolic reprogramming are well documented, the mechanisms through which MYC restricts differentiation are less understood. Multiple studies have shown that MYC inhibits terminal differentiation in multiple cell types, including muscle cells and B lymphocytes [ 9 – 13 ]. MYC has long been thought to inhibit differentiation by regulating the expression of genes, miRNAs, and lincRNAs [ 14 ], which may prevent cells from exiting the cell cycle and undergoing terminal differentiation [ 15 ]. The role of MYC in inhibiting differentiation has important implications for the maintenance of stemness in cancer, as MYC is upregulated in nearly all human tumors [ 16 ]. Although MYC is primarily a transcriptional activator, it can also indirectly repress gene expression through less well-defined mechanisms. For example, loss of MAX leads to substantial upregulation of numerous genes that are normally repressed by members of the MXD (MAX dimerization) family, MNT and MGA [ 17 ]. In addition, MYC can repress gene repression indirectly by transcriptionally inducing epigenetic repressors such as EZH2, a catalytic component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 [ 18 ]. Our lab has investigated the importance of the PAS domain transcription factors hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator (ARNT) and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) as growth-promoting genes [ 19 ] downstream of MYC [ 20 ]. While the oncogenic importance ARNT-AHR has been extensively studied by us and others [ 21 ], the role of aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator 2 (ARNT2), ARNT’s closest homologue, in cancer appear to be context-specific. ARNT2 is directly involved in neural development, particularly in the formation and patterning of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum, retina, and inner ear [ 22 – 24 ]. ARNT2 regulates genes involved in neuronal differentiation, migration, and survival, thereby playing a crucial role in the development and function of the central nervous system [ 25 , 26 ], and dysregulation of ARNT2 expression and function have both been implicated in several neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia [ 22 ]. Several reports found high ARNT2 expression to be linked to reduced cell proliferation and migration, and improved prognosis in breast, lung, gastric, and liver cancers [ 27 – 32 ]. Moreover, recently, ARNT2 was found to be associated with positive outcome in medulloblastoma patients [ 33 ]. Other reports have correlated ARNT2 expression with oncogenic behavior of cancer cells including oral squamous cell carcinoma, TG1 GBM cells, liposarcoma and cervical cancer [ 31 , 34 – 36 ]. To define the role of ARNT2 in GBM, we performed gain- and loss-of-function studies in GBM cells in vitro and in vivo, as well as in induced pluripotent stem cells and human tumor samples. We identified transcriptional and metabolic programs downstream of ARNT2 and validated its function using multiple GBM models. We demonstrate that MYC represses expression transcription of ARNT2, which is normally enriched in the central nervous system but is downregulated in high-grade glioma human samples. Genetic ablation of ARNT2 reduces expression of neuronal and glial lineage genes and enhances tumor growth in vivo, whereas ARNT2 overexpression suppresses tumor growth, establishing ARNT2 as a tumor suppressor downstream of MYC in GBM.
sections.myc represses arnt2, which maintains neu: We previously demonstrated that MYC activates the expression of the growth-promoting bHLH-PAS domain transcription factors AHR and ARNT [ 20 , 37 ]. To define the importance of MYC in broadly regulating the expression of PAS domain transcription factors, we examined an RNA-seq dataset of Rat1 myc -/- fibroblasts expressing empty vector or reconstituted with human MYC [ 20 ], and found that MYC expression not only activated the bHLH-PAS domain transcription factors AHR, ARNT, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor repressor (AHRR), but also suppressed several members of the same family, including neuronal PAS domain protein 4 (NPAS4), single-minded homolog 2 (SIM2), and ARNT2 (Fig. 1 A and Figure S1A). ARNT2 recruits NPAS4 in response to increased neuronal activity, and this dimer induces transcription and increases somatic inhibitory input [ 38 ]. Fig. 1 Repression of ARNT2 expression by MYC. A bHLH-PAS domain transcription factors were regulated by MYC in Rat1 fibroblast RNA-seq dataset (also see Figure S1A). Pink: upregulated by MYC; Blue: downregulated by MYC. B Rat1 fibroblasts myc-/- or myc-/- reconstituted with human MYC were extracted with NP40 lysing buffer, and the total cell lysates were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. C RT-qPCR for the indicated genes in Rat1 fibroblasts with different MYC expression profiles. The expression level of each gene was normalized to the levels of 18S, and the expression level of each gene in wild-type cells was set to 1. Plots show mean +/− SD. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA test, followed up by Dunnett's multiple comparisons test. *Adjusted P ≤ 0.05. D Immunofluorescence of ARNT and ARNT2 in Rat1 fibroblasts myc-/- or myc-/- reconstituted with human MYC. Nuclei were stained with DAPI. E Rat1 fibroblasts myc-/- and myc-/- reconstituted with human MYC or MYC-nick were extracted with NP40 lysing buffer, and the total cell lysates were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. F Rat1 fibroblasts were transfected with control or MYC siRNAs, and total cell lysates were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. G Total cell lysates of human epithelial ARPE-19 cell expressing empty vector and MYC or transfected with control or MYC siRNA were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. H Total cell lysates of human colon cancer cell DLD1 expressing empty vector, MYC, and MYC-nick were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. I Rat1 myc-/- and myc-/- + MYC cells were transfected with Arnt2 siRNAs and cultured in 96-well plate. Cell growth was monitored by Incucyte. Plots show mean +/− SD. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA test, followed up by Dunnett's multiple comparisons test. *Adjusted P ≤ 0.05. J ARPE and ARPE MYC cells were transfected with ARNT2 siRNAs and cultured in 96-well plate. Cell growth was monitored by Incucyte. Plots show mean +/− SD. Statistical significance was assessed by one-way ANOVA test, followed up by Dunnett's multiple comparisons test. *Adjusted P ≤ 0.05. K Total lysates of Rat1 myc-/- cells transfected with control and Arnt2 shRNA were blotted with ARNT2 and tubulin antibodies. L Rat1 myc-/- cells transfected with control and Arnt2 shRNA were subjected to RNA-seq assay. M GO analysis of genes that were upregulated by both MYC and shArnt2 in Rat1 myc-/- cells. N GO analysis of genes that were downregulated by both MYC and shArnt2 in Rat1 myc-/- cells. O Mouse tissues were extracted with NP40 lysis buffer, and total lysates were immunoblotted with the indicated antibodies. P Venn diagram of genes regulated by MYC and Arnt2 KD. Statistical significance of the overlaps was assessed using Fisher’s Exact Test. Q Heatmaps of genes involving in neuron-axon and synapsis functions that were downregulated by both MYC and Arnt2 KD. R iPSCs cell expressing Dox-inducible neurogenin differentiates into neuronal lineages. S - T iPSCs were transfected with siARNT2 and treated with doxycycline for 3 days before lysed for Western blotting analysis We confirmed that human MYC introduction suppressed ARNT2 expression in Rat1 myc-/- fibroblasts and activated AHR and ARNT expression, as demonstrated by using Western blots (Fig. 1 B and Figure S1B) and RT-qPCR (Fig. 1 C). Immunofluorescence (IF) analysis further revealed that MYC expression reduced nuclear ARNT2 levels while increasing ARNT expression (Fig. 1 D). Expression of the cytosolic MYC fragment, MYC-nick, which lacks DNA binding domain [ 12 ], did not affect ARNT2 expression (Fig. 1 E). Conversely, knocking down MYC in Rat1 fibroblasts augmented ARNT2 protein levels (Fig. 1 F). Knocking out MYC from Rat1 fibroblasts increased nuclear ARNT2 staining and decreased ARNT expression (Figure S1C). We confirmed that ARNT2 protein was also repressed in human retinal pigment epithelial cell line ARPE-19 with elevated MYC levels (Fig. 1 G). Like Rat1 fibroblasts, knocking down MYC from ARPE cells also increased ARNT2 level (Fig. 1 H). Our results show that MYC indeed downregulates the expression of ARNT2. Since the MYC-activated bHLH-PAS domain protein AHR promotes cell growth, we examined the effects of ARNT2 loss on cell growth by knocking down ARNT2 in the normal cells Rat1 fibroblast and ARPE epithelial cells using siRNAs. Our results showed that ARNT2 knockdown did not affect the growth of Rat1 myc-/- cells expressing either MYC or empty vector (Fig. 1 I). In contrast, ARNT2 knockdown in ARPE cells increased proliferation in cells expressing empty vector, which have high endogenous ARNT2 levels, but had no effect in ARPE cells expressing MYC, which exhibit low ARNT2 expression and are already highly proliferative (Fig. 1 I–J; knockdown efficiency confirmed in Figure S1F-G). Given that MYC is a transcriptional activator, we explored the mechanisms by which MYC indirectly causes transcriptional repression of ARNT2. MYC had been previously implicated in transcriptional repression via the activation of EZH2 [ 18 ], thus we tested the involvement of the PRC2 in MYC-regulated ARNT2 repression. The PRC2 complex comprises SUZ12, EED, RBBP4, and the histone methyltransferase EZH2 and it represses gene expression by methylating lysine 27 of histone H3 [ 39 ]. We investigate the importance of EZH2 and SUZ12 in repressing ARNT2 in ARPE-19 cells. Given that EZH1 has been reported to compensate for EZH2 depletion [ 40 ], we also interrogated the importance of EZH1. MYC expression upregulated EZH2, EZH1, and SUZ12 protein levels, and the reciprocal knockdown experiments showed that reducing EZH2 indeed increased EZH1 levels in ARPE and ARPE MYC cells (Figure S1D). Consequently, we performed double knockdowns of both genes. Knocking down EZH2, EZH1, and SUZ12 individually in ARPE cells increased ARNT2 expression, whereas only EZH2 and SUZ12 knockdown in ARPE MYC cells elevated ARNT2 protein (Figure S1D). Thus, we concluded that MYC upregulates expression of PRC2 proteins, thereby represses ARNT2 expression (Figure S1E). To investigate the transcriptional functions of ARNT2, we generated a stable ARNT2 knockdown Rat1 myc -/- cell line using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) (Fig. 1 K) and performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis (Fig. 1 L). Gene ontology analysis revealed that ARNT2-regulated genes are enriched in pathways related to cell differentiation, cell development, muscle function, biosynthesis, and signaling (Fig. 1 M-N). Consistent with a role in neural biology, ARNT2 protein was predominantly detected in the brain and cerebellum, as shown by Western blot analysis of mouse tissue lysates (Fig. 1 O). To determine the relationship between ARNT2 loss and MYC-driven transcriptional programs, we cross-referenced the RNA-seq data from ARNT2 knockdown Rat1 myc -/- cells with datasets from Rat1 myc-/- cells expressing MYC. This analysis identified 237 genes that were upregulated by both MYC expression and ARNT2 knockdown, and 539 genes that were downregulated in both conditions, representing 72% of all genes downregulated upon ARNT2 depletion (Fig. 1 P). Remarkably, genes involved in synaptic organization and neuronal axon communication were consistently downregulated by both MYC overexpression and ARNT2 knockdown. These findings suggest that MYC may suppress a differentiated state by repressing ARNT2, a transcriptional regulator of neuronal and developmental gene programs. In the absence of ARNT2, genes required for axonal function and synaptic formation are markedly reduced, reinforcing a role for ARNT2 in maintaining differentiation-associated transcriptional states (Fig. 1 Q). This pattern is consistent with the distribution of ARNT2 mRNA across human tissues (Figure S1H), and with single-cell RNA sequencing data from the Human Protein Atlas, which show that ARNT2 is predominantly expressed in neurons and glial cells (Figure S1I). Accordingly, we identified more than 60 genes involved in neuronal axon and synaptic functions that are downregulated by both MYC overexpression and ARNT2 knockdown (Fig. 1 Q). Given its tissue distribution, we next examined the role of ARNT2 in neuronal differentiation. We used a human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) model expressing a doxycycline-inducible master neuronal transcription factor, neurogenin-2 [ 41 ] (Fig. 1 R). Induction of neurogenin-2 drove rapid differentiation of iPSCs into neuronal populations within 3 days. Western blot analysis of iPSCs before and after differentiation revealed a marked increase in ARNT2 protein upon neurogenin induction (Fig. 1 S-T), paralleling the induction of neuronal differentiation markers β3-tubulin and UCHL1, as well as acetylated tubulin, a marker of stable microtubules in axons and dendrites (Fig. 1 T). To directly test the requirement for ARNT2, we depleted ARNT2 using small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) in iPSCs cultured in the presence of doxycycline. ARNT2 knockdown reduced acetylated tubulin levels and, to a lesser extent, decreased β3-tubulin and UCHL1 expression (Fig. 1 T). In contrast, although glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) expression increased upon neurogenin induction, it was not markedly affected by ARNT2 depletion. Notably, ARNT2 knockdown did not alter expression of the stem cell markers SOX2 or OCT4. Together, these results indicate that ARNT2 promotes neuronal differentiation without affecting maintenance of pluripotency. Our results demonstrate that MYC exerts opposing effects on the transcription of PAS domain transcription factors, upregulating ARNT [ 20 ] and its growth promoting heterodimeric partners from the PAS family AHR [ 20 , 37 ] and HIF1a [ 42 ], while repressing ARNT2. Our findings extend prior studies showing that MYC plays a broad role functionally cooperating PAS domain transcription factors to regulate metabolic and proliferative programs in cancer. Together, these data position MYC as a central regulator of PAS family signaling, selectively activating pro-tumorigenic pathways while repressing lineage-specifying factors such as ARNT2.
sections.knocking out arnt2 decreases the express: Given that MYC is a proto-oncogene, which regulates the initiation and progression of many human cancers [ 8 ], we searched for the tumor types for which repression of ARNT2 by MYC may be the most biologically meaningful. Comparing ARNT2 mRNA levels in tumor and normal tissues from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and GTEx database, we found that ARNT2 levels were elevated in several cancer types including breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA), pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD), and skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM) (Fig. 2 A). In contrast, ARNT2 levels were repressed in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), and most importantly, GBM (Fig. 2 A). Interrogating a previously published single-cell RNA-seq dataset that contains non-tumor cells, IDH mutant gliomas, IDH wild-type glioma, and brain metastatic GBM [ 43 ], we found that ARNT2 levels were specifically downregulated in aggressive tumors (Figure S2A). TCGA data revealed lower ARNT2 levels in higher glioma grades (Fig. 2 B). In addition, the ARNT2 gene had a high frequency heterozygous deletion (up to 45%) in the cancer samples, including 9.2% of low-grade glioma (LGG) and 14.5% of GBM (Figure S2C). Somatic mutations in ARNT2 were also present, although at lower frequency (Figure S2C-D). To examine the relationship between ARNT2 expression and patient survival, we used the Xena Functional Genomics Explorer, which links TCGA survival data to gene expression levels. ARNT2 expression was inversely correlated with poor patient survival in 2 types of cancer: PAAD and glioma when LGG and GBM (LGG-GBM) were analyzed together (Fig. 2 C and Figure S2B). In contrast, ARNT2 expression alone did not significantly impact survival in GBM patients, likely reflecting the uniformly aggressive nature of this disease (Figure S2B). However, when gliomas were analyzed as a continuum (LGG-GBM), loss of ARNT2 expression is more clearly associated with disease aggressiveness. A prior study using TG1 cells suggested that ARNT2 expression correlates with stemness in GBM [ 35 ]. To test this possibility in patient samples, we performed Pearson correlation analyses comparing ARNT2 expression with MYC (Fig. 2 D), the stem cell markers CD133 and CD44 (Fig. 2 E), and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) (Fig. 2 F). ARNT2 expression was inversely correlated with MYC (r = −0.028), CD133 (r = −0.30), and EGFR (r = −0.025). Fig. 2 ARNT2 expression is markedly reduced in glioblastoma (GBM) tumors. Gene function information was obtained from GeneCards ( https://www.genecards.org/ ), and cancer expression (up- or downregulated) and patient survival outcomes were from GEPIA Utilizing GBM cell lines derived from diverse backgrounds (Figure S2E), we found that ARNT2 expression was highest in LN229 cells, followed by U87 cells, and was undetectable in GBM9 and SF188 cells when compared to astrocytes (Fig. 2 G). As expected for a MYC-repressed gene, the levels of ARNT2 and MYC were inversely correlated. Knocking down MYC in LN229 cells increased ARNT2 levels and reduced ARNT levels (Fig. 2 H). Knocking down MYC in U87 and SF188 cells also increased ARNT2 levels, supporting a model of MYC-mediated downregulation of ARNT2. However, ARNT2 remained undetectable in GBM9 cells, even with MYC knockdown (Figure S2F). This suggests that the regulation of ARNT2 by MYC may not be universal across all GBMs. The lack of ARNT2 expression in GBM9 cells might be due to genetic or epigenetic alterations in the ARNT2 gene or other cell-specific regulatory mechanisms independent of MYC. These findings collectively indicate that MYC-mediated regulation of ARNT2 is context dependent and may vary due to intrinsic differences among GBM subtypes. We used LN229 cells, which express the highest levels of ARNT2, to investigate the effects of ARNT2 loss in GBM cells. We knocked out ARNT2 from LN229 cells by CRISPR and selected single clones (Fig. 2 I). ARNT2 KO has no significant effects on protein levels of AHR, HIF-1α, and ARNT/HIF-1β. Two clones (B3 and C4) along with control LN229 cells were subjected to RNA-seq analysis (Fig. 2 J). We identified 129 genes upregulated and 388 genes downregulated with at least 50% expression level changes in both clones compared to control cells ( P ≤ 0.05). Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed that these genes had diverse molecular functions. Of interest, the upregulated genes were enriched in cell and neuron differentiations, various signaling pathways, and viral responses (Fig. 2 K-L). Downregulated genes included signaling pathways, cell proliferation, and biosynthesis (Fig. 2 M-N). Genes involved in neuronal differentiation, development, and function were in both upregulated and downregulated datasets (Fig. 2 L, N).
sections.knocking out arnt2 promotes the growth o: Given our initial observations suggesting that loss of ARNT2 reduces cell differentiation and promotes the expression of growth-related genes, we investigated the impact of ARNT2 loss on cell proliferation. We found that ARNT2 KO in LN229 cells did not significantly alter cell proliferation in vitro (Fig. 3 A). Similarly, knocking down ARNT2 transiently did not globally affect proliferation of Rat1 myc-/- , Rat1 myc-/- + MYC, ARPE, ARPE MYC, DLD1, LN229, U87, and GBM9 cells transfected with up to 4 ARNT2 siRNAs (Fig. 1 I-J, S3A-C). When LN229 cells were induced to differentiate by culturing in low-serum medium, ARNT2 KO increased expression of the stem cell marker Nestin and reduced the neuronal differentiation marker acetylated tubulin (Fig. 3 B). In parallel, ARNT2 loss was associated with elevated Cyclin A1 levels and increased phosphorylation of S6 kinase (Fig. 3 B), consistent with enhanced proliferative potential. Although ARNT2 loss did not impair GBM cell growth in vitro, the upregulation of growth-promoting genes suggests that ARNT2 may be essential for tumor progression in vivo. Consistent with this, when xenografted into NOD-SCID mice (Fig. 3 C) ARNT2 KO in LN229 cells resulted in reduced tumor growth (Fig. 3 D). Tumors derived from ARNT2 KO clone B3 were more than twice the weight of those from wild-type (WT) cells, while clone C4 tumors were less affected (Fig. 3 D). Western blot analysis of UCHL1 revealed reduced expression in both B3 and C4 ARNT2-deficient tumor clones compared with WT tumors, with clone B3 showing the most pronounced loss of UCHL1. Notably, this reduction correlated with the markedly larger tumor size of B3 tumors (Fig. 3 E), supporting the conclusion that ARNT2 expression promotes differentiation and constrains tumor growth. These findings also highlight the essential roles of in vivo studies in uncovering biological functions that are not readily apparent in cell culture models. Plots show mean +/− SD, and p-value was calculated by t-test. * P ≤ 0.05. I Lipid metabolism genes upregulated by both MYC and Arnt2 KD in Rat1 myc-/- cells. Log2FC cutoff 0.585 and t-test p-value < 0.05 By performing hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of paraffin-embedded tumors, we found that the only visible difference between tumors formed from control cells and ARNT2 KO cells was the presence of lipid droplet-like structures in the ARNT2 KO tumors (Fig. 3 F). Recent studies have suggested that an increase in lipid droplets in human tumor tissues, particularly GBM, is correlated with increased disease aggressiveness [ 44 ]. Our metabolomics analyses revealed that tumors derived from ARNT2 KO cells had dramatically higher levels of lipids and to a lesser extent nucleotides (Fig. 3 G), supporting the prior data on lipid droplets in human tumors. Among the lipids upregulated in ARNT2 KO tumors were 2 carnitines associated with long-chain fatty acids, which can be used to generate energy for tumor growth via β-oxidation. Furthermore, metabolomics analyses revealed dramatic increases in the levels of phospholipids in ARNT2 KO tumors. These included 11 phosphatidylcholines (PC) out of 13 readable in the metabolomics platform, 3 out of 7 phosphatidylethanolamines (PE), 1 out of 4 phosphatidylserines (PS), and 2 out of 4 sphingomyelins (SM). PC and PE are the most abundant phospholipids in all membranes of mammalian cells, including the monolayer membrane surrounding lipid droplets. It has been reported that PC and PE regulate the size and dynamics of lipid droplets, and the differentiation of adipocytes [ 45 ]. PS is the major anionic phospholipid of the brain, and it is particularly enriched in the cytoplasmic leaflet in the plasma membrane, functioning as an anionic domain that binds and thereby activates cytosolic neuronal signaling [ 46 ]. SM is highly enriched in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds axons of neurons, as well as the outer leaflet of plasma membrane. Increase in outer leaflet SM content has related to cancer initiation, growth, and immune evasion [ 47 ]. Supporting the increase in phospholipids was the lower expression of phospholipases, including several members of phospholipase A2 (except PLA2G4C), phospholipase D3 (PLD3), and a predicted phospholipase B (PLBD1), in the ARNT2 KO in our RNA-seq dataset (Fig. 3 H and S3D). Phospholipases cleave ester bonds within phospholipids to generate fatty acids and other lipophilic substances [ 48 ]. Phospholipase A2, which hydrolyzes the sn-2 acyl chain of phospholipids to generate free polyunsaturated fatty acids, is considered as the key enzyme and plays important roles in inflammation [ 49 ] and lipid droplet formation [ 50 ]. In addition to decreasing the expression of phospholipases, ARNT2 KO increased the expression level of Annexin A1 (ANXA1) (Figure S3D), which binds phospholipids and inhibits phospholipase A2 [ 51 ]. We also found that ARNT2 regulated the expression of other genes involve in lipid metabolism, including fatty acid desaturase (FADS2), which is essential to maintain stem cells state GBM cells [ 52 ]; acyl-CoA synthetase 5 (ACSL5), which activates fatty acids (FAs) by thioesterification with Coenzyme A (Fig. 3 H). In the Rat1 fibroblasts RNA-seq dataset, we found some genes involved in lipid metabolism increased in ARNT2 KD samples, including phospholipases PLA2G4A and PLCG2, fatty acid desaturase SCD1 and SCD2 (Fig. 3 I). Based on these metabolomics data and RNA-seq analysis, we propose that ARNT2 KO promotes lipid biosynthesis to sustain growth.
sections.ectopic expression of arnt2 reduces the: We generated LN229 cells expressing either empty vector (GFP vector) or GFP-tagged ARNT2 and ARNT2 overexpression had no effect on HIF-1α and ARNT/HIF-1β expression levels. (Fig. 4 A). Consistent with endogenous protein, GFP-ARNT2 localized predominantly to the nucleus, confirming that the tagged construct is functionally competent (Fig. 4 B). Although ectopic ARNT2 expression produced only a modest reduction in LN229 proliferation in vitro (Fig. 4 C), its effects in vivo were striking. In xenotransplantation experiments (Fig. 4 D), tumors derived from ARNT2-overexpressing cells were significantly smaller than those from control cells when evaluated 8 weeks after subcutaneous transplantation into NOD-SCID mice (Fig. 4 E-F and Figure S4). Western blot analysis of tumor lysates revealed markedly increased expression of the neuronal differentiation marker UCHL1 in ARNT2-overexpressing tumors (Fig. 4 G). To define the molecular identity of tumors arising from cells ectopically expressing ARNT2 relative to vector controls, we performed mass spectrometry–based proteomic profiling. Using a cutoff of ≥ twofold change and P ≤ 0.05, we identified 76 proteins significantly upregulated and 260 downregulated in ARNT2-overexpressing tumors (Fig. 4 H). Together, these findings demonstrate that enforced ARNT2 expression suppresses GBM growth in vivo while promoting tumor differentiation, supporting a tumor-suppressive role for ARNT2. Notably, a major fraction of downregulated proteins mapped to mitochondrial pathways, including electron transport chain complex I, the TCA cycle, mitochondrial transport, and lipid biosynthesis (Fig. 4 I–K), suggesting that ARNT2 constrains tumor progression in part by limiting mitochondrial metabolic capacity. sections.ectopic expression of arnt2 reduced the: To extend our findings to additional GBM cell lines, we generated GBM9 cells expressing either empty vector or ARNT2, and found no significant differences in protein levels of HIF-1 family (Fig. 5 A) and the growth of these cells in vitro (Fig. 5 B). However, xenograft tumors (Fig. 5 C) from cells expressing ARNT2 were significantly smaller than tumors from cells expressing empty vector (Fig. 5 D-E and Figure S5A). Western blots of protein lysates from excised tumors revealed modest changes in UCHL1 and Nestin in the ARNT2 expressing tumors, but significantly lower levels of the cell cycle proteins Cyclin A1 and E1 (Fig. 5 F). To better understand the importance of ARNT2 loss in GBM physiology, we performed orthotopic engraftment of either empty vector or ARNT2-expressing GBM9 cells into the brain of NOD-SCID mice (Fig. 5 G). Importantly, we found that mice injected with ARNT2-expressing cells survived longer than those injected with empty vector–expressing cells (Fig. 5 H). We found that empty vector–expressing cells formed significantly larger tumors than the ARNT2-expressing cells. Tumors were distinguishable in dissected brains because of their GFP signal (Fig. 5 I). H&E staining confirmed that tumors arising from vector-expressing cells were larger than the ones arising from ARNT2-expressing cells (Fig. 5 J). The overall morphology of tumors from cells expressing GBM9 empty vector and ARNT2 was similar (Figure S5B). As expected, Nestin was lower in ARNT2-expressing tumors than in empty vector–expressing cells (Fig. 5 K). Comparing the lysates of tumors with those of cells in culture, we found that the change of Nestin was specific to tumors (Fig. 5 L) and that MYC-nick, the cytosolic MYC variant associate with terminally differentiated tissues [ 12 ], accumulated in ARNT2-expressing tumors (Fig. 5 K). M Working model of MYC regulating neuronal identity by repressing ARNT2 Together, our results support a working model in which ARNT2 expression promotes a gene program that enables expression of genes directly involved in axon pathfinding, synapse formation, and neurite outgrowth, thereby supporting the differentiation of central nervous system cell types such as neurons and astrocytes. We propose that MYC upregulation represses ARNT2 transcription, leading to loss of neuronal identity gene expression and facilitating stemness and tumor growth in GBM cells (Fig. 5 M).
sections.discussion: The molecular mechanisms by which MYC promotes the activation of genes that drive metabolic and proliferation in cancer is well established, yet how transformation by MYC limits differentiation in aggressive tumors is not fully understood. Our findings identify repression of the neuronal transcription factor ARNT2 as a critical player through which MYC limits differentiation and promotes GBM progression. Our results suggest that polycomb repressor complex is responsible for repressing ARNT2 downstream of MYC. Interestingly, a similar mechanistic model has been proposed for prostate cancer, where MYC prevents differentiation by upregulating EZH2 [ 53 ]. We propose that regulation of bHLH-PAS transcription factors by MYC plays a vital role in cellular functions [ 54 ]. For example, MYC-mediated deregulation of the circadian clock genes, CLOCK and BMAL1, affects growth specialization in various tissues. Importantly, disruption of the circadian clock by MYC impairs cellular differentiation and promotes tumorigenesis [ 55 ]. The MYC-induced gene ARNT [ 20 ] shares a high degree of similarity with ARNT2, including 61% overall sequence identity and conservation of 12 out of 13 amino acids in the basic region, as well as 80% identity across the HLH and PAS domains. Although ARNT is ubiquitously expressed, ARNT2 is primarily restricted to the brain and has been linked to neuroprotective functions. During neuronal differentiation, ARNT2 expression increases while the ARNT mRNA level decreases [ 56 ], thus further demonstrating that these factors are not functionally similar. The role of ARNT2 in cancer remains complicated, with various studies reporting both pro- and anti-tumorigenic functions. In some contexts, ARNT2 may function as an oncogene in specific tumor types, such as oral cancers [ 31 ]. In other studies, ARNT2 expression is linked to reduced cell proliferation and improved prognosis, as shown in gastric cancer and liver cancer [ 27 , 28 ]. Our findings stand in contrast with prior reports that proposed ARNT2 as a positive regulator of GBM malignancy, which identified ARNT2 in a screen comparing 2 cell models (TG1 and TG1-miR) and suggested a link between ARNT2 and a stem-like phenotype based on its co-expression with stem cell markers and its association with a HIF-like signature [ 35 ]. Our study aligns with a single-cell RNA-seq study that reported co-expression of ARNT2 with stemness genes in GBM specimens [ 57 ]. In contrast, we established downstream effectors (transcriptional and metabolic) of ARNT2 and demonstrated its function through gain- and loss-of-function experiments in vitro and in vivo using non-stem GBM models. We recognize that ARNT2’s role in GBM may be context dependent. Differences between our study and previous reports may reflect the use of different models (e.g., stem-like vs. non-stem), tumor subtype heterogeneity, or variable microenvironmental influences. Similar to GBM, human breast cancer tissues have lower ARNT2 expression, and overexpressing ARNT2 inhibits breast cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and tumor growth and metastasis in vivo [ 29 , 30 ]. Collectively, our findings reveal that MYC-mediated repression of ARNT2 is a key axis for suppressing lineage commitment in GBM. Restoring ARNT2 expression or mimicking its downstream effects could offer a new strategy to reduce tumor aggressiveness in MYC-driven brain cancers. Ectopic expression of ARNT2 suppresses tumor growth and reactivates differentiation programs, positioning ARNT2 as a tumor suppressor-like gene in GBM. We now show that ARNT2, which is thought to be closely related to ARNT, is repressed by MYC. Studies by others showed that GBM requires a large amount of lipids for rapid growth and that substantial quantities of lipids are stored as the form of lipid droplets, which are undetectable in normal brain tissues [ 58 , 59 ]. Lipid droplets play critical roles in GBM growth and survival [ 60 ], which we suggest being at least in part, regulated by ARNT2. Our findings integrate several key features of gliomagenesis: the role of MYC in blocking lineage specification, the loss of neuronal identity in high-grade gliomas, and the metabolic rewiring required to sustain tumor growth. It remains to be determined how loss of ARNT2 in MYC-dependent tumors influences the expression and functional interactions of other PAS domain transcription factors, including HIFs and the circadian regulators BMAL1 and CLOCK.
sections.sex as a biological variable: We used female NOD-SCID mice for our xenograft experiments. No sex differences have been observed in xenografting cells in males and females.
sections.cell cultures: Embryonic Rat1 fibroblasts, human epithelial cell ARPE-19, human colon cancer cell DLD1, and human GBM cells GBM9, SF188, U87 and LN229 were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS, 100 U/mL pen/strep. Human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) with doxycycline-inducible neurogenin-2 (NGN2), gifted from Dr. Erik Ullian (UCSF), were cultured in Essential 8 (E8) medium. Neuronal differentiation was induced using induction medium (DMEM/F12, HEPES + N2 Supplement + Non-essential Amino Acids + L-Glutamine + 2 µg/mL doxycycline) for 3 days [ 41 ]. siRNA was reverse transfected to cells with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX reagent following the standard protocol. Briefly, on the day of transfection, 2.5 × 10 5 cells were seeded per well in 6-well plates and transfected with 5 µL siRNA (20 µM) and 5 µL Lipofectamine previously mixed in Opti-MEM for 15min. After 72 h of transfection, cells were collected and analyzed.
sections.stable cell lines: ARNT2 knockout (KO) cells were generated by transfecting ARNT2 CRISPR/Cas9 KO Plasmid (Santa Cruz sc-403101) into LN229 cells with Lipofectamine LTX&Plus reagent. Three days after transfection, GFP-positive cells were sorted using flow cytometry, and single clones were selected to verify the knockout by using Western blots. For cell lines stably expressing ARNT2, the ARNT2 gene was constructed into pIRESpuro vector with N-terminal GFP tag, and the construct with the empty vector was transfected into LN229 cells. The cells that stably expressed these constructs were selected with 5 μg/mL puromycin. The ARNT2 gene was also constructed into pIRESneo vector with no tag. This construct with the empty vector was transfected into GBM9 cells. The cells stably expressing these constructs were selected with 1 mg/mL G418.
sections.cell viability assays: Cell proliferation was measured using the Incucyte live-cell imaging system. Cells were seeded at 1,000 cells per well in 96-well plates and cultured for 5 days. Time points immediately prior to plateau of the growth curves were selected for presentation. Cell growth was quantified as percent confluence and normalized to control samples at time 0. Six replicates per condition were run concurrently, and the average values were graphed.
sections.immunofluorescence staining and microsco: Immunofluorescence was performed as previously described [ 20 , 61 ]. In short, cells grown on glass coverslips were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 15 min at RT, and permeabilized in blocking buffer (0.1% Saponin, 3% BSA in PBS) for 20 min at 4 °C. Primary antibodies in blocking buffer were added and incubated 1 h at RT. Cells were washed 3 times with 0.1% Saponin in PBS and incubated with secondary antibodies in blocking buffer for 1 h at RT. The nuclei were stained with DAPI. Images were acquired with a Zeiss LSM780 microscope.
sections.western blots of total cell lysates and: Total protein was extracted with lysis buffer containing 10 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.7), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% Nonidet P-40, proteinase inhibitor cocktail (SIGMAFAST™ Protease Inhibitor Cocktail Tablets, EDTA-Free), and 1 mM DTT. For fractionation, the cells were extracted with Buffer A (10 mM HEPES–KOH pH 7.9, 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.5% Nonidet P-40) plus proteinase inhibitor cocktail and 1 mM DTT by vortex. The samples were spun at 4,000 rpm for 4 min, and the supernatants were collected as cytoplasmic fractions. The pellets were washed twice with Buffer A and then extracted with Buffer B (20 mM HEPES–KOH pH 7.9, 400 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.2 mM EDTA, 15% glycerol) plus proteinase inhibitor cocktail and 1 mM DTT with sonication. The samples were spun at 15,000 rpm for 10 min, and the supernatants were collected as nuclear fraction. Protein concentrations were measured by using the Bradford protein assay, and the samples were normalized to same protein concentration. Proteins were separated by SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and then transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Thermo Fisher), probed with specific antibodies, and detected by using chemiluminescence with the Bio-Rad Image lab.
sections.rna-seq: Rat1 myc-/- shControl and Rat1 myc-/- shARNT2 cells, WT and ANRT2 KO LN229 cells were processed for RNA extraction and sequencing (GENEWIZ). RNA-seq assessment of the raw sequencing reads was done using the NGS-QC-Toolkit [ 62 ]. The reads were aligned to the genome RGSC 6.0/rn6 using HISAT2 (v 2.1.0) aligner. A minimum read count filter of 10 total reads was applied to remove low-expressed genes. Filtered reads were then normalized using DESeq2. DeSeq2 employs a negative binomial distribution to estimate data variability and uses an error model for a more robust statistical test for significance. An FDR cutoff of ≤ 5% was used to select significantly altered genes between experiment conditions. GO analysis was performed with Enrichr ( https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/ ). LN229 RNA-seq data was deposited in GEO with ID GSE236486 .
sections.rt-qpcr: RNA was extracted from cells with QIAGEN RNeasy Mini Kit and reverse transcribed to cDNA with High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Thermo Fisher). Relative RNA levels were measured by qPCR with iTaq™ Universal SYBR® Green Supermix (Bio-Rad) and the Bio-Rad CFX96 device and normalized to 18S rRNA gene.
sections.bioinformatics analysis: ARNT2 mRNA expression in tumor and normal tissues across multiple cancer types was analyzed using the Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis (GEPIA) web server, based on TCGA and GTEx datasets. The cutoff values were set at |log2FC|≥ 0.585 and P ≤ 0.01. Kaplan–Meier survival curves comparing patients in the top 25% versus bottom 25% of gene expression were generated using GEPIA2 ( http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn ). Gene expression across glioma grades was obtained from TCGA datasets. Figures 2 L, N and 4 K were generated using gene function information obtained from gene cards https://www.genecards.org/ ) and cancer expression (up or down) and patient survival outcomes from GEPIA.
sections.subcutaneous xenografts: LN229 or GBM9 cells suspended in 30% Matrigel were injected into one flank of each female NOD-SCID mouse (purchased from Jackson lab). Prior to injection, viable cell numbers were determined using Trypan Blue exclusion quantified with Cellomics imaging, which allows for precise and reproducible counting of live cells. Tumor-bearing mice were sacrificed when the largest tumors in the cohort reached ~ 2 cm. At the end of each experiment, tumors were harvested, weighed, and either snap frozen in liquid nitrogen for protein extraction or fixed with 10% formalin for histology. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (approval number: 2017–101798).
sections.orthotopic xenografts: GBM9 cells suspended in HBSS (Ca-, Mg-) were injected orthotopically into the striatum of 9 weeks old NOD-SCID mice using the following coordinates (AP, 0 mm; ML, −2.5 mm; DV, −3 mm) using bregma as the starting cranial landmark (Note that although the injection took place at a depth of −3 mm in the dorsal/ventricle plane, cells were injected at −2.5 mm in the dorsal/ventricle plane to allow for a 0.5 mm gap in which cells could accumulate). Cells were injected at a rate of 1 µL/20 s over 1 min, followed by a 30-s hold before removing the syringe. All injections were facilitated through the use of a stereotactic frame. Viable cell numbers were determined using Trypan Blue exclusion with Cellomics imaging, which allows for precise and reproducible counting of live cells. Mice were monitored weekly using bioluminescent imaging to confirm tumor engraftment and progression. Mice were euthanized based on co-morbidities, including weight, seizures, hunched back, matted fur, and head swelling.
sections.histology: Tumor tissues from xenografts experiments were fixed with 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 2 days and then transferred to 70% ethanol. Tumors were then embedded in paraffin and sectioned into 5-μm thick sections. The sections were stained with H&E performed by the UT Southwestern Medical Center (UTSW) tissue core as previously described [ 63 ].
sections.metabolomics analyses: Metabolomics were performed as previously described [ 64 ] using 20 mg of xenograft tumor tissues were homogenized and extracted with 300 μL of ice-cold methanol/water 80:20 (vol/vol), and then dried in a speedvac. Qualitative assessment of global metabolites by GC–MS were performed by the metabolomics facility at the Children’s Research Institute (UTSW) using a cutoff of 30% changes and p-value under 0.1. VIP scores were calculated using Metaboanalyst 5.0 and used to obtain pathways and heatmaps.
sections.lc\u2013ms/ms: Xenograft tumor samples of LN229 cells expressing GFP vector or GFP-tagged ARNT2 were homogenized in lysis buffer (10 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.7), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% Nonidet P-40), and total lysates were sent to UTSW Proteomics Core for complex identification on Orbitrap Fusion Lumos instrument. MS scans were acquired at 120,000 resolution in the Orbitrap and up to 10 MS/MS spectra were obtained in the ion trap for each full spectrum acquired using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) for ions with charges 2–7. Dynamic exclusion was set for 25 s after an ion was selected for fragmentation. The data were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer 3.0 and were searched using the human protein database from UniProt. The false-discovery rate (FDR) cut-off was 1% for all peptides. Proteins identified by at least 2 peptides were used for the analysis. Fold changes and p-values were calculated using the peptide abundance values, and in general changes with |Log2FC|> 1 and P ≤ 0.05 were considered significant.
sections.quantification and statistical analysis: All statistical analyses were performed using two-tailed student T-test or ANOVA test. P ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All values are reported as mean ± SD in each figure.
sections.supplementary information_1: Supplementary Material 1. Supplementary Material 2.

title: Economic Evaluation of PCV21 Use in Populations with Increasing Serotype 4 Invasive Pneumococcal Disease in the US: An Attributable Fraction Threshold Analysis
abstract: Introduction The 21-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV21) covers 83–88% of IPD in US adults but does not include serotype 4 (ST4), which is covered by previously recommended vaccines (PPSV23, PCV15, PCV20). Recent increases in IPD cases due to ST4 have been observed, particularly among adults under 65, including Native American/Alaskan Native and those with social risk factors. As a result, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends ST4-containing vaccines (PPSV23, PCV15, and PCV20) for populations with ≥ 30% ST4 IPD cases. In this study, we aimed to analyze ST4 attributable fraction (AF) thresholds for health and economic outcomes of PCV21 versus PCV20 vaccination in US adults aged 19–49 and 50–64 years with underlying medical conditions. Methods We used a validated Markov model to estimate incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for PCV21 versus PCV20 and identified ST4 AF thresholds in which the ICER shifted from ‘cost-saving’ to ‘not cost-effective’. The analysis involved a hypothetical 1 million at-risk adults aged 19–49 and 50–64 years. Results PCV21 remained cost-saving compared to PCV20 when ST4 accounted for ≤ 27% (age 19–49) or ≤ 36% (age 50–64) of IPD. When ST4 increases were applied to both IPD and NBPP, these thresholds decreased to ≤ 21% and ≤ 28%, respectively. Conclusion For populations experiencing moderate increases in the proportion of ST4 (i.e., < 30%), PCV21 may offer health and economic benefits over PCV20 for US adults aged 19–64 years with underlying medical conditions. However, in populations with ≥ 30% ST4, ST4-containing vaccines should be used as per ACIP guidance.
