sections.relationship between sfc/dti-alps and co: Among the 216 ID patients who completed cognitive assessments, we investigated the associations between SFC and WM performance using partial correlation analyses. The results revealed that only Sub-SFC showed a significant positive correlation with WM performance ( r = 0.28, pFDR < 0.001; Figure 3h) , while no significant partial correlations were observed for other measures ( Figure 3d – f ). Using the same partial correlation analysis, the DTI-ALPS was also found to be significantly associated with WM performance ( r = 0.30, pFDR < 0.001; Figure 3i ), supporting the association between better WM and stronger glymphatic clearance. This pattern was fully preserved when analyzing the two hemispheres separately, with significant associations observed for both the left ( r = 0.33, pFDR < 0.001) and right ( r = 0.26, pFDR < 0.001) DTI-ALPS indices ( Figure S4 ). Based on these findings, no significant association was observed between global SFC and WM performance. To further explore the neural mechanisms underlying the relationship between sleep quality and WM performance in ID patients, subsequent mediation analyses in this study focused on examining the mediating roles of Sub-SFC and the DTI-ALPS in the association between sleep quality and WM performance in individuals with ID.
sections.network-specific effects of sfc on worki: We first established a mediation model with PSQI as the independent variable, TEML as the dependent variable, and the DTI-ALPS as the mediator. The results showed that the DTI-ALPS significantly negatively mediated the relationship between PSQI and TEML ( β = −0.048 [23.65% of the total effect], SE = 0.018, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.086 to −0.017, Figure 4a ). Next, we modified the mediation model by changing the mediator to the Sub-SFC while keeping PSQI as the independent variable and TEML as the dependent variable. The results showed that Sub-SFC significantly negatively mediated the relationship between PSQI and TEML ( β = −0.051 [25.12% of the total effect], SE = 0.020, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.090 to −0.012, Figure 4b ). These findings indicate that poorer sleep quality was associated with worse WM performance in ID patients, with Sub-SFC partially mediating this association. To assess whether the moderation pattern reported in healthy older adults (Ma et al., 2025 ) also appears in our clinical insomnia sample, we conducted an exploratory moderated mediation analysis. Participants were divided into lower- and higher-PSQI subgroups based on a median split, indexing relatively less versus more severe sleep disturbance. In PROCESS Model 14, DTI-ALPS served as the predictor, Sub-SFC as the mediator, TEML as the outcome, and the PSQI subgroup as a moderator of the association between Sub-SFC and WM. The interaction showed a trend-level effect ( β = −0.225, p = 0.076; index of moderated mediation = −0.058, bootstrapped 95% CI =[−0.140, 0.009]; Figure S5a ), suggesting potential variation in the coupling–memory relationship across PSQI levels. Follow-up mediation analyses further indicated that the indirect effect via Sub-SFC emerged only in the lower-PSQI subgroup ( Figure S5b–c ). Figure 4. Mediation of working memory. Finally, to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying WM impairment through the combined effects of network-specific SFC and DTI-ALPS, we established a serial mediation model with sleep quality as the independent variable, WM performance as the dependent variable, and DTI-ALPS and Sub-SFC as mediators. The results revealed a significant direct effect of PSQI on TEML, indicating that poorer sleep quality is associated with worse WM performance ( β = −0.129 (63.55% of the total effect), SE = 0.053, 95% CI = −0.233 to −0.025). Importantly, the relationship between PSQI and TEML was significantly mediated by both DTI-ALPS and Sub-SFC ( β = −0.074 [36.62% of the total effect], SE = 0.025, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.127 to −0.030, Figure 4c ). Specifically, the indirect effect via DTI-ALPS was significant ( β = −0.040 [19.71% of the total effect], SE = 0.015, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.073 to −0.012), while the indirect effect via Sub-SFC was also significant ( β = −0.026 [12.44% of the total effect], SE = 0.026, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.061 to −0.001). Furthermore, a serial mediation path was identified, where PSQI influenced TEML through both DTI-ALPS and Sub-SFC ( β = −0.008 [4.09% of the total effect], SE = 0.006, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.023 to −0.001). Among the three models, the single-mediator model involving Sub-SFC (Model 2) yielded the lowest AIC and BIC (AIC = 994.41, BIC = 1017.50), and was therefore considered the best-fitting model according to information criteria ( Table S4 ). We additionally confirmed that the mediation effects remained robust when left and right DTI-ALPS values were analyzed separately, yielding patterns highly consistent with the results based on mean DTI-ALPS ( Figure S6 ). Given prior evidence that handedness can influence hemispheric structural and functional asymmetries (Tejavibulya et al., 2025 ), we repeated both the partial correlation analyses and the serial mediation model while controlling for handedness. When handedness was included as a covariate, the partial correlations among the main variables remained highly consistent with the original results. Similarly, adding handedness to the serial mediation model produced an indirect effect that was virtually identical to the primary analysis ( β = −0.075, 36.94% of the total effect, SE = 0.025, bootstrapped 95% CI = −0.127 to −0.030). These findings suggest that the influence of sleep quality on WM performance is partially transmitted via alterations in DTI-ALPS and Sub-SFC, which serve as key neurophysiological mediators.
sections.discussion: This study systematically investigated the complex relationships between sleep quality, DTI-ALPS, and SFC, as well as their impact on WM in ID patients, based on multimodal neuroimaging data. First, we found that poor sleep quality in ID patients was significantly associated with reduced DTI-ALPS and SFC. Second, DTI-ALPS showed specific associations with multimodal brain network features, particularly stronger SFC within the visual network and subcortical network, which were linked to higher DTI-ALPS, while the opposite pattern was observed in the limbic network. Most importantly, both DTI-ALPS and SFC within the subcortical network were positively associated with WM performance and jointly mediated the relationship between sleep quality and WM. To our knowledge, this is the first clinical study to apply DTI-ALPS and SFC analysis in ID patients, providing novel evidence for the neurobiological mechanisms underlying WM impairment in this population.
sections.sleep quality and dti-alps: There is a close physiological relationship between sleep and the brain’s glymphatic function. Recent studies have found that the activity of the glymphatic system exhibits significant circadian rhythmicity, with a substantial increase during sleep and a marked suppression during wakefulness (Voumvourakis et al., 2023 ). In this study, we observed that poorer sleep quality was associated with reduced glymphatic function, a phenomenon that has been validated in multiple independent studies (Ma et al., 2025 ; Taoka et al., 2024 ). This result suggests that a decline in sleep quality may interfere with fluid convection in perivascular spaces, thereby affecting the efficiency of metabolic waste clearance (Carley & Farabi, 2016 ). The neuroprotective role of sleep largely depends on glymphatic clearance of neurotoxic substances, such as Aβ (Reddy & van der Werf, 2020 ). This study used the DTI-ALPS as an imaging marker for evaluating glymphatic function. This technique offers the advantage of being completely noninvasive and has shown good consistency with results obtained from traditional intrathecal contrast agent injection methods (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Notably, the high correlation between bilateral DTI-ALPS indices indicates robust spatial consistency and minimal hemispheric asymmetry in glymphatic measurements. This finding aligns with previous studies reporting comparable left–right consistency in both healthy individuals and patients with insomnia disorder (Xiong et al., 2025 ), supporting the reliability of the DTI-ALPS method. In addition, the overall DTI-ALPS values in our sample were within the expected range reported in prior literature, further validating the robustness of our measurement approach (Ma et al., 2025 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ). At the same time, the cross-sectional nature of our study does not allow us to determine the directionality of these associations. A bidirectional relationship between sleep and glymphatic function is also plausible (Hauglund & Nedergaard, 2025 ; Xiao, Marshall, & Yin, 2025 ). Chronic dysregulation of glymphatic clearance could promote the accumulation of neurotoxic metabolites, neuroinflammation, and vascular stiffness, which may in turn fragment sleep, alter sleep architecture, or increase nocturnal arousals (Cai et al., 2024 ). From this perspective, reduced glymphatic efficiency might not only be a consequence of poor sleep but could also contribute to the maintenance or worsening of sleep disturbances. Longitudinal and interventional studies that track changes in both sleep and DTI-ALPS over time will be needed to disentangle these potential causal pathways (Gottesman et al., 2024 ). PSQI subdimension analyses showed that both decreased sleep efficiency and increased frequency of hypnotic medication use were significantly associated with reduced glymphatic function. This finding may be because low sleep efficiency is often accompanied by prominent features of sleep fragmentation (Dashti et al., 2016 ), including prolonged wake time after sleep onset and increased micro-arousal frequency. Existing research has shown that such fragmented sleep can significantly suppress slow-wave activity during non-REM sleep (Ferri et al., 2010 ). Given that the glymphatic system’s metabolic clearance function relies heavily on the rhythmic expansion of perivascular spaces driven by neurovascular coupling during slow-wave sleep, reduced slow-wave activity caused by sleep fragmentation directly hinders the cerebrospinal–interstitial fluid exchange process (Fultz et al., 2019 ). Additionally, although frequent use of sedative medications may improve difficulties in initiating sleep, it may also interfere with glymphatic clearance by altering sleep architecture (Antila et al., 2024 ). However, it should be noted that in the present study sleep quality was assessed solely through subjective reports. Subjective ratings of sleep efficiency and medication use can be affected by recall bias and insomnia-related sleep misperception (Lv, Zhang, Fan, Chen, et al., 2025 ), and therefore, our findings should be interpreted as reflecting associations between perceived sleep quality and glymphatic function rather than objectively quantified sleep architecture. Future multimodal studies integrating questionnaires with actigraphy and/or polysomnography are needed to determine whether similar glymphatic alterations emerge when sleep is characterized using objective parameters, such as total sleep time, slow-wave activity, or arousal indices.
sections.the role of sfc in supporting glymphatic: At the global level, we observed a significant positive correlation between SFC and the DTI-ALPS, suggesting that stronger structural-functional coupling is associated with better glymphatic function. The SFC reflects the degree to which anatomical connections support functional communication, and may be particularly sensitive to the efficiency and adaptability of inter-regional information transfer. This integrative property likely contributes to SFC’s predictive advantage in cognitive performance and its sensitivity to pathological disruptions in brain networks (Liu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ). At the network level, the association between SFC and glymphatic function showed distinct patterns across RSNs. Notably, VN-SFC and Sub-SFC were positively correlated with the DTI-ALPS, whereas LN-SFC was negatively correlated. These findings indicate that the relationship between structure–function alignment and glymphatic efficiency is network-specific and may vary along the brain’s functional hierarchy. This pattern aligns with the concept of a unimodal-to-transmodal gradient of structure–function decoupling (Facca, Del Felice, & Bertoldo, 2024 ; Valk et al., 2022 ). In unimodal systems such as the VN and somatosensory-related networks, higher SFC may support more stable neurovascular dynamics and facilitate glymphatic clearance, which could help maintain glymphatic efficiency even in the context of poor sleep. In contrast, elevated SFC within transmodal networks such as the LN may reflect a more rigid or maladaptive coupling pattern, potentially associated with reduced network flexibility and impaired glymphatic function (Deco et al., 2021 ). In patients with ID, such a network-specific imbalance may have particular relevance for pathophysiology (Fasiello et al., 2022 ). Stronger coupling in limbic circuits that are involved in emotional salience, arousal regulation, and rumination could contribute to persistent hyperarousal and difficulties disengaging from internally focused or affectively laden processing during the night, which in turn may be linked to both reduced glymphatic efficiency and poorer WM performance (Baglioni et al., 2014 ; Riemann et al., 2010 ). Thus, our findings suggest that altered SFC patterns in insomnia may reflect an insomnia-specific reconfiguration of SFC that affects both nocturnal clearance processes and daytime cognition.
sections.wm performance correlates of sfc and gly: Our results demonstrated a positive correlation between the DTI-ALPS and WM performance. A growing body of evidence indicates that maintaining glymphatic clearance of neurotoxic waste (e.g. Aβ) is essential for preserving cognitive function and promoting brain health, with memory performance appearing especially sensitive to such effects (Shen et al., 2022 ). Impairments in glymphatic function can lead to abnormal accumulation of Aβ, which has been identified as a central mechanism underlying memory decline (Voumvourakis et al., 2023 ). Notably, studies in animal models have demonstrated that enhancing glymphatic outflow reduces Aβ and tau deposition and improves memory performance in Alzheimer’s disease models (Lee et al., 2020 ). Collectively, these findings highlight the clinical potential of targeting glymphatic function as an intervention strategy to improve memory and possibly prevent dementia progression in ID patients. At the global level, no significant association was found between SFC and WM performance. Although previous studies have reported associations between SFC and cognition, these findings are primarily based on nonclinical populations (Medaglia et al., 2018 ; Siow et al., 2022 ), limiting their generalizability. For instance, one study involving healthy older adults showed that sleep quality, as measured by the PSQI, moderated the relationship between global SFC and memory performance: the association was significant only among individuals with good sleep, and not among those with poor sleep quality (Ma et al., 2025 ). Our findings in a clinical insomnia sample are consistent with this perspective, showing that global SFC does not significantly predict WM performance under impaired sleep conditions. Moreover, the literature remains inconclusive regarding the relationship between global SFC and cognitive function. While some studies report that increased global SFC is associated with cognitive decline (Wang et al., 2018 ), others have suggested that it may support cognitive flexibility (Medaglia et al., 2018 ) and facilitate complex task execution (Griffa et al., 2022 ). These inconsistencies point to the limitations of using whole-brain average SFC measures, which may obscure critical regional variations in SFC. In contrast, network-specific SFC indices may provide more sensitive and informative markers of the neural basis of cognitive processing and offer better predictive utility for individual cognitive performance (Baum et al., 2020 ; Popp et al., 2024 ). Supporting this hypothesis, our further analysis revealed a significant positive association between Sub-SFC and WM performance. This finding underscores the importance of considering network-specific coupling metrics, particularly under pathological conditions such as ID, where the brain’s network dynamics may become more spatially localized and functionally specialized.
sections.potential mechanisms underlying the impa: The main finding of this study is that glymphatic function and the Sub-SFC jointly mediate the relationship between sleep quality and WM performance in ID patients. Working memory, one of the core cognitive functions, refers to the ability to temporarily store and manipulate task-relevant information. It plays a crucial role in executive functions and emotional regulation, thereby setting fundamental limits on an individual’s cognitive abilities (Miller, Lundqvist, & Bastos, 2018 ). A wealth of research has shown that sleep deprivation negatively affects WM performance (Almarzouki et al., 2022 ; Wardle-Pinkston, Slavish, & Taylor, 2019 ; Xie et al., 2019 ). From a cognitive process perspective, several hypotheses have been proposed to explain this relationship, such as sleep deprivation potentially increasing retroactive interference or diverting attention, which in turn impairs memory capacity (Rasch & Born, 2013 ). However, there is still no consensus on the neural mechanisms underlying how sleep quality impacts WM. This study provides new insights through multimodal imaging data. As previously mentioned, poor sleep quality typically leads to a reduction in extracellular volume, which decreases the rate of molecular transport (L. Xie et al., 2013 ), thereby impairing glymphatic system function. This impairment in the glymphatic system’s clearance ability results in the accumulation of toxic proteins (e.g. Aβ) and misfolded proteins, a process considered to be one of the core neural mechanisms underlying memory impairment (Voumvourakis et al., 2023 ). Therefore, our first mediation model suggests that poorer sleep quality was associated with reduced glymphatic function, which in turn was associated with worse WM performance. The second mediation model suggests that Sub-SFC partially mediated the association between sleep quality and WM performance. According to the Brainnetome Atlas, subcortical regions, including the hippocampus, thalamus, basal ganglia, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, and insula, are responsible for coordinating perception, memory, emotion, motor control, and motivation. These regions are crucial for WM, particularly in maintaining information, directing attention, and filtering irrelevant stimuli (Fan et al., 2016 ; Sander, Lindenberger, & Werkle-Bergner, 2012 ). Previous studies have shown that regional SFC within subcortical regions (e.g. thalamus) is negatively correlated with insomnia severity in female patients (Wu et al., 2023 ), supporting our finding that poorer sleep quality is associated with lower Sub-SFC. Subcortical regions are typically part of unimodal networks and exhibit lower SFC than multimodal networks (e.g. DMN; Valk et al., 2022 ). However, for unimodal regions, tight structural-functional alignment is vital for efficient neural processing (Taoka et al., 2017 ; Zamani Esfahlani et al., 2022 ). High SFC enhances the capacity of structural pathways to support local functional demands, thereby improving the speed and fidelity of information transfer (Gu, Jamison, Sabuncu, & Kuceyeski, 2021 ). Thus, a stronger Sub-SFC may provide greater structural support and metabolic efficiency, enabling subcortical regions to execute WM-related tasks more effectively. In this way, sleep quality indirectly influences WM performance through its modulation of Sub-SFC. Poor sleep disrupts this coupling, thereby impairing the execution of information maintenance, attentional control, and emotional regulation within these regions. Finally, this study identified that both glymphatic function and Sub-SFC jointly mediate the relationship between sleep quality and WM performance, with a positive association observed between glymphatic efficiency and Sub-SFC. Previous research has shown that glymphatic dysfunction impairs CSF clearance along perivascular pathways by narrowing perivascular spaces and reducing aquaporin-4 activity, which in turn hinders the removal of metabolic waste and contributes to white matter injury, including demyelination (Iliff et al., 2012 ). Such impairment may also lead to the accumulation of neurotoxic proteins, triggering neuroinflammatory or neurodegenerative processes, particularly in subcortical regions where clearance is less efficient (Voumvourakis et al., 2023 ; Wang & Holtzman, 2020 ). These pathological changes can damage the white matter tracts within the subcortical regions, thereby disrupting SFC. Notably, glymphatic dysfunction has been linked to tau accumulation predominantly in subcortical regions, rather than cortical areas, with this subcortical tau burden mediating the relationship between clearance impairment and clinical severity in neurodegenerative conditions (Hsu et al., 2024 ). Similarly, acute sleep deprivation has been shown to increase amyloid-β accumulation in subcortical regions such as the hippocampus and thalamus, negatively correlating with total sleep time (Shokri-Kojori et al., 2018 ). These findings suggest a plausible mechanism through which impaired glymphatic clearance, as a consequence of poor sleep, may contribute to WM deficits by affecting subcortical white matter pathways and disrupting the SFCs they support. In this way, our results highlight a potential sleep–glymphatic–SFC pathway that may underlie cognitive impairments in ID patients. Nevertheless, interactive or bidirectional relationships between glymphatic function and SFC remain biologically plausible. One possibility is that glymphatic clearance and SFC form a mutually constraining system: impaired clearance may increase metabolic burden and compromise white-matter–dependent communication, whereas altered coupling may also relate to structural vulnerability in regions where clearance is less efficient. This perspective implies that glymphatic function could moderate the cognitive consequences of network coupling (or vice versa), rather than acting solely as an upstream mediator. However, because the data are cross-sectional, this pathway should be interpreted as an associational pattern rather than a causal sequence, and the temporal directionality among sleep quality, DTI-ALPS, SFC, and cognition cannot be definitively established. Future studies employing longitudinal designs, experimental manipulations, or both can directly test potential interaction effects and clarify the temporal ordering of these processes.
sections.limitations: This study has several limitations that should be noted. First, the cross-sectional design limits the ability to draw causal inferences. Although mediation models can characterize statistical associations, they cannot establish temporal precedence or determine whether alterations in DTI-ALPS or SFC directly contribute to memory deficits. Future longitudinal or sleep-manipulation studies will be necessary to clarify the causal directionality among sleep quality, glymphatic dynamics, SFC, and cognitive performance. Second, the study lacked a healthy control group. Without a comparison sample, it remains unclear whether the observed levels of glymphatic function, SFC, or WM performance in ID patients are significantly altered or pathological. This absence limits the interpretability of group-level abnormalities and prevents inferences regarding the relative impairment of glymphatic dynamics in insomnia disorder. Moreover, because the glymphatic system remains insufficiently characterized in human neuroscience (Voumvourakis et al., 2023 ), and DTI-ALPS is an indirect proxy rather than a direct measure of glymphatic dynamics (Tzschätzsch et al., 2018 ), the biological mechanisms underlying the observed associations cannot be specified with certainty. In particular, DTI-ALPS does not allow us to determine whether the links to cognition reflect direct effects or indirect pathways related to homeostatic regulation and neuroinflammation. Accordingly, mechanistic interpretations should be made with caution, and future work combining complementary glymphatic-sensitive measures with longitudinal or experimental designs will be important for clarifying these pathways. Third, WM was assessed using the digit span backward task, which may primarily reflect short-term memory capacity rather than dynamic WM processes (St Clair-Thompson, 2010 ). Future studies should consider established paradigms like the N-back task for validation. Fourth, sleep quality was measured solely through self-report, which may be affected by individual biases and emotional states (Pierson-Bartel & Ujma, 2024 ) and, therefore, may attenuate the strength of brain–behavior associations observed in this study. The absence of objective sleep measures such as actigraphy or polysomnography also limits our ability to determine how specific physiological aspects of sleep, such as total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave activity, or arousal burden, relate to glymphatic function and SFC. Future studies incorporating both subjective questionnaires and objective sleep assessments would provide a more comprehensive characterization of sleep disturbances and strengthen the interpretability and generalizability of sleep–brain relationships in ID. Finally, glymphatic function was estimated using DTI-ALPS indices from the lateral ventricles. Although previous work supports this approach (Zhang et al., 2021 ), regional heterogeneity in glymphatic pathways (McKnight et al., 2021 ) means that lateral ventricular measures may not fully capture whole-brain glymphatic dynamics.
sections.conclusion: This study provides novel evidence linking reduced DTI-ALPS and disrupted SFC to WM deficits in patients with insomnia disorder. Using multimodal neuroimaging, we demonstrate that poorer sleep quality is associated with reduced DTI-ALPS, which in turn correlates with lower SFC within the subcortical network and diminished WM performance. Importantly, these two neurophysiological mechanisms jointly mediate the effect of sleep disturbance on WM. Our findings highlight a network-specific, biologically plausible pathway through which disrupted sleep physiology contributes to domain-specific cognitive impairments. These results underscore the clinical value of DTI-ALPS and SFC as potential neuroimaging biomarkers for identifying insomnia-related cognitive vulnerability.

title: Renal replacement therapy in patients under extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: a narrative review
abstract: Background The use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has expanded for severe respiratory and circulatory failure. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is one of the most frequent complications. Up to 85% of ECMO patients develop AKI and approximately half of them require renal replacement therapy (RRT) making a comprehensive understanding of both therapies and their interaction essential for patient management. However, evidence to guide ECMO-specific RRT strategies remains limited. Main body ECMO-related AKI arises from a complex interplay between patient and circuit factors that promote inflammation, endothelial injury, and tubular damage. Timing of RRT initiation in ECMO patients often relies on criteria used in the general critically ill population. Fluid overload is consistently associated with worse outcomes, and observational data suggest that earlier RRT, primarily to control fluid balance, may improve survival although randomized trials in ECMO patients are lacking. All RRT modalities can theoretically be used, but continuous techniques are preferred. RRT can be delivered via a parallel circuit using a dedicated venous catheter or integrated into the ECMO circuit. Integrated configurations reduce the need for additional vascular access and may prolong filter lifespan but require careful pressure management and team expertise to avoid alarms, hemolysis, and air embolism. Anticoagulation strategies must balance bleeding and thrombosis risk across both circuits; unfractionated heparin remains standard, while regional citrate anticoagulation can safely extend filter lifespan in selected patients although data is lacking in patients under veno-arterial ECMO. RRT during ECMO is associated with higher short-term mortality and an increased burden of chronic kidney disease among survivors. Conclusions The management of AKI in ECMO patients remains a major clinical challenge. While RRT is often required in this population, optimal strategies for its initiation, modality selection, and integration with ECMO circuits are still evolving. Current evidence underscores the need for individualized approaches based on patient characteristics. Future research should focus on defining standardized protocols for RRT implementation in ECMO, use of regional citrate anticoagulation, optimizing patient selection, and evaluating long-term renal and survival outcomes.

sections.background_1: Overthe last decades, the use of extracorporeal organ support (ECOS) systems has expanded. Venovenous (VV-) and venoarterial (VA-) extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) may be required in selected patients with refractory respiratory or cardiac failure. Although survival after ECMO has improved over recent years, complications still contribute importantly to morbidity and mortality. Among them, acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequent, with reported rates between 60 and 85% [ 1 – 5 ]. Yet, the pathophysiology of AKI in the context of ECMO remains poorly understood and incidence rates have remained largely unchanged since the early 2000s [ 6 ]. The development of AKI is associated with increased morbidity and in-hospital mortality in ECMO patients [ 2 , 7 ]. Notably, ECMO patients who develop AKI often require prolonged mechanical ventilation and experience longer intensive care unit (ICU) stays [ 3 ]. Many factors including fluid accumulation, refractory acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, uremic complications, and progression of AKI may necessitate the initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT); this need concerns approximately 50% of ECMO patients [ 8 ]. RRT indication and management thus represent a daily concern for clinicians involved in the care of ECMO patients. Despite the growing need to combine multiple ECOS systems in selected patient populations, the optimal strategies for implementing integrated therapies remain poorly defined. In the present review, we explore and summarize the current evidence regarding indications and timing for RRT initiation, RRT modalities, technical considerations concerning ECMO and RRT combination, anticoagulation strategies and outcomes of ECMO patients receiving RRT.
sections.methods: This narrative review was informed by a structured literature search. We searched MEDLINE (via PubMed), the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2010 and September 2025; the search was updated in February 2026 prior to manuscript submission. The search strategy combined controlled vocabulary (when applicable) and free-text terms, using Boolean operators (“AND”, “OR”, “NOT”), and focused on three main concepts: ECMO, AKI and RRT. Keywords and variants included: “acute kidney injury”, “renal replacement therapy/kidney replacement therapy”, “extracorporeal membrane oxygenation/extracorporeal life support”, “continuous renal replacement therapy”, “continuous veno-venous hemofiltration”, “continuous veno-venous hemodialysis/hemodiafiltration”, “intermittent hemodialysis”, “prolonged intermittent renal replacement therapy/sustained low-efficiency dialysis”, as well as terms related to fluid overload/ultrafiltration and anticoagulation (“fluid balance/fluid overload”, “ultrafiltration”, “heparin”, “regional citrate anticoagulation”, “bivalirudin”, “argatroban”). We included original studies (randomized and observational), systematic reviews/meta-analyses, and clinical guidelines addressing indications/timing for RRT, modality choice, technical integration of RRT with ECMO, anticoagulation strategies, and outcomes in ECMO patients. Small series were retained when reporting technical aspects not covered by higher-level evidence studies. Given the narrative design, no formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis was planned.
sections.pathophysiology of aki in ecmo patients: When considering the pathogenesis of AKI in ECMO patients, contributing factors can be categorized into patient-related determinants, factors related to the underlying cardio-respiratory failure, and ECMO circuit–related mechanisms. The severity of pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD) is among the strongest predictors of acute kidney injury, likely reflecting diminished renal reserve and a reduced capacity to tolerate physiological stress. Other well-established risk factors include older age and comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, and heart failure. Sepsis also confers substantial risk, as do markers of acute illness severity, including hypotension or shock and the requirement for vasopressor support [ 9 ]. In both VV and VA-ECMO patients, hemodynamic instability, systemic venous congestion, and shock prior to ECMO cannulation reduce renal perfusion and create a vulnerable substrate for injury [ 10 – 12 ]. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the leading indication for VV-ECMO [ 13 ]. In this setting, mechanical ventilation may contribute to AKI through lung-kidney cross-talk. Gas-exchange disturbances, including hypoxemia and hypercapnia, can alter renal vascular tone and reduce renal perfusion [ 14 ]. Ventilation-induced lung stress may further amplify systemic inflammation, contributing to tubular injury [ 15 ]. In addition, positive-pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure, which can impair venous return or cardiac output and compromise renal blood flow [ 16 ]. In patients with cardiogenic shock who require VA-ECMO, a rapid deterioration in cardiac function can precipitate AKI through a combination of hemodynamic and non-hemodynamic pathways. Reduced forward flow and venous congestion increase renal venous pressure and lower renal perfusion pressure, activating intrarenal mechanisms that can decrease glomerular filtration. In parallel, neurohumoral activation and systemic inflammatory signaling contribute to the bidirectional amplification of cardiac and renal dysfunction [ 17 ]. In post-cardiotomy patients requiring VA-ECMO, AKI is multifactorial involving ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurohumoral activation and mechanical factors related to cardiopulmonary bypass [ 18 ]. The underlying acute illness and pre-existing comorbidities likely influence individual susceptibility to homeostatic disruption. The contact of blood with non-biological surfaces in extracorporeal circuits and high shear stress activate inflammatory and immunological cascades, further amplifying the risk of developing ECMO-related AKI. Mass spectrometry-based serum proteomic analyses have identified differentially expressed proteins known to be involved in coagulation and inflammation in patients treated with VA-ECMO compared to controls [ 19 ]. Activation of the contact and complement system induces leukocyte activation, which leads to endothelial damage and organ injury [ 20 , 21 ]. Along with coagulation-induced activation of endothelial cells leading to increased expression of P-selectin and E-selectin, this altogether leads to adherence, activation, and transmigration of neutrophils. Neutrophil infiltration is thought to be central for the end-organ damage associated with ECMO [ 21 ]. Circuit-related factors such as the induction of shear stress and the occurrence of non-pulsatile blood flow in VA-ECMO contribute to ECMO-related AKI. Shear stress-induced hemolysis leads to the release of cell-free hemoglobin, which promotes oxidative and nitrosative stress, ultimately contributing to tubular injury [ 22 ]. Furthermore, high concentrations of cell-free hemoglobin have been clinically associated with a higher incidence of AKI in ECMO patients [ 23 ]. The pathophysiology of AKI in ECMO patients is summarized in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 Pathophysiology of AKI in ECMO Patients
sections.indications and timing for rrt initiatio: ECMO patients represent a distinct population, yet robust data regarding the optimal timing for RRT initiation in this group remain lacking. The major trials on RRT initiation were all conducted in the general ICU population with AKI [ 24 – 26 ]. None of these studies demonstrated a survival benefit when using an early initiation strategy. Nevertheless, ECMO patients were either excluded, under-represented, or not explicitly reported. In a recent survey, the primary reported indications for initiating RRT in ECMO patients were persistent anuria (44%) and fluid overload (20%) [ 27 ]; according to most respondents (96%), the same criteria as those applied in the general ICU population were used. According to the ELSO (Extracorporeal Life Support Organization) guidelines [ 28 ], RRT should be considered when euvolemia cannot be achieved medically or when metabolic disturbances may “decrease the chance of recovery from cardiopulmonary failure”. Fluid overload (FO) may negatively impact outcomes in ECMO patients as multiple studies have reported a consistent association between FO and increased mortality [ 5 , 29 , 30 ]. More specifically, patients developing early FO—defined as >10% positive fluid balance within 72 hours after ECMO cannulation—experience a two-fold increase in 30-day mortality [ 5 ]. Among patients receiving RRT, 90-day mortality appeared lower when a negative fluid balance was achieved at 72 hours post-cannulation. These findings support a potential link between fluid balance management and survival in ECMO patients, yet the extent to which RRT timing influences this relationship is unclear. Several studies have explored this hypothesis. A retrospective study conducted in Japan [ 31 ] compared mortality between early (< 48 hours) and late initiation of RRT in 2513 VA-ECMO patients identified from a nationwide health claims database. Early RRT initiation was associated with reduced hospital mortality at both 28 and 90 days (HR 0.59, 95% CI [0.53;0.68] and HR 0.67, 95% CI [0.61;0.75], respectively). However, early initiation of RRT was consistently associated with a higher risk of 90-day RRT dependence. In a single-center randomized controlled trial (RCT), patients with postcardiotomy cardiogenic shock were randomized to early (<12 hours) versus standard RRT initiation timing [ 32 ]. Early RRT was associated with significantly improved lactate clearance. These findings support a potential link between fluid balance management and survival in ECMO patients, yet the extent to which RRT timing influences this relationship is unclear. Conversely, a retrospective cohort study found no significant association between the timing of RRT initiation and mortality [ 33 ] and a recent meta-analysis could not determine the optimal timing of RRT, as results were not consistent between studies [ 34 ]. Although FO is often associated with worse outcomes, this relationship may be confounded by severity: patients with ongoing shock, inflammatory capillary leak, or bleeding often cannot safely undergo early net fluid removal. In these patients, fluid removal is particularly challenging because hemodynamic changes may be both beneficial and harmful: while decongestion and afterload reduction may improve cardiac performance, excessive preload reduction or hypotension may also impair organ perfusion [ 35 ]. Overall, the available data do not clearly show that starting RRT earlier improves outcomes in this setting. Starting before recommended indications may simply expose patients to extracorporeal therapy unnecessarily and could even compromise subsequent renal recovery.
sections.modalities: All RRT modalities can theoretically be used in ECMO patients, including intermittent hemodialysis (IHD), prolonged intermittent renal replacement therapy (PIRRT), and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Current guidelines do not recommend one modality over another [ 28 ]. While intermittent modalities such as IHD and PIRRT offer advantages like scheduled circuit downtime, lower costs, and facilitated rehabilitation, they may be associated with hemodynamic instability and disequilibrium syndrome due to higher solute removal rates [ 36 ]. In hemodynamically unstable ECMO patients, CRRT remains the preferred option [ 37 ]. Two surveys have reported a widespread use of CRRT while IHD is rarely performed, accounting for only 3% and 7% of cases [ 27 , 38 ]. Although a few small-scale studies have demonstrated the feasibility of PIRRT or peritoneal dialysis in ECMO patients, data remain limited and do not support the use of such techniques as first-line therapies [ 39 , 40 ]. In contrast, CRRT not only provides superior hemodynamic stability but may also be associated with improved renal recovery compared to intermittent techniques although data specific to ECMO populations are lacking [ 41 , 42 ]. No large-scale study has assessed the optimal clearance mode during CRRT [ 43 ] so that the choice of CRRT modality often relies on local expertise. In ECMO patients, convective modalities appear to be more frequently employed [ 27 , 38 ]. A retrospective study using Taiwan’s national healthcare database compared continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH) and continuous veno-venous hemodialysis (CVVHD) in patients receiving either VV- or VA-ECMO. CVVH was associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality (68.4% vs. 76.9%; OR 0.65, 95% CI [0.50; 0.85]), and shorter ICU length of stay (mean difference -4.59 days, 95% CI [-9.15; -0.03]) [ 44 ]. The superior clearance of middle-molecular-weight solutes such as cytokines with convective therapies may partly explain these findings however the clinical relevance of this mechanism remains uncertain and the relationship between cytokine removal and patient-centered outcomes has not been consistently demonstrated [ 45 , 46 ]. Finally, no study has specifically assessed the optimal RRT dose in ECMO patients. In clinical practice, most clinicians prescribe a dose of 25–30 mL/kg/day, in line with the KDIGO (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes) recommendations for the general ICU population [ 27 ].
sections.parallel connection: In a parallel configuration, CRRT runs independently from the ECMO circuit through a dedicated venous catheter [ 47 ]. The parallel connection avoids any interference between the ECMO and CRRT circuits. A key advantage is the absence of pressure perturbations between devices: the CRRT can run with standard settings without the pressure alarms being triggered, which can occur when it is connected directly to the ECMO circuit [ 47 ]. Furthermore, the connection and disconnection of the CRRT circuit can be performed without specialized training. However, the parallel connection requires the insertion of an additional central venous catheter, which may be challenging in patients already cannulated for ECMO and under anticoagulation therapy [ 47 ]. This additional vascular access may also increase the risk of mechanical complications, insertion-related bleeding, and catheter-associated infection or thrombosis [ 47 ]. Despite these drawbacks, the use of parallel connections remains common, with 40% of centers reporting its use [ 27 ] - possibly due to insufficient team training or the absence of compatible ECMO ports to enable direct connection on the ECMO circuit.
sections.integrated connection: When using an integrated connection, the CRRT machine is directly connected to the ECMO circuit. Various configurations have been described: both the CRRT access and return are connected to the high-pressure section of the circuit after the pump, both are connected to the low-pressure venous cannula before the pump, or the access is connected to the arterial section and the return to the venous section [ 36 , 39 , 47 – 57 ]. Integrated connection of the CRRT machine provides full dialysis capabilities (precise ultrafiltration, dialysis or hemofiltration modes, fluid and electrolyte management) with monitoring of pressures and filter integrity. This connection also avoids a second venous access and its associated complications [ 36 ]. The major disadvantage is related to the “cross-talk” between the two machines: the CRRT device is exposed to pressures outside its normal range as the ECMO pump’s high pressures (often +150 to +400 mmHg post-pump and up to -100 mmHg pre-pump) can exceed the CRRT machine’s normal operating range, which can trigger frequent high or low pressure alarms depending on the CRRT machine used [ 36 ]. With certain configurations, recirculation may occur within the CRRT circuit. However, this phenomenon is considered negligible as the RRT blood flow is typically more than ten times lower than the ECMO flow. The principles for safe ECMO-CRRT integration include selecting appropriate connection sites with the CRRT return line positioned before the oxygenator, ensuring pressures remain within safe operational limits, preventing air entrainment and hemolysis, and adjusting equipment settings to accommodate non-standard pressure environments [ 58 ]. To ensure maximum safety, the connection should always be performed by trained staff; this implies that physicians or perfusionists are readily available to prevent errors in ECMO circuit manipulations. Then, connecting the CRRT after the ECMO pump minimizes the risk of air embolism, which can lead to pump airlock and interruption of ECMO flow. Any connection on the negative section of the ECMO circuit should be performed on one-way valves to prevent air embolism. The CRRT return line should also be positioned before the oxygenator to prevent any arterial or venous embolism to the patient, post-oxygenator return should be avoided. Finally, ECMO circuit modifications should be limited (e.g., added stopcocks or Luer-type sampling/injection ports). In centers that routinely use a dedicated CRRT bridge, it should be built into the initial ECMO tubing at the time of circuit set-up, as each added junction increases circuit complexity, creating structural weak points in the circuit and increasing the risk of blood leak or thrombus formation (Fig. 2 ). sections.technical considerations for integrated: Proper connection configuration and pressure management are crucial when combining ECMO with a CRRT device. The goal is to maintain adequate blood flow through the CRRT device without disturbing ECMO function or causing device alarms. In an integrated ECMO-CRRT configuration, ECMO pump flow is the primary determinant of circuit pressures; higher ECMO flows drive proportionally elevated pressures throughout the CRRT circuit [ 49 , 50 ]. The arterial cannula diameter and any cannula or oxygenator obstruction further modulate pressures, with larger cannula minimizing an increase in pressure [ 55 ]. In contrast, changes in CRRT pump flow have a smaller effect, slightly decreasing access pressure while raising return pressure [ 58 ]. Monitoring pressures within the ECMO circuit is essential to effectively perform an integrated connection. When the CRRT circuit is connected after the ECMO pump and before the oxygenator, the main limiting factor is often the CRRT return pressure: if this pressure exceeds the maximum threshold of the CRRT machine, therapy cannot proceed. The CRRT blood pump generates an increase in pressure downstream of the CRRT circuit that approximately equals the drop pressure measured by the CRRT machine (∆P RRT ). Consequently, the return pressure on the CRRT circuit can be estimated as CRRT return pressure ≈ ∆PRRT + P2, where P2 corresponds to the existing pressure in the ECMO circuit at the connection site. ∆P RRT typically ranges from 20 to 50 mmHg. This estimation allows clinicians to anticipate whether CRRT machine pressure limits will be exceeded prior to connection. If the predicted return pressure exceeds the device’s allowable threshold, an integrated connection at that site may not be feasible [ 58 ]. In case of persistent high pressure on the CRRT return line, other adaptations have been proposed. Pressure alarms can be modified on some CRRT devices but this is not feasible for all of them [ 54 ]. The use of pressure regulators could help maintain pressure within an adapted range, which is necessary if the CRRT return line is placed before the ECMO pump. A 2024 single-center observational comparative study evaluated adding a pressure control line (regulator) on the CRRT return line in an ECMO-integrated setup [ 59 ]. By partially restricting flow at the return line, the pressures within the CRRT circuit changed from strongly negative to mildly positive, thereby protecting the filter. Specifically, when using a regulator, the CRRT circuit filter pressure was maintained around +45 mmHg compared to -69 mmHg without a regulator (p < 0.001) [ 59 ]. This nearly eliminated the pressure swings that cause frequent alarms and filter collapse. The impact on filter longevity was significant: filters lasted ~38 hours with a regulator vs. ~27 hours without (mean use time per filter set, p < 0.01) [ 59 ]. Similarly, a larger observational study by Na et al. observed that patients with pressure-relief valves on both access and return lines had significantly longer CRRT filter lifespan than those with no pressure control (or one-sided control) [ 53 ]. However, the use of clamps on the CRRT circuit could be associated with hemolysis or thrombosis on the RRT line and needs further research [ 36 ]. Overall, the configuration choice for integrated connections should be individualized based on the RRT machine and ECMO circuits available (Fig. 3 ). A thorough understanding of both ECMO and RRT functionality is essential to ensure procedural safety and efficiency. Fig. 3 Figure 3. Algorithm for pressure management of integrated CRRT-ECMO. These findings support that high, stable ECMO blood flow protects against flow stasis, alarms, and downtime which are common in parallel catheter-based CRRT. However, evidence is not entirely consistent and could also depend on the anticoagulation used. A retrospective COVID-19 VV-ECMO study (n=105) using dual anticoagulation (systemic heparin plus regional citrate) found no filter survival difference between integrated and parallel connections (~60% reaching 72 h without clotting) [ 48 ]. Integrated circuits showed higher access and return pressures, yet transmembrane pressures remained stable and therapy uninterrupted under careful anticoagulation [ 48 ]. Large registry data and case series confirm that integration does not increase oxygenator failure or embolic events compared with parallel connection [ 48 ]. The randomized E-CRRT trial found no difference in median CRRT circuit lifespan between integrated and separate connections (approximately 72h in both arms) [ 60 ]. However, a substantial proportion of circuits were maintained beyond the manufacturer’s 72h, potentially increasing infectious risk [ 62 ]. Notably, crossovers from separation to integration were frequent because dialysis catheter placement was unsuccessful or deemed unsafe, likely reflecting that accessible sites for catheter insertion are often more limited in ECMO patients than in the general ICU population. Finally, infectious complications could be associated with the type of connection. The concern for infection risk is twofold: bloodstream infections related to circuit manipulation and local infections at cannulation sites. Interestingly, current data do not demonstrate a clear difference in rates of bacteremia or sepsis between integrated and parallel CRRT strategies [ 48 ]. In Schönfelder’s cohort, the incidence of catheter-associated infections was comparable (~10–15%, p = 0.47) regardless of whether a separate dialysis catheter was used [ 48 ]. sections.anticoagulation: Although anticoagulation is required for both the RRT and the ECMO machine, anticoagulation targets may differ depending on the mode of ECMO. The ELSO guidelines [ 63 ] do not endorse a specific first-line anticoagulation strategy for ECMO circuits, though unfractionated heparin (UFH) is the most prescribed anticoagulant. An international survey reported exclusive use of UFH in 96% of centers for ECMO patients [ 64 ]. Despite its widespread use, UFH has notable limitations, including reduced efficacy in inflammatory states and the risk of heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Other anticoagulants such as direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs) are also used in this population, notably in case of HIT. Bivalirudin binds to both circulating and clot-bound thrombin. Approximately 80% of the drug is metabolized through proteolysis, while the remaining 20% is eliminated unchanged by the kidney. This metabolism results in a predictable anticoagulant effect according to the administered dose and a short half-life, facilitating precise titration of anticoagulation. However bivalirudin is cleared by RRT and thus requires close monitoring and dose adjustment in this situation [ 65 ]. Recent evidence, including systematic reviews and network meta-analyses, suggest that bivalirudin may be associated with lower rates of thrombotic complications compared with UFH without a clear excess of major bleeding. However, the available data remain largely observational so that definitive superiority across all ECMO populations cannot be assumed [ 66 ]. Bivalirudin anticoagulation requires constant blood flow, therefore zones of low flow or stasis at connection sites in integrated ECMO–CRRT configurations may represent a specific risk for local thrombosis and should be closely monitored. In case of renal dysfunction or RRT, argatroban is the recommended treatment for HIT [ 67 ], the therapy should be started at 2 µg/kg/min up to 10 µg/kg/min, to achieve a 1.5- to 3-fold prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). Since argatroban is metabolized by hepatic cytochrome P450, its half-life may be prolonged in case of hepatic impairment. Several case reports show the feasibility of this anticoagulation in ECMO patients, also with concurrent RRT [ 68 – 70 ]. Although approximately 20% of the drug is eliminated during hemodialysis, the overall impact of RRT on argatroban pharmacokinetics appears clinically negligible. A systematic review confirmed the efficacy and safety of argatroban in both IHD for CKD and in CRRT [ 71 ]. A recent randomized controlled pilot trial showed that maintenance anticoagulation with argatroban is feasible and does not increase the risk of thrombosis or hemorrhage in ECMO patients without HIT [ 72 ]. In ECMO patients, the RRT circuit is most commonly anticoagulated using UFH, as it simultaneously ensures anticoagulation of the ECMO circuit. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has been associated with longer hemofilter lifespan than UFH in the general ICU population but these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to ECMO patients as comparative data are scarce [ 73 ]. RCA offers the advantage of maintaining effective anticoagulation of the RRT circuit, even when systemic anticoagulation must be interrupted due to bleeding. In a single-center retrospective study of 29 patients on VV-ECMO, RCA-CVVH was associated with a mean hemofilter lifespan of 27 hours, with no evidence of citrate accumulation or circuit/oxygenator thrombosis [ 74 ]. Similarly, a retrospective study reported a lower rate of RRT circuit clotting (11% vs. 38% in the UFH group, p < 0.001) and an improved hemofilter lifespan in patients receiving RCA + UFH compared to UFH alone, with no reported metabolic complications related to RCA [ 75 ]. These findings suggest that RCA is a feasible and safe anticoagulation strategy for the RRT circuit in ECMO patients, particularly when systemic anticoagulation is contraindicated. However, its use in VA-ECMO remains limited, as patients with circulatory failure and refractory shock may be at greater risk of citrate accumulation [ 76 ]. In centers experienced with RCA, specific reduced-citrate or stepwise initiation protocols have been proposed to limit citrate load and potentially mitigate the risk of citrate accumulation in selected high-risk patients [ 77 , 78 ]. Such strategies rely on strict algorithms and close biochemical surveillance and should be applied cautiously, particularly in patients with refractory shock or multi-organ failure in whom the risk of citrate accumulation is increased.
sections.short-term outcomes: The short-term outcomes of ECMO patients who develop AKI and/or require RRT remain heterogeneous across studies. Several studies have investigated the impact of AKI occurrence and severity on survival in ECMO patients. A prospective French study involving 60 patients on VV-ECMO found that those who developed KDIGO stage 3 AKI had significantly lower survival at hospital discharge compared to those with stage 0–2 AKI (27.6% vs. 67.7%, p = 0.02) [ 79 ]. Similarly, a retrospective Korean study reported increased mortality only among patients with stage 3 AKI, with no significant difference observed for stages 1 or 2 [ 80 ]. Notably, this Korean cohort included both VA- and VV-ECMO patients, with a predominance of VA-ECMO (72%) and a high proportion of patients undergoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation within 24 hours before cannulation (43%), reflecting substantial baseline severity. Outcomes also appeared time-dependent: mortality within the first two weeks after ECMO initiation was higher in the VA-ECMO group, whereas overall in-hospital mortality was lower than in the VV-ECMO group. The authors suggested that VA-ECMO patients may follow distinct trajectories, with early deaths clustering among the most severe presentations, while those surviving the initial phase may experience clinically meaningful recovery once cardiac dysfunction is reversed. This illustrates how differences in indication and underlying pathophysiology can modify the observed association between AKI severity and mortality. In contrast, a cohort study of 190 patients, also including both VA- and VV-ECMO with a predominance of VA-ECMO (83%), reported no significant difference in ICU or hospital mortality between patients with and without AKI. A possible explanation for these conflicting results is that, unlike the first two studies, the latter did not stratify patients by AKI severity; stage 3 AKI thus appears to be the main driver of the association between AKI and mortality in ECMO patients [ 3 ]. Furthermore, pre-existing AKI is a major determinant of poor short-term outcomes; in a study of 329 patients, those with AKI prior to ECMO initiation faced an in-hospital mortality rate of 73%, which was significantly higher than the 42% mortality seen in patients who developed AKI after initiation [ 81 ]. An association between the need for RRT during ECMO and worse outcomes has been repeatedly reported. In two meta-analyses including a majority of VA-ECMO patients, approximately 50% of ECMO patients required initiation of RRT, with overall mortality rates of 63% and 68%. Both studies reported an increased risk of mortality in patients receiving combined ECMO and RRT compared to ECMO alone, with a relative risk (RR) of 1.81 in one and an odds ratio (OR) of 3.73 in the other [ 6 , 8 ]. However, mortality rates differ markedly between studies, probably due to variations in patient selection, ECMO modality, and underlying clinical profiles. Importantly, VA-ECMO is frequently initiated for clinical phenotypes associated with profound hemodynamic collapse and multi-organ failure, including post-cardiotomy shock after cardiopulmonary bypass and refractory cardiogenic shock, whereas VV-ECMO is primarily used for severe ARDS. Such differences are expected to influence both AKI incidence and the likelihood of requiring RRT. In this context, RRT requirement may primarily represent a marker of illness severity and confounding by indication rather than a direct mediator of outcome. This is illustrated by a Belgian studyof 135 patients in which ICU mortality was comparable among three groups: ECMO without AKI, ECMO with AKI not requiring RRT, and ECMO with AKI requiring RRT (43%, 53%, and 60%, respectively; p = 0.21) [ 82 ]. In this study, the absence of an excess mortality signal with CRRT remained consistent when AKI stages and VA/VV-ECMO were analyzed separately and after adjustment for confounders. The authors also suggested that the prognostic weight of AKI may be attenuated in the most severe presentations, such as cardiogenic shock with established multi-organ failure, where outcome is largely driven by the underlying disease. Similarly, a US-based retrospective study found no statistically significant difference in ICU discharge mortality between patients treated with ECMO alone and those receiving both ECMO and RRT (31.4% vs. 39.5%, p = 0.074) [ 83 ]. Overall, these findings support interpreting RRT use during ECMO as a marker of illness severity and underlying clinical context rather than a treatment-related determinant of outcome, and highlight the need for modality-specific analyses and adequately adjusted studies when assessing its prognostic impact. Interpretation is also complicated by practice variation across centers, as thresholds and indications for initiating RRT during ECMO are not standardized and may differ substantially between institutions.
sections.renal recovery and long-term outcomes: Renal recovery in patients who required both RRT and ECMO, remains highly variable across studies. In a large Taiwanese cohort (mean follow-up 2.4 years (SD 2.5)) of VV-ECMO patients, those with dialysis-requiring AKI had significantly higher rates of new-onset CKD (13.7% vs 8.1%) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) (5.2% vs 0.5%) compared to those who did not require RRT [ 84 ]. In a UK-based cohort of 300 VV-ECMO patients, CKD was observed in 33.3% of those who had received RRT during ICU stay, versus 4.3% among those without AKI ( p = 0.004). At 6 months post-discharge, 2.2% remained dialysis-dependent, and 1.4% had progressed to ESRD by 1 year [ 85 ]. Long-term data from a French single-center retrospective study (n = 158) showed that major adverse kidney events occurred in 60% of VA-ECMO patients at 30 days, 60% at 90 days, and 85% at 1 year. Among ICU survivors, 6.7% remained dialysis-dependent at 12 months [ 86 ]. The most comprehensive long-term data come from a Korean nationwide study of adult ECMO survivors, which reported that 7.6% developed new ESRD within 1-year post-discharge. In this study, the risk of incident ESRD was associated not only with pre-existing renal disease (OR 2.83) and longer duration of in-hospital continuous RRT (OR 1.16), but also with the underlying ECMO indication, with higher risk in the cardiovascular group (vs. respiratory; OR 1.78) and in post-cardiac arrest patients (vs. respiratory; OR 2.52) [ 87 ]. These findings underscore that long-term renal outcomes after ECMO are strongly influenced by the pre-cannulation clinical context and the severity of shock-related end-organ injury, variables that are incompletely captured in administrative observational datasets. Accordingly, the observed associations should be interpreted as prognostic signals rather than causal effects of ECMO or RRT exposure. They also emphasize the importance of differentiating VA- and VV-ECMO populations when discussing renal recovery and long-term kidney risk. The main studies reporting the incidence of AKI and RRT use during ECMO, and their association with mortality and/or renal recovery, are summarized in Table 2 . sections.perspectives: Recovery or preservation of renal function before VA-ECMO decannulation is an indicator for hospital survival [ 88 ]. Consequently, protecting kidney function and limiting AKI progression are crucial to improve outcomes in ECMO patients [ 89 ]. This requires timely recognition of AKI, avoidance of nephrotoxic agents, and prevention of FO through judicious fluid administration and promotion of diuresis when appropriate. Beyond these general principles, the timing and practical delivery of RRT on ECMO should be considered within a broader trajectory that integrates cardiac or pulmonary recovery, the strategy for ECMO weaning, and the expected course of renal recovery. In this setting, decongestion is not solely a renal objective but part of a global approach to optimize hemodynamics and treat pulmonary edema, including consideration of left ventricular unloading in VA-ECMO patients [ 90 ]. However, the optimal net ultrafiltration target during RRT remains undefined in this population, and the achievable rate is often constrained by hemodynamic tolerance [ 91 ]. A major unmet need remains the ability to better predict renal recovery, especially in patients under VA-ECMO, an issue with direct implications for decisions such as transition to durable mechanical circulatory support or heart transplantation. Finally, while biomarker-based approaches are appealing for risk stratification and guide decision-making, available data are largely derived from non-ECMO cohorts; at present, there is insufficient ECMO-specific evidence to support routine clinical implementation or to recommend any biomarker-driven strategy in this population [ 92 ].
sections.conclusions_1: The management of AKI in ECMO patients remains a major clinical challenge. While RRT is often required in this population, optimal strategies for its initiation, modality selection, and integration with ECMO circuits are still evolving. Current evidence underscores the need for individualized approaches based on patient characteristics and fluid balance status. Moreover, the integration of RRT into ECMO circuits, particularly with appropriate pressure management, appears safe and may improve filter lifespan and circuit efficiency. Future research should focus on defining standardized protocols for RRT implementation in ECMO, use of RCA, optimizing patient selection, and evaluating long-term renal and survival outcomes.

title: Advanced liposomal nanoplatforms for flavonoid delivery: a mechanistic and comparative perspective in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a common and life-threatening type of liver cancer, and its treatment results are frequently restricted by late diagnosis, drug resistance, systemic toxicity, and limited specificity of traditional treatment methods, including chemotherapy, surgery, and targeted therapy. Flavonoids, which are a family of naturally-occurring polyphenolic compounds, have been of significant interest in the past few years, based on their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic characteristics. These compounds can control major signaling pathways related to tumor development and progression and are good candidates for the treatment of HCC. Poor aqueous solubility, high metabolism, and low bioavailability, however, greatly limit the clinical use of flavonoids. The delivery system of flavonoids based on liposomes is the possible solution to these restrictions as they preserve the stability, solubility, and tumor-targeting characteristics and protect the flavonoid against degradation, encasing it directly into a vesicle of phospholipid. The improvement of therapeutic performance has been implemented through various approaches to formulation, which are inclusive of thin-film hydration, PEGylation, ligand-mediated targeting, and stimuli-responsive systems. The review has provided the latest developments in liposomal delivery of flavonoids as a tool in the application of HCC which include formulation, physicochemical characterization, and therapeutic effects of flavonoids based on in vitro and in vivo experiments. It is also applied by giving a comparative study with conventional therapies. Moreover, such crucial issues about clinical translation as formulation stability, regulatory standards, expandability, and lack of clinical evidence are severely tackled. Lastly, the outlook of the future in the areas of targeted delivery, combination therapy, and clinical validation are described. In general, the liposomal delivery of flavonoids is a compelling approach to enhancing the therapeutic response of hepatocellular carcinoma. Graphical Abstract
