title:
Preformulated, Shelf-Stable, Dendritic Cell-Targeting
Nanogel mRNA Vaccine Delivery Platform
abstract:
Current mRNA-based
vaccine platforms are limited by complex fabrication,
stringent cold-chain dependence, and off-target in vivo delivery, restricting their global accessibility and targeting precision.
Here we show a modular mRNA delivery platform; our approach integrates
inverse microemulsion-derived polymeric nanogels with adsorption-based
mRNA loading and the capability for ligand-directed targeting to develop
targeted reductively cleavable acrylate-based inverse microemulsion
nanogels (TRAINs). By decoupling nanoparticle fabrication from mRNA
loading, preformed TRAINs can be stockpiled and later combined with
newly designed mRNA, enabling a plug-and-play strategy for rapid adaptation
to emerging pathogens, which is particularly advantageous for pandemic
preparedness. This architecture supports efficient mRNA association
and robust cellular uptake and translation in HEK293T cells. TRAIN
also enables postsynthetic surface functionalization; as a proof of
concept, CD206-targeted TRAINs promoted selective delivery to antigen-presenting
cells (APCs), producing sustained and localized protein expression
in BALB/c mice and preferential mRNA delivery to myeloid APCs in heterogeneous
human peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Together, these results
demonstrate TRAINs as a surface-customizable, adsorption-based mRNA
delivery platform with potential for APC-targeted vaccination and
rapid, adaptable vaccine deployment.

sections.introduction:
Vaccines are among the most effective
public health interventions
for preventing infectious disease and reducing global mortality. mRNA vaccines have emerged as a transformative
platform, as exemplified by the Pfizer-BioNTech (BNT162) and Moderna
(mRNA1273) SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, which have shown high levels of antigen
expression and robust immune responses, with clinical efficacy exceeding
90%. − Compared to traditional vaccines, mRNA platforms enable rapid manufacturing
and reduced risk of genomic integration and offer the ability to encode
various proteins, leading to a growing pipeline of candidates across
infectious diseases. − Despite these advances, their broader deployment remains limited
by their fabrication constraints and in vivo delivery,
including cold-chain dependence and off-target effects. − Currently, mRNA-based vaccines predominantly rely on encapsulation-based
fabrication strategies such as LNPs. − However, during this
process, mRNA incorporation is tightly coupled to nanoparticle fabrication,
where mRNA must be loaded during particle formation. While effective,
this fabrication design restricts independent control over formulation
and cargo, limiting modularity, adaptability, and storage flexibility. − In addition, these commercial mRNA-based vaccines offer limited
control over biodistribution, often spreading from their injection
sites, and accumulation in off-target organs such as the liver and
spleen. This off-target biodistribution raises concerns about adverse
effects arising from ectopic-antigen expression and highlights the
need for delivery strategies that enhance local retention and preferential
uptake by immune cells. − In order to enhance mRNA
vaccine delivery, a decoupled approach
where mRNA is loaded onto the particle after fabrication is emerging
as an attractive clinical alternative strategy, such as an adsorption-based
fabrication strategy. By independently synthesizing and optimizing
nanoparticle fabrication from mRNA loading, this adsorption-based
strategy can enable nanoparticles to be synthesized and stockpiled
in advance to serve as ready-to-use delivery scaffolds with RNA adsorption
performed immediately prior to administration. This strategy may help streamline manufacturing, improve
storage flexibility, and eliminate the need to reformulate the nanoparticle
construct for each new mRNA cargo or application. , Moreover, it can enable tunable mRNA association and postsynthetic
targeting, providing a more flexible and targeted strategy for mRNA
delivery. In 2022, India granted emergency use authorization for an
adsorption-based COVID-19 mRNA vaccine, GEMCOVAC-19, which elicited
increases in antispike IgG titers in early phase clinical studies,
highlighting the capability to induce humoral immune responses in
humans. − Despite their potential, adsorption-based RNA delivery strategies
remain comparatively underdeveloped for mRNA delivery, particularly
as intentionally designed platforms, and have not been widely developed
for targeted immune-cell applications. Here, we present TRAINs (targeted
reductively cleavable acrylate-based inverse microemulsion nanogels),
an adsorption-based mRNA delivery platform that decouples RNA loading
from nanoparticle fabrication. This design enables independent control
over mRNA incorporation and surface functionalization, addressing
the key limitations of encapsulation-based systems. We systematically
evaluate mRNA association, stability, and functional delivery and
demonstrate the modularity of the platform through ligand-mediated
targeting of antigen-presenting cells (APCs). As a proof of concept,
we customize the TRAIN surface with anti-CD206 antibody to demonstrate
APC-targeted delivery within heterogeneous human peripheral blood
mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Together, this work presents a versatile
framework for tunable and targeted mRNA delivery.
sections.design\nand synthesis of the train platf:
TRAINs build
from prior work in our group and are
designed as a modular, polymeric nanogel scaffold for mRNA adsorption
and ligand-directed targeting ( Figure ). The platform is formulated with three well-established
and commercially available monomers, bis­(2-methacryloyl)­oxyethyl
disulfide (DSDMA), 2-acryloxyethyl­trimethylammonium chloride
(AETMAC), and N -(3-aminopropyl)­methacrylamide
hydrochloride (APMA), as shown in Figure A and Figure S1 . We chose DSDMA, a redox-responsive cross-linker, whose disulfide
bond undergoes cleavage in reducing intracellular environments, such
as the cytoplasm, where elevated glutathione (GSH) levels can trigger
structural destabilization of the nanogel network necessary for endosomal
release and subsequent cytoplasmic mRNA translation. , AETMAC provides a permanent cationic charge to enable electrostatic
adsorption of mRNA and promotes interactions with the negatively charged
cell membrane, enabling a more efficient entry into cells and downstream
translation. , Finally, APMA was incorporated
to introduce surface-accessible primary amines, that serve as versatile
handles for ligand conjugation via standard bioconjugation chemistries
to support receptor-mediated targeting. , , − TRAINs were synthesized via a templated inverse microemulsion (water-in-oil)
polymerization to produce nanometer-sized, cross-linked polymeric
particles with narrow size distributions. , In this water-in-oil (w/o) system, the aqueous monomer solution
is confined within surfactant-stabilized droplets dispersed in a continuous
heptane “oil” phase ( Figure B). These droplets
act as confined reaction vessels or “nanoreactors” for
free-radical polymerization to produce spherically shaped, covalently
cross-linked nanogels. In prior work
from our group, the successful synthesis of polymeric nanogels via
inverse microemulsion polymerization was demonstrated and key structure–property
relationships were defined. Cross-linking
density strongly influenced particle size, with higher cross-linking
(>25 wt %) restricting network swelling and yielding smaller nanogels
(∼50 nm), while lower cross-linking (<5 wt %) resulted in
swelling and larger particle size (∼125 nm). Nanoparticles in the 50–250 nm range are most efficiently
internalized by cells via endocytosis, thus, we selected a cross-linking density of 12 mol % to generate
particles within the 50–100 nm range. In parallel, incorporation
of cationic monomers was required for nucleic acid association and
cellular uptake; however, excessive charge increased cytotoxicity.
Our previous optimization studies identified 25 wt % cationic monomer
as sufficient for efficient nucleic acid binding without compromising
cell viability. Therefore, TRAINs were
synthesized with 12 mol % cross-linker and 25 mol % cationic monomer
to balance particle size, mRNA association, cellular uptake, and biocompatibility.
sections.characterization of train nanoparticles:
TRAINs were
characterized for their z -average size, polydispersity
index (PDI), zeta potential, and colloidal stability to assess their
suitability as an adsorption-based mRNA delivery platform ( Figure ). In Dulbecco’s
phosphate-buffer saline (DPBS), a solution that closely mimics physiological
ionic strength, TRAIN’s z -average diameter
was around 86.6 ± 1.3 nm ( Figure A; P > 0.05) and the PDI of TRAIN
remained ∼0.2 across three independent batches, indicating
a moderate uniform nanoparticle size distribution. These observations were further supported by transmission
electron microscopy (TEM), which showed dispersed nanoparticle features
with no observable large aggregates or fused structures ( Figure B and Figure S2 ). Notably, DLS measurements yielded
a larger hydrodynamic diameter than TEM, which is consistent with
the hydrated state of particles in solution and the absence of a hydrodynamic
shell in dry-state TEM imaging. The net
surface charge of TRAIN, a critical parameter in colloidal stability
was measured by electrophoretic light scattering (ELS). TRAIN exhibited
a zeta potential of +33.5 ± 1.3 mV in UltraPure water ( Figure C), within an optimal
range (+15.0 to +35.0 mV) for minimizing aggregation and promoting
cellular uptake. Consistent with this,
TRAIN maintained colloidal stability with minor change in z -average diameter over one month at 25 °C in DPBS
( Figure D). While PDI increased from ∼0.2 to ∼0.25
over 4 weeks, values remained below 0.25, a range generally considered
indicative of reasonably uniform nanoparticle size distributions. TRAINs were designed to remain stable extracellularly
while undergoing redox-responsive cleavage under intracellular reducing
conditions. DSDMA, a well-characterized disulfide cross-linker used
in the TRAIN design is known to cleave under reducing conditions. , After incubation in 10 mM reduced glutathione (GSH) at 37 °C,
we observed an increase in particle heterogeneity, with PDI values
greater than 0.3 ( Table S1 ), suggesting
possible disruption of the nanogel structure. , This increase in PDI is likely the result of GSH-mediated disulfide
cleavage, which can promote network swelling causing changes in particle
heterogeneity, whereas as TRAINs in DPBS without GSH demonstrated
a PDI below 0.3 ( Figure A). ,
sections.train-fluc mrna association\nvia n/p rat:
Firefly luciferase (FLuc) mRNA was
used as a model reporter to characterize
TRAIN-mRNA association. TRAINs were incubated with FLuc mRNA at 4
°C for 30 min to facilitate electrostatic surface adsorption
( Figure A). mRNA association
was systematically tuned by varying the nitrogen-to-phosphate (N/P)
ratio, defined as the molar ratio of cationic quaternary ammonium
groups on TRAIN to anionic phosphate groups along the mRNA backbone.
DLS was employed to evaluate changes in z -average
diameter and PDI as a function of N/P ratio. As the N/P ratio decreased,
we observed a progressive increase in the z -average
diameter, consistent with increasing RNA-mediated bridging and aggregation.
PDI values remained low and within an acceptable range (below 0.2)
until the N/P ratio dropped below 1, at which point the PDI increased
by ∼70% ( Figure B). At low N/P ratios (<1), excess FLuc mRNA in solution promotes
RNA-mediated aggregation, producing larger, heterogeneous particles
that lack colloidal stability ( Figure B). In contrast, at higher N/P ratios (≥1),
the relative excess of cationic TRAINs both reduced free FLuc mRNA
in solution and increased net surface charge ( Figure B and Figure C). Together, these effects minimized aggregation by
limiting RNA-mediated bridging and promoting electrostatic repulsion
between particles, resulting in smaller, more compact, and uniform
TRAIN-mRNA formulations ( Figure B). Zeta potential measurements further supported these
trends. At N/P ratios below 1, TRAIN-FLuc mRNA exhibited a net negative
charge ( Figure C),
consistent with excess free mRNA in solution. At an N/P ratio of 1,
the zeta-potential approached near-neutral, indicating charge neutralization
in solution ( Figure C). As the N/P ratio increased above 2, the zeta potential became
increasingly positive, approaching the value of TRAINs alone (+33.5
± 1.3 mV), suggesting the presence of excess TRAINs relative
to mRNA in solution ( Figure C). We next quantified FLuc mRNA association with TRAINs
across N/P
ratios using the QuantiFluor RNA assay to measure the proportion of
free FLuc mRNA remaining in solution after 30 min adsorption at 4
°C. Based on a constant input concentration of 3.2 ng/μL
FLuc mRNA in each sample ( Figure E; see also Equation S1 and Table S2 ), we observed at low N/P ratios (≤2) incomplete association
(∼23% at N/P = 0.5, ∼62% at N/P = 1, and ∼73%
at N/P = 2), whereas N/P ≥ 5 resulted in complete association
with ∼100% of the input mRNA to TRAINs and no detectable free
FLuc mRNA remaining in solution ( Figure E). Agarose gel electrophoresis results ( Figure D) are supported
by the more sensitive QuantiFluor assay. Notably, residual free FLuc mRNA detected at N/P = 2 by QuantiFluor
was not readily visible on the gel, consistent with the qualitative
nature and higher detection threshold of gel-based analysis. Next, to confirm that mRNA adsorption was reversible,
TRAIN-FLuc mRNA was treated with heparin sulfate (50 μg in DPBS,
15 min at 4 °C). Heparin sulfate induced competitive dissociation
of surface-adsorbed mRNA ( Figure S3A ) , as evidenced by the reappearance of free FLuc mRNA at ∼2000
bp on the agarose gel ( Figure S3B ). This
observation was further confirmed by the QuantiFluor RNA assay results,
which showed complete release of FLuc mRNA from TRAINs across all
N/P ratios following the addition of heparin sulfate ( Figure S4 ).
sections.protection and storage\nperformance of t:
Based on physicochemical characterization
( Figure ), an N/P
ratio of 10 was selected for all
following studies unless specified. We evaluated TRAIN-FLuc mRNA under
a controlled degradation challenge using RNase A as a model enzyme,
applying increasing enzyme amounts (0.25–20 ng total), consistent
with low ng RNase challenge conditions reported to induce rapid degradation
of unprotected RNA, from a 0.5 μg/mL stock solution for 15 min
at 25 °C. − Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer analysis showed that TRAINs can protect
surface-adsorbed FLuc mRNA from RNase-mediated degradation up to 5
ng, while higher enzyme levels resulted in rapid degradation, evidenced
by the loss of FLuc mRNA peak and electropherogram smearing ( Figure A and Figure B). Next, we assessed short-term storage performance of TRAIN-FLuc
mRNA at −20 °C (freezer), 4 °C (refrigerator), and
25 °C (room temperature) over 1 week. At −20 °C,
FLuc mRNA remained well-preserved with minimal degradation ( Figure C; see also Figure S5 ). At 4 °C, gradual degradation
was observed, with ∼83% intact mRNA remaining on day 1 and
∼61% by day 7 ( Figure C; see also Figure S5 ), likely
due to the intrinsic RNA hydrolysis at elevated temperature, , leading to the slow breakdown of exposed or weakly bound FLuc mRNA.
In contrast, storage at 25 °C led to rapid degradation, with
only ∼40% intact mRNA remaining by day 3, accompanied by the
appearance of a broad peak at 25–35 s on the electropherogram,
indicating degraded FLuc mRNA ( Figure C; see also Figure S5 ).
By day 5, no detectable FLuc mRNA peak was observed on the electropherogram
( Figure C; see also Figure S5 ), consistent with enhanced intrinsic
RNA hydrolysis at 25 °C. Colloidal
stability during storage was monitored by DLS ( Figure D). At 4 and 25 °C,
the z -average diameter increased over time ( Figure D, red dashed line; P > 0.05), likely coincident with mRNA degradation, which
can destabilize the surface association of FLuc mRNA with TRAINs ( Figure D). , No significant changes in PDI ( Figure D; P > 0.05) were observed
across any of the tested conditions. Moreover, storage at −20
°C led to an overall increase in z -average diameter
relative to the initial sample ( Figure D), consistent with literature showing nanoparticle
growth following freeze–thaw cycles due to cryoconcentration-induced
aggregation. − Increases in hydrodynamic size into the ∼200–300 nm
regime may alter cellular uptake pathways, as nanoparticles below
∼200 nm are generally internalized via clathrin-mediated endocytosis,
whereas larger particles may exhibit reduced uptake efficiency or
shift toward another cellular pathway mechanism. , This size-dependent shift could alter intracellular trafficking,
thereby potentially reducing mRNA translation. , Further temperature studies are required to systematically assess
storage-induced size changes of TRAIN on cellular uptake, intracellular
trafficking and functional protein expression. Together, these initial
findings suggest that inverse microemulsion-derived TRAINs could provide
short-term protection for surface adsorbed mRNA, maintaining integrity
at 4 °C and −20 °C, potentially through electrostatic
confinement of the poly­(A) tail to the cationic particle surface,
as proposed in other adsorption-based systems.
sections.train-fluc mrna delivery to cultured cel:
To benchmark
the biological performance of TRAIN-FLuc mRNA delivery, human embryonic
kidney (HEK293T) cells, known for their transfectability, robust protein
expression, and well-characterized behavior with a variety of nanoparticle
platforms, were used. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the PrestoBlue
assay, which quantified cell viability through the reduction of a
resazurin-based dye by metabolically active cells, producing a detectable
color change from blue to red. HEK293T cells were treated with TRAINs
at concentrations up to 200 μg/mL for 72 h. Cell viability remained
above 80% at concentrations of ≤120 μg/mL after 72 h
of exposure ( Figure A), indicating low toxicity within this range. However, at concentrations
exceeding 120 μg/mL, cell viability decreases below 80%, which
is denoted as a healthy cell culture ( Figure A). Based on these results, subsequent experiments
were performed with TRAINs at 120 μg/mL, with the N/P ratios
standardized accordingly. Cellular uptake of fluorescein (FITC)-labeled TRAINs
associated
with FLuc mRNA was quantified in HEK293T cells by flow cytometry,
using trypan blue (TB) quenching to distinguish membrane-bound from
internalized TRAIN ( Figure B). TRAIN volume was fixed (50 μL per well) and FLuc
mRNA loading was varied to achieve N/P ratios ranging from 0.5 to
15, the median fluorescence intensity (MFI) changed with incubation
time (1–12 h) ( Figure C). At early time points (1 h), TB quenching led to a substantial
reduction in fluorescence across all N/P ratios, demonstrating that
the majority of TRAIN-FLuc mRNA were initially membrane-associated
due to electrostatic interactions ( Figure C). By 4 h, uptake efficiency diverged based
on formulation, with N/P ratios <1 showing poor internalization,
likely due to excess free mRNA increasing electrostatic repulsion,
while N/P ratios >1 exhibited increased internalization ( Figure C). Interestingly,
by 12 h, TRAIN-FLuc mRNA with N/P ratios ≥ 5 maintained stable
MFI post-TB addition, indicating effective and complete internalization
( Figure C). A decrease
in MFI between 4 and 12 h pretrypan blue was observed in most formulations,
especially N/P ratios 1 and 2, which may reflect reduced surface-associated
signal, intracellular redistribution, or partial attenuation of FITC
fluorescence in the intracellular environment. , Next, we investigated in vitro mRNA delivery
by
measuring FLuc mRNA expression. We compared TRAINs associated with
0.1 μg FLuc mRNA per well to Lipofectamine 2000, a well-established
and standardized in vitro gene delivery carrier,
containing FLuc mRNA at an N/P ratio of 10, comparable to our TRAIN-FLuc
mRNA formulation. Naked FLuc mRNA and TRAIN-FLuc mRNA at N/P ratios
less than or equal to 2 demonstrated low transfection efficiency ( Figure D; P > 0.05), with protein expression barely above the experimentally
determined background, while higher N/P ratios greater than 2 led
to efficient translation into functional luciferase ( Figure D; P <
0.0001). Moreover, TRAINs were well-tolerated with cell viability
remaining above 100% at all tested N/P ratios ( Figure S6 ). We observed the highest expression level at an
N/P ratio of 10, demonstrating an approximate 4.5-fold increase in
transfection efficiency over Lipofectamine 2000 ( Figure D).
sections.mechanism of uptake and\nrelease:
We next explored the
intracellular delivery mechanism of FITC-labeled TRAIN-FLuc mRNA by
quantifying cellular uptake via flow cytometry under conditions that
either permitted or inhibited endocytosis. At 37 °C, where endocytic activity is intact, TRAIN uptake
was highly efficient (∼84 to 100% relative fluorescence) ( Figure E). In contrast,
uptake was significantly reduced at 4 °C (∼24 to 31%),
where ATP depletion and reduced membrane fluidity suppress endocytosis, confirming that TRAIN internalization is predominantly
endocytosis-dependent ( Figure E; P < 0.0001). To define the specific
endocytic pathway involved, we employed small-molecule inhibitors
of clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Pitstop 2), macropinocytosis (EIPA),
and caveolae-mediated endocytosis (Nystatin). , Uptake was quantified as the percentage of FITC + cells
and normalized to the uninhibited controls. Pitstop 2 caused the largest
reduction in TRAIN uptake (∼73%), identifying clathrin-mediated
endocytosis as the dominant internalization pathway for TRAIN-FLuc
mRNA in HEK293T cells ( Figure F, P < 0.0001). EIPA produced modest inhibition
(∼24%), indicating a minor secondary contribution from macropinocytosis,
while Nystatin had minimal effect (∼3%), suggesting negligible
involvement of caveolae-mediated uptake ( Figure F). Next, we proceeded to evaluate
the ability of TRAIN-FLuc mRNA to evade endo-lysosomal degradation,
with confocal microscopy analysis performed using live staining LysoTracker
Red DND-99 for marking lysosomal compartments, and FITC-labeled TRAINs
( Figure A). After
6 h of incubation, TRAIN-FLuc mRNA at an N/P ratio of 10 exhibited
low colocalization with lysosomes (∼17–22%), indicating
that TRAINs do not remain trapped in the lysosomal compartments of
HEK293T cells and suggesting efficient endo-lysosomal escape ( Figure B). We calculated
the Pearson’s correlation coefficient and found that TRAINs
exhibited a negative correlation (∼−0.15 to −0.37),
indicating an inverse relationship with lysosome staining and supporting
the colocalization finding that TRAINs do not preferentially accumulate
in the lysosomes ( Figure C). Positive charge is an
effective way for intracellular nucleic acid
delivery and endosomal escape. On the other hand, positive charge
may also hinder RNA release into the cytosol. The positive surface charge of TRAINs (+33.5 ± 1.3 mV) can
help to promote endosomal escape through electrostatic interactions
with anionic endosomal membranes, leading to membrane destabilization
and increased probability of cytosolic access. In addition to these
charge-mediated membrane interactions, the presence of a reductively
cleavable disulfide cross-linker in our nanogel design may further
promote endosomal-to-cytosolic transfer through intracellular cleavage,
enabling cytoplasmic RNA release. To further probe the role of the
cross-linker, we produced a control nanogel design by replacing DSDMA
with a nonresponsive cross-linker, poly­(ethylene glycol) diacrylate
(PEGDA). Nanoparticles cross-linked with PEGDA are known to form more
hydrolytically stable networks that degrade slowly over days through
erosion, and upon cellular internalization, tend to become entrapped
within lysosomal compartments. As anticipated,
the replacement of the cross-linker with PEGDA led to a higher lysosomal
entrapment, displaying a higher colocalization ratio with the lysosomal
compartment (∼27–48%), and a positive Pearson’s
correlation coefficient (∼0.38 to 0.60) ( Figure B and Figure C; P < 0.01 and P < 0.0001). This comparison study was further validated
using the Bright-Glo assay to assess transfection efficiency. Nanogels
cross-linked with PEGDA produced negligible FLuc mRNA expression ( Figure D; P > 0.05), whereas those formulated with DSDMA generated a strong
bioluminescence signal under identical conditions ( Figure D; P <
0.0001), highlighting the potential role of DSDMA in nanogel destabilization,
endosomal-to-cytosolic transfer, and downstream mRNA translation.
sections.modulating trains for preferential apc t:
The
TRAIN platform decouples particle fabrication from surface modification,
enabling postsynthetic, plug-and-play ligand conjugation. This modularity
supports cell-specific targeting without reformulation of the underlying
nanoparticle construct, ideally suited for targeted mRNA vaccine delivery. As a proof of concept, we functionalized the
TRAIN surface with anti-human CD206 antibodies for APC targeting.
CD206 (mannose receptor, MR) is highly expressed on myeloid-derived
APCs, such as dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages, which are
central to initiating and directing adaptive immunity. CD206-mediated endocytosis can route TRAINs
to early endosomal compartments rather than directly to degradative
lysosomes, which may enhance mRNA translation. , CD206-conjugation was achieved by reacting surface exposed
APMA amines on TRAINs with a succinimidyl-[( N -maleimido­propionamido)-tetraethylene
glycol] ester (NHS-PEG 4 -maleimide) linker, followed by
coupling to reduced anti-human CD206 antibodies ( Figure A). Successful conjugation
was confirmed using anti-human CD206 Alexa Fluor (AF)­647-labeled secondary
antibodies and compensation beads, indicating that the CD206 antibody
remained structurally intact and accessible following attachment ( Figure S7 ). The z -average diameter
of AF488-labeled CD206-TRAINs was ∼110.5 nm and increased further
to ∼165.6 nm upon mRNA association, consistent with ligand
conjugation and surface-adsorbed mRNA ( Figure S8 ). Functionalization also reduced the surface charge; unmodified
TRAINs exhibited a zeta potential of +33.5 mV, which decreased to
+16.8 mV for AF488-labeled CD206-TRAINs, and slightly further to +11.3
mV upon mRNA association ( Figure S8 ), agarose
gel electrophoresis illustrates signal retained in the well relative
to free mRNA, consistent with mRNA association to TRAINs ( Figure S9 ). Since receptor-mediated targeting requires close
proximity to target
cells, we first performed preclinical in vivo studies
to evaluate CD206-TRAINs using intramuscular (IM) injection, a clinically
relevant route known to recruit both tissue-resident and infiltrating
APCs. , , Anti-mouse
CD206-TRAINs and isotype controls (1 μg of FLuc mRNA) were administered
IM into female BALB/c mice, and luciferase expression was monitored
over 72 h ( Figure B and Figure S10 ). CD206-TRAINs exhibited
a delayed kinetic profile, with signal gradually increasing from 24
to 48 h, then beginning to decline at 72 h while remaining detectable
( Figure B), consistent
with timing of CD206 + APC recruitment following IM injection. , In contrast, Isotype-TRAINs showed no detectable signal ( Figure B), confirming that
expression was not driven by nonspecific uptake. While unfunctionalized
TRAINs produced only weak, transient expression ( Figure B). These results suggest that
CD206-mediated targeting can provide a distinct, and delayed expression
profile in vivo , suggesting more selective uptake
by recruited APCs. This behavior may be advantageous for mRNA vaccines
requiring localized antigen expression and targeted immune activation. To assess translational relevance, we next evaluated CD206-TRAIN
targeting ex vivo in human peripheral blood mononuclear
cells (PBMCs), which contain both CD206 – lymphocytes
(T cells and B cells) and CD206 + myeloid subsets (monocytes
and dendritic cells). Notably, myeloid cells comprise only ∼5–7%
of PBMCs in healthy individuals, providing
a stringent model for assessing selective delivery. PBMCs were incubated
for 24 h with either unfunctionalized TRAINs (TRAINs), CD206-functionalized
TRAINs (CD206-TRAINs), or Isotype-functionalized TRAINs (Isotype-TRAINs),
the latter serving as a baseline for nonspecific interactions. Flow
cytometry revealed that CD206-TRAIN uptake was restricted to the myeloid
population, with minimal uptake by lymphocytes ( Figure S11 ). Cells were gated using forward scatter (FSC)
versus side scatter (SSC) to identify PBMCs, followed by singlet discrimination
and exclusion of dead cells using Zombie Aqua ( Figure S11A ). Double-positive (DP) cells, identified by co-staining
of TRAIN (AF488-labeled) conjugated to anti-human CD206 antibody (AF647-labeled),
were found exclusively within the myeloid population and expressed
mCherry ( Figure S11B ), confirming receptor-specific
uptake and functional mRNA delivery. Further phenotypic analysis
demonstrated preferential internalization
of CD206-TRAINs by monocytes and dendritic cells, with minimal uptake
in T cells and B cells ( Figure C and Figure D). Compared to Isotype-TRAINs, CD206-TRAINs showed enhanced uptake
in CD206 + APCs, consistent with receptor-mediated endocytosis.
CD206 engagement is known to route cargo to early endosomal compartments
rather than degradative lysosomes, providing
a favorable intracellular pathway for TRAIN. This endosomal localization
positions any translated antigen for efficient MHC-II loading and
presentation to effectively activate CD4 + T cells. Functional
delivery was confirmed by mCherry expression, with CD206-TRAINs performing
comparable to the model system Lipofectamine 2000, with expression
primarily observed in monocytes and dendritic cells ( Figure E). Together, these findings
suggest that receptor-mediated targeting could help to direct TRAINs
to desirable intracellular trafficking pathways that support functional
mRNA delivery and antigen presentation.
sections.conclusions:
In
summary, we have developed TRAINs, as a surface customizable,
polymeric nanogel platform for adsorption-based mRNA loading and the
capability for targeted delivery. By decoupling nanoparticle fabrication
from mRNA association, TRAINs can be preformulated and stockpiled
in advance to serve as ready-to-use scaffolds for mRNA vaccine delivery.
With TRAINs we have demonstrated near-complete mRNA loading at N/P
ratios ≥ 5, while preserving mRNA integrity and transfection
competency without the need for extensive formulation optimization.
The surface-associated FLuc mRNA demonstrated protection from RNase-mediated
degradation through a RNase degradation challenge assay. In HEK293T
cells, TRAINs exhibited efficient cellular uptake predominantly via
clathrin-mediated endocytosis with minimal lysosomal sequestration,
resulting in a 4.5-fold enhancement in FLuc mRNA translation relative
to Lipofectamine 2000. Importantly, the preformulated inverse microemulsion-derived
nanogel architecture provides a chemically addressable scaffold that
supports postsynthesis ligand conjugation using standard bioconjugation
techniques. In preclinical studies, IM administration of CD206-TRAINs
in mice produced a gradual and localized FLuc mRNA expression compared
to unfunctionalized TRAINs, likely driven by recruitment of CD206 + immune cells and lymphatic trafficking. This delayed kinetic
behavior supports selective uptake by infiltrating APC populations
at the injection site. As a proof of concept, leveraging the platform’s
modularity, CD206-TRAINs selectively delivered adsorbed mCherry mRNA
to APCs in human PBMCs, a low-abundance yet critical immune population
for DC-targeted vaccination. CD206-TRAINs preferentially transfected
CD206 + monocytes and DCs. Together, these results highlight
the adaptability of adsorption-loaded, inverse microemulsion-derived
TRAINs for mRNA delivery. Future studies will further explore the
stability and targeting nature of TRAINs as well as induction of cellular
and humoral immunity as a result of efficient APC targeting and mRNA
vaccine delivery.

title: Factors associated with variations in the 6-minute walk distance during the follow-up of patients with systemic sclerosis
abstract: Introduction The 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) is commonly used to assess functional capacity in patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), but its ability to reflect changes in cardiopulmonary status during follow-up remains uncertain. This study aimed to investigate whether variations in the 6MWD accurately mirror changes in organ involvement over time in SSc patients. Methods We conducted a longitudinal study on a global cohort of 227 consecutive SSc patients, including a subgroup of 88 patients with ILD or PH, over a two-year follow-up period. Statistical analyses were performed to assess associations between variations (Δ) of 6MWD (Δ6MWD) and evolution of organ involvement. Results The 6MWD varied only mildly during follow-up (mean Δ6MWD − 11.6 ± 67.5 m), including in patients with ILD or PH (mean Δ6MWD − 16 ± 74 m). Significant associations were noted between Δ6MWD and variations of several SSc parameters, mostly with modifications in functional status (changes in ΔBorg (ΔΔBorg) score, p = 0.002; ΔNYHA, p < 10 − 3 ), PH parameters (Δright atrial area, p = 0.045; persistently elevated Nt-pro-BNP levels, p < 10 − 3 ), chronotropic function (ΔΔheart rate, p = 0.015; Δinitial heart rate, p = 0.024), musculoskeletal involvement (occurrence of joint symptoms, p = 0.006) and perceived quality of life (ΔHAQ-DI score, p = 0.023). In most cases, the strength of these associations was mild to moderate (R 2 = 0.53, adjusted R 2 = 0.36 in multivariate analysis), suggesting the influence of additional factors to explain the majority of Δ6MWD. Conclusion While it remains valuable as a marker of disability and functioning, the variation in the 6MWD does not seem to be a robust surrogate for modifications in organ involvements of SSc patients. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13075-026-03821-x.

sections.introduction_1: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is the most severe systemic immune-mediated diseases. Classified within the spectrum of connective tissue diseases, it is responsible for inflammatory, vascular and fibrosing symptoms that significantly alter patient quality of life and prognosis. In recent decades, the cardiorespiratory complications of the disease, notably pulmonary hypertension (PH) and interstitial lung disease (ILD), have emerged as the leading cause of mortality among SSc patients [ 1 , 2 ]. Improving their prognosis is thus a major unmet need in the field of SSc, that relies on early diagnosis to allow for timely treatment initiation, and rapid detection of treatment failure for immediate readjustment. Among the array of tools available for evaluating SSc patients, the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) stands out for its simplicity, non-invasiveness, cost-effectiveness, and reproducibility, making it a common practice in clinical settings. Originally developed to assess submaximal exercise capacity in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic heart failure, the 6MWT has since been transferred to various conditions, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (iPAH) [ 3 – 5 ]. In these mono-organ conditions, the variation (Δ) in the 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) is an accurate reflection of modifications in the severity of the cardiorespiratory disease [ 6 – 9 ]. However, unlike these situations, SSc is a systemic condition characterized by various extra-cardiopulmonary manifestations (e.g., skin fibrosis, musculoskeletal pain, left-heart disease, anemia) and significant disability, that can impact the 6MWT. As such, in this multi-organ context, it is unclear what exactly is reflected by a modification of the 6MWD during follow-up [ 10 , 11 ]. While several cross-sectional studies have focused on identifying predictors of the 6MWD at a given timepoint [ 12 ], data relating to Δ6MWD over time and the meaning of its variation have seldom been reported in SSc patients. To try and fill this gap, we assessed factors associated with Δ6MWD over time to investigate whether these variations could accurately mirror changes in organ involvement in SSc patients.
sections.patient selection: We performed a longitudinal study and screened consecutive patients aged 18 years and older followed in our National Referral Centre for SSc at Lille University Hospital between November 2014 and August 2022. Consecutive patients were included if they met the following criteria: [ 1 ] a diagnosis of SSc according to the 2013 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) classification criteria; [ 2 ] at least two visits separated by a 2-year (± 6 months) interval with 6MWD data available. There was no exclusion criterion.
sections.data collection: Data were systematically collected at both timepoints by a physician using a standardized case-report form for all patients referred to our day-patient clinic. Each patient underwent a comprehensive evaluation conducted on the same day, except for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and pulmonary function tests (PFTs), which could be performed up to 6 months before or after the visit. Patients underwent a 6MWT at both time points in a calibrated corridor, as per recommendations [ 13 ]. Various parameters including the total 6MWD expressed as absolute (m) and relative (% predicted) values, modified Borg score, peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and heart rate (HR) were recorded at the beginning and end of the test. Changes in Borg score, SpO 2 , BP, and HR during each test were calculated as the difference between their final and initial values. Additional data were collected at both time points: patient and SSc characteristics, clinical parameters (such as modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS) and New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class), biological results (including C-reactive protein (CRP), N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide (Nt-pro-BNP), and creatine kinase (CK) levels), TTE findings (including estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP), right atrium (RA) area and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)), PFT results (including forced vital capacity (FVC), total lung capacity (TLC), and diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO), expressed as absolute values and %predicted according to ECSC standards), composite scores (such as the European Scleroderma Study Group Activity Index (EScSG-AI), Medsger severity score, and Health Assessment Questionnaire-Disability Index (HAQ-DI)) and treatments (immunosuppressants (IS) and vasodilators (VD)). Interstitial lung disease (ILD) was diagnosed on high-resolution CT-scan (HRCT); and staged as limited (if HRCT extent < 20% and forced vital capacity (FVC) ≥ 70%) or extensive (if HRCT extent > 20% or FVC < 70%) according to Goh’s system [ 14 ]. ILD was considered as progressive if one of the following criteria were met: [ 1 ] relative decline of FVC ≥ 10% of predicted value; or [ 2 ] relative decline of FVC between 5% and 10% of predicted value associated with a relative decline of DLCO ≥ 15% of predicted value [ 15 ]. PH was diagnosed by right-heart catheterization (RHC) and classified into causative groups according to the updated clinical classification of PH [ 16 ]. Although the hemodynamic definition of PH changed during follow-up, all patients validated the following set of criteria: mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 25 mmHg, mean pulmonary arterial wedge pressure ≤ 15 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance > 3 Wood units. PH worsening was defined as the occurrence of any one of the following event: all-cause death, lung transplantation, atrial septostomy, hospitalization for worsening PH, initiation of parenteral prostanoid therapy, or clinical deterioration (decrease of at least 15% in 6MWD from baseline, combined with either [ 1 ] worsening of WHO FC from baseline, or [ 2 ] the addition of approved PAH treatment [ 17 ].
sections.statistical analysis: Characteristics of the population were be described using mean ± standard deviation (SD), or median [interquartile range (IQR)] in case of non-normality, for quantitative variables, and number (percentage) for qualitative variables. Patient characteristics were compared between V1 and V2 using paired Student t tests, or paired Wilcoxon signed rank tests in case of non-normality, for quantitative variables, and McNemar’s χ 2 tests for qualitative variables. To study the associations between the difference in 6MWD between V2 and V1 (Δ6MWD) (in absolute value) as the dependent variable and the various explanatory variables, in a first step we conducted linear regressions analyses adjusted with the main potential confounding factors (Δtime, 6MWD at V1, gender, age, body mass index (BMI), disease duration and SSc subtype), which were defined a priori (before the analyses were performed). β coefficients [95% CI] were expressed in meters. Next, we conducted a multivariate regression model adjusted with the same potential confounding factors, and clinical variables of interest (RA area at V1, ΔRA area, FVC at V1, ΔFVC, ΔHR at V1, ΔΔHR, muscle symptoms, joint symptoms, number of IS at V1, ΔIS, number of VD at V1, ΔVD), selected for clinical relevance. We selected these clinical variables by considering one variable per potential organ involvement (e.g. FVC for lung involvement), taking into account the number of missing values, ensuring that there were no collinear variables (all variance inflation factors were less than 1/(1- R²)), no mediation variables and that the number of variables included in the model was consistent with the number of patients. All independent clinical variables were entered into the model simultaneously. The multiple R-squared (R²) was computed and regression diagnostics were performed. In addition, we conducted sensitivity analyses focusing on patients meeting the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) in 6MWD (dichotomizing the dependent variable as Δ6MWD ≤ -30 m vs. > -30 m based on previous studies [ 18 , 19 ]), and on those with ILD or PH. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, version 4.2.2 [ 20 ]. The threshold for statistical significance was set to p < 0.05.

tricuspid regurgitant velocity, VA alveolar volume, Δ variation of At the baseline visit (V1), most of the usual SSc complications were represented (Table 1 , “V1” columns ): musculoskeletal involvement (joint symptoms in 46%, muscle symptoms in 19%), ILD (38%), digital ulcers (19%) and RHC-proven PH (4%) (classified as group 1, i.e. PAH, in all cases). Most patients displayed minimal functional impairment, many of them being classified as NYHA class I or II (79%) with no significant PFT anomalies (mean FVC 102 ± 20%; mean DLCO 71 ± 19%); and treatment by immunosuppressants (10%) or vasodilators (3.5%) was uncommon. All patients performed a 6MWT, with a mean distance of 448 ± 97 m (83 ± 16% of predicted value), a median decrease in SpO 2 of 0 [ 1 ] %, a mean increase in HR of 10.4 ± 11.5 bpm, and a median increase in the Borg score of 2 (2.5). At the follow-up visit (V2), after a 24 (± 6)-month interval, the main characteristics of the population remained mostly unchanged (Table 1 , “V2” columns ). An additional 9 patients developed ILD (prevalence of 41% at V2 vs. 38% at V1, p = 0.008); 3 patients developed group 1 PH (11% at V2 vs. 8% at V1, p = 0.25); and 24 new patients reported occurrences of digital ulcers (57% at V2 vs. 46% at V1, p < 0.001).Significant variations were observed in PFT (mean ΔFVC − 1.4% ± 7.7%, p = 0.009; mean ΔDLCO − 2.2 ± 8.6%, p < 10 − 3 ) and TTE parameters (mean ΔTRJ + 0.1 ± 0.52 m/s, p = 0.04), although these changes remained mild. A larger proportion of patients were treated by immunosuppressants (34% at V2 vs. 10% at V1, p < 0.001) and vasodilators (13% at V2 vs. 4% at V1, p < 0.001). During the V2 6MWT, the 6MWD was significantly but modestly decreased when considering its absolute value (mean Δ6MWD − 11.6 ± 67.5 m, p < 0.01), and stable when expressed as a percentage of the predicted value (mean Δ6MWD − 0.006 ± 0.14%, p = 0.54). Other parameters measured during the test (such as initial and final HR, SpO 2 and Borg scores) were similar between V1 and V2.
sections.associations between \u03b46mwd and clin: Univariate analyses revealed multiple associations between Δ6MWD and several clinical parameters (Table 2, Fig. 1). To identify relevant explanatory variables, these analyses were adjusted for potential confounding factors (gender, age, body-mass index, SSc subtype, disease duration at V1, 6MWD value at V1 and time elapsed between V1 and V2). Fig. 1 Splines modelling the relationship between Δ6MWD and ΔFVC, ΔKCO, ΔsPAP, ΔRA area First, we identified multiple associations between Δ6MWD during follow-up and clinical parameters at V1. Negative associations were noted with age at V1 ( p < 10 − 3 ), 6MWD value at V1 ( p < 10 − 3 ), NYHA functional class III or IV at V1 ( p = 0.031), change in the Borg score during the V1 6MWT ( p < 10 − 3 ), history of PH at V1 ( p = 0.009), elevated Nt-pro-BNP levels at V1 ( p < 10 − 3 ), and sPAP at V1 ( p = 0.015). Positive associations were also observed, with FVC at V1 ( p = 0.023) and FEV1 at V1 ( p = 0.017). Second, the Δ6MWD during follow-up was also significantly associated with the variation of several clinical parameters between V1 and V2. Negative associations were found with ΔmRSS ( p = 0.011), ΔeGFR ( p = 0.013), NYHA functional class III-IV at both visits ( p < 10 − 3 ), PH at both visits ( p = 0.008), elevated Nt-pro-BNP levels at both visits ( p < 10 − 3 ), ΔRA area ( p = 0.045), ΔHAQ-DI score ( p = 0.023), and addition of vasodilating drugs between V1 and V2 (ΔVD, p = 0.018). Positive associations were identified with changes in the chronotropic response (defined as the difference in HRs at the beginning and the end of the test) between the V1 and the V2 6MWT (ΔHR change during test) and in the perceived exertion (defined as the difference in Borg scores at the beginning and the end of the test) between the V1 and the V2 6MWT (ΔBorg change during test) ( p = 0.01 and p = 0.002, respectively).

Building upon the results of our univariate analyses, we designed a multivariate model to identify the factors independently associated with Δ6MWD during follow-up (Table 2 ). Aside from age at V1 (β=-2.6 [-3.9;-1.3] m per 1-year increment, p < 0.001) and 6MWD at V1 (β=-0.3 [-0.5;-0.2] per 1-m increment, p < 0.001), significant and independent associations were found with ΔRA area (β=-6.2 [-12;-0.6] m per 1-cm 2 increment, p = 0.03), FVC at V1 (β = 1.4 [0.4;2.4] m, p = 0.006), HR change during the V1 6MWT (β = 1.9 [0.3;3.6], p = 0.02) and ΔHR change during 6MWT (β = 1.8 [0.4;3.2] m, p = 0.015), and occurrence of joint symptoms during follow-up (β=-67 [-114;-20] m, p = 0.006). This model accounted for 36% of the variance of Δ6MWD.
sections.clinical associations of the 6mwd minima: As previous studies identified a threshold value of approximately 30 m as a clinically meaningful variation of the 6MWD in PAH and ILD patients [ 18 , 19 ], we performed a sensitivity analysis considering Δ6MWD as a dichotomized variable ( Supplemental Table 1 ). Compared to those who remained stable or improved their 6MWD (Δ6MWD > -30 m), patients with a worsened 6MWD at V2 (Δ6MWD ≤ -30 m) were more likely to have PH ( p = 0.04), NYHA functional classes III-IV ( p = 0.005) and elevated Nt-proBNP levels ( p = 0.01) at both visits; and less likely to increase their chronotropic response (ΔHR change during 6MWT, p = 0.01) and their perceived exertion (ΔBorg change during 6MWT, p = 0.003) to exercise during follow-up. We did not observe an increased likelihood of developing ILD or PH during follow-up in patients with Δ6MWD ≤ -30 m compared to those > -30 m, although these were rare occurrences in our cohort.
sections.clinical associations of the \u03b46mwd: As the 6MWT is of particular interest in SSc patients with ILD and/or PH, we performed a subgroup analysis focusing on this specific population. Due to its sample size, only univariate analyses were performed.

capacity; TRV: tricuspid regurgitant velocity; VA : alveolar volume; Δ: variation of At the baseline visit (V1) (Table 2 , “V1” columns ), 84 (96%) patients had ILD, and 8 (9%) had RHC-proven PH (group 1, i.e. PAH, in all cases). Most of them were classified as NYHA class I or II (76%). Lung volumes were mostly normal (mean FVC 92 ± 22%), but with a significant diffusion impairment (mean DLCO 62 ± 20%). PH parameters on TTE remained within normal range for most patients (mean peak TRV 2.6 ± 0.7 m/s, mean RA area 15.6 ± 4 cm 2 ). Musculoskeletal complaints were also frequently reported (joint symptoms in 40%, muscle symptoms in 20%). Treatment included immunosuppressants in 14% and vasodilators in 6% of patients. During the V1 6MWT, patients walked a mean distance of 445 ± 100 m (80 ± 20% of predicted value), with a mean decrease in SpO 2 of 1 ± 2%, a mean increase in HR of 12.2 ± 12.2 bpm, and a median increase in the Borg score of 2 (IQR 2). At the follow-up visit (V2) (Table 2 , “V2” columns ), 1 additional patient developed ILD, and 2 others developed group 1 PH. Overall, 9 (10%) patients had progressive ILD and 6 (7%) had worsening PH. The main characteristics of the population remain stable, except for more frequent history of digital ulcers (70% at V2 vs. 55% at V1, p < 0.001 vs. V1), a mild decrease in TLC (mean − 1.6 ± 6.3%, p = 0.02) and a moderate increase in RA area (mean + 1.4 ± 3.3 cm 2 , p = 0.007). A larger proportion of patients were treated by immunosuppressants (44% at V2 vs. 16%, p < 0.001) and vasodilators (24% at V2 vs. 7% at V1, p < 0.001). A mild decrease of the 6MWD at V2 was observed when expressed in absolute value (mean Δ6MWD − 16 ± 74 m, p = 0.05), but not when considering its relative value (mean Δ6MWD − 0.01 ± 0.16%, p = 0.44). Aside from the Borg score at the beginning of the V2 6MWT (which mildly increased from its V1 value), other parameters measured during the test remained similar between the 2 visits. There was no significant difference in Δ6MWD between patients with and without progressive ILD or worsening PH (mean Δ6MWD − 35 ± 68 m vs. -12 ± 75 m respectively, p = 0.28) ( Supplemental Table 2 ).
sections.associations between \u03b46mwd and clin: We identified several significant associations between the Δ6MWD and clinical parameters at V1 in the SSc-ILD/PH subgroup (Table 3 ), most of which were already observed in the global SSc population. Negative associations were found with age at V1 ( p < 10 − 3 ), dcSSc subset at V1 ( p = 0.018), 6MWD value at V1 ( p = 0.01), change in Borg score during the V1 6MWT ( p = 0.007), history of PH at V1 ( p = 0.012), elevated Nt-pro-BNP levels at V1 ( p = 0.001), and sPAP at V1 ( p = 0.006). Positive associations were also found with ILD status at V1, especially with limited ILD ( p = 0.023), initial SpO 2 at the beginning of the V1 6MWT ( p = 0.026), and estimated GFR at V1 ( p = 0.026). sections.the 6mwd varies mildly during the follow: We observed a significant but modest variation of the 6MWD during follow-up in our unselected cohort of SSc patients. Similar findings were made in a Belgian cohort of 165 SSc patients without ILD or PH, where only non-significant changes in the 6MWD, ranging from a mean − 15.04 to + 3.37 m, were noted over more than 5 years [ 10 ]. Interestingly, the 6MWD variation over time remains similarly mild in our SSc-ILD/PH subgroup. Data from previous studies are in line with these results: the mean Δ6MWD over 1 year was estimated at + 9 ± 84 m in SSc-ILD patients included in the placebo group of the BUILD-2 trial [ 21 ]; and at -8.6 ± 39.3 m in SSc-PAH patients from the PHAROS registry [ 22 ]. This relative stability of the 6MWD over time must also be interpreted considering the low proportion of patients with progressive ILD and/or PH in our cohort. In this specific subgroup, no significant difference was detected compared with patients with stable ILD or PH, a result that may also have been limited by our small sample size.
sections.changes in the 6mwd in ssc patients disp: The 6MWT is routinely used during the follow-up of SSc patients, not only to assess their exercise capacity, but also to detect changes in their cardiopulmonary status. Our work yielded several results that challenge this common clinical practice. First, while we identified several correlations between Δ6MWD and changes in organ involvements, they were usually weak to moderate. Second, the 6MWD trajectory over time does not just reflect variation in organ involvement, but is also influenced their baseline status: indeed, the walk distance appears to decrease faster in patients displaying baseline markers of PH (such as sPAP and elevated Nt-pro-BNP at V1) and ILD (such as FVC at V1), in both our work and previous studies [ 23 – 25 ]. Overall, while it keeps value for functional and prognostic evaluation, these data question the relevance of the 6MWT as a surrogate for changes in cardiopulmonary complications during SSc. Although predictors of the baseline 6MWD have been thoroughly investigated [ 12 ], few studies have focused on identifying relevant associations with Δ6MWD. Interestingly, our work highlights that, among the numerous organ involvements occurring in SSc, only a few complications seemed to contribute to the change in the walk distance during follow-up in these patients. Indeed, in our study, consistent associations of Δ6MWD were found with markers of PH and chronotropic function, in both the global SSc cohort and the ILD/PH subgroup. Previous studies have already suggested an impact of pulmonary vascular impairment on the variations in exercise capacities in SSc: modest correlations of the Δ6MWD were observed with baseline echocardiographic parameters related to right ventricular systolic dysfunction in SSc patients [ 26 ]; and with modifications in hemodynamics [ 27 ] and in Nt-pro-BNP levels [ 28 ] in SSc-PAH patients. In this context, the negative association observed between the number of vasodilators and Δ6MWD may seem surprising at first, given that clinical trials have shown their efficacy in improving the walk distance in SSc-PAH patients [ 29 ]. This however probably reflects an indication bias, with SSc patients prescribed with these drugs more likely to have more severe forms of the disease and more limited exercise capacities. Similar to PAH, autonomic dysfunction has also been linked to exercise intolerance in SSc, with moderate associations found between baseline 6MWD and markers of both vagal withdrawal and sympathetic hyperactivation [ 30 ] in SSc patients; and between Δ6MWD and ΔΔHR in patients with non-idiopathic PAH [ 31 ]. Conversely, variation in lung functional capacities did not significantly impact the 6MWD trajectory during follow-up, in both the overall SSc population and the ILD/PH subgroup. Similar findings were made in other interstitial lung diseases, where only modest associations were noted between Δ6MWD and ΔFVC in IPF [ 3 , 32 ] and non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis [ 33 ]. These results should be interpreted with caution due to the small proportion of patients with progressive ILD in our cohort. Interestingly though, there was no significant difference in the 6MWD annualized decline between progressors and non-progressors in a cohort of patients with various types of pulmonary fibrosis [ 34 ]. As such, the ACR/Chest 2023 guidelines for ILD in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases recommend against monitoring patients using 6MWD during follow-up [ 35 ]. Our multivariate model also suggested that the occurrence of joint symptoms during follow-up negatively impact the 6MWD trajectory over time. Previous studies have shown an influence of musculoskeletal involvement on the walk distance in SSc, when expressed as objective variables (goniometric measures, quadricipital strength) [ 23 ] but not as subjective complaints [ 23 ]. Similar findings have been made in other respiratory diseases, such as COPD where the improvement of the 6MWD during rehabilitation was associated with the change in quadricipital strength [ 36 ]. As we did not collect the nature and location of joint symptoms in our work, further interpretation of this result is challenging. Several mechanisms could explain this finding: degenerative articular and/or peri-articular lesions located to the lower limbs and/or the lumbar spine, chronic inflammatory joint disease associated to the underlying scleroderma, and/or general exercise deconditioning with musculoskeletal limitation. Taken together, these data suggest that the evolution of exercise impairment in SSc remains multifactorial. Specific organ involvements seem to impact the 6MWD over follow-up, mainly relating to pulmonary vascular impairment and chronotropic incompetence, but with a modest influence. The weakness of these correlations may also be explained by the submaximal nature of the exercise testing performed during the 6MWT: stronger associations might be observed with exercise hemodynamics and maximal incremental exercise testing parameters [ 37 ].
sections.the \u03b46mwd as a measure of global di: Our work identified consistent correlations of Δ6MWD with several patient-reported outcomes, namely markers of functional limitation (NYHA III/IV at V1, ΔNYHA), perceived exertion (Borg change during V1 6MWT, ΔBorg change during test) and quality of life (ΔHAQ-DI). These measures not only reflect the objective severity of SSc organ involvements but also its broader impact on patient functioning and daily life [ 38 ]. Consequently, we suggest that the Δ6MWD could be considered as a relevant indicator of global disability rather than only a marker of organ involvement severity in these patients.
sections.strengths and limitations: Our study draws strength from its large SSc population, its longitudinal prospective data collection and the large number of variables available. However, it also has several limitations. First, due to methodological considerations, the follow-up duration had to be pre-determined and was set to 24 (± 6) months to maximize sample sizes. Longer follow-up could have allowed to increase the occurrence of additional SSc complications. However, a sensitivity analysis performed on a smaller population with a 36 (± 6)-month follow-up yielded mostly similar results (data not shown). Second, due to a low proportion of patients with progressive ILD or PH, the study was not sufficiently powered to test correlations in this population. Finally, the interpretation and generalizability of our results are also limited by the mild variation of the 6MWD and the infrequent occurrence of new organ involvement during the follow-up period.
sections.conclusion_1: Our work showed little variation of the 6MWD during the follow-up of SSc patients, and modest correlations with the evolution of organ involvements. Rather, it probably reflects a more global and integrative measure of functional capacity and disability in SSc patients. While it remains valuable for functional and prognostic evaluation, the variation in the 6MWD does not seem a reliable surrogate for modification in organ involvements in these patients.

title: Histological evaluation of hysterectomy specimens after NovaSure ® endometrial ablation in patients with atypical endometrial hyperplasia or endometrial carcinoma
abstract: Background Treatment with NovaSure® endometrial ablation is approved for patients with heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) without evidence of malignant or premalignant lesions. This analysis addresses the rare but clinically relevant situation in which endometrial carcinoma (EC) or atypical hyperplasia (AEH) is identified histologically after endometrial ablation in premenopausal patients. Objective Histological evaluation of hysterectomy specimens with correlation to clinical parameters in patients undergoing hysterectomy after incidental histological diagnosis of AEH or EC following NovaSure® endometrial ablation. Methods A retrospective single-center analysis was conducted on more than 400 patients who underwent NovaSure® endometrial ablation at our center between January 2020 and February 2025. Patients with AEH or EC for whom subsequent hysterectomy specimens were available were included. Histological evaluation was performed and independently reviewed to assess residual endometrium, residual endometrial atypia or carcinoma, and ablation-related histomorphological changes. Results A total of 11 patients (AEH n = 8; EC n = 3) underwent subsequent hysterectomy after NovaSure® endometrial ablation. Six out of eight patients with AEH showed no residual atypia in the hysterectomy specimens (2/8 with focal residual atypia), and no residual invasive carcinoma was detected in any of the three carcinoma cases. Histopathological analysis showed pronounced postablative changes, including necrosis, fibrosis, zonation, and vascular and lymphatic alterations. Conclusion This descriptive study provides a clinicopathological characterization of patients with EC or AEH who underwent hysterectomy after endometrial ablation. In these patients, no preprocedural evidence of endometrial pathology was present, and the diagnosis was established solely through routine histopathological examination of curettage specimens obtained immediately before the ablation procedure. Histological assessment revealed pronounced changes, highlighting specific diagnostic challenges and underscoring the importance of careful patient selection and thorough diagnostic evaluation before NovaSure® ablation. Within the limitations of this study, no evidence was found that prior endometrial ablation compromises oncological outcome.

sections.introduction: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) affects approximately 10–20% of all women, and is defined as deviations from the normal menstrual pattern in terms of frequency, regularity, duration, or volume. Depending on the underlying cause, there are various conservative treatment options (e.g., hormonal) [ 1 , 2 ]. In cases of failure, rejection, or inapplicability of conservative therapy, NovaSure® endometrial ablation is a less-invasive treatment option compared to hysterectomy in women with HMB. The NovaSure® system applies bipolar radiofrequency energy to thermally ablate the endometrial lining [ 3 ]. Limited data are available on histological changes following NovaSure® endometrial ablation. Available studies describe pronounced alterations, including stromal fibrosis, vascular changes, and a characteristic zonal pattern. These changes are described as being most prominent shortly after ablation, while diminishing over time [ 4 , 5 ]. The incidence of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) and endometrial cancer (EC) in premenopausal patients with abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is substantially lower than in patients with postmenopausal bleeding, but still occurs in approximately 1.3% of cases [ 6 ]. NovaSure® endometrial ablation must not be used if there are indications of (pre-) malignant lesions in the endometrium. However, small or focal EC and AEH may remain undetected despite adequate examination, indicating the limited sensitivity of endometrial biopsy. Concordance between Pipelle biopsy and final hysterectomy specimens has been reported to be as low as 60%, particularly in patients without preprocedural clinical suspicion of malignancy [ 7 ]. To date, data are lacking on whether EC or AEH remain histologically detectable after NovaSure® ablation and whether diagnostic or therapeutic limitations may arise. This study aims to characterize the histological patterns following ablation in NovaSure® hysterectomy specimens. It will investigate whether residual atypia or carcinoma can be reliably identified and whether there are indications of potential diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.
sections.cohort and study design:
A retrospective database analysis was conducted at our center between January 2020 and February 2025. Among more than 400 NovaSure® procedures, the pathological findings of curettage specimens obtained immediately before ablation were analyzed. AEH was detected in 8 patients, and EC cells were detected in 3 additional cases. In all cases, hysterectomy specimens from subsequent treatment were available at our center and were evaluated for histopathological characteristics. Patient and procedural characteristics of the 11 corresponding patients are presented in Table 1 . The study was conducted in accordance with the approval of the Ethics Committee of Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nürnberg (approval number: 24-41-Br). This study presents a descriptive analysis of patient characteristics, treatment modalities, and histomorphological features. sections.pathological evaluation of specimens: During routine pathological workup, representative resection specimens were photographed. Paraffin-embedded blocks from all cases were selected, and corresponding H&E-stained sections were digitized using a Hamamatsu S210 slide scanner at 40 × magnification (0.1213 µm/pixel). Two pathologists with several years of experience (A.H. and C.M.) digitally reviewed all cases. Specific histologic alterations were subsequently discussed in joint review until a consensus diagnosis/classification was reached. Specifically, consensus values were obtained for estimated percentage of residual vital endometrium, quality of inflammatory pattern, as well as blood and lymphatic vessel alterations. Additionally, presence of residual atypia, necrosis, fibrotic and myxoid changes, as well as the zonation phenomenon described previously were assessed [ 4 ]. Representative image cutouts of the WSI scans were obtained to illustrate the respective histologic changes.
sections.results_1: A total of 11 patients were included: 3 with EC and 8 with AEH. In all 3 EC cases, endometrioid endometrial carcinoma was diagnosed, with histopathological grade 1 (G1) tumors in two cases and a grade 2 (G2) tumor in one case. Molecular characterization, including immunohistochemical assessment of mismatch repair (MMR) proteins and p53 expression, was available in 2 of the 3 cases. Both analyzed cases demonstrated MMR proficiency (pMMR) and a wild-type p53 expression pattern. All patients with carcinoma underwent guideline-based oncological treatment, including hysterectomy combined with either sentinel lymph-node biopsy or pelvic lymphadenectomy. Sentinel lymph-node mapping after intracervical injection of indocyanine green (ICG) showed adequate intraoperative detection rates in all 3 cases. Postoperatively, all carcinoma patients were classified as FIGO stage IA, with no evidence of lymph-node involvement. All eight patients with AEH underwent hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy. Histopathological examination of the hysterectomy specimens revealed that 6 of the 8 patients with a preoperative diagnosis of AEH showed no residual atypia. Similarly, in all 3 patients with histologically confirmed EC, no remaining invasive lesions were detected in the final hysterectomy specimens. Overall, most cases showed only limited residual vital endometrium. Necrotic and fibrotic changes were common, as were ectatic and thrombotic blood vessels. Most cases showed a typical zonation consisting of a superficial necrosis zone inside the endometrium, a subendometrial hemorrhagic zone with ectatic blood vessels and extravasation of blood, and a deeper fibrotic zone with lightly ectatic lymph vessels, giving the endo- and myometrium a characteristic histological trizonal structure. An overview of the distribution of consensus histologic alterations is provided in Table 2 and illustrated in Fig. 1 . Further histopathological evaluation of the endocervical region revealed no relevant alterations of the lymphatic vessels. The endocervical glands appeared completely viable, with preserved glandular architecture and no evidence of thermal damage or ablation-related changes. Representative histological findings are shown in Fig. 2 . sections.discussion: Only a few studies have investigated the morphological features of hysterectomy specimens following endometrial ablation. Karpathiou et al. described time-dependent histological changes after thermal endometrial ablation, with hysterectomies performed early showing pronounced necrosis, fibrosis, vascular alterations, and a zonation effect. Specimens obtained at later time points demonstrated less prominent changes, and an almost normal endometrial lining; necrosis of myometrial origin and a high prevalence of adenomyosis were observed irrespective of the time interval [ 4 ]. In line with these observations, our cohort likewise exhibited high rates of necrosis, fibrosis, zonation, and alterations in vascular and lymphatic vessels. However, evaluating the time course of these changes was not possible, as all hysterectomies in our study were performed within a limited window of up to 96 days after endometrial ablation. To date, data specifically characterizing hysterectomy specimens from patients with confirmed EC or AEH following endometrial ablation are lacking. In our cohort, only 2 of 11 cases showed focal residual atypia in the hysterectomy specimen, which is consistent with the overall low amount of residual endometrium, as in 73% of cases, there was little or no endometrial tissue remaining. Histological confirmation prior to ablation is essential, as relevant premalignant or malignant lesions may be obscured by the procedure. This is particularly important as a considerable proportion of patients with biopsy-confirmed AEH also have EC in the subsequent hysterectomy specimen, with reported rates ranging from approximately 10% up to more than 50% [ 8 – 12 ]. Kurosawa et al. reported comparable rates, with concurrent EC detected in 41% of patients despite preoperative hysteroscopic inspection and total curettage, demonstrating that even combined hysteroscopic visualization and extensive endometrial sampling may miss focal malignant lesions or underestimate the extent of disease [ 13 ]. These findings are further supported by the study of Parsons et al., who investigated nearly 7000 patients undergoing hysterectomy for benign indications and identified 13 cases of occult EC (0.19%). Of these, 10 patients had undergone prior endometrial assessment by endometrial biopsy or dilation and curettage, and none had shown atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma preoperatively [ 14 ]. These findings support the need for thorough histologic evaluation prior to endometrial ablation and careful clinical treatment planning, while also underlining the inherent limitations of preoperative endometrial assessment. In our cohort, pronounced histological alterations of the lymph vessels and blood vessels attributable to the thermal effects of NovaSure® treatment were observed (Table 2 ), which are of immediate relevance for pathological assessment. However, there was no evidence that these features pose a significant risk of misinterpretation as malignant, as they are not usually located within the central necrotic zone and can be reliably distinguished from malignant glands by their flat endothelial lining and characteristic architectural features. The main diagnostic challenge for pathologists is distinguishing residual malignant cells from non-neoplastic cellular remnants within the necrotic ablation zone, where pronounced thermal and crush artifacts can markedly distort tissue morphology and thereby compromise histopathological interpretability. An illustrative example is shown in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3 Thermally altered endometrial glands with cell nucleus crushing (star) and distortion of glandular architecture (triangle), HE The absence of histologically detectable residual carcinoma should not be interpreted as a treatment effect of endometrial ablation . It may also be explained by complete removal during curettage, superficial tumor spread, or postablative sampling effects. It should also be noted that subsequent endometrial assessment may be compromised after prior thermal endometrial ablation. Both endometrial sampling and sonohysterography have been reported to fail more frequently in this patient group, thereby complicating further diagnostic evaluation [ 15 ]. Sentinel lymph-node biopsy is an established component of oncologic surgical treatment in endometrial cancer [ 16 ]. Sentinel tracer injection is performed intracervically and follows distribution along paracervical lymphatic pathways [ 17 ]. As NovaSure® endometrial ablation is confined to the uterine cavity and, consistent with our histomorphological findings, does not induce thermal alterations in the adjacent endocervical region, preserved cervical lymphatic architecture would be expected (Fig. 2 ). Adequate intraoperative detection of the sentinel lymph nodes was achieved in all 3 EC cases, and sentinel lymph-node biopsy was, therefore, performed in accordance with guideline-based surgical management. Systematic lymphadenectomy was carried out in cases with a specific clinical indication, such as intraoperatively suspicious lymph nodes. In this context, our findings provide no evidence of a limitation of the sentinel lymph-node mapping procedure following NovaSure® endometrial ablation.
sections.conclusion_1: This study provides a descriptive analysis of clinical and histological parameters in a unique patient cohort. Pronounced histomorphological changes were observed after ablation, which are relevant for pathological assessment as they are relevant for delineating ablation-related changes and highlight diagnostic challenges. In particular, within the necrotic ablation zone, thermal and crush artifacts can impair histological interpretability. Preserved endocervical lymphatic structures suggest that sentinel lymph-node mapping based on intracervical tracer injection after NovaSure® ablation is not fundamentally impaired. However, these observations must be interpreted with caution, given the cohort’s descriptive nature and limited size. While the rarity of this clearly defined patient group and the detailed clinical–pathological correlation are significant strengths, the small sample size limits the generalizability. Accordingly, this study aims to provide a descriptive framework rather than therapeutic recommendations.

title: Clinical and sociodemographic correlates of body mass index in a large multicenter obsessive–compulsive disorder sample
abstract: Purpose This multicenter study aims to investigate associations between body mass index (BMI) and sociodemographic and clinical characteristics in a clinical sample of individuals with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD). Methods Data were analyzed from 947 adults diagnosed with OCD, recruited through the Brazilian Research Consortium on Obsessive–Compulsive Spectrum Disorders. BMI was calculated from self-reported weight and height and categorized according to WHO definitions. Sociodemographic and clinical data were obtained using standardized instruments. Associations between BMI and sociodemographic/clinical variables were examined using linear regression models. Results The mean BMI in the sample was 24.55 kg/m 2 (SD = 4.65), with 5.5% of participants classified as underweight, 58% as normal weight, 25% as overweight, and 11.5% as obese. In the multivariate linear regression model, higher BMI was significantly associated with older age ( β = 0.09, p < 0.001), current psychiatric treatment ( β = 1.4, p < 0.001), and binge eating disorder ( β = 4.4, p < 0.001). Lower BMI was significantly associated with female sex ( β = – 1.6, p < 0.001) and body dysmorphic disorder ( β = – 1.2, p = 0.005). No significant associations were found with educational level, OCD severity, comorbid depression, anxiety, bulimia, or anorexia. Conclusion Although BMI was unrelated to OCD severity, it was associated with demographic, clinical, and treatment-related variables, underscoring the need for evaluation beyond symptom-based assessment. Level of evidence: III, as it is based on an observational analytic design using a large cross-sectional multicenter sample.
