Most healthcare providers believed describing symptoms was not difficult for participants (94%, n = 32). 70.6% ( n = 24) believed self-administered pulse oximetry was easy for participants, and 76.5% ( n = 26) believed it was easy for participants to read and report Sp0 2 measurements. One SESAL physician believed waiting to be enrolled in the study was a burden for some patients. Several study nurses explained that if patients felt burdened by calls, they might complain or disenrol, which was rare. Most (91.2%, n = 31) healthcare providers did not believe enrolling participants was difficult; three SESAL respondents believed it was difficult. They believed enrolment involved some ( n = 12) or small effort ( n = 22). During in-depth interviews, SESAL physicians believed the work to implement interventions would be minimal, which some perceived as acceptable and led others to suggest increasing personnel. Study staff reported feeling overburdened by the demands of enrolling and calling patients during the height of COVID-19 waves.
sections.appropriateness: Providers were asked about intervention appropriateness for the problem and context, given limited available resources and other challenges facing the population and health system. Many interview respondents shared participant approval as evidence of appropriateness, in that the interventions fit patient needs and patients appreciate the interventions. Respondents worried that while it was possible to teach participants to use pulse oximeters, they might not understand the results. One respondent expressed doubts about scalability, saying …[implementing this] would imply personnel, it would imply technology and many things that SESAL does not have, there are other priorities…. Medicine, personnel… Another SESAL doctor believed other interventions are more urgent, like those for chronic diseases, but emphasized that monitoring high-risk COVID-19 patients is crucial because people with chronic diseases are at risk for complications.
sections.discussion: This mixed-methods study found that remote patient monitoring and self-administered pulse oximetry were highly acceptable to participants and healthcare providers. Both groups understood the interventions, and participants were satisfied with the quality of care. Some providers expressed concerns about patient capacity to perform pulse oximetry and understand results, but participants did not share those worries. Patient educational attainment was associated with greater likelihood of reporting difficulty with an intervention, but not acceptability. While participants and providers believed monitoring patients at home was valuable, some providers wondered whether the intervention was appropriate for the context, given other urgent, non-COVID-19, health needs. Grounding this investigation in the Sekhon et al. framework facilitated the investigation of defined healthcare acceptability constructs from diverse perspectives and data collection methods. Examining multiple viewpoints can provide lessons about the extent to which respondents are good judges of their own and others’ acceptance and capabilities. The joint display enabled cross-source comparison to highlight convergence or divergence in perspective and experience, rather than triangulation. Intervention coherence was well understood by participants and providers. This knowledge likely was imparted by study staff and indicates a strong ability to convey its mechanism and objectives. Both groups believed providing mental and emotional support was an objective of the intervention. Affective attitude was positive; however, while participants reported nearly universal satisfaction, providers held more diverse viewpoints. Providers indicated that they would be less willing to refer patients versus family members for the interventions. We discovered that this was due to the perceived higher levels of education and support available to healthcare providers’ relatives. These findings indicate that while providers report a positive attitude towards the intervention, that did not translate into willingness to refer patients in the future, despite seeing participants successfully engage with interventions. Participants were more likely to perceive the interventions as effective as healthcare providers. Provider perceptions of effectiveness were informed by perceived intervention objectives, belief in remote monitoring effectiveness and appropriateness, and perceptions of participant experience. Multiple SESAL physicians perceived reduction in unnecessary return patient visits. Although data were not collected to confirm this, similar findings have been observed in other remote patient monitoring studies, where reduced return visits are frequently cited as a positive outcome (Vudathaneni et al. , 2025 ). Providers anticipated remote monitoring would substantially burden patients. Most study participants described a minimal burden and valued the education and support provided. The mismatch between provider perception and participant experience could be due to an underestimation of participant capacity by providers and/or participants underreporting challenges. Providers identified possible barriers participants may have experienced in their return for evaluation: burden (cost, transportation, accompaniment, time) and emotional responses to interacting with the healthcare system (fear of hospitalization, dying, mistreatment, or disbelief in warning sign severity). While similar participant information is unavailable, of the 52 participants who reported seeking care after a referral, 24 (46%) did not do so. The reasons are unclear but could be due to social desirability bias or barriers experienced while seeking care. The appropriateness of relying on participants to return for additional care without providing additional support or linkage to care is uncertain, given significant barriers to access. Most participants reported no difficulty with participation; however, the odds of reporting difficulty significantly increased relative to educational attainment. Participants successfully measured and reported pulse oximeter readings, with at least one measurement provided on 97% of calls, an indication of appropriately held perceptions of self-efficacy. While providers expressed doubts about participant self-efficacy first, many became convinced that participants were capable of self-administering pulse oximetry. However, positivity during in-depth interviews does not negate the anonymous CASI data, where SESAL and study providers indicated greater willingness to refer family than patients for intervention participation, due to doubts about capacity to perform and understand intervention procedures. While appropriateness was not queried directly with participants, positive affective attitude and perceived efficacy provide some evidence that they believed the intervention was the right fit for the problem. The results of this study raise concerns about the appropriateness of referring participants for additional care without facilitating that process, given low rates of successful return for care. Additionally, two providers provided a systems perspective, raising concerns about whether this intervention would be feasible and a suitable investment to provide remote care for COVID-19 patients, given other, non-COVID-19, health priorities. Remote patient monitoring has been shown to be a safe and effective way for stable patients at high risk for adverse outcomes to receive care, with or without the addition of self-administered technology, as well as reducing health facility burden, risk of nosocomial infection, and cost (Camacho-Leon et al. , 2022 ; Mahmoud et al. , 2022 ). Staffing such an intervention is challenging because infection rates and staffing needs increase concurrently; however, with an emergency preparedness plan and training, healthcare staff were willing and believed themselves capable of implementing these strategies (Task shifting healthcare services in the post-COVID world: A scoping review | PLOS Global Public Health). Previous concerns included lack of access to technology, unreliable mobile and electricity networks, and low health and technology literacy, which may be exacerbated among marginalized groups (Gaeta et al. , 2020 ; Agarwal et al. , 2021 ; Diseases, 2021 ; Maghrabi et al. , 2021 ; Vindrola-Padros et al. , 2021 ; Arora et al. , 2022 ; Camacho-Leon et al. , 2022 ). High participation rates demonstrate the penetration of mobile phone technology and the ability of participants to access a phone, even if they do not own one. While concerns about equity in healthcare technology are vital and warranted, assumptions about the capacity of people with lower educational attainment to learn and use new technology should be based on experiences with the target population, rather than assumptions or perceptions, even those of experienced healthcare providers. With those considerations in mind, intervention adaptation will be crucial if these interventions are adopted in the future. Avenues for adaptation are expansive and might include implementation during future health emergencies to monitor high-risk, stable patients, reduce onward transmission, and conserve health facility resources or adaptation to provide short-term remote monitoring of patient post-acute health events, such as monitoring blood glucose after a diabetes diagnosis, including with internet-enabled devices (Salehi et al. , 2020 ; Alboksmaty et al. , 2022 ; DeRogatis et al. , 2024 ). Conceptualizing this approach broadly expands its utility and potential applications, including adapting methods of patient contact and warning sign identification based on the context, patient population, and disease manifestation. Future implementers and researchers adapting this remote monitoring and warning sign identification intervention could focus on (1) selecting a disease, infectious or chronic, with warning signs detectable through self-administered technology, (2) identifying a medically stable yet high-risk population, (3) collaborating with the target group to ensure appropriate communication and technology, (4) developing an educational approach, (5) addressing provider concerns about patient ability to use self-monitoring tools, and (6) tracking provider referral rates to prevent doubts about self-efficacy from limiting participation. Including mental and emotional health support may also enhance patient and provider satisfaction. The success of participant and provider education in this study underscores the importance of health systems’ capacity to rapidly deploy targeted training during health emergencies. Building surge capacity for just-in-time patient and provider education should be a priority in emergency preparedness planning, as novel diseases and interventions cannot be anticipated through continuing education infrastructure alone. The rigorous methodology of this investigation allows the presentation of credible and transferable results, although further investigation would be needed to understand perspectives and capacities of a different target population. This study has limitations. The lack of qualitative investigation with participants limits our understanding of the rationale behind their perceptions of the interventions. Additionally, because study staff administered the disenrolment questionnaires, including questions about acceptability, social desirability bias could positively skew participant responses. Limits of the CASI include the restriction of enrolment to SESAL staff and enrolment to those present on data collection days, which excludes SESAL staff not working on those days or during that shift, and those who no longer worked at the triage centre when data collection was carried out. In-depth interview limitations include that study personnel conducted the interviews, which could positively bias in-depth interview responses, although they were conducted by senior study staff, rather than staff who previously provided patient care. Participant engagement beyond a ten-day period, or beyond the acute phase of a health concern, is unknown and could decrease due to a reduced sense of urgency. It is possible that high participation levels were mediated by the isolation mandate for COVID-19 positive patients, where people were eager to participate, talk to study staff, and report symptoms because they were socially isolated during their infection. More broadly, within implementation science, a recent review of acceptability assessments found they often lack standardized approaches and rigorous methodologies. While this assessment of acceptability does align with the best practices identified in this review, it does not rely on validated scales to calculate acceptability metrics (Ortblad et al. , 2023 ). Finally, due to their extensive use, the evidence base around the limitations of fingertip pulse oximeters was expanded upon during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to an FDA investigation (Food and Drug Administration, 2022 ; Health C for D and R, 2022 ; McFarling, 2023 ). Pulse oximeters were found to measure Sp0 2 1.1% lower among self-identified Black patients and 1.2% lower self-identified non-Black Hispanics, findings that are likely applicable to Hondurans and study participants, 97% of whom self-identified as Mestizo or Mestizo and an additional ethnicity, most frequently Lenca or Maya, during enrolment. While the relatively high referral threshold of 94% Sp0 2 may have avoided under-referrals, better understanding the impact of skin colour on pulse oximeter precision and adjusting warning and referral levels appropriately is essential prior to their use in a population that includes members with darker skin, to avoid delays in identification of hypoxia and referral to appropriate care (Fawzy et al. , 2022 ). In summary, while the intervention was designed to mitigate COVID-19-associated morbidity and mortality, widespread adoption is no longer needed due to the pronounced decrease in severe outcomes. Nonetheless, remote patient monitoring and self-administered technology are powerful tools that can be leveraged to provide remote monitoring of acute conditions, such as when systems are overwhelmed during future epidemics or post-acute health events, whether due to chronic or infectious diseases. Our findings provide evidence for how these interventions may be implemented in a lower resource setting during a pandemic, and how patients and implementors perceive these interventions. Given that successful implementation of healthcare interventions can be grounded in how they are perceived, generating rigorous data to understand and dissect these perceptions is a critical building block in preparing for the next epidemic or pandemic.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Switching to Dolutegravir/Lamivudine in Virologically Suppressed HIV-1 Infected Adults with TDF-Related Renal or Bone Toxicity
abstract: Introduction Long-term use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is associated with renal tubular dysfunction and bone mineral loss. In virologically suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH), optimizing antiretroviral therapy requires maintaining viral suppression while minimizing cumulative drug-related toxicity. We therefore evaluated the efficacy and safety of switching to dolutegravir/lamivudine (DTG/3TC) in Chinese PLWH with TDF-related renal or bone toxicity. Methods This prospective, single-center, open-label cohort study enrolled adults with HIV-1 RNA < 40 copies/ml for ≥ 6 months on TDF-based regimens and evidence of TDF-associated renal or bone toxicity. Participants were switched to DTG/3TC and followed for 48 weeks. The primary endpoint was virological failure at week 48 (FDA Snapshot algorithm). Secondary endpoints included changes in CD4 + T-cell counts, renal tubular biomarkers, bone mineral density (BMD), metabolic parameters, and safety outcomes. Results One hundred participants were enrolled; 91 completed the study per protocol. Median age was 45 years and 90% were male. At week 48, virological suppression was maintained in 90% of the intention-to-treat–exposed population and 99% of the per-protocol population. CD4 + T-cell counts increased significantly at week 48 (+ 77.4 cells/μl; p < 0.001). Markers of proximal tubular dysfunction improved significantly, including reductions in urinary β2-microglobulin-to-creatinine ratio, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and urinary retinol-binding protein-to-creatinine ratio (all p < 0.001). BMD increased in the lumbar spine and hip (both p < 0.001). Modest weight gain (+ 2.17 kg) and small increases in total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were observed at week 48. Conclusions In virologically suppressed Chinese PLWH with TDF-related renal or bone toxicity, switching to DTG/3TC maintained viral suppression and was associated with significant improvements in renal tubular and bone metabolic markers over 48 weeks. DTG/3TC represents a well-tolerated toxicity-driven switch strategy in routine clinical practice. Trial Registration ClinicalTrial.gov ID: NCT05493969 .

sections.introduction: Long-term use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is associated with renal tubular dysfunction and bone mineral loss. In virologically suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH), optimizing antiretroviral therapy requires maintaining viral suppression while minimizing cumulative drug-related toxicity. We therefore evaluated the efficacy and safety of switching to dolutegravir/lamivudine (DTG/3TC) in Chinese PLWH with TDF-related renal or bone toxicity.

sections.key summary points: Why carry out this study? Long-term tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) use is associated with renal tubular injury and bone mineral loss, underscoring the need for clinically effective toxicity-driven switch strategies in virologically suppressed people living with HIV (PLWH). This study investigated whether switching to dolutegravir/lamivudine (DTG/3TC) in PLWH with TDF-related toxicity could maintain virological suppression while improving renal and bone metabolic parameters. What was learned from the study? Switching from TDF-based regimens to DTG/3TC maintained high rates of virological suppression through 48 weeks in Chinese PLWH with documented TDF-related toxicity. The switch was associated with significant improvements in renal tubular biomarkers and bone mineral density, supporting DTG/3TC as an effective toxicity-driven optimization strategy for virologically suppressed PLWH.
sections.introduction_1: The scale-up of antiretroviral therapy (ART) has transformed HIV infection into a chronic, manageable disease. In China, the National Free Antiretroviral Therapy Program (NFATP) has enabled broad access to ART with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)—based regimens, which are the most widely used first-line and maintenance therapies [ 1 , 2 ]. As the treatment duration increases, long-term drug-related toxicities have become a major driver of regimen modification in virologically suppressed patients. TDF-associated renal and bone toxicity are among the most frequently encountered concerns. TDF-related proximal renal tubular dysfunction often manifests as elevated urinary low-molecular-weight proteins before a decline in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) becomes apparent [ 3 ], while progressive reductions in bone mineral density and abnormalities in bone turnover markers are commonly observed during prolonged exposure [ 4 – 6 ]. These complications are particularly relevant in Chinese people living with HIV (PLWH), where long-term TDF use is common. In this setting, ART optimization has shifted toward maintaining viral suppression while minimizing cumulative toxicity. Dual therapy with dolutegravir and lamivudine (DTG/3TC) offers a simplified regimen with a high genetic barrier to resistance, favorable tolerability, and minimal drug–drug interactions. Large randomized trials and real-world studies have demonstrated the non-inferiority of DTG/3TC compared to standard three- or four-drug regimens in virologically suppressed PLWH [ 7 – 9 ], leading to its recommendation in international and Chinese treatment guidelines [ 2 , 10 , 11 ]. Withdrawal of TDF represents a clinically meaningful strategy for patients with TDF-related renal or bone toxicity. Our previous studies have suggested improvements in bone metabolism and stabilization of renal parameters following discontinuation of TDF-containing regimens [ 12 ]. However, most available evidence is derived from randomized trials with strict inclusion criteria or retrospective cohorts with limited assessments of renal tubular and bone metabolic biomarkers. Prospective data focusing specifically on PLWH with documented TDF-associated renal or bone toxicity, particularly in the Chinese clinical context, remain limited. Therefore, we conducted this prospective cohort study of virologically suppressed Chinese PLWH with evidence of TDF-related renal or bone toxicity to evaluate the efficacy and safety of switching to DTG/3TC.
sections.study design and study setting: This was a single-center, prospective, open-label, single-arm cohort study conducted at the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center (SPHCC) in Shanghai, China. SPHCC is the designated center in Shanghai responsible for HIV diagnosis, ART, and long-term clinical follow-up. The center manages a large cohort of over 16,000 PLWH. All patients in this cohort undergo routine follow-up with systematic monitoring of virological, immunological, renal, bone, metabolic, and other relevant parameters. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of switching to a dual regimen of DTG/3TC in virologically suppressed PLWH who developed TDF-associated renal and/or bone toxicity. Participants were not enrolled through population-based random screening; instead, they were selectively identified from the well-characterized longitudinal cohort based on predefined criteria indicating a high likelihood of TDF-related renal or bone toxicity.
sections.participants: The study enrolled PLWH aged 18–75 years who maintained plasma HIV-1 RNA levels below 40 copies/ml for at least 6 months prior to screening while on a TDF plus 3TC/FTC-based regimen. The participants were required to show clinical or laboratory evidence of TDF-associated renal or bone toxicity. Renal impairment was defined by meeting at least one of the following criteria: a sustained decline in eGFR of ≥ 5 ml/min/1.73 m 2 per year for ≥ 3 consecutive years, or a confirmed ≥ 25% reduction in eGFR from baseline; a urine β2-microglobulin-to-creatinine ratio (U-β2-MG/cr) ≥ 300 μg/g; a urine microalbumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) > 30 mg/g; non-diabetic glycosuria; or serum phosphorus level < 0.8 mmol/l after at least 8 h of fasting. Bone toxicity was defined as either a bone mineral density (BMD) T-score < − 1.0, a Z -score < − 2.0, or the occurrence of a fragility fracture after initiation of TDF after exclusion of other contributing factors. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy, breastfeeding, or intention to become pregnant or breastfeed during the study period; active opportunistic infections or malignancies; significant hepatic impairment, defined as alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ≥ 5 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), ALT ≥ 3 × ULN with bilirubin ≥ 1.5 × ULN) or end-stage liver disease; coinfection with hepatitis B virus (HBV), defined as HBsAg positivity and/or detectable HBV DNA (excluding isolated anti-HBc positivity with undetectable HBV DNA); coinfection with hepatitis C virus; known hypersensitivity or resistance to DTG or 3TC; concomitant use of medications contraindicated with the study regimen; and an eGFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m 2 .
sections.data collection and measurements: Data were prospectively collected according to a predefined schedule: screening, baseline (day 1), and follow-up at weeks 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 48.
sections.clinical evaluations: At baseline and all follow-up visits, we documented medical history, concomitant medications, adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs), and body weight. Treatment adherence was assessed at each follow-up visit.
sections.virological and immunological assessment: Plasma HIV-1 RNA levels were quantified at screening, baseline, and weeks 12, 24, and 48 using reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (COBAS ® AmpliPrep/COBAS ® TaqMan ® HIV-1 Test, v2.0, ABI7500). CD4 + T-cell counts were measured at screening, baseline, and weeks 24 and 48 by flow cytometry using a BD FACS Canto II system with BD Multitest™ CD3/CD8/CD45/CD4 reagents (BD Biosciences).
sections.metabolic parameters: Fasting lipid profiles (triglycerides, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C], and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [HDL-C]) and fasting blood glucose were measured at baseline and all follow-up visits.
sections.renal and bone metabolism markers: Serum cystatin C, osteocalcin, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)VitD), retinol-binding protein (RBP) and urinary markers (urinalysis, UACR, U-β2-MG/Cr, and N -acetyl-β- d -glucosaminidase [NAG]) were measured at baseline and all follow-up visits. Cystatin C-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFRcysc) was calculated using the 2012 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) equation.
sections.bmd: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans (Lunar Prodigy; GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) were performed at screening and at weeks 24 and 48 to assess BMD at the lumbar spine and hip, following standardized procedures in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.
sections.study endpoints: The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants with virologic failure at week 48 as defined by the FDA Snapshot algorithm. Virological failure was defined as: (1) HIV-RNA ≥ 40 copies/ml at week 48; (2) discontinuation of treatment due to lack of efficacy; and (3) discontinuation of treatment due to reasons other than AEs and last available HIV-RNA ≥ 40 copies/ml. The secondary endpoints included changes in CD4 + T-cell counts, renal and bone biomarkers, and the incidence of AEs and SAEs. Renal biomarkers included eGFR, serum creatinine, serum cystatin C, UACR, U-β2-MG/cr, urine NAG-to-creatinine ratio (UNAG/cr), and urine RBP-to-creatinine ratio (URBP/cr). Bone biomarkers included BMD and serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin, and 25(OH)VitD levels.
sections.data analysis: All participants receiving ≥ 1 dose of DTG/3TC were included in the intention-to-treat–exposed (ITT-E) population, whereas the per-protocol (PP) population comprised those who completed the study without major protocol deviations. Data distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Normally distributed variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), non-normal variables are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR), and categorical variables are shown as number (%). Changes in CD4 + T cell counts and body weight at weeks 24 and 48 were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, whereas renal, bone, and lipid parameters were assessed using the paired nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The adverse events were summarized descriptively. A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0.
sections.ethical statement: All participants provided informed written consent before being enrolled in the study. All data were de-identified and analyzed anonymously. This study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05493969 ). This study was performed in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration of 1964 and its later amendments and received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of SPHCC (approval number: 2021-S023-04).
sections.participant baseline characteristics: A total of 114 individuals were screened, of which 100 were enrolled, including 70 with TDF-related renal toxicity, nine with bone toxicity, and 21 with both conditions. Nine participants withdrew owing to AEs or other reasons, leaving 91 participants for the per-protocol analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow diagram of patient enrollment. The median duration of ART was 77 months. Most participants received non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens (86.0% in the ITT-E population and 85.7% in the PP population), predominantly efavirenz (EFV). The median baseline CD4 + T-cell counts were high (565 and 573 cells/μl, respectively), with more than 56% of the participants having counts ≥ 500 cells/μl (Table 1 ). sections.aes and saes: AEs were reported in 36% of the participants in the ITT-E population, with hepatic dysfunction (eight cases), hyperuricemia (six cases), and COVID-19 (four cases) being the most common. Other reported AEs included rash (three cases), upper respiratory tract infection (three cases), and insomnia (two cases). Six SAEs occurred but were deemed unrelated to the study treatment, including (1) multiple myeloma; (2) enlarged prostate accompanied by a urinary tract infection; (3) a malignant tumor in the left breast; (4) herpes zoster of the external ear with associated peripheral facial nerve palsy; (5) a fracture of the distal right radius with a concurrent contusion of the skin and soft tissue; (6) and a complex anal fistula. Only one participant discontinued treatment because of insomnia, which was considered to be drug-related.
sections.discussion: In this prospective cohort of virologically suppressed Chinese PLWH with documented TDF-associated renal or bone toxicity, switching to DTG/3TC maintained virological suppression and immunological stability, while being associated with significant improvements in renal tubular and bone metabolic biomarkers. These findings address a common clinical scenario in routine HIV care in China, where long-term TDF exposure is widespread, and regimen modification is increasingly driven by cumulative toxicity rather than virological failure. Our results are consistent with existing evidence supporting DTG/3TC as an effective maintenance strategy and extend these findings to patients with established TDF-related renal or bone toxicity, further supporting its use in clinically vulnerable populations. Boosted protease inhibitors are known to increase TDF nephrotoxicity risk [ 13 ]. In our cohort, however, only 13% of participants received ritonavir-boosted lopinavir, while the majority (86%) were on NNRTI-based regimens, mainly efavirenz. Despite this, they still developed renal/bone toxicity, likely due to longer cumulative TDF exposure (median 77 months), and potential host susceptibility in Chinese individuals. Thus, our findings extend the evidence to unboosted TDF regimens in a real-world Chinese setting. Due to the limited number of patients in the LPV/r group, we were unable to separately assess whether this subgroup exhibited the greatest changes in renal and bone markers. Renal outcomes showed a transient increase in serum creatinine and cystatin C levels after switching, which stabilized by week 48 and is consistent with the known effect of dolutegravir on tubular creatinine secretion rather than true nephrotoxicity [ 14 ]. In contrast, the markers of proximal tubular dysfunction, including U-β2-MG/cr, UACR, and URBP/cr, improved significantly, indicating recovery from TDF-associated tubular injury. Given that TDF-related nephrotoxicity typically manifests as proximal tubular dysfunction rather than reduced glomerular filtration, these changes are clinically relevant and align with previous studies demonstrating renal recovery following TDF discontinuation [ 15 , 16 ]. Bone health also improved after switching, as reflected by significant increases in BMD at both the lumbar spine and hip, along with reductions in bone turnover markers, such as ALP and osteocalcin. These results mirror prior study findings suggesting that DTG/3TC may contribute to skeletal recovery once TDF-related bone loss is halted [ 17 ]. In addition, we observed a modest decrease in vitamin D levels, which may reflect normalization of TDF-related disturbances in mineral metabolism following recovery of renal tubular function and reduction in secondary hyperparathyroidism. Modest increases in body weight were observed following the switch to DTG/3TC, consistent with observations reported with integrase strand transfer inhibitor-based regimens [ 18 – 20 ]. However, it has also been suggested that such weight gain following a switch from TDF-containing regimens to TDF-free regimens may be attributable to the discontinuation of TDF [ 21 ]. We acknowledge that longitudinal reference data on average weight change in our clinic population are not systematically collected, which limits the interpretation of these findings. Additionally, we did not measure waist circumference or calculate body mass index (BMI), so we cannot determine whether the weight gain was centrally distributed. This is another limitation of our study. Small increases in total cholesterol and LDL-C levels were noted, whereas HDL-C and triglyceride levels remained stable [ 20 ]. These findings are consistent with previous observations from our center showing that TDF-based regimens are associated with a more favorable lipid profile compared with non-TDF regimens, likely reflecting the lipid-lowering effect of TDF [ 22 ]. Therefore, the modest lipid increases observed after switching may primarily reflect the withdrawal of this effect rather than an adverse metabolic consequence of DTG/3TC [ 23 ]. The clinical significance of these metabolic changes warrants further evaluation with longer follow-up and controlled studies. DTG/3TC was well tolerated overall, with most adverse events being mild or unrelated to the treatment. Only one participant discontinued treatment because of insomnia. The overall safety profile reinforces the utility of DTG/3TC in patients at risk of drug-related toxicity. This study has several limitations. First, its single-center, open-label design and the lack of a control group limit the generalizability and causal inference of the findings. Second, the cohort was predominantly male (90%), which restricts the applicability of our results to female patients. Third, the follow-up duration was insufficient to determine whether the observed improvements in surrogate biomarkers would ultimately translate into reduced risks of major clinical events (e.g., end-stage renal disease or fragility fractures). Longer-term studies are needed to establish such correlations.
sections.conclusions_1: In summary, switching to DTG/3TC maintained virological suppression and was associated with improvements in renal tubular and bone metabolic markers in virologically suppressed Chinese PLWH with TDF-associated toxicity, supporting the use of DTG/3TC as a safe and effective switch strategy in routine HIV care.

title: Gas6 restores microglial efferocytosis and limits neuroinflammation in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy by activating MerTK and the PI3K–Rac1 pathway
abstract: Aim Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is a major cause of neonatal disability and mortality. Its core pathology involves extensive neuronal apoptosis and persistent inflammatory responses. Microglia play a crucial role in maintaining brain homeostasis and promoting injury repair by recognizing and clearing apoptotic neurons. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear. Method This study employed a co-culture model of apoptotic neurons, phagocytic function assays, cytokine analysis, transcriptome sequencing, Gas6 gene knockout and rescue experiments, combined with a mouse model of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, to elucidate the role of microglia in the phagocytic process and the regulatory function of Gas6. Result Injured neurons induced an early phase of pro-inflammatory activation and enhanced phagocytic capacity in microglia, followed by a shift towards an anti-inflammatory function. Transcriptome analysis suggested that co-culture with injured neurons activated pathways such as PI3K-AKT and NF-κB in microglia, concomitant with a significant upregulation of Gas6. Furthermore, we found that Gas6 deficiency significantly reduced the phosphorylation level of TAM receptors, leading to impaired downstream PI3K/AKT activation and a marked decrease in Rac1-GTP, thereby suppressing cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic function. In parallel, Gas6-deficient microglia exhibited a sustained pro-inflammatory response, with both their efferocytic capacity and ability to regulate inflammation being significantly compromised. In vivo experiments showed that Gas6-KO mice displayed more severe neurological deficits, increased neuronal apoptosis, and stronger inflammatory responses after HIE. Supplementation with exogenous Gas6 elevated TAM receptor phosphorylation and the PI3K/AKT–Rac1 signaling pathway, partially restoring the phagocytic capacity of microglia. Conclusion This study demonstrates the important role of the Gas6–TAM–PI3K/AKT–Rac1 signaling axis in modulating microglial efferocytic function and inflammatory state transition. It provides a potential therapeutic strategy for improving HIE prognosis by targeting the regulation of microglial phagocytosis. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12964-026-02911-2.

sections.aim: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is a major cause of neonatal disability and mortality. Its core pathology involves extensive neuronal apoptosis and persistent inflammatory responses. Microglia play a crucial role in maintaining brain homeostasis and promoting injury repair by recognizing and clearing apoptotic neurons. However, the regulatory mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear.
sections.method: This study employed a co-culture model of apoptotic neurons, phagocytic function assays, cytokine analysis, transcriptome sequencing, Gas6 gene knockout and rescue experiments, combined with a mouse model of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, to elucidate the role of microglia in the phagocytic process and the regulatory function of Gas6.
sections.result: Injured neurons induced an early phase of pro-inflammatory activation and enhanced phagocytic capacity in microglia, followed by a shift towards an anti-inflammatory function. Transcriptome analysis suggested that co-culture with injured neurons activated pathways such as PI3K-AKT and NF-κB in microglia, concomitant with a significant upregulation of Gas6. Furthermore, we found that Gas6 deficiency significantly reduced the phosphorylation level of TAM receptors, leading to impaired downstream PI3K/AKT activation and a marked decrease in Rac1-GTP, thereby suppressing cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic function. In parallel, Gas6-deficient microglia exhibited a sustained pro-inflammatory response, with both their efferocytic capacity and ability to regulate inflammation being significantly compromised. In vivo experiments showed that Gas6-KO mice displayed more severe neurological deficits, increased neuronal apoptosis, and stronger inflammatory responses after HIE. Supplementation with exogenous Gas6 elevated TAM receptor phosphorylation and the PI3K/AKT–Rac1 signaling pathway, partially restoring the phagocytic capacity of microglia.
sections.conclusion: This study demonstrates the important role of the Gas6–TAM–PI3K/AKT–Rac1 signaling axis in modulating microglial efferocytic function and inflammatory state transition. It provides a potential therapeutic strategy for improving HIE prognosis by targeting the regulation of microglial phagocytosis.
sections.supplementary information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12964-026-02911-2.
sections.background: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is one of the leading causes of neonatal death and long-term neurological sequelae [ 1 ]. Following cerebral ischemia and hypoxia, a complex cascade of events is triggered, ultimately leading to extensive programmed neuronal death [ 2 – 4 ]. The timely and efficient clearance of damaged neurons during HIE recovery is particularly critical [ 5 , 6 ]. Within the recovery window, the phagocytic function mediated by microglia determines the success of inflammation suppression and tissue repair. Neuronal programmed cell death can occur in various forms, such as apoptosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis [ 7 , 8 ]. Among these, apoptosis is one of the predominant modes of neuronal death in HIE, especially within the ischemic penumbra [ 9 , 10 ]. A hallmark of apoptotic cells is the maintenance of membrane integrity and the exposure of "eat-me" signals such as phosphatidylserine, enabling their recognition and clearance by professional phagocytes [ 11 ]. This process is known as efferocytosis [ 12 ]. In the central nervous system, microglia are the primary phagocytes responsible for efferocytosis [ 13 – 15 ]. They can sensitively recognize, engulf, and phagocytose apoptotic neurons [ 16 ], thereby preventing their progression to secondary necrosis and the consequent massive release of inflammatory factors. This is vital for maintaining brain microenvironmental homeostasis [ 17 , 18 ]. Studies indicate that the efferocytic function of microglia is not static but is finely regulated [ 19 ]. Fully functional efferocytosis not only accomplishes debris clearance but also drives microglia to transition from a pro-inflammatory to a repair state, secreting cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β, thereby indirectly promoting tissue repair [ 20 ]. Conversely, dysregulated efferocytosis leads to the accumulation of apoptotic cells, exacerbates inflammatory responses, and induces secondary damage [ 21 ]. Thus, given the limited intrinsic repair capacity of neurons, targeted regulation of microglial efferocytic function—enhancing their phagocytic capacity and steering them toward an anti-inflammatory role—has emerged as a highly promising direction in HIE neuroprotective strategies [ 22 ]. Elucidating the key molecular mechanisms governing efferocytosis is of paramount significance for developing interventions to halt HIE progression and improve long-term outcomes in affected children. Among the molecular regulators of efferocytosis, growth arrest-specific protein 6 (Gas6) has emerged as an important signaling molecule. Gas6 is a vitamin K-dependent secreted glycoprotein that serves as a ligand for the TAM receptor tyrosine kinase family, which includes Tyro3, Axl, and MerTK [ 23 ]. Binding of Gas6 to TAM receptors induces receptor phosphorylation, thereby activating downstream signaling pathways involved in cytoskeletal remodeling, cell survival, and immune regulation [ 24 ]. Gas6 can function as a bridging molecule by simultaneously binding phosphatidylserine exposed on apoptotic cells and TAM receptors expressed on phagocytes, thereby facilitating the recognition and engulfment of apoptotic targets [ 25 ]. Beyond promoting phagocytic uptake, activation of Gas6-TAM signaling has also been shown to suppress excessive inflammatory responses and promote immune homeostasis [ 22 ]. In the central nervous system, TAM receptors are expressed in microglia and have been implicated in the clearance of apoptotic neurons and maintenance of neural tissue integrity [ 26 ]. However, the specific contribution of Gas6-mediated TAM signaling to the regulation of microglial efferocytosis and inflammatory balance following hypoxic–ischemic brain injury remains incompletely understood. In this study, we employed an in vitro co-culture model, phagocytosis assays, cytokine analysis, multi-omics sequencing, pathway enrichment analysis, and Gas6 gene knockout and rescue experiments to validate the functional changes in microglia following neuronal injury and the role of the key regulatory factor Gas6. Specifically, we established a glutamate-induced HT-22 neuronal injury model and performed co-culture with primary microglia. Experiments demonstrated that microglia could phagocytose apoptotic neurons (Acs) and exhibited a typical shift from a pro-inflammatory clearance state to an anti-inflammatory repair state upon stimulation. Flow cytometry further confirmed that the phagocytic activity of microglia toward Acs increased over time, reaching a plateau at 3–4 h. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant reprogramming of the microglial expression profile under different conditions, with the co-culture group with Acs activating multiple pathways related to phagocytosis and inflammation regulation, including efferocytosis and PI3K-Akt. Furthermore, based on our established HIE mouse model, we found that Gas6 was significantly upregulated after hypoxic-ischemic injury and was primarily expressed by microglia. In vivo experiments showed that Gas6-knockout (Gas6 −/− ) mice exhibited more severe neurological deficits, increased neuronal apoptosis, and stronger inflammatory responses after HIE. Correspondingly, Gas6 −/− microglia displayed reduced phagocytic capacity, upregulation of pro-inflammatory factors, downregulation of anti-inflammatory factors, and significantly decreased phosphorylation levels of TAM receptors. Supplementation with exogenous recombinant Gas6 reversed these defects. Moreover, Gas6 deficiency also impaired downstream PI3K/AKT activation and led to a marked decrease in Rac1-GTP, thereby suppressing cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic function. Exogenous Gas6 supplementation restored TAM receptor phosphorylation and the PI3K/AKT–Rac1 signaling pathway, partially rescuing phagocytic function. Therefore, this study elucidates the dynamic biphasic response of microglia to injured neuron stimulation and provides new insights into systematically clarifies the central role of the Gas6-TAM axis in regulating microglial phagocytic function and inflammatory balance, providing an important theoretical foundation for microglia-targeted neuroprotective strategies.
sections.mice: The C57BL/6 J mice and pups used in this study were purchased from Shanghai Jihui Laboratory Animal Breeding Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Gas6 knockout mice were obtained from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, Jiangsu, China). All animals were randomized in a standardized manner and housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility at Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center. The environmental conditions were maintained at a temperature of 22± 2 °C, relative humidity of 50%–60%, a 12-h light/dark cycle, with free access to food and water. Standard chow and water were provided ad libitum. Pups were nursed by their dams prior to weaning. All experimental procedures were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center (IACUC approval No. JYIEC-2020–25). The neonatal HIE model was established in postnatal day7 (P7) C57BL/6 J mouse pups, as previously described with modifications [ 27 ]. Briefly, after anesthesia with isoflurane, the right common carotid artery was permanently ligated with a 5–0 silk suture. Following a 1-h recovery period, the pups were placed in a hypoxic chamber maintained at 37 °C and exposed to a gas mixture of 8% oxygen and 92% nitrogen for 2.5 h to induce HIE. After the hypoxic exposure, the pups were returned to their dams. Control animals underwent only separation of the common carotid artery without ligation or hypoxia exposure. Upon completion of behavioral testing, mice were euthanized by decapitation under deep anesthesia on an ice-cold platform. For molecular analysis, dissected tissues were immediately snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and subsequently stored at − 80 °C until use. For histology, samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by cryoprotection in graded sucrose solutions, and then processed for frozen sectioning.
sections.cell culture: Primary microglia were isolated from the brains of postnatal day 1–4 (P1–P4) C57 mouse pups following the protocol described by Du et al. [ 28 ]. The HT‑22 neuronal cell line was obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC; catalog No. CRL‑2900). Cells were cultured in DMEM medium (HyClone, SH30243.01) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, 10,270,106) and 1% penicillin‑streptomycin (Hyclone, SV30010), and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. For indirect co‑culture, a Transwell system (polycarbonate membrane, pore size 0.4 μm; Corning, 3450) was used. HT‑22 neurons were seeded in the upper chamber at a density of 2 × 10 4 cells per well, while microglia were plated in the lower chamber of a 24‑well plate at a density of 1 × 10 5 cells per well.
sections.recombinant gas6 (rgas6) treatment: Recombinant Gas6 was administered via intracerebroventricular (i.c.v.) injection at 1 h after HIE induction. Mice received a dose of 20 μg/kg of rGas6 in a total volume of 4 μL. To maintain sustained central exposure, rGas6 was administered once every two days throughout the experimental period [ 29 ]. Control animals received an equal volume of vehicle (sterile phosphate-buffered saline [PBS] containing 0.1% bovine serum albumin) following the same schedule. For in vitro experiments, primary microglia were treated with rGas6 at a final concentration of 100 ng/mL. rGas6 was added to the culture medium at the initiation of co-culture or stimulation. Cells were then incubated for the indicated time periods. Control groups received an equal volume of vehicle (culture medium or PBS containing 0.1% BSA) under identical conditions.
sections.cell viability assay: For each experimental condition, cells were plated in 96-well plates at a concentration ranging from 5 × 10 3 to 10 × 10 3 cells per well. Viability was evaluated using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Beyotime, Shanghai, China; Catalog No. C0039), with absorbance readings obtained at 24-h intervals.
sections.lactate dehydrogenase activity assay: Cell injury was evaluated using an LDH assay kit (Beyotime, C0017). Briefly, culture supernatants were collected, centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C to remove debris, and incubated with the working solution at 37 °C for 30 min. The reaction was terminated, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm. LDH release was calculated as (experimental group/control group) × 100%. All experiments were performed in at least three independent replicates.
sections.apoptosis assay: Apoptosis was assessed using the Annexin V, 633 Apoptosis Detection Kit (AD11, Dojindo) following the manufacturer's instructions. Cells were stained with Annexin V-633 and propidium iodide (PI), and the percentage of Annexin V⁺/PI⁺ cells was analyzed by flow cytometry (Beckman Gallios, Beckman Coulter, USA).
sections.microglial phenotypic analysis: Microglia were collected and subjected to Fc receptor blocking. Cells were then stained with APC-conjugated anti-CD86 (BioLegend, 159,215) for surface markers and PE-conjugated anti-CD206 (BioLegend,141,706) for intracellular markers. The proportions of CD86⁺ and CD206⁺ cells were analyzed by flow cytometry.
sections.transcriptome sequencing and bioinformat: Total RNA was extracted from microglia samples using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen). RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific). Sequencing libraries were constructed from 3 μg of total RNA per sample following the manufacturer’s protocol and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform to generate paired-end reads. Three independent biological replicates (derived from independent microglial isolations) were included for each experimental group. Raw sequencing reads were processed using fastp (v0.22.0) to remove adapter sequences and low-quality reads. The clean reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (GRCm39) using HISAT2 (v2.1.0). Gene-level read counts were generated using HTSeq (v0.9.1), and gene expression levels were normalized as fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (v1.39.0) based on raw count data, with thresholds of |log₂ fold change|> 1 and adjusted P < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg correction). Principal component analysis (PCA), sample correlation analysis, and hierarchical clustering were performed in R to evaluate the overall transcriptomic differences among samples. Functional enrichment analysis of DEGs was performed using clusterProfiler (v4.6.0) for Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis, with pathways satisfying adjusted P < 0.05 considered significantly enriched. Pathway activity inference was performed using the PROGENy algorithm to assess the regulatory states of major signaling pathways based on the expression of pathway-responsive genes, enabling comparison of pathway activities between experimental groups.
sections.western blot: Total proteins were extracted from mouse cortical tissues. After separation by 10% SDS-PAGE (Epizyme, PG211), proteins were transferred onto a PVDF membrane (Merck). The membrane was blocked with QuickBlock blocking buffer for 30 min, incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, and then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized by chemiluminescence. The levels of phosphorylated proteins were normalized to their corresponding total protein levels for quantitative analysis. Antibody information is provided in the Supplementary Materials.
sections.rac1 activation assay: Rac1 activation was assessed using an Active Rac1 Detection Kit (#8815, Cell Signaling Technology) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Microglia were harvested after co-culture with apoptotic neurons and lysed. GTP-bound Rac1 was selectively captured using GST-tagged PAK1-PBD fusion protein beads, washed, and eluted. Active GTP Rac-1 and Total Rac-1 in whole-cell lysates were analyzed by Western blotting. Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ and normalized to total Rac1 levels.
sections.righting reflex test and negative geotax: Pups were placed in a supine position on a flat surface, and the time required to completely turn over to a prone position with all four limbs touching the surface was recorded as the righting reflex latency [ 30 ]. In negative geotaxis test, Pups were placed head-down on a 45°-inclined textured surface. The latency to complete a 180° turn (head-up orientation) within 60 s was recorded [ 31 ].
sections.rotarod test: Motor coordination and endurance were assessed using a rotarod apparatus [ 32 ]. Prior to formal testing, mice underwent a 3-day acclimation training (twice daily) at a constant speed of 16 rpm. During the test, the latency to fall from the rod rotating at 16 rpm was recorded, with a maximum cut-off time of 300 s. Each mouse was tested three times, and the average value was taken as the final score.
sections.balance beam test: A narrow beam (120 cm long, 1 cm wide, 50 cm above the floor) was used to assess motor balance [ 33 ]. Mice underwent a 3-day pre-training period prior to formal testing. During the test, the time required for the mouse to traverse the beam from the start to the end point was recorded, and the number of hindlimb slips was counted.
sections.novel object recognition test: The experiment consisted of two phases [ 34 ]. In the habituation phase, mice were allowed to freely explore two identical objects placed in a square arena for 5 min. After a 1-h interval, during the test phase, one of the objects was replaced with a novel object, and exploration was allowed for another 5 min. The time spent exploring the novel and familiar objects was recorded. The preference index (PI) was calculated as: PI = time exploring novel object/(time exploring novel object + time exploring familiar object). The discrimination index (DI) was calculated as: DI = (time exploring novel object − time exploring familiar object)/total exploration time.
sections.catwalk gait analysis: Gait parameters were evaluated using the Catwalk automated gait analysis system [ 35 ]. Mice were acclimated to the testing environment for 30 min prior to the experiment. Each mouse was allowed to walk freely across the glass walkway, and three valid runs were recorded. Gait parameters were automatically extracted and analyzed using the built-in software.
sections.neurological deficit score: The neurological functional status was quantitatively assessed using the Neurological Deficit Score system proposed by María I. Ayuso et al. [ 31 , 36 ], with scores ranging from 0 (normal neurological function) to 10 (most severe neurological deficit). The evaluation items included: state of consciousness, ocular signs, respiratory pattern, motor performance, and deep sensory reflexes.
sections.immunofluorescence: For cell staining, cells were seeded on poly-L-lysine-coated coverslips. After 12 h, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min and permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 1 h. Subsequently, samples were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by incubation with corresponding fluorescent secondary antibodies at 37 °C for 1 h in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Servicebio, G1012-10ML). After mounting, images were acquired using a laser scanning confocal microscope and fluorescence intensity was analyzed. Cellular identity was determined based on positive staining for cell type-specific markers. For brain tissue immunostaining, frozen Sects. (20–30 μm thick) were collected from the ipsilateral cortex at the level of the dorsal hippocampus (approximately bregma -1.5 mm to -2.5 mm according to the mouse brain atlas of Paxinos and Franklin). Three consecutive sections per animal were analyzed. Sections were washed in PBS, blocked with 5% BSA for 1 h at room temperature, and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C. Appropriate fluorescent secondary antibodies were applied for 1 h at room temperature in the dark, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. Sections were mounted using anti-fade medium, and images were captured with a laser scanning confocal microscope under consistent settings. For quantification, three random fields per section were imaged, and fluorescence intensity or positive cell counts were analyzed using ImageJ software (NIH, USA). The average of all fields per animal was used for statistical analysis. Detailed antibody information is provided in the Supplementary Materials.
sections.phagocytosis assay: Microglia were pre-labeled with CMFDA (Thermo Fisher, C34554) and co-cultured with Far Red-labeled (Thermo Fisher, C34564) HT-22 neurons [ 37 ]. After co-culture, cells were collected and analyzed by flow cytometry. The proportion of CMFDA⁺/Far Red⁺ double-positive cells was quantified to calculate the phagocytic index.
sections.elisa: Cell culture supernatants were collected and analyzed for the concentrations of ARG-1, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α according to the manufacturer's instructions using commercially available ELISA kits (ARG-1: catalog No. JL13668; IL-6: catalog No. JL10484; IL-10: catalog No. JL20268; TNF-α: catalog No. JL20242). Absorbance was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm, and the cytokine concentrations were calculated based on the standard curve.
sections.statistical analysis: All experiments were performed with 3 (cellular assays) or 5 (animal studies) independent replicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS 21 software (IBM, USA). Differences among groups were examined by one‑way ANOVA, and when a significant difference was detected, post‑hoc comparisons were performed using Tukey's HSD test. A p ‑value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001).
sections.following co-culture with injured neuron: To investigate the response of microglia to neuronal injury, we first established an in vitro model of glutamate-induced neuronal apoptosis. HT-22 neurons were treated with 5 mM glutamate for 24 h to induce excitotoxicity, as confirmed by Annexin V/PI staining, CCK-8 assay, and LDH release assay (Supplementary Fig. 1). Primary microglia were isolated from neonatal C57BL/6 mouse brains(Supplementary Fig. 2) and co-cultured with glutamate-treated neurons at a 1:5 ratio immediately after two washes with pre-warmed PBS to completely remove residual glutamate [ 38 ]. A schematic timeline summarizing glutamate treatment, washing steps, co-culture initiation, and subsequent analyses is provided in Fig. 1 A. Immunofluorescence staining performed after co-culture revealed co-localization between microglia and damaged neurons (Fig. 1 B). After co-culturing microglia with differently treated neurons, we examined the expression of CD86 and CD206 on microglia (Fig. 1 C-E). The results showed that healthy neurons did not alter the proportion of CD86⁺ or CD206⁺ microglial subpopulations, whereas co-culture with Acs led to a significant increase in both subpopulations. This finding suggests that microglia exhibit a heterogeneous and context-dependent activation pattern in response to injured neurons, rather than a uniform polarization toward a single phenotype. To further explore the temporal dynamics of this response, we measured the levels of inflammation-related cytokines in the culture supernatant at different time points (0 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h after co-culture initiation) (Fig. 1 F-I). During the early co-culture period (0 h-6 h), injured neurons significantly induced an increase in the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 (Fig. 1 F) and TNF-α(Fig. 1 G). As the co-culture time extended, the levels of these two cytokines gradually declined. Meanwhile, the secretion of the anti-inflammatory markers IL-10 (Fig. 1 H) and ARG1 (Fig. 1 I) increased significantly between 6 and 24 h. Collectively, these results indicate a time-dependent shift in the overall inflammatory profile of microglia following stimulation by injured neurons. However, given that our data are derived from population-level analyses, they do not directly demonstrate phenotypic switching at the single-cell level. Instead, the observed changes may reflect dynamic alterations in the relative proportions or activation states of distinct microglial subpopulations. sections.the phagocytic activity of microglia tow: To investigate the temporal dynamics of microglial phagocytic activity toward Acs, we established an in vitro co-culture system. Microglia and injured neurons were specifically labeled with CellTracker™ Green CMFDA and CellTrace™ Far Red, and co-cultured at a 1:5 ratio. Phagocytosis by microglia was then assessed via flow cytometry at various time points (0, 30 min, 1, 2, 3, and 4 h) (Fig. 1 J-K and Supplement 3A) [ 39 , 40 ]. The results demonstrated that phagocytic activity increased in a significant time-dependent manner. At the start of co-culture (0 h), no statistical difference in phagocytic capacity was observed between groups. With prolonged co-culture time, phagocytic activity in the MG + Acs group continued to increase (Supplement 3B), reaching 16.8%, 22.9%, and 41.7% at 1, 2, and 3 h, respectively. Subsequently, we analyzed the phagocytic index and its increase rate for both groups at different time points (Supplement 3C-F). Notably, the phagocytic index in the MG + Acs group increased by 54.8% from 2 to 3 h, whereas the increase rate declined markedly to 17.7% between 3 and 4 h. This pattern suggests that the rate of microglial phagocytic increase slowed during the later phase of co-culture and may indicate a tendency toward saturation. The factors contributing to this apparent slowing remain unclear. Possible explanations include a reduction in available target cells, temporary saturation of the phagocytic machinery, or metabolic constraints associated with sustained phagocytic activity.
sections.transcriptomic analysis revealed signifi: To investigate the underlying mechanism, transcriptomic sequencing was performed on microglia cultured alone (MG group), microglia co-cultured with healthy neurons (MG + Neuron group), and microglia co-cultured with Acs (MG + Acs group). Transcriptomic profiling was performed using three biological replicates per group. Principal component analysis (PCA, Fig. 2 A) and correlation analysis (Fig. 2 C) showed good intra-group reproducibility among samples. However, the MG + Acs group exhibited significantly lower correlation with the other two groups, indicating that injured neurons could reshape the overall gene expression program of microglia. Cluster analysis (Fig. 2 B) revealed that the MG + Acs group had the most distinct overall expression pattern compared to the other groups, with its corresponding region in the heatmap displaying a unique color distribution, suggesting extensive transcriptional reprogramming under this condition. To systematically evaluate the regulatory states of key signaling pathways under different conditions, pathway activity analysis was conducted on the MG + Neuron and MG + Acs groups using the PROGENy method. The results indicated significant differences between the two groups across multiple important signaling pathways (Fig. 2 D), suggesting they might be in distinct functional states. Subsequently, focusing on key regulatory molecules among the differentially expressed genes, volcano plot analysis showed that the expression of Gas6 was significantly upregulated in the MG + Acs group (Fig. 2 F). Meanwhile, KEGG enrichment analysis demonstrated significant activation of several pathways closely related to microglial phagocytosis and inflammatory regulation, such as PI3K-Akt and NF-κB (Fig. 2 E). Therefore, we hypothesized that Gas6 expression might be induced and play an important role during the recognition and clearance of apoptotic neurons by microglia. We proceeded to further explore the specific function of Gas6 in both in vitro and in vivo models to elucidate its precise mechanism in microglial efferocytosis. sections.gas6 deficiency exacerbates neurological: A HIE model was established in neonatal mice [ 37 , 41 ], and behavioral tests were performed at different time points. Righting reflex and negative geotaxis assays [ 42 , 43 ] were conducted from two days before to two days after modeling. Prior to induction (P5-P6), no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups in these tests (Fig. 3 A-B). On the day of modeling and during the following two days (P7-P9), pups in the Model group required significantly more time to complete both the righting reflex and negative geotaxis tasks compared with the NC and Sham groups. During the chronic phase, motor and sensory functions were evaluated using the balance beam test and a neurological deficit score [ 44 , 45 ]. In the balance beam test, Model group mice traversed the beam faster than NC and Sham mice (Fig. 3 C) and showed significantly fewer hindlimb slips during crossing (Fig. 3 D). Neurological scoring revealed significantly higher deficit scores in the Model group relative to the NC and Sham groups (Fig. 3 E). Immunofluorescence staining indicated markedly stronger Gas6 signal intensity in the Model group (Fig. 3 F-G). Gas6 protein showed clear co-localization with the microglial marker Iba1, suggesting predominant expression in the cytoplasm of microglial cells (Fig. 3 H-I) [ 46 ]. Western blot analysis further confirmed that Gas6 protein levels were significantly elevated in the Model group compared with the NC and Sham groups (Fig. 3 J-K). Model mice showed prolonged traversal time and increased hind-limb slips. E Neurological assessment at P28. The Model group displayed a significantly higher neurological deficit score. Statistical analysis was performed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test The HIE model was then replicated in Gas6 −/− mice, followed by behavioral assessments, the timeline of behavioral assessments performed after HIE induction is summarized in. In the negative geotaxis (Fig. 4 B) and righting reflex tests (Fig. 4 C), no difference was observed between WT Sham and Gas6 −/− Sham groups. Both WT Model and Gas6 −/− Model groups exhibited significantly longer task-completion times compared with their respective sham groups; moreover, Gas6 −/− Model mice performed worse than WT Model mice. In the balance-beam test, traversal time (Fig. 4 D) and hindlimb slips (Fig. 4 E) were evaluated. No differences were found between WT Sham and Gas6 −/− Sham mice. Compared with WT Model mice, Gas6 −/− Model mice showed significantly prolonged traversal time and increased hindlimb slips. Similarly, in the rotarod test (Fig. 4 F-G), Gas6 −/− Model mice displayed poorer grip strength scores and shorter latencies to fall. In the novel-object recognition test, discrimination index (Fig. 4 H) and preference index (Fig. 4 I) were assessed. Both indices were significantly lower in Gas6 −/− Model mice compared with WT Sham and Gas6 −/− Sham mice. Neurological deficit scoring further indicated more severe impairment in the Gas6 −/− Model group (Fig. 4 J). Additionally, gait parameters wee analyzed using the Catwalk system, including print length (Fig. 4 K), print width (Fig. 4 L), maximum contact area (Fig. 4 M), and mean maximal pressure (Fig. 4 N). Statistical analysis revealed that, compared with WT Model mice, Gas6 −/− Model mice exhibited more pronounced locomotor deficits, particularly in the left forelimb and left hindlimb. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed a significant increase in neuronal apoptosis in the brains of Gas6 −/− Model mice compared with Gas6 −/− Sham mice (Fig. 5 A–B). To evaluate the effect of post-injury Gas6 supplementation in vivo, recombinant Gas6 was administered to Gas6 −/− Model mice following HIE induction, and neurological outcomes were subsequently assessed. Behavioral analyses demonstrated that rGas6 treatment significantly improved neurological performance, as evidenced by enhanced righting reflex (Fig. 5 C), negative geotaxis (Fig. 5 D), rotarod performance (Fig. 5 E-F), and overall neurological scores (Fig. 5 G). To further investigate the effects of rGas6 at the cellular level, primary microglia were isolated from neonatal Gas6 −/− mouse brains and their phagocytic function was assessed by flow cytometry, a schematic diagram illustrating the experimental design is shown in Fig. 5 H. sections.gas6 modulates microglial phagocytic fun: Gas6 is a key ligand for the TAM receptor family (primarily Axl, MerTK, and Tyro3) [ 47 ] and typically transduces extracellular signals by binding to and activating these receptors [ 48 ]. In our experiments, we found that Gas6 exerts its effects by modulating the phosphorylation levels of TAM receptors without altering their total protein expression (Fig. 6 A). Specifically, Gas6 knockout led to a significant reduction in TAM receptor phosphorylation, most notably in p‑MerTK, while supplementation with exogenous recombinant Gas6 restored phosphorylation levels in Gas6⁻/⁻ microglia co-cultured with Acs (Fig. 6 B). These results indicate that Gas6 activates downstream signaling by promoting TAM receptors phosphorylation, with a relatively stronger phosphorylation signal observed for MerTK compared to other TAM receptors; however, this does not necessarily indicate functional dominance. We next examined the PI3K/AKT pathway, a key downstream signaling cascade of TAM receptors (Fig. 6 C). In WT microglia co‑cultured with apoptotic neurons, levels of p‑PI3K and p‑AKT were significantly elevated compared to controls, indicating that intact Gas6 signaling effectively promotes PI3K/AKT pathway activation. In contrast, Gas6 knockout markedly reduced the phosphorylation of both PI3K and AKT, which was partially restored upon exogenous Gas6 supplementation. Further downstream, we evaluated the activation state of the effector molecule Rac1,which regulates cytoskeletal remodeling during phagocytosis (Fig. 6 D). GTP Rac-1 levels were significantly lower in Gas6 ⁻/⁻ microglia after co-culture with apoptotic neurons compared with WT microglia, and exogenous Gas6 supplementation raised GTP Rac-1 levels toward those of the WT group. To investigate the role of Gas6 in regulating the inflammatory phenotype of microglia during efferocytosis, we measured the expression of inflammation‑related molecules in microglia under different treatments (Fig. 6 E). Compared with WT microglia co-cultured with apoptotic neurons, Gas6 ⁻/⁻ microglia in the same setting showed significantly increased expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α, along with decreased expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β. Exogenous recombinant Gas6 supplementation reversed these changes, restoring cytokine expression profiles toward WT levels. We further quantified cytokine secretion in cell culture supernatants by ELISA at 0 h and 24 h after co-culture initiation (Fig. 6 F-I). The 0 h time point represents the immediate post-induction baseline, defined as the moment immediately after apoptotic neurons were added to microglia, before detectable co-culture-induced responses occurred. Consistent with the intracellular protein expression data, Gas6 ⁻/⁻ microglia co-cultured with apoptotic neurons secreted significantly higher levels of IL-6 (Fig. 6 F) and TNF-α (Fig. 6 G), and significantly lower levels of IL-10 (Fig. 6 H) and TGF-β (Fig. 6 I) compared to WT microglia. Exogenous Gas6 supplementation restored the secretion of these cytokines to levels comparable to those observed in WT microglia. Together, these findings demonstrate that Gas6 promotes TAM receptor phosphorylation and activates the PI3K/AKT-Rac-1 signaling axis in microglia, thereby enhancing efferocytosis and promoting a shift toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype following interaction with apoptotic neurons.
