As well as direct effects described for these nutritional components remains their indirect effect via the microbiota, with fibre-rich diets supporting a diverse microbiota capable of producing high levels of short chain fatty acids known for their immunomodulatory effects, whereas high-fat diets support secondary bile acid generation and intestinal permeability known to promote inflammation ( Rohr et al., 2020 ; Zeng et al., 2019 ). Certain translocated bacterial species have also been shown to directly induce TI in mouse models ( Robles-Vera et al., 2025 ). Therefore, dietary associations with TI are very complex, with both direct and indirect associations to increased immune cell priming as well as primary immune responses reported. What appears clear from these studies is that Western diets promote TI and an increase in inflammatory phenotypes through a range of mechanisms. The metabolic consequences of each of these mechanisms require further study.
sections.post-transcriptional regulation: Cell metabolism can also be regulated by post-transcriptional mechanisms. For example, miRs affect cell metabolism by directly targeting metabolic enzymes or transporters, as well as by controlling pathways involved in the control of metabolic processes, such as mTOR signalling ( Virga et al., 2021b ; Carrà et al., 2024 ). Different metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, the TCA cycle, OXPHOS, lipid, and amino acid metabolism, have been shown to be controlled by miRs such as miR-210 ( Virga et al., 2021a ), miR-146a ( Runtsch et al., 2019 ), miR-33 ( Ouimet et al., 2015 ), among others, in a cell-specific and context-dependent manner ( Virga et al., 2021b ; Carrà et al., 2024 ). Notably, miRs are regulated by training stimuli, such as β-glucan, suggesting that they might be involved in TI. In the monocyte-like THP-1 cell line, β-glucan induces the expression of miR-193-5p, miR-5787, miR-146a, miR-210-3p, miR-30a-5p, and miR-8072 ( Du et al., 2017 ), while in the macrophage-like Raw264.7 cell line, β-glucan induces miR-32-5p ( Yang et al., 2025 ). Similarly, miRs expression profiles of β-glucan-trained peripheral blood mononuclear cells from human and mouse specimens show distinct pattern of differentially expressed miRs upon training. Specifically, miR-9-5p, let-7i-5p, miR-223-3p, and miR-155 are consistently upregulated while miR-152-3p, miR-328-3p, and miR-29a-5p are consistently downregulated upon training in both human and mouse ( Su et al., 2021b ). An in-depth study of role of miR-9-5p, one of the miR consistently upregulated in both species upon training, shows that its depletion reduces training phenotype both in vitro and in vivo and reduces mice survival during C. albicans infection. This evidence provides the first proof-of-concept of the functional relevance of miRs in TI ( Su et al., 2021b ). Molecularly, miR-9-5p directly targets IDH3α (isocitrate dehydrogenase 3α), an enzyme of the TCA cycle involved in the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to αKG, reducing αKG levels, stabilising HIF-1α and promoting the glycolytic switch upon training ( Figure 2 ). Conversely, the depletion of miR-9-5p in trained macrophages widely affects cell metabolism by reducing glucose consumption, glycolysis, and NAD, while increasing the ratio of αKG to succinate and fumarate. Due to this increased αKG/fumarate ratio, depletion of miR-9-5p in trained macrophage enhances the activity of the demethylases KDM5, an enzyme involved in the removal of lysine trimethylation of H3K4me3, influencing the methylation status at the promoter of inflammatory and metabolic genes such as Tnf , Il6 , Hk2 , and Slc2a1 (Glut1 ) limiting the glycolytic switch and enhanced cytokine expression. Another interesting mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation is provided by the essential glycolysis component GAPDH. In monocytes, it has been described that GAPDH protein can bind to the 3’ untranslated region (UTR) of several mRNA species, such as Tnf , to induce post-transcriptional repression ( Millet et al., 2016 ). Notably, this mechanism had previously been shown in T cells in the regulation of Ifng mRNA ( Chang et al., 2013 ). Therefore, although not investigated in training setting, the increased glycolysis may also increase TNF levels via the occupation of GAPDH with glycolytic machinery, preventing its secondary inhibitor function. In line with the potential importance of post-transcriptional regulation, inhibiting the glycolytic burst observed upon TLR stimulation in dendritic cells was shown to have no effect on cytokine transcription, but to inhibit FAS required for the increased protein synthesis and cytokine export ( Everts et al., 2014 ). As well as regulating glycolysis, mTOR is a master regulator of many biological functions, including protein translation and mitochondrial activity ( Morita et al., 2013 ). Given the importance of mTOR in the induction of TI, its role may be multifaceted, extending beyond glycolysis induction and HIF stabilisation ( Cheng et al., 2014 ).
sections.metabolic stress: The concept of TI highly resembles the concept of transcriptional memory in which external stimulus can prime a cellular state that results in altered expression of primed genes upon re-exposure to inducing signals ( Tehrani et al., 2025 ). It is characterised by transient gene activation leading to a primed state maintained in the absence of active transcription ( Tehrani et al., 2025 ). In other words, stimuli trigger behaviours, a complex process of mechanisms and features that are employed by living organisms to adapt to the constantly changing environment. When applied to the innate immune system and its ability to react to subsequent pathogenic challenges, this process can be called TI. Transcriptional memory occurs in a diversity of organisms, including both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Nutrients and stress conditions are common triggers of this phenomenon ( Tehrani et al., 2025 ). An illustrative example is found in plants, in which dehydration, infection, high salt, and temperature shock induce primed transcriptional states to control future stressors ( Fu and Dong, 2013 ; Ding et al., 2012 ; Lämke et al., 2016 ). TFs are important contributors to transcriptional and epigenetic memory and they cooperate with local chromatin-based mechanisms like histone-modifying enzymes to induce memory ( Tehrani et al., 2025 ). In line with this, stress-mediated TFs are associated with TI induction. Interestingly, ATF factors were reported in several works regarding TI and tolerance induction. For instance, ATF7 phosphorylation and subsequent release from chromatin was found to be involved in innate immune memory, by decreasing repressive histone marks ( Yoshida et al., 2015 ). ATF4 TF motifs are enriched in the accessible regions generated upon TI mediated by low-dose LPS, compared with high-dose LPS that induces tolerance ( Zhang et al., 2022 ). Accordingly, chronic psychological stress led to a heightened state of readiness in the innate immune system, characterised by increased production of proinflammatory cytokines and an enhanced response to secondary immune challenges ( Barrett et al., 2021 ). Moreover, regarding long-term memory traits, it was found that cardiac stress produced after heart failure influenced the epigenetic landscape of hematopoietic stem cells, thereby affecting their ability to produce different cardiac macrophage subpopulations with enhanced proinflammatory activity. This highlights the potential implications of metabolic stress in TI induction and the contribution of the stress response and adaptations to the epigenetic rewiring ( Rettkowski et al., 2025 ).
sections.technical approaches to study the metabo: Until now, most analyses in TI are performed at a single timepoint, or at a limited set of time intervals at best. As discussed earlier, it is important to discriminate between early and late metabolic changes in TI and we would therefore advocate for more extensive kinetic profiling of the epigenetic and metabolic state of myeloid cells in future studies. Currently, the technologies that are applied to profile metabolic and subsequent epigenetic changes in TI range from very simple multi-well-plate-based assays to high-end OMICs analyses. To investigate epigenetic changes in response to metabolic reprogramming, western blotting can be performed using antibodies directed against histone modifications of interest. This approach has the capacity to detect broad epigenetic changes but doesn’t provide insight into the epigenetic landscape of regulatory region of specific (inflammatory) genes. To obtain such information, one should perform chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) with antibodies targeting specific epigenetic marks of interest. Next, a quantitative PCR can be performed with specific primer pairs to compare DNA fragment abundance in precipitate versus non-precipitated (input) samples. A more sophisticated unbiased approach is to sequence the immunoprecipitated chromatin (ChIP-seq). These ChIP-seq experiments are frequently accompanied by ATAC-seq and RNA-seq to obtain complementary information about specific epigenetic marks, chromatin accessibility, and the expression of the associated genes. ChIP-based studies come with the difficulty that they rely on good antibody clones, and that protocols are not fully standardised and may require trial-and-error-based optimisations that complicate progress and comparison with the field. Also, it remains difficult to probe the relative abundance, and hence importance of, the multitude of histone modifications that can occur and how they influence each other, and eventually how they regulate TI. Both ATAC-seq and RNA-seq are becoming regularly used at the single-cell level and together with the emergence of cell-based metabolic techniques, it is clear that TI research is making the transition towards investigations at single-cell resolution. Another apparent evolution in the field is the study of epigenetic architectures and long-range contact between regulatory regions in the genome. For example, Ziogas et al. recently showed how glycolysis-derived H3K18la marks affect long-range contacts in the regulatory regions of inflammatory genes like Il1b , thus identifying a role for metabolic rewiring and subsequent histone lactylation in modifying gene architecture ( Ziogas et al., 2025 ). Moreover, it should be emphasised that most current techniques are still largely candidate-based targeted approaches that come with the limitation that they provide a biased and non-comprehensive view. Newer mass spectrometry (MS)-based characterisation of PTMs can reveal a more complete and quantitative analysis of histone marks in TI ( Noberini et al., 2022 ; Thomas et al., 2020 ). While MS can reveal the existing modifications and their relative abundance in great detail, it does not provide information about their position. As such, a combination of complementary techniques will be needed to uncover a complete picture containing unbiased quantitative information about histone marks and their relative contributions (MS), distribution of specific marks across the genome (ChIP-seq), how this affects DNA accessibility (ATAC-seq), and finally gene transcription (RNA-seq). For immunometabolic profiling, commercial colourimetric or fluorimetric assay kits can be used to measure intracellular and extracellular levels of lactate, acetyl-CoA, and other key metabolites that govern epigenetic modifications in TI. A broader range of metabolites can be assessed using MS-based targeted and untargeted metabolomics. Importantly, those bulk techniques do not reveal the localisation of metabolites across different organelles in the cell. Subcellular fractionation, followed by metabolite measurements, can be performed to obtain such information. This is relevant since multiple metabolic enzymes that generate metabolites needed for histone modifications have been shown to travel to the nucleus where they can increase concentrations at the location where they are consumed by histone-modifying enzymes ( Lazaropoulos et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ). While metabolomics data can provide a snapshot of metabolite abundance at a certain timepoint, applying 13 C stable isotopes enables the quantification of intracellular fluxes through diverse metabolic pathways and is often termed fluxomics or 13 C metabolic flux analysis. Most of the metabolic readouts applied in TI are bulk analyses and it should be noted that novel approaches that interrogate metabolism at the single-cell level are becoming more regularly applied in the immunometabolism field ( Artyomov and Van den Bossche, 2020 ; Cosgrove et al., 2024 ). These include cytometry-based approaches like ‘Met-Flow’ ( Ahl et al., 2020 ) and single-cell metabolic profiling (scMEP Hartmann et al., 2021 ) via CyTOF in which fluorescently labelled or heavy-metal-tagged antibodies against key transporters and rate-limiting enzymes across multiple metabolic pathways are applied to estimate the metabolic configuration of immune cells at a per-cell level. So far, both Met-Flow and scMEP haven’t been applied in the TI context, but the recent use of SCENITH and CENCAT approaches indicate the field is moving from bulk towards single-cell metabolic analyses. Aside from analysis of expression levels, there also exist functional readouts of metabolic activity. The most commonly used of these is the Seahorse extracellular flux analysis. This technique is commonly used in immunometabolism and TI research to measure glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism via real-time measurements of protons and oxygen to calculate the extracellular acidification rate and oxygen consumption rate, respectively. However, this analysis requires a certain cell number which can be difficult to achieve in scarce populations and does not give single-cell data. A complementary single-cell approach is SCENITH – a flow cytometry-based methodology that uses puromycin incorporation as a proxy for protein synthesis, a process that is responsible for a large proportion of total ATP usage by a cell ( Argüello et al., 2020 ). Using the glycolysis inhibitor 2-deoxyglucose and mitochondrial ATP synthase inhibitor oligomycin and assessing their effect on puromycin incorporation, one can thus calculate the glycolytic versus mitochondrial dependencies of immune cell subsets. This approach was recently applied to explore metabolic changes in ‘trained’ γδ T cells upon measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccination ( Röring et al., 2024 ). CENCAT is an alternate click chemistry-based measurement of protein synthesis via biorthogonal noncanonical amino acid tagging to profile the metabolic dependencies of cell subsets ( Vrieling et al., 2024 ). This new method was recently applied to measure the bioenergetic profile of BCG-trained versus LPS-tolerised macrophages ( Ziogas et al., 2025 ), albeit at a bulk level. The power of the cytometry-based metabolic profiling approaches is that they allow the assessment of metabolic and immune phenotypes simultaneously and a single-cell or subset resolution. They thus have the potential to address key outstanding questions in the field by uncovering how specific monocyte subsets and phenotypes are ‘trained’ and differentiate into macrophages.
sections.conclusion: There is now a large body of evidence that TI is the result of a coordinated epigenetic and metabolic rewiring. Many of the metabolic pathways mentioned here are not specific to training stimuli. Indeed, LPS, the canonical driver of endotoxin tolerance and immune paralysis, is well known for its activation of mTOR, glycolysis, and HIF stabilisation, as well as cytokine and growth factor receptor signalling ( Tannahill et al., 2013 ; Covarrubias et al., 2015 ; Borriello et al., 2017 ). Whether these metabolic pathways support all macrophage activation and the difference lies in epigenetics, or whether the exact combination of metabolic pathways upon training stimuli is crucial for enhanced long-lasting responsiveness to activation, remains to be deciphered. Although a wide range of epigenetic modifications have been described in the context of TI, their possible interconnections and their relative contributions to TI remain poorly defined, and some epigenetic modifications have not yet been studied in this context ( Baldensperger and Glomb, 2021 ; Xie et al., 2016 ). While there are many unanswered questions in this field, with each new discovery, the common factors become clearer. With the increasing use of new state-of-the-art technologies, these answers become more within reach, and their importance in human disease can be exploited.

title: Real‐World Outcomes of FFRangio ‐Guided Treatment for Coronary Artery Disease in Acute Versus Chronic Coronary Syndromes
abstract: Background The use of angiogram‐based fractional flow reserve technologies in routine clinical practice is increasing steadily. Available data suggest that it is associated with comparable clinical outcomes compared with wire‐based fractional flow reserve (FFR), but evidence is still limited, especially in patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACSs). The aim of this study was to examine the real‐world clinical outcomes of an angiogram based fractional flow reserve technology (FFRangio; CathWorks, Kfar‐Saba, Israel) to guide treatment for coronary artery disease in patients presenting with acute versus chronic coronary syndromes (CCSs). Methods This is a retrospective, observational study. Our cohort included consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography in 7 centers (Japan, 6; Israel, 1), whose treatment was guided by FFRangio between January 2021 and December 2023. The primary end point was 2‐year cumulative incidence of major adverse cardiac events, stratified by presentation (ACS/CCS) and treatment strategy (revascularization/deferral). Results Overall, 2245 patients (ACS, 756; CCS, 1489) were included. Patients with ACS were younger and more likely to be diabetic. At 2 years, ACS presentation resulted in higher risk of major adverse cardiac events (9.8% versus 5.6%; HR, 1.80; P <0.001). Stratified by presentation and treatment, deferred patients had similar risk of major adverse cardiac events (ACS, 5.4%; CCS, 4.7%; HR, 1.08; P =0.672) for treated patients, ACS presentation associated with increased risk for major adverse cardiac events (11.7% versus 7.3%; HR, 1.64; P <0.001). Conclusions In a real‐world setting, FFRangio‐guided treatment yields 2‐year outcomes comparable with current data for wire‐based fractional flow reserve for both patients with ACS and patients with CCS. ACS presentation is associated with increased risk for major adverse cardiac events in patients undergoing FFRangio‐guided revascularization but not deferral. These results demonstrate the clinical utility of FFRangio‐guided treatment across the spectrum of coronary artery disease presentation excluding ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction. Registration URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05648396?term=FFRangio%20&viewType=Card&rank=3 ; Unique Identifier: NCT05648396 .
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.methods_1: Anonymized, deidentified data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.study design: The Japan FFRangio registry ( NCT05648396 ) is a prospective registry of consecutive patients undergoing FFRangio‐guided treatment at 6 Japanese centers and 1 Israeli center. At each center, consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography, which included physiology assessment of at least 1 coronary lesion (the decision to use physiology was at the discretion of the operator) using FFRangio between January 2021 and December 2023, were included. Anatomic and clinical scenarios not included were left main disease or presentation with ST‐segment–elevation myocardial infarction (MI). Patients were also excluded if the eventual treatment strategy chosen by the operator was discordant to the FFRangio analysis (ie, deferral for FFRangio ≤0.8 and revascularization for FFRangio >0.8), if wire‐based FFR was measured concomitantly to FFRangio, or if intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography were used to assess the severity of the coronary lesion(s). For ACS cases, culprit lesions (based on angiographic appearance and clinical scenario) were not assessed using FFRangio, which was used to assess residual intermediate stenoses, after successful treatment of the culprit lesion.
sections.study end points: The primary end point was major adverse cardiac events, defined as the composite of all‐cause death, MI, and any repeat revascularization (RR) at 2‐year follow‐up. Secondary end points included the individual components of the primary end points, as well as target‐vessel MI and target‐vessel RR.
sections.data collection: Data on baseline characteristics, index admission, procedure, in‐hospital follow‐up, and discharge were collected at each participating center using a prespecified standard case review form. Participants were followed after discharge through outpatient clinic visits. For those not attending outpatient visits, data were collected through telephone interviews when possible as well as review of the electronic medical record.
sections.statistical analysis: Patients and lesions were stratified according to the treatment strategy (deferral/revascularization) and clinical presentation (ACS/CCS) into 4 groups (ACS revascularization/deferral and CCS revascularization/deferral). Baseline characteristics are presented as count (percentage) for categorical variables and mean±SD/median (interquartile range) for continuous variables and compared between groups using the independent sample t ‐test, Mann–Whitney U test, and the χ 2 test as appropriate. Since the cohort included patients with multivessel disease who underwent FFRangio assessment of >1 lesion/vessel, lesion characteristics (eg, diameter, length) are presented as a lesion‐level analysis, while patient‐level variable (eg, age, sex, comorbidities) data are presented as a patient‐level analysis. Cumulative incidences of the clinical outcomes were calculated for each group using the Kaplan–Meier method and presented as time‐to‐event plots. Comparisons were made between groups using multivariate adjusted Cox proportional hazard ratio models adjusted to relevant baseline characteristics. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 29 software (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY). The study was approved by the institutional review board at the participating centers, and the study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05648396 ). Given the retrospective study design, a waiver from attaining patients' informed consent was granted by the institutional review board at each participating center.
sections.results_1: During the study period, a total of 2427 patients (1618 CCS and 809 ACS) with 3507 lesions (2323 CCS and 1184 ACS) underwent FFRangio assessment in the participating centers. In 182 patients (271 lesions), the treatment decision was discordant with the FFRangio value, and these patients were excluded from the study. The final study cohort included 2245 patients (1489 CCS and 756 ACS) with 3236 lesions (2138 CCS and 1098 ACS). The rates of concordance between treatment decision and FFRangio value were 92.5%, 92.0%, and 93.3% in the overall, CCS, and ACS subgroups, respectively. The corresponding rates for lesion level analysis are 92.3%, 92.0%, and 93.7% in the overall, CCS, and ACS subgroups, respectively, similar to previous reports. 11 Baseline characteristics stratified by clinical presentation are presented in Table 1 . Compared with patients with ACS, patients with CCS were older (70.1 versus 65.1 years; P <0.001) and had a higher prevalence of hypertension (69.1% versus 59.3%; P <0.001), previous MI and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI; 10.8% and 32.8% versus 7.9% and 24.0%; P =0.038 and P <0.001, respectively). Patients with CCS had lower rates of active smoking (14.5% versus 25.2%; P <0.001) and diabetes (35.6% versus 43.1%; P <0.001). In terms of coronary anatomy, patients with CCS had a lower prevalence of multivessel disease (34.6% versus 43.1%; P <0.001), more lesions involving the right coronary artery (34.8% versus 20.2%; P <0.001), and shorter lesion lengths (21.4 versus 26.1 mm; P <0.001). The mean FFRangio of the CCS group was higher compared with that of the ACS group (0.85 versus 0.77; P <0.001). Baseline characteristics stratified by treatment strategy (deferral versus revascularization) and clinical presentation (CCS versus ACS) are presented in Table 2 . The proportion of deferred patients was higher in CCS compared with ACS cases (66.1% versus 48.1%). Within the deferral and revascularization groups, the differences in clinical characteristics between the CCS and ACS groups were consistent with those observed in the entire cohort.
sections.clinical outcomes: Follow‐up was complete for all patients. After a median follow‐up of 730 (interquartile range, 684–730) days, the primary end point occurred in 79 patients with ACS and 105 patients with CCS (cumulative incidence of 9.8% and 5.6%; adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.80 [95% CI, 1.31–2.46]; P <0.001; Table 3 , Figure 2 ). The cumulative risk for the individual components of the primary end point between ACS and CCS were 1.4% and 0.9% for death ( P =0.33), 4.5% and 2.7% for MI ( P =0.08), and 6.1% and 3.2% for RR ( P <0.01). Cumulative incidences of target‐vessel MI were 0.9% and 0.6% in the ACS and CCS groups, respectively (adjusted HR, 1.65 [95% CI, 0.89–3.56]; P =0.11), whereas rates for target‐vessel RR were 3.3% and 1.8%, respectively (adjusted HR, 1.93 [95% CI, 1.06–3.62]; P =0.02). Following stratification by treatment strategy and clinical presentation, cumulative incidence of the primary end point at 2 years was similar in deferred patients (5.4% versus 4.7% in the ACS and CCS groups, respectively; adjusted HR, 1.08; P =0.67), yet significantly higher for patients with ACS in the revascularization group (11.7% versus 7.3%, in the ACS and CCS groups, respectively; adjusted HR, 1.29; P <0.001; Figure 3 ).
sections.discussion: Our study is the first to present large‐scale results on outcomes of FFRangio‐guided treatment for CAD and the first to examine the effect of clinical presentation on these outcomes. Our main findings are as follows. First, ACS presentation was associated with worse clinical outcomes, which was primarily driven by greater needs for RR. Second, FFRangio‐guided deferral (ie, when FFRangio >0.8), resulted in similar (and low) rates of clinical outcomes at 2 years for patients with ACS and patients with CCS. Third, FFRangio‐guided treatment yielded 2‐year clinical outcomes in line with those associated with wire‐based FFR–guided treatment. Angiogram‐based FFR technologies were developed with the aim to provide an alternative to the cumbersome nature of wire‐based FFR tools. Angiogram‐based FFR provides a seamless procedure without the need for additional equipment/medications and has been shown to be faster compared with wire‐based FFR. 16 All these factors may help address the barriers responsible for the significant underuse of physiologic assessment in everyday clinical practice. 17 , 18 Several technologies have shown excellent diagnostic performance compared with wire‐based FFR and are already available for clinical use, but for angiogram‐based FFR tools to replace wire‐based FFR and fulfill its potential to promote the integration of physiologic assessment to everyday clinical practice, robust data on clinical outcomes of angiogram‐based FFR guided treatment are required. Since each angiogram‐based FFR tool is based on different scientific principles (computational fluid dynamics, mathematical models, etc), outcome data specific for each platform are required, and a class effect cannot be assumed to exist. Currently, randomized comparative outcome data are available only for the quantitative flow ratio (QFR) technology (Medis Medical Imaging, Leiden, The Netherlands), where QFR was found to be superior to angiography‐guided treatment in the FAVOR III (Comparison of Quantitative Flow Ratio Guided and Angiography Guided Percutaneous Intervention in Patients With Coronary Artery Disease) China trial. 12 This trial resulted in QFR receiving the same class recommendation (class I) as wire‐based physiology in the European CCS guidelines. 8 However, more recently, when QFR was compared with wire‐based FFR–guided treatment in the FAVOR III Europe trial, QFR‐guided treatment failed to meet the prespecified noninferiority margin for 1‐year death/MI/RR. 13 These discordant trials reinforce the need for high‐quality prospective and observational data specific for each angiogram‐based FFR technology. Currently, only observational data are available for FFRangio‐guided treatment, whereas a large‐scale randomized trial is ongoing (see below). Real‐world data on FFRangio from 2 early‐adopting centers (1 in Israel and 1 in Japan) evaluated a cohort of 492 patients and found favorable 1‐year results (major adverse cardiac events of 4.1% and 2.5% for revascularization and deferral, respectively) that approximated existing outcomes data with wire‐based FFR–guided treatment. 11 Moreover, the current analysis builds off this prior registry data by providing prospective data collection, a larger sample size, multicenter involvement, and longer‐term follow‐up. Furthermore, inclusion of both patients with ACS and patients with CCS provides an additional aspect of novelty compared with previous data. Since our cohort does not include a comparator group of wire‐based FFR‐guided treatment, our results need to be put in the context of similar studies describing outcomes of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment in real‐world patients. A good example is the study by Cerrato et al, 15 which used individual patient‐level data from 5 national/international registries of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment and stratified the results according to clinical presentation. Their cohort included 8579 patients; the primary end point was the composite of death/MI/RR at 1 year. The fraction of patients with ACS was higher in our cohort (33% versus 25%) but the fraction of deferred patients was identical (40% in both cohorts). When comparing the outcomes of FFRangio‐guided treatment in our study with wire‐based FFR–guided treatment in the study by Cerrato et al, the results are very reassuring: similar risk for 1‐year death/MI/RR (5.1% versus 4.5% and 3.4% versus 2.8% for patients with ACS and patients with CCS in our cohort and Cerrato et al, respectively). Likewise, the HR for patients with ACS versus patients with CCS was similar (1.76 versus 1.72 at 1 year in our cohort and Cerrato et al, respectively). The numerically higher rate of events in our cohort can be explained by a higher prevalence of diabetes in our cohort (39% versus 30%). To further put our results in context, one can also examine outcomes of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment restricted to specific clinical presentation: Parikh et al 7 studied a cohort of 17 989 patient undergoing angiography for CCS presentation and compared outcomes of angiography versus wire‐based FFR–guided treatment. The wire‐based FFR–guided treatment group included 2967 patients. The 1‐year risk for the composite of death/MI/RR was 6.8%, compared with 3.2% at 1 year in our cohort of FFRangio‐guided treatment. For patients with ACS, the DANAMI III PRIMULTI (Third Danish Study of Optimal Acute Treatment of Patients With STEMI—Complete Revascularization Versus Infarct‐Related Artery Only) trial 19 randomized patients presenting with ST‐segment–elevation MI and multivessel disease to PCI of the culprit lesion only versus wire‐based FFR–guided complete revascularization. In the wire‐based FFR–guided revascularization arm, the risk for death/MI/ischemia‐driven RR at a median follow‐up of 27 months was 13%. compared with 9.8% at 2‐year follow‐up in our cohort, a difference that is most likely explained by the difference in baseline risk between an all‐comers ACS population and a dedicated acute MI trial. Overall, we believe that when viewed in context of the existing data for wire‐based FFR, our results suggest that FFRangio‐guided treatment seems to yield favorable midterm outcomes that are in line with those of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment. Another interesting finding from this study is the difference in the interaction between clinical presentation and treatment strategy on outcomes between wire‐based FFR and FFRangio. Cerrato et al 15 found that ACS presentation is associated with increased risk for death/MI/RR in deferred patients but not patients with PCI, while in our cohort ACS presentation was associated with increased risk for death/MI/RR for patients with PCI, not deferred patients. Two major explanations have been postulated for the increased risk associated with deferral of nonculprit lesions in ACS cases: lower diagnostic yield of wire‐based FFR due to transient modification of hemodynamic and microcirculatory status during ACS, and higher prevalence of vulnerable plaques in the coronary vessels of patients with ACS. The different findings of our study compared with those of Cerrato et al may stem from the difference between the calculation of FFRangio and the measurement of wire‐based FFR: Since FFRangio is not dependant on direct measurement of pressure/flow in the coronary tree and does not require hyperemia, it is plausible that the hemodynamic and microcirculatory changes associated with ACS have a lesser effect on its diagnostic accuracy compared with CCS, making it a safer tool for choosing the lesion for deferral. The increased risk for subsequent events in ACS cases in the PCI group may be related to more vulnerable plaques found negative for ischemia by FFRangio, which is consistent with previous data showing worse outcomes for patients with ACS undergoing PCI. 20 , 21 , 22 Although encouraging and reassuring, randomized data are required to ascertain the efficacy and safety of FFRangio compared with wire‐based FFR. The ongoing pivotal ALL‐RISE (Advancing Cath Lab Results With FFRangio Coronary Physiology Assessment; NCT05893498 ) trial is randomizing 1924 patients to FFRangio versus wire‐based FFR–guided treatment with the primary end point of 1‐year death/MI/RR and aims to definitively prove the noninferiority of FFRangio to wire‐based FFR in terms of clinical outcomes. Enrollment was completed in January 2025, and it is anticipated that results will be available early 2026. Our study has several strengths and limitations. Regarding strengths, this study is the largest real‐world outcomes study to date, is multinational, and includes an all‐comers population of patients with CAD (33% ACS presentation, 39% multivessel disease). Furthermore, the follow‐up period is longer than previously reported for outcomes of FFRangio‐guided treatment for CAD.
sections.limitations: The main limitation of our study is its design: a retrospective observational study that does not include a comparison arm of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment, thus requiring further validation from comparative studies (both real‐world and randomized trials). Second, it includes mainly Japanese patients, so results may not be representative of other populations. Finally, the sample size and follow‐up period is smaller and shorter compared with data on real‐world outcomes of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment.
sections.conclusions_1: In real‐world clinical practice, FFRangio‐guided treatment yields excellent 2‐year clinical outcomes that approximate previously reported outcomes of wire‐based FFR–guided treatment. Expectedly, ACS presentation was associated with worse outcomes compared with CCS presentation in cases of FFRangio‐guided revascularization, while FFRangio‐guided deferral of nonculprit lesions in ACS cases was associated with similar outcomes to those of FFRangio deferral in patients with CCS.

title: Longitudinal Transitions between Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms and Associations with Substance Use among US Young Adults, 2016–2023
abstract: Background: Internalizing and externalizing symptoms are key mental health indicators that frequently co-occur in young populations. This study examined transition probabilities between none/low-symptom, exclusive internalizing (e.g., depression, anxiety), exclusive externalizing (e.g., aggression, impulsivity), and co-occurring states in young adulthood and assessed associations with substance use. Methods: Using four waves (Wave 4–7) of the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study (2016–2023), this prospective cohort study applied Markov multistate transition modeling to estimate transition probabilities across 4 mental health states based on self-reported past 12-month symptoms. We then examined how current (daily, non-daily) nicotine use, past 30-day binge drinking, cannabis use, prescription drug misuse, and sociodemographic characteristics were associated with transitions between mental health states among baseline young adults (18–24 years). Results: In the sample (N=5,575), the baseline prevalences of none/low symptom, exclusive internalizing, exclusive externalizing, and co-occurring states were 62.5%, 12.1%, 10.4%, and 13.9%, respectively. Sizable transition probabilities from internalizing or externalizing symptoms to co-occurring symptoms were observed in both short-term (21.6% and 19.7% at Wave 2) and long-term (14.7% and 14.4% at Wave 4) analyses. Co-occurring states demonstrated greater stability (43.9% short-term; 16.4% long-term) than internalizing or externalizing symptom states. Nicotine use was associated with transitions from none/low to internalizing symptoms; binge drinking and prescription drug misuse with transitions to externalizing symptoms; and cannabis use with transitions to both internalizing and externalizing symptoms. Conclusions: Transitions to co-occurring symptoms are frequent in young adulthood, and may be associated with patterns of substance use.

title: Outcomes of spontaneous antepartum fetal subdural hematoma: a case report
abstract: Background Fetal subdural hematoma diagnosed antenatally is an extremely rare condition associated with high rates of fetal mortality and long-term neurological morbidity. The underlying mechanisms are poorly understood, and early prenatal diagnosis remains challenging, especially in low-resource settings. The author describes two cases of antepartum fetal subdural hematoma diagnosed by ultrasound in a low-resource African setting, highlighting the diagnostic features, management challenges, and outcomes. Case presentation This paper discusses two Black African pregnant women aged 33 and 24 years with singleton pregnancies diagnosed with fetal subdural hematoma by ultrasound. Both cases presented between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound revealed hyperechogenic, oval subdural masses exerting mass effect on cerebral structures, associated with signs of fetal anemia and reversed middle cerebral artery diastolic flow. Both patients were evaluated for potential underlying etiologies, including trauma, infections, coagulopathies, and vascular anomalies; however, the etiology could not be identified. In one case, intrauterine death occurred two days after diagnosis. In the second case, an intrauterine transfusion was attempted but resulted in stillbirth on the same day. These findings suggest a likely spontaneous origin of the hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available at the time of diagnosis. Conclusion Antepartum fetal subdural hematoma is a rare and often fatal condition with limited therapeutic options once significant hemorrhage has occurred. Prenatal detection may not significantly alter outcomes in advanced cases. Further research is needed to better understand its etiology, improve early diagnosis, and explore potential management strategies.

sections.background: Fetal subdural hematoma diagnosed antenatally is an extremely rare condition associated with high rates of fetal mortality and long-term neurological morbidity. The underlying mechanisms are poorly understood, and early prenatal diagnosis remains challenging, especially in low-resource settings. The author describes two cases of antepartum fetal subdural hematoma diagnosed by ultrasound in a low-resource African setting, highlighting the diagnostic features, management challenges, and outcomes.
sections.case presentation: This paper discusses two Black African pregnant women aged 33 and 24 years with singleton pregnancies diagnosed with fetal subdural hematoma by ultrasound. Both cases presented between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound revealed hyperechogenic, oval subdural masses exerting mass effect on cerebral structures, associated with signs of fetal anemia and reversed middle cerebral artery diastolic flow. Both patients were evaluated for potential underlying etiologies, including trauma, infections, coagulopathies, and vascular anomalies; however, the etiology could not be identified. In one case, intrauterine death occurred two days after diagnosis. In the second case, an intrauterine transfusion was attempted but resulted in stillbirth on the same day. These findings suggest a likely spontaneous origin of the hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging was not available at the time of diagnosis.
sections.conclusion: Antepartum fetal subdural hematoma is a rare and often fatal condition with limited therapeutic options once significant hemorrhage has occurred. Prenatal detection may not significantly alter outcomes in advanced cases. Further research is needed to better understand its etiology, improve early diagnosis, and explore potential management strategies.
sections.introduction: Fetal subdural hematoma (SDH) is one form of fetal intracranial hemorrhage characterized by the accumulation of blood between the dura mater and arachnoid membrane occurring either antepartum or intrapartum. Antepartum fetal SDH is rare, affecting 0.6–1 of fetuses per 1000 pregnancies, while the prevalence increases to 4.6–5.1% among stillbirths undergoing autopsy studies [ 1 , 2 ]. The prevalence is higher among SDH occurring intrapartum than antepartum, affecting 37.8–46% of normal deliveries; in addition, survival without sequelae is higher among intrapartum SDH than antepartum [ 3 – 5 ]. Antepartum fetal SDH is associated with significant mortality and morbidity, with a mortality rate of up to 30% and up to 42% adverse neurologic outcomes among survivors [ 1 – 3 , 6 ]. Fetal SDH can be caused by maternal trauma from either a motor vehicle accident, a fall down injury, intimate partner violence, maternal bleeding disorders, or the use of anticoagulant drugs; invasive antepartum procedures like chorionic villus sampling; and amniocentesis [ 2 , 3 , 6 ] Additionally, fetal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and vascular anomalies can increase the risk of fetal SDH [ 7 ], while in some of the cases, the causes are unknown. Larger SDH hematomas may cause midline shift, fetal anemia, reversed middle cerebral artery (MCA) diastolic flow, and death [ 3 , 8 ]. Although usually detected during ultrasound scans without any symptoms, sometimes they may present with decreased fetal movement or abdominal trauma including [ 2 ]. Diagnosis is usually made by ultrasound scan with further characterization of the hematoma using magnetic resonance imaging MRI [ 3 , 9 ]. Treatment of the fetal SDH depends on the gestational age, size of the hematoma, and antenatal fetal surveillance results [ 10 ]. In this paper, we are going to present two Black African women diagnosed with fetal anemia secondary to subdural hematoma, both of whom died in utero. These two cases are important because they contribute to the limited evidence on antenatally diagnosed fetal subdural hematoma, a rare yet frequently fatal condition with a poorly understood etiology. By presenting two cases with similar clinical features and consistently poor outcomes, it underscores the aggressive course of the disease and the limited effectiveness of current management once significant hemorrhage has occurred. These observations enhance clinical awareness, support earlier recognition, and aid in more accurate prognostic counseling for affected pregnancies. Furthermore, the report highlights critical gaps in knowledge, emphasizing the need for further research to better understand the underlying mechanisms, improve early diagnostic approaches, and explore more effective treatment strategies.
sections.case 1: A 33-year-old gravida IV para III Black African woman at 30 weeks and 4 days of gestation was referred from a nearby hospital for detailed fetal anatomic assessment after an intracranial mass was detected on ultrasound. All three of her previous deliveries were by cesarean section without complications: the first for failed induction, the second for a failed trial of labor after a cesarean section, and the third performed electively in accordance with national guidelines that do not support a trial of labor after two prior cesarean deliveries. During the current pregnancy, she attended five antenatal care (ANC) follow-ups, during which history, physical examinations, and ultrasound assessments were performed and reported as normal, with appropriate fetal growth. However, at her sixth ANC follow-up, an obstetrician identified an intracranial mass on ultrasound and referred her to a fetal medicine clinic for further evaluation. Upon arrival at the clinic, she denied any history of abdominal trauma, intimate partner violence, bleeding disorders, use of anticoagulant medications, invasive procedures, or external cephalic version. Her vital signs were stable. Obstetric examination revealed a fundal height equivalent of 30 weeks’ gestation with cephalic presentation and a positive fetal heartbeat. Ultrasound evaluation demonstrated a singleton intrauterine pregnancy in a breech position, with an average gestational age of 30 weeks and 5 days. Detailed fetal neurosonography identified a 5 × 3 cm hyperechoic unilateral subdural mass causing significant mass effect, with midline shifting toward the contralateral side (Fig. 1 ). Doppler assessment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) showed reversed diastolic flow, with elevated peak systolic velocimetry of 77.54 cm/s (1.9 multiples of median), suggestive of fetal anemia (Fig. 2 ). No other structural abnormalities were detected on comprehensive sonographic evaluation. Fig. 1 Neurosonography of case one, showing unilateral subdural hematoma with midline shift Fig. 2 Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler of case one shows increased peak systolic flow and reversed diastolic flow Based on these findings, a diagnosis of severe fetal anemia secondary to a subdural hematoma was made. Further evaluation with fetal MRI was planned for better characterization, along with intrauterine transfusion to treat the anemia. However, MRI was not available at our hospital. As the patient presented on a Friday afternoon, intrauterine transfusion was scheduled for the following Monday morning. On Sunday, the patient reported absence the of fetal movements. An urgent ultrasound examination confirmed intrauterine fetal demise. She subsequently delivered a stillborn infant two days later.
sections.case 2: A 24-year-old primigravida Black African woman with an unknown last menstrual period was having antenatal care (ANC) follow-up at a private clinic starting at 10 weeks’ gestation. She attended four regular antenatal contacts before the current presentation. Both the first and second trimester scans showed normal fetal anatomy. At her initial visit, routine laboratory investigations showed a blood group of A positive, with negative screening results for Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL), hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), and human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV). Her hemoglobin level was 12.1 g/dl, and her platelet count was 320 × 10 3 /µL. After the 16th day of her fourth visit, she reported a decrease in fetal movement lasting one day at a gestational age of 29 weeks and 2 days. An ultrasound examination revealed a 1.5 × 1.8 cm hyperechoic crescent-shaped mass in the left subdural space of the fetus (Fig. 3 ). A Doppler examination indicated an increased MCA-PSV of 62.23 cm/s (1.6 MOM), suggesting fetal anemia; however, there was no midline shift of the brain or ventriculomegaly (Fig. 4 ). She denied any history of trauma, medications, or coagulopathy. A complete blood count was conducted, which was within the normal range. Fig. 3 Neurosonography of case two shows a unilateral subdural hematoma Fig. 4 Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler of case two shows increased peak systolic flow and reversed diastolic flow Based on the ultrasound findings, a diagnosis of severe fetal anemia secondary to acute fetal subdural hematoma was made, and intrauterine fetal transfusion was planned. However, O-negative blood was not available for two days. During this interval, the fetus developed signs of hydrops, including ascites, pericardial effusion, ventriculomegaly, progressive midline shift, and tricuspid regurgitation. On the third day, the fetus began to develop ascites, pericardial effusion, ventriculomegaly, midline shift, and tricuspid regurgitation. Compatible blood became available on the third day, and an intrauterine transfusion of 60 ml of O-negative blood was performed via transplacental intravascular approach. Pre-transfusion hemoglobin was critically low at 1.5 g/dl, with a hematocrit level of 4%. Following the procedure, she was admitted for close monitoring with cardiotocography. Unfortunately, the fetus developed bradycardia, and intrauterine fetal demise occurred on the same day. Labor was induced the following day, resulting in the delivery of a freshly stillborn infant. This following table compares two cases of antenatally diagnosed fetal subdural hematoma with similar presentations, including decreased fetal movements, hyperechoic subdural masses, midline shift, fetal anemia, and abnormal MCA Doppler findings (Table 1 ).
