title: Funders' Expectations for Open Science in Cardiovascular Research: A Scoping Review of the Largest Cardiovascular Research Funders
abstract: Open science practices, including data sharing, open access, and prospective study registration, have been increasingly recognized to improve transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility in research, yet their uptake and implementation by cardiovascular research funders is unclear. We conducted a scoping review of publicly available policies, guidance, and grant instructions from 12 members of the Global Cardiovascular Research Funders Forum to assess expectations, monitoring, and support for open science in cardiovascular research. We included 105 documents from 9 funders; no relevant documents were identified for 3 funders. Data sharing (67%) and open access (58%) were the most common mandates by funders, followed by prospective registration (50%) and patient and public involvement (50%). Requirements for other practices, including code sharing, use of reporting guidelines, preprints, and open peer review, were uncommon. Monitoring compliance was inconsistent, with many funders not specifying any mechanisms, even for widely required practices. Where available, support was most often provided through financial assistance, guidance, or infrastructure, particularly for open access, data sharing, and patient and public involvement. These findings suggest that while cardiovascular funders are engaging with open science, policies remain uneven in scope, monitoring, and support. Coordinated efforts to strengthen and harmonize open science expectations, particularly around compliance monitoring and researcher training, will be essential to realizing the full potential of open science in cardiovascular research.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.methods: All data and materials underlying this study are publicly available on the Open Science Framework at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9JEFW .
sections.protocol and registration: We conducted a scoping review to identify and analyze publicly available policies and guidance related to open science practices from cardiovascular research funders. This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute's methodology for scoping reviews and is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews. 12 The study protocol was registered prospectively ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9PZTA ).
sections.eligibility criteria: We included documents that addressed at least 1 open science practice (eg, open access, open data, prospective registration, preprints) and were publicly available from cardiovascular research funders. Eligible document types included official policies, guidance documents, grant requirements, application instructions, and relevant web pages. Documents were included if written in English or if a reliable translation could be produced using DeepL Translate. Opinion pieces, blogs, and nonofficial funder communications were excluded.
sections.information sources: We focused on members of the Global Cardiovascular Research Funders Forum, an international coalition of 12 major cardiovascular research funders: American Heart Association (United States) British Heart Foundation (United Kingdom) Danish Heart Foundation Dutch Heart Foundation (Hartstichting) German Centre for Cardiovascular Research (DZHK) Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada Institute of Circulatory and Respiratory Health (Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Canada) Leducq Foundation National Heart Foundation of Australia National Heart Foundation of New Zealand National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (National Institutes of Health, United States) Swiss Heart Foundation We defined open science as an umbrella term encompassing practices that promote transparency, reproducibility, accessibility, and collaboration in research. Documents were included if they referred to at least 1 of the following practices: open access, open data, data management, open code, open materials, prospective registration, transparent reporting, reproducibility practices, preprints, citizen science (including patient and public involvement [PPI]), open peer review, or researcher identifiers (eg, Open Researcher and Contributor ID [ORCID]). Table 1 presents the descriptions of each of the investigated practices. We restricted our analysis to cardiovascular research funders and included only documents available on official websites, without date restrictions.
sections.search strategy: Two reviewers independently conducted searches between January and April 2025. Searches were performed on funders' websites using internal search tools and supplemented with Google queries combining funder names with targeted keywords (eg, “open science,” “open data,” “data sharing,” “preprints,” “preregistration,” “reporting guideline,” “ORCID,” “patient involvement,” “open access,” and “reproducibility”). The first 100 Google hits per funder were screened for relevance.
sections.data extraction and analysis: We developed a customized data extraction form and piloted it on 5 documents to ensure clarity and consistency. One reviewer extracted all data, and a second reviewer conducted quality control on all records. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus or with input from a third reviewer when necessary. Data extraction was performed using Airtable, a cloud‐based database platform. We extracted the following information: Funder name and country Document type (eg, policy, grant call, guidance) Year of publication or last update Cardiovascular research focus (if specified) Open science practices mentioned Whether practices were required, recommended, mentioned without further detail, or not mentioned Monitoring or compliance mechanisms Forms of support (eg, training, financial resources, infrastructure) Some funders developed multiple documents corresponding to different funding opportunities, which varied in their expectations for open science practices. For example, 1 funder's clinical trial program explicitly required data sharing, while its early‐career investigator program only recommended it. These documents also differed in scope, with some providing a high‐level perspective on open science and others outlining specific policies for a certain practice. To ensure consistency and synthesize information from multiple documents at the funder level, we used an inclusive coding approach and applied an ordinal coding reflecting the level of stringency of each open science practice: (1) “required,” (2) “recommended,” (3) “mentioned but not discussed,” and (4) “not mentioned.” Coding was first conducted at the document level. We then summarized each funder per practice by selecting the most stringent level observed across all eligible documents (the minimum value on the ordinal scale). For example, if a practice was required in at least 1 document but only recommended or not mentioned in others, it was classified as “required” at the funder level. The same approach was applied to the assessment of monitoring and support mechanisms for open science practices. When multiple documents from a funder described monitoring or support, we summarized the funder by keeping the most comprehensive level of information reported across documents. This approach reflects the presence of at least 1 formal requirement or mechanism within the funder's policy landscape. Quantitative data were summarized descriptively using counts and proportions. For qualitative data, we conducted a thematic analysis following the approach by Braun and Clarke. 13 Two reviewers independently reviewed and coded the extracted text, refined the codes through discussion, and organized them into overarching themes. Any disagreements were resolved with input from an additional reviewer. Thematic synthesis was conducted using Microsoft Excel (Research Resource Identifier: SCR_016137).
sections.results: We identified 145 documents from 11 (of the 12) cardiovascular research funders across 9 countries in the Global Cardiovascular Research Funders Forum based on searches on the funders' websites and Google. For 1 funder, no potentially relevant documents could be located. After duplicates were removed, a total of 142 documents were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 38 documents were excluded for not meeting the inclusion criteria (eg, documents lacked relevance to open science expectations or did not pertain to research funding). This resulted in 105 documents from 9 funders included in this review (Figure 1 ). The 3 funders for whom we did not locate relevant documents were the Leducq Foundation, the National Heart Foundation of New Zealand, and the Swiss Heart Foundation. Most documents were classified as general guidance or instructions (59 [56%]), followed by policy or formal statement (23 [22%]), grant guidelines (11 [10%]), grant calls (7 [7%]), and other (5 [5%]). Where available, most documents were published or updated in 2024.
sections.open science expectations: We investigated 12 cardiovascular research funders for their expectations on open science practices. To calculate the proportion of funders addressing each open science practice, all 12 funders were included in the denominator. However, the 3 funders without any documents were not assigned classifications (eg, required, recommended, or not mentioned). The extent to which various practices were required, recommended, mentioned, not mentioned, monitored, or supported is presented in Figure 2 . The most commonly required practices were data sharing (8 funders [67%]) and open access (7 funders [58%]), followed by prospective registration (6 funders [50%]). Data management plans were required by 4 funders (33%) and recommended by 1 (8%). Similarly, PPI was required by 4 funders (33%) and recommended by 2 (17%). Use of ORCID identifiers was required by 3 funders (25%), and code sharing was required by 2 funders (17%) and recommended by 1 (8%). Use of reporting guidelines was required by 2 funders (17%), and open materials were required by 1 (8%) and recommended by 1 funder (8%) (Figure 2 ). Preprints were not required by any funders but were recommended by 4 (33%). Open peer review was rarely addressed, mentioned by only 1 funder (8%). Rigor and reproducibility were explicitly required by just 1 funder (8%). When restricting the denominator to funders with retrievable eligible documents (n=9), the proportion of funders addressing each open science practice was higher (see Table S1 ).
sections.monitoring and support of open science p: The extent to which funders monitored compliance with open science expectations varied across practices. In some cases, monitoring mechanisms focused on verifying whether required elements (eg, patient involvement plans) were included in project proposals rather than assessing their implementation during the project. Among funders that required or recommended a given open science practice, monitoring mechanisms were inconsistently reported (Table 2 ). For data sharing, 2 of 8 funders (25%) reported monitoring, 2 (25%) mentioned monitoring without further detail, and 4 (50%) did not mention monitoring. For open access, 2 of 7 funders (29%) indicated that compliance was monitored, 4 (57%) mentioned monitoring without further detail, and 1 (14%) did not mention monitoring. Monitoring was more frequent for data management plans (3/5 [60%]), ORCID use (3/3 [100%]), and rigor and reproducibility requirements (1/1 [100%]). Prospective registration and PPI were monitored by half of the relevant funders (3/6 [50%]), whereas monitoring of code sharing was reported by 1 of 3 funders (33%). No monitoring mechanisms were identified for preprints, material sharing, or the use of reporting guidelines. Support mechanisms also varied widely across practices (Table 3 ). Financial support to cover related costs, either through dedicated funding, fee reimbursements, or by allowing these costs to be included in grant budgets, was most frequently offered for open access (86%), data management (80%), data sharing (50%), and PPI (50%), reflecting the resource demands of these practices. One funder (14%) explicitly stated that it does not cover article processing charges. Funders also provide implementation support, such as training, infrastructure, or guiding materials. Guiding materials were widely provided across several practices, including open access (43%), data sharing (38%), prospective registration (67%), and data management plans (80%). Infrastructure included platforms or resources that facilitate implementation, such as data repositories, patient engagement platforms to identify patient partners, or systems that automatically make an article open access via PubMed Central. Infrastructure was provided for data and code sharing (38% and 33%, respectively), open access (29%), and PPI (17%). Formal or informal training was less commonly reported overall but was most commonly provided for data management plans (40%), PPI (33%), and prospective registration (17%).
sections.discussion: This scoping review provides a comprehensive assessment of open science expectations among 12 major cardiovascular research funders globally. Our findings show that while many funders have incorporated some key open science practices, formal requirements remain unevenly applied across the range of open science practices. Notably, data sharing and open access were the most frequently required practices (67% and 58%, respectively), reflecting broad recognition of their central role in fostering accessibility and transparency of science. The creation of data management plans was also required or recommended by nearly half of the funders (42%). As structured frameworks for planning data collection, storage, and sharing, data management plans operationalize the commitment to data sharing and reproducibility. In addition, practices such as PPI and prospective registration were required or recommended by half of the funders, suggesting a growing emphasis on patient‐centered research and research transparency. The increasing attention to PPI reflects its recognized importance across clinical practice, guideline development, and research, particularly in cardiovascular research, where patient organizations, scientific societies, and major funders have increasingly advocated for its integration. 14 , 15 Beyond patient involvement, prospective registration expectations also illustrate how policy development may be shaped by existing regulatory frameworks. While most funders required prospective registration for clinical trials, it was often only recommended or not mentioned for other types of studies. This pattern likely reflects the longer‐standing regulatory and ethical frameworks governing clinical trials, where prospective registration is widely recognized as essential to reduce selective reporting and publication bias. 16 In contrast, expectations for other study designs, such as observational studies or secondary analyses, remain less consistently defined. This variability has important implications for how funder policies are interpreted and applied. Requirements that apply only to specific study types or funding mechanisms may not be apparent to applicants navigating different programs and can contribute to inconsistent adoption of open science practices. More broadly, this example also reflects a challenge in open science policy development: ensuring that expectations are specific enough to be meaningful yet consistent enough to promote transparency across all study types. Prospective registration reduces bias and increases transparency by requiring researchers to declare their hypotheses, design, and analysis plan before outcomes are known. 17 Expanding its use to other study designs, such as observational studies and secondary analyses, could contribute to improving the reproducibility and integrity of a broader range of cardiovascular research outputs. However, open science encompasses a broader set of practices than those currently prioritized by funders. Practices such as code sharing, use of reporting guidelines, open peer review, and preprints received far less attention, suggesting that funder policies have yet to fully reflect the scope of what transparent and reproducible research requires. The gaps in policy scope are further reflected in how funders approach compliance: Monitoring of compliance with open science policies was inconsistent and often lacking, even for widely required practices. Without (continuous) monitoring, it is likely difficult for funders to use data to better disseminate and implement open science mandates and recommendations among their grantees. For example, while data sharing and open access are among the most frequently required practices, monitoring is only sporadically implemented; fewer than one third of funders with requirements for open access publishing or data sharing actively monitor adherence. Monitoring was somewhat more common for data management plans (60%), the use of ORCID (100%), PPI, and prospective registration (50%), which may reflect their stronger ties to administrative infrastructure or grant reporting mechanisms. The lack of monitoring mechanisms for practices such as preprints and material sharing indicates a potential disconnect between funder expectations and enforcement, raising questions about the effectiveness of current policies in promoting sustained behavior change among researchers. Despite variable monitoring, many funders provide important support mechanisms to facilitate implementation. Financial assistance to cover related costs was more frequent for open access (86%), data sharing (50%), and PPI (50%), highlighting funders' recognition of cost barriers for these practices. Guiding materials and infrastructure, including repositories and technical platforms, were also frequently made available for data sharing, code sharing, and data management plans, supporting researchers in meeting policy requirements. However, formal or informal training opportunities were less consistently reported, highlighting a notable gap. Given that prior surveys 8 have identified a lack of training and resources as key barriers to open science uptake in cardiovascular research, increasing capacity‐building initiatives may be critical to achieving more widespread adoption. This limited and uneven adoption of open science reflects a lack of coordination that could limit the global cardiovascular research community from fully benefiting from open science. Given that cardiovascular research is inherently international, investigators in any single region rely on access to publications, data, and protocols produced worldwide. Without harmonized policies and consistent enforcement, the potential for open science to accelerate discovery and improve patient outcomes remains unrealized. Open science promotes equitable access to knowledge, fosters transparency, and helps prevent or detect research misconduct. 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 In a climate where public trust in science has been challenged, 22 open science can be a tool to maintain institutional and public trust. 23 , 24 Funders occupy a unique position as gatekeepers of research quality, able to set clear expectations for open science practices that support scientific validation and broader scrutiny of research outputs. Strong, publicly accessible policies, combined with monitoring and support, signal a commitment to accountability and provide incentives for the research community to adopt best practices. In this way, funders not only shape the behavior of their grantees but also influence the wider cardiovascular research ecosystem, fostering a culture of openness that could meaningfully advance cardiovascular health globally.
sections.limitations: This study has several strengths, including its novel focus on cardiovascular research funders, a systematic and rigorous approach to identifying and analyzing policies, and an assessment of a broad range of open science practices within a single review. However, some limitations must be acknowledged. Our search was limited to publicly available documents, excluding those accessible only behind password‐protected platforms such as grant application portals. Many funders make their requirements available only at these later stages. We did not contact funders to verify the completeness of the documents, including cases in which no documents were identified. As a result, the absence of publicly available documents does not necessarily indicate the absence of relevant policies, and our findings may underestimate the prevalence of open science expectations while overstating policy gaps. Nonetheless, we consider it essential that open science expectations be made publicly available and easily accessible. Clear communication of these requirements before application is crucial to ensure transparency and to allow researchers to prepare adequately. Additionally, our funder‐level coding approach was based on the most stringent classification observed across all eligible documents, meaning that a practice was classified as required if at least 1 document mandated it, even if other documents from the same funder only recommended it or did not mention it. While this approach captures the presence of at least 1 formal requirement within a funder's policy landscape, it may overestimate the consistency and extent of open science expectations across a funder's funding mechanism. For example, a practice required specifically for clinical trials was classified as required at the funder level, even if no such requirement existed for other study designs. Readers should therefore interpret funder‐level classifications as reflecting the most stringent expectation documented, rather than a uniform expectation across all programs. The complete document‐level data set is publicly available, allowing readers to examine how requirements vary across individual documents and funding mechanisms. Finally, our searches were conducted using keywords in both English and French, and we included documents for which reliable translations could be obtained using automatic tools such as browser‐based translators available on funders' websites. Despite these efforts, documents published exclusively in other languages or lacking accessible translations may have been missed and underrepresented in our review.
sections.conclusions: In conclusion, our findings suggest that cardiovascular funders are engaging with open science but face challenges in translating policies into practice. The observed gaps in monitoring and support highlight opportunities for funders to strengthen their policies by integrating clearer compliance mechanisms and expanding resources for researchers. Coordinated efforts among funders, aligned with evolving best practices and researcher needs, will be essential to fostering a culture of transparency and reproducibility that can accelerate discovery and ultimately improve cardiovascular research findings. Future work should explore how funder policies interact with institutional and researcher‐level factors to influence open science behaviors in cardiovascular research. For example, if a funder mandated data sharing but the grantee's institution did not, this might be seen as a barrier to implementing the practice. Better communication between funders and research‐performing organizations will likely foster greater uptake and implementation of open science practices. Additionally, qualitative research engaging key interest holders could help identify practical barriers and facilitators to policy implementation, informing more tailored and effective interventions. As open science continues to evolve, funders' roles as leaders and enablers will remain critical in shaping a more open, collaborative, and trustworthy cardiovascular research ecosystem. If cardiovascular research wishes to reap the benefits afforded by open science, funders will want to ensure that they set policies; monitor implementation; and provide resources, training, and guidance for researchers.

title: A Community-Level Digital Health Readiness Index for the US
abstract: Key Points Question Can a census tract-level Digital Health Index (DHI), developed from public data, quantify community readiness for digital care beyond existing indices? Findings In this cross-sectional study of 85 396 US census tracts, the DHI (21 socioeconomic, health care access, and digital connectivity indicators) was strongly correlated with established indices (ie, Social Vulnerability Index, Area Deprivation Index, and Digital Divide Index). However, the DHI prioritized different communities as having the lowest digital health readiness, with only 33% to 44% overlap among highest-decile tracts compared with comparator indices. Meaning This study found that the DHI provides a tract-level measure of digital health readiness to enable targeted support and to monitor health accessibility as digital health scales.

sections.question: Can a census tract-level Digital Health Index (DHI), developed from public data, quantify community readiness for digital care beyond existing indices?
sections.findings: In this cross-sectional study of 85 396 US census tracts, the DHI (21 socioeconomic, health care access, and digital connectivity indicators) was strongly correlated with established indices (ie, Social Vulnerability Index, Area Deprivation Index, and Digital Divide Index). However, the DHI prioritized different communities as having the lowest digital health readiness, with only 33% to 44% overlap among highest-decile tracts compared with comparator indices.
sections.meaning: This study found that the DHI provides a tract-level measure of digital health readiness to enable targeted support and to monitor health accessibility as digital health scales.
sections.importance: Digital health services are expanding, yet community readiness for digital care varies widely. Without a validated, granular measure of readiness, health systems and policymakers cannot reliably enable targeted support or monitor equitable deployment.
sections.objective: To develop and validate a reproducible census tract–level index of community digital health readiness integrating socioeconomic conditions, access to care, and digital connectivity.
sections.design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional index development and validation study analyzed public data from 2018 to 2022. The Digital Health Index (DHI) was constructed from 21 indicators with equal weighting representing 3 domains: socioeconomic, health access, and connectivity. Content validity was assessed using a 2-round Delphi panel including 37 experts. Structural validity was assessed with exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Convergent validity was assessed against the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), Area Deprivation Index (ADI), and Digital Divide Index (DDI). External validity was assessed using health care spending. Robustness was assessed using leave-one-out, weight-perturbation, and group-based cross-validation analysis. Data were analyzed between June 2023 and April 2026.
sections.main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were validation metrics, including factor structure fit indices, correlations with established indices, association with health care spending per capita, and Delphi consensus rates for each indicator. Robustness outcomes included stability of tract rankings under indicator removal or weight changes.
sections.results: The DHI was computed for 85 396 US census tracts across all 50 states. DHI scores correlated with SVI, ADI, and DDI scores (Spearman ρ = 0.61-0.84) but prioritized different low-readiness communities, with only 33% to 44% overlap between tracts in the highest DHI decile and those in the highest SVI, ADI, or DDI deciles. Health care spending showed similar inverse associations across indices. DHI rankings remained stable in sensitivity analyses. All 21 indicators met Delphi consensus criteria after 1 or 2 rounds.
sections.conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional index development and validation study, a reproducible measure of community digital health readiness was constructed at the census tract level, integrating socioeconomic, access, and connectivity factors. The DHI may help health systems, public agencies, and researchers identify communities requiring support and track readiness over time as digital health and artificial intelligence initiatives expand.
sections.introduction: Approximately 100 million US residents live in areas with inadequate access to health care. 1 Limited access to health care is amplified in rural communities, which account for 20% of the population, and where 80% of residents lack a sufficient health care workforce to meet local demand. 2 , 3 Digital health tools can extend access, but adoption and effective use remain uneven across communities. These tools encompass both clinically integrated platforms, such as telemedicine and remote monitoring, and those not directly linked to clinical care, such as patient-facing artificial intelligence tools, including large language models. 4 , 5 Rural and socioeconomically disadvantaged areas often lag in adoption, suggesting that community-level digital readiness, defined as the community-level capacity for residents to access and benefit from digital services, varies widely. 6 , 7 , 8 Currently, decision-makers lack a comprehensive metric to quantify this readiness gap. 9 Digital health readiness reflects modifiable, upstream determinants that shape whether digital care can be used equitably. 8 , 10 , 11 We conceptualized readiness across 3 domains: socioeconomic constraints that affect affordability and time, local access to health care that shapes opportunities to engage with the health system, and reliable digital connectivity required to use most digital health services. Deficits in any of these domains are consistently associated with reduced adoption and effectiveness of digital health tools. 12 , 13 Existing indices capture these determinants only partially. The Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Area Deprivation Index (ADI) summarize socioeconomic disadvantage but do not include local health care access measures relevant to digital care delivery. 14 , 15 The Digital Divide Index (DDI) focuses on connectivity but does not incorporate health care access or socioeconomic barriers. 16 While these indices have been used by health systems to support targeted health interventions, decision-makers lack a single, census tract–level measure that integrates the major determinants of digital health readiness to guide where deployments are likely to succeed and where enabling supports are needed. 16 , 17 , 18 This measurement gap impedes evidence-based decision-making as digital health transitions from pilot programs to routine care delivery. It limits the ability to target resources, identify communities at risk of exclusion, and evaluate equity in digital health deployment. Health systems, reimbursement policies, and implementation initiatives frequently require targeting and evaluation, yet available metrics do not differentiate between communities that can benefit immediately and those requiring foundational investments. 19 , 20 National maturity frameworks benchmark policy and governance readiness, but they cannot quantify within-country variation at the community level. 21 To address this gap, we developed the Digital Health Index (DHI), a census tract–level composite measure that summarizes community readiness for digital health across socioeconomic conditions, access to care, and digital connectivity. The aim of this index is to enable health systems, public agencies, researchers, and community partners to prioritize rollouts; pair services with enabling supports, such as outreach, device assistance, and digital literacy; allocate resources effectively; and monitor progress with a focus on expanding digital health access. The myriad applications of the DHI position it as a planning tool for health systems targeting underserved communities and a standardized exposure measure for researchers evaluating the reach of digital health programs. We addressed 2 questions: (1) whether a census tract–level readiness index can be constructed based on nationally available data using a reproducible approach suitable for periodic updates and (2) whether it demonstrates content validity, structural validity, and external validity while providing a distinct implementation signal compared with established indices.
sections.methods: This cross-sectional study was deemed exempt from review and informed consent by the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill institutional review board according to the regulatory category cited under 45 CFR 46.104. A prespecified protocol and codebook guided all decisions on variable handling, scoring, and validation (eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 ). This study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline for cross-sectional studies.
sections.study design: We conducted a mixed-methods cross-sectional index development and validation study at the US census tract level to create and validate the DHI, a composite measure of community digital health readiness. The DHI development was informed by our prior work measuring community characteristics in North Carolina to support the implementation and utilization of telehealth services 22 and our systematic review of digital health measurement approaches. 18 The DHI combines 21 indicators across socioeconomic, access, and digital domains, producing county-, state-, and national-level scores. The unit of analysis was the census tract. 23
sections.data sources: The DHI was constructed using 2018 to 2022 data from 3 sources aligned to 3 domains: socioeconomic indicators from the American Community Survey, 24 health care access indicators from multiple federal databases, 25 and digital connectivity metrics from the Federal Communications Commission National Broadband Map. 26 Data sources and variable selection followed SVI methods but prioritized health care access and digital domain measures. Full variable definitions and data source details are provided in eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 . Datasets were harmonized to census tracts using the Federal Information Processing Standards codes, measurement years were aligned, and sentinel values used by source datasets were treated as missing. For external comparisons and modeling, we also assembled the ADI, 27 SVI, 28 and DDI 16 matched at the census tract level.
sections.dhi development: We constructed the DHI using equal weighting for all 21 indicators, reflecting the a priori assumption that socioeconomic conditions, access to care, and connectivity each contribute materially to digital readiness, ensuring transparency and reproducibility ( Figure 1 ). These indicators were selected from a pool of 32 potential indicators due to their pre-existing associations with digital health (eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 ). Each indicator was coded so that higher values indicated worse conditions (lower readiness). Indicators were then transformed to a common scale and aggregated within domains to create 3 domain scores. The overall DHI score was calculated as the mean of the 3 domain scores, yielding a tract-level index in which higher values reflect lower digital health readiness ( Figure 1 ). Detailed variable coding, transformations, and scoring steps are provided in eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 . Each domain captures well-documented barriers. Lower socioeconomic status reduces digital health access and utilization 29 ; racial and ethnic minority communities, such as Black or African American and Hispanic or Latino populations, face compounded disadvantages from intersecting factors, including lower broadband access, digital literacy gaps, and limited insurance coverage 30 ; and geographic barriers are associated with delayed care-seeking, worse health outcomes, and higher emergency department utilization. 31
sections.weighting approach: We applied equal weighting across indicators to maximize transparency and reproducibility and because no established empirical basis exists for differential weighting of readiness determinants at the tract level. 32 , 33 The Delphi process was used to establish content validity and domain coverage rather than to assign weights. Sensitivity analyses evaluated rank stability under alternative weighting schemes (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ).
sections.statistical analysis: Because digital health readiness is a multidimensional construct without a single reference standard, we used a prespecified, multistage validation framework to assess convergent, discriminant, criterion, and known-groups validity. We also assessed robustness and sensitivity to alternative analytic choices. To improve comparability across indices, the DHI, ADI, SVI, and DDI were aligned so that higher values indicated worse conditions. We standardized the scale to range from 0 to 1. Convergent validity was assessed using Spearman correlation analysis, overlap of worst-decile tracts summarized by the Jaccard index, and decile-based agreement analyses with weighted κ statistics. To assess whether the DHI captured information beyond socioeconomic deprivation, we estimated partial Spearman correlation coefficients adjusted for prespecified covariates. Criterion relevance was evaluated using health care spending per capita from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality Medical Expenditure Panel Survey 34 as an external health economic indicator. Because spending was right-skewed, adjusted associations were estimated using robust linear regression models with log-transformed spending as the dependent variable; results are reported as slopes with 95% CIs. Discriminant validity among DHI domains was assessed using the heterotrait:monotrait (HT:MT) ratio with bootstrapped 95% CIs. Known-groups validity was assessed by comparing the DHI across quartiles of health care spending using the Kruskal-Wallis test, with effect size estimates and Dunn-Bonferroni–adjusted post hoc comparisons. Robustness and sensitivity analyses evaluated whether results depended on weighting, indicator selection, preprocessing, or spatial clustering. First, we assessed weighting sensitivity by perturbating weights with randomly generated weight vectors and compared the resulting rankings with the baseline specification. To further examine sensitivity to factor weighting, we refit regression models under each reweighted DHI and evaluated the distribution and directional consistency of corresponding effect estimates. Second, we evaluated indicator dependence using leave-one-out analyses that sequentially excluded each indicator, recomputed the index, and reassessed tract rankings and spending-model coefficients; multicollinearity was summarized using variance inflation factors. Third, we examined preprocessing sensitivity by varying normalization and winsorization choices and by perturbing normalization parameters to quantify ranking uncertainty. For each alternative specification, we refit criterion models and examined the magnitude and direction of effect estimates. Finally, to reduce optimism due to spatial clustering, we evaluated out-of-sample performance using group-based cross-validation with county- and state-level groupings. To assess the content validity of individual DHI indicators, we conducted a modified, in-person Delphi process 35 at a national connected health conference, with panelists representing implementation, clinical operations, policy, informatics, and digital health research. Interested individuals used a quick response code to voluntarily register for the workshop. Only those in a professional role related to digital health were included; no trainees were included in the workshop. Preconference communications included materials on the DHI construct and the Delphi method for attendees to read prior to attendance. Using an online survey instrument that first collected panel participants’ demographic data, panelists independently and anonymously rated each candidate indicator across structured rounds. After each round, aggregated, nonattributable results were shared to support refinement. Facilitated sessions were used to clarify indicator definitions and resolve wording ambiguities before independent rerating; consensus was not generated through open debate. Based on literature, we prespecified consensus as at least 70% agreement at the somewhat agree or strongly agree level. 36 Indicators below threshold were revised based on feedback and rerated in a subsequent round without access to other panelists’ individual ratings. We followed the Delphi Studies in Social and Health Sciences—Recommendations for an Interdisciplinary Standardized Reporting ( DELPHISTAR ) reporting guidelines. Analyses were conducted in Python version 3.13.5 (Python Software Foundation) and R version 4.5.2 (R Project for Statistical Computing) between June 2023 and April 2026. P values were 2-sided, and P < .05 was considered to indicate statistical significance for all tests. Additional details of statistical analysis are provided in eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 .
sections.results_1: The DHI was computed for 85 396 US census tracts across all 50 states and the District of Columbia. National coverage allows for consistent comparison of digital health readiness across geographic regions and administrative levels.
sections.convergent and discriminant validation: At the census tract level, DHI scores correlated strongly with SVI (ρ = 0.84; P < .001) and DDI (ρ = 0.82; P < .001) scores and moderately with ADI (ρ = 0.61; P < .001) scores ( Figure 2 ). Decile-based agreement analyses showed high ordered concordance for the DHI vs the SVI and DDI (DHI vs SVI: quadratic-weighted κ = 0.83; DHI vs DDI: quadratic-weighted κ = 0.81) and more moderate concordance for the DHI vs the ADI (quadratic-weighted κ = 0.60), while exact same-decile agreement remained limited (0.29, 0.29, and 0.20, respectively) (eAppendix 3 in Supplement 1 ). Among tracts in the highest DHI decile (lowest readiness), overlap with the highest deciles of comparator indices was limited (intersection: 3606 tracts with the SVI; 3428 tracts with the ADI; 4258 tracts with the DDI; Jaccard indices: SVI, 0.35; ADI, 0.33; DDI, 0.44), corresponding to only 33% to 44% concordance in identifying low digital health readiness communities. At the county level, the DHI showed systematic deviations from comparator indices, consistent with geographic reordering when health care access and connectivity were explicitly integrated alongside socioeconomic conditions within a single readiness measure ( Figure 3 ). After adjustment for socioeconomic characteristics, partial correlations attenuated. The partial correlation between the DHI and ADI was weak (ρ = 0.14; P < .001), whereas partial correlations between the DHI and SVI (ρ = 0.55; P < .001) and between the DHI and DDI (ρ = 0.57; P < .001) remained moderate, suggesting that the DHI captures information beyond socioeconomic deprivation alone (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ).
sections.external validity and known-groups valid: In external validation using a health economic indicator, the DHI was negatively correlated with log-transformed health care spending per capita in robust linear regression models (β = −0.635; 95% CI, −0.643 to −0.626). This association was stronger than that observed for the DDI (β = −0.606; 95% CI, −0.634 to −0.578; P < .001), SVI (β = −0.478; 95% CI, −0.483 to −0.474; P < .001), and ADI (β = −0.222; 95% CI, −0.227 to −0.216; P < .001) ( Figure 4 ; eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). The DHI differed across quartiles of health care spending (Kruskal-Wallis P < .001). Areas with higher healthcare spending had better digital health readiness, indicated by lower DHI scores (Spearman ρ = −0.473; P < .001) (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). Using the HT:MT criterion, discriminant validity among the 3 DHI domain scores showed that all bootstrapped CIs were less than the 0.90 threshold (socioeconomic vs access: HT:MT, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.62-0.64]; socioeconomic vs digital: HT:MT, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.73-0.75; access vs digital HT:MT, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.85-0.87). Known-groups validity was assessed across quartiles of health care spending. The DHI differed significantly across health care spending groups (Kruskal-Wallis H = 65 415; P < .001; effect size η 2 [H] = 0.94; κ = 4). Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc Dunn tests revealed that all pairwise differences were significant ( P < .001), indicating graded separation; higher-spending areas were more likely to have lower DHI scores, ie, greater digitalization (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). For example, median DHI increased from 0.285 in the highest spending quartile to 0.423, 0.545, and 0.692 in progressively lower spending quartiles.
sections.robustness and sensitivity analyses: Tract rankings were highly stable under weight perturbation centered on equal weights (median Spearman ρ = 0.999; median Kendall τ = 0.975), with stable top decile membership (median Jaccard = 1.000) (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). Dirichlet-based β-stability analysis showed that across 1000 positive weight draws, the association between the DHI and spending per capita remained negative, indicating a consistently negative association across plausible weightings (β percentiles: 2.5th, −0.141; 50th, −0.098; 97.5th, −0.026) (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). Leave-one-out analysis showed minimal change in rankings when any single indicator was removed (mean Spearman ρ = 0.964), and multicollinearity diagnostics suggested limited redundancy, corresponding to no severe redundancy among indicators (median VIF = 1.92) (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ). Rankings were also stable under normalization uncertainty (median Spearman ρ = 0.985), and group-based cross-validation showed similar performance by county and state (both root mean square error = 0.068) (eAppendix 2 in Supplement 1 ).
sections.qualitative validation: A total of 37 individuals participated in the Delphi consensus-building workshop. Of the participants, 30 (81%) were female, 19 (52%) were health care professionals, and 16 (43%) had 2 to 5 years of experience in their field (eAppendix 1 in Supplement 1 ). By race and ethnicity, there were 12 participants (32%) who identified as Asian, 5 (14%) as Hispanic or Latino, 18 (49%) as White, and 2 (5%) as other race or ethnicity (no further specification). Consensus was achieved for all 21 DHI variables at the Delphi workshop. Of 21 indicators, 17 (80.9%) met the prespecified consensus threshold after 1 round. Following a facilitated discussion, 3 socioeconomic indicators met the threshold after a second round (tract-level Hispanic population percentage, 72.2%; tract-level Black or African American population percentage, 86.1%; tract-level percentage of uninsured residents, 88.9%). One access indicator (emergency department access) did not meet the threshold in round 1 (68.6%) but met the threshold in round 2 following group discussion (89.6%). Digital domain indicators met the consensus threshold in round 1. Item-level results are shown in the Table .
sections.discussion: In this national cross-sectional index development and validation study, we developed the DHI, a census tract–level measure of community digital health readiness that integrates socioeconomic conditions, health care access, and digital connectivity. The DHI showed strong correlations with established area-based indices, yet it identified a different set of communities prioritized as lowest readiness, with limited overlap in the highest-decile tracts vs comparator indices. The index also demonstrated stability across multiple sensitivity analyses, supporting its use as a reproducible community-level measure. These findings address a practical measurement gap in digital health implementation and evaluation. Commonly used indices capture important aspects of vulnerability or connectivity but do not jointly represent the socioeconomic, health care access, and infrastructure conditions that shape whether digital health services can be used effectively in a given community. By incorporating these domains in a single tract-level score, the DHI may help distinguish communities likely to benefit from digital health services without additional support from those where foundational constraints may limit uptake or effectiveness. Health systems lack the capacity to systematically assess digital health readiness in communities to effectively target interventions. 37 Comparator indices, such as the ADI, can help inform telehealth strategies and identify priority areas for patient digital navigator support, but health systems lack a unified, comprehensive framework within the digital health landscape. 38 , 39 Divergence between the DHI and comparator indices is expected, given differences in construct focus. 9 Two communities with similar levels of socioeconomic deprivation may differ in critical factors, such as local access to care or digital connectivity, which can substantially influence their readiness for telemedicine and other digitally mediated services. The 3-domain structure of the DHI supports a novel interpretation of readiness as inherently multidimensional rather than something that can be reduced to deprivation or connectivity alone. The DHI may be useful for both practice and research. For health systems and public agencies, the DHI may support targeting and prioritization by identifying communities with low overall readiness, where enabling supports or infrastructure investments may be needed. Additionally, the domain scores may serve as complementary subindices to help distinguish whether readiness constraints are driven more by socioeconomic conditions, health care access, or digitalization, thereby supporting more tailored planning and intervention design. For researchers, the DHI provides a standardized tract-level exposure that could strengthen study design and evaluation, including stratified sampling, assessment of effect modification by place, and benchmarking across jurisdictions. The domain scores may also support analyses of how different readiness dimensions contribute to outcomes. Furthermore, annual updates to the DHI dataset will sustain its relevancy across stakeholder interests. Readiness should be treated as a modifiable set of conditions, not a fixed trait. The DHI supports a measurement-to-action pathway that is useful for both translational research and implementation. Investigators can use the measure to stratify sites in community-based trials, to prespecify subgroup analyses for effect modification by place, to allocate resources within stepped-wedge designs, and to evaluate natural experiments in which digital services are introduced unevenly across communities. 22 , 40 , 41 For quality improvement and service design, the DHI can enable health systems to inform codesigning interventions with communities, select complementary digital health tools, and conduct ongoing evaluation to determine whether access and use improve among the intended populations. The Delphi panel, after clarification that only validated public data were used and that indicators reflected contextual barriers, affirmed the relevance of the findings to the construct. For instance, emergency department access functions as a tract-level proxy for the local care infrastructure that shapes when and how telehealth substitutes for or complements in-person care. 42 , 43 The DHI may help align digital health deployments with community needs by identifying areas where readiness is low and where additional enabling supports or infrastructure investments may be warranted. It may also support monitoring of readiness over time as policies and resources change. For research, the DHI provides a standardized tract-level measure that can support stratified sampling, assessment of effect modification by place, and benchmarking across jurisdictions and years. Because the DHI is based on public data and a documented scoring approach, it can be replicated and updated to support planning and evaluation. For example, health systems scaling telehealth follow-up or remote monitoring may use the DHI to identify low-readiness communities where additional enablement supports may be needed.
sections.limitations: Several limitations merit consideration. First, the DHI captures community-level determinants available at the national scale and does not directly measure health system implementation capacity or operational telehealth maturity. Second, several candidate readiness measures are unavailable or inconsistently measured at the census tract level, and input measures may contain errors, including broadband availability estimates. Third, validation analyses were cross-sectional; associations should not be interpreted causally, and longitudinal responsiveness to investments remains to be established. Fourth, the DHI should be interpreted as a screening and planning tool and may benefit from supplementation with local context when used to guide decisions. Future research may apply the DHI in clinical and translational settings to guide digital health and artificial intelligence rollouts and assess the uptake and impact of these interventions on health disparities and outcomes.
sections.conclusions: In this cross-sectional index development and validation study, a reproducible census tract–level measure of community digital health readiness was created by integrating socioeconomic conditions, health care access, and digital connectivity. The DHI may help identify readiness gaps, guide targeting of enabling supports, and support evaluation of digital health initiatives as they expand. This index may be of particular interest to health systems designing or implementing digital health programs, and policymakers examining gaps in services and infrastructure to promote better access to health care.

title: Retinal and Choroidal Vascular Alterations in Carotid Dissection Versus Atherosclerosis: Insights Into Divergent Ischemic Mechanisms
abstract: Background To contrast retinal and choroidal vascular alterations between carotid artery dissection (CAD) and carotid artery stenosis (CAS), and analyze their associations with cerebral infarction patterns and stenosis severity. Methods This observational study included stenotic‐degree‐matched patients with CAD and patients with CAS. Retinal ischemic signs—cotton wool spots, retinal artery occlusion, and paracentral acute middle maculopathy—were evaluated using fovea‐centered optical coherence tomography/angiography. Retinal vascular density and choroidal metrics (choriocapillaris density, thickness, vascular volume, and index) were analyzed. Results The final analysis included 863 eyes from 467 participants (85 with CAD, 274 with CAS, 108 controls). Patients with CAD showed a significantly higher prevalence of paracentral acute middle maculopathy than Patients with CAS (6.4% versus 0.61%, P <0.001). Although ipsilateral eyes in both groups showed reduced retinal vascular density ( P <0.017), a divergent pattern was observed in the choroid: CAD‐affected eyes demonstrated significantly higher choriocapillaris density, choroidal vascular volume, and choroidal thickness relative to both control and CAS‐affected eyes ( P <0.017). Clinically, retinal ischemic signs in CAD were significantly associated with cerebral infarction ( P =0.022) and severe stenosis/occlusion ( P =0.008). Notably, retinal signs correlated with cerebral infarction topography: subcortical infarctions were predominantly associated with paracentral acute middle maculopathy, whereas cortical infarctions were linked to cotton wool spots and retinal artery occlusion ( P =0.004). Conclusions Compared with atherosclerotic stenosis, CAD exhibits a distinct oculovascular phenotype characterized by a higher burden of acute retinal ischemia but compensatory choroidal hyperperfusion. Retinal imaging serves as a noninvasive window into CAD pathophysiology, offering biomarkers for assessing hemodynamic stability and thromboembolic risk. Registration URL: www.chictr.org.cn ; Unique identifier: ChiCTR2300074640.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.what is new?: Compared with the diffuse microvascular decline typical of atherosclerotic carotid artery stenosis, carotid artery dissection exhibits a distinct oculovascular phenotype characterized by a higher burden of acute retinal ischemia alongside compensatory choroidal hyperperfusion.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Noninvasive retinal imaging using optical coherence tomography and angiography provides a unique window to differentiate the distinct hemodynamic and thromboembolic pathophysiologies underlying different causes of large‐artery stenosis. Detecting specific acute retinal ischemic signs, such as paracentral acute middle maculopathy, can help clinicians identify patients with carotid artery dissection who are at elevated risk for severe stenosis and topography‐specific cerebral infarctions, thereby facilitating tailored neurological risk stratification.
sections.data availability statement: The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
sections.study design and setting: This study is part of an ongoing, multicenter cohort study (ChiCTR2300074640) aimed at investigating ophthalmic and neuroimaging features. The parent study has been consecutively enrolling patients with cerebral large‐artery stenosis from the Neurology Departments of 3 hospitals in China from April 2021 to February 2025. The rationale and detailed methodology of the study have been previously published. 8 , 10 In brief, cerebral large‐artery stenosis or occlusion was initially screened using computed tomography angiography, magnetic resonance angiography, or ultrasonography, and confirmed by digital subtraction angiography (DSA). All participants underwent a comprehensive neurological examination, visual acuity assessment, and OCT/OCTA imaging. The present analysis focuses specifically on carotid stenosis resulting from different causes—namely, dissection and atherosclerosis. The study was approved by the West China Hospital Research Ethics Committee [2020(922)], and written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
sections.participants: We included adult patients (>18 years) with CAD, regardless of the presence of ischemic events, but excluded those with concomitant trauma. Neuroimaging data were centrally reviewed by principal investigators (B.W. and F.Y.H.). The imaging diagnosis of CAD required at least 1 of the following features 11 : crescent‐shaped hyperintensity within the vessel wall; double‐lumen sign; dissecting pseudoaneurysm, intimal flap, or vessel irregularity; flame‐shaped or tapered stenosis or occlusion at a typical dissection site; and absence of atherosclerotic characteristics. Exclusion criteria comprised incidental chronic dissection, dissection from other causes, emergency endovascular thrombectomy, coexisting neurological disorders (such as dementia, optical neuritis, or migraine), and cerebral atherosclerotic stenosis. For comparison, patients with carotid atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion were randomly selected from the cohort and matched to patients with CAD in a 1:3 ratio based on stenotic degree, as detailed in Data S1 . Additionally, controls were randomly selected from individuals undergoing routine physical examinations at our hospital and matched to the group with CAD by age and sex.
sections.clinical evaluation: Demographic characteristics (sex and age), vascular risk factors (including history of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, alcohol use, and smoking), along with medical history and neurological symptoms/signs, were collected through standardized interviews and physical examinations. In patients suspected of cerebral infarction, brain magnetic resonance imaging was performed, including T1‐weighted, T2‐weighted, fluid‐attenuated inversion recovery, and diffusion‐weighted imaging. Infarct locations were classified as either cortical or subcortical. Detailed protocols for magnetic resonance imaging have been described in our previous publications. 6 Clinical information, neurological imaging, and OCT/OCTA imaging were obtained within 1 week before DSA.
sections.oct and octa imaging: Swept‐source OCT/OCTA (SS‐OCT/OCTA, VG200S; SVision Imaging, Henan, China; version 2.0.106) was used, as detailed in earlier studies. 9 , 10 A raster scan protocol (512 B‐scans × 512 A‐scans, repeated 4 times) covering a 6 × 6 mm 2 macula‐centered area was applied to acquire retinal and choroidal OCT/OCTA images. Both eyes were imaged, and the eyes ipsilateral and contralateral to the CAD were designated accordingly. Retinal and choroidal vasculature were automatically analyzed using the built‐in OCTA software, consistent with our prior methodology. The following parameters were analyzed: vessel density (%) and perfusion area (mm 2 ) of the superficial vascular complex (SVC), deep vascular complex, and choriocapillaris, as well as the foveal avascular zone area (mm 2 ). In addition, the OCT system automatically derived choroidal thickness (μm), choroidal vascular volume, choroidal stromal volume, and the choroidal vascular index.
sections.retinal ischemic signs evolution: We assessed all patients for established retinal ischemic signs or diseases reported in the literature, including cotton wool spots (CWS), central/branch retinal artery occlusion (RAO), central/branch retinal vein occlusion, paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM), ischemic optic neuropathy, and retinal ischemic perivascular lesions (RIPL). In our cohort with CAD, 3 types of acute ischemic signs (CWS, RAO, and PAMM) and the chronic retinal ischemic sign RIPL were identified. CWS appeared as grayish clouds with fimbriate borders on infrared fundus imaging. OCT revealed focal thickening of the retinal nerve fiber layer with hyperreflectivity, and corresponding OCTA showed nonperfusion in the retinal pericapillary plexus (Figure 1A ). RAO presented as a darkened retina with obscured choroidal texture along the retinal artery path on infrared fundus images. OCT displayed hyperreflectivity and edema of the inner retinal layers, accompanied by hypoperfusion on OCTA (Figure 1B ). PAMM was observed as multiple dark macular patches on infrared fundus imaging. OCT demonstrated band‐like hyperreflectivity in the inner nuclear layer (INL), and OCTA revealed diffuse areas of low vessel density in the retinal vasculature (Figure 1C,D,E ). RIPL was characterized by focal INL atrophy and compensatory expansion of the outer retinal layer, resulting in a wavy appearance on OCT sections. The retinal ischemic signs were centrally and independently assessed by 2 neuro‐ophthalmologists (L.C. and H.W.), who were masked to all clinical information. Intergrader agreement was high for CWS (κ=0.94, P <0.001), RAO (κ=0.96, P <0.001), PAMM (κ=0.91, P <0.001), and RIPL (κ=0.93, P <0.001). Any discrepancies between the 2 graders were adjudicated by a third independent ophthalmologist (G.N.L.). Images with signal quality <7, motion artifacts, or other retinal disorders (eg, diabetic retinopathy, age‐related macular degeneration) were excluded. All OCT/OCTA data adhered to the OSCAR‐IB quality criteria 12 and Advised Protocol for OCT Study Terminology and Elements recommendations. 13
sections.statistical analysis: Descriptive characteristics of enrolled participants are presented as mean±SD, median with interquartile range, or frequency with percentage, as appropriate. Baseline characteristics were compared specifically between the groups with CAD and CAS using the t test, χ 2 test, or Wilcoxon test, depending on data distribution and variable type. To mitigate Simpson's paradox and multicollinearity, we employed an indirect standardization approach. First, a multivariable logistic regression model was established in a reference cohort derived from the overall patient population, excluding the participants enrolled in the current study. This model was used to predict the expected probability of retinal ischemic signs based on vascular risk factors (age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, and drinking). These predicted probabilities served as the “expected” risk for patients with CAD and CAS. Subsequently, to assess the difference in standardized prevalence between the groups with CAD and CAS groups, a binomial generalized linear model was fitted with the logarithm of the expected probability included as an offset. In subgroup analyses where complete separation (zero events) occurred, Firth's penalized logistic regression was used to assess associations between retinal ischemic signs and variables such as eye side, cerebral infarction patterns, ocular symptoms, or stenosis degree. The relationship between the subtype of retinal ischemic signs and infarction location was evaluated using the χ 2 test. Furthermore, linear regression models were applied to compare retinal and choroidal vascular metrics. Specific comparisons were performed between ipsilateral and contralateral eyes within the groups with CAD and CAS, as well as between patients with CAD and CAS within the ipsilateral and contralateral eye subgroups, respectively. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.2.3). A 2‐sided P ‐value <0.05 was generally considered statistically significant. For comparisons across 3 groups, the significance level was adjusted using the Bonferroni method, with a P value <0.017 denoting statistical significance.
sections.patients' characteristics: A total of 2432 patients with cerebral large‐artery stenosis were initially identified in the overall cohort, among whom 107 were diagnosed with CAD. Following the application of exclusion criteria and matching for stenotic degree (Figure S1 ), the final analysis included 85 patients with CAD (170 eyes), 274 patients with CAS (497 eyes), and 108 controls (196 eyes). The baseline characteristics of the enrolled participants are summarized in Table 1 . Compared with the group with CAS, patients with CAD were significantly younger (50.91 versus 64.66 years, P <0.001) and had a lower proportion of male participants (74.12% versus 87.55%, P =0.005). Furthermore, patients with CAD exhibited a significantly lower prevalence of vascular risk factors, including hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and alcohol consumption (all P <0.05). Notably, despite the lower burden of risk factors, patients with CAD presented with a significantly higher prevalence of ocular symptoms (25.88% versus 9.85%, P <0.001) and cerebral infarction (56.47% versus 41.61%, P =0.023) compared with those with CAS.
sections.retinal ischemic signs in cad and cas: After adjusting for demographic and vascular risk factors via indirect standardization, patients with CAD demonstrated a markedly higher risk of composite acute retinal ischemic signs compared with patients with CAS (11.05% versus 5.66%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 3.32 [95% CI, 1.79–6.15]; P <0.001; Table 2 ). Specifically, regarding individual signs, the group with CAD exhibited a strikingly higher prevalence of PAMM (6.47% versus 0.61%; aOR, 17.25 [95% CI, 4.75–62.67]; P <0.001) and RAO (2.91% versus 0.81%; aOR, 5.64 [95% CI, 1.50–21.26]; P =0.011). Although the prevalence of CWS did not differ significantly between the 2 groups (aOR, 1.23; P =0.624), the severity of CWS, as indicated by the number of spots, was significantly higher in the group with CAD (adjusted incidence rate ratio, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.25–4.87]; P =0.011). Conversely, regarding chronic ischemic changes, although the raw prevalence of RIPL was lower in patients with CAD (19.19% versus 32.39%), this difference was not statistically significant after adjusting for confounding factors (aOR, 0.77 [95% CI, 0.51–1.18]; P =0.228).
sections.retinal vascular metrics in cad and cas: Regarding retinal parameters, specifically within SVC, a reduction in vascular density and perfusion was observed on the stenotic side, irrespective of the cause (CAD or CAS). In the group with CAD, ipsilateral eyes exhibited significantly reduced SVC density and perfusion compared with both contralateral eyes and control eyes (Table 3 and Figure 2 ; all P <0.017). A parallel pattern was observed in the group with CAS, where ipsilateral eyes demonstrated decreased SVC metrics relative to both contralateral and control eyes (Table S1 ; all P <0.017). Direct comparison between the 2 pathologies revealed no significant difference in the ipsilateral eyes ( P >0.017). However, in the contralateral (nonstenotic) eyes, patients with CAD showed a trend toward preserved or higher SVC density ( P =0.060) and perfusion ( P =0.053) compared with patients with CAS, although these differences did not reach the Bonferroni‐adjusted significance threshold.
sections.choroidal vascular metrics in cad and ca: In contrast to the retinal findings, choroidal vascular metrics exhibited distinct, opposing patterns between the 2 groups. Patients with CAD demonstrated a generalized hyperperfusion profile: both ipsilateral and contralateral eyes exhibited significantly higher choriocapillaris density and perfusion, as well as greater choroidal vascular volume, choroidal stromal volume, and choroidal thickness compared with control eyes (Table 3 and Figure 2 ; most P <0.017). Conversely, patients with CAS displayed a hypoperfusion profile: both eyes demonstrated significantly lower choriocapillaris metrics and reduced choroidal vascular index relative to control eyes (Figure 2 and Table S1 ; most P <0.017). Consequently, in direct subgroup comparisons (both ipsilateral and contralateral), CAD eyes consistently displayed significantly higher choroidal vascular metrics and thickness compared with CAS eyes (Table S1 ; P <0.001 for most metrics).
sections.association between retinal ischemic sig: Subgroup analysis within the cohort with CAD revealed distinct clinical associations. First, regarding laterality, the occurrence of acute retinal ischemic signs (CWS, RAO, and PAMM) was strictly confined to the ipsilateral side (0% versus 20.65% for composite signs; P <0.001; Figure 3A ), whereas chronic RIPL showed no significant lateral predilection ( P =0.357). Second, regarding stenosis severity, patients with severe stenosis or occlusion exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of CWS (7.81% versus 0%; P =0.020) and PAMM (15.62% versus 3.57%; P =0.035) compared with those with mild‐to‐moderate stenosis (Figure 3B ). Third, the presence of retinal ischemic signs was significantly associated with concurrent cerebral infarction. Specifically, the prevalence of composite acute signs (28.30% versus 10.26%; P =0.022) and PAMM alone (16.98% versus 5.13%; P =0.049) was higher in patients with cerebral infarction than in those without (Figure 3C ). Notably, the specific subtype of retinal sign correlated with the topography of cerebral infarction ( P =0.004; Figure 3D ): CWS and RAO were predominantly observed in patients with cortical infarctions, whereas PAMM was strongly clustered with subcortical infarctions.
sections.discussion: This study characterizes the distinct retinal and choroidal vascular phenotypes in CAD, differentiating them from the chronic ischemic profile of CAS. Our findings reveal that CAD is defined by a predominance of acute retinal ischemic signs, specifically PAMM and RAO, rather than the chronic vascular scarring (RIPL) typical of atherosclerotic disease. Furthermore, we identified a novel “divergent” hemodynamic pattern in CAD: ipsilateral retinal hypoperfusion coexisting with compensatory choroidal hyperperfusion, which contrasts sharply with the global vascular suppression seen in CAS. Crucially, these retinal manifestations were strictly ipsilateral and correlated topographically with cerebral infarction patterns. Collectively, these findings suggest that multimodal retinal imaging can serve as a noninvasive window into the unique pathophysiology of CAD, offering potential surrogate markers for assessing cerebral ischemic risk and hemodynamic status. CAD and CAS represent 2 distinct causes of cerebral large‐artery stenosis, each characterized by a unique temporal and pathophysiological profile. CAD typically originates from a spontaneous or trauma‐induced intimal tear, resulting in acute hemodynamic disruption and thromboembolic cascades. 14 In contrast, CAS arises from progressive atherosclerotic plaque burden, leading to chronic, insidious luminal narrowing. 15 This fundamental mechanistic divergence likely explains our observation that patients with CAD exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of acute retinal ischemic signs, specifically PAMM and RAO. PAMM, identified here as a hallmark of CAD 16 , 17 , 18 signifies acute hypoperfusion of the intermediate and deep capillary plexuses, reflecting the sudden hemodynamic compromise inherent to dissection. 19 , 20 Conversely, although patients with CAS presented with a higher raw frequency of chronic signs like RIPL, this likely reflects the older age and clustered vascular risk factors typical of atherosclerotic cohorts rather than a mechanism specific to stenosis itself. 21 , 22 A pivotal finding of this study is the divergent pattern of retino‐choroidal vascular alterations between the 2 conditions. Although both CAD and CAS eyes exhibited reduced retinal perfusion (reflecting the shared downstream effect of internal carotid artery stenosis), patients with CAD uniquely demonstrated preserved, or even hyperperfused, choroidal metrics (greater choroidal vascular volume, choroidal vascular index, and thickness) compared with both patients with CAS and controls. We postulate that this discrepancy stems from differential collateral recruitment. In the setting of acute internal carotid artery dissection, the abrupt flow reduction triggers a robust compensatory surge via the external carotid artery. The choroid, which receives significant supply from external carotid artery anastomoses (via the ophthalmic artery), benefits from this “reactive hyperemia.” 18 , 23 , 24 , 25 In contrast, CAS represents a state of chronic hemodynamic exhaustion. The prolonged, gradual course of atherosclerosis allows for vascular remodeling but often leads to generalized microvascular rarefaction and compromised compensatory reserve, resulting in the diffuse “pan‐layer” hypoperfusion (involving both retina and choroid) observed in our cohort with CAS. 9 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 Thus, the “choroidal hyperperfusion” seen in CAD may serve as a specific biomarker distinguishing acute dissection from chronic atherosclerosis. Our study further elucidates the link between specific retinal phenotypes and cerebral infarction mechanisms. PAMM was strongly associated with subcortical infarctions, suggesting a shared hemodynamic mechanism: both the deep retinal layers and the cerebral watershed zones are exquisitely sensitive to perfusion failure. 30 Conversely, CWS and RAO were spatially correlated with cortical infarctions, implicating an embolic cause where dislodged thrombi travel to distal arterioles in both the retina and cerebral cortex. These findings reinforce the utility of retinal imaging not merely as a screening tool but as a window into the pathophysiology of the stroke itself, distinguishing between hemodynamic failure and embolism. Given the high prevalence of asymptomatic retinal signs and their correlation with stenosis severity and cerebral infarction, we advocate for the integration of routine retinal evaluation into the management of CAD. Noninvasive imaging, particularly OCT/OCTA, offers a unique opportunity to stratify hemodynamic risk. The detection of signs like PAMM may alert clinicians to a higher likelihood of hemodynamic instability and watershed ischemia, potentially guiding more aggressive perfusion‐preserving strategies. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings. First, as an observational, cross‐sectional, and noninterventional study, the design does not permit inference of causal relationships. Second, although the current analysis focused on short‐term retinal alterations, the long‐term influence of carotid dissection on retinal structure, perfusion, and function remains underexplored. Also, the current study included only patients with DSA confirmation, which may introduced a selection bias. Finally, our cohort consisted exclusively of Chinese patients; thus, the generalizability of the results to other ethnic or geographic populations requires validation in future studies.
sections.conclusions_1: In conclusion, this study delineates a distinct ocular vascular phenotype in CAD, characterized by a higher prevalence of acute retinal ischemic signs—specifically PAMM—and a unique hemodynamic profile. Unlike the diffuse, pan‐layer vascular decline observed in CAS, CAD is marked by a divergent pattern: significant retinal hypoperfusion coupled with compensatory choroidal preservation. These findings underscore the fundamental pathophysiological differences between the acute, embolic nature of dissection and the chronic, progressive nature of atherosclerosis. Consequently, retinal imaging serves as a valuable noninvasive window into the cerebral hemodynamics of CAD, offering potential biomarkers for risk stratification and the early detection of cerebrovascular consequences.
