The cut-off mean level of adhesion to Fg at 5 µg/mL was 0.25615089. The confidence intervals (CI) of the relative risks (RR) were determined using the Koopman asymptotic score. The P values calculated using Fisher’s exact test. In contrast, Fn adhesion did not significantly affect survival (31.3% vs. 43.0%; P = 0.08), highlighting Fg binding as the dominant predictor of outcome (Supplementary Table 2 ). These findings suggest that high-adhesion, low-toxicity phenotypes elicit controlled inflammation that promotes bacterial clearance and improved recovery. The survival benefit of strong Fg adhesion was evident across multiple lineages, but was particularly pronounced in CC5 isolates, which exhibited low α-toxin activity (Table 1 ; Supplementary Fig. 9 ). In this lineage, high adhesion was associated with a sixfold reduction in mortality (8.7% vs. 50.0%; P = 0.002). When isolates were further stratified by α-toxin activity, the survival benefit linked to high Fg adhesion was confined to α-toxin–deficient strains ( n = 104). In this subgroup, mortality was markedly lower among patients infected with high-adhesion isolates than among those with low-adhesion isolates (16.6% vs. 38.7%; P = 0.018), corresponding to a 57% relative risk reduction. By contrast, among α-toxin–producing isolates, mortality did not differ significantly between high- and low-adhesion groups (37.3% vs. 47.9%; P = 0.289), underscoring the opposing contributions of α-toxin activity and fibrinogen-binding–mediated protection. Collectively, these findings identify strong Fg adhesion as an independent predictor of survival, particularly in infections caused by α-toxin–deficient strains. They support a virulence trade-off model in which highly adhesive, low-toxicity isolates elicit moderate inflammation conducive to immune clearance, whereas poorly adhesive and/or α-toxin–producing strains suppress host activation, favoring persistence and increased mortality.
sections.polymorphisms in a range of loci affect: To uncover the genetic basis of variation in adhesion phenotypes, we performed a k-mer-based GWAS on the genomes of 236 isolates, enabling detection of variants in both the core and accessory genome while controlling for population structure. No k-mers surpassed the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold (1.05 × 10⁻⁷) in the analysis of Fg adhesion (5 µg/mL coating concentration) (Fig. 3 ). To capture potentially relevant signals, we applied a relaxed exploratory threshold of 10⁻⁴, yielding 586 top-associated k-mers, which we annotated and investigated further (Supplementary Data 2 ). We then functionally validated candidate loci for which mutants were available in the NTML 43 . Fig. 3 K-mers associated with adhesion to Fg. Manhattan plots of k-mers linked to adhesion to Fg (at 5 µg/mL) aligned to reference genomes of ( A ) MRSA252 and B NCTC8325. Horizontal dashed lines represent the Bonferroni-corrected genome-wide significance threshold (1.05 × 10⁻⁷). Loci containing k-mers below our exploratory threshold (10⁻ 4 ) are labeled on the plot. Several top-associated k-mers for Fg binding mapped to known adhesion-related genes. Two repetitive k-mers (kmer_198 and kmer_441), present in 18.4% of isolates and with positive effect sizes, mapped to the coding regions of sdrC (SAR0566), sdrE/bbp (SAR0567), and clfA (SAR0842), the latter two encoding fibrinogen-binding proteins 17 , 44 . Functional validation confirmed reduced adhesion for clfA but not for sdrC or sdrE/bbp mutants (Supplementary Fig. 13 ; Supplementary Data 2 .). Additional k-mers associated with increased Fg binding mapped to sdrH (SAR2119), an MSCRAMM not previously implicated in Fg or Fn binding, present in 3.4% of isolates. However, the sdrH- defective mutant (NE1840) showed no phenotype in adhesion assays. Nevertheless, isolates carrying all these variants exhibited higher mean Fg binding (0.406) compared to the population average (0.255). The GWAS for adhesion to Fg revealed additional genetic variants outside known adhesion loci. A large group of k-mers ( n = 331) present in 91.9–96.6% of samples that mapped to 26 different loci and was associated with decreased binding to Fg (see tab 1 in Supplementary Data 2 ), suggesting their negative impact on adhesion. Among the k-mers in this group, the two with the lowest P -values mapped to the intergenic region upstream of spa and to the N-terminal fragment of the gene encoding SpA. Specifically, these k-mers spanned positions −8 to −61 bp within the core spa promoter region, extending from just downstream of the proximal SarA box through the −35/ − 10 σ A elements and into the coding sequence, up to +49 bp beyond the start codon, suggesting the association between spa expression and lowered adhesion. To validate the GWAS signal for the spa intergenic variant, we identified isolates negative for spa variant ( n = 16) that did not carry other Fg-associated k-mers ( n = 8) as controls and a phylogenetically related isolate from the same clonal complex carrying the spa variant. These eight genetically related isolate pairs belonged to distinct clonal complexes (CC5, CC8, CC15, CC30, and CC45). We experimentally confirmed that the levels of SpA in the cell wall were consistently higher in isolates carrying this spa intergenic variant compared to the control strains lacking this variant, across clonally diverse isolates (Fig. 5 ). Consistently, only the spa knock-out mutant (NE286), among all available transposon knockouts in loci related to this k-mer group, exhibited a significant increase in Fg binding (Supplementary Fig. 13 ). These findings validated the interpretation that the spa -mapping k-mer (conserved sequence present in >91.9% of genomes in the studied cohort) represents the causal variant negatively affecting Fg adhesion. In contrast, the remaining k-mers in the group were likely in linkage disequilibrium with it and did not contribute directly to adhesion. We also found a group of top-associated k-mers ( n = 53, with 3.42 to 9.4% frequency) associated with increased binding that mapped to ISL3 transposons annotated in the NCTC8325 reference genome (Fig. 3 ). Also related to mobile genetic elements (MGEs), we found a k-mer (kmer_210) (3.85% frequency) associated with increased binding to Fg that mapped to the locus encoding a terminase small subunit in SaPIpT1028 (SAR0382), a phage-inducible chromosomal island 45 . Of note, this same k-mer was also found to be associated with increased Fn adhesion (kmer_2206), and other k-mers in the same locus associated with reduced Fn adhesion (with opposite effect sizes, see text below). Altogether, these results point to a role of MGEs in influencing Fg and Fn binding. Outside annotated MGEs, we found groups of top-associated k-mers mapping to a few other loci, but testing the available transposon knockouts of these loci for Fg binding showed no differences compared to the wild-type strain (Supplementary Fig. 13 ; Supplementary Data 2 ). The functional screening was expanded to a group of GWAS hits identified using the D value parameter of adhesion, which validated one additional gene associated with increased adhesion to Fg, the csbB gene encoding a putative glycosyltransferase (locus SAR0757). The GWAS for adhesion to Fn (at 20 µg/mL coating concentration) also revealed genetic variants in cell wall-anchored proteins (Supplementary Data 2 , tab 4 ; Fig. 4 ). Among the top-associated k-mers (with a P value lower than 10 –4 ), we found a group of k-mers that mapped to the coding region of sdrH (SAR2119) with 3.42% frequency and associated with an increased binding to Fn—the same k-mers associated with increased binding to Fg (see above). In addition, we found a k-mer that mapped to the intergenic region upstream of sdrC (SAR0566) (in 3.42% of samples); and k-mers mapping to the intergenic region upstream of ebh (SAR1447) (in 11.1% of samples), both associated with increased Fn binding. The Ebh protein is known to specifically bind human Fn 46 whereas the SdrC has not been associated with binding to either ligand but shown to promote biofilm formation through homophilic interactions 47 . We found a common k-mer (in 38.5% of samples) associated with increased binding that mapped to the coding region of the fibronectin binding protein B ( fnbB ) (locus SA2290 in the reference strain N315). Altogether, our GWAS identified four genetic variants in the coding ( sdrH and fnbB ) or regulatory ( sdrC and ebh ) regions of cell wall-anchored proteins, including known Fn-binding proteins, all associated with increased adhesion to Fn. Indeed, the four isolates carrying all four variants (ST20120206_S1_L001, ST20101791_S1_L001, ST20101789 and ST20112208) had much higher binding values on average (0.617) than the whole population (0.329). The GWAS for adhesion to Fn at 5 µg/mL coating concentration also found top-associated k-mers in the coding region of sdrH and intergenic region upstream of ebh (Supplementary Data 2 , tab 3 ), and additionally identified k-mers in the intergenic region upstream of fnbA (15.8% frequency) and fnbB (17.5% frequency), both associated with increased binding, and in the coding region of ebh (78.2% frequency) associated with reduced binding. Fig. 4 K-mers associated with adhesion to Fn. Manhattan plots of k-mers linked to adhesion to Fn (at 20 µg/mL) aligned to reference genomes of ( A ) MRSA252 and B NCTC8325. Horizontal dashed lines represent the Bonferroni-corrected genome-wide significance threshold (1.05 × 10⁻⁷). Loci containing k-mers below our exploratory threshold (10⁻ 4 ) are labeled on the plot. Beyond known adhesion-related loci, we found a large group of k-mers ( n = 5579) present in 12 isolates (5.1% frequency) and associated with increased adhesion to Fn that mapped mostly ( n = 5417) to a putative new phage on a 5.5k kb contig in the genome assemblies of all these 12 isolates. We used BLASTn to query this contig against the NCBI core nucleotide database. This identified highly similar phage sequences in other staphylococcal species: Staphylococcus cohnii ATCC 29974 (Genbank accession LT963440.1 ), S. haemolyticus K8 ( LT963441.1 ), and S. simulans ATCC 27848 ( LT963435.1 ); and in the complete sequence of Escherichia coli Φ-X174. PHASTEST annotated intact phages of 7.8, 6, and 44.9 Kb in these three staphylococci genomes, all closely related to the E. coli Φ-X174 ( NC_001422.1 ). This putative novel phage may be integrated close to an rRNA or tRNA locus, as other k-mers of the same k-mer group mapped to these loci. Also related to MGEs, we found a group of k-mers with 13.7% to 25.2% frequency associated with reduced binding to Fn that mapped to SaPIpT1028 45 . Of note, we found different k-mers with opposite effect sizes (associated with both increased and decreased binding) in the same locus (SAR0382, terminase small subunit) of this phage-inducible chromosomal island. Outside characterised cell wall-anchored proteins and MGEs, we found a few other loci with top-associated k-mers. Testing the available transposon knockouts of these loci validated the negative association between glcA (locus SAR0190) and binding to Fn which encodes a glucose-specific PTS transporter protein (Supplemental Fig. 16 ; Supplementary Data 2 ).
sections.protein a hinders clfa-mediated adhesion: GWAS revealed an inverse correlation between the spa variant and Fg binding. To validate this finding, we analyzed eight genetically related clinical isolate pairs from distinct clonal backgrounds, differing by the presence or absence of the spa variant. Isolates harboring the variant exhibited elevated levels of cell wall–associated SpA, supporting the conclusion that variant-driven SpA overexpression inhibits ClfA–mediated Fg binding (Fig. 5 ). In line with this, spa::Tn insertion mutants and isogenic Δ spa strains of S. aureus USA300 (LAC) and Newman showed increased binding to both Fg and Fn compared to their wild-type counterparts (Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Fig. 13 ). Fig. 5 The spa variants determine SpA levels, which are inversely correlated with adhesion to Fg. A Western immunoblot analysis of SpA and peptidoglycan (PGN) in cell wall fractions of selected isolate pairs representing different clonal complexes, each comprising a strain lacking the k -mer and a strain carrying the k -mer-containing variant: CC30 (strains 1–10 and 1–7), CC45 (2–84 and 2–88), CC5 (1-15 and 1-28), CC15 (7-4 and 2-21), CC8 (7–2 and 2–69), CC7 (3–22 and 7–3), and CC5 (2–77 and 2–1). B Adhesion of wild-type and Δ spa mutants to immobilized Fg and Fn. Data are presented as mean ± SD from n = 3. Statistical significance was assessed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test. P values were as follows: Fg, 1.25 µg/mL, * P = 0.0369; Fg, 5 µg/mL, ** P = 0.0036; Fn, 10 µg/mL, ns P = 0.1012. To further explore the mechanism, we examined Fg adhesion in strains engineered for inducible expression of clfA and spa . ClfA overexpression promoted Fg binding in a dose-dependent manner, while overexpression of SpA suppressed it in both genetic backgrounds, suggesting direct interference between the two proteins (Fig. 6 ). This effect was absent in Δ spa and clfA -deficient strains under these conditions, consistent with altered culture conditions and the known stationary-phase regulation of clfA expression (Fig. 6 ; Supplementary Fig. 14 ). Fig. 6 Protein A dose-dependently hinders ClfA- mediated Fg binding. Panels show ( A ) adhesion to Fg by strain Newman variants with inducible expression of spa or clfA , B representative Western immunoblot of the ClfA, SpA, and peptidoglycan (PGN) bands and C , D normalized densitometry relative to PGN and wild type in respective cultures. Panels A and B share labeling. One-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple comparisons test was used; A for pRMC2 spa ** P = 0,002227 and for pRMC2 clfA **** P < 0.000001, ( C ) for pRMC2 clfA **** P = 0.00001 and D for pRMC2 spa * P = 0.002227. Western blotting and densitometric analyses confirmed that SpA overexpression did not affect ClfA protein levels. Initially, apparent reciprocal changes in the protein bands were attributed to reduced lysostaphin digestion efficiency in samples overexpressing either SpA or ClfA. However, normalizing signal intensity to peptidoglycan levels eliminated this artifact. These findings indicate that SpA does interfere with the ClfA abundance but likely impairs ClfA–Fg binding through steric hindrance. Supporting this model, overexpression of a sortase-deficient SpA ΔLPXTG variant, lacking the cell wall–anchoring motif, failed to inhibit Fg binding (Supplementary Fig. 15 ).
sections.csbb glycosyltransferase modulates fg ad: GWAS highlighted SAR0757, encoding a predicted Group 2 glycosyltransferase (CsbB), as a locus associated with Fg binding. Strikingly, disruption of csbB in different background strains gave opposite phenotypes (Fig. 7AC). In USA300 (LAC), the csbB::Tn mutant showed significantly reduced adhesion to immobilized Fg and Fn compared with the wild type, whereas in Newman, the same mutation enhanced Fg binding. To determine whether these contrasting phenotypes reflect altered surface display of adhesins, we quantified ClfA abundance in the cell wall by immunoblotting (Fig. 7BD). In USA300, inactivation of csbB reduced ClfA levels in the cell wall, while in Newman, the mutation increased the ClfA abundance (Fig. 7 ). Together, these findings demonstrate that CsbB modulates the cell wall localization of ClfA in a strain-dependent manner, thereby interfering with Fg adhesion. Fig. 7 CsbB glycosyltransferase modulates ClfA abundance and adhesion capacity in a strain-specific manner. Panels show adhesion to Fg of ( A ) USA300 LAC and C Newman variant strains and B , C their respective ClfA amounts in the cell wall fractions. ClfA levels were determines by Western immunoblot and normalized to peptidoglycan (PGN) and wild type. Data are mean ± SD of biological experiments ( n = 3). Statistical significance was assessed using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test; A * P = 0.0126 B ** P = 0.0074, C **** P < 0. 000092, D * P = 0.0195.
sections.glca inhibits adhesion to fn: Genome-wide association mapping identified glcA , encoding the glucose phosphotransferase system (PTS) IIC component, as a locus associated with reduced Fn binding. Specific allelic variants of glcA correlated with significantly increased adhesion to immobilized Fn (Supplementary Fig. 16 ). We compared growth and adhesion phenotypes of wild-type USA300 (LAC) or Newman and their glcA mutant strains. The wild-type LAC doubled in 18.86 ( ± 0.6) minutes, whereas the glcA mutant displayed a slightly slower doubling time of 21.06 ( ± 1.9) minutes ( P = 0.219). On the other hand, the wild-type Newman doubled in 25.05 ( ± 0.35) minutes, whereas the glcA mutant displayed a significantly quicker average doubling time of 23.25 ( ± 1.8) minutes ( P = 0.2095). Therefore, the glcA mutants showed no consistent growth defects under respiratory conditions, with neither change reaching statistical significance. These results indicate that glcA disruption does not confer a growth defect in vitro, though its metabolic role modulates the capacity for adhesion to Fn.
sections.discussion: We observed variation in S. aureus adhesion to Fg and Fn among bloodstream isolates, consistent with previous reports 48 , 49 . Although GWAS analyses have not reached genome-wide significance, likely reflecting the genetic heterogeneity and the limited size of the strain collection, the top-associated variants were found in known and relevant adhesin genes clf and fnb , supporting the validity of our approach. The functional characterization of known and novel determinants provided direct experimental validation of the associations. Among these, spa emerged as a key determinant of reduced Fg binding across SAB isolates. We confirmed that the presence of an intergenic spa variant resulted in an increase of SpA expression across clinical isolates. Moreover, SpA overexpression inhibited ClfA-mediated adhesion in a dose-dependent manner without altering ClfA-mediated surface abundance, whereas a secreted, sorting-deficient variant did not. Our results pointed to direct SpA interference with ClfA–Fg interaction resulting in inhibition of the latter. This finding complements previous evidence that SpA limits S. aureus adhesion via immunoglobulin bridging 50 . Because most invasive isolates coexpress SpA and ClfA, such antagonism is likely widespread. Furthermore, agr loss-of-function mutations, which are common in invasive lineages, further enhance SpA while suppressing other adhesins, promoting a low-adhesion, immune-evasive phenotype 51 . This aligns with our observation that weakly adherent isolates elicited less inflammation and were associated with poorer clinical outcomes. We also found that inactivation of csbB , encoding lipoteichoic acid (LTA) glycosyltransferase, produced contrasting effects in the adhesive capacity of Newman and USA300 strains. Deletion of csbB increased ClfA-mediated Fg binding in Newman but reduced adhesion in USA300, consistent with differences in cell wall teichoic acid (WTA) glycoforms. Newman predominantly produces α-O-GlcNAc–modified WTA, while USA300 synthesizes β-O-GlcNAc–modified WTA 52 , 53 . Although LTA and WTA are modified by distinct enzyme systems, they share common precursors, such as UDP–GlcNAc, and are coordinately regulated during envelope stress. CsbB initiates an LTA-specific glycosylation pathway ( csbB–gtcA–yfhO ) that influences surface charge and the spatial display of surface proteins 54 , 55 . Loss of LTA glycosylation may increase ClfA exposure in Newman, while in USA300, some glycosylation appears necessary for optimal presentation. These results reinforce that LTA and WTA modifications, though distinct, act in concert to maintain envelope homeostasis 54 . A further connection was highlighted between central metabolism and adhesion. Disruption of glcA , encoding a glucose-specific phosphotransferase system (PTS) transporter, resulted in enhanced Fn binding, indicating that metabolic flux may modulate adhesin expression. This phenotype may result from altered nutrient sensing and global transcriptional regulation. A glcA deletion has previously been shown to attenuate metabolic adaptation of S. aureus to invasive infections and consequently virulence in vivo 56 , 57 , implying a link between metabolic efficiency and virulence. Although we were unable to observe a growth defect associated with the glcA mutants, which would directly link the mutation with metabolism in vitro, their defect in adhesion to fibronectin was consistent with previously reported attenuated virulence due to glcA deletion 57 . Potential mechanisms include reduced Agr activity, known to elevate adhesin expression in metabolically stressed variants 58 , and relief of CcpA-mediated carbon catabolite repression, which derepresses fnbA/B transcription and promotes Fn binding 59 . Clinically, we found that patients’ inflammatory responses, measured by peak CRP, correlated with the adhesion capacity of the infecting S. aureus isolates. High-adhesion strains were associated with stronger inflammation and better outcomes. This aligns with the ability of adhesins such as ClfA and FnBPs to trigger cytokine release (e.g., IL-6) 2 , 27 , 29 , 60 . Although ClfA-mediated Fg binding is classically viewed as immune-evasive 33 , 61 , our observations underscore a protective role in bacteremia 30 , 33 , 61 – 64 . The ClfA–Fg interactions promote bacterial aggregation, immune shielding and facilitate host defense by promoting fibrin network formation that traps bacteria and recruits immune cells 61 , 62 , 65 . High-adhesion isolates likely induce an immunothrombotic response that walls off infection foci and enhances clearance 63 , 64 , whereas low-adhesion isolates may evade early containment and disseminate, resulting in poorer outcomes. Pre-existing adaptive immunity may further modulate this relationship. Although we did not measure anti-ClfA titers, most individuals carry antibodies against S. aureus adhesins 66 , 67 . Only antibodies that both opsonize and neutralize ClfA–fibrin(ogen) binding improve bacterial clearance in vivo 68 . Hence, pre-existing anti-ClfA antibodies may amplify early inflammation through Fcγ receptor and complement activation, but clinical benefit likely depends on functional neutralization of ClfA adhesion 68 – 70 . The protective effect of high adhesion disappeared in α-toxin-producing isolates, consistent with the growing evidence on its immunosuppressive activity 14 , 71 . α-Toxin disrupts platelet and neutrophil function, impairs cytokine release, and induces microthrombi and thrombocytopenia 4 , 5 , 72 , thereby dampening CRP responses even when bacteria remain adhesive. In contrast, ClfA–Fg engagement activates platelets and amplifies platelet - leukocyte signaling 73 , 74 , promoting effective inflammation and bacterial clearance. Consequently, in α-toxin–deficient infections, strong adhesion elicits robust inflammation and improved outcomes, whereas in α-toxin–producing infections, cytotoxicity may override these benefits. Notably, others reported that an admission CRP > 161 mg/L predicted complications in community-associated S. aureus bacteremia 75 . This points to a more nuanced relationship in which high CRP may signal overwhelming infection and/or dysregulated inflammation, whereas adhesion-associated CRP elevations, observed here, may instead indicate a coordinated, clearance-promoting host response. Limitations of our study include the modest sample size for detecting small genetic effects in the GWAS. However, our collection encompassed all major clonal complexes circulating in Europe, mitigating major geographic biases. It was based on an observational patient cohort, limiting causal inference. In vitro adhesion assays may not fully capture in vivo conditions such as shear stress or tissue microenvironments. Relying on a library of transposon mutants to prioritise GWAS hits has several limitations: lineage-specific effects of GWAS-associated variants may not be recapitulated in the JE2 NTML background strain; gain-of-function effects of variants may not be reproduced by testing transposon knockouts (which test the effect of loss-of-function mutations) or expected phenotypic changes in transposon knockouts may be masked by the contributions of other loci to the phenotype. Moreover, while we functionally validated key genetic loci using the NTML library, many of the GWAS associations remain to be explored. Together, these data reveal the genetic determinants of S. aureus adhesion capacity and a fundamental virulence trade-off in bacteremia, governed by an inverse relationship between adhesion to Fg and α-toxin activity. High-adhesion, low-toxin strains provoke protective inflammation that limits dissemination, whereas low-adhesion, high-α-toxin strains evade immune containment and drive systemic disease. This model is consistent with the regulatory dynamics of the Agr system, which favors adhesin expression during early infection and upregulates α-toxin production during dissemination 76 – 78 . Our findings suggest that profiling an isolate’s adhesive and toxigenic characteristics could enhance risk stratification in bacteremia. High-adhesion, low-α-toxin isolates may present as contained infections with strong inflammatory responses but a lower risk of sepsis, while low-adhesion, high α-toxin strains may require enhanced therapeutic vigilance, potentially including anti-α-toxin agents. Importantly, adhesion capacity did not correlate with methicillin resistance, underscoring that virulence potential is largely independent of antibiotic resistance. Developing rapid diagnostic tools, such as targeted proteomics 79 , to assess expression of virulence markers like spa , clfA , and hla could support timely, phenotype-guided therapeutic decisions.
sections.ethics statement: This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. A combined dataset of 236 S. aureus bloodstream isolates collected in Poland ( n = 185) and additional isolates ( n = 51) from the French multicenter VIRSTA cohort 80 were used for all primary analyses in this study. Collection of Polish clinical isolates and metadata was approved by the Medical University of Warsaw Bioethics Committee (KB/97/2020) and the Bioethics Committee of the Regional Medical Chamber in Kraków (144/KBL/OIL/2020). The French VIRSTA cohort was approved by the Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile-de-France IV (#2010/05NICB). Both cohorts applied shared inclusion criteria for adult S. aureus bacteremia with matched clinical metadata. The French isolates, representing the same dominant clonal complexes (CC5, CC30, CC45), enriched lineage diversity without introducing new genetic backgrounds, and contained harmonized patient-level data, justifying integration for combined genomic–phenotypic analyses.
sections.sample and metadata collection: Blood cultures were processed using the Bactec FX system (Becton-Dickinson) for up to seven days, and isolates were identified by MALDI Biotyper (Bruker Daltonics). Methicillin resistance was determined according to EUCAST guidelines using a 30 µg cefoxitin disk (MSSA ≥ 22 mm). Infections were classified as healthcare-associated (HA; admission with healthcare exposure in the preceding 30 days or if >48 h after admission or within 30 days of discharge), or community-acquired (CA; onset ≤ 48 h without recent healthcare contact). Clinical variables, including demographics, infection source, acute-phase biomarkers, complications (endocarditis, metastatic abscesses), and outcomes (in-hospital, 30- and 90-day mortality) were recorded in REDCap (University of Warsaw).
sections.genomic sequencing and comparative conte: Genomic DNA was extracted from S. aureus isolates by lysostaphin digestion followed by purification with Norgen Biotek kits. For individual samples, the Genomic DNA Isolation Kit (spin column format; cat. no. 24700) was used, and for high-throughput processing, the Bacterial Genomic DNA Isolation 96-Well Kit (cat. no. 17950). Whole-genome sequencing was performed by Eurofins Genomics Germany on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using paired-end reads (2 × 150 bp). Sequencing libraries were prepared following the manufacturer’s standard protocol. Resulting assemblies were deposited in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) under BioProject PRJEB55240, with isolate-level accessions and whole collection metadata provided in Supplementary Data. Genomes of 51 French isolates from the VIRSTA collection 80 , 81 were retrieved from ENA BioProjects PRJEB48298 and PRJEB49354 and processed identically. For comparative and evolutionary contextual analyses, additional 308 S. aureus genomes from a previously described European collection 77 were included.
sections.bacterial strains, mutants, and plasmids: S. aureus strains were cultured at 37 °C on tryptic soy agar (TSA) or in tryptic soy broth (TSB) with aeration. A complete list of strains used in functional assays is provided in Supplementary Table 1 . Growth kinetics were monitored in microtiter plates over 24 h, and doubling times were calculated by fitting an exponential growth model to absorbance values obtained during the early logarithmic phase (relative absorbance <0.1). Each experiment was performed in three independent biological replicates, each measured in technical triplicate. Experimental uncertainty was expressed as the standard deviation of the corresponding technical replicates. The NTML mutant library, including strain NR-49947, was obtained from BEI Resources (NIAID, NIH) 43 . Targeted gene deletions were generated using the allelic replacement vector pIMAY 82 . All mutants were verified by PCR and evaluated in the corresponding phenotypic assays. Selected NTML alleles were transduced into erythromycin-sensitive S. aureus USA300 LAC and Newman using phage ϕ11 to validate genotype–phenotype associations. For inducible expression studies, spa variants lacking the sortase A recognition motif (LPXTG) were amplified from USA300 and cloned into pRMC2 under an anhydrotetracycline (aTc)–inducible promoter. Resulting plasmids were electroporated into S. aureus Newman and USA300 (LAC) Δ spa mutants.
sections.western immunoblotting: Expression of cell wall (CW) proteins in wild-type and mutant S. aureus strains was assessed following growth in tryptic soy broth (TSB) for 18 h at 37 °C. For analyses involving CW protein variants or strains harboring the inducible expression plasmid pRMC2, overnight cultures were diluted to an initial OD₆₀₀ of approximately 0.1, grown to OD₆₀₀ ≈ 0.7, and induced with 0, 0.2, or 1 µg/mL anhydrotetracycline (aTc) for 5 h. Under either growth condition, cells were harvested by centrifugation (4000 × g , 10 min), washed in 100 mM PBS containing 5 mM EDTA and 1 mM PMSF, adjusted to OD₆₀₀ = 10, and treated with lysostaphin (60 µg/mL) in 30% raffinose buffer for 30 min at 37 °C to solubilize the cell wall fraction. Cell wall extracts were resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes (0.45 µm; Pierce™) using a wet transfer system (Bio-Rad; 100 V, 1 h). Equal protein loading was verified by Ponceau S staining. Membranes were blocked for 1 h at 37 °C in PBST (Th. Geyer 8418-100PCE; pH 7.4, 0.05% Tween-20) supplemented with 10% (w/v) skimmed milk, and then incubated with primary antibodies diluted in PBST containing 5% milk. The following antibodies were used: rabbit anti-SpA (Sigma-Aldrich, cat. no. P3775-1VL), rabbit anti-ClfA (Invitrogen, cat. no. PA5-144428), and mouse anti-PGN (Bio-Rad, cat. no. 7263-1006), the latter serving as a loading control. Incubations were performed either overnight at 4 °C or for 1–2 h at room temperature with shaking. Following three 15-min washes in PBST, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit Fab, Invitrogen, cat. no. A24531; or Thermo Fisher Scientific, cat. no. 31431), washed as above, and developed with Clarity™ Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad). Chemiluminescence was detected using a ChemiDoc™ Imaging System (Bio-Rad). The Bio-Rad anti-PGN antibody recognizes a discontinuous glycan and/or peptide epitope and yielded multiple distinct bands when applied to cell wall fractions. The most prominent band, observed at approximately 40 kDa, was used as an internal reference to verify loading consistency, and its signal intensity was used to normalize the intensities of the ClfA and SpA bands in each sample.
sections.hemolytic assays: α-Toxin (Hla, encoded by hla ) activity was assessed by measuring the hemolytic activity of S. aureus isolates on rabbit blood-containing agar plates. Human blood lysis was also investigated. Isolates were grown in tryptic soy broth (TSB) for 18–20 h (stationary phase), washed, resuspended in PBS, and normalised to an OD₆₀₀ ≈ 5.0. Supernatants were obtained by centrifugation (6000 × g , 10 min), and filtration through 0.2 µm membranes. Fifteen microlitres of each supernatant was spotted onto sterile filter paper discs placed on TSA plates containing 5% rabbit blood (TCS Biosciences, UK) and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Hemolysis zones were imaged with a ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad), and radii were measured in Fiji 84 . Isolates with no detectable hemolysis were classified as non-hemolytic. The Regional Blood Donation Center in Warsaw approved the use of human blood from healthy donors.
sections.genome sequencing and assembly: Genomic DNA was extracted following lysostaphin digestion using a bacterial genomic DNA isolation kit (Norgen Biotek Corp.). Libraries were prepared for Illumina sequencing, and reads were either assembled de novo or mapped to a reference genome as appropriate. Quality control thresholds required sequencing depth >300× and assembly N50 > 40 kb for all genomes. Genome identifiers and metadata are listed in Supplemental Data File 1 . For context, a previously published European collection of 308 invasive S. aureus genomes (Aanensen et al. 42 ) was included. Illumina paired-end reads were assembled using a custom pipeline combining SPAdes v3.15.3 (de novo assembly), the improve_assembly pipeline (refinement), and QUAST v4.6.0 (quality assessment; https://github.com/francesccoll/assembly_pipeline ). Annotation was performed with Bakta v1.5.1 and the Bakta database v4.0 (release date: 2022-08-29; DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.7025248). Multi-locus sequence types (STs) were assigned by extracting the seven housekeeping genes of the S. aureus MLST scheme via BLAST ( https://github.com/sanger-pathogens/mlst_check ) and comparing against the PubMLST database ( www.pubmlst.org ). Clonal complexes (CCs) were inferred by allowing up to two allelic mismatches from the reference ST profile. For comparative genomics, Illumina reads were mapped to the S. aureus MRSA252 reference genome (CC30, GenBank BX571856 ) using Snippy v4.6.0 ( https://github.com/tseemann/snippy ). Consensus sequences were generated by incorporating substitutions and resolving missing calls with a custom script (create_snippy_consensus.py; https://github.com/francesccoll/scripts/ ). Whole-genome alignments were constructed by concatenating consensus sequences, with core-genome alignments retaining only reference regions conserved across isolates. Pairwise core-genome SNP distances were calculated using pairsnp v0.0.1 ( https://github.com/gtonkinhill/pairsnp ). We used an independent collection of 800 genetically and geographically diverse S. aureus strains isolated from various host species 84 to derive the species core genome using Roary with default settings, as previously defined 85 , which consists of 1,766 genes and covers 1.76 Mb (62%) of the reference genome. Maximum likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE v1.6.10, using Model Finder for model selection (best-fitted model TVM + F + R4 chosen according to Bayesian information criterion) and ultrafast bootstrapping for branch support. The type and frameshift mutations in the agr operon were determined from genome assemblies with AgrVATE v1.0.1 with default settings 86 , 87 .
sections.gwas: K-mer-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) were performed to identify genetic variants linked to adhesion phenotypes and other traits. Adhesion phenotypes—including binding to Fg and Fn under multiple conditions (three parameters per ligand)—were quantified experimentally for each isolate and used as quantitative traits in GWAS. We used the raw absorbance measurements of Fg and Fn adhesion to the ligand concentrations that gave the most discriminatory measurement as the outcome variable quantitative and continuous trait, that is, the one that provided the widest range of values and best normal distribution. K-mers (30–100 bp) were generated from polished assemblies using fsm-lite v1.0 ( https://github.com/nvalimak/fsm-lite ). Association testing was carried out with Pyseer v1.3.3, applying a linear mixed model that incorporated both k-mer presence/absence and a similarity matrix derived from core-genome SNP distances. The continuous flag was used for quantitative trait modeling. Population structure was corrected using a kinship matrix, and significance thresholds were set by Bonferroni correction ( P < 0.05/number of unique k-mers; computed via count_patterns.py). As no or very few k-mers achieved a p value below the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold, we applied an arbitrary threshold of 10 –4 to filter, annotate and investigate the top-associated k-mers. The top 1% of associated k-mers were visualised in Manhattan plots. Significant k-mers were mapped to annotated genes or intergenic regions with script annotate_hits_pyseer.py in a sequential manner using a set of 27 reference genomes (See Supplementary Data 2 ) followed by the genome assemblies k-mers were derived from. Mapped k-mers were then annotated and aggregated at the gene level using annotate_kmers_pyseer.py and summarise_kmers_pyseer.py, respectively. In Manhattan plots we plotted k-mers that mapped to MRSA252 and NCTC8325 reference genomes as we noted most k-mers mapped to either of these genomes. To resolve specific variants (SNPs or small indels), k-mer sequences were converted to FASTQ, aligned to reference genomes using bwa mem v0.7.17, and variants called with bcftools mpileup v1.16, parsed via a custom script (link_kmers_to_variants.py). Functional annotations and orthologue mapping were supported by AureoWiki ( https://aureowiki.med.uni-greifswald.de/ ). To interpret top-associated k-mers and delineate individual causal variants, k-mers were grouped if carried by a high overlapping set of samples ( > 80%). For any pair of k-mers, the proportion of samples that carried both k-mers was calculated to create a k-mer similarity matrix. Next, k-mers were clustered using the function groupSimilarityMatrix of the R package MsFeatures , using the k-mer similarity matrix as input and an 80% threshold. This analysis effectively allowed us to delineate groups of redundant k-mers in linkage disequilibrium mapping to multiple loci with the same or very close frequency and effect sizes. K-mer groups are expected to represent the putative causal variant and other genetic variants in linkage disequilibrium with the former that probably do not contribute to the phenotype.
sections.statistics and reproducibility: All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 11 and R (v 4.3.2). Data are presented as mean ± SD. Adhesion measurements were compared between groups (e.g., CA vs. HA, MRSA vs. MSSA) using unpaired two-tailed t tests or ANOVA for normally distributed data, and Pearson’s correlation for normally distributed clinical variables (e.g., CRP). Fisher’s exact test assessed categorical outcomes (e.g., in-hospital mortality by adhesion level and hemolysis phenotype). Relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals was calculated via the Koopman asymptotic score method. Statistical significance was set at two-tailed P < 0.05. We tested if the presence of frameshift mutations in the agr operon were associated with differences in toxicity and adhesion phenotypes using a Wilcoxon rank sum test.

title: Negative-pressure wound therapy versus conventional dressings following stoma reversal: a GRADE-based systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials with predefined subgroup analyses by closure technique
abstract: Background Surgical site infection (SSI) after stoma reversal remains common (15–40%), prolonging hospitalization and potentially delaying adjuvant therapy. Prophylactic negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) is increasingly used for closed incisions; however, its efficacy with different skin-closure techniques remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing NPWT with conventional non-pressure dressings after stoma reversal, with prespecified subgroup analyses by skin-closure technique and certainty of evidence appraised using GRADE. Methods The review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251182767). We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP without language restrictions. Eligible randomized controlled trials enrolled adults undergoing elective ileostomy or colostomy reversal and compared negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) with conventional (non-pressure) dressings with a specified skin-closure technique (purse-string or primary). The primary outcome was incisional surgical site infection within 30–42 days of surgery. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, time to complete wound healing, operative duration, and estimated blood loss. Two reviewers independently screened the studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using RoB 2. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted with sensitivity analyses and pre-specified subgroup comparisons based on closure techniques. The certainty of evidence was appraised using GRADE. Results Seven randomized trials ( n = 429) met the inclusion criteria (NPWT, n = 220; conventional dressings, n = 209). The primary pooled analysis showed no significant reduction in incisional SSI with NPWT versus conventional dressings (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.14–1.30; I²=46%). By closure technique, the effects were larger with primary closure (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06–0.67; I²=0%) than with purse-string closure (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.14–3.35; I²=48%), although the interaction was not statistically significant ( P = 0.23). The risk of bias was generally rated as “some concerns,” primarily due to open-label care, and heterogeneity was low after the sensitivity analysis. Prespecified leave-one-out analyses identified influential studies for SSI, length of stay, and wound healing; however, these findings were interpreted as exploratory influence diagnostics and did not replace the primary pooled analyses. Conclusions In this primary pooled analysis, prophylactic NPWT did not significantly reduce incisional surgical site infection after stoma reversal, although the effect favored NPWT. Exploratory sensitivity and subgroup analyses suggested possible benefits in selected contexts, although these findings should not supersede the nonsignificant primary pooled analyses. Larger, standardized randomized trials are needed to clarify which closure techniques and patient groups derive the greatest benefit. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12893-026-03957-2.

sections.introduction: Stoma reversal, although technically less complex than index colorectal surgery, carries substantial postoperative morbidity, with surgical site infection (SSI) rates of 15–40% in contemporary series [ 1 – 3 ]. Surgical site infections (SSIs) are defined as infections occurring up to 30 days after surgery (or up to one year after surgery in patients receiving implants) that affect either the incision or deep tissue at the surgical site [ 1 ]. Restoration of intestinal continuity predisposes the wound to bacterial contamination, subcutaneous dead space, and impaired perfusion [ 4 – 6 ]. These complications lead to longer hospitalizations, delayed adjuvant therapy, and reduced quality of life [ 5 – 7 ]. Despite refinements in techniques and perioperative care, SSI rates often exceed 30% even in specialized centers [ 7 – 12 ]. The persistently high burden underscores the need for effective and evidence-based prophylaxis [ 13 ]. Negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) is increasingly used as prophylaxis for closed surgical incisions, acting through wound-edge approximation, interstitial fluid evacuation, improved tissue perfusion, and a sealed microenvironment that limits bacterial contamination [ 1 – 3 , 14 , 15 ]. This rationale is particularly salient after stoma reversal, where bacterial burden, tissue edema, and seroma predispose patients to infection [ 6 – 8 , 16 ]. Randomized controlled trials have reported mixed findings, with several showing directionally lower SSI reductions [ 6 , 7 , 9 – 11 ] and others reporting marginal or no benefit [ 8 , 12 , 17 ]. Contemporary meta-analyses have been limited by methodological heterogeneity, protocol variability, and non-standardized outcomes [ 1 – 3 , 14 – 16 ]. These factors and possible effect modification by clinical context underscore the need for rigorous pre-specified subgroup analyses [ 16 , 18 ]. Existing evidence on NPWT after stoma reversal remains difficult to interpret because prior syntheses included heterogeneous study designs, variable NPWT protocols, inconsistent SSI definitions, and limited stratification by skin-closure technique [ 1 – 3 , 14 – 18 ]. Because purse-string and primary closure may have different baseline SSI risks and wound-healing profiles, closure-technique–specific analysis is clinically relevant [ 7 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 19 ]. This systematic review synthesized randomized controlled trial evidence comparing NPWT with conventional dressings after stoma reversal, with prespecified subgroup analyses by skin-closure technique and GRADE assessment of evidence certainty [ 1 – 18 ].
sections.study design: We conducted a protocol-driven, PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing prophylactic negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) with conventional non-pressure dressings after elective stoma reversal. The review protocol, including the statistical analysis plan, was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251182767) before study selection and data extraction. The prespecified protocol included the eligibility criteria, primary and secondary outcomes, subgroup analysis according to skin closure technique, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses.
sections.literature search strategy: A comprehensive search was performed from database inception to November 1, 2025, with no language or date restrictions. We queried MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and WHO ICTRP. Google Scholar supports forward/backward citation chasing (first 200 results screened). Search strings combined controlled vocabulary and keywords for the intervention (e.g., “negative-pressure wound therapy,” “NPWT,” “vacuum-assisted”) and context (e.g., “stoma closure,” “stoma reversal,” “ileostomy,” “colostomy,” “purse-string,” “ primary closure” ) , using RCT filters where available and manual screening otherwise. The full search strings and hit counts are shown in Supplementary Table 1, which also records the number of results returned by each database. We also hand-searched the reference lists of eligible studies and pertinent reviews to identify additional trials.
sections.inclusion criteria: We included RCTs enrolling adults undergoing elective stoma reversal (ileostomy or colostomy), in which the intervention was NPWT applied to the skin incision after reversal, and the comparator was a conventional (non-pressure) dressing. Trials had to (i) report at least one early wound-related outcome, including incisional surgical site infection (SSI) assessed at 30 days or the closest available trial-defined follow-up within 30–42 days, or complete epithelialization/healing at a prespecified time point; (ii) specify the skin-closure technique (purse-string or primary); and (iii) provide sufficient arm-level data to compute the effect estimates. Only randomized parallel-group studies were eligible; multi-arm trials were included if at least one arm met the NPWT definition and at least one arm used a conventional nonabsorbent dressing.
sections.exclusion criteria: We excluded non-randomized studies, including cohort, case–control, before-and-after, single-arm series, and conference abstracts without extractable outcomes. We also excluded pediatric populations, emergency stoma closures, procedures involving concomitant laparotomy or other major operations that materially altered postoperative wound care, and studies in which the comparator involved any form of pressure- or suction-assisted system. Studies exclusively evaluating suture or skin closure techniques without a direct NPWT versus conventional non-pressure dressing comparison were excluded from the study. Studies were also excluded if they lacked sufficient outcome data after unsuccessful attempts to contact the corresponding authors of the studies. At the trial level, the included RCTs commonly excluded patients with active infection or dermatologic disease at the incision site and clinical factors that are likely to impair wound healing or adherence to the wound-care protocol, such as uncontrolled diabetes or immunosuppression.
sections.data extraction and outcome measures: Two reviewers (W.M. and A.M.H.) independently screened the titles/abstracts and full texts, extracted data using a piloted form, and cross-checked the data entries. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer (M.B.M.D.). The extracted items included trial identifiers (year, country, and setting), sample sizes, demographics (age, sex, and BMI), stoma type and indication, skin-closure technique (purse-string vs. primary closure), perioperative antibiotics, NPWT device/type, pressure setting, application details and duration, and comparator dressing protocols. For the primary outcome, incisional SSI was extracted preferentially after 30 days. When the 30-day SSI was not reported, the closest available SSI assessment within 30–42 days was used for the analysis. This window was selected because the included randomized trials assessed early SSI and wound outcomes at slightly different postoperative intervals, most commonly at 30 or 42 days. Restricting the analysis to a 30-day window would have excluded otherwise eligible randomized trials and reduced the available evidence. Composite wound outcomes were not used as SSI events unless the incisional SSI component was separately extractable or clearly included according to the trial definition. Where available, superficial and deep incisional SSIs were analyzed together as overall incisional SSI outcomes. The definitions and assessment methods for SSI used in the included studies are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. When a study reported both composite wound management complications and SSI, the SSI-specific data were prioritized for the primary analysis. Additional outcomes, when available, included complete wound healing/epithelialization by a fixed time point, time to wound healing, wound management complications, length of stay, operative duration, and estimated blood loss (EBL).
sections.quality assessment: The risk of bias was evaluated independently by W.M. and A.M.H. using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for randomized trials (randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results). Domain-level judgments informed the overall RoB ratings for each outcome measure. Disagreements were resolved through discussions with M.B.M.D. Documentation of judgments and justifications was maintained to ensure transparency and to conduct subsequent sensitivity analyses.
sections.statistical analysis: All meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4. Random-effects models were used for all pooled analyses. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using the Mantel–Haenszel method to calculate the RR. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were pooled using the inverse variance method when the outcomes were reported on the same scale. When studies reported medians with measures of dispersion, values were converted to means and standard deviations using established methods described by Wan et al. [ 20 ] Luo et al. [ 21 ]. When only ranges were available, the method described by Hozo et al. was used. Zero-event cells were handled using a continuity correction of 0.5. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Prespecified analyses included subgroup analysis by skin-closure technique and a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis to assess the influence of the individual studies. Publication bias was not formally assessed because fewer than 10 studies were available for each outcome.
sections.sensitivity analysis, subgroup analysis,: We prespecified a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis only, sequentially omitting each TRIAL to assess robustness and single-study influence. The primary subgroup analysis stratified the trials by skin closure technique (purse-string vs. primary) to explore the clinical heterogeneity attributable to the closure method. Between-subgroup differences were examined using Cochran’s Q-test for subgroup differences. The certainty of evidence for each critical outcome was assessed using GRADE across the domains of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias, with summary judgments (high, moderate, low, and very low) and rationale provided in the Summary of Findings table.
sections.results_1: The database search identified 1,773 records, which were reduced to 1,011 unique records after the removal of 762 duplicates (Fig. 1 ). Title/abstract screening excluded 958 citations, leaving 53 reports for full-text review, all of which were retrieved. Of these, 46 were excluded, most commonly for non-randomized design ( n = 27), followed by wrong intervention/comparator or no stoma reversal ( n = 12), and insufficient data/duplicate populations ( n = 7). Ultimately, seven randomized controlled trials met all the criteria and were included in the qualitative and quantitative syntheses (Fig. 1 ). sections.characteristics of included studies: Seven randomized trials of elective stoma reversal enrolled broadly comparable adult populations, with five using purse-string closure and two using primary closure, consistent with our pre-specified subgroups (Table 1 ). Eligibility frameworks were broadly similar across trials, although individual studies varied in their trial-level exclusions, including emergency closures or concomitant laparotomies, active dermatologic conditions at the incision site, and factors that could impair wound healing or adherence, such as uncontrolled diabetes or immunosuppression. The primary endpoints were early wound outcomes, including incisional SSI or complete epithelialization within 30–42 days. The secondary measures included healing quality, resource use, and complications. sections.methodological quality and study integri: The methodological quality of the seven randomized trials was generally acceptable but not unequivocally low-risk. The randomization processes were clearly described and judged to be at low risk in three studies (Carrano 2021, Tiang 2024, Wierdak 2020), while the remaining trials provided insufficient detail on sequence generation and/or allocation concealment, yielding some concerns in D1. Because incisional NPWT cannot be blinded and peri-incisional care was delivered in open-label settings, every study had some concerns for D2 (deviations from intended interventions), despite protocolized dressing schedules. Missing outcome data were minimal and balanced, leading to a low risk of D3 in all trials. Outcomes (SSI within ~ 30–42 days and time/healing) were defined a priori, clinically objective, and assessed using standard criteria, indicating a low risk for D4. Selective reporting (D5) was low risk in six studies; Kojima 2021 had some concerns due to multi-arm reporting with limited outcome details. Consequently, the overall risk of bias was rated as “some concerns” for each study, driven primarily by unavoidable open-label care and incomplete descriptions of randomization, whereas other domains were consistently robust, supporting confidence in the direction and stability of the pooled effects (Fig. 2 ). This suggests a trend toward fewer SSIs with NPWT; however, the difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.13). Overall, Fig. 3 indicates no definitive difference, although heterogeneity was moderate. sections.length of postoperative hospital stay (d: The pooled MD is − 0.33 days (95% CI − 1.30 to 0.64) with I²=61%. The direction favors NPWT (shorter stay), but the effect is not statistically significant ( p = 0.51). Figure 4 shows moderate to substantial heterogeneity across the trials. Fig. 4 Forest plot of length of hospital stay (days) for NPWT vs. nonpressure dressings (random-effects MD)
sections.operative time (minutes): The pooled MD was 1.98 min (95% CI − 2.89 to 6.85) with I²=0%. There was no significant difference in operative time between the groups ( p = 0.42), and the results were consistent. Figure 5 indicates neutrality with minimal heterogeneity in the funnel plot. Fig. 5 Forest plot of operative time for NPWT vs. non-pressure dressings (random-effects MD)
sections.estimated blood loss (ml): The pooled MD is − 3.78 mL (95% CI − 6.26 to − 1.31) with I²=27%. NPWT was associated with a statistically significant reduction in blood loss ( p = 0.003) and low heterogeneity. Figure 6 supports the small but consistent perioperative benefit of NPWT. Fig. 6 Forest plot of estimated blood loss for NPWT versus non-pressure dressing (random-effects MD)
sections.time to complete wound healing (days): The pooled MD was 0.88 days (95% CI − 3.02 to 4.78) with I²=45%. This was not statistically significant ( p = 0.66), and the direction was equivocal with moderate heterogeneity. Figure 7 shows no clear difference in the healing speed. Fig. 7 Forest plot of time to complete wound healing for NPWT versus non-pressure dressings (random-effects MD)
sections.postoperative patient-reported wound cos: Pooled across three RCTs, the random-effects mean difference in patient-reported wound cosmesis was 0.69 (95% CI − 1.23 to 2.62, p = 0.48), showing no statistically significant difference between NPWT and non-pressure dressings (Supplementary Fig. 1).
sections.sensitivity analysis: Leave-one-out analyses were performed as prespecified influence diagnostics to evaluate whether any single trial disproportionately affected the pooled estimates. Uchino 2016 was not excluded from the primary analysis; instead, it was sequentially omitted within a leave-one-out framework. This trial was the most influential study for the SSI estimate because it reported a directionally unfavorable SSI pattern for NPWT, with incisional SSI/wound infection occurring in 3/28 patients in the NPWT group versus 1/31 patients in the control group. After excluding Uchino 2016, heterogeneity decreased, and the pooled estimate became statistically significant in favor of NPWT (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.11–0.89; I²=30%; p = 0.03). However, this result was interpreted strictly as a sensitivity-derived, hypothesis-generating finding and not as a replacement for primary pooled estimates. A strict 30-day-only SSI sensitivity analysis was also performed. Most trials reported SSI or wound infection within approximately 30 days, whereas Tiang 2024 assessed SSI during a 42-day follow-up period and reported no SSI events in either group. Because this was a double-zero study for SSI, its exclusion for a strict 30-day-only sensitivity check did not materially change the direction or interpretation of the pooled SSI effects. Therefore, the primary SSI analysis was retained as SSI within 30–42 days, with timing variation acknowledged as a limitation. For length of stay, exclusion of Carrano 2021 eliminated heterogeneity and showed a statistically significant reduction with NPWT (MD − 0.85 days, 95% CI − 1.51 to − 0.19; I²=0%; p = 0.01). For the time to complete wound healing, the exclusion of Xu 2024 resolved heterogeneity and showed faster healing with NPWT (MD − 2.80 days, 95% CI − 4.75 to − 0.85; I²=0%; p = 0.005). These secondary sensitivity findings were also interpreted as influencing diagnostics rather than definitive pooled effects (Table 3 ). sections.subgroup analysis: The subgroup analysis by skin-closure technique suggested that the protective effect of NPWT against incisional SSI was concentrated in trials using primary closure (LPC), where the pooled risk ratio was 0.20 (95% CI 0.06–0.67) with I²=0%, indicating a statistically significant and consistent reduction in SSI. In contrast, among purse-string closure (PSC) trials, the pooled effect was 0.68 (0.14–3.35) with I²=48%, showing no clear benefit and moderate heterogeneity. The test for subgroup differences did not reach statistical significance (χ²=1.44, df = 1, P = 0.23; I²=30.4%); therefore, while LPC showed a stronger signal, a formal interaction could not be claimed. The overall pooled estimate across both subgroups was 0.42 (0.14–1.30) under a random-effects model, consistent with the main analysis and highlighting the technique-dependent variability in effect (Fig. 8 ). Fig. 8 Subgroup meta-analysis of incisional surgical site infection (≤ 30–42 days) comparing NPWT versus conventional dressings stratified according to skin closure technique. Purse-string and primary closure studies were analyzed separately using random-effects models. Squares represent study-specific estimates weighted by inverse variance, and diamonds represent the pooled effects
sections.grade-certainty of evidence: For the primary outcome of incisional SSI, certainty was based on the primary pooled analysis, which showed a directionally lower SSI risk with NPWT but did not reach statistical significance. The certainty was downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision because most trials had RoB 2 “some concerns” and the confidence interval crossed the null. Sensitivity analyses showed stronger effects after excluding influential studies; however, these sensitivity-derived estimates were not used as the basis for the GRADE certainty judgments. For secondary outcomes, the primary pooled analyses showed no statistically significant difference in length of stay, operative time, time to complete wound healing, or patient-reported wound cosmesis, while estimated blood loss was statistically lower with NPWT but of small clinical magnitude and sensitive to study exclusion. Overall, certainty was limited mainly by study-level risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency for selected outcomes (Table 4 ). Imprecision downgrading was primarily driven by wide confidence intervals crossing the null and limited event numbers. Inconsistency downgrades were applied when statistical heterogeneity was substantial or when the effect estimates varied meaningfully across studies. sections.risk of bias: Downgraded one level because most trials were rated as having RoB 2 “some concerns,” mainly due to open-label care and incomplete reporting of randomization/allocation procedures.
sections.inconsistency: Downgraded for length of stay because of substantial heterogeneity in the primary pooled analysis (I²=61%). Other outcomes were not downgraded for inconsistency because the heterogeneity was low to moderate and did not preclude interpretation.
sections.indirectness: Not downgraded because the included populations, interventions, comparators, and outcome definitions matched the review PICO.
sections.imprecision: Downgraded when confidence intervals crossed the null or included both clinically meaningful benefits and no effect/harm. The estimated blood loss was downgraded because the absolute difference was clinically trivial and sensitive to study removal.
sections.publication bias: Formal testing was not performed because fewer than 10 studies were available for each outcome; therefore, publication bias was judged as undetected but could not be excluded.
sections.discussion: This GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of seven randomized controlled trials found that prophylactic negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) was associated with a directionally lower risk of incisional surgical site infection (SSI) after stoma reversal, but the primary pooled estimate did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.14–1.30; I²=46%) [ 1 – 3 ]. Primary analyses of length of stay, operative time, time to complete wound healing, and patient-reported wound cosmesis also did not show statistically significant differences, while estimated blood loss was statistically lower with NPWT but of small absolute magnitude [ 1 – 3 , 14 – 16 ]. Exploratory leave-one-out analyses demonstrated the sensitivity of pooled estimates to individual studies; however, these analyses were intended as influence diagnostics rather than confirmatory evidence. These findings suggest uncertainty around the pooled estimates and should not be interpreted as replacing the primary analysis. The absolute effect estimates from the primary pooled analysis corresponded to approximately 88 fewer SSI events per 1,000 patients, although the confidence interval ranged from 131 fewer to 45 more events per 1,000 patients. In the leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, the estimated NNT was approximately 10; however, this was derived after excluding Uchino 2016 and should, therefore, be interpreted as exploratory rather than definitive [ 1 – 3 , 16 , 18 , 22 , 23 ]. The potential clinical relevance should be considered in the context of SSI-related morbidity, delays in adjuvant therapy, and costs [ 1 – 3 , 18 , 22 – 26 ]. Future studies should clarify whether the benefits differ according to closure technique, wound characteristics, baseline SSI risk, and perioperative care protocols [ 7 – 12 , 16 , 19 , 22 , 23 , 27 – 29 ]. Subgroup analyses by closure type showed primary closure RR 0.20 (95% CI 0.06–0.67; I²=0%) versus purse-string RR 0.68 (95% CI 0.14–3.35; I²=48%) [ 1 – 3 , 6 – 8 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 22 , 23 ]. Although the magnitude of the effect appeared greater in the primary closure cohorts, the interaction test was not statistically significant; therefore, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory rather than confirmatory [ 7 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 19 ]. Residual heterogeneity may reflect device/pressure settings, duration, baseline SSI risk, antibiotic protocols, and outcome windows [ 1 – 3 , 6 – 8 , 10 , 11 , 16 , 22 , 23 ]. Clinical heterogeneity may have influenced the pooled estimates, including variation in NPWT systems, pressure settings, wear duration, antibiotic protocols, and SSI assessment windows. Compared with previous meta-analyses, the present review differs in that it restricted inclusion to randomized controlled trials, incorporated prespecified subgroup analyses according to closure technique, applied formal GRADE certainty assessment, and emphasized sensitivity analyses as influence diagnostics rather than confirmatory evidence. These methodological refinements were intended to improve interpretability and reduce the bias introduced by observational data. The methodological strengths included exclusive RCT inclusion, prespecified outcomes focused on early SSI and healing, random-effects modeling, prespecified subgroup analysis by closure technique, leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, RoB 2 assessment, and formal GRADE certainty appraisal. GRADE certainty was low for SSI, operative time, estimated blood loss, and wound-healing outcomes, and very low for length of stay, primarily because of study-level risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency [ 14 – 16 , 18 , 24 – 26 ]. Sensitivity analyses identified influential studies, particularly Uchino 2016 for SSI, reinforcing that sensitivity-derived findings should be interpreted cautiously rather than as replacements for the primary pooled analyses [ 10 , 14 – 16 ]. Removal of individual studies also reduced heterogeneity for length of stay and wound healing [ 6 , 12 , 17 , 27 , 28 ]. The effects of estimated blood loss were directionally unstable and clinically negligible (< 5 mL), reinforcing their low certainty and limited clinical value [ 2 , 14 – 16 ]. Several limitations should be acknowledged, including the modest sample size, device heterogeneity, variability in perioperative protocols, and unavoidable lack of blinding. These factors may have contributed to the imprecision and clinical heterogeneity across the pooled estimates. Variations in the SSI follow-up windows, including assessments at both 30 and 42 days, may also have contributed to modest clinical heterogeneity. As fewer than 10 studies were available for each outcome, formal publication bias testing was not feasible. Therefore, small-study effects and publication bias cannot be excluded. Taken together, these findings do not establish a definitive clinical benefit but suggest that NPWT may warrant further evaluation in selected higher-risk patients, particularly when primary closure is planned. Future large multicenter RCTs employing standardized NPWT protocols, economic evaluations, and patient-reported outcome measures are essential for refining clinical indications and facilitating the integration of NPWT into enhanced recovery pathways [ 30 – 33 ].
sections.strengths and limitations: To our knowledge, this review is the first GRADE-assessed synthesis restricted to randomized trials comparing NPWT with conventional dressings after stoma reversal, reducing the selection bias inherent in observational studies. A prespecified protocol guided comprehensive, language-unrestricted searches, duplicate screening and extraction, and standardized RoB2 appraisal across all domains. Technique-stratified subgroup analyses (purse-string vs. primary closure) offer clinically relevant insights into potential effect modifications. Leave-one-out analyses demonstrated that Uchino 2016 had a notable influence on the SSI estimate, although the overall direction of effect continued to favor NPWT. GRADE summaries provide transparent certainty ratings for the risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias in the studies. The inclusion of trials from multiple health systems supports external validity across different perioperative practices and NPWT availability. Limitations include a modest overall sample (429 patients), which constrains the power for definitive subgroup conclusions, especially for the purse-string versus primary closure interaction, where the difference was not statistically significant, despite a larger apparent effect with primary closure. Device heterogeneity (e.g., portable systems with varying pressures, interfaces, and wear times) precludes the provision of device-specific recommendations. Open-label care and incomplete reporting of randomization procedures contributed to “some concerns” regarding the risk of bias and GRADE downgrades. Clinical protocols varied, including antibiotic regimens, and blinding of outcome assessment was impractical due to visible devices, introducing potential ascertainment bias. Because fewer than ten studies were available per outcome, formal publication bias testing was not feasible. Therefore, small-study effects and publication bias cannot be excluded. Unmeasured factors, such as the timing of stoma closure, postoperative wound care practices, nutritional status, glycemic control, and smoking, may also have influenced outcomes. The generalizability of our findings beyond elective ileostomy and colostomy reversals is limited; emergency closures, pediatric populations, and procedures performed concomitantly with laparotomy were not represented.
sections.conclusions_1: In this meta-analysis, prophylactic NPWT did not significantly reduce incisional SSI in the primary pooled analysis. Exploratory subgroup and sensitivity analyses suggested possible benefits under selected conditions; however, these findings require confirmation in larger, adequately powered randomized trials. Although the current evidence does not definitively establish clinical benefits, NPWT may represent a reasonable adjunct in selected high-risk patients, particularly when primary closure is used.

title: 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline: Missing the Boat on CYP2C19 Genotyping
abstract: The 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/American College of Emergency Physicians/National Association of Emergency Medical Services Physicians/Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions acute coronary syndrome guideline focuses on strategies to reduce bleeding risk with antiplatelet therapy yet lacks any recommendation related to CYP2C19 genotyping. The impact of CYP2C19 loss‐of‐function alleles on the effectiveness of clopidogrel is well documented, and although prasugrel and ticagrelor more effectively reduce the risk for atherothrombotic events compared with clopidogrel in patients with a CYP2C19 loss‐of‐function allele, clopidogrel reduces bleeding risk without an increase in atherothrombotic events compared with prasugrel or ticagrelor in those without a loss‐of‐function allele. Accordingly, an American Heart Association Scientific Statement supports CYP2C19 genetic testing before oral P2Y 12 inhibitors are prescribed. This commentary summarizes the evidence in support of CYP2C19 ‐guided P2Y 12 inhibitor selection in the context of other 2025 acute coronary syndrome guideline recommendations and urges future guidelines to incorporate recommendations for CYP2C19 genotyping, especially for those at high bleeding risk.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

title: Patient and public involvement in health and social care doctoral research: recommendations co-produced by doctoral researchers, public contributors, and a public involvement coordinator
abstract: Background Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) is a continually growing component of health and social care research in the UK and internationally, ensuring that research is conducted with and by the public rather than simply about them. Doctoral research represents a critical opportunity to embed meaningful PPI early in researchers’ careers, yet practical recommendations tailored to this context remain limited. Existing studies often focus on individual case reflections or programme-level evaluations, with few capturing the collective experiences of doctoral researchers, PPI contributors, and coordinators. This paper aims to co-produce practical recommendations to support meaningful patient and public involvement in doctoral health and social care research. Main body This paper presents co-produced reflections and recommendations to support PPI in doctoral research. The writing process was approached collaboratively, with a team incorporating public contributors, doctoral researchers, and a public involvement coordinator working together through iterative discussion and revision. The approach aligns with the principles of authentic co-production, creating both “space to talk” through open, respectful dialogue and “space to change” through mutual adaptation. The team’s experiences highlighted both shared benefits and challenges within the process. PPI enriched doctoral research by refining study design, questions, enhancing recruitment, and improving accessibility of outputs, while also offering PPI contributors opportunities for learning and impact. Challenges included managing emotional topics, balancing timelines, and recognising that not all suggestions could be implemented. The coordinator’s role proved vital in bridging between researchers and public contributors, supporting communication, reimbursement processes, and continuity of relationships. Doctoral researchers emphasised the importance of building trust, using accessible language, and developing distinct relational skills alongside academic expertise. From these collective insights, the team developed practical recommendations for three key audiences: doctoral students, PPI contributors, and PPI coordinators. Conclusion PPI in doctoral research offers mutual benefits for contributors and early-career researchers, strengthening both research quality and personal and professional development. Genuine co-production requires time, respect, and institutional support, but can foster strong partnerships and more relevant, impactful research. The recommendations presented here aim to help doctoral researchers, PPI contributors, and coordinators embed authentic, equitable, and sustainable involvement across health and social care research.
