Informed Consent: Formal patient consent was not required for this retrospective study.

title: Pathogenic Characterization of a Novel G47R Transthyretin Mutation in Early‐Onset Amyloid Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy driven by the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from destabilized transthyretin (TTR). Although several pathogenic TTR variants have been characterized, the clinical significance and molecular behavior of rare mutations remain poorly understood. Methods A 31‐year‐old woman with early‐onset transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy and her family members were evaluated. Whole‐exome sequencing identified the G47R variant, which was validated and quantified in the proband and relatives using droplet‐digital polymerase chain reaction and amplicon‐based next‐generation sequencing. Biophysical assays assessed the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of G47R‐TTR. Aggregate formation assays evaluated the ability of small‐molecule kinetic stabilizers, exemplified by tafamidis, to suppress amyloid aggregation in vitro. Plasma TTR tetramer concentrations in the proband and her asymptomatic heterozygous sister were measured using an ultraperformance liquid chromatography–based assay. Results A heterozygous G47R substitution was confirmed in the family. Both homozygous G47R‐TTR and heterozygous G47R: wild‐type TTR exhibited significantly reduced thermodynamic and kinetic stability, comparable to the aggressive L55P variant. Tafamidis effectively suppressed aggregate formation of G47R‐TTR in vitro. Plasma TTR tetramers were markedly reduced in both the symptomatic proband and the asymptomatic carrier, with tafamidis treatment in the proband restoring tetramer concentrations toward physiological levels and improving exercise tolerance and heart failure symptoms. Conclusions G47R represents a pathogenic TTR mutation characterized by substantial structural destabilization and amyloidogenicity, consistent with early‐onset disease. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of genotype‐informed biochemical characterization and support the potential of TTR tetramer concentration as a biomarker for disease severity and therapeutic response.
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Disease

sections.background: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy driven by the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from destabilized transthyretin (TTR). Although several pathogenic TTR variants have been characterized, the clinical significance and molecular behavior of rare mutations remain poorly understood.
sections.methods: A 31‐year‐old woman with early‐onset transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy and her family members were evaluated. Whole‐exome sequencing identified the G47R variant, which was validated and quantified in the proband and relatives using droplet‐digital polymerase chain reaction and amplicon‐based next‐generation sequencing. Biophysical assays assessed the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of G47R‐TTR. Aggregate formation assays evaluated the ability of small‐molecule kinetic stabilizers, exemplified by tafamidis, to suppress amyloid aggregation in vitro. Plasma TTR tetramer concentrations in the proband and her asymptomatic heterozygous sister were measured using an ultraperformance liquid chromatography–based assay.
sections.results: A heterozygous G47R substitution was confirmed in the family. Both homozygous G47R‐TTR and heterozygous G47R: wild‐type TTR exhibited significantly reduced thermodynamic and kinetic stability, comparable to the aggressive L55P variant. Tafamidis effectively suppressed aggregate formation of G47R‐TTR in vitro. Plasma TTR tetramers were markedly reduced in both the symptomatic proband and the asymptomatic carrier, with tafamidis treatment in the proband restoring tetramer concentrations toward physiological levels and improving exercise tolerance and heart failure symptoms.
sections.conclusions: G47R represents a pathogenic TTR mutation characterized by substantial structural destabilization and amyloidogenicity, consistent with early‐onset disease. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of genotype‐informed biochemical characterization and support the potential of TTR tetramer concentration as a biomarker for disease severity and therapeutic response.
sections.what is new?: TTR mutation G47R markedly diminished kinetic stability, supporting its association with early disease onset and pronounced clinical manifestations in patients with amyloid transthyretin cardiomyopathy. Tafamidis treatment could restore transthyretin (TTR) tetramer concentrations toward physiological levels in patients with G47R.
sections.what are the clinical implications?: Plasma TTR tetramer concentration shows potential as a clinically useful biomarker for both disease severity and therapeutic response in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy. Evaluating its level may provide valuable information for the management of these patients.
sections.methods_1: This study complies with the ethical guidelines of the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki, and the protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University (institutional review board approval number 2024‐KY‐0217‐002). In accordance with institutional and ethical requirements, informed consent for the use of clinical information and biological specimens was obtained from all participants included in the study, either directly or via their legally authorized relatives. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding authors on reasonable request.
sections.clinical assessment: A 31‐year‐old female patient presented with recurrent symptoms of heart failure and received a diagnosis of ATTR‐CM in our hospital. The patient received a routine physical assessment on hospital admission. Multiple diagnostic evaluations were performed to determine the patient's clinical status and confirm the diagnosis, including blood biochemical analyses, echocardiography, cardiac‐enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, technetium‐99m pyrophosphate nuclear scintigraphy, and endomyocardial biopsy. Ultimately, the diagnosis was verified through genetic testing. When the TTR mutation was confirmed, we recommended and executed genetic screening for the patient's first‐degree relatives because this disease is inherited.
sections.detection of gene variant load by drople: Droplet‐digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) was performed using a TD‐1 Droplet Digital PCR system (TargetingOne, China) to assess the variant allele frequency (VAF) in genomic DNA extracted from whole‐blood samples. The ddPCR mixture for each sample was composed of 15 μL of 2×SuperMix, 3 μL of probes (final concentration of 200 nM), 2 μL of DNA templates, and 10 μL of deionized water. The thermal profile included an initial step of 10 minutes at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles consisting of 30 seconds at 95°C and 1 minute at 60°C, concluding with a final cycle at 12°C for 5 minutes. Amplicon next‐generation sequencing (NGS) (polymerase chain reaction [PCR] amplicon‐based NGS) was also used to detect the gene variant load. In brief, genomic DNA was extracted from whole‐blood samples using the Solpure Blood DNA Kit II (Magen). Gene target regions were amplified using PCR. The enriched DNA samples were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 with 150 cycles of single‐end reads. Average coverage depth exceeded 20 000×. The sequencing reads have been mapped to the reference human genome, hg19, released in February 2009 ( http://genome.ucsc.edu/ ). Nucleotide alterations in aligned reads were analyzed with NextGENe software (version 2.4.1.2). Variant load was assessed based on VAF.
sections.myocardial pathology: Endomyocardial biopsy was performed from the right ventricular septal wall or the apical portion of the left ventricle using an Argon disposable endomyocardial biopsy forceps (Jawz). ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry were continuously monitored during the procedure. Echocardiography was conducted after the procedure to exclude the possibility of pericardial effusion attributable to the biopsy. Amyloid accumulation was assessed in endomyocardial biopsy specimens using Congo red staining, immunohistochemistry, electron microscopy, and laser‐microdissection liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry proteomics. The methodological procedures for laser‐microdissection liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry–based proteomics were performed as previously described. 16
sections.plasmid construction and protein purific: The Escherichia coli TTR genes were codon optimized, synthesized by GenScript, and subsequently inserted into pET‐29b (+) expression vectors. Plasmids encoding wild‐type (WT), L55P, G47R, G47E, and G47V variants were individually transformed into BL21 (DE3) E. coli cells. Then, TTR and the pathogenic mutants were expressed, respectively, following previous literature. 17 The purity of the purified TTR was ≈98% by SDS‐PAGE gel analysis, which could be used for subsequent experiments.
sections.thermodynamic and kinetic stabilities in: The thermodynamic and kinetic stabilities of WT‐TTR, L55P‐TTR, G47R‐TTR, G47E‐TTR, G47V‐TTR, and the corresponding heterozygous protein (3.6 μM) were measured at different urea concentrations ranging from 3 to 9 M in phosphate buffer, as previously reported. 18 The kinetics data fit well with a single exponential function: I 355/335 =I 355/335 N +A (1–e −kdiss t ), from which the dissociation constant k diss can be obtained. The linear lnk diss versus urea concentration plot enables extrapolation to 0 M urea to determine a half‐life t. All measurements were performed in triplicate (n=3), and the error bars represent the SEM. The 95% CIs for C m and t 1/2 , along with the details of the fitting models and the corresponding goodness‐of‐fit (R2) values, have been added in Table S1 .
sections.aggregate formation assay: TTR (7.2 μM) was preincubated at 37°C for 0.5 hours with various concentrations of tafamidis in a phosphate buffer containing 10 mM sodium phosphate, 100 mM potassium chloride, and 1 mM EDTA at a pH of 7.4. Then, an acidic buffer (200 mM NaOAc and 100 mM KCl, pH adjusted to 4.4 with AcOH) was added in equal volume to initiate amyloid formation. After all samples were incubated at 37°C for 72 hours, the extent of TTR amyloid formation was measured by assessing the average optical density at 330 nm, the fluorescence intensity of ThT/AggStain. Aggregation observed in the presence of only the solvent (dimethyl sulfoxide) was designated as 100% aggregate formation. All measurements were performed in triplicate (n=3), and the error bars represent the SEM.
sections.measurement of plasma ttr tetramer conce: Ultraperformance liquid chromatography (UPLC) with fluorescence detection and Protein‐Pak Hi Res Q (5 μm, 4.6×100 mm) were obtained from Waters. The A2 molecule was synthesized in the laboratory. 19 Plasma samples from the patient and asymptomatic carrier were incubated with A2 for covalent labeling, followed by UPLC separation to detect tetramer TTR, as described in a prior study. 20 Fasting venous blood was drawn from all subjects and collected in vacuum blood collection tubes containing serum‐separating gel. Subsequently, samples were centrifuged at 1800 g for 10 minutes within 6 hours of collection. Serum samples were stored at −70 °C until analysis. A total of 20 μL of serum was precisely pipetted. To this, 2 μL of A2 (400 μM) was added, followed by 100 μL of 0.1 M PBS (pH=7.4). The mixture was vortexed at 2000 rpm for 1 minute to ensure thorough mixing and initiation of the reaction. The derivatization was then allowed to proceed by incubating the mixture at 25 °C for 3 hours to achieve complete reaction. Following incubation, the sample was centrifuged at 4 °C with a relative centrifugal force of 15 000 g for 5 minutes to precipitate any precipitated proteins or potential aggregates. Finally, 100 μL of the clear supernatant was carefully collected for subsequent instrumental analysis. Tetramer concentrations were calculated directly based on the standard curve generated from the A2/UPLC assay (Figure S1 ). The UPLC calibration curve was established over a range of 1 to 10 μM, demonstrating excellent linearity (Table S2 ).
sections.transmission electron microscopy imaging: Aggregated protein suspension (1 mg/mL) was deposited on the carbon coated copper grid (Beijing Zhongjingkeyi Technology Co, Ltd, China) and incubated for 80 seconds, followed by removal of most of the protein suspension. The grid was dried under an infrared baking lamp (Elitech, TPM‐910+, China), stained with 2% (w/w) phosphotungstic acid aqueous solution, and baked with digital display infrared baking lamp before imaging. The grids were subjected to transmission electron microscopy imaging (JEM‐2100, JEOL, Japan) at 200 kV.
sections.proteolytic resistance experiment: Proteinase K was used in the proteolytic resistance experiment for aggregated sortase and aggregated TTR (G47R). To measure the fluorescence decrease kinetics profile on proteolysis, 100 μL aggregated protein solution (1 mg/mL protein, 2.4 μM AggStain) was centrifuged and resuspended in buffer (NaOAc 200 mM and KCl 100 mM, acidified by AcOH to pH=6.23). Proteinase K was introduced to the mixture, and the final concentration of proteinase K was 0.1 mg/mL. The reaction mixture was incubated at room temperature for indicated durations. Fluorescent spectra were collected from 0 to 170 minutes with 5‐minute intervals. All measurements were performed in triplicate (n=3), and the error bars represent the SEM.
sections.subunit exchange experiment: Samples were thawed on ice and stored as needed at −80 °C (experiments with plasma were started within 1 week of thawing). In some experiments, tafamidis (10 mM stock in dimethyl sulfoxide) was added to sample ex vivo, and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 30 minutes before being further processed. All samples were centrifuged for 5 minutes at maximal speed in a tabletop microcentrifuge, and the supernatant was then filtered through a 0.22‐μm polyvinylidene fluoride filter. To initiate subunit exchange, dual‐FLAG‐tagged G47R at the indicated concentration was added to the sample. Unless otherwise indicated, the reaction mixture was incubated at 25 °C for the duration of the subunit exchange period. At each time point (0, 24, 48, 96, 120, and 150 hours) during the incubation, the subunit exchange reaction mixture was removed and added to a sample vial of the fluorogenic small molecule A2 in dimethyl sulfoxide. After completion of the A2 conjugation reaction, the sample was diluted by adding PBS, flash frozen with liquid nitrogen, and stored at −20 °C for later UPLC analysis. All measurements were performed in triplicate (n=3), and the error bars represent the SEM.
sections.analysis of the subunit exchange experim: The expected distribution of tetramers at equilibrium was modeled using the binomial distribution formula, Pr X = k = n k p k 1 − p n − k , where Pr(X = k) represents the proportion of tetramers containing k flag‐tagged subunits. From this model, the “exchange coefficient” was derived as the theoretical proportion of heterotetramers with exactly 2 flag‐tagged subunits (n=2, k=2). Experimentally, this coefficient is represented by the relative area of peak 3 in the ion exchange chromatogram at equilibrium. For all experimental time points, the fraction of exchange was calculated by dividing the relative area of peak 3 (ie, peak 3 area/total area) by this exchange coefficient. The resulting values are 0=no exchange and 1=100% exchange. Rate constants of exchange (K ex ) were calculated using Origin 2022 by plotting the fraction exchange data as a function of time and fitting the results to the first‐order single exponential kinetic equation y = A * 1 − e − kt + B .
sections.clinical features of the identified pati: This patient was a 31‐year‐old woman, presenting palpitations and shortness of breath on exertion, chronic dry cough, and lower‐extremity edema over 4 months. Laboratory analyses indicated a markedly increased concentration of brain natriuretic peptide (4387 pg/mL), a mildly elevated level of cardiac troponin T (0.02 ng/mL), along with normal creatinine levels (57 μM) and normal serum electrolyte and complete blood cell count values. Echocardiographic evaluation identified enlargement of both atria, concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle (septal, 29 mm; and posterior wall, 24 mm), granular sparkling of myocardium, moderate pericardial effusion, and mildly reduced systolic function of the left ventricle (left ventricular ejection fraction, 52%) (Figure 1A ). The electrocardiographic findings demonstrated diminished amplitude in the limb leads, a characteristic indicator commonly associated with cardiac amyloidosis. Serum immunofixation electrophoresis did not detect monoclonal immunoglobulins, and the free light chain concentration and κ/λ ratio remained within standard limits. Technetium‐99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy was conducted together with single‐photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography imaging, which demonstrated intense cardiac radiotracer accumulation classified as grade 3, along with an increased heart/contralateral ratio of 1.9 at 3 hours, indicating strong evidence of TTR amyloid deposition. (Figure 1B ). Cardiac‐enhanced magnetic resonance showed subendocardial delayed gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1C ). Endomyocardial tissue sampling followed by Congo red staining and immunohistochemical analysis verified the presence of amyloid deposits (Figure 1D and 1E ). Electron microscopy analysis showed shrinkage of cardiomyocytes accompanied by disorganized, deteriorated, and necrotic myofibrillar structures. Additionally, numerous amyloid fibrils were observed in the intercellular spaces and along vascular walls, displaying an irregular distribution (Figure 1F ). Scanning laser ophthalmoscopy showed vitreous opacities in the right eye (Figure 1G ), resembling the vitreous abnormalities previously reported in patients carrying the G47R mutation. 14 , 21 Laser‐microdissection liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry proteomics of the endomyocardial biopsy specimens (Figure 1H ) showed that, among the currently recognized amyloid‐typing proteins, TTR exhibited the highest relative abundance, supporting classification as the ATTR subtype. In addition, proteins commonly associated with various forms of amyloidosis, including serum amyloid P‐component (SAP) and apolipoproteins E, A‐I, and A‐IV, were detected as components of the amyloid deposits, as previously described. 22 When interpreted in conjunction with the genetic testing results, the mass spectrometry data confirmed the presence of both wild‐type and mutant TTR peptides. However, it was surprising that the wild‐type species was predominant. The low abundance of the mutant peptide may be attributable to the R mutation coincidentally occurring at a proteolytic digestion site before mass spectrometry analysis. Based on these observations, a clinical diagnosis of ATTR‐CM was considered adequate for this patient.
sections.genetic analysis of the proband and pedi: To differentiate ATTRwt and ATTRm subtypes, genetic sequencing of the patient (proband) was performed. Whole‐exome sequencing of the proband identified a heterozygous missense mutation at nucleotide position 199 within exon 2 of the TTR gene (c.199G>C), leading to the substitution of glycine with arginine (G47R). Figure 2A illustrates the hereditary pedigree of the proband. The proband's father passed away at the age of 35 years because of an unspecified cardiac incident. The genetic sequencing results were normal for the proband's mother and children. The genetic change was subsequently confirmed through Sanger sequencing and was also detected in the proband's asymptomatic sister (Figure 2B ). At the beginning, the mutation frequency of TTR gene in the proband indicated by whole‐exome sequencing was ≈27%, and her asymptomatic sister had not been confirmed as a mutation carrier; it was necessary to rule out the case that the proband carried somatic mosaicism for this variant. To this end, ddPCR and amplicon NGS were performed to detect the variant load in the proband and her family members. ddPCR analysis revealed that the VAF in the proband's peripheral blood was 32.79%, whereas that in her asymptomatic sister was 33.80%. And there was no pathogenic mutation detected in the peripheral blood from her children (Figure 2C ). In addition, the results of amplicon NGS showed that the VAFs were 33% in both proband and her sister (Figure 2D ).
sections.thermodynamic and kinetic stability of t: Our study selected WT‐TTR, L55P‐TTR, G47E‐TTR, and G47V‐TTR as comparative controls to evaluate the stability profiles alongside G47R‐TTR. The X‐ray crystal structures of G47R‐TTR, G47E‐TTR, and G47V‐TTR are shown in Figure 3A and Figure S2 . Glycine's miniature side chain enables optimal core packing (Figure S2A ). G47R introduces steric clash and electrostatic repulsion with its bulky, positively charged guanidinium group (Figure S2B ); G47E creates charge repulsion with its negatively charged carboxylate (Figure S2C ); and G47V disrupts hydrophobic packing and solvation with its bulky, nonpolar side chain (Figure S2D ). The mutation of a local residue disrupts the stability of the distant dimer‐dimer interface, ultimately leading to tetramer destabilization. The experimental findings indicated that G47R‐TTR (C m =2.3 M) exhibited significantly lower thermodynamic stability than that of WT‐TTR (C m =3.4 M) and was comparable to that of L55P‐TTR (C m =2.3 M), an early‐onset mutation. The thermodynamic stability of G47V‐TTR (C m =2.4 M) and G47E‐TTR (C m =2.7 M) was comparable to that of G47R‐TTR (Figure 3B and 3D ; Figure S3 ). On the other hand, G47R‐TTR (t 1/2 =1.9 h) exhibited the worst kinetic stability, compared with that of G47V‐TTR (t 1/2 =3.1 h), G47E‐TTR (t 1/2 =16.0 h), L55P‐TTR (t 1/2 =4.4 h), and WT‐TTR (t 1/2 =42.0 h) (Figure 3C and 3D ; Figure S3 ). Overall, G47R‐TTR exhibited significantly reduced thermodynamic and kinetic stability than WT‐TTR, partially accounting for its early onset of disease and associated pathogenic potential. To more accurately mimic the clinical condition of patients with a heterozygous TTR mutation in their blood plasma, the thermodynamic and kinetic stability of the G47R: WT‐TTR heterozygous variant was evaluated (Figure 3B and 3D ; Figure S3 ). Intriguingly, heterozygous exchange between WT‐TTR and G47R‐TTR clearly improved the thermodynamic stability from 2.3 M to 3.2 M, close to the level of WT‐TTR (C m =3.4 M), but only marginally improved the kinetic stability from 1.9 to 6.0 hours, still far from the WT‐TTR (t 1/2 =42.0 hour). In comparison to other mutations on the G47 residue, for the G47E mutant, the heterozygous substitution with WT‐TTR only slightly enhanced the thermodynamic stability (2.7 M to 2.8 M) and the kinetic stability (16.0 to 21.9 hour) compared with its homozygous G47E‐TTR. However, for the G47V mutant, substitution with WT‐TTR led to a modest improvement in the thermodynamic stability of G47V‐TTR (2.4 M to 2.6 M), but further compromised its kinetic stability (3.1 to 1.4 hours). In addition, for the L55P mutant, the heterozygous substitution with WT‐TTR enhanced the thermodynamic stability (2.3 M to 3.2 M) and the kinetic stability (4.4 to 10.1 hours) compared with its homozygous L55P (Figure 3B and 3D ). Taken together, these data suggested that both homozygous G47R‐TTR and heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR showed compromised thermodynamic and kinetic stability, similar to the early‐onset L55P‐TTR mutant.
sections.g47r : wt \u2010 ttr and g47e : wt \u201: Tafamidis, a widely used small‐molecule kinetic stabilizer, has been authorized in numerous countries for the management of TTR‐related amyloidosis. In this study, we investigated the inhibitory effect of tafamidis on G47R‐TTR amyloidogenesis using both homozygous G47R‐TTR and heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR variants. The transmission electron microscopy revealed that G47R aggregates formed dense, elongated amyloid aggregates (Figure S4 ). Furthermore, oligomeric intermediates were observed during aggregate formation. The reported aggregation sensor AggStain 23 , 24 showed superior sensitivity over ThT, exhibiting a strong, time‐dependent fluorescence increase that supports G47R's aggregation (Figure S5 ). AggStain bound‐G47R‐TTR amyloid aggregates exhibited slower fluorescence intensity decay compared with the amorphous sortase aggregates on proteolysis, confirming their more compact aggregate structure resistant to proteolytic digestion (Figure S6 ). These aggregates are more resistant to proteinase degradation, suggesting its pathogenicity. The heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR showed a similar satisfactory response to tafamidis compared with the homozygous G47R‐TTR (Figure 4A and 4B ). The heterozygous G47E: WT‐TTR and homozygous G47E‐TTR demonstrated the same trends. However, for both homozygous G47R‐TTR and heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR, as the concentration of tafamidis increased, no dose‐dependent inhibitory effect was observed beyond 7.2 μM (Figure 4A and 4B ). The observed inhibition plateau beyond 7.2 μM tafamidis indicates the previously reported negative cooperativity of TTR mutants for the second binding sites, rather than solubility or assay ceiling. As reported by Penchala et al, 25 acoramidis exhibits weaker binding affinity when occupying the second T4‐binding site because of negative cooperativity. Furthermore, the ability to access the second T4‐binding site varies with mutation type, reflecting differential drug‐binding affinities across TTR variants. These findings underscore the importance of characterizing biochemical properties before implementing precision medicine treatments for patients carrying different TTR mutations. Furthermore, greater kinetic destabilization may lead to a poorer stabilization response to tafamidis. In heterozygous samples, higher kinetic stability correlates with a stronger tafamidis response. The order is G47E: WT>G47R: WT>G47V: WT (Figures 3C , 3D , and 4 ). In homozygous variants, the kinetic stability order is G47E>G47V>G47R. However, their drug response order is G47E>G47R>G47V (Figures 3C , 3D , and 4 ). The difference likely stems from mutation‐specific structural factors, such as changes at the dimer‐dimer interface or altered interactions within the tetramer. Acoramidis and diflunisal exhibited consistent inhibitory effects on aggregate formation across wild‐type TTR, homozygous tetramers (G47R, G47V, and G47E), and their corresponding heterozygous tetramers (G47R‐WT, G47V‐WT, G47E‐WT), mirroring the results observed with tafamidis (Figure S7 ). These results underscore the need for mutation‐specific treatment strategies in ATTRm cardiac amyloidosis, as distinct point mutations at the same residue also lead to markedly different clinical outcomes.
sections.quantification of tetrameric ttr concent: Tetramer concentration quantification is important for accurately assessing pathogenic risk in carriers and for monitoring the true mechanistic efficacy of stabilizer therapies (Figure S8 ). 26 Variations in tetramer levels in blood plasma could potentially act as markers for disease progression and the effectiveness of treatment with kinetic stabilizers. An orthogonal subunit exchange UPLC assay was used to measure the kinetic stability of TTR in vitro and ex vivo (patient's plasma) (Figure S9A ). G47R‐TTR exhibited faster K ex compared with WT‐TTR, confirming its intrinsic kinetic instability (Figure S9B,E ). Tafamidis significantly slowed down the subunit exchange rate (K ex ) 20 , 27 of G47R (Figure S9C,E ). Furthermore, introduction of tafamidis in either buffer or patient's plasma environment both stabilized tetramer dissociation, as reflected by improved K ex (Figure S9D,E ). Tafamidis' direct kinetic stabilization provided additional evidence that increased tetramer concentration may reflect enhanced kinetic stability and reduced amyloidogenicity. However, the potential impact of other factors (eg, hepatic synthesis, degradation, nutritional status, inflammation, and amyloid burden) cannot be ignored. Consequently, we examined the TTR tetramer concentration in the patient's plasma using the UPLC technique (Figure 5A ). Formation of the heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR was validated through a subunit exchange assay (Figure 5B ). To accurately replicate the TTR composition in the patient's plasma, we initially derived a standard correlation curve with the heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR tetramer for subsequent quantification (Figure 5C and 5D ). Then, we measured the TTR tetramer concentration in the plasma of the patient and her asymptomatic sister (Figure 5E and 5F ). The TTR tetramer concentration in the G47R patient before tafamidis treatment (61 mg once a day) was found to be 1.48 μM, notably lower than the normal range (3.6–7.2 μM). 28 , 29 , 30 Interestingly, after 2 months of tafamidis therapy, the tetramer concentration increased significantly to 2.55 μM, surpassing that of her asymptomatic sister (2.32 μM). Furthermore, following an extended follow‐up period, the TTR tetramer concentration was reassessed 8 months after starting the medication, yielding a value of 3.65 μM, which approached the normal range. In addition, we compared the clinical parameters (Table S3 ) and symptom changes before and after treatment. We found that after 8 months of oral tafamidis therapy, both pro‐B‐type natriuretic peptide levels and the 6‐minute walk distance showed clear improvement, whereas left ventricular global longitudinal strain demonstrated only minimal improvement and cardiac troponin T levels remained mildly elevated without further change. Meanwhile, the patient reported improved exercise tolerance and reduced palpitations and dyspnea after 8 months of therapy. A mild cough persisted, and intermittent mild lower‐extremity edema was still noted. These findings indicated the considerable instability of the G47R mutant and suggest that TTR tetramer concentration may serve as a potential biomarker for disease onset and treatment monitoring in mutation carriers, as well as for informing the therapeutic window for pharmacologic intervention. However, monitoring of total serum TTR concentration cannot be ignored. In clinical practice, it offers a convenient, low‐cost tool for initial screening during large‐scale or routine follow‐up. 31 , 32 Subsequent evaluation of TTR tetramer concentration then allows for a detailed assessment of the folding state of TTR. This 2‐step strategy of initial screening followed by targeted clinical verification may provide a robust and clinically feasible approach to monitor therapeutic response.
sections.discussion: The TTR G47R mutation was first described by Murakami et al in Japan. 11 In this initial case, the proband was a 38‐year‐old Japanese man presenting with symptoms suggestive of familial amyloid polyneuropathy. Subsequently, the G47R mutation has been reported in 2 Italian families, 12 1 Chinese family, 13 1 Japanese family, 14 and 1 British family. 15 The clinical manifestations observed in these families included peripheral neuropathy, restrictive cardiomyopathy, vitreous opacity, and leptomeningeal involvement, with all affected individuals exhibiting an early onset of the disease. Among them, the youngest patient developed symptoms at the age of 13 years. 14 In addition, a retrospective analysis of patients with hereditary ATTR‐CM conducted in China 5 suggests that G47R appears to be more prevalent than previously anticipated, especially when compared with the 2 other common mutations (V30M and V122I) observed in Western populations. This observation reinforces the idea that the diversity of mutations is influenced by ethnic and geographic factors. In this study, we presented a case of ATTR‐CM associated with a G47R mutation. The proband presented with symptoms of cardiac failure, including edema and dyspnea on exertion, accompanied by blurred vision in the right eye attributable to vitreous opacities, part of which is similar to previous reports. 14 , 21 However, no clinical symptoms of polyneuropathy were observed. Additionally, we are the first to describe a patient with the G47R mutation who exhibited a persistent dry cough, a symptom also noted in individuals with other mutation types. 33 , 34 Furthermore, we consistently observed a VAF of ≈33% for the TTR variant in genomic DNA from the proband and her sister by both high‐depth PCR‐NGS and ddPCR. A literature search did not identify published reports of germline TTR variants with consistently reduced VAF (~30%–35%) in peripheral blood. Although several technical factors may lower the observed VAF from the expected 50% for a heterozygous germline variant (eg, allele‐specific amplification bias and suboptimal primer or probe binding), 35 these technical artifacts generally cause modest deviations and are unlikely to result in a stable VAF of ~33% consistently reproduced across different assay platforms and individuals, as demonstrated in our case. Given this, the finding is more plausibly explained by biological rather than technical causes. After reviewing the relevant literature and consulting with experts in medical genetics, we are inclined to hypothesize that the reduced VAF observed in this family is most plausibly attributable to a postzygotic interallelic gene conversion event, in which the wild‐type allele served as the donor to correct the mutated allele. Similar phenomena of revertant mosaicism have been reported in multiple genetic disorders 36 , 37 ; however, within TTR ‐related diseases, such an occurrence has thus far been documented only in a Sicilian family in which several individuals were affected by familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy associated with the E109Q mutation. 36 Next, we examined the biochemical and biophysical characteristics of the G47R variant to elucidate its underlying pathogenic mechanisms. The thermodynamic and kinetic stability assessment for G47R‐TTR revealed reduced stability compared with WT‐TTR and a level similar to the early‐onset L55P‐TTR. These findings suggest that the structural instability of G47R‐TTR is a key contributing factor to the development of TTR amyloidosis, and that the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of TTR variants partially correlate with the clinical onset and disease severity. TTRs are heterotetramers in patients' plasma attributable to subunit interchange dynamics. Thus, our results also indicate that both the homozygous G47R‐TTR and the heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR variants exhibit compromised thermodynamic and kinetic stability, resembling that of the L55P‐TTR mutant. These findings offer a possible explanation for the early onset and pronounced clinical manifestations observed in our proband. In recent years, some novel therapeutics aimed at stabilizing TTR and reducing its synthesis have been developed. Of these, tafamidis is currently the only one approved for clinical application in China. 26 In our study, we compared the response of 3 different point mutations at position 47 to treatment of tafamidis. Previous reports indicated that the G47R, 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 21 G47E, 38 , 39 , 40 and G47V 26 , 41 variants can each involve the nervous system, heart, and gastrointestinal tract. Notably, some individuals with G47R exhibit ocular involvement, 14 , 21 whereas a subset of those with G47E demonstrate renal involvement. 38 , 39 We also provide a table (Table S4 ) summarizing the reported clinical involvement and the available evidence for biochemical characterization and therapeutic response among the 3 TTR G47 variants. Our results indicated that both heterozygous G47R: WT‐TTR and heterozygous G47E: WT‐TTR showed satisfactory response to tafamidis stabilization. In contrast, heterozygous G47V: WT‐TTR exhibited much poorer response to tafamidis. Consequently, our results highlight the potential importance of treatment approaches and ongoing assessment of therapeutic efficacy, areas that warrant further investigation. Using the A2‐UPLC quantification technique, we measured the plasma concentration of TTR tetramers in both the G47R patient and the asymptomatic carrier. Multiple studies, 28 , 29 , 30 together with our own findings (Table S5–S7 ), have shown that the typical levels of TTR in the plasma or serum of healthy individuals fall within the range of 3.6 to 7.2 μM. Earlier research has reported that serum TTR concentrations are decreased in individuals with ATTRm amyloidosis. 42 , 43 Moreover, in cases of ATTRwt, lower initial serum TTR levels have been independently linked to reduced survival time. 44 Similarly, a recent population‐based study from Denmark indicated that diminished plasma transthyretin levels are associated with a heightened risk of developing heart failure in the general population. 45 Additionally, patients exhibiting higher TTR tetramer concentrations generally demonstrate a more favorable response to TTR kinetic stabilizing therapies. 30 , 46 , 47 In this study, our findings revealed that the TTR tetramer concentration in the proband was markedly reduced compared with that of healthy individuals. Following 2 months of tafamidis therapy, the tetramer concentration showed a substantial increase. With continued treatment over an extended follow‐up period of 8 months, tafamidis further elevated the TTR tetramer concentration to a level approaching the normal physiological range. On the other hand, the proband's sister, identified as an asymptomatic carrier, exhibited a noticeable decline in TTR levels compared with those observed in healthy individuals. These observations may suggest that reductions in TTR tetramer concentrations could signal the potential progression from an asymptomatic state to symptomatic disease. In such individuals, close surveillance of TTR tetramer levels, alongside clinical manifestations and deviations in additional biomarkers, is needed. Additionally, K ex value is obtainable in a semi‐high‐throughput manner and may serve as a powerful proxy for both inherent pathogenicity and responsiveness to kinetic stabilizers like tafamidis. By establishing a correlation between K ex values measured in patient plasma and clinical outcomes in future large‐scale studies, a rapid clinical tool can potentially be created.
sections.conclusions_1: This study described a Chinese patient with ATTR‐CM carrying the TTR mutation G47R. This mutation's markedly diminished kinetic stability supports its association with early disease onset and pronounced clinical manifestations. Tafamidis also exhibited favorable benefits for this type of mutation.

title: Pilot of a blended learning model on medical students’ communication skills in the context of digital innovations
abstract: Background Effective physician–patient communication is essential for high-quality medical care. However, digital transformation and the increasing use of tools based on artificial intelligence (AI) require new competencies that are not yet systematically integrated into medical curricula. Blended learning formats may offer a promising approach to addressing both patient-centered and technology-related communication skills. Methods In this pilot study, sixth- and eighth-semester medical students ( n = 6) participated in an NKLM-based blended learning elective course. The course combined H5P online modules on narrative and AI-related communication with face-to-face sessions involving standardized patients and structured feedback. A mixed-methods evaluation was conducted to assess feasibility and explore learning outcomes. This included a pre–post questionnaire assessing subjective competence gains and an objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) comparing intervention participants with a control group. Results The blended learning format was successfully implemented and completed by participating students. Pre–post analyses showed increases across all assessed domains, with larger absolute gains in competencies related to digital innovations than in narrative communication skills. In the OSCE, communication competencies were generally demonstrated across both groups, with the largest performance differences observed in AI-related counselling tasks and consultation closing. Conclusions This pilot study supports the feasibility and acceptability of the integrated blended learning course. Exploratory findings suggest potential benefits for both narrative and digital communication competencies, with the strongest gains observed in digital communication competencies. These findings highlight the need to integrate AI- and technology-related communication skills more systematically into medical curricula. Given the exploratory design and small sample size, results should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12909-026-09662-1.

sections.background_1: Successful physician–patient communication is a key determinant of high-quality medical care. Research demonstrates that empathetic and patient-centered communication is positively associated with treatment outcomes [ 1 , 2 ], coping, self-regulation, treatment adherence and patient engagement, as well as health-related quality of life [ 2 ]. Ongoing curricular transformations, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, have highlighted the limitations of purely lecture-based, campus-centered teaching and increased the relevance of digitally-transformed and technology-enhanced learning environments [ 3 – 6 ]. Against this background, research on digital, blended, and hybrid learning approaches in medical education has expanded considerably [ 7 ]. Comparative studies suggest that blended learning approaches [ 8 , 9 ] can be more effective than exclusively online or face-to-face formats and have already been successfully implemented across multiple medical disciplines [ 10 – 12 ]. Reported benefits include higher learner satisfaction, increased engagement, and improved learning outcomes [ 13 – 15 ]. A random controlled trial found that blended learning improved medical students’ communication skills and satisfaction compared with lecture-based teaching [ 16 ]. However, there is still limited evidence on how blended learning designs must be structured to optimize learner acceptance, usability, and educational effectiveness [ 17 , 18 ]. Gamification-based instructional approaches are increasingly used in medical education to enhance learner motivation, engagement, and repeated interaction with learning content [ 19 ]. In some cases, they may also support learning outcomes [ 20 – 22 ]. Within this context, interactive digital authoring tools such as H5P ( https://h5p.org/ ) are gaining relevance [ 23 ], particularly within flipped classroom designs and formative feedback processes [ 24 ]. H5P-based learning activities allow students to engage with content in a self-paced manner, receive immediate feedback, and reflect on their own learning progress. Although empirical findings regarding performance improvements are inconsistent, studies report high user satisfaction, streamlined learning workflows, and didactic benefits [ 25 , 26 ]. At the same time, standardized patient–based training remains the gold standard for teaching patient-centered communication skills [ 27 ]. While conventional lectures and digital tools primarily serve preparation in advance, knowledge acquisition, and reflection, communication competence itself develops through practice in authentic interpersonal interaction [ 28 ]. Standardized patient encounters therefore provide an opportunity to apply communication strategies in realistic clinical scenarios, receive structured feedback, and transfer conceptual knowledge into observable communicative behavior. Recent evidence shows, that AI-based tools may further extend this approach by exposing students to virtual patients, digitally mediated communication scenarios, and interactions with increasingly informed, technology-using patients [ 29 ]. Taken together, face-to-face, digital, blended and hybrid learning formats each offer distinct educational strengths, but their specific contributions to communication skill acquisition have not yet been systematically aligned with medical communication training. The present blended learning concept was therefore designed to combine these complementary mechanisms: digital modules to support knowledge acquisition and self-reflection, gamified H5P activities to promote engagement and formative learning, AI-related tools to address emerging digital communication competencies, and standardized patient training to enable experiential practice and feedback. Against this background, the primary objective of this pilot study was to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary educational effects of an NKLM-based blended learning course for medical communication training. The evaluation consisted of a pre–post assessment, an OSCE [ 30 ], and qualitative focus groups. However, the present article reports exclusively on the learning design and the results of the quantitative evaluation.
sections.study design and participants: In the elective course “Medicine Meets AI: Rethinking Medical Communication Training”, sixth- and eighth-semester medical students at the University of Rostock were taught medical communication using a blended learning format. Recruitment for both the elective course and control group was conducted through flyers and university social media channels. In total, eight students initially enrolled; one student withdrew at the beginning of the study for time-related reasons, and another student, although participating in the elective course, was excluded from the pilot analysis due to non-participation in the pre-test and the e-learning components. The sample size was determined by the number of students enrolling in the elective course.
sections.self-directed learning phases: The course was designed as a blended learning format combining traditional face-to-face sessions with digital self-directed learning phases. H5P-based learning units ( https://h5p.org/ ) provided students with immediate feedback on the interactive learning content and supported the ongoing assessment of their own learning progress. Content was delivered through interactive input followed by structured reflection and consolidation activities, including quizzes, drag-and-drop tasks, and interactive videos. The digital component comprised three online modules (Table 1 ): Module 1 addressed “ Narrative communication ” and introduced key principles of patient-centered physician–patient communication. It covered both theoretical foundations and practical techniques, including active listening, narrative elicitation, and structured consultation opening and closing. Module 2 focused on “ Techniques of structured information gathering ”, introducing the WWSZ technique (Wait-Repeat-Reflect-Summarize) [ 31 ] and the four-sides model of communication [ 32 ]. Module 3 addressed “ Technological advancements and informed patients ”, covering digital health applications and generative AI (genAI) tools such as chatbots. The modules were delivered via the learning management system ILIAS, providing students with unrestricted access to the sequentially released content. sections.learning management system analytics: Due to local institutional data protection regulations, individual usage data from ILIAS, such as access frequency, time-on-task, or H5P interaction logs, could not be collected or analyzed. Feasibility and engagement with the online modules were therefore assessed through participant self-report during the course evaluation.
sections.face-to-face sessions: The face-to-face component comprised four sessions that were aligned in timing and content with the online modules (Fig. 1 ). In accordance with the flipped-classroom model, these sessions focused on discussion and consolidation of previously covered content, as well as its application in practice-oriented scenarios.
sections.first session (90\u00a0min): The session began with an introduction, clarification of expectations, and presentation of the learning objectives and organizational framework. The pre-test was then administered. Module 1 was subsequently released, initiating the first self-directed learning phase.
sections.second session (90\u00a0min, four weeks: The session focused on training in narrative communication. Through a series of exercises, students practiced active listening, open-ended questions, targeted questioning and note-taking techniques using common topics (e.g., holiday experiences or illness experiences). Roles alternated between narrator, listener, and observer. The aim of the session was to enhance sensitivity to patient-centered communication and further develop students’ communication competencies. A plenary discussion was conducted to reflect on the experiences.
sections.third session (135\u00a0min, two weeks l: The session focused on communication training with standardized patients. Using uncomplicated cases (cough and low back pain), students conducted general practice history-taking consultations. The focus was on applying the communication techniques introduced in Modules 1 and 2. Facilitators and peers observed the consultations and provided structured feedback.
sections.fourth session (180\u00a0min, four weeks: The final session focused on practical engagement with digital tools relevant to physician–patient communication. Students explored mobile health applications, including the symptom-assessment app Ada Health [ 35 ] and the consultation support tool arriba [ 36 ], and applied them in consultation scenarios involving symptom-oriented information gathering, patient education, and communication of individualized risk information. In addition, despite obvious limitations on the use of chatbots in therapeutic communications [ 37 ], students interacted with a custom-designed patient chatbot on the Character.AI platform [ 38 ] and reflected on symptoms, patient concerns, communication challenges, and the emerging role of AI-mediated communication in healthcare. Fig. 1 Study flow
sections.pre-post assessment: Based on the Communication Skills Attitude Scale (CSAS) [ 39 ], general attitudes were assessed. In addition, NKLM-related learning objectives were derived from the online modules. These were used to develop a pre–post questionnaire assessing subjective competence gains in theoretical understanding and applied communication skills, based on Bloom’s taxonomy of educational objectives [ 40 ]: General attitudes (GA, 9 items): baseline attitudes toward the importance of communication competencies in doctoral practice, openness to technological change in medicine, and self-assessed learning ability [ 39 ]. Theoretical understanding (TU, 35 items ) : knowledge related to narrative communication, patient-centered communication, questioning techniques, and managing digital innovations. Applied communication skills (ACS, 18 items): translation of TU-related into practical communication contexts. Self-assessments were recorded using a 6-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly disagree” [ 1 ] to “strongly agree” [ 6 ], assessing agreement with statements (e.g., “I can explain the principles of narrative communication”). Negatively worded items were reverse coded. In addition, sociodemographic data were collected, including gender, age, semester, prior vocational training, and clinical experience. Items from the three domains were aggregated into a total of 22 mean score scales (Tables 3 , 4 and 5 ). Based on these scale scores, an absolute gain was calculated for each scale, reflecting the subjective competence gain from pre-test to post-test. For further analysis, scales were grouped into the categories “ Narrative communication ” and “ Managing digital innovations ,” for which mean absolute gains were calculated as the average of the corresponding scale-specific absolute gains.
sections.osce: Practical skills were assessed using an OSCE based on a standardized history-taking scenario involving the case vignette “diarrhea.” Performance of the intervention group was compared with that of a control group of seven medical students from the sixth ( n = 4) and eighth semester ( n = 3). Control participants were informed about the general study context but not the case vignette. Trained standardized patients were selected from the professional standardized patient program at the Rostock University Medical Center. OSCE performance was evaluated using a standardized communication rubric comprising eleven evaluation criteria (Table 2 ) rated on a 3-point scale (0–2 points). Two teams of two examiners were instructed using a shared assessment framework prior to the examination. Formal inter-rater reliability statistics (e.g., ICC or Cohen’s K) could not be calculated because individual encounters were assessed by separate examiner teams without overlapping ratings of the same performance. However, students were randomly assigned to the study arms, such that potential differences between examiner teams were distributed unsystematically across groups. Table 2 OSCE evaluation criteria Number Criterion 1 Friendly Greeting 2 Open Conversation Initiation 3 Agenda Setting 4 Trust-Building Communication 5 Transparent Structure 6 Active Listening 7 Conversational Expansion 8 Content Summary 9 AI Tool Counselling 10 Appropriate Closing 11 Information Gathering
sections.sociodemographic characteristics: A total of six students were included in the analysis (three male, two female, one not reported). Four students were in their sixth semester and two in their eighth semester. The mean age was 24.2 years (SD = 2.99). Two students had completed prior vocational training, and the mean duration of clinical experience was 3.67 (SD = 4.27) weeks.
sections.pre-test: Concerning GA, participants reported openness toward the topic of physician–patient communication and interest in learning patient-centered communication techniques. Scale scores for openness to medical change (M = 4.50) and valuation of physician–patient communication (M = 5.63) are presented in Table 3 . Within the domain of TU, students reported confidence levels above four (“somewhat agree”) on the 6-point Likert scale for active listening (M = 4.50) as well as conversation setting, including consultation opening and closing (M = 4.38) (Table 4 ). In contrast, confidence ratings below this threshold were observed for knowledge of narrative communication, narrative elicitation, questioning techniques and information gathering, agenda setting, and all scales related to managing digital innovations. In the domain of ACS (Table 5 ), confidence ratings below four were observed for agenda and conversation structure, information gathering and narrative elicitation, self-reflection in communication, and all scales related to managing digital innovations. Confidence ratings were comparatively higher in conversation setting and initiation (M = 4.33) as well as active listening (M = 4.08).
sections.pre-post comparison: Tables 3 , 4 and 5 show the absolute gain from pre-test to post-test. With regard to GA (Table 3 ), only minor differences were observed, which do not indicate clear changes. sections.osce_1: The OSCE evaluation shows that most basic communication skills (greeting, conversation initiation, conversation setting, active listening, and information gathering) were reliably demonstrated by all participants (Table 6 ). The highest scores were observed for active listening (criterion 6) and conversation opening (criteria 1 & 2). In contrast, lower scores were found for agenda setting and conversation structure (criteria 3 & 5). sections.discussion: The primary purpose of this pilot study was to assess the feasibility and acceptability of a novel NKLM-based blended learning course on medical communication training. As a first exploratory evaluation, students’ self-assessments in a pre-post design were combined with a controlled OSCE. At pre-test, students reported comparatively higher confidence in active listening and consultation initiation and setting [ 41 ]. In contrast, lower confidence levels were reported for other narrative communication techniques, including knowledge of narrative communication, agenda setting, narrative elicitation, information gathering, and self-reflection in communication. Although certain communication skills were perceived as challenging prior to training, post-intervention self-assessments indicated confidence ratings near 5 on the 6-point Likert scale. These findings may be interpreted in light of the stage model proposed by Zöll et al. [ 42 ], which classifies communication learning objectives according to their complexity and the level of instruction and guidance required to achieve them. Other studies have likewise identified variation across specific communication domains when using standardized assessment tools such as the SEGUE questionnaire [ 43 , 44 ]. However, given the small sample size and therefore limited robustness of the findings within individual scales, domain-level comparisons with existing studies should be interpreted with caution. Instead, the present findings primarily highlight the overall positive effect of the blended learning format on the development of narrative communication skills, which is consistent with previous research [ 16 , 45 – 48 ]. Notably, competencies related to digital innovations in physician–patient communication showed the lowest baseline confidence levels but the strongest subjective learning gains following the intervention. In particular, students’ theoretical understanding of AI-based communication support tools and confidence levels of the practical use of digital health applications increased in the self-assessment. The OSCE findings support this observation, as the largest performance differences between intervention and control group were observed in AI-related competencies and consultation closing, which largely accounted for the overall group difference. These findings also highlight the importance of distinguishing between knowledge acquisition, self-perceived competence, and objectively demonstrated communication competence. While theoretical understanding and self-assessed confidence increased across both digital and traditional communication domains, performance-based differences in the OSCE were more limited and most pronounced for AI-related counselling tasks and consultation closing. Recent research describes the increasing digitalization of healthcare and the integration of AI-based applications as transformative developments that are reshaping the professional roles and competencies expected of physicians [ 46 , 49 , 50 ]. Conversely, students in the present study reported limited confidence in digital aspects of interaction, suggesting a gap between emerging professional demands and current training. This discrepancy highlights the need to integrate digital communication competencies more systematically into medical curricula [ 13 , 46 , 51 ]. In line with this, a growing body of literature advocates the early integration of AI-related competencies within medical education [ 52 – 54 ]. The findings of this pilot study support the feasibility and acceptability of integrating H5P-supported self-directed learning, AI-related content, and face-to-face communication training within a blended learning format. While conclusions regarding effectiveness cannot be drawn from the present exploratory study, the observed learning outcomes provide preliminary signals that warrant further investigation in larger studies. Students first acquired theoretical knowledge through H5P-supported self-directed learning before applying this knowledge in face-to-face seminars. Independent exploration of narrative communication techniques as well as AI-based tools prior to in-class discussion may promote experiential learning and perspective-taking, including adopting the role of a patient using digital communication support systems.
sections.limitations: This study is subject to certain methodological limitations. The small sample size highly limits statistical power and generalizability and precluded inferential statistical analyses, resulting in findings that are primarily descriptive, explorative and hypothesis-generating. Also, although OSCE performance was assessed using a standardized communication rubric and examiner training, formal inter-rater reliability could not be established. Furthermore, although the OSCE provided a performance-based measure and was supported by access to an established standardized patient program at Rostock University Medical Center, ensuring a high level of consistency and professionalism in the simulations [ 55 , 56 ], data collection still relied in part on self-assessments, which may be affected by known biases, particularly discrepancies between perceived and actual competence [ 57 ]. In addition, scale construction followed content-based item groupings, and internal consistency was not assessed, limiting the reliability of the measures [ 58 ]. Future iterations of the elective course with a larger sample and the use of a standardized questionnaire would therefore be desirable. In addition, objective learning management system analytics could not be included due to local data protection regulations. Engagement with the digital modules was therefore assessed through participant self-report rather than platform-derived usage metrics. Although all students reported full completion of the online modules and positive experiences with the digital learning activities, objective measures of module usage or interaction intensity were not available. Moreover, participation in the elective course was voluntary, likely resulting in a self-selection bias toward highly motivated students with positive attitudes toward patient-centered communication. Although the control group was recruited through the same channels, the elective course was additionally advertised via the university course catalogue, which may have contributed to differences in motivation and interest between groups. However, participants were recruited from the same semesters to minimize differences in prior training. Beyond this selection effect, self-reported competence gains after the intervention may also be influenced by increased awareness and reflection triggered by engagement with communication-related content.
sections.conclusion: Overall, the findings of this pilot study should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Future studies with larger samples are required to further evaluate the sustainable integration of blended learning formats into medical curricula. This study aims to provide a conceptual stimulus for further research on blended learning. It also highlights the potential of integrating digital innovations, such as digital health applications and AI, into medical communication training and may support future curricular development. Complementary qualitative focus groups were conducted within the same project to capture students’ learning experiences and perceptions and will be reported separately. This will allow for a more detailed examination of the course design and its perceived strengths and limitations.

title: Unmasking residual cardiovascular risk: the paradoxical interaction between remnant cholesterol and calculated LDL-C in a tertiary-care cohort
abstract: Background Residual atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk often remains even after low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels have been brought down to target levels. Remnant cholesterol (RC) and inflammation have been increasingly linked to the residual risk. We aimed to investigating whether the discriminative value of RC the ability of RC to discriminate and its claimed interactions with LDL-C are due to a real clinical phenotype or are affected by formula-dependent biases between the Friedewald and Sampson-NIH equations. Methods We performed a cross-sectional analysis of consecutively tested adults ( n = 3,342) using residual serum samples from routine clinical monitoring. To reduce analytical variability, all lipid profiles were analyzed using a single, dedicated reagent lot. We contrasted risk models with Friedewald-calculated versus Sampson-NIH-calculated LDL-C to assess equation-dependent differences. Lipid parameters, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured. ASCVD was defined using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Edition (ICD-10) codes. Missing covariate data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (m = 50), with additional complete-case sensitivity analyses for CRP-related models. To reduce bias, the observed ASCVD status was included as an auxiliary variable; the outcome itself was not imputed. The discriminative performance of nested logistic regression models was assessed through the pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and pooled DeLong p-values. Results The primary clinical focus was the presence of documented pre-existing ASCVD diagnoses, identified in 11.4% of the cohort, while 9.4% of participants met the criteria for atherogenic dyslipidemia (AD). In the primary analysis with Friedewald LDL-C, we detected a statistically significant ( p < 0.001) negative interaction between LDL-C and RC, while logCRP remained an independent correlate in the adjusted model. Interestingly, when we verified this using the more accurate Sampson-NIH equation to minimize the possibility that the result would be solely due to calculation bias, the paradoxical interaction was still statistically significant ( p = 0.003) along with a strong model performance (AUC: 0.729). This indicates that the interaction is not entirely explained by the mathematical artifact of the Friedewald formula, but rather represents a consistent statistical pattern in this cohort. Conclusion RC adds statistically significant value to risk discrimination. The continuous inverse relationship of LDL-C with high RC identifies a statistical pattern consistent with persistent atherogenic burden despite apparently optimal calculated LDL-C levels. Awareness of this potential suppressor effect may aid in refining risk stratification in tertiary-care settings. sections.background: Residual atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk often remains even after low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels have been brought down to target levels. Remnant cholesterol (RC) and inflammation have been increasingly linked to the residual risk. We aimed to investigating whether the discriminative value of RC the ability of RC to discriminate and its claimed interactions with LDL-C are due to a real clinical phenotype or are affected by formula-dependent biases between the Friedewald and Sampson-NIH equations.
sections.methods: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of consecutively tested adults ( n = 3,342) using residual serum samples from routine clinical monitoring. To reduce analytical variability, all lipid profiles were analyzed using a single, dedicated reagent lot. We contrasted risk models with Friedewald-calculated versus Sampson-NIH-calculated LDL-C to assess equation-dependent differences. Lipid parameters, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) were measured. ASCVD was defined using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Edition (ICD-10) codes. Missing covariate data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (m = 50), with additional complete-case sensitivity analyses for CRP-related models. To reduce bias, the observed ASCVD status was included as an auxiliary variable; the outcome itself was not imputed. The discriminative performance of nested logistic regression models was assessed through the pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and pooled DeLong p-values.
sections.results: The primary clinical focus was the presence of documented pre-existing ASCVD diagnoses, identified in 11.4% of the cohort, while 9.4% of participants met the criteria for atherogenic dyslipidemia (AD).
