sections.key points: • Early breast cancer • Magnetic resonance imaging • Preoperative staging • Practice patterns • Guidelines • International survey
sections.introduction: The preoperative assessment of early breast cancer (EBC) aims to achieve complete tumor resection with optimal cosmetic outcomes. EBC represents stage I and stage II invasive cancers according to a narrow definition and includes ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and stage IIIA or even operable stage IIIB according to a broader oncological definition. While mammography and ultrasound are standard imaging modalities to assess disease extent, breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior sensitivity, with a median incremental cancer detection rate of 16% compared to conventional imaging ( 1 ). This has fueled a rising trend in preoperative MRI use, particularly in the United States, where preoperative breast MRI application rates in EBC reached 60% for women under 65 years of age in 2020 ( 2 , 3 , 4 ). The clinical benefit of routine preoperative MRI, however, remains controversial. While it improves surgical planning, randomized trials have shown it can increase mastectomy rates by 8% without demonstrating a significant improvement in local relapse-free or overall survival ( 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ). Other studies suggest this initial increase in mastectomies may be balanced by a reduction in reoperation rates ( 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ). The largest and most recent meta-analysis demonstrated both improved recurrence-free survival (hazard ratio = 0.77) and better overall survival (hazard ratio = 0.89) with the use of pre-operative contrast-enhanced MRI ( 13 ), though some of this benefit may reflect patient selection (with healthier women having MRI). This conflicting evidence is reflected in heterogeneous national and international guidelines, which largely advise against routine use, reserving it for specific scenarios, such as histologically-proven invasive lobular carcinoma, dense breasts, suspicion of multifocality/multicentricity or imaging inconsistencies ( Table 1 ). This creates clinical ambiguity. While national trends for preoperative MRI are documented for the United States, comprehensive data on global practice patterns are lacking. The present study aimed to map current global practices, perceived benefits, and challenges associated with preoperative breast MRI in EBC among members of the Senologic International Society (SIS) and SIS Working Group to identify key drivers and areas for improvement.
sections.study design and survey distribution: This study was performed according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. After reviewing several international guidelines, a cross-sectional, web-based survey was conducted. The authors developed a 20-question English-language questionnaire, designed to be completed within 10 minutes. The questionnaire was distributed via email to members of the SIS and its working groups. A total of 120 recipients at an expert level were asked to answer and to forward the survey to other experienced colleagues. Communicative hubs among the experts helped to extend the reach of the survey. However, due to data protection regulations, we were not given information on the number or identities of the experts contacted, making it impossible to calculate an exact response rate. The SIS is a worldwide federation of over 100 societies devoted to breast care, and its associated SIS working group comprise groupings of individual experts.
sections.data collection: The survey was hosted online using a survey and feedback platform named PM+ (Performance Management Plus), and responses were collected over 14 days (October 28-November 11, 2024).
sections.statistical analysis: Data from 114 respondents were analyzed using SPSS, version 31 (IBM Inc., Armonk, NY, USA). Analyses included descriptive statistics, chi-square test, Kruskal-Wallis tests, cross-tabulation and ordinal logistic regression (PLUM, Polytomous Universal Model). The threshold for significance was p <0.05.
sections.survey content: The survey was divided into five sections: Section A: Respondent demographics (specialty, continent, country). Section B: Affiliation and center characteristics (certification status, type of institution, annual breast cancer operation volume). Section C: Local and national MRI use (annual MRI volume, national infrastructure, reporting, reimbursement, access times). Section D: MR policy and guidelines (guideline recommendations, personal adherence, perceived patient benefit, comparison with other modalities, eg CEM). Section E: Specific indications (patient characteristics, risk factors, and planned treatment options qualifying for MRI). All questions included in the questionnaire are shown in Table 1 of the Supplementary Material 1 , 2 .
sections.guideline recommendation: Several international guidelines have been reviewed and judged whether they recommend routine preoperative breast MRI. The summarized results are shown in Table 1 . All guidelines were judged to indicate that preoperative MRI was appropriate but only in specific circumstances with none recommending routine use in all patients. These guidelines suggest preoperative MRI for specific conditions, where conventional mammographic and ultrasound imaging is limited, and/or the risk for additional cancers is increased, such as in invasive lobular carcinoma, dense breasts, suspicion of multifocality/multicentricity, or larger size on ultrasound than mammography. Further, most guidelines require that centers should also have the facilities to perform correlation with prior breast imaging, to offer MRI-guided biopsy, and to have the capacity for multidisciplinary discussion and assessment of imaging-pathology concordance. We did not review protocol specifications such as abbreviated MRI or inclusion of diffusion-weighted imaging.
sections.respondent characteristics, heterogeneou: Of 114 respondents, 50.0% ( n = 57) were radiologists and 46.5% ( n = 53) were breast surgeons and 3.5% ( n = 4) oncologists ( Table 2 ). Most participants were from Europe (52.6%, n = 60) or Asia (40.4%, n = 46), all of whom were from Japan. The countries with the highest numbers of respondents were Japan (40.4%, n = 46), Germany (28.9%, n = 33), Belgium (9.6%, n = 11), the USA (3.5%, n = 4) and Türkiye (3.5%, n = 4). The majority (89.5%, n = 102/114) worked in certified breast centers, distributed across community-based hospitals (33.3%, n = 38), university hospitals (31.6%, n = 36), and private institutions (29.8%, n = 34) or other institutions (5%, n = 5, and one missing answer). In general, the answers to all questions were significantly heterogeneously distributed (all p <0.05).
sections.center volume, breast mri turnaround tim: Center Volumes: The mean number of annual breast cancer operations per center was 355. The mean number of annual breast MRI examinations was 514. In Europe and North America, MRI use was concentrated in fewer centers with high annual examination volumes (“high‑volume, concentrated use”). In contrast, Asia (Japan) showed broader diffusion, with more centers adopting preoperative MRI but each performing fewer examinations (“low-volume, diffuse adoption”) ( Table 2 of the Supplementary Material 1 , 2 ). MRI Turnaround Times: 98% ( n = 112/114) of total respondents reported a significant variation across continents in timespan between request of the breast MRI to the MRI report (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.002). Rapid access to MRI results (within 7 days) was reported by 67.5% ( n = 77/114) of respondents, with 19.6% ( n = 9/46) in Japan having access on the same day. MRI Infrastructure: The knowledge about national MRI infrastructure was limited, with 38.6% ( n = 44/114) of respondents not answering this question. Reimbursement by the public health system was more comprehensive in Japan (79.5%, n = 35/44 public health coverage) than in Europe (64.4%, n = 58/90).
sections.indications for preoperative mri: Indications are detailed in Table 3 . Overall, the most common indications based on patient characteristics were invasive lobular carcinoma (93.0%, n = 106/114) and suspicion of multifocality/multicentricity on conventional imaging (84.2%, n = 96/114). For risk factors, family history of breast cancer (76.3%, n = 87/114) and high breast density (73.7%, n = 84/114) were the most cited. In terms of treatment planning, neoadjuvant therapy (78.1%, n = 89/114) and breast-conserving therapy (71.1%, n = 81/114) were the primary drivers. Significant variation was seen for T1 staging, supported by 76.1% ( n = 35/46) of Japanese respondents but only 13.3% ( n = 8/60) of Europeans ( p <0.001). Detailed cross calculations are included in the Supplementary Material 1 , 2 .
sections.guideline perceptions and personal pract: Guideline Perception: Half of the respondents (50.0%, n = 57/114) reported that their national guidelines recommend preoperative MRI for EBC. This perception was more frequent among breast surgeons (67.9%, n = 36/53) than radiologists (31.6%, n = 18/57). Further, this perception was stronger in Japan (78.3%, n = 36/46) compared to Europe (30.0%, n = 18/60) ( Table 4 ), a remarkable contrast to the actual guideline positions shown in Table 1 . The practice guidelines of the American College of Radiology (ACR) and the Japanese are liberal in evaluating the extent of disease with newly diagnosed breast cancer and both include DCIS as an indication. However, most guidelines at the time of the survey suggest limiting the use of preoperative MRI to only a few select patient populations. Personal Practice: Strikingly, among those 57 respondents who perceived guidelines as supportive, 52.6% ( n = 30/57) reported performing more MRIs than guidelines recommend, 36.8% ( n = 21/57) reported strictly following the guideline indications and 8.8% ( n = 5/58) performed fewer MRIs than recommended ( Table 5 ). These liberal or restrictive personal practice patterns could not systematically be explained by continent, specialty, payer, institution type or MR examination numbers in logistic models. Personal Judgement: A majority (84.2%, n = 96/114) believed preoperative MRI provided patient benefit, with none believing it caused harm. This belief was positively correlated with the perception of positive guideline support for the practice ( p <0.05) ( Table 6 ). This divergence between widespread perception of guideline endorsement in daily practice and restrained guideline content ( Table 1 ) was a key finding. Associations with perceived positive guidelines recommendations: Centers in countries where guideline endorsement was perceived for preoperative EBC MRI demonstrated shorter MRI turnaround times compared to those without such ( p <0.02). This association between perceived guideline endorsement and reporting efficiency does not imply causality because structural or resource‑related factors may also contribute.
sections.availability of preoperative staging too: The availability of staging tools is detailed in Table 7 . Overall, ultrasound (97.4%, n = 111/114) and mammography (93.9%, n = 107/114) were nearly universally available. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) was less often available (58.8%, n = 67/114) and contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) was even less often available (21.9%, 25/114). Among the Japanese respondents, more than half reported availability of dedicated breast CT (54.3%, n = 25/46) compared to the whole collective (26.3%, n = 30/114), while CEM was not used for preoperative staging at all in Japan. For the small subgroup of 25 (21.9% of all respondents) CEM users in Europe, USA and Latin America, preoperative MRI was judged to be more beneficial than CEM by 56% ( n = 14/25), equal to CEM in 32% ( n = 8/25) and worse in 12% ( n = 3/25).
sections.discussion and conclusion: Preoperative breast MRI consistently detects additional cancers that remain occult on mammography and ultrasound. Whether these additional findings translate into improved clinical outcomes in EBC had been a matter of debate until 2024. In that year, the largest metaanalyses available to date reported improved recurrence-free and overall survival associated with the use of preoperative MRI ( 1 , 12 , 13 ). Our SIS global survey was performed in 2024 and reveals both striking variation and notable consensus. The most prominent finding was the profound interdisciplinary and intercontinental disparity in guideline perception and practice: 50% of respondents reported that guidelines in their region positively recommended preoperative MRI in EBC. At the same time, more than four fifths (84.2%, 96/114) of all respondents expressed belief in a patient benefit, a sentiment transcending geography and specialty. Clinical decisions appear to be driven not only by the reported survey indications and the traditional guideline interpretation, but also by local culture and resources, health system organization, and deeply held personal conviction that often diverge in our survey respondents from the guidelines recommendations, which were out of date after the publication of the 2024 meta-analysis ( 13 ). The Evidence-Guideline-Practice Gap: The observed global heterogeneity underscores a fundamental disconnect between guideline recommendations and clinical practice. Most international guidelines advise against routine preoperative MRI, citing historical concerns about increased mastectomy rates and the absence of level‑1 evidence for a survival benefit if they do not respect newest evidence ( 13 ). The American Society of Breast Surgeons (ASBrS) Choosing Wisely® Campaign is the most explicit, stating: “Don’t routinely order breast MRI in new breast cancer patients” ( 14 ). In contrast, responses from Japan suggest a different picture. A majority (78.3%, 36/46) of Japanese respondents reported that national guidelines recommend preoperative breast MRI in EBC, compared with 30% (18/60) of European and 50% (2/4) of U.S. respondents. What do the Japanese guidelines actually say? The 2013 Japanese Breast Cancer Society guidelines do not advocate routine use of MRI and do not mention EBC at all but recommend (Grade B) MRI for three scenarios: to determine diagnosis and treatment policies for intra‑breast lesions, to diagnose the extent of breast cancer and to detect multifocal breast cancer undetectable by mammography and ultrasound ( 15 ). The Japanese breast cancer society clinical practice guidelines for breast cancer screening and diagnosis, 2022 edition, adds: “For MRI-detected lesions that are suspected to be malignant on preoperative contrast-enhanced breast MRI, histological examination should be performed if there is an impact on the surgical procedure”. The rationale has been outlined; the decision on the surgical approach should not be based on preoperative MRI findings alone ( 16 ). This recommendation to perform additional biopsy prior to surgery is shared by all current guidelines. Today, in Japan, treatment policies for T1 stage cancers include radiofrequency ablation (RFA). MRI is required not only to select and monitor patients for RFA versus breast‑conserving therapy (BCT), but also as a prerequisite for reimbursement under public health insurance ( 17 ).This is the reason for widespread acceptance of MRI in EBC in Japan. This national context likely explains the sharp contrast in acceptance of T1 stage as an indication for preoperative MRI, observed in 76% (35/46) of Japanese respondents compared with only 13% (8/60) of Europeans. The 2026 published German S3-Guidelines emphasize the better recurrence-free and overall survival after preoperative MRI according to the latest meta-analysis ( 13 ) and justify the routine use of MRI, or alternatively CEM in all patients with newly diagnosed, locally limited breast cancer in the setting of dense beasts or difficult assessment with mammography and ultrasound ( 18 ). Reported clinical practice across continents exceeds the authors’ expectations. Clinical adoption of preoperative MRI in EBC appears more liberal than guideline recommendations, as reflected in our survey for Japan 50% (18/36), Europe 61.1% (11/18), and reported real-world rates in the literature of 60% preoperative breast MRI of EBC in USA for women under 65 years of age ( 2 , 3 , 4 ). The Drivers for Use of Preoperative MRI beyond Guideline Recommendations: Firstly, although our survey answers do not provide a clear explanation for the overuse of preoperative MRI compared to guideline intentions, it is reasonable to assume that general resources, financial aspects and rapid access to MRI may encourage the willingness to perform a preoperative MRI examination. Secondly, the evidence base continues to evolve and is open to interpretation. While early trials raised concerns, recent meta‑analyses by Eisen et al. ( 13 ) indicate that preoperative MRI significantly reduces re-operation rates (odd ratio = 0.73), re‑excisions (odd ratio = 0.63), and increases recurrence-free survival (hazard ratio = 0.77) and overall survival (hazard ratio = 0.89). The benefit in preventing re‑excisions may outweigh the initial increase in mastectomy rates, particularly in invasive lobular carcinoma and non-calcified DCIS ( 13 , 19 , 20 , 21 ). Moreover, improved detection of synchronous contralateral breast cancers has been associated with a reduction in metachronous contralateral disease (hazard ratio = 0.71) ( 13 ). Thirdly, this nuanced benefit where the outcome metric has shifted from survival to surgical precision and patient burden resonates strongly with clinicians, as reflected in the 84.2% (96/114) belief in patient benefit reported in our survey. Historically, pioneers of BCT achieved survival outcomes equivalent to mastectomy through wider excisions and radiotherapy, relying solely on mammography for breast staging ( 22 ). Contemporary surgical paradigms, however, favor smaller excisions to optimize cosmesis and multimodal preoperative breast staging. In this context, MRI is increasingly perceived as a modern tool to offset reduced surgical margins, enabling “first‑pass” clear margins in an era of precision surgery. Combined with advances in systemic therapy that improve overall survival, this reframes the value of MRI not as a determinant of survival, but as a tool of enhancing surgical quality and reducing patient burden, a rationale not fully captured by traditional evidence hierarchies ( 12 , 13 ). Fourthly, emerging data on molecular subtypes further complicate a one‑size‑fits‑all guideline approach. For example, MRI has been shown to reduce mastectomy rates in HER2‑positive disease ( 21 ). Respondent comments and recent publications emphasize that the indication for preoperative MRI in hormone-negative HER2+ and triple‑negative cancers is driven more by planned neoadjuvant systemic therapy than by biological aggressivity alone ( 23 , 24 , 25 ). Both subtypes are prone to multiple occult ipsilateral invasive lesions, higher local recurrence rates and nearly all patients with HER2+ or triple‑negative disease, as well as those with invasive lobular carcinoma, are potential guideline candidates to undergo preoperative breast MRI in U.S. centers. Currently the Alliance A11104/ACRIN 6694 phase III trial is examining the hypothesis that preoperative breast MRI improves staging and selection of stage I and II patients with ER/PR- negative tumors for BCT, thus lowering rates of local regional recurrence ( 26 ). The Drivers of Decision-Making: Survey Indications and “Fast Thinking”: Our data show that the decision for preoperative breast MRI in EBC varies by the traditional patient and tumor characteristics, but now also depends on medical specialty, subjective beliefs and local infrastructure. The strong contrast between Japan (predominantly surgeon respondents) and Europe (predominantly radiologist respondents) suggests the perceived value of MRI is viewed through different professional lenses. The reliance on risk factors such as previous history of breast cancer, despite their limited evidence base for preoperative planning, illustrates the influence of intuitive “fast thinking” in clinical decision-making. Nobel laureate Kahneman ( 27 ) examined this “fast thinking mode” in economic contexts and demonstrated that it is prone to several systematic biases, including optimism bias and a tendency to overestimate benefits while underestimating costs. Breast MRI remains the most sensitive modality for detecting breast cancer in high-risk women and as supplemental screening in those with extremely dense breasts ( 28 , 29 , 30 ). Given this sensitivity, it is understandable that breast surgeons may favor MRI in a proven cancer; to determine tumor size, identify additional foci in either breast, and assess potential extension to the chest wall or lymph nodes. In the absence of precise risk stratification for preclinical and clinical scenarios, surgeons and radiologists seem to intuitively prioritize the anticipated individual benefit for the patient over restrictive guideline recommendations. Practical factors further reinforce this decision pattern, including rapid access to breast MRI, reimbursement policies, and the ease of achieving interdisciplinary consensus for performing preoperative MRI ( 30 ). We hypothesize that intuitive reasoning and contextual facilitators shape practice beyond the boundaries of still valid guidelines that are not adapted to the latest evidence. The Continent-Specific Context: The underlying geographic differences are shaped by the distinct ways in which guidelines are interpreted, contextualized, and implemented across continents ( 31 ). Japan represents a model where perceived guideline support, favorable reimbursement, rapid MRI access, and a strong belief in technological advancement converge. The frequent application of preoperative MRI may explain the moderate use of DBT (26.1%, 12/46) and absence of CEM in our survey. Europe embodies a more restrictive approach, more closely aligned with the intention of the guidelines, likely influenced by cost-control and a higher reliance on radiologists as gatekeepers. Overall availability of ultrasound (100%, 60/60) and high dissemination of DBT (80%, 48/60) and to a lesser degree CEM (31.7%, 39/60) substituting breast MRI may explain this pattern. In Europe, a milestone survey conducted by the European Society of Breast Imaging on the use of clinical breast MRI has reported a restrictive approach of north European countries as far back as 2016 ( 32 ). In Southern European countries, preoperative breast MRI was more frequently performed in all breast cancer patients rather than being limited to those with invasive lobular carcinoma (32.1% versus 6% in northern Europe) ( 32 ). A similar pattern has been observed for patients with DCIS, where 50.9% of respondents in southern Europe reported routinely using preoperative MRI, compared with 22.2% in northern European countries ( 32 ). United States: Although our U.S. survey data remain limited, the reported studies provide a coherent picture. In the United States, preoperative breast MRI continues to be used at comparatively high rates in EBC, despite divergent professional recommendations ( 2 , 3 , 4 ). The ACR quite generously supports preoperative MRI for evaluating disease extent, characterizing additional ipsilateral and contralateral lesions including DCIS and invasive lobular carcinoma and assessing chestwall involvement or response to neoadjuvant therapy ( 33 ). In contrast, surgical guidelines from the ASBrS strictly has argued against any routine use of preoperative MRI dating back to 2018 ( 14 ). Today MRI is most frequently requested for women with dense breasts in Australia ( 34 ). To the best of our knowledge, none of the major U.S. studies or registries (SEER, NCDB, Medicare datasets) report a national percentage of preoperative MRI use stratified by breast density. In the U.S., however, levels of public and provider awareness is high regarding the masking effect of dense breast tissue and its associated increased cancer risk. This awareness has been actively shaped by scientific societies, advocacy groups, and dedicated educational platforms, exemplified by DenseBreastInfo.org, which disseminate information on breast density, supplemental screening, and statelevel legislation ( 35 ). The recent Food and Drug Administration National Dense Breast Reporting requirement, mandating that all mammography facilities inform patients whether their breast tissue is “dense” or “not dense” and include an official density assessment in clinician reports, has further institutionalized this awareness ( 36 ). The authors hypothesize that these expectations on supplemental imaging in women with dense breasts may extend beyond screening and influence decisionmaking in the preoperative setting, contributing to higher preoperative MRI use in the United States compared with other countries. Realworld surveys suggest that feeforservice reimbursement structures, defensive medical practices, and a strong emphasis on individualized surgical planning further contribute to this persistent utilization pattern ( 2 , 3 , 4 ). Guidelines themselves are complex instruments balancing evidence, harm, benefit, and socio-economic factors aiming to provide support for physicians and patients to utilize shared decision making ( 31 , 33 ). When evidence for a clear survival benefit is weak, as is the case with preoperative MRI before the time of the 2024 survey, recommendations naturally lean towards case-by-case discussion. This inherent ambiguity creates space for “instinctive judgement”, as described above ( 27 ). A clinician’s perspective can shift the historic calculus from “no survival benefit” (arguing against MRI) to “prevents reoperations and optimizes cosmesis” (arguing for MRI), especially for subtypes like invasive lobular carcinoma or in patients planned for neoadjuvant therapy. This survey confirms that in practice, the indications often extend beyond the core scenarios incorporating best subjective intentions (assumed patient benefit), risk factors such as dense breasts, planned neoadjuvant therapy and a desire for comprehensive pre-surgical mapping.
sections.implications for future guidelines and r: Scientifically, such ambiguity can be resolved and nuanced by subgroup analysis with reference to metanalysis or new trial data, such as the current phase III Alliance A011104/ACRIN 6694 study, which to date does not suggest an oncologic benefit from routine preoperative MRI in early-stage hormone-negative cancers, i.e. HER2+ and triple negative disease ( 13 , 26 ). This is not surprising in the era of powerful radiation oncology and improving adjuvant/neoadjuvant therapy, both of which can eliminate residual malignant lesions in patients without preoperative MRI. Future trials need to focus on stage-specific surgical endpoints as re-resection and conversion from breast-conservative surgery to mastectomy, and whether deescalation of surgical therapy will progress further with improvement in systemic therapy. The Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI‑RADS) 2025 manual represents a major step forward to obtain up-scaled real-world data ( 37 ). By recommending audits of breast MRI examinations after cancer diagnosis (BI‑RADS MR 6), it provides a unified framework to define and validate expected performance parameters of preoperative MRI ( 38 ). Those data are needed for more nuanced, international guidelines that explicitly address stage dependent specific clinical scenarios (e.g., molecular subtypes) for oncoplastic planning. The final goal will be harmonizing preoperative imaging guidelines with preexisting treatment guidelines, updated evidence on survival benefit for early and advanced breast cancer within an integrated holistic concept ( 39 , 40 , 41 ).
sections.study limitations: This study has several limitations. All data are self‑reported, and the survey format primarily captures “fast‑thinking” clinical judgments. As the term EBC was not explicitly defined in the questionnaire, respondents may have interpreted it differently. A standard definition of EBC shared by most guidelines refers to invasive breast cancer confined to the breast and/or axillary lymph nodes without distant metastases (stage I to IIIA). However, some experts favor broader or narrower borders divergent to the mainstream and include DCIS (stage 0) or operable stage IIIB or restrict EBC to nodenegative or small T1 or T2 tumors. These divergent definitions complicate international comparisons and may influence how clinicians interpret survey questions related to EBC. Although international, the sample size is too small to be representative for most countries, and a selection bias toward clinicians using breast MRI in certified centers is likely. A substantial proportion of respondents came from Japan and Europe. This uneven geographic distribution limits the global generalizability of the results, particularly for less developed regions. Imbalances in respondent specialties between Japan and Europe, together with low participation from other continents, may further skew the findings. All statistical analyses assess associations only; they do not establish causation. For example, a positive perception of guidelines may correlate with faster reporting, but structural factors such as resources, workflow, or infrastructure could equally account for this difference. Another limitation is that, unlike therapy guidelines with stage‑ or subtype‑specific recommendations, most preoperative breast MRI guidelines remain broad and do not differentiate between early and advanced disease. Our survey did not attempt to define a universal standard for what constitutes the presence or absence of preoperative MRI guidance in EBC, acknowledging differing interpretive traditions. A more holistic reading, common in some Asian contexts, may treat broad recommendations as implicitly inclusive of early‑stage disease, whereas a more selective, scenario‑driven interpretation, typical of Western scientific traditions, may conclude that no explicit recommendation exists. This distinction aligns with established findings in cultural psychology, which demonstrate that East Asian cognition tends to be more holistic and context‑oriented, whereas Western cognition is typically more analytic and object‑focused ( 42 ). In conclusion, this SIS survey maps the current global practices and demonstrates that the use of preoperative breast MRI is shaped more by geography, different cultural approaches and resources, and clinical interpretation of evolving evidence than by strict adherence to the current guidelines. Overall, 84.2% of all respondents believed preoperative MRI provided a patient benefit, with none believing it caused harm. The most frequent overall indications were invasive lobular carcinoma (93.0%, 106/114), mammographic/sonographic suspicion of multifocality/multicentricity (84.2%, 96/114), and planned neoadjuvant therapy (78.1%, 89/114), and in Japan, assessing the extent of DCIS (97.8%, 45/46). Among respondents who reported using positive guidelines, 52.6% (30/57) performed more MRI examinations than the guidelines advised. Key influencing factors included specialty reimbursement, and rapid access to MRI. These findings highlight the need for standardized guidelines including the newest evidence and further research to clarify the role of MRI in the modern multidisciplinary management of EBC. Functional and abbreviated MR specifications and CEM should be integrated in future international guidelines updates ( 42 , 43 ).
sections.ethics: Ethics Committee Approval: Not necessary. Informed Consent: No personal patient data were used for this survey. No informed consent necessary.

title: The Role of Inflammatory Biomarkers in Disease Severity and Treatment Response across Psoriasis, Atopic Dermatitis, and Hidradenitis Suppurativa—A Narrative Review
abstract: Chronic inflammatory skin diseases (CISDs) such as psoriasis (PsO), atopic dermatitis (AD), and hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) involve both cutaneous and systemic immune dysregulation, whereas commonly used scores rely largely on subjective clinical features and insufficiently reflect underlying inflammatory activity or cardiovascular risk. This review summarizes evidence across three biomarker domains: tissue–level pathways (the Fas/FasL and interleukin (IL)–21/IL–21R), circulating inflammatory mediators, and hematology–derived indices (the neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet–to–lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte–to–lymphocyte ratio (MLR), pan–immune–inflammation value (PIV), derived neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio (d–NLR), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), systemic immune–inflammation index (SII), and aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI)) in relation to disease activity, therapeutic response, and cardiometabolic burden. A targeted literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (January 2000 to November 2025), supplemented by artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted retrieval, manual screening of reference lists, and citation tracking. Studies providing patient–derived clinical or translational data were included and summarized in structured comparative tables. The findings indicate that dysregulated Fas/FasL signaling contributes to keratinocyte apoptosis resistance and chronic epidermal inflammation in PsO and AD, with limited data in HS. IL–21 is elevated in PsO and AD, correlating with clinical severity and epidermal hyperplasia, whereas its role in HS remains unexplored despite the strong Th17 and B–cell signature of the disease. Complete blood count–derived indices demonstrate associations with systemic inflammation and increased cardiometabolic risk, particularly in PsO and HS, yet diagnostic performance varies and methodological standardization is lacking. Taken together, these biomarkers provide insights into local and systemic aspects of disease biology but are not yet validated for clinical use. Integrating tissue–specific mediators, soluble biomarkers, and hematologic indices into multimodal panels may ultimately strengthen precision monitoring of disease activity, treatment response, and cardiovascular risk in CISDs. Prospective, multicenter studies are needed to establish clinically actionable, biomarker–driven strategies that enable more mechanism informed and personalized care.

sections.key summary points: Chronic inflammatory skin diseases (CISDs), including psoriasis (PsO), atopic dermatitis (AD), and hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), involve systemic immune activation that is insufficiently reflected by current clinical severity scores, emphasizing the need for objective biomarkers. The Fas/FasL axis appears to contribute to sustained cutaneous inflammation through non–apoptotic, pro–inflammatory signaling, although evidence, particularly in HS, remains limited. IL–21 represents a pleiotropic cytokine linking Th1 and Th17 activation with epidermal and inflammatory remodeling, with supportive data in PsO and AD but a clear knowledge gap in HS. Complete blood count (CBC)–derived inflammatory indices are accessible markers of systemic inflammation that show potential associations with disease activity and treatment response, though findings are heterogeneous and require standardization. Integrating tissue expression profiles, serum biomarkers, and CBC–derived indices in prospective studies may enable the identification of biomarker panels for disease monitoring, response prediction, and personalized management across CISDs.
sections.introduction: Chronic inflammatory skin diseases (CISDs), such as psoriasis (PsO), atopic dermatitis (AD), and hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), are prevalent conditions that collectively affect millions of people worldwide, making them some of the most common diseases in the western world [ 1 ]. PsO is estimated to affect approximately 4.4% of the global adult population [ 2 ]. It is a multifaceted dermatological condition. The most common variant is PsO vulgaris which accounts for more than 80% of cases and usually manifests as itching and painful, erythematous, scaly plaques on the skin [ 3 , 4 ]. A significant subset (about 20% of patients) also develops psoriatic arthritis [ 5 ]. The second CISD is AD, ranked first among skin diseases by disability–adjusted life–years [ 6 ]. According to Tian et al., the global prevalence is estimated at 2.6% [ 7 ]. It is characterized by chronic, relapsing eczematous lesions with intense pruritus. AD often coexists with other atopic conditions such as asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergies, contributing to its overall clinical burden [ 6 ]. HS is less prevalent, with an estimated prevalence of around 0.3–0.4% on average in the general population, but it is a highly debilitating disease [ 8 ]. Clinically, HS presents with recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, and skin tunnels in apocrine gland–bearing areas (axillary, groin, perianal, and inframammary regions), often leading to purulent malodorous discharge and fibrotic scars [ 9 ]. All three of these diseases have a profound impact on patients’ quality of life and psychological well–being, due to their visible chronic nature, associated pain or itch, and social stigma. Despite their differing clinical presentations, PsO, AD, and HS share the common features of immune–mediated pathways driving chronic skin inflammation [ 10 ]. However, each condition is characterized by distinct immunological pathways. PsO is an immune–mediated disorder dominated by T helper 1 (Th1), Th17 and Th22 cell responses. In psoriatic lesions, keratinocytes (KCs) proliferation is fueled by pro–inflammatory mediators secreted mainly by T cells, such as interleukin (IL)–17, IL–21, IL–22, and interferon (IFN)–γ, as well as by dendritic cells (DCs), notably tumor necrosis factor (TNF)–α, IL–6, IL–20, IL–23, nitric oxide, and KCs themselves, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), IL–20, and chemokines [ 11 ]. In contrast, AD is classically a Th2–skewed inflammatory disease, with high levels of IL–4, IL–13, IL–5, and associated IgE responses. Notably, chronic or severe AD can also exhibit a mixed Th2/Th1/Th17 profile, indicating a more complex immune microenvironment in long–standing disease [ 12 ]. Inflammation in HS is highly complex, involving both innate and adaptive immune dysregulation. While it is often described as a Th17–driven disease, with IL–17 playing a major pathogenic role similar to PsO, additional mechanisms contribute, including activation of mast cells, DCs, monocytes, B cells, and plasma cells. Inflammatory activity extends beyond visible lesions, affecting even non–lesional skin through persistent immune activation and fibroblast involvement. Moreover, chronic HS leads to structural remodeling with epithelial mesenchymal transition, fibroblast activation, and the formation of tertiary lymphoid organs that perpetuate local immune responses [ 13 ]. Despite these differences, there are converging inflammatory pathways across these inflammatory dermatoses. For example, the Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK/STAT) signaling cascade is activated. Notably, AD and HS have been shown to utilize the JAK/STAT pathway in propagating inflammation, which provides a rationale for the efficacy of JAK inhibitor therapies in these diseases [ 14 – 16 ]. Additionally, certain cytokines (such as IL–36 or IL–1 family members) have been implicated as shared drivers in CISDs. These common immune mediators suggest that, while the upstream triggers may differ, downstream inflammatory circuits in the skin have areas of overlap [ 17 ]. This is further exemplified by the success of targeted biologic drugs that can treat different diseases. As highlighted by, TNF–α blockade, for instance, is a therapy that can benefit both PsO and HS, reflecting the role of TNF–α in both diseases [ 14 ]. Studies indicate that IL–21 represents a universal immunological cytokine involved in PsO, AD, and other CISDs, where it contributes to aberrant T–cell activation and sustained cutaneous inflammation [ 18 ]. Another universal pathway presumably contributing to shared pathogenesis and representing an interesting target for future investigation is the Fas (CD95)/FasL (CD178) system [ 19 – 21 ]. The Fas/FasL axis is classically known as a trigger of programmed cell death (apoptosis) [ 22 ]. Within PsO lesions, Fas expression on KCs is increased, yet its’ signaling appears to be shifted toward anti–apoptotic and pro–inflammatory pathways, rather than the physiological pro–apoptotic response [ 21 ]. In HS, a single study reported that Fas and FasL were significantly overexpressed in lesional skin of Pyoderma gangrenosum, Acne, and Suppurative Hidradenitis (PASH) syndrome patients compared with healthy controls [ 19 ]. In AD, limited data from small cohorts likewise suggest a potential role of the Fas/FasL axis in disease pathogenesis and its possible value as a biomarker [ 23 – 25 ]. IL–21 has pleiotropic effects, generally activating various inflammatory pathways. In the context of dermatologic disease, studies strongly suggest that IL–21 is involved in the pathogenesis of inflammatory skin disorders such as AD, lichen planus, PsO, lupus erythematosus, pemphigus, Sjögren's syndrome, and systemic sclerosis [ 18 ]. While IL–21 has been studied in PsO and AD, its role in HS remains unexplored. Identifying shared immunological pathways, particularly involving IL–21, the Fas/FasL axis, and their soluble forms could have not only pathogenetic relevance by enhancing understanding of the immunophenotypic diversity of CISDs but also predictive value in terms of disease course and treatment response. Furthermore, such insights may enable the identification of objective biomarkers reflecting disease activity. The scoring systems that are currently used for PsO, AD, and HS severity assessment are usually subjective or semi–quantitative measures. Moreover, they do not assess the systemic immune mediated inflammation, which is an inseparable part of CISDs. The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) for PsO, the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) for AD, and IHS4 (International Hidradenitis Suppurativa Severity Score System) for HS are subject to several limitations and need to be replaced or complemented with objective markers. Robust biomarkers would ideally be more sensitive in disease assessment and detection of disease exacerbation, comparable between the institutions, may quantitatively reflect the systemic inflammation, capture the underlying immunological activity, and contribute to personalization of treatment strategies. Biomarkers can take many forms. However, despite intense research, no biomarker has yet been validated for routine clinical use in PsO, AD, or HS. Emerging data suggest that not only IL–21, and the Fas/FasL axis and related soluble mediators, as well as systemic inflammatory indices derived from complete blood count (CBC), may reflect key immunological pathogenesis processes underlying PsO, AD, and HS. Ratios such as the neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet–to–lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte–to–lymphocyte ratio (MLR), pan–immune–inflammation value (PIV), derived neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio (dNLR), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), systemic immune–inflammation index (SII), aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI) reflect both innate and adaptive immune activation. Recent studies have demonstrated that these indices correlate with disease severity and treatment response in CISDs and may complement scoring systems by providing a cost–effective, repeatable measure of systemic inflammatory burden [ 26 – 34 ]. Nevertheless, their role as reliable disease biomarkers or therapeutic indicators remains to be confirmed. This review aims to integrate current evidence on three complementary biomarker domains, Fas/FasL signaling, IL–21/IL–21R immunologic pathways, and CBC–derived systemic inflammatory indices, in the context of disease severity, treatment response, and cardiometabolic risk across PsO, AD, HS. By synthesizing data from tissue, circulating, and hematologic markers, we highlight convergent pathogenic mechanisms, identify knowledge gaps (particularly in HS), and propose directions for biomarker–driven precision monitoring in CISDs. This article is based on previously published studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by the authors.
sections.pso: PsO is characterized by sustained chronic inflammation. Histologically, this manifests as uncontrolled KC proliferation and dysfunctional differentiation, acanthosis, neovascularization, and infiltration of the affected skin by immune cells such as DCs, macrophages, T cells, and neutrophils. Both innate and adaptive immune responses are involved. Although inflammatory pathways share common features, they may partially differ depending on the phenotype, which may result in individual treatment outcomes [ 35 ]. Psoriatic inflammation appears after external factors affect genetically predisposed individuals. More than 70 susceptibility loci have been identified, including genes involved in antigen presentation ( HLA–Cw6 ), IL–23 signaling and promotion of Th17 responses ( IL12B , IL23R , IL23A , and TRAF3IP2 ), IFN signaling, and nuclear factor kappa–light–chain–enhancer of activated B cells (NF–κB) signaling ( TNFAIP3 , NFKBIA , NFKBIZ , TNIP1 , and RELA ) [ 36 ]. Triggering factors that can elicit the disease in genetically predisposed individuals include extrinsic factors: mechanical stress (Koebner phenomenon), air pollutants, sun exposure, drugs, infections, and lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol consumption, dietary habits), and intrinsic factors: obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, or mental stress [ 37 ]. In general, the pathogenesis can be conceptualized as comprising an initiation phase and a maintenance phase characterized by a chronic clinical progression. Trigger factors damage the skin, which activates Toll–like receptors (TLRs) on different cells, mainly KCs and DCs, through the release of damage–associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including double–stranded RNA (dsRNA), single–stranded RNA (ssRNA), and DNA or pathogen–associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Among the most studied PsO–associated AMPs are LL37, β–defensins, and S100 proteins. Activation of plasmacytoid DCs (pDCs) is key in initiating the development of psoriatic plaques by triggering the cascade of cytokine release. Production of IFN–α and IFN–β by pDCs and KCs, with activation by LL37 RNA complexes, causes phenotypic maturation of myeloid DCs (mDCs). Activated mDCs migrate into draining lymph nodes and secrete TNF–α, IL–12, and IL–23. These cytokines are also released by activated slan + monocytes, together amplifying the inflammatory milieu. They promote the differentiation, proliferation, and cytokine release of Th1 (IFN–γ), Th17 and Tc17 (IL–17, IL–21, and IL–22), Th9 (IL–9), and Th22 (IL–22) cells, which, along with TNF–α, stimulate KC proliferation in the epidermis. Moreover, DCs and Langerhans cells (LCs) can present autoantigens, stimulating autoreactive T cells. The impaired skin microbiome can activate γδ T cells, leading to IL–17 and IL–1β production that occurs independently of IL–23 signaling. In the early phase of PsO, neutrophils infiltrate the skin and release extracellular traps, exosomes, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9, and IL–17. Furthermore, KCs themselves participate actively in the inflammatory cascade through secretion of cytokines (IL–1, IL–6, and TNF–α), chemokines, AMPs, and alarmins, which drive the vicious cycle of PsO. Th1 and Th2 cytokines act through JAK/STAT signaling pathways, which is later reflected in targeted treatment, whereas Th17 responses are mediated by NFκB activator 1 (Act1) and NF–κB. However, as already mentioned, pathophysiological pathways may differ depending on PsO subtypes. For example, in pustular PsO, in addition to IL–17 signaling, there is increased expression of IL–1β, IL–36α, and IL–36γ. Some research delves into the autoimmune mechanism of PsO, in which a potential autoantigen candidates include LL37, lipid antigens generated by phospholipase A2 (PLA2) group IVD (PLA2G4D), and hair follicle–derived keratin 17 [ 35 ]. Novel insights into PsO pathogenesis reveal that its mechanism of action involves not only the cytokine expression and release but also a complex network of interactions between cells [ 11 ]. Apart from immune dysregulation involving the IL–23/Th17 axis, some authors have hypothesized that PsO is induced by paradoxical FasL/Fas signaling by activated lymphocytes, resulting in inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., TNF–α and IL–8), persistent inflammation, and KC proliferation. Although there is increased local expression of Fas and peripheral soluble forms of this axis, inflammatory cells and KCs do not undergo apoptosis [ 21 , 38 ]. This mechanism is further discussed in the following section.
sections.ad: AD is a disease caused by defects in the epidermal barrier due to dysfunction of structural proteins, particularly filaggrin (FLG), transglutaminases, keratins, and other intercellular junction components, eg.., claudin–1, as well as alterations in epidermal lipid layers (cholesterol, ceramides, lipids), neuroimmune interactions, and the microbiome (decreased diversity and Staphylococcus aureus domination). Of note, the barrier damage does not necessarily have to be one of the first elements in the pathogenesis of AD, as this mechanism can be reversed, meaning that disorders in type 2 immune activation may themselves cause disturbance of the epidermal barrier. Nevertheless, the key pathogenic element of AD is increased permeability of the epidermal barrier to allergens, pathogens, and irritants, resulting in increased transepidermal water loss, causing dryness and desquamation, and increased skin pH, which enhances increased bacterial proliferation. All these elements together can trigger an exacerbated inflammatory response [ 39 ]. The predominant risk factor for increased skin permeability is genetic predisposition, accounting for 82% of the risk of developing AD, compared with 18% attributable to environmental factors. Numerous susceptibility loci have been identified in AD, involved in pathways regulating IFNγ, innate immunity, T–lymphocyte activity, and epidermal barrier integrity. Depending on the location of filaggrin mutations, onset of AD can be earlier (loci NLRP10) or later ( AFF1 and EHMT1 ). Mutations in the SIDT2 and RBBP8NL genes, i.e., those involved in the response of KCs to herpes virus infection, cause a higher incidence of eczema herpeticum. Genetic susceptibility has been linked to polymorphisms in genes regulating Th2 signaling and cytokine pathways, including IL–4, IL–13, IL–31, IL–33, their receptors (IL–4R, IL–13R), STAT6, thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), and genes involved in vitamin D metabolism. The link with the onset of disease also occurs in the case of epigenetic changes, which may or may not be hereditary. Gene expression depends on several environmental factors, such as exposure to tobacco smoke, environmental pollution, or chemicals. The most studied genes are those associated with exposure to tobacco smoke: NLRP2 (involved in macrophage activity) and PITPNM2 (associated with neutrophils) [ 12 ]. Disrupted epidermal barrier and environmental triggers stimulate KCs to release alarmins (IL–1β, IL–25, IL–33, TSLP), which activate DCs and LCs. DCs are activated by NF–κB and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) pathways and release macrophage–derived chemokine (MDC, CCL22) and thymus and activation–regulated chemokine (TARC, CCL17). The cytokine burst and interaction between OX40L and OX40 on T cells recruit and stimulate Th2 lymphocytes. Differentiated Th2 cells produce IL–4, IL–5, IL–13, IL–31, and IL–33. This leads to perpetuation of barrier dysfunction, decreased production of AMPs, impaired differentiation of KCs, and itch symptoms [ 39 ]. IL–4 and IL–5 promote B–cell class switching to immunoglobulin E (IgE), thereby enhancing mast cell sensitization. Subsequent allergen–mediated crosslinking of IgE bound to mast cell receptors triggers their degranulation and the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators, while IL–5 additionally contributes to eosinophil recruitment and activation. This amplifies local inflammation and intensifies symptoms of AD [ 40 ]. IL–4 and IL–13 increase collagen deposition in the dermis, which results in skin remodeling and lichenification. Simultaneously, elevated pH probably caused by filaggrin gene mutations, which may impair skin acidification and lipid homeostasis, alterations in key acidification pathways such as phospholipase A 2 and the sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE1, barrier disruption, exposing the stratum corneum to extracellular fluid, and exogenous factors such as alkaline soaps lead to enhanced serine protease activity and activation of kallikreins, which in total deteriorate barrier repair, increase corneodesmosome cleavage, and amplify inflammation [ 41 , 42 ]. Scratching, driven by IL31, aggravates disruption of the skin barrier and intensifies inflammation. Over time, a chronic phase occurs and a mixed immunologic profile emerges: Th2 persists, but Th1, Th17, and Th22 cells are recruited to the skin and start to express OX40. This results in epidermal thickening and abnormal KC proliferation [ 12 ]. Given the extensive research on AD, its pathogenesis has been elucidated in detail by numerous studies that describe complex interactions. Therefore, the present section provides only a concise overview of the key mechanisms, without an exhaustive discussion of all known cytokine interrelations. However, beyond the well–established Th2–driven immune response, emerging evidence suggests that additional pathways, including the Fas/FasL apoptotic axis and IL–21 signaling may also contribute to disease pathophysiology [ 18 , 20 , 28 , 43 ]. Alterations in Fas/FasL expression and signaling have been associated with dysregulated KC apoptosis and sustained inflammation, whereas recent reports have described the presence of IL–21 in close proximity to IL–13 and IL–4R expressing T cells in AD–affected skin [ 18 , 20 ].
sections.hs: Patients with HS are suspected of having a genetic predisposition, with approximately 30% of individuals reporting a positive family history. The genetic basis is complex and polygenic with a variety of mutations seen in cases of syndromic alterations, including GEB2 , MEFV , NCSTN , NLRC4 , NOD2 , OTULIN , POFUT1 , PSENEN , PSTPIP1 , and WRD1 mutations. Current genomic studies emphasize that more research is needed to evaluate these complex patterns. Most cases appear to be nonfamilial, suggesting the existence of important coexisting pathogenetic factors that are environmental or lifestyle–related, with smoking and obesity being the most common [ 44 ]. Other factors that are mentioned as playing a role in pathogenesis are hormonal disturbances, mechanical traction, and immune disorders. In addition, the pathomechanism indicates the role of autoinflammatory regulation due to increased cytokine production (TNF–α or Th17–related cytokines). Furthermore, changes in the local microbiome are observed. However, they may be secondly to skin lesions. Although the exact pathomechanism remains incompletely understood, current studies indicate a complex multifactorial process leading to an autoinflammatory reaction in which follicular occlusion initiates cyst formation. Then, subsequent rupture provokes an intense, chronic immune response, ultimately leading to abscesses, sinus tracts, and scarring. The contents of the occluded follicle, such as keratin debris and microbes, which are released into the dermis, initiate a hyperreactive innate inflammatory cascade through simultaneous activation of inflammatory pathways, including Th17/IL–23, the inflammasomes, and innate receptors (TLRs such as TLR2). Inflammasome activation is accompanied by infiltration of neutrophils, macrophages, B cells, Th1 and Th17 cells, plasma cells, and natural killer (NK) cells, leading to erythematous nodules or fluctuating abscesses [ 45 ]. Activation of TLRs on macrophages and DCs by DAMPs and PAMPs enhances production of pro–inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including TNF–α, IFN–α, IL–1β, IL–6, and IL–8, which further stimulate DCs. In turn, activated DCs initiate adaptive immune responses by promoting differentiation of Th1 and Th17 cells. These populations amplify inflammation through the secretion of cytokines such as IL–17, IL–23, and TNF–α, thereby establishing a self–perpetuating inflammatory loop [ 46 ]. Fibrosis, scarring, and the formation of sinus tracts and fistulas occur owing to an imbalance between MMPs and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs), upregulation of profibrotic mediators such as transforming growth factor (TGF)–β1, β2, and β3, and the presence of epithelial strands in the dermis. These partially epithelialized tunnels create a favorable microenvironment for biofilm–forming bacteria, which can sustain chronic inflammation and persistent purulent discharge [ 45 ]. There is also a study indicating increased expression of the pro–apoptotic Fas/FasL pathway in lesional skin of patients with pyoderma gangrenosum, acne, and HS (PASH) syndrome, suggesting that dysregulated apoptosis may contribute to local inflammation and tissue damage [ 19 ]. Furthermore, we hypothesize that IL–21 may represent a relevant immunological mediator, given its ability to amplify the Th17 response and sustain chronic inflammation through enhanced production of IL–17 and TNF–α. Nevertheless, no studies have directly investigated its role in HS.
sections.fas/fasl axis in inflammatory dermatoses:
Across CISDs such as PsO, AD, and HS, dysregulation of the Fas/FasL apoptotic axis emerges as a key immunopathogenic mechanism. Fas (APO–1), a member of the TNF receptor family, was originally described by Trauth et al. as a protein that induces apoptosis by binding of FasL on activated T cells or NK cells to Fas on target cells. Nowadays, it is known that Fas can also activate non–apoptotic signaling [ 47 ]. Soluble Fas (sFas) and soluble Fas ligand (sFasL) act as dynamic modulators of cell death and immune signaling. They can either inhibit apoptosis by acting as decoy receptors or provoke inflammatory and proliferative responses by engaging non–apoptotic signaling pathways [ 48 ]. Recent studies suggest that Fas axis death receptors can trigger pro–inflammatory and proliferative signaling through NF–κB and mitogen–activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways. For instance, activation of Fas/FasL in KCs induces NF–κB–dependent expression of cytokines and chemokines such as TNF–α, IL–6, IL–1β, and C–X–C motif chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL10), indicating that these receptors can mediate non–apoptotic, immunomodulatory effects relevant to the inflammatory response in AD [ 43 ]. Aberrant Fas/FasL signaling in KCs contributes to resistance to apoptosis despite increased Fas expression, sustaining epidermal hyperplasia and chronic inflammation [ 49 ]. In PsO, elevated circulating levels of sFas and sFasL levels, as well as increased tissue expression of FasL, correlate with disease severity and may function as systemic indicators of immune activation. However, topical treatment appears to only partially restore this imbalance [ 50 ]. Lesional skin studies demonstrate upregulated Fas expression on NK cells and T lymphocytes, enhanced FasL on dermal lymphocytes and KCs, and overexpression of Bcl–xL, Bax, inhibitor of caspase–activated DNase (ICAD), and active caspase–3. Despite this, KCs fail to undergo apoptosis, highlighting their apoptotic resistance [ 21 , 49 – 52 ]. Serum analyses similarly report increased concentrations of sFas, sFas/sFasL ratio, and sFasL [ 53 , 54 ]. Both soluble and tissue level alterations in Fas/FasL signaling appear to correlate with disease activity and metabolic or cardiovascular comorbidities such as obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, as well as with treatment modality [ 50 , 51 ]. Anthralin has been shown to reduce Fas expression, diminish FasL and Bcl–x levels, increase Bax expression, and decrease the proportion of apoptotic KCs [ 51 ]. Myśliwiec et al., in their systematic review, emphasized that multiple therapeutic approaches, including ultraviolet B (UVB) phototherapy and systemic drugs such as methotrexate, novel biologics, and anthralin, consistently downregulate Fas/FasL and Bcl–family proteins [ 21 ]. Dysregulated Fas and FasL–mediated apoptosis of T cells, eosinophils, and KCs contributes directly to AD pathogenesis. Cytokines and components of the extracellular matrix promote apoptosis resistance in lesional skin [ 20 ]. IFN–γ upregulates Fas, FasL, and activated T cells, collectively driving KC apoptosis via soluble or membrane–bound FasL. This mechanism was confirmed by blocking IFN–γ/IFN–γR, Fas/FasL, or caspases, which suppressed KC apoptosis [ 23 ]. Fas– or FasL–deficient mice developed aggravated AD with increased epidermal and dermal thickness, collagen deposition, and infiltration by CD4 + T cells, macrophages, and neutrophils, as well as with elevated IgE and Treg counts, increased Th2 cytokine mRNA (IL–4, IL–5, IL–13, and TGF–β1), and reduced expression of CXCL9, CXCL10, and IL–17 [ 43 ]. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from patients with AD demonstrate enhanced apoptosis. FasL mRNA expression on PBMCs correlates with clinical severity [ 25 ]. KCs also show increased Fas/FasL expression. Studies on electromagnetic field exposure indicate modulation of apoptotic and inflammatory signaling. Short–term reductions in Fas, IL–12p70, IL–17A, IL–31, and TNF–α, as well as long–term decreases in IL–4, IL–10, and IL–13, have been reported, together with increased Fas/FasL expression in healthy KCs and enhanced reactive oxygen species–mediated apoptosis [ 24 ]. Moreover, some authors suggest that elevated cord blood sFas is associated with the later development of AD in children [ 28 ]. In summary, in AD, Fas/FasL signaling contributes both to KC apoptosis and to the regulation of immune cell survival. Dysregulated activation of this pathway promotes epidermal damage and barrier disruption, while impaired Fas–mediated immune cell apoptosis may amplify Th2–driven inflammation. In HS, available data remain limited. However, particularly in PASH syndromes, Fas and FasL engagement appears to interact with IL–1, TNF, and IL–17 pathways, linking epithelial apoptosis with neutrophilic inflammation. Collectively, these findings indicate that the Fas/FasL axis functions as a key regulator of both apoptosis and inflammation and that its imbalance contributes to disease chronicity and systemic inflammatory burden. This highlights its potential as a diagnostic and therapeutic target across inflammatory dermatoses [ 19 ]. To summarize current knowledge on the Fas/FasL apoptotic and inflammatory signaling pathway in CISDs, a targeted literature search was performed using the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by Elicit (an AI–assisted tool), manual screening of reference lists, and citation tracking. These sources provide comprehensive coverage of biomedical and clinical research and were considered sufficient for the scope of this study. The search strategy applied the terms (“Fas” or “FasL” or “sFas” or “sFasL” or “CD95” or “CD178”) and (“psoriasis” or “atopic dermatitis” or “hidradenitis suppurativa”), restricted to the publication period between January 2000 and November 2025. After screening titles and abstracts, a total of 15 studies were identified, including 13 original publications (basic, translational, clinical interventional or observational) and 2 reviews or theoretical papers. An overview of the included studies evaluating the Fas/FasL pathway is presented in Fig. 1 . In this subsection, only primary studies providing experimental or clinical data on Fas and FasL expression, sFas, sFasL, or related apoptotic signaling pathways are summarized. Among the original studies, the majority investigated PsO ( n = 7), while fewer studies included AD ( n = 5) and HS ( n = 1). Reviews and theoretical articles are omitted from the tables, as they do not present independent datasets. Nevertheless, their key conclusions are cited within the main text to illustrate the biological framework of Fas/FasL dysregulation and its role in the pathogenesis of CISDs. sections.the role of il\u201321 in chronic skin i: IL–21 is a 15–kDa immunomodulatory cytokine belonging to the common γ–chain family, and it is predominantly produced by T follicular helper cells, Th17 cells, and NK cells. Its production is stimulated by cytokines IL–6, IL–7, and IL–15, or even by itself through activation of STAT3. IL–21 has pleiotropic effects. In general, it activates various inflammatory pathways and helps to generate and differentiate T–cells, as well as promoting B–cells maturation and antibody production [ 18 ]. A parallel, systematic approach was used to identify studies investigating the immunological role of IL–21 and its receptor (IL–21R) in CISDs. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, with additional records identified via Elicit, hand–searching of reference lists, and citation chasing. The search strategy applied the terms (“IL–21” OR “IL–21R”) AND (“psoriasis” OR “atopic dermatitis” OR “hidradenitis suppurativa”), restricted to the publication period between January 2000 and November 2025. After screening titles and abstracts, a total of 14 studies were identified, including 8 original publications (translational, or clinical interventional or observational) and 6 reviews or meta–analyses (3 focused on AD, 2 on PsO, and 1 broader review on CISDs excluding HS), as summarized in Fig. 2 . Among the 8 original studies, 6 investigated PsO, and 2 addressed AD, while none focused on HS. In this subsection, only primary studies providing experimental or clinical data are tabulated. The purpose is to focus on data directly derived from patient samples, enabling a quantitative assessment of IL–21 and IL–21R expression patterns in lesional and nonlesional skin, serum, and peripheral blood. Reviews and theoretical articles are omitted from the tables, as they do not present independent datasets. However, their main conclusions are integrated narratively within the main text to provide broader context and to support the interpretation of findings from primary research. Extracted records were compiled into a structured comparative table (Table 2 ) containing information on author, year, disease type, key markers, sample size, methodology, level versus control, and effect of treatment. This integrative summary enables cross–comparison between disease entities and highlights gaps in current understanding of the immunologic role of IL–21 and its receptor in CISDs. In PsO, IL–21 plays a central pathogenic role by linking T–cell–driven inflammation with KC hyperproliferation. Its expression correlates with disease severity and declines following effective therapy. Experimental work demonstrates that IL–21 promotes PsO–like inflammation through activation of CD4 + T cells and induction of IFN–γ–dependent epidermal hyperplasia [ 26 , 55 – 59 ]. IL–21 blockade attenuates skin pathology and reduces inflammatory infiltrates, highlighting this cytokine as a potential therapeutic target. Xenograft and mouse studies confirm that IL–21 induces epidermal thickening and amplifies inflammatory cytokine networks [ 55 – 57 ]. Histological analyses indicate that IL–21 is predominantly increased in immune cells within psoriatic lesions, while IL–21R is strongly expressed on KCs. The IL–21/IL–21R axis correlates with clinical erythema scores and microvessel density. Mechanistically, IL–21 indirectly promotes psoriatic angiogenesis by stimulating KCs to produce ICAM–1, enhancing endothelial migration and tube formation. Thus, targeting IL–21 signaling may reduce vascular remodeling in PsO [ 59 ]. One review describes high IL–21 expression in psoriatic lesions compared with controls. Moreover, intradermal IL–21 administration in mice induces epidermal hyperplasia, while IL–21 inhibition reduces Th1 and Th17 cytokines and skin thickening [ 60 ]. The isolated discrepancy reported by De Oliveira et al. (2015) reflects that IL–21 is primarily a tissue–restricted cytokine, and its serum level may fluctuate. Combined biological factors (local action, low circulatory levels) and methodological issues (sample size, assay sensitivity, cohort heterogeneity) may have masked true differences. Despite the nonsignificant p –value, the upward trend in IL–21 levels and its tendency to correlate with PASI remain consistent with the broader literature, demonstrating the involvement of IL–21 in psoriatic inflammation [ 61 ]. Reviews highlight that IL–21 contributes to the pathogenesis of AD and may represent a promising therapeutic target, a concept supported by several experimental studies [ 62 , 63 ]. IL–21 is significantly elevated in patients with AD and correlates with clinical severity, particularly with acute lesion morphology, showing strong associations with erythema and edema/papulation. These findings indicate that IL–21 participates in Th2–skewed inflammation and may amplify disease flares [ 27 ]. Murine models further demonstrate that IL–21/IL–21R signaling is required for the mobilization of skin DCs to draining lymph nodes and for the development of allergic inflammation following epicutaneous sensitization. Notably, blockade of IL–21R effectively suppresses AD–like skin inflammation, underscoring the pathway’s functional importance [ 64 ]. Unlike PsO and AD, in which IL–21 and IL–21R upregulation is well documented, HS remains largely unexplored in this context. To date, no studies have assessed IL–21 expression in HS tissue or serum. Given the strong Th17 and B–cell signatures described in HS, IL–21 may play a role, but this remains hypothetical and requires direct investigation.
sections.classical and novel inflammatory markers:
Several systemic inflammation markers, including C–reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), NLR, PLR, MLR, PNR, PIV, and SII, have been associated with cardiometabolic diseases [ 65 ]. However, the use of these inflammatory markers in CISDs remains underexplored as a complement to clinical assessment in determining disease severity. Because these biomarkers and indices are readily measurable and can be incorporated into routine evaluations, further research is necessary to clarify their role in grading disease severity and their potential utility in detecting systemic inflammation and metabolic syndrome. A systematic extraction was conducted to identify publications addressing CBC–derived inflammatory indices (NLR, PLR, MLR, d–NLR, SII, SIRI, AISI, and PIV) in CISDs. The search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library, and was supplemented by Elicit, manual screening of reference lists, and citation tracking. The search strategy applied the terms (“complete blood count derived indices” OR “hematology–derived indices” OR “neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio” OR “derived neutrophil–to–lymphocyte ratio” OR “platelet–to–lymphocyte ratio” OR “monocyte–to–lymphocyte ratio” OR “systemic immune–inflammation index” OR “systemic inflammation response index” OR “aggregate index of systemic inflammation” OR “pan–immune–inflammation value”) AND (“psoriasis” OR “atopic dermatitis” OR “hidradenitis suppurativa”), restricted to the publication period between January 2000 and November 2025. After screening titles and abstracts, a total of 62 studies were identified, including 56 original publications (clinical interventional or observational) and 6 reviews or meta–analyses (5 focused on PsO, and 1 on HS) as summarized in Fig. 3 . Among the original studies, the majority investigated PsO ( n = 37), while fewer studies included HS ( n = 12) and AD ( n = 7). In this subsection, only primary studies providing experimental or clinical data were tabulated. The purpose was to focus on data directly derived from patient samples, enabling a quantitative assessment of CBC–derived inflammatory indices (NLR, PLR, MLR, d–NLR, SII, SIRI, AISI, and PIV) in relation to disease severity and treatment response. Reviews and theoretical papers are omitted from the tables, as they do not present independent datasets. However, their conclusions are narratively integrated into the main text to provide broader clinical and pathophysiological context and to support the interpretation of primary findings. Furthermore, studies that did not specifically evaluate the diagnostic or prognostic value of these indices in CISDs or lacked analysis of their correlation with disease activity or therapeutic response are excluded from the summary tables. Extracted records were compiled into a structured comparative table (Table 3 ) containing information on author, year, disease type, key hematologic markers, sample size, methodology, comparison with control, and treatment effects. This integrative summary enables cross–comparison between CISDs and highlights existing gaps in the clinical utility and standardization of CBC–derived inflammatory indices as biomarkers of disease activity and treatment response. Moreover, certain indices appeared to be disease–specific (for instance, the eosinophil–to–neutrophil ratio, ENR, was primarily relevant in AD). To address this, we first conducted a preliminary literature screening using the terms “CBC–derived indices” and “hematology–derived indices” in order to identify the inflammatory indices most frequently investigated in dermatologic inflammatory diseases. On the basis of this initial screening, we selected indices that appeared consistently across studies and could be derived from routine complete blood count parameters. Subsequently, a targeted literature search was performed for these selected indices within the context of AD, HS, and PsO. To ensure comparability and focus on universally applicable hematologic markers, we selected the following indices for further analysis in future clinical studies: NLR, PLR, MLR, d–NLR, SII, SIRI, AISI, and PIV. These parameters have been repeatedly reported as reflections of systemic inflammation and disease activity across multiple inflammatory skin disorders. This decision was made to maintain methodological consistency and to focus on reproducible CBC–derived markers with established clinical applicability across different CISDs. Systemic inflammatory biomarkers derived from routine blood counts, particularly NLR, PLR, MLR, SII, SIRI, AISI, and PIV, alongside CRP and ESR are mostly elevated in HS, PsO, or AD, correlating with disease activity and systemic inflammatory burden. Several of these indices also reflect metabolic and cardiovascular comorbidities and may support early risk stratification. However, not all indices have been systematically investigated across all three diseases, and the available evidence remains unevenly distributed among PsO, HS, and AD. Their simplicity, low cost, and availability make them promising complementary tools for screening, staging, and monitoring treatment response, especially under biologic therapy (e.g., TNF–α and IL–17 inhibitors). However, variability in their diagnostic performance and limited validation, often based on a relatively small number of studies and modest patient cohorts, highlight the need for further methodological standardization and longitudinal studies before widespread clinical implementation. In HS, hematologic indices most strongly reflect deep tissue inflammation, draining fistula activity, and cardiometabolic burden, making them useful for detecting high–risk patients [ 66 , 67 ]. In PsO, these markers correlate well with systemic inflammation and arthritis risk, and they consistently decrease with effective biologic therapy [ 68 , 69 ]. In AD, their elevation is less strongly linked to clinical severity, particularly in children, suggesting that they may better reflect chronic systemic immune activation rather than skin disease intensity alone [ 70 – 72 ]. Clinical evidence indicates that selected CBC–derived inflammatory indices may also be associated with cardiometabolic and cardiovascular risk, an aspect that is discussed in a separate section of this review [ 73 ].
sections.cardiovascular risk and systemic inflamm: CISDs are increasingly recognized as systemic disorders that accelerate atherogenesis rather than being confined to the skin [ 117 – 119 ]. Persistent low–grade inflammation promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and plaque instability via cytokine–driven activation of monocytes, neutrophils, and platelets [ 120 ]. In this context, circulating inflammatory biomarkers can be viewed not only as markers of cutaneous disease activity, but also as surrogates of subclinical atherosclerosis and cardiovascular risk. Sánchez–Díaz et al., in a study from 2025, reported that SII and NLR may serve as simple, inexpensive screening tools for detecting patients with HS at higher risk of hypertension, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome [ 73 ]. Utlu (2023) highlighted that both SII and SIRI are significantly higher in HS and correlate with CRP, indicating their potential use as accessible inflammatory markers for disease monitoring [ 75 ]. Holgersen et al. suggested that a combination of CRP, ESR, and PIV works as the best predictor of metabolic syndrome [ 68 ]. Çetinarslan et al. (2021) reported that MHR may better reflect chronic inflammatory status or disease duration than acute activity [ 69 ]. Numerous studies indirectly reveal that CBC–derived indices correlate with cardiovascular risk (Tables 4 , 5 , 6 ).
