title: An in vitro comparison of cold atmospheric plasma and methylene blue-mediated antimicrobial photodynamic therapy with 660 nm laser on Streptococcus mutans biofilms
abstract: This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the antimicrobial and antibiofilm efficacy of helium-based cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) and methylene blue–mediated antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (MB-aPDT) against mature Streptococcus mutans biofilms formed on human enamel surfaces. In this study, standardized enamel slabs prepared from extracted human premolars were inoculated with S. mutans ATCC 35,668 and incubated for 7 days to allow mature biofilm formation in the presence of sucrose and human saliva. Specimens were randomly allocated to nine experimental groups ( n = 10): negative control, 0.2% chlorhexidine (CHX), laser only (660 nm, 100 mW, 20 J/cm², 100 s), 0.02% methylene blue (MB) only, MB-aPDT (0.02% MB + 660 nm laser), and CAP applied for 90, 120, 150, and 180 s. Quantitative assessment of biofilm viability was performed by colony-forming unit (CFU/mL) counting. Structural alterations were qualitatively analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA and Tukey post hoc tests (α = 0.05). Both MB-aPDT and CAP significantly reduced S. mutans biofilm viability compared with the untreated control ( p < 0.001). MB-aPDT achieved a 90.7% reduction in CFU counts. CAP demonstrated a time-dependent antibacterial effect, with progressive reductions from 53.5% at 90 s to 87.0% at 180 s. MB-aPDT was significantly more effective than CAP at 90, 120, and 150 s ( p < 0.001), whereas no significant difference was observed between MB-aPDT and CAP at 180 s ( p = 0.266). SEM analysis corroborated quantitative findings, revealing marked disruption of biofilm architecture following MB-aPDT and CAP-180 s treatments. Both MB-aPDT and helium-based CAP exhibit significant antibiofilm activity against mature S. mutans biofilms on enamel surfaces. While MB-aPDT demonstrated superior efficacy compared with shorter CAP exposures, prolonged CAP treatment achieved comparable antibacterial effects. These findings support the potential integration of both modalities as adjunctive, minimally invasive strategies for biofilm control in preventive and restorative dentistry.

sections.introduction: Dental caries persists as a globally prevalent and economically burdensome chronic disease, exerting substantial pressure on healthcare infrastructures worldwide [ 1 ]. The pathogenesis of caries is intrinsically linked to ecological imbalances within the dental plaque biofilm—a dynamic, polymicrobial consortium adhered to the tooth surface [ 2 ]. Within this complex ecosystem, Streptococcus mutans is established as a principal cariogenic pathogen. Its pathogenicity is due to three key features: proficient adhesion to the pellicle-coating enamel, robust synthesis of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) that scaffold the biofilm architecture, and vigorous fermentation of dietary sugars into organic acids. This concerted acidogenic and aciduric metabolism drives localized enamel demineralization, thereby initiating the carious process [ 3 ]. Consequently, the effective management of cariogenic biofilms, especially those with significant S. mutans bioburden, is a critical objective in preventive and therapeutic dentistry [ 4 ]. Conventional caries management primarily relies on mechanical disruption and removal of dental biofilms through personal oral hygiene measures and professional debridement. However, the effectiveness of these approaches is often limited by inadequate patient compliance, restricted access to dental care, and the persistence of microorganisms within anatomically protected sites such as deep pits, fissures, and dentinal tubules [ 5 ]. Although adjunctive antiseptic agents, particularly chlorhexidine, demonstrate substantial antimicrobial efficacy against oral biofilms, their prolonged use has been associated with several undesirable effects, including tooth discoloration, taste alteration, mucosal irritation, disruption of the commensal oral microbiome, and the potential emergence of microbial adaptation or tolerance [ 6 ]. These limitations have driven increasing interest in the development of innovative non-antibiotic therapeutic modalities capable of selectively targeting pathogenic biofilms while minimizing adverse effects on oral tissues and microbial ecology. Two promising alternative antimicrobial approaches that have emerged are cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) and antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT) [ 7 ]. Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) was specifically selected in the present study because it represents one of the most promising emerging non-thermal antimicrobial technologies in dentistry. CAP consists of a partially ionized gas generated at near-ambient temperatures and contains a complex mixture of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), charged particles, UV photons, and transient electric fields. Its antimicrobial activity is multifactorial, primarily mediated through oxidative damage to microbial membranes, proteins, nucleic acids, and the extracellular biofilm matrix, ultimately leading to bacterial cell death and biofilm disruption irrespective of conventional resistance mechanisms. In addition to its direct bactericidal effects, CAP has demonstrated the ability to degrade extracellular polymeric substances, reduce microbial adhesion, and suppress the acidogenic activity of cariogenic bacteria. These unique properties make CAP particularly attractive for the management of biofilm-mediated oral diseases, especially in situations where conventional antimicrobial agents may exhibit limited biofilm penetration, undesirable adverse effects, or reduced long-term effectiveness [ 8 ]. Conversely, aPDT is a light-activated modality utilizing a photosensitizing agent (e.g., methylene blue, MB) excited by light of a specific wavelength (e.g., 660 nm). This photoexcitation triggers the generation of cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (predominantly singlet oxygen), inducing rapid, targeted oxidative lethality within the illuminated field and enabling precise spatial control [ 9 ]. Both modalities present compelling advantages for dental applications: broad-spectrum activity, a low propensity for engendering microbial resistance due to their multi-targeted physical/chemical mechanisms, and potential for selective biofilm targeting [ 10 , 11 ]. Despite accumulating in vitro evidence supporting the individual efficacy of CAP and aPDT against various oral pathogens [ 12 – 14 ], a direct and systematic comparative analysis of these two physical modalities against biofilms of S. mutans —the quintessential cariogenic pathogen—remains insufficiently explored in the literature. Prevailing investigations often assess each technology in isolation or employ planktonic cultures, models that fail to recapitulate the enhanced antimicrobial recalcitrance characteristic of the biofilm phenotype [ 15 ]. A rigorous, side-by-side evaluation of their antibiofilm performance against standardized, mature S. mutans biofilms is therefore essential. Such a comparison is pivotal for elucidating their relative efficacies, potential synergies, and translational feasibility, thereby informing the development of optimized, non-invasive clinical strategies against biofilm-mediated dental diseases [ 7 , 16 , 17 ]. This study aims to systematically compare the antimicrobial and biofilm-disrupting efficacy of CAP and MB-aPDT with a 660 nm laser against mature S. mutans biofilms. We hypothesize that: (i) both CAP and MB-aPDT will significantly reduce the viability and structural integrity of S. mutans biofilms compared to an untreated control; and (ii) a statistically significant difference will exist in the efficacy profile between the two treatment modalities, with one demonstrating superior biofilm eradication or disruption capacity under the defined experimental parameters.
sections.sample size calculation: The sample size was determined based on the study by Garcia et al. [ 18 ] using one-way ANOVA power analysis performed with SPSS software (version 11, IBM, USA). Considering an alpha error of 0.05, a beta error of 0.2 (power = 80%), a standard deviation of 0.72 for the mean log colony-forming units (CFU) count, and an effect size of 0.46, the minimum required sample size was calculated as 10 specimens per group. A total of 9 experimental groups were included in this study ( n = 10 per group).
sections.bacterial strain and culture conditions: Streptococcus mutans ATCC 35,668 was obtained from the Iranian Biological Resource Center (Tehran, Iran). The lyophilized bacteria were reconstituted according to the manufacturer’s instructions and cultured on Mitis Salivarius agar (Merck, Germany) supplemented 1% sucrose (w/v). The plates were incubated under capnophilic conditions (5% CO₂) at 37 °C for 48 h to obtain isolated colonies. For preparation of bacterial suspensions, colonies were inoculated into Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth (Merck, Germany) and incubated at 37 °C under 5% CO₂ until reaching the logarithmic growth phase. The optical density was adjusted spectrophotometrically (BioTek Instruments, USA) at 600 nm to achieve a suspension equivalent to 0.5 McFarland standard (approximately 1.5 × 10⁸ CFU/mL). The final cell concentration was confirmed by serial dilution and colony counting on BHI agar (Merck, Germany) plates.
sections.enamel slab preparation: Human premolar teeth extracted for orthodontic purposes were collected and stored in 0.1% thymol solution at 4 °C until use. Teeth with visible cracks, caries, enamel hypoplasia, or white spot lesions on buccal or lingual surfaces were excluded. Enamel slabs measuring 3 × 3 × 1 mm were prepared from the buccal and lingual surfaces using a water-cooled diamond saw (Isomet, Buehler, USA) [ 19 ]. The outer enamel surface was polished with 600-, 800-, and 1200-grit silicon carbide papers under water irrigation to remove approximately 100 μm of the outermost enamel layer, creating a standardized flat surface [ 19 ]. The slabs were ultrasonically cleaned in distilled water for 10 min to remove debris and then sterilized by exposure to 40 kGray Gamma irradiation.
sections.saliva collection and preparation: Unstimulated whole saliva was collected from healthy volunteers who had no active caries, periodontal disease, or systemic diseases, and had not taken antibiotics within the preceding 3 months. The collected saliva was centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C, filter-sterilized through a 0.22 μm membrane filter, and stored at -20 °C until use.
sections.biofilm development: S. mutans biofilms were formed on enamel slabs following the protocol described by Pourhajibagher and Bahador [ 20 ] with modifications. Sterile enamel slabs were placed in 96-well microtiter plates containing 200 µL of bacterial suspension (1.5 × 10⁸ CFU/mL) in BHI broth supplemented with 1% sucrose (w/v) and 50% filter-sterilized human saliva. The plates were incubated at 37 °C under 5% CO₂ on a shaking incubator for 7 days to allow mature biofilm formation. The culture medium was replaced every 48 h with fresh BHI broth containing 1% sucrose, and biofilms were treated with 10% sucrose for 3 min daily to promote extracellular polysaccharide production [ 20 ].
sections.experimental groups: The enamel slabs containing S. mutans biofilms were randomly allocated into ten experimental groups ( n = 10 per group) as follows: Group 1 (Negative control): Biofilms were treated with sterile physiological saline solution in culture medium without S. mutans . Group 2 (Positive control): Biofilms were treated with 0.02% chlorhexidine (Plastrin, Iran) for 1 min. Group 3 (Laser only): Biofilms were irradiated without a photosensitizer with a 660 nm continuous-wave diode laser (Sirona, Germany) at 100 mW power output, an irradiance of 0.20 W/cm², and an energy density of 20 J/cm² for 100 s. The laser beam, with a spot diameter of 8 mm, was delivered perpendicularly to the enamel surface from a standardized non-contact distance of 1 cm. This configuration ensured complete coverage of the enamel slab surface, promoted homogeneous energy distribution across the biofilm area, and minimized the risk of localized thermal accumulation or uneven irradiation during photodynamic treatment. The laser output power was verified before each experimental session using a calibrated laser power meter (Laser Point srl, Milano, Italy). Group 4 (Photosensitizer only): Biofilms were treated with 0.02% MB (Merck, Germany) dissolved in sterile distilled water for 5 min in the dark without laser irradiation. Group 5 (aPDT): Biofilms were incubated with 0.02% MB for 5 min pre-irradiation time, followed by irradiation with a 660 nm diode laser, similar to group 3. Groups 6–9 (CAP): Biofilms were treated with CAP for different exposure durations: 90, 120, 150, and 180 s. CAP was generated using a helium-based plasma jet system (PlasmArt, Nariatech, Tehran, Iran). The device operated with helium as the working gas at an inlet pressure of 4.5 bar, while the handpiece outlet pressure was maintained at atmospheric pressure. A transistor regulated the voltage to 10 kV (peak-to-peak) with an operating frequency of 100 kHz and power output of 8 W. The gas flow rate was adjusted to number 3 (3.8 L/min) and intensity of 4 (0.780 KV) using a precision low-pressure manometer to monitor the outlet gas pressure. The plasma plume length measured 21 mm with a diameter of 2.5 mm at the nozzle exit.
sections.microbiological analysis: Immediately after the treatments, the enamel slabs were transferred to sterile tubes containing 1 mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4). The biofilms were detached by vortexing for 30 s. Serial 10‑fold dilutions were prepared in PBS, and 100 µL aliquots were plated on BHI agar. The plates were incubated under capnophilic conditions at 37 °C for 48 h, after which the number of CFU/mL was determined [ 20 ].
sections.scanning electron microscopy (sem) analy: To assess the effect of the experimental groups on the microbial biofilm formed on the enamel surface, three separate specimens per group were analyzed qualitatively using SEM. The specimens were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 2 h at 4 °C, dehydrated through graded ethanol series (30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100%), and dried in a critical point dryer. After gold sputter-coating, specimens were examined under a SEM (ZEISS, Germany) at 15 kV accelerating voltage.
sections.statistical analysis: Data were analyzed using SPSS software version 26 (IBM, USA). The normality of data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare mean CFU/mL counts among groups, followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. All experiments were performed in triplicate to ensure reproducibility.
sections.quantitative analysis of s. mutans biofi: S. mutans biofilm viability across experimental groups is presented in Fig. 1 . The negative control showed the highest bacterial count (26.61 ± 1.36 × 10⁶ CFU/mL). Among treatments, 0.2% CHX exhibited the strongest antibacterial effect, reducing viability to 0.118 ± 0.012 × 10⁶ CFU/mL (99.6% reduction). aPDT (MB + 660 nm laser) also significantly reduced bacterial counts to 2.47 ± 0.34 × 10⁶ CFU/mL (90.7% reduction). Fig. 1 The effects of different treatments on the cell viability of Streptococcus mutans . The treatment resulted in significant reductions compared to the untreated control group (* P < 0.05) CAP treatment demonstrated a time-dependent antibacterial effect, with mean CFU/mL progressively decreasing as exposure time increased: CAP-90 s (12.36 ± 1.06 × 10⁶), CAP-120 s (7.98 ± 0.65 × 10⁶), CAP-150 s (6.24 ± 0.46 × 10⁶), and CAP-180 s (3.45 ± 0.30 × 10⁶), corresponding to 53.5%, 70.0%, 76.5%, and 87.0% reductions, respectively. In contrast, methylene blue alone (22.60 ± 1.26 × 10⁶ CFU/mL) and laser alone (25.58 ± 1.29 × 10⁶ CFU/mL) showed minimal reductions. Statistical analysis confirmed that all treatment groups except laser alone ( p = 0.204) differed significantly from the control ( P < 0.001). Post hoc analysis (Tukey HSD) comparing aPDT with CAP treatments (Fig. 1 ) revealed that aPDT was significantly more effective than CAP-90 s, CAP-120 s, and CAP-150 s, with mean differences of 9.89, 5.51, and 3.77 × 10⁶ CFU/mL, respectively (all P < 0.001). However, no significant difference was observed between aPDT and CAP-180 s (mean difference: 0.98 × 10⁶ CFU/mL; P = 0.266; 95% CI: -2.24 to 0.29 × 10⁶ CFU/mL). These findings indicate that while aPDT is superior to shorter CAP exposures, prolonged CAP treatment (180 s) achieves comparable antibacterial efficacy to aPDT. Additionally, a comparison of the colonies grown on the culture medium across the different treatment groups is presented in Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Colonies of Streptococcus mutans grown on brain heart infusion (BHI) agar enriched with 1% sucrose following different treatments: ( a ) Negative control, ( b ) 0.2% chlorhexidine (CHX), ( c ) Laser only (660 nm), ( d ) 0.02% Methylene blue (MB) only, ( e ) Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT; MB + 660 nm laser), ( f ) Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) with an exposure duration of 90 s, ( g ) CAP with an exposure duration of 120 s, ( h ) CAP with an exposure duration of 150 s, and ( i ) CAP with an exposure duration of 180 s
sections.qualitative analysis of s. mutans biofil: The SEM images (Fig. 3 ) demonstrate distinct differences in S. mutans biofilm architecture following various treatments, in agreement with the quantitative CFU/mL findings. In the negative control group (a), a dense and well-organized biofilm structure is evident, corresponding to the highest bacterial counts. Treatment with 0.2% CHX (b) results in a markedly disrupted biofilm with sparse bacterial aggregation, indicating the strongest antimicrobial effect among the tested groups. The laser-only irradiation at 660 nm (c) exhibits a biofilm structure comparable to the control group, suggesting a negligible antibacterial impact. Similarly, the MB-only treatment (d) shows no apparent structural disruption, with biofilm morphology resembling that of the untreated control. In contrast, aPDT (e) produces a pronounced reduction in biofilm density and structural integrity, demonstrating substantial antimicrobial activity. For CAP treatments, a time-dependent decrease in biofilm density is observed. CAP applied for 90 s (f) shows partial disruption of the biofilm structure. Increasing the exposure time to 120 s (g) results in further architectural breakdown and reduced bacterial clustering. At 150 s (h), the biofilm appears more dispersed with fewer intact microcolonies. The 180-s exposure (i) leads to marked structural disintegration and minimal residual biofilm formation. Comparatively, aPDT exhibits greater biofilm disruption than CAP at shorter exposure times (90–150 s), while demonstrating comparable efficacy to CAP applied for 180 s. Fig. 3 Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of Streptococcus mutans biofilms on enamel slabs following different treatments: ( a ) Negative control, ( b ) 0.2% chlorhexidine (CHX), ( c ) Laser only (660 nm), ( d ) 0.02% Methylene blue (MB) only, ( e ) Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT; MB + 660 nm laser), ( f ) Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) with an exposure duration of 90 s, ( g ) CAP with an exposure duration of 120 s, ( h ) CAP with an exposure duration of 150 s, and ( i ) CAP with an exposure duration of 180 s
sections.discussion: The present study provides a direct comparative evaluation of CAP and MB-mediated aPDT against mature S. mutans biofilms formed on human enamel slabs. The findings confirm our first hypothesis that both CAP and aPDT significantly reduce biofilm viability and disrupt structural integrity compared with the untreated control. Furthermore, the second hypothesis is partially supported, as aPDT demonstrated superior efficacy compared with shorter CAP exposure times (90–150 s), while CAP applied for 180 s achieved a comparable antibacterial effect. MB was selected as the photosensitizer because of its well-documented antimicrobial efficacy, strong absorption peak near 660 nm, high singlet oxygen generation efficiency, favorable water solubility, and extensive prior validation in oral aPDT studies [ 21 ]. Moreover, MB remains one of the most clinically accessible and cost-effective photosensitizers for dental applications, facilitating comparison with existing literature [ 6 ]. The significant reduction in S. mutans biofilm viability following MB-aPDT observed in the present study aligns with the growing body of evidence supporting photodynamic therapy as an effective antibiofilm strategy, though comparative analysis reveals considerable variability in reported efficacy attributable to differences in photosensitizer type, concentration, light parameters, and biofilm models [ 21 , 22 ]. Nemezio et al. [ 21 ] evaluated MB-aPDT (0.01% MB, 94 J/cm²) against S. mutans biofilms and reported significant reductions in bacterial viability, although the extent of reduction varied with biofilm maturation stage and experimental conditions. Similarly, Liang et al. [ 22 ] compared MB-aPDT and hematoporphyrin monomethyl ether (HMME)-aPDT against S. mutans biofilms, demonstrating that both modalities significantly reduced CFU counts at energy densities of 30.4 J/cm², with MB-aPDT showing superior efficacy compared to HMME-aPDT, underscoring the importance of optimizing light parameters. The 90.7% reduction achieved with MB-aPDT in this study is consistent with the well-established mechanism of aPDT, which relies on the photoexcitation of a photosensitizer by light of a specific wavelength to generate cytotoxic ROS [ 23 , 24 ]. Upon irradiation at 660 nm, MB undergoes transition to an excited triplet state, subsequently interacting with molecular oxygen through two primary pathways: Type I reaction involving electron transfer to produce superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals; and Type II reaction involving energy transfer to generate highly reactive singlet oxygen (¹O₂) [ 23 ]. Singlet oxygen is considered the predominant cytotoxic species mediating aPDT efficacy, with a diffusion radius of approximately 10–20 nm in biological systems, causing rapid oxidative damage to bacterial membranes and intracellular components [ 24 ]. The spatial precision of aPDT, confined to areas where both photosensitizer and light are present, offers potential for selective biofilm targeting with minimal effects on adjacent healthy tissues [ 23 ]. This targeted mechanism contrasts with the broader, non-selective oxidative action of CAP, though both approaches share the advantage of multitarget physical/chemical mechanisms that reduce the risk of inducing microbial resistance [ 7 , 25 ]. The time-dependent antibiofilm effect of CAP observed in the present study—with S. mutans viability reductions progressing from 53.5% at 90 s to 87.0% at 180 s—aligns with findings from recent investigations employing various plasma sources and experimental models, and reflects the cumulative oxidative damage inflicted by reactive oxygen and nitrogen species generated during plasma exposure. Figueira et al. [ 26 ] demonstrated that a helium low-temperature plasma jet applied to multispecies cariogenic biofilms achieved greater than 2 log₁₀ reduction in viable counts at 5–7 min, with shorter exposures producing more modest effects. Although their exposure durations exceeded those tested in the present work, the progressive increase in efficacy with extended treatment time corroborates our observation of time-dependent CAP activity, with differences in log reductions potentially attributable to variations in biofilm maturity, microbial composition, or plasma source parameters [ 26 ]. Similarly, Puca et al. [ 27 ] reported that an air-based CAP soft jet applied to S. mutans biofilms for 120–180 s induced extensive cell death and reduced biofilm thickness on confocal microscopy, with longer exposure times yielding greater antimicrobial effects—a pattern paralleling the enhanced biofilm disruption observed at 150–180 s in our study and reinforcing the critical role of treatment duration in CAP efficacy. Beyond direct bactericidal activity through RONS-mediated oxidative assault on bacterial membranes, proteins, and nucleic acids, CAP may exert additional carioprotective effects through metabolic modulation. Zhao et al. [ 28 ] investigated argon-based CAP against S. mutans UA159 biofilms and reported significant antibacterial effects, with CAP demonstrating stronger antiproliferative activity than ultraviolet irradiation under comparable conditions. Importantly, their study revealed that CAP inhibits acid production by biofilms and enhances enamel acid resistance, suggesting mechanisms that extend beyond simple bacterial killing to include interference with cariogenic metabolism—findings that complement our results by indicating that CAP not only reduces bacterial viability but may also attenuate the pathogenic potential of residual biofilms [ 28 ]. Liguori et al. [ 29 ] evaluated dielectric barrier discharge plasma against S. mutans biofilms on soft reline materials, reporting that 120-s CAP exposure reduced mature biofilm viability by approximately 2 log₁₀. This efficacy exceeds the 87.0% reduction observed in our study at 180 s, which may reflect differences in plasma source configuration, substrate material, biofilm maturation protocols, or quantification methods. Nevertheless, the consistent demonstration of significant antibiofilm activity across diverse experimental systems supports CAP as a promising adjunctive technology for managing S. mutans biofilms [ 26 – 29 ]. In the current enamel-based model, CAP applied at 8 W with helium flow produced substantial biofilm inactivation while maintaining overall enamel surface integrity. Nevertheless, SEM observations following longer CAP exposures suggested possible mild surface morphological alterations or roughening compared with aPDT-treated specimens. Previous studies have similarly reported time-dependent enamel surface modifications after plasma exposure, potentially related to oxidative etching and physicochemical interactions between reactive plasma species and hydroxyapatite surfaces. Therefore, although severe destructive changes were not observed in the present study, the possibility of subtle enamel surface alteration after prolonged CAP exposure should be carefully considered when optimizing clinical treatment parameters. Variability across CAP studies—including differences in single-species versus multispecies biofilms, biofilm age, plasma physics, and application protocols—helps explain variations in reported log reductions [ 26 , 27 , 29 ]. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Sanesi et al. [ 25 ] confirmed the antimicrobial effect of direct CAP application against oral pathogens, reporting a pooled standardized mean difference of 4.51 for Enterococcus faecalis reduction, while highlighting considerable heterogeneity across studies regarding treatment parameters, gas composition, and clinical application protocols. Despite methodological differences, the convergent evidence from these investigations reinforces the potential of CAP as a versatile antimicrobial approach for challenging dental applications where mechanical debridement may be insufficient, such as deep fissures, dentinal tubules, periodontal pockets, and implant surfaces [ 25 – 29 ]. Yeganehfard et al. [ 7 ] recently conducted a direct comparative investigation of PDT at two wavelengths (660 nm with MB and 810 nm with indocyanine green) alongside CAP treatment (90–180 s) against S. mutans . Their findings closely parallel our results, demonstrating that CAP-180 s achieved substantial bacterial reduction (36.75 ± 18.87 CFU) comparable to PDT 660 nm + MB (39.25 ± 5.62 CFU), with no statistically significant difference between these modalities. Interestingly, their study revealed that PDT 810 nm + ICG showed numerically lower CFU counts (23.5 ± 11.67 CFU) than both CAP-180 s and MB-aPDT, suggesting that near-infrared wavelengths with ICG may offer enhanced efficacy for certain applications [ 7 ]. This aligns with our observation that both physical modalities achieve significant antibiofilm effects, while also highlighting the potential for optimizing photosensitizer-light combinations to maximize therapeutic outcomes. Within restorative and preventive dentistry, CAP and MB-aPDT could be integrated into minimally invasive caries management to disinfect demineralized pits and fissures or residual carious dentin prior to sealing or restoration, potentially reducing residual S. mutans loads and secondary caries risk [ 30 , 31 ]. From an economic and translational perspective, CAP systems currently require higher initial equipment investment compared with conventional antiseptic approaches. Nevertheless, CAP does not require exogenous photosensitizers or disposable antimicrobial agents, potentially reducing long-term consumable costs. Moreover, the multifunctional applicability of CAP in dentistry—including biofilm decontamination, implant surface disinfection, wound healing support, and endodontic applications—may improve overall cost-efficiency in specialized clinical environments. The broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity of CAP, combined with its low likelihood of inducing microbial resistance, further supports its potential long-term clinical value. However, additional clinical and health-economic studies are still required to determine the cost-effectiveness of CAP in routine dental practice [ 8 , 11 ]. In orthodontics, adjunctive aPDT around brackets and bands may help control biofilm accumulation in patients with suboptimal hygiene, offering an alternative to repeated CHX use and mitigating bracket-associated white spot lesions [ 20 , 32 ]. For high-risk or medically compromised patients, targeted applications on root surfaces, around restoration margins, or in fissures could be scheduled at recall visits as part of personalized caries risk–management protocols, complementing fluoride, dietary counseling, and mechanical plaque control [ 33 , 34 ]. Given the comparable efficacy of MB-aPDT and longer CAP exposures in the present work, device-level considerations become important: CAP systems may be particularly attractive in clinical environments already using plasma tools for soft tissue or wound applications [ 35 ], whereas MB-aPDT may be easier to adopt in practices equipped with diode lasers and familiar with laser safety [ 25 ]. Future development of combined or sequential protocols—for example, MB-aPDT followed by short CAP exposure—could theoretically exploit complementary mechanisms to maximize biofilm eradication while keeping individual doses within safe and practical limits, although such combinatorial strategies require rigorous experimental validation [ 36 , 37 ]. Beyond antimicrobial efficacy, the biological safety and host-tissue compatibility of these emerging therapeutic modalities are equally important for their successful clinical translation [ 8 , 11 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that appropriately optimized CAP protocols generally exhibit acceptable cytocompatibility toward gingival fibroblasts, oral keratinocytes, and other mammalian oral cells, while in some cases promoting wound healing and tissue regeneration through controlled redox signaling [ 8 , 11 , 12 ]. However, excessive plasma exposure duration or high concentrations of reactive species may induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, or apoptosis in host tissues [ 8 , 12 ]. Similarly, methylene blue-mediated aPDT has shown favorable biocompatibility because reactive oxygen species generation remains localized to irradiated photosensitizer-containing areas [ 6 , 38 ]. Nevertheless, high photosensitizer concentrations or excessive light fluence may negatively affect host-cell viability [ 6 ]. Therefore, optimization of treatment parameters remains essential to maximize antimicrobial efficacy while preserving the integrity and viability of surrounding oral tissues [ 6 , 11 , 38 ]. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. This investigation employed a monospecies S. mutans biofilm on standardized flat enamel slabs. While this model offers a controlled and clinically relevant platform for initial efficacy assessment, it does not fully replicate the complexity of multispecies, saliva-bathed plaque in vivo, which involves dynamic nutrient flow and host-derived factors. Additionally, only a single MB concentration, one irradiation parameter set, and one CAP configuration were tested; therefore, the findings may not be directly extrapolated to other photosensitizer doses, light fluences, plasma sources, or clinical geometries. Future investigations should evaluate CAP and MB-aPDT against mature multispecies biofilms in dynamic models, optimize dosing regimens for shorter chairside application, and assess their effects on enamel and dentin, pulp safety, and the balance between pathogenic and commensal flora. Randomized clinical trials in high-caries-risk and orthodontic populations will be essential to determine whether the substantial in vitro/ex vivo reductions observed translate into meaningful decreases in lesion incidence and progression.
sections.conclusion: We conclude that both helium‑based CAP and MB‑aPDT at 660 nm significantly reduced S. mutans biofilm viability and disrupted biofilm structure, with 0.2% CHX remaining the most potent modality and CAP‑180 s achieving antibacterial effects comparable to MB‑aPDT. These findings support the clinical potential of these non‑antibiotic physical approaches as adjuncts to mechanical biofilm control and conventional chemotherapeutics in caries‑preventive and restorative dentistry.

title: The predictive value of multidimensional frailty instruments for postoperative adverse outcomes in cancer patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Purpose To systematically review the predictive performance of Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI), Groningen Frailty Indicator (GFI), and Edmonton Frailty Scale (EFS) for adverse outcomes including postoperative complications, unplanned readmission, 30-day mortality, prolonged length of stay among cancer patients. Materials and methods A comprehensive search was conducted across English and Chinese databases until October 2, 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 tool. Predictive performance was evaluated by pooling sensitivity, specificity, and summary receiver operating characteristic curves. Results There were 21 studies (4,435 individuals) that were included for the meta-analysis. TFI demonstrated pooled sensitivities of 0.64 (for postoperative complications), 0.77 (for unplanned readmission), and 0.50 (for prolonged hospital stay), with corresponding specificities of 0.67, 0.54, and 0.64 respectively. The areas under the curve (AUC) were 0.70, 0.71, and 0.60. GFI demonstrated sensitivities of 0.59, 0.65, and 0.55 for complications, 30-day mortality, and functional decline, with specificity of 0.73, 0.63, and 0.77, and the AUC of 0.71, 0.68, and 0.74. EFS had sensitivity 0.39, specificity 0.87, and AUC 0.57 for complications. Subgroup analysis revealed that TFI had reasonable predictive value for adverse outcomes with sensitivity 0.61–0.81 and specificity 0.60–0.68 among most gynecological and gastrointestinal cancer subgroups. In most subgroups, GFI showed higher specificity (0.64–0.84) relative to sensitivity (0.43–0.68). Conclusion TFI and GFI demonstrated moderate predictive validity for adverse outcomes, whereas EFS exhibited poor predictive performance. These findings highlight the necessity for caution interpretation of frailty assessments in clinical practice and underscore the importance of further validating these tools within diverse oncological contexts. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12957-026-04365-9.

sections.introduction: With the global aging population steadily increasing, both the incidence and mortality rates of cancer are rising annually [ 1 ]. According to global cancer statistics [ 1 ], approximately 20 million new cancer cases were reported in 2022, with this number projected to exceed 35 million by 2050, representing a 77% increase from 2022. Frailty is highly prevalent in cancer patients, with an occurrence of rate as high as 86%, often resulting from factors such as disease-related deterioration, treatment side effects, and malnutrition [ 2 ]. It is a biopsychosocial syndrome characterized by deficits in physical, cognitive, psychological, and social components, exhibiting multidimensional, dynamic, and potentially reversible features [ 3 ]. The presence of frailty significantly elevates the risk of adverse outcomes in cancer patients, including postoperative complications, increased mortality, prolonged length of stay, unplanned readmission, and chemotherapy intolerance [ 4 – 6 ]. Therefore, the early assessment of frailty is crucial, as it helps to identify its multidimensional characteristics and guide the implementation of targeted intervention strategies [ 7 , 8 ]. Furthermore, research suggests that frailty is a potentially reversible process, and the timely use of effective assessment tools can help identify high-risk patients, slow or reverse its progression, and ultimately improve clinical outcomes [ 9 – 11 ]. Frailty assessment tools are generally classified into two categories: physical dimension assessments and multidimensional assessments. The former includes tools such as the Frailty Phenotype (FP) and Frailty Index (FI), while the latter encompasses tools like the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI) [ 12 – 14 ]. While uni-dimensional tools primarily focus on the physiological domain, they may overlook psychological and social factors. In contrast, multidimensional tools take into account physiological, psychological, and social domains, thus offering a more comprehensive evaluation of frailty in cancer patients and providing deeper insights into its underlying mechanisms [ 15 ]. On the other hand, many multidimensional tools also rely on questionnaires and basic functional tests, making them practical for use in hospital, community, and home settings [ 16 ]. At present, three multidimensional frailty assessment tools—TFI, GFI, and EFS [ 14 , 17 , 18 ]—have gained increasing attention in oncology [ 19 , 20 ]. They have shown effective predictive validity for frailty among cancer patients across multiple countries [ 19 , 21 ]. Both TFI and GFI are self-reported scales, assessing three (physical, psychological, social) and four (physical, psychological, social, cognitive) domains respectively, each with 15 items and taking under 15 min [ 14 , 17 , 22 ]. Moreover, EFS combines objective measures with self-reports, covering nine dimensions—cognition, general health status, functional independence, social support, medication use, nutrition, mood, continence, and functional performance—with 11 items [ 18 ]. Of these, cognition and physical performance are objectively measured via clock-drawing and Timed Up and Go. It is clinically practical and takes under 5 min [ 23 ]. All three tools are cross-culturally validated and clinically suitable [ 15 – 17 ]. Recently, an increasing number of studies have explored the predictive performance of TFI, GFI, and EFS for adverse outcomes in cancer patients, but the results remain controversial. For instance, some studies have suggested that TFI can predict the risk of unplanned readmission within 30 days in patients with gastrointestinal tumors, while others have contested this finding [ 24 , 25 ]. Similarly, controversies exist surrounding GFI and EFS. For example, Bras et al. reported that GFI could not predict postoperative complications, whereas another study identified frailty as an independent predictor of such complications [ 26 , 27 ]. Regarding EFS, Fan et al. found that its ability to predict postoperative complications became non-significant after adjusting for covariates, while another study confirmed its efficacy in predicting these complications [ 28 , 29 ]. Although previous systematic reviews have emphasized the value of frailty assessment tools in predicting prognosis, most of the existing evidence has concentrated on older populations and uni-dimensional frailty tools [ 30 , 31 ]. Since that frailty in cancer patients involves multiple dimensions, there is a notable lack of systematic research specifically targeting multidimensional frailty scales. To address this gap, the present study aims to systematically synthesize existing research through a meta-analysis. This will assess the predictive performance of TFI, GFI and EFS in predicting adverse health outcomes in cancer patients, thereby providing valuable insights for clinicians in selecting appropriate frailty assessment tools.
sections.materials and methods_1: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the updated PRISMA guidelines and the MOOSE guidelines (meta-analyses of observational studies in epidemiology) (Supplement 1) [ 32 , 33 ]. The review protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025630364). Available from https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42025630364 . Data collection for this review occurred from November 1 to 7, 2025. This study adhered to the TITAN Guidelines 2025 for ethical AI use in research [ 34 ].
sections.inclusion and exclusion criteria: Studies that met the established inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) studies involving adult patients (18 years or older) with any type of cancer; (2) frailty assessment conducted using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI), Groningen Frailty Indicator (GFI), or Edmonton Frailty Scale (EFS); (3) reporting of at least one of the following postoperative adverse outcomes: postoperative complications (most commonly defined as Clavien-Dindo ≥ 2 grade, or categorized as medical/surgical or infectious/non-infectious events), 30-day mortality, prolonged length of stay (usually defined as hospitalization beyond the 75th percentile, with one study attributing it to chemotherapy intolerance), unplanned readmission (generally defined as readmission within 30 days after discharge), or postoperative functional decline (assessed using different scales such as Katz Index, Lawton IADL, ADL, or Barthel Index, all reflecting new or worsened impairment in daily activities); (4) availability of a four-grid diagnostic test table, including true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives; and (5) study design classified as cross-sectional or cohort. Studies were excluded based on the following criteria: (1) reports in the form of conference abstracts, reviews, posters, animal experiments, guidelines, commentaries, case reports, study protocols, or letters; (2) duplicate publications; and (3) studies for which the full text was unavailable.
sections.information sources and search strategy: A systematic search was conducted in nine databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, CNKI, WanFang, VIP, SinoMed) from inception to October 2, 2025, limited to articles in Chinese and English. Search terms were developed by combining medical subject headings (MeSH) with free-text keywords. The following terms were used: “neoplasms,” “Tilburg Frailty Indicator,” “Edmonton Frail Scale,” and “Groningen Frailty.” The full search strategy has been provided in Supplement 2. Two independent reviewers conducted the search to ensure the comprehensiveness and accuracy of the results.
sections.study selection: The studies were independently assessed for eligibility by the two authors based on the titles and abstracts, following the removal of duplicate records. After applying the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, full-text articles were thoroughly reviewed. In addition, the reference lists of all eligible studies, as well as grey literature from OpenGrey ( www.opengrey.com ) and Grey Literature Report from the New York Academy of Medicine Library( www.greylit.org ), were systematically screened to identify additional studies. When necessary, discrepancies regarding decisions were solved through discussion among the three authors.
sections.data extraction: Data extraction was subsequently conducted by two independent authors, with any disagreements resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. The extracted data included: author, year, country, mean age, sex distribution(male/female), study design, sample size, frailty assessment tool and tool cut-off values, cancer type, adverse outcomes, true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN), false negatives (FN), sensitivity, and specificity. If TP, TN, FP, and FN are not directly reported, they were derived from sensitivity and specificity using the following formulas: sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), specificity = TN / (FP + TN). All data were compiled into a standardized table. Missing data were obtained by contacting the authors of the original studies.
sections.risk of bias and applicability: Two independent authors assessed the risk of bias for the included studies and then compared their evaluation results. The risk of bias was evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool within the Review Manager (5.3) software [ 35 ]. This tool consists of two main components: risk of bias assessment and applicability assessment, with the evaluation focusing on four key domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. The risk of bias assessment covers all four domains, while the applicability assessment corresponds to the first three domains. In cases where there was disagreement between the two authors, the third author facilitated resolution through discussion, working toward a consensus.
sections.statistical analysis: Meta-analysis was performed using Stata 15.0, RevMan 5.3, Meta-Disc 1.4 and R software (version 4.4.1). Pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio (PLR), negative likelihood ratio (NLR), diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated and presented in forest plots. Meanwhile, summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curves were plotted, and the area under the curve (AUC) was computed to evaluate predictive performance of TFI, GFI and EFS for adverse outcomes. AUC values were classified as: excellent (0.9-1.0), good (0.8–0.89), fair (0.7–0.79), poor (0.6–0.69), or non-discriminatory (0.5–0.59) [ 36 ]. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I² statistic, with I² ≥ 50% or P < 0.05 showing moderate-to-high heterogeneity. Due to the high heterogeneity, subgroup analysis and meta-regression were conducted to explore the potential sources. We prioritized variables supported by previous evidence, such as cancer type, frailty tool cut-off score, patient age, timing of assessment, sample size, and study design, given the insufficient data reported for other parameters like tumor grade or stage [ 37 ]. Sensitivity analysis was carried out to examine the robustness of the pooled results. Due to the inconsistency in the threshold values of frailty assessment tools across the studies, we further assessed threshold effect. A P-value of < 0.05 was considered indicative of such an effect. A Fagan nomogram was performed to evaluate the clinical utility. Given the varying incidence of adverse events across cancer types, we followed established frameworks for measuring diagnostic uncertainty to visualize how frailty tools modify pre-test probabilities into post-test probabilities [ 38 ]. Specifically, we modeled three clinical scenarios with pre-test probabilities of 25% (low clinical suspicion), 50% (intermediate clinical suspicion), and 75% (high clinical suspicion) [ 39 , 40 ]. Finally, publication bias was evaluated using Deeks’ funnel plot, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
sections.study selection_1: Figure 1 illustrated the comprehensive search process and the results derived from the search strategy, presented in a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram. A total of 1167 records were retrieved from the initial electronic search across various databases: PubMed ( n = 89), Embase ( n = 213), Cochrane Library ( n = 27), Web of Science ( n = 150), Clinical Trials.gov ( n = 50), CNKI ( n = 175), VIP ( n = 80), WanFang Data ( n = 315), and SinoMed ( n = 68). No records were retrieved from two grey literature sources. After the removal of duplicates, 724 records remained for further evaluation. Following the screening of titles and abstracts, 687 records were excluded, leaving 37 studies for full-text review. Ultimately, 21 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis. Fig. 1 PRISMA flowchart of study inclusion and exclusion
sections.characteristics of included studies: Table 1 s ummarized the characteristics of the included studies. These studies were published between 2012 and 2025, with ten conducted in China, six in Switzerland, and one each in Belgium, Romania, Poland, Australia, and Turkey. Seventeen studies were prospective in design, while four were retrospective. TFI was utilized in seven studies, with thresholds of ≥ 4 ( n = 1) and ≥ 5 ( n = 6). Among the thirteen studies using GFI, the thresholds were distributed as follows: ≥3 ( n = 11), ≥ 4 ( n = 1), and ≥ 5 ( n = 1). For the four EFS studies, thresholds of ≥ 7 and ≥ 8 were applied in three and one study, respectively. Notably, Chen et al. employed all three tools, while Fan et al. used both GFI and EFS [ 28 , 44 ]. Furthermore, all included studies were approved by their respective ethics committees and adhered to corresponding ethical standards. sections.risk of bias and applicability of studie: Supplement 3 presented the overall risk of bias and applicability concerns across the included studies. In the “patient selection” domain, two studies were rated as unclear risk due to unspecified sampling methods, while one study was rated as high risk because colorectal cancer patients undergoing stoma reversal surgery were excluded. In the “reference standard” domain, four studies were rated as unclear risk for failing to report whether the standard accurately identified frailty. In the “flow and timing” domain, four studies were rated as high risk, and sixteen were rated as unclear risk. Among high risk studies, four were assessed as high risk since the use of multiple reference standards without fully including all cases. The remaining studies were rated as unclear, primarily owing to the lack of reporting on the time interval between the index test and the reference standard. Lastly, all studies were rated as low concern for applicability.
sections.threshold-effect analysis: Threshold effects were assessed using Meta-Disc 1.4 software. No significant threshold effects were observed for TFI (postoperative complications, prolonged length of stay, unplanned readmission), for GFI (postoperative complications, 30-day mortality, functional decline), or for EFS (postoperative complications) (all P > 0.05).
sections.predictive performance of tilburg frailt: Seven studies assessed frailty with TFI [ 24 , 25 , 41 – 45 ]. For postoperative complications (five studies), pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.64 (95% CI 0.50–0.77; I²=89.2%) and 0.67 (95% CI 0.48–0.82; I²=98.1%), with an AUC of 0.70 (95% CI 0.66–0.74). For prolonged length of stay (four studies), sensitivity and specificity were 0.50 (95% CI 0.27–0.73; I²=94.8%) and 0.64 (95% CI 0.44–0.81; I²=98.0%), AUC 0.60 (95% CI 0.56–0.64). For unplanned readmission (three studies), sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI 0.63–0.90; I²=38.1%) and specificity 0.54 (95% CI 0.40–0.68; I²=93.0%), AUC 0.71 (95% CI 0.61–0.81). Publication bias was not significant except for unplanned readmission ( P = 0.05).
sections.predictive performance of groningen frai: Thirteen studies evaluated GFI [ 26 – 28 , 44 , 46 – 54 ]. For postoperative complications (seven studies), sensitivity was 0.58 (95% CI 0.41–0.72; I²=92.8%) and specificity 0.70 (95% CI 0.57–0.80; I²=93.5%), AUC 0.69 (95% CI 0.65–0.73). For 30-day mortality (five studies), sensitivity was 0.65 (95% CI 0.40–0.83; I²=44.8%) and specificity 0.63 (95% CI 0.51–0.74; I²=90.2%), AUC 0.68 (95% CI 0.64–0.72). For functional decline (three studies), sensitivity was 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.75; I²=88.7%) and specificity 0.77 (95% CI 0.57–0.89; I²=92.8%), AUC 0.74 (95% CI 0.47–0.93). No publication bias was detected.
sections.predictive performance of edmonton frail: Four studies applied EFS for postoperative complications [ 28 , 29 , 44 , 55 ]. Pooled sensitivity was 0.39 (95% CI 0.27–0.52; I²=73.3%) and specificity 0.87 (95% CI 0.70–0.95; I²=87.6%), with an AUC of 0.57 (95% CI 0.53–0.62). No publication bias was observed. The comprehensive diagnostic analysis results for all outcomes could be found in Supplement 4, Fig. 2 , and Table 2 . Deeks’ funnel plots are further illustrated in Supplement 5. sections.predictive performance of multidimension: Considering that gastrointestinal cancers (GI) accounted for a large proportion of the included studies [ 27 – 29 , 41 , 43 – 45 , 47 , 52 , 55 ] and that frailty is more prevalent among GI cancer patients compared to other cancer types, with a reported prevalence of 42% [ 56 ]. we therefore performed a diagnostic meta-analysis focusing on GI cancers. This approach enables a more homogeneous assessment of frailty tools’ predictive performance in a clinically meaningful population. The detailed results are presented in Supplement 6.
sections.outcomes: postoperative complications an: Five studies evaluated TFI in gastrointestinal cancer patients [ 24 , 41 , 43 – 45 ], with pooled AUCs of 0.68 (95% CI 0.64–0.72) for postoperative complications and 0.67 (95% CI 0.57–0.78) for prolonged length of stay, indicating moderate predictive performance. But one study by Chen et al. focused solely on complications [ 43 ]. Three studies assessed GFI for postoperative complications, yielding a pooled AUC of 0.67 (95% CI 0.61–0.73), reflecting limited accuracy [ 27 , 28 , 44 ]. Four studies investigated EFS, with a pooled AUC of 0.57 (95% CI 0.53–0.62), suggesting weaker predictive ability [ 28 , 29 , 44 , 55 ].
sections.other outcomes: unplanned readmission, 3: Meta-analysis was not feasible due to the limited number of studies about unplanned readmission, 30-day mortality, and postoperative functional decline; therefore, a qualitative synthesis was presented. In gastrointestinal cancer frailty assessed by the Chinese TFI was associated with higher unplanned readmission (7.9% vs. 1.9%, P < 0.05) [ 24 ]. For 30-day mortality, results were inconsistent: Tegels et al. reported that gastric cancer patients with GFI ≥ 3 exhibited significantly increased risk (OR 4.0, P = 0.03) [ 52 ], whereas another reported no significant association in colorectal cancer (OR 0.68, P = 0.72) [ 47 ]. For postoperative functional decline, GFI showed reasonable predictive ability, with reported AUCs of 0.79 (95% CI 0.73–0.85) and 0.74 (95% CI 0.66–0.78) [ 28 , 44 ].
sections.meta-regression analysis results: Meta-regression was conducted to explore heterogeneity across cancer type, frailty tool cut-off score, patient age, timing of assessment, sample size, and study design. For sensitivity, TFI prediction of postoperative complications showed no significant heterogeneity, whereas its prediction of prolonged length of stay varied with cancer type, cut-off score, age, timing, and sample size. GFI sensitivity for postoperative complications was affected by cut-off score and study design, while its prediction of 30-day mortality varied with sample size. EFS sensitivity for complications was influenced by outcome definition, cut-off score, and sample size. Regarding specificity, TFI performance was affected mainly by sample size. GFI varied by cut-off and study design both for complications and 30-day mortality. However, no significant heterogeneity was detected for EFS specificity in predicting complications. Detailed results are provided in Fig. 3 and Supplement 7. sections.subgroup analysis: Subgroup analysis by cancer type showed variable predictive performance. TFI sensitivity for postoperative complications was numerically higher in the cervical cancer (0.74, 95%CI: 0.61–0.85) than gastrointestinal cancer (0.68, 95%CI: 0.44–0.86), although specificity was only 0.60 (95%CI: 0.52–0.68). TFI predicting prolonged length of stay with moderate accuracy, in gastrointestinal cancer subgroup with sensitivity of 0.61 (95%CI: 0.41–0.78) and specificity of 0.65 (95%CI: 0.38–0.86), showing numerically superior performance compared to cervical cancer. Meanwhile, TFI achieved the pooled sensitivity of 0.81 (95%CI: 0.65–0.94) for predicting unplanned readmission in gastrointestinal cancer, but its relatively worse specificity (0.44, 95%CI: 0.39–0.49) indicated a high false positive rate. In contrast, the gynecologic cancer subgroup demonstrated a more balanced performance. GFI presented relatively poor predictive performance across different cancer subgroups in our study. The pooled sensitivity of eight studies ranged from 0.43 to 0.64 in gastrointestinal, head and neck, or skin, lung, and breast cancer; GFI demonstrated the specificity of only 0.47 (95%CI: 0.36–0.59) in predicting 30-day mortality in the breast cancer While other subgroups exhibited moderate values (0.64–0.84), indicating some predictive value of GFI for these adverse outcomes. Given insufficient sample sizes in most subgroups, these subgroup findings should be considered exploratory. Furthermore, EFS presented low predictive performance across evaluated cancer types in our study. Detailed results are provided in Table 3 . By contrast, the overall effect estimates for the remaining outcomes were generally stable following the exclusion of individual studies. Detailed contents are shown in Fig. 4 . sections.summary of main results: This meta-analysis systematically integrated the performance of three multidimensional frailty assessment tools for predicting adverse outcomes in cancer patients. It was shown that TFI demonstrated diagnostic value for postoperative complications, prolonged length of stay and unplanned readmission; GFI could predict postoperative complications, postoperative functional decline and 30‐day mortality; whereas EFS showed relatively poor predictive value for complications. In gastrointestinal cancer, unlike EFS, both TFI and GFI retained the diagnostic utility for postoperative complications, and TFI also could predict prolonged length of stay.
sections.analysis of our main study results: TFI showed different predictive performance: acceptable discrimination for postoperative complications (AUC = 0.70) and unplanned readmission (AUC = 0.71), but poor performance for prolonged length of stay (AUC = 0.60). These findings align with its performance in predicting 30-day complications after lumbar degenerative surgery [ 57 ]. Multidimensional frailty tools outperform uni-dimensional indices such as modified frailty index‐5 (mFI-5) and the revised Risk Analysis Index (revised-RAI), which reported areas under the curve of 0.63 and 0.54 respectively in cancer patients [ 58 , 59 ]. This advantage likely reflects the ability of TFI to stratify patients by severity across physical, psychological and social domains. Meta-regression identified multiple complex sources of heterogeneity, which could be partly explained by the theory basis and measurement characteristics of TFI. Firstly, the original theoretical framework for TFI assumes interactive effects among physical, psychological, and social frailty, empirical evidence remains inconclusive [ 3 , 14 , 60 ]. For instance, Ye et al. found a bidirectional but asymmetrical relationship between physical and psychological frailty, with a weaker association to social frailty [ 61 ]. This finding suggests that the original three-dimensional interaction hypothesis of TFI has yet to be fully validated in the population. As cancer populations being assessed diversify, the interactions among the three frailty dimensions may introduce ambiguity, potentially impacting the predictive stability of the tool. Additionally, TFI may have certain limitations in the reliability and validity within the psychological and social domains, making the tool optimal cut-off value unclear [ 62 ]. Differences in cultural interpretation of social and psychological items could therefore potentially influence the predictive accuracy of the tool. Moreover, research indicated that the incidence of social frailty in cancer patients is significantly higher than in the general elderly population and is associated with shorter survival, further suggesting that the current social dimension items in TFI may not fully capture the true condition of frailty among cancer patients [ 63 ]. To address these limitations, future research should concentrate on validating and refining the items to enhance the tool’s cross-cultural applicability. Furthermore, as age and the risk of postoperative adverse events increases, the risk of frailty among cancer patients also rises [ 64 ]. Subgroup analysis of cancer type showed TFI was primarily studied in gastrointestinal and gynecological cancers for predicting above three adverse outcomes, with sensitivity of 0.61–0.81 and specificity of 0.60–0.68. The seemingly modest predictive results across different cancer types may, as previously discussed, be attributed to the use of generalized tool items [ 20 ]. However, these generalized items may not adequately capture cancer-specific frailty phenotypes. For example, some gastrointestinal cancer patients post-surgery may experience chronic digestive dysfunction that requires ongoing monitoring, whereas gynecological cancer patients may present with temporary, treatment-toxic related gastrointestinal symptoms [ 65 , 66 ]. These differences in physical frailty could impact the timing and predictive accuracy of the TFI. Meanwhile, the small sample size in cervical cancer means current evidence does not support using TFI for these patients. Further studies are needed to confirm whether TFI performs differently in gynecological and gastrointestinal cancer subgroups. GFI demonstrated moderate predictive performance for postoperative complications in cancer patients, with an AUC of 0.71. Sources of heterogeneity contained variations in the tool cut-off thresholds and study designs. Firstly, GFI used different cut-off values across studies. Subgroup analysis showed that when the threshold is set at ≥ 4 points, both sensitivity and specificity are 0.65, whereas at ≥ 5 points, sensitivity drops to 0.25, indicating that inconsistent thresholds could affect the validity of frailty identification. Moreover, GFI assessment of cognitive frailty appears to focus predominantly on memory-related items, which may restrict its capacity to comprehensively detect impairments in executive function, attention, and other cognitive domains when applied to cancer populations [ 67 ]. Studies further have indicated that cognitive frailty is a significant predictor of postoperative complications, even outperforming overall frailty assessments [ 68 ]. Therefore, incomplete evaluation of frailty subtypes by GFI may contribute to variations in predictive efficacy. Although the outcome definition for GFI varied across studies on postoperative complications, this was not identified as a source of heterogeneity. Lastly, study design significantly influenced the sensitivity and specificity of complications prediction. Prospective studies showed more stable sensitivity and specificity than retrospective. GFI predicted the postoperative 30-day mortality in frail cancer patients, with AUC of 0.68. This result aligns with the findings of Linda et al., whose study reported an AUC of 0.64 [ 69 ]. The predictive performance of GFI is partially influenced by factors such as tumor staging and grading. For instance, Shaw et al. demonstrated that in patients with lower-grade tumors and early-stage cancers, the correlation between frailty and survival rate is stronger, which partially accounted for differences in predictive efficacy [ 70 ]. Furthermore, while GFI includes dimensions related to psychological frailty, such as anxiety and depression, the role of these factors in predicting short-term mortality remains unclear [ 71 ]. Additionally, significant heterogeneity existed between studies due to differences in study design and sample size. GFI demonstrated moderate predictive performance in predicting postoperative functional decline, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.74, indicating performance between moderate and good. This result is comparable to the predictive efficacy of other frailty scales, such as the Physical Frailty Phenotype (FFP), Frailty Index (FI), and Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), with AUC values of 0.66, 0.76, and 0.77, respectively [ 72 ]. The performance of GFI may be to some extent attributed to its broad assessment scope. Research has shown that factors such as activities of daily living, cognitive status, and depressive symptoms significantly affect postoperative functional decline [ 73 ]. Therefore, the inclusion of multidimensional items in GFI may improve its capacity to capture the diverse characteristics of functional decline, potentially enhancing overall predictive performance. Subgroup analyses by cancer type provide preliminary insights into predictive performance of GFI. Across most subgroups, specificity estimates were consistently higher than sensitivity, which may result from some patients having normal GFI scores despite significant cancer or treatment-related risks. This may attribute to some easily overlooked factors like postoperative psychological health burden and medical decision-making burden, which are difficult for the tool to quantify [ 26 ]. Because of the small number of studies, the predictive value of GFI across gastrointestinal, breast, lung, head, neck or skin cancer merits further investigation. EFS demonstrated relatively poor predictive capability for postoperative complications in cancer patients, with an AUC 0.57. This finding aligns with the study by Czajka et al. [ 74 ], which reported an AUC of 0.50. We considered followed reasons for this poor results. First, while an EFS score ≥ 7 is commonly used as the threshold for frailty, some studies have shown improved predictive performance when cut-off is lowered to ≥ 4, yielding an AUC of 0.67 [ 75 ]. This suggests that variations in cutoff values may influence the predictive accuracy of EFS. Additionally, EFS is predominantly applied to cardiac surgery patients, particularly those with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) [ 76 – 78 ]. For example, EFS achieved AUCs of 0.66 and 0.65 for predicting postoperative adverse outcomes among cardiac patients separately [ 79 ], supporting its utility in cardiac surgery setting. Beyond cardiac surgery, You et al. reported EFS demonstrated an AUC of 0.61 for predicting postoperative complications in elderly patients undergoing major abdominal surgery, suggesting a certain predictive value in other non-cancer surgical population [ 80 ]. Thus, its established utility in non-cancer surgical contexts may not fully apply into cancer patients. Furthermore, postoperative complications in cancer patients are also influenced by outcome definitions and sample size, potentially affecting EFS predictive performance. And lastly, frailty has been described in oncogeriatric practice as a cancer-specific vulnerability state driven by tumor-host interactions and accelerated aging process [ 81 ]. The general nature of EFS may explain its suboptimal predictive value in older individuals with cancer. Therefore since its inconsistent diagnostic accuracy, stemming from threshold variability and these broader applicability concerns, our findings do not support the use of EFS as a tool for predicting postoperative complications in cancer patients.
sections.clinical utility of three multidimension: TFI with sensitivity of 0.77 is suitable for screening of frail cancer patients at risk of unplanned readmission; TFI balanced sensitivity (0.64) and specificity (0.67) supports general risk stratification, rather than definitive decision alone for postoperative complications; GFI of high specificity (0.73 and 0.77) demonstrates reliable for confirming positives, thereby guiding intensified perioperative management and early rehabilitation; balanced sensitivity and specificity of 0.65 and 0.63 indicate moderate discrimination for 30-day mortality; Similarly, EFS with high specificity of 0.87 identifies frail cancer patients at high risk of complications and supports enhanced postoperative monitoring. In Fagan nomograms under low suspicion of clinical scenario, negative posterior probabilities for TFI (15%), GFI (16%), and EFS (19%) showed limited ability to rule out the risk of postoperative complications. On the other hand, under a high suspicion of clinical scenario, positive posterior probabilities substantially increased, with TFI (85%), GFI (87%), and EFS (90%) demonstrating meaningful to confirm the risk of postoperative complications. Detailed information are shown in Fig. 5 . sections.strengths and limitations: This study has several strengths and limitations. First, it is the first to synthesize the commonly used multidimensional frailty tools for cancer patients, examining the predictive performance of TFI, GFI, and EFS for outcomes such as postoperative complications, 30-day mortality, and unplanned readmission. Second, this study provides preliminary insights into the sources of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis by cancer type in the predictive performance of multidimensional frailty scales, as well as the differences in predictive efficacy within gastrointestinal cancer. These findings might lay a methodological foundation for the future development of cancer-specific frailty assessment tools. However, there are several limitations to consider. Firstly, the integrated literature exhibited heterogeneity, and some of our overall summary results have wider confidence intervals, suggesting that clinical applicability should be carefully considered when interpreting the results. Meanwhile, due to the limited number of included studies and heterogeneous cancer types, we were not able to conduct stratified or subgroup analyses for other detailed factors like age groups and cancer stages. Secondly, we have not further clarified clinical utility from other predictive parameters and across factors above. Thirdly, the existing evidence indicated that the predictive efficacy of the three scales is moderate to low. and so caution is required when applying these scales in clinical settings. Fourth, included studies may not have been powered to detect certain complications especially for rare events, which may impact the pooled estimates. In addition, current evidence on common uni-dimensional frailty tools is focused on specific cancers, making direct comparison with TFI, GFI, EFS across cancer population difficult. Lastly, these tools could not account for the broader social, economic, and political factors in health ecology theory, nor can they track the real trajectory of cancer patients within their lived environment. Further research is needed to assess the predictive performance of these tools and compare uni- and multi-dimensional frailty assessments in cancer populations, strengthening the evidence for their effectiveness and establishing their clinical utility.
sections.conclusion_1: Our findings showed that TFI is useful for identifying postoperative complications, prolonged length of stay, and unplanned readmission, while GFI shows value for complications, 30-day mortality, and functional decline. In contrast, EFS demonstrated limited utility for complications.Thus, we recommend TFI and GFI as decision supports, but do not consider EFS when used to assess frailty for the purpose of predicting postoperative complications in cancer patients. Future studies should further validate these three tools predictive performance in cancer patients and assess their real-world applicability. We also recommend developing cancer specific frailty tools that combine objective measures and subjective scales, incorporating frailty subtypes, to enhance assessment accuracy and clinical decision-making.

title: Surgical Management and Outcomes of Carotid Body Tumors in a High-Altitude Region of Yemen: A Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose Carotid body tumors (CBTs) are more prevalent in high-altitude populations, possibly owing to chronic hypoxia-induced carotid body hyperplasia. This study evaluated the clinical characteristics and surgical outcomes of CBTs at a tertiary center in Sana’a, Yemen, located approximately 2,250 m above sea level. Materials and Methods This prospective observational study included 24 patients who underwent CBT resection between October 2023 and November 2025 at our institution. We analyzed patient demographics, tumor volume, Shamblin classification, operative details, and surgical outcomes. Factors associated with cranial nerve injury (CNI) were evaluated using Fisher exact and non-parametric tests. Results The cohort had a mean age of 37.8±11.3 years, with marked female predominance (87.5%) and a high prevalence of blood group O (83.3%). Most tumors were advanced, with Shamblin class II or III tumors accounting for 91.7% of cases. External carotid artery (ECA) management, including permanent ligation in three patients and temporary clamping in one patient, was required in 16.7% of cases. The overall transient CNI rate was 29.2% (7/24), and no permanent neurological deficits or perioperative stroke occurred. Transient CNI was numerically more frequent in patients with Shamblin class III tumors than in those with Class I/II tumors (45.5% vs. 15.4%; P=0.182). Intraoperative ECA management was significantly associated with transient CNI (100.0% vs. 15.0%; P=0.003), whereas tumor volume was not significantly associated with CNI (P=0.820). Conclusion In this cohort, surgical resection of CBTs in a high-altitude region of Yemen was feasible without preoperative embolization, with no permanent neurologic deficits or perioperative stroke. The observed high prevalence of blood group O may suggest a distinctive demographic feature in this population, although this finding requires further investigation. Shamblin class III tumors showed a numerically higher rate of transient CNI, and the need for ECA management appeared to reflect greater surgical complexity. Long-term follow-up and larger studies are needed to validate these findings.
