sections.gene enrichment associations with sfc: PLS2- genes associated with SFC differences were most enriched for BP in regulation of neuron projection and nervous system development, for CC in synaptic and postsynaptic membrane, and for MF in extracellular ligand-gated monoatomic ion channel activity and amyloid-beta binding. Conversely, PLS2+ genes were primarily enriched for BP related to small GTPase-mediated signal transduction and temperature homeostasis, for CC involving adherens junctions and collagen-containing extracellular matrix, and for MF associated with nucleoside-triphosphatase regulator activity and GTPase regulator activity. KEGG analysis revealed significant enrichment in pathways of neurodegeneration-multiple diseases and retrograde endocannabinoid signaling pathway for PLS2- genes, and in neuroactive ligand signaling and axon guidance pathway for PLS2+ genes ( Figure 4d , e and Supplemental Table S4 ).
sections.discussion: Using a multimodal imaging fusion method based on Laplace eigendecomposition, we characterized for the first time abnormal patterns of whole-brain-scale SFC in PTSD patients, and revealed their relationship to multidimensional brain biology. The participant cohort used in this study has been previously described in several publications focusing on identifying imaging biomarkers of PTSD subjects, although in a single-modal fashion (Lei et al., 2015 ; Li et al., 2016 ; Li et al., 2016 , 2021 ). While these studies provided insights into specific aspects of PTSD neuropathology, they were inherently limited by their single-modal experimental design. Going beyond this, the present work investigates potential PTSD biomarkers from a new perspective by combining structural and functional images to identify changes in SFC, and then linking these to the underlying molecular architecture. This new analysis yields a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis and molecular mechanisms of PTSD. We have shown that PTSD patients have region-specific alterations in SFC across multiple brain regions, some of which are significantly correlated with the severity of PTSD; the regional distribution pattern of SFC is associated with the spatial distribution of biological properties of brain tissue; and genes associated with altered SFC in PTSD are enriched in various BPs related to neural development and neural signaling. These findings provide insights into the structural and functional interactions and network wiring rules of PTSD and offer potential biomarkers for diagnostic and therapeutic research. The integrated measure SFC contains more information than the sum of its structural and functional components, and so variations in SFC may arise from diverse neurobiological mechanisms, the interpretation of which depends on the disease context and clinical circumstances. Rather than being directly mapped onto a single mechanism, increases or decreases in SFC are better understood as a manifestation of rebalancing between structural constraints and functional demands within brain networks (Fotiadis et al., 2024 ). To define their complex interdependencies we used the eigendecomposition approach, which models functional signals as a diffusion process on the underlying structural network (Abdelnour, Voss, & Raj, 2014 ). In predicting FC through eigenmode mapping of SC, we simulate how neural activity propagates to form the observed functional patterns. This physics framework, grounded in topology, enhances the neurobiological interpretability of SFC (Abdelnour et al., 2018 ). As in earlier studies using this approach (Facca, Del Felice, & Bertoldo, 2024 ; Wang, Owen, Mukherjee, & Raj, 2017 ), a small number of eigenmodes sufficed for accurate FC reconstruction, which improves sensitivity to subtle changes, and simplifies investigation of structure–function relationships in disease (Lu et al., 2025 ). We found heterogeneous whole-brain SFC distribution aligning with established hierarchies (Baum et al., 2020 ; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019 ): the gradient of gradual SFC decoupling from unimodal (VN, SMN, and SUBs) to transmodal regions (DMN, FPN, and VAN) reflects decreasing functional specialization from modality-specific processing to cognitive flexibility (Preti & Van De Ville, 2019 ). Areas with relatively high SFC, including the cerebellum, have high heritability (Gu, Jamison, Sabuncu, & Kuceyeski, 2021 ). Consequently, high SFC not only reflects structure-constrained variation in dynamics (Fernandez-Iriondo et al., 2021 ), but also underpins stability across individuals and generations. Group comparisons revealed multiple regional SFC alterations. Among the higher-order networks, both DMN and FPN showed extensive SFC changes, consistent with their known roles in PTSD (Alexandra Kredlow et al., 2022 ; Bao et al., 2021 ; Patriat, Birn, Keding, & Herringa, 2016 ). DMN abnormalities overlapped with earlier findings from graph theory in the same cohort (Lei et al., 2015 ), while SFC alterations in right FPN may be related to excessive threat attention bias in PTSD (Berg et al., 2021 ), a further manifestation of dysregulated fear and threat control. PTSD also showed lower SFC in the right visual regions and thalamus. The thalamus is thought to modulate activity across fear-processing regions during high-threat states (Venkataraman & Dias, 2023 ), and amygdala–thalamus connectivity is correlated with PTSD severity (Ben-Zion et al., 2020 ). Threatening visual signals are transmitted to the amygdala via the superior colliculus and occipital lobe (Koller, Rafal, Platt, & Mitchell, 2019 ), and this circuit takes part in fear learning (Wei et al., 2015 ). Notably, variability in threat-visual circuitry connectivity partially underlies susceptibility to PTSD (Harnett et al., 2025 ), and intervention in high visuospatial demand tasks following trauma can alleviate intrusive painful memories (Iyadurai et al., 2018 ), so treatment targeting visual neural circuits shows promise. In addition, PTSD patients with lower VAN connectivity show clinically significant attentional impairment (Esterman et al., 2020 ). In connectome gradient analysis, PTSD patients show higher system segregation in SMN and lower participation coefficients in DAN, correlating with global gradient variance and CAPS scores (He et al., 2025 ). The observed alterations in SFC within these network regions suggest corresponding functional abnormalities. It is of course difficult to establish causation in cross-sectional studies. Due to statistical power limitations, the associations between regional SFC and clinical measures across the SMN, VAN, DAN, DMN, and SUB did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Nevertheless, these findings also provide valuable insights into the potential contribution of SFC alterations to the neural mechanisms underlying PTSD. On the one hand, network configuration abnormalities reflected by SFC may underlie core PTSD symptomatology (Lanius et al., 2015 ; Nicholson et al., 2020 ). For instance, functional alterations in the DMN have been associated with excessive self-referential processing, which may facilitate the intrusive recollection of traumatic memories, manifesting as flashbacks and reexperiencing symptoms (Lanius, Terpou, & McKinnon, 2020 ). Similarly, dysregulated modulation of attention-related networks may lead to attentional rigidity, potentially accounting for threat hypersensitivity and hypervigilance observed in PTSD patients (Koch et al., 2016 ). On the other hand, these findings also suggest that PTSD exhibits clinical heterogeneity that can obscure group-level effects and the directionality of associations (Ben-Zion et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ), highlighting the need for future studies with larger samples to identify potential biological subtypes of PTSD. In any case, more information on these regions may improve our understanding of PTSD severity trajectories. Spatial colocalization analysis demonstrated broad negative correlations between SFC and various aspects of brain tissue biology: specifically, regions enriched for neurons, glia, neurotransmitter systems, and metabolic activity show lower SFC. This may reflect the greater functional flexibility enabled by complex microcircuitry and higher metabolic demands (Chen et al., 2023 ; Luppi et al., 2022 ). PTSD pathophysiology involves various substrates: recent high-throughput single-cell sequencing studies implicate dysregulation in inhibitory neurons, endothelial cells, and microglia across multiple neurotransmitter pathways (Hwang et al., 2025 ). Interestingly, in our study, spatial SFC–neurobiological correlations were highly consistent between PTSD and TENC, with only weak correlations with intergroup SFC differences. Cortical chemoarchitecture shares key organizational traits with functional and structural brain anatomy (Hänisch et al., 2023 ), and a recent study attributed cortical SFC variability to the overlapping distributions of various neurotransmitter systems (L. Jiang et al., 2025 ). Our results may therefore shed new light on the biological substrate of SFC spatial heterogeneity: intrinsic cellular and molecular architecture provides a fundamental constraint framework for the distribution of SFC, persistent regardless of disease status. They also support the idea that the variability in the relationship between white matter structure and neural activity constitutes an inherent property of brain networks (Fotiadis et al., 2024 ). Finally, gene association analysis revealed significant correlations between PTSD-related SFC alterations and PLS2 gene co-expression patterns. Brain genes showed differential expression across regions characterized by varying SFC profiles. PLS2- genes were predominantly enriched in terms related to neuronal synapses, neurodegenerative disease pathways, and ion channel activity. Proper development and regulation of neuron are essential for constructing accurate neural circuits (Tau & Peterson, 2010 ). The widespread lower SFC observed in PTSD may be associated with dysregulation of synaptic regulatory genes, potentially contributing to anatomical–functional decoupling, while alterations in ion channel activity further disrupt synaptic information transmission. These findings resonate with recent large-scale transcriptomic analyses of postmortem brain tissue from PTSD patients, which identified downregulation in a co-regulated set of genes marking interneuron function (Girgenti et al., 2021 ), raising the possibility that SFC-associated gene patterns may reflect pathological synaptic dysfunction in PTSD. Abnormalities in the endocannabinoid signaling pathway, which have been reported in PTSD patients, may promote the retention of aversive emotional memories (Hill et al., 2013 ). Furthermore, enrichment in amyloid-beta-binding functions suggests the involvement of molecules participating in neurotoxicity and protein aggregation, offering a potential link to chronic neurodegenerative mechanisms underlying PTSD (Kritikos et al., 2023 ). By contrast, PLS2+ genes showed enrichment patterns suggestive of compensatory signaling mechanisms in PTSD. As key regulators of cytoskeletal dynamics, GTPase-related proteins directly participate in synaptic structural and functional plasticity (Hedrick et al., 2016 ). Neuroplasticity enables the brain to reorganize and adapt, enhancing resilience to trauma and adversity (Udeh-Momoh et al., 2025 ). It is known that genetic variants can increase trauma vulnerability, and that a supportive environment can mitigate this effect (Clukay et al., 2019 ). Collectively, these findings suggest that transcriptional profiles, being more plastic and responsive to environmental and pathological processes, better capture abnormalities in brain organization, and may be responsible for SFC alterations. However, it is important to note that the enriched pathways identified here are relatively broad and that the interpretations remain speculative at this stage. Therefore, our findings provide exploratory transcriptomic correlates of SFC alterations that suggest candidate molecular pathways that may interact with trauma-related pathophysiology and warrant further mechanistic investigation. This study has some limitations. First, the cross-sectional design precluded determination of whether the SFC alterations represent trait-like or state-like effects, and their dynamic evolution throughout PTSD progression. Second, given the heterogeneity in trauma exposures and individual baselines, the generalizability of findings from our relatively limited sample size requires verification, ideally combining longitudinal follow-up with individual deep phenotyping. Third, in our sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Figures S1, S2) the choice of parameters in constructing SFC has a non-negligible influence on the analytical outcomes, no doubt largely due to necessary trade-offs in the methodological pipelines, familiar from other studies (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020 ; Schilling et al., 2021 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ). The sensitivity analyses also make an indirect argument for the brain network perspective (Osmanlıoğlu, Alappatt, Parker, & Verma, 2020 ): unimodal cortical regions are generally quite sensitive to parameter selection, while ROIs distributed in transmodal association cortices are more robust. This makes sense in terms of the hierarchical organization of brain networks: neural activity in primary sensory areas is more tightly coupled to local anatomical structures, while higher-order association cortices support functional integration through distributed networks, thus depending more on global properties. In the absence of a definitive methodological consensus, we adopted parameter ranges used in similar studies (Baum et al., 2020 ; Facca, Del Felice, & Bertoldo, 2024 ; Honey et al., 2009 ). Future research should systematically evaluate the potential effects of methodological variability on SFC estimation. Fourth, the spatial neurobiological maps and AHBA gene expression data originated from distinct healthy cohorts, which constrains interpretation of their correlations with SFC. Future analyses would benefit from multimodal data acquisition within the same participant population. Fifth, while spatial colocalization and gene association analyses provide valuable insights into neurobiology and brain organization in neuroimaging contexts, inferences remain at a correlative, noncausal level. Precise regulatory mechanisms necessitate further validation using animal models and molecular studies.
sections.conclusion: This study explored SFC deviations associated with PTSD. We found that PTSD, compared to TENC, is characterized by extensive alterations in SFC across multiple brain networks, including SMN, VN, DMN, DAN, VAN, FPN, and thalamus, and that the aberrant SFC patterns are associated with specific molecular and transcriptomic profiles. By integrating macroscale in vivo imaging with microscale biological substrates, our results advance the understanding of SFC in the psychopathology of PTSD and may help to establish targeted diagnosis and treatment measures.

title: Hair Loss in Patients on Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists: Understanding Risks and Managing Outcomes
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1RAs are used to improve glycaemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus; some of these drugs are also used to help with weight loss. In recent years, safety signals concerning a possible link between GLP-1RA therapies and hair loss have been emerging in the USA. The volume of prescriptions for these drugs in Europe is now increasing, and it can be expected that the number of cases of GLP-1RA-associated hair loss will therefore also increase in Europe over the coming years. In this commentary, we consider the pharmacological context and market expansion for GLP-1RAs, examine the evidence for an association between GLP-1RAs and hair loss, explore potential pathophysiological mechanisms, and propose clinical recommendations. Most evidence suggesting a potential association between GLP-1RAs and hair loss comes from pharmacovigilance database analyses and retrospective cohort studies. No prospective, controlled studies have specifically evaluated this issue. The evidence suggesting an increased risk of hair loss is strongest for semaglutide and tirzepatide. However, although cases of hair loss have been noted across diverse settings and multiple analyses, causality has not been established. One potential underlying mechanism is the rapid weight loss seen with these drugs, which could induce telogen effluvium. Further research is needed to evaluate causality, underlying mechanisms, the role of dosing and route of administration, and patient factors that may increase the risk. Clinicians need to be aware of the possibility of hair loss occurring with GLP-1RAs and patients should be informed about the potential risk and monitored for hair loss.

sections.key summary points: Pharmacovigilance database analyses and retrospective studies suggest a potential risk of hair loss with glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), particularly semaglutide and tirzepatide. Similar findings reported by multiple independent analyses strengthen the possibility of an association. However, the evidence is not conclusive, causality has not been established, and further research is needed. One potential underlying mechanism is the rapid weight loss seen with these drugs, which could induce telogen effluvium. Clinicians should be vigilant for GLP-1RA-associated hair loss and should warn patients of the potential risk.
sections.introduction: Glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and weight management for more than 10 years in the USA. They are effective at improving glycaemic control in patients with T2DM and aiding weight loss in patients with obesity [ 1 – 3 ]. Nonetheless, like all medications, GLP-1RAs can be associated with adverse effects, the most common of which are gastrointestinal in nature, such as diarrhoea and nausea [ 1 , 2 ]. Recently, there has been considerable interest on social media about aesthetic changes after the use of GLP-1RAs for weight loss, particularly facial volume depletion and facial aging (“Ozempic face”) [ 4 , 5 ]. In addition, safety signals concerning a possible link between GLP-1RAs and hair loss/alopecia have been emerging in the USA [ 6 ]. Hair loss can be distressing for affected individuals and have a negative effect on their quality of life [ 7 , 8 ]. Among the GLP-1RAs that are available in Europe, several are now approved for use in the management of weight loss as well as the treatment of T2DM. The volume of prescriptions for these drugs is increasing each year [ 9 ]. It can therefore be expected that the number of cases of GLP-1RA-associated hair loss might increase in Europe over the coming years. In this commentary, we consider the pharmacological context and market expansion for GLP-1RAs, examine the evidence for an association between GLP-1RAs and hair loss, explore potential pathophysiological mechanisms, and propose clinical recommendations.
sections.pharmacological context: Endogenous GLP-1, which is released from intestinal endocrine cells, is involved in glucose regulation. Its principal actions include enhancing insulin secretion, inhibiting glucagon secretion, delaying gastric emptying (which reduces the rate that dietary glucose enters to bloodstream), and promoting a feeling of satiety [ 10 , 11 ]. GLP-1RAs were developed to mimic the effect of endogenous GLP-1. They bind to and activate the GLP-1 receptor in a similar manner to endogenous GLP-1 and provide the same beneficial effects on glucose metabolism and food intake. Therefore, treatment with GLP-1RAs leads to improved glucose-dependent insulin secretion, decreased glucagon release, delayed gastric emptying, and a sense of satiety with subsequent reduced food intake [ 10 , 12 , 13 ]. GLP-1RAs are used to improve glycaemic control in patients with T2DM, with all drugs in this class being effective at reducing HbA1c and fasting plasma glucose levels [ 1 , 2 ]. Most GLP-1RAs act only on the GLP-1 receptor; however, tirzepatide is a dual gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP)/GLP-1RA and therefore targets additional glucose regulatory pathways compared with other GLP-1RAs [ 10 ]. Meta-analysis indicates that tirzepatide is the most effective for the treatment for T2DM, followed by the GLP-1RAs semaglutide and liraglutide [ 2 ]. In addition to treating T2DM, some GLP-1RAs are also approved to help with weight loss in patients with obesity. This is achieved through their effects on gastric emptying, satiety and food intake [ 12 , 13 ]. Evidence suggests that tirzepatide and semaglutide provided greater reductions in body weight than other GLP-1 agonists in patients who also have T2DM [ 2 ], and in patients who have overweight or obesity irrespective of the presence/absence of T2DM [ 3 ]. With respect to safety and tolerability, the most common adverse events seen with GLP-1 agonists are gastrointestinal, such as diarrhoea and nausea [ 1 , 2 ]. A benefit–harm modelling study involving non-diabetic adults with overweight/obesity found that abdominal pain, cholelithiasis, constipation, diarrhoea, alopecia, hypoglycaemia, injection site reactions and vomiting were more frequent with GLP-1 agonists compared with placebo, but that achieving a 10% weight loss outweighed the cumulative harm, with a net benefit probability of 0.97 at 1 year [ 14 ].
sections.epidemiological context in europe: GLP-1RAs were first launched in key European markets in 2009–2011 [ 15 ]. GLP-1RAs currently available in Europe for the treatment of T2DM include dulaglutide, liraglutide and semaglutide, with liraglutide and semaglutide also approved for the management of obesity. The dual GIP/GLP-1RA tirzepatide is approved for the treatment of both T2DM and weight loss. Studies from various European countries have demonstrated an increase in the use of GLP-1RAs over time [ 9 , 15 – 18 ]. For example, in Denmark the annual number of initiators of GLP-1RAs increased sixfold between 2016 and 2023 [ 18 ]. Analysis of GLP-1RA annual sales data indicated that the volume of standard units sold across Europe increased by 56.6% between 2021 and 2025 [ 9 ]. This was most evident for semaglutide, for which there was an increase of 171.7%. This sales growth will be reflected in an increasing number of patients being exposed to GLP-1RAs in Europe.
sections.public perceptions: An analysis of Google searches using the TRAJAAN platform found that searches related to GLP-1RAs increased by 45% between December 2024 and November 2025 (data on file), suggesting growing public interest. Most growth was seen in searches concerning price and side effects. Overall, searches mainly focused on weight loss benefits (96.8% of searches) and side effects, including fatigue, hair loss and tooth loosening. Analysis of the Reddit social media platform over the same period, using Brandwatch, found a 19% increase in patients sharing their experiences with GLP-1RAs (data on file). Most users were being treated by healthcare professionals. Users reported that side effects affecting the skin and hair caused emotional stress, particularly skin dryness, cracks, facial ageing/sagging, loss of body skin tone, hair loss, hair thinning/loss of density, and hair breakage. Individuals receiving GLP-1RAs for medical reasons tended to regard side effects as more acceptable than individuals who had purchased a GLP-1RA without a prescription and were taking it for aesthetic reasons. These findings indicate that possible hair loss associated with GLP-1RAs is of increasing concern for patients.
sections.association between glp-1ras and hair lo: Most data on the risk of hair loss with GLP-1RAs or GIP/GLP-1RAs come from database analyses and other retrospective studies. In the clinic, dermatologists tend to use the term alopecia along with a descriptor to define the final pattern/type of hair loss (e.g. alopecia areata, scarring alopecia, whereas when the symptom is increased hair shedding it is described using the terms telogen effluvium; see Sect. “ Clinical Forms of Drug-Induced Hair Loss ”). However, in this section, which discusses safety data from observational studies assessing drugs, the terms used are those stated in the source papers.
sections.pharmacovigilance data: converging signa: Analyses of pharmacovigilance databases, including the US FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) database and WHO global database (VigiBase), indicate that hair side effects are one of the most common dermatological adverse events reported for GLP-1RAs (Table 1 ) [ 19 – 22 ]. However, hair side effects are generally referred to with the generic terms “alopecia” or “hair loss”, without further explanation, making it difficult to understand which type of hair loss it is, and thus providing very generic prevalence data. sections.retrospective studies: increased risk of: Retrospective observational studies have reported mixed results. These studies tended to use more specific hair loss terms than the pharmacovigilance database studies. A small retrospective cohort study involving 283 recipients of GLP-1RAs seen at a dermatology clinic found no significant associations between specific drugs and development of either androgenetic alopecia or telogen effluvium, although non-significant trends were seen for semaglutide and tirzepatide [ 26 ]. However, analyses of large databases have found increased incidences of certain types of hair loss with some GLP-1RAs (Table 2 ) [ 27 – 31 ]. retrospective analysis of a US nationally representative database found that any GLP-1RA use was associated with a significantly increased risk of any alopecia (OR 1.18, p ≤ 0.001) and androgenetic alopecia (OR 1.80, p ≤ 0.001) but not of alopecia areata or telogen effluvium [ 28 ]. Consistent with this, a retrospective analysis of the US TriNetX database found that among specifically evaluated patients with T2DM those treated with GLP-1RAs had an increased risk of androgenetic alopecia compared with recipients of metformin (hazard ratios, HR; tirzepatide 5.67, semaglutide 4.43, dulaglutide 2.75, liraglutide 2.34) (Table 2 ) [ 30 ]. The risk was greater with tirzepatide compared with semaglutide (HR 1.53), dulaglutide (HR 2.17) or liraglutide (HR 2.50) [ 30 ]. Looking at patients specifically being treated for weight management (Table 2 ), a retrospective analysis of Canadian health claims data found a higher incidence of hair loss with semaglutide compared with bupropion-naltrexone (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1.52, 95% CI 0.86–2.69), with the risk being greater in women than in men [ 27 ]. Another analysis of the same database found that use of semaglutide or liraglutide for weight loss was associated with an increased risk of alopecia areata compared with bupropion-naltrexone (aHR 2.09, 95% CI 1.20–3.65), although a direct link between these drugs and the pathogenesis of alopecia areata has not been established [ 29 ]. A retrospective analysis of the US TriNetX database found an increased risk of telogen effluvium with GLP-1RA weight-loss treatment compared with other weight-loss interventions, but subgroup analyses showed this was due primarily to a significantly increased risk with tirzepatide compared with other weight-loss medications (not versus bariatric surgery), with no significant increase in risk seen for semaglutide or liraglutide [ 31 ].
sections.other data sources: As discussed above, real-world data indicate that, amongst GLP-1RAs, the risk of alopecia may be highest with tirzepatide and semaglutide [ 14 , 21 , 23 , 24 ]. Alopecia was not generally reported as a notable adverse event in papers summarizing major phase 3 randomized controlled trials of these drugs (which usually reported events with an incidence of ≥ 5%) [ 32 – 36 ]. However, in a phase 3 trial in non-diabetic patients with obesity, alopecia occurred in approximately 5% of tirzepatide recipients versus 0.9% of placebo recipients [ 37 ]. Moreover, the summary of product characteristics (SmPC) for tirzepatide lists hair loss as a common adverse reaction (incidence ≥ 1/100 to < 1/10), noting that it mainly occurs in patients with overweight/obesity with or without T2DM [ 38 ]. The SmPC for semaglutide used for weight management also lists hair loss as a common adverse reaction, stating that it occurred in 2.5% of semaglutide recipients versus 1.0% placebo recipients, and that it was more common in patients with a greater weight loss (≥ 20%) [ 39 ]. Hair loss is not listed as an adverse reaction in the SmPC for semaglutide used for the treatment of T2DM [ 40 ]. No meta-analyses evaluating hair loss with GLP-1RAs have been published. Systematic reviews have not been able to draw firm conclusions, noting the limited data available, and highlighting that although cases of hair loss have been reported across diverse settings, causality has not been established [ 41 – 43 ]. For example, a systematic review of five studies involving 2905 patients treated with GLP-1RAs (predominantly tirzepatide) that reported hair loss outcomes yielded conflicting findings; some studies reported hair loss with semaglutide or tirzepatide, while others reported improvements in patients with pre-existing hair loss [ 41 ]. The authors concluded that further research was needed. Factors that may affect the risk of hair loss with GLP-1RAs include the specific drug used; the dose, route and frequency of administration; and the indication for treatment (T2DM or weight loss) [ 20 , 44 ].
sections.clinical forms of drug-induced hair loss: In general, several types of hair loss/alopecia may be associated with different types of drugs, including telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, alopecia areata and scarring alopecia [ 45 , 46 ]. As discussed above, the available data suggest that the most common forms of hair loss reported with GLP-1RAs are telogen effluvium and worsening of androgenetic alopecia. Acute telogen effluvium is the most common cause of reversible drug-induced hair loss, with diffuse hair shedding usually occurring approximately 3 months after drug initiation [ 47 ]. A wide range of drugs can cause telogen effluvium, including monoclonal antibodies, kinase inhibitors, and other targeted therapies, oral contraceptives, endocrine therapies, retinoids, antihypertensive agents, anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antipsychotics, anticoagulants, and antifungal and antiviral drugs [ 45 , 47 ]. Anagen effluvium is caused by a sudden halt of anagen hair follicle growth, with hair loss occurring within days or weeks, and is commonly caused by chemotherapeutic agents [ 48 ]. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disorder that causes non-scarring alopecia, which can range from discrete patches to total scalp or body hair loss. Although it is usually idiopathic, alopecia areata can occasionally be triggered by drugs that interfere with immune system activity, including monoclonal antibodies targeting cytokines such as tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-4, checkpoint inhibitors, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors [ 45 , 49 ]. In addition, although rare, some drugs (especially epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors) can cause scarring alopecia [ 45 ]. In most cases of drug-induced hair loss, i.e. telogen and anagen effluvium, hair regrowth occurs after cessation of the offending drug [ 45 ]. However, the course of alopecia areata triggered by drugs may not be influenced by drug withdrawal. Androgenetic alopecia (male-pattern/female-pattern hair loss) is caused by a combination of genetic, hormonal and environmental factors, which can also include excess androgen intake (e.g. anabolic androgenic drug use) [ 50 ]. It is possible that androgenetic alopecia may become more visible if diffuse effluvium caused by GLP-1RA therapy occurs, although the androgenetic alopecia itself is not directly caused by the drugs.
sections.potential pathophysiological mechanism f: The main hypothesis about potential mechanisms underpinning an association between GLP-1RA use and hair loss is stress from rapid weight loss leading to telogen effluvium. Rapid and substantial weight loss due to low calorie intake can act as a stressor on the body, affecting the growth cycle of hair follicles and inducing telogen effluvium [ 51 – 53 ]. For example, hair loss is seen in some patients after bariatric surgery, a procedure that can lead to substantial weight loss and changes in nutritional status [ 54 – 56 ]. GLP-1RA drugs may also lead to micronutrient deficiencies associated with altered and decreased food intake; for example, levels of iron, calcium and some vitamins may be reduced [ 57 – 59 ]. In turn, micronutrient deficiency can be associated with hair loss [ 60 – 62 ]. The possibility of a direct effect of GLP1-RAs on the hair follicles has not been proven, although an in vivo and in vitro study showed expression of GLP-1 receptor in mouse skin hair follicles, suggesting the possibility of similar expression in human skin [ 63 ]. It should also be noted that it is theoretically possible that GLP-1RAs could have an indirect beneficial effect on hair loss, particularly in metabolically compromised patients (e.g. those with obesity, T2DM and peripheral insulin resistance) [ 64 ]. In T2DM, vascular damage from prolonged hyperglycaemia can lead to chronic hair loss [ 65 ]. In addition, androgenetic alopecia has been associated with insulin resistance [ 54 ], and GLP-1R expression is partly mediated by androgens [ 66 ], suggesting close interaction between the hormonal pathways. GLP-1RAs may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce hyperinsulinemia, improve microvascular function and enhance blood scalp flow, thereby targeting pathways involved in follicular miniaturization [ 54 , 64 ]. It has been proposed that by improving metabolic regulation and vascular responsiveness, GLP-1RAs could potentially reduce both diabetes-related hair shedding and androgenetic alopecia [ 64 , 65 ].
sections.summary and limitations of data: Recent evidence suggests a possible association between some GLP-1RAs and GIP/GLP-1RAs, particularly semaglutide and tirzepatide, and hair loss. Limited data suggest telogen effluvium and worsening of androgenetic alopecia may be the most common types of hair loss seen with these drugs. Most evidence on the potential association between GLP-1RAs and hair loss comes from pharmacovigilance analyses and retrospective cohort studies, which mainly mention alopecia or hair loss as a side effect without a specific diagnosis of the type of hair loss. No prospective, controlled studies have specifically evaluated this issue. Similar findings reported by multiple independent analyses strengthen the possibility of an association, but causality has not been established. In addition to the general lack of dermatological confirmation of an alopecia diagnosis, other limitations of the available data include heterogeneous definitions of hair loss/alopecia outcomes, possible under-reporting and reporting biases, and potential confounding due to factors such as T2DM, rapid weight loss and associated nutritional deficiencies. Looking ahead, it is possible that reporting of hair loss associated with GLP-1RAs may increase as these drugs become more widely used to manage weight in addition to their use in diabetes, and this may provide additional information about the risk. In Europe, annual sales of semaglutide and dulaglutide have increased substantially since 2021 [ 9 ], particularly semaglutide, which is approved for both diabetes and weight loss.
sections.recommendations for clinicians: To provide the best management for patients, it is important that clinicians are aware of the possibility of hair loss/alopecia occurring with GLP-1RAs. Patients undergoing treatment with a GLP-1RA should be informed about the potential risk of hair loss. They should also be provided with advice on adequate nutrition to help mitigate the risk, such as maintaining adequate intake of protein and micronutrients [ 52 , 54 ]. Rigorous clinical monitoring of patients for signs of hair loss is important, especially after rapid weight loss. Clinicians should implement proactive management of adverse effects. The specific type of hair loss should be identified, and patients should be referred to a dermatologist if appropriate. Dose reduction or withdrawal of the causative drug should be considered. With respect to prognosis, further studies are needed to confirm whether, if hair loss is due to a GLP-1RA drug, the hair regrows if the drug is stopped. In cases of telogen effluvium, the hair loss will stop after the weight loss stops, aided by counselling on appropriate nutrition.
sections.research perspectives: Further research is needed to evaluate causality, which should include prospective trials that control for weight loss and nutrition. This should include prospective controlled trials comparing weight loss achieved by different means, such as bariatric surgery and different pharmacotherapies (including different GLP-1RAs), and the effect on hair loss. Patients experiencing hair loss as a side effect should be dermatologically evaluated for a specific diagnosis and possible causes should be traced. Research into underlying mechanisms is needed, which could involve studies on GLP-1 receptors in human hair follicles. Stronger signals have been seen for once-weekly drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide), suggesting a potential role for dose and pharmacokinetics; therefore, additional research into the effect of different doses of GLP-1RA and route of administration on the risk of hair loss would be of interest. Studies to identify patient factors that could affect the risk of GLP-1RA-associated hair loss (such as the amount and speed of weight loss, the type of nutrition and serum mineral levels), and to delineate appropriate dose adjustments for patients who experience hair loss would help guide clinical practice.
sections.conclusion: Recent evidence suggests a possible association between some GLP-1RAs and hair loss, mainly telogen effluvium. However, the evidence is not conclusive, causality has not been established, and further research is needed. An international observational study is underway to better understand the impact of these drugs on the skin and appendages. In the meantime, consideration should be given to the balance between benefits and risks when using these drugs. Clinicians should be vigilant for hair loss in patients receiving these drugs. The overall aim should be to ensure the best quality of life and dermatological care for patients using this therapeutic class, which is an essential treatment option for patients with T2DM and individuals with obesity.

title: Endometriosis, subclinical cardiac remodeling, and cardiovascular risk: mechanistic insights from cardiac magnetic resonance and mediation analysis
abstract: Background Endometriosis is a systemic gynecological disorder affecting ~ 10% of reproductive-aged women and shares pathophysiological features with cardiovascular disease (CVD). However, its associations with cardiac remodeling and CVD risk, as well as underlying mechanisms, remain unclear. Methods This study utilized data from the UK Biobank, comprising 6,158 women diagnosed with endometriosis and 229,453 women without the condition. To validate our results, we employed a hospital cohort from the Second Affiliated Hospital of the University of South China, which included 612 women with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis and 612 age-matched controls. We applied multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models to investigate the association between endometriosis and the risk of CVD. Additionally, generalized linear models were used to evaluate cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) metrics. Mediation analyses were conducted to quantify the contributions of 32 biomarkers, with a particular emphasis on metabolic indices (e.g., triglyceride-glucose (TyG)-related indices, lipid accumulation product (LAP)), inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein (CRP), inflammation score (INFLA)), oxidative stress indicators (urate, bilirubin), and hormonal status markers (sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)). Results Over a median 13-year follow-up, 23,239 CVD events occurred. Endometriosis was associated with increased risks of CVD (HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.09–1.29) and coronary heart disease (CHD) (HR 1.25, 95% CI 1.12–1.40). These findings were robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and consistently replicated in the external Chinese cohort, with an additional significant association observed for stroke (HR: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.03–1.40). CMR imaging revealed subclinical concentric remodeling, including increased interventricular septal thickness (1.11%, 95% CI 0.13–2.11), relative wall mass (1.11%, 95% CI 0.05–2.17), and septal-to-lateral wall thickness ratio (0.64%, 95% CI 0.00–1.29). Mediation analyses identified metabolic dysfunction as the primary pathway, with TyG-related indices (15.4%–17.3%), LAP (11.8%), and triglycerides (8.9%) accounting for the largest proportions, followed by inflammation (CRP: 11.1%; INFLA: 3.7%) and oxidative stress (urate: 6.0%). Conclusions Endometriosis is associated with increased CVD risk and early subclinical cardiac remodeling, largely mediated by metabolic and inflammatory pathways. These findings underscore the necessity of cardiovascular risk stratification and metabolic monitoring in the clinical management of women with endometriosis. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12958-026-01564-7.

sections.introduction: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) continues to be the leading cause of mortality among women, accounting for 35% of female deaths globally [ 1 ]. In the United States and Europe, CVD results in more deaths among women than the combined impact of breast cancer, lung cancer, and chronic lung disease [ 1 ]. The majority of cardiovascular-related deaths in women are attributed to CVD and myocardial infarction (MI), as well as heart failure and stroke [ 2 ]. Despite ongoing efforts to raise awareness and improve cardiovascular health among women, progress in mitigating the impact of CVD has stagnated over the past decade [ 3 – 5 ]. Although traditional risk factors contribute to a woman's vulnerability to clinically significant CVD, conventional risk stratification methods, which employ various scoring systems, have proven insufficient in accurately assessing both short-term and long-term or lifetime risk in women [ 6 ]. Moreover, emerging research highlights the importance of female-specific conditions and reproductive history in shaping long-term cardiovascular health [ 7 ]. Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory gynecologic condition affecting ~ 10% of women of reproductive age, often characterized by delayed diagnosis and inadequate treatment [ 8 – 10 ]. Traditionally viewed as a pelvic disorder, it is now increasingly recognized as a multisystem disease [ 11 ]. Mounting evidence suggests that women with endometriosis may be at greater risk for CVD later in life [ 7 , 9 , 12 – 15 ]. Further, treatments for endometriosis, such as hormonal medications, hysterectomy, and oophorectomy, may modify CVD risk [ 9 , 16 , 17 ]. Despite growing evidence linking endometriosis to CVD, it remains uncertain whether endometriosis independently associates with adverse cardiac structural and functional phenotypes. Prior investigations have primarily targeted isolated cardiovascular outcomes, often lacking comprehensive scope and mechanistic exploration. Addressing this gap is crucial for developing integrated approaches that consider both reproductive and systemic health in women with endometriosis. In this study, we leveraged the population-based UK Biobank (UKB) and a hospital-based cohort of laparoscopically confirmed cases to investigate the relationship between endometriosis and CVD. Specifically, our aims were to: 1) systematically examine the prospective associations between endometriosis and incident CVD risk; 2) investigate the associations between endometriosis and subclinical cardiac structural alterations as measured by cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging; and 3) elucidate underlying mechanisms by evaluating the potential mediating roles of metabolic dysfunction, systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and hormonal imbalance in the relationship between endometriosis and CVD.
sections.uk biobank cohort: The UK Biobank is a prospective cohort study that gathered data from more than 500,000 participants aged 40 to 69, sourced from 22 assessment centers across England, Scotland, and Wales. From 2006 to 2010, participants completed a series of questionnaires, underwent diverse physical measurements, and provided biological samples. Participants provided informed consent for linking their data to national records of hospital admissions, cancer diagnoses, and death records. UK Biobank has approval from the North West Multicenter Research Ethics Committee ( https://www.ukbiobank . ac.uk/learn-more-about-uk-biobank/about-us/ethics). This study utilizes data from the UK Biobank baseline assessment conducted between 2006 and 2010. Among the 502,128 participants enrolled in the UK Biobank, 273,155 women aged 40 to 69 years with available information on endometriosis were identified. Initially, 36,206 women with a history of coronary heart disease (CHD), myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), atrial fibrillation (AF), or stroke at baseline were excluded. Subsequently, 1,338 women diagnosed with endometriosis during follow-up were excluded. Ultimately, 235,611 women were included in the main and mediation analyses, among whom 6,158 were diagnosed with endometriosis and 229,453 without endometriosis ( Fig. 1 ) . Fig. 1 Study design
sections.external validation hospital cohort: To address potential misclassification of endometriosis in the UK Biobank due to reliance on self-reported and registry-based diagnoses, we conducted an external validation study using a retrospective-prospective hospital-based cohort from the Second Affiliated Hospital of University of South China, a tertiary referral center for gynecologic diseases in Hengyang, China. This hospital-based cohort included women who underwent laparoscopic surgery for suspected endometriosis between January 2008 and December 2012. Eligibility criteria included: (i) women aged ≥ 20 years at the time of diagnosis, (ii) laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis based on intraoperative visual inspection and histopathological examination, and (iii) absence of clinically evident cardiovascular disease prior to laparoscopic confirmation. Women were excluded if they were pregnant, had pathologically or clinically confirmed leiomyoma, adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, kidney disease, cancer, or autoimmune disorders, or had previously undergone hysterectomy or oophorectomy. The control group comprised women from the same hospital and time period who had no evidence of endometriosis on transvaginal ultrasound or laparoscopy. Controls were frequency-matched to cases in a 1:1 ratio by age and met the same exclusion criteria as cases. In total, 621 women with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis were included as cases, and 621 matched controls comprised the comparison group ( Figure S1 ) . Participants were followed up until May 2025. Because imaging and biomarker data were unavailable in this cohort, validation was limited to the association between endometriosis and incident cardiovascular events. The hospital-based study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of University of South China (Approval No. 2025006), and informed consent was obtained from all participants.
sections.definition of endometriosis: To maximize case ascertainment, we defined endometriosis using both UK Biobank electronic health records (EHR) diagnoses and self-reported physician diagnoses. Specifically, EHR diagnoses were based on ICD-10 codes N80.x, which are commonly used for identifying endometriosis in large-scale epidemiological studies and have been validated in prior research [ 18 ]. Additionally, self-reported cases were obtained during a structured, nurse-led interview at baseline assessment [ 19 ]. This dual approach of combining clinical records with self-reported diagnoses has been shown to improve case identification and is consistent with established methodologies in the literature [ 18 ]. A total of 6,158 women with endometriosis were identified: 3,627 through health records, 3,384 through self-report, and 853 by both sources. While laparoscopic confirmation with histological verification remains the diagnostic gold standard [ 20 ], such information is not systematically available in population-based cohorts. Previous validation studies have shown that registry- and self-report–based definitions of endometriosis, although less sensitive, have high specificity, and thus are more likely to result in under-ascertainment rather than false-positive misclassification [ 21 ]. To strengthen diagnostic validity, we further conducted an external validation study in the Second Affiliated Hospital of University of South China, where all diagnoses were confirmed by laparoscopy and histopathology. This external dataset not only corroborated the accuracy of our case definition but also enabled a sensitivity analysis restricted to laparoscopically confirmed cases, thereby ensuring the robustness of our findings.
sections.definition of cardiovascular disease: The primary outcome in both the UK Biobank and the hospital-based validation cohort was incident CVD, which includes CHD, MI, HF, AF, and stroke. In the UK Biobank, CVD events were ascertained through linkage to national hospital admission databases in England, Wales, and Scotland, with follow-up from baseline assessment until the first occurrence of a CVD event or October 31, 2022, whichever occurred first. The definition of CVD events, including CHD, MI, HF, AF, and stroke, is based on ICD-10 codes. In the hospital-based cohort, CVD events were identified through electronic medical records and clinical follow-up up to the most recent available date. All events in both cohorts were classified according to ICD-10 codes: CHD (I20–I25, including fatal ischemic heart disease and nonfatal MI I21–I23), AF and related arrhythmias (I48–I49), HF (I50), and stroke encompassing all cerebrovascular diseases (I60–I64, I69) (Table S1). The ICD-10 diagnostic codes for all outcomes have been validated in the UK Biobank and other large cohorts, demonstrating their reliability as diagnostic tools for identifying relevant health conditions [ 22 – 25 ].
sections.cmr outcomes: A detailed CMR protocol and analytical methodology have been previously described [ 26 ]. Of the ~ 500,000 original UKB participants, four imaging centers conducted a CMR enhancement study for individuals within travel proximity. By August 2023, over 48,000 participants had undergone CMR imaging, with ~ 40,000 scans included in this analysis, performed on average 9.0 ± 1.7 years after baseline assessment. The CMR scans were primarily utilized to evaluate cardiac anatomy and biventricular function, offering comprehensive assessments of cardiac structure, function, tissue characteristics, and prognostic markers. Metrics were indexed to body surface area (BSA) and, given BSA's limitations in obesity, also to height^1.7 due to ~ 30% of the UKB cohort having a BMI > 30 kg/m 2 . The post-processed parameters included left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), end-systolic volume (LVESV), stroke volume (SV), ejection fraction (LVEF), and myocardial mass. Relative wall mass was defined as the ratio of left ventricular mass to LVEDV. Myocardial volume (MV) was calculated assuming a myocardial density of 1.05 g/mL, and myocardial contraction fraction (MCF) was determined as the ratio of SV to MV. Indexed volumes and mass resulted in the derivation of LVEDV index (LVEDVi), LVESV index (LVESVi), and left ventricular mass index (LVmassi). Wall thickness (WT) across the 16 segments defined by the American Heart Association (AHA) was measured at end-diastole using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model. Both mean and maximal WT were computed, alongside interventricular septal WT (segments 2, 3, 8, 9, 14), lateral wall WT (segments 5, 6, 11, 12, 16), and the septal-to-lateral wall thickness ratio (SLWR); an SLWR greater than 1.3 or less than 0.7 was considered indicative of abnormality. Given the myocardial fiber architecture (oblique, circumferential, longitudinal), LV deformation was assessed via circumferential, radial, and longitudinal strains, both globally and regionally, indexed to LVmassi. Strains were derived from a 3D deformable myocardial model. Regions were defined as basal (segments 1–6), mid (7–12), and apical (13–16); however, mid/apical longitudinal strain data were unavailable at the time of analysis. Absolute strain values were used, with lower values indicating impaired myocardial mechanics.
sections.peripheral biomarkers: Biological samples from participants were collected at the assessment center using 4 mL EDTA vacuum containers. These samples were subsequently stored at 4 °C and transported overnight to the UK Biocentre in Stockport, UK, utilizing a temperature-controlled container to ensure sample integrity. Hematological analyses of whole blood were conducted using the Beckman Coulter LH750 System hematology analyzers to quantify hemocytes. At baseline, twenty biochemical markers in serum were selected for assay using immunoassay analyzers (DiaSorin Liaison XL and Beckman Coulter DXI800) and clinical chemistry analyzers (Beckman Coulter AU5800 and Siemens Advia1800). For further analysis, we categorized blood biomarkers into four groups: metabolic disorders, inflammation, hormones, and oxidative stress. The metabolic biomarkers included triglycerides (TG), total bilirubin (TBIL), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), total cholesterol (TC), the triglyceride-glucose index (TyG), TyG-body mass index (TyG-BMI), TyG-waist circumference (TyG-WC), waist-to-height ratio (WtHR), and lipid accumulation product (LAP). Composite indices were calculated based on established formulas: TyG = ln [triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting blood glucose (mg/dL)/ 2 ], TyG-BMI = TyG × BMI (kg/m 2 ), TyG-WtHR = TyG × waist-to-height ratio, TyG-WC = TyG × waist circumference (cm), LAP = (waist circumference [cm] – 58) × triglycerides (mmol/L). For inflammatory biomarkers, except for single indicators, i.e., C-reactive protein (CRP), counts and percentages of leukocyte, lymphocyte, monocyte, neutrophil, and platelet, five systemic inflammation biomarkers were considered and calculated as follows: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) = neutrophils/lymphocytes, monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR) = lymphocytes/monocytes, platelet to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) = platelets/lymphocytes, systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) = (neutrophils * platelets)/lymphocytes, systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) = (neutrophils * monocyte)/lymphocytes, and the low-grade inflammation score (INFLA-score). The INFLA-score integrates four key inflammatory biomarkers, including WBC count, PLT count, CRP, and NLR. Each biomarker was categorized into deciles, and scored from –4 to + 4 based on its distribution: values in the lowest four deciles received scores from –4 to –1, while values in the highest four deciles were assigned scores from + 1 to + 4. The INFLA-score was then calculated by summing the scores of the four biomarkers, yielding a total score ranging from –16 to + 16, with higher values indicating greater levels of low-grade inflammation. Hormones consisted of sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG). The urate, bilirubin, albumin, and oxidative balance score (OBS) as alternative biomarkers of oxidative stress, were also included in our analysis. Details for calculating the OBS are provided in the Supplementary Methods (Table S2).
sections.uk biobank cohort_1: We included the following factors in the analyses as covariates according to evidence from previous studies [ 9 , 27 ]: (1) Sociodemographic variables assessed at baseline, including age, ethnicity, educational level, and the Townsend Deprivation Index (TDI); (2) Lifestyle factors, such as alcohol consumption, smoking status, physical activity level, and a composite healthy diet score; (3) CVD risk factors, including the use of relevant medications (i.e., antihypertensive, lipid-lowering, glucose-lowering agents, and aspirin); (4) Reproductive and hormonal factors, including age at menarche, use of oral contraceptives (OC) and hormone replacement therapy (HRT). The TDI is a composite measure based on unemployment, non-car ownership, non-home ownership, and household overcrowding, with negative values indicating higher socioeconomic status. Self-reported information on smoking status and alcohol intake was collected. Smoking status was categorized as never, former, and current smokers. Alcohol intake was categorized into the following four groups: never, former, < 1 drink/week, 1–2 drinks/week, and ≥ 3 drinks/week. Physical activity was assessed using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire and categorized as low (< 600 metabolic equiva lent task/min per week), moderate (≥ 600 metabolic equiva lent task/min per week), or high (≥ 3000 metabolic equiva lent task/min per week metabolic equiva lent task/min per week) [ 22 ]. A healthy diet score was established based on total fruit intake (≥ 4.5 pieces per week), total vegetable intake (≥ 4.5 servings per week), total fish intake (≥ 2 servings per week), processed meat intake (< twice per week), and red meat intake (≤ 5 times per week) [ 28 ]. Each favorable diet factor was coded as 1 and unfavorable diet factor was coded as 0, and the total diet score was calculated by summing the individual scores of the five factors, with a range of 0–5. Further details regarding covariates are provided in Table S2.
sections.external validation hospital cohort_1: Sociodemographic information was obtained from medical records and patient interviews. Lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol, physical activity, diet) were collected via standardized questionnaires administered at baseline. Medication use and reproductive factors (age at menarche, contraceptive or hormone therapy use) were abstracted from medical records. Measurement categories were harmonized as closely as possible with the UKB cohort.
sections.statistical analysis: Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD or median with interquartile range (IQR), and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. To achieve normality and minimize heteroscedasticity, all continuous variables underwent log-transformation and subsequent Z-score standardization. Multiple testing was rigorously controlled using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models were constructed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the association between endometriosis and incident CVD. We implemented a hierarchical modeling strategy: 1) Model 1: Adjusted for age at baseline; 2) Model 2: Further adjusted for Townsend deprivation index, race/ethnicity, educational attainment, smoking status, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and healthy diet score; 3) Model 3: Further incorporated reproductive history, including age at menarche, and use of oral contraceptives (OC) and hormone replacement therapy (HRT). The proportional hazards assumption was verified via Kolmogorov-type supremum tests, with no violations observed (all P > 0.05). To strengthen our findings, we conducted five sensitivity analyses: 1) Excluding early-incident cases (< 5 years of follow-up) to mitigate potential reverse causation; 2) restricting case definition to ICD-10 codes only to reduce misclassification; 3) adjusting for menopausal status to account for reproductive aging; 4) excluding participants with prior hysterectomy or oophorectomy to isolate the effect of surgically induced hormonal shifts; 5) cross-geographic validation in an independent, international hospital-based cohort (outside of the UK) using only laparoscopically confirmed cases to ensure maximum diagnostic precision. Given the right-skewed distribution of CMR metrics, generalized linear models (GLM) with a gamma distribution and log link were utilized to evaluate cardiac structural and functional phenotypes. For mediation analysis, we employed a causal mediation framework using the R package “mediation” to quantify the proportions of the endometriosis-CVD association explained by identified biomarkers. Significance was determined via non-parametric bootstrapping with 5,000 iterations, adjusting for all aforementioned covariates. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.3.3).
sections.participant characteristics: Tables 1 and S4 summarize the baseline characteristics of participants from the UK-based Biobank cohort and the independent China-based hospital cohort, respectively. In the UK Biobank cohort ( n = 235,611; mean age 55.7 years), women with endometriosis were younger and less likely to have a college education. Also, they exhibited a slightly elevated prevalence of current smoking, an increase in low to moderate alcohol consumption, and diminished levels of physical activity (all P < 0.05). Moreover, these women experienced menarche at an earlier age and more frequently utilized oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy (all P < 0.05). sections.prospective association between endometr: During a median follow-up of 13.0 years, women with endometriosis had higher risk of CVD than those without endometriosis after fully adjustment for age, ethnicity, education level, Townsend deprivation index, alcohol consumption, smoking status, physical activity, healthy diet score, age at menarche, OC and HRT use (HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.09–1.29; Fig. 2 A). With further in-depth analyses examining subtypes of cardiovascular outcomes, endometriosis was associated with an increased risk of CHD (HR = 1.25, 95% CI: 1.12–1.40; Fig. 2 A). However, no significant associations were observed for myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, or stroke after full adjustment (Fig. 2 A). Sensitivity analyses, such as excluding participants with less than 5 years of follow-up, focusing on ICD-10 endometriosis diagnoses, and adjusting for menopausal status, showed no significant change in associations (Figs. S2-S4). Even after excluding women with previous hysterectomy or oophorectomy, endometriosis was still significantly linked to heart failure (HR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.01–2.03; Fig. S5). Similarly, in the hospital-based external validation cohort of laparoscopically confirmed cases, endometriosis was associated with higher risks of composite CVD (HR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.08–1.36; Fig. S6) and CHD (HR = 1.25, 95% CI: 1.08–1.40; Fig. S6). While associations with myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure were not significant, stroke risk remained elevated (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.03–1.40; Fig. S6), highlighting the consistency of key cardiovascular findings across both cohorts. sections.potential mechanism contributing to the: A linear regression model revealed significant links between endometriosis and various biomarkers, including 11 metabolic, 16 inflammatory, 4 oxidative stress, and 1 hormonal (Table S6). Endometriosis was significantly associated with a pro-atherogenic metabolic profile. Specifically, significant positive associations were observed for triglycerides (β: 0.14, 95%CI: 0.11–0.16), TyG indices (β: 0.11–0.13, 95%CI: 0.08–0.16), LAP (β: 0.11, 95%CI: 0.08–0.13), and LDL-C (β: 0.09, 95%CI: 0.06–0.11). Conversely, HDL-C (β: −0.07, 95%CI: −0.09–−0.04) and total bilirubin (β: −0.05, 95%CI: −0.07–−0.02) showed a significant inverse relationship. The inflammatory markers were also markedly elevated in women with endometriosis, as evidenced by higher levels of CRP (β: 0.11, 95%CI: 0.09–0.14), lymphocyte count (β: 0.04, 95%CI: 0.01–0.06), and the composite INFLA score (β: 0.04, 95%CI: 0.02–0.07). Regarding oxidative stress and hormonal pathways, endometriosis was positively linked to urate concentration (β: 0.07, 95%CI: 0.04–0.10), while significantly lower levels of DBIL (β: −0.06, 95%CI: −0.09–−0.03) and SHBG (β: −0.05, 95%CI: −0.07–−0.02) were observed. We further used the Cox proportional hazards model to examine the relationship between peripheral biomarkers and CVD risk (Tables S7-S8). Metabolic dysfunction emerged as a robust predictor of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Specifically, each SD increment in TyG indices (CVD: HR: 1.13–1.28, 95%CI: 1.12–1.30; CHD: HR: 1.26–1.34, 95%CI: 1.23–1.37) and LAP (CVD: HR: 1.17, 95CI%: 1.16–1.18; CHD: HR: 1.36, 95%CI: 1.33–1.39) was associated with a substantially higher risk of CVD and CHD. Similarly, elevations in triglycerides (CVD: HR: 1.11, 95%CI: 1.10–1.13; CHD: HR: 1.23, 95%CI: 1.21–1.26) and FPG (CVD: HR: 1.09, 95%CI: 1.07–1.10; CHD: HR: 1.12, 95%CI: 1.10–1.14) conferred increased risks for both outcomes. In terms of the lipid profile, HDL-C exhibited a consistent protective association (CVD: HR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.85–0.88; CHD: HR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.78–0.82), while higher LDL-C (CHD: HR: 1.08, 95%CI: 1.06–1.10) and total cholesterol (CHD: HR: 1.04, 95%CI: 1.02–1.06) were specifically linked to increased CHD risk. For inflammatory markers, CRP (HR 1.20, 95% CI: 1.18–1.21) and the composite INFLA score (HR 1.16, 95% CI: 1.15–1.18) showed potent associations, with each SD increase corresponding to a 20% and 16% higher risk of incident CVD, respectively. Furthermore, a spectrum of leukocyte-derived indices, including SIRI (HR: 1.13, 95%CI: 1.11–1.14), NLR (HR: 1.09, 95%CI: 1.08–1.11), and SII (HR: 1.07, 95%CI: 1.06–1.09), consistently signaled increased cardiovascular vulnerability. similar markers were linked to CHD. Conversely, a higher lymphocyte percentage (CVD: HR: 0.92, 95%CI: 0.91–0.93; CHD: HR: 0.93, 95%CI: 0.92–0.95) was associated with reduced risks of both CVD and CHD. In addition, markers of oxidative stress and hormonal status also provided significant prognostic value. Urate levels were positively correlated with increased CVD (HR: 1.17, 95%CI: 1.15–1.18) and CHD (HR: 1.19, 95%CI: 1.17–1.22) risk. In contrast, serum albumin (CVD: HR: 0.91, 95%CI: 0.90–0.93) and SHBG (CVD: HR: 0.93, 95%CI: 0.91–0.94; CHD: HR: 0.86, 95%CI: 0.84–0.88) appeared to be independent protective factors. Mediation analyses showed that the association between endometriosis and cardiovascular outcomes was primarily driven by metabolic pathways, with additional contributions from inflammation, oxidative stress, and hormonal factors (Fig. 4 and Tables S9-S10). For incident CVD, TyG-related indices were the dominant mediators, including TyG-WC (17.3%), TyG-BMI (17.2%), and TyG-WHtR (15.4%), followed by LAP (11.8%) and triglycerides (8.9%), while HDL-C showed an inverse effect (5.6%). Inflammatory markers, particularly CRP (11.1%) and the INFLA score (3.7%), also contributed, along with oxidative stress markers such as urate (6.0%). Similar patterns were observed for CHD, with metabolic markers again accounting for the largest mediation proportions (e.g., TyG-WC 13.5%, CVAI 13.4%, TyG-WHtR 13.1%). CRP (9.0%) and INFLA score (3.3%) remained key inflammatory mediators, while urate (5.0%) and SHBG (2.8%) contributed to oxidative stress and hormonal pathways, respectively.
